# Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library

Complete, uniform, comprehensive, economical, and convenient, containing all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the times of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions completed during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly placed within the text, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be surveyed at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, by which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on the individual texts of each scriptural book and in which passages of their works.

The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes—uniformly similar throughout the whole work—the low price, and above all this collection itself are taken into account: one unified, methodical, and chronological gathering of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but assembled for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which are published the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.

Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the Complete Courses in each branch of ecclesiastical scholarship.

Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin.

The 1,200 volumes of the Latin edition are sold for 1,000 francs; the 1,300 volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for 800 francs.

The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are supplied in it only in Latin translation.

# Expositions of the Epistles of Blessed Paul

[Column 0009]

## Book Nine of the Expositions of the Epistles of Blessed Paul

### Exposition of the First Epistle to the Corinthians

[Column 0009]

## Argument

[Column 0009A]

**(Jerome.)** The Corinthians are Achaeans, and they likewise heard the word of truth from the apostles. Having been overthrown in many ways by false apostles, some were led by the verbose eloquence of philosophy into the sect of the Jewish law. The Apostle recalls them to true and evangelical wisdom, writing to them from Ephesus through Timothy, his disciple.

**(Ambrose.)** Warned by the Lord’s command, the Apostle remained among the Corinthians for a year and six months, teaching the word of God. Hence he deals with them with great confidence and affection, sometimes admonishing, sometimes reproving, and sometimes speaking gently to them as to children.

There are many reasons why he writes to them. The first is that, like heretics, they were dissenting from one another and, devoted to human beings, wished to be called Paulinians, Peterians, and Apollonians rather than Christians. The Apostle strongly reproves this. Yet there were also among them some who dissented from these groups and were devoted to Christ alone.

The second reason is that they had begun to delight in eloquence and earthly philosophy, so that under the name of Christ they might be imbued with doctrines contrary to the faith.

The third is that they were puffed up because the Apostle did not go to them.

The fourth concerns the fornicator whom they allowed to remain among them.

The fifth is that he might remind them of the previous epistle which he had written before this one, which is called the First.

The sixth is that they had begun to inflict injuries and commit frauds against one another, and preferred to seek the judgment of unbelievers.

The seventh is that he indicates that he is permitted to receive support, but refrains from doing so, lest he provide an example for the rapacious [Column 0009C] false apostles.

The eighth is that he may answer their letter, since they had begun to be troubled by heretics concerning marriage.

The ninth is that he declares that each person ought to remain as he believed.

The tenth concerns virgins, since he had received no command regarding them; and there are the remaining matters that will be seen in the body of the letter.

# Chapter One

## The Apostle Praises the Corinthians and Exhorts to Concord Those Who Say They Were Baptized by Different Ministers; and He Shows That God Has Made the Wisdom of This World Foolish

**Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God.**

**(Ambrose.)** He began differently in the Epistle to the Romans, because [Column 0010A] the situation is different. Here, however, he writes that he is an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, because everything he did he did by the will of the Son of God, who said to him: “Go; I shall send you far away to the Gentiles” (Acts 22).

For this reason he was called an apostle—that is, sent to the Gentiles by the will of God. By this he also touches upon those whom neither Christ had sent nor whose teaching was true.

He frequently names God and Christ for this reason: to show that Christ is God, but not the Father himself; that Christ is the Son of God and that God is also the Father; and that the Father and Son are not one person merely because the Son is named.

“Jesus” has one meaning and “Christ” another, although Jesus Christ our Savior is one. Jesus, nevertheless, is a proper name. Just as Moses is called by his proper name, and Elijah, and Abraham, so the Lord Jesus is called as by a proper name. “Christ,” however, is the name of a sacrament, just as one may say “prophet” or “priest.” Thus Christ is proclaimed as the one in whom the redemption of the whole people of Israel was to exist.

**Through the will of God.** He was called to the faith by God’s will, but he believed willingly and by his own choice, as he says in the Acts of the Apostles: “I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision” (Acts 26).

**(Ambrose.)** Many sects had arisen that asserted Christ’s Gospel according to their own understanding. Dry branches of these still exist today, and their advocates were overthrowing the churches. Therefore the Apostle sets forth everything opposed to heresies and affirms that he is a true preacher, since he was sent by Christ according to the will of God.

[Column 0010C]

**And Sosthenes, a brother.** He also commends this man by associating him with himself.

**(Rabanus.)** He says “brother,” not “apostle.” He introduces him as writing with him because Sosthenes was a teacher among the Corinthians themselves and was deeply concerned for them.

**To the church of God that is at Corinth, sanctified in Christ Jesus.**

**(Ambrose.)** He writes to the church because rulers had not yet been appointed over the individual churches. Although he reproves them in many matters, he says, “sanctified in Christ Jesus.” They had been sanctified because they had been reborn in Christ; afterward, however, they began to conduct themselves badly. Thus he shows that the whole Church had been sanctified in Christ, but that some of its members had been overthrown by the corrupt teaching of false apostles and led away from the tradition of [Column 0011A] truth.

**Called saints.**

**(Augustine.)** This means: you have been called so that you may be saints; that is, so that you may not depart from the rule of sanctification.

“My faith calls upon you, Lord, the faith that you gave me and inspired in me through the humanity of your Son and through the ministry of your preacher. And how shall I call upon my God, my God and my Lord? Certainly, when I call upon him, I shall call him into myself.”

**With all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, both theirs and ours.**

It belongs to priests to call upon God, for they are told: “Thus shall you bless the children of Israel, calling my name upon them” (Numbers 6). The Psalmist also says: “And Samuel among those who call upon his name” (Psalm 98). The fact that Samuel was a priest is proved by this: he succeeded a priest and offered sacrifices. Concerning him it is also said according to the historical account: “I shall raise up for myself a faithful priest” (1 Samuel 2). Although he was not of Aaron’s family, he is nevertheless read in Chronicles as being of the tribe of Levi, because the one who appointed him also appointed Aaron. For he chose Aaron in such a way that he did not lose the power to choose others afterward.

**In every place, both theirs and ours,** because priests serve in their own place and in that of the apostles. For this reason they are also called apostles of the churches.

**(Ambrose.)** There is another sense in the statement: “with all who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, in every place, both theirs and ours.” He joins the Jews and the Gentiles together, because “salvation is from the Jews” (John 4), so that in every place where there are Gentiles who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and where the Jews mentioned above are found, all may likewise be one.

The false apostles who preached the name of Christ through worldly wisdom—that is, who mixed in philosophy and rejected the Old Law and the prophets—denied that Christ had truly been crucified, claiming that he had only appeared to be crucified, as Marcion and Manichaeus did. Hence the Apostle says: “But we preach Christ crucified.” Nor did they acknowledge the resurrection of the flesh, concerning which the prophet Isaiah cries out: “Those who are in the tombs shall not rise” (Isaiah 26).

**Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.**

Since he had said, “those who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,” lest he appear to have kept silent about the Father’s name or gift, or to provide some suspicion or occasion for the doctrine of union, he teaches [Column 0011D] that Christ is indeed rightly invoked, but that all grace belongs to the Father. Thus he shows that the two are one in divinity while also giving precedence to the Father’s authority.

**I give thanks to my God always for you.**

Although he writes to everyone in the Church, he expresses himself in such a way—sometimes reproving and sometimes praising—that, when each person hears the epistle read, he understands what is said for him and what against him. For he writes to two peoples within one community, so that when he reproves those who behave badly, they may know that these words are written to them; and likewise, when he praises, the person who remains within the rule may know that the praise is addressed to him.

Therefore he says: “I give thanks to my God always for you, because of the grace of God that has been given to you in Christ Jesus.” This grace was given in Christ Jesus because God established that whoever believes in Christ should be saved without works, by faith alone, through which he freely receives the forgiveness of sins.

**Because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge.**

**(Ambrose.)** This signifies that, having received the grace and the teaching of the word of truth, they continued to possess spiritual knowledge. Therefore he gives thanks to God for them. First, according to his customary manner, he urges them toward progress by praising them. He says that he rejoices in their knowledge, but that they must understand that true wisdom does not puff itself up and does not dissent.

They had become rich in him in every virtue, through the wisdom that establishes the friends of God and the prophets—in every word and in all wisdom, that is, in both the New and the Old Testament.

**As the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you.**

**(Rabanus.)** The testimony in which he says: “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old” (Matthew 13).

**So that you lack nothing in any grace.**

Hence Solomon says: “All good things came to me together with her” (Wisdom 7), that is, together with wisdom.

**(Ambrose.)** The testimony of Christ was confirmed in them because, strengthened in faith, they hoped in no human beings, but all their hope was in Christ, and they had been captured by no allurements of pleasure.

**As you await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ.**

**(Rabanus.)** The person who awaits the coming of Christ is one who is prepared for all things. His coming is called “revelation” because he is now hidden from us.

**(Ambrose.)** It is clear that the person who is watchful and concerned awaits the day of judgment: the future judgment of God, in which our Lord will be revealed to the faithful and the unfaithful alike, so that unbelievers may recognize and know that what they refused to believe was true and may perish, while the faithful rejoice, finding more good than they had expected.

**Who will also confirm you to the end, blameless on the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.**

**(Rabanus.)** Through teaching, as blessed David says: “Strengthen me in your words” (Psalm 118); and again: “Great peace belongs to those who love your name, and there is no stumbling-block in them” (ibid.).

**(Ambrose.)** Confident in spirit and secure in their hope, he is certain that they will remain unviolated until the future judgment. For those who could not be changed amid so many conflicts of opinion and disturbances arising from diversity plainly show that they will remain in the same state.

When he praises these people, he invites those who had been corrupted by the error of the false apostles. By proclaiming the faith of the former, he calls the latter to repentance.

**Who will also confirm you,** he says, **to the end, blameless at the coming of the Lord.**

**(Gregory.)** It is written in the Epistle of John: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1). If it is deception to think oneself without sin, how are we confirmed by the Lord as blameless at his coming, especially since even an infant of one day cannot be without sin?

Is a crime, then, also a sin, without which someone can be confirmed by the Lord? We must certainly know that not every sin is a crime, although every crime is a sin—just as every ungodly person is a sinner, but not every sinner is ungodly.

Thus sins are called both lesser and greater; crimes, however, are scarcely ever spoken of except in the case of serious sins. Human life, with God’s confirmation, can therefore be without crime, but it cannot be without sin—not even for one day.

**God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord.**

**(Rabanus.)** God is faithful, and he confirmed this by calling you into the fellowship of his Son. John explains this fellowship when he says: “God is light, and there is no darkness in him. If we say that we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie” (1 John 1). Paul likewise says: “If we have died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him” (2 Timothy 2).

This passage is directed against the Arians, who wish the Son to be lesser on the grounds that all things are said to have been made through him, although this also applies to the Father, through whom believers are said to have been called into fellowship with his Son.

**(Ambrose.)** Who could doubt God’s promises and faithfulness, since things will not be otherwise than he has said? He makes us adopted sons when we believe in Christ. He grants us what we believe, so that, because we believe that Christ is the Son of God, we may begin to be sons of God, remaining in the same dignity in which Christ remains—the Christ whom we believe to be the Son of God.

Fellowship is brotherhood. Thus, just as he shows that God’s faithfulness will remain unharmed for us in this matter, so we must be found not distrustful or faithless, but persevering in adoption.

**Now I beseech you, brothers, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing.**

Now he urges them to be of one mind—specifically, in that in which, having been reborn, they were called sons of God. For he is now speaking to the whole Church, so that those who had begun to dissent might return to the faith they had begun, which they saw praised in those who persevered in it.

**And that there be no schisms among you, but that you be perfected in the same understanding and in the same knowledge.**

He wants them to be perfect in the same understanding that he had handed down to them, so that they might not differ from one another. He calls them to follow the example of those whom he praised above, so that they may think and defend the same things. Schisms always arise from contention.

**For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those who belong to Chloe, that there are contentions among you.**

**(Gregory.)** See how he had praised them as possessing every word and all knowledge and had said that they lacked nothing in any grace. After speaking for a little while, he gently approaches reproof: he reproves those who are divided against one another, and after first describing their salvation, he later exposes their wounds.

An experienced physician, seeing that a wound must be cut but recognizing that the patient is fearful, touched it for a long time and then suddenly struck. First he laid upon them the gentle hand of praise; afterward he drove in the iron of reproof.

Unless timid minds are first reproved by gentle touch, so that they may hear from other matters something they can take as consolation, they immediately fall into despair when reproved.

But did Paul lie when he first said that they lacked nothing in any grace, although he would later say that they lacked unity? Certainly not. Who, even if foolish, could believe such things about him? Rather, because among the Corinthians some were filled with every grace while others had been cut away through favoritism toward persons, he began with praise of the perfect, so that by a restrained attack he might reach the reproach of the weak.

**(Ambrose.)** Although they had been overthrown, he still calls them brothers. Likewise, in the prophet Isaiah, God says to those who were with him that they should say to those who believed the false prophets, “You shall be our brothers,” so that by this means they might not dissent from them as from brothers.

As for the phrase “by those who belong to Chloe,” some understand these to be people who lived there and bore fruit in the faith of God. Others understand it as referring to a place, as if one said, “by those who are from Antioch.” Others think that Chloe was a woman devoted to God, with whom many worshipers of God lived, whose faith was not denied; thus what they reported about the Corinthians—that there were contentions among them—was true.

He says that there were contentions among them in order to show the diversity of their minds concerning the Lord’s discipline.

**(Rabanus.)** It may be asked how the Apostle believed something about absent people, since it is written: “Do not believe a vain report”; and again: “Speak what your eyes have seen,” and so forth (Proverbs 25).

But he possessed this grace: he knew, even while absent, what was happening in each church, just as he says to the Colossians: “Although I am absent in body, I am present in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order” (Colossians 2).

Since, therefore, he knew that the Corinthians were acting as he had heard, he did not believe this without reason, as though it concerned absent people whose conduct he examined in the Spirit.

**Now I say this because each of you says: I belong to Paul; I belong to Apollos; I belong to Cephas; I belong to Christ.**

**(Ambrose.)** He reveals the error but does not disclose the names of the authors. They were not remaining in one place but were moving about to overthrow the simple. Those whom he names were certainly good teachers, but under their appearance he touches upon false apostles. If he denies that anyone should glory in the former, how much more does he deny it concerning evil teachers, whose corrupt teaching he indicates below?

Among them, however, he points out those who persevered and said that they belonged to Christ, not to a human being—those whom he praises above.

**Is Christ divided?**

The body is divided when its members dissent. He said that Christ was divided because human beings had divided his glory among themselves, just as heretics do not shrink from being called Photinians, Arians, Cataphrygians, Novatians, Donatists, or Manichaeans.

So the Corinthians also had begun to be subjected to the names of various heretics, so that they appeared to venerate human beings in place of Christ. By receiving different doctrines about Christ, they divide Christ.

One person accepts Christ as merely human; another confesses him as pure God without a body; one says that Christ was foretold through the prophets; another denies that the prophets spoke about Christ.

Since Christ is one, God and human, these people, each claiming something different for him, divide Christ. And because they establish many churches under their own names, he adds:

[Column 0015A]

**Was Paul crucified for us?**

He begins with himself, lest it be thought that he rejected the persons of others in order to commend his own. If Christ, he says, died for us, how do we attribute his grace and benefit to human beings, thereby insulting him?

**Were you baptized in the name of Paul?**

If, he says, we believers are baptized into Christ so that we may be justified in his name, why do we make human beings the authors of this faith, forgetful of the faith we began?

**(Augustine.)** When people divide the Church among themselves and attempt to make factions out of unity, maternal charity, bringing forth little ones in the Apostle, lays open her inner parts, tears, as it were, her breasts with words, mourns the children whom she sees being carried away, recalls to one name those who wished to make many names for themselves, and drives them away from her own love so that Christ may be loved.

She says: “Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” What does she mean? “I do not want you to be mine; be with me: we all belong to him who died for us, who was crucified for us.”

**I give thanks to God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name. I also baptized the household of Stephanas; beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.**

**(Ambrose.)** He gives thanks to God because he did not baptize many of them, lest the error that had begun under this pretext become widespread in his name. By this he reproves those who deserved reproach, both the baptizers and the baptized, who, to the injury of the Savior, attributed the grace of baptism to human beings, while the baptizers connived at this for the sake of glory.

For if they were like the Novatians and Donatists of today, who claim baptism for themselves and reject those baptized by us, the baptized among them glory in the persons of those who baptized them. Finally, having renounced the name of Christ, they glory in being called Novatians and Donatists.

Crispus and Gaius were Corinthians, whom he names as witnesses because they were baptized by the Apostle in such a way that they learned that no glory should be assigned to him on this account.

The household of Stephanas, however, were the firstfruits of Achaia, as he indicates near the end of the Epistle. He bears witness to them that they had devoted themselves to the ministry of the saints.

**For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to evangelize.**

Because evangelizing is greater than baptizing, he says that he was not sent to baptize but to evangelize. For in a bishop lies the dignity of all ordinations: he is the head of the other members.

By this he also humbles those to whom they attributed great importance because they had been baptized by them. Thus they might learn from this that baptizing is not a great matter, since not everyone who baptizes is capable of evangelizing. The words spoken in baptism are ceremonial formulas.

Thus the Apostle Peter ordered Cornelius and those with him, once they had believed, to be baptized (Acts 10), but he did not deign to perform this act while ministers stood by. Had they been absent, necessity would have compelled him to do it himself.

He therefore shows how much better than those whom they revered he is, yet he did not allow this honor to be assigned to his own name, knowing that it is dangerous to claim for a human name the glory belonging to God. This is a kind of idolatry.

[Column 0016A]

**Not in the wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied.**

Christian preaching does not need pomp or ornament of speech. Therefore uneducated fishermen were chosen to evangelize, so that the truth of the teaching might commend itself, with power as its witness, lest they seem acceptable through human cleverness and the subtlety of worldly wisdom rather than through truth.

This is like teachings invented by human beings, in which neither reason nor power is sought, but only the arrangement of words. Consequently, whoever wishes to adorn the faith of Christ with words seeks his own glory: he obscures the faith with the brilliance of language, so that he, rather than the faith, may be praised.

Likewise, the false apostles preached Christ in human wisdom in two ways, lest they appear foolish to the wise of this world: they cultivated eloquence and avoided those things that the world judges foolish in us. Thus they taught neither that the Son of God had become incarnate and been born of a virgin nor that there would be a future resurrection of the flesh, because the wisdom and reason of the world considers these things foolish and rejects them.

**Lest the cross of Christ be emptied,** he says, because whoever announces Christ in human wisdom denies the truth of the preaching, as I mentioned above.

**For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing.**

It is clear that those for whom the cross of Christ is foolishness are in perdition, for they have not been rescued from the death of hell.

**But to those who are being saved it is the power of God.**

The meaning is clear: to those who believe, it is the power of God. They believe that the cross of Christ is not weakness but power, understanding that death was conquered on the cross. Those who bear its sign are saved, because death cannot retain them.

**For it is written in Isaiah: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the prudent.”**

He destroys the wisdom of the wise—not his own wisdom in them. He does not destroy and reject the wisdom that he himself gave, but the wisdom arrogated by those who do not possess his wisdom. They make happen what that wisdom denies can happen.

He rejects the understanding of the prudent when he proves that God, whom they call unconcerned, undertook what they consider foolish: that the Son of God should become incarnate, be born of a virgin, and be crucified for human salvation. The reality of this is attested by power, not by words.

**Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe? Where is the investigator of this age?**

With these words he attacks both Jews and Gentiles. The scribes and teachers of the law among the Jews consider it foolish to believe that God has a Son. Likewise, the Gentiles assign this to ridicule.

But the Jews distrust it because it is not so openly signified in the Law. The Gentiles reject it because worldly reason does not admit it; for it says that nothing can happen without mixture and therefore judges it foolish.

The debater of the age is the person who determines that the world is governed by constellations and that risings and settings occur through the twelve signs, calculating that absolutely nothing can happen without the movement of these things.

**Has God not made the wisdom of this world foolish?**

The wisdom of this world has been made foolish. Thinking that it was wise, it was found to be foolish. What it judged impossible has been shown to be possible, while it considered God unconcerned.

Is anything more foolish than the assertion that God made the world but does not care for it? Why did he make it, if what he made does not belong to him?

But because they see some people enjoying the world happily, others being oppressed, the good being despised, and the wicked exulting, they have believed that God is unconcerned.

Whoever calls God unconcerned does not deny that he is malevolent or unjust. For he will judge the world, and he is unjust if he overlooks the good and allows evil to be done.

If they set aside their hatred of the divine law, they can see that we resolve this question by awaiting God’s judgment. In that judgment those who have been oppressed will be exalted, and the violent will be humbled, because there is no partiality with God.

**For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe.**

**(Augustine.)** What is so like imprudence as this? One who had the power, by a single word, to overthrow his persecutors allowed himself to be seized, scourged, spat upon, struck on the face, crowned with thorns, and fastened to wood. This seems like imprudence and foolishness, but this foolishness surpasses all the wise.

**(Gregory.)** The Word of God is wisdom, but the flesh of the Word was called the foolishness of this wisdom. Since carnal people, through the wisdom of their flesh, could not reach the wisdom of God, they were healed through the foolishness of preaching—that is, through the flesh of the Word.

**(Ambrose.)** “The world did not know”—that is, human beings did not know—God in his wisdom. They assigned his one majesty to images or to the elements, disregarding him and, through the wisdom of the flesh, thinking that those things ought to be worshiped which are visible.

Therefore it pleased God to establish a form of preaching [Column 0017C] that would appear foolish to them, so that those who believed what they distrusted might be saved, while those people were condemned.

This, then, is the reversal by which, according to God’s counsel, falsehood is condemned by truth.

**For Jews ask for signs, and Greeks seek wisdom.**

**(Ambrose.)** The Jews ask for signs because they do not doubt that such things could happen; they ask whether they have happened.

They know that Aaron’s dry staff blossomed and produced fruit, that Jonah, swallowed by the sea creature, remained in its belly for three days and three nights and was cast out alive. Yet they especially seek something like what Moses saw when he saw God in the fire. Hence they say: “We know that God spoke with Moses,” although it is a greater thing that the dead and stinking Lazarus came alive from the tomb on the fourth day.

The Greeks, however, seek wisdom because they refuse to hear anything except what is possible according to the reasoning of the world.

**But we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling-block, and to the Gentiles foolishness.**

**(Rabanus.)** He shows that his teaching differs greatly from their understanding.

**To the Jews a stumbling-block.** They are scandalized when they hear that Christ could die, for they await him as immortal—that is, they say: “We have heard from the Law that Christ remains forever” (John 12). They do not understand that he first had to suffer and then enter into his glory.

**To the Gentiles foolishness.** According to worldly wisdom, it appears foolish to believe that God was crucified.

**(Ambrose.)** It is a stumbling-block to the Jews when they hear Christ confessing himself to be the Son of God and abolishing the Sabbath. It is foolishness to the Gentiles because they hear things preached which, since they do not accord with worldly reason, appear senseless: the birth from a virgin and the resurrection of the dead.

**But to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God,** because he is always with God, since “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

Those who believe in Christ understand this through the power that persuades—a power superior to words. The Jews, who first sought a sign, recognize that Christ is the power of God; and the Greeks likewise see that Christ is the wisdom of God. The worldly wisdom that they had previously considered prudence is thereby shown to be the greatest [Column 0018B] foolishness.

**(Ambrose.)** He is therefore the power of God because through him God the Father made all things. He is wisdom because through him God was known. For God could not be known except through one who was from him.

“No one knows or has seen the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Luke 10).

For what is foolish in God is wiser than human beings. (MAUR.) What is considered foolish in God surpasses all human wisdom, because those who have been saved through the mystery of the cross could not be liberated by their own wisdom. (Greg.) For it seemed foolish to human beings that the author of life should die for human beings; and from the very point at which a person ought rather to have become more indebted to him, that person took offense against him. For God is to be honored by human beings with the greater dignity, the more undignified were the things he undertook on behalf of human beings. [Col. 0018C]

(Ambr.) “The foolishness of God,” he says—not because it is truly foolish, but because it is considered foolish by human beings, since it does not accord with worldly reason, although it is spiritual reason. Thus it is recognized as wiser than human beings, because spiritual things possess greater wisdom than bodily things. For spiritual things do not derive from bodily things; rather, bodily things subsist through spiritual things, and therefore bodily things are subject to spiritual things.

And what is weak in God is stronger than human beings. (MAUR.) The weakness of the crucified one overcame death, which even the Giants could not escape. (Ambr.) Without doubt, heavenly things overcome earthly things. Therefore what is weak in God is not weak, because Christ’s weakness is a great victory. For he conquered when he seemed conquered, as he says in the psalm [Col. 0018D] L: “That you may conquer when you are judged.” For the one who is killed unjustly proves himself victorious, making guilty the one by whom he is killed.

See, brothers, your calling: not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble. It is clear that few are those who are puffed up more by worldly reasoning than instructed—that is, those who observe and distinguish the movements of the stars. He also calls these people strong according to the flesh, and wise; and strong for this reason: they assert that the passion of Christ’s cross is weak. For iniquity is strong and seems, for a time, to prevail.

They are also “noble,” through whom they assign antiquity as the origin of their superstition, calling us newcomers. God therefore did not choose this assertion, which is held by the few. Rather, he chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise. The foolish things of the world are that a virgin gave birth and that the Son of God was crucified. For the world considers it foolish to believe this; therefore God chose those who believe what the world judges foolish, in order to confound him. The wise are confounded when they see many professing what the few deny. For it is not doubtful that the opinions of the many are preferred to the opinions of the few.

(Greg.) Alternatively: for the acquisition of knowledge of the faith, the foolish things of the world were gathered first, so that afterward they might also be called clever, as Paul attests when he says: “Not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise.” For the earliest times of the holy Church are said to have been ignorant of letters, so that the Redeemer might show through all his preachers that it was not speech but the substance of the matter that persuaded peoples to believe in life. [Col. 0019B]

And God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong. (Ambr.) The meaning is the same: what the few consider weak—those who regard themselves as wise in this world and, lacking confidence, distrust the hope—is asserted by many to be power, because many believe what unbelievers do not believe, to their shame. For they see those things called Christ’s weaknesses commanding demons and performing wonders. To the world, however, the injuries and passion of the Savior are weaknesses, since it does not know that these contribute to power; for he permitted himself to suffer these things in order to conquer death. To suffer unjustly and, though powerful, to refuse to resist is the glory of the one who suffers and the condemnation of the one who kills.

And God chose the ignoble things of this world and the despised, the things that are not, to destroy the things that are. He chose the ignoble and despised not because they are truly ignoble and despised, but because the world judges them so: they reject worldly arguments by believing in Christ. Thus he might destroy the things that truly are ignoble and despised, because those who judge are themselves more liable to be judged and condemned. Their assertion was invented by error and did not exist from the beginning; whereas our discipline is from the beginning. Their position is therefore destroyed when it is asserted in bare words without testimony. Ours, however, is proved not by words alone but also by the testimony of power.

Why, then, did the Lord first choose a few ignoble, uneducated, and uncultivated people, when before his eyes he had a great crowd—fewer in comparison with those poorer people, certainly, but in their own class many rich, noble, learned, and wise people, whom he afterward also gathered? The Apostle explains the mystery: “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and God chose the foolish things of this world to confound the wise; and God chose the ignoble things of this world, and the things that are not”—that is, that are not counted—“to bring to nothing the things that are.”

For he had come to teach humility and to overthrow pride. He had come in humility and, having come so humbly, in no way sought the lofty first. First, he chose to be born of that woman who was betrothed to a carpenter. He therefore did not choose illustrious ancestry, lest nobility should become proud on this earth. He did not even choose to be born in the most splendid city; rather, he was born in Bethlehem of Judah, which would not even be called a city, and whose inhabitants today call it a village. It is so small, so insignificant, almost nothing, unless it were ennobled by the Lord Christ’s former birth. [Col. 0020A]

He therefore chose the weak, the poor, and the unlearned—not because he abandoned the strong, rich, wise, and noble, but because, if he had chosen those people first, they would rightly have seemed to have been chosen on account of their wealth, their possessions, and their birth; puffed up by these things, they would not have received the salvation of humility, without which no one can return to that life from which one would not have fallen except through pride. (Aug.)

But perhaps someone might say: “Although he himself was born humbly, he wanted to boast in the nobility of his disciples.” He did not choose kings, senators, philosophers, or orators. Rather, he chose common people, the poor, the unlearned, and fishermen. Peter was a fisherman; Cyprian, an orator. If the fisherman had not gone ahead faithfully, the orator would not have followed humbly. Let no one who is lowly despair of himself: let him hold fast to Christ, and his hope will not be false.

So that no flesh may boast in the sight of God. (Ambr.) That is, so that the wisdom of the flesh may be put to shame in its error, with God as judge. For it is the sense of the flesh to distrust the power of God to have caused a virgin to give birth, because the reasoning of the world—which is kin to the flesh—does not accept this.

(Aug.) See how he took glory away from us in order to give glory; he took away ours in order to give his; he took away empty glory in order to give fullness; he took away what wavers in order to give what is solid. Therefore you must not glory in yourself—something Truth prohibited—but in what the Apostle said, which Truth commanded: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (II Cor. X).

For from him you are in Christ Jesus. (Ambr.) “From him”—that is, from God, who is almighty—we are in the faith of Christ. For God’s purpose is that through Christ we should learn his truth and mercy. Truth is the mystery of the Trinity; mercy is that, although we were captives, he redeemed us.

Who was made for us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption. To strengthen believers, he says that Christ accomplished what he accomplished by the will of God, so that we may know that we have truly learned wisdom, have been sanctified, justified, and redeemed by God through Christ. For no one redeems anything except what had belonged to him.

Whether, therefore, we have been redeemed; or sanctified—that is, cleansed from the works of the flesh and the impurity of idols; or justified—for it is right to worship the Creator while rejecting all others; or made wise because through this we have learned that worldly people are unlearned: all this is God’s gift through Christ.

Yet our redemption is this: Christ offered himself to the devil who desired him, in order to remove from himself the opposition of sin and thus free his captives. (Greg.) He was made wisdom for us by God, and righteousness—namely, by that righteousness through which, when he came into this world against the ways of sinners, we conquered the ancient enemy by whom we were held captive.

(Aug.) The Son was made wisdom and justification for us by God, because in time we are converted to him—that is, from a certain point in time—in order to remain with him forever. And he himself, from a certain point in time, became the Word made flesh and dwelt among us.

That righteousness which lives in itself is undoubtedly God and lives unchangeably. Just as life, although it exists in itself, also becomes life for us when we become in some measure participants in it, so, although righteousness exists in itself, it also becomes righteousness for us when we live by clinging to it. We are therefore more or less righteous according as we cling to him more or less.

Hence it is written of the only-begotten Son of God: although he is certainly the Father’s wisdom and righteousness and always exists in himself, he was made for us wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption.

So that, as it is written: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord.” He is plainly the Most High God, true righteousness—or that true God who is supreme righteousness—which we ought to hunger and thirst for. It is our righteousness in this pilgrimage, by which we afterward desire to be filled; it is our full righteousness in eternity. [Col. 0021B]

(Cass.) For if we wish to borrow all things from one person, examples suitable for imitation will either be difficult or certainly never be found, because, although, according to the Apostle, we do not yet see Christ become all in all, nevertheless we can find him in all things in this way—that is, in parts, in all people. For it is said of him: “Who was made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption.”

When, therefore, wisdom is found in one person, righteousness in another, holiness in another, gentleness in another, chastity in another, humility in another, Christ is now divided limb by limb among each of the saints. But when all are brought together into the unity of faith and virtue, he is restored as a perfect man, completing the fullness of his body in the joining and particular character of the individual members. [Col. 0021C]

Until that time comes when God is all in all, God can be in all people in the present in the manner we have described—that is, through the several parts of the virtues—even though their fullness is not yet all in all. For although the end of our religion is one, the professions by which people strive toward the Lord are diverse, as must be discussed more fully in the Conferences of the Elders.

Therefore we ought especially to seek from those people a pattern of discernment and self-restraint in whom we have seen these virtues flow more abundantly through the grace of the Holy Spirit—not because anyone can acquire alone what has been divided among many, but so that, in those good things of which we are capable, we may strive to imitate those who have obtained them in a more distinctive degree.

(Ambr.) “So that, as it is written: ‘Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord.’” This is written in the prophet Jeremiah (Jer. IX). What the prophet says is worthy: that we should glory in the Lord. For the one who glories in God cannot be put to shame; his works and magnificence are apparent in his deeds. Therefore, he says, “Let those who do not make rain and did not make heaven and earth be confounded in their idols.”

Similarly, those who glory in human beings—whom they know certainly to possess no virtue—are rightly addressed by Scripture: “Vain is hope in a human being” (Eccli. XXXIV). Thus the one who glories glories only in the Lord when he recognizes that it is not his own but the Lord’s—not only that he exists, but also that it goes well with him only through the one from whom he has existence.

## CHAPTER II

The Apostle shows that he did not use excellence of worldly speech, because only the perfect—those who are spiritual—can grasp it.

And I, when I came to you, brothers, came not with excellence of speech or wisdom, proclaiming to you the mystery of God. For I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.

(Greg.) It is as though he were saying: “Because I considered that you were unable to grasp the mysteries of his divinity, I spoke to you only of the weaknesses of his humanity.” For above he gradually displayed the form of our discipline; now he proves that he did not present himself to them in any other way than he had shown. In the humility of speech and the foolishness of preaching, as it appears to the world, he spoke to them the mystery concerning Christ.

He calls it a mystery because what was incarnate—the Word of God who is God—had been hidden with God from the ages. They were heretics in whom they gloried, because by means of corrupt eloquence they commended false doctrine, following worldly prudence and emptying Christ’s cross. They were ashamed to be called foolish by the world, so that they would neither proclaim that Christ was born of a virgin nor teach that he was truly crucified, because it seems foolish to confess that the Son of God was born as a human being and was crucified.

The Apostle John also identifies them when he says: “Whoever denies that Christ has come is the Antichrist; and whoever denies the Son does not have the Father” (I John II). For they said that the very one called the Son was the Father; from them Marcion derived his error.

These matters seem closed because he does not make them explicit, but wants them to be understood from his attack on worldly prudence, which is hostile to religion. What he rebukes he wishes to be learned from his judgment, so that he may show that everything our opponents ridicule as foolish is rebuked by him among the Corinthians. For he mentions the body itself, so that the structure of its members may be discerned from it. These things, however, were clear to the Corinthians, because they were not unaware of the causes for which they were being rebuked.

And I was with you in weakness and fear and much trembling. (Amb.) For, preaching Christ in the foolishness of human wisdom, he provoked hatred and persecution against himself, as though announcing something empty, and incurred hostility from Jews and Gentiles.

And my speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of wisdom. He shows that, in order not to win human favor, he did not wish to please human wisdom or devote himself to the art of words, but offered faith to the author, who did not wish his teaching to be made acceptable by the adornment of human tradition or by verbal noise, but by the things themselves, because things precede words. [Col. 0022D]

For the demonstration of the Spirit and of the power of God. Since, by words that are weak in comparison with power, foolish things appear pleasing to the wise, God did not wish his preaching to be commended by the testimony of words but by powers, so that, once the foolishness of the word had been indicated, deeds might show it to be wisdom founded on spiritual reason.

We speak wisdom among the perfect. That is, among those who confess the cross of Christ to be wisdom through the testimony of its power. For those are wise and perfect who possess faith not more in words than in realities.

But wisdom not of this age. He rightly says “not of this age,” but of the future one, in which God’s truth will appear to those who deny it. For this age, because of the weakness of its earthly thought, cannot grasp this reasoning.

Nor of the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing. It is clear that this is not the wisdom of the rulers of this world, because they are destroyed by it. Christianity destroys all the errors that the Apostle enumerates elsewhere—that is, idolatry, greed, and the other vices—as the Apostle John says: “For this reason the Son of God appeared, to destroy the works of the devil” (I John III).

But we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the wisdom that has been hidden. He declares that he was sent to reveal a hidden meaning which neither rulers nor powers knew and which the world had not heard. Hence it is considered foolish because it is unknown; yet it is rational and salvific, as power bears witness, before which all human reasoning gives way.

God’s wisdom was therefore hidden because it consists not in words but in power. It cannot be achieved by human reasoning, but is believed through the efficacy of the Spirit.

Which God predestined before the ages for our glory. It is shown to be true wisdom, and to have always been with God, to such a degree that it is said to have been predestined before the ages for our glory—we who believe. For God, foreknowing the errors that would arise in the world he was going to make, decreed this for the confounding of those who were going to make foolishness their wisdom, but for our glory, who were going to believe and who do believe.

Which none of the rulers of this age knew; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. The rulers of this age should be understood not only as the human rulers of the Jews and Romans, but also as those rulers and powers whom he mentioned above, to whom the following statement truly applies: “Our struggle is against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. IV), because Christ was crucified by their counsel and will.

Finally, after the temptations the devil withdrew, as it says, “until an opportune time” (Luke IV). And the Lord himself says: “The prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV).

The rulers of this age therefore crucified the Lord of glory through ignorance. For how can the rulers of the Jews be understood as the rulers of this age, since they were subject to Roman rule? Nor did the Roman rulers crucify Christ, especially since Pilate said: “I find no cause of death in him” (John XIX). Hence he also washed his hands, saying to the Jews: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man; you will see to it” (Matt. XXVII).

Those rulers, therefore, crucified the Lord whom he openly triumphed over in himself. Although the evangelist Luke says of the demons: “For they knew that he was Christ himself, Jesus” (Luke IV), they did indeed know that he was the one promised in the Law; yet they did not know his mystery, by which he is the Son of God.

The Apostle Peter also says this to the Jewish people (Acts III): “I know, brothers, that you acted in ignorance in doing this evil, as did your rulers”—not, however, the rulers of the age. If servants killed the Lord through ignorance, then sin ought not to be attributed to them; but it is not permissible to be ignorant of this. And although they did not know that he was the Lord, nevertheless, because they were committing an impious act, they were not without knowledge of what they were doing.

Yet he is called the Lord of glory who was crucified, although he cannot die. But because the Word became flesh—that is, the Son of God was incarnate and became human—the death was attributed to him. For the Jews did not persecute flesh as such, but the one who worked through the flesh. Thus, although the Lord of glory is ignorant of death, insofar as the desire of the Jews and the rulers of this age is concerned, they killed the Lord in the flesh.

He was crucified in the form of a servant, and yet the Lord of glory was crucified. For that assumption was such as to make God human and the human being God.

(Aug.) What is said, and why, and according to what aspect, the prudent and diligent reader understands with the Lord’s help. For behold, we have said that, according to what he is as God, he glorifies his own—according to this same reality, he is the Lord of glory—and yet the Lord of glory was crucified. For it is rightly said that God was crucified, not through the power of divinity but through the weakness of the flesh.

But as it is written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him.” (Ambr.) This is written in the Apocalypse of Elijah, among the Apocrypha. Through this example he speaks of an unexpected event, one that not only could not enter the human mind but was hidden even from the heavenly powers: namely, that the Son of God was incarnate. In this way he confirms what he had said above: if the rulers of this age did not understand that the Lord had become human, how much less did human beings understand it.

But if words caused offense or scandal, faith nevertheless ought not to have been denied because of powers and signs. Power ought to have been placed before human weakness and ignorance, and what seemed impossible to human reason ought to have been believed. Therefore he prepared this gift for those who love the Lord—that is, for believers.

(Aug.) Alternatively: “What eye has not seen,” because it is not a color; “nor ear heard,” because it is not a sound; “nor has entered into the human heart,” because the human heart ought to ascend there.

But God has revealed these things to us through his Spirit. (Hier.) If eye has not seen and ear has not heard what God prepared for those who love him, how does the same Apostle add, “But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit”? If it was revealed to the Apostle, should we understand that he revealed it also to others?

The brief answer is that we ought not to ask what it is that eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and the human heart has not conceived. For if it is unknown, how can what is promised in the future be known? It is not seen in the present. For hope that is seen is not hope, but an already certain possession.

It would be like someone saying, “Show me what cannot be shown; speak what cannot be heard; explain what human thought cannot comprehend.” The Apostle should therefore be understood to have said that spiritual things cannot be grasped by bodily eyes, bodily ears, or mortal thought.

For although “we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him” (II Cor. V), it is also written in John’s Epistle: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be, for we shall see him as he is” (I John III).

Nor does his testimony that it was revealed to him and to the saints through the Spirit immediately imply that he himself revealed it to others. Otherwise, he also heard in paradise unspeakable words that he could not report to others; or, if he reported them, they would not be unspeakable.

(Ambr.) Because the rulers of the age were ignorant of this, God revealed it through his Spirit to believers, since God’s reality cannot be learned without the Spirit of God. For he says that this mystery was sent to be declared not only to human beings but also to the rulers and powers in the heavenly places who crucified the Lord, so that, when it was preached on earth, those who are in the corporeal heavens—those who dwell under the elements of the firmament—might learn it.

This Apostle is therefore unique, and he is the one who received this grace, because no one was able to explain the mystery of the Trinity in this way. Hence, by divine judgment, he was also called the vessel of election.

For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. (Aug.) Not, of course, in order to discover what it does not know, but because it leaves absolutely nothing unknown.

(Ambr.) Because this Spirit is from God, it knows everything. He says “the depths of God” because it knows all his power and foreknowledge, something altogether impossible for a creature. For who knows the things of a human being except the human spirit that is in that person? It is clear that our thoughts are known by no one except our own mind, which he called spirit.

(Aug.) Finally, in the Gospel, among other things, he says: “And his spirit returned to her” (Matt. IX). In Scripture, the human spirit is called the rational power of the soul itself, by which it differs from animals and rules them according to the law of nature. Concerning this the Apostle says: “No one knows the things of a human being except the human spirit that is in him.”

For no one knows what is happening in a human being except the human spirit that is in that person, until the Lord comes, enlightens the hidden things of darkness, and reveals the thoughts of the heart, so that each person may see not only his own thoughts but also those of others.

The Apostle said that no one knows what is happening in a human being except the human spirit that is in him according to what we observe in ourselves. For according to what we believe, we do not see: we know that many are faithful, and we are known to many, although it is written, “For who among human beings knows?”

(Greg.) If no one knows the things of a human being except the human spirit that is in him, how is it that it is written in Job: “Certainly I know your thoughts” (Job XXI)?

The human spirit is unknown to another person when it is not revealed by words or deeds. But when it is written, “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. VII), whatever lies hidden within is disclosed by what is done outwardly. Hence it is rightly said through Solomon: “As the faces of those who look into water answer to one another, so the hearts of human beings are manifest to the prudent” (Prov. XXVII).

Accordingly, blessed Job, when he said that he knew the thoughts of his friends as they spoke with him, added, “and the opinions you hold against me are unjust,” thereby showing from an evident matter that he had discovered what lay hidden within them.

So also no one has known the things that are in God except the Spirit of God. (Amb.) This Spirit [Col. 0026A] of God taught us what it knows by nature, not as one taught; and it taught us about the mystery of Christ, because it is not only the Spirit of God but also the Spirit of Christ.

But we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God. From this we know that we have received the Spirit who is from God: the spirit of the world cannot know the things that have been made known to us by this Spirit.

The spirit of the world, however, is the spirit by which fanatics who are without God are seized. For among worldly spirits it is the more powerful one, and it usually divines worldly things by conjectures; they call it the python. This is the spirit that is deceived and deceives through probabilities. It is the one that spoke through the Sibyl, following our understanding and wishing to have a place among the heavenly beings.

So that we may know the things given to us by God. Since the Spirit of God has been given to us, we know the things given to us by God. We could not know these things if we possessed the spirit of the world, because the spirit of the world cannot know them.

For no one knows the mind of God except the one who is from God, the Spirit of God. Lower things cannot know the counsel of higher things, nor can a creature recognize the will of its Creator.

Which we also speak. This makes it clear that we know what has been given to us by God, because we also speak these things, so that others may learn through spiritual teaching. For what was divinely made known to preachers—that is, to the Apostles—was to be handed on to the peoples, and the rulers of this age were to learn what evil they had committed.

(Aug.) For when the Lord says, “The servant does not know what his master is doing” (John XV), we, beloved, can know what our Lord is doing so that we may be his friends. For he himself makes us not only human beings but also righteous people; we do not make ourselves righteous. And in order that we may know this, who but he himself brings it about?

For we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know what has been given to us by God. Whatever good there is is given by him. Since this too is good, it is certainly given by him: that we should know from whom every good thing is given, so that in all good things the one who glories may glory in the Lord.

“For whoever has, to him it will be given” (Luke VIII). What does it mean to have fully? It means to know from whom one has received. But whoever does not have—that is, whoever does not know from whom he has received what he has—will have even what he has taken away from him.

Finally, as he himself says, it belonged to wisdom to know whose gift this gift also was (Wis. VIII). Thus the Apostle Paul, when he commended God’s grace in the Holy Spirit, said to us: “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God.” And as though someone had said to him, “From where do you distinguish this?” he continued: “So that we may know the things given to us by God.”

The Spirit of God, therefore, is the spirit of love; the spirit of this world is the spirit of arrogance. Those who have the spirit of this world are proud and ungrateful to God. They possess many of his gifts, but they do not worship the one from whom they possess them; therefore they are miserable.

(Greg.) He preferred this wisdom to be displayed not in the teaching of human wisdom’s words but in the teaching of the Spirit; for he wished to show this wisdom through the purity of truth alone, not to smear it with the coloring of eloquence.

(Amb.) For human words of wisdom do not perceive this meaning, nor is it grasped through literary studies; it is conceived through spiritual reasoning by faith, as the prophet Isaiah says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. VII).

It is learned more by the law of nature than by the course of the stars and the calculations of the signs marked in the firmament. Finally, believers see that what they believe accords not with human words but with its own nature. For the work recognizes its maker.

Therefore the Gospel speaks spiritual things to our minds, rousing them to knowledge of their Creator.

Comparing spiritual things with spiritual things. That is, transmitting to those who reject worldly prudence the spiritual efficacy contained in the mystery of faith, in order to enlighten the understanding of well-disposed people. For those who believe what the wisdom of the world judges foolish are spiritual.

But the animal person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him. Like animals, such a person presses his understanding down into the earth. Therefore he grasps only what he sees and thinks that nothing can happen except in the way he knows.

Thus, whatever he hears that is different from what he knows, he judges foolish. For he considers that nothing can happen without mixture. Hence he laughs when he hears that God begot a Son, although he knows God to be simple and incorporeal; that a virgin gave birth; and that bodies dissolved by death are restored to life.

Yet these things contribute all the more to the praise of God, so that he may be believed to have done what cannot be investigated by reason. For it is God who did it.

Human weakness considers foolish what its knowledge cannot contain. Yet it ought rather to consider its own judgment foolish, and prudent that which, because it is said to have been done by God, cannot be comprehended. While following human tradition, they deny faith in the one God. Thus what they think cannot happen, because they are puffed up by the reasoning of the flesh, has been accomplished spiritually; and in this way those marked as reprobate have been spiritually condemned.

(Aug.) That they do not possess this Spirit who have separated themselves from the Church, the Apostle Jude most clearly declares when he says: “They separate themselves, being natural people and not having the Spirit.”

Hence, in the Church itself, when the Apostle Paul rebuked those who, although established within its unity, were attempting certain schisms under the names of human beings, he said among other things: “The animal person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God.” For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned.

He shows what he means by “does not perceive”: that is, “does not grasp through knowledge.”

Yet he calls these people, who are established in the Church, little ones—not yet spiritual, but still carnal—and says that they must be nourished with milk, not solid food. “As to little ones in Christ,” he says, “I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able; indeed, even now you are not able” (I Cor. III).

Where it says “not yet” or “not even now,” there is certainly no despair, if the person is striving toward becoming at some time what he is not yet. For he says, “Even now you are carnal,” and, showing from what they are carnal, continues: “For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human ways?”

And explaining the same point more clearly, he says: “When one says, ‘I indeed am of Paul,’ and another, ‘I am of Apollos,’ are you not human beings?”

These people—Paul and Apollos—were united in harmony through the unity of the Spirit and the bond of peace. Yet because these others began to divide them among themselves and to become puffed up in favor of one against the other, they are called human, carnal, and animal, unable to perceive the things of the Spirit of God.

Nevertheless, because they had not separated themselves from the Church, they are called little ones in Christ. He wanted those whom he rebuked to be angels or gods, but they were human beings—that is, amid these contentions they understood not the things of God but the things of human beings. [Col. 0028A]

Of those, however, who have separated themselves from the Church, it is not said that they do not perceive the things of the Spirit, lest this be referred to the perception of knowledge; rather, it is said that they do not have the Spirit.

It does not follow that whoever has the Spirit also perceives through knowledge what he possesses. Therefore the little ones in Christ who are established in the Church possess this Spirit, although they are still animal and carnal, unable to perceive what they possess—that is, unable to understand and know it.

For how could they be little ones in Christ unless they had been reborn from the Holy Spirit? Nor should it seem strange that someone may possess something and be unaware of possessing it. To say nothing of the divinity of the omnipotent and unchangeable Trinity, who can easily perceive through knowledge what the soul is, and who does not have a soul?

Finally, so that we may know most certainly that the little ones in Christ, although they do not yet perceive the things of the Spirit, nevertheless possess the Spirit of God, let us shortly afterward observe how he rebukes those same people, saying: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” He would in no way say this of those who had separated themselves from the Church, of whom it was said: “They do not have the Spirit.”

[Col. 0028C] “But the spiritual person judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one.” (Amb.) Since the true principle of spiritual persons—that is, of believers—is this—for each person is designated by what he believes—they themselves therefore judge all things. For by their example unbelief will be judged, while they themselves will be judged by no one; for who would condemn one who speaks the truth? Since it is evident that all enemies of the faith hold falsehoods as truths, their accusation has already been rendered void, condemned by the judgment of truth; for, as the Lord says, “Whoever has not believed has already been judged” (John 3).

[Aug.] Thus a person is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created him, and, having become spiritual, judges all things that ought indeed to be judged; while he himself is judged by no one. That he judges all things means that he has authority over “the fish of the sea, the birds of the heavens, and all cattle and beasts, and all the earth, and all the serpents that creep upon the earth.” For he does this through the understanding of the mind, by which he perceives the things that belong to the Spirit of God. Otherwise, “a human being placed in honor did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48).

The spiritual person also judges by approving what is right and disapproving what he finds wrongly done in the works and conduct of the faithful—in chastity, fasts, and pious thoughts concerning those things perceived through bodily sensation. For he is now said to judge these matters in which he also has authority to correct. “For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him?”

(Amb.) The mind of God is that by which he commanded these things to be done spiritually, through which the wisdom of the world was proved foolish, denying that what has been done could be done. No one has known this mind in such a way as to find fault with it and correct God’s plan; for whoever has known it praises God’s power, whereas one who denies that he can do all things does not even believe that he made the world. For what great thing is it to believe that he generated from himself, when it is not doubted that he made all things from nothing? Indeed, the Savior says: “With God all things are possible” (Luke 18).

It is clear to all that God has no need of counselors, since he himself supplies counsel even to the counselors of human wisdom. Of him it is also written: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” But just as, when bread or clothing is given to one in need, the Lord testifies that he himself has received it, so, when sound counsel is given to anyone who is ignorant, he himself receives it whose member is the person being instructed. For all the faithful are members of our Redeemer, and just as he is nourished in us through the mercy of generosity, so he is assisted in us through the counsel of teaching.

“But we have the mind of God.” He says this because, as believers, we are participants in that same divine judgment.

## CHAPTER III

He removes the Corinthians’ error, because they were attributing too much to certain ministers; and he treats of building with wood, hay, and stubble, and of the foolish wisdom of the world.

“And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual persons, but as carnal.” (Amb.) He is now speaking to those who, because they were still serving the pleasures of the world, were carnal. Although they had already been baptized and had received the Holy Spirit, because after baptism they had immediately returned to the old person whom they had renounced, they are called carnal. For the Holy Spirit then remains in the one into whom he had poured himself if that person remains in the purpose of his new birth; otherwise he departs—yet in such a way that, if the person reforms himself, he returns to him. For he is always ready for what is good, loving repentance.

“As to infants in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food.” Although they had been reborn in Christ, it was nevertheless not fitting that spiritual things should be entrusted to them. For, having received faith, which is like a spiritual seed, they produced no fruit worthy of God by which they might deserve to learn the words of perfection; instead, like infants, they occupied themselves with imperfect understanding. But the Apostle, a divine man and a spiritual physician, supplied each person according to his strength, lest anyone, through imperfection and inexperience, should suffer scandal concerning spiritual matters.

“For you were not yet able.” He plainly shows that they ought not to have heard what is to be said to those who are established in the faith. “But neither can you now, for you are still carnal.” Here he severely reproves the rashness of those who had earlier complained that they had not heard spiritual things, although they were still unworthy to hear them.

For the false apostles indiscriminately taught everyone in one and the same manner, making no distinction among persons, so that they might become acceptable by being commended through hypocrisy. Yet it is clear that the Lord and our author, Christ, addressed the crowds in one way and the disciples in another, and that there was even a distinction among the apostles themselves. For he showed his glory to three disciples on the mountain, telling them to keep silent about what they had seen until he had risen from the dead.

(Greg.) Holy preachers are, as it were, doors for us, leading us to the interior understanding of eternal wisdom. But when they preach to beginners not lofty and mystical things, but matters that they are able to grasp, they are exterior doors; when, however, they speak profound and mystical things to the perfect, they are interior doors.

Let us see how the exterior door is opened: “I could not speak to you as spiritual persons, but as carnal; as infants in Christ, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food.” Let us see how the interior door is opened: “We speak wisdom among the perfect.” Let us see whether the interior and exterior door are the same: “I am a debtor both to the wise and to the foolish” (Rom. 1); and again: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are sober, it is for you” (2 Cor. 5).

In that, by contemplating and speaking, he is beside himself for the wise, he is an interior door; but in that he soberly adapts himself to preaching for the infants, and does not reveal how great an intoxication of the Spirit is poured into the mind when he preaches, he shows himself to be an exterior door. Thus they are both exterior and interior doors for us: they instruct us at the first entrance of faith, hope, and charity, and, when they preach the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom to those already advancing, they lead us inward by a subtler understanding.

(Aug.) Christ, preached as crucified by the apostles, was a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, he was the power of God and the wisdom of God. Carnal infants hold to this merely by believing; spiritual persons, who are more capable, also perceive it by understanding.

Once this has first been recognized—that spiritual and carnal persons each grasp the very things they hear together according to their own capacity, the former as infants and the latter as adults, the former as nourishment of milk and the latter as solid food—there seems to be no necessity for certain secrets of doctrine to be withheld and concealed from the faithful, to be spoken separately to the more mature, that is, to those more capable of understanding. Nor should this be thought necessary because the Apostle said: “I could not speak to you as spiritual persons, but as carnal.”

For the very fact that he judged himself to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ, and him crucified, means that he could not speak to them as spiritual persons, because they were unable to grasp this as spiritual persons do. Whoever among them was spiritual—that is, whoever spiritually understood what the others heard as carnal persons—could grasp it. Thus the statement “I could not speak to you as spiritual persons, but as carnal” is to be understood as though he had said: “You could not grasp what I was saying as spiritual persons, but only as carnal persons.”

Therefore we must hasten, so that, once we have renounced the world and ceased to be carnal—that is, once we have begun to withdraw from worldly conduct and cease from the manifest pollution of the flesh—we may strive with all our strength immediately to attain a spiritual condition. Otherwise, perhaps, while flattering ourselves because we seem, according to the outward person, to have renounced this world or abandoned the contagion of carnal fornications, as though by this we had attained the height of perfection, we may thereafter become more lax and lenient in correcting our other passions. Held between the two, we may be unable to attain the stage of spiritual progress, supposing that it is sufficient for us to possess perfection because we appear, in our outward person, to be separated from the conduct and pleasures of this world.

“For since there are jealousy and contentions among you, are you not carnal and walking according to the human way?” (Amb.) He shows the causes of their unworthiness: whoever hopes for help from a human being is carnal, whereas whoever, having rejected human power, hopes in God is spiritual, because God is spirit.
