(Aug.) What does it mean to walk according to the human way—that is, to be carnal? The word “human” is understood from “flesh,” that is, from a part of the human being. And he had called these same people “animal” above, and afterward “carnal,” speaking in this way: “The animal person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him.”

To such people, therefore, that is, to the animal, he says shortly afterward: “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual persons, but as carnal.” In both passages he speaks in the same manner, namely, by a part standing for the whole. For from the soul and from the flesh, which are parts of the human being, the whole can be signified, namely, the human being. Thus an animal person is not one thing and a carnal person another; rather, the same person is described by both expressions, namely, a human being living according to the human way.

The same is true where it is written, “By works of the law no flesh will be justified” (Rom. 3), and where it is written, “Seventy-five [seventy] souls went down with Jacob into Egypt” (Gen. 46). This is even clearer in what follows: “When one says, ‘I am of Paul,’ and another, ‘I am of Apollo,’ are you not human beings?”

(Greg.) Although Holy Scripture sometimes uses “human beings” for those who think human thoughts, as the Apostle says, “Since there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal?” and shortly afterward adds, “Are you not human beings?”, it nevertheless sometimes uses the term for those whom it distinguishes from beasts by reason—that is, those whom it does not show to be governed by a bestial movement of the passions. To them the Lord says through the prophet: “You are human beings, the flocks of my pasture” (Ps. 94), because the Lord feeds those whom carnal pleasure does not pursue in the manner of beasts.

By contrast, those who succumb to carnal affection are no longer called human beings but beasts, as the prophet of God says concerning certain people dying in their sin: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel 1).

Sometimes, however, when people recognize that they are not openly committing a vice, they come more quickly to correction if they are put to shame by another, more obvious fault, sought out from the side and brought forward as a reproach. Thus, from what they cannot defend, they may recognize that they are wickedly holding to what they do defend.

Accordingly, when Paul saw that the Corinthians were arrogantly puffed up against one another, each saying that he belonged to Paul, Apollo, Cephas, or Christ, he brought forward the sin of incest, which had been committed among them and left uncorrected.

(Amb.) Just as those who glory in God and hope for grace from him are called gods, adopted by God, so those who glory in a human being are called both human and carnal, enclosed by the judgment of God, which says: “I said, ‘You are gods’; but you shall die like human beings” (Ps. 81).

He therefore begins with his own person, lest it should be thought that he was destroying their persons out of envy. He shows that it is a grave error, insulting to God, when, although God is preached, glory is given to human beings. What, then, is less removed from paganism, so long as hope is still placed in human beings?

“What, then, is Apollo, and what is Paul? Ministers of the one in whom you have believed.” Since they are ministers, hope should not be placed in them but in God, whose ministers they are. Gratitude is due to him whose gift it is; they are servants, whom it is sometimes necessary to compel to administer their office even against their will. Was not Moses compelled to go to Pharaoh (Exod. 2)? Was not Jonah unwillingly sent to preach to the Ninevites (Jon. 1)? Was not Ananias, though objecting, sent to lay his hand upon Saul (Acts 9)?

“And to each one according as the Lord has given.” That is, according as he willed and knew, he divided the duties of ministry among individuals.

“I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth.” To plant is to evangelize and draw people to the faith; to water is to baptize with solemn words. But to forgive sins and to give the Spirit belongs to God alone. If, therefore, God gives the effect of salvation, no glory of salvation belongs to a human being in this matter. For we know that the Holy Spirit has been given by God even without the laying on of hands, and that an unbaptized person has obtained the remission of sins. Was this person not invisibly baptized when he received the gift of baptism?

(Greg.) Great are the things that the Lord accomplishes through his voice, but they would be less great if they could be scrutinized. He therefore does, according to blessed Job, “great and unsearchable things” (Job 37), because he displays the perfection of the work outwardly, while the very nature of the operation remains hidden within.

Outwardly he also sounds forth through the apostles by his voice, but inwardly he himself illuminates the hearts of those who hear. Paul bears witness to this when he says: “I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth.” “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth.”

“Therefore neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth.” (Amb.) What is planted can wither, and what is watered may fail to reach the effect of fruitfulness, unless God gives it vigorous life. Thus, as far as the honoring of God is concerned, a human being is nothing; but as far as ministry is concerned, he is necessary, so that he may be honored as a servant, not so that anything should be hoped for from him to the dishonor of God.

(Aug.) What did Simon desire except to be praised for his miracles and exalted in pride? For pride itself compelled him to suppose that the gift of the Holy Spirit could be purchased with money (Acts 8). In contrast to this pride, the Apostle, remaining in humility, burning with the Spirit at midday and shining with prudence, says: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth.”

He had said: “I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth”; and again: “Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” See how he refuses to be honored in place of Christ and does not wish to display himself to a soul committing fornication as though he were its bridegroom.

Does it not seem a great thing to plant and to water? Yet “neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters.” How cautious he was! He does not call himself anything with respect to the salvation of those whom he desired to build up in Christ.

(Greg.) For we are God’s assistants. When, by the voice of exhortation, we cooperate with the one into whom he himself pours inward grace, we assist outwardly through the ministry of the voice in what he accomplishes inwardly through the Spirit. Our exhortation is brought to perfection only when God is present in the heart, the one who is being assisted. Hence he says elsewhere: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth.”

To plant and to water is to assist; both forms of ministry will be empty if God does not give the growth in the heart. But those who think lofty thoughts from their own understanding do not wish to be humbly God’s assistants. While they consider themselves useful to God, they alienate themselves from the fruit of usefulness.

Hence the Voice of Truth says to the disciples: “When you have done all that was commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were bound to do’” (Luke 17).

“Now the one who plants and the one who waters are one.” (Aug.) They are one because both are hired servants, although their duties are different. I do not know whether Scripture says that those whose nature is different are “one.” If several persons are of the same nature but think differently, they are not one insofar as they think differently.

For if they were already one simply because they were human beings, he would not say that they should be one, “as we are one,” when he commended his disciples to the Father. But Paul and Apollo, because they were both human beings and thought alike, are said to be one: “The one who plants and the one who waters are one.”

Why, then, are they called one without its being added what they are one in? When several are called one, the meaning is that they share the same nature and essence without disagreement or dissent. But when what they are one in is added, something made one from several may be signified, even though their natures differ. Thus soul and body are not simply one—for what is so different?—unless “one” is added or understood, namely, one human being or one animal. Hence the Apostle says: “The one who clings to a prostitute is one body” (1 Cor. 6).

[Col. 0033D] “But each one will receive his own reward according to his own labor.” (Amb.) Although they are one, because the one who evangelizes is greater than the one who baptizes, he distinguished their rewards. This also pertains to the sincerity of teaching, so that the one who transmits doctrine inviolate is worthy of the greater reward.

“For we are God’s assistants; you are God’s agriculture, God’s building.” This pertains to the persons of the apostles, whom we know to be God’s assistants because they are Christ’s vicars.

(Greg.) But we must consider whether the statement of blessed Job might appear contrary to this passage, when he says to his rivals: “Whose assistant are you? Is it the assistant of one who is weak?” (Job 26.) The Apostle, however, says: “We are God’s assistants.”

If it is good to be God’s assistants, why is Elihu reproved for assisting God? The answer is that we must certainly know that some offend God while defending him, whereas others, insofar as they are able, defend God’s cause. The latter are truly God’s assistants when they preach truthfully; the former, by falsely reproving the saints on God’s behalf, strive for God but offend him in their striving.

The latter speak of God not as unknown but as known; the former, even while speaking truth, are not known by God. The Lord says concerning Elihu (Job 38): “Who is this who wraps up judgments in unlearned words?” What does the Lord mean by asking, “Who is this who wraps up judgments?” Yet by asking he condemns him, adding: “In unlearned words.”

Elihu did speak true judgments, but he wrapped them in unlearned words, because he turned the statements of the Holy Spirit against Job, although the Lord had borne witness concerning Job that he was without blame.

We therefore do not use the words “God is our helper forever” in the same sense in which we say, “We are God’s assistants.” He does not need our assistance, whereas we can do nothing without him.

“You are God’s agriculture, God’s building,” because the city already has here a great building in the conduct of the saints. In a building, one stone bears another, because one stone is placed upon another; and the one who bears another is himself borne by another. Thus, in the holy Church, each person both bears another and is borne by another. For neighbors bear with one another, so that through them the building of charity may rise.

“According to the grace that was given to me, as a wise architect I laid the foundation.” (Amb.) He says that grace was given to him so that he might be worthy to preach the Gospel, thereby showing that this too came from God, not from a human being. According to this grace, therefore, he says that, as a wise architect, he laid the foundation.

A wise architect is one who lays the foundation according to the discipline of the author—that is, one who evangelizes according to the tradition of the Savior.

“Another builds upon it.” The superstructure consists of what is handed down after the preaching of the apostles by later teachers, whether bad or good. “But let each one take care how he builds upon it,” that is, let the superstructure correspond to the foundation, lest, if it is crooked and frivolous, it cause ruin while the foundation remains unharmed. For if someone teaches badly, the name of Christ, which is the foundation, remains; but bad doctrine will perish, as the Lord says: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (Matt. 15).

“For no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.” (Greg.) Christ Jesus bears the foundation, and the stones are borne by him; he is not borne by the stones, because our Redeemer bears all our burdens, whereas there was no evil in him that needed to be borne.

(Ambr.) No one can lay another foundation because, although there are certain heretics, they nevertheless teach only under Christ’s name. Otherwise they cannot commend the fabrications of their error unless they preach them with the Savior’s name inserted, so that the dignity of the name may make contrary and absurd matters acceptable.

“But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones…” (Amb.) Precious stones are those that fire does not corrupt. He set forth three kinds of things splendid in the world, by which he signified good doctrine: gold, silver, and precious stones. Wood, hay, and stubble are the three other kinds, but frivolous ones; in these, corrupt and vain doctrine is recognized as being represented.

(Aug.) Those who live well, honor and praise God, are patient in tribulations, and desire their homeland build gold, silver, and precious stones. But those who still love worldly things, are entangled in earthly affairs, and are devoted to certain bonds and affections of the flesh—to their houses, marriages, possessions—and nevertheless are Christians, so that their heart does not depart from Christ, build wood, hay, and stubble.

For in building nothing is placed before the foundation. But what follows? “The work of each person will be revealed by fire.” The fire is the fire of tribulation and temptation. This fire tested many martyrs here, but it will test the entire human race at the end.

There have been martyrs who possessed these worldly things. How many rich men and senators suffered! Yet some of them were building wood, hay, and stubble in their affections for carnal and worldly concerns. Nevertheless, because they had Christ as the foundation upon which they were building, the hay burned, while they themselves remained in the foundation, as the Apostle says: “If anyone’s work remains, he will receive a reward.” He loses nothing, because he will find what he loved.

What, then, did the fire of tribulation do to them? It tested them. “If anyone’s work remains, he will receive a reward; if anyone’s work burns, he will suffer loss.” Thus it is one thing not to be harmed by fire, and another to be saved through fire. And why? Because of the foundation.

Therefore, let the foundation not depart from your heart. Do not place the foundation upon hay—that is, do not put hay before the foundation, so that hay has the first place in your heart and Christ the second. But if hay must already be there, let Christ have the first place there and hay the second.

“Each one’s work will become manifest; the day of the Lord will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire.” This means that bad doctrine will appear to everyone in the fire. For now it deceives certain people. Nothing is placed before the foundation in the building.

Whoever therefore has Christ in his heart in such a way that he does not place earthly and temporal things—even those that are lawful and permitted—before Christ has Christ as his foundation. But if he places such things first, then, even if he seems to possess faith in Christ, Christ is nevertheless not the foundation in him, since such things are placed before Christ. How much more is this true if, while despising saving commandments, he commits unlawful acts: he is shown not to have placed Christ first, but last.

If a Christian loves a prostitute and, clinging to her, becomes one body with her, he no longer has Christ in the foundation. But if someone loves his wife according to Christ, who could doubt that Christ is in his foundation? If, however, he loves her according to this world, carnally, in the disease of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God, the Apostle—or rather Christ through the Apostle—grants even this by way of concession.

Such a person, therefore, may have Christ as his foundation. For if he places nothing of that affection and pleasure before Christ, although he builds wood, hay, and stubble upon the foundation, Christ is the foundation; for this reason he will be saved as through fire.

The pleasures of this world and earthly loves, which are not to be condemned when they arise from the marital union, are consumed by the fire of tribulation. To this fire belong bereavements and all calamities that take these things away. Thus, for the one who built, this building will be harmful, because he will no longer possess what he built upon it, and he will be tormented by the loss of those things in which he had rejoiced by enjoying them.

Yet he will be saved through this fire by the merit of the foundation, because, if the persecutor proposed to him the choice between retaining those things and choosing Christ, he would not place them before Christ.

See in the Apostle’s words a person building upon the foundation gold, silver, and precious stones: “The unmarried person thinks about the things of God, how he may please God.” See another building wood, hay, and stubble: “The married person,” he says, “thinks about the things of the world, how he may please his wife.”

“Each person’s work will be made manifest; for the day of the Lord will declare it”—the day, certainly, of tribulation—“because it will be revealed in fire,” he says. He calls that same tribulation fire, as it is written elsewhere: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation through tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. 27).

“And the fire will test each person’s work, of what kind it is.” If anyone’s work remains—for what each person thinks remains, namely, how to please God through the things of God—“he will receive a reward for what he built upon it”; that is, he will receive what he thought about. But if anyone’s work burns, he will suffer loss, because he will not have what he loved. Yet he himself will be saved, because no tribulation moved him from the stability of that foundation—“but only as through fire.” For what he did not possess without enticing love, he does not lose without burning grief.

“And the fire will test each person’s work, of what kind it is.” (Amb.) Since the examination will take place through fire, if it finds nothing in anyone that can be consumed, it shows that he was a good teacher. For bad and adulterous doctrine is signified by wood, hay, and stubble precisely so that it may be shown to be fuel for fire.

(Aug.) It is not incredible that something of this kind may also happen after this life; and it may be asked whether it is so. Some of the faithful may be saved, more slowly or more quickly according as they have loved perishable goods to a greater or lesser extent, through a certain purgatorial fire. Yet this does not apply to those of whom it is said that they will not possess the kingdom of God, unless those same sins are remitted to them after suitable repentance.

“For no one can lay any other foundation besides the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.” (Greg.) Will the apostles themselves also be tested by fire, although they are said not to be judged but to judge the twelve tribes of Israel? Or will fire test even those with whom Saint Paul counted himself, saying: “But we who are left will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4)?

If we weigh the meaning of Christ’s words, we bring this obscurity into the light, with Christ himself illuminating it. For he said: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it should burn?” (Luke 12.) And the Holy Spirit, descending upon the apostles, appeared in the form of fire. Appearing as a sign to unbelievers, he tested believers inwardly like fire.

Therefore “the fire will test each person’s work, of what kind it is,” because those whom the spiritual fire does not examine in the present time will be tested by fire in the future judgment. “For whoever are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God” (Rom. 8). Although they are tested by fire, they have been examined by the Holy Spirit; for, having received him through the laying on of the bishop’s hands, they did not in any way depart from him. But if they sin in some matter, they are corrected by recognizing and confessing it.

“For everyone,” says the Lord, “will be salted with fire” [the printed text has *salietur*]. Either here he will be tested by spiritual fire, or there by bodily fire.

Clearly, then, just as not everyone will be tested by fire on the day of judgment, so on that same day not everyone at all will be judged. The Lord bears witness to this when he says: “Whoever believes in the Son will not be judged; but whoever is unbelieving has already been judged” (John 4).

Whom, then, will the future fire test, if God will judge neither believers nor unbelievers? But as though we were questioning him, “What, then, will the judgment be?”, he immediately added: “This is the judgment: that light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than light.”

Therefore only those will be judged on the day of judgment who, although they knew that light had come, are nevertheless said to have loved darkness more. For those who remain in darkness have already been judged, while those who have nothing of darkness belong to the light without any judgment.

But those who, although baptized, will be judged in the future judgment are the ones concerning whom judgment will be rendered, so that it may be shown whether they ought to belong more to the light or to the darkness. These, therefore, will rise to be judged; the righteous will rise to judge, and the wicked to be condemned. For the latter too will rise, but not for judgment, as the Psalmist bears witness when he says: “The wicked do not rise in the judgment” (Ps. 1).

If anyone’s work that he has built upon it remains, he will receive a reward.

**(Amb.)** For when no stain of corrupt teaching is found in it, it will be like fine gold; he will be like the three brothers in the fiery furnace, and will receive the reward of eternal life with glory. For just as the gold, silver, and precious stones which the fire did not consume, [Col. 0037D] so also the good teacher will remain incorruptible.

If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss. The work that is said to burn is evil doctrine, which will perish; for all evils will perish, like the way of the wicked, because they are not substances but perverse assertions. To suffer loss, however, is to endure punishments; for who, placed in punishment, does not incur loss?

Yet he himself will be saved, but only as through fire. He says that he will be saved because the substance of which he consists will not perish, just as evil doctrine will perish, since an accident is the cause. He therefore said, “but only as through fire,” so that this salvation would not be without punishment. For he did not say, “He will be saved through fire,” as though he were saved by his own merit, unburned by the fire after being tested through it; [Col. 0038A] rather, by saying, “but only as through fire,” he shows that he will indeed be saved, but will suffer the punishments of fire, so that, purified through fire, he may become saved, and not be tormented by everlasting fire like the unbelievers. Thus, in some respect, it is worthwhile to have believed in Christ.

For the one who sees that he has defended what was false in place of what was true must always be ashamed; and likewise the one who, having cast away what was false, followed what was true, and having rejected impiety, submitted to piety, will always have confidence in God. For whatever lies outside catholic truth is contrary to it.

**(Aug.)** There are many who, misunderstanding this passage through their reading, are deceived by a false security, believing that if they build capital crimes upon the foundation of Christ, the sins themselves can be cleansed through a temporary fire and that they may afterward attain everlasting life. This interpretation, dearest brothers, must be corrected, because those who flatter themselves in this way are deceiving themselves. For by that temporary fire of which the Apostle said, “He himself will be saved, but only as through fire,” not capital sins but lesser sins are purged.

And although—what is worse—there are not only greater sins but also very many lesser ones, nevertheless, concerning the greater sins, even if not all, at least some must be mentioned, lest anyone attempt to excuse himself pointlessly by saying that he does not know which are lesser sins and which are capital crimes. Although the Apostle listed many capital sins, we, so that we may not appear to cause despair, shall briefly say what they are: sacrilege, murder, adultery, false witness, theft, robbery, pride, envy, [Col. 0038C] greed; and if someone has maintained anger for a long time; and drunkenness, if it is habitual, is counted among them.

For whoever recognizes that any of these sins rules over him, unless he worthily reforms himself—if he has the opportunity, performs penance for a long time, gives abundant alms, and abstains from sins—cannot be purified by that temporary fire of which the Apostle speaks; rather, everlasting flame will destroy him without any remedy.

As for lesser sins, although they are known to all, nevertheless, since it would take too long to review them all, it is necessary to name at least some of them. Whenever anyone takes more food or drink than is necessary, he should know that this belongs to lesser sins; whenever he speaks more than is proper, or is silent more than is beneficial; whenever he irritates a poor person who asks at an inconvenient time; whenever, although physically healthy, he wishes to eat while others are fasting, or, being devoted to sleep, rises late for church; whenever, apart from the desire for children, he has intercourse with his wife; whenever he is slow to visit those confined in prison, or slow to visit the sick; if he neglects to restore those who are at odds to harmony; if he irritates a neighbor, wife, child, or servant more than is proper; if he flatters more than is proper; if anyone wishes to flatter a person of higher rank, either willingly or under compulsion; if he prepares excessively elaborate or expensive banquets while the poor are hungry; if he occupies himself, whether in church or outside church, with idle stories for which an account must be rendered on the day [Col. 0039A] of judgment; if, while we swear carelessly, we then are unable to fulfill what we have promised because of some necessity and thus commit perjury; and if we curse with complete ease or recklessness—for it is written, “Nor will those who curse inherit the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI); and if we rashly suspect something that nevertheless often proves not to be as we believe—then, without doubt, we commit sin.

It is clear that these and similar things belong to lesser sins. As I have already said, they can scarcely be enumerated, and not only the Christian people but no saint has ever been, or could be, immune from them. Although we do not believe that these sins kill the soul, nevertheless, by filling it as though with pustules and a dreadful scab, they make it so deformed that they scarcely, or only with great shame, permit it to come to the embrace of that heavenly Bridegroom, of whom it is written: “He prepared for himself a Church without spot or wrinkle” (Ephes. V).

Therefore, by continual prayers, frequent fasts, more generous almsgiving, and especially by the forgiveness of those who sin against us, let them continually be redeemed, lest, gathered together, they perhaps form a heap and overwhelm us. For whatever of these sins has not been redeemed by us must be purified by fire, concerning which the Apostle said that it will be revealed in fire, and that the one whose work burns will suffer loss.

To summarize everything briefly: all the saints who faithfully serve God strive to devote themselves to reading and prayer and to persevere in good works. They build upon the foundation of Christ neither capital crimes nor lesser sins—that is, wood, hay, and straw—but good works, namely gold, silver, and precious stones. Through that fire of which the Apostle says, “It will be revealed in fire,” they will pass without any violence.

But those who, although they do not commit capital crimes, are nevertheless prone to committing lesser sins and negligent about redeeming them will come to eternal life because they believed in Christ and did not commit capital sins. Yet first they must either be refined in this age through the most bitter tribulations by God’s justice or mercy, as has already been said; or, through many acts of almsgiving—and especially while mercifully forgiving their enemies—they must be delivered by God’s mercy; or, certainly, they must be tormented for a long time by that fire of which the Apostle spoke, so that they may attain eternal life without spot or wrinkle.

But those who have committed murder, sacrilege, adultery, fornication, or other similar sins, as has already been said, if worthy repentance does not come to their aid, will not deserve to pass through purgatorial fire into life; rather, they will be cast into eternal burning and death.

## “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?”

**(Ambr.)** He calls us God’s temple so that we may know that God dwells in us; for he must dwell in his own temple. And because he says that God’s Spirit dwells in us, he signifies that the Holy Spirit is to be understood as God.

**(Greg.)** What kind of wood belongs to this temple, the bride describes in the *Song of Songs*: “Our beams are cypress, the wood of our houses is cedar” (Cant. I). For this reason such kinds of wood are chosen for God’s temple: they possess a good fragrance, are incorruptible, and cannot be subjected either to corruptible decay or to the ravages of worms.

## “If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him; for God’s temple is holy, and that is what you are.”

**(Ambr.)** He prefaced this in order to pierce those who, living shamefully, had corrupted their bodies by violating them—especially the man who had his father’s wife, so that he might be guilty before his case came into the open. Finally, when he judges his case, he speaks in a similar, indeed identical, manner, saying: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God?” Above he called it God’s temple, but here he calls it the temple of the Holy Spirit. Who could doubt from this that he signified the Holy Spirit to be God?

**(Greg.)** Who, then, are the priests who guard God’s temple, except those who, by praying, preaching, and keeping watch through spiritual actions, defend the holy Church from the assaults of evil spirits, from the persuasions of the wicked, and from the errors of heretics?

Was he not a guardian of the temple who, enumerating the labors of his passion, says: “In labor and hardship, in many vigils, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness,” and immediately adds: “Apart from those external things, there is my daily burden, my concern for all the churches” (II Cor. XI)?

Consider, I ask, with how great a concern the guardian of the temple keeps watch. For behold, he suffers immeasurable things in himself and shares the concern of his heart with others. What virtue is this, I ask, to think more about the welfare of one’s neighbors than about one’s own affliction? Who can estimate it worthily? Who can weigh it worthily? He labors, mourns, hungers, thirsts, is cold, fasts, and keeps vigil, yet while keeping vigil he thinks about the concern of all the churches.

Behold, an exceptionally diligent guardian of the temple has been set before us as an example; let whoever is able imitate him. To suffer adversity for the sake of truth, to expend good things for one’s neighbors, to keep watch with concern for souls, to investigate and observe lest anyone slip into unbelief, pride, robbery, or impurity—this is to guard the temple of God, that is, the holy Church.

## “Let no one deceive himself.”

**(Ambr.)** That is, let no one think that his own judgment or human counsel benefits him. He returns to the preceding sense: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish so that he may be wise.” He says this because, if anyone understands the promised salvation and the mystery of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, he should become foolish—that is, flee the wisdom of the world—so that he may be judged foolish by it, and then will be wise, because the one who is foolish to the world is wise to God, believing that God has done what the world’s reason cannot comprehend, as I mentioned above.

But the pseudo-apostles, wishing to become wise in the world, preached neither that God has a Son, nor that the Incarnation was real, nor that the flesh could rise again.

**(Cass.)** Morally speaking, you, O man, are to make yourself foolish according to the Apostle’s command so that you may be wise in this world: discerning nothing and judging nothing among the things commanded to you, but always displaying obedience with complete simplicity and faith; judging to be holy, useful, and wise only whatever either God’s law or the judgment of your elder has prescribed for you. Founded upon such instruction, under this discipline you will be able to endure forever.

**(Greg.)** We must know that some within the holy Church are called foolish, but nevertheless noble; others are foolish and ignoble. They are called foolish, but cannot be ignoble, who, despising the wisdom of the flesh, seek the foolishness that will benefit them and are raised to the nobility of their inward offspring by the newness of virtue. They despise the foolish wisdom of the world and desire the wise foolishness of God. For it is written: “What is foolish in God is wiser than human beings” (I Cor. I).

Paul urges us to grasp this foolishness, saying: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish so that he may be wise.” Those who have perfectly attained this foolishness deserved to hear from the voice of Wisdom: “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX).

Behold: by abandoning temporal things, they purchased the glory of eternal power. What, then, is more foolish in this world than to abandon one’s own possessions? And what is nobler in eternity than to come as judges with God? Their nobility is recalled by Solomon’s testimony when he says what I have already mentioned: “Her husband is noble at the gates, when he sits with the senators of the land” (Prov. XXXI). For he regards as very noble those whom he calls senators.

Paul had seen this nobility in himself when, joined in spirit to the Creator’s family, he said:

> “Since, then, we are God’s offspring, we ought not to suppose that the divine is like gold or silver, or like a stone carved by the art and thought of man.”

We are called God’s offspring, not because we have been born from his nature, but because we have been created by his Spirit and will and restored through adoption. Therefore, each person is raised to this nobility to the degree that, through the image he has received, he is renewed into his likeness by imitation.

By contrast, there are foolish and ignoble people who, while fleeing heavenly wisdom and following themselves, fall asleep in their ignorance as though in the baseness of a rejected offspring. For, because they do not understand the purpose for which they were created, they also lose kinship with the nobility received through the image. They are therefore foolish and ignoble whom slavery of mind excludes from participation in the eternal inheritance.

For it is written: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII); and the distinguished preacher says: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.”

**(Greg.)** Those who, while savoring earthly things, were rejected from their inner nobility were foolish and ignoble at once. When many imitate their deeds, they become children of the foolish and ignoble; and while they follow them in understanding and conduct, they are foolish because they do not understand true wisdom, and ignoble because they are not renewed by any freedom of the spirit.

**(Ambr.)** The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God because, when God does what the world denies can be done, he proves its wisdom to be foolishness. And since they say that there are many gods, while faith proves that there is one, they will be confounded in their own prudence, as the power of truth testifies.

For it is written: “I will rebuke the wise in their craftiness”; and again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.” This is found in Psalm XCIII. The sense is the same: knowing that their thoughts were futile, he rebuked their wisdom in order to prove them foolish, showing that what they said was false and that what they thought true was false.

**(Aug.)** “The Lord,” he says, “knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are futile.” But you do not know God’s thoughts, that they are just. He knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are futile; and human beings have known God’s thoughts—but those to whom he has already become a friend and to whom he reveals his counsel.

Abandon, brothers, human thoughts, because they are futile, so that you may grasp God’s thoughts, which are wise.

Therefore, let no one glory in a human being.

**(Ambr.)** Since human thoughts and plans are improvident and weak, one must not glory in a human being but in God, whose counsel cannot be overturned. For whatever human beings devise without God is foolish.

## “For everything is yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas”—that is, Peter—“whether the world or life or death, whether things present or things future; everything is yours, but you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.”

Elsewhere he speaks of the same meaning: “We are your servants for Jesus’ sake” (II Cor. IV). He calls them servants in place of ministers, so that they would not claim individuals for themselves while using everything, just as the Lord also says: “I am among you not as one who is served, but as one who serves” (Mark X; Luke XXII).

The world is certainly ours, but so that we may understand it according to God’s will and place its appointed course within God’s will. The present life has been granted to us, but so that we may pass through it modestly and for God’s glory. Death is ours, so that we may gladly die for Christ and have hope in the future promise. Things present are ours, so that we may use present things in such a way that we do not give offense. Things future are ours, so that, believing in the future, we may entrust ourselves more fully to it, because it is better.

But you are Christ’s, because, since these things have been granted and subjected to us by our judgment, we should likewise subject ourselves to Christ, especially since through him we began to exist, both in our first creation and in regeneration.

Christ is God’s: Christ is God’s own Son, belonging to his Father, doing his will so that we too may do his will.

If, then, we are Christ’s servants, why should we hope for anything from human beings to Christ’s dishonor?

If anyone is striving toward perfection, he will ascend by advancing from that first degree of fear, which we properly called servile, concerning which it is said: “When you have done everything, say, ‘We are unprofitable servants’” (Luke XVII), to the higher path of hope. There he is compared not to a servant but to a hired laborer, because he awaits the reward of recompense. As though secure from penal fear concerning the forgiveness of sins and conscious of good works, he may seem to seek the reward of pleasing God; nevertheless, he cannot attain to that affection of a son who, trusting in the generosity of his father’s indulgence, does not doubt that everything belonging to his father is his.

We must therefore hasten to ascend to the third degree, that of sons, who believe that everything belonging to their Father is theirs. By the unbreakable grace of love, we must merit to receive the image and likeness of that heavenly Father, and, in imitation of the true Son, to proclaim: “Everything that the Father has is mine.” The blessed Apostle also professes this concerning us, saying: “Everything is yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas, whether the world or life or death, whether things present or things future; everything is yours.”

The commandments also call us to this likeness: “Be perfect,” he says, “just as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. V).

In those earlier stages, the affection of goodness is sometimes interrupted, when the strength of the mind is relaxed by some passing moment of the Savior, or by joy or pleasure; or when the fear of Gehenna for the present, or the desire for future things, is withdrawn. Yet there is indeed in those stages a certain degree of perfection that forms us, so that, when we begin to avoid vices either through fear of punishments or hope of rewards, we may pass to the degree of love. For he says: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment; and whoever fears is not perfect in love.” Therefore, “let us love, because God first loved us” (I John IV).

We cannot ascend to that true perfection in any other way than this: just as he first loved us for no reason other than our salvation, so we too must love him for no reason other than love of him alone.

# CHAPTER IV  
## The Apostle rebukes rash judgment, concerning contempt for certain ministers, and persists in correcting them.

## “Let a person regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of God’s mysteries.”

**(Ambr.)** This signifies that some of the Corinthians thought too little of him. But so that a person might think of him as God who had chosen him thought of him, he calls us servants of Christ and stewards of God’s mysteries. For when they did not rely upon a clamor of words or upon human wisdom, it ought to have been understood that they were administering the sacrament of Christ, in which not words but power shone forth, and through which not a human being but God appeared glorious.

As a companion of fishermen, he preached Christ in no other way than they did. Therefore, by proving himself a servant of Christ and of God’s sacraments, he marks out those pseudo-apostles and denies that what they hand on belongs to Christ, because they disagree with the apostolic tradition.

## “Now it is required among stewards that each be found faithful.”

**(Maur.)** This is the voice of one asking: that is, “Do you now think that consciences can be judged?”

**(Ambr.)** What he says applies not only to the person of the pseudo-apostles but also to the others who, having received a stewardship, hesitated consistently to rebuke either evil opinions or evil conduct, whether through shame, fear, or because of their own certain condemnation. This man was so steadfast that he spared not even his own life, provided that he carried out everything faithfully.

## “But it is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day.”

He calls it miserable to be judged by those whom he reproves for such great vices, especially since he knew that he was not to be judged even by the just—or by a human day, that is, because he was not to be judged by the laws believed in by the world. For he had surpassed human justice and devoted himself to heavenly justice, as the Lord says: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of God” (Matt. V).

When he says “a human day,” he also signifies the divine day on which Christ will judge. For just as jurists or pontiffs, whom they call priests, have appointed certain days on which judgments are rendered, so the Lord’s day has also been appointed on which he will judge the world.

## “But I do not even judge myself.”

“For I am conscious of nothing.” It is clear that, possessing a pure conscience, he was not anxious about himself.

## “But by this I am not justified.”

He now humbles himself and speaks as a human being who could unknowingly incur guilt.

## “But the one who judges me is the Lord.”

**(Greg.)** As if he were saying: “I remember that I have acted rightly, yet I do not presume upon my merits, because our life is brought before his judgment.”

**(Ambr.)** He speaks rightly. Although he humbled himself, he nevertheless attributed very much to the Lord Christ, because he can reveal what is hidden from human beings when he judges what is secret—not in order to make someone guilty, but to make him prudent. Although he is holy, he is still human, and it is impossible for something not to be hidden from him.

Sometimes we think something useful that is useless. Nor do we have every member or aspect of human conduct fully described. We have plainly been forbidden things that are serious, but certain circumstances arising from other circumstances are accustomed to deceive us, so that we think useful what is not useful; this, indeed, is a slight matter, because the intention is free.

It is impossible that sin should not occur through ignorance, negligence, vanity, surprise, thought, necessity, or forgetfulness. For even if someone should rise to so lofty a summit of virtue that he could proclaim, without boasting, the Apostle’s words, “It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day; but I do not even judge myself, for I am conscious of nothing,” nevertheless he should know that he cannot be without sin.

For the same teacher did not add this pointlessly: “But by this I am not justified”—that is, “If I have believed myself to be just, I will not immediately possess true glory; nor, because my conscience is not pierced by the reproach of any sin, am I therefore unstained by contact with any impurity. Many things lie hidden from my conscience which, although unknown and obscure to me, are known and manifest to God.”

Therefore he adds: “But the one who judges me,” he says, “is the Lord”—that is, from him alone, to whom the secrets of hearts are not hidden, will the true examination of judgment concerning me proceed.

## “Therefore do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes.”

**(Ambr.)** He warns them not to judge when they themselves are to be judged, lest they have a double sin, as the Lord says: “Do not judge, and you will not be judged” (Matt. VII). Rather, let them await the day of God’s judgment, as though they were faithful and good. For it is an insult to the judge if a judgment or sentence proceeds from a servant before the judge has conducted his examination.

## “He will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts, and then each person will receive praise from God.”

He says this because on the day of judgment nothing will remain hidden of the things that have been done or thought. Simplicity and hypocrisy will appear there, so that the one who was regarded with contempt may perhaps appear worthy, while the one thought to be something may be found reprobate.

Everything will be known on the day of judgment, and then the one who acts or thinks well will receive praise. For here, when someone is praised, it is uncertain whether he is worthy, as he says elsewhere: “It is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends” (II Cor. X)—the Lord from whom nothing is hidden.

**(Aug.)** For mortal human beings do not know the hearts of mortal human beings. But then the Lord will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the thoughts of the heart, and then each person will receive praise from God, because what will be praised and loved by one’s neighbor, in one’s neighbor, will be that which God himself will illuminate so that it is not hidden.

**(Greg.)** Whoever in thought deviates from uprightness sins in darkness. Therefore, the more we know that by our sight we cannot illuminate the darkness of another person’s thought, the less boldly we ought to rebuke the hearts of others.

But we should carefully consider with what severity the father Job was able to correct his sons’ actions, since he devoted himself so earnestly to cleansing their hearts. He said of his sons: “Perhaps my sons have sinned and blessed God in their hearts” (Job I).

What do the rulers of the faithful say to this, who do not know even the evident deeds of their disciples? What do they think in their defense, who do not heal the wounds of their subjects’ actions?

**(Maur.)** The question arises why Paul forbade the Corinthians to judge before the time, when, writing to the Philippians, he says: “For many walk—of whom I often told you, and now say even with tears—that they are enemies of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction” (Phil. III). Thus he who forbade others to judge before the time seems here to have judged before the time those of whom he said, “whose end is destruction.”

**(Greg.)** The answer can be given that Christ, who spoke through Paul, recognizes future things as though they were already past; therefore, even when Paul said this, he judged nothing before the time. The Holy Spirit likewise said through the Apostle Peter to Simon Magus: “You have neither part nor share in this life” (Acts VIII), because the future of Simon Magus had been revealed to Peter in the Spirit as though it were past.

But those to whom future things do not at all appear as past are forbidden by the Lord to judge before the time. Concerning them it is also said by the prophet in rebuke: “Woe to those who prophesy from their own heart” (Ezek. XIII). For to prophesy from the heart is to speak something from mere presumption, not through the Spirit.

## “I have applied these things to myself and Apollos for your sake, so that in us you may learn not to go beyond what is written, so that none of you may be puffed up on behalf of one person against another.”

**(Ambr.)** He applied these things to himself and Apollos by emptying, under his own person and that of Apollos, the glory of the pseudo-apostles and their perverse traditions. He indicated them collectively, not individually, lest an even greater discord arise among the people. For no one who hears his own name attacked, or the name of the person whom he favors, is content to remain silent. But when the name is kept silent, anyone who hears it as though it had been said about himself pretends not to understand.

Under this presentation, therefore, he emptied their persons when he said: “I planted, Apollos watered,” and so forth, so that through these words they might learn that nothing should be attributed to human beings.

## “For who makes you different?”

That is, there are some who, receiving more in baptism or doctrine, say that the others have received less. He says this to those who thought that people baptized by others were somehow superior and who were seduced by their eloquence, so that by a kind of cosmetic coloring they regarded what was wrong as right.

There was such great discord among the people that there were many factions of different parties. The Apostle therefore adapted all his words to all the parties by the use of names, so that, when the Epistle was read, each party would accept that it had been addressed, recognizing that he was attending to its cause.

## “And what do you have that you did not receive?”

He says that this person attained nothing good from others beyond what he had received from him. Therefore, it is pointless to ask, since what they possessed they had received from the Apostle.

He seems to address one person, who speaks to a faction of the people: “But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” The Apostle’s detractors behaved in this way through ignorance: hearing the same things they had already learned from the Apostle, they emptied him of authority and gloried in the teaching of these men. Commended by eloquence, they transferred the glory of preaching to themselves. But the Apostle wished to appear contemptible, provided that he made the glory of God acceptable.

**(Maur.)** Above all, then, the Apostle commends humility to his hearers, so that, established and strengthened in it, they may beware of the ruin of pride and arrogance. Hence elsewhere he says (I Cor. III): “Let no one glory in a human being”; and shortly before: “Let the one who glories,” he says, “glory in the Lord.” For James also says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration” (James I).

**(Aug.)** But those heretics who think that they are made just by themselves, as though they themselves, rather than God, had given this to them, glory not in the Lord but in themselves.

To such people the Apostle says: “For who makes you different?” He says this because no one but God distinguishes a human being from the mass of perdition that came from Adam, making him a vessel for honor rather than dishonor.

But because a carnal and vainly puffed-up person, hearing “Who makes you different?”, could answer, either in words or in thought, “My faith makes me different; my prayer makes me different; my righteousness makes me different,” the Apostle immediately confronts his thoughts and says: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?”

For those who think they are justified by themselves boast as though they had not received anything, and therefore glory in themselves rather than in the Lord.

**(Greg.)** These holy men know that after the fall of our first parent they were born from a corruptible stock, and that they were changed toward better desires or works not by their own virtue but by preceding heavenly grace. Whatever evil they recognize in themselves, they understand as the deserving condition of mortal descent; whatever good they see in themselves, they recognize as the gift of immortal grace. They therefore become debtors to the one who gave them the good will they had not wanted by preceding them, and, by following them, granted them the ability to do the good they desire.

Hence it is rightly said through John: “They worshiped the one who lives forever and ever, casting their crowns before the Lord’s throne” (Apoc. IV). To cast their crowns before the Lord’s throne is not to attribute the victories of their struggles to themselves but to their author, referring the glory of praise to the one from whom they know they received the strength for their struggles.

## “Already you are filled; already you have become rich; you reign without us.”

**(Amb.)** This is irony, as though he were saying: These are the words of someone who is angry, not of someone confirming them. For, since he rebukes such great vices in them, he says that they reign; for they thought this while boasting about what was handed down by the pseudo-apostles.

## “And would that you did reign, so that we might reign with you!”

Like a loving father, he wishes good even for ungrateful children. For how could they reign without the apostles? Whatever has not been handed down by the apostles is full of crimes.

The proper order would have been to say, “so that you might reign with us,” but because he had prefaced it with “would that you did reign,” he could not say it otherwise than, “so that we might reign with you.”

To reign is to be secure in the hope and promises of Christ and to rejoice in the adversities that come for Christ’s name. For they bring profit, not loss. Hence he says elsewhere (II Cor. XII): “When I am weak, then I am strong.”

## “For I think that God has displayed us apostles as the last, as men sentenced to death.”

He attributes this to his own person because he was always in need and suffered persecutions and pressures more than the others, just as Enoch and Elijah will suffer, who will be apostles at the end of time. They must be sent before Christ to prepare God’s people and fortify all the churches to resist Antichrist. The reading of the Apocalypse also testifies that they will suffer persecution and be killed.

The Apostle therefore compared their time with his own when he said, “as men sentenced to death”; for they will come for the purpose of being killed.

Because we have become a spectacle to this world, and to angels and human beings. For Enoch and Elijah also will be a spectacle, to such an extent that their bodies will be thrown into the street, in the sight of the entire unbelieving people. In the same way the apostles became a spectacle, because they were publicly mocked and subjected to the disgrace and death that they endured. He called the world “angels and human beings” because both angels and human beings can be evil, as David says in the psalm: “He troubled them through evil angels” (Psalm 77). Evil, unbelieving people take pleasure in the apostles’ sufferings. The world is called “unbelief” because it follows visible things.

We are fools for Christ. This is true, because those who love Christ are fools in the world’s judgment. But you are wise in Christ. Whoever is judged wise in Christ by the faithless does not rightly affirm Christ. Thus Marcion, because he denies that the Son of God exists and that God could become incarnate, is wise in the world’s eyes; and Photinus, because he does not confess that Christ is God by virtue of the fact that he was born, appears wise to worldly people.

We are weak, but you are strong. They were weak because, preaching Christ without flattery and with what appears to worldly people as foolishness, they were subjected to insults. But you are strong: strong because they professed Christ in such a way as not to offend people, so that they might remain secure.

You are noble. For whoever does not confess that Christ was promised to Abraham and proclaimed from the beginning is noble in opposition to Christ, because he assigns the antiquity of Christ’s promise to others. But we are ignoble. A person is ignoble in the world’s eyes who confesses from the beginning the Christ whom the world denies. Thus all the things stated above—which he appears to deny—he confirms, and what he appears to confirm he denies. These are the words of one who is angry: by denying, he confesses; and by confessing, he denies.

Until this very hour we are hungry and thirsty, naked, and we labor, working with our own hands. For, preaching Christ freely and according to the true faith, without any flattery, and reproving the deeds of an evil life, they found no favor with people. They were struck with blows—that is, treated insultingly—and they were unsettled because they were driven away, lest by remaining long in one place they teach more people.

For this reason they also worked with their hands: not only did they find no favor with people, but it was also unworthy to receive anything from those who devoted themselves to error, as he says in the psalm: “May the oil of the sinner not fatten my head” (Psalm 140). For the one who accepts from a sinner, in order not to be reproved, both loses the freedom to reprove and sins.

We are cursed, and we bless. For while people were treating them badly, they encouraged them toward goodness.

We endure persecution and bear it patiently. For they did not resist those who persecuted them.

We are blasphemed, and we entreat. For they asked those who blasphemed them to allow them to give an account of themselves.

We have become like the refuse of this world, the offscouring of everyone, even until now. By resisting no one, repaying no one’s evil in kind, but always submitting themselves so that through patience they might urge people toward goodness, they became contemptible and despised. “Even until now” means until the present time—even among the Corinthians, for whose sake he endured the evils he has mentioned above. And because he saw that his humility accomplished nothing among them, he complains, moved by grief, that such submission and insults had been unable to produce any fruit, but—what is worse—had produced an even more harmful result.

I do not write these things to shame you. That is, I do not write them to make you blush, but so that you may correct yourselves. But I admonish you as my dearest children. He again makes himself a suppliant, lest, when reproved and provoked to anger, they reject his admonitions. He acts like a healing physician who, cutting away the peelings [putamina; read: putredinem, “putrefaction”], eases the pain he has inflicted with hope and soothing words, so that the sick person may allow himself to be treated.

For even if you have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for through the Gospel I became your father. By these words he shows that no one could love them with the affection with which he loved them. For who would place another’s children before his own in love? Consequently, they ought not to despise the admonitions of one who had endured such great evils for their sake.

I entreat you: become imitators of me. O the holy apostle’s benevolence, that he entreats his children to imitate their father—that is, he willingly asks the sick to accept medicine! In this, however, he wants them to be his imitators: just as he endured many dangers for their salvation at the hands of unbelievers and did not yield, provided that he might evangelize to them day and night the gift of God’s grace, so they too, remaining in his faith and teaching, should not accept the corrupt inventions of the false apostles. Rather, they should resist them, despising insults and slanders, so that they might preserve inviolate their affection for their spiritual father.

For this reason I sent Timothy to you, who is my dearest and faithful son in the Lord. He urges them by means of this same Timothy, whom he calls his dearest and faithful son in the Lord, to recognize in him what they were doing wrong. For when he bore witness to Timothy, he reproved them.

He will remind you of my ways, which are in Christ Jesus, just as I teach everywhere in every church. Through this faithful son, whom he confirms in the Lord, he wants them to return to the rule of truth that he had handed down, so that, reminded by Timothy’s words and example of his conduct, they might come to their senses, recognizing that they had not been wrongly taught by the apostle, since they would learn that he taught the same things in all the churches.

As though I were not coming to you, some have become arrogant. Some of the Corinthians were indignant because he was not going to them—not from longing, but out of pride, as though he considered them unworthy—although the apostle’s greater concern had been to make the unworthy worthy. He therefore desired to go, but the things he was doing were more important.

I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills. After admonishing them, he promises that he will go to them, but only if the Lord permitted it. Since God knows more than a human being, if he knew that it would be worthwhile, he would permit it; and if Paul did not go, the Lord would show that he had not allowed it, certainly because of their unworthiness.

And I will find out not the speech of those who have become arrogant, but their power. He puts them to shame, because although they were behaving indirectly and wrongly, they were indignant as though they were worthy to be visited by the apostle.

For the kingdom of God does not consist in speech but in power. Just as the kingdom of God is commended not by verbal splendor but by the power of signs, so they too should show themselves worthy to be visited by the apostle not by bare words but by the power of spiritual works.

What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness? He introduces words of terror so that those who had become arrogant, having been put to shame, might be humbled. If they truly desired the apostle’s presence, they should prepare themselves to receive him—that is, cleanse themselves of every stain of wrongdoing—so that when he came to them he might rejoice as with his dearest children.

## CHAPTER V

The apostle reproves the vice of fornication, together with its punishment, and censures the root of the offense, namely, negligence in correction.

Fornication is actually reported among you, and such fornication as does not even occur among the Gentiles. (Ambrose.) To show how serious this sin was, he said that it was not even committed by those who do not know God, thereby indicating what punishment ought to be imposed here upon one who, subject to both earthly and divine justice, had committed so great a crime.

So serious that someone has his father’s wife. He disclosed the kind of crime previously mentioned, so that he might not only openly make that man liable to death but also show that those who adhered to him were not free from guilt. For where sin is difficult to commit, it makes a person more guilty.

(Gregory.) Accordingly, the deeds of the shameless must be carefully examined by the one who reproves them, so that in the very things in which they take pleasure they may be shown to be displeasing to God. We correct the shameless more effectively when we demonstrate that the things they believe they have done well were done badly, so that from the place where they believe they have gained glory, useful shame may follow. Sometimes, however, when they recognize that they have not committed the vice of shamelessness at all, they come more quickly to correction if they are put to shame by another, more obvious fault, sought out from the side, so that from what they cannot defend they may recognize that they are acting wickedly in maintaining what they do defend.

Thus, when Paul saw the Corinthians shamelessly puffed up against one another, with one saying that he belonged to Paul, another to Apollos, another to Cephas, and another to Christ, he brought forward the crime of incest, which had both been committed among them and still remained uncorrected, saying: “Fornication is heard among you, and such fornication as does not even occur among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife; and you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that the one who did this deed might be removed from among you.”

It is as though he openly said: “Why do you speak arrogantly of this one or that one, when through the desolation [dissolution] caused by your negligence you show that you belong to no one? And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned?”

(Ambrose.) He humbles their pride so completely that he makes them no longer complainants but suppliants. For they themselves were also participants, since they allowed a person guilty of so enormous a crime to associate with them without correction. They should all, with one mind, have cast him out if he refused to amend himself. But if someone does not have the authority to cast out one whom he knows to be guilty, or is unable to prove the charge, he is free from guilt and is not a judge who can condemn without an accuser. For the Lord did not cast out Judas, although he was a thief, because he had not been accused.

So that the one who did this deed may be removed from among you. Once this deed had become known, he says, the man should have been expelled from the fellowship of the brethren. Everyone knew his crime and did not reprove him; publicly he was keeping his stepmother in the place of a wife. In this matter there was no need for witnesses, nor could the crime be concealed by any evasion.

Although absent in body, I am present in spirit. Absent in person but present through the authority of the Spirit, whose power is present, I have already judged, as though present, the one who committed this deed.

When you are assembled, and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus, hand such a person over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh. Since every carnal pleasure comes from the devil, when a person is handed over to this pleasure, he is handed over to Satan. For the flesh has this in its nature: that it perishes. When the soul joins itself to the flesh’s desire and weakens its spiritual vigor, it too suffers destruction.

Therefore, if the man reproved for the fornication he had committed had been ashamed at being expelled, he would not have perished, since repentance would have followed. Not merely by the consent and presence of everyone, but by the power of the Lord Jesus—that is, by the sentence of the one whose legation the apostle was carrying—he judged that the man should be expelled from the Church.

When he is expelled, he is handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord. The soul and body perish when things contrary to the law are done. In this case, however, the destruction of the flesh is assigned to the man in a different sense. Although all sins produce a carnal person, this desire is especially a desire of the flesh: it hands the soul, stained by filth, over to Gehenna together with the body. For when the soul is overcome by the lust of the flesh, it becomes flesh; and a body rightly governed is called spiritual.

It is nevertheless the mind that either, overcome by enticements, makes the whole person carnal, or, remaining in the vigor of its nature, governs the flesh so that the person is called spiritual.

So that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. He commands that the person described above, who has been defiled, be handed over to Satan, so that the Spirit may be saved in the people of the Church on the day of judgment. For unless he had been expelled, the spirit of the Church would not be saved on the day of judgment.

For because of the contamination, the Spirit was abandoning them all, so that on the day of the Lord they might be found stripped of the Holy Spirit and hear from the Lord the judge: “Depart from me; I do not know you” (Matthew 7). As he says to the Romans: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Romans 8); and in another Epistle: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God.” For if he is grieved, he departs, and he will not be saved—not for his own sake, since he is incapable of suffering, but for ours, since he was given to us so that through him we might be proved to be children of God. For what is lost is not kept safe—not, of course, for its own sake, since wherever it may be it must exist, but for the person from whom it is lost.

(Cassian.) We must firmly believe two things: first, that no one is tempted by them at all without God’s permission; second, that everything inflicted upon us by God, whether it appears for the present to be sorrowful or joyful, is imposed for our benefit by the most merciful Father and the most compassionate physician. For this reason, those who have been handed over to them as to tutors should be humbled, so that, departing from this world, they may either be transferred to the next life more purified or suffer a lighter punishment—those who, according to the apostle, have been handed over in the present time to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Your boasting is not good. (Ambrose.) That is, it is not good, for they were joyful when they ought rather to have been sorrowful over their brother, who had sinned so grievously, just as Samuel was sorrowful when Saul sinned (1 Samuel 15). In this crime evil teachers either concealed the matter or reproved it negligently, as Eli the priest did with his sons when they sinned against God, lest they become hateful to human beings (1 Samuel 2).

Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump? In the same way, the sin of one person, when it is known and not reproved, contaminates many—or rather, all who know of it and do not avoid it, or who, although they could reprove it, conceal it. For a person does not seem to himself to be sinning when no one corrects or avoids him.

Cleanse out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump. This must be understood in two ways, because there is also the leaven of human teaching, as the Savior says: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Matthew 16), that is, of evil doctrine. Therefore evil doctrine must be avoided. For this reason he said this: when the fornicator has been expelled, the old leaven is expelled.

It is called old because it is the sin of ancient error; the new lump, however, is Christ’s teaching.

Since you are unleavened. The term “unleavened” arose from the circumstance of flour not being fermented. When the children of Israel were expelled from Egypt, leaven was taken as a symbol of antiquity, while unleavened bread signified newness. For, having rejected the ancient errors of the Egyptians, they were introduced into the new law. In the same way, after the errors of the pagans, the Corinthians were introduced into the Gospel of Christ.

He therefore urges them to live, in accordance with the profession they had received from the apostle under the name of Christ, as worshipers of the new life. This is what it means to be unleavened.

For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed. According to the law, he teaches that the newness of Passover consists in its meaning, and that Christ was therefore killed so that from him a new proclamation might produce a new way of life. Since we celebrate the meaning of Passover, we must not follow our former life.

Passover, therefore, is a sacrifice, not a passing-over, as some suppose. First comes the Passover, and then the passing-over, because the Savior is first an example and then a sign of salvation. There cannot be a sign before the cross. For after the lamb had been killed in the evening in Egypt, the children of Israel celebrated Passover. They marked the doorposts with its blood, so that at night the angel passing through would not touch those places that had been smeared with the lamb’s blood.

Therefore, let us celebrate the feast [let us feast], not with the old leaven. (Ambrose.) That is, possessing the joy of renewal, let us flee from our former deeds, rejecting every impurity from ourselves, which is corruption. For just as leaven corrupts the whole lump, so an evil life corrupts the whole person.

Therefore, so that we might guard ourselves not only from the shamefulness of life but also from devotion to iniquity, he added:

Not with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. That is, sincerity should produce a clean life, while truth should exclude every kind of fraud.

I wrote to you in the letter not to associate with fornicators. He indicates that he had written earlier, warning them not to join themselves to people of evil life. Since they perhaps seemed not to understand what he had written, he now interprets in this Epistle what he had written, saying: “Certainly not with the fornicators of this world,” but he wrote that they should withdraw from their brothers.

Or with the greedy, or rapacious, or those who serve idols; otherwise you would have had to leave this world. He therefore reproves their understanding, since they perhaps thought that he had forbidden association with unbelieving fornicators, greedy people, rapacious people, or idolaters, but not with brothers. For this reason they did not take it badly that the man who had his father’s wife remained among them.

If, then, you associate with such people, he says, it would have been better for you to die. For death is an advantage for those who act wickedly if they die sooner rather than continue longer in sins.

But now I wrote to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother, if he is a fornicator, or greedy, or serves idols, or is a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a rapacious person; with such a one you should not even eat.

He forbids eating with a brother, but he did not forbid it with an unbeliever, since he says: “If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner, go, and eat whatever is placed before you” (1 Corinthians 10). For this reason he says: “For what have I to do with judging those who are outside?”

This is true, because a bishop cannot judge the faithless. But with a brother in whom these vices are found, he teaches that one should not only refrain from sharing the sacraments but also from ordinary food, so that the person may be ashamed when he is avoided and may correct himself.

Are you not judging those who are within? A person judges when he distinguishes which brother he should associate with, whom he should reprove, and whom he should avoid.

For those who are outside, God will judge. Earlier he said: “Do not judge before the appointed time.” Here he does not prohibit judgment, but earlier he especially prohibited judging a ruler on the basis of unknown matters and suspicion, because it belongs to God alone to judge hidden things. Here, however, he already commands that a brother should examine his brother, as he says elsewhere: “Test yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; examine yourselves” (2 Corinthians 13).

Those who are outside will be condemned on the day of judgment, because the Lord said: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3). For a person in whom there is no hope must be regarded as dead.

# BOOK TEN

[Column 53]

## CHAPTER VI

He reproves his people concerning the judges before whom they bring lawsuits and concerning the cases they have among themselves, and returns to correcting the vice of fornication.

Remove the evil person from among yourselves. (Ambrose.) He continues to admonish them to distinguish themselves from evil both in deeds and in persons.

Does any one of you dare, when he has a case against another, to be judged before the unrighteous and not before the saints? He signifies the unrighteous in two ways: those who do not believe, and those who frequently interpret the laws believed to have been given by God to the world with flattery, assigning their authority to idols. They are therefore unrighteous. And because the law is more truly present in the Church, where God, the giver of the law, is feared, he says that it is better to conduct the case before God’s ministers. They pronounce a true legal judgment more readily out of fear of God.

(Augustine.) Here it might be possible to judge that having a case against another is not a sin, but only wishing to be judged outside the Church, unless he then added: “It is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another.” And lest anyone excuse himself in this way, saying that he had a just case but was suffering injustice and wished to have the judges’ sentence remove it from him, he immediately confronts such thoughts or excuses, saying: “Why not rather suffer injustice?
