Why not rather be defrauded?”

Thus we return to what the Lord says: “If anyone wishes to take your tunic and bring you to court, let him have your cloak as well” (Matthew 24); and elsewhere: “From the one who takes away what is yours,” he says, “do not demand it back” (Luke 6).

He therefore prohibited his people from having lawsuits with others over secular matters. From this teaching the apostle says that it is a fault. Nevertheless, since such lawsuits exist in the Church, he permits them to be settled among brothers, with brothers acting as judges; outside the Church, however, he strictly forbids them. It is clear what is here granted according to indulgence to the weak.

Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? The apostle says nothing offensively. For this reason he called it “this world,” to show that there is another, since the apostle John also says: “Do not love this world” (1 John 2), and the Lord says in the Gospel: “God so loved this world,” and so forth (John 4).

This world, then, is in error; it is not that higher world in whose likeness this one was made. Hence the human being placed here was made in the image of God, so that, just as in the higher world everything comes from one God, so in this world all might have their origin from one human being.

For this reason Moses says in Deuteronomy: “When the Most High divided the nations, when he dispersed the children of Adam, he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God” (Deuteronomy 32).

What could more clearly show that this world is an image of the higher one, established for a definite reason? There is a lower Jerusalem and a higher Jerusalem, which the same apostle calls our mother. There is also a lower paradise, in which the human being was placed and received the command to work and guard it. There is also the heavenly paradise, into which the apostle was caught up and heard secret words (2 Corinthians 12).

The saints will therefore judge this world, because by the example of their faith the world’s unbelief will be condemned.

And the world will be judged in you. This world will then be judged in us if the work of faithless people is found in us. Such persons are therefore unworthy even to judge the smallest matters. That is, those who will judge the world itself are certainly not unworthy to judge the things that belong to the world.

Do you not know that we shall judge angels? He adds something greater by saying, “We shall judge angels,” that is, spiritual powers, which he teaches elsewhere dwell in the heavenly places. Angels will be judged by us in the same manner in which the world will be judged.

(Gregory.) The minds of the saints look down upon all transitory things and contemplate beneath themselves whatever is proud and whatever passes away. As though established at a certain summit of reality, they see everything subject to them all the more clearly because they submit themselves more truly to the Author of all things. From that point they transcend everything—from which they prostrate themselves before the Creator of all in true humility.

(Augustine.) In the Gospel, therefore, the Lord says: “You will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19). If there are twelve seats there, there is no place for the thirteenth apostle, Paul, to sit, and there will be no way for him to judge. But he said that he would judge not only human beings but angels. Which angels, if not the apostates? “Do you not know,” he says, “that we shall judge angels?”

The crowd might answer: “Why do you boast that you will judge? Where will you sit?” The Lord spoke of twelve seats, and one of the twelve apostles fell away; the holy Matthias was appointed in his place. The number twelve of the seats has been completed. First find a place where you may sit, and then threaten that you will judge.

How, then, are there not twelve people alone in the twelve seats, but a great number of the perfected? Just as in the case of the five brothers of the man who was tormented in hell there is understood to be the multitude of the Jewish people, and just as the one hundred and fifty-three fish signify thousands upon thousands of saints, so in the twelve seats a great number of perfected people is understood, not merely twelve individuals.

If you have secular lawsuits, appoint those who are contemptible in the Church to judge them. (Ambrose.) Secular lawsuits are matters concerning the body, or bodily matters. And because this should not be understood as something to be done in that way, he added: “I say this to your shame.”

Since he had mentioned a case above without specifying what kind, and since there are also divine cases—for the same apostle says, “My fellow worker in my case” (Colossians 4)—and since they might perhaps have thought that secular lawsuits, although he had forbidden them to be conducted before the faithless, could nevertheless be heard or settled in the Church by anyone at all, he says, to their shame: “Appoint those who are contemptible in the Church.”

That is, appoint wooden vessels. For he indicated that they were so intractable and inconsiderate that they might perhaps choose three inexperienced persons as judges. The apostle wrote this from experience, for he knew how lukewarm and imprudent they had been found in their other cases.

(Gregory.) Paul was inflaming his hearers toward the virtue of wisdom, the varieties of tongues, and the investigation of the mysteries of prophecy, saying: “Desire the greater gifts, but especially that you may prophesy” (1 Corinthians 14). But because they could not receive spiritual gifts if earthly affairs weighed them down, he had long before said: “Appoint those who are contemptible in the Church to judge.”

It is as though he openly said: “Let those who have lesser merit in the Church and possess none of the powers of great gifts judge earthly matters, so that through those who cannot accomplish great good, lesser matters may nevertheless be supplied.” He calls them contemptible, and yet calls them wise when he says: “Is there no wise person among you who can judge between his brothers?”

What is gathered from this except that those who have acquired wisdom in external matters should examine earthly cases? Those who have been enriched with spiritual gifts ought not to become entangled in earthly affairs, so that, while they are not compelled to administer inferior goods, they may be able to devote themselves to superior goods.

Nevertheless, great care must be taken that those who excel in spiritual gifts do not entirely abandon the external concerns of their neighbors who need help. They should entrust these matters to others to whom it is appropriate to assign them.

Thus Moses also appointed seventy men from among the people to act in his place (Exodus 24), so that, the more he withdrew himself from external cases, the more eagerly he might penetrate inward things. In this way the highest-ranking men make greater progress in spiritual gifts, since their minds are not trampled down by lowly matters; and, in turn, the lesser men in the Church do not live without good works, since in external matters they find righteous tasks to perform.

For holy Church is constituted by the unity of the faithful just as our body is united by the joining of its members. Some members of the body serve the purpose of looking upon the light; others are not separated from contact with the earth. The eye is directed toward the light and is guarded from dust so that it may not become blind. The foot rightly performs its function when it does not refuse to receive the dust of the earth. Yet these members of the body are joined together by mutually sharing their functions, so that the foot runs for the eyes and the eye looks out for the foot.

In the same way, in the holy Church the members should be distinct in function but united in love, so that the highest-ranking men may provide for the way of those who are occupied with earthly affairs, enabling the foot to walk as though toward the light of the eyes, and enabling whatever those involved in earthly affairs do to be directed toward greater usefulness.

The foot’s path is watched over; it walks not only for itself but also for the eyes. While they assist one another through alternating service, it wonderfully comes about that, because each of the chosen does what he can for the others, their works include even what they themselves cannot do.

In all this it must be understood that when those who can suitably attend to the external affairs of their neighbors are lacking, those who are full of spiritual gifts must also accommodate themselves to the weakness of others and serve their earthly needs, insofar as they appropriately can, through the condescension of charity.

The mind ought not to become weary if, although always intent upon spiritual contemplation, it is sometimes bent down as though diminished in order to administer lesser matters, since the Word through whom all created things exist assumed human nature to benefit us and was willing to become for a little while lower than the angels.

What is surprising, then, if a human being bends himself for the sake of another human being, when the Creator of human beings and angels assumed the form of a human being for the sake of human beings? The mind is not diminished when it is thus drawn downward; indeed, it penetrates higher things more subtly the more humbly, for the love of the Creator, it does not despise lower things.

What is unworthy or difficult for us if we direct our mind both above and below, when with the same hand of the body we wash our face and put shoes on our foot?

Is there no wise person among you who can judge between his brother? (Ambrose.) Since, then, he says, there are wise brothers, let some of them be chosen to judge—those whose judgment the world itself deserves. For it is a great disgrace if among those who are said to have come to know the Lord no one is found who can examine a case according to the law of the Gospel.

He says that a brother should be chosen as judge because their Church’s ruler had not yet been appointed. But brother goes to law with brother, and this before unbelievers. It is clear that by unbelievers he means either arbitrators whom people customarily request, or a public judge to whom one might say: “Today is a sacred day; judgment cannot be pronounced.”

It is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another. He indicates that it is a sin because brother litigates with brother, when they ought to strive to be harmonious like brothers, especially since our faith is devoted to peace.

Although a Christian ought not to litigate, nevertheless, if something serious occurs, something that cannot be disregarded, let him bring the case to the Church, lest he incur both present loss and perhaps offense.

Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather allow yourselves to be defrauded? But you do wrong and defraud—and this against brothers. Now he rebukes those whose injustice gives rise to quarrelling, because they are guilty not only of the fraud they have committed, but also share in the wrongdoing of those who, compelled by their injury or fraud, appeal to unbelievers for judgment. Although they ought not to pursue the fraud or injuries inflicted upon them, they not only seek redress but themselves commit fraud and injuries, thus furnishing their brothers with examples for punishment. [Col. 0057A] And what may one suppose such people do to others, when they do not spare their own?

Or do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God? By saying this he shows that they are not ignorant that they are sinning, and therefore that they deserve a more severe punishment. For if the merciless are guilty before God, how much more the unrighteous?

Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idol-servants, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God. [Col. 0057B] He did not mention these things as though they were unknown to people among whom he had stayed for a year and six months, teaching the gospel of God; rather, he admonished them in order to revive in them reverence for the law and the worthiness required for the kingdoms of heaven.

And these indeed were you. Lest he seem to ascribe all these things to everyone—or certainly to make everyone free from these crimes by keeping silent, since he would then appear to have forbidden them without exposing their crimes—he therefore says: “And these indeed were you.” And, lest he provoke them to anger, he adds: “But you were washed,” so that, recognizing themselves as guilty of these crimes, they might immediately breathe again when they heard, “But you were washed.” Some people are ashamed and reform when they hear good things said about themselves.

But you were sanctified; but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God. It is known that all these benefits of purification are received in baptism, [Col. 0057C] which is the foundation of evangelical truth. There the believer is washed after laying aside all sins, is justified in the name of the Lord and in the Spirit of our God, and is adopted as a son of God. By these words he reminds them how great and how excellent is the grace which they obtained through the true tradition. Afterwards, however, under the influence of evil teachers, they adopted opinions contrary to this rule of faith and stripped themselves of these benefits. Hence the purpose is to call them back to their original conviction, so that they may recover what they had obtained.

“Everything is lawful for me,” but I will not be brought under the power of anything. He says that everything is lawful for him—namely, those things which were lawful both for his fellow apostles and for the natural law, not for the law of Moses. Moses prohibited many things because of the hardness of heart of the unbelieving and stiff-necked people. Yet, if one considers the Apostle’s purpose, [Col. 0057D] his meaning in saying these things was different. He introduced the subject beforehand and later intended to deal with it, as he did also in the case of the man who had committed incest; he sets out the point, indicating what he would discuss afterward.

Finally, he immediately returns briefly to the preceding thought, having meanwhile entrusted the matter to their consideration. He says this because it was lawful for him to receive support from them. But because he knew that the pseudo-apostles were seeking an opportunity to receive money, he did not wish to accept anything from them, lest the vigor of evangelical truth should grow weak for the sake of the belly. For if he accepted from those whom he accused of such great vices, he would bend toward them the authority of the teaching office entrusted to him by the Lord. One cannot rebuke firmly the person from whom one receives support, especially when he is eager to give precisely in order to humble the superior.

[Col. 0058A] Hence he also says: “But I will not be brought under the power of anyone.”

(Aug.) Something may be lawful and yet not expedient. But what is not lawful cannot be expedient. Accordingly, not everything lawful is expedient, whereas nothing unlawful is expedient. Something lawful is not expedient when it is permitted, but the exercise of that power brings an obstacle to the salvation of others. In my view, those things which are permitted by the justice that stands before God may nevertheless be inexpedient; if, by being displayed before human beings, they impede them from attaining salvation, they ought to be avoided. Those things, however, are unlawful which are forbidden in such a way that they must not be done.

(Greg.) Often those who are in authority, because they do not know how to restrain themselves even from lawful things, fall into what is unlawful and disorderly. For the only person who will not fall into unlawful things is the one who sometimes cautiously restrains himself even from lawful things. By this very restraint, [Col. 0058B] the blessed Paul shows himself to be bound when he says: “Everything is lawful for me, but not everything is expedient.”

And in order to show, through this very restraint, how far he extended himself in freedom of mind, he immediately adds: “Everything is lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anyone.” For when the mind follows desires it has conceived, it is shown to serve the things whose love has conquered it. Paul, to whom everything is lawful, does not bring himself under the power of anything, because by restraining himself even from lawful things he rises above, as despised, the things that would press upon him through delight.

“Food is for the belly and the belly for food; but God will destroy both the one and the other.”

(Amb.) The destruction of the belly occurs when its function of eating ceases; the destruction of food, however, will occur when birth has come to an end. The pseudo-apostles, who traveled about not for the sake of religion but for profit, [Col. 0058C] did not wish to be harsh toward sinners.

(Aug.) We repair the daily ruins of the body by eating and drinking, until you destroy both foods and the belly through a marvelous satiety, when you have put death to want and this corruptible body has put on incorruption.

“But the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord.”

(Amb.) He now returns to the preceding thought. “And the Lord is for the body.” What does “the Lord is for the body” mean? It is understood that he will grant immortality to the body when it has been raised. For the body dedicated to God will be rewarded with a spiritual gift, in accordance with the merit of its leader, that is, the mind.

“And God both raised up the Lord and will also raise us up by his power.” The meaning is the same as that by which he wished to strengthen the argument through the example of the Lord’s resurrection. For Christ is the power of God, by which he will raise us and the Lord himself. He said this because the Lord himself raised his own body, [Col. 0058D] just as the Lord himself says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” This he said concerning the temple of his body (John 2).

Some, however, think that the Apostle said, “Everything is lawful for me, but not everything is expedient,” because of the freedom of the will that has been granted: fornication is lawful, they say, although it is not expedient. But how can what is forbidden be lawful? Or, if everything is lawful, nothing can be called unlawful; it is lawful, though not expedient. Such people whisper rather than assert this, whether through forgetfulness or negligence.

John the Baptist says to Herod: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Mark 6). But perhaps John was ignorant of human eloquence, although he had been inspired in the womb. If this were the case, he ought to have said: “It is lawful for you, but it is not expedient.”

[Col. 0059A] The Lord likewise says to the Canaanite woman: “It is not lawful to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs” (Matthew 15). And again the Lord says to the Jews: “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, how he entered the house of God and took the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat,” and so forth (Matthew 12).

Therefore everything that is forbidden is unlawful, and everything unlawful is forbidden. Yet sometimes, when some circumstance intervenes, something may be lawful but not expedient.

Or do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Our bodies are members of Christ in the new human being who was created according to God, because he is the head of the Church. Shall I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Far be it!

“Far be it,” he says, because members joined to a prostitute cease to be members of Christ.

Or do you not know that the one who joins himself to a prostitute [Col. 0059B] becomes one body? He says this because whoever joins himself to pollution becomes one with the person to whom he joins himself. For fornication makes the two one, so that in their defilement they are one just as they are one by nature.

“For the two,” he says, “will be one flesh.” It is clear that, since the woman is from the man, the two are one flesh.

But the one who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit.

(Aug.) Since the Spirit of God is in those who act rightly, he is shared by God and human beings. When “one” is said without adding what is one, and several things are called one, a common nature and essence, without disagreement or dissent, is signified. But when what is one is added, something made one out of several things may be signified, even though they differ in nature. Thus soul and body are certainly not one by themselves; for what is so different unless [Col. 0059C] “one” is added or understood—that is, one human being or one animal?

Accordingly, the Apostle says that the one who joins himself to a prostitute is “one body.” He did not say “they are one” or “he is one,” but added “body,” as though one body had been composed from two different beings, male and female. And he says that the one who joins himself to the Lord is “one spirit.” He did not say “the one who joins himself to the Lord is one” or “they are one,” but added “spirit.” For the spirit of a human being and the Spirit of God differ by nature, but through adherence one spirit is made from two different spirits.

Thus, even without the human spirit, the Spirit of God is blessed and perfect; but the spirit of a human being is blessed only with God. Therefore, whether one says “God,” or “of God,” so that this name applies to each individually, it is not to be understood that together they are two gods, but one God. [Col. 0059D] For they adhere to one another, as the Apostle testifies that this can occur even among substances that are distant and different.

The Lord alone is spirit, and the spirit of a human being alone is also spirit; yet if it adheres to the Lord, it is one spirit. How much more is this true where there is an entirely inseparable and eternal union? The mind is ordered according to the order of natures, not of places, so that above it there is none but God. Finally, when it has adhered to him completely, it will be one spirit, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “But the one who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit.”

By entering into a share in that nature of truth and blessedness, the human spirit does not cause God to increase in his nature, truth, or blessedness. In that nature to which it has happily adhered, it will see [Col. 0060A] the immutable in everything that it sees. Then, as divine Scripture promises it, its desire will be satisfied with good things—unchangeable good things—with the Trinity itself, its God, whose image it is. And, so that it may never afterward be violated anywhere, it will be hidden in the concealment of his face, filled with such abundance of him that it will never take pleasure in sinning.

Flee fornication.

(Amb.) He rightly urges them to flee fornication, through which the sons of God become sons of the devil.

“Every sin that a person commits is outside the body, but the one who fornicates sins against his own body.” He shows that this is a very serious sin, because through it the whole body is destroyed, whereas in other sins only a part is destroyed, not the whole. For the whole body is the man and the woman, because the woman is a part of the man.

Whoever commits any other sin sins outside himself; but the fornicator [Col. 0060B] sins against his own flesh. Suppose that someone ends his life by a noose or kills himself with a sword: does he not seem to sin against his own body? He does not sin against his body but against his soul, to which he does violence.

Fornication, however, is a bodily offense, which affects both body and soul. It does not occur without the desire of the flesh, because the flesh also has its own movement; the soul desires in such a way that it sins against the flesh, although nothing can happen without the soul. Thus, because he sins against the flesh that comes from him—for he referred to its origin—he is said to sin against his own body, so that he may cease from fornication as though sparing himself.

According to Novatian, however, the one who fornicates does not seem to sin against his own body but against Christ’s body. He interprets the passage differently, so that he also says that the fornicator sins against the Holy Spirit, on account of the reason [Col. 0060C] for which he was separated from the Church.

This cannot in any way be established. The body of Christ is not one or two Christians, but all of them; each individual is a member. How, then, does the fornicator sin against the body of Christ, when he does not contaminate everyone?

If Novatian’s view were correct, all other sins would be outside God, and only through fornication would a person sin against God. Even the one who goes to idols would not sin against God, nor would the one who denies him during persecution, because every sin that a person commits would be outside the body of Christ, as Novatian thinks.

But if he wishes to interpret the matter differently and deny that any sin exists outside the body of Christ, he will be forced to say that everyone who commits any sin sins against God and against the Holy Spirit, so that the thief, the perjurer, and the liar [Col. 0060D] would also be said to sin against the Holy Spirit.

How, then, is it true when the Lord says: “All sins and blasphemies will be forgiven human beings; but whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matthew 12)? It is evident that, apart from the other sins, there is another sin which is called sin against the Holy Spirit.

Some again think that the fornicator is said to sin against his own body because he is a member of the Church and, by contaminating himself, sins against the Church, of which he is a member. Therefore, when a member of the Church fornicates, it should be said to him that he sins not against himself but against the Church.

But the Apostle says that the fornicator sins against his own body because he sins against his own portion.

(Aug.) [Col. 0061A] “Or do you not know,” he says, “that the one who joins himself to a prostitute is one body? For the two,” he says, “will be one flesh.”

Could this be said of all the other crimes and offenses of human beings? In the case of every other crime, the human mind is free both to commit one particular act and, at that very time, to be elsewhere in thought. But during the very act and time of fornication, the mind is not free to think of anything else. The whole human being is absorbed by the act and in the body, so that it can no longer be said to possess its own mind; rather, the entire human being may be said to have become flesh, a spirit that goes away and does not return.

Thus we can understand the saying, “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body, but the one who fornicates sins against his own [Col. 0061B] body,” as meaning that the Apostle wished to exaggerate the evil of fornication so greatly that, in comparison with it, he said all other sins are to be regarded as outside the body, and that only through the evil of fornication does a person sin against his own body. For the pleasure of the body, arising from the greater heat of lust—than which there is no greater—holds a person as a servant and makes him a captive.

Or do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit whom you have from God?

(Ambr.) Above he called it the temple of God; here he calls it the temple of the Holy Spirit, because in substance the Spirit is what God is. He said this so that we might keep our bodies undefiled, in order that the Holy Spirit might be able to dwell there.

“And you are not your own, for you were bought with a price.” It is clear that one who has been bought is not his own [Col. 0061C] master but belongs to the one by whom he was bought, so that he must do not his own will but that person’s. And because we were bought at a price, we ought to serve our Lord more zealously, lest, being offended, he hand us over to the death from which he redeemed us. For with what a precious price did he buy us, giving his blood for us?

“Glorify and bear God in your body.” To glorify and bear God in the body means to walk according to his law, for through his law he himself is seen in us. Yet to bear God also means to display the image of God through good deeds.

(Aug.) There are two sins and two kinds of sin: a person either sins against God or against another human being. A person also sins against God by corrupting and violating his temple within himself. For God redeemed you by the blood of his Son, although, even before you were [Col. 0061D] redeemed, you belonged to him who created all things. In a particular way he wished to possess you as one redeemed by the blood of his Son.

“You are not your own,” he says; “you were bought at a great price. Glorify and bear the Lord in your body.” Therefore the one by whom you were redeemed made you his house. Do you wish to overthrow your own house? In doing so you would also overthrow God’s house—that is, yourself. If you do not spare yourself, spare yourself for your own sake, or for the sake of God, who made you his temple.

“For the temple of God is holy, which you are. And whoever violates the temple of God, God will destroy.”

—Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman.”

(Ambr.) The pseudo-apostles, agitating them through false interpretations, taught that marriage should be rejected by hypocrisy, [Col. 0062A] so that they might appear purer than others. They therefore asked the Apostle about this in their letter. Since they did not take pleasure in this teaching, they set aside the other matters and asked only about this one.

He replied: “It is indeed good for a man not to touch a woman,” although they did not state the matter to him simply. Yet he added: “Because of fornications, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband.” This was so that nothing contrary to the law should be admitted, while what the law does not prohibit is avoided.

Let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband.

(Greg.) When Paul saw some people in the Church lacking self-control, he conceded the lesser good so that greater evils might be avoided. “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife.” And because spouses are free from guilt in marital intercourse only when they unite not to satisfy lust but to receive offspring, he immediately added, in order to show that even what he had conceded was not entirely without fault, though it was the lesser fault: [Col. 0062B] “But this I say by way of concession, not by way of command.” For what is forgiven and not commanded is not without fault. He clearly saw a sin which he foresaw could be forgiven. Yet when we are constrained in matters of uncertainty, we profitably submit to lesser things, lest in greater things we sin without forgiveness.

(Ambr.) Those who seek a shortcut often go astray. For how could it be possible for people whom he found involved in such great vices to abstain from their wives? Therefore he does not permit them to abstain, lest, while abstaining from what is lawful, they presume upon what is not permitted, as the Manichaeans do.

“Let the husband render the marital due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband.” He says that they are mutually subject to one another in this matter, so that, because they are one [Col. 0062C] body, their will may also be one according to the law of nature.

The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife. He says that neither the husband nor the wife is permitted to hand his or her body over to someone else. In this matter they are mutually indebted to one another, so that no occasion for sin might be given.

Do not defraud one another. He says this so that they may agree in the marital matter and disagreement may not produce fornication.

Except by mutual consent for a time. That is, they should abstain by agreement for the sake of acts of thanksgiving.

So that you may devote yourselves to prayer. Although one ought to pray without ceasing—for this meditation must be practiced every day—nevertheless, in order to give attention to prayer, he commands them to devote themselves to this matter, setting aside periods of time to please the Lord. In order that he may have mercy, he must be entreated with greater purity. Although marriages are pure, one must nevertheless abstain even from lawful things [Col. 0062D] so that prayer may more easily be brought to completion.

Thus those who wished to be sanctified under the law also abstained, among other things, from raisins at the Lord’s command, so that they might become holier. For when someone touches even what has not been granted, he shows that he wishes to receive what he prays for.

And again return to the same. Since he gives the married a rule that, after the days of prayer, they ought to return to natural intercourse.

So that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control. He urges them to abstain for the intervening days, lest an opportunity be given to the devil, as the Apostle Peter says: “Behold, the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour.”

For if a wife is taken for the sake of producing children, [Col. 0063A] the time allowed for the same intercourse does not seem extensive, because the feast days, the days of procession, and the very conditions of conception and childbirth show, according to the law, that intercourse ought to cease at such times.

But this I say by way of concession, not by way of command. It is clear that he gives this advice in order to exclude fornication, not to close the way for those striving toward a better life.

(Aug.) What are light sins and what are grave sins must be weighed not by human judgment but by divine judgment. For we see that certain things were granted even by the apostles themselves as concessions to those who were forgiven. Such is what the venerable Paul says to married couples: “Do not defraud one another, except by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer. And return again to the same, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.”

One might think that it is not a sin to have intercourse with one’s spouse not for the purpose of producing children—which is the good proper to marriage—but also for carnal pleasure, so that the weakness of the incontinent may avoid the deadly evil of fornication, adultery, or any other impurity, shameful even to mention, into which Satan can tempt and lust can draw it. [Col. 0063B]

This could indeed, as I have said, be thought not to be a sin, unless he had added: “But this I say by way of pardon, not by way of command.” Who, then, would now deny that it is a sin, when the authority of the Apostle acknowledges that pardon is granted to those who commit it?

(Greg.) Married couples must be admonished to remember that they were joined for the sake of receiving offspring. When, while serving immoderate intercourse, they turn the occasion of procreation into an occasion of pleasure, they should consider that, although they do not go outside the marriage bond, they nevertheless [Col. 0063C] transgress within marriage the rights of marriage itself.

Hence it is necessary for them, through frequent prayers, to erase what they defile by mingling the beautiful appearance of marital union with pleasures. For this reason the Apostle, skilled in heavenly medicine, instructed not so much the healthy as the sick, and showed them remedies, saying:

## CHAPTER VII

He instructs those who are married and teaches that it is a greater good to live in the virginal state.

Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman.” But because of fornications, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. For the one who permitted this because of fear of fornication clearly gave a command not to those who were standing firm, but showed the fallen a bed, lest they perhaps [Col. 0063D] fall headlong to the ground.

Therefore, to those who were still weak he adds: “Let the husband render the marital due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband.” While granting something of pleasure within the great honor of marriage, he added: “But this I say by way of concession, not by way of command.” For what is said to be forgiven is found to be a fault. Yet it is forgiven all the more quickly when no unlawful thing is done through it, but what is lawful is not maintained under proper restraint.

Lot expresses this well in himself (Genesis 19). He fled burning Sodom, but, although he found Zoar, he did not immediately ascend into the mountains. To flee burning Sodom is to avoid the unlawful fires of the flesh; the height of the mountains is the purity of those who practice continence. Or, as it were, [Col. 0064A] those are on the mountain who cling to marital intercourse but are not loosened by any pleasure of the flesh beyond the proper union for receiving offspring.

What does it mean to stand on the mountain except not to seek the fruit of propagation in the flesh? To stand on the mountain is not to cling to the flesh carnally.

But because there are many who indeed abandon the crimes of the flesh yet, once placed in marriage, do not preserve solely the rights of the lawful use, Lot leaves Sodom but does not immediately reach the mountains. This is what happens when a life already subject to condemnation is abandoned, but the height of marital continence is not yet carefully maintained.

There is, however, between them the city of Zoar, which saves the fugitive who is weak: when spouses unite in incontinence, they flee the fall into crimes and are nevertheless saved through pardon. [Col. 0064B] They find, as it were, a little city in which they are defended from the fires.

For this married life is not remarkable in virtues, but it is nevertheless safe from punishments. Hence Lot says to the angel: “This city is nearby; I can flee to it—it is small—and I shall be saved there. Is it not little, and shall my soul not live in it?”

It is therefore called nearby and nevertheless declared safe for salvation, because married life is neither far removed from the world nor alien to the joy of salvation. But spouses preserve this life of theirs in action as though in a little city when they intercede for one another through continual prayers.

Hence the angel rightly says to that same Lot: “Behold, I have also accepted your request in this matter, so that I will not overthrow the city for which you have spoken.” For when prayer is poured out [Col. 0064C] before God, such a married life is not condemned. Paul also gives instruction concerning this prayer when he says: “Do not defraud one another, except by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer.”

But I wish all people to be as I myself am.

(Ambr.) Insofar as it belonged to a benevolent and solicitous teacher, he wished all people to be able to become like himself. What sort of person he was, however, he immediately shows in what follows.

But each person has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that. This means that each person has God’s gift according to his own vow, so that, if he wishes, he may obtain the ability through God’s will. Therefore no one should be compelled, lest, being forbidden what is lawful, he admit what is unlawful. Let each person choose for himself what he will follow.

But I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they [Col. 0064D] remain as I am. He would not say, “It is good for the unmarried to be as I am,” if he were not chaste in body. Nor would he say, “I wish all people to be as I myself am,” if he had had a wife, since in that case he would not have wished them to be virgins.

But far be that from us. From childhood he burned with the Spirit in such a way that he had no inclination toward this matter, since the grace of God had overtaken him while he was still a young man.

After saying that each person has his own gift from God, he shows in what respect it is better to be more devoted: a person is helped in that which he appears to desire with the eagerness of his mind.

But if they cannot exercise self-control, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn.

(Cass.) It should be noted that there are three kinds of fornication.

The first is accomplished through the union of both sexes. [Col. 0065A]

The second occurs without the female, for which reason Er, the patriarch Judah’s son, is read to have been struck down by the Lord (Genesis 38). In the Holy Scriptures this is called impurity. Concerning it the Apostle says: “I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they cannot exercise self-control, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn.”

The third is conceived in the soul and mind. Concerning it the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5).

The blessed Apostle declares that these three kinds must be extinguished in the same way: “Put to death,” he says, “your members that are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust,” and so forth.

(Ambr.) In this matter he wishes them to strive to exercise self-control. But if, under the impulse of the flesh, they see that they cannot [Col. 0065B] persevere, because they are not sufficiently eager in that very struggle to be helped by God—for God helps the person whom he sees striving with all his strength—then let them marry if they fear burning. Perhaps afterward they will be able to attain this. For once the impediment has been removed, the will restores itself with stronger virtue.

Thus it is written (Matthew 19): “Let the one who is able to receive it receive it.”

(Aug.) “But I cannot,” you say. You cannot? “I cannot” takes up a certain remedial authority of the Apostle: if they cannot exercise self-control, let them marry. Let something be done by which they may attain forgiveness; let it contribute to forgiveness, so that they do not rush into eternal punishment.

Let what is lawful be done, by which it may be recognized what is not lawful. This is indicated by what follows: “I would rather have them marry than burn.” He conceded something to incontinence because the evil person feared eternal punishments and feared what awaits and remains [Col. 0065C] for adulterers. This includes even the situation in which married people, overcome by desire, use one another beyond the necessity of producing children—a penalty belonging among the matters for which the prayer is said daily: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

(Greg.) It is written: “It is better to marry than to burn.” They come to marriage without guilt, that is, if they have not yet vowed themselves to better things. For whoever has resolved to undertake the greater good makes the lesser good, though lawful, unlawful for himself.

It is written: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9). Therefore, whoever had devoted himself to a stronger discipline is shown to be looking back if, abandoning greater goods, he turns again toward lesser ones.

(Ambr.) He did not say, “It is better to marry than to burn,” as though burning were a good thing and marriage were therefore [Col. 0065D] better. He followed customary speech. We commonly say, “It is better to make a profit than to suffer a loss.”

To burn, then, is to be driven or overcome by desires. When the will consents to the heat of the flesh, it burns. To suffer desires without being overcome by them, however, belongs to an illustrious and perfect man.

To those who are joined in marriage I give this command—not I, but the Lord. After speaking to the unmarried and widows, he now addresses those joined in marriage with the Lord’s own authority. “A wife must not separate from her husband”; but if she has separated, she must remain unmarried. This is the Apostle’s counsel: if she has separated because of her husband’s bad conduct, she remains unmarried. “Or let her be reconciled to her husband.” For if, he says, she cannot exercise self-control because she does not wish to struggle against the flesh, let her be reconciled to her husband. A woman is not permitted to marry if she has dismissed her husband on account of fornication or apostasy, or if he, driven by lust, seeks to pervert the marital use of his wife, because the inferior party does not altogether come under the same law as the superior. If, nevertheless, the husband apostatizes or seeks to overturn the marital relationship, the woman can neither marry another nor return to him. “And let the husband not dismiss his wife.” The exception of fornication is understood, and therefore he did not add it, as he did when speaking of the woman. “But if she has separated, let her remain so,” because a man is permitted to take a wife if he has dismissed a sinful wife, since he is not bound by the law in the same way as the woman. For the husband is the head of the wife.

(Aug.) The Lord, therefore, in confirming that a wife should not be dismissed lightly, excepted only the cause of fornication. As for all other troubles, if any should arise, he commands that they be endured steadfastly for the sake of marital fidelity and chastity. He also calls the man an adulterer who marries a woman released from her husband. The Apostle Paul shows the limit of this matter, saying that it must be observed as long as her husband lives. After his death, he grants permission to marry. He himself also maintained this rule, and in it he presents not his own counsel, as in certain other instructions, but the commandment of the Lord who gives orders, when he says: “To those who are married I give this command—not I, but the Lord: that a woman must not separate from her husband; but if she has separated, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband; and let the husband not dismiss his wife”—I believe in a similar form, so that, if he has dismissed her, he should not take another, but should be reconciled to his wife. It can happen that he dismisses his wife on account of fornication, which the Lord wished to be excepted. But if she is not permitted to marry another while the husband from whom she withdrew is alive, nor he to take another while the wife whom he dismissed is alive, then it is much less lawful to commit illicit sexual acts with anyone.

“For the rest I say, not the Lord.”

(Ambr.) He says this to show what the Lord commanded with his own mouth and what he entrusted to this authority, since the Lord also speaks through him. For he says: “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. XIII).

(Aug.) Here we must first consider to whom he was referring when he said, “the rest.” Earlier he had spoken in the person of the Lord to those who are married; now he speaks in his own person to the rest. Perhaps, then, he means those who are not married—but the text does not support this. For he immediately adds: “If any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her.” Thus he is still speaking to those who are married. What, then, does he mean by “the rest,” except that earlier he was speaking to those united in such a way that both were in the faith of Christ, while now he speaks to those united in such a way that both are not believers?

“If any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her. And if any woman has an unbelieving husband and he consents to live with her, let her not leave her husband.”

(Ambr.) He said this because in those beginnings, when both were Gentiles, it happened that one of them came to believe. Since unbelievers abhorred the worship of God, and believers likewise feared contamination from their former error, he therefore commanded that, if they were content to live with those who had been changed, they should also be content to remain faithful with them.

(Aug.) One thing is commanded, another is advised, and another is forgiven. The woman is commanded not to separate from her husband; but if she has separated, she is to remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. Otherwise, then, she may not act. The faithful husband, however, is advised, if he has an unbelieving wife who consents to live with him, not to dismiss her. He is therefore permitted to dismiss her, because the Lord’s command is not that he must not dismiss her, but the Apostle’s counsel is that he should not. The virgin is similarly advised not to marry; but if she marries, she does not follow the counsel, yet she does not act against a commandment.

Forgiveness is expressed when he says: “I say this by way of concession, not by command.” Therefore it is permitted that an unbelieving spouse be dismissed, although it is better not to dismiss the spouse. Yet, according to the Lord’s command, a spouse may not be dismissed except on account of fornication. Unbelief itself is also fornication. For what do you say, Apostle? Certainly, that a faithful husband should not dismiss an unbelieving wife who consents to live with him. “Yes,” he says. Since, then, the Lord also commands that a man should not dismiss his wife except on account of fornication, why do you say here, “I say, not the Lord”? Because the idolatry followed by unbelievers, and every harmful superstition, is fornication. The Lord permitted a wife to be dismissed on account of fornication; but because he permitted it rather than commanded it, he gave the Apostle room to advise that whoever wished should not dismiss an unbelieving wife, since she might perhaps become faithful.

“For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through the believing husband.”

(Ambr.) He shows that they possess the benefit of good will, although they do not possess the honor of Christ’s name; and this pertains to the protection of hospitality, in which the sign of the cross is made—the sign by which death was conquered—for it is a sanctification.

“Otherwise your children would be unclean.” Their children would be unclean if they dismissed those unwilling to live with them and joined themselves to others. They would thereby be adulterers, and their children illegitimate; for this reason they would be unclean. I believe that it had already happened that some women came to the faith through believing husbands, and men through believing wives. Although he does not name them, he nevertheless encouraged them by examples in order to confirm his counsel.

Then he continues: “But now they are holy.” There were already Christian children, sanctified whether through the agency of one parent or with the consent of both. This would not have happened if, when one spouse believed, the marriage had been broken up and the unbelief of the other spouse had not been tolerated until the opportunity for belief arose.

“But now they are holy.” They are holy because they were born from lawful marriages and because, for the greater part, they were born under the worship of the Creator. For just as whatever is done under the proclamation of idols is unclean, so whatever is done under confession of God the Creator is holy.

“But if the unbeliever separates, let him separate.” He safeguards the purpose of religion by commanding that Christians not abandon their marriages. But if the unbeliever departs out of hatred for God, the believer is not guilty of dissolving the marriage; for the cause of God is greater than that of marriage.

“For the brother or the sister is not subject to bondage in such a case.” That is, reverence for marriage is not owed to one who abhors the author of marriage. A marriage that exists without devotion to God is not valid; consequently, the person who is abandoned for God’s sake does not sin if he or she joins another. The insult against the Creator dissolves the marital right with respect to the person who is left, so that the one who has been joined to another is not accused. The unbeliever who departs is recognized as sinning both against God and against marriage, because he was unwilling to maintain the marriage under devotion to God. Therefore he is not owed marital fidelity, since he departed for this reason: he did not want to hear that the God of Christians is the author of marriage.

For if Ezra caused unbelieving wives or husbands to be dismissed so that God might be appeased, and was not angered if they took others from their own nation—for they were not commanded to take back those dismissed and never marry others—how much more, if an unbeliever departs, will the believer have free choice, if he wishes to marry a spouse of his own law? For a union made outside God’s decree ought not to be reckoned a marriage. But when the person later recognizes this and grieves that he abandoned the marriage, he corrects himself so as to merit forgiveness. If both come to believe through knowledge of God, they confirm the marriage.

“But God has called us to peace.” It is evident that one should not quarrel with the person who departs, because he departs out of hatred for God and therefore is not even worthy of consideration.

“For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?” He says this because perhaps those who do not abhor the name of Christ may come to believe.

“Except to each one as the Lord has allotted.” The Lord allotted to each person when he would be saved—that is, when he would be able to believe—and he sustains him. Here too he teaches that such people are to be awaited and that one ought not to be scandalized by them, because their hope must be preserved. If they themselves depart, one must be patient with them.

Let each one walk as God has called him. That is, if the believer is joined in marriage, let him not abandon it, whether husband or wife, but let him remain as he is, whether Jew or Greek. This is what I teach in all the churches. He says this to persuade them that he does not hand down one teaching to them and another to the rest. When they hear that the others are taught this same faith, they accept it more readily; for a person is easily inclined when he sees his companion agreeing.

Was someone called while circumcised? Let him not draw on the foreskin. This is what he said: let him walk as he was called. A Jew who has become a Christian should not think himself perhaps inferior because he does not have a foreskin, nor give glory to the foreskin.

Was someone called while uncircumcised? Let him not be circumcised. A Gentile who has been called should not think that he ought to be circumcised because he hears that the sons of Abraham are preferred. They are not preferred because they are circumcised, but because of Abraham’s merit, whose children they are in both groups if they believe; otherwise they will be worse than the Gentiles. For it is worse to have been and not to be than never to have been.

Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing. It is clear that neither harms nor benefits. But the observance of God’s commandments—that is, faith—makes God favorable, if it is approved by good works.

Let each one remain in the calling in which he was called. This confirms what he said above.

Were you called as a slave? Do not let it trouble you; but if you can become free, make use of it. He encourages the slave, by serving well and fearing God, to make himself worthy of freedom from his earthly master, lest, on hearing “Were you called as a slave? Do not let it trouble you,” he should become more negligent regarding good works toward his earthly master, Christ’s teaching should be blasphemed, and he should fail to win God’s favor. For one who serves well in earthly matters stores up merit with God, because the Lord said: “The one who is faithful in very little will also be faithful in much.”

But the one who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman. Rescued from sins, which prove people to be true slaves, he becomes a freedman. For the truly complete slave is the one who acts foolishly; likewise, the ancients called all wise people free, but all foolish people slaves. Hence Solomon says: “Slaves will serve the wise servant” (Ecclus. X). Thus the person who believes, even if he is temporarily a slave, becomes the Lord’s freedman because he acts wisely by believing in Christ.

If sins make slaves, just as Ham, the son of Noah, became a slave because of sin and folly (Gen. IX), then when someone receives remission of sins, he becomes a freedman.

Likewise, the one who was called free is Christ’s slave. It is progress for a person to pass from being free to becoming Christ’s slave. For he was free from God—which is the greatest crime. Therefore, having lost that bitter and harmful freedom, he received a condition that would benefit him, as the Lord says: “Take my yoke upon you, because it is gentle, and my burden, because it is light” (Matt. XI). Thus he cut away pride and made unity possible, so that the slave would not think himself despised because of his condition, nor the free man, inflated by arrogance of mind, set himself above the slave.

You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings. This is true, because we were bought at so great a price that no one could redeem us except Christ, who is rich over all. Therefore whoever is bought at a price ought rather to serve, so as to repay the buyer, at least in some measure. Bought by God—that is, by Christ—we must not be slaves of human beings. Those are slaves of human beings who subject themselves to human superstitions.

Nevertheless, the Apostle recalls the matter that he condemned at the beginning of the Letter, because some said, “I belong to Paul,” and another, “I belong to Apollos.” Yet he added the article of faith that Christ must be acknowledged as God, when he showed that they should be called Christ’s slaves, not the slaves of a human being.

Let each brother remain with God in the condition in which he was called. This is what he said above; he repeats it in order to commend it fully.

[Col. 0069D] “But concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord.” This answers what they had written, as he said above: “Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me,” etc.

“But I give counsel, as one who has received mercy from the Lord to be faithful.” He denies that he has received a command concerning virgins, because the author of marriage could not command something opposed to marriage, lest he condemn his own former work. Yet he gives counsel—not because marriage displeases him, nor as a result of flattery—because he has received grace for this purpose, that he may be fit to give salutary counsels.

“I therefore judge this to be good because of the present necessity: that it is good for a person to remain as he is.” He says that remaining a virgin is good; and, to show this more absolutely, he says, “because of the present necessity,” because it is best. Thus it may be known that, between what is good and what is best, nothing is so distinguished and useful as virginity. For he teaches that virginity is more commendable not only before God but also in the present life, since it does not know the necessities of the time which marriage suffers—the sorrows of childbirth and likewise the loss of children. Therefore, to exhort women to seek it, he teaches that those who love virginity gain deliverance from the calamities of the present necessity. Thus, when they learn that it has not only a better place with God but also advantages in the present life, they may seek it with every effort.

[Col. 0070A] There is only one thing that labors: to overcome the inclination of the flesh; in all else it is free. Since the flesh is present in its origin and nature, its use is pleasant and its inclination sweet; therefore it is no brief glory to overcome these things.

“Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release.” These are counsels of remedy. For he says that no one ought to be released from his wife except for the cause of fornication. Often, under the pretext of continence, those who dismiss their wives deceive other women when their purpose grows cold. But if someone who has a wife wishes to live better, let him exhort her first to live without scandal.

“Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife.” Knowing this to be more acceptable to God and free from necessity, let him not seek a wife, provided, nevertheless, that he abstains from other things as well. Otherwise, what profit is there in suppressing the desire of the flesh—that is, in rejecting what is lawful and becoming subject to what is unlawful?

“But if you take a wife, you have not sinned.” Certainly he does not sin, because he does what is permitted. But if he has despised this permission, he stores up merit and a crown for himself; for it requires great patience not to do what is not forbidden.

“And if a virgin marries, she will not sin,” because before God she is free in this respect. “Yet such persons will have tribulations of the flesh.” That is, although they are plainly free from sin, they will nevertheless have, in this life, tribulations: pains of the womb, the support of children, food, clothing, dowries, illness, the furnishing of the house, the needs of a wife, and the dominion of a husband.

(Greg.) Those who live spiritually may also suffer tribulation of the flesh. Why, then, is tribulation of the flesh said to belong especially to married persons, when it is not far removed even from the life of spiritual people, except because those who delight in pleasures of the flesh frequently receive greater tribulations from the flesh? Job fittingly says: “His soul shall mourn over himself” (Job XIV), because whoever desires to rejoice in himself is already thereby in grief, in that he has departed from true joy; for the Creator is the true joy of the mind. It is fitting, therefore, that a person should always find himself in sorrow when, having abandoned the Creator, he sought joy in himself.

[Col. 0070D] “But I spare you.”

(Amb.) He spares them when he urges them rather toward those things that exclude the aforementioned tribulations and anxieties of the flesh. He can also seem to spare them when he permits and does not oppose those who desire what he has shown to be burdensome.

“But this I say, brothers: the time has been shortened. What remains is—” By saying that the time is shortened and that it remains, he indicated that the end of the world is imminent. Although he knew that times still remained, he ought not to write otherwise because of those who would read this when a very short time remained, lest the day of judgment, always thought far off, either not be feared or be judged false. Yet it greatly benefits people to say that something is imminent even when it is still far off, for it instills fear for living a better life. Indeed, how anxious are those here in the present who have business before judges when the day of the proceedings is said to be near? This is the sense here of what he says elsewhere: “As deceivers, yet true” (II Cor. VI).

[Col. 0071A] “That those who have wives may be as though they had none.” Since the end of the world is near, they ought not to be anxious to beget children or devoted to sexual use itself, but, being more ready and watchful and exercised in divine works, they should fight concerning the care of the law when battle is imminent. For there will be afflictions such as never were, and many will fall into the snare of the devil. Indeed, none of us wants these things to occur in his own time, fearing the afflictions foretold by the Savior. Therefore, as we wish for ourselves, let us provide for others too, that we may abstain from the begetting of many children, be more given to prayer and God’s service, and foresee the day of judgment, lest we ourselves be unprepared through the hindrances of the present necessity and they incur what we fear.

He therefore wishes believers to abstain even from lawful things, that they may appear not only innocent but also glorious. For to pass over what is permitted belongs to the greatest virtue, and not to desire what is forbidden is not far from it.

(Aug.) Marriages are certainly to be judged happier when, whether after children have been begotten or even after this earthly offspring has been despised, they have been able to preserve continence between themselves by equal consent. For this does not conflict with the command by which the Lord forbids a spouse to be dismissed: one does not dismiss her with whom one lives not carnally but spiritually. And that is observed which is said through the Apostle: “What remains is that those who have wives should be as though they had none.”

[Col. 0071C] (Greg.) Thus the mind of Christian spouses is both weak and faithful: it cannot wholly despise all temporal things, yet it can join itself to eternal things by desire. Although meanwhile it lies in love of the flesh, it is strengthened by the refreshment of heavenly hope; and, though it has the things of the world for the use of the journey, it hopes for the things of God as the fruit of arrival. Let it not devote itself wholly to what it does, lest it utterly fall away from what it ought steadfastly to hope for. Paul aptly and briefly expresses this when he says: “Let those who have wives be as though they had none; those who weep, as though they did not weep; and those who rejoice, as though they did not rejoice.”

A man has his wife as though he did not have her when he uses her for carnal consolation in such a way that he is never, through love of her, bent from the rectitude of his better intention toward evil deeds. He has his wife as though he did not have her when, seeing all things to be transitory, he bears the care of the flesh from necessity, yet awaits by desire the eternal joys of the Spirit. To weep as though not weeping is to lament outward adversities in such a way as nevertheless to know how to rejoice in the consolation of eternal hope. Again, to rejoice as though not rejoicing is to raise the mind over low things in such a way as never to cease fearing the highest things. Accordingly, shortly afterwards he aptly adds: “For the form of this world passes away,” as though he openly said: Do not love the world steadfastly, since the very world that you love cannot stand. You fix your heart in vain as though on something abiding, while that which you love itself flees away.

[Col. 0072A] “And those who weep, as though they did not weep.”

(Amb.) Knowing that the end of the world is near and that the consolation of those who are perhaps oppressed for God’s justice will soon come, let them comfort themselves among themselves with this hope.

“And those who rejoice, as though they did not rejoice.” Those who rejoice in the present should know that grief will soon come—namely, to those who rejoice in the world while uncertain about God’s judgment.

“And those who buy, as though not possessing.” Believers who buy, believing that little time remains to the world, act so as not to spend all their care on something soon to perish; rather, they care for their soul, which they know to be eternal.

“And those who use this world, as though not using it.”

(Greg.) That is, they should not presume upon the use of what will soon perish when the world falls. A person buys yet as though not possessing when he prepares earthly things for use, yet foresees with cautious thought that he will leave them soon. He uses the world yet as though not using it when he brings all outward necessities into the service of his life, but does not allow these same things to rule his mind, so that, subject outside, they may serve and never break the purpose of a mind tending toward things above. Therefore all earthly things are for such people not objects of desire but objects of use. They use necessary things, but desire to have nothing connected with sin. From the very things they possess they daily acquire rewards, and rejoice more in a good work than in a good possession.

[Col. 0072C] “For the form of this world has passed away.”

(Amb.) Since he said that the world will end, he shows that its form passes away, and that this is the end: not that its substance passes away, but its form.

(Aug.) Therefore, if the form of the world will perish, there is no doubt that all things which are in the world will perish. It passes away because the world daily grows old. When judgment has been completed, this heaven and this earth will then cease to be, when a new heaven and a new earth begin to be. This world will pass away through a change of things, not through an utter destruction. Hence the Apostle also says: “For the form of this world passes away; but I want you to be without anxiety.” The form, therefore, passes away, not the nature. For, when those not written in the book of life have been judged and cast into eternal fire, the form of this world will then pass away in the conflagration of worldly fires, just as it came about through the flood of worldly waters.

In that worldly conflagration, as I have said, the corruptible qualities of the elements that suited our corruptible bodies will wholly perish by burning; and the substance itself will possess those qualities which, by a marvelous change, suit immortal bodies. Thus the world, renewed for the better, will be suitably adapted to human beings whose flesh too has been renewed for the better.

[Col. 0072D] “But I want you to be without anxiety.”

(Amb.) For when worldly anxiety is diminished, people keep more eagerly watch over the things of God.

“The unmarried man is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please God.” He shows how we may be without anxiety when he says: “The unmarried man is concerned with the things of the Lord.” For when the anxiety of a wife’s affairs—which alone is heavier than the rest in the world—has been removed, the mind is trained to win God’s favor, provided that in this hope it strips itself of these troubles in order to serve God more.

“But the married man is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife.” Concern for a wife and thought for children are worldly concerns. Among other things, people sometimes commit acts deserving punishment lest they offend them, as Zerubbabel, one of the three chamberlains of King Artaxerxes, relates (III Esdr. III). For a sorrowful wife in the house is a great bitterness.

[Col. 0073A] “A wife and a virgin are divided.” They are divided not in nature but in activity, since in Numbers we read that women were called virgins (Num. XXXI). Therefore the concern of a wife is one thing, that of a virgin another. Yet when “woman” is said, what it signifies is uncertain unless a further indication follows; when “virgin” is said, the expression is plain. For this reason, after “woman” the Apostle placed “virgin,” so that by “woman” he might signify not a virgin. By this he wished to show the virgin free from the weariness and labors which a woman joined to a husband suffers.

“She who is unmarried is concerned with the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and spirit.” Since, in hope of heavenly things, she does not undertake concern for husband and children, she thinks of the Lord, that she may preserve the purpose devoted to God—provided that, with a pure body, her mind, rejecting earthly things, strives for heavenly things. For it is the mind that either sanctifies or defiles the body. What advantage is there in having a pure body and a defiled soul, when the body is either honored or condemned according to the merit of the soul?

[Col. 0073C] “But she who is married is concerned with the things of this world, how she may please her husband.” Bound by the marital law, she is concerned how to fulfill the claim of the marital duty, being subject to worldly necessities.

“But I say this for your benefit, not to cast a snare upon you, but to call you to what is honorable and what affords opportunity to entreat the Lord without hindrance.” Because what is more useful or better seems harsh and burdensome to some people because of their habitual temporal use, he therefore, after giving the reason, exhorts them with the affection of charity that this is simply more useful and more honorable. It is honorable because it is holy and pure; useful because it is most worthy before God and light in the world.

What, then, are we to say? If virgins think of God and women joined to husbands think of the world, what hope remains before God for those who marry? If this is so, their salvation is doubtful. But we see virgins thinking of the world and married women devoting themselves to the works of the Lord. For such virgins, their holiness will not be reckoned by God; and for such marriages there will be a reward with God, because, although bound by earthly ties, they gave themselves to obtaining some reward of immortality in the future.

[Col. 0074A] For the others, not only will virginity not be reckoned to them, but they will also be subjected to punishment: under the cover of a better hope, they occupied their life and conduct with worldly care and anxiety and made themselves sluggish in performing God’s works. As Jeremiah the prophet says: “Cursed is he who performs the work of God negligently” (Jer. XLVIII). These are those of whom he says in another Epistle: “Having indeed an appearance of truth, but denying its power” (II Tim. III).

But the Apostle speaks to those who desire with remarkable devotion to obey heavenly commands, showing and teaching by what short path one goes more swiftly to God. For one who wishes to remain a virgin in order to win God’s favor, knowing what reward he may receive, abstains from what is lawful so as to become better, and at the same time despises every hindrance of the flesh, knowing that these are the things which, like the weights of fetters, hold back the steps of one who runs.

Those not bound by marriage should be admonished to serve heavenly commands all the more rightly because the yoke of carnal union does not incline them toward worldly cares. Those not burdened by the weight of lawful marriage should not be oppressed by the unlawful weight of earthly anxiety. Let the last day find them as much more ready as they are more unencumbered, lest, by neglecting the better things that they are free to do, they deserve the worse punishments.

[Col. 0074B] Let them hear that the Apostle, when instructing some for the grace of celibacy, did not despise marriage but rejected the worldly cares arising from marriage, saying: “I say this for your benefit, not to cast a snare upon you, but to call you to what is honorable and what affords opportunity to entreat the Lord without hindrance.” Worldly anxieties arise from marriages; therefore the Teacher of the Gentiles persuaded his hearers toward better things, lest they be bound by earthly anxiety. What, then, has a celibate person escaped who is impeded by the hindrance of secular cares? He has not subjected himself to marriage, yet he has not escaped the burdens of marriage.

“But if anyone sees himself behaving improperly toward his virgin, if she is beyond puberty and it ought so to be, let him do what he wishes: he does not sin if she marries.” Because above he exhorted, with reasons given, that virginity and continence should be maintained, so that by comparison marriages almost seem useless and to be rejected, he now shows, lest he appear to forbid marriage, that a virgin does not sin if she marries. Yet she undertakes a matter of the greatest labor which has no reward before God, just as it has no punishment; for he wishes Christians to be better in every respect. Therefore, if any woman is desirous of marriage and already mature for its use, it is better that she marry publicly according to the permitted law than that she act shamefully in secret and be put to shame in it.

[Col. 0074D] “But he who has resolved in his heart, having no necessity, and has authority over his own will, and has judged this in his heart, to keep his virgin, does well.” He says this so that one who has a virgin whose mind is not toward marriage may keep her and not offer her an incentive to marriage when he sees that she has no pleasure [will] for marrying. For if benefits ought to be bestowed, how much more should they not be taken away!

“Therefore he who gives his virgin in marriage does well.” He does well because what he does is permitted. “And he who does not give her in marriage does better,” because he stores up merit for her before God and frees her from worldly anxiety.

“A woman is bound by the law for as long a time as her husband lives.” He continues this in order to teach that a woman, even if she has been cast out by her husband, has no permission to marry. “But if her husband falls asleep, she is released from the law.” These matters too pertain to the causes mentioned above, in order to show how blessed a virgin is, since she is subject to no one but God alone. For she seems to overcome natural subjection when what is humbled by nature is raised up.

[Col. 0075A] “Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord.” That is, let her marry the man whom she judges suitable for herself, because unwilling marriages commonly have bad outcomes. “Only in the Lord” means that she should marry without suspicion of disgrace and should marry a husband of her own religion; this is to marry in the Lord.

“But she will be happier if she remains as she is, according to my counsel.” When he says, “Let her marry,” he speaks according to natural law. Although first marriages are from God, second marriages are permitted. Thus, because first marriages are celebrated under God’s blessing, they are exalted. But second marriages lack glory even in the present; they are permitted because of incontinence and because younger widows are prone to fall. Therefore he permits second marriages. But because it is better for her to remain continent, so that she may be worthier in the future, he gives the preeminent counsel, with spiritual reasoning, that she should remain continent.

[Col. 0075B] “But I think that I too have the Spirit of God.” To show that his counsel is valid and provident, he commends it, through humility of expression, with lofty meaning.

## CHAPTER VIII

The Apostle shows that knowledge is of no value unless it is ordered according to charity; he teaches the truth concerning foods sacrificed to idols and reproves the recklessness of those who cause scandal.

“Now concerning things sacrificed to idols, we know that we all possess knowledge.”

(Ambr.) He is now going to speak about knowledge, but he does not immediately say what sort of knowledge it is. He shows this in what follows, saying that an idol is nothing.
