“Knowledge puffs up.” It is clear that a person who possesses knowledge takes pride in that very fact, whether before others because he is considered wise or privately before himself. This kind of knowledge is such that it takes pride in itself; therefore it puffs up.

“But charity builds up.”

(Aug.) This is rightly understood in no other way than that knowledge is beneficial only when charity is present in it. Without charity it puffs up—that is, it raises a person in the emptiness of a most vain, airy pride.

(Ambr.) Knowledge is therefore great and useful to itself when it is humbled by charity, so that it may grow further. It is tempered by love, lest it remain too unmixed and intoxicate the person who possesses it, making him exalt himself. Just as unmixed wine alienates the mind unless it is diluted with water, so knowledge makes a person proud unless it is tempered. Everything by itself is unpleasant and harmful: bread alone is not eaten well, nor are other foods agreeable without admixture; rather, they are harmful. Thus charity builds up. Charity itself, although called by one word, consists in many things; it cannot exist without patience, without humility, or without simplicity of heart.

These people, then, were puffed up by knowledge because an idol is nothing. Knowing that it was permitted to eat meat and that an idol was nothing, they ate the flesh of sacrificial victims against the salvation of their uninstructed brothers, thinking that the food did not defile those who ate it. They were a scandal to their brothers because they did not keep charity before their eyes. It was more pious to refrain from eating meat than to cause a brother to stumble. Their knowledge was destroying the minds of uninstructed brothers, who thought that some grace was present there at the idol because they saw more knowledgeable brothers attending and showing no horror.

Therefore he says, “Charity builds up,” so that, by devoting themselves to the salvation of their brothers, they would not exercise their knowledge there according to its strict rights and cause those brothers to stumble.

(Greg.) Since charity raises us by building us up, knowledge perverts us by puffing us up. Hypocrites often afflict themselves with remarkable abstinence, wear away all the strength of the body, and, as though living in the flesh, extinguish the life of the flesh completely. Through abstinence they approach death, so that they live while almost dying every day. Yet they seek human eyes for these practices and desire the glory of admiration, as the Truth attests when he says: “They disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting” (Matt. VI).

If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know (Ambrose). He shows that those who glory in knowledge have not known in the manner in which they ought to know. For since they do not pursue charity, which is the mother of all good things, they do not know as they ought. Therefore, if knowledge is to bear fruit, it must subject itself to charity.

But if anyone loves God, he is known by him. He loves God who, for the sake of charity, moderates his knowledge so that it may benefit the brother for whom Christ died.

He now takes up the matter of foods sacrificed to idols, in order to show by reasoning that knowledge, when charity is disregarded, not only fails to profit but also does harm. [Col. 0076C] We know that an idol is nothing, and that there is no God but one. This is true: among Christians there is one God, although there are those who are called gods and lords, whether in heaven or on earth. The pagans call the sun, the moon, and the other stars heavenly gods. On earth they call Apollo, Aesculapius, Hercules, and Minerva gods and lords.

For us, however, there is one God, the Father, from whom all things come and we exist in him. All things that exist, wherever they exist, come from him. But when he says, “and we in him,” he distinguishes us from the others who, although they come from him, are not in him, since they still do not believe.

And there is one Lord, Jesus, through whom all things exist, and we through him. Everything comes from the Father but was created through the Son. When he says, “and we through him,” he signifies that, although we were created [Col. 0076D] through him along with the others, through the dullness of our minds and our ignorance we have come to recognize through him the mystery of the one God. Thus he named one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ his Son, so that, since God cannot fail to be Lord, the Lord likewise might be understood to be God; he demonstrated that God and Lord are one, preserving the order of one principle.

But knowledge is not in everyone. That is, not all believers know the mystery of the one God. Therefore some of those who believe think that there is some divine power in idols. Others, still conscious of the idol, eat what has been sacrificed to it as though it had been sacrificed to an idol. Some of the common people, while still venerating the idol, ate what had been sacrificed with reverence, as though some [Col. 0077A] divinity were present there. And their conscience, being weak, is defiled. A conscience is stained if it is weak with respect to God.

Food, however, does not commend us to God. This is true: we shall not therefore please God if we eat everything, nor shall we offend him if we abstain from certain things. For neither shall we abound if we eat, nor shall we lack if we do not eat. If the food of sacrifices is rejected, there will certainly still be something to eat; but if it is taken, there will not be such abundance that nothing further is needed. For this reason it should be rejected, because life cannot be sustained without food, yet it is a source of scandal to the brothers.

See to it, however, that your liberty does not somehow become an offense to the weak. That is, because you say that you are permitted to eat meat from a sacrifice, your knowledge that an idol is nothing must not generate offense among brothers [Col. 0077B] who do not yet know that an idol is nothing.

For if someone sees a person who possesses knowledge reclining in an idol’s shrine, will not his conscience, being weak, be strengthened to eat food sacrificed to idols? He said this because, when someone sees a knowledgeable brother invited to an idol’s shrine and reclining there to eat sacrificial meat, he thinks that some grace is present there and begins himself to eat sacrificial meat. He does not do so with the conscience of the knowledgeable man, who knows that the idol is nothing; rather, when he sees the knowledgeable brother eating there without horror, he thinks that a divine power is present.

And the weak brother for whom Christ died will perish through your knowledge. The weak person will perish if he eats sacrificial food contrary to faith in the one God. These words are, as it were, the words of one who is angry and showing what evil knowledge can produce if it is [Col. 0077C] not restrained by charity.

“Through your knowledge”—that is, your expertise kills him when he sees you doing what he understands differently. You will therefore be the occasion of death to a brother for whom Christ permitted himself to be crucified in order to redeem him. Thus he teaches that, for the sake of charity, one must sometimes conceal one’s knowledge, because the brother’s salvation is undoubtedly more important than food: the food is permitted, but it is not beneficial. This is to know and understand as one ought.

Thus, when you sin against your brothers in this way and wound their weak conscience, you sin in Christ. For when they are not zealous for the charity by which Christ freed us, they sin in Christ—not “against Christ,” since to sin against Christ is to deny Christ; rather, they sin in those things that belong to Christ. Just as one who is under the law is said to sin in the law, so those who are [Col. 0077D] under Christ are said to sin in Christ.

Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat, so that I may not cause my brother to stumble. He teaches that charity must be pursued to such an extent that permitted things are to be treated as forbidden, lest they harm a brother. For how great an evil it is not to transgress through forbidden things, yet to give offense through things that have been permitted—so that the law is observed in permitted matters but not observed in forbidden ones, when they are eaten without consideration?

The law permitted what it permitted with a proper limit that must be observed. It is certainly permitted to have a wife, but if she commits fornication, she must be dismissed. So too it is permitted to eat meat, but if it has been offered to idols, it must be rejected.

## CHAPTER IX

The Apostle leads the Corinthians toward perfection in virtue by his own example and by the example of those who run in the stadium.

“Am I not an apostle? Am I not free? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?” (Ambrose.) When he appears to deny it, he confirms it, for he speaks in anger. He proves that he is an apostle because he was sent to the Gentiles, as the Lord said to him: “I will send you to the Gentiles” (Acts 22). He shows that he is free because he coveted nothing from anyone and did not teach through flattery. He saw Jesus our Lord while he was praying in the temple at Jerusalem.

“Are you not my work in the Lord?” They are his work because he himself planted them in the Lord, evangelizing the word of the Lord among them for a year and six months (Acts 18).

“And if I am not an apostle to others, yet surely [Col. 0078B] I am to you.” The believing Jews who nevertheless continued to observe the law denied that he was an apostle. He was already teaching that circumcision ought no longer to be practiced and that the Sabbath ought not to be observed, while the other Apostles, because of the scandal it might cause, were refraining from speaking openly about this matter. He therefore seemed to teach differently. For this reason they denied that he was an apostle, although he was an apostle to those who had seen in him the distinctive signs of virtue.

“For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.” Under his preaching they had turned from idols to faith in the one God. “My defense before those who examine me is this.” He now begins to present the case that he introduced above when he said: “All things are permitted to me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything. Food is for the belly and the belly for foods” (above, chapter 6).

“My defense before those who examine me is this,” and he adds what it is: [Col. 0078C] “Do we not have authority to eat and drink?” This is what he had said: “All things are permitted to me.”

“Do we not have authority to lead about a woman as the other Apostles, the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas do?” He added “and Cephas” because, although he was first among the Apostles, he did not reject the expenses that were offered to him. Cephas is Simon Peter himself.

Women followed the Apostles out of a desire for the Lord’s teaching and a longing for virtue, providing them with expenses and services, just as they followed the Savior and ministered to him from their own resources.

“Or do only Barnabas and I lack authority to do this?” That is, we do have authority to do it, but we do not wish to. He says “to do” instead of “to receive,” in order to speak more courteously. To confirm this, he adds examples:

“Who [Col. 0078D] ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not partake of its milk?” Do I say these things merely on human authority? Or does the law not say the same?

He teaches that the testimonies quoted above agree with divine evidence, so that he may show that he does not refuse to accept expenses without reason, since so many examples demonstrate both that they should be given and that they may be accepted.

For it is written in the law (Deuteronomy 25): “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is threshing.”

(Gregory.) Under the figure of the ox, at different times are expressed the madness of the luxurious, the laborious strength of preachers, and the humility of the Israelites. Since the madness [Col. 0079A] of the luxurious is signified by the name of the ox and by comparison with it, Solomon judges thus. After first describing the shamelessness of the woman who gives evil counsel, he adds: “At once he follows her, like an ox led to the slaughter” (Proverbs 7).

Again, since the labor of the preacher is expressed by the name of the ox, the words of the law bear witness, where we read: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is threshing,” as though it openly said: Do not prevent the preacher of the word from receiving his wages.

Again, since the people of Israel are represented by the name of the ox, the prophet declares, announcing the coming of the Redeemer: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger” (Isaiah 1). By the ox he signifies the Israelite people, tamed beneath the yoke of the law; by the donkey he indicates the Gentile people, devoted to pleasures and more brutish.

[Col. 0079B] “Is God concerned about oxen?” (Ambrose.) For the moment let us settle this briefly. In the prophet Jonah it is written: “Shall I not spare the city in which there are more than one hundred and twenty thousand human beings, and many animals?” (Jonah 4). And the Psalmist says: “You save human beings and beasts” (Psalm 35). How, then, does God not care about oxen and cattle?

He does not care about oxen and cattle for their own sake, but for our sake, since they were made for us. Therefore he cares about us, not about them. Or rather, he says this precisely for our sake. For our sake it was written—for everything spoken figuratively passes over to us: “The one who plows and threshes in hope ought to receive the fruit of his hope.” This is true, because one labors in hope of receiving the fruit.

“If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material [Col. 0079C] things?” He does not call it great, nor does he say that it is equal, if those who evangelize the kingdom of God and feed the Church with heavenly food receive bodily sustenance, so that, while handing on eternal things, they may obtain temporal ones.

“If others share in your authority, do we not share in it even more?” If those who are not your fathers through the Gospel, and who do not have the same affection toward you, have the authority to receive, how much more do we? The implied meaning is: we, your Apostles, since Barnabas was an apostle.

“But we have not used this authority; rather, we endure everything, so that we may place no obstacle in the way of the Gospel of Christ.” He has disclosed a meaning long kept hidden. He shows that he refuses to accept expenses, although he is permitted to do so, lest the force of evangelical authority become sluggish.

The pseudo-apostles, when people sinned, flattered them because they wanted to receive from them, and they did not seem [Col. 0079D] to themselves to be sinning by becoming subject to them. But because this conduct was contrary to evangelical discipline, Paul does not wish to receive, so that he may rebuke freely and not be found among their number. In order that the force of the Christian rule might remain lawful, he made what was lawful unlawful for himself, since they offended through their liberty.

“Do you not know that those who work in sacred places eat from the sacred place, and that those who serve at the altar share in the altar?” By “sacred places” he signifies the law of the Gentiles, and by “the altar,” that of the Jews. For the Lord decreed through Moses that the priests should take a portion of the things that had been offered.

Thus the Lord Jesus ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel. God therefore did not follow the pattern of the Gentiles through Moses; rather, natural reason itself teaches that a person should live [Col. 0080A] from the place where he labors. He therefore established this principle in accordance with nature itself and human society.

He nevertheless adds this as a further accumulation, reinforcing the case so that he may not make it seem trivial or offensive, since he commends it with so many testimonies; yet he does not wish it to profit him, lest his freedom to rebuke be weakened.

“But I have used none of these things.” After showing in many ways that it is permitted to accept support, he nevertheless declares that he does not need it, since it is harmful to accept it from sinners, as I mentioned above.

“I have not written these things so that they should be done to me. For it is better for me to die than for anyone to deprive me of my glory.” He calls his glory the preservation of the severity of the Gospel. He chooses death rather than violating the rights of the Gospel, knowing that this benefits him more for future salvation. He refuses to accept the service that is owed to him from them, [Col. 0080B] lest by accepting it they gain confidence to sin.

“For if I preach the Gospel, there is no glory for me, since necessity is laid upon me.” As the Lord says: “When you have done all that I command you, say: We are unworthy servants; we have done what we were obliged to do.” “Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel.” A servant sent by the Lord does what he has been commanded even unwillingly; otherwise he must necessarily be bound by blows. Thus Moses was sent unwillingly to Pharaoh, and Jonah was compelled to preach to the Ninevites.

“For if I do this willingly, I have a reward.” It is clear that no one receives a reward for something he does unwillingly. If he acts voluntarily, he is worthy of a reward, because he consents to his master, and what is done willingly is done better.

“But if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship.” [Col. 0080C] This too is not obscure: whoever does something without devotion does it not willingly but under compulsion. Since he is not master of his own power, he unwillingly does what has been commanded him.

“What, then, is my reward? That, when I announce the Gospel, I may offer the Gospel without expense, so as not to abuse my authority in the Gospel.” Having restrained the boastfulness of his words, he glories and wishes it to be understood how great a reward he deserves, because he does not use his authority in the Gospel but rejects the expenses offered to him, lest he weaken the force of preaching.

This means: the practice is permitted, but it is not beneficial for the sake of the salvation of the brothers, so that they may be corrected. He therefore wishes to be an example to the others, so that when they see something is not beneficial, they too may refrain even from what is permitted.

“Otherwise, they will become guilty through an offense”—that is, they take what does not benefit them but causes harm.

(Augustine.) The Apostle says that it is indeed permitted and granted to him by the [Col. 0080D] Lord that those who announce the Gospel should live from the Gospel, that is, should receive from the Gospel what is necessary for this life. Yet he says that he did not use this authority. For there were many who wanted an opportunity to acquire and sell the Gospel. Wishing to cut off this opportunity from them, the Apostle supported himself by the labor of his own hands.

He says elsewhere concerning them (2 Corinthians 11): “That I may cut off the opportunity from those who seek an opportunity.” Although, like the other good Apostles, he was permitted by the Lord to live from the Gospel, he did not make his purpose in evangelizing consist in that support. Rather, he placed the purpose of his support in the Gospel itself. That is, he did not evangelize in order to obtain food and whatever else was necessary, but accepted these things [Col. 0081A] in order to fulfill his mission, so that he would evangelize not unwillingly but willingly.

This is what he rejects when he says: “Do you not know that those who work in the temple eat what comes from the temple, and that those who serve at the altar share in the altar? So also the Lord ordained that those who announce the Gospel should live from the Gospel.”

“But I have used none of these things.” Here he shows that it was permitted, not commanded; otherwise he would be held to have acted contrary to the Lord’s command.

Then he continues: “I have not written these things so that they should be done to me. It is better for me to die than for anyone to make my glory empty.” He said this because he had decided, for the sake of certain people seeking an opportunity, to support himself by the labor of his own hands.

“For if I preach the Gospel, there is no glory [Col. 0081B] for me.” That is: if I preach the Gospel so that these things may be done for me—if I preach in order to attain them and place the end of the Gospel in food, drink, and clothing—why is there no glory for him? “Necessity is laid upon me,” he says. That is, he would evangelize because he had no means by which to live, or in order to acquire a temporary profit from preaching eternal things. In that case there would already be necessity in his evangelizing, not willingness.

“Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel.” But how ought he to evangelize? Surely in such a way that he places his reward in the Gospel itself and in the kingdom of God. In this way he can evangelize not under compulsion but willingly.

“For if I do this willingly, I have a reward. But if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship.” That is, if I preach the Gospel because I am compelled by poverty and by the necessities required for temporal life, [Col. 0081C] others will have the reward of the Gospel through me, those who love the Gospel because I preach it. I, however, will not have it, because I do not love the Gospel itself but have placed its price in temporal things.

It is wicked for someone to minister the Gospel not as a son but as a servant who has been entrusted with a stewardship, so that, as though distributing another’s property, he himself takes nothing from it except provisions. These are given from outside, not as participation in the kingdom but as support for miserable servitude.

Although elsewhere he also calls himself a steward, a servant can be adopted into the number of sons and faithfully administer the matter in which he has merited a coheir’s share to his fellow participants. But here, when he says, “If unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship,” he wishes such a [Col. 0081D] steward to be understood as one who administers another’s property and receives nothing from it himself.

“For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win the more.” (Ambrose.) He is free from all because he has not handed the Gospel over to anyone through flattery, has desired nothing from anyone except salvation, and has not accepted from anyone, under the pretext of hypocrisy, greater expenses for the enjoyment of pleasures.

He says that he has made himself the servant of all by presenting himself, through humility, as like all those whose minds were weak, so that by patience he might strengthen them for future salvation. He encouraged their spirits because they either sinned or followed divine things slowly; and so that they would not take correction harshly, he rebuked them gently.

“And I became [Col. 0082A] to the Jews as a Jew, in order to win Jews.” For it seems as though he pretended, in order to become all things to all people, as flatterers commonly do. But this is not the case. As a divine man and spiritual physician who knew the causes and wounds of all, he encouraged them and sympathized with them with great care.

Since he had certain things in common with all human beings, he became as a Jew to the Jews. Because of their scruples, he circumcised Timothy and, after being purified, went up to the temple, so that they would not receive through him an occasion for blasphemy. He therefore did something that ought already to have ceased, but he did it according to the law. He agreed with them that the law and the prophets were from God, and from these he showed them that Christ was the one who had been promised, so that his agreement with them might produce its effect.

[Col. 0082B] “To those who are under the law, as though I were under the law—although I myself am not under the law—in order to win those who are under the law.” Those who are under the law are known as Samaritans, for they accept only the law, that is, the five books of Moses. They are descended from the Persians and Assyrians, whom the king of Assyria placed in the regions of Samaria after he had taken the children of Israel into captivity. For this reason they also worship fire in the Persian manner.

To these people the Apostle became as one under the law, since he did not deny that the law was from God. In gentle language he drew from it the understanding of Christ. So too that Samaritan woman who said to the Lord, “I know that the Messiah is coming” (John 4), was taught through the law.

“To those who are without the law, as though I were without the law”—although I am not without the law of God, but am under the law of Christ. He says this because, since he is under the law of Christ, he is [Col. 0082C] under the law of God; for what belongs to Christ belongs to God, and what belongs to God belongs to Christ, as he says: “All mine are yours, and yours are mine” (John 17).

“In order to win those who are without the law.” For when he agrees with them—that is, with the Gentiles—that the world and the things in it were made by God, that the soul is immortal, and that we derive our origin from him—for in the Acts of the Apostles he says: “As some of your own poets have said: For we are indeed his offspring” (Acts 17)—he became as one without the law. Through this he introduced to them the claim that Christ himself was the one whom God had chosen to judge the world, and that he was the one through whom God had made all things.

(Augustine.) To both groups he owed charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (1 Timothy 1). Thus he became [Col. 0082D] all things to all people in order to win them all, not by the craft of a liar but by the affection of one who sympathizes. That is, he did not deceptively perform all the evils of human beings, but, as a merciful physician, carefully attended to all their evils as though they were his own.

Therefore, when he did not refuse to observe even the sacraments of the Old Testament himself, he was not deceiving them mercifully, but was not deceiving them at all. Rather, he commended that these rites had been commanded by the Lord God for a certain period of stewardship, and distinguished them from the sacrilegious rites of the Gentiles.

He became as a Jew to the Jews, not through the craft of a liar but through the affection of one who sympathized, when he wished to free them from the error by which they refused to believe in Christ and thought that they could be cleansed from sins and saved through their ancient sacrifices and observance of [Col. 0083A] ceremonies. He wished to free them from that error as though he himself were held by it, loving his neighbor as himself and doing for others what he would wish others to do for him if he needed it. When the Lord had given this instruction, he added: “For this is the law and the prophets” (Matthew 7).

In the same epistle to the Galatians he commanded this compassionate affection, saying: “If someone is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, keeping watch on yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Galatians 6). See whether he did not say that one should become as that person in order to win him—not by deceptively committing the same transgression or pretending to possess it, but by considering what could also happen to oneself through another’s transgression.

[Col. 0083B] In this way one would wish mercifully to help another as oneself had been helped by another. This is not the craft of a liar but the affection of one who sympathizes. Thus Paul became as a Jew to the Jew, as a Gentile to the Gentile, and as any other person established in error or sin—not by pretending to be what he was not, but by sympathy, because such a condition could have been his own. As one who remembered that he was human, he became all things to all people in order to win them all.

For the distinguished preacher did not fall into unbelief in order to become as a Jew, nor did he return to carnal sacrifice in order to become as one under the law. Nor, in order to become all things to all people, did he adapt the simplicity of his mind to the variety of error. Rather, by condescending he approached unbelievers without falling, so that, receiving each person into himself and transforming himself into each person through sympathy, he might gather them together.

[Col. 0083C] If he became as they were, he did so in order to consider what he would rightly wish others to do for him; and the more truly he would meet each person in error, the more he would learn from his own reflection the way of that person’s salvation.

“I became weak to the weak, in order to win the weak.” He became weak when, for the sake of weak brothers, he abstained from permitted things so as not to generate offense among them.

“I have become all things to all people, in order to save all.” This was the conduct of a prudent and spiritual man: he became all things to all people without exceeding the purpose of religion. For whenever he yielded, he yielded in order to make progress, and he did nothing other than what the law commanded.

(Cass.) What else does he show than that he always condescended according to the weakness and measure of those being instructed, relaxing something from the rigor of perfection [Col. 0083D] when destruction seemed to demand it, but preferring what the benefit of the weak required?

If, investigating these matters more attentively and reviewing one by one the distinctive marks of apostolic virtue, someone asks how the blessed Apostle is proved to have adapted his conduct to all people in every respect, where did he become as a Jew to the Jews? Surely, there, while preserving that saying in the depths of his heart which he had proclaimed to the Galatians: “Look, I, Paul, say to you that if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Galatians 5).

Yet in the circumcision of Timothy he assumed, in a certain manner, the appearance of Jewish superstition. Again, where did he become as one under the law to those who were under the law? Surely there, when James and all the [Col. 0084A] elders of the Church feared that the multitude of believing Jews—or rather, of Christians who were Judaizing—would descend upon him. They had accepted the faith of Christ in such a way that they still remained within Judaism. They came to his aid in his danger through this plan and persuasion, saying:

“You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law. They have heard about you that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to abandon Moses, saying that they should not circumcise their children.” And below: “Therefore do what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow. Take them and purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads. Then everyone will know that the things they have heard about you are false, but that you yourself walk orderly and keep the law” (Acts 21).

Thus, for the salvation [Col. 0084B] of those who were under the law, he temporarily trampled upon the strictness of the position he had declared when he said: “Through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God” (Galatians 2). He was compelled to shave his head, to be purified according to the law, and to offer Mosaic vows in the temple.

The same matter also occurred for the salvation of those who were entirely ignorant of the law of God, when he became as one without the law and used, in Athens, where the impiety of the Gentiles flourished, the following beginning for his preaching:

“As I passed by,” he said, “I saw your images and an altar on which was written: IGNOTO DEO—‘TO AN UNKNOWN GOD’” (Acts 17).

Having begun to speak about their superstition as though he too were without the law, he introduced the faith of Christ under the pretext of that profane inscription, saying: “What therefore you worship without knowing it, this I proclaim [Col. 0084C] to you.” And shortly afterward, as though he were entirely ignorant of the divine law, he preferred to cite a verse of a Gentile poet rather than a saying of Moses or the prophets.

“And as some of your poets have said: For we are indeed his offspring.” After attacking them with testimonies of their own that they could not reject, and thus confirming true things from false ones, he added: “Therefore, since we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that divinity is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and thought of human beings” (Acts 17).

He became weak to the weak when, according to indulgence and not command, he permitted those who could not contain themselves to return to one another; and when, feeding the Corinthians with milk rather than food, he says that he was among them in weakness, fear, and much trembling.

He became all things [Col. 0084D] to all people in order to save all when he says: “The one who eats must not despise the one who does not eat, and the one who does not eat must not judge the one who eats”; and: “The one who joins his virgin in marriage does well, and the one who does not join her in marriage does better” (Romans 14).

And elsewhere: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not inflamed?” In this way he fulfilled what he had commanded the Corinthians: “Be without offense to Jews and Greeks and the Church of God, just as I also please everyone in everything, not seeking my own benefit but that of many, so that they may be saved” (1 Corinthians 10).

[Col. 0085A] It would undoubtedly have been useful to him not to circumcise Timothy, not to shave his head, not to undertake Jewish purification, not to practice the barefoot rite, and not to offer legal vows. Yet he does all these things because he does not seek what is useful for himself but what is useful for many. Although this was done with regard to God, it nevertheless was not free from pretense.

For he who had died to the law through the law in order to live to God, and who had counted as loss the righteousness of the law in which he had lived blamelessly, regarding it as refuse in order to gain Christ (Philippians 3), could not offer what belonged to the law with a sincere affection of heart.

Nor is it right to believe that he who had said, “If I rebuild the things that I destroyed, I prove myself a transgressor” (Galatians 2), fell into the very thing he had condemned. In such matters, not the deed itself but the disposition of the one performing it is weighed.

(Augustine.) Let us therefore offer to the person whose weakness [Col. 0085B] we wish to bear what we would wish him to offer to us if we happened to be in that weakness and he were not. This is what the Apostle himself means when he says: “I have become all things to all people, in order to win all.” He considered that he too might have been in the fault from which he desired to free another. He did this by sympathizing, not by lying, as some suppose—especially those who, in defending their own lies, which they cannot deny, seek the protection of some great example.

“But I do everything for the sake of the Gospel, so that I may become a participant in it.” (Ambrose.) That is, I do all the things mentioned above so that I may become a participant in the will of the Gospel, which is directed toward human salvation.

“Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but only one receives the prize?” He now begins to explain something else. By this example [Col. 0085C] he shows how great is the benefit of our law, in which the prize is promised not to one person but to all.

“Run in such a way that you may obtain it.” (Theologus.) He wishes us to run attentively toward the promise, because it is great. We ought not, because of the delays of the slow and sluggish, to halt when we are prepared and eager. It is more fitting for the sluggish to be urged on by those running ahead than for those hurrying forward to be held back by those who remain behind.

“Everyone who competes in the contest exercises self-control in all things.” By “all things,” he means those matters that the same discipline teaches must be avoided. Since they know that only one will be crowned, how much more must we be attentive, since salvation has been promised to all?

Let us inquire what he means by “all things,” so that by comparison with the bodily contest we may acquire instruction for the spiritual contest.

(Cass.) Those who in this visible contest [Col. 0085D] strive to compete lawfully do not have the freedom to use every food suggested by the appetite of desire, but only those foods established by the discipline of the contests themselves. They must abstain not only from forbidden foods, drunkenness, and every form of gluttony, but also from all laziness, idleness, and sloth, so that their strength may increase through daily exercises and continual practice.

They therefore become strangers to every worldly care, grief, and business, and even to marital affection and activity, so that they know nothing besides the practice of their discipline and are not entangled in any worldly concern. From the one presiding over the contest they hope to receive only the sustenance of daily life, the glory of the crown, and worthy rewards [Col. 0086A] for victory.

Therefore, if we understand the discipline of the worldly contest, by whose example the blessed Apostle wished to instruct us, teaching with what vigilance we ought to conduct ourselves, with what purity must we guard the chastity of our body and soul, since we must daily feed upon the sacred flesh of the Lamb—flesh which the precepts of the old law do not even permit an unclean person to touch?

For in Leviticus it is prescribed: “Every clean person shall eat the flesh, but the person who eats flesh from the sacrifice of well-being, which belongs to the Lord, while uncleanness is upon him, shall be cut off from the presence of the Lord” (Leviticus 7).

How great, then, is the gift of integrity, without which even those who lived under the Old Testament could not participate in the symbolic sacrifices, and those who desire to obtain the corruptible crown of this world cannot be crowned!

Therefore, with every possible vigilance, [Col. 0086B] the hiding places of our heart must first be rooted out. What they seek to attain in bodily purity, we must possess also in the conscience of our heart. In that conscience the Lord, seated as judge and presider over the contest, continually awaits the struggle, the race, and the contest.

We must not allow, through careless thought, the things we dread admitting openly even to take root within us; nor may we be polluted by hidden desire in matters over which we are confounded in human judgment. Although such things may escape human notice, they cannot be hidden from the knowledge of the holy angels or of almighty God, from whom no secrets can be concealed.

“And they do this to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one.”

[Col. 0086C] (Ambrose.) In this too the gift is very different, and therefore we ought to be more diligent, since a spiritual crown is reserved for us—not woven from earthly and fading flowers, but set with eternal gems in the form of a royal diadem.

I therefore run in this way, not as though toward uncertainty. He professes to run with great hope, being certain of what has been promised. Thus I fight, not as one striking the air. That is, I contend not so much with words as with deeds. But I discipline my body and bring it into subjection. To discipline the body means to treat it with fasts and to give it what contributes to life, not to luxury; it is brought into subjection when it does not carry out its own will but the will of the spirit. Lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected. He therefore shows that he restrains his body, so that he too may be considered worthy of the reward that he preaches to others, lest, while caring for others, he himself should remain wounded. He thus affirms the reliability of his hope in preaching when he shows by his deeds that he pursues what he teaches: for one who acts otherwise than he preaches makes his hearers suspicious, so that they doubt the promises. By his own example, therefore, he exhorts them to practice not merely in words but in deeds.

**(Cass.)** You see what sum of struggles he has established in himself—that is, in his flesh—as though on a most secure base, placing the outcome of the contest solely in the discipline of the flesh and the subjection of his body. “I therefore run,” he says, “not as though toward uncertainty.” He does not run toward uncertainty because, contemplating the heavenly Jerusalem, he has fixed before him the destination toward which the unwavering insight of his heart must be directed. He does not run toward uncertainty because, forgetting what lies behind, he stretches himself toward the goal, pursuing the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus. Directing the gaze of his mind continually toward him, and hastening toward him with all the eagerness of his heart, he proclaimed with confidence: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith.” And because he knew that, after the fragrance of Christ’s ointments, he had run unweariedly through devotion of conscience and had conquered the contest of the spiritual struggle by disciplining his flesh, he confidently adds: “From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award me on that day.” Thus he also opened for us a similar hope of recompense, if we wish to imitate him in the contest of this course. And he added: “Not only to me, but also to all who love his coming,” declaring that we shall be sharers in his crown on the day of judgment, if, loving Christ’s coming, we acquire victory in the struggle through discipline of the body—not merely that coming which will appear even to those unwilling to see it, but also this coming, by which he daily brings victory into holy souls.

Concerning this coming the Lord says in the Gospel: “I and my Father will come and make our dwelling with him” (John 14); and again: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3).

Yet he does not describe himself as having completed only the contest of the course when he says, “If I run, not as though toward uncertainty.” This refers specifically to the intention of his mind and the fervor of his spirit, with which he followed Christ with all his ardor, singing together with the bride: “We run after you in the fragrance of your ointments”; and again: “My soul has clung to you.” But he also testifies that he conquered another kind of struggle when he says: “Thus I fight, not as one striking the air, but I discipline my body and bring it into subjection.” This properly concerns the pains of continence, bodily fasting, and the affliction of the flesh. Through these he presents himself as a vigorous fighter against his own flesh and indicates that he did not exercise the blows of continence in vain against it, but gained the triumph of the struggle through the mortification of his body. By blows, by the discipline of continence, and by the steps of fasting, he crushed it and gave the victorious spirit the crown of immortality and the palm of incorruption.

You see the proper order of the struggle and contemplate the outcome of spiritual contests: how, having gained victory over vices through the rebellious flesh, the athlete of Christ proceeds as a sublime victor, with that flesh subjected, as it were, beneath his feet. For this reason he does not run toward uncertainty, because he trusted that he would immediately enter the holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem. Thus he fights through fasts and bodily affliction, not as one striking the air—that is, not extending the blows of continence in vain. Through them he struck not empty air but the spirits that move within it, by disciplining his body. For one who says, “not as one striking the air,” shows that although he was not striking empty and insubstantial air, he was nevertheless striking certain beings in the air. And because he had overcome these kinds of contests and proceeded enriched by the rewards of many crowns, he not undeservedly began to undertake struggles against stronger enemies. Having triumphed over his earlier rivals, he confidently proclaims and says: “Now there is no struggle for us against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6).

## CHAPTER X

**The Apostle rejects participation in sacrifices offered to idols and teaches how things sacrificed to idols are to be used.**

For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.

By the example of the Jews, who offended through their negligence, he wants us to be watchful. Therefore he says that they were under the cloud, because everything that happened was done as a figure of us, so that they might possess an image of our reality. Covered by the cloud and protected from their enemies while they were delivered from death, they are said to have been baptized. For when the Egyptians—that is, their enemies—were drowned in the sea, these people, led by Moses, passed safely across and were rescued from death, which baptism accomplishes. Their former evils were not counted against them; rather, purified through the sea and the cloud, they were prepared to receive the Law and the form of our future sacrament.

And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ.

**(Amb.)** He calls the manna and the water that flowed from the rock spiritual because they were not prepared according to the law of the world, but were created for a time by God’s power, without any mixture of the elements, possessing within themselves the figure of the future mystery that we now receive in remembrance of Christ the Lord. For this reason it was also called the bread of angels, because it was created by the power by which the angels exist, signifying that he was to come from heaven who would nourish us spiritually.

Thus the manna first came from heaven on the Lord’s Day, to satisfy the people. Yet the rock that followed is mentioned, and this is understood to be Christ. For wherever human assistance failed them, Christ was present. Therefore he followed them, so that wherever that assistance failed, he might come to their aid. The rock itself did not give the water; Christ did.

The Red Sea signifies baptism; Moses, the leader through the Red Sea, signifies Christ; the people who crossed signify the faithful; the death of the Egyptians signifies the abolition of sins. Did they not believe the same things through which these signs were displayed, through which the things we believe were prophetically foretold? Certainly they believed—but they believed in things that were to come, whereas we believe that they have come.

Therefore he says that they drank the same spiritual drink—but the same spiritual drink, not the same bodily drink. What, then, did they drink? “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ.” See, therefore: while the faith remains, the signs have changed. There the rock was Christ; for us Christ is what is placed upon God’s altar. They drank water flowing from the rock as a great sacrament of that same Christ; the faithful know what we drink. If you consider the visible form, it is something else; if you consider the intelligible significance, they drank the same spiritual drink. “The rock was Christ.”

Concerning this rock it is written in the Book of Job: “The rock poured out streams of oil for me.” This rock now pours out streams of oil for the use of the holy Church, because the Lord, speaking in it, causes the teachings of inner anointing to flow forth. From this rock the stream of oil came forth: the book of Matthew, the book of Mark, the book of Luke, and the book of John. In the various regions of this world, however many teachings he gave, so many streams this rock poured forth through the mouths of all the Apostles. And even now the stream of oil flows from this rock as often as the things spoken about Christ in the ancient books are explained to the minds of hearers to be anointed by the Holy Spirit. They are called streams of oil because they flow down and anoint; whoever is immersed in them is anointed, and whoever is inwardly immersed is enriched.

But God was not well pleased with most of them.

**(Amb.)** He said this because they did not understand the benefit they had received. For they were struck down in the wilderness. It is right that one who has obtained great things but distrusts in small matters should not only fail to attain these things but also lose those he had already received.

How, then, did he previously exhort them to better things? He also says that he labors so that he may be found worthy to reach the promise. Now, in order to restrain them through the terror of this example and persuade them, he says that the Jews then received God’s gift and grace in the same way as we do, but because they were negligent and doubted God’s providence, they were struck down in the wilderness. He shows that he afflicts himself for this reason, lest he be found among their number; therefore we must labor so that we may become imitators of him.

Now these things happened to them as a figure of us, so that we might not be desirous of evil things, as they desired them.

This is the meaning and explanation I mentioned above.

Nor should we become idolaters, as some of them did. Here he touches those who reclined in an idol’s shrine and thought that there was no sin in doing so. As it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exodus 32). They were certainly before the idol, so that those who feasted in the idol’s shrine would not think themselves free from guilt. For while Moses was on the mountain with God, after the image of the calf had been made and the offering had been presented for its dedication, the people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.

This is luxury, by which they were always delighted and were found faithless in the things of God.

**(Greg.)** Therefore he instructs us lest, through assent to the luxury of the idol, we fall into this distrust. We are led from vanity to iniquity when we first slide through light offenses and, since habit smooths everything, cease to fear committing even more serious offenses. For when the tongue neglects to restrain idle words, seized by the customary laxity, it bursts forth boldly into harmful speech. When one gives himself over to gluttony, he immediately proceeds to madness through softness; and when the mind refuses to subdue the pleasure of the flesh, it often rushes toward the beginning of apostasy.

Accordingly, Paul, seeing the losses of the Israelite people and wishing to restrain the evils threatening his hearers, took care to recount past events in order, saying: “Nor should we become idolaters, as some of them did, as it is written: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.”

Eating and drinking drove them to play; playing drew them into idolatry. For if the fault of vanity is not carefully restrained, the unwary mind is immediately devoured by iniquity, as Solomon testifies when he says: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclesiasticus 19). If we neglect to care for small matters, being imperceptibly led astray, we also commit greater ones boldly.

Nor should we commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and twenty-three thousand men fell in one day.

This was repaid to them when they defiled themselves with the women of Midian. For the anger of God arose against them, and it was quieted by the zeal of Phinehas the priest, who possessed zeal for God, so that more would not die.

Nor should we tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him and perished by serpents.

They are said to have tempted Christ by speaking against God, because it was Christ who spoke to Moses. Finally, lest we be found in the same situation, he warns us not to be handed over to the devil, whose figure the serpents bear; Christ commanded us spiritually to tread upon every kind of serpent.

**(Aug.)** For he himself is also the God of the prophets. To signify the sins of the faithless people, sins by whose poison they were dying invisibly, he sent visible serpents among them to attack them; and through the deaths of their bodies he represented, as a corrective punishment, the deaths of their souls.

Nor should we murmur, as some of them murmured.

**(Ambr.)** To murmur means falsely to complain to one another about those set over us and our rulers, insofar as this concerns the meaning of the passage, because murmuring can also arise from a just cause.

And they perished by the destroyer.

That is, they yielded their place to Judas by anticipating him; for Judas, after betraying Christ, was destroyed from the number of the Apostles by God the Judge.

Through these examples he calls us to a more corrected life, so that by obeying his admonitions we may deserve a reward, but by disobeying them a more severe punishment. For there is no doubt that those who sin are subjected to greater torments when the punishments of sinners have been related for the very purpose of preventing us from sinning.

Now all these things happened to them as a figure; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

We are the ends of the ages, because it is known that these things happened to them concerning their recompense so that they might be an example to us, who were destined to exist in faith in Christ at the end of the age. They were done for our benefit, so that if, terrified by these examples, we remain in fear of God, we may receive the glory promised to them. If not, their punishment will be doubled for us, because greater knowledge of the Law makes one more guilty.

**(Aug.)** He says: “All these things happened to them as a figure, but they were written for us.” Here he himself has disclosed why those writings are received by us and why it is no longer necessary for us to observe those signs of events. When he says, “They were written for us,” he clearly demonstrates with what care we must read and understand them and with what authority we must hold them, since they were certainly written for us. But when he says that they were figures of us and that these things happened to them as a figure, he shows that it is no longer necessary, when we enact the realities themselves openly, for us to adhere to the observance of the celebration of the prophetic figures.

Therefore, let the one who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall.

**(Ambr.)** He says this to those who, presuming on their knowledge that everything is lawful to eat, were a stumbling block to their weaker brothers. Thinking that they were advancing through the teaching of the pseudo-apostles, they had become worse and judged the Apostle, although they themselves were guilty. He therefore cuts off pride, lest they be tempted by it, just as the Jews were tempted and perished.

**(Greg.)** Through this sentence, therefore, the hope of the humble is nourished and the arrogance of the proud is crushed: the former may lose the good things of which they are proud, while the latter may attain those things that are despised because they do not possess them. Let us therefore fear in the midst of the things we receive, lest we drive into despair those who have not yet attained them. We know what we are today, but we do not know what we may become shortly afterward. Those whom we perhaps despise may begin late and nevertheless surpass our life through more fervent efforts.

It must therefore be feared that, when we fall, one may rise whom we ridicule while we stand—although one who knows how to ridicule someone who is not standing no longer knows how to stand.

Let no temptation seize you except what is human.

**(Ambr.)** Accordingly, those who speak against the Apostle seem to tempt the Lord, because when they once spoke against Moses and doubted him, they are said to have tempted God. For everything that has not been proved is tested. Therefore, to tear away this temptation, he warns them with terror; but he exhorts them to let a human temptation seize them. A human temptation is to distrust a human being because of hope in God, since hope in a human being is vain, so that in need or distress one does not despair of God by seeking human help.

Thus the Jews, doubting God, sought the aid of idols—that is, human assistance—because the gods of the pagans are earthly, and human error invented the worship of idols. To suffer for Christ, therefore, is a human temptation, through which one advances before God.

**(Aug.)** There are also, I believe, human temptations when someone, with good intention but nevertheless according to human weakness, slips in some counsel, or becomes irritated with a brother out of a desire to correct him, yet somewhat more than Christian tranquility permits. Concerning such things the Apostle says: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human.”

This sentence can also be understood in another way.

**(Cass.)** “Let no temptation seize you except what is human.” We do not deserve, through strength of mind acquired by effort, to experience the heavier struggles of the heavenly powers of wickedness, since we have not been able to subject the fragile flesh, which resists our spirit. Some people, not understanding the Apostle’s testimony, have put the optative mood in place of the indicative: “May temptation not seize you except what is human.” But it is clear that he speaks not with the feeling of one wishing for something, but with the feeling of one declaring or reproving.

**(Greg.)** A human temptation is one by which we are often touched in thought even against our will, so that unlawful things sometimes come into the mind. This, then, we possess within ourselves because of the burden of corruptible humanity. But a temptation is demonic, and not human, when the mind binds itself by consent to what the corruptibility of the flesh suggests.

But God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear; rather, with the temptation he will also provide a way through, so that you may be able to endure it.

**(Ambr.)** He calls God faithful because he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, since God promised to give the heavenly kingdoms to those who love him, and he must give them because he is faithful. Therefore he will be present with those who suffer for him, and he will not permit so much to be inflicted that it cannot be endured. Rather, he will cause the temptation either to cease quickly or, if it is prolonged, will give the strength to endure it.

Otherwise he would not give what he promised, because the one who suffers is overcome, being subject to human weakness, and there would be no one to receive it. But because God is faithful, he helps in order to fulfill what he promised.

Finally, the Lord says that the days will be shortened so that the elect may be saved and may attain the kingdom of God.

Yet how is someone helped by God if he is permitted to be tempted only as much as he can bear? He is clearly helped when he is not permitted to be burdened beyond what he is known to be able to endure—for example, when someone known to be unable to endure more than three days is not permitted to suffer on the fourth day.

**(Greg.)** Against this statement, which says, “God is faithful and will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way through, so that you may be able to endure,” Paul elsewhere seems to think differently. He says to the Corinthians: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning our affliction that came upon us in Asia, for we were burdened beyond measure and beyond our strength” (2 Corinthians 10).

If we are burdened beyond our strength, since God allows us to be burdened, and if we are not burdened beyond our strength, since we are said to be burdened beyond our strength, let us resolve this apparent discrepancy quickly by returning to the prophetic testimony where it says: “Since human salvation is vain, through God we shall act with strength” (Psalm 59).

We are therefore often said to be burdened beyond human weakness because human salvation is vain; yet we are never burdened beyond strength, because he is the physician. A sick person under the hands of a physician sometimes cries because he does not know how he will reach health. But the wise physician often cuts in order to bring the sick person to health.

Paul, therefore, considering human weakness, said that he was burdened beyond his strength; nevertheless he also says: “I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4).

Thus it is written in Job: “His fury is angry against me, and he has treated me as his enemy” (Job 19). For we have learned through the testimony of the outstanding preacher that God is faithful and does not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear, but with the temptation provides a way through, so that we can endure.

The Lord also says through the prophet: “I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel chastisement” (Jeremiah 13). Therefore, when someone is struck so that his strength is overcome by the blow, the Lord no longer strikes him as a son through discipline but as an enemy through anger.

When the scourges exceed the strength of our endurance, we must greatly fear that, because our sins demand it, we are being struck by the Lord not as sons by a Father but as enemies.

And because it often happens that evil spirits suggest many things to the hearts of the afflicted and, amid the outward blows, pour harmful thoughts into their minds, the following is rightly added after the Lord’s fury: “At once his robbers came and made a way for themselves through me.”

His robbers are evil spirits, who occupy themselves with investigating human movements. They make a way for themselves in the hearts of the afflicted when, amid the adversities endured outwardly, they do not cease to introduce perverse thoughts as well.

Of them it is further said: “And they surrounded my tent on every side.” They surround the tent on every side when they encircle the mind with their temptations, persuading it now to mourn temporal things, now to despair of eternal things, now to rush into impatience, and to hurl blasphemous words against God through their most evil suggestions.

Yet, as we have already said, these words also fit blessed Job according to the historical sense. When he gathered before his eyes the evils he had suffered, he judged that he had been struck not as a son being corrected but as an enemy. Through him his robbers also made a way for themselves, because the evil spirits received permission to strike him. They surrounded his tent on every side because, after his possessions and children had been taken away, they also afflicted his entire body with wounds.

But it is very surprising: when he called them “robbers,” why did he add “his,” clearly showing that he wished to indicate that these same robbers belonged to God? If the will and power of evil spirits are distinguished in this matter, it becomes clear why they are called God’s robbers.

Evil spirits constantly long to harm us. But although they possess an evil will from themselves, they do not possess the power to harm unless the supreme will permits them. And although they themselves desire to harm us unjustly, they are not permitted by the Lord to harm anyone except justly.

Because in them there is both an unjust will and a just power, they are called both robbers and God’s: what they unjustly desire to inflict comes from themselves, while what they justly complete of what they desire comes from God.

Therefore, my beloved, flee from the worship of idols.

**(Ambr.)** He now again exhorts them to abstain from every association with idolatry, so that not only their hope but also their mind may be raised toward God, lest through this a temptation against God arise. For no one who is constantly in an idol’s shrine hopes for nothing from God; rather, to hope there is to doubt God, as Saul, after abandoning God, who had become angry with him because of his sin, turned to idolatry, hoping for something from it. This harmed him in the present and prepared for him in the future the avenging punishment of Gehenna.

I speak to prudent people; judge for yourselves what I say.

He adds examples so that he may persuade more easily, because examples commonly persuade those whom words do not sufficiently convince.

The cup of blessing that we bless—is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? And the bread that we break—is it not a participation in the body of the Lord? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.

Because we are one, members of one another, he says that we ought to have one mind, so that one faith may possess one understanding and one work.

Consider Israel according to the flesh. That is, learn, you who see God, how those who are carnal conduct themselves—that is, in idolatry. Are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar?

For just as we, receiving from one bread and one cup, are participants and companions of the Lord’s body, so those who eat sacrifices are participants in the altar of error.

What am I saying, then? That something sacrificed to idols is anything? Or that an idol is anything? But what the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God.

An idol truly is nothing, because an image is seen of a dead thing; but beneath the covering of idols the devil is worshiped.

I do not want you to become companions of demons.

He shows them that what appears in an idol’s shrine is not all there is, but that an occult mystery of iniquity is present, which Satan devised in order to corrupt faith in the one God. Therefore the Apostle John also says in his Epistle: “For this the Son of God appeared, to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3).

He was forbidding them idolatry, and for this reason he wished to show them that they became companions of demons if they ate the sacrifices of idol offerings.

Just as carnal Israel was a companion of the altar in the temple because it ate from the sacrifices, so it was carnal and according to the flesh. There is also Israel spiritually, or according to the spirit, which no longer follows the ancient shadows but the reality that was signified by those preceding shadows.

Here he began, in order to say this: “Therefore, beloved, flee from the worship of idols.” Then he continued by showing to which sacrifice they ought now to belong, saying: “As to prudent people I speak; judge for yourselves what I say. The cup of blessing that we bless—is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break—is it not a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body. For we all partake of the one.”

For this reason he added: “Consider Israel according to the flesh. Are not those who eat from the sacrifices companions of the altar?” Thus they might understand that they were now companions of Christ’s body in the same way as those people were companions of the altar. And because he said this in order to forbid idolatry, this passage of his speech, as I have mentioned, took its beginning from the following words: “Therefore, beloved, flee from the worship of idols.”

They were not to think that it was unnecessary to take care if they ate from the sacrifices of idols merely because an idol is nothing, imagining that these things, as though superfluous, could not harm them. He himself confirmed that an idol is nothing, and that he did not prohibit these things because they had been sacrificed to idols, which possess no understanding. Rather, he says that those who sacrifice them—that is, the worshipers of idols—sacrifice to demons and not to God. “I do not want you to become companions of demons,” he says, because “we who are many are one bread, one body, and all partake of one bread and one cup.”

The one who suffered for us commended his body and blood to us in this sacrament; he also made us to be this. For we have become his body, and through his mercy we are what we have received.

Recall also that you did not exist, but were created. You were brought to the Lord’s threshing floor through the labors of oxen—that is, through those who announce the Gospel. You were threshed, because you were delayed as catechumens. You were stored in the granary; you gave your names; you began to be ground through fasts and exorcisms. Afterwards you came to the water and were sprinkled, and you became one. With the fervor of the Holy Spirit added, you were baked and became the Lord’s bread.

Behold what you have received. Just as you see that what has been made is one, so you must be one by loving one another, holding one faith, one hope, and undivided charity.

When heretics are confronted with this testimony against themselves, they seek division, whereas this bread indicates unity. So too the wine was once in many grapes, but now it is one. After the pressure of the winepress, it is one in the sweetness of the cup. And you, after those fasts, labors, humility, and contrition, have now come in Christ’s name to the Lord’s cup. There you are at the table; there you are in the cup; you are there with us. For together we are this; together we drink, because together we live.

You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons.

As the Lord says: “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matthew 6). For whoever drinks the cup of demons insults the Lord’s cup, and whoever shares in the table of demons speaks against the Lord’s table—that is, against the altar—and crucifies the Lord’s body. Christ was crucified because he destroyed the works of the devil; therefore whoever does the works of the devil opposes Christ.

Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?

It rarely happens that a humble person is jealous of someone powerful, for he knows that he cannot rival him in the matter in which he might envy him. One is either jealous of an unequal person or of one who is nearly equal. Therefore the Apostle said that human beings cannot be jealous of the Lord Jesus. Moreover, those who know him would not consider him worthy to be called Lord if they were jealous of him, as though to prevent him from being Lord.

Through jealousy Satan devised idolatry, so that by denying God as Lord, human beings might serve idols as though they were gods and lords.

Everything is lawful for me, but not everything is beneficial.

He says that everything is lawful according to the law of nature, for everything is clean. The discussion concerned foods and meat sacrificed to idols. For how could things that are prohibited and forbidden be said to be lawful? Even here he indicates that what is permitted is sometimes not beneficial, as the Apostle Peter says: “If this is the reason for a man’s situation with his wife, it is not beneficial to marry” (Matthew 19).

Everything is lawful, but not everything builds up.

The meaning is the same: it is lawful to eat everything, but what is sacrificed to idols does not build up, because it causes a stumbling block for a brother, as was said above. Therefore one must sometimes abstain even from lawful things, so that they may be beneficial.

This is why, although it was lawful for him, he refused to accept payment from them, knowing that it was not beneficial.

Let no one seek his own advantage, but that of the other.

**(Cass.)** Charity does not seek what is its own but what belongs to others. Concerning himself he says: “I do not seek what is beneficial to me, but what is beneficial to many, so that they may be saved.”

If we seek what is ours and stubbornly insist on retaining what is beneficial to us, then, even in such necessities, we must speak the truth and become guilty of another’s death. But if, placing what is salutary for others before our own advantages, we fulfill the Apostle’s command, we will unquestionably have to undertake the necessity of lying. For this reason we will be unable to possess the undivided entrails of charity or to seek what belongs to others according to the Apostle’s discipline unless, relaxing somewhat those things that suit our strictness and perfection, we prefer with willing affection to accommodate ourselves to the interests of others. Thus, with the Apostle, we become weak to the weak, so that we may win the weak.

Whatever is sold in the market, eat, asking no questions for the sake of conscience; for “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness.”

**(Ambr.)** To show that everything is clean, he strengthened this with the example of the twenty-third Psalm, because what belongs to the Lord cannot be unclean. And just as above he says concerning foods, “Everything is lawful,” he immediately adds: “Whatever is sold in the market, eat, asking no questions for the sake of conscience.”

He added this so that the conscience might be free. Although something may be polluted incidentally—that is, by an idol’s offering—the buyer, who does not know this, suffers no scruple and is innocent before God.

If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner, go. Eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions.

That is, eat simply what is placed before you, without asking where it came from.

“Ask no questions for the sake of conscience.” But if someone says, “This was sacrificed to idols,” do not eat it, for the sake of conscience. I say “conscience,” not your own, but the other person’s.

He speaks to the perfect, who are able to disregard idolatry because eating from a sacrifice is nothing, being certain that what is eaten in the name of God the Creator cannot defile. But because the other person, who serves idols, might boast when he sees you eating from the sacrifices, as though you were venerating idols, it should not be eaten.

For in his own conscience he will rejoice, because he has seen you eagerly desire what was sacrificed to idols.

Why should my freedom be judged by another conscience?

He says this because, since his conscience is free from devotion to the idol, why should it be necessary for him to be thought to eat what was sacrificed to idols as an act of veneration? He is judged not to differ from the idolater when he does not recoil from what was offered to the image.

For if I partake with thanksgiving, why am I blasphemed for that for which I give thanks?

That is, if I partake by God’s grace because I eat in his name, why should anyone think that I am devoted to an idol merely because I do not recoil from what was offered to the idol? Why am I “blasphemed”?

He blasphemes me, while the other rejoices in his idol’s shrine. When he thinks that I am a participant, he has an opportunity to remain in error, and a harmful example is given to the brothers.

For if the Law commands that groves, altars, inscriptions, and the idols themselves be destroyed, see whether it is not a sin not only to fail to do these things but also to attend banquets of this kind. Therefore it is not beneficial to eat what has been sacrificed.

Therefore, whether you eat or drink or do anything else, do everything for the glory of God.

Through what follows he made clear that eating in an idol’s shrine, whatever one’s conscience may be, is hostile to God. These things are dedicated to the devil as an insult to the one God. To eat, drink, or do anything for the glory of God means that a meal is held with moderation under invocation of the Creator. Something is done for the glory of God when God is praised in the actions and conduct of a Christian.

Be without offense to Jews, Greeks, and the Church of God. He teaches that one must regulate one’s conduct so that no one is scandalized by it. Offense is given to the Jews when they see a Christian—who says that he accepts the Law and the Prophets—not recoiling from the idols they abominate. To the Greeks, that is, to the Gentiles, offense is given if, instead of being reproved for what they are, they are even encouraged by the failure to avoid their idolatrous rites. An impediment is given to the Church of God when it sees some of its own number cleaving to things hostile to God.

Just as I also please everyone in every way, seeking not what is advantageous to myself but what is advantageous to many, so that they may be saved.

**(Cass.)** To please everyone in every way means to act without giving anyone cause for scandal, for the sake of their benefit, so that what is done may be useful both to them and to this person. It would certainly have been useful to him—as was said above—not to circumcise Timothy, not to shave his head, not to undertake Jewish purification, not to practice barefoot walking, and not to offer legal vows. Yet he does all these things because he does not seek what is useful to himself but what is useful to many. Although this was done in contemplation of God, it was nevertheless not free from pretense. For he who had died to the Law through the law of Christ, so that he might live for God, and who had suffered the loss of the righteousness of the Law in which he had lived blamelessly, counting it as refuse in order to gain Christ, could not offer what belonged to the Law with a genuine affection of heart. Nor is it right to believe that the man who had said, “For if I rebuild the things that I destroyed, I show myself to be a transgressor” (Gal. II), had fallen into the very thing he himself condemned—since in such matters the action itself is considered less than the disposition of the one performing it. Thus, conversely, truth is sometimes found to have harmed certain people, and falsehood to have benefited them.

For Doeg the Idumean truthfully betrayed David to King Saul, when Saul was complaining of David’s flight in the presence of his servants. On account of that truth he deserved to be uprooted from the land of the living, and the Prophet says of him: “Therefore God will destroy you forever; he will tear you away and uproot you from your dwelling, and your root from the land of the living” (Ps. LI).
