**(Aug.)** The Apostle also says, “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. I), while elsewhere he says, “Just as I also please everyone in every way” (1 Cor. X). Those who do not understand this think the statements contradictory, although he said that he did not please human beings because he did not do what was right for the purpose of pleasing human beings, but for the purpose of pleasing God. He wished to turn human hearts toward God precisely through what pleased human beings. Thus he rightly said that he did not please human beings, because in that very matter he was intent on pleasing God; and he rightly commanded that one should please human beings—not so that this should be sought as the reward of right conduct, but because one could not please God if one did not offer oneself as an example to those whom one wished to be saved. No one can imitate the one who did not please himself.

Thus, just as someone could speak without absurdity by saying, “In this work, in which I seek a ship, I am not seeking a ship but my country,” so the Apostle could appropriately say, “In this work, by which I please human beings, I do not please human beings but God,” because I do not seek this for its own sake; rather, I direct it toward the end that those whom I wish to be saved may imitate me.

**(Ambr.)** It should also be understood that good leaders ought to desire to please human beings, but in such a way that, through the sweetness of their reputation, they draw their neighbors toward an affection for the truth—not because they desire to be loved, but because they make their love into a kind of road by which they may lead the hearts of their hearers into love of the Creator. It is difficult for even a preacher who proclaims what is entirely right to be heard willingly if he is not loved.

Therefore, the person in authority ought both to strive to be loved, so that he may be heard, and yet not seek love for his own sake, lest he be found, by a hidden tyranny of thought, to rebel against the person whom he is seen to serve through his office. Paul makes this clear when he reveals the hidden purpose of his devotion, saying, “Just as I also please everyone in every way,” while again saying, “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.” Paul therefore both pleases and does not please: in seeking to please, he seeks not that human beings should please him, but that through him they should please the truth.

“Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.”

**(Greg.)** It is a human matter when he says that we should be his imitators, since a teacher has been granted to us by God. If he is an imitator of God, why should we not be imitators of a human being? Because, just as God the Father sent Christ as teacher and author of life, so Christ sent the Apostles to us as teachers, so that we might be their imitators, since we cannot be imitators of him directly. Thus the Lord says to the Father: “Just as you sent me into this world, so I also sent them into this world” (John XVII). And because it was fitting that they should become his imitators, he adds: “And for their sake I sanctify myself.”

Whatever there is in them of inward compassion, whatever of gentleness of spirit, whatever of zeal for righteousness, whatever of vigilance in humility, whatever of the fervor of charity—they drew all this from the very fountain of mercy, from the very root of gentleness, from the very power of righteousness, that is, from the mediator between God and human beings, the Lord God. The outstanding preacher shows that he bears the likeness of this man when he says, “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.” He urges us to rise toward Christ’s likeness when he says: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly. Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of him who descended from heaven” (1 Cor. XV).

For every holy person is led toward the likeness of this man insofar as he imitates the life of his Redeemer. To disagree with his commandments and works—what else is this than to depart far from his likeness?

# BOOK ELEVEN

[Col. 0099]

## CHAPTER XI. The Apostle rejects errors concerning the celebration of the most holy Eucharist and the preeminence of the man; he sets forth the dignity of the Eucharist and the proper and fitting manner of receiving it.

I commend you, brothers, because you remember me in every respect and, just as I delivered them to you, hold fast to my instructions.

**(Ambr.)** After reproving their morals and conduct, he now wishes to correct their traditions. Therefore he does not confirm this but rebukes them, because, although he was their Apostle, they had forgotten his traditions; nor were they following what they had not yet learned from the tradition of the other Churches. Consequently, as though he were giving them the tradition anew, he says: “But I want you to know that the head of every man is Christ.”

He referred this to authority, because man is from God, but through Christ.

“The head of a woman is the man.” For although the woman also came through Christ, she was nevertheless made from the man, and therefore is subject to the man.

“The head of Christ is God.” It is fitting that the Father should be called the head of the Son, as his begetter. Yet Christ is the head of the man in one way, the man is the head of the woman in another, and God is the head of Christ in another. God is the head of Christ because Christ was begotten from him or by him. The man is the head of the woman because she was formed from his rib by the power of God. Christ is the head of the man because the man, who did not previously exist, was created through him.

Thus one expression has different meanings, because the persons and substances differ.

**(Aug.)** If God is not anything other than all three together, how is God the head of Christ—that is, how is the Trinity the head of Christ—when Christ is in the Trinity, so that the Trinity exists? Or is the Father together with the Son the head of that which is the Son alone? For together with the Son the Father is God, whereas the Son alone is Christ, especially since the Word, already made flesh, is speaking. According to the humility of his condition, the Father is also greater than he, as he says: “For the Father is greater than I.” Thus the very fact that he is God, which he shares with the Father as one, is the head of the human mediator, which he alone is.

For if we rightly call the mind the governing principle of man, that is, as the head of human substance, although the human being is human together with the mind, why should it not be much more fitting, and much more so, that the Word together with the Father, who is God with him, be the head of Christ? Yet Christ as man cannot be understood apart from the Word who was made flesh.

**(Greg.)** For John’s Gospel relates that the napkin which had been over his head was not placed with the linen cloths but was wrapped separately in one place. What, brothers, do we believe this means—that the Lord’s head-cloth was not found in the tomb with the linen cloths? It means that, as Paul bears witness, “the head of Christ is God,” and that the incomprehensible mysteries of the divinity are distinguished from the knowledge available to our weakness; his power transcends the nature of the creature.

Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head.

**(Ambr.)** By “praying” he means making supplication; by “prophesying,” declaring after prayer, in the language of a sign, that the Lord’s coming will take place.

“But every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head.” For it is one and the same thing as if she were shaved. If a woman is not veiled, let her also be shorn. But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her cover her head.

A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God. Although man and woman have one substance, nevertheless, because the man is the head of the woman, he is handed down as superior, so that he is greater in cause and reason, not in substance. The woman is therefore inferior to the man; for she is his portion. The origin of the woman is the man, since she is from him, and therefore the woman appears liable to the man, so that she is subject to his authority.

He says that the honor and dignity of the man prevent him from covering his head. Since he is the image of God, it is inappropriate that he should be concealed; he ought not to be hidden, for the glory of God is seen in the man.

“But the woman is the glory of the man.” There is a great difference between the glory of God and the glory of the man. The man was made in the image of God, not the woman. The image of God exists in the man because the one God made one man, so that, just as all things come from one God, so all human beings might come from one man. Thus the one visible man might bear on earth the image of the one invisible God, so that the one God might be seen in one man, preserving the authority of one principle as a reproach to the devil, who, after neglecting the one God, wished to usurp dominion and divinity for himself. The prophet Ezekiel signifies this, and the Apostle likewise says: “So that he takes his seat in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God” (2 Thess. II).

**(Aug.)** To the Romans he says as follows: “For all of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal. III).

Have faithful women, then, lost the sex of their bodies? Rather, because there they are renewed according to the image of God, where there is no sex, there man was made in the image of God where there is no sex—that is, in the spirit of his mind.

Why, then, ought the man not to cover his head because he is the image and glory of God, while the woman ought to do so because she is the glory of the man? Is the woman not renewed in the spirit of her mind, which is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created it? Rather, because she differs from the man in sex, that part of reason which is turned toward the governance of temporal matters could rightly be represented by her bodily covering, so that the image of God remains only in that part by which the human mind clings to the contemplation or consultation of eternal realities. It is evident that this is possessed not only by males but also by females.

Therefore, their minds reveal a common nature, while their bodies represent the distribution of that one mind.

“Man is not from woman, but woman from man; for man was not created for woman, but woman for man. Therefore the woman ought to have authority over her head, because of the angels.”

**(Ambr.)** The veil signifies authority. By “angels” he means bishops, as is taught in the Apocalypse of John (Apoc. II–III). Since they are certainly human beings, they are rebuked for failing to correct the people, and what is right in them is praised.

The woman ought therefore to cover her head because she is not the image of God, but so that her subjection may be displayed. And because transgression began through her, she ought to bear this sign: in the Church, out of reverence for episcopal authority, she should not have her head free but covered with a veil, nor should she have authority to speak, because the bishop bears the person of Christ. Thus, as before a judge, so before the bishop—for he is the Lord’s representative—the woman ought to appear subject because of the origin of her guilt.

“Nevertheless, neither is woman without man, nor man without woman, in the Lord.” He says “in the Lord” because God made both and made them one. They are one flesh and one body in the Lord—that is, according to the Lord who created them.

Finally, those who do not believe that the woman was taken from the man do not believe in the Lord, or do not believe according to God concerning the origin of human beings. For just as the woman is from the man, so also the man is through the woman. This confirms what he said: both are one in nature, because the origin of the woman is the man, as we read that the Lord the Creator made it in Genesis.

“But all things are from God.” After he had explained each point step by step, so that he might subject everything to God while preserving one principle, he said, “But all things are from God,” so that neither the woman would be saddened because of her subjection nor the man, as though exalted, would become proud.

**(Aug.)** Just as the woman is from the man, so also the man is through the woman, because the woman was made from the man, so that afterward the man might also be born through the woman.

But if Victor divides the matter in such a way as to say that the woman is from the man according to the body, but from God according to soul and spirit, how will the Apostle’s statement, “But all things are from God,” be true? Therefore, in order that the Apostle should speak the truth rather than this person’s interpretation be attributed to the Apostle, the woman is from the man, whether according to the body or according to the whole of that which constitutes human nature. We affirm none of these points as certain; we are still seeking which of them is true. And the man is through the woman, whether the whole of human nature, which is born through the woman, is derived from her in part, or only the flesh—on which there is still a question.

Nevertheless, all things are from God, and on this there is no question: the body, soul, and spirit of both man and woman. Even if they were not born or drawn from God, or did not flow from him in such a way as to be of his nature, they are nevertheless from God, since they were created, founded, and made by him; from him they have their being.

“Judge among yourselves: is it fitting for a woman to pray to God unveiled?”

**(Ambr.)** This is why above he rebukes them ironically, saying: “I praise you because you remember me in every respect, and because, just as I teach everywhere, you hold fast to my traditions.” Since this was the substance of the tradition, and veiled women were present in the Church, they nevertheless permitted them to be unveiled in the Church. Therefore he now endeavors to persuade them of the truth, not by the authority of the tradition they had neglected, but by nature itself, saying: “Does not nature itself teach you?”

For if a man has long hair, he has spoken according to the Law, since the Law forbids a man to wear long hair. But if a woman has long hair, it is her glory, because her hair was given to her as a veil. He wishes this to be understood naturally as honorable and almost as an ordinance, so that a veiled woman may fulfill her duty and give thanks to God. Her hair is therefore an indication of her veil, so that the will of nature may be added. Finally, no woman who is unveiled has authority.

“But if anyone seems contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God.” After giving the reason, he introduces authority in order to overcome the contentious, because Judaism also did not have this custom. Hence he says, “Neither we nor the Church of God,” meaning that neither Moses nor the Savior handed down such a practice.

“But in giving this instruction, I do not praise you, because you come together not for the better but for the worse.” Just as he corrects their conduct point by point through reproof, so also he does not praise their traditions, but rather censures them.

For, in the first place—

By saying “in the first place,” he indicates the kind of sin from which the errors he reproves arose. Wherever there is disagreement, nothing is right.

When you come together in the Church, I hear that there are divisions among you, and to some extent I believe it. For there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you.

Knowing that certain people, corrupted in mind by the devil’s cunning, were behaving in this way, he says, “There must be heresies.” He certainly did not desire or wish this; rather, because he knew it would happen, he said it, just as the Lord said: “It is necessary, he says, that scandals come, and it is necessary for the Son of Man to suffer” (Matt. XVIII). He knew beforehand that Judas would be a traitor.

When he says, “so that those who are approved may become manifest among you,” he indicates those who persevered in the tradition they had received. They were examples of proven adherence to evangelical discipline, for the condemnation of the others. These are the people whom he refers to at the beginning of the epistle when they said, “But we belong to Christ,” while others said, “I belong to Paul,” or “I belong to Apollos.”

**(Aug.)** Reading the Scriptures with a sinful and misguided desire, they are compelled to understand them wrongly. Yet the death of such people serves to awaken the children of the Catholic Church from sleep, as though by thorns, and to advance them toward understanding the divine Scriptures.

“For there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved,” he says, “may become manifest among you”—that is, among human beings, although they are manifest to God.

When you come together into one place, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper. For each person takes his own supper beforehand to eat; one is hungry, while another is drunk. Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the Church of God and shame those who have nothing?

**(Ambr.)** He censures those who came together in the Church in such a way that, when they brought their offerings, each person who had made an offering claimed the whole for himself when the presbyters arrived—for at that time rulers had already been established in all the Churches. The false apostles had sown divisions among them, so that they were jealous over their offerings.

Although the offerings of all were blessed with one and the same prayer, those who had not offered, or who had nothing with which to offer, were overcome with shame and confusion and did not take their portion. They acted so quickly that those who arrived later found nothing to eat.

Therefore, he says, if you come together in such a way that each person takes his own portion, this ought to be done at home, not in the Church, where people come together for the sake of unity and mystery, not for division and the belly. For the offering that is made becomes the possession of the whole people, because all are signified in the one bread; and because we are one, we ought all to partake of one bread.

What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you.

The error has been exposed and reproved, so that henceforth they may correct it and understand the truth they themselves had learned at the beginning. He repeats for them the pattern given by the Savior in such matters, saying:

“For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and, giving thanks, broke it and said: ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which will be delivered for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the New Testament in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.’”

He shows that the mystery of the Eucharist, celebrated during the meal, is not itself a meal. It is spiritual medicine which, tasted with reverence, purifies the person devoted to it. It is the memorial of our redemption, so that, remembering the Redeemer, we may deserve to receive greater things from him.

For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you will proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. Since we have been freed by the Lord’s death, by remembering this in eating and carrying the flesh and blood offered for us, we signify that we have obtained the New Testament in these things. This is the new law, which delivers those obedient to it into the heavenly kingdoms.

Moses also took the blood of a calf in a basin and sprinkled the children of Israel, saying: “This is the covenant which God has established for you” (Exod. XXIV). This was a figure of the covenant which the Lord, through the Prophet, called “new”; that which Moses delivered was therefore old.

A covenant is established by blood because the blood is witness to the divine benefit. As its type, we receive the mystical cup for the protection of our body, blood, and soul, because the Lord’s blood redeemed our blood—that is, it saved the whole human being. The Savior’s flesh was poured out for the salvation of the body, and his blood for our soul, just as Moses had previously prefigured it. For he says: “The flesh is offered for your body, but the blood for the soul”; therefore blood was not to be eaten.

If, then, among the ancients there was an image of the truth that has now appeared and been manifested in the Savior’s coming, how can heretics regard the Old as contrary to the New, when the two themselves bear witness to one another?

Therefore, whoever eats this bread or drinks the Lord’s cup unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.

He calls the person unworthy of the Lord who celebrates the mystery otherwise than it was delivered by him. For one cannot be devoted who presumes to act otherwise than the author gave it. Therefore he warns that, according to the order handed down, the mind of the person approaching the Lord’s Eucharist must be devout.

Since there will be a judgment, each person will have to give an account on the day of the Lord Jesus Christ of how he approaches. Those who approach without the discipline of tradition and conduct are guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.

What does it mean to be guilty except to suffer the punishment of the Lord’s death? For he was killed on behalf of those who nullify his benefit.

**(Aug.)** Why, then, are you surprised if the bread of Christ was given to Judas, through which he might be handed over to the devil, when you see, conversely, that an angel of Satan was given to Paul, through which he might advance in Christ? Thus good harmed the evil person, and evil benefited the good person.

Remember, then, where it is written: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.” The Apostle was speaking of those who treated the Lord’s body as though it were any other food, taking it indiscriminately and carelessly.

If the person who does not judge—that is, who does not distinguish the Lord’s body from other foods—is reproved, how is the person not condemned who approaches the Lord’s table as an enemy while pretending to be a friend?

Let a person examine himself, and then let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body.

**(Ambr.)** He teaches that one must approach communion with a devout spirit and with fear, so that the mind may know that it owes reverence to the one whose body it approaches to receive. One must judge within oneself that he is the Lord, whose blood one drinks in the mystery, the blood that bears witness to God’s benefit. If we receive him with discipline, we will not be unworthy of the body and blood of the Lord; we will appear to give thanks to the Redeemer.

That is why many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep: to demonstrate the truth that there will be an examination of those who receive the Lord’s body. Even now he displays an image of the judgment against those who had received the Lord’s body thoughtlessly, since they were struck by fevers and illnesses and many died, so that the rest might learn from them and the example of the few might frighten the others into correction. They were to understand that they could not carelessly receive the Lord’s body without punishment, and that the person whom punishment had delayed here would be treated more severely because he had despised the example.

If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged. While we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world.

He says this because, if we ourselves corrected our errors, we would not be judged by the Lord. Since we are corrected, however, this is for our benefit, so that we may be amended by that very fear. In the few, all are corrected: “that we may not be condemned with the world,” that is, with unbelievers.

For there is no difference between the unbeliever and the person who approaches the Lord’s table thoughtlessly. The Lord would not place sins worthy of lament before the eyes of those who have transgressed if he intended to strike them with strict judgment through himself. It is clear that he wished to conceal them from his judgment, anticipating them in mercy and making them judges of themselves. Hence it is written: “Let us come before his face with confession” (Ps. XCIV).

**(Cass.)** Hence Paul says: “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged.”

With every possible care, and insofar as it lies within us, we ought to strive to preserve the purity of unblemished chastity, especially at the time when we desire to stand before the venerable altars. With the most vigilant watchfulness we must take care that the integrity of the flesh, preserved beforehand, is not violated especially on the night in which we prepare ourselves for communion in the saving banquet.

But if that most wicked enemy, in order to deprive us of the medicine of heavenly healing, has mocked the guard of our sleeping mind, provided that no reprehensible itching has intervened, no consent to pleasure has defiled us, and provided that the discharge has been produced either by natural necessity or, certainly, by the devil’s attack, without any sense of pleasure, and has been presented as an impediment to our sanctification, we may and ought to approach the grace of the saving food with confidence.

But if this discharge has been caused by our own fault, let us, with a conscience rightly troubled, fear the Apostle’s words: “Whoever eats the bread and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.”

“Let a person first examine himself, and then let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body”—that is, not at all separating that heavenly food from the baseness of ordinary foods, nor judging it to be such that it may be received only with a pure mind and body.

Finally he adds: “For this reason many among you are weak and feeble, and many sleep.” By this he clearly says that spiritual weaknesses and deaths arise particularly from this presumption. For many who presume to take it unlawfully become weak in faith and feeble in mind, entangled in the passions and their diseases; and they sleep in the sleep of sin, never rising from this deadly slumber through a saving vigilance.

Then follows the statement that, if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged. That is, if, whenever we are forestalled by the wound of sin, we judged ourselves unworthy of receiving the sacraments, we would certainly take care, through repentance’s correction, to be able to approach them worthily, and would not, as unworthy persons, be chastised by the Lord with the harshest scourges of infirmities; so that, at least as those pierced with remorse, we might have recourse to remedies for our wounds, lest, not being deemed worthy of the very brief correction of the present age, we be condemned in the future together with the sinners of this world.

Therefore, brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home.

**(Ambr.)** He says that they should wait for one another so that the offering of many may be celebrated together and all may be served. If anyone is impatient, let him feed himself at home with earthly bread.

“So that you may not come together for judgment.” That is, so that you may not conduct the mystery reprehensibly and with offense.

“I will arrange the remaining matters when I come.” He indicates that the first matter to be dealt with is the order of salvation, and he has already explained how both sexes should come together in the Church. If there is error in these matters, it is no slight sin. The remaining matters, which concern the edification of the Church, he promises to arrange by his presence.

## CHAPTER XII. The Apostle commends the grace of God by a general exposition of freely given grace, comparing the body of the Church with the body of nature.

Now concerning spiritual matters, brothers, I do not want you to be ignorant. You know that when you were Gentiles, you went to the form of idols, as you were led.

**(Ambr.)** Before handing down spiritual teaching, he recalls an example from their former conduct. Just as, when they worshiped idols, they were shaped according to the form of idols and were led by the will of demons as their guide, so, when they worship God, they should be an embodiment of the Lord’s law, walking as pleases the Lord. For the form of every law ought to be visible in the profession and conduct of its worshiper. The person in whose faith and conduct the truth of the Gospel shines is the form and image of God’s law.

Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says, “Anathema to Jesus,” and no one can say, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit.

Because they were ignorant of the nature of spiritual gifts, they attributed glory for each charisma to human beings rather than to God. They had not grasped that this gift was administered through the Holy Spirit, nor that the person who calls Jesus “Lord” says this only through the Holy Spirit. He possesses grace in the very fact of his faith, for the glory of Christ’s name. For it is not without God’s gift that one says, “Jesus is Lord.”

By this he shows them that in all things praise and grace belong to God. Just as the image of the idols exists in their ministers and has its order through its various ranks, yet is altogether a human creation, so also in the Lord’s law there are ranks of charismata belonging to the offices of the Church. They were not granted according to human merits, but as members belonging to the edification of the Church, which possess glory in and through themselves, as is also the case with human offices.

For offices are like schools: those placed in them receive dignity, so that the honor of the position makes a person glorious, not his own praise.

Thus he says: “No one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus.’” The voice that says “Anathema to Jesus” is uttered through human error. For whatever is false comes from human beings.

“And no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit.” The very utterance by which Jesus is designated as Lord is not poured forth through human flattery—as idols are called gods—but through the truth of the Holy Spirit. Whatever is true, whoever says it, is said by the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, lest they suppose that the Christian order rests on human favor, and for that reason refuse to be reproved, as happens with idols—for a human being invented the notion that one who is not God should be called God, and therefore the priests are subject to them—he shows them that there is nothing human in the benefit when one says, “Lord Jesus.” Rather, it is the gift of God, who has deigned to reveal his mystery to human beings.

Indeed, the very confession obtains remission of sins, just as the dedication of idols increases guilt. He therefore teaches them that, by saying “Lord Jesus,” they do not confer a benefit upon religion but receive one. They were not to suppose, after the manner of human idols, that grace existed in the Lord’s law because one calls God what is not God.

Finally, because they did not understand that the gift of God exists in faith, each of them had chosen particular human beings to follow, saying: “I belong to Paul,” or “I belong to Apollos.” He therefore humbles their pride, so that they may allow themselves to be reproved.

**(Aug.)** Since we read in the Gospel that the Lord said, “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII), it is rightly asked how this agrees with the Apostle’s statement: “No one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus,’ and no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit.”

For we cannot say that some who have the Holy Spirit will not enter the kingdom of heaven if they persevere to the end. Nor can we say that those who say, “Lord, Lord,” and yet do not enter the kingdom of heaven have the Holy Spirit.

How, then, does no one say, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit? It is because the Apostle specifically used the verb “says,” so as to signify the will and understanding of the speaker, whereas the Lord used the verb generally when he said, “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven.”

Even the person who neither wills nor understands what he says may appear to say it; but the person truly says it who expresses his will and mind through the sound of his voice.

Moreover, the apostolic declaration is: “No one says ‘Lord Jesus’ except in the Holy Spirit.” And who says “Lord Jesus” except the person who loves him—if he says it in the sense that the Apostle intended?

Many say it with their voice but deny him in heart and deeds, as he says of such people: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him.” If he is denied by deeds, then undoubtedly he is also confessed by deeds. No one, therefore, says “Lord Jesus” in mind, word, deed, heart, or work except in the Holy Spirit; and no one says it in this way except the one who loves him.

“But there are divisions of graces.”

**(Ambr.)** He does not wish this to be attributed to human merits, but to the grace of God, for the honor of his name. Just as the person who says “Lord Jesus” speaks in the Holy Spirit, whatever his capacity may be, so also the person placed in a particular rank of ecclesiastical office possesses grace, whatever his capacity may be—not his own grace, certainly, but that of the office, through the efficacy of the Holy Spirit. Hence at the beginning he says: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth.”

The same Spirit, and there are divisions of ministries [Col. 0107D]. Through the same Spirit, he says, different gifts are bestowed. Yet the same Lord, and there are divisions of operations. Here he joins Christ to the Holy Spirit. Yet it is the same God who works all things in all. He asserts so strongly that this is not to be attributed to human beings as their own, but to God alone, that he calls even the gift of the Holy Spirit and the grace of the Lord Jesus the operation of one God, lest grace and gift be divided among the persons of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but that the one work of the three may be understood to be of undivided unity and nature, so that he may refer all glory and divinity to one.

“Yet there are divisions of graces”: they are assigned to the offices of the Church, not to human merits. For if the Holy Spirit is the same Lord, and the Lord is the same God, the three are one [Col. 0108A] God. Since the grace, power, and nature of the Holy Spirit are God’s, and the Lord Jesus is the same in nature as God is, the Holy Spirit, the Lord Jesus, and God the Father are assuredly one. Each individually is the one God, and the three are the one God. Finally, when one acts, the three are said to act, so that the mystery of the Trinity may be contained within the nature and power of the one God, though that mystery is immeasurable.

“But to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.” That is, he receives a gift so that, governing his life by divine restraints, he may be useful both to himself and to others, while displaying an example of good conduct.

“For to one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom.” That is, prudence is given to him, not from letters, but through the flashing light of the Holy Spirit, so that he may have an enlightened heart and be prudent, discerning what must be avoided [Col. 0108B] and what must be pursued.

“But to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit.” That is, so that he may possess knowledge of divine things.

**(Gregory.)** There are some who, through the gift of grace, understand even those things which they have not heard expounded by teachers; these, plainly, have received a word of wisdom. There are others who cannot understand by themselves what they have heard, but retain what they have read in commentators and present with knowledge what they have learned from their reading. With what, then, are these filled, if not with a word of knowledge? This may also be understood in another way, because wisdom pertains to life, while knowledge pertains to teaching. Therefore, one who lives well and preaches prudently is rightly called a treasury of the spiritual building, because riches are distributed from his mouth.

“To another, gifts of healings in the one Spirit”—that is, so that he may provide healing to the infirm or sick.

“To another faith in the same Spirit.” By this he means that he receives the ability to confess and defend the faith without being overcome by shame.

“To another the working of powers.” This signifies that power is given for driving out demons or performing signs.

“To another prophecy”—that is, so that the Spirit may declare future things.

“To another the discernment of spirits.” By this he means that he may understand and judge whether what is said is from the Holy Spirit or from an unclean spirit.

“To another the interpretation of languages.” To interpret means that, through the gift of God, they faithfully explain the words of those who speak in languages or through written texts.

Practical knowledge, therefore—called by the Apostle by another name, charity—is placed above all the languages of human beings and angels, above the fullness of faith that can even move mountains, above all knowledge and prophecy, above the distribution of all one’s possessions, and finally even above glorious martyrdom itself [Col. 0108D]. For after he had enumerated all the kinds of gifts and had said, “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge, to another faith, to another gifts of healings, to another the working of powers, and so forth,” observe briefly how he places charity above all the gifts. He says: “And I will show you a still more excellent way.” By this he clearly shows that the summit of perfection and blessedness consists not in the performance of those miracles, but in the purity of charity. Nor is this without reason: all those things are to be emptied and destroyed, but charity will remain forever. For this reason, our fathers were never seen to seek after such works, or even these signs [Col. 0109A]. Indeed, although they possessed the grace of the Holy Spirit that enabled them to perform them, they never wished to exercise it unless perhaps extreme and unavoidable necessity compelled them.

“But all these things one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each as he wills.”

**(Ambrose.)** What he earlier attributed to the three persons, he now professes to be accomplished through the one Holy Spirit. Since they are one in nature and power, what one works, the three work. Yet God is one, whose grace is distributed to each as he wills—not chiefly according to human merit, but for the building up of his Church. Thus, whatever the world wishes to imitate but cannot accomplish because it is carnal, may be seen in the Church, which is the house of God, through the offices of individuals, granted by the gift and teaching of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0109B], as a demonstration of the truth in those who are despised by the world.

**(Cassian.)** For this reason it is confirmed by unwavering faith and, so to speak, tangible experience that the God of the universe, like a most loving Father and most kindly physician, works all things impartially in all, according to the Apostle. At one time he inspires the beginnings of salvation and implants in each person the fervor of a good will; at another he grants the effect and completion of the very work, and the fulfillment of virtues; at another he recalls even the unwilling and ignorant from an already imminent fall and headlong collapse; at another he introduces occasions and opportunities for salvation and restrains violent and precipitate impulses from deadly dispositions. He receives some who willingly and eagerly run toward him, while he drags others who are unwilling and resisting [Col. 0109C] and compels them toward a good will. Yet the whole of this is not always granted to those who resist, nor to those who persistently remain unwilling; and the sum of our salvation must be attributed not to the merit of our works but to heavenly grace.

Thus we are taught by the words of the Lord himself: “You shall remember your ways and all your crimes by which you polluted yourselves, and you shall be displeased with yourselves in your own sight, because of all your evil deeds which you committed; and you shall know that I am the Lord, when I have dealt well with you for my name’s sake, not according to your evil ways nor according to your worst crimes, O house of Israel” (Ezek. XX).

**(Augustine.)** When the Apostle says of the Holy Spirit, “But all these things one and the same Spirit works,” this is not said because the Father and the Son do not cooperate with him [Col. 0109D], but because in these works there are not many spirits, but one Spirit. Nor is he different from himself in his various works. When he adds, “distributing to each as he wills,” does he not make clear that the Holy Spirit too possesses power, though plainly inseparable from the Father and the Son?

**(Jerome.)** It is asked how the Savior, according to John, breathes the Holy Spirit upon the apostles, while according to Luke he says that he will send him after the Ascension. The solution to this question is very easy if, following the teaching of the Apostle Paul, we recognize the different graces of the Holy Spirit. For he writes in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “There are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God who works all things in all,” and so forth [Col. 0110A].

Therefore, the Lord, who after his resurrection had said according to Luke’s Gospel (Luke XXIV), “I will send the promise of my Father upon you; but remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high,” and who, according to the same author in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts I), “gave them orders not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the promise of the Father, which you have heard from my mouth: for John baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now”—again, at the end of the Gospel according to John, on the day of his resurrection, that is, on the Lord’s Day, is related to have entered to the apostles through closed doors (John XX) and said to them a second time, “Peace be with you,” and added, “As the Father sent me, so I send you.” When he had said this, “he breathed upon them [Col. 0110B] and said to them: Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; whose sins you retain, they are retained.”

Thus, on the day of his resurrection, they received the grace of the Holy Spirit by which they might forgive sins, baptize, make people children of God, and bestow the Spirit of adoption upon believers, as the Savior himself said: “Whose sins you forgive, they will be forgiven them, and whose sins you retain, they will be retained.” But on the day of Pentecost it was promised to them more fully that they would be baptized with the Holy Spirit and clothed with power from on high, because they were to preach Christ’s Gospel to all nations. In accordance with this we read in the sixty-seventh Psalm: “The Lord will give the word to those who evangelize with great power,” so that they might possess the working of powers and the grace of healings, and, as they were to preach to many nations [Col. 0110C], receive various kinds of languages, so that it might already then be known which apostles ought to announce the Gospel to which nations.

Finally, the Apostle Paul, who preached from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum and from there was hastening through Rome to Spain, gives thanks to God that he speaks in more languages than all the apostles. Since he was going to announce the Gospel to many nations, he had received the grace of many languages. This promise of the Holy Spirit was fulfilled on the tenth day after the Savior’s Ascension, as Luke reports when he writes (Acts II): “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, they were all together in the same place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and one rested upon each of them [Col. 0110D]. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various languages, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance.”

Then what is read in Joel was fulfilled (Joel II): “And it shall be in the last days, says the Lord, that I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions.” The word “pouring out” signifies the abundance of grace, and means the same as what the Lord promised: “You shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”

They were baptized with the Holy Spirit so fully that the entire house where they were sitting was filled, and the fire of the Holy Spirit found in them its desired dwelling, divided their tongues, and, according to Isaiah, purified their lips—for he had said that he possessed unclean lips [Col. 0111A]—so that they might preach Christ’s Gospel more purely. In Isaiah (Isa. VI), the lintel of the temple is said to have been shaken, and the whole house filled with smoke, that is, with error, darkness, and ignorance of the truth. But at the beginning of the Gospel, the Church is filled with the Holy Spirit, so that by his grace and fervor all the sins of believers may be cleansed, and the tongue of those preaching Christ may be healed by the fire of the Holy Spirit which the Lord had said he would send.

For John and Luke do not disagree, so that one would indicate that the Spirit was given on the first day of the resurrection while the other described him as having come on the fiftieth day. Rather, this is the progress of the apostles: those who first received the grace of forgiving sins later received the power to perform works, together with all the kinds of gifts which, as we have recalled, were described by the Apostle, and—what was more necessary—the diversity of languages of all nations, so that, when they were going to announce Christ, they would need no interpreter [Col. 0111B].

Hence, in Lycaonia, when they heard Paul and Barnabas speaking in their own languages, they believed that gods had been turned into human beings. And truly, the clothing of power is the grace of the Spirit; possessing it, they did not fear the tribunals of judges or the purple robes of kings.

For before suffering, the Lord had promised this and said (Luke XXV): “When they hand you over, do not consider how or what you shall speak; for what you are to speak will be given to you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.”

I boldly and openly declare that, from the time when the apostles believed in the Lord, they always had the Holy Spirit and could not perform signs without the grace of the Holy Spirit, though according to a certain measure and degree. Hence the Savior cried out in the temple, saying: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.” He said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive (John VII). In the same passage he adds: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.”

This does not mean that the Holy Spirit did not exist, since the Lord and Savior said (Matt. XII): “But if I cast out demons by the Holy Spirit.” Rather, the Spirit who was in the Lord did not yet wholly dwell in the apostles. For this reason they were terrified at his passion, denied him, and swore that they did not know Christ. But after they were baptized with the Holy Spirit and the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out upon them, they spoke freely to the rulers of the Jews: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts V). They raised the dead, rejoiced amid scourging, poured out their blood, and were crowned by their sufferings.

The Spirit was not yet in the apostles, nor did spiritual graces flow from their bellies, because the Lord had not yet been glorified. But what that glory is, he himself says in the Gospel: “Father, glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world existed” (John XVII). The glory of the Savior is the triumphal cross: he is crucified as a human being, glorified as Lord. Finally, the sun flees, the moon is changed into blood, the earth trembles with an unprecedented earthquake, the underworld is opened [Col. 0112A], the dead walk, and the rocks split. This is the glory of which he spoke in the Psalm: “Rise up, my glory; rise up, harp and lyre” (Ps. CVII).

And that very glory—the dispensation of the assumed flesh—answered concerning itself: “I shall rise at dawn,” so that the title of the twenty-first Psalm, “for the morning assumption,” might be fulfilled.

We say these things not because we believe that there is one God and another human being, or make two persons in the one Son of God, as the new heresy falsely accuses us. Rather, the one and same Son of God is also the Son of Man. Whatever he says, we refer one statement to his divine glory and another to our salvation. For our sake “he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II); and “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I).

I am amazed at Montanus and his insane women, abortive prophets, when the Lord promises and says, “I am going away and sending another Paraclete to you,” and later Luke the evangelist relates that the apostles received what had been promised, while Montanus claimed that it had been fulfilled in himself much later. For the promise was made to the apostles: “I will send the promise of my Father upon you, and you shall remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke XXIV). Rising, he breathed upon the apostles—not upon Montanus, Priscilla, or Maximilla—and said to them: “Whose sins you forgive, they will be forgiven; whose sins you retain, they will be retained.” To the apostles, I say, he commanded that they should not depart from Jerusalem but await the promise of the Father. And afterward we read that what had been promised was fulfilled [Col. 0112C]: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance.”

For the Holy Spirit breathes where he wills. And when the Lord says, “I will send another Paraclete to you,” he shows himself to be the Paraclete, who is called the Comforter. Hence God the Father too is designated by this name, “the God of mercy and of all consolation.” But if the Father is Comforter, the Son is Comforter, and the Holy Spirit is Comforter, and believers are baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—which is understood to mean God—and the name of the one Godhead and Comforter is one, then the nature too is one.

This Holy Spirit was not only in the apostles but also in the prophets. David prayed concerning him, saying: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. L). Daniel is reported to have possessed the Spirit of God (Dan. IV, V), and David spoke in the Spirit when he said that the Lord had said to his Lord: “Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. CIX).

The prophets did not prophesy without the Holy Spirit. “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. XXXII). Whatever belongs to the Father and the Son likewise belongs to the Holy Spirit. And when the Spirit is sent by the Father and comes in place of the Son, in different passages he is called the Spirit of God the Father and the Spirit of Christ.

Hence, in the Acts of the Apostles, those who had been baptized with John’s baptism and believed in God the Father and Christ, because they did not know the Holy Spirit, are baptized again—or rather, they then truly receive baptism [Col. 0113A]. For without the Holy Spirit the mystery of the Trinity is incomplete. And in the same book Peter is related to have said to Ananias and Sapphira (Acts V) that, by lying to the Holy Spirit, they had not lied to human beings but to God.

“For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free, and we were all given to drink of one Spirit” (Ambrose).

Through this he teaches that no person is to be despised as though insignificant, nor anyone preferred as though perfect, and that glory owed to God alone must not be attributed to human beings, since the one and same God is glorified in all. For we all possess one baptism and one and the same Holy Spirit. He says this because some were taking pride in certain people while despising others as contemptible [Col. 0113B].

**(Augustine.)** Speaking of the members of Christ—that is, of the faithful—he does not say “so also the members of Christ,” but called the whole of what he had described “Christ.” For just as there is one body with many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also Christ has many members in one body. Therefore, all of us together with our head are Christ, for without the head we are powerless.

Why? Because we are, with our head, a vine; without our head—God forbid—we are branches cut off, destined not for any farmer but only for the fire. Hence he also says in the Gospel: “I am the vine, you are the branches, and my Father is the farmer. Without me,” he says, “you can do nothing” (John XV).

“For the body is not one member, but many.”

**(Ambrose.)** By saying this he shows that unity possesses varieties of offices, and that this diversity does not conflict with unity of power, since the unity of the body does not consist in singularity but in many members, so that they may provide one another with what they owe.

If the foot should say, “Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body,” is it for that reason not of the body? That is, one who appears weak cannot be denied membership in the body because he is not powerful.

If the ear should say, “Because I am not the eye, I am not of the body,” is it therefore not of the body? He says that one who is somewhat lower must not be considered unnecessary to the body because he is not among the first. For if all had one office and one function, how would the remaining needs of the body be fulfilled, since it is clear that many offices are required for the governance of the body?

“If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the sense of smell be?” He says that the will of God, because it is provident and rational, fitted the members to the body so that nothing would be lacking in the perfection formed by many members.

“But now God has placed the members, each one of them, in the body as he willed.” It is evident that, if all had possessed one dignity, they would not be called members, nor would they constitute a body. Therefore, they are governed by the various offices of the members [Col. 0114A]. For all could not be one member. They are many because they differ from one another in dignity.

“But if all were one member, where would the body be? But now there are many members, yet one body.” He says this because, although the many members need one another, they do not differ in the unity of nature. Though they are diverse, this diversity converges into one, so that the usefulness of the body may be fulfilled.

The same is true of the things from which the world itself is composed. Though they differ not only in functions but also in natures, they nevertheless contribute to the perfection of one world; and from all of them arises a certain balance in the fruits that serve human use.

“The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I do not need your work’; nor again the head to the feet, ‘You are not necessary to me.’” That is, the superior cannot say to the inferior, “I have no need of you,” because the eyes see, but the hands are the ones that work. Indeed, the members of the body that seem weaker are much more necessary.

That is, one who is higher in rank and dignity cannot do without the one who is humble, because the humble person can do something the exalted person cannot. Iron can do what gold cannot; and therefore the feet confer honor upon the head.

“And the members of the body which we think less honorable, on these we bestow more abundant honor.” It is evident that, although someone may be exalted in dignity, if a subordinate is lacking who makes him glorious by his services, the dignity itself will be contemptible. Office is what establishes dignity. It is as though an emperor lacked an army. Although the emperor is great, he nevertheless needs an army, for it is a member of his body, with tribunes, counts, and commanders before it. Soldiers are inferior to all these and yet more necessary, like the members of the body which, although they appear lower, are more useful. Without eyes, the hand works; and the foot, as it walks, seeks food [Col. 0114C].

“And the members of our body which we consider less honorable, we surround with greater honor.” The meaning is similar: in those who are thought to lack dignity, we find something to praise, just as we do in the members of the body, and it pleases us more than what we find in the others. What honor would hands deserve if, by them, we could not hold what we want? What honor would feet deserve if, by them, we could not go where we want? Therefore we add honor to them—for example, to the feet, which, because they are humble and without dignity, we adorn with shoes [Col. 0114D].

“And our less honorable members have greater propriety.” It is evident that our private parts, which appear shameful, cover themselves with propriety by avoiding public view, lest through indecency they inspire horror.

In the same way, some of the brethren, although poor and shabby in dress, are nevertheless not without grace, because they are members of our body. They often walk wearing a short, ugly garment and with bare feet. Although they appear contemptible, they are more worthy of honor, because they often lead a purer life. What appears despised to human beings is often judged beautiful by God.

“But our honorable members have no need.” God has arranged the body so that the member lacking honor receives greater honor [Col. 0115A]. It is clear that the head, face, and hands do not need anything added to adorn them. So too, in brothers whose diligence in learning and whose conduct are honorable, there is nothing for us to add; the honor due to them is already rendered. But those who are despised or humble require encouragement, by which some honor may be added to them, so that they may become useful. Otherwise, through contempt itself, they will become more negligent toward themselves, even though they are the ones who most need improvement.

“So that there may be no schism in the body, but that the members may have the same concern for one another.” He says that the Lord arranged the human body in such a way that all its members are necessary and therefore concerned for one another, because one cannot exist without the other. What is considered lower is more necessary, as has been explained and discussed concerning the brethren, because no one should be despised as useless.

**(Gregory.)** “The members of the body which we think less honorable, on these we bestow more abundant honor, and our less honorable members have greater propriety. But our honorable members have no need.” Just as the dishonorable members are in the body, so within the holy Church there are powerful and arrogant people. Since they cannot be struck by open denunciation, they are, as it were, covered by the honor of concealment. We are speaking here of the hidden sins of the powerful. But when they sin in a way known to others, they must be rebuked in the presence of those who know, lest, if the preacher remains silent about the fault, he appear to approve it, and lest the fault, growing into an example, remain uncut by the shepherd’s tongue.

“And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it.”

**(Ambrose.)** This is unambiguous when applied to the members of the physical body. If the eye, foot, or hand is seized by some sickness or weakness, the whole body suffers with it. So we too ought to suffer with our brethren if some such circumstance or need arises.

“Or if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it.” It is clear that the head, or the other members, are glad when the feet are well cared for or healthy. Thus we ought to rejoice when we see a brother more refined in conduct and distinguished by honorable behavior—that is, sound in judgment.

“Now you are the body of Christ and members individually.” He openly shows that he has treated our situation through the analogy of bodily members, because we cannot all do the same things, but each has received grace according to the measure of faith [Col. 0115D].

**(Cassian.)** If we possess this knowledge—or rather, this faith—which I have explained above, so that we believe that all things are done through God and that everything is distributed for the benefit of souls, we will not only never despise them but will also pray for them unceasingly as for our own members, and will sympathize with them with all our inward being and with the fullest affection. For when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. We know that without them, as our members, we cannot in any way be made complete, just as we read that even our predecessors could not attain the fullness of the promise without us, as the Apostle declares concerning them (Heb. XI): “And all these, though commended by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promises, since God had provided something better for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us.”

“And God has appointed certain ones in the Church, first apostles.”

**(Ambrose.)** As the head, therefore, he placed the apostles in the Church. They are the ambassadors of Christ, as the same Apostle says (2 Cor. VI): “We are acting as ambassadors for him.” They are bishops, as the Apostle Peter confirms when, among other things, he says concerning Judas: “Let another receive his episcopate.”

“Second, prophets.” We should understand prophets in two ways: those who announce future things and those who reveal the Scriptures. Apostles too are prophets, since the first rank contains all the ranks subject to it. Finally, the wicked Caiaphas prophesied because he was high priest (John XI), on account of his office, certainly, not his own merit [Col. 0116B]. Nevertheless, there were prophets in a special sense, interpreters of the Scriptures and announcers of future things, such as Agabus (Acts XI, XXI), who prophesied the sufferings and chains awaiting this Apostle in Jerusalem, and foretold the famine that occurred under Claudius.

Therefore, although the apostle is greater, he sometimes needs prophets. And because all things come from one God the Father, he decreed that individual bishops should preside over individual churches.

“Third, teachers.” He calls teachers those who, in the Church, instructed children in letters and in memorizing readings, after the custom of the Synagogue, since their tradition has passed down to us.

“Then powers, and afterward gifts of healings.” Someone may not be a bishop and yet possess within himself the gift of powers or healings.

“Helps, administrations.” These are given so that a person may be vigilant in understanding divine matters, yet in such a way that, concerning certain things which he is not permitted to fulfill, he receives from another what he does not possess, since everything cannot be granted to one person [Col. 0116C]. There are also administrators who serve as examples to people through spiritual restraints.

“Kinds of languages.” This means that it is a gift of God to know many languages, so that God may bestow this grace upon someone and grant him skill in interpreting languages.

“Are all apostles?” It is true that there is one bishop in a Church.

“Are all prophets?” There is no doubt that prophecy is not granted to everyone.

“Are all teachers?” He is a teacher to whom this is granted.

“Are all powers?” The one to whom God gives the power to cast out demons may possess this power.

“Do all possess gifts of healings?” How could it happen that all should possess gifts of healings?

“Do all speak in languages?” Certainly not, except the one who receives the gift of this ability [Col. 0116D].

“Do all interpret?” The one to whom God gives it can interpret languages. These statements must be inserted according to the sense given above. He explained, by supplying the reason, that all possess different graces and that the whole cannot be granted to one person, using the example of the members. By the example of the physical body, he introduces the spiritual body, and thereby teaches that God must be blessed in all things and gloried in the name of him whose grace this is.

We find the same principle even in physical things. Gold is better than silver, yet silver is more widely used. Bronze is necessary, but iron is needed still more; almost nothing is done without iron, although it is inferior.

And afterward: “But eagerly desire the better gifts.” He immediately completes this in what follows: “And I will show you a still more excellent way” [Col. 0117A]. Step by step he leads them toward what is more useful, showing them that the grace of all the gifts mentioned above—which are seen in human beings, whether speaking, healing, or prophesying—does not belong to human merit but to the honor of God.

Therefore he now says that he will show them a clearer way, by which one goes to heaven, and which places merit with God. Since the things mentioned above do not always pertain to merit, the Savior says: “Many will say to me on that day”—that is, the day of judgment—“Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and perform many powers?” (Matt. VII). And because this does not pertain to merit but consists in offices of the Church, for the confusion of the nations and the proclamation of God’s honor, the Lord says to them: “Depart from me [Col. 0117B], you workers of iniquity; I do not know you.”

Secure in seeing God’s work manifested in them, they were negligent toward themselves. Likewise, when the seventy-two disciples rejoiced that demons had been subjected to them, the Savior said: “Do not rejoice in this, that the demons are subject to you, but rejoice in this, that your names are written in heaven” (Luke X). Why, unless because they had been subjected to the name of God, not through human merit? And why does this not now happen in such a way that people possess the grace of God? It was necessary for it to happen at the beginning, so that the foundations of the faith might receive firmness. Now it is not necessary, because one people brings another people to faith when their good works and simple preaching are seen.

**(Augustine.)** “The one who says that he remains in Christ ought to walk as he himself walked, and that one should walk” (1 John II). What is this way on which Christ walked? What else is it but charity, concerning which the Apostle says: “I will show you a still more excellent way”?

If, therefore, we wish to imitate Christ, we must run along the very way on which Christ deigned to walk even while hanging upon the cross. For he was fixed upon the cross, and, running along the way of charity, he prayed for his persecutors. Finally, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII). Therefore, let us too continually pray this for all our enemies, that the Lord may grant them amendment of conduct and forgiveness of sins.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Excellence, Benefit, and Permanence of Charity.

[Col. 0117D] If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. (Ambr.) It certainly seems a great grace to speak in different tongues; yet something greater is to know even the language of angels, if that is possible. That is, if one can possess a spiritually understood angelic movement. But he shows that this is not to be credited as merit, but to the glory of God, subject to Him, saying that such a person is like “sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal”: for just as bronze resounds when struck by another, and a cymbal clangs, so also the one who speaks in tongues possesses the effect and movement of the Holy Spirit, enabling him to speak. “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X). Indeed, [Col. 0118A] the she-ass also spoke with a human tongue to Balaam son of Beor (Num. XXII), so that he might learn the majesty of God; and infant children burst forth in praise of God, to the confusion of the Jews. The Savior showed that not only these, but even these stones, could cry out for the condemnation of the faithless and the glory of God; and at the very beginnings, as a commendation of faith, those who were being baptized spoke in tongues.

(Greg.) “If I speak,” he says, “in the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal.” For one who speaks good things but does not follow those same good things through love gives back a sound like bronze or a cymbal, because he himself does not feel the words that he utters. “And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, but do not have love, [Col. 0118B] it profits me nothing.”

(Ambr.) Truly it profits nothing. Prophecy is uttered for the glory of God, as the Prophet says: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. CXIII). Balaam also prophesied, although he was not a prophet but a diviner; Caiaphas prophesied, not by merit but by virtue of the dignity of the priestly office; and Saul prophesied when he had already been filled with an evil spirit on account of his disobedience, yet for God’s purpose, so that he might not capture David and kill the one he wished to kill.

“And if I know all mysteries.” It profited Judas nothing to have learned the mysteries with the apostles, since, an enemy of love, he betrayed the Savior. The prophet Ezekiel also showed that the devil knew the heavenly mysteries, when he testifies in reproving language that the devil had been in paradise with God and had possessed precious [Col. 0118C] stones; and the same Apostle signified by those stones the mysteries of divine teaching. Yet this profited him nothing, because, forgetful of love, he rushed into pride.

“And if I have all knowledge.” Knowledge profits nothing if love is absent. Thus it profited the scribes and Pharisees nothing when the Savior said: “You have the key of knowledge, and you neither enter yourselves nor allow others to enter” (Luke VI). For by envy they corrupted love and reduced its knowledge to nothing. Tertullian and Novatian also possessed no small knowledge; but because through zeal they lost the bonds of love, they turned to schism and created heresies to their own destruction.

“And if I have all faith, so that I remove mountains.” To perform miracles or to cast out demons through faith is the power and glory of God; it contributes nothing to merit unless one is devoted to good conduct, as I mentioned above.

“And if I distribute all my possessions.” The matter is clear: even if all one’s possessions are expended, it profits nothing when love is neglected, because love is the head of religion, and whoever lacks the head lacks life.

“And if I hand over my body so that I may be burned, it profits me nothing.” Without love nothing profits, because love is the foundation of religion. Whatever, therefore, is done without love is fleeting.

(Cass.) Without it no one can ascend to perfect purity of heart and to the contemplation of God. Hence we have seen some people despise the greatest resources of this world—not only many talents of gold and silver, but even the magnificence of estates—and afterward become agitated over a knife, a stylus, or a pen. If they had kept the contemplation of a pure heart steadfast, they would certainly never have admitted, over small things, what they had preferred to reject utterly lest they incur it over great and precious possessions. Indeed, some people often guard a book with such zeal that they do not allow anyone even lightly to read or touch it, and thereby incur occasions of impatience and death; whereas they are moved to acquire the rewards of patience and love.

Although they have scattered all their riches for Christ’s love, they nevertheless retain their former affection for small things and sometimes grow violently angry over them. As though they did not possess apostolic love, they become unfruitful and barren in everything. The blessed Apostle foresaw this in the Spirit, saying: “And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and hand over my body so that I may be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing.”

Thus it is clearly proved that perfection is not immediately attained through nakedness and the deprivation of all possessions, or through the rejection of ranks and dignities, unless that love is present whose members the Apostle describes and which consists solely in purity of heart. For what else is it not to be jealous, not to be puffed up, not to be irritated, not to act wrongly, not to seek one’s own interests, not to rejoice over iniquity, not to think evil, and the rest, than always to offer God a perfect and most pure heart and to guard it untouched by every disturbance?

All things belonging to this grace must therefore be done and sought by us. For its sake we must undertake fasts, vigils, labors, bodily nakedness, reading, and the other virtues, so that through them we may prepare and preserve our heart unharmed from every harmful passion and, relying on these steps, ascend to the perfection of love. You see, therefore, that nothing more precious, nothing more perfect, nothing more sublime—and, so to speak, nothing more enduring—can be found than love. For love never fails; without it not only the most excellent kinds of spiritual gifts but even the glory of martyrdom itself is emptied.

Whoever, therefore, has been founded in the perfection of this love must ascend by a higher degree to that more sublime fear of love, which is generated not by the terror of punishments or the desire for rewards, but by the greatness of love. By it a son reveres a most indulgent father, a brother reveres a brother, a friend a friend, and a wife her husband with anxious affection, fearing not his blows or insults but even the slightest offense against love. In everything—not only in deeds but also in words—he is continually filled with awed piety, lest the warmth of that affection toward him grow even slightly cold.

One of the prophets elegantly expressed the magnificence of this fear (Isa. XXXIII): “Riches,” he says, “of salvation are wisdom and knowledge; the fear of the Lord is itself his treasure.” He could not have expressed the dignity and merit of this fear more clearly than by saying that the riches of our salvation, which consist in true wisdom and knowledge of God, cannot be preserved except by the fear of the Lord. To this fear, therefore, holy sinners are summoned by prophetic utterances, as the Psalmist says: “Fear the Lord, you his saints, for there is no lack for those who fear him.” Whoever fears God with this fear is certain to lack nothing necessary for perfection.

Love is magnanimous; it is kind. Love is not jealous, is not puffed up, does not act wrongly, is not ambitious, does not seek what belongs to itself, is not irritated, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity; rather, it rejoices with the truth, endures all things, believes all things, hopes all things, bears all things. Love never fails.

(Ambr.) He taught such great praises of love that it was not without reason that he seemed to place it before all other things, and to say that those who devote themselves to other commandments labor in vain if they do not obey this one. Hence the apostle John also says: “God is love,” and whoever does not have love should know that he does not have God. Therefore Paul says in another Epistle (Eph. II): “But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great mercy showed mercy to us.” Whoever therefore does not have love is ungrateful toward God’s mercy, because he does not love that by which he was saved. Thus they should learn how grievously those sin who place food before brotherly love. For love benefits us in the present and remains with God forever.

(Cass.) All gifts are granted for use and necessity for a time; when their dispensation has been completed, they will unquestionably pass away. Love, however, will not be interrupted by any period. Not only does it work profitably in us in the present world, but in the future, when the burden of bodily necessity has been cast off, it will remain much more effective and excellent. It will never be corrupted by any weakness, but through perpetual incorruption will cling to God with greater ardor and more intense devotion.

(Aug.) What is as magnanimous as to die for the impious? What is as kind as to love even one’s enemies? Love alone is not oppressed by another’s happiness, because it is not jealous; love alone is not exalted by its own happiness, because it is not puffed up. It alone is not pricked by knowledge of evil, because it does not act wrongly; it endures all things, believes all things, hopes all things, bears all things.

It endures everything in the present life because it believes everything concerning the future life; it bears everything inflicted here because it hopes for everything promised there. It does not seek what belongs to itself. Indeed, people would not be lovers of money unless they thought themselves superior in proportion as they were richer.
