Love is opposed to this sickness: it does not seek what belongs to itself, that is, it does not rejoice in private superiority. Therefore it is rightly not puffed up. Love believes all things, at least among those whom it joins together and makes one.

(Greg.) “Love,” he says, “is patient, is kind, is not jealous, is not puffed up, does not act wrongly, is not ambitious, does not seek what belongs to itself, is not irritated, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth.” Love is patient because it endures the evils inflicted upon it with equanimity. It is kind because it generously supplies good things in return for evils. It is not jealous because, since it desires nothing in the present world, it does not know how to envy earthly successes. It is not puffed up because, while it anxiously desires the reward of inward recompense, it does not exalt itself over outward goods.

It does not act wrongly because, as it expands itself solely in love of God and neighbor, it ignores whatever departs from uprightness. It is not ambitious because, while it eagerly strives inwardly toward its own goods, it in no way covets the possessions of others. It does not seek what belongs to itself because it neglects as alien all the transitory things it possesses here, recognizing that nothing is properly its own except what remains with it.

It is not irritated because, even when provoked by injuries, it does not arouse itself to any movement of vengeance, while it awaits greater rewards after great labors. It does not think evil because, grounding its mind in the love of purity and uprooting all hatred from its roots, it does not know how to turn over in the mind what defiles it. It does not rejoice over iniquity because, having begun with love alone toward everyone, it does not exult over the destruction of its adversaries. It rejoices with the truth because, loving others as it loves itself, it becomes glad at whatever uprightness it sees in them, as though rejoicing in the increase of its own progress.

(Aug.) Among the other virtues that the apostle Paul enumerates—love does not envy, does not act wrongly, is not irritated, does not think evil, and so forth—he gathers four of its virtues at the end, saying: “It endures all things, believes all things, hopes all things, bears all things; love never fails.”

Of these four virtues of holy love, therefore, it is fitting to speak to your holiness. It is pleasing first to consider how, like four hinges embracing the world, it has possessed the whole world. Let us therefore, if you please, seek examples of certain saints—those who were possessed by these virtues of holy love—and assign one virtue to each, so that we may recognize that all are present in all. For everyone who endures piously believes rightly; everyone who believes rightly hopes for something; and whoever hopes bears up, lest he fall away from hope.

But now let us see who these people are, whose faith we may be able to attain insofar as we are helped from above. The virtue of love that endures all things shone forth in holy Noah; that believes all things, in holy Abraham; that hopes all things, in our fathers, that is, in the people of Israel; and that bears all things, in our very head, the Lord Jesus Christ, who is true love, which never fails. Nor should your love consider the other saints alien to these virtues. Know that, because of the brevity of time and the discourse undertaken, they have been passed over in such a way that you nevertheless know with absolute certainty that all are in Christ and Christ is in all.

But now let us see how holy Noah possessed—or was possessed by—the virtue of love that endures all things. God foretold to him that, as human wickedness increased, He would destroy the world by a flood. Immediately warned, Noah took refuge in wood and, leaving behind the beauty of the open fields, confined himself within the narrowness of the ark. He endured the roar of heaven, the sound of the waters, and the crashing of the storms. After all this, he who was accustomed to rejoice in human companionship became, in a way, the companion of serpents and wild beasts.

Nor was this man terrified that beasts were with him in the ark. Rather, once wildness recognized its order, because humanity had recognized its own, the animals obeyed the commanding man, because they understood that the man had obeyed the higher Lord. In Noah it was shown what Adam had lost by despising the commandment, and it was demonstrated that human beings can even rule beasts if they submit obedience to their Creator.

This holy man awaited and endured the end of the flood; the ark was not abandoned before the cause of the beasts had come to an end. The good man bears the wicked, and until, at the end, he is separated bodily, he remains inwardly and is not separated in heart.

If you are a soul that desires to possess the virtue of love that endures all things, leave the world and take refuge in the wood of the cross. Do not fear the storms and whirlwinds of this flood. You will not be drowned if you are carried by the wood; he who deigned to create knows how to steer. Let only the virtue of love be present, the love that endures all things; let no circumstance tear you away from the solidity of the ark. Remain good and endure the wicked. For it is better, remaining inside, to endure the wicked for the sake of the good than to go outside, perish, and abandon both the good and the wicked.

If beasts are with you—that is, if there are with you in the Church heretics or schismatics teaching perverse things and holding false opinions, or even wicked Catholics themselves, who seek, like beasts, to devour souls—let them be endured until the end of the age, like the end of the flood. Even if they roar and gnash their teeth and try to break apart the ark itself, do not be afraid. When the flood is over, let an empty and thorny forest receive them, while fertile earth receives you.

After the end of the age the impious will be carried off to the outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth; the godly will be received by the land of the living. Holy Noah himself also offered sacrifice to God after the end of the flood, but from clean animals, not from unclean ones. Clean and unclean animals were able to float together in the ark, but the wicked did not reach the sacrifice of God.

But let us now move on, so that we may examine the remaining matters. Let that holy man Abraham come forward and teach us by his example to possess the virtue of love that believes all things. At a single summons he did not hesitate to leave his native land, home, and family. Everything is abandoned so that he may obey the Lord’s command. God said to him: “Go out from your kindred and from your house, and come to whatever land I shall show you” (Gen. XII).

This holy man did not think or say to himself: “Where shall I go? To whom shall I entrust myself? To what land shall I travel?” Rather, as soon as he heard, he rose, ran, hastened, and hurried onward. He did not see the promised land, but by believing he held it firmly. He walked on the right path and did not turn aside elsewhere with wandering steps, because the one who sent him to an unknown land did not abandon him. Nor did He deceive him. The reward was given to the believer: he reached the land, was enlarged and multiplied, became rich from poverty, powerful from insignificance, and was enriched with every good.

In him was fulfilled what the Lord promised His disciples in the Gospel, saying: “If anyone has left a house, or a field, or parents [the reading “varentes” is uncertain] for the sake of my name, in this life he will receive a hundredfold, and in the age to come he will obtain eternal life.”

The reward of this faith was still increased, and a son was promised to the old man. The virtue of love that believes all things was present: he heard, rejoiced, and loved more greatly. He received a son from a barren wife, whom barrenness and age had already deprived of hope of bearing, and in that son he held most firmly the promised blessing of all the nations.

Yet love still tests him, commends him once tested, and shows his descendants that he placed nothing before God. The Lord called him from heaven, saying (Gen. XXII): “Abraham, Abraham.” And he, like an obedient servant, said, “Here I am.” The Lord said: “Take your son, the one you love, Isaac, and go into the high land, and offer him as a burnt offering on one of the mountains that I shall tell you.”

Even this command did not disturb or break the faithful servant. For the virtue of love that believes all things was present in him. He rose, went home, saddled the ass, gathered wood, took the sword and fire, brought the boy with him, and went to the place.

Then Isaac, now attentive, questioned his father, saying: “Father.” He replied: “What is it, son?” The son said: “Behold, here are the fire and the wood; where is the sheep that you are going to sacrifice as a burnt offering?” The father answered: “God will provide Himself a sheep for the sacrifice, my son.”

Here I see a great and profound mystery. Abraham carried one thing in his heart and promised another to his son; yet neither did the things he promised deceive the son, nor did any weakness change his heart from its purpose.

It is pleasing to consider another virtue of love, the virtue that hopes all things. We recognize that above we assigned this to the people of Israel and to our fathers. For this virtue’s voice is heard in that familiar prophetic passage: “In you our fathers hoped; they hoped, and you delivered them” (Ps. XXI).

They themselves were commanded to flee from Egypt, and a land flowing with milk and honey was promised to them. They crossed the Red Sea and came into the wilderness. The hope of love led them, so that they might learn to love God freely. The reward of faith was given to them also; for He cannot fail to repay who deigns to make Himself a debtor. After the wilderness they sucked honey from the rock and ate the bread of heaven. They were not deprived of what they desired and hoped for; they also received the promised land.

Let every soul that has been embraced by the virtue of this love arise and flee from Egypt—that is, from the desire for this age—and proceed to the Red Sea, namely, the baptism of Christ, red because it has been dyed with Christ’s blood. Let enemies pursue: sins together with their author, the devil, like the Egyptians with their king Pharaoh. Let them rage and follow the fugitives. What do you fear? They rage only as far as the water. You will enter, and they will enter after you; but the water, turned against them, will be their destruction, while it will contribute to your salvation. It will overwhelm them and wash you; it will condemn them and free you.

Afterward, receive honey from the rock, with which you may satisfy your thirst. For the rock was Christ, from whose commandments, as from springs of sweetness, you will be satisfied. You will also taste the bread of the one who said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John VI). You will taste and see how sweet the Lord is.

And if the virtue of love that hopes all things is prominent in you, you must pass through the wilderness; that is, use this world as though you did not use it, and recognize that you are a stranger on this road if you desire to enter the promised land. This is the land of which the Prophet sings and says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVIII).

The final virtue of love remains, the virtue that bears all things and never fails. We see that this belongs to our very head, the Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore it is placed last, since Christ is the end of the law.

How much He Himself endured for us, I think your love cannot fail to know. Nevertheless, I shall say something about it—something worthy, at least, concerning so great a subject. First, that God became man, that the Word became flesh; that He did many good things and suffered evils; that He raised the dead and died; that His singular patience endured the devil as tempter and the disciple as betrayer; that He endured Judas himself as a thief before he showed himself a betrayer, and before the experience of chains, the cross, and death, He did not deny him the kiss of peace on his deceitful lips.

But how much did He endure in death itself? He bore the flames of hatred and the tongues of ministers of an evil heart. The Jews cried out, “Crucify, crucify!” And, in order that the Jews might remain guilty, the innocent One was crucified by them. The Son of God is led to the cross and struck in the face, He who is the true palm of victory. He is crowned with thorns, He who came to break the thorns of sins. He is bound, He who frees the fettered. He is hung upon wood, He who raises the fallen. The fountain of life is given vinegar to drink. Discipline is scourged; salvation is wounded; life dies. Death killed life for a time, so that death might be killed by life forever.

What did the Jews gain by exulting in this death of Christ as though they were victorious? While they feared to lose an earthly and fleeting kingdom, they did not hesitate to kill the King of heaven and earth. Yet they did not become victors as they thought. If they conquered, how did they lose the kingdom? How have they remained servants to this day? This is the reason: Christ was killed by them.

The rulers of the Jews said among themselves, as the Evangelist relates: “You see,” they said, “that the whole world has gone after him. If we let him live, the Romans will come and take away both our place and our kingdom” (John XI). They killed Christ, and they lost both their place and their kingdom.

What did it profit you, O mad Jews, that you committed so great a crime? Because you refused to serve Christ the Lord as was fitting, did you therefore escape His dominion? While kings serve Him, you serve them; you have become wicked servants of the good servants of Christ. Through them He crushes your obstinacy, through them He scatters your counsels, and through them He will repay your crimes upon your own heads.

Thus far Augustine.

Whether prophecies will be abolished, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be destroyed—for we know in part and prophesy in part; but when what is perfect has come, what is in part will be abolished.

(Ambr.) He said that all the gifts of the spiritual powers would be abolished because they cannot comprehend as much as the truth itself contains, nor can we grasp or express the fullness of truth. For how can a human tongue encompass everything that belongs to God? Therefore our imperfection will be destroyed. What is true will not be abolished; rather, when what is lacking is added to the imperfect, the imperfect will be destroyed. The destruction is of imperfection, when what is imperfect is completed into what is true.

“When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child; when I became a man, I abolished the things that belonged to childhood.” He said this because the saints, when they depart from this world, necessarily find more than they now think, just as the apostle John said concerning the Savior: “Then we shall see him as he is.”

In this life, therefore, we are children in comparison with the future life. For just as this life is imperfect, so also is knowledge. “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face.” It is clear that now images are seen through faith, but then the realities themselves.

(Greg.) Let us look upon Paul, as though wrapped in a certain darkness, covered with the swaddling clothes of infancy. He says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then I shall know as I am known.”

If he had not seen himself to be an infant in age when compared with the apprehension of heavenly things, he would in no way have prefaced this comparison by saying: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child, understood as a child, and thought as a child.” We therefore ascend to youthful strength when, with a strong understanding, we behold the life toward which we are striving. But now, because the sharpness of our intention is blunted by its weakness from the inward light, our mind is held bound in the swaddling clothes of infancy.

(Aug.) For it is written in the Psalm: “Your knowledge has been made wondrous beyond me; it has prevailed, and I cannot attain it” (Ps. CXXXVIII). “Beyond me,” I understand to mean: I perceive how wondrous and incomprehensible is your knowledge, by which you made me, since I cannot even comprehend myself, whom you made. Yet “in my meditation the fire shall burn” (Ps. XXXVIII), so that I may always seek your face.

I know that Wisdom is an incorporeal substance and that it is the light in which those things are seen that are not seen by bodily eyes. Yet such a great and spiritual man says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face.”

If we ask what this mirror is and of what kind, surely the answer occurs that nothing but an image is seen in a mirror. We have therefore tried to see through this image, which is what we are, however imperfectly, the one by whom we were made, as through a mirror.

But because he added “in an enigma,” this is unknown to many who do not know the letters in which there is a certain teaching concerning modes of expression, which the Greeks call *tropoi* (τρόποι). It is extremely difficult and unusual to pronounce the names of each of these modes, or tropes, in Latin. Hence some of our translators, unwilling to use the Greek term, interpreted the Apostle’s expression “which things are in allegory” by circumlocution, saying: “which things signify one thing through another.”

There are several forms of this trope, that is, of allegory, among which is what is called an enigma. What, then, is allegory except a trope in which one thing is understood through another? An example is the passage to the Thessalonians: “Therefore let us not sleep as the rest do, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night; and those who are drunk, are drunk at night. But let us who are of the day be sober” (1 Thess. V).

This allegory, however, is not an enigma, for unless someone is very dull, its meaning is readily apparent. An enigma, to explain it briefly, is an obscure allegory, such as “the leeches had three daughters,” and other similar sayings.

But when the Apostle named allegory, he found it not in a word but in an event. From the two sons of Abraham, one by a slave woman and the other by a free woman—something that was not merely said but actually done—he showed that two covenants were to be understood (Gal. IV). Before he explained it, it was obscure; therefore that allegory, which is the general name, could specifically be called an enigma.

Accordingly, as it seems to me, just as by the name “mirror” he wished an image to be understood, so by the name “enigma” he wished a likeness to be understood, yet one that was obscure and difficult to discern.

Since, therefore, by the names “mirror” and “enigma” the Apostle’s various likenesses can be understood—likenesses suited to the understanding of God in whatever way this is possible—nothing is more suitable than that which is not without reason called His image.

Let no one therefore be surprised that even in this mode of seeing, which has been granted to this life through a mirror, namely, in an enigma, we labor to see in some fashion. The word “enigma” would not sound here if vision were easy.

In the Gospel also the Lord says to the disciples: “I tell you that their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.” Therefore, just as they see, so shall we see; but we do not yet see in that way. For this reason the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face.”

This vision is therefore reserved for us as the reward of faith. Concerning it John also says: “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John III).

The face of God must be understood as His manifestation, not as some bodily member such as we possess and call by that name. The saints will therefore see God in this body; but whether they will see Him through it as through the body we now use to see the sun, moon, stars, sea, earth, and the things in it is a considerable question.

For it is difficult to say that the saints will then have such bodies that they will be unable to close and open their eyes whenever they wish. It is more difficult still to say that there anyone who closes his eyes will not see God. For if the prophet Elisha, while absent in body, saw his servant Gehazi receiving the gifts given to him by Naaman the Syrian (2 Kings V), how much more will the saints in that spiritual body see all things—not only when they close their eyes, but even from places where they are bodily absent?

And that expression of the Apostle, “face to face,” does not compel us to believe that we shall see God through this bodily face, where bodily eyes are located. We shall see Him by the Spirit without interruption. For unless there were also a face of the inner person, the same Apostle would not say (2 Cor. III): “But we, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.”

Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, just as I have been fully known.

**(Ambrose.)** That is, I shall see what has been promised, just as I am seen—that is, as present before God, where Christ is.

**(Augustine.)** Let us not try to transfer to that vision of God, which is promised to us in the resurrection, the lust of the eyes belonging to this world. Rather, let us devote ourselves with pious affection to cleansing our hearts, and let us not imagine a bodily face when the Apostle says, “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face,” especially since he expressed himself more clearly: “Now I know in part, but then I shall know fully, just as I have been fully known” [Col. 0127B]. If, then, we shall know God with a bodily face, we have now been known by his bodily face; for he says, “Then I shall know fully, just as I have been fully known.” Who, therefore, would not understand that in this passage he also wished to signify that face of ours of which he says elsewhere: “But we, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord”? From the glory, that is, of faith into the glory of eternal contemplation. For this is what he means: this is the transformation by which the inner person is renewed from day to day.

**(Gregory.)** It is likewise written in Job: “As if by stealth my ear receives the veins of his whisper” (Job 4). The ear of the heart secretly receives the veins of the heavenly whisper, because the mind, breathed upon by the subtlety of inward speech, recognizes it suddenly and secretly [Col. 0127C]. Unless it withdraws itself from outward desires, it does not penetrate inward things. It hides itself in order to hear, and it hears in order to hide itself, because, withdrawn from visible things, it sees invisible things, and, filled with invisible things, it completely despises visible things.

It should be noted, however, that when he says, “As if by stealth my ear receives the veins of his whisper,” A whisper is the speech of a hidden word, the very utterance of an inward inspiration; the veins of the whisper are said to be the origins of the causes by which this inspiration is conveyed to the mind. God opens, as it were, the veins of his whisper when he secretly reveals to us by what ways he comes to the ear of our understanding. Sometimes he pierces us with love; sometimes with fear; sometimes, by showing that present things are nothing, he raises us to love eternal desires [Col. 0127D]. Sometimes he first reveals eternal things, so that temporal things may afterward appear worthless. Sometimes he discloses our own evils to us and extends us so far that we grieve even over the evils of others. Sometimes he sets the evils of others before our eyes and, having wonderfully pierced us, corrects us from our own perversity.

To hear secretly the veins of the divine whisper is therefore to recognize faintly and inwardly the hidden ways of divine inspiration. Yet we may also understand “whisper” and “the veins of the whisper” in another way. One who whispers speaks secretly and does not make his voice distinct, but merely imitates one.

So long as we are weighed down by the corruption of the flesh, we cannot see the brightness of divine power as he himself remains immutable, because the sharpness of our weakness cannot endure even that which shines upon us intolerably from the ray of his eternity [Col. 0128A]. When almighty God reveals himself to us through fissures of contemplation, he does not speak to us, but whispers; for although he does not disclose himself fully, he nevertheless manifests certain things about himself to the human mind.

Then, however, he no longer whispers but speaks, when his definite appearance is revealed to us. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “I shall openly announce the Father to you” (John 16); hence John says: “We shall see him as he is” (1 John 3); hence Paul says: “Then I shall know fully, just as I have been fully known.” But now the divine whisper has as many veins reaching us as there are created works over which the divinity itself presides. For while we behold all created things, we are lifted up in wonder at the Creator.

[Col. 0128B] Just as flowing water, entering fissures, seeks channels through which to increase, and spreads more widely the more open the channels it finds, so we, while gathering knowledge of the divine through careful consideration of his creation, open to ourselves, as it were, the veins of his whisper. For through what we see made, we marvel at the power of its maker; and through those things that are publicly visible, what lies hidden in secret flows out to us.

“But faith, hope, and charity remain, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.”

**(Ambrose.)** Charity is rightly the greatest, because it brought it about that faith should be preached and that there should be hope of the future life, as I mentioned above. Hence the Apostle John also says: “By this we know his charity, because he laid down his life for us” (1 John 3). Charity is therefore rightly the greatest, since through it the human race has been restored [Col. 0128C].

**(Augustine.)** Thus there are three things by which all knowledge and prophecy serve: faith, hope, and charity. Faith is succeeded by the vision that we shall see, and hope by the blessedness itself to which we shall come; but charity will rather increase when those two fall away. If we love by believing what we do not yet see, how much more shall we love when we begin to see it? And if we love by hoping for what we have not yet reached, how much more when we have reached it? “Faith, hope, and charity remain,” he says, “these three; but the greatest of these is charity.” For when each person has reached eternal things, and those two have fallen away, charity will remain greater and more certain.

Faith is what makes us avoid the contagion of vices through fear of the future judgment and punishments [Col. 0128D]. Hope, withdrawing our mind from present things, makes us despise all bodily pleasures in expectation of heavenly rewards. Charity, kindling us with the ardor of the mind toward love of Christ and the fruit of spiritual virtues, makes us detest with utter hatred whatever is contrary to them. Although these three may appear to tend toward one end, they are nevertheless separated from one another by great degrees of excellence.

The first two properly belong to human beings who, striving toward progress, have not yet conceived an affection for the virtues. The third belongs especially to God and to those who have received within themselves the image and likeness of God. For he alone does what is good without being urged by fear or by the prospect of reward, but solely out of love for goodness. “The Lord has made everything for himself,” as Solomon says (Prov. 16). By the excellence of his own goodness he grants an abundance of good things to the worthy and the unworthy alike, because he cannot be wearied by injuries or moved in a suffering manner by human iniquities, remaining always perfect goodness and an unchangeable nature.

## CHAPTER XIV

**He demonstrates the superiority of prophecy over the gift of tongues and explains how both gifts are to be used.**

“Pursue charity; desire spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy.”

After charity he urges that the pursuit of prophecy should be held in greater esteem. For although the spiritual degrees that he enumerates are great, this gift is nevertheless better because it benefits the Church, so that all may learn the meaning of the divine law. Whatever someone devotes his mind to, in that very thing he receives a gift, as Solomon says: “To know the law is the highest understanding.” Knowledge supported by charity is not puffed up but gentle, benefiting everyone for the common good.

“One who speaks in a tongue does not speak to human beings but to God; for no one hears him, though in the Spirit he speaks mysteries.”

**(Ambrose.)** This is what he means: one who speaks in an unknown tongue speaks to God, because God knows everything, whereas human beings do not. Therefore there is no benefit from this activity; he speaks in the Spirit, not with understanding, because he himself does not know what he says.

“But one who prophesies speaks to human beings for edification, exhortation, and consolation.” A person is edified when he learns the solution to questions. Exhortation takes place when he is inspired to desire the gift of prophecy. He is consoled because in hope he sees contempt for discipline. Knowledge of the law strengthens minds and urges them toward progress in a better hope.

“One who speaks in a tongue edifies himself, but one who prophesies edifies the Church.” Because he alone perhaps knows what he is saying, he edifies only himself; but one who prophesies edifies the whole people. Everyone understands what he says.

He calls prophets interpreters of the Scriptures. Just as a prophet speaks of future things that are unknown, so here, when someone reveals the meaning of the Scriptures—which is hidden from many—he is said to prophesy.

“I want you all to speak in tongues, but especially that you may prophesy.” He could not forbid speaking in tongues, because above he had said that this gift was of the Holy Spirit; but the pursuit of prophecy was to be preferred because it is more useful. “The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in a tongue, unless he interprets.” If he is able to interpret, he is not inferior, because he edifies the Church. What benefits everyone is greater. He speaks in tongues through God’s gift and also interprets, as did those twelve in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 4).

“Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what benefit shall I bring you, unless I speak to you either in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in teaching?”

All these expressions have one meaning: no one can teach unless he is understood. Yet these four forms can be applied to the fourfold understanding of sacred Scripture: history, tropology, allegory, and anagogy.

Of these four kinds of interpretation the blessed Apostle says: “Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what benefit shall I bring you unless I speak to you either in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in teaching?”

Revelation belongs to allegory, by which what the historical narrative conceals is disclosed through spiritual meaning and exposition. For example, if we attempt to explain the passage: “Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. 10), and likewise, “They all ate the same spiritual food” and “all drank the same spiritual drink from the rock that followed them”—“and the rock was Christ” [Col. 0130B]. This exposition, when compared with the prefiguration of the body and blood of Christ, which we receive daily, contains the principle of allegory.

The knowledge likewise mentioned by the Apostle is tropology. Through it we discern with prudent examination everything pertaining to practical judgment—whether things are useful or honorable. Thus, for example, we are instructed to judge among ourselves whether it is fitting for a woman to pray to God with her head uncovered. As has been said, this reasoning contains a moral meaning.

Prophecy, which the Apostle placed third, signifies anagogy, by which speech is transferred to invisible and future things. Thus: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus. For this we say to you by the word of the Lord: we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first” (1 Thess. 4). The figure of anagogy is set forth in the form of exhortation.

Teaching, however, unfolds the simple order of historical exposition. It contains no more obscure meaning than what resounds in the words themselves, as in the passage: “For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he rose on the third day, and that he appeared to Cephas” (1 Cor. 15); and: “God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. 4). Or: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deut. 6).

“Yet even lifeless things that produce sound, whether flute or lyre, if they do not give distinct notes, how will it be known what is played on the flute or what is played on the lyre? For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle?”

Because examples persuade more easily than words, he commends the point by examples, so that they may readily understand that those who cannot interpret should not speak in tongues in the Church. For why does someone speak if no one understands him? [Col. 0131A] “So also you, unless you give through the tongue a meaningful utterance, how will it be known what you are saying? For you will be speaking into the air”—that is, accomplishing nothing.

There are, so to speak, many kinds of languages in the world, and nothing is without a voice. There are indeed many kinds of languages, he says, but they have their own meaningful sounds, so that they may be understood. “Therefore, if I do not know the power of the sound, I shall be a barbarian to the one to whom I speak, and the one who speaks shall be a barbarian to me.”

He does not urge them to strive toward a situation in which they appear to one another as barbarians through an unknown language. Rather, since this concerns concord, they must strive so that, through unanimity of understanding, they may rejoice together in a common joy.

“So also you, since you are zealous for spiritual gifts, seek to excel in them for the edification of the Church, so that you may prophesy.” For it is beneficial to explain the Scriptures. The mind is stirred and rejoices when it grasps something from the Scriptures; and the more eagerly it applies itself to this, the more it abandons vices. Therefore he urges them to devote their effort to this.

“Therefore, let the one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret.” He says that the person who desires to speak in tongues ought to pray that he may receive the gift of interpretation, so that his effort may benefit others.

“If I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my understanding is without fruit.”

It is evident that our mind does not know what is being said when our tongue speaks a language it does not know, just as Latins sometimes sing in Greek, delighted by the sound of the words while nevertheless not knowing what they are saying. The spirit, therefore, which is given in baptism, knows what the mind is praying while it speaks or prays in a language unknown to it; but the mind, which is the soul, is without fruit. For what benefit can someone have who does not know what he is saying? [Col. 0131C]

“What then? I shall pray with the spirit; I shall pray also with the understanding. I shall sing a psalm with the spirit; I shall sing a psalm also with the understanding.”

He means that when someone speaks in a language he knows, he prays both with the spirit and with the understanding. Not only does his spirit—which, as he said, was given in baptism—know what is being prayed, but his mind also knows it. Augustine explains the matter similarly concerning the psalm: the mind is not ignorant of what is being sung.

The spirit is distinguished from the mind by this very clear testimony: “If I pray in a tongue,” he says, “my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful.” When “tongue” is understood in this passage to mean obscure and mystical signs, no one is edified by hearing what he does not understand if the understanding of the mind is removed from them.

Hence he also says: “The one who speaks in a tongue does not speak to human beings but to God; for no one hears him, although in the spirit he speaks mysteries.” This sufficiently indicates that here he calls “tongue” that in which there are signs like images and likenesses of things, which require the attention of the mind in order to be understood. Once they are understood, he says that they are in the Spirit, not in the mind.

Thus he says more plainly: “If you bless in the spirit, how will the one who occupies the place of the unlearned say ‘Amen’ at your blessing, since he does not know what you are saying?” Since the tongue—that is, the bodily member which we move in the mouth when we speak—produces signs of things rather than the things themselves, he used the word “tongue” figuratively for any utterance of signs before they are understood.

When understanding, which belongs properly to the mind, is added, there is revelation, recognition, prophecy, or teaching. Therefore he says: “If I come to you speaking in tongues, what benefit shall I bring you unless I speak to you in revelation, or in recognition, or in prophecy, or in teaching?” That is, once understanding has been added to the signs—that is, to the tongue—what is being done is carried out not only in the spirit but also in the mind.

Accordingly, when signs were shown in the spirit through certain likenesses of bodily things, if the activity of the mind had not been added so that they might also be understood, there was not yet prophecy. The one who interpreted what another had seen was more truly a prophet than the one who had seen it.

It is therefore clear that prophecy reaches the mind more than that spirit which, in a particular sense, is called “spirit”: a certain power of the soul inferior to the mind, in which likenesses of bodily things are represented [Col. 0132B]. Thus Joseph was more truly a prophet, because he understood what the seven ears of grain and the seven cows signified, than Pharaoh, who saw them in a dream (Gen. 41). The spirit of the latter was shaped so that he might see; the mind of the former was illuminated so that he might understand. Hence in the one there was a tongue, in the other prophecy: in the one, the imagination of things; in the other, the interpretation of the imagination.

The one who sees in the spirit only the signs of the things signified, through images of bodily things, is therefore a lesser prophet; greater is the one endowed solely with their understanding; but greatest is the prophet who excels in both, seeing in the Spirit the meaningful likenesses of bodily things and understanding them through the vitality of the mind [Col. 0132C].

Daniel’s excellence was tested and proved in this way. He both told the king the dream which the king had seen and disclosed what it signified (Dan. 4–5). The bodily images themselves had been expressed in his spirit, and their meaning had been revealed in his mind.

“Yet if you bless in the spirit—”

**(Ambrose.)** That is, if you praise God in a tongue unknown to those listening, “how will the one who occupies the place of the unlearned say ‘Amen’ at your blessing, since he does not know what you are saying?” The unlearned hearer, not understanding what he hears, does not know the end of the prayer and does not respond “Amen”—that is, “true”—so that the blessing may be confirmed. For those who respond “Amen” complete the confirmation of the prayer, so that all that has been said may be confirmed in the minds of the hearers by the testimony of truth.

“For you indeed give thanks well.” He speaks of the person who says what he himself knows, because he knows what he is saying. “But the other is not edified.” If you come together for the edification of the Church, things must be said that the hearers understand. For what benefit is there in someone speaking in a tongue known only to himself, so that the one who hears gains nothing? He ought therefore to remain silent in the Church, so that those may speak who benefit the hearers.

“I thank my God that I speak in the tongue of all of you.”

Since above he said that speaking in tongues was a gift of the Holy Spirit, he therefore attributes to God the fact that he speaks in the tongues of them all. And lest he seem to say this out of envy, as though he were a rival, he shows that he speaks in all these tongues, but because this is not greatly beneficial he adds: “But in the Church I would rather speak five words with my understanding, so that I may instruct others also, than ten thousand words in a tongue.”

He says that it is more useful to speak a few words in an intelligible exposition—words that everyone understands—than to give a lengthy discourse in obscurity. These people were Hebrews, who sometimes used the Syriac language and more often Hebrew in their discourses or offerings, as a mark of distinction. They gloried in being called Hebrews because of the merit of Abraham; but the same Apostle regarded this as nothing, saying: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

“Brothers, do not become children in your understanding. Be infants in malice, but be mature in your understanding.”

He wants them to be mature, so that they may know what is necessary for the instruction of the Church; abandoning malice and errors, they should pursue what benefits their brothers. For the person who acts so as to benefit someone—especially a brother—is mature in understanding.

“In the law it is written: ‘By people of other tongues and by lips of others I shall speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.’”

The Lord said this concerning those whom he foresaw would not believe in the Savior. To speak in other tongues and with other lips means to preach the New Testament, as the prophet Jeremiah says: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I established with their fathers” (Jer. 31). That is, he would speak in an altered manner, with the arrangement changed from the way the words of the old law had stood.

When they heard that the Sabbath was being annulled, the new moons abolished, circumcision brought to an end, sacrifices changed, foods previously forbidden permitted to be eaten [Col. 0133C], and Christ preached as God from God—this was to speak with other lips and in other tongues—but the faithless did not wish to obey God.

This may also be understood as follows: many of the Jews were malicious, and therefore it was not fitting that the Gospel should be spoken to them openly in revelation. He spoke to them in parables, so that they might understand that it was not being revealed to them because they were evil, and that they were not correcting themselves so as to make themselves worthy to hear the words of God through explanation.

Hence the disciples say to the Lord: “Lord, why do you speak to them in parables?” And the Lord replies: “Because it has been given to you to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to them it has not been given, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand” (Luke 8). This was so that the unworthy might not receive salvation; yet, even when they recognized that it had happened according to their deserts, they did not turn and seek to satisfy God.

“Thus tongues are for a sign.” That is, through the veil of an unknown tongue the words of God have been obscured, so that they may not be seen by the faithless. When unknown tongues are heard, it is a sign that this has happened because of faithlessness, so that the hearer may not understand.

“Not for believers but for unbelievers.” That is, tongues serve to conceal meanings from unbelievers. “But prophecy is not for unbelievers but for believers.” It is not fitting for believers to hear tongues they do not understand; they are fitting for unbelievers, who are not worthy to understand, as the prophet Isaiah says: “Go and say to this people: ‘You shall hear with your ears and shall not understand,’” and so forth (Isa. 6).

“Therefore, if the whole Church comes together in one place and all speak in tongues, and unlearned people or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are mad?”

It is clear that if everyone speaks in different tongues, a kind of disordered tumult arises among the people, as though they were suffering from frenzy.

“But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or an unlearned person enters, he is convicted by all, he is judged by all; the secrets of his heart are also made manifest, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you.”

When the hearer understands and is understood, sees God praised and Christ worshiped, he recognizes that the religion is true and worthy of reverence. He sees that nothing deceptive and nothing hidden in darkness is being done, as among the pagans, whose eyes are veiled lest, looking upon what they call sacred rites, they perceive themselves to be mocked by various vanities.

Every deception seeks darkness and displays false things as true. Among us, therefore, nothing is done cunningly or under a veil; rather, one God is simply praised, from whom all things come, and one Lord Jesus, through whom all things exist.

For if there were no one who understood, or by whom the person himself might be examined, he could say that it was some sort of deception and a unity sung in tongues because it would be shameful for it to be disclosed.

Prophecy concerns the present. The Apostle Paul says: “But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or an unlearned person enters, he is convicted by all, he is judged by all; the secrets of his heart are made manifest, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you.”

**(Gregory.)** When the secrets of his heart are made manifest, it is plainly shown that, in this form of prophecy, the Spirit does not foretell what is going to happen but reveals what already is [Col. 0134C].

But in what way can the prophecy of the Spirit be called prophecy when it reveals nothing future but speaks of the present? In this matter we must observe that it is rightly called prophecy not because it foretells what is to come, but because it brings hidden things to light. Just as time withdraws any future event from our eyes, so in the present a cause withdraws a thought from our eyes. A future event is hidden in future time, whereas a present thought is concealed in the secrecy of the heart.

There is also prophecy concerning the present when some matter is hidden not in the mind but by the distance of a place, yet is unveiled through the Spirit. In this way the mind of the prophet becomes present where his body is not present. Giezi, for example, had gone far away from the prophet when he received the gifts of Naaman the Syrian; nevertheless the prophet said to him: “Was not my heart present when the man turned back from his chariot to meet you?” (2 Kings 5).

“What then, brothers? When you come together, each of you has a psalm?”

**(Ambrose.)** That is, he proclaims the praise of God through song.

“He has a teaching”—that is, he possesses an exposition of meanings through spiritual wisdom.

“He has an apocalypse”—that is, he possesses a prophecy of hidden things which, with the favor of the Holy Spirit, may reach everyone’s understanding.

“He has a tongue.” So as not to sadden those who were able to speak in tongues, he permitted them to speak in tongues, but only in such a way that interpretation followed. Therefore he says, “He has an interpretation,” so that if an interpreter were present, an opportunity would be given to those speaking in tongues [Col. 0135A].

“Let everything be done for edification.” This is the conclusion: nothing should be done uselessly in the Church. They should work especially for this purpose, so that the unlearned may also make progress and nothing in the body may remain dark through ignorance.

For this reason he wants everyone to come prepared, with different spiritual gifts, so that, alert through the very eagerness of their minds and encouraging one another, they may desire the better gifts for the enlightenment of their brothers.

“If anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be by two or, at most, three, and one at a time, and let someone interpret.” That is, two or three—no more—should speak in tongues, and individually, not all at once, lest they appear to be insane. He therefore says “at most, three,” so that they would not occupy the day speaking in tongues while lacking interpreters and depriving the prophets of time to expound the Scriptures, since the prophets are the enlighteners of the whole Church.

“But if an interpreter [the source is lacunose here] is not present, let him remain silent in the Church, but speak to himself and to God.” That is, let him pray silently within himself or speak to God, who hears all things, even those that are mute. In the Church, the person who benefits everyone ought to speak.

“Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge.” He maintained the same limit when he said, “Let two or three speak,” each individually, as above. He permitted the others to question them about matters that might arise in uncertainty or that someone might be unable to grasp, since abilities differ, so that such matters might be clarified through fuller discussion.

“But if something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent.” That is, let the superior give way to the inferior, so that, if he can, the latter may speak, and let the former not be troubled, because the gift may also be given to the other, so that he may say what, although he appears inferior, was not granted to the superior.

For just as everything cannot be granted to one person, even if he is superior, so it is impossible that nothing should be imparted to someone, however inferior he may be, so that no one is without the grace of God.

“For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may be encouraged.”

This is the tradition of the synagogue, which he wants us to follow; for he writes to certain Christians who came from the Gentiles, not from the Jews: they sat while disputing, with elders of rank in chairs, those following in benches, and the last on the floor upon mats. If something was revealed to one of them, he commanded that space be given for him to speak, and that he not be despised, because they are members of the body.

“And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.” Since there is one and the same Spirit who gives himself both to prophets speaking of future things and to those who reveal the Scriptures, according to the nature and circumstances of the matters involved, he therefore said that the Spirit is subject to the prophets. He wished to kindle their minds with the hope that the Spirit would not resist by contradicting them, lest discord arise in the body. Those who are called in peace ought to devote themselves to patience, lest the laws of peace be broken.

“For God is not a God of dissension but of peace, as I teach in all the churches of the saints.” By saying this, he urges them to do what he has commanded, since he testifies that he teaches the same things in the churches of the saints.

“Or did the word of God come forth from you, or did it reach you alone?”

These are words of rebuke. They were so puffed up as though this salvation had been promised to them alone, and as though all the other nations were called to faith through their example—or as though there were no others who could receive the grace of God when the Apostles preached [Col. 0136A].

They boasted as though they were conferring a benefit rather than receiving one when they approached the faith. Hence he says: “Or did the word of God come to you alone?” Anyone who wants to buy something that he knows is not being sought by others approaches the purchase with a certain disdain, as though he were conferring a benefit on the seller. Thus the Apostle rebukes the Corinthians, who were weighed down by such pride and vanity, as though, if they did not obey the words of faith, no one else would believe. He says to the Jews: “It was necessary that the word of this life be spoken to you first, but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

“If anyone thinks that he is a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize that the things I am writing to you are the Lord’s commandments.”

By saying this, he touches upon the false apostles mentioned above, by whom they had been corrupted. At the prompting of human desires, these men taught earthly things rather than divine things. Therefore he says that he is transmitting nothing of his own but the Lord’s, so that those whom he persuades may appear to have been won for God, not for human beings. With this confidence he preaches steadfastly, possessing a clear conscience, because he does not wish to please human beings but God. Hence he does not flatter sinners so that they may increase in their sins, but admonishes them to cease.

“But if anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored.” Rightly so: one who does not know that what the Apostle says are the Lord’s commandments will himself be ignored by the Lord on the day of judgment, as the Lord says: “Truly I tell you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25).

“Therefore, brothers, desire to prophesy.” Although he rebukes them, finds fault with them in many respects, and corrects them because they had departed from his tradition, he nevertheless calls them brothers. For Isaiah says to the people of the Lord: “Say to those who do not walk rightly in my ways: ‘You are our brothers.’”

Thus, in order to console them after his corrections, he calls them brothers and urges them to desire prophecy, so that through continual discussion and exposition of the divine law they may become more firmly instructed and learn that the preaching of the pseudo-apostles was perverse.

“And do not forbid speaking in tongues.” Because of charity, those who are able to speak in tongues should not be forbidden when an interpreter is present, lest dissension arise.

“But let everything be done properly and according to order.” That is, according to the order stated above. What is done properly is what is done with peace and discipline.

[Col. 0136D] “Let women keep silent in the churches.”

Here he supplies what he had omitted. Above he commanded that women be veiled in the Church; now he shows that they must be quiet and modest, so that their veiling may be worthwhile.

If the man is the image of God and the woman is not, and if she is subject to the man according to the law of nature, how much more ought women to be subject in the Church out of reverence for the one who is God’s representative and who is also the head of the man?

“For they are not permitted to speak, but must be subject, as the law also says.” What does the law say? “Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.” This is the specific law. Hence Sarah called Abraham her lord, her husband (Gen. 18). For this reason they are commanded to remain silent, lest the sentence of the law mentioned above be weakened. Sarah was subject to her husband, as has been said, although husband and wife are one flesh.

Yet she is commanded to be subject for two reasons: because she comes from the man and because sin entered through her.

“But if they want to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home, for it is shameful for a woman to speak in the Church.”

It is shameful because it is contrary to discipline for women to presume to speak about the law in the house of God, where they have been commanded to be subject to their husbands, when they know that men have primacy there. It is more appropriate for women to devote themselves to prayer in the house of God, restraining their tongues and opening their ears, so that they may hear how the mercy of God, through Christ, conquered the death that had reigned through them.

For if they dare to speak in the Church, it is disgraceful, since they are veiled precisely so that they may appear humbled. But they show themselves shameless, which is also a reproach to their husbands; for in the insolence of women the husbands too are marked with blame.

## CHAPTER XV

**The Apostle treats of the grace of the resurrection, beginning with commendation of evangelical teaching.**
I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel that I preached to you, which you also received, in which you also stand, through which you are also being saved—if you hold fast to the manner in which I preached it to you, unless you believed in vain. (Ambr.) He shows them that if, in this matter under discussion, they have been led astray from his tradition, they have lost what they believed. For the whole hope of believers consists in this understanding: that the dead will rise. When he says, “in which you also stand,” he is speaking of those who were firm in the faith of this tradition [Col. 0137C]; for he speaks indiscriminately, so that those who are steadfast in faith may rejoice, while those who waver may grieve at being corrected and may be restored.

For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures. He refers to the Scriptures of the Old Testament, which sang beforehand of the Lord’s future passion. For the prophet Isaiah says (Isa. LIII): “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter,” and, among other things, “For his life will be taken from the earth; because of the iniquities of my people he was led to death.” These things are known to have been fulfilled in Christ. But because the wording appears to signify past time, this is not contrary to the truth, since for God, who knows all things beforehand, nothing is future. Therefore he speaks of what is future for us as though it had already happened. For in the Apocalypse of the apostle John [Col. 0137D] it is said (Apoc. XVII): “The Lamb,” he says, “who was slain from the foundation of the world.” Since it will not happen otherwise than God knows, it is said to have happened: for it becomes so for us, not for God, since with God there is nothing that can be called future.

And in the Psalm he says: “The Lord has reigned from the wood” (Ps. XCV); and Moses likewise signified his cross, saying: “Then you shall see your life hanging before your eyes, and you shall not believe” (Deut. XXVIII). Therefore, in this same matter, an expression signifying future time is sometimes also introduced, lest the wicked defend that the statement was not spoken about Christ if everything were expressed as though it belonged to the past.

And that he was buried. No one doubts that a dead man was buried, as the prophet Isaiah says (Isa. LIII): “And I will give the wicked for his burial.”

[Col. 0138A] And that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures. Everything is enclosed within faith. Therefore, under the person of the people, the Lord’s resurrection on the third day was described as future; for the prophet Hosea says: “After two days he will revive us, and on the third day we shall rise and live in his sight” (Hos. VI). No believer denies that all have risen in Christ, just as they were dead in Adam. Likewise, in the Psalm, under the person of a man, he signifies Christ also, saying: “You have subjected all things under his feet; you have crowned him with glory and honor” (Ps. VIII).

And that he was seen by Cephas, that is, Peter; this is also attested by Cleopas and Emmaus in the Gospel according to Luke, which says that he appeared to Peter alone. And afterward to the eleven. This too is contained in the Gospel. Then he was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once. He speaks this on the basis of his own testimony [Col. 0138B]. Of these, many remain until now, but some have fallen asleep. Of those to whom the Lord appeared after the resurrection, he then says that many were still in the body.

Then he was seen by James. He appeared separately to James, just as he did to Peter. I think this happened so that the many appearances might strengthen faith in the resurrection. Then to all the apostles. Again he appeared to all the apostles on the mountain where Jesus had appointed them, as Matthew the Evangelist reports. Earlier, in Jerusalem, eight days after his resurrection—that is, on the Lord’s Day—he entered to the disciples while the doors were shut, so that Thomas’s mind might be strengthened, as the apostle John says. By “the mountain” it is understood that he gave them commandments.

(Aug.) He did not say, “first he appeared to Cephas,” since that would conflict with the fact that the Gospel records that he appeared first to the women [Col. 0138C]. “Afterward,” he says, “to the eleven,” at whatever hour one wishes, but still on the very day of the resurrection. Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once—whether these were gathered together with the eleven behind closed doors because of fear of the Jews, so that, when Thomas had gone out, Jesus came to them, or whether it happened after those eight days, it makes no difference. “Afterward,” he says, “he appeared to James.” For we should understand that he was then first seen by James, but by some particular manifestation, separately. “Then to all the apostles”—not to them for the first time then, but already so that he might converse more familiarly with them until the day of his ascension.

Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. (Ambr.) He appeared to him first in heaven, and afterward, when he was praying, in the temple. He called himself “untimely born” because, born outside the proper time, he received the apostolate in Christ after Christ had been received bodily into heaven.

For I am the least of the apostles. He humbles himself and attributes the matter to time: he is lesser in time, not in dignity. But because he had also been a persecutor, he lowers himself, saying: Who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God.

(Greg.) Let us see how Paul had been touched by the wings of the apostles and roused to repentance. Considering the evils of his former persecution and the apostles’ innocent life, he said: “For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God.” He considered the apostles’ innocence, and, because of his former wickedness, all the care that he displayed in the Church became worthless in his eyes. He did not consider how many he surpassed through the understanding he had received, because, weighing their innocence, he grieved that he had once been a persecutor.

But let us see whether any of the apostles admired in Paul the understanding that had been given to him. We must first seek the chief of the apostles, who, admonishing his disciples, says: “As also our most beloved brother Paul wrote to you according to the wisdom given to him, as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them about these matters. In them there are certain things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort” (II Pet. III). Thus Paul admires the innocence of all the apostles, while the first apostle admires in Paul his wisdom. Therefore they touch one another with their wings, since they mutually stir one another to progress by that from which they fly.

Thus almighty God acts in human hearts as he does in the regions of the earth. He could have given every region all fruits. But if one region did not need the fruits of another, it would have no fellowship with the other. Hence he grants abundance of wine to one, but of oil to another; he makes this one abound in flocks, and that one in the richness of crops, so that when one brings what the other does not have, and the other returns what the first did not bring, through the fellowship of grace the lands, though divided, may also be joined together.

Just as the regions of the earth are, so are the minds of the saints. As they mutually contribute what they have received, the regions, so to speak, offer their fruits to one another, so that all may be joined together in one charity [Col. 0139C]. Yet amid these things we must understand that, just as all the elect always observe in others what they have received better from God than they themselves have received, so that they prefer them in their thoughts and subject themselves to them in humility, so the mind of the reprobate never considers what good another possesses more abundantly than itself, but what good it possesses more abundantly than another. They do not weigh what good the other spirit has received and they lack, but what good they possess and what evils the others possess.

When almighty God distributes virtues to individuals for this purpose—that one may humble another in thought—the reprobate turn the good they have received toward their own ruin in pride. They constantly consider the good things they themselves have and others do not, and never strive to weigh how many good things others have which they themselves lack. What divine mercy arranges for the increase of humility, depraved minds turn toward the increase of pride; and through the diversity of gifts they fall away from the good in which they ought to have grown in humility.

Therefore, most beloved brothers, it is necessary that you should always look at what you possess less abundantly, but in your neighbors at what they have received more abundantly than you, so that, while you regard them as superior to yourselves because of the good that they possess and you do not, you too may grow through humility in order to obtain it. For if you weigh the good things received by them, while they consider in you the gifts you possess, you touch one another with your wings, so that, always roused toward heavenly things, you may fly [Col. 0140A] upward.

But by the grace of God I am what I am. (Ambr.) He gives glory to God, who chose him, and does not defend his own dignity, but calls himself unworthy. Thus he truly merits more, knowing that the Lord said: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke XIV).

And his grace toward me was not empty. He says this because, although he had been a persecutor, he did not therefore receive a lesser measure of grace in the apostolate. But I labored more abundantly than all of them. He adds the reason: he was not merely made inferior, but, because of the steadfastness by which he was strong in Christ, he suffered more labor; and, not bearing this unwillingly, he became more worthy.

Yet not I, but the grace of God with me. Lest he be thought to have exalted himself boastfully, he immediately humbles himself, attributing this very thing not chiefly to himself but to the grace of God, so that he may always return all glory [Col. 0140B] to God, from whom he is rightly to receive exaltation.

(Aug.) Not because he himself was doing no good, but because he would do nothing if God did not help him.

(Cass.) For when he says, “I labored,” he signifies the effort of his own free choice; but when he says, “not I, but the grace of God,” he shows the power of divine protection. When he says, “with me,” he declares that grace cooperated with him not while he was idle or secure, but while he was laboring and sweating.

This is also proved in Job, his most approved athlete, when the devil sought him for single combat. We read that divine justice provided for him. For if he had confronted the enemy not by his own strength but protected solely by God’s grace, and, without any strength of his own endurance, supported only by divine aid, had endured the many masses of temptations and destructions sought with the enemy’s entire cruelty, how would the devil not have more justly repeated against him the calumnious statement he had previously uttered: “Does Job worship God for nothing? Have you not hedged him around, and his house, and all his possessions? But stretch out your hand, that is, let him contend with me by his own strength; unless he blesses you to your face” (Job I)?

But since the slanderous enemy did not dare to repeat any such complaint after the struggle, he confessed that he had been overcome not by God’s strength but by Job’s.

(Greg.) Therefore heavenly mercy first acts in us without us, so that afterward it may also act with us, through our free choice, the good that we already desire. Yet through the grace it expends, it rewards this in us at the final judgment as though it had proceeded from us alone.

Because divine goodness precedes us in order to make us innocent, Paul says: “But by the grace of God I am what I am.” And because our free choice follows that same grace, he adds: “And his grace toward me was not empty, but I labored more abundantly than all of them.” When he saw that in himself he was nothing, he said: “Yet not I.” But because he discovered that, together with grace, he was something, he added: “But the grace of God with me.” For he would not say “with me” if, together with prevenient grace, there were not also a following free choice. Thus, to show that without grace he is nothing, he says, “not I”; but to demonstrate that grace worked together with him through free choice, he adds, “but the grace of God with me.”

[Col. 0141A] Whether, then, it was I or they, this is how we preach, and this is how you believed. (Ambr.) This is what he indicated above: that he received no inferior grace in preaching than the other apostles, but one and the same grace. Therefore he charges the Corinthians’ faithlessness more severely, because, although this belief had been made manifest among all the churches, they had departed from this faith and hope. He then says:

But if Christ is preached as risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ risen. But if Christ has not risen, your faith is empty, and our preaching is empty.

These things had been handed down by false apostles, who asserted that Christ had neither been born, nor suffered in the flesh, nor risen again. The apostle John also marks them out, because they denied that Christ had come in the flesh. Hence he says: “Whoever denies that Christ has come in the flesh is the Antichrist; and whoever denies the Son does not have the Father” (I John II).

These men went about and overturned the faith of certain people, lest, because they were judged by the wise of the world, they should be considered foolish. For the wise of this age judge a person foolish when they hear of the resurrection of the dead. “But if,” he says, “it is true that Christ has not risen, we are false preachers, and your faith will be empty.” For they believed this when the apostle preached: that the dead would rise; and drawn by this hope, they came to faith.

He asserts that this would certainly work to their detriment if they believed what will not happen. It is shameful for anyone to profess that he believed what is false. Therefore he also brings shame upon them and declares their labors fruitless if what they heard from the false apostles is true—namely, that the dead will not rise. No one willingly hears this said about himself; thus, when they saw that it was against them, they might return to their first faith.

We are also found to be false witnesses of God, because we testified against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise. Whoever asserts that God raised Christ from the dead is a false witness if this did not happen. Yet he preaches God’s power, not as an enemy, since he attributes so remarkable a deed to God’s power. But if it is true that he raised Christ from the dead, what should be said of the one who is both a false witness against God and declares his work foolishness? For if the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen.

[Col. 0141D] But if Christ has not risen, you are still in your sins; therefore those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. He terrifies them so that, since no one wishes evil for himself, they may grieve that they have begun to believe what is against them. For who would not wish to hear that his sins have been forgiven? And those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. He adds this to increase their terror, because they do not wish to regard the departure of their loved ones as perdition. Those who departed from the world under this hope—or who did not fear being killed because they believed they would rise according to Christ’s example—and if this is not true, have perished. He tells them what, because of their love for their deceased, they do not wish to hear, so that he may cut away from them what they previously wished to hear through error.

(Aug.) There are also true chains of reasoning whose conclusions are false, following from the error of the person with whom one is arguing. A good and learned person introduces them so that the one whose error they follow may be ashamed and abandon that same error; for if he wishes to remain in it, he must also be compelled to hold the things he condemns.

The Apostle was not asserting truths when he said, “Neither has Christ risen,” and then, “Our preaching is empty, and your faith is empty,” along with the other statements that follow, all of which are entirely false. For Christ has risen, the preaching of those who announced this was not empty, and the faith of those who believed it was not empty. But these false statements were most truly connected to the proposition that there is no resurrection of the dead. Once those false assertions have been rejected—since the contrary facts are true—the resurrection of the dead follows [Col. 0142B].

Since there are true connections not only of true propositions but also of false propositions, it is easy to learn the truth of connections even in the schools outside the Church. But the truth of propositions must be sought in the sacred books and in ecclesiastical teaching. The truth of connections itself, however, was not instituted by human beings but observed and noted by them, so that they might learn or teach it; for it exists perpetually in the rational structure of things and was established by God.

For just as someone who recounts the order of times does not himself compose it, and one who points out the arrangement of places or the natures of animals, serpents, or stones does not display things instituted by human beings, and one who demonstrates the stars and their movements does not demonstrate something instituted by himself or by any other person, so also the one who says, “When what follows is false, what precedes must be false,” speaks most truly. He does not make it so, but merely demonstrates that it is so.

From this rule comes the point we have recalled from the Apostle. The proposition that there is no resurrection of the dead comes first; this was asserted by those whose error the Apostle wished to destroy. The proposition that follows necessarily from it is: “Neither has Christ risen.” But this conclusion is false, for Christ has risen. Therefore what precedes is false; and what precedes is the assertion that there is no resurrection of the dead.

There is therefore a resurrection of the dead. The whole matter is expressed briefly as follows: “If there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ risen. But Christ has risen; therefore there is a resurrection of the dead.”

Thus, the fact that, when the conclusion is removed, what precedes must also necessarily be removed, was not instituted by human beings; they merely demonstrated it. This rule pertains to the truth of connections, not to the truth of propositions. But in this passage, where the resurrection was being discussed, both the rule of connection is true and the proposition concluded from it is itself true.

If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are more pitiable than all human beings. (Ambr.) It is clear that we hope in Christ both in the present life and in the future. For Christ does not abandon his servants here, but gives them grace; and in the future they will be in eternal glory. But if there were no hope of the future life, we would be more pitiable than all human beings, as he says. For what purpose would there be fasting, vigils, deaths, a pure life, justice, mercy, and death, if no reward for these things is to exist in the future? Unbelievers, at least, enjoy this life.

(Cass.) This question commonly disturbs the minds of those who possess little faith or knowledge. They think that the merits of the saints, or the rewards that are not given in the present but laid up for the future, are repaid within the brief span of this temporal life.

But we, who do not hope in Christ only in this life—for otherwise, according to the Apostle, we would be more pitiable than all human beings, since we receive none of the promises in this world and, because of our unbelief, would also lose them in the future—must not be led astray by their opinions. Otherwise, ignorant of the truth of the proper definition, we would be shaken by temptations, wavering and fearful, when we saw ourselves also subjected to the same conditions. We might then attribute to God either fickleness or neglect of human affairs—which it is even wicked to say—because he does not protect the saints who live uprightly in temptation, does not repay the good with good and the wicked with evil in the present, and because we might deserve to be condemned along with those whom the prophet Zephaniah rebukes:

“Those who say in their hearts, ‘The Lord will not do good, nor will he do evil’” (Zeph. I);

or else we might be found among those who are said to have blasphemed God with such complaints:

“Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such people please him”; or, “Where is the God of justice?” (Mal. III).

We would also be adding the blasphemy described in what follows:
