“It is useless to serve God; and what profit is there that we have kept his commandments and walked mournfully before the Lord?” “Therefore now we call the arrogant blessed, for those who practice wickedness have been enriched; they have tempted God and have been saved.”

Therefore, in order that we may escape this ignorance, which is the root and cause of this most perverse error, we must first know what is truly good and what is evil. Then, holding not the false definition of the crowd but the true definition of the Scriptures concerning these matters, we will not be deceived by the error of unbelieving people.

Everything that exists in this world falls into three categories: good, evil, and intermediate. We must therefore know what is properly good, what is evil, and what is intermediate, so that our faith, strengthened by true knowledge, may remain unshaken in all temptations.

Nothing, then, among merely human things is to be believed the chief good except virtue of soul and sincere faith alone, which leads us to divine things and makes us continually cling to that immutable good. Conversely, nothing is to be called evil except sin alone, which separates us from the good God and joins us to the evil devil.

Intermediate are those things which, according to the disposition and choice of the person using them, can be turned toward either side: wealth, power, honor, bodily strength, health, beauty, life itself, or death, poverty, bodily weakness, injuries, and other things like them. According to the quality and disposition of the user, these can either advance toward the good or toward the evil.

For wealth also frequently advances the good, according to the Apostle (I Tim. VI), who commanded the rich of this world to give freely, to share with those in need, and to lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that through these things they might seize true life. According to the Gospel (Luke XVI), wealth is good for those who make friends for themselves from unrighteous mammon.

But wealth is again turned toward evil when it is amassed merely for storing away or for luxury, and is not distributed for the use of those in need.

Power and honor, bodily strength and health are likewise intermediate and suitable to either side. This is easily proved by the fact that many saints in the Old Testament, placed amid all these things—in the greatest wealth, at the height of dignity, and in bodily strength—are known to have been most acceptable to God. Conversely, those who abused these things and turned them toward the service of their wickedness were rightly punished or destroyed, as the Book of Kings frequently indicates.

Birth and death themselves are also intermediate, as the birth of Saint John and that of Judas testify. The life of one was so beneficial to him that it is said to have brought joy at his birth to others as well, according to the statement: “And many will rejoice at his birth” (Luke I). But of the other it is said: “It would have been good for that man if he had not been born” (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV).

Of the death of John and of all the saints it is said: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV). But of Judas and those like him: “The death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. XXXIII).

The blessedness of Lazarus, the poor man covered with sores, demonstrates how useful bodily weakness can sometimes be. Scripture mentions no other merits of his virtues (Luke X), yet solely because he endured poverty and bodily weakness with the greatest patience, he deserved, in a most blessed lot, to possess Abraham’s bosom.

Poverty, persecutions, and injuries, which the opinion of the whole populace regards as evils, are shown clearly to be useful and necessary by the fact that holy men not only never wished to avoid them, but, either seeking them with the greatest virtue or enduring them courageously, became friends of God and obtained the rewards of eternal life. The blessed Apostle agrees, saying: “For this reason I am pleased with weaknesses, insults, necessities, persecutions, and distresses for Christ” (II Cor. XII); “for when I am weak, then I am strong,” because power is perfected in weakness.

Therefore those who are exalted by the greatest wealth, honors, and powers of this age are not to be thought to have obtained from these things the chief good, which is defined as existing only in virtues. They have obtained something intermediate. For just as these things are found useful and advantageous for the just who use them for necessary purposes, since they produce an opportunity for good works and their fruit in the eternity of the life to come, so for those who abuse their resources wickedly they are useless and disadvantageous, producing an opportunity for sin and death.

But now Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep, since, indeed, through a man came death, and through a man the resurrection of the dead. (Ambr.) In saying this he touches upon the false prophets who denied that Christ was born, and consequently denied that the flesh had risen, because one who had not been born could not have died. He therefore proves that Christ rose from the dead by proving that he was a man, so that there may be no doubt that a man was raised from the dead by God. For since death was introduced through human sin, the justice of Christ merited the resurrection of the dead.

For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ. He says this because, just as Adam, having sinned and discovered death, held all those descended from him so that they would be dissolved, so Christ, not sinning and therefore conquering death—for whoever does not sin conquers death—acquired life, that is, resurrection, for all who are from his body.

Although, therefore, he granted a general resurrection—so that, just as all, whether just or unjust, die in Adam, so in Christ all, both believers and unbelievers, may rise, though unbelievers rise for punishment—they nevertheless appear to be made alive because they will receive their bodies, no longer to die, but to suffer in them without end the punishment they refused to believe in.

(Aug.) “Just as all die in Adam,” he says, “so also all will be made alive in Christ.” For just as no one is outside Adam in the kingdom of death, so no one is outside Christ in the kingdom of life; just as through Adam all human beings became mortal in punishment, children of the age, so through Christ all righteous human beings become immortal in the grace of the Son of God.

But each in his own order. (Ambr.) He now wishes to explain the orders of the resurrection, lest they think it fabulous because it has not yet happened in the others. He explains to them the orders and the times—when it happened and when it will happen—that the dead may rise.

Christ the firstfruits. As it is also attested in the Acts of the Apostles, where it is written in Moses: “Whether Christ is subject to suffering, whether he is the first to rise from the dead,” and so forth. He rose first, therefore, so that he might become a pattern for those who believe in him.

Then those who belong to Christ, who believed at his coming. This is to be understood in two ways: both because at his second coming the saints will rise according to the faith of the Apocalypse of John, and because at his first coming, when he rose, many bodies of saints rose in testimony to death’s defeat and despoiling. Under one signification, therefore, he encompasses the Lord’s two comings.

[Col. 0145D] Then the end, when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished every principality, authority, and dominion. (Cass.) We can gather by clear reasoning why they are called principalities or authorities: either because they rule over and preside over various peoples, or because they exercise their principalities over lower spirits and demons. The fact that there are also evangelical legions is testified by their own confession. For they cannot be called Dominions unless they have those over whom they exercise the authority of their dominion; nor can they be called authorities and principalities unless there are those over whom they claim principalities. We find this also most clearly designated in the Gospel by the blaspheming Pharisees: “By Beelzebul, the prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Luke XI).

For we read that they are called “rulers of the darkness,” and that another is called “the prince of this world.” Yet the blessed Apostle asserts that these ranks will be abolished in the future, when all things have been subjected to Christ: “When he has handed over,” he says, “the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished every principality, authority, and dominion.” This cannot happen in any other way unless those over whom they are known in this age to exercise powers, dominions, or principalities have been removed from their dominion.

But he must reign until he has placed all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death; for he has subjected all things under his feet.

(Ambr.) He says this because, when the kingdom has been handed over, the end of the world will come, with the resurrection fulfilled. Some, frightened by the harshness of the statement, wish to appear devout and therefore depart from the proper meaning. They recoil when they hear the words, “when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father,” thinking that, if this handing over of the kingdom is understood according to the sound of the words, the matter would be left empty—as though, if he hands it over, he himself no longer possesses it, just as though the Father, handing all things over to the Son, had emptied himself.

But the Lord himself says: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” (Luke X). And afterward: “This is eternal life,” he says, “that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII). Behold: while the Son reigns, the Father also reigns.

How could the Son be thought to empty himself by handing over the kingdom, when the angel says to Mary: “And the Lord God will give him the throne of David [Col. 0146C] his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke I)? And Daniel says of the same kingdom, among other things: “The God of heaven will raise up another kingdom that will never be destroyed, and this kingdom will be eternal” (Dan. II).

Therefore no one should doubt that the Son will always reign with the Father. This handing over of the kingdom means that, when all things have been subjected to the Son and have worshiped him as God, and death has been destroyed, the Son will show them that he is not the one from whom all things are, but the one through whom all things are. This will be handing over the kingdom to God and the Father: to show that he himself is the one from whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named. Then the end will come. The destruction of death is indeed the resurrection of the dead.

(Aug.) Then the end, when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father. Our Lord Jesus Christ will therefore hand over the kingdom to God and the Father, without separating himself from him, or the Father, or the Holy Spirit, since he will lead believers to the contemplation of God, where there is the end of all good works, everlasting rest, and joy that will not be taken from us. This is what the Lord signifies when he says: “Again I will see you, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John XVI).

His faithful, whom he redeemed with his blood, are called his kingdom. “When he has abolished,” he says, “every principality, every authority, and every power.” That is, so that there may no longer necessarily be a dispensation of representations through angelic principalities, authorities, and powers. From their person it is not improperly understood to be said in the Song of Songs to the bride: “We will make for you likenesses of gold with ornaments of silver, until the king is in his chamber” (Song I); that is, until Christ is in his secret place, because “our life is hidden with Christ in God.” “When Christ,” he says, “your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. III).

Nor should we think that Christ will hand over the kingdom to God and the Father in such a way as to take it away from himself; some empty talkers have believed this. When it is said that he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father, he is not separated from him, because together with the Father he is one God. But the word “until,” which has been placed here, deceives those who are careless about the divine Scriptures and eager for disputes. For the passage continues: “For he must reign until he has placed all his enemies under his feet” [Col. 0147B], as though, once he has placed them there, he would not reign. They do not understand that it is said in the same way as: “His heart is established; he will not be moved until he sees his enemies” (Ps. CXI); for when he has seen them, he will not then be moved.

When he says, “All things have been subjected to him,” clearly this excludes the one who subjected all things to him. “But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all.” (Ambrose) The meaning is the same as that which he now unfolds, to show what it means to hand the kingdom over to God and the Father. He adds this to the meaning: since the Father, in handing the kingdom over to the Son, is not subjected to him, as the Son is subjected to the Father—for it is incongruous that the Father should be subjected to the Son—the Father therefore subjected all things [Col. 0147C] to the Son, so that the Son might likewise be honored as the Father is honored.

When all things have confessed Christ as God and have been laid beneath his feet, then Christ the Lord himself will also be subjected to God the Father, so that God may be all in all. He says this because, when the pride of all Principalities, Powers, and Dominions has been crushed and they have worshiped Christ as God, then Christ, because of the Father’s unique authority, will indeed show himself to be God, but to be from God, so that the authority of the one sublime and ineffable principle may remain. This is what it means for the Son to subject himself to the Father.

(Augustine) When he has said that all things have been subjected to him, it is clear that this excludes the one who subjected all things to him. Thus no one should understand that the Father subjected all things to the Son in such a way as to suppose that the Son himself subjected all things [Col. 0147D] to the Father. For the operation of the Father and the Son is inseparable. Otherwise, it was not the Father himself who subjected all things to him, but the Son subjected them to the one who hands the kingdom over to him and abolishes every Principality, every Power, and every Virtue.

These words are spoken of the Son: “when he has handed the kingdom over to God and the Father, when he has abolished every Principality, every Power, and every Virtue.” For it is he who subjected them, since he abolishes them. But the statement, “When all things have been subjected to him, then he himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him,” was made so that no one might suppose that Christ’s form, assumed from human creation, was later converted into divinity itself, as though it had more clearly expressed the deity—which is not a creature, but the incorporeal, immutable, consubstantial, and coeternal unity [Col. 0148A] of the Trinity.

(Ambrose) This is what it means for God to be all in all: when every creature learns that Christ is its head, and that God the Father is Christ’s head, God the Father is all in all. This means that every creature should have one understanding, and that every tongue of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings should confess with one voice that there is one God, from whom all things exist.

If he had said, “so that God may be in all,” it would indeed be understood that he is in all, but through affection or a common understanding, not also that those things themselves exist from him. But when he said, “all in all,” he signified that they both come from him and that he is in them: they come from him because they were created by him; he is in them because, in the confession of all, there is one God.

Yet [Col. 0148B] the Son is not subjected to the Father in the same way that creation is subjected to the Son. “So that God,” he says, “may be all in all.”

(Augustine) For what else is meant by what he said through the prophet, “I will be their God, and they will be my people” (Jer. XI), except: I will be what satisfies them; I will be whatever human beings rightly desire—life, salvation, nourishment, abundance, glory, honor, peace, and every good thing? Thus also that statement of the Apostle is rightly understood: “so that God may be all in all.”

He himself will be the end of our desires: he will be seen without end, loved without weariness, and praised without fatigue. This gift, this affection, this activity will certainly belong to all, just as life itself will be eternal for all.

Otherwise, what will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all?

(Ambrose) He wishes to show the resurrection of the dead to be so certain and firm that he gives as an example those who were so confident about the future resurrection that they even baptized themselves for the dead [Col. 0148C]. If someone had perhaps been overtaken by death, they feared that the one who had not been baptized might either rise badly or not rise again; someone living was baptized in the name of the dead person. Hence he added: “Why are they also baptized for them?” By this example he does not approve their action, but demonstrates the firmness of their faith in the resurrection.

“Why are we also in danger every hour? I die daily for your glory, which I have in the Lord.” By saying, “Why are we also in danger?” he distinguished the persons, showing that those who were baptized for the dead were not Catholics. Finally, above he said: “Why are they also baptized for them? Are we also baptized for them?” Jephthah too, although he was found faithful in a matter that could not be acceptably done [Col. 0148D]—when he offered his daughter according to his vow, which he had foolishly made (Judg. XI)—is an example. Thus the action itself is not approved, but the perseverance of faith is brought forward as an example.

He recalls the dangers and labors of preachers when he says:

“Why are we also in danger?” The implied continuation is: unless we hope for the future resurrection, as he mentioned above. Confident that true life would follow this death, they did not fear the dangers inflicted by unbelievers on account of their zeal for those whom they grieved to have lost because they had believed. Thus he shows his concern for their salvation, on account of the glory promised by the Lord, as it is also said in the Law: “Raise your voice like a trumpet; if they hear you, you will have won their souls” [Col. 0149A]. The Apostle was always hastening toward this, ever concerned that his glory before God might increase through the salvation he had won for many.

(Augustine) “Every day,” he says, “I die for your glory, brothers.” No one should understand this as though it meant, “Your glory made me die every day,” just as one says, “He was made learned through that teacher’s instruction,” that is, “It came about through that teacher’s instruction that he was thoroughly taught.”

The Greek manuscripts decide the matter: they read, **νὴ τὴν ὑμετέραν καύχησιν**, “by your boasting.” This expression is used only by one who is swearing an oath. Thus it is understood that he commanded that one should not swear, lest anyone, seeking an oath as though it were a good thing, should slip into perjury through the habit of frequent swearing.

Accordingly, the Lord teaches that nothing among God’s creatures is so insignificant that anyone should think it permissible to swear falsely by it. [Col. 0149B] Since divine providence governs all things, from the highest to the lowest—from the throne of God even to a white or black hair—other things are also understood from this. Not all of them could be mentioned, just as in the statement we have cited from the Apostle: “I die every day for your glory,” to which he added the oath in order to show that he owed it to the Lord, “which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

“If, according to human judgment, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what benefit is there for me if the dead do not rise?” (Ambrose) This means: if, according to human understanding—which, seeing that it does not fall within the nature of things that flesh once dissolved should be restored to life, scarcely believes in the future resurrection of the dead—I did not fear being handed over to beasts [Col. 0149C], I gained nothing.

But that is not the meaning. Because he was certain of the promised life, he not only did not fear, but willingly allowed himself to be handed over to beasts, as he says among other things in the Acts of the Apostles: “For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts XXI).

“Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.” This was spoken by the prophet Isaiah (Isa. XXII) concerning those who, as though nothing existed after death, devoted themselves solely to the belly like animals, just as those did who were corrupting the Corinthians.

“Do not be deceived: bad conversations corrupt good morals.” He signifies that a good resolution can be overthrown by conversation with wicked people. Constant association with corrupt speech damages the mind, and therefore such people must be avoided. [Col. 0149D] Whoever wishes to preserve the faith he has received must especially avoid those who make a tumult at the very beginning, so that he may fulfill what he has judged useful.

“Be sober, be vigilant, you righteous, and do not sin.” He urges vigilance, lest they be captured by the deception of a corrupt understanding, drawn away from the faith, and corrupted by refusing to believe in the resurrection of the dead. He commanded them to be righteous so that they might cultivate not merely earthly righteousness but also heavenly righteousness, because earthly righteousness neither establishes merit nor makes one guilty.

For what great thing is it not to take what belongs to another, especially since this arises from fear? But it is a great thing to give from one’s own possessions to someone who has nothing; this is true righteousness. And, so that they might not sin, he added the following. From this he wished it to be understood that he had not commanded them to preserve temporal righteousness, but [Col. 0150A] divine righteousness, because whoever preserves heavenly righteousness is undoubtedly perfect in the present life.

“For some have ignorance of God: I say this to your shame.” Those among them who were being converted, while ignorant of God’s purpose, were saying that it was foolish to believe that the dead would rise. Therefore he brings shame upon them as though they were imprudent. They believed people who, possessing ignorance of God, taught contrary to God’s decrees.

“But someone will say: How are the dead raised? And with what sort of body do they come?” He said that those whose corrupted opinion he had expressed had ignorance of God, saying: “How will the dead rise, and with what sort of body will they come?” He appropriately answered them, saying: “Fool! What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies.”

He is not dealing with the merely natural human being by the authority of Scripture, using [Col. 0150B] examples to persuade him—examples which, if he accepted them, would keep him from error—but by the physical reasoning in which he takes pride, so that he may refuse to believe that dissolved and dead bodies rise again. For he shows that the dead are restored to life and multiplied, so that human error may be confounded.

“And what you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare [Col. 0150C] grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other kind. But God gives it a body as he wills, and to each of the seeds its own body.”

(Gregory) When the Apostle says, “You do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare grain,” he indicates what we see: a grain grows with a stalk and leaves, although it is sown without a stalk and leaves. Therefore, in the increase of the glory of the resurrection, he did not say that the seed-grain lacked what it had; rather, it possesses what it did not have.

(Ambrose) If, then, a bare grain is sown and, by God’s command, is clothed in a certain manner through the ministry of the elements and rises again with many additions useful to human beings, why should it not be believable that, through God’s power, the dead can rise, with the substance improved but not multiplied in number?

What, then, does the unbeliever demand concerning the body in which the dead will rise, when examples proclaim the basis of faith: a resurrection in which the substance is improved, not lost, and in which each person will receive his own body, the body in which Adam was created?

(Augustine) In accordance with this, he had said, “You do not sow the body that is to be.” For it is not that wheat will not come from wheat; rather, no one sows the grass, or the stalk, or the many coverings of chaff that enclose the grains, although the seeds rise together with them. Therefore he says, “but a bare grain.” By this he wishes to show that [Col. 0150D] if God can add to the bare seed what was not there, much more can he restore what was present in the human body.

What he adds now concerns the distinction among those who rise, because of the different glories of the faithful and the saints.

“Not all flesh is the same flesh. There is one kind of flesh of human beings, another of animals, another of birds, and another of fish. There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. But one is the glory of heavenly bodies, and another of earthly bodies. One is the brightness of the sun, another the brightness of the moon, and another the brightness of the stars; for star differs from star in brightness. So also is the resurrection of the dead.”

The meaning throughout is this: if kinds of flesh, although all are mortal, nevertheless differ [Col. 0151A] from one another according to the various kinds of living creatures; and if bodies, although all are visible, nevertheless differ from one another according to the diversity of their places, so that the glory of heavenly bodies is one and that of earthly bodies another; and if, in the sublime regions, although all are heavenly, they themselves also differ in the brightness of their lights, it is not surprising that in the resurrection of the dead the glory of merits will differ.

(Ambrose) Since all flesh comes from the same mass, how and why is there such great diversity among these things, so that one substance has produced different kinds? Let the sophists of the world and the investigators of the stars now say, if they can comprehend what lies outside themselves, while they do not know what is within themselves.

Finally, all the philosophers of the world, who refused to humble their minds before the law of God in order to accept its faith, constantly asserting diverse and contradictory positions, wounded one another [Col. 0151B] in their empty debates, because in none of them was the sign of attested truth recognized—truth that could commend the doctrine by being placed before words. God likewise ordained this for our instruction: it is not proved by words but by power, and words cannot resist it.

Therefore, just as flesh of different living creatures comes from one substance, so also the dignities of human beings, though they are of one flesh, will be different in the resurrection, so that each person will appear according to the quality of his merit, especially since even here we see the diversity of bodies.

“And bodies,” he says, “heavenly and earthly. But one is the glory of heavenly bodies, and another of earthly bodies.” The heavenly bodies are those of the risen; the earthly bodies are those they possess before they die or rise. Since Christ is heavenly, bodies are called heavenly from him; but from Adam, because he is earthly [Col. 0151C], they are called earthly bodies.

“One is the brightness of the sun, another the brightness of the moon, and another the brightness of the stars; for star differs from star in brightness.” He uses a comparison within one nature to explain distinctions within a substance that is not essentially divided. Just as the sun, moon, and stars, although of one nature, nevertheless differ in brightness, so human beings, although of one kind, will nevertheless be unlike one another in glory according to merit.

Their dignity will correspond to the brightness of the sun who possess the hundredfold number, those who, in order to be perfect, were rivals of the first rank. Of them it is said: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII).

Those should be compared with the brightness of the moon who have acquired the sixtyfold number through good works, so that they may possess the merit of the second rank.

The merits of those who have sought, through righteous labors, the dignity [Col. 0151D] of the third rank—the thirtyfold number—should be compared with the brighter stars.

Those human beings who, although sinners, chose to attain the honor of no rank among the three should be likened to the stars that follow, which are midway between the bright and the darker stars.

The resurrection of the faithless is like that of the dark and lowest stars, because, having followed error, they are to be compared with stars that lead others into error, as the Apostle Jude says in his Epistle. Unbelief cannot have a bright resurrection. Just as a coal covered with its own ash is darkened, so they, surrounded by the darkness of their error through their faithlessness, will be deprived of light.

“So also is the resurrection of the dead.” He gives examples so that there may be no doubt [Col. 0152A] that the dead will rise, and so that, once the reason has been received, no one may hesitate.

“It is sown in corruption; it rises in incorruption.” To sow is to bury, so that the body may decay; to rise in incorruption means that, once raised, it can no longer decay but possesses the splendor of immortality.

“It is sown in dishonor; it rises in glory.” It is sown in dishonor because, while it is punished in a dark and loathsome state, it becomes foul and swarms with worms. But it will rise in glory because, once raised, it will be light and will suffer no injury from filth.

“It is sown in weakness; it rises in power.” It is sown in weakness because it is immobile and unable to govern itself. But it rises in power because it will then be wholly alive and vigorous.

“It is sown an animal body; it rises a spiritual body.”

(Cassiodorus) Although [Col. 0152B] we acknowledge that some natures are spiritual, such as Angels, Archangels, and the other Powers, as well as our own soul, or certainly this subtle air, they should nevertheless in no way be considered incorporeal. For they possess, according to their own mode, a body by which they subsist—although it is far more subtle than our bodies, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies”; and again: “It is sown an animal body; it rises a spiritual body.”

From these words it is clearly gathered that nothing is incorporeal except God alone. Therefore all spiritual and intellectual substances can be penetrated only by him, because he alone is wholly and everywhere, and is in all things, so that he sees and examines both human thoughts and the inward movements of the mind [Col. 0152C], entering into every recess of the mind.

For concerning him alone the blessed Apostle declared, saying (Heb. IV): “For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. And no creature is invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open to his eyes.”

And blessed David says (Ps. XXXII): “He fashions their hearts individually”; and again: “He himself knows the secrets of the heart” (Ps. XLIII).

(Ambrose) The body is an animal body while it is sustained by food so that it may live; but it is a spiritual body when it will need none of these things, having been transformed into life. All the preceding statements are enclosed within this meaning. An animal body cannot always possess the Holy Spirit here; but then, that is [Col. 0152D], in the resurrection, he will always remain among the saints. A spiritual body will rise, one that can go to meet Christ.

As it is written: “The first man, Adam, was made a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit.” It should be noted that, when he speaks of two Adams, he shows that both are of the same nature. This opposes the Manichaeans and the Apollinarians, who deny that a complete human being was assumed by the Word of God.

“And not first the spiritual, but the animal, and afterward the spiritual. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so also are the earthly.”

He is called heavenly because he was conceived and born not according to the pattern of human weakness, but by the command of divine majesty. For he was conceived [Col. 0153A] and possessed our nature to such a degree that he is called the second Adam—and a human being.

“And as was the heavenly, so also are the heavenly.” If, as the heretics wish, the one who is called heavenly did not assume a human being of our race, then neither are those who are called heavenly of our nature. But if no one doubts this concerning them, there should be no uncertainty concerning him either.

(Augustine) In these words of the Apostle—“It is sown in corruption, it rises in incorruption,” and the rest—is it permissible to think that our bodies will rise in a better condition than Christ’s, when he is proposed as the example on whom we ought faithfully to fix our attention and in whose grace we ought to hope? Consequently, Christ’s body could in no way have risen with corruption if [Col. 0153B] our body is promised a resurrection in incorruption.

It is therefore certain, and there should be no doubt, that Christ’s body—which, although it did not experience the corruption of putrefaction in the tomb, as it is written, “You will not allow your holy one to see corruption,” could nevertheless be pierced by nails and a lance—now exists wholly in incorruption. What was sown in the dishonor of passion and death now exists in the glory of eternal life; what could be crucified in weakness now reigns in power; and what was an animal body, because it was taken from Adam, is now a spiritual body, inseparably joined to the spirit.

When the Apostle wished to introduce scriptural testimony concerning the animal body, he used the passage that is read in Genesis: “If there is,” he says, “an animal [Col. 0153C] body, there is also a spiritual one,” just as it is written: “The first Adam was made a living soul.” Recall how it is written: “And God breathed into his face the breath of life, and the man became a living soul” (Gen. II).

It is also said concerning animals: “Let the earth bring forth a living soul” (Gen. I). Thus the animal body is understood to be called similar to other animals because of the dissolution and corruption of death. It is renewed daily by food, and afterward, when the living being is overcome, its bodily structure is dissolved.

The spiritual body, however, is a body that is already immortal together with the spirit. Although some suppose that the body then becomes spiritual when the body itself is changed into spirit, and that the human being, who consisted of body and spirit, will wholly and entirely become spirit—as though the Apostle had said, “The body is sown; the spirit will rise”—the Apostle [Col. 0153D] said: “It is sown an animal body; it rises a spiritual body.”

Therefore, just as an animal body is not a soul but a body, so we must not think that a spiritual body is spirit, but rather a body. Who, then, would dare to suppose either that Christ’s body did not rise as a spiritual body, or that, if it rose as a spiritual body, it was no longer a body but a spirit, when he himself refutes the opinion of the disciples? When they saw him, they thought they were seeing a spirit, but he said: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke XXIV).

That flesh, therefore, was already a spiritual body; yet it was not a spirit, but a body that could no longer be separated or divided from the soul by any death, as was the animal [Col. 0154A] body. The animal body was animated by God’s breath when the man became a living soul; it too would have become spiritual without the intervention of death, had transgression of the commandment not first imposed the punishment of sin, before God granted the crown of preserved righteousness.

Thus the Lord Christ came through us and to us, finding us sinners while he was righteous, assuming in a certain manner the condition of our humility. For he appeared to us in an animal—that is, mortal—body. If he had wished, he could have come first with an immortal body; but because it was necessary for us to be healed through the humility of the Son of God, he descended to the level of our weakness and displayed the merit and reward of our faith through the power of his resurrection.

Therefore the Apostle continues: “The last [Col. 0154B] Adam became a life-giving spirit.” Whether this is understood of the first Adam, who was formed from dust, or of the last Adam, who was born from a virgin, or whether both are fulfilled in each individual human being, so that the first Adam is the human being in a mortal body and the last Adam is that same person in an immortal body, he nevertheless wished this difference to exist between a living soul and a life-giving spirit: in the former there is an animal body, in the latter a spiritual body.

A soul indeed lives in an animal body, but it does not give life so as to remove corruption. In a spiritual body, however, because it adheres perfectly to the Lord and is one spirit with him, it gives life in such a way as to make the body spiritual, consuming all corruption and fearing no separation.

Accordingly he continues: “But not first the spiritual, but the animal, and afterward the spiritual. The first man was from the earth, earthly [Col. 0154C]; the second man from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so also are the heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven.”

What does “As was the earthly, so also are the earthly” mean except “mortals from a mortal”? And what does “As is the heavenly, so also are the heavenly” mean except “immortals through immortality”—the former through Adam, the latter through Christ?

The Lord became earthly for this purpose, although he was heavenly: to make those who were earthly heavenly. That is, he became mortal from immortality by assuming the form of a servant, without changing the nature of the Lord, so that he might make those who were mortal immortal by imparting the Lord’s grace, without retaining the condition of a servant.

Therefore, just as we have borne the image of that earthly one, let us also bear the image of this heavenly [Col. 0154D] one.

(Ambrose) The sinner bears the image of Adam, but the righteous bears the image of Christ. Therefore, just as before baptism we bore the old human being, so after baptism let us bear the new one.

This, however, I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor can corruption possess incorruption. Scripture frequently uses “flesh” for the works of the flesh, as in the passage: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Rom. VIII). [GR.] Otherwise, flesh as it is will not possess the kingdom of God unless it is clothed with immortality. In sacred language, “flesh” is spoken of in one way according to nature and in another according to guilt, or corruption. Flesh according to nature is meant where it is written: “This now is bone from my bones and [Col. 0155A] flesh from my flesh” (Gen. II); and: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I). But flesh according to guilt is meant where it is written: “My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh” (Gen. VI); and as the Psalmist says: “He remembered that they are flesh, a spirit that goes and does not return” (Ps. CII). Hence Paul also said to the disciples: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit.” They were not outside the flesh, though he was sending them letters; rather, because they had overcome the passions of carnal desires, they were already, through the power of the Spirit, free from being “in the flesh.” Therefore, when the apostle Paul says, “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God,” he wishes “flesh” to be understood according to guilt, not according to nature. [Col. 0155B] Accordingly, immediately afterward, since he had spoken of flesh according to guilt, he shows this by adding: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.” In the glory of that heavenly kingdom, therefore, flesh will exist according to nature, but it will not exist according to the desires of passion, because, once the sting of death has been conquered, it will reign in eternal incorruption.

(Aug.) Since the Apostle, discussing the resurrection of the body, had taught that our bodies would become from corruptible bodies incorruptible, from contemptible bodies glorious, from weak bodies strong, and from animal bodies spiritual—that is, from mortal bodies immortal—he added and said: “This, however, I say, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God.” And lest anyone should think that the Apostle had defined this according to the substance of the flesh, he made clear what he meant by adding: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption,” as though he were saying: “I said that flesh [Col. 0155C] and blood will not possess the kingdom of God for this reason: corruption will not possess incorruption.” In this passage, therefore, by the terms “flesh and blood” he wished corruption and mortality to be understood. Finally, as though someone were saying to him, “How will there be flesh, and yet flesh will not be there?” he answers: There will indeed be flesh, because after his resurrection the Lord said, “Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me having” (Luke XXIV). Yet flesh will not be there, because “flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.” He explains what he had said by adding: “Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed.” Or, as the Greek manuscripts have it: “We shall all sleep, but we shall not all be changed.”

(Aug.) [Col. 0155D] Whether he wished this change to be understood as for the worse or for the better, the following passages make clear. “Behold, I tell you a mystery” signifies obscurity by naming the mystery. “We shall all rise,” he says, “but we shall not all be changed.”

(Ambr.) All human beings will rise, but only those who are going to reign will be changed into glory. Or it may be understood in this way: “We shall all rise,” namely, those of us who are found dead at Christ’s coming; “we shall not all be changed,” namely, those who are found in the body, because only the saints will attain the glory of blessedness.

“In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.” By “the twinkling of an eye” he wishes to signify the extreme brevity of the moment, so that you may recognize the greatness of God’s power from the speed of the resurrection. “At the last trumpet, and the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.” The last coming of Christ is understood. [Col. 0156A] The dead, however, are to be understood either as sinners, who are also said to be dead while they are living, so that they may rise for punishment; or as immortals, so that they may rise without any diminution of their members. Or, certainly, he simply says that all the dead will rise, and that only the saints, together with those who are found alive and righteous, will be changed into glory.

(Aug.) “In an atom,” he says—that is, in a point of time that cannot be divided; “in the twinkling of an eye”—that is, with the utmost speed; “at the last trumpet”—that is, at the final sign that will be given so that these things may be accomplished. Many of you do not know what an atom is. *Atom* is from the Greek τόμι, “section”; *atom* is the Greek term for that which cannot be cut. But an atom in a body is a small body, so minute that there is no longer anywhere for it to be divided. An atom in time is a brief moment that no longer has any place where it can be divided. [Col. 0156B] For example, a stone is divided into parts, and those parts into pebbles; the pebbles are divided into grains of sand, and the grains of sand into the tiniest dust. You reach some minuteness that you can no longer cut. This, then, is how an atom exists in a body.

In time, however, consider how a year is divided into months, the months into days, and the days can still be divided into hours. The hours still admit divisions into certain, somewhat longer portions of moments, until you come to such a point of time, and to such a drop of a moment, that it cannot be extended because it has no middle. This is an atom in time.

When he had said “in an atom,” he added how much action and movement can take place in that atom of time: “In the twinkling,” he says, “of an eye.” How great is the twinkling of an eye? [Col. 0156C] He does not mean the movement by which we close or open the eye by moving the eyelid. Rather, by “the twinkling of the eye” he means the emission of rays for seeing something. As soon as you have opened your eye, your ray is emitted—not merely to the nearby wall, but to a mountain far away. Nor do I mean only a mountain on earth, which is visible because it is near; I mean the stars, the sun, and the moon, which are separated from the earth by so great an interval. As soon as you have emitted the ray, it is there, because it traverses distances so quickly: in an atom, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, when that sign is given from heaven on the day of judgment. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.

Therefore, this change must without doubt be understood as a change for the better, because both the righteous and the unrighteous will rise, as the Lord says in the Gospel [Col. 0156D]: “Those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John V). He calls judgment eternal punishment, as he says elsewhere: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John III). Accordingly, those who will rise for judgment will not be changed into that incorruption which cannot suffer any corruption of pain. That incorruption belongs to the faithful and the saints. These others, however, will be tormented by perpetual corruption, because “their fire will not be extinguished, and their worm will not die” (Mark IX).

What, then, does this distinction mean—“the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed”—unless it means that all will rise incorruptible, but that among them the righteous will also be changed into that incorruption which absolutely no corruption can harm? [Col. 0157A] Those, therefore, who will not be changed into it will indeed rise incorruptible in the integrity of their members, but they will nevertheless be corrupted by the pain of punishments when they hear: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV)—an evil report which the righteous person will not fear.

Having said of the change of the righteous, “We shall be changed,” as though we were asking how this would happen or what that change would be, he adds and says: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.” In my judgment, there can be no doubt that the statement, “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God,” is to be understood in this sense: corruption and mortality of flesh and blood will not be there. For it is according to these qualities that he has called it “flesh and blood” in this passage.

(Ambr.) [Col. 0157B] There is that which puts on, and there is likewise the clothing.

(Aug.) Since resurrection cannot occur unless death has preceded it, and since in that passage “sleep” cannot be understood except as death, how will all either sleep or rise if so many whom Christ will find in the body will neither sleep nor rise? If, therefore, we believe that the saints who are found alive at Christ’s coming will, in that same rapture by which they are caught up to meet him, depart from their mortal bodies and immediately return to the same bodies made immortal, we will encounter no difficulty in the Apostle’s words—whether where he says, “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies,” or where he says, “We shall all rise,” or “We shall all sleep.” For even those will not be made alive through immortality unless each of them first dies for a little while; [Col. 0157C] and thus they will not be excluded from the resurrection, which they precede in that sleep, although it will be extremely brief, yet not nonexistent.

When “this mortal” has put on immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.”

(Ambr.) Once the causes of death have been emptied through divine victory, death itself will perish as though swallowed up.

“Where is your sting, O death? Where is your victory, O death?”

(Aug.) The prophet speaks in the person of the righteous, who taunt death. “Then,” he says, “the saying that is written will come to pass: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where is your contention, O death? Where is your sting, O death?’” The sting of death is sin.

I think that in this passage death signifies the carnal habit that resists the good will through the enjoyment of temporal things. For it would not be said, “Where is your contention?” if it had not resisted and fought back. [Col. 0157D] Its contention is also described in that passage (Gal. V): “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do the things you wish.” Through perfect sanctification, therefore, it comes about that all carnal appetites, once our spirit has been enlightened and brought to life, are subjected to that same good will.

We incurred this death through sin. Sin was altogether a matter of free choice, since in paradise no pain arising from denied pleasure resisted the good will of the human being. “The sting of death is sin.”

(Ambr.) The arrow of death is sin, by which souls are slaughtered. “The power of sin is the law.” Sin becomes stronger and greater through knowledge. Therefore, the sting of death is sin, because through sin pleasure came into existence—pleasure that could now [Col. 0158A] resist the will and restrain it with pain. Since this pleasure arose from the soul’s decline and from its becoming worse, we rightly call it death.

“The power of sin is the law,” because the things prohibited by the law are committed with much greater wickedness and shamefulness than they would be if no law prohibited them. Death, then, will be swallowed up in victory when, through sanctification perfected in every part of the human being, the pleasure of spiritual things overwhelms carnal pleasure.

The sting of death is sin, by whose puncture death came about. Sin is like a scorpion: it stung us, and we died. But how can it be said, “Where is your victory, O death?” This is not promised to us in the present life but in the resurrection. Then it will be granted to the saints that they will neither wish to sin at all nor be able to sin.

[Col. 0158B] “But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.” The victory is over that sin through which the law had been weakened by our carnal will, and which Christ immediately destroyed by the cross.

Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast and immovable, abounding always in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not in vain in the Lord. Having given the reason for the resurrection, concerning which they had been uncertain, he exhorts them to remain in God’s work, now assured of the future reward.

## CHAPTER XVI

The Apostle teaches how one should conduct oneself with strangers and neighbors, and at the end of the Epistle adds a greeting.

[Col. 0158C] “Now concerning the collection that is made for the saints, as I ordained for the churches of Galatia, so also do you. On the first day of the week.”

(Ambr.) He speaks of the contributions that were collected in each church and sent to Jerusalem for the poor saints. “The first day of the week” is the Lord’s Day, as it is said in the Gospel that the Lord rose on the first day of the week.

“Let each one of you set aside and store up with himself whatever he has judged appropriate, so that when I come the collections may not then be made.” By reserving contributions little by little, they should not think themselves burdened all at once, since God loves cheerful givers.

“When I am present, I will send those whom you approve by letter to carry your gift to Jerusalem; and if it is worthy that I should go also, they will go with me.” It is clear in itself that he leaves both matters to their judgment: both that what they give should be carried and that those by whom they send it should themselves go.

[Col. 0158D] “And if it is worthy,” he says, “that I should go also, they will go with me”—that is, if your offering is such that it ought also to be conveyed under my sponsorship.

“I shall come to you when I have passed through Macedonia, for I shall pass through Macedonia; but I shall perhaps remain with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me on wherever I go. For I do not want to see you now merely in passing; I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits.” The Macedonians conduct themselves in such a way that it is not necessary for me to remain with them longer; with you, however, it is necessary for me to remain or spend the winter, for there are many things among you that require correction, just as a physician remains where more people are sick.

“I shall remain at Ephesus until Pentecost, for a great and evident door has been opened to me [Col. 0159A], but there are many adversaries.” I shall remain there for this reason: although a clear opportunity for preaching has been granted to me, there are many who resist.

“If Timothy comes, see that he is without fear among you, for he is carrying out the work of the Lord, as I am. Let no one despise him.” Let him be without fear of tribulation or even of your contempt.

“Send him on his way in peace, so that he may come to me, for I am waiting for him with the brothers.” Do nothing that might contribute to wounding his spirit.

“Now concerning the brother Apollos, I inform you that I strongly urged him to come to you with the brothers, and certainly it was not his will to come at this time; but he will come when the opportunity arises.”

“Watch, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, be strengthened, let all your affairs be done in charity.” Watch with the eyes of the mind, to guard against the devil’s cunning. [Col. 0159B] Stand firm, because sleep does not easily creep upon those who are standing. Act manfully, for every fickleness and changeableness is judged characteristic of a woman. Be strengthened, so that there may be progress in your virtue. Hasten to do everything not for the sake of empty glory but for the sake of charity.

“I appeal to you, brothers: you know the household of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, that they are the firstfruits of Achaia, and have devoted themselves to the service of the saints. Be subject to such persons, and to everyone who cooperates and labors among you. I rejoice at the presence of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they have supplied what was lacking on your part. For they are present with you, and you can derive great benefit from them; or rather, they came to me to perform for you the service of charity. They have refreshed both my spirit and yours.”

[Col. 0160A] Out of charity for you they refreshed your spirit, and for my joy they refreshed mine. “Therefore, recognize such persons.” Hence he says elsewhere (Phil. III): “Recognize those who walk in such a way that you may have our example.” Recognize and honor them, recognizing their zeal or labor.

“The churches of Asia greet you. Aquila and Priscilla greet you warmly in the Lord, together with the church that is in their house, with whom I also lodge.” He called the household gathering a church because it was a domestic congregation of the brotherhood.

“All the brothers greet you. Greet one another with a holy kiss. The greeting is by my own hand—Paul’s. If anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed: Maranatha.”

(Aug.) [Col. 0160B] He uses a word that is at once Greek and Syriac. “If anyone,” he says, “does not love the Lord, let him be accursed: Maranatha.” In the Greek language he called him “condemned” by the word *anathema*; he defined *Maranatha* as “until the Lord returns.”

(Ambr.) Just as Christ will come as redemption for those who love him, so for those who do not love him he will pronounce a curse—that is, he will abominate and destroy them. *Maranatha* is more Syriac than Hebrew, although, because the two languages are neighboring, it has something that sounds Hebrew; and it is interpreted as “Our Lord has come.”

“The grace of the Lord be with you.” This is the customary subscription written by his own hand.

“My charity be with all of you.” Just as I love you, so may you love one another in Christ.

“In Christ Jesus. Amen.” Not according to the charity of the world. This statement confirms the blessing, as he himself shows above: “How will he say ‘Amen’ over your blessing?”

# BOOK TWELVE

## EXPOSITION OF THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0159]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0159C]

After the Corinthians had performed penance, the apostle Paul writes them a consolatory Epistle from Troas. Praising them, he exhorts them to better things, showing that although they had been saddened, they had been corrected. The principal reason for this Epistle, therefore, is that in the first Epistle he had especially rebuked their teachers because of the sins of certain persons, and they had been greatly saddened. Now he consoles them, setting his own example before them and teaching that they ought not to take it badly that they had been rebuked for the salvation of others, since he himself is daily subjected to dangers and death for the salvation of others.

## CHAPTER I

He wins the Corinthians’ goodwill through his tribulations in order to arouse their attention, and excuses himself concerning the promise he had made to them.

“Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God.”

(Aug.) Paul loves us to learn his sins, so that the one who healed such a sickness may be glorified. The physician’s hand cut away and healed the magnitude of the wound. That voice from heaven struck down the persecutor and raised up the preacher; it killed Saul and brought Paul to life. [Col. 0160C] Saul was the persecutor of the holy man; he received this name because he persecuted Christians. Later he was changed from Saul into Paul.

What does *Paul* mean? “Little.” Therefore, when he was Saul, he was proud and exalted; when he was Paul, he was humble and little. This is why we say, “I shall see you shortly,” that is, “after a little while.” Hear that he became little: “For I am the least of the apostles” (1 Cor. XV), and elsewhere he says, “to me, the least of all the saints” (Eph. III). Thus he was among the apostles like the fringe of a garment, but the church of the Gentiles touched him as a woman suffering from a flow of blood, and was healed.

(Ambr.) It is asked why, contrary to the custom of letters, he places his own name first in all his Epistles, before the names of those to whom the letters are addressed. This is a matter of the authority of the apostolic order, by which [Col. 0160D] he writes to those beneath him, just as secular judges also customarily direct writings to those whom they govern.

“Through the will of God.” Through the will of God, not of human beings, so that he might show at the same time that he was sent by Christ not without the Father’s will.

“And Timothy, the brother, to the church of God that is at Corinth.” He did not say “Paul and Timothy,” because both were not apostles. In the Epistle to the Philippians, where such authority was not necessary, [Col. 0161A] both are designated servants.

“With all the saints.” Here “saints” may be understood as priests, who in the first Epistle are placed among those who invoke the Lord, and in the Epistle to the Philippians are mentioned with bishops and deacons. They are named afterward so that the less intelligent would not think that they had been listed beforehand, when they are already included in the church.

“Who are in all Achaia,” whose metropolis is Corinth.

“Grace to you and peace from God.” They give thanks to God, rejoicing that they are being consoled for the purpose of consoling others.

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies.” Because every mercy comes from him.

“And the God of all consolation”—that is, of perfect consolation, because comfort in tribulation is not something lesser.

“Who consoles us in our pressure.” [Col. 0161B] Not in some pressures, but in all.

“So that we ourselves may also console those who are in every distress, through the exhortation by which we ourselves are exhorted by God.” For this reason we are delivered, so that we may console others and free them from sadness. Or, in this way, he gives us a model for consoling others; and through the exhortation by which we ourselves are consoled by God, we recognize that God abandons none of those who fear him, and that in the future he rewards even more greatly those whom he does not forsake in the present.

“For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds.” Thus Peter was freed from prison (Acts XII), and Paul himself was strengthened in the temple by a vision and a voice of the Lord (Acts XXII).

“Whether, then, we suffer distress for your exhortation and salvation [Col. 0161C].” We suffer either because we exhort you toward salvation or so that we may provide you with an example of endurance. For it is clear that the one for whose sake we suffer is present with us, consoling us and rescuing us from our distress through deliverance brought about by the intervention of his majesty.

“Whether we suffer pressure, it is for your exhortation and salvation; whether we receive exhortation, it is for your exhortation, which operates through the endurance of the same sufferings that we also suffer; and our hope for you is firm, because we know that if you are companions in suffering, so also you will be companions in consolation.”

He speaks generally: because they were suffering persecutions for the sake of believers, being subjected by the unbelieving to insults and slaughter, they would likewise be delivered by God’s help, for the consolation of believers, lest, having been scandalized, they should fall away from the faith. The apostles’ injuries were therefore trials for believers [Col. 0161D], as it is written in the prophet Zechariah: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zech. XIII).

Although the faithful believe in future things, during the very beginnings of distress these things cause scandal to the inexperienced. They think the promise empty if they see the preacher oppressed by violence. But if the believer is already firm, he suffers together with his teacher, trusting in future hope, so that he may be consoled together with the one with whom he suffers.

“For we do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning our pressure that occurred in Asia, that we were weighed down beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we were even weary of living.” He indicates that the suffering of distress had been brought almost to the point of death, in order to show what evils they endured for the sake of the Corinthians’ salvation [Col. 0162A], so that the Corinthians would not bear it more heavily if their errors were rebuked by those who endured such harsh things for them. For what physician would not rebuke his patient for treating himself too carelessly, lest the physician’s medical care remain without effect?

“But we ourselves had within us the sentence of death, so that we might not trust in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead.” He signifies that such an outrage of wickedness had risen up against the preachers of the faith that they had death before their eyes. Finally, having been rescued from that very distress, they say that they had been raised again. They had been afflicted in such a way that they despaired of their present life. But because God does not deny his protection to those placed in necessity, especially to his own, he rescued those who were despairing of themselves but trusting in God [Col. 0162B]. For they declared that they would have failed under the excessive pressure unless God had been present.

“Who delivered us from such great dangers and delivers us; in him we hope that he will still deliver us, with you also helping in prayer for us, so that thanks may be given for us by many persons for the gift bestowed on us through many.”

He says this because the grace of God consoled the apostles on account of many persons—that is, on account of all believers, for whose sake those pressures were also inflicted upon them. And therefore, because it is for the sake of all, let all give thanks to God when temptation ceases; or, when it arises, let all together make supplication.

“For our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience.” He says this because they trusted in their conscience, which was pure from every pretense; therefore they did not despair of God’s assistance.

(Greg.) [Col. 0162C] In the Gospel (Matt. XXV), holy Church is declared to be like ten virgins. Since the wicked are mixed with the good and the reprobate with the elect, she is rightly said to resemble both wise and foolish virgins. There are many who practice continence, restrain themselves from external desire, and are carried by hope toward what is within; they mortify the flesh and, with their whole desire, yearn for the heavenly homeland; they seek eternal rewards and do not wish to receive human praise for their labors. These plainly do not place their glory in the mouths of human beings but hide it within their conscience.

There are also many who afflict the body through abstinence but seek human approval for that very abstinence. They devote themselves to teaching and give much to the needy, but they are plainly foolish virgins because they seek only the reward of passing praise [Col. 0162D]. Hence it is openly added: “The five foolish ones did not take oil with them, but the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps.” By oil, the radiance of glory is signified; our vessels are our hearts, in which we carry all that we think. The wise have oil in their vessels because they keep the radiance of glory within their conscience, as Paul testifies when he says: “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience.” But the foolish virgins do not take oil with them because they do not have glory within their conscience, seeking it instead from the mouths of their neighbors.

“Because we have conducted ourselves in this world in simplicity and sincerity, not in carnal wisdom but in the grace of God, and more abundantly toward you.”

(Amb.) This is the glory of conscience that he called [Col. 0163A] simplicity and sincerity. And because these things come from God’s teaching, he added, “not in carnal wisdom but in the grace of God,” to show that he had presented a conscience free not to human wisdom but to the preaching of the Gospel.

He renews what had happened previously. For this signifies that in the first Epistle he had accused them of a deceptive preaching adapted to human judgment. He accuses its preachers of carnal wisdom in two ways: they preached according to the judgment of the world so as not easily to offend people, and they did this for the sake of profit, pursuing their own carnal gains. For this reason the Apostle never wished to accept support from the Corinthians, so that he would not give them the opportunity to say that he was like them in this matter. Hence he says, “We conducted ourselves among you with greater simplicity [Col. 0163B],” because, although he had accepted from others, he did not wish to accept from them, lest he lose the authority to rebuke them.

“For we have written nothing else to you than what you read and understand.” He says that he writes what they would not merely see in letters but also find manifest in his actions, so that he might prove that he fulfilled by his deeds what he says—deeds by which each person’s mind and purpose may be learned.

“I hope that you will understand fully to the end, just as you have understood us in part, because we are your glory, just as you are ours on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.” He hopes that they will progress because they had already begun to become better, having recognized the Apostle’s affection toward them; and they gloried in him as sons in a most beloved father. Hence the Apostle also testifies that his glory is seen in obedient sons, and that it ought to be seen when it is [Col. 0163C] beneficial—that is, on the day of God’s judgment. By saying this, he urges them to persevere.

“And in this confidence I had wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second grace, and through you to pass into Macedonia, and again from Macedonia to come to you, and to be sent on my way by you into Judea.” This confidence arose from their reformed life. For he now signifies that he also desired those whom previously it had been unworthy to see. They would therefore have received full grace from his arrival, because a letter is an image, whereas presence is reality.

It is not without purpose that he wished to go and did not go. He wishes it to be understood that there were some among them on whose account he did not fulfill his intention, so that, once they had applied themselves to the work, they might be purified.

[Col. 0163D] “Therefore, when I was considering this, did I use fickleness? Or do I make my plans according to the flesh, so that with me it is ‘Yes, yes’ and ‘No, no’?” Because he had said, “I had wanted to come to you,” and did not go, he therefore says: “Did I use fickleness? Or do I make my plans according to the flesh, so that with me it is ‘Yes’ and ‘No’?”

As though he were openly saying: Let not a breath of changeability move you concerning this, because I do not yield to the fault of fickleness. A person who says one thing and does not do it appears to be acting from fickleness. Therefore, lest they should think this about the Apostle, he clears it away: he did not do this lightly but deliberately, so that he would not fulfill what he had planned.

“Or,” he says, “do I make my plans according to the flesh?” For someone who thinks according to the flesh does not fulfill what he plans when he is overcome either by showing deference to more powerful persons [Col. 0164A], or by profits, or certainly by displays—things the Apostle always despised.

A spiritual plan, however, is not fulfilled when someone more prudently considers something for the salvation of the soul, just as the Apostle did not fulfill what he had wanted in order that through this very thing they might become better, knowing that he had postponed his visit because certain people among them had not yet purified themselves from their sins.

“Let what is with me be ‘Yes, yes’ and ‘No, no.’” This signifies that he did nothing other than what ought to be done, because usefulness must be placed before desire. This is the spiritual sense. The carnal sense changes in such a way that it places desire before usefulness.

“But God is faithful, because our word toward you is not ‘Yes’ and ‘No.’” Rather, it is “Yes” in him. This is what he also says to the Galatians: “If I rebuild the things I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor” (Gal. II).

[Col. 0164B] Therefore, he calls God’s preaching faithful in him, for flatterers do these things: they frequently omit what is true so as not to offend people.

“For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you through us—through me and Silvanus and Timothy—was not ‘Yes’ and ‘No,’ but ‘Yes’ has been in him.”

(Amb.) As far as suitable preachers are concerned, this ought to be the case: with them there should be “Yes, yes” and “No, no,” so that they do nothing except what they know to be useful. Since we frequently desire something other than what is useful, the Apostle placed usefulness before his desire, so that he would not go to them.

“For in Christ Jesus there was not ‘Yes’ and ‘No,’ but ‘Yes’ was in him,” because he never desired anything other than what is useful. His will is always joined to usefulness [Col. 0164C]. He was not changed so as to do unwillingly what is useful, nor did he hesitate about anything, nor did he change his will.

“For however many the promises of God are, in him they are ‘Yes.’ Therefore, through him also comes the ‘Amen’ to God, for our glory.” It is clear that truth is always in God—that is, “Amen”—made manifest through Christ and afterward preached through the apostles for the glory of God, with the powers of signs bearing witness that the things God promised through Christ our Lord are true. The glory of God consists in the statement that all things are from him, through him, and in him.

“Now the one who confirms us with you in Christ, and who anointed us, is God; he also sealed us and gave us the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts.” He says that Christ confirms the Gentiles in the faith promised to the Jews [Col. 0164D], because he is the one who made both one—that is, circumcision and uncircumcision—making peace in one new human being.

The Lord, therefore, confirms, and so does God, who anointed us—that is, who gave us royal honor, as the apostle Peter says: “We are a royal race” (1 Pet. II)—through a spiritual anointing, whose type was found in the kings of the Jews.

“He also sealed us,” giving us his Spirit as a pledge, so that we may not doubt his promises. For if he has entrusted his Spirit even to mortals, there is no doubt that he will already add it to immortals for glory.

He nevertheless speaks of one work of the Father and the Son, because he says that Christ confirms and God does so. Whomever the Son confirms, the Father also confirms [Col. 0165A]; and when the Father gives the Spirit, the Son also gives him, because the Holy Spirit belongs to both, as he says to the Romans: “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. VIII).

Since, therefore, he has spoken of human perfection, he has made mention here of the Trinity. For the whole fullness of perfection consists in the Trinity.

“But I call God as witness upon my soul, that, in sparing you, I did not come again to Corinth.” Now he makes clear the reason why, although he had wanted to go to them, he postponed his visit: he would go when he found nearly all of them already corrected. He is now speaking to those who seemed to wish to correct themselves but were not making the effort to fulfill that wish. Since it was therefore necessary to rebuke them, he turned his journey elsewhere, lest he sadden many; and this was his way of sparing them.

To impress this upon their minds, he calls God as witness [Col. 0165B], lest they should think themselves unworthy or despised by him. Once they learned this, they would correct themselves so as to deserve his presence.

“Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are fellow workers for your joy, for by faith you stand.” Since faith is a matter not of necessity but of will, he says, “not that we lord it over your faith,” for domination belongs to necessity.

“We are fellow workers,” he says, “for your joy”—that is, just as there is sadness in an evil work, so there is joy in correction. “We are fellow workers for this joy,” because, when they wished to correct themselves, they offered opportunities by which they could fulfill what they had begun to desire.

“Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are fellow workers for your joy.” Immediately he added, “for by faith you stand,” as though he were explaining what he had said: “We do not lord it over your faith because you stand by faith [Col. 0165C].” We are equal to you in the matter in which we recognize you standing. It was not as though he did not know himself to be placed above the brothers, since he said: “We became little ones in the midst of you” (1 Thess. II), and again: “We are your servants through Christ” (2 Cor. IV).

## CHAPTER II

The twofold reason why the Apostle did not come: lest he should sadden them, and so that he might produce greater fruit elsewhere; he then explains what that fruit was.

But I determined this within myself, not to come to you again in sorrow. (Amb.) It is clear that he did not wish to go lest, perhaps, while rebuking a few, he should grieve many, and himself also be grieved; for all the members share in the sorrow of one. For if I grieve you, who is there to make me glad except the one who is grieved by me? [Col. 0165D] He says this because he does not wish to grieve them; but because they had devoted themselves to sins, it was necessary that they should be grieved against the Apostle’s will, yet in such a way that thereafter, having become obedient, they might gladden those who were grieving together with them—so that he who had grieved them by rebuking them might rejoice in them when they corrected themselves. And I wrote this very thing to you so that, when I come, I may not have sorrow upon sorrow because of those over whom I ought to rejoice, confident in all of you, because my joy is the joy of you all. Therefore he says that he wrote this so that, when he came afterward, there might be nothing over which he would be grieved, their vices having been removed, but that he might rejoice with them as with most beloved sons—so that he who was afflicted by tribulations from unbelievers might rejoice because of those who had believed. [Col. 0166A] For the Apostle’s joy is the purification of the people. He rejoices for this reason: there is no reproach in those with whom he ought equally to rejoice.
