For out of great tribulation and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears, not so that you might be grieved, but so that you might know the abundant love that I have for you. It is evident that when someone rebukes another in such a spirit that he grieves more deeply than the sinner does over his sins, he certainly does not rebuke him in order to grieve him, but to show him with what love he loves him. For whoever does not rebuke his brother in this spirit grieves him; he insults his brother if he does not grieve with him. But if anyone has caused me sorrow, he has not caused me sorrow alone, but in part, so that I may not burden you all. All these [Col. 0166B] whom he says are “in part” are holy; for there are two parts among the people, as I mentioned in the First Epistle. These, then, belong in part to the holy, whom he indicates were grieved by their brother’s error, just as he himself was. By saying this he burdened the sinner, or the one who had sinned: for one whose offense causes many to suffer becomes more guilty. And therefore: This rebuke, which has been inflicted by the majority, is sufficient for such a person. A person surely suffers great pain when he sees that his offense displeases many.

So that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive and console him, lest such a person be swallowed up by excessive sorrow. He commanded that a person afflicted because of his own sin should be helped, because repentance, if it proceeds from a true heart—that is, if the person who has been rebuked immediately grieves inwardly—at once bears fruit. Accordingly, the history in the Books of [Col. 0166C] Kings records that when Ahab had been rebuked by the prophet, he was moved in heart and immediately obtained forgiveness (III Kings XXI); and David, when rebuked in the matter of Uriah the Hittite, because he recognized that he had sinned, had his offense blotted out (II Samuel XII). So also the Apostle commands that the man who had committed incest by having his father’s wife, after being rebuked and cast out, should be recalled when grieving, lest, seeing himself for a long time grieved and despised, he should despair of himself and give his soul over to the enjoyment of the world, as though he no longer had a place with God. This is to be swallowed up by greater sorrow: the despairing person turns to the commission of sins, by which, weighed down, he is swallowed up by the second death. For this is true repentance: to cease from sin; for he proves that he grieves for himself if thereafter he stops sinning. Therefore I beseech you to confirm your love toward him. [Col. 0166D] I wrote to you for this reason, to learn by experience whether you are obedient in all things. It can be understood that he approves these people as having become obedient in other matters, for they had corrected what concerned ecclesiastical order. Hence he also wishes them to be obedient in this matter, by confirming their brother in love and receiving him into communion.

But if you have forgiven anyone anything, I forgive also. It is clear that he himself does what he commands to be done, and that he cannot refuse this when he writes urging that it be done, although he had the authority to command. But in the First Epistle he exposed the man’s grave offense so that everyone would shudder at him. Now he wishes him to be received, and he asks that, although their minds toward him had been embittered, it should not remain difficult for them to share ecclesial communion with him. [Col. 0167A] For they did not possess as much foresight as the Apostle, so as immediately to understand that what the Apostle was saying in this case ought to be done. Therefore he begs them to forgive him, indicating that God had forgiven him, because the Apostle did nothing without the Spirit of God. (Greg.) Well, in the vision of Ezekiel (Ezekiel XL), when the lips of the tables are measured and the measure of a palm is mentioned, “one” is added, so that, just as unity is maintained in faith through the preaching of teachers, so unity of mind may also be preserved in conduct, lest, because of the good work one person performs, another break out into the evil of discord. We ought to perform good works in such a way that through them also we preserve, as far as we rightly can, unanimity with those among whom we live—that is, not abandoning the good that we are doing, but forestalling by good persuasion the evil of discord that we fear.

[Col. 0167B] Thus Paul, preserving in his works the unity of the palm, prevented discord from arising when he saw that the Corinthians wished to receive again a certain man who had already fallen and been expelled from the Church, saying: If you have forgiven anyone anything, I forgive also; for if I have forgiven anything, I have done so for your sake in the person of Christ, lest we be outwitted by Satan. He is accustomed, that is, to generate evil from good and to turn into discord what is done through love. Hence he immediately added concerning him: For we are not ignorant of his designs. But a teacher who, through the good things he preaches, forms right conduct in his hearers, if he does not bind the minds of those who act together in unanimity, has a palm on his lips, but does not possess the unity of the palm that has been mentioned. [Col. 0167C]

For if I have forgiven anything, I have done so for your sake in the person of Christ. (Amb.) By saying this he places a burden upon them: if [Al. quasi, “as though”] a teacher, he forgave, at his disciples’ request, the sin of the one whom they wished, how much more ought the disciples to obey their teacher? And to show that what he had forgiven was ratified before God for the one whom he had forgiven, he says that he forgave it in the person of Christ—that is, he counted Christ as approving it, since he exercised Christ’s legation, so that what the Apostle did might be Christ’s deed, just as he said: Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven (Matthew XVIII). But if Christ forgave the one for whom they had asked through the Apostle, how much more had he already been forgiven whom the Apostle himself urges them to forgive? Lest we be outwitted by Satan, for we are not ignorant of his designs. He says what I mentioned above: [Col. 0167D] consolation ought to follow a brother who weeps over his offense, lest, having long been grieved and despised by the Church’s love, he begin to despair of himself. Then the subtle devil, who is always lying in wait, seeing that his mind has been made worthless, may approach and suggest that he should at least enjoy present things, since he has been cast down from hope of the future reward; and the brother, possessed by the devil, may perish, although repentance had been given him for this purpose, that, when converted, he might restore himself. As the prophet Ezekiel says: I do not desire the death of the one who dies, but rather that he should turn back and live (Ezekiel XVIII); and again: Let them turn back, he says, and I will replant them (Ezekiel XXXII).

(Greg.) With great skill in his teaching, he was handed over to the one who was compelled to punish him, although he had voluntarily subjected himself to guilt, so that he who had voluntarily subjected himself to guilt was handed over under compulsion for punishment to the one to whom he had submitted, so that he who had been the author of the vice of wickedness might himself become the lash of discipline. [Col. 0168A] But when this repentance had been rightly carried out, and he learned that the Corinthians had already been moved toward him with mercy, he said: If anyone has been forgiven anything, I forgive also. For if I have forgiven anything, I have done so for your sake in the person of Christ. Thinking, therefore, of the grace of communion, he says, If anyone has been forgiven anything, I forgive also—as though he were saying: I do not dissent from your goodness; whatever you have done, let it be mine also. Then he added: And if I have forgiven anything, I have done so for your sake—as though he were saying: I have added goodness to your actions; whatever I have done mercifully for your sake—my goodness—is therefore your benefit; your goodness is my benefit.

Immediately adding the very bond of hearts by which this unity is maintained, he continued: In the person of Christ. As though someone might dare to ask: Why do you so carefully join yourself to your disciples? Why do you conform yourself to their actions, or them [Col. 0168B] to yours, with such attentive concern? He immediately added: Lest we be outwitted by Satan. He indicates how sharply he pierces Satan’s [Al. sagaces, “shrewd”] snares by adding: For we are not ignorant of his designs—as though he were saying in other words: With the Lord as our author, we are sharp stakes, and by carefully examining we penetrate the nostrils of this Behemoth, lest he turn into an end of wickedness what the mind has begun well.

When I came to Troas for the Gospel of Christ, and a door had been opened to me in the Lord, I had no rest for my spirit because I did not find Titus my brother; but, taking leave of them, I departed for Macedonia. (Hier.) He tells the Corinthians what he did, what he suffered, and how in all things he gives [Col. 0168C] thanks, so that by his example he may urge them to strive. I came, he says, to Troas, which was formerly called Troy, to preach the Gospel of Christ in Asia. And when a door had been opened to me in the Lord—that is, when very many had believed, whether through the signs and wonders that God worked in me, so that there was hope of a faith being born and growing in the Lord—I had no rest for my spirit. That is, I could not find the consolation I had hoped for, because I did not find Titus my brother, whether the one whom I thought would be found there, or whom I had heard was living there, or who had said that he would come there.

But what was this great consolation, and what rest for the spirit could Titus’s presence provide, so that, because he did not find him, Paul took leave of them and departed for Macedonia? We have said several times that the Apostle Paul [Col. 0168D] was a most learned and educated man, trained at the feet of Gamaliel, who preached in the Acts of the Apostles and said: What have you to do with these men? For if it is from God, it will stand; but if it is from men, it will be destroyed (Acts V). Although he possessed knowledge of the holy Scriptures and the gift of speech in various languages, for he himself boasts in the Lord and says: I thank God that I speak in tongues more than you all (I Corinthians XIV), he could not adequately express the majesty of divine meanings in the language of Greek eloquence. Therefore he had Titus as an interpreter, just as Blessed Peter had Mark, whose Gospel was composed with Peter narrating and Mark writing. Indeed, the two epistles attributed to Peter differ from one another in style, character, and the structure of their words; [Col. 0169A] from this we understand that, according to the necessity of circumstances, he made use of different interpreters.

Thus the Apostle Paul was saddened because he had not found the channel and instrument of his preaching through which he might sing to Christ at that time, and he proceeded to Macedonia. For a Macedonian man had appeared to him, saying: Cross over and help us (Acts XVI), so that there he might find Titus and visit the brothers, or be tested by persecutions.

This may also be understood in another way. (Amb.) Paul had gone to Troas to preach the Gospel of Christ, and when he had begun preaching, there were people who received the word of faith. But because Titus’s assistance was lacking, the labor was intolerable because of the uproar of those who opposed him. Although some of them had opened their hearts to receive the word of God, [Col. 0169B] the insolence of the unbelievers was nevertheless considerable, rising up against the Apostle out of zeal for those who believed. One person could not fulfill both tasks: either instructing the faithful or resisting the unbelievers. Therefore, after taking leave of those who had received him, he departed for Macedonia.

But thanks be to God, who always triumphs through us in Christ Jesus. Instead of saying, “who triumphs over us,” or “who accomplishes his triumph through us,” he speaks as he had said elsewhere: We have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings. For when I came to Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we suffered every kind of tribulation—battles outside, fears within. But God, who comforts the humble, comforted us by the arrival of Titus—not only by his arrival, but also by his [Col. 0169C] consolation (I Corinthians IV; II Corinthians VII).

Therefore, after taking leave of the Trojans, or people of Troas, he departed for Macedonia, so that he might find Titus there and have the consolation of his interpretation and of the Gospel. We understand that Titus was not found there, but came afterward amid the Apostle’s tribulations and persecutions. Before Titus arrived, therefore, Paul endured many hardships and gave thanks to almighty God in Christ Jesus, whom he preached to the nations, because God had chosen him as one in whom he might accomplish the triumph of his Son. God’s triumph is the suffering of the martyrs: the shedding of blood in Christ’s name and joy amid torments. For when someone sees martyrs standing firm with such perseverance, being tortured and glorying in their sufferings, the fragrance of the knowledge of God is spread among the nations, and the silent thought arises that, unless the Gospel were true, [Col. 0169D] it would never be defended with blood. This confession is not delicate, wealth-loving, and secure; rather, this is the triumph of the apostles and their victory—in prisons, in wounds, in persecutions, in hunger, nakedness, and thirst.

But someone hearing this might answer: How, then, did not everyone believe? Before he asks the question, therefore, he resolves it, and according to his custom he explains beforehand whatever another person might object. And he manifests the fragrance of his knowledge through us in every place: For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God, among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing. To some, indeed, an odor of death unto death; to others, an odor of life unto life.

(Hieron.) The meaning is that, in every place, we are the good fragrance of the knowledge of Christ’s name before God, and that the fragrance of our [Col. 0170A] preaching spreads far and wide. But because human beings have been left to their own choice—for they do not do good by necessity but by will, so that believers may receive a crown and unbelievers be given over to punishment—our fragrance, which is good in itself, passes by the virtue or vice of those who receive or do not receive it either into life or into death: those who believe are saved, and those who do not believe perish.

(Amb.) The fragrance of the knowledge of God is in Christ and through Christ. He called it a fragrance for this reason: just as certain things, although unseen, are nevertheless recognized by their smell, and one understands that something is present in a place even though one does not see it, so God, because he is invisible, wished to be understood through Christ. Thus the preaching of Christ, which reaches the ears invisibly just as fragrance reaches the nostrils, [Col. 0170B] was to reveal God the Father to creation, together with his only-begotten Son. The apostles, entrusted with this embassy—just as the Lord says to God, the Son to the Father, “Just as you sent me into this world, so I also send them into this world”—were to manifest the fragrance of the knowledge of God and of Christ through signs and wonders.

The truth of the preaching concerning God and Christ is demonstrated by the testimony of power. It is represented by fragrance because, although God is not seen, through this power, which works invisibly, he is understood to be present in the apostles, so that the truth of the doctrine may be made manifest. Therefore whoever rightly proclaims Christ is a good fragrance before God, worthy of praise among the one who believes and not blameworthy in the one who does not believe. But whoever does not rightly proclaim Christ is a bad fragrance before God, both among those who are faithful and among those who distrust; for he will be guilty on behalf of both. [Col. 0170C] The one who distrusts seems not to believe because what he hears is perverse, while the one who believes believes wrongly.

The Apostle therefore spoke according to the reasoning of the Law: just as in the Law the one who offered sacrifices with a good intention was a good and acceptable fragrance to God, so now the power of preaching supplies to God the fragrance of a doctrine that is sweet-smelling. For this reason God supplied the apostles with all his assistance, so that they might pour out the words of his knowledge into receptive ears, whether Jewish or Gentile, adding to these the mystery of the Lord Jesus’ birth according to the will of God and his Father, in the unity of saving faith, for the salvation of believers and the destruction of those who distrust.

To some, he says, an odor of death unto death. He says this because to unbelievers the preaching of Christ’s cross is an odor of death. For when they hear the word of God, they receive it as though [Col. 0170D] it were a plague from which death arises, and it is necessary that, according to their faith, it should become so for them. But to others an odor of life unto life. It is true: the word of faith that is heard is a divine message of eternal salvation, and according to their faith it will happen to them. Therefore, whether among those who perish or among those who are saved, the apostles were the good fragrance of Christ before God, because they preached sincerely. Those who did not believe were themselves tying the noose around their own necks.

To them, as the Lord says to the prophet Ezekiel: You preach; if they listen to you, you will gain their souls; but if not, let them look to themselves. You, nevertheless, will be free from their destruction.

(Greg.) Just as a good fragrance arises from virtue, as Paul testifies when he says, “He manifests the fragrance of his knowledge through us in every place,” and “We are the good fragrance of Christ [Col. 0171A] before God,” so, conversely, stench arises from vice. The root of all evils is greed; and because every evil is generated through avarice, it is fitting that the house of avarice should be built in stench. Happy are those who live by a good fragrance; but what is more wretched than those who die by a good fragrance?

(Aug.) And who, someone may say, is killed by a good fragrance? This is what the Apostle says: And who is sufficient for these things? In marvelous ways God has arranged that by a good fragrance the good should live and the wicked die. The fame of the Apostle Paul, who acted well, lived well, proclaimed righteousness in word and demonstrated it in deed, an extraordinary teacher and faithful steward, was spread everywhere. Some loved him; some were envious of him. You loved the one who acted well—you lived by a good fragrance. You envied the one who acted well—you died by a good fragrance. Behold why the most vigorous soldier [Col. 0171B] and unconquered defender of grace gives thanks. Behold why he gives thanks: because the apostles are the good fragrance of Christ before God, among those who are saved by his grace and among those who perish by his judgment. But lest this should provoke too much anger in those who understand it poorly, he himself admonishes them and says:

And who is so sufficient for these things? For we are not like the many who adulterate the word of God, but in sincerity, as from God and before God, we speak in Christ. (Amb.) In this verse he touches upon the false apostles, who adulterated the words of God by corrupt interpretation, removing the divine meaning and substituting a human one. Some of them, zealous for Jewish tradition, did not teach rightly about Christ; therefore he calls them less competent. The apostles, however, preached sincerely, [Col. 0171C] as it had been given from God; before God—that is, as God had given it, with God himself as witness—they spoke in Christ, not seeking their own glory but God’s. To speak in Christ is to proclaim his honor and power.

(Hier.) For it is difficult to find someone worthy to proclaim the virtues of Christ who does not seek his own glory [Note: [Col. 0171D] Here a member of the phrase seems to be missing; perhaps something of this kind: “rather than his glory . . .” EDIT.] in announcing them. By denying that he is like the many who sell the word of God, he shows that there are very many who consider piety a means of gain and do everything for the sake of disgraceful profit—those who devour widows’ houses. He, however, speaks in sincerity, as one sent by God, and in the presence of the one who sent him, speaking all things in Christ and for Christ, so that the purpose of God’s preaching may be Christ’s triumph and his glory.

And it should be noted that at the end of this chapter the mystery of the Trinity is displayed. For we speak from God, in the Holy Spirit, before God the Father, in Christ. [Col. 0171D]

(Greg.) An adulterer in carnal intercourse is concerned not with offspring but with pleasure. Likewise, anyone who is perverse and serves empty glory is rightly said to adulterate the word of God, because through sacred speech he desires not to beget children for God but to display his own knowledge. Whoever is drawn to speak by the lust for glory devotes himself more to pleasure than to generation. To adulterate the word of God is either to think about it otherwise than it is, or to seek from it not spiritual fruits but adulterous offspring of human praise. To speak in sincerity, on the other hand, is to acquire nothing through one’s speech beyond what is fitting. [Col. 0172A]

He speaks as from God who knows that he does not possess from himself what he says, but has received it from God. He speaks before God who, in everything he says, does not seek human favor but directs his attention to the presence of almighty God, seeking not his own glory but that of the author. But the person who knows that he has received from God what he says and nevertheless seeks his own glory by speaking does speak as from God, but not before God, because when he preaches he treats as absent the one whom he does not set before his heart.

Holy men, however, speak both from God and before God, because they know that from him they have what they say, and they regard him as present in their words, both judge and hearer. Hence it happens that, when they recognize that they are despised by those close to them and that their words do not benefit the lives of their hearers, they conceal [Col. 0172B] how great their virtues are, lest, if speech uselessly reveals the secret of the heart, it should break out into empty glory.

## CHAPTER III. The Apostle shows that he does not need, nor seek, human commendation. He commends the ministers of Christ to the Church with regard to the dignity of their office and the excellence of their knowledge.

Are we beginning again to commend ourselves? (Amb.) Since he is criticizing the false apostles and pointing out the perverse commendations they received, while testifying that he himself is a true preacher, he seems once again to commend himself, as in the First Epistle. And lest he should appear to do this through some worldly cunning for the sake of earthly profit, he added: Do we perhaps need, like some, letters of commendation to you or from you? In saying this he both purifies his own intention [Col. 0172C] and continues to criticize the false apostles, whom he proves to travel around the churches for the sake of their own honor and profit, to take away salvation rather than to bestow it. They were among those of whom the Lord says: You devour the houses of widows and orphans, praying at length; therefore you will receive the greater judgment (Matthew XXIII). Paul, however, neither touched their possessions nor endangered them, but saved their souls by the truth of his doctrine. He therefore commended himself to their benefit, not in a scandalous but in a spiritual manner, so that they might believe of him what he was; for whoever thinks badly of what is good sins. Thus this commendation benefits them more.

You are our letter, written in our hearts. A letter is an indication of salvation. He therefore rightly says this, because the salvation of the Corinthians was in the heart of the Apostle and of those who were with him; for he was always [Col. 0172D] thinking about their salvation. Since the apostles and those who were with him had them in their hearts, they were letters written in their hearts, because whoever is always mindful of someone has that person written in his mind.

Known and read by all people, since you are shown to be Christ’s letter, delivered by us. It is clear that when Christians are spoken of, they are Christ’s letter, indicating the salvation that God gave in Christ to all human beings, with the apostles writing it. For while they teach, they write.

Written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God. Since the things promised are eternal, they are said to be written by the Spirit of God, who always is; temporal things, however, are written with ink, which grows old and loses its [Col. 0173A] memory.

Not on stone tablets, but on tablets of fleshly hearts. He now strikes at the old Law, which, having first been given on stone tablets, was abolished when Moses broke the tablets beneath the mountain. The new Law, however, is written in the mind—that is, in the heart—not by a pen but by the Spirit, because faith is an eternal reality and is written by the Spirit so that it may remain. The old commandments, however, will cease when the world comes to an end. Therefore, just as one law differs from another, so the stewards of that Law differ from the stewards of the law of faith.

We have such confidence through Christ toward God. He shows how great is the dignity of the apostles when he says, “We have such confidence through Christ toward God,” indicating that the ancients did not have this confidence toward God, because their ministry was of a lesser kind.

[Col. 0173B] Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God, who also made us competent ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life. Although he gives precedence to apostolic dignity, he nevertheless breaks forth into the praises of God, attributing this not to human merits but to the grace of the one who deigned to establish a saving proclamation for human life—a proclamation that would save those whom the old law held guilty, remission of sins having been granted through Christ our Lord.

For the letters were given to Moses for this purpose: that, according to the law of nature, they might kill those who despised the law. But the Spirit—that is, the law of faith, which is not written but held within the mind—gives life to those deserving death when they turn back, so that, having been justified, they may no longer sin.

[Col. 0173C] The law, then, was rightly given so that there might be fear of sinning. But because the human race is frail, God’s mercy was given through the apostles’ preaching, so that, their sins having been forgiven, those who believe in Christ might escape death. This is the preaching of the New Testament, which God had promised through the prophets.

The Teacher of the Gentiles likewise, recognizing that he had been made competent for the ministry of the New Testament, proclaims that this was not by his own merit or labor, but by God’s compassion.

**(Cassiodorus.)** “Not that we are,” he says, “competent to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God”—which is less idiomatic in Latin, but can be expressed more clearly as: “Our competence is from God.” Finally, what follows says: “Who also made us competent ministers of the New Testament.”

So greatly did the apostles perceive that everything pertaining to salvation had been granted to them by the Lord that they even asked the Lord to provide them with faith itself, saying, “Increase our faith” (Luke 17), its fullness—not presuming upon free will, but believing that it would be bestowed upon them as God’s gift.

**(Augustine.)** The law, when merely read and not understood, or not fulfilled, certainly kills; it is then called “the letter.” But the Spirit gives life, because the fullness of the law is love, which has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

Now if the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stones, was glorious—so glorious that the children of Israel could not look intently at Moses’ face because of the glory of his countenance, a glory that is being brought to an end—how much more will the ministry of the Spirit be glorious?

It is evident that the grace of the law of faith is greater than that of the law of Moses. Although the law of Moses was given for the purpose of being beneficial, when it was despised it became a law of death. Therefore, because it could not provide for sinners, the law of faith was given—a law that would save them, not merely by forgiving but also by justifying them.

There was therefore a great difference between the one law and the other. At that time, those stained by sin could not look upon Moses’ face as he descended from the mountain with the law he had received on the tablets (Exodus 34), because his face had become glorious, so that sinners could not look upon it, since they were worthy of death. That glory is now brought to an end through the law of the Spirit: once they have received forgiveness of sins and been made righteous, they are worthy—and able—to behold the glory of God, just as Peter, John, and James saw the glory of Christ on the mountain (Matthew 17).

**(Augustine.)** Why is it called “the ministry of death” if the law is good? Because “sin, in order that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good” (Romans 7). Nor should this surprise us, since the same thing is said concerning the preaching of the Gospel: “We are the good odor of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing; to some, an odor of life leading to life, but to others, an odor of death leading to death.”

The law was called the ministry of death to the Jews, to whom it was also written on stone, to signify their hardness—not to those who fulfill the law through love. For the fullness of the law is love: “Whoever loves another has fulfilled the law. For, ‘You shall not commit adultery, you shall not murder, you shall not steal,’ and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (Romans 13).

Since this too is written in the same law, care must be taken not to understand figurative language literally. This is also what the Apostle means when he says, “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” When something said figuratively is accepted as though it had been said literally, one thinks carnally. No death of the soul can more appropriately be named than this: when even that which distinguishes the soul from beasts is subjected to the flesh by following the letter.

For example, whoever follows the letter, upon hearing of the Sabbath, understands nothing except one day among the seven, which recur in an unbroken sequence. Upon hearing of sacrifice, he does not go beyond the thought of what is customarily done with animal victims and earthly produce.

For if the ministry of condemnation was glorious, the ministry of righteousness abounds much more in glory.

**(Ambrose.)** He says this because the gift of God’s righteousness through faith in Christ is greater than that of the old law: glory is greater in salvation than in death. Although condemnation is just, it contributes more to praise when it forgives, so that the guilty person may be able to correct himself.

[Col. 0174D] **(Augustine.)** Although the law was just, holy, and good, it brought death upon transgressors, whom God’s grace did not assist in fulfilling the righteousness of the law. For in the old covenant it was necessary that the law be imposed upon the proud, who trusted in the power of their own will—a law that did not give righteousness but issued commands—so that, entangled in the death of transgression, they might flee to grace, which was revealed in the New Testament as not merely commanding but also assisting.

What wonder, then, if that was called the ministry of death, in which the letter kills by prohibiting the evil that is done, but does not command the good that is done? This, however, is called the ministry of the Spirit, who certainly gives life, so that we may rise from the death of transgression and possess righteousness—not as guilty persons reading it on tablets, but as free persons possessing it in our hearts and conduct.

This is the distinction between the New Testament and the Old: there, the old person is confined by the narrowness of fear; here, the new person moves freely in the breadth of love.

As for what was said about Moses, the minister of the Old Testament—that the children of Israel could not look intently at his face because of the glory of his countenance—it signified that they would not understand Christ in the law. Therefore a veil had been placed over Moses’ face before them, so that they would not look intently, as it is written: “The children of Israel to the end.”

But what is the end of the law? Let not I, but the Apostle himself answer: “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10)—the end that perfects, not the end that destroys.

The end is called such because of that for which all things are done, whatever is done through some other office. For there is this difference between an office and an end: an office concerns the things we ought to do, while the end is that for which we do them. All those things were done for Christ, whom the children of Israel did not understand in the things that were being done.

This is what the veil signified: it did not permit them to look intently to the end, that is, to Moses’ face, which signified Christ. Yet it was said that this glory would be brought to an end because all the shadows signifying something are brought to an end when the reality signified arrives.

Just as the knowledge that exists now will be brought to an end, as the same Apostle says, when that which he calls “face to face” has come (1 Corinthians 13), so too it was necessary that what had been given to the Jews in shadows in the Old Testament be brought to an end through the revelation of the New Testament.

Certainly, not everyone in that people failed to understand Christ, who was prefigured through those shadows of the Old Testament. For Moses himself and the other prophets understood him, since they foretold him to others. Nor was that which shone forth in this respect glorified because of its surpassing glory.

**(Ambrose.)** It is evident that what was seen gloriously in Moses’ face did not become truly glorious. For when the glory of his face benefited no one, it bore no fruit of glory; rather, it was harmful—not through any fault of its own, but because of sinners. In this respect, therefore, it was not glory.

The greater glory is that which abounds in grace, so that people purified by God’s gift, once their darkness has been wiped away, may be able to see the glory of Christ. For if that which is being brought to an end is through glory, much more is that which remains in glory.

He does not deny that there was glory in the law or in Moses’ face, but it did not remain in Moses because what appeared was a figure. The truth remains forever. Thus, as great as the difference between image and truth, so great is the difference between the glory of Moses’ face and the glory of Christ.

Therefore he previously said, “because of the surpassing glory.” The former glory was as great as was appropriate to be believed of a servant; the latter is as great as belongs to his begetter, because the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father.

Just as the stars are glorious in the evening, but their brightness is brought to an end when the sun rises, so Moses’ glory is brought to an end when the glory of Christ appears.

“Therefore, having such hope, we use great confidence.” He says that we have the hope of seeing glory—not such as was in Moses’ face, but the glory that the three apostles saw on the mountain when the Lord revealed himself. From this, then, we should infer how much divine clemency has bestowed upon us, and how much richer a gift of the higher grace it has deigned to grant us than it had given to the Jews.

The Jews, therefore, could not gaze upon the glory of Moses’ face, though it was lesser. We, however, believe that we shall see not the lesser glory of Moses but the surpassing glory of the Savior.

The Jews did not deserve to see the glory of a servant; we shall see the glory of our common Lord. Therefore we too ought, insofar as we can, to repay God’s benevolence by being more devoted to his love, since he has given us confidence—cleansing us from sins—to see the glory of God.

Now, therefore, confidence must grow in us, prepared by good works; for we shall see only as much as we believe.

“And not as Moses placed a veil over his face, so that the children of Israel might not look intently at the end of what was being brought to an end.”

Because by God’s grace we have been made worthy to see the glory of Christ, he says, “not as Moses,” who placed a veil over his face so that the children of Israel would not look upon it. He placed the veil because they could not bear the splendor of his face on account of sin. Once that sin has been removed, the power to see the glory of God is granted to the end.

The veil is not revealed as long as they remain under the law; when they turn to the grace of faith, it is brought to an end. With the dignity that comes through faith, indignity is removed.

But their minds were dulled to this very day. He calls them dulled as long as they do not believe. This dullness arose because of unbelief. Therefore, when they turn to faith, the sharpness of their mind is restored so that they may see the splendor of the divine light.

The same veil remains unremoved in the reading of the Old Testament, because it is brought to an end in Christ. He says that this dullness remains in the reading of Exodus as long as they do not believe; for it is not revealed unless they believe. In Christ it is brought to an end—that is, through faith in Christ the veil is removed. Once the offense has been taken away, they begin to see what, while sin obstructed them, they could not see.

But “to this very day, when Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart.” It is evident that when this part of the law is read, the judgment of those who are under the law is being recited.

**(Gregory.)** Hence it is written in Job: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there” (Job 1). The Redeemer’s mother, according to the flesh, is the Synagogue, from which he came to us visibly in bodily form. Yet it kept him concealed within itself under the covering of the letter, because it neglected to open its eyes to his spiritual meaning.

Because it did not wish to see God hidden in human flesh, it refused, as it were, to behold him naked in his divinity. But he came forth naked from his mother’s womb, because, proceeding from the flesh of the Synagogue, he came visibly to the Gentiles.

This was aptly signified when Joseph fled, leaving behind his garment. When the adulterous woman wished to use it improperly, he left the garment and fled outside. In the same way, when the Synagogue, believing the Lord to be merely human, wished to hold him in an adulterous embrace, he left the covering of the letter to its eyes and presented himself visibly to the Gentiles, so that they might recognize the power of his divinity.

Hence Paul also says: “To this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart.” For the adulterous woman kept the garment with herself, and lost naked the one whom she had held improperly. Therefore, coming from the Synagogue, he appeared visibly to the faith of the Gentiles; naked he came forth from his mother’s womb.

But when one turns to the Lord, the veil will be removed.

**(Ambrose.)** To turn to the Lord means to believe in Christ, so that, recognizing the Lord, one may deserve to receive forgiveness—that is, that the veil may be removed and the sentence by which one was held guilty under the law may be brought to an end.

“The Lord, however, is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.” Since God is Spirit, through Christ he gave a spiritual law, certainly not written in letters but impressed upon souls through faith. It does not teach visible things, but urges that invisible things be believed; the soul grasps them spiritually, not through what the eye sees.

This law gives freedom, asking only for faith, so that, because one believes what one does not see, one may deserve to be freed from bondage. Yet there is no freedom in guilt, for it is written: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.”

“But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.”

He says “we all” who have obtained freedom through the gift of God’s grace. Beholding the glory of the Lord through faith, we are transformed into the same image that we hope for—that is, after this life has passed, we shall be found like the image of Christ’s glory, as the Apostle John says: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3).

“From glory to glory,” as from the Spirit of the Lord: that is, we are raised by God’s gracious gift from the glory of Moses, which we were unable to see because of guilt, to the glory that we believe will be given to us by the Spirit of the Lord. Glory will be given in such measure as it is fitting for God to give through his Spirit.

For this reason he said, “as by the Spirit of the Lord,” to show that such glory would be given as corresponds to the greatness of the giver. Moses’ glory was neither so great nor everlasting; he received glory according to the measure of the law. Likewise, according to the measure of the law of faith, in which the Spirit of God is present, glory will be given to believers.

God has granted the faithful so much that he gives them his Spirit, the pledge of the glory he has promised.

**(Augustine.)** “Now we see through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13). If we ask what this mirror is and what sort it is, surely the answer presents itself: in a mirror nothing but an image is seen. Therefore we have tried, through this image, to see to some extent what we are, and through it, as through a mirror, to see from whom we were made.

This is also signified by what the same Apostle says: “But we, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.”

He said “beholding,” meaning seeing through a mirror, not looking out from a watchtower. In the Greek language this is not ambiguous; hence the apostolic letters, when translated into Latin, use the word for a mirror in which images of things appear, not the word for a watchtower, from whose height we look at something farther away. The words themselves also differ in sound, so that it is entirely and sufficiently clear that the Apostle said “beholding the glory of the Lord” by means of a mirror, not from a watchtower.

When he says, “we are transformed into the same image,” he certainly wishes the image of God to be understood. By “the same” he means this very image that we contemplate, because this image is also the glory of God, as he says elsewhere: “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God” (1 Corinthians 11).

Therefore, when he says “we are transformed,” he means that we are changed and pass from one form to another—from an obscure form to a radiant form. For the obscure image is itself also the image of God; and if it is an image, it is certainly also a glory, in which we human beings were created, surpassing the other animals.

It is of this human nature that it was said: “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God.” This nature, the most excellent among created things, when it is justified from impiety by its Creator, is transformed from a deformed form into a beautiful form. Even in impiety itself, the more condemnable the vice, the more certainly praiseworthy is the nature. For this reason he added, “from glory to glory”: from the glory of creation to the glory of justification.

This may also be understood in other ways: “from glory to glory”—from the glory of faith to the glory of sight; from the glory by which we are children of God to the glory by which we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.

By adding, “as by the Spirit of the Lord,” he shows that the good of so desirable a transformation is conferred upon us by God’s grace.

Yet this belongs to this image when the good Teacher instructs us, through Christian faith and the doctrine of piety, to attain the future perfection. Thus, with unveiled face, freed from the veil of the law—which is the shadow of future things—we behold the glory of the Lord and are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.

The Jews have a veil over that face because they do not pass over to Christ; for when anyone passes over to Christ, the veil is removed. It is with that face unveiled that we are transformed into the same image.

He says most explicitly that a veil has been placed over their heart. There, therefore, is the face which, once unveiled now in faith, although through a mirror and in a riddle, we behold; but then we shall see face to face.

## CHAPTER IV

**The Apostle commends the ministry of the New Testament, both with regard to the performance of good and with regard to the endurance of evil.**

“Therefore, since we have this ministry according to the mercy we have received, we do not lose heart.”

**(Ambrose.)** He speaks of such great hope in this ministry that, strengthened by it, he does not lose heart under afflictions. He uses the “great confidence” mentioned above because those who trust in what has been promised endure whatever adversity occurs. He attributes this not to human merits but to God’s mercy, which first cleanses a person, then justifies him, adopting him as a son for God, so that it may grant him a glory like the glory of God’s own Son.

“But we renounce the hidden things of shame.” He teaches that all disgraceful and polluted things that can be done or imagined must be removed, so that a person may be worthy of that glory, and that they may be expelled not only from one’s actions but also from one’s thoughts.

These are words of exhortation. Speaking in his own name and that of his companions, he urges a better life because of the vices mentioned above, which he often reproves in them. These hidden things of shame may also be the schemes that they devise with a perverse intention for preaching, in order to deceive. Hence he adds: “Not walking in craftiness, nor adulterating the word of God.”

One contributes to his own disgrace and disfigurement when, with a deceitful mind, he corrupts the teaching in order to deceive the hearts of the simple. He will be found shameful on the day of God’s judgment. Through the craftiness of an evil mind, in order to accomplish whatever pleases it, a person adulterates the words of God so as to reverse their meaning. To adulterate is to attempt to exclude the true meaning through a false one.

“But by the manifestation of the truth, commending ourselves to every human conscience before God.” He says that in evangelical preaching he made himself suspect to no one. He adds “before God” to show that he proves this to be manifest not only to human beings but also to God, to whom nothing is hidden.

He therefore calls upon God as witness, so that he himself may be believed to preach as it was given by its author. God also bears witness to this before the world by causing signs and wonders to be performed through his hands.

“But even if our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing.” This is true, because unbelievers do not see: through their unbelief they blind themselves to the splendor of God’s power. A veil lies over their heart, and the dullness of unbelief—especially among the Jews.

“In whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, may not shine.”

He calls him the god of worldly people because they are hostile to faith in Christ. He blinds their understanding so that they will not see the truth of the Gospel of Christ’s majesty. In this way he grants them what they want.

Because people are hostile and lack understanding, they call the truth false; by this very act they are aided in being unable to believe what they do not wish to believe. Although Christ is the image of God, they assert that he is merely corporeal, leaving aside his deeds and mentioning only his flesh. Concerning them Isaiah said: “He has blinded their eyes, so that they may not see, and their ears, so that they may not hear, to this very day” (Isaiah 6).

**(Augustine.)** Many of us distinguish this sentence in such a way that they say the true God blinded the minds of unbelievers. When they read the words “in whom God,” they suspend the sentence there and then add: “the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers.” Even if one does not distinguish it in this way, one may alter the word order for the sake of explanation and understand it as: “In whom the God of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers.”

What meaning becomes clear in that distinction? It is possible that an action by which the minds of unbelievers are blinded may, in a certain sense, pertain even to the true God—not because of malice, but because of justice. As the same Paul says elsewhere: “Is God unjust, who inflicts wrath?” (Romans 3).

Some hidden matter precedes this hidden judgment, in which God carries out the most just examination of his judgment, so that the minds of some are blinded and those of others are enlightened. To him it is most truly said: “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Psalm 35).

“For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord.”

**(Ambrose.)** This means that we do not announce our own glory, lest anyone say that we preach the Gospel for our own sake, perhaps so that it might benefit us temporarily. Rather, we announce Jesus our Lord, submitting ourselves to his power and majesty.

When, therefore, we shake no one, burden no one, and confess Christ our Lord, why should we be judged arrogant, as though we were preaching for our own advantage, so that we might appear glorious?

“But ourselves as your servants through Jesus.”

He proves himself to be Christ’s servant to such a degree that, at Christ’s command, he testifies that he is their minister in preaching, so that, for their benefit, he and his companions may be subject in the ministry of the Gospel. By calling himself their servant, he signifies “minister”; but he speaks humbly, showing truly that he does not preach the Gospel for his own glory, but for the glory of the Lord Christ, whom he obeys and serves, just as the Lord himself says: “I am among you as one who ministers” (Luke 22)—not because of the merit of those whom he serves, but because of the Lord’s command.

**(Gregory.)** The humble are placed on high, because when they humble themselves in submission, they pass in mind beyond all temporal things through the lofty judgment of their spirit. When they consider themselves unworthy in every respect, they rise above and trample upon the glory of this world by the examination of right thought.

Let us look at the humble Paul. Behold, he says to the disciples: “For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord, and ourselves as your servants through Christ.” Let us see this man placed in a high position through humility, for he says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Corinthians 6). And again: “He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 2).

Perhaps an external chain then bound him, but in his mind he had been placed in high things; through the certainty of his hope he was already seated in heaven. Thus holy men are despised outwardly and endure everything as though unworthy, but confessing themselves worthy of heavenly seats, they await the glory of eternity with certainty.

While they labor outwardly under the adversity of persecution, they retreat inwardly to the fortified citadel of the mind, and from there look down upon everything beneath them, seeing that even they themselves are bodily passing among these things.

“For God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts for the illumination of the knowledge of God’s love in the face of Jesus Christ.”

**(Ambrose.)** He says that it was accomplished by God’s mercy. “We,” he says, “who were unbelieving in our ignorance”—that is, in darkness—“were made by God to be light for the other Gentiles.”

See how he still humbles himself, preferring the glory of God alone and of Christ. They are illuminated so that they may possess knowledge of God’s glory through Christ. Therefore he says “knowledge of the glory of God,” meaning not of God alone but also of Christ, who is his glory. He indicates that it is not God alone who is known, but also his works, mercy, and providence, by which he both created and saved the human race, appearing in Christ through the glory of his power.

**(Augustine.)** He even attributes to the writer the folly of saying that darkness existed eternally without beginning, while light began from darkness—as though he had read in the book he attacks that darkness was everlasting, when it is written: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth. But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss” (Genesis 1).

Darkness therefore began from the time when the confused mass of heaven and earth began to exist, before light was made to illuminate what, without light, had been dark. What is inappropriate, then, if the beginnings of worldly matter were dark, so that, when light was added, what had been made might be rendered better, and the condition of the human being who was later to come might be signified in this way as one who progresses?

Moreover, if this person dislikes the idea that light began from darkness, let the same Apostle say this to him, since, writing to believers, he says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5).

Who accomplished this except the one who, when darkness was over the abyss, said, “Let there be light,” and light was made? The same Apostle Paul expressed this more clearly elsewhere, saying: “God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts.”

“But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing power may be of God and not from us.”

**(Ambrose.)** By “treasure” he signifies the mystery of God in Christ, which is revealed to believers but covered by a kind of veil from unbelievers. Just as a treasure is placed in hiding, so the mystery of God is hidden within a person, that is, in the human heart.

He says that this treasure was given by God in mind and body, so that the greatness of God’s power might appear through human preachers alone, in order that every tongue might be reconciled to its Creator—not for the honor of human beings but of God, who reveals himself through human beings.

Although they were humble and uneducated, they received power from God both to speak great things and to accomplish them. By calling them “earthen vessels,” he signifies the weakness of nature, which can do nothing unless it receives power from God. Thus God proclaims himself through these weak things for his own praise, so that glory may be given to him, not to the human being formed from clay.

**(Gregory.)** Contemplating within himself these riches of knowledge, Paul humbles his contemplation by considering human frailty and says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels.”

We therefore find many riches within ourselves when, by investigating the sacred writings, we receive gifts of abundant understanding and perceive in them many things that are nevertheless not mutually contradictory.

But there is no secure joy in knowing great or many things in the divine writings; the true joy is in keeping what one has learned. For whoever understands well recognizes what understanding requires him to do. The more widely understanding extends, the more earnestly it binds a person to fulfill works.

Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “From everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required; and from the one to whom they have entrusted much, they will demand more” (Luke 12).

Let us therefore regard the understanding given to us as money lent to us. The more that is entrusted to us through benevolence, the more deeply we are held as debtors in our works. Often, even the money of understanding that we have received is lost when it is lent out at interest to hearers, unless it is distributed cautiously.

“In everything we suffer affliction, but we are not crushed.”

Now he shows why the preachers were competent: God was always present with them in their need. Therefore, he says, although they suffered pressure, they were not hemmed in—that is, God did not permit them to be oppressed so greatly that they would cease to believe.

“We are in need, but not abandoned”: that is, when they were placed in poverty, God the shepherd was present with them.

“We suffer persecution, but are not forsaken.” This is true, because God watched over them so that their enemies would not satisfy their own desires against them.

“We are struck down, but do not perish.”

**(Ambrose.)** That is, they were thrown down by blows but, because God opposed it, were not killed. Whether imprisoned or bound, they escaped the hands of their enemies through God’s help.

Finally, when Paul and Silas were imprisoned, already beaten and with their feet fastened in the stocks, they sang a hymn to God with joy (Acts 16), having become stronger than those who had not been beaten.

“Always carrying in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies.”

There is no doubt that Christ is killed in the martyrs, and that in those who suffer for the faith, whether their end, imprisonment, or scourging, these are the sufferings of Christ, so that his life may be openly manifested in their bodies.

These are the sufferings that demonstrate their merit for the future life that Christ promised. Hence he says elsewhere: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12); and again: “Through tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14).

Always indeed we, who are alive, are handed over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our mortal flesh. It is clear what he says: “For this reason,” he says, “we do not refuse to be handed over to death for Jesus’ sake, although we could live, so that the life by which Christ rose from the dead may be bestowed upon this mortal flesh of ours”—that is, so as not to fear dying because of the resurrection that has been promised.

Thus death works in us, but life in you. He says this because they were subjected to death for their salvation; yet, while preaching to the Gentiles, they provoked hostility against themselves from both Jews and Gentiles, even to the point of death. But having the same spirit of faith—that is, the common spirit by which faith is strengthened—we have it with you also. For this reason they endured such great evils on behalf of those people [Col. 0182D], so that they might be joined together in faith.

As it is written: “I believed, and therefore I spoke”; and we also believe, and therefore we speak. He gave the example from Psalm 115 in order to show that he was ready to endure everything precisely because he believed in the future resurrection. Therefore, secure concerning the future life, he has no care for the present life—since this is believed so that the blessed life may then be hoped for, if this present life is despised. Secure, then, because what he believed is true, he dares to preach it so as to make others share in his hope.

(Aug.) He would not have said “the same spirit of faith” unless he were also reminding us that the ancient righteous possessed that same spirit—namely, the spirit of Christ’s incarnation. But because what was future was foretold to them, whereas what has already happened is announced to us [Col. 0183A], and because what was veiled in the time of the Old Testament would be revealed in the time of the New Testament, its mysteries were varied, so that some things were in the Old Testament and others in the New, although faith itself is not varied.

The blessed apostle Paul brought forward a testimony from the Scriptures in which he commended to us the glory of the martyrs. “For this reason,” he says, “it is written: ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke’; and we also believe, and therefore we speak.” For if they had believed only and had not spoken, they would not have suffered. By believing they seized hold of death, and by speaking they encountered it: a death in which the corruptible body would be sown and incorruption reaped.

This meaning—namely, “we believe, and therefore we speak”—the same apostle explained elsewhere [Col. 0183B] in this way: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X). The same faith in the Mediator saved the ancients, the little ones together with the great—not the Old Testament, which gives birth to slavery.

Knowing that he who raised Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and establish us with you. (Amb.) In this hope he says that they labor for the sake of faith, because the resurrection of the Lord Jesus goes before as an example of what those who believe will become: for just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ. Adam is a figure of death, the cause of sin; but Christ is a figure of life because of righteousness, since he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (I Pet. II).

And because he called these people participants in the common faith, he says, “He will establish them with you,” so that, sharing one faith, they may be together in one house of peace. For when they understand that they suffer deadly things on behalf of those people [Col. 0183C], and these people in turn are concerned about their sufferings, they will be together as fellow sufferers and participants in the promised life, so that, having grieved together, they may rejoice together. He speaks in this way on account of those who denied the resurrection, whom he also reproves in the First Epistle.

For everything is for your sake, so that grace, abounding through many, may abound in thanksgiving to the glory of God. God did not wish anyone to be excluded from his gift. And because not everyone receives the word of faith, the Apostle, knowing God’s will, did not fear suffering persecutions and dangers, provided that he preached faithfully to all, so that more might be able to believe. Thus God’s abundant gift would not be diminished through the thanksgiving of only a few, to God’s dishonor, but would benefit many through the thanksgiving of many [Col. 0183D], to the glory of God.

How worthy, then, is this man of honor, who always subjected his soul to death, lest God’s gift produce a result altogether different from that for which it was given! Is it not a great insult to one who prepares an abundant banquet and invites many, yet has only a few present at the end?

Therefore we do not lose heart. It is evident that this belongs to the preceding sense. For, in order to show his devotion to the things of God as still more earnest, he adds these words, by which he proves that in no respect does he fail to fulfill what is pleasing to God, being nevertheless secure concerning the promised resurrection.

But although our outward self is being corrupted, our inward self is being renewed day by day. Through pressures [Col. 0184A], wounds, hunger, thirst, cold, and nakedness the flesh is corrupted, but the soul is renewed by hope of the future reward, because it is purified through continual tribulations. For it makes progress under pressure and does not perish, so that, as temptations increase, it daily gains toward merit; indeed, this corruption of the body also contributes to immortality through the merit of the soul.

(Aug.) This renewal does not take place in a single moment, at the time of conversion, as that renewal in baptism takes place in a single moment through the remission of all sins. For not even the smallest remnant remains that is not forgiven. Rather, just as it is one thing to be free from fevers and another to recover from the illness caused by the fevers, and as it is one thing to remove an embedded weapon from the body and another to heal, by a second treatment, the wound made by it, so the first treatment is to remove the cause of illness [Col. 0184B], which occurs through the forgiveness of all sins. The second is to heal the illness itself, which happens gradually as one makes progress in the renewal of this image.

These two things are demonstrated in the Psalm, where we read: “He who forgives all your iniquities” (Ps. CII)—which occurs in baptism. Then it follows: “Who heals all your diseases” (ibid.)—which occurs through daily advances, as this image is renewed.

In knowledge, therefore, of God and in the righteousness and holiness of truth, the one who is renewed by making progress day by day carefully strives to transfer his love from temporal things to eternal things, from visible things to intelligible things, and from carnal things to spiritual things; from these things he strives to restrain and diminish his desire, and to bind himself in love to those others.

The image, then, which is renewed by the spirit of the mind in the knowledge of God [Col. 0184C], will be perfected not outwardly but inwardly, day by day, through the vision that will then be face to face after the judgment. For now it makes progress through a mirror in an enigma.

(Greg.) It must be understood that sometimes the adversary crushes us, and sometimes God crushes us. Through the crushing inflicted by the adversary we fall away from virtue; but through the Lord’s crushing, broken away from vices, we are strengthened in virtue. The prophet had seen this crushing when he said: “You shall rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you shall crush them” (Ps. II).

The Lord rules and crushes us with a rod, because, through the strong uprightness of his ordering, while he restores us inwardly, he afflicts us outwardly. For insofar as he humbles the strength of the flesh, he exalts the purpose of the spirit. Hence this same crushing also serves the potter’s vessel, as is said through Paul: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” [Col. 0184D]. Expressing both crushing and governance, he says: “Although our outward self is being corrupted, our inward self is being renewed day by day.”

For this momentary and light affliction of ours is producing in us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure. (Ambr.) He calls the tribulations of the present time, which are inflicted on account of faith, momentary and light because they are temporal. Nevertheless, for those who suffer, they produce an eternal weight of glory in supreme measure. For great reward is given for small labors, and in place of light tribulation the sublimity of everlasting glory will be weighed out beyond measure.

[Col. 0185A] While we do not contemplate the things that are seen, but the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal. Having a desire for heavenly and spiritual things, he professes that these present and earthly things are to be despised, since in comparison with spiritual things they are nothing. For these things stand in relation to heavenly things as a figure stands in relation to the truth: the figure passes away, but the truth remains. Therefore the righteous do not fear leaving this world, but rejoice.

## CHAPTER V. He discusses the reward of the righteous and their desire and preparation for it.

For we know that if our earthly house, this habitation, is dissolved, we have a building from God [Col. 0185B], a house not made by human hands, eternal in the heavens.

(Greg.) The holy preachers of the Church contemplate in the present, through the joy of the spirit, the future that awaits them. Once they pass from their bodies, they are not delayed by intervals of waiting, as the ancient fathers were delayed from attaining the heavenly homeland. For as soon as they leave the bonds of the flesh, they rest in the heavenly abode, as Paul testifies when he says: “We know that if our earthly house, this habitation, is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made by human hands, eternal in the heavens.”

Before our Redeemer paid, by his death, the penalty of the human race, even those who had followed the paths of the heavenly homeland were held in the prison of hell after departing from the flesh—not so that they might be punished as sinners, but rather because, resting in more remote places [Col. 0185C], they were prevented from entering the kingdom by the guilt of the first sin, since the Mediator’s intervention had not yet come.

Hence, according to the same Redeemer’s testimony, the rich man who is tormented in hell sees Lazarus resting in Abraham’s bosom (Luke XVI). Surely, if Lazarus were not still in the lower regions, the rich man, placed in torment, would not see him there.

Therefore the same Redeemer, dying on account of the debt of our guilt, enters the regions below, so that he may lead his own, who clung to him, back to the heavenly places. But wherever redeemed humanity now ascends, there it would certainly have reached even without redemption, if it had not wished to sin.

The holy man would therefore sit there, since, if he had not sinned, he would have ascended there even without redemption—a place to which the holy preachers, after redemption, must arrive with great labor.

[Col. 0185D] (Ambr.) With this confidence the Apostle says that one must not fear being violently separated from the body by unbelievers, or by the lot of life, because an eternal dwelling in heaven has been prepared for such people, so that, expelled from a temporal and earthly dwelling, they may be received into an everlasting house.

Therefore this is also something to be desired. But because it is not to be desired lest another perish for the sake of your glory, nevertheless, if it should happen, it must be willingly endured. For he calls this flesh an earthly house because it is mortal, so that, if we are dissolved from it, we shall find an eternal house built for us in heaven. This house signifies the immortal body in which we shall always exist after rising again, whose form has already been displayed in heaven in the body of the Lord.

[Col. 0186A] (Aug.) Although we desire to cling to Christ, we nevertheless do not wish to die. Yet we willingly—or rather patiently—suffer for Christ, because no other passage is given by which we may cling to him. For if we could reach Christ by another means, who would wish to die?

Explaining our nature—that is, a certain fellowship of soul and body, and a certain intimacy of their union and articulation—the Apostle says that we have “a house not made by human hands, eternal in the heavens,” that is, immortality prepared for us, with which we shall be clothed at the end, when we have risen from the dead.

For in this also we groan, desiring to be clothed over with our habitation that is from heaven, if indeed, once clothed, we shall be found not naked. For we who are in this dwelling also groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life [Col. 0186B].

But he who brings this about for us is God, who has given us the pledge of the Spirit.

(Ambr.) For this reason he says that we groan in our prayers, so that the glory promised from heaven may clothe us when we rise. Thus, desiring this, they persist in prayer, lest, when they rise and receive the body, they be found naked—that is, strangers to the promised glory.

For this is necessary: that the soul, clothed with the body, may by God’s judgment be clothed over with glory, which is transformation into brightness. Death is from the earth, but resurrection is from heaven—provided that we are transformed into glory.

Some manuscripts have: “if indeed, having been unclothed, we are found not naked.” That is, if, when we depart from the body, we have been clothed with Christ, because whoever is baptized in Christ puts on Christ.

If, therefore, we remain in the form and tradition of baptism, when unclothed of the body we shall not be found naked [Col. 0186C], because Christ dwells in the inner person. When we are seen clothed with him, or with the Holy Spirit given to us, we shall be worthy to be clothed over with the promised glory. For the promised brightness falls upon the one whom he sees to possess the sign of adoption.

“For while we are,” he says, “in this body,” that is, the mortal body, “we groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that this mortal thing may be swallowed up by life.” The meaning is the same.

For this reason he says that, burdened by the sufferings of the body and by the storms of the world, we direct our petitions to God, lest we be changed by being overcome and become unworthy; but also so that, whatever the manner of our departure, we may be found persevering in faith and clothed with the Holy Spirit, who in substance is Christ.

Then we shall be able to be clothed over with the promised glory, if, when unclothed of the body, we have not been stripped of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0186D]. Thus what is mortal is swallowed up by life: that is, when we rise, we are clothed over with immortality together with glory, so that we can no longer die or be entangled in sufferings. This is to be swallowed up by life, because one rises for the purpose of no longer being driven by punishments.

But he who perfects us for this very purpose is God, who has given us the pledge, the Spirit. He says that God will perfect on the day of judgment what we ask for with groaning—namely, that we may be found worthy not to be unclothed but to be clothed over—in accordance with the preceding meaning, because he has promised and is faithful, giving the pledge of the fulfillment of this matter, the Spirit. He himself is the seal of our adoption.

(Aug.) We are therefore weighed down by a corruptible body, knowing that the cause of this burden is not the nature and substance of the body but its corruption. We do not wish to be stripped of the body [Col. 0187A] but to be clothed with its immortality. Then there will be a body, but because it will not be corruptible, it will not weigh us down.

For it is written in the Psalm: “You have saved my soul from necessities” (Ps. XXX). What shall I now say about the necessity of mortality itself? It is necessary to die, yet no one wishes for what is necessary. Hard is the necessity of not wishing for what cannot be avoided.

For if it could happen in this way, we would certainly not wish to die and become what the angels are said to be willing to become; but we would wish for a change without death, as the Apostle says: “For we who are in this habitation groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be stripped, but to be clothed over.” We wish to reach the kingdom of God, but we do not wish to die. We groan, being burdened, in accordance with what Scripture says elsewhere: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation presses down the mind that thinks of many things [Col. 0187B]” (Wis. IX).

Therefore, he says, “we groan, being burdened.” Under the burden, that is, of corruptible flesh, we groan, being burdened. If you groan, willingly lay down this burden. Certainly he said that he groans under this load; he said that he is weighed down under the burden of the corruptible body. See whether he wishes to be stripped of this burden under which he is weighed down and groans.

This does not follow. Rather, he says that we do not wish to be stripped. O voice of nature, confession of punishment! The body is heavy, the body is burdensome, the body is corruptible; he groans beneath it, yet does not willingly abandon it.

“We do not wish,” he says. “Are you going to remain this way, groaning?” And if you groan, burdened, why do you not wish to be stripped? He says, “No.” See what follows: “We do not wish to be stripped, but to be clothed over.” Beneath an earthly tunic I groan; I hasten toward a heavenly garment. I want to receive that one; I do not want to lay down this one [Col. 0187C]. This is what it means: “We do not wish to be stripped, but to be clothed over.”

Therefore, Paul, let me understand you: will such an injury be done to that heavenly garment that it comes upon these rags of mortality and corruption, so that this is beneath and that above, this within and that outside?

“Far from it,” he says. “I do not speak in this way. I do not wish to be stripped, but to be clothed over—not, however, so that corruption may lie hidden beneath incorruption, but so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.”

You have exclaimed well, since you know the Scriptures. But lest anyone ignorant of the Scriptures suppose that these are my words, Paul’s words follow. All these are apostolic words: “We groan, being burdened, in which we do not wish to be stripped, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.”

You rightly remember what he says elsewhere when speaking of the resurrection of the body: “This corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality” [Col. 0187D]. But when this corruptible thing has put on incorruption, and this mortal thing has put on immortality, then the saying that is written will take place: “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (I Cor. XV).

What he says there—“so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life”—he says here: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” Nowhere is death: not below, not above, not within, not outside. For death has been swallowed up in victory. “Where is your contention, O death?”

“But he who,” he says, “perfects us for this very purpose is God, who has given us the pledge, the Spirit.” The answer has already been given when we were speaking of the difference between the present age and the future age.
