Here, through the pledge of the Spirit, we receive strength for struggling and conquering; there, without any external or internal enemy, we shall enjoy ineffable and everlasting peace [Col. 0188A].

(Greg.) Whoever, therefore, wishes to have here everything that is to be possessed there shows that he does not have faith. In sacred Scripture the designation “pledge” sometimes signifies the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and sometimes the confession of sin.

A pledge is understood as the gift of the Holy Spirit, as is said through Paul: “He who gave us the pledge, the Spirit.” For we receive this pledge so that we may hold certainty concerning the promise made to us. The gift of the Holy Spirit is therefore called a pledge because through it our soul is strengthened toward certainty of inward hope.

Again, by the name “pledge” the confession of sin is usually understood, as it is written in the Law: “When your brother owes you anything, and you take a pledge from him, return the pledge to him before sunset” (Exod. XXII). For the one who confesses the sin he has committed and asks forgiveness [Col. 0188B] has already given, as it were, a pledge for a debt. We are commanded to return this pledge before sunset because, before the sun of righteousness sets in us through the sorrow of the heart, we ought to return to him the confession of forgiveness from whom we received the confession of guilt.

Therefore, always having confidence and knowing that while we are in this body we are away from the Lord—for we walk by faith and not by sight. (Ambr.) It is clear that by faith we are with the Lord, not by presence; and therefore we are away from him not by faith but by sight [the source reads *non fide, sed specie*, apparently contrary to the immediate context]. And why, when he says the same thing in the Acts of the Apostles—“For in him we live and move and exist” (Acts XVII)—does he say here that we are away from the Lord? If he is everywhere, how are we, placed here, away from the Lord?

Without doubt he is everywhere; indeed, everything is in God. But because God’s dwelling is in the heavens [Col. 0188C], and he is always seen there, we who are placed here, where he is not seen, are said to be away from him. For when we do not see him, although he is present, we are absent from him.

But we have confidence and a good will, preferring to be away from the body and present with the Lord. He rightly says “we have confidence.” For, having confidence in God’s promise and knowing that it is much more advantageous to be there than in this world, they agree and desire to depart from the body, so that they may rest beneath God’s altar until the day of resurrection.

And therefore we strive, whether absent or present, to please him. He says that this is what must be done and that we must persist in good works, so that, whether we are still placed in this life or present before Christ’s tribunal, we may please him. Therefore, if discipline is preserved, we shall please him both here and there, because whoever pleases him here [Col. 0188D] will not displease him there.

For we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to his own body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil. Therefore, if, when Christ judges, each of us will receive the deeds of the body, he will certainly not be assigned to good or evil without the body. And he did not say “the deeds of the flesh,” because the vices of the flesh are always to be punished, but “the deeds of the body,” because one sometimes acts spiritually and sometimes carnally.

(Aug.) These things, therefore, which the Church frequently performs for commending the dead, are not contrary to that apostolic judgment by which it was said: “For we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil.” For each person acquired this merit for himself while he lived in the body [Col. 0189A], so that these things might be of benefit to him; they are not beneficial to everyone.

Why are they not beneficial to everyone? Surely because of the difference in the life each person led in the body. Judgment and righteousness must be carried out in such a way that it may benefit us afterward, when each receives according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil.

For the Apostle said “through the body,” meaning through the time during which he lived in the body. For if someone blasphemes with an evil and impious mind and thought, and does not carry it out through any bodily members, he will not for that reason be guiltless, because he did not perform it by bodily movement, since he performed it during the time in which he also possessed a body.

It is appropriate to consider the Apostle’s words. He did not say that the one judged must receive according to what he did before the body. It is evident that souls did not exist before bodies [Col. 0189B]. For if they had existed beforehand, the Apostle would certainly have said: “Just as through the body, so also before the body.”

Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade human beings, but we are manifest to God.

(Ambr.) Since, therefore, God’s judgment is to come through Christ in order to distinguish the works of individuals, the Apostle says that he persuades them toward sound understanding and life, so that his hearers may be secure concerning future punishment and he himself may glory in them, possessing the fruit of his lips. For the evil speech of some brings God’s day of judgment into doubt: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (I Cor. XV).

“We persuade human beings,” he says, so that they may believe and take care not to fall into sin and then repent when repentance bears no fruit. “But we are manifest to God.” For he preached what God had commanded [Col. 0189C], and God is said to know what is good. Finally, he says to those who act wickedly: “I do not know you” (Matt. XXV).

And I hope that we are also manifest in your consciences. Their purity was evident to the Corinthians, because they had never been caught in flattery, nor had their preaching displeased the holy ones, nor had they ever attempted to elicit secretly from anyone something—as is customary—so that outwardly they might appear simple among the crowds but inwardly be impostors. Therefore he strikes their consciences so that they themselves might be witnesses to the truth of the apostles.

We do not commend ourselves to you again. Since earlier, while affirming his true preaching, he seemed to praise himself, he now indicates that he is saying the same thing not for his own praise [Col. 0189D] but for their glory, so that they may rejoice that they have learned the integrity of the preaching from those who announced it.

But we give you an occasion to glory on our behalf, so that you may have something to use against those who glory in appearance and not in heart. He says this because many, through arrogance, gloried in themselves on account of the apostles, professing that they had been taught by those who had always been with the Lord. Therefore here also he says that he gives them a basis by which they too might glory against those people, because he was an apostle from whom they had learned.

Hence elsewhere he says (II Cor. XII): “I have done nothing less than those who are very apostles,” which he says under compulsion, lest his silence harm these people. For whoever glories in his heart restrains pride, knowing that God gives grace to the humble but resists the proud [Col. 0190A] (Jas. IV). The mind of the proud does not produce fruit worthy of God.

Whether, then, we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober-minded, it is for you. He says this because, if he is thought to have spoken loftily or arrogantly, since he seemed to praise himself, this should be attributed to God, because he spoke the truth. But if he is understood not to have spoken arrogantly, but to have spoken for the glory of his hearers, he says that this benefits the Corinthians, so that what has been said is sound for the hearers if it is understood in the way it was spoken. But if it is thought to have been said boastfully, it should be dismissed as madness from God, for all pride is regarded as a kind of madness.

Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: “You will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending above the Son of Man” (John I). Hear the Apostle himself ascending and descending in one sentence [Col. 0190B]: “Whether,” he says, “we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are temperate, it is for you.”

What does “we are beside ourselves” mean? That we see those things which it is not lawful for a human being to speak. What does “we are temperate for you” mean? “Did I judge myself to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified?” (I Cor. II.)

If the Lord himself ascended and descended, it is evident that his preachers also ascend in illumination and descend in preaching.

The word *extasis* is Greek; in Latin, insofar as it can be understood, it may be expressed in one word as *excessus*, “going beyond” or “departure.” In this departure of the mind, two things are understood: either terror or an attentiveness directed toward heavenly things, so that earthly things somehow slip from memory.

All the saints experienced this *extasis*, to whom the mysteries of God, surpassing this world, were revealed. Concerning this departure of the mind [Col. 0190C]—that is, *extasis*—Paul, when speaking and indicating himself, says: “Whether,” he says, “we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are temperate, it is for you. For the love of Christ compels us.”

That is: if we wished only to do and contemplate those things that we behold in the departure of the mind, I would not be with you, but would be in the heavenly realms, as though despising you. And when would you, weak as you are, follow us in those higher and inward things, unless the love of Christ again compelled us? Although he existed in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. II).

Let us also consider ourselves servants, and let us not be ungrateful to him from whom we have received higher things on behalf of the weak. We should not despise lower things, but should adapt ourselves to those who cannot see sublime things with us.

This, then, is what he says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God.” For he sees what we see in the departure of the mind; he alone reveals his secrets [Col. 0190D]. Indeed, he says that he was caught up and taken away as far as the third heaven, and heard ineffable words that it is not lawful for a human being to speak.

So great, moreover, was that departure of the mind that he said: “Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (II Cor. XII).

For the love of Christ urges us, since we judge this: that if one died for all. Since Christ, loving the human race, gave himself over to death in order to redeem them, the apostles, in order to repay him in some measure, exhort human beings to serve him. And, in order to draw them [Col. 0191A], they must testify that they preach the truth, while others teach perverse things; nor must they conceal their own merit, so that they may point out the punishment of evil teachers.

They were not doing these things, therefore, through arrogance of mind, but so that Christ’s gift might be understood by human beings and that, faithfully devoted to him, they might offer thanksgiving. For the sake of Christ’s love, they do not remain silent about how great and how numerous his gifts are toward those who love him—not for the sake of boasting, but to invite their hearers to devotion to him, lest Christ’s death appear fruitless, not so that the apostles’ praise might be recognized.

For through the merit and glory of the apostles, Christ’s grace and God’s benefit are recognized.

Therefore all have died, and Christ died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose again for them. Since all must die because of Adam, Christ died for all [Col. 0191B] in order to free them from the second death. Therefore those who live in the body, knowing that Christ died for them, should be subject to him and confess him as Lord. For because his death is beneficial, his resurrection bears witness to it.

Thus the one who is ready to do the will of his Lord does not live for himself.

(Aug.) It is good for everyone to hear the voice of the Son of God and to live for a life of piety, passing from the death of impiety. Concerning this death the apostle Paul says: “Therefore all have died, and he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose again for them.”

All, therefore, were dead in sins, no one at all being excepted, whether through original sins or through sins added by the will, either through ignorance or through knowledge, by failing to do [Col. 0191C] what is just. And for all the dead, the one living man died—one who had no sin at all—so that those who live through the remission of sins might no longer live for themselves but for him who died for all on account of our sins and rose again on account of our justification (Rom. IV).

Therefore from this point onward we know no one according to the flesh. And even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, now we no longer know him.

(Ambr.) It is true that, when Christ rose from the dead, carnal birth in him ceased, bodily weakness ceased, and the suffering of death ceased. Until the cross there was an appearance of weakness in Christ; afterward, what had not been believed appeared, as he himself also says: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am [Col. 0191D]” (John VIII).

The Apostle recalls this for the purpose of showing with what devotion Christ must be served. For, for the salvation of human beings, he not only did not disdain to be born as a human being, but also willed to be treated with insults and to die, so that, understanding how precious his death is, they might serve him more eagerly—not as though repaying a human being, but God. For services must be rendered to each according to his person and merits.

Therefore, if there is any new creation in Christ, the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new. It is evident that all things have been renewed through Christ, if they consider his dignity. For he becomes new to those to whom previously he seemed merely human, when he is understood to be God. As weakness withdraws, divinity is recognized; and as the former error ceases—the error that, by introducing belief in many gods, had led the human race away from faith in the one true God [Col. 0192A]—all things return to the profession of simplicity, worshiping one God in the Trinity.

“We,” he says, “from now on know no one according to the flesh. And even if we knew Christ according to the flesh, we no longer know him.”

(Aug.) It is now certainly apparent to everyone that the Apostle said this because of Christ’s resurrection, since these words were preceded by the statement that those who live should no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them and rose again.

For what else does “not for themselves but for him they should live” mean except that they should not live according to the flesh in hope of earthly and corruptible goods, but according to the Spirit in hope of the resurrection, which has already taken place in Christ?

Therefore, concerning those for whom Christ died and rose again, and who were now living not for themselves but for him, the Apostle knew no one according to the flesh, because of the hope of future immortality in expectation of which they lived [Col. 0192B]. In Christ this was not hope but reality. Although he had known him according to the flesh when he was still destined to die, he no longer knew him in that way, because he knew that he had risen and that death would no longer rule over him. And because in him we all are—although not yet in reality, nevertheless already in hope—what he is, we also are.

He continues and says: “Therefore, if there is any new creation in Christ, the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new. But all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ.”

Every new creation, therefore—that is, the people renewed through faith—already possesses in hope what will afterward be perfected in reality in Christ, and already has within itself what it hopes for [Col. 0192C].

Thus the old things have now passed away according to hope, because it is no longer the time of the Old Testament, in which a temporal and carnal kingdom was expected from God. And all things have become new according to hope, so that we may hold fast to the promised kingdom of heaven, where there will be neither death nor corruption.

But in the resurrection of the dead the old things will pass away not according to hope but according to reality, when the last enemy, death, will be destroyed (I Cor. XV), and all things will become new, when this corruptible thing puts on incorruption and this mortal thing puts on immortality (II Cor. IV).

This has already happened in Christ, whom Paul no longer knew according to the flesh in reality. But among those for whom he died and rose again, he knew no one according to the flesh not in reality but according to hope [Col. 0192D], because, as he says in the same way to the Ephesians, we have been saved by his grace.

“Even if we knew Christ according to the flesh,” he says, “we now no longer know him.” For even Christ’s flesh is not known according to the flesh by the one who knows spiritually the Word made flesh.

Everything, however, is from God. (Ambrose.) Although Christ redeemed us, everything nevertheless comes from God, because all fatherhood is from him; therefore the person of the Father must necessarily be placed first. He reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation. For God was indeed in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them. And he placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore, on behalf of Christ we act as ambassadors [Col. 0193A], as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God. He who knew no sin, for our sake he made sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

God almighty, the Father of Christ, when all the things he had made through Christ had become perishable through error, having forgotten their Creator, deigned to send Christ our Lord from the sacred dwellings to earthly things, made flesh in the appearance of a man, so that he might be an example to human beings of how they should make God their Creator favorable toward them.

God, then, was in Christ—but how? As though in a vicar or ambassador, as he was in the prophets, or in some other way? Can it be understood that he was in the Son in the same way as he was in the prophets? For the Son is naturally the ambassador of God the Father; hence he says: “Because the Father is in me, and I am in the Father” (John XIV). [Col. 0193B] The Father is understood to be in the Son because their substance is one. There is unity where there is no difference; and for this reason they are mutually in one another, because their image and likeness are also one, so that whoever sees the Son is said to have seen the Father: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father also” (John XIV).

Rightly, therefore, it is said: “God was in Christ”—that is, the Father was in the Son—reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them. For creation sinned against God and did not repent so as to return to him. God, unwilling that his work should perish, sent his Son, through whom, after the forgiveness of sins had been proclaimed to them, he might reconcile them to himself through the very one through whom he had created us.

Whether, therefore, through the Son or through servants, God exhorts the people, because the whole matter must be referred to him, by whose will and providence [Col. 0193C] Christ was incarnate for the redemption and salvation of human beings. When he wished to return to the Father, Christ gave the disciples the dispensation he had received from the Father. Urging reconciliation with God on Christ’s behalf—this is what I said—Christ gave the apostles as his vicars, so that they might preach reconciliation with God on his behalf.

(Augustine.) “On behalf of Christ,” he says, “we act as ambassadors, as though God were exhorting through us; we beseech you on behalf of Christ”—that is, as though Christ himself were beseeching us to be reconciled to God. If the Apostle exhorts and beseeches us to be reconciled to God, then we were God’s enemies; for no one is reconciled except after enmity. Yet sins, not nature, made us enemies.

How are we reconciled, unless that which separates us from him is removed? There is something that separates, but there is also a mediator who reconciles. [Col. 0193D] Sin is the separating intermediary; the Lord Christ is the reconciling mediator: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (I Timothy II). Therefore, so that the separating substance—which is sin—might be removed, that mediator came. He himself became both priest and sacrifice, and because he became a sacrifice for sin, he offered himself as a burnt offering on the cross of his passion.

The Apostle continues and says, after he had said, “We beseech you on behalf of Christ to be reconciled to God,” as though we were asking, “How can we be reconciled?”: “We beseech you,” he says, “on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.”

(Gregory.) Behold: by sinning we created discord between ourselves and God, yet God first sent his ambassadors to us, so that we who sinned might be entreated to come to God’s peace. [Col. 0194A] Therefore let human pride blush, and let anyone be ashamed if he does not first make satisfaction to his neighbor, when, after our fault, God himself—the one who was offended—entreats us through ambassadors that we should be reconciled to him.

He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us. (Ambrose.) He says that God the Father made his Son Christ sin, since the one who knew no sin—that is, who had not sinned—was made flesh, not changed, but incarnate. Just as one who is made prefect does not lose what he was, but assumes what he was not, so Christ became human because of sin. The lot and dignity of being born as a human being did not touch him; but because all flesh is under sin, he became flesh and thus became sin.

And because he was offered for sins,[Col. 0194B]  he is not improperly said to have been made sin, since the sacrifice in the Law that was offered for sins was called “sin.” Thus we might become the righteousness of God in him who knew no sin, as Isaiah says: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isaiah LIII; I Peter II). He was killed as though he were a sinner, so that sinners might be justified before God in Christ.

Satan suffered jealousy against the Savior when he saw him teaching human beings how to make God favorable toward them by renouncing the devil; and for this reason he killed him, not knowing what would follow against himself. For after the cross Christ descended to the underworld, having conquered death; for the one who knew no sin could not be held by death, because death emptied hell through sin, so that the death of the righteous might benefit sinners and henceforth death might not be able to hold those who bear the sign of the cross. [Col. 0194C]

(Augustine.) In the Old Testament, sacrifices for sins were called “sins.” Christ truly became this, of which those sacrifices were shadows. Hence, after the Apostle had said, “We beseech you on behalf of Christ to be reconciled to God,” he immediately added: “He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that we might be the righteousness of God in him.”

He does not say, as it is read in certain corrupt manuscripts, “He who knew no sin made sin for us,” as though Christ himself had sinned for us. Rather, he says, “He who knew no sin”—that is, Christ—God made sin for us; and to this God we are to be reconciled. That is, Christ became a sacrifice for sins, through which we might be able to be reconciled.

He, therefore, became sin,[Col. 0194D]  so that we might become righteousness—not our righteousness, but God’s; not in us, but in him. Likewise, he demonstrated that sin—not his, but ours—was established not in himself, but in us, through the likeness of sinful flesh in which he was crucified. Since sin was not present in him, he in a certain manner died to sin while dying to the flesh in which there was the likeness of sin.

## CHAPTER VI

The Apostle exhorts his own people concerning the good they are to practice in the future, both in outward conduct and inward devotion, and concerning the avoidance of unbelievers.

As fellow workers, we also exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain. (Ambrose.) The Apostle seeks to undertake the care of human salvation in a twofold manner: both by showing devotion to God’s providence and by performing the duty of charity toward human beings. [Col. 0195A] For he says: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.” This is written in the prophet Isaiah; it teaches that God’s grace was predestined for the time of Christ. For God determined that his mercy should flow abundantly in such a way that he would grant help to those who sought it in the name of Christ.

“Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation,” giving no one any occasion for offense, so that our ministry may not be blamed. He says that the time has arrived in which sinners may advance toward forgiveness; he says that the time has arrived in which medicine may be applied to mortal diseases. Therefore he shows himself concerned for the salvation of the sick, lest through some negligence the grace of medicine should fail to produce the effect of his good will.

By his faith and vigilance, therefore,[Col. 0195B]  he removes every occasion for offense from the negligent, lest their sluggishness should perhaps create an occasion of offense for the disciples. In this way they show themselves free, because they preach plainly and with complete earnestness what is salutary. Hence he adds: “So that our ministry may not be blamed.” Their ministry would indeed be blamed if they did not give, by their own works, examples for the things they taught in words to be done.

But in everything let us present ourselves as God’s ministers. God’s ministers teach without flattery, so that they may please the one whose ministers they are. The false apostles, knowing that they had not been sent by God, pursued present advantage instead.

In great patience. Patience is what saves human beings. For unless he had made use of patience, how would he have saved the Corinthians, whom after his preaching he had found entangled in such great moral vices and errors of various sects? [Col. 0195C] Through his patience he gradually brought them back to true doctrine.

In tribulations. He endured afflictions, knowing what had been promised by God for these things.

In necessities. Necessity consisted also in teaching one who was placed under affliction, because he had been sent by the Lord.

In distresses. Though distressed by the opposition of the faithless through hope of the future, he did not yield.

In beatings. Though frequently beaten by Jews and Gentiles, he did not remain silent about the grace of Christ.

In imprisonments. Often sent to prison, he disregarded his own safety and preached God’s gift even there.

In riots. He was so devoted to God that not even turmoil diminished the confidence he had in God.

In labors. He did not cease laboring with his own hands, so as not to be burdensome to anyone, confident that this was profitable for him before God.

In vigils. He was so concerned with the duty entrusted to him that he did not cease even at night. [Col. 0195D]

In fastings. Sometimes voluntarily, sometimes out of necessity because of poverty, he endured fasts and gave thanks to God, who fed him spiritually; for he was content for this reason, lest he be bent toward the concerns of the belly.

In chastity. By defending chastity, whether of the body or of the Gospel, he made not a few enemies.

In knowledge. By asserting the knowledge of the Law and the Gospel, not in human wisdom or pretense, he showed himself to God as a faithful steward of Christ.

In long-suffering. He was great-hearted in carrying the weaknesses of his brothers and in despising this world. Hence elsewhere he says (Galatians VI): “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

In kindness. He was kind, because just as he reproved, so also he consoled, [Col. 0196A] so that after correction he might comfort them with gentle exhortation.

In the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit flees what is counterfeit. Therefore, because he taught sincerely, he conveyed God’s gift in the Holy Spirit.

In unfeigned love. Love is feigned in those who abandon their brothers in necessity. Hence, because he always made the necessities of his brothers his own, he was sincere in love. For he sympathized with everyone, as he says elsewhere (II Corinthians XI): “Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?”

This is true love: when, disregarding one’s own advantage, one cares for the person whom one professes to love. The Apostle always did this.

In the word of truth. The word of truth was in his teaching, because he transmitted nothing other than what he had received from the Lord.

In the power of God. The power of God was in him, and through signs and wonders of God this power proved him to be an able minister. [Col. 0196B]

Through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left. (Cass.) Through the weapons of righteousness that are on the right and on the left, one must pass under proper moderation; and one must walk between both extremes with discretion governing the way, so that we neither allow ourselves to be led away from the path of continence handed down to us, nor again fall through harmful indulgence into the desire for food and the belly.

He signifies that he was a balance both for the faithful and for the unfaithful and unbelieving. For the weapons of righteousness destroy iniquity.

(Gregory.) Adversity did not break him, nor did prosperity lift him up into fearlessness of mind. Therefore he carried the palm on both sides, because he remained strong in adversity and humble in prosperity.

Whoever is lifted up by prosperity does not know how to have the palm in his right hand; whoever is broken by adversity does not know how to carry the palm on the left side. [Col. 0196C] Therefore, so that the palm may be carried on both sides, confidence in adversity and fear in prosperity must always be present in our minds: lest adversity drag us into despair, or prosperity lift the mind up in confidence in itself.

Again, when one strives only toward what is inward, he should not bend toward any lowly object of love, lest prosperity elevate him, adversity disturb him, flattering things charm him according to his will, or harsh things press him into despair. Thus, while he humbles the intention of his mind under no passions, he shows how he is covered on both shoulders by the beauty of the priestly shoulder-piece.

For rightly the shoulder-piece is also commanded to be made of gold, hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and twisted linen, [Col. 0196D] so that it may be demonstrated how greatly the priest ought to shine through the diversity of virtues.

Often, when praise of one who acts well is insolently brought to his ears and resounds outwardly in words, it generates inwardly in the mind a certain persistent storm of exaltation. The result is that, although the mind does not readily display outwardly the joy it takes in human favor, it nevertheless feels inwardly, and not slightly, the force of corruption.

(Cass.) Therefore, whoever wishes to walk along the royal road through the weapons of righteousness that are on the right and on the left must, according to apostolic discipline, pass through glory and dishonor, through infamy and good reputation. He must do so with such caution that, while the swelling waves of temptations rise, discretion guides us and the Spirit of the Lord blows for us, directing our course along the way of virtue.

If we incline even slightly to the right or left, [Col. 0197A] we must know that we shall be dashed against destructive songs of conduct. Hence we are warned through the wisest Solomon: “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left” (Proverbs III). That is, do not flatter yourself because of your virtues or exalt yourself because of successes on the right and spiritual achievements; nor, turning aside to the left along the path of vices, seek glory for yourself from them, according to the Apostle, to your own shame.

Through glory and dishonor. (Ambrose.) To those who regarded the Gospel of God as glorious, he plainly declares himself to be an upright and faithful preacher. In the same way, to those who considered the words of divine teaching dishonorable and deformed, he showed himself to be a faithful minister of God, since he was neither frightened nor ashamed to say to them what they dreaded hearing.

Through infamy and good reputation. He also showed himself to be an upright steward of God before those who formed a good opinion of the faith and before those who formed a bad one, since he did not fear their envy but remained steadfast.

(Cass.) Therefore, all the things thought to be prosperous,[Col. 0197B]  which are called the right-hand side and which the holy Apostle designated by the terms “glory” and “good reputation,” are weapons of righteousness for the perfect man. Likewise, those things that are considered adverse, which he clearly expressed by “dishonor” and “infamy,” and which he describes as being on the left, become weapons of righteousness for the perfect man, if he bears them magnanimously in his broad heart.

By fighting through these things, and by using these very adversities by which he seems to be attacked as weapons, and by being fortified against those who inflict them as though with bow, sword, and a very strong shield, he acquires for himself, through endurance, the advancement of virtue and the most glorious triumph of steadfastness. [Col. 0197C] He takes this triumph from the very things inflicted as deadly blows by his enemies.

He is neither lifted up by prosperity alone nor cast down by adversity, but always walks along a level road and the royal way. He is never moved from that state of tranquility as though to the right when joy comes upon him, nor driven again to the left when adversity presses in and sadness prevails.

“For there is great peace for those who love your name, and there is no scandal for them” (Psalm CXVIII).

As deceivers and truthful. (Ambrose.) Unbelievers called them deceivers; the faithful, on the contrary, declared them truthful and sincere. Yet this does not yield to hatred so as to impose a false appearance upon the truth.

As unknown and known. They were unknown to the wicked but known to the good, for the good recognized the truth in them.

As dying, and behold, we live. [Col. 0197D] Those who hated them thought every day that they would not escape the threats of iniquity. But these men, teaching by the favor of God, awaited deliverance from present and future death, protected by the help of Christ.

As chastised, and not killed. They seemed to be tested when they were treated in such a way that people thought they might yield; but because they were not conquered, they were not handed over to death. The one who does not remain in the faith is handed over to death—not to this death, but to the future one.

This may also be understood of present death: God allowed them to be tested so that they might grow in merit through afflictions, but he did not permit them to be killed.

As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing. This is true, because this sorrow produces joy, and those who saddened them with insults increased their joy.

As poor, yet making many [Col. 0198A] rich. Insofar as the present life is concerned, they seemed poor, but they bestowed spiritual riches on believers: poor on earth, rich in heaven.

As having nothing, and possessing everything. This was glorious in the apostles: without the anxiety and title of possessing, they possessed not only the things that were in possessions, but also their very owners. For everything had to be placed at their feet because of their virtues, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts IV).

(Gregory.) In the midst of these things I am glad to raise the eyes of the mind toward God’s elect, oppressed outwardly, and to see what great citadels they guard inwardly. Everything that stands out externally lies beneath their hidden gaze in contempt.

For, snatched inwardly above themselves, they fix their mind on high; and whatever they suffer in this life they see as slipping far below and as foreign to them. [Col. 0198B] So, to put it this way, while they strive to become outside the flesh in their mind, they almost fail to notice the very things they endure.

In the eyes of such people, nothing that rises high in time is truly high. For, as though seated on the summit of a great mountain, they look down upon the plains of the present life. Transcending themselves through spiritual elevation, they see inwardly beneath them everything that swells outwardly through carnal glory.

Hence they spare no power opposed to the truth. Those whom they see lifted up through pride, they press down by the authority of the Spirit.

Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians. (Ambrose.) He says this because of liberty and a clear conscience. For a mind conscious of wrongdoing hesitates to speak, loses its meaning, and falters in its words.

Our heart is enlarged. [Col. 0198C] The hearts of those who rejoice in themselves through the confidence of good conduct are enlarged—or certainly, through hope of the future reward, they are not narrowed by tribulation. For just as in this life there is no repayment unless labor has preceded it, so in divine matters there is no reward unless difficulties have first come before it.

Do not be narrowed by us, but be enlarged in your own hearts, having the same recompense in return. He says this because it was no fault of the teachers if the disciples went astray, despising the vigor of the teaching. Each person will receive a reward according to his works.

As far as the teachers were concerned, they had not been silent, as the Lord says to the prophet Ezekiel: “Raise your voice and speak to the people; and if they listen to you, you will gain them” (Ezekiel III).

(Gregory.) “If not,[Col. 0198D]  you will save your own soul.” When they see that they cannot be understood by weak hearers, even righteous people commonly praise the good things they say—not because they themselves crave praise, but in order to stir their hearers to attentive listening. Thus, when they have brought forth many things from the hidden places of their hearts, he added: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged.”

But arrogant people, because they do not understand the heart of the good and sometimes imitate only their words, praise what they say—not because the sluggishness of their hearers displeases them, but because they themselves enjoy craving approval. They imitate the voices of the righteous and pretend, but they do not understand the force of the voice. They see what the righteous utter, but they do not know what the righteous seek.

I speak as to children:[Col. 0199A]  be enlarged yourselves, and do not be yoked together with unbelievers. (Ambrose.) He exhorts them to good conduct and hope, so that, trusting and cleansing their consciences, they may rejoice in themselves, possessing the confidence of a pure mind, as their teachers do. They are to separate themselves from the fellowship of unbelievers in evil works.

Thus he rightly wishes those who work and hope for the future to be enlarged in spirit. For one who labors but does not believe in the future is narrowed, like an unbeliever, by despair of what is to come.

(Augustine.) The breadth of the commandment is love, because where there is love there is no narrowness. The Apostle was in this breadth when he said: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged; you are not narrowed within us.” Therefore: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad.”

What is the broad commandment?[Col. 0199B]  “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another.” Love, therefore, is not narrowed.

Do you wish not to be narrowed on earth? Live in a broad place. Whatever a human being does to you does not narrow you, because you love that of God which does not harm you. You love God, you love brotherhood, you love the law of God, you love the Church of God. It will be eternal. You labor on earth, but you will reach the promised fruit. Who can take away from you what you love?

For what partnership is there between righteousness and iniquity? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness? What agreement does Christ have with Belial? Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever? What agreement is there between the temple of God and idols? (Ambrose.) It is clear that the things he lists are opposed to one another; consequently, he teaches that one must flee from them, because the Lord says: “No one can serve two masters.”

The Law preaches righteousness,[Col. 0199C]  so that iniquity may be fled. It displays light, which is truth, so that one may depart from ignorance, which is darkness. It announces Christ in the mystery of God, so that one may withdraw from the devil, who wishes to lie that he is God. It promises believers eternal life, so that, freed from faithlessness, they may be separate from every error of unbelievers. It forbade the worship of idols because they are enemies of the temple of God.

(Cassiodorus.) Each vice has its own station in our heart. Claiming this station for itself, it expels Israel—that is, contemplation of the highest and holy things—from the recesses of our soul, and it will not cease to oppose them.

For virtues cannot dwell together with vices. “What partnership is there between righteousness and iniquity? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness?”

But when the vices have been conquered by Israel’s people—that is, by the virtues fighting against them [Col. 0199D]—the place that lust or fornication had occupied in our heart will thereafter be held by chastity; the place seized by anger will be reclaimed by patience; the place occupied by sorrow that produces death will be possessed by healing and joy-filled sorrow; the place devastated by listlessness will be cultivated by courage; the place trampled down by pride will be honored by humility.

Thus, once the individual vices have been expelled, their places—that is, their effects—will be possessed by the opposing virtues. These virtues are rightly called the children of Israel, that is, of souls who see God. When they have expelled all the passions of the heart, they should be believed not so much to have invaded another’s possessions as to have recovered their own.

For you are the temple of the living God.[Col. 0200A]  (Ambrose.) Nothing is so hostile to the human being as idols, because they compel one to depart from faith in the one God.

As God says: “For I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people. Therefore, come out from their midst and be separated, says the Lord, and do not touch what is unclean; and I will receive you, and I will be a father to you, and you will be my sons and daughters, says the Lord almighty.”

For the present, let us explain the meaning of the original source, so that we may declare whose words they are: “For I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people.”

These are the words of Christ. For this is also what Jeremiah testified among other things, saying: “Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch III). [Col. 0200B] He dwelt among us, as the Apostle John says: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I).

And because he is our God, Jeremiah says again: “This is our God.” And because we are his people, there is no doubt; for the Church is Christ’s. Therefore he wishes us to be separated from every contamination, so that he may receive us as sons, as he says: “Little children, I am with you a little while longer” (John XIII).

And because he is almighty, I think there should be no doubt. For if, as he himself says, “Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise” (John V), this means that the Son is able to do everything that the Father can do. If the Father cannot do something, neither can the Son. But the Son is competent to say of the Father: “With God all things are possible” (Matthew XIX).

By this testimony he also exhorted us to pure living,[Col. 0200C]  and he showed that our Lord Jesus—who was long ago our God—had already been predestined to receive us in the affection of his love.

## CHAPTER VII

A useful admonition of the Apostle is set forth first, and the Corinthians are commended for their former good conduct.

Therefore, since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God. (Ambrose.) What he says is clear; yet the defilement of the flesh must be understood in many ways. For this reason he did not say merely “from the defilement of the flesh,” but “from every defilement,” so that we might flee all carnal vices.

Everything that the Law forbids is carnal,[Col. 0200D]  so that we may perfect the holiness of the Spirit in the fear of God. We perfect the holiness of the Spirit in this way: if, in the fear of God, we follow what is right, so that, abstaining from sins under the name of Christ, we may be holy.

Those who appear to restrain themselves from vices without Christ’s promise are sanctified according to the world, not according to the Spirit of God. For, according to God, those are clean who are faithful; all the rest, whatever they may be, are unclean. Whatever is without Christ is unclean, as he says to Titus: “To the unbelieving nothing is clean, for their mind and conscience are defiled” (Titus I).

Receive us. We have wronged no one, corrupted no one, defrauded no one. He wishes them to consider what he says,[Col. 0201A]  so that, taking these words into their hearts, they may acknowledge that what he says is true. Then, rejecting those whom he touches upon, they may direct their whole mind toward those whom they see that he loves with true affection.

For they were false apostles, who harmed them by corrupting their understanding and burdened their purses through the serpent-like cunning of fraud.

I do not say this to condemn you. That is, I do not reject you; I admonish you so that you may correct yourselves. For whoever despises someone does not forgive him.

For we have already said that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together. From what has been said, he wishes them to recognize with what disposition he speaks to them. Those whom he wishes to have as partners both in present sufferings for Christ and in future life, he certainly does not reject; rather, he exhorts them to make themselves worthy of participation.

I have great confidence in you;[Col. 0201B]  I have great reason to glory on your behalf. I am filled with consolation; I overflow with joy in all our tribulation. This confidence comes from the correction in the First Epistle. Because they did not receive that correction harshly, they gave him confidence to admonish them.

They seemed willing to correct themselves, and therefore he glories. He declares that his own spirit is consoled by this, to such an extent that he affirms that he overflows with joy in every affliction. Seeing that there is hope in those for whom he suffers distress, he rejoices even while he is afflicted, certain that he will receive from God a reward for the salvation he has gained for them.

For when we came to Macedonia, our flesh had no rest. He recalls the afflictions and beatings they endured for the sake of believers, so that he may provoke them more strongly to love.

“Our flesh had no rest,” he says. [Col. 0201C] He says this so that they may sympathize with them, since they were certain to give their lives even unto death for the salvation of the faithful. Before one tribulation and bodily injury had subsided, another came, so that there was no rest for the sufferer.

And because all flesh is without understanding, he signifies that it had no rest, or has no rest, in suffering. The soul, however, although it suffered in the body, nevertheless had rest in this respect: it hoped that God would grant a reward for these tribulations inflicted by the faithless on account of the faith. Indeed, in the very midst of the affliction they sang hymns to God.

But we suffered every tribulation. According to the historical account, when the Lord called them, they entered Macedonia. After not a few had believed, and after they had found comfort through Lydia, a woman who believed together with all her household, [Col. 0201D] it happened that they drove out of a maidservant the spirit of Python—that is, a divining spirit—belonging to certain men.

When those men saw that they had lost the considerable profit that the girl brought them by fortune-telling, they stirred up a riot against Paul and Silas and dragged them to the marketplace before the magistrates. The magistrates inflicted many blows on them and sent them to the innermost part of the prison, even fastening their feet in a wooden restraint.

This is the affliction they suffered in Macedonia, and this is why he says: “Our flesh had no rest.”

Outside were conflicts; inside were fears. The conflicts were in the body while it was being beaten; the fears were in the mind. For fear is present where understanding is also present. Yet this fear was on account of those who had believed, lest they should be scandalized by his suffering.

For what could he now fear for himself, when he suffered?[Col. 0202A]  Besides, he says in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XXI) that he was ready not only to be bound but also to die for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.

It therefore appears that he signified the whole human being as afflicted in the flesh, so that the Spirit, which is given to a human being in order to remain and is impassible, should not be understood to have been afflicted. Rather, the whole human being is said to have been afflicted in the flesh with respect to body and soul, but with respect to the Spirit he remained impassible.

It may also be understood in this way: “Outside were conflicts”—that is, in public the faithless were fighting against the faithful, resisting the truth while filled with fury. News of this generated fears inside, where the Apostle was.

(Gregory.) Who would not fear afflictions? But because he was more intent upon the things of God, he overcame this fear through hope.

When holy men are caught in the battle of tribulations,[Col. 0202B]  they strike some while others are being persuaded, at one and the same time. They oppose to the former the shield of patience; against the latter they hurl the weapons of teaching. Through a remarkable art of courage they rise to fight on both fronts, so that they may wisely teach what is perverse within and bravely despise adversity without. By teaching, they correct some; by enduring, they suppress others.

For they despise the hostile forces that rise against them by suffering patiently. But by sympathizing with weakened fellow citizens, they lead them back to salvation. They resist the former, lest they carry others away as well; they fear for the latter, lest they completely lose the life of righteousness.

Let us look at the soldier of God fighting on both fronts. He says: “Outside were conflicts; inside were fears.” He describes the innumerable battles he endured externally: “In dangers from rivers, in dangers from robbers, in dangers from my own people, in dangers from the Gentiles, in dangers in the city, in dangers in the wilderness, in dangers at sea, in dangers among false brothers” (II Corinthians XI).

Let us consider what labor it is to endure adversity outside and protect the weak within at one and the same time.[Col. 0202C]  Outside he suffers conflicts, because he is torn by blows and bound with chains; inside he endures fear, because he fears that his suffering may harm not himself but his disciples.

Hence he also wrote to them, saying (I Thessalonians III): “Let no one be shaken by these tribulations, for you yourselves know that we have been appointed to this.” For he feared the fall of others in his own suffering, lest, when the disciples saw him afflicted and beaten for the faith, they should refuse to profess themselves believers.

O immense depths of love! He despises what he himself suffers and takes care that the disciples should suffer no wound of false persuasion in their hearts. In himself he disregards the wounds of the body; in others he heals the wounds of the heart.

The righteous have this particular quality:[Col. 0202D]  when placed in the pain of their own tribulation, they do not abandon concern for another’s welfare. While they grieve over the adversities they themselves endure, they anticipate what is necessary for others by teaching them. Like great physicians who have themselves been struck, they suffer the tears of their own wounds while offering medicines of health to others.

But he who comforts the lowly, God comforted us also by the arrival of Titus. (Ambrose.) Since God does not forget his own, but always gives them consolation in tribulation, he hastened Titus’s arrival, so that it might bring relief to those placed in the heat of affliction; for great is the comfort of one who suffers if he has someone with him to console him. Not only by his arrival [Col. 0203A], but also by the consolation with which he comforted us concerning you. He adds still more to the consolation, signifying that he had heard from Titus of their ready willingness to repent, to such an extent that Titus, who had been grieved by their disobedience, received consolation from their repentance. The Apostle shows how great his affection was for them: he did not count the lowest depths of prison, nor the pain of beatings, nor the laceration of his body, nor the fetter by which his feet had been confined; rather, when he heard of their correction, he rejoiced and, forgetting his sufferings, gave thanks to God for their salvation, regarding it as though it were a recompense for his tribulations.

Reporting to us your longing, your weeping. Titus announced that they had a desire to amend themselves. For, learning what had been promised [Col. 0203B] to those who live well, they were stirred to desire these things. Your weeping, he says: when reproved, they wept in sorrow because they had sinned, and they did not seek to excuse themselves; hence he glories in them. Your zeal on my behalf. Learning of the Apostle’s love toward them, they began to defend him against his opponents.

So that I rejoiced the more. For even if I grieved you by the letter, I do not regret it. It is clear that he ought not to regret this matter, since such an outcome followed from it, for in the first Letter he had rebuked their errors rather severely. “I do not regret,” he says, “having written more harshly, because the situation required it.” And if I did regret it, seeing that although that letter grieved you for a time, now I rejoice. He says this because, if he regretted it on account of his love—because he had grieved them—consolation would follow from joy [Col. 0203C], since it had been beneficial that he grieved them.

Not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved unto repentance; for you were grieved according to God. He says that he rejoiced because they were grieved with shame, not with anger. For one who, when reproved, feels shame promises to correct himself; but one who becomes angry shows that he will become worse.

So that you might suffer no loss through us. “Everything,” he says, “that we do may have its effect in you; even the fact that we grieved you is for your benefit.”

For godly grief produces repentance leading to lasting salvation. It is clear that the one who is grieved because he has sinned is grieved according to God: he is sorrowful because he has done what God hates, and this pertains to the stability of salvation.

(Cassian.) The grief, therefore [Col. 0203D], that produces repentance leading to lasting salvation is obedient, gentle, humble, meek, gracious, and patient, as proceeding from the love of God; extending itself tirelessly toward every bodily and spiritual pain and contrition, with a desire for perfection; and in a certain manner joyful and invigorated by the hope of progress. It retains the entire sweetness of graciousness and patience, possessing within itself all the fruits of the Holy Spirit that the same Apostle enumerated: “Love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, faith, meekness, kindness, self-control” (Gal. 5). But the other grief is exceedingly harsh, impatient, fruitless, full of bitterness and sorrow, hard, and destructive through the punishment of despair. It breaks and draws back from diligence and salutary [Col. 0204A] sorrow the one whom it has embraced, being irrational and destroying not only the efficacy of prayers but also all the spiritual fruits mentioned above, which that other grief knows how to confer.

Therefore, apart from that grief which is undertaken either for salutary repentance, or for the pursuit of perfection, or from desire for future things, every grief—as worldly grief and grief that brings death—must equally be rejected and driven utterly from our hearts, like fornication, or the spirit of avarice (*philargyria*), or anger. We can expel this most destructive passion from ourselves in this way: by keeping our mind continually occupied with spiritual meditation, raising it through hope of the future and contemplation of the promised blessedness. In this manner we shall be able to overcome every kind of sorrow—whether arising from preceding [Col. 0204B] anger, or coming upon us through loss of profit or injury inflicted upon us, or generated by an insult received, or proceeding from a reasonable confusion of mind, or imposing upon us a deadly despair—when, always remaining joyful and steadfast through contemplation of eternal and future things, we are neither cast down by present misfortunes nor lifted up by prosperity, regarding both as fleeting and soon to pass away.

But worldly grief produces death. He says this because godly grief produces life: one repents and hopes in God’s mercy. In the same way, worldly grief produces death: the exposed sinner is sorrowful as though he were destined for punishment and had no one from whom to hope for mercy. Even if for the present [Col. 0204C] there should be no one to punish him, he will nevertheless be unable to escape God’s judgment.

For behold, this very thing—that you were grieved according to God—what earnestness it has produced in you. It is true, for the one who repents is concerned lest he sin again.

But defense. Correctly so, because repentance has no excuse but shame.

But fear. He shows the fear in the sinner who, because of his offense, asks pardon.

But longing. The one who knows that sin has disfigured him desires to be restored.

But zeal. The one who understands that the rebuke is for his benefit begins to feel zeal for the completion of good works.

But vengeance. It is necessary that a person avenge the one whose affection toward him he perceives; and he takes vengeance upon himself when he afflicts himself as the cause of his offense.

In everything you have shown yourselves [Col. 0204D] to be pure in the matter. When they seem to meditate upon everything that pertains to progress toward a better hope, possessing zeal for the Apostle, and striving through faith to show themselves upright in all the duties of human conduct toward their teacher, they demonstrate that they are pure in every respect.

Therefore, although I wrote to you, it was not on account of the one who did the wrong. He calls the one who acted wickedly and unjustly the man who had committed incest; he also touches upon those whom he indicates in the first Letter to have committed wrongs and frauds against their brothers.

Nor on account of the one who suffered wrong. These men were treated unjustly because they suffered things contrary to their rights from their brothers. This is the sense that he recalls at the beginning of the Letter, where he says, “If you forgive anyone anything, I also forgive.” For he shows that he did not write chiefly on behalf of those who had sinned [Col. 0205A], so that they should be forgiven, but rather on behalf of the Church: when one person acts wickedly, many are put to shame; and when one suffers insult or fraud, many are indignant, because “if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it.”

But in order to make manifest our concern for you before God. By correcting the unjust and defiled, sanctifying them, and reconciling them to the Church, he shows that he has concern for the entire people, in accordance with what I mentioned above.

For this reason we received consolation. He says that he received consolation and, through this, gives consolation. He received it when he learned that those whom he had rebuked wished to correct themselves, so that through patience they might be reformed. He gives it when he recalls them to the Church, lest, being grieved for too long, they should despair of themselves and turn aside to a public and deadly [Col. 0205B] way of life.

And in our consolation we rejoiced more abundantly over the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by all of you. When he heard that those rebuked in the first Letter wished to correct themselves, he received consolation. But when he learned from Titus that they were suffering sorrow because of their error, his consolation increased and he was filled with joy, because their will had begun to be proved by their actions, with Titus as a reliable witness reporting this with gladness of heart.

And if I have boasted to him about you, I have not been put to shame. Before Titus went to the Corinthians, he heard from them—that is, from the Apostle and those who were with him—that the Corinthians had a good will [Col. 0206A] toward correcting their faults. Therefore, when Titus returned and reported the same things, the Apostle was certainly not put to shame but became more joyful, because Titus had found them no different from what he had heard about them.

But just as we have spoken everything to you in truth, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true. The Apostle writes these things exulting in the Spirit, rejoicing over them in such a way that he finds their efficacy as true as his preaching to them had been, at least in its correction of them. For the truth of the one who rebukes is then shown to be manifest, if those who are rebuked begin to amend themselves. When the rebuked are changed, they bear witness to the one who rebuked them.

And his heart is more abundantly disposed toward you. He says that Titus’s mind and affection are toward them, because he saw their progress. For the mind of a holy man is directed toward every good thing.

Remembering [Col. 0206B] the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling. The Corinthians knew that Titus had been sent to them by the Apostle, by whom they had been rebuked for such great faults. They were therefore frightened at his arrival; and, because they had begun to amend their way of life, they were anxious to obey his commands, so that when he returned he might make the Apostle’s attitude toward them more favorable. For this reason he indicates that they honored Titus: in Titus they reverenced the Apostle.

I rejoice that in everything I have confidence in you. He rejoiced not only in their good will, but also in the good works by which they were correcting what they had done wrong. Therefore, he says, “I have confidence in you in everything.”

## BOOK THIRTEEN

[Col. 0205]

### CHAPTER VIII. The Apostle exhorts the Corinthians to send alms to Jerusalem and discusses those who collect these alms.

Now we make known to you, brothers, the grace of God that has been given in the churches of Macedonia: that amid a great trial of tribulation, their abundant joy overflowed. (Ambrose.) Because the Macedonians received the word of faith with devoted hearts, he says that grace was given them by God, so that amid the tribulation of Paul and Silas mentioned above they would not suffer scandal, but would receive the word with exultation of mind, confident in the promised hope, and show themselves approved through these sufferings.

And their deep poverty abounded in the riches of their generosity. He praises their resolve, because although their material [Col. 0205D] resources were scanty, their spirit was found rich in service to the saints. For they acted with a pure conscience, seeking to please not human beings but God.

For I bear them witness according to their ability, and beyond their ability they were willing. As much as was worthy and pleasing to God, who knows their strength, they gave from their resources for the service; and because they had given themselves to God with their whole heart, they wished to offer more than their means allowed.

Begging us with much exhortation for the favor and fellowship of the service that is performed for the saints. He praises them for having offered the service so simply and devotedly, even though it exceeded their means, that they begged us with tears [Col. 0206C] to accept what did not seem acceptable to receive, because it was more than their resources could bear, lest poverty afterward persuade them to regret the good work.

But because they showed themselves to be such that, already setting aside present things with pure hearts, they strengthened themselves by the confidence of faith in future promises, it seemed right to accept from them, lest the grace of their good heart should lose its fruit.

And not as we had hoped, but they gave themselves first to the Lord, and then to us by the will of God. “For this reason,” he says, “their offering ought to have been accepted: they had first corrected their former errors and the faults of their life and conduct, and had vowed themselves to God beyond what had been expected [Col. 0206D].” It seemed that they acted simply, so that the one to whom the offering was made would not fear to accept it, since they were not offering with the intention of buying off their superiors and thereby having to endure their faults without rebuke; for gifts blind the eyes and weaken the force of authority.

Thus, by giving themselves to God while correcting their faults, and afterward to their brothers by offering material support, they ought not to have been grieved, since even before they began they had wished to be perfect.

By their example, therefore, he invites the Corinthians to complete with attentive minds what they had begun, strengthened by this exhortation.

So that we urged Titus that, just as he began [Col. 0207A], so also he might complete this grace among you. Since he knew Titus’s sincere affection toward them, as well as their obedience to him, he signifies that through Titus he could more easily exhort them to this work. Just as Titus had borne fruit among them in other matters through his exhortation, so he might also bear fruit in this grace, making them ready for the service of the saints; and, since they were already correcting their faults, they might obtain the fruit of this generosity. Those who give for the purpose of avoiding rebuke will receive no fruit from the deed.

But just as you abound in everything—in faith, speech, knowledge, all earnestness, and your love for us—so also abound in this grace. He exhorts them so that he may boast of them before the other churches. For this is the proof of their correction: whether they are ready for service [Col. 0207B] to the saints.

I do not speak as one commanding, but by the earnestness of others also testing the genuineness of your love. It is clear that he does not command, but exhorts them to send support to those suffering poverty and to relieve their distress. By showing their good disposition to God and to human beings, they will certainly receive a reward.

For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: although he was rich, for your sake he became poor, so that by his poverty you might become rich. He says that Christ became poor because God deigned to be born as a human being, humbling the power of his majesty so as to acquire for human beings the riches of divinity, so that, as the Apostle Peter says, they might become “partakers of the divine nature.” He therefore became human in order to take humanity up into God, as it is written: “I said [Col. 0207C], You are gods” (Ps. 81).

In this way he exhorts them to become poor, as it were, by giving, so that their poverty may be beneficial, just as Christ’s poverty benefited us. Christ became poor for our sake, not for his own; we become poor so that it may benefit us.

And I give my advice in this matter, for this is beneficial to you, who not only began to do but also to desire it from the previous year. Now complete the work as well. So that, just as the readiness of your will is present, so also may its completion be according to what you have.

He says this so that their will may appear in their work, if it is genuine, according to their means: let each give as much as his spirit can and wishes, so that his conscience may be pure and not hypocritical, seeking to please human beings while receiving no reward from the Lord. For if the will is ready, it is accepted according to what one [Col. 0207D] has, not according to what one does not have.

Since the Corinthians are being urged to this work of service, this is prescribed for them: they should not give more than they are able, lest, offering more than they can afford under compulsion rather than voluntarily, they should appear burdened and destined to receive no reward; for one who does something under compulsion has no reward.

The churches of Macedonia, however, offered voluntarily and with entreaties. They showed that they were doing this with their whole will, offering more than they could afford; therefore it was acceptable. For the more they offered, the more they will receive. If someone gives as much as he wishes or is able, it is accepted, for he appears to do this deliberately. Therefore, let him give as much as his will both can and wishes, so that he may receive a reward for this deed.

Not so that there may be relief for others and tribulation for you. It is true, for one must give in such a way that giving does not produce poverty for the givers.

But by equality at the present time. He says this so that, according to what one has for the present, one may distribute it to the saints. For more is not demanded than one ought to retain for oneself [Col. 0208A].

(Gregory.) “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 19). Hence Zacchaeus says: “Behold, I give half of my possessions to the poor” (Luke 19), so that we may carefully consider that those whom we now see in poverty we shall one day see in abundance, and that those whom we behold in abundance will one day be in poverty if we neglect to give generously.

Therefore, whoever now gives temporal assistance to the poor, expecting afterward to receive what is everlasting from him, cultivates the earth, so to speak, for harvest; and it returns more abundantly [Col. 0208B] whatever it has received. It follows, then, that pride should never arise from a gift, since the rich person, from what he gives to the poor, is acting so that the poor may not remain poor forever.

Let your abundance supply their poverty, so that their abundance may also supply your poverty. (Ambrose.) This means that, since at the present time the saints suffer poverty after abandoning everything in the world and devoting themselves solely to divine works, so that they may attend to teaching and prayer for the benefit of many, those who believe and who devote themselves to crafts or business, or who at least possess inherited resources, should minister to the needs of the saints. Then, when the saints are rich in spiritual things and these others are poor in them, the saints may share with them in return, repaying them, as it were, for their service, just as the Lord says: “As long as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me” (Matt. 25).

So that there may be equality, as it is written [Col. 0208C]: “He who had much did not have too much, and he who had little did not have too little” (Exod. 16). This is the equality spoken of: since these people minister to the saints in the present time, their turn will be repaid to them in the future. For they make the saints their debtors.

The one who has much will not have too much, and the one who has little will not have too little. This is read in Exodus. The saints possess more in the hope of the future age than those who appear rich in the present age; nevertheless, there the two will be made equal. Just as the poverty of the saints is sustained here by the benefit of the rich, so in the future age, in which those who now appear poor will be rich, the rich will become wealthy through the benefit of the saints.

For they have not given themselves entirely to God, so as to be poor here and rich there. Rather, because they are rich here, they are poor there; and they will be enriched through the support of the saints, who, although placed here, are already there in mind. For it is no ordinary merit [Col. 0208D] to minister to the saints through righteous labor.

“He who had much will not have too much,” because he gave what he had in excess to the needy. “And he who had little will not have too little,” namely, the one who received from the one who had abundance, “so that,” he says, “there may be equality.”

(Gregory.) It greatly helps to tame the pride of the giver if, when he gives earthly things, he carefully weighs the words of the heavenly Teacher, who says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16).

If we acquire eternal dwellings through their friendship, then surely those who give must consider that they are offering gifts to patrons rather than bestowing presents upon the needy. Through Paul he says: “Let your abundance supply their [Col. 0209A] poverty, so that their abundance may supply your poverty,” so that, as was said above, we may carefully consider that those whom we now see in poverty we shall one day see in abundance, while those whom we behold in abundance, if we neglect to give generously, will one day be poor.

Blessed Job, therefore, wishing to show carefully how humility and mercy were joined together in him, says: “If I have despised one passing by because he had no clothing, and the poor man without a covering, if his sides did not bless me and he was not warmed by the fleeces of my sheep” (Job 31). It is as though he were saying: In love of my neighbor, following one and the same rule, I both suppressed the vice of pride and practiced compassion: I did not despise the passerby, but looked upon him humbly and warmed him mercifully.

For whoever, over the one [Col. 0209B] to whom he gives something, exalts himself in arrogant pride commits a greater fault inwardly through his pride than he gains merit outwardly through his generosity. He becomes naked of inner goods while clothing one whom he despises as naked, and thus makes himself worse than he was by considering himself better than his needy neighbor. For the one who lacks clothing is less poor than the one who lacks humility.

Therefore, when we see those who share our nature lacking external goods, we must consider how many interior goods are lacking in us, so that our thoughts may not exalt themselves over the poor, when they carefully see that we are all the more truly needy the more inwardly needy we are.

(Jerome.) O what blessedness it is to receive great things for small ones, eternal things for fleeting ones, things that live forever for things that die, and to have the Lord as one’s debtor.

But if any widow has children [Col. 0209C], especially if she has a household dependent upon her, let her not abandon her needy children. Rather, according to equality, let her remember first her own soul and consider it one of her children, and let her divide with her children instead of leaving everything to them. Indeed, let her make Christ a coheir of her labors.

You will reply, “It is difficult; it is harsh; it is contrary to nature.” But you will hear the Lord responding to you: “Let the one who is able to receive it receive it”; and, “If you wish to be perfect” (Matt. 19), he does not impose the yoke of necessity upon you, but grants free choice to your own power.

Do you wish to be perfect and to stand at the highest summit of dignity? Do what the apostles did: sell everything you have, give it to the poor, and follow the Savior; follow naked and alone the naked and solitary virtue.

Do you not wish to be perfect, but to hold the second degree [Col. 0209D] of virtue? Leave all that you have, and give to your children and relatives. No one reproaches you if you pursue what is lower, provided that you know that the path chosen first has rightly been placed before you.

You say, “This belongs to the apostles and to men; a noblewoman cannot sell everything, since she needs many supports for this life.” Hear the Apostle exhorting you: “Not that there should be relief for others and tribulation for you, but according to equality let your abundance support their poverty, and their abundance be the supplement of your poverty.”

Hence the Lord also says: “Let the one who has two tunics give to the one who has none” (Luke 3). What if there are the cold blasts of Scythia and the snows of the Alps? They are repelled not by two or three tunics, but scarcely by the skins of animals.

Whatever, therefore [Col. 0210A], can protect our bodies and assist human weakness, for those whom nature has sent forth naked, should be called one tunic. Whatever is necessary for present nourishment is called one day’s food. Hence the command is given: “Do not worry about tomorrow” (Matt. 5)—that is, about the future. And the Apostle says: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (1 Tim. 6). If you have more than is necessary for food and clothing, distribute it; know that in this you are a debtor.

Ananias and Sapphira incurred the Apostle’s sentence because they guarded their possessions distrustfully (Acts 5). “Then,” you ask, “is the one who does not give his possessions to be punished?” Certainly not.
