They were punished because they wished to lie to the Holy Spirit; while reserving what was necessary for their livelihood, as though they had perfectly [Col. 0210B] renounced the world, they pursued empty glory as though they had renounced the world perfectly. Otherwise, one is free either to give or not to give. Yet for one who wishes to be perfect, present poverty is compensated by future riches.

But how a widow ought to live, the Apostle comprehended in a brief statement when he said: “She who lives in pleasures is dead” (1 Tim. 5).

But thanks be to God, who put the same concern for you into the heart of Titus, for he indeed accepted the exhortation. (Ambrose.) God, who is just and knew that the Corinthians wished to make progress, kindled Titus’s affection for them, so that by his exhortation he might bring their will to good work. Seeing their progress, he was comforted and rejoiced in them.

But, being even more concerned, he went to you of his own accord. That is, seeing [Col. 0210C] them progress in good conduct, he became more concerned for their disposition, so that he went to them voluntarily. Earlier, even when asked, he had excused himself from going to them because of their faults.

We also sent with him our brother, whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the churches. Not only this, but he was also appointed by the churches as our traveling companion in this grace that is administered by us for the glory of the Lord and the expression of our willing purpose. They commend this man, who was unknown to them, so that they might know how favorable an opinion already existed of them, since such men were sent to them. These men would rejoice with them and increase them in the faith by which God works, for whose glory the vicars of Christ diligently carried out this work, so that God, the creator of heaven and earth, might be acknowledged in them.

Avoiding this, that anyone [Col. 0210D] should reproach us in this abundance that is administered by us for the glory of God. Since the service was under discussion, he adds this lest he be judged negligent in caring for the poor or the saints, if he carried out this work too sluggishly. For the Apostles had agreed among themselves concerning this matter, that they should remember the poor, as he indicates in the Letter to the Galatians.

Since the Apostle was above reproach in everything, he signifies that he was taking this precaution lest he be judged negligent in this matter, so that, once this work had been completed, his concern and foresight might be evident in every respect.

For we take thought for what is good not only before God but also before human beings. He provides what is good before God when he teaches what God commands concerning service to the saints or the poor. Before human beings [Col. 0211A] he provides what is good by sending men of such character to exhort them to this work that, through their integrity, they would not cause them scandal but would encourage them, lest the Apostle’s good teaching fall into disrepute through its careless ministers.

But we sent with them our brother whom we have often tested as being concerned in many matters; but now much more concerned, because of his great confidence in you—whether on account of Titus, who is my companion and your helper, or on account of our brothers, the apostles of the churches, the glory of Christ. He calls Titus his companion because he too was a bishop, to whom he entrusted a ministry known throughout all the churches of his province. Along with him he adds a third brother, approved in many good works and concerned for them. Through Titus’s report they conveyed the Corinthians’ good will, and he calls the other messengers “the apostles of the churches, the glory of Christ.”

He shows that he had become more eager to see them and exhort them to the service of the saints, for he had gained confidence from hearing that the Corinthians [Col. 0211B] had become better. Hence he hastened to come to them, certain that they would obey him and do good works.

Therefore, show before them and before the face of the churches the evidence of your love and of our boasting about you. He admonishes them to show their love in the persons whom he sends, so that the good things they had heard about them might be proved true. They would show that they had progressed through the Apostle’s admonitions if they received his messengers with honor, so that the other churches might recognize that the good things being said about them were true. He thus stirs their hearts, because one [Col. 0211C] who is well regarded commonly strives to show himself better.

### CHAPTER IX. The Apostle, removing suspicion, teaches that alms should be given promptly, cheerfully, and abundantly.

For concerning the ministry that is performed for the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you: for I know your readiness, on account of which I boast about you among the Macedonians.

(Ambr.) These are also words intended to please. He says that it is superfluous to write about the ministry performed for the saints, so that he may appear to think well of them. It is indeed superfluous to remind someone whom you know will act; but, in order to display his diligence, it is necessary for him to write, both to make them more ready and to reveal what he proclaims about them to the others—for things that seem superfluous commonly produce greater concern. [Col. 0211D] Thus the Lord, although he did not doubt the love of the apostle Peter toward him, says to him three times: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John, final chapter). This threefold repetition seems almost superfluous, but it contributes to the completion of the admonition, so that he may know that he must attend with great diligence to what he frequently commands.

For Achaia has been ready since the previous year.

(Greg.) In those from whom he required not so much deeds as pious intentions, he undoubtedly praises the pious intentions more than the deeds. It must nevertheless be noted that this very consolation contains a reproach when he says, “since the previous year”: it was good, certainly, but they had done it late; therefore the teacher praised it not without criticism. For he is a physician: he applies medicine to the wound, which both soothes what has been cleansed [Col. 0212A] and bites what is found to be putrid.

(Ambr.) After Macedonia he mentions Achaia—that is, the churches of the province of Achaia—not all of them, since the Corinthians too are Achaeans. They had prepared themselves, moved by emulation of the Macedonians, to minister to the saints. By saying this, he exhorts the Corinthians all the more, when he says that they had been ready since the previous year, but were now awaiting the distribution of their ministry according to the need of each person.

And your emulation has stirred up very many.

After the Macedonians he says that Achaia was ready. Then he adds that the Corinthians too should become ready according to their promise. The other churches, meanwhile, were stirred to good works by emulation of the Corinthians when they heard that those who had previously been entangled in many errors had afterward corrected themselves and become people of good will: for if those who had behaved badly after receiving the [Col. 0212B] faith had begun to have this intention, how much more should those in whom such vices had not been found!

But we have sent the brothers, so that what we boast about concerning you may not be rendered empty in this matter, and so that, as I said, you may be ready.

He refers to the brothers mentioned above, namely Titus and those whom he added as assistants. They were to exhort the Corinthians more earnestly to fulfill their promise concerning the ministry to the saints, so that they might encourage them not only by letter but also face to face, through frequent admonitions, lest the Apostle’s exultation—which arose from his boasting about the excellence of their spirit—should be rendered empty. By mentioning this so often, therefore, he displays his concern for them, unwilling that they should be put to shame.

Lest, when the Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we—and not to say you—should be put to shame in this undertaking. [Col. 0212C]

It is clear that, if what he had testified about them should not be found, he himself would be put to shame in them, and they would be even more confounded, since they had not been willing to do what the Apostle had testified about them, either to make his testimony true or out of regard for so great a man.

Therefore I considered it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you, so that they might prepare this promised blessing, so that it might be ready—not as an act of greed.

To make his concern still more evident, he says that he urged the brothers through whom they might be reminded to fulfill what they had promised but were not fulfilling. Above, he calls Titus’ departure voluntary: that is, it had not been forced upon him, but as soon as he heard, he gladly embraced it, so that he might appear to have gone voluntarily to them because of his hope in them. [Col. 0212D]

Now he does not signify that he urged these men because they were unwilling to go; rather, he demonstrates his affection for them by urging even those who wished to go, so that what both they desired and he requested might take place without any delay. This, then, is what he is doing with them: he wants them to be faithful to their promise, and he says that he is reminding them for the sake of their reputation—not to deceive them, but so that they might offer only as much as they would not regret.

But I say this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly.

He calls the sparing person greedy, one from whom the offering must be extorted; for he regrets it because he promised. He also infers this from their delay: they had promised long ago but had deliberated for a long time. Such a sparing person has a very small harvest, because he sows hesitantly; he does not know how to make his deed beneficial.

And whoever sows in blessings [Col. 0213A] will also reap from blessings.

(Greg.) He sows in blessing who does this with good will, in hope of future recompense. Therefore the excellent preacher, in order to kindle the depths of our compassion toward generosity, said: “For your sake he became poor, although he was rich.” When he also says, “not that there should be relief for others and affliction for you,” he undoubtedly spoke by accommodating himself to the weak, since for some who cannot bear poverty it is more tolerable to give less than, after their generosity, to murmur because of the distress of want.

Then, to kindle the minds of his hearers toward great eagerness in giving, he added shortly afterward: “But I say this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly.” Yet sometimes, we say that compassion from the heart is greater than giving; for whoever [Col. 0213B] perfectly pities the needy considers everything he gives to be little. If the giver’s good will did not prevail, the same excellent preacher would not have said to his disciples that they had begun not only to do but also to desire it from the previous year. It is easy even for an unwilling person to obey in a good work; but this was a great virtue in the disciples: they had first desired to do the good deed that had been commanded them.

Each person should give as he has determined in his heart, not with sadness or from necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver.

(Ambr.) He teaches that this will benefit them in the future if it is done with a joyful spirit. From those who make offerings, God chooses the one to whom he will repay: the one who acts with a devoted heart, as though storing up treasure for himself with God. For whoever acts unwillingly, out of present shame—lest he appear disgraceful when others are making offerings—has no reward. [Col. 0213C]

God is able to make every grace abound toward you.

He wishes God’s power to be present with them, so that, just as God pierces their hearts in correcting their vices and through the truth of doctrine, so also in this matter he may favor their undertakings, so that by God’s grace they may abound in every good.

So that, always having all sufficiency in everything, you may abound in every good work.

(Ambr.) He says and wishes that, by God’s will, they may always be sufficient for themselves in everything and may not lack what is necessary for salvation. If, therefore, they choose sufficiency for themselves alone, they will be able to abound in God’s work. They must retain for themselves only what is sufficient and spend the rest for the needs of the saints or the poor; and this will be to abound in every good work. Although what a poor person gives may be small, it nevertheless abounds because [Col. 0213D] it is done with right judgment; for not only the amount is considered, but also from what source and with what intention it is given.

Thus the widow in the Gospel was praised for giving little, while those who put in much were not praised. Her little was much, because she gave more than she could; the rich gave less, although they could give more. Consequently, her small gift, because she gave beyond her means, was found to be greater than the rich person’s large gift, because they gave from what they had in abundance. Whoever gives as much as he can does rightly; yet he places that widow before himself, because she gave everything she had (Luke XXI).

As it is written: “He scattered; he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever and ever.”

This is written in Psalm 111. By this example he adds to the concern for the poor, [Col. 0214A] so that they may abound in every good work. For if the righteousness of the one who gives generously to the poor remains forever, how much more that of the one who ministers to the saints? The poor may be called those who are publicly needy; the saints, however, are distinguished from them, because they are servants of God, devoted to prayers and fasts and leading a pure life. So too the prophetess Anna, who did not depart from the temple, serving with fasts and prayers day and night (Luke II), setting aside every concern of the world.

This mercy is therefore called righteousness, because the giver knows that God gives everything in common to all: his sun rises for everyone, he sends rain on everyone, and he gave the earth to everyone. For this reason he shares with those who do not possess an abundance of the earth, lest they appear to have been deprived of God’s benefits. He is therefore righteous who does not keep for himself alone [Col. 0214B] what he knows has been given to everyone; and he is righteous not only now but also forever, because in the future age he will have this righteousness with him perpetually.

Now he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will also supply and multiply your seed and increase the produce of your righteousness, so that you may be enriched in every respect and abound in complete sincerity.

Everything belongs to God: both the seeds and the things that grow increase and multiply by God’s will for human use. God, therefore, who gives these things also commands that they be shared with those in need. Consequently, the person who gives according to God’s will cannot fail, by God’s will, to be increased with such increments, so as to enlarge the fruit of righteousness; for to the giver he adds more, so that he may have more from which to give.

This is righteousness: since God gives, a person should in turn give [Col. 0214C] from what he has to the one who lacks. For God wishes these people to be ministers of those who choose better things and despise the abundance of the present age, devoting themselves entirely to the things of God. God gives assistance to each person according to his good will.

The saints, who wish to possess nothing here except food and clothing, God has appointed those who wish to possess these things to be their protectors, so that the one who ministers to them well and sincerely may be increased by God’s will, in order always to have something to give—being enriched both for the present and for the future. For the one who sows once will reap twice. Thus, if he is concerned for future hopes, he should not wish to have the saints subject to him, but should rather humble himself before them, because he will receive from God the reward for this conduct. If he wishes to humble them before himself for the present, he loses the hope of the future. Here he has received the reward for his work, [Col. 0214D] since he is not acting sincerely, as the Lord says: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matthew VI).

Which produces through us thanksgiving to God: for the ministry of this service not only supplies what the saints lack but also abounds through many thanksgivings to the Lord, by the testing of this ministry. They glorify God for your obedience to the confession of the Gospel of Christ, and for the sincerity of your sharing with them and with everyone, while they themselves pray for you and long for you because of the surpassing grace of God in you. Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift.

He says this because whoever performs this work through the stewards of God’s gift—so that God may be thanked by those who receive the necessary expenses [Col. 0215A] in Christ’s name, not subject to begging but to God, from whose goods they know themselves to be nourished—not only receives thanks from them, but also from the remaining brothers, who will give thanks to God for them and commend their deed to the Lord. Thus, although they give to a few, they are commended to God by the prayers of many.

By testing their disposition in this work, they magnify the Lord in them. Strengthened by the hope of him, they obey the Gospel of Christ in submission of mind, not wishing the saints to humble themselves before them so that they may provide what is necessary. This will be to give thanks sincerely for their sharing, while commending themselves to the prayers and desires of the saints.

For who would not wish to see with his own eyes people made subject to their needs for the name of God? Indeed, these are called God’s gifts: the one who ministers through them gives to God, [Col. 0215B] because what is given is attributed to the one who commands it to be done. Giving thanks to God in these matters, and for his ineffable gift—for it is God’s gift that stirs people to good works, since the promised hope urges them toward the ministry mentioned above.

## CHAPTER X. Paul excuses himself from the false accusations made against him by the evidence of his deeds, by reason, and by examples.

Now I myself, Paul, appeal to you by the gentleness and modesty of Christ—who in person am humble among you, but when absent am confident toward you.

(Ambr.) This is what he now says: he is such when absent as he is when present. He was not humble in appearance through flattery or submission to anyone or anything; rather, he guarded his steadfastness so jealously that he sometimes even abstained from what was lawful [Col. 0215C] lest he be bent. Hence he says in another Epistle (1 Corinthians VI): “Everything is lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything. Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food, and God will destroy both the one and the other.”

Therefore he appeals to them while absent and introduces the modesty of Christ, lest, when present, he should be found harsher on account of their vices than he is in the Epistle. By composing themselves, those who had not yet reformed might soften the Apostle’s severity toward themselves, so that, finding them moderate, he might rejoice in them rather than be burdened by severity.

By “confidence,” therefore, he signified the assurance of severity, which perhaps they thought he possessed only in the Epistle, not also when present in person. For in the first Epistle he appears severe and exceedingly strict. Therefore he warns them not to expect him to use the same severity when present.

I ask that, when present, I may not be bold with the confidence [Col. 0215D] by which I am thought bold against some who suppose that we walk according to the flesh.

The meaning is the same, but in order to make it clear he repeats it. He is asking to find them in such a condition that he will not be compelled to become angry, but may rest with them. Here, therefore, he has disclosed what he signified above, and in what follows he makes it still clearer: this is the confidence that he has here called assurance, namely, the authority given to him by Christ, whose representative he is, to punish those who, acting under Christ’s name, do not obey so as to correct the things for which they are reproached.

He refers to those who, by not receiving the spiritual matters spoken by the Apostle, regarded him as though he were speaking about carnal matters that ought not to be accepted. Therefore he says: “Who suppose that we walk according to the flesh,” because whoever despises spiritual things thinks that they are carnal. [Col. 0216A]

For although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh.

That is, although we are placed in the body, we live spiritually. The person who does what pleases God lives spiritually; the person who obeys his desires wages war according to the flesh. For every error is called flesh. But the person who obeys Christ in faith and discipline wages war for Christ.

For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God.

They are powerful because they are incorruptible. Everything carnal is corruptible; therefore these are called weapons because they resist vices, bearing the sign of their emperor, Christ, who is the enemy of vices. Just as an emperor vindicates his kingdom through soldiers, so the Savior through us, his servants, defends the confession and discipline of the one God.

For the destruction of strongholds, destroying arguments and every height [Col. 0216B] that exalts itself against the knowledge of God.

The spiritual weapons are faith in incorruptible preaching. Through these God conquers the principalities and powers, which, seeking to usurp dominion for themselves, are known to exalt themselves against the faith of Christ, inserting themselves into human thoughts in order to draw people away from God’s rule. The truth of faith destroys these thoughts.

Therefore by “strongholds” he means the principalities and powers, and the spiritual forces of wickedness, which exalt themselves and arm the minds of unbelievers to oppose Christ. Against them God’s law fights, scattering their arguments.

And taking every understanding captive into obedience to Christ.

It takes the understanding captive when it conquers reasoning that contradicts it, bringing and preparing it to be humble and gentle toward the faith of Christ, which it had previously resisted.

And being ready to avenge [Col. 0216C] every disobedience, whenever your obedience has been fulfilled.

It is clear that he avenges disobedience when he condemns it through obedience, destroying it when he brings those who resist to the faith, so that unbelief may be condemned by those who had defended it.

Look at what is evident according to appearance.

Now he wants them to consider what is plain—that is, to judge openly what he is about to say. He therefore says:

If anyone is confident that he belongs to Christ, let him consider this again within himself: just as he belongs to Christ, so do we.

He speaks to those whose pride he is touching. They presumed upon themselves and, through the inflation of their minds, thought less of the Apostle than was proper, as though they did not need his instructions. He warns them that, if they were confident that they were servants of Christ, they ought not to doubt the Apostle [Col. 0216D]; rather, they should think of him similarly, although he was their inferior—or, in fact, they ought to prefer the teacher of the Gentiles to themselves.

Here he teaches them humility by making himself equal to them, although he was a chosen vessel and the teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth. He wants them to consider what is plainly visible: no believer should think more highly of himself than of the Apostle; how much less should anyone think less highly of him than of himself?

He therefore bears witness against them and teaches them not to lose the merit of a good life through pride of mind. For whoever knows that he is something humbles himself so that he may become greater.

For even if I should boast somewhat more about our authority, which the Lord gave for building up and not for destroying you, I shall not be put to shame.

Now he signifies [Col. 0217A] that above he humbled himself by comparing himself with them. If he should raise himself up, he would not be put to shame, because he received from the Lord the authority to preach so as to save those who obey, not destroy them.

If, then, the one who was sent by the Lord lowers himself and compares himself with inferiors, how much more should those who possessed no testimony of their own refrain from comparing themselves with their superiors—not to mention preferring themselves to them?

And so that I may not appear as though I were frightening you through letters.

The person who appears to frighten through letters is one who possesses neither authority nor confidence when present, but dares to act when absent because he is afraid when present. They say: “His letters are severe and powerful, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible.” Let such a person consider that, whatever we are in word through letters when absent, we are the same [Col. 0217B] when present in deed.

He therefore proves that he is not one person when absent and another when present. He was not presumptuous, for he had received authority from the Lord. A person to whom authority has not been given can be bold when absent, but when present suffers shame. The Apostle, therefore, is not ashamed when he rebukes, because he acts with the confidence of authority.

He says these things concerning those who preached without being sent, flattering people because they wished to commend themselves.

(Greg.) But often holy preachers wish to display themselves in order to be of benefit, yet they cannot; often they desire to remain quiet, yet they are not permitted. No one, therefore, knows when God will command the clouds of rain to display his light, because no one comprehends when God gives the power of preaching so that the glory of those who preach may shine forth.

Thus the Lord says to Job: “Do you know when God commanded the rains to display the light of his clouds?” [Col. 0217C] (Job XXXVII). It is as though he were saying openly: “When you already see preachers who are about to come into the world, do you comprehend when the Lord will impel them to preach by a fullness of the Spirit, or by what means he now makes the brightness of their lives known?”

Accordingly, he aptly adds: “Do you know the paths of the great clouds and perfect knowledge?” (ibid.). These clouds have very subtle paths, namely, the ways of holy preaching; for narrow is the gate that leads to life. They restrain people along these paths when they do not depart from the track of their intention by wandering through the world’s broad desires. The strict discipline of living well is not a broad road but a path, in which each preacher is carefully confined, constricting himself anxiously under the guardianship of the [Col. 0217D] commandments.

For we do not dare to insert ourselves among, or compare ourselves with, some who commend themselves.

(Amb.) These are the people who commend themselves: those who, without having received authority, wish to exercise dominion, claiming authority for their own name. The person who is sent claims authority not for himself but for the one by whom he is sent, thereby also showing that he has been chosen by the Lord as a steward.

Thus he neither joins nor compares himself with those who preach without being sent, since he presumes nothing beyond what has been granted.

But they, measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves with themselves.

We, however, will boast beyond measure—but according to the measure of the rule that God has measured out to us, a measure extending as far as you.

He says that he exercises as much authority [Col. 0218A] as has been granted by its author, and he does not wish to exceed the measure. Therefore, he says, our boasting will not be proud when it does not go beyond the limit of the authority given.

He uses “glory” for the authority he exercised in correcting sinners, so as to save them. Yet he says that he does not glory in the exaltation of authority, but for their building up. He demonstrates that, if he wished to glory in the authority given to him by the Lord, he would not be ashamed. But he uses it in such a way that he glories only in the progress of believers, consistently correcting those who are vicious so that he may glory in their salvation. The authority given to him is thereby directed toward salvation, not arrogance.

Thus he testifies in two ways that he does not boast beyond measure: first, because he acts according to the authority given, as he said; and second, because he claimed authority only as far as his preaching [Col. 0218B] extended.

For he was confident concerning those whom he himself had founded in the faith of Christ. He says that the preaching field was assigned to each person, so that each might have certain cities of his own in which to glory on account of their faith. By God’s will this Apostle was called to preach to the Macedonians, and he was instructed by the Lord to evangelize the Corinthians.

He therefore speaks boldly to those whom he himself founded and to whom he came by God’s will. He does not have such confidence toward the others, because they were within another’s rule—that is, within the portion of another evangelist.

For we are not extending ourselves beyond you, as though we had not reached you.

That is, we have not reached you in preaching as people who were not sent; rather, we were appointed to you, with God sending us. To be extended beyond measure means to be extended farther than is permitted [Col. 0218C]; but he has not gone beyond the measure God gave his evangelists, and he testifies that he has preserved it.

He makes this clear so that they may know that he was directed to them by God and therefore ought to obey his admonitions, lest, by despising him, they appear to resist the God by whom he was sent.

For we have reached even you in the Gospel of Christ, not boasting beyond measure in the labors of others.

Here what he says appears more clearly: he himself had founded them, and therefore speaks to them with such confidence. They had not been acquired for the faith through another’s labor, as he says in another Epistle (1 Corinthians IV): “In Christ I begot you through the Gospel.” Therefore he does not boast beyond measure who boasts in his own labor.

And having hope that, as your faith grows, we shall be magnified among you according to our rule, even to evangelize beyond you.

Because he hopes for the fruit of the faith he has sought [Col. 0218D], he declares that he does not act negligently, lest he yield to weariness and troubles. He believes that he will be magnified before God if his hearers increase in faith, as the Lord says: “Father, just as you sent me into this world, I also sent them into this world, and for their sake I sanctify myself” (John XVII). He says this because the obedience of disciples is the testimony of their teacher.

Hence he says: “To be magnified among you according to our rule, in abundance, even to evangelize in regions beyond you.”

Rejoicing more greatly in their faith, he necessarily professes that he will preach beyond them, in order to increase the glory of his preaching where Christ had not yet been preached.

Not boasting in another’s rule, in places prepared by others.

It is clear that a prudent man [Col. 0219A] neither places his confidence in nor hopes for glory from things that have been established through the labors of others. Therefore the Apostle does not dare to act among those who believed through the preaching of others, lest he appear to glory in another’s labors. Rather, he strives to preach to those to whom the message had not been announced, so that he may seek glory through his own labor.

But “whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord.”

By saying this he signified that both this confidence and this glory must be given to the Lord, whose grace it is. Whoever is confident in evangelical authority should be confident by God’s authorship, so that all profit from the divine work may accrue to the Lord.

But whoever has not received authority from God cannot boast in the Lord, because he seeks his own glory. For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends.

It is true: the Lord commends the one who is approved, [Col. 0219B] whom he considers worthy and sends to preach his gift. But the one whom he does not send he does not commend. The person who preaches without being sent commends himself; consequently, he is not worthy but presumptuous and rejected.

## CHAPTER XI. By first setting forth his case, the Apostle presents his commendation from his works and from the evils he has endured.

Would that you could bear with a little of my foolishness—and indeed, bear with me.

(Ambr.) As he begins to speak truthfully about himself, he calls himself foolish because this seems to pertain to his praise. Hence it is said: “Let your neighbor’s lips praise you, and not your own.” [Col. 0219C] But here he is compelled by grief because those who ought to have thought better of him than of anyone else were thinking of him unworthily.

For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God; for I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.

He shows that he is about to speak out of love for them, so that what he says may contribute not so much to his own praise as to their progress. They must learn how to favor their father in the Gospel, because the reproach of a father is the disparagement of his children, while the praise of children is the glory of their father.

He calls them virgins in the faith, and therefore is jealous of them lest corruptors of the faith should lead them astray, so that he may present them undefiled to Christ the judge on the day of judgment. Hence we read in the Apocalypse of John: “These are the ones who did not defile themselves with women, [Col. 0219D] for they remained virgins; these follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Revelation XIV).

By “women” he signified error, because error began through a woman. Thus he also calls Jezebel a woman, referring to the wife of Ahab, who in her zeal for Baal killed the prophets of God (1 Kings XVIII), although idolatry is understood—the idolatry by which morals and the truth of faith are corrupted.

For if you understand “women” literally, so that you think they are called virgins because they kept their bodies undefiled, you exclude the saints from this glory. All the Apostles except John and Paul had wives. Consider whether it would be fitting to accuse the Apostle Peter, who is first among the Apostles—how much more so among the others!

(Aug.) As for the virgins whom he said in the evangelical parable were going out to meet the bridegroom (Matthew XXV), I think this should be understood so that the one called the bride consists of those very virgins. It is like saying that, when all Christians run together into the Church, sons run together to their mother, although the one called “mother” consists of those very sons. [Col. 0220A]

For now the Church is betrothed and is a virgin who is to be led to the wedding—that is, while she keeps herself from worldly corruption. At that time she will marry, when all mortality has passed away and she bears offspring through immortal conception.

“I betrothed you,” he says, “to one husband, to present a chaste virgin to Christ.” He says “you,” drawing them from the plural into the singular. Therefore they may be called both virgins and a virgin.

But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ.

(Ambr.) He shows why he is compelled [Col. 0220B] to testify truthfully about himself. He declares that glory has been given to him not so that he may praise himself, but so that he may expose those who, under Christ’s name, preached against Christ, and by whom the Corinthians were being led astray. The truth would benefit them more than it benefited him.

He is acting so that the seducers may not be heard. He compares them to the devil because of the cunning of their wickedness, since they attempt to corrupt the hearts of the faithful away from the truth of Christ. Fearing this, he is always concerned for them, lest they be violated.

(Aug.) Few women in the Church possess bodily virginity, but all the faithful possess virginity of heart in the faith itself. The Apostle feared that the virginity of their hearts would be corrupted by the devil. Those who have lost this virginity are virgins in body without cause.

A Catholic woman precedes a heretical virgin: the former is not a virgin in body [Col. 0220C], while the latter has become a woman in heart—and a woman not through a husband but through the serpent. But what does the Church say? “You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk”—the basilisk is the king of serpents, just as the devil is the king of demons—“and you will trample upon the lion and the dragon” (Psalm XC).

For if the one who comes preaches another Christ whom we did not preach, or you receive another spirit that you did not receive, or another Gospel that you did not accept, you rightly put up with it.

(Ambr.) Why does he say, “You rightly put up with it,” if another Christ had been preached to them, or if another spirit or another Gospel had been handed down to them, when he says to the Galatians: “If anyone announces to you something other than [Col. 0220D] what you received, let him be accursed” (Galatians I)?

If it was wrong for the Galatians to accept anything other than what had been handed down by the Apostles, how would it have been right for the Corinthians if another Christ had been preached to them? But the Apostle knew that no other Christ than the one who was crucified would ever be preached. Therefore he says, “You would rightly put up with it” if those who come had preached to you another and superior Christ. To the Galatians, however, he said “let him be accursed” if they heard something else—not something greater, certainly, but something contrary.

“Moreover,” he says, “the very Christ whom we proclaim is preached by them, as is this Gospel. Why, then, should we be regarded as inferior, when nothing more is learned from them?”

Above he speaks about false apostles, corrupters of the faith; here, however, [Col. 0221A] he speaks about true preachers. The Corinthian people were wavering amid various errors: some favored the false apostles; some favored those from whom, in carefully composed words, they heard the same things they had heard from the Apostle; and others favored the Apostles because they had been with the Lord, disparaging their own Apostle Paul because he had not seen the Lord in the flesh.

I consider that I have done nothing less than the great apostles. He does not wish God’s grace to appear inferior in him, since he taught similarly and did the same things as the apostles who seemed more prominent because they had begun teaching earlier and had been with the Lord. Hence they were thought to possess greater authority, although this Apostle’s election was accompanied by testimony, he labored more than the others, saw the Lord while praying in the temple [Col. 0221B], and spoke with him. And if unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge. This does not apply to the apostles, since they were not eloquent—for example, they were unlettered—yet they were filled with the Holy Spirit. Rather, he touches upon those whom the Corinthians preferred because of their polished speech, although in religion the force of speech is necessary, not its pleasing sound.

How, nevertheless, does he humble himself by saying that he is unskilled in speech, and what of the statement Festus makes: “Paul, Paul, your many letters are driving you out of your mind”? (Acts XXVI). By saying this, then, he did not wish it to be understood that he did not know how to speak; rather, because of those who wished to be commended not by faith but by eloquence, he said that in this respect he was unskilled—though this involved no fault. In what does involve fault and brings salvation, however, he did not declare himself unskilled [Col. 0221C]. For one who is unskilled in speech is not guilty before God, whereas one who does not possess knowledge of God is guilty of ignorance, since it is not permissible to be ignorant, especially of what pertains to salvation. Therefore the Apostle, having rejected eloquence, acted so that faith might be acceptable through the testimony of virtue: not that eloquence should commend faith, but virtue, to which eloquence yields.

But in every respect I have been made manifest to you. He says that he was manifest to the Corinthians in every respect, because they were not unaware that he also possessed that skill in speaking. Some favored him for this reason, while others, who did not know that he was inferior in anything, favored the others. Therefore he speaks with agitation, because it was worse that, although they knew he lacked nothing, they humbled him before the others, even though they had seen that through him not only preaching was fulfilled [Col. 0221D], but also apostolic signs and wonders were performed.

Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself so that you might be exalted? Because I preached the Gospel of God to you free of charge? Since they were puffed up because he had refused to accept support from them, and for this reason preferred others to him, he says: “Did I sin because I humbled myself, judging myself unworthy to receive it?” Is this why you are angry with me, although it was not a sin but a glory?

Thus he humbled himself when he did not demand what was owed him. It was indeed owed him that he should receive support from those to whom he preached the Gospel of God, as the Lord established when he said: “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke X). But for their benefit he refused it. He refused the support offered for two reasons: first, so that he would not be found like the false apostles, who preached not for the glory of God but for their own advantage, and so that they would not receive an opportunity to plunder them—for when one person does not accept, another cannot demand much; and second, so that the vigor of evangelical authority would not grow slack. For one who accepts from sinners loses the authority to rebuke them.

Thus they are exalted when he does not accept from them for the purpose of correcting them, so that they may be improved and raised from death to life.

I robbed other churches, receiving support for your service, and when I was with you and was in need, I was no burden to anyone. He shows that he not only did not wish to accept from them, but also accepted from others and ministered to them. To show how extensive this was, he says—not a little: “I robbed other churches for your service” [Col. 0222A]. He therefore indicates that he spent no small amount on them. When he says “I robbed,” he indicates that much was received and given, not extorted. Hence he adds, “receiving support.” Support is what a soldier receives for his expenses in place of pay.

Thus he brought shame upon them, since he certainly did not refuse through deceit, when he himself ministered to them; and by this ministry, which they had promised, he wanted them more easily to fulfill their obligation, knowing themselves to be debtors, so that their service would no longer be a matter of great glory but of duty, lest they should boast even of this.

And when I was present, he says, with you, and when I was in need, I was a burden to no one. He wanted to benefit them so greatly that he consoled his own poverty for the sake of their salvation. For he endured poverty contentedly, lest they should suffer any scandal. Whoever gives thinks that he is exalted and no longer allows himself to be rebuked.

For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I lacked. He always received from the Macedonians because they had first corrected their faults. Just as he ought not to accept from the Corinthians, lest it result in scandal for them, so he ought again to accept from the Macedonians, lest those who sowed well lose their fruit.

And in every respect I kept myself, and will keep myself, from being a burden to you. He says that he will remain committed to this even if they correct themselves, because of the false apostles who were seeking an opportunity to plunder them.

(Gregory.) Let us consider, if we can, the Apostle Paul, who was as patient among persecutors as he was gentle among disciples. Certainly, when he came to Corinth, he drew the Corinthians away from the service of idols and made known to them who the true God was. He preached to them the joys of eternal life [Col. 0222D]. After he had gathered a great multitude of people into the faith, he endured such poverty there that he suffered severe need for food. He did not receive earthly bread from the disciples to whom he preached heavenly bread. He persisted in preaching for the life of his hearers; he persisted in the labor of his hands for the life of his body. Support from other lands was also sent to him by disciples, so that he might be able to preach to the Corinthians.

Indeed, he later speaks to those same Corinthians in a Letter, saying: “When I was with you and was in need, I was a burden to no one; for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I lacked.” He prefaced this with a great reproach, saying: “I robbed other churches, receiving support for your service” [Col. 0223A].

Let us therefore consider, if we can, how great was the gentleness of this man: to preach the bread of the spirit and not receive the bread of the flesh; to instruct the hearts of his hearers concerning eternal riches and yet suffer hunger among those same faithful and prosperous disciples; to endure want among the well-fed and nevertheless not speak of what he endured; not to speak of what he suffered and yet not grieve; to see the hard hearts of miserly hearers toward him and not cease preaching.

For, as the Acts of the Apostles testify, he preached continuously in the same city for a year and six months (Acts XVIII). After he had departed from those same Corinthians, he later wrote to them about what he had endured while he was among them. Why did he never tell them this while he was living among them? So that what had not been done toward him from good will might not be done from command, and so that, when their mercy became known, their willingness might not remain unknown.

Why, then, did he write this later, when he was far away? So that the disciples would not remain altogether uncorrected, and so that, whatever they had been toward their teacher in their stinginess, they might not be the same toward other brothers.

Truly, in this also Paul, truly the teacher of the Gentiles, neglecting what was his own and caring for what belonged to others, fulfilled what he had preached: “Let no one seek his own, but what belongs to another,” and, “Let each of you consider not his own interests, but those of others.”

How great, then, is this virtue of gentleness; how great the tranquility of spirit! Which one of us, if he had converted one person from this world’s life to the service of almighty God, and saw himself in need while that person did not provide him with the means of life, would not immediately have despaired of that person’s life? Who would not say that he had labored in vain? Who would not fall silent in exhorting someone whom he did not see bearing the fruit of good works first in himself?

But Paul, made firm at the summit of virtue through gentleness, persisted, preached, loved, and completed the good work he had begun. By bearing with them and persevering, he led the hearts of the disciples to mercy.

Indicating later that he knew of their progress, he writes in the same Letter (above, chapter IX): “Regarding the ministry that is carried out for the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you. For I know your readiness, about which I boast of you among the Macedonians: that Achaia has been prepared since the previous year, and your zeal has stirred up very many.”

The truth of Christ is in me: this glory of mine will not be taken away in the regions of Achaia [Col. 0223D].

(Ambr.) He urges all Achaia to minister to the saints, but does not permit himself to do so, lest he fail to complete the glory he had begun. For it is a glory to abstain from what is permitted, especially for the salvation of others. In the regions of Achaia, therefore, he did not wish to make use of support; elsewhere he did use it. And he promises still more under the testimony of Christ, saying that he will remain committed to this, lest he ever receive anything from the regions of Achaia.

Why? Because I do not love you? God knows. Having given the reason, he also calls God as witness to the love he had for them: he did not refuse to accept because he did not love them, but rather because he loved them, so that this very act might benefit them, as I have said.

And what I do, I will continue to do, so that I may cut off the opportunity of those who seek an opportunity, so that in what they boast they may be found to be like us [Col. 0224A]. The glory of the false apostles consisted in accepting money. Therefore the Apostle refused this, lest he appear like them. For unless this had been avoided by the Apostle, a greater opportunity would have been given them to accept—or rather, to extort—money, when they could point to the example provided by the Apostle in this matter.

For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. They are deceitful because they preach Christ out of greed, not with a religious mind, and without being sent, usurping for themselves the name of apostle.

And no wonder; for Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light. It is evident that Satan often deceives many, appearing to them as though he were an angel of God in order to mislead them. Hence Jesus son of Nave, being cautious, asked who the one was who had appeared to him (Joshua V). And the apostles, terrified in the boat, thought that he was a phantom. Therefore, when the Lord said, “Do not be afraid; it is I,” and Peter readily believed him, he said: “If it is you, command me to come to you upon the water” (Matthew XIV), so that, if he firmly set his foot upon the water, he would know that the one who appeared was real, since it was not a phantom.

It is therefore no great thing if his ministers disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness. The ministers of righteousness are the apostles, and these men falsely claimed to be their associates in order to deceive their hearers.

Their end will be according to their works. Without doubt, such men will be judged according to the wickedness of their minds, since they pretend to be ministers of God not for God’s sake but for the sake of their own belly. Yet he said that their end would be according to their works, so that they might be understood to perish just as their works and care for the belly perish.

(Gregory.) The ancient enemy tests the religious minds of human beings in different ways: to the wicked he openly presents the evils they desire, but he secretly lies in wait for the good and deceives them under the appearance of holiness. To the wicked, as to his familiar associates, he presents himself openly as evil; but to the good, as though they were strangers to him, he conceals himself beneath the pretext of some kind of respectability, so that he may introduce evils which he cannot openly impose, hidden beneath the veil of good action.

Thus, when his members are unable to cause harm through open wickedness, they often assume the appearance of good action. They reveal themselves as corrupt in their deeds, but falsely claim holiness in their outward appearance. For if the wicked were openly evil, the good could not receive them at all. But they take something from the appearance of the good, so that while good people accept in them the appearance they love, they may also unknowingly receive the poison they avoid.

Therefore, observing certain people who served the interest of the belly under the guise of preaching, the Apostle Paul says: “For Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light” (II Corinthians XI). What wonder, then, if his ministers disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness?

Again I say, lest anyone think me foolish; otherwise, receive me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little.

(Ambr.) Above he had already said: “Would that you could bear with a little of my foolishness.” Here he repeats it, for he always sets forth beforehand what he will later develop after many intervening matters. What he set forth above he now begins to explain. Since he is about to say things that seem to belong to his praise, he calls himself foolish: “so that I too,” he says, “may boast a little.” He says “a little” because this is in the words, not in the meaning.

He is therefore not truly saying these things for his own glory, but wishes to show them that those whom they think glorious possess nothing more than he does. Thus, if they are thought glorious, “I too,” he says. He calls this foolishness because he is pursuing something in his own praise. Yet he shows that he has been compelled to speak in this way, for he grieves that they considered those men exalted while despising him, although they possessed nothing more than he did.

What I am saying, I am not saying according to God. He does not speak according to God because these things pertain to the swelling of the flesh, and glory does not arise from pride before God, since humility is glorious before God.

But as though in foolishness, in this matter of glory [Col. 0225B]. He did not say “complete foolishness,” but foolishness in part. What he says is true, but because arrogance is a vicious thing, even though what is said is true, it is nevertheless as though in foolishness for anyone to praise himself. Complete foolishness would be for someone to praise himself with falsehoods: one person is proud on account of the truth, the other is foolish on account of falsehood. Yet the substance of boasting in this matter is carnality, since this glory falls away like the flower of hay.

Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast. He says this because some of the Jews who were becoming believers were already presuming upon the fact that they were children of Abraham—that is, they were boasting according to the flesh and claiming the nobility of their flesh. They defended their privilege of descent because they were called children of the one who believed God, even though “the soul that sins, it shall die.”

“If this, then, is glory,” he says, “I too will boast, because I too am a son of Abraham.” But being a son of Abraham is of no benefit before God, because it is faith that saves, not descent from Abraham. Therefore this is the glory of the flesh—just as it would be called glory if someone were said to be the son of a nobleman.

For you gladly tolerate fools, since you yourselves are wise. He calls foolish those who boast of carnal circumcision. Because the Corinthians tolerated them so that they might appear glorious, the Apostle also wishes them to tolerate him, so that he might show himself to be what they were, while nevertheless not boasting of this aspect according to God.

Hence he calls this glory foolishness. He says that he boasts according to the flesh, but professes this to be foolish, both to empty this glory of its force and to show that he had been compelled to burst forth into praise of the flesh.

This is therefore irony. For how are they wise when they are often reproved? Is not the Apostle’s foolishness wiser than their wisdom? For he, being wise, tolerates the unwise; by his patience he bears with them so that they may make progress, lest by provoking or rejecting them he make them worse—or, if he cannot make progress in them, he preserves his own restraint. There is none of this among the Corinthians.

How, then, do they gladly tolerate the unwise, when they themselves are wise? Only because he does not wish this to be understood as the words sound. It lies in the meaning and in the manner of delivery: the same words do not always have the same meaning. He pronounces them one way but intends another; sometimes he confirms what he says, and sometimes he denies it.

For they, as unwise and foolish people, were tolerating false apostles.

For you tolerate it if someone brings you into slavery. This is true, because they were being brought into slavery—not through wisdom but through foolishness—so that they might serve the false apostles.

If someone devours you. Nor is this false, because they were content to have their possessions devoured by false teachers.

If someone takes from you. To “take” is to seize someone by deceit. Therefore he indicates that these people were being captured by deceitful teachers and were enduring what was not beneficial.

If someone is exalted. [The reading “extoditur” is evidently corrupt; the sense requires “extollitur,” “is exalted.”] Exaltation is pride. Thus he touches upon those who were proud, who wrongly censured the Apostle and did not displease these others.

If someone strikes you in the face. Someone is struck in the face when an insult is directed at his mouth. Here he refers to those who, because they belonged to Abraham’s race, reproached the others for being uncircumcised, putting themselves above them and humiliating them [Col. 0226B].

(Augustine.) The face is that by which each person is recognized. We read in the Apostle: “For you tolerate it if someone brings you into slavery, if someone devours you, if someone takes from you, if someone is exalted, if someone strikes you in the face.” Immediately afterward he added: “I speak according to dishonor,” to show what it means to be struck in the face: namely, to be scorned and despised. The Apostle does not say this so that they would not tolerate those men, but so that they might tolerate him all the more, since he loved them so much that he wished to spend himself for them.

I speak according to dishonor. He calls “dishonor” what he said above: “I too will boast according to the flesh.” He does not say that this pertains to praise, for he was not weak in the matter in which those whom he secretly touches boasted. Hence he added: “As though we had been weak in this respect” [Col. 0226C].

(Ambr.) It is evident that he was not weak in this glory in which the believing Jews, whom these Corinthians tolerated, put themselves first—as though the Apostle were unlike them in this respect. For he too was descended from Abraham, and therefore they were not weak in this glory of the flesh.

Those who had attached themselves to the race of Abraham were considered weak. For the others regarded themselves as strong in the very matter in which they put themselves first because they were Israelites; they wish themselves to be tolerated in order to show that in this glory of the flesh they are neither unlike nor weak.

When he speaks of his own case, he introduces the person of Barnabas, his companion. Hence in the First Letter he says (I Corinthians IX): “Or do only Barnabas and I not have the authority to do this?” They were therefore not inferior in this glory in which the Jews boasted, but they did not applaud themselves because of it.

Finally, he says: “In whatever anyone dares—in foolishness I speak—I also dare.” That is, he was not weak in the glory in which the Israelites boasted, nor indeed was he to be judged wise on that account, since he did not wish to place himself above the wise.

In foolishness, therefore, he says that he dares in what those dare who boast that they are children of Abraham, so as to empty their glory of its force. He declares himself unwise so that they would not appear wise.

They are Hebrews? So am I. They are Israelites? So am I. They are the seed of Abraham? So am I. In these matters he shows himself equal to those whom he mentioned above, so that he might demonstrate the falsity of the disparagement by which they judged him unworthy [Col. 0226D].

They are ministers of Christ?—I speak as one less wise—I am more. Speaking truly about himself, he declares himself foolish, so that it may be understood that he had been compelled to burst forth into his own praise. For one who voluntarily relates things that contribute to his praise does not call himself unwise.

He therefore shows what things make him more a minister of Christ than the other preachers. Having found an opportunity, he touches upon everyone, even the persons of the apostles, grieving that God’s grace was judged inferior in him, although he performed the same works as the other apostles and endured greater sufferings for the sake of the faith. Hence in another Letter he says (I Corinthians XV): “I labored more than all of them.”

(Gregory.) Hence it is that good preachers both flee honor because of pride and yet wish to be honored for the sake of imitation. Thus the Apostle Paul, speaking to his disciples, fled honor and nevertheless showed how much honor was due him.

When he said to the Thessalonians: “For we never came with words of flattery, as you know, nor with an occasion for greed—God is witness,” he immediately added: “Nor seeking glory from human beings, either from you or from others, although we could have been burdensome as apostles of Christ; instead, we became little ones in your midst” (I Thessalonians II).

Again, fleeing honor, he says to the Corinthians: “For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord, and ourselves as your servants through Jesus Christ” (II Corinthians IV).

Yet when he saw them turning away from the path of true faith through the persuasion of false apostles, he showed them most fully how much honor was due him, saying: “In whatever anyone dares—in foolishness I speak—I also dare. They are Hebrews? So am I. They are Israelites? So am I. They are ministers of Christ?—I speak as one less wise—I am more.” He also adds that the secrets of the third heaven had been revealed to him, and that, having been caught up, he had penetrated the mysteries of paradise.

Behold, while fleeing honor, he proclaims himself the servant of the disciples; behold, while seeking honor for the benefit of his hearers, he places the merits of his life above those of the false apostles. The excellent teacher acted so that, when his character became known, the life and speech of the wicked preachers might be made worthless by comparison with him.

He would have commended them if he had hidden himself; by not displaying himself, he would have given error an opportunity. In a wonderful way, therefore, he both displays the grace of humility and seeks an increase of usefulness: he proclaims himself the disciples’ servant and shows himself superior to his adversaries. He shows the disciples what humility he has received; he shows his adversaries what exaltation he possesses.

It becomes known to his adversaries what he has received as a gift; it becomes known to the disciples what his inward thought remains. It becomes known to his adversaries what he appears outwardly in his actions. For holy men, when compelled to recount the good things they do, do not serve pride but usefulness.

In many labors. (Ambrose.) He says “in many labors” because the others also labored, but not as much. For this man sought food by the labor of his hands from morning until the fifth hour, and from then until the tenth hour he debated publicly with such exertion that he persuaded those who contradicted him.

In prisons more abundantly. It is clear that he was sent to prison more frequently than they were.

In beatings beyond measure. He says “beyond measure” because they exceeded what was appropriate. They too were beaten, but not as much.

In deaths frequently. This is true, because he endured dangers more frequently than the others.

Five times I received from the Jews forty lashes less one. He says this because he was scourged by the Jews five times, receiving thirty-nine blows according to the law of Moses, as it is written in Deuteronomy XXV. Thus he briefly recounts what happened on five occasions.

Three times I was beaten with rods. He suffered this at the hands of the Gentiles.

Once I was stoned. He was stoned by the Jews in a city of Lycaonia (Acts XIV).

Three times I suffered shipwreck. Since he is everywhere said to have sailed amid adverse storms, it was easy for him to suffer shipwreck three times.

A night and a day I was in the depths of the sea. This happened when he was sent to Rome after appealing to Caesar. Then, in the open sea—that is, in the depths of the sea—he was in danger of death, with death before his eyes. For it is written in that very passage: “So that we despaired even of living” (II Corinthians I).

Often in journeys. He now recounts other dangers, showing that he was harassed for Christ according to the flesh both on land and at sea.

In dangers from rivers. If he is recounting the dangers of journeys, why does he say “dangers from rivers”? While traveling in winter, when the rains are constant, he encountered danger from rivers overflowing their banks.

In dangers from robbers. When the devil could have killed him in the city, he stirred up robbers against him on the road, although he carried nothing that the robbers desired.

In dangers from my own people. He means the persecutions of the Jews, who were his brothers according to the flesh. They grieved because, having abandoned the Law, he had converted to the Gospel of Christ.

In dangers from the Gentiles. He suffered persecution from those who acted against him because of the mystery of the incarnation of the Lord Jesus Christ and the preaching of the one God.

In dangers in the city. He was in such danger in the city that he escaped through a window from the hands of those lying in wait for him.

In dangers in the wilderness. This danger had been arranged by the Jews when, having prepared an ambush, they wanted to kill him on the road.

In dangers at sea. Above he had already said: “Three times I suffered shipwreck; a night and a day I was in the depths of the sea.” What other danger was there at sea? This refers to the danger that occurred at sea, that is, in the ship, when the soldiers had planned to kill all the prisoners, lest anyone swim away and escape [Col. 0228D]. The centurion prevented this danger from being carried out, so that Paul would not be killed and might be brought alive to Rome (Acts XXVII).

In dangers from false brothers.

(Augustine.) These false brothers are those of whom he says to the Galatians: “But because of the false brothers secretly brought in, who slipped in to spy on our freedom which we have in Christ Jesus” (Galatians II). They were partly Christians and partly Jews, perfect in neither identity. Out of zeal for the Law they stirred up hostility against the Apostle, because he said that, once Christ had been preached, the Law had ceased.

Finally, when they pressed him, he was compelled to circumcise Timothy. A Christian who persecutes a Christian out of zeal for the Law is therefore a fictitious Christian; this is a false brother.

For if these men were merely Jews, and he called them false brothers because of Judaism, what need would there be to repeat the point? He had already said it above. “Dangers from my own people,” however, does not refer to false brothers according to the flesh; in Christ they are false, because they are not Christians with their whole mind. There were also other false brothers, such as Demas and Hermogenes.

(Gregory.) The holy man was surrounded on every side by persecutions and scourges, as it is said through blessed Job: “At least now understand that God has not afflicted me with a just judgment and has surrounded me with his scourges” (Job XIX).

To be struck with scourges is one thing; to be surrounded by them is another. We are struck with scourges when, even in our pains, we possess consolation from other things. But when such affliction weighs us down that our spirit can find no relief from the consolation of anything, then we are not merely struck with scourges but surrounded by them, because we are encircled on every side by the blows of tribulations.

Paul had been surrounded by scourges when he said: “Outside, fights; inside, fears” (II Corinthians VII). He had been surrounded by scourges when he said: “In dangers from my own people, in dangers from the Gentiles, in dangers in the city, in dangers in the wilderness,” and so forth. He enumerates them in such a way as to show that he never had rest.

When holy Church is surrounded by the scourges of her tribulations, all the weak among her are brought into a state of faintheartedness, so that they consider themselves all the more hopeless the longer they see themselves delayed in being heard.

In labor and distress. (Ambrose.) This is true, because there can be labor without distress. But here he adds “and in distress” to show that the labor itself was destructive.

In many sleepless nights. His vigils were many, but some were voluntary and others necessary. Placed under pressure, he had to remain awake, seeking God’s help. He taught not only by day but also by night, as he says in the Acts of the Apostles.

In hunger and thirst. Frequently driven into flight while the Jews persecuted him, he necessarily suffered hunger and thirst through want.

In many fastings. He fasted often so that he might deserve to be protected by God’s aid. One fasts when one has nothing to eat and abstains.

In cold and nakedness. He experienced cold and nakedness when he suffered shipwreck. Finally, he says: “The barbarians kindled a fire and restored us because of the rain that was coming down and the cold” on the island of Malta (Acts XXVIII).

Besides those external hardships, there is my daily preoccupation: concern for all the churches. This concern, which he calls daily, arises from the practice of tradition, so that he might instruct the people entrusted to him every day. The hardships mentioned above, however, were imposed by necessity. The day was given for work, and the night for rest. But because necessity pressed him to attend to everyone, he also taught at night. He did not hesitate to afflict himself, lest God’s grace be idle.

Who is weak, and I am not weak? He says that he sympathizes with everyone and grieves with them, with the affection by which he provides medicine for their wound. He pursues this point so that he may show with what care he protects and governs the Church entrusted to him, and therefore that he should be judged inferior to none of the other apostles—especially since, as was evident, he labored more than all of them [Col. 0230A].

For he was subject to greater hostility among the Jews than the other apostles. When he was persecuting the Church, he was suddenly changed and became its defender, testifying and affirming that he had heard Christ, whom he had previously regarded as a dead man, speaking with him from heaven. Many would necessarily follow this testimony, knowing that he had become a defender from being a persecutor, not without reason. For this reason the Jews were tormented and always sought to kill him.

Who is scandalized, and I am not burning? To be scandalized, in this passage, is to suffer the desire of the flesh. Since people are often scandalized unwillingly, enticed by the form or beauty of the body or by the heat of their own flesh, the Apostle, considering the necessity of human nature, says that he burns, so that, sympathizing with their weakness, he may care for such people [Col. 0230B].

He does not condemn them, but admonishes them in humble language, so that in hope of the promised reward they may resist the impulses of the flesh. Otherwise some of those who hear him, overcome by fleshly desires and despairing of themselves, might think that God would no longer accept them if they corrected themselves, and might perish by remaining in the same state.

(Gregory.) Through the inward organs of charity, whatever the minds of the perfect endure in the injury of the little ones causes them grief. The harms suffered by the weak pass into the hearts of the strong through compassion. Hence Paul says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?” The more perfect someone is, the more perfectly he feels the pains of others.

Therefore holy Church, distressed when the weak fall under the scourges of tribulation, will rightly say, when she recalls these times:

If it is necessary to boast, I will boast of the things that belong to my weakness. He says this because, if a Christian is to boast, he must boast in humility, through which one grows before God. Hence elsewhere he says (II Corinthians XII): “When I am weak, then I am strong”—that is, when I humble myself for the salvation of my brother, then I am exalted.

This is where one must boast, not in descent from the flesh, because someone is from the seed of Abraham.

(Ambr.) The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying. He calls God as witness so that what he says may readily be believed, especially because these people did not honor him as a true apostle.

The governor of the people of King Aretas was guarding the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me. And I was let down through a window in a basket along the wall, and so I escaped his hands.

[Col. 0230D] “If it is necessary to boast” (though indeed it is not expedient). The governor of Damascus, seeing the Jews laying an ambush for the Apostle, wished by evil power to carry out their wicked design, so that he himself might capture him if he could, both to please the Jews and to appear diligent in the duty entrusted to him, if, for the sake of public order, he killed one whom he heard publicly disturbing it. This happened at the very beginning, when the Lord appeared to him on the road as he was going to Damascus. The Jews were incensed when they saw the man who had come to bring believers in Christ bound to Jerusalem now preaching the sect that he had come to condemn. Thus it happened that he was lowered by the disciples through a window, over the wall, in a basket, and escaped.

Some consider this an improper thing, because he was not freed by God’s help. Since he was liberated by what human beings could accomplish, they ask what need there was for him to be delivered by divine assistance, when God’s assistance is necessary only if human help fails. In what sense, then, does he not say that it is expedient for him to boast? The joy of the present life is fragile: if he had not escaped, he would have suffered martyrdom. But because flight in persecution was commanded, he deliberately escaped; for no one ought to wait until he is sinned against in his own person. Therefore he says that one may boast because he escaped, but he adds, “it is not expedient,” because of pride: one grows through humility, and God’s help benefits the gentle, not the arrogant. Moreover, since the one who boasted of having escaped the death inflicted for the sake of faith seems to regard suffering for Christ as something empty, it is for this reason also not expedient to boast.

(Aug.) We recall the words of the Lord: “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matt. XX). Who, then, would believe that God wished this to happen in such a way that the flocks whom he purchased with his own blood would be abandoned to the necessary ministry without which they cannot live? Did he himself do this when, carried by his parents into Egypt, he fled as a little child—he who had not yet gathered the churches that we could say had been abandoned by him? Or when the Apostle Paul, so that the enemy might not seize him, was lowered through a window in a basket and escaped his hands, was the church that was there abandoned to the necessary ministry? Was what had to be accomplished not completed by the other brethren established there?

The Apostle did this with their consent, so that he might preserve himself for the Church, since that persecutor was seeking him personally. Let Christ’s servants, therefore, the ministers of his word and sacrament, do what he commanded or permitted: let them flee entirely from one city to another whenever one of them is specifically sought by persecutors, so that the Church may not be abandoned by the others who are not being sought in this way, but that those others may supply food to their fellow servants, whom they know cannot otherwise live.

When, however, the danger is common to all—that is, to bishops, clergy, and laity—those who need the others should not be abandoned by those whom they need. Either all should withdraw to fortified places, or those who have the necessity of remaining should not be abandoned by those through whom the Church’s need among them must be supplied, so that they may either live together or suffer together whatever the Master of the household wishes them to endure.

## CHAPTER XII. The Apostle commends himself on the basis of visions and places there a remedy against the danger of pride, etc.

“But I shall come to visions and revelations of the Lord.” (Amb.) Now he will show to what height he was taken up, so that from this it may be understood how great and how extraordinary were the things shown and spoken to him, lest, as some seemed to think, he be regarded as inferior to the other apostles.

“I know,” he says, “a man in Christ fourteen years ago—whether in the body, I do not know; or outside the body, I do not know; God knows—caught up as far as the third heaven.” He affirmed both possibilities, because he did not deny that either could happen: that he might have been caught up without the body, or in the body. Perhaps some might think it insignificant if a man in Christ was caught up as far as the third heaven, since the moon is said to be in the third sphere. But that is not the meaning, because he is understood to have been caught up beyond all the stars of the world. It is therefore something magnificent and wondrous that he reports. He signifies that he himself was caught up above the firmament, to the third heaven, among the spiritual heavens.

“And I know such a man—whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows—because he was caught up into paradise and heard secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter. On behalf of such a man I shall boast.”

He says that he was caught up twice: first, from here as far as the third heaven, and then into the heavenly paradise, where the Lord told the thief that he would be with him. He says that this is the paradise of the Father, there where the city Jerusalem, our mother, is also said to be.
