What wonder is it, then, if after the resurrection the body, already purified and made refined, is believed to become immortal and to be in the heavens, when the Apostle does not doubt that a body still mortal could have been lifted to the heavens and taken up into the heavenly paradise of God the Father? On behalf of such a man—that is, one so worthy of God as to experience this—he says that he boasts, and he does not wish to say openly that he is speaking about himself, lest he seem to praise himself.

The Apostle John likewise, although it is known that he was speaking about himself, says: “This is the disciple whom Jesus loved, who also reclined at supper upon his breast” (John ult.), lest he appear to speak boastfully about himself.

(Greg.) Because at times we strive to advance in virtue and receive certain gifts, while, having been repulsed from others, we lie prostrate in the depths—for no one apprehends as much virtue as he desires—the almighty God, discerning the inner person, sets a measure even to spiritual progress. Thus, from the fact that a person attempts to apprehend something and cannot, he may not exalt himself in those things which he can attain.

Therefore that exceptional preacher, who had been caught up to the third heaven and had penetrated the secrets of paradise, did not wish to remain tranquil and untroubled after the revelation. But because the almighty God establishes limits for human beings that cannot be passed, he both raised this man to know sublime things and then brought him back to endure lowly things. Thus, as he observed the measure of his condition, while attempting to attain security and unable to do so, he was prevented from going outside himself through exaltation and was compelled by humility always to return within his proper bounds.

In this way a ruler is near to each person through compassion and elevated above all through contemplation: through the inward organs of pity he transfers the weakness of others into himself, while through the height of contemplation he transcends even himself by desiring invisible things. He must neither despise the weaknesses of his neighbors while seeking lofty things, nor, by accommodating himself to their weaknesses, abandon the desire for lofty things.

This is why Paul is led into paradise and searches out the secrets of the third heaven, yet recalls the mind, suspended in contemplation of invisible things, to the bedchamber of the flesh, and administers in his hidden teachings how people ought to conduct themselves, saying: “But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render the wife her due, and likewise the wife to her husband” (1 Cor. VII). A little later: “Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same” (1 Cor. VII).

Behold, he is already inserted into heavenly secrets, yet through the inward organs of condescension he examines the bedchamber of the flesh. The one whom, lifted up to invisible things, he raises to what is beyond sight, he mercifully turns the eye of his heart toward the hidden places of the weak. He transcends heaven in contemplation, yet does not abandon the bed of the flesh through concern for it, because, joined to the highest and the lowest by the bond of charity, he is powerfully caught up to lofty things in himself through the strength of the Spirit, and in others he is calmly made weak through compassion.

For this reason he says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burned?” (1 Cor. IX). Again he says: “To the Jews I became as a Jew” (ibid.), clearly not by abandoning faith but by showing compassion. By taking upon himself the role of unbelievers, he learned from his own experience how he ought to have mercy on others, so that he might give them what he would rightly have wished to be given to himself if he were in their condition.

Again he says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you” (2 Cor. V), because he knew both how to transcend himself through contemplation and how to adapt that same self to his hearers through condescension.

“But for myself I shall boast of nothing except my weaknesses.” Thus he does not boast about himself, since he does not openly declare that he is speaking about himself. “In my weaknesses,” he says, “I shall boast.” For to explain the pressures of sufferings and the weaknesses of distress does not seem glorious but rather tearful. For this reason he says that he boasts in them, knowing nevertheless that they lead to the reward of heavenly recompense.

What could be more glorious for a Christian in the future than to recount the punishments inflicted on him for Christ? “For if I should wish to boast, I shall not be foolish, for I shall speak the truth.” He says this because, if he were to proclaim the merit that he possesses before God, he would not be imprudent, since he would be speaking the truth. Therefore, if someone speaks of the merits shown to him, he is certainly not foolish; but if he remains silent, he is also prudent.

For what reason, then, does he now boast openly? He immediately adds: “But I refrain, lest anyone think of me beyond what he sees in me or hears from me.” Thus he shows why he does not boast openly: “lest anyone,” he says, “think me to be extending my boast beyond what the boundary of my merits permits.”

He refers to those whom he had as detractors on account of the law, as I mentioned above. For certainly it is good not to conceal the glory of one’s merits, so that believers may be encouraged.

(Greg.) He still had something to say about himself, which he refrains from saying. But the excellent teacher does both: by speaking of what he had done, he instructs his disciples; by keeping silent, he guards himself within the limits of humility. He would have been excessively ungrateful if he had been entirely silent about himself for the sake of the disciples, and perhaps excessively incautious if he had disclosed everything about himself to the disciples. But, wonderfully, as has been said, he did both: by speaking, he educated the life of his hearers; by remaining silent, he guarded his own.

It should be understood that holy men, whenever they make something about themselves known to those who come after them, imitate the custom of their Creator. For God, who forbids us to praise ourselves with our own mouth, speaks his own praises through sacred Scripture—not because he needs those praises, since he does not advance through praise, but because, while he tells us of his greatness, he lifts our ignorance toward him. By speaking of his goodness, he teaches us about the one whom no human being would know if he had wished to remain silent about himself.

For this reason he makes his praises known, so that, hearing him, we may be able to know him; knowing him, love him; loving him, follow him; following him, attain him; and, having attained him, enjoy his true vision. Hence the Psalmist says: “He declared the power of his works to his people, that he might give them the inheritance of the nations” (Ps. CX). It is as though he were saying openly: He makes known the works of his strength so that the one who hears him may become rich in gifts.

Therefore, imitating the custom of their Creator, holy men sometimes reveal certain things about themselves, so that their hearers may be instructed, not so that they themselves may advance. Yet in these matters they guard themselves with deep consideration, lest, while raising others from earthly preoccupation, they themselves be submerged in the desire for earthly praise.

Hypocrites often imitate their words, but they completely fail to understand the meaning of those words. What the righteous do for the benefit of their neighbor, they do for the extension of their own reputation.

The holy Job, looking upon hypocrites, says that they do not desire future glory but wish to possess the present: “For what is the hope of the hypocrite?” (Job XXVII). Since he loves present things, he has no hope for the future. For it is written: “What a person sees, why does he still hope for?” (Rom. VIII). Thus the hypocrite does not reach toward eternal rewards through hope, because he boasts that he possesses here what ought to have been sought elsewhere.

Since his fault has been stated, the punishment is also added, when it immediately follows: “May God not deliver his soul,” and the rest.

“And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me.”

(Amb.) He testifies that God provides for good merits when he permits the good to be brought low by temptations—not only so that they may not be deprived of the fruits of their labors, but also so that these may increase for them to the fullness of their eternal possession. This remedy, then, was given to the Apostle so that, pressed by insults, his mind might not be exalted because of the greatness of the revelations; for an idle heart necessarily had a tendency to become exalted over the things it had seen.

(Aug.) Here you recognize an Apostle possessing the greatness of revelations and fearing the precipice of exaltation. If you hold his honor in high regard, then listen to what the physician applied to his swelling, so that you may know that even the Apostle himself, who wished to save others, was still being treated: “Lest,” he says, “the greatness of the revelations should exalt me.”

Now I can say to the Apostle Paul: “Do not be exalted, holy Apostle!” Is it still necessary for you not to be exalted? Is it still necessary for you to fear exaltation? He says to me: “Why do you speak to me in this way? Listen to what I am, and do not think highly of yourself, but fear. Hear how the little lamb enters where the battle line is in such danger. ‘Lest the greatness of my revelations should exalt me,’ he says, ‘there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me.’”

What sort of swelling did he fear, who received such a most biting counter-irritant? Come now, then, and say that there was in this man as much righteousness as there is in the holy angels. Or does the holy angel in heaven also receive an angel of Satan as a thorn, so that he may be buffeted and not become exalted? Far be it from us to suspect this of the holy angels. We are human beings; let us acknowledge that the holy apostles were human beings—chosen vessels, but still fragile; still living as strangers in this flesh, not yet triumphing in the heavenly homeland.

(Greg.) One kind of striking is inflicted on a sinner so that he may be punished without reprieve. Another is inflicted so that he may be corrected. Another is inflicted sometimes not so that he may correct past sins, but so that he may not commit future ones. Another neither corrects past fault nor prevents future fault, but serves so that, when unexpected salvation follows the blow, the power of the one who saves may be known and loved more ardently; and when an innocent person is worn down by the scourge, the reward of patience may be greatly increased.

At times a sinner is struck so that he may be punished without reprieve, as is said to doomed Judea: “I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel chastisement” (Jer. XXX); and again: “Why do you cry out over your affliction? Your pain is incurable” (ibid.).

At times a sinner is struck so that he may be corrected, as the Gospel says: “Behold, you have been made well; now do not sin anymore” (John V). The words of the Savior show that the preceding sins had demanded the force of suffering as their penalty.

At times someone is struck not to cleanse a past fault but to prevent a future one. Paul plainly says this about himself: “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me.” He does not say “because it exalts me,” but “lest it should exalt me.” He aptly indicates that through that blow he is restrained from a fault that might occur, not cleansed from one that has occurred.

Sometimes, however, someone is struck neither because of past nor future iniquity, but so that the power of divine virtue alone may be displayed through the removal of the blow. Thus, when the disciples say to the Lord in the Gospel concerning the man born blind, “Did this man sin, or his parents, that he should be born blind?” the Lord answered: “Neither did this man sin nor his parents, but that the works of God might be revealed in him” (John IX).

What is accomplished by this revelation except that, through the scourge, the strength of his merits may be increased, and, when no past iniquity is being wiped away, great strength may be generated through patience?

“For this reason I besought the Lord three times that it might depart from me, and he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.’”

(Amb.) He testifies that the thorn of the devil—which he treacherously implants in human minds to harm the servants of God, inciting them to abandon God’s service—was something about which he had entreated the Lord three times, yet had not obtained its removal. He does not say that he was despised, but that, unknowingly, he was asking against himself, namely, that the temptations through which he was becoming more perfect should cease.

For this reason he says to the Romans: “We do not know how to pray as we ought” (Rom. VIII). He says that this was answered to him so that God’s grace might be sufficient for him, either by adding strength to endure or by shortening the time of distress. Thus his devotion, not being broken by the weakness of the affliction that had come upon him, might be shown to have been tested.

(Aug.) We find that the wicked have asked and received, while the good have asked and not received. What is worse than demons? Yet they asked for the swine and received them, and it is found that God did not fulfill the desire of the demons (Mark V).

What, then, shall we say, except that “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. II), and that he grants the request of those who ask? Yet a question about the Apostle still remains. Was he not himself among those who are his, he who said: “The Lord knows those who are his”? Therefore all who are his ask and receive.

But we ask what the things requested for this temporal life accomplish. Sometimes they benefit, sometimes they harm. When God knows that they will harm, he does not give them to his own who desire and request them—just as a physician does not give a sick person everything he asks for, and in love refuses what he would grant without love.

He hears all his own for eternal salvation, but he does not hear all of them according to temporal desire. For this reason he does not hear them in one matter, so that he may hear them in another.

Finally, consider the very words. When he did not receive what he had asked the Lord to remove, the Lord said to him: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.”

“What do you desire from me—that the thorn in your flesh should be taken away, the thorn you received so that you would not become exalted in your revelations? You ask this because you do not know that it benefits you. Trust the physician: what he has applied is painful but useful; it causes pain, but it brings forth health. ‘Power is perfected in weakness.’ Endure weakness if you desire health; endure weakness if you desire perfection, because power is perfected in weakness.”

(Greg.) Behold, when we are afflicted by some suffering or bodily trouble, we may wish to know its hidden causes, so that, through knowledge of the matter itself, we may find consolation in what we suffer. But because no individual answer is given to each of us individually concerning our particular temptations, we turn to sacred Scripture. There we find that Paul, tempted by bodily weakness, heard: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.”

This was said to him specifically in his weakness so that it would not have to be said separately to each of us. In sacred Scripture, therefore, we have heard the voice of God addressed to afflicted Paul, so that, when we are perhaps afflicted, we would not each seek to hear it through a private consolation.

The Lord did not answer all our questions with individual words, because he speaks once and does not repeat the same thing a second time. That is, through what he delivered in sacred Scripture to our fathers, he took care to instruct us.

“I shall therefore gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.”

(Amb.) It is clear that he teaches that one should boast when one is humbled by insults. Christ supplies the power to endure, so that insults, which previously seemed harsh and therefore intolerable, may afterward be willingly accepted and softened by Christ’s assistance.

Thus he says that he is glad to be struck, provided that Christ heals him, knowing that Christ’s medicine adds more to salvation than weakness takes away from health.

“For this reason I am pleased with myself in weaknesses, in insults, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses, for Christ. For when I am weak, then I am strong.”

It is true that the Christian conquers when he is thought to be losing, and that faithlessness loses when it rejoices that it has conquered. Therefore he applauds when he is insulted and rises when he is oppressed.

(Cass.) That poverty, persecutions, and insults—which in the judgment of the whole populace are considered evils—are useful and necessary is also clearly demonstrated by the fact that holy men not only never wished to avoid them, but, whether eagerly seeking them or enduring them courageously with the greatest strength, became friends of God and obtained the rewards of eternal life, as the blessed Apostle declares:

“For this reason I am pleased with myself in weaknesses, in insults, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses, for Christ. For when I am weak, then I am strong, because power is perfected in weakness.”

And for this reason those who are exalted by the great riches, honors, and powers of this world should not be thought to have obtained from these the principal good, which is defined as existing in virtues alone, but something intermediate. For just as these things are found to be useful and advantageous to the righteous who use them properly—they produce the opportunity for good works and for the fruit of eternal life—so to those who abuse their wealth wickedly they are useless and harmful, and they furnish an opportunity for sin and death.

What could be grievous, what could be hard, for one who has accepted Christ’s yoke with his whole mind? One grounded in true humility and always looking toward the Lord’s sufferings rejoices in every insult inflicted upon him, saying: “For this reason I am pleased with myself in weaknesses, in persecutions, in distresses, for Christ; for when I am weak, then I am strong.”

By what loss of a familiar possession, I ask, will one be tormented who is glorious in perfect nakedness, voluntarily offering himself for Christ, rejecting all the resources of this world, and generally reckoning all its desires as dung, “that he may gain Christ”?

Through continual meditation on that Gospel command, he despises and excludes the heat of every loss: “For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange will a person give for his soul?” (Matt. XVI).

Over the loss of what will the person grieve who knows that everything that can be taken away from others is not his, proclaiming with unconquered strength: “We brought nothing into this world, and there is no doubt that we can take nothing away” (1 Tim. VI)?

By what necessity of poverty will the strength of one be overcome who does not know how to have a purse for the road, money in his belt, or a garment unsuitable to the season, but boasts with the Apostle in many fasts, hunger, thirst, cold, and nakedness?

[Col. 0237D] “I have become foolish; you compelled me.” (Amb.) He says that he was compelled to show what he was. Certainly, one who has spoken the truth about himself is not foolish; but he lowers himself to show that he did not display his merits willingly.

“For I ought to have been commended by you.” It is clear that they ought to have borne witness on his behalf against his detractors, among whom he had established the Church and displayed the wonders of his apostleship, so that, while he remained silent, they might defend the one whom they had as their father in the Gospel of Christ.

“For I was in no way inferior to those who are very apostles.” “Very” here means “exceedingly,” as some think. For they were what the Apostle Paul also was. He says this because he is not inferior to the earlier apostles, either in preaching or in performing signs—not in dignity, but in time.

For if priority of time is thought to establish a claim, John began to preach before Christ, and it was not Christ who baptized John, but John who baptized Christ. Does God judge in this way? Indeed, Andrew followed the Savior before Peter, yet Andrew did not receive primacy; Peter did.

Why, then, did some not regard him as an apostle, when by God’s grace he could do the same things as the apostles? For this reason he grieves, and under compulsion he shows what he has deserved through the Lord’s favor. Thus he was compelled not only to declare that he was not inferior, but also that he had labored more than all the others.

They were displeased with him and did not consider him an apostle because, out of zeal for the ancestral law, they rejected his preaching, treating him as an enemy of Moses’ tradition because he said that the law had already ceased. They favored the other apostles more and humbled him in comparison with them, because those apostles did not assert anything against the law with such steadfastness.

“And if I am nothing, nevertheless the signs of an apostle were performed among you in all patience, in signs, wonders, and mighty works.” Thus he humbles himself in order to raise them up. Yet he mentions patience first, because for a long time he endured them like impatient sick people, so that, by applying the medicine of signs and mighty works, he might heal the wounds of their error.

“For what is there in which you were inferior to the other churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong.” He continues to commend himself through humility. He shows that they were not inferior to the other churches in anything, but rather had something more: he preached the Gospel of God to them without charge, something granted to no other churches, since the Lord says: “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke X).

“If, therefore,” he says, “I am worthy of an insult because of a good work, forgive me.” Every fool is an accuser of what is good. To show them to be ignorant, he asks forgiveness from them for an act for which he deserves praise.

“Behold, this is the third time I am ready to come to you, and I shall not burden you.” Lest they think that he had done this at the beginning merely to commend himself, but afterward wished to receive payment for his evangelical preaching, he shows that he remains in the same disposition, so that he would not appear later to be correcting his action and thus provide his detractors with something to criticize.

“For I do not seek what is yours, but you.” He shows that he does not wish to receive anything from them in order to win them for himself, so that, when they understood that he valued them above money, they might finally recognize his affection for them.

“For children ought not to lay up treasure for their parents, but parents for their children.” He presents himself as their spiritual father, as he says in the first Epistle: “Through the Gospel I begot you” (1 Cor. IV). Yet parents in the flesh are the ones who lay up treasure for their children; spiritual children, however, ought properly to provide their spiritual parents with the expenses necessary to sustain the present life. For it is not a great thing that those who impart spiritual things should receive bodily things.

Here he proves at such length that he does not wish to receive from them that he transfers the role of the bodily father to the spiritual father, so that he not only does not receive from them but, if possible, himself gives to them, just as he has already said above: “I robbed other churches, receiving support for your service.”

By saying this he touches them, so that they may understand how great he is, and what those deserve who have neglected the care of so great an apostle.

“But I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls.” Now he openly reveals the affection and charity that he had for them, when he says that he is prepared not only to spend what is his for them, and to spend it more generously, but also to die himself for the salvation of their souls, as the Apostle John likewise says: “Following the example of the Savior, we ought even to lay down our lives for the brethren.”

“Although loving you more, I am loved less.” He urges them to love, because they ought to love him more, especially since through him they had learned the way of salvation, through him had been acquired for God, and from unbelieving had become believing, from defiled had been purified.

“But let it be so: I did not burden you; yet, being crafty, I caught you by deceit.” He does not omit anything that could be proposed against him, so that he may clear himself in every respect. For he had done nothing by deception among them, but in simplicity had looked after himself once and them in two ways: he had provided for them before God, and here had not sought their wealth, while for himself he considered sufficient what had been promised by God for the future.

Perhaps they might suspect that he had refused what they offered because it was small, in order to obtain greater things; that, examining his own merits, he rejected not money itself but despised the amount as unworthy of him. They might suppose that, by looking around for something more suitable, he had acted through cunning, so that what he did would appear to have been done not from contempt but from greed.

“Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you?” This is what he means: those whom he sent did not tell them that, if they wished to keep the Apostle peaceful toward them, they should offer an amount worthy of his person; nor did they say that he had refused because what was offered was less than was appropriate. Such a story would have been devised by the Apostle’s cunning, so that what he did would appear to have been done not from contempt but from avarice.

“I appealed to Titus and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did we not follow the same footsteps?” It is clear that, since nothing of this kind was said or done by those whom he sent, their unanimous judgment is shown to be honorable, and every suspicion of avarice is excluded.

“Do you think once again that we are defending ourselves to you?” This is what he says: “For a long time you have doubted us, thinking that we were not dealing with you sincerely.” The false apostles had been stirring them up, asserting that the Apostle was acting in this way through evasion because they wished to plunder them.

“Before God, in Christ, we speak.” Everything, however, beloved, is for edification.

(Greg.) He speaks before God from God who both understands the word of preaching and what he receives, and seeks through it to please God, not human beings. Let them hear what is written: “Every arrogant person is an abomination to the Lord” (Prov. XVI). For when someone seeks his own glory in the word of God, he seizes the right of the giver and does not hesitate to place the one from whom he receives this very gift behind his own praise.

(Amb.) He wants them to think correctly and well of him, and therefore satisfies them both by reason and by testimony. He does not present himself in this way for his own benefit but to complete their edification, and so to stir their love toward him—both by not burdening their resources and by not weakening the authority of his power in reproving vices. For it certainly benefits the one who is reproved that he may be corrected if the superior refuses what is offered precisely so that he may reprove freely.

“For I fear that when I come, I may perhaps not find you as I wish, and that I may be found by you to be such as you do not wish.” Since not all those whom he rebuked in the first Epistle had yet corrected themselves in the vices for which they had been reproved, he wishes to appear to be going to them with authority, so that, frightened, they may reform and he may find them as he wishes.

He says this so that they may present themselves in such a way that they may be in harmony with the Apostle and rejoice together with him. For one person finds another as he does not wish when that other makes himself such as to be out of harmony with him.

“Lest there be among you quarrels, rivalries, animosities, dissensions, slanders, whisperings, swellings, and disturbances.” Now he recalls the errors that he censured in the earlier Epistle, when they showed partiality to persons, preferring one to another, and were divided among themselves.

“Lest, when I come again, God should humble me before you, and I should mourn over many of those who sinned before and did not repent of the impurity, fornication, and shamelessness that they committed.” He warns them so that he may not find them as he found them earlier, involved in various vices of impure actions—or rather of names, since every action is without blame, but the name of disorder makes it a crime. It is unlawful when it is done otherwise than was permitted.

He says that he is humbled by their sins because, like a loving father, he begins to mourn the sins of his children. For what father would not rejoice when his children act well? In the same way, he must necessarily mourn if they conduct themselves wickedly.

Therefore he admonishes them: if some who had committed earlier fornication, or some other impurity or shamelessness, had not repented—as he indicates that some had not—they should now repent, so that when he came he might be with them without sorrow.

When he says, “and I should mourn over many of those who sinned before and did not repent,” he proves that some of them had repented and some had not. This is contrary to Novatian, who says that fornicators cannot complete repentance and be received into communion. Here he proves that they did complete repentance and were therefore received into the peace of the Church.

He identifies three forms of sin when he names fornication, shamelessness, and impurity.

## CHAPTER XIII. The Apostle censures those who adhere to false prophets, commending those who persist in true doctrine; a greeting is placed at the end.

Behold, this is the third time I am coming to you. (Ambrose.) Earlier he said that he had prepared himself; now he says that he is already coming. “Every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” He said this according to the Law, so that someone might either be acquitted or condemned by two or three witnesses. Thus he warns them that, at the Apostle’s third coming, they should be found purified. “I have already said, and I say beforehand”—he indicates that he said this previously while present, so that they might correct themselves and not be reproved with shame; and now, while absent, he declares that he is saying the same thing again, so that, if they do not amend after the second reproof, they should not be spared. “Or do you seek a test of Christ speaking in me?” They seek proof of Christ speaking in the Apostle, since they do not obey his commands, wishing to test whether he dares to exercise punishment, so that they may understand that he possesses trustworthy authority and thereafter fear him. For whoever despises his teacher is seeking to be corrected.

(Cassian.) We ought to know above all that there are three sources of our thoughts: from God, from the devil, and from ourselves. Thoughts are from God when he deigns to visit us with the illumination of the Holy Spirit, raising us toward more exalted progress; when, by the most salutary compunction, he chastises us in those matters in which we have acquired too little or have been overcome through acting sluggishly; or when he discloses heavenly mysteries to us and turns our purpose toward better actions and our will toward them. Thus, when King Ahasuerus, chastised by the Lord, is prompted to search out the annual records [the wording is uncertain], he remembers the services of Mordecai (Esther 6), raises him to the highest rank of honor, and immediately revokes the most cruel decree against the Jewish people (Esther 6). Or it is when the Prophet says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Psalm 84). Elsewhere he says: “The angel who spoke within me” (John 14). Or it is when the Son of God promises that he will come together with the brother and make his dwelling with us. “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10). And the chosen vessel says: “Do you seek a test of Christ speaking in me?”

From the devil, however, a succession of thoughts arises when he attempts to overthrow us both by the pleasure of vices and by hidden snares, displaying evils fraudulently as though they were goods with the utmost subtlety, and transforming himself for us into an angel of light. Or it is when the Evangelist reports: “And when supper had taken place, the devil had already put it into the heart of Simon Judas Iscariot to betray the Lord”; and again: “After the morsel,” he says, “Satan entered into him” (John 13). Peter also said to Ananias: “Why has Satan tempted your heart, that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?” (Acts 5). We also read that saying, foretold long before in the Gospel through Ecclesiastes: “If the spirit of one who has power rises up against you, do not leave your place” (Ecclesiastes 10). And there is that which is spoken to God against Ahab in the Third Book of Kings, in the person of an unclean spirit: “I will go out, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets” (1 Kings 22).

Thoughts arise from ourselves when we naturally remember things that we are doing, have done, or have heard. Concerning these blessed David says: “I have considered the days of old, and I have held the eternal years in mind; and I meditated by night with my heart, I was exercised and I swept my spirit” (Psalm 76). And again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain” (Psalm 93). In the Gospel also the Lord says to the Pharisees: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matthew 9).

We must therefore continually observe this threefold distinction and examine with vigilant discernment all the thoughts that arise in our flesh, first investigating their origins, causes, and authors, so that we may consider, according to the merit of those who suggest them, how we ought to present ourselves toward them.

He who is not weak in you, but is powerful in you. (Ambrose.) Christ is powerful in them, because they saw the dead raised in his name, demons driven out, paralytics restored, the deaf hearing, speech returned to the mute, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. All these things belong to power, not weakness; indeed, for this reason they were drawn to the faith. For although he was crucified in weakness, he lives by the power of God. It is true that Christ was crucified because of our sins, so that, by destroying death, he might free those who believe in him from it. He therefore consented to become weak for our sake, so that he might conquer death for us. Descending into the underworld, although he knew no sin at all, he was killed as though he were a sinner and erased Adam’s bond, so that thereafter the dead, under his name, would not be held by death but would have confidence to go to heaven. Thus, killed because of our weakness, he rose again by the power of the Father, proving to the disciples by an example enacted in himself that what he had taught was true.

(Gregory.) For this reason it is said through blessed Job: “For I know that my Redeemer lives” (Job 19). It is as though he were saying plainly: Let every unbeliever know that the one who was scourged, mocked, struck with blows, crowned with a crown of thorns, smeared with spittle, crucified, and killed lives after death. With firm faith I believe and with free voice I confess that my Redeemer lives—the one who fell among the hands of the ungodly.

For we too are weak in him. (Ambrose.) This refers to the person of the apostles, who became weak while preaching him, that is, Christ, when they were subjected to insults, imprisoned, and beaten. But we live with him through the power of God in us. It is clear that if they were weakened by unbelievers among believers, this was not weakness but advancement, because the faithful become stronger through their weakness. The death inflicted by unbelievers is therefore life with respect to believers; for through the power of God they will rise again, so that they may live with Christ.

Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith; examine yourselves. He commands the brothers to examine one another, for they become more attentive if they confer with one another. He therefore wished this “testing” to be understood as examination, because every examination is a testing, although not every testing is an examination. If God is said to test, it is an examination; but if the devil is said to test, it is a temptation, because he attempts to overthrow. A human being, too, sometimes tests in order to examine and sometimes in order to ensnare.

(Gregory.) For an evil anticipated by deliberation is brought under the control of the mind struggling against it by reason; everyone is overcome by adversity to a lesser degree when he is found all the more prepared for it through foreknowledge. Often the heavy burden of fear is lightened by experience; often death itself, just as it disturbs when unexpected, so delights when anticipated by deliberation. Thus it is rightly said of this horse in Job: “He boils and roars; he swallows the earth, and does not reckon the sound of the trumpet’s blast. When he hears the trumpet, he says, ‘Ha!’” Then it follows: “He smells the battle from afar”; as though it were said more plainly: He overcomes every contest for this reason, because he prepares his mind for battle before the battle.

To smell the battle from afar is to foresee by thought every adversity while it is still far off, lest unforeseen events should perhaps overcome him. Paul was urging the disciples to smell this battle from afar when he said: “Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith; examine yourselves.” It is as though he were openly commanding them: Bring the struggles of persecutions back to mind, and, weighing the innermost and hidden places of your hearts, discover what sort of people you will be able to prove yourselves amid punishments.

Holy men smell this battle from afar when, even while established in the peace of the universal Church, they perceive either the battles of heretics or the impending torments of persecutions from unbelievers. While living rightly, they often receive evil for good and endure the insults of slander with equanimity, so that, if an occasion for persecution should arise, open enemies may find them all the stronger, inasmuch as the darts of false brothers within the Church have not overcome them. For the one who collapses from the state of patience before the wounds inflicted by tongues is himself a witness that he will not withstand the sword of open persecution.

Do you not know yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you—unless, perhaps, you are reprobate? (Ambrose.) He says this because, if you do not know how to examine one another, you do not recognize that Jesus Christ is in you; and this is what it means to be reprobate: not to know the faith of one’s religion and profession. For whoever possesses the understanding of his faith in his heart knows that Jesus Christ is in him.

But I hope that you will recognize that we are not reprobate. He provokes them to knowledge of the faith and of upright living. For when they begin to recognize the sure authority and merit of their apostle before God, they will also be able to be attentive to themselves.

Now we pray to God that you do no evil—not so that we may appear approved, but so that you may do what is good, while we may seem to be reprobate. He prays for them with that affection with which he always prays that they abstain from evil. “Not,” he says, “so that we may appear approved,” that is, not so that we may seem authoritative while you are sinning, “but so that you may do what is good, while we may seem to be reprobate.” What does this mean? Is the Apostle praying that he might be reprobate? Certainly not; rather, he prays that, when they are acting well, they may be humbled, as it were, since they would not dare to reprove them, and that, once humbled, they might appear reprobate.

Those who are approved by God appear so when they judge sinners, by the authority granted to them. Therefore, if there are no people whom they must judge, their authority ceases, and they appear, as it were, reprobate. For we can do nothing against the truth, but only for the truth. He says this because power is not given against the truth, so that they may accuse one who lives well, but for the truth, so that they may punish one who is an enemy of the Law. Thus power will cease if they do what is good. Hence he says to the Romans: “Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it” (Romans 13). Therefore, when someone does good and does not fear, authority has been made void in relation to him. This is what it means to appear reprobate: that the authority by which he is shown to be approved ceases in him.

We rejoice when we are weak, but you are powerful. To be weak means not to exercise authority. He wishes them to be strong, so that, by acting well, they may conquer their vices and prevent punishment or correction from being directed against them.

And what wonder is it if the chosen vessel, for the glory of Christ, the conversion of his brothers, and the privilege of his people, should wish to become accursed from Christ, when the prophet Micah also wished to become a liar and to be alienated from the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, provided that the Jewish people might escape those blows and disasters of captivity that he had foretold by his prophecy? “Would that I were not a man possessing the Spirit,” he says, “and that I might rather speak a lie!” (3 Kings 22.)

This also we pray for: your perfection. He asks in prayer that they may be perfected in this, so that, perfected in the strength of a good life and an incorrupt faith, they may not sin. For this reason I write these things while absent, so that I may not act harshly while present. It is clear that he warns them while absent so that he may find them more corrected and not, while present there, rebuke them with shame, causing the one who sins in the assembly of the brothers to blush.

According to the authority that the Lord gave me for building up and not for destroying. This is the authority that earlier he wishes to remain idle if they act well. If they do not, he exercises it so that, when they are corrected, they may be built up and not killed. Those who are rebuked so that they may be corrected are not destroyed but built up for life.

For the rest, brothers, rejoice; be perfected; encourage one another; think the same thing; live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you. This joy will arise from their correction, and from it perfection will also be able to proceed. But first there will be consolation, so that, through hope of future things, they may abandon present pleasure. “Think the same thing,” he says, because of their former disagreement, so that they may now have one mind. Live in peace. When they are in agreement, they will have peace. “And the God of peace and love,” he says, “will be with you.”

Christ is the God of peace, who said: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14). He is also the God of love, who again says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another. And by this,” he says, “everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another, the love with which I have loved you.”

Yet the peace of God is one thing, and the peace of the world another, because the wicked and the impure also have peace, but to their condemnation. The peace of Christ, however, is free from sins: it flees faithlessness, rejects deceit, and resists evil deeds. This peace is pleasing to God and hostile to the devil; whoever possesses it will also possess love and God himself for their perpetual protection.

Greet one another with a holy kiss. This is an ecclesiastical greeting, because these kisses are not carnal but spiritual; through the embrace of bodies they join souls together, not through the desire of the flesh but of the spirit.

All the saints greet you. He urges them toward holiness, so that they too may dare to return the greeting of the saints; for this reason they are greeted by the saints, so that they may imitate them.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. Amen. Here there is a summation of the Trinity and a unity of power, which is the perfection of complete salvation. The love of God sent us Jesus the Savior, by whose grace we have been saved. The fellowship of the Holy Spirit enables us to possess this grace of salvation; for he protects those who are loved by God and saved by the grace of Christ, so that the perfection of the Three may be the consummation of the human being in salvation.

## BOOK FOURTEEN. EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS

[Col. 0245]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0245A]

(Ambrose.) Anyone who believes in Christ and observes the law of works understands Christ wrongly. So do the Symmachians, who derive their origin from the Pharisees and, while observing the whole Law, call themselves Christians, defining Christ, after the manner of Photinus, not as God and human being but as human being alone. For if they understood Christ to be God, they would expect nothing from the law of works—that is, from new moons, the Sabbath, circumcision, and distinctions among foods—because whoever worships God and the Lord of the Law is above the Law; nor can the Law judge one who agrees with the Lawgiver.

Indeed, the Law was not given for those who worshiped God, but for those who both believed and acted wickedly, to the contempt of the Creator. Hence he says to Timothy: “For the Law was not established for the righteous, but for the unrighteous and those who behave wickedly” (1 Timothy 1). And Moses says: “You shall make the children of Israel fear.”

Therefore the Galatians, or those who were subverting them, still having hearts covered by the mist of error, do not perceive the meaning of the prophet Isaiah, who among other things says: “For he will complete and abbreviate the word in equity, because the Lord will make an abbreviated word upon the earth” (Isaiah 10). If they understood these words, they would withdraw from the Law, knowing that from the preaching of John the Baptist the Law had already ceased, so that faith alone might suffice for salvation, abbreviated from the Law. For the Law contains teaching about God the Father, Christ his Son, and the Holy Spirit.

(Augustine.) The reason why the Apostle wrote to the Galatians is that they might understand that the grace of God accomplishes this: they are no longer under the Law. When the grace of the Gospel had been preached to them, certain people from the circumcision appeared. Although they bore the name of Christians, they had not yet grasped the benefit of grace itself and still wished to remain under the burdens of the Law that the Lord God had imposed on those serving not righteousness but sin—that is, by giving a just law to unjust people in order to demonstrate their sins, not to remove them.

For grace alone, the grace of faith that works through love, removes sins. Since the Galatians had already been established under this grace, those people wished to place them under the burdens of the Law, insisting that the Gospel would benefit them nothing unless they were circumcised and submitted to the other bodily observances of the Jewish rite. For this reason they began to regard the Apostle Paul, from whom the Gospel had been preached to them, with suspicion, as though he did not observe the discipline of the other apostles, who compelled the Gentiles to Judaize.

The Apostle Peter had yielded to the scandal caused by such people and had been led into dissimulation, as though he too held that the Gospel benefited the Gentiles nothing unless they fulfilled the burdens of the Law. The Apostle Paul recalls him from this dissimulation, as he teaches in this very Epistle.

A similar question is found in the Epistle to the Romans. Nevertheless, there appears to be this difference: there he resolves and settles the dispute that had arisen between those who had believed from the Jews and those who had believed from the Gentiles. The former thought that the reward of the Gospel had been rendered to them on account of the merits of the works of the Law, and they did not wish this reward to be given to the uncircumcised as though they were undeserving; the latter, by contrast, were eager to put themselves above the Jews, as though above the murderers of the Lord.

In this Epistle, however, he writes to people who had already been disturbed by the authority of those who were from the Jews and who were compelling them to observe the Law. For they had begun to believe those people, as though the Apostle Paul had not preached the truth because he had not wished them to be circumcised.

(Jerome.) This is distinctive of the Epistle to the Galatians: he does not write to those who, being from the Jews, had believed in Christ and thought that the ceremonies of their ancestors ought to be observed. Rather, he writes to those who, being from the Gentiles, had received the faith of the Gospel and, having afterward fallen back, had been deterred by the authority of certain people who asserted that Peter, James, and all the churches of Judea had mixed the Gospel of Christ with the Old Law; that Paul himself practiced one thing in Judea and preached another to the nations; and that it was useless for them to believe in the Crucified One if they thought that what the chief of the apostles observed could be neglected.

For this reason he proceeds so cautiously and keeps to a middle course between the two sides that he neither betrays the grace of the Gospel, pressed by the weight and authority of his elders, nor does injury to his predecessors while defending grace. Yet he proceeds indirectly and, as it were, secretly through winding passages, so that he may teach that Peter acted on behalf of the people of the circumcision entrusted to him, lest, suddenly abandoning their ancient way of life, those who had been scandalized by the cross should not believe; and, since the preaching to the Gentiles had been entrusted to Paul, that it was right for him to defend as truth what another was pretending for the sake of administrative accommodation.

Therefore he began in this way: “I am astonished that you are so quickly transferring yourselves from the one who called you into the glory of Christ to another gospel.”

(Augustine.) In this opening, therefore, he briefly indicated the question at issue, although he also showed it sufficiently in the greeting itself when he said that he was an apostle “not from human beings nor through a human being”—a statement that is found in no other Epistle. He thus showed that those who were persuading them of such things were not from God but from human beings, and that, insofar as the authority of the Gospel testimony is concerned, he ought not to be regarded as inferior to the other apostles, since he knew himself to be an apostle not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father.

Accordingly, beginning from the very vestibule of the Epistle, with the Lord permitting and assisting our efforts, we have undertaken to consider and explain each point in this manner.

## CHAPTER ONE

The Apostle rebukes the Galatians for their rapid transfer from the Gospel of Christ, which the Apostle received not from a human being but from Christ.

Paul, an apostle not from human beings, nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead.

(Ambr.) He testifies that he was not chosen by human beings and sent to preach, as were certain men who were chosen by the apostles and sent to strengthen the churches; nor like others who were sent by the Jews to disturb the churches—men whom he calls false apostles—but that he was sent by the Son of God. In this context he seems for that reason to deny that Christ is a human being: because Christ gave commandments as God, not as a human being, and chose him by divine judgment. By this he declares himself an authorized and reliable preacher, since the one whom God chooses is certainly much better than the one whom a human being chooses.

“Nor,” he says, “through a human being,” as they supposed concerning Christ, those who compelled these people to be circumcised, but “through Jesus Christ,” that is, through the one who is both God and human. He immediately makes this clear when he says, “and God the Father, who raised him from the dead.” By saying this he condemned two heresies, those of Mani and Photinus: Mani denies that Christ is human, though he does not deny that he was crucified; Photinus does not allow that Christ is God, yet he does not dare deny that Christ himself—that is, his body—raised himself from the dead. Thus, since Mani does not deny the crucifixion, he appears foolishly not to acknowledge Christ as human; while Photinus, in a kind of impiety, denies the God whom he confesses to have raised himself from the dead.

For he reads that the Lord said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”; “but he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2). Therefore, by saying that he himself raised himself from the dead, he indicates that he raised his own body from the dead; nevertheless, he is also said to have been raised by his Father, because all the Son’s power comes from the Father, so that the Son’s deeds are the Father’s deeds, from whom all things derive.

(Hier.) Nor should we pass over the fact that the Hebrews say that even among the prophets and holy men there are some who are both prophets and apostles, while others are prophets only. Thus they say that Moses, to whom it is said, “Behold, I shall send you to Pharaoh” (Exodus 3), and who replies, “Provide another whom you may send” (ibid.), and Isaiah, to whom God says, “Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?” (Isaiah 6), are both apostles and prophets.

From this we too may understand that John the Baptist should be called both a prophet and an apostle, since Scripture says: “There was a man sent from God, whose name was John” (John 1). For this reason, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, Paul customarily placed neither his name nor the title “apostle” at the beginning, because he was going to speak about Christ: “Therefore, having Jesus, the high priest and apostle of our confession” (Hebrews 3). It would not have been appropriate that, where Christ was to be called an apostle, Paul also should be named an apostle.

There are four kinds of apostles. The first is one who is neither from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father. The second is one who is indeed from God, but through a human being. The third is one who is from a human being and not from God. The fourth is one who is neither from God, nor through a human being, nor from a human being, but from himself.

Isaiah, the other prophets, and the apostle Paul himself may belong to the first kind: they were sent neither from human beings nor through a human being, but by God the Father and Christ. Joshua son of Nun belongs to the second kind: he was appointed an apostle by God, but through Moses. The third kind occurs when someone is appointed through human favor and ambition, as we now see many being placed in the priesthood not by God’s judgment but through the purchased favor of the crowd. The fourth kind belongs to false prophets and false apostles, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Such men are false apostles, workers of iniquity, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ,” who say, “Thus says the Lord,” although the Lord did not send them (2 Corinthians 11).

Paul the Apostle, however, is not such a one: he was sent neither from human beings nor through a human being, but by God the Father through Jesus Christ. From this it is also demonstrated that the heresy of Ebion and Photinus must be refuted here: our Lord Jesus Christ is God, since the Apostle, who was sent by Christ to preach the Gospel, denies that he was sent by a human being.

At this point other heresies also creep in—those that claim that Christ’s flesh was merely apparent and say that Christ is God, not human. There is also a new heresy that asserts that Christ’s dispensation was only partial. Thus the faith of the Church, standing amid the shipwrecks of so many false doctrines, is assailed from every side: if it confesses Christ to be human, Ebion and Photinus creep in; if it insists that he is God, Mani, Marcion, and the authors of the new doctrine boil up.

Let them therefore hear together that Christ is both God and human—not that there is one God and another human being, but that the one who was always God graciously became human for our salvation.

(Aug.) The one who is sent by human beings is a liar; the one who is sent through a human being may be truthful, since the truthful God can also send through a human being. Therefore, the one who is sent neither by human beings nor through a human being, but through God, is truthful because of the one who sends him; he also makes truthful those who are sent through a human being.

The earlier apostles, then, were truthful: they were sent not by human beings but by God through a human being, namely, through Jesus Christ while he was still mortal. The final apostle is also truthful: he was sent through Jesus Christ when, after his resurrection, he was wholly God. The other apostles came through Christ while he was still partly human, that is, mortal; Paul is the final apostle sent through Christ when he was already wholly God, that is, immortal in every respect.

Therefore, the authority of his testimony must be equal, since the Lord’s glorification completes whatever the order of time may seem to lack in his honor. For this reason, after saying “and God the Father,” he added, “who raised him from the dead,” so that he might briefly indicate that he had now been sent by the glorified one.

And all the brothers who are with me, to the churches of Galatia.

(Ambr.) After commending his authority, he still adds to the argument, so that he might show that all the others who were with him were likewise moved against them. Although his authority would have sufficed and could not have been refuted, nevertheless, in order to aggravate the seriousness of their deed—since they had abandoned their original faith—he indicates that many others were stirred up with him to condemn their error. For someone can easily understand that he is in error if he sees himself reproved by many.

(Hier.) In other Epistles, Sosthenes and Silvanus, and sometimes Timothy, are placed at the beginning. In this one alone, because the authority of many was necessary, the name of all the brothers is assumed. Perhaps they too were from the circumcision and were not held in contempt by the Galatians. Indeed, the judgment and agreement of many concerning one matter contributes greatly to correcting a people.

When he says “to the churches of Galatia,” this too should be noted: here alone he writes generally, not to the church of a single city but to the churches of the entire province, and he calls “churches” those which he later accuses of having been corrupted by error.

From this we should understand that “church” can be used in two ways: for the church that has neither stain nor wrinkle and is truly the body of Christ, and for the assembly that gathers in Christ’s name without possessing complete and perfect virtues. In the same way, “wise” is used in two senses: both for those who possess full and perfect virtue and for those who are beginning and are progressing.

Of the perfect it is said: “I will send wise men among you” (Matthew 23). Of the foolish it is said: “Reprove a wise man, and he will love you” (Proverbs 9). For the one who possesses full and perfected virtue has no need of correction. According to this meaning, we should understand the other virtues as well: “strong,” “prudent,” “pious,” “chaste,” “just,” and “temperate” are sometimes used properly and sometimes in an extended sense.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

(Aug.) The grace of God is that by which sins are given to us, so that our sins may be forgiven and we may be reconciled to God; peace is that by which we are reconciled to God.

(Ambr.) He shows that the human race has been lifted up through the benefit of both the Father and the Son. He does not signify that the Son is lesser when he calls him “our Lord,” nor that the Father is greater because he calls him “our God,” since the Father would not be truly God unless he were also Lord, nor the Son truly Lord unless he were also God.

If, then, the grace of the Father and the Son toward us is one, why is it, he asks, that those who think less of the Son equate him with the law, so that you serve partly Christ and partly the law, when you read the Lord saying: “For the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath” (Luke 6)? Through this they may see what insult they inflict upon the Lord when they compare the Lord with a servant.

He gave himself for our sins, to rescue us from the present evil age.

(Aug.) “The present evil age” should be understood as referring to the evil people who are in it, just as we speak of an evil house because of the evil inhabitants who live in it.

(Ambr.) He clearly shows that the law is of no benefit when he says that Christ offered himself to suffer for us, so that he might justify us, whom the law held guilty; thus, delivered from the law through faith in Christ, we would no longer be sinners but, justified by a second birth, would be called children of God.

Since the human race was held under the power of the devil, the Savior offered himself to the devil’s will, so that, mocking him by the power of his strength, when the devil accepted the one whom he could not hold, the Savior might take away from him those whom the devil held subject under an evil claim. Having thus stripped the lower world, he carried the trophy of souls to the Father, from whom all things come—something the law certainly could not do.

Although the law was given for our benefit, when we sinned it was turned against us and became an enemy; it began to kill rather than give life. Christ, however, by forgiving offenses, not only gave us life but also joined us to himself, so that we might be called children of God through faith.

What an enormous error it is, therefore, after grace to return under the law—that is, after receiving freedom, to wish to become slaves again—like a man rescued from the sword who, forgetful of the benefit, sells himself once more to the gladiatorial trainer (*lanista*). For the buyer’s accuser is the one who abandons him and returns again to his former master.

“To rescue us,” he says, “from the present evil age.” He says this because the Lord surrendered himself to death in order to free us from the error of the age: that is, so that, having become strangers to the understanding of this age—which, growing old through the course of its years, moves toward its end—we might share in the future age, which knows no decline, in the knowledge of the one God.

The evil of the present age consists in this: it does not render fitting reverence to God the Creator and to Christ the Restorer, while human error invents many gods for itself, or while believers fail to reserve for Christ the honor owed to him.

According to the will of God the Father, to whom be glory for ages of ages. Amen.

(Aug.) How much more, then, should human beings not arrogantly attribute to themselves whatever good they do, when even the Son of God himself said in the Gospel that he did not seek his own glory and had not come to do his own will, but the will of the one who sent him. The Apostle now recalls that will and glory of the Father, so that he too might signify, following the example of the Lord by whom he was sent, that he did not seek his own glory or do his own will in preaching the Gospel, just as he says shortly afterward: “If I were pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.”

(Ambr.) To make what he says firm and full of authority—that Christ freed us—he adds that Christ did this with the Father’s will.

(Hier.) Nor did the Son give himself for our sins without the Father’s will, nor did the Father hand over the Son without the Son’s will. But this is the Son’s will: to fulfill the Father’s will, as he says in the psalm: “To do your will, my God, I desired” (Psalm 39).

The Son gave himself so that he might overthrow by his own righteousness the injustice that was in us; Wisdom handed himself over so that he might conquer folly; holiness and strength offered themselves so that they might destroy filth and weakness.

Thus he freed us not only in the future age, according to the promised hopes that we believe, but also here from the present age: by dying with Christ, we are transformed into newness of understanding and are not of this world, by which we are rightly not loved.

The question arises how the present age came to be called evil. Heretics commonly seize upon this as an opportunity to assert that one creator belongs to the age of light and the future age, and another to the age of darkness and the present age.

We, however, say that it is not the age itself—the period that runs through day and night, years and months—that is called evil, but, by homonymy (ὁμωνύμως), the things that take place in the age. Thus it is said that “the day’s evil is sufficient for it.” Jacob’s days are also described as few and evil (Genesis 47), not because the span of time in which Jacob lived was evil, but because the things he endured exercised him through various trials.

Indeed, at the time when Jacob served for his wives (Genesis 29) and was afflicted by many hardships, Esau was at rest. Thus the same period of time was good for one person and evil for another. Nor would Ecclesiastes have said, “Do not say, ‘Why were former days better than these?’” (Ecclesiastes 7), unless this referred to the distinction between good and evil.

Hence John says: “The whole world is set in the evil one” (1 John 5), not because the world itself is evil, but because evil things are done in the world by human beings, who say, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isaiah 22). The Apostle himself says: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.”

Forests too are disgraced when they are full of robberies—not because the earth and woods sin, but because places also acquire the disgrace of murder. We detest the sword by which human blood was shed, and the cup in which poison was mixed—not because the sword or cup sinned, but because those who used them badly deserve hatred.

In the same way, the age, which is a span of time, is neither good nor evil in itself; it is called good or evil because of those who are in it.

Therefore the ravings and fables of Valentinus must be rejected. From the fact that Scripture speaks of “ages,” he fabricated his thirty αἰῶνες, claiming that they were living beings and that, through tetrads [or “quadrads”], ogdoads, decads, and duodecads, they produced as many numbers of ages as the sow of Aeneas produced piglets.

It must also be asked what distinction exists between “age,” “the age of the age,” and “ages of ages,” and where the term is used for a brief period of time and where for eternity. For in Hebrew, “age,” that is, *olam*, when it contains the letter *vav*, signifies eternity; when it is written without *vav*, it signifies the fiftieth year, which they call the jubilee.

For this reason, the Hebrew who, because of his love for his wife and children, has his ear pierced and submits himself to servitude under his master is commanded to serve “for the age,” that is, until the fiftieth year. The Moabites and Ammonites do not enter the assembly of the Lord until the fifteenth generation and “for the age,” because every harsh condition was released with the arrival of the jubilee.

Some say that “ages of ages” has the same meaning as “holy of holies,” “works of works,” and “Song of Songs.” Just as heaven differs from those things whose heavens they are, and the holy things that are holier by comparison with the holy, and works that are better by the superiority of works, and songs that surpass all songs, so too the ages are ages in comparison with the ages.

They explain the present age as beginning from the time when heaven and earth were created and continuing until the consummation of the world, when Christ will judge all things. They extend the term even farther back and advance it into earlier times, discussing whether past ages were good or evil and whether future ages will be good or evil. They fall into such profound questions that they have composed books and endless volumes on this subject.

As for the fact that Paul’s prologue concludes with “Amen,” a Hebrew expression: the Septuagint translated it as γένοιτο, that is, “let it be done”; Aquila as πεπιστωμένως, “truly” or “faithfully.” The Savior also constantly uses this expression in the Gospel, confirming his words with “Amen.”

I am astonished that you are so quickly transferring yourselves from the one who called you into the grace of Christ Jesus to another Gospel—which is not another.

(Aug.) If the Gospel is something other than what the Lord gave, either through himself or through someone else, it can no longer rightly be called the Gospel. He carefully said, “You are transferring yourselves from the one who called you into the glory of Christ,” which they wanted to nullify, as though Christ had come in vain if circumcision of the flesh and similar works of the law were so effective that human beings could be saved through them.

Except that there are some who disturb you and want to change the Gospel of Christ.

They do not change the Gospel of Christ in the way they disturb you, because it remains absolutely firm. Nevertheless, they want to change it: they call back the attention of believers from spiritual things to carnal things. When their attention has been turned toward these things, the Gospel itself remains unchanged; therefore, after saying “those who disturb you,” he did not say “those who change it,” but “who want to change the Gospel of Christ.”

(Hier.) Paul first marvels that they have been transferred from the freedom of the Gospel into the slavery of legal works; then he marvels that they have been transferred so quickly. For it is not the same offense to be transferred by someone with difficulty and to be transferred easily. In martyrdom, the one who immediately sprang forward to deny without struggle or torture does not suffer the same punishment as the one who, twisted among racks, cords, and fires, was compelled to deny what he believed.

The preaching of the Gospel was still recent; not much time had passed since the Apostle had brought the Galatians from idols to Christ. He therefore wonders how they could so quickly have departed from the one in whose name they had only recently become Christians.

The passage also contains a hyperbaton, and can be read in its proper order as follows: “I am astonished that you are so quickly transferring yourselves from Christ Jesus, who called you into grace, saying, ‘I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance’” (Luke 19); for “by grace you have been saved,” and not through the law.

“You have been transferred,” he says, “to another Gospel, which is not another,” because everything false does not endure, and what is contrary to the truth does not exist. Thus Scripture says: “Do not hand over, Lord, your scepter to those who are not” (Esther 14); and God called things that were not, so that he might make what was not come to be.

If this is said of those who held the same God and the same Scriptures—that they had been transferred to another Gospel, which is not the Gospel—what should we think of Marcion and the other heretics, who reject the Creator and pretend that Christ belongs to another God? They do not fall and collapse merely through an interpretation of the law and the letter, or through a conflict between flesh and spirit; they disagree with the whole order of the Church.

He aptly says: “Except that there are some who disturb you and want to change the Gospel of Christ.” “They want,” he says, “to change, alter, and disturb the Gospel of Christ,” but they cannot, because its nature is such that it cannot be other than what is true.

Everyone who interprets the Gospel with a spirit and mind different from what is written disturbs believers and changes the Gospel of Christ: he makes what is before the face into what is behind the back, and turns what is behind the back into what is before the face.

If someone follows only the letter, he places what is behind on the face. If someone accepts Jewish interpretations, he places behind him those things which by their nature have been established before the face.

It is also fitting that the word of “transfer” has been adapted to the Galatians: for *Galatia* signifies “transfer” in our language.

But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you something beyond what we have preached to you, let him be accursed. As we said before, so now I say again: if anyone preaches to you something beyond what you received, let him be accursed.

(Aug.) Truth must be loved for its own sake, not because of the human being or angel through whom it is announced. For the one who loves it because of its announcers can also love lies, should those announcers happen to present some of their own.

“As we said before,” he says, “and now I say again: if anyone preaches to you something beyond what you received, let him be accursed.” Perhaps he had said this earlier in the present letter; or, because he repeated what he had said, he wished to say, “as we said before.” In any case, the repetition most beneficially directs the mind toward firmly retaining the faith commended in this way.

(Hier.) It may also be understood hyperbolically—not that the Apostle or an angel could preach anything different from what they had once said, but that even if it were possible for apostles and angels to change, one nevertheless must not depart from what had once been received. This is especially so since the Apostle himself elsewhere demonstrates the firmness of his faith, saying: “I know that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8).

“I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness to me.” These are not the words of one who could ever depart from the faith and love of Christ.

(Ambr.) They had been called into a Gospel different from the one preached by those who had subverted them, but not different from the one announced by the apostles. The false apostles claimed that it was different in order to arouse hostility against the Apostle who had instructed them. To ensnare the Galatians through this deception, they had to say that the Apostle’s Gospel was different from what the Savior’s reasoning taught, while claiming that their own teaching was true because it agreed with the old law.

These are the people who raised this question with Paul and Barnabas, as is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles. They taught believers from the Gentiles that they could not be saved unless they were circumcised according to the custom of Moses and became Jews.

“Except that there are some,” he says, “who disturb you and want to change the Gospel of Christ.” It is clear that they said this in order to change the Gospel of Christ, altering its traditions so that they might be Jews under the name of Christ—that is, to turn the Gospel of Christ into the law.

No one should be surprised that the Apostle, who softened the harshness of conduct, was so deeply moved. He grows indignant on behalf of the Galatians’ salvation against the enemies of Christian discipline. His indignation shows that it is no slight sin, after receiving faith, to turn back to the law. For he asserts the Gospel he had preached to them to be so firm and true that he says they should not listen even to the apostles themselves if they should perhaps preach something different after having been changed.

Their reputation—that they were apostles of Christ—had spread everywhere. Or if the devil, pretending to be an angel of God so that he might easily be heard, were to appear from heaven preaching against these things, he would be recognized as an adversary and regarded as an abomination.

(Hier.) The word “anathema” properly belongs to the Jews. It is used both in Joshua and in Numbers, when the Lord commanded that everything in Jericho and among the Midianites be regarded as detestable and devoted to destruction (Numbers 21; Joshua 6).

Let us ask those who assert that Christ and the Apostle Paul belong either to the good God, previously unknown until that time, as his son or servant—those who say that he does not know how to curse or condemn anyone—how the Apostle can now use a word belonging to the Jews, that is, to the Creator, and wish an angel or apostle to perish, when he himself is not accustomed to take vengeance.

When he adds, “As we said before, and now I say again,” he shows that at the beginning he had already warned them and pronounced anathema upon those who were going to preach otherwise, and that now, after the preaching had occurred, he decrees the anathema that he had previously announced.

For this reason he pronounced anathema both upon himself—since they accused him of doing one thing in Judea and teaching another among the Gentiles—and upon an angel, whom they understood to be greater even than their earlier apostles. This was so that the authority of Peter and John would not be thought great, since neither Paul, who had previously instructed them, nor an angel was permitted to preach anything different from what they had once learned.
