He therefore named himself and the angel explicitly, while mentioning the others without names: “If anyone,” he says, “preaches to you.” By using this general expression he avoided insulting his predecessors while nevertheless covertly indicating their names.

Now am I seeking the approval of human beings or of God? Or am I trying to please human beings? If I were still trying to please human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.

(Ambr.) He indicates that those by whom the Galatians had been overthrown were seeking to please human beings, not God, in subverting them. In order to be praised by the Jews, they said that the law had to be observed according to the Jews’ wishes; otherwise, if they preached the true Gospel of Christ, they would make the Jews their enemies.

But the Apostle Paul, who taught that one must please God with complete devotion, did not fear offending human beings, provided that he commended God’s glory. Setting aside all present things in favor of future ones, he commended himself to hope as a worthy servant of Christ. Those who pursue their own profits under the name of the Lord cannot be worthy servants.

(Hier.) We should not think that the Apostle is teaching us, by his example, to disregard human judgment, since elsewhere he says: “Knowing therefore the fear of the Lord, we persuade human beings, but we are manifest to God” (2 Corinthians 5); and again: “Be without offense to Jews and Gentiles and the Church of God, just as I also please everyone in everything, not seeking my own advantage but that of many, so that they may be saved” (1 Corinthians 10).

If it is possible for us to please both God and human beings at the same time, we should please human beings as well. But if we cannot please human beings except by displeasing God, then we must please God rather than human beings. Otherwise, Paul himself would not explain why he pleases everyone in everything by adding, “not seeking what is useful to me but what is useful to many, so that they may be saved.”

The person who, out of charity—which does not seek its own interests but those of others—pleases everyone so that they may be saved, pleases God first, since God is concerned for the salvation of human beings.

The word specially added here, “now,” also has its force: at the present time one may please or displease human beings, just as one may have pleased them at another time for the salvation of many. Paul once pleased the Jews when, as a zealot for ancestral traditions (Galatians 1), he lived irreproachably within the law. He had such ardor and faith in the ceremonies of his ancestors that he became a participant in Stephen’s death and went to Damascus to bind those who had departed from the law (Acts 9).

But after he was transferred from persecutor into a vessel of election and began to preach the faith that he had once attacked, he also began to displease the Jews whom he had previously pleased.

This, then, is what he says: “Am I seeking to please the Jews, whom I pleased by displeasing them and thereby pleased God? If I were pleasing them, I would not yet be a servant of Christ; for I would be asserting the law and destroying the grace of the Gospel.”

Now, therefore, I am not even led into pretending to observe the law, because I do not seek to please both God and the Jews at once; whoever pleases them displeases God.

The word “persuade” itself is taken from ordinary human usage, when someone attempts to implant in others what he himself possesses and has once absorbed. It is read in many passages of Scripture, including this one: “This persuasion is not from the one who called you” (Galatians 5). Likewise in the Acts of the Apostles: “The Jews came to him at his lodging in great numbers, and he explained to them, testifying about the kingdom of God and persuading them about Jesus from the law of Moses and the prophets, from morning until evening” (Acts 28).

All this was because a report had been spread about him that he secretly observed the law and had joined himself in Jerusalem to those who practiced Judaism.

(Aug.) No one persuades God, because everything is manifest to him. But the person who persuades human beings well is the one who does not wish to please them personally but wishes them to accept the truth that he persuades them to embrace.

The one who pleases human beings, seeking not his own glory from them but God’s glory so that they may be saved, no longer pleases human beings but God. Or rather, when he also pleases God, he pleases human beings at the same time—but not merely human beings. For it is one thing to please human beings and another to please both God and human beings.

Likewise, the person who pleases human beings because of the truth does not himself please them; the truth pleases them. When Paul says “please,” he means insofar as it depends on him and concerns his intention, as though he were saying, “I would wish to please.” For if someone is pleased without his agency, as though on his own account and not because of God and the Gospel he announces, this should be attributed to the pride of the person who is wrongly pleased, rather than to the error of the one who pleases him.

The meaning, therefore, is this: “Am I now persuading human beings or God? Or, because I am persuading human beings, am I seeking to please human beings? If I were still seeking to please human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.”

For Christ commands his servants to learn from him to be gentle and humble of heart (Matthew 11). No one can do this who seeks to please human beings for his own sake—that is, for his own private and personal glory.

He says elsewhere also: “We persuade human beings, but we are manifest to God” (2 Corinthians 5). Thus, when he says here, “Am I persuading human beings or God?” the meaning is not that one should persuade God, but that one should persuade human beings.

Nor should it disturb us that elsewhere he says: “Just as I also please everyone in everything” (1 Corinthians 10). For he adds: “not seeking what benefits me, but what benefits many, so that they may be saved.”

It benefits no one toward salvation if a human being pleases him for his own sake. Such a person pleases beneficially only when he pleases because of God—that is, so that God may please and be glorified through him, when God’s gifts are recognized in the human being or received through the human being’s ministry.

When a human being pleases in this way, it is no longer the human being but God who pleases. Thus both statements can rightly be made: “I please” and “I do not please.” If there is a good interpreter and a devout knocker at the door, both meanings will become clear, and neither will repel the one who enters through any contradiction.

For I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel that was preached by me: it is not according to man. For I neither received it from man nor learned it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ.

(Ambr.) Now he opens the beginning of the Epistle. For he wishes the very point to be made clear: he had not learned from man the things he taught, lest doubt arise concerning what he taught. Nor had his preaching been fashioned according to human judgment, so that it might appear unworthy of divine authority; rather, he says that he learned it from the Son of God through revelation, when Christ was already in heaven after the resurrection.

(Aug.) The Gospel that is according to man is false, for “every man is a liar” (Psalm 115). Whatever truth is found in man is not from man, but from God through man. Therefore what is according to man ought not even to be called the Gospel—such as that brought by those who were drawing into slavery, from freedom, those whom God was calling from slavery into freedom.

(Hier.) From this passage the doctrine of Ebion and Photinus is refuted: namely, that Christ is God and not merely man. For if Paul’s Gospel is not according to man, and he neither received nor learned it from man, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ, then Jesus Christ, who revealed the Gospel to Paul, is certainly not merely man. And if he is not man, consequently he is God—not that we deny that he assumed humanity, but that we reject the notion that he was merely human.

Nor should we think that the Gospel lies in the words of Scripture, but in its meaning; not on the surface, but in the marrow; not in the leaves of expressions, but in the root of reason. It is said in the prophet concerning God: “His words are good with him.” Scripture is useful to those who hear it when it is not spoken without Christ, when it is not uttered without the Father, and when the one who preaches does not communicate it without the Spirit. Otherwise even the devil, who speaks from the Scriptures, and all heresies—according to Ezekiel (Ezek. 13)—sew cushions for themselves from them, to place beneath the elbow of every age.

There is great danger in speaking in the Church, lest, through a perverse interpretation, the Gospel of Christ become the gospel of a man, or, worse, of the devil.

The difference between receiving and learning is this: the one receives the Gospel to whom it is first communicated and who is brought to faith, so that he believes the things written to be true; but the one learns who comes to understand those things which in the Gospel are represented through riddles and parables, once they have been explained and expounded. And he understands them not through a man revealing them, but through Christ, who revealed them to Paul, or through Paul, in whom Christ speaks.

The very word *ἀποκαλύψεως*, that is, “of revelation,” properly belongs to Scripture, and was used by none of the wise men of the world among the Greeks. Hence it seems to me that, as in other words which the translators of the Septuagint transferred from Hebrew into Greek, so also here they made a great effort to express the peculiar character of a foreign speech, devising new words for new realities. The word suggests that, when something covered and veiled is uncovered by removing the covering above it, it is shown and brought into the light.

To make this clearer, accept an example. When Moses spoke with God with his face revealed and uncovered—that is, without a veil—he placed a veil over his face when speaking to the people, because they could not look upon his countenance. Before the ark of the covenant also a veil had been spread; when it had been drawn back, the things previously hidden were disclosed, and—to use the very word—they were “revealed.”

The apostle Paul says that he received the Gospel neither from men nor through man. In the present passage this is also understood indirectly as referring to Peter and to the other apostles who preceded him: no one’s authority or teaching is to move him, since Christ alone is his teacher of the Gospel.

Moreover, he indicates that revelation when, as he was going to Damascus, he was granted on the road to hear Christ’s voice and, after his eyes had been blinded, to behold the true light of the world (Acts 9).

For you have heard of my former manner of life in Judaism: how excessively I persecuted the Church of God and ravaged it; and how I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries among my people, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers.

(Ambr.) He briefly recalls his former purpose, which had previously flourished according to the flesh in opposition to the Church.

(Hier.) This account is highly beneficial to the Galatians: how Paul, once the destroyer of the Church and the fiercest defender of Judaism, was suddenly converted to faith in Christ—and this at the very time when the crucified Christ was first being proclaimed throughout the world, when the new doctrine was being driven out to the ends of the whole world by both Gentiles and Jews.

For they could say: “If the man who from childhood was trained in the disciplines of the Pharisees, who surpassed all his contemporaries in Jewish tradition, now defends the Church which he once persecuted with the greatest force; and if, amid the hatred of all, he prefers to possess the grace and newness of Christ rather than the antiquity of the law with the praise of many, what ought we to do, who have begun to be Christians from paganism?”

He fittingly added, “I persecuted the Church of God excessively,” so that from this too wonder might arise: it was not just anyone who had lightly persecuted the Church, but the man who surpassed the others in persecution, who had been converted to the faith.

And wisely, while narrating one matter, he inserts that he had served not so much the law of God as the traditions of his fathers—that is, the traditions of the Pharisees, who teach the doctrines and commandments of men and reject the law of God in order to establish their own traditions.

How elegant, moreover, is the observation and the weight of the words: “For you have heard,” he says, “of my former manner of life in Judaism?”

(Aug.) If, by persecuting and ravaging the Church of God, he was advancing in Judaism, it is evident that this was opposed to the Church of God—not through that spiritual law which the Jews received, but through their carnal manner of life in bondage.

And if Paul, as a zealot—that is, an imitator—of his ancestral traditions persecuted the Church of God, then his ancestral traditions are opposed to the Church of God. The fault, however, is not that of the law. For the law is spiritual and does not compel itself to be understood carnally; rather, the fault belongs to those who interpret even what they received carnally and who also handed down many things of their own, dissolving, as the Lord says, the commandment of God because of their traditions.

(Hier.) “Manner of life,” not grace; “formerly,” not now; “in Judaism,” not in the law of God.

How excessively I persecuted the Church of God and ravaged it! He did not persecute as the others did, but excessively. Nor was even a vehement persecution sufficient for him; rather, like some brigand and plunderer, he devastated the Church.

He does not say “the Church of Christ,” since at that time he considered Christ contemptible and persecuted him, but, as he now believes, “the Church of God,” either signifying that Christ himself is God or that the Church belongs to the same God who was formerly the giver of the law.

“And I advanced,” he says, “in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries among my people, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers.”

Again, he calls it advancement not in the law of God but in Judaism; not beyond all, but beyond many; not beyond the old, but beyond his contemporaries—both reporting his zeal for the law and avoiding boastfulness. By mentioning the traditions of his fathers rather than the Lord’s commandments, he showed that he was a Pharisee from Pharisees and that he had zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.

Even to this day those who understand the Scriptures in a Jewish manner persecute the Church of Christ and lay it waste, corrupted not by zeal for the law of God but by human traditions.

But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the Gentiles—

Not only here, but also in the Epistle to the Romans, Paul writes that he was set apart for the Gospel of God. Jeremiah too, before he was formed in the womb and conceived in his mother’s belly, is said to have been known to God and sanctified (Jer. 1). And concerning the righteous—or, as some think, from the person of the Savior—it is said: “Upon you I was cast from the womb; from my mother’s womb you are my God” (Psalm 21).

Conversely, David sings concerning sinners: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Psalm 50); and elsewhere: “Sinners have been estranged from the womb” (Psalm 57).

And in both respects, before the children were born, “God loved Jacob, but hated Esau” (Mal. 1; Rom. 9).

Heretics find here an opportunity to claim that there are different natures—namely, a spiritual nature, an ensouled nature, and a material nature [*χοίκην*]—one to be saved, another to perish, and another to occupy an intermediate position. They argue that otherwise the righteous would never be chosen before doing anything good, nor would the sinner be hated before committing sin, unless the natures of those who perish and those who are saved were different.

A simple answer may be given: this comes about through God’s foreknowledge, so that he loves the one whom he knows will become righteous before he comes forth from the womb, and hates the one whom he knows will be a sinner before he sins. This does not mean that there is injustice in God’s love or hatred, but that he cannot regard otherwise those whom he knows will become either sinners or righteous. We, as human beings, judge only concerning present things; but for him to whom future things are already accomplished, judgment concerns the end of things, not their beginnings.

It is not, however, the same thing that he says—“to reveal his Son in me”—as if he had said, “to reveal his Son to me.” For to the one in whom something is revealed, that thing can be revealed which was not previously in him. But in the one in whom it is revealed, what is revealed is something that was previously in him and was later disclosed.

The same is found in the Gospel: “There stands among you one whom you do not know” (John 1); and elsewhere: “He was the true light which enlightens every person coming into the world.” From this it becomes evident that knowledge of God is naturally present in everyone, that no one is born without Christ, and that no one lacks within himself the seeds of wisdom, justice, and the remaining virtues.

It may also be understood otherwise: the Son of God was revealed in Paul because, when Paul preached, the Gentiles came to recognize the one whom previously they did not know.

Immediately I did not yield to flesh and blood—or, as the Greek more accurately has it, “I did not confer with flesh and blood.”

(Ambr.) Thus, through God’s foreknowledge, he was set apart from his mother’s womb—that is, before he was born—or God knew him as destined to be good immediately after his birth, just as he says to the prophet Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you,” and so forth (Jer. 1).

In the same way, God, knowing what the apostle Paul would become, went before him and called him before his conversion, because he was necessary. Therefore, he immediately undertook the administration of God’s gift, setting aside every carnal concern. For he neither sought anyone’s counsel nor referred to anyone what he was about to do; rather, he immediately preached Christ, because he is the Son of God. For just as those who will later be evil are often good beforehand, so those who will later be good are often evil beforehand.

(Hier.) I know that many think this was said concerning the apostles. Porphyry also objects that, after Christ’s revelation, Paul did not deign to go to men and confer with them, lest, after God’s teaching, he should be instructed by flesh and blood.

But far be it from me to think that Peter, John, and James were flesh and blood—things that cannot possess the kingdom of God. After Christ’s revelation, Paul did not confer with flesh and blood because he did not wish to cast pearls before swine or give what is holy to dogs.

Someone may say: “Even if he did not immediately confer with flesh and blood concerning the Gospel, it is nevertheless understood that later he did confer with flesh and blood.” On this interpretation, which excuses the apostles from being called flesh and blood, the passage cannot stand: for the one who at the beginning did not confer with flesh and blood would nevertheless, as I have said, later have conferred with blood and flesh.

The preposition therefore constrains us to punctuate the passage differently, so that “immediately” or “at once” is not joined with “flesh and blood,” but is connected with what precedes. It should be read as follows:

“When it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb, and then to reveal his Son in me, and finally to preach him among the Gentiles, immediately”—so that the account may begin from its proper origin—“I did not confer with flesh and blood.”

(Aug.) Whoever is separated, in a certain manner, from the womb of his mother is separated blindly from the custom of carnal parents. Whoever yields to flesh and blood assents to his carnal relatives and kindred when they give him carnal advice.

Nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me; rather, I went away to Arabia and returned again to Damascus.

(Amb.) He says that he was not chosen by necessity to go to the apostles who preceded him, as though he were to learn something from them, because God had revealed through his Son how he was to teach.

He says this in order to show that nothing other than what he taught was to be held, and that men were not to be believed, but God, from whom he testifies that he had learned. Consequently, those who had brought them under the law were false teachers, because what they taught had not been handed down by God.

From Damascus, therefore, he went to Arabia to preach, where there were none of the apostles, so that he might establish the Churches there himself, lest Judaism be introduced by stealth through false apostles. From there he returned again to Damascus, to visit those to whom, while they were still inexperienced, he had preached the Gospel of God’s grace.

Then, after three years, I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and I remained with him fifteen days.

It was fitting that he should wish to see Peter, because he was first among the apostles, to whom the Savior had entrusted the care of the Churches. He did not go in order to learn anything from him, since he had already learned from the Author himself, by whom Peter too had been instructed, but out of affection for the apostolate and so that Peter might know that the permission given to Paul was the same as that which Peter himself had received.

When he came to him, therefore, he was received as a guest and stayed with him fifteen days, like a fellow apostle of one mind with him.

He makes these things known in order to show that he was in harmony with the apostles and had disagreed with them in nothing, as the false apostles whispered about him, in order to disfigure him before the Churches of the Gentiles and implant their own evils in the more simple-minded by saying that these agreed with the teaching of the greater apostles.

(Hier.) The order of the history does not seem to agree with this, according to Luke’s account in the Acts of the Apostles. Luke reports that, after Paul’s faith in Christ, when he had boldly preached the Gospel in Damascus for many days, plots were made against him, that he was lowered by night through the wall in a basket, and that he came to Jerusalem, attempting to join himself to the disciples.

When they avoided him and were afraid to approach him, Barnabas brought him to the apostles. There he related how he had seen the Lord on the road and had acted boldly in Damascus in the name of Jesus: “He was with them,” Luke says, “going in and going out in Jerusalem and acting boldly in the name of the Lord. He also spoke and disputed with the Greeks; but they sought to kill him. When the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him to Tarsus” (Acts 9).

Here, however, Paul says that he first went to Arabia and then returned to Damascus; that after three years he came to Jerusalem, saw Peter, and stayed with him fifteen days; and that he met no other apostle except James, the brother of the Lord.

To make these statements credible—for in the absence of witnesses they could seem doubtful—he confirms them under oath, saying: “As for what I am writing to you, behold, before God, I am not lying.”

We may therefore suppose that Paul did indeed go to Jerusalem, according to Luke’s account, not as though he were going to the apostles who preceded him in order to learn something from them, but to escape the force of the persecution which had been stirred up against him in Damascus because of the Gospel of Christ. Thus he came to Jerusalem as he would have come to any other city. From there he immediately withdrew because of the plots, went to Arabia—or Damascus—and then, after three years, returned from there to Jerusalem to visit Peter.

Or certainly the sequence may be understood as follows. Immediately after he was baptized and had been strengthened by taking food, he was with the disciples who were in Damascus for several days. To the astonishment of everyone, he immediately preached in the synagogues of the Jews that Jesus was the Son of God. Then he went to Arabia, returned from Arabia to Damascus, and remained there for three years.

Scripture attests that these were “many days,” saying: “When many days had passed, the Jews took counsel to kill him. Their plot became known to Saul, and they guarded the gates day and night in order to kill him. Therefore his disciples took him by night and lowered him through the wall, letting him down in a basket. When he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join himself to the disciples.”

Luke omitted Arabia for this reason: perhaps Paul accomplished nothing in Arabia worthy of the apostolate, and Luke preferred, in his concise account, to mention those things which seemed worthy of Christ’s Gospel.

Nor should this be attributed to the apostle’s negligence, as though he had stayed uselessly in Arabia; rather, some dispensation and command of God required him to be silent. For later too we read that Paul and Silas went out and were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia.

Alternatively:

“But I went away to Arabia and returned again to Damascus.” What benefit does this account offer me if I read that Paul, after Christ’s revelation, immediately went to Arabia and immediately returned from Arabia to Damascus, without knowing what he did there or what benefit his going and returning brought?

The Apostle himself gives me an opportunity for a higher understanding in this same Epistle, when, discussing Abraham, Hagar, and Sarah, he says: “These things are spoken allegorically; for these are two covenants: one indeed from Mount Sinai, producing slavery, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, joined to the Jerusalem that now is” (Gal. 4).

He teaches that the Old Testament—that is, the son of the slave woman—was placed in Arabia, whose interpretation is “humble” and “declining.”

As soon, therefore, as Paul believed, he turned toward the law, the prophets, and the mysteries of the Old Testament, already situated in decline. He sought Christ in them, the one whom he had been commanded to preach among the Gentiles; and, having found him, he did not remain there longer. Rather, he returned to Damascus—that is, to the blood and passion of Christ—and, strengthened by prophetic reading, proceeded to Jerusalem, the place of vision and peace, not so much to learn something from the apostles as to confer with them concerning the Gospel that he had preached.

Then, after three years, I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter.

He did not go in order to look upon his eyes, cheeks, and face, to see whether he was thin or fat, whether he had a hooked nose or a straight one, or whether his forehead was covered by hair or, as Clement reports in his *Periods*, whether he was bald on the head.

Nor do I think it was consistent with apostolic dignity that, after so great a preparation lasting three years, he should have wished to look upon something merely human in Peter. Rather, he saw him with those eyes with which he also appears now in his Epistles. With those eyes Paul saw Cephas with which Paul himself is now seen by all who possess understanding.

If this does not seem convincing to someone, let him join all these statements with the preceding meaning: that the apostles contributed nothing to him. The fact that he appeared to go to Jerusalem means that he went to see the apostle, not from a desire to learn—for he too had the same source of preaching—but to pay honor to the first apostle.

“And I remained with him fifteen days.” He did not need extensive instruction, since he had prepared himself for so long to see Peter.

Although to some it may seem excessive to observe even the numbers found in Scripture, nevertheless I think it is not without reason that he places the number fifteen for the days Paul lived with Peter. It signifies complete knowledge and perfected teaching, since there are fifteen songs in the Psalter and fifteen steps by which the righteous ascend to sing to God and stand in his courts.

Hezekiah too, when fifteen years were granted to him for life, deserved to receive a sign in the steps; and the solemnities of God begin on the fifteenth day.

Moreover, because we follow a twofold understanding, he specifies fifteen days in order to show that the period during which he could have learned anything from Peter was not long, so that everything might be referred back to the meaning with which he began: that he had not been taught by man, but by God.

But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the brother of the Lord.

(Ambr.) He saw James in Jerusalem because he had been appointed there by the apostles as bishop. James himself had previously been an unbeliever, as the Evangelist says: “For even his brothers did not yet believe in him” (John 7).

(Hier.) This may also be understood otherwise: because of his outstanding conduct, incomparable faith, and wisdom that was not ordinary, he was called the Lord’s brother, and because he was the first to preside over the Church which, as the first to believe in Christ, had been gathered from the Jews.

The other apostles too are called the Lord’s brothers, as in the Gospel: “Go, tell my brothers: I am going to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (Matt. 18; John 20). And in the psalm: “I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will sing [praise] to you” (Psalm 21).

But he is called “brother” in a special sense to whom the Lord, as he went to the Father, had entrusted the sons of his mother.

And just as Job and the other patriarchs were indeed called servants of God, but Moses possessed something especially distinguished, as it is written concerning him, “Not as Moses, my servant,” so the blessed James was specially called the Lord’s brother, as we said earlier.

As for the things I am writing to you, behold, before God I am not lying.

(Hier.) This may be taken simply, so that the meaning is: “The things I am writing to you are true, and I confirm them with God as witness; they have not been embellished by any verbal art or disguised by any lie.”

Or it may be understood more profoundly, so that it reads: “The things I am writing to you are before God,” that is, they are worthy of God’s sight.

Why are they worthy of God’s sight? Because I am not lying. And just as “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Psalm 33), while he turns his face away from the sight of the impious, so now the things written are before the Lord because I, who write them, am not lying; they would not be before the Lord if I were lying.

This may be understood not only of the things he is now writing to the Galatians, but also generally of all the Epistles: what he writes is not false, and his heart and his words do not disagree.

(Aug.) The one who says, “Behold, before God I am not lying,” certainly swears an oath. But what of the holy man—was this oath permissible?

An oath is not contrary to the commandment when it arises from evil—not from the one who swears, but from the unbelief of the one whom he is compelled to persuade by an oath. From this it is understood that the Lord prohibited swearing in such a way that, so far as it depends on each person, no one should swear.

Many people do this, keeping oaths in their mouths as though they were something great or pleasant. The Apostle certainly knew the Lord’s commandment, and yet he swore. We should not listen to those who refuse to regard such expressions as oaths. For what will they make of the saying, “I die daily, by your glory, brothers, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord” (1 Cor. 15), which the Greek manuscripts very clearly establish as an oath?

So far as it depends on him, the Apostle does not swear. He does not seek an oath out of desire or affection for swearing, for an oath is something more than “Yes, yes; No, no,” and therefore it arises from evil. Rather, he swears because of the weakness or unbelief of those who are not otherwise moved to faith.

Then I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia.

(Hier.) After the vision at Jerusalem he came to Syria, whose name among us means “lofty” or “sublime.” Then he crossed into Cilicia, which he desired to bring into the faith of Christ, preaching to it the call to repentance. For Cilicia is interpreted as “assumption” or “a lamentable calling.”

But I was unknown by face to the Churches of Judea that are in Christ.

(Aug.) It should be noted that it was not only in Jerusalem that Jews believed in Christ. Nor were they so few that they were merely mixed among the Churches of the Gentiles; rather, they were so numerous that Churches were formed from them.

They had heard only this: “The one who formerly persecuted us now preaches the faith which he once tried to destroy”; and they glorified God because of me.

(Aug.) This is what the Lord also says: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).

(Hier.) The Churches that were in Judea knew Paul only by report. Most of them had seen him more as a persecutor than as an apostle. But Syria and the regions of Cilicia, Arabia, and Damascus perhaps knew him by his appearance as well, because the teacher of the Gentiles preached the Gospel of Christ not to Jews but to Gentiles.

Everything he does has this purpose: to teach that he could never have become glorious among those very people whom he had formerly persecuted, unless his preaching had also been approved by the judgment of those who previously knew him as an evil man.

He secretly returns to his main point by confirming that he had spent so short a time in Judea that even those who believed there did not know him by face. From this he shows that neither Peter, nor James, nor John had been his teachers, but Christ, who had revealed the Gospel to him.

At the same time, it should be noted that above he says he persecuted the Church, whereas here he says he persecuted the faith: there, people; here, the matter itself. Thus it could now more aptly be added: “He preaches the faith which he once tried to destroy.” The same could not have been said of the Church.

(Amb.) Since the law of Christ offers something different from Judaism: there is circumcision of the flesh, here circumcision of the heart; there, service under the elements through new moons and the Sabbath, here service to God alone in the Spirit, because one believes with the heart; there, bondage is the cause of sin, here, freedom comes from the remission of sins. There is therefore a great difference between them.

## CHAPTER II

The Apostle shows, from the approval and authority of the other apostles, that circumcision is not necessary. He opposed the apostle Peter, who seemed in some measure to cloak circumcision, concluding that the legal observances were not to be kept.

Then, after fourteen years, I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also with me. I went up in response to a revelation, and I conferred with them concerning the Gospel that I preach among the Gentiles.

(Cass.) Who, then, could be so presumptuous and blind as to dare entrust himself to his own judgment and discernment, when the vessel of election testifies that he himself needed the counsel of his fellow apostles?

From this it is most clearly established that no one is shown by the Lord the way of perfection if, having the means by which he can be instructed, he despises the teaching or institutions of his elders, making light of that saying which must be guarded with the greatest care: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will declare it to you” (Deut. 32).

But separately to those who seemed to be something, lest I should be running, or have run, in vain. (Jerome) Thus, after fourteen years he went up to Jerusalem; and whereas previously he had gone only to see Peter and had stayed with him fifteen days, he now says that he went in order to confer with the apostles about the Gospel, taking with him Barnabas, who was circumcised, and Titus from the Gentiles, who had his foreskin, so that “every word might stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” But to confer is one thing, and to learn another. Among those who confer there is equality; between teacher and learner, the learner is the inferior.

At the beginning of his faith, he saw the apostles only in passing; after seventeen years, as he himself says, he speaks with them fully. He humbles himself and inquires lest he should be running or have run in vain. He does this for a twofold reason: both to display the humility of Paul, who, already a teacher throughout the whole world of the Gentiles, had nevertheless hastened to the apostles who preceded him; and so that the Galatians might learn that those too who presided over the churches in Judea had not rejected his Gospel.

At the same time he teaches that, for the sake of the faith of Christ and the freedom of the Gospel, he dared to bring Titus, an uncircumcised man, to those very people who knew more about him—namely, that he violated the law, destroyed Moses, and utterly abolished circumcision. He brought him among so great a multitude of Jews and among his enemies, who, as though out of zeal for the law, desired to drink his blood. Neither he nor Titus was overcome by any fear so as to yield to a necessity that might have been excused on account of the place, the authority of the elders, the number of the churches that believed in Christ from among the Jews, or the time, lest they should at once endure so great a hatred.

Some say that he went up to Jerusalem after fourteen years on the occasion described in the Acts of the Apostles, when disagreement arose among the believers at Antioch concerning which requirements of the law ought to be observed or set aside, and it was decided to go to Jerusalem and await the judgment of the elders. Paul and Barnabas themselves were sent on that occasion. They say that this is what is read in the Latin manuscripts: “To whom we yielded submission for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain among you.” That is, Paul and Barnabas allowed themselves to be sent to Jerusalem concerning a matter that was manifest, as though it were doubtful, so that the grace of the Gospel might be confirmed to believers by the judgment of the elders also, and so that no further doubt might remain about the omission of circumcision, since the apostles had commanded by letter that the yoke of the law be removed from those among the Gentiles who believed in Christ. [Col. 0265B]

(Augustine) The fact that he expounded the Gospel privately to those who were prominent in the Church, after he had already expounded it before everyone, does not mean that he had said something false and therefore told the truth privately to a smaller number. Rather, he had omitted certain things that the little ones could not yet bear—just as he says that he gave the Corinthians milk, not solid food (I Cor. III). For it is never permissible to speak falsely; but at times it is useful to keep silent about something true. It was necessary that the other apostles should know of his perfection.

For it did not follow that, if he was faithful and held the true and correct faith, he must already also be an apostle. But what he adds—“lest perhaps I should be running, or have run, in vain”—is to be understood not as referring to those with whom he privately conferred about the Gospel, but to those to whom he is writing, as though it were expressed in the form of a question. It thereby becomes evident that he was not running, or had not run, in vain, since, by the testimony of the others also, he was shown to differ in nothing from the truth of the Gospel.

(Ambrose) Since his reputation had spread widely among all the Jews, although he was not seen face to face—for he was going about with his customary steadfastness establishing and strengthening the churches among the Gentiles—among the Jews, because of the law, an unfavorable opinion of him arose, as though he disagreed with the preaching of the other apostles. Hence many were troubled, and the Gentiles could fear that he was leading them into something different from what the apostles who had been with the Lord had handed down.

On this very account the Galatians were subverted by Jews who said that Paul taught something different from Peter. Therefore, instructed by a revelation from the Lord, he went up to Jerusalem with witnesses to his preaching, namely Barnabas and Titus, one a Jew and the other a Gentile, so that, if anyone had taken offense at him, their testimony might remove it. He disclosed to them the meaning of his preaching; with the apostles, however, he conferred privately, so that they might know that he did not depart from the evangelical rule. This was so that they would not think that he had been running, or had run, in vain, as some of the believing Jews supposed.

Nor could he learn anything from them, since he had been instructed by God. But, for the sake of concord and peace, it happened by God’s will that the doubt or suspicion of the brothers and of his fellow apostles might be removed, and that it might benefit the Gentiles to know that his Gospel agreed with that of the apostles.

Moreover, when they had decreed that those from the Gentiles who believed should not be troubled, but should observe only these requirements: abstention from blood, sexual immorality, and idolatry—let the Greek sophists who claim for themselves expertise and say that they flourish by the natural subtlety of their intellect now say what was handed down for the Gentiles to observe. Were these things unknown to them, or known? But how can anyone learn what he already knows?

Therefore those things which the Gentiles thought permissible were shown to them to be unlawful. Consequently, when they were commanded to abstain from blood, they were not thereby prohibited from murder; rather, they received what Noah had learned from God: that they should abstain from eating blood together with flesh. For how could it have happened that Romans, trained in Roman laws—whose authority in the observance of commands is so great—did not know that murder must not be committed, since Roman laws punish adulterers, murderers, false witnesses, thieves, sorcerers, and perpetrators of other evils?

Finally, these three commands are found to have been given by the apostles and elders, although Roman laws do not know them: that they should abstain from idolatry, from blood, as Noah did, and from sexual immorality. The Greek sophists, not understanding this, yet knowing that one must abstain from blood, corrupted Scripture by adding a fourth command, namely that one must also abstain from what has been strangled. I think that now, by God’s will, they will understand this, since what they added had already been stated above. [Col. 0266A]

But not even Titus, who was with me, was compelled to be circumcised, although he was a Gentile. This means: “At that very time when I was in Jerusalem,” he says, “Titus, who was with me, was not compelled to be circumcised, although we were among the apostles and those who had believed from the Jews. No one compelled him”—that is, Titus—“to be circumcised.” The implied question is: Why, then, are you being circumcised, when Titus was not compelled by the apostles, who seemed to be something, to be circumcised, but was received uncircumcised?

But because of the false brothers who had been secretly brought in, who slipped in to spy out our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might enslave us, we yielded to submission for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain among you.

Because Titus was a Greek, just as the Galatians were, Paul denies that he was circumcised. By saying this he rebukes those who allowed themselves to be circumcised although they were Greeks. But lest someone object that he himself had circumcised Timothy, he now explains why he did what he denied ought to be done, saying:

“But because of the false brothers who had been secretly brought in, who slipped in to spy out our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might enslave us, we yielded to submission for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain among you.”

The Greeks, on the contrary, say, “We did not yield even for an hour.” They say that this agrees with the case, because, they maintain, the man who forbade it ought not to have said that he had done it, lest he prove that it ought to be done. But the apostle, a man of God, knowing that this could be brought against him, puts it forward himself in order to anticipate his accusers, and gives the reasons that compelled him to do what he did not wish to do.

“Because of the false brothers who had been secretly brought in,” he says. He calls them “secretly brought in” because they entered deceitfully, presenting themselves as brothers although they were enemies. “Who slipped in”—that is, they entered humbly while feigning friendship—“to spy out our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might enslave us.”

To spy out means to enter in such a way that one pretends one thing but seeks another, by which one may accuse our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus. Freedom in Christ Jesus means not being subjected to the law. “So that they might enslave us”: this is why they entered with deceit and fraud, namely, to subject our freedom to slavery by forcing us to submit to the law of circumcision.

“We yielded to submission for an hour”: that is, for a time we subjected ourselves to slavery, humbling ourselves before the law, so that, after Timothy had been circumcised, the deceit and scandal of the Jews might cease. For, as may be understood, they were prepared to stir up tumult and sedition against him.

The reason was that they had an opportunity for making accusations, because Timothy’s mother was a Jew, but his father a Greek. Thus it happened that, according to the law, the child had not been circumcised. But because the apostle wished to take him with him and ordain him bishop, as he did—for, he says, all those in that region gave him a good testimony—he suffered the plots of the Jews.

They were testing whether he would receive the uncircumcised son of a Jewish woman, preparing a sedition. For if he maintained that Gentiles ought not to be circumcised, as the letter from the apostles on this matter had decreed, or if he did not forbid the children of Israel to be circumcised—since the apostles had indicated nothing about them in that same letter—the believing Jews would have raged all the more on the authority of that letter, because it did not forbid Jews to circumcise their children.

“Then,” he says, “taking him, he circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places.” But the Gentiles did not take offense; therefore Titus was not compelled to be circumcised.

Thus he yielded for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain among the Gentiles, since they do not subject themselves to circumcision. But among the Jews the truth of the Gospel was not present, because believers circumcised their children. “For in Christ Jesus neither foreskin nor circumcision has any value, but faith working through love” (Gal. VI).

(Augustine) It can also be read according to what the Greek manuscripts have: “To whom we did not yield submission even for an hour.” For this reason he circumcised Timothy: so that the Jews, and especially his maternal relatives, would not think that those who had believed in Christ from the Gentiles detested circumcision in the same way that idolatry must be detested—although the Lord commanded circumcision to be performed, whereas Satan persuaded people to idolatry.

He did not circumcise Titus for this reason: lest he provide an occasion to those who said that the Gentiles could not be saved without circumcision, and who might falsely claim that Paul held this view for the deception of the Gentiles. He himself makes this sufficiently clear when he says:

“But not even Titus, who was with me, although he was a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised, because of the false brothers who had secretly entered, who slipped in to spy out our freedom, so that they might reduce us to slavery. To them we did not yield submission even for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain among you.”

Here it becomes clear what he understood them to be seeking, and why he did not do what he had done in the case of Timothy. He could act with that freedom by which he showed that these sacraments ought neither to be sought as necessary nor condemned as sacrilegious.

But from those who seemed to be something—whatever they once were—it makes no difference to me. God does not accept the person of a human being.

(Ambrose) This means that the apostles were formerly simple and inexperienced men, possessing no distinction in the law; but this was not an obstacle. For who could accuse one whom God excuses? It is not asked what someone was, but what he is. Past things neither condemn nor vindicate them. Nevertheless, he wishes it to be understood that he was learned in the law, renowned in life, and consequently an outstanding minister in the administration of the Gospel.

“Those who were thought to be something contributed nothing to me.” He says that he received nothing from the apostles, but from God. For the one who granted the unlearned understanding of Christian teaching also, he says, graciously granted me, although I was learned in the law, understanding of this kind of reasoning.

How, then, could he have learned from them, when Christ’s grace found him learned and made him more learned? But, on the contrary, when they saw that the Gospel of the uncircumcision had been entrusted to him, just as the Gospel of the circumcision had been entrusted to Peter—for the one who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me among the Gentiles—and when they recognized the grace of God that had been given to me, Peter, James, and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave the right hands of fellowship to me and Barnabas, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision.

(Augustine) Those who seem to be something seem to be something only to carnal people; for they themselves are not something. Even if they are good ministers of God, Christ is something in them, not they themselves by their own power. For if they were something by themselves, they would always have been something—whatever they once were—which means that they too had once been sinners.

He says that it makes no difference to him because God does not accept the person of a human being. That is, God called everyone to salvation without partiality, not counting their sins against them. Therefore, even in the absence of those who had first become apostles, Paul was perfected by the Lord, so that when he conferred with them there was nothing they could add to his perfection. Rather, they saw that the same Lord Jesus Christ, who saves without partiality, had given Paul the ministry among the Gentiles, just as he had given Peter the ministry among the Jews.

They were therefore not found to disagree with him in anything. When he said that he had received the perfect Gospel, they did not deny it or wish to add something to him as though he were imperfect. On the contrary, instead of reprovers of imperfection, they became approvers of perfection. They gave the right hands of fellowship—that is, they consented to fellowship and obeyed the Lord’s will—agreeing that Paul and Barnabas should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision, which seems contrary to the foreskin, that is, to the Gentiles. [Col. 0269B]

For what he says—“on the contrary”—can also be understood in this way, so that the order is: “Those who seemed to be something added nothing to me; but, on the contrary, they agreed that we should go to the Gentiles, who are opposed to circumcision, while they should go to the circumcision. They gave the right hands of fellowship to me and Barnabas.”

Let no one think that he said this as an insult to his predecessors: “Those who seemed to be something—whatever they once were—it makes no difference to me.” They, as spiritual men, wished to resist those who were carnal, who thought that they themselves were something, rather than Christ in them. They greatly rejoiced when it was impressed upon people that they themselves, as Paul’s predecessors, had been justified by the Lord from sins, just as Paul himself had been—by the Lord who does not accept the person of a human being—because they sought God’s glory, not their own.

But because carnal and proud people become angry if anything is said about their former life and receive it as an insult, they form their judgment of the apostles from their own disposition. Peter, James, and John, however, were more honored among the apostles because the Lord showed himself to those three on the mountain as a sign of his kingdom, when six days earlier he had said: “There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man in the kingdom of his Father” (Matt. XVI; Mark IX).

Yet they themselves were not pillars; they only seemed to be. For Paul knew that Wisdom had built herself a house, and had not established three pillars, but seven. This number refers either to the unity of the churches. For seven is commonly used to signify the whole, as it is said in the Gospel: “He will receive sevenfold in this age,” as though he were saying, “As having nothing, yet possessing all things” (II Cor. VI).

For this reason John also writes to seven churches (Apoc. I), which certainly represent the whole Church. Or the number seven of the pillars refers more specifically to the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit: wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge and piety, and the fear of God (Isa. XI). Through these operations the house of the Son of God, that is, the Church, is held together.

As for what he says, “Only that we should remember the poor, which I was also eager to do”—the apostles all shared a common concern for the poor among the saints who were in Judea, those who had placed the prices of their sold possessions at the apostles’ feet.

Thus Paul and Barnabas were sent to the Gentiles, so that the churches of the Gentiles, which had not done this, might minister through their prayers to those who had done it. As he says to the Romans (Rom. XV): “But now I am going to Jerusalem to minister to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem. They have been pleased to do so, and they are their debtors. For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in material things.”

Paul therefore did not fall into any deception, because everywhere he observed what he saw being maintained, both among the churches of the Gentiles and among those of the Jews, so that he would never remove customary practice from the kingdom of God. He merely warned that no one should place hope of salvation in superfluous matters, even if, for the sake of avoiding offense to the weak, he wished to preserve a custom in such matters.

Thus he says to the Corinthians (I Cor. VII): “Was someone called while circumcised? Let him not draw back his foreskin. Was someone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the observance of God’s commandments. Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called.” He referred this to those customs or conditions of life that do no harm to faith and good morals.

(Jerome) If someone was a thief when he was called, he ought not to remain a thief. This is a hyperbaton; after removing the many words inserted in the middle, it can be read briefly as follows: “Those who seemed to be something contributed nothing to me; but, on the contrary, they gave the right hands of fellowship to me and Barnabas.”

(Augustine) He says that he came to Jerusalem and conferred about the Gospel with the apostles, and that the right hands were given to him—that is, a sign of concord, a sign of agreement—because in no respect did it differ from what they themselves had learned.

(Jerome) Or perhaps his meaning, concealed without self-display, is this: “Those who seemed to be something contributed nothing to me; but, on the contrary, I contributed something to them, making them stronger in the grace of the Gospel.”

The whole meaning of what he says is that the same Gospel of the uncircumcision was entrusted to him, and the Gospel of the circumcision to Peter. He sent me to the Gentiles and appointed Peter in Judea. The Gentiles, already grown to maturity, could not be afflicted with the useless pain of circumcision, nor abstain from foods to which they had always been accustomed and which God had created for use. Nor could those who had believed from the Jews and had been circumcised, and who thought by custom, as though by a second nature, that they possessed more than the other nations, easily despise the things in which they gloried.

Accordingly, by God’s providence one apostle was given to the circumcised, appearing to acquiesce in the shadows of the law; another was appointed to those in uncircumcision, so that he would not regard the grace of the Gospel as slavery but as free faith. Thus no impediment to faith would arise under any pretext, and people would not fail to believe in Christ because of circumcision or uncircumcision.

Nor do we say that Peter, who himself in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts X) testified that no human being should be regarded as common or unclean, and who was taught through the vessel lowered from heaven by its four corners that it makes no difference whether someone is a Jew or a Gentile, forgot what came before and thought that the law ought to be observed in addition to the grace of the Gospel.

Rather, he pretended that he too was keeping the law in order gradually to lead the Jews away from their ancient manner of life. They could not suddenly reject so great a burden of observance and the most cautious conduct of their former life as though these were refuse and loss.

From this we understand why Peter, James, and John gave the right hands of fellowship to Paul and Barnabas: so that, amid different observances, the Gospel of Christ would not be thought to be different, but so that there might be one fellowship both of the circumcised and of those who had the foreskin.

He fittingly prepared the way by saying: “The one who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision.” This was so that no one would think that he was disparaging Peter. Rather, after first praising him, he showed that Peter accepted circumcision to some extent in order to win those who had been entrusted to him from the Jews and preserve them in the faith and Gospel of Christ.

He implies also that, if Peter did this blamelessly and observed for a time what was not lawful so as not to lose those entrusted to him, then Paul ought even more to do what had been entrusted to him for the truth of the Gospel among the uncircumcised, lest the Gentiles, deterred by the burden and difficulty of the law, withdraw from faith in Christ and belief in him.

(Ambrose) He names Peter alone and compares himself with him because Peter received primacy for founding the Church, while Paul too was chosen in like manner to have primacy in founding the churches of the Gentiles. Nevertheless, Peter would also preach to the Gentiles if the occasion required it, and Paul to the Jews; for each is found to have done both. Yet Peter’s full authority is recognized as having been given for preaching to Judaism, while Paul’s perfect authority is found in preaching to the Gentiles.

Hence he calls himself the teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth. Each received his portion according to his abilities and his assigned administration. For it was more difficult to draw those who were far from God to faith than those who were near.

(Jerome) “Peter,” he says, “and John and James, who seemed to be pillars.” Three times above we read this said about the apostles: “But separately to those who seemed to be something”; “From those who seemed to be something”; and “Those who seemed to be something contributed nothing to me.” I was therefore concerned to ask what he meant by “those who seemed.” But now he has freed me from every doubt by adding, “who seemed to be pillars.”

The apostles are therefore the pillars of the churches, especially Peter, James, and John. Two of these were deemed worthy to ascend the mountain with the Lord. One of them introduces the Savior speaking in the Apocalypse: “The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God” (Apoc. III), teaching that all believers who conquer the adversary can become pillars of the Church.

Writing to Timothy, Paul says: “So that you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth” (I Tim. III).

By these passages and others we are taught that the apostles, all believers, and the Church itself are called a pillar in Scripture. It makes no difference whether the reference is to the body or to its members, since the body is divided into members and the members belong to the body.

Thus Peter, James, and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave the right hands of fellowship to Paul and Barnabas, but they did not give them to Titus, who was with them. For he had not yet reached that measure at which the Lord’s wares could be entrusted to him on equal terms with his elders, nor could he occupy the same place in this commerce that Barnabas and Paul occupied.

“So that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcision—only that we should remember the poor, which I was also eager to do.”

(Jerome) The holy poor whose care was especially entrusted by the apostles to Paul and Barnabas are those who believed from the Jews and carried the prices of their possessions to the apostles’ feet, to be distributed to the needy. Or they may be those who, because they were regarded by their fellow tribesmen, relatives, and parents as deserters from the law and as believers in a crucified man, were considered objects of hatred and abomination.

The epistles of Paul bear witness to how greatly the holy apostle labored in their service: his letters to the Corinthians, to the Thessalonians, and to all the churches of the Gentiles, instructing them to prepare this gift and convey it to Jerusalem either personally or through others whom they approved. Hence he now says confidently that he was also eager to do this very thing.

The poor may also be understood in another way: those of whom it is said in the Gospel, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). Such people deserve to be remembered by the apostles.

There are also those poor of whom Solomon writes: “A man’s wealth is the ransom of his life, but the poor man does not endure a threat” (Prov. XIII). For he cannot hear the terror of future punishments—the poor man in faith, poor in grace, possessing neither spiritual riches nor knowledge of the Scriptures, which is compared with gold, silver, and precious stones.

Since “the healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Luke V), it was therefore fitting for the apostles also, in the communication of the right hands, not to despise the poor or look down on sinners, but always to remember them. Paul remembered the Corinthian man in this way: in his first epistle he had saddened him for a time, so that, while his body suffered through repentance, his spirit might be saved; in the second, lest he should be swallowed up by excessive sorrow, he recalled him to the Church, asking everyone to confirm their love for him and to forgive the brother, just as he himself had forgiven each of them in the presence of Christ. In this way he fulfilled the agreement he had made in Jerusalem, always to remember the poor. [Col. 0273A]

When Peter had come to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he was blameworthy. (Ambrose) After the harmony of their fellowship and the honor of primacy which, by God’s grace, they mutually accorded one another, the Apostles now appear to disagree among themselves because of an intervening matter of negligence or error—not in a private cause, but out of concern for the Church. “To his face,” he says, “I opposed him.” What does this mean except that I contradicted him in his presence? And for what reason does he add, “because he was blameworthy”? He was blameworthy, certainly, in relation to evangelical truth, which this action opposed. For who would dare resist Peter, the first of the Apostles, to whom the Lord gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven, unless it were another of such standing—one who, confident in his own election and knowing that he was not inferior, steadfastly condemned what Peter had done without consultation? [Col. 0273B]

(Gregory) There are, however, some who understand this not of Peter, the chief of the Apostles, but of another man named Peter, who was reproved by Paul. If they had read the words of the Apostle Paul more carefully, they would not say this. For when Paul was about to say, “When Peter had come to Antioch, I opposed him to his face,” in order to show of which Peter he was speaking, he prefaced his account with these words: “The Gospel of the uncircumcision was entrusted to me, just as the Gospel of the circumcision was entrusted to Peter; for he who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me among the Gentiles.” It is therefore clear which Peter Paul means: the one whom he calls an Apostle and whom he says presided over the Gospel of the circumcision.

There were also some who said that the second Epistle of Peter, in which Paul’s Epistles are praised, was not Peter’s. But if they had been willing to weigh the words of that Epistle, they could have formed a very different judgment. For it is written there: “A voice came down to him from the magnificent glory, of this kind: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’” (Matt. XVIII); and it is immediately added: “And we ourselves heard this voice when we were with him on the holy mountain.” Let them therefore read the Gospel, and they will immediately recognize that, when this voice came from heaven, the Apostle Peter was standing with the Lord on the mountain. It was therefore he who wrote this Epistle—the man who heard this voice from the Lord on the mountain.

Before certain men came from James, Peter ate with the Gentiles; but when they came, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision. The other Jews joined him in his dissimulation, so that even Barnabas was led along with them into that dissimulation. [Col. 0273C]

(Ambrose) All these Jews who consented to Peter’s and Barnabas’s dissimulation were people of good faith. But because of the scandal of those who came from James—for they were zealous for the Law and venerated the Law and Christ with equal devotion, which is contrary to the discipline of faith—they did not associate with the Gentiles in their presence. For they feared the attack of those who were zealous for the Law. If that had been all, it would not have been blameworthy; but what the error consisted in he shows in what follows. For Peter himself yielded to the hostility and boldness of the Jews, fearing that, through what is easy to introduce, a scandal might arise which would be difficult to settle. Thus he was compelled to purify himself according to the Law, and he circumcised Timothy against his will.

But when I saw that they were not walking by a straight path toward the truth of the Gospel, I said to Peter before them all. He attacks Peter alone so that the others might learn through the one who was first. “If you, though you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?”

Now he has disclosed the reason for the rebuke. There would have been no error if, in the presence of the Jews, Peter had refrained from associating with the Gentiles out of fear of scandal. But the whole reason for the rebuke is this: when the Jews came from James, Peter not only separated himself from those with whom he had lived as a Gentile, but also compelled them to Judaize, because of his fear of those men. Thus the Gentiles did not know which position was true. For they knew that he himself had not lived among them as a Jew; but afterward, hearing from him that they ought to follow the pattern of the Jews, they naturally hesitated about what was true. If it was true that they ought to Judaize, they regarded Peter as a transgressor, because he had lived as a Gentile. But if the other position was better and true—namely, that they should live simply and freely—then his cowardice was the ruin of the Gentiles, since, after the good had been taken away from them, a burdensome and ineffectual way of life was imposed upon them. [Col. 0273D]

The Apostle Paul, however, when he yielded for a time, did not approve this course; rather, he loudly declared that he was doing something superfluous and futile because of the fury of the Jews. He would not have yielded to this matter unless a circumstance had intervened in which the boldness of many Jews was making a show of itself. Timothy was the son of a Jewish woman but of a Greek father. For this reason, as an infant, he had not been circumcised according to the Law. They were therefore lying in wait, investigating whether Paul would receive as uncircumcised one who had been born a Jew—a thing they considered unlawful for the Jewish people—and seeking an opportunity by which they might regard him as a subverter of the Law. For this reason he yielded for a time to their fury.

(Jerome) An example from Jehu, king of Israel, teaches us that a useful dissimulation may be assumed at the proper time. Jehu could not have killed the priests of Baal unless he had pretended that he wished to worship the idol, saying: “Gather all the priests of Baal for me. For if Ahab served Baal a little, I will serve him much” (2 Kings X). So too David, when he changed his appearance before Abimelech, who dismissed him and let him go. Nor is it surprising that righteous men should sometimes dissimulate for a time for the sake of their own salvation and that of others, since the Lord himself, although he had no sin and no sinful flesh, assumed the likeness of sinful flesh, so that, by condemning sin in the flesh, he might make us the righteousness of God.

Paul had certainly read in the Gospel that the Lord commanded: “If your brother sins against you, go and correct him between yourself and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother” (Matt. XVIII; Luke XVII). Since the Lord had commanded that this should be done even in the case of the least of the brethren, how did Paul dare to rebuke the greatest of the Apostles so openly, so boldly, and so steadfastly, unless Peter himself had been willing to be rebuked in this way and Paul was not doing him an injury? Paul had previously said: “I went to Jerusalem to see Peter, and I remained with him fifteen days; but I saw none of the other Apostles” (Gal. I). [Col. 0274A]

“If you,” he says, “though you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?” By an unanswerable argument he binds Peter—or rather, through Peter, those who were compelling him to do contradictory things. “If you, Peter,” he says, “are a Jew by nature, circumcised from childhood and observing all the precepts of the Law, and now, because of the grace of Christ, know that these things have no usefulness in themselves but are patterns and images of things to come; and if you eat with those who are from the Gentiles, living no longer superstitiously as before but freely and without distinction, how can you now withdraw from those who have believed from among the Gentiles, separating and distinguishing yourself from them as though they were contaminated, and compel them to Judaize?

“For if those from whom you withdraw are unclean, and you withdraw from them because they do not have circumcision, then you compel them to be circumcised and to become Jews, although you yourself, born a Jew, have lived as a Gentile.” He also discreetly reveals the reason why he argued against Peter: namely, that by his dissimulation he was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize, since they wished to imitate him.

(Augustine) When Peter came to Antioch, Paul rebuked him—not because Peter observed the customs of the Jews, in which he had been born and educated, although he did not observe them among the Gentiles, but because he wished to impose them upon the Gentiles when he saw that certain people had come from James, that is, from Judea; for James presided over the Church of Jerusalem. Fearing those who still thought that salvation consisted in those observances, Peter separated himself from the Gentiles and pretended to consent to the others in imposing those burdens of servitude upon the Gentiles. This is sufficiently clear from the words of his rebuke. Paul did not say, “If you, though you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, why do you return again to the custom of the Jews?” Rather, he said, “How do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?”

The fact that he said this to Peter before them all was necessary, so that all might be healed by Peter’s rebuke. It was not useful to correct in private an error that was openly harmful. In addition, Peter’s weakness and charity—for the Lord had said to him three times, “Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep”—readily endured such a rebuke from a later shepherd for the salvation of the flock. For the one who was rebuked was himself more admirable than his rebuker and more difficult to imitate. It is easier to see what ought to be corrected in another and to correct it by blaming or rebuking him than to see what ought to be corrected in oneself and willingly to be corrected—whether by oneself, and still more by another; and that another a later figure, and before them all. [Col. 0274B]

This provides a great example of humility, which is the supreme discipline of Christianity. Charity is preserved by humility, for nothing violates it more quickly than pride. Therefore the Lord did not say: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I raise four-day-old corpses from the tomb, drive all demons from human bodies, and remove diseases, and other things of this kind.” Rather, he said: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI). Those signs are signs of spiritual realities. But to be gentle and humble, as the preserver of charity, belongs to the spiritual realities themselves. Through those signs, people whose bodily eyes are devoted to visible things are led toward them; since they cannot seek faith in invisible things from familiar and customary matters, they seek it from new and sudden visible signs.

If those who were compelling the Gentiles to Judaize had learned to be gentle and humble in heart—the lesson Peter had learned from the Lord—then, at least when such a great man was corrected, they would have been invited to imitate him. They would not have thought that the Gospel of Christ had been repaid to them as though it were a debt owed to their own righteousness. Rather, knowing that a person is not justified by works of the Law except through faith in Jesus Christ, and that the works of the Law are fulfilled with faith assisting human weakness—not by one’s own merit but by God’s grace—they would not have demanded from the Gentiles the carnal observances of the Law. They would have understood that through the very grace of faith the Gentiles could fulfill the spiritual works of the Law.

For when anyone attributes the works of the Law to his own powers, rather than to the grace of the merciful God, “no flesh will be justified” (Rom. III). This means every human being, or all who understand things carnally. Therefore those who, although already under the Law, believed in Christ did not come because they were righteous, but in order to be justified, and so they came to the grace of faith. [Col. 0274C]

The Jews had imposed the name “sinners” upon the Gentiles out of an ancient pride, as though they themselves were righteous, seeing the splinter in another’s eye and not the beam in their own. Following their manner of speaking, the Apostle says: “We are Jews by nature and not sinners from the Gentiles.”

(Augustine) That is, we are those whom they call sinners, although they themselves are sinners. “We,” he says, “who are Jews by nature, not being Gentiles whom they call sinners, nevertheless believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ. They would not have sought to be justified unless they had been sinners. Or did they sin because they wished to be justified in Christ? If they were already righteous, then by seeking something else they certainly sinned.”

Knowing, however, that a person is not justified by works of the Law but through faith in Jesus Christ, we too believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ and not by works of the Law.

(Jerome) “A Jew by nature” is one who is descended from Abraham and was circumcised by his parents on the eighth day. He is not a Jew by nature who was later made one from among the Gentiles.

(Ambrose) He demonstrates by a clear argument that they had been deceived into observing the Law, in which no one is justified before God. For those who are Jews by nature, wishing to be justified, abandon the Law and flee to faith in Christ, since “no flesh will be justified by works of the Law.” He says that no human being is justified by works of the Law; for whoever is righteous is justified by faith, as were Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other saints.

(Jerome) To gather the whole argument into a brief statement, its sense is as follows. “We”—that is, I and you, Peter—for Paul joined himself to Peter so that he would not appear to be doing him an injury—“when we were Jews by nature, doing what the Law commanded, and not sinners from the Gentiles”—who are sinners either generally because they serve idols or because, as we now suppose, they were considered unclean—“knowing that we could not be saved by the work of the Law but by the faith of Christ, believed in Christ, so that what the Law had not given us, faith might provide, the faith we possessed in Christ.
