“But if, leaving the Law in which we could not be saved, we have passed over to faith, in which circumcision of the flesh is not sought but the pure devotion of the heart, and if by now withdrawing from the Gentiles we act as though everyone who is not circumcised is unclean, then the faith in Christ in which we previously thought we were saved is more a minister of sin than of righteousness, since it abolishes circumcision, and whoever does not possess circumcision is unclean.

“But far be it from me to claim again what I once destroyed and knew had not benefited me. Once departing from the Law, I died to the Law so that I might live in Christ. I was fastened to his cross and, reborn as a new person, subsisted by faith rather than by the flesh, and went out of the world with Christ. What I once undertook, I hold fast. Christ did not die for me in vain; my faith in him would be futile if I could have been saved without his faith while remaining in the old Law.

“Knowing,” he says, “that a person is not justified by works of the Law except through faith in Jesus Christ, we too believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ and not by works of the Law.”

Some say that, if what Paul asserts is true—namely, that no one is justified by works of the Law but by faith in Jesus Christ—then the patriarchs, prophets, and saints who lived before Christ’s coming must have been imperfect. We must remind them that Paul is speaking here of those who have not attained righteousness because they believe they can be justified by works alone. The ancient saints, however, were justified by faith in Christ. Abraham “saw Christ’s day and rejoiced” (John VIII); Moses “considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt” (Heb. XI), for he looked toward the reward; and Isaiah saw the glory of Christ, as the evangelist John recalls (John XII). Jude speaks generally of all of them: “I wish to remind you, though you know all things once for all, that Jesus, having saved the people from the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe” (Jude 5).

Thus it is not so much the works of the Law that are condemned as those who trust that they can be justified by works alone. The Savior also says to the disciples: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). [Col. 0274D]

In this passage we must consider how many precepts there are in the Law, which no one can fulfill. Conversely, we must say that some things prescribed by the Law are also done by those who do not know the Law; but those who perform them are not justified because they do them without faith in Christ. For example: not sleeping with another man with the intercourse proper to a woman; not committing adultery; not stealing; rather, honoring father and mother and performing the other things that are commanded.

If they bring forward examples from holy men, saying that men versed in the Law carried out the things prescribed by the Law, we reply that “the Law is not laid down for the righteous but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the unholy and profane” (1 Tim. I). Whoever has been taught by God does not need even to be taught charity, since Paul says: “Concerning charity, I have no need to write to you, for you yourselves are taught by God to love one another” (1 Thess. IV).

Therefore no flesh will be justified by works of the Law. (Jerome) That flesh will not be justified by works of the Law of which it is written: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. XL). But that flesh will be justified by faith in Jesus Christ of which it is said in the mystery of the resurrection: “All flesh will see the salvation of God” (Luke III). In a humbler interpretation, however, it was formerly not all flesh that was justified by the Law, but only those people who were in Palestine; now all flesh is justified by faith in Christ, while his Church is established throughout the whole world.

But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves were also found to be sinners, is Christ therefore a minister of sin? Far from it. [Col. 0278B]

(Ambrose) How can Christ be a minister of sin, when he forgives sins? “Far from it,” he says. But if, while wishing to be justified through faith in Christ, we serve the Law, we confess that we are under sin, because faith draws a person away from the Law so that he may be righteous. Therefore, if we give ourselves to the Law, we are found to be sinners, because those who are under the Law are under a curse. But if this is so, he says, is Christ therefore a minister of sin?

(Augustine) They certainly cannot say this, because even those who wished the Gospel to be delivered only to circumcised Gentiles had believed in Christ. Therefore, when Paul says “Far from it,” he says it not alone but together with them. He destroyed the pride that gloried in works of the Law—pride that ought to be and could be destroyed—lest the grace of faith appear unnecessary if people believed that the works of the Law could justify even without it. [Col. 0278C]

Therefore he is a transgressor if he builds those things again, saying that the works of the Law justify even without grace, so that Christ is found to be a minister of sin. “For if I rebuild the things that I destroyed, I establish myself as a transgressor.”

(Ambrose) The matter is clear: when a person approaches Christ, he abandons the Law, for from being a slave he becomes free. If he returns again to the Law, he himself becomes his own accuser, because he condemns his own action.

(Augustine) What then? Because you previously opposed the faith of Christ, O Paul, do you make yourself a transgressor by building up what you now build? But Paul did not destroy the Law, because it cannot be destroyed; rather, he had truly destroyed—and steadfastly continued to destroy—the pride that gloried in it, because that pride could be destroyed. Therefore the transgressor is not the one who, having tried to destroy something true and afterward recognizing it to be true and indestructible, holds fast to it so that it may be built upon. The transgressor is the one who, having destroyed something false because it can be destroyed, builds it again.

For through the Law I died to the Law, so that I might live for God. (Ambrose) He says this because through the law of faith he died to the Law of Moses. For the person who is liberated from the Law dies to the Law and lives for God, whose servant he becomes after being purchased by Christ.

(Augustine) He says that he died to the Law so that he would no longer be under the Law, but nevertheless he died through the Law—either because he was a Jew and had received the Law as a tutor, as he later makes clear. The purpose of a tutor is that the tutor eventually becomes unnecessary, just as an infant is nourished by breasts so that he may no longer need breasts, and one reaches one’s homeland by ship so that the ship is no longer needed.

Or he died to the Law through the Law understood spiritually, so that he would not live under it carnally. For he wished them to die to the Law in this manner when he shortly afterward says to them: “Tell me, you who wish to be under the Law, have you not read the Law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons,” and so forth (Gal. IV; Gen. XXI)—so that, through the same Law understood spiritually, they might die to the carnal observances of the Law.

When he adds, “so that I might live for God,” he lives for God who is under God; but he lives for the Law who is under the Law. A person lives under the Law insofar as he is a sinner, that is, insofar as he has not been changed from the old person. He lives by his own life, and therefore the Law is above him, because whoever does not fulfill it is beneath it. [Col. 0279A]

For the Law is not laid down for the righteous—that is, it is not imposed so that it may be above them. The righteous person is rather in the Law than under the Law, because he does not live by his own life, the life against which the Law is imposed as a restraint. To put it another way, the person who lives justly with love of righteousness lives, in a certain sense, by the Law itself—not rejoicing in a private and transient good, but in a common and abiding good.

Therefore the Law did not need to be imposed upon Paul, who says: “I live, yet no longer I; Christ lives in me.” Who, then, would dare impose the Law upon Christ, who lives in Paul? No one would dare say that Christ does not live rightly, so that a Law would have to be imposed upon him to restrain him.

(Jerome) It is one thing to die through the Law and another to die to the Law. Whoever dies to the Law was previously living for it, observing Sabbaths, new moons, and feast days, the typological elaboration of sacrifices, Jewish fables, and genealogies. But after Christ came, and after the Law of which it is written, “We know that the Law is spiritual” (Rom. VII), he died to the former Law through the evangelical Law.

The soul which, according to what is written to the Romans, “if it had married while her husband was alive, was called an adulteress” (Rom. VII), after the death of her husband—that is, the old Law—married the spiritual Law, so that she might bear fruit for God. Hence in Hosea it is said to her: “From me your fruit has been found” (Hos. XIV). To this is beautifully added that mystical saying: “Who is wise and will understand these things? Or intelligent and will know them?”

Whoever, therefore, dies through the spiritual Law to the Law of the letter lives for God, since he is not without the Law of God but is in the Law of Christ. Whoever dies to the Law because of sins is indeed dead, but it cannot be said of him that which follows: “so that he might live for God.” [Col. 0279B]

The Apostle also teaches elsewhere that there is another spiritual Law beyond the Law of the letter, saying: “Therefore the Law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good” (Rom. VII). Ezekiel likewise speaks in the person of God: “I brought them,” he says—that is, the people of the Jews—“out of the land of Egypt, and I led them into the wilderness, and I gave them my commandments and showed them my judgments, which a person shall do and live by them” (Ezek. XX).

But concerning that Law which produces wrath, to which the Apostle also died, he afterward says: “I also gave them commandments that were not good, and judgments by which they would not live.” The same distinction is signified in the Psalter: “For I did not understand the writing; I will enter into the strength of the Lord.”

I have been crucified with Christ. Because he had said that through the Law he had died to the Law, he now shows how he had died: “I have been crucified with Christ.” He took up his cross and followed Christ, and in that very passion he prayed: “Remember me when you come into your kingdom.” Immediately he heard: “Today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke XXIII).

If someone, with his members mortified upon the earth and dead to the world, has been conformed to the death of Jesus Christ, he is crucified with Jesus and fastens the trophy of his mortification to the wood of the Lord’s passion.

(Ambrose) Whoever does not do the things of the world or of error is dead to the world.

I live, yet no longer I; Christ lives in me. There is no doubt that, in one who is liberated from death through faith, Christ lives. While he gives forgiveness to one who deserves death, Christ himself lives in that person, since the person has been rescued from death by Christ’s protection. [Col. 0280B]

(Jerome) The one who formerly lived in the Law does not live—he who persecuted the Church. But Christ lives in him: Christ who is wisdom, strength, the Word, peace, joy, and the other virtues. Whoever does not possess these cannot say: “Christ lives in me.” Paul says all this in his own person while arguing against Peter about Peter.

(Augustine) Hear the Apostle Paul denying himself: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.” Hear him still denying himself: “I live, yet not I.” “Not I live”—an explicit denial of himself. But now follows the glorious confession of Christ: “Christ lives in me.” What, then, does “deny yourself” mean? Do not yourself live in yourself. What does “do not yourself live in yourself” mean? Do not do your own will, but the will of him who dwells in you.

But the life that I now live in the flesh, I live in faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me. [Col. 0280C]

(Ambrose) Since future life has been promised to Christians, whoever now lives in this life fortified by the helps of God lives in faith in the promised life. Here he contemplates an image of that life, possessing, as it were, a pledge of the future life, which has been obtained for us through God’s will by the love of Christ.

(Jerome) It is one thing to be in the flesh and another to live in the flesh. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God; hence it is said to those who live well: “But you are not in the flesh” (Rom. VIII). “In faith,” he says, “I live in the Son of God and in Christ, who loved me and gave himself for me.”

In the Epistle to the Romans he speaks of God, saying that he did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us. Here, however, he speaks of Christ, saying that Christ himself gave himself up: “He loved me,” he says, “and gave himself for me.”

In the Gospel, where the Apostles are listed, it is added: “and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.” Again, in the same Gospel: “Behold, he has drawn near who will betray me” (Mark X; Matt. XXVI). Concerning the chief priests and elders of the people, Scripture records that they condemned Jesus to death, bound him, led him away, and delivered him to Pilate the governor. And afterward concerning Pilate: “He released Barabbas to them, but Jesus he scourged and delivered to them to be crucified” (Matt. XXVII).

Thus the Father delivered up the Son, the Son himself delivered himself up, Judas delivered him, and the priests delivered him to the rulers; finally, Pilate himself, after receiving him to be delivered up, delivered him up. But the Father delivered him up in order to save the lost world; Jesus himself delivered himself up in order to carry out the will of the Father and his own will; Judas, the priests, the elders of the people, and Pilate delivered the author of life to death without understanding what they were doing. [Col. 0280D]

(Augustine) Since Christ himself also gave himself up for our salvation, you see that we must consider not what a person does but with what disposition and will he does it. In the same action we find God the Father and Judas: we bless the Father and detest Judas; we bless the charity and detest the wickedness.

For how great a benefit was bestowed upon the human race when Christ was delivered up! Did Judas think of this when he delivered him? God thought of our salvation, because we have been redeemed. Judas thought of the price for which he sold the Lord. The Son himself thought of the price he gave for us; Judas thought of the price he received in order to sell him. Thus different intentions make different actions, even when the external deed is one. If we measure it by the intentions, we find one thing to be loved and the other condemned, one glorified and the other detested.

“But the life that I now live,” he says, “in the flesh”—because he could not say that Christ was still living a mortal life; and life in the flesh is mortal—“I live in faith in the Son of God,” so that Christ may also live in the believer by dwelling in the inner person through faith, and afterward fill him through vision, when mortality has been swallowed up by life.

To show that Christ lives in him, and that while living in the flesh he lives in faith in the Son of God, Paul makes clear that this is not his own merit but Christ’s grace: “He loved me,” he says, “and gave himself for me.” For whom did he give himself, if not for a sinner, in order to justify him? Paul says this although he had been born and educated as a Jew and had been even more zealous for the traditions of his fathers. Therefore, if Christ gave himself even for such people, they too were sinners. Let them not say that this was given to them because of the merits of their righteousness, as though what was not needed had been given to the righteous. For the Lord says: “I have not come to call the righteous but sinners”—specifically so that they might no longer be sinners.

(Jerome) Very blessed and fortunate is the person in whom Christ lives and who, through each thought and action, can say: “I live in faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.”

I do not reject the grace of God. For if righteousness comes through the Law, then Christ died for nothing. [Col. 0281C]

(Ambrose) Therefore the person who perseveres in Christ’s faith is not ungrateful to Christ. He knows that he has received no benefit except from Christ, and that it would be an insult to Christ if he compared him with another whose help he could not have received. “For if righteousness comes through the Law,” he says, “then Christ died for nothing.”

Nothing could be clearer. If a person could have been justified through the Law, Christ ought not to have died. But because the Law could neither grant remission of sins nor, triumphing over the second death, strip the captives whom the cause of sin held captive, Christ died in order to provide what the Law could not. Therefore he did not die for nothing, for his death is the justification of sinners.

(Jerome) The one who rejects the grace of God is both the person who, after the Gospel, lives according to the Law and the person who, after baptism, defiles himself with sins. But whoever can say with the Apostle, “His grace toward me was not empty” (1 Cor. XV), can also say confidently: “I will not reject the grace of God.”

What follows is especially necessary against those who think that, after faith in Christ, the precepts of the Law must still be observed. We must say to them: if righteousness comes through the Law, then Christ died for nothing. Or else let them explain how Christ did not die for nothing if works justify. But although they are dull-witted, they will not dare say that Christ died without cause.

Accordingly, from the part of the syllogism proposed here—“For if righteousness comes through the Law, then Christ died for nothing”—we must take up what follows necessarily and cannot be denied: Christ did not die for nothing. We must then conclude: righteousness therefore does not come through the Law. [Col. 0282A]

Up to this point he has argued against Peter; now he returns to the Galatians.

## CHAPTER III

The Galatians are rebuked; the Apostle demonstrates the imperfection of the Mosaic Law and says that righteousness comes through faith, while also explaining the usefulness of the Law.

O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you? [Col. 0282B]

(Ambrose) These are the words of an angry man, expressed with astonishment, because they had been so corrupted that they did not even recognize that they had been deceived. He has used a proem, for everyone who is bewitched passes from good to evil. So too they had passed from freedom and security into servitude and anxiety.

(Jerome) This passage can be understood in two ways. The Galatians may have been called foolish because they came from greater things to lesser ones, having begun with the Spirit and now being brought to completion in the flesh. Or the reason may be that each province has its own characteristics. The Apostle confirms that the Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies, as the poet Epimenides truly called them. The Latin historian attacks the frivolous Moors and fierce Dalmatians; all poets disparage the timid Phrygians. Philosophers boast that more capable intellects are born at Athens. Cicero taunts the Greeks before Gaius Caesar as “either frivolous Greeks or savage barbarians.” In his speech For Flaccus he says, “Inborn frivolity and cultivated vanity.” All Scripture reproves Israel for being heavy-hearted and stiff-necked.

In this way, then, I think the Apostle also attacked the Galatians on account of the characteristic of their region. Some, however, involving themselves in profound questions, almost under the pretext of avoiding the heresy that posits different natures, say that Tyrians, Sidonians, Moabites, Ammonites, Idumeans, Babylonians, and Egyptians, and all the nations named in Scripture, possess certain peculiarities derived from preceding causes and from the merit of their former deeds. Otherwise, they say, God’s justice would be called into question, since each nation is asserted to possess either some good or some evil that another does not possess. [Col. 0282C]

Avoiding these lofty speculations, we shall follow what was said above. We may say either that the Galatians are accused of foolishness because they cannot distinguish the spirit of the Law from its letter, or that they are rebuked for the fault of their nation because they are unteachable and senseless, slower to attain wisdom.

As for what follows—“Who has bewitched you?”—we should explain it in a manner worthy of Paul, who, although untrained in speech, was not untrained in knowledge. We should not suppose that he knew there was a form of bewitchment popularly believed to cause harm; rather, he used a familiar expression and, as elsewhere, adopted here too a word from ordinary conversation.

We read in Sirach: “The gift of the envious tortures the eyes” (Ecclus. XX). The person whom we call “envious” is more expressively called in Greek a *fascinator*—one who casts the evil eye. And in the Wisdom written under Solomon’s name: “The bewitching of wickedness obscures good things” (Wis. IV). These examples teach us either that the envious person is tormented by another’s happiness, or that a person who possesses some good is harmed by another who bewitches him—that is, envies him.

It is said that the evil eye especially harms infants and young children, and those who have not yet planted their steps firmly. Hence one of the Gentiles also said:

> I do not know what eye bewitches my tender lambs.

[Col. 0283A]

[Col. 0283B] Whether this is true or not, God will see to it; for it may happen that demons also serve this sin, and that, whenever they recognize that someone has begun or made progress in God’s work, they turn him away from good works. For the present, the point at issue is that we think the example has been taken from popular belief: just as tender age is said to be harmed by the evil eye, so the Galatians, newly born and nourished in faith in Christ with milk rather than solid food, may have been harmed as though by some such fascination, and, with the stomach of their faith nauseated, may have vomited up the food of the Holy Spirit.

If anyone objects, let him explain how the following were likewise taken from common opinion: the Valley of the Titans in the Books of Kings (II Kings XXIII), sirens and onocentaurs in Isaiah (Isa. XIII, XXXIV), Arcturus, Orion, and the Pleiades in Job (Job XXXVIII), and other things of this kind—names which certainly have their causes and origins in the fables of the Gentiles.

“Before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly displayed.” (Amb.) It is clear that Christ appears publicly displayed before the eyes of fools—that is, stripped or condemned. Before the eyes and understanding of the wise, however, he appears not only not condemned, but himself to have condemned death by his cross. For the Lord’s passion is our life and the destruction of death.

But because these people had begun to think wrongly after being transferred to the law, he complains that Christ seemed to their minds to have been condemned; therefore he added: “He was crucified among you.” That is, he was crucified according to your understanding, as though he were merely a man. For where there is no complete hope, there is a man. Thus they did not think that salvation was complete in Christ, because they equated the law with him. But in those who understand Christ rightly, Christ lives in them.

“In Photinus he was crucified.” For Photinus is truly dead, in whom Christ is said to have been crucified, since this is brought forward here as an accusation.

(Hier.) Alternatively: “He was crucified among you.” Christ was rightly publicly displayed before us, for the entire chorus of the prophets foretells his gibbet and passion, with blows and scourging, so that we may know his cross—not merely from the Gospel, in which he is reported to have been crucified, but from long before he deigned to descend to earth and assume the human being who was crucified.

Nor is the praise of the Galatians small, since they believed in the crucified one in such a way that he had already been publicly displayed before them: that is, by diligently reading the prophets and recognizing all the mysteries of the old law, they came to faith by a proper path and sequence.

[Col. 0284A] (Aug.) After saying, “Jesus Christ was publicly displayed,” he added, “crucified,” so that this would move them especially when they considered at what price he had purchased the possession that he was losing in them—for it would have been little merely that he had died freely, as he had said above. The former statement sounds as though he had not reached the possession for which he had given his blood. When someone is publicly proscribed, however, even what he possessed is taken away.

Yet this proscription does not harm Christ, who even in this way is, through his divinity, Lord of all; it harms the possession itself, which lacks the cultivation of this grace. From this point he begins to demonstrate how the grace of faith is sufficient for justification without the works of the law, lest anyone should say that he did not attribute the whole justification of humanity solely to the works of the law, but neither to the grace of faith alone; rather, that salvation was perfected from both.

But, for this question to be treated carefully, lest anyone be deceived by ambiguity, he must first know that the works of the law are of two kinds. Some belong to ritual observances, others to morality. Circumcision of the flesh, the temporal Sabbath, new moons, sacrifices, and all the countless observances of this kind belong to ritual. To morality belong: “You shall not kill,” “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not bear false witness,” and the other commandments of this sort.

Can the Apostle therefore be so unconcerned whether a Christian is a murderer or adulterer, or chaste and innocent, as he is unconcerned whether he is circumcised in the flesh or uncircumcised? Here, then, he is dealing chiefly with those works of the law that belong to ritual observances, although he indicates that he sometimes introduces the others as well.

Toward the end of the epistle he will treat separately those matters that belong to morality. He treats the former at greater length and the latter briefly. For the ritual observances impose burdens especially upon the Gentiles, whose usefulness lies in understanding them: all these things are explained to Christians so that they may understand what they signify, although they are not compelled to perform them.

In observances, however, if they are not understood, there is only slavery, as there was among the Jewish people and still is to this day. But if they are both observed and understood, they do no harm; indeed, they can be of some benefit if they correspond to the proper time, just as Moses himself and the prophets observed them in ways appropriate to that people, for whom such slavery was still useful, so that they might be kept under restraint by fear.

Nothing terrifies the soul so devoutly as an uninterpreted sacrament; once understood, however, it produces devout joy, and it is celebrated freely if the time requires it. If it is not required, it is merely read and discussed with spiritual delight. Every sacrament, when understood, refers either to contemplation of the truth or to good morals. Contemplation of the truth is founded upon love of God alone; good morals upon love of God and neighbor, upon which two commandments the whole law and the prophets depend.

Let us therefore see how circumcision of the flesh and the other works of the law of this kind are not necessary where the grace of faith is already present.

“This alone I wish to learn from you: did you receive the Spirit from the works of the law, or from hearing with faith?” The answer is certainly: from hearing with faith. For faith was preached to them by the Apostle, and in that preaching they surely perceived the coming and foreknowledge of the Holy Spirit, just as at that time, at the beginning of the invitation to faith, the presence of the Holy Spirit was also manifested through visible miracles, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles.

This had happened among the Galatians before these people came to corrupt and circumcise them. The meaning, then, is this: if your salvation depended upon those works of the law, the Holy Spirit would not have been given to you until after you had been circumcised.

Then he added: “Are you so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now being completed by the flesh?” This is what he had said earlier, at the beginning: unless some people are disturbing you and wishing to transform the Gospel of Christ. Disturbance is contrary to order. The order is to rise from carnal things to spiritual things, not to fall from spiritual things to carnal things, as had happened to them. This is a backward transformation of the Gospel; and since it is not good, it is not the Gospel when this is proclaimed.

“So foolish,” he says, “are you, that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now being completed by the flesh?”

(Amb.) He is still speaking with the metaphor of the stomach, for he is deeply grieved over their error: he saw that the structure he had built in them through the Gospel was being destroyed. He was not so disturbed by the Corinthians, because, although he called them carnal, they had not been so completely deranged in mind as to allow themselves to be circumcised.

Thus these people are also called foolish and without understanding, because they were unable even to take care of the pain of their flesh; for a person is usually led as far as what gives pleasure or does not cause pain. The words, therefore, are those of one asking a question, and what he asks confirms his point in part, when he says: “This alone I wish to learn from you: did you receive the Spirit from the works of the law, or from hearing with faith?”

He asks them about something in which they also gloried and which they could not deny, because they had received the Holy Spirit through faith, not through the law. Thus, coming to their senses, they might recognize that they had received the gift of God in which they gloried not from the work of the law, but by believing in Christ, and so, at least in this way, might show gratitude to Christ by abandoning the law, which they had learned was of no benefit to them.

He sets before them what at that time could not be denied: that the Spirit of God dwells in believers. For this gift of God was manifested to human beings in order to commend the rudiments of faith, just as it happened at the very beginning among the Apostles and the other disciples.

It also happened among those twelve who, because they had not been baptized but polluted in an adulterous baptism under the name of John’s baptism, were commanded by the Apostle Paul to be baptized in the name of the Trinity. When hands were laid upon them, the Holy Spirit fell upon them and supplied them with speech in various languages, together with their interpretation, so that no one would dare deny that the Holy Spirit was in them.

For this reason he calls the Galatians without understanding: although they knew and were conscious of this fact, they degraded themselves by submitting to the care of the flesh.

“Having begun,” he says, “with the Spirit, are you now being completed by the flesh?” He says this because, although the ascent of faith is from lower things to the highest, they, in contrast, had fallen from the heights to the depths. For having become spiritual through faith, they turned back to the law and lost the grace of the Spirit that they had obtained. “Completion” signifies destruction—that is, the loss of faith.

(Hieron.) Let us consider carefully that he did not say: “I wish to learn from you whether you received the Spirit from works,” but added, “from works of the law.” For he knew that the centurion Cornelius (Acts X) had received the Spirit from works, but not from works of the law, which he did not know.

But if the contrary is asserted—“Then can the Spirit also be received without hearing with faith?”—we shall answer that Cornelius did indeed receive the Spirit, but from hearing with faith and from the natural law, which speaks in our hearts of the good things that ought to be done and the evils that ought to be avoided. Through this law we previously reported that Abraham, Moses, and the other saints were justified. The observance of works and the righteousness of the law can subsequently increase it, but not the carnal law that has passed away; rather, the spiritual law.

[Col. 0286B] For the law is spiritual. Nor, because we give faith precedence, do we destroy the works of the law; nor do we say, as some do, “Let us do evil until good things come” (Rom. III), whose condemnation is just. Rather, we place grace before slavery, and say that what the Jews do out of fear, we do out of love: they are slaves, we are sons. They are compelled to do good; we willingly embrace the good.

Therefore, faith in Christ does not produce license to sin. Instead, love arising from faith increases the desire for good works: we do good not because we fear the judge, but because we know that these things please the one in whom we believe.

Someone may ask: if faith comes only from hearing, how can those born deaf become Christians? A person can understand God the Father from the greatness and beauty of created things, and the Creator can consequently be recognized from his works. But Christ’s birth, cross, death, and resurrection cannot be known except through hearing. Therefore either deaf people are not Christians, or, if deaf people are Christians, what the Apostle says elsewhere is false: “Thus faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of God” (Rom. X).

To anyone content with a simple answer to this difficulty, one may say that he did not speak generally, saying, “Everyone’s faith is from hearing,” but rather, “Faith is from hearing,” which can be understood both in part and in whole—namely, the faith of those who hear and who believe.

But whoever tries to resolve this difficulty will first attempt to assert that deaf people can learn the Gospel through signs, daily interaction, and, so to speak, through the speaking gestures of the whole body. Then he may also say that the word of God, to which nothing is deaf, speaks especially to those ears of which he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. XI); and in the Apocalypse: “Whoever has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Apoc. II).

And Isaiah says: “The Lord added an ear to me.” This is the other human being, to whom God speaks in secret, who cries out in the heart of the believer, “Abba, Father.” And, as we have often explained, just as the body has all its members and senses, so the soul also has all its senses and members, including ears. Whoever has these will have little need of the ears of the body to understand the Gospel of Christ.

[Col. 0287A] At the same time, observe also that here “spirit,” without any addition, is understood to mean “Holy Spirit,” whom we receive as God’s gift and not as a human gift. Of him it is written elsewhere: “The incorruptible Spirit is in all things” (Wis. XII). And: “The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit” (Rom. VIII). And in another place: “No one knows the things that are in a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him.” And in Daniel: “Bless the Lord, spirits and souls of the righteous” (Dan. III).

“So foolish,” he says, “are you, that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now being completed by the flesh?” If the Galatians had received the Holy Spirit, how were they foolish? The answer is immediately given: they had indeed begun with the Spirit, but when they were being completed by the flesh, the Spirit had been taken away from them.

Therefore they suffered all those things they suffered for no reason. To prevent this from happening to him after sin, David prays: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. L).

Pay close attention: the person who follows the Scriptures according to the letter is said to be completed by the flesh. Therefore what is written to the Corinthians—“Though living in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh” (II Cor. X)—can better be understood in this way: those who explain the Old Testament in a humble manner are said to wage war in the flesh; those who follow the spiritual meaning are indeed in the flesh, because they have the same letter as the Jews, but they do not wage war according to the flesh, since they pass over from flesh to spirit.

“You suffered so many things for no reason—if indeed for no reason.”

(Amb.) He indicates that they suffered many things for the sake of faith from unbelievers. At that time those who believed were a reproach to the others, whether household members or outsiders, for they were pointed out with the finger as though guilty of treason against the divine majesty. Thus the Galatians likewise suffered many things and experienced people who were even more irrational; they had lost the reward of these sufferings by submitting themselves to the law.

(Aug.) They had already endured many things for the sake of faith, not through fear, as though placed under the law, but rather, in their very sufferings, they had overcome fear through love, because the love of God had been poured into their hearts through the Holy Spirit whom they had received.

Therefore, he says, you suffered so many things for no reason—you who, after so much had been endured in you through love, wish to fall back into fear? But because he added, “if indeed for no reason,” he showed that he hoped they could be restored.

(Hieron.) Let us consider the wretched Jews, how superstitiously and laboriously they live under their observances among the other nations, saying: “Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle.” Thus we shall prove true what he says: “You suffered so many things for no reason.” Yet the sentence is not immediately softened or made doubtful by the words “if indeed for no reason,” because this is said of those who are able to return from the law to the Gospel.

It can be understood better in this way: the Galatians, having first believed in the Crucified One, suffered many reproaches from Jews and Gentiles and endured no small persecutions. They are rightly accused of having suffered these things in vain if they withdraw from the grace of Christ, for whose sake they suffered so much.

At the same time there is this hope: whoever has labored for the faith of Christ and afterward fallen into sin is said, while he sins, to have suffered his former trials in vain; but if he returns to his former faith and [Col. 0288A] former devotion, he will not lose those sufferings.

“Therefore, does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do this from works of the law, or from hearing with faith?”

“Supplies” means “administers”; it should be read as a present-tense verb, so that it may be shown that the Holy Spirit is continually ministered to those who are worthy, hour by hour and moment by moment.

The more someone advances in God’s work and love, the more he has within himself the powers of the Holy Spirit. These powers are brought to completion by hearing with faith, not by works of the law—not because the works of the law are to be despised and a simple faith sought without them, but because those very works are adorned by faith in Christ.

That wise man’s saying is well known: it is not the faithful person who lives from righteousness, but the righteous person who lives from faith.

At the same time, he shows that the Galatians, after receiving the Holy Spirit through faith, possessed gifts of power—namely prophecy, kinds of tongues, healings of diseases, and other gifts listed among the spiritual gifts in the letter to the Corinthians. Yet after all this, perhaps because they did not possess the grace of discerning spirits, they were ensnared by false teachers.

(Amb.) The distinguishing marks of power are added as witnesses to the faith, showing that it is a faithful and reasonable hope. But no power accompanies the law that might draw people to hope in it; for things that are seen are not hoped for, but are temporal, like the law of works, as we showed above.

“As it is written: ‘Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.’”

(Amb.) By the example of Abraham, who is the father of faith, he shows that righteousness is not reckoned from works of the law, but through faith. For Abraham was justified by believing. Accordingly, they had foolishly and recklessly subjected themselves to the law, which was not given for justification. This is discussed more fully and clearly in the Epistle to the Romans.

(Aug.) The especially victorious point here is that his faith was reckoned as righteousness before he was circumcised. To this is most properly referred what was said to him: “All nations shall be blessed in you”—through imitation of his faith, since he was justified even before receiving the sacrament of circumcision, which he received as a seal of faith, and before the whole slavery of the law, which was given much later.

(Hieron.) Abraham believed God when he left his homeland for a land he did not know, trusting that Sarah, ninety years old and barren, would give birth. After hearing God’s promise that his seed would be called in Isaac, he offered Isaac himself as a victim, yet did not doubt the Lord’s promise. Such faith is rightly reckoned as righteousness: he surpassed the works of the law and won God’s favor not through fear, but through love.

“Know, therefore, that those who are of faith—these are sons of Abraham.”

(Amb.) This is true: believers are sons of Abraham. If Abraham was first justified by faith, then all who believe after him are his sons, whether from the Jews or from the Gentiles.

(Hieron.) He discusses this more fully in the Epistle to the Romans: Abraham’s faith was reckoned as righteousness not in circumcision but in uncircumcision. Carefully observing this, he teaches that those are sons of Abraham who believe with the disposition with which Abraham believed while uncircumcised. Abraham “rejoiced that he would see the day of the Lord; he saw it and rejoiced.”

Hence it is said to the unbelieving Jews: “If you are Abraham’s sons, do the works of Abraham” (John VIII). What other works was the Lord expecting from them at that time, when he said this, except belief in the Son of God whom the Father had sent and who was speaking? “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in him who sent me” (John XII).

Therefore, in another passage, when people were boasting about the antiquity and nobility of their lineage, they were answered: “Do not say, ‘We have Abraham as our father’; for God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. III). No one doubts that the stones there signify the hard hearts of the Gentiles, which were later softened and received the seal of faith.

[Col. 0289A] “For Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, announced the Gospel beforehand to Abraham: ‘All nations shall be blessed in you.’ Therefore those who are of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham.”

(Amb.) He says this because Abraham is the model of all believers, so that those who believe are blessed in him. By following his faith, they become participants in the same blessing. It is clear that the faithful will be blessed with the faithful, just as the unfaithful are punished with the unfaithful.

“Scripture, foreseeing,” he says, “that God would justify the Gentiles by faith,” and so forth.

(Hieron.) This does not mean that Scripture itself—namely, ink and parchment, which are insensible—could foresee the future. Rather, the Holy Spirit and the meaning concealed in the letters foretold what would come many centuries later.

Moreover, the example taken from Genesis is contained in its own book in this form: “And all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in your seed” (Gen. XXVII). Interpreting this concerning Christ, the Apostle says: “It does not say, ‘and to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: ‘and to your seed,’ who is Christ.”

We must observe this in nearly all the testimonies taken from the ancient books into the New Testament: the evangelists or Apostles relied upon memory and, while explaining the meaning, often changed the order; sometimes they removed words and sometimes added them.

No one can doubt that all the nations were not blessed in Isaac, Jacob, the twelve Patriarchs, or the others descended from Abraham’s stock, but in Christ Jesus, through whom all nations praise God and a new name is blessed upon the earth.

The Apostle may also have taken his example concerning the seed from another passage in Genesis, where it is written: “God”—with no doubt referring to Abraham—“brought him outside and said to him, ‘Look toward heaven and count the stars, if you are able to count them’; and he said to him, ‘So shall your seed be’” (Gen. XV). “And Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”

Therefore all who believe will be blessed with faithful Abraham, who, because of his remarkable faith in God, is said to have been the first to believe in him. Likewise, Enos is written to have hoped to call upon the Lord God because of his pre-eminent and outstanding hope in God (Gen. IV).

This does not mean that Abel—of whom the Lord says, “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me” (Gen. IV)—and the others thereafter did not hope to call upon God. Rather, each person is named according to the quality that is especially characteristic of him.

[Col. 0290A] “For all who are of the works of the law are under a curse of the law.”

“For all who are of the works of the law are under a curse of the law.”

(Aug.) He wishes this to be understood as referring to fear, not freedom: namely, that those who persisted in all the things written in the book of the law in order to do them would be punished by bodily and present vengeance, and that, in addition, within the punishment of their bodies they would fear the disgrace of the curse.

But the person who is justified before God is the one who worships him freely—not out of desire to obtain something from him other than himself, nor out of fear of losing something. For our true and perfect blessedness is in him alone. Although he is invisible to bodily eyes, he is worshiped by faith as long as we live in this flesh, just as he said above: “But the life I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God.” This is the righteousness to which the statement refers: “For the righteous person lives by faith.”

“For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them.’”

(Hieron.) I have the practice that whenever the Apostles take something from the Old Testament, I return to the original books and examine carefully how it is written in its own place.

I therefore found this very passage in Deuteronomy (Deut. XXVII) written among the Septuagint interpreters as follows: “Cursed is every person who does not continue in all the words of this law, to do them”; and all the people shall say, “So be it, so be it.”

Aquila has it this way: “Cursed is the one who does not establish the words of this law, to do them.” [Col. 0290C] And all the people shall say, “Truly.”

Symmachus: “Cursed is the one who does not make firm these words, to do them.” And all the people shall say, “Amen.”

Theodotion translated it as follows: “Cursed is the one who does not raise up the words of this law, to do them.” And all the people shall say, “Amen.”

From this we understand that the Apostle, as elsewhere, gave the meaning of the testimony rather than its exact words. We are uncertain whether the Septuagint interpreters added “every person” and “in all,” or whether these expressions were present in the ancient Hebrew and were afterward deleted by the Jews.

The following consideration presses me toward this suspicion: the Apostle, a man skilled in Hebrew and thoroughly learned in the law, would never have produced the word “every” and the phrase “in all,” as though they were necessary to his meaning in proving that all who are of the works of the law are under a curse, unless they were found in the Hebrew books.

For this reason, when rereading the Hebrew books of the Samaritans, I found that *Chol*, which means “every” or “all,” was written there, in agreement with the Septuagint interpreters.

The Jews therefore removed that word without cause, lest they should appear to be under a curse if they could not fulfill everything that was written, even though the more ancient writings of another people also testify that it was present.

Since no one can fulfill the law or do everything that was commanded, the Apostle also testifies elsewhere, saying (Rom. VIII): “For what was impossible for the law, weakened as it was through the flesh, God did by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh; and, because of sin, he condemned sin in the flesh.”

[Col. 0291A] If this is true, someone may object: “Then Moses, Isaiah, and the other prophets who lived under the works of the law are also under a curse.” Whoever has read the Apostle’s statement will not hesitate to agree, and will answer that each of the saints, in his own time, became a curse for the people.

Nor will attributing this also to righteous men immediately seem to detract from the Savior, as though he had done nothing special or excellent by becoming a curse for us, since others too became a curse for others. For none of those men, although he himself became a curse, liberated anyone from the curse—except the Lord Jesus Christ, who by his precious blood redeemed all of us, and those men themselves—I mean Moses and Aaron, all the prophets, and the patriarchs—from the curse of the law.

Do not think that this is merely my own opinion. Scripture is witness: “Because Christ, by the grace of God” (II Cor. V)—or, as it is read in certain copies, “apart from God, died for all.”

But if he died for all, then he died also for Moses and for all the prophets, none of whom was able to erase the ancient bond written against us and fasten it to the cross (Col. II).

“All have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. III). Ecclesiastes also confirms this judgment: “There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccl. VII).

Finally, the Apostle’s statement farther below clearly teaches that neither Moses nor any distinguished man of antiquity could be justified before God through the law. For it follows: “But because no one will be justified before God by the law, it is manifest that the righteous person lives by faith.”

(Ambr.) Accordingly, he teaches that one must depart from the law, lest the righteousness sought through faith perish.

But the law does not proceed from faith; rather, “the one who has done these things will live by them.” The law does not proceed from faith, because it commands nothing to be believed: all its requirements are evident, so that the person who observes the law may live; otherwise, he must necessarily be punished, because he has committed what he knew was to be avoided.

An objection may be raised from the opposite direction: If no one is justified by the law, why is the person who neglects something prescribed by the law accursed? The answer is that no one is justified before God by the law; yet he is justified before the world, so that he may be secure in the present life. But if he wishes to be justified before God, so that this may contribute to his merit on the day of God’s judgment, let him follow faith; otherwise, though secure here, he will be guilty in the future. The law is therefore useful—but the law written on the tablets; the other requirements, as he said, were given to be a burden. (Jerome)

He took the example proving that the righteous live by faith and not by works from the prophet Habakkuk (Habakkuk II), whose words the Septuagint translators rendered as follows: “But the righteous shall live by my faith.” Aquila and Theodotion have: “But the righteous shall live by his faith,” that is, by God’s faith. It should certainly be noted that he did not say, “A man” or “A person lives by faith,” lest he provide an occasion for despising works of virtue; rather, he says, “The righteous lives by faith,” so that whoever is faithful and is to live by faith could not come to faith or live in it unless he had first been righteous and had ascended, as though by certain steps of a pure life, to faith.

It can therefore happen that someone is righteous and yet does not live without the faith of Christ. If this presents a difficulty to the reader, let him accept Paul’s words, in which Paul says of himself: “According to the righteousness that is in the law, blameless” (Philippians III). Paul was therefore at that time righteous according to the law, but he could not yet live, because Christ was not yet speaking within him: “I am life” (John XI). Afterward, believing in him, Paul began to live.

Let us too formulate something similar to the statement “The righteous lives by faith,” and say: “The chaste person lives by faith; the wise person lives by faith; the courageous person lives by faith”; and from the other categories of virtue let us produce a corresponding statement against those who, not believing in Christ, think themselves courageous, wise, temperate, or righteous. Let them know that no one lives without Christ, without whom every virtue is a vice.

The present testimony can also be read in this way: “because the righteous is from faith,” with “he lives” then following. When he says, “The law does not proceed from faith, but the one who has done these things will live by them,” it is shown most clearly that “life” is not being mentioned in the abstract, but life referred to something. For “the righteous lives by faith,” and nothing is added—neither “in these things” nor “in those things.” But the person living under the law, who has done these things, “will live by them,” that is, in the things he has done and considered good. His reward for his labor consists only in the works he has performed—whether in length of life, as the Jews think, or in avoidance of punishment, by which the transgressor of the law is killed.

Let us not suppose that the words “to live by them” belong to the Apostle; they belong to the prophet Ezekiel, who says: “I led them out into the wilderness, and I gave them my commandments and showed them my statutes, which a person shall do and shall live by them” (Ezekiel XX).

(Augustine) Understand, therefore, that in this passage “the law” is used for the works themselves. Those who lived by these works were certainly afraid that, if they did not perform them, they would suffer stoning, crucifixion, or something of that kind. “The one who has done them,” he says, “will live by them”—that is, he will receive a reward, so that he will not be punished by this death. This does not mean life before God, since whoever has lived by faith in God during this life will possess the most immediate reward after departing from it.

Therefore, whoever desires or fears present, visible things does not live by faith, because the faith of God concerns invisible realities, which will be given afterward. There is, then, a certain righteousness in the works of the law, since it is not left without its reward: “the one who has done them will live by them.”

Hence he also says to the Romans: “For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God” (Romans IV). It is one thing not to be justified, and another not to be justified before God. The person who is not justified at all preserves neither those things that have a temporal reward nor those that have an eternal one. But the person who is justified by the works of the law is not justified before God, because he expects from them a temporal and visible reward. Nevertheless, this too is, as I have said—or, so to speak, a kind of earthly and carnal righteousness. For the Apostle himself calls it righteousness when elsewhere he says: “The righteousness that is in the law, in which I lived blamelessly.”

For this reason, when the Lord Jesus was about to give freedom to believers, he did not observe certain of these practices according to the letter. Thus, when the disciples, being hungry on the Sabbath, plucked heads of grain, he replied to those who were indignant that the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath (Luke VI). By not observing those practices in a carnal manner, he consumed the envy of carnal people and indeed accepted the punishment appointed for those who did not observe them; but he freed those who believed in him from fear of such punishment. This is the point of what he adds: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us, because it is written: Accursed is everyone who hangs on a tree, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.”

(Ambrose) Since no one could fulfill the law, everyone was liable to the curse of the law, so that it might exact vengeance from them. But Christ, born as a human being and offered by the Father for us, redeemed us from the devil. By willingly offering him to death on behalf of those who were subject to the curse of the law, he made him a curse in this manner: just as in the law the victim offered for sins was called “sin,” so, because he was offered for those under the curse, he became a curse, being killed as though he were a sinner.

For this reason he did not say, “Having become accursed for us,” but “having become a curse.” The person who was offered to death on account of his own sin became accursed, for he was dying in his own case. If you examine the matter more closely, you will see that Christ became the curse of those by whom he was killed. The Savior’s cross is the sin and curse of the Jews, because it is written: “Accursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deuteronomy XXI).

Moses said this in Deuteronomy concerning those condemned to death, so that it would suffice for those suspended on a tree to remain there until evening and then be taken down for burial. “Accursed,” he says, “is everyone who hangs on a tree.” It was enough for a person condemned to death that, because he had been suspended, he died on the tree; otherwise, if he remained suspended longer, his death would bear greater disgrace than it deserved, and it would become a stain upon his family if his death were publicized further.

Accordingly, the innocent Savior, suspended on a tree, is not accursed, but is the curse of those by whom he was suspended. Yet, as far as the Jews are concerned, by handing him over to Pilate to be killed as though he were a sinner, they made him a curse, so that he might be killed as though guilty, although he was innocent; for according to the law, the person deserving death is accursed.

When they saw many people gathering around his teaching, they were jealous and said: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John XII). Thus he is said to have been killed for us, and for us in two ways. Although they thought he ought to be killed so that he would not teach, they accomplished nothing, because his teaching grew and he nullified death through his Passion. Descending to the underworld, he delivered the human race. For this reason also he allowed himself to be killed, knowing that he was acting for us and against the devil.

(Augustine) Let the person who denies that Christ was accursed also deny that he died. But whoever confesses that he died cannot deny that death comes from sin, and therefore that death itself is also called sin. Let him hear the Apostle himself saying: “Our old person was crucified together with him” (Romans VI), and let him understand whom Moses called accursed.

Therefore the Apostle, following this, says of Christ: “He became a curse for us,” just as he did not hesitate to say, “He died for us all.” For “he died” means the same as “he became a curse,” because death itself comes from the curse. Every sin is also a curse—whether the sin itself, which is committed so that punishment may follow, or the punishment itself, which is called “sin” in another sense because it results from sin.

Christ accepted our punishment without guilt, so that from it he might release us from our guilt and also bring our punishment to an end. “God sent his Son,” he says, “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans VIII). Since he was mortal, he possessed the likeness of sinful flesh. He also consequently calls this “sin,” saying: “So that, through sin, he might condemn sin in the flesh” (ibid.). Why, then, would Moses fear saying “a curse,” when Paul did not fear saying “sin”?

As for the addition, “Everyone who hangs on a tree,” Moses certainly did not fail to foresee that righteous people would also be on crosses; rather, he foresaw the heretics who would deny the true death of the Lord and who, wishing to separate Christ from this curse, would thereby separate him from the reality of death as well.

For if that death was not real, no curse hung upon Christ crucified on the tree, because he was not truly crucified. Accordingly, the word “everyone” was added, so that Christ would not be said to have no part in true death if, through foolish reverence, he were separated from the curse joined to death.

Some among us, less well instructed in the Scriptures, greatly fear this statement. While approving the ancient Scriptures with due piety, they do not think that it was spoken concerning God but concerning Judas, his betrayer. They say that for this reason Scripture did not say, “Accursed is everyone who is fastened to a tree,” but “who hangs on a tree,” because the Lord is not signified here, but the one who hanged himself with a noose. They are greatly mistaken and do not notice that they are arguing against the Apostle, who says: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us; because it is written: Accursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.”

Therefore, the one who became a curse for us is the very one who hung on the tree: Christ, who freed us from the curse of the law, so that we would no longer be justified by fear through the works of the law, but by faith before God—a faith that operates not through fear but through love.

The Holy Spirit, who spoke this through Moses, provided for both things: that those who were not yet able to live by faith in invisible realities would be restrained by fear of visible punishment, and that he himself would abolish this fear by accepting what was feared. Having removed fear, he could give the gift of love.

Nor should it be thought an insult to God that the one who hangs on a tree is called accursed. He hung on the tree in that part of him that was mortal. The origin of mortality is known to believers: it comes from the punishment and curse of the first sin of humanity. The Lord accepted this condition and bore our sins in his body upon the tree.

If it were said, “Death is accursed,” no one would recoil. What, then, hung upon the tree except the Lord’s death, so that by dying he might overcome death? The very curse, therefore, was overcome.

Likewise, if it were said, “Sin is accursed,” no one would be surprised. What, then, hung upon the tree except the sin of the old person, which the Lord accepted for us in the very mortality of the flesh? Thus the Apostle neither blushed nor feared to say that God made him sin for us, adding: “So that he might condemn sin concerning sin.” For our old person would not have been crucified together with him, as the same Apostle says elsewhere (Romans VI), unless, in that death of the Lord, the figure of our sin had hung, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might no longer serve sin.

In the likeness of that sin and death, Moses also raised a serpent upon a tree in the wilderness (Numbers XXI). Through the serpent’s persuasion, humanity fell under the sentence of death. Accordingly, the serpent was fittingly raised upon the tree as a sign of death itself; in that figure, the Lord’s death hung upon the tree.

(Jerome) Marcion also intrudes at this point, attacking the power of the Creator, whom he slanders as bloodthirsty, cruel, and vengeful. He asserts that we were redeemed through Christ, who is the Son of another, benevolent God. If Marcion understood the difference between buying and redeeming—for the person who buys purchases what belongs to another, whereas the person who redeems purchases specifically what was his own and ceased to be his own—he would never twist the simple words of Scripture into an accusation against his doctrine.

Christ therefore redeemed us from the curse of the law, which was established for sinners. Through the prophet he rebukes them, saying: “Behold, you were sold because of your sins, and in your iniquities I dismissed your mother” (Isaiah L). The Apostle repeats this same point, saying: “I am carnal, sold under sin” (Romans VII).

The curses of the law written in Leviticus and Deuteronomy are not fulfilled because God is their author; rather, through the prophetic Spirit, what was going to happen is announced to those who were going to sin.

But if someone wishes to constrain us by the Apostle’s testimony, which says: “All who are of the works of the law are under a curse. For it is written: Accursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the law, to do them,” and wishes to assert that all who were under the law were accursed, let us ask him whether those who are under the Gospel of Christ and do not carry out his commandments are accursed or not.

If he says that they are accursed, then the Gospel contains what we have in the law. If he denies that they are accursed, then the Gospel’s commandments were established in vain, and those who fulfill them will receive no reward.

The two positions are resolved in this way: just as Christ Jesus freed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, so he also rescues us from the curse of the Gospel, which is established against those who do not fulfill its commandments, by himself becoming a curse for us. He knows that he does not forgive even the smallest portion of the talent and exacts the last quadrans.

(Ambrose) He says this because, after the Jews had reproached and cursed the Savior while flattering themselves on the righteousness of the law—as though he were guilty of violating the Sabbath—the blessing of the promise made to Abraham passed through faith in Christ Jesus to the Gentiles. Hence the Lord says to the Jews: “The kingdom will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.”

(Jerome) This is a very famous question, and the Jews regularly bring it against us as a reproach: that our Savior and Lord was under God’s curse.

First, therefore, we must observe that not everyone who hangs on a tree is accursed before the Lord, but the person who has sinned, has been condemned to death because of his crime, and has been lifted upon a cross. He is not accursed because he was crucified, but because he fell into such guilt that he deserved crucifixion.

Next, we must set against them the point that will be explained more fully below: Scripture reports that he was crucified because of a curse and blasphemy against God. Symmachus translated the passage more explicitly, saying: “Because he was hanged on account of blasphemy against God.”

Finally, let us ask them whether, if Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, because they refused to worship Nebuchadnezzar’s idol (Daniel III), had been hanged on a tree, they would have considered them accursed or worthy of every blessing; and whether they would have judged the ninety-year-old Eleazar under Antiochus, king of Syria (2 Maccabees VI), and the glorious mother with her seven sons (2 Maccabees I), to be accursed or entirely deserving of blessing.

Certainly, if Haman had not himself, by his own deserving, mounted the cross that he had prepared for Mordecai (Esther VII), I think Mordecai would have ascended it not as an accursed man but as a holy one.

These and other similar examples establish that the accursed person is the one who has committed a crime worthy of the gallows, not the one crucified through the injustice of judges, the power or shouting of enemies and the crowd, envy of his virtues, or a king’s anger.

So much against the Jews. But to return to our discussion: we cannot know why the Apostle, in the passage written as “Accursed by God is everyone who hangs on a tree,” either omitted something or added something.

If he was following the authority of the Septuagint translators, he ought to have added the name of God, as they rendered it. But if, as a Hebrew of Hebrews, he considered what he had read in his own language to be most accurate, he should not have included either “everyone” or “on a tree,” since neither is found in the Hebrew.

It therefore seems to me either that the ancient Hebrew books differed from those now in circulation, or that the Apostle, as I have already said, presented the meaning of the Scriptures rather than their words; or—and this is more likely—that after Christ’s Passion someone added the name of God both to the Hebrew manuscripts and to our copies in order to brand us with infamy, since we believe that Christ was accursed by God.

I therefore enter this contest boldly and appeal to the books: nowhere is anyone written to be accursed by God, and wherever a curse is mentioned, the name of God is never added.

“To the serpent: You are accursed above all beasts.” To Adam: “Accursed is the earth in your works.” To Cain: “You are accursed upon the earth.” Elsewhere: “Accursed is Canaan; he shall be a servant to his brothers.” And in another passage: “Accursed is their anger, because it was bold, and their wrath, because it was harsh.”

No one should be troubled by the fact that Christ became a curse for us. The God who is said to have made him a curse also made him sin for us, although Christ knew no sin. The Savior, from the fullness of the Father, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians II); life was put to death, and the Wisdom of God was called foolishness, so that what was foolish in God might become wiser than human beings.

In Psalm LXVIII he speaks concerning himself: “God, you know my foolishness, and my offenses are not hidden from you.”

The Lord’s dishonor is therefore our glory. He died so that we might live; he descended to the underworld so that we might ascend into heaven; he became foolishness so that we might become wisdom; he emptied himself of the fullness and form of God, taking the form of a servant, so that the fullness of divinity might dwell in us and we might become servants of the Lord. He hung upon the tree so that, by being hung upon it, he might erase the sin we had committed through the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

His cross changed bitter waters into sweetness (Exodus XV), and it raised up the lost axe that had sunk into the depths when it was thrown into the current of the Jordan (2 Kings VI).

Finally, he became a curse—he became one, I say; he was not born one—so that the blessings promised to Abraham might, with him as their author and guide, be transferred to the Gentiles, and so that the promised Spirit might be fulfilled in us through his faith.

## BOOK FIFTEEN

[Col. 0297]

### CHAPTER III FOLLOWS

“Brothers, I speak according to human considerations.”

(Ambrose) He says this because he wishes to commend the logic of the divine promise by the example of a human case. Hence he also mentions a human testament, which is certainly much weaker than the divine one. Yet no one disregards or overrides a testament confirmed by a human being.

It is true that a testament of the deceased, legally executed, cannot be annulled.

(Augustine) “Yet no one,” he says, “annuls or overrides a human testament once confirmed,” because when a testator changes a testament, he does not change a confirmed testament; the testament is confirmed by the testator’s death.

The death of the testator confirms his testament because he can no longer change his decision. In the same way, the unchangeableness of God’s promise confirms the inheritance of Abraham, whose faith was reckoned as righteousness.

The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say “seeds,” as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: “and to your seed,” who is Christ.

(Ambrose) This is what is written in Genesis to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Genesis XXII). This was certainly fulfilled in Christ, in whose name all the nations are blessed through faith. Therefore the promise was confirmed not in many but in one, who is Christ.

By this argument the Apostle identifies as falsifiers of the testament those who, while believing in Christ, still hope for something from the law, so that salvation would be promised not only in Christ but also in the law. He therefore proves that the promise of blessing was made in Christ alone.

(Augustine) Christ is one, both head and body. The Apostle teaches this when, speaking of Abraham’s seed, he says: “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed,” after having said above: “He does not say ‘and to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as though referring to one, ‘and to your seed,’ which is Christ.”

If Abraham’s seed is Christ, what else was said to those to whom it was said, “Therefore you are Abraham’s seed,” except, “Therefore you are Christ”? And so, when the Apostle calls Christ the seed of Abraham to whom the promises were spoken, he means all Christians who imitate Abraham through faith.

He reduces this to the singular by emphasizing that it was not said “and to seeds,” but “to your seed.” For there is also one faith, and those who live carnally from works cannot be justified in the same way as those who live spiritually from faith.

“Now this is what I say: a testament confirmed by God is not annulled by the law made four hundred and thirty years later, so as to abolish the promise.”

(Ambrose) He teaches that the promise of blessing was confirmed in Christ alone, so that he may show that the law was given four hundred and thirty years later. Once the promise had been established, the law was subsequently given—not to weaken the promise, but to signify what would happen and when it would happen.

(Jerome) The Apostle, who became all things to all people in order to win them all, indebted to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and also to the Galatians whom he had shortly before called foolish, became foolish to them as well.

He did not use with them the arguments he used with the Romans, but simpler ones—arguments that foolish people could understand and that were almost taken from the street. Lest he seem to have done this through incompetence rather than skill, he first appeases the prudent reader and moderates what he is going to say by the preface: “Brothers, I speak according to human considerations.”

What he is going to say, he says, is not according to God, not according to hidden wisdom, and not to those who can eat solid food, but according to those who, because of the weakness of their stomach, are fed with the dew of milk and are in no way able to hear what is weighty.

Thus, to the Corinthians, among whom fornication was reported—a fornication so serious that it was not found even among the Gentiles—he says: “I speak, not the Lord” (1 Corinthians VII). And to the same people in the second letter: “What I am saying, I am not saying according to the Lord, but as though in foolishness” (2 Corinthians XI).

Some think that, because he was about to discuss a human testament, the death of the testator, and other examples based on human analogy, he said: “Brothers, I speak according to human considerations.” But it seems to me that this was indeed prefaced for the reason they suppose, yet especially because of what follows: “He does not say ‘and to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as though referring to one, ‘and to your seed, which is Christ.’”

Traversing all the Scriptures in meaning and memory, I have never found “seed” written in the plural, but whether the reference is favorable or unfavorable, it is always singular.

Moreover, if anyone carefully compares the Hebrew volumes and the other editions with the translation of the Septuagint, he will find that where “testament” is written, the word does not sound like “testament” but like “covenant”—the term called *Berith* in the Hebrew language.

It is therefore clear that the Apostle did what he promised: he did not use hidden meanings with the Galatians, but ordinary and lowly ones, which could displease the prudent unless he had first said, “I speak according to human considerations.”

At this point the years must be reckoned from the time when the Lord spoke to Abraham, saying, “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed,” until the lawgiver Moses. The question is whether the period was four hundred and thirty years, and how this corresponds to the Lord’s promise to Abraham in Genesis that his descendants would come out of the land of slavery after four hundred years.

This is no small matter, and many have investigated it. I do not know whether anyone has discovered the answer.

It is nevertheless indisputable that the law had not yet been given and could not, after so many years, have been given in such a way as to annul the ancient promises made to Abraham. For if the law justifies, then Abraham, who lived long before the law, was not justified. Since they cannot say this, they are forced to confess that a person is not justified by the works of the law but by faith.

At the same time, this compels us to understand that all the ancients who were justified were justified by that same faith. What we shall attain by believing—partly in what is past, namely the Lord’s first coming, and partly in what is future, namely the Lord’s second coming—they believed entirely as future, that is, both comings, the Holy Spirit revealing this to them so that they might be saved.

Hence also the statement: “Abraham desired to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John VIII).

“If the inheritance comes from the law, it no longer comes from the promise; but God granted it to Abraham through the promise.”

(Ambrose) The Jews defend two mutually opposed positions. For no argument or reasoning can persuade them that the promise made to Abraham was annulled by the law—and rightly so.
