Yet, through an ill-considered presumption, they defend another position against this one, thinking that justification cannot arise without the works of the law, even though they know that Abraham, who is the pattern of this matter, was justified without the works of the law through faith alone.

Blinded by a kind of rivalry, they neither understand nor consider that if justification comes through the law, the promise is excluded. And if the promise is excluded, Abraham’s faith will undoubtedly be frustrated.

The Jews cannot even bear to hear this, knowing that the promise given to Abraham comes from faith, and that this promise justifies through faith, not through the law, just as Abraham himself was justified by faith.

Therefore those are heirs of Abraham’s promise who succeed him by receiving the faith in which Abraham was blessed and justified. The testimony of Abraham’s promise is consequently called a testament, so that after his death his heirs might possess the promise, having become his children through faith.

This process continued until Christ, who had been promised to Abraham, so that after Christ’s death believers might be heirs of Abraham’s faith through the testament of Christ’s blood. The gift promised to Abraham was therefore fulfilled for his children in Christ, although Abraham himself also obtained this gift in the place where he was found.

(Jerome) The simple meaning developed in this passage has this force: the Apostle teaches that the promises previously made to Abraham cannot be destroyed by the law given afterward, and that what came later cannot prejudice what came before. The promises were given to Abraham four hundred and thirty years earlier, namely, that all nations would be blessed in him.

The observance of the law—according to which the person who performed it would live by it—was given to Moses on Mount Sinai four hundred and thirty years later.

The opposite objection could be raised: Why, then, was it necessary for the law to be given after such a long interval following the promise, since the giving of the law might give rise to the suspicion that the promise had been destroyed, while, if the promise remained, the law seemed to have been given without benefit?

The Apostle, anticipating this question, himself raises and explains it in what follows, saying:

“What, then, is the law? It was laid down because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom he had promised, ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not of one party, but God is one.”

Since the promise made to Abraham remained, and the law was afterward given through Moses, its introduction might seem pointless. He therefore explains why it was given: “It was laid down because of transgressions,” he says.

After the people’s offense in the wilderness, after they worshiped the calf and murmured against the Lord, the law came to prohibit transgressions: “The law is not laid down for the righteous but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners” (1 Timothy I).

To go back further: after the idolatry to which they had been enslaved in Egypt, so that they forgot the God of their fathers and said, “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus XXXII), the rites for worshiping God and the punishment of those who sinned were established by the hand of the mediator, Christ Jesus.

For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (John I)—not only heaven, earth, the sea, and all that we see, but also those things that were imposed through Moses upon the stubborn people as a kind of yoke of the law.

(Ambrose) The law of works—that is, the law of Moses—was placed between the beginning of the promise and the seed to whom the promise was made, that is, between Abraham and the Savior.

It was therefore given long after the promise had been made, so that by this very distinction one thing might be understood as law and another as promise; and so that it might instruct God’s people, separated from the nations, under the fear of God, making them worthy to receive the promise, which is Christ.

It is nevertheless called a law of works because it teaches what is to be done bodily at God’s command: concerning sacrifices, firstborn creatures, tithes, and other such matters.

“Ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator.”

By “angels” he means God’s messengers: Moses, Joshua son of Nun, and the other prophets up to John the Baptist, concerning whom God says: “Behold, I send my angel before your face” (Malachi III).

Through these messengers, therefore, the law was ordered and arranged by God in the hand—that is, in the authority—of the Savior. He is the mediator, or reconciler, of God and human beings, so that he may save those whom he wishes from among those who received the law through the angels mentioned above.

For he himself says: “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wishes” (John V).

The mediator, however, is not of one party. Without doubt, a mediator—that is, an arbiter—is not of one, but of two. For when two peoples were always fighting against one another, continually divided and hostile because of their differing doctrine, the Savior came as their arbiter, removing from both peoples the things over which they disagreed, so that they might be able to live in peace. Thus he took away from the Gentiles their multitude of gods and their service of the elements, which was a stumbling block to the Hebrews; and from the Jews he took away the works of the law—that is, new moons, circumcision, observance of the Sabbath, distinctions of foods, and the other practices that the Gentiles detested. In this way those who had previously been enemies became peaceful.

If this is so, why do the Galatians, through dullness of mind, corrupt this arbitration by turning to Judaism? They nullify the Savior’s judgment when, after peace has been made, they subject themselves to those things that had previously been hostile to peace, as though repenting of the peace. According to the Galatians’ understanding, then, Christ is not an arbiter, because, having been brought under the law, they made one people out of two; and no one, surely, is the arbiter of a single people. He develops this same meaning for the Ephesians when he says: “For he himself is our peace, who made both one and, in his flesh, broke down the dividing wall of the barrier, abolishing the enmity, the law of commandments expressed in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself as one new man, making peace” (Eph. II). If he made peace in one new man, he certainly took away from both the things over which they had been divided, and by giving them his law he established that by which they might be at peace. The Galatians have rushed into this by turning to Judaism.

But God is one. He says this lest, by preaching Christ as God and calling him the arbiter of the one God, he might be thought to have preached against the law and the prophets. He teaches, therefore, that this arbiter is to be understood through the assumption of flesh, as he says to Timothy: “The arbiter of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. II). But insofar as he is God, he is not separated from the Father, but is one with the Father: whether the Father or the Son, there is one God. For “God” is the name of nature and power, and the very meaning of the names teaches that this remains undivided in the Father and the Son.

*(Jerome.)* After, for our salvation, the mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, deigned to be born from a virgin’s womb, he was called a mediator. But before he assumed a human body, when he was with the Father in the beginning as God the Word, he was called merely a mediator in relation to all the saints to whom the word of God came—namely, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and afterward Moses and all the prophets whom Scripture mentions—without the addition of the humanity that he had not yet assumed.

When he says, “The law was ordained through angels,” he wishes this to be understood: throughout the whole Old Testament, wherever an angel is first reported to have appeared and afterward is introduced as speaking like God, the one who appeared was indeed an angel from among the many ministers, whoever he may have been; but in him the mediator spoke, saying: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. III). Nor is it surprising that God speaks through angels, since God also speaks through angels who are in human beings—that is, through the prophets—as Zechariah says: “And the angel who was speaking in me said” (Zech. II, IV, V); and afterward he adds: “Thus says the Lord Almighty.” For the angel who was said to be in the prophet did not dare to speak in his own person: “Thus says the Lord Almighty.”

By “the hand of the mediator,” we must understand his power and might. Although, according to his divinity, he himself is one with the Father, according to the office of mediator he is understood as distinct from him. Since the order of the reading is confused and disturbed by inversion, it seems that it should be restored for us as follows: “The law was established through angels in the hand of the mediator; it was ordained through angels because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made.” There can be no doubt that the seed signifies Christ, as is also confirmed from the beginning of Matthew: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.”

*(Augustine.)* We find between what and what the mediator stands, when the Apostle himself says: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.” If you were not lying prostrate, you would not need a mediator; but because you lie prostrate and cannot rise, God has, in a certain sense, extended his arm to you as mediator: “And the arm of the Lord—to whom has it been revealed?” (Isa. LIII).

A sufficiently necessary question arises. If faith justifies, and if the earlier saints who were justified before God were justified through that same faith, why was it necessary for the law to be given? He introduces this question by asking and saying: “What, then?” Up to this point there is a question; afterward the answer follows: “The law was set forth because of transgressions, until the seed should come,” he says, “to whom the promise had been made, ordained through angels in the hand of the mediator.”

“The mediator, however, is not of one, but God is one.” That Jesus Christ is called mediator according to his humanity becomes clearer from that other statement of the same Apostle: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. II). A mediator, therefore, could not be between God and God, because God is one. But the mediator is not of one, because he stands in the middle between more than one.

The angels who have not fallen from the sight of God do not need a mediator through whom they might be reconciled. Likewise, the angels who fell through voluntary transgression, with no one persuading them, are not reconciled through a mediator. It remains, then, that the one who was cast down by the mediator of pride, the devil, persuading him to pride, should be raised up by the humble mediator, Christ, persuading him to humility.

For if the Son of God had wished to remain in the natural equality of the Father and had not emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, he would not have been the mediator of God and human beings, because the Trinity itself is one God, the same in the three—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—remaining constant in the eternity and equality of its divinity. Thus the only Son of God became the mediator of God and human beings when the Word of God, God with God, lowered his majesty to the level of humanity and raised human humility to the level of divinity, so that he might be mediator between God and human beings: human through God, yet beyond human beings.

“For he is beautiful in form beyond the sons of human beings, as one anointed with the oil of gladness beyond his companions” (Ps. XLIV). Therefore all those people who, by believing, loved Christ’s humility—through revelation before it occurred and through the Gospel after it occurred—and by loving it imitated it, were healed from the impiety of pride and reconciled to God.

But this righteousness of faith, since it was given to human beings not on account of merit but through the mercy and grace of God, was not widespread before God, the human being, was born among human beings. The seed to whom the promise was made signifies a people, not those very few who, seeing through revelations that this righteousness would come, were saved through the same faith but could not save the people.

That people, if considered throughout the whole world—for from the whole world the Church gathers the heavenly Jerusalem—is indeed few, because the narrow way belongs to the few. Yet all who have been able to exist, gathered into one from the time the Gospel has been preached, and all who will be able to exist among all nations until the end of the age, together with those very few who, through faith in the Lord and through prophecy before both his comings, received the salvation of grace, complete the blessed condition of the saints in the eternal city.

Thus the law was placed upon a proud people so that, since they could not receive the grace of love unless they had been humbled, and could in no way fulfill the commandments of the law without this grace, they might be humbled by transgression and seek grace. They were not to imagine that they were saved by their own merits—which is pride—but were to be righteous not through their own power and strength, but in the hand of the mediator who justifies the ungodly.

The whole dispensation of the Old Testament was administered through angels, with the Holy Spirit acting in them, and with the very Word of truth—not yet incarnate, but never departing from any truthful administration. That dispensation of the law was arranged through angels, who sometimes acted in their own person and sometimes in the person of God, as the prophets also customarily did. Through that law, which revealed illnesses without removing them, pride was also crushed by the charge of transgression.

It was arranged through angels, but in the hand of the mediator, so that he himself might free from sins those who, already compelled by transgression of the law to confess their condition, acknowledged that they needed the grace and mercy of the Lord, so that their sins might be forgiven and that in a new life they might be reconciled to God through him who had poured out his blood for them.

Among these people pride had to be broken through transgression of the law. They boasted of their father Abraham and arrogantly claimed to possess righteousness by natural descent, setting their merits in circumcision above those of the other nations with all the greater harm because of their arrogance. The Gentiles, however, could be humbled much more easily even without this kind of transgression of the law. For when the Gospel of grace found human beings who recognized that they derived no origin of righteousness from their parents, it also found them servants of idols.

The Jews, however, could not be told what could be said to the Gentiles: that the righteousness of their parents in worshiping idols had not existed, although they supposed that it did. Nor could they be told that the righteousness of their father Abraham was false. Thus they are told: “Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance, and do not say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father’; for God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. III).

To the Gentiles, on the other hand, it is said:

> “Therefore remember that formerly you were Gentiles in the flesh, called the uncircumcision by what is called the circumcision, made in the flesh by human hands; remember that at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants, having no hope of the promise and without God in this world.”

Finally, the former are shown as unbelievers broken off from their own olive tree, while the latter are shown as believers grafted from the wild olive tree into that of the former.

Their pride, therefore, had to be worn down through transgression of the law. Thus, after he had magnified their sins with the words of Scripture, he says to the Romans: “You know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become accountable to God” (Rom. III)—the Jews through transgression of the law, and the Gentiles through ungodliness without the law. Hence he says again: “For God has shut up all things in unbelief, so that he might have mercy on all” (Rom. XI). He says this now as well, reopening the question itself: “Is the law, then, against the promises of God? Certainly not.”

*(Ambrose.)* Certainly not, because the law is not hostile to the promise, especially since it confirms it. For Moses first said: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers” (Deut. XVIII). The Apostle Peter proves in the Acts of the Apostles that this was spoken of Christ (Acts III).

“For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly have come from the law.” He calls this the righteousness that is reckoned as righteousness before God—that is, the righteousness of faith. The law, too, possessed a kind of righteousness, but only for the present age, not one that justified before God. For it could not remit sins and thereby make righteous people out of sinners. It was given for this purpose: to inspire fear, urging human beings toward a good life and punishing the irreverent. Therefore the law was not given as something that could give life, but as something that could condemn.

But Scripture confined all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ. He expressed this same meaning to the Romans when he said: “God has shut up all things under sin, so that he might have mercy on all” (Rom. XI). He said what I mentioned above: that the law was given so that sinners might know themselves to be guilty before God.

Once their sins had been revealed, they were confined so that they could not excuse themselves, but would seek mercy. Then, when the one who had been promised to Abraham came, he would ask from them the faith that Abraham possessed, so that they might obtain forgiveness for their evils and justification.

God had revealed this through the prophet Isaiah when he said: “He will come from Zion, who will rescue and turn ungodliness away from Jacob; and this shall be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins” (Isa. LIX).

*(Augustine.)* When you hear “promise,” expect the one who makes it to act. Human nature was capable, through free choice, of wounding itself; but once wounded and injured, it is no longer capable of healing itself through free choice. The law is good if one uses it lawfully.

What, then, is it to use the law lawfully? It is to recognize one’s illness through the law and seek divine help for healing. For, as I have said, if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would altogether have come from the law; there would have been no need to seek a Savior, Christ would not have come, and he would not have sought the lost sheep with his blood.

The same Apostle says elsewhere: “For if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Gal. II). The law, therefore, was not given to take away sin, but to confine all things under sin. The law showed that there was sin where those who had been blinded by habit might suppose there was righteousness. In this way, once humbled, they would recognize that their salvation was not in their own hand, but in the hand of the mediator.

Humility, above all, calls us back from the place where pride cast us down; and this very humility is suited to the reception of the grace of Christ, who is the unique example of humility.

Nor should anyone here, in such ignorance, say: “Why, then, did it not benefit the Jews that the law was administered through angels and arranged in the hand of the mediator?” It benefited them beyond anything that can be expressed. For what churches of the Gentiles placed the prices of their possessions at the feet of the apostles? What other people produced so many thousands of human beings so suddenly? Nor should one consider the crowds of unbelievers, since every threshing floor has, by many times, a greater share of chaff than of grain.

From where else do those words of the same Apostle to the Romans come, except from the sanctification of the Jews? “What, then? Has God rejected his people? Certainly not. For I too am an Israelite, from the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Rom. XI).

When he praised the church of the Thessalonians above the churches of the Gentiles, he says that they had become like the churches of Judea, because they had suffered many things from their fellow countrymen for the sake of faith, just as those churches had suffered from the Jews. Hence also what I mentioned shortly before, which he says to the Romans: “If the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in material things” (Rom. XV).

Before faith came, they were being guarded under the law, confined within the faith that was to be revealed. This is what he says: before the Savior came, we lived under the guardianship of the law so that we would not sin and might be worthy of the promise when it came. For through this hope the law kept us safe, so that it might present us—that is, the Jews—to Christ when he came.

*(Jerome.)* Just as the mediator of God and human beings stood between the giver and the recipient of the law, so the law itself, which was given after the promise, slipped in between the promise and its fulfillment. It must not for that reason be thought to exclude the promise, because, following afterward, it appears to abolish what came before. Rather, from the fact that it could not give life or bestow what the first promise had pledged, it is evident that it was given to guard the promise, not to overthrow it.

If a law had been given that could provide life and exhibit what the promise had pledged, the promise would truly be thought to have been excluded by the law. But now, having been placed—as we said above—because of transgressions, it more strongly accuses those of being sinners who, after the promise, were given the law as a guard and, so to speak, as a prison. Because they had not wished, through the freedom of their will, to await the promise innocently, they were hindered by legal bonds and reduced to the servitude of commandments, so that they might be guarded until the coming of the future faith in Christ, which would bring the promise to fulfillment.

Nor should Scripture be considered the author of sin because it is said to have confined all things under sin. A commandment prescribed by right reveals and exposes sin rather than causing it. Likewise, a judge is not the author of crime when he binds wicked people; rather, he confines them and declares them guilty by the authority of his judgment, so that afterward, if he wishes, the sovereign’s mercy may release those who are liable to punishment.

*(Augustine.)* The law itself brought it about that they should be found so near and should approach God from such close proximity, selling their possessions and bringing the proceeds, as the Lord commanded those who wished to be perfect. Under the law they were guarded, confined within that faith—that is, within the coming of the faith that was later revealed.

At that time, confinement consisted in fear of the one God; and the fact that they were found to be transgressors of that law proved useful, not destructive, to those who believed. For knowledge of a greater illness made them desire the physician more intensely and love him more ardently: “To whom more is forgiven, he loves more” (Luke VII).

Accordingly, the law was our pedagogue toward Christ Jesus, so that we might be justified by faith.

*(Ambrose.)* The meaning is the same: we were under the care of the law until Christ came, who justifies those who believe. But when faith came, we were no longer under a pedagogue.

“For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus.” One who is under a pedagogue is not master of his own power. A child, being unstable and inclined to sin, is kept under the care of a pedagogue. But when Christ came, making adults, as it were, out of minors, we were freed from the power of the pedagogue and, through the washing away of sins, became sons of God, although we had been slaves of sin.

*(Jerome.)* A pedagogue is assigned to children so that a wayward age may be restrained and hearts inclined toward vices may be held in check, while tender childhood is trained through study; and so that, disciplined by fear of punishment, it may be prepared for the more advanced disciplines of philosophy and the governance of the state.

Yet a pedagogue is neither teacher nor father, and the one being educated does not expect to receive the pedagogue’s inheritance or knowledge. A pedagogue guards another man’s son, from whom he will withdraw after the boy has reached the lawful age for receiving his inheritance.

Indeed, the very name *pedagogue* says this: it is formed from Greek *παῖς* (*pais*, “child”) and *ἄγω* (*agō*, “I lead”), because he leads—that is, guides—children. Thus the law of Moses was imposed upon the wayward people like a stricter pedagogue, to guard them and prepare them for the future faith. After that faith came and we believed in Christ, we were no longer under a pedagogue. Tutor and guardian withdrew from us, and, entering the lawful age, we were truly called sons of God. It is not the abolished law that gives us birth, but faith, our mother, which is in Christ Jesus.

*(Augustine.)* Whoever follows the letter holds translated words as though they were proper and does not refer what is signified by the literal word to another meaning. If, for example, he hears “Sabbath,” he understands nothing except one day of the seven, repeated in continuous succession; and when he hears “sacrifice,” he does not extend his thought beyond what is customarily done with the victims of animals and the fruits of the earth.

Yet this servitude differed greatly among the Jewish people from the practice of the other nations, since they were so subjected to temporal things that one God was commended in all these practices. Although they observed signs of spiritual realities in place of the realities themselves, not knowing what they signified, they nevertheless had this implanted in them: that through such servitude they were pleasing the one God whom they did not see.

The Apostle writes that this guardianship was like that of a pedagogue over children. Therefore those who stubbornly clung to such signs could not endure the Lord’s contempt for them when the time of their revelation had come. From this they devised accusations because he healed on the Sabbath.

For “all who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ.”

*(Ambrose.)* He says this because believers, while being changed, put on Christ, when they are called what they believe.

“There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” He speaks of no distinction among believers, so that no one may be prejudiced by what he was before he believed. For one gift has been decreed for all these people. With God there is no distinction of persons, except that arising from character and life, so that people of one faith may be distinguished by their merits, not by their persons.

*(Jerome.)* That Christ is clothing is proved not only from the present passage but also from another, where the same Paul exhorts us: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. XIII). If those who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ, it is clear that those who have not put on Christ have not been baptized in Christ.

For the words “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” were spoken to those who were considered believers and had received Christ’s baptism. If someone receives only the bodily washing of water, visible to the eyes of the flesh, he has not put on the Lord Jesus Christ. Simon, too, in the Acts of the Apostles, had received the washing of water; but because he did not have the Holy Spirit, he had not put on Christ. Heretics and hypocrites, and those who live sordidly, appear indeed to receive baptism, but I do not know whether they possess Christ’s clothing.

Let us therefore consider whether someone among us may perhaps be discovered who, because he does not possess Christ’s clothing, may be convicted of not having been baptized in Christ.

When someone has once put on Christ and, having been sent into the flame, has shone white through the fervor of the Holy Spirit, it is not discerned whether he is gold or silver. As long as the heat possesses the mass, there is one fiery color, and every diversity of origin, condition, and body is removed by such clothing.

“For there is neither Jew nor Greek.” In place of “Greek,” we should understand “Gentile,” because *Ἕλλην* (*Hellēn*) signifies both “Greek” and “pagan.” The Jew is not better because he is circumcised, nor is the Gentile worse because he has the foreskin. Rather, according to the quality of faith, a Jew or a Greek is better or worse.

Likewise, slave and free are not separated by social condition but by faith, because a slave can be better than a free person, and a free person can surpass a slave in the quality of faith. Similarly, male and female are distinguished by the strength and weakness of their bodies; but faith is judged according to devotion of mind. It often happens that a woman becomes the means of salvation for a man, and that a man surpasses a woman in religion.

Since this is so, and the entire diversity of origin, condition, and body is removed through Christ’s baptism and his clothing, we are all one in Christ Jesus, so that, just as the Father and the Son are one in themselves, so we too may be one in them.

*(Augustine.)* Have believing women therefore lost the sex of their bodies? No. But because there they are renewed according to the image of God, where there is no sex—there humanity was made according to the image of God, where there is no sex, namely, in the spirit of the mind—all are clothed in her.

Will her husband be concerned about the nakedness of his servants when he is staying somewhere, having such a wife? Who is this husband except Christ? And who is the wife except the Church?

They are clothed—and clothed most excellently. Do you wish to know how excellently? “All who have been baptized in Christ have been clothed; you have put on Christ.” All who have put on Christ are completely clothed in her presence.

They put on Christ not only according to the form of the sacrament, but also in the practice of example, following the footsteps of their Lord. Human beings put on Christ sometimes only up to the reception of the sacrament, and sometimes also up to the sanctification of life. The first can be shared by both the good and the wicked; the second belongs to the good and devout.

Thus he says: “The law was our pedagogue toward Christ.” This is what he means when he says: “We were guarded under the law, confined within it; after faith came, we are no longer under a pedagogue.”

He does not, therefore, condemn those who nullify the grace of Christ, as though the one who calls people into freedom had not yet come and they still wished to remain under a pedagogue. When he says that all are sons of God through faith because they have put on Christ, all who have been baptized in Christ, his purpose is that the Gentiles should not despair because they had not been guarded under a pedagogue and therefore should not think themselves sons. By putting on Christ through faith, all become sons—not by nature, as does the only Son, who is also the Wisdom of God, nor through the power and singularity of the assumption by which he naturally possesses and acts as the person of Wisdom, as the mediator himself, made one with the Wisdom that assumed him without the intervention of any mediator.

Rather, they become sons by participation in Wisdom, prepared and granted through the faith of the mediator; and this grace of faith he now calls clothing. Those who believed in Christ put on Christ and therefore became sons of God and brothers of the same mediator. In this faith there is no distinction: neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female. For insofar as all are believers, all are one in Christ Jesus.

And if faith, through which one walks justly in this life, accomplishes this, how much more perfectly and abundantly will the reality itself accomplish it when we see face to face? For now, although we possess the first fruits of the Spirit, who is life because of the righteousness of faith, the body nevertheless remains dead because of sin. The difference of nation, condition, or sex has indeed already been removed from the unity of faith, but it remains in mortal conduct.

The order of these distinctions must be observed along the journey of this life, and the apostles give instructions concerning it, providing most salutary rules about how people should live with one another according to the distinction of nation—Jews and Greeks; according to the distinction of condition—masters and slaves; and according to the distinction of sex—husbands and wives; or according to whatever other such circumstances arise.

The Lord himself first said: “Give back to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XII; Luke XX). Some things we preserve in the unity of faith without any distinction, while other things belong to the order of this present life, as on a journey, lest the name of the Lord and his teaching be blasphemed.

This is done not only because of anger, so that we may avoid offending people, but also because of conscience, so that we may not act hypocritically, as though merely before human eyes. Rather, we act with a pure conscience of love, for the sake of God, who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. II).

But if you are one in Christ Jesus, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise.

*(Ambrose.)* All believers are Abraham’s seed, because Abraham is the father of all believers. And if they are sons, they are necessarily heirs of his promise, so that through faith they may obtain what was promised to Abraham and become participants in his justification in the kingdom of heaven.

*(Jerome.)* Since the promises were made to Abraham and to his seed, which is Christ Jesus, consequently those who are Christ’s sons—that is, his seed—are also called Abraham’s seed, since they are his seed from the Seed.

But whenever our Lord Jesus Christ is called Abraham’s seed, this should be understood bodily: he was generated from Abraham’s stock. Whenever, however, we who, having received the Savior’s word, have believed in him and have received the nobility of the race of Abraham, to whom the promise was made, are called seed, we should understand this spiritually, as the seed of faith and preaching.

Moreover, this should also be considered: when he speaks of the Lord, he says that the promises were made to Abraham and to his seed—that is, to Christ Jesus—and he uses the plural “promises.” But when he speaks of those who, through Christ, are Abraham’s seed, he uses “promise” in the singular, as in the present passage: “Therefore you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise.”

It was fitting, of course, that what was spoken in the one Christ in the plural should be applied in the singular to the many human beings.

*(Augustine.)* Above he had said: “He does not say ‘and to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: ‘and to your seed,’ which is Christ.” Here, therefore, he shows that the one seed is Christ. But Christ is not to be understood as the mediator alone; the Church is also to be understood, of which he is the head, so that all may be one in Christ and receive the inheritance according to the promise through faith.

The people had been confined within that faith—that is, guarded like children under a pedagogue until the coming of the faith—until the appropriate time of maturity, because those who had been called in that people according to the purpose were to be called into freedom: namely, those who were found to be grain on that threshing floor.

## CHAPTER IV

The Apostle demonstrates the cessation of the legal observances through two comparisons, with the ingratitude of the Galatians inserted between them.

I mean that as long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a slave, although he is lord of everything; but he is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by his father. (Ambrose.) It is true that they established the father’s legal authority and determined up to what age a subject ought to remain under authority, so that, as long as he is a child, he cannot exercise his freedom or rule as an heir; rather, in the condition imposed by his guardians or stewards, he is almost like a slave. By this example he proves that those who were under the law were children with respect to merit and did not possess freedom, because in the condition of the law they were subjected on account of sin. Thus we too, when we were children, were enslaved under the elements of this world. By “elements” he means the new moons and the sabbath: the new moons are lunar days, which the Jews observe, while the sabbath is the day of rest. Before the promise came—that is, the gift of God’s grace which purifies and justifies believers—we were imperfect and childish, subjected by God’s law to fellow servants, as though to pedagogues; for our freedom was held in bondage because of sin. Yet the Jews did not expect anything from the elements, as the pagans did, but worshiped God the Creator in the creature.

(Jerome.) This child-heir, who differs in nothing from a slave although he is lord of everything, but is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by his father, signifies the entire human race up to the coming of Christ—and, to say more, up to the consummation of the world. For just as all who have not yet been born die in the first-created Adam, so also all who were born before Christ’s coming are made alive in the second Adam. And thus it will happen that we served the law in the fathers, while they are saved by grace in the children. This interpretation accords with the Catholic Church, which asserts one providence for the Old and New Testaments and does not separate in time those whom it has joined in condition. We have all been built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Jesus Christ our Lord as the cornerstone holding us together. He made both peoples one, and, by destroying the dividing wall in his flesh, abolished the hostility between the two peoples; he changed the difficulty of the ancient law through the integrity of evangelical doctrines.

[Col. 0310C] Guardians and stewards may also be understood as the prophets, whose words instructed us daily in anticipation of the Savior’s coming, just as the law of Moses, explained above, was a pedagogue. The angels of the little ones may likewise be understood—those who daily see the face of the Father and intercede for them—of whom it is said: “He will send the angel of the Lord around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Psalm 33). Priests and rulers may also be understood, for at that time they ruled over the people and are now considered to provide a pattern.

Those are rightly said to be under guardians who, possessing the spirit of fear, have not yet deserved to receive the spirit of freedom and adoption. For infancy fears sins, is afraid of its pedagogue, and does not trust that it is free, although by nature it is [Col. 0311A] a mistress. According to both interpretations—whether we have called the guardians and stewards prophets or angels—this child remains under stewards and guardians until he has completed the proper time of the mature man.

As the proper age, under Roman law, is fixed at twenty-five years, so, for the perfection of the human race, Christ’s coming is reckoned as the appointed time. As soon as he comes, and we have all grown into a mature man, the pedagogue and guardian depart from us. Then we shall enjoy the authority of the Lord and possession of the inheritance, in which, because we were born earlier, we had in a sense been considered strangers.

Thus we too, he says, when we were children, were enslaved under the elements of the world. He called the elements of the world the same beings whom above he had called guardians and stewards. Because we were first placed under these rulers, and were not yet able to receive the coming of the Son of God among us, we were instructed in their midst. Some think that these are angels who preside over the four elements of the world—earth, water, fire, and air—and that, before anyone believes in Christ, he must be governed under their authority.

Most think that by the elements of the world he means heaven and earth and what is within them: the sun, moon, seas, and the gods of forests and mountains—things worshiped by the sages of Greece, the barbarian nations, and the Romans, the sewer of every superstition. When Christ comes, we are freed from these things, understanding them to be creatures, not divinities.

Others interpret the elements of the world as the law of Moses and the utterances of the prophets, because through these beginnings and elementary stages of learning we receive the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom. Accordingly, to those who ought already to have been mature but, having neglected the truth, still clung to the rudiments of instruction, the Apostle writes in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Although by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need someone to teach you what are the elementary principles of the words of God” (Hebrews 5).

(Augustine.) It may be asked how, according to this comparison, the Jews were under the elements of this world, since through the law they received, they were instructed to worship the one God who made heaven and earth. But there may be another resolution of this passage. Earlier he made the law a pedagogue, under which the Jewish people were placed; now he may call the elements of the world the procurators and stewards under whom the nations served. Thus the one child—the people belonging through one faith to the one seed of Abraham, because it has been gathered from both Jews and Gentiles—was partly under the pedagogue of the law during its childhood, namely, in the part gathered from the Jews; and partly under the elements of this world, which it served as procurators and stewards, in the part gathered from the Gentiles.

Thus, when the Apostle mingles his own person into the statement—not saying, “When you were children, you were enslaved under the elements of this world,” but saying, “When we were children, we were enslaved under the elements of the world”—this does not refer to the Jews, from whom Paul derives his origin, but rather [Col. 0312A] to the Gentiles, only in this passage. He can fittingly join himself to their person, since he was sent to evangelize them.

Then he says that, when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son to free the child-heir who was enslaved, partly to the law as to a pedagogue, and partly to the elements of this world as to procurators and stewards.

But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. (Ambrose.) The fullness of time is the completed period appointed by God the Father, when he would send his Son, so that, having been made from a virgin and born as a human being, he might subject himself to the law until the time of baptism, giving the pattern by which sinners, washed and freed from the yoke of the law, would by God’s gracious favor be adopted as his sons, as he had promised, having been redeemed by the blood of his Son.

It was necessary for the Savior to be made under the law, as a son of Abraham according to the flesh, so that he might appear circumcised—the one who had been promised to Abraham and had come to justify the nations through faith, bearing the sign of the one to whom he had been promised. Therefore no one else ought to be circumcised after him, because the sign continued only until the one who had been promised to restore the faith in which Abraham had been justified in uncircumcision came. Thus circumcision is not necessary for believers. Abraham, however, was circumcised because he believed that he would have a son in whom all the nations would be blessed.

(Jerome.) Pay careful attention to the fact that he did not say “made through a woman,” as Marcion and the other heresies wish, since they pretend that Christ’s flesh was merely apparent, but “of a woman,” so that he would be believed to have been born not through her but from her. As for his calling the holy and blessed mother of the Lord “a woman,” not “a virgin,” the same is written in the Gospel according to Matthew, when Joseph’s wife is mentioned and when the Lord himself rebukes her as a woman. It was not necessary always to call her “virgin” cautiously and timidly, since “woman” signifies sex more than union with a man.

Just as he was made under the law in order to redeem those who were under the law, so, on behalf of those who were born from a woman, he wished to be born from a woman. For this reason also he received baptism in the flowing waters of the Jordan, as though he were a penitent, although he was free from sins, in order to teach the others that they must be cleansed through baptism and born as sons through the new adoption of the Spirit.

John the Baptist, not understanding this, tried to prevent him from approaching the washing, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you” (Matthew 3). Immediately the mystery is taught: “Let it be so for now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Mark 1; John 1), lest the one who had come for the salvation of humanity omit anything from the conduct of human beings.

(Augustine.) The phrase “made of a woman” causes offense, because we confess that he was born of a virgin, but we confess that “made” refers only to his humanity. God is always the one who makes; he does not become something in order to exist. God does not become, but something comes to be for someone, as it is said: “Lord, you have become our refuge” (Psalm 89), and: “The Lord has become my helper” (Psalm 29).

When was the one who was never made made? The Lord Christ was made human so that he might exist as what the Creator, who had always been, was not: a creature. Remaining God, he was made human, so that what he was not might come to be, not so that what he was might perish.

Why, then, is what was made from the virgin called “of a woman”? Among the Hebrews, in whose language Scripture was first written, “woman” is the name indicating sex, not lost virginity. Read when woman was formed. “God,” it says, “took one of his ribs”—that is, of the man—“and built it into a woman.” Thus Mary is a woman; thus it was said to her before she gave birth, before she conceived: “Blessed are you among women” (Luke 1).

When, therefore, he says, “God sent his Son, made of a woman,” he sufficiently shows that the Son was sent precisely by being made of a woman. As one born from God, he was already in this world; as one born from Mary, he was born into this world and came as one sent.

Thus, although without any beginning in time the Word was in the beginning, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word, within the Word itself, without any temporal beginning, there was the time when the Word would become flesh and dwell among us. When this fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman—that is, made in time—so that the incarnate Word might appear to human beings.

(Jerome.) Another person will examine the words themselves more acutely, “to redeem,” and will say that those are signified as redeemed who first belonged to God’s side and afterward ceased to do so. Those who were not under the law, however, are not so much redeemed as purchased. Thus, concerning the Corinthians, among whom fornication—and such fornication as is not even heard of among the Gentiles—was being committed, he writes: “You were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 7), not “redeemed,” since they had not been under the law.

(Augustine.) Behold, Christ came for this purpose: to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might no longer be under the law but under grace. Who, then, gave the law? The one who gave the law also gave grace. But he sent the law through a servant, while he himself descended with grace.

How had people come to be under the law? By failing to fulfill the law. Therefore, whoever fulfills the law is not under the law but with the law; whoever is under the law is not lifted up by the law but weighed down by it. Thus the law makes all who are placed under it guilty, and it is over their heads for this purpose: to display sins, not to remove them.

Because they could not fulfill the law by their own strength, having become guilty under the law they implored the help of a liberator. The guilt imposed by the law made the proud sick, and the sickness of the proud became the confession of the humble. The sick now confess that they are sick, so that the physician may come and heal the sick. Who is the physician? Our Lord Jesus Christ.

He says “adoption” so that we may clearly understand the one and only Son of God. We are sons of God by his gift and merciful graciousness; he is Son by nature, being what the Father is. He did not say “let us receive,” but “let us receive again,” to signify that we had lost this in Adam, from whom we are mortal.

Therefore what he says—“to redeem those who were under the law”—refers to freeing the people who, as a child, served under a pedagogue, and it relates to what he said, “made under the law.” But what he says—“so that we might receive adoption as sons”—relates to what he said, “made of a woman.”

From this we receive adoption: that the only Son did not disdain participation in our nature. He was made of a woman so that he would not only be the only-begotten Son, where he has no brothers, but also the firstborn among many brothers.

He proposed two things: “made of a woman” and “made under the law.” But, reversing the order, he answered by now joining to it the people who, as children, served under procurators and stewards—that is, under the elements of this world—so that they would not think they were not sons because they were not under a pedagogue.

And because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba, Father.” (Ambrose.) He began with those to whom he was writing, saying: “Because you are sons of God,” and then he includes the Jews when he says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts.”

When he called the Gentiles who believe in Christ sons of God—those who had previously been enemies—there was no doubt that he also meant believing Jews to be called sons of God, since they are known already to have been called by this name. They received the name long ago, as an image, so that afterward it might be confirmed through Christ, because without the Spirit it was not complete.

This is what he also says to the Romans: “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are sons of God” (Romans 8). To prove that we had been adopted by God as sons, he gave us his Spirit, which displays the sign of the Father in his sons. Since in our weakness and unworthiness we would not dare to say this, the Spirit prompts us to dare to say, “Abba,” which means “Father.” In former times the Jews were not permitted to say this.

(Jerome.) Clearly the Apostle Paul names three spirits: the Spirit of the Son of God, as in the present passage, “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts”; the Spirit of God, as in the statement, “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Romans 8); and the Holy Spirit, as in, “Your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, who is in you” (1 Corinthians 6).

That the Holy Spirit is someone other than the Son of God is most clearly demonstrated in the Gospel: “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Luke 12).

I shall briefly show the three spirits named in Psalm 50, where the Prophet says: “Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit.”

He calls the princely Spirit the Father, because the Son is from the Father and not the Father from the Son. By the right Spirit—the Spirit of truth and righteousness—he signifies Christ the Lord, because the Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5). It is also written in the Psalms: “Give the king your judgment, O God, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Psalm 71).

Then, using its explicit name, he calls the Holy Spirit the Holy Spirit. Although these titles and persons differ, they are united in substance and nature; and, because of their shared nature, the same Spirit is indifferently called at one time the Spirit of the Father [Col. 0315A] and at another the Spirit of the Son.

The argument by which he attempts to assert that we are no longer under the law but under the grace of the Lord Jesus he concludes in this way. Earlier he had said that we might receive adoption as sons; now he proves from the Spirit we possess within us that we are sons of God.

He says that we would never dare to say, “Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name,” unless the Spirit dwelling within us, with the great voice of understanding and doctrine, were crying: “Abba, Father.”

“Abba” is Hebrew and means the same as “Father.” Scripture preserves this practice in many places, placing the Hebrew word together with its interpretation. It should also be noted that in Scripture “crying out” does not mean emitting a loud voice, but understanding and the greatness of doctrine.

For in Exodus the Lord answered Moses, “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exodus 14), although no voice at all had previously come from Moses. Rather, Scripture called his wounded heart and his tearful groaning for the people a cry.

Therefore, just as the one who has the Spirit of the Son of God is a son of God, so, conversely, the one who does not have the Spirit of the Son of God cannot be called a son of God. “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8).

(Augustine.) Here he did not say that the Spirit itself cries out in prayer, but “in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’” Elsewhere, however, he says: “Because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Galatians 4). Here he does not say “in whom we cry,” but preferred to say that the Spirit itself cries out, by which it comes about that we cry.

So also with the statements: “The Spirit himself intercedes with inexpressible groanings”; and: “It is the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.”

Therefore you are no longer a slave but a son. (Ambrose.) He is not a slave because, having been removed from the power of the law, he has become a partner in the blessing of God’s proper Son.

And if a son, then also an heir through God. There is no doubt that a person adopts a son for the purpose of leaving him as an heir. But inheritance comes through someone’s death. How, then, are mortals called heirs of one who always lives? Scripture speaks according to our custom, so that we may understand. To show that the Father will give his sons his goods, it calls the things he will give an inheritance.

(Jerome.) What we say in this passage we must also observe elsewhere: the entire human race is discussed in the singular number. For all believers are one in Christ Jesus and members of his body. Reduced to a perfect man, we have him as our head, because Christ is the head of man.

But at that time, when you did not know God, you served those who by nature are not gods. (Ambrose.) Because previously they sinned through ignorance by serving idols, he indicates that their ignorance was easily pardoned, as Abimelech says to God in Genesis: “Lord, will you destroy an ignorant nation?” (Augustine.) It is quite probable that the earlier statement also concerned the Gentiles, that they were enslaved under the elements of this world, as under procurators and stewards.

For the elements themselves are certainly not gods by nature, whether in heaven or on earth: although there are “many gods and many lords,” for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him (1 Corinthians 8).

When he says, “You served those who by nature are not gods,” he sufficiently demonstrates that the one true God is God by nature. By this name the Trinity is received within the most faithful and Catholic embrace of the heart.

As for those who are not gods by nature, he previously calls them procurators and stewards because no creature exists—whether one that remains in the truth, giving glory to God, or one that did not remain in the truth, seeking its own glory—that does not serve divine providence, willingly or unwillingly. The creature that is willing does with providence what is good; from the creature that is unwilling, what is just is brought about.

For if the transgressing angels themselves, with their prince the Devil, were not rightly called procurators or stewards of divine providence, the Lord would not call the Devil the ruler of this world, nor would apostolic authority itself employ him for the correction of human beings. Paul says elsewhere: “I handed them over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Timothy 1). And elsewhere, for their salvation, he says: “Although absent in body, I am present in spirit, and I have already judged, as though present, the one who has acted in this way. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are assembled, and my spirit with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, you are to hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus” (1 Corinthians 5).

But an officer under so great a commander does only what is permitted to him, and the procurators and stewards of this world do nothing unless the Lord allows it. Nothing escapes him as it would escape a human being, nor is he deficient in power, so that procurators and stewards who are under his authority could accomplish anything, in the matters subject to them according to their rank, either without his permission or without his knowledge.

Yet they are not recompensed according to what is justly done through them, but according to the intention with which they act. For God has not denied free will to his rational creature, and yet he has retained for himself the power that justly orders even the unjust.

We have treated this passage more fully and extensively in other books. Therefore, whether the nations worshiped the sun, moon, stars, heaven, earth, and other such things, or demons, they are rightly understood to have been under procurators and stewards.

Nevertheless, what follows again entangles the question as though it had already been explained. For throughout the entire Epistle he shows that no one troubled the Galatians’ faith except those who came from circumcision and wished to lead them toward the carnal observances of the law, as though salvation were found in them. Yet in this one passage he appears to address those who were attempting to return to the superstitions of the Gentiles.

But now that you have come to know God—or rather, to be known by God—how can you turn back again to the weak and impoverished elements, to which you wish to be enslaved anew? (Ambrose.) He marks the gravity of their offense, because after knowing God they had begun to follow what belonged to the pagans; and he adds something further: “For they did not themselves know God, but rather were known by God.”

Since they were not seeking God, he summoned them to his grace; yet, ungrateful, they had begun to turn back to the things they had worshiped when they did not know God, so that they might venerate weak and impoverished elements rather than Christ with their whole mind, in whom all divinity dwells.

He calls the elements weak and impoverished because they are imperfect; for in governing the world they need one another. In Christ, however, salvation is perfect.

(Jerome.) I therefore think that, as long as a person is a child and has not completed the time appointed by the father so that he can be called a son and heir, he is under the elements of the world—that is, under the law of Moses.

But when, after freedom, adoption, and the inheritance owed to a son, he returns again to the law, wishing to be circumcised and to follow the whole letter of Jewish superstition, then what had previously been merely the elements of the world for him are also called weak and impoverished beginnings. For they are so useless to their worshipers that they cannot even provide what they had previously provided, after Jerusalem, the temple, and the altar have been destroyed.

Someone might reply: If the law and the commandments written in the law are weak and impoverished elements, and if those who have come to know God—or rather have been known by him—ought not to observe the law, lest they begin not so much to worship God, by whom they have been known, as to return to those who are not gods by nature, then either Moses and the prophets observed the law but did not know God and were not known by him; or, if they knew God, they did not fulfill the commandments of the law. Both alternatives are dangerous to assert: either that they did not do what belongs to the law and thus knew God, or that they did not know God while they guarded the weak and impoverished elements of the law.

This can be resolved by saying that, just as Paul became a Jew to the Jews in order to win Jews, and at Cenchreae cut his hair because of a vow, and practiced going barefoot and shaving his head in the temple at Jerusalem (Acts 10), in order to calm the jealousy of those who had been instructed against him because they thought he acted contrary to the law of Moses and the God of the prophets, so holy men also did what belonged to the law while following the meaning of the law more than its letter.

They desired, no less than Abraham, after removing the veil from their face, to see the day of Christ; they saw it and rejoiced (John 8). They became weak to the weak, in order to win the weak; and to those who were under the law they became as though they themselves were under the law, so that they might separate them from the idols to which they had become accustomed in Egypt.

The law of Moses, which before the Gospel was rich, prosperous, and illustrious, after Christ’s coming became, by comparison with him, weak and impoverished, diminished and destroyed by the one who was greater than Solomon, the temple, and Jonah (Matthew 12).

In another interpretation, we shall affirm that the weak and impoverished elements are the traditions of the Jews and the contemptible understanding according to the letter. These are “ordinances that are not good” and “commandments that are not good.” The spiritual understanding of the law is strong and rich, so that either it should not be called an element at all, or it is an element only in comparison with the future age and life in Christ Jesus, in which the angels and heavenly powers now live.

Compared with the Jewish understanding, however, it is called not so much an element—that is, a beginning—as perfection.

When he says, “Now that you know God, or rather are known by him,” he shows that after worshiping idols the Galatians came to understand God, or rather were judged worthy of his knowledge. This does not mean that God the Creator of all things is ignorant of anything, but that those alone are said to be known by God who have changed error into piety: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2).

And the Savior says in the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd, and I know my own and my own know me” (John 10). But to the impious he says: “I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity” (Luke 13); and to the foolish virgins: “I do not know you—who you are” (Matthew 25).

[Col. 0318B] You observe days and months and seasons and years. (Ambrose.) He now explains which elements he meant. The sun makes the day; the courses of the moon make the months; the seasons are spring, summer, autumn, and winter. These four, when their proper number has been completed, make a year.

Those observe days who say, for example: “One must not set out tomorrow”; “Nothing should be begun the day after tomorrow”; and they are accustomed to be deceived in this way. Those observe months who examine the course of the moon, saying, for example: “On the seventh moon, tools should not be made”; or again: “On the ninth moon, a purchased slave should not be brought home.” Through such practices adverse events more readily tend to occur.

They observe seasons when they say: “Today is the beginning of spring”; “Today is a festival”; “The day after tomorrow is the Vulcanalia”; and they say such things as: “It is an inauspicious day; one may not leave the house.”

They observe years when they say: “On the Kalends of January it is a new year,” as though the years were not completed every day. To preserve the memory of Janus with two faces, they use this superstition, which ought to be far from the servants of God. For if God is loved with the whole heart, then, with him propitious, there ought to be neither fear nor suspicion of such things.

Another interpretation follows.

(Jerome.) Whoever does not worship the Father in spirit and truth does not know the sabbath-rest prepared for the saints, concerning which God says: “If they shall enter into my rest” (Psalm 94). Nor does he remember those times of which it is written: “Remember the days of eternity” (Isaiah 46); and elsewhere: “I remembered the ancient days, and I kept eternal years in mind” (Psalm 76).

He observes Jewish days, months, seasons, and years: days such as sabbaths and new moons; from the tenth day of the first month until the fourteenth, when the bodily lamb is reserved for sacrifice; and from the fourteenth until the twenty-first of that same month, when unleavened bread is eaten—not the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5), but in the old leaven of the malice and wickedness of the Pharisees.

He also observes the seven weeks which, following Jewish practice, he counts after the unleavened bread, the days of Israelite Pentecost. He observes likewise the blowing of trumpets in the seventh month, on the first day of the month. He observes Jewish days according to custom by setting aside the tenth day of that same month for atonement and fasting, and by setting up booths for the Feast of Tabernacles.

Those guard the months who observe the first and seventh month without understanding the mystery of truth.

[Col. 0319A] They also observe seasons who come to Jerusalem three times each year, believing that they fulfill the Lord’s command: “Three times in the year you shall keep a feast for me: the feast of unleavened bread, the feast of the firstfruits of the harvest, and the feast of ingathering at the end of the year” (Exodus 23). And elsewhere: “Three times in the year every male of yours shall appear before the Lord your God” (Exodus 34).

When he says “and years,” I think he means the seventh year of remission and the fiftieth year, which they call the Jubilee.

Someone may say: If it is not permitted to observe days, months, seasons, and years, then we too incur a similar offense when we observe the fourth day of the week, the preparation day, the Lord’s Day, the fast of Lent, the festival of Easter, the joy of Pentecost, and, according to the variety of regions, different seasons established in honor of the martyrs.

To this question someone who answers simply will say that the days of Jewish observance are not the same as ours. We do not celebrate the Passover of unleavened bread, but the Passover of the resurrection and the cross. We do not count seven weeks at Pentecost according to Israelite custom, but venerate the coming of the Holy Spirit.

And, so that an unregulated gathering of the people might not diminish faith in Christ, certain days were established so that we might all come together at the same time. This is not because the day on which we assemble is more celebrated, but because, on whatever day we ought to assemble, greater joy arises from seeing one another.

The person who attempts to answer the opposing question more acutely asserts that all days are equal. Christ is not crucified only on the preparation day, nor does he rise only on the Lord’s Day; rather, every day is a day of holy resurrection, and he is always to be eaten as the Lord’s flesh.

Fasts and gatherings during the days were established by believing men for the sake of those who devote themselves more to the world than to God, and who cannot—or rather do not wish—to gather in the Church throughout the whole course of their lives and offer God the sacrifice of their prayers before their human activities.

For how many people are there who regularly practice even the few appointed times of prayer or fasting? Therefore, just as it is permitted for us either always to fast or always to pray, and to celebrate continually, with joy, the Lord’s Day by receiving the Lord’s body, so it is not permitted for the Jews at every time to sacrifice the lamb, celebrate Pentecost, set up the tabernacles, or fast every day.

(Augustine.) There are certain things that would be considered very slight unless Scripture showed them to be more serious in its judgment. Who, for example, would think how great a sin it is to observe days, months, seasons, and years in the manner of those who, on particular days, months, or years, wish either to begin or not to begin something because, according to the empty teachings of human beings, they consider certain times favorable or unfavorable?

We can measure the magnitude of this evil from the fear of the Apostle, who says to such people:

I fear for you, lest somehow I have labored among you in vain.

**(Ambrose.)** The Galatians had been overthrown in a twofold manner: after receiving the grace of God, they were turning not only to the Law but also to their former errors. For, having been led astray or overturned, they readily inclined toward observance of the Law—its observance of days and new moons had drawn them to these practices. Therefore he says: “I fear for you, lest somehow I have labored among you in vain.” For he saw them progressing toward what was worse, so that they might even withdraw altogether from Christ.

**(Jerome.)** He has moderated his words with sufficient prudence between the Apostle’s authority and the gentleness of a holy man, adding: “I fear for you, lest somehow I have labored among you in vain.” For if he had wished to condemn them abruptly, he would certainly have said: “I fear you, for I have labored among you in vain.” But now, seeing that they had zeal for God, though not according to knowledge (Rom. X), he did not entirely despair of the salvation of those who had been deceived by a pious error; nor, on the other hand, did he leave them without correction, lest he give both them an opportunity to persevere in error and others an opportunity to err similarly.

“I fear for you” is put for “I fear concerning you.” A teacher labors in vain when he himself summons his disciples to greater things, while they, falling backward, return to lesser and lowly things.

**(Augustine.)** Our assemblies are full of people who take from astrologers the times for carrying out their affairs. Indeed, when something is about to be begun—whether a building or any other such work—they often do not hesitate to warn us against beginning it on the days they call “Egyptian days,” not knowing, as the saying goes, where they are walking.

But if this passage is to be understood of the superstitious observance of the Jews, what hope do those people have who wish to be called Christians while steering their shipwrecked life by an ephemeris? For if, following Jewish custom, they observed times according to the divine books that God gave to the still-carnal people, the Apostle would say to them: “I fear for you, lest somehow I have labored among you in vain.” And yet, if someone is discovered—even a catechumen—observing the Sabbath according to the Jewish rite, the Church is thrown into an uproar.

But now innumerable members of the faithful say to us with great confidence to our faces: “I do not set out after the Kalends.” And we scarcely and timidly prohibit such things, smiling lest they become angry and fearing that they might regard us as marveling at something new. Woe to the sins of human beings, which we shudder at only when they are unusual, while those customary sins—for the cleansing of which the Son of God’s blood was poured out—however great they may be, and however completely they shut the kingdom of God against themselves, we are often compelled to tolerate by seeing everything, and by tolerating certain things even to do them ourselves. And would that, O Lord, we did not do everything that we have been unable to prohibit!

But now let us see what follows. Indeed, we had passed over the statement: “But now, having come to know God—or rather, having been known by God.” It seems that in this passage also the Apostle’s manner of speaking wishes to accommodate human weakness, and that the mode of divine speech appears not to have descended only in the books of the Old Testament, even to the level of earthly human thoughts.

Since he corrected what he had said—“having come to know God”—this ought not to trouble us. For it is clear that, as long as we walk by faith and not by sight, we have not yet come to know God; rather, we are purified by that faith so that at the proper time we may be able to know him. But when, in the very correction, he says, “or rather, having been known by God,” if this is taken strictly, God may seem to come to know something in time that he had not known before.

Therefore the statement should be understood figuratively, so that we take the “eyes” of God to mean his love itself, which he demonstrated by sending his only Son to be killed for the ungodly. For we commonly say of those who are loved that they are held before someone’s eyes. Thus “having come to know God—or rather, having been known by God” means what John also said: “Not that we loved God, but that he himself loved us” (I John IV).

## Be as I am, because I also am as you are.

**(Ambrose.)** He says this so that they may take care to correct these things, since it is not impossible for them to be as he is. For he too was this—that is, a human being—just as they were; and although he had been in error while persecuting the Church, once corrected he turned himself around.

**(Jerome.)** His meaning is this: “Just as I became weak for you who were weak, and could not speak to you as spiritual people but as carnal people and little children in Christ, and because you were not yet able to eat solid food I fed you only with the milk of the Gospel, not wishing you to remain forever in the age of infancy, but gradually to lead you on to adolescence and youth so that you could receive solid food, so you too ought to be as I am: namely, to think of more perfect things, leaving milk behind and passing on to stronger foods and greater nourishment.”

He says this as an imitator of the Savior, who “did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and being found in human appearance” (Phil. II), so that we might become gods from human beings and no longer die; but, rising again with Christ, might be called his friends and brothers, so that the disciple might be as the teacher and the servant as the lord.

This may also be understood as follows: “I beseech you, brothers,” he says, “that, having rejected the Jewish observance of days, months, seasons, and years—which are shadows of things to come—you imitate me. I lived in the Law without complaint, but I considered everything as refuse and rubbish, in order to gain Christ” (Phil. III). For I too was once as you are now, when I was held bound by these same observances and, because Christ’s Church did not practice them, was persecuting and ravaging it.

## Brothers, I beseech you: you have done me no wrong.

**(Augustine.)** It is as though he were saying: “Therefore do not think that I wish to harm you.”

**(Ambrose.)** He now deals more gently with them and begins to recall their good qualities, so that, after hearing severe reprimands, they might be refreshed by hearing of their good works and deliberately reform themselves, lest, being pressed too long by harsher rebukes, they become embittered.

Yet he says that they had done him no harm, for their offense harmed themselves. The Apostle had fulfilled the duty of the stewardship entrusted to him, preaching to them with all diligence, just as the Lord says to the prophet Ezekiel: “You preach; if they listen to you, you will gain them; if not, you will save your own soul” (Ezek. III).

## You know that because of the weakness of the flesh I preached the Gospel to you formerly, and you did not despise or reject your trial, which was in my flesh; rather, you received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.

He recalls to them the time when he first preached the Gospel of God to them. At that time the Apostle was being subjected to insults and weakened by beatings. He appears weak because he is humbled and does not resist for the sake of the Gospel of God.

In this he praises their steadfastness, because they were not drawn away from the faith. The Apostle’s sufferings were a trial for the Galatians, in which they were found firm and did not waver in faith. For, having been scandalized, they might have said: “What power or hope is there in this faith, when its minister is so humiliated?” But because they had already filled their minds with hope for the future, they did not fear present dangers for Christ’s name. They were certain that our faith has its dignity not on earth but in heaven, and that great rewards are repaid for these tribulations.

**(Jerome.)** These words both summon us to humility and strike down the arrogance of bishops who, as though stationed on some lofty watchtower, scarcely deign to look upon mortals or speak to their fellow servants.
