Let the erring and foolish Galatians learn from the Apostle that they are called brothers; let them learn gentle words after rebuke from one who says: “I beseech you.” And what he beseeches is that they should be his imitators, as he is Christ’s.

Indeed, to follow the present passage, he asks nothing great: just as he himself became lesser for their sake, descending from greater things, so they should rise from lesser things to greater.

“You have done me no wrong,” he says. A disciple wrongs his teacher if through his negligence he destroys the teacher’s commands and labor. The Galatians had not wronged the Apostle up to the present time, since they were preserving his Gospel and commandments.

Or it may be understood thus: “When I first announced the Gospel to you, and because of the weakness of your flesh—for you were not able to receive greater mysteries—I preached to you as to little children and pretended that I myself was weak in order to win you, who were weak. Did you not receive me as an angel, as Christ Jesus?

“Since, therefore, you never wronged me in anything, and since, for your sake, you regarded me as humble and cast down, like the Son of God, how is it that, now that I summon you to greater things, I am wronged by you? You are losing my labor and making void that stewardship in which I had pretended to be little; now you grieve over it as though it had been fruitless.”

By “the weakness of the flesh,” he means not his own weakness but that of his hearers. Paul preached to the Galatians, who could not subject the flesh to the word of God; being, as it were, fleshly, they were entirely unable to receive spiritual understanding.

To make this clearer, let us give an example. The one who says, “If they cannot contain themselves, let them marry” (I Cor. VII), teaches on account of the weakness of the flesh; and likewise: “If a woman’s husband has died, she is free; let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (ibid.). But he does not teach on account of the weakness of the flesh when he says: “You are released from your wife; do not seek a wife”; and: “It is time that those who have wives should be as though they had none.” Some commandments are given to spiritual people, others to carnal people. And one thing is commanded according to authority, another according to indulgence.

“And you did not despise,” he says, “your trial in my flesh.” This is an obscure passage and requires closer attention. “I,” he says, “preached to you formerly, as to little children and infants, because of your weakness of flesh, beginning with lesser things and, so to speak, almost stammering among you. This arrangement and simulated weakness of preaching was my management, but your trial: whether you would approve of these things and regard as great what, in accordance with your condition, was lesser and was presented by me as humble. Yet you received them not as little things but as great ones, and admired them so greatly that you received me, who spoke these things, as an angel—or, to say more, as the Son of God.

“Thus your trial, by which I was testing you in the carnal announcement of my teaching, was neither despised nor worthless. It possessed more dignity than I had estimated.”

This passage may also be explained as follows: “When I came to you, I did not come with a discourse of wisdom, but as a humble and despised man, bringing nothing great except the Crucified One.

“When, therefore, you saw me established in a body subject to illnesses, promising the kingdoms of heaven, you did not mock me or consider me worthy of contempt. You understood that the humility of my flesh and the lowliness of my appearance were presented as a trial for you: whether you would despise one whom unbelievers considered pitiable. But, on the contrary, you received that humble, lowly, and despised man as an angel, and more than an angel.”

Or certainly we may conjecture that, at the time when he first came to the Galatians, the Apostle was ill and afflicted by some bodily weakness; nevertheless he did not cease or suppress his voice in silence, so as not to preach the Gospel that he had begun. For they report that he often suffered the most severe headache, and that this was the “angel of Satan” assigned to him to buffet him in the flesh, lest he become exalted (II Cor. XII).

This weakness and bodily illness was a trial among those to whom the Gospel was being announced: would they despise one who promised sublime things while they saw him subject to bodily ailments? It may also be said that, at the beginning of his coming to the Galatians, he endured insults, persecutions, and bodily blows from those who opposed the Gospel. This was certainly a great trial for the Galatians, who saw Christ’s Apostle being beaten.

When he says, “You received me as an angel, as Christ Jesus,” he shows Christ to be greater than an angel, although, according to the dispensation of his body, the Psalmist had sung that he was made lower: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. VIII). And he shows that his words at the beginning possessed such power that he was regarded as both an angel and Christ.

## Where, then, is your blessedness?

**(Ambrose.)** He says that they had been blessed in comparison with the other Churches because the Apostles’ sufferings did not break them but caused them to grow in faith.

## For I bear you witness that, if possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me.

**(Augustine.)** Why could this not happen, except because it could in no way happen justly? Job likewise says: “Would that I could kill myself!” (Job X). And the Lord says to Lot: “I cannot do the thing until you have entered there” (Gen. XVIII). He said that he could not do what, without doubt, he could do in power, but could not do in justice.

**(Ambrose.)** He shows that their devotion to religion had been so complete that they had not only received him well but had also been found strong in faith. And, what contributes still more to their praise, they had offered almost all that was theirs to be destroyed for his sake. This is why he grieves the more: such great love had been overthrown by evil teaching.

## So I have become your enemy by telling you the truth?

He says this because, “I cannot,” he means, “become the enemy of you, from whom I have experienced such great services.” But because no one wishes to be rebuked when he is in error, I seem to you to be an enemy when I rightly correct you.

**(Jerome.)** Blessed is the one who walks in the way of the virtues. But even if he reaches the virtues, it does not profit him to have withdrawn from vices unless he grasps what is best; for in good pursuits it is not the beginnings so much as the end that ought to be praised.

Just as in a vineyard there are many stages of the grapes’ progress toward the winepress, so first the vine must put forth shoots and promise hope in its blossoms; then, when the flower has fallen, the form of the future cluster must emerge, and the swelling grape gradually come to birth, until, pressed in the winepresses, it pours out sweet must. So too in teaching there are successive stages of blessedness: one hears the word of God, conceives it, and it grows in the womb of the soul until it reaches birth. Once it has given birth, the soul suckles and nourishes it, and leads it through infancy, childhood, adolescence, and youth to the full-grown human being.

Therefore, since each stage, as we have said, possesses its own blessedness according to its progress, if the end—and, so to speak, the final touch to the work—is lacking, the whole labor will be rendered useless, and it will be said: “Where, then, is your blessedness?”

“Although,” he says, “I called you blessed at the time when you received the Gospel according to the flesh, because you were fervent at the beginning, now, because I do not see a roof placed upon the building, and because the foundations were laid almost in vain, I am compelled to say: ‘Where, then, is your blessedness?’—that blessedness for which I formerly considered and praised you as blessed.

“For I myself truly confess that, when I preached humble things to you, or was struggling amid persecutions, you loved me at the beginning so greatly that, if it had been possible—for the things he says are to be understood hyperbolically—you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me, so that I might see more than all your eyes could see. You wished to become blind through your unspeakable love for me, so that the light of the Gospel might rise more fully in my heart. You wanted my benefit to increase through your losses.

“And this was at the time when, as to little children and infants, I was announcing small and humble things to you—either because of the weakness of your flesh or because, owing to the injuries suffered by my flesh, I seemed unworthy of faith. But now, because I have begun to summon you from elementary matters, syllables, and childish reading to greater studies, so that you may hold books in your hands and learn words full of instruction and meaning, you resist and grow angry. The perfection of doctrine seems burdensome to you, and you have been so changed into other affections that you now regard as an enemy the one whom you received as an angel and as Christ, to whom you wished to give your eyes, because I announce the complete truth to you.

“He ended the sentence elegantly when he said: ‘So I have become your enemy by telling you the truth?’ For he showed that the beginnings of his preaching were not so much the truth as shadows and an image of the truth.”

This resembles that famous saying of the Roman poet:

> “Compliance wins friends; truth breeds hatred.”

But see how much better the Apostle is here than that poet. The Apostle tempered this saying for those whom he had called foolish and little children, and made it particular by directing it specifically to the persons of the Galatians. The poet, however, declared it generally and asserted that it applied to himself among all people, and he was greatly mistaken.

For the compliance by which he thought friends were made, once truth is removed, is not so much compliance as flattery and fawning. It is clear that these should be called secret enmities rather than friendships.

At the same time, we should consider that even today, as long as we explain the Scriptures according to the letter to little children and infants—to those in whose hearts Christ has never grown and who do not advance in age, wisdom, and grace with God and human beings—we are praised, honored, and admired. But as soon as we begin to urge them to advance toward better things, they become hostile and malicious toward our preachers.

## They are zealous for you, but not well; they want to shut you out so that you may be zealous for them.

**(Augustine.)** That is, they envy you. Those who wish to make you carnal rather than spiritual are zealous, but not well. “They want to shut you out,” he says, “so that you may be zealous for them”—that is, imitate them. And how? Unless it is so that you may be held fast by the yoke of slavery, just as they themselves are held fast.

## But be zealous for what is good, always in what is good—and not only when I am present with you.

**(Ambrose.)** He signifies that they had been overthrown by the envy of the Jews. For when they saw them progressing in the Gospel in this way and showing such great love for the Apostle, they acted so as to deceive them. They were enemies of the Apostle because of the Law, wishing, while the name of the Savior remained, to make them Jews and rejoicing in their downfall.

They could not bear to hear that the grace promised to them had been given to uncircumcised Gentiles. Therefore they wanted the Galatians to become their imitators, so that they might be circumcised according to their custom.

“Be zealous for better gifts; be zealous always for what is good, and not only when I am present with you.” The better gifts are spiritual gifts, which those who imitate them will possess as an affection before God. These spiritual things are good, and he wishes them always to imitate them—not temporarily, as before, or only while he is present, after which they would turn to something else. Rather, he wants them henceforth to persevere in the good.

**(Jerome.)** Those who are zealous, but not well, do not so much desire to become better themselves, so that they may imitate those worthy of emulation, as they wish to make those very people worse and drag them backward through perverse emulation.

For example, let us suppose that there is a Christian who reads Moses and the Prophets; he knows that everything occurred beforehand in shadow and image for that people, but was written for us upon whom the ends of the ages have come. He understands circumcision not so much of the foreskin as of the ears and heart. He has risen with Christ and seeks the things above. He has been freed from the burden and slavery of the Law: “Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle.”

If someone wishes to persuade this man, using the words of Scripture, to accept what is written not through tropological interpretation but according to the letter that kills, so that he may become openly a Jew rather than secretly one, that person is zealous for him, but not well. He hastens to drag back one who is moving swiftly toward greater things, so that the man may imitate him instead—one who is going backward—or at least may no longer advance very far.

He therefore speaks to the Galatians, who had been induced by advocates of the Law to imitate them, although those advocates ought rather to have imitated the Galatians. For it is natural for what is greater to arise from what is lesser, not for what is lesser to arise from what is greater.

He says: “Be zealous for what is good, in what is good”—that is, do not imitate the advocates of Jewish observance, but imitate the things that are good.

For just as someone who imitates another’s wealth, power, or rank does not so much emulate what is good as what ought to be avoided, so you, on the contrary, should be zealous for what is good in what is good. Seek spiritual things rather than carnal things, so that they may not teach you to be Jews, but you may teach them to be Christians.

Do this always, so that by a steadfast advance you may reach the end of a good work. For you formerly were zealous for what is good in what is good when I was with you. But after I departed from you, you lost everything I had handed down. From a secure station and a faithful harbor, you were again swept out to sea by the receding wave.

Nor is it surprising that, when the Apostle—the vessel of election and the one in whom Christ the Lord spoke—departed, the Galatians were changed, since even now we see the same thing happening in the Churches. Whenever a teacher appears in the Church who is eloquent in speech and upright in life, and who spurs his hearers toward the virtues as though with goads, we see the whole people hastening, burning with zeal, and running about in acts of almsgiving, fasting, chastity, receiving the poor, burying the dead, and other similar works. But when he has departed, we see them gradually wither, grow thin from the loss of nourishment, grow pale, languish, and follow the destruction of all that previously flourished.

## My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.

**(Ambrose.)** He first begot them through faith in baptism. But because they were found to have been born, as it were, through miscarriage—deformed and weak—he now reforms them into Christ with the anguish of his concern.

For, although they conceived faith, they did not at all attend to the meaning of faith; therefore they are said not to have Christ formed in their souls. If they had understood God’s grace in Christ, they would not, after faith, have been led over into Judaism.

**(Augustine.)** He spoke this more in the person of Mother Church. For elsewhere also he says: “I became little in the midst of you, as a nurse cherishes her own children” (I Thess. II).

Christ is formed in the believer through faith in the inner person, who is called into the freedom of grace: gentle and humble in heart, not boasting of works and merits, which are nothing and amount to nothing, but beginning some merit from grace itself.

It may be puzzling that he says, “For whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you,” unless we understand this labor as referring to the anguish of cares by which he brought them forth so that they might be born in Christ, and by which he is again in labor because of the dangers of seduction that he sees disturbing them.

The concern of such cares—which he says in a certain sense causes him labor—can continue until they reach “the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (cf. Eph. IV), so that they may no longer be carried about by every wind of doctrine.

Therefore he did not say this because of the beginning of faith by which they had been born, but because of strength and perfection: “for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” He commends this labor elsewhere in other words when he says: “My daily burden is the care of all the Churches” (II Cor. XI).

**(Jerome.)** The first curse declares with how many difficulties and how much pain children are brought forth from the womb: “In sorrow you shall give birth to children” (Gen. III). Wishing, therefore, to show the concern of teachers for their disciples and what feelings they suffer lest their followers fall away from salvation, Paul says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor.”

In another passage he had spoken as a father: “Even if you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you do not have many fathers” (I Cor. IV). Here, however, he speaks in Christ not as a father but as a mother, so that they may recognize in him the anxiety and devotion of both parents.

Moses also spoke similarly about the people: “Did I conceive this entire people in my womb?” (Num. XI).

Who among us, do you suppose, is so anxious for the salvation of his disciples that he is tormented not for a few hours or, at most, two or three days, but throughout his entire life, until Christ is formed in them?

Christ is also formed in the hearts of believers when all the mysteries are disclosed to them and the things that had seemed obscure become clear.

We must also observe that the one who, through sin, had in a certain sense ceased to be human is conceived by the teacher through repentance, and the formation of Christ in him is again promised. This stands against the Novatians, who do not wish those whom sins have once crushed to be reformed.

## I wish I could be present with you now and change my voice, because I am perplexed about you.

**(Jerome.)** Divine Scripture builds up when it is read, but it is much more beneficial when it is turned from writing into speech, so that the one who taught through a letter may instruct his hearers while present.

For a living voice has great power—a voice resounding from the mouth of its author, uttered and distinguished by the very pronunciation with which it was generated in the human heart.

Knowing, therefore, that speech delivered in person has greater force, the Apostle wishes to change his apostolic voice—the voice contained in writing—into his presence. Since this would be more useful for those who had been corrupted into error, he wishes to recall them to the truth by living speech.

He says this because he is “perplexed” about them. Indeed, the Greek expression is more precise here: ἀποροῦμαι (*aporoumai*) does not signify so much the confusion that among them is called αἰσχύνη (*aischynē*) or σύγχυσις (*synchysis*) as it signifies need and want.

The meaning, therefore, is: “I wish to be present with you now and to utter in person the voice of the written word, because I am in need concerning you.” For I do not have the fruits that teachers usually receive from their disciples, and the seed of teaching has been sown in vain, since I suffer such utter poverty among you that I might burst into Jeremiah’s words: “I have benefited no one, nor has anyone benefited me” (Jer. VII).

The passage may also be understood more simply. “Until now I have used gentle words with you, saying: ‘Brothers, I beseech you,’ and: ‘My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.’ But I, who have spoken to you gently and tenderly as a father, out of the love by which I cannot bear to see my children perish and remain perpetually in error, wish now to be present, if the chains of my imprisonment did not restrain me, and to change my gentle voice into words of rebuke.”

Nor is it fickleness if I am now gentle and now angry. Love impels me; grief impels me to speak with different emotions. For I do not know into what words I should first break forth, or with what medicine I ought to heal you, because I am perplexed about you.

Tell me, you who wish to be under the law: have you not heard the law? (Hier.) It should be noted that “law” here means the account of Genesis—not, as people commonly think, the things that must be done or avoided, but the whole account woven together concerning Abraham, his wives, and his children, which is called “the law.” We read elsewhere also that the prophets are called “the law.” He therefore hears the law who, according to Paul, examines not its surface but its marrow; he does not hear the law who, like the Galatians, follows only its external shell.

(Ambr.) This is found in Genesis: since Sarah could not bear children—for she was barren—she offered her maidservant Hagar to her husband Abraham as a concubine, so that she might adopt as her own whatever Hagar bore (Gen. XXI). Thus it happened that Ishmael was born of Hagar. Afterwards, by God’s command, a son was promised to Abraham from his wife Sarah, who was barren; she bore Isaac to Abraham. Then Abraham began to have two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman: but the one born of the slave woman was born according to the flesh, whereas the one born of the free woman was born through the promise. These things are spoken allegorically.

Ishmael, who was born of the slave woman Hagar, was born according to the flesh; Isaac, however, was born not according to ordinary custom but according to divine providence and by God’s power, since Sarah was both old and barren. Isaac was born as a type of Christ. Therefore he asserts that these things were spoken allegorically, so that one thing might signify another through the persons of Ishmael and Isaac. Ishmael signifies the birth of the Jews, or of those who are slaves of sin; Isaac, however, signifies Christians, because they are born in freedom. One who receives the forgiveness of sins becomes free.

For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. But the one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, whereas the one by the free woman was born through the promise. These things are the two covenants, which are spoken allegorically.

Moses, taking the blood of a calf in a bowl, sprinkled the people, saying: “This is the blood of the covenant which God established with you” (Exod. XXIV). This is what he said: “One, indeed, from Mount Sinai, generating for slavery, which is Hagar.” For the law was given on Mount Sinai, and Moses, reciting it to the people, called this book the Covenant; then he sprinkled the people with blood, as I have said. This law held sinners guilty, and they began to be slaves of sin, having become children of Hagar, as of a slave woman.

Now Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, which borders the Jerusalem that now exists, “serving with her children.” By saying that Hagar signifies earthly Jerusalem, that is, the synagogue, he means that she generates for slavery: for those whom she generates are under sin.

But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. The one whom he calls our mother is the rule of the Lord’s mystery, through which we are reborn into freedom, just as she herself is free. For this reason she is called heavenly, because heaven is her dwelling; and those whom she generates will be there with her, as the Lord says: “Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII).

She is also life, because those who believe and are reborn through her are endowed with immortality. For it is said of the Lord (John I, V): “What was made in him was life”; and, “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life.” And “the life was the light of human beings.” This life and light is the mother of the faithful.

As it is written—for in Isaiah this passage is found, which follows: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. LIV).

He says that earthly Jerusalem has a husband because she generates according to the flesh; but he calls the heavenly Jerusalem, whom he says is our mother, barren because she does not bear according to the flesh and does not suffer labor pains—that is, she does not travail. She generates spiritually, without suffering, crying aloud in joy, because although once deserted—for by whom, if not by Adam? Since life was deserted and death followed—she now has more children than she who has a husband, that is, than she who generates carnally. For Christians are far more numerous than Jews, as he says in the Apocalypse (Apoc. VII): “And I saw a great multitude which no one could number, from every tribe and nation.”

(Hier.) It is exceedingly difficult to demonstrate that only Isaac, who was born of Sarah, was generated through the promise, and not Ishmael also, who sprang from Hagar, the Egyptian slave woman. Scripture reports that when Hagar, pregnant, fled from Sarah who was persecuting her, and an angel came to her in the desert and urged her to submit to her mistress’s authority, that same angel also said these words: “I will multiply your offspring exceedingly, and it shall not be numbered because of its multitude” (Gen. XVI). And later, concerning Ishmael, words are given which no one would doubt are words of promise: “He shall be a rustic [wild] man; his hand shall be against everyone, and everyone’s hand against him, and he shall dwell opposite all his brothers.”

But one may answer that the promise of an angel is of less authority than the promise of God himself. For just as a star does not shine brightly once the sun has risen, so the words of angels, compared with God’s promise, are obscured, vanish, and are counted as nothing.

This answer does seem to have some force, but it is immediately crushed by the authority of the Scripture that follows. For it is written (Gen. XVII): “Abraham said to God: ‘Would that Ishmael might live in your sight!’ And God answered him: ‘Behold, Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac; and I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant, and with his offspring after him.’ But concerning Ishmael: ‘Behold, I have heard you, and behold, I have blessed him, and I will increase him and multiply him greatly. He shall beget twelve nations, and I will make him into a great nation. But I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear for you at this time in the coming year.’”

From this it is evident that, even according to God’s own words, Ishmael too was generated through a promise. But this is resolved by saying that the promise is properly fulfilled in the granting of the covenant, whereas to bless, increase, and multiply greatly—as is written concerning Ishmael—is one thing, and to make someone an heir through a covenant—as is said concerning Isaac—is another: “I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant, and with his offspring after him”; and later: “I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear for you.”

And just as gifts are one thing and substance another, bequests one thing and inheritance another—for we read (Gen. XXV) that gifts were given to Abraham’s sons by his concubines, but that the inheritance of the whole substance was left to Sarah’s son—so, as we have said, blessing and bequests are one thing, and a covenant another.

It may also be said concerning Ishmael that either the angel or God spoke after he had been conceived, whereas concerning Isaac God made the promise before he was conceived in Sarah’s womb.

Now we must turn briefly to higher matters, so that we may say that each of us is initially born not according to the promise, so long as he is instructed by the simple words of Scripture and still delights in Jewish interpretations. But when he has advanced to higher things and understood the law spiritually, then he is generated through the promise. To speak more plainly: every day those who perform the works of Abraham are born from Abraham; but those who have the spirit of slavery again in fear are generated from the Egyptian slave woman, whereas those who have received the Spirit of adoption are generated from Sarah the free woman, by the freedom with which we have been endowed by Christ.

“These things,” he says, “are spoken allegorically.”

Allegory properly belongs to the art of grammar, and in our elementary schooling we learn how it differs from metaphor and the other tropes. It presents one thing in its words but signifies another in its meaning. The books of orators and poets are full of allegories. Divine Scripture too is woven together to a considerable extent through this device.

The apostle Paul understood this; and since he had also touched, to some extent, upon secular literature, he used the very term “figure,” calling it “allegory,” as it is called among his people, so that he might thereby indicate more clearly the unusual character of the Greek expression in this passage. That Paul knew secular literature, though not perfectly, is testified by his own words: “One of their own prophets said: Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies” (Titus I). This is a heroic verse of the poet Epimenides, whom Plato and the other ancient writers also remember.

Likewise, when he was speaking at the Areopagus among the Athenians, he added: “As some of your own poets have said: For we are indeed his offspring” (Acts XVII). This half-line is attributed to Aratus, who wrote about the heavens and the stars.

And also: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (I Cor. XV). This iambic trimeter was taken from Menander’s comedy.

From these and other passages it is evident that Paul was not ignorant of secular literature, and that what he calls “allegory” here he elsewhere calls “spiritual understanding.”

(Cass.) It should be understood that practical instruction extends to many professions and disciplines, while theoretical instruction is divided into two parts, namely, historical interpretation and spiritual understanding. Hence Solomon too, after enumerating the manifold grace of the Church, added: “All who are with her are clothed doubly” (Prov. XXXI).

There are three kinds of spiritual knowledge: tropology, allegory, and anagoge. Concerning these it is said in Proverbs: “But describe them for yourself threefold, according to the breadth of your heart” (Prov. III and XXII).

History therefore embraces knowledge of past and visible things. It is recalled in this way by the Apostle: “For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and the other by a free woman. But the one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, whereas the one by the free woman was born through the promise.”

The things that follow belong to allegory, because the events that truly took place are said to have prefigured the form of another mystery: “For these,” he says, “are the two covenants: one indeed from Mount Sinai, generating for slavery, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, which corresponds to the Jerusalem that now exists and serves with her children.”

Anagoge, ascending from spiritual mysteries to certain higher and more sacred secrets of heaven, is then set forth by the Apostle: “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is the mother of us all.” For it is written: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband.”

Tropology is a moral explanation pertaining to the correction of life and the practical formation of conduct. Thus, if we understand these same two covenants practically and wish to take them as the practical and theoretical disciplines of the human being; or certainly if we wish to understand Jerusalem or Zion as the human soul, according to the words: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion” (Ps. CXLVII).

Thus, if we wish, the four aforementioned figures converge into one, so that one and the same Jerusalem may be understood in four ways: according to history, as the city of the Jews; according to allegory, as the Church of Christ; according to anagoge, as the city of God, that heavenly city which is the mother of us all; according to tropology, as the human soul, which the Lord frequently reproves or praises under this name.

(Hier.) It should also be noted that nearly everyone gives the following explanation of this passage: they interpret Hagar the slave woman as the law and the Jewish people, but Sarah the free woman as the Church gathered from the Gentiles, who is the mother of the saints, as Paul says, “who is the mother of us all.”

She was barren for a long time, before Christ was born of the Virgin, and she was barren because Isaac, the laughter of the world, had not yet been born from the chosen father with the voice of sublime doctrines resounding—for in our language Abraham is understood as “chosen father,” with the sound included.

But Hagar, whose name is interpreted as *paroecia*, that is, “sojourning,” “pilgrimage,” or “stay,” gives birth to Ishmael, who merely hears God’s commandments but does not do them—a rustic, bloodthirsty man, pursuing deserted places—who is hostile to all his brothers born from the free woman and resists them with an adverse countenance.

Nor is it surprising that the Old Testament, which was established and written on Mount Sinai, which is in Arabia and borders the Jerusalem that now exists, is not perpetual, since sojourning differs from permanent possession, the name of Mount Sinai signifies temptation, and Arabia means “setting” or “decline.” Conversely, the Jerusalem above, which is free and the mother of the saints, shows that the Jerusalem presently existing below is sunk down in a low and humble condition.

Some understand the two covenants differently. They interpret divine Scripture, both the Old and the New, according to the diversity of its meanings and the judgment of those who read it, as either the slave woman or the free woman. They wish those who still serve the letter and possess the spirit of fear to have been generated for slavery from Hagar the Egyptian; but those who ascend to higher things and wish to understand allegorically what has been written to be children of Sarah, whose name in our language is interpreted as ἄρχουσα, that is, “ruler” or “princess,” in the feminine gender.

They claim that they resort to this interpretation because it would be unjust to understand Moses and all the prophets as generated from the slave woman, while regarding any Gentiles as generated from the free woman. It is therefore better, as we said above, not only to regard different people within the Church as slaves or free according to the diversity of their interpretations, but also to regard one and the same person as the son of the slave woman so long as he follows the historical account. But when Jesus opens the Scriptures for him, his heart burns, and in the breaking of the bread he sees the one whom previously he did not see, then he too may be called a son of Sarah.

“Rejoice,” he says, “barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband.”

The synagogue had the law as its husband, and, according also to the prophecy of Hannah (I Sam. II), once fruitful in children, it was formerly rich in offspring. But the Church was barren, without the husband Christ, without any address from the Bridegroom’s word, because she lay for a long time in the desert.

But after the synagogue received the writ of divorce into its hands and turned all the husband’s ornaments into the adornment of an idol, then, while the former belt was rotting (Jer. XIII), the husband wove another girdle around his loins from the Gentiles, another loincloth. As soon as she was joined to the husband, she conceived and bore.

And in Isaac the Lord cries out through the prophet: “Has a nation been born all at once?” (Isa. LXVI)—when, in a single day in the Acts of the Apostles, three thousand and five thousand people believed (Acts II and IV).

I do not think it necessary to speak of the multitude of Christians and the small number of Jews, since throughout the whole world the standards of the cross shine forth, while scarcely any Jew, rare and notable, appears in the cities.

But we, brothers, are children of the promise according to Isaac.

(Ambr.) This means that we are not children of the flesh but of God, because Isaac was born as a type of the Son of God. He wishes us to understand that, having become children of God, they turned back so as to become children of the flesh; but if they repent, they are children of God.

But just as then the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the spirit, so it is now. Not only was Ishmael born according to the flesh, but Esau also, because he too was born as a type of the Jewish people. Of him it is written in the prophet Malachi: “I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau” (Mal. I). He persecuted Jacob, who was born as a figure of the Christian people and was called Israel, that is, “a man who sees God.” In the same way, this signified that the Jews, through envy, persecute Christians.

For this reason they deliberately overthrew the Galatians by carnal cunning. But what does Scripture say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son. For the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman.”

These are Sarah’s words. She bears the type of the heavenly Jerusalem, generating Isaac through the promise. Thus, once the son of the slave woman—that is, the Jewish people—has been cast out and rejected because of unbelief—for they are slaves of sin, to whom forgiveness has not been granted—the son of the free woman, that is, the new people of the heavenly kingdom, is to be the heir of that Jerusalem above.

Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman, with the freedom with which Christ set us free. We were therefore children of the slave woman while we were subject to sins; but after receiving forgiveness of sins from Christ, we were set free.

(Hier.) I do not think that we can find anywhere that Ishmael persecuted Isaac. We find only that, when the son of the Egyptian woman, who was the elder, was playing with Isaac, Sarah became indignant and said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with my son Isaac” (Gen. XXI).

And surely an ordinary game among children is unworthy of expulsion and disinheritance. But the Apostle, as a Hebrew of Hebrews, educated at the feet of the teacher Gamaliel, who once restrained the Pharisees raging against the Lord by his counsel, understood from Sarah’s words—“The son of the slave woman shall not inherit with my son Isaac”—that the play had not been ordinary.

Perhaps Ishmael, as the elder and as one circumcised at an age when he could already understand and feel what he suffered, was claiming the privileges of the firstborn. Scripture therefore called the quarrel of the children “play.” Hence Sarah, unable to endure these words and unwilling from childhood to tolerate the custom of the slave woman’s son claiming the privileges of the firstborn, burst forth: “Cast out the slave woman with her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with my son Isaac.”

When this seemed harsh to Abraham—for greater things are always owed to the firstborn—since Ishmael was not only to cease being first but was not even to receive an equal portion with his younger brother, God, who wished the free woman to remain within and the slave woman to be expelled, confirmed Sarah’s words and said to Abraham: “Let it not be harsh in your sight concerning the boy and the slave woman. Everything that Sarah has said to you, listen to her voice, because in Isaac your offspring shall be called.”

Therefore, just as then Ishmael, the elder brother, persecuted Isaac, still nursing and a little child, claiming for himself the privilege of circumcision and the rights of the firstborn, so now Israel according to the flesh rises up, is puffed up, and exalts itself against its younger brother, the Christian people from the Gentiles.

Let us consider the madness of the Jews, who killed the Lord, persecuted the prophets and apostles, oppose God’s will, and we shall see—history itself teaches us this—that much greater persecutions were stirred up by the Jews against Christians than by the Gentiles.

(Aug.) Let us ask what he says in Genesis: “And it happened, when Ishmael and Isaac were playing, that he saw them playing.” Who persecuted whom? Sarah saw them playing and said: “Cast out the slave woman and her son.” Why? Because she saw them playing.

But Paul calls that play persecution, because the play was mockery. If it was mockery, it was seduction and deception. Every game of children is an imitation of a more serious affair. When an older child plays with a younger one, it is as though the younger is being deceived: the older, knowing that he has other business on which he is intent, pretends and plays certain games with the child, that is, with the weaker one.

Ishmael was older and strengthened in wickedness. But while playing with the child Isaac, he was deceiving Isaac and practicing certain tricks of play upon the weaker child. The mother noticed that play; the Church understands that play.

Sarah said: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.” The Church says: “Cast out the heresies and their children, for heretics shall not be heirs with Catholics.”

But why will they not be heirs? Were they not born from the seed of Abraham? And how do they possess the baptism of the Church? They possess baptism, which would make Abraham’s seed heir, were it not that pride excludes them from the inheritance.

You are born by the same word, through the same sacrament, but you do not attain the same inheritance of eternal life unless you return to the Catholic Church. You are born from the seed of Abraham, but outside you are the son of the slave woman because of pride.

## Chapter V. The Galatians are urged not to observe the legal precepts in order to escape evils and attain blessings; and the works of the flesh and of the Spirit are distinguished.

Stand firm, therefore, and do not again be held back by the yoke of slavery.

(Ambr.) He urges them to stand firm in the grace they have received, lest, returning to former things, they lose the gift of freedom which they had obtained.

(Hier.) When he says “stand,” he urges firm and steadfast faith in Christ, so that the Church of Galatia may remain with a fixed foot in the Savior. Concerning this the righteous man also speaks elsewhere: “He set my feet upon a rock” (Ps. XXXIX)—that is, upon Christ—so that they may not be carried about by every wind of doctrine and swept in different directions.

By “the yoke of slavery” he means the harsh, difficult, laborious law, which consumes its worshipers with burdensome labor day and night. Thus Peter also says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Why do you test God by placing upon the necks of the brothers a heavy yoke which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?” (Acts XV).

When he adds “again,” he does not mean that the Galatians had previously kept the law, but that the yoke of idolatry too is heavy—the yoke under which the Egyptian people were oppressed and, like lead, submerged in the Red Sea. With the same meaning he had said above: “How are you turning back again to the weak and beggarly elements, to which you wish to be enslaved anew, observing days and months and seasons and years?”

Behold, I, Paul, tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you.

(Ambr.) Now he does not conceal the force of the manifest truth or of his own authority, saying: “Behold, I, Paul, tell you”—that is, I, the teacher of the Gentiles, whose work you are in Christ, openly tell you that Christ will be of no benefit to you if you are circumcised.

For the Lord himself says: “The law and the prophets were until John; from then on the kingdom of heaven is preached” (Luke XVI). Before the new preaching began, therefore, it was necessary to be circumcised. But now, with the law of faith succeeding, those things must be followed which the unadorned truth commands. For the old and the new ought not to be mixed, according to the authority of the Lord who preaches; for he says: “No one sews a patch of new cloth onto an old garment, for it tears away the strength of the garment, and the rent becomes worse” (Matt. IX).

Accordingly, circumcision added to a believer will not only be of no benefit but will also be harmful. For it is a greater evil to become a slave from being free than to be born one.

(Hier.) Since, after first saying in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, “To the married I give this command—not I but the Lord” (I Cor. VII), he immediately added, “To the rest I give my command,” lest his authority should be thought worthless, he says: “I think that I too have the Spirit of God.” Thus, with the Spirit and Christ speaking in him, he would not be despised when, imitating the prophets, he said: “Thus says the Lord Almighty.”

What has been said becomes still more forceful if it is joined to the opening in which he says: “Paul, an apostle not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ,” and so forth, so that those who hear may be moved not so much by the authority of the one sent as by the authority of the one who sent him.

Someone may say that this passage contradicts what is written to the Romans (Rom. III): “Circumcision indeed is of value if you observe the law”; and below: “What advantage, then, has the Jew, or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way. First, indeed, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them.”

If Christ is of no benefit to those who have been circumcised, how is circumcision beneficial to those who keep the law?

This is resolved by answering that the Epistle written to the Romans was addressed to those who had believed from both the Jews and the Gentiles. Paul acted so that neither people would be offended, in order that each multitude might retain its own privilege: the Gentiles were not to be circumcised, and those who were circumcised were not to be brought to the foreskin.

But in writing to the Galatians he used a different argument. They were not from the circumcision but from the Gentiles who had believed, and circumcision could not benefit those who, after the grace of the Gospel, were returning again to the rudiments of the legal system.

The statement, “If you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you,” must be understood more subtly. It means not only that circumcision itself is of no benefit to them if they are circumcised, but also that, even if they appear to possess other virtues in Christ apart from circumcision, all of them perish when they have been circumcised after faith in Christ.

What, then? Was circumcision of no benefit to Timothy? It was of great benefit in every way. For he was circumcised not so much in order to think that he could obtain some advantage from circumcision itself, as to win others: becoming a Jew to Jews, so that by his circumcision he might lead Jews to faith in Christ.

Circumcision is therefore of no benefit when it is thought to confer usefulness by itself.

(Aug.) I say, then, that circumcision of the foreskin and other practices of this kind were divinely given to the former people through the covenant called the Old Covenant, as signs of future things which had to be fulfilled through Christ. When those things arrived, these practices remained for Christians to read only for the understanding of the prophecy that had been promised, but not as things that necessarily had to be done, as though the revelation of faith—which was signified here as something still to come—were still awaited.

Although these practices were not to be imposed upon the Gentiles, they ought not, however, to have been removed from the custom of the Jews as though they were detested and condemned. They were therefore to disappear gradually and little by little, while the preaching of the grace of Christ was growing—the grace by which alone believers knew that they were justified and saved.

Those shadows of things that had previously been future, but were then already arriving and present, were to be consumed in the calling of those Jews whom the bodily presence of the Lord and the apostolic age had found in that condition. This was sufficient to commend the practices, so that they would not be avoided as detestable and equivalent to idolatry.

Beyond this, however, they were not to progress, lest they be thought necessary, as though salvation came from them or could not exist without them. This is what the heretics thought: wishing to be both Jews and Christians, they were able to be neither Jews nor Christians.

He says that Christ will profit them nothing if they are circumcised, but in the manner in which these people wished them to be circumcised—that is, so that they placed the hope of salvation in circumcision of the flesh.

For Christ was not of no benefit to Timothy because Paul himself circumcised him when he was already a Christian young man. He did this because of the scandal of his own people, without pretending anything at all, but out of that indifference expressed in the words: “Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing.” This circumcision does no harm to one who does not believe that salvation is in it.

I testify again to every person who circumcises himself that he is obligated to perform the whole law.

(Ambr.) Some can keep the law to a certain extent without being circumcised. For many Romans in Judea kept the law while uncircumcised. Hence the apostle Paul says to King Agrippa of Judea: “Do you believe the prophets, King Agrippa? I know that you believe” (Acts XXVI).

And there was the centurion whose servant was near death. He sent to Jesus and asked him to come and heal his servant, and the Jews, bearing witness on his behalf, said to Jesus: “He is worthy that you should grant this, for he loves our nation, and he himself built our synagogue for us” (Luke VII).

Yet no one who is circumcised fails to keep the whole law. He is obligated because the law was given to the circumcised. He said this because they were showing themselves so dull-witted that they deserved to bear all the burdens of the law.

(Hier.) The God who first commanded circumcision to Abraham and then, through Moses, in the law, established not only circumcision but also many other things to be observed: festivals to be attended frequently at Jerusalem; burnt offerings of victims every morning and evening; the sacrifice of a lamb in one place only; a rest for the land every seventh year; the fiftieth year of remission; and other matters which each reader can easily extract from the Scriptures.

We shall therefore press Ebion and his followers, who, after believing in Christ through the Gospel, think that people must be circumcised, either to perform circumcision and the other things commanded in the law, or, if it is impossible to perform everything, to let circumcision also cease, since, along with the other practices, it has been omitted as useless.

If they answer that they ought to do only what is possible—for God does not demand from us what we cannot do, but what we can fulfill—we shall say to them that it is not the same God who wishes them to keep the law and who abandons those who keep the law.

Or how will he make those guilty because they have interrupted the law who, even if they wished, could not complete everything?

But we follow the spiritual law, which says: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing” (Deut. XXV); and with the Apostle we understand: “Is it oxen that God cares about?” (I Cor. IX). Rather, he says this on our account.

And we observe the delicate Sabbaths—not so that our ox, donkey, and lowly animals may rejoice on the Sabbath, but so that those human beings and animals may rejoice of whom it is written: “You will save human beings and animals, Lord” (Ps. XXXV): human beings, namely, those who are rational and spiritual; animals, those who are slower in understanding and are instructed by spiritual people to keep the Lord’s Sabbaths.

Nor is this contrary to what was said above: “If you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you,” and to what follows: “I testify to every person who circumcises himself that he is obligated to perform the whole law,” nor to what we add here. For “the hearers of the law are not righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” (Rom. II).

That person is a doer of the law who can say: “We are the circumcision”; and: “A Jew inwardly”; and: “We know that the law is spiritual.”

But the one who follows the mutilation and the murderous letter is not a doer of the law but an enemy of the true law, especially after the coming of the Savior, who, for those who turn to him, removes the veil from the heart, so that all of us, with unveiled face contemplating the glory of the Lord, may be transformed from the oldness of the letter into the newness of the Spirit (II Cor. III).

You have been severed from Christ, you who are justified in the law; you have fallen away from grace.

(Ambr.) Those to whom Christ is of no benefit have been severed from Christ. They had been full of his grace; when it departed, they were emptied of it. He speaks to those who, after receiving the gift of God’s grace, preferred to be circumcised.

“You who glory in the law have fallen away from grace.” The righteousness of the law consists in observing the things that were given. Therefore, whoever wishes to be justified by these things after faith loses grace, because the gift of God came for this purpose: so that, when the burdens of the law had ceased, it might justify believers before God.

(Hier.) Just as no one can serve two masters, so it is difficult to fulfill both the shadow and the truth of the law at the same time. In the old law there is a shadow until the day dawns and the shadows are removed. The truth is in the Gospel of Christ: “For grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.”

Therefore he loses the grace of Christ, and forfeits the Gospel which he had held, whoever thinks that he is justified by any observance of the law. Once he has lost grace, he is deprived of the faith of Christ and rests in his own work.

For κατηργήθητε ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ means not, as it has been wrongly translated into Latin, “you have been emptied of Christ,” but “you have ceased from the work of Christ.”

It is better understood as referring generally to the whole law: what he had earlier commanded spiritually concerning circumcision—saying, “If you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you”—he now comprehends in relation to the entire law. Those who believe that they are to be justified by any observance of the law make no progress in the work of Christ.

We, however, by the Spirit, from faith await the hope of justification, for in Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any power nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love.

(Ambrose.) It is clear what he says: the hope of justification is in faith through the Spirit, not through the works of the law; for in faith one serves God spiritually, with devotion of mind and purity of heart. Hence the Lord says to the Samaritan woman: “God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in Spirit and truth” (John 4). Therefore neither uncircumcision nor circumcision is of any value, but faith alone is needed for justification, working through love. Faith must be strengthened by brotherly love, so that the believer may be perfect.

Finally, when the scribe asked what the first commandment was, the Savior replied: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and your neighbor as yourself.” “On these two commandments,” he says, “the whole law and the prophets depend” (Luke 10). The other commandments are therefore imperfect, since perfection is contained in these two commandments.

(Jerome.) Those who wish to live in Christ Jesus must desire virtues and flee vices. The intermediate things that lie between virtues and vices are neither to be fled nor desired, such as circumcision and uncircumcision and other things like them. Therefore in Christ Jesus neither bodily circumcision nor uncircumcision has value, since they are placed in the middle, that is, between vices and virtues; but faith, which works through love, has value, so that the faith credited to Abraham as righteousness may be approved and every work of faith may be placed in love, since the whole law and the prophets depend upon love.

Indeed, in these two commandments—“You shall love the Lord your God” and “You shall love your neighbor”—the Savior declared that the law and the prophets consist. Paul likewise says elsewhere: “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not covet”; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Romans 13). If every commandment is summed up in what was said, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” and faith working through love is of great effect, it is evident that the activity of faith through love contains the fulfillment of all the commandments.

Just as, according to the apostle James, “Faith without works is dead” (James 2), so without faith, even if works are good, they are reckoned dead. Those who do not believe in Christ, yet are upright in conduct—what do they possess more than the works of virtue?

Let that prostitute in the Gospel provide an example of faith working through love. After she had washed the Lord’s feet with her tears while he reclined in the Pharisee’s house, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with ointment, and after the Lord had proposed to the murmuring Pharisee the parable of two debtors, one owing fifty denarii and the other five hundred (Luke 7), he added: “Therefore I tell you, her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much”; and, turning to the woman, he said: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth?

(Ambrose.) He testifies that their progress in the work of faith had been good, but that the wickedness of evil men detained them, so that they did not complete their course with effective perseverance. Therefore he exhorts them to come to their senses, henceforth believing none of those who, by persuading them that the works of the law had to be observed, prevented them from obeying the truth of the Gospel.

“Consent to no one: this persuasion is not from him who calls you.” This is true, because the Jews were doing this on human advice, in order to place them under the yoke of the law, not by the judgment of God, who was calling them through his apostle to grace.

“A little leaven leavens the whole lump.” He says this because, although they mix some element of the law with faith, they violate faith, so that it bears no fruit and is not acceptable. He added this lest they perhaps consider themselves to possess the grace of faith intact if they observed only a few points of the law.

(Jerome.) One thing is the work of God, another the work of human beings. God’s work is to call; the human work is either to believe or not to believe. Thus, wherever else human free choice is affirmed in Scripture, as in: “If you are willing and obey me,” and again: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you?” (Deuteronomy 10), this passage especially confirms it.

Some simpler people, thinking that they were honoring God by making even our persuasion subject to his power, removed the word “not” from the sentence and gave it a meaning contrary to the Apostle’s. Whether for good or for evil, then, neither God nor the devil is responsible: our persuasion is not from him who called us, but from ourselves, who either consent or do not consent to the one calling us.

Alternatively: “This persuasion that you are now following is not from God, who called you at the beginning, but from those who later troubled you.”

“A little leaven leavens the whole mass.”

(Jerome.) What other doctrine of the Pharisees is this, except observance of the law according to the flesh? The meaning, then, is: Do not think that the plots of a few men who have come from Judea and teach something else should be disregarded. A spark is a small thing and, while it is visible, is scarcely noticed; but if it takes hold of fuel and finds material to feed it, even a small fire will consume walls, cities, forests, and whole regions.

I am confident in the Lord concerning you that you will think nothing else.

(Ambrose.) He says that he trusts them in this hope because they had entered upon the path of error not willingly but after being deceived. Once the true road had been shown to them, he is confident that they could easily return.

(Hieronymus.) Paul does not declare this by conjecture, as some wish, but by the prophetic Spirit: the Galatians would return to the path of truth, which they had lost. For he who urged others to strive for spiritual gifts, and especially to prophesy, was himself also filled with the same grace when he spoke: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Corinthians 13).

Foreseeing, therefore, in the Spirit that they would believe nothing except what they were taught through the Epistle, he says: “I am confident in the Lord concerning you that you will think nothing else.” The addition of the Lord’s name also signifies this. If he had judged it by conjecture, he could have said, “I am confident concerning you”; but by adding “in the Lord,” he prophetically declared what he knew would happen, trusting in a certain divine inspiration.

“But whoever is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.”

(Ambrose.) Just as one who converts a sinner is to be rewarded, as the apostle James says in his Epistle, “Whoever brings a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul and cover a multitude of sins” (James 5), so whoever forces one walking on the straight road to turn aside onto a crooked path receives condemnation, whoever he may be.

He adds this concerning such people lest they claim merit for themselves on the grounds that they were sons of Abraham according to the flesh. For, exalting themselves, they say to Jesus: “We are Abraham’s sons” (John 8).

(Jerome.) “To bear the judgment” means what he says in the following passage in other words: “Each person will bear his own burden.” I think that in Scripture “burden” can be understood both in a good and in a bad sense: both of those who are weighed down by serious sins and of those who bear the light burdens of virtues.

The penitent speaks of sins in the Psalm: “My iniquities have risen above my head; like a heavy burden, they have become too heavy for me” (Psalm 37). Of virtues and the teaching of virtues the Savior says: “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11).

That doctrine may also be understood as a burden is made clear in the Gospel: “For they bind heavy burdens that cannot be carried and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are unwilling to move them with a finger” (Matthew 23).

How serious it is to disturb someone from tranquility and to agitate the peaceful hearts of people with waves, as it were, is testified by the Savior’s words to the apostles: “Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid” (John 14). Indeed, for one who disturbs and scandalizes anyone in the Church, it is better that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be thrown into the sea than that he scandalize one of these little ones whom the Savior points out (Matthew 18).

The Galatians, therefore, had been troubled between spirit and letter, circumcision and mutilation, hidden and manifest Judaism, not knowing what they should do.

The passage may also be understood more briefly in this way: Whoever he is who draws you back to the teaching of the Pharisees and desires you to be circumcised in the flesh, even if he is eloquent and boasts of his learning in the law, I say nothing more than this, which you yourselves cannot deny: that he will bear judgment for this work and receive the reward due to his labor.

(Augustine.) This is the disturbance contrary to the proper order: that spiritual people should become carnal. Since it must be understood that there were some who wished to persuade them to this slavery, and who saw that they were being recalled by the authority of the apostle Paul, they even said that Paul himself held this opinion but did not wish to disclose it to them easily. He therefore most appropriately adds his own position:

“But I, brothers, if I preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted?”

(Ambrose.) What he says is clear. He was heard by the Jews as an enemy for this reason, and they did not cease persecuting him: because he taught that circumcision had already come to an end. Finally, when the Jews repeatedly compelled him and brought false accusations against him, seeing the judge to be partial, he was forced to appeal to Caesar.

“Then the offense of the cross has been abolished.” The preaching of the cross was an offense to the Jews because it abolished the Sabbath and circumcision. If he had admitted circumcision, there would have been no offense, and the Jews would have been at peace with us. For they said of the Savior: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John 9).

(Jerome.) We read in the Acts of the Apostles, and the apostle Paul himself often recalls in his Epistles, that he endured very frequent persecutions from the Jews because he taught that those from the Gentiles who had believed in Christ ought not to be circumcised.

These people, then, concerning whom he had said above, “Whoever troubles you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be,” added this also in order to deceive the Galatians: “Not only Peter and James and John and the other apostles in Judea observe circumcision and the other precepts of the law; Paul himself also, who taught you differently from the truth of the matter, circumcised Timothy and frequently became a Jew to the Jews, compelled by the truth.”

Now wishing to remove this opinion from the minds of the Galatians, Paul says: “But I, brothers, if I preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted?” All the hatred of the Jews against me, he says, and all the madness with which they rage against me, is for no other reason than that I teach the Gentiles not to be circumcised and not to observe the burdens of the law, which are superfluous and have already been abolished.

Since I suffer persecution, it is evident that I do not preach circumcision, which I destroy. For I do not suffer persecution from the Jews so much because I preach Christ crucified and say that Jesus is the Christ whom the law and the prophets foretold, as because I teach that the law has been fulfilled.

That the cross is an offense to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles, our Lord himself shows, since he is called a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense. I think this is for no other reason than that when the preaching advances among its hearers with full sails, as soon as it reaches the cross it strikes against it and can proceed no farther on its unhindered course.

Yet this cross, which is an offense to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles, is to us who believe power and wisdom: “For Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1). Thus, because it was called foolishness, the foolishness of God became wiser than human beings; and because it was called weakness and an offense, the weakness of God became stronger than human beings.

“Then the offense of the cross has been abolished. Would that those who are troubling you would even mutilate themselves!”

(Ambrose.) “Would that those who are subverting you would be cut off!” This is like what he says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus, let him be accursed” (1 Corinthians 16).

These people too belong to that diseased flock, and he joins them to their opinion, so that they may be cut off from the mercy of God, having stripped the Galatians of God’s grace. He curses them not only spiritually but also physically: since they were compelling the Galatians to be circumcised, they themselves should be cut off, so that the pain of the body might be increased for them.

(Augustine.) “Would that those who are troubling you would be cut off!” he says—not merely circumcised, but cut off. Thus they will become eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven and will cease sowing carnal things.

(Jerome.) It is asked how Paul, a disciple of the one who said, “Bless those who curse you” (Luke 6), and who himself said, “Bless and do not curse” (Romans 12), and elsewhere, “Nor will the abusive possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6), now cursed those who were troubling the churches of Galatia, and cursed them with the wish: “Would that those who are troubling you would be cut off!”

The suffering of mutilation is so detestable that even one who inflicts it on another against his will is punished by public laws, while one who castrates himself is regarded as infamous. For although this saying may be true: “Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2), and this one also: “Do you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me?” (2 Corinthians 13), certainly the voice of a curse cannot be understood as belonging to the one who says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble, and meek in heart” (Matthew 11).

It is rather thought that Paul, driven by Jewish fury and a certain unrestrained madness, could not control himself, instead of having imitated the one who, “like a lamb before its shearer, did not open his mouth,” and who did not return curses to those who cursed him, but “gave himself to death,” condemned.

To this, whoever answers on Paul’s behalf will say: These words express not so much rage against his adversaries as love for the churches of God. He saw that the whole province, which he himself had transferred from idolatry to faith in Christ through his blood and dangers, had been thrown into confusion by a sudden persuasion. In apostolic grief, the grief of a father, he could not restrain himself. He changed his tone and became angry with those whom he had previously flattered, so that those whom he could not retain by gentleness he might at least retain by rebuke.

Nor is it surprising if the Apostle, as a human being still enclosed in a fragile vessel, seeing another law in his body taking him captive and leading him into the law of sin, once said this—something we clearly see holy men frequently fall into.

It may also be said, although it may seem superfluous to some, that Paul did not so much curse them as pray for them: that they might lose those parts of the body through which they were compelled to sin. Just as the Gospel says that it is better for someone to enter the kingdom of heaven without an eye, without a hand, without a foot, or without any other bodily member than to go whole into Gehenna (Matthew 18), so here he might wish them to lose one part of their body rather than, through the opportunity afforded by an intact body, be condemned to everlasting fire.

When this passage is criticized by pagans, we have shown how it may be answered. Now let it be wielded by us against heretics—Marcion, Valentinus, and all those who bark against the Old Testament—for this reason: how can those who accuse the Creator of being bloodthirsty, severe, warlike, and merely a judge excuse this passage in the apostle of the good God?

Certainly, I think there is no sentence in the Old Law against anyone so savage and bloody as this: “Would that those who are troubling you would be cut off!” Nor can they say that the Apostle prayed for the enemies of Christ, who were troubling his churches, or that the words were spoken out of love, since their very weight demonstrates that they are filled with swelling anger and indignation. Whatever defense they bring forward for the Apostle, we shall use in defense of the Old Law.

(Augustine.) Curses are called prophetic not because they arise from the evil wish of one invoking harm, but because they are declarations made by the Spirit who knows beforehand. For when the Apostle says, as though angry and indignant, “Would that those who are troubling you would be cut off!”, he seems indeed to have wished them harm. Yet if you consider the person of the writer, you will understand through a most elegant ambiguity that he wished them well: they are eunuchs who have mutilated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.

## BOOK SIXTEEN

[Col. 0343]

## CHAPTER V FOLLOWS

[Col. 0343B]

For you were called to freedom, brothers; only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another.

(Ambrose.) They were called to freedom because, although they were subject to sins, they received the grace of God, were forgiven their offenses, and were set free.

“Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh.” He says this lest the flesh deprive them of the freedom they had received. For this reason they wished them to be circumcised: so that they might enter into subjection to the law. Therefore he warns them not to make themselves an opportunity for this by consenting to them.

“But through love serve one another.” He urges them to possess love not through a carnal affection but through the Spirit, so that they may be subject to one another.

“For the whole law is fulfilled in you by one saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” This is written in Leviticus, as was said above: the perfection of salvation operates through love, because whoever does not love his brother does not love God, as the apostle John says (1 John 4).

“But if you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another.” It is clear that dissension among brothers is hostile to love. Therefore he urges them to be peaceable and to advance in what is good. Contentions generate quarrels, whose fruit is the destruction of life.

(Theodoret.) Whoever, therefore, strives to keep the perfection of evangelical teaching is established under grace and is not oppressed by the dominion of sin. For this is what it means to be under grace: to fulfill what grace commands. But whoever refuses to be subject to the fullness of evangelical perfection should know that, although he may seem to himself to be baptized and a monk, he is not under grace but is still hindered by the bonds of the law and weighed down by the burden of sin.

The purpose of the one who adopts by the grace of adoption all those by whom he is received is not to destroy but to build up, not to abolish but to fulfill the Mosaic decrees. Some, entirely ignorant of this and neglecting the majesty of Christ’s counsels and exhortations, are so released by the security of presumptuous freedom that they not only fail to approach Christ’s commandments as difficult, but also despise as obsolete the very minor commands given by the Mosaic law to the foolish and immature.

They say, with the harmful freedom that the Apostle condemns: “Shall we sin because we are not under the law but under grace?” (Romans 6). Whoever, therefore, is neither under grace, because he has in no way ascended to the summit of the Lord’s teaching, nor under the law, because he does not accept even those minor commandments of the law, is oppressed by the twofold dominion of sins. He thinks that he has received Christ’s grace merely in order, through harmful freedom, to become alienated from him, falling into what the apostle Peter warns us not to incur: “Live as free people, not using freedom as a covering for evil” (1 Peter 2).

The blessed apostle Paul likewise says: “You were called to freedom, brothers,” that is, so that you might be released from the dominion of sin; “only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh,” that is, do not suppose that the frustration of the legal commandments is permission for vices.

The Apostle teaches that this freedom exists nowhere except where the Lord dwells: “The Lord is Spirit,” he says, “and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3).

Therefore I do not know whether I have been able to express and clarify the meaning of the blessed Apostle as those who have experienced it understand it. I know one thing: it is most plainly preserved, even without anyone’s exposition, by all who have perfectly maintained practical—that is, active—discipline. They will not labor to understand through disputation what they have already learned by practice.

“But through love,” he says, “serve one another.”

(Augustine.) Whoever serves through love is free, and serves, and without misery obeys God, doing with love what is taught rather than through fear what is compelled. Love makes us free from the yoke of guilt when, through mutual love, it subjects us to one another’s service, and when we consider the goods of others to be our own, offering and presenting our own things to others as though they were theirs.

(Jerome.) Since this passage, in which he says, “You were called to freedom, brothers,” and so forth, is very obscure, it seemed appropriate to transfer here, word for word, material from the tenth book of the *Stromata*—not because individual points cannot be explained in their own places and according to their meanings, but because, separated from the preceding discussion, they form one difficult whole. If they are understood merely as they sound, they seem inconsistent, abrupt, opposed to one another, and full of contradictions.

(Origen.) These, then, are Origen’s words:

“This is a difficult passage, and it seems that it must be discussed by us in this way. Whoever is free and follows the spirit and truth with a higher understanding despises the preceding types and the letter. Yet for that reason he ought not to despise those who are inferior or give an opportunity to those who cannot perceive higher things to despair completely of themselves. Although they are weak and are called flesh in comparison with the spirit, they are nevertheless the flesh of Christ.
