“If he understands the mystery of love serving the weak, let him do something for the sake of the weak, lest his brother perish through his knowledge—the brother for whom Christ died.

“Pay close attention, therefore, to whether this meaning can be woven from what follows. ‘You were called to freedom, brothers,’ he says. Perhaps this is because not everyone could grasp the calling to freedom; hence you now hear: ‘Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh.’

“For the greater ought to serve the lesser through love, since whoever wishes to be greater will be the servant of all. Therefore let the spiritual person not tear the flesh of Christ, nor give them an opportunity to bite one another in retaliation against the one who provokes them, lest they be consumed by one another.”

(Augustine.) This is our hope: that we may be freed by the Free One; and in freeing us, he made us servants. We were servants of desire; once freed, we become servants of love.

The Apostle says this also: “You were called to freedom, brothers; only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another.”

Let no Christian therefore say: “I am free; I was called to freedom. I was a slave, but I have been redeemed, and by that redemption I have become free. I shall do what I wish; no one should prevent me from doing my will if I am free.”

But if you commit sin by that will, you are a slave of sin. Do not therefore abuse freedom as an opportunity to sin freely; use it as an opportunity not to sin. Your will will be free if it is devout; you will be free if you are a servant: free from sin, servant of righteousness.

“But through love,” he says, “serve one another.” This cannot happen unless each person regards the weakness of another as his own, so that he may bear it patiently until the one whose salvation he cares for is freed from it.

“For the whole law is fulfilled in one saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

It may be asked why the Apostle here also mentioned only love of neighbor, by which he said that the law is fulfilled, and likewise in the Epistle to the Romans, when he was dealing with the same question: “Whoever loves another,” he says, “has fulfilled the law. For, ‘You shall not commit adultery, you shall not murder, you shall not steal, you shall not covet’; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Love does no evil to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfillment of the law” (Romans 13).

Since perfect love exists only in the two commandments of love of God and love of neighbor, why does the Apostle, both in this Epistle and in that one, mention only love of neighbor? Is it not because people can lie about loving God, since fewer temptations test that love? But in love of neighbor they are more easily proved not to possess it, when they act unjustly toward others.

It follows that whoever loves God with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his mind also loves his neighbor as himself, because this is commanded by the one whom he loves with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his mind.

Likewise, who can love his neighbor—that is, every human being—as himself unless he loves God, by whose command and gift he can fulfill love of neighbor? Since the two commandments are so constituted that neither can be kept without the other, it is often enough to mention one of them when the subject is works of righteousness—more appropriately, the one by which each person is more easily convicted.

Hence John says: “Whoever does not love the brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4). Some claimed to possess love of God, but their hatred of their brother proved that they did not possess it. This is easy to judge in daily life and conduct.

(Jerome.) The Apostle, therefore, although free from all things, made himself the servant of all for the sake of love, so that he might win more people. Accordingly, he rightly exhorts the others also to serve one another through love, which seeks not its own but the neighbor’s good.

Whoever wishes to become first will be the servant of all. Just as the Savior, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; and, being found in human appearance, humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2), so we too should now understand that whatever we formerly seemed compelled to do under the law must now be done freely, through love.

So great is love that the whole law is summed up in it. In another place the Apostle enumerates the blessings of love, saying: “It is not jealous; it does not act wrongly” (1 Corinthians 13). After repeating many things in the middle, he concludes at the end: “It hopes all things, endures all things; love never falls away.”

The Savior also says in the Gospel that this is the sign by which his disciple is recognized: if he loves his neighbor. I think this applies not only to human beings but also to angels.

The same thing is said in other words: “Whatever you do not want people to do to you, do not do to them; and whatever you want people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matthew 7).

I do not want my wife to be adulterated; I do not want my property to be seized; I do not want to be oppressed by false testimony. To sum everything up in a brief statement, I resent having anything unjust done to me.

If, through love working in me, I either do or desire these same things to another, the whole law has been fulfilled.

Nor is it difficult to show how all the commandments—“You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness,” and others like them—are maintained through the single observance of love.

It is difficult to show how even the sacrifices commanded in Leviticus, and the abstinence from or permission to eat foods, since some are called clean and others unclean, as well as the recurring annual festivals, are summed up in the one commandment of love—unless someone takes refuge in the claim that the law is spiritual and that, before the true high priest came, we served heavenly things through images and patterns.

After he offered himself once as a victim and redeemed us by his blood, all the ancient law’s variety and difficulty was fulfilled in his love for humanity. “For God so loved the world that he gave his beloved and only-begotten Son for us” (John 3).

But for one who, living once for all by the Spirit, has put the works of the flesh to death and, loved by the Savior, is called not a servant but a friend (John 15), no further law has been laid down—the law established for the impious and sinners, the insubordinate and the wicked.

Yet now, although we perform at least part of all the more difficult things, we fail to do this one thing, which is easier to do and without which everything we do is empty.

The body feels the hardship of fasting; vigils torment the flesh; alms are acquired through labor; in martyrdom blood is poured out, and although faith burns, it is not shed without fear and pain. There are people who do all these things. Love alone is without labor.

And because it alone makes the heart pure, the devil attacks it in us, lest we see God with a pure mind.

When I sit speaking against my brother and place a stumbling block before the son of my mother; when I am distressed by another’s happiness and make another’s good into my own evil—is not what follows fulfilled in me? “But if you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another.”

Possession of love is rare. Who wishes, following the Apostle, to become accursed from Christ for the sake of his brothers? Who, weeping with those who weep and rejoicing with those who rejoice, is wounded by another’s wound? Who is struck down by the death of a brother?

We are all more lovers of ourselves than lovers of God.

See how great a good love is. If we perform martyrdom in such a way that we wish our relics to be honored by human beings; if, pursuing popular opinion, we shed blood fearlessly and give our property away until we ourselves are reduced to begging, this work deserves not so much a reward as punishment; it bears the torments of treachery rather than the crown of victory.

“But if you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another.” This may be understood simply: let us not slander one another; let us not think that we avenge ourselves by cursing; let us not, when we have been saddened, desire to sadden others; and, like beasts, let us not bite and be bitten in turn, so that destruction and consumption follow the bites.

[Col. 0347D] **“But I say: Walk by the Spirit, and you will not carry out the desire of the flesh.”** (Ambrose.) After prohibiting them from the law of works, in which there are carnal commandments, he now commands them to abstain from the vices of the flesh. For that person walks by the Spirit who flees sins. “For the flesh desires against the Spirit, but the Spirit against the flesh. These two oppose each other, so that you do not do whatever you wish.” He sets forth two laws, as he also does in the Epistle to the Romans, which oppose each other: one of God, the other of sin. The latter is signified by the flesh because it delights in visible things and, greedy for sins, seeks them, so that the inner person, caught between these opposing forces, does not do what he wishes.

The divine law presses down and drives away the law of sin, advising a person to preserve the vigor of his nature, lest he be captured by enticements. The other, acting in ambush, assails a person with blandishments so that he may despise the commandment of the divine law. When, therefore, a person has consented to the law of God, the law of sin contradicts him, persuading him not to do what the divine law commands. Conversely, the law of God restrains a person from doing what the law of sin suggests. A person does not regard this as absurd: he knows that it accords with his nature to do what the law of God commands, and ultimately he rejoices when he does these things. But when he performs what the law of sin suggests, he sees himself to be shameful and recoils afterward. Therefore the commandments of the law of the Spirit must be kept, and carnal things must be fled. Conscience itself accuses a person if he consents to that law, knowing that what the law of sin suggests is abhorrent.

(Hieronymus.) “I say,” he says, “walk by the Spirit, and you will not carry out the desires of the flesh.” This too must be understood in two ways, in accordance with what precedes. We may say that those who have mortified the works of the flesh by the Spirit and have sown in the Spirit, so that they may reap eternal life from the Spirit, whenever they feel the flesh’s pleasure titillating them, do not carry out its desire—which, if fulfilled, seems for a time to flatter them—but restrain it by the Spirit and, according to the judgment of the historian, live more by the command of the mind and the service of the body.

We may also understand it in this way: since the law is spiritual, and since it is not the one who is a Jew outwardly but the one who is a Jew inwardly, and since circumcision is that of the heart, in the Spirit and not in the letter, we say that those walk by the Spirit and do not carry out the desire of the flesh who depart from Egypt spiritually and draw spiritual food and drink from the spiritual rock; who are judged neither in food nor drink, nor in respect of a festival, a new moon, or a sabbath, but walk spiritually in all things, not fulfilling the desire of the fleshly law or of the letter, but reaping the fruits of spiritual understanding.

A third interpretation has also been offered by some concerning this passage. It does not differ greatly from the second: they assert that the desire of the flesh is found in those who are infants in Christ, whereas the way of the Spirit belongs to mature men. The sense, they say, is: “Walk in the gravity of the Spirit, that is, on the path of a mature man, and you will not carry out the desires of children.”

“For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. These oppose each other, so that you do not do whatever you wish.” The flesh delights in present and fleeting things; the Spirit in eternal and future things. Between these two conflicts the soul stands in the middle. It has in its power good and evil, to will or not to will; but it does not possess an enduring will or refusal, because it can happen that, after consenting to the flesh and performing its works, it again reproaches itself through repentance, joins itself to the Spirit, and brings forth its works.

This, then, is what he says: “These oppose each other”—that is, the flesh and the Spirit—“so that you do not do whatever you wish.” He does not mean that our free choice has been taken away, by which we may assent either to the flesh or to the Spirit; rather, what we do is not properly our own, but the work itself is assigned either to the flesh or to the Spirit. It is a great labor and requires exceedingly difficult discussion, after the works of the flesh and of the Spirit have been displayed, to discover certain intermediate things that seem to belong neither to the flesh nor to the Spirit.

We are called carnal when we give ourselves wholly to pleasures; spiritual when we follow the Holy Spirit as our guide—that is, when we think with him instructing us and are taught by him as our master. I believe philosophers to be “soulish” or natural people, who think their own thoughts to be wisdom. Of them it is rightly said: “The natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit, for they are foolishness to him” (I Cor. II).

To make this clearer, let us take an example. Let the flesh be called earth, the soul gold, the Spirit fire. As long as gold remains in the earth, it loses its own name and is called by the name of the earth with which it has been mixed. But when it has been separated from the soil and has received both the appearance and name of gold, it is indeed called gold, but has not yet been tested. If it has been refined and purified by fire, then it receives the splendor of gold and the dignity of its adornment.

So too the soul, standing between earth and fire—that is, between flesh and Spirit—when it gives itself to the flesh is called flesh; when it gives itself to the Spirit is called spirit. But if it trusts in its own thought and thinks that it can discover the truth without the grace of the Holy Spirit, it will be marked, like dirty gold, with the designation “natural person.”

(Cassian.) The flesh delights in luxury and lust; the Spirit does not even yield to natural desires. The flesh wants to be satisfied with sleep and filled with food; the Spirit is so nourished by vigils and fasts that it would not even admit sleep and food for the necessary use of life itself. The flesh desires to overflow with every resource; the Spirit strives not even to possess the daily substance of a little bread.

The flesh seeks to shine through baths and to be surrounded by daily throngs of flatterers; the Spirit rejoices in the filth of squalor and the vastness of an inaccessible desert. The flesh is comforted by honors and the praises of men; the Spirit glories in injuries inflicted upon it and in persecutions.

Between these two desires, therefore, the will of the soul stands in a certain more blameworthy middle position. It is delighted neither by the crimes of vices nor by the pains of virtues. It seeks to restrain itself from carnal passions, yet is entirely unwilling to endure the necessary pains without which the desires of the Spirit cannot be possessed. It desires to obtain bodily chastity without chastisement of the flesh; purity of heart without the labor of vigils; an abundance of spiritual virtues while the flesh rests; the grace of patience without anyone’s harsh reproach; the humility of Christ without the loss of worldly honor; the simplicity of religion while pursuing secular ambition; to serve Christ with the praise and fear of men; to proclaim the strictness of truth without even the slightest offense to anyone.

Finally, it prefers to obtain future goods in such a way that it does not lose present ones. Such a will could never bring us to true perfection, but would place us in a certain most wretched condition and make us like those who in the Apocalypse are rebuked and corrected by the Lord: “I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, I will begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Apoc. III)—unless these mutually rising battles immediately tore apart this extreme lukewarmness.

For when, serving this will of ours, we wish to relax ourselves a little in its service, the flesh’s goads immediately rise up. Wounding us with their vices and passions, they do not allow us to remain in that quality of purity in which we delight, but drag us toward that cold path, full of thorns, which we dread. Again, when inflamed by the fervor of the Spirit we wish to extinguish the works of the flesh, and in no consideration of human weakness we attempt to devote ourselves wholly to immoderate zeal for virtue, unless the flesh intervenes and recalls and restrains the Spirit from that blameworthy excess, it comes about that the two desires, opposing each other in such alternating struggle, moderate the will of the soul by a kind of just balance. The soul does not wish to owe itself entirely to carnal desires, nor does it wish to labor at the works of virtue; and while this conflict excludes the more destructive will of the soul, it places a certain balance of equality upon the scales of our body. This balance rightly distinguishes the boundaries of Spirit and flesh, permitting neither the mind inflamed by the fervor of the Spirit to outweigh the right side, nor the flesh, pierced by the goads of vices, to outweigh the left.

This battle is usefully stirred up within us day after day. We are healthfully compelled to approach the condition we do not desire, so that we may acquire purity of heart not through idleness or security, but through continual sweat and contrition of spirit; and so that we may preserve chastity of the flesh through strict fasts, hunger, thirst, and vigilance. We must also obtain uprightness of heart through reading, vigils, continuous prayer, and the squalor of solitude; retain patience in tribulations through exercises; serve our Creator amid blasphemies and an abundance of insults; and, if necessary, pursue truth amid the envy and hostilities of this world.

While such a struggle wages war in our body, drawing us away from this indolence and security and calling us toward the labor and zeal for virtues that we do not desire, the middle course is best maintained. The lukewarm arbitrariness of our will is tempered by a most measured warmth: on one side by the fervor of the Spirit, on the other by the coldest rigor of the flesh. Thus the desire of the Spirit does not allow the mind to be dragged toward unrestrained vices, nor does the weakness of the flesh permit the Spirit to be exalted toward irrational desires for virtue. Otherwise the sources of every kind of vice might spring up from the former, or from the latter the chief disease—elation—might arise and pierce us with the heavier weapon of pride. But when this battle is followed by a just balancing, it opens a sound and moderate way of virtue between the two, teaching the soldier of Christ always to proceed on the royal road.

**“But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.”** (Ambrose.) The meaning is not obscure: one who has the Holy Spirit as guide does not go astray. For the law rules over those who go astray, as he says elsewhere (I Tim. I): “The law is not laid down for a righteous person.”

(Hieronymus.) It must therefore be noted that here “Spirit” is not read with the article or with any addition, as in the other passages where we read “the spirit of gentleness” and “the spirit of faith,” but is simply called “Spirit.” These small distinctions, which are observed more carefully in Greek than in our language, seem to have some importance, since we have no articles at all. [In Greek, ἄρθρα means “articles.”]

A question arises here: if everyone who is led by the Spirit is not under the law, whether Moses and the prophets were also led by the Spirit and lived under the law—which the Apostle denies—or, possessing the Spirit, were not under the law—which the Apostle affirms here—or, as a third possibility, while living under the law they did not possess the Spirit, which it is impious to believe of such great men.

We shall answer briefly that “to be under the law” is not the same as “to be as though under the law,” just as “to be in the likeness of sinful flesh” does not mean the same as “to be in sinful flesh.” Nor do “a true serpent” and “the likeness of a serpent made of bronze,” which Moses hung in the desert, mean the same thing.

Thus, Moses and the holy prophets, walking by the Spirit and living by the Spirit, lived not under the law but as though under the law. They seemed indeed to be under the law, but they did so in order to win those who were under the law and summon them from the lowliness of the letter to the height of the Spirit. Paul too, who became a Jew to the Jews and all things to all people in order to win all (I Cor. IX), did not say that he became “under the law,” but “as though under the law,” showing that he observed not the reality of the law but its likeness. We seem to have resolved the proposed question.

But what shall we do with that passage of Paul which says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law”? (Gal. IV.) If Christ was under the law and not as though under the law, the whole preceding argument will be rendered void.

Yet this objection too will be resolved in its proper place. He who was made under the law in order to redeem those who were under the law, although free from the law, voluntarily subjected himself to the law. He was much freer than Paul, who testified that he was not under the law but as though under the law. And just as, for our sake, he descended into the filth and abyss of death, while we cried out, “Who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII), so he also willed to be born of a woman and to be under the law, in order to save those who were born of a woman and lived under the law.

(Augustine.) “Walk by the Spirit,” he says, “and do not carry out the desires of the flesh.” He did not say, “Do not have them,” because they could not avoid having them; rather, he said, “Do not carry them out”—that is, do not fulfill their works by the consent of the will.

What is said in Galatians, “Do not carry out the desires of the flesh,” corresponds by contrast to what is said in Romans: “I do not find how to accomplish the good.” The desires of the flesh are not fulfilled in evil, because the assent of our will does not join them; nor is our will fulfilled in good, so long as the movement of those desires, to which we do not consent, remains.

“For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. These oppose each other, so that you do not do whatever you wish.” When the flesh desires against the Spirit and the Spirit against the flesh, so that we do not do what we wish, the desires of the flesh are not fulfilled, although they occur, nor are our good works fulfilled, although they occur.

The desire of the flesh is fulfilled when the Spirit also consents to evil works, so that it no longer desires against the flesh but together with it. The good works likewise are fulfilled when the flesh so consents to the Spirit that it no longer desires against it. This is what we wish when we desire the perfection of righteousness.

For it is most truly and most faithfully written: “The flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh.” Yet I think that the flesh can desire nothing without the soul—something which every learned and unlearned person accepts without doubt. Accordingly, the cause of carnal desire is not in the soul alone, but still less is it in the flesh alone. It arises from both: from the soul, because without it no pleasure is perceived; from the flesh, because without it carnal pleasure is not perceived.

When, therefore, the Apostle speaks of the flesh desiring against the Spirit, he undoubtedly means carnal pleasure, which the Spirit possesses from the flesh and with the flesh, a pleasure which it possesses alone. For, unless I am mistaken, the Spirit alone possesses desire—not mixed with the pleasure of the flesh or with the appetite for carnal things—by which the soul longs and pines for the courts of the Lord (Ps. LXXXIII).

The Spirit alone also possesses that of which it is said: “You have desired wisdom; keep the commandment, and the Lord will provide it for you.” When the Spirit commands the members of the body to serve this desire with which it alone burns—as when a book is taken up, something is written, read, discussed, or heard, and finally when bread is broken for a hungry person and other duties of humanity and mercy are performed—the flesh offers obedience; it does not stir up desire.

When something that delights the same soul according to the flesh opposes these desires, by which the soul alone desires, then it is said that the flesh desires against the Spirit and the Spirit against the flesh.

“But if you are led by the Spirit,” he says, “you are not under the law.” This seems to me a great question: what does it mean to be “under the law,” in the sense in which the Apostle condemns it? He does not mean this because of circumcision or those sacrifices formerly performed by the patriarchs but now not performed by Christians, or other things of that kind. Rather, he means the very commandment the law gave: “You shall not desire”—which we certainly acknowledge Christians to observe and to proclaim especially through the light of the gospel.

He calls the law holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good. Then he adds: “Therefore, did what is good become death to me? Certainly not; but sin, so that sin might be shown to be sin, worked death in me through what is good, so that sin might become exceedingly sinful, or sin through the commandment” (Rom. VII).

What he says here—that sin became exceedingly sinful through the commandment—is expressed elsewhere as: “The law entered so that the offense might abound. But where the offense abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. V). Elsewhere, when he had spoken above about the dispensation of grace, which justifies, he asks as though inquiring: “What then is the law?” He immediately answers: “It was added because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made.”

He condemns as being under the law those whom the law makes guilty because they do not fulfill it. They do not understand the benefit of grace for carrying out God’s commandments, and in proud arrogance presume upon their own strength. “The fullness of the law is love” (Rom. XII); and “the love of God has been poured into our hearts,” not through ourselves, but “through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V).

Thus, if human weakness is not aided by God’s grace, the commandment “You shall not desire” holds a person guilty beneath it and condemns him as a transgressor rather than freeing him as a sinner. Circumcision and the other things commanded for the sake of signification, which had to be abolished once the revelation of grace had become more widely known, could justify no one. Yet for that reason they were not to be avoided as though they were the sacrileges of the Gentiles, even when the grace that had been foretold through such shadows began to be revealed. They were to be permitted for a little while, especially to those who came from that people among whom they had arisen; afterward, however, they were to be abandoned irreproachably by all Christians, as though they had been honorably buried.

**“Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity, luxury, the service of idols, magical practices, hostilities, contentions, rivalries, anger, quarrels, dissensions, sects, envies, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.”**

(Ambrose.) All these things and those like them are members of the law of sin, which the Apostle calls “works of the flesh,” because these errors are from the world, and the flesh is from the world. For all sins arise from outside, from the side of the flesh and not from the side of the Spirit; therefore they are not improperly called works of the flesh.

(Augustine.) Consideration of this entire passage of the Epistle can resolve the question of what it means to live according to the flesh. Among the works of the flesh—which we said were manifest and which he condemned by listing them—we find not only those that pertain to the pleasure of the flesh, such as fornication, impurity, luxury, drunkenness, and revelries, but also those by which vices of the mind are displayed, although they are unrelated to the pleasure of the flesh.

Who would understand the service rendered to idols, magical practices, hostilities, contentions, animosities, dissensions, heresies, and envies as anything other than vices of the mind rather than of the flesh? It can happen that, because of idolatry or the error of some heresy, a person abstains from bodily pleasures, and yet even then, although he may appear to restrain and control the desires of the flesh, apostolic authority proves that he lives according to the flesh. Thus, in abstaining from the pleasures of the flesh, he is shown to perform damnable works of the flesh.

Who does not harbor hostilities in his mind? Or who speaks in such a way that he says to his enemy, or to one whom he thinks his enemy, “You have an evil flesh against me,” rather than “You have an evil mind against me”? Why, then, does the teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth call all these things and those like them “works of the flesh”? It is because, by that mode of speech in which the whole is signified by a part, he wishes the human being himself to be understood by the name “flesh.”

If someone says that the flesh is the cause of bad conduct in every vice because the soul, affected by the flesh, lives in this way, he is certainly paying careful attention to the whole nature of the human being. For the corruption of the body, which weighs down the soul, is not the cause of the first sin but its punishment. Nor did corruptible flesh make the sinful soul corruptible; rather, the sinful soul made the flesh corruptible. Although certain incentives to vice and the vices themselves arise from this corruption of the flesh, not every vice of an evil life is to be attributed to the flesh. Otherwise we would absolve the devil from all these things, although he does not have flesh.

Who is more hostile than the devil? You know. Who is found to be more contentious, more animated, more rivalrous, and more envious against us? Since he possesses all these things without flesh, how are they “works of the flesh” unless they are works of the human being, whom, as I said, the Apostle calls “flesh”? He did not become like the devil by possessing flesh—which the devil does not possess—but by living according to himself, that is, according to the human being.

(Hieronymus.) It is also elegantly expressed that he placed works in the flesh but fruit in the Spirit, because vices end and perish in themselves, whereas virtues sprout and abound like crops.

Let us not think that the soul has no work if vices are assigned to the flesh and virtues to the Spirit. As we said above, the soul is placed in a certain middle position: it either joins itself to the flesh and is called flesh, as in the statement, “My Spirit will not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. VI), or it is joined to the Spirit and passes into the name of spirit. For “whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI).

The first work of the flesh, therefore, is fornication. He placed it first and made it manifest at the outset, so that we would not be uncertain about the middle items. “Everything whatever a person does is outside the body, but the one who fornicates sins against his own body” [I Cor. VI]. “We are not our own; we were bought with a price. Therefore let us glorify God and bear God in our body.”

The fornicator is guilty of a greater crime because he takes Christ’s members and makes them members of a prostitute: “The two will be one flesh.” The unbeliever who does not believe in Christ makes his own members members of a prostitute; the believer who fornicates makes Christ’s members members of a prostitute. Conversely, in the case of an unbeliever who fornicates, I do not know whether he violates or builds a temple to an idol; for demons are especially worshiped through vices. This one thing I know: whoever fornicates after faith in Christ violates God’s temple.

The second work of the flesh is called impurity, and luxury follows it. Just as the ancient law, concerning unspeakable crimes committed secretly—crimes whose very naming is most shameful, lest both the mouth of the speaker and the ears of the hearers be polluted—embraced them generally by saying, “Make the children of Israel reverent [or respectful] toward every impurity” (Lev. XV), so here it calls the other extraordinary pleasures, including even the acts of marriage if they are performed without modesty and decency, as though under the eyes of God and with service rendered only to children, “impurity” and “luxury.”

In the catalog of the works of the flesh, idolatry holds the fourth place. Whoever has once surrendered himself to luxury and pleasure no longer looks to the Creator. Otherwise, all idolatry delights in festivals, gluttony, the belly, and the things beneath the belly.

And lest anyone perhaps think that magical practices and sorcerous arts are not prohibited in the New Testament, they too are named among the works of the flesh, because through magical arts it often happens both that wretched people love and that they are loved.

Hostility, which is placed after magical practices, is shown by the crime to which it is attached to have what kind of guilt. As far as lies with us, we ought to have no enemy and to be at peace with everyone. If, however, by speaking the truth we incur some enemies, we are not so much their enemies as they are enemies of the truth.

For when it is said in Genesis to Abraham, “I will be an enemy to your enemies and oppose those who oppose you” (Gen. XII), it should be understood as above: Abraham was not so much their enemy as they were enemies of Abraham’s virtues and religion, through which, after trampling down idols, he worshiped the God who had become known to him.

There is also the command given to the people of Israel (Num. XXV) that they should be enemies of the Midianites with perpetual hatred and discord transmitted to their descendants. This is addressed, as it were, to those who were under a pedagogue, and who elsewhere deserved to hear: “Hate your enemy” (Lev. XIX).

Or certainly the disagreement was not so much between persons as between ways of life. Just as God usefully placed enmity between the serpent and the woman, so that their friendship would not be harmful to the human being—through that friendship he had been cast out of paradise—so among the Israelites and the Midianites it was a dissimilar way of life, rather than one nation as such, that was condemned.

Contention holds the seventh place among the works of the flesh. It is placed among the vices as though in a kind of sacred and eminent number. “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward everyone, qualified to teach, patient, correcting with gentleness even those who argue against him” (II Tim. II).

After contention comes rivalry, which in Greek is more significantly and more familiarly called ζῆλος (*zēlos*). I do not know which of us is free from this evil. The patriarchs envied Joseph their brother (Gen. XXXVII); and Miriam and Aaron, the prophetess and priest of God, were deceived by this passion against Moses. So far did this extend that Miriam, of whom Scripture had related, “Miriam the prophetess took a tambourine,” and so forth, was afterward cast outside the camp, defiled by the disease of leprosy, and marked her repentance by seven days of separation (Num. XII).

Next comes anger, which does not produce the righteousness of God (Jas. I) and is a form of rage. There is this difference between irascibility and anger: an irascible person is always angry, whereas an angry person is stirred up for a time. I do not know who could possess the kingdom of God when the person who becomes angry is separated from the kingdom.

Quarrels too, which the Greeks significantly call ἐριθείαι (*eritheiai*), exclude people from the kingdom of God, since a quarrel is called μάχη (*machē*). Ἐριθεία (*eritheia*) occurs when someone is always ready to contradict, delights in another’s irritation, engages in womanish quarreling, and provokes the person who is arguing. Among the Greeks this is also called φιλονεικία (*philoneikia*), “love of contention.”

Dissensions too are works of the flesh, when someone, not being perfect, does not speak with the same understanding and the same judgment, but says: “I am of Paul,” “I am of Apollos,” “I am of Cephas,” and “I am of Christ.” The same dissension is found among households: husbands against wives, fathers against sons, brothers against brothers, fellow servants against fellow servants, soldiers against comrades, artisans against artisans of the same trade.

It sometimes happens that dissension arises in the interpretation of Scripture. From these dissensions heresies also boil up, which are now placed among the works of the flesh. If the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God (Rom. VIII), and all doctrines of falsehood that oppose God are hostile to him, then heresies too, being hostile to God, are consequently referred to the works of the flesh.

“Heresy” in Greek is derived from “choice,” because each person chooses for himself the discipline that he thinks best. Therefore, whoever understands Scripture differently from the meaning demanded by the Holy Spirit, by whom it was written, can be called a heretic even if he has not withdrawn from the Church. Such a person belongs to the works of the flesh because he chooses what is worse.

Heresy is followed by envy. We should not think that envy is the same as zeal, because zeal can be understood in a good sense, when someone strives to imitate what is better. Envy, however, is tortured by another’s happiness and is divided into a twofold passion: either a person himself possesses what he does not want another to possess, or, seeing another to be better, he grieves that he is not like him.

A certain recent poet cleverly translated a Greek verse and played with envy in elegiac meter, saying:

> Nothing is more just than envy: for it immediately
> gnaws and tortures the mind of its own author.

The blessed Cyprian also wrote a very fine book on Zeal and Envy. Whoever reads it will not hesitate to number envy among the works of the flesh.

There is this difference between an envious person (*invidus*) and one who is envied (*invidiosus*): the envious person envies someone more fortunate; the envied person suffers envy from another.

Drunkenness holds the fourteenth place among the works of the flesh. “Drunkards will not possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI). The Lord also says to his disciples: “Beware lest your hearts become weighed down with wine and drunkenness” (Luke XXI). Through wine a person’s senses are overturned, his feet collapse, his mind wavers, and lust is kindled. Hence the Apostle cries out: “And wine, in which is luxury” (Eph. V).

Everyone has authority over his own judgment. I follow the Apostle in saying that luxury and drunkenness are in wine, and in naming drunkenness and luxury among the works of the flesh. Nor can the person who is overcome by these passions deny it.

Although some may think that I deserve criticism for saying in the book I wrote on preserving virginity that young women ought to flee wine as they would poison, I shall not regret that opinion. There the work of wine, rather than the creature of God, was more strongly condemned by us. We granted a restriction to a virgin burning with the natural heat of youth, so that under the pretext of drinking little she might not drink more and perish. Otherwise, we knew that wine is consecrated in the blood of Christ and that Timothy was commanded to drink wine (I Tim. V).

Drunkenness can arise from wine as well as from other kinds of drink prepared in various ways. Hence it is also said of the holy person: “He will drink neither wine nor strong drink” (Luke I). *Sicera* is interpreted as “drunkenness.” Thus, lest anyone who did not drink wine think that some other drink was permitted to him, the excuse is removed: everything capable of causing intoxication is taken away together with wine.

The fifteenth and final work of the flesh is revelry. “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (I Cor. X; Exod. XXXII). Luxury is always joined to drunkenness.

A certain not undistinguished orator, writing about a drunk person awakened from sleep, expressed the matter elegantly: “Once awakened, he could neither sleep; drunk, he could not remain awake.” By this saying he somehow expressed that the man was neither dead nor alive.

It would be a long task to repeat all the works of the flesh and make a catalog of vices. He therefore summed them all up in one statement by saying, “and things like these.” Would that we could avoid them as easily as we understand them.

“I warn you,” he says, “as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.” Earlier he had said: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires” (Rom. VI). Sin possesses all these forms, in distinguishing which we have perhaps lingered longer than was necessary.

Therefore, in the soul in which sin has reigned, the kingdom of God cannot reign. “What partnership is there between righteousness and iniquity? What fellowship does light have with darkness? What agreement does Christ have with Belial?” (II Cor. VI.) Do we suppose that we shall inherit the kingdom of God if we are free from fornication, idolatry, and magical practices? Behold: hostility, contention, anger, quarrels, dissension, drunkenness, and the other things we regarded as small exclude us from the kingdom of God.

It makes no difference whether someone is excluded from blessedness by one thing or by many, since all exclude him in the same way. In the Latin manuscripts, adultery, acts of shamelessness, and murders are also reported as written in this catalog of vices. But it should be understood that no more than fifteen works of the flesh are enumerated, and these are the ones we have discussed.

(Augustine.) Those who do these things are the ones who, consenting to carnal desires, decide that they ought to be done, even if the ability to fulfill them is not granted. Those, however, who are touched by movements of this kind yet remain unmoved and stand in greater love—who not only do not offer the members of their body for evil action, but do not even consent by a nod of the will to offer them—do not perform these works and therefore will possess the kingdom of God.

Sin no longer reigns in their mortal body so as to obey its desires, although sin dwells in their mortal body. The force of the natural habit by which we were born mortal, and of our own life, has not yet been extinguished; by sinning, we ourselves have increased what we carried from the origin of human sin and condemnation.

It is one thing not to sin; it is another not to have sin. The person in whom sin does not reign does not sin—that is, he does not obey its desires. But in the person in whom these desires do not exist at all, there is not only no sin, but sin itself is absent. Although this can be achieved in many respects during the present life, it is not to be hoped for in every respect except in the resurrection and transformation of the flesh.

The statement “as I warned you” may cause concern. If one asks where he had warned them before, it is not found in this Epistle. Therefore, either he had warned them of this when he was present, or he knew that the Epistle sent to the Corinthians had reached them. There he says:

“Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI).

Here, therefore, after listing the works of the flesh by which the kingdom of God is closed, he added the works of the Spirit, which he calls the fruit of the Spirit.

The fruit of the Spirit, however, is love, joy, peace, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, faith, gentleness, patience, and self-control; against such things there is no law. Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires (Ambrose).

He did not say, “The works of the Spirit are love,” but “the fruit of the Spirit.” For the law of the Spirit [Col. 0358B] bears fruit in these things mentioned above, so that through them the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom may be sought. Those who are devoted to Christ he calls “Christs,” that is, “anointed ones.” They crucify the flesh—that is, the world—when they condemn those things from which errors arise. The apostle John likewise follows this interpretation when he says: “Do not love this world, nor the things that are in this world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, because everything that is in this world is the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes” (1 John 2). Therefore, whoever does not desire the world and what is in the world crucifies the flesh.

These vices—idolatry, sorcery, heresies, envy, enmity, anger, quarrels, and the like—should not be attributed to the human body. They are called “carnal” for this reason: [Col. 0358C] they belong to the portion of the world, as I mentioned above. In the meantime, he set down no more than ten qualities signified by the fruit of the Spirit, so that he may appear to have encompassed everything in them, in accordance with the tablets of God’s covenant, in which no more than ten commandments were delivered.

(Jerome.) Which other quality among the fruits of the Spirit ought to hold the first place except love, without which the other virtues are not reckoned virtues, and from which all good things arise? For love holds the first place both in the Law and in the Gospel: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” How full of good things love is, we briefly touched on above; and for the present it is enough to have said even a little: love does not seek what is its own, but [Col. 0358D] what belongs to another.

Even if someone is hostile through his own fault toward the person who loves him, and attempts to stir his tranquility into waves of hatred, the latter is never disturbed and never judges God’s creature worthy of hatred; “for love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4). Likewise, when the Savior says, “A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a bad tree bear good fruit” (Matthew 7), I believe that this was said not so much of human beings as of the fruit of the flesh and of the Spirit. For the Spirit can never commit those vices that have been enumerated among the works of the flesh, nor can the flesh overflow with those fruits that arise from the Spirit.

Yet through the negligence of its possessor it can happen that the Spirit dwelling [Col. 0359A] in a person does not have its own fruits; and, conversely, when the works of the flesh have been put to death, the flesh ceases to sin. Nevertheless, they do not proceed so far that the neglected tree of the Spirit should produce the works of the flesh, or that the cultivated tree of the flesh should put forth spiritual fruits.

In second place among the spiritual fruits is joy, which even the Stoics—who distinguish more subtly among words—consider something different from gladness. They say that joy is the uplifting of the soul exulting over things that deserve exultation, whereas gladness is an unrestrained elevation of the soul that knows no limit and rejoices even in things mingled with fault.

Others, by contrast, set pleasure against joy—not pleasure that arouses the body to lust, tickles the senses, and flatters them with a sweet affection, but another pleasure, homonymous with this one—*ὁμώνυμον*—which, without moderation or any dignity [Col. 0359B] of rejoicing, raises its voice in laughter. If this is true, and if their distinction between the words neither deceives nor is itself mistaken, let us consider whether this may be why it is said: “There is no rejoicing for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isaiah 48).

At the same time, we should note that joy follows love. Whoever loves someone always rejoices in that person’s happiness. If he sees the beloved deceived by some error and fallen into the slippery path of sins, he will indeed grieve and hasten to rescue him; but he cannot change joy into sorrow, knowing that none of God’s rational creatures perishes forever.

The third fruit of the Spirit is peace, from which Solomon also received his name, since he preceded Christ in a typological figure. Concerning the Church [Col. 0359C] the Psalmist sings: “His place has been made in peace” (Psalm 75). Among the eight blessings of the Gospel it is written: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5). In the first Psalm of Ascents we also sing: “With those who hated peace I was peaceable” (Psalm 119).

Let us not think that peace is to be sought only in this, that we do not quarrel with another. The peace of Christ—that is, our inheritance—is with us when a tranquil mind is disturbed by no passions.

After peace comes long-suffering, or patience, since we may interpret *μακροθυμία* in either way. Its opposite is faintheartedness, concerning which it is written: “The fainthearted man is exceedingly foolish.” But the one who is patient and endures everything is a wise man. And with *ἐπίτασις* he is called “very wise.” Thus it is also written in Proverbs: “A long-suffering man is abundant in prudence.”

Kindness, or gentleness [Col. 0359D]—for among the Greeks *χρηστότης* conveys both meanings—is a mild, agreeable, tranquil virtue, suited to fellowship with every good thing; it invites others into intimacy with itself, is sweet in speech, and temperate in conduct. The Stoics accordingly define it as follows: “Kindness is a virtue naturally disposed toward doing good.”

Goodness is not greatly different from kindness, since it too appears disposed toward doing good. It differs in this respect, however: goodness may be somewhat stern, with a severe expression and austere manners; it may do good and provide what is requested, yet not be pleasant in companionship or invite everyone through its own sweetness.

The followers of Zeno likewise define it in this way: “Goodness is a virtue that is beneficial, from which usefulness arises; or a virtue pursued for its own sake; or [Col. 0360A] an affection that is the source of benefits.”

Among the fruits of the Spirit, faith holds the seventh and more sacred place. Elsewhere too it is placed among three qualities: hope, faith, and love. It is not surprising that hope is not included in this catalogue, since what is hoped for is contained in faith; and the Apostle, writing to the Hebrews, defines it in this way: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not yet seen.” Whatever we hope will come, and which is not yet present, we possess through faith, hoping to hold what we believe.

It is also asked how faith is placed within love. Whoever loves never thinks himself injured, never suspects anything except what he loves and what loves him; but when love has departed, faith also departs at the same time.

After faith, gentleness is listed. It is opposed [Col. 0360B] to anger, quarrels, and dissensions, and it is never provoked into its opposites. Truly, it grows good fruits from the good tree of the Spirit. Through it Moses, the servant of God, deserved to receive the testimony of Scripture, which says: “Moses was gentler than all the people who were upon the earth” (Numbers 12).

It says “upon the earth,” for he could not be gentler than those who saw God face to face, since we are often compelled to do many things through the weakness of the flesh. Concerning David also, although many believe that what follows was prophesied of our Lord—and we do not deny this—the Holy Spirit sings typologically of the one who was to come: “Remember, Lord, David and all his gentleness” (Psalm 131).

David’s gentleness was especially evident toward Saul, Absalom, and Shimei. One of them wished to kill him; another, plotting revolution, [Col. 0360C] sought to deprive him of his kingdom; another threw stones at him, scattered dust, and shouted, saying: “Go out, go out, you wicked man” (1 Kings 19 and following; 2 Samuel 15–16).

Self-control is placed last among the fruits of the Spirit. We must understand it not only with respect to chastity, but also with respect to food and drink, anger, mental agitation, and the desire to disparage others.

The difference between modesty and self-control is this: modesty belongs to perfect men and to completed virtue. Of such people the Savior says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matthew 5); and of himself: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matthew 11).

Self-control, however, is on the way of virtue but has not yet reached its goal. For desires still arise in the thoughts of the person who exercises self-control [Col. 0360D] and pollute the ruling faculty of the mind, although they do not overcome him or draw the person thinking them into action.

Self-control is necessary not only against desires and lust, but also against the three remaining disturbances: grief, joy, and fear.

“Against such things there is no law.” For the law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the unrighteous and the disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners (1 Timothy 1). The Law says to me: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not defraud; you shall not desire another’s possessions; you shall not swear falsely; you shall not steal.” If, while the fruit of the Spirit—love—reigns in me, I do none of these things, the commandments of the Law are superfluous for me.

Finally, the wise men of the world also held this opinion concerning philosophy: [Col. 0361A] what the laws publicly compel people to do by necessity, philosophy persuades them to do willingly.

(Augustine.) These spiritual fruits therefore reign in the person in whom sins do not reign. These good things reign when they delight us so greatly that, amid temptations, they themselves hold the mind lest it fall into consent to sin.

Whatever delights us more must determine our conduct. For example, the form of a beautiful woman appears and moves us toward the pleasure of fornication. But if the inner and sincere beauty, the beauty of chastity through the grace that is in the faith of Christ, delights us more, then we live and act according to it. Thus, when sin does not reign in us so as to make us obey its desires, but righteousness reigns through love, [Col. 0361B] we do with great delight whatever we know pleases God in that righteousness.

What I have said about chastity and fornication I wish to be understood of the other matters as well. Therefore love is rightly set against fornication, since in love alone is chastity guarded. All disturbances conceived from that fornication are forms of uncleanness; against them is set the joy of tranquility.

The service of idols is the final fornication of the soul. Because of it, a most furious war was waged against the Gospel with those reconciled to God; although its remnants were long ago crushed, they still remain hot.

Peace, therefore, is opposed to this fornication—the peace by which we are reconciled to God. When that same peace is also maintained with human beings, the vices of sorcery, enmity, contention, rivalry, hostility, and dissension are healed in us. [Col. 0361C] So that these matters may be dealt with among those among whom we live according to a proper moderation, long-suffering serves for endurance, kindness for healing, and goodness for forgiveness.

Faith resists heresies; gentleness resists envy; self-control resists drunkenness and banquets.

Let no one suppose that rivalry is the same as envy. They are neighboring qualities, and because of that proximity one is often used in place of the other: rivalry for envy, or envy for rivalry. But since both are mentioned here in their respective places, they certainly demand that we distinguish between them.

Rivalry is pain of mind when another attains something that two or more people were seeking, and which [Col. 0361D] cannot be possessed by more than one person. Peace heals this rivalry, because we seek what all who desire it become one in when they attain it.

Envy, however, is pain of mind when someone appears unworthy of attaining something, even something that you did not desire. Gentleness heals this, when each person, referring the matter back to God’s judgment, does not resist his will and trusts more that the thing was rightly done than himself, who had judged the person unworthy.

Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified their flesh with its passions and desires, as he says in what follows. How did they crucify it, except by [Col. 0362A] preserving that chaste fear which endures forever and by which we avoid offending the one whom we love with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind?

An adulterous woman does not fear in the same way that a chaste woman fears. The adulteress fears that her husband may guard her; the chaste woman fears that he may abandon her. The husband’s presence is grievous to the one, his absence to the other. Therefore the former fear is corrupt and does not wish this age to pass; the latter is chaste and endures forever.

The prophet desires to be crucified by this fear when he says: “Pierce my flesh with nails because of your fear” (Psalm 118). This is the cross of which the Lord says: “Take up your cross and follow me” (Mark 8).

(Jerome.) Therefore, if our bodies are members of Christ, our flesh too is consequently the flesh of Christ. We crucify it by putting to death upon earth fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire, and greed. And now, as a matter of praise, it is said of us that we have crucified the flesh of Christ Jesus [Col. 0362B] with its vices and desires, and that we always carry the mortification of Jesus in our body, so that his life may also be manifested in our flesh.

It is no small labor to live in the present age in such a way that the life of Jesus is already now manifested in our flesh. For in this way our mortal bodies too will be made alive through the Spirit dwelling in us.

I almost forgot the second interpretation. I had said that everything that follows should be referred to the Law and circumcision. The meaning, therefore, is this: those in whom there is the fruit of the Spirit—love, joy, and the rest—have crucified the bodily understanding of Scripture, which is now called the flesh of Christ, together with its passions and desires, which generate [Col. 0362C] nourishment for vices in little ones and infants.

Such flesh of Christ is crucified by the person who does not serve the history according to the flesh but follows the guiding Spirit of allegory.

(Augustine.) It accords with our devotion that, since we are about to celebrate the approaching passion of the crucified Lord, we ourselves should make a cross for the suppression of carnal pleasures, as the Apostle says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.”

Upon this cross, throughout the whole of this life—which is lived amid temptations—the Christian ought continually to hang. For on this earth there is no time for removing the nails of which the Psalm says: “Pierce my flesh with nails because of your fear” (Psalm 118). The flesh is carnal desire; the nails are the commandments of righteousness. [Col. 0362D] The fear of God fastens those desires to the cross and crucifies us as an acceptable sacrifice to him.

Hence the Apostle likewise says: “Therefore I beseech you, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living, holy, and pleasing sacrifice to God” (Romans 12).

(Gregory.) “Those who belong to Christ,” he says, “have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.” We crucify the flesh with its vices and desires if we restrain the appetite so that we no longer seek anything from the glory of the world.

For whoever disciplines his body but pants after honors has brought the cross upon his flesh, but through desire lives even more wickedly for the world. Often, through the appearance of holiness, though unworthy he attains a position of authority which, unless he had displayed some virtue within himself, he would not have deserved to obtain by any effort [Col. 0363A]; but what he obtains with pleasure passes away, while what follows remains with punishment.

## CHAPTER 6

The Apostle urges the Galatians to mutual support and confirms what he has said about the cessation of the legal observances.

If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. Let us not become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another and envying one another.

(Amb.) He says this because, if we live well and honorably, we ought also to have good conduct; for this is to live by the Spirit: to have an undefiled life. And we walk by the Spirit if we strive for peace, for peace produces charity. Empty glory, however, is wanting to win where there is no reward, so that one should not be eager for contention, knowing that such things generate disagreements and quarrels: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel” (II Tim. II). For it makes the fruits of a good life barren, destroying the promised hope of a chaste manner of life. A good and chaste life must be adorned by good conduct and enriched by benevolence.

(Hieron.) “If we live by the Spirit, let us obey the Spirit.” Let us use this testimony against those who do not wish to understand the Scriptures spiritually. Who is it that lives by the Spirit, unless it is our hidden man, who also sometimes tends to live according to the flesh? But when he has lived by the Spirit, he walks by the Spirit; when he has wished to walk according to the flesh, although living, he is dead. The perfect man in Christ always lives by the Spirit: he obeys the Spirit and never lives according to the flesh. On the other hand, he who has given himself wholly to the flesh and assigned himself to the passions never lives by the Spirit. Between these are those whom we can call neither spiritual nor carnal: they fluctuate between virtues and vices, now drawn back toward better things and becoming spiritual, now tripped by the slippery path of the flesh and becoming flesh.

“Let us not become desirous of empty glory, provoking one another, envying one another.” The Greeks have one word, κενόδοξοι, which the Latin translator expressed by a circumlocution of three words. The countless books of philosophers and the two volumes Cicero wrote on glory show how many definitions and meanings the word glory possesses. But since we are attempting to explain not the etymologies of words but the meaning of Scripture, we shall connect this passage with what precedes it in the following way: If we live by the Spirit, let us obey the Spirit, serving one another in charity, not through the law. We must not contend over the interpretation of the Scriptures, saying, “Circumcision is better.” “No, the foreskin is.” “History must be rejected and allegory followed.” Or rather: “Allegory is empty and shadowy, supported by no foundations of truth.” Hence it happens that envies arise among us. “For,” he says, “they wish to exclude you, so that you may emulate them” (Gal. IV), not so much wishing to teach the truth of the law as to conquer.

But lest we leave the word glory entirely untouched, while leaving the philosophers their absurdities, let us recall something from the Scriptures. The name glory denotes the opinion of the common people and praise sought through human favor where it is said: “They do all their works so that they may be glorified by men” (Matt. XXIII); and elsewhere: “How can you believe, who seek glory from one another?” (John V). Yet in the same passage it is taken in a good sense when he says that they do not seek glory from the one who alone is God. From this we understand that the same word now signifies virtue and now vice. If I seek glory from men, it is vice; if from God, it is virtue. He also urges us toward true glory when he says: “Those who glorify me, I will glorify” (I Sam. II).

(Aug.) “Let us not,” he says, “become desirous of empty glory, envying one another and provoking one another.” This is altogether magnificent and ordered in a wholly divine manner. After instructing them against those by whom they were being seduced into the servitude of the law, he takes care that, having become more instructed and now wishing to answer the accusations of carnal people, they should not devote themselves to contentions and, through a desire for empty glory, serve empty cravings instead of serving the burdens of the law.

Nothing proves a spiritual person so much as the way he handles another’s sin: whether he thinks rather of that person’s liberation than of insult, rather of assistance than of abuse, and, insofar as opportunity is granted, undertakes his restoration. Therefore he says: “Brothers, if someone is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual, restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens.” Nothing inclines one so greatly toward mercy as the thought of one’s own danger. Thus he did not wish them either to neglect the correction of their brothers or to pursue contention.

Many people, when awakened from sleep, want to quarrel; or, when they are forbidden to quarrel, want to go back to sleep. Therefore peace, love, and the thought of our common danger must be preserved in the heart. The manner of speech—whether it is expressed more sharply or more gently—must be moderated according to what the salvation of the person being corrected appears to require. For elsewhere he also says (II Tim. II): “The servant of Christ must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, teachable, patient.” And lest anyone think from this that he must cease correcting another’s error, he adds: “Correcting with modesty those who think differently.”

How “with modesty”? How “correcting”? Only if we retain gentleness in our heart while applying some medicinal severity through the word of correction. Nor do I see any other way to understand what is written in the Epistle: “Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, exhort, rebuke with all patience and instruction” (II Tim. IV). For being “out of season” is certainly contrary to being “in season,” and no medicine heals unless it is applied at the proper time.

Nevertheless, the passage can also be divided in this way: “Be urgent in season,” so that the sense is, “Reprove out of season”; then the rest follows: “Exhort, rebuke with all patience and instruction.” In that case you are considered timely when you press forward by building up, but when you tear down by reproving, you should not care even if you appear untimely, if this is untimely to such people. Thus the two following commands can be referred individually to the two preceding ones: “Exhort when you press forward out of season; rebuke when you reprove out of season.” Then the final two can likewise be referred to them in reverse order: “with all patience,” in order to endure the indignation of those whom you are tearing down, and “with instruction,” in order to teach the aims of those whom you are building up.

Yet even if the passage is divided in the more customary way—“be urgent in season, and, if you make no progress in this manner, out of season”—it must be understood that you should never abandon what is timely. Thus understand “out of season” in such a way that you appear untimely to the person who does not willingly hear what is said against him. You, however, should know that this is timely for him, and you should preserve love and concern for his healing in a gentle, modest, and fraternal spirit.

For many people afterward, reflecting on what they had heard and how justly they had heard it, reproached themselves more seriously and severely. Although they appeared to leave the physician more agitated, they were gradually healed as the force of the word penetrated to their inmost parts. This would not happen if we always waited for the person in danger, with his members festering, to decide when he wished to be burned or cut—something that even physicians of the body, who treat people with a view to an earthly reward, do not do. How many people are found who have not experienced the physicians’ knife or fire while bound, when even those who willingly submit to being bound are rarer? For many, resisting and shouting that they would rather die than be treated in that way, have had all their limbs bound, with scarcely even their tongues left free—not at their own decision or that of the resisting patient, but according to the judgment of the art itself (the printed construxerunt is perhaps constrinxerunt, “bound”). Yet the physician’s spirit is not moved by the cries and abuse of those who suffer, nor does his hand rest.

But the ministers of heavenly medicine either want to see the splinter in their brother’s eye through the beam of hatred, or consider it more tolerable to see the sinner die than to hear the word of one who is indignant. This would not happen if we brought to the mind of another whom we are treating a spirit as healthy as the hands with which physicians handle another person’s limbs. Therefore one must never undertake the task of rebuking another’s sin unless, examining our conscience through inward questioning, we have clearly answered before God that we are acting out of love.

But if the abuse, threats, or even persecutions of the person you have rebuked have wounded your spirit, and if he still appears capable of being healed through you, say nothing until you yourself are healed. Otherwise you may consent, through carnal impulses, to harm him, and present your tongue as a weapon of iniquity to sin, returning evil for evil or curse for curse. Whatever you say with a wounded spirit is the impulse of one who punishes, not the charity of one who corrects.

Love, and say what you wish: what sounds in the form of a curse will in no way be a curse if you remember and feel that, through the sword of God’s word, you wish to be the person’s liberator from the siege of vices. But if, as often happens, you undertake such an action out of love and approach it with love in your heart, yet during the process something creeps in—when resistance causes you to turn away from pursuing the person’s vice and makes you hostile to the person himself—then afterward, washing away this dust with tears, you must remember, for your greater healing, that we ought not to pride ourselves over the sins of others when we sin in rebuking them. For the misery of the sinner more easily makes us angry than compassionate.

(Greg.) “Bear one another’s burdens.” Because the keeping of the Old Testament contains fear, nothing could signify more clearly that charity is the gift of the New Testament than this passage, where the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ.” This is understood as the law of Christ because the Lord himself commanded that we love one another, establishing such weight in that commandment that he said: “By this it is known that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John XIII).

The service of this love is to bear one another’s burdens. But this service is not eternal; it will indeed lead to eternal blessedness, in which there will be none of the burdens that we are commanded to bear for one another. For what can the law of Christ be understood to be more appropriately than charity, which we truly fulfill when, out of love, we endure the burdens of our brothers?

Yet this same law is called manifold, because charity, through diligent concern, expands into every work of virtue. It begins with two commandments but extends itself into countless others. The beginning of this law is love of God and love of neighbor. The love of God is divided into three, since the Creator is commanded to be loved with all the heart, with all the soul, and with all the strength. Here we must observe that, when divine speech commands that God be loved, it not only tells us from what source he is to be loved but also indicates to what extent: it adds “with all,” so that whoever desires to please God perfectly may leave nothing of himself to himself.

The love of neighbor is derived into two commandments. On the one hand, it is said through a certain righteous man: “What you hate to have done to you by another, see that you do not do to another” (Tob. IV). On the other hand, the Truth says through himself: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them” (Luke VI). Through these two commandments of the two Testaments, malice is restrained by one and benevolence is bestowed by the other: each person, by not doing the evil he does not wish to suffer, ceases from harmful action; and, by bestowing the good he desires to have done to himself, he exercises himself in benevolence for the benefit of his neighbor.

As these two commandments are considered with vigilant attention, the heart is stretched toward countless services of virtue, lest the restless mind burn with desires to inflict what it ought not, or, sluggish through idleness, grow numb toward rendering what it ought. When a person takes care not to do to another what he himself would by no means wish to endure from another, he watches himself attentively lest pride raise him to contempt of his neighbor, or, by casting down his spirit, make him exalt himself; lest ambition tear his thoughts and, while expanding them toward the desire for what belongs to others, constrict them; lest luxury pollute the heart and corrupt it by subjecting it to unlawful desires; lest anger embitter it and inflame it even to the utterance of insult; lest envy bite it and, rivaling the happiness of others, consume itself with its own fire; lest immoderate talkativeness draw out the tongue and extend it even to the wantonness of slander; lest hatred arouse malice and provoke the mouth to the dart of cursing.

Again, when he considers doing to another what he himself expects another to do to him, he weighs how to return good for evil and better things for good; how to show the gentleness of patience toward the insolent; how to offer the grace of kindness to those languishing from the plague of malice; how to unite the discordant in peace; how to bind the harmonious to the desire for true peace; how to give the needy what is necessary; how to show the way of uprightness to those who err; how to soothe the afflicted with word and compassion; how to restrain through rebuke those inflamed by the desires of this world; how to mitigate the threats of the powerful by reasoning; how, insofar as he can, to relieve the distress of the oppressed; how to oppose patience to those resisting from without; how, with patience, to offer discipline to those who are proud within; how to temper zeal with gentleness toward the faults of those under one’s authority, so that gentleness does not weaken the devotion to justice; how zeal may burn for punishment without, in its burning, crossing the boundary of compassion; how to provoke the ungrateful to love through benefits; how to preserve the grateful in love through services; how to remain silent about the evils of neighbors when one cannot correct them; and how, when they can be corrected by speaking, to fear that silence may be consent.

He must tolerate in such a way what he keeps silent about that he does not conceal the poison of grief in his heart; offer the gift of kindness to the ill-disposed in such a way that he does not, through favor, depart from the rule of uprightness; expend on his neighbors everything he can, but, in expending it, not become swollen with pride; fear the precipice of self-exaltation in the good things he displays, but not grow sluggish in the practice of goodness; give what he possesses in such a way that he considers the greatness of the rewarder’s generosity; and, when he gives earthly things, not think more than necessary about his own poverty or obscure, through sadness, the light of cheerfulness in the offering of his gift.

The law of God is therefore rightly called manifold, because, although charity is one and the same, when it has fully taken possession of the mind, it kindles it in many forms toward innumerable works. We briefly express its diversity if, by touching on them in passing, we enumerate its good works in individual chosen people.

Through Abel, charity offered gifts chosen for God and endured his brother’s hatred without resistance (Gen. IV). Through Enoch, it taught him to live spiritually among human beings and also bodily removed him from human beings into a sublime life (Gen. V). Through Noah, having despised everything else, it showed him pleasing to God alone, exercised him in the construction of the ark through the devotion of long labor, and preserved the world’s survivor by his pious work (Gen. VI). Through Shem and Japheth, it humbly blushed at their father’s shame and, by placing a cloak upon their backs, concealed what they did not see (Gen. IX).

It raised Abraham’s right hand because he lifted it obediently against his son’s life, and made him the father of innumerable offspring and nations (Gen. XXII). It enlarged Isaac’s mind because it had always kept it pure, so that, although his eyes were dimmed by age, he could see things far in the future (Gen. XXVII). It compelled Jacob both to mourn from the depths of his being for the loss of his good son and to endure with submissive humility the presence of his wicked sons (Gen. XXXVII).

It taught Joseph, sold by his brothers, to endure servitude with an unbroken freedom of spirit and afterward to rule over those same brothers without an exalted mind (Gen. XLII and following).
