It cast Moses, when the people had sinned, prostrate in prayer even to the point of asking for his own death (Exodus); and yet, through the zeal of righteous anger, it raised him to the slaughter of the people, so that he both offered himself to death for the people who were perishing and immediately raged against the sinner in the place of the angering God.

It raised Phinehas’s arm for vengeance upon sinners, so that, seizing a sword, he pierced the couple who were joined together and, in his anger, appeased the Lord’s anger (Num. XXV). It taught Joshua, the scout, first to defend the truth in speech against lying fellow citizens and afterward to wield it with the sword against enemies (Josh. II and following).

It made Samuel humble even in leadership and preserved him blameless in his deposition. Because he loved the people who persecuted him, he himself bore witness that he did not love the height from which he had been cast down (I Sam. III). It moved David, before an unjust king, to flee through humility and filled him with mercy for forgiveness. He fled from his persecutor, fearing him as his lord, yet, when he found the power to strike him, he did not regard him as an enemy (I Sam. XXIV and elsewhere).

Through Nathan, it raised him against the sinning king to the authority of free rebuke; and when the king’s guilt was absent, it laid him humbly prostrate in petition (II Sam. XII and following). Through Isaiah, it did not blush to display the nakedness of the flesh in preaching (Isa. XX), and, having removed the carnal veil, it penetrated to heavenly mysteries.

It taught Elijah to live spiritually through the zeal of fervor and also bodily removed him to life (IV Kings II). It filled Elisha twofold with his master’s spirit because it had taught him to love his master simply (ibid.). Through Jeremiah, it resisted lest the people descend into Egypt; yet, loving the disobedient, he himself descended to the place from which he had forbidden them to go (Jer. XLII).

It lifted Ezekiel first from earthly desires and afterward balanced him in the air by the lock of his head (Ezek. VIII). In Daniel, because it restrained his appetite from royal food, it also shut the mouths of hungry lions for him (Dan. XIV). In the three boys, because it subjected the fires of vice to them while they were at peace, it also moderated the flames in the furnace at the time of tribulation (Dan. III).

In Peter, it bravely resisted the threats of intimidating rulers and humbly listened to the words of his inferiors concerning the abolition of circumcision (Acts V). In Paul, it humbly endured the hands of persecutors, yet, in the matter of circumcision, boldly rebuked the view of one far inferior to himself (Acts XV).

This law of God is therefore manifold: it accords with each circumstance without being changed, and joins itself to changing situations without itself being changed.

(Hier.) Paul knew that he was a worshiper of that God who does not desire the death of the sinner but repentance. And, with the Trinity excepted, every creature, although it may not sin, is nevertheless capable of sinning. Therefore Paul exhorts even the spiritual person, through fear of himself, not to sin and to extend a hand to the fallen.

He beautifully calls a person “overtaken in transgression,” showing from the very name the frailty of his condition and indicating that he is worthy of pardon: like a human being deceived by error and plunged into a gulf, he cannot raise himself without help and assistance. The word “man” is not added to “spiritual”; rather, it is as though God is commanded to restore a man overtaken in transgression—or, as it is better expressed in Greek, to perfect him in a spirit of gentleness.

But a person who is perfected does not lack everything; he lacks only certain things. Accordingly, if he has not gone astray through many sins but has been overtaken by some particular fault, the spiritual person should apply a spirit of gentleness and mildness in correcting the sinner. He should not wish to correct the erring person harshly, angrily, or sadly, but should encourage him by promising salvation and promising pardon. He should bring forward Christ’s testimony, which invites those weighed down by the heavy burden of the law and sins to his easy yoke and light burden, so that they may learn that he is humble, gentle, and meek in heart, and may find rest for their souls (Matt. XI).

Let us use this testimony against heretics who, inventing stories about different kinds of nature, say that the spiritual is a good tree and does not produce bad fruit. Behold, the Apostle, whose authority they themselves follow, says that those who are spiritual can sin if they are puffed up by the arrogance of their heart and fall. We also admit this, and we admit that the χοϊκοί—those who are earthly—can become spiritual if they turn toward better things.

Someone may oppose us with what is written to the Corinthians: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?” (I Cor. IV.) If there he says that he will come to sinners not in a spirit of gentleness but with a rod, how is it that here, for those who have been overtaken in some sin, he applies not a rod but a spirit of gentleness?

The answer is that he is speaking there to people who, after sinning, did not recognize their error and did not wish to submit to their superiors or be corrected through repentance. But when a sinner recognizes his wound and hands himself over to the physician for healing, a rod is not necessary; a spirit of gentleness is.

The following question may also arise: If someone ought to restore a sinner in a spirit of gentleness because he considers himself, lest he also be tempted, should the righteous person who is sure of his own mind and knows that he cannot fall therefore not restore the sinner in a spirit of gentleness?

We answer: Even if the righteous person has conquered, knowing how great a struggle was required for his victory, he will grant forgiveness to the sinner all the more readily. For this reason the Savior was tempted, “in every respect like us, without sin” (Heb. IV), so that he might have compassion and sympathy for our weaknesses, taught by his own example how difficult victory is in the flesh.

If a virgin has remained so into old age, let him forgive the person who was once deceived by the heat of youth, knowing through how many difficulties he himself passed through that age. If someone has been tortured for confessing the Name and sees another deny the faith under torture, let him have compassion on the denier’s wounds and not so much marvel that the other was defeated as that he himself conquered.

Observe also the caution of the writer. He did not say, “Considering yourself, lest you also fall,” but, “lest you also be tempted.” To be defeated or to conquer is sometimes in our power; but to be tempted is in the power of the tempter. For if the Savior was tempted, who can be secure that he will cross the seas of this life without being tempted?

Those who think that Paul spoke according to humility and not truthfully when he said, “Even if I am unskilled in speech, yet I am not in knowledge” (II Cor. XI), should defend the grammatical consequence of this passage. He ought, according to their order, to have said: “You who are spiritual, restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourselves, lest you also be tempted,” and not have introduced a singular number after a plural.

The Hebrew, therefore, a Hebrew of Hebrews and highly learned in his native language, could not express profound meanings in a foreign tongue and did not greatly care about words, since he had the meaning secure.

For if anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone and not in another.

(Amb.) This is true and hidden from no one: if we consider our actions and our mind, we place ourselves above no one and do not readily judge anyone. But whoever exalts himself as though he were something is in error, for he does not know that growth comes from humility.

He does not keep before his eyes the words and deeds of the Savior, who, although he is Lord of all, humbled himself in order to give us an example of what we ought to follow if we wish to grow. If we raise ourselves up, we are brought low; this is what the inexperience of an inflated heart produces, so that a person may appear more esteemed among human beings.

For, despising and looking down on sinners, he strives to appear righteous, like that Pharisee whom the Lord condemns (Luke XVIII). Is someone not truly inexperienced who desires present glory? Does he not truly despair of future things who wishes to obtain the reward of righteousness in the present? Why? Because he is not righteous in his conduct but falsely pretends to righteousness. For whoever wishes to be righteous places another before himself, so that he may truly be righteous. Each person knows his own evils better than those of another.

“Each person will carry his own burden.” Finally, he wished to make this known to the proud: a person is not defiled by another’s sin, provided that he dissents from it. Thus no one should fear joining himself to a sinner or receiving someone who approaches him, in order to win him. For if anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.

(Hieron.) If someone does not wish to bear another’s burdens and, without compassion, is content only with his own work and virtue, not seeking what belongs to another but what belongs to himself—that is, being a lover only of himself and not also of God—he deceives himself.

The passage can be read and divided in two ways: either, “If anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself”; or, “If anyone thinks himself to be something,” with “when he is nothing” following afterward. This distinction is heard more clearly in Greek than in Latin.

The sense of the first division is: He who thinks himself to be something when he is nothing deceives himself. The second sense is deeper and more pleasing to us. If anyone thinks himself to be something in the very fact that he considers himself something, judging himself not from mercy toward his neighbor but from his own work and labor, content with his own virtue, then through this very arrogance he becomes nothing and deceives himself. This is expressed better in Greek by φρεναπατᾷ, that is, “he deceives his own mind,” whereas the Latin translator rendered it, “he seduces himself.”

He deceives his own mind who thinks himself wise and, according to Isaiah, “is wise in his own eyes and intelligent in his own sight.” The meaning of this passage is connected with circumcision and the law as follows: the person who is spiritual but has no mercy toward his neighbor, despising the humble because he himself is higher, deceives himself, not knowing that this is the law of the Spirit: that we love one another.

“But let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone and not in another.” The sense is this: You who consider yourself spiritual and stronger because of another’s weakness must consider not the weakness of the one who lies fallen but your own strength. For if another cannot pass perfectly from Judaism to Christianity, it does not follow that you are therefore a perfect Christian. But if your own conscience does not accuse you, you have glory in yourself and not in another.

An athlete is not strong because he defeats a weak opponent and overcomes the languid limbs of his adversary, but only if he is strong and glories in his own strength, not in another’s weakness.

The passage can also be understood in another way. He who has a conscience of good work and, examining himself, does not condemn his work should not glory in this before another, pour out his praise publicly, share it with everyone, and seek boastfulness through human favor. Rather, he should have glory in himself and say: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

Whoever seeks glory from another has neither the world crucified to him nor himself crucified with Christ; for he has received from human beings the reward he was seeking.

“Each person will carry his own burden.” This appears to contradict what precedes, where he says: “Bear one another’s burdens.” If each person will carry his own burden, one person cannot carry another’s burden. But we must observe that there he commanded us to support one another in this life when we sin, and to be mutual assistance to one another in the present age. Here, however, he is speaking of the Lord’s judgment upon us: we shall be judged as sinners or saints not from another’s sin and comparison with someone worse, but according to our own work, with each person receiving according to his work.

Although obscurely, we are taught by this brief statement a new doctrine that remains hidden: while we are in the present age, we can help one another through prayers and counsels; but when we have come before the judgment seat of Christ, neither Job, nor Daniel, nor Noah will be able to plead for anyone. Each person will carry his own burden.

(Aug.) Let us be recalled to conscience, of which the Apostle says: “For our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I). Let us be recalled to the conscience of which he says: “Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another.”

Therefore let each of us test his own work: whether it flows from the vein of charity, whether branches of good works sprout from the root of love. “Let each person test his own work,” he says, “and then he will have glory in himself and not in another”—not when another’s tongue bears witness to him, but when his own conscience bears witness.

Question your heart: what have you done, and what did you desire there—your salvation or the empty praise of human beings? Look within. For a human being cannot judge what he cannot see, unless, under the different meanings of the word burden, you suppose that he is unquestionably contradicting himself in speech, placing words so close together in one statement: shortly before he said, “Bear one another’s burdens,” and afterward he said, “Each person will carry his own burden.”

But some burdens are those of shared weakness, while others are those of rendering an account to God for our actions. The former are shared with our brothers and borne together; the latter are carried individually by each person.

Let the one who is being instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him.

**(Ambrose.)** He says this so that those who listen may share all good things with their teachers. But if they act otherwise than they teach, one must not share in those things with them, but dissent, so that the law may be your guide rather than a human being. He will harm himself, not you, because you observe what you are taught.

**(Jerome.)** Marcion interpreted this passage as though he thought that the faithful and catechumens ought to pray together, and that the teacher should share prayer with the disciples. He was especially encouraged by what follows: “in all good things.” Yet, if the subject had been prayer, the command ought certainly to have been given to the one who catechizes, not to the one being catechized—namely, not to the disciple but to the teacher. Moreover, the other statements that follow do not agree with his interpretation: “Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap,” and, “Let us not grow weary in doing good; for in due season we shall reap, if we do not give up.”

The meaning, therefore, is this: because above he had commanded spiritual people to instruct those who had been overtaken in some offense in a spirit of gentleness, and to bear one another’s burdens, fulfilling the law of Christ, he now, conversely, commands those who were still weaker—disciples and carnal people—to provide material things to their teachers, just as they themselves reap spiritual things from them. The teachers, devoting themselves wholly to divine instruction and study, need the necessities of this life; and what is written concerning the manna should be fulfilled: “He who had much did not abound, and he who had little was not diminished” (Exod. XVI).

In the present passage he calls “good things,” according to popular usage and common custom, food and clothing and the like—things that people ordinarily count among goods: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content.” Nor is it surprising that Paul designated the things necessary for the body as “good,” since our Savior also said to those who had not yet ascended to the summit of the virtues, but were still walking at a lower level and asking that faith be added to them: “If you then, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him?” (Matt. VII).

I think that Job also, when he spoke to his wife as though to one of foolish women, referred to bodily riches in view of her opinion: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord” (Job II). And again, concerning hardships, afflictions, and temptation, through which victory is won: “Why should we not endure evils?” Yet “evils” and “goods” are properly located not in riches and afflictions but in virtues and vices, as the righteous man says in the psalm: “Who is the man who desires life and longs to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXIII and following).

Strictly speaking, “evil” is what we ought to avoid; “good” is what we ought to do. That rich man in the Gospel, who had no knowledge of good and evil, rightly considered the abundance of his fields a good, saying: “Soul, you have good things laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, be merry” (Luke XII). And another man, who lay in purple and was rich in luxuries, heard Abraham say to him in the underworld: “You received good things during your life” (Luke XVI).

One must also consider whether this might perhaps be understood as a command given to disciples to share the word with those who instruct them, to obey them, and to make themselves teachable and agreeable—but only in matters that are good, spiritual, and not distorted by heretical or Jewish perversity.

Do not be deceived: God is not mocked.

**(Ambrose.)** No one doubts that God cannot be deceived, but that each person receives from him what he deserves. “Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.” For “he who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh.” Here he signifies carnal vices, which are ordinarily committed in the flesh, so that anyone who has corrupted himself in his flesh may know that he will become subject to corruption. He corrupts the body who presumes upon what is forbidden.

But “he who sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit.”

**(Augustine.)** Sowing in the spirit is serving righteousness from faith with love, and not obeying the desires of sin, although those desires arise from mortal flesh. The harvest of eternal life will come when death, the last enemy, has been destroyed, when what is mortal will be swallowed up by life, and this corruptible body will put on incorruption (I Cor. XV).

In this, therefore, the third stage, in which we are under grace, we sow in tears when desires arise from the animal body. By refusing to consent to them, we resist them, so that we may reap in joy when, after the body has also been transformed, no distress from any part of us and no danger of temptation will trouble us.

**(Ambrose.)** A Christian human being consists of spirit and flesh; for, in comparison with the Holy Spirit, the human being is flesh. Therefore, when a person gives assent to the spirit while restraining himself from things that are contrary to it, he sows spiritually, so that he may be able to reap eternal life. By the testimony of the spirit he receives immortality as his reward. Just as the one who corrupts himself by dishonoring his body will belong not to eternity but to corruption, so the one who keeps himself undefiled will obtain eternal life.

“Do not be deceived,” he says; “God is not mocked. Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap.”

**(Jerome.)** Foreseeing that those who were being taught—and who ought to supply their teachers with expenses and the necessities of life—might plead poverty and say, “My field dried up this year from drought; hail destroyed my vineyard; the revenues that might have been available for tribute were seized; I have no means by which to contribute what is commanded,” he added: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked.”

He knows, he says, your hearts; he is not ignorant of your resources. A plausible excuse may somehow satisfy a human being, but it cannot deceive God. At the same time he urges them to provide what has been commanded, calling it “seed,” so that no one may think lost what he will receive back with multiplied increase.

To the Corinthians also he taught the principle of giving and receiving by a similar example: “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows with blessings will also reap with blessings. Let each one give as he has determined in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX).

“For he who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh; but he who sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit.”

Everything that we say, do, or think is sown in two fields, flesh and spirit. If the things that proceed from the hand, mouth, and heart are good, having been sown in the spirit, they will overflow with the fruits of eternal life. If they are evil, having been received from the field of the flesh, they will cause a harvest of corruption to spring up for us.

Alternatively: Whoever understands the law carnally also expects carnal promises—things that are corrupted in the present age. But whoever is a spiritual hearer sows in the spirit and will reap everlasting life from the spirit.

**(Ambrose.)** This is eternal life: to live without punishment and to possess glory. For if a person who is now in anxiety denies that he is living, how much more will he suffer fire and a torturer when he is alienated from God?

Let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due season we shall reap, if we do not give up.

He says this because the one who is strong in sowing will also be strong in reaping—that is, he will receive in the manner in which he acts. Therefore he urges us to be ready to do good and not to become weary, confident that we shall receive great things in return for small things, and eternal things in return for earthly things, at the time God promised.

**(Jerome.)** “Let us not grow weary in doing good,” he says, “for in due season we shall reap, if we do not give up.” He urges those who await the reward of good work in this life to devote themselves to perseverance, not knowing that, just as in seed there is one time for sowing and another for harvest, so in the present life the work is the sowing—whether it is now reaped in the spirit or in the flesh—but the harvest of works is the future judgment. According to the quality and diversity of the sowing, we shall produce different harvests: a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold. No one can reap that crop if he gives up, for “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X).

And in another passage: “Be,” he says, “one who does not give up.” But what does that mean? When sinners increase daily in evil works, should we grow weary in doing good?

Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to everyone.

**(Ambrose.)** The Gentiles have time for doing evil. For how can people without God do good? But those who have become Christians have time to do good to all people, so that after receiving faith, good work may advance toward the promised reward. Time is granted for life for this reason: so that we may now conduct ourselves justly, giving an example to the Gentiles.

And especially to those who are of the household of faith.

**(Augustine.)** Whom else should we understand him to mean except Christians? Eternal life is to be desired for all with equal love, but the same services of love cannot be shown to everyone.

**(Ambrose.)** It is true: we ought to be more ready and more inclined toward good with regard to our brothers, because we are members of one another.

**(Jerome.)** As we have said, the time of sowing is the present time and the life through which we are passing. In this life we may sow whatever we wish; when this life has passed, the time for working will be taken away. Hence the Savior also says: “Work while it is day; the night is coming, when no one can work any longer” (John IX).

The word of God, the true sun, has risen for us, and the beasts have gathered into their dens. Let us go forth like human beings to our work and labor until evening, as it is mystically sung in the psalm:

“You appoint darkness, and it becomes night; in it all the beasts of the forest move about, the young lions roaring to seize their prey and to seek their food from God. The sun rises, and they gather themselves together and lie down in their dens. A man goes forth to his work and to his labor until evening” (Ps. CIII).

Whether we are sick or healthy, humble or powerful, poor or rich, obscure or honored, hungry or eating, let us do everything in the name of the Lord with patience and equanimity. Then what is written will be fulfilled in us: “For those who love the Lord, all things work together for good.”

If I restrain anger itself, lust, and the injury that desires revenge; if I remain silent for God’s sake; if, through every sting of agitation and every incitement to vice, I remember God watching me from above, these things become occasions of triumph for me.

Let us not say when we give: “He is my friend; I do not know this man. This one ought to receive; that one ought to be despised.” Let us imitate our Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matt. V).

The fountain of goodness is open to all: slave and free, commoner and king, rich and poor drink from it alike. When a lamp has been lit in a house, it shines equally for everyone. If the restraints of generosity are loosened indiscriminately toward all, how much more toward those who are of the household of faith and toward Christians, who have the same Father and are reckoned under the title of the same teacher?

It seems to me that this passage can also be connected with what precedes, so that he calls “those of the household of faith” the teachers to whom above he had commanded that their hearers should supply all things considered good.

The course of this life is brief. This very thing that I speak, say, write, correct, and reread either increases or diminishes my time. Titus, the son of Vespasian, who entered Rome in triumph in vengeance for the Lord’s blood after Jerusalem had been overthrown, is said to have been so good that, when he remembered late one night at dinner that he had done nothing good that day, he said to his friends: “Today I have lost a day.”

We think that we do not lose an hour, a day, moments, time, or years when we speak an idle word, for which we shall give an account on the day of judgment.

If that man said and did this naturally, without the law, without the Gospel, and without the teaching of the Savior and the apostles, what ought we to do, when even Juno’s once-married women, Vesta’s virgins, and other chaste idols stand to condemn us?

Blessed John the Evangelist, when he remained at Ephesus into extreme old age and could scarcely be carried to church in the hands of his disciples, being unable to form many words with his voice, used to say nothing else at each gathering except this: “Little children, love one another.”

At last the disciples and brothers who were present, wearied because they always heard the same thing, said: “Teacher, why do you always say this?” He replied with a saying worthy of John: “Because it is the Lord’s commandment, and if it alone is done, it is sufficient.”

This is relevant to the Apostle’s present command: “Let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith.”

See with what large letters I have written to you with my own hand.

**(Ambrose.)** He wishes these letters to be obeyed. For where there is a handwritten original, it cannot be said to be false. Otherwise, perhaps, having been deceived, they might excuse themselves concerning the Epistle, as though it were false or not the Apostle’s, unwilling to be reproved.

**(Jerome.)** Those who wanted to circumcise the Galatians had spread the claim that Paul did one thing and preached another, and that by his conduct he destroyed his own teaching, since he who asserted that the law had been abolished was himself found to be living within the law.

Because Paul could not overturn this opinion in person before everyone—for he was prevented by the chains he was enduring for Christ’s martyrdom—he made himself present through a letter. And so that no suspicion of a forged Epistle might arise, from this point to the end he wrote it out himself, showing that the preceding portion had been written by another.

That Epistles were sent under his name by false teachers he also demonstrates when writing to the Thessalonians: “We ask you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together to him, not to be quickly shaken from your understanding or alarmed, either by spirit, or by word, or by a letter supposedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were already present, so that no one may deceive you in any way” (II Thess. II).

And to remove from suspicion of falsity the entire Epistle he was sending, he subscribed it at the end in his own hand, saying: “The greeting of me, Paul, with my own hand; this is the sign in every Epistle: so I write. The grace of our Lord [Col. 0376D] Jesus Christ be with you all.”

To the Colossians also, to whom he had dictated the letter, he similarly added a note in his own hand: “The greeting of me, Paul, with my own hand. Remember my chains” (Col. IV).

And wherever he knew that false teachers were present who might sow new doctrines under the authority of the Apostle, he subscribed the Epistle in his own hand. Finally, when writing to the Corinthians, among whom there were schisms and heresies, with each person saying, “I am of Paul,” or “I am of Apollo,” or “I am of Cephas,” he marked his Epistle with this notation: “The greeting of me, Paul, with my own hand. If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed: Maranatha,” and so forth (I Cor. XVI).

For this reason, wishing to remove every opportunity from the false teachers who had corrupted the Galatians away from the truth of the Gospel, he completed the end of the Epistle with a note in his own hand, saying: “See with what large letters I have written to you.”

This does not mean that the letters were physically large—for this is what the Greek word *πηλίκοις* signifies—but that the traces of his own hand were recognizable to them. Thus, when they recognized the strokes of the letters, they would think that they were seeing the very man who had written them.

Those who wish to please in the flesh compel you to be circumcised, only so that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ.

**(Jerome.)** Above he showed from what point he had written with his own hand; now he repeats what he had written.

Gaius Caesar, Octavian Augustus, and Tiberius, the successor of Augustus, had promulgated laws allowing the Jews who were dispersed throughout the entire Roman Empire to live according to their own rite and to devote themselves to their ancestral ceremonies.

Therefore, whoever was circumcised, even if he believed in Christ, was regarded by the Gentiles as a Jew. But whoever, without circumcision, showed by his foreskin that he was not a Jew became subject to persecutions both from Gentiles and from Jews.

Wishing to avoid these persecutions, those who had corrupted the Galatians persuaded the disciples to adopt circumcision as a defense. The Apostle now calls this “confidence in the flesh,” since they preferred circumcision during persecution both to the Gentiles whom they feared and to the Jews whom they wished to please. The Jews could not persecute them, nor could the Gentiles, who saw them circumcising even proselytes and observing the precepts of the law themselves.

**(Ambrose.)** “To please in the flesh” means “to please human beings.” In order to live with the Jews—whom he calls false apostles—appeased or at least not hostile to them, they preached Christ in such a way that they also taught the law was to be observed. The Apostle, however, never feared this; steadfastly, he did not remain silent about what is true, providing both for himself and for those whom he taught. Thus he says: “I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts XXI).

**(Jerome.)** For those who are circumcised do not keep the law; rather, they want you to be circumcised so that they may boast in your flesh.

Because of the weakness of the flesh, he says, the law cannot be fulfilled. Hence the Jews observe the precepts and teachings of human beings more than the commandments of God. They fulfill neither the law bodily—for that is impossible—nor spiritually, because they do not understand it.

Thus everything they study, do, and strive for has this purpose: that among the Jews they may boast of the injury done to your flesh and boast that, through their teaching, they have circumcised the Gentiles. They do all this so that they may please the Jews and so that resentment against the law, which has been defeated, may subside.

**(Ambrose.)** This is like the statement addressed to the Apostle Peter: “If you, though you are a Jew, live like a Gentile, how can you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?” (Gal. II).

So these men, although they themselves did not keep the law and lived unjustly, were zealous for circumcision, so that they might thereby appear to be defenders and lovers of the law. Yet it is clear that the one who defends and keeps the law is the person who performs its righteous requirements and does not neglect the commandment given for life.

Such, then, was the excuse of the Galatians. He says these things so that they may at least understand that they were being mocked like foolish and dull-witted people, whose sufferings they made the occasion of their boasting.

But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.

**(Augustine.)** “The world has been crucified to me,” he says, so that it may not hold me; “and I to the world,” so that I may not hold it. That is, neither can the world harm me, nor do I desire anything from the world.

Whoever boasts in the cross of Christ does not wish to please in the flesh, because he does not fear the persecutions of carnal people. Christ first endured those persecutions in order to be crucified and to provide an example for those who follow his footsteps.

**(Ambrose.)** Just as the false apostles, through hypocrisy, treated tribulations endured for Christ’s name as though they were useless, being ashamed of them, so the Apostle boasted of them, knowing that a great reward would result from them. The same was true of his fellow apostles, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “Then,” it says, “the apostles went out from the council rejoicing that they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Christ” (Acts V).

Therefore, the person whose entire hope is in Christ boasts in his cross. For that person the world has also been crucified, since he is certain that the love of Christ’s cross is life, while love of the world produces death.

**(Jerome.)** Only the person who takes up the cross and follows the Savior can boast in the cross of Christ; the person who has crucified his flesh with its vices and desires, who has died to the world, and who does not contemplate the things that are seen but those that are unseen, seeing the world crucified and its form passing away.

The world is crucified to the righteous—the world of which the Savior says: “I have overcome the world”; and, “Do not love the world”; and, “You did not receive the spirit of the world.”

The world has been crucified to the one for whom the world has died. The consummation of the world has come for him, and he has become worthy of a new heaven, a new earth, and the New Testament. He sings a new song and receives a new name written on a stone, which no one knows except the one who receives it (Rev. II).

**(Gregory.)** Paul therefore rightly says, when he had perfectly despised the age and saw himself made such that this age could no longer desire him at all, that he was free from the bonds of this life: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

The world had been crucified to him because he no longer loved it, since it was already dead to his heart. But he had also crucified himself to the world because he strove to present himself to it as one whom, being like a dead man, it could not desire.

If a dead person and a living person are in one place, although the dead person does not see the living one, the living person nevertheless sees the dead. But if both are dead to each other, neither sees the other at all.

Likewise, one who no longer loves the world may still be loved by it against his will. Although he himself, like a dead man, does not see the world, the world, not yet dead, still sees him. But if he neither retains the world in his love nor is himself retained by the world’s love, both are mutually dead to one another, because neither desires the other and, being dead, pays no attention to the other.

Since Paul neither sought the glory of the world nor was himself sought by the glory of the world, he boasts that he is crucified to the world and that the world is crucified to him.

**(Jerome.)** But it may be asked how Paul now says, “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ,” when elsewhere he boasts concerning other things, as when he says: “By your glory, which I have in Christ Jesus” (I Cor. XV); and again: “I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (II Cor. XII); and elsewhere: “It would be better for me to die than for anyone to deprive me of my glory” (I Cor. IX), along with the other statements written in this manner.

But it must be understood that all that boasting, when referred to the cross, is the glory of the cross. Whatever worthy deed is accomplished in the virtues is done because of the Lord’s passion.

For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.

And upon all who follow this rule, peace and mercy be, and upon the Israel of God.

**(Augustine.)** By “new creation” he means a new life through faith in Jesus Christ. The word deserves notice, for it is difficult to find even those who have already come through believing into adoption as sons called a “creation.”

**(Ambrose.)** The new creation is our regeneration. It is this that gives progress to those who persevere. Upon them is the peace of God, for the person who is at peace with God fears no one’s hostility. He is safe under the protection and mercy of God, which was promised and remains upon the Israel of God—not upon the Israel of a human being.

The unbelieving Jews are Israelites according to the flesh. He therefore signified two groups upon whom the peace and mercy of God remain: believing Jews and faithful Gentiles.

**(Jerome.)** Just as the faithful and the unfaithful, although one in substance, are divided into two according to their differing understanding, as the Apostle says, “Having stripped off the old man with his deeds and having put on the new, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of his Creator” (Col. III), so also, although the world is one according to substance, it becomes one thing or another according to perception.

To the sinner the world is old; to the holy person it is new. When the world has been crucified to the holy person, circumcision and uncircumcision are of no account to him—neither Jew nor Gentile—but a new creation, into which the body of our humiliation is transformed according to the body of Christ’s glory.

“For the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new.” And just as the glory of the sun is one, the glory of the moon another, and the glory of the stars another, and star differs from star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead (I Cor. XV).

Daniel agrees with this in the same voice, saying: “Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will rise: some to eternal life, and some to eternal disgrace and eternal confusion” (Dan. XII); and, “Those who understand will shine like the brightness of the firmament” (Matt. XIII); and concerning the righteous: “Many will shine like the stars forever.”

For neither in the sun, moon, firmament, nor stars does circumcision or uncircumcision have any value; rather, there is a new condition without those parts of the body that can be cut away.

Thus we too, who love God and for whom those things have been prepared that “eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and have not entered into the human heart” (Isa. LXIV; I Cor. II), when we have been transformed from the body of our humiliation into the body of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, will have that body which neither a Jew can circumcise nor a Gentile preserve with its foreskin. This does not mean that it is different according to substance, but that it is different according to glory.

“For this mortal body must put on immortality, and this corruptible body must be clothed with incorruption” (I Cor. XV).

The blessed Evangelist John, sensing something similar, also said: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be. We know that when it is revealed, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III).

Since, therefore, the glorious body of Jesus Christ has not yet been revealed—the body that, after the resurrection, still bore the marks of the nails and entered through closed doors—we, who have already risen with Christ in baptism and have been reborn into the new human being, must serve neither circumcision nor uncircumcision. Rather, let us believe that we already are what we shall be.

And upon all who follow this rule, peace and mercy be, and upon the Israel of God.

Everything is directed according to a standard, and when the rule has been applied, it is shown whether things are crooked or straight. So also the teaching of God is a kind of rule of speech, judging between what is just and what is unjust. Whoever follows it will have peace within himself, the peace that surpasses all understanding, and after peace, mercy, which is the chief quality of the Israel of God.

He is called the Israel of God in distinction from the one who has ceased to be the Israel of God. They say that they are Jews, and they are not, but they lie, since they are a synagogue of Satan (Rev. II).

Nor should you be surprised that, in imitation of the spiritual Israel, there is a carnal Israel, which possesses neither peace nor mercy. Concerning this it is also written to the Corinthians: “See Israel according to the flesh” (I Cor. X), just as, in imitation of God and the Lord, there are also many gods and many lords, whether in heaven or on earth.

Beautifully, in a single expression, so that he might conclude the Epistle according to the subject proposed, he called them “the Israel of God,” thereby teaching that everything said above had been discussed not outside the matter but in relation to it.

From now on let no one cause me trouble.

This does not mean that he had failed in teaching, but that, just as a farmer has this labor if the plants he has planted dry up, and a shepherd has this anxiety if the sheep he has gathered are scattered and torn apart, so he no longer wished to endure such trouble.

**(Ambrose.)** He did not want to be troubled any further, lest he perhaps be compelled to write again. He now wishes them to become more corrected, so that, after their errors have been cut away, he might have rest following so many difficulties.

But if they should prove harder and inflexible in their conversion, they should withdraw from him, so that he might devote his labors and effectiveness to those from whom he could hope for reward or profit.

**(Jerome.)** It is better read in Greek: “Let no one henceforth exhibit labors to me”—that is, so that I may not again have to labor on your behalf.

A teacher is burdened by the student who lives and thinks differently from what the teacher has taught and done. The statement may also anticipate their contention, should some of them wish to contradict him later. Thus, after discussing the veiling of a woman’s head and the non-veiling of a man’s head, he concludes to the Corinthians: “If anyone thinks he is contentious, we have no such custom, nor the churches of God” (I Cor. XI).

That is: We have said what seemed to us honorable and just. But if anyone, unwilling to submit to the truth, seeks what he may answer and what arguments he may use against it, let him know that he is not worthy of a response, since he is more prepared to quarrel than to be taught.

For I bear the marks of Jesus in my body.

**(Augustine.)** “Marks” (*stigmata*) are certain signs of servile punishments. If, for example, a slave had been placed in chains because of some offense—that is, because of some fault—or had suffered something of this kind, he was said to bear marks; and therefore, under the law of manumission, he belonged to an inferior order.

The Apostle therefore wished to call the marks of the punishments he endured through persecutions “the marks of Jesus.” He knew that these were repaid to him because of the offense of his persecution, since he had persecuted the churches of Christ. Thus the Lord himself said to Ananias, when Ananias feared him as a persecutor of Christians: “I will show him,” he said, “what he must suffer for my name” (Acts IX).

Nevertheless, because of the remission of sins in which he had been baptized, all those tribulations did not bring destruction upon him but advanced him toward the crown of victory.

**(Jerome.)** Whoever is circumcised after the coming of Christ in the flesh does not bear the marks of the Lord Jesus but possesses glory in his own shame. But the one who was beaten beyond measure, frequently imprisoned, beaten with rods three times, stoned once, and endured the other things recorded in the catalogue of his boasts—that person bears the marks of the Lord Jesus in his body.

Perhaps also the person who disciplines his body and brings it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, he himself should be found disqualified (II Cor. IX), bears the marks of the Lord Jesus in his body.

The apostles rejoiced (Acts V) that they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus.

**(Ambrose.)** He says this in anger, because he saw that the sufferings he endured for the sake of believers were ineffective among them. For the sake of Christ, he had not feared to suffer wounds and chains through the steadfastness and faith of his teaching. Rather, he endured, out of love for the believers, to bear the scars of wounds in his body, so that he might preach to them no less faithfully than the false apostles who had deceived the Galatians.

He therefore does not want anyone who is not devoted to this matter to cause him trouble. These marks—that is, the scars of wounds—are testimonies concerning the believers who suffer, showing that they are worthy of the future promise.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.

He does not speak of the grace of the law, but says that the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ is with the spirit of those whom he calls spiritual brothers; for not all of them had been completely overthrown.

**(Jerome.)** Let it not be dissension, servitude to the law, quarrelling, or strife with your spirit, but the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let it be with your spirit—not with the flesh, not with the soul—either because, having become spiritual, you have ceased to be flesh and soul, or because, in what is principal, even what is lesser is included.

The soul and flesh are subject to the spirit, concerning which Ecclesiastes says: “The spirit will return to him who gave it” (Eccl. XII). And Paul says elsewhere: “The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit” (Rom. VIII).

This grace of the Lord Jesus is not with everyone, but with those who deserve to be called brothers by the Apostle: faithful brothers and genuine brothers. This is what the word “Amen” signifies, a Hebrew word.

The Seventy translated *Amen* as “Let it be” (*Fiat*); Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated it as “faithfully” or “truly.” Just as in the Old Testament, by a certain custom of swearing, God confirms his words by saying, “As I live, says the Lord,” and people also swear by saying, “As your soul lives,” so our Savior in the Gospel demonstrates through the word “Amen” that the things he says are true.

That “Amen” signifies the agreement of the hearer and is the seal of truth, the First Epistle to the Corinthians also teaches us. There Paul says: “Otherwise, if you bless in the spirit, how will the one who occupies the place of the uninstructed say ‘Amen’ over your blessing, since he does not know what you are saying?” (I Cor. XIV).

From this he shows that the uninstructed person cannot respond that what is said is true unless he has understood what is being taught.

Amen.

# BOOK SEVENTEEN. COMMENTARY ON THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS

[Col. 0381]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0381D]

(Ambr.) The Apostle did not found the Ephesians in the faith, but strengthened them in it, suffering many evils on their behalf from the unbelieving, as he says: “For if, after the manner of men, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what does it profit me if the dead are not raised?” (1 Cor. XV). And because he foresees that his struggle will not be without the effect of their advancement, rejoicing in them, he exhorts them to better things in writing concerning his confinement in the city of Rome; for, having come from Jerusalem under guard with a guarantor, he is understood to have lived there, remaining outside the camp in his own rented lodging (Acts XXVIII).

[Hier.] He was writing to the Ephesians, who worshipped Diana—not this huntress who holds a bow and is girded, but that final [multimammiam, “many-breasted”], whom the Greeks call πολύμαστον, “many-breasted,” so that by the image itself they might falsely represent her as the nurse of all beasts and living creatures. He was writing to the metropolis of Asia, a city in which idolatry and the magical arts’ deceptions—which always follow idolatry—had flourished to such a degree that Demetrius said: “The temple of the great goddess Diana will be counted as nothing, and her greatness also will be destroyed, whom all Asia and the whole world worship” (Acts XXIX). [Col. 0383A] Finally, the Apostle remained there for three years, preaching the Gospel night and day, so that, once the citadel of idolatry had been destroyed, the temples of the smaller cities might easily be captured. Scripture itself reports how Paul spoke to the Ephesians, saying: “Therefore keep watch, remembering that for three years, night and day, I did not cease admonishing each one of you with tears; and now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, who is able to build up and give you an inheritance among all the sanctified” (Acts XX). For those whom the error of demons had held for so long needed the Apostle’s commendation to God, and they knew that there were spiritual powers to which they had attributed a certain likeness of divinity in entrails, auguries, and divinations. Hence he speaks to them again: “Therefore I testify to you on this day that I am pure from the blood of all. For I have not held back from announcing to you the whole will of God” (ibid.). And in the same place: “How I held back nothing of what was profitable to you, so as to announce and teach you publicly and privately” (ibid.). He had read in Ezekiel (Ezek. XXXIII) that, if the watchman did not announce the enemy’s arrival to the people, the blood of the citizens would be required from his hands; therefore he recalled that he had announced to them the whole will of God and everything that would be useful to them, so that he might be free from their blood.

But that you may know that those who had believed at Ephesus were bound by demonic deceptions and magical practice, the same Acts of the Apostles repeats and says: “Many also of those who had practiced curious arts brought their books together and burned them before everyone; and when their value had been calculated, they found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver. Thus the word of the Lord grew powerfully and was strengthened” (Acts XIX). [Col. 0383C] We have recalled all these things for this reason: to show why the Apostle gathered obscure meanings and mysteries unknown through the ages in this Epistle especially, and, contrary to the custom of the holy Scriptures, taught about their power [Note: [Col. 0383D] a In Jerome: “and concerning the power of the holy and opposing virtues.”]: who the demons are, what power they possess, what they formerly were, and how after Christ’s coming they were overthrown and destroyed. Of them he says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this darkness, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI). And elsewhere: “I will remain at Ephesus until Pentecost. For a great and effective door has been opened to me, but there are many adversaries” (1 Cor. XVI). He remained at Ephesus until Pentecost, the season of joy and victory, in which we do not bend our knees or bow down to the earth, but, rising with the Lord, are lifted up to the heights of heaven. He remained because a door was open to him—not a small door, but a great one—so that, having bound and overcome the strong man, he might invade, plunder, and overthrow his house, and lead away captivity captive (Matt. XII): the one who, gathering the ranks of his attendants, fought against the Apostle with his entire battle line. And [he was defeated. Who the Ephesians were is especially demonstrated by this]: [Col. 0384A] just as John, when he was about to relate the mystery of the Lord’s ancient birth, reclined upon his breast and drew a stream of teachings from the purest fountain (John XIII, XXI), so these people, rushing upon Paul’s neck as he departed (Acts XX), showed by their eyes and embraces that they possessed with him one treasury of knowledge, and by their tears testified to their longing for their teacher.

## CHAPTER ONE

Some are predestined by God; and God’s benefits bestowed upon the apostles and the Ephesians are recalled.

### Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God.

(Ambr.) He writes in his customary manner: he testifies that he is an apostle of Jesus Christ by God’s will.

(Hier.) If the preposition *through* indicates the ministry of the one through whom the action is carried out, this meaning seems to me to agree with that saying: “No one comes to the Father unless my Father has drawn him” (John VI). Thus also what is read in John’s Gospel—“All things were made through him,” unquestionably through the Son—does not prejudice our Lord Jesus Christ, as though he were lesser because he obeys the Father’s will. Similarly, here it does not prejudice the Father that Paul is an apostle of Jesus Christ through his will.

Others understand this passage as showing that Paul is the apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, who is Christ: just as he is called the Wisdom, Word, Power of God, Truth, Resurrection, and Life, so he is also called the Will.

Some think it makes no difference whether he said “through the will of God” or “from God’s will,” because he uses these prepositions interchangeably and “through the will of God” means the same as if he had said “from the will of God.”

“To all the saints who are at Ephesus and faithful in Christ Jesus.” Some, more inquisitively than necessary, think that, because it was said to Moses, “You shall say this to the children of Israel: ‘He who is’ has sent me” (Exod. III), those who are saints and faithful at Ephesus are also named by the term of essence: just as from the holy come holy people, from the just, just people, and from the wise, wise people, so from him who is, those who are are called; and in accordance with the same Apostle, God chose what was not, in order to destroy what was.

They also explain the very Scripture cited as testimony in such a way that we understand the destruction of what was from what follows: “So that,” he says, “no flesh may boast in the sight of God.” For, they say, if someone, advancing from what he was not into what he is by God’s making him exist, does not give thanks to the giver but considers his existence the result of his own merit, then what is immediately destroyed is his being, and what he had been begins not to be.

Others simply think that the passage was written not about those who “are,” but about those who are holy and faithful at Ephesus.

“And faithful in Jesus Christ.” Because “the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the believing husband, and the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the believing wife” (1 Cor. VII), and there are also holy vessels and speechless animals sacrificed to God in the temple, he therefore called those whom he had called holy also faithful. Faith descends from the judgment of one’s own mind, whereas sanctification is sometimes received from the generosity of the one who sanctifies, without our will. But when he says “faithful in Christ Jesus,” this has been added with the greatest care for the sake of distinction. There are many faithful people, but not faithful in Christ Jesus: if someone returns a deposit; if someone does not deny what has been entrusted to him; if he shows himself a faithful friend, ready to betray his life rather than his faith—as we read of certain philosophers—that person is indeed faithful, but he is not faithful in Christ Jesus. Catechumens too may be called faithful, but they are not faithful in Christ, because they have not been baptized in Christ: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III).

### Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus.

(Ambr.) He says that God’s grace is with the saints and faithful, and calls him our Father, because all things were both created and restored by him; but he calls Christ our Lord, because he redeemed us by offering himself for us.

(Hier.) Either both expressions are to be referred jointly to both persons—that is, both grace and peace are from God, both from God the Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ—or the individual expressions are to be referred individually: grace to God the Father, and peace to Christ. For it immediately follows: “To the praise of the glory of his grace, in which he graced us in the Beloved,” so that the Father’s grace consists in his deigning to send the Son for our salvation, while the Son’s peace consists in our being reconciled to the Father through him, and in his making the two one by destroying the intervening wall and abolishing enmity in his flesh.

Alternatively, God’s grace benefits us only if we are not ungrateful for our salvation [Perhaps something is missing from the author], attributing our good qualities to our own merits. We shall preserve the peace of reconciliation if we do nothing contrary to the will of him who made peace for us in his blood.

### Blessed is God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, in Christ Jesus.

(Ambr.) He has blessed us with every spiritual blessing—that is, not with an earthly but with a heavenly blessing, and not with a corruptible but an eternal one—because Christians’ glory is not on earth but in heaven, and it is in Christ. For every gift of God’s grace is in Christ; thus, if anyone thinks that he can be blessed by God while despising Christ, let him know that he is in error.

(Hier.) Just as, according to his substance and nature, God, who is good, made us good by sharing himself and says to Israel, “Be holy, for I also am holy” (Lev. XX), so he himself makes us blessed because he is blessed. The lawgiver gives blessings, and “the blessing of the Lord is upon the head of the righteous”; from this blessing Baruch has his name, which in our language means “blessed.”

He blessed us not with one blessing but with all—not because we all obtain everything, but because, while each person has one or several blessings from among them, through the individual blessings we all possess them, and not in earthly but in spiritual blessings. There are also earthly blessings: to have children, to abound in wealth, to enjoy honor and health. This earthly blessing descends even to irrational animals. For it was said of them: “The Lord blessed them,” and he said, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. I).

But spiritual blessings are in the heavenly places, because the earth cannot contain spiritual blessing. Indeed, we do not see those blessings fulfilled in the prophets who kept God’s commandment in Deuteronomy—for example, lending at interest to foreign nations, having granaries full of grain, being blessed in the cities and blessed in the fields, and other things of this kind. They wandered in sheepskins and goatskins, in poverty and distress, in deserts and mountains, in caves and caverns of rocks, avoiding the attacks of persecutors (Heb. XI).

Everything must therefore be understood spiritually, and spiritual blessings must be awaited not in earthly but in heavenly places. But when he says, “He has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places,” as though it had already happened in the past and had not been promised for the future—that is, “he has blessed,” and not “he will bless”—the question arises how, while we are still placed on earth, he has blessed us with a heavenly blessing.

Either, then, because “our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III), and we are not of this world, but, having laid aside the image of the earthly, bear the image of the heavenly, and do not live in the flesh but in the spirit (1 Cor. XV), and store up treasures for ourselves in heaven, where we also have our heart, we are said now to be blessed with a heavenly blessing; or certainly because every spiritual blessing, although it is on earth, is nevertheless reckoned as coming from the heavenly places.

“He has blessed us,” he says, “with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ”: in the word of God, in knowledge, in truth, and in the other virtues.

The sentence may be read in two ways: “Blessed is God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” so that “blessed is God,” who is the creator of all things, concludes this section; then what follows is introduced: “who is also the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Or it may be read so that “God and Father” is referred jointly to our Lord: “Blessed is the God of him who assumed humanity, and the Father of him who in the beginning was God the Word with God.” This does not mean that the man assumed is one person and the Word who assumed him another, but that one and the same person is proclaimed now exalted and now humble according to the diversity of circumstances.

### Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him.

In Greek, instead of “before the foundation of the world,” it is written πρὸ καταβολῆς τοῦ κόσμου, “before the καταβολή of the world.” But καταβολή is not precisely the same as *constitutio*, which means “foundation” or “establishment.” Therefore, because of the poverty of our language, the novelty of the subject, and—as someone has said—the broader expression and richer language of the Greeks, we shall try not so much to translate word for word, which is impossible, as to explain the force of the word by a kind of circumlocution.

Καταβολή properly means when something is thrown downward and sent from a lofty place into a lower one, or when something takes its beginning. Thus those who lay the first foundations of future buildings are said to have καταβεβληκέναι—that is, to have “thrown down the beginnings of the foundations.”

Paul therefore wished to show that God had fashioned all things from nothing. He did not refer to a condition, creature, or created thing, but to καταβολή, that is, to the beginning of a foundation, so that, contrary to Manichaeus [Col. 0387A] and the other heresies that posit both a maker and matter, nothing from which creatures were made preceded the creatures; rather, all things came into existence from nothing.

When he testified that he chose us to be holy and blameless before him—that is, before God—before the world’s formation, this pertains to God’s foreknowledge. For all future things are already accomplished for him, and before they happen all things are known, just as Paul himself was predestined in his mother’s womb and Jeremiah was sanctified in the womb.

(Ambr.) God, who foreknows all things, knows who would believe in Christ, as he says to the Romans: “Those whom he foreknew, he also called” (Rom. VIII), not only from the Jews but also from the nations. Those, then, whom God is said to call persevere in faith. These are the ones whom he chose in Christ before the world, so that they might be undefiled before God in [Col. 0387B] love—that is, so that the love of God might make their conduct holy.

(Hier.) When he says, “that we should be holy and blameless before him,” there is this difference between “holy” and “blameless”: one who is holy may also be understood to be blameless, but one who is blameless is not immediately holy. Little children are blameless, because, with bodies still innocent, they have committed no sin; yet they are not holy, because holiness is acquired through the will and through effort. One who has not sinned may be called blameless, whereas one who is full of virtues is holy, in accordance with what is written in a certain psalm: “He who walks without blemish and practices righteousness” (Ps. XIV), and in the Song of Songs: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song IV).

### In love, predestining us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, unto himself.

(Ambr.) He says that God decreed that those who believe in Christ should be adopted as sons of God, so that Christ, the true Son of God, might be their head.

(Hier.) When he says, “In love, predestining us,” the words may be read in two ways, so that “in love” is joined either with what precedes or with what follows.

Joined with what precedes: “that we should be holy and blameless before him in love,” followed by “predestining us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ unto himself.”

Joined with what follows: “in love predestining us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ in him”—that is, in Christ, who was never anything other than a son, whereas we were not sons before we were predestined in him.

He predestined this: that everyone who wished to believe in him might have power to become a son of God, because no one can become a son of God unless he possesses faith and love, which works through affection.

### According to the purpose of his will.

Or, “according to the good pleasure of his will.” The word εὐδοκία, which Latin speech has translated as *placitum*, “pleasure,” is composed in Greek from two complete words, ἀπὸ τοῦ εὖ and τοῦ δοκεῖν—“well” and “to seem.” We can call it *beneplacitum*, “good pleasure,” because not everything that pleases is immediately approved as pleasing in a good way. Rather, εὐδοκία—that is, “good pleasure”—is said only where what has pleased is shown to have pleased rightly.

(Ambr.) He says that God had such a good pleasure that the grace given to human beings might advance the praise of his glory, so that our salvation might be the glory of God.

### To the praise of the glory of his grace, in which he graced us in the Beloved.

God gave us grace because we believed in his Son Christ. For, loving his Only-Begotten, he generously bestows divine gifts upon those who love him.

(Hier.) Every grace that we obtain for the glory and praise of him who graced us in the Beloved is accomplished in the Lord our Savior. For no good can be understood apart from wisdom and truth, justice, peace, redemption, and the other virtues. Nor should the Latin manuscripts be read as “in his beloved Son,” but simply “in the Beloved,” so that the meaning is “in the Beloved,” with something understood by all [Note: [Col. 0387D] a This is treated more fully in Jerome.].

This is the Beloved of whom it is sung in Isaiah: “I will sing for my beloved” (Isa. V). When he says “he graced,” that is, “he made us acceptable in Christ,” he not only redeemed us but, by forgiving our sins, made us righteous without any merit of ours.

### In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins.

(Ambr.) He demands a twofold grace, because he both redeemed us by his blood and did not count our sins against us: that is, he both redeemed us and set us free.

(Hier.) The one who is redeemed is a captive who, having come under the power of enemies, has ceased to be free. So we too served under the yoke of sin and were bound, as Truth itself says in the Gospel: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII). Before the Redeemer came, we could not unbind our hands from their chains or raise our eyes upward. He came, broke our bonds, and set us free. But who could do this except Jesus our Lord, who redeemed the whole world in his own blood?

Christ’s blood and flesh are understood in two ways: either as that spiritual and divine flesh of which he himself says, “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John VI), and, “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have eternal life” (ibid.); or as the flesh that was crucified and the blood poured out by the soldier’s lance.

In accordance with this distinction, a difference of blood and flesh is spoken of in his saints: one flesh is that which will see the salvation of God; another flesh and blood are those that cannot possess the kingdom of God. Accordingly, after Christ’s blood has redeemed us, we are written as having received forgiveness of sins: for unless we have been redeemed, our sins are forgiven us in vain, nor can we receive pardon for our offenses; and we cease to be slaves only if the once-bloody Victor has received a price for us.

### According to the riches of his grace, which has superabounded in us.

He said “has abounded” so that he might not only free us from death but also give us such wisdom that we might know his wills and hidden mysteries. Whoever understands God’s truth in the forgiveness of our sins, especially in the Church gathered from the nations—which was alien to the covenant and promises of Israel—understands what kind of abundance of God’s grace exists in those who believed in him.

He does not make these riches of grace empty in himself who, as far as human frailty permits, strives, labors, and contends, and says with the Apostle: “His grace toward me was not empty” (1 Cor. XV). But whoever, not remembering the greatness of the benefit, sinks into worse things, in that person the wealth of God’s grace and abundant generosity is weakened by poverty.

### In all wisdom and prudence.

We may understand wisdom as knowledge of invisible things, and prudence as knowledge only of visible things.

(Ambr.) He adds this to grace, because after the benefits mentioned above there comes the gift of wisdom and prudence concerning spiritual things.

### To make known to us the mystery of his will.

This pleased God, whose counsel cannot be reconsidered, to reveal in Christ the mystery of his will at the time when he wished it to be revealed through the creature’s knowledge. His will was this: that, when he manifested Christ, he might then show favor to all who were in error, whether in the heavens or on earth; that this might be regarded as the gift of believers, so that their sins would not be counted against those who received the faith of Christ.

(Hier.) The Stoics also think that wisdom and prudence are different, saying: “Wisdom is knowledge of divine and human things; prudence, however, concerns mortals alone.” According to this distinction, we may understand wisdom as knowledge of invisible and visible things, but prudence as knowledge only of visible things.

The question therefore arises: how did God make known to us the mystery of his will in all wisdom and prudence? First, it should be understood simply that the mystery of his will is our redemption through the blood of his Son and the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which abounded in us. In other words, by believing in the Lord’s Passion—which is foolishness to unbelievers—we possess wisdom and prudence.

Next, he made all the mysteries known to us through the holy Scriptures: how he first fashioned heaven and earth, and made, ordered, and distinguished everything within them; how the world was filled with the fashioned human being up to Christ’s Passion; and how invisible things are known through visible things.

Finally, even the things that are on earth require wisdom and prudence.

### According to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him for the administration of the fullness of times.

Above he had said, “according to the good pleasure of his will”; now he says, “according to his good pleasure,” with the word “will” omitted. There he placed προόρισμον, that is, “predestination,” for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ; here he places πρόθεσιν, that is, “purpose” or “setting forth.”

Those who are accustomed to scrutinizing words assert that there is this difference between predestination and purpose: the predestination of something prefigures much earlier in the mind of the one who predestines what is going to happen; but purpose occurs when the execution is already near and the result almost follows the thought.

When he says “which he purposed in him,” this must refer to the mystery. For above he had said, “to make known to us the mystery of his will.” This mystery is the administration of the fullness of times, so that at the appointed time all things might be completed that had previously been prefigured in the Law or foretold by the prophets.

### To restore all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth, in him.

Nothing is said to be restored unless it has fallen. Thus we may say that the joy of the angels in the salvation of human beings is restored in heaven—the joy they had before human beings wholly turned away from righteousness.

On earth, no one is ignorant that the human race has been restored in Christ. It may also be believed that the number of the angels was restored through the souls of the saints who were brought into heaven by our redemption.

(Aug.) Things in heaven are restored when what fell among the angels is supplied from human beings. Things on earth are restored when the human beings who were predestined for eternal life are renewed from the old age of corruption.

(Hieron.) Some say that by “heaven” souls are to be understood, and by “earth,” bodies. Thus the restoration of souls is now in their *conversatione* (“conduct of life”) [or *conversione*, “conversion”] to God; the restoration of the body will be in the resurrection, when the dead rise.

Some manuscripts have “to recapitulate” instead of “to restore.” For the entire administration—which began both before the world and afterward in the world—of invisible as well as visible creatures promised the coming of the Son of God. Adam, expelled from paradise, was to be recalled through the Savior (Gen. III); the division of the unity of languages in the building of the tower (Gen. XI) prefigured the gift of languages in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts II); Isaac, as a type of the Lord, himself carried his cross (Gen. III); Samson, nourishing his holy hair, loved the embrace of the poor Delilah and confessed to her all the secrets of his heart (Judg. XVI): this signified the mystery of the Savior and the Church from the nations, truly poor and needy.

Thus, in the Lord’s cross and in his Passion, all things were recapitulated—that is, everything was reckoned together in this ἀνακεφαλαίωσις, “recapitulation.”

To make this clearer, let us give an example from daily practice. Suppose I paid out twenty denarii, then another five and another fifteen; I also gave thirty and three times ten at different times. If I want to reckon these together, the sum of one hundred grows for me, and in one number I have everything I listed before. So all the mysteries and the entire dispensation of antiquity—not only what took place on earth but also what took place in heaven—are completed in Christ’s Passion.

Once Christ has suffered, been buried, risen, and ascended victoriously to the Father, I no longer need the old number, because I hold everything in one. Observe carefully that not only all the histories of the Scriptures that the Holy Spirit recounts as having taken place on earth, but also those in the heavenly places that are hidden from us, are held to have been recapitulated in Christ’s Passion.

(Ambr.) Every creature in heaven and on earth, when it learns the knowledge of Christ, is restored to the state for which it was created. When it is instructed in faith in the one God, once it has recognized the Savior’s mystery, it is restored from the error it had received, knowing with certainty that its creator is one God and Lord.

For this reason it is said in John’s Apocalypse: “I saw Michael and his angels fighting in heaven with the dragon and his army” (Rev. XII). This opposition arises partly from error and partly from the presumption of usurped tyranny.

### In whom we too have been called by lot, predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will.

(Aug.) By “lot,” as I believe, he meant grace, by which we have been saved. Why does he call grace by the name “lot”? Because in a lot there is no selection, but the will of God. For where it is said, “This one does, and that one does not,” merits are considered; and where merits are considered, there is selection, not lot.

But when God found no merits of ours, he saved us by the lot of his will, because he willed it, not because we were worthy: “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God” (Eph. II). This lot is, in a certain sense, God’s hidden will regarding the human race. With him there is no iniquity; he does not show partiality, but his hidden justice is a lot to you.

(Hier.)
