The words “inheritance” and “lot,” through which we have come to share in Christ, show that we have migrated from one power to another: that is, we have been transferred from the power of evil angels into the power of God. Those who had previously been captives unto destruction Christ captured unto life, so that he might lead them back on high. In a certain sense captivity itself was captured, since through a second captivity those who had previously been captives are set free.

It should be considered that here προορισμός and πρόθεσις—that is, predestination and purpose—are placed together, according to which God works all things, according to the counsel of his will. This does not mean that everything that happens in the world is carried out by God’s will and counsel; otherwise evils too could be attributed to God. Rather, whatever he does, he does with counsel and will—that is, with full reason and power.

He wills all things that are full of reason and counsel: he wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. II). But because no one is saved without his own will—for we possess free choice—he wills us to will what is good, so that, when we have willed it, he himself may also will to fulfill his counsel in us.

### That we should be to the praise of his glory, who first hoped in Christ.

(Ambr.) This is what he says: the administration of preaching was ordained by God for those from the Jews who believed in Christ. Therefore no one from the nations was chosen for the apostolate; for it was fitting that preachers be chosen from those who had first hoped for the salvation that had been promised to them in Christ.

(Hier.) “Who first hoped in Christ” refers to those to whom Christ was foretold through the Law or the prophets. Yet it may seem beforehand to pertain to all who believe in Christ, so that those who hope in Christ in this present life may in the future life be to his praise and glory.

But one is the reward of the person who hopes in Christ voluntarily, and another of the person who believes in him from necessity.

### In whom you also, when you had heard the word of truth, the Gospel of your salvation—in whom, having believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise.

“In whom,” unquestionably, means “in Christ.” Among the others who heard, you too, Ephesians, heard the word of truth.

“The Gospel of your salvation”: by believing in it, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise.

According to the order of reading, however, the sentence does not seem to stand properly. Nothing corresponding to the preceding phrase “in whom you also, having heard the word of truth, the Gospel of your salvation” follows, since “in whom” is immediately repeated a second time. Because this is superfluous, removing it from the middle can restore the text to the order of the reading.

Paul endured this because of his excessive love for Christ: he always named again, even superfluously and extraordinarily, the one whom he loved. A diligent reader can find this throughout all his Epistles. Thus the second occurrence of “in whom” is found to have disturbed the order of the sentence and to have left the earlier proposition hanging.

Nor is the praise of the Ephesians small: they heard not merely preaching but the word of truth. What is the word of truth except the Son of God, who is the Truth, since he says, “I am the way and the truth” (John X)? What is it to hear this truth except to believe in Christ and obey him, as it is said in the Gospel: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God” (John V)?

What is it for the dead to hear except for sinners to believe in the Son of God and obey his voice—that is, his commandments? In this you nations are now shown to be one with us, because you have received the same Spirit, whose gifts are the pledge of the future inheritance.

For if the pledge is so great, how great will the inheritance of the eternal promise be?

A person is sealed if he has heard the word of truth and believed in the Holy Spirit of promise. For many have heard and, remaining unbelieving, have by no means received the seal of the Holy Spirit.

It is also said to the prince of Tyre: “You are the seal of the likeness of God” (Ezek. XXVIII). The seal of God is this: just as the first human being was created in the image and likeness of God, so in the second regeneration whoever receives the Holy Spirit is sealed by him and receives the form of the Creator.

It must be asked where else “the Holy Spirit of promise” is written, or what it signifies. I think that, just as the Holy Spirit makes holy the one into whom he has been infused; the spirit of wisdom makes wise; the spirit of understanding makes understanding; the spirit of counsel makes cautious and prudent; the spirit of fortitude makes strong; the spirit of knowledge makes knowledgeable; the spirit of piety makes pious; and the spirit of fear makes fearful and trembling with fear of God, so the spirit of promise—or the Spirit of God—makes the person in whom he dwells a guarantor and a god.

Conversely, an unclean spirit makes someone unclean and, as an unclean inhabitant, prepares a filthy house for himself. The spirit of fornication makes fornicators, concerning whom the prophet says: “You have been led astray by the spirit of fornication” (Hos. IV). An evil spirit makes people evil and perverse, and a demonic spirit makes them demonic. Whatever the liquid poured into a new vessel may have been, the vessel long retains its smell and taste.

Who is the pledge of our inheritance for the redemption of adoption, to the praise of his glory.

The Latin translator rendered *arrhabo* as “pledge” (*pignus*); yet *arrhabo* does not mean the same thing as *pignus*. For an *arrhabo* is given as a kind of testimony and bond toward a future purchase, whereas a *pignus*, that is, an ἐνέχυρον, is given in exchange for money lent, so that when the money has been repaid, the creditor returns the pledge to the one who repaid the debt.

Whoever, therefore, has received not merely the Holy Spirit [but the Holy Spirit] of promise will consequently also receive the pledge of the inheritance; and that inheritance is eternal life. Just as the nature of a future purchase and possession is estimated from the pledge—for example, a villa worth one hundred solidi from a pledge of ten solidi, or a possession worth one thousand solidi from one hundred solidi—so from the variety of the pledge the greatness of the inheritance that will afterward follow is also recognized.

Although someone may be holy and perfect, and in everyone’s judgment considered worthy of blessedness, he has nevertheless now received the Spirit as a pledge of the future inheritance. If the pledge is so great, how great will the possession be? And just as the pledge given to us is not outside us but within us, so the inheritance itself, that is, the kingdom of God, which is within us, is present inwardly in us.

For what inheritance could be greater than to contemplate and behold, through perception, the beauty of Wisdom, the Word, Truth, and Light; to behold its ineffable substance and the magnificent nature of God; and to gaze upon the substance of all things created in the likeness of God?

This Holy Spirit of promise, then, who is the pledge of our inheritance, is given now to the saints so that they may be redeemed and joined to God for the praise of his glory—not because God needs anyone’s praise, but because the praise of God benefits those who praise him. As they come to know his majesty and greatness through each of his works, they burst forth in praise of it, overcome by wonder. (Ambrose.) The praise of God’s glory consists in the acquiring of many converts to the faith, just as the glory of a physician consists in curing many. It therefore belongs to the glory of God that he called the nations, so that through the faith promised to the Jews they might obtain the healing of their salvation, bearing the sign of redemption and of the future inheritance: the Holy Spirit given after baptism. For those who have been redeemed have been designated heirs, if they persevere in their regeneration, so that initial faith may merit forgiveness, while holy conduct persevering together with faith may merit a crown.

Therefore I too, having heard of your faith, which is in the Lord Jesus, and of your love toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers. Since, in accordance with God’s decree by which he determined that the nations should become participants in the promise made to the Jews, the Ephesians, after hearing the word of God, received the faith of Christ, loving all the saints, as the Lord commanded. For this reason he gives thanks to God for their conversion and love, because God deigned to incorporate the nations with the Jews. (Maurus.) Love for the saints of God is therefore a great proof of faith; for this faith the Apostle also praises the Ephesians. Accordingly, he says elsewhere (Gal. V): “Faith that works through love,” showing that faith accomplishes nothing without love in the age of reason.

(Jerome.) “That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, the eyes of your heart having been enlightened.” Although a word-for-word translation might excuse the Apostle to a careful reader, since the whole sentence appears to overflow with confused construction and to produce a solecism, nevertheless, because the defect is audible in Greek, we shall attempt, in answering our detractors, to arrange the order of the reading according to its meaning, so that we may say:

“Having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus Christ and in all his saints, and seeing the distinction between your faith in the Lord and in all his saints, I do not cease giving thanks and remembering you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation.”

What follows—“the eyes of your heart having been enlightened”—can likewise be rendered by hyperbaton in this way:

“Therefore I, having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus Christ for the knowledge of him, the eyes of your heart having been enlightened, and in all the saints, do not cease, giving thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation for knowledge, so that you may know what is the hope of your calling, and so forth.”

(Ambrose.) It is clear that he says he prays for them so that they may know the hope of their faith in the heavenly reward. Once they have fully understood what fruit belongs to believers, they will become more eager to cultivate religion. Yet there appears to be progress of this kind: if they are already so devoted before they know the glory of the promise, they will necessarily become more devoted when they have come to know it.

He calls God the Father of glory and the God of Christ, although God is truly the Father of Christ and the God of creation. The Lord himself also says the same thing: “I am going to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John XX). He is therefore the Father of all glory, because all glory, power, and dignity come from him.

He is also the Father of Christ, but in another way, because Christ is the true Son and the God of all, though God is not God of Christ in the same manner. He is God of Christ because Christ is God from God; but he is God of the others as the cause of terror. Thus he says through the prophet Malachi (Mal. I): “If I am God, where is my fear?”

(Jerome.) Moreover, “the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory,” should be understood in such a way that, just as our Lord Jesus Christ himself is the speech of wisdom, truth, peace, justice, and strength, so he is also glory, according to what is said elsewhere: “The glory of God will appear.” Throughout almost the entire Old Testament it is written that the glory of God was seen above the tabernacle of testimony, and the Psalmist sings: “Rise up, my glory” (Ps. CVII).

This glory, illuminating the world with its radiance, fashioned for itself a temple from the Virgin’s womb. God becomes the Father of the glory of this temple; and where Christ is, he alone is called “Father,” whereas where Jesus is, his God is named without any qualification.

This God of the assumed man, however, and Father of glory, wisdom, and truth, gives believers in his Son a spirit of wisdom and revelation, so that they may become wise and, with unveiled face, contemplate the glory of the Lord. When this wisdom and revelation have made them wise and have uncovered those hidden mysteries, it immediately follows that they possess “the eyes of the heart” enlightened.

The present words also establish that, according to the members of the outward man, the inward man likewise has members. For plainly he called them “the eyes of the heart,” which we cannot understand apart from perception and mind. To this corresponds the Psalmist’s saying: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Ps. XII). And elsewhere: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Eccl. II). If we take “eyes” simply as bodily eyes, then certainly the eyes of the foolish as well as of the wise are in his head. The head of the wise is therefore understood as perception, which is also called by another word the mind, the spirit, and the governing faculty of the heart.

As for the phrase “in the knowledge of him,” that is, ἐπίγνωσιν αὐτοῦ, some understand it as meaning that there is a distinction between γνῶσις and ἐπίγνωσις, that is, between knowledge and recognition: knowledge or awareness concerns things that we did not previously know and afterward began to know; recognition, however, concerns things that we previously knew but later ceased to know, and of which we afterward regain memory. They suppose that we once possessed an earlier life in the heavenly realm, but after being cast into these bodies and forgetting God the Father, now come to know him through revelation, according to the saying: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Ps. XXI), and by repeating other similar passages.

So that you may know what is the hope of his calling, what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of the might of his power, which he worked in Christ, raising him from the dead.

Whoever, in accordance with Paul’s prayer, has once received the spirit of wisdom and revelation, so that with the eyes of his heart opened he may behold, will know what has been laid up for those who are called and what the saints of God should hope for—what he will give abundantly and generously to those who possess his inheritance. For those who, believing in the likeness of Paul, are called, the greatness of God’s power is necessary for attaining this knowledge. By that power God acted in Christ Jesus our Lord, whom he raised from the dead.

The inheritance is to be understood in two ways. Either the firstborn of all creation is the inheritance of the soul of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the man assumed from body and soul, and we inherit the Word together with the inheritance of that soul; or our inheritance in Christ is the one divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Just as houses and villas are called inheritances—that is, the very things possessed by heirs—so God himself is the inheritance of believers and saints.

It is also written in the Old Testament: “You shall not give an inheritance to the sons of Levi among their brothers, because I am their portion” (Num. XVIII). And elsewhere: “The Lord is their inheritance.” The saint who knows that he possesses nothing apart from God speaks boldly: “The Lord is my portion,” and: “You are the portion of my inheritance and my cup” (Ps. XV).

It is therefore no small matter to know the hope of the calling and the riches of the glory of God’s inheritance among the saints. For to know these things we need the power by which God also acted in raising his Son—the one whom he raised not merely once, but continually, from the dead—and made him “free among the dead,” untouched by any contamination of death.

Christ rises daily from the dead; he is raised daily in penitents. This does not mean that, even according to the flesh, he did not have authority to lay down his soul and take it up again (John X)—for no one took it from him unless he himself laid it down—but that, according to the dispensation of the flesh and of the Son, the man and the Son are said to have been raised by God the Father.

And he established him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, authority, power, and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come.

(Ambrose.) He declares that the salvation of believers and their glory consist in the resurrection of the Savior, so that from it the faithful may learn what has been promised to them. In like manner they will be exalted above the heavens in the future, together with Christ, as he himself says: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me, and may see my glory” (John XVII).

This is because of the incarnation of the Son of God: even after becoming man, he is said to be above all the heavens and, seated at God’s right hand, above every creature. He has the name of God by nature, not by adoption, so that those who crucified him may know that he is the Son of God. The honor that the Father gave him through generation was manifested when, having been born a man and having suffered, he conquered death and rose, ascending to the place from which he had descended, above all the heavens.

Hence it is said: “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. LXXXIV). Because the Father gave all judgment to the Son, he is said to sit at God’s right hand as judge.

(Jerome.) He demonstrated God’s power by means of human analogy—not that a throne is set up and God the Father sits upon it with the Son seated beside him, but because we cannot understand him as judging and reigning in any other way except through our own language.

This also applies to what is written in the hundred and ninth Psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand,” and so forth. If the Son sits at the Father’s right hand according to the manner of a reigning figure, it would necessarily follow, according to the same analogy, that he is greater than the one who sat on the left. But the same Psalm teaches us that it must be understood otherwise than the literal wording sounds, when it says later: “You are a priest forever; the Lord is at your right hand.”

For how, if the Son sits at the Father’s right hand, can the Father again be said to be at his right hand? Or how can the earth be his footstool and heaven his throne, when Isaiah says that he holds the earth in his fist and measures heaven with the span of his hand? What is contained cannot be inside that which contains it, nor can one hold within his hand the one by whom he himself is surrounded according to the manner of one seated.

Just as being near to God or withdrawing far from him must be understood not according to spatial distances but according to merits—so that the saints are near him, while sinners, of whom the prophet says, “Behold, those who distance themselves from you will perish” (Ps. LXXII), are removed from all his nearness—so “being at God’s right or left” must be understood as meaning that the saints are at his right, while sinners are at his left. The Savior confirms the same thing in the Gospel (Matt. XXV), when he speaks of the sheep as being at the right and the goats at the left.

The very word “sit” also signifies the power of kingship, by which God grants a benefit to those over whom he deigns to sit: namely, that he both governs them and has them in his chariot, turning their previously wandering and free necks toward his own command.

After this, the question arises how what follows can be understood: “above every principality, authority, power, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come.” What has been said about God’s right and left hands, and about sitting, is already clear. Now it must be asked where the Apostle found these four names—I mean principality, authority, power, and dominion—and from where he brought them forth.

For it is not permissible to suppose that a man instructed in divine reading spoke something that is not found in the sacred books. I therefore think that he either brought forth from the traditions of the Hebrews matters that are secret, or else, understanding the law to be spiritual, perceived more sublimely what had been written in a manner resembling historical narrative. He recognized that what is recounted in Numbers and in the books of Kings concerning kings, princes, commanders, tribunes, and centurions is an image of other princes and kings—namely, that in the heavenly realm there are principalities, authorities, dominions, powers, and other designations of ministries that neither we can name nor, I think, Paul himself, confined in a frail body, was able to enumerate.

If there are principalities, powers, dominions, and authorities, they must also have subjects—those who fear them, serve them, and are strengthened by their might. These distributions of offices will exist not only at present but also in the future age, so that through successive advances and honors, ascents and descents, someone may either increase or decrease, and may come under one power, then another authority, principality, or dominion.

We little human beings, soon to be dissolved into ash and dust, if we are raised to kingship by the consent of men, have such great varieties and hierarchies of ministries that we can more easily perceive them than describe them. For example, a prefect in civil administration has judges throughout the provinces and according to his own order; the military, in turn, is divided among so many counts, commanders, tribunes, and a multiplicity of armies. Do we suppose that the Lord of lords and King of kings is satisfied with only one simple ministry?

And he subjected all things beneath his feet and gave him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body, the fullness of him who is fulfilled in all things.

(Jerome.) This appears to contradict what is written elsewhere: “For we do not yet see all things subjected to him” (Heb. II); and also: “For he must reign until he has put his enemies under his feet” (1 Cor. XV). If all things have not yet been subjected to him, and he must reign until all things have been subjected to him, how has God now subjected everything beneath his feet? Especially since Paul says elsewhere: “When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (1 Cor. XV).

Either, then, he mentions according to the present what is future as though it had already happened, in accordance with the meaning we explained above, where he says: “He blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus”; or, if it must be understood as referring to the past, we should take it in this way: even those things that are not subject to him by their will serve him by the condition of their nature. For example, demons, Jews, and gentiles are not subject to Christ willingly; for they do not serve Christ, nor are they subject to his feet. Yet because they were created by him for a good purpose, they are subject against their will to his power, although by the freedom of their will they struggle against him.

This interpretation also fits what follows: “And he gave him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body.” Just as a head has many members subject to it, some of them diseased and weak, so our Lord God Jesus Christ, the Son, being the head of the Church, has as members all who are gathered in the Church: the saints, certainly, as well as sinners. The saints are subject to him willingly, but sinners are subject to him by necessity. Thus even his enemies are subject beneath his feet.

Accordingly, when he says “all things,” he appears to raise a question. The statement, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet,” and elsewhere, “He must reign until he puts his enemies beneath his feet,” requires no elaborate interpreter: things that are hostile, once conquered, are subjected beneath his feet and pass under the power of the victor.

But why should all things—that is, angels, thrones, dominions, authorities, powers, and the other beings that have never been opposed to God—be subjected beneath his feet? This seems obscure.

It can therefore be answered that no one is without sin, and that those stars are not clean in God’s sight, and that all creation trembles before the Creator’s coming. Hence the cross of the Savior is said to have purified not only the things on earth but also those in heaven.

Another person refers “all things” not to the totality but only to those things about which the discussion has taken place. In this way, “the whole city cried out” does not mean that no one in the city remained silent, but that even lesser parts are designated from the majority. Likewise the Apostle says: “All seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. II). And again: “All abandoned me,” not because Timothy and the other disciples who were with him at the time the Epistles were written had abandoned him, but because he had been deserted by many; he complains that he had been abandoned by all, that is, by the greater part.

The same expression occurs in the Psalm: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. XIII). For if all have turned aside, then the one speaking has turned aside as well. Elsewhere: “I said in my alarm: Every man is a liar” (Ps. CXV). Either everything he said is true or it is false. If every man is a liar, then the one speaking is also a liar. But if he is also a liar, then the statement that every man is a liar is not true either. If the statement is true, “all” must be understood as we have said: a large portion of humanity lies.

The Apostle also writes elsewhere (Col. I and III): “teaching every person,” and again, “admonishing every person.” This does not mean that he taught every human being—for how many there are even today who have heard neither the Apostle’s teaching nor his name—but that he teaches and admonishes all who are in the Church and desire to know the things of God.

There follows: “the fullness of him who is fulfilled in all things.” The statement, “then the Son himself will be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all,” is understood in the same way. For now God the Father is present by parts in individuals: in one person as justice, in another as chastity, in another as temperance, in another as wisdom, and in another as strength. Even in holy and perfect men it is difficult to find all the virtues together.

But when, at the end of all things and at the consummation of the world, everything has been subjected to him, “all” will be fulfilled “in all,” so that, just as God is full of every virtue, everything may be fulfilled in everyone, and all may possess what previously each possessed individually.

The statement, “He gave him as head over all things to the Church, which is his body, the fullness of him who is fulfilled in all things,” can also be understood not only of human beings but of angels, all powers, and rational creatures. Nor should the phrase “who is fulfilled in all things” be understood simply as it sounds. He does not say, “who fills all things in all,” but “who is fulfilled in all things.” To fill and to be filled are different: in the one case the verb concerns the agent, in the other the recipient.

Just as an emperor is fulfilled when his army increases daily, new provinces are added, and the multitude of peoples grows, so our Lord Jesus Christ, insofar as all believe in him and come daily to his faith, is himself fulfilled in all. This is so, however, in such a way that everything may be fulfilled in everyone—that is, that those who believe in him may be filled with every virtue and, according to the Gospel (Luke II), cause him to increase in age, wisdom, and grace.

(Ambrose.) In another way, he says that the Father subjected every creature to the Son, so that, because he made all things through him, the Son might be the head and Lord of all. He subjected everything to him when he begot him before all things, so that through him he might make what did not exist.

By saying “the whole Church,” he comprehensively includes everything that is in heaven and on earth, so that its members may become members of the new man while confessing that this is the one through whom they were made by God. They are subjected to him as members to the head, from whom they derive their origin, so that everything may be fulfilled in all.

When they have returned to the confession of the one God, bending the knee to Christ, “all” is fulfilled in all, so that he may be all things, because all things are from him, and therefore he himself is in them, because they subsist by his power. For when they withdraw from God, they seem to empty him; hence he says elsewhere (Col. II): “That all things may grow into the increase of God.”

## Chapter II

The Ephesians are led to give thanks because they have been freed from sin and separated from the other nations.

And you, when you were dead in your trespasses, in which you once walked according to the age of this world.

(Ambrose.) He calls them dead because they follow the errors of the world. Whatever departs from the confession of the one God is considered dead, because it does not remain in the root from which it derives its origin.

(Jerome.) “And you,” he says, “nations, when you were spiritually dead because of the excessive burden of your sins, he made alive together with Christ,” as he says in what follows. The distinction between trespasses and sins can be explained in this way: trespasses occur when we fail to do what ought to be done; sins occur when we do what we ought not to do.

According to the prince of the power of this air, the spirit that now works in the sons of distrust.

(Ambrose.) By “the prince of the power” he means the devil. He signifies that the devil corrupted the understanding of the world, so that people would depart from the one God and adopt the opinion of many gods, making them companions in his conspiracy, since they are found denying the one God in the same impiety.

He therefore calls this prince of error a spirit of the air in order to show that he has seized this realm for the exercise of domination. Air is one thing and prince another; but because he rules in the world or in the air, he is called the spirit of the air.

Among them we too all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of our thoughts, and we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest.

(Cassian.) Although blessed Paul has generally declared all vices to be carnal—since he has numbered enmities, anger, and heresies among the works of the flesh—we nevertheless distinguish them by a twofold division in order to collect their remedies and natures more carefully.

We say that some are carnal and others spiritual. Those are carnal that specially belong to the incitement and perception of the flesh, which takes such pleasure and nourishment in them that it even arouses tranquil minds and sometimes drags them against their will into assent to its desire. Of these the blessed Apostle says: “Among whom we all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of our thoughts, and we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest.”

We call those spiritual that arise solely from the impulse of the soul. They not only bring no pleasure to the flesh but afflict it with the gravest sufferings, while feeding the soul, sick as it is, with a most wretched pleasure. For this reason, those who strive for purity need a simple medicine of the heart for these passions, whereas carnal passions can reach health only through the twofold treatment we have described.

Accordingly, it greatly benefits those who strive for purity to remove from themselves at the outset the very materials of these carnal passions, by which either their occasion or their recollection can be generated in the still-sick soul. A double illness necessarily requires a double treatment. For the body, so that desire may not attempt to burst into action, the image and enticing material must necessarily be removed; and for the soul, so that it may not conceive desire even in thought, diligent meditation on the Scriptures and watchful concern must likewise remain alert.

(Ambrose.) He refers to unbelief when he mentions the desires of the flesh. The pleasure of the flesh is to delight in visible things, so that it calls the elements—which God established as the governing structures of the world—gods, although this name is owed to the one God, from whom all things come. Just as he has no partner among these in power, so he has no associate in name.

The name is not denied to Christ, however, because just as they share a common nature, so they will also share a common name. Yet there is this difference between the Father and the Son: the Father received this from no one, while the Son received everything belonging to the Father through generation, so that in power, substance, and name the Son differs in nothing from the Father. Hence he says: “All that the Father has is mine, and what is mine is the Father’s.”

Is it therefore unworthy or contradictory for Christ also to be called God? He is called God from God the Father, so that the authority of the one God may be preserved.

If anyone thinks that the Apostle means something else when he speaks of doing the will of the flesh, let him know that the Apostle lived a pure life, since he lived blamelessly according to the righteousness of the law. But because he persecuted the faith of Christ, he says: “We once lived in the desires of our flesh.” Every sin is called flesh, especially unbelief, which is the mother of every crime. No one will benefit from good works or chastity if he is unbelieving; unbelief stains all these things.

This is why he added: “And we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest.” When an evil will is added to nature, nature becomes a nature of wrath—that is, one subject to vengeance—while the substance itself is not changed, but the evil will is.

For this is attributed to nature, as what follows shows. Hence he says in Isaiah: “A wicked seed” (Isa. I), and he then explains why it is a wicked seed: “For you have forsaken the Lord,” he says, “and provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger.” Thus a nature that abandons God is called a wicked seed.

To degenerate is to depart from one’s author; and when it gives the others a bad example, it is a bad seed, for it produces very bad fruits. But if it returns to its author, nature will be good, according to the Apostle, who, having been changed as he recognized his Creator, is called a vessel of election.

(Jerome.) Earlier he had placed two things together: “You, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins,” and he had referred to sins when he said, “in which you once walked.” But concerning trespasses, nothing similar seemed to follow that could complete the sense. Now he says: “In these trespasses we too all once lived.” And lest, in saying “and in your sins, in which we too all once lived,” he should appear through pride to exempt himself from sin, he added: “In which we too all once lived.”

Whoever says that he lived in past trespasses and does not confess present ones says: “We once lived,” not in one desire but in the desires of our flesh. For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Gal. V). We did not do one will of the flesh but many, and not only the wills of the flesh but also those of the minds. In Latin manuscripts this is given as “thoughts.”

I think the distinction between the sins of the flesh and those of the minds is this: sin of the flesh is impurity and luxury, and the acts by which such things are fulfilled through its service in lust; the offense of the minds concerns doctrines opposed to truth and heretical perversity. Thus we can say that many heretics—although this is rare—do the wills of their minds rather than the wills of their flesh, while many churchmen, on the contrary, do the wills of the flesh rather than those of the mind. There are also many who do the wills of both flesh and mind alike.

We have said this not because heretics do not do the wills of the flesh—for among them there are more bodily vices than among our people—but so that, by giving an example, what we wished to explain might be understood more easily.

“And we were by nature,” he says, “children of wrath, like the rest.” Let the heretics who maintain that there are different natures answer how Paul—who was certainly of a spiritual nature, as there can be no doubt—could have been by nature a child of wrath, like the rest who were still placed in error.

We, however, say that all human beings are first by nature children of wrath, either because of the body of our humiliation and the body of death, and because from youth the human mind has been inclined toward evil; hence Solomon says: “There is no just person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccl. VII); or because, at the time when we are able to have knowledge of God and reach puberty, we all sin either in deed or in thought.

We were therefore by nature children of wrath, like the rest, including all the saints who have been redeemed from the wrath by the blood of Christ. For if Paul, who lived blamelessly according to the righteousness that was in the law, says that he was by nature a child of wrath, why should we fear testifying that even the holy men of earlier times were children of wrath?

Of all of them it could truly be said: “When the commandment came, sin revived, but they themselves died.” “Children of wrath” should be understood in the same way as “children of destruction,” “children of iniquity,” and “children of death.” This does not mean that wrath, death, iniquity, and destruction exist as substances by nature and possess children, but that people are called children of whatever operates in them, just as those who are to be consumed by the fires of Gehenna are called children of Gehenna.

Otherwise, children of wrath are understood as children of the devil. For the devil is destruction, wrath, and death: “Death grew strong and devoured”; and: “The last enemy to be destroyed is death”; and to the devil: “You have become destruction.” He became this, he says, by his own will, not because he was created this way from the beginning.

How, then, is death said to have entered the world through the devil’s envy (Wis. II), so that through him those who previously lived died, and how is he called destruction because he destroys whoever he deceives? In the same way he is called wrath because of the savagery that he exercises against human beings.

But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ. (Ambrose.) These are the true riches of mercies: that mercy should be freely bestowed upon those who did not seek it, as Isaiah says, “I was revealed to those who did not seek me.” For this is to abound in mercy: that it should be granted even to those who do not ask. Yet this is God’s love toward us: because he made us, he does not wish us to perish; [Col. 0403A] for he loves his own work. Indeed, he acts in such a way as to love what he has made; no one hates his own labor. And when we were dead, he made us alive together with Christ. (Jerome.) Because of his love with which he loved the human race—and not with a simple love, but a great one—when we were dead on account of our offenses, he made us alive. And he did not merely make us alive—for that was too little for his goodness and greatness—but he made us alive together with Christ Jesus, granting us one and the same life with Christ.

(Ambrose.) We were dead, alienated from God; but by his grace he called us back, that is, he made us alive together with Christ. For because through him he made us, again through him he restored us in him—that is, so that we might be his members. [Col. 0403B] He is our head, and, by God’s favor, we have him as the author of our life, as the apostle Peter says: “But you killed the author of life” (Acts 3).

(Albert.) As for what he says, “because of his great love”: great love is to love rebellious servants as sons. Hence we should consider how greatly he loves those who have now become holy, since he deigned to love sinners so greatly that he did not spare even his own Son for their salvation.

By grace you have been saved. (Jerome.) If “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8), then we have been saved more by grace than by works. For we can repay God nothing for all that he has repaid us.

And he raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in [Col. 0403C] Christ Jesus. (Ambrose.) He says what I mentioned above: that the saints, including those from the Gentiles, will be there where Christ also is their head.

(Jerome.) Above he had said that God raised Christ from the dead and made him sit at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, power, virtue, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. Now he adds that he has also raised us with him and made us sit in the heavenly places at his right hand.

The question therefore arises: how has God, who saved us and raised us up, also made us sit with Christ? The one who answers more simply maintains that, according to God’s foreknowledge, he has spoken of what is future as though it had already happened. This is the custom of Scripture: sometimes future events are expressed in the past tense. [Col. 0403D] For example, concerning the Lord’s cross: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 21); and elsewhere concerning his passion: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isa. 53); and again concerning the insults of the scourging: “By his bruise we were healed” (ibid.); and elsewhere: “Because of the sins of my people he was led to death” (ibid.).

This is so that, because future things are uncertain to human beings, hope might not waver or falter. Things that God knew would occur—before whom nothing is uncertain—are therefore recalled as though they had already happened. Or it is because, according to the philosophers also, what has happened cannot be made not to have happened; thus those who hear may regard as already accomplished what is still future.

Another person, who understands Christ’s resurrection and kingdom spiritually, [Col. 0404A] does not hesitate to say that the saints already sit and reign with Christ. For just as a saint is no longer in the flesh, although he lives in the flesh, and has his manner of life in heaven although he walks on earth, and, ceasing to be flesh, is wholly transformed into spirit, so he sits in the heavenly places with Christ. For “the kingdom of God is within us,” and “where our treasure is, there our heart will be also” (Luke 17). We sit firmly and securely with Christ—in wisdom, the Word, righteousness, and truth.

This too may be said: just as we have received the pledge of the Holy Spirit without yet attaining its entire fullness, so also we sit and reign with Christ without yet possessing the perfect session in the heavenly places.

(Augustine.) For he previously said, “He made us alive together with Christ.” He said this to the Corinthians: those who [Col. 0404B] live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them. And when he says, “by whose grace we have been saved,” he speaks as though it were already accomplished, because he holds it in hope. For elsewhere he says most plainly: “For in hope we were saved.” Therefore here also he proceeds and enumerates as though already accomplished what is still future: “He raised us up together and made us sit in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.”

It is certain that Christ already sits in the heavenly places, but we do not yet. Yet because by certain hope we already possess what will be, he says that we sit together in the heavenly places—not yet in ourselves, but already in him. And so that we may understand that something still remains future, he continues: “So that in the ages to come he might show the surpassing riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.”

(Jerome.) How [Col. 0404C] great is the benefit, and how manifold the grace, by which the Lord has freed us from the disturbances of this age and made us sit and reign with Christ—this is demonstrated above all by the fact that in the ages to come he will show his glory and display his riches toward us, not to one rational creature alone, but to all rational creatures. We, who were formerly held by the law of hell and were destined, because of our vices and sins, to punishments as well as to the works of the flesh, will now reign in Christ and sit with him.

We shall sit not in some lowly place, but above every principality, power, virtue, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. For if Christ, raised from the dead, sits at God’s right hand [Col. 0404D] in the heavenly places above every principality, power, virtue, and the rest, and if we sit and reign with Christ, we must sit above those things over which he sits.

But the diligent reader immediately asks: “What then? Is a human being greater than the angels and all the powers in heaven?” Because it is dangerous to answer this way, he will refer the principalities, powers, virtues, dominions, and every name that is named—not only in this age but also in the age to come—especially since all things have been subjected beneath Christ’s feet, not to the good order but to the contrary one. He will say that they are fallen angels, the prince of this world, and Lucifer, who rose in the morning; and that at the end the saints will sit with Christ above them, granting even those beings [Col. 0405A] a benefit who now roam about without restraint, abusing their freedom wickedly and falling headlong into sins.

When such beings have those sitting above them, they will begin to be governed according to the will of those who sit.

But what he says—“so that in the ages to come he might show the surpassing riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus”—he will transfer to the interpretation that we were saved not by our merit but by his grace. It is a greater proof of goodness to die for sinners rather than for the righteous: “For perhaps someone would dare to die for a good person.” He will give us what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart.” He has already granted all these things in part in Christ Jesus, because nothing apart from Christ can be called good.

For by grace you have been saved through faith, [Col. 0405B] and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast. Therefore, he says, he will show the surpassing riches of his grace in the coming ages, because you have been saved by grace through faith, not by works. And this faith itself is not from you, but from him who called you.

This is said so that perhaps a hidden thought might not creep upon us: “If we were not saved by our works, surely we were saved at least by faith; and in another respect what saves us belongs to us.” Therefore he added and said that faith itself is not of our will but God’s gift—not that human free choice is taken away, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement to the Romans, “It depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9); rather, the freedom of choice itself has God as its author, [Col. 0405C] so that everything may be referred to his benefit, since he himself has permitted us even to will what is good.

All this is said so that no one may boast that he was saved by himself and not by God.

(Augustine.) And lest they arrogate even faith to themselves in such a way that they fail to understand that it was divinely given, the same Apostle says elsewhere that “he obtained mercy in order that he might be faithful.” Here too he added: “And this is not from yourselves, but it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast.”

(Ambrose.) It is true that all thanksgiving for our salvation must be referred to God, who grants us his mercy so as to recall us, though wandering and not seeking the true way, to life. Therefore we should not glory in ourselves, but in God, who regenerated us through a heavenly birth by the faith of Christ, [Col. 0405D] so that, trained in good works, we might be deemed worthy to receive the promises that God decreed for us who have already been reborn.

For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we might walk in them.

(Jerome.) He gives the reasons why we have been saved by grace through faith, and why this itself is not from us but from God’s gift, saying: “For we are his creation.” That is, the fact that we live, breathe, understand, and are able to believe belongs to him, because he is our creator.

But observe carefully that he did not say, “We are his representation and molding,” but “We are his workmanship.” Molding derives its origin from the clay of the earth, whereas workmanship has its beginning according to likeness and image. This distinction is also set forth together in Psalm 118, [Col. 0406A] where different meanings are conveyed: “Your hands made me and fashioned me.” “Workmanship” holds the first place, and “molding” follows.

And because the terms “creation” and “formation” are customarily joined to great works—for example, “that city was founded,” and “the world was created from the beginning”—and because each of the saints, through various doctrines and virtues, is a whole world in himself, we are therefore now said to have been created in Christ and created for good works. This may mean the works we ourselves have done or will do, or other creatures to which our manner of life must be transferred, so that we may walk in the works God prepared. Great hope has already been given to us, since we are destined to walk in the things God has prepared with great care.

And since we have once come to the term “creation,” and Wisdom in the Proverbs of Solomon [Col. 0406B] says that she was created as the beginning of the Lord’s ways (Prov. 8), many people, fearing that they might be compelled to call Christ a creature, deny the whole mystery of Christ and say that this Wisdom signifies not Christ but the wisdom of the world.

We openly declare that there is no danger in calling him a creature whom, with complete confidence in all our hope, we confess to be worm and man, crucified and accursed—especially since, in the two verses preceding, Wisdom itself promises that she will speak of things that are after the ages. Since Christ made the ages, and since what follows consists of things that he promised he would speak after the ages, they must be referred to the mystery of the incarnation, not to the nature of God.

The Hebrew codices, moreover, do not have, “The Lord created me [Col. 0406C] as the beginning of his ways,” but, “The Lord possessed me.” There is a great difference between possession and creation. For what is possessed exists, subsists, and belongs properly to its possessor; but a creature is one that did not exist before it was made, or is transferred from what it was into something else. Thus we too are now said to have been created in Christ Jesus—not because we did not previously exist, but because we were created for good works.

David also prays for this in the Psalm, saying: “Create a clean heart in me, O God” (Ps. 50). Certainly he had possessed a clean heart before God when the Lord spoke of him: “I have found David the son of Jesse, a man according to my heart” (Acts 13). But just as creation there signifies restoration, so in us and in Christ, through each individual work and progress, “creation” and “formation” may be [Col. 0406D] understood. Thus every day, among believers—who are variously called, according to their merits, mountains, valleys, hills, and plains—Christ is created, born, and formed.

Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles were in the flesh. You were called uncircumcision by what is called circumcision, made in the flesh by hands, because at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world.

(Ambrose.) He admonishes the Gentiles to remember what they once were. They were carnal and without hope, sharing in none of the Jews’ promise in Christ—for Christ had been promised to the Jews, not to the Gentiles—so that they might give more abundant thanks to God through Christ, who in his mercy [Col. 0407A] made them, though carnal, participants in spiritual things.

He says “circumcision made in the flesh by hands” in order to signify that there is another circumcision, spiritual and not made by hands.

(Jerome.) By calling the Ephesians Gentiles “in the flesh,” he shows that in the spirit they are not Gentiles. Conversely, the Jews are Gentiles in the spirit and Israelites in the flesh.

The Jews and Gentiles are divided in four ways. Some are circumcised both in the flesh and in the spirit, such as Moses and Aaron, the apostles, and Nathanael, whose hidden Judaism the Lord perceived when he said: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 1).

Others are circumcised neither in flesh nor in spirit, such as Nebuchadnezzar and Pharaoh, and today the multitude of barbarian and Roman peoples who do not believe in God.

A third group is circumcised only in the flesh and has an uncircumcised [Col. 0407B] spirit. To them the prophet says: “Be circumcised to your God, and do not circumcise the flesh of your foreskin” (Jer. 4); and elsewhere: “All the nations are uncircumcised in the flesh, but the house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart” (Jer. 9).

The last group is that of which he now speaks: “Because at one time you Gentiles were in the flesh, called uncircumcision by what is called circumcision, made in the flesh by hands.” Such today is the whole multitude of believers, and the entire world from the Gentiles is filled with them.

Accordingly, to distinguish spiritual Gentiles from Jews, the Ephesians are called Gentiles in the flesh, because according to the Spirit they are Israelites. Scripture also mentions Israel according to the flesh [Col. 0407C] elsewhere: “See Israel according to the flesh” (1 Cor. 10), because in the spirit it was not Israel.

He has beautifully moderated his words: “You were called uncircumcision by what is called circumcision, made in the flesh by hands”—not that this is circumcision, but that it itself assumes the name and is truly circumcision made by hands, not by the Spirit.

At the same time, we must note that we who, as he recalled, were once without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the promises and covenant of God, now, after we have believed in Christ, are said to receive not only his promises and covenants but also to possess the commonwealth of Israel. Thus the whole legal manner of life is fulfilled in us.

For the law is spiritual, and we are more truly circumcised and keep Sabbaths in the spirit. We offer spiritual sacrifices; when their temple and altar have been destroyed, we offer to God the tithes of our fruits. [Col. 0407D] We sacrifice the spotless lamb; with our loins girded and prepared, we eat the Passover. Just as circumcision is said to be made in the flesh by hands, so, by way of distinction, another circumcision is understood to exist—one that is not made by hands, as we have said, but by the Spirit.

When he says, “having no hope and without God in this world,” this does not mean that the Ephesians had not had or worshiped many gods before they believed in Christ. Rather, whoever is without the true God has no god. The addition “without God in the world” is significant. They did have a God whom God had foreknown they would possess; according to God’s foreknowledge they were not without God, but in the world they were without God.

But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away, [Col. 0408A] have been brought near in the blood of Christ.

God is everywhere, and he is wholly everywhere. How can anyone be separated from him, since all things are in him? He himself also speaks through the prophet: “I am God who draws near and not from far away.” The Psalmist testifies: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present.”

Since all things are in him, nevertheless he is said to be far from the ungodly, in accordance with the saying, “The Lord is far from the ungodly.” He from whom the ungodly are far is near to the saints. Thus, although he was far from the Ephesians, he was made near to them in the blood of Jesus.

It must be examined carefully that no one draws near to God without the blood of the Lord Jesus.

(Ambrose.) He continues to commend God’s gift and grace, to whom he always wishes us, as though bound to him, to render thanks. For this reason he recalls that we have been made near to God through Christ’s blood: [Col. 0408B] to show how great God’s affection is toward us, since he permitted his Son to die for us. Thus, remaining steadfast in his faith, we should not yield to all the destruction inflicted upon us for his sake, knowing that he deserves more from us than enemies can inflict.

Although he is Lord and lacks nothing, he offered himself for us—not for his own benefit, but for ours. Even if it benefited us nothing, we might perhaps be compelled to die for the Lord, since we are servants; how much more, then, when the death not only of him but also of us produces an effect beneficial to us!

For he himself is our peace, who made both one. (Jerome.) He says: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14). For just as wisdom makes people wise, righteousness makes them righteous, sanctification makes them holy, and life makes them living, so he himself, who is peace, makes us peaceful, [Col. 0408C] so that we may say: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceable” (Ps. 119).

But if Christ is the peace of believers, whoever is without peace consequently does not have Christ.

Who made both one, and by abolishing the middle wall of the partition, the hostility, in his flesh. (Ambrose.) The Savior’s passion made peace between circumcision and uncircumcision. He abolished the hostility that was like a middle wall, separating circumcision from uncircumcision and uncircumcision from circumcision. He gave the law so that neither the Jew, presuming upon circumcision, would reject the Gentile, nor the Gentile, trusting in uncircumcision—that is, in paganism—would despise the Jew. Rather, both, renewed, were to follow the faith of the one God in Christ.

Everything the Savior taught he confirmed when he rose again. Yet by the middle wall [Col. 0408D] dividing the law of works from paganism, he signified a stone fence or enclosure—that is, not a stable or sturdy wall. For paganism was not a firm reality, having been invented by human beings, and neither were circumcision, new moons, dietary regulations, sacrifices, or the observance of Sabbaths stable and fixed. They were given in such a way that they would cease when Christ came. Although God gave them, he gave them for a time; the preaching of faith, however, is firm and has no successor.

By abolishing the law of commandments in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself as one new human being, making peace.

This is what I briefly mentioned above: he abolished the law that had been given to the Jews in circumcision, new moons, foods, sacrifices, [Col. 0409A] and the Sabbath—that is, he caused it now to cease, because it was a burden—and in this way he made peace.

Hence the apostle Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Why are you placing upon the neck of the brothers a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?” (Acts 15).

So that he might present and reconcile both in one body to God through the cross. Having removed the hostility by his death, Christ first reconciled the peoples to one another; then he made them peaceful toward God the Father, so that human beings of one nature, who had been made different through error, might become members of one new body, whose head is Christ.

Putting the hostility to death in himself, and coming, he proclaimed peace to you who were far away, and peace to those who were near, because through him we both have access [Col. 0409B] in one Spirit to the Father.

(Ambrose.) The meaning is the same: he put the hostility to death in himself when he died for all, both Jews and Gentiles. The Savior’s death benefits everyone. Rising from the dead, after condemning the death that held everyone, he showed what hope those who believe in him possess.

From this he commanded the preaching by which all were summoned to God the Father in the unity of the Spirit, discord having been torn apart. Whether they were Jews, who are called near because the promise was made to their fathers, or Gentiles, who are called far away because they did not receive the law given through Moses, once the former observance had been removed, they were to receive the faith of Christ, through which they would become one.

(Jerome.) After the Savior destroyed in his flesh the wisdom of the flesh, [Col. 0409C] which is hostile to God, and changed the legal precepts into evangelical teachings, so that he might make one Christian people from Jew and Gentile, he proclaimed peace to us who were far away and to the remnant of the Jews who believed from Israel through the apostles.

Then through him we approached God and recognized that we have one Father in the Spirit. The Lord’s saying in the Gospel was fulfilled: “So that there may be one shepherd and one flock” (John 10). And again: “I have other sheep that are not from this fold” (ibid.), signifying us, who were to be gathered from the Gentiles.

The hostility that was destroyed in the Savior’s flesh was also put to death through the cross. For it is written that he should reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, putting the hostility to death in it—not, [Col. 0409D] as the Latin codices have it, “in himself,” because of the ambiguity of the Greek pronoun. For ἐν αὐτῷ may be understood both as “in himself” and as “in it,” that is, in the cross, because the cross—σταυρός in Greek—is masculine.

The law of commandments was also overturned in doctrines after circumcision, the Sabbath observance left to God’s people, Passover, Pentecost, and the command not to appear empty-handed before God came to be understood more deeply than their surface wording suggests. We withdrew from the letter that kills and began to follow the life-giving Spirit.

When he says, “Coming, he proclaimed peace to you who were far away,” that is, to the Gentiles, “and peace to those who were near,” that is, to the Jews, it seems to me that he has presented testimony from Isaiah in different words and used the sense of Scripture as though it were his own. [Col. 0410A]

For it is written there: “I have seen his ways and healed him, and I comforted him and gave him true comfort, peace upon peace to those who were far away and to those who were near” (Isa. 57). These words are according to the common edition.

But anyone who reads the Apostle’s statement elsewhere, where he recalls Christ—“making peace through the blood of his cross for those who are on earth and those who are in heaven,” together with what is said in that passage—will not think that we, who according to the Spirit are called Israel, were far away, while the Jews, who are called Israel only according to the flesh, were near.

Rather, he will apply the whole interpretation to the angels, the heavenly powers, and human souls, understanding that Christ joined earthly and heavenly things in his blood, although they had previously been at odds with one another.

The good shepherd, carrying the sick sheep back to the mountains, [Col. 0410B] made it be with the others; and he joined the drachma that had been lost to the drachmas that had remained safe (Luke 15). He also drew the legal commandments back to those doctrines whose type and image Moses saw when he observed what was to be made in the tabernacle.

Thus the Lord’s cross benefited not only the earth but also heaven, not only human beings but also angels; and every creature of the Lord was cleansed by its Lord’s blood.

When he says, “so that he might create the two in himself as one new human being,” [Col. 0410C] which seems to correspond more closely to the interpretation above concerning Jews and Gentiles, he adapts it to his own understanding in this way: the human being made according to the image and likeness of God will receive, after reconciliation, the same form that the angels now possess, but that he himself lost.

He calls him a new human being because he is renewed every day and will dwell in the new world, when there will be a new heaven and a new earth. He will drink the new cup of Jesus in the kingdom of God, sing a new song, and rejoice in the reading of the Old and New Testaments.

Elsewhere it is written: “Behold, I am making all things that will now arise” (Isa. 43). He will understand this to mean that the beginning of renewal takes place in the present age. But he will not think that perfect and complete newness can yet be fulfilled in this age.

And just as now “we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13), so the renewal of the new human being will then be fully and perfectly completed, when heavenly and earthly things have been joined and we have approached the Father in one Spirit, with one mind and one judgment.

I do not [Col. 0410D] know whether he intimates something of this kind in another Epistle—if, indeed, anyone accepts it—when he says to discerning readers: “All these, having received testimony through faith, did not receive the promise, since God had provided something better for us, so that they might not be perfected without us” (Heb. 11).

For this reason the whole creation groans together with us, who groan in this tabernacle, and suffers with us, because we have conceived the fear of God in the womb; we grieve and await the revelation of the children of God, so that it may be freed from the bondage of vanity to which it is now subject. Then there will be “one shepherd and one flock,” and the prayer of God will be fulfilled: “Let your will be done in heaven and on earth.”

Therefore you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.

To what he had said above—“strangers to the covenants and promise”— [Col. 0411A]he now responds: “Therefore you are no longer strangers,” that is, sojourners. And to what he had previously said—“alienated from the commonwealth of Israel”—he now responds: “You are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.”

(Maurus.) Because you who were once far away, having no promises concerning Christ or your salvation, are now near—not merely near, but also fellow citizens with the saints.

Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets. (Ambrose.) This means that you have been placed upon the New and Old Testaments. What the apostles preached, the prophets foretold. Although he says to the Corinthians, “God placed first in the Church apostles, second prophets” (1 Cor. 12), those prophets are different ones. There he is discussing the ordering of the Church; here, the foundation of the Church. [Col. 0411B] The prophets arranged and prepared, but the apostles laid the foundations.

Hence the Lord says to Peter: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16); that is, I will establish the faithful for life upon the confession of the catholic faith. David also arranged the house of God and marked the place where it was to be built, while Solomon founded it.

Upon the chief cornerstone, Christ Jesus, in whom the whole building, constructed together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, in whom you too are built together into a dwelling place of God in the Holy Spirit.

(From Jerome.) In him you Ephesians also are built into a temple for the supreme God, from living stones. If the whole building, whether constructed from Jews or Gentiles and joined together through the cornerstone that unites the two walls, grows into one temple [Col. 0411C] of the one God, should we not labor with all our strength to become those stones of which it is written: “Holy stones are rolled upon the earth” (Zech. 9)?

And when we have become living stones, hewn smooth on every side, even and polished, possessing no roughness, let us be built into a temple and make within ourselves a dwelling place for God, so that he may deign to dwell in us through the Holy Spirit.

(Ambrose.) The Savior took the two peoples into himself and made them one in the Lord, just as the cornerstone holds two walls together in the unity of a firmly established house. The faithful are the visible surfaces of the temple of God, living in the Spirit so that they may become heirs of the heavenly dwelling.

(Alban.) The whole building constructed upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets may signify not only us but also the heavenly powers, [Col. 0411D] so that all together may become a dwelling place of God in the Holy Spirit.

The highest stone, through which all things are joined, is Christ the Son of God—the stone cut from the mountain without hands (Dan. 2). Concerning him the Psalmist testifies: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the head of the corner; this was done by the Lord” (Ps. 117).

He was rejected by the Pharisees, who seemed to possess knowledge of the Lord’s law and to build God’s temple with legal commandments. But he was taken up by God as the cornerstone, so that he himself might hold the two walls together in the middle, and through him each people might have access to God, while the Gentiles might be built together with God’s people into one spiritual house and a dwelling place worthy of God.

## Chapter 3

The Apostle first sets forth his intention of praying for the Ephesians, and prays for them, attributing all their good to God.

For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles—if indeed you have heard of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you, since by revelation the mystery was made known to me, as I wrote above briefly, so that, when you read, you can understand my insight into the mystery of Christ. (Jerome.)

As far as the sequence of the discourse and the wording of the passage are concerned, despite the most diligent inquiry into what he has prefaced—“For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, on behalf of you Gentiles”—we could find nothing that he completed in relation to it. For he did not say, “For this reason I, Paul, did this or that, or taught that,” but, while the sentence remained suspended, he passed on to other matters—unless perhaps we should excuse him because he himself confessed, saying, “And if I am unskilled in speech, yet I am not so in knowledge” (II Cor. XI), and should seek in him an order of meaning rather than of words. This may be rendered as follows:

“For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ—and imprisoned for you who are from the Gentiles—came to know the mystery, so that I might also hand it on to you, as I have spoken at some length [variant: a little earlier] in this same Epistle. You ought, however, to hear of the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you who are from the Gentiles, for whom also I am a prisoner of Jesus Christ.”

That Paul was a prisoner of Jesus Christ on behalf of the Gentiles can also be understood of the mystery [or martyrdom], because, having been thrown into chains at Rome, he sent this Epistle at the time when we have shown that those to Philemon, the Colossians, and the Philippians were written elsewhere [Col. 0412B]. Or certainly, because it is read in many places that the bond of the soul is called this body, by which the soul is held as if shut up in a prison, we say that Paul was therefore restrained by the bonds of the body and did not return to be with Christ, so that the preaching entrusted to him among the Gentiles might be completed. Some, however, introduce another meaning here: that Paul, predestined and sanctified from his mother’s womb for the preaching of the Gentiles before he was born, later received the bonds of the flesh.

I think, however, that the expression in this passage is also faulty. For instead of what he ought to have said—“For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ on behalf of you Gentiles, came to know the mystery, as I wrote briefly, so that, when you read, you can understand”—he says, “For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner according to revelation: the ministry [mystery] was made known to me,” and so forth. But if someone can show, even in accordance with the sequence of the discourse and its wording, that the Apostle was accomplished and did not fall into the faults of grammatical expression, that person should rather be heard.

Whenever we point out a solecism or something of that kind, we are not attacking the Apostle, as malicious people accuse us of doing; rather, we are especially defenders of the Apostle. For, being “a Hebrew from Hebrews,” without the polish of rhetorical speech, the arrangement of words, and the beauty of eloquence, he could never have brought the whole world over to the faith of Christ unless he had evangelized it “not in the wisdom of speech, but in the power of God” [Col. 0412C]. For he himself says to the Corinthians (I Cor. II):

“And I, when I came to you, brothers, came not with lofty speech or wisdom, proclaiming to you the testimony of Christ”; and again: “My word and my preaching were not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in a demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of human beings but in the power of God.”

This man, then, who makes solecisms in his words, who cannot produce a hyperbaton or bring a sentence to completion, boldly claims wisdom for himself and says: “Since by revelation the mystery was made known to me, as I wrote briefly.” Indeed, if anyone considers the earlier parts of this Epistle, he will see that mysteries were revealed to him, of which he touched upon a certain small portion in his discourse—not so much bringing forth everything he knew as showing, from what little he said, what he left unspoken [Col. 0413A].

“You can understand,” he says, “when you read my meaning,” or “my insight into the mystery of Christ.” This is the same as what we said in the preface: that none of Paul’s Epistles contains so many mysteries, wrapped in such hidden meanings—mysteries of which the Apostle boasts that he knows and which he briefly shows to have been disclosed to us—so that we may read the things written with greater attentiveness.

( Ambrose.) Since he has shown what the stewardship of divine clemency toward the salvation of the Gentiles had been before the world existed, he now declares that, by God’s providence and with Christ sending him, he is carrying out the embassy of this gift. For after his resurrection the Lord sent his Apostles to preach in his place, directing this man toward the conversion of the Gentiles. Thus he said to him: “Go; I will send you far away to the Gentiles.” Therefore he used the Lord’s own words when he says, “Peace to you who are far away, and peace to those who are near,” and, “If indeed you have heard of the stewardship of grace that was given to us for you.” He wants them to know that by God’s judgment he was sent by Christ to preach to the Gentiles the mystery of God’s grace.

“By revelation the mystery was made known to me, as I wrote previously in brief, so that, when you read, you can understand my insight into the mystery of Christ.” He indicates that the revelation of God’s mystery was shown to him, a mystery about which he recalls having written briefly earlier—that is, moderately, to the extent that they were able to grasp the Apostle’s insight into Christ’s sacrament.

## What in other generations was not made known to the children of human beings, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus through the Gospel, of which I became a minister according to the gift of God’s grace that was given to me according to the operation of his power.

(Jerome.) The mystery of Christ, which the Apostle has obtained in part above, and the question how it was unknown to other generations, seem to require fuller reconsideration. Did Abraham, Jacob, Moses, Isaiah, and the other Prophets know nothing of it, or did they? Scripture records that they foretold the Lord’s coming and the calling of the Gentiles.

Abraham saw his day and rejoiced (John VIII), and it was said to him: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII). Jacob, too, prophetically speaks of the one who would arise from Judah: “He himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX). Moses also considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt. And Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son” (Isa. VII); and elsewhere: “A shoot from Jesse, and the one who shall arise to rule over the nations; in him the nations shall hope” (Isa. XI).

And, lest this become lengthy, let it suffice to say a few things from the Psalms: “All the families of the nations shall worship before him” (Ps. XXI); and again: “All nations shall serve him” (Ps. LXXI); and still more clearly concerning the people of Israel and the Lord the Savior: “Visit this vineyard and perfect it, which your right hand planted, and upon the son whom you strengthened for yourself” (Ps. LXXIX). The stewardship of his body is also indicated in what follows: “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand.”

Either, then, we must accept the view of Montanus, that the patriarchs and prophets spoke in ecstasy and did not know what they were saying [Col. 0413D]; or, if that is impious—for the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets—they certainly understood what they spoke. And if they understood, the question arises how Paul can say that what was unknown to other generations was revealed to Christ’s Apostles.
