Perhaps we should answer that the Apostle carefully and deliberately testified that the mystery was unknown to the children of human beings, not to the children of God to whom he speaks: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. LXXXI). Those who received the Spirit of adoption, among whom the patriarchs and prophets were numbered, knew God’s sacrament.

Or, if this is not accepted and seems too forced and artificial, the discussion will move to the position that Paul did not state absolutely and generally that the Lord’s sacrament had been entirely unknown to other generations, but that the ancient patriarchs and prophets did not know it in the manner in which it has now been revealed to the saints and Apostles. For it is one thing to know beforehand in the Spirit what is to come, and another to see those things completed in reality.

Thus John is called greater than all the prophets because he saw and pointed out with his finger the one whom the others had prophesied, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sins of the world” (John I). In accordance with this meaning, the following can also be explained: “Many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Luke X). They desired to see and hear these things because they knew them as future. For if they did not know what was to come, how could they desire what they entirely ignored?

We read in the Books of Kings that the Lord promised Solomon in a dream, saying: “Because you asked this thing of me and did not ask long life for yourself, nor requested riches, nor the lives of your enemies, but asked that you might understand and hear judgment, behold, I have done according to your word and have given you a wise heart, so that you may be wise; and afterward no one like you shall arise” (III Kings III) [Col. 0414D]. How, then, do some people think that the mystery revealed to Christ’s Apostles had been unknown to Solomon, when Solomon was wiser than all the Apostles, and the divine voice had earlier promised this to the patriarchs? He also confidently speaks of himself: “God taught me wisdom, and I know the understanding of the holy ones” (Wisdom VII).

David, too, boasts of his knowledge of the hidden mystery, saying: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom” (Ps. L); and to the one who vaunted himself over his wisdom, God speaks through the prophet: “Are you wiser than Daniel?” (Ezek. XXVIII).

Either, then, we must retain the meaning discussed above: that the patriarchs and prophets were ignorant of Christ’s mystery in the way it has now been revealed to the Apostles, because it is one thing to hold something in one’s hands and another to foresee in the Spirit what is still future. Or we must say that, just as faces are not like faces, so hearts are not like hearts, and, according to the Apostle, gifts are diverse: one person has prophecy, another kinds of tongues, another gifts of healing, another acts of assistance and administration; one is wise, another faithful; one excels in awareness of secrets, another is content with simple faith.

For not everyone, like Solomon, spoke in the same way about the natures of beasts, birds, and plants, so as to discuss everything “from the cedar of Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall.” Conversely, perhaps Solomon did not see all the kinds of sacrifices and forms of divine worship as Moses did; nor did the Lord speak to him face to face; nor did he possess or understand such a wealth of vessels and furnishings, whose pattern the Lord showed Moses on the mountain.

And just as we must believe that the patriarchs and prophets possessed certain things that the Apostles did not possess, so, conversely, according to the needs of the time and the preaching of the Gospel, the Apostles had a fuller knowledge of Christ’s mystery. The holy men of ancient times certainly knew it, but not in the manner of the Apostles, upon whom the necessity of preaching had been laid.

What is this mystery, then, which “as it has now been revealed” was not made known to other generations? Surely it is what follows: “that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and fellow sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus through the Gospel,” of which Paul became a minister according to the gift of God’s grace that was given to him according to the operation of God’s power.

I know that the addition of the conjunction, by which the text says “fellow heirs, members of the same body, and fellow sharers,” makes the sentence inelegant in Latin. But because it is found in the Greek, and because each word, syllable, letter, and point in the divine Scriptures is full of meaning, we prefer to risk something in the arrangement and structure of the words rather than in the understanding.

The Gentiles are therefore fellow heirs with Israel—or, as we consider better, fellow heirs with Christ—so that God may be our inheritance and we may be fellow heirs of Christ. This is also written elsewhere (Rom. VIII): “Heirs of God, and fellow heirs of Christ.” This does not mean that some possession is divided among us, but that he himself is the Lord, our inheritance and possession. For the Lord says: “The Lord is our inheritance.” And elsewhere: “The Lord is my portion and my inheritance” (Ps. XV).

“Members of the same body” signifies that, just as in one body there are many members—for example, eyes, hands, ears, feet, belly, and knees—and, although they are in one body, they have their own distinctions, so that they rejoice and suffer for one another, so those who have believed in Christ possess diverse gifts, yet are gathered together into the one body of the Church.

In the two preceding words—that is, in his saying “fellow heirs” and “members of the same body”—one might still suspect some difference within the one body. But by adding, “and fellow sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus,” he has entirely removed every difference. For where there is one common participation, everything is shared.

He also fittingly added, “through the Gospel,” of which I became a minister according to the gift of grace that was given to me according to the operation of his power, so that he might display God’s grace rather than his own merit. He knew that he had been a persecutor and had ravaged Christ’s Church. By this humility he completely excludes the charge of arrogance, which some think should be brought against him because he said that the mystery had been revealed to him, whereas it had been unknown to the patriarchs and prophets. For the disciple of humility would never swell with arrogant words, saying that the Gospel of which he was the minister was due not to his own merit but to the grace of God.

Those who wish the prophets not to have understood what they said, and to have spoken as if in ecstasy, also draw into support of their doctrine the passage found in many copies of the Epistle to the Romans:

“To the one who is able to strengthen you according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept silent through eternal times but has now been manifested through the prophetic Scriptures and the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and what follows (Rom. XVI).

They should be answered briefly that Christ’s mystery was kept silent in past ages, not among those who promised that it would come, but among all the Gentiles, to whom it was afterward manifested. It should also be noted that the sacrament of our faith cannot be revealed except through the prophetic Scriptures and the coming of Christ.

Let those who do not understand the prophets, nor desire to understand them, and who assert that they are content with the Gospel alone, know that they do not understand Christ’s mystery, which had been unknown to all the Gentiles from eternal times.

(Ambrose.) The Apostle asserts that this was shown by the Lord in the time of Christ: what had been hidden was that the Gentiles would become participants in the grace promised in the Law. He says that it was shown to the holy preachers and prophets—that is, to the Apostles and interpreters of the Law—not to the ancient prophets.

Although Gentiles had earlier been admitted to the Law, they were commanded to be circumcised. The prophets knew that the Gentiles would become participants in God’s gift, for they signified this in many places. But this remained hidden: that they would become participants in God’s grace without circumcision, Sabbaths, new moons, and other such observances, so that they might receive the faith of Christ and be saved without the Law.

This is what he says: “In the Spirit the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and participants in his promise in Christ.” For the one who worships God in the Spirit has no need of the works of the Law.

“Through his Gospel I became a minister according to the gift of God’s grace that was given to me according to the operation of his power.” Through the preaching of his ministry he asserts that the gift was made known which God appointed for the Gentiles according to the operation of his power. The operation of his power is evident in this: he raised Christ from the dead, conquering death, in which he saved everyone. The stewardship of his Gospel, however, is this: through it God’s will was recognized, because he decreed to save the Gentiles without the works of the Law.

## To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given.

(Ambrose.) He humbles himself when he calls himself the least, knowing that humility produces progress. For he says that such great grace was given to him that this gift—which had previously been unknown in past ages—was granted to him so that he might make it known to the Gentiles. How can he appear to be the least of all the saints, when, before he was baptized, he was called a vessel of election?

## To evangelize among the nations the unsearchable riches of Christ.

He proves that he was chosen to preach God’s gift in the incomprehensible riches of Christ, which Christ deigned to bestow upon the Gentiles, who had already been without hope, so that they might be saved through faith without the works of the Law [Col. 0417B]. It is clear that no one sends an eminent and very great gift through an unworthy person. Thus, while showing how much he deserved from God, he nevertheless humbles himself, so that his merit may increase.

## And to enlighten everyone concerning the stewardship of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things.

He says that he was sent to teach the Gentiles the mystery in two ways: the mystery that was in God, from whom all things exist, so that through him they might learn and understand that Christ is always in God and with God, and that God had determined to save the Gentiles without circumcision and the other commandments of the Law.

The Jews were found unworthy to have such a great teacher. For the Jews believed in Christ in such a way that they nevertheless continued to observe the Law, which is hateful to God. Thus the Apostles say to their fellow Apostle Paul: “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the Law” (Acts XXI).

It therefore came about that the vessel of election was sent to teach the Gentiles, so that they might have the fullness of their faith, placing their hope in Christ alone and in nothing from the Law. For it was by the manifest sacrament of Christ that such a gift was given, one that would bring salvation to its complete effect.

Just as great gifts are given for great vows, so, when a magnificent mystery was revealed, human beings were endowed with so distinguished a gift as a cause of joy and gladness—one sufficient for them to possess the abundance of salvation.

(Jerome.) I do not think that the Apostle Paul agreed with the secret judgment of his own mind when he truly said that he was the least of all the saints—for example, of those who were in Ephesus, Corinth, Thessalonica, or who had believed throughout the whole world. Although saying that he was the least of all the saints is an indication of humility, it would be a charge of falsehood if he held one thing hidden in his heart and brought another forth on his tongue.

We must therefore find an explanation by which Paul was truly the least of all the saints and yet did not fall from apostolic dignity. The Lord says to the disciples in the Gospel: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him become the least of all; and whoever wishes to be first, let him be the last of all” (Mark IX). Paul fulfilled this in deed when he said: “For I think that God has displayed us Apostles as the last, as men condemned to death.”

Therefore, to all who desired to become weak for Christ’s sake, the Apostle Paul was weaker—and for that reason greater. For he says: “I labored more than all of them, yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me” (I Cor. XV).

Because of this humility, although he was the least of all the saints, this grace was given to him among the Gentiles: to evangelize the unsearchable riches of Christ and to teach the stewardship of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things.

If the riches of Christ are unsearchable, how are they evangelized among the people? If the mystery was hidden from the ages in God, how is it brought forth through Paul among the Gentiles? But “unsearchable” and “hidden” must be understood in two ways: either the riches were formerly unsearchable and have now been opened after the Lord’s Passion; or, certainly, they were by their nature unsearchable for human beings, but have become known because God revealed them.

For it is one thing to reach a secret through one’s own curiosity: once it has been found, it ceases to be unsearchable. It is another thing to be able, by one’s own diligence, to comprehend that secret as well, but through the grace of God. When you know it and show it to others, it nevertheless remains unsearchable, since, as far as you were concerned, it was hidden before it was shown.

The Psalmist testifies that the unsearchable riches of Christ refer also to Christ himself, saying: “How immeasurable is the abundance of your goodness, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. XXX.) These riches of goodness had been hidden from all past ages in the Lord, who is the Creator of all.

Where are Marcion, Valentinus, and all the heretics who assert that one is the creator of the world—that is, of visible things—and another the creator of invisible things, calling the former just and the latter some perpetually unknown and wholly good being who is the Father of Christ? Behold, the God in whom Christ’s mystery was hidden from all past ages is proclaimed to be the Creator of all things. From this it is shown that the God of the New and Old Testaments is the same.

The mystery hidden from the ages can also be understood in another way: the ages themselves were ignorant of it—that is, all the spiritual and rational creatures who existed in the ages. For “the age” is often understood to mean those things that exist in the age, just as Paul says to the Galatians: “That he might rescue us from the present evil age” (Gal. I); and elsewhere (Eph. II): “So that he might show in the ages to come,” meaning, “to all the things that were to exist in the ages that would follow.”

## So that the manifold wisdom of God might be made known through the Church to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places, according to the predetermination of the ages that he accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord.

(Ambrose.) God had such a good purpose concerning this that he not only gave the Gentiles this teacher, but also arranged for the truth of Christ to be made known through him to the spirits in the heavenly places who are called principalities and powers.

They are called powers because they are more powerful among the other spirits; they are called principalities because they rule over the powers. Through the Church—which has been drawn toward life in many different ways—they recognize that the mystery of the one God remains in Christ, and they cease from error.

The same thing is accomplished here: ecclesiastical preaching benefits even them, and they abandon their agreement with the tyranny of the devil, by which he armed himself against faith in the one God through impious presumption. This interpretation is set forth in the twenty-third Psalm, where God is shown to be Lord of the universe, as the Spirit of God says through David: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it.”

(Augustine.) This mystery was therefore hidden from the ages in God in such a way that the manifold wisdom of God might nevertheless be made known through the Church to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places, because the Church first existed there, where after the resurrection this Church also is to be gathered, so that we may be equal as sons of God.

(Jerome.) According to the gift of grace that was given to the Apostle so that he might evangelize the unsearchable riches of Christ and teach among the Gentiles the mystery that had been unknown from the ages, that same sacrament was revealed to him so that the manifold wisdom of God might be made known not only to the Gentiles but also through the Church to the principalities and powers [Col. 0419B]. This wisdom, according to the purpose of the former ages, had long been appointed and now appears to have been brought to completion in Christ.

But if the manifold wisdom of God was unknown to the principalities and powers in heaven—which we ought to understand as the holy ministering powers, although some interpret them as the prince of this air and his angels—and has now been revealed to them through the Church, how much more was it unknown to the patriarchs and prophets, whom we showed above not to have been ignorant of Christ’s mystery, but not to have known it in the manner of the Apostles?

The manifold wisdom of God, called in Greek *πολυποίκιλος* (*polypoikilos*), that is, “manifold” or, so to speak, “variegated in many ways,” has now been revealed through the Church to the principalities and powers. God had formerly determined in his own mind that it would come to be, and we recognize that it has now been perfected from what we see.

The cross of Christ, therefore, benefited not only us but also the angels and all the powers in heaven, and it disclosed a sacrament that they had not previously known. Accordingly, when they see the Lord returning to heaven in the body, they marvel and say: “Who is this who comes up from Edom, whose garments are bright from Bozrah [variant: Bosra], so beautiful in his white robe?” (Isa. LXIII.) And elsewhere: “Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts—he is the King of glory” (Ps. XXIII).

Let us not think, then, that there is a simple faith in the Church, but rather a manifold and varied wisdom, so that it is not merely diverse but distinguished by great variety.

You look upon Christ’s cradle: look at heaven as well. You behold the infant crying in the manger, but at the same time listen to the angels praising. Herod persecutes him, but the Magi worship. The Pharisees do not know him, but the star points him out. He is baptized by a servant, but the voice of God thundering from above is heard. He is immersed in the waters, but a dove descends—or rather, the Spirit in the form of a dove.

He comes to his Passion and fears to suffer; he wishes the cup to pass from him, and he reproves Peter because Peter feared the cup. What is wiser than this seeming folly, or more distinct in variety, or more obscure in wisdom, than what God accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord?

Although, according to the order and connection of the discourse, the Church may be understood by many to have been made, and *πρόθεσις* (*prothesis*), that is, “proposition”—which in Latin expression we have rendered in the neuter gender as *propositum*—nevertheless, “wisdom made in Christ” may resonate more strongly than the other possibilities. For “the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings” (I Cor. I).

If, according to mystical interpretations, it is said that wisdom was made in Christ, let the Arians understand that they vainly boast of the testimony in which Wisdom speaks of herself as created, begotten, and founded at the beginning of God’s ways. Certainly, according to them, if she was created, she could not have been born. But if she was born, how is she also said to have been founded and created?

## In whom we have boldness and access with confidence through faith in him.

It is a great thing, therefore, not only to have boldness, but also to have it with confidence. Nor is it enough merely to have access; for access itself should be firmer, and we should have it with confidence. The beginning and source of this confidence and access is faith in Christ.

Whoever, therefore, does everything with reason and order believes in Christ as Word and Reason. Whoever is able to comprehend wisdom believes in Christ as Wisdom. Whoever understands truth believes in Christ as Truth. Whoever understands righteousness believes in him as Righteousness. There is no need to say more, since I have often been compelled to discuss Christ in the same way.

# BOOK EIGHTEEN

[Col. 0419]

## CHAPTER III FOLLOWS

[Col. 0419D]

## Therefore I ask that you not lose heart because of my tribulations on your behalf, which are your glory.

(Gregory.) Behold, while placed in tribulation, he exhorts others; and by what he himself endures, he strengthens others. He had not, like an ostrich, forgotten his children; rather, he feared greatly that his disciples, seeing in their preacher the disgrace of so many persecutions, might despise the faith in God displayed in him, as though the countless insults of his sufferings might prevail against it.

For this reason he was less troubled by the torments themselves, but feared more for his children because of the temptation caused by his torments. He thought little of the wounds of his own body while he feared wounds of the heart in his children. He himself received the wounds of torments by suffering, but by consoling his children he healed the wounds of their hearts.

Let us therefore consider how great his love must have been, since amid his own pains he feared for others. Let us consider how great a love it is to seek the salvation of one’s children amid one’s own losses and to preserve the state of mind of one’s neighbors even through one’s own humiliation.

(Ambrose.) He warns them not to be scandalized because of the tribulations inflicted upon the saints by the faithless. It belongs to their glory if the disciples are not scandalized by the tribulation of their teacher, being strengthened by this hope: that the oppression of the faithful will be raised up into the glory of the age to come. This is the testing of the faithful: whether they direct their attention to the hope of their faith.

(Jerome.) What the Latin translator expressed as “that you may not lose heart” can, according to the ambiguity of the Greek expression, also be read as “that I may not lose heart,” giving the following meaning: “Therefore I ask that I may not lose heart in my tribulations,” and so forth.

This, then, is what the Apostle asks and earnestly begs from the Lord: that he may not fail amid his afflictions. He saw that he had preached the Gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, had gone to Rome, and either had gone on to Spain or was preparing to go there. The whole world was being lifted from the power of its prince by his teaching; idols were being abandoned; and the temples, deserted by their worshipers, were being filled with squalor and filth.

For this reason the entire army of demons and the whole host of hostile powers, forming a battle line against him, fought so that through tribulations and distress he might cease preaching the Gospel of Christ and eventually, exhausted, take rest.

This is therefore what he says: “I ask that I may not lose heart in my tribulations on your behalf.” Everything I suffer, everything that troubles and constrains me, is for the sake of your salvation, while I desire to announce the Gospel to you; and my tribulations are your glory.

He spoke as though unskilled, joining a singular “glory” to the plural number of “tribulations” when he said, “in my tribulations on your behalf, which is your glory,” instead of saying, “which are your glory.” Unless someone more forcefully and profoundly refers this through a hyperbaton either to “boldness,” or “access,” or “faith,” and says: “In whom we have boldness and access and faith; and this boldness, access, and faith is your glory,” the meaning above should rather be followed.

According to what the Latin expression gives us—“Therefore I ask that you may not lose heart in my tribulations on your behalf, which are your glory”—the passage can also be explained as a request on behalf of the Ephesians, that they should not grow weary and fail amid the Apostle’s pressures, since what follows is more consistent with this meaning.

For this reason I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord [Col. 0421C] Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, so that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, and that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts.

**(Ambrose.)** He says that he prays with bent knees, asking that, since God has deigned to call the Gentiles to know the mystery of his will, he may also grant this, because he is rich: that by his command they may be strengthened in the Spirit. That is, let the bodily calamities inflicted by the faithless not disturb them, but let them remain steadfast, awaiting its reward in the future.

“Christ dwelling through faith in your hearts, in the inner person.” He asks that they be strengthened in this respect, so that they may not doubt but rather believe that Christ dwells within them, although they do not see him with these eyes. He asks that the Spirit given to them may instill this in them as a gift of God, [Col. 0421D] so that they may be certain about Christ: that he lives, that he is the Son of God, and that he dwells through faith in our hearts. When we possess faith in him in our hearts, we seem to possess Christ himself. This advances us insofar as we are secure concerning his help, because he does not abandon us but is always present on account of the faith he sees in us. For this reason his Spirit, who is also the Spirit of God the Father, is given to us, so that in his place he may keep us safe, if we assent to him, and may also reveal hidden things. Through him, therefore, we ought not to doubt that Christ himself dwells in us.

For this is another Paraclete; among them there is a distinction of persons, not of nature, because he receives from him and proceeds from God. For where there is unity of nature, they belong to one another. Hence the Lord says: “Everything that belongs to the Father is mine, and everything that is mine belongs to the Father.” Therefore, he says, I bend my knees to the Father, so that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened.

**(Albert.)** He rightly asks, therefore, that the faith of the Ephesians not fail amid the pressures and hardships that he suffers because he preaches the Gospel to the Ephesians. These pressures are punishments among unbelievers, but glory and victory among the faithful, because to overcome is not to yield to adversaries in hardship.

It must therefore be observed that, just as anyone subject to the Savior is said to bend his knee to him, so one who is the slave of sin and has the spirit of slavery again in fear is written as having bent his knee to sin. Yet when we explain these things spiritually, we do not immediately abolish the literal practice of prayer, by which, with the knee fixed to the ground, we adore God [Col. 0422B] and obtain more readily what we ask of him.

“To the Father,” he says, “of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.” We must therefore ask how every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named from God the Father. He does not say, “from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth was born or created,” but “from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named,” because it is one thing to deserve the name by the designation “fatherhood,” and another to possess fellowship by nature—which belongs to the Son of God alone.

God is both creator and father of Adam, whom he first formed. Hence also, in the Gospel according to Luke, when the genealogy was gradually reckoned upward from Christ through David and Abraham, Scripture says at the end: “The son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God” (Luke 3). This showed that the designation of fatherhood on earth first arose from God [Col. 0422C]. Thus those who are called sons of God receive from him, who is supremely and properly Father, the grace of fatherhood.

But it is asked for what reason every fatherhood in heaven is also named from him. Just as we, who are not descended from Abraham, are called children of Abraham if we have faith, and just as we call the patriarchs and prophets our fathers, provided that sins do not separate us from them, so perhaps angels and the other heavenly powers have rulers of their own kinds whom they rejoice to call fathers.

It may also be said that God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, is Father according to substance, and that the Only-Begotten is not a son by adoption but by nature; whereas the other creatures possess the name of fatherhood by adoption [Col. 0422D].

“That he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit, and that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, in the inner person.” Therefore, he says, I bend my knees to the Father, in whose likeness every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, beseeching and entreating him to grant you the power of his glory—that is, knowledge of and fellowship with his majesty—and to strengthen and confirm you through the Holy Spirit. For there is no strength apart from the Spirit of God.

He strengthens and confirms you in the inner person—for we seek not bodily strength but that of the soul, and we desire the inner rather than the outer person to be strengthened—so that, after Christ has dwelt [Col. 0423A] in the inner person, he may dwell in the ruling faculty of that inner person, that is, in the rational mind, and establish his dwelling and seat there. All this will happen through faith, if we believe in him. This dwelling, which is built through the beginning of faith, has its roots and foundation in love. Concerning this he begins to speak more fully, saying: “Rooted and founded in love, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth.”

**(Gregory.)** God has breadth, because he extends his love even to the gathering of persecutors. He has length, because by patiently enduring us he leads us to the homeland of life. He has height, because he transcends even the understanding of those who have been received into the heavenly assembly [Col. 0423B]. He has depth, because below, among the condemned, he incomprehensibly exercises the judgment of his strictness.

He exercises these four aspects individually in us who are placed in this life: breadth by loving, length by enduring, height by surpassing not only our understanding but also our desires, and depth by displaying his judgment before our eyes and strictly judging the unlawful movements of our thoughts.

Yet no one recognizes how unfathomable his height and depth are unless he has either begun to be lifted by contemplation to the highest things or, resisting hidden impulses, begun to be disturbed by the persistence of temptations. Hence it is said to blessed Job: “He is higher than heaven; what will you do? He is deeper than hell; how will you know?” (Job 11). It is as though it were said plainly: How can you be sufficient to know his depth and excellence, when you do not know either how to rise to the heights by virtue or how to correct yourself amid temptations? 

**(Ambrose.)** It follows: “That you may be rooted in love,” and so forth. He says that the indwelling Spirit or Christ grants this to us, so that we may be founded in the love of God, bound to him by his benefits, and may be able, with the saints—that is, the apostles and prophets—to know God, immeasurable and beyond estimation, exceeding all things by the majesty of his power.

For when he says, “breadth, length, height, and depth,” he signifies this: just as in a sphere length is as great as breadth, and height as great as depth, so in God everything is equal in the immensity of infinity. A sphere is enclosed within a defined boundary; but God not only fills all things, he surpasses them. He is not enclosed, but contains all things within himself, so that he alone is ineffable and infinite. Insufficient thanks are offered for this grace: although he is so great, he deigned through Christ to visit the human being subject to sin and death.

“To know the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge.”

**(Ambrose.)** After the infinite and incomprehensible knowledge and inexpressible clemency of God the Father, he also wishes us to recognize the love of Christ, because it surpasses knowledge—knowledge, that is, human knowledge is understood—so that the love of Christ may be regarded as beyond human understanding.

For who can comprehend the reason for this mystery of love: that God should become human for the sake of humanity, and then die for human beings; that the Lord should do so for servants, the Creator for his creature, the pious one for the impious? Why did he love us in this way? Or what did he seek to possess from us, since he needs nothing? Is this love not beyond human knowledge? Or could any human being show such love to another, although it is unequal and therefore surpasses human imaginings?

He therefore wishes us to know this: our understanding cannot attain it or perceive the depth of Christ’s benefits toward us. Thus we should always be suppliant and devoted to him; and although we cannot in any way repay what we owe, we should persevere in his faith even unto death. For in the magnificence of his majesty he did for us things unworthy of himself, so that we too may serve him insofar as we can.

“That you may be filled with all the fullness of God.”

**(Albinus.)** When we have come to know, with complete trust of mind, that Christ dwells in the inner person, rooted and founded in love, then, together with the other saints, we shall begin to strive toward those things: with a discerning mind we shall comprehend what are breadth, length, depth, and height. Not only this, but we shall also desire to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that after all these things have been completed in us in proper order and due arrangement, we may then be filled with all the fullness of God.

We may understand the height as the angels and the heavenly powers, and the depth as the underworld and the things beneath it. Length and breadth may refer to the intermediate regions situated between the heights and the depths. Since it follows that someone is near either the heavenly regions or the infernal ones, those who begin to advance toward better things, rising toward heavenly and lofty realities, may be called “length”; whereas those who are close to the lower region and fall into vices may be assigned the name “breadth.” For “broad and spacious is the way that leads to death” (Matthew 7).

All these things may also be understood in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ: breadth in the transverse wood, where his arms were extended; height in the part of the wood above the breadth, to which his head was joined; length in the lower part extending beneath the breadth of the wood, to which his whole body was attached; and depth in that part of the cross which was fixed in the earth.

Breadth signifies the extension of love, which is commanded to extend not only toward friends, represented by the right side, but also toward enemies, understood by the left. Height pertains to hope, because all works of love are made firm in the hope of eternal recompense [Col. 0424D]. Length signifies perseverance in good works, concerning which it is said: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10). The invisible depth of the cross demonstrates the divine grace from which all these things proceed and grow.

**(Ambrose.)** Because faith is neither complete in the Father alone nor perfect in the Son alone, he therefore added: “that you may be filled,” he says, “with all the fullness of God.” Thus, through confession and thanksgiving, honor is reserved for the Son just as for the Father, and all things that are from God the Father are believed to have been made and restored through the Son, so that the full perfection of divinity may exist in the confession of believers.

Nothing will be lacking to the Christian when he recognizes that God the Father is altogether immeasurable and confesses the love of Christ as ineffable and surpassing human knowledge.

“Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us—to him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, for ever and ever. Amen.”

**(Jerome.)** To what he had said above—“I bend my knees to the Father,” and so forth—he now adds: “To him who is able,” and so forth. By this he shows that, according to human weakness, he asked for what seemed beneficial to them; but, as concerns the truth of the matter itself, God is able to give more than is asked of him. For we do not know how to pray as we ought, and often ask for things against ourselves, thinking that they are for our benefit.

We read this concerning Paul himself. When he begged that the angel who tormented him might depart from him, he was told: “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12). God is therefore able to grant not only more than we ask, but also more than we understand.

Accordingly, he will grant more than we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us, so that, just as now he gives us certain things not according to our merit but beyond our desires—things that we did not dare ask for and that, even if we had asked, we would not have thought ourselves worthy to receive—so he may also grant the other things that the mind cannot conceive and the tongue cannot express.

Therefore, glory belongs to God himself, first in the Church, which is pure, without spot or wrinkle, and which can therefore receive the glory of God because it is the body of Christ; then in Christ Jesus, because in the body of the assumed human being, whose members are all believers, the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily [Col. 0425C]. This glory does not extend merely through the present age and end with future ages, but remains, grows, and increases throughout all generations and for ever and ever in ineffable eternity.

**(Ambrose.)** “To him,” he says, “who is able to do abundantly beyond all things that we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us—to him be glory in Christ Jesus and in the Church throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

He refers this to the person of the Father, so that, because he knows better what is beneficial and what should not be asked, and when things should be given and what kind and how great they ought to be, he himself may govern those who believe in him by his providence and power.

Glory is therefore given to him in Christ Jesus because through Christ he provides everything for us, and because the Father’s honor is in the Son and in the Church—that is, in the people whom he deigned to adopt. For the glory of the Father is in the splendor of his children, as the Lord says: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5). “For ever and ever. Amen,” that is, in eternity, truly.

## CHAPTER IV

The Apostle instructs the Ephesians to preserve ecclesiastical unity through the connection and distinction of the members; then he leads them toward moral uprightness.

“I therefore, a prisoner in the Lord, beseech you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called.”

**(Ambrose.)** He exhorts them, so that by walking rightly in the Lord’s commandments they may be able to attain the promised glory. For just as a skilled physician beseeches the sick to conduct themselves properly so that they may recover sound health, so the teacher of the Gentiles [Col. 0426A] exhorts them, by performing works worthy of their faith, to receive what has been promised to the saints, knowing that this progress contributes to his own glory.

“With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”

**(Ambrose.)** Here he forbids dissension. He urges them to pursue love, lest they lose the Spirit of power and peace, and therefore to bear with one another patiently. For modesty produces progress: when they tolerate one another, correcting one another with gentleness of spirit, they are brought to improvement, and peace will remain in them. Through peace they will rightly be called children of God, because the Lord said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.”

Disturbance or unrest produces contention, which is accustomed even to defend things it knows to be evil, lest it appear to yield [Col. 0426B]. From this discord arises, and discord corrupts the bonds of peace.

**(Albinus.)** The Apostle, established in the bonds of Christ and in prison for martyrdom, could indeed write this. But it is better to say that he was bound in the love of our Lord Jesus Christ, as Clement also testifies in writing to the Corinthians: “Who can declare the bond of the love of God?” Those who love Christ follow him, bound by the ties of love.

As for his saying, “that you may walk worthily of the calling with which you were called,” one should be considered to walk worthily of his calling who enters through him who says: “I am the way”; who does not turn to the right or the left; who turns his foot away from every evil way; and in whom this is fulfilled: “The steps of a human being are directed by the Lord” (Psalm 36).

“With all humility and gentleness, with patience.” Whoever knows that he is earth and ashes, and that shortly he will be dissolved into dust, will never be lifted up by pride. Whoever, having contemplated God’s eternity, considers the brief span of human life, almost the length of a moment, will keep death always before his eyes and will be humble and cast down.

Therefore, let us say with complete humility and truth: “Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor are my eyes lifted up” (Psalm 130). True humility exists not so much in speech as in the mind, so that our conscience knows us to be humble; we should never think that we know, understand, or are anything.

Gentleness is likewise that which is disturbed by no passion and is not especially broken by anger or fury. Whoever possesses it will attain the blessedness promised by the Lord’s word, so that he may possess the earth—that is, command and rule his own body. When the body has been subjected, this is his first inheritance: to live in the flesh, but not according to the flesh.

“Bearing with one another in love” with patience: the patient person returns injury to no one and repays evil to no one with evil, fulfilling what the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good” (Romans 12).

We ought to bear with one another in love, not merely so that we may be praised, but so that the person whom we support may benefit unto salvation. If someone helps another in any tribulation, he will be praised in love for carrying another’s burden. But whoever has done none of these things does not possess brotherly love.

“Eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” This passage is especially directed against heretics, who, after destroying and corrupting the bond of peace, think that they possess the unity of the Spirit, although the unity of the Spirit is preserved in the bond of peace. We, however, must diligently guard the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, because nothing pleases God without peace—not even an offering at the altar.

“One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling.”

**(Ambrose.)** He added this on account of peace and harmony: because the Church is one body, the people should have one mind, since what is believed is one.

“One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in us all.”

Here he continues to commend unity. Since the unity to which we are called is one, we should disagree in nothing. For if there is one Lord—that is, Christ—as he himself says in the Gospel, “Your teacher is one, Christ”; one faith; one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is over all, through all, and in all believers, then the people should have one mind and one heart, because the things he enumerates belong to unity and agree in every respect.

He says that God the Father is over all because he owes his existence to no one, and therefore is over all and through all. He is through all because all things are from him, and it is necessary that he be above all these things that are from him. “And in us all,” that is, in the faithful. He is in us through confession, because we confess him, and because he has given us his Spirit, through whom he is undoubtedly in us. He is not in the pagans, because they deny that he is the Father of Christ.

**(Albinus.)** There is one Lord and one God, because the dominion of the Father and the Son is one, and their divinity is one. Therefore faith is also called one, because we believe alike in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. There is also one baptism, for we are baptized in the same way into the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and we are immersed three times, so that the one sacrament of the Trinity may be made manifest. We are not baptized into the names of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but into one name, which is understood to be God.

The diversity of these prepositions—“over,” “through,” and “in”—demonstrates the distinction of the persons in God: the Father is over all, because he is the source of all; the Son is through all, because all things were created through the Son; and the Holy Spirit is in all, because he is given to believers, and we are the temple of the Holy Spirit, with whom the Father and the Son dwell in us.

“But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift.”

Although God, the holy Trinity, is over all, through all, and in all, grace is nevertheless given to believers according to a measure. This does not mean that the Holy Spirit has a measure—for there is no end to his magnificence—but that he is given to each according to a measure, according to what is useful for the recipient. That is, he bestows as much of the gift as the one to whom it is given is able to receive. For God, the giver of gifts, knows what is appropriate to give to each person.

**(Ambrose.)** Now, lest the diversity of gifts among human beings harm unity, he removes this objection by showing that the diversity lies in the functions of the gifts, not in nature. He says that each person is given as much grace as the Lord has deigned to bestow, but not without a measure of equity, because he will grant to each according to his abilities, so that each may draw as much as he thirsts for.

Therefore he says: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings.” This is written in Psalm 67. Yet he began to bestow these gifts after his triumphs. For, conquering death, he was exalted on the cross, as he himself had said: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw everything to myself” (John 12).

He stripped the underworld when he took away those captives whom it held under bondage because of Adam’s transgression or their own sins, as they consented to him; and, ascending from there into heaven, he brought them with him. Some of them, rising in their bodies, appeared; many appeared as a testimony that death had been defeated, so that those who perhaps would not have believed in Christ’s resurrection might be convinced by the resurrection of people whom they knew to have died.

They saw people whom they recognized as having lived previously. Although captives are led away unwillingly and as belonging to another, the Savior nevertheless led them as his own and as willing captives. For when his appearance provoked those who desired liberation, he is said to have captured them.

**(Albert.)** Since he had said above, “Grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift,” in order to confirm these same gifts, which he shortly afterward also enumerates by saying, “And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers,” he showed that they too were given by the Savior. He drew testimony from Psalm 67, so that we might know that the spoils distributed among human beings were those which Christ, the victor, had won.

“For ascending on high, he led captivity captive.” We who now believe in Christ, gathered from the Gentiles, although we were creatures of God, had been captured by the devil and distributed among his minions. Our Lord Jesus Christ therefore came, according to Ezekiel [Ezek. 12], carrying the vessels of captivity with him. With his head covered so that his adversaries would not recognize him, he preached to the captives release and to those held in chains liberation. He freed us from the chains and fetters of our enemies, and, once liberated and rescued from the old captivity through a new captivity, he led us with him into heaven.

To those very people whom he victoriously rescued from the enemy’s hand he granted diverse gifts of grace. The Apostle repeats all this so that, because he had said above, “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace,” he might teach that the Church is harmonious in its diverse charisms. That is, just as there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God the Father, so we too should be one in love in the bond of peace, preserving the unity of the Spirit.

“But what does ‘he ascended’ mean except that he also descended into the lower parts of the earth?”

**(Ambrose.)** It is true that he descended in order to ascend—not like human beings, who descended in order to remain there. For they were held in the underworld by sentence, but that sentence could not hold the Savior, who conquered sin.

After triumphing over the devil, he descended into the heart of the earth, so that his manifestation might be a preaching to the dead, and so that all who desired him might be freed. He could not fail to ascend, because he had descended for this purpose: by the force of his power to trample death and rise with the captives for whose sake he had permitted himself to suffer [Col. 0429A].

**(Jerome.)** The one who is now said to have ascended is said to have ascended because he had previously descended. This is what the words mean: “But what does ‘he ascended’ mean except that he also descended?”

We must therefore inquire concerning what is written elsewhere: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3). How did he ascend after first descending? When he said these things after the descent from heaven, he showed that he had once ascended to heaven.

We must also reconsider how this descent and ascent should be understood: whether bodily, locally; spiritually, above the body; or in both ways. The lower parts of the earth are understood as the underworld, to which our Lord and Savior descended, so that, ascending victoriously with him into heaven, he might lead away the souls of the saints who were held enclosed there.

Hence, after his resurrection, many bodies of the righteous were seen in the holy city. That the underworld is in the lower part of the earth is also testified by the Psalmist, who says: “The earth opened and swallowed Dathan and covered the assembly of Abiron” (Psalm 105); the same matter is explained more fully in the Book of Numbers. Elsewhere too we read: “Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into the underworld” (Psalm 54).

“The one who descended is also the one who ascended above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things.”

**(Ambrose.)** This is what the Lord says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.” This is also contained in the Psalm, which says: “His going forth is from the summit of heaven, and his course reaches to its summit” (Psalm 18).

Thus, descending from heaven, he was born as a human being on earth. After his death he descended into the underworld; rising from it on the third day, he ascended before all mortals above all the heavens, so that he might show creation that death had been mocked.

**(Maurus.)** When he says “the one,” he indicates that the one who descended and the one who ascended are one person.

**(Albinus.)** Did he pass bodily through all the heavens, through all the heights and the circles of the heavens that philosophers call spheres, and, transcending them, stand at the summit of heaven? Or should he rather be believed to have transcended and surpassed all corporeal things, and, contemplating eternal realities, to have remained above the heavens—that is, above invisible things? I consider the latter view better.

The Son of God therefore descended into the lower parts of the earth and ascended above all the heavens, so that he might fulfill not only the Law and the Prophets but also certain other hidden dispensations, which he alone knows, accomplishing them with the Father. For we cannot fully know how the blood of Christ benefited both the angels and those who were in hell; nevertheless, we cannot be ignorant that it benefited them.

**(Maurus.)** “But what does ‘he ascended’ mean except that he descended?” This is effective against the heretics who say that Christ did not exist before the birth of the blessed Virgin Mary. Christ is not God by development; rather, out of the mercy we needed, he graciously became human.

“And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ.”

He explains why Christ is said to have ascended, although he was everywhere: clearly, this is according to the form of a servant, into which he had descended graciously, not locally. He then shows that through the same person God’s elect received gifts according to various ranks in the Church.

The first order in the Church of Christ is the authority of the apostles, who were sent by the Lord himself, the Son of God, and are therefore called apostles. To them the Lord himself said after his resurrection: “Go, teach all nations” (Matthew 28).

Second are the prophets—not those who predict future events, as did the prophets of the Old Testament, but those who rebuke and judge the faithless and ignorant and proclaim the destruction that awaits them if they remain unconverted. Those who inspire human minds through preaching with the sweetness of the kingdom of God are also prophets.

Third are the evangelists, whose feet are beautiful for announcing peace (Romans 10). Whoever faithfully announces the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding, whether to one person or to many, is an evangelist.

“Others as pastors and teachers”: whoever is a pastor should also be a teacher, so that no one, however holy, may dare assume the name and office of pastor unless he is able to teach those over whom he appears to preside.

**(Ambrose.)** The apostles are bishops; the prophets are interpreters of the Scriptures, although in the earliest beginnings there were prophets such as Agabus and the four prophetic virgins, as is contained in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 11; 21), for the instruction of beginners in the faith.

Now interpreters are called prophets. Evangelists are deacons, as Philip was. Although they are not priests, they can nevertheless evangelize without a chair, as did Stephen and the aforementioned Philip (Acts 8).

Pastors may be lectors, who nourish the listening people through readings, because “a human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word” (Matthew 4). Teachers are exorcists, because in the Church they restrain and chastise the disorderly; or they are those who customarily instruct children who are to be taught through readings, as is the custom of the Jews. Their tradition passed over to us, but through negligence it has grown obsolete.

Among these, after the bishop, the one who is said to prophesy because the hidden meaning of Scripture has been opened to him is understood to hold the greater place, especially because he brings forth words of future hope. This order may now be that of the presbyterate.

For all orders exist in the bishop, because he is first a priest—that is, chief of priests—and also a prophet and an evangelist, along with the other offices to be fulfilled in the ministry of the faithful. Yet after churches had been established in every place and their offices ordered, the arrangement became different from what it had been at the beginning.

At first everyone taught and everyone baptized whenever an opportunity arose, on whatever day or at whatever time. Philip did not seek a time or day on which to baptize the eunuch (Acts 8), nor did he insert a fast. Paul and Silas did not delay the time when they baptized the jailer and all his household (Acts 16). Peter did not have clerics or seek a day when he baptized Cornelius and his entire household (Acts 10). Nor did he himself baptize them; rather, he ordered the brothers who had gone with him from Joppa to Cornelius to baptize them. For at that time no one had yet been ordained except the seven deacons.

Therefore, so that the people might grow and multiply, at the beginning everyone was permitted to evangelize, baptize, and explain the Scriptures in the church. But once the Church had spread throughout all regions, assemblies were established, and rulers and the other offices were ordered in the churches, so that no one from the clergy who had not been ordained would dare assume an office that he knew had not been entrusted or granted to him [Col. 0431B]. The Church began to be governed by another order and form of oversight.

For if everyone could do the same things, it would be irrational, and the matter would appear common and utterly worthless. Hence it is that now deacons do not preach among the people, nor do clerics or laypeople baptize, nor are believers immersed on just any day, except when they are ill.

For this reason the Apostle’s writings do not entirely correspond to the ordination that now exists in the Church, since they were written during the earliest beginnings. He even calls Timothy, whom he had appointed a presbyter, a bishop, because the first presbyters were called bishops, so that when one departed, the next would succeed him. Finally, in Egypt the presbyters confirm people when the bishop is absent.

But when later presbyters began to be found unworthy of holding primacy, the arrangement was changed through the foresight of a council, so that merit rather than rank would create a bishop, established by the judgment of many priests. This was done so that an unworthy person would not rashly usurp the office and become a scandal to many.

Under the Law, priests were born from the tribe of Aaron, the Levite tribe. Now all are of priestly descent, as the Apostle Peter says: “You are a royal and priestly race” (1 Peter 2). Therefore a priest may be made from the people.

“For the building up of the body of Christ.” He says that the ordering of the Church was arranged according to the joining together of the human body, into the unity of its confession, so that although they differ in dignity, all may be one in Christ, having one head, Christ—that is, the author of life.

Until we all attain the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God. (Ambrose.) He says that this order is to remain for as long as all those destined for life are of one faith in the knowledge of Christ. To a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ. He exhorts us to labor in such a way that the perfection of faith may be grasped. Its principle is this: faith must hold Christ to be perfect and fully God, and must not measure him by human standards, but regard him as perfect God in the fullness of divinity. For by saying “perfect man,” he does not signify temporal age and measure; rather, by this expression he wishes us to become perfect in the fullness of our understanding of the divinity of the Son of God.

(Albinus.) There are some who think, on the basis of the apostle’s statement, that all will rise again to the age of Christ—the age he had when he suffered—so that each person will receive the measure of his own body, whether the measure he had in youth, even if he died an old man, or the measure he would have attained had he not died before reaching the full stature of his body. Or, if this view is not acceptable because of the idea of perfection, let us understand it as referring to the whole body of Christ, into which all the saints must come together, so that there may be one body through its various members. Christ holds the office of the one head; therefore he prefaced the statement with “to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God.” This unity of Christ’s body exists only in the knowledge of Christ and in the unity of the Catholic faith.

Thus we must labor with every effort, first to attain the unity of faith, and then, within that same unity, to possess the knowledge of the Son of God. When possession of these things has become secure, we shall cease to be little ones and shall receive the measure of the inner man—the measure of the fullness, which is the measure of Christ—and shall receive the name of perfect men. [Col. 0432B] Yet this is so that the whole multitude of believers may reach the consummate age of the fullness of Christ. Then he immediately added, saying: So that we may no longer be little ones, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine, by the wickedness of men, by cunning directed toward the deception of error.

(Ambrose.) He wishes us to be founded and established in the discipline of the Catholic faith, which the apostle Peter professed after God had revealed it. He does not want us to be blown about in error by the pestilential assertions of various heresies, inventions of human wickedness, so that through them the error of the deceiver may be introduced under the name of truth. This is the remedy of falsehood: that it introduces error under the pretext of truth. He also warns us not to wander, once we have become believers, as fragile and uncertain concerning the promised hope, as we wandered before receiving the faith—humble in understanding and drifting through various errors. Since we have become Christians, we ought to be founded, for there is no ambiguity in our faith; it is commended by the power of miracles.

(Jerome.) Since he says, “so that we may no longer be little ones, tossed about,” and so forth, while also confessing himself to be tossed about and little, it should be considered whether he spoke in humility, or whether, seeing in part and knowing in part, he understood how far he was from perfect knowledge and burst forth in words expressing his true consciousness. If someone wishes to say that he spoke in humility, let him use this example: “When I was a little one, I spoke as a little one, I understood as a little one, I thought as a little one; but when I became a man, I put away the things of a little one.” Another may respond to this by saying that, in comparison with many, the Apostle had reached the age of a perfect man, but that, in relation to the things laid up for the saints, he was still called little.

Indeed, the prophet calls all the apostles who believe in Christ little ones, saying: “Behold, I and the little ones whom the Lord has given me” (Genesis 33). After this, the matter must be discussed more attentively, lest perhaps, in humility, the Apostle should have called himself not only little but also tossed about and carried in different directions by every wind of doctrines, into the deceit of men, into wickedness directed toward the deception of error.

But the one who wishes him to have spoken not from humility but from consciousness says: The apostle Paul was a man of sharp and keen intelligence, and, at the first attempts of disputants, he foresaw with discerning mind what arguments would need to be introduced. He therefore often saw both sides arguing in such a way, and asserting propositions so plausible in matters opposed to one another, that they caused the hearer to doubt. For this reason, as a human being still enclosed in a fragile body, he was indeed carried about by every wind of doctrine, but he was not dashed to pieces.

He stood at the stern, holding the helm, and broke the foaming waves of heresies against the security of faith; yet he was not altogether fearless, secure, tranquil, or calm. He watched the winds blowing from every side, caught their contrary arguments with attentive ear, and overcame them, but his victory was not secure for him. Since he saw that the words and arguments of his adversaries, by which they attempted to overturn the truth, could not easily be overcome, and were full of every kind of cunning, woven together by the art of dialectic—or rather by the art of the devil—he hoped for God’s help, so that God might drive every doubt from his mind and enable him to believe the truth firmly and immovably, without that distress, and to increase in love for Christ, whom he knew to be the head of the whole body of the Church.

But doing the truth in love, let us grow in every way into him who is the head, Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and held together through every supporting joint, according to the working apportioned to each individual member, makes the body grow for its own upbuilding in love.

At the end of all things, when we have begun to see God face to face, and have reached the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ, from whose fullness we have all now received, so that Christ may not be only partly in us but wholly in us; and when, having left behind the beginnings of little ones, we have grown into that man of whom the prophet says, “Behold, a man; Orient is his name” (Zechariah 6), and whom John the Baptist recalls in the words, “After me comes a man who was made before me, because he was before me” (John 1)—then, at the meeting in one faith and one knowledge of the Son of God, whom now, because of the variety of minds, we do not all know with one and the same understanding and knowledge, the whole body, which had previously been scattered and torn apart in different directions, will be restored to its proper framework and union.

Then one ministry and the consummate perfection of one age will cause the whole body to grow equally, and all its members will receive the increase of age according to their measure. This entire edifice, by which the body of the Church grows in its several parts, will be completed through mutual love, when the true physician, Christ Jesus, comes to heal the body of the whole Church, now scattered and torn apart, and to restore to each member its proper dignity according to the quality of its merits, so that one love may flourish in all and perfect blessedness may be brought to perfection.

All these things will happen in such a way that the members are joined to one another in love; and while one member rejoices with another and takes pleasure in another’s joy, the body of Christ—that is, the Church of the saints—will dwell in the heavenly Jerusalem, which the Apostle elsewhere calls the mother of the saints.

(Ambrose.) He explains why he said that Christ is the head of all. For, he says, from him the whole body—that is, the entire company of archangels, powers, principalities, and authorities—subsists. Although each of these has its own number and consists of legions, as the Lord himself said, nevertheless, because all are from one and through one, he calls them all together one body.

For just as the members, although belonging to one body, are nevertheless diverse in activity and dignity, so creation was made by God through Christ. From the cherubim and seraphim—the mighty ones [“powers”] who are beneath God’s throne—and from the angels whom the Lord himself calls holy, there is, as it were, a kind of concatenation, ordered and descending as far as the firmament, so that everything is joined together while nevertheless being distinguished according to merits. I say “according to merits” not only of offices but also of natures.

For when he says that all things are joined together, he does not mean that they will all have one nature. Rather, just as the members of a body are distinguished by their functions, not by their nature, so in all these things it is not the members but the natures themselves that make the distinctions.

This, then, is the work being accomplished: that all may be brought back to one understanding and that there may be one body in understanding, while the confession of all creation is one, so that it may agree in love of the Creator for its own advancement. For it rebuilds itself into the temple of the Lord; it had been destroyed by the madness and fury of the devil.

Therefore I say this and testify in the Lord: you must no longer walk as the Gentiles walk, in the vanity of their understanding, having their intellect darkened, alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them because of the blindness of their hearts. They, having become despairing, have given themselves over to shamelessness, to the practice of every impurity and greed.

Once the Creator has been revealed and the reason shown that creation ought to follow, he bears witness against them before their God, so that they may not walk or think otherwise than they have been taught. They must not be found like the Gentiles, who neither receive the faith nor possess the conduct commanded by the law, whose understanding is darkened, and who do not esteem the truth of the divine name.

For while they pursue vanities—that is, idolatry—they are restrained by the devil from walking in the way of the one God, so that he may make them companions in his own destruction. He signifies that the Gentiles have blindness of heart because they despair of the future resurrection. As though they would not exist thereafter, they defile their lives with the most shameful actions, unwilling to submit themselves to the law of faith, because it forbids pleasure for the sake of the hope of the future life. They therefore judge that hope worthy of mockery, so that they may seem, with good reason, to dishonor themselves and desire what belongs to others with greedy lust, as though after this life there were no life.

(Albinus.) “Therefore,” he says, “I say this to you, Ephesians, and I testify to you that, since you are going to attain the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ, you must not walk as the Gentiles walk.” They serve idols and misuse, perversely in mind and understanding, the gifts of God. They received soul and understanding for the purpose of knowing God, but they have been alienated from his way, and we know no other way apart from Christ; and they walk in the blindness of their hearts.

Would that it were enough merely to have sinned, and that they might, even at a late hour, do penance and condemn the vices to which they have continually panted, so that there might be a remedy in looking back [or, repenting] after error. But now, despairing and plunging themselves, in the irrational manner of beasts, into filth and the abyss, they have given themselves over to shamelessness and lust. They do whatever the body wishes, the mind desires, and lust suggests; and, since they have omitted nothing at all that is unclean, they have done all this in greed, for they are never satisfied by indulging their lust. Their pleasure has no limit.

Or else, going beyond the union permitted between man and woman, they proceed to greater excesses, men committing shameful acts with men and receiving in themselves the due reward of their error.

(Maurus.) He introduces two kinds of sin, both exceedingly destructive: lust in the desire of the flesh, and greed in worldly ambition. To these two evils he adds a third, the abyss of despair, because they are unwilling to do penance for such deeds. There can be no doubt that this is the most destructive element in all sins.

But you did not learn Christ in this way, if indeed you heard him and were taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus.

(Ambrose.) It is clear that Christians have not learned despair after this death, but hope concerning both outcomes. Life is promised to the faithful, but death—eternal punishment—to the faithless. Thus, whether death or life is in view, it is learned in Christ: whoever follows him will rise through him to life, but whoever separates himself from him will through him be handed over to Gehenna, for he will be condemned by Christ as judge.

And since there are some in the Church who, under the name of Christ, do not follow the truth, he says, “as the truth is in Jesus,” so that, if they have been taught in the way that the truth is in Jesus, they may be seen to have learned Christ, heard him, and been taught in him. Christ teaches concerning himself what he is, how great he should be believed to be, what hope exists in him, and what those who believe ought to be like.

Whoever has learned Christ knows that he rose from the dead so that he might be an example to believers. Therefore there is great hope after this death for those who love God.

(Albinus.) To learn Christ is the same thing as to know him: that is, to know and love holy virtues. It is as though he were saying: To learn Christ is to hear wisdom, justice, fortitude, temperance, and the other virtues in which Christ is understood—or rather, because Christ is all these things, to know Christ is to practice these and similar virtues, especially love, which is the head and perfection of all virtues.

Therefore, if someone has heard, learned, and loves Christ, he will not walk in the vanity of his understanding, nor will he walk with his mind darkened, nor will he be alienated from the life of God. He will also possess knowledge once ignorance has been dispelled; and, when light has been introduced into the darkness, all blindness will be removed from the eyes of his heart. If he possesses this, he will not give himself over to carnal impurity or worldly ambition.

As the truth is in Jesus: for the fullness of truth—that is, the whole truth—dwelt in none of the patriarchs or prophets, but only in Jesus. The others knew in part and prophesied in part, and through a mirror, in an enigma; in Jesus alone all the truth of God appeared, and it speaks boldly: “I am the Truth” (John 14).

(Maurus.) This may also be understood in another way. Just as a shadow differs from a body, and the shadow is a kind of sign of the true body, so the law was a shadow, while Christ was the truth. From his fullness we all receive, and grace upon grace, because “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.”

To put off, with respect to your former way of life, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error.

(Ambrose.) Whoever has heard Christ—that is, learned him—has learned to depart from his former way of life, which he calls the old man because of the past time of ignorance. The one and the same person is therefore called old if he follows his former vices; but if he walks in the newness of life, alienated from worldly error, whether in conduct or in understanding, he is called new—not in the substance of flesh and soul, but in understanding and manner of life.

The old man is nevertheless called corrupted because of adulterous understanding and shameful life.

(Albinus.) Since, according to the order and wording of the passage, the sentence appears to overflow and to involve hyperbaton, it should be read in this way: “But you did not so learn Christ, if indeed you heard him and were taught in him, to put off, with respect to your former way of life, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error, as the truth is in Jesus.” The sense is: As the truth is in Jesus, so it will also be in you who have learned Christ, heard him, and been taught to put off, with respect to your former way of life, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error.

I think that the old man whom he commands to be put off is called old because he has grown old in wickedness. For, always erring according to his former way of life and the desires of error, and failing in the work of corruption, he is corrupted and violated. Since he is continually engaged in the desires of error and never ceases from vice, he is not merely called “corrupted,” but “being corrupted,” because each day, each hour, each point and moment, he is corrupted, violated, and continually becomes worse.

But be renewed in the spirit of your mind.

(Gregory.) To accomplish these things, the examples of the fathers and the precepts of sacred speech greatly assist us. For when we look upon the deeds of the saints and lend our ear to divine commands, some things that we contemplate and others that we hear set us ablaze; and our heart is not constricted by sluggishness when it is stirred to imitation.

And put on the new man, who was created according to God in the justice and holiness of truth.

(Ambrose.) It is just and true to follow the right way. The one who follows the right way is devoted to his Creator and walks in his will, which the Gentiles do not know. Renewed in the spirit of his mind, he is said to have put on the new man, who is Christ. For the one who has been reborn through faith in Christ puts on Christ and strives after the life Christ handed down, so that he may appear to have been created according to God.

A person is created in that which he understands; therefore the truth and justice of God are unknown to the Gentiles. When believers acknowledge God as Creator and keep his commandments, they are created in justice and truth.

(Albinus.) We are not renewed in understanding without the spirit, nor in the spirit without understanding. Rather, we are renewed when the spirit of our understanding is joined together, so that, just as we sing with the spirit, we may also sing with understanding; and just as we pray with the spirit, we may also pray with understanding.
