Thus may the spirit of our understanding be renewed, so that, when our understanding has become clean and purified and has been separated from every stain of sordid co-creation, the spirit may also be joined to it. In this way they are united with one another by a kind of bond of unity, so that it is no longer called a simple spirit but the spirit of understanding.

When we have been renewed in the spirit, which is the spirit of our understanding, then we shall put on the new man, who was created according to God. I think that this is the same thing expressed in other words as is said elsewhere: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 13).

This is the new man with whom all believers ought to clothe and cover themselves. For what was not new in the man assumed by our Savior? His conception, birth, delivery, infancy, teaching, life, virtues, and finally the cross and passion, by which he stripped the principalities and opposing powers; also his resurrection and ascension into heaven.

He, therefore, was truly created in justice and holiness of truth, because he was the true Son of the true God, and the whole worship and justice of God was completed in him in truth.

(Augustine.) What he says—“created according to God”—is expressed elsewhere as “according to the image of God.” But by sinning he lost the justice and holiness of truth, and therefore this image became disfigured and discolored. He receives it again when he is reformed and renewed.

When he says, “in the spirit of your mind,” he did not intend two things to be understood there, as though the mind were one thing and the spirit of the mind another. Rather, because every mind is spirit, though not every spirit is mind. There is also the Spirit who is God, who cannot be renewed because he cannot grow old. And there is a spirit in human beings that is not mind, to which belong imaginations resembling bodies; concerning this he says to the Corinthians: “But if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful” (1 Corinthians 14).

He says this when what is spoken is not understood, because it cannot be spoken unless images of bodily sounds in the spirit precede, in thought, the sounds of the mouth.

The human soul is also called spirit. Hence we read in the Gospel: “He bowed his head and gave up his spirit” (John 18), by which the death of the body is signified when the soul departs.

A little later, therefore, because spirit is spoken of in so many ways, he wished “the spirit of the mind” to mean that spirit which is called mind. Thus, when the same Apostle says, “in the putting off of the body of the flesh,” he did not intend two things to be understood, as though flesh were one thing and the body of flesh another, but because “body” is a name applied to many things, none of which is flesh.

Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak the truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members of one another.

(Albinus.) Far be it from us to understand this as though he had permitted us to speak falsehood to those who are not yet members of the body of Christ. Rather, it is said because each of us ought to regard another as what he wishes that person to become for him, even if he has not yet become so.

In this passage he truly calls every human being a neighbor, since every person is generated from the same parent as we are, namely Adam. The Gospel parable makes this clear in the case of the man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among robbers, and, while the priest and Levite passed by, was cared for by a Samaritan and brought to an innkeeper (Luke 10).

After this, the Lord affirms that the neighbor is the one who showed him mercy, wishing to demonstrate that all people are neighbors to all others. But what follows—“because we are members of one another”—seems to me rather to signify a mystery and to be spoken of those who are our neighbors in faith and virtue. For people are not members of one another except the faithful of the faithful and Christians of Christians.

Therefore he commands that each person proclaim to another the things of God, which are full of truth, and speak truth with his neighbor—that is, proclaim Christ, who is the truth.

(Augustine.) Every human being is a neighbor; we are all neighbors by the earthly condition of our birth. In another sense, because of the hope of the heavenly inheritance, you ought to regard every human being as your neighbor, even before he is a Christian. For you do not know what he will become before God. Someone who is now a Jew, heretic, or pagan may perhaps, through God’s mercy, be converted to the Lord in such a way that he may deserve to hold the first place among the saints.

(Ambrose.) Since we have been created in truth and justice and reborn in baptism, we are commanded to put away falsehood so that we may remain in that condition, taking up truth and doing nothing deceitful with our brother. Because we are members of one body, we should support one another in truth in matters affecting us.

Be angry and do not sin.

Since a person cannot be forbidden to become angry—especially because anger is a natural impulse arising from causes and can often contribute to the correction of the offender—he says that one should become angry, but he warns that one must not sin through anger.

For we are accustomed to overstep the bounds when we become angry, and we ourselves are found to sin while reproving sinners, when we become more angry and burden the sinner more heavily than he deserves. He therefore teaches that anger itself must be exercised with moderation.

Nor should anyone display excessive justice toward the offender. Some people sin in such a way that they seem to deserve blows so severe that they cannot endure them; and one who might perhaps have been corrected is removed from life—not without sin on the part of the angry person.

Hence Solomon also says: “Do not be excessively righteous, for there is one who perishes through his own righteousness” (Ecclesiastes 7). We ought to imitate God, who exercises justice with restraint. Although it would be just for the wicked to be punished, in his patience he bears with them so that some of them may be corrected. He bears with us, his own servants, when we sin, and does not quickly strike anyone.

(Jerome.) There is no doubt that what he says—“Be angry and do not sin”—is taken from the fourth Psalm. It seems contrary to what is said elsewhere: “But now put away from yourselves all anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, and shameful speech from your mouth” (Colossians 3).

Yet even a simple interpretation is harmful if people think that the reins of anger have been loosened. The word “anger” has a twofold meaning, not only among us but also among philosophers: either when, having been provoked by an injury, we are stirred by natural impulses; or when the initial surge and fury have subsided, the mind is able to exercise judgment and nevertheless desires vengeance against the person thought to have caused the injury.

I therefore think that the present passage refers to the former kind of anger. It is granted to us as human beings that, at the sight of something undeserving, we may be moved and that the tranquillity of our mind may be disturbed like a gentle breeze. Yet we must never be lifted up by swelling waves through the force of fury.

(Albinus.) Perhaps both kinds can be understood in this passage, because at times the anger of a teacher benefits a pupil, and a father’s anger teaches his son more than unrestrained indulgence. Anger is natural to human beings when they become angry over sins, as is the will to desire what is good. But reason, which has been given to human beings as their mistress, must regulate both, so that neither goes beyond what necessity requires.

For this reason he immediately adds: Let not the sun go down upon your anger.

(Augustine.) Accordingly, the Apostle here commands that the sun of reason not be darkened by excessive anger and become enveloped in the full darkness of resentment.

The statement may indeed be understood according to time: if anger, arising from the condition and weakness of mortality that we carry, steals upon a Christian, it ought not to be held for long or allowed to become yesterday’s anger. Cast it out of your heart before this visible light sets, lest that invisible light abandon you.

But it is better understood in another way: our sun of justice and truth is Christ, whose truth illuminates the human soul and toward whom the angels rejoice. Although the weakened vision of human hearts trembles beneath his rays, it is nevertheless purified by the commandments so that it may contemplate him.

When that sun begins to dwell in a person through faith, he must not allow such anger to be seen in him that the sun sets upon his anger—that is, that Christ abandons his mind, because Christ does not wish to dwell together with his anger.

(Jerome.) Since the true sun sets upon wicked prophets, according to what is written, “The sun has set at noon upon your prophets” (Amos 8), and likewise sets upon all sinners, granting them none of the light of his rising, the Apostle now commands that we must not, overcome by fury, do things through which the sun may set upon us and the ruling power of the heart be enveloped in darkness.

Some think that this should be understood simply in the same way as the passage from the fourth Psalm, from which it appears to have been taken: “What you say in your hearts, in your chambers, be pierced”—that is, whatever you sin in the day by deed, word, or thought, cleanse it through repentance during the night. Let anger be brief and not be postponed until the following day.

And do not give place to the devil.

(Ambrose.) He wants anger to pass away and not be retained in the breast, so that it may rise and set with the day. For if it remains in the mind, it gives the devil an opportunity to boast. An angry mind must think evil, which is what the devil desires. He finds a mind prepared for evil, and by inserting himself into it through his own inclination, he deceives the human being who was made for life; for it is characteristic of a human being to think, but of the devil to bring the thought to completion.

“Therefore,” he says, “do not give place to the devil.”

(Jerome.) He is like a roaring lion, seeking an entrance through which he may burst in (1 Peter 5). Just as the Father and the Son stand before the door and knock, so that they may enter and dine with the one who receives them, so the adversary is always ready to burst in upon us; and when we give him an opening, he enters.

Before he comes, he commonly sends certain darts ahead and makes a thought the forerunner of his arrival. If we receive this thought in our heart, nourish it inwardly, and cause it to grow, then, when he sees that his offspring has grown within us, he himself will dare to enter.

Thus, in the heart of Judas Iscariot, he first cast the arrow that he should betray the Savior. If that wretched man had not cherished the arrow after receiving it, Satan would never, after the dipped bread had been placed in the dish, have entered into him (John 13).

At the same time, observe carefully that the devil found no place to enter Judas—whose breast he had already struck—except at the Savior’s meal. For we are especially given over into his power when we are not overcome by the Savior’s humanity, mercy, or gentleness, even though we unjustly hate him.

To this command now given, “Do not give place to the devil,” the following passage from Ecclesiastes may be compared: “If the spirit of one who has power rises against you, do not give him your place” (Ecclesiastes 10). That proud and presumptuous spirit wishes to rise and enter; but even if he thinks that he has overwhelmed you and exalts himself, you will retain [“do not yield”] your place. For the devil’s power lies not in his presumption and boastfulness but in your own will.

(Augustine.) People give place to the devil through their own desires. They do not see the devil with whom they are fighting, but they possess an easy remedy: let them conquer themselves within, and they will triumph over him without.

Whoever was stealing must steal no longer, but rather labor, working with his own hands, so that he may have something to give to one suffering need. (Jerome.) Since those who conduct themselves in the business of this life are compelled, for the sake of profit and necessary use, either to buy or sell something and to pursue gains through commerce—and since it is difficult even for those who are free from other passions, namely fornication, idolatry, adultery, and homicide, not to be held by this vice—for this reason he now admonishes the Ephesians not to incur the crime of theft under the pretext of profit. He calls theft everything that is acquired to another’s loss; but he says that it is just for each person, working with his own hands and obtaining his livelihood by labor, to give to those who have nothing.

Nor does he say, “Let him rather labor, working with his hands at what is good,” so that he may not be in need himself and may have a livelihood for those in need, and trouble no one; rather, he says, “Let him labor with his own hands at what is good, so that he may have something to share with those in need.” Therefore, whoever labors only so that he himself may not be in need, and withdraws his hand from others, although he applauds himself, has not fulfilled the Apostle’s command.

(Ambrose.) The Christian is therefore commanded not only not to take away what belongs to another, but also to supply from his own labor the necessities of those suffering want, so that, devoted to good works, he may repay what he previously took away and henceforth store up treasure for himself for the future. Whoever ceases from theft may receive pardon, but not glory. For what is great, or what merit is there, in abstaining from what belongs to others? One advances toward merit when he gives from his own possessions to the needy.

(Jerome.) Another meaning may also be understood: “Whoever was stealing must steal no longer,” and what follows, in view of what is written about the false prophets: “Each one steals the words of God from his neighbor” (Jer. XXIII); and in the Gospel: “All who came before me are thieves and robbers” (John X); and to the Romans: “You who preach against stealing, do you steal?” (Rom. II). We are thus forbidden to commit spiritual thefts.

For what follows—“but rather let him labor, working with his own hands at what is good”—cannot properly be referred to the necessities of this life, so that whatever is destined to perish should be called good and should belong to the mammon of iniquity. Even if just labor possesses wealth acquired without deceit, it is enough if such wealth is not called evil; it cannot otherwise be called good.

He therefore does good who turns away from evil and does good, and who works in the field of his own soul so that it may be filled with spiritual bread and may be able to lend to the hungry and assist the one suffering need, giving food at the proper time to his fellow servants.

Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only such speech as is good for building up when there is need, so that it may give grace to those who hear. A good word is one that teaches virtues to be pursued and vices to be avoided; an evil word is one that provokes to sins and incites those already inclined toward ruin. Whenever another person makes progress through our speech, and whenever, according to the suitability of place, time, and person, it builds up those who hear, a good word has proceeded from our mouth. But whenever we speak either at the wrong time, or in an unsuitable place, or in a manner inappropriate to those who hear, an evil word proceeds from our mouth for the destruction of those who listen.

Let us therefore consider what we say, since we shall give an account for every idle word on the day of judgment (Matt. [Col. 0441C] XII); and even if we do no harm, yet if we do not build up, we shall have to pay the penalty of an evil word.

(Ambrose.) In God’s servant everything ought to appear good, and his purity ought not to be stained in any respect. For what benefit is there in having a clean life and a filthy mouth, since the Lord says that each person will either be justified or condemned by his words? Nor can it be believed that someone lives well who speaks badly. Evil speech draws one into many vices. A person may speak badly by uttering obscenities, by slandering the good, by speaking deceitfully, or by lying; such things produce error. Good and sober conversation, however, gives grace and an example to those who hear, so that they may honor God in their words, being built up in the faith of Christ.

And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. (Jerome.) The grieving of the Holy Spirit is to be understood in the same way as the wrath, repentance, jealousy, and other passions attributed to God by analogy with human experience—not because the Spirit of God can be grieved or because divinity experiences any disturbance, but because from our words we learn about God’s disposition: that he grieves whenever we sin and mourns over sinners.

(Maurus.) Or this is a mode of expression like that which the same Apostle uses elsewhere: “The Spirit himself intercedes for us with unspeakable groanings” (Rom. VIII). The Holy Spirit does not groan, but makes us groan in our prayers.

(Jerome.) We have been sealed with the Holy Spirit of God so that our spirit and soul may be impressed with God’s seal and may receive that image and likeness in which we were formed at the beginning.

(Maurus.) The day of our redemption is the day on which, through the sacrament of baptism, we were redeemed and adopted by God as sons; or the day of our redemption is also the day when “this corruptible will put on incorruption, and this mortal will put on immortality” (1 Cor. XV).

(Ambrose.) When we act well, the Holy Spirit given to us rejoices in us, seeing his admonitions advancing our welfare, as it is said by the Lord: “There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke XV). The Holy Spirit therefore rejoices in our salvation, not in his own, since he has no need of joy. Conversely, if we do not obey him, he is grieved because he bears no fruit in us. He wants us to belong to life; yet he is not grieved in such a way as to suffer, since he is impassible. When he is said to be grieved, this signifies something on our account: he abandons us because we have offended him by despising his admonitions. His grief, therefore, is our unworthiness, which prevents us from being called God’s children. For he is the Holy Spirit who sanctifies God’s children by remaining in us.

(Augustine.) The substance of the Holy Spirit itself, insofar as it is whatever he himself is, cannot be grieved, since it possesses eternal and unchangeable blessedness and is itself rather that eternal and unchangeable blessedness. But because he dwells in the saints in such a way that he fills them with the love by which human beings must, in time, rejoice at the progress of the faithful and at their good works, they must also grieve at the fall or sins of those whose faith and devotion had made them rejoice. This grief is praiseworthy because it proceeds from the love that the Holy Spirit pours out. Therefore the Spirit himself is said to be grieved by those who act in such a way that the saints are grieved by their deeds—not for any other reason than that they possess the Holy Spirit. By this gift they are so good that the wicked cause them sorrow, especially those whom they either know or believe to have been good. Such grief is certainly not merely free from blame; it is especially worthy of praise and proclamation.

Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, along with all malice. (Albinus.) Here he shows the things by which the Holy Spirit is grieved and abandons the heart in which he had dwelt through love and moderation. Bitterness is opposed to the gentleness and sweetness of the Holy Spirit. Fury is anger in its beginning, and a disturbance growing hot in the soul. Indignation arises from pride, when we judge someone unworthy and therefore do not wish to endure him.

(Jerome.) Anger is that whose forms are bitterness, fury, and indignation. Once its fury has subsided, it desires vengeance and wishes to injure the one whom it thinks has caused harm. Therefore all bitterness, fury, and indignation must be removed from us. After all these, shouting and blasphemy are rightly also forbidden among us, because whoever has once been overcome by fury very often breaks out into shouting and, raging turbulently, is tossed about like a leaf.

Blasphemy occurs when false things are fabricated about God, or when someone, deceived by heretical depravity in the Catholic faith, is proved to have gone astray.

(Augustine.) Blasphemy is the utterance of falsehoods about God himself. For this reason blaspheming is worse than perjury: by perjury God is presented as a false witness, whereas by blasphemy falsehoods are spoken about God himself.

(Ambrose.) Fear ought to moderate and impose a limit upon accidental causes. But because some people, suppressing anger and shouting within their hearts, may retain malice in order to repay it when an opportunity arises, he therefore adds that these things must be removed along with all malice. For it is not only blasphemy that is malice; it is also the pretense of peace in one’s face while meditating discord in one’s heart.

(Cassian.) When he says, “Let all anger be removed from you,” he leaves out no anger whatever as necessary or useful to us. If it is necessary to care for a sinning brother, one must hasten to do so in such a way that, while perhaps attempting to apply medicine to someone suffering from a mild fever, one does not, through anger, involve oneself in the blindness of a more serious disease.

The person who wishes to heal another’s wound must remain free from every disease and healthy, lest the Gospel saying be applied to him: “Physician, first heal yourself” (Luke IV), and lest, seeing the speck in his brother’s eye while failing to see the beam in his own eye, he be unable to remove the speck from his brother’s eye because he carries a beam of fury in his own. Moved and inflamed by whatever cause of anger, the fury of the heart blinds a person; and the huge beam of a more destructive disease prevents the mind’s sight from beholding the sun of righteousness.

It makes no difference whether a golden plate, a leaden plate, or one of any other metal is placed before the eyes: the preciousness of the metal does not alter the condition of blindness. We have, in fact, a ministry implanted within us that is useful and salutary for us to receive for this one purpose: when we angrily rage against the unruly movements of our heart, and are ashamed that we have acted or spoken before human beings, we should be indignant that such things have ascended from the hidden places of our breast into the presence of the angels and of God himself, who is everywhere, penetrates all things, and whose eye we tremble before with complete dread, since the secrets of our conscience can never be hidden from him.

But be kind to one another, compassionate, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you. (Ambrose.) He urges us to become kind and compassionate toward one another after the example of God the Father, as the Lord also says: “Be merciful, so that you may be like your Father who is in heaven” (Luke VI). If the Lord has had mercy through his Son upon servants, how much more ought the servants themselves to have mercy on one another and forgive one another if one sins against another?

(Albinus.) The Apostle commands us to be gentle, kind, and gracious, and to invite people voluntarily into our friendship, so that no one may fear approaching us; such familiarity is acquired above all through mercy. Nor, when we give to others, do we immediately cease to possess what we have given.

(Jerome.) He continues, “forgiving one another,” because what is done well toward another is stored up more for the one who performs it than for the one who receives it: “He who has mercy on the poor will himself be filled,” and “he who gives to him lends to God” (Prov. XIV; XIX). Or it should be understood in this way: when we are gentle and compassionate, and, abandoning the disturbances that had provoked us, pass over into gentleness and self-control, what has been given and forgiven is given to us ourselves, as we turn from evil things to good and grant ourselves those very things that God the Father granted in Christ.

For if, having abandoned vices, we possess virtues, we also acquire them for ourselves through our own effort and cause ourselves to have what God granted us in Christ. Another person will simply understand the words “forgiving one another” in the same way as the earlier statement, “Be kind to one another”: that is, “forgiving each other.” Just as God forgave us our sins in Christ, so we should forgive those who have sinned against us.

To prove that the forgiveness of sins is called a gift in Scripture, he will take the example written in Luke (Luke VII), where one debtor owed five hundred denarii and another fifty, and the creditor released both of them. When the Savior asked which of them would have greater gratitude, the one questioned answered that it would be the one to whom more had been forgiven. It is also said in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

God forgave us in Christ, not as one situated outside him, but as one dwelling in him, because the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. Nor is the one in whom forgiveness is given immediately inferior to the one who gives it in himself, since the Apostle also says: “If I have forgiven anything, it was for your sake in the presence of Christ and God” (2 Cor. II).

## CHAPTER V

He urges the Ephesians to follow Christ in the fervor of love, in the beauty of holiness, and in the truth they have come to know; and he instructs married persons.

“Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children.” (Jerome.) Whoever understands how it was said, “Be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. V), will know how it is now also said, “Be imitators of God.” Writing to the Corinthians he says: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Cor. XI). They could not immediately become imitators of Christ; it was a great thing for them if they could become imitators of Christ.

But to the Ephesians, as people whom he had already taught such great mysteries, he does not say, “Be imitators of me,” nor “imitators of Christ,” but “imitators of God”—not because being an imitator of Christ is less than being an imitator of God. For Christ is God; rather, the distinction is that one thing is to imitate him according to his humanity and another according to his divinity. For although we once knew Christ according to the flesh, now we know him no longer in that way.

The Savior also speaks, displaying the humility of his dispensation: “Whatever he sees the Father doing, the Son does likewise.” This does not mean that the Father made one heaven and one earth, while Christ made another heaven and another earth and the remaining elements in their likeness; it means that whatever the Father does, the Son does the same.

In what way we can become like God, he testified above when he said: “Forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you.” I do not think that in everything else God has done a human being can imitate God. But, for example, just as he is compassionate and makes his rain fall on the good and the evil (Matt. V), so let us pour out our goodness upon all people. When we have done this, we shall be beloved children.

(Ambrose.) This person is truly the father’s beloved son who imitates his good qualities.

And walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling fragrance. Just as he wants us to be imitators of God the Father in kindness and mercy, so also of Christ his Son in love, so that, just as he loved us by giving himself for us, we too ought to lay down our lives for one another. The Apostle John also said this, teaching by the Lord’s example that lives must be laid down for the brethren.

(Jerome.) Whoever struggles against sin for the salvation of others even to the shedding of blood, so that he gives his own life for them, walks in love, imitating Christ, who loved us so greatly that he endured the cross for the salvation of all. Just as he gave himself for us, so that person too, willingly dying for those whom he can help, will imitate him who gave himself to the Father as an offering and sacrifice for a sweet-smelling fragrance; he himself will also become an offering and sacrifice of God for a sweet-smelling fragrance.

(Ambrose.) If, then, Christ’s death is a sweet-smelling fragrance to God, God willingly accepted his death. If this is true, those who crucified him according to God’s will did not sin. But this is not so, because Christ is said to have offered himself to God by allowing himself to be killed while remaining in the will of God his Father. Whoever is justly killed offers himself to the devil, for he does the devil’s will so that he deserves to be killed. Likewise Christ, while adhering to God’s will, displeased the devil; and therefore the devil killed him, because Christ offered himself to God by carrying out righteousness. In the offering, righteousness and truth are signified. God looks to these, and this is his acceptable sacrifice.

Thus the innocent person who is killed pleases God, not because he is killed, but because he preserved righteousness even to death. God Christ therefore accepted this death for the sake of life, and for this reason it is called a sweet-smelling fragrance to God.

Yet to the Romans he says: “God delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII). We must now ask how God delivered him up, or how he offered himself to God, since, as far as the words are concerned, this seems contradictory. God is said to have delivered him up when he permitted him to be killed, as the Lord says to Pilate: “You would have no authority over me unless it had been given you from above” (John XIX). Authority was indeed given to him, but to one who was willing: that is, he was permitted to do what he wished. This is what it means to deliver someone up; for when he does not intervene, he delivers him up.

If God had not wished to permit it, Christ would not have been killed. He therefore permitted him to be killed, but by those who wanted to kill him—not under compulsion, but voluntarily. They are therefore not free from punishment because they were permitted to do what they wanted. Condemnation applies to them because they willed it. God nevertheless permitted it because he knew that this would become, for the sake of many, a deed against the devil. It was fitting that what the enemy, ignorant of the future, thought he was doing against himself as though for his own advantage should be permitted to him, so that, imputing his ignorance to himself, he might be tormented by repentance for his deed.

But that Christ himself offered himself, or that God delivered him up, is one and the same thing, because the will of both is one.

But fornication and every impurity, or greed, must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints. (Ambrose.) What he says is clear. Yet he shows how serious a matter greed is, although we conceal it, when it is compared with fornication and impurity and appears to us as though it were some insignificant fault, even though it is a grave sin.

(Albinus.) He briefly comprehends all crimes by designating two roots of crimes: fornication and greed, adding impurity to fornication and associating greed with impurity as belonging to the other category. He indicates not only the desire for money but also the greed he had designated above when he said: “Let no one transgress against and defraud his brother” (1 Thess. IV).

“As is fitting,” he says, “for saints.” Of them the Lord says through the prophet: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. XI). Every bodily impurity and every instability of mind wandering through the various fluctuations of the will must be avoided by saints. Nor can one rightly be called holy who is involved in such crimes.

Nor obscenity, nor foolish talk, nor coarse joking, which is not fitting, but rather thanksgiving. (Ambrose.) Since some people are accustomed to do something disgraceful or to provoke laughter with foolish talk, as though it were not a sin, he forbids this, because God’s servants ought always to appear sober and modest. Everything that ordinarily provokes laughter and loud amusement is unfitting for Christian seriousness, because it is fitting for God’s servant to think about heavenly things and about how he will come crowned before Christ’s tribunal. I think that “foolish talk” should be understood as referring to silly and pointless stories.

(Jerome.) The difference between foolish talk and coarse joking is that foolish talk contains nothing wise or worthy of the human heart. Coarse joking, however, proceeds from a prudent mind and deliberately seeks certain urbane, rustic, obscene, or foolish expressions—what we can call joking in another word—in order to provoke laughter in those who hear. Yet this too must be utterly banished by holy men, for whom it is more fitting to weep and mourn, as the Gospel says: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall be comforted” (Luke VI).

(Ambrose.) Sin is committed through foolish talk; hence Solomon says: “The fool practices evil through laughter” (Prov. X). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. XII). Nor can things said for the purpose of insulting someone be regarded as harmless; therefore such things do not contribute to what is salutary. He therefore advises us to do and say what advances our benefit and God’s praise, meditating day and night on his law, as it is written in the first psalm.

(Albinus.) Having rejected all these things from the Christian, he next adds what is fitting for him, saying, “but rather thanksgiving.” He signifies that the Christian’s words ought to be seasoned with the salt of wisdom, so that they may give grace to those who hear, as he said above. In this passage, however, “thanksgiving” seems to refer more to the words of the speaker and the understanding of the hearer than to the thanksgiving customarily offered to God for his benefits.

(Ambrose.) From their conduct and morals, God’s servants ought to be recognizable even when silent, so that, as truth differs from falsehood, so God’s servants may differ from the servants of the devil.

For this you must know: no fornicator, impure person, or greedy person—which is idolatry—has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. He shows why these things must be removed: whoever is such will have no share in the kingdom of heaven, which belongs to the Father and the Son. To teach that greed is a dangerous matter, he calls it idolatry, than which there is no greater sin.

Let us therefore examine why greed is called idolatry. Idolatry takes the honor due to God and claims it for a creature, when, in the name of divinity—which belongs to the Creator alone—it asserts that the creature shares in it. Greed is equated with this because the greedy person similarly appropriates and hoards for himself the things that belong to God, denying through greed what God granted for the common use of all. He gathers these things to himself so that others may not use them; this causes them to be sold at a high price, so that the poor cannot live. If they were not hoarded, the abundance of all things would make them useful to everyone. Indeed, among the ancients, because greed was absent, there were no high prices either.

It is rightly compared with idolatry because it harms many and is likewise hostile to the Creator. God wants and commands that the poor be assisted from the things he created; greed contradicts him.

(Jerome.) It should be noted that although he had forbidden six vices above— fornication, impurity, greed, obscenity, foolish talk, and coarse joking—he now lists only three: fornication, impurity, and greed. Whoever is subject to these cannot have an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.

For if the foolish talker and the coarse joker were excluded from the kingdom of God, how would the judgment appear to be harsh when he has specifically separated three, refusing to forgive the weakness of human frailty? After all, our own words condemn us even when spoken in jest: “Whoever does not stumble in speech is perfect.” Nor, by saying these things, are we making room for foolish talk and coarse joking, since they are not excluded from the kingdom; rather, because there are different dwellings with the Father (John XIV), and star differs from star in glory (1 Cor. XV), so too it is in the resurrection of the dead. Even if someone is free from fornication, impurity, and wantonness, nevertheless, if he is a foolish talker and a coarse joker, he will not occupy the place he would have possessed had he not had these vices.

Someone may object: “Foolish talk and coarse joking do not bear the same guilt as fornication, impurity, and greed. Should he not also have named obscenity along with the three preceding vices?” The answer is that here “obscenity” signifies a hidden thought, when our senses are inflamed with lust and the soul is set ablaze by the titillations of the flesh, yet is restrained by the fear of God and the judgment of the mind.

Indeed, above he also named three together without obscenity, saying: “Fornication, every impurity, and greed must not even be named among you.” Subsequently obscenity was named together with foolish talk and coarse joking. Therefore, just as foolish talk and coarse joking do not destroy or permanently exclude a person from the kingdom, neither does this kind of obscenity.

But because above, on the basis of what we had read elsewhere—“Let the greedy person not transgress against and defraud his brother in business”—we had said that greed was used in place of adultery, we now ask whether the present statement, “or the greedy person, which is the service of idols,” agrees with that interpretation or with the common translation.

In many passages of the prophets we find idolatry called fornication: “They fornicated after their idols,” he says, and, “They were seduced by the spirit of fornication” (Judg. II; Ezek. XXIII, and elsewhere). Fornication can therefore also be understood as referring to idolatry.

But if the greedy person is understood as one who acquires money by any means and desires to possess coins by right or wrong, delighting in a full purse, then he is an idolater because he worships the image of the coin itself and venerates the idolatry engraved upon it. Just as the belly is the god of the gluttonous, so money can most justly be called the god of the covetous—especially since in another passage the Apostle calls covetousness idolatry.

We must also examine what he intended by saying, “in the kingdom of Christ and of God.” Is the kingdom of Christ one thing and the kingdom of God another, or is it the same kingdom of the Father and the Son? If he had said, “in the kingdom of the Son and of the Father,” we would come through the Son to the Father. Although there would be a distinction of persons, there would nevertheless be one majesty of those who reign.

But when he says, “in the kingdom of Christ and of God,” let us understand God and Christ as one, because even when Christ hands over the kingdom to God the Father, the Father will not be “all in all,” but God will be “all in all.” Wherever God is, both the Father and the Son can be understood. Moreover, what we say about the Father and the Son, let us understand in the same way about the Holy Spirit.

(Augustine.) I ask, then, who sins more gravely: the person who unknowingly falls into heresy, or the person who knowingly does not withdraw from greed—that is, from idolatry? According to the rule by which sins committed knowingly are placed above sins committed in ignorance, the knowing greedy person surpasses the other in wickedness. But lest the magnitude of the crime itself in the case of heresy do what the loss suffered by the knowing person does in the case of greed, the ignorant heretic may be considered equal to the knowing greedy person.

No one should deceive you with empty words; for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience. Therefore do not become their fellow-participants. (Ambrose.) Empty speeches are vain; and the vanity of idols is the worship of idols, which certainly does not have its beginning from God but from error. He therefore teaches that assent must not be given to their words. For they are always clamorous and, through a certain seductive deceit, oppose the faith; they put forward the custom of antiquity, judging that the reasoning of present things should be asserted rather than the hope of things to come. Therefore vengeance from heaven comes upon them, so that they may know that what they refused to believe is true. He teaches that God’s servants ought to be kept far apart from this vanity, lest they become participants in their punishment.

(Jerome.) The words that deceive and overthrow are empty and void, whereas those that build up their hearers are full, abundant, and richly supplied. Since, then, there are many who say that punishments for sins are not future, nor are torments to be inflicted from outside, but that sin itself and the consciousness of the offense constitute the punishment—while the worm in the heart does not die (Mark IX) and fire is kindled in the soul—in the manner of a fever, which does not torture the sick person externally but, seizing the bodies themselves, punishes what it possesses without the infliction of outward torments: these convictions and fraudulent snares he therefore called empty and void words. They seem to possess a certain flower of eloquence and to flatter sinners, but, while they give them confidence, they lead them all the more toward eternal punishments, because God is angry at nothing so much as when a sinner becomes proud and, standing erect and stiff-necked, is not bent toward weeping nor asks mercy for his offense.

For this reason the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience, or of unpersuadability. The sons of unpersuadability, or disobedience, are so called in the same way as the sons of destruction, the sons of fornication, the sons of death, the sons of Gehenna, and other similar expressions, which it is very easy to find in various places of Scripture. Therefore do not become their fellow-participants. A person becomes a participant, or fellow-participant, in the sons of disobedience when he is found in fornication, uncleanness, and greed, on account of which the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience.

He is indeed a participant in them because he participates in and shares their evil works. But a fellow-participant is so called because he is a participant together with others; and in *fellow-participant* the notion of *participant* is included, whereas in *participant* the person is not immediately understood to be a fellow-participant. Observe carefully the words *fellow-participant* and *participant*. For I think that in Scripture *participant* is always taken in a good sense, and *fellow-participant* in a bad one. For example: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your participants” (Psalm XLIV); and elsewhere: “For we have become participants in Christ, if only we hold the beginning of his substance firm to the end” (Hebrews III). Moreover, I do not remember having read *fellow-participant* anywhere else except in the present passage; yet here it is clearly placed not in a good sense but in the contrary one.

For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. (Ambrose.) Darkness is ignorance, because no one sees in darkness. Ignorance, moreover, is paganism or unbelief, from which they were drawn by God’s grace to faith and made light, that is, truth, because in the light the things that exist are made manifest. Thus pagans, celebrating their mysteries in darkness, are deceived in a cave with their eyes covered. Having become Christians from among them and having come to know the truth, they are called sons of light, because God is light, and they receive his faith in truth.

(Jerome.) Just as the righteous are the light of the world, so consequently the ungodly are called darkness. The righteous, because they are light, will see light in light; but the unrighteous, because they are darkness, are a people sitting in darkness and seeing nothing. We understand their difference and distinction from their fruits. For everyone who does evil hates the light (John III), and, not coming to the light, is dark, and is a son of night and darkness. But whoever does the truth comes into the light, and is light, and is a son of light and of day. Those who are luminous and those who are dark are recognized by the light or darkness of their hearts.

Furthermore, you may ask whether, for the sake of distinguishing those who are light but not light in the Lord, it is said of the righteous: “Now you are light in the Lord.” It is fittingly written to the Ephesians, who had ascended to the summit of knowledge, that they are light in the Lord. Nor is darkness itself changed into light, or light into darkness; rather, those who, from what they are, have also acquired a name of virtue or vice, if they are converted from one state to another, will receive, in accordance with the things by which they are possessed, the name either of darkness or of light—*homonymously* (ὁμωνύμως, “by the same name”).

Walk as children of light, for the fruit of light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth. (Ambrose.) He says this so that they may conduct themselves in such a way that they may rightly be called children of light. For the works of light are done openly and without fear, whereas the works of darkness are done secretly because they are unlawful; every sin fears being brought into the open.

(Alb.) If God is light and there are no darknesses in him, the children of God are children of light. Likewise, if Christ is the true light, his children also—to whom he says, “My little children, I am with you yet a little while” (John XIII)—are children of the true light. From this it follows that those who are children of God the Father are the same as those who are children of Christ Jesus.

“The fruit,” he says, “of light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth.” These are the fruits by which we are recognized as children of God. The fruit of light is found not only in goodness but also in righteousness and truth. Where goodness is, there also is righteousness; where righteousness is, there consequently is truth. Goodness is recognized in love, righteousness in good works, and truth in catholic teaching.

(Jerome.) Against Marcion, who separates the just God from the good God and thinks that the Creator is just, while some other god—of whom this Christ who came is the son—is good alone, let us bring forward this testimony: the fruit of light consists not only in goodness but also in righteousness and truth. Where goodness is, there also is righteousness; where righteousness is, there consequently is truth.

Therefore, in the good Father of Christ, as they themselves also confess, there are goodness and truth. But where goodness and truth are, there—in him and not in another, as the Apostle now teaches—there is righteousness. Let Marcion understand that Christ himself is called goodness, truth, and righteousness: goodness, in that he gives grace to those who believe in him, not according to works but according to mercy; righteousness, in that he gives each person what he deserves; and truth, in that he alone knows the causes of all creatures and of all things.

Prove what is well-pleasing to God. (Alb.) He exhorts us to do everything with deliberation, so that, being cautious and attentive, we may do only what we understand to be pleasing to God. But because in this passage the sequence of the discourse appears disturbed and the whole sentence seems disordered, the speech should be restored to this arrangement: “Therefore do not become their fellow-participants, proving what is well-pleasing to God; for although you were once darkness, now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light, showing the fruit of light in all goodness, righteousness, and truth.”

(Ambrose.) From the magnificence of holiness and goodness it can be judged by what works God is delighted. For he himself said: “Be holy, just as I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Leviticus XI). And the Lord says: “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Luke VI). These things are pleasing to God. For in holiness there is purification, while in mercy there is complete and perfect righteousness.

And do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness. (Jerome.) In the Letter to the Galatians (Galatians V), he used the word *fruit* for the Spirit but *works* for the flesh, saying: “He has made known the works of the flesh, which are fornication,” and the rest. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, long-suffering,” and so forth. In the present passage, however, the works of darkness are called unfruitful, and those who have done them are joined to them by participation.

(Ambrose.) He warns us not to pollute ourselves by consenting to the deeds of the wicked, because they are unfruitful with respect to the good.

(Alb.) By “the unfruitful works of darkness” he means evil habits in sins. He forbids Christians to participate in them but rather urges them to reprove them wherever they are understood to exist. Therefore he immediately adds: “But rather also reprove the things that are done by them in secret; for it is shameful even to speak of them.”

(Ambrose.) He now wants them not only to be separate from evil deeds but also to reprove the misdeeds of those who act shamefully in secret. Sins are then shown to be sins when they are reproved, so that the sons of light may be admired. When they are justly reproved by them, the guilty will not be able to contradict them but will rather revere them.

(Alb.) Among the other commandments, the ability to reprove sinners is a mark of the greatest freedom. But this can be done by the person who does not deserve to hear: “Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your eye, and then you will be able to remove the speck from your brother’s eye” (Matthew VII). From this it must be understood that the person is able to reprove others who is not himself reproved in his own conscience.

But when he says here, “It is shameful even to speak of them,” he refers back to what was said above about the sons of disobedience, so that the meaning may be: “The things that are secretly done by the sons of disobedience—namely, fornication, uncleanness, and all greed—it is shameful to speak of.”

But everything that is reproved is made manifest by the light; for everything that is made manifest is light. (Jerome.) Without doubt, “everything” means the things that are secretly done by the sons of disobedience. These are made manifest when reproved by the light. The light reproves the things that were previously darkness and afterward became light in the Lord, so that, through being reproved, they may be changed for the better, and, once changed, may be made manifest in public and become light when brought into the open, because everything that is made manifest is light.

(Ambrose.) This is true, because sins become visible when they are reproved. For as long as the sinner is not corrected, he scarcely seems to himself to be sinning. Everything that is made manifest is light; in what is brought into the open there is no ambiguity, and what is openly a transgression cannot be excused. Just as, when the sun appears, it can no longer be denied that it is day, so, when sin has been revealed, its reproof cannot be considered false.

For this reason he says: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will illumine you.”

(Ambrose.) This sleep signifies the stupefaction of the mind, which is alienated from the true way. Such alienation is a kind of death, from which the person is urged to rise, so that, coming to his senses, he may recognize the truth, which is Christ. Therefore the unbelieving and vicious, sunk in filth and despairing of life, are admonished to rise, or rather to emerge, and to have a share with Christ, passing from darkness to light and from death to life.

(Jerome.) Since the works of darkness, once reproved by the light, are made manifest in the light, and the things that were reproved are transformed, this is said to those who were sleeping and dead because they were doing the works of darkness: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead.”

Someone may ask who it is that says, “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead,” or whose testimony the Apostle used. The person content with a simple answer will say that he brought forward something read in hidden prophets and in writings called apocryphal, just as it is evident that he did elsewhere as well—not because he approved the *apocrypha* (ἀπόκρυφα, “hidden writings”), but because he used verses of Aratus, Epimenides, and Menander to establish at the appropriate time what he wished to establish. Yet the whole of what Aratus, Epimenides, and Menander wrote is not holy merely because he testified that they had truly said something.

Another person, supposing that the Holy Spirit had fashioned a *prosopopoeia* (προσωποποιΐα, “personification”) for the exhortation to repentance, will recall that these words were spoken in that manner.

For my part, according to my limited ability, having carefully examined all the editions of the ancient Scriptures, including the very volumes of the Hebrews, I have never found this written anywhere—unless perhaps we explain it in this way: just as formerly the prophets spoke in the assembly of the people, “Thus says the Lord,” and, “Because the Lord has spoken,” so the Apostle, filled with the Holy Spirit, suddenly broke into words that Christ was speaking within him and said, “Thus says the Lord.”

The matter must also be discussed of how one and the same person can be addressed as though sleeping: “Rise, you who sleep,” and as though dead: “Arise from the dead.” Since there is a human spirit, which I remember always to be written of in a good sense, and a soul, whose weaknesses and deaths as a result of sins we read about, what is now said—“Rise, you who sleep”—refers to the spirit, while what follows—“Arise from the dead”—is fitted to the soul. “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel XVIII); but we never read that the spirit dies at all.

Therefore Christ, the true light, will rise for the person who has risen from sleep and has been raised from the dead.

See, then, how carefully you walk—not as unwise people but as wise. It is rightly said to the Ephesians that they should walk carefully, since they had trained senses for discerning good and evil and, testing everything, retained what they had determined to be good. Whoever watches how he walks and how carefully he places his step, lest he perhaps strike his foot against a stone, and says, “Your word is a lamp for my feet, Lord, and a light for my paths” (Psalm CXVIII), is certainly wise.

For I do not think that any simpleton, even if he wishes to walk carefully, can fulfill this command, which is enjoined upon the wise and the unwise. From this we understand that even the moral commands, which most people consider obvious, require prudent and careful exposition, on the basis of what is said in Psalm XVIII: “The commandment of the Lord is lucid, enlightening the eyes.” For that lucid commandment enlightens the eyes of those who, having abandoned folly, have devoted themselves to the pursuits of wisdom.

Redeeming the time, because the days are evil. (Ambrose.) Since above he commanded that unbelief and the vices of life be reproved by God’s servants, he now adds that they should be reproved prudently, because of the danger of scandal, so that one must conduct oneself wisely among the unbelieving, especially at a time when the unbelieving rule, relying upon a profane ruler.

If a Christian sees an unruly and angry opponent, he should withdraw from him and pretend not to notice him, lest he provoke him to blasphemy and to stirring up a disturbance. He should speak where an opportunity is given. For just as, when questioned among powerful unbelievers, he must not remain silent or deny what is true, so, if there is danger in disputing among them, he must refrain, since it is harmful to sow upon thorns. This is the mark of a prudent person: to know how to answer each individual.

There is someone who, although unbelieving, is not completely unapproachable, so that he will not even tolerate hearing words of faith. Again, there is someone in whom the zeal of unbelief burns so fiercely that one should discuss the faith not only not with him but not even in his presence, since, by clamoring and blaspheming, he becomes a source of scandal to many. Thus Paul and Barnabas, when they heard those who were blaspheming against them (Acts XIII), shook out their garments and withdrew from them.

(Jerome.) When we spend time in a good work, we redeem it and make our own what the wickedness of human beings had sold. No one who seeks the necessities of this life and thinks about wealth and anxieties—which the Gospel calls thorns—can redeem time for himself.

By redeeming the time that is contained in evil days, we in a certain sense change it, turn evil days into good days, and make them belong not to the present age but to the future one.

This passage can also be explained in another way: “O Ephesians, for whom Christ, the sun of righteousness, has risen as you have risen from the sleep of this age, walk carefully and prudently. Having cast away folly, hold fast to wisdom, through which you may not be changed with the variation of times, but may make the diversity of times into one time for yourselves.”

And since there are very many persecutions—for at the beginning the churches were harassed almost every day—hold to one course and know that it must be preserved. Do not change like the moon in the manner of a fool (Ecclesiasticus XXVII), but hold firmly in mind what you once began, lest, if you see a persecuting judge, you also change along with the judge’s will.

Again, if someone who praises your doctrine comes, confess that you are Christians, but preserve what you are at all times.

Let us set forth an example from Scripture, so that what we are saying may become clearer. Joseph had resolved to please God (Genesis XXXVII and following). This resolve was not changed by any variation of circumstances—not by the envy of his brothers, nor by the condition of servitude, nor by the allurements of youth, nor by the promises of his mistress, nor by the squalor of prison, nor afterward by the pride of Egyptian power. He was always one and the same, and, as we have said, redeeming for himself the variation of times, he turned evil days into good ones.

The same must be understood of Job. Though afflicted by various trials, he was not changed by wealth, losses, bereavement, wounds, the reproaches of his friends, solitude, or afterward the restoration of all his goods (Job II and following). For he had redeemed the time for himself and had made the evil days good.

Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is. (Ambrose.) The Lord Jesus urges us to pursue peace (John XIV), and the chosen vessel says: “If it can be done, so far as it depends on you, live in peace with everyone” (Romans XII). And to Timothy he says: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all” (II Timothy II).

This is the will of the Lord: that the things his servants ought to do should be done with modesty. For disturbance, clamor, or contention accompanied by anger produces hostility. He therefore added this on account of what was said above, where God wishes [the variant reads, “God’s”] servants to reprove the sins of sinful people: since disagreement and quarrel commonly arise from this, they should reprove sinners with restraint and gentleness, lest, provoked to anger, they leap into conflict. Therefore he prudently urges that this be carefully observed, so that there may be progress.

(Jerome.) Since the time is evil and, as we said above, must be redeemed, wisdom should first be sought, so that through it we may be able to understand what the will of God is. For we cannot walk carefully unless we have first understood God’s will.

Therefore, in every work, one must first consider what God wishes; and, after judgment has been exercised, one must then do what has been shown to please him.

And do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit. (Ambrose.) Sober people can have confidence in reproving others. For good conduct strikes fear into the delinquent, and the person being reproved will not be able to take the correction harshly when he knows that the conduct of the one admonishing him is excellent. Where there is drunkenness, there is debauchery; and debauchery provokes shameful behavior. Therefore it is fitting to be sober, so that the standards of good conduct may be preserved.

(Jerome.) Just as we cannot serve two masters, God and Mammon (Matthew VI), so we cannot be filled simultaneously with the Spirit and with wine. The person filled with the Spirit possesses prudence, gentleness, modesty, and chastity; the person filled with wine possesses folly, rage, shamelessness, and lust. I think that all this is signified by the one word “debauchery.”

We have often noted that the word *spirit*, when used without an added qualification, is taken in a good sense; this too seems to be observed here.

Speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord. (Ambrose.) The Holy Spirit loves a rational life. For if we live well, we shall be filled with him, as he recalls, so that we may confess and exalt God’s gift with varied vocal melody, and praise may be sung to God by every tongue.

For wherever the Spirit is, he is always meditating on spiritual things, so that they may not be only on the lips but may burst forth from the heart, in accordance with the ancient saying of the Lord through the prophet: “This people honors me with its lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah XXIX).

(Jerome.) Whoever abstains from the drunkenness of wine, in which there is debauchery, and instead is filled with the Spirit, can receive the psalms, hymns, and songs spiritually in every respect. He will therefore be able to sing, make melody, and praise the Lord more with the mind than with the voice.

This is what is meant by “singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord.” Let young men hear this; let those hear it whose duty it is to sing psalms in the Church: one must sing to God more with the heart than with the voice.

Let the servant of Christ sing in such a way that it is not the voice of the singer but the words of the Lord being spoken that please him, so that the evil spirit who was in Saul (1 Samuel XVI) may be driven out from those who are similarly possessed by him.

There seems to be this difference among psalms, hymns, and songs: hymns are spoken in praise of God; psalms display the moral life; songs occur when the Creator is proclaimed from the created things.

Giving thanks always for everything in the name of Jesus Christ to God and the Father, submitting to one another in the fear of Christ. (Ambrose.) We are commanded to give thanks to God in all his gifts. He has also deigned to adopt us through Christ his own Son, through whom we have come to know him and have learned in the Spirit about God, because God is Spirit and must be worshiped in the Spirit. Each person is to submit to the other on account of the fear of Christ, who commanded that humility be practiced.

(Jerome.) What he says, “Giving thanks always for everything,” must be understood in two ways: we are to give thanks to God both at every time and for everything that happens to us. Thus, not only for what we consider good, but also for what constrains us and comes against our will, the joyful mind should break forth into praise of God.

This act of thanksgiving is observed by prudent people both generally and particularly. Generally, so that we give thanks to God for all the good things that this world supplies us; particularly, when we rejoice in God’s benefits that come to us, or even, if adversities occur, when we give thanks to God in them. This virtue belongs only to Christians.

Whoever, as we have said, gives thanks for everything to God the Father through the mediator of God and human beings should give thanks through Christ Jesus, because unless it is through him, we cannot approach God the Father.

(Alb.) What he says, “Submitting to one another in the fear of Christ,” let bishops hear it, let presbyters hear it, let every order of teachers hear it: they are to be subject to those subject to them. Let them imitate the Apostle who says: “Although I was free from all, I made myself a servant to all, so that I might gain all” (1 Corinthians IX).

This is the difference between the rulers of the nations and Christians: they rule their subjects, whereas we serve; and we are greater if we have become least of all.

But what he says, “in the fear of Christ,” must be understood in this way: this submission itself should not take place for the sake of human glory but for the fear of Christ, so that we fear offending him.

(Jerome.) Another person will interpret “submitting to one another in the fear of Christ” by saying that this general statement is divided and distributed in what follows: “Wives, be subject to your husbands”; “Children, obey your parents in the Lord”; and “Servants, obey your fleshly masters with fear and trembling.”

Thus not only are wives to be subject to husbands, children to parents, and servants to masters, but husbands also to wives according to the duty that has been commanded; fathers to children, so that they do not provoke them to anger; and masters to servants, so that they withdraw threats and provide them with what they need. They should be subject to one another, and should do this out of the fear of God. Just as Christ was subject to his servants, so those who appear to be greater should submit to those beneath them by rendering the duties that are commanded.

Here we may understand fear in place of *eulabeia* (εὐλάβεια), that is, reverence, which is closer to love. For it is by no means fitting for the Ephesians to do anything from fear and not from love of Christ.

Let wives be subject to their own husbands as to the Lord, because the husband is the head of the wife, just as Christ is the head of the Church.

The words “let them be subject,” which have been added in the Latin copies, are not found in the Greek manuscripts. For the statement refers back to what precedes, and “let them be subject” is understood from “submitting to one another in the fear of Christ,” so that, by a common construction (*apo koinou*, ἀπὸ κοινοῦ), *subject* resounds with both clauses: “wives to their husbands, as to the Lord.” But this is more readily understood in Greek than in Latin.

Wives are commanded by natural law to be subject to their husbands, because the husband is the source or authority of the wife. Hence, he says, just as to the Lord, so they ought to be subject to their husbands. For this reason Sarah called Abraham “lord” (Genesis XVIII).

Just as Christ is the head of the Church, so the husband is the head of the wife. For the Church took its beginning from Christ, and therefore is subject to him; so also the woman took her beginning from the man, so that she should be subject to him.

There is nevertheless this difference: the woman is of the same substance as the man, whereas the Church can participate in Christ in name, but not in nature.

(Alb.) It must be considered that, just as there is a holy union in Christ and in the holy Church, so there should be a holy bond between man and woman. There is a just reason why the woman should be subject to the man: in the first creation the woman came from the man, not the man from the woman. Therefore her turning should be toward the man.

Some interpret this passage according to the allegorical sense, saying that the wife is understood as the body and the husband as the mind. Just as the Church is subject to Christ, so bodies ought to be subject to the understanding and reduced to one spirit, if they have been joined to the Lord, because “the person who clings to the Lord is one spirit.”

Therefore it is added: “He himself is the Savior of his body.”

(Alb.) He preferred to call the Church the body of Christ rather than his flesh. It is clear that whatever is flesh is consequently also body, but not everything that is body is consequently flesh. Therefore he preferred to call the Church the body of Christ, whose body Christ Jesus is the Savior—that is, the Word, Wisdom, and the other virtues in which he is understood.

But just as the Church is subject to Christ, so also wives are subject to their husbands in everything.

(Jerome.) The Church is glorious, having no spot or wrinkle (Ephesians V), or anything of that kind. Therefore the sinner who is stained by any impurity cannot be called a member of the Church of Christ, nor can he be said to be subject to Christ.

It is possible, however, that just as the Church, which previously had wrinkle and spot, was afterward restored to youth and purity, so the sinner may run to the physician, because “those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matthew IX; Luke V), so that his wounds may be healed and he may become part of the Church, which is the body of Christ.

He also speaks to the Ephesians with sufficient elegance and caution when he says: “As the Church is subject to Christ, so wives are subject to their husbands in everything.” If a wife is to be subject to her husband as the Church is to Christ, then there is a holy union between husband and wife, and the body must never serve its passions.

If someone should oppose us with what is written to the Corinthians—that a husband should render the due to his wife and a wife to her husband—he should recognize that there is a great difference between the Corinthians and the Ephesians.

The Corinthians are addressed as little ones and infants, among whom there were disagreements and schisms, and fornication was heard of such a kind as was not even found among the nations (1 Corinthians V). Therefore they are permitted, after prayer, to return to the same union, lest they be tempted by Satan, although there in what follows he says that he grants them this indulgence not according to his will, but according to their gifts (*charismata*).

The Ephesians, however, among whom he spent three years and disclosed all the mysteries of Christ, are instructed differently. Each person possesses the free power of choice either to follow the Corinthians or the Ephesians and to be saved either by Corinthian servitude or by Ephesian freedom.

“Woe,” says the Savior, “to those who are pregnant in that day” (Luke XXI), that is, the day of judgment; and these are, properly speaking, the works of marriage. Therefore every effort must be made to imitate the Ephesians rather than the Corinthians, lest we be found, as in the Flood, buying, marrying, selling, and joined in marriage. Instead, with our loins girded, let us hold lamps.

Men, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself up for her, in order to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word of life, so that he himself might present to himself a glorious Church, not having stain or wrinkle or anything of that kind, but holy and immaculate.

(Greg.) She has no stain or wrinkle who is free both from shameful conduct and from duplicity of speech. But because she now holds within the bosom of faith many who are also reprobate, when the time of persecution blazes up, she suffers from the very enemies whom she had previously seemed to nourish with the words of her preaching. Let blessed Job therefore speak in the person of the Lord: “My wrinkles [Col. 0457C] bear witness against me” (Job XVI)—that is, they themselves, by persecuting me, reproach me; although now placed within my body, they do not cleanse from themselves the malice of their duplicity. Hence it is suitably added: “And the liar is raised up against my face, contradicting me.” Even in the time of her peace the holy Church suffers falsehood, since there are many in her who distrust the promise of eternity and yet pretend to be faithful. Because they do not dare openly to contradict her preaching, she suffers their falsehood not against her face but, as it were, behind her back. But when the time of wickedness breaks out, the one who now detracts through fear comes forward to contradict her face-to-face, because he opposes the words of true faith with open utterance.

(Ambr.) Women are commanded to be subject and to show reverence to their husbands; [Col. 0457D] men, however, are admonished to love their wives so greatly that they even lay down their lives for them, possessing, for the sake of love, a jealous concern for their affection and discipline, so that they may be religious and holy. He who loves his wife loves himself. By natural reason a woman is a portion of the man’s body; therefore, in loving the woman, the man loves himself. When he commits fornication, he sins against himself, because the two are one flesh. They do not divide the substance of nature so that number may arise through the persons; rather, they exist in the unity of nature.

(Hier.) Although husband and wife are bound to one another by mutual love—such as that remembered in the case of Hasdrubal’s wife, who, when her husband was captured, threw herself into the flames of her country, and of the other women who refused to outlive their dead husbands—nevertheless a wise man will never compare [Col. 0458A] that love with the love of Christ and the Church. This, then, is to be understood as a holy love: the love with which Isaac loved his wife Rebekah, whose name is interpreted as “patience,” and brought her from the land of Mesopotamia, which is surrounded on every side by the waves of this age, into the promised land, so that he might be comforted after the death of his mother. He tempered the destruction of the Synagogue through the union with the Church.

(Alb.) The Apostle therefore admonishes that the love between man and wife be holy, so that they may not be among themselves in the passions of desire like the nations that do not know God, but that their bond may be holy and immaculate in the faith of chastity, just as all chastity consists in the union of Christ with the Church. He cleansed her by the washing of his blood, so that she might be wholly without wrinkle or stain, purified from every portion [Col. 0458B] of vice. Yet we must consider when the Church is the bride of Christ without any stain or wrinkle: this will certainly be when she appears in glory with Christ, when Christ himself appears glorious. For Christ himself was not glorified before the resurrection in the form of a servant. Therefore the Evangelist says of him: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII).

(Hier.) Since, according to the tropological interpretation, we have said that men signify souls and wives bodies, let the soul love the body so that, like Christ, it may give itself up for its salvation and sanctify it by the word of teaching, presenting it to itself without any stain or wrinkle of old age—especially since it knows that the body will be saved in the resurrection and will see the salvation of God. Such a man [Col. 0458C] has Christ as his head. When, for the salvation of the flesh, he humbles himself and becomes one flesh with his wife, he draws her back to the spirit; and, joined to the Lord, he ceases to be flesh.

He also beautifully derived “stain” and “wrinkle,” since he was speaking of marriage, from the example of women for the adornment of the Church. Just as women’s bodies may be soiled by blemishes [*naevi*], contracted by wrinkles, or discolored by freckles, and just as all women’s concern is to wipe away whatever appears disfiguring and to display the beauty of their bodies to their husbands, so souls must be cleansed from every filth of sin, so that the wrinkle of the old man may be stretched out by youth and that the new man may be renewed from day to day.

(Aug.) Do you not wish to have a stain? Do what is written: “Wash yourselves, be clean; remove your wickednesses from your hearts [Col. 0458D]” (Isa. I). Do you not wish to have a wrinkle? Stretch yourself out upon the cross. For it is not enough merely to be washed; you must also be stretched out, so that you may be without stain or wrinkle. Through washing sins are removed; through being stretched out, desire for the future age is produced, for which Christ was crucified.

Hear Paul after he was washed: “Not from works of righteousness that we performed, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration” (Titus III). Hear him also after he was stretched out: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue according to the goal toward the prize of the heavenly calling in Christ Jesus” (Phil. III). Therefore he is rightly without the stain of iniquity and without the wrinkle of a double heart, like the good and faithful friend of the bridegroom. [Col. 0459A] “For I betrothed a pure virgin to one man, to present her to Christ without stain or wrinkle” (II Cor. XI).

Then, through his mercy, the righteous, fully and perfectly cleansed, will shine in the kingdom of their Father. Then the Church will fully and perfectly be without stain or wrinkle or anything of that kind, because then she will also truly be glorious. For when he says not merely, “that he might present the Church to himself without stain or wrinkle,” but adds “glorious,” he clearly indicates when she will be without stain or wrinkle or anything of that kind: namely, when she is glorious. For it cannot be said that she is now glorious amid such great evils, such great scandals, such a great mixture of the worst people, and such great reproaches from the ungodly. Although kings serve her, that is where the more dangerous and greater temptation lies. [Col. 0459B] Rather, she will then be glorious when what the same Apostle says comes to pass: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians III).

Likewise, men ought to love their wives as their own bodies.

(Alb.) It is said in Genesis concerning the union of man and woman: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II).
