Likewise, in the Gospel the Lord repeats the same statement, saying: “He who created them from the beginning made them male and female, and said: For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Matt. XIX). Since, therefore, husband and wife are one flesh, wives must be cared for in all chastity and honor as our own bodies.

(Hier.) No one loves his body shamefully or loves himself for the sake of intercourse; rather, he cherishes and nourishes his body as a vessel [Col. 0459C] of his soul, lest, when the vessel is broken, what it contained should flow out and burst forth. According to the literal sense also, as long as a woman is devoted to childbirth and children, she bears the same relation to her husband that the body bears to the soul. But if she should prefer to serve Christ rather than the world, she will cease to be called a woman and will be called a man, because we all desire to attain to the perfect man.

If we refer this also to the tropological interpretation, we shall love our body and the senses of the body—indeed of a lower condition than the mind, but through which the disciplines of the liberal arts and virtues pass into the understanding. He who loves his wife loves himself. For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church.

(Ambr.) By the example of the Savior he exhorts [Col. 0459D] men to love their wives: just as Christ nourishes and cherishes his body, so should a man nourish and cherish the woman, because she is his flesh.

(Alb.) As far as the simple meaning is concerned, we are now commanded to observe holy precepts of charity between man and wife, so that we may nourish and cherish our spouses—that is, provide them with food, clothing, and whatever is necessary. As for those who are said to inflict death upon themselves because of some unbearable pain caused by an excessive illness, no one doubts that they do this not out of hatred for the flesh but because of the affliction of pain, wishing to end the prolonged torture of suffering by a swift death. Yet we cannot rightly call them wise or say that they have sound judgment concerning their souls.

(Hier.) The statement should therefore be referred more to the tropological meaning. Let us say [Col. 0460A] that the soul should love, nourish, and cherish that flesh which will see the salvation of God, instructing it in disciplines, fattening it with heavenly bread, and irrigating it with the blood of Christ, so that, refreshed and clean, it may follow the man with free movement and not be weighed down by any weakness or burden.

The comparison with Christ nourishing and cherishing the Church is also beautiful, as he says to Jerusalem: “How often I desired to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling!” (Matt. XXIII). Souls likewise cherish their bodies, so that this corruptible body may put on incorruption and, suspended by the lightness of wings, be more easily lifted into the air.

Let us therefore cherish both wives, as men, and our bodies, as souls, so that wives may be transformed into men and bodies into souls, and there may be no distinction of sex at all. [Col. 0460B] Just as among the angels there is neither male nor female, so let us, who are destined to be like angels, already begin to be what has been promised to us in heaven.

Because we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones.

(Amb.) This is to be understood spiritually. He called us his members because he himself is the head of the whole Church. Since through him we began to exist, he is called our head, as the one from whom the whole body subsists. Thus every spiritual creature is his member, provided that it bends the knee in his name.

(Hier.) We are members of the body of Christ not according to the nature of his eternal divinity, but in accordance with the humanity which he deigned to assume. Although the man who was assumed possesses the nature of our bodies, [Col. 0460C] he does not possess their origin. We are formed from human seed; he was born of the Holy Spirit.

It may also be said otherwise: the body of Christ is the Church, and the Church is assembled from all believers. Paul and the Ephesians are members of the body—that is, of the Church of Christ.

For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.

(Ambr.) To commend unity, he gave an example of unity, so that just as man and woman are one by nature, Christ and the Church might likewise be understood to be one through faith.

(Hier.) Thus, to encourage mutual affection between wife and husband, he took the example of Adam and Eve, so that just as a rib is taken from Adam and built into a wife, and the wife is again reduced into one flesh with the man—[Col. 0460D] because he who loves his wife loves himself—so we too should love our wives.

The same thing is interpreted allegorically in Christ and the Church, so that Adam might prefigure Christ and Eve the Church. For the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. And just as the whole human race is born from Adam and his wife, so the entire multitude of believers has been generated from Christ and the Church. Having become one body of the Church, it is again placed in Christ’s side and fills the place of the rib, becoming one body with the man, while the Lord himself requests this in the Gospel: “Father, grant that just as you and I are one, so they too may be one in us” (John XVII).

This is a great mystery, but I speak of [Col. 0461A] Christ and of the Church.

(Ambr.) He signifies that the sacrament of the mystery is great in the unity of man and woman. He does not reveal this, however, but seeks from the mentioned mystery another meaning that does not conflict with it, one that he knows pertains to the advancement of the human race—namely, to the Church and the Savior. Just as, after leaving his parents, a man clings to his wife, so, after abandoning every error, the Church should cling to and submit herself to her head, which is Christ.

(Aug.) Who does not recognize that Christ left his Father in this sense: although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. II)? He also left his mother, the Synagogue of the Jews, which clung carnally to the Old Testament, and clung to his holy wife, the Church, so that through the peace of the New [Col. 0461B] Testament the two might be one flesh. For although he is God with the Father, through whom we were made, he became through the flesh a partaker of us, so that we might be his body.

Thus, as it were, from two there is formed a single person consisting of head and body, bridegroom and bride. The prophet Isaiah also commends the wondrous and excellent unity of his person, for, speaking in him, Christ says: “As a bridegroom he bound the turban upon me, and as a bride he adorned me with ornament” (Isa. LXI). He called himself bridegroom; he called himself bride. Why? Unless because the two were one flesh, why should two speak in one? For in Christ the Church speaks, and in the Church Christ speaks; the body speaks in the head and the head in the body.

(Hier.) Nevertheless, contrary to what many think, not every part of the history written about Adam and Eve in [Col. 0461C] Genesis can easily be referred to Christ and the Church. Only what is placed in the present passage can be so referred: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.”

For the first man and first prophet, Adam, prophesied this concerning Christ and the Church: our Lord and Savior left his Father, God, and his mother, the heavenly Jerusalem; he came to the earth for the sake of his body, the Church; he fashioned her from his side; and for her sake the Word became flesh.

Since not all mysteries are equal, but one mystery is greater and another lesser, he therefore now says, “This is a great mystery,” while at the same time indicating his humility by adding, “[Col. 0461D] But I speak of Christ and of the Church.”

Gregory Nazianzen, a highly eloquent man and especially learned in the Scriptures, when he discussed this passage with me, used to say: “See how great the mystery of this chapter is. When the Apostle interprets it of Christ and the Church, he does not assert that he has expressed it in a manner equal to the dignity of the testimony; rather, he seems to say in a certain way: ‘I know that this passage is full of ineffable mysteries, and that it seeks a divine heart as its interpreter.’ But for my part, given the smallness of my understanding, I think for the present that it should be understood of Christ and the Church—not because anything is greater than Christ and the Church, but because it is difficult to interpret in Christ and the Church everything that is said about Adam and Eve.”

Nevertheless, let each one of you [Col. 0462A] love his own wife as himself.

Someone may suppose that the Apostle commands the same love between husband and wife as was commanded toward one’s neighbor, for it is written: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” and now it says: “Let each one love his own wife as himself.” Therefore the same love would exist toward one’s neighbor and toward one’s wife.

But if, according to the Savior’s interpretation, every human being is a neighbor to every other human being, then there would be no difference in the love owed to one’s wife and to any other person. To say this is highly absurd. With one’s neighbor, the comparison is made so that you may love him as yourself and desire that he be saved. But with one’s wife, the adverb “as” does not express similarity but approval and confirmation, spoken with a certain force.

Thus we say [Col. 0462B] of a man, “He acted as a man,” and of the Savior it is written: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten” (John I). This does not mean that the Savior possessed glory by comparison with another only-begotten one; he himself is the Only-begotten. And if there were another only-begotten one, he could not be called only-begotten. Therefore he did not need the example of another only-begotten, but possessed glory as the Only-begotten—that is, glory appropriate to himself.

(Alb.) Although it is said figuratively concerning Christ and the Church, “The two shall be one flesh,” nevertheless, in the historical sense, it is said to men: “Love your wives in all chastity and holiness.”

And let the wife fear her husband.

(Ambr.) Since man and woman have one nature, the man is therefore admonished to love the woman as himself. But because the woman is inferior in person [Col. 0462C] by reason of condition, not of nature, she is commanded to be subject to the man and to fear him.

(Hier.) It should also be noted that the man is commanded to love his wife, while the woman is commanded to fear her husband. Love is appropriate to the man and fear to the woman; to the slave, however, not only fear but trembling is added. Hence he says in what follows: “Slaves, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling.”

But he says, “Let the wife fear her husband.” If fear of God, because of fear of punishment, does not allow the one who fears to be perfect, how much more imperfect will a woman be who fears not only God but also her husband? For this reason it must be asked whether wife and the wife’s fear are to be understood carnally, since wives are often found to be much better than their husbands: they command them, manage the household, raise the children, and maintain discipline in the family, while their husbands [Col. 0462D] indulge themselves and run after prostitutes. Whether such women ought to rule their husbands or fear them I leave to the reader’s judgment.

But if, according to the allegory, as we said above, the wife is understood as the body and the man as the mind, there is nothing inappropriate in her fearing him as a handmaid fears her master, since she is established in a secondary rank and in a lower substance. For, as Crispus says, “We make greater use of the mind’s command and the body’s service.”

Whoever follows the simple meaning concerning woman and husband will show that the word “fear” has two meanings. One is the meaning of which John says: “He who fears has punishment,” and, “He who fears is not perfect” (I John IV). In accordance with this, slaves have a spirit of servitude in fear—the fear required of them by the Lord, who says to them: “And if I am Father, [Col. 0463A] where is my glory? And if I am Lord, where is my fear?” (Malachi I.)

The other meaning is what philosophers call εὐλάβεια (*eulabeia*), which among us may be called “reverence,” although the word does not fully convey its force. The prophet also knows the fear of the perfect, and whoever fears with this fear is perfect, as he says in the thirty-third Psalm: “There is no lack for those who fear him” (Psalm XXXIII). Thus this fear may simply be commanded of the wife, so that she may fear—that is, revere—her husband.

## CHAPTER VI

The Apostle teaches the mutual conduct of parents and children and returns to instructing the Ephesians generally concerning all the virtues.

Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is just. Honor your father and [Col. 0463B] mother.

(Ambr.) A law is also given to children: because they exist through their parents as authorities, they must obey them. For it is just that they show reverence to those through whom they exist.

(Alb.) It is ambiguously stated whether children ought to obey their parents in the Lord—that is, parents who begot them in the Lord, as Paul did the Ephesians—or their carnal parents, if the latter are good and do not educate their children contrary to God’s will. Both are understood to be required: we are commanded to obey our carnal parents in the Lord’s will and our spiritual parents.

Which is the first commandment with a promise: “So that it may be well with you and you may be long-lived upon the earth.”

(Ambr.) This promise is contained in Exodus (Exod. XX): parents are to be honored so that things may go well with their children and they may reach a more advanced age.

How, however, did he call this the first commandment, when [Col. 0463C] it is clear that the first commandment is stated thus: “You shall have no other gods besides me”; then: “You shall not make for yourself any likeness of those things that are in heaven above or on the earth below”; third: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain”; fourth: “You shall observe my Sabbaths”; but fifth: “Honor your father and mother,” and so forth?

The reason is that the first four commandments pertain to the Lord and are therefore understood to be contained on the first tablet. The remaining commandments pertain to the human being: that he honor his parents, not kill, not commit fornication, not steal, not bear false witness, and not covet anything belonging to his neighbor. These six commandments appear to have been written on the second tablet, the first of which is: “Honor your father and mother.”

For this reason he said, “which is the first commandment with a promise”: to distinguish [Col. 0463D] between the commandments that pertain to God and those that pertain to human beings.

(Alb.) Perhaps this promise was given carnally to the Jews, whereas to us it is spoken spiritually: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. V). Not this earth, on which even the ungodly sometimes commit crimes against their parents and nevertheless grow old, but that earth which the Lord promises to the meek and in which the righteous will dwell. Its blessings the Psalmist believes he will see when he says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm XXVI).

And fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.

(Alb.) The sin of children is disobedience to their parents. Because parents might command [Col. 0464A] something perverse, he added “in the Lord.” But the sin of parents is to provoke little children and infants to anger, or at least to command adolescents and those of more mature age to do things that are burdensome.

Just as the reward of obedience and submission has been displayed in the case of children, so restrained authority is commanded in the case of parents, so that fathers may know that they preside over their children not as over slaves but as over sons. They must not become worse through being exasperated by your impatience, for by your example they ought to have learned patience.

(Ambr.) In anger no one recognizes what is useful. Therefore children ought to learn temperance from the example of their parents, so that they may pursue what is beneficial. Fathers ought to remember that they too were once children and certainly did not wish to be embittered by their fathers. Children likewise ought to recognize that they will become [Col. 0464B] fathers and would not wish to be dishonored by their own children. Therefore both should show one another what they seek from one another.

(Alb.) But in Greek *correction* is better read, a word that conveys admonition and instruction more than austerity. The priest Eli himself was holy, but because he did not educate his sons in all discipline and correction, he fell backward and died (I Kings II).

Slaves, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, in the simplicity of your hearts, as you would Christ.

(Ambr.) Since our religion is higher than all others and alone possesses power, promising the kingdoms of heaven to believers, lest pride should arise in people on this account, all are commanded to discharge the duties owed according to their present conditions and offices. In this way they may encourage the minds of unbelievers toward the worship of God, whom [Col. 0464C] they see to be both just and humble.

When masters see that slaves have improved and have faithfully advanced in rendering service, they freely render to them what they deserve. Slaves, when they perceive the gentleness of their masters, eagerly desire the faith whose power governs human duties with such peaceful restraints.

Even one who occupies a subordinate condition, if he has a servant, does not wish to be despised by him. Therefore he himself ought not to despise his own master. Just as he wants his master to treat him, so he ought to treat his servant, and thus he will be able to please God.

(Hier.) To distinguish him from the spiritual Lord, the master is now called “earthly,” so that a slave who has believed in God but has not yet attained the summit of knowledge may properly serve an earthly [Col. 0464D] master with fear and trembling, in the simplicity of his heart, and serve him faithfully as Christ.

He must not serve merely for appearance, as those do who desire to please human beings, but must turn necessity into willingness and make a reward out of servitude—especially since the lord of the flesh does not command anything different from the Lord of the spirit.

This is what he says: “Not serving for appearance, as those who please human beings, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God.” The slave should also possess this fidelity not under compulsion but voluntarily and from the heart, serving his master as Christ, from whom he will receive the faithful reward of servitude, no less than if he had served as a free man by his own choice.

“Not serving for appearance, as those who please human beings, [Col. 0465A] but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, serving with kindness as to the Lord and not to human beings, knowing that whatever good each person does, he will receive this from the Lord, whether slave or free” (Ambr.)

Because of the fear of God, he wishes just and faithful service to be shown to human beings. The slave serves God, whose rights he preserves in the service owed to his earthly master; he hears that God will repay him for his just deeds on the day of judgment and bears witness to this concerning all others.

This can also contribute to the salvation of masters. When they see that, through God’s grace, it is difficult for slaves to become faithful servants, they will be able to praise the glory of God.

(Hier.) Just as he had written to the Corinthians according to the circumstances of the time (I Cor. VII), so that, if one of two spouses wished to believe, [Col. 0465B] divorces might not arise between husbands and wives under the pretext of faith in Christ, so also to the Ephesians and Colossians—because at the beginning of the faith many thought that gentile masters ought to be despised—he now establishes moderate instructions concerning social conditions. Thus he neither appears to incite slaves against their masters nor, on the other hand, teaches masters that they should be obeyed if they command vicious and abominable things.

It should also be noted that he added different instructions concerning the obedience of children and slaves. To children he says: “Obey your parents in the Lord.” To slaves, however: “Obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling.” Thus, just as fear distinguishes the relationship between a slave and a wife, so obedience differs between children and slaves.

When commanding slaves to obey their masters, he beautifully added “as Christ,” and again, “as servants of Christ, doing [Col. 0465C] the will of God,” so that a slave should not obey an earthly master if he wishes to command anything contrary to the precepts of God.

And you, masters, do the same toward them, giving up threats, knowing that both their Lord and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with God.

(Ambr.) Earthly masters, certainly knowing that God is the common Lord of all, should demand such service as they would not find burdensome if it were demanded of them. For with whatever measure one measures, it will be measured back to him. The Lord is a just judge who distinguishes causes, not persons.

(Hier.) What are these things that he earlier commanded slaves, so that he now tells masters to do the same things toward slaves? I think he means what he had said: “in the simplicity of the heart,” “doing the will of God,” “from the heart,” and “with fidelity [Col. 0465D],” or “benevolence” toward slaves, since εὔνοια (*eunoia*) can signify both.

For each person will receive from the Lord whatever good he has done, whether a servant has served, as was said above, or a free person has exercised mastery, as is fitting. He must not be terrifying or quick to beat, knowing that he too has a Lord in heaven, with whom there is no partiality, who alone judges intentions and, according to them, prefers the better to the worse, choosing deeds rather than persons.

Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the power of his might.

(Ambr.) After all the admonitions and exhortations, after the order of discipline has been religiously handed down and the arrangement of the mystery has been revealed, he wants them to be strong in faith through confidence in God’s power. Knowing that [Col. 0466A] the hope of the promise is firm, they should be ready for the service of God, raising their helm against the waves stirred up by the enemy’s folly. He raises a storm against God’s servants, but he himself suffers shipwreck.

(Hier.) What he says—“Be strong in the Lord and in the power of his might”—is understood entirely in Christ, so that those who believe may be strengthened in all the virtues that are understood to belong to him.

After the specific commands concerning what men and wives, fathers and children, masters and slaves ought to observe, he wisely now commands all people generally and collectively to strengthen themselves in the Lord and in his power and prepare themselves against the devil. Concerning him he writes in what follows:

Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.

From what we read below, and [Col. 0466B] from all that is said in the Scriptures concerning the Lord and Savior, it is most clearly proved that all the weapons of God with which we are now commanded to be clothed signify the Savior. Thus he says one and the same thing as though he had said: “Put on all the armor of God,” meaning, “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ.”

For if the belt is truth and the breastplate is righteousness, while the Savior is called both Truth and Righteousness, there is no doubt that he himself is the belt and the breastplate. Therefore, according to the Apostle, he will be the preparation of the Gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God—living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword (Hebr. IV).

What other weapons of God can we consider necessary for one who must fight against the devil’s cunning, except the power [Col. 0466C] that is Christ? Whoever is clothed with him according to all that is understood concerning him will be able to resist all the devil’s wiles.

Because he is girded with truth, he will not easily be led into doctrines of falsehood. Because he is clothed with the breastplate of righteousness, he cannot be pierced by the darts of iniquity. When he has been shod with the most beautiful footwear in the preparation of the Gospel of peace, as one who has prepared his works at the end and has therefore become a man of peace, he neither undertakes anything warlike or tumultuous nor will be condemned with those who are unprepared.

Unbelief, too, which is the enemy of faith, will have no power where the shield of faith is present. The head, and the chief part of the heart and soul in which all the senses have spoken, will not be shaken when surrounded by the helmet of salvation [Col. 0466D]. Finally, like a strong and warlike man, he will cut down, kill, and slaughter all sects opposed to the truth, holding in his hand the sword of the Spirit—that is, the word of God.

Therefore, wishing to display the devil’s manifold devices by which he tries to seize us, the Apostle called his methods—that is, his inventions or cunning—by reference to those places where we do not guard our heart with complete vigilance.

If we abstain from bodily pleasure, he captures us when we are insufficiently cautious concerning avarice. If we also despise avarice along with pleasure, he slips in through luxury, makes our belly into our god, and through this conquers even those things that had seemed strong.

Just as commanders skilled in warfare customarily attack especially those parts of cities [Col. 0467A] that are poorly fortified, so that, after entering through them, they may easily capture the fortified places, so the devil seeks to break in through whatever he sees lying open or not firmly closed and to enter the very citadel of the heart and soul.

It is unnecessary to speak of his other ambushes, since from these examples the other kinds of his cunning can be recognized.

*Diabolus* is a Greek name, interpreted as “the accuser.” According to the characteristic usage of the Hebrew language, because the tribe of Zebulun also bears a certain resemblance to this word, it can be called καταρύων (*kataryōn*), that is, “flowing downward.” This signifies that he gradually flowed from virtue into vice and fell from heavenly things to earthly ones.

(Amb.) The armor of God is steadfast faith, through which alone Satan has always been conquered.

Since our struggle is not against flesh and blood, [Col. 0467B] but against rulers and authorities, against the world-governors of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

The Apostle is certain that the harms inflicted by faithless servants of God are administered at the instigation of the devil. His height is great and impossible for human beings to reach; therefore he urges us to take up the weapons of God, by whose power alone all his devices are overcome and destroyed. He is the one whose satellites they are, whom he calls “the rulers of this darkness”: the most wicked spirits who dwell in the heavenly places, in the firmament of the world. These are the leaders of error, the rulers of darkness—that is, those set over ignorance and faithlessness.

(Aug.) “Rulers of darkness” must be understood as ruling perversely, as though they were teachers of unbelief.

[Col. 0467C] Therefore the Apostle Paul, warning us how cautious we ought to be toward our enemies, says to the servants of God who were suffering tribulations, namely, through human rebellions, wickedness, and hostilities:

“Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities and the rulers of the world.”

Of what world? Of heaven and earth? Far from it. There is no ruler of this world except the Creator. But what world does he mean? The lovers of the world. Finally, he adds and explains what world he means: “of this darkness.” Of what darkness, surely, except that of unbelievers and the impious? For when the impious and unbelieving had become pious and faithful, the same Apostle addressed them in this way: “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V).

“Against the spiritual forces of wickedness,” he says, [Col. 0467D] “in the heavenly places”: you fight against the devil and his angels; you do not see your enemies, yet you conquer them. “Deliver me from the hands of my enemies and from those who persecute me” (Ps. CXLIII).

He called them “rulers of the world” because they rule the lovers of the world. They do not rule the world as though they were rulers of heaven and earth; rather, he calls sinners “the world”: “and the world did not know him” (John I). Such a world is ruled by those who do not know Christ. For just as Christ governs and rules those who are light, so the devil drives and incites those who are darkness toward every evil. The Apostle therefore exhorts us not to pray against an evil human being, but against the devil who works together with him, and to do everything we can so that the devil may be expelled and the human being set free.

For just as, if an armed man mounted on a horse from the opposing side should come against someone stationed in battle, that person does not become angry with the horse but with the rider, and does everything in his power to strike the rider and seize the horse, so we must act toward evil people: we must not work against them, but with all our strength against the one who incites them, so that, when the devil is conquered, the wretched person whom he had begun to possess may be set free.

(Hier.) I do not think that Paul, writing to the Corinthians, could have said, “Our struggle is not against blood and flesh,” when he says: “No temptation has overtaken you except what is human; but God is faithful and will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear” (1 Cor. X). I think, rather, that the struggles against flesh and blood are those which are there called “human temptations,” when the flesh desires against the spirit and urges us to do its works: fornication, uncleanness, wantonness, idolatry, enmities, quarrels, heresies, ambushes, drunkenness, revelries (Gal. V), and the rest of the things like them.

But the temptation is not human, nor is the struggle against flesh and blood, when Satan himself, transformed into an angel of light, attempts to persuade us to regard him as an angel of light; or when he does something similar through every kind of power, signs, and lying wonders, and through every deceit of wickedness. For when the enemy has ensnared someone so that he may enter into him and speak through him, the Lord says that this is not as though flesh and blood, or a human temptation, had deceived him, but as though it were a principality and authority, a ruler of darkness, [Col. 0468C] and a spiritual wickedness.

Therefore let us not give place to the devil; and even if a spirit possessing authority rises up against us, let us give him no place, according to what is written: “Do not give him place” (Eccl. X).

Someone may say that what he says—“Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and authorities,” and the rest that follows—is said in order to teach us that even those vices which we think are supplied to us by the flesh do not belong to flesh or blood, but are suggested by certain spiritual wickednesses.

For there are certain demons who serve lusts and love songs, as the prophet also recalls when he says: “They were led astray by a spirit of fornication” (Hos. IV). They are also said to have certain barbarous names, as those who are truly called sorcerers by the common people have often confessed. Incantations, prayers, various colors, and different kinds either of metals or of foods are said to be things at which demons, when invoked, attend and seize wretched souls.

Others preside over anger, rages, and wars; others preside over enmities and stir up hatred among human beings. Since, they say, the Apostle wishes to teach us that these kinds of vices are not produced by the nature of the body or from the matter of flesh and blood, but by the prompting of demons, he therefore says: “Our struggle is not against blood, but against principalities and authorities,” and the rest.

But we have now brought forward examples of those who serve wretchedly in magical arts and are reported to do these things [or: “are forbidden to do these things”; the reading is uncertain], so that we may recall [or: “blunt”; the reading is uncertain] the opinion of those who [Col. 0469A] think that all vices belong to flesh and blood and that demons have no power to incite us to sin.

We think that Jacob also had such a struggle: namely, that he did not contend against flesh and blood when he remained alone and a man wrestled with him, helping and strengthening him against another who was fighting with great exertion (Gen. XXXII).

At the same time, consider whether those who think that Jacob wrestled all night in the ordinary manner of wrestlers are not perhaps ridiculous. For what is so remarkable if, as they say, in wrestling he either prevailed or was defeated? But according to the rational and appropriate understanding of the patriarch’s wrestling, we must believe that he had such a struggle as those have who can say: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood.”

Nor is it necessary to examine the whole mystery of that passage, since, in its proper place, if I live, it must be discussed more fully.

We ask, however, where Paul read these things in the Old Testament, or by what authority he published matters that were nowhere written. We infer from the things written in the Law, in Joshua, in the Book of Judges and Kings, and in Chronicles concerning battles and single combats—for example, David against Goliath, and the sons of Israel against foreigners and the other nations—that the Apostle understood them more profoundly and perceived in them a spiritual war corresponding to the bodily one, in which the combatants were either defeated or victorious.

The satraps of each place, then, were indications of the heavenly powers; the kings of the individual nations were images of those who are now called the rulers of the world and of darkness; while evil human beings demonstrated the spiritual forces of wickedness [Col. 0469C] in the heavenly places.

It seems to us that the Apostle is saying this in other words:

“O Ephesians, the things you have heard about Israel’s battles against the nations seem indeed to speak of flesh or blood—for example, of the Egyptians, Idumeans, Ammonites, Moabites, and the other nations. But if you truly wish to know, understand that all those events happened to them figurally. They were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, so that from them we may understand that our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against certain spiritual and invisible powers: against the rulers of this darkness, which lies upon this world and inflicts upon human beings the error of unbelief; and against the spiritual forces of wickedness which dwell [Col. 0469D] in the heavenly places.

“This does not mean that demons dwell in the heavenly places, but that the air above us has received this name. Hence the birds that fly through the air are called ‘the birds of heaven’ (Ps. VIII; Luke VIII, IX, XIII).”

In another place the Apostle says of demons that they wander in this air (Eph. II): “In which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the sons of disobedience.”

This is the opinion of all teachers: that this air, which divides heaven and earth by lying between them and is called the void, is full of opposing powers.

After this it must be reconsidered from whom the principalities, authorities, rulers of the world of this darkness, and spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places received the power to be what they are.

Another person may say that the apostate devil assigned various offices to his satellites, and that God is not the author of these classifications. An attentive reader can oppose to him the following: How is it written, “There is no authority except from God” (Rom. XIII)? If this is said of human beings, how much more of those who are of a subtler and better nature?

Nor does someone who thinks this immediately incur the charge of blasphemy, since each one may have received different ministries according to his own will. For just as in cities we see those who have committed some shameful deed assigned either to care for animals, to cut marble, to clean the filth of sewers, or to preside over gladiators and be appointed to shed the blood of criminals, so demons, through the freedom of their own choice, have received the province of ambushes, frauds, crimes, perjury, and the remaining vices, so that they are rulers of darkness because they did not wish to be rulers of light.

When these rulers of the world and of darkness have wrestled against someone, tripped him, and made him fall, they immediately attach him to the world and darkness over which they preside.

For this reason we must labor more vigorously, so that, having once heard, “I chose you out of this world, and you are no longer of this world; for if you were of the world, the world would love what was its own” (John XV), we may not return to the world or subject ourselves to it. Rather, let the world be crucified to us and we to it, so that Jesus, the ruler of light, may join us to his own world and place us under the authority of his Father, rescuing us from the power of spiritual wickedness and from their heaven, which will pass away and cannot be called God’s throne.

For it is impious to believe that the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places hold possession of the heaven of which God says: “Heaven is my throne” (Acts VII).

Thus, whoever understands the things that happen to us in this world, both when we are present and when we are absent, while we cannot see them—either because of this fragile and earthly body of our lowliness in which the soul is enveloped, or because a subtler nature is not disclosed to bodily eyes—will see what the darknesses are that the Apostle now mentions.

It may be that this entire earthly life is called darkness: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John I). Or perhaps the light and understanding of the soul is overshadowed, covered, and blinded by the earthly body, the body of death and lowliness [Col. 0470D].

Let us know, however, that apart from the present passage we have never read κοσμοκράτορες—“world-rulers”—anywhere in either the Old or the New Testament. Paul coined this word because, in arguing with the Ephesians, he needed to adapt new names to new and invisible realities.

Moreover, because he says “in the heavenly places,” which seems ambiguous, we must say that the phrase may be understood as applying to everything, so that the sense is:

“Our struggle is not against the authorities in the heavenly places, and against the rulers of this darkness in the heavenly places, and against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places”—not merely against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

This is especially so if we understand, as was explained above, why birds are called “heavenly,” and why common usage says that rain comes from heaven, although rain does not come down from heaven.

For philosophers say that the clouds from which rain is poured and showers fall are no more than two thousand paces from the earth. In accordance with this understanding, the floodgates of heaven are also said to have been opened during the Flood.

Nevertheless, the worse someone is, the nearer he will be to earthly places and to denser substance. For both the earth and the air surrounding us have their own density.

Some say that souls freed from their bodies, if they have been refined in the present life and worn down, as it were, by the file of ἄσκησις—“ascetic discipline”—and virtues into a subtle body, will not dwell in denser regions, but will be near God, who is incorporeal.

But if they are such as those of whom it can be said, “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Ps. VI)—or “fat of heart,” according to the weight of their grossness—they are dragged down to the lowest places and weighed down by their grossness.

After this, it must likewise be discussed whether there is some place denser than this earth and air, called by most people “hell” (Infernus), in which those called the inferi dwell. Who these are, and what knowledge or distinction they possess in relation to those who are called the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, is not for the present discussion.

It remains for us to learn more clearly from two groups mentioned by the Apostle what difference there is between the struggle against flesh and blood, and the rulers of this darkness and the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

When he wishes to indicate human temptations—that is, the struggle against flesh and blood—he speaks of them with contempt and disdain: “Who will separate us from the love of God? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution?” (Rom. VIII).

But when he wishes to teach us about the opposing powers, the rulers of darkness, and the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, he begins from another point, as though from another head, and says: “For I am certain that neither death nor life,” and the rest.

Perhaps this chapter has been discussed at greater length than the reader would wish. But I ask him to forgive the difficulty of that passage and of the Ephesians, who, after their magical practices, ought to have known by whom they had once been deceived.

Therefore take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and, having done everything, to stand firm.

(Hier.) “The evil day” either indicates the present time, of which he had said above, “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil,” on account of the distress and labors of this life, since we do not reach the palm of victory without sweat and struggle;

or certainly the day of consummation and judgment, when the devil, our enemy and avenger, will wish to retain us on his side. From it will be delivered the one who considers the poor and needy: “On the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Ps. XL).

This is the day of which it is also written elsewhere: “Behold, the day of the Lord’s wrath is coming” (Isa. XIII); and elsewhere: “For the day of the Lord will come, insatiable in fury and wrath” (Isa. XXII); and again: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord! Why do you desire the day of the Lord? It is darkness and not light, just as if a man were to flee from the face of a lion and encounter a bear, and enter his house and rest his hands upon the wall, and a serpent were to bite him. Is not the day of the Lord darkness and not light, gloom without brightness?” (Amos V).

For how could this day not be evil, since it is wrapped in darkness and gloom? The prophet Joel also recalls it, saying: “Blow the trumpet in Zion; proclaim it on my holy mountain. Let all who inhabit the earth be confounded, because the day of the Lord is coming, because the day of darkness and tempest is near, the day of cloud and gloom” (Joel II).

And Zephaniah speaks of the same day: “Great is the day, very near and exceedingly swift; the voice of the day of the Lord is bitter, harsh, and mighty: a day of wrath, that day, a day of distress and necessity” (Zeph. I), and the rest.

After these words he adds: “And I will afflict human beings, and they will walk like the blind, because they have sinned against the Lord” (Rev. XII).

Therefore, so that someone may be able to resist the devil on this day—for he is the accuser of our brothers—let him take up all the weapons of God. For this is what πανοπλία means: not merely “weapons,” as it has been translated simply in Latin, but being girded with every kind of missile and weapon.

Of these weapons he explains in what follows. Let him know that he can stand only if he has done everything, so that, full of every virtue, he may plant his feet firmly and not be moved from the battle line. Let him be among those of whom the Lord says, “There are some of those standing here” (Matt. XVI); and elsewhere, “For you stand by faith” (2 Cor. I); and the Psalmist says, “He established my feet upon a rock” (Ps. XXXIX).

A third interpretation is also introduced by some, who say that not every battle against the devil ends in death, but that when we have departed from this world, a stronger and more open struggle will then take place for us, with those present against those present. They explain in this sense what we discussed shortly before: “Neither things present nor things future,” saying that the “future things” are the struggles that must be undertaken after this life.

Likewise they interpret the words, “Therefore we strive, whether in the present or in the future, to please him” (2 Cor. V), as signifying by the present time this life and by the future the time after death.

They refer also what is now said—“having done everything, to stand”—to the same sense, as though no one could do everything in the present life, but only do a part, just as he sees in part and prophesies in part; and as though he could stand perfectly only when he had done everything.

Another person explains these things more simply, saying that Paul was exhorting and warning the Ephesians concerning future temptations and persecutions which, in the prophetic spirit, he saw would come upon them after this Epistle, so that they might do everything by which they could stand firm in the faith of the Gospel and not fall during persecution.

We think, however, that the evil day is specifically taken here from Psalm forty-eight.

Therefore stand, with your loins girded in truth.

It is beyond doubt that in Scripture all the members of the soul are called by reference to the members of the flesh and body. I think that the loins are one such member, and we are commanded to gird them with truth.

It is also written in the Gospel according to Luke: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands” (Luke XII).

Since the loins are always understood in relation to generation and seed, according to the words, “I will set the fruit of your loins upon your throne” (Ps. CXXXI), and elsewhere, “Levi was still in the loins of his father Abraham when Melchizedek met him” (Heb. VII), it seems to us that the person who does not render to his wife what is owed and does not serve lust, but imitates the unbegotten God and does not minister to the business of generation, has girded his loins.

I think that this also signifies the fact that John had a leather belt around his loins (Matt. III). He was not one of those unclean persons who, because of the discharge of semen, were cast outside the camp and could not dwell with the ark of the Lord; nor was he among those of whom it is written in Numbers: “Let his garments be torn” (Num. VIII).

Whoever is girded with Christ in truth gathers these garments up high, draws them upward, and covers, binds, and encloses the shamefulness of naked sides with a spiritual belt. He is ready for battle and possesses works that shine, which are called burning lamps.

And having put on the breastplate of righteousness.

Just as a person who wears a breastplate densely woven from hooks and iron rings joined together is difficult to wound in those places that preserve life most particularly, so the person surrounded by the manifold garment of righteousness will neither, like a deer, receive an arrow in the liver nor fall into desires and rages.

Instead, he will be pure in heart, having God as the craftsman of this breastplate, the one who fashions every weapon for each of the saints and does not allow him to be struck and burned at once by the flying arrow of the day or by the fiery arrows.

And having your feet shod in the readiness of the Gospel of peace.

[Col. 0473C] Observe more carefully that he has called a certain power of the soul “feet,” by which we enter into the one who says, “I am the way,” and which we ought to shoe with the readiness of the Gospel of peace.

As a figure of these shoes, the shoes in Exodus came first: those which the people eating the Passover are commanded to have, together with those who are prepared to make a journey.

“For thus,” he says, “you shall eat it: your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staffs in your hands; and you shall eat it in haste. For it is the Passover of the Lord” (Exod. XII).

To eat with haste and with one’s feet shod is a sign of readiness, so that, strengthened by the paschal food, one may cross the broad and dreadful wilderness.

Therefore, whoever is still walking should put on shoes. But whoever, having crossed the Jordan, has already entered the promised land should uncover his foot. “Remove,” he says, “the shoe from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground.”

If someone is not Jesus son of Nun [Joshua], nor an apostle, let him shoe his feet in the readiness of the Gospel of peace. But if someone is an apostle and may be numbered among the Twelve, let him by no means take off his shoe on the road, nor cover his heel in order to avoid scorpions and snakes. Rather, already perfected and complete, let him stand on holy ground, live in Christ, and follow the Lamb wherever he goes.

It is asked whether he now said “the Gospel of peace” to distinguish it from another gospel, or whether it is proper to this Gospel that it be called the Gospel of peace.

Whoever therefore has peace is shod with the Gospel of Christ. Once he has been shod, he is prepared; and when prepared, he must not think himself perfect, but must prepare himself for this purpose: to proceed, and by proceeding to come to the end.

Above all, take up the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the fiery arrows of the evil one.

It is as though he had said: “Carry the shield of faith in every work, so that, covered and protected, you may receive the arrows that come against you and skillfully deflect them here and there by the art of war.”

This is the faith which even Abraham, after many works and virtues, scarcely was able to obtain, so that Scripture could say of him: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. IV).

The arrows of the evil one are obvious: he wishes to shoot them into our hearts through the worst thoughts. It was of these that he cast one into the heart of Judas, so that he might betray the Savior.

Therefore the enemy cannot even obtain an opening by which to wound the soul if we hold the shield of faith. On this shield not only are the weapons that come against us broken, but the fire itself of the weapons is extinguished—the fire of which the prophet also complains when he says: “All are adulterers; their hearts are like an oven” (Hos. VII).

Whoever holds this shield of faith with a strong hand and, trusting in the Lord, knows that he is safe from the arrows that come against him, will speak fearlessly:

“I trust in the Lord. How can you say to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountain like a sparrow’? For behold, sinners have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at those who are upright in heart” (Ps. X).

Therefore, he says, since I trust in the Lord, by what reasoning do you give me the advice not to stand against the assault of my enemies and against the arrows that they have prepared in their quivers against me, wishing to strike not only me but all who are upright in heart?

Behold, I stand upon the rock and do not flee to the dark mountains; and all the weapons of the enemies, repelled, turn back upon those who direct them.

And take up the helmet of salvation.

Because of this helmet of salvation, all the senses in our head remain sound, especially the eyes, of which Solomon says in Ecclesiastes: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Eccl. II).

For he knew what the head of a human being was and which eyes were placed in a human being’s head. If Christ is his head, and the eyes of the wise are in his head, it follows that all our understanding, mind, thought, speech, and counsel—provided that we are wise—should be in Christ.

In Christ, that is, in the Word, the light, the truth, righteousness, and all the virtues.

(Amb.) Since we wage war against the most savage enemies, skilled in every kind of evasion, we must therefore keep watch with every caution and care, so that whatever they attempt may find us fortified and prepared.

For God must help those whom he sees keeping watch in prayers and awaiting victory from his weapons.

In this kind of war, therefore, a sober mind and a pure conscience are necessary, because the battle is not against bodily wickedness but against spiritual forces.

Against earthly enemies the body is strengthened by food, and the mind is inflamed by drink, so that it may take courage for resistance. But against spiritual forces of wickedness we must fight spiritually, and the weapons of sobriety and abstinence must be taken up, so that, filled with the Holy Spirit, we may overcome unclean and wandering spirits.

Thus we shall gird our loins in truth if we are prepared to resist error. For everyone who wishes to work girds himself, so that, removing impediment, he may work more diligently.

And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, with every prayer and supplication, praying at all times in the Spirit, and keeping watch in this very thing with all perseverance and supplication for all the saints, and for me.

(Hier.) The word of God flows from the Holy Spirit; but the contrary voice speaks from the earth and takes its beginning from there. “The one who is from the earth is from the earth and speaks from the earth. The one who comes from heaven is above all, and what he has seen and heard, this he testifies” (John III).

The word of God is the sword of the Spirit, concerning which Paul now says: “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” [Col. 0475B] (Heb. IV).

For the word of God is living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword, and penetrating to the dividing of soul, bones, and marrow.

This Spirit cuts and divides, accomplishing much through the prayer of those who at all times beseech the Lord in the Spirit, according to the saying: “I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray also with the mind” (1 Cor. XIV).

By this means the Apostle advances, so that through vigils and persistent prayer he may be enriched in the word of God and in teaching, and so that all this abundance may contribute to the salvation of others, benefiting even those who make supplication on his behalf.

At the same time, the Apostle’s humility is admirable: he asks the Ephesians to make supplications for him. For he says: “with all perseverance and supplication for all the saints and for me,” so that he might mention the saints separately and himself separately.

[Col. 0475C] That speech may be given to me in the opening of my mouth, so that with confidence I may make known the mystery of the Gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains, so that in it I may dare to speak as I ought.

(Hier.) What he now says, “in the opening of my mouth,” and elsewhere, “opening his mouth, he taught them, saying” (Matt. V), and “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. CXVIII), and “I will open my mouth in parables” (Ps. LXXVII), and other similar passages, must be understood as though he had said:

“Let the treasures be opened, and let the mysteries hidden from the ages be disclosed, so that the Holy Spirit may enter in order to bring forth the things that lie concealed.”

The following words prove that this is the meaning of this testimony, namely, “that speech may be given to me in the opening of my mouth.” He says: “with confidence to make known the mystery of the Gospel.”

Not in proverbs and parables, as the prophets and the Lord himself spoke while he was still in the body, saying: “The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs, but will announce the Father to you openly” (John XVI).

Only the person who does not have a condemning heart can obtain this speech of confidence. “For if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God, and whatever we ask, we receive from him” (1 John III).

Rare, therefore, is the person who makes the mystery of the Gospel known with confidence, because rare is the person who has confidence toward God. “For who will boast that he has a pure heart, or who will stand and say that he is clean from sins?”

After this, what he means when he says, “for which I am an ambassador in chains,” must be briefly touched upon: namely, that he was making the mystery of the Gospel known.

The person who understands this simply will say that he wrote this from Rome while he was in prison and chains, on account of the testimony of Christ. But another will contend that he said it on account of the body of our lowliness and the chain with which we are surrounded, since we do not yet know according to what we ought to know and see through a mirror in an enigma.

According to this view, he could truly open the mysteries in the confidence of the Gospel only when he had laid aside the chain and gone forth free from prison—unless perhaps even one who is in chains must be counted as being without chains if he has his manner of life in heaven, and if it can be said of him: “But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Rom. VIII).

(Ambr.) If we live rightly, the Holy Spirit remains in us, and we can obtain what we ask.

Therefore, to pray always in the Spirit means to direct prayer to God with a clean conscience and unshaken faith. The person who prays with a polluted mind and intends to sin again prays in the flesh—not because of an unforeseen event or a sudden lapse, but by deliberate intention.

Yet one may avoid sin unto death if one prays perseveringly, so that the mind, with constant attention, may always be intent upon the law of God, meditating day and night on the things that God loves.

Then they can also pray for the saints; for it is not unworthy that the members should be concerned for one another. Nor can it seem rash if capable disciples intercede for their teacher, assisting him so that, after laying aside impediments, he may use freedom to preach, as was handed down by the author, lest, oppressed by the force of tribulations, fear itself blunt the sharpness of his teaching and cause him to lose his strictness.

Therefore he urges prayer for himself in two ways: that his understanding may be filled with the Spirit for fully expressing the mystery, and that the ability to speak boldly may be granted him in its defense. God gladly hears such a prayer, for he sees his own embassy despised in his apostle; and therefore, angered on his own behalf, he will not deny its fulfillment.

For if it is the custom and law among human ambassadors not to inflict harm upon them, with what presumption and boldness are not only injuries but death inflicted upon the ambassadors of God?

Therefore he says, “for which I am an ambassador in chains.” He was not permitted to speak freely, but, proclaiming the words of God under subjection and necessity, he was subjected to chains, scourges, and deaths. He was stoned, and he himself also fought with beasts at Ephesus (1 Cor. XV).

[Col. 0476D] But so that you too may know what concerns me and what I am doing, Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make everything known to you. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that you may learn what concerns us and that he may comfort your hearts. (Jerome.) Understand this in two ways. Either Tychicus was sent to Ephesus so that he might announce to them that the Apostle’s imprisonment had become known throughout the entire praetorium, and that his chains had advanced the cause of the Gospel, at the time when he wrote to the Colossians, saying: “Everything concerning me Tychicus, the beloved brother, minister, and fellow servant in the Lord, whom I have sent to you for this very purpose, will make known to you, so that you may learn what concerns us and may comfort your hearts,” together with Onesimus, the most dear and faithful brother, who is one of you, and so forth. For it was a great [Col. 0477A] consolation to hear that Paul was triumphing in Rome, the mistress of cities and the citadel of Roman power, from prison and chains.

Or certainly Tychicus was sent for this reason: to announce to them Paul’s manner of life, which they did not know, and, as it were, to provide those who were learning with a model of life by recounting the Apostle’s deeds and virtues, for those who wished to imitate him. It could not have been a small consolation for those desiring to emulate him to learn what the Apostle had done.

(Ambrose.) Through Tychicus the Ephesians learn what the Apostle is doing, and he likewise learns what the Ephesians are doing. There could be no doubt concerning the Apostle, since what he was doing was divine; but it was necessary to know what he was doing among the faithless and amid their plots. Concerning the Ephesians, however, it was necessary to learn whether or not they were making progress. Therefore, so that they might obey Tychicus and listen to his words willingly, he commends him, [Col. 0477B] calling him this most beloved brother and an able minister of God.

Peace to the brethren and love with faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. He wishes peace, which is the gateway of love, to be with the brethren, and love with faith, so that, having entered through peace, they may remain in love, which comes from faith. For this is from God the Father and his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

(Jerome.) For if there are other gifts that are bestowed by God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, among these peace holds no small place. It surpasses all understanding and guards the hearts and minds of the saints: a certain serenity and tranquility of the resting soul, driving away every storm and whirlwind of disturbances. Similar to this is love with faith, which God the Father and the Son likewise grant together, so that we may love God with our whole heart, our neighbors as ourselves, and pray for our enemies. This peace and love, which the Apostle invokes upon believers, are possessed only by those who deserve to be called brethren; [Col. 0478A] for it is “peace to the brethren, and love with faith and peace.” Therefore the Father grants both love and faith just as the Son does, and the heresy that refuses to allow the Son to do what the Father can do is silenced.

Grace be with all who love the Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption. (Ambrose.) The Apostle, foreseeing that many would in desperation abandon the understanding of faith concerning the Lord Jesus Christ, says that eternal grace will remain with those who love Christ and think rightly about him, in accordance with the will of God the Father. For those who call him degenerate, the grace given to them will be taken away.

(Jerome.) Some have interpreted this in such a way that they thought the one who loves our Lord Jesus Christ is a person who is free from works of corruption, understanding works of corruption as sexual intercourse. Hence common usage and ordinary speech call those who do not know intercourse with women “uncorrupted,” namely virgins, and those who have tasted such pleasure “corrupted.” They also apply the testimony: “If anyone corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt him” (I Cor. III). But I do not know whether they can explain what is written: “Each person has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (I Cor. VII). Let us therefore see whether it may be better to understand every sin as corruption of the soul, and to call those who are free from sin uncorrupted, so that those who love the Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption are those who are not held by the bonds of sin, and the grace of God is with them.

At the same time, I think that, to distinguish those who love the Lord Jesus Christ but not “in incorruption,” as the phrase now stands, from those who love him in incorruption, he says that those who love him in incorruption have the grace of God in Christ. For how many love the Lord, ready for exile, ready for martyrdom, ready to endure poverty and every kind of insult for him, and nevertheless are overcome by the passion of the flesh? Yet the Apostle does not invoke grace upon these, because the Lord’s grace is with all who love him in incorruption.

# BOOK NINETEEN. EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS

[Col. 0477]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0477C]

The Philippians were refined men, and in the contemplation of virtues they were better than many others. They always devoted great care to the necessities of blessed Paul, considering themselves his debtors, both because he was an apostle and because he seemed to endure much labor for the benefit of others. Anyone can recognize this from what the same Paul wrote at the end of the epistle. But a dispute about precedence arose among some of them, and this among those who seemed especially adorned with virtues. They were drawn into this dispute, as often happens among human beings, particularly when they possessed those qualities that could grant them precedence. Virtue can contribute this above all, although there are also certain other things that can confer it. Yet the more they perceive themselves to be better than others, the more vehemently [Col. 0478C] they claim it for themselves—unless someone, considering the weakness of human nature, has driven every kind of pride from his heart.

To this was added the fact that those who were from the circumcision were hastening to persuade the faithful who had believed from among the Gentiles to keep the Law. The Apostle seems to have written much about these people in the second epistle to the Corinthians and in the epistle to the Galatians. Some of them also came to the Philippians, attempting to steal away [Col. 0478D] those who had believed in Christ. They taught them that it was not fitting for those who believed in Christ to neglect the Law. Therefore blessed Paul writes in the present epistle about the humility that must be maintained, setting down what was appropriate to write to them, and at the same time writing about those who urged them to keep the Law, so that they would not heed their words. He also includes certain matters that he thought suitable for them in forming their judgment. All these points will be demonstrated more carefully in the interpretation that will proceed section by section, together with what he says to them and all the remaining matters that he appears to have stated in the epistle. It is worthwhile to add only this much, to clarify the text of the epistle: he writes these things to them from the city of Rome while he was in chains, at the time when he appealed to Caesar and was therefore brought from Judea to Rome, Nero reigning at that time.

## CHAPTER ONE

The Apostle gives thanks for the benefits conferred by the Philippians; indicating his own situation, he distinguishes among preachers and expresses his love, while urging his people to endure persecution.

Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ. (Augustine.) Just as there are two kinds of fear, which produce two kinds of people who fear, so there are two kinds of servitude, which produce two kinds of servants. There is a fear that perfect love casts out, and there is another, chaste fear, enduring forever and ever. In that fear which love casts out there is also a servitude that must be cast out together with the fear itself. For the Apostle joined the two, namely servitude and fear, saying: “You have not received the spirit of servitude again in fear” (Rom. VIII).

The Lord was looking upon a servant belonging to this servitude when he said: “I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his lord is doing” (John XV). He did not mean the servant who belongs to chaste fear, to whom it is said: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV), but the servant who belongs to the fear that must be cast out by love, concerning whom he says elsewhere: “A servant does not remain in the house forever, but the son remains forever” [Col. 0479C] (John VIII).

Since, therefore, he has given us the power to become children of God, let us be children of God, not servants, so that, in a marvelous and ineffable—but nevertheless true—way, we may be servants who are not servants: servants, that is, in chaste fear, to which belongs the servant who enters into his Lord’s joy; but not servants in the fear that must be cast out, to which belongs the servant who does not remain in the house forever.

To all the saints who are in Philippi, with the bishops and deacons: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. (Ambrose.) This is the epistolary heading. He associated Timothy with himself because he had once sent him into Macedonia with Erastus and because Timothy was known to them. It should be noted that he called those who are now called presbyters “bishops,” naming them in this way. For it was not yet the custom for many in one city to be those who are now called bishops; indeed, in ancient times there were not persons in every city fulfilling this office. Yet, when he mentioned bishops, he immediately also mentioned deacons. He would not have mentioned deacons as inferior to them while leaving presbyters unmentioned. But anyone can recognize this more clearly from what is written to Titus, where he says: “Appoint presbyters in every city, as I commanded you” (Tit. I), and, adding what sort they should be, he says: “A bishop must be blameless” (I Tim. III), clearly calling presbyters bishops.

In this passage we must observe that he said “with the bishops.” He did not say “with fellow bishops,” as some have understood it, just as we are accustomed to write “with fellow presbyters.” For he did not return to his own person and say “with fellow bishops,” so that it could be understood as “with our fellow bishops”; rather, he referred to what he had said, “to all the saints in Christ Jesus.” The meaning can therefore be understood as “with all who are in Philippi,” namely, with their bishops and deacons among the saints there. He does not designate their names explicitly, but because the exhortation to humility seemed more appropriate to those who could instruct the others and, before the rest, offer themselves as a model to them in what was fitting and ought to be done, he addresses them in this way.

I give thanks to my God upon every remembrance of you, always making my prayer for you all with joy, making my prayer for your fellowship in the Gospel from the first day until now. He frequently begins writing with thanksgiving. Here, however, he also seems to attest to a virtue of theirs, if he not only declares that he always gives thanks for them in every prayer, but also makes a common prayer for them with joy in the Gospel from the first day until now, expressing his wonder.

For his declaration that he rejoices for them in his prayers appears to be an indication of their virtue. His statement “from the first day until now” indicates their most steadfast constancy, since they had never undergone any change. And because it might seem careless to rejoice for everyone whose outcome was uncertain, he adds: “Being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will perfect it until the day of Christ Jesus.”

He is also clearly right to have adapted both the beginning and the end to the grace of Christ—not only because the faith that is in Christ was thereby confirmed, and because this made them more steadfast toward the good as they learned that the cause of what was being done must be attributed to God, but also because they themselves ought to give thanks for what had already occurred. For their continuing in this way appeared to provide them with assurance concerning the future.

As it is right for me to think this of you all, because I have you in my heart, and because, both in my chains and in the defense and confirmation of the Gospel, you are all sharers in grace. He referred this to what he had said above, where he said, “With joy, making my prayer for your fellowship in the Gospel.” He wished to say: It is especially fitting for me to believe such things about you, since I always have you in my heart, even though I am in chains, even though I am detained because of my defense and because of my work. For this makes me regard you in such a way that I know you have confirmed my preaching and teaching through your faith.

Because he had received the grace of the apostolate so that others might believe, he says that they became sharers in that grace by believing. For one who believed shared in grace. Showing his abundant affection for them, he says: “For God is my witness, how I long for you all in the compassion of Christ Jesus. And this I pray: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and every kind of discernment, so that you may approve what is excellent, that you may be sincere and without offense on the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.”

When he said “in the compassion of Christ,” he meant “in that love which is according to Christ.” And when he said “your love,” he meant the love that exists both toward God and toward one another [Col. 0481B]. He therefore wishes to say: God is my witness regarding the affection I hold toward you, and I pray at every moment that the love which is directed toward God and toward one another may abound more and more in you. I want you to possess suitable knowledge of the things that pertain to virtue, approving what is excellent, and to devote greater care to those things, so that on the future day you may appear without any reproach, possessing an abundant supply of upright conduct. Through this God can be glorified in you even in the present life, as all people praise him above your virtue, in whose name you do these things.

He wrote these things to them to show the affection he held toward them, and he used the truest praises to exhort them. In what follows, however, he begins to make known to them matters concerning himself, addressing them as affectionate people who were very concerned for him, since they seem to have sent him financial support. It was fitting to make known to such people the matters concerning himself, and these matters could also contribute to their instruction. For since they were under severe necessity, the Apostle was sufficient, by contemplating piety, to teach them to endure even heavier burdens for the sake of virtue by imitating him. He begins in this way:

I want you to know, brothers, that the things concerning me have turned out rather for the advancement of the Gospel, so that my chains have become manifest in Christ throughout the whole praetorium and to all the rest, and that most of the brethren, confident in the Lord because of my chains, dare much more fearlessly to speak the word.

Blessed Paul, after appealing to Caesar when Festus wished to hand him over to the Jews, was brought to Rome in chains. Having been brought before Nero and having made his defense, he remained there for two years and obtained complete security. Therefore, in the second epistle to Timothy, which he wrote to him from Rome—not at the time when he was writing to the Philippians, for he wrote to them while he was there, but on a second occasion, when he was punished by death there—he says: “At my first defense no one stood by me, but everyone deserted me; may it not be counted against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled and all the Gentiles might hear, and I was delivered from the lion’s mouth” (II Tim. IV), [Col. 0482A] indicating Nero.

At that time everyone thought that blessed Paul would be killed by Nero, because he was exceedingly cruel, and especially because Paul seemed at that time to be teaching certain new doctrines, very foreign to those rites by which the Romans then worshiped their gods. Yet, contrary to all expectation, he was brought in to defend his case. Not only did he suffer nothing, but he also obtained complete security, so that he later departed from Rome and continued his customary work of teaching.

What had happened moved everyone to amazement and gave the faithful great confidence, so that, free from all fear, he taught the doctrines of piety. When he said “throughout the whole praetorium,” he meant “in the royal quarters and among those around him.” He called that place the praetorium which, according to the usage of our time, we call the palace.

Therefore he said: I want you to know that the things belonging to my teaching receive increase day by day. Although bound, I became known to everyone; brought in, I appeared in my own defense; and I was freed from every danger, so that many of the faithful, receiving confidence from what had happened to me, might teach with confidence the things that belong to piety.

Some indeed preach Christ out of envy and rivalry, but some also out of goodwill. Explaining more fully what he meant by “out of envy and rivalry,” he adds: Some preach Christ out of rivalry, not sincerely, thinking that they can bring affliction upon my chains.

Some, he says, envying what had gone well for me, and because I had suffered no harm when brought before Nero, but had even earned release by stating what had happened to me, are exercising their rivalry against me. They rush about, not acting from any confidence, but, so to speak, from the wickedness of impiety, hastening to teach their doctrines. They want those who hold authority and power, stirred by their confidence, to consider that the reason for all these things is that I passed through the affair without danger, so that they may again turn against me and correct the others through my punishment.

Anyone who understands that this was the effect produced against blessed Paul will not be surprised, as though he had suffered something because of envy.
