Then, when he said that they preach Christ “out of goodwill,” he clearly indicated this by adding: Some indeed do so out of love, knowing that I have been appointed for the defense of the Gospel. That is, some preach the love they have toward Christ, confident that it is my work that piety should be preached. They make use of the confidence granted because, by the grace of God, matters concerning me were arranged in such a way that everyone obtained confidence.

He makes the choice of both groups even clearer by saying: “What then? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is being preached.”

(Augustine.) These men were hirelings who envied the Apostle Paul. Why did they envy him? Because they were seeking temporal things. But listen to what he adds: “What then? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice, and I shall rejoice.” Christ is the truth. The truth is proclaimed by hirelings in pretense, and by sons in truth. The sons patiently await the Father’s eternal blessedness; the hirelings hastily desire the temporal wage of the one who hires them. Let human glory, which I see the hirelings envying, be diminished for me, and nevertheless let the glory of Christ be spread abroad through the tongues of hirelings and sons of God.

We see that these men proclaimed a holy and chaste matter, but not chastely. Why, then, does the Apostle rejoice? Not in their evil, but in the good of Christ’s name.

(Ambrose.) What was said to Paul is worthy of great amazement, although there is something else similar to it. He says: I do not examine their intention, even though what is being done is done out of envy to my harm; provided that all teach people to believe in Christ. For blessed Paul does not, as some have thought, grant license to those who desire to pervert the doctrine of piety. Rather, he wishes us to have hatred toward heretics, as he himself writes: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second correction” (Tit. III).

But here he is speaking about those who teach sound doctrine in their beliefs, yet do this not for the sake of piety itself, but in order to stir up plots against him. He shows that, with good reason, he continues to speak in this way about those who do not do the work wholeheartedly but desire to plot against him: “And in this I rejoice, and I shall rejoice.” For I know that this will result in my salvation through your prayer and the provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ.

With matters standing thus, I am filled with joy, knowing that in the future age I shall rejoice even more when I receive a reward for these things, while you pray and Christ, through the Spirit, abundantly grants us grace for their sake. For they expected that the resurrection would occur through the Holy Spirit and that they would attain the enjoyment of future blessings, since they hoped to obtain them beforehand. It is evident that they also expected the splendor of future glory to be granted to them by the Spirit according to the measure of their faith or labors.

He therefore rightly said “the provision of the Spirit,” signifying an abundant reward and the greatness of the recompense that it is fitting for the Spirit to grant. Although the things hoped for are great, the present tribulations were also great, since such plots were being prepared against him by those who shared the same faith.

According to my expectation and hope, I shall be put to shame in nothing, but with all confidence, as always and now, Christ will be magnified in my body, whether through life or through death. He clearly speaks of despair, saying that he cannot hope for what is present. He wishes to say: Although I am confined by such great evils that I despair of present circumstances and think that no hope of safety remains, nevertheless I hope not to be put to shame. I have been thoroughly instructed that through what concerns me Christ will appear great, whether I live or die; nor will my death occur with Christ merely permitting it, or in vain.

And because he said that Christ would be magnified, although this did not yet have proof in what had happened to him, he showed that it would be sufficient for him if Christ were magnified and added: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” Even if I live, he says, I have concern for nothing except what pertains to Christ’s glory. Although I die for him, I am confident that I have gained greatly. For I am going to be with him. Therefore he adds, with the greatest amazement: “But if living in the flesh means fruit from my labor, and what I should choose I do not know.”

I am hard pressed between the two, having the desire to depart and be with Christ, which is much better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake. Thus I am also turned toward uncertainty, not knowing what is fitting for me to choose. The departure from this life delights me, because it makes me present with Christ; yet it is also pleasing to me to remain alive, because I can bring many of those who are strangers to Christ to faith in him. Therefore, although it is better for me to depart from here and be with Christ, I judge that my presence is more necessary for your sake, so that I may lead you, who are approaching the faith.

(Gregory.) And yet elsewhere he says: “We who are in this dwelling groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (II Cor. V). Behold, he desires to die, and yet he fears being stripped of the flesh. Why is this? Because although victory rejoices forever, the punishment itself nevertheless disturbs him in the present. Although love of the reward to come prevails, the pain of being driven away still touches the soul without sorrow.

For just as a brave man, when he is girding himself with weapons for a battle that is already near, both trembles and hastens, both shudders and rages, and seems to be afraid, as his pallor shows, yet is driven forward with great force by anger, so a holy man, when he sees himself drawing near to suffering, is both struck down by the weakness of his nature and strengthened by the firmness of his hope. He trembles at approaching death, yet rejoices that by dying he will live more truly. For he cannot pass to the kingdom except through death. Thus, while trusting, he seems to doubt; while seeming to doubt, he trusts; he rejoices and fears, and fears and rejoices, because he knows that he cannot reach the prize of rest unless he crosses with labor what lies between.

So when we desire to drive illnesses from the body, we indeed sadly drink the bitter cup of purification, but we also rejoice in the health that follows. Since the body cannot otherwise reach health, we willingly take in the drink even what displeases us. When the soul sees that life is contained in bitterness, it is troubled by sorrow but becomes cheerful.

(Cassian.) Finally, when blessed Paul saw himself being enriched by such and so many fruits, and, on the other hand, weighed in his heart the good of contemplation, placing, as it were, the profit of so many labors in one balance and the delight of divine contemplation in the other, after his heart had been examined and disciplined for a long time, he was delighted on one side by the immense rewards of his labors, while on the other the desire for unity and inseparable fellowship with Christ invited him even to the dissolution of the flesh. At last, in anxiety, he cried out and said: “What I should choose I do not know. I am hard pressed between the two, having the desire to depart and be with Christ, for that is much better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake.”

Although in many ways he had preferred the excellence of this good to all the fruits of his preaching, nevertheless he submits himself to the consideration of love, without which no one wins the Lord’s favor. For the sake of those to whom he was still, like a nurse, giving milk from the breasts of the Gospel, he does not refuse separation from Christ, harmful to himself but necessary for the others. Indeed, he is compelled to choose this above all by that excessive virtue of piety through which, for the salvation of his brothers, he would, if possible, have wished to undergo even the ultimate evil of anathema.

(Ambrose.) And because he said these things while making his own choice public, lest he seem to be making plans without sound reason or to be unaware of what concerned him and of where he stood, he adds: “And being confident of this, I know that I shall remain and continue with you all, for your progress and joy in the faith, so that your boasting in Christ Jesus may abound in me through my coming again to you.”

I have spoken these things according to my own affection. Yet I know that I shall remain in this life, so that I may come to you again and that the things concerning you too may make progress in faith, with a great multitude being added to you and led to faith through me. Thus I shall have an even greater occasion for boasting about you according to Christ.

When he says “your,” he does not speak fully of the person of the Philippians, but means those among the Gentiles who would believe through him. He speaks in their person, as though they themselves had believed in this way.

Only live in a manner worthy of the Gospel of Christ. Here he begins to discuss concord and humility with them, teaching them not to contend over precedence. He strongly invites them to modesty by that statement in which he says, “so that your conduct may be worthy of the Gospel of Christ.” If this is what he asks of them, namely, that they should act consistently with their promise, consider the admirable addition he makes: whether, when I come and see you, or when I am absent and hear about you, you are standing firm in one spirit, with one mind, struggling together for the faith of the Gospel, and not being frightened in anything by your adversaries.

Whether he is present or absent, he is equally concerned that they recognize what is better and therefore always desire to devote themselves with equal zeal to the better course.

What is his counsel? That they should stand firm in one spirit, that is, agree among themselves. Explaining the usefulness of concord, he says that they should struggle together for the faith of the Gospel and not be frightened in anything by their adversaries. This is a sign of destruction for the adversaries, but of salvation for you.

You will be able, he says, by agreeing among yourselves, to provide one another assistance in the faith, so that you do not yield to what your adversaries inflict upon you. These things are evidence of destruction for them, since they will justly suffer the penalties for which they do such things against you; but for you they will be salvation, which you acquire because in the present life, for the sake of piety, you take delight in sufferings.

He also encourages them to undertake suffering: “And this is from God, because it has been granted to you for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him.” By these words he sufficiently supplied them with courage, since it is good to suffer for Christ, so that it is also fitting to give thanks to him for this because of the gains that arise from it for them.

(Cassian.) “And this,” he says, “is from God, because it has been granted to you for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him.” Here he declares that both the beginning of our conversion and faith and the endurance of sufferings are granted to us by the Lord. David likewise understood this and prayed that the same thing be granted to him as a mercy, saying: “Establish, O God, what you have worked in us” (Ps. LXVII). He showed that the beginnings of salvation, bestowed by God’s gift and grace, are not sufficient if they are not perfected by his mercy and daily action.

For it is not free choice but the Lord who releases those in chains; it is not our strength but the Lord who raises up those who are crushed; it is not the diligence of reading but the Lord who enlightens the blind. In Greek it is said: “The Lord makes the wise blind.” It is not our caution but the Lord who guards strangers; it is not our strength but the Lord who lifts up, or supports, all who fall.

We say these things not so that we may empty our zeal, labor, and diligence by expending them vainly and uselessly, but so that we may know that without God’s help we are neither able to strive nor able to make our efforts effective in attaining so immense a reward of purity, unless God’s assistance and mercy are granted to us.

Then, by his own example, he exhorts them still more:

Having the same struggle that you saw in me and now hear about me.

## CHAPTER II

He instructs his people in unity of faith, true humility, and holiness, and sends his messengers to them.

Then he takes up an exhortation, saying: “If, therefore, there is any consolation in Christ, any encouragement from love, any fellowship of the Spirit, any tenderness and compassion, complete my joy.” (Ambrose.) He rightly said “if, therefore,” because they seemed to be concerned for him on account of his pressing need, even sending him whatever they knew was necessary for his use. “If,” he says, “you truly care for our consolation, and, because you love us, suffer with us as we endure such things, do those things which will be able to return to us perfect joy concerning you.”

He expressed these requirements in various ways: they were to be harmonious and loving toward one another. Then, rejecting the practices he had observed among them, he admonished them: “Do nothing out of rivalry or vainglory.” You ought not to quarrel, from a desire for empty glory, over precedence, but do what is more fitting: “In humility consider one another superior to yourselves.”

“It is better,” he says, “through humility to regard even those who are our equals as better than we are, and thus to assign them every honor with eagerness.” And because he knew especially well what could cut off such rivalry, he added advice: each person should consider not only his own interests, but also those of the other. “Do not,” he says, “consider how you yourself may hold the first place; reflect rather that, if it is pleasant for you to preside over the others, it is much more intolerable for someone else to hold the second place. If you think about matters in this way, you will also exercise greater care for the others out of equality.”

“Do nothing,” he says, “out of rivalry or vainglory, but in humility of mind regard one another as superior to yourselves, and anticipate one another in showing honor.” Thus each person, attributing more knowledge and holiness to his companion, should believe that the highest exercise of true discernment lies more in the other’s judgment than in his own.

Often, whether through the devil’s deception or through human error—for no one in this flesh can fail to be deceived as a human being—one who has sharper intelligence and greater knowledge may sometimes conceive something false in his mind, while one of slower understanding and lesser standing may perceive something more rightly and truly. Therefore no one, however well supplied with knowledge, should persuade himself in the empty swelling of pride that he has no need of another’s judgment. Even if the devil’s deception does not mislead his judgment, he will nevertheless not escape the more serious snares of arrogance and pride. Who could claim such a thing for himself without immense ruin? For the chosen vessel, in whom Christ, as he himself confessed, was speaking, declares that he went up to Jerusalem for this sole reason: to submit, in a private examination, to his fellow apostles the Gospel which he preached to the Gentiles with the Lord revealing and cooperating. By this it is shown not only that unanimity and concord are preserved through these commandments, but also that all the plots of the opposing devil and the snares of his deception are not to be feared. (Ambrose, Augustine.)

Then he makes use of a very necessary example for teaching humility, saying what belongs to Christ: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus.” We ought not to understand this as though we were merely pretending to think in such a way, but should truly believe that there may be something hidden in another person by which that person is superior to us, even if the good in which we seem superior to him is not hidden.

These thoughts, which bring down pride and add love, cause us to bear one another’s burdens not only with equanimity but with the greatest willingness. Nothing makes us gladly undertake this dutiful labor of carrying the burdens of others unless we reflect on how much the Lord endured for us.

For this reason the Apostle, admonishing us not to look each to his own interests but to those of others, says: “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” and so forth.

This is so that, just as he, when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” and, although without sin, took our sins upon himself, did not attend to his own interests but to ours, so we too, willingly imitating him, may bear one another’s burdens.

Some say that the Son is less than the Father because it is written, in the Lord’s own words, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14). The truth, however, shows that the Son was also, in a proper sense, made less than himself. For how was he not made less than himself when he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant?

He did not take the form of a servant in such a way as to lose the form of God. If, therefore, the form of a servant was taken without the form of God being lost, and if, both in the form of a servant and in the form of God, he himself is the only-begotten Son of God the Father—equal to the Father in the form of God, and, in the form of a servant, “the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2)—who would not understand that, in the form of God, he is greater even than himself, while in the form of a servant he is less even than himself, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being?

The Son of God is therefore equal to God the Father by nature, but less in appearance: in the form of a servant that he took, he is less than the Father; in the form of God which he possessed before taking that form, he is equal to the Father. “Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as a thing to be seized.”

(Gregory.) That he “emptied himself” means that he made himself visible from the greatness of his invisibility, so that the form of a servant might conceal the fact that, by his divinity, he penetrated all things without limitation.

(Ambrose.) It is customary for human beings to seize those things from which they think they can acquire something. We frequently say that someone thought a certain thing ought to be seized—that is, that he took it up quickly, as though it could bring him great profit. Thus, concerning Christ, the Apostle says that he “did not regard it as a thing to be seized, to be equal with God”: that is, he did not regard equality with God as a great acquisition, nor, puffed up, remain in his own dignity; rather, for the benefit of others, he chose to endure lower conditions than those proper to himself.

And indeed, when he existed in the form of God, this means that he existed as God, Lord, ruler, and author of the whole universe. All these descriptions, truly understood, seem to follow from the name “God.” What did he do? “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.”

Divine Scripture calls being emptied “being made nothing,” as it is written elsewhere (Romans 3): “Faith has been emptied”—that is, it has been shown to be nothing. “Have the same mind,” therefore, “having the same love, united in soul and of one mind.” Our preaching has been emptied—that is, it is nothing and vain.

When it says that he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” it indicates that he concealed that dignity. Those who saw him thought him to be only what could be seen, since his divine nature was hidden from all. “The form of a servant” means the nature of a servant; human nature is so called because it is servile. Likewise, when he says “in the form of God,” he speaks of the divine nature, that is, of one existing in the divine nature.

But since he said “the form of a servant,” and this was common both to human beings, animals, and angels—for all are forms of servants, and all were made—he added what would indicate the distinctive character of the matter. He wished to explain what he meant by “the form of a servant”: “being made in the likeness of human beings.”

When he says “being made,” he uses the term in the sense of *habitus* (“condition” or “garb”). When he says “in the likeness of a human being,” he means “in a human being,” since the likeness of a human being is a human being. He joined all these expressions concerning the Word of God, and therefore added: “And being found in appearance—or form—as a human being.”

This is in comparison with that nature which cannot be perceived in any appearance or form. He used both “appearance” and “form” to say that, although invisible and free from every form, as was fitting, he nevertheless willed to be seen in a human being.

In certain copies, however, it is read: “And being found in appearance as a human being.”

(Augustine.) “Appearance” is used of something that happens to us in order to be possessed by us. Yet there is a distinction: some things that happen to us and produce appearance are not changed by us, but change us while remaining themselves intact and unmoved. Thus, when wisdom happens to a human being, wisdom itself is not changed; rather, it changes the human being, making the foolish wise.

Other things happen in such a way that they both change and are changed, such as food. Food itself loses its form and is changed into our body, while we, restored by food, are changed from weakness and languor into strength and vigor.

There is a third kind, in which the things that happen are themselves changed and produce appearance, and are in some way changed by those in whom they produce appearance, as with clothing. When clothing is put on, it receives a form which it did not have when it was removed, while the limbs themselves remain in their own condition both when they are clothed and when they are unclothed.

There may also be a fourth kind, in which the things that happen to produce appearance neither change those to whom they happen nor are themselves changed by them, as with a ring on a finger.

When, therefore, the Apostle was speaking of the only-begotten Son of God, insofar as his divinity is concerned, according to the truth that he is God, he said that he was equal to the Father. This was not for him like a seizure—that is, like desiring something alien—if, while always remaining in that equality, he did not wish to take on humanity and appear among human beings as a human being. But “he emptied himself,” not changing his own form, but taking the form of a servant.

He was not converted or transformed into a human being, losing his unchangeable stability. Rather, although he truly took on a human being, he himself, the one who took him on, was made in the likeness of human beings—not for himself, but for those among whom he appeared in human form. “Being found in appearance as a human being” means that, by possessing a human being, he was found as a human being.

He could not be found as a human being by those who had impure hearts and could not see the Word who was with the Father, unless he took on that which they were able to see and through which they might be led to the inner light.

This appearance does not belong to the first kind. The human nature, remaining what it was, did not change the nature of God. Nor does it belong to the second kind, since a human being did not change God, nor was changed by him. Nor does it belong to the fourth kind, since humanity was not assumed in such a way that neither it changed God nor was changed by him. Rather, it belongs to the third kind: it was assumed in such a way that it was ineffably changed, and in a more excellent and intimate manner.

For when clothing is put on by a human being, it receives the form of the human being. By this term “appearance,” therefore, the Apostle sufficiently indicated how he said “being made in the likeness of human beings”: not by a transformation into a human being, but by appearance, as when someone is clothed with a human being, uniting him to himself in some way and conforming him so as to associate him with immortality and eternity.

But the appearance that consists in the acquisition of wisdom and discipline the Greeks call ἕξις (*hexis*); the appearance according to which we speak of being clothed or armed they call rather σχῆμα (*schēma*). From this we understand that the Apostle was speaking of this kind of appearance, since in the Greek copies σχῆμα is written, while in the Latin copies we have *habitus* (“appearance,” “condition,” or “form”).

By this term we must understand that the Word was not changed through the assumption of humanity, just as limbs are not changed when clothed. When the Apostle commended his obedience as extending to death, it was not enough for him to say, “becoming obedient unto death.” For it was not just any death; he added, “even death on a cross.”

Among all kinds of death, nothing was worse than that death. Hence, when the sharpest pains torment someone, the suffering is called *cruciatūs* (“torture”), a name derived from the cross. Those hanging on wood, fastened to it by nails through hands and feet, were killed by a prolonged death. They remained alive on the cross for a long time—not because a longer life was chosen, but because death itself was prolonged, so that the pain would not end quickly.

We say too little when we say that he wished to die for us: he deigned to be crucified, and by dying the worst death he destroyed every death. It was the worst death in the eyes of the Jews who did not understand; for it had been chosen by the Lord. He was to have the cross itself as his sign and to place that cross, like a trophy after the devil’s defeat, upon the foreheads of the faithful, so that the Apostle might say: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6).

“He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross.”

(Ambrose.) “He humbled himself,” he says. Up to this point he seems to have spoken of things befitting the divine nature; in what follows he passes to those things which can be applied to human nature: “Becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross.”

Such language is fitting for a human being, but cannot at all be applied to the divine nature. That nature cannot suffer death, since it promised to raise the dead, as the Lord himself clearly says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2). He applies the destruction to the temple, but attributes the action of resurrection to himself.

From the very beginning he speaks distinctly of the one Christ, and, as was customary when speaking of one person, he nevertheless recalls both the distinction and the nature: the one who existed in the form of God took the form of a servant. In saying “the form of God,” he indicates one thing; in saying “the form of a servant,” another: the former is that which is taken, the latter the one who takes it.

Yet, lest this division of the expressions cause someone other than Christ to be understood in full, he refers the form of a servant back to the same person. Thus it can readily be seen that everything he says about the one who exists in the form of God and all the other expressions are understood as referring to Christ’s person.

He prevents the form of a servant from being thought to be something other than Christ by saying that it was received from him. While saying whatever was necessary concerning the divine nature, he added, for the increase of humility, those things proper to his humanity, and, speaking of the honor that came to him after the Passion, he added that the Lord Jesus Christ was exalted. In this way he clearly shows that he does not think that a human being other than Christ was assumed, and by their powers he indicates the difference between the natures.

Since he says everything in the passage concerning Christ as one person, he sufficiently displays their union. He gathers into one all the things that differ in power according to the distinction of natures, while preserving the union of the person.

In this passage, and especially here, he seems to have acted both wisely and necessarily. For both the meticulous doctrinal method he customarily employs and the present argument made this manner of exposition especially fitting for him. His purpose was to teach the Philippians that humility is good and entirely sufficient to bring profit to the person who practices it, and he confirms this by an example drawn from Christ. The example had to be enlarged in every respect for the sake of fuller instruction.

If he had mentioned only the deity, he could indeed have sufficiently shown that it is altogether fitting to think humbly. He would have shown only the divine nature, making humility a matter far removed from its dignity. But he could not in any way have demonstrated that humility is profitable to the one who practices it, since he could not prove that this nature could acquire anything through such an act.

If, on the other hand, he had mentioned only the human nature, he would have shown that humility is profitable because of the things acquired by that nature, but he could not have confirmed that it is fitting to think humbly when one possesses a comparable dignity. Nor could the statement “becoming obedient unto death,” applied to a human being, prove anything that pertains to humility. This would be so unless the divine nature in him had also been shown, through which he could have avoided submission to death.

For, considered in himself, he did not fulfill an act of obedience by succumbing to death: he endured death unwillingly, according to the limit previously assigned to nature. But wisely, as he said, he referred everything to one person, gathering together into one the things that seemed to differ in power according to the distinction of natures, so that from both he might draw what was useful for exhortation.

From the statements concerning his deity he persuaded us that we must necessarily display humility in our thoughts, since the Word, who is God, seemed voluntarily to have done such things, considering humility preferable to all else for the salvation of others. From the things done according to his humanity he showed that humility is profitable to the one who wishes to practice it, since after the Passion he was established in such great glory.

Therefore, when he says, “becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross”—which properly belongs to his humanity, since that humanity also appeared to have undergone suffering—he shows from the statements concerning his divinity that humility is to be commended, since he could have avoided suffering had he wished. He adds:

“Therefore God also exalted him.”

I do not know whether anyone could be found so foolish as to think that the Word of God was exalted after the Passion. What, then, is this exaltation? “And gave him the name which is above every name.”

The meaning of “name” is clear: he does not mean merely a designation, but something acquired by him, just as in the statement: “And let them know that the Lord is your name” (2 Chronicles 6)—that is, “that you are Lord.”

He himself explains what that name is: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.”

God gave him this: that all should adore him, and that all should confess Jesus Christ to be God, established in the glory of God the Father—that is, that he should possess the kind of glory which it is fitting for one who calls God his Father to possess, because of the union he has with the only-begotten Son.

No one who is aware of the matter can doubt that these things were acquired after the Passion by the one who was assumed. But they were present from the beginning to the Word of God, since he was the maker of all things. I think no one would dispute this unless he were surrendering to utter madness.

By “those in heaven” he means the invisible powers; by “those on earth,” living human beings; and by “those under the earth,” the dead, who themselves will confess the Lord, the author of their resurrection, through the resurrection.

One further matter among these things must be explained. Certain heretics, wishing to distort the testimony which says, “he did not regard equality with God as a thing to be seized,” have understood it in this way: “Christ,” they say, “thought it appropriate for himself not to seize that equality which God appeared to possess.”

The statement itself shows great foolishness. When could Christ have conceived such a thought, if, according to their opinion, he was made out of nothing? He would know both that his author was his maker and that his creator was his creator. Unless perhaps they say that he did not usurp equality with God in the manner of demons. That interpretation indeed suits heretics, who always speak words filled with madness.

But such words do not suit Paul, as though he were saying something great about Christ—even if someone should claim that the things they say concerning the Son are of such a kind. They seem not to have understood the Apostle’s meaning when he says: “Considering one another in humility as superior to yourselves.”

It is evident that in these words he does not teach inferiors to render due honor to superiors. Rather, he admonishes those who are equal in honor to regard one another as surpassing themselves through humility. Hence he used “one another,” so that each group—the former toward the latter and the latter toward the former—might hold the same attitude.

He also seems to have fitted the example to this. Christ, claiming equality with the Father according to his divine nature, consented to dwell in a human being and thereby to acquire a lowly reputation among human beings. They did not then think him to be anything other than what he seemed to be on account of his humanity; beyond that, they did not recognize him.

The point would not have been suitable if, having no equality with the Father, he had merely been fulfilling a command, with nature itself imposing the necessity of obedience upon him. It would therefore have been ridiculous, according to the Apostle’s intention, to say that Christ did not rise up against the Father, nor attempt to seize the equality which he possessed with the Father, while giving them advice to regard themselves as equals and, through the cooperation of good works, to consider themselves superior to one another by humility.

Thus blessed Paul, exhorting them throughout, adds:

“My beloved, therefore, just as you have always obeyed—not only in my presence, but much more now in my absence—work out your salvation with fear and trembling.”

He very effectively persuaded them, by recalling the past, not to think anything unworthy of themselves, but to do the things they had done at the beginning. He made them more even-tempered in his presence, and then, commending the zeal appropriate to them, he adds:

“For God is the one who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure.”

In this way your eagerness will find God’s grace cooperating with it. He must cooperate with you so that you may think and do the things pleasing to God. This is why he says, “according to his good pleasure.”

(Augustine.) Then he leads the word toward exhortation. It is astonishing that, when the crucified one is preached, two people hear: one despises him, the other ascends. Let the one who despises him blame himself; let the one who ascends not claim the ascent for himself, lest the proud lose what the humble deserved.

Even those who were already walking on the right path should not attribute it to themselves or to their own strength, lest they perish from that path. Therefore Holy Scripture, teaching us humility, speaks through the Apostle: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.” And lest they derive any self-confidence from the fact that he said “work out,” he immediately adds: “For God is the one who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure.”

God is the one who works in you; therefore, with fear, make a valley, receive the rain. Depressed places are filled; high places become dry. Grace is rain. Why then are you surprised if God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble? Therefore “with fear and trembling”—that is, with humility—“do not think highly of yourself, but fear” (Romans 11). Fear, so that you may be filled; do not think highly of yourself, lest you become dry.

“But do everything,” he says, “without grumbling or disputing, so that you may be blameless and innocent, children of God without reproach in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life, for my glory on the day of Christ.”

Thus, among those people whose concern is largely directed toward what is worse, you will appear blameless, as it is fitting for those who have been made members of the order of God’s children to appear. Enlightened by virtues, you will shine among them like lights, awaiting that eternal life in the future day in which I too will have occasion to glory, while showing that their progress will provide great confidence to me also, who will be made better through it.

“For I did not run in vain, nor labor in vain. But even if I am poured out as a libation over the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice and rejoice together with you all. In the same way, you also rejoice and rejoice together with me.”

(Ambrose.) Since you are concerned for virtue, I rejoice with you, and I rejoice in that hope by which I shall also exult over you in the future age. I know that I did not labor for the faith in vain; rather, I endure everything for a just reason, even though I am prepared to undergo death for you. You offer your faith to God as a sacrifice, while I pour out my own blood for you like a libation.

He rightly said, “Do this very thing yourselves.” This is both just and fitting: by doing so, you will appear as companions in my joy. Then he adds:

“I hope in the Lord Jesus Christ to send Timothy to you shortly, so that I too may be encouraged when I know how things are with you. For I have no one so like-minded who will sincerely be concerned for you. For all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ.”

“I hope,” he says, “to send Timothy to you shortly, so that through him I may be in better spirits when you have been carefully instructed concerning yourselves. For I have no other person so like-minded and so affectionately concerned for you, while everyone considers only his own interests.”

He is referring to those who are from the circumcision. Wishing to show that he does not say this merely to favor Timothy, he uses their testimony, since they knew him, and says:

“But you know his proven character, how, as a son with his father, he served with me in the Gospel.”

And again he adds:

“This, therefore, is whom I hope to send to you as soon as I see what concerns me.”

He immediately indicates that he will send him to them once he has seen and learned what concerns him—namely, the circumstances in which I find myself—without putting off the matter any longer.

“But I trust in the Lord that I myself also will come shortly to you.”

He adds that he too strongly trusts God that he will come to them, and therefore continues:

“But I considered it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier, and your apostle and minister of my need. For he was longing for you all and was troubled because you had heard that he was ill. Indeed, he was ill almost to the point of death; but God had mercy on him, and not only on him but also on me, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow.”

“Since for the present I considered it necessary to send Epaphroditus to you, he is my fellow worker according to the Gospel, and your apostle and minister of my needs”—that is, the one through whom you sent the things that were necessary for my use.

Then, commending him to them, he says that Epaphroditus himself longed for them, and especially for the things concerning them. He had learned through no one else that they had heard of his illness; for he was distressed, reckoning the distress which they seemed to feel on his account. He had truly been ill, even approaching death. But God had mercy on him—and more on me and on him—delivering him from illness, so that, surrounded by much sorrow, I would not have to bear the addition of another sorrow through his death.

He adds:

“I have therefore sent him more promptly, so that when you see him again you may rejoice.”

He sent him quickly so that, seeing him, they might be filled with joy, and so that he himself might no longer be sorrowful, knowing that Epaphroditus’s arrival would console them.

He then adds:

“Receive him therefore in the Lord with all joy, and hold such people in honor, because for the work of the Lord he came near to death, risking his life, to make up for your deficiency in serving me.”

He asks them to receive him willingly and advises them to honor fully those who are such as he is. He shows that Epaphroditus is rightly worthy of honor among them by saying that he served their will, carrying to Paul the things sent by them, and in doing so fell into such danger.

He calls this service itself “the work of the Lord.” He also calls it the fulfillment of their deficiency in serving him, since they had wished to send what was necessary for his use but could not do so adequately: each person could not personally carry everything he wanted to give him. Thus he says that Epaphroditus made up what was lacking on their part. Receiving something from everyone, and fulfilling everyone’s wishes, he brought it all.

In saying this, he mentioned that he would send Timothy, but concerning Epaphroditus he said that he had sent him together with his letter. He added to all this:

## CHAPTER III. He shows the abolition of the legal observances by word and example; then excuses himself and urges them to imitate him.

“Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord.”

(Ambrose.) He says this while praying for them. That is: may divine grace enable you to endure everything in such a way that you are always filled with joy in the good things granted to us by him.

He rightly added “in the Lord,” because there is both rejoicing and improper rejoicing. A person rejoices improperly when he seems to delight in present goods, judging that his good consists in possessing and enjoying them.

“To write the same things to you is not burdensome for me, and it is a safeguard for you.”

Here he begins to rebuke those who were from the circumcision and were trying to persuade them to live according to the Law. When he says “to write the same things,” he does not mean that he had already written them, for nowhere in this Epistle does he seem to have said so. Nor have we learned that he wrote another letter to them. Rather, he says this because he had taught them very earnestly about these matters when he was with them.

He means: “It is not burdensome for me to write to you about the matters concerning which I have often spoken to you, since frequent admonition seems to provide you with greater caution.”

What matters are these? “Beware of the dogs; beware of the evil workers.”

He called them “dogs” because they had no sense of shame and, although frequently rebuked for their perverse and empty teaching, seemed to persist in the same practices. He calls them “evil workers” because they do not hasten to teach those things which accord with piety.

He calls doctrine “work,” just as he says elsewhere (1 Corinthians 3): “If anyone’s work which he has built upon it remains, he will receive a reward; if anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss.” It is clear that he was speaking there about doctrines.

“Beware of the mutilation.”

He rightly called it “the mutilation,” because when circumcision was pleasing to God, it was circumcision indeed. But now, since it is not performed according to God’s will and they merely mutilate the body to its harm, he compares them with himself, saying:

“For we are the circumcision.”

That is, we are those who do the things pleasing to God and carefully guard what pleases God. This is proper to those who claim to possess circumcision. Confirming it from the practices themselves, he adds:

“We serve God in the Spirit and glory in Christ Jesus, and do not put confidence in the flesh.”

We serve God in the Spirit and glory in Christ, who has become the author of these things for us. Yet we do not define piety as consisting in things according to the flesh.

Thus the Lord also says in the Gospels: “The Father seeks such people to worship him. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4). He said this to the Samaritan woman, who thought that the divine nature ought to be worshiped in a particular place. He taught that the divine nature is incorporeal and that it is fitting for it to be worshiped by such a disposition.

This is especially clear in the passage where we are commanded not to serve the creature but the Creator.

(Augustine.) Not in the way in which we are commanded through love to serve one another—which in Greek is δουλεύειν (*douleuein*)—but in the way in which service is rendered to God alone, which in Greek is λατρεύειν (*latreuein*).

Hence idolaters are so called because they offer images the service that is owed to God. In this sense it is said: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matthew 4).

The Greek text distinguishes this more clearly, for it has λατρεύσεις (*latreuseis*, “you shall serve ritually”). Moreover, if we are forbidden to serve the creature with this kind of service, since it is said, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve,” the Apostle likewise condemns those who “worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator.”

The Holy Spirit is certainly not a creature, since all offer him this kind of service. The Apostle says: “For we are those who serve God in the Spirit,” which in Greek is λατρεύοντες (*latreuontes*). Many Latin manuscripts also read this way: “who serve God in the Spirit.”

All the Greek copies, or nearly all of them, and some Latin copies, however, have not “we serve in the Spirit of God” but “we serve God in the Spirit.” But those who err in this matter and refuse to trust the more authoritative testimony—do they not also find the following variation among the manuscripts?

“Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?” (1 Corinthians 6.)

(Ambrose.) And lest he seem to accuse them without cause, he himself has nothing of that kind, but possesses for his own defense the things in which they boast.

Indeed, I have confidence even in the flesh. If anyone else seems to have confidence in the flesh, I have still more. If, he says, it was good to take pride in such things, I am inferior to none of them in this respect. Then, point by point, he states all those things that seemed great to those who lived according to the law.

[Col. 0496D] Circumcised on the eighth day. He rightly specified the eighth day, to show that he was not an outsider, among whom circumcision is customarily celebrated later. (Aug.) From the beginning, and according to the law, the circumcision of infants was commanded to take place on the eighth day in the ancient sacraments, because Christ—in whom the stripping away of carnal sin takes place, which circumcision signifies—rose on the Lord’s Day, which is the eighth after the seventh.

Of the stock of Israel. From whose stock all those seem to descend who belong to any tribe. Of the tribe of Benjamin. It was also necessary to add the tribe, to show that he was not an outsider but had derived his origin from the beginning of that people. Therefore, indicating this more clearly, he says: A Hebrew of Hebrews. He did not say, “A Jew of Jews.” For that designation was recent; but by saying “a Hebrew of Hebrews,” he confirmed the antiquity of his origin through an ancient designation.

Then he also states those things that belong to his purpose: According to the law, he says, a Pharisee. Those who adhered to this sect were considered careful interpreters of the law, and they hastened to teach what appeared to be contained in the law. Hence he shows this by saying: According to zeal, persecuting the Church. And because his persecution provided complete proof—for it could have happened that he did this merely through ferocity, under the pretense by which he appeared to do it out of zeal for piety—he adds: According to the righteousness that is in the law, having become blameless. He rightly said “that is in the law,” since it was impossible for anyone to attain complete blamelessness.

[Col. 0497B] Running through everything and showing that he lacked nothing good among the things that belonged to the law, he says: But whatever things were gain to me, these I have considered loss for the sake of Christ. He calls them “gains” to show that at that time they were necessarily practiced. Then, adding what serves to establish his point, he says that the concern he had for those matters was regarded as gain. Now, however, in comparison with Christ, they are considered losses.

Thus he says, in comparison with Christ: But I also consider everything to be loss because of the surpassing knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord. He rightly added “my Lord,” as though recognizing the difference itself by comparison with him. Moved by love, therefore, he called his Lord God, since he was the cause of greater goods.

Then he adds:

[Col. 0497C] For whose sake I have suffered the loss of all things, and consider them refuse. And because it might seem insulting to call the things of the law “refuse,” he immediately adds: That I may gain Christ. He shows that the comparison with those who belong to Christ makes such things appear in this way. How, then, or in what manner?

And that I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which comes from the law, but that which comes through the faith of Christ, the righteousness that comes from God through faith. I desire, he says, to attain that righteousness which comes from God, which we can attain through the faith that is in Christ. Therefore I despise my own righteousness, which comes from the law, knowing that it is both laborious and impossible to set right. For it is easier for me to sin under the law than to be made upright. He makes still clearer what that righteousness from God is:

[Col. 0497D] It is acquired through the faith that is in Christ.

(Aug.) Paul had said this about the Jews: they possessed what was evil, and especially this—that, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they were not subject to the righteousness of God (Rom. 10). Then, after Christ’s passion and resurrection, when the sacrament of grace according to the order of Melchizedek had been given and revealed, they still thought that the ancient sacraments had to be celebrated not merely by force of customary solemnity but from necessity for salvation. Yet if these things had never been necessary, the Maccabean martyrs would have suffered death for them fruitlessly and pointlessly.

Finally, he says that he condemns and regards as refuse the error and vice by which the Jews persecuted Christian preachers of grace as enemies of the law:

[Col. 0498A] in order that he might gain Christ. He does not mean that the observances of the law, if celebrated according to ancestral custom, were to be rejected—as he himself celebrated them—without any necessity for salvation, as the Jews thought they had to celebrate them, nor does he mean the deceptive pretense that he had reproved in Peter.

For whoever thinks that he fulfills the precepts of the law by the choice of his own will, without the Spirit of grace, wishes to establish his own righteousness rather than receive the righteousness of God. For why does the same Apostle say, “That I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which comes from the law, but the righteousness that comes through faith, righteousness from God”? Why does he call it his own righteousness, which comes from the law, and approve that righteousness, but call the righteousness that comes through faith not his own but from God?

Is the law not from God? Who but an unbeliever would say this? But he calls it his own righteousness “from the law,” because in it a person thinks that the law is sufficient for him to perform the divine commandments, trusting in his own strength. He says that righteousness from faith is from God because God apportions to each person a measure of faith. It belongs to faith to believe that God works in us even the willing, just as he worked in that seller of purple whose mind God opened so that she might attend to what Paul was saying.

[Col. 0498B] Accordingly, even those Jews who believed in Christ—including Paul—must not be said to be heirs from the law at all, but rather from the promise. For this reason it was said, “In Isaac shall your seed be called” (Heb. 11), because “not the children of the flesh are the children of God,” but the children of the promise are counted as the seed.

That I may know him and the power of his resurrection. He did not say merely “his resurrection,” but “the power of his resurrection.” What, then, is the power of his resurrection? It is that it was accomplished for the sake of all, so that all might attain a similar resurrection. For, believing in Christ, I also believe that I shall know the power of his resurrection—that is, attain the resurrection in which, made immortal and impassible, I shall be freed from every sin and shall no longer need the law.

For it would not be fitting that, at the same time, while laboring and sweating, I should direct my affections toward the law and its power. Rather, I shall be guarded by divine grace in what is good, since then I shall no longer be able to sin.

And the fellowship of his sufferings, being conformed to his death, if somehow I may attain the resurrection that is from the dead. For this reason, he says, I also desire to share in his sufferings, being made like his death, because, in imitation of him and through contemplation of piety, I am drawn from what is alien toward death, with the hope by which I trust that I shall share in his resurrection, which is also filled with great and immeasurable glory.

Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect; but I pursue it, if indeed I may apprehend that for which I was also apprehended by Christ Jesus. Because Christ appeared to him from above, and from heaven displayed his glory to him, he says this concerning that which is perfect, although he has not yet been established in it; for he still awaits it.

[Col. 0498D] In all things, however—[the text here is corrupt or uncertain]—he strives to attain participation in those things in which he himself saw Christ with his own eyes, when Christ, coming before him through his revelation while he was persecuting him, summoned him into his knowledge, and he persists in those very things.

Brothers, I do not consider myself yet to have apprehended it.

(Greg.) Therefore, like travelers, we should not look at how much road we have already traversed, but at how much remains for us to complete, so that what is continually and fearfully regarded as future may soon become past. We ought, therefore, to examine more closely the good things we have not yet done than those we rejoice that we have already done.

But human weakness has this characteristic: it prefers to look at what pleases it in itself rather than at what displeases it in itself. For when the sick eye of the heart fears the labor caused by its own lack of consideration, it seeks, as it were, a couch of pleasure in the soul where it may lie hidden softly. Thus it understands what advantages it has gained from good deeds already completed,

[Col. 0499B] but does not know what losses it suffers from those it has neglected. Often even the elect are tested by this fault. Often their hearts are prompted to recall whatever good they have done and already to exult in the joy of security. But if they truly are elect, they turn the eyes of their minds away from whatever pleases them in themselves; they suppress all joy in themselves over the good they have accomplished and seek sadness over what they understand themselves to have done inadequately. They consider themselves unworthy and, almost alone, fail to see their own good deeds, which they offer to all for imitation and observation.

This is why Paul, while setting aside the good things accomplished in himself and thinking only of those that still remained to be accomplished, says: “I do not consider myself to have apprehended.” This is also why, so that he might humble himself concerning the good things he was doing, he strove to bring his former sins back to mind, saying: “Who formerly was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent” (1 Tim. 1).

Although he once also said, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Tim. 4), it must be carefully observed that he said this at the time when he already knew that he was about to depart from the body. For there he had prefaced it by saying: “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand.” Thus he recalled the completion of his work only when he foresaw that no time for further activity remained within the span of life.

Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the goal, toward the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus.

(Amb.) I do not announce myself truly perfect in achievement, for I do not yet stand in possession of the things that are awaited. Nevertheless, knowing their greatness, I make no account of all former things, consigning them completely to oblivion. I extend my thought toward future things and those that are awaited, having one single aim toward which I look. In everything I do, I seek to attain the rewards set before me in the heavenly calling.

By “heavenly calling,” he means the heavenly dwelling to which we have all been called in order that we may attain it; hence it is also called the kingdom of heaven. For, rising incorruptible and immortal, we hope, according to the promise given to us, to dwell in heaven.

(Aug.) A new life, therefore, is now begun and lived in faith. For it will come when death is swallowed up in victory, when that last enemy is destroyed (2 Cor. 15), when we have been changed and made equal to the angels. For now we have been apprehended in fear through faith; then we shall apprehend in love through sight.

For as long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord (2 Cor. 5); for we walk by faith, not by sight. The Apostle himself, therefore, who says, “I shall apprehend as I have been apprehended,” openly confesses that he has not apprehended:

[Col. 0500A] “Brothers,” he says, “I do not consider myself to have apprehended.” Yet because this hope is certain for us through the promise, when he had said, “We have been buried with him through baptism into death,” he added: “So that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6).

We therefore walk in the reality of labor, but in the hope of rest; in the flesh of old age, but in the faith of newness.

(Amb.) By comparison he wished to show how greatly those things that are ours appear to surpass the law. Since he had spoken of his own attitude toward these matters, he attempts to teach what judgment ought to be held concerning them, and adds this exhortation:

Let us, then, as many as are perfect, think this way. Therefore, if we desire to enjoy what is perfect, we ought to understand these things. Rejecting all those things that are temporal, we ought to think in agreement with the future state.

Let as many of us, then, as are perfect, think this way.

(Aug.) That is, let as many of us as run perfectly think this: that we are not yet perfect, so that we may be perfected there toward which we are still running perfectly. When the perfect has come, then what is partial will be destroyed (1 Cor. 13)—that is, it will no longer be partial but complete, because reality itself will take the place of faith and hope: not something to be believed and hoped for, but something to be seen and possessed.

Love, however, which is greater than these three, will not be taken away but increased and brought to completion, contemplating what it believed and attaining what it hoped for. In that fullness of love the commandment will be fulfilled: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.”

For while there remains any carnal desire that must be restrained by self-control, God is not loved with the whole soul. For the flesh does not desire without the soul, although the flesh is said to desire; it is the soul that desires carnally.

[Col. 0500D] Then the righteous person will be entirely without any sin, because there will be no law in his members resisting the law of his mind. Rather, with his whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind he will love God, which is the first and greatest commandment.

Why, then, should this perfection of human beings not be commanded, even though no one possesses it in this life? For one does not run correctly if one does not know where one must run. How, however, could it be known if it were not shown through commandments?

And if you think anything otherwise, God will reveal this also to you.

(Amb., Aug.) For if we do not know how great and what sort of things the future will be, God shows them to us through the realities themselves. If we have reached a point, let us walk in that same direction—not only concerning what we do not know but ought to know, but also concerning anything we think otherwise, God has revealed this same thing to us.

We have reached the way of faith; let us hold to it with the greatest perseverance. It leads to the king’s chamber, in which all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Col. 2). We must walk, advance, and believe, so that our hearts may become capable of those things that we cannot now contain. If the last day finds us advancing [the manuscript has *proficientes*; the transmitted reading is *proficiscentes*], there we shall learn what we could not learn here.

Nevertheless, in whatever we have attained, let us think the same way and remain within the same rule.

(Amb.) Meanwhile, he says, we must remain in the things in which we are and to which we have been called, showing toward them a fitting attitude, not departing from the expectation of future things, but directing our life according to that expectation. For this is the meaning of the preceding words.

Some, however, failing to attend to the sequence, received these words as though the Apostle were speaking about virtue. They understood “forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead,” and all the rest in the same way. For they do not connect these words properly with the place where he says, “To write the same things to you is not burdensome for me”; yet this teaches them throughout that it is not fitting to obey those who persuade them to live according to the law, as we have also shown in the interpretation. This is made clearer still by what follows.

Imitate me, brothers. That is: do not live under the law, just as I do not live under the law. And to show that he says these things not for his own sake but because he desires them to possess such a manner of life, he added:

[Col. 0501C] And observe those who walk in this way, as you have us for an example. Look carefully, he says, at those who live as we do; obey them and hasten to imitate them.

Then, vigorously rebuking his opponents, he presses the matter upon them:

For many walk, of whom I often told you, and now I say even with tears, they are enemies of the cross of Christ. It would have been sufficient to invite the Philippians to hatred of them, since they were trying to teach things contrary to the cross. Therefore he adds:

Their end is destruction. For what else should one expect concerning those who resist Christ and hasten to diminish him, devoting to the law the concern that belongs to Christ?

Their god is their belly. “Eat this; do not eat that.” They turn their attention to such practices as though directing themselves toward a certain god—their belly—and consider this to be piety toward it, striving to offer some things to it and not to offer others. For what is no longer done according to the will of God is mere observance, containing no goodness.

Yet they complete iniquity, as he sees. Therefore he also diminishes its importance by saying:

[Col. 0501D] Their glory is in their shame. They think it something great that some things are eaten and others are not eaten, failing to consider that every kind of food, whatever it may be, once consumed is turned into excrement, which they themselves would be ashamed to look upon. Behold the end of their pursuits!

And fully accusing them, he adds:

They set their minds on earthly things. For legal observances are necessary for the present life—whether circumcision, sacrifice, dietary observances, or the keeping of Sabbaths. All these things, however, will be useless in the future age. Those who are established in that age and await it are already thought to exist according to its pattern.

[Col. 0502A] But our citizenship is in heaven. Therefore we also await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will reform the body of our humiliation, conforming it to the body of his glory, according to the operation by which he is able also to subject all things to himself.

Our citizenship is not earthly but heavenly, and we await our departure there. Therefore we await Christ himself as our firstfruits, the one who will transfer this body, now humbled under death, to immortality, making it like his own body. For he can do not only this, but, renewing all things, he joins them to himself,

[Col. 0502B] so that every corruption may be dissolved and all things may look toward him as their ruler and the author of incorruption.

For when he says in this place that he will “subject” things to himself, he is not speaking of the servitude that arises from necessity. That is not the point here. Rather, he means that he joins all things to himself through the benefits he provides for them, so that all things look toward him as their ruler and the author of good things.

The same is true of what is written to the Corinthians: “Then the Son himself will be subject” (1 Cor. 15). This does not mean that he will serve, but that he remains joined to him, offering all things through himself. He says this concerning the humanity he assumed.

Then, in the following chapter, he strengthens his exhortation and consolation.

## Chapter IV

The Apostle strengthens endurance by exhorting his people to spiritual joy and perseverance in good works. A greeting is placed at the end.

Therefore, my most beloved and greatly desired brothers, my joy and crown, stand firm in the Lord, beloved.

(Amb.) That is: live in this manner. He shows in these words how greatly he loved them and revered them, calling them diligent, most beloved, and greatly desired brothers, declaring that they were his joy and crown, and adding again to all these expressions: “Beloved.”

I exhort Euodia and I entreat Syntyche to think the same way in the Lord. It is clear that these women themselves were contending against one another, striving for precedence, as women adorned with virtues, and, as usually happens in such disputes, were being provoked.

Therefore he mentioned them by name,

[Col. 0502D] but with great respect, persuading them to do what was good while also giving them the consideration appropriate to their persons.

Here especially it is possible to observe that at that time there was no distinction between men and women, since both were equally impelled by the contemplation of piety. When he wrote to the whole people, he did not hesitate to mention these women by name, testifying to the greatest respect for them in his discourse and fearing nothing—not even that he might thereby incur some reproach.

It is also clear that he did not distrust the women, fearing that they might be distressed because they had been rebuked in the presence of everyone. Such was the instruction among those who were there at the time, and everything was done among them in charity, that the women who needed rebuke were rather pleased to be rebuked before everyone, and no one accused what was done on any account.

I also entreat you, true companion, help them. Some have thought that blessed Paul had a wife and that he was writing to her, as though she were living at Philippi. They did not attend to the fact that he used *affectiose*, not *affectiosa*: the former is a form that can be applied to a man, but not to a woman.

They should also have considered that divine Scripture nowhere calls the man who has joined himself to a wife “conjugal,” but rather calls him one who shares the same faith. For the Lord also calls that way of life which is under the law a yoke: “Take my yoke upon you, for it is gentle” (Matt. 11).

[Col. 0503B] It therefore appears that he is writing to someone joined to him by affection and faith, whom he urges to restore them to concord through his own efforts. He discusses peace with them in order to offer them good counsel and to do everything with the greatest care, so that he may bring them back to unanimity. He shows that they are worthy of great care by adding:

They labored with me in the Gospel. It is clear that they followed him somewhere on his journey and ministered to him as he fulfilled the teaching of piety.

And lest he appear to be speaking of some ordinary contest, he adds:

Together with Clement and my other fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life. That is, they worked together with me in teaching piety, just as those others did.

It is also clear from this that when he says to the Corinthians, “Do we not have authority to lead about a woman?” (1 Cor. 9), he is not saying that he never led one about, but that he did not always do so. We have noted this more cautiously and demonstrated it in the exposition of that Epistle.

And again he prays for them:

Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice. That is: may such things always be present to you from God that you may be filled with joy.

Then he turns to exhortation, which could be fitted to the exhortation that had been given with humility:

Let your moderation be known to all people. Just as I want you to be moderate, so that everyone may rejoice in you because of your moderation.

And because moderate people are often harmed, he adds:

The Lord is near; do not be anxious. Even if you suffer injury, do not be anxious. God is near, and he will bring help to you in your need; he is also powerful enough to punish those who harm you.

What, then, should those who are harmed do?

But in every prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known before God.

(Isaac.) He teaches them four kinds of supplication. The Lord also deigned to initiate us into these by his own example, fulfilling in this respect as well what is said of him: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1).

He assumes the form of supplication when he says: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26); or in what is sung concerning him in the Psalm: “God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 21).

[Col. 0504A] Prayer is expressed when he says: “I have glorified you on earth; I have completed the work that you gave me to do” (John 17); or: “For their sake I sanctify myself, so that they also may be sanctified in truth” (ibid.).

Petition is expressed when he says: “Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me, so that they may see my glory, which you have given me” (ibid.); or certainly when he says: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23).

Thanksgiving is expressed in the words: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, because this was pleasing before you” (Luke 10); or certainly when he says: “Father, I thank you because you have heard me. I knew, however, that you always hear me” (John 11).

[Col. 0504B] Although the same Lord distinguished these four kinds of supplication as things to be offered separately and at different times, according to the manner we have understood, he nevertheless also showed through his examples that they can all be included together in a perfect supplication. He did this especially through the prayer that we read at the end of the Gospel according to John, which he poured forth at great length.

Since it would be too long to go through everything in its entirety, the diligent investigator can learn from the sequence of that reading that these things are so. The Apostle likewise expressed the same point in his Epistle to the Philippians, placing these four kinds of supplication in a somewhat altered order and showing clearly that they should sometimes be offered together in the fervor of a single supplication. He says:

But in every prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known before God.

(Aug.) Through this he wished especially to teach us that thanksgiving ought also to be mingled with petition in prayer.

When he says, “Let your requests be made known before God,” this should not be understood as though they become known to God, who knew them even before they existed. Rather, they should become known before God for our sake through endurance, not before human beings through boasting. Or perhaps they should also become known before the angels who are with God, so that, in a certain sense, they may offer them to God, consult him concerning them, and report back to us, openly or secretly, what they have learned must be fulfilled at God’s command.

For the angel said to a man: “When you were praying, I offered your prayer in the presence of the glory of God” (Tob. 12).

And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus. That is: may he himself grant you perfect peace, who is more powerful than all things. He said that the peace of God surpasses everything, so that he might speak of God himself.

Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are chaste, whatever things are just, whatever things are holy, whatever things are lovable, whatever things are of good repute—if there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline—think about these things, which you have both learned and received, heard and seen in me. Do these things, and the God of peace will be with you.

(Amb.) Apply diligence to truth, he says, to chastity, justice, and purity. Thus he says: “Abstain from wicked dealings,” just as he also said there, “In every matter you have shown yourselves to be pure,” conducting yourselves in such affairs as to do what pleases everyone—

[Col. 0505A] that is, what everyone recognizes as good. For among all people there is a similar acknowledgment of good things. From such deeds a good reputation can follow you.

Whatever works belong to virtue, whatever can secure praise for you from everyone—seeing this in us, learning this from us—do these things, and you will always have God with you, providing you with his deep peace.

Having completed all that belonged to exhortation, he writes further about the things that had been sent to him by them:

I rejoiced greatly in the Lord because at last you have flourished again in your concern for me; indeed, you were concerned, but you lacked opportunity.

He rightly said “in the Lord,” so that he would not seem to rejoice because money had been sent to him. Rather, he says that he rejoiced because of the intention of those who sent it,

[Col. 0505B] because their concern for him had returned. He knew that they had long been concerned for him, but that they had not had the opportunity to do what they wished.

For when he said, “You lacked opportunity,” he means that they had been prevented, despite having the opportunity, from doing what they wished.

For even among those who provide such things, it is not the things they give that constitute the fruit, but the spirit in which they give them. Therefore, he who served God rather than his belly—I clearly see why he rejoiced, and I greatly rejoice with him—had received from the Philippians what they had sent through Epaphroditus. Yet I see why he rejoiced: from that source he rejoices, and from that source he is nourished.

For speaking the truth, he says: “I rejoiced greatly in the Lord, because at last you have flourished again in your concern for me, in which indeed you were concerned.” But you had lacked opportunity. Therefore, through that long lack of opportunity, they had withered and, as it were, dried up with respect to this fruit of good work. He rejoices that they flourished again, not because they had relieved his need.

[Col. 0505C] For this reason he continues:

Not that I say this because of need. For I have learned to be content with whatever I have. I know how to be humbled, and I know how to abound. Everywhere and in all things I have been instructed both to be filled and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things through him who strengthens me. Nevertheless, you did well to share in my tribulation.

(Aug.) Why, then, do you rejoice, great Paul? Why do you rejoice, and from what are you nourished? What is it that feeds your joy? Let us hear what follows:

Nevertheless, he says, you did well to share in my tribulation. This is why he rejoices; this is what nourishes him: because they did well, not because his distress had been relieved. He is the one who says to you, “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. 4), because he knows both how to abound and how to suffer need in you who strengthen him.

(Ambr.) I say these things not because I bear poverty heavily. I have trained myself to be content with the things found in the present, and I am not disturbed in any respect by what happens to me. I received both the things that brought rest and the things that brought sadness, with a prudent and sober understanding.
