In difficult circumstances I had become accustomed not to bear them heavily; in prosperous circumstances I did not relax into luxury. Rather, I set each thing that happened to me in its proper place.

And lest, by saying this, he appear to think highly of himself, he adds: I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me. He himself, he says, enables me to do this: to use rest with fitting judgment, to endure sadness with courage.

And lest he be thought to despise what had been sent by them, since he had such a discipline, he adds:

Nevertheless, you did well to share in my tribulation. You are worthy of all praise because you shared in my tribulations, sending provisions and relieving my need. Through this sharing, it is necessary that you should also share in the reward.

You know also, Philippians, that in the beginning of the Gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church shared with me in the matter of giving and receiving except you alone, because even when I was in Thessalonica you sent supplies for my needs once and twice.

(Aug.) He now rejoices that they have returned to these good works and is glad that they have blossomed again, as though the field’s fertility had lain dormant. Did he rejoice because of his own needs, since he said, “You sent for my needs”? Did he rejoice for that reason? No; and how do we know this? Because he immediately continues, saying: “Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the fruit.” My God has taught me to distinguish between the gift and the fruit. The gift is the thing itself that the giver bestows; this is something necessary, such as money, food, drink, clothing, shelter, or assistance. The fruit, however, is the giver’s good and upright intention.

The gift is to receive a prophet, to receive a righteous man, to extend a cup of cold water to a disciple; but the fruit is to do this in the name of the prophet, in the name of the righteous man, in the name of the disciple. Elijah is nourished by the widow’s fruit, because she knew that she was feeding a man of God (III Kings XVII); but by the raven he was fed by the gift; it was not the inner Elijah but the outer Elijah who was nourished, who could even be harmed by the lack of such food.

(Ambr.) Then he says that, when he first preached piety to you, together with the other Macedonians, and afterward departed, no one gave me anything—not even did I receive anything from another—except from you alone. For when I was staying in Thessalonica, you sent me once and twice what was necessary for my needs.

Did he say, “You shared in the matter of giving and receiving”? He means this: not that he himself gave some things and they gave others, but that they gave while he received. He called it a sharing in giving and receiving because they gave and he received. And again he shows that he is not saying this on account of the things that had been given to him: “Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the abundant fruit accruing to your account.”

[Col. 0506D] “I say this,” he declares, “not because of the things that were given, but I praise your purpose, whose fruits are evident. By giving, you have secured for yourselves a great reward and recompense.” Thus, among good preachers, preaching is not undertaken for the sake of livelihood; rather, livelihood is received for the sake of preaching. And whenever necessities are supplied to preachers by their hearers, they do not usually rejoice over the gift of the things themselves, but over the reward of those who supply them. Hence it is also said through the Apostle: “I do not seek the gift, but I seek the fruit.” The gift is the thing itself that is supplied; the fruit of the gift is that something is supplied with a kindly intention and with a view to the reward to come.

Therefore, we understand the gift as residing in the material thing, and the fruit in the heart. And because the Apostle was nourished by the reward of his disciples rather than by their gift, he declares that he seeks not the gift but the fruit.

Therefore he immediately adds, saying: “I have all things and abound; I have been filled, having received from Epaphroditus the things that you sent, an odor of sweetness, an acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God.” Since I have received everything that was sent from you—and indeed I have received even more and greater things, which were sent from you through Epaphroditus—he shows that he also gives them many thanks for what they had given, honoring their purpose above the things that had been sent.

He prays for them that those very things may appear before God as a sacrifice of good odor: he receives their purpose and repays them with the favor that proceeds from himself.

“My God will fulfill every desire of yours according to his riches in glory, in Christ Jesus.” He prays that, in the present life as well, every necessity of theirs may be fulfilled by God, so that they may suffer no deprivation.

“Now to our God and Father be glory for ever and ever. Amen.” For it is fitting to return glory to God the Father for all things.

“Greet every saint in Christ Jesus. The brothers who are with me greet you. All the saints greet you, especially those who are of Caesar’s household.” He greets every saint among them; he also sends greetings from the brothers who are with him and from all the saints who are in Rome, saying that they are believers and belong to Caesar’s household. For there were some from there who had come to believe. And he adds the customary conclusion with which he ends his Epistles:

“The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.”

# BOOK TWENTY. EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS

[Col. 0507]

## Argument

[Col. 0507B]

Blessed Paul writes to the Colossians just as he wrote to the Ephesians, whom he had not seen before writing to them. He himself demonstrates this in his writings, when he says: “Having heard of your faith in Christ and the love that you have for all the saints.” And again, when he writes: “I want you to know what a struggle I have for you and for those who are in Laodicea, and for all who have not seen my face in the flesh.”

The subject of the Epistle is as follows. It is his custom, wherever or to whomever he writes—when he has not seen those to whom he writes before—to exalt the things that belong to Christ and to demonstrate the greatness of those who have been directed through him. For it was otherwise impossible to demonstrate anything great or beneficial to people who follow the faith that is in him.

Here, however, he saw that this approach was necessary to him not only for that reason, but also because of those who were from the circumcision. They traveled everywhere, attempting to persuade those from the Gentiles who had believed that, together with the faith that they had in Christ, they should also keep the decrees of the Law. Since these people had also come to the Colossians and had all but persuaded some of them to serve the legal decrees, Paul, by showing the superiority of the things directed by Christ, necessarily showed the Law to be weak, while at the same time demonstrating that its careful observance and guardianship were superfluous and vain.

For both reasons, therefore, he writes in this way: first, because such a method could be suitable to him when writing to them for the first time; and second, because, on account of those who were from the circumcision, he hastened to exalt the things that belong to Christ, as was appropriate while explaining the greatness of the deeds that had been accomplished.

After this, he also clearly exhorts them, declaring persuasively that they no longer need to observe the Law in any respect because of those who were teaching them such things. Then, turning to exhortation, he speaks to them all about many necessary matters. In what follows, we shall begin to give the exposition, which appears to proceed in sections, since the matters belonging to the argument of the Epistle have been sufficiently set forth here.

## Chapter One. Having gained their goodwill, he introduces the authority of the Gospel, which must be firmly believed.

Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy the brother, to the holy and faithful brothers who are in Colossae, in Christ Jesus. Grace to you and peace from God our Father.

(Ambr.) Having made the customary heading of the Epistle, he begins in this manner:

“We give thanks to God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, always praying for you, having heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and the love that you have for all the saints.”

Thus also, in the Epistle that he wrote to the Romans, he began writing to them with thanksgiving. Here he adds, “praying for you,” showing that he gives thanks not only for the fact that they have believed, but also prays for the time that remains.

And what is his prayer? “Because of the hope that has been laid up for you in heaven,” so that you may attain the heavenly blessings whose firm hope is being preserved for you, provided that the things proceeding from you have also accompanied it. He shows that he is saying nothing other than what they had learned, which they had previously heard “in the word of the truth of the Gospel, which has come to you.”

I say that, by receiving the teaching with the truth of the Gospel, they learned these things for their greater encouragement. He shows that they alone, in contrast with other people, did not learn these things; otherwise he could have held them more firmly in the faith by showing that the piety held in common by everyone was held also by them, as it is throughout the whole world. At the same time, he displays the greatness of the matter, saying that it is “bearing fruit and increasing.”

“Not only,” he says, “has it been made known to those who are throughout the whole world, but the Gospel has also increased day by day.” Then, lest they should think that the Gospel does not achieve increase among everyone, as he had said, “in all,” he adds:

“As among you, from the day on which you heard and came to know the grace of God in truth.”

“You came to know piety,” he says, “as did everyone; and it has also increased everywhere, day by day. Just as it is among you, so everywhere the Gospel displays its power and receives increase each day, both among you and among all who are in the world.” This was sufficient both to encourage them and to persuade them to remain in the faith, if only all had come to know these things to be true by common agreement.

Then he indicates by whom they had been taught:

“As you learned from Epaphras, our beloved fellow servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ Jesus on your behalf; who also made known to us your love in the Spirit.”

Clearly in these words he shows that they received the Gospel from Epaphras, whom he rightly praised, presenting him to them as worthy of honor. He also commended him to them because he had made known to him the things concerning them. For he knew that it was necessary and beneficial in every respect that a teacher should be worthy of honor and beloved by his disciples.

He seems to have acted most appropriately toward Epaphras in this matter, so that they ought to remain steadfast in his teaching with great affection. He had delivered the Gospel to them while setting aside the Law. Therefore, he would not have praised his teaching if it had not been of this character. For how could he have praised the teaching of one who taught that these things ought not to be observed?

Then, taking up again what he had said—“always praying for you”—he says:

“Therefore we also, from the day on which we heard, do not cease praying and asking for you, that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, so that you may walk worthily of God, pleasing him in all things, bearing fruit and increasing in every good work, strengthened with all power according to the might of his glory, in all patience and long-suffering with joy.”

He appears, under the form of prayer, to have wished every good thing for them, while teaching them what was suitable for them. He says that, from the moment we heard the things concerning you, we prayed without delay, so that, filled with every spiritual understanding, you might be able to know the will of God, conduct yourselves worthily of him, and hasten to please him in every respect. Thus good works might also be multiplied in you day by day together with the knowledge of God, who, as you look toward him according to his power, can fill you with his own patience, so that you may patiently endure all the things that bring sorrow and may have joy in them because of the reward that will be repaid to you for them in the age to come.

As I have said, he declares that he wished these things for them. And, while saying the things that belong to prayer, he teaches them to apply themselves diligently to what is appropriate. Then, taking up also the thanksgiving that he had fulfilled on their behalf, he makes it the beginning of his teaching, just as he did in the Epistle to the Ephesians, where, under the appearance of thanksgiving, he seemed to instruct them in matters of doctrine. Therefore he says:

“Giving thanks to God the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in light.”

“These things,” he says, “we ask above all, giving thanks to God for you, because through his knowledge he has declared you worthy to belong to the company of the saints, although you had been strangers to piety and followers of idols.”

For when he said “in light,” he means through his knowledge; and when he said “who has considered you worthy,” he means that he has declared you worthy. The gain is that they have been joined to the company of the saints.

“He rescued us from the authority of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love.”

“Not only,” he says, “has he taken you away from error and from the power of demons, but he has also declared you to be participants in Christ’s kingdom.” For when he says, “transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love,” he means what he says elsewhere: “If we endure, we shall also reign with him” (II Tim. II).

Therefore it is good that he did not say merely “Son,” but “Son of his love.” For we do not become participants in the kingdom of God the Word—how could we be joined to the Maker of the universe? Rather, he speaks of the man who was assumed, whose honor we shall also share because of the likeness of nature, when we are able to demonstrate our affection for him by our very works.

(Aug.) When he says “Son of his love,” let it be understood as nothing other than “his beloved Son,” and finally, “the Son of his substance.” For the Father’s love, which exists in a nature that is ineffably simple, is nothing other than that nature itself; and consequently, the Son of his love is none other than he who was begotten from his substance. Hence he called him the Son of his love, because he is not a son according to nature, but has attained the love belonging to adopted sons.

(Ambr.) In every respect he intends to show the greatness of the things that belong to Christ, as we said earlier in the argument, and he hastens to prove the greatness of the things that have been corrected by him. Therefore he discusses the man who was assumed as though he were the firstfruits of our nature, and because he became for us the provider of many blessings.

Hence he adds:

“In whom we have redemption and the forgiveness of sins.”

Through him we have obtained complete security from sins. He speaks of the future condition, in which, through the resurrection, our nature having become immortal, we shall no longer be able to sin. The same is meant by what was said to the Ephesians, “so that we may be holy and without blemish.”

Then he also speaks of the dignity that belongs to him:

“Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature.”

The catholic faith, which distinguishes between the Creator and the creature, permits no difficulty in understanding these two titles. It receives him as the Only-Begotten according to what is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I).

But it understands “firstborn of every creature” according to what the Apostle says: “So that he himself might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. VIII), whom the Father generated for fraternal fellowship with him, not by equality of substance but by adoption through grace.

Thus Jesus Christ is both Only-Begotten, insofar as he is the Word of God, God with God, equally unchangeable and equally eternal, not considering it robbery to be equal with God; and he is the firstborn of every creature, insofar as all things were created in him, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible.

He rightly adds “invisible,” not because God is also visible, but to demonstrate the greatness of the matter. If, that is, in this one who is like an image we see the invisible nature, it is because he has been joined to God the Word. He will judge the whole world, appearing in the future age according to his own nature, as is fitting, with great glory, coming from heaven. In this he preserves the order for us, clearly showing that we all direct our nature toward him as toward a kind of divine image, in which the greatness of the things that are brought into being is reflected, as we ascribe authority to the judge whose nature is not visible.

I have been astonished at those who have accepted this as referring to the divine nature. First, they did not see that blessed Moses also says of man, “He made him in the image of God” (Gen. II), and blessed Paul says: “A man ought not to veil his head, since he is the image and glory of God” (I Cor. XI). This would never have been said of human beings if it were proper to the divine nature alone.

Moreover, they did not consider that every image, when it is itself seen, displays what is not seen. How, then, could an image be made that is not seen, when it is evident that images are customarily made among those who make them either for the sake of honor or out of affection, so that they may serve as a reminder of those who are not seen for those who are nevertheless able to see?

Then he adds: “The firstborn of every creature.” From this, certain people of great prudence have especially inferred that the words “image of the invisible God” refer to the divine nature, as though, because the firstborn cannot be seen or received in relation to humanity, the phrase must refer to divinity. They ought to have perceived that this cannot be applied to the divine nature. For if he were firstborn as a creature, he should necessarily be said to have been created first. But if they say that he was begotten, the statement itself will appear to contain many contradictions, if one who is not created is called the firstborn of creatures.

For when someone is called “firstborn” of others, he can properly be called firstborn of those who evidently preserve that likeness to him which they necessarily possess. The Apostle clearly demonstrates this when he says to the Romans:

“For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he himself might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. VIII).

He plainly calls him the firstborn brother of those who are conformed to him because of the likeness that they have from God. They rightly claim him as their firstborn, since he surpasses them in this respect. For even there he did not say “conformed to the Son,” but “to the image of the Son,” clearly calling the image of the Son the visible nature.

But they ask how the man who was assumed can be seen as the firstborn of the whole creation, since he did not exist before every creature but received existence in the last times. They do not understand that “firstborn” is not spoken only with reference to time, but often also with reference to honor. The one called firstborn is indeed the firstborn of those who were generated after him; yet the one who was born earlier is necessarily also accorded precedence in honor, just as both the order of nature and the law of divine Scripture have established.

Sometimes Scripture uses this name by transference with reference to time, but often also with reference to honor. For blessed David, recalling the things that had been done for him, by which God promised to receive those descended from him into his fellowship, says as though God himself were speaking:

“He called upon me, ‘You are my Father,’ and I will make him firstborn” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

God does not say that he will make each one of them earlier than the others in time, but that he will give them very great assistance.

The Apostle also clearly demonstrates the same thing in the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying:

“But you have approached Mount Zion, and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the assembly of many thousands of angels, and the church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven” (Hebr. XII).

He means those who have been considered worthy of great honor. He does not mean that some sons are earlier than other sons.

And elsewhere: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. IV), that is, “honorable to me.” For there were others before Israel who had been considered worthy to be called sons of God. Moses speaks of them:

“When the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, they took wives for themselves from all those whom they chose” (Gen. VI).

So also in this passage, when he had said “the firstborn of the whole creation,” he means “honorable above every creature.” If he had simply said “firstborn,” he would have spoken only of one who was honorable. But because he added “of every creature,” he designated the one who is honored by every creature.

Indeed, the Christ who is according to the flesh is truly called, in time, the firstborn of the whole creation, which was made in him. Blessed Paul appears to have spoken of this in the present passage.

Therefore, interpreting his statement “the firstborn of the whole creation,” he adds:

“Because in him all things were created.”

He did not say “through him,” but “in him.” For he is not speaking of the first creature, but of that division of creation which took place in him, according to which all things that had long been dissolved were brought together into unity, just as he says elsewhere: “To recapitulate all things in Christ, those in heaven and those on earth.”

Because of human wickedness, the whole creation, so to speak, appeared to be torn apart. The angels and all invisible powers turned away from us because of our impiety toward God. Moreover, we ourselves were released into death, by which the soul was separated from the body; and thus the whole connection of creation was also dissolved.

From the beginning, man had been formed as a kind of creature joined by kinship to all things: his body consisted generally of all things, that is, of the four elements, while his soul appeared to have an affinity with the invisible powers. A single kind of union of all things appeared to arise from this, as all things converged toward one another, so that with one accord they might render the worship owed to God with careful attention, and all might hasten to obey those things that accorded with his laws.

But because of sin we became mortal, and the soul was separated from the body. The bond of kinship was thereby dissolved, so that the invisible powers no longer considered that they had any communion with us in view of the condition of our body. In addition, we had become hateful to God because of the sight of sin, and he also turned away from us.

Therefore even those who presided over visible natures and moved them for our benefit according to the limit appointed to them no longer wished to fulfill these functions, unless they received the promise that all harsh things would be dissolved.

Death and corruption also ceased when all things were restored to one accord, just as he writes to the Romans:

“For the creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope; because the creation itself will also be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. VIII).

In our renewal, therefore, through which the connection of all things is also restored—and whose firstfruits are those who belong to Christ according to the flesh, in whom the finest and, so to speak, most comprehensive renewal of all things will be accomplished—blessed Paul says: “If anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new.”

For the harmony, concord, and connection of all things that continue to exist will be saved in incorruption for all. The invisible powers will also love us thereafter, as being relatives and friends of God.

He therefore rightly said, “All things were created in him,” not only because, through the things that were accomplished concerning him, we have attained the promise of future things, but also because the perfect union of all things will be preserved in him because of the indwelling of the divine nature, so that nothing of what is common to us can ever again be torn apart.

On the one hand, all things will love him because of the intimacy that they were able to have with him, as with a man consisting of visible nature and with God consisting of invisible nature; on the other hand, all things will turn toward him with great fear because of the inseparable Word of God joined to him.

Therefore, when he said “all things,” he added: “Those in heaven and those on earth.” Since it was uncertain whether “those in heaven” and “those on earth” referred to visible or invisible things—for there are also things in heaven that are seen, such as the sun, moon, and stars, which he placed in the firmament of heaven—he made the division clear by adding: “Visible and invisible.” That is, all these things have subsequently been joined and bound together in him.

But whether because of knowledge, or also because of dignity, and because visible things appeared more certain, since the intimacy that existed with the man himself, who is seen, was manifest, he passes over this and proceeds to invisible things, because what was said about them appeared greater.

Here he clearly possesses proof of the greatness of those things that have been directed through Christ, and the invisible nature received renewal in him.

“Thrones, or dominions, principalities, or powers.”

He did not mention angels, because that name appeared to signify the function of ministry. Instead, he said “thrones,” “dominions,” “principalities,” and “powers,” because these names are also applied to them according to the function that they appear to fulfill. They also possess some indication of the dignity that belongs to them, since they have received the role of surpassing others invisibly.

Some of them are superior to the air, others to the sun, others to the moon, and others to the stars; still others are assigned to particular stars, so that they may move all things according to the limit imposed on them by God, in order that all things may be able to remain in existence.

They were called “principalities” and “powers” because they had received authority to rule and to exercise power over some affair. Thus, writing to the Ephesians concerning the devil, he says: “According to the prince of the power of the air, of the spiritual realm” (Ephes. I, III). And in Daniel: “The prince of Persia resisted me, and your prince” (Dan. X), calling forth the angel who expended his care on their behalf.

Therefore he expands the meaning when he says “thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers,” speaking of the same thing in various ways. “If,” he says, “there is anything that rules, or claims dominion for itself, or holds a principality, or exercises power—however one may wish to speak of the authority assigned to them by God—all things were created in him.”

At first they were weary on account of human beings and unwilling to complete their own work for our sake; but now they accomplish everything with eagerness, honoring that property of our nature which has been united to him. They do not hesitate to worship it because of the nature present in him in the age to come, since all things have been gathered together in him by a kind of union returning into itself.

This will occur especially at the time when corruption and death have been wholly dissolved. And because it seemed in some way unbelievable that, when speaking of a man, one should say that all things were created in him, he confirms this by adding:

All things were created through him and in him. (Ambrose.) “Do not be surprised,” he says, “for this dignity does not belong to him from himself, but on account of the nature that dwells in him, through which all things were made and toward which all things also look, considering him who is their one and the same Lord.” And, enlarging the point further, he says: “He himself is before all things, and all things subsist in him”—that is, he existed before all things, produced them all, and they appear to subsist through his power.

(Ser.) No believer doubts that, before the creation of this visible universe, the Lord made the spiritual and heavenly powers. Since they knew that they themselves had been brought forth from nothing, through the Creator’s beneficence, to such a glorious blessedness, they continually gave him thanks and clung unceasingly to his praises. We must not suppose that God first began the beginnings of creation and of his own work with the establishment of this world, as though during those inner and innumerable ages he had been idle, deprived of all divine providence and administration, and as though, being solitary and having no one on whom to exercise the benefits of his goodness, he had been estranged from all munificence. It is sufficiently low and incongruous to think this of that immense, beginningless, and incomprehensible majesty.

The Lord himself says this concerning those powers: “When the stars were made together, all my angels praised me with a loud voice.” Therefore those who took part in the creation of the stars are most clearly shown to have been created before that beginning in which heaven and earth are said to have been made, since they are said to have praised with great wonder the Creator who preceded all these visible creatures that they saw brought forth from nothing.

Before, then, that temporal beginning which is mentioned by Moses, and which, according to the historical—or rather Jewish—sense, signifies the age of this world, while our own interpretation remains intact, namely, that Christ is the beginning of all things, in whom the Father created everything, according to the statement, “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1), before that beginning, he says, it is beyond doubt that God created all those heavenly powers and spiritual virtues. The Apostle enumerates and describes them in order as follows: “For in Christ all things were created, those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible, whether angels or archangels, thrones or dominions, principalities or powers; all things were created through him and in him.”

That some of their number—namely, certain princes—also fell is made perfectly clear by the lament of Ezekiel and Isaiah (Isaiah 14; Ezekiel 28). In these passages we recognize, mourned in grievous lamentation, the prince of Tyre and that Lucifer who was rising in the morning.

(Ambrose.) It is not surprising that, while arguing as though about a human being, he passed from human matters to teaching about divinity. We can show that the Apostle did the same when writing to the Philippians, where he says: “Who, existing in the form of God,” and so forth (Philippians 2). There the Apostle plainly passed from divine matters to human ones, and indeed spoke of everything as though it concerned one and the same person.

Likewise, when writing to the Hebrews, he says: “He has spoken to us in the Son, whom he appointed heir of all things” (Hebrews 1). Here he plainly speaks of a human being, whose speech we heard, and who assumes dominion over things that previously did not belong to him. Yet he passed over to the divine, in order thereby to establish their greatness; and then he returns again to the human, still speaking of everything in that section of the letter as though it concerned one person. The same Lord is often found to have done this in the Gospels. Anyone may recognize this more cautiously if he follows our interpretation through that passage of John’s Gospel in which he appears to have spoken to the Jews concerning the paralytic who had been healed. Thus, in this passage also, he has mentioned the divine nature in order, from its greatness, to establish what belongs to human beings.

(Ambrose.) From there he again returns to the human, saying: “And he himself is the head of the body, the Church.” That is, he assigns to us in common as head this one in whom all things were created, while the Church became his body through spiritual regeneration. It bears the form of the future resurrection, according to which we hope to share with him and become participants in his immortality, having been baptized as though fulfilling a certain likeness of those whose prince he himself became for us. For this reason, then, we also ascribe that head to ourselves.

Hence he adds: “Who is the firstborn from the dead”—that is, the first of all who rise again, reborn into that life. Since he calls the firstborn from the dead a human being whom he has assumed, this is clear. It is also possible to see plainly from the very wording that he speaks as though of one person, both in what precedes and in what is now said.

Those who attempt to interpret the Apostle’s words incorrectly, and who take the statement “who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation” as referring to the divine nature, will in no way be able to entangle our interpretation with their accusations. We have said that he passes from the divine nature to the human, and again from the human to the divine; indeed, necessity compels them to do the same. The reality itself forces them to take the words spoken above as referring to the divine nature. But although they may contend wickedly about everything, they will never be able to take the phrase “firstborn from the dead” as referring to the divine nature.

The Apostle, however, clearly showing that he had also said above “firstborn of all creation,” again spoke of the same matter: “firstborn from the dead.” Hence he adds: “So that he himself might hold the first place in all things.” He did not state “so that” as a cause, but expressed what followed in his customary manner. He means that he is first in every respect—not only because he appears to have initiated the resurrection, but also because he holds the first place in all things.

All those things named among created beings, as though granting him greater honor, and as though interpreting what he had said above and wishing to make that statement clearer, he says: “For in him all things were created,” and so forth. “For in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether those on earth or those in heaven.”

He calls the Church the fullness of God, and likewise “all things,” since he is in all things and fills all things. This can clearly be learned from what he appears to have said when writing to the Ephesians: “And he gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all things in all.”

This, then, is what he says: that it pleased God that all fullness should dwell in him—that is, in Christ. He means that every creature, which has been filled by him, was approved for union with him. Explaining the same point at greater length, he says: “And through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, through him, whether those on earth or those in heaven.”

“All things,” he says, “were reconciled and joined together in his death”—for this is what he means by “blood” and “cross”—both those above the earth and those above the heavens, because he died and rose again. Rising, he bestowed on all alike the promise of resurrection and immortality.

Everything is thereby brought together into harmony, as we also said above, and begins from him as the author of concord. This is what he has said most appropriately concerning him: that through his death he joined all things together and established them in peace through the union that exists with him.

He plainly appears here to have repeated what he had said—“in him all things were created, those in heaven and those on earth.” He will also carefully establish that he spoke there of the same person of whom he appears to have spoken here, whom he plainly called “firstborn from the dead,” thereby showing that he gave this name to the human being assumed by the Father.

In these statements, therefore, while showing that the things belonging to Christ are great and transcendent, and that the nature he assumed claims for itself things far greater than those belonging to a human being, he has also sufficiently demonstrated the greatness of the things accomplished through him by means of the general statements. He now turns the discourse further to their own person, since they had obtained the benefit that had been bestowed on all in common. Thus he would lead them not only, through their participation in it, to reverence, so that they would not depart from the faith that is in Christ, but also to consider what belongs particularly to them, since they too have been greatly exalted through these benefits along with the others.

(Augustine.) Through that singular sacrifice in which the Mediator was offered—the one sacrifice foreshadowed in the Law by many victims—heavenly things are reconciled with earthly things and earthly things with heavenly things, since, as the Apostle says, “in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him all things were reconciled to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether those on earth or those in heaven.”

This peace surpasses, as it is written, all understanding; nor can it be known by us except when we have come to it. For how are heavenly things reconciled except for our sake, that is, by being brought into concord with us? For there is always peace there, both among all intellectual creatures themselves and between them and their Creator. That peace, as has been said, surpasses all understanding—certainly ours, not that of those who continually behold the face of the Father.

Whether, then, I say “head and body” or “bridegroom and bride,” understand one thing. For this reason the same Apostle, while he was still Saul, heard: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9). The body is joined to its head, and the preacher of Christ suffered from others what he himself had done as a persecutor.

He says: “I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ,” referring to the sufferings of Christ. This shows that he suffered in a way that cannot be understood with reference to the head, which now suffers nothing of the kind in heaven, but with reference to the body, that is, the Church; and that body, together with its head, is one Christ. He did not say “the sufferings of my Christ,” because he was a member, and in his own persecutions he completed, according to his portion, the sufferings that Christ had to endure throughout the whole body.

“And you, though you were once alienated and enemies in mind through evil works, he has now reconciled in the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy, blameless, and irreproachable before him.” (Ambrose.) Here too he appears to have preserved the sequence of what he had written in the Epistle to the Ephesians. There, after first recounting magnificently the things concerning Christ, he then added the union of the Church that had been made with him, and, passing to what was particular, mentioned the persons to whom he was writing, saying: “And you, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world,” and so forth.

So here also, after recounting what belongs to Christ—as it was fitting that these things should be recounted—and then adding the union of the Church that had been made with him, he passes to what is particular, namely, to the persons of the Colossians. He says that the things accomplished concerning Christ are great and excellent, and that you too have obtained such benefits: for, although you were alienated from God and placed among his enemies because of the devotion you showed toward wickedness, he reconciled you to God through his death, removing mortality from you and granting you immortality. Once established in that state, you are secure from every sin and can no longer do anything improper.

You remain without enduring any accusation, but conduct yourselves in a manner pleasing to him in every scrupulous respect. We have observed this throughout all the Epistles: the Apostle displays, from the future, the greatness of what Christ has done for us, and all his correction rests upon the promises—the renewal that will take place in the future age. We have shown that he said the same thing when writing to the Ephesians.

He then passed further to his own person, indicating what they had been persuaded by those who urged them to devote themselves to observing the Law. “Provided that you remain grounded and steadfast in the faith, and not moved away from the hope of the Gospel that you heard,” and so forth.

Just as, in the passages where he exhorted them to believe firmly, he mentioned them with thanksgiving, saying that the glory of the Gospel was asserting its power throughout the whole world, so here also he indicates that they had been led astray from that glory which appears to be firm among all, and he mentions it in order to make them feel greater shame.

“Which has been proclaimed in every creature under heaven.” It would have been exceedingly serious for them to depart from that which all alike loudly proclaimed to be good. Wishing to make this point clearer, he adds: “Of which I, Paul, became a minister.”

It was God’s work that he should preach the Gospel among the Gentiles, apart from the observance of the Law, just as he divided the preaching between blessed Peter and the others. He mentions this when writing to the Galatians, and shows that he is conscious of teaching what is good: “Now I rejoice,” he says, “in my sufferings for you; I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ.”

(Gregory.) He takes care, through all his scriptural arguments, to proclaim the Redeemer of the world, and sought to signify him through all the elect, as though through his members. Hence blessed Job is said, in the Latin expression, to lament, so that through both his name and his wounds the passion of our Redeemer might be signified. Concerning him the prophet says: “Truly he himself bore our sicknesses, and he carried our sorrows” (Isaiah 53).

When the tempter had taken everything away, he killed both Job’s servants and his children, because, at the time of Christ’s passion, he struck not only the Jewish people, who served through fear, but also the Apostles themselves, who had been reborn through love alone, with the weapon of faithlessness.

Blessed Job’s body is afflicted with wounds because our Redeemer did not disdain to be fastened with nails to the gibbet of the cross. He receives wounds from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head because the tempter, raging through persecution, afflicts the holy Church, which is his body, not only in its outermost and lowest members but even up to its highest members.

Hence Paul also says: “I fill up what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ in my flesh, for the sake of his body, which is the Church, of which I, Paul, became a minister.”

(Ambrose.) Therefore I also rejoice while suffering for you, because Christ suffered beforehand in order to confer a benefit on you, declaring his body to you through the resurrection. What was lacking in his tribulations, I myself complete by those which will be for you.

(Rabanus.) What does “what was lacking” mean? By learning what things were appointed for you, you may receive the promise from them. This, however, cannot happen without labor and tribulations. For this reason I suffer, going about and preaching to everyone the things that have been corrected, so that, believing with the affection of your hearts, you may receive that closeness which exists with him. For I became their minister.

And so that he might not appear presumptuously to ascribe the direction of this ministry to himself, he says: “According to the stewardship given to me for you, to fulfill the word of God, the mystery that was hidden from ages and generations but is now manifest to his saints, to whom God willed to make known the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles.”

(Ambrose.) Anyone may find these matters expressed in the very words of the Epistle he wrote to the Ephesians, since he wrote both that Epistle and this one to people who had not seen him. For this reason he appears to have placed many similar ideas in both Epistles.

He says, then, that this ministry was entrusted to him by God, so that he might teach everyone what had formerly been unknown to all, but is now known to his saints: namely, that what was such a gift, because of its great goodness and the generosity of its glory, was likewise granted to the Gentiles for their enjoyment.

In former times, all piety was regarded as confined within the Jewish people; the Gentiles had no fellowship with them. But the Gospel promised to all alike the gift of things to come. He calls this a “mystery” because it was formerly hidden but is now manifest.

Since he says, “to his saints, to whom God willed,” he is speaking of the Apostles and of those who were then leaders, concerning whom he also appears to have spoken plainly when writing to the Ephesians.

And since he says, “what are the riches of the glory of the mystery,” he adds: “Which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.” This is the great wealth—namely, Christ—and the fact that we believe in him. He is the hope of future glory, and he became for us the cause of good things by granting us the expectation of them.

“Him we proclaim, admonishing every person and teaching every person in all patience, so that we may present every person perfect in Christ Jesus.” “Him,” he says, “we preach, teaching everyone to have such an affection for him that they may be able to attain perfection in the future through the faith that is in him.”

He calls the future condition “perfection.” He appears to say the same in the Epistle to the Galatians and in this one to the Ephesians: in that state nothing good will be lacking.

Since he referred all these matters to what he had said—“Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you”—he takes up the same point again: “In this I also labor, striving according to his working, which works in me in power.” “For these things,” he says, “I desire to labor in every way, striving because of the power granted to me from heaven for this purpose.”

One may find this also entirely similar in meaning to the Epistle he appears to have written to the Ephesians, where he says: “For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus,” and so forth (Ephesians 2).

Since he clearly showed that this teaching belonged to him, inasmuch as he appeared to have been entrusted with the ministry to the Gentiles and created by God for this purpose, he hastens to address them, because he had not yet come to them.

## CHAPTER II

He teaches them to beware of deceptions through false prophecy, through the authority of the Law, and through a pretence of holiness.

“For I want you to know what concern I have for you, for those who are in Laodicea, and for all who have not seen my face in the flesh.” (Ambrose.) “I do not want you to be ignorant of this,” he says: “although I have not seen you, I nevertheless endure a very great struggle on your behalf. I am no less concerned for you than for those whom I have seen.”

What does he mean by saying that he suffers a struggle for them? “So that their hearts may be comforted, instructed in love, and in all the riches of the fullness of understanding.” He means that, coming together in the love that exists toward Christ, they may attain the enjoyment of those good things that are awaited through a firm understanding.

“In the knowledge of the mystery of God the Father of Christ Jesus, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.” He means that they may share in the unspeakable good things granted to us by God, which are now hidden in Christ; when he appears in the future age, the generosity shown toward us will then also be seen in its works.

As we have often said, he calls the grace extended toward the Gentiles a “mystery,” because it was originally unknown. He declares that knowledge of the mystery means participation in it. He also declares that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ, since they have been established through great prudence by Christ for our benefit. They are now unknown, but will be seen then, when he himself appears.

The Apostle knew these treasures, but who can know how far he penetrated into them and how far he advanced within them?

(Augustine.) Yet, according to what is written—“To each of us is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good; to one is given through the Holy Spirit a word of wisdom, and to another a word of knowledge, according to the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12)—if these two differ from one another so that wisdom is attributed to divine matters and knowledge to human matters, I recognize both in Christ, and so does every one of his faithful.

When I read, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” I understand in the Word the true Son of God, in the flesh the true son of man, and both together united in one person, God and man, through an ineffable generosity of grace.

Therefore Christ is our knowledge, and Christ is also our wisdom. He implants faith in us concerning temporal things, and he displays truth concerning eternal things. Through him we proceed toward him; through knowledge we strive toward wisdom. Yet we do not depart from the one and same Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom are hidden.

“But I say this so that no one may deceive you with subtle words.” (Ambrose.) What does he mean by “I say this,” and why do I have this struggle on your behalf? For I fear that at some time you may undergo a change by giving your attention to persuaders. You will then be able, as I said, to attain the promises made to you, when you remain firm in piety.

Showing that he also shares in their joy if they conduct themselves well in the matters concerning them, he says: “For although I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.” Although I am absent, I am with you in affection of heart, rejoicing in you, provided that you are willing to remain in the faith of Christ with firm conviction. Then he begins openly to exhort them:

“Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus, walk in him, rooted and built up in him, and established in the faith, as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.”

Through all these words he wished to say: Remain in what you received, conducting yourselves according to it, so that it may be clear that you received these things from Epaphras apart from the observance of the Law. For this reason he also praised his tradition at the beginning.

He did well to add thanksgiving, showing that the teaching is good in such a way that it is fitting for those through whom they came to know him to give thanks.

Then, condemning the adversaries, he says: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit.” By “philosophy” he meant a pompous doctrine of words, which the adversaries habitually employed with a certain pretence to seduce their hearers. He thereby shows that it was not true philosophy, but words of seduction devised and invented to deceive their listeners.

(Gregory.) God therefore teaches us, in accordance with blessed Job’s statement, concerning the beasts of the earth and the birds of the sky: when we recognize what we are, the weakness of the flesh does not cast us down, nor does the spirit of pride lift us up. We are neither brought low by sinking into the depths nor inflamed by pride over exalted things.

Whoever falls through the flesh is cast down by the appetite of beasts; whoever is lifted up in mind is raised up, like a bird, as though on the feather of lightness. But if one watches attentively, maintaining both humility of mind and chastity of flesh, he quickly recognizes that one is guarded through the other.

For pride has often been the seedbed of lust. While the spirit raises such people aloft as though to a height, the flesh sinks them into the lowest places. They are first secretly lifted up, but afterward fall publicly, because, while they swell inwardly through hidden movements of the heart, they fall openly through bodily lapses.

Thus the exalted deserved to be struck with a just retribution: because they place themselves above human beings through pride, they sink through lust to the likeness of beasts.

“For a human being, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Psalm 48).

“According to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ.” (Ambrose.) By “the elements of the world” he means the observance of days and seasons, since these things are determined by the elements of the world. By the world’s element he means the sun and the moon, from which the cycles of days and seasons also appear to arise.

Writing to the Galatians, he likewise called it a human tradition. He did not call the Law itself human, but the teaching of those who were present at that time, saying that it was human because it was not carried out according to God’s judgment. To show its perversity, he added, “and not according to Christ,” setting the person of Christ against it and exposing the perversity of the doctrine.

(Augustine.) “Beware, therefore,” he says, “lest anyone deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit according to the elements of this world.” He was addressing those who, as though more learned, explain idols. Therefore, after saying “through philosophy,” he immediately added, “according to the elements of this world.” He warns them to beware not of ordinary worshipers of images, but of supposedly more learned interpreters of signs.

“For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily.” Not “bodily” because God is corporeal, but either he uses a metaphorical expression, as though God did not dwell bodily in a temple made by human hands—that is, through signs that prefigured him. He calls all those observances “shadows of things to come,” using the word metaphorically.

For, as it is written, the Most High God does not dwell in temples made by human hands (Acts 17). Or “bodily” was said because God dwells also in Christ’s body, which he assumed from the Virgin, as in a temple. Hence, when he said to the Jews who were asking for a sign, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (Matthew 14), the Evangelist, explaining what this meant, says: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body.”

(Ambrose.) Here also he says “the whole fullness of deity” to mean the entire creation filled by him. He expresses the sense that he appears to have set forth above: that every creature dwells in him, that is, is joined to him, and that he holds it within himself as a kind of body fitted together because of the union that exists with him.

It is therefore altogether inappropriate to attend to anyone who teaches anything other than what he taught, in whom all things have been fitted and joined together. Making the impropriety still clearer, he adds: “And you have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power.”

He summarizes again what was said above. You, too, having him within you, have been deemed worthy of his union; he also stands as head over all invisible powers. Everything has been joined to him for knowledge of him, as a body is joined to its head.

Then, bringing the greatness of their gifts to bear upon their shame, he says: “In whom you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand, in the removal of the body of flesh, in the circumcision of Christ.”

(Augustine.) He certainly did not intend us to understand two separate things, as though flesh were one thing and the body of flesh another. “Body” is a name applied to many things, not all of which are flesh; for there are many heavenly bodies and earthly bodies apart from flesh. He said “body of flesh,” meaning the body that is flesh. Thus he also speaks of “the spirit of your mind,” meaning the spirit that is the mind: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Ephesians 4).

(Ambrose.) “In him,” he says, “and through the faith that is in him, you have been instructed concerning the mortality imposed upon you, and with that mortality he also removed your sins.”

He means: You have attained immortality, and, once established in it, you will no longer sin, because mortality imposes the necessity of sinning. It is therefore fitting, for this reason also, that you should not appear ungrateful toward him who became the provider of such great benefits for you.

He rightly called the removal of mortality “circumcision,” showing its difference by comparison. There, a small portion of the body is removed, without producing any benefit; here, such great mortality is removed for the better, as our body is transformed.

Hence he called it “a circumcision not made by hand,” showing from the manner of its operation how different it is. There, a human hand performs the circumcision; here, it is divine grace that effects the removal of mortality.

The addition “in the circumcision of Christ” is also necessary. He means that you were circumcised with the circumcision whose promise Christ gave you. Since the things that had been said were great, but had not yet been brought into operation, he continues:

“Having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.”

Although you have not yet obtained these things in reality, you have already been made like them in form: you died with him in baptism and rose with him. It is therefore evident that you attained baptism by believing—first believing that God is powerful enough to do these things and that he has already done so, since he raised Christ from the dead, accomplishing in him the firstfruits of the common resurrection.

We have shown in many passages of apostolic teaching that he habitually establishes proofs of the things concerning Christ from future realities. He also mentions the form that is fulfilled in the present, so that they may be seen to possess now certain pledges of the things they await. For this reason we receive the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit in baptism.

Since he said “form,” he takes up again what he had said, in order to explain more fully the grace that proceeds from it.

And when you were dead in trespasses and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made you alive together with him, forgiving you all trespasses. (Augustine, Ambrose.) He called “uncircumcision” that which is signified by uncircumcision, namely, carnal sins, from which we are to be stripped. In this passage he does not speak of bodily uncircumcision, but just as he called circumcision the removal of mortality, so he called uncircumcision that which still carries mortality about with it. This, then, is what he says: Since you had been put to death by sins because of the mortality imposed upon you, he raised you together with Christ, effecting in him the common resurrection, [Col. 0524A] through which every form of your sin will be destroyed. For this is what he says: “forgiving you all trespasses,” because he has placed us beyond the ease of sinning; for through the resurrection, once we have become immortal by nature, we shall no longer be able to sin.

Then he joins to this another benefit acquired for us, which he thought also suited his present argument: “Blotting out the bond of the decree that was against us, which was contrary to us, and he took it away from our midst, fastening it to the cross.” (Ambrose.) He calls the law a bond, whose every requirement we ought to fulfill, since it was established by God. Yet it was harsh—indeed, impossible—for us to be justified according to the strictness of the law, because the law commanded that the sinner be punished whenever [Col. 0524B] and however he sinned. To refrain from sinning completely, however, was exceedingly impossible for a human being in his present condition. Consequently, those who lived under the law could by no means be made secure from punishment.

He therefore calls the law a bond against us because it was contrary to us—that is, because, through its strictness, it did not permit us to attain justification. And he erased this bond by his decrees, meaning by the resurrection and immortality. For he shows that these are doctrines when, writing to the Ephesians, he says that he abolished “the law of commandments contained in decrees.” Why? Because the law was necessary for those who were subject to sin, restraining and preventing them from sinning. But those who have risen and have become immortal will no longer be able to sin. Thus the law is superfluous for those who are such; and in [Col. 0524C] this, he says, he makes us secure, so that we may no longer live under the law, through which we were especially liable to fall easily under punishment.

He aptly said, “fastening it to the cross,” because, in the present life, the law is useful to us, since we are able to sin; but the end of this life is death. “He fastened it,” he says, “to the cross”: for by dying he brought the law to its end. Nor can the law have any further place among those who have risen. In this respect we too are made to be outside the law, insofar as, through the form of baptism, we pass into the things that are to come, ordering our conduct according to baptism.

And what is greater still: “Stripping off principalities and powers, he led them forth openly, triumphing over them confidently in himself.” By “principalities and powers” he here means the hostile powers, [Col. 0524D] which would never have had any power against us if we could not sin. For, he says, he laid aside mortality, which he removed for the common benefit of all; and he stripped them also of that authority which they had abused against us, displaying a great and unquestionable victory over them. Thus they are put to shame, since those vain powers had endured so much labor against us without being able to gain any advantage, while we have passed into a better condition, so that we can no longer sin.

For he has joined everything to the resurrection. After we have been removed from mortality and made incorruptible, we are indeed made free from sin, and we are also delivered from subjection to the law. We are likewise made secure from every assault of the demons. [Col. 0525A] All these things necessarily follow those who have become immortal and have been made secure from every condition of sinning; they also preserve divine grace in an everlasting disposition toward goodness. And because he showed through the things accomplished by Christ that we have also been made secure from life under the law, he adds:

“Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink, or in a portion of a feast day, or of a new moon, or of Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is Christ’s.”

And by showing the difference between the observance of these things and the conduct that is according to Christ, [Col. 0525B] he shows by comparison that the former are almost nothing else than a shadow of things to come. He says that they are weaker than the things belonging to Christ to the same degree that a shadow is weaker than a body. A body is substance, whereas a shadow merely appears; yet even the shadow cannot appear unless there is a body. For a body produces whatever makes a shadow and allows it to be seen.

Thus all things belonging to the present life, together with their observance, are shadows when compared with the things that belong to Christ, because Christ’s things have been established and endure no end, since after the resurrection we shall become immortal and incorruptible. The things belonging to the law, however, are, in comparison with future things, like a shadow, because they possess their proper status only in the present life. Food, drink, a festival, a new moon, and a Sabbath were observed for a brief time and then passed away, [Col. 0525C], since those who have once died no longer need this observance. Christ’s gift, however, once it has begun, remains unmoved and never undergoes any change. For when he says “a shadow of things to come,” he means that, in comparison with future things, all these observances are shadows. Therefore he adds the body to the image of the shadow, saying that in Christ there is the truth possessing everlasting life.

(Augustine.) When he says, “Let no one judge you in food,” he declares that it is no longer necessary for these things to be observed. When he says that they are “a shadow of things to come,” he shows why they were appropriate to be observed at the time when the things that have now shone forth clearly for us were being foretold through such figures and shadows.

“Let no one deceive you, wishing, in humility and the worship of [Col. 0525D] angels, to walk in what he has not seen, vainly puffed up by the mind of his flesh, and not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, supplied and joined together through its ligaments and connections, grows with the increase of God.”

In these words a certain expression of the face and manner of voice is required. For he spoke ironically, putting the words into the mouths of those who say, “Do not touch, nor taste,” although all things are clean to the clean.

(Ambrose.) By touching upon this concern for vain observances under the name of knowledge, he perceived that one must beware of those who were called philosophers and of Judaism, where the shadows of things to come had to be removed, since their light, Christ, had already come. The law was said to have been given through angels, as though they had ministered at the time when the law [Col. 0526A] was given, just as blessed Paul says: “For if the word spoken through angels was firm” (Hebrews II).

Those who persuaded others to keep the law also maintained that the angels would be angry if the law were not observed. Then, pretending a certain humility, they hastened to display it, as though they observed the law they had despised out of fear. “Do not,” he says, “pay attention to those who display this humility and wish to put angels before you. Yet, in the arrogance of their minds, they say things that are not true and pretend that they are acting rightly: ‘and not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, supplied and joined together through its ligaments and connections, grows with the increase of God.’ You ought instead to pursue the things that belong to Christ, in whose effect the common body is held together, [Col. 0526B], according to the grace supplied to them, by which that growth which is according to God can be produced.”

Then he hastens to offer an exhortation based on the things he had previously set forth:

“If, then, you have died with Christ to the elements of this world, why, as though you were living in the world, do you submit to decrees such as: ‘Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle’?”

If, then, you have been instructed as those who have already died together with Christ and risen with him, and have been transferred beyond the condition of this life—for this is what he means by “the elements of this world”—why, as though you were living in the present life, do you tolerate those who establish laws for you and say, “Eat this,” “Do not touch that,” and other things of this kind?

And, exposing the vanity of their tradition, he says:

“All of which perish in their very use, according to the commandments and doctrines of human beings. [Col. 0526C]”

Their end, he says, is corruption and digestion, for this happens with all foods. These are human traditions, just as he said above; he does not call them the legislation of the law, but “the commandments and doctrines of human beings.”

“Which have indeed an appearance of wisdom in superstition and humility, and in not sparing the body, not in any honor, for the satisfying of the flesh.”

The statement is obscure. He means that, when these practices are handed down, they seem to possess some display of the teachers’ knowledge, and that those who are suitably disposed toward such things appear to be cultivating humility. But he shows that they also seem unwilling to spare their own bodies and consider them unworthy of any honor, so as to fill the body with everything; rather, they abstain from many things because of the tradition of the law.

He said this because they attached great importance to abstinence and, as it were, despised foods on account of the law. In what follows he exposes the pitiable character of the practice itself. [Col. 0526D]

(Gregory.) Here one should observe that, in his discussion, the outstanding preacher joins the appearance of humility to superstition. When the flesh is worn down by abstinence beyond what is necessary, humility is displayed outwardly; but inwardly one takes great pride in that very humility. And unless the mind often became swollen with pride because of the virtue of abstinence, the arrogant Pharisee would never have carefully counted it among his great merits, saying: “I fast twice in the week” (Luke XVIII).

(Jerome.) We now confirm what we have often said: although Paul was unskilled in speech, he was not unskilled in [Col. 0527A] knowledge (II Corinthians XI), and he spoke not of humility but of the truth of conscience. For the tongue cannot express profound and hidden meanings. Even when a person himself understands what he feels, he cannot transfer it clearly into another’s ears in pure speech. Paul, although extremely eloquent in his native language—for he was “a Hebrew of Hebrews” and educated at the feet of Gamaliel, a man most learned in the law (Acts XII)—becomes entangled when he wishes to interpret even that language.

If this happens to him in Greek, which he had learned from childhood when he was raised at Tarsus in Cilicia, what should be said about Latin translators, who, attempting to express word for word, make his meaning more obscure?

“Therefore let no one surpass and defeat you, wishing to follow the humility of the letter and the worship and cult of angels, [Col. 0527B] so that you do not serve spiritual understanding but representations of future things, which even the one who desires your defeat does not see—or, if he does see, the Greek has both possibilities.”

Especially since he walks swollen with pride and proceeds puffed up, displaying arrogance of mind in the gesture of his body—for this is what ἐμβατεύων means—while he is vainly inflated and swollen with the understanding of his flesh, interpreting everything carnally and investigating the delirious traditions of the Jews. He does not hold fast to the head of all the Scriptures, of which it is said: “The head of a man is Christ” (I Corinthians XI), the head and beginning of the whole body, of those who believe, and of all spiritual understanding.

From this head the body of the Church, through its joints and connections, receives the living sap of heavenly teaching, so that all its members are gradually [Col. 0527C] quickened. Through the hidden passages of the veins, the purified blood of food is poured out and administered; bodily temperance grows, or rather is maintained, so that, with the limbs watered from the fountain of the head, they may grow toward the perfection of God. Thus the Savior’s prayer may be fulfilled: “Father, I will that, as I and you are one, so they also may be one in us” (John XVII), so that, after Christ has handed us over to the Father, “God may be all in all” (ibid.).

Hence Paul also says above: “Let no one judge you”—those who boast that they are teachers of the law—in food and drink (I Corinthians XV), claiming that some things are clean and others unclean, or that some days are festivals and others are not. For us who believe in Christ risen, there is a continual and eternal festival. Or let them judge you regarding the Kalends and the new month, when the waning moon [Col. 0527D] comes to an end and is exposed to the shadows of night: for the light of Christians is eternal and is always illumined by the rays of the sun of righteousness.

Or let them judge you regarding a portion of the Sabbaths, so that you may not perform servile work or carry burdens, since we have been given the freedom of Christ and have ceased to carry the burdens of sins. “All these things,” he says, “are shadows of things to come and images of future blessedness.” Thus, while the Jews remain clinging to the earth according to the letter, we pass through Christ to Christ. For, to distinguish the shadows, the body is now named: just as truth is in a body and falsehood in the shadow of a body, so, in spiritual understanding, every kind of food and drink, the whole festival, perpetual Kalends, and eternal rest are to be awaited.

[Col. 0528A] We ask what he intended by “the humility and worship of angels.” Or what meaning does it have when the Lord said to the disciples, “Rise, let us go from here,” and, “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matthew XXIII), and when the place where the Lord was crucified is spiritually called Egypt or Sodom?

The whole cult of Jewish observances has been destroyed. Whatever victims they offer, they offer not to God but to fallen angels and unclean spirits. It is not surprising that they do this after the Lord’s Passion, since through the prophet Amos it was also said to them: “Did you offer sacrifices and victims to me for forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? And you took up the tabernacle of Moloch and the star of your god Remphan, the images that you made in order to worship them?” (Amos V).

The martyr Stephen explained this more fully in his dispute with the Jews, [Col. 0528B] reviewing the ancient history, and spoke as follows (Acts VII): “And they made a calf in those days, and offered sacrifice to the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their hands. But God turned away and delivered them up to serve the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets.”

The “host of heaven” does not refer only to the sun, moon, and shining stars, but also to the whole angelic multitude and their army, which in Hebrew is called Sabaoth, that is, “of virtues” or “of armies.” Hence in the Gospel according to Luke we read: “And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II).

For God makes his angels spirits and his ministers [Col. 0528C] a burning fire. And so that we may know that those who worshipped idols, although they appeared to offer victims in the temple, did not offer them to God but to angels, we learn more fully through Ezekiel: “I gave them statutes that were not good, and commandments that were not good” (Ezekiel XIII). For God does not seek the blood of goats and bulls, but “the sacrifice of God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Psalm L).

Therefore those who made the calf at Horeb and worshipped the star of their god Remphan, concerning which we have discussed more fully in the prophet Amos, worshipped images that they themselves had made. And God delivered them up to serve the host of heaven, which the Apostle now calls the “worship of angels,” [Col. 0528D] in place of humility. In Greek, ταπεινοφροσύνῃ means “humility of mind” or “of understanding,” as well as pitiable superstition: namely, the belief that God is pleased by the blood of goats and bulls and by the odor of incense, from which human beings often turn away.

What follows is:

“If you have died with Christ to the elements of this world, why, as though living in the world, do you submit to decrees: ‘Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle,’ all of which perish in their very use, according to the commandments and doctrines of human beings; which indeed have an appearance of wisdom in superstition and humility, and in not sparing the body, not in any honor, for the satisfying of the flesh.”

(RAB.) This seems to us to be the meaning. Let us proceed through each point and, with Christ resounding, [Col. 0529A] disclose the obscurity of the meanings and words.

If you have been baptized in Christ and buried with Christ in baptism, having died to the elements of the world—that is, to what is meant by “element”—why do you not say with me: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world” (Galatians VI)?

Have you not heard the Lord saying: “They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world” (John XVII)? Yet, on the contrary, as though living in the world, you submit to decrees such as: “Do not touch the body of a dead person, nor the garment or stool on which a menstruating woman has sat; do not taste the flesh of swine, hares, cuttlefish, squid, moray eels, freshwater eels, or any fish that lacks scales and fins.” All these things are subject to corruption and perish in their very use, [Col. 0529B] and are digested into excrement: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for foods” (I Corinthians V); and, “Everything that enters through the mouth does not defile a person, but the things that come out of us” (Mark VII).

“According to the commandments,” he says, “and doctrines of human beings,” in accordance with what Isaiah says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of human beings” (Isaiah XXVII).

Therefore the Lord also rebukes the Pharisees, saying (Matthew XV): “You have nullified the commandment of God in order to establish your traditions.” For God said: “Honor your father and your mother; and whoever curses father or mother, let him die the death.” But you say: “Whoever says to his father or mother, ‘Whatever gift is from me will profit you,’ does not honor his father or his mother,” and so forth. [Col. 0529C] He concludes: “And you have nullified the commandment of God because of your tradition.”

I cannot review how many traditions the Pharisees have—traditions which today they call δευτερώσεις, “second traditions”—nor how many old-womanish tales there are, for the size of the book does not permit it. Many of them are so shameful that I am embarrassed to mention them.
