Yet I shall mention one disgrace of that hostile nation: they appoint the wisest men as leaders of the synagogue and assign them to a shameful task, so that, if they cannot determine with their eyes whether the blood of a virgin or menstruating woman is clean or unclean, they test it by taste.

Moreover, it was commanded that on the Sabbaths each person should sit in his own house and not go out, nor walk from the place where he lives. If we begin to press them according to the letter, so that they may neither lie down, walk, nor stand, but only [Col. 0529D] sit, they customarily reply: “Barachibas, Simeon, Helles, our teachers, have handed down to us that we may walk two thousand feet on the Sabbath,” and other things of this sort—placing human doctrines before the doctrine of God.

This does not mean that we say one must always sit on the Sabbath and never withdraw from the place in which one happens to be. Rather, whatever is impossible in the law, in which it is weakened through the flesh, must be fulfilled through spiritual observance.

It follows: “Which indeed have an appearance of wisdom.” Here the word “indeed” is a superfluous conjunction [Col. 0530A], a usage which we find the Apostle employing in many places because of his lack of grammatical training. For the conjunction “or,” which commonly responds to the preposition with which “indeed” is associated, does not follow.

Jewish observances therefore appear, among the uneducated and the common people, to possess an image of human reason. Their sages and teachers are called σόφοι, that is, “wise men.” Whenever they expound their traditions to their disciples on appointed days, they usually say: “The wise men teach the traditions.”

For “superstition,” the Greek has ἐθελοθρησκεία, “self-chosen worship” or false religion. For “humility,” it has ταπεινοφροσύνη, a word which generally conveys a virtue rather than a vice. Here it must be understood to mean that they think humble and earthly thoughts.

Ἀφειδία σώματος, whose name the Latin language does not express, means among us “not sparing the body.” The Jews do not spare their bodies in taking food: sometimes they despise what they have and seek what they do not have. From this necessity they occasionally contract weakness and illness. Nor do they honor themselves, since all things are clean to the clean [Col. 0530B] and nothing can be unclean when it is received with thanksgiving (I Timothy IV). For this reason it was created by the Lord, so that, through the nourishment and satisfaction of the flesh, human limbs might be invigorated and sustained.

By “the elements of the world,” through which we live—or rather, through which we have died—we must understand the law of Moses and the whole Old Testament. [Col. 0530C] Through these elements, as through the beginnings of religion, we learn about the Lord. Letters too are called elements, since through them we join syllables and words and proceed through prolonged meditation toward constructing an argument.

The art of music likewise has its elements, and geometry begins with the elements of lines; dialectic and medicine also have their own principles and systems. In the same way, through the elements of the Old Testament, holy men educate infancy so that it may come to the fullness of the Gospel. Hence Psalm 118 and all the other psalms prefaced by letters lead us through ethics to theology, and cause us to pass from the elements of the letter, which is being destroyed, to the life-giving Spirit.

Therefore, since we have died to the world and to its elements, we ought not to observe the things that belong to the world, because in one there is a beginning and in the other perfection.

## CHAPTER III

The Apostle gives general instruction concerning conduct, teaching the putting away of vices and the acquisition of virtues, and gives particular instruction concerning parents, children, married couples, and slaves.

“Therefore, if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.” (Ambrose.) This is what he means: in comparison with you, who have already risen with Christ according to the promise, the concern directed toward earthly things is pitiable. After completing all these matters, you ought to be concerned with heavenly things and imitate that which is in heaven, where Christ has deigned to sit at the right hand of God, having attained, so to speak, great honor in his condition.

(Augustine.) Certainly we have not yet risen as Christ did; nevertheless, according to the hope that exists in us concerning him—or in him—he has already testified that we have risen with him. Hence he also says [Col. 0531A] (Titus III): “According to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration,” as though that salvation had already been given. Elsewhere he says most clearly: “For by hope we have been saved.”

The transformation that will not possess corruption will belong to the saints, to those who now possess the resurrection of the spirit. Concerning this resurrection the Apostle says: “If, then, you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are on earth; for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.”

Just as we die according to the spirit and rise according to the spirit, so later we die according to the flesh and rise according to the flesh. What is the first death? Not doing what you used to do, not believing what you used to believe. He served idols; he came to know the one God. [Col. 0531B] He died in idolatry and rose in faith. He was a drunkard; he became sober. Drunkenness died; sobriety rose.

Thus all the evil deeds that we cease to do are, as it were, a death within us. For nothing will be lacking from our desire when God is all in all. Such an end has no end: no one dies there. No one reaches that place unless he dies to this age—not the death of all, by which the body is deserted by the soul, but the death of the elect, by which, even while the mortal flesh still dies, the heart is raised above.

“Set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth.”

(Ambrose.) Since he saw that the manner of those who dwell upon the earth was opposed to this, he says that they should set their minds on the things that are in heaven.

“For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.”

(Augustine.) Perhaps this is why it was said: “Love is strong as death” (Song of Songs VIII). [Col. 0531C] For through this love it comes about that, while we still exist in corruptible flesh, we die to this age and our life is hidden with Christ in God. Indeed, love itself is our death to the age and our life with God. For if death occurs when the soul departs from the body, how can it not be death when our love departs from the world? Love is therefore as strong as death. What is stronger than the love by which the world is conquered?

(Ambrose.) “You have died,” he says, to this present life, insofar as nature will endure this; but you have risen. For this too has been accomplished in Christ, so that it might also be accomplished in us. There can be no ambiguity about these things, but for the present [Col. 0531D] they remain uncertain, because we do not see Christ himself. They are accomplished, therefore, by the power of God, who also brings this to completion, and with Christ, who is the firstfruits of these things. For the present he is not seen, nor is that which is to come seen.

(Gregory.) Holy men, therefore, do not cease to put themselves to death with the sword of the sacred word: they mortify themselves with respect to the importunity of bodily desires, the tumult of useless cares, and the clamor of troubling disturbances. [Col. 0532A] Within, before the face of God, they hide themselves in the bosom of the mind.

Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “You shall hide them in the secret place of your face from the disturbance of human beings” (Psalm XXX). Although this will be accomplished perfectly hereafter, it is even now carried out to a great extent, when they are snatched away from the tumult of temporal desires by delight in inward things, so that, while their mind is wholly directed toward the love of God, it is not torn apart by any useless disturbance.

This is why Paul saw his disciples, through contemplation, as dead and hidden as though in a tomb, and said to them: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” Therefore whoever seeks death rejoices when he finds a tomb, because whoever desires to mortify himself greatly rejoices when he discovers the rest of contemplation. Thus, having been extinguished to the world, he remains hidden from all disturbances of outward things and conceals himself within the bosom of intimate love.

“What then? When Christ your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.”

(Ambrose.) He means: when the one who is the source of the immortality of your life appears from heaven, then you too will appear in the same condition, having obtained the enjoyment of eternal life and future glory. [Col. 0532B]

Thus, having again cast aside the conduct that belongs under the law through the things hoped for in the future, he proceeds to exhortation and shows that it is not merely unfitting for them to sin because they are not under the law; rather, it is much more fitting for them to accomplish the things that belong to the truth, provided that they wish to do the things corresponding to what is hoped to be accomplished through Christ.

Mortify, therefore, your members that are upon the earth. For once we have been made immortal after the resurrection, we will no longer be able to sin; but it follows that mortals sin. Thus, just as he posits a mortal man composed of the various members of sins, so also mortals can do such things. For he said “members that are upon the earth” in order to indicate the wicked acts that mortals are accustomed to pursue. (Augustine.) [Col. 0532C]

When these members have therefore been mortified, we rise first in faith. But just as death according to the spirit precedes resurrection according to the spirit, so death according to the flesh will precede the resurrection that is to come according to the flesh.

Fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols. (Jerome.) For the blessed Apostle does not compel us by his command to cut off hands, feet, or genitals; rather, he earnestly desires that the body of sin—which plainly consists of members—be destroyed as quickly as possible through zeal for perfect holiness. Concerning this body he says elsewhere, “that the body of sin may be destroyed” (Romans 6), and he consequently explains what its destruction is: “so that we may no longer serve sin.” From this body he also begs to be delivered with a lament, saying: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Romans 7.)

This body of sin, then, is shown to be constructed from many members of vices; whatever is sinned by deed, word, or thought belongs to its portion. Its members are most appropriately said to be “upon the earth.” For those who employ their service cannot truthfully profess, “Our manner of life is in heaven.” Describing the members of this body in the present passage, the Apostle says: “Mortify your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols.”

He therefore places fornication first, by which he means that which is accomplished through carnal intercourse. He names uncleanness as the second member, meaning that which sometimes, without any contact with a woman, creeps in through the negligence of an inattentive mind, whether during sleep or wakefulness. For this reason it is marked and prohibited in the Law, which not only excluded the unclean from participation in the sacred meats, but also commanded that they be separated from the camp, lest they pollute holy things by their contact. It says: “Any person who eats of the flesh of the sacrifice of well-being, which belongs to the Lord, while uncleanness is upon him, shall perish before the Lord; and whatever the unclean person touches shall be unclean” (Leviticus 7). Likewise in Deuteronomy: “If there is among you a man who has been polluted by a nocturnal emission, he shall go outside the camp and shall not return before he has washed with water; and after sunset he shall return to the camp” (Deuteronomy 23). [Col. 0533A]

Next he sets down lust as the third member of sin. This grows in the hidden recesses of the soul and can approach someone without bodily passion. There is no doubt that *libido* is so called from that which pleases.

After this, descending from greater sins to lesser ones, he introduces evil desire as the fourth member. This may be referred not only to the aforementioned uncleanness of passion, but generally to every harmful desire; it is the sickness of a corrupted will alone. Concerning it the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” It is much more difficult to restrain the desire of a slippery mind when an opportunity for seductive sight is presented to it. By this it is most clearly demonstrated that, for perfect purity, bodily chastity alone cannot suffice unless integrity of mind is added to it.

After all these, he identifies the final member of that body as greed, plainly showing that the mind must be restrained not only from desiring what belongs to others, but also that one’s own possessions must be scorned with greatness of spirit. The multitude of believers is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles as having done this. It is said: “The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one claimed that anything belonging to him was his own, but they had everything in common. For as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what they sold [Col. 0533B] and laid them at the apostles’ feet; and distribution was made to each as anyone had need” (Acts 4).

And lest this perfection appear to belong only to a few, he testified that greed is the service of idols—and not without reason. Whoever does not share with the necessities of the poor, and preserves his money with faithless tightfistedness, places Christ’s commandments after his own desires and incurs the crime of idolatry, preferring love of worldly material to divine charity.

(Ambrose.) It should be noted that he called greed the worship of idols, as though it could separate them from the likeness of God. For it is impossible for anyone to abstain from wicked dealings when he is held by the desire to possess more.

(Augustine.) For this reason he compares greed to the service of idols, saying: “Greed, which is the service of idols.” The blessed Cyprian amplified this meaning in his letter to Antonius to such an extent that he did not hesitate to compare greed with the sin of those who, during the persecution, had declared in certificates that they would offer incense. Yet although it is utterly clear that one sins much more gravely when he knows than when he does not know, I would like someone to tell me this: if one person falls into heresy without knowing how great an evil it is, while another knowingly does not depart from greed, knowing how great an evil it is, which of them is worse? I can put the question this way also: if one person unknowingly rushes into heresy, while another knowingly does not depart from idolatry—for the Apostle says, “Greed, which is the service of idols”—which is worse?

(Serapion.) Nor do I think the following should be passed over: just as there are three kinds of fornication—the first, accomplished through the intercourse of both sexes; the second, without female contact, on account of which the son of the patriarch Judah is recorded as having been struck down three times by the Lord, and which is called uncleanness in the holy Scriptures, concerning which the Apostle says (1 Corinthians 7), “But I say to the unmarried and to widows that it is good for them to remain as I am; but if they cannot exercise self-control, let them marry, for it is better to marry than to burn”; and the third, which is conceived in soul and mind, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel, “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5)—so there are three kinds of *philargyria*, love of money.

The first does not permit those who renounce their riches and possessions to be stripped of them. The second persuades us, with greater desire, to take back what we have dispersed or distributed to the needy. The third compels us to desire or acquire what we did not possess even before. And to show that no one can do these things without guilt, he says: “Because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience.”

(Ambrose.) It is not only absurd for us to sin; even if we rise again and sin, we shall await the necessary punishment.

Among whom you also once walked, when you lived in them. These things were formerly practiced by you, when you measured your entire hope by the present life and expected nothing more. But now you too must put away all these things. It is no longer fitting for you to live according to them, since you will chiefly exist in immortality, in which you are now considered to have your standing. We must therefore depart from all these things and put away anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, and shameful speech from our mouths. [Col. 0534D]

(Serapion.) It should be understood that there are three kinds of anger. One burns inwardly; another bursts forth into word, deed, and action, and is called hatred. Concerning these the Apostle says: “Now put away from you all anger and indignation.” The third is not discharged hotly at the moment like the others, but is stored up for days and periods of time; it is said to last a hundred years. All these must be condemned by us with equal horror.

Therefore, if we desire to attain that highest divine reward of which it is said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5), not only must these things be cut away from our actions, they must also be uprooted from the innermost roots of the soul. For it will be of little benefit if the fury of anger is restrained in speech and does not break out into action, if God, who is not unaware of the secrets of hearts, perceives that it remains hidden in our breast. The Gospel word commands that the roots of vices be cut away rather than their fruits; once their sources have surely been torn out, they will never sprout again. Thus the mind will be able to remain continually in complete patience and holiness when these things have been uprooted not merely from the surface of conduct and actions, but from the inner chambers of thought. For this reason anger and hatred are cut down, lest homicide be committed; without them the crime of homicide cannot in any way be perpetrated.

“Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5); and “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3). Although he is known among men not to have shed his brother’s blood with his own hand or by a weapon, he is pronounced a murderer by the Lord through the disposition of anger, insofar as in his heart he desires that the other should perish. For God will render to each person either reward or punishment not only for the result of an action, but also for intention and desire.

(Albert.) Hence the Apostle likewise says, writing to the Ephesians: “Let all bitterness and anger and indignation and clamor and blasphemy be taken away from you, with all malice” (Ephesians 5). Here he shows by what things the Holy Spirit is grieved and leaves the heart in which he had dwelt through charity and gentleness.

Bitterness is opposed to the sweetness and delight of the Holy Spirit. Fury is a foolish anger, a disturbance boiling in the depths. Indignation arises from pride, when we judge someone unworthy and therefore do not wish to endure him. Anger is the general condition whose forms are bitterness, fury, and indignation; after the fury has subsided, it desires vengeance and wishes to injure the one whom it thinks has caused harm. Therefore all bitterness, fury, anger, indignation, and clamor must be removed from us.

After all these things, clamor and blasphemy are rightly prohibited among us as well. For one who has once been overcome by fury often breaks out into shouting and, growling tumultuously, is scattered about like a leaf. Blasphemy occurs when false things are fabricated about God, or when someone is shown to have erred after being deceived by heretical perversity in the Catholic faith. Finally, he adds that these vices, together with all malice, must be removed from us. Malice is whatever is contrary to virtue, and it may be called vice by another name.

Do not lie to one another. (Ambrose.) He did not say *alterutrum* (“to one another”), but *in invicem* (“among yourselves”): that is, it is not right for you to speak to each other with pretense, but with a sincere mind. And because he mentioned members, he adds actions that follow from them:

Stripping off the old man with his actions. Completely, he says, it is fitting for you, in putting off the mortal man, to put off also the actions that follow him.

And put on the new man, who is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created him. You ought to do things consistent with this new man whom you have put on, having been renewed and made according to the image of the one who was the author of this restoration for you. Thus he says that it is fitting for you to remain unchangeable in goodness in every respect, for this will belong to you in the future in proportion to what is possible in the present life. [Col. 0536A]

Then, showing the goodness of this restoration, he adds:

Where there is neither Gentile nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all.

When, he says, we have come to stand in that transformation, Jew and Gentile will no longer be distinguished. The distinction between circumcision and uncircumcision has been abolished because we have been made immortal. Thus neither barbarian nor free person nor slave will any longer be discernible, with Christ appearing in all. According to his likeness we shall possess immortality. He therefore wishes to observe what is fitting in those who have put on this kind of man and have been made according to that form in him.

(Augustine.) If, then, we are renewed in the spirit of the mind, and the new man is himself the one who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created him, there is no doubt that it is not according to the body, nor according to any other part of the soul, but according to the rational mind—where knowledge of God can exist—that man was made according to the image of the one who created him. According to this renewal we also become children of God through the baptism of Christ; and, putting on the new man, we put on Christ through faith.

Who, then, is the person who excludes women from this fellowship, since they are co-heirs with us of grace? Elsewhere the same Apostle says (Galatians 3): “For you are all children of God through faith in Christ Jesus. For all of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.”

Have faithful women, then, lost the sex of their bodies? No. Rather, because they are renewed there according to the image of God, where there is no sex, man was made according to the image of God where there is no sex—that is, in the spirit of his mind. For just as, after the fall into sin, man is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created him, so in the very creation he was created before he grew old through sin, so that he might be renewed again in that same knowledge. This renewal and reformation is “according to God,” or “according to the image of God.” It is said to be “according to God” so that it will not be thought to be made according to some other creature. It is said to be “according to the image” so that it may be understood that this renewal takes place where the image of God is—that is, in the mind.

We should not therefore understand the phrase “according to the image of the one who created him” as though there were another image according to which he is renewed, rather than the very image that is being renewed.

Put on, therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience. (Jerome.) Concerning the bride it is said in the Psalm: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, surrounded by variety” (Psalm 44). What is more beautiful than this variety? Job also spoke of it: “Who gave women wisdom in weaving, or skill in varied work?” (Job 38). And the high priest, once a year, when he burned incense on behalf of the people and entered the Holy of Holies, wore garments of various kinds.

Certainly, if wealth rather than holiness produced variety in clothing and diversity in virtues, Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar would be said to have possessed these garments, and not Joseph, who, under a foreigner and shepherd father, could not have had garments of varied colors and royal garments. [Col. 0537A]

(Ambrose.) Through all these things he exhorted us to preserve among ourselves that charity which exists toward one another. These are works of charity. Continuing in the same vein, he adds:

Bearing with one another and forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another. And wishing to persuade them by example, he says: “Just as the Lord forgave you, so also do you.”

Then, as a concise confirmation of what he has said concerning all this charity, he wishes to say: “Be diligent in charity,” for by it the ordering of these things is accomplished. Showing the usefulness of charity, he adds:

Which is the bond of perfection. For, he says, in the future age, when we have come to stand there, we shall remain bound to one another by what is still commanded—that is, charity—enduring no further separation. We shall be held together in that harmony which exists toward one another, each being the same toward the other.

And let the peace of Christ rejoice in your hearts. The blessed Paul knew that, while charity remains, everything is easily set in order, whereas nothing fitting can be accomplished by those who hold to things contrary to it. He therefore seems in every passage to make much of charity, and, showing the usefulness of the exhortation, he adds:

To which you were also called in one body; and be grateful. We have become one body through regeneration. It is evident that we have been called in peace, since no body ever knows division within itself. [Col. 0537C] It is therefore fitting that, because of this very calling, you show yourselves grateful through your deeds, preserving that calling toward one another intact.

Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly. Let the abundant teaching of Christ, he says, dwell very richly among you, as you teach and admonish one another in all wisdom. Keep such continual remembrance of these things that you may always appear to be teaching and admonishing one another, showing a manner of life corresponding to that teaching. For his teaching will be very rich among you if you are always willing to preserve it in your understanding by thinking on these same things.

When he said “in all wisdom,” he called wisdom that understanding which arises from these things.

With psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to God. Always, he says, give thanks to God in your understanding for the benefits he has bestowed upon you.

Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him. Whatever you say or do, he says, looking to Christ, hasten to offer due thanksgiving to God and the Father for the things that have been bestowed upon you through Christ. For by psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs he called this thanksgiving, saying: “Give thanks to God in your hearts.” Or whatever you say or do, speak and act as it is right for those who have been deemed worthy to obtain such things. For this is true thanksgiving.

Then, imitating in this section what he had written to the Ephesians, he turns to particular exhortation, saying:

Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. He commands wives to be subject to their husbands.

Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh toward them. He admonishes husbands to love their wives and not treat them bitterly.

Children, obey your parents in all things, for this is pleasing in the Lord. He urges children to obey their parents.

Fathers, do not provoke your children to indignation, lest they become discouraged. He advises fathers not to grieve their children excessively.

Slaves, obey your earthly masters in all things, not serving merely for appearance, as those who please human beings, but in singleness of heart, fearing God. Whatever you do, work from the soul, as for the Lord and not for human beings, knowing that you will receive from the Lord the reward of an inheritance. Serve the Lord Christ.

He also commands slaves to obey their masters, looking toward that recompense of reward which will be given them by God for faithful service. Act, therefore, as it is right for those who expect God to grant them a reward.

Not as serving human beings, but as serving the one from whom they also expect to receive a reward in return. He adds:

For whoever does wrong will receive back what he has done unjustly, and there is no partiality with God.

Even if masters should in some way wish to afflict them unjustly, they will not be innocent; for God accepts or respects no person.

## CHAPTER FOUR

The Apostle instructs masters and commends himself to the prayers of the Colossians, showing how they ought to conduct themselves toward unbelievers; and the conclusion of the Epistle is given in the form of a greeting.

Masters, provide your slaves with what is just and equitable, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven. (Ambrose.) He advises masters to grant their slaves what is appropriate, treating them humanely, showing them love in their conduct, and applying diligence toward them as far as possible. They should also grant forgiveness to those who transgress when it happens that they sin. For this is what he calls just and equitable: that they should not consider them equal to themselves; for it may happen that slaves serve, and serve with undivided devotion.

He wrote at such length because he also urges masters to preserve these things in remembrance, since they too are under that Master who is in heaven.

And again he turns to fellowship and says:

Devote yourselves to prayer, keeping watch in it with thanksgiving. He commanded them to pray continually with sober minds and to give thanks for the good things granted to them by God.

Praying at the same time for us also, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also bound, so that I may make it manifest as I ought to speak. Pray for us also, he says, that Christ may work with us, so that we may be able to teach everyone the truth that is in Christ, for which I am presently bound.

Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, making the most of the time. With prudence, he says, dispute with those who are strangers to the faith, using the present time as is appropriate for you, since one who purchases something acquires it for the use of his own advantage. [Col. 0539A] This is what he wished to say: in the present time, in which evils abound, hasten, according to the measure of your strength, to do what you recognize to be expedient for you, so that you may also prepare rewards for yourselves in the future through the manner of life for which you remain in the present age.

Let your speech always be in grace, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person. Hasten, he says, to utter things that are always full of prudence, considering what answer ought to be given to each person and discussing matters appropriately, so that something like a gift may rather seem to be accomplished through your words. With these words he added the following:

Tychicus, the most beloved brother, faithful minister, and fellow servant in the Lord, will make known to you everything that concerns me. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that he may learn what concerns you and may console your hearts, together with Onesimus, the beloved and faithful brother who is one of you. They will make known to you everything that is being done here.

For this reason he was sent by me with Onesimus, the brother who had come from you, so that they might make known to you what concerns us and cheer you by their arrival, making manifest to you everything that is being done here.

Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, concerning whom you received instructions. If he comes to you, receive him.

He greets them, then, on behalf of Aristarchus, whom he declares to be his fellow prisoner, as one bound with him, and on behalf of Mark, whom he says is Barnabas’s nephew. Concerning Mark, he declares that they have received instructions, so that they should receive him when he comes. He says that they received the instruction not from anyone else, [Col. 0539C] nor from himself, since that could not have happened because he had not yet seen them, but from the one who had preached the Gospel to them.

And Jesus, who is called Justus, who are of the circumcision—these alone are my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.

He also greets them on behalf of Jesus, who is surnamed Justus. He says that these alone among those of the circumcision who believed are his fellow workers in the Gospel, and that they have provided him consolation.

Epaphras, who is one of you, greets you, a servant of Christ, always striving for you in prayers, so that you may stand perfect and filled in every will of God. For I bear him witness that he has much labor on your behalf and on behalf of those who are in Laodicea and Hierapolis.

He next greets them on behalf of Epaphras, who preached to them, saying that he is greatly concerned for them, so that he prays that they may remain firm in the faith. The Apostle says that he bears witness that Epaphras is concerned for them, and also for those who are in Laodicea and Hierapolis.

Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas greet you. He also greets them on behalf of Luke the physician, who wrote the Gospel, and likewise on behalf of Demas.

Then he writes to them:

Greet the brothers who are in Laodicea, and Nympha, and the church in her house. Greet, he says, those who are in Laodicea, and Nympha with all her household who are in her house. He adds:

When this Epistle has been read among you, see that it is read in the church of the Laodiceans, and that you also read the one from Laodicea.

Thus he commands that, after this Epistle has been read by them, it should also be read in the church of the Laodiceans. He tells them to read the one that is from Laodicea—not because he is writing to the Laodiceans. Hence some have thought that a false Epistle to the Laodiceans was fabricated in the name of the blessed Paul, for it was not a genuine Epistle. Some, however, thought that it was the one signified in this passage.

But the Apostle does not say “to the Laodiceans”; he says “from Laodicea,” meaning the letter that they had written to the Apostle, in which certain things deserving reproof were set forth. For this reason also he ordered it to be read among them, so that they might reprove themselves upon learning what had been written concerning them. And for this reason, as may be understood, he did not consider them worthy of having a letter written to them. Rather, he commanded that the one written to the Colossians be read among them, so that they might likewise receive the admonition concerning good things and be converted for the better, since they had been reproved by Paul and had not been considered worthy even to receive a letter written by him. [Col. 0540C]

Then he says to them:

And say to Archippus: “See to the ministry that you have received in the Lord, so that you may fulfill it.” He then tells them to say to Archippus that he should fulfill the ministry he received.

But since it seemed that they might infer from the letter that Archippus was residing among the Laodiceans and had been entrusted with the ministry of teaching, he adds:

The greeting of me, Paul, by my own hand. Since he wrote the greeting with his own hand, he says:

Remember my bonds. That is: Do not shrink from suffering for the truth, following my example.

He added the customary conclusion:

Grace be with you. Amen.

In this designation he appears to have brought the Epistle to completion.

# BOOK TWENTY-ONE

## COMMENTARY ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 0539]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0539D]

The blessed Apostle Paul traveled through various cities preaching the faith that is in Christ. Instructed by a divine revelation, he came to the cities of Macedonia; from there he also came to Thessalonica, as can be learned with the greatest care from the book of the Acts of the Apostles. Among others, therefore, he preached to the Thessalonians the teaching of piety.

When his adversaries became indignant over this, it happened that the Apostle suffered many things in that same city of the Thessalonians, and those who believed in Christ also endured many evils from their fellow countrymen. Thus the blessed Apostle was compelled, when he departed from Thessalonica, to proceed to Athens. Fearing, however, for those who had believed, lest they should be driven by the severity of their adversaries to depart from their purpose, he was compelled to send Timothy to them, both to learn what had taken place and to strengthen the minds of the faithful by his presence, as well as to admonish them through salutary exhortation to persist in the faith.

Timothy, having fulfilled everything that had been entrusted to him by the blessed Apostle, returned to him and reported that they had endured many evils inflicted by their adversaries, yet had not departed from the faith. Among other things, he also reported that there were certain matters among them that ought to be corrected.

Learning these things from Timothy, the Apostle writes this first Epistle to the Thessalonians, praising them because in adverse circumstances they had endured so faithfully while contending for the faith. He also instructs them concerning the matters that he had learned were being conducted improperly among them. We shall be able to recognize all these things much more eagerly and clearly from the interpretation that proceeds section by section.

## CHAPTER ONE

The Apostle gives thanks for the Thessalonians’ good beginning and the spread of this goodness.

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians. (Augustine.) The assembly of the Jews is properly accustomed to be called a synagogue, although it too has been called a church. Our Apostles, however, never called ours a synagogue, but always a church, either for the sake of distinction or because there is some difference between a gathering—from which *synagogue* takes its name—and a convocation—from which *church* takes its name. Animals are accustomed to be gathered together, whereas a convocation more properly concerns beings who use reason, such as human beings.

In God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: grace to you and peace. (Ambrose.) Here he shows above all that when he says “grace to you,” he uses the expression in the same way that we customarily place “salvation” in the heading of an Epistle. He also says “in God the Father,” just as we are accustomed to write “in the Lord.”

We give thanks to God always for you all, remembering you in our prayers without ceasing, mindful of your work of faith, labor of charity, and endurance of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ before our God and Father.

And we give thanks, he says, for you, and without ceasing we pray for you. For we remember what you have done on behalf of the faith, the labor that you endured for the charity of Christ, and the endurance that you demonstrated in the very tribulations, because of the things that you hope will be present for you on account of the faith that you have in Christ.

He rightly added “before our God and Father,” in order to say: “Do these things in a manner pleasing to God,” so that the faith that is directed toward Christ and that affection may be seen to accord with God’s will. He thereby teaches them that they justly endure everything for the sake of the faith.

Knowing, beloved brothers, your election by God, that our Gospel came to you not in word only, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with great fullness.

You know, he says, how you were chosen—that is, how you came to the faith—not believing merely our words. For we did not speak only, but also performed great and glorious miracles through the power of the Spirit, by which you were confirmed in what was being proclaimed to you by us. Therefore, hold most carefully and justly to what you have learned, and do not abandon your purpose because of the evils that befall you. Then, persuading them by what concerned himself, he adds: “As you know what sort of people we were among you for your sake.” [Col. 0542A]

You also recognize very well what concerned us: the pressures under which we ourselves lived and how much we endured for your sake. He rightly added “for your sake,” in order to invite them more strongly to reverence. For if he himself suffered on their behalf, they themselves were all the more bound, with sound reason, to suffer for themselves. This also, when spoken truthfully, seemed likely to encourage them greatly. Praise is especially welcome when it has not been bestowed on someone without cause, but ordinarily rouses the mind to virtue on the basis of deeds already performed.

And you became imitators of us and of the Lord. Since he had said that similar things had also occurred among them, he could strongly persuade them to remain steadfast in their faith on that account. Thus, by very appropriately mentioning the Lord as well, he appears to have made his exhortation stronger: for in their sufferings they seemed to imitate not only the apostles but the Lord himself. Then he makes the imitation explicit when he says: “Receiving the word amid great tribulation with the joy of the Holy Spirit.” [Col. 0542B]

The Lord, he says, suffered for us through the cross, bringing salvation to us; and you, enduring tribulation for the faith that is in him, should know that you imitate both us and God. You endured the things that were grievous with joy, not bearing heavily the troubles that came upon you, but being encouraged by the good things that are expected to be repaid to you for them. He rightly added “of the Holy Spirit.” Otherwise, how could those who were presently suffering have rejoiced over things not yet seen, unless the miracles performed by the Spirit had prepared in them a firm faith in future realities, so that, looking toward those powers, they could easily endure what at present seemed full of sorrow?

Increasing their praise, and adding what could also appropriately serve to encourage them, he says: “So that you became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia.” For those in Macedonia and Achaia, seeing you, both believing and enduring persecution, were ashamed to seem unlike you in this world; and in a certain sense they became examples to those who had not seen them. [Col. 0542C]

For from you the word of the Lord has been proclaimed not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but in every place your faith toward God has gone forth. Here “the word of God” does not mean faith, for faith did not take its beginning from them. Rather, he says, everyone learned how much you had suffered for the faith, and everyone marveled at the steadfastness of your faith, so that they also encouraged others. And, binding the point together even more forcefully, he says: “So that we have no need to say anything.” [Col. 0542D]

For they themselves report concerning us what sort of entrance we had among you and how you turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God and to await his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus, who delivers us from the coming wrath.

We do not need, wherever we may be, to say anything about you, because what was done among you is known to everyone. Thus there is no jealousy in those who report how promptly you received us. This is what he means by “what sort of entrance we had among you,” and by “how you turned”: you departed from the worship of idols in accordance with the doctrines pleasing to us, and you recognized your Lord, who truly lives and is the true God. You also believed what was told you concerning Jesus: that he rose from the dead, so that he might deliver all of us who believe in him from the punishment we expect, and that he will come from heaven, bestowing benefits on us all. [Col. 0543A]

He rightly mentioned his coming from heaven first, and then the resurrection, even though the latter would seem to come first in chronological order. This was because, for the confirmation of faith, it was especially fitting that he would appear in glory from heaven at the end of the age.

It should be noted that, in speaking of the renunciation of idols, he asserted that God is living and true, in order to show by contrast that idols are neither living nor true gods, but are called such only by a false name. Therefore, whenever you encounter this expression, you should understand that it cannot be said of the Father in such a way as to exclude the Son, nor of the Son in such a way as to exclude the Father. Rather, both the Father and the Son are believed by all the devout to be God. [Col. 0543B]

Having said these things for their encouragement, he goes on to recall what concerned himself, especially those matters whose occurrence among them he knew they themselves had witnessed. By recalling what had happened to him among them, he sought to persuade them not to yield to sorrow.

## CHAPTER II. He consoles his people in adversity by comparing them with himself and with the Church of Jerusalem.

For you yourselves know, brothers, our entrance among you, that it was not fruitless. Rather, after we had suffered and been treated shamefully, as you know, at Philippi, we acted boldly in our God to speak to you the Gospel of God amid great struggle. (Ambrose.) [Col. 0543C]

You know, he says, that we did not come to you casually or by chance. Although we had suffered many evils at Philippi, we nevertheless did not fail to come to you and confidently preach true religion, even though great necessity pressed upon us from every side. He rightly said that we acted boldly “in God,” lest he seem to attribute that confidence to himself; therefore he attributed it to divine cooperation.

It is also remarkable that the Apostle said that our entrance was not fruitless, because he had previously suffered much—as though one who reckons gain to himself in sufferings considers that he has done nothing fruitless whenever he happens to suffer for the sake of true religion. And because he mentioned sufferings, he also describes the manner of his teaching: [Col. 0543D]

For our exhortation was not from error, nor from impurity, nor from deceit. But just as we were approved by God to be entrusted with the Gospel, so we speak—not as pleasing human beings, but God, who tests our hearts.

Here he calls the teaching itself “exhortation,” for this is how, he says, we instructed you—not as those customarily teach who wish to lead their hearers astray or to convey something untrue to them, often concealing by deceit the things they say. Rather, we taught a true doctrine, endowed with the greatest care and purity, which you approved and which also appeared to have been entrusted to us. Accordingly, we continued to act with approval, saying these things boldly, as was fitting for those who seek not to please human beings but God, who knows the mind most carefully. He has joined all these points together to show that his confidence was rightly grounded. Continuing to recount what concerned himself in order to instruct them, he declares: [Col. 0544A]

For we were never found using flattering speech, as you yourselves know.

On the contrary, we used to say that those who wish to live devoutly will suffer the tribulations of the present life. He rightly added “as you know,” hastening to produce those very people as witnesses to his words.

Nor did we act under a pretext of greed, nor seek gain. In saying this he did not add, “as you know,” but rather, “God is witness.” With good reason he used God as the witness of his life, as the more suitable witness. [Col. 0544B]

Nor did we seek glory from human beings, either from you or from others. We never considered how we might acquire praise, whether from you or from anyone else. He very carefully said “not seeking”—that is, not setting this as our aim, nor having it as the intention of our actions. For this is what we ought to do: not to act with a view to human glory. Nor can blame attach to us when we do what agrees with the divine law, even if glory from human beings should follow us.

Although we could have been a burden, as apostles of Christ. He applied this to what he had said about not acting under a pretext of greed. It would have been more fitting for them, as apostles, to make use of their authority and to receive from them what was necessary for their sustenance; yet they had not wished to accept it. [Col. 0544C]

But we became gentle among you.

(Gregory.) That is, we conducted ourselves with complete moderation and humility, unwilling to appear burdensome to anyone. The impious person is a leader who departs from the path of truth and, while rushing headlong himself, invites those who follow him toward the precipice. The impious person is a leader who shows the way of error through examples of arrogance.

Paul feared becoming an impious leader when he restrained the height of his authority, saying: “Nor seeking glory from human beings, either from you or from others, although we could have been a burden as apostles of Christ; but we became little ones among you.” [Col. 0544D]

He became little among them because he feared that, if he claimed the honor belonging to his exalted position among his disciples, he would display examples of pride. He feared, surely, that while he sought for himself the power of pastoral authority, the subject flock might follow him over the precipice; and that he who had undertaken the ministry of piety might lead his followers into impiety.

Therefore, the person in authority must carefully consider what examples he offers to those under him. He should know that he ought to live as well as those over whom he vigilantly presides, lest he become inflated by being placed above others, lest he demand the rights of authority beyond measure, lest the force of discipline be changed into the harshness of pride, and lest, from the very point at which he could restrain his subjects from perversity, he pervert the hearts of those who look to him. Otherwise, as has been said, he may become a leader of impiety through the office of piety. [Col. 0545A]

One who does not know how to lead people by living well should not undertake the leadership of human beings, lest the person chosen to correct the faults of others himself commit what ought to be cut away.

Those in authority should therefore look carefully in every direction, so that they may live both for themselves and for those under them; so that they may conceal within the bosom of their mind the good they do, yet through it provide their followers with examples of right action for their advancement; so that, while noticing the faults of their subjects, they may correct them without becoming inflated by the force of that correction; so that they may tolerate certain matters corrected gently without, through the same gentleness, loosening the bonds of discipline; so that they may overlook certain things by tolerating them, but not allow them to grow through such concealment.

These duties are burdensome, and difficult to preserve unless divine grace supports one in carrying them out. Rightly, therefore, the Book of Wisdom says concerning the coming of the strict Judge: “He will appear terribly and swiftly, for a very severe judgment will fall upon those who rule.” (Wisdom 6.) [Col. 0545B]

Since the power of governance very often gives rise to the fault of pride, and since pride itself is regarded as impiety by the strict Judge, it is rightly said of the Lord through Elihu: “He calls leaders impious.” For, while they grow proud because of that very leadership, they draw their subjects into impiety by their example.

Accordingly, great care must be taken that the person placed over human beings for their governance preside within the secret chamber of his mind upon the seat of humility. While he is attended externally as one who judges others, he should constantly observe with vigilant eyes before what Judge he himself will one day stand to be judged concerning these matters. The more anxiously he now trembles before the One whom he does not see, the more securely he will behold him when he sees him.

Let him therefore consider that he may scarcely be sufficient to satisfy the strict Judge for his own soul alone; so that, in the time when he must render an account before him for governing his subjects, he may, so to speak, have as many souls to answer for as those over whom he presides. If this thought continually burns within his mind, it suppresses every swelling of pride. Then the prudent ruler will all the less be called either an apostate king or an impious leader, the more carefully he considers the power he has received to be not an honor but a burden. [Col. 0545C]

For the person who now desires to be a judge does not then desire to see the Judge. The faults committed out of love for possessing authority cannot be counted. Authority is governed well only when it is retained not because it is loved but because it is feared. In order that it may be exercised rightly, it must first be imposed not by desire but by necessity. [Col. 0545D]

Once received, authority should be neither abandoned out of fear nor embraced out of desire. Otherwise, someone may become proud under the guise of humility by fleeing contemptuously from the order of divine providence, or may cast off the yoke of the heavenly Ruler because he delights in private governance over others.

Authority, therefore, when received, must not be loved out of desire but endured with patience, so that it may then be light at judgment because it is now recognized as patiently burdensome in ministry.

As a nurse cherishes her own children, so, longing for you, we were pleased to share with you not only the Gospel of Christ but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.

(Ambrose.) He wishes to say that we were so far from being unwilling to bear the weight of tribulations that, amid those evils, we hastened with great longing to teach you, willingly placing even our souls at risk for your sake, because we loved you steadfastly and were held toward you by complete affection. [Col. 0546A]

He confirmed what he intended to say by the quality of the example he offered, which is worthy of admiration. Mothers customarily offer their milk to their children with great eagerness, considering that they are helping when they are able to nurse their children. Here he called the nurse a mother—the woman who nourishes her children—and made this clear by adding, “as she cherishes her own children.” He then further heightened his meaning by indicating that he had wished to receive nothing from them.

(Augustine.) He did not say “as a mother,” because sometimes mothers are either more indulgent or less loving toward their children, and after giving birth they hand them over to others to be nursed. [Col. 0546B] Again, if he had said only “as a nurse cherishing” and had not added “her own children,” he might have seemed to have received children born by another woman to be nourished. He called himself a nurse because he nourished them, and called them his own children because he himself had given them birth, saying: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4). He gives birth as the Church gives birth—from her own womb, though not from her own seed.

For you remember, brothers, our labor and weariness: working night and day so as not to burden any of you, we proclaimed to you the Gospel of God.

(Ambrose.) You yourselves know how much labor we endured, so that we would not seem burdensome to you because of our needs. We persisted, and we did not appear to be occupied with your instruction during the day alone. Nor could we devote the entire day to our work in such a way as to provide sufficiently for ourselves. In all these matters he invokes their own testimony and that of God: [Col. 0546C]

You are witnesses, and God also, of how devoutly, justly, and blamelessly we behaved toward you who believed.

As you know how we exhorted and consoled each one of you, as a father does his own children. He uses their own testimony because they knew how patiently he exhorted them like a father and consoled them amid the sorrows that came upon them, entreating them not to depart from the faith. He also mentioned God, because he said that he had behaved devoutly, justly, and blamelessly toward those who believed—before God, who above all seemed to possess careful knowledge of these things.

And we testified that you should walk worthily of God, who called you into his own kingdom and glory. [Col. 0546D]

He rightly said “we testified,” thereby showing that he had spoken these very things to them from the beginning: that they ought to possess deeds worthy of the One who called them to his knowledge with the great promise of future things. In proportion to the greatness of that promise, they ought also to perform corresponding deeds.

When he speaks of “his” kingdom and glory, he again passes to their person. At one moment he recalls what concerned himself, in order to lead them to revelation; at another he adapts himself to their praise, so that he may seem by such zeal to arouse their eagerness still more.

And for this reason we also give thanks to God without ceasing: because, when you received from us the word of the hearing of God, you received it not as the word of human beings, but—as it truly is—as the word of God, which also works in you who have believed.

The things we preached were indeed ours in the sense that they came through us; yet there were also things that came from you. Therefore, we do not cease to give thanks to God for you, because, when you received the teaching of God from us, you received it not as though human beings were speaking to you, but as it was fitting for those to receive it who were receiving divine teaching. This teaching is also shown to be present among you by your deeds. He explains how it is manifested in your deeds: [Col. 0547A]

For you, brothers, became imitators of the churches of God that are in Judea in Christ Jesus, because you also suffered the same things from your own countrymen as they did from the Jews.

You suffered, he says, things similar to those who in Judea believed in Christ. For just as they suffered many evils from the Jews, so you suffered from your own countrymen—that is, from the Gentiles. [Col. 0547B]

He rightly encouraged them by recalling those who had believed in Judea, so that they too might endure their labor with courage, since they were not the only ones to suffer for the sake of true religion. For the complete churches throughout Judea also fluctuated amid various persecutions.

Accordingly, explaining the Jews’ wickedness more fully, he shows how great and what kind of things they suffered from those who lived among them:

They killed the Lord Jesus and their own prophets, and persecuted us.

He appropriately placed “the prophets” in the middle, since they prove that the Jews, driven only by wickedness, undertook to kill both the Lord and the apostles. They also appear to have acted in this way toward their own prophets. And what is more serious: [Col. 0547C]

They do not please God and are hostile to all human beings, forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles so that they may be saved, thus always filling up their sins. But the wrath of God has come upon them unto the end.

It is no wonder, he says, whatever they attempt to do, so that they seem to lack no evil; yet they will receive from the eternal Judge the complete punishment for which they are responsible.

He joined all these statements together with particular reference to the person of the Jews, accusing them with good reason. He necessarily recalls them in the present context both to show what the faithful in Judea suffer, living as though in the midst of a contest, and to show that the Thessalonians have suffered nothing so harsh from the Gentiles—if they are willing to compare what they endure with what is taking place in Judea. [Col. 0547D]

He included all these points to encourage the Thessalonians. Since, among other things, he had spoken of his coming to them, he now begins to discuss what happened after his departure, at the same time making known in these matters the affection he held for them:

But we, brothers, having been bereft of you for a short time—in presence, not in heart—like orphans, hastened all the more eagerly to see your face, with great longing. For we wished to come to you—I, Paul, both once and again—but Satan hindered us.

In every respect he appears to have increased the expression of his affection for them by saying that he had not departed from them in heart but only in presence, and that, though separated from them for a time, he immediately desired above all things to see them again. By saying that he had been separated from them like an orphan, he displayed his affection greatly. Earlier he had said, “As a father I exhorted each one of you.” There the image of a father seemed appropriate; here, in his absence, he uses the expression “separated like orphans.” For this kind of absence especially arises from the very circumstance that causes children to seek their father. [Col. 0548A]

And what proves this longing? The fact that “we wished to come to you.” Since he said “we wished” in the plural, he adds, speaking of himself: “I, Paul, both once and again.” And what prevented this? “Satan hindered us.” Since the Thessalonians would have been helped by his presence, he rightly attributed every harmful obstruction to Satan, and showed that his affection for them was not empty. [Col. 0548B]

For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of boasting? Is it not you before our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming? For you are our glory and joy.

Whatever good we expect on the future day, when our Lord Jesus Christ comes to examine all things, we expect a reward from him then for the labors that we endure for your sake. The uprightness of those under his care is a priest’s great glory.

(Gregory.) Therefore the distinguished preacher rightly says to his disciples: “What is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Are you not this before the Lord?” But when priests neglect the lives of their disciples and bring no fruit from their progress before the Lord, what are they other than inglorious? Before the strict Judge they will surely not find then the glory that, through the labor of preaching, they do not now seek in the conduct of those under them. [Col. 0548C]

It is rightly said, “He brings down the nobles,” because when the mind of rulers is abandoned by just judgment, it does not seek the inward reward of recompense. A person is brought down in the very thing by which he is deceived: instead of eternal glory, he rejoices in temporal leadership. Thus he brings down the nobles, because, while neglecting to preach the future heavenly homeland, they fall here into their own desires.

## CHAPTER III. The Apostle sends Timothy to console the Thessalonians; the benefit of his return is set forth, and so forth.

Therefore, when we could bear it no longer, we thought it good to be left alone in Athens, and we sent Timothy, our brother and minister of God in the Gospel of Christ.

(Ambrose.) He returns to what he had said earlier: “I wished to come to you.” Since, therefore, he could not fulfill that intention, he chose to remain alone in Athens and to send Timothy to them. For what purpose? [Col. 0548D]

To strengthen you and console you concerning your faith, so that no one might be shaken by these tribulations.

Timothy would strengthen them by the exhortation of his words and make them more even-tempered by his presence, so that they would not yield, defeated by their tribulations. For he calls being moved “yielding.” He shows that what he says is reasonable:

For you yourselves know, he says, that we have been appointed for this.

And how do they know? Because, when we were with you, we told you beforehand that we would suffer tribulation. “And so it happened, as you know.” I told you this when I said that the obstacles to our affairs were obstacles caused by Satan; and the event itself followed. [Col. 0549A]

For this reason I also, no longer able to bear it, sent to learn about your faith, lest somehow the tempter had tempted you and our labor should prove fruitless.

Again he takes up the reason for which he had sent Timothy. What did you learn when he returned?

But now that Timothy has come to us from you and has brought us good news of your faith and love, and that you always have a good remembrance of us, longing to see us just as we long to see you, for this reason we were comforted, brothers, concerning you in all our tribulation and distress through your faith.

Since Timothy came and reported the steadfastness that you have toward us, and that you always remember us, longing for us just as we long for you, we have received sufficient consolation amid all our tribulation: namely, the report about you that we have learned. And, showing how the good things he learned about them delighted him, he adds: [Col. 0549B]

For now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord.

Now we consider ourselves to live if you have persevered in the faith, thereby increasing our own life as well.

What thanksgiving, he says, can we render to God for you, for all the joy with which we rejoice because of you before your God?

We regard as our own whatever good things belong to you. Thus, because we heard such things about you through Timothy’s report, we have great joy concerning you, and we consider ourselves unable to give thanks to our God worthily enough for them. In saying this, he appears also to have spoken from the longing with which he desired to come to them: [Col. 0549C]

Night and day we pray exceedingly that we may see your face and supply what is lacking in your faith.

We persist in praying that we may see you and supply whatever may seem lacking in you. Explaining his longing, he adds:

May God himself, our Father, and our Lord Jesus direct our way to you.

He especially desires this: that what he longs for may also be requested in prayer. In this way, by speaking of his prayer, he strengthens them for enduring the most severe tribulations.

May the Lord multiply you and make you abound in love for one another and for all, just as we do for you, so that he may strengthen your hearts, blameless in holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.

May he add to you, he says, such love for one another and for everyone as he has brought about in you through our love for you; and may he strengthen your mind in faith, so that you remain without accusation, restraining yourselves from every unsuitable act. This is what he means by “in holiness”: through holiness you will be able, on the future day, to obtain confidence before God together with all the others who live acceptably in virtue. [Col. 0549D]

## CHAPTER IV. He rebukes his people for the vices of fornication, greed, idleness, and immoderate mourning for the dead.

For the rest, brothers, we ask and beseech you in the Lord Jesus: just as you received from us how it is fitting for you to walk and to please God, so may you abound more and more. (Ambr.) We said earlier in the argument that Timothy, having returned from Thessalonica, had reported to him the steadfastness of their faith, which they had preserved inviolate when they encountered the necessity of persecution, and also that there were among them certain matters requiring correction. The Apostle therefore writes this Epistle concerning those things reported to him by Timothy, saying what was appropriate in praise of them, on account of which they had remained firm amid adversity; at the same time exhorting them to persevere in the same resolve. In the matters already mentioned, he seems to have completed this with a prayer, bringing his discourse to a close.

Here, however, he begins to discuss those things which he had learned were being done improperly by them. He therefore says this: “We beseech you to make your conduct correspond to the teaching which you received from us, hastening to please God and advancing according to the direction of his law.” He made an excellent beginning with the words, “For the rest, then, brothers,” after completing the praises he had spoken concerning the steadfastness of their faith. His meaning is this: “Since you demonstrate by your very deeds that you possess the disposition appropriate to the contemplation of piety, let us therefore henceforth apply diligence to your life, so that nothing may seem lacking in you of those things which appear useful—and indeed necessary—for your perfection.” He added here, “just as you received from us,” demonstrating that they did not now hear these things from him for the first time, but had already long ago been instructed concerning them. Hence, enlarging upon this, he says: “You know what commandments I gave you through the Lord Jesus,” showing everywhere that he writes nothing new to them today.

“For this is the will of God, your sanctification.” He necessarily said, “This is the will of God,” since it is fitting to do those things which God wills to be done, and sanctification is fully understood as the renunciation of everything improper. Explaining more clearly what he is presently discussing, he adds:

(Cass.) And lest he leave us in doubt or obscurity about what he wished to call sanctification—whether justice, or charity, or humility, or patience, since sanctification is believed to be acquired through all these virtues—he continues and plainly indicates what he specifically wished to call sanctification: “This is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain,” he says, “from fornication; that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in honor and sanctification, not in the passion of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God.”

Observe with what praises he commends it, calling the honor of the vessel—that is, of our body—and sanctification by this name. Conversely, then, whoever is in the passion of desire remains in dishonor and uncleanness and conducts himself as a stranger to sanctification. A little later, for the third time, he again speaks of this holiness, declaring: “For God did not call us to dishonor, but to holiness.” Therefore, whoever rejects these things rejects not man but God, who also gave his Holy Spirit in us. He joined inviolable authority to his command when he said: “Whoever rejects these things”—that is, the matters concerning holiness which I have just discussed—“rejects not man”—that is, not me, who command these things—but God, who speaks through me, and who also appointed our heart as a dwelling place for his Holy Spirit.

You see, in simple and pure words, with what proclamations and how great praises he has exalted it: first, by assigning the name sanctification specifically to this virtue; then, by asserting that through it the vessel of our body is to be freed from uncleanness; third, by declaring that, once dishonor and disgrace have been cast aside, it will remain in honor and sanctification. Finally, he indicated the highest perfection of reward and the recompense of blessedness by showing that, through this dwelling in our breast, the Spirit will be holy.

“Abstain,” he says, “from all fornication.”

(Ambr.) Timothy had reported to him, among other things, that they were indifferent regarding sexual intercourse and were living licentiously, so that some of them, even though they had wives, were not content with their own wives. He reported that certain others even had intercourse with other men’s wives. The Apostle now writes to them, beginning with this excellent correction of their conduct.

When he says “from all fornication,” he wished to display more clearly the different kinds of fornication. For it would not otherwise have been possible to help those who were sinning unless he had specifically spoken about the matters that needed correction.

“That each one know how to possess his own vessel in holiness and honor, not in the passion of desire.” He says this concerning those who, although they had wives, were not content with them. He called a man’s own wife his “vessel,” saying that he should possess her in holiness—that is, when she is not defiled by adultery—and in honor, because he should not despise his own wife and look toward another man’s wife. More plainly, he said “not in the passion of desire,” since one who acts in this way does not appear to be joined to her as to his wife, but acts solely for the sake of intercourse, which he called the passion of desire.

Desire cannot be called a crime when a man appears to fulfill the movement of nature with his own wife. But he called it “the passion of desire” when those who have intercourse with other women also wish to use their own wives after the manner of those women. Then, by comparison, he sufficiently condemned the contrary practice: “like the Gentiles who do not know God.”

In saying this, he referred to those who, although they had wives, had intercourse with other women. In what follows, however, he also discusses those who presumed to have intercourse with women who were lawfully joined to their husbands in marital affection:

“Let no one transgress and defraud his brother in the matter.” He spoke with great modesty when he said “in the matter,” but he earnestly sought in every respect to condemn the injustice of the act. When he says “let no one transgress,” he accuses one who invades boundaries that have been established. By saying “defraud,” he accuses one who takes away another’s possession. And by saying “his brother,” he has heightened the crime still further: for it is a greater offense if he has intercourse with the wife of one who is his brother through faith. He called him “brother” in order to show the crime of the usurpation as even greater, since among all peoples it has been regarded as a matter of shame, to the extent that no one is permitted to take another man’s wife, not even the wife of a deceased brother.

Then, wishing to bring them into fear, he adds: “Because the Lord is an avenger concerning all these things.” He rightly added “all,” so that the statement might appear to apply to the earlier matters as well. And again, as though bearing witness that he had already said these same things to them, he added: “As we told you beforehand and solemnly affirmed,” showing that it was necessary for them to hear this teaching also.

“For God did not call us to uncleanness, but to sanctification.” Therefore, if we restrain ourselves from these things, we have done what is fitting for our calling. For he called us to the sanctification of possession, in which we also hope to exist in the future age, when we shall rise and become incorruptible and shall no longer be able to sin. We ought also to imitate this, as far as possible, in the present life.

Then he adds: “Therefore, whoever rejects these things rejects not man but God, who also gave his Holy Spirit in us.” Thus, whoever does these things rejects God himself, doing one thing while having been called to another. The addition he made here concerning the Spirit that was given is necessary, since future goods are bestowed upon us by him.

“It is sown,” he says, “an animal body; it rises a spiritual body.” Therefore, if, having received this pledge of future things—that is, the firstfruits of the Spirit—we do other things besides those to which we have been called in hope, this is an evident contempt of God, who appears to have given us the pledge.

Having discussed these natural sexual relations, he passes to another subject.

Concerning brotherly charity, we have no need to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another. Indeed, you do this toward all the brothers throughout the whole of Macedonia. But we beseech you, brothers, to abound more and more, to make it your ambition to be quiet, to attend to your own affairs, and to work with your hands, just as we commanded you, so that you may walk honorably before those who are outside and may have need of no one.

He learned that there were also some among them who seemed extremely disorderly: they did no work that contributed to the usefulness of others, lived idly, and busied themselves with the lives of others, stirring up certain disturbances on this account.

(RAB.) He discussed these matters more plainly in the Second Epistle as well. Here he writes concerning them because idleness itself and freedom from work caused them to misuse their leisure for nothing useful. For while the generosity of others, without investigation, offered assistance to all who were in need, provided they were thought to belong to the same faith, he first praises those who gave help with this intention and who rightly fulfilled it. At the same time, he commends them because they hastened to complete this effort not only toward their own people but also toward other believers who appeared to be living in different places.

He therefore commands the others not to misuse their freedom for improper purposes. They were unwilling to perform any work and, through idleness itself, hastened to occupy themselves with matters that were inappropriate. Just as we praise those who minister to the needy and display such an intention toward their faithful brothers, so we wish the others also to attain growth: that they should be quiet, attend to their own affairs, and work with their hands, so that they may be able not to need another’s assistance and may not be put to shame among outsiders on account of indecent conduct. He adds similarly here: “Just as we commanded you,” and so forth.

(Ambr.) He shows that he is not now imposing this upon them as something new.
