He then proceeds to matters that it was appropriate to mention, persuading them not to grieve dishonorably over those who depart from this life. For this reason he also discusses the future state there and explains the glory that will belong to the saints at that time. Because of the need for instruction, he recounts what he considered appropriate to the present subject. For the greater the things that were expected, the more could those who were held by profound grief be consoled.

(Cass.) The blessed Paul, as a true and spiritual physician, saw that this disease, which arises from the spirit of weariness, was already beginning to spread—or, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, foresaw that it would arise—and hastened to forestall it with the salutary medicines of his commandments.

Writing to the Thessalonians, he first, as a highly skilled and perfect physician, soothed the weakness of his patients with the gentle and mild treatment of his words. Beginning with charity, he commended them in that respect, until the fatal wound, softened by a gentler remedy and with the indignation caused by its swelling laid aside, could more easily endure stronger medicines. Thus he says:

“Concerning brotherly charity, we have no need to write to you, for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another. Indeed, you do this toward all the brothers throughout the whole of Macedonia.”

He first applied the gentle soothing of praise, making their ears calm and ready for the treatment of the saving word.

Again he continues: “But we beseech you, brothers, to abound more and more.” He still caresses them with the gentle softness of his words, lest he find them not yet suited to receive a complete cure. What is it that you ask, Apostle, that they abound more and more in? Surely in charity, about which you said above: “Concerning brotherly charity, we have no need to write to you.” And why is it necessary for you to say, “We beseech you to abound more and more,” when they do not even need anything to be written to them concerning this, especially since you give the reason why they have no need of it, saying: “For you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another”?

You add a third and greater point: they have not only been taught by the Lord but also fulfill in deed what they are taught. “Indeed, you do this,” he says—not toward one or two, but toward all the brothers; not merely toward your fellow citizens or acquaintances, but throughout the whole of Macedonia.

Tell us, then, at last: why do you introduce this at such length? Again he continues: “But we beseech you, brothers, to abound more and more.” And only after a long while does he break forth into what he had been laboring toward: “and to make it your ambition to be quiet.”

He stated the first reason; then he adds a second: “and to attend to your own affairs.” A third as well: “and to work with your hands, just as we commanded you.” A fourth: “and to walk honorably before those who are outside.” A fifth: “and to desire nothing from anyone.”

Now the hesitation that he had delayed expressing through so many preliminary statements is revealed: what it was bringing forth in his heart—“and to make it your ambition to be quiet.” That is, remain in your own cells and do not become restless through various rumors, which are usually generated by the vices [or, according to another reading, the desires] or stories of idle people, or bring disturbances upon others.

“And to attend to your own affairs”: do not, out of curiosity, wish to investigate the affairs of the world, or, examining the conduct of various people, devote your efforts not to your own correction and the pursuit of virtue but to slandering your brother.

“And to work with your hands, just as we commanded you.” He had earlier warned them not to be restless, not to concern themselves with other people’s affairs, not to walk dishonorably before outsiders, and not to desire anything belonging to another. Now he adds: “and to work with your hands, just as we commanded you.”

For he clearly showed that idleness was the cause of the things he had condemned earlier. No one can be restless or concerned with another’s affairs except one who is unwilling to persist contentedly in the work of his own hands.

He also introduces a fourth disease born from this same idleness: that they should not walk dishonorably. He says: “and to walk honorably before those who are outside.” One who is not content to remain within the enclosure of his cell and devote himself to the work of his hands can never walk honorably, even before worldly people. It is necessary for him to behave dishonorably while seeking the necessities of life: to devote himself to flattery, to pursue the latest happenings in households, and to seek occasions for conversations and stories by which he may prepare for himself an entrance and opportunity to penetrate the houses of various people.

“And desire nothing from anyone.” One who does not take pleasure in the pious and quiet labor of his own work, by which he obtains the substance of his daily livelihood, cannot help longing for the gifts and presents of others.

You see how many causes—so serious and so shameful—are generated by the single corruption of idleness.

But we do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest who have no hope.

(Ambr.) He did well, for he did not remove grief but forbade it to be excessive. He especially exposed their opponents to shame by comparison, since they have no hope. It would indeed be improper for those who expect better things after death than belong to the present condition to grieve like those who expect nothing further after death.

Then he also speaks of those who are in hope: “For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus.”

(Greg.) Why does the distinguished preacher call the Lord’s death “death,” but call the death of the Lord’s servants not death but sleep? It is because, observing the weakness of his hearers, he composes the medicine of his preaching with remarkable skill. He does not hesitate to present as dead the one whom he knew had already risen, but, in order to instill the hope of resurrection, he calls those who had not yet risen not dead but sleeping.

He was not afraid to say “dead” of one whom his hearers knew had already risen, but he was afraid to call “dead” those whom they scarcely believed would rise.

(Ambr.) If we believe in the resurrection of Jesus, then we must necessarily also believe concerning those who sleep, since he will raise them through Jesus so that they too may be with him. This is what he means by “he will bring them with him.” For the words “through Jesus” must be connected with what follows, where he says, “he will bring them with him.” The statement should therefore correspond to the words: “For since through a man came death, through a man also comes the resurrection of the dead.” We must understand that through Jesus he will grant us resurrection as well, since he is the cause of these things for us.

We must also attend to this point: when he speaks of Jesus, he says “dead,” because there death still existed in him and had not yet been abolished. Here, however, he speaks of sleep because death itself had already been abolished, whether according to the promise or according to the deed, whenever one wishes to examine the matter with regard to Christ rising from the dead.

For the confirmation of his greater statements he introduces these words: “If,” he says, “Christ, having died, rose again, and nothing hindered his resurrection because God willed it—and at first death had not yet been abolished—then with much greater reason we believe that this is justly true in us after its abolition.”

We must also attend to this: while discussing Christ’s resurrection, he leaves aside the word “sleep” and discusses the assumption. Clearly, confession of the resurrection is joined to the assumption.

For he hastens to persuade them, in the present matter, concerning those things that seemed to surpass the others. Explaining this more fully, he shows the greatness of future things:

“For this we say to you by the word of the Lord.” He rightly says “by the word of the Lord,” that is, according to the revelation which appears to have been accomplished in us through divine action. For he could not have expected belief when speaking of future things unless this had also been spoken beforehand:

“For we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord.”

When he says “we,” he is not speaking of himself or of those who were then living in the present life, but of those believers who will be alive at the time when the resurrection is to occur. He says “we,” that is, “believers,” because he himself was such a believer and was writing to people like them.

Hence he adds: “who remain until the coming of the Lord,” showing that he is not speaking of those who were living in his own time, but of those who will be alive at the consummation.

“We shall not precede those who have fallen asleep.” He means that, at the time of the assumption, those believers who have already died will not be preceded by those who are then found alive. Making this clearer, he adds:

“For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord.”

(Aug.) These apostolic words most clearly demonstrate that the resurrection of the dead will take place when Christ comes to judge the living and the dead. Yet it is customary to ask whether those whom Christ will find alive—whose person the Apostle represented in himself and in those who were then living with him—will never die at all, or whether, at the very moment when they are caught up with the risen in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, they will pass through death into immortality with marvelous speed.

For it must not be said that it is impossible that, while they are being carried upward through the air, they should die and live again within that interval. The words “and so we shall always be with the Lord” should not be understood as though he said that we would remain forever with the Lord in the air, since he himself will certainly not remain there, because, when he comes, he will pass onward. One goes to meet someone who is coming, not someone who is remaining.

Rather, “so we shall always be with the Lord” means that we shall be such as possess everlasting bodies, wherever we may be with him. According to this understanding—that we should believe that those whom the Lord will find alive here will, within that brief interval, both undergo death and receive immortality—the Apostle himself does not seem to object when he says: “In Christ all will be made alive,” while elsewhere, speaking of the resurrection of bodies, he says: “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies.”

(Ambr.) By “the dead in Christ” he means those who both believed in Christ and died for Christ. He said that they would rise first, just as he wrote to the Corinthians: “Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ’s, who believed in his coming, then the end” (I Cor. XV).

He clearly showed the speed of the resurrection in that Epistle when he said: “In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; for the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.”

This is what he says here as well: Christ will indeed descend from heaven with a terrifying trumpet and with a great voice resounding at that time, according to divine operation. As is customary, he calls the archangel who precedes and commands everyone, “Rise,” a trumpet. He calls the command the voice of that same archangel, because he will say, “Rise.”

When these things have occurred, everything will happen swiftly, so that those who died for the faith will rise before the others, and with the believers who are then found in this present life they will be carried above the clouds, as though in vehicles, and led into the air to meet the Lord, so that they may always be with the Lord.

He indicated the great and extraordinary speed that will then occur: when the Lord Christ appears from heaven, the trumpet sounds, and the angel cries, “Rise,” everything will be completed swiftly. The dead will rise together and the living will be caught up with them, and the living will no longer be able to precede them. Thus all things will be brought together at once through a certain divine and terrifying operation.

It is also clear that when he says, “The dead in Christ will rise first,” he is not speaking of the exclusion of those righteous people who came before Christ’s advent. For it may be that the one who plainly said, writing concerning those Hebrews, “And all these, having obtained testimony through faith, did not receive the promise” (Hebr. XI)—God having determined something better for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us—shows that they too are to be made perfect with us.

Rather, since he was writing after Christ’s advent, he said this to distinguish those who did not believe in Christ. The righteous who existed before his advent, insofar as they were concerned, labored according to their own time; and for this reason they were justly reckoned with them.

(Hieron.) Certain people ask about the Apostle’s statement that, at the advent of the Lord and Savior, some who are alive will be caught up in the clouds to meet him, so that they will not be preceded by those who sleep in Christ. They wish to know whether these will meet him in their bodies without dying beforehand, since our Lord also died and Enoch and Elijah are said, according to the Apocalypse of John, to be destined to die, so that no one might be found who had not tasted death.

This can be learned from the context of the passage itself. The saints who are found bodily present at the Savior’s advent will meet him in those same bodies, but in such a way that what is inglorious, corruptible, and mortal will be changed into glory, incorruption, and immortality. Just as the bodies of the risen will be, so will the substance of the bodies of the living be transformed.

Hence the Apostle says elsewhere: “For this reason we do not wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (II Cor. V). This is so that the body may not be abandoned by the soul, but that, while the soul dwells in the body, what was previously inglorious may become glorious.

As for Enoch and Elijah, whom the Apocalypse reports will come and will die, that is not a matter for the present discussion. The whole book must either be understood spiritually, as we think, or, if we follow a literal interpretation, we must submit to Jewish fables: that Jerusalem will again be built, sacrifices will be offered in the temple, and, with spiritual worship diminished, carnal ceremonies will prevail.

(Hier.) For this reason, the statement that Paul makes concerning the resurrection to the Corinthians should be read in this way: “We shall all sleep, but we shall not all be changed.” If all die in Adam, and death involves sleep, then we shall all sleep, or we shall all die.

According to the idiom of the Scriptures, the one who has died sleeps in the hope of the future resurrection, and everyone who sleeps certainly awakens—provided that the sudden force of death has not overwhelmed him and death has not been joined to sleep. When all have thus slept according to the law of nature, only the saints will be changed for the better in soul and body. Thus incorruption belongs to all who rise, but glory and transformation properly belong to the saints.

As for what follows, according to the Greek readings, “in an atom,” [*en atomō*], and “in the twinkling of an eye”—for both are read—and as our translators have rendered it, “in a moment and in the twinkling of an eye,” or “in the movement of an eye,” he explained it thus: with the resurrection of all joined together, they will be caught up to meet Christ—but those whom death has dissolved.

But why do I investigate these matters and bring accusations against the apostolic words, when he himself plainly writes: “We who remain at the coming of the Lord”? Who these “remaining” ones are, we learn from the Savior’s words (Matt. XXVI): “As in the days of Noah they were taking wives and giving in marriage, and suddenly the flood came and took them all away, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.” These words establish that, at the end of the world, many will be found alive and still in their bodies.

It follows: “with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and the dead will rise first.” The Savior again speaks of this in the Gospel: “At midnight the bridegroom came” (ibid.). He will certainly find people living in the body, when “two will be in one bed: one will be taken and the other will be left; two will be grinding: one will be taken and the other will be left” (Matt. XXIV). By these words it is shown that the consummation of the world will come at midnight, when everyone is secure, as Origen says in his third volume.

Then: “we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord.”

Although the preceding discussion of Acacius treated this matter more fully, we must nevertheless state what others think—namely Theodore, Apollinaris, and Diodorus, who follow one opinion. Diodorus wrote as follows:

“Paul the Apostle calls them ‘those who remain’ and ‘those who are alive,’ not because he wishes it to be understood that he himself and others will be found among those resurrected in the body, but he said ‘we’ in place of ‘the righteous,’ among whom I too am numbered. They will be caught up to meet Christ, not sinners.

“We understand ‘alive’ not tropologically, as referring to the saints who have not died to sin, but as referring to all those whom Christ will find in the body when he comes. And what follows—‘we shall not precede those who have fallen asleep’—we must by no means refer to sinners, but to the righteous. For sinners will have no share with the righteous in that resurrection.”

In explaining Paul’s First Epistle to the Thessalonians, after discussing many matters in varied and prudent discourse, he added the following. There can be no doubt that Acacius drew upon much of it:

“What, then, is the meaning of what Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy write to the Thessalonians in the word of God: ‘We who are alive, who remain at the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep’? Who are these who, being alive, speak such things?

“Certainly Paul, an Apostle not from men nor through a man; Timothy, his beloved son in the faith; and Silvanus, who was united with them both in affection and in virtues—not they alone, but anyone who resembles Paul in knowledge and conduct—can say: ‘We who are alive,’ whose body is dead because of sin, but whose spirit is life because of righteousness; whose members are mortified upon the earth, so that the flesh no longer lusts against the spirit.

“For if the flesh still desires, it is alive; and because it is alive, it desires, and its members have not been mortified upon the earth. But if they have been mortified, they by no means lust against the spirit, since through their mortification they have lost such desire.

“Therefore, just as those who have lost the present life and have been transferred to better things live more fully after laying aside the body of death and the incentives of every vice, so those who carry the mortification of Jesus in their body and do not live according to the flesh but according to the spirit live in him who is life. Christ lives in them, of whom it is written: ‘The word of God is living and effective,’ and he is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

“For those in whom the power of God lives are alive, having laid aside all human weakness; and those in whom wisdom lives are alive, wisdom which is hidden by God; and those in whom righteousness lives and works are alive. For Christ has become for us not only righteousness from God but also wisdom, and everything that is virtue.”

Although, in the present passage, the writers of this Epistle separate themselves from those who sleep and are dead in Christ, this observation might seem superfluous, and testimony drawn from a single passage might not be sufficient. But now the same meaning is found because he speaks with the same spirit in the First Epistle to the Corinthians:

“We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the movement of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.”

What is written in the present passage—“he will descend from heaven with the trumpet of God”—he compares with what is said to the Corinthians: “at the last trumpet, for it will sound.” And what is read in the Epistle to the Thessalonians—“the dead in Christ will rise first”—corresponds to what is written to the Corinthians: “the dead will rise incorruptible.”

What follows concerning us—“we who are alive, who remain”—corresponds to the words: “and we shall be changed.” Both statements can be understood in this way: “we who are alive, who remain, at the coming of the Lord,” and “we who shall be changed.” We are not among those who are called dead, but are alive.

For this reason we await the Lord’s presence not in death but in life, because we are of the Israelite race, and a remnant has been chosen from among us. Concerning them the Lord spoke long ago: “I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal” (III Reg. X).

In the Gospel of John (John XI), as well, a twofold order of the living and the non-living is described: “Everyone who believes in me, even if he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die.”

If we understand “the living” as we have already explained, then we should believe that those who sleep and are dead in Christ are those who, although they wish to live in Christ, are nevertheless dead through sin. But if “the remnant” and “the election according to grace” are called the living, those who do not believe in this way and were not born from Israel’s nobility will be called those who sleep and are dead in Christ.

(Ambr.) Nevertheless, because the recollection of his words had sufficiently brought them to shame, he instructs them at the same time not to lose heart concerning those who depart from this life, since they are expecting such things. They should grieve only out of affection and customary attachment.

Hence he adds: “Therefore comfort one another with these words.” “When you are placed in tribulations,” he says, “repeat these things to one another.” The very recollection of them will be sufficient to bring consolation to those who hear, provided that they belong to the household of faith and do not doubt concerning future things.

## CHAPTER V

He admonishes his people concerning the future day of death and the general judgment, and urges them to conduct themselves well toward God and their neighbor.

Concerning the times and seasons, brothers, you have no need to have anything written to you. For you yourselves know very well that the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night. (Ambrose) Here another chapter begins. They had been asking when the end of this age would be. He therefore writes to them appropriately, so that they should not inquire further or suppose that they could say anything definite, since they had once heard that the time of the Lord’s coming is uncertain. He says “like a thief in the night,” because a thief comes without announcing himself. And because the adversaries mocked precisely what he was saying to them, declaring that it could never happen, he adds: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will overtake them, like labor pain upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.” He means that unbelievers ought not to look forward to these things, since what we say will necessarily happen, even if they think a thousand times that nothing of the kind will occur. Even if they suppose themselves secure and act as they wish according to the freedom of their will, the judge will suddenly come upon them, just as labor pains come upon pregnant women, so that it will not be possible for them to escape punishment.

He has therefore applied this example very aptly to everything, since they too will be subjected to a severe punishment. Labor is indeed severe for a pregnant woman; and by this he shows that the time of consummation has been fixed by God, although, because it occurs suddenly, it may appear uncertain to us. For women too seem to have a definite time for childbirth: they ordinarily expect delivery according to the course of the months, yet the very day of delivery is uncertain to them, since they cannot know it until labor pain suddenly overtakes them.

Then, taking up an exhortation from what has preceded and addressing them as children, he says: “But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that that day should overtake you like a thief. For you are all sons of light and sons of day; we are not of night or of darkness.” Since he had said, “He will come like a thief in the night,” here he says that they are not in darkness, because they have recognized the truth. Therefore, although that day comes suddenly, it does not claim over you the role of a thief, since you are to be helped by his coming; it does so only over those who await a punishment of wrongdoing. And so that they may consider this recognition sufficient for themselves, he adds: “Therefore let us not sleep as the others do, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who become drunk, become drunk at night. But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and the helmet of the hope of salvation. For God has not appointed us for wrath, but for the acquisition of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that, whether we watch or sleep, we may live together with him.”

It is therefore fitting that, rewarded with such knowledge, we should watch and be sober concerning the careful observance of those things that are appropriate for us to guard. Nighttime is more suitable for us also for drunkenness; for one who is such can easily remain hidden. But those who, through knowledge, already stand as though in the daytime ought to be sober and watchful concerning the practices of the virtues, as people who conduct themselves in the daytime, when it is not possible for anyone to remain hidden if he has done anything improper.

What are those works, then, that we should assign to ourselves as people conducting themselves in the daytime? He says faith, in which he also places love. From these we acquire the hope of salvation, which the Lord God, through Christ—who chose to undergo death for us—has handed over to us: salvation, not punishment, although we are still held according to this present life. For this is what he says: “Let us watch,” even if we have departed from this life; for this is what he means by “let us sleep.” He wishes to say that those who will then be living at Christ’s coming, and those who have already died, will all acquire eternal and incorruptible life: those who departed earlier into death will rise again in this way, while those who are then living will be changed into incorruptibility, just as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “We shall all be changed.”

Nothing, therefore, prevents us from enjoying the salvation that is to come, provided that those things which proceed from us do not in the least hinder us. For this reason he adds: “Therefore comfort one another and build one another up, just as you are doing.” From the point at which he said that they should not inquire curiously into the consummation of the age and its time, he necessarily added this here—that is, leaving those matters aside, do these things and be concerned about them; and discuss them with one another for the common benefit. After this he exhorts them, saying:

“We ask you, brothers, to recognize those who labor among you, who preside over you in the Lord and admonish you; esteem them exceedingly in love because of their work. Be at peace with them.” Thus consider those who appear to have been entrusted with the work of teaching worthy of the greatest honor, and do not resist them when they wish to correct you. For this is what he means by “be at peace with them.”

This was also accustomed to happen among those who lived without discipline. In the preceding passage, when he wrote to them, he seems to have indicated their insolence: while he wished to correct those who were sinning and to teach those who were doing what was improper, these people thought themselves burdened by the teachers’ reproof. Thus, while addressing them, he turns his speech toward the teachers and instructs them: “We exhort you, brothers: admonish the disorderly, comfort the fainthearted, support the weak, and be patient with everyone.” It was necessary to exhort them not to withdraw from their work because of the insolence of some. He also commanded the teachers to do, in due order, everything he himself had prescribed concerning them, about which he had also written in his Epistle, urging them to apply diligence to these matters and, briefly, to instruct the disorderly, to whom he himself also seems to have written.

“Comfort the fainthearted,” those who sorrowfully endured the separation of those who had fallen away. “Support the weak.” He is speaking of those who were being cast down by fornication; he teaches that they should not reject them because of the reproach of the sin itself, but should also apply the necessary diligence toward them and take greater care of them so that they may be converted. Thus also, writing elsewhere, he says (II Cor. XI): “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” That is, I consider the sins of others to be my own.

He rightly adds, “Be patient with everyone,” because this is extremely necessary for teachers: they must not readily despair because of sins, but patiently fulfill their teaching, always awaiting improvement in their disciples and considering it their own gain even if they are able to recall them to what is honorable only after some delay. Then, proceeding to a general exhortation, he commands:

“See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always pursue what is good toward one another and toward all.” He says that evil must be repaid to no one, but that the good should be pursued as far as virtue gives assistance, so that they may offer one another benefits more generously, including those things which may seem to us to arise from earthly material. (Augustine) When a man sees someone living badly and perhaps contributing something to the Church, and does not rebuke him, he flees in his heart. What does it mean to flee in one’s heart? To fear. Fear is an inward flight. Why does he fear? Because he is a hireling, afraid that the man may not accept the rebuke and may not give what he is accustomed to give.

He sees the wolf coming—that is, the devil breaking the neck of the man who lives badly—and he flees, inwardly refraining from useful correction, full of fear. But one who is a shepherd, and who cares for the sheep, does not abandon him (John X), but does what the Apostle says: “Reprove the disorderly, comfort the fainthearted,” and so forth.

Let no shepherd, then—or anyone who calls himself a shepherd—suppose that he does not repay evil for evil, when he instead repays evil for good. For although that man may be a sinner and a criminal, he gives some of his goods to the Church; but the other repays him evil for good when he withholds correction from him.

But since all this must be done out of love, while people sometimes regard their correctors as enemies, for this reason, after saying, “Reprove the disorderly,” he added, “Comfort the fainthearted.” Perhaps the person begins to fail and becomes troubled because of the correction; then you ought to comfort him. “Support the weak,” lest they fall through weakness. If weakness has caused him to stumble, let love receive him into its bosom. And after saying these things he added at the end: “See that no one repays anyone evil for evil.” Correction, therefore, is not evil if it is given properly. But what does the good sheep say when he is corrected by his superior? “Let the righteous correct me in mercy” (Ps. CXL).

Then he adds: “Rejoice always.” That is, in place of all the sadnesses that befall you, be of good courage, made more even-tempered by the expectation of future things. After this he commands: “Pray without ceasing; give thanks in all things, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.” He commanded them to pray without interruption, and always to give thanks in their prayers, because God wills these things and especially demands them from us: that we should be grateful to him and render him the thanks owed for those good things that he has bestowed upon us.

(Isaac in Cassian’s *Conferences*) And therefore, so that prayer may be uttered with the fervor and purity it ought to have, the following must by all means be observed. First, concern for carnal matters must be cut away altogether. Then, for the sake of no business whatsoever, not only anxiety but even memory itself must be entirely excluded. Slander, empty talk—or mutilated speech—must be cut off, as must also buffoonery. Above all, the disturbance of anger or sadness must be uprooted from the depths. The harmful tinder of carnal desire and love of money must be torn out by the roots.

When these and similar vices have been entirely expelled and cut off—even those that may be exposed to human eyes—and when such cleansing purification has preceded, a purification accomplished by the purity of simplicity and innocence, then the firm foundations of profound humility must first be laid, foundations capable of supporting a tower that will enter the heavens. Afterward the spiritual structure of the virtues must be placed upon them, and the mind must be restrained from every slippery wandering and roaming, so that it may gradually begin to be exalted toward the contemplation of God and spiritual vision.

For whatever our soul has conceived before the hour of prayer must necessarily come before us in prayer through the intrusion of memory. Therefore, if we wish to be found a certain kind of person when praying, we must prepare ourselves beforehand, before the time of prayer, to be such. The mind is shaped in supplication by its preceding condition, and the image of our earlier actions—or even of our earlier words and thoughts—preludes before our eyes as we fall down to pray. It may make us angry according to our previous disposition, or sad, or cause us to reconsider earlier desires or causes; or, what one is ashamed even to say, it may make us be assailed by the tickling of some buffoonish word or deed and a foolish laugh; or it may make us fly back to our former wanderings.

For this reason, whatever we do not want to cling to us when we pray, let us hasten to exclude beforehand from the hidden places of our heart, so that we may fulfill the apostolic command: “Pray without ceasing, lifting up pure hands in every place, without anger or disputation” (I Tim. II). Otherwise we shall not be able to fulfill this command unless our mind has been purified from the contagion of every vice and, devoted only to the virtues—which are natural goods—is nourished by the continual contemplation of almighty God.

“Do not extinguish the Spirit; do not despise prophecies; test everything, and hold fast to what is good.” (Augustine) Not that the Spirit can be extinguished, but, insofar as it lies with them, those who act in such a way that they wish it extinguished are rightly called its extinguishers.

(Ambrose) This is directed to those who held in high esteem the persons who then possessed spiritual gifts. There were also others who put forward certain things for persuasion, pretending that what they did came from divine revelation—just as we learn from the Acts of the Apostles that the Jews also undertook to exorcise demoniacs in the name of Christ (Acts XIX).

Since, then, among the Thessalonians there were some who did not accept what was professed as proceeding from spiritual operation, feigning that they avoided it out of cautious concern because of deceivers—and since this was done by disorderly persons, whose disorder was often exposed by what the prophets said—he therefore said: “Do not reject the prophets, nor prohibit spiritual activity.” For when he said that the prophets were to be rejected and that the things said by them were not to be accepted, he means that the Spirit’s activity was being despised.

But if, he says, you fear deceivers, accept what is said after testing it; and if anything in what is said is found to be contrary to the divine laws, reject only that, but hold fast to what is better. Then he adds: “Abstain from every form of evil,” as though they were also craftily doing this very thing.

“May the God of peace sanctify you completely, and may your spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.” He prays for them so that they may be guarded as holy in every respect and be without blame in soul and body, so that the grace of the Holy Spirit, once granted to them, may also be preserved whole in them, suffering no diminution because of their wickedness, and so that they may attain eternal rewards at Christ’s coming.

(Jerome) A beautiful question arises here, to be treated in a brief discussion. Above he had said, “Do not extinguish the Spirit.” If this is understood, we shall immediately know which Spirit this is who is to be preserved with soul and body on the day of the Lord’s coming. Who could believe that the Holy Spirit can be extinguished like a flame which, once extinguished, ceases to be what it was, and that he can suffer the abolition of his own being—he who once spoke in Israel through Isaiah, Jeremiah, and each of the prophets, saying, “Thus says the Lord,” and who now speaks in the Church through Agabus, “Thus says the Holy Spirit”?

“There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but the same God, who works all things in all. To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for what is useful: to one, through the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healings in one Spirit; to another, works of powers; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing them to each as he wills” (I Cor. XIII).

Concerning this Spirit David prayed that he not be taken away from him, saying: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. L). When he is taken away, it is not in his own substance that he is extinguished, but he is extinguished in the person from whom he is taken away.

I think that “Do not extinguish the Spirit” means the same thing as what he writes elsewhere (Rom. XII): “Being fervent in spirit.” For when the fervor of the spirit does not grow lukewarm through multiplied iniquity and the cooling of love, the spirit is in no way extinguished.

Therefore, “May the God of peace sanctify you completely,” or “in all things”—that is, may he make you full and perfect; for this is what the Greek word ὁλοτελής (*holotelēs*) signifies. God is called the God of peace because through Christ we have been reconciled to him. Christ is our peace, “who has made both one” (Eph. II), and in another place he is called peace surpassing all understanding (Phil. IV), which guards the hearts and thoughts of the saints.

Whoever is sanctified, or made perfect, in all things has spirit, soul, and body preserved on the day of the Lord. The body makes use of the functions of its individual members: for example, the hand works, the foot walks, the eye sees, the ear hears, the teeth grind food, the stomach digests, and another organ assimilates it. Or, if no part of the members has been cut off, can anyone believe that the Apostle is praying for believers that, on the day of judgment, Christ may find the body of all of them complete, when everyone’s bodies have either been dissolved by death or, as some wish, are found still breathing and retain their infirmities—especially the bodies of martyrs and of those who for Christ’s name have had their eyes put out, their noses cut off, or their hands severed?

The complete body, therefore, is the one of which we spoke in another question: it does not retain the head from which the whole body, joined and compacted together, receives its growth in the service of Christ. This is the body of the Church. Whoever holds the head of this body and preserves the remaining members will possess a complete body, insofar as human nature can receive it.

According to this same pattern, the integrity of the soul must also be preserved. It can say: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, who heals all your diseases” (Ps. CII). Of the soul it is also written: “He sent his word and healed them” (Ps. CVI). The spirit too is preserved whole when we do not err in spiritual matters, but live by the spirit, yield to the spirit, and put the works of the flesh to death by the spirit, bringing forth all its fruits—love, joy, peace, and the rest.

In another way Solomon gives us a command, saying: “But describe these things for yourself three times in counsel and in conscience, so that you may answer words of truth to those who put questions to you” (Prov. XXII). There is a threefold inscription in our heart and a threefold rule of the Scriptures. The first is that we understand them according to history; the second, according to tropology; the third, according to spiritual understanding.

In history, the arrangement of the things written is involved. In tropology, we rise from the letter to greater things, interpreting morally whatever was done carnally among the former people and turning it to spiritual profit for our soul. In θεωρία (*theōria*), we pass to higher things, leaving earthly matters behind and discussing the blessedness of future things and heavenly realities, so that meditation on the present life may be a shadow of the future blessedness.

When Christ finds people of this kind, preserved whole in body, soul, and spirit, and possessing in themselves the truth of this threefold knowledge in its perfection, he will sanctify them with his peace and make them perfect.

Many understand this passage simply as referring to the resurrection, so that spirit, soul, and body may be preserved whole at the Lord’s coming. Others wish to affirm here a threefold substance in the human being: the spirit, by which we perceive; the soul, by which we live; and the body, by which we walk.

There are those who argue that the human being subsists only from soul and body and wish to understand the spirit in him not as a third substance but as an activity, by which what is called mind, perception, thought, and spirit in us is designated. Certainly there are not as many substances as there are names.

When the passage is brought forward, “Bless the Lord, spirits and souls of the righteous” (Dan. III), they do not accept the text, saying that the Hebrew does not contain it.

But in the present passage, as we said above, by “spirit,” which is preserved whole together with soul and body, we understand not the substance of the Holy Spirit, which cannot perish, but his graces and gifts, which in us are both kindled and extinguished by our virtue or our fault.

(Augustine) It is one thing to be without sin, which in this life was said of the only-begotten Son alone; it is another thing to be without blame, which could be said even of many righteous people in this life, since there is a certain manner of good living about which no just complaint can be made even in this human society.

For who could justly complain about a person who wishes evil to no one, faithfully gives counsel to those whom he can help, and does not retain a desire for vengeance against anyone’s injuries, so that he can truthfully say, “As we also forgive our debtors”?

And so that no one may be uncertain concerning prayer, he adds: “Faithful is he who has called you, and he will also do it.”

(Ambrose) This means: He who calls you is true; he promised you good things and has also filled you with his blessing.

“Brothers, pray for us.” After this he writes in such a way as to ask them to pray for him also, binding them together in his love. For the law fixes love in such a way that they should pray for one another; indeed, we cannot pray for those whom we do not love. At the same time, he teaches us that we ought both to ask this from one another and to do it for one another.

“Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss.” He then commands them to greet all the brothers with a holy kiss, calling it holy because it is made perfect by love.

“I adjure you by the Lord that this Epistle be read to all the holy brothers.” He adjures them to have the Epistle read to all the holy brothers, suspecting from certain reports that had reached him that what he had written would not be brought to everyone’s knowledge. After this he adds: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.” The Apostle appears to have brought his Epistle to completion with this word.

# BOOK TWENTY-TWO. EXPOSITION OF THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 0565]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0565D]

After the blessed Apostle Paul had written his first Epistle to the Thessalonians, he learned that, although the stubbornness of the adversaries had persisted in the same savagery and had attacked those who had believed with various temptations, nevertheless those who remained steadfast in the faith had proved superior to every temptation in all the harsh trials that had befallen them.

He also learned that some, having been persuaded, supposed that the end of the present age was imminent, and that certain people were reporting this to the others as though they had been taught it by the Apostle himself. They added that those who lived disorderly lives had in no respect been improved by the Apostle’s earlier letters, in which he had given them counsel concerning what they ought to do, but had persisted in their former evil purpose.

He therefore writes this second Epistle, first praising them highly because, while contending against every assault of the adversaries, they had not been overcome. He also exhorts them to persist in the same purpose in the present time and to overcome through patience every storm brought upon them by the adversaries.

Then he instructs them not to suppose that the consummations of the ages are already pressing upon them. Among other matters, he instructs them concerning the coming of Antichrist and how and in what manner he will appear. He writes forcefully concerning the disorderly, reproving them because they had gained no benefit from the earlier writings in which he had given them counsel about what they ought to do. We shall be instructed more carefully about all these matters from what follows.

## CHAPTER ONE. The Apostle gives thanks for the good conduct of the Thessalonians and prays for a better consummation.

“Paul, and Silvanus, and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

(Ambrose) Having made this superscription of the Epistle, he begins as follows: “We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is fitting.” The same Apostle was often accustomed to begin with thanksgiving. Here, however, he seems to have expanded the thanksgiving itself, not saying simply, “We give thanks,” but “we ought to give thanks,” as though he would also be worthy of blame if he did not render what was owed for them, for whom they ought to give thanks and concerning whom thanksgiving appears to be required.

The addition he makes is clear when he says, “As is fitting.” This itself also increases the thanksgiving, since their circumstances are such that thanksgiving ought justly to be rendered to God for them. Showing, therefore, that he says these things with good reason, because the things concerning them were great, he says: “Because your faith is growing exceedingly, and the love of each and every one of you for one another is increasing.”

In every respect he shows that the things concerning them were great. He said that their faith was increasing, meaning that they possessed something beyond steadfastness. For steadfastness can be spoken of even when someone remains in the same condition. But when he says that it has grown exceedingly, he shows that they have also received an increase within faith itself.

Likewise, saying that their love for one another abounds shows that their progress had become better with each passing day. Wishing to assert that this too was something greater, he says: “The love of each and every one of you all for one another.” For he says that all of them are alike in this respect.

And what is the proof of this? “So that we ourselves boast of you in the churches of God because of your patience and faith in all your persecutions and tribulations that you endure.” Finally, we report our boast concerning you everywhere, praising the steadfastness of your faith, because, although afflicted by various tortures, you remained in the same condition.

He rightly says, “that you endure,” because it was worthy of admiration that they bore the torments inflicted upon them with a brave spirit. Then he speaks of the benefit of the suffering itself: “As an indication of God’s righteous judgment, so that you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you also suffer.” In the future age you will appear to enjoy the kingdom of heaven justly on account of these things, provided that you are also willing to suffer for it, considering the enjoyment of it to be a great good.

And showing that it will not go unpunished for the adversaries who do such things to them, he adds: “Since it is righteous with God to repay tribulation to those who afflict you, and to you who are afflicted, rest with us.” For when he says, “since it is righteous,” he means, “if indeed it is righteous.” He wishes to say: At that time God will justly subject to punishment those who in the present life have done such things to you, while to you, for whom you suffer, he will offer a great reward in his generosity.

Making public the weight of that punishment, he also says what the coming of the judge himself will be like: “At the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of his power, in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

He shows in every respect that his coming will be terrible: by the nature of the place, since he is seen to come from heaven; by the power of his ministers, since he says that he will come with the angels of his power; and by the form of the torments, since he says that it will be a flame of fire.

Asserting also who will be subject to these torments, he names those who do not know God and those who have not obeyed the Gospel, thus providing a greater proof of the severity of their torments. If punishment awaits those who have merely failed to obey the faith, how much more will it await those who impose slanders and accusations upon believers?

Then he heightens the form of the torments as far as he can, saying: “They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction.” By the very character of the punishment he shows that the torments are severe. They are destruction, and are completed in the ruin of extermination; and they last not for a time but eternally.

Again he returns to the person of the judge, showing from him the greatness of the punishment: “Away from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his power.” And because he has shown throughout that the torments destined for the adversaries are great, he says where those who have believed will then be: “When he comes to be glorified in his saints and to be marveled at in all who have believed, because our testimony among you was believed on that day.”

The phrase “on that day” must be referred back to what he had said, “and to be marveled at in all who have believed,” so that the words “because our Gospel was believed among you” stand in the middle and appear to belong, according to the final sense, with what follows.

He means this: On that day he will appear glorious and marvelous in those who believed in him, because of the good things he will do for them—good things in which you too will share, since you received our teaching. In this way he exhorts them throughout by recalling the revelation they await, since great torments will be inflicted upon the adversaries and those who believe may expect to attain the enjoyment of great blessings.

He adds: “For this reason I also pray always for you, that our God may make you worthy of his calling and fulfill every good purpose and work of faith with power, so that the name of our Lord Jesus may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Because of such things, we continue praying for you, asking that God may display you as worthy of those good things, to whose enjoyment you have also been called; that he may fill you with every good and strengthen you, so that you may show your faith in your works and easily endure the things inflicted by the adversaries.

Thus Christ will also appear glorious in you according to the present age, when you gladly consent to suffer for him. And you, who have believed so firmly in him, will enjoy the future glory that by his grace he promised to those who believe in him.

He appears to have completed, at this point, the knowledge appropriate to the praise of those who remained steadfast amid adversity and to the exhortation that they should continue in the same steadfastness. From here, however, he begins to discuss the consummation of the age, teaching them not to suppose that the end of the world is imminent.

## CHAPTER TWO. The Apostle instructs his people concerning the coming of Antichrist and demonstrates the truth of this matter in several ways.

[Col. 0569C] “But we ask you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and by our gathering to him, that you not be quickly shaken, either by a spirit, or by a word, or by a letter supposedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were already present.” (Gregory.) When Paul recognized that the Thessalonians, persevering in the preaching they had received, had been disturbed by a certain faintheartedness concerning the approaching end of the world, he first praises in them what he sees to be strong, and then, by carefully admonishing them, strengthens what is weak. For he says: “We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is fitting, because your faith is growing greatly and the love of each one of you for one another is increasing, so that we ourselves boast of you in the churches of God because of your endurance and faith.” After prefacing these flattering praises of their way of life, he shortly afterward added:

“But we ask you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and by our gathering to him, that you not be quickly shaken from your understanding, nor be terrified, either by a spirit, or by a word, or by a letter supposedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were already present.”

The true teacher arranged that they should first hear the praise with which they could recognize themselves, and afterward the exhortation which they were to follow. Thus, lest the subsequent admonition disturb their minds, the preceding praise might strengthen them; and he, who knew that they had been shaken by suspicion of the approaching end, no longer rebuked them as already shaken, but, as though unaware that this had happened, forbade them to be shaken any further. [Col. 0570A] In this way, while they believed that the lightness of their agitation was unknown to their preacher, they would become all the more blameworthy because they feared that he knew of it.

(Ambrose.) That, at the Lord’s coming, all the righteous are to be caught up in clouds to meet him, and that they are to be with him forever, the Apostle clearly asserted in the First Epistle. Therefore he says here: “And our gathering to him.” For he says that Christ’s coming and their gathering to him will then take place.

(Rabanus.) Do not allow yourselves to be persuaded by those who mislead you, as though that time were near. Whether someone claims to speak of it as a spiritual operation, or as though he had learned it from a word or letter of ours, do not be persuaded by him. And, wishing to make them even more cautious, he adds: “Let no one deceive you in any way.” This means: however anyone may speak these things to you, do not believe him.

“For unless the apostasy comes first and the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God.”

(Ambrose.) He means to say that these things cannot happen before Antichrist comes. For he must first come, and afterward the things that are mentioned will follow. He called that time “the apostasy,” because then almost everyone will depart from piety and rush to him. He called him a man for a fitting reason, because he will be a human being, with the demon operating everything in him, just as God the Word appears to have perfected everything in that man who was assumed for our salvation. [Col. 0570B]

For he will attempt in every respect to imitate the things of Christ, even saying that he himself is Christ. He called him the man of sin because he will serve sin and will become the cause of sin for many people. He calls him the son of perdition because he will afterward be handed over to perdition, as he states more clearly below. He calls him “the adversary,” because he will act contrary to the divine will and strive to lead everyone over to himself. He calls him one who “exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped,” because, persuading all people to depart from their own religion, he will make himself worshiped, saying that he is Christ, and will justly demand that divine honor be paid to him by everyone.

Thus, entering even the temples of God—that is, houses of prayer—he will sit [Col. 0570C] as though he himself were Christ and therefore ought to be worshiped by human beings in the place of God. And, showing that he is saying nothing new to them, he says: “Do you not remember that, when I was still with you, I used to tell you these things?” Then he adds: “And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time.”

He says “what now restrains him” because the devil had long wished to do this very thing, but God meanwhile restrains him, since he has appointed the time for the consummation of this age, according to which he permits him to appear. The Apostle called this “what now restrains him,” saying that God’s decree restrains him. Hence he adds: “So that he may be revealed in his own time.” It is as though he is forbidden to appear now until that time, because by divine decree he is being held back for the present. [Col. 0571A]

He will appear then, at the end of the age, when the Lord also permits him to display his wickedness. Therefore he rightly adds: “For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work.” That is, although the devil does not openly carry out the apostasy, he now accomplishes it secretly, moment by moment, through his agents, attempting to tear away from piety those who approach the faith. And, taking up the same point again, he says: “Only let the one who now restrains continue to restrain, until he is removed from the midst; and then the lawless one will be revealed.”

The minds of the Thessalonians, therefore, had been moved and disturbed either by an occasion arising from their failure to understand the Epistle, or by a fabricated revelation that had deceived them while they slept, or by someone’s conjecture interpreting the words of Isaiah, Daniel, and the Gospels concerning Antichrist as referring to that time, so that they expected Christ to come then in his majesty. [Col. 0571B]

(Jerome.) The Apostle remedies this error and explains what they should expect before the coming of Antichrist, so that, when they see those things happen, they may know that Antichrist—the man of sin and the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped and who sits in the temple of God—is to come.

“Unless,” he says, “the departure comes first,” which in Greek is called ἀποστασία (*apostasia*), “so that all the nations subject to the Roman Empire withdraw from it, and he is revealed”—that is, he is shown forth—“whom the words of all the prophets announce: the man of sin,” in whom is the source of all sins, “and the son of perdition,” that is, of the devil. [Col. 0571C] For he is the perdition of all, who opposes Christ; and for this reason he is called Antichrist. He exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped, whether this means the God of all the nations, or all gods; or whether he tramples underfoot every false and true religion. And he will sit in the temple of God—either in Jerusalem, as some think, or, as we more correctly judge, in the Church—displaying himself as though he were Christ himself and the Son of God.

“Unless,” he says, “the Roman Empire has first been desolated and Antichrist has come beforehand, Christ will not come,” for he is to come in order to destroy Antichrist. “You remember,” he says, “that these very things which I am now writing in a letter I was telling you in person when I was with you, and I was saying that Christ would not come unless Antichrist had come first. And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time”—that is, you know very well what prevents Antichrist from coming at present. He does not wish to say openly that the Roman Empire must be destroyed, since those who rule it consider it eternal. Hence, according to John’s Apocalypse, the name of blasphemy—namely, “eternal Rome”—is written on the forehead of the purple-clad prostitute. [Col. 0571D]

For if he had said openly and boldly, “Antichrist will not come unless the Roman Empire is first destroyed,” there would then have seemed to be a just cause for persecution to arise against the Church in the East.

The following words, “For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work; only let the one who now restrains continue to restrain until he is removed from the midst, and then the lawless one will be revealed,” have this meaning: Through the many evils and sins by which the most impious Caesar oppresses the world, the coming of Antichrist is being brought to birth, and what he will do is being partially accomplished in the present age. [Col. 0572A] Only let the Roman Empire, which now holds all the nations, cease to hold them, and let it become half [*dimidio*; *de medio fiat*, “be removed from the midst”]; then Antichrist will come, the source of lawlessness. The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth—that is, by divine power and the command of his majesty, for his command is his deed—not by a multitude of armies, not by the strength of soldiers, and not by the assistance of angels. As soon as he comes, Antichrist will be killed; and just as darkness is driven away by the sun’s arrival, so the Lord will destroy and wipe him out by the radiance of his coming.

His works are the works of Satan. And just as the fullness of divinity was bodily present in Christ, so in Antichrist there will be every kind of power, sign, and wonder, but all of them lies. For just as the magicians resisted the signs of God performed through Moses with their own lies, and Moses’ rod swallowed their rods, so the truth of Christ will swallow the lie of Antichrist. Those who have been prepared for perdition, however, will be deceived by his lie. [Col. 0572B]

(Augustine.) Others, however, think that both “you know what restrains him” and the mystery of lawlessness at work refer only to the wicked and false people who are in the Church, until they reach such a number as to make a great people for Christ [or: “who would make a great people for Antichrist”]. They believe this to be the mystery of lawlessness, which appears hidden. They think that the Apostle exhorts the faithful to persevere firmly in the faith they hold, saying: “Only let the one who now restrains continue to restrain until he is removed from the midst”—that is, until the mystery of lawlessness, which is now hidden, departs from the midst of the Church. They believe that this mystery is also indicated by what John says in his Epistle: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2). [Col. 0572C]

(Gregory.) The same John says: “Now many Antichrists have arisen,” because all the wicked are already his members. By living wickedly, these members, perversely brought forth, have gone before their head. Hence Paul says: “So that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work,” as though he were saying: “Then Antichrist will appear openly, for now he secretly works his hidden deeds in the hearts of the wicked.”

To say nothing of more obvious crimes, behold: one person silently envies his brother in his heart, and, if he finds an opportunity, strives to overthrow him. Whose member is he, if not of the one of whom it is written: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wisdom 2)? Another, thinking himself to possess great merit and, through the swelling of his heart, preferring himself to everyone, believes all others inferior to himself. Whose member is he, if not of the one of whom it is written: “He beholds every high thing; he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41)? [Col. 0572D]

Another seeks the power of this world, not in order to benefit others, but so that he himself may not be subject to anyone else. Whose member is he, if not of the one of whom it is written: “He said: I will sit on the mountain of the Covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14)?

For the Most High alone so rules over all things that he cannot be subject to another. The Devil perversely wished to imitate him when, seeking his own dominion, he refused to be subject to him. Therefore, whoever desires power for this reason—that he disdains to be subject to the one placed over him by heavenly ordinance—imitates the Devil. [Col. 0573A]

(Ambrose.) Attention must be given to the point that he called the revelation of Antichrist his manifestation. Above he said, “When the man is revealed,” and here, “The lawless one will be revealed,” because, from the Lord’s coming onward, the Devil has always been planning to do this for the harm of human beings. He certainly would have done it, had God not restrained him according to his ineffable providence. But then he will act and bring into the open what he had long contemplated, when he is permitted to put his will into action.

And, showing that he too will not be without punishment, he adds: “Whom the Lord will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the radiance of his coming.” [Col. 0573B]

(Ambrose.) It is evident that he is speaking of a human being. For it would not be fitting to say this of Satan, whom he is going to hand over to eternal punishment; rather, he speaks of that man, because the demon found him to be a suitable instrument for carrying out such great wickedness according to his thoughts. He made this clearer below when he said: “Whose coming is according to the working of Satan.” He indicates that this is someone other than Satan, someone who will display himself by Satan’s working.

But what he says is terrifying: while that man is doing such things and persuading people throughout the whole world to depart from piety, Christ will suddenly appear from heaven and, merely by crying out, make him cease from his work, utterly consuming him. This is what he means by “the breath of his mouth,” that is, by his voice, taking the expression from things familiar to us, since we use the breath cooperating with us for articulate speech. [Col. 0573C]

He now begins to relate the things that belong to this man: “Whose coming is according to the working of Satan”—that is, Satan will be present there, working everything in him. Then he adds what Satan works in him:

“With every power and signs and lying wonders.”

He will display through him many great signs and wonders. He rightly adds “lying,” showing that he performs them more in appearance than in reality. By what means does he do this?

“And with every deceit of unrighteousness among those who are perishing, because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved.”

He calls those who are to receive him people for whom the love of truth was not accepted, so that they might be saved. He means that they should have remained in the truth’s love and not departed from it, since through it they could have been saved.

“Therefore God sends them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie and may all be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to unrighteousness.”

It is evident that, by God’s permission, he attributes this as though it were God’s work. He means that, because they did not remain in the truth, they turn their attention to deception and believe the lie, undergoing a just punishment because they abandoned the truth and turned toward unrighteousness. It is as though he were saying: “They worshiped the Devil,” calling this unrighteousness because those who do it do not act according to justice. And since he had spoken of those who would then be unbelieving, he rightly adds: [Col. 0574A]

“But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose us from the beginning for salvation, in sanctification of the Spirit and faith in the truth, to which he also called you through the Gospel, for the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

“Therefore,” he says, “for this reason too we give thanks to God for you: because he chose you so that you might attain the salvation you await, sharing with you the grace of the Spirit and granting you faith in the truth. For the calling of the Gospel offered you the future glory, promising it through the faith that is in Christ.”

And afterward:

“Therefore, brothers, stand firm and hold fast to the traditions that you have learned, whether by word or by our letter.”

He applies this to the whole matter. That is: do not allow yourselves to be persuaded by those who wish to deceive you, but remain in what we delivered to you, whether by word when we were present or by letters when we were absent.

Then again he prays for them:

“May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal consolation and good hope by grace, console your hearts and strengthen you in every good word and work.”

“He,” he says, “who by his grace granted us that eternal consolation—that is, the hope of future blessings—may he also prosper this present life, strengthening your hearts, so that you may be able both to say and to do whatever is good.”

(Paphnutius, in Cassian’s *Conferences*.) The same Apostle teaches that God also fits or strengthens our minds for every good work and works in us what is pleasing to him (Hebrews 13): “Now may the God of peace, who brought forth from darkness the great shepherd of the sheep, Jesus Christ, in the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you in every good thing, working in you what is pleasing in his sight.” He prays that this may also happen to the Thessalonians, saying:

“May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal consolation and good hope by grace, encourage your hearts and strengthen you in every good work and word.”

After this he writes to them.

## CHAPTER III

The Apostle asks for the support of prayer, instructs them concerning the reform of the wicked, and urges them to work with their hands.

“Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified, as it is among you, and that we may be delivered from unreasonable and wicked men.”

(Ambrose.) He asks them to pray for him and for his desire that the teaching may everywhere advance, as it had among them, and that he may be rescued from all the plots of his adversaries. He adds:

“For not all have faith.”

That is: not everyone believes; there are also those who resist the truth. Therefore, so that he may be rescued from their plots, he considers their prayers necessary. [Col. 0575A]

“But the Lord is faithful, who has strengthened you and will guard you from evil.”

He returns to the words of the prayer he had offered, wishing that firmness of faith might be present in them, and saying at the same time: God, who truly called you to the hope of goodness, will himself strengthen you in faith, so that you may attain those good things while departing from every improper deed. To this he adds:

“But we have confidence in the Lord concerning you, that you both do and will do what we command.”

By saying that he has good confidence in them, because they diligently carry out all his teaching, he sufficiently exhorts them to show by their deeds that his opinion of them is firm. And again he prays for them, saying:

“May the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and into the endurance of Christ.”

May it be granted to you to remain in that love which is directed toward him, enduring even if something must be suffered for him. For when he said “of God and of Christ,” the expression seems to be set in common, that is, “in love and endurance.”

“But we solemnly charge you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition which they received from us.”

It is evident that he is speaking here about the undisciplined, whom he also rebukes severely, commanding them to refrain from conversing with such people. For this is what he means by “separate yourselves” or “withdraw yourselves”: hasten to distinguish yourselves from those who are such. And, so that he might not seem to communicate this merely by word, he says:

“For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not restless among you.”

And, since these matters were still not sufficiently weighty, he adds:

“For we did not eat anyone’s bread without paying for it,”

and, what is greater:

“But in labor and weariness, working night and day, so as not to burden any of you.”

And, adding what could be considered greater still:

“Not because we did not have the right, but in order to give you an example for imitation.”

We certainly had the right to receive support, since we appeared to be free for the sake of the teaching, but we did not wish to do so, in order to teach you by our very conduct how one ought to live. And, showing that he remained among them while doing such things, he recalls his instruction again:

“For even when we were with you, we used to proclaim to you: if anyone is unwilling to work, neither should he eat.”

We were saying this when we were present: that the lazy are not worthy even to eat. He is not saying generally that whoever does not work should not eat. For, writing at length to the Corinthians, he appears to have explained that support is owed to those who devote themselves to teaching, so that they may receive material provision from their disciples. Rather, he says that the person who is not a worker is the one who is concerned neither with higher things nor willing to do any bodily work. Being idle, he scrutinizes the lives of others with curiosity; for he is speaking about the undisciplined.

(Cassian.) Finally, these very people whom he had gently encouraged in the First Epistle with a soothing caress of words, he now undertakes in the Second to heal with harsher and, as it were, cauterizing medicines, as though they had not improved through milder remedies. He no longer prefaces his words with the tender and flattering expression found there: “We ask you, brothers,” but says here: “We solemnly charge you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly.”

There he asks; here he commands. In the former letter there is the affection of one who soothes; in this one there is the severity and threat of one who insists: “We solemnly charge you, brothers.” Since you previously despised our requests and refused to listen, obey us now that we command you. And he makes the command terrifying not by a bare word, but by invoking the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, lest they again despise it as though it had been spoken merely in a human voice and attach little importance to observing it.

Immediately, like a highly skilled physician who, unable to cure rotting limbs with gentle medicine, attempts to heal them by cutting with spiritual iron, he says: “Withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition which they received from us.”

Thus he commands that they withdraw from those who refuse to devote themselves to work, and that they be cut away like limbs corrupted by the rottenness of idleness, lest the disease of inertia, like a deadly contagion, infect even the healthy parts of the body as the decay spreads. Since he is about to speak of those who refuse to work with their hands and to eat their own bread quietly, from whom he also commands that they withdraw, observe with what reproaches he brands them from the outset.

First, he calls them disorderly and says that they do not walk according to the tradition; in other words, he designates them as rebellious, since they refuse to proceed according to his instruction, and as dishonorable—that is, as people who pursue no proper and honorable order in their conduct, visits, speech, or use of time. For anyone who is disorderly must necessarily be subject to all these vices.

“And not according to the tradition which they received from us.”

By this he marks them, in a certain sense, as rebels and despisers: they disdain to keep the tradition they received from him and refuse to imitate what they remember their teacher not only to have taught by word, but also to have accomplished by deed.

“For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us.”

He greatly intensifies the accumulation of his reproach when he asserts that they fail to observe something which had remained fixed in their memory and which they had learned to imitate not only through verbal instruction, but also received through the provocation of his example.

“Because we were not restless among you.”
