By wishing to prove through the exercise of work that he was not restless among them, he abundantly marks those who refuse to work as always restless through the vice of idleness.

“Nor did we eat anyone’s bread without paying for it.”

With each word, the teacher increases the force of his interpretation. The preacher of the Gospel says that he did not eat anyone’s bread without paying for it, although he knew that the Lord had commanded that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel (1 Corinthians 9), and again: “The laborer is worthy of his food” (Luke 10). Since the one who preached the Gospel, performing so exalted and spiritual a work, could lawfully claim food for himself by the authority of the Lord’s command, and could not be said to eat without payment, what shall we do, to whom not only has no preaching of the word been entrusted, but we are not even charged with any care except that of our own soul? With what confidence shall we dare to eat bread freely with idle hands, when the chosen instrument, constrained by the concern and preaching of the Gospel, does not presume to eat without the work of his hands?

“But in labor,” he says, “and weariness, working day and night, so that we might not burden any of you.”

He continues to intensify the additions to his correction. He did not simply say, “We do not eat bread from any of you,” and stop there. For it could have seemed that he was supported by his own idle resources and stored-up money, or by contributions or gifts from others, even if not from these people. “But in labor,” he says, [Col. 0577B] “and weariness, working night and day”—that is, we were supported specifically by our own work. And he says that we did not do this according to our own preference or for pleasure, whenever rest and bodily exercise invited us to it, but because necessity and lack of food compelled us to do it, not without immense bodily fatigue.

For not only throughout the whole day, but also during the night, which appears to have been granted for bodily rest, I pursued this manual labor unceasingly out of concern for food. Yet he does not testify that he lived among them entirely by himself, lest this example appear insignificant or merely individual if it were offered as the example of one person alone. He also asserts that all who had been assigned to the ministry of the Gospel with him—that is, Silvanus and Timothy, who are writing these same things with him—labored at similar work.

In saying, “so that we might not burden any of you,” he also instills great shame in them. If the one who preached the Gospel, commending it by signs and mighty works, did not dare to eat bread without paying for it lest he burden anyone, how can they fail to consider themselves burdensome when every day, while idle and inactive, they presume to eat bread without payment?

“Not as though we did not have the right,” he says, “but so that we might give ourselves to you as an example for imitation.”

He discloses the reason why he imposed so much labor upon himself: “so that,” he says, “we might give you an example for imitation.” If you should perhaps consign to forgetfulness the teaching of words frequently impressed upon your ears, at least you might retain in your memory the examples of conduct delivered to you before your eyes.

He also reproves them in this respect, when he says that he undertook this labor and bodily weariness day and night for no other reason than to provide an example, and that nevertheless they were unwilling to be instructed, although he had imposed such fatigue upon himself for their sake without being under any necessity to do so.

“And indeed,” he says, “although we had the right, and the resources and possessions of all the brothers were open to us, and although I knew that our Lord had permitted me to use them, I nevertheless did not use this right, lest something rightly and lawfully done by me should provide others with an example of harmful idleness. For this reason, while preaching the Gospel, I preferred to support myself by my own hands and work, so that I might also open the way of perfection for you who wished to walk along the path of virtue and offer you, by my labor, a model of conduct.”

But lest he seem to have worked silently, wishing to teach them by examples while failing to instruct them by the admonitions of his commands, he adds:

“For even when we were with you, we used to proclaim to you: if anyone is unwilling to work, neither should he eat.”

He further emphasizes the laziness of those who, knowing that he worked with his own hands as a good teacher for the sake of teaching and instruction, nevertheless refuse to imitate him. He also magnifies his own diligence and caution, saying that he not only gave them this example while present, but also continually proclaimed in words that, if anyone is unwilling to work, neither should he eat.

He no longer offers them the counsel of a teacher or physician, but attacks them with the strictness of a judicial pronouncement. Resuming his apostolic authority, he delivers sentence against the contemptuous as though from a tribunal—the authority which he asserted had been given him by the Lord when, writing to the Corinthians with a threat, he warned those who were living in sin to hasten to correct themselves before his arrival. Thus he commanded:

“We ask you not to force me, when I am present, to act against some with that authority which has been given to me over you” (2 Corinthians 10).

And again:

“For if I should wish to boast somewhat of the authority which the Lord has given me for your edification and not for your destruction, I shall not be ashamed” (2 Corinthians 13).

With that authority, then, he pronounces: “If anyone is unwilling to work, neither should he eat.” He does not consign them to a carnal sword, but by the authority of the Holy Spirit forbids them the means of sustaining this present life, so that, if they should remain rebellious through love of idleness without considering the punishment of future death, they may at least be compelled by natural necessity and fear of present destruction to accept the commands that lead to salvation.

Indicating this more clearly, he says:

“For we hear that some among you walk restlessly, doing nothing but acting as busybodies.”

(Ambrose.) By saying “acting as busybodies,” he means that they abuse their idleness by devoting themselves to scrutinizing the lives of others. He rejects this as improper and commands them to separate themselves from such people, saying that they are not even worthy to eat if they are unwilling to work. Expounding the matter more fully, he adds:

“Now those who are such we command and beseech through our Lord Jesus Christ to work quietly and eat their own bread.”

He does not simply say that they should work, but adds “quietly,” referring to what they were removing: they were not to busy themselves inquisitively with the lives of others. For he wanted them to work without any curiosity at those tasks by which they could provide for their own support.

(Cassian.) After so much evangelical strictness, he now explains why he had prefaced all these matters:

“For we hear that some among you walk restlessly, doing nothing but acting as busybodies.”

He is never content to declare that those who refuse to devote themselves to work are corrupted by only one disease. In the First Epistle he calls them disorderly and says that they do not walk according to the tradition they received from him. He also defines them as restless and as eating bread without paying for it.

Here again he says: “We hear that some among you walk restlessly,” and immediately adds the second sickness, which is the root of this disorder: “doing nothing.” He also names a third disease, which grows from the second like a little branch: “but acting as busybodies.”

Therefore he hastens to apply an appropriate correction to the fuel of so many vices. Setting aside the apostolic authority he had used shortly before, he returns again to the heart of a compassionate father or merciful physician. As though addressing his sons and adopted children with a salutary prescription, he applies the remedies of health, saying:

“Now those who are such we solemnly charge and beseech in the Lord Jesus to work quietly and eat their own bread.”

Like a highly skilled physician, he cures the causes of so many ulcers, which arise from the root of idleness, by one saving command to work. Knowing that the other unhealthy conditions springing from the same root must immediately be extinguished once the principal source of the disease has been destroyed, he deals with them in the same way.

And because those who were such, refusing entirely to work, were carrying out in a seditious manner things that were improper, taking advantage of the fact that the generosity of others supplied them with what they needed—as though they belonged to the same faith, a point which, as we seemed to indicate in interpreting the First Epistle, he also makes clear—he adds something addressed to those who were providing for them:

“Now you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good.” (Ambrose.) This means: carry out your own proper work, and do not abandon the good work because of the wickedness of others. Even if they are evil in their purpose, your reward will be equal on account of your own purpose, when you give to them. [Col. 0579C]

(Cassian.) “Do not,” he says, “grow weary in doing good”—that is, continue to extend your kindness toward them if, perhaps, they neglect to observe what we have said. Just as he rebuked those who were weak, lest, dissolved in idleness, they devote themselves to restlessness and meddling, so he warns those who are sound that the kindness which, by the Lord’s command, we are obliged to extend to good and evil alike must not be withheld from them if some wicked persons should refuse to turn to sound teaching. Rather, they should not cease to benefit and encourage them, both by words of consolation and correction and by their customary acts of kindness and humanity.

Yet, again, lest some, provoked by this leniency, should disdain to obey his commands, he mingles apostolic severity with it and says: “But if anyone does not obey our word through this letter, mark him, and [Col. 0579D] do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed.” And, warning them—for the sake of his own reverence and the common good—what they ought to observe and with what caution [Col. 0580A] they should keep the apostolic commands, he immediately adds the leniency of a most indulgent father and teaches them what affection, as toward their brothers, they ought likewise to retain toward those mentioned above: “Do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother.”

(Ambrose.) “I want you,” he says, “to do this: not to treat him as an enemy, but in every way—by rebuke, exhortation, and instruction—to bring him back to what is honorable.”

(Cassian.) He mingled paternal affection with judicial severity and tempered the sentence pronounced with apostolic rigor by merciful gentleness. For he commands that the person who has scorned to obey his instructions be marked and that they not associate with him; nevertheless, he does not command this to be done out of hatred, but with a view to brotherly love and their correction. “Do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed”: he who was not corrected by my gentle commands may at least, being shamed by your public separation from him, begin at last to be recalled to the path of salvation.

“Now may the God of peace himself give you peace always in every way. The Lord be with you all. Amen.”

(Ambrose.) Then he prays that peace be granted to them by God, so that they may always possess it and so that it may always be present with them in every way through God.

“My greeting is in the hand of Paul.” He called the subscription the greeting. For in place of what we customarily write—“In health,” and so forth—he always writes, “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Thus he calls this the greeting; for he does not appear to have greeted anyone in his letter: “This is the sign in every letter. This is how I write: The grace [Col. 0580C] of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.”

Therefore I use this as a kind of seal in every letter, writing with my own hand what I have also done in this letter, so that no one may doubt that these are my letters. He seems to have added this at this point not without a specific reason, but because those who were speaking about the consummation of the age and saying that it was near were persuading them as though they were also claiming, on the basis of the Apostle’s letter, that he had indicated the same thing. He himself had already indicated this above, writing that they should not be persuaded by those who promised, through the Apostle’s letter, that they were saying such things. Therefore, at this point he necessarily indicated which things he had written to them, since it was sufficient to show that the letter was his by means of the greeting; and also that it was his custom to subscribe in his own hand, so that they should accept nothing contrary to what had been written here if anyone should persuade them of the same things.

# BOOK TWENTY-THREE: EXPOSITION OF THE FIRST LETTER TO TIMOTHY

[Col. 0579]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0579D]

“The holy apostle Paul left the blessed Timothy at Ephesus”—namely, so that, traveling throughout all Asia, he might govern all the churches there. Accordingly, in the first letter which we are now undertaking to interpret, he writes to him, at the very beginning of the letter immediately admonishing him to instruct his people with the utmost care not to heed those who wish to introduce the observance of the law among Christians. In what follows he teaches him what it is appropriate for him to do, having undertaken the administration of the churches.

For this reason he instructs him about everything, teaching him what sort of person each one ought to be who is appointed in any way to the ecclesiastical order or appears to exercise a ministry. Explaining this most carefully, he instructs him about what is becoming to a presbyter and what to a deacon, what sort of widows ought to be, and likewise instructing him about all the rest that was appropriate, he appears to have drawn forth a complete teaching in the letter itself. In the middle portion of the letter he also recalled certain matters concerning doctrine, [Col. 0581B] about which he clearly saw that instruction was especially necessary for him.

He left out nothing that could contribute to the common adornment, provided that someone should wish to read or preserve his writings with suitable care. In my judgment, therefore, all bishops ought to memorize this letter with the greatest care. Thus instructed diligently, they could learn to govern or administer the churches of the Lord God as is fitting, serving the laws of the blessed Paul. For no one should doubt that what he then wrote to Timothy, leaving him at Ephesus and appointing him over all the churches that appeared to be in Asia, can be applied to every bishop who is believed to govern the church of God.

The exposition must therefore be begun which it is fitting for us to unfold in sections, since the argument seems to have been sufficiently expressed by us in these introductory remarks.

## CHAPTER ONE

The Apostle warns Timothy not to attend to genealogies and legal observances. He gives thanks to God for his call to the apostolate and urges him to resist teachers of falsehood.

“Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus according to the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, to Timothy, his beloved son in the faith: grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.”

(Ambrose.) The blessed Paul appears, in the superscription of this letter, contrary to his custom, to have added “grace,” “peace,” and “mercy,” using this addition of words because of the greater affection which he seemed to have for Timothy. Having completed the superscription, he begins in this way:

“As I urged you to remain at Ephesus when I was going to Macedonia, so that you might instruct certain persons not to teach otherwise, nor to attend to myths and endless genealogies, which produce questions rather than God’s stewardship, which is in faith.”

Above all, the humility of the blessed Paul deserves admiration. Writing to his disciple, he did not say, “As I commanded,” or “approved,” or “said,” but simply said, “As I urged,” or “As I entreated.” Thus it was the practice of those holy men to invite everyone to the work of piety by entreaty, so that they might also instill eagerness in them with a certain delight of spirit. Entreaty, indeed, knows how to encourage even the very sluggish, whereas the weight of a command often appears to have made even one who is already eager sluggish.

But attention must also be paid to the meaning of the words. For he does not mean what the surface meaning seems to indicate: that he urged Timothy to remain at Ephesus so that he might command certain persons not to teach otherwise. He did not leave him there for this alone, but so that he might do everything with that solicitude which he had been appointed to exercise toward the churches of God. He also appears to have written to him in the letter about all these matters.

Two meanings are intertwined here. First, the exclamation is expressed incompletely, in such a way that what has been said might nevertheless appear to be a single statement. He means: “As I urged you, when I was setting out for Macedonia, to remain at Ephesus, giving careful attention to those who are there—and this is what you are doing—fulfilling the task entrusted to you and diligently completing everything that pertains to their common correction.”

This, then, is what he wishes to signify by the words, “As I urged you to remain at Ephesus when I was going to Macedonia.” I have shown that the statement is expressed incompletely, because the blessed Paul uses his customary manner of speaking to him, explaining as best he could what seemed appropriate to him. He had not studied rhetorical discipline, nor did he think it suitable for him to devote himself to such a style.

Then he added, “So that you might instruct certain persons,” and what follows. By this he says what he especially wished to arrange above all else. What, then, was it? “I want you,” he says, “above all to dissuade those who desire to teach something else in the church, contrary to what the rule of piety requires.”

It is evident what he means by “that you might instruct certain persons”: he is speaking of his own people, not outsiders. It was not Timothy’s principal task at that time to instruct foreign teachers of piety, not merely to rebuke those who made no use of contrary doctrines, but rather to endure many things from them in return.

He says that they ought not to teach otherwise, speaking of those who had believed from the circumcision and who, speaking of many things as though on behalf of the law, attempted to teach the Gentiles contrary to the practice of Christian doctrine. In nearly all the letters one may find the blessed Paul writing at length about them, because at that time there were many who proposed such teaching. Anyone may recognize this more clearly by reading through our interpretation, which we appear to have unfolded in almost all the letters, in which we showed that the blessed Paul spoke at length about these matters.

When he says, “not to attend to myths and endless genealogies,” he speaks generally about everyone, but especially about those who are from the Gentiles. By attending to the things said by the Jews, they often appeared to do harm to the doctrine of piety. The Galatians are also found to have suffered this, since, along with observing the other things prescribed in the law, they did not even refrain from circumcision.

He says that they ought not to attend to genealogies because at that time the Jews devoted great effort to showing that Christ had descended from Abraham and David in accordance with the succession of the promises. For this reason they also attempted to recall ancient lineages, saying, “How this one arose from that one,” and, “How that one was born from this one.” Many were consequently thrown into confusion by these things, especially those who had believed from the Gentiles and were unable to know anything about the ancient books with sufficient care.

“Command these people,” he says, “not to attend to genealogies.” He rightly calls them “endless,” because those who explained such things could turn their discourse now in one direction and now in another: now speaking of the ancestry of one person, now of another, and again passing from the first to the second. This necessarily happens in genealogies whenever someone wishes to explain a lineage descending through many generations.

He calls them endless because they have no limit, nor can opportunities for speech cease in such questions. He also calls these opportunities for narration “myths,” because they contain nothing necessary in themselves, but only a certain empty and fabulous account: that one person begot another from this woman.

Explaining what he means by “endless,” he rightly adds: “Which produce questions rather than God’s stewardship, which is in faith.” The narration and concern devoted to such matters, he says, seem to produce abundant and endless questions, but they prevent people from knowing God’s stewardship, by which God graciously chose to accomplish our salvation through Christ. Those who hear ought especially to attend to this with complete faith, since they can possess proof of it in the realities themselves.

Since their teaching has by no means been omitted, it is not appropriate to investigate the succession of families. That these things were then harmful is clearly proved by the accounts of the Evangelists Matthew and Luke. Both explained how Christ’s generation descended from antiquity, yet they did not arrive at David by the very same genealogy. Matthew appears to have traced one genealogy descending from David, whereas Luke was compelled to arrive at another account, because of the questions that were then especially being raised. Anyone may learn this with the greatest care by reading through our interpretation, which we appear to have set forth concerning the Gospels.

After saying what it was appropriate to command them and from what they ought to restrain themselves, he briefly states what he saw that needed correction among the faithful, so that he might direct their diligence:

“The goal of the commandment is love from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith.”

“I especially want you to command them what is also the goal of our teaching: that they should withdraw from every empty question, should not attend to those who wish to tell certain fabulous tales, and should preserve sound and whole love toward the common Lord, with a pure heart and a perfect conscience.”

Showing what great harm arises among those who do not stand rightly in relation to the doctrine of piety, he adds:

“From these things some have gone astray and turned aside to empty talk, desiring to be teachers of the law, though they understand neither what they say nor the matters about which they make assertions.”

“By pursuing this,” he says, “some have indeed become outsiders to piety, while devoting themselves to empty talk. They pretend to teach the things of the law, although they have no understanding of what they themselves say.”

And since it seemed likely that they did not understand the matters about which they spoke, he rightly adds, “nor the matters about which they make assertions.” For those who do not know what they ought to speak about appear to be ignorant of their own concerns.

And lest he should appear to accuse the law, he adds:

“We know that the law is good, if someone uses it lawfully.”

“I say this not to accuse the law, but to rebuke their foolishness, since they do not know how to use it. If someone uses it as is fitting, I acknowledge that the law is exceedingly worthy of praise and venerable.”

And lest he should again appear to introduce the observance of the law as though it had some continuing use, he adds:

“Knowing this: that the law is not laid down for the righteous but for the unrighteous and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the wicked and defiled, for parricides and matricides, for murderers, for fornicators, for those who have intercourse with males, for kidnappers, liars, and perjurers.”

I know this: the law contains the renunciation of improper actions, for it was given to prohibit every iniquity. The law’s definition is necessary for those who sin, since it teaches them not to do such things. But for those who have once been justified and have become superior to every sin, the law is superfluous, since they possess the direction of the law in the highest degree.

This is the case with us, who await the resurrection and incorruption [Col. 0584C], together with which we shall remain in everlasting immutability, no longer able to sin. For this reason we do not need the law. Therefore, for us who have believed and have already come to exist in those realities through the form of baptism, the definition of the law is superfluous. We are no longer instructed by the law to abstain from sins; rather, we are taught to imitate those realities in whose form we now already stand.

After listing the sins, he states the matter even more clearly:

“And whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine, according to the gospel of the glory of the blessed God, which was entrusted to me.”

He means that everything evil is contrary to our doctrine, which we rightly make conform to the gospel of glory. By “glory” he means that which will be present for human beings in the age to come, when they will pass into a better condition:

“For what is sown in corruption will rise in incorruption; what is sown in weakness will rise in power; what is sown in dishonor will rise in glory.”

He calls the preaching concerning the gospel “the gospel,” and he rightly says that it was entrusted to him, so that he might teach all people to await these things through the faith that is in Christ.

He calls it the glory of the blessed God because he says that it is bestowed on us by him. In this passage he rightly calls God blessed, because he possesses blessedness in his own nature on account of his immutability, while he grants the same to us freely.

This, then, is the preaching concerning the future realities which we are all taught to await. By following the corresponding teaching, we prepare in the present age to imitate that life, guarding ourselves from sins as far as we are able. For, by the form of baptism, those who believe are permitted to become sharers in those good things. The law is superfluous for such people: first, because they await the enjoyment of those very realities in which they already exist and therefore do not need the law’s definition; and second, because the faith concerning those realities appears to surpass every form of lawful teaching and can lead them to every precaution of virtue.

Then, as though proceeding from what he has said, he turns to giving thanks to God, because the gospel was entrusted to him although he was not worthy. He uses what had happened to him as an illustration of his words and at the same time shows that Christ saved everyone, establishing them in the future good things in which they will remain immutable and henceforth without sin, so that the law will appear superfluous for them.

After saying, “According to the gospel of the glory of the blessed God, which was entrusted to me,” he adds:

“And I give thanks to him who strengthened me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he considered me faithful and appointed me to the ministry, although I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent.”

“I give,” he says, “many thanks for these things to Christ, who strengthened me for such a work, so that I might preach the gospel to the whole world. This could not have happened if I had not been made worthy of his cooperation. And because, by his revelation, he handed me over to piety and was pleased to impose another ministry upon me for salvation, he considered me worthy, even though I was still devoted to persecuting, blaspheming, and insulting those who believed in him.”

Emphasizing this, he says:

“But I received mercy because I acted ignorantly in unbelief. Yet the grace of our Lord abounded exceedingly, together with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.”

“But such was I,” he says. “Yet having obtained mercy, I was deemed worthy of great things. God assigned my sins to my ignorance, while receiving me, through his goodness, into faith and love.”

(Gregory.) Even when the saints stand upon the heights of virtues, they consider the place from which they have been raised, and they do not despise the lowliness of another’s weakness. Hence it is written in Job: “He commands the snow to descend upon the earth, and the winter rains and the rain of his strength” (Job 37).

Thus, just as waters return to the earth from which they were taken, so the righteous, condescending to sinners, do not cease to remember what they once were. Paul was certainly still on earth when he understood the law in a carnal way, but when he was led to heavenly things he was changed into snow, because what he had previously understood in weakness he transformed into the solidity of true understanding. Yet, condescending to his brothers, he returned, as it were, to the lowly places like snow. And because, after reaching the heights of virtues, he recognizes how unworthy he had been, he says:

“Although I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent, I received mercy because I acted ignorantly in unbelief.”

See how gently he remembers his weakness, so that he may bear patiently with the weakness of others. For, just as water returned to the earth from which it had been taken after rising into the heavens, so Paul, after the many mysteries of his contemplation, remembers that he was a sinner, in order that he might humbly benefit sinners.

(Ambrose.) After giving thanks for himself, as he appears to have done in order to demonstrate the foregoing matters, recounting what had happened to him, he adds:

“This saying is trustworthy and worthy of complete acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.”

It is therefore true that Christ came for the salvation of sinners, as can be perceived from my own case. By calling it a trustworthy saying, he says that the word is true. He calls it worthy of acceptance because everyone, whoever he may be, will receive it if he believes that God saves human beings through mercy, when he permits sinners to remain because of their weakness.

God’s goodness is especially acceptable to everyone, since it is exceedingly great and has become much more abundant toward us. And everyone who delights in these words—being human himself and wishing to hear good things about human beings—does so all the more. Developing the same point more fully, he adds:

“But for this reason I received mercy, so that Christ Jesus might first display in me complete patience as an example for those who would believe in him for eternal life.”

For this reason he chose me as a minister of the calling of the Gentiles, so that through me he might make it clear to everyone that, through God’s mercy and goodness, all who believe in him will be saved as they seek eternal life.

If such a person was chosen as a minister of the teaching, what will those be like who are called to piety through him? And, as though showing by these words that all will then truly be saved through mercy, when they have become outsiders to sin and appear no longer to need the law, he confirms what he had proposed: that it is not appropriate to quarrel about the law, but that the believer in Christ should await the future and, according to his ability, order his life in the present age in conformity with those future realities.

Thus the law is not so necessary for them in the present, provided that, looking toward the future, they wish to take care concerning virtue. He concluded his discourse with thanksgiving, since he showed that great blessings are present for us. Therefore he says:

“Now to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, to God alone, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.”

That is, it is right for us to praise him for all the good things, since he appears to be the author of such great blessings for us. Yet the hymn does not set down any name in an absolute form. It calls God the King of the ages because of the eternity of the future realities; it calls him incorruptible because of the incorruption which we await for ourselves; and it calls him invisible because the good things that are awaited are not seen. Thus, from the attributes belonging to God, he skillfully suggests that we should believe in the things that will come to us from him, just as above he called him blessed in confirmation of the blessedness that will come to us.

But because the Apostle did not establish any of these matters according to his own judgment, rather gathering them together—as we showed in the interpretation—against those who attempted to corrupt the simplicity of doctrine by their teaching of the law, he wrote to Timothy so that he might command his people not to tolerate those who teach such things and not to attend to those who wish them to be taught. He shows this more clearly in what follows, after adding:

“This command I entrust to you, my son Timothy.”

“This,” he says, “I entrust to you”—that is, I give you this command: teach these things and command your people not to attend to those who wish to deceive them and lead them over to the sect of the law.

And, showing that he did not appear to impose these things upon him without qualification, he adds:

“According to the prophecies previously made concerning you.”

By this, he says, I made your election known through divine revelation and entrusted to you the work of teaching. Then, lest he should appear to give him counsel uselessly after the prophecies, as though he no longer needed it, he adds:

“So that you may wage the good warfare in them, having faith and a good conscience.”

He elegantly shows prophecy to be a gift, but it will be your task to confirm that election by your work. Election, however, does not ordinarily exercise force over our will, since election could not help Judas, who possessed a wicked will.

Therefore remain firm in the doctrine. By this he means: have faith, and conduct yourself in them with a good conscience, so that you yourself are not led astray, that you do not shrink from teaching others, and that you are willing to suffer something for their sake if necessary. This will provide you with great assistance, and these graces will correspondingly choose such things.

Showing how great the disgrace is if someone does not possess a good conscience toward the doctrines, he says:

“Some, having rejected it, have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith.”

They possessed an unsuitable conscience concerning these matters, accepted the teaching of their opponents, and were thereby placed outside the faith. Since they remained uncertain in parts, they were shown to be outsiders to all piety.

And, in order to bring him into still greater fear, he specifically names those who had been such persons, whom he knew especially, beyond the others, to have written for the worse:

“Among them,” he says, “are Hymenaeus and Alexander.”

And what happened to them?

“I handed them over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme.”

For when he says, “I handed them over to Satan,” he means, “I alienated them from the church.” In writing to the Corinthians he appears likewise to have said that such a person should be handed over to Satan, because those who are excluded from the church appear to be placed under Satan’s power. He calls alienation from the church “handing over to Satan,” thereby showing how great an evil it is to be excluded from the church.

And lest he should appear to have handed them over through some severity or to have been unwilling to receive their correction, he adds:

“So that they may learn not to blaspheme.”

He did not present this as the cause, but used the expression according to its ordinary sense. “I excluded them,” he says, “from the church, not preventing their correction, but even greatly hoping that this might happen: that, somehow, having been made better by rebuke, they might learn not to blaspheme, but return to the truth.”

Writing similarly to the Corinthians, he adds: “For the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved.”

By this he means: “For this reason I drove him away from the church, so that, if somehow by repentance he should afflict himself in the present life and thereby become worthy, he might be able to attain future salvation.”

Having spoken thus far about the precaution concerning doctrine which he considered necessary for many in the present life, he now begins to speak further about those matters that seemed to pertain to the common adornment and about what must necessarily be fulfilled in the church—that is, prayers. He says these things first because he considered it necessary first to teach them what they ought suitably to do. Then he discusses the conduct of life, beginning in this way.

## CHAPTER TWO

Timothy is instructed about the practice and manner of prayer, and he speaks of prayer with regard to the people under his care.

[Col. 0588B] “I urge, then, first of all, that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made.” Above all, he says, I urge that which you ought especially to know as a matter of practice, so that, knowing what is appropriate, you may be able to do what is appropriate. He speaks of prayers, supplications, and petitions according to the variety of petitions; there is also an abuse of terms through their changeability. For either we ask God to grant us good things—which he called “prayers”—or for release from evils—which he named “supplications.” And when he also said “petitions,” he spoke with complete consistency, for above all we strive to advance toward works of virtue, whereas the things opposed to this are many and persistent. One reason is that the assault of demons seeks in various ways to turn us away from the good; another [Col. 0588C] is the distress of the passions that seems to dwell within us. Through these we are excluded from good things and, against our purpose, are often shut up in things that are not fitting for us. But it is necessary for us, who endure much struggle on this account, to have recourse to God, who is able by his assistance to calm everything that contributes to our distress.

(Augustine.) He called this “petition,” because we continually pray to God on behalf of the things that oppose us; he compared this to the widow who asked to be freed from the power of her adversary. Many things may be said here that ought not to be rejected, but I choose to understand these words as referring to what the whole—or nearly the whole—Church regularly does. Let us take “supplications” to mean those that we make in the celebration of the sacraments, before that which is on God’s table begins to be blessed; “prayers,” when it is blessed and sanctified and broken for distribution—a petition that nearly the whole Church concludes with the Lord’s Prayer; and “intercessions,” or, as your copies have it, “petitions,” when the people are blessed. For then the bishops or advocates commend those entrusted to them, through the laying on of hands, to the most merciful power. When these things have been completed and so great a sacrament has been received, thanksgiving concludes everything; the Apostle also commended it as the final element in these words.

The principal reason for saying this was that, having touched upon and indicated these matters briefly, no one might think that what follows was to be neglected: “for all people, for kings [Col. 0589A] and all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all godliness and charity.” For no one, in accordance with the weakness of human thought, should suppose that these things ought not to be done for those through whom the Church was suffering persecution, since the members of Christ were to be gathered from every kind of human being. Hence he adds and says: “For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” And lest anyone should say that there could be a way of salvation in good conduct and in the worship of the one almighty God without participation in the body and blood of Christ, he says: “For there is one God and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus.” Thus what he had said—“he desires all people to be saved”—is not to be understood as accomplished in any other way except through the mediator: not the God who was always the Word, but the human being Jesus Christ, when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. [Col. 0589B]

(Isaac.) I think that all the forms of prayer cannot be comprehended without great contrition of heart, purity of soul, and illumination by the Holy Spirit.

(RAB.) There are as many forms as there are states and qualities by which a single soul—or rather, all souls—can worship God. And therefore, although we know that, because of the dullness of our heart, we cannot discern all the forms of prayer, nevertheless we have attempted to arrange them as far as the modest extent of our experience has been able. For according to the degree of purity in which each mind advances, and according to the quality of the state into which it is either inclined by what has preceded or renewed through its own diligence, these forms themselves are also reshaped at every moment. It is therefore absolutely certain that no one can always offer prayers of one uniform kind.

For one person prays in one way when he is cheerful, in another when he is weighed down by grief or despair; in one way when he flourishes through spiritual progress, in another when he is crushed beneath the burden of assaults; in one way when he seeks forgiveness of sins, in another when he asks for the acquisition of grace or of any virtue, or certainly when he pleads for the destruction of some vice; in one way when he is pierced by consideration of Gehenna and fear of the coming judgment, in another when he is inflamed by hope and desire for future blessings; in one way when he is in necessities and dangers, in another when he is living in tranquility and security; in one way when he is illuminated by revelations of heavenly mysteries. He prays differently when he is constrained by barrenness of virtues and dryness of understanding.

And so, having arranged these matters concerning the quality of prayer—not as fully as the magnitude of the subject demands, but only as the shortness of time permits, or as the weakness of our intellect and the dullness of our heart are able to contain—we now face a greater difficulty: to explain individually the forms of prayer that the Apostle distinguished in four parts, saying: “I urge, then, first of all, that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made.” It must by no means be doubted that these were divided by the Apostle in this way for a reason. First, we must investigate what is signified by supplication, prayer, petition, and thanksgiving; then we must inquire whether these four forms are to be taken up equally by the one who prays—that is, whether everyone ought to utter each of the supplications, petitions, or thanksgivings—or whether one person should offer supplications to God, another petitions, and another thanksgivings, according to the measure of his age, in which each mind advances through directed effort. Therefore, the properties of the nouns and verbs themselves must first be examined, and the difference between prayer, supplication, and petition discussed; then it must similarly be investigated whether they are to be offered individually or together. Third, we must inquire whether the order itself, which has been arranged in this way by the Apostle’s authority, teaches the hearer anything further, or whether this distinction is to be taken simply and thought to have been arranged by him without further significance. [Col. 0590A]

“I urge,” he says, “first of all, that supplications be made.” Supplication is an imploring, or a petition for sins, by which each person, pierced by remorse over sins committed either recently or in the past, begs for forgiveness.

Prayers are those by which we offer or vow something to God. In Greek this is called εὐχή, that is, a vow. Each of us fulfills this when, renouncing the world, we promise that, dead to all worldly actions and conduct, we will serve the Lord with the full intention of our heart. We pray when we promise that, content with renouncing secular honor and despising earthly riches, we will cling to the Lord in complete contrition of heart and poverty of spirit. We pray when we promise that we will offer perpetual purity of body or steadfast patience. Or we pray when we vow that the roots of anger or sadness, which bring about death, have been utterly torn from our heart. If we fail to do this, though we long to be set free and return to our former vices, the reason for our prayers and vows is recited against us. It is therefore better for us not to make a vow than to make one and fail to fulfill it. In accordance with the Greek, this may be expressed: “It is better for you not to pray than to pray and fail to fulfill your vow.” [Col. 0590C]

In third place are placed petitions, which we are accustomed to utter on behalf of others when we are in spiritual fervor: for our loved ones, certainly, or when we ask for the peace of the whole world. To use the Apostle’s own words, this is when we supplicate for all people, for kings, and for all who are in high positions.

In fourth place, then, are placed thanksgivings. The mind offers these either when it recalls God’s past benefits, or when present benefits are being fulfilled, or when it looks forward to what great things God has prepared for those who love him. In ineffable transports it gives thanks to the Lord; and sometimes prayers are poured forth with greater abundance for this reason, when, gazing with pure eyes upon the rewards reserved for the future, our spirit is stirred to pour out thanks with immense joy.

From these four forms the occasions for rich supplications are usually generated. From the form of supplication, which arises from remorse for sins; from the state of prayer, which flows from confidence in one’s offerings and from the completion of future things through purity of conscience; from petition, which proceeds from the ardor of charity; and from thanksgiving, which is generated by consideration of his benefits, greatness, and compassion—we very often know fervent prayers and fiery petitions to emerge.

Thus all the forms mentioned above are found to be useful and necessary for all people, so that one and the same person may at one time emit pure and fervent supplications, at another prayers, at another petitions, and may express varied affections. Nevertheless, the first seems especially to belong to beginners, who are still pierced and tormented by the goads and memory of their vices; the second to those who, already advancing spiritually and desiring virtues, stand at a certain elevation of mind. [Col. 0591A] The third belongs to those who, fulfilling their vows through their deeds, are moved by consideration of the fragility of others and by the zeal of charity to intercede for them. The fourth belongs to those who have already driven the thorn of a guilty conscience from their hearts and, in worldly affairs, recall with the purest mind the Lord’s acts of generosity and mercies—which he either granted in the past, bestows at present, or prepares for the future. They are carried with the most fervent heart toward that fiery prayer which the mouth of all people can neither comprehend nor express.

Sometimes, however, the mind that advances toward that true disposition of purity and has begun to take root in it conceives all these things together. Sweeping through them all like an incomprehensible and most consuming flame, it pours out ineffable prayers to God with the purest strength. The Spirit himself, interceding with inexpressible groanings, sends these prayers to God, while we remain ignorant. In the single moment of that hour the mind conceives and pours out in supplication things so great that, I do not say, it cannot recount them fully with its mouth, but at another time it cannot even recall them in its own mind.

Hence, at whatever level a person may stand, he is sometimes found to utter pure and intent prayers. For from that first and humble order, which consists in the remembrance of the future judgment and is established in the souls of those who still lie under the punishment and fear of terror, he is sometimes so pierced for a moment that he is filled with no less spiritual joy through the richness of supplication than the one who, surveying and traversing God’s acts of generosity through the purity of his heart, is dissolved in ineffable joy and gladness. For, according to the Lord’s saying, he begins to love more because he recognizes that more has been forgiven him.

(Ambrose.) Since he said “thanksgivings,” it is evident that thanksgiving can differ from prayer. For in one way a person makes a petition for what is lacking in daily use, whereas thanksgiving is offered for what has already been granted. You are taught for whom these things ought to be done.

“For all people.” He commands them to be concerned in common for all. For the person who is commanded to do these things for all people is evidently commanded also to extend concern to all. Then he proceeds to those who seem to be highest among human beings. [Col. 0592A]

“For kings,” he says, “and all who are in high positions.” And, showing that this too is their advantage, he adds: “so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all godliness and sobriety.” For if they live in peace, as is appropriate, it is possible for us also to devote ourselves to godliness and to a sober life, bringing tranquility about and persuading them to act in this way, just as he himself commanded. The common concern for all people throughout the whole world ought to be extended, and common benefits ought to be regarded as those things that belong to everyone.

“But this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior.” He has sufficiently persuaded them to think in this way, since this also pleases God. Therefore, demonstrating that these things please God, he adds: “who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” Since God desires these things for all people, no one can contradict them. It is evident that he desires all to be saved, because he also watches over all. It is therefore necessary for us to imitate his care for all, if indeed we are hastening fully to think in a manner like God’s. And, showing this in every respect, he adds: [Col. 0592B]

“But there is one God.” That is, because he is Lord of all—not Lord of some but not of others. Therefore, it is impossible for him to despise certain people as though they were alien to him.

“There is one mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus.”

(Augustine.) Thus the false mediator—the Devil—through whom, by God’s secret judgments, human pride deserves to be deceived, has one thing in common with human beings, namely, sin; he wants to appear to have something else in common with God, so that, since he is not covered by the mortality of flesh, he may display himself as immortal. But because “the wages of sin is death” (Romans 6), this is what he has in common with human beings, so that together they may be condemned to death.

But the true mediator, whom your hidden mercy, Lord, revealed to human beings and sent so that, by his example, they might also learn humility itself—the mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus—appeared between mortal sinners and the immortal Just One: mortal with human beings, just with God. Thus, since the wages of justice are life and peace, by the justice united to God he might abolish the death of the justified wicked, a death that he chose to share with them. He was shown in this way to the ancient saints, so that they might be saved through faith in his future passion, just as we are saved through faith in his past passion. Insofar as he is human, he is a mediator; insofar as he is the Word, he is not a mediator, for he is equal to God, is God with God, and, together with the Holy Spirit, is one God.

(Ambrose.) But that mediator who endeavors to join us human beings to God is also one and the same person, and for this reason he is human according to nature. Most appropriately, and especially in this passage, he called him human, so that he might demonstrate from nature the community of the gift, since all must necessarily confess that, being a part of the whole according to a nature common to all, he can bestow the gift through likeness of nature.

Therefore, taking this as though it had already been brought into confession, he adds: “who gave himself as a redemption for all, a testimony at his appointed times.” For he gave himself for all; he did not consent to undergo death for only some, but, wishing to confer a common benefit upon all, he deigned to undergo suffering. According to the time at which he suffered, he calls the suffering itself a “testimony,” while by “his appointed times” he means the time at which he suffered. He asserts that it was necessary for them in every respect, showing that it is appropriate to extend common concern to all people, since God also cares for all. For not only is he Lord of all in common, but, what is greater, Christ himself also seems to draw near to all alike through the particularity of his nature. He bestowed a benefit upon all by undergoing suffering for all; and he confirms this further [Col. 0593B] through the things that concern him.

“In this,” he says, “I was appointed a herald and an apostle—I speak the truth, I do not lie—a teacher of the nations in faith and truth.” Therefore I too was appointed an apostle for their sake, so that I might bring this teaching itself to the knowledge of all people and bring everyone to approach the faith of Christ, through whom these things have been bestowed upon us. I was appointed an apostle especially for the instruction and introduction of the nations, so that he may mean all people who are in every place.

He appropriately inserted the words “I speak the truth, I do not lie,” so that what he was saying might also make his affirmation credible. When he said “in faith and truth,” he means: I was appointed teacher of the nations for this purpose, so that I might teach them both faith and truth. Thus, having established in every respect that it is necessary and appropriate for those who come together for the same purpose to pray in common for all, extending providence toward all in imitation of God, he proceeds to discuss what their discipline ought to be. He distinguishes them according to sex, dividing them into men and women. First, appropriately, he speaks about men, explaining the reason for distinguishing them while endeavoring to establish common laws of virtue for them, as we shall be able to learn more clearly from what follows.

“I therefore want men to pray in every place, lifting pure hands”—or, according to another edition, “raising holy hands”—“without anger and dispute.” [Col. 0593D] What he said, “in every place,” should be referred to the statement “raising holy hands.” For he means: I want their discipline to be such that, whenever they appear to pray in whatever place, they raise holy hands to God.

It is evident that by “holy hands” he meant a disposition of mind. Therefore, explaining how the raising of hands can be holy, he adds “without anger and dispute,” briefly defining perfect virtue in these words. When he said “without anger,” he meant hating no human being. When he said “dispute,” he meant that they should not doubt in a faithful mind that they will receive what they ask for. In the one case he appears to have confirmed the love that is directed toward one’s neighbor; in the other, the love directed toward God. For the person who firmly believes that God, without envy, gives us whatever we ask of him will naturally also love him as the giver of good things.

(Isaac.) For this reason, whatever we do not want to interrupt our prayer, we should hasten to drive out from the inner shrine of our breast, so that we may fulfill the Apostle’s command: “Pray without ceasing, and in every place lift pure hands without anger and dispute.” Otherwise we shall not be able to fulfill this command unless our mind, purified from the contamination of every vice and devoted only to the virtues as natural goods, feeds continually upon contemplation of almighty God. When, in this purity, the mind’s understanding is absorbed, so to speak, it is transformed from an earthly condition into a spiritual and angelic likeness. Whatever it begins to insert, whatever it considers, whatever it does, will be the purest and most sincere prayer.

Then, speaking about women, he adds: “Likewise also the women.”

(Ambrose.) He rightly said “likewise,” showing that he did not distinguish them for this reason. For he wants this quality to be present in women just as in men. But he also speaks of other matters by which he especially seemed to need to exhort women. Hence he adds: “in dress, adornment, with modesty and chastity.” They are not to adorn themselves with braided or plaited hair, gold, pearls, or costly clothing, but with what is fitting for women who profess to worship God through good works.

Through all these words he means that women too ought to exercise the same diligence, saying that women who strive to worship God should display modesty and chastity together even in the appearance of their clothing. This is what he says: “in dress, with adornment, with modesty and sobriety.” They should not hasten to impose an external ornament upon themselves, as is customary, from gold, pearls, the arrangement of the hair, or costly clothing.

That it was necessary to exhort women about this more than men is evident. What he called “through good works,” in the phrase “in good works,” he appropriately set against the command “to adorn themselves.” Let it therefore be understood that they are not to adorn themselves with the things mentioned above, but with good works—the adornment fitting for those who profess to worship God. He rightly opposed good works to that adornment, since they are manifestly very different from it. Those ornaments are more deserving of blame, whereas this ornament necessarily earns praise.

Attention must be paid to the Apostle’s words: in rejecting the contrary things, he placed the worse first, saying, “not with curled or braided hair,” and then added the rest, saying, “with gold or silver or pearls or costly clothing.” The former may sometimes be done because of an inappropriate vanity, whereas the latter is done solely for adornment.

Having said what he especially considered appropriate to exhort women about, he adds something else that he could say to them but not to men in the same way:

“Let a woman learn in silence with all submission.” And, interpreting his statement more clearly, he adds: “I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over her husband, but to remain in silence.”

It is evident that he adds this concerning the state of affairs that existed in common assembly, since it was not appropriate for them to teach in the Church. Such an instruction was necessary at that time, when prophecies were also considered worthy of divine grace, through which women seemed to acquire—not merely, I should say, confidence to speak, but confidence to speak publicly. Therefore they necessarily had to be instructed not to misuse spiritual grace for the disturbance of the Church; what they ought to display for the benefit of others, they were to display within the walls of their homes.

For Paul in no way imposed these regulations upon their domestic conduct, nor did he forbid women to invite or teach their unbelieving husbands toward godliness, or to encourage believing husbands whose conduct was improper to perform works of virtue. For where would the statement be found: “For how do you know, woman, whether you will save your husband?” (1 Corinthians 7).

He therefore speaks, as I said, about the common order. For in a large part of the epistle he appears to have said many things that concern common assembly. Thus, abundantly demonstrating that it is not appropriate for women to teach in the common gathering but that they should remain in silence, he first establishes a proof from nature, asserting: “For Adam was formed first, then Eve.”

(Ambrose.) Second, he argues from what happened: “And Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, became a transgressor.” And indeed he too was deceived. But because he was arguing about the common order, distinguishing which sins had been committed by women and which by men, he rightly says that the man was not deceived but that the woman truly was deceived, since she appeared to have been the cause of his deception. They could not turn the accusation against her in this way, and he wished to avoid seeming to pronounce a judgment against the female sex as though that practice and authority belonged to every woman and made her useless for godliness.

She was deceived; justice and reason demand that this very thing be seen in all women.

“But she will be saved through the bearing of children, if she remains in faith, love, and sanctification with chastity.”

The origin, however, is not to be rejected. By saying “through the bearing of children,” he will demonstrate in what follows what he means concerning women: offspring may be considered worthy of salvation through those women who look toward godliness and remain in faith and love, living also in sanctification with chastity and exercising care over their lives.

When he said “she will be saved through the generation of children,” he is not speaking of Eve but of the female sex. For, while discussing the sex as a whole, he turns to the persons of Adam and Eve and proves from them that it is not appropriate for women, like men, to claim for themselves a role in the common assembly. And lest this appear to be an accusation against the sex, he rightly shows through what was said about the persons that the sex as such was not condemned, nor were women who wished to exercise proper diligence rejected from godliness. Rather, he means that they are to be admitted to godliness in the same way as men, but that in the common assembly they ought to occupy the later place.

He established from many matters that this is how it should be done. Thus, dividing the Church according to sex, he mentioned men separately and women separately. He appears to have included in a common exhortation even those things that could properly be applied to women, and in this way his common exhortation embraced everyone who belongs to the Church. For since he mentioned both men and women, it is evident that he included them all together.

From there he proceeds to distinctions of rank, because, as I said, he discusses everything for the common benefit. He mentions their order according to this division, showing that there are certain things which are appropriate for one person to perform and other things which are appropriate for another, so that nothing may seem lacking among the matters that ought to be done for the common benefit.

### CHAPTER III

Timothy is taught to arrange the ranks of the Church, both with respect to bishops and deacons and their wives; and the reason for the foregoing is set forth.

“Faithful is the saying.”

(Ambrose.) This saying is like the one expressed in the Gospel: “Amen, amen, I say to you.” Just as that expression is spoken as an affirmation and placed there for greater certainty, so this too is said to mean: “The saying is true and worthy of belief.” He says: “If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work.”

He rightly said “work,” and not “dignity.” For ecclesiastical functions are not dignities but work, since each of these offices—whether the episcopate, the diaconate, or anything else—has been established for the common benefit. The person who is appointed to one of them gives clear evidence that it is a work: when he is brought forward publicly, he assumes a function for the necessity and benefit of others.

(Gregory.) Therefore, while praising the desire, the Apostle immediately turns what he has praised into fear when he suddenly adds: “Therefore a bishop must be above reproach.” As he subsequently enumerates the virtues that are necessary, he makes clear what this blamelessness is. Thus he both encourages the desire and terrifies by his command, as though he were plainly saying: I praise what you seek, but first learn what you are seeking, lest, while neglecting to measure yourselves, your blameworthiness appear all the more disgraceful because you hasten to be seen by everyone at the summit of honor.

For the great craftsman of governance urges his hearers forward by encouragement and draws them back by fear, so that, by describing the height of blamelessness, he may restrain them from pride, and, by praising the office they seek, shape them toward a life worthy of it.

(Ambrose.) The foresight of blessed Paul is worthy of admiration in this passage. He did not say that no one should desire it, lest, by condemning every form of reverence in another way, he encourage everyone to rush toward it. Instead, he gave a middle formulation: “If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work.” He did not say only this: “I do not forbid the one who desires it.” For the person who desires it also strives toward an excellent work.

But he immediately shows what kind of person the one who wishes to attain this must be. From the very beginning he makes them anxious, even by what he said—that the person desires a good work. For he taught them first to understand that the work of the episcopate is indeed a work and that the person called to it is called to a task which he must necessarily fulfill with care.

He leads them into still greater fear through the statements that follow, since he expressed each requirement individually, indicating with what virtues of life the one who desires the episcopate must be adorned. His purpose was to persuade them to understand that the office must not be desired carelessly; rather, they must learn how it is appropriate to desire it, in accordance with his teaching.

What then? “A bishop must be above reproach.” It is evident that, by saying “above reproach,” he was not considering the intention of accusers but looking to the person’s life. For even Paul himself was unable to escape the accusations of his accusers.

[Col. 0597B] “The husband of one wife.” Some have understood this differently; but what is commonly observed is truly ridiculous. For if someone who has lived chastely takes a second wife, they do not admit such a man into the clergy; but if someone has lived licentiously and has lawfully taken one wife, he is both admitted and advanced in the clergy—although blessed Paul has plainly indicated elsewhere that second marriages ought to take place.

Every union contracted outside legitimate marriage is manifest fornication. For the moment I pass over the fact that, even after they have openly taken two legitimate wives, they baptize such men and indiscriminately advance them into the clergy, although in other matters they are thought to observe this rule—as though baptism caused a man no longer to have had two wives. They frequently do the same with men of corrupt judgment, thinking that they are doing an excellent thing if, after baptizing a man who has lived a licentious life, they advance him to clerical office, although he appears never to have possessed any diligence either in virtue or in piety.

To pass over in silence the question of baptism, for what purpose it is given—a matter which many do not even wish to examine—they ought to know this: blessed Paul is discussing the kind of civic and social life according to which, as he himself holds, a bishop ought to have lived; he is not discussing the remission of sins which is granted by grace to those who have received baptism. If they think that matters should be handled in this way, then all Paul’s legislation is superfluous, since the situation permits a man who has lived in any manner whatsoever to be baptized and immediately [Col. 0597D] advanced into the clergy—something Paul expressly rejected.

He wishes the man who is brought to the episcopate to appear to possess a testimony to his goodness from his former life: a man who has adhered throughout his life to the pursuit of virtue, or at least who has shown, through repentance, that he has passed from a worse life to a better condition. We shall be able to understand this more clearly from what follows.

Even today many do this, as though they were performing some great good. What he said, “the husband of one wife,” some understood in the following way—a view which I accept as more probable—because at that time there were many who legally had two wives at once, something which the Mosaic law permitted them to do. Many, however, who had one legitimate wife were not content with her. They also consorted with others, whether their own slave women or other women, indulging openly in lust; and this still happens today among those who are unwilling to exercise any care for chastity.

They therefore say that Paul meant this: the man who is advanced to the episcopate should be one who, after taking a wife, lived chastely with her, content with her alone and moved by natural desire only toward her; and if, having lived in this way, he lawfully took a second wife after the death of the first and continued to live with her in the same manner, he ought not, according to Paul’s definition, to be prevented from entering the episcopate.

Some have claimed that this was both defined and established by blessed Paul. I strongly reject their assertion and am not persuaded by them. The same man who commanded that second marriages should take place would not prohibit a man who, after the loss of his first wife, lawfully took a second wife according to due order from being advanced to the episcopate. For when he said, “I say to the unmarried and to widows,” joining the two together, he appears to have set forth one law for both. It is evident that he considered the condition of both to be the same. For what difference is there between having no wife at all because of the natural course of events and having had one, losing her, and then no longer having one?

Such reasoning rests more on circumstance than on the intention of the matter. The man who had a suitable wife for a long time certainly possessed her for as long as he wished; but the man who lost the same wife after a short time necessarily proceeded to a second marriage. These things happen through circumstance rather than through the direction of the will. Blessed Paul, examining this matter fully, therefore concluded that the man who is to be advanced to the episcopate must be known by such a life.

It is ridiculous to suppose that blessed Paul established a law which approves neither will nor intention, but makes distinctions according to circumstance and accident. If someone says that the Apostle, caring little about circumstance and accident, nevertheless wished to establish a rule about bishops with great care and precision—namely, that they must have had intercourse with only one wife—let him understand that, on this reasoning, it would likewise not be right to advance such a man even after baptism.

Baptism does not make it true that he has not had intercourse with two wives, nor does it cause people to think that he had only one wife—much less does it make them overlook the man who had one legitimate wife but lived licentiously with many others and was shown to have lived such a life, and therefore ought not to be advanced to the episcopate, even if, according to their claim, he has received baptism.

For if a man lawfully joined to two wives and, by the choice of his own purpose, lived chastely with them ought not to be received into the episcopate, then, because of the scrupulousness required in this matter, it is much more improper to advance to it a man who lived licentiously, on the grounds that he has received baptism.

These statements are sufficient concerning what he said: “the husband of one wife.” Necessity itself compelled us to explain its meaning more clearly, while rejecting the custom which appears to prevail among many. In what follows we shall disclose the Apostle’s fuller meaning from the very words, demonstrating above all the force of what has been said. For the rule of virtue and equity demands that the person who speaks about such a matter should not place custom above justice, but should examine Paul’s laws and apply to God those things which ought appropriately to be applied to him—since he always tests everything according to justice, not according to circumstance or accident, and knows how to judge each person according to his purpose and will.

Frequently, even the circumstances surrounding baptism come about in different ways: one person receives it earlier because of weakness or some other occasion, perhaps from childhood; another receives the grace of baptism after a long old age, having lived licentiously throughout his life but receiving baptism at the time of death. Meanwhile, the person who received baptism in childhood may have practiced virtue with great diligence, yet may have sinned in some matters—as a human being, and as commonly happens—and may even have fallen into a serious sin, having stumbled more through weakness than through the inclination of his soul.

It would be ridiculous if this person were harmed by circumstance and received no benefit from his diligence in good works simply because he received the grace of baptism in childhood, while the other, although he had suffered none of the things for which he sinned, should nevertheless appear illustrious in the life to come, and this because he happened to receive baptism at the end of his life, despite having shown no diligence in goodness.

These matters should be understood by those who do not know the reason for which baptism is given, nor have wished to examine the divine Scriptures. From them they could learn that Simon received no benefit from the gift of baptism because of the perversity of his purpose, since the Holy Spirit did not rest upon him; whereas it placed no obstacle in the thief’s way to his entering the dwelling of paradise, because of the excellence of his purpose, even though he had not received baptism.

I say this not to undermine baptism, but because of those who, under the pretext of baptism, strive to introduce great negligence into the judgment of the just God. Baptism is indeed great, because it contains the bestowal of so many blessings; and the purpose of each person is necessarily judged by the Lord God, from whom especially the gift of baptism can bring much assistance to those who receive it. It is not the nature of the water, but the faith of those who receive it, that ordinarily draws the perfect generosity of God into baptism.

Let us also examine the other things he says concerning the bishop.

“Sober.” That is, he must carefully attend to the things which ought to be done.

“Chaste.” Necessarily so, because he is appointed as a teacher jointly of men and women.

“Orderly.” By his conduct, bearing, and appearance, he shows in every respect what a bishop ought to be.

“Hospitable.” The bishop ought to be hospitable—not indiscriminately to every stranger, but to those who share the same faith. He ought to receive them, as people known to him and belonging to him, with the greatest care.

“Teaching.” His task is to teach people both virtue and piety. If he does not know how to teach these things, he appears not to understand what he professes to instruct others in. By “teaching,” however, he does not mean only a man capable of delivering a lengthy exposition of words in church—a task which very few are able to perform—but one who can, by whatever kind of speech, instruct everyone both generally and individually in the doctrines of piety, in piety itself, in virtue, and in the ways in which they ought to practice these things, through which they could especially attain growth.

If the bishop does not know these things, he will appear to differ in no way from the others, merely assuming the outward appearance of a teacher. Accordingly, writing shortly afterward, among the other things he said concerning the bishop, Paul says that he must “hold fast the faithful word according to the teaching, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it.” Thus he wishes the bishop to lack none of the qualities pertaining to teaching.

“Not given to wine.” He says this rightly. If it is necessary for every person, how much more for a bishop, who ought at all times to be ready for the performance of those duties which ought to be carried out.

“Not a striker.” He must not strike anyone indiscriminately, without cause, or through continual reproach. He wishes him to deal with each matter rather with moderation, as he also says in the Second Epistle: he must be moderate toward all, not remembering wrongdoing, teaching those who resist with gentleness. Even if it is sometimes necessary to rebuke, he should appear to do so because necessity itself requires it, and not from the ferocity of his own will. Thus he says, “but to be moderate.”

“Not quarrelsome.” He adds another qualification:

“Not greedy for money.” This is more necessary for a bishop than all the other qualities. If he lacks it, he will never exercise care concerning what is fitting, since greed for money urges people to do many things which ought not to be done.

“Managing his own household well.” That is, administering it and exercising care. Then, further demonstrating what this management means, he adds: “having his children in submission, with all chastity.” He immediately continues:

“If someone does not know how to preside over his own household, how will he care for the church of God?” Whoever does not know how to govern his own properly will be much less able to govern or teach the church.

When he said, “having children in submission,” he was not speaking about the children’s will, but about the father’s care: he must himself hasten to train them chastely and keep them obedient and submissive to him, giving them counsel concerning what is fitting. If, while the father’s will is of this character, the children wish to persist in what is worse, this is due to the perversity of their own will, not to the father’s fault.
