For he is speaking here about the father’s purpose, namely, that he should devote care to his own so that they may be trained with moderation, discipline, and seriousness.

From this it can be shown that he will likewise be concerned for everyone. The sons of Samuel are also seen to have lost their justice through love of money, yet we certainly do not blame Samuel for their purpose.

“Not a recent convert, lest, being puffed up, he fall into the judgment of the devil.” Some have judged very foolishly in this passage that by “recent convert” the Apostle meant a man who is young in age. They ought at least to have considered that Timothy, to whom he was writing these things, was not merely young but extremely young, so that he might appear liable to contempt on that account. Therefore he wrote to him—“Let no one despise your youth” (2 Tim. 4)—and he himself, while still young, was chosen for the apostolate, as Luke indicates in the Acts of the Apostles.

By “recent convert,” then, he meant either someone who had only recently come to faith or someone who had only recently received baptism. For he calls faith a planting, as he writes elsewhere: “I planted,” that is, “I brought them to faith.” He speaks similarly of baptism in Romans 8: “If we have been planted together in the likeness of his death,” speaking of baptism.

These things were not so separated in the time of the Apostles that people first believed and were baptized later; those who were not baptized were not then called believers. Hence, following the same custom, even today those who have been baptized are called believers. In many regions, moreover, people do not call those who have not received baptism Christians.

The Apostle also says in the same passage: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his.” It is evident that the person who does not receive baptism does not have the Spirit. He therefore wishes the man who is advanced to the episcopate to have been a believer and baptized for a considerable time. Accordingly, he gives many necessary and highly appropriate reasons for this requirement.

He adds the first reason: “Lest, being puffed up, he fall into the judgment of the devil.” A man is said to be puffed up when he exalts himself and thinks highly of himself because of things which he does not actually possess.

Someone who has only recently come to faith and received the grace of baptism, but has not yet furnished proof of his purpose or been properly instructed in the matters that concern him, if he is advanced so that he himself may teach others, may be puffed up by the very ordination and become greatly foolish. Since he has been appointed a teacher, he may no longer tolerate learning from anyone else; yet he does not know how to teach, because he did not first learn.

He is puffed up by qualities which, in truth, he does not possess. In his vain exaltation because of the appearance of authority imposed upon him, he will appear to differ in no way from the devil. The devil was created as a minister of God, but sought to think highly of himself, appropriating to himself God’s name and honor and exalting himself in qualities which did not belong to him; he awaits the just punishment of the Judge.

From this it is clear what we said earlier: Paul requires proof of one’s purpose in every respect. He wishes the bishop likewise to be a man who can furnish evidence of his purpose through his conduct—something that baptism cannot provide. Baptism grants remission of sins; but, if it is safe to state the matter so absolutely, apart from purpose it does not produce a virtue which has not been practiced.

He then gives another reason: the man who is to be advanced to the episcopate must have been trained in virtue in every respect and in piety.

“He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside, lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil.” By “those who are outside,” he means those who are outside the Church. Among them, he necessarily ought to have an unimpeachable reputation as far as possible, and he teaches at the same time that he must take care of his reputation.

For what he says means this: there are professions which, by their very nature, cause the person who practices them to be subject to reproach—for example, a tax collector, an innkeeper, a procurer, or some other occupation which many people might criticize or condemn. We frequently see people poorly regarded on account of certain matters, because they have stained the reputation of their life with blemishes and their conduct has become known to many: either they lived licentiously, or they were greedy in financial matters, or they engaged in commerce for the sake of unjust and shameful profits.

This, then, is what he means: if there are men who, because of their former life and profession, have been considered by people to have shown the most corrupt disposition, such men ought to be avoided and not advanced to the episcopate, even if they appear to have come faithfully to the Church and to have adorned their lives through the pursuit of better things—until, over a long period of life and conduct, they have demonstrated their improvement, so that they appear to have enhanced their reputation among those outside the Church.

Thus, although someone may appear worthy because of his faithful contemplation, faith, or baptism, his former life deprives him of confidence among those outside the Church, so that he not only cannot help outsiders but may be reproached on account of the disgracefulness of his life.

When he said, “lest he fall into reproach,” he adds a third reason: “and the snare of the devil.” This reason is in no respect weaker than those already mentioned. It is not prudent to entrust the care of others to such a man or suddenly grant him such great power, because he has not yet provided a secure demonstration of his life and conduct. It is uncertain whether he will not repeat something resembling his former life, since the devil may devise many schemes against him in order to plunge him again into his former offenses.

He appears to have only recently withdrawn from worse things, and he cannot be corrected toward what is better while he is under the care of another in a position not suited to him, since he himself appears to have been entrusted with the care of others. Thus, in every respect, Paul shows that the man who is advanced to the episcopate ought to be proven and adorned with those virtues which belong to piety.

He must not be considered worthy of this office merely because of faith or the grace of baptism, unless he is also supported by the testimony of his life and conduct.

He has set forth three necessary reasons why this should be so. The first is that a man may easily be puffed up by the authority through which he is appointed to teach others. The second is that he must have a good testimony from those who are outside. The third is that people could not safely form a judgment about him, since it is uncertain whether he remains firm in a better purpose or whether he may return to his former and worse condition, rather than being made radiant through the pursuit of better things.

These, then, are the things stated by Paul—things which ought to be stated to a man believed to possess divine grace. But those who think themselves superior to Paul’s decrees are unwilling to consider any of this. They advance many men to the episcopate without requiring an examination of their former life or purpose, and offer this single defense of themselves: that the man has only recently come to faith or has only recently been baptized.

If someone wishes to recognize the difference between Paul’s decrees and the judgment of these men, let him consider the reasons for which Paul instructed that matters ought not to be handled in this way. Then he will perceive the usefulness of Paul’s decree. Let him examine the matter in actual practice and see whether, among those who have been made bishops in this fashion, he will not find either all these reasons or at least one of them.

He will find them puffed up with immense pride, so that they consider those who have been called to the same grace neither like themselves nor worthy—although these latter have always adorned their lives with the best pursuits and have not departed from that excellent purpose which they appeared to have maintained throughout their former life.

He will find them, above all, eager because of their greed for money to gather wealth from every direction, if indeed they were previously of this character. Or he will find them harassed by reproaches from those outside the Church because, not long before, they had practiced such-and-such a profession, possessing no testimony of integrity from their life which could enable them to strengthen others or exercise care for their own office.

It is evident from what we have said earlier that blessed Paul admits into ecclesiastical office the man who has passed from a corrupt life to a better one and has furnished proof of this through his actual conduct. He does not reject him on account of his former way of life but considers him worthy because of the second. Such a man will necessarily receive a good testimony because his life has been corrected: he has voluntarily transferred himself to what is better and has cast off from himself the reproach of his former life.

There is no need to fear that he will easily return to his former ways if, by his own choice, he has voluntarily preferred to depart from them, considering it best to devote himself to the care of better things. In the same way we shall find that blessed Matthew was chosen from among the tax collectors and passed into the apostolate, because their former life caused no impediment to those who undertook this office, since they adorned themselves through a wholehearted devotion to the pursuit of better things.

“Deacons likewise.” Anyone ignorant of the usage of the divine Scriptures may suppose that blessed Paul passed over the presbyters. But the matter is not so. What he said earlier concerning the bishop he also says concerning those who are now called presbyters, because in ancient times both were called by these names.

We noted this when writing about the Philippians in that Epistle, where the Apostle, beginning his letter, mentioned “bishops” together with deacons. Clearly, it would not have been possible for there to be many bishops in one city.

The matter can be understood more clearly from what the Apostle wrote to Titus. He says: “That you should appoint presbyters in every city, as I instructed you,” and, describing the kind of men he ought to appoint, he adds: “The bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward” (Titus 1). Yet it would have been appropriate for him to call him a presbyter; nevertheless, he clearly called him both bishop and presbyter.

It is not right to pass over in silence the reason for this, namely, the change in the names which appears to exist at present, and the reason why the names have been distinguished, so that now neither may a bishop be called a presbyter nor may a presbyter claim for himself the designation of bishop, so long as he remains a presbyter.

In ancient times, when presbyters devoted themselves to piety, they were appointed everywhere and received the name of presbyter as an honorific designation, just as among the Jews those who presided over the people were called presbyters. They were also called bishops because of the work which they appeared to perform: they had been appointed to oversee everything that pertained to the worship of piety, so that the administration of all things was entrusted to them.

At that time they possessed the complete administration and authority of ecclesiastical ministry, and everything was governed according to their judgment. Luke can also teach us this more clearly. In the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 10), among other things, he says that Paul sent to Ephesus and summoned the presbyters to himself. He also reports the exhortation which he delivered to them when they arrived. Paul speaks to them in this way:

“Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to govern the church of God.”

It is evident that those whom Luke himself called presbyters Paul declared to have been summoned as bishops.

Those who now possess the power of ordination and are now called bishops, however, were not appointed as bishops of a single church. They governed entire provinces and were then called by the name of apostles. Thus blessed Paul placed Timothy over all Asia and Titus over Crete.

It is evident that he likewise placed others over other provinces in different regions. Each of them, having been entrusted with the care of an entire province, would travel through all the churches, ordaining clergy where they were lacking and resolving whatever difficult cases arose among them. At the same time, by the word of teaching they corrected them, and by reconciling them to God they appeared, through grace, to dissolve even the most serious offenses of sinners, accomplishing fully everything that the person appointed to this position ought to do.

At that time, as I said, all the cities had presbyters, each of whom governed his own church. Those who are now called bishops were then called apostles.

When those who had received episcopal ordination were appointed over individual cities or districts, the churches were at that time governed in this way. But as piety appeared to increase, and not only cities but entire regions were filled with believers, the blessed Apostles died. Those who were ordained after them to preside over those original churches could not be made equal to them, nor did they possess an equal testimony of miracles; indeed, they appeared weaker than the Apostles in many other respects.

They therefore considered it burdensome to claim for themselves the designation of apostles. They divided the names: to the presbyters they left the name of presbyter, while others were called bishops—those who were endowed with the power of ordination, so that these same men might fully recognize themselves as the heads of the churches.

Bishops also became more numerous when circumstances demanded it. Later, others were added through the generosity of those who carried out the ordinations. At first, only two or at most three bishops were appointed in each province. This practice also appeared to be maintained, until not long ago, in many provinces in the western regions; in some places one will find it preserved even to the present.

As time advanced, however, men were appointed not only in the cities but also in individual localities where there was not even sufficient need to demand that they be ordained to fulfill this office.

These things have been said by us to make clear the meaning of the apostolic Scripture, and also to bring into the open the custom—or the reason for the change—which had existed previously.

It remains to consider what he says about deacons, since it is evident that what was said about bishops was intended to signify those who at that time governed as presbyters—so that there was one in each province—and that these instructions apply especially to the present and are observed with all diligence by those who are now called bishops, all the more earnestly because they seem to have been entrusted with the greater office. What, then, does he say? With regard to deacons, he seems likewise to have preserved approximately the order that he had followed in this passage concerning women and men. For when he had first spoken about men, he added, “Likewise also the women,” showing that he wishes the qualities that belong to virtue to be common to them. He did the same here: after stating what he had previously said about the bishops—those who are now called presbyters—he adds, “Likewise the deacons,” that is, “I desire all that pertains to virtue to be present in them also.”

Then he adds: “Chaste.” (Ambr.) With good reason: since they were mediators and ministers of the priestly office, not only toward men but also, necessarily, toward women, it was fitting that they should be such.

[Col. 0605D] “Not double-tongued.” He says this also with good reason. If they convey what is entrusted to them by the presbyters, whether to men or to women who are admitted to them, it is right that they should carry out sincerely and appropriately what they are told and what they hear through those who give them instructions. Anyone will then be able clearly to perceive the usefulness of blessed Paul’s decrees, if he is willing to examine them together in the realities themselves.

“Not devoted to much wine, not seeking dishonest gain.” Both these qualities are necessary for deacons, just as for presbyters. For in the case of presbyters also he included this, saying that they must not be drunken or greedy for money. When he says “likewise,” he seems sufficiently to have indicated that all the qualities belonging to virtue ought to be common to them in every respect.

[Col. 0606A] Yet he adds certain things specifically, in order to confirm the matter more and more; then he adds generally: “Holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience.” In brief, he has stated the qualities that deacons ought to observe. He says that, serving in the ministry of the faith—that is, proclaiming the doctrines of piety—they should have a pure conscience in the office that they appear to fulfill. For he often calls the doctrine concerning Christ a “mystery,” as we shall be able to recognize more clearly from what follows in this epistle.

Then he adds: “And let these also first be tested, and so let them serve, having been appointed without accusation.” When he said “let them serve,” he means, “let them be advanced into the diaconate,” since they could not serve unless they had first been ordained. Thus blessed Paul seems throughout to write concerning one who is to be advanced into the ministry: he must have a good testimony from his past life, and he must not be advanced into the ministry absolutely or at random.

[Col. 0606B] Moreover, since he spoke of deacons, and this is also a common designation for women who are appointed to this work, he appropriately adds: “The women likewise must be chaste.” He does not mean here that they should have wives of such a character, but that the women who are appointed to fulfill the office of deacons should likewise be such, distinguished equally by their zeal for virtue. For he also added here, “Not slanderers,” because it commonly happens that other women confidently report to them matters concerning themselves. Therefore, he says, they must not be slanderers, so as not to repeat to others what some women tell them and thereby give rise to disputes or separations.

[Col. 0606C] “Sober.” That is, intelligent and ready, so that they may promptly fulfill everything that properly belongs to them. Then he states the matter fully: “Faithful in all things.”

He inserts in the middle the points he had mentioned concerning women who perform the office of the diaconate, because of the commonality of the name, thereby showing that he wishes these women also to devote themselves similarly to the pursuit of virtue. Then he resumes the discussion he had begun earlier concerning deacons, adding what remains: “Let the deacons,” he says, “be husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own households well.”

He has stated briefly the same point that he had made above concerning presbyters, showing throughout that he wishes the same zeal for virtue to be present in them. Then, because they seem to be inferior to presbyters according to rank, he shows that they are in no respect inferior to them if they are willing to fulfill their own office as is fitting, and he adds: “For those who have served well acquire for themselves a good rank and great boldness, which is in Christ Jesus.”

[Col. 0606D] Those who have fulfilled their office appropriately, although they may appear in the present to hold the lower rank, will, if they prove themselves excellent stewards for the future, attain very great boldness from Christ. He does not say that “good rank” refers to the present age; nor would he have said, “They acquire for themselves a good rank,” since the rank of the diaconate is itself good, but he would certainly have said “a greater one.” Now, however, by adding “good,” he does not mean that the rank of the diaconate is not good, but that he acknowledges that rank to be good and encourages those who are willing to attain it.

For no one can benefit another unless he has also agreed to those things that can preserve our conscience whole. He adds: “And great boldness in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.” He plainly shows that he is speaking of what will then be. He wishes to teach them that an inferior rank can bring no harm to those who are found worthy to attain great and perfect blessings, provided that their conscience is preserved undefiled by those very things, as is fitting.

Having surveyed in this way the orders that are held in ecclesiastical service, he adds: “I write these things to you, hoping to come to you shortly; but if I delay, so that you may know how it is fitting for you to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.”

[Col. 0607A] “I have written these things to you,” he says, “hoping above all to come to you soon. But if it should happen that I delay, I have written them so that you may know what it is fitting for you to do and how you ought to govern the Church of God.” He added most appropriately, “of the living God,” thereby showing the dignity of the Church.

It should be understood that when he calls the Church the house of God, he does not mean a house of prayer, according to the opinion of many, but the congregation of the faithful, just as he says when writing to the Hebrews: “Whose house we are.” For this reason he also called it “the pillar and foundation of the truth,” because the firmness of the truth is found in it. Since the Church is the congregation of the faithful, the doctrine of piety must necessarily be preserved in it. If they remain in the faith as is fitting, the doctrine of piety will certainly remain undefiled; but if those who belong to the Church turn away from their purpose, the precision of the doctrine will necessarily waver, since, in the present life, the knowledge of the truth is visibly found among human beings.

It is also worthy of being added to our remarks that one should not be surprised that the Apostle appears to have made no mention either of subdeacons or of the “elect.” Those grades of service that are necessarily found in the Church were added later, chiefly for the usefulness of the ministry, because the multitude of believers later required that the need be fulfilled by others.

[Col. 0607B] Hence they do not receive ordination before the altar, since they are not appointed to minister at the mysteries. Some of them fulfill the office of readers; others prepare below the deacon the things that belong to the deacons’ ministries, and they also attend to the lamps. For presbyters and deacons alone fulfill the ministry of the mystery: some of them carry out the priestly work, while others minister at the sacred rites.

We have marked this point so that no one may think that Paul omitted them through forgetfulness, although it was appropriate that he should remember them. Attention should also be given to what follows. Since the Apostle called the Church “the pillar and foundation of the truth,” he thought it best to insert doctrinal statements as well, in order to show what that truth is.

He prepares Timothy to discuss these matters with them also. In referring to doctrine, he recalled those words whose mention was especially demanded by the circumstances of that time. Therefore he says:

[Col. 0607C] “And confessedly great is the mystery of piety,” or “the sacrament of piety.” That is, he means “the doctrine.” This is what we indicated above: he often calls the doctrine concerning Christ a “mystery,” because the divinity of the Only-Begotten was present in a human being, and for this reason it could not easily come to the knowledge of many. Mysteries, too, are customarily not known equally by everyone.

Thus, writing to the Corinthians, he also said: “But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, which was hidden” (1 Cor. VII). He was plainly speaking of the proclamation that is according to Christ. A little later he adds: “For if they had known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.” So also here: “Confessedly,” he says, “great is the mystery of piety.” There is no doubt about this, for it had indisputable proof in the facts themselves. Hence he adds: “Which was manifested in the flesh.”

That is, the one who is the object of piety’s ministry, because he is great and surpassing—the invisible God, the Word, the Only-Begotten of the Father—manifested himself to human beings by appearing in the flesh for the common salvation of all.

He very appropriately does not say here “in a human being,” but “in the flesh,” although above he had plainly said: “For there is one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus.” This was the matter that at that time we received with uncertainty, and for this reason he was compelled to descend to these words.

[Col. 0608A] At that time, a doctrine opposed to the teaching of piety seemed to be spreading more and more: it attempted to alienate all visible things from the work of God and therefore also denied that an assumption of flesh had taken place. It said that the Lord had appeared in the flesh only as a phantom, so that, on this account, the flesh did not appear worthy of such honor and care—even though it had been worthy to be the dwelling place of the divine nature.

Then, saying “who was manifested in the flesh,” he uses an expression that seemed rightly to be spoken of God. For it was the divinity that had been seen in Christ’s flesh. He then passes to those things that could be said about a human being, in order to confirm through a fuller development of the argument what was then being called into question.

[Col. 0608B] “Justified in the spirit.” This plainly cannot refer to the divinity, but it can evidently be applied to human nature, which also received the indwelling of the Spirit at baptism. At that time the Spirit came upon him in the form of a dove; he was then led by the Spirit into the wilderness to contend against the devil in combat; and by the Spirit of God he cast out demons, as he himself says in the Gospels. He also accomplished fully those things that, according to the Spirit dwelling in him, were expedient for our salvation.

Those things celebrated according to Christ were the firstfruits of our salvation. Therefore the Spirit receives the indwelling of God the Word for the perfection of all good things, since through participation in the Spirit the cause of all good things is acquired for us, both in the present age and in the future.

Nor is it surprising if, while discussing the same person, he appears to pass from statements about the divinity to statements about humanity. This is the custom of the divine Scriptures. We have shown this not only in our interpretation of the apostolic writings, but also, as those who witnessed it know, in our interpretation of the Gospels.

[Col. 0608C] “Manifested to angels.” That is, he became visible to angels. By saying “manifested,” he shows how his greatness also became an object of wonder to the angels.

“Proclaimed among the nations.” “He was announced,” he says, “to human beings.” Then he adds what is greater: “Believed on in the world.” For what was proclaimed would not in itself have been anything great if the faith of the hearers had not followed.

By this he was speaking of a sufficient proof of Christ’s greatness: human beings who were in every place received faith concerning him. They would never have consented to believe what was said about him if they had not received, from the facts themselves, satisfactory testimony concerning what was proclaimed.

[Col. 0609A] “Taken up in glory.” He speaks of that taking up by which he was taken up from among human beings. He placed this last, as though it were sufficient to invite them to faith: he had been made visible to angels, proclaimed to human beings, and received by them through faith.

Having said these things about Christ—as matters that must necessarily be known and preserved, and from which one must not be moved—he concludes, provided that a firm and not merely bare confession of these things remains among the faithful.

## CHAPTER IV  
The Apostle excludes the erroneous manner of teaching and sets forth the true manner of teaching.

“Now the Spirit expressly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, having their own conscience seared, forbidding to marry and commanding abstinence from foods,” and so forth.

(Greg.) For there are some who devote themselves so zealously to bodily virginity that they condemn marriage. There are also some who praise abstinence so extravagantly that they detest those who consume necessary nourishment. Concerning them Paul says: “Forbidding to marry and to abstain from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful.”

Since he calls them back from the fleshly intention of their superstition, the heretics, when they see these people living differently from what they taught, declare that their powers have been broken by the activity which they formerly maintained in the Church. Therefore, even in the present time of discipline, if any adversity befalls the Church, they suspect that it has happened as a fitting repayment for sins.

(Ambr.) It is evident that blessed Paul says these things not because such professions had already begun among certain people at that time, but because they were later to have their beginning among human beings. He indicates that he learned of these things through the Spirit and foretold that they would occur in the last times.

He joined them to the statements that had been made about Christ, not without qualification, but because he knew that those very people would in the future remove both marriage and foods, while at the same time denying that flesh had been assumed by God the Word.

[Col. 0609D] He therefore joined these matters together most appropriately, as though he were attacking one purpose from both sides. For anyone can clearly see that the Manichaeans, the Marcionists, those belonging to the heresy of Valentinus, and all who are like them both condemn marriage and accuse the use of foods as dishonorable, while striving to show that flesh was not assumed by God.

Attention should be given to the bitterness with which he remembers them and to the force with which he establishes that those who will begin to teach these things in the last times are seductions of evil spirits. He calls them “doctrines of demons,” showing how grave he considered their profession to be.

[Col. 0610A] He rightly said, “speaking lies in hypocrisy.” For all such people pretend to be Christians and, through their teaching, promise that they possess a higher form of chastity. They strive to teach much about piety and Christ to those who obey them. Yet they themselves hasten with every effort to engage in all those things that are full of lust and contain every form of depravity, matters about which they seem especially eager to remain completely silent.

But once, through the pretense they adopt, they have succeeded in persuading someone to obey them in everything, they then introduce those matters into their speeches, persuading their followers to carry them out as though they were performing works of piety, although they are full of every kind of uncleanness.

Anyone will find this to be so if he wishes to examine with the greatest care all the things just mentioned, although they cannot easily be detected, since such people strive to conceal these practices from the majority.

[Col. 0610B] Accordingly, he adds: “Having their own conscience seared.” Those who pretend to chastity are found to practice every form of uncleanness within themselves. It is evident that those who do such things cannot possess integrity, for they are conscious within themselves of the contradiction between their words and their conduct: they practice these things themselves and teach them to others.

It is also evident what he means by “forbidding to marry and to abstain from foods”: he shows that not marrying or not eating food is not itself worthy of accusation, but that the crime consists in their striving to forbid these things by law. For someone to abstain from them by personal choice is not improper. To forbid them, however, belongs to necessity rather than to personal purpose. One cannot say the same where personal choice is involved: there is continence in that case, but here there is manifest execration.

[Col. 0610C] It should also be noted that when he says “to abstain from foods,” we may observe, as we shall also note elsewhere, his lack of concern for rhetorical completeness, since he often says much imperfectly. Here too, by saying “forbidding,” as though he understood the matter to be done by compulsion, he leaves the subsequent construction incomplete. From this, too, one may understand whom he accuses: those who compel abstinence from foods.

Then, by stating the judgment that he also condemns—because it will be made publicly among human beings—he adds proof that they do not propose these things appropriately: “Which God created to be received with thanksgiving.”

For it was exceedingly improper for God, who created these things for this purpose, to prohibit human beings from using them by law. He necessarily added “with thanksgiving,” indicating that a manner of use had also been added, in accordance with the things’ creation. This sufficiently proves the wickedness of those who forbid them. For if it is good to give thanks to God for foods, it is impious to accuse them while leaving no further occasion for thanksgiving to those who believe that these foods have been granted to them.

[Col. 0611A] Whoever confesses that these things were created by God for this purpose, even if he abstains from them by his own choice, nevertheless recognizes that it is fitting to give thanks to God for them. Explaining their perverse choice more fully, he adds: “For the faithful and for those who have known the truth.”

He does not say simply “for all human beings.” It might seem that the use of foods is likewise appointed for all, since God made them part of the universe. But he wishes to show more clearly the wickedness of those who think in this way about foods, since they also presume to say other things about them, although their use appears above all to be both necessary and suitable for everyone.

He accuses them more severely by adding “with thanksgiving.” Foods were made for this reason: that each person should consume them with thanksgiving. For it is right that those who enjoy them should give thanks to the one who graciously bestowed them. But he does not say this about everyone; he speaks only of the faithful, for unbelievers do not know how to give thanks.

[Col. 0611B] Thus, although the use of foods appears, according to the reason of creation, to have been appointed generally for all, it appears especially applicable to the faithful when it is carried out as it ought to be. Through this he shows their great perversity: although they ought to give thanks for the rest granted to them, whether they consume these foods or abstain from them as faithful people, they instead accuse the foods, claiming that they were not well made, and strive by law to reject their use.

Then, saying that they were made by God, he appropriately adds: “Because every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected.”

“How,” he says, “could that which was made by God appear worthy of accusation?” He states the matter well and generally: “For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected.” All things are useful. Therefore those things that were given for use as food are not to be rejected but rather received, since they were made by God for this purpose.

(Theoph.) For if we fast with such a sense and intention that we believe sin is contracted through participation in food, we gain no fruits at all from our abstinence; rather, according to the Apostle, we contract the greatest guilt and the crime of sacrilege by abstaining from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known the truth, because “every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving.”

For whoever thinks that some thing is common, to that person it is common. Therefore, merely because someone has consumed food, we read of no one being condemned—unless some accompanying or subsequent act occurred through which he deserved condemnation.

(Ambr.) He again adds the manner in which these same foods ought to be consumed: “Which is received with thanksgiving.”

[Col. 0612A] Then he adds what benefit can arise from them: “For it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer.” When foods are consumed with thanksgiving, one no longer participates in ordinary food but in holy food; for when thanks are given to God, the foods too are sanctified.

Having thus moved on to doctrinal statements, inserting them for the confirmation of the truth whose pillar and foundation he had asserted the Church to be, he spoke especially of those things that at that time most needed to be said because of the questions then being raised. Since Timothy would often teach the faithful about these matters, Paul admonishes him in these words:

“By setting these things before the brethren, you will be a good minister of Christ Jesus.” “You will be,” he says, “a trustworthy minister of Christ if you teach these things diligently to those who are joined to us by faith.” At the same time he shows that such diligence is useful to Timothy himself: “Nourished by the words of faith and of the good doctrine that you have followed.”

[Col. 0612B] “This,” he says, “will also advance you toward what is better. For when you strive, with the necessary diligence, to teach others the things that belong to faith, you yourself acquire greater firmness in them, as one nourished by their continual meditation.” He wishes to show that it is fitting for Timothy to teach others continually what follows, as though he were saying: “These things, which you have often heard and learned while always living with me, you ought to teach to others.”

After sufficiently exhorting him in these words to devote himself to teaching with every diligence, he likewise warns him not even slightly to attend to things that are contrary.

[Col. 0612C] “But avoid profane and old-womanish fables.” This was spoken by the Apostle especially profitably above all else. If, then, someone wishes to devote himself to apocryphal books—the books that those who profess such doctrines claim to possess, published under the names of the most blessed apostles but filled with the writings of demonic people—he will recognize the usefulness of Paul’s words.

All those profane statements and old-womanish fables inserted in those books are thus not merely fables but even more detestable than old-womanish fables. They contain filth and uncleanness that human ears could not endure.

After appropriately speaking of the dishonor of the things fabricated by his opponents, and in keeping with what he had said previously, he adds again: “Exercise yourself toward piety.”

Earlier he said, “Teach these things with the necessary diligence.” Frequent meditation on them will help not only those being taught but also you. Since he had inserted this exhortation into the statements by which he warned against the opponents, he now returns to that same subject.

[Col. 0612D] He rightly called the exercise of piety diligence in teaching: the person who hastens to instruct others in these matters with every care makes the practice of piety an exercise for himself, since he performs the works of piety. He calls it “exercise” in order to indicate that he should instruct others in these things with complete diligence.

Frequent meditation is ordinarily practiced through the labor of piety. Since he compared this exercise with bodily combat, he showed by the comparison the difference between them and said: “For bodily exercise is profitable for a little, but piety is profitable for all things, having the promise of the present life and of the life to come.”

[Col. 0613A] Those who engage in bodily combat and train themselves for it throughout their present life ordinarily derive their consolation from it. But the struggle and exercise of piety provide us with great assistance in many respects and promise to bestow great benefits upon us in the future age. They can also bring us no small benefit in the present life.

When he spoke of “the present life,” he meant that even if the godly have sometimes endured hardship, they obtain very great assistance in the present life as well.

(Moyses.) Piety, which undoubtedly is understood as love, is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of the life to come. Therefore, when bodily exercise is said to be profitable “for a little,” it is plainly declared that it is neither practiced throughout all time nor able, by itself, to confer the fullness of perfection upon the one who labors.

The word “little” can refer to either of two things: to the shortness of time, since bodily exercise cannot be coeternal with a human being both in the present and in the future; or certainly to the smallness of the benefit gained from bodily exercise, since bodily affliction produces certain beginnings of progress but not the perfection itself of love, which has the promise of both the present and the future life.

For this reason we consider the exercises of the works mentioned above necessary, since without them one could not ascend to the heights of love. These works of piety and mercy that you mention are also necessary in the present age, while unequal disparity still prevails. Their activity would not be expected here if the condition of the poor, needy, and weak did not abound so greatly—a condition produced by human injustice, namely, by those who seize for their own use alone the things granted to everyone by the common Creator, while not even keeping them for use in the proper manner.

[Col. 0613B] Therefore, as long as this inequality rages in the world, this action will necessarily be useful to the person who practices it. It restores to a good disposition and pious will the repayment of the inheritance of eternal life. In the future age, however, when equality reigns, it will cease, since there will no longer be inequality on account of which these works ought to be performed. Instead, all will pass from this manifold activity—that is, from activity in deeds—to the love of God and the contemplation of divine things in perpetual purity of heart.

[Col. 0613D] “The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance.”

(Ambr.) That is, he has said true things, which could admit no doubt, since piety appears to bestow upon its followers an abundance of many blessings. After confirming his statements, he turns again to the continuation of his exhortation and says: “For to this end we labor and are reviled, because we have hoped in the living God, who is the Savior of all human beings, especially of the faithful.”

Thus, since piety can provide many blessings, it is no wonder that we who believe in the ever-living God both labor and are reproached for its sake. It is excellent to suffer for him, since he knows how to save all by his goodness, and knows how to grant the faithful many rewards because of the eagerness of their soul.

[Col. 0614A] Since he has shown throughout that this zeal is necessary and that, while teaching others, they should exercise themselves in piety, he resumes the exhortation he had begun and adds: “Command and teach these things.”

He did not simply say “command,” but indicated that Timothy ought to insist earnestly whenever the matter itself compelled him to do so.

Then, because Timothy was young and his age seemed to be despised by many, he added: “Let no one despise your youth.” That is: “Do not be fainthearted on account of your age, nor hesitate to teach with authority, since you were chosen for this purpose while still young.”

His next addition is truly admirable: “But be an example of the faithful in word, in conduct, in love, in faith, and in purity.”

[Col. 0614B] “Do not,” he says, “look to your age. Rather, devote yourself to these things, so that you may say and do what ought to be said and done; so that they may conduct themselves as is fitting; so that they may maintain the love that extends toward everyone; so that they may be firm in faith; and so that they may practice purity.”

In this way, you yourself should present yourself as a pattern to the faithful for whom you govern your life, instructing them how it is fitting to conduct themselves and providing them, through your own actions, with a testimony to your life. Do not leave the dignity of teaching to your age; hasten to say everything with confidence.

(Greg.) “Command,” he says, “and teach with all authority.” He does not advise a domination of power but the authority of life. For what is taught with authority is first practiced and only afterward spoken.

Conscience hinders the tongue and deprives teaching of confidence. Therefore he did not suggest authority in speech but confidence in good action.

[Col. 0614C] Hence it is also written concerning the Lord: “For he was teaching them as one having authority, and not as the scribes and Pharisees” (Mark I). For he alone spoke uniquely and supremely with good authority, because he committed no evil through weakness. From the power of his divinity he possessed what he ministered to us through the innocence of his humanity.

But because we are weak human beings, when we speak to human beings about God, we ought first to remember what we are, so that from our own weakness we may consider how, in the order of teaching, we should care for weak brothers.

Let us therefore consider whether we are such as those whom we correct, or whether we were once such, although by the operation of divine grace we are no longer so. Let us correct with humble hearts all the more gently as we recognize ourselves more truly in those whom we amend.

[Col. 0614D] But if we are neither now nor ever were such as those whom we wish to correct, let us take care lest our heart grow proud and fall more disastrously because of that very innocence. While correcting their vices, let us recall their virtues to our eyes. If they have no virtues at all, let us have recourse to the hidden judgments of God.

For just as we received the good that we possess without any merits of our own, so grace from the power on high can also be poured into them, so that the virtues that we previously received may later be awakened in them as well.

Who would have believed that Saul would surpass Stephen in apostolic merit, when Saul had guarded the garments of those who stoned Stephen at his death? The heart must first be humbled by these thoughts, and only then should the wickedness of those who sin be rebuked.

Then, exhorting him generally concerning the matters that belong to him, he adds: “Until I come, attend to the reading, to exhortation, and to teaching.”

(Ambr.) Devote care to reading, so that you may learn what it is fitting for you both to do and to teach others. By continually instructing yourself through reading, you will be able to devote yourself to teaching and exhortation.

For he does not simply say “narration,” but “exhortation” or “instruction”—that stirring of the mind that ordinarily arises from certain matters that are brought forward. At times it is especially necessary to do this publicly, when we encounter a discourse that the matter itself compels us to explain to individuals.

[Col. 0615A] Persuading him to persevere diligently in teaching and exhortation with gentle persuasiveness, he adds: “Do not neglect the gift that is in you.”

He could have sufficiently persuaded Timothy to carry out the work of teaching with diligence by pointing out that he had been found worthy to attain this divine gift because of that very cause. Wishing to increase the gift already given and to exhort him still more strongly, he adds: “Which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.”

You obtained the divine gift for this reason, receiving it through revelation—through, I say, the laying on of the hands of many men, and not of the least among them, who appeared to minister that grace at your ordination.

[Col. 0615B] Therefore, in every respect, you have no excuse for neglecting what was entrusted to you, whether because of the revelation through which you received it or because of the dignity of those who, ministering for this very purpose, laid their hands upon you.

In this passage he did not call “presbyters” those who are now called presbyters. Nor did the circumstances permit these men to lay hands upon him for the ordination to this office. Rather, he speaks of the assembly of apostles that was with the Apostle Paul and that laid hands upon him at his ordination.

He called it a presbytery in consideration of its honor. Even now, according to this custom, they continue to act in this way: at the ordination of bishops, not one person but many complete an ordination of this kind.

Then, continuing to offer counsel, he adds: “Meditate on these things; be devoted to them, so that your progress may be evident to all. Attend to yourself and to the teaching; persist in them. For by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.”

[Col. 0615C] In every respect he says that it is fitting for Timothy to exercise diligence concerning himself and to make himself illustrious through the virtues, so that above all he may devote himself to reading and carry out the work of teaching with every diligence. In this way he will be a provider of goodness both for himself and for many others.

Having completed his exhortation on these matters and filled it out with many statements, he proceeds to write what sort of person it is fitting for Timothy to be toward each individual.

## CHAPTER V  
The Apostle instructs Timothy concerning the elderly, the young, and widows; he teaches who true widows are and speaks about the provision for the ministers of the Church, and so forth.

“Do not rebuke an elder, but exhort him as a father.” [Col. 0616A] (Ambr.) By “elder” he means not one according to the order of his office, but according to age—that is, an old man. He is saying: Do not appear harsh to the old, but speak to them with gentleness, as to your fathers. “Young men as brothers.” He included under the general term what he had said, “exhort.” He means: Do not attack anyone, and do not be harsh or bitter; rather, show your affection toward everyone with mercy and kindness, loving the aged as fathers and the younger as brothers. Since he had said this about men, wishing to show that he ought to have a fatherly affection toward both men and women, he passes to the latter group and says correspondingly: “Older women as mothers.” Toward women, he says, show yourself in such a way that you regard their elders as your mothers.

Then, speaking similarly about younger women, he adds: [Col. 0616B] “Younger women as sisters, with all purity.” Love these also, he says, as your own sisters. He showed that the division of the sexes should be made according to age, although he could have stated the matter more generally and without distinctions. He did this so that, by treating the groups separately, he might show that he wants his affection to be displayed equally toward all, both men and women, whether they are old or young. He most appropriately divided men and women not only according to sex but also according to the ages that ordinarily arise from the nature of things. Hence he mentioned names appropriate to age, so that he would show affection toward the aged in the manner of parents and toward the young in the manner of brothers.

To increase his affection toward them for the better, he said something resembling what the Lord had said to the one who reported to him [Col. 0616C] that his mother and brothers were waiting outside. He replied: “My mother and my brothers are these who do the word of God.” So he too commanded Timothy to regard the faithful in the same order.

Careful attention should be paid to the caution he used when speaking of young women: he said “as sisters” and added “with all purity.” Thus he both showed that his counsel toward persons of that age should be cautious and instructed him that it is possible to have a fervent affection toward women out of devotion, even when they are young, without bringing that affection into the worst kind of action. For when he said “as sisters,” he placed the same expression here as in the preceding passage, giving the counsel that he should not only love them, as he had said above, but also, to demonstrate integrity, should add this qualification, so that the rights of chastity might not be violated through affection.

If, however, someone deliberately disregards what is better and wishes to fall into what is worse, women are nevertheless sisters, sharing the same nature and capable of suffering similar things. We shall love them because of the closeness of nature, and we shall take care not to do anything improper toward them, honoring that natural kinship with due reverence. [Col. 0616D]

“Honor widows who are truly widows.” Everything that the blessed apostle Paul seems to have inserted from the point where he said, “Great indeed is the mystery of godliness,” up to the statement, “young women as sisters, with all purity,” he presented as dogmatic teaching for the proof of the truth, since he said that the Church is the pillar and foundation of the truth. Other matters he stated for the instruction of blessed Timothy, judging that it was right for him to carry them out, whether for his own sake or for the benefit of the others.

He began at the point where he said: “I urge, then, first of all, that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made.” All of these appeared to concern the usefulness and adornment of the universal Church. For when he says “first of all,” he chiefly indicates that he considered it necessary for the congregation of the Church as a whole to be formed by these things—namely, that every worship owed to God should be rendered with the appropriate thanksgiving owed to him for the things he has given us. Moreover, when we pray, we must not pray only for ourselves but also for all human beings.

Therefore, in what follows, he necessarily adds what they ought to be like in life, conduct, and behavior. First he used the common division of human nature, saying some things for the instruction of men, teaching what they ought to be like, and other things for women. In this way he appeared to give everyone, in common, counsel concerning the fulfillment of the virtues. Then he passes to the order of those who do not seem to fulfill the ministry of the Church, considering that they need a private exhortation, since the Church as a whole is appropriately served by their ministry. When these people act well, the others can be greatly helped; conversely, when they fail to provide what is fitting, it appears that very great harm is inflicted on many.

Thus he seems first to have discussed presbyters, instructing what they ought to be like; then deacons; afterward men and women. After completing these matters, he appears to have extended his instruction to this subject, which we have said was inserted and interposed. It was appropriate, after the common exhortation that he appeared to have addressed to everyone, to join to it what ought to be said specifically about widows. It was fitting to mention them in their own order because of the care that ought to be provided for them.

From this point, as I said, he departed from the proposed insertion [Col. 0617D] and continued with what followed. It was his custom, after the sequence of his statements, to make further insertions; thus he came to the words that had to be spoken about widows. “Honor,” he says, “those who are truly widows.” He did not wish to refer to an absolute profession on their part, but to the point at which the profession appears to be fulfilled in practice. For when he says here “honor,” he means, “show them care.” This becomes evident from what follows, where he teaches more clearly who are to be regarded as true widows.

Again he speaks of those who ought not to be supported at the Church’s expense, adding concerning them: “If any widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to manage their own household and to repay their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.” What he says—“let them learn”—he says of the children and grandchildren, not of the widows. He was eager to teach that only those widows should be nourished at the Church’s expense who could not obtain support from any other source. Therefore, if a widow has children or grandchildren, let those born from her support their mother or grandmother, because this is more pleasing to God: that they should be nourished by them and not require the Church’s assistance.

Then he speaks of those widows whom he considers truly widows, saying: “But she who is truly a widow and desolate has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day.” It is evident that he wants a true widow to be supported at the Church’s expense for two reasons: first, so that she may be well ordered in conduct [Col. 0618B] and adorned with virtues; second, because she appears to have no one at all who can fully care for her. This is the true widow who has no relative and spends the whole time of her life devoted solely to prayers.

“But she who lives in luxury is dead while she lives.” If a woman, after losing her husband, professes that she remains in widowhood while living luxuriously, she is more dead than alive, even if she appears to live. She is held neither by marital responsibility nor adorned by the pursuit of virtue; rather, hastening to devote herself only to feasts and pleasures, she will be able to do nothing that is proper for her.

(Moyses) For just as the kingdom of the Devil is received through the connivance of vices, so the kingdom of God is possessed through the practice of virtues, purity of heart, and spiritual knowledge. Where the kingdom of God is, there is without doubt eternal life; and where the kingdom of the Devil is, there is death and hell. No one doubts this. Whoever is there cannot praise the Lord, according to the saying of the Prophet: “The dead will not praise you, nor all those who go down into hell” (Ps. 113)—that is, those dead through sin. “But we,” he says, “who live,” not in vices or in this world, but for God, “will bless the Lord from this time forth and forever” (ibid.).

“For there is no remembrance of you in death; in hell, who will confess to you?” That is, no one. For no one, even if he professes himself a soldier, a Christian, or a monk, confesses God while he sins. No one who admits what the Lord detests remembers God, nor does he truly profess himself to be that Lord’s servant when, in stubborn recklessness, he despises his commands. It is in this death that the blessed Apostle declares the luxurious widow to be: “The widow who lives in luxury,” he says, “is dead while she lives.”

There are therefore many who, while living in this body, are dead and, lying in hell, cannot praise God. Conversely, there are those who, although dead in body, bless and praise God in spirit, according to the saying: “Bless the Lord, spirits and souls of the righteous” (Dan. 3), and, “Let every spirit praise the Lord” (Ps. 150).

“And command these things also, so that they may be irreproachable.” (Ambr.) That is: say this also to them, so that by living excellently they may remain irreproachable. Then he adds: “If anyone does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.”

He referred this to the statement, “If any widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to manage their own household,” since he said that such a woman ought to be supported by her children and grandchildren, so that nothing necessary for her would be lacking. He said this to admonish them to be diligent toward their parents, since we ought to care for all who are joined to us by kinship, especially members of our household. By these he means those who appear to be joined to us by the closest bonds of relationship, such as a father, mother, grandfather, or grandmother.

If anyone despises such people, it is evident that he has no concern at all for the faith but is worse than an unbeliever, because he does not wish to keep the law of nature laid down for one who professes to preserve godliness. Beginning his instruction from the statement, “Honor widows who are truly widows,” he explained what those women ought to be like who are cared for under ecclesiastical provision. He inserted a discussion of widows who have children or grandchildren, assigning their care to those relatives and completing what he had said less fully above.

Then, returning to the sequence of his own subject, he clearly explains what he wants those widows to be like who are to be maintained both under ecclesiastical discipline and through ecclesiastical care: “Let a widow be enrolled who is not less than sixty years old.”

Above all, he believed that their age should be specified, at which women were to be admitted into the order of widows. Some, however, failing to consider why he wished the age to be indicated, established the rule that women ought not to be ordained deaconesses before reaching this age. They thought that this requirement especially had to be observed for deaconesses, because they were to be advanced to a higher order than widows. They did not understand that, if he had decreed that this should be observed in their ordination, he would have commanded it much more strictly in the case of presbyters and bishops—something they were entirely unable to see.

The blessed Paul, however, never believed that office should be determined by age. For he placed Timothy himself, although very young, over churches of great importance, entrusting him with a great task that appeared to surpass all others. This is indicated by the letter that he addressed to him, saying: “Let no one despise your youth.”

What, then, does he mean here? He does not wish diligence in virtue to be established by age, for he appears chiefly to be testing that very matter. The age that has already provided extensive and careful proof of each person’s purpose is sufficient.

Since true widows were enrolled in the ecclesiastical order so that they might receive ecclesiastical provision, there were many women who had lost their husbands but did not wish to remain among the widows because of the pursuit of virtue. Rather, by enjoying the Church’s provision and having secure access to what concerned bodily use, they wished to pass their lives in comfort. From this motive, as commonly happens, many evils arose, because they did not strive to live as they ought. They did not wish to be enrolled as widows for the sake of virtue, but only out of a desire for security, so that without any labor or work they might easily obtain their daily sustenance.

The blessed Paul, therefore, wishing to establish this matter with the utmost caution, determined that the woman who wished to be enrolled among the widows should be tested by age and virtue: by age, because before that time of life they could obtain their sustenance through the work of their own hands; and by virtue, because he did not consider it right that ecclesiastical funds should simply be spent on any widows whatsoever. Rather, he judged it more fitting that those who were to be sustained by ecclesiastical care should be adorned with virtue.

Therefore, after speaking about age, he adds in what follows what he wished their conduct to be like. First he says: “She must have been the wife of one husband.” Here, when he says “the wife of one husband,” he does not mean a woman who has married a second husband. Paul himself gave counsel that remarriage should be permitted, and he nowhere treated it as something that could rightly be condemned as indecent. Rather, he means a woman who has lived chastely with her husband, whether she had only one husband or had also married a second, provided that while she had a husband she never directed her attention toward another.

For he requires chastity from such widows. Those women also practice chastity who live chastely with their husbands within marriage, whether with a first husband or a second. It would be unreasonable to exclude from ecclesiastical care women who, after entering a second marriage, had been adorned by the pursuit of virtue as was fitting and had then reached an advanced old age, leaving them to be worn down by poverty merely because they had been joined to a second husband. Paul appears to have prohibited this nowhere; rather, by excluding fornication, he allowed this to take place.

Then he adds: “Having a testimony in good works.” He explained this briefly, but in what follows he treats it point by point, saying: “If she has brought up children.” A woman who has not cared for her own children clearly possessed great inhumanity in her soul.

“If she has shown hospitality to strangers.” He is not speaking of just any strangers but of the faithful, and of faithful people who pursue virtue. Finally, wishing to explain more fully the kind of hospitality he especially wants them to practice, he adds: “If she has washed the feet of the saints.” He did not simply say “strangers,” but “saints,” so that he might encourage them to wash the feet even of those whom they receive as guests, keeping the saints in mind.

As I said, he adds this to exhort them, showing that they ought to receive guests with the greatest care and not neglect anything belonging to honorable service.

“If she has assisted those suffering tribulation.” Again he stated the matter briefly: “If she has followed every good work.” It is evident that he recommends that these things be done according to one’s strength.

It is clear from these statements that he wants faithful women who are married to be like this as widows. For when he says that widows ought to have lived such lives, he wants them to have fulfilled the same obligations while they were married. Otherwise, how could they be found to possess this kind of life if they had not been like this while married?

Showing why he also specified an age according to which he commanded them to be admitted to the order of widows, he adds: “But refuse younger widows.” He does not say this because youth is unworthy of practicing virtue, but he explains the reason in what follows: “For when they have grown wanton against Christ, they desire to marry, incurring condemnation because they have annulled their first faith.”

He rightly says “grown wanton against Christ.” That is, after they have been received among the widows and have obtained ecclesiastical support, once they are secure with regard to bodily necessities, they care for nothing except to indulge idly in bodily pleasures, since they have nothing about which they need to be anxious. Such pleasures also tend to weaken the human understanding. Having become idle and despising their profession, they begin to think about marriage, making themselves gravely liable because they have judged that the promise they made to Christ ought to be disregarded, thus annulling their first faith.

He did not say this about marriage, as some have foolishly supposed, but about the profession of widowhood. For it would not have been right for him to declare liable to condemnation women who were doing what he himself appeared to have permitted. Explaining the evil of their idleness, he adds: “At the same time they learn to go around from house to house, and not only to be idle but also to be gossips and busybodies, saying things they ought not.”

By all this he means that, having no concern for bodily necessities and securely obtaining what is required for their use, they learn, precisely because of that abundance, to cultivate idleness. There is nothing else that can urge them toward work. Remaining idle, they devote themselves to excessive talk and hasten to carry the words of some people to others and those of others back to them. From this arise sorrows, as they meddle inquisitively in other people’s affairs and strive to say what ought not to be said.

For this reason he indicated above both their age and their conduct, decreeing that those who do not devote themselves to the pursuit of virtue should not be nourished at ecclesiastical expense. Women who are still young and of this character ought to devote themselves to the care of their bodily sustenance, since such care can also benefit them greatly in the pursuit of godliness. Concern for food can restrain them from excessive frivolity, so that, humbling their thoughts, they may become concerned for themselves.

For this reason, when speaking of presbyters and deacons, he did not mention age, but mentioned it only in the case of widows who were hastening to be enrolled in the order of widows for the reason I have described. He also showed why he had commanded that younger widows not be admitted—not because youth is not faithful and useful for the pursuit of virtue, but because many of them did not appear to practice it appropriately. They pretended that they intended to remain widows only so that they might be nourished at ecclesiastical expense.

“Therefore I want younger widows to marry, bear children, and manage households.” Why? So that the impulse of youth, occupied with extensive responsibilities, might be restrained.

He did not say this to exclude younger widows from the pursuit of virtue, but rather to invite them to it. Having said that women who were adorned neither by age nor by virtue ought not to be admitted to the order of widows who are supported at ecclesiastical expense, he prepared them by this statement not to attempt such a course. His words appropriately confirm this, since he wants them in every way to preserve what is proper.

Thus he does not appear completely to reject younger widows who order their lives cautiously. He continues: “Giving the adversary no occasion for reproach.” For I do not want them, after pretending to widowhood for this reason, to be found later in other circumstances and thereby to give an opportunity to those who hasten to disparage us, on the ground that we make no effort to live properly but only pretend to practice virtue outwardly.

And so that he might not appear to have inferred this merely from suspicion, he states the cause itself and says: “For some have already turned back after Satan.” In every way he seems to exclude from the order of widows those who do not use widowhood well, removing every occasion for pretense from the profession itself.

It would also appear ridiculous to admit virginity if someone did not wish to profess it, as may be seen from the letter that he appears to have written to the Corinthians. Yet he does not admit young women deprived of their husbands, even if they wish to pursue widowhood appropriately. Nor will those who profess virginity be waiting until old age to make that profession.

It is just at this point to mention those who devote all their effort to excluding people from marriage. They also try to bring certain people into this profession. Paul’s teaching appears to be so far removed from such practices that he even forbids admission to the profession until a person has displayed great virtue and diligence in conduct.

He therefore adds: “If any faithful man—or any faithful woman—has widows, let him or her provide for them, and let not the Church be burdened.” Just as above he said concerning those who have children or grandchildren that they should be nourished by them, so here he wants those who have widows in their households to care for them, so that the Church would not have to bear much concern for such people.

And so that he might not appear to establish this as a law by which those who govern the churches could collect money under such a pretext while freeing themselves from the multitude and care of widows who need provision, he rightly adds: “So that it may be sufficient for those who are truly widows.”

By true widows he means those who are completely desolate and have no one to care for them. Thus the Church could provide for those who were desolate without having to bear responsibility for many, since the faithful, if they were able, would assist the few from their own resources. As for those widows whom individual people have in their own households, he exhorts them to provide for them themselves. If they have a mother or grandmother, they should care for them according to the measure of their strength, because of their very close relationship.

He has discussed at such length the support of widows because, although he had said above what presbyters ought to be like, he had not mentioned anything about their services or their support. Since at that time those men themselves were fulfilling the care of the churches, he appropriately adds something about them as well. [Col. 0623A]

“Let the presbyters who preside well be considered worthy of double honor.” By “double,” he means abundant. For, he says, sound reason demands that presbyters be considered worthy of greater provision. Hence he adds, “who preside well.” Yet he did not speak absolutely of the care owed to those who merely belong to the order and rank of presbyters, but of those who appear to fulfill the function of their rank as is fitting.

Therefore he adds: “Especially those who labor in word and teaching.” He did not say absolutely that these men were worthy of provision, but for the reason that they expend very great labor—provided that they are willing to fulfill the work of teaching as is fitting. They must show concern for everyone in common, teach them to do what ought to be done, and labor greatly on behalf of each person, bringing everyone to what is proper through excellent counsels and exhortations.

For the blessed apostles also appear to have placed the work of teaching before every other work. Therefore, when a dispute arose at one time concerning the widows (Acts 6), they said that it was not right for them to abandon the word of teaching and serve the widows’ tables, since they considered the work of teaching more appropriate to them.

Wishing to confirm through the testimony of Scripture what he had said about presbyters, asserting that they especially labor in teaching, the Apostle adds: “For Scripture says: ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing,’” and, “The laborer is worthy of his wages.” As though he were saying plainly: You shall not prevent the preacher of the word from receiving his support.

(Greg.) In speaking of the care that ought rightly to be provided for them, he adds: “Do not accept an accusation against a presbyter except on the testimony of two or three witnesses.”

(Ambr.) The Apostle is worthy of all admiration, because he was concerned even about this matter. It had been said generally: “Every word shall be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (2 Cor. 15). But here, rejecting an accusation in the opposite direction, he said: “Do not receive it except before two or three witnesses,” because, whereas in other matters the case may meanwhile suffer and the matter may be judged otherwise, this matter ought not to be handled in that way for two reasons.

First, a presbyter must care for everyone as a common father, both men and women. Since he fulfills the care of both sexes alike, he is necessarily required to see women and speak with them whenever the reason of godliness demands it. Second, various accusations were brought against them on many different occasions because the same presbyters were sometimes compelled to rebuke those who were guilty of sins and to reprimand those who were not behaving properly.

The Apostle therefore foresaw that accusations could easily arise against presbyters from such people. Their own actions would assist their accusers, so that whatever they wished to say against them might be regarded as a genuine accusation, since the presbyters were permitted to see women and speak with them for legitimate reasons—something that appeared to give malicious people an opportunity for accusation.

What, then, does he decree should be observed? He says: Do not listen in any other way unless two or three witnesses appear to be witnesses to the very matter about which the accusation is made.

And so that he would not appear, by saying this, to wish to conceal the sins of wrongdoers, he adds: “Those who sin, rebuke in the presence of all, so that the rest may have fear.” I want the matter to be examined with the greatest care, and I do not want a charge against them to be accepted without scrutiny. But if some are found truly to have sinned, let them be rebuked openly, so that the others may become chaste by their example. He rightly said that this also serves the correction of others. It would not have been necessary for this to happen unless it were for the amendment of others, concerning whom we read in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone” (Matt. 18).

[Greg.] But when, at the dictation of the disciple, the sinner is to be rebuked “in the presence of all,” what did the teacher of truth himself mean when he said, “between you and him alone”? We shall resolve this question quickly if we consider the force of the statements more carefully.

There he said “those who sin,” but he did not add against whom. Here he said, “If your brother sins against you.” Therefore, if your brother sins secretly against you and you wish to rebuke him before everyone, you are not a corrector but a betrayer. Those who sin against God, however, are to be rebuked “in the presence of all.” [Here take a breath so that the word “rebuke” may be joined to what follows.]

Hence Paul says (Gal. 2): “When Peter came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he was not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel”; and shortly afterward: “I said to Peter before everyone”—as though he had said, because Peter had practiced pretense before everyone—“If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?” (ibid.).

Secret sins, therefore, may be rebuked secretly, while public sins ought to be rebuked before everyone, “so that the rest may have fear.” Whatever has moved the minds of others must by no means be kept silent, but must be brought forward with great humility.

Then, addressing all of them solemnly, he adds: [Col. 0624D]
