“I testify before God and Christ Jesus and his elect angels that you observe these things without prejudice, doing nothing by inclining to one side.”

(Ambr.) That is, do not readily pronounce judgment against anyone out of hatred before he has been proved guilty by sound reasoning, nor, conversely, conceal sins out of regard for some friends. This is what he means by doing nothing through partiality. Such an adjuration is especially necessary in matters of this kind.

Then he turns to Timothy, giving him counsel, and says: “Do not lay hands quickly on anyone.” Do not readily bring anyone forward for ordination at all, without extensive examination. Showing the seriousness of the matter, he adds: “Nor share in the sins of others.”

If, he says, after you have examined him as is fitting, that person sins, it is not your crime. But if you bring him forward for ordination easily and without careful examination, you become a partner in his sins. He will be punished justly for the sins he has committed; but you will be punished for having acted carelessly, for not having thoroughly tested his judgment, and for having brought him into the ministry without adequate examination.

And, further impressing fear upon him, he adds: “Keep yourself pure.” Then he also gives the instructions that concerned Timothy himself: “No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses.”

It is evident that he also gives him counsel concerning this matter because he saw that Timothy was very weak in body. Out of regard for self-control, Timothy had continued to drink only water. We often do such things for the sake of others, so that we may not appear indifferent toward their conduct, knowing that the things made or given for our use cannot harm us when properly taken.

(Greg.) For the outstanding preacher Paul, when he came to Mitylene and knew the island to be full of unbelievers, saved Publius’s father, who was suffering from dysentery and fevers, by praying (Acts 28). Yet when Timothy was ill he instructed him, saying: “Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses.”

What is this, Paul? You restore an unbeliever who is sick to health by prayer, but you treat so great a helper of the Gospel, as though you were a physician, through nourishment. The answer is that outward miracles are performed so that people’s minds may be led to inward realities, so that through what is visibly shown as marvelous, invisible things that are even more marvelous may be believed.

The father of Publius had to be healed by a sign of power so that he might revive inwardly when he returned to health through the miracle. But there was no need for an outward miracle to be performed for Timothy, because he was already wholly alive inwardly. What is surprising, then, if miracles do not occur frequently as faith spreads, when the Apostles themselves did not perform them for certain people who were already faithful? He rightly adds:

“The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment, but those of others also follow. Likewise, good works are manifest, and those that are otherwise cannot remain hidden.”

(Ambr.) He means that the sins of people who offend and do not live rightly are manifest and will secure for them the punishments prepared in the age to come, even if they do some things that may remain hidden from many. Similarly, among those who have decided to live rightly, many of their deeds are manifest to people, while some also remain hidden from many. This is what he indicates when he says, “those that are otherwise.” Not everything can be uncertain.

Therefore, do not fear that you will fail to acquire a good reputation because you make use of water as a drink. Instead, use a little wine because of the necessity caused by your illness, knowing well that the things people surmise, provided that we live rightly, will for the most part be seen to be good.

[Col. 0625D]

(Greg.) We shall suffer no harm from these things, even if many of our deeds are unknown to many people. When the Apostle Paul was instructing his beloved disciple concerning the establishment of the Church’s offices, so that he would not perhaps promote people to the sacred orders irregularly, he said: “Do not lay hands quickly on anyone, nor share in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.” Then, immediately turning his words to Timothy’s bodily weakness, he said: “No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses.” At once he adds: “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment, but those of others also follow.”

What connection does the prohibition against drinking water by one who is ill have with what he added about the hidden sins of some people and the manifest sins of others? It is this: after making his judgment concerning Timothy’s illness, he returns at the end to what he had said above: “Do not lay hands quickly on anyone, nor share in the sins of others.”

To show with what care those sins ought to be investigated, after giving a warning concerning discretion in the face of bodily weakness, he immediately added that in some people they become evident and in others remain hidden, saying: “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment, but those of others also follow.” Thus Paul, in this statement, does not use the same words that he had just used when speaking of Timothy’s weakness; afterward he also adds something about slaves.

## CHAPTER VI. The Apostle urges bishops to care for the poor in the service of masters and urges them to pursue humility, godliness, and the other virtues.

“Let all who are under the yoke of slavery regard their masters as worthy of every honor, so that the name of the Lord and the teaching may not be blasphemed” (Ambrose). He writes this concerning those who have unbelieving masters, commanding them to render every service to their masters, even though they are strangers to godliness, so that no blasphemy or reproach may thereby be attached to the teaching of godliness, on the assumption that we instruct them in such a way that they despise their masters. Since he speaks of slaves who have unbelieving masters, this is evident also from the words, “so that the teaching [Col. 0626D] of God may not be blasphemed on this account.” It is shown still more clearly by what follows, for he adds:

“But those who have believing masters must not despise them because they are brothers, but must serve them all the more, because they are believers and beloved, as those who share in the benefits.”

It is right, he says, that these too should not, under the pretext of godliness, despise their masters, who treat them kindly; rather, they ought to serve them much more, as believers, who should be loved by them for that very reason and especially because they treat them kindly. This is what he means by “those who share in the benefits”: that is, those who hasten to support them with benefits in consideration of the godliness that they practice. Thus the kindness of masters must not become an occasion for the slave’s contempt, but should rather retain them in greater affection. He adds again:

“Teach and urge these things.”

In every way he stimulates him to hasten to set this teaching before them with great concern. And since he runs through everything that he thought generally appropriate for the correction of the Church, as we have indicated more carefully in what we interpreted earlier, he again recalls those who attempt to teach things contrary to godliness. He speaks of those who had believed from the circumcision, who endeavored to do everything by imposing observance of the Law upon believers; he had said much about them at the beginning of the Epistle. Thus, after moving on to corrective instructions applicable to all in common, he again takes up what he had said at the beginning about these very people and concludes with it, inserting the other matters into the middle part of the Epistle:

“If anyone,” he says, “teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the teaching that accords with godliness, he is conceited and understands nothing.”

He rightly joined ignorance to arrogance. Arrogance is properly said to be that which makes people think highly of themselves concerning things that are not present in them. It is a very great disgrace to them that they promise to teach others while they themselves understand nothing. Indeed, they deserve to be mocked for this very reason: while promising to teach others, they themselves know nothing.

The proof of this is more clearly evident from what precedes. If they do not attend to the teaching that accords with godliness, it is clear that they understand nothing of what they ought to know. Thus they promise to teach in vain, being ignorant of what they ought to know. Then, censuring their activity, he adds:

“Being sick with questions and disputes about words [quarrels].”

They frequently raised questions because they wished by this method to establish their own positions. He rightly says that they are sick, calling their thinking a sickness because, abandoning godliness, they turned over inappropriate questions. And to show that many other shameful things arose from their zeal for questioning, he adds:

“From these arise envy, strife, blasphemies, evil suspicions, conflicts among people corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth, who suppose that godliness is a means of gain.”

From this envy results, since each person envies anyone who can in any way appear capable in teaching. Many quarrels also arise, because they speak about matters that ought not to be discussed—especially since those who are not united with us in faith blaspheme us and idly seek accusations against us. It also necessarily happens that they have an evil suspicion of us, particularly those who are outsiders to our faith, while they love those men, delighted by their words and eager to imitate them, doing the things that they see those men doing. These are people corrupted in mind, possessing no desire for truth, who endeavor to do everything for the sake of profit. They consider godliness a means of gain, an evil from which many other evils arise. [Col. 0627D–0628A]

He adds most appropriately: “Withdraw from such people.”

After showing their wickedness and the shameful things they produce, it would have been sufficient simply to advise separation from them. Then, leaving the remaining matters aside, he returns to the point at which they hastened to gather money, and here he expands his discourse at greatest length, since he did not think it easy for them to despise money.

Knowing also that the desire for money permits no one to do what ought to be done—for contempt of money easily enables a person to accomplish what is better—he says:

“Godliness with contentment is great gain.”

Godliness is great profit, great riches, a profitable business, so that we may be concerned with those things sufficient for our needs. He rightly adds, “godliness with contentment,” so that he might neither appear to remove necessity nor encourage a desire for excess, and so that concern for money might be taken away in every respect.

“For we brought nothing into this world, and there is no doubt that we can take nothing out of it.”

A great and powerful meaning seems to be contained in this concise statement. Those who are devoted to money labor for what they already possess, so that it may remain and be preserved; and for what they do not yet possess, they consider how they may acquire it. He excludes both concerns, so that they should spend no effort on what they already have. For when he says, “We brought nothing,” he means that we came naked into this world and this life, and therefore forbids us to labor for the things that we possess, as though they were our own, since we find them here when we enter this life. He also shows that it is altogether futile to labor for them, saying, “because we can take nothing out of it.” What benefit is there in laboring when, even if we can acquire everything, we will leave here what we have gathered? What, then, should be done, since one thing is necessary and the other excessive?

“But having food and clothing, with these we shall be content.”

It is sufficient to have what is necessary for our use, since we shall enjoy only these things; everything else, even if it has been accumulated, we leave to others in this world.

“But having food and coverings, with these we shall be content.”

He says “coverings,” not “garments,” as is not properly rendered in some Latin copies—that is, things that merely cover the body, not things that flatter the glory of dress. For, he says, it is excessive for us, who brought nothing with us, to wish to acquire much in order to carry it away from here.

Then, showing how harmful such concern is to one who wishes to devote himself to godliness, he adds:

“For those who want to become rich fall into temptation and a snare of the devil, and into many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge people into destruction and perdition.”

The person who desires to acquire riches must become entangled in many troubles, endure many dangers, and give way to harmful and foolish desires—desires by which they are accustomed to increase and multiply their wealth. These desires prepare great destruction for those who are once seized by them. Who could adequately describe the evils that commonly arise from the desire for riches? Therefore he adds:

“For avarice is the root of all evils.”

And, he says, to put it briefly, there is no shameful thing, no evil, that is not admitted through the desire for money.

Showing that he had learned this by experience, and knowing that many had been seriously deceived by this desire, he adds:

“By desiring it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.”

Through this desire, he says, many appear to have fallen away from the faith, so that even in the present life they could not be found among better things; instead, they continued mourning and grieving over the sorrows that had befallen them because of it.

(Gregory) Concerning sinners, this too is said through blessed Job: “The root of the junipers was their food” (Job 30). What is signified by the root of the juniper except avarice, from which the thorns of all sins grow? Concerning it Paul also says: “The root of all evils is desire.” It secretly arises in the mind, but visibly produces the pricks of every sin in action. The excellent preacher immediately discloses these pricks rising from this root when he adds: “By desiring it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.” By saying “many sorrows,” he made known that the pricks arising from this root are like things growing from it. In the junipers, therefore, we understand sins; but in the root of the junipers, what else do we understand but avarice—that is, the material of sins?

(Cassian) For this reason, let no one regard this disease as insignificant or contemptible. Just as it can very easily be avoided, so, if it takes possession of anyone, it scarcely permits him to reach the remedies of health. It is a storehouse of evil vices; it becomes the root of all wickedness and the inextricable fuel of evil, as the Apostle says: “The root of all evils” is *philargyria*, that is, the love of money.

When this has taken possession of a person’s mind in a lax and lukewarm manner, it first troubles him concerning a small sum and describes for him certain apparently just and reasonable pretexts by which he ought either to keep some money for himself or acquire it. He complains that what is supplied in the monastery is not sufficient and can scarcely be endured even by a sound and robust body. What should be done if poor health of the flesh should arise and nothing personal has been stored away with which the illness might be supported? He complains that the monastery’s provision is extremely meager and that its negligence toward the sick is very great. If he has nothing of his own with which care can be provided for the body, he says that he will miserably die of hunger. Even the clothing that is supplied, he claims, is insufficient unless he arranges for another garment to be provided for himself. Finally, he says that he cannot remain long in the same place or monastery; and unless he has prepared travel expenses and the cost of transportation overseas, he will be unable to move whenever he wishes. Constricted by the necessity of poverty, he will continually endure a laborious and wretched life without any progress, always poor and naked, and, not without reproach, sustained by another’s property. [Col. 0629D–0630A]

“But you, man of God, flee these things.”

(Ambrose) He appears rightly to have exhorted him to flee these things, calling him a man of God. It is fitting for one who is such to guard himself against every evil. Then, as to a most beloved disciple, he writes to him and indicates what he ought to do:

“But pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, gentleness.”

Spend your concern, he says, on these things. And since labor is necessary for those who strive to practice virtue, he adds:

“Fight the good fight.”

He necessarily adds “the good fight,” or “contest,” to faith, so that here above all he might show that such labor is necessary—a labor undertaken for many good things. Then, disclosing the profit of the labor itself, he adds:

“Take hold of eternal life.”

The reward of these contests or struggles is eternal life; through them he will be able to attain it. He urges him to act zealously in these matters, in which, he says, he was called and confessed the good confession—for on account of this he also believed.

This is what he means by: “In which you were called and confessed the good confession.” Because of this calling, you confessed godliness; that is, he says, you suffered for it. For when he said, “You confessed,” he means, “You suffered.” Therefore, exhorting him still more to endure labor for these things, he adds:

“Before many witnesses.”

Many knew that blessed Timothy had been joined to Paul because of godliness and that he had suffered no little. Therefore, he says, it is necessary for you in every respect to endure labor for eternal life, for which you both believed and confessed godliness, having often been exposed to dangers. It is right that what was acquired at the beginning should not be destroyed by later indolence.

Then, exhorting him still further, he adds:

“I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and before Christ Jesus, who bore witness to the good confession before Pontius Pilate, to keep the commandment without stain, blameless until the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

The commandment is, he says, the things that I commanded you. He shows well here the reason why he also commanded him to fight in the contest for the faith. Therefore, recalling Christ’s coming and confirming and establishing that it will certainly take place, he adds:

“He will display at his proper times—the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone possesses immortality, dwelling in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see, to whom be honor and eternal dominion. Amen.”

From the greatness of the divine nature he confirmed the future things concerning it. Accordingly, he set down in the present tense those things that concern God, because they could provide a kind of confirmation of future realities.

He seems to have done this very thing also at the beginning of the Epistle, where he says: “To the King of the ages, incorruptible, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.” Therefore, here too he calls him blessed in order to confirm the future blessedness that will come to us, since he is such by nature that he possesses blessedness and cannot undergo any change.

He called him powerful so that no one might doubt that he can grant us resurrection. He also called him King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule, to show by this that he subjects all things, and that he is powerful enough to subdue demons, destroy death, and remove everything that presently afflicts us.

Therefore he said that he alone possesses immortality, because it is sufficient for him to grant us what he alone possesses by nature, having received it from no one else. When he said, “Dwelling in inaccessible light,” he confirmed that he abides in an immeasurable and inaccessible light, and that he will also, in the true sense, cause the bodies of the righteous to be illumined by light.

But he also said, “Whom no human being has seen or can see,” to show that it is not at all astonishing if the things that will then exist for us are not presently seen. For the one who will bestow these things upon us is himself invisible to us by nature. Thus he appears to have brought his discourse to completion by confirming future realities, so as to persuade Timothy all the more to attend carefully to the things written for him.

(Gregory) We shall therefore see God, and he himself will be the reward of our labor, so that after the darkness of this mortality we may rejoice in access to his light. But when we say that his light is accessible, what Paul says opposes itself to the mind: “Who dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see.” Behold, again I hear what the Psalmist says: “Draw near to him and be enlightened” (Ps. 33). How, then, are we enlightened by drawing near if we do not see the very light by which we can be enlightened? But if, by drawing near to him, we see the very light by which we are enlightened, how is it said to be inaccessible?

In this matter we must consider that he said “inaccessible,” but meant inaccessible to every person who reasons according to human understanding. Holy Scripture commonly designates all followers of carnal humanity by the term “human.” Thus the same Apostle says to certain people who were quarreling (1 Cor. 3): “Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human ways?” Shortly afterward he adds: “Are you not human beings?” Elsewhere he brought forward the testimony that “what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him” (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2). After saying that this was hidden from human beings, he immediately added: “But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit,” distinguishing himself from the human condition, since, having been caught up above human beings, he already understood divine things.

So also here, when he declared God’s light inaccessible, he added, to show to whom it was inaccessible: “Whom no human being has seen or can see.” In his customary manner he calls “human beings” all who understand human things; those who understand divine things are, in a sense, above human beings.

We shall therefore see God if, through a heavenly way of life, we deserve to be above human beings. Yet we shall not see him in the manner in which he sees himself. The Creator sees himself in a manner altogether different from that in which the creature sees the Creator.

As far as the immensity of God is concerned, a certain measure of contemplation is appointed for us, because we are circumscribed by the very weight by which we are creatures. Thus we certainly do not behold God as he beholds himself, just as we do not rest in God in the manner in which he rests in himself. Our vision or rest will be in some way similar to his vision or rest, but it will not be equal to it.

So that we may not, so to speak, lie inert within ourselves, the wing of contemplation lifts us up; from ourselves we are raised to behold him. Carried away by the concentration of the heart and by the sweetness of contemplation, we in some manner go from ourselves into him. Yet this very going is less than resting; nevertheless, to go in this way is to rest perfectly.

It is therefore perfect rest, because God is seen; yet it cannot be made equal to his rest, because he did not pass from himself into another in order to rest. It is therefore a rest both similar and dissimilar, because what his rest is, ours imitates. In order that we may be eternal and blessed forever, we imitate the eternal; and great for us is eternity, the imitation of eternity. We are not excluded from the one whom we are able to imitate, because by seeing him we become participants, and by participating we imitate him.

This vision begins now through faith, but then it is perfected in direct sight, when we drink from the very fountain of God’s coeternal Wisdom, whom now we receive through the mouths of preachers as through flowing streams.

(Ambrose) He also adds a word about the rich, realizing that he had omitted saying this in the middle part of the Epistle, where he had discussed the other matters with him, and says:

“Command the rich in this present age not to be high-minded.”

He rightly said “in this present age,” to show that the riches themselves are temporal, and that it was especially inappropriate for them to be high-minded because of them.

“Nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches.”

He adds this also to show that, even in this present age, riches are not held securely by the rich.

“But in the living God, who richly supplies us with all things for enjoyment.”

He most appropriately set against temporal riches that abundance which is given to us by God. Who is so foolish as to doubt that it is better to hope in God than in riches? Therefore he added “living,” in order to emphasize the point still further.

He compared the temporal use of riches with God’s eternity and called the use of riches itself uncertain. When he said, “He richly supplies us with all things,” this is true. It is evident from the place where he had said earlier that we enjoy all things from him. And to show that we ought rather to look to God, from whom we have the enjoyment of every good, despising those riches that are presently ours, it is appropriate that we should always give thanks to God, who appears to be the author and giver of all the good things we enjoy.

Then he instructs them concerning what they must necessarily do after this, saying:

“To do good, to be rich in good works, to give readily, to share”—and what profit will result from this? He says—“storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of eternal life.”

In the age to come they will receive a great reward for doing these things in the present age. Indeed, they will receive such a reward as can never undergo any change. By “foundation,” he meant their firm support.

He wished to say this briefly: Command them not to be high-minded because of what they possess, but to recognize that the Lord is their giver and to give him thanks continually for everything granted to them. Let them devote themselves to good works, so that by giving little in the present life they may receive great things in the age to come.

(Gregory) The poor must be admonished in one way, and the rich in another. To the poor we must offer the consolation of comfort against tribulation; to the rich we must introduce fear against arrogance.

To the poor person the Lord says through the prophet: “Do not fear, for you will not be put to shame” (Isa. 54). Not long afterward he speaks encouragingly to her: “O poor little one, tossed about by the storm,” and again consoles her, saying: “I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty.”

But Paul says to his disciple concerning the rich: “Command the rich of this age not to be arrogant in mind or to hope in the uncertainty of their riches.”

Here we must note very carefully that the teacher of humility, when recalling virtues, does not say “ask,” but “command,” because although compassion must be shown to weakness, honor is not owed to arrogance. What is rightly said to such people is applied all the more rightly because they swell with pride of thought over transitory things.

Concerning them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to you who are rich, because you have your consolation” (Luke 6). Since they do not know the joys that are eternal, they console themselves with the abundance of the present life.

Consolation, therefore, must be offered to those whom the furnace of poverty purifies, while fear must be brought upon those whom the consolation of temporal glory exalts, so that the former may learn that they possess riches that they ought not to possess, and the latter may recognize that they can by no means retain the riches they see.

(Paphnutius in the *Collationes*) In the Holy Scriptures riches are understood in three ways: evil, good, and intermediate.

Evil riches are those of which it is said: “The rich have become poor and hungry” (Ps. 33), and: “Woe to you who are rich, because you have received your consolation.” To cast away such riches is the highest perfection.

In contrast to these, the poor are those who are praised by the voice of the Lord in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5); and in the psalm: “This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him” (Ps. 33); and again: “The poor and needy shall praise your name” (Ps. 73).

There are also good riches, the acquisition of which is a great virtue and merit. The righteous man who possesses them is praised, as David says: “The generation of the upright shall be blessed. Glory and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever and ever” (Ps. 111); and again: “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own riches” (Prov. 13).

Concerning these riches it is said in the Apocalypse to one who, not possessing them, is blamefully poor and naked:

“I am about to vomit you out of my mouth, because you say, ‘I am rich and wealthy and lack nothing,’ and you do not know that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked. I advise you to buy from me gold refined by fire, so that you may become rich, and that you may be clothed in white garments, and the shame of your nakedness may not appear” (Rev. 3). [Col. 0634A]

There are also intermediate riches, that is, riches that can be either good or evil. They can be transferred to either side according to the will or character of those who use them.

Concerning these the blessed Apostle says:

“Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment; to do good, to give readily, to share, to store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of true life.”

The rich man in the Gospel (Luke 16), retaining these riches and by no means supplying them to the needy, while poor Lazarus, placed before his door, desired to be filled with the crumbs from his table, was assigned to unbearable fires of Gehenna and eternal burning.

Therefore, when we abandon these visible riches of the world, we cast away not our own possessions but those of others, even though we boast that we acquired them either through our own labor or by inheritance from our parents. For, as I have said, nothing is ours except that which, possessed in the heart and joined to our soul, cannot be taken away by anyone at all.

Concerning those visible riches, Christ rebukingly speaks to people who retain them as though they were their own and refuse to share them with the needy:

“If you were not faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke 16).

Daily experience clearly teaches that these riches belong to others; indeed, the Lord’s saying itself marked this by the very designation.

Concerning the invisible and worst riches Peter speaks to the Lord:

“Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what, then, will there be for us?” (Matt. 19).

It is certain that they left nothing more than very cheap and torn nets. Unless all these things are understood in this renunciation of vices—which is truly great and supreme—we find neither that the apostles left anything valuable nor that the Lord possessed anything for which he would grant them such great glory of blessedness that they would deserve to hear from him:

“In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

If, therefore, those who perfectly renounce these earthly and visible possessions for definite reasons cannot attain to that apostolic love, nor by the vigor of their decision climb with ease to that higher and exceedingly rare third degree of renunciation, what must those judge concerning themselves who do not even grasp perfectly the first degree, which is very easy, but retain their former filth of money together with their former unbelief, and imagine that they ought to glory merely in the bare name of human beings?

The first renunciation, then, which we mentioned, is a renunciation of things belonging to others. By itself it is therefore insufficient to confer perfection upon the person who renounces, unless he proceeds to the second renunciation, which is truly a renunciation of our own things. Once we have attained this by expelling all vices, we shall also climb to the summit of the third renunciation. Through it we despise in mind and spirit not only everything that is done in this world or possessed by people in separate portions, but even the fullness of all the elements, which is considered magnificent, as subject to vanity and soon to pass away.

We look only, according to the Apostle, “not at the things that are seen, but at the things that are not seen; for the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4). Thus at last we may deserve to hear what was said to Abraham: “Go into the land that I will show you” (Gen. 12).

This clearly shows that unless someone fulfills those three higher renunciations with the full ardor of his mind, he cannot reach this fourth one, which is given as the reward and recompense of the person who renounces perfectly: namely, that he may deserve to enter the promised land, which will no longer produce for him thorns and thistles of vices, but which, after the expulsion of all passions, will be possessed in this body through purity of heart.

It is not the virtue or diligence of the laboring person that will show this land to him; rather, the Lord himself promises that he will show it, saying: “Go into the land that I will show you.”

This clearly proves both that the beginning of our salvation takes place through the Lord’s calling, when he says, “Go out from your land,” and that the completion of perfection and purity is likewise granted by him, when he says, “Go into the land that I will show you.” That is, it is not a land that you can discover by yourself or through your own diligence, but one that I will show you when you are not only ignorant of it but not even seeking it.

(Ambrose) Having spoken again about the rich, he turns to Timothy’s person and suitably adds what had been mentioned above:

“O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words and the oppositions of falsely named knowledge, which some, promising it, have fallen away from the faith.”

Here he speaks about those people. You, he says, must guard the faith with every virtue, avoiding those who teach contrary things and who are always devising something new and inappropriate to say. They invent controversies against the truth under the name of knowledge, falsely claiming to possess knowledge, while they are very far removed from faith.

He rightly also spoke of the commendation of the doctrines through their carefulness, to show that it is especially necessary for him to guard what he received from him, since what has been entrusted to him will also be required of him.

(Gregory) Whoever prepares himself for the words of true preaching must take the origins of his arguments from the sacred pages, so that everything he says may be referred back to the foundation of divine authority and the structure of his speech may be established upon it.

As we have often said, heretics, while striving to establish their own perverse positions, bring forward things that are in fact contained in the pages of the sacred books. Therefore the excellent preacher admonishes his disciple, saying:

“O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words.”

Because heretics desire to be praised as possessing outstanding intelligence, they produce things that appear new. Thus it happens that, while they wish to appear wise, they scatter seeds of folly among their wretched hearers.

(Cassian) Concerning those who seem to acquire a certain appearance of knowledge, or concerning those who devote themselves diligently to reading the sacred volumes and memorizing the Scriptures but nevertheless do not abandon carnal vices, the following is elegantly expressed in Proverbs:

“Like a gold ring in a pig’s snout, so is the beauty of a badly behaved woman” (Prov. 11).

What benefit is it for anyone to attain the adornment of heavenly eloquence and that most precious beauty of the Scriptures if, by clinging to muddy works or thoughts, he breaks it by subjecting it to filth, as though it were utterly unclean, or pollutes it in the foul mire of his lusts?

The result will be that what is customarily an ornament to those who use it rightly will not only be unable to adorn these people but will become filthy through an even greater accumulation of mud. For praise is not beautiful from the mouth of a sinner, to whom the prophet says:

“Why do you recite my ordinances and take my covenant upon your mouth?” (Ps. 49).

(Ambrose) Bringing the Epistle to completion in these matters, he adds the customary greeting at the end of the Epistle, saying:

“Grace be with you. Amen.”

# BOOK TWENTY-FOUR. EXPOSITION OF THE SECOND EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY

[Col. 0635]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0635D]

Paul’s Epistle to Timothy is here explained according to its meaning. As is our custom, we shall first explain its argument. For it is evident that he did not write this Epistle immediately after the First Epistle, nor did he write it from the same places from which he had written the first. In writing the First, he says: “As I urged you to remain at Ephesus” (1 Tim. 1), showing that he had left him there, and thus he writes the Epistle to him as though Timothy were still residing in those places. In this Epistle, however, at the end he writes: “I have sent Tychicus to you at Ephesus” (2 Tim. 4), as though Timothy were still at Ephesus when he wrote this Epistle to him.

In the first Epistle he had made it clear that he wrote to him in such a way as to indicate that he himself would come to him not long afterward. For he says: “I am writing these things to you, hoping to come to you soon” (1 Tim. 3). But in writing this one, he indicates that he expects soon to depart this life in confession of Christ. For he says: “I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand” (2 Tim. 4). He also orders him to come to him quickly, saying: “Make haste,” he says, “to come to me soon.”

He writes this Epistle to him from the city of Rome, at the time when, after appealing to Caesar, he had been brought to Rome in chains from the region of Judaea (Acts 24). For after remaining in Rome for two years, as Luke says, and after Nero—before whom he had been brought to give an account of himself—had released him by his authority, because Nero had found that he had committed no other act deserving accusation, Paul, once released, immediately fulfilled his work. For he hastened to traverse the whole world in order to impart the knowledge of piety to everyone, and it is not uncertain that wherever Timothy was then residing, he was residing there according to the will of blessed Paul, for the benefit of others.

For it would not have been possible for the Apostle to write to him in this way, praising him, approving his work, and showing concern for everything that concerned him, if Timothy had left him against the Apostle’s will and remained in other places wherever it pleased him. He therefore writes this Epistle to him—not as in the First Epistle, instructing him how he ought to organize each matter that could contribute to the common adornment of the Church, but as one who had sufficiently instructed him in the First Epistle about everything in which it was fitting for him to be instructed. He therefore composed this Epistle for him, giving him counsel and at the same time reminding him that with the utmost diligence he should carry out whatever was useful to others, and with complete eagerness; and that, for the sake of the preaching itself, even if circumstances demanded it, he should not hesitate to expose himself to dangers.

Indeed, much of this Epistle seems to express precisely that point. For this reason he also endeavors to recount how many and how great were the sufferings he had endured in many places, so that he might encourage Timothy to endure similar things in imitation of him. In the middle of the Epistle, where he seems especially to exhort him, he also mentions those who were attempting to advance toward what was worse, reproving them in no mild terms. He further indicates that, as time progresses, wickedness increases greatly among human beings, teaching Timothy not to withdraw from his work because of those who are advancing toward what is worse.

At the end of the Epistle he intimates the things that he carries with him, and the circumstances in which he has been or is. Meanwhile, he also gives instructions concerning matters about which it was fitting for Timothy to be instructed, since he was writing to his beloved disciple. We shall learn all these things most carefully from the interpretation that will be produced section by section; the time also urges us to undertake their interpretation, since the argument has now been sufficiently explained.

## CHAPTER ONE. The Apostle urges Timothy to preach Christ’s Gospel steadfastly, on the grounds of episcopal dignity and the scarcity of preachers.

> “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, according to the promise of life that is in Christ Jesus, to Timothy, my most beloved son: grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.”

*(Ambr.)* What he says, “according to the promise of life that is in Christ Jesus,” refers back to what he had said, “an apostle.” That is: I was made an apostle in order to preach the immortal life promised to all in the future age through Christ, who was also the first to appear to have risen for all, and to teach all human beings throughout the whole world, so that, receiving instruction concerning these things, they might also attain the enjoyment of the promised blessings.

These matters are written in the preface of the Epistle. He begins as follows:

> “I give thanks to God, whom I serve from my forefathers with a pure conscience.”

That is: I hasten to serve him with a pure conscience. For he did not say this as though he were bearing witness to himself, although he truthfully professes that these things were so. Hence he also adds:

> “As without ceasing I remember you in my prayers night and day, and desire to see you.”

This entire statement seems to have been inserted into an already completed thought. The Apostle now returns to what he had said: “I give thanks to God,” and so forth, “remembering your tears, that I may be filled with joy.”

He wishes to say: Because I always remember you in my prayer, whether I pray at night or by day, I give many thanks to God for you, remembering those tears which you shed at the time when you were departing from me. The memory of those tears brings me very great joy. For when he says, “that I may be filled with joy,” the expression “that” does not state the cause, but, in the customary manner, indicates what follows. And lest he seem to rejoice simply over tears, he says:

> “Receiving the memory of the faith that is in you without hypocrisy.”

From these things, he says, I especially consider how sincerely you offer your faith to God, and how great an affection you show toward us, who became your teachers in the words of piety, so that you cannot even bear our separation with magnanimity.

And, showing that diligence in piety was necessary for him in many respects, he adds:

> “Which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice.”

Since this still did not seem to contribute to Timothy’s praise—if his grandmother or parents had been such—he adds:

> “But I am certain that it is also in you.”

That is: you yourself are such. And, wishing to show in every respect that diligence in piety belonged to him, since it had descended to him from his grandparents and parents, and since he himself practiced similar things, he says:

> “For this reason I remind you to rekindle the grace of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands.”

Thus, in every respect, this word addressed to you is appropriate, so that in your work you may show the very grace which you were found worthy to receive through the ordination of my hands.

He sufficiently exhorts him to hasten with all his strength to help others, calling his ordination “grace.” For it was not right that one who had received the divine gift for this purpose should neglect the grace entrusted to him. Since he had sufficiently exhorted him in all these matters concerning what was fitting for him—by recalling his grandparents and parents, his own intention and will, and the grace which he had received at his ordination—and since the task itself seemed arduous, especially because many dangers were being inflicted on them by adversaries at that time, he therefore adds:

> “For God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.”

For we ought not to fear those evils which are inflicted on us by outsiders. Why? Because the grace of the Spirit that is in us is entirely sufficient to strengthen us, bind us to the love of God, and make us pure even in our thoughts.

Finally, the blessed Apostle, who had long ago transcended that servile degree of fear through the power of the Lord’s love, despising lower things, professes that he has been enriched by the Lord with greater blessings:

> “For God did not give us,” he says, “a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.”

He also exhorted those who burned with perfect love of the heavenly Father, and whom divine adoption had already made sons instead of servants, in these words:

> “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again into fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8).

When the prophet described this fear together with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit—which undoubtedly descended upon that Lordly man according to the dispensation of the incarnation—and had said:

> “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety” (Isa. 11),

he finally introduced something as though it were especially important, saying:

> “And the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.”

Here we must first observe carefully that he did not say, “The spirit of the fear of the Lord shall rest upon him,” as he had said of the preceding gifts, but, “It shall fill him,” he says, “with the spirit of the fear of the Lord.” For its abundance is so great that, once it has taken possession of someone through its power, it occupies not merely a part but the whole of his mind.

And rightly so. For, cleaving to the love that never fails, it not only fills the person but also possesses him continually and inseparably, without being diminished by any pleasures of temporal joy or delights—something that sometimes happens with the fear that is cast out.

This, then, is the fear of perfection, with which that Lordly man is said to have been filled—the one who came not only to redeem the human race but also to offer the form of perfection and examples of virtue. For the true Son of God, who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found, could not possess that servile fear of punishments.

Then, inviting him to modesty, he adds:

> “Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord Jesus Christ, nor of me, his prisoner.”

By these words he strongly drew him toward modesty, saying that he should not be ashamed, as though he ought to be ashamed of the things that belong to piety unless he were also willing voluntarily to endure them with some regard for piety. Hence he did not say, “Do not be ashamed of the Lord,” but “of the testimony of the Lord”—that is, of the passion. Nor was it sufficient for him to say this; he also added that he himself was a prisoner, sufficiently reminding him that, while remembering Christ and the things that concerned Christ, he should not shrink from suffering, if he desired to share both with the Apostle and with Christ in these sufferings.

Hence he also adds:

> “But labor together with the Gospel.”

Thus the Gospel itself has been perfected through sufferings. It is necessary that you share in it through the sufferings you endure for the benefit of others, showing that the Gospel is such that it is worthy to suffer for it.

> “According to the power of God, who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works but according to his own purpose and grace.”

This form of expression, in which he says “according to the power of God,” is similar to the wording he used earlier, “according to the promise of life that is in Christ Jesus,” which he placed in the preface of this Epistle. Just as there he says “according to the promise of life”—that is, I was made an apostle to preach the life promised to you—so here also he says, “according to the power of God,” that is, through the power of God, “who saved us.”

Therefore strive, labor, and subject yourself to sufferings, so that you may make known to everyone what has been ordained for our sake. He wishes to say that the Gospel is a great thing, for the power of God is in it—the power of the one who saved us and called us into holiness and into that incorruption which we await. He did this not because of our merit but because of his mercy.

The same is expressed in what was said to the Romans:

> “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes” (Rom. 1).

Labor, then, in a manner worthy of the greatness of the promised blessings.

Then, showing the greatness of the Gospel, he also wishes to exalt it on account of its antiquity. He says:

> “And the grace that was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times, but has now been manifested through the appearing of our Savior Jesus Christ.”

Although the Gospel appears to be new in the outcome of events, it is ancient in the will of the giver. God had long ago approved that these things would take place in Christ. Therefore, when Christ himself appeared to us, he brought it forth in action.

And, to confirm the Gospel, he adds the greatness of the blessings ordained for our sake:

> “Who indeed destroyed death, but brought life and incorruption to light through the Gospel.”

This is what he did, he says: he destroyed death and revealed to us a new kind of life, entirely free from corruption. Such is the life which we await to be granted to us through the resurrection.

And since he had sufficiently stirred him up by the greatness of the doctrines, he adds:

> “For which I was appointed a preacher, an apostle, and a teacher of the Gentiles.”

And, to stir Timothy up by his example, he says: I was appointed an apostle for these things, so that, by doing them yourself, you may also appear to share in my work. Then, continuing to exhort him fully on the basis of his own example, he adds:

> “For this reason I suffer these things, but I am not ashamed.”

He rightly says, “I am not ashamed,” because earlier he had also said to him, “Do not be ashamed.” And, showing that he rightly teaches him not to be ashamed, he says:

> “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to guard my deposit until that day.”

For I am very certain, he says, that the one who gave me the Spirit as a pledge of future things, as a kind of deposit, will preserve this pledge inviolate, so that then we may attain the perfect grace of the Spirit. In that hope we have now received the grace of the Spirit as a pledge.

*(Greg.)* Thus, whatever labors holy men now entrust to the Truth, so many pledges of their reward do they also keep shut within the chamber of hope. Yet the heat of labor is now felt grievously, so that at some time refreshment may be received from rest.

> “You have the pattern of sound words that you heard from me, in faith and love in Christ Jesus.”

*(Ambr.)* Remember my teaching and the things you have often heard from me, when I spoke to you about the faith that we ought to offer to God and the love that is according to Christ. He rightly said, “You have the pattern of my teaching.”

Then, concerning himself, he also gives Timothy the same advice:

> “Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.”

Hasten to preserve unimpaired the grace of the Spirit which you have received, through concern and diligence in doing what is fitting. And, again recalling his own example, he urges him to fulfill his teaching energetically, considering the sorrows that seem to befall him day by day to be of no importance.

> “You know that all those who are in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Philetus and Hermogenes.”

Those who are mentioned here seem to have pretended to hold the faith, but turned away from him while he was residing in Asia. For no external conflict is more grievous than an internal one—that is, when one’s own people abandon him.

Nothing, he says, should make you sorrowful among the sorrows that occur. Consider instead what has happened to me: those who seem to share our faith, all of them in Asia, have abandoned me. Among them are Philetus and Hermogenes. He mentions them by name because perhaps they showed the worst disposition toward the Apostle at Ephesus. He said this for Timothy’s consolation and instruction, so that he would not bear heavily those sorrows that befell him.

Then, exhorting him toward better things, he also mentions one who showed a different disposition and says:

> “May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chain; but when he arrived in Rome, he diligently sought me and found me. May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day; and how much service he rendered at Ephesus, you know better.”

For, by recalling Onesiphorus, he also urges Timothy to exercise diligence in piety. Hence here too he says, “He was not ashamed of my chain,” appropriately joining this to what he had said for Timothy’s exhortation: “Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of the Lord.” And, confident in the progress of his exhortation, he adds:

## CHAPTER TWO. The Apostle urges Timothy to carry out the ministry of preaching and warns him to flee youthful desires.

> “You, therefore, my son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus; and what you have heard from me through many witnesses, entrust to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.”

*(Ambr.)* In every respect, therefore, show in actual deeds, for the benefit of others, that grace which was given to you by Christ. Let your concern be to carry out every great undertaking with diligence, and also to teach others the things you frequently heard from me while I was teaching them. For by saying “through many witnesses” he means that you too should teach these things—not just anyone, but those whom you consider capable of learning them, so that they may also pass on the profit of these teachings to others.

Then, exhorting him by an example, he says:

> “Labor as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.”

Imitate the soldiers of this age, and, considering yourself a soldier of Christ, hasten to endure everything difficult and laborious for the sake of piety. Giving him counsel by the same example, he adds:

> “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one who enlisted him.”

Know, he says, that those who are found worthy in their military service through good will restrain themselves from every worldly business, directing their attention solely to their work. He rightly says, “entangles himself,” and says it very precisely, because one who is such and is concerned with these things cannot attend to what is better, since he has once become entangled in worldly affairs.

Then he turns to another example:

> “And if anyone competes in the games, he is not crowned unless he competes lawfully.”

It is impossible to attain the blessed crowns unless one not only gives attention to the discipline of justice but also perseveres in its laws. So much more fitting is it for you, whether as an athlete or as a soldier of Christ, to restrain yourself from bodily affairs and devote yourself solely to piety.

Since he has exhorted him not to concern himself with worldly business, but to attend only to those things that pertain to the benefit of others, human necessity requires that he also inquire about matters relating to food and clothing.

*(Greg.)* We rightly call the angelic spirits soldiers of God, because we know that they wage war against the aerial powers. Yet they carry out these battles not through labor but by command, because whatever they seek to accomplish against unclean spirits, they are able to accomplish through the assistance of the one who governs all things.

Concerning this army, when our King was born, it is written:

> “Suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army” (Luke 2).

The number of chosen human beings is also joined to this army. Through the lofty desire of their minds, they are freed from the conduct of earthly servitude. Of them Paul says:

> “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs.”

Although they now appear few, in the invisible homeland they reign beyond number. For even if they are few in comparison with the wicked, they cannot be measured by the multitude of their assembly.

Often some people, as though forgetting that they have been placed over their brethren for the sake of their souls, devote themselves with all the effort of their hearts to worldly concerns. When these concerns are present, they rejoice that they are occupied with them; when they are absent, they pant after them day and night amid the fever of troubled thought. And when, perhaps because opportunity has ceased, they are free from these concerns, they are even more grievously wearied by their very freedom from them.

They consider it pleasure if they are weighed down by activities; they count it labor if they are not laboring in earthly affairs. Thus it happens that, while they rejoice in worldly tumult, they remain ignorant of the inward things which they ought to have taught others.

Consequently, the lives of those under them undoubtedly grow sluggish. For when a subordinate desires to advance spiritually by following the example of the one set over him, he encounters that example as an obstacle in the road. When the head is weak, the members are vigorous in vain; and when an army is reconnoitering the enemy, it follows swiftly in vain if the commander himself has gone astray from the route.

No exhortation lifts the minds of those under authority, and no reproof corrects their faults, because, while the ruler of souls exercises the office of an earthly judge, the shepherd’s care is absent from the custody of the flock. Those under him cannot grasp the light of truth, because, while the thoughts of shepherds are occupied with earthly pursuits, the dust driven by the wind of temptation blinds the eyes of the Church.

In contrast, the Redeemer of the human race, when restraining us from gluttony, says:

> “Take heed, lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke 21).

Immediately he adds, “or with the cares of this life,” and, at once adding fear, says:

> “Lest that day come upon you suddenly.”

He also announces the character of its arrival, saying:

> “For it will come like a snare upon all who sit upon the face of the whole earth” (ibid.).

Again he says:

> “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6).

For this reason Paul, by solemnly warning—and rather, by admonishing—the minds of religious people away from fellowship with the world, says:

> “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one who enlisted him.”

For this reason he both commands the rulers of the Church to devote themselves to leisure for spiritual things and shows them remedies for consolation, saying:

> “If you have worldly lawsuits, appoint as judges those who are despised in the Church” (1 Cor. 6),

so that, namely, those whom spiritual gifts do not adorn may serve earthly administrations. It is as though he said more openly: Since they cannot penetrate inward things, let them at least perform the necessary tasks outside.

> “The farmer who labors ought first to receive a share of the fruits. Understand what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in all things.”

*(Ambr.)* He wishes to say: Acquire without hesitation from the faithful who provide for you the things that necessarily pertain to your use. He urged him especially by this very example. Just as a farmer cultivates and teaches the faithful through your teaching, so it is right for you to offer God the fruit of virtue and good works and to receive it before all others, since others also seem to obtain it through your labor.

Hence he says:

> “Understand what I say,”

as though he had expressed the matter somewhat obscurely; at the same time, he wishes him to be granted understanding in all things.

> “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my Gospel, for which I suffer even to chains as though I were a criminal.”

He rightly said, “from the seed,” in order to indicate more clearly the assumption of a body. Nor did he state these things without purpose, for at that time he was especially striving to teach them. Simon and all those who belonged to his heresy had begun to say that Christ was not in the flesh but appeared in some kind of phantasm, so that even a true resurrection was not accepted. For how could the resurrection be believed to be real if the flesh had not truly been assumed?

This, then, is what he says: Remember to teach, as far as your strength permits, that Jesus Christ was born from the seed of David, truly made human according to nature, and that he rose from the dead—a fact which the Gospel also testifies will happen to all.

For this reason I consent to endure what evildoers endure, because I know that great gain can be acquired from it. And, to show that the piety of the Gospel cannot be harmed in any way by the sorrows that befall him, he adds:

> “But the word of God is not bound.”

That is: Although I endure many evils, no harm thereby arises for the truth of the matter. The promise of God remains unimpaired, even if I seem to be subjected to innumerable torments.

He appropriately joins this to what precedes:

> “Therefore I endure all things for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with heavenly glory.”

For the sake of those who have been chosen and set apart for this purpose, I endure everything, so that through Christ they may attain salvation and dwell in everlasting glory. And, exhorting Timothy, he adds:

> “The saying is trustworthy: for if we have died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him.”

There is no doubt, he says, that we who share in things that are worse will necessarily share with him also in things that are better. Showing the gains that usually come from sharing in suffering, he also mentions the loss that usually befalls those who do not wish to remain in the faith:

> “If we deny him, he also will deny us.”

Then, lest it seem that he himself would be harmed in equal measure when we deny him, he adds:

> “If we do not believe, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself.”

The things that we do improperly harm us; he, however, is harmed in no way. For he remains stable and firm in his glory, and these things cannot be denied, since they are discerned in the very events themselves.

> “Remind them of these things, bearing witness before the Lord.”

He rightly says “bearing witness,” in order to bring him into fear:

> “Do not quarrel about words, for it is useful for nothing except the ruin of those who hear.”

Remind them, he says, to pursue these things, setting the judgment of God before them. But do not devote yourself to quarrels, for nothing arises from quarrels except that some desire to confirm lies, to the ruin of many.

> “Take care to present yourself to God as approved, a worker who is not ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth; but avoid profane and empty speech.”

Attend to the safeguarding of the doctrines. Remind them of the things that belong to the truth, teaching them according to a sound rule, and do not shrink from laboring for these things. Reject the novel expressions of the adversaries, which are full of every impurity and have been devised for the sake of novelty by many.

> “For they advance toward greater ungodliness, and their speech spreads like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have departed from the truth by saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they overthrow the faith of some.”

He wishes to say: Do not regard them as having made any new progress, nor suppose that they presently possess advancement according to piety merely because many follow them. Just as gangrene spreads through the body, so they too, enticing many of the faithful with their words, draw them toward ungodliness. Such were Hymenaeus and Philetus, who denied the true resurrection of Christ and dream of another resurrection—one that must necessarily consist in burning.

The Apostle seems to have said these things for Timothy’s consolation, since those who have been appointed to care for the benefit of others are accustomed to become very sorrowful when they see many of the faithful advancing toward what is worse. Therefore, continuing to persuade him not to fail in spirit through distress, nor to be thrown into stupefaction on account of the wickedness of others, he adds:

> “But God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are his.’”

Let these two things console you, he says. First, the seduction of others does not destroy the truth of things. Second, God has long known his own—those who truly belong to him. Thus, those whom you now see being led astray, God already knew to be reprobate. Nothing new is happening, then, so that you should be thrown into stupefaction; rather, what is happening is what God knew long ago would happen.

He also established what care we ought to exercise, saying:

> “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.”

That is, let such people depart from every form of ungodliness.

Since he knew that excellent teachers, such as blessed Timothy, were deeply distressed by these matters—because they saw many of their own people rushing toward what was worse—for this reason he added another consolation and said:

> “In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay; some indeed are for honor, while others are for dishonor.”

The great house, he says, is the Church, consisting of many people. Therefore it is necessary that not all who are there be alike. For even in a great house all the vessels cannot be found to be similar, however large the house may be. Among vessels of gold and silver, wooden and earthen vessels are also seen; some are worthy of honor, while others are contemptible and set apart for a particular use.

Then, since the division of vessels was natural, so that Timothy would not suppose that the same thing must be true among us, he adds:

> “If anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the Master, prepared for every good work.”

There, material nature produces the distinction; here, it is produced by the will. For the one who separates himself from inferior things becomes a useful vessel. This lies within our own will and power.

Showing that the matter depends upon intention, he again turns to Timothy’s exhortation, which he pursues almost throughout the whole Epistle. Hence he says:

> “Flee youthful desires.”

Keep far from yourself every pleasure and empty delight that does not befit you, especially those by which youth is accustomed to be captivated.

> “Pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who call upon the Lord from a pure heart.”

Give attention to righteousness, to faith in God, to love, and to peace with those who pursue the virtues of life. In speaking very well about these matters, he urges him to strive to preserve peace wherever it is proper and possible to do so.

> “Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they produce quarrels.”

He called “foolish and uneducated” those questions that are not undertaken for any useful purpose. Turn away, he says, from those who wish to make themselves shine solely through questions. Quarrels arise from such questions, because their intention is not right. And he shows that such conduct is neither fitting nor becoming for him:

> “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel.”

Then, explaining to him how he ought to devote himself to teaching, he says:

> “But he must be gentle toward everyone, able to teach, not quarrelsome, teaching with gentleness those who resist the truth.”

Showing the usefulness of this approach, and how much better it is to teach those who resist in this way, he adds:

> “Perhaps God may grant them repentance leading to the knowledge of the truth, and they may recover from the devil’s snare, having been held captive by him for his will.”

It is impossible to pacify adversaries through quarrels, but teaching commended by gentleness often knows how to persuade and soften the hardness of the mind. It also prepares them to perceive the truth, when they have departed from presumption. Seized by that presumption, they are held fast as though by a certain diabolical snare, dragged toward what is worse and unwilling to accept any correction for the better.

Then, recalling the future at the end of time, he consoles blessed Timothy, so that he may not lose heart because of the most wicked times and people, as follows in the next chapter.

## CHAPTER THREE. Because false preachers are multiplying, the Apostle exhorts Timothy to preach, and an admonition concerning steadfastness is set before him.

“Now understand this: in the last days difficult times will come.” (Ambrose) For it is customary that the recollection of worse conditions console those who are living in evil ways. And, showing what these difficult times will be, he adds: “People will be lovers of themselves”—doing everything for their own advantage or because of their apostasy—“lovers of money,” because they devote all their zeal to gathering money; “boastful,” those who boast of possessing what they do not possess; [Col. 0647A] “proud,” those who think highly of themselves because of what they appear to have; “blasphemers,” devoting themselves to disparagement and directing all their care toward disparagement; “disobedient to parents.” What he adds is evident: “ungrateful”—toward those who do good to them. For he also places among the wicked those who have been raised up by benefits if they do not give thanks to those who bestowed the benefits; “wicked,” meaning those who show no diligence toward justice; “without affection,” meaning those who deliberately wish to have affection for no one; “slanderers,” those who carry the words of these people to those others, and the words of the others to these, so as to stir them up against one another; “without self-control,” meaning those who are weaker in the grip of their passions; “harsh,” and he considers harsh those who wish to show diligence toward no good thing; “ungrateful,” [Col. 0647B] those who do not willingly pursue the endeavors of good people; “traitors,” that is, of friends; “reckless,” ready for evil; “puffed up,” because they think highly of themselves in matters that are entirely absent from them. There is, however, a difference between “boastful” and “puffed up”: “puffed up” is designated by one’s own judgment, whereas “boastful” describes someone accustomed to vaunting himself in speech. “Lovers of pleasures rather than lovers of God,” those who think pleasures ought to be honored before piety.

He says these things not about outsiders but about members of the Church, who will be such. For from the beginning his discourse concerned such people—those who usually creep toward what is worse—from the point at which he said, “Remember Jesus Christ risen from the dead,” in that exhortation by which, giving advice to Timothy, he endeavored to rebuke the adversaries who also seek to overthrow many of those who belong to the Church. For their sake he fully consoles him, so that he may not bear it too heavily, but may indeed devote himself to his own work and separate himself completely from wicked people. Thus now too, as though speaking about such people, he says that these things will occur at some time in the last days or times: people who, under the appearance of members of the household, will do what ought not to be done.

(Gregory) From this heart is born the arrogance of the proud. If, in their pride, they did not despise God, they would by no means penetrate so many slippery paths through their wantonness. By such vegetation Behemoth is fed: hungry for the punishment of eternal death in them, he is satisfied by their ruined morals. The proud of this world, even when at times they are hindered by the order of eternal providence from completing wicked deeds and therefore cease from them, nevertheless multiply wickedness in thought—sometimes so as to display themselves as more powerful than others in possessions and honors, sometimes so as to exercise that same power in seeking to harm another, and sometimes, driven by slippery impulses, so as to dissolve themselves in frivolous actions and pleasures. While they continually intend to do not what is right but what is wicked with the things divinely granted to them, what else do they do but wage war against the Lord with his own gifts? Since, therefore, this Behemoth continually recognizes himself in the minds of the proud through their desires, he finds in them, as it were, the grasses of the mountains, by which he stretches out his belly, refreshed by his own wickedness.

Thus he appropriately adds: “Having the appearance of piety, but denying its power.” (Ambrose) They pretend, indeed, to possess piety, but are very far removed from the actual practice of it. And because those who will then exist will be such people, he says to him: “And avoid these people. For among them are those who creep into households and captivate little women, burdened with sins, who are led by various desires, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth.” Accordingly, since such people will exist in the last days—of whom these present ones are an enigmatic representation—hasten, as far as your strength permits, to withdraw from them. By their wickedness they plunge themselves into the households of others, so that, seducing certain women, they may draw them toward what is worse. He does not mean women who are truly pious and faithful, for that is impossible, but those who are thought to belong to us. They are filled with every wickedness, and although they are always learning from us what they ought to do, they receive no benefit from our teaching because of the wickedness of their purpose and judgment. For this is especially why they attend to those teachers: they perceive that their words coincide with their own desires.

While terrifying him by recalling future events, he also consoles him by recalling things that have already happened. “Just as,” he says, “Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these people also resist the truth, men corrupted in mind and disqualified in faith.” Remember, he says, what formerly happened in the time of Moses, against whom wicked men resisted. Therefore it is no cause for astonishment if even now people corrupted in mind resist the truth. And since, in a certain sense, such people—especially at the beginning, when they pretend to faith—appear to many to be hidden, people do not recognize who or what they are.

“But they will not advance any further,” he says, “for their folly will be manifest to all, as theirs also was.” Those people, whoever they are, will no longer be able to conceal themselves. Time will make them manifest, just as it made the folly of those earlier men manifest, and in the time that followed. For when some ask how the blessed Paul could have known the names of those who resisted Moses, that question deserves to be regarded as great folly. It is ridiculous to suppose that Moses, although he appears to have declared beforehand such things as had been uncertain to many, could also have remembered the names of men whom no one at that time could have known, while Paul should be regarded with astonishment if he was able to name two men who had lived before him. Moreover, according to the tradition of the ancients, there was nothing new in his knowing these things.

One point, however, deserves notice: it appears to raise a question among many as to how, in the preceding passage, he said that they would “advance greatly,” while here he says, “they will advance no further.” He does not say these things according to the same empty reasoning. There he says that they will advance, speaking of those who follow them, and indicating that those who act according to their words will never fail. Finally, he adds: “And their word spreads like gangrene.” But here, speaking of those who are able to corrupt the truth, he says that they will not advance, because at the beginning many people, not knowing them, recognize only their outward appearance and form. As time goes on, however, they will necessarily come to recognize the subversion contained in their doctrines. Therefore, when he said “they will not advance,” he meant that their error could remain hidden for a time; hence he added: “For their folly will be manifest.”

Through all these statements, therefore, he consoles Timothy, so that he may not be excessively distressed on account of those who are creeping toward what is worse. Then he encourages him by his own counsels, saying:
