“But you have followed my teaching, my conduct, purpose, faith, patience, love, piety, endurance, persecutions, and sufferings.” Always dwelling with me, he says, you have experienced these things: what sort of teaching I was accustomed to give to others; how I disciplined myself; how I hastened each day to practice these things with regard to faith; how I persisted in it without any wickedness; how I loved and endured everyone; and how, with great delight, I endured the persecutions that my adversaries inflicted upon me. Imitate these things, therefore, and devote your concern to them, considering the adversaries to be of no consequence.

Then, to encourage Timothy, he also speaks of the sufferings themselves: “What things happened to me in Antioch, in Iconium, and in Lystra; what persecutions I endured.” And, to make him still more courageous in enduring sufferings, he adds: “And the Lord delivered me from them all.” You know, he says, that in various circumstances God’s providence toward us has been proved. You ought not to depart from it, provided that you are willing to persist patiently in these things.

“And all who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution. But wicked people and impostors will advance toward what is worse, erring and leading others into error.” Again here he uses “advance” of those who are deceived, because such people can never fail. Anyone who wishes to examine the matter by the facts themselves will find that this happens throughout all time: every heresy, when it first appears, becomes suspect to many, but is exposed with time, because whenever a new doctrine arises, there can never be found fewer people who are deceived by it.

“But you, remain in the things that you have learned and believed.” And, urging him to hold fast and persevere, he adds: “Knowing from whom you learned them.” The dignity of the teacher is sufficient to encourage disciples. Then he gives another reason: “And because from childhood you have known the sacred writings.” This too was sufficient to exhort him. For it seems shameful that someone who had been nourished in good things from childhood should, at the end, after a long period of training, begin to do what is unworthy. He also shows that the teaching itself is exceedingly sublime when he calls the sacred writings divine Scriptures, which ought to be believed in every respect. Therefore, adding to the excellence of the teaching itself, he says: “Which are able to instruct you for salvation through faith in Jesus Christ.” He shows that Timothy must remain in the teaching of piety for several reasons: first, because of the greatness of the teacher; second, because he had learned these things from childhood; third, because the teaching itself is divine; and fourth, because it can bestow great benefits upon those who are willing to believe in Christ, as they attain the salvation that comes through faith.

(Hieronymus) It belongs to the discipline of a priest to answer one who asks about the law. If, while displaying diligence concerning other matters, he pleads ignorance and negligence concerning the holy Scriptures, he boasts of his dignity in vain, since he does not exhibit the works appropriate to it. This is what the apostle Paul writes to Titus: that he should be able to refute those who contradict. And to Timothy: “Since from infancy you have known the sacred writings, which are able to instruct you for salvation,” so that he may rebuke sinners before everyone. And because he said, “the sacred writings, which are able to instruct you,” he added: “Every Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work.”

(Ambrose) Such, he says, is all Scripture, which was given by the divine Spirit, so that it is sufficient to provide for every useful purpose: whether it is appropriate to teach what ought to be done, whether sinners ought to be rebuked, whether some correction ought to be applied to penitents, or whether it is necessary to instruct people concerning what can lead them to righteousness. Thus whoever wishes to devote himself to God can, through the usefulness of the Scriptures, become perfect in every respect. And after exhorting him concerning all these things, wishing to make his exhortation more terrifying, he adds in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER IV. The Apostle foretells the multiplication of evil hearers, together with the announcement of his martyrdom. He requests Timothy’s arrival and greets his friends.

[Col. 0650C]

“I therefore testify before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who is going to judge the living and the dead, according to his appearing and his kingdom.” (Ambrose) That is, he will judge everyone then, when he appears according to the dignity in which he exists.

“Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season.” He does not say this so that Timothy should be urgent at an inopportune time—for whatever is inopportune ought not to be done by any reasoning—but he says: leave no time without instruction; consider every time suitable for this purpose. He says this concerning those who ought to be instructed. But because it happens that some, through laziness, do not persevere in instruction, he says: “Reprove, rebuke, exhort.” Reprove those who persist in sin, so that they may be able to understand their sin. “Rebuke,” he says, the one who recognizes his sin, and place him under judgment. “Exhort”: lead him back again, after repentance, to his former state.

He also teaches the manner in which this ought to be done: “With all patience and teaching.” Do not omit anything appropriate to be done, whether in reproof or in rebuke. And because it happened that some did not accept these things because of the wickedness of their character, he again recalls those people: “There will be a time,” he says, “when they will not accept sound teaching, but according to their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears, and they will turn their hearing away from the truth and turn instead to fables.” He called “fables” those words that are contrary to piety.

This recollection was necessary for him in the present situation. For after exhorting Timothy to reprove, rebuke, and exhort, he wished him not to lose heart if some people, rushing toward what is worse, were unwilling to pay attention to him when he did these things. Therefore he indicates that those who will live in the final times will be much worse than these, creating greater labor for their teachers. Hence he adds:

“But you, be sober in all things; endure hardship; do the work of an evangelist; fulfill your ministry.” That is: if some people are not helped, do what you ought to do, and do it with every diligence. Endure labor for the Gospel and perform what belongs to you. For it is for this that he will also give an account, not for the will of others. He rightly said, “Fulfill your ministry”: diligently complete the work entrusted to you, being content with your own task, even if the things belonging to the disciples do not appear to correspond.

And because he had testified concerning these things, after the exhortation he wishes to show that the appropriate time has come for his testimony. Therefore he says: “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand.” My departure from this present life is near, and I will no longer have time to admonish you concerning what ought to be done. For this reason I have given you this exhortation, with God as witness. He did not simply say, “I am being poured out,” but because he was about to undergo death for confessing Christ, he spoke of a libation. For a libation is the pouring out of wine, performed in expiation for divine honor.

“I have fought the good fight; I have completed the course; I have kept the faith.” He does not say these things boastfully, but for Timothy’s encouragement. That is: for the time I had in this life, I fulfilled everything that appeared to belong to me.

(Cassian) Since he knew that, after the fragrance of Christ’s ointments, he had run tirelessly through the devotion of a swift-moving conscience, and had conquered the contest of spiritual struggle by disciplining the flesh, he says with confidence: “From now on the crown of righteousness is reserved for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day.”

(Gregory) Because he had contended against passing evils for the sake of fruit, he confidently anticipated without doubt the joys that endure.

(Ambrose) He rightly called it the crown of righteousness, since it is given in recompense for labors; and he called him the righteous judge to confirm the things that will come to him on account of his labor. He also shows that he alone will not attain such a struggle, but that all who are willing to labor for the Gospel with the same concern will attain it. Hence he says: “And not only to me, but also to all who love his appearing.”

(Cassian) He declares that we will share in his crown on the day of judgment if, loving Christ’s appearing, we acquire victory in the struggle through discipline of the body. He means not only that appearing which will be visible even to those unwilling to see it, but also the appearing that takes place daily in holy souls. Concerning this appearing the Lord says in the Gospel: “I and my Father will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV). And again: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation III).

(Ambrose) Therefore, he says, the prize of the crown is also set before you, if only you are able to labor sufficiently. It is worthy of wonder that he did not say “to those who have labored” or “to those who have suffered,” but “to those who love his appearing.” For the time of struggles and sufferings does not always exist, but the time of love does. If someone hastens to bring salvation as he ought even in a time of peace, he suffers no loss if the time of struggles is absent.

With these words he completes his own counsel and concludes, under solemn testimony, the exhortation concerning the teaching that he appears to have given Timothy. Then he continues to write about matters concerning which reason required him to write, since Timothy was his disciple and especially beloved by him.

“Hasten to come to me quickly.” Explaining the reason why he had ordered him to come quickly, he says: “Demas has abandoned me, loving the present age, and has departed for Thessalonica.” That is, he has turned toward what is worse, entangling himself entirely in the affairs of the present life; for this is what he calls the pleasure of the present age.

“Crescens has gone to Galatia.” By Galatia he means what we now call Gaul; the ancients likewise called all those regions by this name, as one can recognize from many other sources and from the Jewish history that Josephus appears to have written. Those who are now called Galatians are also so named; the account of the ancients indicates that they came from those regions to these places.

“Titus to Dalmatia.” He does not mention that these men departed from him in imitation of Demas or that they had turned toward what is worse, but only that they were not present.

“Luke is with me alone. Take Mark and bring him with you.” And, explaining why Mark should come, he says: “He is useful to me for ministry.” He is suitable for me because he hastens to accomplish everything with the greatest diligence.

“I sent Tychicus to Ephesus.” Then he also instructs Timothy to carry out the things that he ought to do in service:

“When you come, bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus, and the books, especially the parchments.” In Latin he called the parchments *volumina* (“scrolls”), following the usage in which people spoke at Rome. He used this expression without distinction, and it appears that he wrote this Epistle from that city as well. In ancient times people had the custom of writing the divine Scriptures in scrolls, just as even to the present day the Jews appear to possess many things written in scrolls. He called other things “books” according to common usage, because they were in another form.

It is laughable that some have thought that the word *penula* in this passage does not signify the Apostle’s clothing but some kind of book. They have not paid attention to what follows. For it would have been superfluous to say “and the books” if the cloak too were a type of book; it could have been included with the others.

“Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils. The Lord will repay him according to his works. You too, avoid him, for he strongly resisted our words.” He included this for Timothy’s protection and caution, not as an accusation of Alexander. For it did not concern him to pass judgment on Alexander, and therefore he also mentioned the punishment that awaited him from God for the things he was doing. He was not cursing him, as some have thought, but encouraging Timothy, who endured many evils from him, to endure them patiently. For this reason he necessarily mentioned the man and instructed Timothy, as far as his strength allowed, to hasten to avoid his snares.

There is no reason for astonishment that so much disorderly behavior then came from a coppersmith, since ordinary people too rose up against those who preached piety; and the common people especially appeared to stir up every kind of sedition.

“At my first defense no one stood by me, but everyone deserted me. May it not be counted against them.” By “my first defense” he means the occasion when he was first led to Rome in chains from Judea, when he had also made his appeal. He rightly prayed that this sin not be counted against them, since he recognized that some had withdrawn because of weakness and others because of an imminent necessity of their own.

“But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled and all the nations might hear; and I was delivered from the mouth of the lion.” By “the lion” he enigmatically calls Nero the emperor. He wishes to say that he obtained God’s judgment, by whom he was strengthened, and, having given satisfaction concerning the matters that had been brought against him, was ordered to be released, so that he might complete his course and make known the doctrines of piety to many—which he also appears to have done.

“And the Lord delivered me from every evil work, and he will save me for his heavenly kingdom; to him be glory forever and ever. Amen.” He did not say, further, “He delivered me from him.” Earlier he had foretold that he would be killed after not much time, which also happened: he was condemned to death by Nero at the time when he came to Rome for the second time. But he said, “He delivered me from every evil work,” meaning, “He delivered me from every oppression of the present life, saving me for his kingdom, which I also await.”

After this he instructed Timothy: “Greet Priscilla and Aquila and the household of Onesiphorus.” He also informs him about the others, saying: “Erastus remained at Corinth”—indicating that Erastus remained at Corinth. “But I left Trophimus at Miletus sick.” He indicates that he left Trophimus sick at Miletus, and adds: “Hasten to come before winter.”

Then, writing to him, he indicates that the brothers also greet him: “Eubulus greets you, and Prudens [Pudens], and Linus, and Claudia, and all the brothers.” By “all the brothers,” he means those who were at Rome at that time. Those whom he recognized as especially dear to him and righteous he thought worthy of naming individually; the rest he included in the general greeting. First, praying for Timothy himself, he says: “The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.” Then he closes the Epistle with the customary conclusion: “Grace be with you. Amen.” At the end, he also judged himself included with them in the customary greeting.

## BOOK TWENTY-FIVE. EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE TO TITUS.

[Col. 0653]

## ARGUMENT.

[Col. 0653C]

When the blessed Apostle came to Crete, he handed on the way of piety to those who lived there. But because the very demands of piety compelled him to go on to other provinces, so that he might instruct all who lived in different places in the way of piety, he left the blessed Titus in Crete, just as he had left Timothy in Ephesus, placing him over the churches that were there.

He therefore writes to him, to put it briefly, concerning the ordinations that had to be made, instructing him how it was appropriate to make those appointments. At the same time he gives him counsel concerning all the other matters and teaches him how he ought to act in each of them. He also mentions those who were of the circumcision, just as he had mentioned them in the Epistle that he had first written to Timothy, strongly instructing him not to teach anything contrary to piety himself or allow others to teach it.

Finally, this Epistle also appears to bear great similarity to that Epistle. For there was one reason why he wrote both to this man and to that one. The Epistles appear to differ only in this respect: he wrote more fully and cautiously to Timothy about everything, whereas in this Epistle, which he sent to Titus, he appears to have explained everything concisely.

The substance of the Epistle consists in these matters. I, however, taking up the preaching concerning each point, will endeavor to explain it briefly. It is indeed our custom not to prolong the exposition without limit when the meaning of the truth can be sufficiently explained in a few words.

## ANOTHER ARGUMENT.

From Jerome.

Although those who invalidated the first faith are not worthy of belief—I mean Marcion and Basilides, and all the heretics who tear apart the Old Testament—we would nevertheless tolerate them to some extent if they would at least keep their hands off the New Testament and did not dare either to violate the evangelists or the apostles of Christ, whom they themselves loudly proclaim to be the Son of the good God. But now, since they have scattered his Gospels and have made the Apostles’ Epistles not the Epistles of Christ’s apostles but their own, I wonder how they dare to claim for themselves the name of Christians.

Now, since they pronounce judgment with heretical authority and say, “That Epistle is Paul’s, this one is not,” let them understand that they are refuted for the sake of the truth by the very authority with which they themselves are not ashamed to fabricate falsehoods. But Tatian, the patriarch of the Encratites, who himself rejected certain of Paul’s Epistles, considered this one especially—that is, the Epistle to Titus—to be declared apostolic, disregarding the assertion of Marcion and of the others who agree with him on this point.

The Apostle therefore writes, O Paula and Eustochium, from Nicopolis, which is situated on the Actian coast and is now a part—indeed, perhaps the greater part—of your estate. He wrote to his disciple Titus, his son in Christ, whom he had left in Crete to instruct the churches. He instructed him that, when either Artemas or Tychicus had arrived in Crete, Titus himself should come to Nicopolis.

For it was right that the one who had said, “My concern is for all the churches,” and who, setting out from Jerusalem, had established the Gospel of Christ as far as Illyricum, should not allow the Cretans to be abandoned through the absence both of himself and of Titus. From them the seeds of idolatry had first sprung up. Instead, he should send Artemas or Tychicus in his place and that of Titus, so that the Cretans might be strengthened by their teaching and consolation.

## CHAPTER I. Concerning the Lord the Father, who promised the Lord the Son to us before eternal times and later revealed him in his appointed times. Concerning the rule for a bishop, and the fact that those who were once called bishops were the same persons who were called presbyters. And concerning the deceivers of the churches.

“Paul, a servant of God, but an apostle of Christ Jesus.” (Jerome.) In the Epistle to the Romans he began in this way: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle”; but here he calls himself a servant of God and an apostle of Christ Jesus. For if the Father and the Son are one, and whoever believes in the Son believes also in the Father, Paul’s servitude must likewise be referred indifferently either to the Father or to the Son.

This servitude, however, is not that of which the Apostle says (Rom. VIII): “For you have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption, by which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’”; rather, it is the noble servitude of which David also speaks to God: “I am your servant, and the son of your handmaid” (Ps. CXV), and blessed Mary says to the angel: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke I).

Moses also possessed this servitude. Concerning him the Lord says to Jesus son of Nun (Josh. I, XI, XII, XIII): “Moses, my servant, has died.” And elsewhere: “Moses, the servant of the Lord, died in the land of Moab by the word of the Lord.” Surely we must not suppose that Moses and Mary possessed the spirit of slavery in fear rather than in love of God. Nor is it surprising that holy people are nobly called servants of God, since through the prophet Isaiah the Father speaks to the Son: “It is a great thing for you to be called my servant” (Isa. XLIX).

It is therefore not impious to believe that the one who had assumed the form of a servant did what belongs to servants, so that he may be said to have served the Father’s will, since he himself served his servants. This is the servitude of love, by which we are commanded to serve one another. The Apostle himself, although free from all, made himself the servant of all. And elsewhere he says: “Your servant for Christ’s sake.” The servant of God is the one who is not a servant of sin. Therefore the Apostle, who was not a servant of sin, is rightly called the servant of God the Father and of Christ.

Moreover, when he says, “but an apostle of Christ Jesus,” it seems to me equivalent to saying: “the praetorian prefect of Augustus Caesar,” or “the commander of the army of the emperor Tiberius.” Just as the judges of this world, wishing to seem nobler, derive their titles from the kings whom they serve and from the dignity with which they are puffed up, so the Apostle, claiming great dignity for himself among Christians, prefaced his title with the designation “apostle of Christ,” so that the authority of the name itself might terrify those who read it, indicating that all who believed in Christ ought to be subject to him.

[Col. 0656B] “According to the faith of God’s elect and the knowledge of the truth that accords with godliness, in hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before eternal ages; but in his own times he manifested his word in the preaching entrusted to me, according to the command of our Savior God, to Titus, his beloved son according to the common faith: grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.” (Ambrose.) He made the preface of the Epistle long because of that considerable addition which he seems necessarily to have inserted; it is also known that he frequently did this elsewhere, as in the Epistle he had written earlier to the Romans.

The structure of the preface therefore seems to consist in the following: “Paul, a servant of God, but an apostle of Christ Jesus, to Titus, his beloved son,” and the rest that follows. He inserted, however, everything from the point where he had said “according to the faith of God’s elect” up to the point where he said “to Titus, his beloved son.”

This resembles the beginning of the Epistle that he appears to have written a second time to Timothy, where he said: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, according to the promise of life that is in Christ Jesus.” For he says the same thing here: that he was appointed an apostle so that through him all those might believe who had long ago been chosen by God for this purpose because of the goodness of his plan; and that they might also know the truth of godliness, so that they could attain that everlasting life which they await, and which God had long before promised to make present.

“Paul, a servant of God, but an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God’s elect.” (Jerome.) That is, of those who have not merely been called, but also chosen. There is likewise great diversity among the elect themselves according to the variety of their works, thoughts, and words. Nor does everyone who is God’s chosen one immediately possess faith in accordance with his election, or knowledge in accordance with his faith.

Thus the Savior also spoke to the Jews who had believed in him: “If you remain in my word, you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John VII). The Evangelist testifies that he said this to people who had indeed believed, but did not yet know the truth—a truth they could attain if they remained in his word and, having been made free, ceased to be servants.

The question arises why, after saying “according to the faith of the elect and the knowledge of the truth,” he added “which accords with godliness.” Is there some truth that is not grounded in godliness, so that he now introduces the knowledge of a truth that accords with godliness as a distinction from it?

There certainly is truth that does not possess godliness. If someone knows the art of grammar, or dialectic, so as to have a method for speaking correctly and to distinguish between falsehood and truth; geometry, arithmetic, and music also possess truth within their own disciplines—but that is not the knowledge of godliness. The knowledge of godliness is to know the Law, to understand the prophets, to believe the Gospel, and not to be ignorant of the apostles.

Conversely, there are many who possess a true knowledge of godliness but do not immediately possess the truth of the other arts, including those we mentioned above.

[Col. 0657B] This truth, therefore, whose knowledge accords with godliness, is founded upon the hope of eternal life, because it immediately grants the reward of immortality to the one who has come to know it. Without godliness, knowledge of the truth gives pleasure for the present, but it does not possess an eternity of rewards. That eternal life was promised by God, who does not lie, before eternal ages, and he manifested it in his own times in Christ Jesus.

But to whom did he promise it beforehand, and whom did he afterward make manifest, except his Wisdom, which was always with the Father (Prov. VIII), rejoicing when the world had been completed and delighting in the sons of humanity, and promising that all who would believe in it would possess eternal life?

Before he laid the foundations of the world, before he spread out the seas, established the mountains, suspended the sky, and consolidated the earth by casting down its mass, God promised these things—God in whom there is no falsehood. This is not because he could lie but chose not to utter words of falsehood; rather, because, as the Father of truth, he contains no falsehood in himself.

Nor must we pass over in silence how God, who does not lie, promised eternal life before eternal ages. From the time when, according to the account of Genesis, the world was made, and times were established through the succession of nights and days, and likewise of months and years, the periods of time have been constituted. Within this course and wheel of the world, times pass away and come again; some are future and others past.

For this reason certain philosophers do not think that the present exists, but only the past or the future, because everything we speak, do, or think either passes away while it is happening or, if it has not yet happened, is awaited.

Before these times of the world, therefore, we must believe that there was a certain eternity of ages, in which the Father was always with the Son and the Holy Spirit. And, so to speak, all eternity is God’s one time—or rather, there are innumerable times, since he himself is infinite and, existing before times, surpasses every time.

Not yet six thousand years of our world have been completed. How many eternities before this, how many times, how many beginnings of ages must we suppose there were, in which angels, thrones, dominions, and the other powers served God and, at God’s command, continued to exist without the cycles and measurements of time?

Before all these times, therefore—times that neither speech can express, nor the mind comprehend, nor silent thought dare approach—God the Father promised that the word of his Wisdom, his very Wisdom, and the life of those who would believe would come into the world.

Pay close attention to the text and order of the reading, because the eternal life that God, who does not lie, promised before eternal ages is not something other than the Word of God. “For he manifested,” he says, “his word in his own times.” Therefore the life he had promised is his Word, which “in the beginning was with the Father”; “and the Word was God, and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I).

That the Word of God, namely Christ, is himself life, he testifies elsewhere when he says: “I am life” (John XIV). This life is not brief or confined within certain periods of time, but perpetual and eternal. It was manifested in the last ages [Col. 0658B] through the preaching entrusted to Paul, the teacher and master of the nations, so that it might be proclaimed in the world and become known to humanity, according to the command of our Savior God, who desired us to be saved by fulfilling what he had promised.

The Apostle writes to Titus, “his beloved son,” which in Greek is γνησίῳ τέκνῳ, and cannot be fully expressed in Latin. For γνήσιος has this particular sense: someone is called faithful, genuine, and, so to speak, legitimate or true-born, without comparison to another.

From this we understand that there was also considerable difference among Paul’s sons: some were γνήσιοι, that is, most genuine, closely joined to him, and born from a true marriage and a free woman; others, however, were like those born of the slave woman and of Hagar, who could not receive the inheritance with Isaac, the son of the free woman (Gal. IV).

For the discourse, wisdom, and teaching by which Titus instructed the churches of Christ made him the Apostle’s own son and separated him from association with all the others.

Let us next examine what follows: “according to the common faith.” Did he call the faith of all who believed in Christ common, or only his own faith and that of Titus? It seems better to me that the faith of the apostle Paul and Titus was called common than that of all believers. Among the latter, because of the diversity of their minds, faith could not be common but was diverse.

Finally, the preface of the Epistle and the Apostle’s greeting to Titus are completed with this conclusion: “Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.”

This may mean either that both grace and peace come from God the Father as well as from Christ Jesus, so that each may be understood as given by both; or that grace is referred to the Father and peace to the Son.

We must not pass without reflection over the fact that in some cases the Apostle prayed that grace and peace might be multiplied for them, whereas here, in addressing Titus, peace and grace are stated without multiplication.

Noah, a righteous man and the only one saved from the shipwrecked world, is not said to have found many graces but one grace in the sight of God. Moses likewise says to the Lord: “If I have found grace in your sight …”

It belongs to the perfect to purchase one pearl and one treasure at the price of all pearls and all their possessions; beginners, however, and those still on the journey, do not yet possess even one pearl alone, but many.

[Col. 0659A] “For this reason I left you in Crete,” so that you might set right what remained unfinished.

It belongs to the apostolic dignity to lay the foundation of the Church, which no one can lay except the architect. “For no one can lay any foundation other than Jesus Christ.”

Those who are lesser craftsmen can build structures upon foundations. Therefore Paul, as a wise architect, striving with every effort not to glory in what had already been prepared, and after softening the hard hearts of the Cretans toward faith in Christ—subduing and instructing them both by speech and by signs, and teaching them to believe not in their native Jupiter but in God the Father and in Christ—left Titus, his disciple, in Crete to strengthen the beginnings of the newly born Church and to correct whatever seemed to be lacking. He himself went on to other nations in order once again to lay the foundation of Christ among them.

When he says, “so that you might set right what remained unfinished,” he shows that they had not yet arrived at the full knowledge of the truth. Although they had been corrected by the Apostle, they still remained in need of correction. Everything that is corrected is imperfect.

(Ambrose.) He rightly said, “what is lacking.” If the order of godliness had not been handed down to everyone by the Apostle, it remained for the administration of the believers to be completed, so that they might be instructed toward agreement through ecclesiastical ordinances. He also indicates what correction is necessary.

“And appoint presbyters in each city, as I directed you.”

(Jerome.) Let bishops hear this—those who have the power to appoint presbyters in each individual city—and let them learn under what law the order of ecclesiastical appointment must be maintained. Let them not suppose that these are merely the Apostle’s words, but Christ’s, who says to his disciples: “Whoever rejects you rejects me; and whoever rejects me rejects the one who sent me” (Luke X). Likewise: “Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever hears me hears the one who sent me” (ibid.).

From this it is evident that those who, disregarding the Apostle’s law, wish to confer an ecclesiastical rank on someone not because of merit but through favor, act against Christ. Through his Apostle, Christ has explained in what manner a presbyter ought to be appointed in the Church.

Moses was God’s friend, and God spoke with him face to face. He could certainly have made his own sons successors to his authority and left his particular dignity to his descendants. Yet Jesus, a stranger from another tribe, was chosen, so that we might know that authority over peoples is to be given not to blood but to life.

But now we see very many people treating this matter as a favor. They do not seek those who could benefit the Church most, to raise them as pillars of the Church, but those whom they themselves love, or by whose services they have been won over; or those for whom some influential person has made a request; and, to say nothing of worse cases, those who have secured clerical status by gifts.

Let us carefully attend to the Apostle’s words: “So that you might appoint presbyters in each city.”

(Ambrose.) Just as those who are in error need the knowledge of godliness, so it also seems necessary to admonish those who have believed concerning godliness. This cannot otherwise be done unless all assemble together and certain men are appointed for this purpose—men able by their teaching to fulfill the duty of communion.

This could be fulfilled through the appointment of a presbyter, who, when they had assembled, could discuss with them and teach them those matters which it was appropriate for them to learn. Hence in the present passage he mentions only these men, because for this very reason they could provide great benefit in the common assembly.

It is indeed clear that the others were also necessary—those who, together in the clerical order, would fulfill their own duties, and through whom matters pertaining to the common good could be explained.

Then he repeats what he had said: “as I directed you,” teaching what sort of presbyters ought to be appointed.

“If anyone is without reproach”—not someone recognized as a sinner because of the offense of his sins, but someone known for the integrity of his life, so that he may truly and reasonably be judged without reproach, having overcome every ambush of his accusers.

[Col. 0660B] “For a bishop must be without reproach, as God’s steward.”

(Jerome.) Therefore the presbyter is the same as the bishop. Before rivalry was introduced into religion at the devil’s prompting, and people began saying among themselves, “I am of Paul,” “I am of Apollo,” “I am of Cephas” (1 Cor. I), the churches were governed by the common counsel of the presbyters.

But after each person began to regard those whom he had baptized as his own rather than as Christ’s, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one of the presbyters should be chosen and set over the others, and that the entire care of the Church should belong to him, so that the seeds of schisms might be removed.

Suppose someone thinks that the view that bishop and presbyter are one, and that the one is a name of age and the other a name of office, is not derived from Scripture but is our own opinion. Let him reread the Apostle’s words to the Philippians: “Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are in Philippi, with bishops and deacons: grace to you and peace,” and the rest (Phil. I).

Philippi is one city of Macedonia, and certainly there could not have been several bishops in one city in the way they are now called bishops. But because at that time the same men were called bishops as were called presbyters, he spoke indifferently of bishops as presbyters.

Someone may still regard this as ambiguous unless it is confirmed by another testimony. It is written in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XX) that, when the apostle Paul had come to Miletus, he sent to Ephesus and summoned the presbyters of that same Church. Among other things he then said to them: “Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to shepherd the Church of the Lord, which he acquired through his own blood.”

Here too observe carefully how, after summoning the presbyters of the one city of Ephesus, he later called those same men bishops.

If anyone wishes to accept the Epistle written under Paul’s name to the Hebrews, there too the care of the Church is divided equally among several people. For he writes to the congregation: “Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are the ones keeping watch over your souls, as those who must give an account, so that they may not do this with groaning, since that would be of no benefit to you.”

Peter, who received his name from the firmness of his faith, says in his Epistle: “Therefore I appeal to the presbyters among you, as a fellow presbyter and witness of Christ’s sufferings, and as one who shares in the glory that is to be revealed in the future: shepherd the flock of the Lord that is among you, not under compulsion but willingly” (1 Pet. V).

This has been said to show that among the ancients the same men were presbyters as were bishops; gradually, however, so that the shoots of dissensions might be torn out, the entire responsibility was transferred to one person.

Therefore, just as presbyters know that by ecclesiastical custom they are subject to the one placed over them, so bishops should know that they are greater than presbyters more by custom than by the truth of the Lord’s appointment, and that they ought to govern the Church in common, imitating Moses. Although he alone possessed the authority to rule the people of Israel, he chose seventy men with whom he might judge the people (Num. XI).

Let us therefore see what sort of presbyter or bishop ought to be appointed.

“If anyone is without reproach, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not accused of debauchery or disobedient.” (Gregory.) The distinction between sin and crime is this: every crime is a sin, but not every sin is a crime. In this life many people can be without crime, but no one can be without sins.

Thus the holy preacher, when describing a man worthy of priestly grace, did not say, “If anyone is without sin,” but “if anyone is without reproach.” For who can be without sin, when John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I)?

In this distinction between sins and crimes we must consider that some sins pollute the soul, whereas crimes destroy it. Thus blessed Job, defining the crime of sexual immorality, says: “It is a fire that devours unto destruction” (Job XXXI). The guilt of wrongdoing does not merely stain unto pollution but devours unto destruction.

And because, whatever other good works there may be, if the crime of sexual immorality is not cleansed, they are overwhelmed by the enormity of this crime, he added: “and uprooting all its growths.” The growths are the soul’s good works; yet if the flesh rules over it in a perverse order, the fire of sexual immorality burns up everything that has been brought forth well. For in the sight of almighty God no works of justice or piety are of any value if they are shown to be defiled by the contagion of corruption.

What good does it do if someone piously has compassion on the need of his neighbor, when impiously he destroys himself, the dwelling place of God? Therefore, if the flame of lust is extinguished through the impurity of the heart, every virtue that arises is produced in vain.

“For a bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward: not arrogant, not irascible, not addicted to wine, not violent, not pursuing shameful gain.” (Jerome.)

First, then, he must be blameless—whom, I think, he calls by another word “irreproachable” in the Letter to Timothy. This does not mean merely that, at the time when he was ordained, he should be without any crime and should have erased his former stains by a new manner of life; rather, from the time when he was reborn in Christ, no consciousness of sin should gnaw at him. For how can the ruler of the Church remove evil from its midst if he himself has fallen into a similar transgression? Or with what freedom can he rebuke a sinner when, silently, he himself answers that he has committed the very things he rebukes?

Therefore, “whoever desires the office of bishop desires a good work” (1 Tim. III). He says “work,” not honor or glory. “Moreover, he must have a good testimony from those outside, so that he may not fall into reproach and the devil’s snare.”

As for what he says, “the husband of one wife,” we should understand it not to mean that every monogamous man is better than a digamous one, but that the person who can exhort others to monogamy and continence should himself provide an example in his teaching. Suppose, for example, that one man lost his wife as a young man, was overcome by the necessity of the flesh, took a second wife, immediately lost her also, and thereafter lived continently; while another remained married until old age and, as most people consider happiness, enjoyed the use of his wife and never ceased from sexual intercourse. Which of the two seems to you better, more chaste, and more continent? Surely the man who was unfortunate even in his second marriage and afterward lived chastely and holily—not the man who was not separated from his wife’s embrace even by old age. Let no one, then, congratulate himself, when chosen as though monogamous, that he is better than every digamous man, since in him what has been chosen is happiness rather than will.

[Col. 0662A]

Some understand this passage as follows: they say that it was the custom of the Jews either to have two wives or more, as we read in the Old Testament concerning Abraham and Jacob. They therefore take this to be the present commandment: that the man to be chosen as bishop must not have two wives at the same time.

[Col. 0662B]

Many, more superstitiously than accurately, think that even those who were formerly pagans and had one wife, but, after losing her, married another after Christ’s baptism, should not be chosen for the priesthood. Yet if this is to be observed, those should rather be kept from the episcopate who, having previously practiced lust promiscuously among prostitutes, took one wife after being reborn. It is much more detestable to have fornicated with many than to be found digamous, since in the one case there is the misfortune of marriage, while in the other there is a lust readily inclined to sin.

(Augustine.) What food is for the salvation of the body, intercourse is for the preservation of the race; neither is without carnal pleasure, but the different works of the Fathers were determined only by the difference of times. Thus it was necessary for even non-carnal prophets to unite carnally, just as it was necessary for even non-carnal apostles of the Church to eat bodily food.

[Col. 0662C]

Those understood more acutely that a steward may not be ordained unless he is the husband of one wife who judged that even a man who, as a catechumen or pagan, had had another wife should not be ordained. For the issue concerns the sacrament, not sin, since all sins are forgiven in baptism. But the one who said, “If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she does not sin; and let her do what she wishes—she does not sin if she marries” (1 Cor. VII), made sufficiently clear that marriage is no sin.

[Col. 0662D]

Because of the holiness of the sacrament, however, just as a woman, even if she was defiled while still a catechumen, cannot after baptism be consecrated among God’s virgins, so it did not seem unreasonable that a man who had exceeded the single number of wives had not committed some sin, but had lost a certain sacramental norm—not necessary for the merit of a good life, but for the sign of ecclesiastical ordination. Thus, just as the many wives of the ancient fathers signified our future churches from all the nations, subject to one man, Christ, so our bishop, the husband of one wife, signifies the unity of all the nations subject to one man, Christ. This unity will be perfected when he reveals the hidden things of darkness, and so forth; at present, however, there are both open and concealed dissensions—even with charity preserved—among those who will then be one and united, though at that time no such dissensions will exist.

[Col. 0663A]

Therefore, just as it was not then permitted, is not now permitted, and will never be permitted to serve two or more masters, so it was not then permitted, is not now permitted, and will never be permitted to pass from a living husband into another marriage. For to apostatize from one God and go over to another’s adulterous superstition is always evil.

Our holy men therefore did not do, for the sake of more numerous offspring, what Cato the Roman is said to have done—namely, to hand over his living wife to another household so that children might be produced there. In our marriages, the holiness of the sacrament counts for more than the fruitfulness of the womb.

[Col. 0663B]

(Jerome.) Indeed, it lies within our power for a bishop or presbyter to be blameless and to have one wife. But what follows—“having faithful children, not accused of dissipation or disobedient”—does not lie within our will.

[Col. 0663C]

Suppose that parents have properly trained their children and from earliest childhood have continually instructed them in the Lord’s commandments. If afterward these children devote themselves to dissipation, overcome by vices and giving the reins to lust, will the fault rebound upon their parents, and will the children’s sins stain their father’s holiness?

If anyone instructed his children well, I think Isaac was among such men; certainly he must be believed to have properly trained his son Esau. Yet Esau, a fornicator and profane man, sold his birthright for one meal (Gen. XXV, XXVI, and following). Samuel likewise, who was such that he called upon the Lord and the Lord heard him, and who obtained winter rain in the time of harvest, had sons who turned aside after greed, accepted gifts, and became such unjust judges that the people, unable to endure them, asked for a king like the other nations (1 Sam. VIII).

[Col. 0663D]

Therefore, if priests were being chosen, Isaac would be judged unworthy of the priesthood because of Esau, and Samuel because of his sons. And when the sins of parents are not imputed to their children, now that the sentence “The parents have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge” (Ezek. XVIII) no longer prevails, will the vices of children prejudice their parents?

[Col. 0664A]

The first point, then, must be that the name of the priesthood is so holy that even matters outside our control are counted against us—not that we fail to become bishops because of our own vices, but that we may be kept from this rank because of our children’s lack of restraint. For with what freedom can we rebuke other people’s children and teach them what is right when the one rebuked can immediately say to us, “First teach your own children”? Or with what face can I rebuke a stranger fornicating when my own conscience answers me: “Then disinherit your fornicating son; cast away your children who serve their vices”? When a wicked son lives with you under the same roof, do you dare remove the speck from another’s eye while not seeing the beam in your own? (Luke VI.)

[Col. 0664B]

The righteous man is not, then, polluted by the vices of his children; rather, the Apostle reserves for the leader of the Church the freedom to become such a man that he will not fear rebuking outsiders because of the vices of his children.

Furthermore, this must also be brought forward against those who swell with pride over the episcopate and think that they have attained not Christ’s stewardship but sovereignty, because all who have not been ordained bishops are not immediately better than they are, and because they imagine that their election proves them especially approved. Let them understand that some have been removed from the priesthood because the vices of their children hindered them.

[Col. 0664C]

But if the sins of children prevent a just man from becoming bishop, how much more will each person, considering himself and knowing that “the powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wis. VI), withdraw from this position—which is less an honor than a burden—and refrain from seeking to occupy the place of others who are more worthy!

Finally, it must be said that in Scripture “sons” are understood as λογισμοί, that is, thoughts, and “daughters” as πράξεις, that is, deeds. The bishop who must now be appointed is therefore one who has both his thoughts and his deeds under his control, who truly believes in Christ, and who is not stained by any defilement of creeping vices.

[Col. 0664D]

“For a bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward.” Among stewards, therefore, a faithful man is sought—one who does not eat and drink with drunkards, strike male and female servants, but awaits the Lord’s coming at an uncertain hour and gives his fellow servants their food at the proper time. The sole difference between a steward and a household is that the steward is a fellow servant placed over his fellow servants.

[Col. 0665A]

(Ambrose.) In this passage he demonstrates two things that we have already mentioned in the First Letter to Timothy: those who are now called presbyters were then called not only presbyters but also bishops. For when he says, “that you should appoint presbyters throughout the cities,” and, discussing presbyters, adds, “For the bishop must be irreproachable, as God’s steward,” he shows that those who were to be appointed throughout the cities and who could carry out the administration of the churches were called presbyters. They entrusted entire provinces to these men for the same purpose and gave them the authority to ordain. Traveling through the cities, like bishops through their regions, they ordained those who seemed insufficient for service in the Church and taught them what they ought to do, both ordaining and instructing each individual as they thought expedient.

[Col. 0665B]

At that time these same men who presided over ordinations were called apostles. Because of the reverence attached to that title, they considered it burdensome to be called by that name and preferred, according to the custom now in use, to claim for themselves the title of bishops, since they judged it a greater distinction of merit to be called by the name of apostles. If matters had not been so, he would not have said, “that you should appoint presbyters throughout the city,” but would have said, “that you should appoint a bishop throughout the city,” who, once ordained, could fulfill everything that those lesser ministers were able to accomplish.

[Col. 0665C]

(Jerome.) Let the bishop therefore know that the people are his fellow servants, not his slaves. The other matters that follow lie within our control.

“Not arrogant”—that is, not puffed up and pleased with himself because he is a bishop, but, like a good steward, seeking what benefits the greatest number.

“Not irascible.” The irascible man is one who is always angry and is shaken by the slightest breath of an answer or of sin, like a leaf by the wind. Truly, nothing is uglier than a furious teacher who, although he ought to be gentle and, according to what is written, “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, apt to teach, patient, instructing with gentleness those who oppose him,” behaves in the opposite way: with a grim face, trembling lips, furrowed brow, unrestrained insults, and a countenance shifting between pallor and redness, he makes a din with his shouting. By his savagery he drives the erring not so much back toward the good as headlong toward evil.

[Col. 0665D]

Hence Solomon also says: “Anger destroys even the wise” (Ecclus. VII); and, “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James I). Yet a man who becomes angry occasionally is not thereby irascible; the irascible man is one who is frequently overcome by this passion.

He also forbids the bishop to be “addicted to wine.” Concerning this it is written to Timothy: “Not devoted to much wine.” What is it like to see a bishop drunk, so that, with his judgment occupied, he either amplifies his laughter contrary to the dignity of gravity and cackles with relaxed lips, or, if he happens to remember some sad matter, bursts into sobs and tears amid his cups?

[Col. 0666A]

It would take too long to go through each detail and explain the insanities suggested by drunkenness. You may see some turning cups into weapons and throwing a goblet into a fellow guest’s face; another, with his clothes torn, rushing upon another’s wounds; some shouting, others sleeping. The one who has drunk more is considered stronger; it is treated as an accusation if someone, despite being adjured in the king’s name, has not drunk more frequently. They vomit in order to drink, and drink in order to vomit. The digestion of the stomach and the throat are occupied with one and the same service.

For now, let this suffice: according to the Apostle, “in wine is debauchery” (Eph. V); and wherever there are satiety and drunkenness, there lust rules. Look at the belly and the genitals: the arrangement of the members corresponds to the quality of the vices. I shall never consider a drunk man chaste, for even if he has fallen asleep stupefied by wine, he could nevertheless have sinned through wine.

[Col. 0666B]

We may well wonder that the Apostle condemned drunkenness in bishops or presbyters when the Old Law also commanded (Lev. X; Num. VI) that priests, when entering the temple to minister to God, should drink no wine at all; and that the Nazirite, as long as he was growing his sacred hair, seeing nothing defiled or mortal, should abstain from wine, from dried grapes, from the weaker drink usually made from grape pomace, and from every intoxicating beverage that turns the mind away from soundness.

[Col. 0666C]

Let everyone say what he wishes; I speak from my own conscience. I know that abstinence, when interrupted, has harmed me, and, when resumed, has benefited me.

After drunkenness he also commands that the bishop not be violent. Taken simply, this instruction edifies the hearer, so that he does not readily extend his hand to strike, or, mad with anger, break out into blows upon another’s face. Better, however, is it to call non-violent the man who is gentle and patient, knows at the proper time what should be said and what should be kept silent, and does not strike the consciences of the weak with useless speech.

[Col. 0666D]

For when the Apostle forms the leader of the Church, he is not forbidding him to be a boxer or a pancratiast—a fault that would also be condemned in a commoner or any pagan—but, as I have said, he forbids him, by insulting and talkative behavior, to destroy one whom he could have corrected through modesty and gentleness.

The pursuit of shameful gain must likewise be absent from the man who is to become bishop. There are many who teach what ought not to be taught for the sake of shameful gain; they overthrow entire households and think that godliness is a means of profit (1 Tim. VI). Better, according to Solomon (Prov. XVI), is “a small gain with justice than great revenues with iniquity”; and a good name in poverty is to be preferred to an evil name in riches (Ps. XXXVI).

[Col. 0667A]

The bishop who wishes to imitate the Apostle, having food and clothing, ought to be content with these alone (1 Tim. VI). Those who serve the altar should live from the altar (1 Cor. IX)—live, he says, not become rich. Hence money is shaken out of our belt, and we wear only one tunic, and we do not think about tomorrow (Mark VI). To pursue shameful gain is to think about more than the present.

Up to this point, the Apostle’s words have instructed us concerning what a bishop or presbyter ought not to possess. Now, by contrast, what he ought to possess is explained.

[Col. 0667B]

“But hospitable, a lover of good things, chaste, just, holy, continent, holding fast the faithful word that accords with the doctrine, so that he may be able to encourage in sound doctrine and rebuke those who contradict.” (Ambrose.)

“Hospitable,” he says—that is, one who gladly receives strangers united to him in faith. “Kind,” so that he is devoted to goodness. “Chaste,” so that he keeps himself superior to every form of wantonness. “Just,” so that he pursues justice. “Holy,” so that he preserves himself above every evil. “Continent,” one who takes no pleasure in sensual delights. “Holding fast the faithful word that accords with the doctrine”—that is, diligently devoted to the doctrine of godliness. Yet what benefit is there in being diligent about doctrine if one is not also equipped with the ability to teach it? “So that he may be able to encourage in sound doctrine and rebuke those who contradict.”

[Col. 0667C]

He must possess the virtue necessary not merely to teach godliness abundantly to the godly, but also to rebuke those who resist, supported by the truth of the doctrines.

(Jerome.) Above all, hospitality is enjoined upon the future bishop. If everyone desires to hear those words from the Gospel, “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matt. XXV), how much more should the bishop’s house—whose home ought to be a common lodging for all—be hospitable? A layman who receives one, two, or a few people will fulfill the duty of hospitality. Unless the bishop receives everyone, he is inhuman.

[Col. 0667D]

But I fear that, just as the queen of the South, coming from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, will judge the people of her own generation, and the men of Nineveh, having repented at Jonah’s preaching, will condemn those who despised hearing the Savior, greater than Jonah (Matt. XII), so very many among the people, withdrawing from the ecclesiastical rank while practicing activities unsuitable for a bishop, may judge bishops.

I think John referred to such matters when he wrote to Gaius: “Beloved, you act faithfully in whatever you do for the brethren, especially for strangers, who have testified to your love before the Church. You will do well to send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God; for they have gone out for the sake of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles” (3 John 5, 7).

[Col. 0668A]

And truly, while the Holy Spirit spoke through him of what would happen to the churches, he already then rebuked the matter, saying: “I wrote also to the Church, but Diotrephes, who desires to hold the first place among them, does not receive us. Therefore, when I come, I will call attention to his deeds, which he does by speaking evil against us. And not content with refusing to receive the brethren himself, he also prevents those who wish to do so and casts them out of the Church.”

Now, indeed, one may see what was foretold in many cities: when bishops or presbyters see laymen who are hospitable and lovers of good things, they envy, rage, excommunicate, and expel them from the Church, as though it were not permitted to do what a bishop himself does not do—as though the condemnation of priests consisted in such laymen’s existence. They regard them as burdensome, as if placed upon their own necks, and harass them with various persecutions in order to draw them away from good works.

[Col. 0668B]

Let the bishop also be chaste, whom the Greeks call σώφρονα (*sōphrona*). The Latin translator, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, translated it “prudent” instead of “chaste.”

If laymen are commanded to abstain from intercourse with their wives for the sake of prayer, what should we think of the bishop, who must daily offer to God undefiled sacrifices for his own sins and those of the people? Let us reread the Books of Kings, and we shall find that the priest Abimelech refused to give David and his men the bread of the Presence until he had asked whether the men were pure from women (1 Sam. XXI)—not from other women, but from their wives—and until he had heard that they had abstained from marital relations since the day before yesterday. Only then did he grant them the bread he had previously refused.

[Col. 0668C]

How great is the difference between the bread of the Presence and the body of Christ? What difference is there between shadows and bodies, image and truth, models of future things and the very things prefigured by those models?

Therefore, just as gentleness, patience, sobriety, moderation, abstinence from gain, hospitality, and kindness ought especially to be found in the bishop, and as he ought to stand out among all laymen in these qualities, so chastity—indeed, priestly purity, if I may put it so—must be his particular possession. His mind, which is to consecrate Christ’s body, must abstain not only from impure deeds but also from the glance of the eye and the error of thought.

[Col. 0668D]

The bishop must also be just and holy, so that he may exercise justice among the people over whom he presides, rendering to each what he deserves and showing no partiality in judgment. The difference between the justice of a layman and that of a bishop is that a layman may appear just among a few, whereas a bishop can exercise justice among as many as he has under his authority.

“Holy,” which in Greek is called ὅσιος (*hosios*), signifies rather a holiness mingled with piety and referred to God. The one whom we call holy, the Greeks call ἅγιος (*hagios*); the one whom they call ὅσιος, we may call pious toward God.

[Col. 0669A]

The bishop must also be abstinent—not, as some think, merely from lust and the embrace of his wife, but from every disturbance of the soul: he must not be provoked to anger, cast down by sadness, agitated by fear, or lifted up by immoderate joy. Abstinence is also mentioned by the Apostle among the fruits of the Spirit. If it is required of everyone, how much more of the bishop, who must patiently and gently bear the faults of sinners, console the fainthearted, support the weak, return evil to no one for evil, and overcome evil with good?

[Col. 0669B]

Finally, he must hold fast the faithful word that accords with the doctrine, so that, just as God’s word is faithful and worthy of complete acceptance (1 Tim. I), he may present himself in such a way that everything he says is considered worthy of belief and his words become a rule of truth.

He must also be able to console those who are shaken by the storms of this age and, through sound doctrine, destroy weak and defective teachings. It is called “sound doctrine” in contrast with doctrine that is sick and weak. He must also be such as to rebuke those who contradict—heretics, Jews, and the wise men of this age.

[Col. 0669C]

The preceding qualities that he lists among the bishop’s virtues pertain to life. But what he says—“so that he may be able to encourage in sound doctrine and rebuke those who contradict”—pertains to knowledge. For if a bishop’s life alone is holy, his holy life can benefit only himself. But if he is also learned in doctrine and speech, he can instruct others as well—not only his own people, by instructing and teaching them, but also his adversaries, striking them back. Unless they are refuted and convicted, they can easily corrupt the hearts of the simple.

[Col. 0669D]

This passage is directed against those who surrender themselves to idleness and the dream of leisure and think it a sin to read the Scriptures, and who despise as babblers and useless those who meditate on the law of the Lord day and night (Ps. I). They do not notice that, after listing the bishop’s manner of life, the Apostle likewise enjoined doctrine.

“For there are many who are disobedient, empty talkers, and deceivers of minds, especially those of the circumcision. They must be silenced, since they overthrow entire households, teaching what ought not to be taught for the sake of shameful gain.” (Ambrose.)

[Col. 0670A]

There are many, he says, who do not wish to obey the doctrine of truth; by following every kind of verbal emptiness, they lead many astray. Such are those who are of the circumcision, who wish to introduce the doctrine of the Law into Christian teaching. Hence they must be rebuked with greater force, since they teach against equity, so that the simple may be freed from their deception.

Nor can they otherwise be separated from their madness, since they devote all their efforts to overthrowing entire households and leading them toward worse things through the vanity of their words. They do this especially in order to satisfy their greed for money and to acquire funds by such means.

[Col. 0670B]

(Jerome.) The man who is to become the leader of the Church should possess eloquence joined with integrity of life, lest his deeds be silent without speech, and his words blush because his actions fail to support them.

There are not merely a few but many who are disobedient and arrogant, who do not heed the Psalmist’s words: “Is not my soul subject to God?” (Ps. LXI). They corrupt, by empty persuasion, the good seed of minds that naturally possess knowledge of God.

[Col. 0670C]

This is what Paul seems to me to have meant when he says φρεναπάται (*phrenapatȇ*): not, as the Latin translator simply rendered it, “deceivers,” but “deceivers of minds.” Indeed, without the authority of Scripture, their talk would have no credibility, unless they seemed to support their perverse doctrine with divine testimonies as well.

These are the Jews of the circumcision, who at that time were striving to overthrow the emerging Church of Christ and introduce legal precepts. Paul discusses them more fully in Romans and Galatians. A few months ago, we too dictated three volumes in explanation of the Letter to the Galatians.

[Col. 0670D]

Such men the teacher of the Church, to whom the souls of the peoples have been entrusted, must overcome by the reasoning of Scripture and silence them by the weight of its testimonies. They overthrow not one or a few households, but entire households with their masters and families, teaching about distinctions among foods, the abolition of the Sabbath long ago, and the insult of circumcision. If only they did this out of zeal for the faith, they might in some measure be excused, since the Apostle says: “I testify that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. X).

[Col. 0671A]

But now they do it because their god is their belly (Phil. III). For the sake of shameful gain, they wish to make people their own disciples, so that, like teachers, they may be supported by their followers.

We may also interpret “for the sake of shameful gain” in another way. We may suppose that the Apostle used a common expression by which all heretics, while teaching perverse doctrines, customarily claim to be gainers of men, although it is not gain but destruction to kill the souls of those they deceive.

By contrast, whoever rebukes his erring brother according to the Gospel, and the brother is converted, has gained him. What greater gain or anything more precious can there be than to gain a human soul? Every teacher of the Church who persuades people to the faith of Christ by sound reasoning is therefore an honorable gainer; and every heretic who deceives and is himself deceived by various tricks, speaking what ought not to be spoken for the sake of shameful gain, is the opposite.

[Col. 0671B]

“One of them, their own prophet, said: ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies.’ This testimony is true.” (Jerome.)

As regards the wording and the continuity of the passage, the statement “One of them, their own prophet, said” seems to refer to those about whom he spoke above: “especially those of the circumcision, who must be silenced, since they overthrow entire households, teaching what ought not to be taught for the sake of shameful gain.” The sequence would then be: “One of them, their own prophet, said.”

But since this hexameter verse is found in none of the prophets who prophesied in Judea, it seems to me that the passage should be read in two ways. The words “One of them, their own prophet, said” may be joined to what precedes: “For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what was lacking,” followed by, “One of them, their own prophet, said”—that is, one of the Cretans.

[Col. 0671C]

But because much intervenes between the statements, this seems awkward, and perhaps no one will accept it. Therefore it must be connected in another way with the nearer preceding words. We should read as follows:

“There are many who are disobedient, empty talkers, and deceivers of minds, especially those of the circumcision. These many disobedient, empty-talking deceivers of minds, together with those of the circumcision, must be silenced, since they overthrow entire households, teaching what ought not to be taught for the sake of shameful gain. One of them, their own prophet, said”—so that “their own prophet” refers not specifically to the Jews, and especially to those of the circumcision, but to the many who are disobedient, empty talkers, and deceivers of minds. Since they were in Crete, they must certainly be believed to have been Cretans.

[Col. 0671D]

This verse is said to be found in the oracles of Epimenides, the Cretan poet. For the present he called him a prophet, either allusively—since such Christians deserve such prophets, just as there were the prophets of Baal, the prophet of Confusion, and other prophets of offenses whom Scripture mentions as vicious—or because Epimenides truly wrote oracles and responses that foretold the future and announced long beforehand what was to come.

Indeed, the book itself bears the title *Oracles*. Since it appeared to promise something divine, I think the Apostle consulted it to see what the divination of the Gentiles promised and then made timely use of the verse when writing to Titus, who was in Crete, so that he might crush the false teachers of the Cretans by the authority of their own island.

[Col. 0672A]

Paul is also found to have done this elsewhere. In the Acts of the Apostles, when he was addressing the people and arguing at the Areopagus, the court of the Athenians, he said among other things: “As some of your own poets have said: ‘For we are indeed his offspring’” (Acts XVII). This half-line is found in Aratus’s *Phenomena*, which Cicero translated into Latin, as did Germanicus Caesar, and more recently Avienus, along with many others whose names it would take too long to enumerate.

To the Corinthians, who themselves were refined by Attic eloquence and, because of the proximity of their region, seasoned with the flavor of the Athenians, he took an iambic verse from Menander’s comedy: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. XV).

Nor is it surprising that he should make use, according to the opportunity of the moment, of verses by Gentile poets, since he also addressed the Athenians by altering something from the inscription of an altar: “As I passed by,” he said, “and observed your objects of worship, I found an altar on which was written: ‘TO AN UNKNOWN GOD.’ What therefore you worship without knowing, this I proclaim to you.”

[Col. 0672B]

The inscription on the altar, however, was not as Paul stated it, “To an unknown god,” but rather: “To the gods of Asia, Europe, and Africa, to unknown and foreign gods.” But because Paul did not need several unknown gods, but only one unknown God, he used the singular expression to teach that the God whom the Athenians had written at the head of the altar was his own God. They ought rightly to know that they should worship the one whom they had revered without knowing him, and they could not remain ignorant of him.

Paul did this rarely and only when the opportunity of the place, rather than a desire for display, required it—after the manner of bees, which are accustomed to compose honey from various flowers and fit together the cells of their honeycombs.

Some think that this verse was taken from Callimachus of Cyrene, the poet, and in part they are not mistaken. For Callimachus himself, writing in praise of Jupiter against the Cretans, who boasted that they displayed his tomb, says: “Cretans are always liars, who even built his tomb with sacrilegious intent.”

But, as we said above, the complete verse was taken by the Apostle from the poet Epimenides, and Callimachus used its beginning in his own poem. Alternatively, Callimachus may have put into meter a common proverb by which Cretans were called deceitful, without appropriating another’s work.

Some think that the Apostle should be criticized because he made an inadvertent mistake and, while rebuking false teachers, confirmed that verse. Cretans are said to be deceitful because they constructed an empty tomb for Jupiter. If, as Epimenides or Callimachus says, they rebuke the Cretans as deceitful, evil beasts, and lazy bellies because they do not recognize the divine, because they imagine that Jupiter, who reigns in heaven, lies buried on their island, and if the Apostle’s judgment confirms what they said to be true, it follows that Jupiter is not dead but alive.

Thus, they say, Paul, an unskilled destroyer of idolatry, while acting against perverse teachers, asserted the gods whom he was attacking.

The brief answer to them is this: just as, when he says “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” and “For we are indeed his offspring,” he did not thereby approve Menander’s entire comedy or Aratus’s entire book, but made use of a verse because it suited the occasion, so here he did not confirm the whole work of Callimachus or Epimenides—one of whom sings Jupiter’s praises and the other writes about oracles—by means of a single verse. He rebuked only the Cretans as liars because of the vice of their nation, not on account of the opinion for which they were criticized by the poets, but because of their innate readiness to lie, refuting them through the testimony of their own countryman.

Finally, so that we may know that the Apostle did not speak against the Cretans by chance, as those people think, but deliberately, carefully, and with every possible safeguard, he says: “This testimony is true.” He does not mean the entire poem from which the testimony was taken, nor the whole work, but only this testimony, this verse by which they are called liars. And surely one who agreed with only one part of a poem must be understood to have rejected the rest.

We discussed in Paul’s Letter to the Galatians how the Cretans are marked as liars, the Galatians as foolish, Israel as stiff-necked, and each province by its own particular vice.

Since there is nothing more that we can add here, we are content with this.

(Ambrose.) “This testimony is true,” he says—that is, what was said about the Cretans by someone who was formerly considered great among them is true. I also affirm the same thing about them, because they show no concern for the doctrine of truth but, on the contrary, attend to the lies of those who are of the circumcision, who strive to teach them nothing true.

What, then, must be done, since they are such?

“On account of which reason, rebuke them sharply, so that they may be sound in faith, not paying attention to Jewish myths and commandments of men who have turned away from the truth.” He commanded that they be rebuked sharply, so that they might persevere in sound faith and not be led astray by those who report certain fabricated myths and ravings, teaching them to observe the law—a human commandment belonging to those who pay no heed to the truth and do not wish the law to cease through God’s judgment.

(Hier.) Therefore, he says, rebuke them severely: for they are liars, evil beasts, and lazy bellies, who persuade people of falsehoods, who, like wild beasts, thirst for the blood of the deceived, and who, not working quietly, eat their own bread. “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame.” Rebuke them, so that they may be sound in faith. Concerning this soundness of faith he speaks also in what follows: “that the older men be sober, honorable, chaste, sound in faith and charity and patience.” By analogy with the soundness of faith, soundness is also ascribed to doctrine: “For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine.” There are also “words of sound teaching,” about which he speaks to Timothy in the First Epistle: “If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the doctrine that accords with piety” (I Tim. VI).

That is, if anyone, after the coming of Christ, is cut down or mutilated (conciditur) and is not circumcised, he serves Jewish myths and commandments of men who oppose the truth. For it is not the one who is a Jew outwardly, but the one who is a Jew inwardly; nor is it circumcision outwardly, but circumcision of the heart in the spirit, not in the letter. If anyone celebrates Passover not “with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (I Cor. V), so as to remove from his soul every old leaven of malice and wickedness, that person attends to myths and follows shadows while neglecting the truth.
