If anyone, not rising with Christ and not seeking the things above but those below, says, “Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle” things that perish (Coloss. III), that person, by practice according to the commandments and teachings of men, follows rules that are not good and commandments that are not good. But where there is truth and a spiritual law, there are good justifications and excellent commandments; whoever does them “shall live by them” (Ezech. XX).

“Everything is clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean; rather, both their mind and conscience are defiled.”

(Amb.) Because they seemed to act scrupulously regarding the consumption of foods, some of which, according to the terms of the law formerly promulgated, were to be eaten and others rejected, he says: The things made for food have nothing unclean in themselves, provided that someone wishes to consume them with a clean conscience; but if someone, through his unbelief, has a defiled conscience, nothing can be clean for one who is such. Through their own faithlessness they are likewise harmed by all these things.

(Hier.) At Christ’s coming everything was cleansed: what he purified, we cannot partake of. But when treating these matters, we must take care not to provide an opportunity for that heresy which, according to the Apocalypse and to the Apostle Paul himself when writing to the Corinthians, thinks that one ought to eat things sacrificed to idols, because everything is clean to the clean. For the Apostle’s purpose here was not to discuss things sacrificed to demons, but to oppose Jews who, according to the discipline of the abolished law, considered some things clean and others unclean. For he says: “We cannot partake both of the Lord’s table and of the table of demons; nor can we drink both from the Lord’s cup and from the cup of demons.”

It is therefore in us whether we eat clean or unclean things. For if we are clean, creation is clean for us. But if we are unclean and unbelieving, everything becomes common for us, whether because of the heresy dwelling in our hearts or because of the consciousness of our sins. Moreover, if our conscience does not condemn us and we have confidence in piety toward the Lord, “we shall pray with the spirit, and we shall pray also with the mind; we shall sing psalms with the spirit, and we shall sing psalms also with the mind” (I Cor. XIV), and we shall be far from those of whom it is now written: “Both their mind and conscience are defiled.”

“They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him, being detestable and disobedient and rejected for every good work.”

Those whose mind and conscience are defiled profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him, according to what is said in Isaiah: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX; Matth. XV). Just as someone honors with his lips and withdraws far away in his heart, so someone confesses God in speech but denies him in his works.

(Amb.) They deny, he says, knowledge of his works by refusing to obey his laws or to do anything that accords with them.

(Hier.) But one who denies God by his works, with a feigned confession, is rightly detestable and profane; and since he is persuaded by no consideration of truth, he is called disobedient and unbelieving. Hence it happens that he is rejected for every good work. For even those things that he may perhaps have done well, overcome by natural goodness, are not good, since by the perversity of his mind they are rejected.

They think that God is denied only if, during persecution, someone is seized by the Gentiles and refuses to acknowledge himself a Christian. But behold: the Apostle declares that God is denied by all actions that are perverse. Christ is wisdom, justice, truth, holiness, and strength. He is denied through foolishness as wisdom, through iniquity as justice, through falsehood as truth, through disgrace as holiness, and through weakness of spirit as strength. Whenever we are overcome by vices and sins, so often do we deny God; and conversely, whenever we do something good, we confess God.

Nor should we suppose that on the day of judgment the Son of God will deny only those who denied Christ in martyrdom. Through all works, words, and thoughts, Christ, whether denied, denies; or confessed, confesses. I think that it is concerning this confession that he also commands the disciples, saying: “You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (Acts I), so that in all good works and words a mind devoted to Christ may confess him.

There is also a certain praiseworthy denial, of which the Apostle himself says (Tit. II): “That, denying impiety and worldly desires, we may live chastely, justly, and piously in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of our great God and Savior.” Whoever has denied this denial and wishes to follow the Savior who says, “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matth. XVI), having put off the old man with his works and put on the new, will follow his Lord (Ephes. IV).

But how someone should deny himself must be considered. The chaste person denies the fornicator he formerly was; the wise person, the imprudent; the just person, the unjust; the strong person, the weak. And, to speak generally of everything, we deny ourselves as often as, trampling upon our former vices, we cease to be what we were and begin to be what previously we were not.

## CHAPTER II. Titus is instructed to educate older men, younger men, and slaves.

“But you, speak what accords with sound doctrine.”

(Hier.) It is one thing to speak sound doctrine and another to teach what accords with sound doctrine, because in the one case there is merely simple instruction, while in the other, together with what one teaches, there is also correction of life. “Whoever relaxes one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matth. V).

We read that the Savior commanded the disciples not only to labor in meditation upon the Scriptures, so that they might repeat what was written and store it in the treasury of memory, but first to do what was commanded: “Whoever does and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.). Unless our justice surpasses the justice of the scribes and Pharisees, we cannot enter the kingdoms of heaven. They sit upon the chair of Moses, speak but do not act, and bind unbearable burdens, which they place upon people’s shoulders, while they themselves do not wish to touch them with even a finger (Matth. XXIII).

Thus the Apostle now teaches Titus, his son in Christ and his disciple, to speak what accords with sound doctrine, because doctrine is sound when the teacher’s teaching and life are in agreement.

“That the older men be sober, honorable, chaste, sound in faith, charity, and patience.”

(Amb.) The word “teach” is missing. He means: Teach the older men, so that he may say that those who are more advanced in age in the Church should be sober and concerned with those things that accord with both modesty and chastity. “Sound in faith and charity,” according to that firmness which everyone ought to possess.

(Hier.) Having first generally instructed Titus concerning what he himself ought to say to everyone, in the words, “But you, speak what accords with sound doctrine,” he now explains, species by species, what is fitting for each age. First, what is fitting for older men; next, what is fitting for older women; third, what is suitable for the young, both male and female; although, in the command concerning older women, he appended instructions regarding younger women, so that he might not so much teach the younger women himself as explain what they should be taught by the older women. Finally, concerning slaves, and concerning each age and condition, he establishes the commands in such a fitting manner that his speech becomes a rule for life and conduct.

He therefore wishes the older men to be sober, or watchful, because among the Greeks νηφάλιοι signifies both; honorable, so that the gravity of their age may be adorned by gravity of conduct; chaste, so that they may not indulge themselves in the age of others, nor, with blood already cold toward lust, become an example of ruin to the young; sound in faith, concerning whose soundness we have spoken above.

But let them be sound not only in faith, but also “in charity and patience,” so that, once they possess the first soundness of faith, they may hear from the Savior: “Your faith has saved you” (Matth. IX). Charity is warm in those who burn in spirit; but it is cold, icy, and frozen in those who have endured the harshest blasts of the north wind. “For from the north evil will be kindled upon all who inhabit the land” (Jer. I). Because of this coldness of charity, Amnon also grew cold toward his sister Tamar (II Reg. XIII). Therefore we must fear lest we too should at some time be overcome by this weakness of charity.

For it sometimes happens that at first our affection toward a virgin or toward any woman is holy; but when the mind has softened into attachment, gradually the soundness of charity grows pale through languor and begins to weaken, until it brings the lover to final death. Therefore the Apostle also commands Timothy cautiously and prudently to exhort the younger women in all chastity.

All chastity exists in flesh, spirit, and soul: lest the eye be scandalized; lest we remain hanging, fascinated by the beauty of a woman’s face; lest we take pleasure in hearing useless words; lest the mind, first hardened, should afterward grow soft through feigned speeches. Let both young and old men, therefore, and both younger and older women, as we have said, take care and guard their hearts with every diligence, lest through the soundness of love the disease of affection enter, and through holy love there arise a love that is not holy, drawing them to Gehenna.

Whoever is sound in faith and sound in charity should also be sound in patience—patience that is tested especially in temptations. For it is of no benefit to have possessed the things we have listed above unless all the wealth and merchandise with which a ship is laden are preserved in a storm, and, while winds blow from every side, what was well acquired is brought safely through without shipwreck: “For whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matth. X and XXIV).

“Older women likewise are to be in holy behavior, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, teachers of what is good, so that they may train the younger women to be chaste: to love their husbands, to love their children, to be modest, chaste, managing their households, kind, submissive to their husbands, so that the word of God may not be blasphemed.”

(Amb.) By “older women” he means those advanced in age, just as above he spoke of older men; not, as some in the Church mistakenly suppose, women advanced in age who, after the manner of men, should assume the office of the presbyterate. He makes this clear when he says “likewise.” He means that women advanced in age should also be adorned with becoming behavior—that is, should be advanced in reverence and modesty—and should not devote themselves to much wine or drunkenness. Nor should they carry the words of these women to those men, or the words of those men to these women. Let them teach what is good, so that they may not only be able to apply diligence to goodness but also teach the things that are best.

(Hier.) Although the Apostle Peter commanded that husbands should honor their wives as the weaker vessel (I Petr. III), it must not nevertheless be thought that a wife who has a weaker bodily vessel must therefore also be weak in mind. Hence they are now commanded so that in them too the Apostle’s saying may be fulfilled: “Power is perfected in weakness” (II Cor. XII). They are told to possess everything that was commonly commanded to older men, in the words “older women likewise”—that is, just as older men, they should be sober, honorable, chaste, sound in faith, charity, and patience.

And, according to their sex, they should have this distinctive quality: that they be “in holy behavior,” or, as it is better read in Greek, ἐν καταστήματι ἱεροπρεπεῖς—that is, their walk, movements, facial expression, speech, and silence should all display a certain dignity of sacred decorum.

And because this class of women is usually talkative, according to the saying (I Tim. V): “At the same time they also learn to go around from house to house, and not only idle but also gossips and busybodies, saying things that they ought not,” he therefore wishes them not to be slanderers—that is, not accusers, not women who, in order to please some people, disparage others.

Or perhaps, since they themselves have already passed beyond youth, they discuss the ages of younger women and say: “That woman adorns herself in this way; that one dresses herself in that way; so this woman goes out; she loves him; she is loved by him.” Even if these things are true, they ought not so much to accuse them before others as to correct the woman herself privately through the charity of Christ, and to teach her rather not to do such things than to accuse her publicly for having done them.

These ages, because the pleasures of the body have grown cold for them—although there are many who are not ashamed of their gray hair and who, trembling before a flock of grandchildren, arrange themselves like little maidens—are accustomed to surrender themselves to wine according to their desire. When they have seemed wise and eloquent to themselves amid their cups, they assume a kind of austerity of conduct, saying what they imagine themselves to be and not remembering what they once were. Let older women therefore be prohibited from excessive drinking of wine, since what lust is in the young, drunkenness is in the old.

Or how can an older woman teach younger women chastity, when, if a younger woman imitates the drunkenness of an old woman, she cannot be chaste? He says pointedly and explicitly: “Not enslaved to much wine.” For it is a kind of slavery and the lowest condition for a person’s senses to be occupied by wine, so that the person is no longer his or her own but belongs to the wine.

Since he has first taught what sort of women older women ought to be, and then explained what they have in common with older men, he has also set out their particular qualities: that they be full of honorable and holy behavior and of every form of decorum; neither slanderers nor disparagers of others, nor women whose senses are occupied by wine. He now consequently entrusts them with the reins of teaching, so that, when they have become such women, they may have freedom to teach—to teach, that is, what is good.

Although in another place he says, “I do not permit a woman to teach,” this must be understood as removing from them the authority to teach men. Otherwise, they are to teach younger women as their own daughters.

First, let them teach chastity, because against this the enemy fights most fiercely in the flowering of youth, and all his power against women is concentrated in the navel of the womb. Next, let them teach them to love their husbands and cherish their children.

What sort of instruction is it to teach women to love their husbands, when this is established not in the speech of the teacher but in the heart of the lover? He wishes them to love their husbands chastely; he wishes there to be modest affection between husband and wife, so that the wife, with modesty and shame, and as though compelled by the necessity of sex, may render the marital debt rather than demand it from her husband, and may believe that she performs the work of bearing children before the eyes of God and the angels.

In this way she will not be ashamed even of the secrecy of the marriage bed, the darkness of night, and her closed bedroom, when she considers that everything lies open to God’s eyes. They love their children in the proper manner if they train them in God’s discipline. But to refuse to distress them by teaching what is good and to grant them freedom to sin is not to love children but to hate them.

Let the younger women also be trained to care for their households. And because it could happen that household management might be conducted harshly, making a wife more severe toward her servants through this command of the Apostle, he therefore added “kind,” so that she might then consider herself to be governing her husband’s household well if she obtained this from the servants through kindness, not terror.

He also says “submissive to their husbands,” lest, puffed up by wealth and nobility, they forget God’s judgment by which they are subject to their husbands. For he says to the woman: “Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. III).

Here the wisdom of Holy Scripture must be considered. The Lord did not address this to the man, saying, “You shall rule over your wife,” but to the woman, so that he might leave her the reward of obedience, since it lies within her power—if she wishes to obey God’s commands—to serve her husband and be subject to him. Thus her servitude would in a certain way be free and full of love: she serves her husband while fearing to offend him.

For the man was not created because of the woman, but the woman because of the man. And since the man is the head of the woman, while Christ is the head of the man, any wife who is not subject to her husband, that is, to her head, is guilty of the same offense as a man who is not subject to Christ, his head.

The word of the Lord is blasphemed either when God’s first judgment is despised and treated as worthless, or when the Gospel of Christ is brought into disrepute, as a Christian woman—subject according to the law of God—desires to rule over her husband against the law and faith of nature, even though Gentile women also serve their husbands according to the common law of nature.

“Likewise exhort the younger men to be chaste in all things. Present yourself as an example of good works, in teaching, in integrity and chastity, in sound and irreproachable speech, so that the one who is opposed may be ashamed, having nothing evil to say about us.”

(Amb.) Just as, when speaking of those women, he instructed what sort of younger women ought to be, so he added very appropriately concerning younger men, saying “likewise”—that is, teach younger men also to devote themselves to sobriety and chastity.

And because he has mentioned all older and younger people, whether men or women, he consequently adds: “Presenting yourself as an example of good works in all things, preserve incorruptibility in teaching, sound and irreproachable speech, so that the one who is opposed may be ashamed, having nothing wrong to say about us.”

“In all things,” he says, “of which you teach others, present yourself as a model of good works.” Show them every form of chastity in your own deeds, and speak of everything that is good and free from reproach, so that our life may make our adversaries ashamed, since they can say nothing wrong about us.

(Hier.) Just as, when he had commanded above, “Older women likewise in holy behavior,” we said that the likeness of the older women was to be referred to the older men, so now, in what he adds, “Likewise exhort the younger men to be chaste,” we think that the likeness of the younger men should be applied to the older women, and through the older women to the older men, so that the younger men may possess the sobriety of the older men and be honorable, chaste, and sound in faith, charity, and patience.

They should also possess the holiness of behavior belonging to the older women, so that they may not be accusers, may not be enslaved to much wine, and may teach what is good, and so forth.

But he made this particular to the younger men: that they should be chaste in all things—namely, in mind as well as body, in deed as well as thought—so that there may be no suspicion of disgrace in a young man.

Although some Latins think that it should be read: “Likewise exhort the younger men to be chaste,” and then continue, “In all things presenting yourself as a model of good works,” we should nevertheless know that “in all things” refers to what precedes: “Exhort them to be chaste in all things.”

We should also know that continence is necessary not only in the activity of the flesh and in the desire of the mind, but in all matters: so that we do not desire undeserved honors, are not inflamed by avarice, and are not overcome by any passion.

“Presenting yourself,” he says, “as a model of good works.” It is of no benefit for someone to be trained in speaking and to have worn out his tongue in talking unless he teaches more by example than by word.

Thus, if someone is immodest, however eloquent he may be, when he exhorts his hearers to chastity, his speech is weak and he has no authority to exhort. Conversely, however rustic and slow to speak someone may be, if he is chaste, he can urge people by his example to imitate his life.

What he says, “in incorruptibility,” should be understood in the sense that incorruptibility properly signifies virginity. Thus those who are virgins are commonly called incorrupt; and those who have ceased to be virgins are called corrupt. We say: “She who was once a virgin has been corrupted.”

Hence I think that Titus, before he was occupied with the work of the flesh, believed the Gospel, received baptism, and remained a virgin, and that now he is admonished by the Apostle to present himself as a model of incorruptibility. We do not see this incorruptibility in Timothy. For when he said to him, “Let no one despise your youth, but be an example of the faithful in speech, conduct, charity, faith, and chastity,” he said nothing about incorruptibility and mentioned only chastity.

Chastity can be understood even in celibacy without virginity—unless perhaps we understand chastity as referring to the mind and incorruptibility to the body, according to what is written elsewhere in the definition of a virgin: “That she may be holy in body and spirit.”

And he himself now adds in sequence: “In teaching, in incorruptibility, in chastity.” We can interpret both incorruptibility and chastity as referring to integrity in teaching, except that what follows specifically—“in sound and irreproachable speech”—would then constitute a distinct command concerning the instruction of doctrine.

When he says “irreproachable speech,” he does not mean that anyone possesses such eloquence and prudence that no one reproves him—for even the apostles and evangelists are reproved by heretics and Gentiles—but that he should say or do nothing deserving reproach, even though adversaries are ready to reproach him.

And because there are many who are disobedient, empty talkers, and deceivers of minds, who hate the one who reproves at the gates and abhor holy speech, let us therefore present ourselves as examples in all things—in teaching, integrity, chastity, and sound and irreproachable speech—so that adversaries, terrified by the soundness of our life and doctrine, may not dare to accuse us; that is, may not fabricate anything plausible as an accusation.

Indeed, even today we see some people in the Churches—although such a rare bird is seldom found—possessing such gravity and self-restraint that they receive testimony even from adversaries, who say: “That man is great and of holy conduct and upright morals—if only he were not a heretic.”

No one is so outrageously shameless that he could accuse the rays of the sun of darkness or cover bright light with the gloom of night. Therefore the Apostle, also guarding against these things, says (II Cor. XI): “So that I may remove the opportunity from those who desire an opportunity.”

The one who is opposed may also be understood as the devil, who is the accuser of our brothers, as the evangelist John proclaims. When he has nothing evil to bring against us, he is put to shame, and the accuser cannot accuse. The devil, moreover, in Latin means “accuser” or “slanderer.”

“Slaves are to be submissive to their own masters in everything, pleasing, not contradicting, not stealing, but showing complete and good faith, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior.”

(Amb.) In this passage too he teaches that slaves should be submissive to their own masters. He says, “Teach them in everything,” if this is pleasing to their masters. He makes this clearer in what follows when he says “in everything,” referring only to service; but he did not state this so that it might be turned toward impiety. He says: “Not contradicting, not defrauding,” so that they do not despise the commands of their masters, bring any fraud upon them, or steal anything belonging to them, but show complete and good faith, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior.

Teach them, he says, to show every form of good faith toward their masters. For the doctrine of God will thus appear admirable, since it also produces slaves who behave in such a way toward their masters.

(Hier.) Since our Lord and Savior, who says in the Gospel, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matth. XI), considers no condition, age, or sex excluded from blessedness, the Apostle now establishes commands also for slaves, as members of the portion of the Church and of the body of Christ.

And just as above he taught what Titus ought to teach older men, older women, younger women, and younger men, so now he establishes commands suitable for slaves.

First, they are to be submissive to their masters in everything—but in all those things that are not contrary to God. If a master commands something that is not contrary to the Holy Scriptures, the slave should submit to the master. But if the master commands something contrary to them, the spirit must obey God rather than the master of the body.

Pay careful attention to how he assigns commands suited to each person. “Slaves,” he says, “are to be submissive to their masters in everything.” Elsewhere, discussing children, he says: “Children, obey your parents” (Coloss. III). It is fitting for children to obey their parents; for slaves, to be subject to the master who commands.

But just as a poor person can be saved according to his measure, and a woman is not excluded from the kingdom of God because of the weakness of her sex, and every condition can attain blessedness according to its proper order, so slaves should be content that they are slaves. They should not think that they cannot serve God because they are subject to human beings, but should rather wish to please God’s will by being submissive to their masters in everything, by being content with their condition, and by fulfilling what the Apostle next commands, so that they do not contradict or steal.

The greatest vice of slaves is to contradict their masters and, when they have commanded something, to mutter to themselves. Titus therefore warns that through sound teaching he should remove this passion from those who are Christian slaves.

For if a slave must carry out what the master commands, why should he not do this with good will, rather than offend his master while nevertheless doing what he is ordered to do—especially since God was offended by the people at the waters of contradiction? Elsewhere, speaking of the murmuring people, he says: “Let their murmuring cease before me, and they shall not die” (Num. XX).

After contradiction, let the doctrine of Christ correct another vice of slaves: that they not be thieves. A thief is judged not only in great matters but also in small ones. For it is not what has been taken by theft that is considered, but the mind of the thief.

As in fornication and adultery, the act is not different because the prostitute or adulteress is beautiful or rich, deformed or poor; whatever she may be, it is one fornication or adultery. So too in theft: however much a slave may take, he incurs the crime of theft.

Let slaves therefore be submissive to their masters in everything, content with their condition, not bearing slavery harshly, not contradicting their masters, and not stealing. After this, let them show good faith in everything, so that they may adorn in everything the doctrine of God our Savior.

For if they are faithful in small matters before earthly masters, greater matters will begin to be entrusted to them by God. The one who does what is suited to his condition adorns the doctrine of the Lord. Conversely, the one who is not submissive in everything, who is displeased with his condition, who contradicts and defrauds, and who shows good faith in nothing, brings it into disgrace.

For how can someone be faithful in the substance of God who was unable to show faithfulness to an earthly master?

“But the grace of God our Savior appeared to all people, training us to deny impiety and worldly desires and to live soberly, justly, and piously in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us so that he might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself a people of his own, zealous for good works.”

(Amb.) Such, he says, is the grace that has now appeared through Christ, a grace that must be learned by everyone: that, fleeing impiety and wickedness, desire and injustice, we may pass through the present life and display in every respect a modest and chaste life. Thus, being formed as far as possible according to the future state that we await, we may now seem to imitate it, since we await God and our common Savior Christ, who will appear and bestow benefits upon all of us together. For it was for this very reason that he chose to suffer for us: so that he might rescue us from every form of wickedness and acquire for himself a people of his own, always endowed with good works.

(Hier.) After the catalogue of doctrine given to Titus—what he should teach older men, older women, younger women and younger men, and finally slaves—he rightly adds now: “For the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all people.”

There is no difference between free and slave, Greek and Barbarian, circumcised and uncircumcised, woman and man; rather, we are all one in Christ. We are all called to the kingdom of God, and after our offense we are all to be reconciled to our Father—not through our merits, but through the grace of the Savior.

This may mean that Christ himself is the living and subsisting grace of God the Father, or that this grace belongs to Christ, God our Savior, and that we have not been saved by our own merit, according to what is said elsewhere: “You will save them for nothing” (Psal. LV). This grace has therefore appeared to all people in order “to train us, denying impiety and worldly desires, to live chastely, justly, and piously in this age.”

What it means to deny impiety and worldly desires, I trust can be understood from what we explained above: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Tit. I), and the contrary can be understood through opposites.

Worldly desires, therefore, are those suggested by the ruler of this world, and, since they belong to the world, pass away with the cloud of this world. But when we have lived in Christ chastely and justly, sinning neither in body nor in mind, we shall also live piously in this age. This piety awaits the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.

For just as impiety dreads the coming of the great God, so piety, secure in its works and faith, awaits him.

Where is the serpent Arius? Where is the snake Eunomius? Jesus Christ is called the great God and Savior—not the firstborn of all creation, not the Word and wisdom of God, but Jesus Christ; and those are the names of the assumed human being.

Nor do we speak of one Jesus Christ and another Word, as the new heresy falsely accuses us. Rather, we call the same one, both before the ages and after the ages, both before the world and after Mary—indeed, from Mary—the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ. He gave himself for us so that by his precious blood he might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself a people “of his own” (περιούσιον—for this is how it is found in Greek), making them zealous for good works.

Rightly therefore Christ Jesus, our great God and Savior, redeemed us with his blood so that he might make the Christian people his own possession; and it could be his own possession only if it proved zealous for good works.

Hence also what is written in the Gospel, according to the Latin interpreters, “Give us this day our daily bread,” is better expressed in Greek as “our ἐπιούσιον bread,” that is, distinguished, excellent, and special bread—namely, the one who, descending from heaven, says: “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (John VI).

For surely we, who are forbidden to think about tomorrow, cannot be commanded in the Lord’s Prayer to ask for this bread which, shortly afterward, must be digested and cast away into the privy. Nor is there much difference between ἐπιούσιον and περιούσιον: only the preposition has been changed, not the word.

Some think that the bread called ἐπιούσιον in the Lord’s Prayer is so called because it is above all οὐσίαι—that is, above all substances. If this is accepted, it does not differ greatly from the meaning we have explained; for whatever is distinguished and excellent is outside and above everything.

“Speak these things, and exhort, and rebuke with all authority.” (Jerome.) He has set down three terms: “speak, exhort, rebuke.” What he says by “speak” appears to refer to instruction; but what he adds, “exhort”—that is, παρακάλει—means something different in Greek than in Latin. For παράκλησις signifies consolation more than exhortation. He also used this word above concerning young men: “Likewise console the young men, that they be modest in all things”; concerning this we expressed the wording in its proper place as it is read in Latin, as though “exhort” had been written. [Col. 0683A] He therefore consoles the listener who says, “We entreat you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God” (II Cor. V); and he humbles and subordinates himself in order to win the one whom he consoles. But the third term, “rebuke,” seems to me contrary to consolation, so that whoever has despised consolation may be worthy of rebuke and deserve to hear: “You have forgotten the consolation that speaks to you as sons” (Hebr. XII). In the second Epistle to Timothy also we read of one consolation and another rebuke, when the Apostle says: “Be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, console” (II Tim. IV). There rebuke is taken up first, and afterward severity is tempered with consolation. Here, however, he first wishes the disciples to be consoled, and, if they have not benefited from consolation, then to be corrected—and corrected with all authority. [Col. 0683B] For this is how I understand what has been said, “Rebuke with authority”: that it refers specifically to the rebuke, and not collectively to the preceding two. For it is not fitting to say, “console with all authority” or “speak with all authority,” but only, “rebuke with all authority.”

(Ambrose.) “How, then, do these things stand?” I shall explain: teach these things, and, if necessary, do not hesitate to reprove severely those who are not persuaded by these words. And because he had spoken to the doubting, he said that they ought to reprove with authority; he adds: “Let no one despise you.” But when he says, “Let no one despise you,” he does not mean that no one should despise you even if someone is exceedingly fierce; rather, he means that you should rebuke him when he sins, so that by rebuking him you may train others to be modest, sober, and chaste.

(Jerome.) Someone may think that what is now written to Titus is the same as what was said to Timothy: “Let no one despise your youth” (I Tim. IV). But, in accordance with the distinction in the Greek expression, we think that περιφρονείτω, which is written here, means one thing, and καταφρονείτω, which was said to Timothy, another; and that the prepositions περὶ (“around,” “concerning”) and κατὰ (“against,” “down upon”) create a difference of meaning. That the Apostle Paul did not use different names and words fortuitously or arbitrarily, but also used different prepositions according to the variety of circumstances, can be made clear from what he says: “For woman is from man, but man is through woman” (II Cor. XI); and elsewhere: “Because from him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. XI); and likewise: “Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through man” (Gal. I).

We therefore judge καταφρόνησις (“contempt”) to refer properly to the case when someone, stretched upon the rack and between plates, disregards pain and fears neither the judge’s threats nor the uproar of the surrounding crowd, but, for the confession of martyrdom, despises and scorns every punishment. There is, on the other hand, also a wicked contempt, of which Habakkuk likewise testifies, with the Holy Spirit speaking through him: “See now, you despisers, and behold marvels, and perish” (Habac. I). In accordance with this we said that it was written to Timothy: “Let no one despise your youth” (I Tim. IV)—that is, “I do not want you to present yourself in such a way that you could rightly be despised by anyone.”

Περιφρόνησις (“disregard”), therefore, which is used now concerning Titus, has this meaning: Let no one among those in the Church, while you act sluggishly, live in such a way that he thinks himself better than you. For what sort of edification will there be for a disciple if he understands that he is greater than his teachers? Hence not only bishops, presbyters, and deacons ought to take the greatest care to surpass the entire people over whom they preside in conduct and speech, but also those of the lower order—exorcists, readers, custodians, and all who serve the house of God—because nothing so greatly destroys the Church of Christ as laymen being better than clerics.

## CHAPTER III

How the people ought to conduct themselves toward rulers, with an explanation of the passage, and concerning heretics. A greeting is appended.

“Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to obey, to be ready for every good work, to blaspheme no one, not to be quarrelsome, to be modest, showing every gentleness toward all people.” (Ambrose.) He necessarily added the subsequent teaching: that they ought also to be subject and obedient to those who, in the present life, occupy a certain height of dignity, concerning whom he gives commands for the common condition and benefit. For many think that they are doing something good if they despise those who, in the present life, appear to preside over others, especially when they appear to be ruined by some wickedness. Then he says that those who desire to devote themselves to piety must take care concerning this; yet they must not think that there is anything good in their engaging in litigation or contention against others.

“To be ready for every good work, to blaspheme no one, not to be quarrelsome, [Col. 0684C] but modest, showing every gentleness toward all people.” For it is neither virtue nor diligence to speak against those who have been exalted in dignity. It is better to practice what is good with every zeal, attacking no one with blasphemies, but abstaining from every contention, ordering your life with complete modesty and gentleness, which you ought especially to show toward all people—not only toward those who appear to rule over others, but also toward those who belong to their populace and rank. And because, beginning with rulers, he turns his discourse to the others, teaching that it is fitting for them to show their modesty toward all people, they objected to him with the impiety of certain persons; because of this, even to the present day many of the faithful think it good to engage in litigation against such people. He appropriately adds: “For we too were once without understanding,” and so forth.

(Jerome.) Since the doctrine of Judas the Galilean still flourished at that time and had many adherents—the same doctrine that is mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles, where Scripture reports: “For before these days Theudas arose, claiming to be someone great, and men numbering about three thousand joined him; and after him Judas the Galilean arose in the days of the census” (Acts V)—among other things he put forward from the Law as plausible the claim that no one should be called lord except God alone, and that those who brought tithes to the Temple should not pay tribute to Caesar. This heresy had grown so great [Col. 0685A] that it even disturbed the Pharisees and a large part of the people, so that this question was also brought before our Lord: “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matt. XXII; Mark X.) The Lord answered them prudently and cautiously: “Give back to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

In agreement with this answer, the Apostle Paul teaches that believers ought to be subject to rulers and authorities. For the ἀρχαί (“rulers,” more precisely “principalities”) that are read in Greek signify principalities more than persons who rule, and they indicate the authority itself, not the human beings who are in authority. But because he had said, “Remind them to be subject to principalities and authorities,” this could give those who fear torments an opportunity for denial, since they might assert, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement, that they were subject to principalities and authorities and would do what they commanded. Therefore he added, “to obey for every good work.” If what the emperor and governor commands is good, obey the will of the one who commands; but if it is evil and has a meaning contrary to God, answer him with the words from the Acts of the Apostles: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts V).

Let us understand this same principle concerning slaves who are under masters, wives who are under husbands, and children who are under parents: they ought to be subject to masters, husbands, and parents only in those matters that do not contravene God’s commands. But what follows, “to be ready,” may be read in two ways: either “to be ready for every good work” is understood, or it is joined with what precedes, so that the statement is read, “to obey for every good work,” and, that concluded, “to be ready” is understood as another distinct and special command. This accords with what is written in Leviticus (Lev. XVI): “The goat that is sent away, bearing the people’s curse, is to be handed over to the hand of a ready man.” If, therefore, someone is ready to take the scapegoat [ἀποπομπαῖον] and lead it into the wilderness, and there destroy it and, as far as he is able, remove it by the lot of the curse, when he has obeyed every good work he will also be ready.

“Ready” can also be understood in another way: they should form beforehand in their minds whatever may happen, and when such things occur, they should endure nothing as though it were new, but have everything prepared for it.

“To blaspheme no one” is not to be taken simply. For he does not say, “to blaspheme no human being,” but absolutely “no one”—neither an angel nor any creature of God. For everything made by God is very good. When the archangel Michael disputed with the devil about the body of Moses, he did not dare to pronounce a judgment of blasphemy, but said: “God commands you” (Jude 9). If Michael, therefore, did not dare to pronounce a judgment against the Devil—even though he was entirely worthy of a curse—how much more ought we to be pure from every curse? The Devil deserved a curse, but blasphemy ought not to issue from the mouth of an archangel.

Read the ancient books again and see which tribes were appointed on Mount Garizim to bless the people and which were on the other mountain to curse. Reuben, who had defiled his father’s bed, and Zebulun, Leah’s youngest son, and the sons of the maidservants were placed on Mount Ebal, so that they might curse those who were worthy of a curse (Deut. XXVII). It would be lengthy to enumerate now how Jacob, who had called his sons to bless them (Gen. XLIX), saying, “that I may bless you,” later joined something apparently like a curse to the blessing: “Cursed be their anger, because it was fierce”; and how the Lord himself speaks in Genesis: “Cursed is the earth in your works” (Gen. III).

For now, let this alone suffice: the disciples of Christ ought not to blaspheme; nor ought we to be quarrelsome, as the text adds. For if we are sons of peace and wish peace to rest upon us, and have approached the heavenly Jerusalem (Hebr. XII), which receives its name from peace, then let us have peace with those who hate peace (Ps. CXIX), and, as far as depends on us, let us be at peace with all people—not only with the modest, but also with the quarrelsome. For there is no virtue in bearing with the gentle. Let us make room for anger, showing every gentleness toward all people—not because we ought to display gentleness toward everyone out of a desire for empty glory, but because, while we bear with everyone and do not repay injury with injury, our deeds themselves may become known to all.

Someone may, for vainglory, popular opinion, and the favor of the crowd, pretend to be gentle toward some people and feign goodness. But where gentleness is not true, genuine, and substantial, I do not know whether anyone can be persuaded that such a person is gentle toward all.

“For we too were once foolish, disobedient, [Col. 0686C] astray, serving desires and various pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, hating one another.” (Ambrose.) “If,” he says, “you hate him because of his impiety, remember that formerly we were all such.” He appropriately added “hateful”—that is, we were worthy of being hated, although we certainly did not wish to be hated.

(Jerome.) Let someone ask how Paul was foolish, unbelieving, astray, and serving various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating, before the goodness and clemency of our Savior had saved him through the washing of the second birth—not from works of righteousness that he had performed, but according to his mercy, which he poured out abundantly and generously upon the apostles and believers through Jesus Christ by the Holy Spirit, so that, having obtained the inheritance of grace, they might possess the hope of life forever.

Certainly we read that, according to the righteousness that is in the Law, he was circumcised on the eighth day without reproach; that he was a Hebrew of Hebrews, according to the Law a Pharisee (Phil. III), of the tribe of Benjamin, educated at the feet of Gamaliel, and instructed in the sacred writings from infancy. The answer is that the Jews who before the Savior’s coming, passion, and resurrection devoted themselves to the Law possessed some righteousness, though not complete righteousness—as Simeon and Anna the prophetess, serving in the Temple of God, are also found to have possessed it. But after the people cried out, “Crucify him, crucify him; we have no king but Caesar” (John XIX), and, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII), the kingdom of God was taken away from them and given to a nation producing its fruits (Matt. XXI). From that time, whoever did not believe in Christ was foolish, wandering, unbelieving, and serving various pleasures.

Do you not think that Paul was foolish when he had zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Rom. X; I Cor. XV), and persecuted the Church and guarded the garments of those stoning Stephen? (Acts VII.) He had been inflamed with such hatred against the Savior that he received letters from the priests and went to Damascus to bind those who believed in Christ (Acts IX). Or how could he have possessed any virtues without the virtue of God in Christ Jesus, or extinguished the burning flame of pleasures when he was not a temple of God? What greater malice and envy could there be than to obtain letters against people who were absent and everywhere devastate the disciples of Christ? Not to wish him himself to be saved, and to envy the others who could be saved; to hate Christians and consequently deserve hatred from everyone.

And what greater error and senseless disobedience could there be than, after the day had dawned and the shadows had passed, to wish to preserve the abolished Law and say, “Do not handle, do not touch, do not taste,” and, when solid and manly food had appeared, to desire to be fed on the milk of infancy?

“But when the goodness and human kindness of our Savior God appeared, not from works of righteousness that we performed, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us richly through Jesus Christ [Col. 0687C] our Savior, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.” (Ambrose.) What mercy of God, therefore, appeared through Christ’s coming, and what salvation from him we attained—we attained it not from our works. There was nothing good in us; rather, through his mercy, he renewed and set us apart by the power of the Holy Spirit through the form of the washing, and granted us the exceedingly rich enjoyment of good things, so that by his grace we might be found worthy to attain righteousness, which we could by no means attain from our own works. For we attain that perpetual life in which, once established, we shall be free from every corruption and every sin.

He recalled these things in order to teach them that they themselves had been judged worthy of such great goods by mercy alone. It is therefore not right to pursue with hatred, because of their impiety, those who once appeared hateful, since we too ourselves formerly appeared hateful.

(Jerome.) Let us attend more carefully and find in the present chapter the Trinity most clearly expressed. For the goodness and clemency of our Savior God—no other than God the Father—through the washing of regeneration and the renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, justified us for eternal life. The salvation of believers is the mystery of the Trinity.

Others understand this passage in such a way that they think it was spoken not about Paul and the apostles, but, under the person of the apostles, about others: just as, under his own person, he spoke of Apollo and Cephas concerning the dissension and schism that he was correcting among the Corinthians, so here also, naming himself and the apostles, he showed what all who believed in Christ had been like before the regeneration of the life-giving washing. At the same time, his humility is admirable: although he regarded all the usefulness and righteousness of the Law as refuse and rubbish, he rightly recalled that without Christ he had served every vice.

“Faithful is the saying, and concerning these things I want you to affirm strongly, so that those who have believed God may be careful to preside over good works; for these things are good and useful to people.” (Ambrose.) Since it is beyond doubt and true that we have attained such great goods through God’s mercy, he therefore calls this a faithful saying, joining it to what preceded. It is certainly necessary that you yourself teach these things with great confidence and give counsel to those who have believed in God, so that they may apply appropriate care, because these things can help people.

(Jerome.) What he says, “the saying is faithful,” must be joined to the preceding words: “so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.” For the saying concerning God’s inheritance and the hope of eternal life is worthy of faith. Therefore it is necessary not to doubt or fear, but both to believe oneself and to confirm others so that they may believe. Not only this, but this too must be confirmed together with the other things to those who are willing to believe; therefore he says, “and concerning these things I want you to affirm strongly.”

Those who have believed these things to be true must take care of good works, through which the inheritance of God and the hope of eternal life are prepared. And beautifully, in order to produce greater faith, he did not say “those who believe human beings,” but “those who believe God.” For it is necessary that they take care of good works, which, when completed and performed with every zeal, are good and useful to believers.

“But avoid foolish questions, genealogies, contentions, and disputes arising from the Law; for they are useless and vain.” (Ambrose.) Because at that time great harm was being inflicted on the Church by such people, he was compelled by necessity to mention them both at the beginning and at the end of the Epistle. He appears to have done the same in the Epistle that he wrote to Timothy: “Do not permit,” he says, “people to quarrel about the things commanded in the Law; and do not let your work be hindered by attending to genealogies, which they habitually produce because they devote themselves to wordiness.” No one will be able to obtain any benefit from these things; rather, he suffers great harm.

(Jerome.) Because questions are manifold and diverse, Solomon spoke concerning those who seek God, saying: “Those who seek him rightly have found peace.” Therefore those who do not seek God rightly cannot find peace.

There are very many examples of people who do not seek God rightly. The Jews seek God perversely, hoping that they can find him without Christ. Heretics, clanging with the empty noise of words, seek the one whom they cannot find. Philosophers and barbarians also, holding various opinions about God, sought God; but because they did not seek rightly, their questions were foolish, since they thought God could be comprehended by human senses.

Paul therefore calls us back from these questions. On the other hand, he encourages and urges us toward wise questions supported by the authority of Scripture, mindful of the Savior’s commands, in which he says: “Seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you; ask, and it will be given to you. For everyone who seeks will find, and whoever asks will receive, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Luke XI)—provided that our body is not subjected to sins, and wisdom will enter into us. Let the understanding be exercised; let the mind be nourished daily by divine reading; and our questions will not be foolish questions.

But when he says, “Avoid genealogies, contentions, and disputes that arise from the Law,” he is specifically attacking the Jews, who boast and think that they possess knowledge of the Law if they know the names of individuals. Because these names are foreign, and we do not know their etymologies, we often pronounce them incorrectly; and if we happen to err in the accent, the length or shortness of a syllable—either lengthening short syllables or shortening long ones—they customarily ridicule our ignorance, especially in aspirations and in pronouncing certain letters with a scraping of the throat.

Just as we, being Latin speakers, more easily commit to memory Latin names and origins belonging to our own language, so they have absorbed from earliest childhood the words of their native language with their fullest meanings; and from the beginning with Adam to the final generation of Zerubbabel they recite all the genealogies so quickly and accurately from memory that you would think they were merely reciting their own names. We, who have either learned other letters, or at least believed in Christ late, or even, though infants, have been enrolled in the Church, follow the meaning of the Scriptures more than their words.

Dialecticians, whose leader is Aristotle, customarily spread the nets of arguments and confine the freedom of rhetoric in the thorny thickets of syllogisms. Those who spend entire days and nights on this, whether questioning or answering, proposing or accepting, assuming, confirming, and concluding, call certain people contentious—those who dispute as they please, not by reason but by the irritation of quarrellers. If those whose particular art is contention do this, what should a Christian do except flee contention altogether?

Legal disputes too must be utterly rejected and left to Jewish foolishness. For they are useless and vain: they have only the appearance of knowledge, but benefit neither those who speak nor those who listen. What benefit is it to me to know how many years Methuselah lived, or in what year of his age Solomon took a wife, lest perhaps Rehoboam be thought to have been born in the eleventh year of his age? And there are many similar questions, which are either difficult to discover because of the variety of books and the errors that have become established while uncorrected texts are gradually copied from other uncorrected texts; or, even if we found the answers through great effort and labor, we know that learning them would profit us nothing.

It often happens that we engage in disputes about the Law not from a desire for truth, but from a desire for glory, wishing to be considered learned by those who listen; or certainly, from this little rumor, we pursue shameful profits. Then he gives a general instruction, saying:

“After one and a second correction, avoid a heretical person, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being self-condemned.” (Ambrose.) “Avoid fully,” he says, “the person who has deliberately chosen things contrary to piety; for this is whom he calls a heretic. After you have instructed him once and twice and shown him what is appropriate for his salvation, it is superfluous to dispute longer with such a person, since it is evident that he receives no correction: after hearing once and twice the things appropriate for him, he did not wish to recognize the truth. Leave such a person, therefore, to await the just punishment from the judge, since he brings no complete and final decision to fulfillment through instruction.”

(Jerome.) In Greek, heresy is named from choice, since each person chooses for himself what appears to be better. The philosophers too—the Stoics, Peripatetics, Academics, and Epicureans—are called adherents of this or that heresy. It would be superfluous to go through them individually and enumerate Marcion, Valentinus, Apelles, Ebion, Montanus, and Mani with their respective doctrines, since it is very easy for everyone to recognize the errors by which each is led. If only Arius and Eunomius, and the originator of the new heresy, were not so well known; perhaps they would have deceived fewer people!

“After one correction,” therefore—or, as it is better expressed in Greek, νουθεσίαν—“avoid a heretical person.” Νουθεσία signifies more properly admonition and instruction without rebuke. [Col. 0690C] In Latin manuscripts one reads—and Pope Athanasius also approved this as correct—“after one and another correction.” This means that it is not enough to rebuke or admonish only once someone who has been corrupted by some error; a second instruction must also be given to him, so that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses.

But why he must be avoided after the first and second correction, he explains by giving the reasons: “because such a person is perverted and sins, being self-condemned.” For someone who has been corrected once and twice, and, having heard his error, does not wish to be corrected, considers the one correcting him to be in error; and, on the contrary, preparing himself for verbal battles and quarrels, he wishes to win over the person by whom he is being taught. He is therefore said to be self-condemned because the fornicator, adulterer, murderer, and those guilty of other vices are expelled from the Church by the priests. Heretics, however, pronounce judgment against themselves by withdrawing from the Church of their own will; that withdrawal appears to be a condemnation of their own conscience.

They think that the distinction between heresy and schism is this: heresy holds a perverse doctrine, while schism separates itself from the Church because of disagreement with a bishop. This can indeed be understood to some extent at the beginning. But no schism fails to invent some heresy for itself, so that it may appear to have withdrawn rightly from the Church.

“When I send Artemas to you, or Tychicus, hasten to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to winter there.” (Jerome.) We read at the beginning of this Epistle: “For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what was lacking and appoint presbyters in every city, as I instructed you” (“as I arranged for you”). Since the Cretans had recently come to believe, and Paul was departing and passing on to other Churches, they were not to be left orphaned, but were to have an apostolic man who would correct what appeared to be lacking.

Therefore, because Titus was necessary after the foundation of the other Churches, so that he might build the structure above it, Paul writes to him that, after sending Artemas or Tychicus—one of the two who had been with him—to Crete to fill his place, Titus himself should come to Nicopolis, assuring him that he intended to winter there. From this we recognize Paul’s fatherly affection for the Cretans. He needs Titus for the ministry of the Gospel, yet he does not wish Titus to come to him before Artemas or Tychicus, his successor, has arrived in his place.

Nicopolis is the city that received its name because of Augustus’s victory, since he conquered Antony and Cleopatra there.

“Diligently send on Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they may lack nothing.” (Jerome.) This is the Apollos about whom it is also written to the Corinthians: “Each of you says, ‘I am of Paul,’ and ‘I of Apollos,’ and ‘I of Cephas’” (I Cor. III). He was an Alexandrian man of Jewish origin, very eloquent and well versed in the Law, and bishop of the Corinthians. Because of the dissensions that existed in Corinth, he presumably crossed over to the nearby island of Crete with Zenas the lawyer; after Paul’s Epistle had moderated the dissensions that had arisen in Corinth, he returned again to Corinth.

We cannot say from another passage of Scripture who Zenas the lawyer was, except that he too was an apostolic man and carried out the same work as Apollos: building up the Churches of Christ. He therefore commands Titus that, since they were going to sail from Crete to Greece, he should not allow them to lack provisions, but should ensure that they had what was necessary for the journey.

“Let our people also learn to preside over good works for necessary uses, so that they may not be unfruitful.” Above he had said: “Diligently send on Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they may lack nothing.” Since an unspoken objection could arise—so that not Titus alone, but any reader of the Epistle, might say, “And where was Titus to obtain provisions to give to those who had none?”—he resolves and, as it were, removes this objection by saying: “Let our people also learn to preside over good works for necessary uses, so that they may not be unfruitful.”

He calls his own people “our people”—those who had believed in Christ. Since they belonged to Christ, they rightly deserved to be called both Paul’s and Titus’s people. “You have authority,” he says, “over the disciples. Teach them not to be unfruitful, but to minister to Evangelists and apostolic men who serve in good works; and let them minister not for just any purposes, but for necessary uses.”

“For having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (I Tim. VI); and those who serve at the altar should live from the altar, and those who have become participants in our spiritual things ought to share their material things with us. And lest they perhaps easily despise either Paul’s Epistle or Titus’s command, he calls all who have not ministered to the Evangelists unfruitful.

Solomon also says in Proverbs, “The fruit is almsgiving”; and Paul himself calls love the first fruit of the Spirit. Love, however, is demonstrated especially in sharing and service. “So that,” he says, “they may not be unfruitful”: “For every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. III). This too I say: “The one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (II Cor. IX). To refuse to give to apostolic men and evangelizers of Christ what is necessary for their needs is to condemn oneself to barrenness.

“All who are with me greet you.” Either he used his customary expression, saying that Titus was greeted by everyone who was with him, or this was addressed specifically to Titus because he was such a person that he deserved the affection of all who were with Paul. It is great praise of Titus that Paul says he is greeted by everyone.

“Greet those who love us in faith.” If everyone who loves loved in faith, and there were no others who loved without faith, Paul would never have added faith to love by saying, “Greet those who love us in faith.” Mothers also love their children, so that they are ready to die for them, but they do not love in faith. Wives love their husbands, for whom they very often die, but that love is not the love of faith.

Only the love of the saints loves in faith, to such an extent that even if the one who is loved is an unbeliever, the saint nevertheless loves him in faith, in accordance with the saying: “Let all your deeds be done in faith”; and elsewhere: “Love your enemies.” The saint loves his enemies, and therefore loves them in faith, because he believes in the one who promised that, in fulfillment of the commandment, he would repay the reward.

“The grace of our Lord be with you all.” It should be known that in the Greek manuscripts it is written, “Grace be with you all,” so that neither “of the Lord” nor “of our” is found in the authentic books. He therefore invokes grace upon Titus and the others who were with him, as well as upon all the saints and believers. Just as the patriarch Isaac blessed his son Jacob, and Jacob blessed the twelve patriarchs; and as the apostles, when entering a house, said, “Peace to this house,” and, if the house was worthy, their peace rested upon it, but if it showed itself unworthy, their peace returned to those who had invoked it—so now, at the end of his Epistle, the Apostle invokes grace upon believers. Together with the prayer it had its effect, and it lay within believers’ power to present themselves as such as the one blessing wished the blessed to be. Amen.

# THE TWENTY-SIXTH BOOK  
## EXPOSITION ON THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON

[Col. 0693]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0693A]

(Ambr.) The argument of the Epistle which the blessed Apostle Paul wrote to Philemon is as follows. Onesimus, the slave of a certain Philemon, a faithful and religious man, having conceived an evil purpose, left his master by flight. In the course of time, when the blessed Apostle recognized that he belonged to Philemon’s household and family, he saw him while he himself was in chains. By his counsels and exhortations he won him over so completely that, abandoning the former wickedness of his own will, he returned and obeyed his master of his own free will, rendering him every service as was fitting. The Apostle, appeasing and instructing him, sent him back to Philemon, presenting him not only as fit for his service but also teaching him to possess the carefulness of piety.

[Col. 0693B] He therefore writes this Epistle to Philemon, asking that he grant Onesimus forgiveness for the offenses he had formerly committed against him and receive him with affection because of the present correction of his purpose. This, then, is the argument of the Epistle.

The usefulness of this Epistle also lies in this: that all who hold ecclesiastical office, especially those who appear to preside over churches, may know how they ought to deal with those who are joined to us by faith, particularly when matters are at issue that appear properly to belong to them. Anyone will be able to perceive their usefulness most clearly if he considers what is being done by many in our own times.

Now, as those appointed to instruct others for their benefit, we wish to admonish those who are joined to us by faith about matters [Col. 0693C] concerning which it is necessary to agree with the principle according to which Paul wishes, with the greatest pleading, to reach agreement with them. Very many in our own times, not knowing what ought to be done, how, or when, suppose that, out of regard for piety, everything belonging to the present age ought to be confused, and that there should be no distinction between slaves and masters, rich and poor, those subject to rulers and those who appear to rule others. They think that this alone is proper to them: to command, with great authority, those things that seem right to themselves, claiming this power for themselves—I do not know from where.

Paul, on the contrary, considered it best that each thing should remain in its proper order, while the purpose of piety was preserved. Why, then, was he reconciled to this arrangement, since this distinction could by no means exist among human beings unless [Col. 0693D] God had wished it to exist—provided, of course, that he knew it to be expedient for human beings? He knew that such a distinction in no respect harms the principle of piety, since rich and poor, slaves and free persons, can, if they wish, devote themselves to piety. Conversely, they can choose what is worse [Col. 0694A], if what they wish to do is permitted. He therefore wished all these things to remain in their proper order.

Accordingly, exercising appropriate care, he instructed everyone alike. Thus he commands obedience to rulers, saying that all authority has been established by God, and he commands us fully to render to each person what is owed, whether tax, revenue, fear, or honor. He gives the fullest command that whatever is held as a debt or obligation should be paid.

Nor, when writing about generosity toward the poor, does he command that it be practiced as an obligation; rather, he considered it better to allow each person to act according to the judgment of his own purpose. He added that they should give according to their means; nor does he permit some to be at ease while those who provide are crushed by poverty.

[Col. 0694B] He commands slaves to offer every form of servile service to their masters with the utmost diligence, whether they have impious or pious masters. For in the present Epistle also, when that great Paul writes to a faithful man and his own disciple, and writes about a slave who has returned to a better condition and promises that thereafter, with an unimpaired will and complete devotion, he will serve his master, he does not command that the master set the slave free because of this change of will for the better. He merely asks that the slave be forgiven for the offenses he had previously committed, and he makes this request with much entreaty.

If someone among those living now had encountered such a case, he would neither ask nor plead that the master forgive the slave. Instead, he would write with great authority that a slave joined to us by faith and voluntarily hastening toward piety [Col. 0694C] ought to be freed from servitude. For there are many such people in the present age who wish to appear prudent to others by imposing burdensome commands.

In the present Epistle, who could be so unpersuadable, or possess so hardened a mind, that he would not marvel at Paul, so great and distinguished in every respect and surpassing almost all human beings in every virtue of piety, when he sees him writing to his disciple with complete entreaty to obtain forgiveness for a slave—and not to an apostle, but to a faithful man adorned with good character, one who lived the ordinary life, as can be gathered from what Paul writes to him, with wife and son, and indeed about a slave? Those who were perfect at that time, however, were alien to all such things.

Therefore it seems to me that those who at the beginning [Col. 0694D] established and commanded that the Epistles be read in the Church, like the others, had this especially in mind: that this Epistle should be read in the Church because it could teach its hearers humility more than the other Epistles. For it is not plausible that, when writing to the entire Church about matters of such importance, Paul would humble himself [Col. 0695A]; but this is the marvel: that, writing to one person—and to a disciple who was not especially eminent—about so slight a matter, he appears to have acted with such humility and to have commanded him concerning matters whose authority seemed to lie in Philemon’s hands.

(Hier.) Those who do not wish to accept among Paul’s Epistles the one written to Philemon say that the Apostle did not always speak, nor did he say everything, with Christ speaking in him. Human weakness could not have sustained the uninterrupted movement of the Holy Spirit, nor could the needs of this little body always have been fulfilled in the presence of the Lord—for example, arranging a meal, taking food, feeling hunger, being satisfied, digesting what had been consumed, and replenishing what had been expended.

I say nothing of the other points that they carefully and forcibly repeat in order to assert that there was some time when Paul would not have dared to say [Col. 0695B], “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2), or, “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (1 Cor. 13). What sort of proof of Christ, they ask, is it to hear, “When you come, bring with you the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus” (2 Tim. 4), or that saying to the Galatians, “Would that those who trouble you would even cut themselves off” (Gal. 5), or in this very Epistle, “At the same time, prepare a lodging for me”?

They say that this happened not only to the apostles but likewise to the prophets. Hence it is frequently written, “The word of the Lord came to Ezekiel,” or to any other of the prophets, because, after completing his prophecy, the prophet returned again into himself and became an ordinary human being rather than a prophet. The sole exception was our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0695C], in whom the Holy Spirit never ceased to remain. John the Baptist also received this sign (Mark 1), so that he might recognize the one upon whom he saw the Holy Spirit descending and remaining to be that very one. From this it is shown that the Holy Spirit descends upon many, but that it is properly the distinctive mark of the Savior that he remains in him.

On these and similar grounds they wish either to deny that the Epistle written to Philemon is Paul’s, or, if it is Paul’s, to maintain that it contains nothing capable of edifying and was rejected by many of the ancients, since Paul wrote it merely in the capacity of one commending someone, not of one teaching.

But those who defend it as possessing genuine authority say that it was never received by all the churches throughout the whole world unless it was believed to be the Epistle of the Apostle Paul. On the same principle, they say, they ought not to accept even the Second Epistle to Timothy or the Epistle to the Galatians [Col. 0695D], since these too contain examples of human weakness: “When you come, bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus,” and, “Would that those who trouble you would even cut themselves off.” More such examples are found in the Epistle to the Romans and in the other Epistles, especially those to the Corinthians, which were dictated in a more relaxed manner and almost in everyday speech. In them the Apostle says, “To the rest I say—not the Lord” (1 Cor. 7). Since these Epistles too contain such things, either they should not be considered Paul’s Epistles, or, if they are accepted, the Epistle to Philemon should also be accepted by the precedent of similar Epistles that have been received.

They greatly err, however, if they think that buying food, preparing lodging, or obtaining clothing is sin, and assert that the Holy Spirit is driven away if we serve, for a little while, the needs of this little body. [Col. 0696A] “Do not,” says the Apostle, “grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4). The prophet identifies by what actions the Holy Spirit is grieved, arranging many vices and sins in order, and finally declares: “In all these things you were grieving me” (Jer. 8).

Otherwise, would it be a sin to offer a cup of cold water, wash feet, sacrifice a calf, or prepare a meal, when we know that through such things some are adopted as sons of God? But it seems to me that, while they criticize the Epistle for its simplicity, they reveal their own lack of understanding, not perceiving what virtue and wisdom lie hidden in each expression. With your prayers, and with the Holy Spirit himself suggesting to us the meaning of what was written, we shall attempt to explain these things in their proper places.

[Col. 0696B] But if brevity is held in contempt, let Obadiah, Nahum, Zephaniah, and the other twelve prophets also be despised. In them there are such marvelous and lofty things that one cannot know whether one ought to admire their brevity of expression or the greatness of their meaning. If those who reject the Epistle to Philemon understood this, they would never despise brevity, which was composed with evangelical elegance in place of the law’s elaborate burdens, while the Lord makes his word brief and complete upon the earth.

## CHAPTER ONE

On Philemon, Appia, Archippus, and his household church; on Philemon and the Apostle, who always remembered him in his prayers on his behalf; on the aged and imprisoned Apostle commanding Philemon, yet at the same time pleading with him on behalf of Onesimus, his slave, and recommending that lodging be prepared for him; on Epaphras, the Apostle’s fellow prisoner, and on Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, Paul’s assistants.

“Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy the brother, to Philemon our beloved and fellow worker, and to Appia our sister, and to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church that is in your house.”

(Hier.) The question is asked why, or at whose command, Paul either abandoned his former name or took up a new one. That Abram should be called Abraham was accomplished by God’s command; that Sarai should receive the name Sarah was likewise God’s command. And, to come to the New Testament, that Simon should receive the name Peter, and that the sons of Zebedee should be called Boanerges—that is, “sons of thunder”—was commanded by the voice of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0696D] But why Saul was called Paul, no Scripture records. Nor should we suppose, as simpler Latin readers interpret it, that he was previously called Saulus rather than Saul, since he belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, among whom this name was more common. Saul, the king of Judea and persecutor of David, was also from the tribe of Benjamin.

That we call Saul “Saulus” is not surprising.
