Hebrew names are declined according to the likeness of Greek and Roman case forms, so that just as Joseph is called Josephus, and Jacob Jacobus, so Saul is called Saulus in our language and speech. Thus Scipio, after Africa had been subjected, took the name Africanus; and Metellus, after the island of Crete had been conquered [Col. 0697A], brought back the distinction of Creticus for his family. Roman emperors even now are named from the nations they have conquered—for example, Adiabenici, Parthici, and Sarmatici. So Saul, sent to preach to the nations, brought back the trophies of his victory from the first spoil of the Church, the proconsul Sergius Paulus, and raised the banner by which he came to be called Paul instead of Saul.

If an interpretation of the name is also sought, “Paul” sounds in Hebrew as “marvelous.” Truly it is marvelous that, after Saul—whose name is interpreted as “desired,” because he had been requested by the devil for the harassment of the Church—he should become, from a persecutor, a chosen instrument.

Perhaps this has been discussed at greater length than was necessary, but it was necessary. As for what follows, “a prisoner of Jesus Christ,” it is especially worthy of admiration, in the present matter, that the Apostle wrote in this way. He also wrote to several others while he was in chains, as can be seen from the Epistles themselves [Col. 0697B]. Yet nowhere else, in the preface, did he place “prisoner” with his name, saying, “Paul, a prisoner.” Here, however, he did not call himself either a slave or an apostle, as was his custom in writing, but was writing to him about particular matters and about matters that lay within Philemon’s authority.

He thought it better to say this, so that he would not appear to have abused his apostolic authority and to be commanding Philemon presumptuously. Instead, he set down what he judged would be more appropriate and would also be very persuasive. Philemon might have thought it no great thing to provide such small services to a man who was held in chains for the salvation of others, although, if he had wished, he could have avoided suffering these things, as Paul himself says in one place: “For although I was free from all, I made myself a slave to all, that I might win more” (1 Cor. 9).

[Col. 0697C] “‘A prisoner,’ he says, ‘of Jesus Christ.’” He used this title in no other Epistle, although in the body of the Epistles—to the Ephesians, Philippians, and Colossians—he testifies that he was in chains for his confession of Christ. It seems to me a greater mark of boldness to call himself a prisoner of Jesus Christ than an apostle.

The apostles gloried in having been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus Christ; but the authority of chains was necessary here. Since he was about to plead for Onesimus, the one making the plea had to be such as could obtain what he requested.

Happy is the one who glories not in wisdom, wealth, eloquence, or secular power, but in the sufferings of Christ. Not everyone who is imprisoned is a prisoner of Christ. Whoever is imprisoned for the name of Christ and for his confession [Col. 0697D] is truly called a prisoner of Jesus Christ. Blood shed makes a person a martyr only when it is shed for the name of Christ.

He therefore writes to Philemon from Rome, imprisoned in the jail, at a time when it seems to me that the Epistles to the Philippians, Colossians, and Ephesians were dictated.

The Epistle to the Philippians belongs to this period, first because Paul writes it with Timothy alone, as he does this Epistle also. Second, because he says plainly that his chains have become manifest for Christ throughout the whole praetorium. What the praetorium means he indicates at the end of that Epistle: “All the saints greet you, especially those of Caesar’s household” (Phil. 4). Sent by Caesar into prison, he became better known to Caesar’s household and made the house of the persecutor into a church of Christ.

[Col. 0698A] He then says: “Some indeed preach Christ out of rivalry, not sincerely, thinking to raise up affliction for my chains” (Phil. 1).

In the Epistle to the Colossians there is a similar opening: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy the brother” (Col. 1). Later he says: “Of which I, Paul, became a minister, who now rejoice in my sufferings for you and fill up in my flesh what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ, for his body, which is the Church.” At the end he adds: “The greeting is by the hand of Paul. Remember my chains.”

This is so that we may know that these Epistles too were dictated from prison and amid chains.

The Epistle to the Colossians has this particular feature: the same Onesimus who is now commended to Philemon was also the bearer of that message. [Col. 0698B] For Paul says:

“Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord, will make known to you everything concerning me. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that he may learn about your circumstances and comfort your hearts, together with Onesimus, the beloved and faithful brother, who is one of you.”

If Philemon, to whom this Epistle is written, is Onesimus’s master—or rather, if he has begun to be his brother in the Lord—and if it is reported to the Colossians that Onesimus is one of them, reason and the order of the matter themselves lead us to conclude that Philemon too was a Colossian, and that at the same time Onesimus carried to the whole church the common Epistle, while he was carrying the private letter commending him to his master.

There is also another indication: in this same Epistle Archippus is named, to whom Paul writes here together with Philemon. In the Epistle to the Colossians he says: “Say to Archippus [Col. 0698C], ‘See to the ministry that you have received in the Lord, so that you may fulfill it.’”

What ministry did Archippus receive from the Lord? In the Epistle to Philemon we read: “And to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church that is in your house.” From this I think either that he was the bishop of the church of Colossae, being admonished to preside over it zealously and diligently, or that he was a preacher of the Gospel.

Or, if this is not so, for the present it is enough for me that Philemon, Archippus, and Onesimus himself, who carried the letter, were Colossians, and that at the same time the four Epistles mentioned above were written.

The Epistle to the Ephesians belongs to this period [Col. 0698D] because Paul says here also that he is imprisoned for Christ, and because, at the end of this Epistle, he commands the same things that he had commanded in the Epistle to the Colossians: that wives should be subject to their husbands, husbands should love their wives, children should obey their parents, parents should not provoke their children to anger, slaves should obey their earthly masters, and masters, abandoning threats, should provide their slaves with what is just.

Finally, he concludes that Epistle with these words:

“What I am doing, Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make known to you. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that you may know the things concerning me and that he may comfort your hearts.”

Tychicus is the one who is sent to the Colossians with Onesimus, and who at that time had Onesimus as his companion when Onesimus was carrying the letter to Philemon.

“And Timothy the brother.”

(Amb.) Paul ought rightly to be praised in this respect also: in a private Epistle [Col. 0699A] he does not disdain to associate Timothy with himself in writing.

(Hier.) In other Epistles Sosthenes and Silvanus, and sometimes Timothy, are included. In this one, only Timothy is included, either because the Epistles were dictated at the same time or because Timothy and the others were present. I think this was done for two reasons: first, so that the Epistle would have greater authority, since it was not written by one person alone; and second, because there was no rivalry among the apostles. If, while Paul was dictating, something was revealed to another [Col. 0699B], Paul added it to the letter he was dictating without any sadness.

This was in accordance with the instruction he himself gave to the Corinthians: “If something is revealed to another who is sitting by, let the first be silent” (1 Cor. 14). In this way he himself also fulfilled his own command in practice. On account of the few things that another suggested and that Paul added as his own, he also wrote the other person’s Epistle completely.

“To Philemon, our beloved fellow worker.”

(Amb.) He calls him a fellow worker because he showed care in the service of the saints, contributing no small assistance to those to whom the preaching of the Gospel had been entrusted.

When writing to the Philippians he says: “You have done well by sharing in my affliction” (Phil. 4). He calls it “sharing” because, while he was in chains, they sent him what they thought necessary for his daily needs.

(Hier.) The Greek does not have ἠγαπημένῳ (*ēgapēménō*), which means “beloved,” but ἀγαπητῷ (*agapētō*), that is, “worthy of love” or “lovable.” The difference between “beloved” and “worthy of love” is that someone who does not deserve love can nevertheless be called beloved, whereas someone is “worthy of love” only when he is loved deservedly.

Thus we are commanded to love our enemies. They are beloved [Col. 0699C], but not worthy of love. We love them not because they deserve to be loved, but because we are commanded not to hate them.

The expression prefixed in the title of Psalm 44, “for the beloved,” is also better rendered in Greek as “for the lovable” or “for the one worthy of love.” That passage is manifestly understood of Christ. Although the Jews think that Solomon is called *Ididia* [*Idithum*; Jedidiah], that is, “beloved of God,” believing that God bestowed this name upon him because of his wisdom, who can more truly be called beloved of God than the one of whom the Father speaks in the Gospel: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 3, 17).

Paul and Timothy therefore write to Philemon, their most beloved fellow worker, who is called beloved because he is engaged in the same work of Christ; also to Appia their sister [Col. 0699D], who possessed no false or feigned form of sisterhood; and to Archippus their fellow soldier, whom I think proved victorious with Paul and Timothy while fighting against adversaries for the name of Christ. For this reason he is now called a fellow soldier: because he prevailed in the same contest and battle.

The letter is also written to “the church that is in his house.” But this is ambiguous: does it mean the church that is in the house of Archippus, or the church that is in the house of Philemon? It seems to me that it should be referred not to Archippus but to Philemon, to whom the Epistle itself is assigned.

Although Paul and Timothy write together to Philemon, Appia, Archippus, and the church, what follows shows that Paul is writing only to Philemon [Col. 0700A], speaking with one person alone.

(Amb.) The Apostle preserves the order. Just as he named the husband before the wife and the parents before the son, so after the masters he mentioned the other persons who were considered, in one way or another, to belong to their household. He did not say, “to your household,” but “to the church that is in your house,” showing that he regards the house in which all the faithful appear to dwell as a church, and considers them worthy of his writings as though they held the place of a church.

For Paul does not define a church as a multitude of men, but as the purpose of those who meet together in the same pious intention. In the circus and in the theaters also one sees a multitude of people gathering, but that multitude could not be called the Church of God because of the perverse intention of those who had assembled there.

[Col. 0700B] The Church of God is called such even if only two or three have gathered together with pious intent, because what the Lord said is true: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.”

And because Paul believed that the others should be joined to Philemon in the preface of the Epistle, this contributes no small support to the argument for the present matter. For if the communion of faith gave them such confidence that they were joined with their masters, it was right that they should thereafter regard Onesimus with affection, since, through sharing in his purpose, he had undertaken the same care that they had undertaken.

(Hier.) When Paul says, “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,” he is still writing from two persons to several. Nearly all the Epistles have the same opening [Col. 0700C]: he invokes grace and peace upon them from God the Father and from Christ the Lord. From this it is shown that the Son and the Father have one nature, since the Son can grant what the Father grants, and what the Son grants is said to be granted by the Father.

Grace is that by which we are saved without any merit or work of our own. Peace is that by which we have been reconciled to God through Christ, as in the words: “We beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.”

The text continues:

“I give thanks to my God always, making mention of you in my prayers, hearing of your love and the faith that you have in the Lord Jesus and toward all his saints, so that the sharing of your faith may become evident in the recognition of every good thing that is in us in Christ.”

(Ambr.) He begins his writing with thanksgiving, giving thanks to God for Philemon, just as he appears to have done in many Epistles [Col. 0700D]. But, so that he would not seem now to be giving thanks for him merely because of the letter, he very appropriately adds: “Always making mention of you in my prayers.”

“In my prayers,” he says, “I remember you and give thanks to God for you.” And, indicating the very reason for which he gives thanks to God, lest he should seem to say this as an empty gift, he adds: “Hearing of your love and the faith that you have toward the Lord Jesus Christ.”

So that it might not seem uncertain how Paul had learned this, he indicates that these things had been granted to Philemon by the Lord. For love and faith directed toward the Lord reside in the intention of the soul; love toward all the saints, however, is displayed in deeds [Col. 0701A], and from this the former affection is also known. For the love shown in deeds toward the saints proves the affection that one has toward God.

Accordingly, he most appropriately adds: “So that the sharing of your faith may become perfect in the recognition of every goodness that is in us in Christ Jesus.”

(Hier.) Here Paul is no longer speaking as Paul and Timothy to Philemon and the others, but as Paul alone to Philemon alone: “I give thanks,” he says, “making mention of you in my prayers.”

The wording is ambiguous: does he always give thanks to his God, or does he always make mention of Philemon in his prayers? Both meanings can be understood. Whoever commands others to give thanks to God in all things could not be constrained by any troubles so as not himself always to give thanks to God.

But if Paul always prayed for the saints and for those who were especially good—and Philemon was a saint, possessing such faith and love that he was known not merely by report but also by his actions [Col. 0701B]—it is credible that Paul always prayed for Philemon, so that the faith and love that he possessed in Christ and toward all his saints might, through the sharing of faith and the practice of recognition, be preserved in every good thing by the mercy of Christ.

There is no difficult interpretation of the love that he had in Christ Jesus and toward all his saints, since after God we are commanded to love our neighbors. The question now is how someone can have the same faith in Christ Jesus and in his saints.

The phrase is expressed *a communi*—that is, with the verb or sense shared across both objects: “the love that you have in the Lord Jesus and toward all his saints,” and “the faith that you have in the Lord Jesus and toward all his saints.”

For an explanation of this passage, let us take an example from Exodus: “The people believed God and Moses his servant” (Exod. 14). [Col. 0701C] One and the same act of belief is referred to Moses and to God, so that the people who believed in the Lord are also written to have believed in his servant.

This applies not only to Moses but to all the saints: whoever believes in God cannot receive faith in him in any other way than by also believing in his saints. Love and faith in God are not perfect if they are weakened by hatred and unbelief toward his ministers.

What I mean is this: someone may believe in God the Creator, but he cannot believe unless he first believes that what has been written about God’s saints is true.

Even today there are many simple people who perform works of righteousness but do not possess knowledge of what they themselves are doing. Hence Paul adds: “So that the sharing of your faith may become effective in the recognition of every good thing [Col. 0701D].”

By how many stages and advances the apostolic discourse stretches toward higher things! Someone may possess love and faith in God and in his saints, but perhaps he does not share that love equally with everyone. He may share it with everyone, but not complete it in action. Someone may fulfill his intention in action, but still be unable to possess perfect knowledge of his deeds.

There may even be someone who possesses both action and knowledge but does not possess the recognition of every good thing. For while performing many things justly, gently, and diligently, he may still fall short of his virtues in some respect.

Was Philemon not such a person? He possesses the sharing of effective faith and love in the recognition of every good thing. Since this perfection exists in the apostles, however, let us not think that it is perfect merely because it exists in them [Col. 0702A]. Rather, it is wholly present because it belongs to Christ. Thus whatever good is praised in Philemon, and whatever is taken from the example of the apostles, is good because it is drawn from the fountain of Christ.

“For we have had great joy and consolation in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother.”

(Ambr.) “It is right,” he says, “that I rejoice, since you always serve the saints with great affection. From them I also find sufficient consolation in my afflictions when I hear of the earnestness of your zeal.” He says this in praise and encouragement of Philemon. Praise that recounts past conduct generally makes people more eager in what follows.

(Hier.) He states and explains more fully why he had said, “I give thanks to my God, always making mention of you in my prayers [Col. 0702B].” It was indeed worthy to give thanks to God for Philemon’s love, since, by receiving the inward affection of the heart and the deep recesses of the saints’ souls, he had refreshed them.

This also is an apostolic expression: he constantly calls these inward affections “hearts,” wishing to display the fullness of the mind’s love. Therefore, rejoicing with those who rejoice and believing himself refreshed with those who had been refreshed, he possesses a joy that is neither passing nor slight, nor something that might occur by chance, but a great joy, and one as eminent as the love that existed in Philemon. His consolation was increased by the love that descended upon Philemon, full of the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation.

“Therefore, having great confidence in Christ Jesus to command you concerning what is fitting, I appeal to you rather on account of love [Col. 0702C], since you are such a man as Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.”

(Ambr.) First, he did not say, “I have authority to command,” but “confidence.” Second, he did not appeal on the basis of his apostleship or of that dignity with which he seemed to be endowed, but on the basis of the love that he had toward everyone, so that this confidence might be of such a kind that Philemon himself had granted its cause.

Accordingly, in Philemon’s praise and encouragement he adds: “Therefore, having great confidence in Christ,” and so forth. Because Philemon possessed such an established purpose and intention, his disposition encouraged Paul confidently to command him, since Philemon could never resist Paul’s request. Whoever is so generous toward all the saints will never be reluctant, on account of the present matter, to grant the favor being requested.

“Therefore, your purpose and the love that is sufficient toward all [Col. 0702D] give me confidence to command what is fitting. Yet I do not do this; rather, I appeal.”

Then, inviting him also to modesty, Paul says: “Since you are such a man as Paul the aged.” The very name of Paul possessed such force! For whatever supreme good could be understood was present in Paul. When he added “aged,” he did not simply invite Philemon to respect him by mentioning his age and longevity; he also made the very word “Paul” venerable.

For anyone who hears of Paul as aged could understand that his devotion to piety had grown through a long period and that he had suffered much for this reason [Col. 0703A]. He began to preach the Gospel while still a young man; yet he continually advanced in Christ toward old age, persevering in sufferings.

Therefore, lest he appear to be persuading him simply by appeal to age, he very appropriately adds: “And now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.” He is saying, in effect: “Do not merely feel shame before old age and gray hairs nurtured in chains, and before an age so long raised amid those sufferings that are endured for Christ.”

(Hier.) After first offering many praises of Philemon, Paul could have commanded rather than requested, since the matter for which he was asking was useful both to the one who excelled and to the one who was making the request. This confidence arose from the fact that one who had accomplished such great works for Christ could not be unequal to himself in other matters.

[Col. 0703B] But Paul wishes to ask rather than command. He places before Philemon the great authority of the one making the request, by which he pleads as an apostle, as an old man, and as a prisoner of Jesus Christ.

The whole matter for which he asks is this: Onesimus, Philemon’s slave, had compounded flight with theft and had plundered some of his master’s household property. Proceeding toward Italy so that he might not be more easily apprehended in the nearby region, he had squandered his master’s money in luxury.

Let no one think that this has been rashly and arbitrarily invented by us. He may learn it from what follows. Paul would never say, “If he has wronged you or owes you anything, charge it to me. I, Paul, have written this with my own hand; I will repay it.” He would not become surety for property that had been taken unless what had been taken had been squandered.

While Paul was therefore in prison at Rome because of his confession of Christ, Onesimus believed in the Lord Jesus [Col. 0703C]. Baptized by Paul, he wiped away the stains of his former life through worthy repentance, to such an extent that the Apostle who had once rebuked Peter for not walking with the right step in the truth of the Gospel became the witness of Onesimus’s conversion.

Therefore, insofar as the sin and crime by which he had injured his master are concerned, Onesimus does not deserve forgiveness. But insofar as the testimony of the Apostle is concerned—who knows that he has been fully converted—Philemon is placed under a great obligation. He is asked to forgive the one who, from a fugitive and thieving slave, had become the Apostle’s minister.

What other ministry did the Apostle have than the Gospel of Jesus Christ? Onesimus was now to be forgiven not as though by a master, but as though by a fellow slave and fellow evangelist, since he was likewise a slave and minister of Christ.

“I beseech you for my son, whom I have begotten in bonds, Onesimus—who was formerly useless to you, but now is useful both to you and to me—whom I have sent back to you; receive him, that is, my own heart, whom I had wished to keep with me, so that he might minister to me in bonds for the Gospel.” Wishing to obtain what he requests, he now declares that he is pleading not for Philemon’s slave but for his own son; and for that son whom he begot in the bonds of the Gospel, that is, in the sufferings he endured for the Gospel of Christ. Although Onesimus had previously been useful only to his master—for a thieving and fugitive slave harms no one other than his master—now, by the compensation of his usefulness, through which he is useful both to his master and to Paul, and through Paul to others, he deserves more love than he had previously deserved hatred. Hence he says: “Who was formerly useless to you.” “To you,” he says, “alone, not to others; but now useful both to you and to me.” Useful to his master, because he could serve Paul on behalf of his master; useful to Paul, because while Paul was detained in prison and chains, Onesimus could minister to him in the Gospel.

At the same time, the Apostle’s greatness of soul and ardent mind in Christ are worthy of admiration. He is confined in prison, bound with chains, hemmed in by bodily squalor, separation from those dear to him, and the darkness of punishment; yet he does not feel the injury, is not tormented by grief, and knows nothing else except to think about the Gospel of Christ. He knew that Onesimus was a slave, knew that he was a fugitive, knew that he had once been a thief, and knew that he had been converted to faith in Christ. It is a great labor for such a man to persevere in what he has begun. For this reason he repeatedly emphasizes and reiterates that Onesimus is his son, the son of his bonds, and a minister of the Gospel while he himself is in bonds, so that that Philemon—prudently and deliberately praised so highly in the preface—would not dare to refuse, lest he appear unworthy of his own praises.

When he says, “But you, that is, receive him as my own heart,” this means what I said shortly before: “heart” signifies the inward affection of the heart and a complete willingness from the soul, when everything that is within us is received by the person being petitioned. In another sense, all children are the hearts of their parents.

“But without your consent I wished to do nothing, so that your good deed might not be as though compelled, but voluntary.” It did not seem right to me to retain against your will one who belonged to you; for I consider it just that whatever good is done by you should be carried out according to your own decision.

This question, which many people ask and repeatedly reconsider—why God, when making human beings, did not create them good and upright—can be resolved from the present passage. If God is good voluntarily and not by necessity, then, when making the human being in his image and likeness, he ought to have made him such that he too would be good voluntarily and not by necessity. Those who claim that the human being ought to have been made unable to receive evil are saying this: he ought to have been made such that he would be good by necessity and not by will. But if he had been made such that he accomplished good not voluntarily but necessarily, he would not have been like God, who is good because he wills it, not because he is compelled.

It is therefore clear that they demand things contrary to one another. When they say that the human being ought to have been made like God, they are asking that he be made free in his will, just as God himself is. But when they add that he ought to have been made such that he could not receive evil, thereby imposing on him the necessity of goodness, they wish the human being not to be made like God.

The Apostle Paul, then, could have retained Onesimus for his ministry without Philemon’s consent. But if he had done this without Philemon’s consent, it would indeed have been good, but not voluntary. What was not voluntary was, in another respect, shown not to be good; for nothing can be called good unless it is freely chosen.

Here, therefore, we must consider the Apostle’s prudence. For this reason he sends the fugitive slave back to his master: so that he may benefit his master, since he could not benefit him while he was being held apart from his master.

The preceding question is therefore resolved as follows: God could have made the human being good without his will; but if he had done so, the goodness would not have been voluntary, but compelled. What is good by necessity is not good, and in another respect is shown to be evil. Thus, leaving us to our own freedom, he made us more like his image and likeness; and to be like God is absolutely good.

“Perhaps for this reason he departed from you for a while, so that you might receive him forever, no longer as a slave but, more than a slave, as a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord!”

Sometimes evil becomes an occasion of good, and God turns the wicked plans of human beings toward what is right. What I am saying will become clearer through an example. The brothers of Joseph, driven by the goadings of their jealousy, sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of gold. This became the beginning of every good thing for his father, his brothers, and all Egypt. Later he himself said to his brothers: “You intended evil against me, but God intended it for good.”

We can understand something similar in the case of Onesimus: evil beginnings became occasions of a good outcome. If he had not fled from his master, he would never have come to Rome, where Paul was bound in prison. If he had not seen Paul in bonds, he would not have received faith in Christ. If he had not received faith in Christ, he would never have become Paul’s son and been sent to perform the work of the Gospel. Thus, gradually and through the successive stages of the argument, Onesimus became a minister of the Gospel precisely because he fled from his master.

By adding “perhaps,” he appropriately moderated his statement. For the judgments of God are hidden, and it is rash to pronounce with certainty upon something doubtful. “Perhaps,” he says, “for this reason he departed”—cautiously, hesitantly, tremblingly, and without a completely firm step, lest, if he had not inserted “perhaps,” all slaves should have been obliged to flee in order to become apostolic men.

When he adds “for a while,” we should understand “a while” as a period of time. Compared with eternity, every period of time is short.

“So that you might receive him forever.” No master of a slave is eternal, for his power and the condition of both parties end with death. Onesimus, however, who through faith in Christ has become eternal, was received by the eternal Philemon—for Philemon himself had believed in Christ—and, having received the spirit of freedom, began, from being a slave, to be a beloved brother, an eternal brother, both to the eternal Apostle and to his master. As previously Onesimus had been joined to him by the condition of the flesh, so afterward he was joined to him by the spirit. When he was subject to him in the flesh, he was not joined to him in the Lord; but now he is joined to him both in the flesh and in the Lord. From this we understand that a believing slave is bound to his master by a double law: for a time he is joined to him by the necessity of the flesh, but forever he is united to him in spirit.

(Ambr.) We must observe that he did not say, “so that you may have him,” but “so that you may receive him.” He does not mean that, because Onesimus departed, Philemon should henceforth have him as a slave, thereby displaying greater affection toward him—for it would be ridiculous to say this about a fugitive slave—but that he should receive him above the status of a slave. That is, he should receive him not merely as one rendering him the servile service that slaves customarily offer their masters, which Philemon had a right to expect because of Onesimus’s changeable character and purpose.

What, then, does he mean by saying “above a slave, a beloved brother”? He means a brother who loves greatly. It is as though he were saying: Although he departed by flight, he has become so much better that he is prepared not only to render you, with complete faithfulness, the service owed to you as a slave, but also, as a brother joined to you by great love, to suffer everything for you from now on.

And because it was uncertain whether these things were in fact so, he adapts his statement by adding: “Especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.” The statement is obscure because of its extreme brevity. The Apostle often wishes to explain certain matters concisely and consequently wraps his words in obscurity.

He testifies concerning Onesimus that Onesimus had also been useful to him, after receiving exhortation and instruction from him. He means that if Onesimus proved himself such toward Paul, changing his conduct so that he willingly wished to provide him with every kind of servile service, how much more would he prove such toward Philemon? Toward Philemon, he owed the devoted fulfillment of love on account of faith and piety, and, as toward his master, service rendered with complete faithfulness.

This is what he means by “in the flesh,” namely, according to the present arrangement. When interpreting the Apostle’s statements, we have frequently explained that he commonly uses “flesh” to designate the temporal condition possessed in the present life.

“If, therefore, you regard me as a partner, receive him as you would receive me.” Above all his other statements, he sought to persuade Philemon by this one, since it was fitting that Philemon should regard as common to all the faithful, on account of their common faith, everything that belonged to him. The Apostle considered this especially appropriate in his own case, since he was a preacher and teacher of the doctrines of the piety of the true God.

“If,” he says, “you share in the faith and fully consider everything we possess to be common to us, receive this man for my sake.” He does not say that Philemon should receive Onesimus in the rank of an apostle—for how could he have persuaded him to do that?—but rather: “Because I have received him, you too receive him.” That is, if you truly consider everything to be common between us.

(Hier.) Philemon desired to have Paul as a partner. Believing in Christ, he naturally wished to have such progress that he might become like Paul and share with him in his bonds. Let us therefore consider how greatly Onesimus is praised and how much he is said to have progressed, since he is to be received as Paul himself, and since his master is to desire Paul’s companionship in such a way.

Briefly, what he says is this: “If you wish to have me as a companion, have Onesimus also, whom I regard as my companion, my son, and my own heart. If you do not receive him, and are unwilling to have him, you yourself understand that you cannot have me.”

“But if he has harmed you in anything or owes you anything, charge it to me.” “Demand it from me. As an imitator of his Lord, and with Christ speaking in him, he ought, according to his strength, to do what Christ did. For if Christ bore our weaknesses and suffered our wounds, the Apostle rightly places himself in Onesimus’s stead and guarantees what Onesimus owed.”

As we said above, the whole matter concerns what had been taken by theft and squandered through extravagance. It could not be dismissed without compensation. Philemon made compensation at great cost when, in place of a fugitive slave and the money that had been lost, he received a beloved brother and an eternal brother, and through him made the Apostle his debtor.

“I, Paul, write this with my own hand; I will repay it—not to mention that you owe me even your own self.”

(Ambr.) He promised to repay, knowing that a rich reward is reserved with God for masters who exercise such goodness toward their slaves, especially when they are willing to grant forgiveness to those who have offended. He also showed that Philemon ought not to hesitate to grant such favor: “not to mention that you owe me your own self.” “I promise these things,” he says, “knowing that you too will receive abundant rewards through God’s mercy for the goodness you are now exercising toward this man. But you should consider that you owe me your entire self, even though I do not say so.”

(Hier.) What he says means this: “What Onesimus took by theft, I guarantee that I will repay. This letter and my own hand are witnesses to my guarantee. Believe me as I make this promise for Onesimus. I say this as though speaking to someone else; but if I return to my own claim, because of the word of Christ that I preached to you, through which you became a Christian, you owe your very self to me. If you are mine, everything that is yours is mine. If everything that is yours is mine, then Onesimus also, who is yours, is mine. I could therefore have used him as my own; but I leave it to your will, so that you may have the reward of forgiving him.”

“Yes, brother, let me enjoy you in the Lord; refresh my heart in Christ.”

(Ambr.) When he said, “Let me enjoy you in the Lord,” he used the words as an adjuration. He means: “I forgive him his past offenses and receive him; make him rest with me: let me enjoy you in the Lord.” That is, let me see you making spiritual progress in all those things that are according to the Lord, so that I may consider this my gain.

And because it was fitting that Paul should make his request with abundant entreaty, in view of his humility, while it seemed that he suspected Philemon might perhaps not readily consent to his petitions, the Apostle was therefore compelled to plead with him at length and beyond measure.

(Hier.) The Latin language does not express the particular force of the Greek. For when he says, Ναὶ, ἄδελφε, “Yes, brother,” the word Ναὶ is a kind of adverb expressing the affection of one who entreats. But when we translate it “Yes, brother,” we convey, more evenly and clearly [Jerome reads *aquatius et dilutius*, “more watered-down and diffuse”], I know not what other sound than what is written.

Just as the Hebrew expression which the Seventy Interpreters frequently translated as “O indeed” (ὦ δή) signifies in their language the feeling of one who entreats, so that Symmachus sometimes translated it as “I beseech,” so we too encounter in the Greek language the same force that the Greeks encounter in the Hebrew.

When he says, “Let me enjoy you in the Lord,” something quite different is meant from what is generally supposed. The Apostle does not enjoy anyone except one who possesses within himself many virtues harmoniously joined together. Everything that is called Christ according to the variety of circumstances—namely, wisdom, justice, self-restraint, gentleness, temperance, and chastity—he prays that Philemon may possess, so that, when he has abounded in these things, Paul himself may be filled by enjoying him.

And lest you think that this enjoyment is the kind by which we often take pleasure in one another’s presence and enjoy one another, he added “in the Lord.” By adding the Lord’s name, he indicated that there is another kind of enjoyment by which someone may enjoy a person apart from the Lord.

“Refresh my heart in Christ.” Just as Paul wishes to enjoy Philemon in the Lord, so he wishes Philemon to refresh his own heart—Onesimus, whom he had also called by this name above—in Christ. The wording is ambiguous: is Onesimus Paul’s heart in Christ, or is Onesimus Paul’s heart to be refreshed by Philemon in Christ?

If you take the former meaning, Onesimus is rightly called Paul’s heart in Christ, because Paul begot him for Christ in his bonds. If you take the latter, Onesimus is to be refreshed in Christ by Philemon, as he is instructed by Philemon’s words concerning Christ.

“Confident in your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say.”

(Ambr.) I write these things without doubt that you will quickly grant the favor. I would have written in the opposite manner if I did not know that you would do not only this, but also more if I had requested it.

(Hier.) Whoever presumes upon the person whom he is about to ask, by that very presumption in a certain sense prejudges him, so that he cannot refuse what is requested. Moreover, if the one who asks knows that the person petitioned will do more than he has asked, he requests less so that the person petitioned may have the reward of making a voluntary and greater gift.

But if Philemon does this at a human command, how much more will he do it out of love for God? Therefore he is rightly praised in the Apostle’s words because he anticipates his commands by his deed and can say: “May the free offerings of my mouth please you, O Lord” (Psalm 118).

Bringing his request to an end, he adds: “At the same time, prepare a lodging for me.” I do not think that the Apostle was so wealthy or so burdened with luggage that he needed a lodging prepared for him, or that, dissatisfied with a single room, he would regard a house extending only over a small space for his body as vast. Rather, by making Philemon expect that he would come to him, he intended to make him more eager to do what had been requested.

If anyone thinks that this was not a matter of administrative arrangement but a genuine command to prepare lodging for him, lodging should be prepared for the Apostle rather than merely for Paul. He was coming to a new city to preach the Crucified One and to bring unheard-of doctrines. He knew that very many people would flock to him. First, therefore, the house had to be in a prominent part of the city, where people could easily gather; next, it had to be free from every disturbance; it had to be large enough to accommodate many hearers; it must not be near places of public spectacle; it must not be rendered detestable by a shameful neighborhood; finally, it ought to be situated on level ground rather than in an upper room.

For this reason I think that he also stayed in Rome for two years in rented quarters, and I do not suppose that the lodging was small, since crowds of Jews came there every day.

“For I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you.” God, when asked, grants a son to his father, and a brother is often preserved through his brother’s prayer. The Apostle, however, is granted to the whole Church through its prayers, for the benefit of those who are going to hear him. This gift is said to be given not so much for the benefit of one who is being deferred from martyrdom, prepared as he is for martyrdom, as for the benefit of those to whom the Apostle is being sent.

Paul himself says elsewhere that he was frequently in prison and was released from his bonds: “in prisons frequently” (II Corinthians [citation incomplete in the source]). Sometimes, through the Lord’s help, he was released because the persecutors themselves found nothing in him deserving death. For at that time no senatorial decrees had yet been issued against the Christian name, nor had Nero’s sword yet consecrated Christian blood. Rather, because of the novelty of his preaching—either through envious Jews or through those who saw their idols being destroyed and stirred up the crowds to madness—he was sent to prison, and then, when the violence and fury had subsided, he was released again.

The Acts of the Apostles testify that this was as we say. There Felix says to Agrippa: “Paul could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar” (Acts 26). It also says that he had found no cause against him except certain questions concerning his own religion and concerning a certain Jesus whom Paul asserted to be alive. From this we understand that the other judges likewise could have released them, since the Lord was bringing it about that the new preaching might be spread throughout the whole world.

“Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you, as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers.”

(Ambr.) He calls Epaphras his fellow prisoner because Epaphras had shared with him in those sorrows that Paul himself endured for Christ. “Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers”—and also, he says, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke are his fellow workers, because they worked alongside him for the benefit of others.

(Hier.) What we said at the beginning—that the Epistle to the Colossians was written at the same time and carried by the same bearer of the letters as the Epistle to Philemon—is also demonstrated by the names of those introduced as sending greetings. For in that Epistle too we read:

“Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, and Epaphras, who is from among you, a servant of Christ” (Colossians 4).

A little farther on it says:

“Luke, the beloved physician, greets you, and Demas. And say to Archippus: ‘See to the ministry that you have received in the Lord, so that you may fulfill it.’ And: ‘Remember my bonds’” (ibid.).

If anyone does not think that the two Epistles were written at the same time because the Epistle to the Colossians contains a few names that are not included here, let him know that not everyone is a friend or acquaintance of everyone else, and that a private letter to one person is different from a public letter to the whole Church.

“Epaphras,” he says, “my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you.” Concerning Epaphras, who is called Paul’s fellow prisoner, we have received the following account. They say that the parents of the Apostle Paul were from the region of Giscala in Judaea, and that when the whole province was devastated by Roman forces and the Jews were scattered throughout the world, they were transferred to Tarsus, a city of Cilicia. The young Paul followed the condition of his parents. Thus the following statements, which he makes concerning himself, can stand:

“They are Hebrews; so am I. They are Israelites; so am I. They are the seed of Abraham; so am I” (I Corinthians 11).

And again:

“A Hebrew of Hebrews” (Philippians 3),

along with the other statements that indicate him to have been more a Jew than a man of Tarsus.

If this is so, we may also suppose that Epaphras was taken captive at the time when Paul was captured, and that he was settled with his parents in Colossae, a city of Asia, where he later received the word of Christ. Hence, as we said above, it is written to the Colossians:

“Epaphras, who is from among you, a servant of Christ, always laboring anxiously for you in prayers” (Colossians 4).

If this is indeed the case, Aristarchus, who is called his fellow prisoner in the same Epistle, is brought under the same interpretation—unless, as some think, the word “captivity” indicates something hidden and sacred, namely, that they were captured together and brought into this valley of tears.

If neither interpretation is accepted, then, from the fact that “in Christ Jesus” has been added here, we may suppose that Epaphras endured in Rome the same bonds for Christ that Paul endured, and that he could therefore be called not only Christ’s prisoner but also Paul’s fellow prisoner.

Or perhaps the meaning is that he too was distinguished among the apostles, like Andronicus and Junia, concerning whom it is written to the Romans:

“Greet Andronicus and Junia, my relatives and fellow prisoners, who are distinguished among the apostles, and who were in Christ before me” (Romans 16).

This concerns Epaphras.

As for Paul’s fellow workers in the Gospel and in his bonds, when he wrote the Epistle to Philemon he names Mark, whom I believe to be the author of the Gospel; Aristarchus, whom we mentioned above; Demas, concerning whom he complains elsewhere:

“Demas has abandoned me, loving the present age, and has gone to Thessalonica” (II Timothy 4);

and Luke the physician. Luke left the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles to the Churches. Just as the Apostles changed from fishermen of fish into fishers of human beings, so Luke was changed from a physician of bodies into a physician of souls. Concerning him Paul also says elsewhere:

“I sent with him the brother whose praise in the Gospel is throughout all the Churches” (II Corinthians 8).

Whenever his book is read in the Churches, his medicine is taken again and again.

“The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.” Just as the people of Israel are counted from the better part of a human being, the head, as Scripture says, “according to their heads,” so in the whole human being and in every part of the saints there is the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. But from the greater and better part, namely the spirit, the whole human being is designated by synecdoche: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.”

When grace is in the spirit, it makes the whole person spiritual, so that he clings to God, because “whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit.”

According to the Hebrews, the names are interpreted as follows: Paul, admirable; Timothy, beneficent; Philemon, wonderfully gifted, or “mouth of bread”—from *mouth*, not from *bone*; Apphia, self-controlled or freedom; Archippus, length of work; Onesimus, answering; Epaphras, fruitful and seeing, or increasing; Mark, exalted by command; Aristarchus, a mountain of greater work; Demas, silent; Luke, himself rising.

If you wish to understand these names according to their interpretations, it is not difficult to see that he is writing first to one who is admirable and beneficent, to someone to whom all virtues have been granted and whose mouth is open to heavenly bread. Then he writes to one who is self-controlled and free, and to one who is devoted to the length of a work from which he never ceases his holy labor.

He writes on behalf of one who answers according to his testimony, and also to the one to whom the Epistle is especially dedicated. He is greeted by one who is increasing in abundance, and by one who has been made more exalted through commandments, and by the one who has grown through greater works even to the mountain. He is greeted also by the one who has set a guard over his mouth and a fortified door upon his lips—who perhaps was silent because he had abandoned the Apostle for a short time.

Finally, he is greeted by the one who rises in himself, increases daily, and makes progress, while the whole world is filled with his Gospel; he grows each time that his Gospel, heard and read, builds people up. Amen.

# BOOK TWENTY-SEVEN. EXPOSITION ON THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

[Col. 0711]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0711B]

(Hier.) First, it must be explained why the Apostle Paul, in writing this Epistle, did not follow his usual practice by setting down either the designation of his name or the dignity of his office. The reason is that, when writing to those who had believed from circumcision, he did not wish, as the Apostle of the Gentiles rather than of the Hebrews, to deprive his ministry of its authority, since he knew their pride and was demonstrating his own humility.

It is therefore said that the Apostle sent this Epistle to the Hebrews written in the Hebrew language. The evangelist Luke, preserving its meaning and arrangement, composed it in Greek after the death of the Apostle Paul.

## CHAPTER ONE

The excellence of Christ is set forth: he is the giver of the new law, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, equal in power and dignity; and Christ is shown to be superior to the angels.

“In many parts and in many ways,” says John Chrysostom, “long ago God spoke to our fathers in the prophets.”

The blessed Apostle’s entire purpose in this Epistle to the Hebrews—that is, to his own people—was to summon them to faith in Christ and to distinguish the excellence of the grace given through the Son from the legal shadows that had been mediated through angelic ministrations. Since they were greatly afflicted by the many evils that had befallen them and deeply crushed, so that they might consequently think themselves inferior and more miserable than the rest, he showed that they enjoyed a still greater grace, in order to raise his hearers from the very beginning of his discourse. [Col. 0711D]

Therefore he says: “In many parts and in many ways God long ago spoke to our fathers in the prophets.” Why, when mentioning the prophets, did he not set himself over against them? He was so much greater than they as the dispensation entrusted to him was more glorious. Yet he did not do this: first, because he refused to say greater things about himself; second, because his hearers were not yet mature; third, because he wished to lift up their minds and show that the excellence of the present age was great. It was as though he were saying: “What is so great about his having sent prophets to our fathers? To us he sent his own only-begotten Son.”

He began very appropriately with the words “in many parts,” he says, “and in many ways.” For he shows that even the prophets themselves did not earn the grace of seeing God: the Son, however, did see him. By saying “in many parts and in many ways,” he signifies what is said elsewhere: “For I multiplied visions, and I was represented in the hands of the prophets” (Hos. 12). [Col. 0712B] Accordingly, the excellence of the New Testament is declared not only because prophets were sent to the fathers, whereas the Son was sent to us, but also because none of the prophets or patriarchs saw God except in representations, while it is evident that the only-begotten Son became incarnate and was seen in that flesh through which the same man, assumed by the Word of God, is the only-begotten Son of God.

Therefore he immediately added: “In these last days he has spoken to us in the Son.” By saying “in the Son,” he means the same as if he had said “through his Son,” because the preposition *in* can bear the sense of *through*, just as he is found to use these prepositions interchangeably in many places of his Epistles. He still kept silent about Christ’s name because he knew that many of them had denied that he was the Son of God. He did not say “Christ spoke,” although it is plainly established that Christ spoke; thus he had not yet confronted the Jews openly by name. For it was clear that nearly all to whom the prophets spoke were wicked and impious, and he did not yet wish to raise the question of these people. In the meantime, he discusses generally the gifts that were bestowed upon them by divine generosity.

“Whom he appointed heir of all things.” What does “whom he appointed heir of all things” mean? Here he speaks of the incarnate Son, about whom he spoke above, just as it is also written of him in the second Psalm: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.” It is no longer merely Jacob who is the Lord’s portion and Israel alone who is his lot, but rather all nations. [Col. 0712C] This means that he appointed this Son Lord of all things. He uses the title “heir” in order by it to establish and show two things: that he is the proper Son and that no loss of dominion can befall him. He calls him heir of all things—that is, of the whole world.

Then he turns his discourse to higher matters, saying: “Through whom he also made the ages,” to show that the one who came into the world in these last days is the one through whom he also made the world. He displays his greatness, since he was the labor and author of the New Testament. After this, using several elegant steps, he reaches what is much greater than all the things he has said above, proclaiming: [Col. 0712D]

“Who, being the radiance of his glory and the exact representation of his substance.”

Everywhere we need a devout understanding, but especially where we speak or hear about God, because neither is the tongue sufficient to speak worthily about God, nor is the intellect capable of comprehending him. Whenever speech fails or thought cannot adequately express what concerns God, we ought then all the more to glorify God, because we possess such a God as transcends both the intellect and the beginning of thought.

He rightly called him the radiance of glory, since he knew him to be the one who said: “I am the light of the world” (John 8), showing him to be light from light, just as God is from God, illuminating our souls and making the Father known to us. [Col. 0713A] Through “radiance” he declared the unity of essence with God the Father and, in a wondrous manner, showed one substance, while revealing two persons in glory and radiance.

Therefore he also adds: “Who is the exact representation of his substance.” An image is distinct from the one whose form it expresses, but not in every respect—only according to person. For this image gives an altogether clear indication of equality with that whose image it is, and plainly admits no suspicion of even the slightest dissimilarity. Here he calls it “image,” whereas elsewhere he calls it “form,” when he says: “Who, being in the form of God” (Phil. 2). Form, that is, image, declares one equality of essence.

For it is written of the same Redeemer of ours: “Who, being the radiance of his glory and the exact representation of his substance, and upholding all things.” (Gregory.) His hand, therefore, carries our hearts; his hand raises us up in contemplation. For unless, as has been said, the Word of the Almighty became human for the sake of human beings, human hearts would not be able to contemplate the excellence of the Word. Therefore the minds of human beings were exalted from the place where the humble God appeared among human beings.

“And upholding all things by the word of his power.” “Upholding,” that is, governing all things by that Word of power through which he made all things. For governing the world is no less than creating it. In creation, the substances of things were produced from nothing; in governing, what has been made is preserved so that it does not return to nothing. Therefore, while all these things are governed and things opposed to one another are fitted together, a great, very wondrous, and exceedingly powerful sign of God is revealed. [Col. 0713B]

After this glory of the divine majesty in the Son, he descends to the humility of the incarnation, saying: “Having made purification for sins.” He signifies two things: that he cares for us, in saying “upholding all things by the word of his power,” and that, by adding “having made purification for sins,” he cleanses our sins.

In these two matters especially we seem to see the Apostle glorying: he shows that these blessings were brought to us through the Son. After reminding us of the cross and passion of this same Son, through which purification from sins was provided for us, he immediately teaches us about his resurrection and ascension, raising us toward heavenly things and directing us to contemplate his ineffable glory. For he says:

“But he sat at the right hand of his majesty in the heights.”

By “right hand” he did not give God a bodily form, but demonstrated the greatness of his honor. By saying “in the heights,” he showed that he is higher than and superior to all things, and that he has reached even the throne of the Father’s glory. Therefore, just as the Father is in the heights, so also is the Son. Sitting together signifies nothing other than equality of honor. If he had wished to show inferiority, he would never have said that he sat at the right hand, but rather at the left.

“He became as much superior to the angels as the name he inherited is more excellent than theirs.” (John Chrysostom.) [Col. 0713C]

O apostolic wisdom! Or rather, it is not Paul’s wisdom, but the marvelous grace of the Holy Spirit. He did not speak these things from his own understanding, nor did he discover this dispensation by human ingenuity. From where could he have received it? Could he have learned such things from chisels, skins, or that workshop? Certainly not; this was the work of divine majesty.

He did not produce these insights from his own mind, which at that time was so weak and impoverished that he had no advantage over ordinary and common people. How could a man whose whole life and attention were spent on the prices of things sold and on the preparation of skins perceive anything divine? Yet the grace of the Holy Spirit displays the powers of its strength through whomever it wishes.

For just as someone wishing gradually and gently to raise a little child to some lofty place reaching to the very summit of heaven would do so step by step, ascending from lower to higher places; then, when he had reached the heights, would command the child to look down toward the lower regions; and, when he saw the child hesitate and grow weary from darkness and weakness, would lower him again to humbler places so that he might breathe and restore his courage; then, when he had recovered, would lift him again to the heights and once more bring him down to the lower regions—so the blessed Apostle dealt with the Hebrews. You will find him everywhere following the footsteps of his teacher in teaching. [Col. 0713D]

For Christ himself acted in this way: sometimes he lifted his disciples to higher things, and sometimes, out of consideration for their weakness, he brought them down to lower things, never allowing them to remain for a long time on only one side.

Observe again Paul’s wisdom: by what steps he raises them and how he brings them to the very summit of piety. Then, before they grew faint and darkness overwhelmed them, see how he brought them back to lower things, so that they might recover somewhat:

“He spoke to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things.”

The title “Son” is common. Wherever “proper Son” is understood, he is superior and more excellent than all things. But for the moment, whatever the precise meaning may be, he establishes that he is from above. Observe how he says this: “Whom he appointed heir of all things.” The statement “he appointed him heir” indicates humility. Then he rises to a higher and loftier step: “Through whom,” he says, “he also made the ages.” [Col. 0714A]

Next he comes to what is higher than everything else, beyond which no further step can be taken:

“Who is,” he says, “the radiance of his glory and the exact representation of his substance.”

Truly he has led them into inaccessible light, into the radiance of his immense and supreme brightness. Before any darkness could overwhelm them, observe how he once again gradually lowers them to lesser and familiar matters, saying:

“Upholding all things by the word of his power. Through him,” he says, “having made purification for our sins, he caused him to sit at the right hand of his majesty.”

He does not simply say, “He caused him to sit,” but “after purification,” he says, “he caused him to sit.” He undertook the work of the incarnation; then he speaks of humble things; and after saying a little more, he adds: “At the right hand of his majesty in the heights.” [Col. 0714B]

Again he returns to recounting humble matters:

“He became as much superior to the angels as the name he inherited is more excellent than theirs.”

Here he is already speaking of the one who exists according to the flesh. In saying “he became superior,” he did not indicate the Father’s essence. That which is recognized as consubstantial with the Father’s essence was not made but begotten. He is speaking of the bodily substance, for that was made.

But the present discussion does not concern his substance—that is, how he came to exist. Rather, it is as John says: “He who comes after me has become before me” (John 1). This means “more honorable and more excellent.” So here also: “He became,” he says, “as much superior to the angels,” that is, more honorable and more glorious, “as he inherited a more excellent name.”

Do you see that the discourse concerns the one who exists according to the flesh? The name “God the Word” he always possessed; he did not inherit it later. Nor is it established that he later became superior to the angels when, through his purification, he took away our sins. He was always superior—not merely superior, but incomparably superior to all things.

Nevertheless, these statements concern the one who exists according to the flesh. Paul uses this method with us as well when he discusses human nature and speaks both of things lofty and of things lowly. When we say, “A human being is nothing; a human being is earth; a human being is ashes,” we name the whole from its inferior aspects. But when we say, “A human being is a mortal and rational animal, related to heavenly things,” we name the whole from its better aspects. So Paul sometimes speaks of Christ from what is lower and sometimes from what is higher, both wishing to confirm the dispensation and commending the simple nature. [Col. 0714C]

“For to which of the angels did he ever say: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’? And again: ‘I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me’?”

This is said without any doubt about the Son’s incarnation. Therefore he used the future tense: “I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me.” But when he said, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you,” he clearly shows that the same one of whom he says, “I will be a father to him,” was begotten from the very essence of the Father. He used the present word “today” because for God there is neither past nor future; all things are always present.

This may also be understood as having been said according to the flesh, because the flesh shares in what is higher, just as the divinity graciously consented to share in what is humble. Thus in this passage he plainly shows two natures in Christ.

Let us now apply these things as examples for our salvation. If he, though God, Lord, and Son of God, did not refuse to assume the form of a servant, how much more ought we to accomplish everything commanded us and endure all that is humble. Let us remember Christ saying: “When you have done everything, say, ‘We are useless servants’” (Luke 17). [Col. 0714D]

“And when he again brings the Firstborn into the inhabited world, he says: ‘And let all the angels of God worship him.’” (John Chrysostom.)

Our Lord Jesus Christ calls his bodily coming an “exit,” as you find when he says: “The sower went out to sow” (Matt. 13), and again: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16). This can be found in many passages of Scripture.

Paul, however, calls Christ’s entrance his coming, saying: “When he brings the Firstborn into the world.” He calls the assumption of flesh an “entrance.” But someone may ask why he uses such different terms.

The meanings of the statements are clear, and it is evident in what sense each expression is used. Christ rightly calls it an exit. We were outside God, like people bound outside a royal palace who have incurred the king’s displeasure through some offense. Such people are excluded from the royal court. But if someone wishes to obtain pardon for them, he does not first bring them into the palace; rather, he himself goes out and mingles with them there, engaging them in conversation until he makes them corrected and worthy to be presented before the king. [Col. 0715A]

Christ acted in the same way. He came out to us—that is, he assumed flesh—and, speaking with us, made the King’s commandments known to us. Thus, cleansing us from sins and turning us toward God, he brought us, like an excellent mediator, into the royal court. Therefore he calls the coming of his incarnation an “exit.”

Paul calls it an “entrance” by a metaphor drawn from heirs who take possession of an inheritance and assume the right of ruling over a possession. For when he says, “He again brings the Firstborn into the inhabited world,” he means that the inhabited world is entrusted to him. He possessed the whole world when he was recognized by everyone.

These things, however, are not said of the true God, but of the flesh. For if, according to John, he was in the world and the world was made through him, in what other way could he be brought into it except according to the flesh? [Col. 0715B]

“And let all the angels of God worship him.”

Whenever he is about to say something great and lofty, he first prepares it and makes it acceptable by saying that the Father brought in the Son. Above he had said that God did not speak to us through prophets but through the Son, and that the Son is superior to the angels, an argument he established from the Son’s name. Here, however, he wishes to derive arguments from another matter.

From what matter? From worship. He shows him to be so much superior as a lord is evidently superior to servants. It is as though someone brought a person into a house and immediately ordered all the leaders of that household to bow down together and worship him. So also God commanded all the angels to worship Christ according to the flesh, saying: “And let all the angels of God worship him”—even Gabriel himself.

But someone may ask whether only the angels were commanded to worship him. No. Consider what follows:

“And concerning the angels he says: ‘He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire’; but concerning the Son: ‘Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.’” [Col. 0715C]

Here is the greatest difference: they were created, whereas he is uncreated. Concerning the angels he says: “He makes his angels spirits.” Concerning the Son he does not say “who makes.” He could indeed have expressed the distinction in this way: “Concerning the angels he says, ‘He makes his angels spirits’; but concerning the Son, ‘The Lord created me,’” since “God made him Lord and Christ.”

But neither of those statements was said concerning the Son, nor is the latter said of the true God, but of the one who exists according to the flesh. When he wishes to signify the true distinction, he no longer includes only the angels, but all the powers that perform heavenly ministries. Do you see how he divides them and with what clarity he distinguishes creatures from the Creator, calling them ministers and him Lord, servants and him heir and proper Son? [Col. 0715D]

(Augustine.) It must be understood that “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature. They are always spirits, but they cannot always be called angels. Do you ask the name of their nature? It is “spirit.” Do you ask the name of their office? It is “angel.” In what he is, he is spirit; in what he hears, he is an angel, because *angelos* is Greek for what is called *nuntius* (“messenger”) in Latin, just as “human being” is the name of a nature, whereas “soldier” is the name of an office.

Thus those who were created as spirits by God the Creator are made angels when he sends them to announce what he has commanded, and his ministers are made a flame of fire. We read that fire appeared in the bush (Exod. 3); we also read that fire was sent from above and accomplished what was commanded (4 Kings 2).

It may be said that when they are sent to announce gentle things, they are angels; when they are sent for vengeance, they are ministers—that is, burning fire. These offices also exist in the present Church. When holy preachers proclaim spiritual things and announce the joys of God’s kingdom, they are called angels; but when they proclaim the terror of the fire of Gehenna, they are ministers, terrifying sinners with the threat of that fire which will never be extinguished.

“But concerning the Son: ‘Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.’”

Here he speaks of the one who exists according to the flesh, concerning whom the Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son”; and shortly afterward: “He has given him authority to exercise judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5). [Col. 0716A]

Here the throne of God pertains to the future judgment, in which the form of the servant will be seen as judge of the living and the dead. By that judgment Christ truly governs, examines, and judges all things. He says “forever and ever” because the final judgment will stand in eternal separation between the good and the wicked, as the one who will judge testifies in the Gospel: “Then these will go away into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25).

“A scepter of righteousness is the scepter of your kingdom.”

The scepter signifies the rule of divine righteousness, which is rightly called straight because it is bent by no crookedness. This scepter governs the righteous and strikes the impious. It is invincible strength, the most upright righteousness, and inflexible discipline. [Col. 0716B]

In ancient times the scepter was called the insignia of royal honor, signifying by it the King of virtues, the Lord Savior: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity.” It is the straight scepter: to love equity and hate wickedness. No one perfectly loves righteousness except the one who also abhors evil deeds, because love of truth is hatred of falsehood.

Below he explains what rewards were given for this love of goodness and hatred of iniquity, saying:

“Therefore God, your God, has anointed you.”

Christ’s anointing signifies both king and priest, since these dignities were assumed through sacred anointings. The very name “Christ” is derived from holy chrism. But he is said to be anointed in that nature according to which, through the dispensation, he is truly said to have been born, died, and risen as Christ. His divinity, on the other hand, needed no gift and no honor to assist it.

The repetition in “God, your God” displays a proclamation of great love.

“With the oil of exultation above your companions.”

He indicates in two ways that this holy anointing came about. The oil of joy is freedom from the stain of sin. Thus the conscience is always gladdened when it is not bitten by any harshness of recollection. [Col. 0716C]

(John Chrysostom.) Who are these other companions besides human beings? This is what is said elsewhere (John 5): Christ received the Spirit without measure.

Observe how he always joins his discourse to the dispensation of the flesh, even while speaking about the nature of the divinity. What could be said more clearly? Do you see how a creature and offspring are not the same thing? He would not have made this distinction if both were the same, nor would he have introduced, in contrast with the word “made” that he had used, the statement: “But concerning the Son he says, ‘Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.’”

Nor would he have called the Son by a different name if the meaning of “Son” were the same as that of “creature.” For what difference, I ask, would remain if offspring and creature were the same?

(Augustine.) It is said “above your companions” because he is known to have received this blessing above the whole human race—whether kings or priests in the Old Testament, or apostles and martyrs in the New—so that, being uniquely anointed, he might anoint the others. In him is the fountain of blessing, and, according to his will, it appropriately flows through all the elect. [Col. 0716D]

But all these things pertain to the flesh, to which the most perfect and glorious Word was united for the salvation of the saints. In another Psalm (Ps. 132) this ointment is said to have descended upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, down to the edge of his garment; and shortly afterward: “For there the Lord commanded blessing and life forever and ever.”

After the excellence of his humanity, the blessed Apostle once again turns in the same Son of God to the divine eternity, drawing upon the testimony of another Psalm. For he says:

“And you, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands.” (Ambrose.)

When he says, “In the beginning you founded the earth, Lord,” he shows what sound minds cannot deny: that the Creator is recognized as having existed without any beginning, apart from his creature. “And the heavens are the works of your hands.” Here we must understand “hands” as the power of God’s command. For elsewhere it is said: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148). [Col. 0717A]

“They will perish, but you will remain.”

They perish in respect of what they are, as creatures are changed for the better. But you remain, so that just as he showed the Lord’s eternity before he created all things, so after the heavens have been changed he might say that he remains in the glory of his majesty.

“And they will all grow old like a garment.”

That which is consumed by death in the manner of clothing grows old, as does human flesh, which nevertheless will be changed for the better in the resurrection.

He added: “And like a cloak you will change them, and they will be changed.” In these words the prophet perhaps wished the transformation of the heavens to be understood. They are changed like the other elements, as it is read in another prophet: “And there will be a new heaven and a new earth” (Rev. 21). [Col. 0717B]

(John Chrysostom.) To show that the works of the Lord will now remain under eternity, he says: “You will change them, and they will be changed,” because they will never return to this corruptible state. He says, therefore, that he is going to transform the world, and, indicating the ease of the act, adds: Just as anyone wraps up and changes a cloak, so he will both fold up and change the world.

Therefore, if he can so easily bring about transformation and a condition that is made better, who can say that in a lesser work he needed the assistance of another? How long will they persist in such madness without shame? At the same time, it is a greater consolation to know that everything does not remain in the same condition.

They will indeed be changed, but he himself remains the same forever, as it is said: “But you are the same, and your years do not fail.”

(Ambrose.) By the change he indicates that created things will be diminished, while he himself remains what he is, just as he said to his servant Moses: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3). In these three verses the change of creatures and the eternity of the Lord are described with wondrous brevity. [Col. 0717C]

After the majesty of the Son’s divine eternity, the blessed Paul once again directed his discourse to the glorification of his humanity, saying:

“But to which of the angels did he ever say: ‘Sit at my right hand’?”

To the victorious Son, the triumphant conqueror of the whole world through his holy incarnation, the honorable sharing of the Father’s majesty is offered after the glory of the resurrection, so that through this position the glory of the humanity he assumed might be declared.

“Until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.” (John Chrysostom.)

Here again he makes them confident, since he shows that the future will bring about the defeat of their enemies, and that, because their enemies will also be Christ’s enemies, this again reveals both the sign of his kingdom and equality of honor.

I do not think there is any weakness implied by his saying that the Father will be angered over the things that the Son endured unjustly.
