Rather, this is even more a sign of the Father’s great love and honor for the Son. For if he is angered on his behalf, how can anyone maintain that he is a stranger to him?

The same is said of him in another Psalm: “He who dwells in the heavens will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them” (Ps. 2). Again he himself said: “But those enemies of mine who did not wish me to reign over them, bring them here and kill them” (Luke 19). Since these are his words, hear what he says elsewhere: “How often I wanted to gather your children, and you were unwilling? Behold, your house will be left desolate” (Matt. 23). And again: “Whoever falls upon that stone will be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him” (Luke 20). [Col. 0717D]

Moreover, if he himself is going to judge them, all the more will he repay them with what they deserve in this life. Therefore what is said is rather a matter of honor: “Until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”

(Ambrose.) The feet of the Lord signify eternal stability, so that he stands as though with his footsteps planted by the power of his omnipotence. Those are to be placed beneath these feet who, abandoning the opposition of their vices day by day, return to the Lord and, like a footstool beneath his feet, bow before his teachings.

Without doubt this is said of those enemies who, having been converted, are placed at his right hand. Here the adverb “until” does not indicate the end of a period of time, but demonstrates the power of eternity: [Col. 0718A]

“Are they not all ministering spirits sent out for service, for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?”

Why are you surprised if the angels offer their ministry to the Son, when it is also established that they have been made ministers of our salvation? Wishing to raise up the minds of those to whom he speaks, he says that the functions of angels are directed by the Lord for the sake of human salvation. The Son is Lord and Savior; they, as servants, minister to the salvation of those predestined.

The books of both the Old and New Testaments are full of examples of this everywhere. Angels evangelized the shepherds (Luke 2); we read that an angel was sent to the Virgin Mary (Luke 1); at the Lord’s resurrection angels appeared to the women (Mark 15; Luke 24; John 20); and many other such things are read in the divine Scriptures.

Understand, therefore, how great is the honor bestowed upon us: God appoints angels as ministers to us, as he appoints them to his friends. [Col. 0718B]

(Gregory.) It is written in the book of Job: “God, against whose anger no one can stand, beneath whom those who carry the world bow” (Job 9). In this statement the angelic powers may be understood. They carry the world, for they administer the cares involved in governing it, as Paul bears witness when he says: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent out for service, for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?”

He says: “God, against whose anger no one can stand, beneath whom those who carry the world bow,” as though he were contemplating the humility of every creature and, trembling, saying: Which of frail human beings could comply with your commands, when even the angelic powers bow before your dread?

Or certainly, because when we bend down we do not see what is above us. Those most subtle spirits would stand erect if they fully attained the power of his majesty. But those who carry the world are bowed beneath God, because although they see, as far as elevated spirits can, the height of his divinity, even the angelic powers cannot comprehend it. [Col. 0718C]

The just man, unable through weakness to penetrate this mystery but weighing it to some extent from the ministries of the highest spirits, gathers himself back to consideration of his own condition with anxious humility and becomes contemptible in his own sight before the power of the heavenly greatness, saying:

“How great, then, am I, that I should answer him and speak with him in my words?”

As though he were plainly saying: If that creature, which is not weighed down by flesh, is insufficient to contemplate him, with what mind do I debate his judgments, when I am confined by the burden of corruption?

(John Chrysostom.) You see, then, that they render us service for God’s sake and perform great offices on our behalf. Therefore Paul says: “All things are yours, whether life or death, whether the world or things present or things to come.”

The Son also was sent, but not as a servant, nor as one who merely performs someone’s duties, but as the only-begotten Son, willing and desiring the same things as his Father. Indeed, he was not sent at all, for he did not pass from one place to another; he assumed flesh. The angels, however, move from place to place: they leave the first places in which they were and come to others, passing into places where they had not previously been. [Col. 0718D]

This also inspires confidence in them when he says: “Why are you afraid?” For they likewise perform an angelic ministry for us.

Having thus introduced the ministry of the angels, he immediately adds a discussion of the excellence of the grace brought to us through the Son of God, saying.

## CHAPTER TWO

The Apostle shows that the new law given by Christ must be obeyed, and that the humility of his passion does not stand in its way.

“Therefore we ought to pay much closer attention to the things we have heard, lest perhaps we drift away.” Why did he say “much closer”? That is, closer than we were accustomed to under the Law. He therefore urges them to attend more diligently to what they have heard through the Son of God than to what was spoken through the angels, customarily joining his own person to theirs in saying “we have heard” and “we drift away,” unwilling that the understanding of those who hear should flow away from what has been heard through emptiness. He explained this more fully in what follows, saying:

“For if the word spoken through angels became firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward” [Col. 0721D]. What does “became firm” mean? Namely, that it was true—as if he were saying, “faithful at the appropriate time”—wishing it to be understood that the Law given through angels was to be firmly observed in its own time. For it is shown in many passages that the Law was given through angels. Yet he testifies that the one who did not observe it received a just recompense of reward.

Why did he say “recompense of reward”? “Reward” is ordinarily used of something good. (John.) But this is the Apostle’s habit: he does not take great care over his words, but indiscriminately uses expressions that are spoken of good things or of evil things for one another [Col. 0722A]. Thus elsewhere he said, “bringing every thought into captivity to obey Christ”; and again, speaking of a “recompense of reward” in place of punishment, just as in the present passage he called punishment a reward. Likewise elsewhere he said: “For it is just with God to repay tribulation to those who trouble you, and to you who are troubled, rest (II Thessalonians I).” That is, justice will not perish, but God has carried out his judgment and turned it upon sinners, although not all sins are manifest except when the commandments that have been established are despised.

“And how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?” By these words he signifies that there was not so great a salvation in the Old Testament as there is in the grace of God, which the Son of God brought to us. For God has not now promised us, as he did them, the riches of earthly territory, but the grace of heaven; not vengeance against earthly enemies, but deliverance from spiritual ones. He has granted not a temporarily happy life, but one eternally blessed. He briefly indicated all these things by saying, “if we neglect so great a salvation.” Then he added the surpassing greatness of what was spoken through the Son of God:

“Which, having first begun to be proclaimed through the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard.” That is, if we say that these things had their beginning from the very fountainhead, then they were not brought to us by human beings, nor by any created or fashioned power; rather, the only-begotten Son himself bestowed them upon us.

“By those,” he says, “who heard, it was confirmed to us”—that is, it was entrusted to us and brought to completion. “We have a pledge,” he says [Col. 0722C]—that is, this salvation which he assigned to us has not been extinguished or diminished, but remains and prevails forever.

The cause of this is the operation of the divine will: those who heard the Lord confirmed us through their own powers. This is a great work, wholly worthy of faith, which Luke also stated at the beginning of his Gospel: “Just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word delivered them to us.” But someone may say: How was this salvation confirmed? What if those who first heard these things fabricated them?

He refutes this objection, showing that this grace is not human. For if these things had been fabricated, the divine majesty would not have borne witness to them. Therefore he added:

“God also bearing witness by signs, wonders, powers, and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his own will” [Col. 0722D]. They bear witness, and God also bears witness. And how does God bear witness? Not by word or voice—although that too would certainly be worthy of faith—but “by powers and wonders and various manifestations of power he bears witness.” He rightly said “various powers,” signifying the abundance of graces that was not found among the ancients: neither such great signs nor such diverse wonders.

He therefore says that they were not simply believed, but through signs and wonders. Consequently, when we believe them, it is shown that we believe not them but God. “And by distributions,” he says, “of the Holy Spirit according to his will.”

But perhaps someone will say: “What then? Since magicians perform signs, and the Jews said that Christ cast out demons by Beelzebub (Luke XI), should we therefore believe magicians?” But they do not perform such signs. Therefore the Apostle added, saying, “various powers”: for those things should be attributed not to power but rather to weakness, since they are shown to be phantasmal and empty. Therefore he added, saying: “And distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will.”

I think that in this passage he signifies something else as well. For I believe that there were not many among them who possessed divine gifts, but that these gifts had ceased among them because they had become sluggish and negligent. Therefore, in order to comfort them lest they fall into despair, he attributes everything to the divine will and divine purpose—as if he were saying: “He himself knows what benefits each person, and what is suitable for each one; and he himself distributes to each the grace that is beneficial.”

He says the same to the Corinthians: “God placed each one as he willed (I Corinthians VII)”; and again: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good according to his will (I Corinthians XII).”

He therefore shows that this preaching arose according to the will of God the Father. (Ambrose.) He attributes everything to the divine will and his purpose, so that no one might rely upon his own merits—as if he were saying: “He himself knows what benefits each person and what is suitable for each; therefore he bestowed grace upon each according to the foreknowledge of his will.”

It follows:

“For he did not subject to angels the world to come, of which we are speaking.” He did not subject to angels our salvation, which was accomplished in the world at the last time and which the prophets had long foretold as future; rather, he subjected it to his Son, to whom the Father’s voice sounded, as was shown above:

“You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance (Psalm I).”

He confirms this with prophetic examples, saying:

“But someone testified somewhere, saying”—why did he not give the prophet’s name, but conceal it? He does this in other testimonies also, as was said above. I think he did not do this in order to conceal the name, but because they possessed great knowledge of the Scriptures, so that he did not need to state the name of the speaker. Rather, he introduced the testimonies as though they were obvious and readily available:

“What is man that you remember him, or the son of man that you visit him? (Psalm VIII).”

“What is man”—this is to be pronounced with contempt: that is, a fragile and fleeting creature, following Adam, bound by the general perversity of ancient sin. The Lord remembers him when he forgives sins and bestows the gifts of his mercy.

“Or the son of man, that you visit him?” Here the voice must now rise, for this signifies the Lord the Savior. He was not born, like other mortals, from two human beings, but came forth from the Holy Spirit and the womb of blessed Mary, ever Virgin, like a bridegroom from a glorious bridal chamber.

Consider that above he said, “you remember,” but then added, “you visit.” He remembered when, from heaven, he showed mercy to the patriarchs. He visited when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” For someone is said to visit when a physician enters among the sick; and it is clear that this was fulfilled at the Lord’s coming:

“You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor.”

Here the humility and glory of the Lord Savior are narrated. He was made lower not by the necessity of ministerial service, but by the voluntary choice of his compassion, as the Apostle says:

“He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.”

It follows: “a little lower than the angels (Philippians II).” He who accepted the cross for the salvation of all was, in that respect, made lower than the angels—the Creator of the angels being made lower than the angels.

He rightly said “a little lower,” because although he assumed a mortal body, he nevertheless had no sin. He was crowned with glory and honor when, after the exceedingly wondrous resurrection, God, exalted in that he had become man, received the faith of the world. He was crowned with glory in the resurrection and ascension, and with honor in the confession of the Father’s majesty.

“And you appointed him over the works of your hands; you subjected all things beneath his feet.” Above, his glory and honor were narrated; now his power is also set forth, so that the perfect fullness of Christ the Lord’s majesty may be recognized.

By saying “over the works of your hands,” he shows that every creature is subject to him. For just as nothing is excluded from the Lord’s work, so it is proved that nothing is separated from Christ’s power.

“For in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing that was not subject to him.” By saying “all things,” he seems to have excluded neither earthly nor heavenly things, although earlier, because of the humility of the flesh, he had said that he was made a little lower than the angels. After the ascension he says that all things were subjected beneath his feet, so that this distinction may both remove uncertainty from those who hesitate and display the glory of his incarnation [Col. 0724C]. He says, “Under his feet,” so that every creature may rightly be seen to worship and adore him.

“Now we do not yet see all things subjected to him.” He says this concerning those who do not believe in him, because the Gospel’s preaching has not yet obtained everything. Above he said that nothing was left unsubjected to him; here he asserts that not yet do all things appear subject to him. There he designates universal subjection, whether voluntary or compelled; here, only the voluntary subjection of those who faithfully believe in him.

“But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.”

Here he shows that the glory and honor are Christ’s cross, on account of which he was made a little lower than the angels. The Lord himself always calls it this, saying, “that the Son of Man may be glorified.” If he calls glorious those things that he suffered for his servants, then you, a human being, should have no doubt that the things you suffer for the Lord belong to your everlasting glory.

He added, “so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.” He calls him grace itself who tasted death for the salvation of all. It was not owed to us that the Son should taste death for us; grace accomplished this. He indeed died for all. But what if not all believe? He nevertheless fulfilled what belonged to him. Therefore he said “he tasted death,” because he remained in it only for a short time, so that, having conquered it, he might immediately rise again.

“For it was fitting that he, for whom and through whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should perfect the author of their salvation through suffering.”

It was fitting that he should perfect—that is, complete—the salvation of all through suffering, he through whom all things exist: that is, through his death, through which the things in heaven and the things on earth were restored.

You see how much there is between us and him: he is the Son, and we are sons. He is the proper Son; we are adopted. He saves, and we are saved. You see how he both joins us to himself and distinguishes us:

“In bringing many sons,” he says, “into glory”—here he joined us to himself;

“the author,” he says, “of their salvation”—here he distinguished himself from us.

“Both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one.” Here again he joins them, honoring and comforting them by calling them Christ’s brothers, according to his statement that they are from one.

Then, fortifying his argument and showing that he spoke of the one who is according to the flesh, he said:

“He who sanctifies”—that is Christ—“and those who are sanctified”—that is, us.

Observe how great the difference is: he sanctifies; we are sanctified. He added, “all from one.” There is one God from whom all things come; but he is one way, and we another. He is like the proper Son, whereas we are like adopted sons. Nevertheless, we have one God as Father. He, as the proper Son, sanctifies; we, as adopted sons, are sanctified.

“For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: I will proclaim your name to my brothers.”

In saying, “He is not ashamed to call them brothers,” he demonstrates that our brotherhood is not a matter of nature but of his mercy and great humility, because he chose us as brothers for himself. He confirms this by prophetic testimony, lest it be thought something new and not foretold long before:

“I will proclaim [it] to my brothers.”

After the sacred passion and resurrection, he says that the glory of his divinity would be proclaimed throughout the whole world. For “I will proclaim” means, “I will cause it to be narrated,” just as he said to the women in the Gospel: “Go, tell my brothers (Matthew XXVIII).”

Those who love and those who are loved are called brothers.

He added:

“In the midst of the Church I will praise you.”

In the midst of the saints, the Lord’s praise resounds through him who says:

“I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones (Luke X).”

The true praise of the Lord is narrated not only by the mouth but also by the heart of one who loves and fulfills the Lord’s commandments.

“And again: I will put my trust in him.”

This was said of the man he assumed, whose entire confidence is undoubtedly in God the Father, as he himself says in the Gospel when he prayed for them:

“Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me (John XVII).”

He also exhorts them to have confidence, saying:

“Take courage; I have overcome the world.”

[Col. 0726A] “And again: Behold, I and the children whom God has given me.”

The Apostle brought this testimony from Isaiah, referring it to Christ and the apostles, whom he called children because of their innocence. Concerning them the Lord himself says:

“Let the little children come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven (Mark X).”

“Therefore, since the children have shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared in the same.”

Here he establishes the true brotherhood and genuine humanity of Christ, not a fictitious one. Just as the children consist of flesh and blood, so he shared in flesh and blood, in order to have that by which he might taste death for the children’s salvation. He immediately adds the reason for this dispensation:

“So that through death,” he says, “he might destroy the one who had the power of death, that is, the devil.”

(John.) Here he demonstrates something remarkable: the devil was conquered by the very means through which he had possessed power. The weapon that had been strong against the world—namely, death—was the means by which Christ struck him. Here he intimates the greatness of the victor’s power by showing what good death accomplished:

“So that he might free those who through fear of death were subject to slavery throughout their entire life.”

Why do you tremble? Why do you fear it? It has already been condemned; it is no longer terrible, but desirable, like the end of labors and the beginning of rest.

Why does he say, “through fear of death they were subject to slavery throughout their entire life”? All had been servants of death because they feared death. They had not yet been released from fear of death, whose laws held them captive. Now the saints mock it: having completed the contest and conquered death, they are about to pass into the kingdom.

Therefore Paul himself also says:

“I desire to depart and to be with Christ (Philippians I).”

“For he did not take hold of angels anywhere, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham; therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect.”

(Ambrose.) Here he honors the patriarch and those who are descended from him, to whom this Epistle was written. He therefore recalls God’s benefits both from Christ’s carnal kinship and from the promise spoken to Abraham:

“To you and to your seed I will give this land (Genesis XII),”

because all are from one: Christ according to the flesh is from Abraham, as are those to whom he was speaking.

But what he said above—“Since the children have shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared in the same”—he now explains more fully, showing from where he would take flesh and blood. Therefore he says:

“For he did not take hold of any of the angels”—that is, he did not assume the nature of any angel—“but he took hold of the seed of Abraham.”

That dignity was not granted to angels, that the Son of God should be joined to their nature in one person. Rather, God the Son bestowed this honor and dignity upon human nature, so that God and man might be one person.

Why did he say “he took hold”? Because, as though we were withdrawing from him and fleeing far away, he pursued and seized us, and united the nature of our frailty to himself in one person. What a wondrous union, that the eternal and immortal should be joined to what is mortal and temporal!

(Gregory.) For this reason our Redeemer became not an angel but a human being: unquestionably, what he redeemed had to be assumed, so that by not taking hold of the fallen angel he might leave him, while by taking hold of the human being in himself he might restore him.

(John.) And truly it is a great, wondrous, and awe-inspiring thing that our flesh should sit above, be worshiped by angels and archangels, by Cherubim and Seraphim. As I often turn this over in my mind, I am overwhelmed and imagine even greater things concerning the human race. For I see greater and glorious beginnings, and God’s great haste on behalf of our nature.

He did not simply say that he took hold of human beings. Wishing to raise them up and show the greatness and honor of their race, he said:

“But he took hold of the seed of Abraham” [Col. 0727B].

“Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect.” What does “in every respect” mean? He was born, he was brought up, he grew, he suffered everything that was necessary, and in the end he died. This is what “being made like his brothers in every respect” means.

Since he had said many things about Christ’s majesty and former glory, he now turns to speak of the dispensation, so that we may contemplate with what wisdom, and with what great diligence, he showed himself to have desired to become like us. This revealed the greatest care for us.

For above he said, “Since the children have shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared in the same”; and here he said, “being made like his brothers in every respect”—as if he were saying:

“He who is so great, who is the radiance of glory, who is the exact representation of the substance, who made the ages, who sits at the Father’s right hand—he desired and strove to become our brother in every respect. For this reason he left the angels and the other powers, descended to us, took hold of us, and accomplished ten thousand good things: he dissolved death, expelled the devil from his tyranny, led us out of slavery, and set us free. He honored us not only with brotherhood but also with ten thousand other gifts, for he even desired to become our priest before the Father.”

For he continues:

“So that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make atonement for the sins of the people.”

There was no other reason for him to be made like his brothers in every respect except that he might be a faithful high priest for us and make atonement for our sins. He saw us lying prostrate and perishing, suffering the tyranny of death, and he had mercy.

“But that he might make atonement,” he says, “for the sins of the people, so that he might become a merciful and faithful priest”—what does “faithful” mean? True and powerful. For it is the mark of a faithful priest to be able to free from sins those of whom he is priest.

Therefore, in order to offer a sacrifice capable of cleansing us, he became human. He added, “in the things pertaining to God”—that is, for the sake of those matters that pertain to God. For, he says, we had been defeated, guilty before God, and dishonored. There was no one to offer a sacrifice on our behalf. He saw us in this condition and had mercy—not appointing a priest for us, but himself becoming the priest.

“For in that in which he himself suffered, having been tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted.”

(Ambrose.) “In that in which”—that is, as a human being in whom he suffered—he is able to free those held captive and to assist those who are tempted, so that they may not be overcome. He learned our temptations by experience, not only as God but also as a human being in himself. Although God in his own nature is incapable of suffering, the same Son of God was capable of suffering in the nature he assumed, being made like our nature. In the flesh that he took, he suffered many cruel things. He knows what temptation is for those who endure it: he himself was tempted, but was not overcome.

(John.) What does he mean, then, by saying that “he is able to help those who are tempted”? It is as though someone were saying: “He stretches out his hand with great eagerness in order to suffer together with them.”

Since they wanted to possess something great and superior from those who were from the Gentiles, he shows that they possess something greater in a way that did not harm those who were from the Gentiles. What is this? Salvation is from them, because he first took hold of them, since from them he assumed flesh.

“For he did not take hold of angels, but of the seed of Abraham.” Through this he both honors the patriarch and shows who the seed of Abraham is. He recalls the promise made by God, through which it was said:

“To you and to your seed I will give this land.”

He indicates a certain kinship in a small way, because all are from one; but that kinship was not extensive.

He returns again to this recollection of the dispensation according to the flesh and says:

“His very willingness to become human was already a matter of great divine care and love. But now there is not only this; there are also the immortal blessings bestowed upon us through him.”

“For,” he says, “to make atonement for our sins.”

Why did he not say “of the world,” but “of the people”? He bore the sins of all, but for the time being the discussion concerned them. The angel also said to Joseph:

“You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people (Matthew I).”

This had to happen first, and for this reason he came: to save these people, and then through them, the others, although the opposite order has in fact occurred.

From the very beginning the apostles also said:

“To you God, having raised up his Son, sent him to bless you (Acts III)”;

and again:

“The word of salvation has been sent to you (Acts XIII).”

Here he displays the nobility of the Jewish people by saying:

“To make atonement for the sins of the people.”

For the present he spoke in this way. Since he is the one who forgives the sins of all, he made this manifest in the case of the paralytic, saying:

“Your sins are forgiven you.”

And in baptism he said to his disciples:

“Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

But when Paul had “taken hold of the flesh” [the wording is uncertain in the supplied text], he now speaks entirely of lowly things without fear. Pay attention to what he says next.

## CHAPTER III. It is shown that Christ surpasses Moses and must be obeyed steadfastly.

“Therefore, holy brothers, participants in a heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and high priest of our confession, Jesus, who is faithful to him who made him, as Moses also was in all his house” [Col. 0729A].

He is still speaking about the mystery of Christ’s incarnation. For in the Gospel he himself testifies that he was sent only to the lost sheep (Matthew X), that is, to the house of Israel.

The Greek word *Apostle* means “sent” in Latin. Recognize what kind of priest Jesus is, and what he is, and you will have no need of any other consolation or comfort. He called him the high priest of our confession—that is, of our faith—to whom this new people has been entrusted, just as the former people were given to Moses to govern. But greater and far better things have been entrusted to this one.

Blessed Paul wishes to raise the minds of the Israelites to the excellence of God’s promises, so that they may prepare themselves attentively to receive what God kindly promised to bring them. He calls them dearly beloved brothers, called to heavenly things, participants with Christ in God’s inheritance, Christ being faithful to him—that is, to God the Father who made him.

He speaks of Christ’s humanity, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, not of his divinity, which was not made but begotten by the Father, of one substance with him.

“As Moses,” he says, “was faithful in his house.”

Since he was about to place Christ above Moses by comparison in the matter of the priesthood under the Law, he introduced this statement, asserting that Christ was faithful in his house: faithful, that is, devoted, defending what belongs to him, and not permitting it to be corrupted. As he says in what follows, we are that house.

As Moses was faithful in his house—that is, in the former people—he immediately goes on to show how we ought to be Christ’s house:

“For we are his house if we hold firm to the end the confidence and glory of hope,” because “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved (Matthew X, XXIV).”

He calls those who are summoned into the Church a house. He added:

“We are the house of God”—that is, created as God’s workmanship in Christ Jesus.

Up to this point he has compared Christ’s incarnation with Moses. From here he turns to narrate Christ’s higher greatness, saying:

“For this one has been considered worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as the one who built the house has greater honor than the house.”

He did not say that the craftsman has greater honor than the works, but that the builder has greater honor than the house he constructs. You see that he is not speaking of a temple, but of the entire former people whom Moses led out of Egypt, and then of the people whom Christ delivered from the devil’s slavery and acquired as a house for himself.

“For every house is built by someone, but the one who created all things is God.”

Here he distinguishes the builder from the building, wishing it to be understood that God is the author of both houses. Yet he is the author of one in a different way from the other: of the house over which Moses presided in one way, and of the house whose leader and Lord Christ is recognized to be in another.

Therefore he continues:

“And Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony of the things that were to be spoken; but Christ was faithful as a Son over his own house, and we are that house if we hold firm to the end the confidence and glory of hope.”

This one, that is, Jesus, enters into the Father’s possessions as a son; the other, that is, Moses, entered as God’s servant.

Here again he urges them to stand firm and not be overthrown. For we shall be God’s house if we hold firm to the end the confidence of hope and glory. He rightly said “the confidence of our hope,” because all good things for the saints are in this life matters of hope, until they reach the vision of perfect blessedness:

“For by hope we were saved (Romans IX).”

We cannot possess the good things promised to us in this penal life except in hope, patiently awaiting them and holding that hope firm to the end.

“Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says (Psalm 94):

> Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation, on the day of testing in the wilderness, where your fathers tested me, proved me, and saw my works for forty years. Therefore I was angered with that generation, and I said: ‘They always go astray in heart.’ But they did not know my ways; so I swore in my anger: ‘They shall not enter into my rest.’”

The blessed Apostle spoke above about hope, because we ought to hope for what is yet to come: “For hope that is seen is not hope” (Romans 9). The history which the prophet recalls here is well known. When the Israelites had gone out from the land of Egypt, traveled a long way, and received many signs of God’s power—in Egypt, at the Red Sea, and in the wilderness—they decided to send spies to inspect the nature of the land that had been promised to them. These men went forth and returned. They greatly admired the land and said that it was exceedingly fruitful, but that the province was inhabited by unconquerable and powerful men.

The Israelites, however, ungrateful and foolish, ought to have remembered God’s many benefits: how he had rescued them from danger when they were enclosed amid so great an army of Egyptians; how he had given them springs of water without fail; how he had bestowed manna; and how he had performed other miracles for them, so that they might believe in God. But they neither believed God nor remembered any of these things. Terrified by fear, they said: “Let us return to Egypt.”

God was therefore angry with them, because they had so completely forgotten God’s benefits and his wonders, and he swore that that generation would not enter the rest formerly promised to their ancestors. Thus all of them perished in the wilderness, except only two.

The Apostle therefore mentions three rests in this Epistle: the first, the Sabbath, on which the Lord rested from his works; the second, in Palestine, where the Israelites, after entering, were to rest from great misery and toil; and the third, which is the true rest, namely, the kingdom of heaven. Those who are granted the opportunity to reach it truly rest there from their labors and difficulties. It is of this rest that the prophet speaks here to the true Israelites, saying:

> “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts,”

lest you suffer the same things as your ancestors suffered and thereby be deprived of the promised rest. For your fathers once heard his voice through Moses and became hardened. At that time he spoke through a herald; when you hardened your hearts, he now speaks through himself. Let your hearts become tender. He who formerly sent heralds before him has deigned to come himself. He speaks here with his own mouth who spoke through the mouths of the prophets. At the voice of him who sent the herald and now cries out through himself, do not close your hearts. Remember how your fathers became hardened and how they did not enter the promised rest, but perished in bitterness, murmuring against God. Your fathers were the ones who perished.

Do not imitate them. They were your fathers; but if you do not imitate them, they will not be your fathers, although you were born from them, knowing “that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Luke 3).

“For forty years I was angered with that generation.” He chastises them in many ways, yet they always went astray in heart. The Lord fasted in the wilderness for forty days in order to triumph over him through whom they had murmured against God for forty years in the wilderness. After the entire glory of his victory had been completed in his passion and resurrection, he remained with his disciples for forty days before ascending into heaven. In the first forty days he displayed the temptations of this pilgrimage; in the later forty days, the consolation which the saints will have in their homeland. For his body, that is, the Church, must be tested in this world; but that Consoler is not absent who said: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28).

> “To whom I swore because of their unbelief that they would not enter into my rest.”

For God to speak is a great thing; how much greater, then, for him to swear. By an oath he wished to provide confirmation. By whom does God swear except by himself? He has no greater by whom he might swear. By himself he confirms his commands; by himself he confirms his threats. Just as what he promises is true, so what he threatens is certain.

He swore that they would not enter his rest; yet some must enter his rest. Therefore, when those others were rejected, we shall enter, because if some branches were broken off on account of dissimilarity and unbelief, we may be grafted in on account of faith and humility.

(Joannes.) The apostolic exhortation to the people concerning entering the rest follows:

> “See to it, brothers, that there not be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, causing you to depart from the living God.”

Through hardness, unbelief is born. Just as hardened and rigid bodies do not yield to the hands of physicians, so hardened souls do not yield to the word of God.

“For if your fathers,” he says, because they did not hope as they ought to have hoped, suffered the things that are read in the history we mentioned earlier, and perished in the wilderness because of hardness of heart, you have much more reason to fear that such things will happen to you, just as they happened to them. For this word was addressed to those who were present or would later be present. Therefore he says “today.” Indeed, it is always “today” as long as the world endures.

He goes on to speak further about “today,” saying:

> “But exhort one another each day, as long as it is called ‘today,’ so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.”

That is: build one another up; correct one another; take care that similar things do not happen to you; let no one among you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin—that is, by unbelief.

Observe that unbelief produces sin. Just as unbelief gives birth to an evil life, so also, when the soul has descended into the depths of evil, it becomes contemptuous. In its contempt, it does not permit itself to believe, so that it may free itself from fear of everlasting death.

Then the Apostle adds:

> “For we have become partakers of Christ.”

What does “we have become partakers of Christ” mean? “We partake of him,” he says; that is, we have become one with him, since he is the head and we are the members, co-heirs and of one body with him, according to the spiritual human being who was created in him.

> “If only we hold firmly to the beginning of his substance until the end.”

What is “the beginning of his substance”? He signifies faith, through which we subsist and are born from God as sons, and, so to speak, are made substantial. This must be observed with the greatest care, lest we be corrupted by the stain of any doctrine. Then the Apostle continues to speak still of “today.”

(Albinus.) “While it is said,” he says, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in that provocation”—up to—“from the things they heard.”

Here the Apostle begins to explain the prophetic testimony which he quoted above. For he said: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the bitterness.”

(Joannes.) Whose hardening does he mention? That of certain unbelievers? Is it not that of those whose corpses were cast down in the wilderness? For what he says means this:

> “They heard too,” he says, “just as we hear; but what benefit did the word they heard bring them?”

Therefore do not think that you will be helped merely by hearing the preaching, since they too heard through Moses but gained no benefit from what they heard, because they did not believe. The word they heard was not joined with faith. Faith distinguished those who believed the word from those who did not believe.

For he says: “But not all.” Caleb and Joshua, because they did not join the unbelievers, escaped the punishment inflicted upon them. Nor was it the only gift granted them that they escaped the death by which the others perished: they were also granted entry into the promised land and the honorable possession of their allotted portion.

## Chapter IV. On Entering the Heavenly Rest, Toward Which We Must Hasten Because of the Excellence of Christ’s Divinity and Humanity

> “Therefore let us fear lest, while the promise of entering into his rest remains, any of you should be thought to have fallen short.”

(Albinus.) Let us fear their destruction and dread God’s just judgment, which will repay each person according to his works. Everlasting rest is promised to those who have faith, yet to that faith which works through love. Let us therefore fear everlasting punishment if, after leaving behind the promise we made to God in baptism, we should perhaps return again to the works of unbelief which we renounced before many witnesses. Let each person labor on his own account, lest he be found unworthy of entering God’s rest.

> “For indeed we have received the good news just as they did; but the word they heard did not benefit them, because it was not joined with faith in those who heard it.”

We too have been told how we ought to enter God’s rest, just as they were; yet we have been told through the Son, whereas they were told through a servant. The Apostle immediately adds words of exhortation, saying:

> “For we who have believed are entering into the rest, just as he said: ‘As I swore in my anger, they shall not enter into my rest.’”

He urges us to enter the rest, lest what was said to them be said to us as well: “They shall enter,” that is, they shall not enter, into my rest. For he hastens to show that there is another rest to which we have been called, namely, the heavenly one. He does not say that we shall enter the rest which is in Palestine, but that they did not enter it because of the hardening of their hearts—neither the Palestinian rest nor the heavenly rest.

He therefore adds a discussion of the first rest:

> “For somewhere he has spoken of the seventh day in this way concerning the works completed from the foundation of the world: ‘And God rested on the seventh day from all his works,’”

and so forth.

Immediately he adds the second rest, which was promised to the people of God, and says concerning this rest again:

> “They shall not enter into my rest.”

The conjunction “if” may be understood as affirmation, negation, or doubt. Above it was used as a negation, where he said that because of their unbelief God swore that they would not enter the promised rest. He added, “They shall enter,” that is, they shall not enter. Here, however, it can be understood as affirmation, as though he were saying: “If they enter, they will fare well.” Therefore he adds:

> “Since, then, it remains for some to enter it, and those who formerly received the good news did not enter because of unbelief, he again sets a certain day—‘Today’—saying through David, after so long a time, as was said above: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.’ For if Jesus had given them rest, he would never afterward have spoken of another day.”

Since, he says, it remains for some to enter that rest—namely, the one that existed in Palestine—only a few entered it, that is, only two, Caleb and Joshua, out of all those who had departed from Egypt. Accordingly, he says: “And those who formerly received the good news did not enter because of unbelief,” signifying those who had gone out from Egypt, whose corpses were cast down in the wilderness.

Then he begins to discuss, though obscurely, the third rest, which was promised through Christ to those who believe:

> “Again,” he says, “he sets a certain day—‘Today’—through David, saying, after so long a time, as was said above: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts. For if Jesus had given them rest, he would never have spoken afterward of another rest.’”

Here he shows that there is a certain third rest, of which David said “today.” He does not signify the rest into which Jesus led the people, but another rest far more excellent than that one, into which the true Jesus, not a symbolic one, led those who belong to him.

Let us hear why this is certain. After so many years, he says, David again says:

> “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”

For if Jesus had truly given rest to the people whose leader he was, David would not afterward have spoken of another rest.

It is therefore certain that some will receive the rest which was signified by the rest in Palestine, into which the true Jesus will lead his people.

> “Therefore a Sabbath-rest remains for the people of God; for whoever has entered his rest has himself also rested from his works, just as God did from his.”

God’s rest is to be understood as the perfection of his works: on the sixth day he completed the original creation of things, and on the seventh he ceased from creating new natures. Through that rest of God, which is eternal, he earnestly urges us toward eternal rest, which he called the Sabbath-rest.

(Joannes.) Observe how he has reasoned throughout this entire discourse. He says that he swore to those earlier people that they would not enter the rest, and they did not enter it. Then, after them and after a long period of time, speaking to the Jews, he said:

> “Do not harden your hearts as your fathers did.”

It is therefore certain that there is another rest. For this could not be said of the rest that was in Palestine, since they already possessed it. Nor can it be said of the seventh day, since it is not that rest he was discussing; it had already taken place long before. He therefore signifies another rest, which is the true rest.

Indeed, that is truly rest where pain, sadness, and groaning have fled; where there are neither anxieties, labors, struggles, nor fear that causes the soul to grow numb and tremble, but only the fear of God, full of delight. There is not found there:

> “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Genesis 2),

nor thorns nor thistles. There is not found there:

> “In sorrow you shall bear children,”

nor:

> “Your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.”

Instead, everything is peace, joy, gladness, delight, goodness, and gentleness. There is no envy there, nor jealousy, nor bodily illness, nor the death of the soul. There is neither darkness nor night there: always day, always light, always the brightness of day. There is no weariness there, nor satiety or disgust; we shall always persevere in the desire for good things.

(Albinus.) Since he was speaking to Jews, he did not say “rest” in this passage, but “Sabbath-rest,” a proper name associated with what they rejoiced in and hastened toward. He called the kingdom of God the Sabbath-rest. Just as he commanded that on the Sabbath one abstain from all evils and do only those things that pertain to the service of God—things which the priests performed and which benefited the soul, and nothing else—so it will be then.

He does not intend such a Sabbath in the kingdom of God that someone should afterward return from it to laborious works, as they did on the carnal Sabbath. Whoever enters this Sabbath of God rests perpetually from his works, just as God rested from his.

Wishing therefore to instruct them about the resurrection and everlasting rest, he repeatedly inserted the word “today,” so that they would never despair of entering it, as though he were saying: “If anyone has sinned, as long as it is still ‘today,’ let him have hope of returning.” Therefore let no one despair as long as he lives.

> “Let us therefore hasten to enter that rest, so that no one may fall into the same example of unbelief.”

(Joannes.) Faith is indeed a great and saving thing, and without it no one can be saved, as it is said:

> “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 9).

But faith alone is not sufficient. Faith must work through love, and it is necessary also to live worthily of God. Therefore Paul likewise admonishes those who have been deemed worthy to receive the mysteries, saying:

> “Let us hasten to enter that rest.”

Let us hasten, he says, because faith is not sufficient by itself; a life worthy of faith must also be added, and great diligence must be applied lest faith remain idle.

(Albinus.) If those who murmured against God were not found worthy to enter the land, how shall we, living indifferently like the nations, be found worthy to enter heaven? Everyone who wishes to possess heaven must adorn faith with good works.

Nor is this the only loss suffered by one who lives badly—that he does not enter the kingdom of God. What is even more terrifying is that he is handed over to everlasting punishment. Therefore he adds:

> “So that no one may fall into the same example of unbelief.”

He terrified his hearers with the destruction of those who perished in the wilderness, lest they fall under the same judgment, as though he had said: “We are sufficiently instructed by what happened to our ancestors not to fall into similar things and not to suffer what they suffered.” This is what he means by “the same example of unbelief.”

Then, to instill greater fear in sinners, he adds:

> “For the word of God is living and effective, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing as far as the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.”

(Joannes.) Here he shows that the same one performed those deeds and lives; he has not been extinguished. Therefore, since you have heard about the word, do not understand it superficially. For he says that it is sharper than a sword.

Observe Paul’s distinction, and from this consider why the prophets needed to speak of a sword, a rhomphaea (long sword), and a bow:

> “Unless you repent,” he says, “he has sharpened his sword; he has bent his bow and prepared it” (Psalm 7).

If now, after so long a time and after the consummation, he cannot terrify merely by the name “word,” but also requires these expressions in order to show its eminence by comparison, how much more is it then “sharper, piercing as far as the division of soul and spirit”?

What does this mean? He has signified something more terrible: either that the word divides spirit from soul, or that it penetrates and reaches even what is incorporeal, not merely bodies, as a sword does. Here he shows that the soul too is punished and that the inner parts are examined. He shows that we have the same judge who condemned them because of their unbelief.

For he said:

> “The word of God is living.”

The Word of God is the Son of God, who said of himself:

> “If anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.”

Just as they would have lived and entered the promised land if they had kept the word of God, so we shall live and enter the heavenly rest if we keep his word.

> “For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword.”

A sword can divide the limbs from the body and penetrate hidden places and the nature of the flesh. But the word of God is far sharper than it, reaching, as the Apostle says, “as far as the division of soul and spirit.”

We live by the soul; by the spirit we understand. Carnal life is shared by us with the beasts; spiritual reason is shared with the angels. Yet God’s judgment is effective, distinguishing between carnal and spiritual sins: who acts, what he does, with what intention, and with what desire he serves God in his heart. His perception is so penetrating that he knows everything we do or think more certainly than we ourselves do. We always have as the witness of our deeds and thoughts the one whom we shall have as our judge.

Let us fear the presence of him whose knowledge we can in no way escape. For he said that the word of God is a discerner, that is, the providence of God, showing that all our inward and outward things will be judged by him who knows everything about us and penetrates the whole human being completely.

Nor is it surprising that, being wholly everywhere, he knows his entire creation, whether spiritual or bodily, since nothing that was made was made without him. Therefore he added:

> “There is no creature invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open to his eyes.”

(Serapion.) From this it is clearly gathered that nothing is incorporeal except God alone. Therefore all spiritual and intellectual substances can be penetrated by him alone, because he alone is wholly and everywhere and in all things, and thus he examines and surveys the thoughts of human beings and all the inner movements of the mind.

Outward works are open to human eyes, but our inward and most subtle thoughts are incomparably more fully open to the eyes of God.

> “For all things,” as it is written, “are naked and open to his eyes.”

(Gregory.) Often we fear appearing disorderly in an outward action before human eyes, yet in our inward thought we do not fear his regard. We do not see the one who sees everything; for we are much more visible inwardly to God than outwardly to human beings. Therefore all the saints keep watch over themselves outwardly and inwardly, either reproving themselves outwardly or fearing that inwardly they may be seen, though invisibly, as wicked.

(Joannes.) Here he especially terrified them lest, although they were still standing in the faith, they should fail to complete the works of faith with full satisfaction. For he discerns what is in the heart; there he examines and considers it, repaying each person according to his merits.

And why speak only of human beings? Whether you mention angels, archangels, Cherubim, Seraphim, or any other creature, everything is revealed to his eye; everything is open and manifest. What could escape him?

> “All things are naked and open to his eyes.”

But what does “open” mean? It is a metaphor drawn from skins taken from animals, which are removed so that what is inside may be seen. For when someone has killed animals and stripped the skin from the flesh, all the inner parts are revealed and become open to our eyes. So everything lies open before God.

But observe also how he always requires bodily examples. This arises from the weakness of his hearers. Because they were weak, he declared that they were sluggish and needed milk, not solid food.

> “All things are naked and open to his eyes, to whom we must give an account.”

What does “to whom we must give an account” mean? It means that we shall render to him an account of our deeds.

[Col. 0737A] “Since, then, we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God.” (Alb.) Having shortly before discoursed about his divinity, he said: “All things are naked and open to his eyes”; but now, because he is speaking about the flesh, he discusses the priesthood of him who offered himself for the sake of our salvation, and how he entered first of all into rest. “For we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens.” Thus Moses, the leader of the people, to whom a transitory rest was promised, will not enter into the rest which he so often promised to the people. But this our priest, guarantor of a better promise, making a way for those who believe in him, first entered into the rest promised to the people entrusted to him, showing that he is a great priest because he possesses an everlasting priesthood, always living to intercede [Col. 0737B] for us; and he shows that this same one is the Son of God when he says, “Jesus the Son of God”—something he nowhere wished to say of Moses. Rather, he presented Moses as a servant, testifying earlier under the name of Jesus— the name which the angel sent from God announced to the Virgin—that he was the true Son of God and therefore the great priest.

“Let us hold fast also to his confession, for we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses.” What confession does he mean? That he is the Son of God; that Christ is God; that he suffered, was buried, rose again, ascended into heaven on the third day, sits at the right hand of God the Father, and will come from there to judge the living and the dead; through him we possess every good thing: redemption, resurrection, and an everlasting inheritance with him. [Col. 0737C] Let us confess these things. That they are true is made most evident by the fact that the high priest, established within the inner veil, enters sprinkled with his own blood, not with another’s, as did the former priests, who were sprinkled with the blood of a red heifer.

“For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses.” He does not, he says, fail to know the things that belong to us. For he came by way of the human condition, in every respect without sin, bringing with him nothing by which he would be liable to death, as he himself testifies in the Gospel, saying: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.” Many high priests do not know those who are placed in tribulations, nor do they know what the tribulation of any particular person is. For it is impossible [Col. 0737D] for one who has had no experience of affliction, and has not endured all things sensibly, to know the afflictions of the afflicted. Our high priest, however, appropriately endured everything that was imposed upon human misery after the sin of the first man, and then ascended within the inner veil to the throne of the Father’s majesty.

“Tempted in every respect according to the likeness, without sin.” (Theo.) If, then, there can be this communion of our earthly lowliness with that lofty and divine High Priest, so that we too may be tempted without any offense of sin, why does the Apostle distinguish him from human beings by such a division, as though he were accepting this as something unique and singular in him? He is distinguished from all of us by this one exception: we are tempted not without sin, whereas it is established that he was tempted without sin. For what human being, however strong and warlike, is not often exposed to hostile weapons? Who, as though enclosed in impenetrable flesh, can enter into such dangers of battle without danger?

But he alone was “fairer in appearance than the sons of men” (Ps. 44), assuming the condition of human death together with all the frailty of the flesh, yet never stained by contact with any defilement. For he was tempted in the desert by the devil, according to the likeness of our nature, by the vice of gluttony, when it was said to him: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves” (Matt. 4). He was also tempted by vainglory, when it was said to him: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down.” He was also tempted by the disease of avarice, or by the swelling of pride, when the devil promised him [Col. 0738B] all the kingdoms of the world and their glory.

He was indeed tempted in various ways, but he was not overcome: tested in tribulations, everywhere a glorious victor. He was tempted according to the likeness of flesh, without sin. Thus he had the likeness of sinful flesh, although his flesh was entirely without sin. This is the temptation by which he was tempted: he suffered the persecution of many, received spitting, was accused, endured slander, suffered calumnies, was rejected by his own people, and at last was crucified.

“According to the likeness,” he says, “without sin.” When he says “in the likeness of flesh,” he does not mean that there was merely a likeness of flesh in him, but that he assumed true flesh. Why, then, did he say “in the likeness of flesh”? The true nature which he assumed is like our flesh, but he had none of the sins which our flesh contracted from its parents, because original sin was of such a character in the flesh of the first man that from it both punishment and remedy could arise: punishment and sin in the whole human race, except in Christ, in whom alone there was salvation and remedy. Sinful flesh was not so prejudged that a remedy could not arise from it; the power of God foreknew how, from the same substance, the equity of righteousness and the goodness of mercy could emerge.

“Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of grace, so that we may receive mercy and find grace for timely help.” “(Joan.) What seat of grace does he mean?” He means the royal seat itself, of which it is said elsewhere: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109).

What does “Let us approach with confidence” mean? It means that we have a high priest without sin, contending with the world. “Take courage,” he says, “for I have overcome the world” (John 16). For when it is said that he had to suffer all things, yet was free from sins, this is what it signifies: as though he were saying, “We are under sin, but he is without sin.”

(Alb.) Let us therefore approach with confidence, so that we have nothing evil in our conscience—that is, without doubting; for one who doubts cannot approach with such confidence. Let us therefore approach with confidence: that is, let us approach through faith to his throne of grace. Let us have confidence that, although we are sinners, we can be restored through his grace, provided that we produce fruits worthy of repentance and retain firm faith to the end.

Now our true high priest, Jesus the Son of God, sits upon the throne of grace, ready to forgive our sins in this timely assistance. This, then, is the timely season of his help and mercy, as that outstanding teacher said elsewhere: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6). And the Prophet, signifying long beforehand this season of timely help, said: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. 49).

Even now, after baptism, for sinners to find mercy if they repent is a gift of him who sits upon the throne of grace. That he has become timely for us is a great indication of the humility which he assumed from our nature, not of his own substance, which he possesses triumphantly with the Father. Let us therefore bring to him faith together with confidence in his goodness. At this timely season, when he sits upon the throne of grace and grants everything that certainly contributes to our salvation, it is the season of gifts. Let no one despair of himself. Let us fear his throne of judgment when he comes to judge all things according to righteousness. Then will be the time of despair for those who now refuse to turn to the seat of grace, when the bridal chamber will be closed and only those who bring lamps shining with good works will remain with the bridegroom.

(Joan.) “Let us hasten,” he says; for Paul also said: “So I run, not as uncertainly.” Running is necessary, and vigorous running. One who runs sees no one who meets him, whether he passes through meadows or difficult places. One who runs never stands still; for if he neglects even a little, he loses everything. One who runs puts nothing before the goal but presses toward it all the more.

I have said this to those who say: “In my youth I was devoted; in my youth I fasted, but now I have grown old.” You ought rather to have increased your devotion greatly. Let no one enumerate his former virtues; now is the time when a person is most vigorous, and he is not steadfast in youth. For one who runs this bodily course rightly says that gray hair has overtaken him and that he cannot run in the same way, because the whole contest is situated in the body.

But for what reason will you lessen your running? Here what is needed is the soul, with an upright soul. The soul is strengthened rather in old age; then it is vigorous, then it rejoices. Just as the body, while it is held by fevers and succeeding illnesses, is afflicted even if it is strong, but when it has been freed from the siege of diseases, it recovers its proper strength, so the soul in youth labors under fevers: the love of glory oppresses it, as do the love of pleasures, sexual things, and many other imaginings. When old age arrives, it drives away all these passions, some by satiety, others by philosophy, holding them in check.

For one who is so frantic in old age shows that in youth he was such not through ignorance, inexperience, or age, but through negligence. He can say, “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance” (Ps. 24), who conducts himself suitably in old age and changes as age advances. But if he is equally disgraceful in old age, how is he worthy to be called an old man, when he shows no reverence even for his age? For the one who says, “Do not remember the sins of my youth,” says this as one corrected in old age.

Therefore do not defraud yourself of pardon for the things you did in youth on account of what occurs in old age. For how is it not absurd, and beyond pardon, for an old man to sit in taverns, an old man to hurry to the circus, an old man to go up to the theater, running with the crowd like boys? It is truly shameful and ridiculous to be adorned with gray hair outwardly while inwardly possessing a childish understanding. If a young man insults him, he immediately brings forward his gray hairs, saying: “At least show reverence to these gray hairs.” But if you, now an old man, show them no reverence, how do you desire a young man to revere your gray hairs? “You do not revere them,” you say? Rather, you dishonor them. God has honored you and given you the whiteness of hair.

What benefit is there in having the first place at a gathering? How will a young man revere that honor when he sees you more devoted to wantonness? Gray hair is venerable when the person does what is fitting for gray hair; but when he behaves like a youth, he will be more ridiculous than youths.

How will you be able to admonish the young when you old men become drunk through your lack of self-restraint? I do not say these things now to mock the elderly; rather, I mock the young. For you who do these things, even if you reach your hundredth year, appear young to me and like children. Young men, even if they receive only a little discipline and are corrected, are better than their elders.

This is not merely my statement; Scripture too recognizes this distinction. “For old age is honorable, not because of length of time, and a spotless life is the measure of old age” (Wis. 4). We honor [gray hair?]—not because it has a white color, and therefore honor it more than black, but because it is an indication of a life advanced in virtue, and from it we infer an inward old age. But if people do what is contrary to old age, they become objects of ridicule.

Nevertheless, a young man is not free from blame. A young man may have pardon only so long as he is inexperienced and needs time and experience. But when it is necessary to demonstrate self-control or courage, and especially when it is necessary to abstain from money, he is by no means free from blame; indeed, there are circumstances in which a young man is blamed more than an old man. The old man needs much treatment because old age weakens him; the young man, however, is strong if he wishes to govern himself. What pardon does he deserve when he steals more than an old man, when he harbors evil in his heart, when he does not help an old man, when he speaks many superfluous words, when he insults, curses, and becomes drunk?

If he thinks that he cannot be blamed for lack of self-control, observe that in this matter too he has much assistance, if only he wishes to use it. Even if desire does not spur him more powerfully than it spurs an old man, there are many things in which he can struggle more effectively than an old man, so as to charm that beast. What things are these? Labors, reading, and vigils.

“But what have these things to do with us,” he says, “who are not monks?” You say this to me? Say it to Paul, when he says: “Keeping watch with all perseverance and prayer” (Eph. 6), and when he says: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13). He did not write these things only to monks, but to all who were in the cities.

A secular person has nothing more than a monk except intercourse with his wife. In this he has permission; in other matters, not at all, but he must conduct himself in everything equally as monks ought to do. For the beatitudes proclaimed by Christ were not spoken only to monks; otherwise the whole world would perish, and we would accuse God of cruelty. But if the beatitudes were spoken only to monks, while it is impossible for a secular person to fulfill them—even though he himself commanded marriage—then he destroyed everyone. For if a person cannot fulfill, within marriage, the things that belong to monks, everything has perished and been corrupted, and he has confined the things of virtue within a narrow space. How, then, is marriage honorable if it hinders us so completely?

## CHAPTER V

The Apostle explains what is required in a high priest and shows that these things apply to Christ, while intimating the difficulty of speaking about Christ.

“For every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings in matters pertaining to God.” (Joan.) Blessed Paul now wishes to show that this Testament is much better than the old one, because nothing in it is imaginary—for example, no bodily temple, no fleshly victims, no legal observances—but everything is higher and more perfect, since the whole character of this Testament belongs to spiritual things.

Spiritual things, however, do not introduce the weak in the same way as bodily things do. He began his discussion from bodily matters, saying: “For every high priest taken from among human beings is appointed on behalf of human beings.” He first defines what a high priest is and demonstrates what belongs to a high priest, what his ministry is, and what the signs of the priesthood are: namely, that he offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, and that he be able to sympathize with those who are ignorant and err.

“For he himself is also surrounded by weakness.” It was necessary to establish faith in higher earthly things so that they might reach higher spiritual things, and so that the custom of priests according to the manner that existed in the Law might lead them upward, that is, to the priesthood of Christ, since they were still weak. [Col. 0741D] For this reason he introduces the role of a fleshly high priest.

The office of a high priest, then, is to stand between God and the people and to beseech God on behalf of the people’s sins. Christ did this, offering himself for our sins, always living to intercede for us: once taken from among human beings, but always interceding on behalf of human beings.

The Apostle sets forth some things common to Christ and the priests, and other things higher than these. What he says, “Every high priest taken from among human beings,” is common to Christ. “He is appointed on behalf of human beings.” And this [perhaps, “also this”]: “To offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.” This too is common, but not entirely; the remaining points are not common.

“He is able to sympathize with those who are ignorant and err.” Here there is already something superior, about which he discoursed more fully above in the preceding statement. But what he added—“and for this reason he ought to offer for himself also, just as for the people, for sins”—belongs more to the legal priests than to Christ, unless someone should say that Christ and the Church are one body, and that when he offers for the Church, he offers also for his own members. But this may appear a forced interpretation.

Next he undertakes to explain how one ought to approach the priesthood, lest anyone should take the honor for himself, but only one who is called by God, as Aaron was. Here he also strikes at priests desirous of honor and eager for the priesthood, not for the salvation of the people but for worldly ambition.

Aaron, therefore, was called by God. By the sign of the flowering rod he was shown to be a priest chosen by God, and this was also demonstrated by the destruction of those who wished to envy his high priesthood.

“So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but the one who said to him, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’” This is what he himself says in the Gospel: “For I have not come of myself, but he sent me” (John 7). And again: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me” (John 8).

It should be noted that “to glorify,” “to honor,” and “to make glorious” are three words but one reality. The Greek word is δοξάζειν (*doxazein*, “to glorify”), but through the variety of translators it has been rendered differently in Latin. What is said in the Gospel as “I glorify,” the Apostle here calls “glorification.”

The Son, therefore, was glorified by the Father when, after he had been baptized, the Father’s voice was heard from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 4). This glorification, or glorifying, had been foretold much earlier through the Prophet, inspired by the Holy Spirit: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2). “The Lord” signifies the Father.

Let us observe what he says: “He said to me, ‘You are my Son,’” which he was also going to say after the baptism: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” He added this so that you might understand Christ to be one person, the only-begotten Son of God: “Today I have begotten you.” This has nothing in common with the others, since those who are called priests are called sons, of whom it is said: “I said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81). But the whole statement properly belongs to the only-begotten Son.

Likewise, in another place he says: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109). Melchizedek was not a priest according to the legal commandments, but according to the dignity of a certain singular priesthood, offering bread and wine to God rather than the blood of irrational animals. Christ became a priest according to the order of this priesthood—not a temporal priest, but an eternal one.

To him this was said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” All were priests under the Law; he alone was priest according to the order of Melchizedek, by virtue of being born from the virginal womb before the morning star—not according to the fact that he was born as God from the Father, with the Father, coeternal and consubstantial with the one who begot him, but priest on account of the flesh which he assumed, or on account of the victim which he offered for us, received from us—that is, his flesh and blood.

Concerning this victim he himself says in the Gospel: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6). But in this flesh and blood let the human mind conceive nothing bloody, nothing corruptible, lest, as the Apostle says, “the one who eats the body of the Lord unworthily eats judgment for himself” (1 Cor. 11). Rather, let it conceive the life-giving and saving substance in bread and wine, through which, when it is received worthily, the forgiveness of sins and possession of the kingdom of God are granted to us.

The most righteous king Melchizedek established the order of this sacrifice through a mystical likeness when he offered to the Lord the fruits of bread and wine. It is clear that the sacrifice of animals, which belonged to the order of Aaron and not to that of Melchizedek, has now perished; rather, what remains is this institution, which throughout the world is celebrated in the distribution of the sacraments.

Christ is called a priest above all because he offered himself once to be sacrificed for us, just as Holy Scripture mentions Melchizedek and his priesthood only once. When “forever” is said, the Lord Christ is signified, who remains in everlasting glory.

“Who, in the days of his flesh, offered prayers and supplications to the one who was able to save him from death, with a loud cry and tears, and was heard because of his reverence.”

(Alb.) What our high priest accomplished in the priesthood the Apostle expresses here more certainly, saying: “in the days of his flesh.” The days of our Lord’s flesh are those in which he assumed flesh, in which he was tempted and suffered, and in which he offered prayers and supplications to the one who was able to save him from death.

Everything that Christ did in the flesh consists of prayers and supplications for the sins of the human race. The holy shedding of his blood is the loud cry by which he was heard by God the Father on account of the reverence due to that sinless passion. He suffered for the sake of our salvation; although he had no sin, he became sin for us—that is, an offering for our sins.

He accomplished all this in great reverence and perfect love: he who first loved us and gave himself for us as an acceptable offering to God. He was therefore heard by God because he offered an acceptable offering to God, namely, himself.

What is said here is therefore similar to what is read in the Gospel, that he said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not my will, but yours be done” (Matt. 26). For he did not come to do his own will, but the will of the one who sent him; he placed the will of the Father’s dispensation before the will of his flesh, so that he might show the true nature of our humanity in himself.
