Here blessed Paul says that he poured out prayers and supplications, not because of fear of death, but for the sake of our salvation. Hence he also says elsewhere (Heb. 12) that the blood of Christ speaks better things for us than the blood of Abel, which cried from the earth to accuse his brother of crime (Gen. 4); but the blood of Christ cries from the earth to the Father, interceding for us.

“And although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from the things that he suffered; and, having been perfected, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him, having been called by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek.”

I think enough has already been said above about the similarity of the priesthood of Melchizedek. Now let us see what the Apostle wishes to be understood in saying: “Although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from the things that he suffered.” The obedience which he says the Son of God learned—that is, willingly assumed—he also shows elsewhere, where he says: “He became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross; therefore God also exalted him” (Phil. 2).

But when he says, “Having been perfected, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him,” “perfected,” that is, “made complete,” he shows how great is the gain from his passion, which is sufficient for everlasting salvation for all who believe.

Therefore, if the obedience of the Son is the cause of human salvation, how great is our necessity to obey God, so that we may be found worthy of the salvation which he granted to us through his own Son?

“Concerning whom we have much to say, and difficult to explain, since you have become weak in hearing.”

He gives the reason why the discourse which he undertook concerning the incarnate Son was difficult to interpret: namely, because they were weak and fragile in understanding the profound mysteries. Although, for the time, they ought to have been teachers, they had become people who needed milk, not solid food. The difficulty of interpretation lay in their slowness, not in apostolic wisdom, to which the mysteries hidden from the ages had been revealed, as he demonstrates most fully in the Epistle to the Ephesians.

(Joan.) Observe how he creates desire while offering praise. This was always Paul’s wisdom: mingling difficult matters with commendations. He did the same in the Epistle to the Galatians, saying: “You were running well; who hindered you?” and “You suffered so many things in vain, if indeed in vain” (Gal. 5); and again: “I am confident about you in the Lord” (ibid.).

He does the same with these people: “But I am confident about you that you possess better things, and things that accompany salvation.” Then he added: “For although you ought to be teachers by this time, you again need someone to teach you what are the elementary principles of the beginning of the words of God, and you have become people who need milk, not solid food.”

(Alb.) He speaks to those who ought to have possessed, through the Law and the Prophets, a trained understanding of the coming of Christ and of the grace brought through him to believers. If they had believed, they could also have become teachers of others through the mysteries of God that had been given to them. But now they have become like infants, to whom the first elements of letters are taught for reading, whereas they ought to have been strong in faith and vigorous in knowledge, ready to receive the solid food of wisdom, which belongs to the mature. Now they have become people who need milk.

For he calls milk a humble discourse, and testifies that they needed it because they could not ascend to the higher secrets of God’s mysteries. For example, one who cannot understand what the Evangelist says—“The Word became flesh”—how can he reach the height of that discourse where he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”?

“For everyone who partakes of milk is inexperienced in the word of righteousness, for he is an infant. But solid food belongs to the mature, to those who have their faculties trained for distinguishing good and evil.”

The palate distinguishes the flavors of foods; the soul tests the various discourses of teachings, concerning which he says later in this Epistle: “Do not be led astray by various doctrines” (Heb. 13). Just as an infant does not know how to distinguish between one food and another and often comes into danger by consuming harmful things unless an elder restrains him, so every uneducated person does not know how to distinguish doctrines, is easily deceived, and comes into danger on the path of error. What milk and solid food are in one case, the uneducated and the wise are in the other.

As milk suits infants and solid food suits those mature in age, so a humble discourse suits the uneducated, while it is fitting for the wise, who appear to possess trained faculties, to know the secret mystery of God.

“How, then, can our faculties become trained?” Certainly through practice and frequent reading of the Holy Scriptures. Hence the Psalmist calls blessed the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night (Ps. 1).

[J. Chrys.] How, then, do our faculties become trained? Through practice in the Scriptures and through frequent hearing. For when we have set forth their errors, and you hear them today and test tomorrow that they are not sound, you learn everything and come to know everything; and if you do not grasp it today, you will grasp it tomorrow.

“Having faculties,” he says, “trained.” You see that our hearing must be trained by frequent hearing of the divine Scriptures, so that we are terrified by no novelty. “Trained,” he says, “for distinguishing”—that is, to be experienced.

One person says that there is no resurrection; another expects nothing of the future; another posits a second God; another says that he had his beginning from Mary. Observe immediately how all have fallen through excess. Some always go beyond the limit; others confine themselves within the limit—for example, the first of all the heresies was that of Marcion, which introduced another god who did not exist and went beyond the limit.

After that came the heresy of Sabellius, who said that the Son, the Spirit, and the Father are one. Then came Marcellus and Photinus, who proclaimed the same things, and Paul of Samosata, who said that Christ had his beginning from Mary. Then came the Manichaeans, for this teaching was somewhat newer. After them came the Arians. There are others as well.

For this reason we embrace the faith, so that we may not be forced to contend with ten thousand heresies and undergo labor. For when a reader proceeds, he first states whose book it is—for example, that of this prophet or that one—and then says that these matters ought accordingly to have been noted by you, and that you ought to know not only the text itself but also the reasons for what was written and who said these things; but everything is without reason and superfluous.

Every haste concerning the things that belong to this life is emptied out. But concerning spiritual things there is no proper concern. For this reason they do not come to us according to our desire, and there are many difficulties there also. Christ said: “Seek the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6). He says that he will give these things as an addition, but we reverse the order and seek the earth and earthly goods as though they were to be given in the place of the addition. For this reason we possess neither these nor those things.

Let us awaken at last and become desirous of future things; then these things too will follow. For it is impossible that one who seeks the things of God should not also attain the things that belong to human beings. This is the judgment of Truth itself, which says this. Let us therefore act in no other way, but endure Christ’s will with equanimity, lest we fall away from everything.

## CHAPTER VI

The Apostle adds the matters he wishes to leave aside, because of which acceptance of his teaching is impossible, and explains for whom it is appropriate and useful.

«Therefore, leaving behind the elementary teaching about Christ, let us advance to perfection, not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God, of the teaching of baptisms, [Col. 0746C] of the laying on of hands, of the resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment. And this we shall do, if indeed God permits.» (J. Chrys.)

Listen to how severely Paul rebuked the Hebrews for always wishing to learn the very same things—and rightly so: «For although you ought to be teachers by this time,» he says, «you again need someone to teach you what are the elementary principles of the beginning of the words of God.» I fear that the time has also come for me to say this to you, because although by this time you ought to be teachers, you do not even possess the rank of disciples, but, always hearing the very same things and behaving toward those same things as though you had heard nothing, you remain in that condition. Even if someone should question you, hardly any of you would be able to answer, except for a very few who can easily be counted. This, however, is no small loss. [Col. 0746D] For the teacher who wishes to proceed farther and reach more secret and profound teachings is often prevented by the inability of his students to learn. Just as, among schoolteachers, if a boy who is always hearing the elementary lessons does not retain them, the teacher will always be obliged to repeat the same things to him and will not cease teaching him until he has been able to learn them fully—for it would be the height of folly for someone who had not properly implanted the first lessons to wish to lead the boy on to other things—so also in the Church: if, while we continually say the same things, you learn nothing more, we shall never cease saying those same things.

(Alb.) If our purpose were display and love of praise, we would necessarily be always leaping over and passing beyond these matters, caring nothing for your benefit but seeking only your applause. [Col. 0747A] But since we have not set this as our aim, and labor in everything for your assistance, we do not cease discussing these same matters with you until you grasp them as a settled habit. Just as one who is being introduced to literary learning must first hear the elementary lessons, so a Christian must first of all be instructed in the catholic faith, which is the foundation of our salvation. This foundation, which the Christian has in his heart, must be firm and fixed, so that from it he may become worthy to be led on to the perfection of the other virtues. But if someone has heard the word of truth and has been baptized, and after several years needs to hear again about the faith—because he must believe in the resurrection and the coming age—he does not yet have a foundation. He is seeking again the beginning [Col. 0747B] of Christianity, because faith is the foundation, while the other things are superstructures. Blessed Paul makes this clear in the words that follow, saying: «Not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God.»

(J. Chrys.) What, then, is the beginning? Nothing other than this: «The beginning,» he says, «is when life is not yet complete.» Just as one who is being introduced to literary learning must first hear the elementary lessons, so a Christian must know these things completely and have no doubt about them. [Col. 0747B] If he needs instruction in these matters, he does not yet have a foundation; for the foundation must be firm, fixed, standing, and not subject to removal. If someone has heard the word of truth and has been baptized, and after ten years needs to hear again about the faith—because he must believe in the resurrection [Col. 0747C] of the dead—he does not yet have a foundation but is seeking again the beginning of Christianity. For faith is the foundation, while the other things are superstructures. Observe him saying (1 Cor. III): «I laid the foundation, and another builds upon it. If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, and so forth.»

«Not again,» he says, «laying a foundation of repentance from dead works.» What does «let us advance to perfection» mean? «Let us proceed to the very summit,» he says—that is, let us have an excellent life. Just as, among the elementary letters, the first letter, alpha, contains the whole alphabet, and the foundation contains the entire building, so the satisfaction that concerns faith includes purity of life. Without this, one cannot be a Christian, [Col. 0747D] just as a building cannot exist without a foundation, nor can anyone become skilled in letters without the elementary lessons. But if someone always remains occupied with the elementary lessons and never proceeds to the building, he will never possess anything more. Do not suppose, however, that faith has been diminished because it is called an elementary principle. For it is itself the whole of virtue.

(Alb.) We call someone perfect who possesses a rightly ordered life together with faith. If either of these is lacking, he will not be perfect; if both are absent, he may rightly be called a little one. Just as an infant must again be taught letters, so this person must again be instructed in the faith. He secretly wishes to weaken the Law and recall his hearers to the grace of Christ. Whoever is going to proceed toward virtue must first condemn and cast away wickedness, [Col. 0748A] cleanse away dead works through repentance, and then approach God.

«The teaching of baptisms,» he says, «and of the laying on of hands, and of the resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment.» Repentance alone is not sufficient to make sinners clean unless they are immediately baptized, as we read that blessed Peter answered in the Acts of the Apostles: «Repent, brothers, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus (Acts II).» For what a human being cannot accomplish by himself, he can receive through the grace of God in baptism.

What does «the teaching of baptisms» mean? It is not to be understood as referring to many baptisms, but to one; for just as there is one faith, so there is also one baptism. He used the plural because of the variety of those receiving baptism. «And of the laying [Col. 0748B] on of hands,» through which the Holy Spirit can be received. It is believed that this is customarily performed by bishops after baptism for the confirmation of unity in the Church of Christ. Once these matters have been perfectly received in the Church, one must possess faith in the resurrection and in the future judgment. To live like the angels and to need none of the things belonging to this life—this is the promise of this life made to us through the Holy Spirit. The fruit of this promise is the presence of that same life; these two things—that is, faith and judgment—remain for one who has been baptized once, not to be baptized again.

(J. Chrys.) What, then, is «the teaching of baptisms»? Not of many baptisms, but of one. Why, then, did he use the plural? By saying «not again laying a foundation of repentance,» he also needed to say this, as though speaking to those who needed to be baptized again, catechized again, and again taught after baptism what they ought and ought not to do. He used the plural for this reason: he wished to show them that if they needed to be cleansed again, they would remain incorrigible.

«And of the laying,» he says, «on of hands.» Thus they received the Holy Spirit … by laying hands openly upon them. «And of the resurrection of the dead»—for this takes place in baptism and is confirmed in confession. «And of eternal judgment.» Why did he say this? Because perhaps those who already believed might be shaken and begin to live wickedly and negligently. He says: Wake up. One must not say, “If we live negligently, [Col. 0748C] we shall be baptized again, catechized again, and receive the Holy Spirit again. If we now fall away from the faith, we shall again [Col. 0748D] be able to be baptized, wash away our sins, and receive the same blessings that we first received.” You are mistaken, he says, if you think this.

«And this we shall do, if indeed God permits.»

(Alb.) In this faith of baptism, resurrection, and future judgment, with God’s permission, we instruct you fully. But lest anyone should suppose that a second or third baptism could take place after sins, he immediately added, saying:

«For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have become participants in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the coming age, and then have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt.» [Col. 0749A]

«It is impossible,» he says—not difficult. «It is impossible,» he says. He cast them into despair regarding the possibility of being baptized a second time, because “impossible” means what cannot happen, whereas “difficult” means what, although requiring effort, can nevertheless happen.

If, he says, you have once been enlightened through the grace of the Holy Spirit and have tasted the heavenly gift—that is, have received the forgiveness of sins—and have become participants in the Holy Spirit through the distribution of God’s gifts, which blessed Paul enumerates in the Epistle to the Corinthians; and if you have tasted the good word of God—here he means the teaching of the Gospel—and have come to know the powers of the coming age, what revelation of the coming age is there other than the resurrection and the blessed life promised to the saints? You received and came to know all these things in the teaching of faith, [Col. 0749B] having been enlightened by God’s grace through baptism.

Know with complete certainty that if you fall again into sins, it is impossible for you to be renewed again to repentance—that is, through repentance. What then? Is repentance excluded after baptism? Certainly not. But renewal cannot take place a second time through the washing of holy baptism. He said “to be renewed,” that is, to become new. For to make a person new is the work of holy baptism, concerning which the Prophet says: «Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s (Ps. CII).» Its power—that is, the power of holy baptism—is established in the cross and burial of Christ. Therefore he added: «Crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt.» That is: «Our old self was crucified together with Christ (Rom. VI).» As he says elsewhere: «For we have been conformed [Col. 0749C] to his death»; and again: «You were buried with him through baptism into death (Col. II).»

Just as it is impossible for Christ to be crucified a second time—that is, to hold him up to contempt—so one who thinks that he can be baptized a second time seeks to crucify Christ a second time. But Christ was crucified, died, conquered death, rose again, and ascended into heaven with triumph and glory.

«For just as Christ died once in the flesh on the cross, so we die once in baptism—not in the flesh, but to sin.» And just as he cannot die again, so we cannot be baptized again, except perhaps through the tears of repentance, not through the washing of regeneration.

“What then?” you ask. “Is there no repentance?” There certainly is repentance, but there is no other baptism. [Col. 0749D] Repentance, moreover, possesses great power even for one who has been deeply submerged in sins. If he wishes, it can free him from the burden of sins, bring one who is in danger into safety, even if he has reached the very bottom of wickedness. This is clear from many testimonies. Therefore he added: «For shall one who falls not rise again, or shall one who turns away not return? (Jer. VIII).»

What, then, is this medicine of repentance, and how is it compounded? First, by confessing one’s own sins: «I did not conceal my iniquity,» he says, «and I declared my iniquity against myself to the Lord, and you took away the wickedness of my heart (Ps. XXXI).» Second, by mourning one’s sins with great humility and thereafter producing fruits [Col. 0750A] worthy of repentance, so that one may never again fall into the same sins. Then one should begin to redeem oneself through abundant almsgiving, if one possesses the means of this world, as it is written: «The wealth of a man is the ransom of his soul (Prov. XIII).» Finally, one must not become angry with anyone, return evil for evil, but forgive all who sin against oneself, as Truth itself says: «Forgive, and you will be forgiven (Matt. VI).»

«For land that often drinks in the rain falling upon it and produces suitable vegetation for those by whom it is cultivated receives blessing from God; but if it produces thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to a curse, and its end is burning.»

(J. Chrys.) Let us hear the words of God with fear. [Col. 0750B] These are not Paul’s threats; they are not the words of a human being. They are the words of the Holy Spirit, the words of Christ speaking through Paul. Here he makes a comparison between a soul progressing in the teaching of God and one neglecting its salvation. He compares the progressing soul to fertile land watered by heavenly rains and flowering with holy shoots, saying: «For land that often drinks in the rain falling upon it.»

Here he shows that those to whom his discourse was addressed had received and absorbed the word of heavenly teaching. They had received it repeatedly through the Law and through the Prophets, yet even so they had not become ready to produce shoots of faith. He adds further concerning the good land into which the seed of God’s word fell: «Producing,» he says, «suitable vegetation.» Nothing is so suitable as faith in the Son of God and an excellent life.

Such land receives blessing from God [Col. 0750C] so that it may produce thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and even a hundredfold fruit. It should also be noted that all abundance in the crops of the earth and in the fruits of trees can come to cultivators according to their desire only through God’s blessing. For it was not the farmers who aroused the earth to produce fruit, but God’s command, as the same blessed Paul says elsewhere: «I planted, Apollos watered, but God gives the growth (1 Cor. III).»

He therefore appropriately offered this example of a soul flourishing in virtues and in God’s blessing. Then he immediately added another example concerning one who neglects his salvation, saying: «But if it produces thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to a curse, and its end is burning.»

Who, after all, is free from these thorns? [Col. 0750D] Even if we were free from them, we ought not to be presumptuous, but should fear and tremble lest the thorns of sins sprout up within us. How could a soul or flesh full of thorns be proud? Would it not need to uproot them with even greater care?

What, then, are the thorns? Let us hear Christ speaking about thorns: the cares of this world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it becomes fruitless (Matt. XIII). He said “producing thorns,” not “generating”; such land is near to a curse. What great consolation this statement contains! He says “near to a curse,” not “cursed.” Since it has not yet fallen [Col. 0751A] under the curse but is merely near it, it can also be brought far away from it.

Nor did he offer consolation only in this respect, but also in what follows. He did not say: “Rejected and near to a curse, which will be burned.” What did he say? «Whose end is burning.» This burning will occur only if someone remains in his sins to the end. For «on whatever day the sinner turns, he shall live and shall not die (Ezek. XVIII).»

But if we cut away the thorns through repentance, we shall be able to enjoy a thousand blessings, become approved, and share in God’s blessing.

(J. Chrys.) After rebuking them sufficiently, terrifying them, and striking them, he again takes care not to cast them down further and make them lie helpless. For someone who strikes a sluggish person makes him even more sluggish. [Col. 0752A] He therefore neither flatters them in everything, lest he make them worse, nor strikes them in everything, but applies some blows while offering much healing through what follows.

What did he say? “We do not say these things as though we were blaming you, nor as though we thought you were full of thorns, but because we fear that you may become such. It is better to terrify you with words, so that you may not suffer these things in reality.” This is Paul’s wisdom—and a very great wisdom. He did not say, “We suppose,” or “We infer,” or “We expect,” or “We hope,” but with complete confidence of soul, as is shown at the beginning of the following book.

# BOOK TWENTY-EIGHT

[Col. 0751]

## THE SIXTH CHAPTER FOLLOWS

[Col. 0751B]

«But we are confident concerning you, beloved, of better things and things nearer to salvation, although we speak in this way.»

(Alb.) Since blessed Paul had no present grounds on which to praise those to whom he was writing, he began to proclaim to them the hope of future things, saying: «We are confident, brothers, concerning you, of better things and things nearer to salvation, although we speak in this way.» It is as though he had said: “We have confidence concerning you in certain excellent things that contribute to your salvation. We are certainly not saying of you what I said above concerning the rejected land and the land near to burning, because we believe better things concerning you.”

He also recalled their past to them, so that he might draw them from what had already happened toward every good thing. Therefore he added: «For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and the love that you showed in his name, when you ministered to the saints and continue to minister.»

(J. Chrys.) See how he refreshed and strengthened their souls by recalling ancient things to their minds. He made them understand that God had not forgotten them or his former benefits toward them. For the person who lacks hope for the future is bound to sin. Then he urges them in every way to hope for the future. If someone despairs of God’s present benefits, since he has no possession from God, who can strengthen him concerning the future?

He makes a similar reproach to the Galatians, saying: «You were running well; who bewitched you? (Gal. V).» And again: «You suffered so many things in vain.» But in order to soften the present statement, he immediately added: «If indeed in vain.» So also here he moderated his statement, saying: «For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work, while you showed such love toward the saints.»

For we desire you to imitate those who through faith and patience inherited the promises. How great his desire for their salvation was, he showed in the following exhortation, saying: «For we desire each one of you to show the same diligence for the fulfillment of hope to the end, so that you may not become sluggish.»

“We desire,” he says, “that you continue not merely in words but also in virtues—not as though we were blaming your former conduct, but warning you to be concerned about the future. That is, just as you were at first, so we desire you to be now and in the future.”

[Col. 0752B] He did not say “I wish,” which would express the authority of a teacher, but—because this was an expression of paternal affection—«we desire each one of you to have the same diligence that you formerly possessed, for the fulfillment of hope concerning the blessed resurrection unto eternity.” (?)

«But imitators of those who through faith and patience will inherit the promises.»

(Alb.) He urges his hearers to await God’s promises and the inheritances that he promised to his saints with sincere faith and perfect patience. He seeks to strengthen this more firmly by examples, when he says:

«For when God made his promise to Abraham, [Col. 0752C] since he had no one greater by whom he could swear, he swore by himself, saying (Gen. XXII): ‘Surely, blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you’; and thus, patiently enduring, he obtained the promise. For human beings swear by one greater than themselves, and the end of every dispute among them for confirmation is an oath.»

(J. Chrys.) After strongly rebuking the Hebrews and sufficiently terrifying them, he first consoles them with praise. Second—and this is even stronger—he shows by what they are certainly going to receive that they will obtain what they hoped for. He makes this consolation arise from future things, but again also from past things, which made them more ready to believe.

Just as, in the matter of punishment, he terrifies them more through those examples, so also in the matter of rewards he consoles them through these examples, showing God’s customary manner of acting. This is that he does not quickly produce what he has promised, but waits a long time. He did this as an indication of his gentleness and power, and to lead us to faith, since we live amid tribulations [Col. 0752D] and have not yet received the promises. We should not despair of the reward of our labors.

Although he had many examples, he brought Abraham forward for mention, both because of the dignity of his person and because this event occurred especially in him. At the end of the Epistle he also says that all these people, seeing and loving those promises from afar, did not receive them, so that they might not be made perfect without us.

«For when God made his promise to Abraham,» he says, «since he had no one greater by whom he could swear, he swore by himself, saying: ‘Surely, blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you’; and thus, patiently enduring, he obtained the promise.»

[Col. 0753A]

(Alb.) The wisdom of blessed Paul is remarkable. Alternately he raises those to whom he writes with praise; alternately he terrifies them with the threats of the preceding history, lest they should be unbelieving and less trusting in God’s promise; and alternately he urges them by examples toward patience and faith, so that they may believe without hesitation not only when God speaks but also when he swears by himself.

Although he had many examples of saints who through patience inherited God’s promises, he chose the especially faithful Abraham, both because of the dignity of his person and because this occurred particularly in him.

«Who, patiently enduring, obtained the promises in his sons»—not only those of the past, which were fulfilled among the people of God, but also proclaiming those of the future in the sons of Abraham according to faith. The patient endurance of the one who heard and awaited the promised inheritance [Col. 0753B] cooperated with God’s promise. The fainthearted and unbelieving did not obtain it through the words of God, but a very great multitude of them perished in the desert.

How impious it is not to believe God when he swears! «For God swore by himself, since he had no one greater by whom he could swear.» Here, in this oath, the person of God the Father may be understood, who promised the patriarch concerning his Son, saying: «And in your seed all the nations shall be blessed.» He does not say “in your seeds,” as blessed Paul demonstrates in another Epistle (Gal. III), but «in your seed,» that is, Christ.

Christ himself also swears in the Gospel, saying: «Amen, amen, I say to you,» and he swears by himself, since he too had no one greater [Col. 0753C] by whom he could swear.

«Blessing I will bless you»—this may be understood as referring to the stars of heaven, by which the saints who would come from his seed are signified. «Multiplying I will multiply you» may refer to the sand of the sea, by which the sinful peoples of that nation may be signified. For both are said to have been spoken by the Lord, where he says: «And your seed shall be like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the shore of the sea.»

«For human beings,» he says, «swear by one greater than themselves, and the end of every dispute among them for confirmation is an oath.» If, therefore, one must believe human beings in regard to the future, concerning whom the Prophet says: «Every human being is a liar (Ps. XIV),» how much more must one believe God’s oath, since he is truth and can neither be deceived nor lie?

«For human beings swear by one greater than themselves, and the end of every [Col. 0753D] dispute among them for confirmation is an oath.»

(J. Chrys.) It is as though he were saying: “By this the dispute of the whole controversy is resolved—not merely that of some individual, but of the whole matter.” It was indeed necessary to believe God without an oath, but he says that God swore:

«In which God, wishing to show more abundantly to the heirs of the promise the unchangeableness of his purpose, interposed an oath.»

He mentions this promise because it was made commonly to us.

«He interposed an oath.»

(Alb.) Since among human beings something is regarded as trustworthy when an oath has been introduced into their disputes, he added this also. It is not the same for human beings to swear by themselves as it is for God. A human being does not possess authority over himself, but God possesses authority [Col. 0754A] over all things. Yet because the human race is unbelieving, he condescended to us. Just as he swears on our account, although it is unworthy of him not to be believed, so it was said earlier: «And he learned from the things that he suffered,» because human beings think it especially worthy of belief that someone should pass through experience before arriving at faith.

«So that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have the strongest consolation, we who have fled for refuge to hold fast to the hope of the promise, which we have as a sure and firm anchor of the soul.»

He spoke of two things: the promises of God the Father concerning his Son, and the coming of the Son into this world for our salvation. The hope that has been set before us is the truth of events that were promised to the patriarchs and fulfilled for them, so that from what has already happened we may believe what is yet to come.

We have this hope, he says, as a sure and firm anchor of the soul.

(J. Chrys.) Just as an anchor cast out from a ship does not allow it to be driven about, even if the winds shake it, but, once cast out, makes the ship secure, so faith strengthened by hope introduces us into the reality that we now possess through faith and hope. Therefore he added:

«And entering into the interior of the veil.»

A storm and heavy rain shake a small boat, but an anchor does not allow it to sink. So also our hope, which we have fixed within the interior of the veil, cannot be submerged by any unbelief, if we truthfully say with the Prophet: «Cast your care upon God, and he himself will nourish you (Ps. LIV).»

If we did not have this hope, we would be completely submerged, not only in spiritual matters but also in bodily ones. [Col. 0754C] One may find great strength from this in commerce, agriculture, and military service. Unless someone first sets this before himself, he never undertakes anything else: «For the one who plows,» the Apostle says, «plows in hope (1 Cor. IX),» and all our labor is consoled by hope of whatever reward.

Hope penetrates into the interior of the veil when it believes, hopes, and loves heavenly things without any doubt, and demonstrates through works what it believes and what it hopes for.

To add still greater firmness to our hope, he added:

«Where Jesus, having become for us a forerunner, entered within, having been made high priest forever according to the order of Melchisedech.»

(Joan.) A forerunner is the forerunner of certain others, as John was the forerunner of Christ. He did not simply say “entered,” but «where the forerunner entered for us,» as though it were undoubtedly necessary that we should follow [Col. 0754D] our forerunner. For the one who precedes and the one who follows ought to be on the same road.

This is said of him who is according to the flesh, who offered himself as a sacrifice to God for a fragrant offering. He was made high priest according to the order of Melchisedech. Therefore those whose high priest he is must also be better; and whatever difference there is between Aaron and Christ, there is, in a certain sense, the same difference between Jews and Christians.

Let us offer superior sacrifices—sacrifices that can be offered in that heavenly sanctuary: no longer a sheep or an ox, no longer blood and fat. All these things have been set aside, and in their place rational service has been introduced, that which is offered to God through the soul and through the spirit.

«God is spirit,» he says, «and those who worship him must worship in spirit [Col. 0755A] and truth (John IV).»

[Alb.] What is it to worship God in spirit except to worship him in charity and perfect faith, in unwavering hope, and in the holy virtues of the soul, which the Apostle abundantly enumerates elsewhere?

# CHAPTER VII

The excellence of Christ’s priesthood is shown by comparing Christ with Melchisedech, whose priesthood is both superior to the Levitical priesthood and more necessary.

«For this Melchisedech, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, met Abraham as he was returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, and Abraham apportioned tithes to him.»

(J. Chrys.) Wishing to show the difference between the New and Old Testaments, Paul spreads and hurls this argument in many places. Like a kind of bell, he anticipates the ears of his hearers and exercises them. [Col. 0755B] From the very beginning he immediately introduced this point, saying that God spoke to them through the prophets but to us through the Son; to them in many parts and in many ways, but to us through the Son.

Then, after speaking about the Son—who he is, what he has accomplished, and warning that he must be believed lest we suffer what the Jews suffered—he says that he is high priest according to the order of Melchisedech. Wishing repeatedly to enter into this distinction, he first arranged many things and rebuked them as though they were weak, then again restored and refreshed them so that they might recover confidence. At last, when his hearers had become vigorous, he introduces the basis of the distinction. For one who is deaf and despairing does not readily perceive anything. [Col. 0755C]

And so that you may understand, hear Scripture saying: «They did not listen to Moses because of faintheartedness.» Therefore, after first removing their grief through many terrifying yet gentle words, he then undertook to explain the distinction. What did he say?

«For this Melchisedech, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God…» And what is more remarkable, he demonstrates in the very type that there is a great distinction. For what I have said always establishes the truth through the type, drawing upon past events because of the weakness of the hearers.

«For this Melchisedech,» he says, «king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, met Abraham as he was returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him; and Abraham also apportioned to him a tenth from everything.»

(Alb.) The Hebrews report that this man was Shem, the first son of Noah, and that at the time when Abraham was born (Gen. XIV) he was two hundred [Col. 0755D] ninety years old.

It would not be surprising if Melchisedech had gone out to meet the victorious Abraham and had brought bread and wine for the refreshment both of Abraham himself and of his warriors, and had blessed him, since he received from his grandson, by paternal right, tithes of the spoils and of the victory. He was the priest of the Most High God and also king of Salem.

Salem, however, is not, as Josephus and many of our people think, Jerusalem—a name compounded from Greek and Hebrew, which the mixture of a foreign language shows to be absurd—but a town near Scythopolis, which is still called Salem. There the palace of Melchisedech is shown, its ruins displaying the magnificence of the ancient structure by their size.

Jacob is also read to have descended [Col. 0756A] to this city, which was in the land of Canaan, in the region of Shechem. It should also be considered that when Abraham was returning from the slaughter of the enemies whom he pursued as far as Dan, he was not on the road to Jerusalem but on the route to the metropolitan town of Shechem. Concerning this we read in the Gospel: «John was also baptizing at Aenon near Salem [Salim], because there were many waters there (John III).»
“First, because he is interpreted as ‘king of righteousness,’ and then also as ‘king of Salem,’ that is, ‘king of peace’: without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God, he remains a priest forever.”

The blessed Paul frequently introduces this same Melchizedek as a type of God the Savior. Although all the holy Fathers, Patriarchs, and Prophets of earlier times expressed in some respect a figure of the Savior, this Melchizedek, who was not of Jewish descent, more particularly went before as a type of the priesthood of the Son of God. Of him it is said in Psalm 109: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

They interpret his order in many ways: he alone was both king and priest; he exercised the priesthood before circumcision, so that the Gentiles did not receive the priesthood from the Jews, but the Jews from the Gentiles; he was not anointed with priestly oil, as the commands of Moses prescribe, but with the oil of exultation and the purity of faith; he did not sacrifice victims of flesh and blood or receive with his right hand the blood of brute animals, but consecrated the priesthood through the simple and pure sacrifice of bread and wine.

Yet one must not believe that this Melchizedek was without father or mother, since Christ also, according to both natures, has both father and mother. Rather, he is suddenly introduced in Genesis as having met Abraham when Abraham was returning from the slaughter of his enemies, and neither before nor afterward is his name or genealogy found written.

The Apostle affirms by this example that the priesthood of Aaron—that is, the priesthood of the Jewish people—had both a beginning and an end; whereas the priesthood of Melchizedek—that is, of Christ and the Church—is eternal both in the past and in the future.

This Melchizedek is interpreted as “king of righteousness.” Who is the true king of righteousness except our Lord Jesus Christ? Then he is called “king of Salem,” that is, “king of peace,” which pertains to Christ. For he makes us righteous by reconciling all things in heaven and on earth (Colossians 1). He alone is the king of righteousness and peace, our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his divinity, without beginning and without end, is the everlasting King, eternal from the eternal Father, although according to his temporal mother he was temporal.

Just as we do not read the beginning or end of this Melchizedek in Holy Scripture because it has not been written, so we do not know the beginning or end of the Son of God because he has none. The likeness consists in this: neither the beginning nor the end of either is read of. In the case of the one, because it has not been written; in the case of the other, because it does not exist at all.

“Consider how great this man was, to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth from the spoils.”

He therefore turns his discourse toward those who boast that they are Abraham’s children and that their nobility has descended from his origin—those who strive to exalt him with divine praises and, as we read in the Gospel, set him before the Lord when they say: “Are you greater than our father Abraham?” (John 8). It is as though he were saying: The one whom you consider superior to everyone was offering a tenth to Melchizedek, and that from the choicest part of the victory—the one who was made like the Son of God and became a high priest forever.

“And indeed those who receive the priesthood from the sons of Levi had a commandment according to the law to take tithes from the people, that is, from their brothers, although they themselves also came forth from the loins of Abraham.” (J. Chrys.)

So great is the excellence of the priesthood that even those who were like their ancestors and had the same ancestor were nevertheless judged much better than their brothers when they were made worthy of the priesthood. Thus Aaron is read to have stood between the living and the dead in order to appease the anger of God that had broken out; and he could do this from among the people, although all had one ancestor.

Therefore Abraham himself would in no way have given a tenth of the spoils to a foreigner unless his honor had been exceedingly great and supreme, and unless he had discovered that this pleased God. He thereby also showed that an uncircumcised priest is far higher than a circumcised priest.

How, then, did he show this? Because Levi himself, from whom the priestly line arose, was tithed in the loins of his ancestor.

“But he whose generation is not counted among them received tithes from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises; and without any contradiction, what is lesser is blessed by what is greater.” (Alb.)

He who is without genealogy was tithed in Abraham—not Levi alone, but Aaron himself, who used to receive tithes from the people, and through him the whole Levitical priesthood. Nor was he content merely to stand there; he exalted him still further by a greater honor when he said: “And he blessed him who had the promises.”

He showed that this man was more honorable according to the common judgment of all; and “without any contradiction,” he says—that is, it is clearer than daylight to everyone—that what is lesser is blessed by what is greater. Therefore the type of Christ is better even than the one who possessed the promises.

For the one who was made a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek—and Melchizedek himself also bore his type—offered himself as an acceptable sacrifice to God, not from any necessity, but by the will of his own authority. He, who owed nothing to death, therefore cleansed the sins of all through the priestly sacrifice of his own body.

“And here indeed mortal men receive tithes; but there it is testified that he lives—and, so to speak, through Abraham even Levi, who receives tithes, was tithed, for he was still in the loins of his father when Melchizedek met him.” (J. Chrys.)

But lest someone say, “Why do you return to ancient matters? Tell us . . . how it is usually said . . .”—and he rightly called him this—“that through Abraham Levi was tithed, although he received tithes.”

How? “He was still in the loins when Melchizedek met him”; that is, Levi was in Abraham, although he had not yet been born. And he did not say “the Levite,” but “Levi.” Do you see the eminence? Do you see how great the difference is between Abraham and Melchizedek, who bore the type of our high priest?

He showed the excellence of the authority, which did not arise from necessity: the one gave tithes, which belongs to a priest; the other blessed, because he was greater. This excellence also passed to all his descendants. In a marvelous and forceful manner he excluded the Jewish arguments. Therefore he said, “You have become weak,” because he wished to overturn these things so that they would not glory in them. Such is Paul’s wisdom: he first prepares the way and then enters upon the matters he wishes to demonstrate.

“If, therefore, perfection was through the Levitical priesthood—for under it the people received the law—what further need was there for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek, and not to be called according to the order of Aaron? For when the priesthood is transferred, it is necessary that a transfer of the law also take place.” (Alb.)

Here he begins to show the differences between the Old and New Testaments, saying: “If perfection”—that is, completion—“was through the Levitical priesthood,” why was there need for another priest to arise? No one doubts that Aaron was the first priest from the tribe of Levi after the law had been given. Therefore the priesthood which he exercised was called the Levitical priesthood.

Melchizedek, however, who bore the type of our priest—that is, of our Lord, the Savior of the world—was made much greater in the priestly order than that Levitical priesthood. For he would never have said “according to the order of Melchizedek” if Aaron’s priesthood had been better, under which the Jewish people received the law.

If, therefore, there is a transfer of the priesthood, there must also be a transfer of the law. A priest cannot exist without a Testament, without a law, and without commandments.

“For he of whom these things are said belonged to another tribe, from which no one served at the altar. For it is evident that our Lord arose from Judah, concerning which tribe Moses said nothing about priests.”

When he says “he of whom these things are said,” he means “he concerning whom these things were spoken,” signifying the Lord and Savior. When the priesthood was transferred, the Testament also was transferred—not only in its order and commandments, but also in its tribe; for the tribe too had to be changed.

And how was the priesthood transferred from one tribe to another, from the priestly tribe to the royal tribe? So that the same one might be both royal and priestly.

Observe the mystery: first, according to the sequence of this discourse, there was the royal priesthood of Melchizedek; second, there was the priesthood in Aaron; third, in Christ there was again a royal priesthood. He was always King, but became priest when he assumed flesh and offered the sacrifice.

Do you see the change in these things? What was accomplished by transfer appears, as though by the continuity of events, to return in a new form.

“And it is even more evident if another priest arises according to the order of Melchizedek, who was made not according to the law of a fleshly commandment, but according to the power of an indestructible life. For he testifies: ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.’”

Here he establishes a new difference between the Levitical priesthood and the priesthood of Christ: the former is fleshly, the latter spiritual; the former temporal, the latter eternal.

For he says of the priesthood of Aaron: “according to the law of a fleshly commandment.” That law was fleshly in many respects: in the circumcision of the flesh, in the purification of the flesh, in fleshly sacrifices and offerings, in the distinction of foods, days, and seasons, and also in the rewards by which peace and security, prosperity, abundance of crops, and royal power were promised to those who did good and kept the law. All these things, however, were destined to end in death.

But the priesthood of Christ is not like this; it is according to the power of an indestructible life.

Who is this kind of priest? Not Aaron, nor Melchizedek himself, but the one whom that Melchizedek prefigured. God the Father himself bears witness to him with an oath: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek”—that is, not temporal and not having an end, but according to the power of an indestructible life. He possesses indestructible life in himself, although for a time he was dead in the flesh; nevertheless, he lives forever in his divinity and, in his humanity, as mediator between God and human beings, he always lives to intercede for us.

“On the one hand, there is a rejection of the preceding commandment because of its weakness and uselessness, for the law brought nothing to perfection.” (J. Chrys.)

Here the heretics rise up, but observe the passage carefully: he did not say “because of its wickedness,” nor “because of its evil,” but “because of its weakness and uselessness.” Elsewhere also he shows its weakness when he says: “What was impossible for the law, weakened as it was through the flesh” (Romans 8).

It was not therefore the law itself that became weak, but we. “For the law perfects nothing.” What does “it perfects nothing” mean? It accomplished no perfection, because it was not obeyed. Add also that even if it were heard, it would not make anyone perfect or master of virtue. For the present, however, he is not saying this here, but that it was powerless. And rightly so: the letters prescribed, “Do this; do not do that.” These things alone were prescribed; they did not also inspire virtue, because there was no such hope.

What is rejection except exclusion? Rejection means that what possesses authority has now been excluded. Thus he shows what held authority, but has now been despised because it accomplishes nothing.

Did the law therefore accomplish nothing? It was useful—indeed, very useful—but it accomplished nothing toward making people perfect. Thus the law made nothing perfect. Accordingly, he says that all the things of the law were forms and shadows: circumcision, sacrifice, and Sabbath. It could not therefore pass into the soul; for this reason it yields and withdraws.

(Alb.) Its rejection therefore took place so that room might be made for grace, when grace came in which perfection would be accomplished. The law was useful, but for those who had faith in Christ, not for those who placed all their hope in it.

“But the introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God; and insofar as this was not without an oath, priests were made, but he was made so with an oath by the one who said to him: ‘The Lord swore and will not repent: You are a priest forever.’”

He says, “the introduction of a better hope.” The law also had hope, but not such a hope. Those who pleased God and kept his law hoped to possess the land, to suffer nothing grievous, and to live prosperously, as it is said: “The one who does it will live by it” (Galatians 3).

But here we hope that, if we please God and keep the evangelical commandments, we shall possess not earth but heaven. More than this, we hope for what is much better than heaven: to stand near God, to reach the very paternal throne, and to minister to him with the angels.

This priesthood, through which we shall possess this glory, will not be without an oath, so that we may believe God’s promise to be firm. For he promised all these things to us in his own Son, whom he delivered up for us all, and through him he promised all these things—of him it was said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

“To that extent Jesus has become the guarantor of a better Testament; and indeed many others became priests because they were prevented by death from continuing, but he, because he remains forever, possesses an everlasting priesthood.”

He sets forth two differences: our priest has no end, unlike the legal priest. He does this in the person of Christ, who, he says, “entered according to the power of an indestructible life.” He also testifies to this with an oath, as was said above.

Just as he remains, so also the law which he brought will remain, in which there is true forgiveness of sins and the perpetual reception of grace. If the former law was excluded because of its weakness, since it could lead nothing to perfection, this law, which the great high priest brought, has power, is strong, and remains.

He demonstrates this from the high priest. How? Because he is one. He would not be one unless he were immortal. Just as there were many priests under the law because they were mortal, so there is one because he is immortal—one who has become the guarantor of a better Testament to such an extent that it was sworn concerning him that he would always remain.

“Therefore he is also able to save forever those who approach God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them.”

You see that he is speaking of the one who exists according to the flesh. For when he is high priest, then he also intercedes; he intercedes according to that nature in which he is high priest.

(J. Chrys.) Therefore when Paul says, “who also intercedes for us,” he signifies this same thing: the high priest intercedes. Otherwise, how could the one who, like the Father, raises the dead whom he wishes and gives them life—how could he intercede where salvation is needed, when he possesses all judgment over everyone? How could he intercede who sends angels, commanding some to cast people into the furnace and others to save them?

For this reason he said, “he is also able to save”: he saves because he does not die, because he always lives, and because he has no successor. If he has no successor, he can also be present to all.

“This high priest,” as though he had been extraordinary, existed only until that time during which he lived, like Samuel and any others of that kind. Afterward they no longer existed, since they died. But this one is not so; he saves forever.

He signifies a certain mystery: “He saves,” he says, “not only here but also there, those who approach God through him.” How does he save? “He always lives to intercede for us.”

Do you see his humility? Do you see his humanity? He did not say that he had obtained this, but that he always intercedes for them in order to obtain it. What does “forever” mean? Not only for a time, but also there, in the life to come.

He therefore always needs to plead. And how can this be reasonable? Righteous human beings often obtain everything through a single petition, whereas he continually asks. Why does he sit? Observe: this is a disagreement. Do not be afraid, and do not say, “He loves us and has confidence in the Father, but he cannot live forever.” He always lives, he says.

(Alb.) Who is it that intercedes except the union of human nature with that divinity which he brought to the paternal throne—always living and capable of saving?

The other high priests, because they did not always exist, do not always intercede. He saves not only in this life through the intercession of his humanity, but also glorifies in the future, when he will deliver the kingdom to God the Father and lead the saints to the vision of the Father’s majesty.

“For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens.”

It was also fitting that he should be such a high priest for those of whom he says: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15).

Clearly, legal servants had mortal, sinful high priests, who offered sacrifices for themselves; but the sons and friends of God have an immortal high priest, “separated from sinners”—that is, from the former priests—one who is “innocent and holy.”

(J. Chrys.) Innocent, because without wickedness, as the prophet says: “No deceit was found in his mouth” (Isaiah 53). Holy, because outstanding in every goodness. “Undefiled,” because he had no sin. “Made higher than the heavens,” because all the angels of God worship him.

“Who has no daily necessity, as those priests do, first to offer sacrifices for their own sins and then for those of the people; for he did this once for all when he offered himself.”

Here he now distinguishes the excellence of the spiritual sacrifice and declares how great the difference is. He said that Christ was a high priest; he said that he belonged to the Testament, though he did not say everything. He already anticipates and strikes at the sacrifice itself.

Do not therefore suppose, when you hear him called a high priest, that he continually exercises the high-priestly office. He exercised it once; afterward he sits. Do you suppose that he again stands and serves? He thereby shows that the work was an act of his dispensation. Just as he became a servant, so he also became a high priest and minister. For it is not the minister’s place to sit, but to stand.

Here he shows the greatness of the sacrifice: although it was one and was offered once, it suffices forever; it prevailed as much as all other things did not prevail. What he offered, moreover, he did not offer for himself but for the people.

Nor was this sacrifice to be offered daily for the people. Its holiness and honor before God were so great that, once offered, it benefited the people of God forever.

“For the law appoints as priests men who have weakness.” (Alb.)

For this reason they always offered sacrifices for themselves as well as for the people. But this one is so powerful that, once offered in the sacrifice of his flesh, there was no need for anyone who believed to offer anything further on his behalf.

“But the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints the Son, perfected forever.”

Here too the name “Son” is set down in contrast with the servants who existed under the law, because those servants were weak—either because they were sinners or because they were mortal.

He demonstrates that this Son is perfect because he always lives and is always without sin. The Apostle says both things, wonderfully comforting those who hear and sternly frightening those who neglect.

He comforts by declaring that the great high priest makes atonement through a powerful sacrifice. He frightens them so that they may not sin, because that sacrifice will never again be offered for sins. There is no other sacrifice; one sacrifice has cleansed us. After this there will be judgment.

All who have been redeemed by this sacrifice, let us remain in it, preserving our nobility and our honor.

(J. Chrys.) Since, therefore, we have such a high priest, let us imitate him and follow in his footsteps. There is no other sacrifice; one has cleansed us. After this there are fire and Gehenna.

For this reason he repeatedly turns the matter over, saying: one priest, one sacrifice, so that no one, thinking there are many sacrifices, may sin without fear. All who have been made worthy of the seal, all who have obtained the priesthood, all who share in the immortal table, let us remain, preserving our nobility and our honor. For our downfall is not without danger.

But those who have not yet been made worthy of these things should not for that reason presume. When someone sins for the very purpose of receiving holy baptism at his final breath, perhaps he does not obtain it.

And believe me: I am not saying what I am about to say in order to frighten you. I know many who have suffered this, who committed many sins in the hope of baptism but, when the day of death came, departed empty-handed. God granted baptism for this purpose: to wash away sins, not to increase them.

If someone uses baptism for the purpose of committing greater sins, baptism itself becomes the cause of negligence. For if there were no washing, they would live more cleanly, since they would not possess their sins.

Do you see how we ourselves bring about the saying, “Let us do evil so that good may come”? Therefore I beg you, since you have not yet been initiated, to wake up.

Let no one approach virtue like a hired laborer; let no one approach it like an ungrateful person; let no one approach it as though it were something burdensome and unbearable. Let us therefore approach it eagerly and joyfully. For if no reward had been set before us, ought we not to be good? At least let us become good with the reward.

And how are you not ashamed? This is the greater reproach: “Unless you give me a reward,” you say, “I will not become chaste.” Therefore I dare to say something: you will never be chaste—not even when you are chaste—if you do this for the sake of a reward. For if you do not value virtue itself, you do not love it.

But God, because of our great weakness, wished that for the time being virtue might be practiced even for the sake of the reward; yet we do not pursue it even in this way.

## CHAPTER VIII

He shows that Christ is a better minister of the sacred rites than the ministers of the Old Testament.

“But the main point concerning what is being said is this: We have such a high priest, who has sat down at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens, a minister of the holy things and of the true tabernacle which the Lord [God] established, and not man.” (J. Chrys.)

In one passage the Apostle Paul mingles lowly things with exalted things, always following his teacher so that his hearers may be led through lowly matters to higher ones, and through these to those others. Thus, when they come from sublime matters, the way becomes easy for them to learn great things, because those things were matters of disagreement.

After showing him to be a high priest, what did he add? “But the main point,” he says, “in what is being said is this: We have such a high priest, who sits at the right hand of Majesty.” Yet this is not the characteristic of a priest, but of the one for whom the priest must perform his priestly service.

“Minister of the holy things”—and he was not simply called a minister, but “minister of the holy things and of the tabernacle which God established, not man.”

Do you see the distinction? Did he not shortly before make a distinction when he said: “Are they not all ministering spirits?” And for this reason, he says, they do not hear: “Sit at my right hand,” since that belongs to one who sits and is not a minister.

How, then, is he here called a minister, and a minister of holy things? For here he spoke of the tabernacle.

Observe how he instructed the souls of those who had believed from among the Jews. They may perhaps have imagined that we do not have such a tabernacle. “Behold,” he says, “a high priest, and a great one, much greater than that one, who offered a marvelous sacrifice.”

But see whether this discourse might perhaps be merely an assertion, perhaps only an exaggeration and an attempt to animate them. Therefore he first established it by the oath, and then by the tabernacle, which indeed also demonstrates the difference.

He also devised another argument: “which the Lord established,” he says, “and not man.” Where are those who say that heaven is signified here? Where are those who declare that it is spherical and derived from the sphere? Both interpretations are excluded in this passage.

(Alb.) When he says, “The main point in what has been said,” he signifies something supreme and great, like a recapitulation of the preceding discussion, bringing the hearer to the matter itself.

“Such a high priest,” he says, “we have, who sits at the right hand of Majesty”—mingling lowly things with exalted, human things with divine, and showing that the same one is both God and high priest. No one sits at God’s right hand except the one who is “the minister of the holy things and of the tabernacle which God established, and not man.”

This tabernacle is the souls of the saints, for whom he supplies eternal joys, and it is also the veil of heaven—the great high priest who sits at the right hand of the Father’s Majesty on high.

When you hear that the same one sits at God’s right hand and ministers to the saints, sitting signifies divine dignity; ministering signifies the great mercy and love which he bestows upon us. It is a marvelous mystery that the same one sits in the glory of divinity whom his persecutors saw hanging on the cross; and in that cross of his passion there is the ministry of our salvation.

We believe that this took place, and we know that it benefits us for salvation. But what might the carnal human mind think when it is said that he sits at God’s right hand? Holy Scripture accommodates itself to our weakness and our customary way of thinking, so that humanity in its frailty might be instructed, since human thought could not reach the secret glory of divinity.

Thus, after the glory of the resurrection, an honorable seat is offered to the victorious Son and triumphal conqueror of the whole world through the holy incarnation, so that through this position the glory of the humanity he assumed might be declared.

For by the word “sit” this is signified: Christ our head is understood to have been placed at the Father’s right hand, that is, exalted in divine majesty. In that place are to be set those who are separated from the lost by the gift of the same Savior.

“For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; therefore it is necessary that this one also have something to offer.” (J. Chrys.)

Lest, because you hear that he sits, you think that he is called a priest in every respect, that sitting signifies divine dignity, whereas this signifies the great mercy and love which he bestows upon us.

For this reason he repeats the point and dwells on it at greater length. He fears that his hearers may reject it, and therefore now turns his discourse to this matter.

Some were asking why he died. “He was a priest,” he says, “but a priest does not exist without a sacrifice. Therefore it is necessary that he have a sacrifice.” And speaking in another way, because he is above, he shows from every direction that he is a priest: from Melchizedek, from the oath, and from the offering of the sacrifice.

(Alb.) The high priests of the Old Testament were appointed to offer legal gifts and sacrifices for their own sins, as he said above, and also for the sins of the people.

Therefore it was necessary that our Savior, in the days of his flesh, have something to offer for us. In the eternal nature of his divinity he had nothing to offer, so he took from us what he could offer for us—that is, human flesh.

What is so suitable for immolation as mortal flesh for mortals? What is so pure for cleansing the faults of mortals as flesh born without any contamination of carnal desire in a virginal womb, from a virginal mother? What could be offered and received with such favor as the flesh of our sacrifice, made the body of our priest?

And since four things are considered in every sacrifice—to whom it is offered, by whom it is offered, what is offered, and for whom it is offered—therefore sacrifice is owed to no one except the one true God.

Accordingly, our high priest offered himself for us: the same person was priest and sacrifice.

(J. Chrys.) Then from this he also establishes another necessary syllogism:

“For if he were on earth, he would not be a priest, since there are those who offer gifts according to the law, who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things.”

If, therefore, he is a high priest, as indeed he is, he must seek another place. If he existed on earth, he would certainly not be a high priest. How could he be? He neither offered nor exercised the priesthood—and rightly so, for there were other priests.

Thus he shows that it is no longer possible for a priest to exist on earth.

(Alb.) If he were an earthly high priest, like Aaron, he would not be a priest according to the order of Melchizedek forever. Aaron died and is not a priest. Christ, however, because he lives forever, is an everlasting priest—not like those who serve a copy and shadow of heavenly things.

All the priests established under the law bore a priesthood that was a copy and shadow of heavenly things—that is, of spiritual things—signifying the true and everlasting priesthood of Christ.

Is not our faith a heavenly altar, on which we offer our prayers daily? It possesses nothing of a carnal sacrifice that is reduced to ashes, diminished in smoke, or dispersed in vapors.

These sacrifices are made bright and more festive. How could those who are told, “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20), fail to celebrate heavenly sacrifices?

All the sacrifices of the Levitical priesthood were signs of these sacrifices, because “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.”

“As it was answered to Moses when he completed the tabernacle (Exodus 25): ‘See,’ he says, ‘that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain.’” (J. Chrys.)

Because our hearing is less suited to receiving instruction than sight—for we do not impress upon our minds everything we hear as readily as what we perceive with our own eyes—he showed him everything.

Whether, therefore, he is speaking of a pattern and shadow or of the temple, he adds: “See and make everything according to the pattern that was shown to you.”

(Alb.) Here, however, one may ask what he meant by “everything”: whether the construction of the tabernacle or the victims and sacrifices which they were to offer in it. But it is better understood as referring to both.

“But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry, to the extent that he is also the mediator of a better Testament, which has been established upon better promises.”

“See,” he says, “how much better this is than that celebration. That was a copy and form; this is the truth,” as it is said in the Gospel: “The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1).

The Apostle subsequently signifies which grace he means here when he says: “which has been established upon better promises.” As heavenly things are better than earthly, eternal things than temporal, so Christ God is the mediator and priest of a better Testament.

Having passed from place and priest and sacrifice, he finally sets forth the difference between the Testaments.

(J. Chrys.) Here he lifts us toward heaven and shows that, in the promises of God, we have heaven in place of the tabernacle; that the former things were copies of our things; that he elevates our celebration through these realities; and thus the priesthood now fittingly stands forth [the text may read “is raised up”].

But, as I said, what most greatly rejoices them is that he adds: “which has been established upon better promises.”

How is this certain to them? Because the former has been excluded, while this has been introduced in its place. It prevails because it is better.

Just as he says: “Since perfection was through that, what need is there, he asks, for another high priest to be raised up according to the order of Melchizedek?”—so here also he employs the same syllogism, saying:

“For if that first covenant had been blameless, no place would have been sought for a second; for, finding fault with them, he says…”

(Alb.) That is, if those who observed it had been blameless, there would never have been room left for a second. But because the former was not perfect, a suitable place was found for the second Testament, as the Lord says through the prophet:

“Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will bring to completion over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah a new covenant (Jer. 31). And not according to the covenant [Col. 0766B] that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, because they did not remain in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord.”

Here he carefully indicated whom he meant by saying that they did not remain in his covenant, when he added: “On the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt.” He was speaking of the Law given on Mount Sinai, which is known to have been given on the fiftieth day. Their fathers did not remain in that covenant, but made a calf at Horeb and worshiped it. For he was not speaking of the covenant that he proposed to their fathers—that is, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. All the children of faith may be called children of Abraham, as it is written of the Lord himself in the Gospel: “But I say to you that God is able from these stones [Col. 0766C] to raise up children for Abraham” (Luke 3).

And this is the New Covenant, which God will bring to completion—that is, bring to perfection—over all nations, so that all who believe in Christ may truly be children of Abraham according to spiritual generation.

(John.) From where is it certain that it has received its end? He showed this indeed from the priesthood; but now he shows it more clearly from the very word, namely, that it has been excluded. How so? “In better promises.” Where are these, tell me? In earth and heaven. But observe how there too he spoke of promises, so that one might not accuse him in this matter. For there, “because we draw near to God,” he showed a better hope, since there also there is hope; and here he signifies better promises, since there also he made a promise.

Since they were always being blamed: “For behold, the days are coming,” he says, [Col. 0766D] “says the Lord, and I will bring to completion over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah a new covenant, not an old one.” What covenant does he mean? Lest they perhaps be able to say that, he also defined the time. For he does not simply say, “according to the covenant that I made with their fathers,” lest they should say that he meant the covenant made with Abraham, or with Noah; rather, what kind does he identify? “Not according to the covenant that I established with their fathers when they came out of the land of Egypt.” Therefore he also added: “On the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; and they did not remain in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord.”

Observe that evils begin first from us: “They,” he says, [Col. 0767A] “did not remain first.” Negligence is ours, whereas good things are from God—I mean those belonging to his benefits. Here he establishes something like an excuse, showing the reason for which he abandoned them.

“For this is the covenant that I will establish with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will give my laws into their minds, and I will inscribe them upon their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And no one will teach his neighbor, nor each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because all will know me, from the least to the greatest of them. For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.”

(Alb.) Here too there is a great difference between law and law, between Scripture and Scripture, between the letter and grace. [Col. 0767B] For the letter of the Law was written on tablets of stone, which Moses himself broke when he saw the people dancing before the calf; but grace was given in the hearts of believers through the Holy Spirit, through whom love has been poured out in the hearts of believers.

What was hidden in the letter and read by the people through the traditions of their teachers, the Holy Spirit, when he came, taught to the Apostles. And this is what the Prophet says: “No one will teach his neighbor, nor each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ for all will know me, from the least to the greatest of them”; just as it is read in the Gospel concerning the Lord: “Then he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24).

(J. Chrys.) “‘From the least,’ he says, ‘to the greatest of them they will know me,’ and they will not say, [Col. 0767C] ‘Know the Lord.’ When did this happen, except now? For it is evident what has been done among us. What was done among them, however, is not evident, but was concealed in the New Gospel.

Something is called new when it displays something different, or when it possesses more than the old. ‘Behold,’ he says, ‘this too exists as new,’ when some parts of it have been removed while others remain.
