For example, if someone completely alters an old and falling house and lays new foundations, we immediately say, ‘He made it new,’ although he has removed some parts and altered others.

Heaven too is called new in this way—not when it will no longer be airy, but when it gives rain ... when it is not unfruitful; not when it will be changed ... not when some parts of it have been excluded and others [Col. 0767D] have remained. Thus, he says, one rightly calls the covenant new.

[Sic] For if I show that that covenant has become older, in which no one bears fruit, and if you wish to recognize it fully, read what Haggai said, what Zechariah said, what the angel said, and what Ezra also reproves. See how they rebuked him, how no one inquires of the Lord, where they themselves transgressed, and how they themselves did not know.

Do you see how your case suffers violence? But I will show my own, namely, that it is properly called new. Yet I do not concede that the words ‘there will be a new heaven’ were spoken concerning this. Why did he not rather set down what is said in Deuteronomy, ‘There will be an airy heaven,’ to signify the distinction? [Col. 0768A] But if you hear, ‘It will be new’—and for this reason, he says, he promises that another covenant will be given, because they did not remain in the first—then I demonstrate this through what he said: ‘What was impossible for the Law, in which it was weakened through the flesh’ (Rom. 8); and again: ‘Why are you testing God by placing upon the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?’ (Acts 15).

“But they did not remain,” he says. Here it is shown that the transgression of our ancestors makes us worthy of spiritual things: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18); that is, “No one will say to his neighbor, ‘Know the Lord’” (Hab. 2). And again: “The earth will be multiplied [Col. 0768B] so that it may know the Lord, as abundant waters have covered the sea.”

“By saying ‘new,’ he has made the first old; and what is becoming old and aging is near destruction.”

(J. Chrys.) See how he revealed what had been concealed and opened up the very mind of the Prophet. He honored the Law and did not wish to call it old explicitly. Nevertheless, he said this: if that covenant were new, he would certainly not afterward call this covenant new as well. Therefore, while granting something more and introducing another covenant, he says, “It has become old.”

Therefore it too will be dissolved and perish, and will no longer exist. Taking confidence from the Prophet, he proceeds somewhat more forcefully against that covenant, appropriately showing that our things now flourish, whereas those things are old and near destruction. But our youth will be renewed [Col. 0768C] like the eagle’s if we run to the fountain of life, if we extend wings and eyes toward the Sun of righteousness.

Then, taking the designation “old” and adding another term of his own—namely, “age”—and taking what remained from the other expressions, he says: “It is near destruction.” And the old covenant did not simply cease through the coming of the new; rather, it was like something that had grown old, like something useless.

Therefore he said, “because of weakness, because of uselessness, and the Law accomplishes nothing,” and because “if the first had been blameless, no place would have been sought for a second.” He did not speak as though it were liable to crimes, but as though it had failed to achieve its purpose, speaking in the manner of ordinary people. It is as if someone were to say, “This house is not blameless,” that is, “It has a defect; it is weak.” [Col. 0768D] Or, “This garment is not blameless,” that is, “It is already rotten.” Thus he did not accuse it here as wicked, but as having a grievance and a defect.

## CHAPTER IX

The Apostle touches upon the things that belonged to the ministry of the Old Covenant, and from them argues the dignity of Christ and of the new law.

“The first covenant indeed had ordinances of worship and an earthly sanctuary. For a tabernacle was prepared—the first one—in which there were a lampstand, a table, and the presentation of the loaves, which are called the holy things. Behind the second veil was the tabernacle called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant covered on every side with gold. In it was a golden urn containing the manna, and Aaron’s rod that had blossomed, and the tablets of the covenant. Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat, concerning which it is not now possible to speak in detail. [Col. 0769A] With these things thus arranged, the priests continually entered the first tabernacle, carrying out the services of worship; but into the second tabernacle only the high priest entered once a year, not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the people’s ignorance.”

(J. Chrys.) He showed from the priesthood and from the covenant that the former was destined to come to an end. Now he also shows from the very pattern of the tabernacle how this is so. “These are the holy things and the Holy of Holies.” The holy things of the first tabernacle are indications of the former age, for there everything was done through sacrifices; but the Holy of Holies is a sign of the present age, of what now exists.

He says that the Holy of Holies is heaven, the veil is heaven, and the flesh entering within the veil is the veil of his flesh. It is good, however, to return to the earlier passages and speak from them. What then, he says? “The first covenant had ordinances of worship.” What are “ordinances”? Signs and sanctifications that existed at that time. By indicating that it does not have them now, he shows that it has ceased. “For then,” he says, “it did not have them; therefore now it is not, as though they were still present.” [The transmitted wording is difficult.]

[Col. 0769B]

“Then it had an earthly sanctuary.” He calls it earthly because everyone was permitted to enter, and that place in the tabernacle was visible—the place where the priests stood, where the Jews were, as well as proselytes, Gentiles, and Nazarenes. Since it was accessible even to Gentiles, he calls it earthly; for the whole world did not belong to the Jews. [Col. 0769C]

“For a tabernacle,” he says, “was constructed first, the one called the holy place, in which were the lampstand, the table, and the presentation of the loaves.” These were signs of the world.

“Behind the second veil was the tabernacle called the Holy of Holies.” Observe how everywhere he calls it a tabernacle, from what would be contained there.

“Having,” he says, “a golden censer and the ark of the covenant enclosed on every side with gold, in which was a golden urn containing the manna, and Aaron’s rod that had blossomed, and the tablets of the covenant.” All these things were venerable and clear memorials of Jewish ingratitude.

“And the tablets,” he says, “of the covenant”—for he had broken them.

“And the manna”—for they had murmured, and, so that the memory might be handed down to posterity, he commanded that it be preserved in a golden urn. [Col. 0769D]

“And Aaron’s rod,” he says, “which had blossomed, and above it the cherubim of glory.” What are “the cherubim of glory”? Either glorious cherubim, or those who have been established under God.

“Over-shadowing,” he says, “the mercy seat.” By this prayer he also elevates these things, to show that the things which come after them are greater.

“Concerning which,” he says, “it is not now possible to speak in detail.” Here he indicated that these visible things were not all that existed, but that they were certain enigmas.

“Concerning which,” he says, “it is not now possible to speak in detail”—perhaps because they would require a lengthy discourse.

“With these things thus constructed,” he says, “the priests continually entered the first tabernacle, carrying out the services of worship.” That is, these things existed, but the Jews did not enjoy them, for they did not see them. Therefore they were established no more for them than for those to whom they were prophesied. [Col. 0770A]

“But into the second tabernacle once a year only the high priest entered, not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the people’s ignorance.” Do you already see the forms set forth beforehand? Lest they should say, “How is there one sacrifice?” he showed that this had existed from the beginning, since what was holier was one and fearful.

And how did the high priest offer this once, if [the text perhaps reads “he offered,” though the wording is uncertain] they had received the custom from the beginning? For even then, he says, the high priest offered it once. And he rightly said, “not without blood”—not, indeed, without blood, but with this blood. For the matter was not insignificant. He shows that there will be a sacrifice which is not consumed by fire, but which is demonstrated through blood.

Since he called the cross a sacrifice, though it had neither fire, nor wood, nor an offering in the usual form, but was offered once in blood, he showed that the ancient sacrifice too was of this kind, being offered once in blood. [Col. 0770B]

“Which he offered for himself,” he says, “and for the people’s ignorance.” He did not say “for sins,” but “for ignorance,” lest they should think highly of themselves. For if you sinned unwillingly, but were ignorant without intending it, then no one is clean. Everywhere he shows what belongs to him, namely, that Christ is a much greater high priest.

(Alb.) We read in Josephus that the tabernacle was made in the likeness of this world; its exterior parts represented the form of this age. Therefore the holy priests minister daily, kindling the light of teaching and feeding the people of God.

The “loaves” that ought to be present upon the table from Sabbath to Sabbath—that is, from the Sabbath of our hope, in which we are, as it were, secure in Christ from the storms of this world, until that Sabbath in which we retain what we now possess in hope. [Col. 0770C]

The lampstands are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which shine in the Church for those who understand through him upon whom rests the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and godliness, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. 11).

The inner tabernacle, which is called “the Holy of Holies,” signifies heaven itself. The veil is heaven, within which our priest Christ entered, not without blood.

“Having a golden censer,” in which the prayers of the saints are offered. In it are “the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat,” that is, a multitude of knowledge.

The mercy seat is aptly said to have been placed above the ark, because it was specially given by God the Father to the mediator of God and human beings, “so that he might be the propitiation for our sins.” Therefore Paul also says: “Jesus Christ, who died—indeed, who also rose again—who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8). [Col. 0770D]

“And the ark of the covenant.” This is the flesh of our Savior, in which are the manna of divinity, the tablets of the two covenants, and the rod of Aaron that blossomed in the priesthood of Christ—“concerning which it is not now possible to speak in detail.”

“With these things thus arranged, the priests continually entered the first tabernacle, carrying out the services of the sacrifices.” What he said above, namely, that it was an earthly sanctuary, he now shows more clearly: it was the tabernacle in which earthly sacrifices were performed, accomplishing nothing perfect for the one who served in them. [Col. 0771A]

“But into the second tabernacle once a year only the high priest entered, not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the people’s ignorance.” This high priest partly signifies the one who entered heaven once, within the veil, into the Holy of Holies, to stand before the face of God for us.

When he says, “to offer for himself and for the people’s ignorance,” this is what he himself said on the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Far from my salvation are the words of my transgressions” (Ps. 21). What are “the words of my transgressions,” except those of his body?

“This was signifying by the Holy Spirit: that the way into the holy places had not yet been revealed, while the first tabernacle still had its standing. This was a parable for the present time, according to which gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the worshiper according to conscience.” [Col. 0771B]

Therefore, he says, these things were constructed in this way so that we might learn that the Holy of Holies—that is, heaven—is still customarily inaccessible to mortals. Nor should we think that it is impossible to enter there, since our high priest first entered within the veil, not without blood, as the Prophet foretold: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments stained from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63).

But we patiently await the time of our resurrection, when “we know that when he appears, we shall be like him” (Col. 3)—that is, immortal. Just as death will no longer rule over him, so neither will it rule over our flesh.

“It is a comparison,” he says, “for the present time.”

(John.) What does he mean by “the present time”? The time before Christ’s presence. After Christ’s coming it is no longer “present”; how so? For it is pressing toward its end. [Col. 0771C] Indicating something else as well, he said: “This is a comparison for the present time”—that is, it was made as a figure.

“According to which gifts and sacrifices are offered, unable to perfect the worshiper according to conscience.” Observe what this means: “The Law accomplishes nothing,” and “if that first covenant had been blameless.” How so? “According to conscience.” The sacrifices, he says, did not remove the stains of the soul, but concerned only the body, “according to the law of a fleshly commandment.” They could not forgive adultery, murder, or sacrilege.

Do you see what he says: “Eat this, do not eat that”? These were matters of indifference.

“Only with foods and drinks and various baptisms and ordinances of the flesh imposed until the time of correction.” Only with foods and drinks and various baptisms. “Drink this,” he says; “do not drink that.” Yet nothing had really been prescribed concerning drink; rather, by treating these things with contempt, he says, “and with various baptisms and ordinances of the flesh imposed until the time of correction.” [Col. 0771D]

For this was the righteousness of the flesh. By this he cast down those sacraments, showing that they possessed no power and that they existed only until the time of correction—that is, they awaited the time that would correct all things.

(Alb.) These fleshly ordinances concerning foods and drinks and various baptisms were imposed until the time of correction. Observe what this means: “For the Law brought nothing to perfection”; but according to the stains and ignorances of a fleshly commandment it was able to cleanse. [Col. 0772A]

It could cleanse nothing from adultery or capital crimes, but could only condemn offenses committed without mercy. Therefore the Pharisees brought the adulterous woman before Jesus (John 8), so that they might accuse him if he ordered her release contrary to the Law, or so that he might lose his commendable custom if he commanded that the Law’s requirement be observed.

But the wisdom of God avoided both alternatives, as if it had said: “The Law is just, if it has just ministers. Whoever would remove the speck from another’s eye ought first to remove the beam from his own eye.”

Concerning the baptism of the Jews, the Gospel according to Mark (Mark 7) speaks more fully, where the Pharisees criticized the Lord and his disciples [Col. 0772B] for eating with unwashed hands. But the Pharisees wash their hands in vain—indeed, all the Jews do so in vain—and are baptized when they return from the marketplace, so long as they disdain to be washed in the Savior’s font.

But the Pharisees, taking the spiritual words of the Prophets in a fleshly sense, seriously err. The Prophets commanded the purification of heart and conduct when they said, “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. 1), and “Cleanse yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52). The Pharisees, looking only to the washing of the body, greatly err.

For it is certain that Moses and the Prophets, when they commanded that the vessels of the people of God be washed with water, purified with fire, or sanctified with oil, whatever the reason, did not intend to instruct us in the cleansing of material things, but rather in the purification and holiness of minds and deeds, and in the salvation of souls.

“But Christ, appearing as high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made by hands—that is, not of this creation.” [Col. 0772C]

(J. Chrys.) By “the tabernacle not made by hands” he means the flesh. Here he rightly called it both greater and more perfect, since both God the Word and the whole operation of the Spirit dwell in it.

“For God does not give the Spirit by measure.” He called it more perfect because it is blameless and accomplishes greater things.

That is, “not this creation.” See how much greater it is: he did not construct it without the Spirit, nor is it from this creation—that is, it is not from these created things, but is spiritual, from the Holy Spirit.

Do you see how he calls the body both the tabernacle and the veil and heaven? “Through the greater and more perfect tabernacle,” through the veil—that is, “his flesh”; and again, “within the veil”; and again, entering into the Holy of Holies, to stand before the face of God. [Col. 0772D]

Why does he do this? Because the same things have different meanings. For example, I say that the veil is heaven. Just as a veil separates the holy places like a wall, so the flesh, concealing the divinity, does the same. Likewise, the tabernacle has divinity within it. The tabernacle is heaven, for the high priest is within it.

(Alb.) From this we hope that future good things—namely, eternal things that do not pass away—will be given to us.

“Not of this creation”—that is, it is not the form of this tabernacle that human beings pitched in the wilderness, but it was created by God himself in a wholly different way, spiritually rather than carnally. In this tabernacle the souls of the righteous and the angelic spirits now are, awaiting the completion of the number of their fellow servants. [Col. 0773A]

“For Christ,” he says, “coming ...”

(John.) He did not say “having been made,” but “coming,” that is, coming for this very purpose, not succeeding another. He did not first arrive and then become high priest, but came as such at once. Nor did he say, “the high priest who comes with sacrifices,” but “of the good things that have come,” as though language were unable to express the whole reality.

“Nor through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood he entered once for all into the Holy Place, having obtained eternal redemption.” Everything has been transformed.

(Alb.) There the blood of goats washed away the sins of the flesh; here the blood of Christ washes away the sins of the spirit. By saying “having obtained eternal redemption,” he shows that there was no eternal redemption in the earlier sacrifices and legal ceremonies.

“Through his own blood,” he says, “he entered once into the Holy Place.” Here too he called it heaven. [Col. 0773B]

(J. Chrys.) “He entered once,” he says, “into the Holy Place, having found eternal redemption.” By saying “having found,” he shows that this redemption belonged to things that previously had not been found, and that, beyond what had been hoped for, he found eternal redemption through a single entrance. Then he adds the proof.

“For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkling those who are defiled, sanctifies for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God?”

If, he says, the blood of bulls could cleanse the flesh, much more will the blood of Christ wash away the stain of the soul. But lest anyone, on hearing “sanctifies,” should suppose that the washing is perfect [Col. 0773C], he immediately adds the reason for the difference, saying: “Who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God”—that is, an unblemished sacrifice.

For this sacrifice was free from sins. This is what “through the eternal Spirit” means—not through fire or through certain other things.

“And he will cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.”

(Hier.) He rightly said “from dead works.” For if someone touched a dead person, he was defiled; likewise, if someone touches a dead work, he is contaminated through conscience. Sins are dead works.

(Alb.) “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it”; so the person who has been washed from dead works through repentance, if he does the same things again, will be more seriously contaminated. [Col. 0773D]

As the Apostle Peter says: “A dog returns to its own vomit” (2 Pet. 2); so does one who repeats his own folly.

(J. Chrys.) “To serve,” he says, “the living God.” Here he makes clear that those who have dead works cannot serve the true and living God, because those works are dead and false, and rightly so.

Therefore no one who has dead works enters here. For if one who touched a dead body was not permitted to enter the temple, how much more can one who has dead works not enter heaven? The pollution is indeed extremely serious, for all works that do not possess life are dead.

Just as a dead body is useful for no sense, and indeed grieves those who approach it, so sin immediately strikes our rational faculty and does not allow even the understanding itself to rest, but disturbs and agitates it. [Col. 0774A]

It is also said that disease, when it arises, corrupts bodies. Sin is something of this kind; it differs from disease not in that it first corrupts the air and then the bodies, but in that it immediately leaps upon the soul.

Do you not see those who are afflicted with disease—how they are seized by a kind of swelling, how they turn and turn back, how they are filled with foul odors, how their faces are disfigured, how they are unclean throughout? Such too are sinners, even if they do not perceive it.

“And for this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that, death having taken place for the redemption of the transgressions committed under the first covenant, those who have been called may receive the promises of the eternal inheritance. For where there is a covenant, the death of the one who made the covenant must intervene. For a covenant is confirmed over the dead; otherwise it is not yet valid while the one who made the covenant is alive.” [Col. 0774B]

Perhaps many who were more weakly disposed might, because Christ died, especially refuse to believe his promises. Therefore Paul sets this forth abundantly, taking examples from common practice.

What kind of example is it? “For this reason,” he says, “one must have confidence.” Why? Because covenants become firm and receive their force not while those who make them are alive, but when they are dead. Therefore, he says, “he is the mediator of the New Covenant.”

A covenant is made concerning the final day of death. Such a covenant has some as heirs and disinherits others. So also here: “I desire that where I am, these also may be” (John 17), Christ says. [Col. 0774C]

And again hear him speaking concerning those who are disinherited: “I do not ask concerning all, but concerning those who believe through their word in me.”

Again, a covenant ought to have witnesses. Hear him again saying: “I am the one who bears witness concerning myself, and the one who sent me bears witness concerning me”; and again: “He bears witness concerning me”—speaking of the Paraclete—and he sent the twelve Apostles, saying: “Bear witness before God” (Acts 1).

“Therefore,” he says, “he is the mediator of the New Covenant.” What is a mediator? A mediator is not the lord of the matter of which he is mediator. The matter is one thing, and the mediator another. For example, a mediator of marriage is not the one who contracts the marriage, but the one who helps the person who is going to contract it. So here too the Son became mediator between the Father and us. [Col. 0774D]

The Father did not wish to give us this inheritance, but was angry with us and indignant because we had become so alienated. Therefore he became our mediator and the Father’s, and persuaded him.

How then did he become mediator? He conveyed words, bringing to us what came from the Father through messengers; he also added death. For we were under accusation, and it was necessary that we die.

(Alb.) He sent his Son, made from a woman, who could die for those indebted to death; he died for us, undergoing the death that was owed. He makes us worthy of the covenant and of the promised inheritance. In this way the covenant was made firm.

Our sin was so great that we could never have been saved unless the only-begotten Son of God had died for us. [Col. 0775A]

When he says that the covenant is invalid while the one who made it is alive, this means that, as long as the one who made the covenant lives, he can change his decision and bring other heirs into his inheritance.

“Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.”

(J. Chrys.) Hence, he says, “not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood”—that is, it was made firm and strengthened. What he says by “therefore” means this: it was necessary for the solemnity of the covenant to be completed also through Christ’s death.

[Col. 0775B] “After Moses had read the whole commandment of the law to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, together with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying: ‘This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.’ He likewise sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels of the ministry with blood. Almost everything is cleansed with blood according to the law, and without the shedding of blood there is no remission.”

(Alb.) What does it mean that the book, the people, and the tabernacle were sprinkled with blood, unless the precious blood of Christ our Savior was foretold from the beginning by that figure? Why hyssop? Hyssop is a low-growing herb that grows among rocks. Christ’s humility is signified by this herb, as is the power by which our inward parts are cleansed. For this kind of herb is customarily used to cleanse ailments of the lungs. Why water? He shows that the future cleansing would take place through the water of baptism. Why scarlet wool? So that it might retain the blood. Here he shows that the water and the blood are the same thing: our baptism also is his passion. [Col. 0775C] Therefore Paul says elsewhere (Rom. VI; Col. II): “For you have been buried with him in baptism.”

But when he says, “Without the shedding of blood there would be no remission,” why does he say this? Because among them there was not full remission, but only a partial remission in a small measure. Now, however, he says: “This is the blood of the New Testament, which was shed for us for the remission of sins.” What is the book that was sprinkled with mystical blood, and what are the vessels of anointing, and what is the tabernacle, unless they are the people? For they themselves are the book, the vessels, and the tabernacle. Therefore the Lord says: “I will dwell in them, and I will walk among them.” But all the cleansing of the body belonged to the Old Testament. Now the blood of Christ is spiritual, in the soul. Therefore he says: “This is the blood of the New Testament for the remission of sins.”

[Col. 0775D] Among them the blood was sprinkled on the surface and the sprinkled blood was again washed away. For the people did not walk about perpetually covered in blood. In the soul, however, it is not so; rather, the blood is mingled with its very essence, making it a fountain, pure, and leading it to that ineffable beauty. For this reason the lamb was slaughtered and its blood smeared on the lintels of those who were to be delivered. For this reason also all the sacrifices of the Old Testament are read, so that they might designate this one sacrifice through which there is true remission of sins and the cleansing of the soul forever.

“Therefore it is necessary that the copies of the heavenly things be cleansed with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these.”

(Alb.) How are these the copies of the things that are in heaven? He called our manner of life heavenly, for whatever was enacted in the Old Testament was a copy and sign of this manner of life. Hence the Apostle says: “Our way of life is in heaven” (Phil. III). These things, then, which belong to us are in heaven, and these things of ours are heavenly, although they are celebrated on earth.

[Col. 0776A] What is this manner of life of ours? It is true philosophy, which Christ taught and which the apostles followed, leading to heavenly things. Hence the Apostle also says: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so are the heavenly” (I Cor. XIII).

“‘With better sacrifices,’ he says, ‘than these.’” Whatever is better is better by virtue of some good. The copies, therefore, which are in heaven were good; but the heavenly things themselves far surpass the examples of the saints by which they are signified. [Col. 0776B] If, then, we are heavenly and have obtained so great a sacrifice, let us fear remaining on earth.

(J. Chrys.) Yet we seem to be on earth and not to be on earth in a certain sense, when our will is in heaven, although our bodies are on earth. If, then, we draw near to God in our mind, we are in heaven. What concern have I with heaven itself when I see the Lord of heaven, when I myself become heaven? “We will come,” he says, “I and the Father, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John XIV).

Heaven itself is clear and pure by nature; it does not change in winter or at night. Therefore let us not fear suffering this either in the tribulations of the world or in the adversities of the devil, but let us remain immaculate and pure. Heaven has the sun; let us also have Christ, the sun of righteousness, always shining in our hearts.

[Col. 0776C] (Greg.) For the devil himself, overthrowing us in the root of our first parent, held the human being under his captivity as though justly, since, created with free will, he consented to the devil when he urged what was unjust. Created for life in the freedom of his own will, he voluntarily became a debtor to death.

Such guilt therefore had to be destroyed, but it could not be destroyed except by sacrifice. A sacrifice had to be sought, but what sort of sacrifice could be found for absolving human beings? For it was not just that the victims of brute animals should be slaughtered for rational human beings. Hence the Apostle says: “Therefore it is necessary that the copies of the heavenly things be cleansed with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these.”

[Col. 0776D] Therefore, if brute animals were not worthy victims for a rational animal—that is, for a human being—a human being had to be sought who ought to be offered for human beings, so that for the rational sinner a rational victim might be slaughtered. But what of the fact that a human being without sin could not be found? And when a victim was offered for us, how could it cleanse us from sin if it itself were not free from the contagion of sin? What was defiled could not cleanse those who were defiled.

Therefore, for the victim to be rational, a human being had to be offered; but for that human being to cleanse humanity from sins, he had to be both human and without sin. Yet who would be a human being without sin if he descended through the mixture of sin? Accordingly, for our sake the Son of God came into the Virgin’s womb. There he became human for us; he assumed nature, not guilt. He made a sacrifice for us and presented his body as a sinless victim for sinners—a victim that could both die in its humanity and cleanse by its righteousness.

[Col. 0777A] When the ancient enemy saw him after his baptism, he immediately attacked him with temptations. Attempting to break into his inward parts by various approaches, he was defeated and overthrown in the very impregnable integrity of his mind. But since he was unable to reach his inward parts, he turned to his outward parts, so that, because he had been defeated by the strength of his mind and could not deceive him through temptation, he might at least seem to overcome him by the death of his flesh. As was said earlier, he was permitted to act against that which the Mediator had received from us mortals.

[Col. 0777B] But where he was able to do something, there he was defeated on every side. From the place where he received outward power to kill the Lord’s flesh, there his inward power by which he held us was killed. He was defeated inwardly while he seemed to conquer outwardly. He had held us as debtors by right of death, but he justly lost his right of death over us, because through his agents he sought to destroy the flesh of one in whom he found nothing owing to the debt of guilt.

Our Lord therefore paid for us an undeserved death, so that the death owed by us might not harm us.

“For Jesus did not enter holy places made by human hands, copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God for us.”

(Joan.) The Jews held exalted ideas about the temple and the tabernacle, and therefore they said: “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord” (Jer. VII). No such temple had been constructed elsewhere on earth—not because of its wealth, nor for any other reason. For God, who had commanded it, had wished it to be made with great dignity, because they were more readily attracted and enticed by bodily things.

[Col. 0777C] It had golden bricks in its walls; anyone who wishes may learn this from the Second Book of Kings and from Ezekiel, as well as how many talents of gold were expended at that time. The second building was made more splendid both in beauty and in every other respect. Nor was it venerable for this reason alone, but also because it was one. Everyone came there from the ends of the earth, whether from Babylonia or from Ethiopia. Luke makes this clear in Acts when he says: “There were dwelling there Parthians, Medes, and Elamites, and those who inhabited Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene” (Acts II).

[Col. 0777D] All the peoples of the world therefore gathered there from every direction, and the name of that temple was greatly renowned. What, then, does Paul do? Just as there he added Christ’s death, so here he sets all heaven against the temple. And he shows not only this difference, but also a high priest made superior by the act: “That he may appear,” he says, “before the face of God.” Thus he makes the matter more venerable not only by the heaven but also by the entrance. For he did not simply see him there through certain signs, as here, but saw the Lord himself.

Do you see that all these statements are humble because of the descent? Why are you surprised that he intercedes, when he establishes him as a priest?

“Nor [did Christ enter] in order to offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest [does]; nor did Christ enter holy places made by human hands, copies of the true ones.”

[Col. 0778A] Therefore those are the true things, while these are copies. Indeed, the temple was constructed like the heaven of heavens. What do you mean? Unless he enters heaven, will he not appear before God, who is everywhere and fills all things? Do you see that all these things concern the flesh?

“That he may appear,” he says, “before the face of God for us.” What does “for us” mean? He ascended with the sacrifice, he says, being able to propitiate the Father. What then? Tell me: is he himself the enemy? The angels were enemies; he was not an enemy. Since the angels were enemies, hear what he says: “He reconciled the things on earth and the things in heaven.”

Therefore he also entered heaven, now to appear before the face of God for us—now to appear, now to be manifested, but for us.

“Nor does he offer himself often, as the high priest enters the holy places every year in the blood of another.”

[Col. 0778B] (Alb.) Above he called all the copies of the true things “copies”; here he also calls the things into which the high priest enters “true.” This temple alone was more venerable than any other in the entire world. People streamed to it from every direction, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles: on the holy day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit was given to the apostles as they spoke in all languages, people from different parts of the world were present, hearing and seeing the heavenly miracle.

But Paul set all heaven against this temple, and he showed not only this difference but also the great High Priest, so that he might stand before the face of God. Therefore he makes the matter more venerable not only by heaven but also by the entrance. For he does not simply appear through certain signs, as here, but stands before God himself, always living to intercede for us.

[Col. 0778C] (Joan.) Consider how great the differences are: often and once; in another’s blood and in his own blood. The difference is very great. He himself, therefore, is both sacrifice and priest and victim.

“Otherwise he would have had to suffer repeatedly from the foundation of the world. But now, at the consummation of the ages, he has appeared through his sacrifice for the destruction of sin. And just as it is appointed for human beings to die once, and after this comes judgment, so also Christ, having been offered once, will appear a second time without sin for the salvation of those who await him.”

[Col. 0778D] (Joan.) Since sins were abundant, he appeared at the appropriate time. This is also what he says elsewhere: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. V).

If, when offered once, he had not been sufficient to destroy the sins of all who believe in him, he would have had to suffer repeatedly from the foundation of the world. To prevent this, he suffered once, at the consummation of the world, for the destruction of the sins of many.

“And just as it is appointed for human beings to die once, and after this comes judgment”—then he says: “And having died once,” because redemption was accomplished by one death. “It is appointed,” he says, “for human beings to die once.” This, then, is what it means: he died once for all.

What then? Do we no longer die that death? We do die, but we shall not remain in it—which is not truly even death. For the tyranny of death, and death in the true sense, exists when the dead are never permitted to return to life. But when there will be life after death, and a better life, that is not death but sleep.

[Col. 0779A] Since death was going to retain everyone, he died in order to free us.

“So also Christ,” he says, “having been offered once.” By whom was he offered? It is clear that he offered himself. Here he does not say merely that he is the priest, but also the victim and the sacrifice offered through himself.

“Having been offered once,” he says, “to take away the sins of many.” Why “of many,” and not “of all”? Because not all believed. He died for all, insofar as it depended on him. That death is as powerful as the destruction of all; but he did not remove the sins of all because they were unwilling.

What does “he took away sins” mean? Just as in the offering we offer sins upward and say, “Whether willingly or unwillingly we have sinned; forgive us”—that is, we first mention them and then ask for remission—so it happened here as well.

[Col. 0779B] Where did Christ do this? Hear him saying: “And for their sake I sanctify myself” (John XVII). Behold, he offered the sins; he took them from human beings and offered them upward to the Father, not so that he might issue any judgment against them, but so that he might forgive them.

(Alb.) It is appointed for all to die once, and after death each person will be judged according to his merits. So also Christ died once for the sins of others; and because he died both voluntarily and necessarily, he will appear a second time without sin at his second coming.

[Col. 0779C] (Joan.) What does “without sin” mean? As though he did not sin. He did not die as one owing death, nor because of sin. But how will he appear? To punish, he says. Yet he did not say that; rather, he said what is festive and gracious: “He will appear without sin to those who await him for salvation.”

Then they will no longer need a sacrifice in order to be saved, but will accomplish this through their works themselves. Every victim for sin is called “sin.” At that time there will not be a victim for sin, because there will be no sin, but righteousness—whether in the reward of the righteous or in the repayment of sinners.

## CHAPTER X

It is shown that the old law cannot remove sin, by declaring the excellence of Christ’s priesthood and that his priesthood must be obeyed steadfastly.

“For the law, possessing a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the realities.” That is, not the truth itself. [Col. 0779D] For when someone, as in a painting, lays down the outlines of shadows to indicate what he intends to paint, it is a shadow, not an image. But if someone applies the actual colors to the flowers and places them upon the outlines, then it becomes an image. Such was also the law: a shadow of the truth.

“With the same sacrifices that they offer continually year by year, it can never perfect those who draw near. Otherwise they would have ceased offering them, because the worshipers, once cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sin. But in them there is a remembrance of sins year by year. For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.”

(Joan.) This one sacrifice, he says, is one; those sacrifices are many. For this very reason they were not powerful, since they were many. What need was there for many, tell me, if one was sufficient? Therefore the fact that many were offered continually shows that they were never cleansed.

[Col. 0780A] When a medicine is powerful, effective for health, and capable of driving away every illness, once it has been applied it accomplishes everything. If, after being applied once, it accomplishes everything, it shows its power, so that it need not be applied again. This is its function: that it no longer be applied. But if it is applied continually, it is clear evidence that it has accomplished nothing. The power of a medicine is that it is applied once, not frequently. So it is here also. Why were they continually healed by the same sacrifices? If they had been freed from all sins, sacrifices would certainly not have been offered day after day.

Therefore it was a remembrance of sin, not an absolution, since both the priests and the people alike were cleansed daily by the same sacrifices. In Christ, by contrast, one sacrifice was offered, powerful for eternal salvation.

[Col. 0780B] What, then, about us? Do we not offer every day? We do offer, but we do so in remembrance of his death. This is one sacrifice, not many. How is it one and not many? Because that sacrifice was offered once, and was offered in the holy of holies. This sacrifice is its copy. We always offer the same one—not one lamb today and another tomorrow, but always the same one.

Therefore this is one sacrifice. Otherwise, on the reasoning that it is offered in many places, are there many Christs? Certainly not. Christ is one everywhere: here fully present and there fully present, one body. Just as the one who is offered everywhere is one body, not many bodies, so also there is one sacrifice.

[Col. 0780C] Our High Priest is the one who offered the sacrifice that cleanses us. We offer that same sacrifice now, which, having been offered then, cannot be consumed. What we do takes place in remembrance of what was done: “Do this,” he says, “in remembrance of me” (Luke XXII; I Cor. XI). We do not offer another sacrifice, as the high priest does, but always the same one; rather, we enact the remembrance of the sacrifice.

“Therefore, when he entered the world, he said: ‘Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you prepared a body for me. You took no pleasure in burnt offerings for sin. Then I said: Behold, I come. In the heading of the book it is written about me: To do your will, O God.’ Above, when he says: ‘You did not desire sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings for sin, nor were those things offered according to the law pleasing to you,’ then he says: ‘Behold, I come, to do your will, O God.’”

[Col. 0780D] (Alb.) The signs that promised have been removed because the promised truth has been presented. Therefore he says: “You did not desire burnt offerings and sacrifices, but you prepared a body for me.” That is, the legal sacrifices could not atone for the sin of the human race, but you prepared a body for me. This is spoken in the person of the one who assumed the body of our mortality, so that he might have something to offer for us.

“Then I said: Behold, I come.” Then was the time for the signs to be removed and the promised truth to come. “Then I said: Behold, I come”: these things removed, those things offered; these fulfilled.

[Col. 0781A] Where are the sacrifices of the Jews? They have passed away and are not in the Church of Christ, because the one whom those sacrifices prefigured has come, concerning whom it is written at the head—or in the heading—of the book.

Which book? Certainly the Psalter, where it says: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, and has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the seat of pestilence, but his delight is in the law of the Lord” (Ps. I). Some call this psalm the head of the entire book. Therefore the Apostle also says here: “In the heading of the book it is written about me: To do your will, O God.”

That is what is said in the Gospel: “I have not come,” he says, “to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John VI).

[Col. 0781B] “He removes the first in order to establish the second.” That is, he removes the first testament, which was given to Moses on Mount Sinai, in order to establish the second—that is, the Gospel offered through Christ—as firm.

“By this will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.” This offering was made once, but it always has power to wash all who believe and all who desire to be cleansed by it.

Therefore he added and explained more fully the power of this sacrifice, blessed Paul himself saying:

“And every priest stands daily ministering and repeatedly offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But this man, having offered one sacrifice for sins, sat down forever at the right hand of God, from then on waiting until his enemies should be placed as a footstool for his feet.”

[Col. 0781C] (Joan.) He shows that the former sacrifices were useless for complete cleansing; rather, they were a form and possessed much less power. But this objection occurred to him: If they were forms, how is it that, when the truth came, they did not cease and disappear, but are still celebrated?

He therefore says this to them, showing that they are no longer celebrated, not even as forms. For God does not regard them as acceptable; only those who have always resisted the Holy Spirit hold to them. Therefore he refutes them by prophetic testimony, saying: “You did not desire burnt offerings and offerings for sin.” This is said of no one other than Christ.

And what wonder is it if now God’s will is not in the blood of goats and bulls, when he says through the prophet Isaiah: “Who has required these things from your hands?” (Isa. I). “You did not desire these things. Then I said: Behold, I come.”

“By this will we have been saved.” How have we been saved? That is, “through the offering of the body of Jesus once for all.” And every priest stands daily ministering. To minister is the task of servants, but to sit is the task of rulers. Hence he says: “He sits at the right hand of God.”

[Col. 0781D] Therefore, “having offered one sacrifice,” which is able to save, “he sits forever at the right hand of the Father, from then on waiting until his enemies should be placed as a footstool for his feet.”

Who are his enemies? The Jews, plainly, and all unbelievers, who will be condemned by him on the day of judgment. Here he signifies the greatness of his power. He did not say “until they are subjected,” but “until they are placed” beneath his feet.

Let us therefore not become part of the number of his enemies. For not only are unbelievers enemies, but also those whose lives are filled with impurity.

[Col. 0782A] “The mind of the flesh is hostile to God. For it does not submit to the law, nor indeed can it” (Rom. VIII).

“For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are sanctified. The Holy Spirit also bears witness to us. For after saying, ‘This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws in their hearts, and I will write them upon their minds,’ he then says: ‘And I will no longer remember their sins and their iniquities.’ But where there is remission of these, there is no longer an offering for sin.”

(Alb.) One offering of Christ’s body will perfect those who have been sanctified, and it brings complete remission of sins. He also proved this from the testimony of prophecy, saying:

“The Holy Spirit also bears witness to us,” that is, “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws in their hearts.”

[Col. 0782B] Not as the law was written on tablets of stone, but he wrote it permanently on the tablets of their fleshly hearts.

What is this law written in the hearts of each person? Certainly love: that we should not do to another what we do not want done to us. This is what covers a multitude of sins, as it is said in the Gospel: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. VII).

Therefore it is not necessary to cleanse ourselves daily through daily sacrifices, as under the old law.

“Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Christ, which he inaugurated for us as a new and living way through the veil—that is, through his flesh—and since we have a great priest over the house of God—”

[Col. 0782C] (Joan.) Here he shows the difference between the high priest, the sacrifices, the tabernacle, the covenant, and the promise, and the great distinction between them: those things were temporal, but these are eternal; those were weak, but these are perfect; those were forms, but these are the truth.

“For it is not according to the law of a carnal commandment,” he says, “but according to the power of an indestructible life”; and: “You are a priest forever.” Behold the priest’s perpetuity.

And concerning that covenant he said that it was old: “What becomes old and grows aged is near to disappearing.” But this is the New Testament, possessing remission of sins. The former had nothing of this kind. The former was made by human hands, but this is not made by human hands. The former had the blood of goats, but this has the Lord’s blood. The former had a standing priest, but this has one who sits.

[Col. 0782D] Since all those things are lesser and these are greater, therefore he says: “Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence.”

From where does this confidence arise? Just as sins produce shame, so the remission of all sins produces confidence; and so does the fact that we have become co-heirs and enjoy such great love.

“Into the entrance of the holy places,” he says. Here he calls heaven the entrance and access to spiritual things.

“Which he inaugurated.” That is, which he constructed, prepared, and initiated. Dedication means the beginning of use. “Which he prepared,” he says, “and through which he himself proceeded.”

[Col. 0783A] “A new and living way.” Here he declares the fulfillment of hope by calling it new. For he attempts to show that we now possess things greater than before, since the gates of heaven have now been opened—something that did not happen even to Abraham.

He called it the new way of life, but he called that way “living”; that is, the commandments. He himself dedicated the new way; he dedicated it for this reason, because he himself proceeded along it. He rightly called it a veil: when he had been raised on high, then the heavenly things appeared.

“Let us draw near with a true heart in the fullness of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.”

(Joan.) In what way should we draw near? In holiness, faith, and spiritual worship. “With a true heart,” without hypocrisy, “in the full assurance of faith,” because none of these things is visible—neither priest, nor sacrifice, nor altar.

Therefore he says: “In the fullness of faith.” [Col. 0783B] We must believe as firmly as we are certain of visible things, and even more so. For here the senses of the flesh sometimes err concerning the things that are seen; there, however, this is not so, because by the Spirit we perceive spiritual things, and we may not hesitate concerning them.

Therefore he says: “With our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience.” He shows that not faith alone is sought, but also a virtuous life, because faith without works is idle. They cleansed bodies, but we cleanse the conscience.

“And our bodies washed with pure water.” Here he means the bath of baptism. For baptism is not the cleansing of the body, but of the soul, if faith is present in the one baptized—whether the faith of the parents or of the person himself, if he has reached the age of reason.

“Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.”

[Col. 0783C] (Joan.) Do not scrutinize anything; expect no rational proof. All these things require faith, because “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XIII). Just as God is faithful in his promises, so he wishes us to be faithful in our promises—promises by which we know that we oppose the devil and confess Christ.

“And let us consider one another for the provocation of love and good works, not abandoning our assembly, as is the custom of some.”

What does “let us understand one another” mean? If someone is endowed with virtue, let us imitate him and direct our attention to him, so that we may love and be loved. For good works arise from love.

Assembly is a great good. It produces more fervent love, and from it all good works are generated. There is no good thing that is not done through love. Let us therefore strengthen love in one another, because “love is the fullness of the law.”

[Col. 0783D] We do not need labors or sweat. If we love one another, a path freely opens before us, leading to virtue and to heavenly things. Just as on a journey, if someone gains a beginning, he is led along the straight road to where he ought to go, so it is also with love: only grasp its beginning, and immediately it offers you its hand, leads you, and directs you.

“As is the custom,” he says, “of some.”

(Alb.) Here he not only admonished them, but also blamed and terrified those who were dividing the unity of love.

“But encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the day approaching.”

[Col. 0784A] What day does he designate, unless the day of judgment, on which the merits of each person are examined—or even the final day of our life? For elsewhere he says: “The Lord is near; do not be anxious about anything” (Phil. IV), that is, about earthly things. And again: “Our salvation is nearer now than when we believed” (Rom. XIII). For the time has been shortened.

“Indeed, for those of us who sin deliberately after receiving knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins is any longer left.” (Alb.) For when we sin voluntarily, after we have received acknowledgment of the truth, no further sacrifice for sins remains, just as under the old law it was granted that sacrifices might be offered repeatedly for sin. For Christ himself is not to be sacrificed again for our sins: this was done once, and there is no need of a second offering. Rather, after receiving grace, we must remain in faith and in the truth of good works. [Col. 0784B]

(Joan.) Trees that have been properly planted and have received all the care of the farmers, applied by hand and through labor, if they produce no return for the labor, are uprooted and handed over to the fire. Something similar happened in the matter of baptism. For when Christ has established us and we have received spiritual irrigation, if thereafter we bear no fruit, the fire of Gehenna and the unquenchable flame will await us.

Paul therefore urges charity and the production of good works, inviting them by means of useful considerations. What are these useful considerations? “We have access to the holy places, through the new way which he dedicated for us.” After inviting them to good works by useful considerations, he now wishes to do the same by means of fearful and sorrowful things. For after saying, “Let us not abandon our assembly, as some have made a practice of doing, but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the day approaching,” he added:

“For when we sin voluntarily, after we have received acknowledgment of the truth, no sacrifice for sins is any longer left.”

There is need, he says, of good works—indeed, there is need, and very great need. “For when we sin voluntarily, after we have received acknowledgment of the truth, no sacrifice for sins is any longer left.” You have been cleansed; you are free from crimes; you have become a son of God. If you return to your first vomit, another judgment awaits you, unless you are renewed through repentance.

Therefore he subsequently says: “But a certain fearful expectation of judgment and the fury of fire, which will consume the adversaries.” In saying this he did not exclude repentance, nor the reconciliation effected through repentance; nor does he repel and cast down the sinner through despair, for he is not so hostile to our salvation. What, then, did he exclude? He excluded a second baptismal washing. He did not say, “There is no further repentance”; nor did he say, “There is no further forgiveness.” Rather, he says, “There is no further sacrifice”—that is, there is no second cross.

“For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are sanctified,” unlike the Jewish sacrifices. He wishes to make us cautious, so that we do not look for either the cross of Christ or Jewish sacrifices again for our sins. And whoever neglects the remedy of repentance, let the fury of fire devour him. Therefore, while he has time, let each person flee to the remedy of repentance, [Col. 0785A] lest he be handed over to eternal fire.

“Anyone who sets aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses.”

He instills terror in Christians by recalling the punishments of those who sinned under the law: “Without mercy,” he says, so that there may be no pardon and no mercy, although that law belonged to Moses. If two or three, as he ordained, testify against someone, the judges of the people immediately condemn him to death, if he has acted contrary to the law or has disobeyed.

And if this is so under the old law, where the law of Moses is set aside, “how much worse punishment,” says the Apostle, “do you think will be deserved by one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, considered the blood of the covenant—by which he was sanctified—to be profane, and insulted the Spirit of grace?”

As Christ is greater than Moses, and grace greater than the law, so he will deserve greater punishments. And how does someone trample underfoot the Son of God? When someone partakes of him unworthily through the sacraments, does he not commit a great sin? Does he not trample upon him? Does he not despise him? For just as we regard the things we trample upon as worthless, so those who sin freely, without fear and without repentance, consider Christ worthless and do not fear that he will be their judge.

By grace he has become the body of Christ, yet he makes himself the body of the devil; and he makes the blood of Christ profane in himself, although he had been cleansed, when he returns to his former vomit and neglects to cleanse himself again through repentance.

“And insulting the Spirit of grace.” Whoever has not received a benefit has insulted the benefactor. He made you a son; you, however, wish to become a slave of sin. He came to dwell with you; you, however, do not prepare a dwelling worthy of his habitation, but procure another inhabitant for yourself—that is, the devil.

“We know that he said: ‘Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay’; and again: ‘The Lord will judge his people’ (Deut. XXXII; Rom. XIII).” [Alb.] He said this concerning enemies and concerning those who neglect to cleanse themselves through repentance, but who do evil in security. “He will judge” means that he will separate the good from the wicked within his own people, and the faithful from the unfaithful.

“For it is fearful to fall into the hands of the living God.”

A person falls into the hands of God on the day of judgment—that is, into the power of his judgment—when he will repay each according to his merits. Whoever does not now seek to meet his face through confession and repentance, while he has time, will, if he does not repent of his sins, fall into the fearful judgment of almighty God. [Col. 0785D]

“Remember the former days, in which, after being enlightened, you endured a great struggle of sufferings.”

(Joan.) The best physicians, when they have cut deeply and have increased the pain through the incision, immediately bring comfort and a remedy to the place where the pain is present, and they soothe the troubled spirit. After they have restored it, they do not make another incision; indeed, they tend the one already made with milder medicines capable of lessening the severity of the pain.

Paul did the same. After shaking their minds by saying, [Col. 0786A] “It is fearful to fall into the hands of the living God,” and proving that the one who insults the grace of God and treats the Holy Spirit contemptuously must perish in every way, he also demonstrates this from the law of Moses. Accordingly, so that he would not cause someone despairing under excessive fear to be swallowed up by sorrow and despair, he consoles them with praise and exhortations, and places before them the rivalry of their own community.

“After being enlightened”—that is, strengthened through divine grace—“you endured a great struggle of sufferings.” He does not simply say “struggle,” but adds “great”; nor does he say “temptations,” but “combat.” To suffer for the name of Christ is a matter of great praise and a proclamation of the highest praises.

“And on the one hand, you were made a public spectacle through reproaches and tribulations; on the other, you became companions of those who lived in this way. For you also had compassion on the prisoners.” (Joan.)

Now he pursues their praises in detail, saying that they not only endured sufferings for Christ courageously, but also showed compassion to those who were imprisoned.

“And you were made a public spectacle through tribulations and reproaches.” Reproach is a serious matter, capable of overthrowing the strength of the soul and powerful enough to blind the mind. Since the human race is exceedingly desirous of glory, it is therefore easily captured by reproaches. He did not simply say “through reproaches,” but increased the force by saying, “you were made a public spectacle.” When someone is reproached secretly, he is certainly saddened, but much more when it happens before everyone.

Tell me: how great an evil was it for people who had descended from Jewish weakness and passed over to the best way of life, despising their ancestral traditions, to suffer many evils at the hands of their own relations and to have no defense? “I have nothing to say,” he says, “because you suffered these things and perhaps grieved—indeed, you rejoiced all the more.” This is what he signified by saying, “You became companions of those who suffered in this way.” He brings the apostles themselves forward as examples.

“You not only,” he says, “did not feel shame in your own sufferings, but you also became companions of others who suffered in this way.” This is both a consolation and an exhortation. He did not say, “Endure my tribulations and become my companions,” but, “Be ashamed of your own sufferings.”

“And you had compassion,” he says, “on the prisoners.” You see that he is speaking of himself and of the other prisoners. You did not regard those chains as chains, but stood firm like courageous athletes, because you not only had no need of encouragement or consolation in your own circumstances, but also became encouragement and consolation to others. [Col. 0786D]

“And you accepted with joy the seizure of your possessions.” (Alb.) He praises them wonderfully for their faith. For if they had not believed that they had received better things in place of the substance that had been taken from them, they would not have accepted its seizure with joy. Accordingly, he adds the confidence of faith:

“Knowing that you have a better and abiding possession.”

As though he were saying: Seeing your future riches, you endured with joy; you regarded what had not yet appeared as though it were already present. This is wholly the work of the apostles and worthy of those courageous souls: to rejoice in blows, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles:

“After they had left the council, they rejoiced because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts V). [Col. 0787A]

“Knowing,” he says, “that you have a better and abiding possession.” That is, one that is firm and substantial and cannot perish as this earthly possession perished. [Col. 0788A]

## BOOK TWENTY-NINE

[Col. 0787]

### CHAPTER XI. The Apostle shows what it means to be subjected to Christ; in describing faith, he commends it in many ways.

“Therefore, brothers, do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward with God.”

(Alb.) He urges them most earnestly not to throw it away, for it is easier to preserve something whole than to recover it after it has been lost. Nothing is necessary for you except to stand firm and remain in your strength, which has a great reward with God.

“For you need patience, so that, by doing the will of God, you may receive the promise.”

O how great is the exhortation and consolation contained in this statement! You have only one task: to persevere in the contest until you receive a crown worthy of your labor. For not the one who begins will be crowned, but “the one who perseveres in the struggle to the end will be saved” (Matt. X).

“In your patience,” says the Lord, “you will possess your souls.”

(Joan.) “You may receive” means, “you may receive the promises of God.” He consoles them as if someone were speaking to an athlete who had defeated and overthrown everyone, with no opponent remaining to contend against him, and who was about to be crowned, but who, unable to endure the delay while the judge of the contest came to award the crown, wished impatiently to leave and flee because he could not bear his thirst and the flames of the heat.

This is what he himself signifies when he says:

“For yet a little while, and the one who is to come will come and will not delay.”

(Alb.) It is no small consolation to hope that the judge, rewarder, and consoler will soon come to reward the steadfastness of the contest.

(Joan.) And lest they should say, “When will he come?” he consoles them from the Scriptures. For he says, “Our salvation is near.” Thus he consoles them as though only a short time remained. He does not say this on his own authority, but from the Scriptures. For if it has already been a long time since it was said, “Yet a little while, and the one who is to come will come and will not delay” (Hag. II), it is clear that now he is much nearer. Therefore, both perseverance and expectation bring no small reward.

“But my righteous one will live by faith” (Hab. II). “And if he withdraws, my soul will not be pleased with him. But we are not children of withdrawal, leading to destruction, but of faith, leading to the acquisition of the soul.”

(Alb.) The Apostle introduced this prophetic testimony as an exhortation to faith. Just as the one who doubts will be displeasing, so the one who believes will live in his upright faith. Therefore, let us believe that Christ the judge has come swiftly, and let us prepare to meet him in good works, so that we may not be children of withdrawal from eternal light, but of acquisition for glory, hearing with the saints on the great day the desired voice:

“Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV). [Col. 0788A]

“Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen; for by it the elders obtained testimony.”

(Joan.) O how wonderfully he speaks when he says, “the conviction of things that are not seen.” Conviction belongs to matters that are wholly manifest. [Col. 0788B] Faith, therefore, he says, is the vision of things that do not appear, and it leads to the same certainty as that produced by things that are seen.

Accordingly, belief or unbelief cannot properly be spoken of with regard to things that are seen. Nor, again, can faith be spoken of unless someone has greater certainty concerning things that are not seen than concerning things that are seen.

Since things that are hoped for are thought to be without substance, faith gives them substance; or rather, it does not give them substance, but is itself their essence. For example, the resurrection has not yet occurred, and does not yet possess substance, but hope causes it to subsist in our soul. This is what he called “substance.”

If, therefore, faith is the conviction of things that are not seen, why do you wish already to see them, so that you may fall away from faith and cease to be righteous? For “the righteous person lives by faith.” But if you wish to see these things, you will no longer be faithful. You have labored, he says; you have endured many contests. I say the same, he says—but wait. That is, do not seek here the things for which you hope.

(Greg.) Thomas touched the Lord’s side and exclaimed, “My Lord and my God!” Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed” (John XX).

When the Apostle Paul says, “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen,” it is plainly evident that faith is the proof of those things that cannot appear. For things that appear already have not faith but knowledge.

When Thomas saw and touched, why was it said to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed”? He saw one thing and believed another. Divinity could not be seen in a mortal man. He saw the human being, therefore, and confessed God, saying, “My Lord and my God!” Thus he believed by seeing: he considered the true human being and exclaimed that this was the God whom he could not see.

“By faith we understand that the ages were fashioned by the word of God, so that the visible things came into being from the invisible.”

(Joan.) Faith requires a strong and manly spirit, one that rises above all sensible things and surpasses the weakness of human reasoning. No one can otherwise become faithful unless he withdraws himself from ordinary custom.

Since the souls of the Hebrews were weak, and although they had begun from faith were being made faint-hearted by the sufferings of their tribulations, enduring them with too little patience and being shaken, he first exhorted them by those very things, saying, [Col. 0789A] “Remember the former days.” Again, he exhorted them from divine Scripture, which says, “The righteous person lives by faith.” Then he did so by reasoning, saying, “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the conviction of things that are not seen.”

Now he begins to speak of their ancestors, those great and wonderful men, almost saying: If all those people were saved by faith where the good things were already before their feet, how much more shall we be saved?

When the soul finds a companion in the same sufferings, it rests and breathes again. This also usually happens in faith and in tribulation. “Therefore,” he says, “let mutual faith be a consolation among you.”

The human race is exceedingly unbelieving, neither trusting itself nor feeling secure about what it thinks it possesses; yet it is greatly concerned for the glory that is bestowed by many. What, then, does Paul do? He exhorts them from their ancestors, and first from common understanding.

Tell me, he says, is faith accused as something that cannot be demonstrated and is rather a deception? Therefore he shows that the greatest things were perfected through faith, not through reasoning.

And how does he show this? Tell me. It is evident, he says, that God brings into being the things that exist from things that did not exist, and visible things from things that did not appear, and subsisting things from things that did not subsist.

And from where do we know this? Because he made these things by his word. Reasoning contributes nothing to us in this matter; on the contrary, it would suppose that visible things were made from visible things.

Therefore even the philosophers say that nothing comes from things that do not exist, since they are animal-like and grasp nothing by faith. Yet they themselves are also refuted. Whenever they say something great or powerful, they say that it must be apprehended by faith—for example, when they say that God is without beginning and unbegotten.

Reasoning does not support this claim; on the contrary, it opposes it. Observe now their great folly. They say that God is without beginning and that he exists from nothing. This is much more astonishing than saying that God made the things that exist from things that did not exist.

For to say, “God is without beginning because he is unbegotten, because he was generated neither by himself nor by another,” is, as far as reasoning is concerned, more difficult than to say, “God made the things that exist from things that did not exist.” In the latter case, many things are credible: someone made them, and what was made had a beginning. In the former case, however, the unbegotten exists spontaneously, having neither beginning nor time. Do these things not require faith even more? Tell me.

But he did not set forth what was much greater; rather, he did the opposite. “From where,” he says, “do we know that God made these things?” Reasoning does not support it. No one was present when these things were being made; how, then, can it be certain? It is clear that this is a matter of faith.

“By faith,” he says, “we understand that the ages were perfected by the word of God.” Why by faith? Because the visible things were made from things that did not appear. This belongs to faith.

“By faith Abel offered to God a greater sacrifice than Cain, through which he obtained testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts; and through it, though dead, he still speaks.”

After stating what is common, he then explains it through individual persons. For Abel was a glorious man, comparable with the world; this he also indicated later. Since he had established this matter through a hundred or two hundred persons, then, seeing that the number was small, he added, “of whom the world was not worthy.”

Observe whom he places first: the one who suffered evil, and this from his brother. “You,” he says, “suffered the same things from your fellow countrymen.”

Abel was killed by a brother who had received no injury from him, but who was envious because of God. This shows that they too suffered from envy. Abel honored God and died for the honor of God, and he had not yet obtained the resurrection. Yet his desire was manifest, and the things that ought to be done by him were done; but the things he hoped would be granted by God had not yet been bestowed upon him.

Here he calls the sacrifice “more honorable,” “more splendid,” and “necessary.” And we cannot say, he says, that it was not accepted. God did accept it, and said to Cain, “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly.” Therefore Abel both offered rightly and divided rightly.

But what recompense did he receive for these things? He was killed by his brother’s hand. The condemnation that his father had deserved on account of sin, Abel, though upright, was the first to undergo. He suffered so cruelly because he suffered it at the hands of his brother and was the first to be killed; yet he lived honorably and rightly, having no one to imitate.

Whom did he look to and imitate in order to honor God in this way? His father or his mother? They had rather dishonored God despite such great benefits. His brother? He too had dishonored God. Therefore Abel found this good within himself.

What, then, happened to one who was worthy of such honor? He was killed. How, moreover, did he also receive another testimony that he was righteous? It is said that fire descended and consumed his sacrifices.

“He looked upon Abel,” it says, “and upon his sacrifices” (Gen. IV). In the language of the Syrians, it reads, “and he kindled.”

Although God had testified to his righteousness both in his words and in his works, and although he saw him extinguished for his sake, he still did not reward him, but left him in that state. Therefore this was true faith. What miracles had Abel seen that he should believe there would be some recompense of good things from God? Did he not possess this virtue through faith alone?

What does “and therefore, though dead, he still speaks” mean? So that he would not lead them into great despair, he showed that Abel had partly enjoyed his recompense. His contemplation is indeed great.

“And he still speaks”—that is, Cain killed him, but did not kill his glory and memory with him. He is not dead; therefore neither will you die. The harsher the sufferings someone has endured, the more his glory increases.

How does he still speak? This is evidence that he lives: he is in everyone’s mouth, and everyone admires and blesses him. Whoever admonishes others to be righteous speaks. His suffering benefited more than his speech. Just as heaven speaks merely by appearing, so Abel speaks whenever he comes to mind.
