“By faith Enoch was translated so that he should not see death, and he was not found because God had translated him; for before his translation he had testimony that he pleased God; for whoever approaches God must believe that he exists and that he becomes a rewarder of those who seek him.”

By faith Enoch was translated so that he would not see death—the death of which the Lord says in the Gospel, “Whoever lives and believes in me will never die” (John XI).

Therefore, if we desire to attain true perfection, we must hasten so that, just as in body we have rejected parents, homeland, the riches of the world, and our desires, so also in heart, leaving all these things behind, we may not again return in longing to what we abandoned.

In another sense, Enoch was translated because he pleased God; and the reason he pleased God was faith. If he had not known that he would receive recompense, how could he have pleased God?

“For without faith it is impossible to please God.” How so? “He believed that whoever believed that God exists would also receive recompense.” From what, then, does one become pleasing to God? “One must believe,” he says, “that he exists”—not what he is.

If “that he exists” requires faith and not reasoning, then what he is cannot be grasped by reasoning either. If the existence of a reward requires faith and not reasoning, how could matters pertaining to his essence be comprehended by reasoning? What kind of reasoning could reach such things?

Some say that everything that exists came into being by chance and spontaneously. You see that unless we believe concerning everything—not only concerning recompense, but also concerning what God himself is—all things slip away from us and do not stand firm.

Many ask where Enoch was translated, and why he was translated, and why neither he nor Elijah died; and, if they still live, how they live and in what condition. It is superfluous to inquire into these things. Scripture has said that this one was translated and that the other was taken up; but where they are and how they exist, it has not added. For it says nothing beyond what is necessary.

This is what is meant by the statement about the translation: he was translated, not having died, but so that he would not see death. Therefore it added, “He was translated alive because he pleased God.”

At first God allowed death to occur, wishing through the son to terrify the father. Wishing to show that the sentence truly remained firm, he subjected not only the wicked but also the one who had pleased him to punishment—I mean blessed Abel. Almost immediately after this, he translated Enoch and did not raise Abel, lest they become presumptuous and confident; but he translated Enoch alive. Through Abel he terrified them; through Enoch he stirred them to emulate what pleases him.

(Greg.) One does not arrive at faith through virtues; rather, through faith one reaches virtues. The centurion Cornelius, whose almsgiving was praised even before baptism, with an angel bearing witness (Acts X), did not come to faith through works, but came through faith to works.

For the angel says to him, “Your prayers and your almsgiving have ascended before God.” If he had not believed in the true God even before baptism, whom was he praying to? Or how had almighty God heard him, if he was not asking him to perfect him in good things?

He therefore knew God, the creator of all things, but did not know that his almighty Son had become incarnate. For he could not have done good works unless he had first believed; for it is written, “Without faith it is impossible to please God.”

He therefore possessed faith, since his prayers and almsgiving could please God. By good action, however, he earned the privilege of knowing God perfectly and believing the mystery of his incarnation, so that he might reach the sacraments of baptism. Through faith, therefore, he came to works; through works, he was made firm in faith. [Col. 0792A]

“By faith Noah, having received a divine response concerning things not yet seen, and moved by fear, prepared an ark for the salvation of his household; through it he condemned the world and became heir of the righteousness that is through faith.”

(Joan.) Enoch was an example of faith alone, [Col. 0792B] but this was an example both of faith and of unbelief. This is perfect consolation and exhortation: not only are those who believed found to have been approved, but unbelievers also suffered the opposite.

“What, then,” he says, “does this mean: ‘By faith Noah, having received an oracle’?” What does “having received an oracle” mean? It means that it was foretold to him. Why is it called an oracle? For elsewhere he says, “An oracle had been given to him by the Spirit” (Luke II). And again, “What did the divine oracle say?”

Do you observe the equality of honor given to the Holy Spirit? For just as God gives oracles, so also does the Holy Spirit.

Why did he say it in this way? Prophecy is called an oracle. “Concerning things not yet seen,” he says—that is, concerning the rains—“he built the ark in fear.”

Reasoning suggested nothing in this matter. They were marrying and giving in marriage; the air was clear and serene, and there were no signs. Nevertheless, he was afraid.

“By faith,” he says, “having received an oracle concerning things not yet seen, he built the ark in fear for the salvation of his household, through which he condemned the world.” How? He showed that they were worthy of this punishment because they were not corrected even by that construction.

“And he became heir of the righteousness that is through faith.” From this it became evident that he was righteous: from the fact that he believed God. It is certain that faith produces righteousness. For just as we have received an oracle concerning Gehenna, so did he.

Although he was mocked and reproached, he paid no attention to any such thing.

“By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed and went out to the place that he was to receive as an inheritance; and he went out without knowing where he was going.”

Whom did he see, tell me, that he might imitate him? He came from a pagan and idolatrous homeland; he had not heard prophets and did not know where he was going. Since they were looking at those among the Hebrews who had believed, as though ten thousand had already obtained good things, he showed that no one had yet received anything: all were without reward, and no one had yet received recompense.

Abraham left his homeland and his house, and went out without knowing where he was going.

“By faith he dwelt in the land of promise as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, fellow heirs of the same promise.”

What is surprising if he lived in this way, when even his descendants lived so? He saw the promise being contradicted. For it had been said, “I will give this land to you and to your seed.” He saw his son living there as a foreigner; his grandson likewise saw himself wandering in a foreign land, and he was not disturbed.

Perhaps this happened to Abraham for good reason, since the promise was to be brought to fulfillment later. But in the case of his offspring it was sufficiently astonishing, although it too had been said to him, “I will give it to you and to your seed”—not “through your seed,” but “to you and to your seed.” Yet neither he, nor Isaac, nor Jacob possessed what had been promised.

One served in mercenary servitude; another was persecuted; the other almost fell away in fear. At one time he killed enemies in war; at another, unless God had been present, he too would have perished.

Therefore he said, “with fellow heirs of the same promise.” Not he alone, he says, but also the heirs.

“For they were awaiting a city having foundations, whose architect and builder is God.”

Observe that they received the promises for this reason: by waiting and trusting that they would receive them. If trusting is equivalent to receiving, we may understand the passage in this way. Although these people possessed none of these things, they nevertheless looked upon them with desire.

Why did this happen? So that we might be ashamed. They did not fix their attention on the promises made on earth, but sought the future city. God speaks to us above and below about the heavenly city, yet we seek an earthly one.

He said to them, “I will give you present things,” because he saw them—or rather, because they showed themselves worthy of greater things. He did not permit them to receive these things, but granted them greater ones, wishing to show us that they are worthy of greater things because they do not wish to be bound to earthly matters.

It is like someone promising childish things to a wise little child—not so that the child may receive them, but to display the child’s wisdom, while the child asks for greater things. This shows how earnestly they drew their minds away from earth, since they did not even accept the things that were offered.

Indeed, this is why their descendants receive them: those descendants were worthy of the land. What does “a city having foundations” mean? Were these people not foundations? They were not foundations in comparison with those others. “Whose architect and builder is God.”

“By faith Sarah herself also received power to conceive offspring, even beyond the proper time of life, because she considered him faithful who had promised. Therefore, from one man—and one as good as dead—were born descendants as numerous as the stars of heaven and as countless as the sand on the seashore.” [Col. 0793D]

“By faith,” he says, “Sarah herself also.” Here he truly arouses shame in them, since they appeared weaker than a woman. But perhaps someone might say, “How was this through faith, when she laughed?” The laughter arose from unbelief, but the fear arose from faith. For when she said, “I did not laugh,” this was done from faith. Thus unbelief was removed and faith was introduced.

“By faith,” he says, “Sarah herself received power to conceive”—and to retain—offspring. She received power although she was already dead and barren. There were two obstacles: one arising from time, since she had grown old, and another from nature, since she was barren. [Col. 0794A]

“Therefore also, from one man, all were born like the stars of heaven and like the sand on the seashore.” Therefore, he says, all were born from one—not only meaning that she gave birth, but also that she became the mother of as many as even fertile women could not produce.

“Like the stars of heaven,” he says. How, then, does he count them more than once, when he said, “Just as the stars of heaven cannot be numbered, so neither can your seed”? Either he spoke hyperbolically, or certainly he meant all those who are continually begotten from that origin.

“All these died according to faith, without receiving the promises.”

Here it is worthy to ask two questions: first, how, after saying above, “Enoch was translated and was not found, so that he would not see death,” he now says, “All these died according to faith”; and again, after saying above, “not receiving the promises,” he says that Noah received a reward for the salvation of his household, that Enoch was translated, that Abel still speaks, and that Abraham received the land. Yet he says, “According to faith all these died without receiving the promise.”

What, then, does this mean? It seems necessary first to resolve the first question, and then the second.

“All these,” he says, “died according to faith.” Here he says “all” not because all died, but because, apart from that one, all those whom we know to have died did die.

What he said—“without receiving the promises”—is true. For this promise did not concern Noah. Isaac and Jacob perhaps received the land of promise. But what recompenses did Noah, Abel, and Enoch receive? Either he spoke of these three, or, if he also spoke of the others, it was not a promise that they should receive the land, but rather that Abel should be admired, Enoch translated, and Noah saved.

Indeed, these things came to them because of virtue. They were, however, libations and first tastes of future things. From the beginning God knew that the human race needed great humility and condescension. Therefore he not only grants us the things that are to come, but also provides us with the things of this life, just as he said to his disciples:

“Whoever has left houses, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life” (Matt. XIX).

And again:

“Seek the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. VI).

[Col. 0794D] “But seeing them from afar and greeting them.” Here he signifies something mystical: for all the things spoken there concerning the future have come to pass—concerning the resurrection, the kingdom of heaven, and the other matters that Christ, when he came, proclaimed. For he says these are the promises. Either this is what he means, or certainly that they did not actually receive them, but departed from here in confidence because of them. For they trusted by faith alone.

“Seeing them from afar.” They trusted in them so greatly that they even greeted them. He says this by a metaphor drawn from sailors, who, when they look upon cities desired from afar before entering them, anticipate their arrival with a greeting and make those cities familiar to themselves.

“And confessing that they are strangers and sojourners upon the earth.” (Joan.) The first virtue—and the whole of virtue—is to be a stranger and sojourner in this world, to have nothing in common with the affairs of this age, but to remove oneself from them like a stranger, as also did those blessed men of whom he says: “They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, afflicted, tormented, of whom the world was not worthy” (below). For they called themselves strangers. Paul, however, said something more: he did not call himself a stranger, but dead to the world, and the world dead to him. “The world,” he says, “has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI).

[Greg.] But what people sojourns in this world except the one that, running toward the lot of the elect, knows that it has a homeland in heaven, and hopes all the more to find its own possessions there because here it doubts that everything passing away is alien to it? The people, therefore, are strangers—the entire number of the elect—who, regarding this life as a kind of exile, sigh with the whole intention of their hearts for their heavenly homeland. Of them Paul says: “Confessing that they are strangers and sojourners upon the earth. For those who say such things make it clear that they are seeking a homeland.”

The same Apostle endured this sojourn when he said: “While we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (II Cor. V). “For we walk by faith, not by sight.” He sought to avoid the hardships of this sojourn when he said: “Having the desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. I). And again: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (ibid.).

The Psalmist felt the weight of this sojourn when he said: “Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged. I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been a long-time sojourner” (Ps. CXIX). How often he longed to be delivered from it, burning with heavenly desires and saying: “My soul thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of my God?” (Ps. XLI.) But those who fix their hearts upon earthly pleasures do not know this desire. For while they love only visible things, they certainly do not love invisible things—even if they believe that they exist—because, while they follow external things too closely, they become carnal even in mind.

(Joan.) “They were strangers and sojourners,” he says, the saints. In what way and manner? But where does Abraham confess that he is a stranger and sojourner? Perhaps we shall find that he himself also confessed this. David, however, did confess it: “I am a stranger,” he says, “as all my fathers were” (Ps. XXXVIII). Those who lived in tents and purchased burial places with money were plainly strangers, since they did not even possess a place where they could bury their own dead.

What, then, does this mean? Were they saying that they were strangers in that land which is in Palestine? By no means, but in the whole world—and rightly so. For they saw nothing in it of what they desired; everything was foreign and alien to them. They desired to cultivate virtue, but in this world there was much iniquity, and everything was foreign to them. They had no friend and no familiar companion except a few. Their concern was not with the things of this world; and they demonstrated this not only in words but also in their very circumstances and deeds.

[Col. 0796A] How? God said to Abraham: “Leave your homeland”—the land thought to be his homeland—“and come to a foreign land.” He was not held back by affection for his own people; but, like a stranger departing from a foreign land, he left that homeland without any reluctance. He said to him: “Offer me your son”; and he offered him as though he had no son. He possessed his money in common with passersby and regarded it as nothing; he yielded precedence to others; he exposed himself to dangers; he endured ten thousand hardships. He did not build splendid houses, he did not indulge himself, nor was he concerned about clothing, all of which are customary in this life. Rather, he practiced everything that belongs to the heavenly city: hospitality, brotherly love, almsgiving, patience, contempt for money, contempt for present glory, and contempt for all the other things that exist in this world.

[Col. 0796B] His son, too, was of the same character: he was harassed, suffered persecution, was attacked, yielded, and obeyed, as one established among strangers. For strangers endure whatever they suffer, since they are not in their homeland. Even when his wife was taken away, he endured this also, as one living among strangers. Everything he did belonged to the heavenly homeland, displaying chastity and integrity. For after he had betrothed her, he did not live with that woman; only after the vigor of youth had passed did he take her, showing that he did this not for the sake of lust but in service and obedience to the divine promise.

And what of Jacob? Was he not seeking only bread and clothing, the things that belong to strangers who fall into great poverty? Did he not depart under persecution like a stranger? Was he not a hired laborer? Did he not everywhere endure ten thousand hardships like a stranger?

“For those who say such things make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. And indeed, if they had remembered the one from which they had departed, they would certainly have had opportunity to return; but now they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly one.” (Joan.) Oh, what a difference! They were in labor every day, desiring to be freed from this life and to return to their homeland; but we do the opposite. If a fever comes upon us, we abandon everything and, like little weeping children, fear death. And rightly do we suffer this, for we conduct ourselves in this life as strangers, not like those hastening toward their homeland, but like those going to punishment.

Therefore we grieve and fear, because we have not used these things as we ought, but have overturned the proper order; therefore we lament when we ought rather to rejoice. For this reason we are terrified like murderers and leaders of brigands when they are being led before the tribunal, considering all the evils they have committed—and therefore fearing and trembling. But those fathers were not like this; they hastened toward rest.

Paul also groaned together with them: “We ourselves,” he says, “groan while we are in this world, being burdened” (II Cor. V). Such were Abraham and the others. They were strangers in this entire world and were seeking a homeland. Was it the one they had left? By no means. For what prevented them, if they wished, from returning and becoming citizens again? But they were seeking the one that is in heaven, and they hastened to depart from here. Thus they pleased God.

“Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.” Oh, what dignity—that he should deign to be called their God! This is great, truly great, and a sign of immense blessedness. He is called the God of earth and heaven, just as he is called the God of the pagans, because he himself created and established all things. But he is not called the God of those holy men in that manner, but as one would call him the intimate friend of someone.

Just as he can be called not merely the God of the nations but the God of the whole world, so he could be called the God of Abraham. But you do not know how great this dignity is, because we do not even attain to it. For just as the Lord God is now called the God of Christians, and yet this name exceeds our dignity, how much greater is it if he is called the God of one person? Consider the greatness of this: although he is called the God of the world, he is not ashamed to be called the God of three men.

But suppose that these men called themselves strangers because of their sojourning. What of David? Was he not a king? Was he not a prophet? Did he not live in his own homeland? Why, then, did he say: “I am a stranger and a sojourner”? Tell us, holy David, how are you a stranger. “As my fathers were,” he says, “because they too were strangers.” “We have a homeland,” he says, “a true homeland.” How, then, are you a stranger? “On earth,” he says. Therefore they too were strangers on earth. “As they were,” he says, “so also am I.”

As this man was, then, so were they also. Let us therefore become strangers as well, so that God may not be ashamed to be called our God. For it is a disgrace to him when he is called the God of evil people, and he himself brings disgrace upon them, just as he is glorified when he is called the God of good and excellent people who cultivate virtue.

For if we avoid being called the masters of wicked servants and abandon them, and if someone, addressing us, says, “That man does many evil things—is he your servant?” do we not immediately say, “Certainly not,” rejecting the dishonor? For there is a relationship between servant and master, and disgrace passes from one to the other . . . . But they were so illustrious and so full of confidence that God was not only not ashamed when he was called their God, but even said to them: “I am the God of Abraham, and so forth” (Moses in the *Collation*).

In the Gospel, too, the Lord says more explicitly to the Sadducees: “Have you not read what was spoken by God, who says to you: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matt. XXII).

For all those men live. Concerning them the Apostle says: “Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.” That they are neither idle after the separation of this body nor devoid of sensation is also shown by the Gospel parable (Luke XVI), which is told about the poor Lazarus and the rich man dressed in purple. One of them earned the most blessed place—that is, rest in Abraham’s bosom—while the other is burned by the intolerable heat of eternal fire.

And if we also attend to what is said to the thief, “Today you will be with me in paradise,” what else does it plainly signify than that souls continue not only to retain their former understanding, but also to enjoy, by a fitting corresponding recompense, the condition appropriate to the character of their dispositions and actions? The Lord would never have promised this to him if he had known that his soul, after the separation from the flesh, would either be deprived of sensation or dissolved into nothingness. For it was not his flesh but his soul that was to enter paradise with Christ.

“By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested, and he offered his only-begotten son, he who had received the promises, to whom it had been said: ‘In Isaac shall your offspring be called’; for he considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, and from there he received him back in a parable.” (Joan.) Truly great was Abraham’s faith. God’s commandments seemed to contend with God’s commandments; faith seemed to oppose faith; and God’s commandment was contrary to the promise. For it is written: “God said: Leave your land and your kindred, and I will give you this land.” Yet he did not give him that land as an inheritance, not even the space of a footstep.

Do you see how the things commanded appear to be contrary to the promises? Again he said: “For in Isaac shall your offspring be called,” and Abraham believed. And again he says: “Sacrifice him to me”—the one from whose offspring the whole world was to be filled. Do you perceive the conflict between commandments and promises? He commanded things contrary to the promises; yet that righteous man was neither bewildered nor said that he had been deceived.

He heard from the very one who had made the promises things contrary to the promises, and he was not troubled, but acted as though they were harmonious—and in truth they were harmonious. They appeared contrary to human reasoning, but they were harmonious with faith. When the Apostle said, “Considering that God is able even to raise him from the dead,” he showed that, by the very faith through which Abraham had believed that God would give him a son when none existed, he also believed that God could raise the dead. He added that by this same faith he believed that the one who had been killed could be raised.

Human reasoning found it equally doubtful that a son should be given from a dead and aged womb, already incapable of bearing, and that one who had been killed should afterward be raised. But faith is both leader and guide, going before us toward the future.

“By faith,” he says, “he offered Isaac when he was tested.” There was no other reason for that offering than this. Then he unfolds the whole meaning. For lest anyone should say that Abraham had another son and hoped that the promise would be fulfilled through him, and therefore offered Isaac confidently: “He was offering,” he says, “even his only-begotten son, he who had received the promises.”

What do you mean, “only-begotten”? What, then, was Ishmael? “Only-begotten,” he says, I call him insofar as the matter of the promise is concerned. Therefore, after saying “only-begotten,” he added “Isaac,” wishing to show why he was only-begotten: “to whom it had been said, ‘In Isaac shall your offspring be called.’”

Do you see how he marvels at what the patriarch did? “In Isaac,” he says, “shall your offspring be called,” and yet he offered his son to be killed. Then, lest anyone should think that he did this in despair, and that through this command he had lost faith in the promise, he makes clear that this too was truly an act of faith. He possessed that faith even though it appeared to oppose this command; but it did not oppose it.

For he did not measure God’s power by human reasoning; he did everything by faith. Therefore he is not afraid to say: “God is able even to raise him from the dead.” Hence he received him back in a parable—that is, as an example. When the ram had been killed, Isaac was saved. Accordingly, he received him back through the ram, killing the ram in his place.

These things were forms and figures: for here it is the Son of God who is killed. And contemplate the greatness of God’s mercy. Since a great gift was to be given to humanity, he wished not to make it appear a gift but rather something owed. He first persuaded a man to hand over his own son in obedience to God’s command, so that, when he himself handed over his Son, he would not appear to be doing anything great, since a human being had done this before him; thus the act would appear not as grace but as the repayment of a debt.

“Hence,” he says, “he received him back in a parable”—that is, as in a likeness. The ram was, as it were, a parable and a type of Isaac. Since the sacrifice was complete, and Isaac was killed as far as Abraham’s intention was concerned, God therefore gave him back to the patriarch.

“By faith, concerning things to come, Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau.” “Many prophets and righteous people,” he says, “desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luke X). Did the righteous know all future things? If the Son was not revealed to some because of their weakness, since they could not receive him, then he was rightly revealed to those who shone with the glory of virtue. Paul also says that they knew future things, that is, the resurrection of Christ.

But when he says “concerning things to come,” he does not mean the future age, but things future within this age. Do you see that what he said concerning Abraham can also be said concerning Jacob? They did not receive the blessings; those blessings were bestowed upon their descendants, while he himself attained what was future.

For we find that his brother was more prosperous in this world. Jacob, however, passed his entire life in hired service, dangers, ambushes, deceptions, and fears. When questioned by Pharaoh, he said: “My days have become few.” Esau, however, lived in precedence and great confidence. Where, then, did good things come to Jacob, if not in the future?

“Concerning things to come,” he says, “Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau.” Although Esau was the elder, he places Jacob first because of his virtue. Do you see how great his faith was, and from what source such great blessings were promised to their children? Certainly from faith—that is, from believing God.

“By faith Jacob, when he was dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph and worshiped the top of his staff.” Here it is necessary to set out all the blessings, so that his faith and prophecy may also become evident.

“And he worshiped,” he says, “the top of his staff.” Here, he says, he did not merely pronounce a prediction, but trusted concerning the future as though he were demonstrating it by deed. Since another king was to arise from Ephraim, therefore he said: “And he worshiped the top of his staff.”

Behold, even when he was already old, all the peoples worshiped Joseph—signifying the worship that was to belong to him in the future. This had already begun to be fulfilled when his brothers worshiped him. It was to occur again later through the ten tribes. Do you understand how he foretold the future? Do you see how much faith he possessed? How he believed concerning future things?

Some things are examples of patience alone: how evils are to be endured, and that good things are not received here, as happened with Abraham and Abel. Other things are examples of faith, as happened with Noah: that there is a God and that there is retribution. Faith has many forms in this life, because there is retribution, because things are not to be endured in the same manner, and because one must struggle before receiving gifts or crowns.

But what happened in the case of Jacob is an example of faith alone, because God promised Abraham: “I will give this land to you and to your offspring.”

“By faith Joseph, when he was dying, remembered the departure of the children of Israel and gave orders concerning his bones.” Joseph heard this while still established in a foreign land. He had not yet seen the promise fulfilled, yet even so his spirit did not collapse. He believed so firmly that he spoke about their departure and gave instructions concerning his bones.

He did not believe alone; he also led others into faith, so that they would always remember that he would never have given instructions concerning his bones unless he had confidently hoped for their return with complete faith.

“By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they did not fear the king’s command.” It is necessary to speak about Moses’ parents. Pharaoh had ordered all male infants to be killed, and no one escaped this danger. From where, then, did these people hope that they could save the child? “From faith,” he says.

What kind of faith? They saw that the infant was beautiful, and his very appearance drew them toward faith. Thus, from the beginning, from his very cradle, much grace had been infused into that righteous man—not through nature’s action, but through divine grace. This grace also stirred that barbarian Egyptian woman to love him, take him, and seize him. Yet the faith of Moses’ parents did not possess an adequate proof.

What, then, and how much was it, that they should believe merely from his appearance? “But you,” he says, “believe from the events themselves, and you will have many pledges of faith.” That you might receive with joy the seizure of your possessions, and that whatever such things you have suffered was accomplished through faith and patience.

But because these people also believed and afterward were afflicted with faintheartedness, he shows that their faith too was stretched over a long period, as happened with Abraham, although the events themselves appeared to contradict one another: “They did not fear,” he says, “the king’s command.” That command was indeed carried out in deed, whereas this is suspicion and bare fear—and this belonged to the parents.

Then he presents an example familiar and close to them, or rather one greater and more exalted than theirs: “By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter.”

It is as though he were saying to them: None of you has abandoned a spacious and splendid royal palace, or such treasures; none, though he could have been a king’s son, has despised them as Moses did. And to show that he did not simply leave them, he says: “He refused”—that is, he recoiled from them and rejected them.

With heaven set before him, it was pointless to admire the palace of the Egyptian kingdom. And see how wonderfully Paul expressed this. He did not say that he considered heaven, and the things in heaven, greater riches than the treasures of Egypt; rather, he said, “the reproach of Christ.” For he judged it better to endure reproach for Christ than to live in luxury.

“Choosing rather to be afflicted with the people of God than to have the enjoyment of sin for a time.” You suffer for yourselves, but he chose this for the sake of others and willingly threw himself into such great dangers, although he could have lived piously and enjoyed worldly goods, rather than “having,” as he says, “the enjoyment of sin for a time.”

He regarded unwillingness to be afflicted with others as sin; he considered this itself to be sin. If, then, he judged it a sin not to suffer gladly with the others, affliction is clearly a great good, since from the height of royal dignity he threw himself into it.

For he did these things while looking ahead to great matters: “Considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking toward the reward.”

What is “the reproach of Christ”? It means enduring such reproaches as you now endure, such as Christ also endured. And how did Moses endure reproach for Christ? “For the rock was Christ.” Thus he too endured reproach, just as we endure reproach, because we suffer evils while hastening to God.

He also endured reproach when he heard: “Do you intend to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?” This is the reproach of Christ: to suffer evils to the very end and last breath, just as Christ himself also endured reproaches and heard: “If you are the Son of God.” He heard this from those for whom he was being crucified, that is, from his own fellow people.

This is the reproach of Christ: when someone suffers reproach from his own household, or from those to whom he has done a kindness. For Christ too suffered these things in return for his kindness. In this respect the reproach belongs more to Christ than to Moses, because Christ suffered these things from his own people. He endured reproach and patiently bore everything while they shook their heads at him.

Since they might perhaps, after hearing these things, desire a reward for themselves as well, he says that both Christ and Moses suffered such things. Therefore, he says, luxury and ease belong to the portion of sin, but enduring reproaches belongs to Christ.

“By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the king’s anger, for he endured as though seeing the invisible one.” What do you mean, that he did not fear? Yet Scripture says that when he heard, he was afraid, and for that reason he gained safety through flight and returned from flight. Nevertheless, his return again was an act of a spirit that entrusted itself to God.

He did not say: “Since they are seeking me and searching for me, I will not entrust myself to those very people.” Accordingly, the fact that he returned from flight was also an act of faith.

What, then? “He did not remain,” he says, lest he throw himself into manifest danger. For that would already have been an act of testing God: to leap into the midst of dangers and say, “Let us see whether God will deliver me.” The devil said this even to Christ: “Throw yourself down.”

Do you see that it is diabolical for someone needlessly and excessively to cast himself into danger, testing whether God will save him? Moreover, Moses could no longer preside over those people and govern them, so ungratefully were they disposed toward the one who had done so much for them. It was therefore foolish and senseless to remain there.

All these things happened because he endured as though seeing the invisible one. In their actions people fear those whom they see bodily; they do not consider God present to them because they do not see him. In contrast, Moses is praised because, while he despised the king of Egypt and obeyed God’s commands, he endured as though seeing the invisible one.

He cast the perverse ruler of the earth away from the eyes of his heart, as though he did not see him; but he endured the invisible king as though seeing him, because he did not turn the eye of his mind away from fear of him.

If, then, we always see God with the mind, if we continually turn our mind toward his remembrance, everything will easily appear to us, everything will become bearable, we shall endure everything lightly, and we shall become superior to all things.

For if someone sees a beloved person—or rather, remembers him—he lifts up his soul and becomes exalted in mind, so that he can easily endure everything, delighting in the memory of that person. Whoever keeps in mind the one who has deigned truly to love us, and remembers him, cannot feel grief or fear anything terrible or dangerous.

“By faith he celebrated the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so that the one who destroyed the firstborn might not touch them.” Paul commonly argues through many matters even in the midst of his discourse, and his statements are densely packed. Such is the grace of the Holy Spirit: it does not contain a few ideas in an abundance of words, but possesses great and abundant meaning in a brief expression.

Consider, therefore, how, under the occasion of exhortation and while discussing faith, he recalls the types of which they are examples, and how great is the mystery of which we possess the fulfillment.

“By faith,” he says, “he celebrated the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so that the one who destroyed the firstborn might not touch them.” The lamb’s blood was sacrificed in the house, and the doorposts were smeared with the blood; this was protection from the Egyptian destruction.

If, then, the blood of a lamb, in the midst of the Egyptians and amid such great destruction, preserved the Jews unharmed, how much more will it save us, as we smear not doorposts but our souls with the blood of Christ?

Even now the destroyer prowls in the depths and in the night. But let us put on the weapons of righteousness—that is, that sacrifice. He calls the sprinkling of blood an anointing. For God led us out of Egypt, that is, out of darkness and idolatry.

Although what was being done was nothing in itself, what was accomplished through it was great. What was being done was the pouring out of blood; what was accomplished was salvation, protection, and the prevention of destruction. The angel feared that blood, for he knew whose type it was; he trembled, understanding the Lord’s death. Therefore he did not touch the doorposts.

Moses said: “Anoint them,” and they anointed them, and they confessed. But you, possessing the blood of the Lamb himself, do not trust?

“By faith they crossed the Red Sea as through dry land; when the Egyptians attempted it, they were swallowed up.” Again he compares the perfected people with the people of one place, lest they say, “We cannot do what the righteous were able to do.”

“By faith,” he says, “they crossed the Red Sea as through dry land; when the Egyptians attempted it, they were swallowed up.” Here he brings them to the remembrance of the sufferings they endured in Egypt.

How so? Because they hoped by faith to cross the Red Sea, and for this reason they prayed; or rather, Moses was the one who prayed. Do you see that everywhere faith surpasses human reasoning and overcomes human weakness and lowliness?

Do you see that as soon as they believed, they also escaped punishments—at one time through the blood on the doorposts, and now through the Red Sea? This also showed that it truly was water in which those who came against them were swallowed up. From this it became clear that it was not an illusion, but that it demonstrated the reality of events, just as in the case of the lions that devoured them, and as in the furnace in which they were burned (Dan. VI, III).

So now you see the same things proving beneficial to some for salvation and grace, but to others for destruction. So great a good is faith that even when we have reached some kind of despair, we are then delivered—even if we come to the very point of death, even if everyone despairs of us.

For what hope was there? On one side were the Egyptians, on the other the sea, and they themselves were unarmed. If they tried to flee, they would either perish in the sea or fall into the hands of the Egyptians. Nevertheless, he delivered them from the greater despair. The sea itself was spread beneath them like land, while it drowned the Egyptians like the sea: there, it had forgotten its nature; here, it was even armed against them.

“By faith the walls of Jericho fell after they had been encircled for seven days.” It was not the sound of trumpets that cast down the stones of the walls—even if someone sounded trumpets for ten thousand years—but faith accomplishes everything.

Do you see that everywhere the course of events and the law of nature are altered, and that everything takes place beyond hope? Therefore here too everything happens beyond hope. Since he was saying again and again that one must believe and be guided by hopes of the future, he developed this entire discourse, showing that from the beginning all miracles were obtained and accomplished through faith—not only now.

“By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with the unbelievers, having received the spies in peace.” Therefore it would be exceedingly shameful if they had proved more faithless than a prostitute. Yet she heard men announcing these things and immediately believed.

The result also followed upon her faith: while everyone else perished, she alone was saved. She did not say to herself, “I shall perish with the majority.” She did not say, “Can I be wiser than these wise men who do not believe, while I believe?” She said nothing of the kind, but believed their words—that those things could come to pass.

“And what more shall I say? For time will fail me as I enumerate.” (John.) He no longer gives names; but, making an end with the prostitute and arousing their shame by the character of the person, he no longer expands the recollection of the histories, lest he seem to prolong his discourse. Nevertheless, he does not explain them, but passes rapidly over them, doing both things very wisely: avoiding delay without removing the density of his statements. For he neither kept entirely silent nor became burdensome by speaking; rather, he accomplished both. When someone contends bravely, if he persists in the contest, he tires his audience. Whoever wishes to become burdensome to one who already believes through the length of his discourse incurs a reputation for self-display. One must look to usefulness and adapt oneself accordingly.

“Of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David and Samuel, and the prophets, who through faith conquered kingdoms.” In this passage some criticize Paul because he places Barak, Samson, and Jephthah among these men. What do you say? He includes a prostitute, and should he not include these men? Do not now tell me about another life of theirs; ask instead whether they did not believe, even if they did not shine in faith. “And the prophets,” he says, “who through faith subdued kingdoms.” “They practiced righteousness; they obtained promises.” Who are these whom he mentions? Here he means the mercy that David possessed. For I think that he is speaking about him when he says: “They obtained promises.” What promises? Those concerning which it was said that his seed would sit upon his throne.

“They stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the force of fire, escaped the edge of the sword.” Consider how they were in the midst of death: Daniel among the lions; the three young men walking in the furnace; the Israelites, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob amid various trials—and even so they did not despair. This is faith: that when circumstances turn against us, then we believe, because nothing contrary has happened, but everything has come in due sequence and order.

“They escaped the mouths of swords.” I think that he is again speaking of the three young men. “They recovered strength from weakness, became mighty in war, routed foreign armies, received back their dead through resurrection.” He signifies the period after their return from Babylon. “From weakness,” I think, means from captivity, when Jewish affairs were already in despair, when they were scarcely different from the dead. Who did not despair that they could return from Babylon? And I do not mean merely return, but also become stronger.

“They routed foreign armies.” But, he says, nothing of this kind has happened to you. Yet these things are patterns of what is to come.

“Women received back their dead through resurrection.” He refers to what occurred in the case of the prophets, signifying Elisha and Elijah, who raised the dead.

“Others were tortured, refusing release, in order to obtain a better resurrection.” Others, he says, were tortured, refusing release so that they might attain a better resurrection. For why, tell me, did they not wish to live in the present life? Was it not because they were awaiting a better one? When they raised others, they themselves nevertheless desired to die. It is therefore clear that they refused release in order to attain a better resurrection—not, however, one like the resurrection received by the sons of those women. Here it seems to me that he signifies John and James, for “torture” means decapitation. They could have seen the sun; they could have refrained from reproving; but they chose rather to die, even while raising others, in order to attain a better resurrection.

“Others experienced mockeries and scourges, and in addition bonds and imprisonments; they were stoned, they were sawn apart, they died by the slaughter of the sword.” With these he brings the list to an end, because they were joined to his hearers by the closest resemblance, and because these examples especially brought them consolation. When someone is held in the same cause, or in the same suffering and sadness, he receives comfort from the similarity of one who suffers with him. Otherwise, even if one speaks of a worse suffering, if it has not arisen from the same cause, it is of no benefit. Therefore he concludes his discourse here, naming bonds, prisons, scourges, and stonings, signifying Stephen and Zechariah. For this reason he adds: “They died by the slaughter of the sword.”

What do you say? Some escaped the mouths of swords, while others perished by the slaughter of the sword. What does this mean? Which of these things do you praise or admire—this one or that one? “This one,” he says … This is closer to you, while the other is praiseworthy, because faith prevailed even in the face of death itself, and because it is a type of things to come.

“They wandered about in sheepskins, in goatskins.” Always, but especially when I recall the virtues and upright deeds of the saints, despair of myself comes upon me, because we do not even receive in dreams an experience of the good things that those men practiced throughout their lives. They were not suffering punishments for sins, but were always advancing toward righteousness and were always afflicted.

I seem to understand Elijah, to whom our discourse has now reached. For he names him in this passage, and the examples end with him, since this was especially familiar and characteristic of these people. After mentioning what happened to the apostles—that they died by the slaughter of the sword, were stoned, and so forth—he returns to Elijah, who suffered the same things. Perhaps, since they did not yet hold so high an opinion of the apostles, he appropriately makes his discourse from the one who was taken up, who was held in the greatest admiration. Through him, therefore, he wished to bring encouragement and consolation.

“Needy, afflicted, tormented, of whom the world was not worthy.” (Gregory.) Of these the Lord also speaks figuratively to Job:

“Who is it that sent the wild ass free  
and loosed his bonds?  
He made its dwelling a wilderness  
and its shelters salt ground.  
It mocks the multitude of the city  
and does not hear the complaint of the tax collector;  
it surveys the mountains of its pasture  
and seeks every green thing.” (Job XXXIX.)

In the Psalms also:

“Let those redeemed by the Lord say so,  
whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy;”

and shortly afterward:

“They wandered in the wilderness, in a dry place,  
and found no road to an inhabited city.  
Hungry and thirsty,  
their soul fainted within them.  
And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted,  
and he delivered them from their necessities.” (Psalm CVI.)

Jeremiah also describes them in this way:

“Blessed is the one who has borne the yoke from his youth.  
He will sit alone and keep silence,  
because he has borne it upon himself.” (Lamentations III.)

They also echo, in feeling and deed, the words of the Psalmist:

“I have become like a pelican of the wilderness;  
I have kept vigil and become like a solitary sparrow on the roof.” (Psalm CI.)

(John.) There are two miracles of faith: it obtains great things, and it suffers great things, counting suffering as nothing. And you cannot say, he says, that they were sinners and insignificant people. If you compare them with the whole world on the other side, I find them superior in the weight of their virtue, drawing down the balance and standing far more honorable. What, then, could they receive here?

(Rab.) Here he stirs their minds so that they may not cling to present things, but may think on what is above and on what surpasses everything in this life, since the whole world is unworthy in comparison with them. What, then, do you wish to receive in this life? It is an insult if you receive your reward in this life. Let us therefore not think in worldly terms, nor seek repayment in this life; let us not be so impoverished. If the whole world is not worthy of them, why do you seek some part of it? And rightly so, for they are friends of God.

By “the world” here he means either the multitude of human beings, or creation itself, or both; Scripture commonly calls both of these “the world.” If the whole creation, he says, were set alongside all human beings, it would never be worthy in comparison with them. And rightly so. Just as ten thousand measures of straw or hay are not worthy in comparison with pearls, so neither are they worthy in comparison with these men. “Better,” he says, “is one who does the will of God than ten thousand wicked people.” By ten thousand he does not mean merely many, but an immeasurable multitude. Understand, then, how great the righteous person is.

Jesus son of Nave said:

“Let the sun stand still at Gibeon  
and the moon over the valley of Aijalon”;  
and it happened so. (Joshua X.)

Let the whole world come—or rather two, three, four, ten, and twenty—and let them say and do this; they will not be able. But the friend of God commanded the creatures, the friends of his friend. Rather, he asked his friend, and the servants obeyed; and the man who was below commanded those above.

“Wandering in deserts and mountains and caves, and in the holes of the earth.” (John.) They did not even have clothing, he says; such was the excess of their tribulation. They had no city, no house, no shelter. Christ also said this: “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” What do I mean by saying that they had no shelter? They were not even permitted to remain standing. For when they came to the deserts themselves, they were not at leisure. He did not say, “They sat in the deserts,” but that even there they fled and were driven from place to place—not merely out of the inhabited world, but even from uninhabitable places … [lacuna] what happened there.

So it is, he says: they blame us because of Christ. But what fault could they find with Elijah? They drove him away and pursued him, and forced him to struggle with hunger; and these men were then suffering the same things.

“He determined to send them,” he says, “brothers—the disciples who were afflicted. According to the ability each possessed, each of them determined to send aid to the brothers living in Judea.” This also applied to these men.

“Afflicted,” he says, and suffering hardship on journeys and amid dangers.

“And all these, having been approved through the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise, God having provided something better for us, so that they should not be perfected without us.” Like exiles and fugitives, he says, like those caught in disgrace, they seemed to be unworthy. They found no refuge even in the deserts, but were always fleeing and seeking various places of escape; they wished to bury themselves alive and were always in fear.

What, then, is the reward, or what such recompense and return? “They have not yet,” he says, “received their reward,” but still remain. Even though they have died, and amid such great tribulation, they have not yet received it. They have had so much time since they conquered, and still have not received it.

But you, engaged in the contest, are distressed. Understand, therefore, what it means for Abraham and the apostle Paul to sit and wait until the completion, so that then they may be able to receive their reward. For unless we too have gone there, the Father has declared that he will not give them their reward—just as a good father, who loves his children, tells worthy children who have completed their work that he will not give them food until their other brothers have also arrived.

You are anxious because you have not yet received your reward. What, then, will Abel do, who conquered before all the others and still sits without a crown? What will Noah do? What will the others of those times do? For behold, they have waited for you, and they are waiting for others who will come after you.

You see that in this respect we surpass them: for concerning us he said, “God provided something better.” So that they might not seem to possess more than we do, if they were crowned before us, he appointed one time for all the crowns; and the one who conquered so many years ago will receive the crown together with you.

Do you contemplate the divine care and love? He did not say, “So that they might not be crowned without us,” but “so that they might not be perfected without us.” For then they will indeed appear complete. They preceded us in the contests, but they do not precede us in the crown. He did not injure them, but honored us. For they too gladly await you as brothers.

If we are all one body, the joy of the body is thereby increased when it is crowned together and collectively, not in separate parts. Indeed, the righteous are marvelous in this also: just as they rejoice in their own blessings, so they rejoice in the blessings of their brothers. Therefore this too proceeds according to their desire: that they may be crowned with their brothers and glorified together.

## CHAPTER XII

The Apostle urges his people to endure the evils of punishment and avoid the evils of sin, showing the conditions of the old and the new law.

“Therefore, since we too have so great a cloud of witnesses imposed upon us, laying aside every weight and the sin that surrounds us, let us run with endurance the contest set before us.” (John.) In many places Scripture draws consolation from the ancestors through matters that come to hand, just as the prophets commonly speak “of heat and hardship, of rains,” and so forth …

This too he says here: the remembrance of those saints, like a cloud kindled by a fiery ray … thus arouses and refreshes the soul oppressed by evils. He did not say, “Appearing above us,” but “imposed upon us,” which was stronger. Thus he gives us greater confidence through the cloud and mass of witnesses.

And rightly he called them witnesses. He signified not only those who were in the New Testament, but also those who were in the Old. For they too bore witness to the divine majesty: the three young men, Elijah, and all the prophets.

“Laying aside,” he says, “everything.” Everything that he mentions? Sleep, anxiety, low thoughts, everything human. “And the sin,” he says, “that surrounds us.” He said “surrounds,” either because it easily encircles us or because it can itself easily be encircled. I think, however, that the latter is what he means: if we wish, we easily prevail over sin.

“With endurance,” he says, “let us run the contest set before us.” He did not say, “Let us fight as soldiers,” nor “let us struggle in athletic fashion,” nor “let us wage wars,” but named what is lighter than all these things, calling it a race. Nor did he say, “Let us add to our running,” but let us remain in the same course and not collapse.

“Let us run,” he says, “the contest set before us.” Then he adds the sum and head of the discourse. What he had placed first, he also places last: Christ.

“Looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.”

“Looking,” he says—that is, so that we may learn how to run. Just as children attend to their parents, and students in contests attend to their teachers, shaping their minds according to the teachers’ art and receiving certain rules through sight, so here also, if we wish to run and learn to run well toward Christ, let us attend to “Jesus, the author,” he says, “and perfecter of our faith.”

What does this mean? It means that he himself infuses faith into us. For he said to his disciples: “You did not choose me, but I chose you.” (John XV.) Paul also said the same: “Then I shall know, just as I have been known.” (1 Corinthians XIII.) He laid the beginning upon us, and he will also bring it to an end.

“Who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising shame.” It was possible for him, if he wished, to suffer nothing: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.” (1 Peter II.) As he himself also said in the Gospel: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.” (John XIV.)

It therefore lay within his power, if he wished, not to come to the cross: “I have authority,” he says, “to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again.” (John X.) If, then, the one who had no necessity of being crucified was crucified for us, how much more is it right that we should endure everything bravely?

“Who for the joy set before him,” he says, “endured the cross, despising shame.” What does “despising shame” mean? He endured, he says, a disgraceful death. Let us suppose that he was going to die; why also die disgracefully? For no other reason than to teach us to regard as nothing the glory bestowed by human beings. Therefore, although he was not subject to death, he accepted death, teaching us to take our stand against death and to consider it of no importance.

Why did he not say “despising sorrow,” but “despising shame”? Because he did not endure death with sorrow.

And what happened at the end? “He sat down,” he says, “at the right hand of the throne of God.” You see the reward, which Paul also learned, knowing it: “Therefore God highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus Christ every knee should bow.” (Philippians II.)

He signifies the one who is according to the flesh. But even if there were no reward, the example alone would have been sufficient to persuade us to endure everything. Now, however, rewards too are offered—not ordinary ones, but very great and unspeakable ones.

Therefore, whenever we suffer anything of this kind, let us think first of Christ, even before the apostles. Why? Because his whole life was filled with insults. He was always hearing that he was mad, a deceiver, and a magician. The Jews were saying: “No, but he deceives the people”; and again: “That deceiver said while he was still alive, ‘After three days I will rise again.’” (Matthew XXVII.) They again accused him of magical arts, saying: “He casts out demons by Beelzebul.” (Luke XI.) They said that he was mad and had a demon: “Are we not right in saying that he has a demon and is mad?” (John X.)

He heard these things from them while he was conferring benefits, working wonders, and displaying the works of God. If he had done nothing and nevertheless heard such things, it would not be remarkable. But when he was teaching what belonged to the truth, they called him a deceiver; and when he expelled demons, they said that he had a demon. This is a matter deserving great lamentation.

Do you also wish to hear the accusations that he endured, whether secretly or openly, and even from his disciples? To them also he said: “Do you too wish to go away?” (John VI.) Yet even by believers he was already being told, “You have a demon.”

Did he not always flee, at one time into Galilee and at another into Judea? Were not many trials inflicted upon him from his infancy? Did not his mother, while he was still an infant, take him down into Egypt?

For all these reasons he said: “Looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.”

Let us now turn our attention to what his disciples suffered. Let us read Paul’s words and hear him saying: “In great endurance, in afflictions, in hardships, in blows, in imprisonments.” (2 Corinthians XI.) And again: “To this very hour we are hungry and thirsty, naked and beaten, homeless, and we toil, working with our own hands. When cursed, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat.”

I ask: who has suffered even the smallest part of these things?

“As deceivers,” he says, “as dishonored, as having nothing.” And again: “Five times I received from the Jews forty lashes less one; three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; I spent a day and a night in the deep; often on journeys, in dangers, hardships, hunger,” and so forth.

And because these things were pleasing to God, hear him saying: “For this I pleaded with the Lord three times, and he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.’” “Therefore,” he says, “I will glory in my weaknesses, in tribulations, necessities, hardships, blows, and imprisonments, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me.” (2 Corinthians XII.)

Hear Christ also saying: “In the world you will have tribulation.” (John XVI.)

“Consider him who endured such contradiction from sinners against himself, so that you may not grow weary, fainting in your souls.” (John.) If the sufferings of those near us raise us up, how much eagerness do the sufferings of the Lord bring us? What have you not suffered? By passing over everything, he signified the whole through “contradiction.” One must also add such things as the blows he received on the head, mockeries, insults, reproaches, and derision. He indicated all these by the term “contradiction,” and not only these, but also the other sufferings connected with life—the sufferings of Christ and the sufferings of the apostles.

For he knew that this way was the better path of virtue, so much so that he himself, who had no need of it, proceeded along it. He knew to such an extent that tribulation is beneficial to us, and indeed is the cause of rest.

Hear him saying: “Unless someone takes up his cross and comes after me, he is not worthy of me.” (Luke X.) If you are a disciple, he says, imitate your teacher; this is what belongs to a disciple. But if he himself proceeded through tribulations while you wish to go to rest, you do not wish to travel the same road that he traveled, but another. How, then, will you follow without following? How will you be a disciple if you do not pursue the teacher’s footsteps?

Paul also said this: “We are weak, but you are strong; we are dishonored, but you are honored.” (1 Corinthians IV.) And how, he says, can this make sense if you pursue opposites? You are disciples, while we are teachers?

Tribulation, then, is a great good, dearly beloved brothers. For it accomplishes two great things: it cleanses from sin and makes people stronger.

What, someone may say, if it overturns and destroys someone? Does tribulation not do this? But if that happens, our indolence has caused it.

How, he asks? If we are sober-minded; if we entreat God not to let us be tempted beyond what we can bear; if we always hold fast to him; if we stand bravely and form our battle line while we have him as our helper—then, even if temptations rush upon us more violently than all the winds, they will be like straw and a leaf carried through the air.

Hear Paul saying: “In all these things we conquer.” (Romans VIII.) And again: “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us.” (Ibid.) And again: “The momentary lightness of tribulation is producing for us an immeasurable weight of eternal glory.” (2 Corinthians IV.)

Consider, then, what dangers, how many shipwrecks, continual tribulations, and other such things he calls light. Emulate this man of adamant, who conducted himself in this life as though he were already wearing a body to no purpose.

Are you in poverty? But you are not in the poverty in which Paul was, who was also tested by hunger, thirst, and nakedness. Nor did he suffer these things for one day; he endured them continually.

How is this certain? Observe him saying: “To this very hour we are hungry and thirsty and naked.” (1 Corinthians IV.) What a marvelous thing: although he possessed such glory in preaching, he nevertheless suffered so much. Perhaps he was spending the rest of his life in this condition when he wrote: “I know a man fourteen years ago—whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know.” (1 Corinthians XII.) And again: “After three years,” he says, “I went up to Jerusalem.” (Galatians I.) And again hear him saying: “It is better for me to die than for anyone to empty my glory.” (1 Corinthians IX.)

Not only this, but also, writing again, he said: “We have become like the refuse of the world.” (1 Corinthians IV.)

What, I ask, is worse than hunger and thirst? What is more severe than bitter cold? What is more dangerous than the plots of brothers, whom he even calls false brothers? Was he not called the world’s disease and a deceiver? Was he not called a subverter? Was he not beaten until he was bruised?

Let us hold these things in mind, dearly beloved brothers; let us consider them and keep them in our memory. We will never collapse, even if we suffer insults, even if robbery, even if ten thousand terrible things. May we prove worthy to appear approved in heaven, and everything here is bearable. May we fare well there, and the affairs of this life are nothing. These things are a shadow and a dream. Whatever they may be, let us hope for and look toward those things; these will appear as nothing to us, whether considered according to nature or according to time.

“You have not yet resisted to the point of blood in your struggle against sin, and you have forgotten the consolation that speaks to you as sons, saying:

‘My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord,  
and do not grow weary when you are reproved by him.  
For whom the Lord loves, he chastens;  
and he scourges every son whom he receives.’”

There are two kinds of discourse that seem opposed to one another, but which bring one another much assistance. Here he impressed both kinds upon them.

One kind occurs when we say that certain people have suffered many things. The soul in some way rests when it has many witnesses to its own sufferings, just as above he introduced the exhortation by saying: “Recall the former days, in which, after being enlightened, you endured a great contest of sufferings.” (Above, X.)

The other kind occurs when we say that someone has suffered nothing great. The former kind enables the soul overwhelmed by sorrows to rest and recover; the latter turns back and recalls a negligent and supine soul that has been made arrogant.

Therefore, so that the testimony just given might not generate pride in them, consider what Paul says: “You have not yet resisted to the point of blood against sin.” He did not immediately add what followed. First he showed them all who had resisted to the point of blood, and then he stated that the sufferings of Christ are a cause for glory. After that he passed more easily through the remaining points.

He did the same when writing to the Corinthians, saying: “No temptation has overtaken you except what is human.” (1 Corinthians X.) That is, a small temptation. This was highly suitable for lifting up the soul. For when someone thinks that he has reached the limit of everything, he persuades himself, from what has preceded, that he has accomplished no great deeds.

It is as though he were saying: You have not yet suffered death; you have suffered only the loss of money or honor; you have merely been driven about and persecuted. Christ shed his blood for you, but you have not yet suffered anything comparable for yourselves. He struggled for the truth unto death, fighting on your behalf, while you have not yet reached the dangers that threaten destruction.

“And you have forgotten,” he says, “the consolation.” That is, you have surrendered and collapsed.

“You have not yet resisted to the point of blood in your struggle against sin.” Here he also shows that sin was breathing fiercely against them and armed in various ways. The words “you have not resisted” are addressed to those standing there.

“And you have forgotten,” he says, “the consolation by which he speaks to you as to sons: ‘My son, do not be troubled by the discipline of the Lord, and do not grow weary when you are reproved by him.’”

After exhorting them from the events themselves, he then, in abundance, encourages them from the testimonies. “And do not faint,” he says, “when you are reproved by him.” Certainly these are God’s words, and they can bring them no small consolation when they understand that enduring such things is the work of God. For by his permission the righteous suffer various pressures, just as it was said to the apostle Paul: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.” He is the one who permits it.

“For whom the Lord loves, he reproves; and he scourges every son whom he receives.” You cannot say that some righteous person is free from tribulation, even if this seems so to us; we do not know the other calamities that he suffers. It is therefore necessary for every righteous person to pass through pressures and tribulations.

For Christ’s verdict is that “broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, but narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life.” (Matthew VII.) If life is reached by that way, and it is impossible to arrive there by any other route, it is certain that all who have been led to eternal life have passed through this narrow way.

“Persevere in discipline, as God offers himself to you as sons; for what son is there whom the father does not correct?” “In discipline,” he says, “persevere”—not in punishments or tortures.

Observe what Paul says. From the very thing by which they considered themselves abandoned, he says that they should rather believe that they are abandoned. It is as though he were saying: Because you have suffered so much, do you think that God hates or has abandoned you? If you were not suffering these things, then you would have more reason to suppose this. For if he scourges every son whom he receives, the one who is not scourged is plainly not numbered among the sons.

What, then, are the wicked—do they suffer no evils? How, he asks, do you say that every son is scourged? But he did not say that everyone who is scourged is a son; he said that every son is scourged. For he always and everywhere strikes and chastises the son. It cannot therefore be shown that one who is a son is not scourged.

There are indeed many wicked people who are scourged, such as murderers, robbers, sorcerers, and plunderers of tombs. But they suffer punishments for their own iniquity; they are not scourged as sons, but punished as the worst of criminals. We, however, are scourged as sons.

Then he begins to deal with them from common and public custom. Do you see how from every direction he draws arguments—from events, Scripture, various sayings, his own reasoning, analogies and examples, and the conduct of ordinary life?

“But if you are without discipline,” he says, “of which all these have become participants, then you are adulterers and not sons.” If you are without discipline, he says, consider that, as I have already stated, this confirms that one who is not chastised cannot be a son.

Just as in the households of heads of families, fathers neglect illegitimate children, as though they were not being taught and as though they were not being made honorable, but are very concerned for their own children, lest evil should overwhelm them through negligence, so, if not being chastised is characteristic of illegitimate children, we ought to rejoice when we are chastised, since this is applied to legitimate children. Therefore God deals with us as with sons.

“Then, indeed, we had fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we revered them; shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live?” Again he proceeds from the sufferings they themselves endured. For just as above he says, “Remember the former days,” so here also he says: God deals with you as with sons; and you cannot say, “We are unable to endure such things.” For if children revere their earthly fathers, how can you not revere the heavenly Father even more?

**(Seren.)** What could he have defined more clearly by this distinction, since he expressly declares that human beings are the fathers of our flesh, but that God alone is the Father of souls? Yet even in the formation of this body, human beings are to be credited only with the ministry, while the ultimate act of creation belongs to God, the Creator of all. David says: “Your hands made me and fashioned me” (Psalm 118). And blessed Job says: “Did you not milk me like milk, and curdle me like cheese? Did you not furnish me with bones and sinews” (Job 10). And the Lord says to Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jeremiah 1).

Ecclesiastes, moreover, clearly and properly gathers together the nature and origin of both substances—their beginning, from which each came forth, and their end, toward which each tends—and, at the same time, discusses the separation of this body and the soul, saying: “Before the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.” What could he have said more plainly than this: that he declares the substance of the flesh, which he calls dust because it takes its beginning from human seed and seems to be sown through human agency, as though taken from the earth, to return again to the earth; but that the spirit, which is not generated through the union of the two sexes but is bestowed individually by God alone, returns to its author? This is also clearly expressed by that breathing of the Lord by which he first gave life to Adam.

Thus, from these testimonies we plainly conclude that no one can be called the Father of spirits except God alone, who makes them from nothing whenever he wills; whereas human beings are called only the fathers of our flesh.

“We had,” he says, “our fleshly fathers as teachers and educators, and we revered them. Shall we not much more submit to the Father of spirits and live?” **(Joan.)** By “Father of spirits” he means either the giver of spiritual gifts, or of prayers, or of incorporeal virtues. For if we die in this way, then we shall live.

“And they, indeed, for a few days, according to their own will, instructed us; but he does so for what is beneficial, so that we may receive his sanctification.” The difference between them is not merely a distinction of persons—that they are earthly while he is heavenly—but also arises from the very cause and matter of their action. They do not instruct us for the same reason or toward the same ends. They instruct us according to what seems good to them—that is, fulfilling their own pleasure and desire—and they do not always consider what is useful or appropriate. This one, however, cannot be described in the same way. He does not do this for any pleasure of his own, but for our advantage. “They instructed you,” he says, “so that you might be useful to them,” sometimes perhaps even without reason; but here there is nothing of the kind.

Do you see that this also brought them worthy consolation? We are especially intimate with those whom we know do not command or instruct for their own sake, but whose entire and complete effort is expended on our behalf. This is the mark of sincere and perfect love: when the beloved is of no advantage to the lover, and yet the lover is said to instruct, train, and do everything for him—not in order to receive anything, but rather to give—and hastens in every way so that the beloved may become capable of receiving his gifts.

“For they,” he says, “instructed us for a few days according to their own will; but he does so for what is beneficial, so that we may receive his sanctification.” What is “his sanctification”? It is his purity, by which he makes us worthy, insofar as he is able. He therefore hastens so that you may receive it, and does everything in order to impart it to you; but you make no effort to become able to receive it.
