“I have said,” he says, “You are my Lord, for you have no need of my good things” (Psalm 15). “They,” he says, “instructed us for a few days according to their own will, for their will was not useful in all things; but this one trains us for what is beneficial.”

Discipline, therefore, is participation in holiness—especially when it drives away negligence, excludes desires, removes love of worldly things, turns the soul around, and makes it condemn everything belonging to this life. When these things take place, this is indeed affliction; but is holiness not thereby perfected? Does it not draw spiritual grace toward itself?

“Every discipline, however, at the present time seems not to be a matter of joy but of sorrow.” Those who drink bitter medicines patiently endure their unpleasantness at first, and then experience the benefit of health. Virtue is like this, and vice is like this as well. In vice there is pleasure at first, followed by sickness; in virtue there is sorrow at first, and then delight is produced. Yet it is not the same when someone is first saddened and afterward enjoys joy, as when someone first rejoices and afterward falls into sorrow. In the former case, hope of future delight diminishes present sorrow; in the latter, fear of future sorrow disfigures present joy. Consequently, in the one case joy never completely prevails, while in the other sorrow never dominates.

**(Theod.)** Neither a spur is agreeable to a horse nor correction pleasant to one who is at fault. All disciplines are presently felt as bitter by those being trained, just as the Apostle says: “Every discipline at the present time seems not to be a matter of joy but of sorrow, but afterward it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been exercised by it. For whom the Lord loves, he corrects; and he scourges every son whom he receives. For what son is there whom his father does not correct?”

Accordingly, evils are sometimes used to mean afflictions, as in the saying: “And God repented of the evil which he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it” (Jeremiah 26); and again: “For you, Lord, are merciful and compassionate, patient and greatly merciful, and repenting of evils” (Joel 2)—that is, of the tribulations and hardships which you are compelled to bring upon us according to the deserts of our sins. Knowing that these things are useful to some, another prophet, certainly not envying their salvation but caring for it, prays: “Add evils to them, Lord; add evils to the glorious of the earth” (Jeremiah 11). And the Lord himself says: “Behold, I shall bring evils upon them”—that is, sufferings and desolations by which, chastened beneficially in the present, they may at last be compelled to return and hasten to me, whom they despised in prosperous circumstances.

**(Greg.)** Although pain and blessedness cannot, strictly speaking, coexist, it is nevertheless rightly said: “Blessed is the person whom the Lord corrects” (Job 5), because through the pain of correction by which the sinner is oppressed, he is eventually instructed toward the blessedness that is free from pain.

**(Joan.)** From these arguments, then, Paul draws consolations, and again employs a common judgment to which no one can object, since no one can resist a common decree when everyone agrees upon something.

“Be saddened,” he says. For such is usually the character of discipline; such was its beginning. “Every discipline,” he says, “at the present time seems not to be a matter of joy but of sorrow.” He blessed the word “seems,” because discipline is not, he says, a matter of sorrow, but only seems to be so.

“Every discipline,” he says, both human and spiritual. Do you see how he contends from common notions? “It seems,” he says, “to be sorrow.” It is not, therefore. For what kind of sorrow is it when something becomes an occasion of joy, just as pleasure is not truly pleasure when it becomes the cause of sorrow?

“Afterward it yields the most peaceful fruit of righteousness to those exercised by it.” Not merely fruit, but an abundance of fruits. “Those who are exercised by it,” he says. He rightly said, “those who are exercised by it”—that is, those who patiently endure for a very long time. And how does he put it? Is it not more sonorous to call it “exercise”? Discipline, therefore, is exercise. For it makes an athlete stronger, renders him unconquerable in contests, and proves him impregnable.

In battles, then, all such discipline is necessary, and the present discipline must likewise be of this kind. Therefore one must work toward better things and toward an end full of joy and peace. Do not be surprised that, although it is itself bitter, it nevertheless produces sweeter fruits. In trees also the bark is almost always bitter and rough, while the fruits themselves are pleasant in their sweetness.

He took this example from common knowledge. If, then, it is appropriate to hope for such things, why are you sorrowful? Why, after enduring sorrow, do you fail with regard to the better things that it is fitting for you to sustain? If you have endured, you ought not again to grow weak with regard to the reward. He addresses them as people who have competed in a race, or endured blows, or labored in war.

“Therefore lift up the hands that hang down and the weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not go astray, but rather may be healed.”

Do you see how he arms them, how he raises them on high? “Walk straight,” he says. Here he touches upon their thoughts, so that they may persevere without any hesitation. If discipline leads to love, if it ends in something better, and if this is demonstrated both by events and by words, why are you becoming slack? This is what happens to those who fail through despair, who are made firm by no hope of future things.

“Walk straight,” he says; let lameness not increase further, but rather let the person be restored to his former condition. For one who runs while lame remains in wickedness. Do you see that it lies within you to obtain healing by every means?

“Pursue peace with everyone and holiness, without which no one will see God.”

**(Maur.)** There are many things that display the form and character of Christianity, but nothing is greater or better than the affection of mutual love and peace, which unites human hearts. Therefore Christ also says: “I give you my peace” (John 13); and again: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (same place).

For this reason the Apostle Paul also says: “Pursue peace with everyone and holiness”—that is, moral goodness or chastity—“without which no one will see God.”

**(Joan.)** As he also said above: “Not abandoning our assembly,” so here too he touches upon the same point. Nothing makes people so easily overcome and readily subdued, especially in times of temptation, as separation and withdrawal.

“Pursue peace with everyone,” he says. Even with evildoers? “If possible,” he says, “so far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone” (Romans 12). So far as concerns you, he says, maintain peace, doing nothing that harms piety; but when you suffer wrongs, endure them bravely. For patience is a greater weapon in temptations. Christ likewise made his disciples stronger when he said: “I am sending you as sheep among wolves; therefore be wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matthew 10).

“What do you mean? We are among wolves, and you command us to be sheep and doves?”

“Yes,” he says, “for nothing so confounds the one who does evil as the strong endurance of the one who suffers, when he returns no vengeance either in word or deed.” Consider how much you gain from this: you extinguish the evil and acquire a greater reward for yourself.

By holiness he means chastity and moderation in marriage: whether someone is unmarried and marries with chastity, or is married and does not commit fornication but uses his own wife with restraint—for this too is holiness.

How is this holiness? … Marriage preserves the holiness that comes from faith; it prevents the mind from attaching itself to prostitutes.

“Without which,” he says, “no one will see God.” He also says to the Corinthians: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor adulterers, nor idolaters, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor the greedy, nor thieves, nor drunkards, nor slanderers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6). For how could one who has become a single body with a prostitute possess unity of body with Christ?

**(Maur.)** He clearly declared that without holiness—which he usually calls integrity of mind or purity of body—God cannot be seen at all.

**(Cass.)** To pass over all the passages inserted in the holy Scriptures in praise of this virtue—for it is not my purpose to compose a panegyric of chastity, but to explain its character, how it should be acquired and preserved, and what its end is according to the traditions of the Fathers—I shall offer only one sentence of the blessed Apostle, by which it may be evident how, in writing to the Thessalonians, he placed it above all virtues, commending it with such noble wording: “This,” he says, “is the will of God: your sanctification” (1 Thessalonians 4).

And lest he leave us in doubt or obscurity as to what he wished to call sanctification—whether justice, love, humility, or patience, for sanctification is believed to be acquired through all these virtues—he adds and plainly indicates what he specifically wished to call sanctification:

“This is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain,” he says, “from fornication; that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in honor and sanctification, not in the passion of desire, like the nations that do not know God.”

See with what praises he commends it, calling it the honor and sanctification of the vessel—that is, of our body. Therefore, conversely, one who is in the passion of desire remains in dishonor and uncleanness and lives estranged from sanctification.

A little later he again declares this to be holiness: “For God did not call us to dishonor, but to holiness. Therefore whoever rejects these things rejects not a human being but God, who also gave his Holy Spirit within us.” He joined inviolable authority to his command, saying: “Whoever rejects these things”—that is, the matters concerning holiness of which I have spoken—“rejects not a human being”—that is, not me, who command these things—“but God,” who speaks through me and who also appointed our heart as a dwelling place for his Holy Spirit.

You see, in simple and pure words, with what proclamations and how great praises he exalts it: first, by assigning the name sanctification properly to this virtue; second, by asserting that through it the vessel of our body must be freed from uncleanness; third, by showing that, once dishonor and disgrace have been rejected, it will remain in honor and sanctification; and finally, by indicating that the highest reward of perfect blessedness is that through it the Holy Spirit will dwell in our breast.

“Watching carefully lest anyone be deprived of the grace of God.”

**(Joan.)** He speaks to them as though they were traveling long roads with a numerous company of travelers, as if he were saying: Take care that none of you remains behind. I do not require only that you yourselves arrive, but also that you watch over the others.

“Lest any of you,” he says, “be deprived of the grace of God.” What does he mean by the grace of God? Future blessings, evangelical faith, and an excellent manner of life—for these are the graces of God. Do not tell me that only one person will perish, for Christ died even for one. Yet you neglect the one for whom Christ deemed himself worthy to die.

“Watching carefully,” he says—that is, examining diligently, visiting, and recognizing, as is customary with the sick.

“Lest any root of bitterness spring upward and cause hindrance, and through it many be defiled.” This is written in Deuteronomy. He took the expression from the metaphor of shrubs: “Lest any root of bitterness.” He also said to others: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (Galatians 5). I do not say this only because wickedness might be found in that person, but also because harm might grow from his offshoot. That is, if such a root exists, do not allow any shoot to rise from it; cut it off before it defiles others and makes them wicked.

“Lest any root of bitterness,” he says, “spring upward and cause hindrance, and through it many be defiled.”

Here he says that sin is bitter. Indeed, nothing is more bitter than sin, and this is known by those who, after committing sin, are tormented by the sorrow of conscience and consumed by an exceedingly dreadful bitterness. The bitterness of wrongdoing overturns the understanding and reason itself.

The nature of that bitterness is such that it continues to do harm. He rightly said “a root of bitterness”; he did not say “a bitter root,” but “a root of bitterness.” A bitter root can produce sweet fruits, but a root, source, or purpose of bitterness can never produce anything sweet, because everything there is bitter, everything grievous, and everything full of crime and abomination; it brings no sweetness or pleasure.

“And through it,” he says, “many are defiled”—that is, cut off those who are intemperate and lustful.

“Lest there be any fornicator or profane person, like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright.”

What then? Was Esau a fornicator? He does not say here that Esau was a fornicator, but what he said above—“Pursue holiness”—is also signified here: “Lest there be any profane person, like Esau.” That is, a glutton, an intemperate and worldly person, because he rejected spiritual things.

“Who for one meal,” he says, “sold his birthright.” He sold, through his own negligence and desire, the honor he had received from God; for the sake of a small pleasure he lost great honor and everlasting glory. This applies particularly to those who are unclean and profane.

Therefore not only the fornicator is unclean, but also the glutton, who is a slave to his belly. For he too, being a slave to another kind of desire, is compelled to crave many things, compelled to seize what belongs to others, and compelled to appear base and dishonorable, since under that deadly master he bears an exceedingly harsh slavery.

Such a person often considers blasphemy a trivial matter; he regards his birthright as having no value or dignity. That is, he is one who, for the pleasure of temporal things, goes so far as to sell his birthright.

Therefore the birthright is not that of the Jews but ours. These words are also highly effective in relieving their sorrow: he who was first became last, and he who was second became first—the latter through perseverance, the former through negligence.

**(Cassian.)** “Lest there be any fornicator,” he says, “or profane person, like Esau.” Therefore, in proportion to how exalted and heavenly the reward of chastity is, it will be attacked by the more serious snares of its adversaries. For this reason we must apply ourselves diligently not only to bodily continence but also to contrition of heart through continual sighs of prayer, so that the furnace of our flesh—which the king of Babylon does not cease to kindle with the sparks of carnal suggestions—may be extinguished when the dew of the Holy Spirit descends into our hearts.

“Know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no place for repentance, although he sought it with tears.”

**(Joan.)** What are we to say here? Does Paul exclude repentance? Certainly not. How, then, does he say that he found no place for repentance? If he blamed himself, if he groaned with great sighs, why did he not deserve to find a place for repentance?

Because that was not repentance. Just as Cain’s sorrow did not arise from repentance, so here those words were not words of repentance. Cain’s brother’s murder makes this plain; similarly, so far as his will was concerned, Esau too intended to bring death upon his brother Jacob. For he said: “The days of mourning for my father are approaching, and I will kill my brother Jacob.” Tears alone, therefore, were not enough to grant him repentance.

He did not simply say that he sought through repentance, but “that with tears he sought a place for repentance and did not find it.” What are we to say, then, except that he did not repent as he ought? For this is repentance: that it be carried out appropriately. Otherwise, if he condemns repentance, how does he again admonish and exhort those who are sluggish? How does he invite those who have become lame, weakened, and slack—which is the beginning of ruin—to rise?

“He found no place for repentance.” This can also be understood in another way: he committed a sin greater than repentance. There are sins that surpass repentance, as though he were saying: Let us not fall into an incurable ruin. While someone is merely lame, he can easily become upright and healthy; but if he is completely overthrown, what can remain afterward?

He therefore speaks these things to those who have not yet fallen, to press them down through fear—as if he were saying that the one who has fallen can no longer deserve consolation. Here he warned them in another way, so that they would not fall. Elsewhere, however, when he speaks to those who had already fallen, he says the opposite, lest they fall into despair: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4). Elsewhere he says to them: “You who are justified in the law have fallen away from grace” (Galatians 5). Behold, he himself testifies that they had fallen.

Therefore, whoever stands and hears that the one who falls cannot obtain forgiveness will stand more firmly and carefully. But if you use equal severity toward the one who has fallen, he must be reduced to such a state that he can never rise again. With what hope, or with what fruit, would he undertake conversion?

He not only shed tears, he says, but also sought. It seems that he does not exclude repentance, but makes them more cautious and better fortified, so that they may not rush headlong into ruin. Whenever, therefore, people do not believe that Gehenna exists, let them recall these things; and all who think that sins remain unpunished should consider why Esau could not obtain forgiveness: namely, because he did not repent as he ought.

Those tears were not tears of repentance, but arose from a violent spirit and indignation, as his actions make clear.

“For you have not approached a tangible and accessible fire, and storm, and darkness, and tempest, and the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words—which those who heard excused themselves so that the word would not be spoken to them. For they could not bear what was said: ‘And if even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.’ And so terrifying was what appeared that Moses said: ‘I am terrified and trembling.’”

Everything belonging to the old temple was indeed wondrous. The Holy of Holies was there; venerable things were there; and these events reported as having taken place on Mount Sinai—fire, darkness, gloom, and tempest—were there as well. “God was seen,” he says, “on Mount Sinai,” and all these things were remembered with awe.

The New Testament, however, was not given to us with anything of this kind, but was bestowed through the simple word of Christ. Observe, therefore, how he makes comparisons between these things and those, and how he places them at the end. After he had piled up many proofs, after he had shown the difference between the two testaments, and after he had criticized the old one, he finally proceeds to these arguments as though by an easier path.

What does he say?

“For you have not approached a tangible and accessible fire, and storm, and darkness, and tempest, and the sound of a trumpet and the voice of words, which those who heard rejected, so that no further word would be spoken to them.”

It is as though he were saying: Those things are indeed terrifying and so dreadful that the ear itself could scarcely endure them, and no beast would dare approach that place. Nevertheless, the things that later took place will not be like these. For what is Mount Sinai in comparison with heaven? What is a tangible fire in comparison with the intangible God?

“For God,” he says, “is a consuming fire.” “Let God not speak to us,” they said, “but let Moses speak to us.” What was brought before them was so terrifying that Moses himself said that he was terrified and trembling.

“Why are you surprised,” he says, “at the people? He himself who entered the darkness, where God was, himself says: ‘I am terrified and have become trembling.’”

“But you have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the assembly of many thousands of angels, and the Church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and God the judge of all, and the spirits of the righteous who have been perfected, and Jesus, the mediator of the New Testament, and the sprinkling of blood that speaks better than Abel.”

Those things were indeed terrifying; but these are much more wondrous and far more glorious. Here there is neither darkness, nor gloom, nor tempest. It seems to me that these things signify the obscurity of the Old Testament—that is, what was difficult to understand, the shadow of the law, and the veil placed over those writings.

The fire signifies the lawgiver, severe and terrible in fire. The sound of trumpets was rightly employed there, as though an emperor were present. The same thing will occur at the second coming: “At the last trumpet,” he says, “all will rise again” (1 Corinthians 15); for the trumpet will accomplish this through its voice.

At that time, therefore, everything was perceptible both to human hearing and to human sight, whereas now everything has been granted to us spiritually. Then, he says, there was much smoke, because God is said to be fire; he is also said to have appeared similarly in the bush, and the smoke likewise signifies that there was fire.

Darkness and gloom brought terror to those who saw them. Thus Isaiah also says: “The house was filled with smoke” (Isaiah 6).

What does the tempest signify? The human race was negligent and sluggish; it was therefore necessary that it be raised up by these things and made attentive. No one was so dull or foolish that, when these events occurred, his whole heart was not lifted toward higher things. Human minds had to be raised in this way when the ordinances of the law were being delivered.

“And Moses,” he says, “was speaking, while God was answering him.” A divine voice also had to be heard, since the commandments of the law were to be given through Moses; therefore he was made worthy of belief by the divine voice.

They could not see him because of the darkness, and they could not hear because of the weakness of his voice. What, then, happened? God answered with a loud voice … “And they refused,” he says, “so that no further word would be spoken to them.”

From the very beginning, they themselves became the cause of this matter, so that God might appear in the flesh. “Let Moses speak to us,” they said, “and let God not speak to us.”

Those who make comparisons diminish one side so that the realities of the other side may stand out. So here, by comparison with those things, ours are shown to be greater, better, gentler, and filled with greater wonders. They are better in two ways: they are both better and clearer, and therefore more accessible to many.

This is also what he says in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “With unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 3); for Moses “would place a veil over his face.” They, he says, did not deserve to receive things such as those bestowed upon us.

What did they deserve to see? Darkness and gloom. They did hear a voice, but you too have heard a voice—not coming through a cloud, but through the flesh of Christ. You were neither thrown into confusion nor disturbed; you stood and spoke with the mediator.

The darkness also signifies the invisibility of God: “And the cloud,” he says, “was beneath his feet” (Psalm 17).

Then Moses was afraid; now no one is afraid. Then the whole people stood below, whereas we, although we are below heaven, nevertheless draw near to the Son of God. There, as with Moses, was a desert and desolation all around; here there is a city and a multitude of thousands of angels.

In this expression he signifies joy and delight in place of darkness, gloom, storm, and tempest.

“And the Church,” he says, “of the firstborn, which is written in heaven, and God the judge of all.” They did not approach, but stood at a distance; you, however, have approached, he says.

Here he terrifies them by saying, “and God the judge of all”—not merely of the Jews or of the faithful, but plainly of the whole world.

“And the spirits,” he says, “of the righteous who have been perfected.” He means the souls that have proved acceptable to God.

“And the mediator,” he says, “of the New Testament, Jesus, and the sprinkling of blood that speaks better than Abel.”

**(Maurus.)** What is this? Did Abel’s blood speak? Yes, he says. For above he said that, through it—that is, through faith—the one who is dead still speaks; and again God said: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me” (Genesis 4).

Whether it should be understood in this way or in that way, the fact remains that the event is still proclaimed. Nevertheless, it is not like this blood—that is, the blood of Christ. For it cleansed everyone and emits a voice more significant and clearer, inasmuch as it also received a greater testimony from the events themselves.

**(Joan.)** If blood speaks, he says, how much more does he speak who, though slain, lives! What does he say? “The Spirit himself,” he says, “speaks for us with inexpressible groanings” (Romans 8). How does he speak? Having entered a mind purified by sincerity, he raises it up and makes it speak of great things.

**(Greg.)** It had been said of Abel’s blood: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth.” But the blood of Jesus speaks better than Abel’s, because Abel’s blood sought the death of the murderer of his brother, whereas the Lord’s blood obtained life for his persecutors.

Therefore, so that the sacrament of the Lord’s passion may not be fruitless for us, we ought to imitate what we receive and proclaim to others what we venerate. His cry finds a place to hide within us if the tongue remains silent about what the mind has believed. But so that his cry may not remain hidden in us, each person must, according to his measure, make known to those near him the mystery of the life he has received.

“See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. For if those did not escape who refused him who spoke on earth, much more shall we not escape, if we turn away from him who speaks to us from heaven, whose voice then shook the earth, but now makes this promise, saying, ‘Yet once more, and I will shake not only the earth but also heaven.’ And the words ‘Yet once more’ indicate the removal of things that can be shaken, as things made, [Col. 0823A] so that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.”

(John.) “Take heed,” he says, “lest you reject him who speaks,” that is, do not neglect him. “For if those did not escape who rejected him who spoke on earth.” Whom do you think he signifies in this passage? It seems to me that he signifies Moses. What he says amounts to this: If those who rejected the lawgiver established on earth could not escape, how shall we be able to reject him who established for us from heaven the commandments of the law? Do not suppose that in this passage he speaks of one bearer of the law and another of the Gospel. Far from it. He does not say this, but he signifies that, although the same one is indeed both this and that, he appears more terrible when he speaks from heaven than he did at that time. For he does not signify a difference of person, [Col. 0823B] but says that the manner in which he gave us the new law is different.

How do we know this? “For if those,” he says, “did not escape who rejected him who had been established on earth, much more shall we not escape if we turn away from him who speaks to us from heaven.” What then shall we say? Is this one different from that one? How then did he say, “whose voice then shook the earth”? For if his voice shook the earth—he who then gave the law—but now he promises, saying, “Yet once more, and I will shake not only the earth but also heaven,” it is certain that he is the very same one.

“And the words ‘Yet once more’ indicate the removal of things that can be shaken, as things made.” What is signified by these words? Clearly, that everything will be taken away and all things will be changed for the better. This, it seems to me, is what is signified in this passage. Why then do you grieve, he says, when you suffer something in this world, which cannot remain and which will soon pass away? If this world had perhaps possessed rest in the last ages, then it would have been appropriate to grieve over one who is hastening toward the end.

“So that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.” What, then, and of what kind, are these unshakable things? Those that are to come, evidently. Let us therefore do everything for the sake of this end, so that we may attain that life and enjoy those ineffable blessings.

“Therefore, since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us have grace, by which we may serve God acceptably with reverence and awe; for indeed our God is a consuming fire.” Elsewhere he says, “The things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (II Cor. IV), and from this he draws an argument for exhortation and consolation concerning the evils that we endure in the present age. So here also he does and says: We must stand firm so that we may have grace—that is, so that we may give thanks to God. We ought not merely to endure present evils without resentment, but also to offer him thanks for future blessings.

“By which,” he says, “we may serve God acceptably.” That is, we serve God acceptably when thanks are offered to him in all things. “Do everything,” he says, “without grumbling and without hesitation.” For whatever someone does while grumbling will be cut off, and his reward will perish. Consider also what judgment the Israelites received because of their grumbling. Therefore, he says, do not grumble; for it is not pleasing to God when he is served with grumbling and when thanks are not offered to him for everything—for temptations as well as for spiritual blessings. Let us therefore say nothing sluggish, nothing shameless; rather, let us submit ourselves so that we may be worthy of reverence and respect—that is, with reverence and fear of the Lord.

## CHAPTER XIII

He exhorts them to do good toward their neighbors, themselves, and their leaders; asks for their prayers on his behalf; and offers them the benefit of his own prayer, together with a greeting.

“Let brotherly love remain, and do not forget hospitality, for through this some, without knowing it, entertained angels as guests.”

(John.) Observe how he commands them to keep the commandments already given. He does not impose other commandments upon them. He did not say, “Become lovers of the brethren,” but, “Let brotherly love remain.” Again, he did not say, “Become hospitable,” as though they were not already so, but, “Do not forget hospitality.” Perhaps this could have happened because of their tribulations.

“For through this,” he says, “some pleased God”—or, according to another edition, “were unaware”—“by receiving angels as guests.” Do you see how great the honor and how great the gain are? What does “remained hidden” mean? It means that, without knowing it, they received them as guests. Therefore Abraham also received a great reward: without knowing that they were angels, he received them as guests. For if he had known, there would have been nothing remarkable.

Some say that Lot is also signified in this passage.

“Remember those in bonds as though bound with them, and those who are suffering as though you yourselves were still in the body. Let marriage be honorable in all, and let the marriage-bed be undefiled. God will judge fornicators and adulterers.”

Consider how extensively he speaks here about chastity. “Pursue peace,” he says, “with all people, and holiness, lest there be any fornicator or defiled person.” And again: “God judges fornicators and adulterers.”

But let us now see in what way he says that marriage is honorable in all things and that the marriage-bed is undefiled. Clearly, he says this because the faithful person is preserved in the holiness of chastity. Here he also strikes at the Jews, who thought that marital intercourse was defiling and said that a person who rose from the marriage-bed could not remain clean.

Therefore, that which is permitted by nature is not defiled, O most ungrateful and senseless Jews, but that which proceeds from a perverse will. For if marriage is honorable, [Col. 0824D] it is also clean. Why, then, do you think that pollution arises from it? By placing first, “Marriage is honorable in all, and the marriage-bed is undefiled,” he shows that he has rightly introduced what follows. For if marriage is permitted, then fornicators are rightly punished, and adulterers are rightly condemned. Here he contends against the heretics.

And observe how well he does not say here again, “Let no one be covetous,” but, speaking at once [F.: *semel*, “once”], introduces it as a common admonition, as though he were not directing his words only to them. “Let your conduct be free from covetousness, and be content with what you have.” Let your conduct, he says, be free from covetousness. He did not say, “Do not possess anything,” but, “Let your conduct be free from covetousness.” He thus reveals the philosophy of each person’s will [F.: *ostendat . . . voluntas*, “may reveal … will”]. For above he had said, “You accepted with joy the plundering of your possessions” (Hebr. X), thereby showing that they were not devoted to covetousness.

He therefore rightly admonishes them: “Being content,” he says, “with what you have.” For many, after the loss of their possessions, later desire to gather wealth again under the pretext of almsgiving. “Therefore,” he says, “let your conduct be free from covetousness”; that is, let us await what will be useful, and let us care only for necessities.

What, then, someone may say, if we do not even obtain the means necessary for those necessities? Believe me, this is not so; it is not so. “For he himself has said, ‘I will never leave you nor forsake you,’ so that we may confidently say, ‘The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me.’”

Again, there is consolation in temptations. For he himself said it, and he does not lie in any way: “I will not forsake you.” Therefore we can say with confidence, “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me.” You have the promise; you must not hesitate. He himself promised it; do not doubt.

When he says, “I will not forsake you,” he is not speaking only of money, but also of everything else. “The Lord,” he says, “is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me.” And rightly so. Let us therefore also cry out in all temptations, and, having God favorable toward us, let us mock all human things. For just as, when God is angry, nothing will benefit us even if all our friends stand with us, so, when God loves us, we shall lack neither protection nor safety even if all our enemies pursue us with hostility: “I will not fear,” he says, “what man can do to me.”

“Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you. Consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith.”

In this passage, I think he is also speaking about assistance to the brethren. For this is what he says: “Those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith.” What does “consider” mean? It means repeatedly turning it over in your mind, examining it among yourselves, considering it carefully, and investigating, he says, “the outcome of their way of life”—that is, their perseverance to the end, since their way of life had a good end.

“Looking,” he says, “at their life, imitate their faith.” Faith comes from a pure life. Faith signifies firmness. How so? Because they believe in future things; for they would not have displayed a pure life if they had doubted concerning the future.

“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” “Yesterday” signifies the past time, “today” the present, while “forever” signifies the future without end. It is as though he were saying: You have heard of a high priest, but not of one who will cease to be; he is always the same.

It is as if there were some who said that he does not exist, but that another is to come. To this he replies that the one who was yesterday is himself also today and forever. For even today the Jews say that another is to come; by separating themselves from the one who is the true high priest, they have fallen into error and have supposed that the Antichrist is to come.

“Do not be carried away by various and foreign doctrines.” Do not, he says, be carried about by various and novel doctrines—not only by novel doctrines, but also by various ones. He calls doctrines novel when they are outside those that you heard from us; he calls them various because they are many-formed and manifold. For they possess nothing firm, but are multiplied by a diversity of differences; and above all, the teaching concerning foods is extremely entangled.

“For it is good that the heart be established by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those who walked in them.” Here he gradually indicates those who introduce observances concerning foods. For all things are clean to faith. Faith is what is needed, not foods. These doctrines are various; these are novel—especially since Christ says, “Not what enters the mouth defiles a person, but what comes out” (Matt. XV). Observe that he does not dare to say this openly, but speaks as though under some figure of meaning.

“For it is good,” he says, “to establish the heart by grace, not by foods.” Everything depends upon faith. If faith itself is strengthened, the heart also will be fortified. Faith therefore confirms everything, whereas various thoughts disturb; for faith is opposed to a wandering mind.

“In which,” he says, “those who walked had no benefit.” What profit, I ask, comes from such observances? Do they not rather destroy? Do they not place such a person under sin? For this is the true thing to guard against.

“In which,” he says, “those who walked had no benefit”—that is, those who always observe these things. For there is one observance: namely, to abstain from sin. What benefit is there in abstaining from foods, when some are so senseless that they are not even able to refrain from sharing in sacrifices? Therefore nothing saved them. Although they were zealous concerning such observances, because they did not have faith, the keeping of those food regulations profited them nothing.

“We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat.” Our practices are not like those among the Jews, so that not even the high priest is permitted to partake of them. Since he had said, “Do not observe these things,” lest anyone think that he was destroying his own practices, he turns the matter around again: “We observe such things,” he says; indeed, we observe them more earnestly, not granting even to the priests themselves any share in them.

Then he removes the sacrifice from the realm of figures and brings his argument back to the primary reality, saying:

“For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy place by the high priest as a sin-offering are burned outside the camp.” Those things, then, were types of these, although Christ fulfilled them all by suffering outside.

In this also he signifies that Christ willingly deigned to suffer, showing that those things were not instituted in a simple or arbitrary manner, but that even that dispensation was a sign of this passion.

“Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood. Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach; for here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come.”

Do you see the figure shining with great splendor? “For sins,” he says, “he suffered outside the gate.” “Let us therefore go out to him, bearing his reproach”—that is, suffering the same things and sharing in his sufferings. He who was condemned and crucified suffered outside; he suffered outside, but his blood was taken up to heaven.

You see, then, that we share in the blood that is brought into the holy place—but the holy place is the true one. We therefore share in the reality. If, then, we share not in reproach but rather in sanctification, that reproach is the cause of sanctification. For just as he himself endured reproach, so must we. Therefore, if we go out, we share with him.

What does he mean by saying, “Let us go out to him”? Clearly, let us share his sufferings and bear his reproaches. For he did not simply command us to live outside the gate, but, just as he endured reproaches and was condemned, so must we.

(Gregory.) For this reason God became incarnate: to bring us into faith and lead us out to the vision of himself. Thus, in the holy Gospel also, he says: “If anyone enters by me, he will be saved, and he will go in and go out and find pasture” (John X). He will enter, evidently, into faith; he will go out to vision; and he will find pasture in eternal satisfaction.

For this reason the Psalmist also says: “May the Lord guard your going in and your going out” (Ps. CXX). The Lord guards the entrance of each soul by which it enters into faith, and also its exit by which it goes out to vision, so that, neither when entering the Church, may it be overthrown by errors, nor, when going out from this temporal life to the eternal, may it be snatched away by the ancient enemy.

Concerning this exit of ours, which we ought daily to meditate upon in our minds, Paul also speaks of our Redeemer, saying: “In order to sanctify the people through his own blood, he suffered outside the gate. Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach; for here we have no lasting dwelling-place [city], but we seek the one that is to come.”

The man, then, who appeared to the prophet Ezekiel (Ezek. X) stood at the gates and spoke in this way, because Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and human beings, even at the time of his passion gave his disciples the commandments of life, so that those who believe in him may always look toward the gate and, weighing his passion with attentive consideration, may not turn the eyes of their hearts away from their own departure either.

“Through him, therefore, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name.”

(John.) They offered sheep and calves and gave them to the high priest; but we offer none of these things. Let our lips produce only thanksgiving. Let our voice echo nothing blasphemous, nothing sluggish, nothing insolent, nothing defiant, nothing arrogant. Rather, let our conduct be marked by modesty and reverence. For when the soul falls into despair amid tribulations, it also becomes shameless; but let us flee from such things.

Behold, again he says the very thing that he stated above: “Not abandoning our assembly.” For in this way, he says, we can accomplish everything with modesty. Often even people, out of shame, abstain from many evil deeds.

“Do not forget beneficence and communion, for by such sacrifices God is pleased.” I do not proclaim these things only to brothers who are present, but also to those who are absent. If others have seized your possessions, nevertheless show the work of hospitality from what you have. What excuse shall we have when we hear such words addressed to those who clearly endured the plundering of their possessions?

And he did not say simply “hospitality,” but “love of hospitality.” This is found more distinctly in Greek. He did not use ξενοδοχίαν (*xenodochian*), which signifies hospitality, but φιλοξενίαν (*philoxenian*), which indicates love of hospitality—as though he were saying: Do not merely receive strangers, but perform this act with love and charity.

And he did not speak of a future reward stored up for them, lest he make them even more sluggish, but says that the reward has already been granted: “For through this,” he says, “some, without knowing it, received angels as guests.”

“By such sacrifices,” he says, “God is pleased.” Let us offer him such a sacrifice that he himself may offer it to the Father. It is not offered in any other way except through the Son—or rather, also through a contrite mind. All these things are said for the sake of the weak; for it is clear that grace belongs to the Son. Otherwise, how is equal honor given to him? “That all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John V). Where, then, is equal honor if he is not equal?

“The fruit,” he says, “of lips confessing his name.” Let us endure everything with thanksgiving, whether it is poverty, illness, or whatever else befalls us. He alone knows what is beneficial for us. “For we do not know what we ought to pray for” (Rom. VIII). Since, then, we do not even know how to pray for what is proper unless we receive it from the Spirit of God, let us hasten to give thanks for everything and to endure everything courageously.

Are we in poverty? Let us give thanks. Are we in illness? Let us give thanks. Are we suffering slander? Let us give thanks. Are we enduring some evil? Let us give thanks. For this makes us near to God.

“Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over you as those who will give an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning; for this [Vulgate adds: ‘not’] is beneficial for you.”

After he had said above, “Consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith,” he then added: “Obey your leaders and submit to them.” First he established them as leaders, and then he said, “Obey your leaders and submit to them.”

What then, someone may say, if the leader proves wicked? Shall we not obey him? What do you mean by wicked? If the matter concerns the faith, flee from him and avoid him—not only if he is a human being, but even if an angel descends from heaven. But if you call him wicked in his character and conduct, do not investigate this.

I do not say these things on my own, but from divine Scripture. Hear Jesus saying: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat” (Matt. II). After first saying many bad things about them, he then said, “They have sat on Moses’ seat.” “Everything,” he says, “that they tell you, do and observe; but do not do according to their works.”

They possess dignity, he says, even though their lives are ruined. Nevertheless, attend not to their life but to their words. As far as conduct is concerned, no one will be harmed. Why is this so? Because what they do is manifest to everyone, and even if he reaches the summit of iniquity, he will not be able to teach others evil.

But when the matter concerns the faith, what is said is not manifest to everyone, and the wicked person does not hesitate to teach what is contrary. The command, “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged” (Matt. VII), concerns life, not faith; what follows makes this clear: “Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye and do not notice the beam in your own eye?” Therefore, “Everything they tell you to do,” he says, “do.” But doing concerns conduct, not faith. “According to their works, however, do not do.”

Do you see that the subject is not doctrines, but life and works?

“For they keep watch over you, as those who will give an account.” Let rulers also hear this—not only those who are governed by rulers—for just as those who are governed ought to be obedient, so rulers and leaders ought to be watchful.

“I say this,” he says, “so that they may do it with joy and not with groaning, for this is not beneficial for you.” You see that when a leader is despised, he ought not to inflict punishments; his whole vengeance is to weep and groan. For when a physician is despised by a sick person, he does not take revenge but weeps and groans.

But you may say that if he groans, God takes vengeance on you. For if we groan over our own sins, we draw God’s mercy toward ourselves; but when we groan over the arrogance or contempt of others, do we not call upon God even more? A groan, then, will be worse than any vengeance. For when the person himself does not understand, the one who groans calls upon the Lord. Just as, when a teacher is despised by a child, the pedagogue is summoned, who approaches the child more sternly, so also they speak to disobedient disciples … danger.

“Pray for us; for we are confident that we have a good conscience, desiring to live honorably in all things.”

Observe that these are supplications, as though he were writing to people who were distressed [variant: “of the writer”], were turning away from him, and were disposed toward him as toward a petitioner (*praecatorem*; the reading is uncertain), unable even to endure hearing his name. Since, then, he asked such things from those who hated him—things that one might expect from those who loved him—he established this point here, saying, “We are confident that we have a good conscience.”

It is as though he were saying: I do not want you to bring any accusations against me. “Our conscience,” he says, “condemns us in nothing, nor are we conscious of having done anything against you or laid snares for you.”

“We are confident,” he says, “that we have a good conscience in all things”—not only among the Gentiles, but also among you. We have done nothing for the sake of profit, and we have said nothing deceitfully. Perhaps he was accused in such matters: “For they have heard concerning you that you teach apostasy from the law” (Acts XXI).

I am writing these things, he says, not as an enemy or as an adversary, but as a friend. This is also shown by what follows: “But I urge you even more strongly to do this, so that I may be restored to you more quickly.” To pray in this way—not simply, but with complete earnestness and every possible effort—is the mark of one who loves greatly.

“That I may come to you quickly,” he says. This is the attitude of one conscious of no wrongdoing: he hastens to come to them quickly and exhorts them to pray that this may be granted to him. First he asks them for the aid of their prayer; then he himself prays for every blessing for them.

“Now may the God of peace, who brought back from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, our Lord Jesus Christ, by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you in every good work so that you may do his will, accomplishing in you what is pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

“God,” he says, “of peace.” Therefore do not quarrel with us, if you wish to have the God of peace favorable to you.

“Who brought back,” he says, “from the earth the shepherd of the sheep.” This is spoken of the resurrection. From this point to the end of the prayer he confirms to them the doctrine of the resurrection and testifies that greater things will be accomplished for them. For they are among those who have already received the beginning, and all their course is directed toward perfection.

He prays for them, which is characteristic of one who loves. In his other epistles he prays at the beginning; here he does so at the end.

“May he equip you,” he says, “in every good work, so that you may do his will, accomplishing in you what is pleasing in his sight.” Observe how he shows that virtue can be implanted, saying neither that everything comes from God nor that it is accomplished solely by us. For when he says, “May he perfect you in every good work,” this signifies: You possess virtue, but you need completion.

What does he mean by “in every good work and word”? That they should have both an upright life and sound doctrines. “According to his will,” he says, “accomplishing what is pleasing in his sight.” For this is the greatest virtue: to do what is pleasing in the sight of God. Thus the Prophet also says: “And according to the purity of my hands,” he says, “in the sight of his eyes.”

(Paphnutius.) The Apostle also teaches that God equips, or strengthens, our minds for every good work and works in us those things that please him, saying: “The God of peace, who brought back from the darkness the great shepherd of the sheep by the blood of the eternal covenant, Jesus Christ, may he equip you in every good thing, accomplishing in you what is pleasing in his sight.” He also prays that this may happen to the Thessalonians, saying:

“May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal consolation and good hope through grace, encourage your hearts and strengthen you in every good work and word” (II Thess. II).

Finally, the prophet Jeremiah plainly testifies that even the fear of God, by which we may hold firmly to him, is infused into us by the Lord. Speaking in the person of God, he says:

“And I will give them one heart and one soul, so that they may fear me all their days, and it may be well with them and with their children after them. And I will make with them an everlasting covenant, and I will not cease doing good to them; and I will put my fear into their hearts, so that they may not depart from me” (Jer. XXXII).

Ezekiel likewise says:

“And I will give them a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within them; and I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh, and I will give them a heart of flesh, so that they may walk in my commandments and keep my judgments and perform them; and they shall be my people, and I shall be their God” (Ezek. XI).

By these passages we are most clearly taught that the beginning of a good will is granted to us through the inspiration of the Lord, whether he draws us toward the path of salvation by himself, through the exhortation of some person, or through necessity. The perfection of the virtues is likewise bestowed by him. Our part, however, is to carry out God’s exhortation and help, whether more weakly or more earnestly; and for this [variant: “through this”] we deserve either reward or the most fitting punishment, according as we have neglected—or striven, through the devotion of our obedience, to fulfill—the dispensation and providence that he has conferred upon us with the utmost benevolent favor.

This is clearly and openly set forth in Deuteronomy:

“When the Lord your God brings you into the land that you are entering to possess, and drives out before you many nations—the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites—seven nations greater in number and stronger than you, and when the Lord delivers them over to you, you shall strike them down to destruction. You shall not make a covenant with them, nor shall you enter into marriage alliances with them” (Deut. VII).

That they are brought into the promised land, that many nations are destroyed before them, and that nations greater in number and stronger than the people of Israel are delivered into their hands—the Scripture declares to be the grace of God.

But whether Israel strikes them down to destruction or preserves and spares them, whether it makes a covenant with them or not, and whether it enters into marriage alliances with them or not—the Scripture testifies that these things belong to Israel itself.

By this testimony it is plainly distinguished what we ought to attribute to free will and what to God’s dispensation or daily assistance. It is the work of divine grace to provide us with opportunities for salvation, successful outcomes, and victory; but it is our task to carry out the benefits granted by God either more earnestly or more sluggishly.

“Now I ask you, brothers, to bear with the word of exhortation; for indeed I have written to you very briefly.” You see that what he wrote to no others he writes to these people: “For,” he says, “I am not troubling you with a lengthy discourse.” The Apostle called this extensive writing brief, plainly in comparison with what he was about to say, in accordance with what he also said elsewhere: “As I wrote to you briefly, according as you are able, when you read, to understand my prudence in the mystery of Christ” (Eph. III). And observe his wisdom: he does not say, “I beg you to endure a word of admonition,” but, “Bear with the word of consolation,” that is, a word of comfort, a word of exhortation. No one, he says, can reject the length of a discourse except through impatience. This, in fact, was what made them turn away from him. He does not wish to expose this, but says it covertly, as though he were saying: “Although you are fainthearted—for such people are unable to endure the length of a discourse.”

(Greg.) We must also take care how much we say, lest, if we prolong a word of exhortation or reproof to someone unable to bear much, we bring our hearer to disgust. Hence that same distinguished preacher speaks to the Hebrews, saying: “I ask you, brothers, to bear with the word of consolation; for indeed I have written to you very briefly.” This is especially suitable for the weak: they should hear a few things that they are able to grasp, but things that may pierce their minds with the pain of repentance. For if, at one time, a discourse of exhortation is delivered to them in many forms, since they cannot retain many things, they lose everything at once. Therefore physicians too spread the poultices that they apply to weakened stomachs with a suitable medicine, but thinly, lest, if they are filled with too much medication, instead of helping the stomach’s weakness by strengthening it, they should burden and oppress it.

(Joan.) “Know that our brother Timothy has been released; if he comes more quickly, I shall see you.” This was suitable for making them gentler: he declared himself ready to come to them, so that he might see them together with his disciple. I think, however, that they were not particularly hostile toward Timothy; hence he also placed him first: “Know,” he says, “that our brother Timothy has been released; if he comes quickly, I shall see you with him.” But why did he say “released”? I think he had been sent into custody; or, if this is not the case, he says that Timothy had been released from Athens, for this is also recorded in the Acts of the Apostles.

“Greet all your leaders and all the saints. The brothers from Italy greet you. Grace be with all of you. Amen.” Do you see how honorably he treats them? Indeed, he was writing to them on behalf of others. “Grace,” he says, “be with all of you. Amen.” He wishes them grace, which is common to all. But how does grace come to be with us? If we do not wrong it when benefits are conferred upon us, if we are not negligent concerning God’s gifts. What is grace? Namely, the forgiveness and cleansing of sins. This is with us if we act rightly. For who, being injurious, could preserve this grace and not immediately be deprived of it? For example, he forgave you all your sins: how will grace remain with you—or the operation of the Holy Spirit—unless you draw it toward yourself through good works? This is the cause of all good things: that spiritual grace persists in us. It leads us by a straight path to every good thing; and when we depart from it, we perish and are deprived of every good.

Therefore let us not drive it away. It lies with us whether it remains in us or departs from us. The former occurs when we contemplate heavenly things; the latter when we turn toward worldly things. “The world,” he says, “cannot receive him, because it neither sees him nor knows him.” Do you therefore perceive that it does not belong to a worldly soul to possess the Holy Spirit? We consequently need great diligence if we are to retain him within ourselves, make ourselves secure, and place ourselves in peace.

For just as a ship carried across the sea by a favorable wave cannot be hindered or sunk so long as it enjoys a favorable and steady wind, and after the voyage great glory also comes to its sailors and passengers—rest to the former, because they were not wearied by the labor of rowing, and to the latter because it freed them from the distress of the sea, made the voyage itself cheerful, and granted them the pleasing spectacle of a prosperous course—so too the soul assisted by the divine Spirit rises above all things, towers over all the fluctuations of this life, and advances along the road leading to heaven more vigorously than that ship proceeds. It is not driven by wind, but carried by the Paraclete himself; it possesses clean sails, is full of favorable breezes, and drives every relaxation and slackness from its mind.

For just as wind striking slackened sails accomplishes nothing, so the Holy Spirit does not remain in a relaxed and sluggish soul. We need complete strictness and every form of intensity, so that our mind may be ardent within us and all our works may be earnest and strong.

For example, when we pray with great concentration, we must do this by directing our mind toward heaven, not with ropes but with powerful desire. Likewise, when we show mercy, we need intensity, lest concern for the household, care for children and wife, or fear of poverty entering in should make our sails slack for us. If we attend everywhere to the hope of future things, the soul receives the operation of the Holy Spirit well. But when those thoughts and miseries impede it, they allow no grace to fall upon it; and if some grace should happen to fall there, it is not harmed, but the breath is quickly struck back by the soul’s groanings and is shaken out and departs.

Therefore we need great intensity. For already we are sailing upon a great and spacious sea, full of many beasts and many reefs. This sea also brings many storms upon us and, when the sky is covered with clouds, raises greater waves. Therefore, if we wish to sail without distress and without danger, we must raise the sails of our ship—that is, of our will—for this is sufficient for us.

Abraham too, because he kept his desire directed toward God and offered his will to God whole and perfect, needed nothing else: “He believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” Faith is an entire and genuine will. He offered his son; and although he did not kill him, it is certain that he received the reward of one who kills, and though the deed was not performed, the reward was restored to him whole and perfect.

Let our sails therefore be clean; let them not be worm-eaten. For everything that grows old and falls into senility is close to destruction. Let them not be worn out and torn, so that they cannot hold the spiritual breezes. “The natural man,” the Apostle said, “does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit” (1 Cor. II). For just as spider webs do not receive the breath of the wind, so neither can a worldly soul, nor a natural man, receive the grace of the Holy Spirit. Our thoughts differ in no way from those webs: they possess coherence only in appearance, but remain empty of all virtue.

Our thoughts, however, must not be like this, since we are sober-minded. Whatever may happen, the Christian endures everything and is superior to everything, stronger than every blow. Let each person be a spiritual man, and let a thousand evils befall him: he is in no way conquered. And why should I say more? Let poverty, sickness, insults, slander, reproaches, blows, every kind of punishment, every kind of deception, disgrace, and injury befall him. If he regarded all these things with laughter, as though he were placed outside the world and free from bodily passions, he would remain unconquered.

And because I do not wish to magnify these matters merely with words, I believe that even now there are many such people, such as those who have withdrawn into the desert. Yet this is no marvel, for I believe that such people are hidden even in the cities. If I wish, I can point to such people among the ancients. To recognize this, consider Paul: what evil did he not suffer? What did he not endure? He bore everything courageously. Let us imitate him, and thus we shall be able to reach tranquil harbors, bringing back the greatest profits.

Let us therefore stretch out our mind and raise it toward heaven; let us be held by that love and put on the spiritual fire with courage. Let us save ourselves through the burning of the divine flames. No one surrounded by those flames fears the attack of anyone, whether man, beast, or a thousand snares. For as long as a person walks aflame, he overcomes everything, surpasses everything, and despises everything. Flame is an unconquerable thing, and fire is unbearable to all things, for fire consumes everything.

Let us therefore be surrounded by this fire, I exhort you, offering glory to our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom, together with the Holy Spirit, belong glory, dominion, and honor, now and forever and unto the ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0833D]

# Appendix to the Expositions of Rabanus Maurus on the Epistles of the Blessed Apostle Paul

## Jacobus Pamele’s Exposition of the Epistle to Philemon

### Preface

First of all, this must be noted: both Jerome and Chrysostom, Theophylact, Oecumenius, and Theodoret record that there were formerly certain people who refused to admit this Epistle to Philemon among Paul’s Epistles, because it was written about a matter of little importance, or at least, if it was Paul’s, because it contained nothing capable of edifying us. For this reason, most of the ancients rejected it, since it seemed to have been written merely for the purpose of commendation, not instruction.

But, says Jerome, those who defend it as possessing genuine authority say that it was never received by all the churches throughout the world unless it was believed to be the Apostle Paul’s; and by the same reasoning we ought not to receive the Second Epistle to Timothy or the Epistle to the Galatians, in which the Apostle himself is clearly shown—even with the agreement of those very people—to have supplied examples of human weakness. Such is the passage: “When you come, bring the cloak which I left at Troas with Carpus” (2 Tim. IV). And this one: “I wish that those who trouble you would even cut themselves off” (Gal. V).

Many passages can also be found in the Epistle to the Romans and in the other Epistles, especially in those to the Corinthians, written in a more relaxed and almost everyday style. Since these too contain something of this sort, either they must not be regarded as Paul’s Epistles, or, if they are accepted, the Epistle to Philemon must also be accepted on the precedent of similar writings that have been received.

Then Jerome gives his own view. “If,” he says, “he does not think that the small things belong to those to whom the great things belong, then, following Marcion, Valentinus, and Apelles, he ought to introduce one creator for ants, worms, gnats, and locusts, and another for heaven, earth, the sea, and angels.”

And since we have mentioned Marcion, let it at least be established on Marcion’s authority that the Epistle to Philemon is Paul’s. Although Marcion either did not accept Paul’s other Epistles or altered and mutilated certain passages in them, he did not dare to lay hands on this one alone, because its brevity protected it.

It seems to me, however, that when they accuse the Epistle of simplicity, they reveal their own incompetence, not understanding what power and wisdom lie hidden in each of its expressions. We shall try to explain these in their proper places.

But if brevity is to be despised, let Obadiah, Nahum, Zephaniah, and the other twelve prophets also be despised. Their writings contain such wondrous and lofty things that one does not know whether to admire their brevity of expression or the greatness of their meaning. If those who reject the Epistle to Philemon understood this, they would by no means despise its brevity.

The Greeks likewise said that this Epistle was of little importance; yet Chrysostom, above all, explains at great length the various benefits of this Epistle, which you have summarized in these words from Oecumenius and Theodoret:

First, it instructs us to be diligent even in small matters. Second, it teaches that, if a slave so wicked has been converted, no one should despair of any of them [i.e., such slaves]. Third, it teaches that servants should not be withheld from their masters against their masters’ will under the pretext of piety. Finally, it teaches that servants endowed with virtue should not be despised, since Paul calls Onesimus his son.

This was the purpose of my preface: both to prevent anyone from doubting that this is a genuine Epistle of the Apostle Paul and to prevent anyone from despising or devaluing it on account of its brevity. Let us now proceed to its subject, which is as follows.

### Argument

Philemon, a good man, had been left by his slave Onesimus, who had secretly taken money—something slaves commonly do. Onesimus went to Rome, where he was converted and baptized by Paul and served him for some time while Paul was in chains. Paul now sends him back to Philemon with this Epistle, which both pleads the case concerning the theft and commends Onesimus to him; at the same time, the Apostle instructs Philemon to prepare lodging for him.

## Single Chapter

### “Paul”

Here Jerome first discusses from where, at what time, or through what person the Apostle received the name Paul from the name Saul. He notes first of all that one should not think, as simpler-minded Latins do, that he was called Saulus rather than Saul because he belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, in which this name was more common. Saul, the king of Judaea and persecutor of David, also belonged to the tribe of Benjamin.

Saulus is a Hebrew name declined in the manner of Greek and Roman names, just as Joseph becomes Josephus and Jacob becomes Jacobus. Since Jerome treats this matter here, we too shall do so, as briefly as we can.

The ancient commentators offer various opinions here. Since Scripture provides no clear certainty on the matter, none of them can be rejected, since each and every one has distinguished authorities in its support.

Origen, in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, holds that Paul possessed the name Paul from the beginning along with the name Saul, because he was a Roman citizen, and that the name Paul was more pleasing to the Romans—just as we find many people in the books of the Old Testament called by different names.

Augustine and Ambrose hold that he changed his name along with his religion.

Jerome here, and Bede in Book II of his Commentary on the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 9, hold that he adopted the name Paul as a trophy from Sergius the proconsul, whom he won for Christ, as related in Acts XIII. This would be like Scipio Africanus, named from conquered Africa, or Metellus Creticus, who brought back the distinction of his family from the subjugated island of Crete.

Here, then, you have the differing opinions of great authorities. Erasmus, as it seems, attempts to do so unsuccessfully. He follows Origen’s opinion in preference to the others, rejecting not only the second but also the third opinion mentioned, although Jerome’s opinion is preferred by most.

Erasmus’s objection to Jerome is that in Acts XIII Paul is called Paul before he converted Sergius. Bede clearly resolves this in the passage already mentioned by means of a figure common in Scripture, prolepsis or anticipation. “Luke,” he says, “by teaching this, appropriately indicated there that Paul would be called Paul, where he related that after his conversion he first came to Jerusalem.” He is speaking of Acts IX.

Where our Latin text reads, “When he had come to Jerusalem,” the Greek codex of Bede himself inserted: “When Paul had come to Jerusalem.” Bede alludes to this passage, although his own codex seems to have contained an error, since Greek manuscripts today almost universally read not Παῦλος (*Paulos*) but Σαῦλος (*Saulos*) at that point.

The position of Jerome is also strongly confirmed by the fact that, up to the passage in which Luke relates the story of Sergius Paulus, he consistently calls the Apostle Saul; but after he has won over the proconsul, he always calls him Paul and never Saul.

Jerome also discusses here where the etymology of this name should be sought. Omitting the opinions of others, according to which Jerome thinks the name is a Hebrew word with a marvelous meaning, and others derive it jointly from Hebrew and Greek, as those who interpret it as “mouth of a trumpet,” the more probable opinion seems to be that the name is either Greek in origin and means “quiet,” or Latin in origin and means “small.”

Bede holds this opinion in the passage already cited. “Nor should it be thought,” he says, “that Peter or Paul are Hebrew names rather than Latin or Greek ones.” The argument he adds, however—namely, that the Hebrews do not have the letter *P*—does not prove the matter at all; indeed, it shows that he was unfamiliar with the Hebrew language.

Erasmus follows the same opinion in the preface to his paraphrase of the Epistles of Paul.

### “A prisoner of Jesus Christ”

Since the Apostle used this title at the beginning of none of his other Epistles, although in the body of the Epistles to the Ephesians, Philippians, and Colossians he testified that he was in chains, it is not without reason that one asks why he used this title in this Epistle.

The answer is obvious: it seems more impressive to say that he is a prisoner of Jesus Christ than to say that he is an apostle. The apostles gloried in having been considered worthy to suffer disgrace for Christ’s name. Thus, in order to claim greater authority for this Epistle, he began with his humiliation.

For just as being bound on account of sin is a disgrace, so, conversely, enduring chains for Christ is the greatest glory. He then adds “of Jesus Christ” so that no one might think he had been thrown into chains for any other reason than Christ’s name.

From this passage we can also infer the time and place in which this Epistle was written and sent: namely, from Rome during the earlier captivity, of which he says to Timothy, “At my first defense no one stood with me,” and so forth, while Paul was still in chains.

Jerome further believes that at this same time the Apostle dictated the Epistles to the Philippians, Colossians, and Ephesians. He holds this especially concerning the Epistle to the Philippians, first because he writes it to them with Timothy alone, and then because he clearly says that his chains have become known throughout the whole praetorium.

What the praetorium was, he indicates at the end of that Epistle: “Especially those who are of Caesar’s household greet you.” Finally, he says in the same Epistle: “Thinking that they were stirring up affliction for my chains.”

The beginning of the Epistle to the Colossians is likewise similar: “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ, and Timothy, the brother.” Later he says: “Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you,” and at the end: “Remember my chains.” This is why we should understand that these Epistles too were dictated while he was in chains.

The distinctive point concerning the Colossians is that the same Onesimus who is now commended to Philemon carried that Epistle. As it says later: “Tychicus, the most beloved brother, will make known to you everything concerning me,” and so forth, “together with Onesimus, the beloved and faithful brother, who is one of you.”

There is another point in that Epistle’s opening: it also mentions Archippus, just as this Epistle does: “Tell Archippus,” and so forth.

The Epistle to the Ephesians is similarly connected with this circumstance because Paul says there, in chapter I, that he is a prisoner for Christ; and at the end of that Epistle he gives precisely the same instruction as in the Epistle to the Colossians, that servants should obey their masters according to the flesh, and so forth. Finally, he closes his Epistle with the same conclusion as the other: “Tychicus, the most beloved brother, will make known to you what I am doing,” and so forth.

Tychicus is the one who was sent with Onesimus. Thus Onesimus had him as a companion at the very time when he was carrying these letters to Philemon.

### “And Timothy, the brother”

In the other Epistles, Sosthenes and Silvanus are sometimes included, and at times Timothy as well. Timothy alone is included in four: this Epistle, the two already mentioned—to the Philippians and Colossians—and the Second Epistle to the Corinthians. This was because they were dictated either at the same time or in the presence of Timothy and the others.

Jerome thinks this was done for two reasons: first, so that the Epistle might have greater authority, since it was not written by one person alone. Hence Chrysostom also notes here: “He includes another servant, so that, being entreated by many, Philemon may more easily grant the request.”

Second, there was no rivalry among the apostles. If something were perhaps revealed to another while Paul was dictating, Paul would add it to the Epistle he was dictating without resentment, in accordance with what he himself had commanded in 1 Corinthians XIV: “If something is revealed to another who is prophesying, let the one who was previously prophesying be silent.”

The character of this Timothy is not to be discussed here; that subject belongs more properly to the commentaries on the Epistle to Timothy. Paul calls him “brother” because they shared in the preaching of the Gospel.

### “To Philemon, the beloved”

Here we must briefly discuss who this Philemon was, what kind of man he was, and where he came from. We postponed this matter to this point so that the preface might not become too lengthy.

The commentaries generally agree that he was a noble man, Phrygian by nationality. Although that people is generally harsh and servile, according to the proverb, “A Phrygian is corrected by blows,” Philemon himself was gentle in character, faithful in life, shared his possessions with the needs of the saints, and gave abundant alms.

St. Jerome concludes that he was a Colossian—Colossae being a city in Phrygia—both because, in the Epistle to the Colossians, the Apostle says that Onesimus was one of them, that is, originated there, and because he also mentions Archippus there as their bishop, as is stated immediately afterward; Archippus is also mentioned here.

It must also not be overlooked that the Greek does not read ἀγαπημένῳ (*agapēmenō*), “beloved,” but ἀγαπητῷ (*agapētō*), “worthy of love” or “lovable.” The difference between “beloved” and “worthy of love” is that someone who does not deserve love can still be called beloved, whereas “worthy of love” refers only to one who is loved deservedly, as Jerome also attests.

Therefore the phrase written above the title of Psalm XLIV, “For the beloved,” is better rendered in Greek as “For the one worthy of love.”
