Paul and Timothy therefore write to Philemon, their most beloved friend; and he was most beloved because he was engaged in the same work. Hence they add:

### “And our helper”

Although Philemon had been appointed to no ecclesiastical office, as Ambrose notes, the Apostle nevertheless calls him his helper, or, as Ambrose reads it, a participant in his labors. Chrysostom clearly infers this from the fact that, even if Philemon himself did not preach the Gospel, he served the needs of the saints and received them as guests. He infers it both from the Apostle’s statement that the hearts of the saints had found refreshment in Philemon and from the fact that Paul ordered him to prepare lodging, as we shall explain more fully below.

The Greeks meanwhile note that the words “beloved and helper” have great force and that they ought to move Philemon to grant the Apostle’s request readily. If he is beloved, he will gratify the one who asks him; if he is a helper and colleague, he will certainly not restrain the slave when he comes to him. Rather, as Theophylact says, he will send him back to Paul so that Onesimus may serve him as he preaches, and so that the slave may take the place of his master in serving the saints.

### “And to Apphia, our most beloved sister”

Apphia, says Primasius, is believed either to have been Philemon’s sister or his wife. Jerome seems to incline more toward the former opinion, whereas the Greeks follow the latter. According to them, the sense is: “And to Apphia, or Appia, his wife, who is exceedingly worthy of my love because of our kinship in faith.”

Oecumenius urges us to observe carefully the Apostle’s modesty: he not only employs Timothy but also Philemon’s wife and another person as intercessors with him.

The passage in Galatians III, where the faith of Christ is concerned, makes it equally clear here that it makes no difference whether someone is Gentile or Jew, man or woman. The name of Apphia is inserted between two men and apostles, between Paul’s fellow worker and his fellow soldier, so that, supported by the company of both groups, she may not appear to lack rank because of her sex, but rather to possess it through her merit.

### “And to Archippus, our fellow soldier”

Here again Chrysostom emphasizes the Apostle’s humility in writing. He did not wish, he says, to command by authority and power, although he could justly have done so; nor did he disdain it if he was not obeyed. Rather, it was as though an unknown person were writing to unknown people and asking others to assist him on behalf of a little slave as a brother.

For it has great power in obtaining a request not merely to be entreated by many, but also to refer one’s pleas to many. Hence he says, “And to Archippus, our fellow soldier,” as though he were saying: “If you are a companion in military service, you must also show yourself a companion in this matter.”

Jerome thinks that Archippus is called a fellow soldier because he fought with Paul and Timothy against their opponents for Christ’s name and emerged victorious.

Archippus is also mentioned in the Epistle to the Colossians, chapter IV: “Tell Archippus: See to the ministry that you have received in the Lord, so that you may fulfill it.”

Most modern commentators think that this ministry was the episcopate of the Colossians; the ancients speak less openly and as though uncertainly. Jerome infers from the passage that Archippus was either a bishop or a preacher of the Gospel. Oecumenius says likewise concerning the passage in Colossians: “Perhaps he was their bishop, or had received some other ministry for souls.” Theophylact speaks in much the same way.

Primasius gives the more specific view that he was either a bishop or a deacon.

### “And to the church that is in your house”

Both the Greek and Latin manuscripts generally read this way. Ambrose, however, and likewise Jerome, read: “And to his domestic church,” or “the church that is in his house.”

Even according to our reading, but more particularly according to the other, it is ambiguous whether Paul is writing to the church that is in the house of Archippus or to the church that is in the house of Philemon.

Jerome meanwhile prefers to refer the expression to Philemon, to whom the Epistle itself is addressed. Although Paul and Timothy jointly write to Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the church, what follows shows that Paul is writing only to Philemon and conversing with one person alone, when he says below: “Always making mention of you.”

This manner of writing—where several people are addressed in the preface, but afterward one speaker is introduced throughout the body of the Epistle—is also observed in several other Epistles.

The Greeks are inclined to this opinion as well. “By ‘church,’” says Theophylact, “he means all the faithful who were in Philemon’s house, both free persons and slaves.”

Observe, therefore, the humility displayed by the Apostle, who even employs slaves as intercessors. He knew that it often happened that the words of slaves changed their masters’ decisions, especially when someone was pleading on behalf of a slave—particularly if the slaves had perhaps initially incited their master against him.

Observe also how wisely he acted: by mentioning them, he honored them in such a way that their master had no reason to be angry. He does not allow masters to take offense at the name of “church” because slaves are counted among them. For the church knows no distinction between master and slave: “In Christ Jesus there is neither slave nor free,” the same Apostle says in Galatians III.

Chrysostom concludes from this that Philemon was remarkable in virtue, since his house and entire household were faithful—so faithful that the Apostle calls them a church.

### “Grace to you”

He is still writing from two people to several, and almost all the Epistles have an opening similar to this. Although “grace” is a general term, here it is understood as the forgiveness of sins: a general term is being used for a particular one.

The commentators interpret it this way both here and in the other Epistles. Augustine discusses this meaning of grace in Book I of his *Retractions*, chapters 14 and 15. In a similar way, Scripture elsewhere says, “the law and the prophets,” although the prophets too are included in the law.

### “And peace”

That is, “may it be” or “may it increase.” Peace here means friendship established with God. Augustine explains it this way in his exposition of the Epistles to the Galatians and Romans, when he says that peace is that by which we are reconciled to God. St. Jerome explains it similarly here and in his commentary on Galatians.

This interpretation is preferable to the others and seems more plausible if we retain the passage in Romans V: “Having been justified freely, we have peace with God.”

The Greeks likewise interpret this passage as though the Apostle were saying: “I wish you grace and peace; but how will the forgiveness of sins be in you if you do not forgive your debtors their debts? And how will you have peace with God if you are not reconciled with your slave?”

On this occasion one may also see Chrysostom’s beautiful and lengthy discussion of forgiving injuries done by one’s neighbor, using the example of the merciless Gospel servant who, after his master had forgiven him ten thousand talents, most harshly demanded a hundred denarii from his fellow servant.

Among other things, Chrysostom says:

“Someone has grieved you and treated you with insults and injuries. Consider how many similar things you have committed against others and against the Lord himself, and you will be more inclined to forgiveness. Consider what you say when you pray: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive,’ and so forth. Observe how you bind yourself: unless you forgive, you cannot say these words yourself.”

There is much else in the same vein, to which we refer the reader.

### “From God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ”

Here one must observe that he did not say “through Jesus Christ,” as Jerome implies should be understood elsewhere, when in his commentaries on the Epistles to the Galatians and Ephesians he says that peace is granted by the Son because he is the mediator.

Rather, the expression is formulated in this way to show that the Son and the Father possess one nature: the Son can provide what the Father can provide, and what the Son provides is said to be provided by the Father. Jerome explains it in this way here as well.

It must also be noted that “Lord” is Christ’s distinctive epithet in Paul, because by his death he claimed us for himself after freeing us from the tyranny of the devil.

### “I give thanks to my God, always making mention of you in my prayers”

He speaks here according to his customary manner. At the beginning of his Epistles he generally begins with thanksgiving; in the others he immediately commends the grace of God.

Here, however, he is no longer speaking as Paul and Timothy to Philemon and the others, but as Paul alone to Philemon.

The sentence is ambiguous: does he always give thanks to his God, or does he always make mention of Philemon in his prayers? Both can be understood.

The sense may be: “I give thanks for this, that I always make mention of you in my prayers,” in accordance with 1 Timothy I: “I give thanks to my God because I have you continually in remembrance.”

Or it may mean: “I always give thanks to my God whenever I remember you,” in accordance with the command he gave to others, that they should give thanks to God in all things.

He says that he always gives thanks and always prays for Philemon because he never allowed a day to pass without observing appointed times for prayer. Augustine says this in *On Heresies*, heresy 57.

Paul’s devotion is remarkable: amid so many sermons and occupations, he nevertheless prayed for everyone at the proper time.

It must also be noted that there is emphasis in the expression “my God,” whom, as he says, “I worship in my spirit.” He explains this emphasis both in Romans—“whom I serve,” he says, “in my spirit”—and in 2 Timothy: “whom I serve from my ancestors with a pure conscience.”

### “Hearing of your love and faith”

He now explains why he always gives thanks to God whenever he remembers Philemon: “because I hear,” he says, “of your love.” Unless that love were very great, its reputation would never have reached from Phrygia all the way to Rome.

He does not immediately request grace on behalf of Onesimus at the beginning. First he expresses admiration for the man and praises his virtues; he also adds no small contribution from his own affection by saying that he always remembers him in his prayers and that many people have found refreshment in him. Only then does he proceed to the purpose of the Epistle, thus winning Philemon’s goodwill.

Moreover, so that he might not appear to be writing only for this one reason—as though he would not have written on any other account unless Onesimus had compelled him—observe how wisely he adds other reasons for the Epistle: first by insinuating Philemon’s love, and afterward by instructing him to prepare lodging for Paul.

What kind of love this was, he indicates in what follows:

“Which you have toward the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints.” So that everyone may understand that perfect charity by which not only God but also one’s neighbor is loved—and especially charity shown in receiving the saints as guests and assisting their needs—it is clear how someone may have charity toward the saints. But how someone may have faith in the saints, since he also thinks this part belongs to faith, Jerome discusses at considerable length. He considers that having faith in the saints means nothing other than believing what the saints have said and done, just as the same act of believing is referred both to Moses and to God, so that the people who believed in the Lord are likewise said to have believed in his servant: Exodus 19, where it says, “The people believed God and Moses his servant.” Perhaps it could also appropriately be said that someone has faith in his saints, because through faith working by love he comes to their aid.

There is also in this passage a tacit admonition intended to arouse Philemon’s readiness to forgive, as if he were saying: Since you are moved by charity toward all the saints, you ought also to embrace Onesimus with love, since he is now a believer.

“So that the sharing of your faith may become evident.” For *evident*, the Greek has ἐνεργής, that is, “effective”; our translator read ἐναργής, and the Greeks generally read it in the same way. Their meaning, therefore, is that the faith which you share with us may become effective; and it will be effective if it proceeds to every good work. Meanwhile, our reading can also be retained, because faith becomes evident precisely by working. But how it becomes effective, the Apostle adds:

“In the recognition of every good work among you in Christ Jesus.” There is a variant reading here. Most authorities—including Jerome, Ambrose, and the Greeks—do not read the word *work*, nor is it found today in the commonly circulated Greek copies, so that it seems not originally to have been present in our text either. Since, however, all the commentaries interpret this passage of faith working, and almost all tacitly supply that word, I think it also entered our text for the sake of greater clarity. I believe this did not happen recently, but already a thousand years ago, since Primasius reads it; and for that reason I also think some Greek copies came to have the word inserted, as Robert Stephanus noted.

The same explanation probably accounts for the fact that, where our translator reads “among you,” both the Greeks and Ambrose—Jerome does not address this word—read, “which is among us in Christ Jesus.” The Greek copy reads likewise. Indeed, Primasius, although he reads as our translator does, provided that his codex is corrected, also gives an interpretation suited to that reading; because it differs somewhat from the Greek interpretation, we shall present it shortly. Oecumenius, moreover, interprets the Greek εἰς Χριστὸν Ἰησοῦν as “toward Christ Jesus.”

The Greeks interpret the passage in this way: “So that your faith may become effective and more productive,” namely, through this means and by this fact: that you recognize—that is, love and accomplish—every good work which now exists among us toward Christ Jesus. For whoever does good to someone, says Oecumenius, does it to Christ, and especially whoever benefits his saints.

Jerome interprets it almost in the same way, except that he presses the expression “in the recognition,” as though he were saying: “So that your faith may be completed by works; and not only that, but so that this work may also be done according to knowledge.” For it can happen, he says, that someone has faith and completes it by works, but does so simply and plainly, without possessing its recognition and knowledge, according to the Apostle’s words: “They have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Romans 10). Such, he says, are many today who perform works of righteousness but do not possess the true knowledge that produces them.

This explanation, however, seems far-fetched; the preceding Greek interpretation is better, if *recognition* is understood as love. We must meanwhile consider whether another explanation might also fit well: namely, that “to know” is taken as “to do,” according to the saying, “The one who did not know sin,” which Augustine and many others interpret as “did not commit sin.” The meaning would then be: “In the working of every good”; and the word *work* would have been added merely by way of explanation.

Primasius also offers an interpretation which, it seems, should not be entirely dismissed: “So that the sharing of your faith may become evident in the recognition of every good thing among us and in Christ,” that is, so that all those who are good among us may clearly recognize in Christ that you are faithful.

“In Christ Jesus” is added because living well and possessing faith working through love come to us only from Christ, as Jerome also noted in this passage. This text should be noted against those who deny that works are necessary for faith; and in the commentaries on this passage, especially those of Theophylact, there is much that bears upon this point.

[Col. 0842A]

“For I have had great joy and consolation in your charity.” In place of our reading *joy*, modern Greek copies read χάριν, that is, “grace.” But this seems corrupt, since not only the Latins—Jerome, Ambrose, and Primasius—but also all the Greeks consistently read as our translator does; indeed, they interpret this reading. The variation seems to have arisen from the similarity of the word χαράν, which means “joy.”

The meaning is as if he were saying: “I do not give thanks to my God without reason whenever the memory of you comes to me. For we not only rejoice, but your charity brings us such pleasure that it also gives us consolation in our chains.” What kind of charity this was, he explains again in these words:

“Because the hearts of the saints have found rest through you, brother.” Notice that, although he wishes to say, “If you show kindness to others, you should show it much more to me,” he does not say this directly, but in a more tactful way. He knows that the remembrance of benefits shown to others makes those whom we entreat more compliant.

For what we have as “have found rest,” the Greek is ἀναπέπανται, which also means “have been refreshed”; Oecumenius explains it in this way. The meaning, then, is that by receiving the saints you have renewed and refreshed the inward affection of their hearts and the deepest recesses of their souls. This is an apostolic idiom: he always uses the word “hearts” when he wishes to display the fullness of the mind through charity. Thus also in 1 John 3: “And closes his heart against him,” that is, his inward affection.

He deliberately adds “brother,” for by such deeds Philemon truly demonstrated himself to be a brother.

“Therefore, although I have great confidence in Christ to command you what pertains to the matter, I appeal to you rather for the sake of charity.” The version followed by Oecumenius expresses the meaning beautifully: “Therefore, although I have great confidence to enjoin upon you what is proper, I ask you rather for the sake of charity.”

After first offering Philemon many praises, since the matter for which he is about to plead would benefit both the one who is asked and the one who asks, Paul could have commanded rather than requested. He had confidence that someone who had performed such great deeds for Christ could not be unequal to himself in other matters. Yet he wishes rather to ask than to command.

Meanwhile, note that in Oecumenius’s version, where our text has “what pertains to the matter,” he reads “what is fitting,” explaining it in his commentary as “for a matter that is expedient.” Chrysostom likewise reads “what is expedient,” and Jerome, “what is useful.”

According to our text, therefore, he says less while implying more. By adding this, he shows that he commands with greater confidence because the request will benefit not only himself but Philemon above all. This interpretation should be followed. Theophylact’s interpretation is somewhat different and, it seems, less in keeping with the text.

It should not be passed over in silence that Theophylact’s genuine reading was remarkably corrupted here by the first translator, Christopher Porsena. Contrary to Theophylact’s own Greek copy and to the judgment of all the ancients, he translated our reading “what pertains to the matter” as “what does not pertain to the matter.” He seems to have taken τὸ ἀνῆκον as though it contained the privative particle. Continuing in this error, he completely distorted Theophylact’s explanation, as Philip Montanus correctly noted. His translation of this passage must therefore be rejected entirely, and Montanus’s followed, as in many other places.

It is strange how so great an error came upon him, since ἀνῆκον rather signifies “what is appropriate,” namely, “what pertains to the matter,” or “what is fitting” (as Suidas says), “what is suitable.” For ἀνήκω means “I belong,” “I pertain,” or “I concern.”

The expression “in Christ” may refer either to “having confidence,” so that the meaning is: “We do not presume this because you are more distinguished in the world, but because of the faith you have in Christ,” as Chrysostom understands it; or again, the meaning may be: “Since you are such a person toward all the saints, I had much more freedom to command you in Christ—that is, as one who, according to Christ, begot you,” and so forth, as Theophylact explains.

The latter interpretation, however, seems more remote; the former appears more suited to the text.

“Since you are such a man as Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.” Ambrose reads this in the same way, and Primasius likewise, as though Paul were saying: “You ought to hear me, since you are like me in every respect, being of the same age—or, being bound to the Lord’s affairs, or subjected to chains for his name.”

Since this does not adequately explain his meaning, and since we nowhere read that Philemon was imprisoned for the faith, the reading found in the Greek copies, followed by all the Greeks and apparently also alluded to by Jerome, seems much more satisfactory. Otherwise there would also be a solecism, as Erasmus correctly noted.

The Greek reads: Τοιοῦτος ὤν, that is, “being such,” or “since I am such.” The commentaries explain it in this way: “I ask and entreat you to hear me, since I am such as someone ought to be in order to persuade you—Paul already an old man, possessing dignity both from his age and from his authority in teaching, and now having attained something greater still, namely, that I am a prisoner. In entreaties, the misfortune of the one pleading carries great weight. Yet I am not imprisoned for just any reason, but for preaching Jesus Christ. You ought therefore to favor such a prisoner if you favor Christ’s teaching.”

“I appeal to you for my son, whom I begot in my chains.” After preparing and softening Philemon’s mind in so many ways, Paul still does not immediately add Onesimus’s name. Even after such a striking admonition, he delays further, for he knew the anger of masters against runaway slaves, especially when the slave had fled after plundering his master’s property. He therefore strives in every way to moderate Philemon’s anger.

First, he softens him still further by not calling Onesimus Philemon’s slave, but his own son—one therefore highly approved by him—using the same name by which he called Timothy. He was not a son begotten at an ordinary time, but in chains, and thus worthy of greater honor because he had been born amid the very struggles and trials endured for Christ.

When Paul says that he begot him, he means nothing other than that he instructed him in the faith of Christ and baptized him. Having thus quieted Philemon’s indignation, he finally mentions the name and adds:

“Onesimus.” What kind of slave Onesimus was, and where he came from, may be gathered from Jerome on the basis of what is said at the end of Colossians: “Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord, will make known to you everything concerning me. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, so that he may learn how things are with you, together with Onesimus, the beloved and faithful brother, who is one of you.” That is, one of your own people.

Both Onesimus and his master Philemon, as well as Archippus, mentioned above, were therefore Colossians. Onesimus, originally Philemon’s slave, after fleeing from him—as will soon be shown—first became Paul’s minister, and it is certain that he later remained in holiness of life. Oecumenius testifies that he later suffered martyrdom in Rome, when Tertullus held the prefecture, undergoing the sentence of martyrdom by the breaking of his legs. Nicephorus supports this in *Ecclesiastical History*, book 3, chapter 11, where he says that Onesimus suffered martyrdom under Domitian.

Whether this was the same person whom Nicephorus mentions in book 8, chapter 3, saying that he was the second bishop of Byzantium after the apostle Saint Andrew, and governed that episcopate for fourteen years, with only Saint Stachys intervening, may rightly be doubted—especially since the years during which Saint Andrew, Saint Stachys, and Onesimus governed the episcopate appear to extend even to the time of Domitian.

“Who was once useless to you.” This seems to allude to his name and to explain it, for ὀνήσιμος in Greek means “useful.” Paul acknowledges his offense, knowing that confession of guilt softens anger. Moreover, so that the anger would not flare up again, he speaks more mildly than he could have done. He could have said, “who inflicted great loss upon you,” but he merely says, “who was useless.”

What loss Onesimus inflicted upon Philemon, Primasius does not discuss. Ambrose seems to understand that Onesimus injured Philemon in the same way slaves injure their masters when, after offending them for some reason, they flee. The Greeks, followed by Jerome, maintain that Onesimus compounded his flight with theft: he had plundered some of his master’s household property, and, having fled to Italy so that he might not be apprehended nearby, had squandered his master’s money through extravagance.

Eventually reaching Rome, he was converted through the preaching of the apostle Paul while Paul was in prison, and was baptized by him. Thus he wiped away the stains of his former life and afterward lived in such a way that the Apostle did not hesitate to commend him as his own son. Paul alludes here to that theft, and in order to move Philemon more readily to grant forgiveness, he uses the following beautiful antithesis:

“But now he is useful both to you and to me.” The meaning is: “Previously he was useless to no one except you, for a thieving and runaway slave could harm no one other than his master. Now, on the contrary, the loss is compensated by the usefulness through which he is useful both to you and to me. To you, because he can minister to me in your place; and to me, because, while I am confined in prison and held in chains, he can assist me in preaching the Gospel.”

Paul’s greatness of spirit and remarkable fervor of mind toward Christ should be noted here. He is held in prison, bound with chains, confined by bodily squalor, separation from those dear to him, and the darkness of punishment, yet he does not feel the injury or suffer in distress. He thinks of nothing other than the Gospel of Christ.

“Whom I have sent back to you.” Here too Paul moderates Philemon’s anger by placing Onesimus in his hands. Masters are especially accustomed to become angry when petitions are offered on behalf of absent slaves. Once he considered Philemon’s anger sufficiently and abundantly appeased, Paul proceeds to the actual request, adding:

“But you receive him—that is, my own heart.” He presents his request with the greatest affection, for by saying “my own heart” he demonstrates the magnitude of his love for Onesimus. It is as though he were saying: “Receive not so much him as myself represented in him, since he is exceedingly dear to me.”

A friend is, as it were, another self. “Receive him,” he says, that is, treat him with love and honor. He deserves not only forgiveness but also honor, for he is Paul’s son and your brother, as he adds later.

The Greeks interpret this passage in much the same way, and Jerome follows them, although he also notes that all children are the hearts of their parents. Primasius’s commentary is drawn from this, interpreting “my heart” as “my son.”

[Col. 0844D]

“Whom I wished to retain with me, so that he might minister to me in your place in the chains of the Gospel; but without your advice I wished to do nothing.” Observe Paul’s wisdom: he almost puts Onesimus in Philemon’s place when he says, “so that he might minister to me in your place.” Yet he shows that he is also consulting Philemon’s interests, as though he were saying: “If it is in your interest to serve me, and he does so here in your place, you will certainly gain by it.”

By adding “without your advice,” or, as Oecumenius reads it, “without your judgment,” the Apostle greatly softens Philemon. The matter was necessary and very useful, so that Onesimus might minister to the Apostle in chains; yet Paul did not wish to do anything without consulting him.

Why he did not wish to do so, he adds:

“So that your good might not be as though compelled, but voluntary.” He did not simply say “from compulsion,” but “as though from compulsion,” as if he were saying: “I knew that even if I retained him contrary to your judgment, I would by no means cause you grief. Nevertheless, so that the matter would not appear to be done under compulsion, I did not wish to do it.”

On this occasion Jerome treats here the question of why God did not create human beings good by necessity. A related question is whether a human being or an angel could have been created in such a way that he could not be evil. Augustine discusses the same question in the *Enchiridion*, chapters 105 and 106, where he seems to presuppose that God could indeed have created such beings but did not wish to do so.

“For the order,” Augustine says, “was not to be omitted by which God wished to show how good a rational soul is which can also sin, although it is better that it cannot sin.”

Jerome says almost the same: “God could have made human beings good without their will; but if he had done so, their goodness would not have been voluntary but necessary. What is good by necessity is not good, and in another sense it is called evil. Therefore, leaving us to our own free choice, he made us more according to his image and likeness. For God is good because he wills to be good, not because he is compelled.”

If, then, one asks whether there is no good that comes from necessity, the answer is certainly that there is, as is evident in the martyrs. It was good for them to suffer, yet they suffered under necessity, since many would not have escaped death even if they had denied Christ amid their torments. Nevertheless, even that good is in a certain sense voluntary, because it occurs without the will resisting it.

“Perhaps for this reason he departed from you for a time, so that you might receive him forever.” Sometimes evil becomes an occasion of good, and God turns human beings’ wicked plans toward what is right. Thus Joseph said to his brothers: “You intended evil against me, but God intended it for good.”

We can understand something similar in Onesimus. If he had not fled from his master, he would never have come to Rome, where Paul was imprisoned. If he had not seen Paul in chains, he would not have received faith in Christ. If he had not received the faith of Christ, he would never have become Paul’s son and been sent into the work of the Gospel.

By carefully adding “perhaps,” Paul moderates the statement. God’s judgments are hidden, and it is rash to pronounce as certain what is doubtful. He therefore spoke cautiously, hesitantly, and tentatively, lest, if he had not included “perhaps,” all slaves should think that they ought to flee in order to become apostles.

The word “for a time” must be understood as referring to a period of time. For ὥρα in Greek means “time,” but a short period; and in comparison with eternity, every period of time is brief. Paul does not say, “For this reason he fled,” but “for this reason he was separated,” using a more honorable expression.

Since no slave remains his master’s slave forever—the master’s authority and the condition of both parties end with death—Paul adds:

“So that you might receive him forever, no longer as a slave, but in place of a slave as a beloved brother.” The meaning is: “You lost a slave for a short time, but you have found a brother forever, both in this world and in the world to come.”

Ambrose says that Paul adds this so that Philemon would not suffer, as masters commonly do, some disdainful or inflated feeling. For this reason he also humbles Onesimus by calling him Philemon’s brother.

Where our text reads “in place of a slave,” Jerome reads “more than a slave”; the Greeks likewise read “above a slave.” Paul adds “forever,” according to the same Jerome, because Christians will be joined together forever by the spirit of love.

“Especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.” If he is my brother, Paul says, you will certainly not be ashamed to have him as your brother too—both in the flesh and in the Lord—that is, one who can attend both to secular and to spiritual affairs.

There is here also a beautiful and extended discussion by Saint Chrysostom in praise of humility, based on Paul’s example: Paul commends a slave so greatly that he even calls him his brother.

“Therefore, if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would me.” Paul shows such affection for Onesimus that he calls Philemon, whom he had praised so highly above, his partner—Ambrose reads “associate,” and Oecumenius likewise—if Philemon will receive Onesimus as he would receive the Apostle.

This is what the wise man said: “Let the free serve the wise servant.” The statement is intended to frighten Philemon, so that at least for this reason he might accept Onesimus if he did not wish to do so out of charity.

Nothing has such force in commanding as not asking for everything at once. Thus Paul also places this greatest request only after many others: “Receive him as you would me.”

“But if he has harmed you in anything or owes you anything, charge it to me.” Paul did not say, “He stole,” but more mildly, “he harmed you,” or “acted unjustly,” “or owes you something.”

It is plausible that Onesimus had spent what he had stolen. “Therefore,” Paul says, “charge this debt to me; consider me your debtor.” Theophylact understands the Greek word ἐλλόγει in this sense. Jerome likewise infers from this that Onesimus had already spent the money taken by theft. “For,” he says, “he would not become surety for what had been taken unless what had been taken had been squandered.”

Since people are usually most distressed by the loss of money, Chrysostom says, Paul offers himself as surety for it. Yet he prudently adds the fault only at the very end.

“I, Paul, have written this with my own hand; I will repay.” He says this graciously and cheerfully while writing with spiritual grace, as though he were saying: “Here, for greater security, you have my bond: these words have been written in my own hand.” This feature is peculiar to this Epistle.

“Not to mention that you owe me even your own self.” So that Philemon would not think Paul held an unworthy opinion of him in being unwilling to ask him openly to forgive a theft committed by a slave—for that would in some sense show Philemon to be cruel—Paul demonstrates how greatly he trusts him.

“You owe me,” he says, “not merely what belongs to you, but even yourself,” namely, because of the message of Christ which he preached to him. “I could have used that right, but I did not, so that you might have the reward of forgiving.”

“Yes, brother, may I profit from you in the Lord.” In place of “so,” the Greek has ναί, an adverb expressing affirmation or entreaty. Jerome notes that it is the language of one who is flattering, and the other commentaries, both Ambrose’s and the Greek ones, indicate something similar.

Ambrose therefore comments: “He now flatters him, so that his obedience may be voluntary and may therefore have its reward,” and so forth. Jerome notes that this word cannot be conveniently expressed in Latin; likewise, the Greeks could not conveniently translate the Hebrew word, but read “I beseech you” in its place.

Augustine discusses this when distinguishing between *uti* and *frui*, especially in *On Christian Doctrine*, book 1, chapter 4, and similarly in book 83 of the *Questions*, question 30. He says that to enjoy something (*frui*) is to cling to it in love for its own sake, whereas to use something (*uti*) is to do so for the sake of another.

He says similar things in book 1, chapter 22, of *On Christian Doctrine*, and in book 10, chapter 10, of *On the Trinity*. Yet he also says in the same work, chapter 33, that *frui* is often used for enjoying something in the sense of using it with delight, though improperly. He concludes that, since a human being is not to be loved for his own sake but for the sake of something else, one cannot properly enjoy a human being.

Since this passage seemed to conflict with that position, Augustine resolves it by saying that when Paul adds “in the Lord,” he sufficiently indicates that he does not place his hope in a human being. “When,” he says, “you enjoy a human being in God, you enjoy God rather than the human being.”

The Greeks explain the meaning as follows, and Jerome also alludes to it: “I profit from you in the Lord,” that is, “I shall receive benefit from you in matters that accord with Christ; I shall rejoice in your excellent works in the Lord; I shall see you growing rich in every spiritual good.” Thus the following words will in a certain sense explain this expression.

“Refresh my heart in Christ.” He repeats what he said above in order to move Philemon’s affection more deeply, since Philemon should understand how dear he is to Paul. The meaning is therefore the same as before: “Refresh my love for you on account of Christ; for you will not be conferring a benefit upon me, but upon Christ.”

“Confident in your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say.” In this way Paul urges Philemon to do more than is requested. It often happens that someone who sees that others think well of him shows himself to be better still. Thus, if the person making the request knows that the one asked will do more than he has requested, he asks for less, so that the one asked may have the voluntary reward of a greater act of generosity.

Note that “more than I say” means nothing other than “more than I ask.”

“At the same time, prepare a lodging for me.” Philemon might have suspected that, if Paul had not written because of Onesimus, Paul would not have considered him worthy of even a word. Dispelling this suspicion, Paul says: “I have not written only on his account, but also so that you may prepare lodging for me.”

The commentaries, both Greek and Latin, especially Jerome’s, note that the Apostle was not burdened with such baggage that he would literally be concerned with arranging lodging. Rather, while expecting Philemon to come to him, Paul wishes him to do more than he has been asked.

If someone thinks that Paul’s instruction to prepare lodging was not merely a diplomatic expression but a genuine command, then lodging had to be prepared for the Apostle more than for Paul. He was coming to a new city to preach the Crucified One and the doctrines of the New Testament. He writes that many people would flock to him, and therefore the house first had to be situated in a prominent part of the city, where people could easily gather.

It also had to be free from every kind of inconvenience, spacious enough to accommodate many hearers, not near theaters or public games, and not in a disgraceful neighborhood. Finally, it ought to have been situated on the ground floor rather than in an upper room.

For this reason, I think that he also remained in Rome for two years in a rented house; nor, I believe, was it a small dwelling, since crowds of Jews gathered there every day.

[Col. 0847C]

“For I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you.” From this, most interpreters—especially the more recent ones, and Primasius as well as the commentary attributed to Jerome, which I think is by the same author—conclude that this Epistle was written during Paul’s earlier imprisonment, mentioned in 2 Timothy: “At my first defense no one stood by me.” Jerome also indicates this, though less explicitly.

We learn two things here. First, there is great power in the prayers of servants of God, since Paul, so great and eminent a man, needed them. Second, we ought to be humble in spirit, since Paul needed the prayers of his disciples.

“Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you.” Jerome again infers from this that this Epistle and the Epistle to the Colossians were written at the same time and sent by the same person, because Paul mentions the same people in the greeting of that Epistle:

“Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you; and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas; and Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ”; and shortly afterward: “Luke the beloved physician greets you, and Demas.”

Chrysostom likewise infers from this argument that Philemon was a Colossian, because Epaphras was a Colossian, sent by the Colossians to the Apostle, who seems to have first instructed them in the faith, according to what is said in Colossians 1: “As you learned from Epaphras.”

But there is difficulty in the fact that Paul first calls Epaphras his fellow prisoner in Christ, a phrase which the Greeks scarcely touch upon, while Jerome discusses it at great length. He first relates a story—which he himself calls a story—according to which the parents of the apostle Paul came from the region of Siscalis in Judea. When the whole province was devastated by the Romans and the Jews were scattered throughout the world, they were transferred to Tarsus, a city of Cilicia. Paul also followed the condition of his parents, and thus it can be consistent with his testimony that he was “a Hebrew of Hebrews,” together with the other indications that he was from Tarsus.

“If this is so,” Jerome says, “we may suppose that Epaphras was also captured at the time when Paul was captured and was settled with Paul’s parents in the Asian city of Colossae, later becoming a Christian.” If this is so, Aristarchus too, when he is called Paul’s fellow prisoner in the Epistle mentioned, will be understood in the same way.

Jerome indicates that others understand something hidden and mysterious in the word “captivity,” namely, that they were captured together and led into the valley of tears. But because “in Christ Jesus” is added here, neither interpretation is satisfactory. We may therefore suppose, he says, that Epaphras endured in Rome the same chains for Christ that Paul did.

The Greeks come close to this interpretation when they comment on the passage in this way: “With these words Paul puts Philemon to shame: if Epaphras was imprisoned together with him, while Philemon himself would not even show the grace of receiving Onesimus, who was being held captive for the name of Christ.”

“Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers.” This Mark is the one who wrote the Gospel. Aristarchus is mentioned in the Epistle to the Colossians as having been Paul’s fellow prisoner, just as Epaphras is described here.

Demas is the same person mentioned there and again at the end of 2 Timothy: “Demas has deserted me, loving the present world.” Luke is the Evangelist who also wrote the Acts of the Apostles and was Paul’s constant companion.

Since Paul here still places Demas among his fellow workers, although in the Epistle to Timothy he says that Demas deserted him—or, as some say, returned to pagan worship and became a priest of idols, or devoted himself more to his own convenience and leisure—Oecumenius notes that if the Epistle to Timothy was written earlier than this one, Demas later repented; but if it was written afterward, he deserted the Apostle later.

There seems no doubt that this Epistle is the earlier one, both because Paul here hopes to be released from his chains and because Theophylact explicitly says so in this passage. He undoubtedly considers the Epistle to Timothy later than this one.

By calling these men his fellow workers and assistants, Paul shows that they join him in asking Philemon on behalf of Onesimus, as though he were saying: “It is therefore fitting that you should gratify such great men.”

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.” [Note: [Col. 0847D] “Amen,” says Justin, *Apology* 2, addressed to Antoninus, is the same in Hebrew as “Let it be.”]

This subscription belongs to the Apostle as the one confirming that the Epistle was sent by him, since he generally uses such a subscription. Jerome notes here that, just as authority is counted from the better part of a human being—namely, the head, as Scripture says, “according to their heads”—so the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ is present in the whole holy person, but is said to concern the whole person from the better and greater part, namely the spirit. For when grace is in the spirit, it makes the whole person spiritual.

“Sent from Rome by Onesimus the servant.” As in the other Epistles, this subscription is not found at the end of this one in the Latin manuscripts, but only in the Greek manuscripts. Primasius, however, also reads part of this subscription: “Written from the city of Rome.”

[Col. 0849D]

THE ALLEGORIES OF THE BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, ON THE WHOLE OF SACRED SCRIPTURE [Note: [Col. 0849D] a Published now for the first time from an ancient manuscript.] (G)*
[Col. 0849A] Whoever desires to attain knowledge of sacred Scripture should first carefully consider when its narrative is composed historically, allegorically, anagogically, or tropologically. These four modes of understanding—namely history, allegory, tropology, and anagogy—we call the four daughters of Mother Wisdom, [Note: [Col. 0850D] b The passage is corrupt.] for we cannot reach the full disclosure of all the secret contained in her without first investigating knowledge of these. For Mother Wisdom nourishes through these sons of adoption: she gives the foolish [the beginners] and the tender the drink of the milk of history; those progressing in faith she feeds with the bread of allegory; to the good and those who labor diligently and toil at good works she gives satiety in the savory refreshment of tropology; and finally, to those who, lifted from the depths through contempt for earthly things and advanced toward the heights through heavenly desire, she gives the sober intoxication of theoretical contemplation in the wine of anagogy.

History concerns an appropriate narration of things done, which is contained in the surface meaning of the letter and is understood as it is read. Allegory, however, contains something more within itself: through the fact that the passage [F. speaking] concerning the truth of a matter gives something to be understood about the purity of faith and the mysteries of the holy Church, whether present or future, it says one thing and signifies another, but always reveals this through figurative and veiled expressions. Tropology likewise consists, like allegory, in figurative words or deeds; but it differs from allegory in this respect: allegory establishes faith, whereas tropology [Col. 0849C] builds up moral conduct. Anagogy, whether expressed in veiled or open words, concerns the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland and demonstrates, in covered or uncovered language, what reward awaits right faith or holy life.

For history, by narrating the examples of the perfect, rouses the reader to imitate holiness; allegory, by revealing faith, leads to knowledge of the truth; tropology, by instructing morals, leads to love of virtue; and anagogy, by manifesting everlasting joys, leads to desire for eternal happiness. Thus, in the house of our soul, history lays the foundation, allegory raises the walls, anagogy supplies the roof, while tropology paints it with various ornaments, both inwardly through affection and outwardly through the effect of good works.

When this sacred Scripture of which we speak simply narrates the words of history, it casts down, as it were, the beginning foundation of the building; [Col. 0849D] and [Col. 0850A] when, through the exercise of allegory, it discloses the mysteries of faith, it raises the structure of the mind toward love of the truth. When, through the sublimity of anagogy, it discusses the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland, it places on the roof, so to speak. But when, in tropology, it investigates mystical understanding through the exercise of contemplation, it adorns the spiritual building of which we speak with various virtues—both those that belong inwardly to the Lord and those that belong outwardly to the neighbor—like a variety of beautiful colors arranged through the loveliness of mortality.

Since it is established that these four modes of understanding sacred Scripture reveal every secret contained in it [F. ei], we must consider when it wishes to be understood according to only one, when according to two, when according to three, and when according to all four together. Once we have first investigated all these matters in this way, with truth itself as our guide, it is next necessary for us to examine carefully in how many and what ways we can understand the things of which it treats.

For sometimes one and the same thing has nothing naturally inherent in it that, insofar as it concerns merely human bodily advantage or disadvantage, can be judged either praiseworthy or blameworthy. That same thing, therefore, may sometimes have in sacred Scripture not merely a different but even an opposite meaning. To give three examples out of countless ones: there is the water whose streams flow from the belly of the believer, and there is the water against which the Psalmist prays lest the storm overwhelm him; [Col. 0850C] there is the camel that passes through the eye of a needle, and there is the camel from which Rebekah descended when she saw Isaac; there is the lion who conquered from the tribe of Judah, and there is the lion who prowls about seeking whom he may devour. Who does not know how far apart the meanings of these three things are, even though each of the things signifying is one and the same?

When, therefore, we hear sacred Scripture speaking about things in this manner, let us diligently observe the properties of their qualities naturally inherent in those same things. Then we shall clearly be able to know whether we ought to take them in a good or in a bad sense, according to what the sequence of the narrative it has composed requires.

Third, we must inquire in how many and what ways the names it treats—of persons as well as places—are to be interpreted, whether Hebrew [Col. 0850D] or Greek; for this offers great edification in the interpretations of proper names [Col. 0851A]. Concerning the meanings of things and the interpretations of names, it treats for our edification sometimes according to two modes of understanding, sometimes according to three, and sometimes according to all four together.

Since we have briefly said something above about these four modes of understanding, and have decided both to set forth and explain together more of the differences among such things as can presently come to mind, as well as to bring forward some interpretations of such names, we shall instruct our own ignorance—and that of those like us, if any such exist—from what we are able to find in the expositions of the holy Fathers.

So that the Reader may find what is sought more quickly [F. sooner], we present, in the order in which semivowels and mute consonants are joined to vowels, the words [F. voces] belonging to those things whose various meanings we propose to discuss:

## A

Angel. Abyss. Premature birth. Vinegar. Reclining. Young women. Air. Silver. Bracelet. Weapons. Small altar. Craftsman. Field. Lamb. Farmer. Wing. Height. Aloe. Friend. Jar. Spices. Spider. Fields. Stars. Ascent. She-ass. Antius. Carved figures. Forewall. Corner. Wild boar. Water. Arcturus. Atrium. South wind. Ear. Soul. Unleavened bread. Tree. Life. Fir tree. Hawk. Battle line. Needle. Fat. Field. Ram. Sand. Arks. Armed man. Fatty flesh. Asp. She-lambs. Altar. Stranger. White spot. Fattened animals. Female friend. Ring. Small fields. Herds. Plow. Ascent. Donkey. Maidservant. Animals. Bee. North wind. Eagle. Bow. Dawn. Gold. Charioteer. Axis. Adversary.

### Angel

An angel is Christ or the Holy Spirit, as in the Gospel of John: “An angel descended into the pool, and the water was stirred, and whoever descended first into the pool after the stirring of the water became well” [Note: [Col. 0851] 1 John V, 4.]. This means that when Christ came to the Jewish people, the unity of the faithful was healed through the movement of that people, which came to faith through his Passion. Or, when the Holy Spirit descends into the font of Baptism and makes it fruitful, one faithful people is washed.

An angel is John the Baptist, as the prophet says from the person of the Father to the Son: “Behold, I send my angel, who will prepare the way before you” [Note: [Col. 0851] 2 Mal. III, 1.]. He himself went before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways.

An angel is an evil spirit, as in the Psalms: “The angel of the Lord constricting them,” and “the devil binding them” [Note: [Col. 0851] 3 Ps. XXXIV, 5–6.].

Angels are heavenly spirits, as in the Psalms: “You make your angels spirits” [Note: [Col. 0852A] [Col. 0851] 4 Ps. CIII, 4.]. When holy spirits are sent, they are angels.

An angel is any priest, as in Malachi, where it says that “the angel of the Lord is the army” [Note: [Col. 0851] 5 Mal. II, 7.], that is, he announces the Lord.

### Soul

The human soul receives different names because of its various functions. When it gives life to the limbs, it is called soul; when it clings to sensible things, sensuality; when it perceives, sense; when it consents, pleasure; when it remembers, memory; when it contemplates, spirit; when it understands tastefully, intellect; when it understands, mind; and when it discerns, reason.

The soul sometimes means the whole human being, as in Genesis: “Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy souls” [Note: [Col. 0851] 6 Gen. XLVI, 27.], that is, with seventy people.

The soul is sensuality, as in Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews: “The word of God reaches to the division of soul and spirit” [Note: [Col. 0851] 7 Heb. IV, 12.]. The Spirit of the Lord understands how sensuality is divided from reason.

The soul is animal life, as in the Psalms: “He sent satiety into their souls” [Note: [Col. 0851] 8 Psal. CV.], that is, into the animal life sustained by bodily food.

The soul is the present life, as in the Gospel: “The soul is more than food” [Note: [Col. 0851] 9 Matt. VI, 25.].

The soul is courage, as in the Psalms: “I covered my soul in fasting” [Note: [Col. 0851] 10 Ps. XXXIV.], meaning that, so that I might not avenge myself, I concealed my courage.

The soul is Christ himself, as in the Prophet: “He will no longer reject you from my soul” [Note: [Col. 0851] 11 Lev. XXVI, 11.], that is, Christ, my Son, will not reject you.

The soul is that power of God by which he penetrates all things: “His soul—whatever he willed, he did” [Note: [Col. 0851] 12 Ps. CXIV, 3, and CXXXIV, 6.]. That inner power possesses omnipotence in his will.

The soul is called teaching, as in the Prophet: [Col. 0852C] “My soul hates your new moons” [Note: [Col. 0851] 13 Isa. I, 14.], that is, my will has rejected your outward festivals.

The soul is the intention of the mind, as in Job: “My soul chose hanging” [Note: [Col. 0851] 14 Job VII, 15.], that is, my intention chose to withdraw from earthly things.

The soul is the desire of the righteous, as in Job: “He filled the soul of her young” [Note: [Col. 0851] 15 Job XXXIX, 1.]. The Lord brings the desire of the Church’s saints to fulfillment.

The soul is the life of animals, as in Job: “In whose hand is the soul of every living thing” [Note: [Col. 0851] 16 Job XII, 10.]. The life of brute animals is in his power.

The soul is the devil’s will, as in the Song of Exodus: “I will divide the spoils * by my hand” [Note: [Col. 0851] 17 Exod. XV, 9.], that is, I will seize human souls, and my will shall be fulfilled.

### Abyss

The abyss is the Old and New Testaments, as in the Psalms: “Abyss calls to abyss” [Note: [Col. 0851] 18 Ps. XLI, 8.]. The Old Testament announces the New in the preaching of the saints.

The abyss is the company of the apostles, as in * the Psalms: “The abyss gave its voice” [Note: [Col. 0851] 19 Hab. III, 10.]. The apostles uttered their preaching from the depth of their hearts.

The abyss is the darkness of every wicked person, as in Job: “The abyss says, ‘It is not in me’” [Note: [Col. 0851] 20 Job XXVIII, 14.]. His obscure life cries out that patience is not in him.

The abyss is the eternal judgment of God, as in Job: “He will regard the abyss as though it were growing old” [Note: [Col. 0851] 21 Job XLI, 23.]. The devil, in his proud members, does not fear the eternal judgment of God, as though it were weak and unstable.

The abyss is called hell in the Gospel: “The legion begged him not to send them into the abyss” [Note: [Col. 0853] 1 Luke VIII, 31.], that is, not to plunge them into hell.

The abyss signifies the pains of death, as in the Psalms: “Placing the abysses in his treasuries” [Note: [Col. 0853] 2 Ps. XXXIII, 7.], that is, the profound mysteries in the secrets of sacred Scripture.

The abyss signifies those who are utterly despairing, as in the Psalms: “The Lord did everything whatever he willed, in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all abysses” [Note: [Col. 0853] 3 Ps. CXXXIV, 6.]. Just as he raises contemplations, which are heaven, so he makes actions fruitful, which are earth; so he strengthens the unstable, who are the sea; and so he acts in those who are utterly despairing. Likewise, he sometimes exercises his mercy in those who are abysses.

The abyss signifies the confusions of evil deeds, as in the Song of Exodus: “The abysses covered them” [Col. 0853B] [Note: [Col. 0853] 4 Exod. XV, 5.], that is, the confusions of their deeds overwhelmed them.

### Fir tree

The fir tree is the height of contemplation, as in Isaiah: “I will place the fir tree in the desert” [Note: [Col. 0853] 5 Isa. XLI, 19.]. In the world of the Gentiles, the Lord placed contemplation.

Fir trees are the powerful and unfruitful.

The fir tree signifies the holy angels, as in the Prophet: “The fir trees did not equal its height” [Note: [Col. 0853] 6 Ezek. XXXI, 8.]. In comparison with those angels, that first angel was higher.

### Premature birth

Those born prematurely signify the saints before the Law, as in Job: “Like a hidden premature birth” [Note: [Col. 0853] 7 Job III, 16.]. The saints before the Law were largely hidden from this world.

A premature birth signifies human imperfection, as in the book of Numbers: “Like a premature birth brought forth from its mother’s womb” [Note: [Col. 0853] 8 Num. XII, 12.]. Those who murmur are cast out as imperfect from mother Grace [Col. 0853C].

### Hawk

A hawk signifies any of the elect, as in Job: “Does the hawk grow feathers through your wisdom?” [Note: [Col. 0853] 9 Job XXXIX, 39.]. Through God alone the holy man acquires the feathers of virtues.

The hawk signifies the rapacious, as in Daniel: “And claws will grow like those of a hawk” [Note: [Col. 0853] 10 Dan. IV, 40.]. Those who are deceived in mind through pride grow even toward the pangs of rapacity.

### Vinegar

Vinegar is deceit, as in the Gospel: “He filled a sponge with vinegar” [Note: [Col. 0853] 11 Mark XV, 36.]. The devil filled the Jewish peoples with fraud and deceit.

Vinegar is any lazy person, as in Proverbs: “As vinegar is bitter to the teeth” [Note: [Col. 0853] 12 Prov. X, 26.], so the lazy person frequently harms the saints, who are called teeth, with an irritating word; as in Proverbs: “A viper, salt, vinegar in vices, and one who sings with a most evil heart” [Note: [Col. 0853] 13 Prov. XXV, 20.]. When a perverse mind is reproved, it murmurs, just as nitre foams and boils when placed in vinegar.

Vinegar is unbelief, as in the Psalms: “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” [Note: [Col. 0853] 14 Ps. LXVIII, 22.]. That is, I thirsted for their faith, and they gave me their unbelief to drink.

### Battle line

The battle line is the unity of the elect, as in the Song: “Terrible as an army set in battle array” [Note: [Col. 0853] 15 Song VI, 3, 9.]. Through their harmony the elect are terrifying to the devil.

### Heap

A heap of wheat signifies the growth of virtues, as in the Song: “Your belly is like a heap of wheat” [Note: [Col. 0853] 16 Song VII, 2.]. Those who are tender and belong to the holy Church receive growth in virtues.

A heap of testimony signifies the multitude of holy martyrs, as in Genesis: “They called that place Gilead, that is, ‘heap of testimony’” [Note: [Col. 0853] 17 Gen. XXXI, 47–48.]. In the holy Church the multitude of martyrs is honored.

A heap of stones is the rebuke of the last judgment, as in the books of Kings: “They gathered over Absalom a very great heap of stones” [Note: [Col. 0853] 18 2 Kings XVIII, 17.]. To the reprobate it will be said in judgment: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” [Note: [Col. 0853] 19 Matth. XXX, 41.].

A heap of Mercury is unbelief, as in the Proverbs of Solomon: “As one who throws a stone into a heap of Mercury, so is one who gives honor to a fool” [Note: [Col. 0853] 20 Prov. XXVIII, 8.]. Whoever advances a fool to ecclesiastical honor commits, in a certain way, the guilt of unbelief.

### Reclining

Reclining signifies the heavenly homeland, as in the Song: “While the king was at his reclining place, my spikenard gave its fragrance” [Note: [Col. 0853] 21 Song I, 13.]. When Christ sought heaven by ascending, the Church poured forth the fragrance of holiness.

### Needle

The needle is the piercing of pain, as in the Gospel: “For a camel to enter through the eye of a needle” [Note: [Col. 0853] Matt. XIX, 24; Mark X, 25; Luke XVIII, 25.]. Christ endured the piercings of pain on the cross.

### Young women

Young women signify the souls of the saints, as in the Song [Note: [Col. 0853] 23 Song I, 3.]. They are called young women because the devout souls of the saints love Christ.

### Fat

Fat signifies Christ’s divinity, as in the Psalms: “He satisfies you with the fat of wheat” [Note: [Col. 0853] 24 Ps. CXLVII, 14.]. Christ nourishes that heavenly Jerusalem with his divinity.

Fat signifies the simple meaning of Scripture, as in the Psalms: “He fed them with the fat of wheat” [Note: [Col. 0853] 25 Ps. LXXX, 17.]. He refreshed them with a simple understanding.

Fat signifies spiritual desire, as in the Song of Deuteronomy: “With the fat of lambs and rams” [Note: [Col. 0853] 26 Deut. XXXII, 14.], that is, with the spiritual desire of subjects and superiors.

Fat signifies abundance, as in the Psalms: “Their iniquity came forth as though from fat” [Note: [Col. 0853] 27 Ps. LXXII, 7.]. Through their abundance they sinned.

Fat signifies carnal joy, as in the Psalms: “They enclosed their fat” [Note: [Col. 0853] 28 Ps. XVII, 10.], that is, they confirmed their carnal joy.

Fat signifies the goodness of the inner will, as in the Psalms: “Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness” [Note: [Col. 0853] 29 Ps. LXII, 6.], [Col. 0854D] that is, inwardly with a good voice, just as outwardly through good action.

### Air

Air signifies the mind of any worldly person, as in Job: “Suddenly the air will be condensed into clouds” [Note: [Col. 0853] 30 Job XXXVII, 21.]. Through the sudden gift of the Spirit, the worldly mind is brought to holiness.

### Field

The field is the world, as in the Gospel: “To the man who sowed good seed in the field” [Note: [Col. 0855] 1 Matt. XIII, 24.], that is, to Christ, who scattered preaching throughout the world. Prepare your body and diligently cultivate your field: that is, pull up the thorns of iniquities and cultivate the body for the harvest of recompense.

The field is a good work, as in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0855] 2 Matt. XIII, 44.], where the field is bought for the treasure. A good work is undertaken for the sake of heavenly desire.

The field is sacred Scripture, as in Job: “They reap a field that is not theirs” [Note: [Col. 0855] 3 Job XXIV, 6.]. Heretics corrupt sacred Scripture, which is not theirs.

The field is the office of preaching, as in the Song: “Come, my beloved, let us go out into the field” [Note: [Col. 0855] 4 Song VII, 11.]. Christ goes forth from the Father’s hidden place, and the Church from the secret of contemplation, to the office of preaching.

The field is the Jewish people, as in Genesis: “Isaac went out to meditate in the field as evening was falling” [Note: [Col. 0855] 5 Gen. XXIV, 63.]. At the end of the world Christ went forth from heaven to teach among the Jewish people.

The field is the Gentile people, as in the Psalms: “The beauty of the field is with me” [Note: [Col. 0855] 6 Ps. XLIX, 11.]. The holiness of each religious man is with me for recompense.

The field is outward ceremony, as in the Gospel: “The older son was in the field” [Note: [Col. 0855] 7 Luke XV, 25.]. The Jewish people, content with the literal sense, cared for outward things.

The field is the life of any negligent person, as in Proverbs: “I passed by the field of a lazy man” [Note: [Col. 0855] 8 Prov. XXIV, 30.], that is, I examined the life of a sluggish person, “and behold, it was entirely filled with nettles and thorns” [Note: [Col. 0855] 9 Ibid.]. In his heart, itching desires and the prickings of vices sprout.

The field is the present holy Church, as in Genesis: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field” [Note: [Col. 0855] 10 Gen. XXXII, 27.]. The Church has been sanctified by the holiness of Christ, from whose fullness we have all received.

The field is the heavenly homeland, as in Proverbs: “He considered a field and bought it” [Note: [Col. 0855] 11 John I.]. The Church diligently learns what the joys of eternal life are and does not cease to labor for them.

### Lamb

The lamb is Christ, as in Exodus [Note: [Col. 0855] 12 Exod. XII, 5.]: the lamb is sacrificed without blemish, that is, Christ dies without guilt.

The lamb is any licentious person, as in Proverbs: “Following her like a frolicking lamb” [Note: [Col. 0855] 13 Prov. VII, 22.]. The lustful imitate the lustful.

Lambs signify the apostles, as the Lord says to them in the Gospel: “Behold, I send you like lambs among wolves” [Note: [Col. 0855] 14 Matt. X, 16.], that is, among unbelievers.

Lambs signify holy men, as in Isaiah: “And in his arm he will gather the lambs” [Note: [Col. 0855] 15 Isa. XL, 11.], that is, in his strength he will help holy men.

Lambs signify the simple and innocent, as in the Gospel: “Feed my lambs” [Note: [Col. 0855] 16 John XXI, 16.]. These are sinners whom I redeemed with my blood and who, having been made innocent, are nourished by his preaching.

A ewe-lamb signifies the active life, as in Leviticus: “Let him offer a ewe-lamb from the flocks” [Note: [Col. 0855] 17 Lev. V, 6.], that is, let him practice the active life, which is shared by many.

### Farmer

The farmer is God the Father, as in the Gospel: “My Father is the farmer” [Note: [Col. 0855] 18 John XV, 1.]. He spiritually cultivates the elect in his Son.

The farmer is any reprobate person who loves earthly things, as in Genesis: “Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and Cain a farmer” [Note: [Col. 0855] 19 Gen. IV, 2.]. Every elect person nourishes simple * thoughts beneath him, while every reprobate person, bringing forward his inner things *, loves earthly things.

The farmer signifies the rulers of the Synagogue, as in the Gospel: “He will lease it to farmers” [Note: [Col. 0855] 20 Matt. XXI, 33.]. He entrusted that ancient people to the rulers of the Synagogue.

The farmers signify the teachers of the Church, as in the Gospel: “He will lease his vineyard to other farmers” [Note: [Col. 0855] 21 Ibid. V, 41.], that is, he will entrust his Church to other teachers.

### Altar

The altar is divinity itself, as in the Psalm: “Establish the solemn day in the dense growth, up to [the horn of the altar]” [Note: [Col. 0855] 22 Ps. CXVII, 27.], that is, practice virtues frequently, reaching the eminence of the Godhead.

The altar is Christ’s flesh, as in Jeremiah: “God rejected his altar” [Note: [Col. 0855] 23 Lam. II, 17.]. He permitted Christ’s flesh to be crucified.

The altar is the humanity of the Word itself, as in Exodus: “You shall make an altar of earth for me” [Note: [Col. 0855] 24 Exod. XX, 24.], that is, you shall believe that the humanity of the Word was taken from the Virgin.

The altar is the wood of the cross, as in Genesis [Note: [Col. 0855] 25 Gen. XXII, 9.], where Isaac was placed upon the altar: Christ was offered upon the cross.

The altar is the secret place of the mind, as in the Psalm: “I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will surround your altar, O Lord” [Note: [Col. 0855] 26 Ps. XXV, 6.]. I will amend evil works through repentance and adorn the secret place of the mind with virtues.

The altar is faith, as in the Psalm: “They will place them upon your altar” [Note: [Col. 0855] 27 Ps. L, 21.]. They join the innocence of the new life to faith *.

The altar is the life of the righteous, as in Genesis: “Noah built an altar to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0855] 28 Gen. VIII, 20.]. Christ consecrated the life of the righteous to the Father.

The altar is devotion of heart, as in the Gospel: “If you offer your gift at the altar” [Note: [Col. 0855] 29 Matt. V, 23.], that is, if you pour out your prayer through devotion of heart.

The altar is the secret of heaven, as in the Psalms: “I will enter the altar of God” [Note: [Col. 0855] 30 Ps. XLII.], that is, I will reach the secret of heaven.

### Breath

Breath [alitus] is Christ’s humanity, as in Job: “My breath was abhorrent to my wife” [Note: [Col. 0855] 31 Job XIX, 17.], that is, the Synagogue despised my humanity.

Breath is the utterance of the mouth, as in Daniel: “Even my breath is shut off” [Note: [Col. 0855] 32 Dan. X, 17.], that is, I lack not only strength in heart but also fall silent in the very speech of my mouth.

Breath is the devil’s suggestion, as in Job: “His breath makes coals burn” [Note: [Col. 0855] 33 Job XLI, 12.], that is, the devil’s suggestion kindles the thoughts of the reprobate.

### Wings

Wings signify the Lord’s mercy and truth, as in the Psalms: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings,” that is, defend me under the aid of your mercy and truth.

Wings signify the Lord’s commandments, as in the Psalms: “They will hope under the shelter of your wings” [Note: [Col. 0855] 34 Ps. XXXV, 8.], that is, they will hope in the protection of your commandments.

Wings signify the thought of a holy man, as in Job: “He spreads his wings for sexual intercourse” [Note: [Col. 0857] 1 Job XXXIX, 29.], that is, every elect person opens his thoughts to the Holy Spirit through confession.

Wings signify the thoughts of a hypocrite, as in Job: “When the time comes, he raises his wings on high” [Note: [Col. 0857] 2 Job XXIX, 21.]. When he finds opportunities, he displays his thoughts publicly.

Wings signify the desires of the rapacious, as in Zechariah: “They had wings like the wings of a kite” [Note: [Col. 0857] 3 Zech. V, 9.]. The greedy strive to seize what belongs to others.

Wings signify the virtues of the saints, as in Ezekiel: “I heard the sound of the wings, like the sound of many waters” [Note: [Col. 0857] 4 Ezek. I, 24.]. Spiritual virtues, which were previously present in a few, afterward appeared in many.

Foreigners signify demons, as in the Psalms: “Foreigners have risen up against me” [Note: [Col. 0857] 5 Ps. LIII, 5.], that is, demons have fought against me.

### Height

Height is the sublimity of rewards, as in Ezekiel: “The stature and height of the wheels also” [Note: [Col. 0857] 6 Ezek. I, 18.]. In sacred Scripture one learns both uprightness of life and height of glory.

Height is the prince of this world, as in Habakkuk: “The height will raise its hands” [Note: [Col. 0857] 7 Hab. III, 10.]. The exalted rulers of this age raise up their works.

Height is prosperity, as in Paul: “Neither height nor depth” [Note: [Col. 0857] 8 Rom. VIII, 39.], that is, neither prosperity nor adversity.

### White spot

A white spot signifies blindness of heart, as in Tobit: “The white spot began to depart from his eyes” [Note: [Col. 0857] 9 Tob. XI, 14.]. When Christ began to be recognized by the Jewish people at the end of the world, the long blindness of unbelief with which they are now oppressed departs from them.

A white spot signifies arrogance of mind, as in Leviticus: [Col. 0857C] “If he has a white spot in his eye” [Note: [Col. 0857] 10 Lev. XXI, 20.], that is, if he has arrogance in his mind.

### Aloe

Aloe is the virtue of continence, as in the Song: “And aloe with all precious ointments” [Note: [Col. 0857] 11 Cant. IV, 41.], that is, continence together with all the highest virtues.

Aloe is the pleasure of the flesh, as in Proverbs: “I have sprinkled my bed with myrrh and aloe” [Note: [Col. 0857] 12 Prov. VII, 17.], that is, I have filled my mind with sweetness and carnal pleasure.

### Fattened animals

Fattened animals signify the Fathers of the New Testament, as in the Gospel: “My bulls and fattened animals have been killed” [Note: [Col. 0857] 13 Matt. XXII, 4.]. The Fathers of the Old and New Testaments prepare spiritual nourishment for us.

### Friend

The friend is Christ, as in the Song: “He is my friend, daughters of Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0857] 14 Song I, 16.]. He loved his Church so greatly that he died for her.

A friend is any neighbor of ours. In the Proverbs of Solomon: “My son, if you have become surety for your friend” [Note: [Col. 0857] 15 Prov. VI, 1.], that is, for your neighbor.

A friend is our mind, as in the Gospel: “My friend has come to me from the road” [Note: [Col. 0857] 16 Luke XI, 6.], that is, my mind has come to itself.

A friend is sometimes one who is a Christian in name alone, as in the Gospel: “Friend, how did you enter here?” [Note: [Col. 0857] 17 Matt. XXII, 12.] The wicked man is a friend because of the faith he holds, but because he lacks charity, he does not have a wedding garment.

Friends signify the holy angels, as in the Song: “She who dwells in the gardens—the friends listen” [Note: [Col. 0857] 18 Song VIII, 13.]. The holy angels desire to hear the progress of the human soul.

Friends signify holy preachers, as in Job: “Friends will cut him down” [Note: [Col. 0857] 19 Job XL, 25.]. Holy preachers destroy the devil in the elect whom they convert to faith.

Friends signify the other saints, as in the Gospel: “You are my friends if you do what I command you” [Note: [Col. 0857] 20 John XV, 14.], that is, you love me then if you keep my commandments.

### Female friend

The female friend is the holy Church, as in the Song: “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend” [Note: [Col. 0857] 21 Song I, 15; IV, 1, 7; VI, 3.]. The spiritual holy Church shines with beauty.

The female friend signifies the holy angels, as in the Gospel: “She calls together her friends and neighbors” [Note: [Col. 0857] 22 Luke XV, 9.]. The angels of the Lord love the one from whose voice they never depart.

### Jar

The jar is avarice, as in Zechariah: “This is the jar going forth” [Note: [Col. 0857] 23 Zech. V, 6.]. No one is entirely free from avarice.

The jar is measure in contemplation, as in the books of Kings: “He brought him with him with three calves, a measure of flour, and a jar of wine” [Note: [Col. 0857] 24 1 Kings I, 24.]. Our life is then offered well to God when, together with the mortification of vanity, curiosity, and pleasure, we maintain fullness in action and discernment in contemplation.

### Ring

The ring is the seal of faith, as in the Gospel: “Put a ring on his hand” [Note: [Col. 0857] 25 Luke XV, 22.], that is, faith in his work.

The ring signifies the book of the Gospels, as in Exodus [Note: [Col. 0857] 26 Exod. XXV, 12.]. There were four rings at the four corners of the ark; the four parts of the Church are adorned by the four books of the Evangelists.

Rings signify the shoots of eternal blessedness, as in Exodus: “You shall cast golden rings for the poles” [Note: [Col. 0857] 27 Ibid. V, 13.]. In return for the good works we now perform, we shall possess glorious perpetuity and perpetual glory.

### Year

The year is the time of grace, as in Isaiah: “Proclaim the acceptable year” [Note: [Col. 0857] 28 Isa. LXI, 2.], that is, the advent of grace, which presents him to us as favorable.

The year is the multitude of the redeemed, as in Job: “Let it not be counted among the days of the year” [Note: [Col. 0857] 29 Job III, 6.]. Among the elect who are saved, the apostate does not receive hope of salvation.

The year signifies Christ’s eternity, as in the Psalm: “Through generation and generation are your years” [Note: [Col. 0857] 30 Ps. CI, 25.]. The eternity of God endures forever.

The year signifies our life, as in the Psalm: “Our years will be meditated like a spider” [Note: [Col. 0857] 31 Ps. LXXXIX, 9.], that is, our life creaks with empty things and corruptions [Col. 0858D].

### Maidservant

The maidservant is the Church, as in the Psalms: “Save the son of your maidservant” [Note: [Col. 0857] 32 Ps. LXXXV, 16.], that is, me, who am a member of the Church.

The maidservant is corruptible flesh, as in Genesis: “Cast out the maidservant and her son” [Note: [Col. 0857] 33 Gen. XXI, 10.], that is, despise the flesh and its carnal fruit.

The maidservant signifies the preachers of the Church, as in Job: “He will bind it with his maidservants” [Note: [Col. 0857] 34 Job XL, 24.]. Through his preachers the Lord binds the devil.

The maidservant signifies the effeminate minds of the Jews, as in Job: “Your maidservants regarded me as a stranger” [Note: [Col. 0859] 1 Job XIX, 15.]. Through faith the effeminate minds of the Jews recognized me.

The maidservant signifies all the humble, as in Genesis: “And food for her maidservants” [Note: [Col. 0859] 2 Prov. XXXI, 15.]. The holy Church grants spiritual refreshment to the humble.

### Carved figures

Carved figures are the varieties of good works, as in the book of Kings: “And very prominent carved figures” [Note: [Col. 0859] 3 1 Kings VI, 32. *]. In the holy man, who is the temple of God, varieties of good deeds appear to others as examples.

### Caves

The caves of the heart are its secrets, as in Job: “When * he fed in the caves” [Note: [Col. 0859] 4 Job XXXIX, 2.]. Holy men rest not in outward things but in the secrets of their hearts.

### Forewall

The forewall signifies the prophets, as in Isaiah: “The Savior will be placed in it as a wall and a forewall” [Note: [Col. 0859] 5 Isa. XXVI, 1.]. Christ, who in himself was the Church’s wall through the mystery of his incarnation, was, before his incarnation, a forewall for that same Church in the prophets.

### Animals

The animals are the four Evangelists, as in Ezekiel: “The likeness of a human being in the animals” [Note: [Col. 0859] 6 Ezek. I, 5.]. They labor for Christ.

The animals are the saints in the Church, as in the Psalms: “Your animals will dwell in it” [Note: [Col. 0859] 7 Ps. LXVII, 11.]. The righteous live in the Church by faith.

The animals are the greedy; * in Ezekiel, the abomination of animals was depicted on the wall [Note: [Col. 0859] 8 Ezek. VIII, 10.]. In their need, the wicked depict within themselves the depravity of the greedy.
