The animals are the two thieves crucified with Christ, as in * Habakkuk: “In the midst of two animals.” Christ was suspended in the midst of two thieves.

Angulus signifies a humble place, as in Proverbs: “It is better to sit in a corner of the housetop”—that is, in a humble place—“in peace than in a lofty place with discord” [Note: [Col. 0859] 9 Prov. XXI, 9.]. Angulus signifies conjunction, as in the Psalms: “This has become the head of the corner” [Note: [Col. 0859] 10 Psal. CXVII, 22.], because Christ joined the two peoples. By angulus, the ends of this world are signified, as in Exodus: “Two boards shall be erected […] at the rear of the tabernacle” [Note: [Col. 0859] 11 Exod. XXVI, 23.], because, when the end of this world arrives, the holy Enoch and Elijah will be erected against the devil. By anguli are signified the pretended works of wicked minds, as in Zephaniah: “The day of the Lord is against the lofty corners” [Note: [Col. 0859] 12 Zeph. I, 16.], because vengeance will strike the hearts of the wicked, which are lofty because of their exaltation and are called corners because of their duplicity. [Col. 0859D]

Apis is an unclean sinner, as in Isaiah: “The Lord will hiss for the bee” [Note: [Col. 0859] 13 Isa. VII, 18.], because by his inspiration he calls the unclean sinner to himself. Apes are the humble, as in Ecclesiasticus: “The bee is small among flying creatures” [Note: [Col. 0859] 14 Eccl. XI, 13.], because the humble have been made to dwell among the proud. By apes are signified slanderers, as in the Psalms: “They surrounded me like bees” [Note: [Col. 0859] 15 Psal. CXVII, 12.], because they praised me openly but slandered me in secret; for bees have honey in their mouths and a sting in their hind parts. [Col. 0860A]

Aper is the prince of the Romans, as in the Psalms: “The boar from the forest devastated it” [Note: [Col. 0859] 16 Psal. LXXIX.], because Titus, who ruled in Rome, took the Jewish people captive.

Aquilo is the severity of persecution, as in the Song: “Arise, north wind; come, south wind” [Note: [Col. 0859] 17 Song IV, 16.], because the Church sometimes desires that the severity of persecution be softened. Aquilo is the gentile people, as in Isaiah: “I will say to the north: Give; and to the south: Do not hinder” [Note: [Col. 0859] 18 Isa. XLIII, 6.], because I will inspire the gentiles to believe. Aquilo sometimes signifies one converted and chosen for the faith, as in Job: “Gold will come from the north” [Note: [Col. 0859] 19 Job XXXVII, 24.], because splendor of wisdom came both from Paul and from Augustine, who had previously been cold in faith. [Col. 0860B] Aquilo signifies old age, as in the Gospel: “They will come from the north and […] blunt” [uncertain text], because some in old age tend toward rest. Aquilo signifies the suggestion of the ancient enemy, as in Jeremiah, where the face of a heated pot was “from the face of the north” [Note: [Col. 0859] 20 Jer. I, 13.], that is, “I will reign over the reprobate.” Aquilo is the devil, as in Job: “He stretches out the north over the void” [Note: [Col. 0859] 21 Job XXVI, 7.], because God permits the devil to dominate the minds of those who are empty of his grace.

Aqua is the Holy Spirit, as in the Gospel: “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly” [Note: [Col. 0859] 22 John VII, 38.], because the gifts of the Holy Spirit proceed from the memory of the believer. Aqua is Christ, as in the Psalms: “I tested you at the water of contradiction” [Note: [Col. 0859] 23 Psal. LXXX, 8.], that is, by Christ, whom many contradict. [Col. 0860C] Aqua is subtle wisdom, as in Proverbs: “Deep water is from the mouth of a man” [Note: [Col. 0859] 24 Prov. XVIII, 4.], because subtle wisdom is found in the speech of the just. Aqua is loquacity, as in Proverbs: “He who releases water is the beginning of quarrels” [Note: [Col. 0859] 25 Prov. XVII, 14.], because whoever does not restrain loquacity destroys harmony. Aqua is worldly desire, as in the Gospel: “He cast him into fire and water in order to destroy him” [Note: [Col. 0859] 26 Matt. XVII, 15; Mark IX, 22.], because the devil now burns those whom he possesses with the heat of lust, and now defiles them with the filth of desire, in order to destroy them. Aqua is baptism, as in the Psalms: “The water covered those who afflicted them” [Note: [Col. 0859] 27 Psal. CV, 11.], because in baptism the sins of the elect are forgiven. Aqua is the prophetic utterance expressed in riddles, as in the Psalms: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” [Note: [Col. 0859] 28 Psal. XVIII, 12.], because the prophets possess obscure speech. Aqua is Christ’s holy preaching, as in Ezekiel: “I will pour clean water upon you” [Note: [Col. 0859] 29 Ezek. XXXVI, 25.], that is, “I will cleanse you through pure preaching, so that you may be clean because of the word that I speak to you.” Aqua is compunction, as in the Books of Kings: “They drew water and poured it out before the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0859] 30 I Kings VII, 6.], because they brought forth compunction from the depths of their hearts and wept before God. [Col. 0860D]

[Col. 0861A]

Aqua is the prosperity of this world, as in the Psalms: “We passed through fire and water” [Note: [Col. 0861] 1 Psal. LXVI, 12.], that is, through adversity and prosperity. Aqua is adversity, as in the Psalms: “Let not the storm of water overwhelm me” [Note: [Col. 0861] 2 Psal. LXVIII, 16.], that is, “Let not a mass of adversity overcome me.” Aqua is human knowledge, as in Exodus: “Do not eat anything raw or cooked in water” [Note: [Col. 0861] 3 Exod. XII, 9.], because Christ must be conceived neither as a mere man nor as something whose manner of incarnation may be scrutinized. Aqua is the abundance of the world, as in the Apocalypse: “The angel poured out his bowl upon that great river, the Euphrates, and dried up its water” [Note: [Col. 0861] 4 Apoc. XVI, 12.], because the preacher raises his voice against the world and causes its abundance to be despised by many. Aqua is the historical understanding, as in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0861] 5 John II, 9.], where the water at the wedding was changed into wine, because in the union of Christ and the Church the literal meaning is changed into the spiritual. [Col. 0861B]

Aqua is the pleasure of the flesh, as in the Gospel: “Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again” [Note: [Col. 0861] 6 John IV, 13.], because the more frequently the pleasure of the flesh is indulged, the more it is desired. Aqua is eternal refreshment, as in the Apocalypse: “The angel showed me the spring of living water” [Note: [Col. 0861] 7 Apoc. XXII, 1.], that is, Christ revealed to me the abundance of eternal refreshment.

By aqua are signified the holy angels, as in the Psalms: “And the waters that are above the heavens” [Note: [Col. 0861] 8 Psal. CXLVIII, 4.], that is, the angels who dwell in the heights, “let them praise the name of the Lord.” By aqua are signified blessed souls, as in the Psalm: “You cover its upper parts with waters” [Note: [Col. 0861] 9 Psal. CIII, 3.], because we indeed understand sacred Scripture in some measure, but the blessed souls who already see the Lord in the heavens know fully everything of which it treats. By aquae are signified the saints who are [Col. 0861C] now in the Church, as in the Psalms: “The river of God is filled with waters” [Note: [Col. 0861] 10 Psal. LXIV, 10.], because in the holy Church the people serving the Lord increase both in merit and in number. By aquae are signified the laments of humility, as in Job: “If I wash myself as with waters of snow” [Note: [Col. 0861] 11 Job IX, 30.], that is, “If I am drenched with the laments of humility.” By aquae are signified the devotions of the saints, as in Job: “He weighs the waters by measure” [Note: [Col. 0861] 12 Job XXVIII, 25.], because God wondrously regulates the devotions of his saints, so that some cannot perform as much in action as they are able to comprehend in […] effect. By aquae are signified the sins that God forgives his elect, as in Genesis: “The Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters” [Note: [Col. 0861] 13 Gen. I, 2.], because his mercy is greater than their iniquity. [Col. 0861D]

By aquae is signified the knowledge of heretics, as in Proverbs: “Stolen waters are sweeter” [Note: [Col. 0861] 14 Prov. IX, 17.], that is, “Our hidden knowledge is better.” By aquae are signified persecutions, as in the Psalms: “He established his land upon the waters” [Note: [Col. 0861] 15 Psal. CXXXV, 6.], that is, “He founded the Church upon persecutions.” By aquae are signified mortal peoples, as in the Psalm: “The waters saw you, O God” [Note: [Col. 0861] 16 Psal. LXXVI, 17.], because the peoples looked upon you by believing and feared you by making petition. By aquae are signified unstable thoughts, as in the Psalms: “Deliver me from many waters” [Note: [Col. 0861] 17 Psal. CXLIII, 7.], that is, “from many unstable thoughts.” [Col. 0862A]

By aquae are signified the blandishments of temptations, as in Job: “The waters hollow out stones” [Note: [Col. 0861] 18 Job XIV, 19.], because the blandishments of temptations sometimes soften strong men. By aquae are signified the pleasures of the reprobate, as in the Psalms: “He turned their waters into blood” [Note: [Col. 0861] 19 Psal. CIV, 29.], because God sometimes brings the evil desires of the impious to the cruelty of bitterness. By aquae are signified infernal punishments, as in the Song of Exodus: “They sank like lead in mighty waters” [Note: [Col. 0861] 20 Exod. XV, 10.], that is, weighty sinners plunged into infernal punishments.

Aquila is Christ, as in the Song of Deuteronomy: “The eagle stirred up its young to fly” [Note: [Col. 0861] 21 Deut. XXXII, 11.], because Christ does not cease to urge his disciples to advance from virtue to virtue. Aquila is John [Col. 0862B] the Evangelist, as in Ezekiel: “The face of an eagle was above the four of them” [Note: [Col. 0861] 22 Ezek. I, 10.], because, by speaking about Christ’s divinity, he fixed his eyes upon the sun like an eagle; he was not only above the other evangelists but surpassed himself. Aquila is the devil, as in Proverbs: “The way of an eagle in the heavens” [Note: [Col. 0861] 23 Prov. XXX, 19.], because the subtlety of the enemy is difficult for holy men to detect. Aquila signifies the soul, as in Job: “The eagle will be exalted and will place its nest in high places” [Note: [Col. 0861] 24 Job XXXIX, 30.], because through contemplation the soul is exalted and fixes its desire in the heavens. Aguila [sic] signifies the sublime power of this world, as in Ezekiel: “A great eagle, with great wings, long pinions, full of feathers and variegated, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar” [Note: [Col. 0861] 25 Ezek. XVII, 3.], that is, King Nebuchadnezzar, a powerful king with many powers, filled with the varied lightness of worldly glory, besieged Jerusalem and led away the entire captive people. [Col. 0862C]

By aquila are signified the souls of the elect, as in the Gospel: “Wherever the body is, there also will the eagles be gathered” [Note: [Col. 0861] 26 Matt. XXIV, 28.], because where the Lord is in the body, there will be the souls of the saints. By aquilae are signified demons, as in Jeremiah: “Our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0861] 27 Jer. IV, 13.], that is, “Our enemies were more cruel than aerial spirits.”

Arturus is the holy Church, as in Job: “He who makes Arcturus and Orion” [Note: [Col. 0861] 28 Job IX, 9.], because the Lord both founded the Church and produced holy martyrs in it. Arturus is the Old Testament, as in Job: “Can you scatter the circle of Arcturus?” [Note: [Col. 0861] 29 Job XXXVIII, 31.], because the Lord changed the [Col. 0862D] letter of the Old Testament into a spiritual meaning. Arturus is the unbelieving people, as in Job: “From Arcturus the cold will come” [Note: [Col. 0861] 30 Job XXXVII, 9.], because the coldness of unbelief proceeds from an unbelieving people.

Arcus is sacred preaching, as in the Psalms: “Bending and shooting the bow” [Note: [Col. 0861] 31 Psal. LXXVII, 9.], because many in the Church are sent against others with the words of preaching but succumb in temptation. Arcus is human strength, as in the Psalms: “For I will not trust in my [Col. 0863A] bow” [Note: [Col. 0863] 1 Psal. XLIII, 7.], that is, “I will not rely upon my own strength.” Arcus […] as in the Psalms: “The sinners have bent their bow” [Note: [Col. 0863] 2 Psal. XI, 2; and XXXVI, 14.], because the Jews practiced deceit against the Lord. Arcus […] the Evangelist, as in the Psalms: “A bronze bow” [Note: [Col. 0863] 3 Psal. XVII, 35.], that is, “You have made my strong workers unbending.” Arcus is sacred Scripture, as in the Psalms: “He bent his bow” [Note: [Col. 0863] 4 Psal. VII, 13.], because the Lord presented sacred Scripture to us. Arcus is the threat of judgment, as in the Psalms: “Let them flee from the face of the bow” [Note: [Col. 0863] 5 Psal. XXXVI, 14; and LXIV, 4.], that is, “Let them escape the final judgment.” Arcus is hidden malice, as in the Psalms: “They bent the bow, a bitter thing” [Note: [Col. 0863] 6 Psal. LXXVII, 57.], that is, “They practiced hidden malice.” “The bows were turned,” that is, their predecessors had an evil intention. Arcus is threats, as in the Psalms: “They bent the [Col. 0863B] bow, but the Lord […] will weaken it” [uncertain text], that is, “He threatens them so that they may be humbled.” Arcus is the virtue of patience, as in Genesis: “His bow remained strong” [Note: [Col. 0863] 7 Gen. XLIX, 24.], because the patience of a holy man is vigorous. By arcus are signified the ambushes of those who strike, as in the Psalms: “There he broke the powers, the bow” [Note: [Col. 0863] 8 Psal. LXXV, 4.], that is, “There he destroyed the strength of those lying in ambush.”

Argentum is spiritual eloquence, as in Isaiah: “Your silver has become dross” [Note: [Col. 0863] 9 Isa. I, 22.], that is, the spiritual eloquence of the Law is fouled by the dregs of carnal desires. Argentum is the splendor of divine eloquence, as in the Song: “We will make golden ornaments for you, variegated with silver” [Note: [Col. 0863] 10 Song I, 11.], that is, “Through me you will have the teachings of divine wisdom adorned with the splendor of eloquence, through the diversity of very small variations.” Argentum signifies the martyrs, whose voice is this, as in the [Col. 0863C] Psalms [Note: [Col. 0863] 11 Psal. LXVI.]: “You have tested us by fire,” because you removed in tribulation the stains that were in us. Argentum signifies poetic fictions, as in the Apocalypse: “No one will buy the merchandise of your silver any longer” [Note: [Col. 0863] 12 Apoc. XVIII, 12.], because no one thereafter will frequent the jocular words of the impious. Argentum signifies the life of preachers, as in Job: “Nor will silver be weighed in exchange for it” [Note: [Col. 0863] 13 Job XXVIII, 15.], because not even preachers themselves, however just they may be, can in any way be compared with Christ.

Aries is the flesh of Christ, as in Genesis [Note: [Col. 0863] 14 Gen. XXII, 13.], where Isaac is placed upon the altar but the ram is slaughtered, because Christ is crucified but only his flesh dies. Aries is the priestly order, as in Proverbs: “And the ram, and there is no one who can resist him” [Note: [Col. 0863] 15 Prov. XXX, 31.], because both earthly kings and rulers are subject to the holy priesthood that is in the Church. Aries is the movement of anger, as in Leviticus: “He also offered the ram as a burnt offering” [Note: [Col. 0863] 16 Lev. VIII, 28.], because a holy man ought to slaughter every movement of anger within himself. By arietes are signified the holy apostles, as in the Psalms: “The rams of the sheep are clothed” [Note: [Col. 0863] 17 Psal. LXIV, 14.], because the apostles who rule over the faithful are clothed with the Holy Spirit. By arietes are signified the prelates who are in the Church, as in the Psalms: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” [Note: [Col. 0863] 18 Psal. XXVIII, 1.], that is, yourselves, whom [Col. 0864A] the prelates have begotten in Christ. By arietes are signified all rational beings, as in Genesis: “He placed the rods before the eyes of the rams” [Note: [Col. 0863] 19 Gen. XXX, 41.], that is, external goods before the sight of rational beings. By arietes are signified heretics, as in Jeremiah: “Your princes are like rams” [Note: [Col. 0863] 20 Lam. I, 6.], that is, “Your prelates are heretics who have been led astray.”

Armilla is divine mercy, as in Job: “Or will you pierce his jaw with a bracelet?” [Note: [Col. 0863] 21 Job XL, 21.], because divine mercy, embracing us on every side, rescues us from the power of the devil. Armilla signifies justification received from the Just One, as in Genesis: “Recognize whose ring and bracelet these are” [Note: [Col. 0863] 22 Gen. XXXVIII, 25.], because from Christ the Church has both faith and justification. [The preceding source phrase, “a justificato,” is materially uncertain.] By armillae are signified the works of prelates, as in Isaiah: “The bracelet and the earrings” [Note: [Col. 0863] 23 Isa. III, 19.], that is, the works of prelates and the obediences of subjects. By armillae are signified actions [Col. 0864B] pertaining to the Decalogue, as in Genesis: “Two bracelets weighing ten shekels” [Note: [Col. 0863] 24 Gen. XXIV, 22.], because the holy Church receives the works of the Decalogue.

Arena is the calamity of this life, as in Job: “This would appear heavier than the sand of the sea” [Note: [Col. 0863] 25 Job VI, 3.], because the misery we suffer is both weighty and abundant like sand. Arena signifies the humble, as in the prophet: “I set sand as a boundary for the sea” [Note: [Col. 0863] 26 Jer. V, 22.], because God placed the humble in order to conquer the swelling pride of the proud. Arena is the instability of this world, as in the Gospel: “Who built his house upon sand” [Note: [Col. 0863] 27 Matt. VII, 26.], that is, “He always founded his mind upon the instability of this world.” Arena is the heavenly city, as in Genesis: “I will multiply your offspring like the sand that is on the seashore” [Note: [Col. 0863] 28 Gen. XXII, 17.], because almighty [Col. 0864C] God grants his elect such spiritual increase that, insofar as they are able, they may imitate the holiness of those citizens who dwell in the solid foundation of the heavenly homeland.

Arma are spiritual virtues, as in Saint Paul: “With the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left” [Note: [Col. 0863] 29 II Cor. VI, 7.], that is, good works in prosperity and adversity. Arma signify the heart of the reprobate, as in the prophet: “They descended into the broad place with their weapons” [Note: [Col. 0863] 30 Ezek. XXXII, 27.], because they rushed into destruction with their bodies. Arma are open attacks, as in the Psalms: “He will break the weapons” [Note: [Col. 0863] 31 Psal. XLV, 10.], that is, “He will destroy manifest attacks.” Arma are the wickednesses of the devil, as in the Gospel: “He will take away all his weapons” [Note: [Col. 0863] 32 Luke XI, 22.], that is, “He will annihilate all his wickednesses.” [Col. 0864D]

Arca is the body of Christ, as in Exodus: “Join together an ark from the wood of Chettim” [Note: [Col. 0863] 33 Exod. XXV, 10.], that is, “Believe that the body of Christ consists of incorruptible members.” Arca is the Church, as in the Psalms: “Arise, O Lord, to your rest” [Note: [Col. 0863] 34 Psal. CXXXI, 8.], that is, “Arise from the dead, and let the Church also arise, which you have deigned to sanctify.” Arca is any ecclesiastical teacher, as in the Books of Kings [Note: [Col. 0863] 35 II Kings VI.], where the Lord struck Uzzah because he had touched the ark [Col. 0865A] of the Lord; for those who arrogantly touch the prelates of the Church with the hand of criticism are struck by spiritual death. Arca is the holy mind, as in Genesis: “Make yourself an ark of smoothed wood” [Note: [Col. 0865] 1 Gen. VI, 14.], that is, “Make a mind free from the burden of sin.”

Arula is the human heart, as in Exodus: “You shall place four rings upon the small altar” [Note: [Col. 0865] 2 Exod. XXVII, 5.], that is, “Through understanding you shall entrust the books of the four Evangelists to your heart.”

Armatus is the devil, as in Job: “And he will seize him while armed” [Note: [Col. 0865] 3 Job V, 5.], because the devil seizes the impious in death for punishment. Armatus is any proud person who tries to excuse himself, as in the Books of Kings [Note: [Col. 0865] 4 I Kings XVII, 39.], where David did not know how to walk while armed, because every humble person proudly does not know how to excuse himself. By armati are signified tyrants, as in [Col. 0865B] Job: “They go out to meet the armed” [Note: [Col. 0865] 5 Job XXXIX, 21.], because the holy preacher does not fear to resist the pride of tyrants.

Artifex is the Lord, as in the Song: “Which were fashioned by the hand of the craftsman” [Note: [Col. 0865] 6 Song VII, 1.], because spiritual gifts are bestowed upon us through the Lord’s grace.

Arvina is the fatness of things, as in Job: “And fat hangs upon his sides” [Note: [Col. 0865] 7 Job XV, 27.], because in the counselors of the impious […] fatness abounds. [Uncertain text.]

Artus are the innermost members of the Church, as in Job: “All my limbs have been reduced to nothing” [Note: [Col. 0865] 8 Job XVI, 7.], that is, “My weak members take great delight.” [The Latin is textually uncertain.]

Area is the Church, as in the Gospel: “And he will cleanse his threshing floor” [Note: [Col. 0865] 9 Matt. III, 12; Luke III, 17.], that is, “Cleansing his Church.” Area is this world, as in the Book of Judges: “I will place [Col. 0865C] this fleece of wool on the threshing floor” [Note: [Col. 0865] 10 Judg. VI, 37.], because God placed the Virgin Mary in the world for the salvation of humanity. Area is the breadth of the gentile people, as in the Books of Kings [Note: [Col. 0865] 11 II Kings XXIV, 18.], where David established an altar to the Lord on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, because Christ consecrates the Church to the Father in the breadth of the gentile people.

Arbor is Christ, as in the Song: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forests, so is my beloved among the sons” [Note: [Col. 0865] 12 Song II, 3.], because there is a great difference between Christ and the holy sons of the Church, since they are mere human beings. Arbor is the cross, as in the Song: “Under the apple tree I awakened you” [Note: [Col. 0865] 13 Song VIII, 5.], that is, “Through faith in my Passion I recalled you from death.” Arbor is humble knowledge of God, as in the Gospel: “Zacchaeus climbed a sycamore tree in order to see [Col. 0865D] Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0865] 14 Luke XIX, 4.], because unless we grasp the foolishness of God, we do not deserve to comprehend Christ. Arbor is robust faith, as in the Gospel: “The mustard seed grew and became a great tree” [Note: [Col. 0865] 15 Luke XIII, 19.], because faith grew, although previously it had appeared rejected by the world, and received great strength. Arbor is good will, as in the Gospel: “A good tree does not produce bad fruits” [Note: [Col. 0865] 16 Matt. VII, 18.], because an evil action does not proceed from a good utterance. Arbor is evil will, as in the Gospel: “There is no good tree that produces bad [Col. 0866A] fruit” [Note: [Col. 0865] 17 Luke VI, 43.], because the will in the mind is not then good when evil fruits appear in action. Arbor is anyone perfect in faith, as in the Apocalypse: “It was commanded to him” [Note: [Col. 0865] 18 Apoc. VII, 1.], that is, it was enjoined by God upon the disciples of Antichrist, “that they should not harm the grass,” that is, anyone inexperienced in faith, “nor any green thing,” that is, anyone advanced in faith, “nor any tree,” that is, anyone perfect in faith. Arbor is human nature, as in the Gospel: “The tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” [Note: [Col. 0865] 19 Matt. VII, 19.], because the impious person who does not take care to conquer well will be cut off from the fellowship of the just and cast into the fire of Gehenna. Arbor signifies the entire mass of the reprobate, as in the Gospel: “The axe has been laid at the root of the tree” [Note: [Col. 0865] 20 Ibid.], because Christ the Judge, who […] drew you from the handle of his humanity [Col. 0866B] and cut you with the iron of his divinity, will consume all the reprobate. [Text materially uncertain.] By arbor this world is signified, as in the Gospel: “When trees produce fruit from themselves, you know that the kingdom of God is near” [Note: [Col. 0865] 21 Luke XXI, 30–31.]. By arbores are signified heretics, as in the Epistle of Jude: “Autumnal trees” [Note: [Col. 0865] 22 Verse 12.], because the salvation of heretics is despaired of.

Aromata are holy men, as in the Song: “Blow upon my garden, O south wind, and its spices will flow” [Note: [Col. 0865] 23 Song IV, 16.], that is, “Make my Church fruitful, O holy Bridegroom, and its saints will appear.” Aromata are the good works of the saints, as in the Song: “And the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices” [Note: [Col. 0865] 24 Song IV, 10.], because the sweetnesses of the virtues found in the Virgin Mary surpass the good works of the saints. Aromata are pure thoughts [Col. 0866C], as in the Song: “I have gathered my myrrh with my spices” [Note: [Col. 0865] 25 Song V, 1; Mark XVI, 1.], because whoever now mortifies the flesh and purifies the mind will reap eternal life from both in the future. Aromata are the sweetnesses of prayers, as in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0865] 26 Luke XXIV, 1.]: […] “the women came at dawn carrying the spices that they had prepared,” because, once the darkness of the devout mind has been dispelled, souls come bearing prayers prepared beforehand. [Text interrupted in the source.]

Areolae are teachings of the virtues, as in the Song: “His cheeks are like beds of spices” [Note: [Col. 0865] 27 Song V, 13.], that is, his martyrs persist in teachings and virtues. Areola is any humble person, as in the Song: “My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the bed of spices” [Note: [Col. 0865] 28 Song VI, 1.], that is, Christ came to his Church, that is, to the humble person, in order to make his dwelling there. [Col. 0866D]

Aranea is the afflicted soul, as in the Psalms: “And you made his soul waste away like a spider” [Note: [Col. 0865] 29 Psal. XXXVIII, 12.], that is, “You permitted his soul to be afflicted like a spider.” Aranea is the vanity of life, as in the Psalms: “Our years will meditate like a spider” [Note: [Col. 0865] 30 Psal. LXXXIX, 9.], that is, “Our years are full of vanity.”

Armenta are the teachers or rulers of the Church, as in the Song of Habakkuk: “And there will be no herd in the stalls” [Note: [Col. 0865] 31 Hab. III, 17.], that is, “There will be no prelate among the people.” [Col. 0867A] Armenta is the company of the patriarchs, as in the Song of Deuteronomy, […] “a calf from the herd,” that is, Christ born from the patriarchs.

Arva are subjects, as in the Song of Habakkuk: “And the fields will not produce food” [Note: [Col. 0867] 1 Hab. III, 17.], that is, the subjects will not possess the food of obedience.

Aratrum is the practice of righteousness, as in the Gospel: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0867] 2 Luke IX, 62.], that is, no one who turns back from the practice of righteousness to the sins he has abandoned is worthy to be saved. Aratrum is […] a good example, as in the Books of Kings: “And he cooked the flesh with the plow of the oxen” [Note: [Col. 0867] 3 III Kings XIX, 21.], that is, “He mortified carnal works in imitation of the saints.”

Astra are the holy angels, as in Job: “When the morning [Col. 0867B] stars praised me together” [Note: [Col. 0867] 4 Job XXXVIII, 7.], that is, the angels whom I first created. Astra are holy men in the Church, as in Isaiah: “I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0867] 5 Isa. XIV, 13.], that is, “I will cause the reprobate, over whom I rule, to oppress the contemplatives of the Church by their election.”

Ascensus is Christ’s exaltation, as in the Psalms: “You who make the cloud your ascent” [Note: [Col. 0867] 6 Psal. CIII, 3.], because a cloud received him from their eyes.

Ascensus is the affliction of martyrs, as in the Song: “A purple ascent” [Note: [Col. 0867] 7 Song III, 10.], namely, the blind martyr afflicted for the Lord. Ascensus is the progress of the spiritual life, as in Ezekiel: “And its ascent had seven steps” [Note: [Col. 0867] 8 Ezek. XL, 22.], because through the grace of the sevenfold [Col. 0867C] Spirit we acquire progress in good conduct.

Ascensor is the Lord, as in Job: “He will overthrow the horse and its rider” [Note: [Col. 0867] 9 Job XXXIX, 21.], that is, “He will despise the holy man and the Lord who rules over him.” Ascensor is the lover of this world, as in Genesis: “So that its rider may fall backward” [Note: [Col. 0867] 10 Gen. XLIX, 17.], that is, “Just as the world loves against the Lord, so that it may fall into what is behind.” Ascensor is the devil, as in the Song of Exodus: “He cast horse and rider into the sea” [Note: [Col. 0867] 11 Exod. XV, 1.], that is, the devil plunged into hell all the proud and the one who rules over them.

Asinus is the gentile people, as in Isaiah: “And the ass its master’s manger” [Note: [Col. 0867] 12 Isa. I, 3.], that is, the people of the gentiles, who were previously unclean, acquired spiritual nourishment. [Col. 0867D] Asinus is the foolishness of the Jews, as in Genesis: “Stay here with the ass; after we have worshiped, we will return to you” [Note: [Col. 0867] 13 Gen. XXII, 5.], because blindness happened in part to Israel until the fullness of the gentiles enters, and thus all Israel will be saved [Note: [Col. 0867] 14 Rom. XI, 25.]. Asinus is anyone who serves the weak, as in Job: “They drove away the ass of the orphans” [Note: [Col. 0867] 15 Job XXIV, 3.], that is, heretics led away the one who, weak, raged through charity. Asinus is the laziness of fools, as in Deuteronomy: “You shall not plow with [Col. 0868A] an ox and an ass” [Note: [Col. 0867] 16 Deut. XXII, 10.], that is, “You shall not join a diligent and wise person with a foolish and lazy preacher.”

Asina is our flesh, as in the Book of Joshua: “Achsah, riding on an ass, received from her father an upper and a lower spring” [Note: [Col. 0867] 17 Josh. XV, 19.], because the faithful soul, ruling the flesh, receives from the Lord compunction arising from love and fear. Asina is the Synagogue, as in the Gospel: “You will find an ass tied” [Note: [Col. 0867] 18 Matt. XXI, 1–2.], that is, “You will see the Jewish people bound by the cords of sins.” By asinae are signified the lustful, as in the prophet: “Whose flesh is like the flesh of asses” [Note: [Col. 0867] 19 Ezek. XXIII, 20.], that is, their flesh is as lustful as the flesh of asses. By asinae are signified wanton senses, as in […] Job: “You who ride upon shining asses, speak” [Note: [Col. 0867] 20 Judg. V, 10.], because those can rightly praise who know how to rule their wanton senses manfully. [Col. 0868B]

By asinae are signified all heavenly souls, as in the Books of Kings [Note: [Col. 0867] 21 I Kings IX, 3.], where the asses of Kish, Saul’s father, were lost and Saul was sent to seek them, because human souls had been lost and the Lord was sent into this world to save sinners. By asinae are signified the simple, as in Job: “There were five hundred she-asses” [Note: [Col. 0867] 22 Job I, 3.], because the devotion of the truly simple serves our Redeemer, who preserved the […] portion of continence. [Text interrupted and materially uncertain.]

Aspis is the devil, as in the Psalms: “You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk” [Note: [Col. 0867] 23 Psal. XC, 13.], that is, “You will crush him who deceives secretly and rages openly.” Aspis is any reprobate person, as in the Psalms: “Like the deaf asp that stops up its ears” [Note: [Col. 0867] 24 Psal. LVII, 5.], because the reprobate did not incline the sense of his heart to the voice of preaching. Aspis is the [Col. 0868C] hidden ferocity of the devil, as in Isaiah: “He will put his hand into the hole of the asp” [Note: [Col. 0867] 25 Isa. XI, 8.], because the Lord sometimes visits by his grace those who have possessed within themselves the devil’s hidden malice. By aspis is signified the evil spirit, as in Job: “His bread will be changed into the gall of asps” [Note: [Col. 0867] 26 Job XX, 14.], because the pleasure of the impious will be changed into the bitterness of unclean spirits. By aspis are signified the suggestions of the devil, as in Job: “He will suck the head of the asp” [Note: [Col. 0867] 27 Ibid., v. 16.], because along the path of diabolical suggestions the impious person will receive it. By aspis are signified deceitful people, as in the Psalm: “The poison of asps is under their lips” [Note: [Col. 0867] 28 Psal. CXXXIX, 4.], that is, the fraud and malice of deceitful people lay hidden beneath the words of the Jews.

Atrium is the holy Church, as in the Psalms: “Worship the Lord in his holy court” [Note: [Col. 0867] 29 Psal. XXIX, 2; and XCVI, 9.], that is, “Serve [Col. 0868D] him in his holy Church.” Atrium is the world: “The strong man, armed, guards his court” [Note: [Col. 0867] 30 Luke XI, 28.], that is, the devil possessed this world. Atrium is the breadth of the faithful, as in Ezekiel: “And he measured the court in length, one hundred cubits” [Note: [Col. 0867] 31 Ezek. XL, 47.], because the faithful possess the perfection of good works through the long endurance of hope. Atrium is the worldly circuit, as in the Gospel: “Peter stood in the court of the high priest with the attendants at the fire” [Note: [Col. 0867] 32 Mark XIV; John XVIII.], because the denier of God remains amid the worldly [Col. 0869A] circuit, devoted to the desires of the flesh. Atrium is the unbelieving people, as in the Apocalypse: “The court that is outside the temple, cast out” [Note: [Col. 0869] 1 Apoc. XI, 2.], that is, “Show that those who do not wish to enter the faith are to be separated from the communion of the faithful.” By atrium are signified the prophets and apostles, as in the Psalms: “Enter into his courts” [Note: [Col. 0869] 2 Psal. XCV, 8.], that is, “Become conformed to his apostles and prophets.” By atria are signified the commandments of charity, as in the Psalms: “In the courts of the house of our God” [Note: [Col. 0869] 3 Psal. XCII, 14.], that is, “In the commandments through which all things become common.” By atrium are signified the secrets of heaven, as in the Psalms: “My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0869] 4 Psal. LXXXIII, 3.], that is, “My spirit desires to reach the secrets of heaven.”

Aurora is the holy Church, as in the Song: “Like the rising dawn” [Note: [Col. 0869] 5 Song VI, 9.], because the holy Church rises by desire from the darkness of the present life [Col. 0869B] toward heavenly things. Aurora is one who newly begins good works, as in the Psalms: “You fashioned the dawn and the sun” [Note: [Col. 0869] 6 Psal. LXXIII, 16.], because the Lord established both the beginning […] in a good work and its perfection. Aurora is the life of the just, as in Job: “If the dawn suddenly appears” [Note: [Col. 0869] 7 Job XXIV, 17.], because the impious person despises the life of the just. Aurora is the holy mind, as in Job: “And you showed the dawn its place” [Note: [Col. 0869] 8 Job XXXVIII, 12.], because through revelation the Lord shows the devout mind the heavenly homeland, which is its place.

South Wind is the Holy Spirit, as in the Song: “Come, South Wind [Note: [Col. 0869] 9 Song IV, 16],” that is, the fervor of the Holy Spirit comes. South Wind, the Jewish people, as in Isaiah: “And to the South Wind I shall say: Do not hinder [Note: [Col. 0869] 10 Isa. XLIII, 6],” that is, I shall command the Jews not to impede the nations from believing. South Wind, any preacher, as in the Psalms: “He transferred the South Wind from heaven [Note: [Col. 0869] 11 Ps. LXXVII, 26]”: for the Lord chooses a preacher from the sublimity of life. South Wind, the assembly of martyrs, as in the Apocalypse: “From the South Wind, three gates [Note: [Col. 0869] 12 Rev. XXI, 13],” for the faith of the Trinity is preached by the martyrs. South Wind, holy devotion, as in the Psalms: “Restore our captivity, O Lord, like a torrent in the South Wind [Note: [Col. 0869] 13 Ps. CXXV, 4],” for through holy devotion the mind is freed from inward cold. South Wind, the holiness of religious conduct, as in Ezekiel: “Like a structure of a city inclined toward the South [Note: [Col. 0869] 14 Ezek. XL, 2],” for the holy Church is intent upon the fervor of holy conduct. South Wind, the secret place of heaven, as in Job: “Who makes the inner chambers of the South [Note: [Col. 0869] 15 Job IX, 9],” for the Lord has prepared those inner places of the heavenly homeland for his own.

[Col. 0869D]

Gold is the Divinity itself, as in the Song: “His head is finest gold [Note: [Col. 0869] 16 Song V, 11],” for the divinity of Christ is ineffable radiance. Gold, the splendor of the heavenly homeland, as in the Apocalypse: “The city itself was pure gold [Note: [Col. 0869] 17 Rev. XXI, 18],” for that heavenly city will shine with eternal purity. Gold, the wisdom of the first angel, as in Ezekiel: “Gold was the workmanship of your adornment [Note: [Col. 0869] 18 Ezek. XXVIII, 13],” for the first angel was adorned with great wisdom. Gold, the beauty of the good spirits, as in Job: “Refined gold shall not be given for * it [Note: [Col. 0869] 19 Job XXVIII, 15],” for no angel can be made equal to Christ. Gold, the virtue of charity, as in the Apocalypse: “And girded around the breasts with a golden belt [Note: [Col. 0869] 20 Rev. I, 13],” that is, bound within himself by the bond of charity. * Gold, spiritual wisdom, as in Proverbs: “A desirable treasure [Note: [Col. 0869] 21 Prov. XXI, 20],” that is, spiritual wisdom rests in the mouth of the wise. Gold, the wisdom of the Gentiles, as in the Psalms: “And there shall be given to him of the gold of Arabia [Note: [Col. 0869] 22 Ps. LXXI, 15],” that is, the wise among the Gentiles shall serve him. Gold, temporal exaltation, as in Job: “If I thought gold to be my strength [Note: [Col. 0869] 23 Job XXXI, 24],” for the righteous does not trust in his temporal exaltation. Gold, the radiance of the saints in heaven, as in Job: “Gold shall not be compared with it [Note: [Col. 0869] 24 Job XXVIII, 17],” for not even the saints who are already in heaven can be made equal to Christ. Gold, faithful souls coming from the Gentiles, as in Job: “Gold shall come from the North [Note: [Col. 0869] 25 Job XXXVII, 22],” that is, devoted souls shall come forth from the Gentile people. Gold, the assembly of martyrs, as in Job: “There is a place for gold where it is smelted [Note: [Col. 0869] 26 Job XXVIII, 1],” for martyrdom is of no benefit unless it is received within the Church. Gold, the virtue of patience, as in Job: “He tested me like gold that passes through fire [Note: [Col. 0869] 27 Job XXIII, 10],” that is, I was not overcome by the tribulation I endured; rather, I was made more radiant through wisdom. Gold, the royal power of Christ; thus, in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0869] 28 Matt. II, 11] the Magi offer gold to Christ, for the Gentile people believes him to be a powerful king. Gold, the life of a priest, as in Jeremiah: “How the gold has become dim [Note: [Col. 0869] 29 Lam. IV, 1],” for the splendid life of priests is disfigured by vices. Gold, the good conduct of the faithful people, as in Job: “And its clods are gold [Note: [Col. 0869] 30 Job XXVIII, 6],” for not only do priests shine in the Church through the distinction of holiness, but the faithful people in it also gleam through good conduct. Gold, the radiance of those who have despised the world, as in Job: “He shall spread gold beneath him like mud [Note: [Col. 0869] 31 Job XLI, 21],” for he sometimes subjects those who have despised the world to himself just as he does those who love it. Gold, the keenness of subtle understanding, as in the Apocalypse: “I advise you to buy gold from me [Note: [Col. 0869] 32 Rev. III, 18],” that is, give the price of good works if you wish to attain keen understanding, by which through holy action we attain clear perception. Gold, the wisdom of the reprobate, as in the Apocalypse: “No one shall buy your gold’s merchandise any longer [Note: [Col. 0869] 33 Rev. XVIII, 12],” for once the condemned reprobate have been judged, no one will thereafter seek their wisdom. Gold, the splendor of worldly pomp, as in the Psalms: “I have loved your commandments above gold [Note: [Col. 0869] 34 Ps. CXVIII, 127],” and so forth, that is, more than worldly pride. Gold, the eternal life of the elect, as in the Psalms: “The hinder parts of his back were in the pallor of gold [Note: [Col. 0869] 35 Ps. LXVII, 14],” for the Church that follows after him, honoring God, will shine in the splendor of enduring life.

The Ear is God’s power, as in the Psalms: “Your ear has heard the preparation of their heart [Note: [Col. 0871] 1 Ps. IX, 17],” that is, your power has penetrated their hidden thoughts. The Ear, mercy, as in the Psalms: “And his ear,” that is, his compassion, “is toward their prayers [Note: [Col. 0871] 2 Ps. XXXIII, 16].” The Ear, a teacher of the Church, as in Proverbs: “The ear that hears the reproofs of life will dwell in the midst of the wise [Note: [Col. 0871] 3 Prov. XV, 31],” for whoever willingly hears the reproofs of teachers generally ascends to the teachers’ chair. The Ear, the human mind, as in Exodus: “He shall pierce his ear with an awl [Note: [Col. 0871] 4 Exod. XXI, 6],” that is, he shall enlighten his mind with the word of God. The Ear, the understanding of the heart, as in Job: “Does not your ear discern words [Note: [Col. 0871] 5 Job XII, 11]?” for the understanding of the heart inwardly distinguishes the words that sound outwardly. The Ear, any subordinate, as in Proverbs: “The hearing ear and the seeing eye, the Lord has made [Note: [Col. 0871] 6 Prov. XX, 12],” for God is the creator of both: namely, of the subordinate who obeys and of the superior who commands. The Ear is taken for what is hidden, as in the Gospel: “What you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the rooftops [Note: [Col. 0871] 7 Matt. X, 27],” that is, what you receive in secret, pour out publicly. The Ear, inward contemplation, as in Job: “My ear received the veins of his whisper as if secretly [Note: [Col. 0871] 8 Job IV, 12],” that is, my contemplation secretly perceived the signs of inward and divine speech. Through the ear, obedience, as in the Gospel: “Whoever has ears, let him hear [Note: [Col. 0871] 9 Matt. XI, 15; XIII, 9],” that is, let whoever wishes to obey listen to my words. Through the ear, pure understanding, as in the Psalms: “But you pierced ears for me [Note: [Col. 0871] 10 Ps. XXXIX, 7],” that is, you caused me to understand perfectly what you wished. Through the ear, divine judgments, as in Isaiah: “The Lord says this in my ears [Note: [Col. 0871] 11 Isa. V, 9],” that is, these things are in my judgments.

Charioteer is any preacher, as in the Books of Kings: “The chariot of Israel and its charioteer [Note: [Col. 0871] 12 IV Kings II, 12],” for the preacher ought both to carry and to lead the people of God.

Bird is Christ, as in Job: “The bird has not known the path [Note: [Col. 0871] 13 Job XXVIII, 7],” for Judea did not believe that Christ had ascended to heaven. Bird, the human soul, as in Job: “And the bird is born for flight [Note: [Col. 0871] 14 Job V, 7],” for the pure soul stretches itself out in contemplation. Bird, every unstable person, as in Proverbs: “Like a bird that migrates from its place [Note: [Col. 0871] 15 Prov. XXVII, 8],” for every unstable person does not remain in his place. Bird is the frivolity of words, as in Proverbs: “The bird flies across the heights [Note: [Col. 0871] 16 Prov. XXVI, 2],” for frivolous words return upon the one who uttered them. Bird, that proud enemy, as in Job: “Will he mock him as a bird [Note: [Col. 0871] 17 Job XL, 24]?” for the Lord deceived the proud devil through his wisdom. Through birds, spiritual men, as in Genesis: “But he did not divide the birds [Note: [Col. 0871] 18 Gen. XV, 10],” for spiritual men do not divide scandals by themselves. Through the bird, evil spirits, as in the Song of Deuteronomy: “He shall devour them like a bird, with a most bitter bite [Note: [Col. 0871] 19 Deut. XXXII, 24],” for evil spirits will consume the reprobate.

Axles are the hearts of teachers, as in the Books of Kings: “And four wheels, for each base, and bronze axles [Note: [Col. 0871] 20 III Kings IV, 30],” for the evangelists and teachers confirm their preaching through the teachings of the prophets.

Unleavened bread is purity of mind, as in Exodus: “For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread [Note: [Col. 0871] 21 Exod. XII, 15],” that is, throughout the whole time of this life you shall devote yourselves to holiness of mind.

Adversary is the devil, as in Peter’s Epistle: “Your adversary the devil prowls around [Note: [Col. 0871] 22 I Peter V, 8],” for the devil always intends to do harm. Adversary, the unbelieving people, as in the Psalm: “The adversary provokes your name to the end [Note: [Col. 0871] 23 Ps. LXXIV, 10],” that is, the unbelieving people despises your faith. Adversary, sacred Scripture, as in the Gospel: “Be agreeable to your adversary [Note: [Col. 0871] 24 Matt. V, 25],” that is, agree with sacred Scripture, which opposes carnal desires.

## B

Babylon. War. Gill (branchia). Cluster. Behemoth. Bases. Ox. Arm. Boxwood. Basilisk. Locust. Beard. Linen. Staff. Bath. Butter. Bitumen. Belt. Beast.

Babylon is the city of the reprobate, as in the Prophet: “Flee from the midst of Babylon [Note: [Col. 0871] 25 Jer. L, 8; and LI, 6],” that is, despise the customs of the reprobate. Babylon, a perverse mind, as in the Prophet: “We have healed Babylon, and it was not healed [Note: [Col. 0871] 26 Ibid. v. 9],” that is, we endeavored to heal the perverse mind that is spiritually ill, and it does not wish to receive health. Babylon, the Church from the Gentiles, as in Peter’s Epistle: “The elect Church that is in Babylon greets you [Note: [Col. 0871] 27 I Peter V, 13],” the faithful people that has been converted from the Gentiles to the faith. Babylon, sin, as in the Prophet: “When you come to Babylon, there you shall be delivered [Note: [Col. 0871] 28 Mic. IV, 10],” for many, by falling into sin, come to self-knowledge and are cured of the plague of pride. Babylon is the impious who will be condemned at the end, as in the Apocalypse: “Babylon has fallen [Note: [Col. 0871] 29 Rev. XIV, 8],” for the impious will be condemned in body and soul together. Babylon, our flesh, as in the Psalms: “Daughter of Babylon [Note: [Col. 0871] 30 Ps. CXXXVI, 8],” that is, the flesh confused through sins, for Babylon is interpreted as “confusion.” Babylon, this world, as in Daniel [Note: [Col. 0871] 31 Dan. XIV, 22]: Habakkuk was carried to Babylon by his hair; for the preachers of Christ are brought to the world. Babylon, hell, as in the Prophet: “I shall bring you back from Babylon into your land,” that is, from hell to the heavenly homeland.

The Staff is God’s mercy, as in the Psalm: “Your staff comforts [Note: [Col. 0871] 32 Ps. XXII, 4],” that is, your mercy has comforted me. * Staff, the power of government, as when Judah gave Tamar his staff in Genesis [Note: [Col. 0871] 33 Gen. XXXVIII, 18], for the Church received the power of government from Christ. Staff, support, as in Tobit: “The staff of our old age [Note: [Col. 0871] 34 Tob. X, 4],” that is, the support of our weakness. The Staff is the Law, as in the Books of Kings, when Elisha sends Gehazi to the dead man “with a staff [Note: [Col. 0873] 1 IV Kings IV, 28],” for Christ sent Moses with the Law to the human race, dead in sins. Staff, * as in Isaiah: “The Lord has broken the staff of the impious [Note: [Col. 0873] 2 Isa. XIV, 5],” for Christ destroyed the devil, who is lord of the reprobate. Staff, righteousness, as in Genesis: “With my staff I crossed this Jordan [Note: [Col. 0873] 3 Gen. XXXII, 10],” for we must cross this world in our righteousness. Staff, the cross of Christ, as in the Books of Kings, when David came against Goliath with a staff [Note: [Col. 0873] 4 I Kings XVII, 43], for Christ triumphed over the devil on the wood. Through the staff, pastoral cares, as in Exodus: “Holding staffs in their hands [Note: [Col. 0873] 5 Exod. XII, 11],” that is, carrying out pastoral cares in their works.

The Belt is continence, as in Exodus: “And a belt * of embroidered work [Note: [Col. 0873] 6 Exod. XXVIII, 39],” continence of various kinds. The Belt, the virtue of continence, as in Job: “He loosens the belt of kings [Note: [Col. 0873] 7 Job XII, 18],” for in those who glory in chastity, the Lord permits the girdle of that same chastity to be broken. The Belt, mortification of the flesh, as in the First Book of Kings [Note: [Col. 0873] 8 Chapter XVIII, 4; chapter XVIII, 11]: “Jonathan gave David his garments down to the belt,” for we must offer to our Lord, who is the true David, not only our exterior garments but also the mortification of our very flesh. The Belt, unity of faith, as in the Second Book of Kings [Note: [Col. 0873] 9 Chapter II, 5]: “Why did you not pierce him? And I would have given you ten shekels of silver and one belt,” for whoever extinguishes in himself the desire for this world deserves to be strengthened in the perfection of the Decalogue and in unity of faith. The Belt, our very spirit, as in the Third Book of Kings [Note: [Col. 0873] 10 I Kings XXI, 13]: “And he put the blood of battle on the belt that was around his loins,” that is, he placed the cruelty of discord in the spirit, which ought to preside over the wanton movements of the flesh.

The Beard is the divinity of Christ, as in the Books of Kings: “Saliva flowed down upon the beard [Note: [Col. 0873] 11 Ps. CXXXII, 2],” for * low and childish words covered the divinity of Christ. The Beard, the assembly of the apostles, as in the Psalms: “The ointment descended upon the beard, the beard of Aaron [Note: [Col. 0873] 12 Ezek. V, 1],” for the Holy Spirit came upon Christ’s apostles. The Beard, the Jewish people, as in Ezekiel: “You shall pass your sword over head and beard [Note: [Col. 0873] 13 Jer. XLI, 5],” as though by his terrible judgment the Lord cut away from himself the ancient * priesthood and the Jewish people. The Beard, confidence, as in Jeremiah: “Men came * shaven in beard [Note: [Col. 0873] 14 Isa. LIII, 1],” for holy men * admit Christ’s confidence in their own strength.

The Arm is Christ, as in Isaiah: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” [Note: [Col. 0873] 15 Isa. XX, 11] that is, to whom has the Son of God been announced? The Arm, the strength of our Savior, as in Isaiah: “With his arm he will gather the lambs [Note: [Col. 0873] 16 Ps. XLIII, 4],” that is, in his strength he himself will help the simple. The Arm, the weak strength of man, as in the Psalm: “And their arm shall not save them [Note: [Col. 0873] 17 Song VIII, 6],” that is, their strength shall not heal them. The Arm, the work of charity, as in the Song: “Set your arm as a seal [Note: [Col. 0873] 18 Job XXXVIII, 15],” for the bride imitates the bridegroom in the action of charity. The Arm, the pride of the Antichrist, as in Job: “And the exalted arm shall be broken [Note: [Col. 0873] 19 Ps. XVII, 35].” Through the arm, strong works, as in the Psalms: “You have made my arms like a bronze bow [Note: [Col. 0873] 20 Job XXXVIII, 15],” that is, you have made your works tireless.

The gill (branchia) is the devil’s power, as in the Book of Tobit: “Seize his gill (branchia) [Note: [Col. 0873] 21 Ps. XVII, 35],” for God annihilated Satan’s power.

Bases are the divine counsels, as in the Song: “The legs of the bridegroom are like marble columns founded upon golden bases [Note: [Col. 0873] 22 Tob. VI, 4],” for the holy men through whom Christ walks, exalted through contemplation and strong through vigor, are secretly disposed by divine counsels. Bases, the apostles, as in Job: “Upon whom the bases of the earth were solidly founded [Note: [Col. 0873] 23 Song V, 15],” for the apostles of the holy Church are confirmed in Christ. Bases, preachers, as in Exodus: “You shall make four columns and cover their bases with gold [Note: [Col. 0873] 24 Job XXXVIII, 5],” for there are four Gospels, and their interpreters shine with the radiance of wisdom. Bases, the Fathers of the Old Testament, as in Exodus [Note: [Col. 0873] 25 Exod. XXVI, 17, 18, 19]: the boards of the tabernacle are placed upon bases, for the fathers under grace rest upon the shining conduct of the preceding fathers.

The Basilisk is the devil, as in the Psalms: “You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk [Note: [Col. 0873] 26 Ps. XC, 13],” that is, you shall overcome the devil.

The Bath is judgment, as in Leviticus: “The bath shall be just for you [Note: [Col. 0873] 27 Lev. XIX, 36; Deut. XXV, 13, 14, 15],” that is, judge justly. Through the bath, the two substances of man, namely body and soul, as in the Third Book of Kings: “The sea held two thousand baths [Note: [Col. 0873] 28 III Kings VII, 26],” for in baptism we are cleansed completely both in body and in soul. The ephah and the bath are one measure, but the ephah is used for dry things, such as wheat and salt, while the bath is used for liquids, such as wine and oil.

War is persecution, as in the Psalms: “They turned back on the day of battle [Note: [Col. 0873] 29 Ps. LXXVII, 9],” for the unstable fail under persecution. War, worldly adversity, as in Job: “He will rescue you in war [Note: [Col. 0873] 30 Job V, 20],” that is, he will protect you in adversity. War, the battle of vices, as in Job: “From far away he scents war [Note: [Col. 0873] 31 Job XXXIX, 28],” for the prudent person foresees the battle of vices. War, the devil’s temptation, as in the Psalms: “You sheltered me over my head on the day of war [Note: [Col. 0873] 32 Ps. CXXXIX, 8],” that is, you protected my mind amid the heat of diabolical temptation. War, the resisting adversary, as in the Psalms: “You girded me with strength for war [Note: [Col. 0873] 33 Ps. XVII, 40],” that is, you strengthened me with patience against the adversary. War, the adversary’s suggestion, as in Paul: “The saints are strong in war [Note: [Col. 0873] 34 Heb. XI, 34],” for holy men * resist Satan’s suggestion bravely. War, the evil one himself, as in Job: “Remember the war, and do not speak further [Note: [Col. 0875] 1 Job XL, 27],” that is, always remember what the evil one is like, and restrain yourself from murmuring. War, final condemnation, as in Job: “And may he rain upon him his war [Note: [Col. 0875] 2 Job XX, 23],” for God pours eternal condemnation upon the impious.

Behemoth is the devil, as in Job: “Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you [Note: [Col. 0875] 3 Job XL, 10],” for God created that spirit who is now the devil.

The Beast is anyone converted from sin, as in Isaiah: “The beast of the field will glorify me [Note: [Col. 0875] 4 Isa. XLIII, 20],” that is, the sinner who repents of his sin will honor me. The Beast, an irrational mind, as in Exodus: “If a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned [Note: [Col. 0875] 5 Exod. XIX, 13; Heb. XII, 19],” for if an irrational mind raises itself to the heights of contemplation, unable to bear the weight of what is above, it is killed by the heavenly voices. The Beast, the serving Jewish people, as in Genesis: “A beast devoured Joseph [Note: [Col. 0875] 6 Gen. XXXVII, 33],” that is, the persecuting Jewish people killed Christ. The Beast, mortal sin, as in Isaiah: “No evil beast shall pass through it [Note: [Col. 0875] 7 Isa. XXXV, 9],” for the holy mind strives with every effort to avoid mortal sin. The Beast, the society of the reprobate, as in the Apocalypse: “I saw a beast rising from the sea [Note: [Col. 0875] 8 Rev. XIII, 1],” for the followers of the Antichrist emerge from earthly things after him. The Beast, the devil, as in the Apocalypse: “The beast that you saw was, and is not [Note: [Col. 0875] 9 Rev. XVII, 8],” for * before Christ’s coming the devil reigned, but when he came, the devil was overcome. Through the beasts, the blinded Jews, as in the Psalm: “In that very night all the beasts of the forest will pass through [Note: [Col. 0875] 10 Ps. CIII, 20],” for as their blindness increased, the Jews proceeded toward the deed of the Lord’s Passion. Through the beasts, the Gentiles, as in the Psalm: “All the beasts of the field will drink [Note: [Col. 0875] 11 Ibid., verse 11],” for the Jews are intoxicated by the streams of sacred Scripture. Through the beasts, all simple people, as in Genesis: “God created the beasts of the earth [Note: [Col. 0875] 12 Gen. I, 24],” for God placed the simple in the Church. Through the beasts, unbelievers, as in Paul: “I fought against beasts [Note: [Col. 0875] 13 I Cor. XV],” that is, I argued against unbelievers. Through the beasts, evil spirits, as in Job: “All the beasts of the field play there [Note: [Col. 0875] 14 Job XL, 15],” for evil spirits exult in the reprobate mind. Through the beasts, unstable movements of the heart, as in Job: “And the beasts of the earth shall be at peace [Note: [Col. 0875] 15 Job V, 23],” that is, the inward movements of your heart shall not disturb you. Through the beasts, sins: as in the Psalms: [lacuna] thus [lacuna] through confession you ought to [lacuna] the past, and so preserve yourself from what is future.

Linen is righteousness, as in the Apocalypse: “For the linen garments are the justifications of the saints [Note: [Col. 0875] 16 Rev. XIX, 8].” Linen, affliction of the flesh, as in Exodus: “Scarlet twice-dyed, and twisted linen,” that is, twofold charity and afflicted flesh. Linen, virginity, as in Proverbs: “Linen and purple are her clothing [Note: [Col. 0875] 17 Prov. XXXI, 22],” for the holy Church is clothed in some with virginity and in others with martyrdom. As Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, says:

Now it is linen, now a purple garment,

Which through wars brings forth roses, through peace lilies.

Linen, the battle-line of the virtues, as in Exodus: “Tent-cloths of twisted linen [Note: [Col. 0875] 18 Exod. XXVI, 1],” for the saints are adorned with the beauty of virtues. Linen, external observance, as in the Gospel: “Let him be clothed in purple and linen [Note: [Col. 0875] 19 Luke XVI, 19],” for the Jewish people possessed an external observance of life.

Bitumen is the strength of charity, as in Genesis: “You shall coat the ark with bitumen outside and inside [Note: [Col. 0875] 20 Gen. VI, 14],” for the Lord strengthens Christ according to his humanity with the power of charity, both within, in the heart, and outside, in action. Bitumen, virginity, as in Exodus: “She took a basket of reeds and coated it with bitumen and pitch [Note: [Col. 0875] 21 Exod. II, 3],” for he chose what came from wisdom as virginal, and adorned it with virginity and humility. Bitumen, the hardness of discord, as in Genesis: “They had bricks for stone and bitumen for mortar [Note: [Col. 0875] 22 Gen. XI, 3],” for the wicked, abandoning the strength of good action, love the mud of lust; and, rejecting the bond of charity, they embrace the hardness of discord.

The Cluster is Christ, as in Numbers [Note: [Col. 0875] 23 Num. XIII, 24], where two men carry a cluster on a pole, for two peoples confess Christ upon the cross. The Cluster, spiritual joy, as in the Song: “My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus to me [Note: [Col. 0875] 24 Song I, 14],” for flowering joy glorified me through the resurrection; Cyprus is interpreted as “flowering.” The Cluster, the work of righteousness, as in Job: “He shall be harmed like a vine in its first flowering [Note: [Col. 0875] 25 Job XV, 33],” for in the reprobate mind even good work is destroyed through pride. The Cluster, the work of righteousness, as in the Song of Deuteronomy: “And a most bitter cluster [Note: [Col. 0875] 26 Deut. XXXII, 32],” for what the wicked person does proceeds from bitterness. Through clusters, holy preachers, as in the Song: “And your breasts are like clusters [Note: [Col. 0875] 27 Song VII, 7],” for the two peoples of the holy Church imitate their preachers. Through clusters, the impious, as in the Apocalypse: “Gather the clusters of the vine of the earth [Note: [Col. 0875] 28 Rev. XIV, 18],” for the Lord exterminates the wicked who are swollen with earthly pleasure.

The Ox, a preacher, as in the Law: “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass [Note: [Col. 0875] 29 Deut. XXII, 10],” that is, do not join a fool in preaching with a wise preacher. The Ox, a good work, as in the Law: “You shall not work with the firstborn of an ox [Note: [Col. 0875] 30 Deut. XV, 19],” that is, do not * exercise the beginnings of good work in public. The Ox, the Jewish people, as in Job: “Will the ox bellow when it has a full manger [Note: [Col. 0875] 31 Job VI, 5]?” for the Jewish people was freed from its lamentable condition in those matters in which it recognized Christ’s incarnation. The Ox, the Gentile people, as in Isaiah: “The ox knows its owner [Note: [Col. 0875] 32 Isa. I, 3],” for the Gentile people believed in its redeemer. The Ox, Luke the evangelist, as in Ezekiel: “The face of an ox on the left [Note: [Col. 0875] 33 Ezek. I, 10],” for Luke began his Gospel with sacrifice. The Ox, every fool, as in Proverbs: “She follows him like an ox led to the slaughter [Note: [Col. 0875] 34 Prov. VII, 22],” for the fool follows the desire for this world to destruction. Through the oxen, the patriarchs, as in Leviticus: “A calf from the oxen, without blemish [Note: [Col. 0875] 35 Lev. IV, 3],” that is, Christ, born from the patriarchs without fault. Through the ox, all the perfect, as in Job: “The oxen were plowing [Note: [Col. 0877] 1 Job I, 14],” that is, the perfect were doing perfect works. Through the oxen, superiors, as in the Psalm: “Beasts in the minds and oxen [Note: [Col. 0877] 2 Ps. XLIX, 10],” that is, subordinates in virtues and superiors. Through the oxen, gentle thoughts, as in the Third Book of Kings: “Lions on the bases, oxen, and cherubim [Note: [Col. 0877] 3 III Kings VII, 29],” for in superiors there ought to be gentle thoughts together with sternness and knowledge. Through the ox, heretics, as in the Psalm: “Their oxen are fat [Note: [Col. 0877] 4 Ps. CXLIII, 14],” for heretics, called by the feminine gender because of their softness, abound in earthly things. Through the ox, desires of the senses, as in the Gospel: “I have bought a yoke of oxen [Note: [Col. 0877] 5 Luke XIV, 19],” they persist in desire for the five senses. Through the oxen, elevations of the heart, as in the Psalm: “I shall offer you an ox with a goat [Note: [Col. 0877] 6 Ps. LXV, 15],” that is, I shall mortify the elevations of the heart together with the mortification of the wantonness of the flesh. The Ox, the ancient enemy, as in Job: “He shall eat grass like an ox [Note: [Col. 0877] 7 Job XL, 10],” for the devil devours the carnal.

The Trumpet is persecution, as in Job: “When he hears the trumpet, he says: ‘Ha!’ [Note: [Col. 0877] 8 Job XXXIX, 8],” for the holy preacher rejoices over persecution. Through the trumpet, preachers, as in Joshua [Note: [Col. 0877] 9 Josh. VI, 4], where the priests went around Jericho with trumpets; for preachers went around the world with their preaching.

The Locust is gluttonous greed, as in Joel: “The locust shall eat what the grasshopper left [Note: [Col. 0877] 10 Joel I, 4],” for gluttony then infects the reprobate mind when pride abandons it.

Butter is the humanity of Christ, as in Isaiah: “You shall eat butter and honey [Note: [Col. 0877] 11 Isa. VII, 15],” for Christ, in the unity of his person, had both a divine nature, which pertains to honey, and a human nature, which pertains to butter. Butter, the teaching of the patriarchs, as in the Song of Deuteronomy: “Butter from the herd, and milk from the flock [Note: [Col. 0877] 12 Deut. XXXII, 14],” that is, rich teaching from the patriarchs, *[uncertain: amplicem], and from holy conduct. Butter, the contemplative life, as in Job: “He shall not see the streams of the river, the torrent of honey and butter [Note: [Col. 0877] 13 Job XX, 17],” for no wicked person practices works of holiness—neither those pertaining to the contemplative life nor those pertaining to the active life. Butter, the inclination of the flesh, as in the Book of Judges: “And she offered butter to the prince in a bowl [Note: [Col. 0877] 14 Judges V],” for we have no stronger means of overthrowing the prince of this world within us than to maintain steadfast charity in our mind. Butter, the fruitfulness of good action, as in Genesis: “He also took butter and set it before them [Note: [Col. 0877] 15 Gen. XVIII, 8],” for from the fruitfulness of good work we ought to please the holy Trinity within us. Butter, the richness of spiritual virtues, as in Proverbs: “Whoever presses the breasts firmly to draw out milk expresses butter [Note: [Col. 0877] 16 Prov. XXX, 33],” for those who diligently press their body and soul toward the sweetness of holiness * also attain the richness of spiritual virtues. Butter, the anointing of repentance, as in Job: “I washed my feet with butter [Note: [Col. 0877] 17 Job XXIX, 6],” for the Lord, whose figure Job represented, washes the affections of his elect with the ointments of repentance.

[Col. 0878A]

Boxwood is the greenness of faith, as in the Prophet: “I shall place in the desert the fir tree and the boxwood [Note: [Col. 0877] 18 Isa. XLI, 19],” that is, in the Church of the Gentiles I shall establish contemplatives and those who retain the greenness of faith.

## C

Corpse. Heat. Character. Foodstuffs. Footwear. Cheese. Cup. Key. Cachexy (cachessi). * Cinnamon. Basket. Cherub. Cistern. Caper. Supper. Bark. Rib. Color. Conflict. Chariot. Concubine. Darkness. Cedar. Circle. Furnace. Neck. Burning heat. Cyprus. Hair. Straining. City. Choir. [Col. 0878C] Chalice. Carbuncle. Scars. Cry. Camp. Ash. Lampstand. Cave. Cypress. Capitals. Clergy. Citizens. Dove. Consuls. Gnat. Fortress. Masons. Neck. Confusion. Stalk. Framework. Crown. Flesh. Camel. [Col. 0878B] Harmony. Horn. Song. Cartilage. Food. Path. Prison. Cymbal. Ham. Cataracts. Gnats. Head. Lyre. Bowl. Scarlet. Saffron. Sea-monster. Pebble. Grating. [Col. 0878C] Shield. Carmel. Chains. Belt. Basket. Confession. Bedchamber. Locks of hair. Raven. Skin. Hind. Cerastes. Heel. Coals. Oven. Field. Chair. Channels. Heaven. Columns. Counselors. Dog. Cell. Cups. [Col. 0878B] Capon. Desire. Comedies. Elbow. Crystal. Doe. Wax. Thought. Quail. Serpent. Heart. Leg. Reed. Swan. Nails. Puppy. Dog-flies. Brightness. Knife. [Col. 0878C] Concubines. Hills. Body. Guardian. Stag. Neck. Calumniator. Haircloth.

The Corpse is Christ, as in Deuteronomy: “If a corpse of a dead man is found among you [Note: [Col. 0877] 19 Deut. XXI, 1],” that is, if the body of crucified Christ is found among you. The Corpse, anyone fallen into guilt, as in Job: “Wherever the corpse is, the eagle is immediately present [Note: [Col. 0877] 20 Job XXXIX, 33],” for the preacher hastens to expose anyone who has fallen into sin. The Corpse, the devil, as in Isaiah: “Cast out like a rotting corpse [Note: [Col. 0877] 21 Isa. XIV, 19],” for the devil was rejected because of the rot of pride. Through the corpse, our prayers, as in Genesis: “The birds descended upon the corpses,” for the frivolities of phantoms plunge themselves into our prayers. Through the corpse, the crimes of sinners, as in Isaiah: “The stench of their corpses shall rise [Note: [Col. 0877] 22 Isa. XXXIV, 3],” for infamy proceeds from their crimes. Through the corpse, the punishment of the condemned, as in Isaiah: “They shall see the corpses of the men who transgressed against me [Note: [Col. 0879] 1 Isa. LXVI, 24],” for in the future the elect will look upon the punishments of the reprobate.

Darkness is the devil, as in the Psalm: “Darkness is beneath his feet [Note: [Col. 0879] 2 Ps. XVII, 10],” for Christ tramples down the devil. Darkness, prophecy, as in the Psalm: “Cloud and darkness surround him [Note: [Col. 0879] 3 Ps. XCVI, 2],” for what the apostles taught openly, the prophets foretold obscurely. Darkness, the hidden glory of the Lord’s majesty, as in Exodus: “Moses entered into the darkness in which God was [Note: [Col. 0879] 4 Exod. XX, 21],” for only the perfect can attain the contemplation of the glory of the Lord’s majesty. Darkness, confusion of mind, as in Job: “May darkness seize the mind [Note: [Col. 0879] 5 Job III, 5],” that is, may confusion invade the mind’s perverse delight. Darkness, sin, as in Job: “Nor may darkness seize my face [Note: [Col. 0879] 6 Job XXIII, 7],” that is, guilt did not blind the affection of my mind. Darkness, the last day, as in Zephaniah: “That day is a day of darkness [Note: [Col. 0879] 7 Zeph. I, 15],” for that final day will obscure the reprobate. Darkness, the examination of the final judgment, as in Genesis: “A dark darkness came to pass, passing between those divisions [Note: [Col. 0879] 8 Gen. XV, 17],” for that final judgment will separate the wicked from the good.

Calor is the fervor of the Holy Spirit, as in the Psalm: “There is none who can hide himself from his heat” [Note: [Col. 0879] 9 Psalm XVIII, 7], because the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each person according to * measure. Heat is the sweetness of charity, as in Job: “The stone, dissolved by heat, is changed into bronze” [Note: [Col. 0879] 10 Job XXVIII, 2], because one who was hard is softened through the sweetness of charity. Heat is the desire for righteousness, as in Genesis: “It happened at the first heat of mating, while the sheep looked upon the rods and gave birth” [Note: [Col. 0879] 11 Genesis XXX, 39], because all the simple first look upon examples in the very desire for righteousness, and bring the good they desire to fulfillment. Heat is the punishment of the reprobate, as in Job: “Let him pass from the waters of snow to excessive heat” [Note: [Col. 0879] 12 Job XXIV, 19], because the condemned pass from cold to burning heat.

The cup is Christ’s passion, as in the Gospel: “You will indeed drink my cup” [Note: [Col. 0879] 13 Matthew XX, 23], that is, you will imitate my passion. The cup is Sacred Scripture, as in the Psalm: “My cup is made drunk” [Note: [Col. 0879] 14 Mark X, 39], because Sacred Scripture, which intoxicates its hearers, is clear. The cup is God’s judgment, as in the Psalm: “The cup is in the hand of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0879] 15 Psalm XXII, 5], that is, judgment is in God’s power; it is “full of unmixed wine,” without any dregs of * justice, “full of mixture,” repaying good with good and evil with evil. The cup is the tribulation of the saints, as in the Psalm: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup” [Note: [Col. 0879] 16 Psalm LXXIV, 9], because God is the portion of those who suffer tribulation for him. The cup is the passion of the martyrs, as in the Psalm: “I will take the cup of salvation” [Note: [Col. 0879] 17 Psalm XV, 5], that is, I will endure the passion of martyrdom in imitation of Christ. The cup is worldly pleasure, as in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0879] 18 Psalm CXV, 13]: the golden cup of Babylon; for this world of ours is indeed beautiful, but it leads to confusion.

The reed is Christ, as in the Psalm: “My tongue [Col. 0880A] is the reed of a swift writer” [Note: [Col. 0879] 19 Apocalypse XVII, 4], because the Holy Spirit inspired in their hearts those whom Christ taught as disciples. The reed is any preacher, as in Isaiah: “The green shoot of the reed will arise in it” [Note: [Col. 0879] 20 Psalm XLIV, 2], that is, in the Church there will be a teacher of preachers. The reed is the gentile world, as in Isaiah: “He will not break the bruised reed” [Note: [Col. 0879] 21 Isaiah XXXV, 8], that is, he will not condemn the weak gentile people [Note: [Col. 0879] 22 Psalm XLII, 3]. The reed is any hypocrite, as in Job: “In the secrecy of the reed Behemoth sleeps” [Note: [Col. 0879] 23 Job XL, 16], because the devil rests in the mind of one who pretends. The reed is God’s ordering, as in Ezekiel: “A measuring reed was in his hand,” because God has it in his power to order all things. Through the reed, preachers are signified, as in Exodus: “On the shaft of the reed and the cups” [Note: [Col. 0879] 24 Exodus XXXVII, 17], because there are preachers and hearers in the Church.

[Col. 0880B] The slanderer is the devil, as in the Psalm: “And you will humble the slanderer” [Note: [Col. 0879] 25 Psalm LXXVII, 4], that is, Christ will overcome the devil.

The heel is the end of our action, as in Genesis: “You will watch his heel” [Note: [Col. 0879] 26 Genesis III, 15], because the devil strives to corrupt the end of our action. The heel is our progress, as in the Psalm: “They themselves will watch my heel” [Note: [Col. 0879] 27 Psalm LV, 7], because my enemies do not cease to envy my progress. The heel is our flesh, as in the Psalm: “The iniquity of my heel will surround me” [Note: [Col. 0879] 28 Psalm XLVIII, 6].

[Col. 0880C] The pebble is the divine word, as in Isaiah: “And in the hand of the seraph was a pebble” [Note: [Col. 0879] 29 Isaiah VI, 6], because the love of God sets aflame the one who completes the divine word in action. The pebble is the eternity of the heavenly homeland, as in the Apocalypse: “To the one who conquers I will give a white pebble” [Note: [Col. 0879] 30 Apocalypse II, 17], because whoever conquers here by resisting temptation will have bright and everlasting eternity in the future. The pebble is the punishment of the lying tongue, as in Proverbs: “His mouth will be filled with a pebble,” because whoever here sins by lying with his tongue will hereafter be tortured in his tongue by the punishment of burning.

The path is the life of every religious person, as in Isaiah: “The path of the righteous is straight for walking” [Note: [Col. 0879] 31 Isaiah XXVI, 7], because one who lives according to the life of religious people does not stumble into the crookedness of iniquity. Through the pebble, wicked doctrines are signified, as in the Book of Judges: “They walked along crooked paths” [Note: [Col. 0879] 32 Judges V, 6], that is, they followed erroneous doctrines.

[Col. 0880D] The shoe is Christ’s humanity, as in the Psalm: “I will extend my shoe over Edom” [Note: [Col. 0879] 33 Psalm LIX, 10], that is, I will reveal my incarnation to the gentile world. The shoe is preaching, as in Deuteronomy: “Iron and bronze are his shoe” [Note: [Col. 0879] 34 Deuteronomy XXXIII, 25], that is, strength and tribulation follow his preaching. The shoe is action, as in the Books of Kings: “Abner placed the terror of battle in his shoe,” because every wicked person exercises the cruelty of discord in his action. The shoe is a deadly action, as in Exodus: “Loosen [Col. 0881A] the shoes from your feet” [Note: [Col. 0881] 1 Exodus III, 5], that is, cast the work of death away from your affections. Through the shoe, external goods are signified, to advance good works. * Through shoes, external evils are signified, as in the Gospel: “Do not carry shoes” [Note: [Col. 0881] 2 Matthew X, 10], that is, do not arm yourselves with the examples of wicked people. Through the shoe, the mortifications of our members that are upon the earth are signified, as in the Song: “How beautiful are your steps in shoes” [Note: [Col. 0881] 3 Song VII, 1], that is, how beautiful are your works in the mortification of pleasures.

The cry is the blood of our redemption, as in Job: “Nor may my cry find in you a place to hide” [Note: [Col. 0881] 4 Job XVI, 18], because the holy Church of Christ does not conceal the blood. The cry is the desire of any righteous person, as in the Psalm: “May my cry come to you” [Note: [Col. 0881] 5 Psalm CI, 2], because God hears the [Col. 0881B] desire of the righteous. * That is, it is the desire of the reprobate, as in Genesis: “The cry of Sodom has come before me” [Note: [Col. 0881] 6 Genesis XVIII, 20], because the desire of the reprobate clamors importunately in God’s ears. The cry is the violent temptation of the devil, as in Job: “He did not hear the cry of the exactor” [Note: [Col. 0881] 7 Job XXXIX, 10], because the holy man does not consent to the devil’s violent temptations.

The nails are the precepts of charity, as in the Book of Kings: “He fastened the plates with golden nails” [Note: [Col. 0881] 8 3 Kings VI, 21], that is, he strengthened works with the precepts of charity. The nails are reason and understanding, as in Isaiah: “And strengthen your nails” [Note: [Col. 0881] 9 Isaiah LIV, 2], that is, strengthen reason and understanding so that they do not grow weak. The nails are the corrections of the saints, as in Ecclesiastes: “The words of the wise are like nails” [Note: [Col. 0881] 10 Ecclesiastes XII, 11], because their words prick vices through corrections.

[Col. 0881C] The key is Christ, as in the Gospel: “You have taken away the key of the knowledge of Christ; you yourselves did not enter, and those who were entering you prevented” [Note: [Col. 0881] 11 Luke XI, 52]; that is, you strive to take me away, neither believe in me nor permit others to believe. The key is the opening of Sacred Scripture, as in the prophet: “And I will give the key of the house of David” [Note: [Col. 0881] 12 Isaiah XXII, 22], that is, I will establish the unlocking of Sacred Scripture in the Church of Christ. The key is the confinement of the impious heart, as in the Apocalypse: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss” [Note: [Col. 0881] 13 Apocalypse XX, 1], because we believe in Christ humbling himself, who confines our body by his just judgment. Through keys, the powers of teachers are signified, as in the Gospel: “And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0881] 14 Matthew XVI, 19]; the Lord grants the Church the power of binding and loosing.

[Col. 0881D] The field is this world, as in the Song: “I am the flower of the field” [Note: [Col. 0881] 15 Song II, 1], that is, I am the beauty of the world. The field is the gentile world, as in Ezekiel: “Rise, go out into the field” [Note: [Col. 0881] 16 Ezekiel III, 22], because Christ, entering the world at the Father’s command, called the gentiles to faith. The field is the broad life of this age, as in the Psalm: “And the cattle of the field” [Note: [Col. 0881] 17 Psalm VIII, 8], that is, the pleasure-seekers of the world. The field is the Jewish people, as in Daniel: “Habakkuk was going into the field” [Note: [Col. 0881] 18 Daniel XIV, 32], [Col. 0882A] because Christ came to the Jewish people. Through the field, uncultivated gentiles are signified, as in the prophet: “The fields of the wilderness put forth Israel’s fragrant shoot,” because the people of the nations brought forth the fruit of the Law that had been given to the Jewish people. Through the field, the minds of the faithful are signified, as in the Psalm: “And your fields will be filled with abundance” [Note: [Col. 0881] 19 Psalm LXIV, 12], because the minds of the righteous are filled through inward fellowship.
