The camel is Christ, as in the Gospel: “Straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel” [Note: [Col. 0881] 20 Matthew XXIII, 24], that is, demanding the robber’s release and crucifying Christ. The camel is the crookedness of vices, as in Genesis: “When Isaac was seen, Rebecca descended from the camel” [Note: [Col. 0881] 21 Genesis XXIV, 64], because, having recognized Christ, she abandoned the crookedness of vices. Through the camel, the powerful of this age are signified, as in Isaiah: “The flood of camels will cover you” [Note: [Col. 0881] 22 Isaiah LX, 6], because the powerful of the [Col. 0882B] world come to the Church. Through camels, the arrangements of earthly affairs are signified, as in Job: “His possession was three thousand camels” [Note: [Col. 0881] 23 Job I, 3], because the holy man subjects earthly administrations to the understanding of the Holy Trinity.

The bit is the affliction of the flesh, as in the Psalm: “With bit and bridle” [Note: [Col. 0881] 24 Psalm XXXI, 9], that is, restrain their proud words by the affliction of the flesh. The bit is discipline: “A bit for the ass” [Note: [Col. 0881] 25 Proverbs XXVI, 3], that is, discipline for the servant.

The furnace is the tribulation of the righteous, as in the Apocalypse: “And their feet were like burnished bronze, as though in a burning furnace” [Note: [Col. 0881] 26 Apocalypse I, 15], because tribulation refines the righteous. The furnace is charity, as in Isaiah: “And his furnace is in Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0879] 27 Isaiah XXXI, 9], because in the heavenly homeland the ardor of charity reigns. The furnace is infernal life, as in the Gospel: “And they will cast them into the furnace of fire” [Note: [Col. 0881] 28 Matthew XIII, 42, 59], that is, into the burning of infernal [Col. 0882C] flame.

The lampstand is Christ, as in Exodus: “You shall make a beaten lampstand” [Note: [Col. 0879] 29 Exodus XXV, 31], because Christ, who is the light of the world, was afflicted by the blows of his passions. The lampstand is contemplation, as in the Books of Kings: “Let us place a lampstand for Elisha” [Note: [Col. 0879] 30 4 Kings IV, 10], because, if Christ—who is represented by Elisha—is to remain among us, we must have the light of contemplation. The lampstand is the dignity of a preacher, as in the Apocalypse: “Unless you repent, I will move your lampstand from its place” [Note: [Col. 0879] 31 Apocalypse II, 5], that is, I will take your dignity away from you. The lampstand is the condition of our body, as in the Gospel: “But upon a lampstand” [Note: [Col. 0879] 32 Matthew V, 16; Luke VIII, 16, and XI, 33], because we ought to place the word of God above our very body. Through the lampstand [Col. 0882D] the Churches are signified, as in the Apocalypse: “The seven lampstands are the seven Churches” [Note: [Col. 0879] 33 Apocalypse I, 20].

Brightness is innocence, as in the Song: “My beloved is radiant” [Note: [Col. 0879] 34 Song V, 10], that is, pure from sin. Brightness is the beauty of the heavenly homeland, as in the Book of Wisdom: “The brightness of eternal light” [Note: [Col. 0879] 35 Wisdom VII, 16], because in Christ there is perpetual splendor.

The basket is Sacred Scripture, as in Exodus: “The basket [Col. 0883A] with unleavened breads” [Note: [Col. 0883] 1 Exodus XXIX, 23], that is, Sacred Scripture together with pure works.

The channels are Sacred Scriptures, as in Genesis: “He placed rods in the channels” [Note: [Col. 0883] 2 Genesis XXX, 38], because the examples of the saints are in the Scriptures. The channels are the minds of the righteous, as in the Song: “The king’s purple joined to the channels” [Note: [Col. 0883] 3 Song VII, 5], because Christ’s passion is impressed upon the minds of the saints.

The dog is an shameless sinner, as in Proverbs: “A dog returning to its vomit” [Note: [Col. 0883] 4 Proverbs XXVI, 11], that is, a shameless sinner returns to his sin. The dog is any penitent, as in Ecclesiastes: “Better is a living dog than a dead lion” [Note: [Col. 0883] 5 Ecclesiastes IX, 4], because one who humbly confesses his sins is better than one who proudly presumes upon his merits. The dog is any weak person, as in the Book of Kings: “Am I a dog, that you come against me with a staff?” [Note: [Col. 0883] 6 1 Kings XVII, 43], that is, do you consider me so weak that you believe you can overcome me so easily? [Col. 0883B] The dog is any utterly worthless person, as in the Book of Kings: “Whom are you pursuing, king of Israel? Whom but a dead dog?” [Note: [Col. 0883] 7 1 Kings XXIV, 15], that is, me, utterly worthless, who am not even worthy to live. Through dogs, the apostles are signified, as in the Psalm: “The tongue of your dogs” [Note: [Col. 0883] 8 Psalm LXVIII, 4], because the apostles’ preaching was poured into the gentiles. Through dogs, the nations are signified, as in the Gospel: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs” [Note: [Col. 0883] 9 Matthew XV, 26], that is, to give apostolic doctrine to the gentiles. Through dogs, the Jews are signified, as in the Psalm: “Dogs surrounded me” [Note: [Col. 0883] 10 Psalm XXI, 17], that is, the Jews attacked me. Through dogs, faultfinders are signified, as in the Gospel: “Do not give what is holy to dogs” [Note: [Col. 0883] 11 Matthew VII, 6], that is, do not give the mystery of Sacred Scripture to those who criticize mordantly. [Col. 0883C] Through dogs, slanderers are signified, as in Paul: “Beware of dogs” [Note: [Col. 0883] 12 Philippians III, 2], * that is, do not look upon slanderers. Through dogs, those devoted to chatter are signified, as in the Apocalypse: “Outside are dogs, outside are sorcerers” [Note: [Col. 0883] 13 Apocalypse XXII, 15], because those who persist in the crime of loquacity and evil action are excluded from the kingdom of God. Through dogs, good preachers are signified, as in the Gospel: “The dogs licked Lazarus’s sores” [Note: [Col. 0883] 14 Luke XVI, 21], because holy preachers healed the sins of the gentile people. Through dogs, evil preachers are signified, as in the prophet: “Mute dogs, unable to bark” [Note: [Col. 0883] 15 Isaiah LVI, 10], because evil preachers are unwilling to rebuke vices.

The head is Christ’s divinity, as in the Song: “His head is the finest gold” [Note: [Col. 0883] 16 Song V, 11], because in Christ’s divinity there is incomparable radiance. The head is Christ’s humanity, as in the Psalm: “He exalted my head above my enemies” [Note: [Col. 0883] 17 Psalm XXVI, 6], that is, he raised Christ as man above my * enemies. The head is faith, as in the Psalm: “My head,” that is, faith, “grew cold among the * wicked.” The head is the Jewish priesthood, as in Job: “He has taken the crown from my head” [Note: [Col. 0883] 18 Job XIX, 9], because God took dignity away from the Jewish priesthood. The head is any ruler, as in the Books of Kings: “You were made head among the tribes of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0883] 19 1 Kings XV, 17], that is, you were appointed ruler over the peoples of Israel. The head is the principate of the Synagogue, as in Isaiah:

[Col. 0884A] “Every head is sick” [Note: [Col. 0883] 20 Isaiah I, 5], because the entire principate of the Synagogue was spiritually sick. The head is the beginning, as in the Psalm: “At the head of the book it is written” [Note: [Col. 0883] 21 Psalm XXXIX, 8], that is, at the beginning of the Psalter it is written, “It is about me.” The head is any proud person of this age, as in Job: “Or will you fill the fishpond with the head of him?” [Note: [Col. 0883] 22 Job XL, 26], because God draws even the proud to himself through his preachers. The head is the beginning of temptation, as in Job: “He will suck the head of the asp” [Note: [Col. 0883] 23 Job XX, 19], because every wicked person immediately accepts the beginning of temptation by consenting to it. The head is excellence, as in the Law: “The resident alien will be head” [Note: [Col. 0883] 24 Deuteronomy XXVIII, 44], that is, the stranger will surpass you. The head is the devil, as in the Psalm: “The head of their circuit” [Note: [Col. 0883] 25 Psalm CXXXIX, 10], because the devil, who is the head of the wicked, never proceeds rightly. The head is the Antichrist, as in Habakkuk: “You struck [Col. 0884B] the head from the house of the wicked” [Note: [Col. 0883] 26 Habakkuk III, 13], that is, you overcame the Antichrist, who is the dwelling place of the devil. The head is the enemy’s desire, as in Genesis: “* She herself will crush your head” [Note: [Col. 0883] 27 Genesis III, 15], that is, the Virgin Mary will trample upon your desire. The head is the mind, as in the Song: “Your head is like Carmel” [Note: [Col. 0883] 28 Song VII, 5], that is, your mind possesses the thought of spiritual circumcision; for Carmel is interpreted as “knowledge of circumcision.” The head is intention, as in Jeremiah: “His enemies have become the head” [Note: [Col. 0883] 29 Lamentations I, 5], that is, your enemies prevail over him in that very intention. Through heads, the elations of the proud are signified, as in the Psalm: “He will crush the heads upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0883] 30 Psalm CIX, 6], that is, he will destroy the elations of the worst people in the Church. Through heads, criminal vices are signified, as in the Apocalypse: “The dragon had seven heads” [Note: [Col. 0883] 31 Apocalypse XII, 3], because the devil suggests the seven capital [Col. 0884C] vices.

The hair is the subtlety of thoughts, as in the Psalm: “He will crush the crown of the hair of those who walk [in their sins]” [Note: [Col. 0883] 32 Psalm LXVII, 22], that is, he will destroy the sharp subtlety of heretics. The hair is the order of preachers, as in Daniel [Note: [Col. 0883] 33 Daniel XIV, 35]. Habakkuk is said to have been carried by the hair from Judea to Babylon; through Habakkuk, whose name is interpreted as “embracing” or “wrestler,” our Redeemer is represented, who, as though embracing his own, entered the struggle against the devil: “Now Habakkuk was in Judah” [Note: [Col. 0883] 34 Ibid., verse 32], and Christ was spiritually sent to the Jews. “He had cooked a stew,” because Christ, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, prepared the food of life from the water of wisdom. He “had crumbled bread in a bowl”; and Christ, as though into vessels of the Lord’s word for the apostles, had entrusted nourishment of spiritual [Col. 0884D] doctrine by setting it forth as though breaking it. He “entered the field and carried it to the reapers”; and Christ, coming to the Synagogue, preached to the Jews. “And the angel said to him: Carry the meal that you have to Babylon, to Daniel who is in the lions’ den” [Note: [Col. 0883] 35 Ibid., verse 33], because the apostles pleaded that salvation be given to the gentiles by the Lord. Through Babylon, the confused gentile world is signified; through Daniel, the people of the nations; through the lions’ den, the dark way of life of the demons. [Col. 0885A] “The den, therefore, into Babylon” [Note: [Col. 0885] 1 Daniel XIV, 34] is the dwelling place of demons among the gentiles; “Daniel in the den” is the people of the nations dwelling in the region of the shadow of death. “I have not seen Babylon,” says Habakkuk, “and I do not know the den”; and the Lord says: “I was not sent except to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0885] 2 Matthew XV, 24]. Therefore, Habakkuk, carried by the hair to Babylon, brought Daniel the meal that he had prepared for the reapers; and our Redeemer, through his preachers, ministered to the gentiles the word of salvation intended for the Jewish people. “Daniel rose and ate” [Note: [Col. 0885] 3 Verse 38]; and the people of the nations, rising from error, are raised up to faith and refreshed by the nourishment of divine doctrine. After Daniel is left behind, Habakkuk is restored to the place from which he had been carried; and Christ, when the fullness of the gentiles has been completed, will return to the Jews, and then all Israel will be saved. [Col. 0885B] Through hairs, angels are signified, as in the Apocalypse: “His hair was white” [Note: [Col. 0885] 4 Apocalypse I, 14], because the angels of the Lord are visible in perpetual brightness. Through hairs, the sacraments of the Law are signified, as in Job, for Job himself is read [Note: [Col. 0885] 5 Job I, 20] to have shaved the hairs from his head; because Christ is known to have taken the sacraments of the Law away from that first priesthood. Through hairs, superfluous thoughts are signified, as in the Law [Note: [Col. 0885] 6 Numbers VI, 18], where the Nazirites are commanded to place their hair in the fire of the sacrifice; because the perfect ought to set their superfluous thoughts aflame in the flame of the Lord’s love. Through hairs, the faithful peoples who cling to Christ the head are signified, as in the Song: “Your hair is like a flock of goats that have come up from the washing” [Note: [Col. 0885] 7 Song VI, 4], because peoples washed through baptism seek the heights through desire. Through hairs, abundant earthly substance is signified, as in the Gospel, where Mary wiped the Lord’s feet with the hair of her head [Note: [Col. 0885] 8 Luke VII, 38, 44], because [Col. 0885C] every faithful person gives the poor what they need from his abundance.

The capitals are the two Testaments, as in the Books of Kings: “Two capitals above the heads of the columns” [Note: [Col. 0885] 9 3 Kings VII, 16], because the two Testaments are in the minds of teachers.

The fortress is the Virgin Mary, as in the Gospel: “Jesus entered a certain fortress” [Note: [Col. 0885] 10 Luke X, 38], because Christ came into the womb of the uniquely virgin woman. The fortress, * as in the Gospel: “Go into the fortress that is opposite you” [Note: [Col. 0885] 11 Matthew XXI, 2], that is, into the world that is opposed to you. The little chapel is our mind, as in the Gospel: “The Lord entered with the disciples into the chapel of Emmaus, and was recognized by them” [Note: [Col. 0885] 12 Luke XXIV, 13, 15, 31], because when he enters with us, within us, knowledge of him is granted to us.

The caper is the Jewish populace, as in Ecclesiastes: [Col. 0885D] “The caper will be scattered” [Note: [Col. 0885] 13 Ecclesiastes XII, 5], because the Jewish people were cast off on account of their unbelief.

The doe is Christ, as in the Song: “My beloved is like a doe,” because Christ assumed human likeness. The doe is the Church, as in the Song: “Return, be like a doe, my beloved” [Note: [Col. 0885] 14 Song II, 9]; that is, return to purity, my form, which you received from the Church. Through does, the virtues of souls are signified, as in the [Col. 0886A] Song: “I adjure you by the does” [Note: [Col. 0885] 15 Song III, 5], that is, I instruct you in virtues.

The she-goat is the Church, as in Genesis: “Take a three-year-old cow and a three-year-old she-goat” [Note: [Col. 0885] 16 Genesis XV, 9], that is, the Synagogue and the Church, both of which believe in the Trinity. The she-goat is contemplation, as in Leviticus: “Let him offer a lamb from the flocks, or a she-goat” [Note: [Col. 0885] 17 Leviticus V, 6], that is, the active life, which pertains to many, and the contemplative life, which pertains to few.

The prison is the weight of our corruption, as in Job: “You have surrounded me with a prison” [Note: [Col. 0885] 18 Job VII, 12], that is, you have walled me in on every side with the weight of my corruption. * It is the congregation of unbelievers, as in the Apocalypse: “Satan will be released from his place” [Note: [Col. 0885] 19 Apocalypse XX, 7], because he will then emerge from the wicked, from whose * place he is now held. [Col. 0886B] The prison is tribulation, as in the Apocalypse: “He is about to cast you into prison” [Note: [Col. 0885] 20 Apocalypse II, 10], that is, into tribulation. The prison is our flesh, as in the Psalm: “Lead my soul out of prison” [Note: [Col. 0885] 21 Psalm CXLI, 8], that is, free my soul from this body of death. The prison is hell, as in the Gospel: “The judge will send you into prison” [Note: [Col. 0885] 22 Matthew V, 24], that is, into hell.

The flesh of Christ is either that which we receive on the altar, of which it is said: “Our * flesh is truly food” [Note: [Col. 0885] 23 John VI, 55], or that which was fixed to the wood, of which the Psalm says: “My flesh was changed because of God” [Note: [Col. 0885] 24 Psalm CVIII, 24], that is, into the glory of immortality, through spiritual grace. Flesh means sin, as in Job: “I covered my flesh with ashes” [Note: [Col. 0885] 25 Job XVI, 15], that is, I exposed my guilt through the humility of repentance. Flesh is spoken of according to nature: “Flesh of my flesh” [Note: [Col. 0885] 26 Genesis II, 23], because woman [Col. 0886C] is naturally from man. Flesh is any weak person, as in the Psalm: “He remembered that they were flesh” [Note: [Col. 0885] 27 Psalm LXXVII, 39], that is, he knew their root: that they are fragile. Flesh is carnal affection, as in Job: “His flesh will waste away” [Note: [Col. 0885] 28 Job XXXIII, 21], that is, his flesh will wither. Flesh is the corruption of immortality, as in Paul: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0885] 29 1 Corinthians XV, 50], etc.; that is, corruption will not possess incorruption. Flesh is any carnal person, as in Genesis: “My Spirit will not remain in man, because he is flesh” [Note: [Col. 0885] 30 Genesis VI, 3], that is, he cannot be spiritual so long as he strives to be carnal. Flesh is the whole human being, as in Paul: “The works of the flesh are manifest” [Note: [Col. 0885] 31 Galatians V, 19], that is, of the human being; for the vices that are listed belong not only to the flesh but also to the soul. Flesh is carnal wisdom, as in the Gospel: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you” [Note: [Col. 0885] 32 Matthew XVI, 17], that is, the carnal inflation of wisdom and [Col. 0886D] knowledge has not revealed it to you. Flesh is desire, as in Paul: “The flesh desires against the spirit” [Note: [Col. 0885] 33 Galatians V, 17], that is, the desire of the flesh against the soul. Flesh is softness, as in Genesis: “He took one of his ribs and filled it with flesh in its place” [Note: [Col. 0885] 34 Genesis II, 21], because the Lord sometimes removes strength from us and permits softness to exist in us. Through flesh, the meanings of Sacred Scripture are signified, as in Exodus: “They shall eat [Col. 0887A] the flesh roasted by fire that night” [Note: [Col. 0887] 1 Exodus XII, 8], that is, in the obscurity of the present life we ought to be refreshed by the meanings of Sacred Scripture. Through flesh, the disciples of Christ are signified, as in Job: “My bone cleaved to my skin after my flesh was consumed” [Note: [Col. 0887] 2 Job XIX, 20], because, when the disciples fled, soldiers stood by Christ in his passion. Through flesh, humble teachings are signified, as in the Psalm: “He rained flesh upon them like dust” [Note: [Col. 0887] 3 Psalm LXXVII, 27], that is, he gave them humble teachings pertaining to action. Through flesh, weak works are signified, as in Proverbs: “The life of the flesh” [Note: [Col. 0887] 4 Proverbs XIV, 30], because, if innocence is carefully guarded, whatever is weak outwardly is strengthened. Through flesh, the impious are signified, as in Deuteronomy: “My sword will devour flesh” [Note: [Col. 0887] 5 Deuteronomy XXXII, 42], that is, my judgment will condemn the impious. Through flesh, the punishments of the reprobate are signified, as in the Apocalypse: “That you may eat the flesh [Col. 0887B] of kings and tribunes” [Note: [Col. 0887] 6 Apocalypse XIX, 18], that is, that you may take delight in the torment of the reprobate, both great and small.

A song is the praise of God, as in the Psalm: “He put a new song into my mouth, a song [to our God]” [Note: [Col. 0887] 7 Psalm XXXIX, 4], that is, so that in my customary way I may praise my God. A song is heavenly glory, as in Ezekiel: “Lamentations and a song were written in the book” [Note: [Col. 0887] 8 Ezekiel II, 10], because Sacred Scripture announces mourning for us in the present and glory in the future. Through a song, inward consolations are signified, as in Job: “He gives songs in the night” [Note: [Col. 0887] 9 Job XXXV, 1], because the Lord grants his own consolations in tribulation.

Carmel, which is interpreted as “knowledge of circumcision,” is the carnal purification of the Jews, as in the Books of Kings: “Nabal and his possession were in Carmel” [Note: [Col. 0887] 10 1 Kings XXV, 2], because the foolish Jewish people trusted in outward [Col. 0887C] purification; for Nabal is interpreted as “foolish.” Carmel is knowledge of secrets, as in the Song: “Your head is like Carmel” [Note: [Col. 0887] 11 Song VII, 5], that is, your mind possesses knowledge and awareness of secrets.

Cartilage is the members of the devil, as in Job: “His cartilage is like a plate of iron” [Note: [Col. 0887] 12 Job XL, 13], because the devil’s members never cease to trouble those who are members of Christ.

The reed-bed is the Jewish people, as in Exodus: “He placed him in the reed-bed of the river” [Note: [Col. 0887] 13 Exodus II, 3], because Christ first appeared to the harsh Jewish people. The reed-bed is the life of hypocrites, as in Job: “Can the reed-bed grow without water?” [Note: [Col. 0887] 14 Job VIII, 11], because hypocrites receive the greenness of good works only from a heavenly gift.

[Col. 0887D] The carbuncle is the light of great knowledge, as in Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0887] 15 Ezekiel XXVIII, 13], where the carbuncle is said to have covered the first angel; for the light of great knowledge illuminated him.

The caradion is the vice of loquacity, as in the Law [Note: [Col. 0887] 16 Leviticus XI, 19], where God’s people are forbidden to eat the * caradion; for those who strive to please God do not wish to persist in the vice of loquacity.

The hinges are the angelic spirits, as in the Books of Kings, where hinges are said to have been in the inner house of the Holy [Col. 0888A] of Holies [Note: [Col. 0887] 17 1 Kings VII, 50], because the spirits of the saints rejoice in the innermost places of heaven. The hinges are preachers, as in the song: “For the hinges of the earth belong to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0887] 18 1 Samuel II, 8], because the preachers of the Church belong to the Lord. The hinges are the ends of the world, as in Job: “He will also cover the hinges of the sea” [Note: [Col. 0887] 19 Job XXXVI, 30], that is, he will read the ends of the world.

The coals are the virtues that were in Christ, as in the Law: “the high priest carried into the Holy of Holies a censer full of coals [lacuna]” [Note: [Col. 0887] 20 Exodus XXX, 34], because Christ will raise a body full of holy virtues to the heavens. The coals are the saints who will judge with the Lord at the end, as in the Psalms: “Coals will fall upon them” [Note: [Col. 0887] 21 Psalm CXXXIX, 11], because the perfect saints will judge the reprobate with the Lord. The coals are the fires of repentance, as in Proverbs: “You will heap burning coals upon his head” [Note: [Col. 0887] 22 Proverbs XXV, 22], that is, by your good [Col. 0888B] works you will move your enemy to repentance. The coals are the fires of charity, as in the Psalms: “The clouds passed, hail and coals of fire” [Note: [Col. 0887] 23 Psalm XVII, 13], because, when iniquity abounds, both preaching and warnings will cease to be salutary for many, and the flames of charity will grow cold. The coals are holy men, as in Ezekiel: “Like burning coals of fire” [Note: [Col. 0887] 24 Ezekiel I, 13], that is, like holy men who love the Lord in secret. The coals are good examples, as in the Psalms: “With desolating coals” [Note: [Col. 0887] 25 Psalm CXIX, 4], that is, with good examples that lay waste to vices. The coals are sinners, as in the Psalms: “Coals were kindled by him” [Note: [Col. 0887] 26 Psalm XVII, 9], because many who had been extinguished by the heat of righteous desire and had become black through sin were kindled and illuminated by God. The coals are the wicked who persist in their [Col. 0888C] evils, as in Jeremiah: “Their face has been blackened above the coals” [Note: [Col. 0887] 27 Lamentations IV, 8], that is, they have preserved the exceedingly wicked in their perversities.

The grating is the heart of any saint, as in Exodus: “A bronze grating in the form of a net” [Note: [Col. 0887] 28 Exodus XXVII, 4], that is, the mind of a holy man made strong through the multiplicity of virtues.

The bowl is the order of preachers, as in the Song: “A turned bowl, never lacking cups” [Note: [Col. 0887] 29 Song VII, 2], because holy preachers are both free from crime and full of a spiritual drink.

Cheese is firmness of mind, as in Job: “You coagulated me like cheese” [Note: [Col. 0887] 30 Job X, 10], that is, you solidified me in the joining together of sluggish thought.

The camps are the angels, as in Genesis: “The camps of God [Col. 0888D] are here” [Note: [Col. 0887] 31 Genesis XXXII, 2], that is, these are the angels of God in whom God dwells. The camps are holy men, as in Ezekiel: “Like the sound of a multitude and of camps” [Note: [Col. 0887] 32 Ezekiel I, 24], that is, like the fame of many saints. The camps are the whole Church together, as in the Song: “Like an army arranged in battle formation” [Note: [Col. 0887] 33 Song VI, 3, 9], that is, like the harmonious assembly of the Church. The camps are spiritual virtues, as in the Song: “What will you see in the Shulammite except choirs of camps?” [Note: [Col. 0887] 34 Ibid., verse 12], because in the Jewish people, when it has been converted to [Col. 0889A] faith, there will be the adornments of spiritual virtues. The camps are persecutors, as in the Psalm: “If camps should stand against me” [Note: [Col. 0889] 1 Psalm XXVI, 3], that is, when my adversaries resist me, I will trust in God.

A cub is Christ, as in Genesis: “A lion’s cub is Judah” [Note: [Col. 0889] 2 Gen. XLIX, 9], that is, Christ is from the tribe of Judah. A cub is the Jewish people, as in the Psalm: “Like a lion’s cub dwelling in hiding places” [Note: [Col. 0889] 3 Ps. XVI, 12], because the Jewish people persecuted Christ, first lying in wait for him secretly. A cub is the devil, as in the Book of Judges, where Samson kills a lion’s cub [Note: [Col. 0889] 4 Judg. XIV, 5], because Christ overcomes the devil. The apostles are represented by cubs, as in Job: “You will fill the souls of the cubs” [Note: [Col. 0889] 5 Job XXXIX, 1], that is, you will fulfill the desire of the apostles and the Church. Reprobate people are represented by cubs, as in the Psalm: “The cubs of lions roar in order to seize” [Note: [Col. 0889] 6 Ps. CIII, 21], because wicked people, who follow demons, do not cease persecuting the good. Slanderers are represented by cubs, as in Job: “The teeth of the lions’ cubs are broken” [Note: [Col. 0889] 7 Job IV, 10], that is, the words of slanderers have been destroyed. Demons are represented by cubs, as in the Psalm: “Deliver my soul from among the lions’ cubs” [Note: [Col. 0889] 8 Ps. LVI, 5], that is, he redeemed me from the power of demons. Gentiles are represented by little dogs, as in the Gospel: “The little dogs eat from the crumbs” [Note: [Col. 0889] 9 Matt. XV, 27], because the Gentiles seek the inner substance of sacred Scripture.

A chair is, in one sense, that of the world, on which Christ does not sit; in another, that of Moses, in which the Pharisee is to be heard; and in another, that of the elders, in which God is praised. The first is of pestilence, the second of righteousness, and the third of glory. The first is damnable softness; the second, the austerity of spiritual governance; the third, the sublimity of heavenly blessedness. In the first sit the wicked, in the second the good, and in the third the blessed. In the first are sinners, in the second teachers, and in the third rulers.

The first chair is supported by these four feet: neglect of oneself, forgetfulness of God, the beauty of visible things, and the sweetness of pleasurable things. Its backrest is the delight of sin; its cushion, the commission of sin. Neglect of oneself and forgetfulness of God tear out the eyes of the inner soul. The beauty of appearance and the sweetness of affection entangle its feet in deadly snares. The delight of sin ensnares it, while the commission of sin casts it down.

The four feet of the second chair are the four cardinal virtues: prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. Its backrest is love of God; its cushion, the testimony of conscience. Prudence illuminates, fortitude strengthens, justice adorns, and temperance moderates. The love of God gladdens, and the testimony of conscience brings tranquility.

In the third chair there are four feet, namely, the essence, power, knowledge, and love of the elect. Its backrest is the presence of the divine vision; its cushion, the supreme peace of rest. Then, truly, the elect will be: they will exist, be able, know, love, see, and rest. They will exist without mortality, be able without weakness, know without error, love without offense, see in fullness, and rest in supreme peace.

Therefore, the first chair is one of iniquity, the second of equity, and the third of happiness. Those who sit in the first are subjected to the flesh in the commission of every sin; those in the second preside over the Church with the authority of right judgment; those in the third rejoice with God in the eternity of happy joy. Of these chairs, the first is to be avoided, the second loved, and the third desired, because the first is evil, the second good, and the third blessed.

Chains are the bonds of vices, as in the Law: “I broke the chains of your virtues” [Note: [Col. 0889] 10 Lev. XXVI, 13], that is, I scattered the bonds of sin that were weighing down our minds. Chains are afflictions, as in Job: “If they are in chains and bound with ropes of poverty” [Note: [Col. 0889] 11 Job XXXVI, 8], that is, even if they are in afflictions and bound by the fetters of destitution. Chains are the harsh laws of the nations, as in the Gospel: “No one could bind him, not even with chains” [Note: [Col. 0889] 12 Mark V, 3], because not even the harsh laws of the Gentiles could restrain the human race from sins. Chains are spiritual virtues, as in the Books of Kings: “And like the form of a net of chains” [Note: [Col. 0889] 13 III Kings VII, 17], that is, in the form of the multiplicity of spiritual virtues. Chains are present tribulations, as in Ecclesiastes: “Someone comes forth from chains into rest” [Note: [Col. 0889] 14 Eccles. IV, 14], because the saints pass from present tribulations to eternal rest.

Waterfalls are the apostles, as in the Psalm: “At the sound of your waterfalls” [Note: [Col. 0889] 15 Ps. XLI, 8], because sinners hope in the mercy of God through the preaching of the apostles. Waterfalls are the profound judgments of sacred Scripture, as in Genesis: “And the waterfalls of heaven were opened” [Note: [Col. 0889] 16 Gen. VII, 11], that is, the profound judgments of sacred Scripture were revealed.

A burning heat is the zeal of faith, as in Job: “My bones have dried up because of the burning heat” [Note: [Col. 0889] 17 Job XXX, 30], that is, my virtues have withered because of my zeal.

The tail is perseverance, as in the Law, where it is commanded that it be removed in the sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0889] 18 Lev. VIII, 25], so that perseverance in good work may be possessed. The tail is disgrace, as in the Law: “You will be at the tail” [Note: [Col. 0889] 19 Deut. XXVIII, 44], that is, in disgrace and dishonor. The tail is the end of the age, as in Exodus: “Stretch out your hand and seize its tail” [Note: [Col. 0889] 20 Exod. IV, 4], because at the end of the age, through his grace, he will give [what is unspecified] to the Jews. The tail is the Antichrist, as in Job: “He will draw up his tail like a cedar” [Note: [Col. 0889] 21 Job XL, 12], because he will raise that condemned man to the greatest height. Blandishments are represented by the tail, as in Revelation: “The powers of the horses are in their tails” [Note: [Col. 0889] 22 Rev. IX, 19], because the powers of heretics are in their blandishments.

A cave is in the wound in the Lord’s side, as in the Song: “Arise, my friend, in the cavity of the wall” [Note: [Col. 0889] 23 Song II, 14], because through the sacraments of his redemption, which flowed from Christ’s side, the holy Church rose from unbelief. A cave is the heart of any wicked person, as in Isaiah: “He will put his hand into the den of the basilisk” [Note: [Col. 0889] 24 Isa. XI, 8], because the Lord sometimes visits by his grace a perverse mind that had been a dwelling place of demons. The preaching of heretics is represented by a cave, as in Job: “He will dwell in the caves of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0891] 1 Job XXX, 6], that is, the wicked man will remain in the preachings of heretical doctrine.

The cedar is divinity, as in the Book of Kings: “From the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall” [Note: [Col. 0891] 2 III Kings IV, 33], that is, from divinity, which reigns in heaven, to humanity, which proceeded from the Virgin. The cedar is Christ, as in the Song: “The chosen cedars” [Note: [Col. 0891] 3 Song V, 15], because Christ is free from the corruption of sin. The cedar is the wood of the holy cross, as in Isaiah: “I will set a cedar in the desert” [Note: [Col. 0891] 4 Isa. XLI, 19], that is, I will cause the venerable wood of the cross to exist in the Church. The cedar is the height of the saints, as in the Psalm: “He will multiply like the cedar of Lebanon” [Note: [Col. 0891] 5 Ps. XCI, 13], because the holy man, through the growth of inward grace, is raised to the height of righteousness. The cedar is faith in Christ, as in Ecclesiasticus: “I was exalted like a cedar in Lebanon” [Note: [Col. 0891] 6 Ecclus. XXIV, 17], because faith in Christ is held in great veneration in the world.

Angels are represented by cedars, as in Ezekiel: “The cedars were not taller than it” [Note: [Col. 0891] 7 Ezek. XXXI, 8], because the other angels were not taller than that first angel. Gentiles are represented by cedars, as in the Psalm: “The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars” [Note: [Col. 0891] 8 Ps. XXVIII, 5], that is, the preaching of Christ humbling the Gentiles who were exalted [text uncertain]. Jews are represented by cedars, as in the Psalm: “The Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon” [Note: [Col. 0891] 9 Ibid.], that is, he will humble the Jews who glory in the brightness of the world, since Lebanon is interpreted as “whiteness” or “brightening.” Any proud person is represented by a cedar, as in the Psalm: “I saw the wicked man exalted above measure and raised up like the cedar of Lebanon” [Note: [Col. 0891] 10 Ps. XXXVI, 35], that is, I observed the wicked man making himself haughty and exalting himself in the likeness of those proud men mentioned earlier. Powerful worldly people are represented by the cedars of the age, as in the Psalm: “And the cedars of Lebanon, which he planted” [Note: [Col. 0891] 11 Ps. CIII, 16], that is, the Lord sometimes restores them spiritually; although they are worldly, they are nevertheless rooted in faith.

A cherub is a holy angel, as in Ezekiel: “The cherub had two faces” [Note: [Col. 0891] 12 Ezek. X, 21], because the holy angel fulfills both commandments of charity. The cherubim represent the two Testaments, as in Exodus: “Two cherubim, with the faces of the powers, upon the mercy seat” [Note: [Col. 0891] 13 Exod. XXV, 18–20], because the two Testaments concordantly preach Christ.

Heaven is God, as in the Psalm: “They set their mouth against heaven” [Note: [Col. 0891] 14 Ps. LXXI, 9], that is, they blasphemed the Lord. Heaven is Christ, as in the Psalm: “The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0891] 15 Ps. CXIII, 16], that is, Christ is the Son of the Father, to the honor of God. Heaven is heavenly blessedness, as in Isaiah: “How you have fallen from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0891] 16 Isa. XIV, 12], that is, from heavenly blessedness. Heaven is the understanding of angels, as in Job: “He is higher than heaven” [Note: [Col. 0891] 17 Job XI, 8], because God surpasses the understanding of the angels. Heaven is the assembly of heavenly spirits, as in the Psalm: “Forever, O Lord, your word remains in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0891] 18 Ps. CXVIII, 89], because, after the devil’s fall, the assembly of heavenly spirits preserves obedience to the divine word without failing.

Heaven is the holy Church, as in Genesis: “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0891] 19 Gen. I, 14], that is, let there be spiritual men in the strength of the Church. Heaven is this world, as in Revelation: “A great sign appeared in heaven” [Note: [Col. 0891] 20 Rev. XII, 1], that is, a great miracle appeared in the world. Heaven is this air, as in the Gospel: “Consider the birds of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0891] 21 Matt. VI, 26], that is, the birds that fly in the air. Heaven is the faithful soul, as in Revelation: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” [Note: [Col. 0891] 22 Rev. VIII, 1], because rest comes about in the soul in a brief moment. Heaven is sacred Scripture, as in the Psalm: “Stretching out heaven like a skin” [Note: [Col. 0891] 23 Ps. CIII, 2], because sacred Scripture is opened to mortals. Heaven is holiness of life, as in Job: “And who brought forth the frost from heaven?” [Note: [Col. 0891] 24 Job XXXVIII, 29], because after sublime holiness someone sometimes bends toward iniquity.

Angels are represented by heaven, as in the Psalm: “The heavens poured down before the face of God” [Note: [Col. 0891] 25 Ps. LXVII, 9], because angels convey God’s commands to us. The apostles are represented by heaven, as in Job: “His spirit formed the heavens” [Note: [Col. 0891] 26 Job XXVI, 13], because the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, taught the apostles all truth. Preachers are represented by the heavens, as in the Psalm: “The heavens declare the glory of God” [Note: [Col. 0891] 27 Ps. XVIII, 1], that is, the highest preachers announce the grace of God. The wiser people in the Church are represented by heaven, as in Deuteronomy: “Hear, O heavens, what I speak” [Note: [Col. 0891] 28 Deut. XXXII, 1], that is, you who are wise, listen to the great things I am about to say. Spiritual people of every kind are represented by heaven, as in the Psalms: “Who made the heavens with understanding” [Note: [Col. 0891] 29 Ps. CXXXV, 5], because he caused his saints not only to believe divine things but also to understand them. Sublime modes of contemplation are represented by heaven, as in the Psalm: “They ascend up to the heavens” [Note: [Col. 0891] 30 Ps. CVI, 26], that is, they will reach the highest kinds of contemplation.

A chamber is the Church, as in the Song: “He brought me into his chambers” [Note: [Col. 0891] 31 Song II, 4], that is, through contemplation he caused me to enter into inward joys.

Carvings are works of the virtues, as in the Book of Kings: “There were prominent carvings on the walls” [Note: [Col. 0891] 32 III Kings VI, 35], that is, good works set before others by holy men as an example.

Lots are the two Testaments, as in the Psalm: “If you sleep among the midst of the lots” [Note: [Col. 0891] 33 Ps. LXVIII, 24], that is, if you rest between the two Testaments. Portions are the dignities of orders, as in: “Portions will not benefit them if they themselves are wicked.”

Masons are the teachers of the Church, as in the Books of Kings: “Solomon’s masons hewed the stones” [Note: [Col. 0891] 34 III Kings V, 17–18], because the preachers of the Redeemer instructed faithful peoples through preaching.

The evening meal is the sweetness of contemplation, as in the Gospel: “A certain man prepared a great dinner” [Note: [Col. 0891] 35 Luke XIV, 16], and he reclined upon his breast, because every perfect person is refreshed in contemplation by the wisdom of Christ. The evening meal is the refreshment of eternal life, as in the Gospel: “A certain man prepared a great dinner” [Note: [Col. 0893] 1 Luke XIV, 16], because he leads his elect to eternal life for refreshment.

Wax is any sinner, as in the Psalms: “Like wax before the fire” [Note: [Col. 0893] 2 Ps. LXVII, 3], because the sinner fails before him who is a consuming fire. Wax is the old law, as in the Psalm: “Like melting wax,” that is, like the old law, which fails according to the letter.

The stag is the faithful soul, as in the Psalm: “As the stag longs for the springs of water” [Note: [Col. 0893] 3 Ps. XLI, 1], because the faithful soul desires an abundance of spiritual goods. The ancient Fathers are represented by the stag, as in the Song: “My beloved is like a young stag” [Note: [Col. 0893] 4 Song II, 9], because Christ was born from the flesh of the ancient fathers. Great contemplatives are represented by stags, as in the Psalms: “The high mountains are for the stags” [Note: [Col. 0893] 5 Ps. CIII, 18], because the highest modes of contemplation belong to the greatest contemplatives. Those who despise the world are represented by stags, as in the Psalms: “He made my feet like those of stags” [Note: [Col. 0893] 6 Ps. XVII, 54], that is, he directed my works after the likeness of holy men. Sanctities are represented by stags, as in the Song: “I adjure you by the does of the stags” [Note: [Col. 0893] 7 Song III, 5], that is, I urge you to love the holiness of merits.

A doe is a negligent preacher, as in Ezekiel [Jeremiah]: “The doe in the field gave birth and abandoned it” [Note: [Col. 0893] 8 Jer. XIV, 5], because a negligent preacher sometimes cares for those whom he brought forth through preaching. Teachers are represented by the doe, as in Job: “You have watched the does giving birth” [Note: [Col. 0893] 9 Job XXXIX, 4], that is, teachers spiritually bringing forth offspring are to be considered.

The neck is pride, as in Deuteronomy: “I know that your neck is exceedingly stiff” [Note: [Col. 0893] 10 Deut. XXXI, 27], that is, your pride is extremely rigid. The neck is good freedom, as in Job: “He cut my neck” [Note: [Col. 0893] 11 Job XVI, 13], that is, he aided my freedom. The exaltation of the wicked is represented by the neck, as in the Psalm: “The just Lord will cut the neck” [Note: [Col. 0893] 12 Ps. CXXVIII, 4], that is, he will destroy the exaltation of the proud.

A horned serpent is the Antichrist, as in Genesis: “A horned serpent on the path” [Note: [Col. 0893] 13 Gen. XLIX, 17], because the Antichrist will show himself to holy men both poisonous and exalted.

The sea monster is death, as in Jonah: “The sea monster swallowed Jonah” [Note: [Col. 0893] 14 Jonah II, 1], because death seized Christ. The sea monster is the devil, as in Job: “Am I the sea, or a sea monster?” [Note: [Col. 0893] 15 Job VII, 12], that is, I am like neither the reprobate nor their head, the devil. The sea monster is the proud height of worldly power, as in Isaiah: “God will kill the sea monster that is in the sea” [Note: [Col. 0893] 16 Isa. XXVII, 1], that is, he will destroy the unbelief and proud height that exist in the world.

Food is love of the world, as in the Gospel: “Work not for the food that perishes” [Note: [Col. 0893] 17 John VI, 27], that is, do not love worldly pleasure, which fails. Food is Christ, as in the same passage: “But for the food that endures to eternal life” [Note: [Col. 0893] 18 Ibid.], that is, be eager to acquire Christ, who lives forever. Food is the possession of hypocrites, as in Job: “Nothing remained of his food” [Note: [Col. 0893] 19 Job XX, 21], because the possession of hypocrites fails. Food is communion of life, as in Paul: “With such a person, not even to eat” [Note: [Col. 0893] 20 I Cor. V, 11], that is, to have no communion at all. Foods represent doctrine, as in Proverbs: “Do not desire his foods, in which there is bread of deceit” [Note: [Col. 0893] 21 Prov. XXIII, 3], that is, his doctrines, in which there is barrenness. Foods represent inward consolations, as in Job: “What my soul formerly refused to touch, now because of anguish is my food” [Note: [Col. 0893] 22 Job VI, 7], that is, what I formerly did not even deign to consider is now sweet consolation to me.

Provision is spiritual refreshment, as in Proverbs: “She gave provisions to her servants” [Note: [Col. 0893] 23 Prov. XXXI, 15], that is, she bestowed spiritual consolations upon her faithful. Provisions are things belonging to bodily nourishment, as in the Psalms: “He sent it in abundance” [Note: [Col. 0893] 24 Ps. LXXVII, 25], that is, he gave them bodily refreshment to satiety.

Scars are sins, as in the Psalms: “The scars have become corrupt” [Note: [Col. 0893] 25 Ps. XXXVII, 6], that is, my former faults have returned to pleasure.

The swan is pride, as in the Law, where it is forbidden for anyone to eat a swan [Note: [Col. 0893] 26 Lev. XI, 18], that is, lest he display himself as haughty.

Sackcloth is Christ’s flesh, as in the Psalms: “I clothed myself in sackcloth” [Note: [Col. 0893] 27 Ps. XXXIV, 13], that is, I was hidden in flesh. Sackcloth is the Jews, as in the Psalms: “I made my garment sackcloth” [Note: [Col. 0893] 28 Ps. LXVIII, 12], that is, I experienced as exasperating the Jews who had been close to me. Sackcloth is the harshness of repentance, as in the Book of Judith: “Judith had sackcloth over her loins” [Note: [Col. 0893] 29 Judith VIII, 5], because the faithful soul must extinguish the pleasures of the flesh through the harshness of repentance. Sackcloth is the coarse minds of human beings, as in Exodus [Note: [Col. 0893] 30 Exod. XXVI, 7], where haircloth coverings are commanded to be made for covering Christ’s tabernacle, because those who are coarse-minded ought to protect from outward impediments those who devote themselves to inward things.

The furnace is the examination of judgment, as in Genesis: “A burning furnace appeared,” or “smoking” [Note: [Col. 0893] 31 Gen. XV, 17], because the final judgment will darken and burn the reprobate. The furnace is the torment of flesh and soul, as in the Psalms: “You will place them like a furnace of fire” [Note: [Col. 0893] 32 Ps. XX, 10], because the Lord burns the condemned both in flesh and in soul. The heart of any wicked person is represented by the furnace, as in the prophet: “Like a furnace kindled by one who bakes” [Note: [Col. 0893] 33 Hos. VII, 4], because the wicked heart is inflamed by the devil’s prompting. The furnace is good love, as in Leviticus: “You shall offer loaves baked in a furnace” [Note: [Col. 0893] 34 Lev. XXVI, 26], that is, you shall show God the acts of a good life strengthened by true love.

The shield is the standard of the cross, as in the Book of Joshua: “Raise the shield that is in your hand” [Note: [Col. 0893] 35 Josh. V, 18], that is, raise up in the world the cross that is in your power. The shield is an excusing word, as in Job: “He will brandish the spear and the shield” [Note: [Col. 0893] 36 Job XXXIX, 26], because slanderous and excusing words attack the good preacher. Pride is represented by the shield, as in the Books of Kings: “A bronze shield covered his shoulders” [Note: [Col. 0895] 1 I Kings XVII, 6], that is, there is rigid exaltation in those who are highest in the devil’s heart. The shield is the protection of virtues, as in the Song: “A thousand shields hang upon it” [Note: [Col. 0895] 2 Song IV, 4], because sacred Scripture shows us holy protections of the virtues. Holy men are represented by shields, as in the Books of Maccabees: “The sun shone upon the golden shields” [Note: [Col. 0895] 3 I Macc. VI, 39], because Christ illumines religious men. The shield is the virtue of patience, as in Isaiah: “Rise, princes, and take up the shields” [Note: [Col. 0895] 4 Isa. XXII, 5], that is, you who exercise spiritual authority will possess your souls through patience.

The cymbal is the vice of loquacity, as in Paul: “Or a clanging cymbal” [Note: [Col. 0895] 5 I Cor. XIII, 1], that is, if I am without charity, my preaching is nothing but loquacity. The cymbal is the preaching of the Antichrist, as in Isaiah: “Woe to the land of the cymbal of wings” [Note: [Col. 0895] 6 Isa. XVIII, 1], because the Antichrist should be cursed, since he will preach pride and exaltation. The cymbal represents the services of charity, as in the Psalm: “Praise him with cymbals” [Note: [Col. 0895] 7 Ps. CL, 5], because those praise God most greatly who, through the charity of the Spirit, are united to one another.

The cup is heavenly doctrine, as in Genesis: “He found the cup in Benjamin’s sack” [Note: [Col. 0895] 8 Gen. XLIV, 12], because heavenly doctrine was in Paul’s heart. The cup is the Law, as in the Books of Kings: “Take the cup of water” [Note: [Col. 0895] 9 I Samuel XXVI, 11], because the teachers of the Jews do not possess spiritual knowledge of the Law. Hearers are represented by the cup, as in Exodus, where cups are commanded to be made on the stem of the lampstand [Note: [Col. 0895] 10 Exod. XXV, 33], because hearers exist in the Church of Christ.

Ash is failure, as in Job: “Your memory will be compared with ashes” [Note: [Col. 0895] 11 Job XIII, 12], that is, your memory will fail. Ash is repentance, as in Job: “I covered my flesh with ashes” [Note: [Col. 0895] 12 Job XVI, 15], that is, through repentance I mourned my carnal sins. Ash is humility, as in Job: “Man will return to ash” [Note: [Col. 0895] 13 Job XXXIV, 15], that is, he will abase himself in humility. Ash is the corruption of mortality, as in Job: “I repent in dust and ashes” [Note: [Col. 0895] 14 Job XLII, 6], that is, I repent in remembrance of my corruption and mortality. Ash is the sinner, as in the Psalms: “For I ate ashes like bread” [Note: [Col. 0895] 15 Ps. CI, 10], because God incorporates the sinner, provided he is penitent, into himself as a righteous person.

The consummation of the Lord’s Passion is represented by ash, as in Exodus: “Pots for receiving ashes” [Note: [Col. 0895] 16 Exod. XXVII, 3], that is, hearts for retaining the memory of the Lord’s Passion. The perfections of good works are represented by ashes, as in Leviticus: “Take the ashes that the devouring fire has consumed” [Note: [Col. 0895] 17 Lev. VI, 10], because God receives the perfections of good works that ardent love has brought to completion.

The dog-fly is the wickedness of the evil, as in the Psalm: “He spoke, and the dog-fly came” [Note: [Col. 0895] 18 Ps. LXXVII, 45], because by his just judgment God permits the wickedness of the ungodly to exist.

Cinnamon is humility, as in the Song: “And cinnamon with all the trees of Lebanon” [Note: [Col. 0895] 19 Song IV, 14], that is, humility together with all other good works.

Locks of hair are throngs of peoples, as in the Song: “And my locks are full of drops of the nights” [Note: [Col. 0895] 20 Song V, 2], that is, my peoples are filled with the dark flows of sin.

The girdle is the vigor of righteousness, as in Proverbs: “And he gave the girdle to the Canaanite” [Note: [Col. 0895] 21 Prov. XXXI, 24], because the Lord gave the vigor of righteousness to the Gentile people.

Gnats are unrest of heart, as in the Psalm: “He spoke, and the dog-fly and gnats came” [Note: [Col. 0895] 22 Ps. LXXVII, 45], because in the reprobate the Lord permits unrest of heart to exist together with wickedness in action.

Cyprus is the refreshment of heavenly grace, as in the Song: “Cyprus with nard” [Note: [Col. 0895] 23 Song IV, 13], that is, love of inward affection together with the reputation of good action. Cyprus is the Catholic Church, as in the Song: “My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus for me” [Note: [Col. 0895] 24 Song I, 14], that is, Christ, whom I love, is the beautiful fruitfulness of the Church.

The cypress is Christ, as in Ecclesiasticus: “I was exalted like a cypress on Mount Zion” [Note: [Col. 0895] 25 Ecclus. XXIV, 17], because Christ, who is the incorruptible wisdom of the Father, ascended to heaven.

The circle is sacred Scripture, as in Proverbs: “A golden ring in its snout” [Note: [Col. 0895] 26 Prov. XI, 22], that is, the ability of heretics frequently employs sacred Scripture. The circle is heavenly protection, as in Job: “Will you put a ring in its snout?” [Note: [Col. 0895] 27 Job XL, 21], that is, will you restrain its cunning through your protection? The holy books are represented by circles, as in Exodus: “You shall prepare four golden rings” [Note: [Col. 0895] 28 Exod. XXV, 12], that is, you shall understand the four books of the holy Gospel.

The cistern is sacred Scripture, as in Exodus: “If anyone opens a cistern” [Note: [Col. 0895] 29 Exod. XXI, 33], that is, if anyone expounds sacred Scripture. The cistern is the human heart:

“Drink water from your own cistern” [Note: [Col. 0895] 30 Prov. V, 15], that is, receive consolation from your own heart. The cistern is the perverse mind, as in Jeremiah: “The cistern makes its water cold” [Note: [Col. 0895] 31 Jer. VI, 7], because the impious mind makes its thought wicked. The cistern is hell, as in Genesis [Note: [Col. 0895] 32 Gen. XXXVII, 23], where the Jews put Joseph into a cistern that had no water, because Christ descended into hell while the Jews were falling; it possessed no sweetness of grace.

Crystal is hardness of heart, as in the Psalm: “He sends his crystal like morsels” [Note: [Col. 0895] 33 Ps. CXLVII, 17], because just as God incorporates the faithful into himself, so also he sometimes cultivates the hard-hearted. Crystal is the angelic nature, as in Ezekiel: “Like the appearance of terrifying crystal” [Note: [Col. 0895] 34 Ezek. I, 22], that is, after the likeness of the angelic nature, which has already attained the stability of incorruption.

Cups are humble teachings, as in Exodus: “Bowls and cups on the table” [Note: [Col. 0897] 1 Exod. XXXVII, 16], that is, the highest and the humble teachings in Scripture.

The lyre is right action, as in the Psalms: “Give thanks to the Lord with the lyre” [Note: [Col. 0897] 2 Ps. XXXII, 2], that is, in right action. The lyre is the active life, as in the Psalms: “A pleasing psalm with the lyre” [Note: [Col. 0897] 3 Ps. LXXX, 3], that is, the sweetness of contemplation together with action. The lyre is mortification of the flesh, as in the Psalms: “Sing to the Lord with the lyre and with the voice of the psalm” [Note: [Col. 0897] 4 Ps. XCVII, 5], that is, in abstinence from the flesh and holiness of speech. The lyre is joy, as in Job: “My lyre has been turned into mourning” [Note: [Col. 0897] 5 Job XXX, 31], that is, my joy has been turned into sorrow. The lyre is the sweetness of consolation, as in the Books of Kings: “David played the lyre, and Saul’s spirit was refreshed” [Note: [Col. 0897] 6 I Kings XVI, 23], because the fervor of an angry person is moderated by the sweetness of gentle speech.

The city is the heavenly homeland, as in the Psalms: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city” [Note: [Col. 0897] 7 Ps. CXXII, 3], because that heavenly city is constituted from many living in one peace. The city is the holy Church, as in the Song: “I will go around the city through the streets and squares” [Note: [Col. 0897] 8 Song III, 2], that is, in my mind I will survey the Church through religious and secular people. The city is the Virgin Mary, as in the Psalms: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” [Note: [Col. 0897] 9 Ps. LXXXVI, 3], because marvelous things are spoken of holy Mary. The city is human conduct, as in Job: “He despises the multitude of the city” [Note: [Col. 0897] 10 Job XXXIX, 11], that is, he abhors the multiplicity of human conduct.

The city is the holy soul, as in the Gospel: “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” [Note: [Col. 0897] 11 Matt. V, 14], because a soul placed in the eminence of holiness cannot be concealed. Gentile society is represented by the city, as in the Psalms: “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” [Note: [Col. 0897] 12 Ps. XLV, 5], that is, the fruitfulness of the Holy Spirit gladdens the Gentile people. The Jewish people are represented by the city, as in Isaiah: “How has the city, full of judgment, become a prostitute?” [Note: [Col. 0897] 13 Isa. I, 21], because the Jewish people, which once was [text uncertain], withdrew from God through the filth of unbelief. This world is represented by the city, as in Proverbs: “The wise man ascends the city of the mighty” [Note: [Col. 0897] 14 Prov. XXI, 22], that is, Christ conquers this world. The heart of the holy man is represented by the city, as in the Psalms: “In your city reduce their likeness to nothing” [Note: [Col. 0897] 15 Ps. LXXII, 20], that is, in the heart of the holy man, in which you dwell, you set in array the vices that are likenesses of demons. The human body is represented by the city, as in the Gospel: “He set their city on fire” [Note: [Col. 0897] 16 Matt. XXII, 7], that is, he subjected their bodies to punishment. Hell is represented by the city, as in the Psalms: “Who will lead me into the fortified city?” [Note: [Col. 0897] 17 Ps. LIX, 11], because God the Father caused his Son to descend into hell. The five cities represent the bodily senses, as in the Gospel: “You are to be over five cities” [Note: [Col. 0897] 18 Luke XIX, 19], that is, to have dominion over the five bodily senses. The impious are represented by cities, as in the Psalm: “You have destroyed their cities” [Note: [Col. 0897] 19 Ps. IX, 7], that is, you have condemned the impious.

Citizens are the faithful, as in Paul: “You are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” [Note: [Col. 0897] 20 Eph. II, 19], that is, companions of the saints. Citizens are the persecuting Jews, as in the Gospel: “But his citizens hated him” [Note: [Col. 0897] 21 Luke XIX, 14], because the unbelieving Jews persecuted Christ. Citizens are demons, as in the Gospel: “He went and joined himself to one of the citizens” [Note: [Col. 0897] 22 Luke XV, 15], that is, he joined himself to the ancient enemy, who is one of the demons.

Scarlet is the ardor of charity, as in Exodus: “Scarlet twice dyed” [Note: [Col. 0897] 23 Exod. XXV, 4], that is, love of God and of neighbor. Scarlet is the Passion of Christ, as in Genesis, when the midwife tied a scarlet thread on the hand of Zerah, who was born afterward [Note: [Col. 0897] 24 Gen. XXXVIII, 28], because knowledge of the Lord’s Passion reached the Gentile people who were adopted.

A chorus is concord, as in the Psalms: “Praise him with tambourine and chorus” [Note: [Col. 0897] 25 Ps. CL, 4], that is, glorify God in abstinence from the flesh and concord in charity. Congregations of the elect are represented by the chorus, as in the Song: “What will you see in the Shulammite, except choruses of camps?” [Note: [Col. 0897] 26 Song VI, 12], because among those dwelling in the Church there are holy communities that are terrifying to evil spirits.

The basket is servile work, as in the Psalms: “His hands served in the basket” [Note: [Col. 0897] 27 Ps. LXXX, 7], that is, they occupied themselves with servile work. The basket is corruption, as in the Gospel: “Until I dig around it and put in a basket of manure” [Note: [Col. 0897] 28 Luke XIII, 8], that is, until I make the faithful and humble mind recognize the corruption of its sin. The hearts of the righteous are represented by the basket, as in the Gospel: “They filled twelve baskets with fragments” [Note: [Col. 0897] 29 Matt. XIV, 20; Mark VI, 53; Luke IX, 17; John VI, 13], because the hearts of people who have been illuminated through the twelve apostles are filled with the exposition of sacred Scripture.

The neck is the order of preachers, as in the Song: “Your neck is like an ivory tower” [Note: [Col. 0897] 30 Song VII, 45], that is, preachers who transmit the food of life to others are themselves beautiful and chaste. The neck is the word of preaching, as in Proverbs: “That a necklace may be added to your neck” [Note: [Col. 0897] 31 Prov. I, 9], that is, so that the word of preaching may be strengthened in the failing structure of the virtues. The neck is the mind, as in Isaiah: “Loose the bonds of your neck” [Note: [Col. 0897] 32 Isa. LII, 2], that is, cast away your earthly desires, which press your mind downward. The neck is faith, as in the Song: “You have wounded me with one hair of your neck” [Note: [Col. 0897] 33 Song IV, 9], that is, you have moved me toward devotion through the unity of faith, by which the head, Christ, is united to his body, which is the Church. The neck is boldness, as in Job: “He ran against him with an outstretched neck” [Note: [Col. 0897] 34 Job XV, 26], that is, proud boldness resisted him. The neck is the end, as in Habakkuk: “You laid bare the foundation as far as the neck” [Note: [Col. 0897] 35 Hab. III, 13], that is, you opened the hidden things of the devil all the way to the end. The neck is exaltation, as in Job: “Strength will dwell in his neck” [Note: [Col. 0897] 36 Job XLI, 13], because, on account of his pride, the devil judges himself to be strong.

**Dove** signifies the Holy Spirit, as in the Gospel: “[I saw the Holy Spirit descending like a dove and remaining] in him” [Note: [Col. 0899] 1 Matt. III, 16; Mark I, 10; Luke III, 22; John I, 32], meaning that the Holy Spirit came upon Christ in simplicity and gentleness.

**Dove** signifies Christ, as in the prophet: “The land has been made desolate by the face of the wrath of the dove” [Note: [Col. 0899] 2 Jer. XXV, 38], meaning that at Christ’s judgment the reprobate will perish, those whom he now tolerates gently and simply.

**Dove** signifies the Church, as in the Psalm: “The wings of the dove are silver-plated” [Note: [Col. 0899] 3 Ps. LXVII, 14], meaning that the pastors of the Church are adorned with divine utterances.

**Dove** signifies any simple person, as in the Psalms: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, and I shall fly away” [Note: [Col. 0899] 4 Ps. LIV, 7], that is, “from where shall I fly away from troubles, so that I do not lose my simplicity?”

**Dove** signifies any foolish person, as in Hosea: “A dove, deceived and without understanding” [Note: [Col. 0899] 5 Hos. VII, 11], meaning that the deceived, depraved mind—to return to the heart . . . * [Col. 0899B]

**Dove** signifies any person who despises the world, as in Genesis: “The dove found no place where its foot could rest” [Note: [Col. 0899] 6 Gen. VIII, 9], meaning that whoever perfectly despises the world does not fix his affection in it through love.

**Dove** signifies the active life, as in Genesis [Note: [Col. 0899] 7 Gen. XV, 5]: Abraham offered a turtledove and a dove in sacrifice; this means that every perfect person offers solitude to God in contemplation, and public life in action.

**Doves** signify the gifts of the Holy Spirit, as in the Gospel: “He drove out those who were selling doves in the temple” [Note: [Col. 0899] 8 John II, 16], meaning that God expels from the Church those who sell and buy the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

**Doves** signify the groans of repentance, as in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0899] 9 Luke II, 24]: in her purification, blessed Mary offered two young doves; this means that through the twofold groaning of repentance the faithful soul purifies itself, grieving both for the good it omitted and for the evil it committed.

**Pillar** signifies the divinity of Christ, as in Exodus: the pillar of fire went before the people by night [Note: [Col. 0899] 10 Exod. XIII, 21], meaning that Christ raised up the people, shrouded in darkness, through the terror of his divinity.

**Pillar** signifies the humanity of Christ, as in Exodus: the pillar of cloud was over the people by day [Note: [Col. 0899] 11 Ibid., verse 22], meaning that Christ appeared gentle in his humanity to the Gentile people, who were illumined through faith.

**Pillar** signifies Christ’s humble preaching, as in the Psalms: “He spoke to them in the pillar of cloud” [Note: [Col. 0899] 12 Ps. XCXVIII, 7], that is, he instructed them through humble preaching.

**Pillars** signify the holy angels, as in Job: “The pillars of heaven tremble and quake at his command” [Note: [Col. 0899] 13 Job IX, 6], meaning that the angels praise his majesty, the dominions adore it, and the powers tremble.

**Pillars** signify the apostles, as in Paul: “James and Cephas and John, who appeared to be pillars” [Note: [Col. 0899] 14 Gal. II, 9], meaning that they and the other apostles support the Church.

**Pillars** signify preachers, as in Exodus: “You shall make twenty pillars, with an equal number of bases” [Note: [Col. 0899] 15 Exod. XXVII, 10], that is, you shall establish holy preachers who, understanding both Testaments, are initiated into the teachings of the prophets.

**Pillars** signify Christ’s actions, as in the Song: “His legs are like marble pillars” [Note: [Col. 0899] 16 Song V, 15], meaning that Christ’s actions are both upright and strong.

**Pillars** signify the sacred Scriptures, as in the Song: “He made its pillars of silver” [Note: [Col. 0899] 17 Song III, 10], meaning that our peace-making Christ established the Scriptures in the holy Church to give understanding.

**Pillar** signifies uprightness of faith and vigor of life, as in the Books of Kings: “He set up two pillars at the entrance of the temple” [Note: [Col. 0899] 18 3 Kings VII, 21], meaning that we cannot enter the entrance of the heavenly homeland unless we believe rightly and live holily.

**Pillars** signify the inward virtues of the mind, as in the Psalms: “I have strengthened its pillars” [Note: [Col. 0899] 19 Ps. LXXIV, 4], that is, “I have strengthened its inward virtues.”

**Pillars** signify the rulers of the Jews, as in Job: “He shakes the earth from its place, and its pillars tremble” [Note: [Col. 0899] 20 Job IX, 6], meaning that Judea was cast down and its rulers were left desolate.

**Color** signifies the beauty of religion, as in Jeremiah: “Its finest color has changed” [Note: [Col. 0899] 21 Lam. IV, 1], meaning that the beauty of religion is obscured in many people.

**Color** signifies depraved conduct, as in Leviticus: “When a white color appears on the skin” [Note: [Col. 0899] 22 Lev. XIII, 10], that is, when depraved conduct has appeared publicly.

**Color** signifies secular eloquence, as in Job: “Wisdom cannot be compared with all the dyed colors of India” [Note: [Col. 0899] 23 Job XXVIII, 16], meaning that the wisdom of Christ cannot be compared with the eloquences of the fleeting world.

**Serpent** signifies incarnate Wisdom, as in Exodus: “The staff became a serpent, so that Moses fled from it” [Note: [Col. 0899] 24 Exod. IV, 3], meaning that the Jewish people saw Christ in the flesh but fled from him through unbelief.

**Serpent** signifies the devil, as in Job: “The winding serpent was brought out” [Note: [Col. 0899] 25 Job XXVI, 13], meaning that through Christ’s grace the devil, the deceiver, was driven out from humanity.

**Serpent** signifies the Antichrist, as in Genesis: “Let Dan be a serpent on the road” [Note: [Col. 0899] 26 Gen. XLIX, 17], meaning that the Antichrist will present himself as alluring in deceiving those who walk along his road.

**Hills** signify the saints who lived before the Law, as in Genesis: “The desire of his hills” [Note: [Col. 0899] 27 Ibid., verse 26], meaning that many kings and prophets desired Christ . . .

**Hills** signify the holy martyrs, as in the Psalms: “The hills will gird themselves with rejoicing” [Note: [Col. 0899] 28 Ps. LXIV, 13], meaning that the holy martyrs regarded it all as joy when they fell into various temptations.

**Hills** signify holy men, as in the Psalms: “And the hills, righteousness” [Note: [Col. 0899] 29 Ps. LXXI, 3], that is, let faithful people practice the work of holiness.

**Hills** signify the heights of the world, as in Habakkuk’s song: “The hills of the world were bowed down” [Note: [Col. 0899] 30 Hab. III, 6], that is, the lofty powers of the world were humbled.

**Locks of hair** signify companies of saints, as in the Song: “His locks are like the raised branches of palm trees” [Note: [Col. 0899] 31 Song V, 11], meaning that holy men always practice spiritual victory.

**Locks of hair** signify the thoughts of the mind, as in the Song: “His locks, joined in purple by the channels of the king” [Note: [Col. 0899] 32 Song VII, 5], meaning that the thoughts of the devout soul represent Christ’s Passion to themselves as an example.

**Joints** signify intentions, as in Paul: “Of joints and marrow also” [Note: [Col. 0901] 1 Heb. IV, 12], meaning that God discerns thoughts and intentions.

**Harmony** signifies the speech of teachers, as in Job: “And the harmony of heaven that puts one to sleep” [Note: [Col. 0901] 2 Job XXXVIII, 37], meaning that in the future life the speech of teachers will cease, and no one will teach his neighbor.

**Concubines** signify the souls of the impious, as in the Song: “And there are eighty concubines” [Note: [Col. 0901] 3 Song VI, 7], meaning that the wicked indeed believe in the future resurrection, but do not love it by living well.

**Concubine** signifies the Old Law, as in Genesis: “Reuben slept with his father’s concubine” [Note: [Col. 0901] 4 Gen. XXXV, 27], meaning that the Jewish people abused the law of God through a perverse understanding.

**Desire** is good, as in the Book of Wisdom: “The desire for wisdom leads to the everlasting kingdom” [Note: [Col. 0901] 5 Wis. VI, 21].

**Desire** is evil, as in the Epistle of John: “The desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes” [Note: [Col. 0901] 6 1 John II, 16].

**Knowledge** signifies approval, as in Exodus: “I know you by name” [Note: [Col. 0901] 7 Exod. III, 12].

**Knowledge** signifies awareness, as in the Epistle of John: “He knows all things” [Note: [Col. 0901] 8 Gen. IV, I, 25].

**Knowledge** signifies sexual intercourse, as in Genesis: “Adam knew his wife” [Note: [Col. 0901] 9 Ps. LXXVII, 45].

**To eat** signifies to afflict, as in the Psalms: “He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them” [Note: [Col. 0901] 10 Prov. XXIV, 13; and XXV, 16], that is, “it afflicted them.”

**To eat** signifies to learn, as in Proverbs: “Eat honey, my son,” that is, “learn wisdom.”

**To eat** signifies to fulfill, as in the Psalms: “I have forgotten to eat my bread” [Note: [Col. 0901] 11 Ps. CI, 5], that is, “I neglected to fulfill the divine commandment.”

**To eat** signifies to slander, as in Paul: “If you bite and devour one another” [Note: [Col. 0901] 12 Gal. V, 15], that is, “if you slander one another.”

**Confession** signifies praise, as in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Father of heaven and earth” [Note: [Col. 0901] 13 Matt. XI, 25].

**Confession** signifies sin, as in the Psalms: “I will confess my iniquity against myself” [Note: [Col. 0901] 14 Ps. XXX, 5].

**Consuls** signify holy men, as in Job: “I would sleep with the consuls of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0901] 15 Job III, 14], that is, “I would rest with those who offer others counsel for life.”

**Counselors** signify wicked teachers, as in Job: “He leads counselors to a foolish end” [Note: [Col. 0901] 16 Job XII, 17], that is, “he allows wicked teachers to end their lives in folly.”

**Counselor** signifies Christ, as in Isaiah: “His name shall be called Counselor” [Note: [Col. 0901] 17 Isa. IX, 6], meaning that he gave humanity counsel for life.

**Counselors** signify the holy angels, as in the Books of Kings: “The counselors of King David” [Note: [Col. 0901] 18 2 Kings VIII, 16, 17, 18], that is, angels who agree with human beings for salvation, give counsel, and serve God.

**Contention** is good, as in the Gospel: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate” [Note: [Col. 0901] 19 Luke XIII, 24].

**Contention** is evil, as in Paul: “Since there is jealousy and contention” [Note: [Col. 0901] 20 1 Cor. III, 3].

**Heart** signifies the soul of Christ, as in the Psalms: “My heart was troubled within me” [Note: [Col. 0901] 21 Ps. XXXVIII, 11], that is, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” [Note: [Col. 0901] 22 Matt. XXVI, 38].

**Heart** signifies the wisdom of Christ, as in the Psalms: “My heart became like melting wax” [Note: [Col. 0901] 23 Ps. XXI, 15], that is, “my wisdom was manifested in the crucified one.”

**Heart** signifies reason, as in the Song: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” [Note: [Col. 0901] 24 Song V, 2], that is, “I cease from external things and, through contemplation, attend inwardly to rational matters.”

**Heart** signifies the will, as in the Psalm: “And his heart drew near” [Note: [Col. 0901] 25 Ps. LIV, 22], meaning that God’s hidden will appeared in the Scriptures.

**Heart** signifies sublime contemplation, as in the Psalm: “A human being will approach a lofty heart” [Note: [Col. 0901] 26 Ps. LXIII, 7], that is, “he will apprehend sublime contemplation.”

**Heart** signifies prelates, as in Isaiah: “Speak to the heart of Jerusalem and call to her” [Note: [Col. 0901] 27 Isa. XL, 2], that is, “to the highest prelates of the Churches.”

**Heart** signifies the priests of the Synagogue, as in Job: “He changes the heart of the rulers of the people of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0901] 28 Job XII, 24], meaning that God allowed the priests of the Jewish people to be changed from good to evil.

**Heart** signifies the enemy’s pride, as in Job: “His heart will be hardened like a stone” [Note: [Col. 0901] 29 Job XLI, 15], meaning that the devil is always hardened in his pride.

**Heart** signifies the devil’s cunning, as in Tobit: “Disembowel this fish and preserve its heart” [Note: [Col. 0901] 30 Tob. VI, 5], meaning that God both exposed the devil’s wickedness and enclosed his cunning in the sacred books.

**Heart** signifies thoughts, as in the Psalms: “God searches hearts and kidneys” [Note: [Col. 0901] 31 Ps. VII, 10], meaning that he himself sees what each person thinks and what delights each one.

**Body** signifies the person of Christ, as in the Gospel: “Wherever the body is, there also will the eagles be gathered” [Note: [Col. 0901] 32 Matt. XXIV, 28], meaning that wherever Christ now is according to his humanity, there also will be the souls of the elect.

**Body of Christ** also signifies that body which was once crucified on the gallows [Note: [Col. 0901] 33 Matt. XXVII, 35 and following; Mark XV, 25; Luke XXIII, 33; John XIX, 18], and that which is sacrificed daily in the mystery [Note: [Col. 0901] 34 Matt. XXVI, 26; Mark XIV, 22; Luke XXII, 19; 1 Cor. XI, 24], and that which, subject to the one Lord, illumined by one faith, and cleansed by one baptism, is the holy Church [Note: [Col. 0901] 35 Rom. XII, 5; 1 Cor. XII, 13, 27; Eph. I, 23; Col. I, 18, 24].

**Body** signifies sin, as in Ezekiel: “With two wings they covered their body,” that is, “he removed his sin through fear and repentance.”

**Body** signifies corruption, as in Paul: “Who will free me from my body?” [Note: [Col. 0901] 36 Rom. VII, 24], that is, “from the corruption of this mortality?”

**Body** signifies the multitude of the reprobate, as in Job: “His body is like shields” [Note: [Col. 0901] 37 Job XLI, 6], meaning that the reprobate, in whom the devil dwells, excuse themselves by their sins.

**Raven** signifies a preacher, as in Job: “Who prepares food for the raven?” [Note: [Col. 0901] 38 Job XXXIX, 3], that is, “who gives the preacher what enables him to be nourished by the obedience of his subjects?”

**Raven** signifies any stubborn and insolent person, as in Genesis: “He sent out the raven, which did not return” [Note: [Col. 0901] 39 Gen. VIII, 7], meaning that the insolent and stubborn person is expelled from the Church and condemned.

**Raven** signifies any humble person, as in the Song: “His locks are black like a raven” [Note: [Col. 0901] 40 Song V, 11], meaning that the faithful peoples who cling to Christ the head are humble in their own eyes.

**Ravens** signify preachers, as in Proverbs: “Let the ravens of the torrent dig him out” [Note: [Col. 0903] 1 Prov. XXX, 17], that is, “let preachers remove the blasphemer who resists the streams of doctrine.”

**Raven** signifies the Gentiles, as in the Psalms: “And the young ravens that call upon him” [Note: [Col. 0903] 2 Ps. CXLVI, 9], that is, “the children of the Gentiles calling upon or seeking him.”

**Crown** signifies victory, as in Exodus: “You shall make a golden crown over the ark” [Note: [Col. 0903] 3 Exod. XXV, 11], meaning that the Lord grants his faithful victory in temptation.

**Crown** signifies the assembly of the apostles, as in the Psalms: “You placed upon his head a crown of precious stone” [Note: [Col. 0903] 4 Ps. XX, 4], that is, “at the beginning of his preaching you gave him the harmonious assembly of the apostles.”

**Crown** signifies the multitude of the saints, as in the Psalms: “You bless the crown of the year with your goodness” [Note: [Col. 0903] 5 Ps. LXIV, 12], that is, “you will grant an increase of grace to the multitude of the saints.”

**Crown** signifies the reward of the kingdom, as in the Epistle of James: “He will receive the crown of life” [Note: [Col. 0903] 6 Jas. I, 12], that is, “he will receive the eternity of grace.”

**Horn** signifies royal power, as in the canticle: “And he will exalt the horn of his Christ” [Note: [Col. 0903] 7 1 Kings II, 10], meaning that power in heaven and on earth was given to the human Christ.

**Horn** signifies strength, as in the Psalms: “In you we will scatter our enemies with the horn” [Note: [Col. 0903] 8 Ps. XLIII, 6], that is, “by your strength we will overcome your enemies.”

**Horn** signifies eminence, as in the Psalms: “Even to the horn of the altar” [Note: [Col. 0903] 9 Ps. CXVI, 27], that is, “even to the eminence of the Godhead.”

**Horn** signifies pride, as in the Psalms: “Do not exalt the horn” [Note: [Col. 0903] 10 Ps. LXXIV, 5], that is, “do not raise yourselves through pride.”

**Horn** signifies the arms of the cross, as in Habakkuk: “Horns are in his hands” [Note: [Col. 0903] 11 Hab. III, 4], meaning that his hands were fastened to the arms of the cross.

**Horn** signifies the saints who surpass the flesh, as in the Apocalypse: “I saw a Lamb having seven horns” [Note: [Col. 0903] 12 Rev. V, 6], that is, “I contemplated Christ possessing all the saints.”

**Horn** signifies the opponent of the Law, as in the Apocalypse: “I saw a beast rising from the sea, having ten horns” [Note: [Col. 0903] 13 Rev. XIII, 1], that is, “I saw the Antichrist exalting himself through evil people and possessing opponents of the Law.”

**Two horns** signify the two Testaments, as in the Apocalypse: “The beast had two horns” [Note: [Col. 0903] 14 Ibid., verse 11], meaning that the Antichrist will usurp the two Testaments.

**Horns** signify the defenses of the virtues, as in the Psalms: “Producing horns and claws” [Note: [Col. 0903] 15 Ps. LXVIII, 32], that is, “possessing robust virtues and perseverance.”

**Horns** signify the powers of the impious, as in the Psalms: “And I will break all the horns of sinners” [Note: [Col. 0903] 16 Ps. LXXIV, 14], that is, “I will destroy the powers of the impious.”

**Horns** signify the powers of the righteous, as in the Psalms: “The horns of the righteous will be exalted” [Note: [Col. 0903] 17 Ps. LXXIV, 11], meaning that God raises up the powers of the good.

**Curtain** signifies a holy man, as in Exodus: “The length of the curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits” [Note: [Col. 0903] 18 Exod. XXVI, 2], meaning that every saint, fulfilling the Decalogue in love of God and neighbor, passes away toward the reward of the future resurrection *.

**Bark** signifies the sign of the cross, as in the Song: “Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate” [Note: [Col. 0903] 19 Song VI, 7], meaning that the saints allow themselves to be afflicted in imitation of the cross.
