**Bark** signifies pleasures, as in Job: “They were eating the bark of trees” [Note: [Col. 0903] 20 Job XXX, 4], that is, “they loved the external pleasures of visible things.”

**Bark** signifies the historical senses, as in Genesis: “When the bark had been stripped away, the tree appeared” [Note: [Col. 0903] 21 Gen. XXX, 37], that is, “when the historical senses have been removed, the spiritual beauty of understanding becomes known.”

**Saffron** signifies charity, as in the Song: “The shoots of the bride are nard and saffron” [Note: [Col. 0903] 22 Song IV, 13–14], meaning that it performs holy things as an example of good work and pertains to the virtue of charity.

**Quail** signifies the Law, as in the Psalms: “He spoke, and the quail came” [Note: [Col. 0903] 23 Ps. CIV, 40], meaning that God commanded, and the old Law was given to the Jews.

**Quail** signifies carnal pleasures, as in Numbers: “The wind seized quail and brought them across the sea into the camp” [Note: [Col. 0903] 24 Num. XI, 31], meaning that carnal pleasures, which are in the world, . . . to religious men.

**Rib** signifies spiritual strength, as in Genesis: “When he had fallen asleep, he took a rib and filled its place with flesh” [Note: [Col. 0903] 25 Gen. II, 21], meaning that this happens morally when someone, surrendering himself to forgetfulness, allows his spiritual strength to be destroyed and carnal softness to take its place.

**Ribs** signify the senses of the soul, as in Job: “It attacks the middle of his ribs” [Note: [Col. 0903] 26 Job XVIII, 22], meaning that spiritual poverty corrupts the body of the soul of the impious.

**Cubit** signifies a good action, as in the Books of Kings: “The mouth of the basin was one cubit” [Note: [Col. 0903] 27 3 Kings VII, 31], meaning that the preacher’s speech proclaims both the unity of true charity and the vigor of good action.

**Cubit** signifies the multiplicity of the active life, as in Ezekiel: “A cord of six cubits and a handbreadth” [Note: [Col. 0903] 28 Ezek. XL, 5], meaning that Scripture embraces both lives, the active and the contemplative.

**Bed** signifies a depraved mind, as in the Psalms: “He meditated iniquity upon his bed” [Note: [Col. 0903] 29 Ps. XXXV, 5], that is, “he considered evil in his mind.”

**Bed** signifies the devil’s resting-place, as in Isaiah: “It will be the lair of dragons” [Note: [Col. 0903] 30 Isa. XXXIV, 13], meaning that every reprobate person makes himself a dwelling-place for demons.

**Bed** signifies a good mind, as in the Gospel: “Enter into your room” [Note: [Col. 0903] 31 Matt. VI, 6], that is, “love the inner tranquility of your mind.”

**Bed** signifies heavenly rest, as in the Gospel: “My children are already with me in bed” [Note: [Col. 0903] 32 Luke XI, 7], meaning that the souls of the saints, released from their bodies, are already with the Lord in heavenly rest.

**Bed** signifies the rewards of the saints, as in the Psalms: “They will rejoice upon their beds” [Note: [Col. 0903] 33 Ps. CXLIX, 5], meaning that the saints rejoice in the rewards given to them in heaven according to their merits.

**Bed** signifies the gatherings of evil people, as in the Song: “You will be crowned from the lairs of lions” [Note: [Col. 0903] 34 Song IV, 8], that is, “you will carry away victory over the gatherings of the proud.”

**Stalk** signifies the condition of the world, as in Genesis: “Seven ears of grain were sprouting on one stalk” [Note: [Col. 0903] 35 Gen. XLI, 5, 22], that is, “seven years of fertility and infertility were about to occur in the condition of this age.”

**Stalk** signifies any hypocrite, as in the prophet: “There is no standing stalk or germ in it” [Note: [Col. 0905] 1 Hos. VIII, 7], meaning that the hypocrite knows how to live rightly, but true holiness is not in him.

**Gnat** signifies Barabbas the robber, as in the Gospel: “Straining out a gnat” [Note: [Col. 0905] 2 Matt. XXIII, 24], meaning that the Jews were asking for the robber to be released.

**Knife** signifies sharpness of understanding, as in Proverbs: “Set a knife at your throat” [Note: [Col. 0905] 3 Prov. XXIII, 2], that is, “have sharpness of understanding in your speech.”

**Knife** signifies the commandments of God, as in Joshua: “Make stone knives for yourself and circumcise the sons of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0905] 4 Josh. V, 2], meaning that the Lord Jesus gave humanity strong commandments by which the excesses of vices are cut away from them.

**Chariot** signifies the assembly of the saints, as in the Psalm: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold” [Note: [Col. 0905] 5 Ps. LXVIII], meaning that the saints are perfect in the Law.

**Chariot** signifies great sins, as in Exodus: “He cast Pharaoh’s chariot and his army into the sea” [Note: [Col. 0905] 6 Exod. XV, 4], meaning that the Lord overwhelms both small and great sins in baptism.

**Chariot** signifies a gentle prelate, as in the Books of Kings: “The chariot of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0905] 7 4 Kings II, 12], that is, “one who carries the people of Israel through gentleness.”

**Chariot** signifies the unstable things of the world, as in the Psalms: “Some trust in chariots” [Note: [Col. 0905] 8 Ps. XIX, 8], that is, “they delight in things that revolve.”

**Leg** signifies corruption, as in Isaiah: “Uncover your leg” [Note: [Col. 0905] 9 Isa. XLVII, 2], that is, “show how corruptible you are.”

**Leg** signifies good desires, as in Leviticus: “What has longer legs behind” [Note: [Col. 0905] 10 Lev. XI, 21], meaning that we ought to imitate those who extend their desires toward the eternity of the future life.

**Leg** signifies the strengths of steadfastness, as in the Gospel, * and the evil spirits that are sent will be broken, not only in the reprobate but also in the elect, to take away from them the strength of steadfastness.

**Legs** signify holy teachers, as in the Gospel: “They did not break Jesus’ legs” [Note: [Col. 0905] 11 John XIX, 33], meaning that persecutors or evil spirits cannot weaken the holy preachers upon whom the Lord relies in his Church.

**Legs** signify the paths of the Lord’s incarnation, as in the Song: “His legs are like marble pillars” [Note: [Col. 0905] 12 Song V, 15], meaning that whatever Christ undertook in his humanity was upright and strong.

**Watcher** signifies Christ, as in Isaiah: “Watcher, what of the night?” [Note: [Col. 0905] 13 Isa. XXI, 11], that is, “What shall I do about my iniquity? * Christ, [what] shall I do?” [The final words are textually uncertain.]

**Watchers** signify teachers, as in the Song: “The watchers of the walls took away my cloak” [Note: [Col. 0905] 14 Song V, 7], that is, “the teachers of the Churches took my depraved old age away from me.”

**Watchers** signify evil spirits, as in the Gospel: “The watchers were terrified because of him” [Note: [Col. 0905] 15 Matt. XXVIII, 4], meaning that when the Lord comes to judgment, not only reprobate human beings but also wicked spirits will be afraid.

**Skin** signifies every reprobate person occupied with earthly things, as in Job: “My skin has dried up” [Note: [Col. 0905] 16 Job VII, 5], meaning that those who dry up excessively in earthly matters dry up from the moisture of divine love.

**Skin** signifies any sick person, as in Job: “My skin, blackened upon me” [Note: [Col. 0905] 17 Job XXX, 30], meaning that the sick who are in the Church are darkened when persecution comes.

**Skin** signifies softness, as in Jeremiah: “His skin clung to his bones” [Note: [Col. 0905] 18 Lam. IV, 8], meaning that carnal softness invaded spiritual strength.

**Skin** signifies sin, as in Job: “I have made sackcloth over my skin” [Note: [Col. 0905] 19 Job XVI, 15], that is, “through the severity of repentance I have destroyed sin.”

## D

Fawn. Riches. Diadem. Delights. Sleep. Flood. Desert. Drachma. House. Dawn. Failing. Rich. Right hand. God. Back. Beloved. Damascus. Lord. Day. Denarius. Leader. Dragon. Dromedary. Finger. Teeth.

**Doe** signifies the devil, as in Isaiah: “And it will be like a fleeing doe” [Note: [Col. 0905] 20 Isa. XIII, 14], meaning that every reprobate person withdraws from the Church together with his head, the devil.

**Damascus** signifies the devil, as in the Song: “Which looks toward Damascus” [Note: [Col. 0905] 21 Song VII, 4], meaning that our discernment ought to anticipate the devil’s cunning.

**Damascus** signifies the mass of the reprobate, as in Isaiah: “Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city” [Note: [Col. 0905] 22 Isa. XVII, 1], meaning that the reprobate will not always be permitted to remain here.

**Damascus** signifies the Roman Empire, as in Isaiah: “And the strength of Damascus will perish” [Note: [Col. 0905] 23 Isa. VIII, 4], meaning that the power of the Roman Empire will cease, and the power of Christ, which is eternal, will reign.

**Drachma** signifies human nature, as in the Gospel: “I have found the drachma that I had lost” [Note: [Col. 0905] 24 Luke XV, 9], that is, “I restored human nature, which I had lost through fault.”

**Drachma** signifies evangelical and human nature, as in the Gospel: “What woman, having ten drachmas” [Note: [Col. 0905] 25 Ibid., verse 8], meaning that eternal Wisdom of God possessed nine orders among the angels and a tenth among human beings.

**Dragon** signifies the devil, as in the Apocalypse: “Michael and his angels fought with the dragon” [Note: [Col. 0905] 26 Rev. XII, 7], that is, Christ and his ministers fought with the devil.

**Dragon** signifies this world, as in the Psalms: “This dragon, which you formed to play in it” [Note: [Col. 0905] 27 Ps. CIII, 26], meaning that we ought to mock the world’s deceit.

**Dragon** signifies the Antichrist, as in the Apocalypse: “Behold, a great red dragon” [Note: [Col. 0905] 28 Rev. XII, 3], meaning that the Antichrist will be proud and cruel.

**Dragons** signify evil spirits, as in Isaiah: “It will be the lair of dragons” [Note: [Col. 0905] 29 Isa. XXXIV, 13], meaning that the depraved mind permits evil spirits to dwell within it through guilt.

**Dragons** signify the Jews, as in Jeremiah: “They drew in the wind like dragons” [Note: [Col. 0905] 30 Jer. XIV, 6], meaning that the venomous Jews gathered counsel against Jesus.

**Dragons** signify the Gentiles, as in Isaiah: “The beast of the field will glorify me, the dragons” [Note: [Col. 0905] 31 Isa. XLIII, 20], and so forth, that is, “the people of the world, and especially the Gentile peoples, will praise me.”

**God** is understood as referring to the person of the Father, as in the Acts of the Apostles: “The God of our fathers glorified his Son Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0907] 1 Acts III, 13].

**God** is understood as referring to the person of the Son, as in Paul: “Who is God blessed above all forever” [Note: [Col. 0907] 2 Rom. IX, 5].

**God** is understood as referring to the person of the Holy Spirit, as in the Acts of the Apostles: “You have not lied to human beings but to God” [Note: [Col. 0907] 3 Acts V, 4].

**God** is understood as referring to the whole Trinity, as in Exodus: “The Lord your God is one God” [Note: [Col. 0907] 4 Deut. VI, 4].

**God** is spoken of essentially, as in Exodus: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” [Note: [Col. 0907] 5 Exod. III, 6]; and titularly, as also in Exodus: “Behold, I have appointed you as God to Pharaoh” [Note: [Col. 0907] 6 Exod. VII, 1].

God speaks to me by himself, in the Psalms: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” [Note: [Col. 0907] 7 Ps. LXXXIV, 9]; or through angels, as in Genesis: “The Lord God called Adam, and God said to him” [Note: [Col. 0907] 8 Gen. III, 9]; or through an assumed creature of ours, as in Genesis: “I saw the Lord face to face” [Note: [Col. 0907] 9 Gen. XXXII, 30]; or he is placed in the understanding, as in the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” [Note: [Col. 0907] 10 Matt. V, 8].

How God speaks through himself is found in Book VI of the *Moralia*; how he speaks sometimes through angels, sometimes . . . . through a creature subject to him, and sometimes . . . . through the understanding is found in the letter of blessed Augustine to Italica [Note: [Col. 0907] 11 Epistle 6], in the same author’s letter to Paulina on seeing God, in Book XXII of *The City of God*, and in Book XXVIII of the *Moralia*.

**God** signifies the Jews, as in the Psalms: “God stood in the assembly of gods” [Note: [Col. 0907] 12 Ps. LXXXI, 1], that is, Christ dwelt bodily among the Jews.

**God** signifies prelates, as in the Law: “You shall not revile the divine one” [Note: [Col. 0907] 13 Exod. XXII, 28], that is, prelates.

**Delights** signify the divine utterances, as in Job: “Overflowing with delights in the Almighty” [Note: [Col. 0907] 14 Job XXII, 26], that is, “you will abound in delights for knowing the utterance of sacred Scripture.”

**Delights** signify joys, as in Ezekiel: “You were in the delights of God’s paradise” [Note: [Col. 0907] 15 Ezek. XXVIII, 13], meaning that that reprobate angel was in the joys of heavenly loveliness.

**Denarius** signifies Christ, as in the Apocalypse: “Two pounds of wheat for a denarius” [Note: [Col. 0907] 16 Rev. VI, 6], meaning that those who hold to faith and works in . . . belong to Christ.

**Denarius** signifies eternal recompense, as in the Gospel: “Having agreed with the workers for a daily denarius, he sent them into his vineyard” [Note: [Col. 0907] 17 Matt. XX, 2], meaning that if we labor vigorously in the holy Church, we will receive eternal recompense.

**Denarius** signifies the two Testaments, as in the Gospel: “The next day he brought out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper” [Note: [Col. 0907] 18 Luke X, 35], meaning that after his resurrection Christ caused the disciples to understand both Testaments.

**Failing** is understood in an evil sense, as in the Psalms: “My days have failed like smoke” [Note: [Col. 0907] 19 Ps. CI, 4], meaning that the more our life exalts itself, the more quickly it vanishes.

**Failing** is understood in a good sense, as in the Psalms: “My spirit failed” [Note: [Col. 0907] 20 Ps. LXXVI, 4], that is, “my fear fell asleep.”

**Teeth** signify the words of the Church, as in Job: “He gnashed his teeth against me” [Note: [Col. 0907] 21 Job XVI, 10], meaning that the Lord rages against sinners through the words of the Church.

**Teeth** signify preachers, as in the Song: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep” [Note: [Col. 0907] 22 Song IV, 2], meaning that the unanimous and innocent preachers of the Church sometimes lay aside not only what is superfluous but also what is necessary.

**Teeth** signify the inner senses, as in Job: “Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth?” [Note: [Col. 0907] 23 Job XIII, 14], that is, “with my inner senses I rebuke my carnal vices.”

**Teeth** signify the words of the Law, as in Deuteronomy: “Moses’s teeth were not moved” [Note: [Col. 0907] 24 Deut. XXXIV, 7], meaning that the words of the Law cannot be passed over without all things being fulfilled.

**Teeth** signify the strengths of the virtues: [lacuna] “He permits that one to be weakened.”

**Teeth** signify the vices of gluttony, as in Job: “The teeth of the lion’s cubs are broken” [Note: [Col. 0907] 25 Job IV, 10], that is, “the pleasures of gluttony have been destroyed in the sons of the proud.”

**Teeth** signify the persecutions of demons, as in the canticle of Deuteronomy: “I will send the teeth of beasts against them” [Note: [Col. 0907] 26 Deut. XXXII, 24], meaning that the Lord permits the persecutions of demons to rage against the reprobate.

**Teeth** signify the persecutors of the Church, as in Job: “His strength is in the circuit of his teeth” [Note: [Col. 0907] 27 Job XLI, 5], meaning that the weak fear the persecutors through whom the devil bites.

**Teeth** signify harsh things, as in the Psalms: “You have broken the teeth of sinners” [Note: [Col. 0907] 28 Ps. III, 8], that is, “you have destroyed the cruel words of the wicked.”

**Teeth** signify slanderers, as in the Psalms: “God will break their teeth” [Note: [Col. 0907] 29 Ps. LVII, 7], that is, “God will destroy their slanders.”

**Teeth** signify cruelties, as in Job: “From his teeth I took the prey” [Note: [Col. 0907] 30 Job XXIX, 17], that is, “I rescued the humble person from the cruelties of the wicked.”

Desert signifies heaven, as in the Gospel: “I left the ninety-nine sheep in the desert” [Note: [Col. 0907] 31 Luke 15:4]; that is, he left the angelic nature in heaven.

Desert signifies the womb of the Virgin, as in Hosea: “God will bring a scorching wind from the desert” [Note: [Col. 0907] 32 Hosea 13:15]; that is, God the Father brought forth for us Christ, mighty, from the womb of the Virgin.

Desert signifies Judaea, as in the Gospel: “John was preaching in the desert” [Note: [Col. 0907] 33 Matthew 3:1]; that is, announcing Christ to desolate Judaea.

Desert signifies the Gentiles, as in Isaiah: “Let the desert exult” [Note: [Col. 0907] 34 Isaiah 42:11]; that is, let the Gentile people rejoice.

Desert signifies this world, as in the Song: “Who is this who comes up from the desert?” [Note: [Col. 0907] 35 Song of Songs 3:6]—namely, Mary, who is raised up from this world.

Desert signifies the multitude of the ungodly, as in the Apocalypse: “He carried me away into the desert” [Note: [Col. 0907] 36 Revelation 17:3]; that is, he carried me away in contemplation to behold the multitude of the ungodly.

Desert signifies a depraved mind, as in the Book of Tobit: “Raphael bound the demon in the desert of Upper Egypt” [Note: [Col. 0907] 37 Tobit 8:3]; that is, the devil is held shut up in a depraved and darkened mind.

Desert signifies a holy mind, as in Exodus: “When he had driven the flock to the interior of the desert, the Lord appeared to him” [Note: [Col. 0907] 38 Exodus 3:1]; that is, the Lord appears spiritually to us when we bring our thoughts into true unity within a devout mind that consists in holy solitude.

Desert signifies holy conduct, as in Exodus: “We shall sacrifice to the Lord in the desert” [Note: [Col. 0909] 1 Exodus 8:27]; that is, we shall serve the Lord in holy conduct.

Through the desert signify demons, as in the Psalms: “Nor from the deserted mountains” [Note: [Col. 0909] 2 Psalm 73:7]; that is, not even those malignant spirits have a place open to them for fleeing the divine majesty.

Right signifies the Son of God, as in the Psalms: “The right hand of the Lord has wrought power” [Note: [Col. 0909] 3 Psalm 107:7]; that is, the Son of God works miracles.

The right hand of God signifies grace, as in Job: “You will extend your right hand to the work of your hands” [Note: [Col. 0909] 4 Job 14:15]; that is, you will give your grace to the one whom you created.

Right signifies the just, as in Deuteronomy: “In his right hand was a fiery law” [Note: [Col. 0909] 5 Deuteronomy 33:2]; that is, burning charity is in his saints.

Right signifies the salvation of the soul, as in the Psalms: “Let the devil stand at his right hand” [Note: [Col. 0909] 6 Psalm 108:10]; that is, he placed money before the salvation of his soul.

Right signifies good action, as in the Psalms: “Their right hand is filled with gifts” [Note: [Col. 0909] 7 Psalm 25:10]; that is, they sell their righteousness.

Right signifies contemplation, as in the Song: “His right hand will embrace me” [Note: [Col. 0909] 8 Song of Songs 2:6]; that is, contemplation of him will gladden me.

Right signifies power, as in the Psalms: “Their right hand is a right hand of iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0909] 9 Psalm 143:8]; that is, their power is wicked.

Right signifies prosperity, as in the Law: “You shall not turn aside to the right or to the left” [Note: [Col. 0909] 10 Deuteronomy 5:32; 17:11]; that is, do not exalt yourself in prosperity.

Right signifies any friend, as in the Psalms: “I looked to the right” [Note: [Col. 0909] 11 Psalm 141:5], and so forth; that is, I sought among my friends for someone who might help me, and found no one.

Right signifies elation over virtues, as in Job: “If I turn to the right, I shall not see him” [Note: [Col. 0909] 12 Job 23:9]; that is, if I grow proud of my virtues, I cannot contemplate him.

Right signifies eternal life, as in Proverbs: “Length of days is in her right hand” [Note: [Col. 0909] 13 Proverbs 3:16]; that is, heavenly life will never cease through any ending.

Right signifies favor, as in the Psalms: “God is at my right hand, that is, he favors me, so that I shall not be moved” [Note: [Col. 0909] 14 Psalm 15:8].

Right-hand ornaments signify adornments of good works, as in the Law: “Right-hand ornaments and rings” [Note: [Col. 0909] 15 Exodus 25:33]; that is, [lacuna] and the adornment of good works.

Diadem signifies the humanity of Christ, as in the Song: “See King Solomon with the diadem with which his mother crowned him” [Note: [Col. 0909] 16 Numbers 31:50]; that is, honor Christ in his humanity, which he took from his mother without a father.

Diadem signifies judgment, as in Job: “And with the diadem of my judgment” [Note: [Col. 0909] 17 Song of Songs 3:11]; that is, I have been adorned with my judgment as though with a certain diadem.

Day signifies the Father and the Son, as in the Psalms: “Declare the day to the day” [Note: [Col. 0909] 18 Job 29:14]; that is, preach the Father from the Son.

Day signifies the angel Gabriel and the Virgin Mary, as in the Psalms: “Day pours forth the word to day” [Note: [Col. 0909] 19 Psalm 95:2]; that is, the angel announced to Mary.

Day signifies the devil, as in Job: “Let the day perish in which I was born” [Note: [Col. 0909] 20 Psalm 18:3]; that is, let the devil, through whom I was deceived, be condemned.

Day signifies the prosperity of the wicked, as in Jeremiah: “We do not desire the day of a man” [Note: [Col. 0909] 21 Jeremiah 17:16]; that is, I did not desire worldly prosperity.

Day signifies the condition of the wicked, as in the Gospel: “Indeed, in this your day, the things that belong to your peace” [Note: [Col. 0909] 22 Luke 19:42]; that is, in this condition of yours, which you maintain in peace.

Day signifies the pleasure of sin, as in Job: “Let that day be turned into darkness” [Note: [Col. 0909] 23 Job 3:4]; that is, would that it might be foreseen into how great a darkness of sin the pleasure of sin drags a person!

Day signifies time, as in Ecclesiastes: “In the day of good things, do not be unmindful of evils” [Note: [Col. 0909] 24 Ecclesiastes 7:15]; that is, in a time of repose, do not be unmindful of disturbance.

Day signifies the heat of temptation, as in the Gospel: “The burden of the day and the heat” [Note: [Col. 0909] 25 Matthew 20:12]; that is, the burden of temptation and tribulation.

Day signifies the eternity of the day, as in the Psalms: “With you is the beginning in the day of your power” [Note: [Col. 0909] 26 Psalm 109:3]; that is, one essence with you in the eternity of your majesty.

Day signifies the illumination of the mind, as in Job: “Each one on his own day” [Note: [Col. 0909] 27 Job 1:4]; that is, each elect person ought, in the illumination of his own mind, to refresh his neighbor.

Day signifies the brightness of inward repose, as in Genesis: “God sanctified the seventh day” [Note: [Col. 0909] 28 Genesis 2:3]; that is, through the brightness of inward repose, a person is consecrated to God.

Day signifies the heavenly homeland, as in the Song: “Until the day breathes forth” [Note: [Col. 0909] 29 Song of Songs 2:17]; that is, until the brightness of the heavenly homeland breaks forth.

Day signifies the incarnation of Christ, as in the Psalms: “In the day the Lord commanded” [Note: [Col. 0909] 30 Psalm 41:9]; that is, in the light of his incarnation he had mercy on the world.

Through day signify redeemed human beings, as in Job: “Let it not be counted among the days of the year” [Note: [Col. 0909] 31 Job 3:6]; [that is,] let the apostate angel not attain forgiveness among redeemed human beings.

Through day signify good works, as in the Psalms: “The Lord knows the days of the just” [Note: [Col. 0909] 32 Psalm 36:18]; that is, he approves the works of the saints.

Dawn signifies the coming of inward brightness, as in Job: “Rising early, he offered holocausts” [Note: [Col. 0909] 33 Job 1:6]; that is, when inward brightness came, he prayed to God.

Dawn signifies zeal, as in the Psalms: “At dawn they came to him” [Note: [Col. 0909] 34 Psalm 77:34].

Dawn signifies the time of the resurrection, as in the Psalms: “I shall rise at dawn” [Note: [Col. 0909] 35 Psalm 56:9]; that is, in the morning before the light.

Finger signifies the Holy Spirit, as in the Gospel: “If by the finger of God”—that is, by the Spirit of God—“I cast out demons” [Note: [Col. 0909] 36 Luke 11:19].

Finger signifies discernment, as in the Gospel: “He was writing with his finger on the ground” [Note: [Col. 0909] 37 John 8:6, 8]; that is, with humble discernment we ought to examine our earthly heart.

Finger signifies restraint, as in Job: “Put your finger upon your heart” [Note: [Col. 0909] 38 Job 21:5]; that is, restrain your speech.

Through the finger is signified the diversity of persons, as in Isaiah: “Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers?” [Note: [Col. 0909] 39 Isaiah 40:12]. Through “who?” (*quis*), the unity of subsistence; through “three,” the unity of persons.

Through four fingers signify the books of the Gospels, as in Exodus: “Make a rim of gold, four fingers high” [Note: [Col. 0909] 40 Exodus 37:12]; that is, whatever holiness we possess, we learn through our conduct from the books of the Gospels.

Through fingers signify the workers of the Church, as in the Song: “My fingers are full of most exquisite myrrh” [Note: [Col. 0911] 1 Song of Songs 5:5]; that is, my workers glory in tribulations.

Beloved signifies the Father and the Son, as in the Song: “What is your beloved beyond another beloved?” [Note: [Col. 0911] 2 Song of Songs 5:9]; that is, the Son from the Father.

Beloved signifies the Jewish people, as in the prophet: “Why does my beloved commit many crimes?” [Note: [Col. 0911] 3 Jeremiah 11:15]; that is, why does the one whom I love spiritually sin so impiously?

Flood signifies baptism, as in the Psalms: “The Lord makes the flood dwell” [Note: [Col. 0911] 4 Psalm 28:10]; that is, he established baptism in his Church.

Flood signifies the final judgment, as in the Psalms: “In the flood of waters” [Note: [Col. 0911] 5 Psalm 31:6]; that is, in the final judgment, in which the reprobate, who are fluid, will be condemned, while the just will not perish.

Flood signifies sin, as in Genesis: “I will destroy every flesh with the waters of the flood” [Note: [Col. 0911] 6 Genesis 6:7]; that is, God permits carnal people to be consumed by the pleasures of sin.

Rich signifies God, as in the Gospel: “There was a certain rich man who had a steward” [Note: [Col. 0911] 7 Luke 16:1]; that is, God, who [lacuna] has a human being for himself.

Rich signifies the Jewish people, as in the Gospel: “There was a certain rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen” [Note: [Col. 0911] 8 Luke 16:19]; that is, the Jewish people gloried in the cultivation of outward life.

Through the rich signify lovers of the world, as in the Psalms: “The rich have become needy and hungry” [Note: [Col. 0911] 9 Psalm 33:11]; that is, lovers of the world will waste away through poverty and hunger.

Riches signify the words of the Law, as in Job: “He will vomit up the riches that he devoured” [Note: [Col. 0911] 10 Job 20:15]; that is, he will lose the words of the Law that he possessed.

Riches signify counsels, as in Job: “If I rejoiced over my great riches” [Note: [Col. 0911] 11 Job 31:25]; that is, I did not lift myself up in vain joy over the counsels in which there is abundance.

Riches signify contemplations of God, as in the Psalms: “And you will be nourished by his riches” [Note: [Col. 0911] 12 Psalm 36:3]; that is, you will have spiritual refreshment in contemplations of him.

Lord sometimes signifies the Father, sometimes the Son, and sometimes the Holy Spirit, as in this single verse: “The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping; the Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has accepted my prayer” [Note: [Col. 0911] 13 Psalm 6:9–10].

Lord signifies any prelate, as in the Books of Kings: “The Lord will take your lord from you” [Note: [Col. 0911] 14 4 Kings 2:3, 5]; that is, Elijah, your prelate.

Through lord signify sins, as in the Gospel: “And their lords said, ‘Why are you untying the colt?’” [Note: [Col. 0911] 15 Luke 19:33]. The Lord had many colts, because the people of the nation served the enormities of many sins.

House signifies the heavenly homeland, as in the Psalms: “That I may dwell in the house of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0911] 16 Psalm 22:6]; that is, that I may live in the heavenly homeland.

House signifies the Church, as in the Psalm: “Holiness befits your house” [Note: [Col. 0911] 17 Psalm 92:5]; that is, holiness ought to be in the Church.

House signifies the human mind, as in the Psalms: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house” [Note: [Col. 0911] 18 Psalm 25:8]; that is, I desired to make beautiful my mind, in which you ought to dwell.

House signifies the humanity of Christ, as in Proverbs: “Wisdom built herself a house” [Note: [Col. 0911] 19 Proverbs 9:1]; that is, the Son of God assumed flesh for himself.

House signifies this world, as in the Gospel: “And the one who is on the housetop, with his vessels in the house, let him not come down to take them” [Note: [Col. 0911] 20 Matthew 24:17]; that is, let him not return to the desires of the world that he abandoned.

House signifies a household, as in the Books of Kings: “That you might speak concerning the house”—that is, concerning the household—“of your servant” [Note: [Col. 0911] 21 2 Samuel 7:19].

House signifies the pleasure of human approval, as in Job: “He will lean upon his house, and it will not stand” [Note: [Col. 0911] 22 Job 8:15]; that is, in the future he will not look to human praise, but it itself will fail.

House signifies the Jewish people, as in the Gospel: “I will return to my house from which I came out” [Note: [Col. 0911] 23 Luke 11:24]; that is, the devil says this to the Jewish people when they refused to receive Christ. He came out from them when they received the Law.

House signifies the Gentiles, as in the Psalms: “The house of Jacob from a barbarous people” [Note: [Col. 0911] 24 Psalm 103:1]; that is, the Gentile people were once alien from God, but now he himself dwells in them through faith.

House signifies the protection of the Savior, as in the Psalms: “The house of the heron is their leader” [Note: [Col. 0911] 25 Psalm 103:17]; that is, Christ’s progress leads his elect.

House signifies a depraved soul, as in Ezekiel: “A house that provokes to anger”; that is, a depraved soul provokes the Lord to anger through its wickedness.

House signifies death itself, as in Job: “Where the house appointed for every living person is” [Note: [Col. 0911] 26 Job 30:23]; that is, there is no person who will live and not see death.

Through house signify different orders, as in the Psalms: “God is recognized in her houses, in her various prayers” [Note: [Col. 0911] 27 Psalm 47:4].

Through houses signify good consciences, as in Job: “He filled his houses with silver” [Note: [Col. 0911] 28 Job 3:15]; that is, the perfect abound in the brightness of divine utterance within their consciences.

Through houses signify depraved thoughts, as in Job: “In deserted houses, which have been reduced to burial mounds” [Note: [Col. 0911] 29 Job 15:28]; that is, the wicked have thoughts abandoned by God, and in them they bear the corruption and stench of sin.

Through houses signify human bodies, as in Job: “How much more those who dwell in houses of clay” [Note: [Col. 0911] 30 Job 4:19]; that is, as long as we are in this corruptible body, we cannot be entirely free from sin.

Dromedary signifies the Gentiles, as in Isaiah: “The dromedaries of Midian and Ephah” [Note: [Col. 0911] 31 Isaiah 60]. The Gentile people, who formerly belonged to judgment, now honor the Lord on account of mercy.

Back signifies all who follow, as in the Psalms: “Make their back always bent” [Note: [Col. 0911] 32 Psalm 68:24]; that is, permit the subject wicked, who follow evil prelates, to slip toward earthly things.

Back signifies the mind, as in the Psalms: “He turned his back away from burdens” [Note: [Col. 0911] 33 Psalm 80:7]; that is, he lightened his mind from sins.

Back signifies the reprobate, as in the Psalms: “You will place them as a back” [Note: [Col. 0911] 34 Psalm 20:13]; that is, you will cast them behind you—that is, the ungodly.

Back signifies patience, as in the Psalms: “Sinners built upon my back” [Note: [Col. 0911] 35 Psalm 128:3]; that is, I was patient while they inflicted many evils.

Back signifies the rulers of the Church, as in the Psalms: “The rear parts of his back are in the pallor of gold” [Note: [Col. 0913] 1 Psalm 67:14]; that is, the rewards of the ruler of the Church are in the beauty of eternal brightness.

Sleep signifies the repose of life, as in the Song: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” [Note: [Col. 0913] 2 Song of Songs 5:2]; that is, I rest in contemplation.

Sleep signifies torpor, as in Paul: “Rise, you who sleep” [Note: [Col. 0913] 3 Ephesians 5:14]; that is, you who are torpid with respect to useful work.

Sleep signifies death, as in the Gospel: “Lazarus, our friend, is sleeping” [Note: [Col. 0913] 4 John 11:11]; that is, he is dead.

Sleep signifies sickness, as in the Gospel: “They all grew drowsy and slept” [Note: [Col. 0913] 5 Matthew 25:5]; that is, through the weight of sickness one arrives at the sleep of death.

Sleep signifies blindness, as in the Psalms: “All who went up slept” [Note: [Col. 0913] 6 Psalm 75:7]; that is, all the proud are blinded.

To sleep signifies to fall into sin, as in the Psalm: “My soul grew drowsy through [weariness]”; that is, I have often fallen into sin.

Sleep signifies sexual intercourse, as in “he slept with her”—that is, he had intercourse with her.

Leader signifies Christ, as in the Song of Exodus: “You were a leader to the people whom you redeemed, in your mercy” [Note: [Col. 0913] 7 Exodus 15:13]; that is, the Lord mercifully leads his elect to himself.

Through leaders signify the apostles, as in the Book of Numbers: “The leaders offered offerings at the dedication of the altar” [Note: [Col. 0913] 8 Numbers 7:2]; that is, the apostles devoted themselves to building the holy Church.

Through leaders signify wicked teachers, as in Job: “Who calls the wicked leaders” [Note: [Col. 0913] 9 Job 34:18]; that is, wicked teachers, when they do not purify themselves, break out into wickedness.

Through leaders signify heretics, as in Job: “They restrained the leaders with their voice” [Note: [Col. 0913] 10 Job 29:10]; that is, once the truth of Christ has been revealed, the heretics fall silent.

Through leaders signify principal vices, as in Job: “He scents the call to the leaders” [Note: [Col. 0913] 11 Job 39:28]; that is, every perfect person is accustomed to foresee how original vices incite a person to evil.

## E

Ivory. Edom. Palm branches. Emulation. Snuffers. Engadi. Rust. Bronze. Heshbon. Food. Ether. Ethiopia. Exacting creditor. Army. Drunkenness. Kid. Egypt. Electrum. Exit. Sword. Horse. Hedgehogs. Caterpillar. Summer. Eternal. Ethiopians. Explorers.

Ivory signifies the life of the holy Fathers, as in Jeremiah: “Ruddier than ancient ivory” [Note: [Col. 0913] 12 Lamentations 4:7]; that is, they were holier than the ancient fathers were.

Ivory signifies the incorruption of Christ’s flesh, as in the Song: “His belly is ivory” [Note: [Col. 0913] 13 Song of Songs 5:14]; that is, his body is free from the corruption of sin.

Ivory signifies chastity: “Your neck is like an ivory tower” [Note: [Col. 0913] 14 Song of Songs 7:4]; that is, the holy preachers of the Church are commended both by the sublimity of contemplation and by the brightness of chastity.

Ivory signifies strength, as in the Books of Kings: “Solomon made a throne of ivory” [Note: [Col. 0913] 15 1 Kings 10:18]; that is, our peacemaker built his Church from the strength of the saints.

Drunkenness signifies the joy of heavenly grace, as in the Song: “Be drunk, my beloved” [Note: [Col. 0913] 16 Song of Songs 5:1]; that is, the elect will be completely filled with charity when they enjoy the blessedness of both flesh and soul.

Drunkenness signifies the inward satiety of the saints, as in the Psalms: “They will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house” [Note: [Col. 0913] 17 Psalm 64:12]; that is, even here the saints are sometimes nourished by the fullness of your heavenly house.

Drunkenness signifies love of the world, as in Joel: “Awake, you drunkards, and weep” [Note: [Col. 0913] 18 Joel 1:3]; that is, you who love the world, attend to yourselves and grieve.

Drunkenness signifies the anxiety of the present life, as in Jeremiah: “He has intoxicated me with wormwood” [Note: [Col. 0913] 19 Lamentations 3:15]; that is, he permitted me to be so greatly troubled by the bitterness of the present life that I was estranged from myself by punishment.

Drunkenness signifies error, as in Paul: “Those who are drunk are drunk at night” [Note: [Col. 0913] 20 1 Thessalonians 5:7]; and those who err err through the darkness of ignorance.

Church signifies the good, as in the Psalms: “In the midst of the Church I will praise you” [Note: [Col. 0913] 21 Psalm 21:23]; that is, I will proclaim you in the communion of the faithful.

Church signifies the evil, as in the Psalms: “I have hated the assembly of the wicked” [Note: [Col. 0913] 22 Psalm 25:5]; that is, the gathering of the impure.

Kid signifies Christ, as in Exodus: “You shall also take a kid” [Note: [Col. 0913] 23 Exodus 12:5]; that is, you shall sacrifice Christ, who came in the likeness of sinful flesh.

Kid signifies correction, as in Genesis: “Let a kid be brought from the goats” [Note: [Col. 0913] 24 Genesis 37:31]; that is, Christ corrected the Church from the Gentiles through his preachers.

Kid signifies a sinner, as in Genesis, where Joseph’s brothers dipped his tunic in the blood of a kid; that is, the Jews reproached Christ for sin as though he were a sinner.

Through the kid signify the reprobate, as in the Gospel: “The shepherd separates the sheep from the kids” [Note: [Col. 0913] 25 Matthew 25:32]; that is, Christ will separate the elect from the reprobate.

Through the kid signify sins of the flesh, as in Genesis: “He covered me with the skins of the kids” [Note: [Col. 0913] 26 Genesis 27:16]; that is, Christ endured such harsh things as though he had sins in his own deeds.

Through the kid signify impure thoughts, as in the Song: “And feed your kids beside the shepherds’ tents” [Note: [Col. 0913] 27 Song of Songs 1:8]; that is, refresh your impure senses after the likeness of the reprobate.

Through the kid signify groans of repentance, as in Genesis: “So that I may make food for your father from the kids, which he gladly eats” [Note: [Col. 0913] 28 Genesis 27:9]; that is, God is refreshed from the Gentiles [lacuna].

Edom means “blood-red,” and signifies this world: “The one who comes from Edom”—that is, the one who rises from the world.

Edom signifies each carnal person, as in Genesis: “Therefore his name was called Edom” [Note: [Col. 0913] 29 Genesis 25:30]; that is, whoever places the flesh before the spirit ought rightly to be called carnal.

Edom signifies sin: “Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom” [Note: [Col. 0913] 30 Psalm 136:7]; that is, when the brightness of the heavenly homeland appears, the Lord will condemn the deeds generated by sin.

Edom signifies the Jewish people, as in the Book of Numbers: “Edom refused to grant Israel passage through his land” [Note: [Col. 0913] 31 Numbers 20:18]; that is, the Jewish people refused to admit the Gentile people to knowledge.

Edom signifies the Gentiles, as in Genesis: “Kings reigned in Edom before there was a king in Israel” [Note: [Col. 0915] 1 Genesis 36:31]; that is, there were some saints among the Gentiles before the Jewish people was chosen.

Edom signifies the devil, as in Jeremiah: “Hear the counsel of the Lord, which he sent concerning Edom” [Note: [Col. 0915] 2 Jeremiah 49:20]; that is, receive the faith of Christ, whom the Father sent to destroy the devil.

Edom signifies hell, as in Ezekiel: “I will act against Edom according to my anger” [Note: [Col. 0915] 3 Ezekiel 25:14]; that is, I will act against hell as though I were angry with it, stripping it and bringing or leading the elect out from it.

Egypt signifies darkness and signifies this world, as in Genesis: “Do not go down into Egypt” [Note: [Col. 0915] 4 Genesis 26:2]; that is, do not love the world.

Egypt signifies sin, as in the Psalms: “When Israel went out of Egypt” [Note: [Col. 0915] 5 Psalm 113:1]; that is, when the elect, having been delivered from their sins through confession, attain holiness.

Egypt signifies unbelief, as in the Psalms: “When Joseph went out from the land of Egypt: my tongue” [Note: [Col. 0915] 6 Psalm 80:6], and so forth; that is, the Christian people, coming out from the darkness of unbelief, heard the commandments of the New Testament, previously unknown.

Egypt signifies the Gentiles, as in the Gospel: “The child Jesus was taken from Judaea into Egypt” [Note: [Col. 0915] 7 Matthew 2:13–14]; that is, after the Jewish people was left behind, the faith in Christ’s incarnation reached the Gentiles.

Egypt signifies hell, as in Exodus [Note: [Col. 0915] 8 Exodus 12 and 14:24 and following]: Israel was delivered from Egypt through the sacrifice of the lamb; that is, through the passion of Christ the elect were brought back from hell.

Palm branches signify spiritual triumphs, as in the Song: “His locks are like palm branches” [Note: [Col. 0915] 9 Song of Songs 5:11]; that is, the perfect, who cling more closely to Christ the head, bravely conquer the vices that tempt them.

Electrum signifies Christ, as in Ezekiel: “From its midst, something resembling the appearance of electrum” [Note: [Col. 0915] 10 Ezekiel 1:4]; that is, on the last day Jesus Christ will appear as judge of the living and the dead. He is God and man, just as electrum is mixed from gold and silver.

Emulation is good, as in the Song: “Emulation is hard as hell” [Note: [Col. 0915] 11 Song of Songs 8:6]; that is, holy men are severely inflamed by good zeal.

Emulation is bad, as in the Psalms: “Do not emulate those who do evil” [Note: [Col. 0915] 12 Psalm 36:1]; that is, do not be displeased that you are not like the wicked.

Emulation signifies a good example, as in Paul: “And our emulation stirred up many” [Note: [Col. 0915] 13 2 Corinthians 9:2]; that is, our good example aroused very many.

Snuffers signify the two Testaments, as in Exodus: “Let the snuffers be made of purest gold” [Note: [Col. 0915] 14 Exodus 25:38]; that is, each Testament shines with the brightness of wisdom.

Sword signifies the rigor of continence, as in the Song: “Each one’s sword is upon your thigh” [Note: [Col. 0915] 15 Song of Songs 3:8]; that is, through the rigor of continence the elect put to death their members that are upon the earth.

Sword signifies the sharpness of preaching, as in the Books of Kings: “David was girded with his sword” [Note: [Col. 0915] 16 1 Kings 25:3]; that is, Christ was armed with his preaching to overthrow the devil’s wickedness.

Engadi means “the fountain of the kid,” and signifies baptism, as in the Song: “My beloved is to me in the vineyards of Engadi” [Note: [Col. 0915] 17 Song of Songs 5:14]; that is, Christ, whom I love, appears spiritually in those who have been washed in baptism.

Engadi signifies repentance, as in the Books of Kings: “Behold, David dwells in the safest places of Engadi” [Note: [Col. 0915] 18 1 Kings 24:1]; that is, Christ dwells in those whom repentance makes secure.

Horse signifies the humanity of Christ, as in the Apocalypse: “Behold, a white horse” [Note: [Col. 0915] 19 Revelation 6:2]; that is, Christ’s flesh shines with every holiness.

Horse signifies any preacher, as in Job: “Will you give strength to the horse?” [Note: [Col. 0915] 20 Job 39:22]; that is, God alone appears to confer the strength for good work upon the preacher.

Horse signifies any ungodly person, as in the Song: “He will cast horse and rider into the sea” [Note: [Col. 0915] 21 Exodus 15:1]; that is, the Lord plunges any ungodly person, together with the devil who rules him, into hell.

Horse signifies this present age, as in Genesis: “Biting the horse’s hooves” [Note: [Col. 0915] 22 Genesis 49:17]; that is, the Antichrist will exercise his cruelty at the end of the age.

Horse signifies the human body, as in Proverbs: “A horse is prepared for the day of battle” [Note: [Col. 0915] 23 Proverbs 21:31]; that is, the body offered to the danger of death.

Horse signifies secular honor, as in the Psalms: “The horse is deceptive for salvation” [Note: [Col. 0915] 24 Psalm 32:17]; that is, worldly honor cannot confer salvation upon a person.

Blind horse signifies a persecutor, as in the Apocalypse: “And behold, a red horse” [Note: [Col. 0915] 25 Revelation 6:4]; that is, the persecutors of the saints were cruel.

Horse signifies the outward form of heretics, as in the Apocalypse: “And behold, a black horse” [Note: [Col. 0915] 26 Ibid., verse 5]; that is, heretics become black through the ugliness of error.

Horse signifies the Antichrist, as in the Apocalypse: “And behold, a pale horse” [Note: [Col. 0915] 27 Ibid., verse 8]; that is, however great the pride of the Antichrist may be, it will fail at the end.

Horse signifies any lustful person, as in the Psalms: “Do not become like a horse and a mule” [Note: [Col. 0915] 28 Psalm 31:9]; that is, do not be lustful and unfruitful.

Through horses signify the apostles, as in Exodus: “You sent your horses into the sea”—that is, your preachers into the whole world.

Through horses signify the proud and the rich, as in Isaiah: “Woe to those who go down into Egypt, hoping in horses” [Note: [Col. 0915] 29 Isaiah 31:1]; that is, woe to those who love the world excessively and trust in abundant possessions.

Through horses signify works, as in the Apocalypse: “They followed him on white horses” [Note: [Col. 0915] 30 Revelation 19:14]; that is, the saints imitated his passion in their works.

Through horses signify thoughts, as in Deuteronomy: “The king shall not multiply horses for himself” [Note: [Col. 0915] 31 Deuteronomy 17:16]; that is, a prelate shall not have proud thoughts.

Horse signifies any saint, as in Job: “He mocks the horse and its rider” [Note: [Col. 0915] 32 Job 39:21]; that is, the devil despises in his imitators every holy man, and God who rules him.

Rust signifies pride, as in the Gospel: “Where rust destroys” [Note: [Col. 0915] 33 Matthew 6:19–20]; that is, do not seek to please human beings in your work and lose it through pride.

Caterpillar signifies lust, as in Joel: “What the caterpillar left, the locust ate” [Note: [Col. 0917] 1 Joel 1:4]; that is, whenever any wicked person abandons lust, he immediately becomes proud of his chastity.

Hedgehogs signify penitents, as in the Psalms: “The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs” [Note: [Col. 0917] 2 Psalm 103:18]; that is, Christ mercifully receives penitents.

The hedgehog signifies the vice of excuse-making, as in Isaiah: “There the hedgehog has its form” [Note: [Col. 0917] 3 Isaiah 34:15]; that is, the vice of excuse-making lies hidden in a wicked person.

Bronze signifies the strength of the angels, as in Job: “They are like the most solid things, as though cast in bronze” [Note: [Col. 0917] 4 Job 37]; that is, they have been established in great strength.

Bronze signifies good action, as in Exodus: “Gold and silver and bronze” [Note: [Col. 0917] 5 Exodus 25:3]; that is, wisdom, preaching, and good action.

Bronze signifies an insensible heart, as in Job: “Nor is my flesh bronze” [Note: [Col. 0917] 6 Job 6:12]; that is, my heart is not insensible.

Bronze signifies condemnation, as in Job: “He rushes upon a bronze bow” [Note: [Col. 0917] 7 Job 20:24]; that is, he rushes into eternal condemnation.

Bronze also signifies the strength of incorruption, as in Ezekiel: “Behold, a man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze” [Note: [Col. 0917] 8 Ezekiel 40:3]; that is, Christ has been strengthened with every strength of incorruption.

Bronze signifies strengthening, as in Ezekiel: “Like the appearance of glowing bronze” [Note: [Col. 0917] 9 Ezekiel 1:7]; that is, of an inflamed preaching.

Heshbon means “a belt of mourning,” and signifies the holy Church, as in the Song: “Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon” [Note: [Col. 0917] 10 Song of Songs 7:4]; that is, preachers baptize in the Church.

Heshbon signifies a pierced heart, as in the Book of Numbers: “Fire went out from Heshbon” [Note: [Col. 0917] 11 Numbers 21:28]; that is, the love of God proceeds from a pierced heart.

Food signifies the body of Christ, as in the Psalms: “He gave food to those who fear him” [Note: [Col. 0917] 12 Psalm 110:5]; that is, he gave his flesh to those who fear him.

Food signifies the refreshment of the heavenly homeland, as in Job: “From there he observes food” [Note: [Col. 0917] 13 Job 39:32]; that is, he gazes upon how great the satiety in heaven is.

Food signifies simple doctrine, as in the Psalms: “He gives their food to the beasts” [Note: [Col. 0917] 14 Psalm 146:9]; that is, he grants the unlearned doctrine suited to them.

Food signifies desire, as in the Psalms: “He gives them food in due season” [Note: [Col. 0917] 15 Psalm 144:15]; that is, so that their desire may be pleasing.

Food signifies any saint, as in the prophet: “His food is choice”; that is, the devil also strives to incorporate a holy man.

Through food signify the sacrifices of the Law, as in Paul: “Not by foods, which did not benefit those who relied upon them” [Note: [Col. 0917] 16 Hebrews 13:9]; that is, not by shadowy sacrifices, which did not benefit those who trusted in them.

Summer signifies the kingdom of God, as in the Gospel: “You know that summer is near” [Note: [Col. 0917] 17 Matthew 24:32]; that is, the kingdom of God.

Summer signifies the present life, as in Proverbs: “He prepares food in summer” [Note: [Col. 0917] 18 Proverbs 6:8]; that is, spiritual refreshment in the present life.

Summer signifies the day of judgment, as in Proverbs: “He will beg in summer, and it will not be given to him” [Note: [Col. 0917] 19 Proverbs 20:4]; he will ask for the support of life on the day of judgment, and will not receive it.

Summer signifies every perfect person, as in the Psalms: “You formed summer and spring” [Note: [Col. 0917] 20 Psalm 73:17]; that is, you formed the perfect and the foolish.

Ether signifies the angels, as in Proverbs: “When he makes the ether firm above” [Note: [Col. 0917] 21 Proverbs 8:28]; that is, when he confirms the angels in the heavenly city.

Ether signifies the fathers of the New Testament, as in Job: “Consider the ether, how it is higher than you” [Note: [Col. 0917] 22 Job 35:5]; that is, consider the fathers of the New Testament, for God is higher than you.

Eternal signifies what has neither beginning nor end, as in the Book of Ecclesiasticus: “He who lives forever created all things together” [Note: [Col. 0917] 23 Ecclesiasticus 18:1]; and he made the nature of invisible things and the matter of visible things in the angels.

Eternal signifies what has a beginning but no end, as in the Psalms: “I will sing of the mercies of the Lord forever” [Note: [Col. 0917] 24 Psalm 88:1]; that is, the elect will begin to sing of the mercies of the Lord but will never cease.

Eternal signifies the present age, as in the Song of Exodus: “The Lord will reign forever and beyond” [Note: [Col. 0917] 25 Exodus 15:18]; that is, in this age and in the future.

[Col. 0918B] Ethiopia means this world, as in Job: “The topaz of Ethiopia cannot be compared with it” [Note: [Col. 0917] 26 Job 28:19], meaning that no one from this world, however splendid he may be, can be compared with Christ, who is the wisdom of the Father. Ethiopia means the Gentiles, as in the Psalms: “Ethiopia will stretch out her hands to God” [Note: [Col. 0917] 27 Psalm 67:32], meaning that the Jewish people will anticipate them. Ethiopia means the assembly of the reprobate, as in Habakkuk: “On account of iniquity I saw the tents of Ethiopia” [Note: [Col. 0917] 28 Habakkuk 3:7], meaning: I contemplated that the breadth of the reprobate was condemned because of iniquity.

Ethiopians mean sinners, as in the Psalms: “Before him the Ethiopians will fall” [Note: [Col. 0917] 29 Psalm 71:9], meaning that sinners will prostrate themselves before him in repentance.

An exactor is the devil, as in Job: “They did not heed the voice of the exactor” [Note: [Col. 0917] 30 Job 3:18], meaning: they did not consent to the suggestion of the tempting devil. An exactor is the appetite of the belly, as in Job: “He does not heed the cry of the exactor” [Note: [Col. 0917] 31 Job 39:10], meaning that he does not obey the appetite of the belly immoderately. An exactor is an evil habit, as in Isaiah: “How has the exactor ceased?” [Note: [Col. 0917] 32 Isaiah 14:4], meaning: by what action has the violent habit of sin been made to cease?

Explorers are those who rebuke, as in Genesis: “You are explorers; you came to see the weaker parts of the land” [Note: [Col. 0917] 33 Genesis 42:9], meaning that it is characteristic of the wicked to investigate the faults of others, in case they should discover some weakness in them that they can accuse. Explorers mean the Two Testaments, as in Joshua: “Joshua sent explorers to Jericho” [Note: [Col. 0917] 34 Joshua 2:1], meaning that Christ sent the Two Testaments to the Church. Explorers mean preachers, as in the Book of Numbers: “The explorers of the land returned” [Note: [Col. 0917] 35 Numbers 13:26], meaning that preachers return to themselves through their preaching.

An army is a multitude of angels, as in the Books of Kings: “All the army of heaven standing beside him” [Note: [Col. 0917] 36 3 Kings 22:19], meaning that a multitude of angels stands beside God. An army is an assembly of demons, as in the Song of Exodus: “And he cast his army into the sea” [Note: [Col. 0919] 1 Exodus 15:4], meaning that God condemned the multitude of demons to hell. An army means vices, as in Job: “And the howling of the army” [Note: [Col. 0919] 2 Job 39:28], that is, the uproar of vices. By an army, the holy martyrs are meant, as in the Apocalypse: “The armies that are in heaven followed him” [Note: [Col. 0919] 3 Revelation 19:14], that is, the martyrs who were in the world imitated Christ.

Exits mean defects, as in the Gospel: “Go out to the exits of the roads*” [Note: [Col. 0919] 4 Matthew 22:9], and call those who are strong in good works. Exits mean compunctions, as in the Psalms: “My eyes have brought forth exits of waters” [Note: [Col. 0919] 5 Psalm 118:136], that is, the outpourings of tears caused by compunction. Exits mean abandonment of sin, as in the Psalms: “At the departure of Israel from Egypt” [Note: [Col. 0919] 6 Psalm 113:1], that is, when the elect person abandons his sin and withdraws from it.

## F

[Col. 0919B]

Quiver. Face. Bundle. Fig. Daughter. Firmament. Basket. Flower. Opening. Strong. Forehead. Iron. Bridle. Phrygia. Lightning. Thunderbolt. Wave. Sling. Streams. Cold. Grain. Pit. Flame. Flour. Fragment. Honeycomb. Ash. Thigh. Underclothes. Window. Smith. Straw. Phial. Son. Daughter. Fringe. Pipe. Leaf. Spring. Litter. Foundation. End. Radiance. Rivers. River. Smoke. Tongs. Strength. Rope. Thief. Fruit. Ditch. Dregs. Famine. Brother. Spear. Throat. Gall. [Col. 0919C] Woman. Beast.

A quiver is the hidden judgment of God, as in Job: “He opened his quiver” [Note: [Col. 0919] 7 Job 30:11], that is, he brought down his* hidden judgment. A quiver is the plotting of the wicked, as in the Psalms: “They prepared their arrows in the quiver” [Note: [Col. 0919] 8 Psalm 10:2], that is, they devised their evil plans through plotting. A quiver is the counsels of the saints, as in Job: “The quiver will resound over him*” [Note: [Col. 0919] 9 Job 39:26], that is, the counsels of the saints will advance to overcome the devil. A quiver is Sacred Scripture, as in Genesis: “Take your weapons, your quiver and your bow” [Note: [Col. 0919] 10 Genesis 27:3], that is, sanctification—namely, Sacred Scripture—and preaching.

A smith is the devil, as in the prophet: “Behold, I shall send the smith who blows” [Note: [Col. 0919] 11 Isaiah 54:16], that is, I shall permit the tempting devil to afflict them. A smith is any obstinate person, as in Isaiah: “The smith cast a *bundle” [Note: [Col. 0919] 12 Isaiah 40:19], meaning that every obstinate person confirms in his heart whatever he has fashioned. A smith is a flatterer, as in Isaiah: “The smith worked with a file” [Note: [Col. 0919] 13 Isaiah 44:12], that is, the harsh flatterer spoke by *flattering. A smith is Christ, as in the Gospel: “Is this not the smith?” [Note: [Col. 0919] 14 Mark 6:3], meaning that he himself fashioned all things.

[Col. 0920A] A face is God the Father, as in the Gospel: “Their angels always see the face of my Father” [Note: [Col. 0919] 15 Matthew 18:10], that is, they continually gaze upon God the Father. A face is the Son, as in the Psalms: “How long will you turn your face away from me?” [Note: [Col. 0919] 16 Psalm 12:1], that is, how long will you delay sending Christ, whom you are going to send? A face is the presence of God, as in the Psalms: “Do not turn your face away from me” [Note: [Col. 0919] 17 Psalms 26:9; 101:3; 142:7], that is, do not deny me your presence in the future. A face is the knowledge of God, as in the Psalms: “Seek his face always” [Note: [Col. 0919] 18 Psalm 104:4], that is, desire at all times to attain knowledge of God. A face is the benevolence of God, as in the Psalms: “Do not cast me away from your face” [Note: [Col. 0919] 19 Psalm 50:13], that is, do not allow me, once renewed, to be cast away from your face, that is, from your benevolence. A face is the knowledge possessed by God, as in the Psalms: “He turned his face away, lest he see to the end” [Note: [Col. 0919] 20 Psalm 9:32], that is, he does not have the knowledge by which he could know our evils. A face is the protection of God, as in Habakkuk: “Before his face death will go” [Note: [Col. 0919] 21 Habakkuk 3:5], that is, where God protects, the devil cannot prevail. A face is the attention of God, as in Job: “Then I shall not be hidden from your face” [Note: [Col. 0919] 22 Job 13:20], that is, if I am such a person, I do not fear your attention.

A face is each individual faithful person who is known by the Lord. Hence the four Evangelists are described in Ezekiel under the form of four living creatures: “Each had four faces, and each had four wings” [Note: [Col. 0919] 23 Ezekiel 1:6], meaning that the same faith of contemplation and the same contemplation of divinity existed in each one as existed in all. A face is the Church, as in the Apocalypse: “Her face was like the sun shining in its strength” [Note: [Col. 0919] 24 Revelation 17:16], meaning that the holy Church is illuminated by Christ and illuminates her children for the imitation of Christ. A face is the human heart, as in Job: “You will lift up your face to God” [Note: [Col. 0919] 25 Job 22:26], that is, you will raise your heart to God. A face is intention, as in Job: “Fatness covered his face” [Note: [Col. 0919] 26 Job 15:17], that is, excessive abundance corrupted his intention. A face is conscience, as in the Gospel: “When you fast, anoint your head” [Note: [Col. 0919] 27 Matthew 6:17], that is, make your mind joyful, “and wash your face,” that is, lay bare your conscience. A face is any preacher, as in Job: “My face swelled from weeping” [Note: [Col. 0919] 28 Job 16:16], that is, my preachers have been filled with grief. A face is a good action, as in the Song: “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears” [Note: [Col. 0919] 29 Song of Songs 2:14]; let a face be shown to the Lord by doing good, and let a voice also be shown by preaching what brings salvation. A face is the Old Law, as in Exodus: “He placed a veil over his *face” [Note: [Col. 0919] 30 Exodus 34:33], meaning that the Old Law is covered by a *veil. A face is the presence of Antichrist, as in Job: “Poverty precedes his face” [Note: [Col. 0919] 31 Job 41:13], meaning that, as the coming of Antichrist approaches, there will be a lack of holiness in the world.

A bundle is the passion of Christ, as in the Song: “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me” [Note: [Col. 0919] 32 Song of Songs 1:13], that is, Christ sets before me as an example the passion of his death. By a bundle, sins are meant, as in Isaiah: “Loose the bundles that weigh down” [Note: [Col. 0921] 1 Isaiah 53:6], that is, cast away from yourself the sins that oppress you. By a bundle, gatherings of the condemned are meant, as in the Gospel: “Bind the bundles to burn them” [Note: [Col. 0921] 2 Matthew 13:20], meaning that those who were companions in guilt here will be companions in punishment there.

A sickle is the divine judgment, as in the Apocalypse: “And in his hand a sharp sickle” [Note: [Col. 0921] 3 Revelation 14:14], meaning that Christ holds strict judgment in his power. A sickle is death, as in the Gospel: “Immediately he puts in the sickle” [Note: [Col. 0921] 4 Mark 4:29], meaning that the time has come, because whenever any elect person reaches perfect holiness, he is taken away through death to heavenly rest.

A flame is knowledge, as in Exodus: “God appeared to him in a flame of fire” [Note: [Col. 0921] 5 Exodus 3:2], that is, in knowledge of the Law. A flame is any preacher, as in the Apocalypse: “His eyes were like a flame of fire” [Note: [Col. 0921] 6 Revelation 1:14], meaning that holy preachers inflame and set others alight. A flame is pleasure, as in Job: “A flame will dry up his branches” [Note: [Col. 0921] 7 Job 15:30], that is, pleasure will destroy his works. A flame is temporal glory, as in Job: “Nor will the flame of his fire shine” [Note: [Col. 0921] 8 Job 18:5], that is, the glory of his pleasure will not endure. A flame is the intensity of an evil desire, as in the Psalms: “The voice of the Lord cutting through the flame of fire” [Note: [Col. 0921] 9 Psalm 28:7], that is, the preaching of Christ destroying the fervor of evil desire. A flame is the devil’s instigation, as in Job: “And a flame will come forth from his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0921] 10 Job 41:12], meaning that instigation toward evil proceeds from the devil. By a flame, good preaching or good examples are meant, as in the Song: “Its lamps are lamps of fire and flames” [Note: [Col. 0921] 11 Song of Songs 8:6], meaning that holy men burn with love of God and offer good examples to others.

Famine is lack of virtue, as in Job: “Let his strength be weakened by famine” [Note: [Col. 0921] 12 Job 18:12], meaning that every wicked person, because of lack of holiness, does not possess spiritual strength. Famine is temptation, as in Job: “In famine he will rescue you from death” [Note: [Col. 0921] 13 Job 5:20], that is, in temptation he will protect you so that you do not consent. Famine is evil silence, as in the prophet: “Not a famine of bread, but of hearing the word of God” [Note: [Col. 0921] 14 Amos 8:11].

Flour is a pure thought, as in Hosea: “There is no sprout in it, and it will not make flour” [Note: [Col. 0921] 15 Hosea 8:7], that is, there is no good desire in it, and there is no pure heart in it. Flour is the soul, as in Genesis: “Mix three measures of flour” [Note: [Col. 0921] 16 Genesis 18:6], that is, bring the memory, reason, and will of your soul into one harmony. Flour is the thought of the wicked, as in Isaiah: “Take the millstone; grind flour” [Note: [Col. 0921] 17 Isaiah 47:2], that is, take up the circuit of external cares, and never exercise thought within yourself.

By the designation “brother,” Christ is understood, as in the Song concerning the Synagogue that will be converted at the end of the world: “Who would grant me my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother, so that I might find you outside and kiss you, and no one would despise you?” [Note: [Col. 0921] 18 Song of Songs 8:1]. It is as though it said: Would that someone might show me Christ, who was born according to the flesh from the Jews. He heard the teachers of the Law on each Sabbath, so that, understanding him to be a true human being, I may find his complete peace, and so that the Gentiles may no longer call me blinded and rejected.

A brother is any Christian, as in Paul: “If anyone is named a brother” [Note: [Col. 0921] 19 1 Corinthians 5:11], that is, if anyone is regarded as a Christian. A brother is any good person, as in the Gospel: “If anyone does the will of my Father, he is my brother” [Note: [Col. 0921] 20 Matthew 12:50]. By “brothers,” the apostles are meant, as in the Gospel: “Go to my brothers” [Note: [Col. 0921] 21 Mark 3:35], that is, to my disciples. By “brothers,” Christ’s relatives are meant, as in the Gospel: “Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside” [Note: [Col. 0921] 22 Matthew 12:47].

People are called brothers in four ways: by nature, as Esau and Jacob [Note: [Col. 0921] 23 Genesis 25:24–25]; by nation, as all the Jews [Note: [Col. 0921] 24 Romans 9:3–4]; by kinship, as Abraham and Lot [Note: [Col. 0921] 25 Genesis 12:5]; and by affection, as all who preserve faith toward one another [Note: [Col. 0921] 26 1 Kings 18:1; 2 Kings 1:26].

A fragment is the passion of Christ, as in the Song: “Your cheeks are like a fragment of a pomegranate” [Note: [Col. 0921] 27 Song of Songs 4:3], meaning that Christ’s holy martyrs imitate his passion. By a fragment, the more secret matters of the Law are meant, as in the Gospel: “Gather the fragments that remain” [Note: [Col. 0921] 28 John 6:12], meaning that teachers ought to preserve among themselves the more secret matters of the Law, which lesser persons cannot grasp.

A spear is Christ, as in the Psalms: “Pour out the spear” [Note: [Col. 0921] 29 Psalm 34:3], that is, make Christ known to the world, through whom you have conquered the ancient enemy. A spear is the soul, as in the Psalms: “Your spear from the enemies of your hand” [Note: [Col. 0921] 30 Psalm 16:13], that is, rescue the soul from the ungodly. A spear is death, as in the Psalms: “Rescue from the spear” [Note: [Col. 0921] 31 Psalm 21:21], that is, “God, rescue my soul from death.” By a spear, temptations are meant, as in the Psalms: “The enemies’ spears have failed” [Note: [Col. 0921] 32 Psalm 9:7], that is, the devil’s temptations have been weakened through Christ.

A honeycomb is divinity, as in the Gospel: “A portion of broiled fish and a honeycomb” [Note: [Col. 0921] 33 Luke 24:42], meaning that, after giving us the example of his passion, he will refresh us in the resurrection through his divinity. A honeycomb is Christ’s humanity, as in the Song: “I ate the honeycomb with my honey” [Note: [Col. 0921] 34 Song of Songs 5:1], that is, I believed that the greatest humanity existed together with divinity. A honeycomb is the literal understanding, as in Proverbs: “And the honeycomb is sweet to my throat” [Note: [Col. 0921] 35 Proverbs 24:13], that is, the letter of Sacred Scripture is exceedingly sweet to my heart.

Likewise, the honeycomb in which honey lies hidden is Sacred Scripture, which contains the spiritual meaning within the letter. Hence Solomon says: “Eat honey, my *son, and the sweetest honeycomb for your throat” [Note: [Col. 0921] 36 Ibid.], meaning the teaching of preaching. Hence also: “Your lips drip with honeycomb” [Note: [Col. 0921] 37 Proverbs 5:3], that is, preaching that instructs proceeds from your preachers, O Church! A honeycomb is worldly pleasure, as in Proverbs: “A soul that is full will trample the honeycomb” [Note: [Col. 0921] 38 Proverbs 27:7], meaning that the person *whom inward refreshment satisfies through contemplation almost despises worldly pleasure.

[Col. 0923A] Throats are knowledge, as in Job: “And the throat of the eater tests flavor?” [Note: [Col. 0923] 1 Job 12:11], meaning that the knowledge of the reader discerns inward wisdom. Throats are the meditations of the heart, as in the Psalms: “How sweet are they to my throats” [Note: [Col. 0923] 2 Psalm 118:103], that is, his Scriptures are sweet in my meditations. Throats are words, as in Job: “Nor will folly resound in my throats” [Note: [Col. 0923] 3 Job 6:30], that is, foolishness will not be heard in my words.

Ash is remembrance of mortality, as in Job: “I repent in ash and dust” [Note: [Col. 0923] 4 Job 42:6], that is, in remembrance of my mortality. Ash is an iniquitous mind, as in Job: “Like ash scattered by the whirlwind” [Note: [Col. 0923] 5 Job 21:18], meaning that temptation destroys a perverse mind.

Gall is the persuasion of demons, as in Job: “The gall of asps within” [Note: [Col. 0923] 6 Job 20:14], that is, the persuasion of demons in the mind. Gall is unbelief, as in the Psalms: “They gave me gall for food” [Note: [Col. 0923] 7 Psalm 68:22], that is, the Jews fed me with the bitterness of unbelief. Gall is the malice of the devil, as in Tobit: “Disembowel this fish and keep the gall for yourself” [Note: [Col. 0923] 8 Tobit 6:5], meaning that the Lord exposed the devil and enclosed his malice in the sacred books.

A thigh is Christ’s humanity, as in the Psalms: “Gird yourself with your sword upon your thigh” [Note: [Col. 0923] 9 Psalm 44:4], that is, use the word of preaching manfully against the world—you who are most mighty in the humanity you assumed. A thigh means the saints, when John says of Christ in the Apocalypse: “On his garment and on his thigh he has written: King of kings and Lord of lords” [Note: [Col. 0923] 10 Revelation 19:16]. For Christ’s flesh, which he placed at the right hand of the Father, and the saints, begotten by the seed of the divine word, bear witness from him that authority has been given to him over good and evil. A thigh is offspring, as in Genesis: “The souls who came forth from Jacob’s thigh” [Note: [Col. 0923] 11 Genesis 46:26], that is, people descended from Jacob. A thigh is the pleasure of the flesh, as in Exodus: “Let a man put on his sword” [Note: [Col. 0923] 12 Exodus 32:27], that is, let him mortify his heart through severity.

A woman is carnal affection, as in Exodus: *“If it is a female, preserve it” [Note: [Col. 0923] 13 Exodus 1:16], meaning that the devil desires carnal affections to be nourished. “Woman” is also understood according to sex, as in Genesis: “He made them male and female” [Note: [Col. 0923] 14 Genesis 1:27], meaning that he distinguished the human race by two sexes, namely male and female.

Underclothes are the insignia of chastity, as in Exodus: “You shall make linen underclothes” [Note: [Col. 0923] 15 Exodus 28:42], meaning that the Law invites us to the splendor of chastity.

Grass is a transitory thing, as in Isaiah: “All flesh is grass” [Note: [Col. 0923] 16 Isaiah 40:6], that is, every human being is transitory. Grass is temporal support, as in the Psalms: “Bringing forth grass for cattle” [Note: [Col. 0923] 17 Psalm 103:14], meaning that the lower multitude supplies temporal support to its cultivators. Grass is anyone simple in faith, as in the Apocalypse: “So that they should not harm the grass of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0923] 18 Revelation 9:4], that is, so that they should not impede the inexperienced in faith, “nor any green thing, nor any tree,” that is, those who are advanced and perfect. Grass is a good work, as in Genesis: “Let the earth bring forth green *grass” [Note: [Col. 0923] 19 Genesis 1:11], that is, let the devout soul bring forth good action. Grass is any carnal person, as in Job: “Behemoth eats grass like an ox” [Note: [Col. 0923] 20 Job 40:10], meaning that the devil, who is fashioned as a scourge for you, delights like a fool in the life of the carnal.

A window is the mouth of a human being, as in the Book of Joshua: “She tied the scarlet cord in the window” [Note: [Col. 0923] 21 Joshua 2:18, 21], meaning that the holy Church does not cease to preach Christ’s passion with her mouth. A window is the faithful person, as in the Books of Kings: “Open the eastern window” [Note: [Col. 0923] 22 4 Kings 13:17], that is, have Christian faith within yourself. Through a window, Christ’s miracles are meant, as in the Song: “Looking through the windows” [Note: [Col. 0923] 23 Song of Songs 2:9], meaning that through the miracles he performed outwardly, his hidden divinity came forth to us. Through windows, the teachers of the Church are meant, as in the Books of Kings: “Solomon made windows in the temple” [Note: [Col. 0923] 24 3 Kings 6:4], meaning that Christ instructed teachers in the Church. Through windows, inward contemplations are meant, as in Ezekiel: “He made slanting windows in the chambers” [Note: [Col. 0923] 25 Ezekiel 40:16], meaning that the Lord places inward *contemplations in the minds of his elect. Through windows, the senses of the heart are meant, as in Isaiah: “Like doves to their windows” [Note: [Col. 0923] 26 Isaiah 60:8], meaning that holy men keep their external senses simple and unharmed by sin.

A beast is the savagery of the Jews, as in Genesis: “An evil beast devoured Joseph” [Note: [Col. 0923] 27 Genesis 37:20; Psalm 78:10], that is, the savagery of the Jews killed Christ. By a beast, the Gentiles are meant, as in the Psalms: “All the beasts of the forests are mine” [Note: [Col. 0923] 28 Matthew 13:33], that is, the Gentiles throughout the world will believe in me.

Leaven is charity, as in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened” [Note: [Col. 0923] 29 1 Corinthians 5:6]. The kingdom of heaven is the holy Church, in which this likeness is spiritually fulfilled. For Christ, the power of God and wisdom of God, received from the Father *of the Lord’s charity, which he gave to the three orders of the faithful, so that they might *diligently love God and neighbor according to the letter. A satum is a kind of measure, or [uncertain: *]. The woman is Christ’s flesh. Leaven is the Gospel. The three measures are all the nations, *because of the three sons of Noah.

Leaven is pride, as in Paul: “A little leaven corrupts the whole mass” [Note: [Col. 0923] 30 Matthew 8:15], meaning that a wrong choice destroys many good things. Leaven is dissimulation, as in the Gospel: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy” [Note: [Col. 0923] 31 Luke 12:1], that is, do not cover with simulated virtues the faith that you preach in words. Leaven is malice, as in Paul: “Purge out the old leaven” [Note: [Col. 0923] 32 1 Corinthians 5:7], that is, cleanse yourselves from the oldness of malice. Leaven is the desire for praise, as in Leviticus: “Loaves without leaven” [Note: [Col. 0925] 1 Leviticus 2:4; 7:12; 8:26], that is, good works without desire for human praise.

Iron is the gift of understanding, as in the Books of Kings: “The iron floated, and he said, ‘Take it’” [Note: [Col. 0925] 2 4 Kings 6:6]. The gift of understanding returns to the humbled heart; it had been lost through pride. Iron is preaching, as in Job: “He will regard iron as straw” [Note: [Col. 0925] 3 Job 41:18], meaning that the devil will regard the dart of preaching in his minds as though it were something contemptible. Iron is tribulation, as in the Psalms: “Iron passed through his soul” [Note: [Col. 0925] 4 Psalm 104:18], that is, harsh tribulation weighed down his life. Iron is the harsh habit of sin, as in the Psalms: “Bound in misery and iron” [Note: [Col. 0925] 5 Psalm 106:10], meaning that they were in spiritual want and a harsh habit. Iron is holy men, as in Job: “Iron is taken from the earth” [Note: [Col. 0925] 6 Job 28:2], meaning that one who was soft and carnal has now become spiritual and strong. Iron is a harsh word, as in Deuteronomy: “And the iron slipped from the handle and struck his companion” [Note: [Col. 0925] 7 Deuteronomy 19:5], meaning that a harsh word spoken indiscreetly offends the hearer. Iron is spiritual strength, as in Ezekiel: “Take for yourself an iron griddle” [Note: [Col. 0925] 8 Ezekiel 4:3], meaning that every prelate ought to exercise spiritual strength in his zeal. Iron is the necessity of the present life, as in Job: “He will flee iron weapons and rush upon a bronze bow” [Note: [Col. 0925] 9 Job 20:24], meaning that every wicked person, while refusing to endure the harshness of the present life for God, rushes into eternal damnation. Iron is the wickedness of the evil, as in Job: “His cartilage is like plates of iron” [Note: [Col. 0925] 10 Job 40:13], meaning that the wicked oppress the good through hard wickedness.

[Col. 0925C] A litter is the virgin Mary, the holy Church, the faithful soul, and the heavenly homeland, as in this single example from the Song: “King Solomon made himself a litter from *the wood of Lebanon” [Note: [Col. 0925] 11 Song of Songs 3:9]. Christ chose both the body of the Virgin, composed of incorruptible members; built the holy Church from holy men; adorned the human soul with pure thoughts; and gladdens the heavenly homeland, which consists of good citizens.

A bridle is ignorance, as in Isaiah: “And the bridle of error that was in the jaw of the peoples” [Note: [Col. 0925] 12 Isaiah 30:28], that is, the ignorance that was in the hearts of human beings. A bridle is silence, as in Job: “He placed a bridle in my mouth” [Note: [Col. 0925] 13 Job 30:11]. A bridle is affliction of the flesh, as in the Psalms: “Bind their jaws with bit and bridle” [Note: [Col. 0925] 14 Psalm 31:9], that is, humble their hearts through severity and affliction.

A straw is disturbance of the mind, as in the Gospel: “You will see to remove the straw from your brother’s eye” [Note: [Col. 0925] 15 Matthew 7:5], that is, you will be able to rebuke the agitation of another’s heart.

Dregs are the letter of the Law, as in the Psalms: “Its dregs have not been emptied” [Note: [Col. 0925] 16 Psalm 74:9], meaning that the still-carnal letter has been retained among the Jews. By dregs, sins are meant, as in the prophet: “He rested upon his dregs” [Note: [Col. 0925] 17 Jeremiah 48:11].

A phial is the human soul, as in the Book of Judges: “In a phial he offered butter to the prince” [Note: [Col. 0925] 18 Judges 5], meaning that in our soul we ought to possess charity for the destruction of the prince of the world. By a phial, teachers are meant, as in Exodus: “You shall prepare *bowls and phials” [Note: [Col. 0925] 19 Exodus 25:29], meaning that the Lord sent apostles and teachers to the holy Church.

A fig is sweetness of mind, as in the prophet: “I will destroy its vine and its fig tree” [Note: [Col. 0925] 20 Hosea 2:12], meaning that in necessity God sometimes permits both contemplation and sweetness to be impaired in a human being. A fig is the human race, as in the Gospel: “Someone had a fig tree planted” [Note: [Col. 0925] 21 Luke 13:6], meaning that the human race has its nature created by God. A fig is the holy Church, as in the Song: “The fig tree has put forth her *unripe figs” [Note: [Col. 0925] 22 Song of Songs 2:13], that is, the holy Church has brought forth her martyrs. A fig is the Jewish people, as in the song of Habakkuk: “For the fig tree will not blossom” [Note: [Col. 0925] 23 Habakkuk 3:17], that is, the Jewish people will not possess the splendor of faith.
