A fig is the shadow of the Law, as in the Gospel: “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you” [Note: [Col. 0925] 24 John 1:48], that is, placed under the shadow of the Law, I chose you. A fig is the human mind, as in Joel: “He stripped my fig tree” [Note: [Col. 0925] 25 Joel 1:7], that is, he laid bare my mind through human praise. A fig is charity, as in the Gospel: “Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?” [Note: [Col. 0925] 26 Matthew 7:16]. Thorns and thistles are heretics, among whom no one can find spiritual understanding or the sweetness of charity.

[Col. 0926C] A son is Christ, as in the Psalms: “Save the son of your handmaid” [Note: [Col. 0925] 27 Psalm 85:16], namely, of her who said: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0925] 28 Luke 1:38]. A son is any member of the Church, as in the Gospel: “The only dead son of his mother was being carried out” [Note: [Col. 0925] 29 Luke 7:12], meaning that everyone who returns to life through repentance is a son of the Church. A son is the Jewish people, as in the Gospel: “The elder son was in the field” [Note: [Col. 0925] 30 Luke 15:25], meaning that, when the Gentile people were called to faith, the Jewish people remained in external things through error. Foreign sons are the Jews, who have grown old while remaining in the old person. Foreign sons are heretics, that is, those who preach error, “whose mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0925] 31 Psalm 143:8]. A son is the people of the Gentiles, as in the Gospel: “My son was dead and has come to life again” [Note: [Col. 0925] 32 Luke 15:24], that is, the Gentile people fell into death through unbelief and returned to life through faith.

By “sons,” angels are meant, as in Job: “One day, when the sons of God had come” [Note: [Col. 0925] 33 Job 1:6 and 2:1], meaning that the good angels are sons of the supreme Father. By “sons,” the apostles are meant, as in the Gospel: “The sons of the bridegroom cannot mourn” [Note: [Col. 0925] 34 Matthew 9:15], that is, the apostles of Christ cannot grieve. By “sons,” the Jews are meant, as in the Gospel: “It is not good to take the children’s bread” [Note: [Col. 0925] 35 Matthew 15:26], that is, the salvation destined for the Jews.

[Col. 0927A] By “sons,” holy men are meant, as in the Epistle of John: “Now we are sons of God” [Note: [Col. 0927] 1 1 John 3:2], meaning that through faith and good works we are born from God. By “sons,” those who return from a good life to iniquity are meant, as in the Psalms: “Foreign sons have lied to me and have limped away from your* paths” [Note: [Col. 0927] 2 Psalm 17:45–46], meaning that they withdrew from good actions and returned to sins. By “sons,” followers of others are meant, as in Job: “The sons of the wicked will be far from salvation” [Note: [Col. 0927] 3 Job 5:4], meaning that those who follow any wicked person into iniquity do not attain true salvation, in accordance with this passage: “The sons of Ephraim, fitting out and shooting the bow, turned back in the day of battle” [Note: [Col. 0927] 4 Psalm 77:9]. Many in the Church who are called followers of the apostles who produce fruit read the Scriptures attentively and shoot verbal arrows against sinners, but fail amid the fervor of their own temptation.

By “sons,” the hearers of any heretic are meant, as in Job: “If his sons are multiplied, they will be by the sword” [Note: [Col. 0927] 5 Job 27:14], meaning that all who receive a heretic’s teaching, however many they may be, arrive at condemnation. By “sons,” human beings created by God are meant, as in Job: “I entreated the sons of my womb” [Note: [Col. 0927] 6 Job 19:17], that is, I humbly entreated human beings whom I begot by creating them, having myself become human. By “sons,” good works are meant, as in Paul: “The woman will be saved through the bearing of children” [Note: [Col. 0927] 7 1 Timothy 2:15], that is, the faithful soul through the multitude of good works; likewise according to the passage: “And may you see your sons” [Note: [Col. 0927] 8 Psalm 127:5], that is, the rewards of good works.

The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, dead in the house, is a person who sins secretly. “The son of the widow, carried outside the gate” [Note: [Col. 0927] 9 Luke 7:12], is a person who sins publicly. “Lazarus, dead for four days” [Note: [Col. 0927] 10 John 11:39], is one who sins through a stinking habit.

## Daughter

“Daughter” signifies the Church, as David says: “That I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” [Note: [Col. 0927] 11 Psalm IX, 15], that is, that I may proclaim all your praises to others in faith, hope, and charity, by which the holy Church—which is now called “the glory of the Lord”—strives to contemplate God face to face.

Likewise, by the name “daughters of Zion” the Jews are designated, as the primitive Church says in the Song: “Go forth and see, daughters of Jerusalem, King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him” [Note: [Col. 0927] 12 Song of Songs III, 11]. “Come out,” she says, “O Jews who dwell around Mount Zion, from the ignorance of unbelief, and believe in him,” that is, in Christ; for Christ, the king of all, in that crown of thorns which the ancient Synagogue placed upon him, from which he was born according to the flesh, reconciled heavenly and earthly things “on the day of his dispensation,” on the day of the announcement, when the Church was betrothed to him. Understand: “see him,” “on the day of the joy of his heart,” namely, see him “on the day of his resurrection.” It is as though she said: believe in his incarnation, passion, and resurrection.

By “daughter” the flesh is signified, where it says: “O wretched daughter of Babylon” [Note: [Col. 0927] 13 Psalm CXXXVI, 8], O flesh raised amid the confusion of vices, “blessed is he who will repay you with the repayment with which you repaid us,” since, by inciting us to vices, you compel us to be subject to virtues. “Blessed is he who will seize” lest the darkness grow, “and dash” [Note: [Col. 0927] 14 Ibid., verse 9] lest, when shattered, they perish, “your little ones,” that is, the foolish and illicit impulses born from you, O daughter of Babylon, “against the rock”; for wherever the fear of Christ is rooted, whatever illicit thing arises is quickly dashed to pieces.

The weaker members of the Church are called “daughters of Jerusalem,” as the bride says in the Song: “King Solomon made himself a litter from the trees of Lebanon” [Note: [Col. 0927] 15 Song of Songs III, 9]; for Christ established the holy Church for himself from those who are strong, lofty, beautiful, fragrant, incorruptible, and in every respect shining with the brightness of virtues. For “Lebanon” is interpreted as “whitening.” The Church is called a litter either because it carries Christ through the world, or because it lifts souls to the heavenly banquets, or because it [Col. 0928B] cuts and judges for Christ.

“And he made its columns of silver,” because he instructed its supporters, who were to sustain others, with the brightness of divine speech. “Its reclining-place of gold,” because he filled certain persons, upon whom he might incline and rest his head, with the radiant contemplation of himself. “Its seat of purple,” because he makes certain persons, whose example first ascends to the virtues and afterward to the Holy of Holies. He makes others ready for martyrdom, constructing them, as it were, in the middle of the litter by charity, for he adorned the whole life of the Church with love of God and neighbor.

Why “because of the daughters of Jerusalem,” that is, because of the weaker members of the Church? So that those who cannot ascend to the perfect summit of knowledge, contemplation, and patience may remain in charity; and without doubt they will reach the banquet of eternal life.

Likewise, “daughters” can mean any weak persons, as in Ecclesiasticus: “You have daughters; watch over their bodies” [Note: [Col. 0927] 16 Ecclesiasticus VII, 26].

“Daughter” means the soul, as in the Gospel: “My daughter is grievously afflicted by a demon” [Note: [Col. 0927] 17 Matthew XV, 22], that is, my soul is wearied by sin.

By “daughters” secular people are meant, as in Isaiah: “The daughters of Zion walked with outstretched necks” [Note: [Col. 0927] 18 Isaiah III, 16], because secular people have been weakened through pride.

## Fringe

The fringe is Christ’s incarnation, as in the Gospel: “As many as touched the fringe of his garment were made well” [Note: [Col. 0927] 19 Mark VI, 56], because all who believe in his incarnation attain true salvation.

By “fringes” are meant human ways of life, as in the Psalms: “In golden fringes is her glory” [Note: [Col. 0927] 20 Psalm XLIV, 14], because the holy Church glories in the holy ways of life of human beings.

By “fringes” our minds are meant, as in the book of Numbers: “Let the children of Israel place hyacinth-colored cords on their fringes” [Note: [Col. 0927] 21 Numbers XV, 38], because souls who see God through contemplation possess heavenly desires in their minds.

## Firmament

The firmament is God’s protection, as in the Psalms: “The Lord is a firmament for those who fear him” [Note: [Col. 0927] 22 Psalm XXIV, 14], because God protects those who fear him.

The firmament is the angelic nature, as in Ezekiel: “When a voice came from above the firmament, they stood and lowered their wings” [Note: [Col. 0929] 1 Ezekiel I, 25], because, when the divine utterance that surpasses the understanding of angels is silently heard in the mind by the saints as best they can, they humble themselves in all things and do not presume upon their virtues.

The firmament is the eminence of the Church, as in Genesis: “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven” [Note: [Col. 0929] 2 Genesis I, 14], that is, let holy people appear in the eminence of the Church.

The firmament is reason itself, as in Genesis: “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide waters from waters” [Note: [Col. 0929] 3 Genesis I, 6], because there ought to be reason in us, which separates evil thoughts from good ones.

The firmament is temporal assistance, as in the Psalms: “He destroyed every firmament of bread” [Note: [Col. 0929] 4 Psalm CV, 16], that is, he permitted all the strength by which they ought to have been helped to be weakened.

## Pipe

The pipe is suggestion, as in Daniel: “When you hear the sound of the pipe, worship the statue” [Note: [Col. 0929] 5 Daniel III, 5], because the reprobate consent to the devil at his suggestion.

By “pipe” the words of wicked people are meant, as in Job: “His bones are like pipes of bronze” [Note: [Col. 0929] 6 Job XL, 13], because the more sweetly the seductive words of the wicked sound, the more grievously they deceive.

## Basket

The basket is the Virgin Mary: “He took a basket of bronze and placed the infant inside it” [Note: [Col. 0929] 7 Exodus II, 3], because God the Father chose the virgin Mary, who conceived Christ within herself.

## Leaf

The leaf is the word of God, as in the Psalms: “And its leaf shall not wither” [Note: [Col. 0929] 8 Psalm I, 4], because the word of God endures forever.

The leaf is the human being himself, as in Job: “Against a leaf driven by the wind” [Note: [Col. 0929] 9 Job XIII, 25], that is, against a human being who is swept away by the movement of temptation.

The leaf is instability, as in Isaiah: “We have all fallen like a leaf” [Note: [Col. 0929] 10 Isaiah LXIV, 6], that is, weak and unstable, we have been cast down.

## Flower

The flower is Christ, as in the Song: “I am the flower of the field” [Note: [Col. 0929] 11 Song of Songs II, 1], that is, I am the glory of the Church.

The flower is the beauty of the world, as in the book of Wisdom: “Let not the flower of the season pass us by” [Note: [Col. 0929] 12 Wisdom II, 7], that is, let us not cast away from ourselves the beauty of the age.

The flower is the tenderness of early youth, as in Job: “Who comes forth like a flower” [Note: [Col. 0929] 13 Job XIV, 2], and so forth, because the first age of a human being bursts forth like the leaf of a flower.

The flower is the praise of hypocrites, as in Job: “While it is still in flower, it will wither” [Note: [Col. 0929] 14 Job VIII, 12], because even a pretender sometimes fails amid the very praise he receives.

The flower is the beginning of a good work, as in Job: “His cluster will be harmed like a vine at its first flowering” [Note: [Col. 0929] 15 Job XV, 53], because the hypocrite is corrupted at the beginning of a good work by human praise.

By “flowers” the tender and foolish are meant, as in the Song: “Strengthen me with flowers” [Note: [Col. 0929] 16 Song of Songs II, 5], because the faithful soul receives consolation from the fact that others are converted to God.

## Fountain

The fountain is Christ, as in Zechariah: “An open fountain for the house of David” [Note: [Col. 0929] 17 Zechariah III], that is, Christ incarnate from the house of David.

The fountain is eternal blessedness, as in the Psalms: “With you is the fountain of life” [Note: [Col. 0929] 18 Psalm XXXVI, 10], because with God there is eternal happiness, which never fails through death.

The fountain is the holy Church, as in the Song: “A garden enclosed, a sealed fountain” [Note: [Col. 0929] 19 Song of Songs IV, 12], because the holy Church contains within itself the shoots of virtues and does not reveal its secret mysteries to the unworthy.

The fountain is the human soul, as in the Song: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters” [Note: [Col. 0929] 20 Ibid., verse 15], because in a holy soul there is a dwelling-place of useful and life-giving thoughts.

The fountain is the punishment of human mortality, as in the Gospel: “Jesus, wearied from the journey, was sitting beside the fountain” [Note: [Col. 0929] 21 John IV, 6], because, burdened by the weakness he had assumed, he permitted himself to be humbled under the penalty of our mortality.

The fountain is the sin of avarice, as in Genesis: “A fountain rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0929] 22 Genesis II, 6], because from the mind of the avaricious proceeds desire, which is the root of all evils and scarcely permits anyone to remain at peace.

By “fountains” preachers are meant, as in Isaiah: “You shall draw water with joy from the fountains of the Savior” [Note: [Col. 0929] 23 Isaiah XII, 3], that is, you shall receive words of salvation from heralds of the truth.

By “fountains” spiritual teachings are meant, as in the Psalms: “You send forth fountains in the valleys” [Note: [Col. 0929] 24 Psalm CIV, 10], that is, you grant spiritual teachings to the humble.

By “fountains” the sacred Scriptures are meant, as in the Psalms: “In the churches you shall be blessed from the fountains of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0929] 25 Psalm LXVIII, 27], that is, preach nothing in the Church except from the Scriptures of the holy Fathers.

By “fountains” the gifts of inward grace are meant, as in Proverbs: “Let your fountains flow out” [Note: [Col. 0929] 26 Proverbs V, 16], that is, display outwardly, for the edification of your neighbors, the spiritual gifts you have received.

By “fountains” sins are meant, as in Hosea: “God will lay waste its fountains” [Note: [Col. 0929] 27 Hosea XXII, 15], because God destroys in his elect the sins by which their enemies had held them captive.

## Opening

The opening is the anguish of the Passion, through which the camel—who, in order to take away our sins, voluntarily humbled himself—could more easily enter into heavenly blessedness [Note: [Col. 0929] 28 Matthew XIX, 24; Mark X, 23; Luke XVIII, 25] than lovers of the world can attain fellowship with his Church.

The opening is inward compunction, as in the Song: “My beloved put his hand through the opening” [Note: [Col. 0929] 29 Song of Songs V, 4], because he inspired me with his work through hidden compunction. “And my belly trembled at his touch” [Note: [Col. 0929] 30 Ibid.], because my heart, through his inspiration, was terrified that it had not done for its neighbors what God did for his enemies: although he was God, he became human for the salvation of human beings.

The opening is a perverse mind, as in Isaiah: “He will put his hand over the opening of the asp” [Note: [Col. 0929] 31 Isaiah XI, 8], because God sometimes pours his grace into that mind in which the devil previously dwelt.

By “opening” spiritual gifts are meant, as in Ezekiel: “Your openings were prepared for you on the day when you were created” [Note: [Col. 0929] 32 Ezekiel XXVIII, 13], because the apostate angel, in his first brightness, received his first spiritual gifts.

Likewise, by “openings” Christ’s … are understood, as the bridegroom says in the Song: “Arise, my beloved, my bride, and come, my dove, into the openings of the rock” [Note: [Col. 0929] 33 Song of Songs II, 13–14]. “Arise,” he says, [Col. 0931A] from the repose of contemplation; “my beloved,” whom I loved unto death; “my bride,” in whom I have bestowed such great things; “and come” to preach, that is, to the office of preaching. “My dove in the openings of the rock,” nesting and warming chicks for me in the [lacuna] of Christ.

## Tongs

The tongs are Christ with the Father, as in Isaiah: “The coal which he had taken from the altar with the tongs” [Note: [Col. 0931] 1 Isaiah VI, 6], because, through the equality by which the Son is one with the Father, he brought the word of truth from the Father, by which he purified the disciples whom he sent into the world.

By “tongs” the two Testaments are meant, as in Exodus: “You shall make basins and tongs for the use of the altar” [Note: [Col. 0931] 2 Exodus XXVII, 3], because God established teachers and the two Testaments for adorning the holy Church.

## Strong

The strong one is Christ, as in Isaiah: “His name shall be called STRONG” [Note: [Col. 0931] 3 Isaiah IX, 6], because he conquered the devil.

The strong one is the devil, as in the Gospel: “While the strong man, armed, guards his halls” [Note: [Col. 0931] 4 Luke XI, 12], that is, while the devil possesses the world.

By “strong ones” the Jews are meant, as in the Psalms: “The strong have rushed upon me” [Note: [Col. 0931] 5 Psalm LVI, 4], that is, the Jews raged against me.

By “strong ones” demons are meant, as in the Psalms: “The strong have sought my soul” [Note: [Col. 0931] 6 Psalm LIV, 5], that is, demons desired to seize my soul.

## Strength

Strength exists in what is good, as in the Psalms: “The Lord is the strength of his people” [Note: [Col. 0931] 7 Psalm XXVIII, 8], because God made his elect spiritually strong for overcoming the devil.

Strength in evil is meant, as in Job: “Strength will dwell in his neck” [Note: [Col. 0931] 8 Job XLI, 13], because in the members of the devil there is a damnable power.

## Forehead

The forehead is the mind of every righteous person, as in Exodus: “The plate shall always be upon his forehead” [Note: [Col. 0931] 9 Exodus XXVIII, 38], because the memory of the Lord’s Passion ought always to be in the mind of a holy man.

The forehead is the shamelessness of flesh or heart, as in Ezekiel: “The house of Israel is hardened in forehead” [Note: [Col. 0931] 10 Ezekiel III, 7], because any wicked persons are so called on account of the shamelessness of their hearts.

## Furnace

The furnace is the Antichrist, as in Revelation: “Like the smoke of a great furnace” [Note: [Col. 0931] 11 Revelation IX, 2], that is, the doctrine of the arrogant Antichrist, who tests the good and burns up the wicked.

The furnace is tribulation, as in the book of Wisdom: “As gold in the furnace he tested them” [Note: [Col. 0931] 12 Wisdom III, 6], because God examines holy men in tribulation.

The furnace is the burning heat of carnal desire, as in the Law: “I brought you out of Egypt, from the iron furnace” [Note: [Col. 0931] 13 Deuteronomy IV, 20], because God leads his elect out both from the darkness of ignorance and from the terrible fires of carnal desire.

## Pit

The pit is humility, as in Ezekiel: “Let a pit be made in the altar” [Note: [Col. 0931] 14 Ezekiel XLIII, 13], because, if our mind is to preserve the good things within itself, it must not abandon the virtue of humility.

The pit is the memory of a human being, as in the books of Kings: “The pit of the aqueduct was filled” [Note: [Col. 0931] 15 3 Kings XVIII, 35], because every holy person has his memory filled with the moisture of spiritual grace.

The pit is the virtue of patience, as in Isaiah: “Hide yourself in the earth” [Note: [Col. 0931] 16 Isaiah II, 10], because through the humility of patience, which the elect now practice, they will afterward be hidden from the terrible judgment.

The pit is earthly desire, as in Joshua: “I buried the silver in dug-up earth” [Note: [Col. 0931] 17 Joshua VII, 21], because every wicked person hides the brightness of divine speech in the depth of earthly desire.

## Pitfall

The pitfall is the malice of deception, as in the Psalms: “He fell into the pit that he made” [Note: [Col. 0931] 18 Psalm VII, 16], because, while any wicked person sometimes strives to deceive another, he deceives himself.

The pitfall is the vice of excuse-making, as in Isaiah: “There the hedgehog made its pit” [Note: [Col. 0931] 19 Isaiah XXXIV, 15], because, when a proud person is reproved for his sin, he flees into the darkness of excuses.

The pitfall is earthly desire, as in Job: “You will plunge their faces into the pit” [Note: [Col. 0931] 20 Job XL, 8], because the reprobate bend all their attention toward earthly desire.

The pitfall is [lacuna] of death, as in the Psalms: “They dug a pit before my face, and they fell into it” [Note: [Col. 0931] 21 Psalm LVII, 7], that is, they killed themselves in the very thing by which they thought to kill me.

The pitfall is hell, as in the books of Kings: “They cast him into a great pit” [Note: [Col. 0931] 22 2 Kings XVIII, 17], because lovers of this world are plunged into the infernal pit.

## End

“End” is used for something completed, as when one says, “The web is finished.”

“End” is used for something consumed, as when one says, “The food is finished.” For we speak differently of a finished web, which is being woven, and of finished food, which is being eaten.

The end is Christ, as in the Psalms: “The patience of the poor shall not perish unto the end” [Note: [Col. 0931] 23 Psalm IX, 19], because patience cannot perish with Christ, although it perishes among the proud.

The end is fulfillment, as in Paul: “Christ is the end of the law” [Note: [Col. 0931] 24 Romans X, 4], because he came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it.

The end is the death of the flesh, as in the Gospel: “He loved them unto the end” [Note: [Col. 0931] 25 John XIII, 1], that is, he loved them so greatly that he died for them.

The end is eternal life, as in the Psalms: “Make my end known to me, Lord” [Note: [Col. 0931] 26 Psalm XXXIX, 5], that is, make known to me the eternal joy of which it is said: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” [Note: [Col. 0931] 27 Matthew XXV, 21, 23]. Make it known to me for this purpose: that, understanding how great it is, I may love it above all things, and by loving it may reach it.

The pit is eternal destruction, as in the Psalms: “He will labor forever and yet live unto the end” [Note: [Col. 0931] 28 Psalm XLIX, 9], that is, he will always be punished and will remain in eternal destruction. Although he labors in everlasting punishments, he will never be entirely consumed, because he will continue living in labor and punishments. For what purpose? Not so that he may rejoice in life, but so that he may perish eternally.

The end means the Gentiles, as in the Psalms: “God will rule Jacob and the ends of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0931] 29 Psalm LIX, 14], that is, he will exercise his judgment not only over the Jewish people but also among the Gentiles.

By “end” inward thoughts are meant, as in the Psalms: “In his hand are all the ends of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0931] 30 Psalm XCV, 4], that is, it is in his power to dispose all the inward thoughts of the soul.

The end is eternity, as in the Psalms: “The poor man shall not be forgotten unto the end” [Note: [Col. 0933] 1 Psalm IX, 19], that is, God will not forget the humble forever.

By “end” the extremity of the world is meant, as in the song of Hannah: “The Lord will judge the ends of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0933] 2 1 Kings II, 10], because a person will be judged according to how he is found at the end.

## Flight

Flight is fear of slaughter, as in the Psalms: “Flight has perished from me” [Note: [Col. 0933] 3 Psalm CXLII, 5], that is, I did not fear suffering so greatly that I refused to undergo death.

Flight is failure, as in the Psalms: “I will turn those who hate him to flight” [Note: [Col. 0933] 4 Psalm LXXXIX, 24], because those who do not love Christ are heading toward damnable failure.

## Radiance

Radiance is renewal of the mind, as in Job: “Like the midday radiance it will rise for you at evening” [Note: [Col. 0933] 5 Job XI, 17], because, when a holy man is tempted, he is renewed in mind.

## Lightning

Lightning is the threat against sinners, as in Ezekiel: “And lightning came forth from the fire” [Note: [Col. 0933] 6 Ezekiel I, 13], because from the Holy Spirit, on the day of preachers, a threat against sinners proceeds.

Lightning is the terror of fear, as in the Gospel: “His appearance was like lightning” [Note: [Col. 0933] 7 Matthew XXVIII, 3], because, when the Lord comes for judgment, he terrifies the reprobate through his distinction.

By “lightning” preachers are meant, as in Job: “Does he send lightning, and do they go?” [Note: [Col. 0933] 8 Job XXXVIII, 35], because God sent preachers of the truth into the whole world, and they went forth preaching everywhere.

“Lightnings” are miracles, as in the Psalms: “He made lightnings into rain” [Note: [Col. 0933] 9 Psalm CXXXV, 7; Jeremiah X, 13 and LI, 16], because, before God entrusted the word of preaching to the disciples, he gave them the power to perform miracles.

Thunderbolts are the sentences of the Last Judgment, as in Job: “He will send thunderbolts against him” [Note: [Col. 0933] 10 Job XXXVIII, 35], because in judgment he will pronounce a severe sentence against the devil in his members, saying: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” [Note: [Col. 0933] 11 Matthew XXV, 41].

## River

The river is the Holy Spirit, as in the Psalms: “The rush of the river gladdens the city of God” [Note: [Col. 0933] 12 Psalm XLVI, 5]; the grace of the Holy Spirit will gladden the people gathered to live rightly.

The river is the human race, as in Ezekiel: “Among the captives beside the river Chebar” [Note: [Col. 0933] 13 Ezekiel I, 3], because Christ came to wretched human beings who, as a whole race, were burdened alike by guilt and punishment. For “Chebar” is interpreted as “heaviness.”

The river is the instability of this age, as in the Psalms: “They will pass through the river on foot” [Note: [Col. 0933] 14 Psalm LXVI, 6], because, through the lightness [or fickleness] of the world, the saints hasten toward stability; although the saints are in the mortality and desire of this age, they will nevertheless easily reach immortality.

The river is this world, as in Revelation: “And the sixth angel poured out his bowl upon that great river, the Euphrates, and dried up its waters” [Note: [Col. 0933] 15 Revelation XVI, 12], while the herald of truth raises his preaching over the world at that time and foretells that its abundance will be dried up, saying with the Apostle: “The world is passing away with its desire” [Note: [Col. 0933] 16 1 John II, 17]. “Euphrates” is interpreted as “devourer,” and this world consumes everything within itself and daily tends toward decline.

The river is the holy Church, as in the Psalms: “The river of God is filled with waters” [Note: [Col. 0933] 17 Psalm LXV, 10], that is, the holy Church is filled with spiritual gifts.

The river is sacred Scripture, as in Job: “They do not see the streams of the river” [Note: [Col. 0933] 18 Job XX, 17], that is, they do not understand the meanings of sacred Scripture.

By “river” the gifts of the Holy Spirit are meant, as in the Gospel: “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly” [Note: [Col. 0933] 19 John VII, 38], because spiritual heights proceed from the mind of the believer so that others may be instructed.

By “rivers” Christians are meant, as in the Psalms: “The rivers shall clap their hands together” [Note: [Col. 0933] 20 Psalm XCVIII, 8], that is, Christians will labor unanimously and joyfully in good works.

By “rivers” preachers are meant, as in Ecclesiastes: “To the place from which the rivers flow, they return, so that they may flow again” [Note: [Col. 0933] 21 Ecclesiastes I, 7], because holy preachers ascribe all the holiness they possess to God, so that they may be able to persevere in that same holiness.

By “rivers” the Jews are meant, as in the Psalms: “The rivers have raised their waves” [Note: [Col. 0933] 22 Psalm XCIII, 3], that is, the Jews have raised up their contradictions.

By “rivers” the Gentiles are meant, as in the Psalms: “And in the rivers his right hand” [Note: [Col. 0933] 23 Psalm LXXXIX, 26], that is, his power is among the Gentiles.

By “river” proud teachers of the Law are meant, as in the Psalms: “He made rivers into a desert” [Note: [Col. 0933] 24 Psalm CVII, 33], that is, he abandoned the arrogant teachers of the Law.

By “rivers” the transitory things of this world are meant, as in the Psalms: “By the rivers of Babylon” [Note: [Col. 0933] 25 Psalm CXXXVII, 1], that is, we have humbly pressed beneath us the transitory things of this present confusion.

By “rivers” temptations are meant, as in the Song: “Nor will rivers overwhelm it” [Note: [Col. 0933] 26 Song of Songs VIII, 7], because temptations cannot extinguish true charity in a holy mind.

By “rivers” the crimes of the reprobate are meant, as in Isaiah: “Woe to the land of the whirring wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia” [Note: [Col. 0933] 27 Isaiah XVIII, 1], that is, accursed is the proud man, the Antichrist, who surpasses the worst in sinning.

By “rivers” tribulations are meant, as in the Gospel: “The rivers came and beat upon that house,” and so forth [Note: [Col. 0933] 28 Matthew VII, 25, 27]; persecutions flowed in and struck the human mind.

## Stream

The stream is the abundance of inward refreshment, as in Revelation: “He showed me a river of living water” [Note: [Col. 0933] 29 Revelation XXII, 1], that is, he revealed the abundance of eternal refreshment.

The stream is secular life, as in Job: “He will swallow the river and will not be astonished” [Note: [Col. 0933] 30 Job XL, 18], because the devil does not regard it as a great thing that he incorporates secular people into himself.

The stream is the final examination, as in Daniel: “A fiery and swift river came forth from before him” [Note: [Col. 0933] 31 Daniel VII, 10], because that destructive examination will carry the reprobate away into eternal burning.

By “stream” the words of the prophets are meant, as in Job: “He also searches out the depths of the rivers” [Note: [Col. 0933] 32 Job XXVIII, 11], that is, he investigated through the obscurities of prophetic words.

By “stream” secular wisdom is meant, as in the song of Habakkuk: “You will cleave the rivers of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0935] 1 Habakkuk III, 9], because, as the Apostle says: “God made foolish the wisdom of this world.”

## Waves

The waves are persecutors, as in Job: “He walks upon the waves of the sea” [Note: [Col. 0935] 2 Job IX, 8], because God overcomes the persecutions of the world in his elect.

The waves are the malice of the wicked, as in Job: “Here you shall break the swelling waves” [Note: [Col. 0935] 3 Job XXXVIII, 11], because he restrains the malice of the wicked, so that they cannot harm as much as they wish.

## Smoke

The smoke is the holy Church, as in the Song: “Like a column of smoke” [Note: [Col. 0935] 4 Song of Songs III, 6], because the holy Church, Gentile and upright, rises from present things toward those to come.

The smoke is compunction, as in the Psalms: “Smoke rose up in his compunction” [Note: [Col. 0935] 5 Psalm XVIII, 9], because compunction arises in the mind from remembrance of divine anger.

The smoke is evil teaching, as in Revelation: “From the smoke of the pit locusts came forth upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0935] 6 Revelation IX, 3], because wicked heretics were born in the Church from the obscure teaching of the wicked.

The smoke is pride, as in the Psalms: “They will fail as smoke fails” [Note: [Col. 0935] 7 Psalm XXXVII, 20], because the proud tend toward damnable failure.

The smoke is the devil’s temptation, as in Job: “Smoke proceeds from his nostrils” [Note: [Col. 0935] 8 Job XLI, 11], that is, a darkening temptation proceeds from the devil’s temptations and obscures the soul.

The smoke is the brevity of this life, as in the Psalms: “As smoke vanishes, so they will vanish” [Note: [Col. 0935] 9 Psalm LXIX, 3], because the present life vanishes into nothing in an instant.

The smoke is the darkness of damnation, as in Revelation: “The smoke of their torments will rise forever and ever” [Note: [Col. 0935] 10 Revelation XIV, 11], because the darkness of the damnation of the reprobate will never fail. They will rightly never be without punishment, since, while they lived, they did not wish to be without sin.

The smoke is the doctrine of heretics, as in Revelation: “From their mouths came forth smoke and sulfur” [Note: [Col. 0935] 11 Revelation IX, 17], because heretics teach greed, lust, and pride.

## Sling

The sling is the Church, as in Job: “The stones of the sling have become like stubble to him” [Note: [Col. 0935] 12 Job XLI, 14], because the devil, in his members, contemptuously despises the holy men of the Church.

The sling is sacred Scripture, as in the books of Kings: “He took a sling in his hand and went out against the Philistine” [Note: [Col. 0935] 13 1 Kings XVII, 40], because Christ fulfilled sacred Scripture in his works and fought against the devil.

The sling is the instability of the reprobate, as in the books of Kings: “The soul of David’s enemies will whirl like the force and circuit of a sling” [Note: [Col. 0935] 14 1 Kings XXV, 29], because the life of those who do not love Christ always falls from evil to worse.

## Foundation

The foundation is Christ, as in Paul: “No one can lay another foundation besides the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0935] 15 1 Corinthians III, 11].

The foundation is faith, as in the Psalms: “Lay it waste, lay it waste, down to its foundation” [Note: [Col. 0935] 16 Psalm CXXXVII, 7], that is, destroy completely in the Church whatever righteousness there is, until you uproot faith as well.

The foundation is the hidden things of the devil, as in the song of Habakkuk: “You laid bare the foundation as far as the neck” [Note: [Col. 0935] 17 Habakkuk III, 13], that is, you exposed the devil’s hidden things to the end, or as far as his suggestion.

By “foundation” the apostles are meant, as in the Psalms: “Its foundations are placed upon the mountains of Zion” [Note: [Col. 0935] 18 Psalm LXXXVII, 1], because the apostles, founders of the Church, are sent forth from the prophets.

By “foundations” preachers are meant, as in Job: “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?” [Note: [Col. 0935] 19 Job XXXVIII, 4], that is, when I confirmed the teachers of the Church.

By “foundations” the exaltations of the proud are meant, as in the song of Deuteronomy: “He will burn the foundations of the mountains” [Note: [Col. 0935] 20 Deuteronomy XXXII, 22], that is, vengeance will destroy the exaltations of the proud.

By “foundations” the defenders of the Church are meant, as in Revelation: “The wall of the city has twelve foundations, and upon them the twelve names of the apostles of the Lamb” [Note: [Col. 0935] 21 Revelation XXI, 14]. For the defenders of the Church are founded upon the prophets and apostles, and they possessed the faith that they had received. The name of the Lamb is in them because they foretold that he himself would come and suffer for the salvation of the world.

By “foundations” carnal pleasures are meant, as in Job: “The river will overturn their foundations” [Note: [Col. 0935] 22 Job XXII, 16], because the instability of this brief life brings the pleasures of the reprobate to an end.

By “foundations” the supreme rulers of the world are meant, as in the Psalms: “The foundations of the mountains were disturbed and shaken” [Note: [Col. 0935] 23 Psalm XVIII, 8], that is, the chief rulers came devotedly to the faith, seeing that anger would come upon them unless they changed.

## Streams

The streams are the abundance of virtues, as in the Song: “They sit beside overflowing streams” [Note: [Col. 0935] 24 Song of Songs V, 12], because the saints possess an abundance of spiritual virtues in humility.

## Rope

The rope is faith, as in Job: “And will you bind his tongue with a rope?” [Note: [Col. 0935] 25 Job XL, 20], because by true faith we have destroyed the blasphemies of the devil.

By “ropes” the precepts of sacred Scripture are meant, as in Jeremiah: ropes—that is, old cloths—lifted the prophet from the pit [Note: [Col. 0935] 26 Jeremiah XXXVII, 11, 12, 13], because divine precepts and holy examples raise the elect from the depth of the present life.

By “ropes” good outcomes are meant, as in the Psalms: “The ropes have fallen to me” [Note: [Col. 0935] 27 Psalm XVI, 6], that is, good outcomes have appeared to me in luminous goods.

By “ropes” the harshnesses of the world are meant, as in Job: “They are bound with the ropes of poverty” [Note: [Col. 0935] 28 Job XXXVI, 8], that is, they are bound by the hardships of want.

## Cord

The cord is the subtlety of preaching, as in Ezekiel: “And a linen cord was in his hand” [Note: [Col. 0935] 29 Ezekiel XL, 3], because God subtly completed his preaching in action.

The cord is faith, as in Ecclesiastes: “A threefold cord is not easily broken” [Note: [Col. 0935] 30 Ecclesiastes IV, 12], because faith in the Holy Trinity is not easily broken.

The cord is our thought, as in the Psalms: “You have examined my path and my cord” [Note: [Col. 0935] 31 Psalm CXXXIX, 3], that is, you have scrutinized the strict measure of my thought.

By “cord” the Lord’s precepts are meant, as in Isaiah: “Lengthen your cords” [Note: [Col. 0935] 32 Isaiah LIV, 2], that is, fulfill the Lord’s precepts to the end with perseverance.

By “cords” perverse pleasures are meant, as in Isaiah: “Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity” [Note: [Col. 0937] 1 Isaiah V, 18], woe to you who persistently love iniquity in perverse pleasures.

## Thief

The thief is the heretic, as in the Gospel: “The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy” [Note: [Col. 0937] 2 John X, 10], because the heretic strives for this purpose: to lead people astray.

The thief is any hidden enemy, as in Job: “At night he will be like a thief” [Note: [Col. 0937] 3 Job XXIV, 14], that is, unexpectedly and secretly he will try to cause harm.

By “thieves” evil spirits are meant, as in the Gospel: “Where thieves do not break through or steal” [Note: [Col. 0937] 4 Matthew VI, 19–20], because evil spirits can deprive the citizens of goodness of heavenly joys neither by force nor by fraud.

## Cold

Cold is adversity, as in Proverbs: “Because of the cold the lazy man would not plow” [Note: [Col. 0937] 5 Proverbs XX, 4], because any reprobate, on account of the harshness of adversity, scorns to labor for an eternal reward.

Cold is the severity of the Last Judgment, as in the Psalms: “Who will withstand the sight of his cold?” [Note: [Col. 0937] 6 Psalm CXLVII, 17], because, when the Last Judgment appears, even the elect will tremble.

Fructus, by designation, sometimes signifies Antichrist, sometimes the Redeemer, and sometimes a good work, as can be proved by one example: “The earth has given its fruit” [Note: [Col. 0937] 7 Jas. V, 18]: the Virgin Mary bore Christ; Christ’s flesh brought redemption to the world; and the human being redeemed through Christ’s blood brought forth good works naturally proper to him.

Fruit signifies Christ’s body, as is said in the Song from the voice of the bride: “Under the shadow of him whom I desired, I sat”—that is, I found rest under Christ’s protection—“and his fruit was sweet to my throat” [Note: [Col. 0937] 8 Song II, 3], by which I understand life in his heart, while I also receive that fruit visibly.

Fruit signifies reward, as in the Gospel: “A good tree produces good fruits” [Note: [Col. 0937] 9 Matt. VII, 17], meaning that a good action merits a reward. Likewise: “Or make the tree bad, and its fruit bad” [Note: [Col. 0937] 10 Matt. XII, 33]; this does not urge you to do evil, but teaches what reward awaits evildoers.

Fruit signifies a good example, as in the Psalms: “The earth shall be satisfied with the fruit of your works” [Note: [Col. 0937] 11 Ps. CIII, 13], that is, the lower multitude is refreshed by the examples of the saints.

Fruit signifies righteousness, as in Proverbs: “Give her of the fruit of her hands” [Note: [Col. 0937] 12 Prov. XXXI, 31], that is, reward her for the righteousness of her works.

Fruit signifies eternal blessedness, as in the Song: “A man would bring for the fruit of the vineyard a thousand silver pieces” [Note: [Col. 0937] 13 Song VIII, 11], meaning that whoever is manly in spirit despises all worldly things for the blessedness of heaven.

By fruit are meant holy preachings, as in the Song: “That he might eat the fruit of the fields” [Note: [Col. 0937] 14 Song V, 1], that is, that he might be refreshed by the preachings of the saints.

By fruits are meant spiritual virtues, as in the Song: “I will climb the palm tree and take hold of its fruit” [Note: [Col. 0937] 15 Song VII, 8], and I will take up Christ’s cross and acquire the spiritual virtues that are in it.

By fruits are meant eternal rewards, as in the Song: “Two hundred for those who guard its fruits” [Note: [Col. 0937] 16 Song VIII, 12], meaning that those who strive to fulfill the twofold love do so lest they lack eternal rewards.

The name fruit signifies eternal death, which is improperly called fruit: “What fruit,” says the Apostle, “did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of them is death” [Note: [Col. 0937] 17 Rom. VI, 21].

Grain signifies Christ, as in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat dies” [Note: [Col. 0937] 18 John XII, 24], meaning that when Christ fell into the earth through the death of the flesh, he filled the whole world with a manifold harvest.

Grain signifies any righteous person, as in Job: “The grain desires the clouds” [Note: [Col. 0937] 19 Job XXXVII, 11], that is, every righteous person desires preachers. [The Latin appears defective here.]

Grain signifies spiritual work, as in Job: “Let a thorn come forth for me instead of wheat” [Note: [Col. 0937] 20 Job XXXI, 40], that is: if I have not benefited the Church fruitfully and lose spiritual work, I shall incur sin.

Grain signifies Holy Scripture, as in the Psalms: “He satisfies you with the fat of wheat” [Note: [Col. 0937] 21 Ps. CXLVII, 14], that is, he has refreshed you with the spiritual understanding of Holy Scripture.

Grain signifies virtues, as in the Book of Judges: “Jerubbaal threshed wheat from the chaff” [Note: [Col. 0937] 22 Judg. VI, 11 and following], that is, every saint separates virtues from vices. While he was threshing wheat from the chaff, the Angel appeared to him; at his command he immediately cooked a kid, placed the flesh upon a rock, and poured the broth of the flesh over it. The Angel touched it with his staff, and fire coming out of the rock consumed it.

To thresh wheat is to separate virtues from vices. When people do this, the angel appears to them—that is, God supplies grace—who commands the kid to be sacrificed, meaning that the sinner is put to death through repentance. To place the kid’s flesh upon the rock is to set the sinner’s carnal works in exchange for Christ. To pour the broth of the flesh over it is to reject carnal desires completely for Christ’s sake. The angel touched these things with his staff when divine power did not abandon our repentance and conversion. For the fire coming out of the rock consumed the broth, meaning that divine love [the source text has a marked, uncertain reading: +] went forth and consumed the filth of conduct and thoughts.

Grain signifies the word of doctrine, as in Genesis: “May God give you an abundance of grain” [Note: [Col. 0937] 23 Gen. XXVII, 28], that is, may God grant you an abundance of eloquence and spiritual doctrine, “of wine and oil.” Grain, namely, so that you may be taught to conduct yourself rightly in the world; wine, so that you may be intoxicated to the contempt of the Sadducees; and oil, so that you may be drawn to embrace the bridegroom. From what source, surely, does this abundance proceed, except from the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth—that is, from the grace of Christ and the fruitfulness of the Church? Grain is found in Proverbs, wine in Ecclesiastes, and oil in the Song of Songs.

Grain signifies the delight of the flesh, as in the Psalms: “They have multiplied from the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil” [Note: [Col. 0937] 24 Ps. IV, 8], that is, the reprobate have been filled with carnal delight: grain for gluttony, wine for drunkenness, and oil for excessive concern with this life. Concerning these things the Lord says in the Gospel: “Pay attention to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness and the cares of this life” [Note: [Col. 0939] 1 Luke XXI, 34].

Grain is touched by the sun in the field: this signifies that the reason of the heavenly light is illumined within in this life. It receives rains: this signifies that it grows rich through the word of truth. It is exposed to winds: this signifies that it is exercised by temptations. It bears chaff: this signifies that it endures wicked superiors. It is threshed on the threshing floor so that it may be released from attachment to the chaff: this signifies that, while it receives the scourges of corruption, it departs, though not yet purified, from the company of the flesh. After the chaff has been left behind, it is carried to the granary: this signifies that, while the reprobate remain outside, the righteous are raised to eternal joys.

### G

Gilead. Cock. Helmet. Sword. Steps. Grain. Treasury. Cheeks. Nation. Flock. Hunchback. Gomer. Fishpond. Drops. Gratuitous things. Galbanum. Hen. Ice. Footsteps. Gravel. Hail. Frost. Generation. Clods. Giant. Whirlpool. Throat. Galilee.

Gilead, which is interpreted as “heap of testimony,” signifies Christ, when it is said in the Song: “Your hair is like flocks of goats that have gone up from Mount Gilead” [Note: [Col. 0939] 2 Song IV, 1]. The meaning is that your poor, [source text marked +], spontaneously seek the heights, are swift toward good work, love little nourishment, and, with Christ as helper—of whom all the prophets bear witness—ascend from virtue to virtue.

Gilead is also understood as a multitude of martyrs, as is said in the Psalms from the Lord’s person: “Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine” [Note: [Col. 0939] 3 Ps. LIX, 9], meaning that the multitude of martyrs serves me, as does the people forgetting the things that are behind; “and Ephraim is the protection of my head” [source text marked +], meaning that I rest my head upon those who bear fruit.

“Martyr” in Greek means “witness”; with the mouth of all the faithful, the Church bears witness to what is true concerning Christ. Hence it is rightly said through the prophet concerning heretics: “They cut open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge their territory” [Note: [Col. 0939] 4 Amos I, 13]. Heretics, indeed, kill by perverse destruction the minds of the faithful that had already conceived something else from their understanding of the truth, and they extend the name of their knowledge. To enlarge territories that are near at hand is to extend the name of one’s opinion. Thus they cut apart with the sword of error the hearts of little ones already pregnant with the reception of the word, and, as it were, make them their own by the opinion of their doctrine.

Galbanum is the power of prayer, as in Exodus: “You shall offer galbanum of good fragrance” [Note: [Col. 0939] 5 Exod. XXX, 34], that is, “you shall offer to God prayer of good sweetness.”

The cock is the order of teachers, as in Job: “Who gave the cock understanding?” [Note: [Col. 0939] 6 Job XXXVIII, 36] This means that it belongs to God to grant understanding to a teacher.

The cock is the company of the apostles, as in Proverbs: “A cock girded about his loins” [Note: [Col. 0939] 7 Prov. XXX, 31], meaning that the apostles were girded with love; to them it was said: “Let your loins be girded” [Note: [Col. 0939] 8 Luke XII, 35], and so forth.

The hen is the wisdom of God, as in the Gospel: “As a hen gathers her chicks under her wings” [Note: [Col. 0939] 9 Matt. XXIII, 37], and so forth. This means that the wisdom of God leads the elect to salvation through the spiritual gifts it grants.

The helmet is good hope [the source text marks “good” with +], as in Paul: “And take up the helmet of salvation” [Note: [Col. 0939] 10 Eph. VI, 17], that is, acquire for yourselves saving hope.

Ice is the cold Synagogue, as in Job: “From whose womb did ice come forth?” [Note: [Col. 0939] 11 Job XXXVIII, 29]. The Jews are content with the Law; indeed, through unbelief they have become ice [source text marked +].

The sword is the wrath of God, as in the Psalms: “Unless you are converted” [Note: [Col. 0939] 12 Ps. VII, 13], that is, unless you wash yourselves from sin, he will show you his wrath [source text marked +].

The sword is holy preaching, as in Paul: “Take up the sword of the Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0939] 13 Eph. VI, 17], that is, practice spiritual preaching.

The sword of the Spirit is the word of which it is said: “Behold, the bed of Solomon; sixty mighty men from the strongest of Israel surround it, all holding swords and most skilled in warfare” [Note: [Col. 0939] 14 Song III, 7–8]. The bed of the peaceful man is eternal blessedness, in which the king rests with the elect; or it is the peaceful conduct of the faithful in the present life.

The strong men “surround” both beds: preachers defend the present peace of the Church against attacks, while those who are more perfect, with fixed intention, contemplate the eternal rest of the heavenly homeland. They are appropriately said to be “sixty,” because they are perfect both in doctrine and in conduct, and in them work does not disagree with doctrine.

They are “mighty” because they are not corrupted by prosperity and are not broken by adversity. They are “from the strongest of Israel,” whether in preaching, contemplation, or endurance. What is said of “Israel” may be understood both according to the flesh and according to faith. For preachers have been chosen from both peoples.

“All holding swords” means that they never cast the word of God away from themselves, but keep it ready and fulfill it in action. “Most skilled in warfare” means that through long practice they have learned what they ought to proclaim, and why, where, how, and to whom they ought to speak.

“Each one’s sword is upon his thigh”: this means that preaching is upon his humanity, so that he may overcome its impulses. For they chastise their body, just as they teach others, lest, while preaching to others, they themselves become reprobate by living differently.

They do this “because of the terrors of the night,” namely, lest the snares of the devil, if they find them secure and unarmed, strike them down miserably, the present peace of the Church be violated, and eternal blessedness thereby be lost.

By the name of swords, keen intelligence is understood, according to the Apostle, who says: “The word of God is living and effective, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword” [Note: [Col. 0939] 15 Heb. IV, 12]. The Son of God is immortal and almighty, and more perceptive than every intellect, whether in carnal or spiritual matters, [source text marked +] most acute. “It reaches even to the division of soul and spirit.” This occurs ineffably, in the way that sensuality differs from reason, and sensuality itself differs from itself, when that which is more devoted to lower things is superior, or when recalled from them is more worthy, though even then it cannot be compared with reason.

The Son of God also knows how the Holy Spirit is distinct from himself [source text marked +], whether when it longs for God, considers heavenly things below, or by reason reflects upon the right conduct of worldly matters below; and he knows how things are separated by sensuality, when that which is lower in it is surpassed by what is higher.

It is evident that by swords others are designated—persecutors. For it is read in the Books of Kings how David, a ruddy youth and handsome in appearance, while tending his father’s sheep, went forth armed with Saul’s armor to fight Goliath. When he realized that he was burdened rather than helped by that armor, he laid it aside and chose for himself five very smooth stones from the stream. He carried them in a bag—or, as others say, in a milk vessel—together with a staff and sling. Thus he went out against the enemy; and when Goliath had been struck in the forehead by the blow of one stone hurled by the sling’s rotation and had fallen, David drew the sword of the one who had been struck down and cut off his head [Note: [Col. 0941] 1 1 Sam. XVII, 38–51].

In this deed David signifies the Church, whose face all the rich of the people will entreat to behold. She is ruddy in the martyrs and beautiful in all her members. She is young because of the newness of life, nourishing faithful souls through [source text marked +] salutary doctrine.

Goliath is the devil, against whom the faithful must fight as against an enemy. Whoever desires to despise the world advances against him for battle. Saul’s armor is the carnal observance of the Law, which, because it justifies no one, does not help but burdens. The very smooth stones are the purest meanings in the Law.

The Church took these from the stream, doing nothing [the text is defective here], that is, from the Jews, who did not use the spiritual meaning of the Law and, because of the deep desires of their flesh, are compared to a stream [source text marked +].

The bag signifies preachers, who are guests and pilgrims in this world. The milk vessel signifies the simple, filled with the doctrine of faith. The staff is discipline for chastising the insolent, and mercy for supporting the weak.

The sling with its cords is the mouth of the preacher, together with the two stones. “One stone is placed in the sling, by whose rotation the enemy is killed.” Although preachers retain the whole Law within themselves, they nevertheless often turn its unity within themselves to destroy the enemy: one God, one faith, one baptism.

He fell after being struck in the forehead, so that it might be clear to everyone that the enemy had been struck and conquered.

Goliath’s sword signifies the persecutors of the Church, through whom he attempted to remove its head. But when grace arrived, the devil was beheaded with his own sword. Thus many persecutors overcome the devil by attending both to themselves and to others who had become the devil’s body; through the hand of David—that is, through the Church’s agency [source text marked +]—they separated them from their head, and afterward they clung to the side of the Church.

Goliath’s sheath is error enveloping unbelief. Unless the sword were drawn from it [source text marked +], Goliath’s head could never be cut off by means of it.

The sword signifies temporal tribulation, as in the Gospel: “And a sword will pierce his own soul” [Note: [Col. 0941] 2 Luke II, 35], that is, tribulation will torment your soul.

The sword signifies opposition, as in the Psalms: “Sinners have drawn the sword” [Note: [Col. 0941] 3 Ps. XXXVI, 14], that is, the reprobate have exercised opposition.

The sword signifies separation, as in the Gospel: “I have not come to send peace, but a sword” [Note: [Col. 0941] 4 Matt. X, 34], that is, separation.

The sword signifies persecution, as in the Psalms: “Shield, sword, and battle” [Note: [Col. 0941] 5 Ps. LXXV, 4], that is, the Lord removes from his Church both the vice of excuse and the weapon of persecution [source text marked +], as well as the harassment of the enemy.

The sword signifies the malice of the devil, as in Job: “He who made him has brought his sword near him” [Note: [Col. 0941] 6 Job XL, 14], meaning that God, who created him, has restrained his malice.

The sword signifies the word of corruption, as in Isaiah: “The sword will devour you” [Note: [Col. 0941] 7 Isa. I, 20], that is, corruption will rebuke you.

The sword signifies a word of detraction, as in the Psalms: “Their tongue is a sword” [Note: [Col. 0941] 8 Ps. LVI, 5], that is, their speech is full of biting detraction.

The sword signifies perverse persuasion, as in the Psalms: “Deliver me from the evil sword” [Note: [Col. 0941] 9 Ps. CXLIII, 10], that is, rescue me from deadly persuasion.

The sword signifies death, as in Genesis: “He carried the sword and fire in his hands” [Note: [Col. 0941] 10 Gen. XXII, 6], meaning that Christ’s passion and death were in the Father’s power.

The sword signifies vengeance, as in the song of Deuteronomy: “My sword shall devour flesh” [Note: [Col. 0941] 11 Deut. XXXII, 42], that is, my vengeance shall destroy the carnal.

The sword signifies sin, as in Ezekiel: “If he sees the sword and does not blow the trumpet” [Note: [Col. 0941] 12 Ezek. XXXIII, 3]. The sinner is worthy of condemnation [source text marked +] if he ceases from teaching when he sees sin reigning [source text marked +].

The sword signifies Antichrist, as in Job: “When the sword takes hold of him” [Note: [Col. 0941] 13 Job XLI, 17], meaning that when Antichrist has received the devil into himself, severe persecution or tribulation will exist in the world.

The sword signifies the Last Judgment, as in the song of Deuteronomy: “If I sharpen my flashing sword” [Note: [Col. 0941] 14 Deut. XXXII, 41], that is, if in wrath I reveal my judgment.

The sword signifies eternal damnation, as in Job: “If his sons are multiplied, they shall be for the sword” [Note: [Col. 0941] 15 Job XXVII, 14], meaning that all whom the wicked man has as imitators will be condemned.

By the sword are meant the words of God, as in the Psalms: “Two-edged swords are in their hands” [Note: [Col. 0941] 16 Ps. CXLIX, 6], that is, the words of God are in their works.

Gravel signifies an unstable mind, as in Job: “In the caves of the earth or upon the gravel” [Note: [Col. 0941] 17 Job XXX, 6]. Heretics dwell among such hearers, who possess deceitful and unstable minds.

By gravel are meant the reprobate, as in Job: “He was sweet to the gravel of Cocytus” [Note: [Col. 0941] 18 Job XXI, 33]. The devil is sweet in their minds, [source text marked +], because now, through their shifting instability, they move toward eternal lamentation; [source text marked +] for “Cocytus” is said to mean lamentation.

A step signifies human progress, as in the Book of Ezra: “The people stood in their place” [Note: [Col. 0941] 19 Neh. VIII, 7], meaning that the assembly of the saints unanimously perseveres in its progress.

By steps are meant spiritual virtues, as in Job: “I will declare him according to my individual steps” [Note: [Col. 0941] 20 Job XXXI, 37], that is, I will praise him for each of the virtues I possess.

By steps are meant the gifts of the Holy Spirit, as in Ezekiel: “There were seven steps of the ascent of the gate” [Note: [Col. 0943] 1 Ezek. XL, 6], meaning that through the sevenfold gifts of the Spirit one reaches the entrance to the heavenly homeland.

Grass signifies hearers, as in the song of Deuteronomy: “Like drops upon the grass” [Note: [Col. 0943] 2 Deut. XXXII, 2], meaning that faithful hearers receive the subtle drops of holy preaching.

A grain signifies Christ’s humanity, as in the Gospel: “A grain of wheat falling” [Note: [Col. 0943] 3 John XII, 24], that is, Christ’s humanity appearing in the world.

A grain signifies the word of faith, as in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed” [Note: [Col. 0943] 4 Matt. XIII, 11]. The holy Church possesses within herself the word of a strong faith.

A grain signifies the weakness of the human body, as in Paul: “And the body, not what is to be, but a bare grain” [Note: [Col. 0943] 5 1 Cor. XV, 37], meaning that our flesh is not now as it will be, but is corruptible and weak.

Hail signifies the word of correction, as in the Psalms: “The clouds passed by, hail” [Note: [Col. 0943] 6 Ps. XVII, 13], and so forth. In that blessed life, hearers will be taught by neither preaching nor rebuked by correction.

Hail signifies the Synagogue, made harsh by unbelief, as in Job: “Have you seen the treasures of hail?” [Note: [Col. 0943] 7 Job XXXVIII, 22]. Even in the Synagogue’s [source text marked +] perfidy, God keeps the faithful in reserve.

Hail signifies tribulation, as in the Psalms: “He delivered their beasts to the hail” [Note: [Col. 0943] 8 Ps. LXXVII, 48], meaning that through tribulation God permits the supports of the wicked to be destroyed.

Hail signifies violent plunder, as in the Psalms: “And he killed their beasts with hail” [Note: [Col. 0943] 9 ibid., v. 50], that is, he permitted their powers to be deceived through violent plunder.

Hail signifies a grievous affliction, as in Exodus, where hail devastated Egypt [Note: [Col. 0943] 10 Exod. IX, 22–24], that is, a grievous affliction torments the world.

The treasury signifies the heavenly homeland, as in the Gospel: “He watched how the crowd was casting its gifts into the treasury” [Note: [Col. 0943] 11 Mark XII, 41]. God looks with pious regard upon those who despise earthly things in order to attain the heavenly homeland.

The treasury signifies the mind of a holy man, as in Ezekiel: “He shall place the linen garments in the treasury” [Note: [Col. 0943] 12 Ezek. XLIV, 19], meaning that holy men preserve within the mind the subtle forms of devotion.

By the treasury are meant the prelates of the Church, as in Ezekiel: “The treasuries around the pavement” [Note: [Col. 0943] 13 Ezek. XL, 17], meaning that holy prelates guard the lower people with attentive and watchful care.

Frost signifies the Jewish people, as in Job: “And who has begotten the frost from heaven?” [Note: [Col. 0943] 14 Job XXXVIII, 29]. Although that people is faithless, the Lord caused it to proceed from the heavenly stock of the ancient fathers.

Frost signifies the harshness of tribulation, as in Job: “When God breathes, frost is formed” [Note: [Col. 0943] 15 Job XXXVII, 10], meaning that wherever God pours out his inspiration, tribulation sometimes immediately increases.

Cheeks signify the holy martyrs, as in the Song: “His cheeks are like beds of spices” [Note: [Col. 0943] 16 Song V, 13]. The holy martyrs, who blush in Christ’s body, which is the holy Church, emit the greater sweetness before God the more harshly they are tested in their passion.

Cheeks signify the high priests, as in the Song: “Your cheeks are beautiful, like a tower” [Note: [Col. 0943] 17 Song I, 10]. The spiritual beauty of holy prelates consists in bodily chastity and compunction of mind.

Cheeks signify good workers, as in the Song: “Your cheeks are like a slice of a pomegranate” [Note: [Col. 0943] 18 Song IV, 3]. The workers of the holy Church, diverse within the unity of faith, appear publicly for the progress of their neighbors.

By the name of cheeks, modest prelates are portrayed, in whose presence one is ashamed to sin. Hence in the Song, the Bridegroom says to the Bride: “Your cheeks are like a slice of a pomegranate, apart from what is hidden within” [Note: [Col. 0943] 19 ibid.]. For outwardly they are red with martyrdom; inwardly they shine white with virginity, to say nothing of private prayers, vigils, fasts, and almsgiving.

By the name of cheeks, the modesty and piety of the Savior are understood, according to what the Bride says of him: “His cheeks are like beds of spices, planted by perfumers” [Note: [Col. 0943] 20 Song V, 13]. The habits of our Redeemer were [lacuna] and composed, and were bundles of virtues, recorded in harmonious voice by prophets and apostles.

Generation signifies something good, as in the Psalms: “This is the generation of those who seek him” [Note: [Col. 0943] 21 Ps. XXIII, 6].

Generation signifies something evil, as in the Gospel: “An evil and adulterous generation” [Note: [Col. 0943] 22 Matt. XII, 39; XVI, 4]. The former is the gentile people, who sought the Lord through faith; the latter is the Jewish people, who apostatized from God through unbelief.

“This is the generation of the upright, which shall be blessed” [Note: [Col. 0943] 23 Ps. CXI, 2]; but this is “a crooked and embittering generation, a generation that did not direct its heart and whose spirit was not faithful with God” [Note: [Col. 0943] 24 Ps. LXXVII, 8].

Likewise: “Generation and generation shall praise your works” [Note: [Col. 0943] 25 Ps. CXLIV, 4], that is, every succession of the faithful; “or will you extend your anger from generation to generation?” [Note: [Col. 0943] 26 Ps. LXXXIV, 6].

There are two generations: one of Adam, which is carnal; the other of Christ, which is spiritual. Just as evil Christians are expelled from the latter, so good people who lived before Christ’s coming are grafted into it.

“The thoughts of his heart from generation to generation” [Note: [Col. 0943] 27 Ps. XXXIII, 11] means that the divine dispositions, rationally made, remain among Jews and gentiles: among the Jews, because blindness has happened in part to Israel; among the gentiles, so that the fullness might enter and thus all Israel might be saved.

“Your dominion is in every generation and generation” [Note: [Col. 0943] 28 Ps. CXLIV, 13], mortal and immortal.

“The generation of the upright shall be blessed” [Note: [Col. 0943] 29 Ps. CXI, 2], meaning that their imitators, or their works, will be rewarded.

A nation signifies the human race, as in Isaiah: “You have multiplied the nation, but you have not magnified the joy” [Note: [Col. 0943] 30 Isa. IX, 3]. The human race did indeed increase before Christ’s coming, but it descended into hell.

A nation signifies the Jewish people, as in the song of Deuteronomy: “A nation without counsel and without understanding” [Note: [Col. 0943] 31 Deut. XXXII, 28]. The Jews are without discernment of good and evil and without prudence concerning future things, because they have no provision at the end of life.

By nations are meant gentiles, as in the Psalms: “All nations, clap your hands” [Note: [Col. 0943] 32 Ps. XLVI, 2], that is, all gentile peoples, honor God in your works.

By nations are meant those living as gentiles, as in Paul: “You know that when you were gentiles” [Note: [Col. 0945] 1 1 Cor. XII, 2], that is, when you were living as gentiles.

Likewise in the Apocalypse: “All the nations drank of the wrath of her fornication” [Note: [Col. 0945] 2 Rev. XVIII, 3], meaning that all who live as gentiles shared in the vengeance of Babylon’s impurity.

And elsewhere: “The other part, which is outside, cast out,” [source text marked +] meaning: show that unbelievers are to be excommunicated; “and do not measure,” that is, do not give what is holy to dogs, “because it has been given to the nations, and they have fornicated,” by living as gentiles.

By nations are meant vices: “He cast out the nations from before them” [Note: [Col. 0945] 3 Ps. LXXVII, 55], that is, he cast the seven chief vices out of the hearts of his saints. “And by lot he divided the land among them,” meaning that by his grace he granted each person a share in the heavenly homeland, “by the cord of distribution,” that is, according to the measure of divine generosity, “and he made the tribes of Israel dwell in their tents,” so that where vices had reigned, divine virtues might reign.

Clods signify holy men, as in Job: “And its clods are gold” [Note: [Col. 0945] 4 Job XXVIII, 6], meaning that the saints who are in the Church shine with the radiance of true wisdom.

Clods signify the hardened hearts of unbelievers, as in Job: “Or will he break the clods of the valleys?” [Note: [Col. 0945] 5 Job XXXIX, 13]. It belongs to God alone to break from the hardness of unbelief the hearts of those who are still in an impassable place because of unbelief.

A flock is the assembly of the chosen saints, as in the Gospel: “Do not fear, little flock” [Note: [Col. 0945] 6 Luke XII, 32], that is, “Take comfort, my people, who in number [lacuna] are few in comparison with the reprobate.”

A flock is the assembly of the perfect, as in the Song: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep” [Note: [Col. 0945] 7 Song IV, 2], meaning that the prelates of the Church imitate the examples of the saints.

A flock is the order of penitents, as in the Song: “Your hair is like flocks of goats” [Note: [Col. 0945] 8 ibid.], meaning that the lower peoples of the Church, who mourn their sins in repentance, set them before themselves as an example.

By a flock are meant unlearned peoples, as in Job: “They plundered flocks and pastured them” [Note: [Col. 0945] 9 Job XXIV, 2], meaning that heretics seize unlearned peoples and strangle them with their wicked doctrine.

By a flock are meant conventicles of the reprobate, as in the Song: “Go after the footsteps of your flocks” [Note: [Col. 0945] 10 Song I, 8], that is, follow the examples of gatherings of the reprobate.

By a flock are meant the orders of the saints, as in the Psalms: “And he took him from the flocks of sheep” [Note: [Col. 0945] 11 Ps. LXXVII, 70], meaning that God raises a preacher from the orders of the simple.

Footsteps signify good works, as in Job: “You have indeed counted my footsteps” [Note: [Col. 0945] 12 Job XXIV, 16], that is, you have kept my works counted before you in order to reward them [source text marked +].

Footsteps signify the actions of any wicked person, as in Job: “The footsteps of his strength shall be constricted” [Note: [Col. 0945] 13 Job XVIII, 7], meaning that the works of the wicked, which now appear stronger, will be brought to nothing.

Footsteps signify the movements of the mind, as in Job: “And he counts all my footsteps” [Note: [Col. 0945] 14 Job XXXV, 4], meaning that God knows all our inner movements.

Footsteps signify holy merits, as in the Psalms: “Direct my footsteps according to your word” [Note: [Col. 0945] 15 Ps. CXVIII, 133], that is, form good merits in me according to what Holy Scripture teaches.

Footsteps signify spiritual progress, as in the Song: “How beautiful are your footsteps in sandals” [Note: [Col. 0945] 16 Song VII, 1], meaning that the Church’s progress in examples is exceedingly beautiful.

A hunchback signifies any covetous person, as in Leviticus: “If he is hunchbacked, he shall not offer bread to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0945] 17 Lev. XXI, 20], meaning that whoever is subject to covetousness cannot offer a spiritual sacrifice to God.

A giant is Christ, as in the Psalms: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course” [Note: [Col. 0945] 18 Ps. XVIII, 6], meaning that Christ passes through the course of the present life with a certain joyful strength and strong joy.

A giant signifies any saint, as in the Psalms: “A giant will not be saved by the greatness of his strength” [Note: [Col. 0945] 19 Ps. XXXII, 16], meaning that not even a holy soul can be saved in its holiness without God’s help.

A giant signifies the devil, as in Job: “He has rushed upon me like a giant” [Note: [Col. 0945] 20 Job XVI, 14], meaning that the devil has proudly risen up against me.

A giant signifies a grave sin, as in Ecclesiasticus: “Did he not kill the giant?” [Note: [Col. 0945] 21 Sir. XLVII, 4], meaning that every elect person strives to kill the grave sin within himself.

By giants are meant prelates, as in Job: “Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters” [Note: [Col. 0945] 22 Job XXVI, 5], meaning that prelates cannot be concerned for their subjects without sorrow.

By giants are meant proud men, as in Genesis: “The giants ruled over the earth” [Note: [Col. 0945] 23 Gen. VI, 4], meaning that reprobate men rule in the present life.

By giants are meant the princes of the earth, as in Isaiah: “He will raise up giants for you” [Note: [Col. 0945] 24 Isa. XIV, 9], that is, he will raise up lofty princes in the world.

By giants are meant those who despair, as in Isaiah: “The giants shall not rise again” [Note: [Col. 0945] 25 Isa. XXVI, 14], meaning that those who despair do not rise from sins through repentance.

By giants are meant demons: “You will bring down the land of the giants to ruin” [Note: [Col. 0945] 26 ibid., v. 19], that is, you will destroy hell, which is the dwelling place of demons.

A giant signifies any exceedingly strong man, as in the Psalms: “A giant will not be saved by the greatness of his strength” [Note: [Col. 0945] 27 Ps. XXXII, 16], that is, by endurance of sufferings and by being swift in transcending worldly things; nevertheless, he will not be saved by the greatness of his strength without the help of grace.

A gomor signifies the virtue of discernment, as in Exodus: “A gomor for each head” [Note: [Col. 0945] 28 Exod. XVI, 16], meaning that each of the elect ought to practice the virtues of discernment.

A whirlpool signifies the onrush of persecution, as in the song of Habakkuk: “The whirlpool of waters passed by” [Note: [Col. 0945] 29 Hab. III, 10], that is, the onrush of persecuting peoples ceased.

A fishpond signifies the holy Church, as in Job: “Or a fishers’ hut with his head?” [Note: [Col. 0945] 30 Job XL, 26]. God mercifully unites to the holy Church, which was entrusted to fishermen, the very greatest imitators of the devil [source text marked +].

The throat signifies Christ’s doctrine, as the bride says in the Song: “His throat is most sweet” [Note: [Col. 0945] 31 Song V, 16]. Christ’s doctrine both prepares assisting grace and enduring life.

Alternatively, the bridegroom’s throat is the inward savor of Christ’s words, which few taste; but those who taste it hunger for more. Or, just as the words he spoke are evident upon the Lord’s lips, so in his throat the hidden disposition of his goodness is revealed to the understanding—by which it came about that he spoke outwardly to us.

Throat is also used for heart and for voice.

The throat signifies any preacher, as in the Song: “Your throat is like [source text: *] a voice” [Note: [Col. 0947] 1 Song VII, 9], meaning that the preacher of the Church, in whom the Lord’s voice resounds, announces intoxication with heavenly love.

Drops signify the opinions of heretics, as in the Song: “My locks are full of drops of the night” [Note: [Col. 0947] 2 Song V, 2], that is, my peoples have been deceived through the opinions of heretics.

Drops signify anguish, as in the Gospel: “Like drops of blood running down upon the ground” [Note: [Col. 0947] 3 Luke XXII, 44], meaning that the bodily labors of Christ, who is the Church, [source text marked *] are full of anguish.

Galilee, which is interpreted as “wheel,” signifies the world, [source text marked *] which is always turning toward its end. Galilee, [source text marked *] which is also interpreted as “transmigration made,” signifies a change of life: sometimes from an evil life to a good one, sometimes from a good life to blessedness. Very many examples of these are found in the Gospel.

### H

Fishhook. Herbs. Heron. Hermon. Winter. Spears. Hyenas. Neighing. He-goat. Horrible. Reed. Earth. Moisture. Shoulder. Herod. Spear-shaft. Kid. [source text: *] Desert. Dropsical. Today. Holocaust.

Hamus means the humanity of Christ, as in Job: “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook [Note: [Col. 0947] 4 Job 40:20]?” For when the devil bit the bait of Christ’s body, the barb of his divinity, which lay hidden in his humanity, pierced him. The hook is understood as the word of preaching, in which the bait of inner blessedness is found. Hence the Lord, after proving to blessed Peter by a rational * argument that he ought not to pay the didrachma because he was the king’s son, added, saying: “But lest we scandalize them, go to the sea and cast in a hook [Note: [Col. 0947] 5 Matthew 17:27]”; as if he were saying to all the faithful, of whom Peter bears the type in this age: Go into the world and preach him in whom the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom hangs. “And take the fish that first comes up,” that is, embrace Christ in faith and love, who first passed from this world to the Father in heaven. “And when you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater, *”; and when his words have been expounded, you will find not only complete redemption but also reward. For a stater is a kind of * small coin, containing two didrachmas—that is, a double drachma. “Take it,” he says, “and give it to them for me and for you.” “For me,” namely, who pay what I did not seize; “but for you,” who in the first man seized what belonged to God—that is, to be subject to no one. Therefore, whoever is guilty should seek redemption in Christ’s words, and * will live: for God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son; let him present that Son to his exactors on his own behalf, setting him against the evil spirits who gave one drachma to humanity and demand two: they gave it pride and daily demand interest. This is the sudden destruction enveloped in earthly ambition; hence Ecclesiastes says: “A man does not know his end; but just as fish are caught by a hook, so human beings are seized at an evil time [Note: [Col. 0947] 6 Ecclesiasticus 9:12],” when it overtakes them unexpectedly.

A shaft means the holy Church, as in Exodus: “The shaft of the lampstand and its reeds [Note: [Col. 0947] 7 Exodus 25:31],” that is, the Church of Christ and the holy preachers.

By the name “spear,” Christ or the apostles are understood. Hence it is written: “They will go forth in the light of your arrows [Note: [Col. 0947] 8 Habakkuk 3:11],” meaning that, through the authority of your utterances, the apostles will advance throughout the world—that is, through the manifest power of Christ, your Son, who works miracles. Alternatively: “They will go forth in the light of your arrows,” meaning that through the preaching and example of your apostles people will come to faith. “In the brightness * of your spear *,” in the power of your apostles, who have been sent out and work miracles. They are called arrows because they are sent far away; spears because they strike at close range. The first part of the final sentence and the last part of the first, joined together, make a third. A spear means holy preaching, as in Job: “The spear will not be able to stand [Note: [Col. 0947] 9 Job 41:17],” meaning that no preaching will be able to convert Antichrist to life. A spear means royal power, as in the Books of Kings: “Take the spear that is by his head [Note: [Col. 0947] 10 1 Samuel 26:11],” meaning that Christ took royal power away from the rulers of the Jews.
