A spear means persecution, as in Job: “The quiver will sound over him, * the spear will glitter [Note: [Col. 0947] 11 Job 39:26],” meaning that the holy man will be touched by the wickedness of the reprobate and harassed by persecution. A spear means the teaching of heretics, as in the Books of Kings: “The iron of his spear weighed six hundred * shekels of iron [Note: [Col. 0947] 12 1 Samuel 17:7],” meaning that it maturely displays the complete learning or perfection of the teaching of heretics, or of heretical doctrine. A spear means pride, as in the Books of Kings: “When he was in the forest that is in Ramah, holding a spear in his hand [Note: [Col. 0947] 13 1 Samuel 22:6],” meaning that every person who is lifted up exercises pride in action through + excess of delight and delightful elevation.

A dwelling is understood as Christ and the Church, according to the saying: “The sun and moon stood in their dwelling [Note: [Col. 0947] 14 Habakkuk 3:11],” meaning that although the rulers of this age displayed their power in persecution, Christ nevertheless remained in the Church [Col. 0948D] and the Church remained in Christ. A dwelling signifies the mind, according to the saying: “Behold, an angel of the Lord stood by [Note: [Col. 0947] 15 Acts 12:7],” meaning that Christ was ready to help his faithful one: “And light shone in the dwelling of the prison,” meaning that divine grace flashed in the sinner’s mind, in which the affliction of diabolical temptation had found a place. For here, as in many passages, prison signifies tribulation. Herod means the devil. Peter, however, bound in prison with two chains, represents the soul that was formerly steadfast in goodness and afterward, fettered by the bond of love and consent, became entirely subject to the tribulation of the enemy’s temptations. A dwelling means the heavenly Jerusalem, according to the saying: + “They wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place [Note: [Col. 0949] 1 Psalm 106:14],” meaning that they were without God and without the divine word: “They did not find the way to the city of their dwelling,” meaning that they possessed the + image of the faithful Church that bears the heavenly Jerusalem. A dwelling is an action, as in the Book of Numbers: “Indeed, your dwelling is strong,” that is, your action is strong.

Breath. See above, “Alitus.”

A reed signifies sacred Scripture, as it is written in the Apocalypse: “And the angel who was speaking with me [Note: [Col. 0949] 2 Revelation 21:15],” that is, the Son, the messenger of the Father’s will, “had a golden reed,” that is, sacred Scripture, gleaming with divine wisdom, “in order to measure the city,” + to teach the universal Church according to the measure of its capacity, “and its gates,” which defend others. “And the city was set on a + square,” meaning that the Church has four sides: faith, hope, charity, and action. These are said to be equal because as much as one believes, so much does one hope; as much as one hopes, so much does one love; and as much as one loves, so much does one act. A reed signifies unstable people; hence the Lord says concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind [Note: [Col. 0949] 3 Matthew 11:7]?”—which he clearly introduced not by asserting but by denying. For John was not a reed shaken by the wind, since he was neither shaken by terror nor led astray by fear, but remained steadfast in the fear of God. A reed signifies the gentile people, according to the saying: “He will not break a bruised reed [Note: [Col. 0949] 4 Matthew 12:20],” meaning that Christ, coming in the flesh, recalled the gentile people, already despaired of, to forgiveness—he who came to save what had perished. A reed signifies the vicious, according to the saying: “Rebuke the wild beasts of the reed [Note: [Col. 0949] 5 Psalm 68:31],” that is, destroy the heretics who dwell in the swamp of vices, or who deceitfully oppose sacred Scripture.

Sand signifies unfruitful unbelievers, according to the Lord’s saying: “I will number them, and beyond the sand . . . [Note: [Col. 0949] 6 Psalm 139:18],” meaning that the elect will be counted by me in a definite number, as being few; “and more than the sand of the sea,” meaning that the Lord will surpass the unbelievers in merit, and the elect will surpass the faithful in the world. Sand signifies love of the world, in which whatever is built is prepared for ruin. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who hears my words and does not do them is like a man building a house on sand. The rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house; and it fell, and its ruin was great [Note: [Col. 0949] 7 Matthew 7:26–27].” Whoever firmly establishes his mind in love of the world builds his house upon sand; but when bodily allurements, the gravest persecutions, and unclean spirits assail this house, which is established on a weak foundation, from every side, its ruin becomes all the heavier, the more lavish the expenditure on the building has been. Sand signifies the weakness of the things under discussion, according to the saying: “And he rained flesh upon them like dust [Note: [Col. 0949] 8 Psalm 78:27],” that is, abundantly, “and winged creatures like + the sand of the sea,” that is, innumerable quail. The elect are sand, as in Genesis: “I will make your offspring like the sand that is on the shore of the sea [Note: [Col. 0949] 9 Genesis 22:17],” meaning that God will bless the true children of Abraham at the consummation of the age. Sand means the reprobate, as in the Apocalypse: “And the dragon stood upon the sand of the sea [Note: [Col. 0949] 10 Revelation 12:18],” meaning that the devil dominates the unstable minds of the reprobate.

By the name “grass,” Christ incarnate is understood, as Job says: “Will the wild ass bray when he has grass [Note: [Col. 0949] 11 Job 6:1]?” The wild ass finds grass when the gentile people perceive Christ incarnate through faith, which the truly wicked person does not possess, though he brays in his fasts. Alternatively, when someone, burning with desires for the vision + within, refreshes himself through his compunction after a worldly life, he brays like a wild ass without grass; but when he reaches eternal life, he will rejoice without end in the grass he has received. By the name “grass,” the verdure of faith is understood, as the Lord says: “So is the kingdom of God, + when a man casts seed into the ground, and sleeps, and rises night and day, and the seed + reaches its term, and grows while he does not know it. For the earth bears fruit of itself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear [Note: [Col. 0949] 12 Mark 4:26–28].” “The kingdom of God” is the holy Church; “the man” is Christ, “who casts seed into the ground,” meaning that he preached the word of God everywhere through himself and through the apostles. “The man sleeps,” meaning that Christ received the sleep of death on the cross. “The seed rose night and day,” meaning that neither death nor life could delay the word of God. Hence the Apostle says: “I suffer even to chains, + doing evil: + but the word of God is not bound [Note: [Col. 0949] 13 2 Timothy 2:9].” The seed “sprouted” when the word of preaching took root in the honored people. The seed “grew” when the word spread among the Jews and among the gentiles. This happened “while that man did not know,” that is, while Christ was bodily absent, as he says in the Psalms: “A people whom I did not know served me [Note: [Col. 0949] 14 Psalm 18:44]”—“a people whom I did not know,” namely, by bodily presence. “For the earth bore fruit of itself,” meaning that the faithful people, having received the seed of the divine word, propagated within themselves the fruit of righteousness. How did it “first bring forth the blade,” that is, living faith, “then the ear,” that is, good action, though imperfect: [Col. 0950D] “then the full grain in the ear,” that is, good works possessing no imperfection; “and when it has produced the fruit, immediately he puts in the sickle,” meaning that after faith and action, which have + proceeded from the seed of the word, have spread everywhere, Christ will exercise judgment, “because the harvest is present,” that is, the consummation of the age. For when the fullness of the gentiles has entered, the day of judgment will come—that is, the end of the world.

By the name “grass,” every spiritual person can be understood, as the Lord says concerning the sown field: “But when the grass had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds also appeared [Note: [Col. 0951] 1 Matthew 13:26 and following].” The sower is the Son of + Man; the field is the world; the good seed is the sons of light; the weeds are the sons of iniquity; the sleeping men are prelates acting negligently; the enemy is the devil; the growing grass is the + spiritual person progressing toward better things; its fruit is that person’s good work. “Then the weeds appeared,” meaning that when someone has lived well, then he will be able to see who has been evil. The + servants of the householder, seeing people well formed by God but corrupted through the negligence of teachers and by diabolical + instruction, wish to remove from their midst all who live badly, having zeal for God but not according to knowledge. For the Lord wills something else, and he added the reason, saying: “No, lest while gathering the weeds you uproot the wheat together with them.” Here a place is given to repentance, and we are warned not to cut anyone off quickly from the fellowship of the faithful. For it can happen that someone who today seems to be a weed, when repentance intervenes by God’s grace, tomorrow + will become wheat.

“Allow both to grow until the harvest, and at harvest time I will say to the reapers: Gather the weeds and bind them + into bundles for burning; but gather the wheat into my barn.” The harvest is the consummation of the age; the reapers are angels; the binding of the weeds into bundles suggests that those who share one crime will also share one punishment; the wheat means the saints; the barn means the heavenly dwelling.

This command of the Lord—“Allow both to grow until the harvest”—seems to be contrary to what the Apostle says: “Remove the evil person from among you [Note: [Col. 0951] 2 1 Corinthians 5:13],” and that one should have no fellowship with a brother who is called a fornicator or a miser, and so forth. For if separation is forbidden and patience must be maintained until the harvest, how are the wicked to be cast out from among + you? Does the Judge preach one thing while the herald proclaims another? But because between wheat and weeds—which we call darnel, *lolium*—as long as it is still grass and the stalk has not yet come to the ear, there is great similarity and scarcely any difficult distinction in discerning them, the Lord warns us not to deliver judgment quickly concerning ambiguous matters, and therefore to reserve the judgment that is hidden, by which he will cast the wicked out from the assembly of the saints on the day of judgment, not on suspicion of a crime but on the basis of manifest guilt. The Apostle’s word, however, concerns chaff, that is, those who are openly wicked, who either by their own mouth [Col. 0951D] confessed . . . or were convicted by ecclesiastical judgment. The mention itself in the Apostle’s words clearly indicates this. The Lord, for his part, deals with the general separation of all the wicked, which was the subject of their discourse; but Paul deals with the spiritual separation of certain people convicted, as has been said, which must be carried out for their correction as far as possible, with the peace of the Church and without scandalizing the good, “lest,” as the Lord says, “the wheat also be uprooted.”

By the name “grass,” virtues are understood, as Moses says * in the song of Deuteronomy: “Let my teaching gather like rain [Note: [Col. 0951] 3 Deuteronomy 32:2],” so that it may fertilize the minds of hearers; “let your word flow like dew,” so that it may cool the heat of vices—like rain upon grass, making the shoots of virtues grow green, and like drops upon the turf, so that they may never dry up. By the name “grass,” luxurious and slippery desires are designated, as Job says concerning Behemoth: “For him the mountains bear grass [Note: [Col. 0951] 4 Job 40:15],” meaning that proud rich people, at Satan’s pleasure, produce and nourish luxurious and slippery desires. Grass means good knowledge, as in Jeremiah: “Their eyes failed, because there was no grass [Note: [Col. 0951] 5 Jeremiah 14:6],” that is, the prelates of the synagogue vanished because they did not possess spiritual knowledge. Grass means good action, as in Genesis: “Let the earth bring forth green grass [Note: [Col. 0951] 6 Genesis 1:11],” * let a person practice fitting action. [Col. 0952B] Grass means temporal support, as in the Psalm: “And grass for the service of human beings [Note: [Col. 0951] 7 Psalms 104:14 and 147:8],” that is, temporal support for the needs of preachers. Grass means worldly glory, as in the Psalm: “In the morning may it pass away like grass [Note: [Col. 0951] 8 Psalm 90:6],” meaning that when the brightness of the life to come appears, the glory of the world will fail. By grasses, clearer ordinances are meant, as in Job: “They ate grasses and the bark of trees [Note: [Col. 0951] 9 Job 30:4],” meaning that heretics, by understanding perversely, twist both clearer ordinances and the examples of the saints. By grasses, the sayings of the Old Testament are meant, as in the Books of Kings: “He went out into the field to gather wild grasses [Note: [Col. 0951] 10 2 Kings 4:39],” meaning that we ought to read sacred Scripture and, through understanding, follow the ancient sayings. By grasses, carnal pleasures are meant, as in Job: “For him the mountains bear grasses [Note: [Col. 0951] 11 Job 40:15].” By grasses, eternal joys are meant, as in * Jeremiah: “There they rest in green grasses [Note: [Col. 0951] 12 Ezekiel 34:14],” meaning that the elect will have rest in unfading joys.

A kid means Christ, as in Exodus: “You shall also take a kid and sacrifice it [Note: [Col. 0951] 13 Exodus 12:5],” that is, you Jews shall receive Christ—* that is, you shall crucify him—who, not only innocent for the guilty but also righteous for the unrighteous, willed to be crucified, tempted in every respect according to likeness, without sin [Note: [Col. 0951] 14 Hebrews 4:15]. The kids are sinners, who will be on the judge’s left [Note: [Col. 0951] 15 Matthew 25]. Hence the bridegroom rebukes the bride, still young and therefore trembling lest she be deceived by heretics, with a kindly reprimand, saying: “If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women [Note: [Col. 0951] 16 Song of Songs 1:7]”—as if he were saying: If you are so simple [that] you do not know what is right; if you have forgotten what teachings have imbued you and what examples have formed you, “go out from my company and depart after the tracks of the flocks”; follow the various actions of those who wander; “and feed your kids beside the shepherds’ tents”; teach your lost and doomed hearers * after the schools of your foolish teachers—or, to feed kids means to nourish the uncleanness of the flesh. The Lord does not command this, but permits it, and foretells to the one who does not know what will happen.

A kid means repentance, as in Genesis: “I will send you a kid from the goats [Note: [Col. 0951] 17 Genesis 38:17],” meaning that Christ pours repentance for former errors into the Church. A kid means the appetite of the flesh, as in the Book of Judges: “Gideon cooked a kid [Note: [Col. 0953] 1 Judges 6:19],” meaning that those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires [Note: [Col. 0953] 2 Galatians 5:24]. By kids, the pleasurable senses of the body are meant, as in the Song of Songs: “Feed your kids [Note: [Col. 0953] 3 Song of Songs 1:8],” that is, I will permit you to nourish your pleasurable senses. By kids, the reprobate are meant, as in the Gospel: “He will indeed set the sheep at his right hand, but the kids at his left [Note: [Col. 0953] 4 Matthew 25:33],” meaning that the elect will be saved and the reprobate condemned.

The heron means Christ, as in the Psalms: “The house of the heron is their leader [Note: [Col. 0953] 5 Psalm 104:17],” meaning that the Church, which is Christ’s dwelling, leads the elect to life. The heron means any perfect person, as in Job: “The wing of the ostrich is like the wings of the heron [Note: [Col. 0953] 6 Job 39:16],” meaning that at times a hypocrite publicly displays an action such as is practiced by the one who is perfect in all things.

The wilderness means Judea, as in the Psalms: “He split the rock in the wilderness [Note: [Col. 0953] 7 Psalm 78:15],” that is, he broke the hardness in Judea, “and watered them as if in a great abyss [Note: [Col. 0953] 8 Ibid.],” * he poured forth throughout the whole world an abundance of divine gifts. The wilderness means the gentiles, as in the Prophet: “The fields of the wilderness sprouted [Note: [Col. 0953] 9 Joel 2:22],” meaning that the people of the gentiles, having looked upon it, brought forth the law for fruitfulness, which they received as though merely by its fragrance. The wilderness means an austere, tranquil, and secure life, to which the servants of God must truly flee.

Hermon indicates the gentiles, as in the Psalms: “Tabor and Hermon will rejoice in your name [Note: [Col. 0953] 10 Psalm 89:12],” meaning that the Jews, coming through the law and illuminated, and the gentiles, anathematizing the devil and alienated from vices, will rejoice in being subjected to your Lord. * For Tabor is said to mean “coming light”; Hermon is called “anathema” or “alien.” Hermon, which is interpreted as “exalted light,” signifies Christ, as the Psalm says: “Like the dew of Hermon that descends upon Mount Zion [Note: [Col. 0953] 11 Psalm 133:3],” that is, the grace of Christ * who has been exalted and has come to the Church. That brothers dwell together in unity is like the grace of Christ, which descends upon the more eminent members of the Church. Zion, contemplating future things, is interpreted as “watchtower.”

The dropsical person signifies any miser, as in the Gospel: “And behold, there was a dropsical man before him [Note: [Col. 0953] 12 Luke 14:2],” meaning that the miser, the more abundantly he possesses, the more he desires, just as the dropsical person thirsts the more he drinks.

Winter, because it is a season of instability and abounds in storms, signifies an abundance of iniquity. Hence the Lord in the Gospel according to * Mark says: “Pray that your flight may not take place in winter [Note: [Col. 0953] 13 Mark 24:20],” that is, when you have been in abundance, “or on the Sabbath,” a saying which Luke gives as follows: “Watch at all times, praying that you may be considered worthy to escape the things that are to come and to stand before the Son of Man [Note: [Col. 0953] 14 Luke 21].” Those who are then found in an abundance of iniquity, [Col. 0954A] and not in the calling of good works, will not be worthy. Alternatively, winter is unsuitable for * journeys because of the cold; on the Sabbath, however, it is not permitted to go farther, as the law forbids [Note: [Col. 0953] 15 Exodus 16:29]. The meaning is: See to it that you do not then begin to flee from God’s anger, when it is not permitted to walk.

Winter means the cold of unbelief, as the bridegroom says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “Arise, my beloved [Note: [Col. 0953] 16 Song of Songs 2:10],” from the quiet of contemplation, “and come” to the office of preaching: “for winter * has already passed,” that is, the freezing of unbelief from the hearts of the gentiles; “the rain has gone away and departed,” persecution, gradually declining, has ceased altogether. Winter means wickedness, as in the Gospel: “The feast of the Dedication took place in Jerusalem, and it was winter [Note: [Col. 0953] 17 John 10:22],” meaning that when God taught on that feast, their wickedness against him blazed up. Winter means the final judgment, as in Proverbs: “He prepares in summer what he will eat in winter [Note: [Col. 0953] 18 Proverbs 6:8],” that is, in the present life he earns what he will be rewarded for in the * future.

The hyena is the devil, as in the Prophet: “The den of the hyena is my inheritance,” that is, the Jews, whom I chose as an inheritance, rejected me and received the devil into themselves.

The fawns are spiritual virtues, as in the Song of Songs: “Your two breasts are like two fawns [Note: [Col. 0953] 19 Song of Songs 7:3],” meaning that in both peoples—namely, the Jewish and the gentile—there are spiritual men.

The neighing is preaching, as in Job: “You will surround the horse’s neck with neighing [Note: [Col. 0953] 20 Job 39:22],” that is, you will enrich the preacher’s mind with holy preaching.

The swallow means perseverance in prayer, as in Isaiah: “Like a young swallow [Note: [Col. 0953] 21 Isaiah 38:14],” that is, I will pray continually and hastily, in the manner of a swallow. By swallows, the proud are meant, as in the Book of Tobit [Note: [Col. 0953] 22 Tobit 2:14], where warm dung from a swallow’s nest fell into the eyes of the sleeping man: that is, burning lusts from the nourishment of the proud occupied the inner senses.

The he-goat means Christ, as in Leviticus, where the scapegoat carried the sins of the people [Note: [Col. 0953] 23 Leviticus 16:22]; meaning that Christ, sent into the world by the Father, carried the sins of the human race. Those two he-goats, one of whom is killed and the other sent into the wilderness, mystically signify Christ and * Barabbas. For Christ suffers death for the sins of the people, and * Barabbas descends into hell. Likewise:

> Before the temple doors the law brings two he-goats:
>
> * One is sent away “from iron” (*de ferro*, reading uncertain); the other dies.
>
> [Col. 0954D] Christ is each of the two he-goats in different respects:
>
> For he bore on the wood and lives in the citadel of heaven.

For just as Christ is figured in the lamb because of innocence, so also in the he-goat because of the multitude of sinful flesh. A he-goat means the movement of lust, as in the law: “Take a he-goat for sin [Note: [Col. 0953] 24 Leviticus 9:3],” that is, extinguish in * us the movement of lust before you rush headlong into the actual deed. A he-goat means the uncleanness of the flesh, as in the Psalms: “I will offer you cattle together with he-goats [Note: [Col. 0953] 25 Psalm 66:15],” that is, to your honor I will slaughter within myself the pride of the mind together with the wantonness of the flesh. By a he-goat, works of repentance are meant, as in the Song of Deuteronomy: “And he-goats with the marrow of wheat [Note: [Col. 0955] 1 Deuteronomy 32:14],” that is, he will perform works of repentance when he receives the body of Christ.

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0955] 2 Verse 13]: “He established him”—that is, the people led out of Egypt—“upon a high land, that he might eat the fruits of the fields, that he might suck honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone; butter from the herd, and milk from sheep with the fat of lambs and rams, the sons of Bashan, and he-goats with the marrow of wheat, and drink the purest blood of the grape.”

Mystically, the “people of the Jews” is the people of Christians who confess God. “Egypt” is unbelief; the “Red Sea” is baptism consecrated in the blood of Christ; the “wilderness” is the world; the “land of Bashan,” which is mountainous and is interpreted as “dryness,” signifies the Church, entirely dried up from love of the world * and understood as higher than the whole world. The “fruits of the fields” are the virtues and works of the faithful. “Honey from the rock” is the sweetness of evangelical teaching about Christ before his Passion. “Oil from the hardest stone” is the * anointing of the Holy Spirit from Christ made immortal. “Butter from the herd” is the rich and subtle teaching of the strong. “Milk from sheep” is the light teaching of the simple. The “fat of lambs and rams” is spiritual desire, which is still supplied to us by the example of the simple and of the strong sons of the Church set before their subjects. A he-goat means works of repentance necessary at every level of the virtues. “He would drink the marrow of wheat and the purest blood of the grape”: the purity of Christ’s body and his most sweet blood, through which the people of God are sent to salvation; for the he-goat, being wanton, indicates those devoted to lust.

God the Father is “a man,” as in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son” [Note: [Col. 0955] 3 Matt. XVIII, 23], that is, like God the Father, who joined the Church to Christ. For God the Father made a wedding feast for his Son when he united his own nature to his Word.

“Man” is understood as Christ, as in the Gospel: “A certain man going abroad called his servants and handed over his goods to them” [Note: [Col. 0955] 4 Matt. XXV, 14]. For Christ, according to the flesh, when he was about to ascend to heaven, bestowed various gifts on his disciples, whom he had chosen, according to each one’s [*capacity]. “To one he gave five talents,” that is, knowledge of outward things, which are subject to the bodily senses [Col. 0955D]; “to another one,” that is, understanding of inward things; “to another two,” that is, both. The five talents are doubled when some are also taught faithfully to administer outward things. The two talents make another two whenever some are formed both to govern outward matters well and likewise to serve spiritual understanding. To bury a talent in the earth is to entangle all understanding solely in earthly business. Moreover, whoever reveals to no one the understanding he has received from God hides the talent.

“Man” means the Redeemer of the world, as in Job: “My eye shall not see me” [Note: [Col. 0955] 5 Job VII, 8], that is, the Redeemer’s mercy shall not call me back. [Col. 0956A] By the designation “man” are signified [the following], as is read in the Psalms: “The sun has risen” [Note: [Col. 0955] 6 Ps. CIII, 22], that is, the Lord has risen again, “and they have gathered together,” namely, the Jews into the unity of faith; “and they shall be placed in their chambers,” meaning that the baptized shall rest in their consciences. “Man shall go forth to his work,” because, when Christ rose again and a multitude of Jews came to the faith, the choir of the apostles went forth into all the earth to preach the gospel; previously they had remained inactive because of fear of the Jews. “And to his labor until evening,” that is, to continual preaching until the darkness that will come at the end of the age through Antichrist. Labor is the continuation of work.

“Man” means any preacher, as in the Gospel: “Go into the village that is opposite you, and you will find an ass tied up, [Col. 0956B] on which no human being has sat” [Note: [Col. 0955] 7 Matt. XXI, 2]. This means that no preacher had yet taught the gentile people. For, entering the world, the apostles found that opposing people—the nations—were entangled in the bonds of sins. No teacher endowed with reason ruled them, one who might restrain them from evil by the bridle of correction or compel them to hold fast to the good.

By “man” the just person is understood, as in: “All who saw him were troubled” [Note: [Col. 0955] 8 Mark VI, 50]. This means that those were pierced in heart who, after the Savior’s resurrection had been accomplished, understood that the Jews were ineffective; “and every man feared,” meaning that every just person endowed with reason shuddered at association with them.

“Man” means the evangelist Matthew, as in Ezekiel: “The face of a man” [Note: [Col. 0955] 9 Ezek. I, 5, 10]. Because Matthew began to write about a human being, he was represented by the human face [Col. 0956C].

“Man” means the mind’s reason, as in the Gospel: “I have no man, so that, when the water has been troubled, he may put me into the pool,” that is, [lacuna] I lack the inward [means] by which the meditation on the Lord’s Passion may heal me.

“Man” means any wicked person, according to: “To judge the orphan and the humble” [Note: [Col. 0955] 10 Ps. X, 18], that is, so that the wicked man may no longer presume to be proud in earthly matters. For this is the desire of the poor, which the Lord heard; or, to the extent that this world has died for them, let the humble person be judged, so that no wicked person may thereafter presume to exalt himself above the saints, who, retaining the seed of the divine word, bear fruit in patience.

“Man” means Antichrist, as in Paul: “For unless the dissension first comes, and the man of sin, the son of perdition, is revealed, who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God” [Note: [Col. 0955] 11 II Thess. II, 3]. The words “the day of the Lord will not come” are to be supplied. The Apostle calls “dissension” the separation of the ten kings from the Roman Empire: the Persians, Saracens, Vandals, Goths, Lombards, Burgundians, Franks, Huns, Alemanni, and Suebi. Antichrist [lacuna]; although he will have caused himself to be regarded as the Lord and Son of God, he will possess no divinity in himself beyond the fact that he is a mere human being. He is called “the man of sin” because, conceived and born in sins, he will devote himself to increasing sins [Col. 0957A]. He is “the son of perdition” because he is born into the world for this purpose: to destroy others and finally to perish himself forever. “He will oppose every good,” since he will be full of every evil; indeed, the entire wickedness of diabolical deceit will dwell in him. Finally, he will burst forth into such madness that he will presume to remove himself not only from Jove and Mercury and the other so-called gods, but also from the holy Trinity, which all believers worship in true faith. But, as the Psalm declares concerning him, his sin will be sought, until the stroke of the eye has been brought to nothing, and he himself will not be found; that is, he will be destroyed without end. He is called “the man of sin” because he will subject himself entirely to sin.

The devil is called “man,” not because of his nature but because of his [Col. 0957B] guilt and weakness. Hence it is written in the Gospel that, while the men were sleeping, an enemy man sowed weeds in the midst of the wheat. This plainly means that, when prelates act negligently, the ancient enemy makes sons of darkness from the sons of light, and what was sweet is turned into bitter. “An enemy man has done this” [Note: [Col. 0957] 1 Matt. XIII, 25, 28], because it is always the devil’s task to mingle evil with good.

By “man” the human race is understood, according to what John says in the Apocalypse: “By these three plagues a third of mankind was killed, by the fire, smoke, and sulfur that came forth from their mouths” [Note: [Col. 0957] 2 Apoc. IX, 18]. Two parts of the human race are to be saved, namely, the active and the contemplative; the third consists of the rejected. Different punishments are assigned to these in hell according to the different offenses by consciously committing which they were killed in this world—offenses that proceed from the preaching of Antichrist’s ministers. Those will experience eternal fire who here placed no limit on their desires. There they will be afflicted with smoke who here are blinded by the darkness of pride. They will have the stench of sulfur who, while they lived, without remedy subjected themselves to the stench of lust.

By “man” the patriarchs are signified, according to: “From heaven he looked upon the sons of men” [Note: [Col. 0957] 3 Ps. XIII, 1]. This means that the Word of God visited the Jews, descended from the stock of the patriarchs, by assuming humanity. Elsewhere: “God looked down from heaven,” meaning that Christ visited the entire offspring of the first parents through the apostles, who are called “heavens,” because “their sound has gone forth into all the earth.”

Some passages also speak of “men” in an evil sense, as in: “Nevertheless, the sons of men” [Note: [Col. 0957] 4 Ps. LXI, 10], meaning those who hope in worldly things and imitate worldly people. “The sons of men are liars in the balances” [Note: [Col. 0957] 5 Ibid.], meaning that they practice fraud not only in promises but also in petitions or judgments, so as to deceive whomever they can; thus they proceed from vanity to the same thing, that is, to vanity. For they proceed from vanity to vanity who come to riches through fraud or raise themselves to pride through riches.

It should be noted that every son of man is a man, but not every man is a son of man. Adam was made when God created him; hence men and sons of men are sometimes distinguished. Those who imitate Adam, the man, are called “men”; those who imitate Christ, the Son of Man, are called “sons of men.” Hence it is written: “You will save men and beasts” [Note: [Col. 0957] 6 Ps. XXXV, 8]. Carnal people enjoy temporal salvation, which, through the abundance of divine mercy, is shared also by beasts. But the sons of men, who imitate not Adam the man but Christ the Son of Man, “will hope under the shelter of your wings” [Note: [Col. 0957] 7 Ibid.], not, that is, in the things given to the wicked, but in the protection of your mercy and compassion.

It must be understood that “man” is sometimes spoken of by nature, sometimes by guilt, sometimes by reason, sometimes [Col. 0958B] by weakness, sometimes by likeness, sometimes by virtue, and sometimes by folly.

By nature, as in Genesis: “Let us make man according to our image” [Note: [Col. 0957] 8 Gen. I, 26], meaning that man was made in the image of God in his soul. And elsewhere: “A man was born in her,” meaning that Christ assumed human nature in the Church.

By guilt, in Paul: “Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not men?” [Note: [Col. 0957] 9 I Cor. III, 3], that is, are you not guilty? And likewise: “Are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to man?” [lacuna].

By reason, as there: “If, according to man, I fought with beasts at Ephesus” [Note: [Col. 0957] 10 I Cor. XV, 32], meaning: first I argued wisely against unbelievers; “what does it profit me if the dead do not rise?” To fight with beasts “according to man” is to argue rationally against unbelievers.

By virtue, as in the Psalms: “Man shall approach the deep heart” [Note: [Col. 0957] 11 Ps. LXIII, 8], that is, any virtuous person shall approach profound contemplation; or: “Man shall approach the deep heart” [Note: [Col. 0957] 12 Ps. VI, 4, and CVII, 8], meaning that Christ will willingly come to the profound counsel of his Passion. Likewise: “I will not fear what he will do” [lacuna], and so forth.

By weakness, as in Jeremiah: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man” [Note: [Col. 0957] 13 Jer. XVII, 5], that is, who hopes in one who is weak.

By folly, as in Proverbs: “The bread of deceit is sweet to a man” [Note: [Col. 0957] 14 Prov. XX, 17], that is, the teaching of [lacuna] is sweet to a fool.

By likeness, as in the [Gospel]: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who is a king” [Note: [Col. 0957] 15 Matt. XVIII, 23], and so forth.

Demons are “horrible,” as in Job: “They will go and come upon him, horrible” [Note: [Col. 0957] 16 Job XX, 25]. This means that, although evil spirits sometimes or rarely depart from a wicked person, they nevertheless continually return to him [Col. 0958D].

“Earth” is the holy Church, as in the Psalms: “And he will make them rest upon his earth” [Note: [Col. 0957] 17 Isa. XIV, 1], meaning that God grants his elect spiritual rest in the holy Church.

“Earth” means sacred Scripture, as in Genesis: “God brought forth from the earth every tree beautiful to the sight” [Note: [Col. 0957] 18 Gen. II, 9], meaning that in sacred Scripture God reveals to us the lives of the holy fathers.

“Earth” means the mind of any saint, as in the Prophet: “Upon the earth of my people shall come up thorns and briers” [Note: [Col. 0957] 19 Isa. XXXII, 13]. This means that even the mind of a holy man is sometimes disturbed by the pricks of vices [Col. 0959A].

“Humility” expresses the virtue of gentleness, according to: “See my humility” [Note: [Col. 0959] 1 Ps. CXVIII, 153], meaning: attend to how humble I am before the proud who persecute me; “and deliver me” from the persecution of others, “for I have not forgotten your law,” which commanded humility to be observed and charity to be shown even to enemies. It signifies the affliction of persecution, according to: “This has comforted me in my humility” [Note: [Col. 0959] 2 Ibid., v. 50], that is, hope raised me up in my affliction; for unless consoling hope raised us up, affliction would completely destroy us. “Let us glory,” he says, “in tribulations, knowing that if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” [Note: [Col. 0959] 3 II Tim. II, 11–12]. Hence he was comforted: “For your word has given me life” [Note: [Col. 0959] 4 Ps. CXVIII, 50], meaning that your promise encouraged me to endure suffering.

“Humility” denotes delight, according to: “The enemy has persecuted my soul” [Note: [Col. 0959] 5 Ps. CXLII, 3]. This means that a carnal impulse rose up to crush “my soul,” that is, my reason. “He has humbled my life to the earth,” that is, he has cast my way of life down into the desire for earthly things; by drawing me away from love of eternal things, he cast me into the desire for earthly things.

“Humility” indicates satisfaction, according to: “I am afflicted” [Note: [Col. 0959] 6 Ps. XXXVII, 9], meaning that I torment my body with fasts, vigils, and many afflictions, “and I have been humbled exceedingly,” meaning that I take care to oppress my soul with the bitterest severity, shaking it with continual sighs and lamentations and piling before its eyes the filth of all my crimes.

[Col. 0959C] “Moisture” means the lust of the flesh, as in Job: “Behemoth sleeps in moist places” [Note: [Col. 0959] 7 Job XL, 16], that is, the devil rests in those who love carnal desires.

“Shoulders” are the proclamations of the prophets, as in the Books of Kings: “Ten shoulder-pieces at the corners of the base” [Note: [Col. 0959] 8 III Kings VII, 34], that is, throughout the four regions of the world, the proclamations of the prophets are honored.

A “shoulder” is social life, as in Job: “May his shoulder fall from its joint” [Note: [Col. 0959] 9 Job XXXI, 22], that is, if I have done this evil, may my social life fall away from the structure of charity.

A “shoulder” is the work of justice, as in Job: “That I may carry him on my shoulder” [Note: [Col. 0959] 10 Ibid., v. 36], that is, I shall carry the Lord in my work.

A “shoulder” is one’s own deed, as in Isaiah: “Uncover your shoulder” [Note: [Col. 0959] 11 Isa. XLVII, 2], that is, show your wicked action [Col. 0959D].

A “shoulder” is labor, as in Genesis: “He placed his shoulder under the burden” [Note: [Col. 0959] 12 Gen. XLIX, 15], that is, he undertook a laborious life.

A “shoulder” is the flesh of Christ: “whose rule is upon his shoulder” [Note: [Col. 0959] 13 Isa. IX, 6]. This means that he himself endured in his own flesh the cross that he preached to others, and through the cross which, at his death, he bore on his shoulders, power was given to them in heaven and on earth.

By “shoulder,” sufferings are meant, as in the Gospel: “Which of you is a man who has a hundred sheep?” [Note: [Col. 0959] 14 Luke XV, 4 and following], and so forth. The man had a hundred sheep, meaning that Christ possessed the nature of angels and of human beings in perfection. “He lost one sheep,” meaning that human nature perished. “Therefore he left the ninety-nine in the desert in order to find the one,” meaning that he left, as it were, the highest choirs of angels in heaven in order to restore the human race. “He found the lost sheep” when he assumed human nature in himself. “Having found the sheep, he placed it joyfully on his shoulders,” when he willingly permitted, or caused, the human nature he had assumed from us to be fastened to the cross on his shoulders. This means that God expiated the sin of the human race through his own sufferings. “He returned home” when he ascended to heaven. “He called together his friends and neighbors” when he invited the holy angels, as if to rejoice with him over human salvation. They are “his friends” because they perfectly keep his word. They are “his neighbors” because they continually behold him face to face.

A “shoulder” is the mind, according to: “Shem and Japheth placed a garment upon their shoulders and covered their father’s nakedness with their faces turned away” [Note: [Col. 0959] 15 Gen. IX, 23, 20]. “Noah,” then, “a just man, planted a vineyard,” and Christ, who committed no sin, released the synagogue through the law. “Noah drank of the wine of his vineyard” [Note: [Col. 0959] 16 v. 21], and Christ experienced the harshness of the synagogue. “Noah became drunk,” and Christ was filled with many insults. “Noah was stripped,” and Christ, when the apostles fled, was left alone; or [lacuna] it is Judaic, because weakness appeared “in his house,” that is, in the Jewish house. “Noah slept,” and Christ died.

“But when the father of Canaan”—namely, Ham—“saw the nakedness of his father, he reported it outside and mocked him” [Note: [Col. 0959] 17 v. 22]. This plainly means that the reprobate, who are cunning to do evil, dishonor Christ’s shameful Passion by declaring friendship only in the sound of their voice while dishonoring him by their evil lives. For Ham is interpreted as “cunning.”

“But Shem and Japheth placed a garment upon their shoulders and covered the nakedness of their father with their faces turned away” [Note: [Col. 0959] 18 v. 23]. This means that the good faithful, whether from the Jews or from the nations, possess in their minds—not merely in the sound of their voice, as do the reprobate—so great a mystery of faith, and they honor the lowly and foolish things of God with great reverence, that is, with “faces turned away,” because it is stronger and wiser than human beings.

Shem, whose name is interpreted as “named,” represents the Jews, who were famous for many rewards [Col. 0960D]. Japheth, however, who is called “enlargement,” signifies the nations spread everywhere.

“Then Noah, awakening from sleep, [lacuna] his son Ham” [Note: [Col. 0959] 19 v. 24], not in Ham himself but in his son, [lacuna], because Christ will rise from the dead and hate all the reprobate who mock his Passion—not in what they are perfected in, but in the work they do. Hence Canaan is appropriately interpreted as “their movement,” that is, their work. Canaan is the servant of his brothers, because the work of the reprobate serves the faithful either for the exercise of patience or [Col. 0961A] for the advancement of wisdom.

“Shoulder” signifies strength, according to: “He spread out his wings” [Note: [Col. 0961] 1 Deut. XXXII, 11], meaning that he gave them his mercies; “and he took them up,” from the number of the lost into the number of the saved; “and carried them upon his shoulders,” meaning that he supported them in his strength.

“Shoulder” signifies strong people, according to: “I shall exult and divide Shechem” [Note: [Col. 0961] 2 Ps. CVII, 8] [lacuna]. Shechem is interpreted as “shoulder,” as though Christ were saying: I shall joyfully fulfill obedience, and thus I shall take some from the nations, fit to bear all my burdens, into my portion.

By “shoulders,” ways of life are meant, as in the Gospel: “They bind unbearable burdens and place them upon people’s shoulders” [Note: [Col. 0961] 3 Matt. XXIII, 4], that is, excessively burdensome commandments upon the ways of life of their subjects.

“Holocaust,” which is called “wholly burnt,” signifies the married man or the contemplative life. In Greek, ὅλον means “whole” in Latin; καυστόν or καυστίς in Greek means “burnt” in Latin. Concerning both it is written: “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, when the walls of Jerusalem have been built” [Note: [Col. 0961] 4 Ps. L, 21]. This means: if impassibility and immortality, the fortifications of the other virtues, have been restored to the sons of the Church, “then you will accept with favor and often receive the sacrifice,” which each person will offer not from another’s property but from his own—not, that is, slaughtering a goat or bull outside himself, but destroying lust and pride within himself.

“You will accept offerings,” namely, the many benefits of the active life; “and holocausts,” namely, the contemplative life or martyrdom, in which nothing is reserved for the world but everything is directed toward God here in the present. What in the future? “They will only place calves upon your altar,” meaning that they will offer you new and innocent peoples who will never again bear the yoke of sin.

Likewise: “I will enter your house” [Note: [Col. 0961] 5 Ps. V, 8], the eternal house in heaven, “in holocausts,” purified in body and soul. What follows? “I will offer you holocausts full of marrow” [Note: [Col. 0961] 6 Ps. LXV, 15], that is, my inward parts blazing with the fire of divine charity. For nothing is better than marrow [lacuna].

Herod signifies the devil, according to the figure of the Church in the Acts of the Apostles: “King Herod laid hands on some members of the Church to afflict them” [Note: [Col. 0961] 7 Acts XII, 1]. This means that the devil, who is king over all evils, never ceases to send the wicked troops of his warriors to afflict the faithful.

“For he killed James, the brother of John, with the sword” [Note: [Col. 0961] 8 Ibid., v. 2]. This means that, through a deadly persuasion, he slaughtered some who had become intimate with divine grace because they had subdued their vices by wrestling against them. For James is interpreted as “wrestler,” and John as “the grace of God.”

“When he saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to seize Peter also” [Note: [Col. 0961] 9 Ibid., v. 3]. This means that the devil endeavors to tempt not only lesser or ordinary men in the Church but also its highest men, endowed with knowledge of God and strength of steadfastness. He attacks them as though they were unwilling and resisting, considering that this would be displeasing to the Christian faith over which he himself presides as enemy. Peter is interpreted as “knowing” or “firm.”

By “Jews,” all the enemies of Christ or of the Church are signified [Col. 0962A].

“Now it was then the days of Unleavened Bread” [Note: [Col. 0961] 10 Ibid.]. This means, without doubt, that the great tribulation of the faithful is a great solemnity for their enemies.

“When he had seized him, he put him in prison” [Note: [Col. 0961] 11 Ibid., v. 4]. After the enemy has entangled the faithful soul in the snares of temptations [lacuna], he immediately confines it in every kind of tribulation and, as is appropriately added, guards it through temptations, evil spirits, and wicked people: “He handed him over to four squads of soldiers to be guarded” [Note: [Col. 0961] 12 Ibid.]. Having summoned his attendants, who throughout the four regions of the world never cease to disturb the faithful inwardly and outwardly, the enemy guards the soul, although it is struggling and not yet fully consenting, until, bringing it to complete conformity with his will, he is able to devour it. For as long as some spark of goodness shines in it, it is bitter to the enemy’s teeth.

Hence it follows: “Intending after Passover to bring him out before the people” [Note: [Col. 0961] 13 Ibid.]. He intended to give those subject to him—who, through their evil pleasure and the consent of the faithful soul, had made, as it were, a Passover celebration for themselves—a full and perfect joy by bringing the consenting soul all the way to action. This would have happened, had not the devotion of the Church, which was pleading for this man, come to his aid. For “while Peter was being kept in prison, prayer was being made without interruption to God for him” [Note: [Col. 0961] 14 Ibid., v. 5] [lacuna]. There is no doubt that the continual prayer of the whole Church is of very great benefit to those in tribulation.

“When Herod was about to bring him out, on that very night Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains” [Note: [Col. 0961] 15 Ibid., v. 6]. When the enemy had harassed the faithful person for so long with temptations [lacuna], bringing him, through negligence, into such a deep, dark, and thickened temptation, [lacuna]. He had already been surrounded by demons and wicked people and bound by the fetter of affection and consent.

“And guards before the door were guarding the prison.” This means that evil spirits keep watch in every way so that, once the door of confession has been closed to the sinner, the tribulation of temptation may in no way be diminished but rather, increased, may be strengthened.

But what hope is there in so great a necessity? What benefit did the prayers of the Church bring him? Listen: “And behold, an angel of the Lord stood beside him” [Note: [Col. 0961] 16 Ibid., v. 7]. This means that Christ, the angel of great counsel, was ready to help his faithful servant [Col. 0962D].

“And a light shone in the dwelling of the prison.” This means that divine grace flashed in the mind of the sinner, in which the distress of anxious temptation had previously held its place.

“And striking Peter’s side, he awakened him.” This means that, rebuking his sluggishness, he urged him toward conversion, saying: “Rise quickly,” as though he were saying to the soul: Resist quickly the temptation to which you have consented too long. “Rise,” that is, prepare yourself to confess. “Rise quickly,” that is, do not delay turning to the Lord; do not put it off, for death does not delay.

“And the chains fell from his hands.” This means that, when divine grace enlightens the sinner’s heart and awakens it through the admonitions just mentioned, consent and pleasure fall away from the practice of iniquity.

“Then the angel said to him: Gird yourself and act manfully” [Note: [Col. 0963] 1 Acts XII, 8]. “Gird yourself”: prepare yourself for good works. “Gird yourself”: gather yourself by tightening the folds of desire.

“And put on your sandals” [Note: [Col. 0963] 2 Ibid.]. That is, apply defenses to your actions, so that they may no longer be wounded by the thorns of carnal desires.

After this he added: “Wrap your garment around you” [Note: [Col. 0963] 3 Ibid.], that is, put on the faith and righteousness you formerly possessed, which you cast aside while sleeping. “And follow me” [Note: [Col. 0963] 4 Ibid.], so that, rising from death, you may never again die but may always walk in newness of life.

“And going out, he followed him” [Note: [Col. 0963] 5 Ibid., v. 9]. This means that the faithful soul, inspired by such divine admonitions, casts aside the wicked pleasures in which it was entangled and begins, by desiring good things, to follow the Lord who calls it, although not yet perfectly.

Hence it follows: “And he did not know that what was happening through the angel was real; but he thought he was seeing a vision.” For it often happens that a soul, long and greatly wearied by diabolical temptations, when it feels itself divinely admonished toward patience and conversion, does not think that the admonition it hears within is divine, but rather some fantastic delusion of the kind it was accustomed to hear. Therefore it is necessary for the Lord to act toward it in such a way that it may know with complete certainty that it is not being fantastically deceived but divinely admonished.

It follows: “Passing through the first and second guard, they came to the iron gate, which opened of its own accord for them” [Note: [Col. 0963] 6 Ibid., v. 10]. He passes through the first and second guard who, by repenting and confessing, abandons the first consent and the harmful pleasure by which he was guarded by the devil.

The iron gate still remains. This means that, when the soul has decided to turn away from evil and do good, the stubborn habit of sinning sometimes resists it, producing difficulty in living well. This habit, unless divine grace [lacuna], leads a person on earth to the city over which Herod presides—that is, to the dwelling of Tartarus. But when the angel goes before and leads, the iron gate is found to open of its own accord [lacuna]. This means that, with the grace of Christ going before and accompanying it, however long-standing and hard the evil habit may have been, it is easily shattered, and an exit is opened for the penitent soul.

“And going out, they proceeded along one street.” The sinful soul leaves through the iron gate when it abandons the hard habit of sinning. It proceeds along a street when, in the freedom and breadth of good works, it completes the proper measure and order of living well.

“And immediately the angel departed from him” [Col. 0963D]. This does not mean that Christ entirely abandons the repentant soul that lives well, but that, with grace accompanying it, he entrusts it to its free will, so that, once left to itself, it may learn from whom it has received the ability to live well and may give him unceasing thanks.

Hence it is plainly added: “And Peter, returning to himself, said: Now I truly know that the Lord sent his angel and delivered me from the hand of Herod and from all the expectation of the Jewish people” [Note: [Col. 0963] 7 Ibid., v. 11]. The soul has withdrawn very far from itself when, taking pleasure in an evil suggestion, it consents to it. It returns to itself when it earnestly strives to abandon evil and do good. Or it returns to itself when it truly sees what it once was when made by God, what it made itself by sinning, and what it has become again through God’s grace.

Finally, when the consent to wickedness has been cast aside, and the soul, now completely returning to itself from harmful pleasure and a life made wretched by habit, recognizes and remembers in what ways it was evil, it confesses that it has been snatched—not through any prerogative of its merits but through grace sent to it from heaven—from the power of the prince of darkness and of his attendants [Col. 0964B], who were maliciously waiting to bring it even to death [lacuna].

Herod, who killed the innocent children, figuratively represents the leaders of the persecutors who rage against the Church. The report that the innocent children were killed [Note: [Col. 0963] 8 Matt. II, 16] signifies that the glory of martyrdom is attained through innocence of life and the merit of humility. The fact that they were killed two by two indicates those perfected in doctrine and action. The fact that [lacuna] it equally declares the simple and uneducated to be strong in faith, though not in the faith of steadfastness. The fact that they were killed “in Bethlehem and in all its borders” shows that not only in Judea, where the Church began, but also [lacuna] the faithless throughout the earth will be subjected and the faithful crowned. The fact that they were killed while Christ escaped indicates that martyrs may indeed be killed in body, but Christ can in no way be taken away from them, whether living or dead. Hence the Apostle says: “Whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s” [Note: [Col. 0963] 9 Rom. XIV, 8].

Herod also represents hypocrites when he sends the magi to Bethlehem to inquire carefully about the child. For he pretends that he too wishes to worship him, so that he may destroy him. But human malice can do nothing against the divine plan.

“Today I have begotten you” [Note: [Col. 0963] 10 Ps. II, 7], the Father says to the Son. Although that day may appear to have been spoken prophetically of the time when he was born according to the flesh, so that “I have begotten” may be understood as “I caused to be born,” nevertheless “today” signifies the present, and in eternity nothing is past, as though it had ceased to exist, nor future, as though it did not yet exist, but only the present: whatever exists is eternally present in the divine nature [Col. 0964D].

The saying may therefore be understood as “I have begotten you today.” Or it may refer specifically to the day on which he was born from his mother without a father, according to what the angel said to the shepherds: “I announce to you great joy, for today a Savior has been born for you” [Note: [Col. 0963] 11 Luke II, 10]. But since it was night when he was born, one may ask why the angel said “today.” Yet one who was born at night is most appropriately said to have been born “today,” since it is known that his birth drove away the darkness of the world’s antiquity.

The same applies to what the evangelist Mark reports the Lord saying to blessed Peter, more confident than the others: “Amen, I say to you, today, in this night, before the cock crows twice, you will deny me three times” [Note: [Col. 0965] 1 Mark XIV, 30]. “Today” indicates the benefit of the Passion; “in this night,” its bitterness.

“Today” signifies all time in general, according to: “Today, if you hear his voice” [Note: [Col. 0965] 2 Ps. XCIV, 8]. The following is to be supplied from what precedes: then you will be his people and his sheep. “Do not harden your hearts”; rather, soften them, so that, like soft wax, they may be able to receive the image of our King.

I

Hyacinth. Within. I command. Hell. Justice. Jerusalem. Young men. Judges. [Col. 0965B] Door. Reed. Intestines. Youth. Rain. Image. Idumea. Fire. Ibexes. Judgment. Yoke. Jordan. Jasper. India. Wicked. Islands. Infant. Merchants. Anger.

Hyacinth means heavenly desire, as in Exodus: “Gold and silver and bronze and hyacinth” [Note: [Col. 0965] 3 Exod. XXV, 3–4], that is, wisdom and eloquence, predestination and heavenly desire.

By “hyacinth,” eternal rewards are meant, as in the Song: “The bridegroom’s hands are rounded works of gold, full of hyacinths” [Note: [Col. 0965] 4 Song V, 14]. This means that the works Christ performed in action shine with the splendor of wisdom and are worthy of eternal rewards.

Jasper is faith, as in Isaiah: “I will make your fortifications of jasper” [Note: [Col. 0965] 5 Isa. LIV, 12]. This means that God works miracles in the Church in order to multiply faith.

**The Gate** is Christ, according to the passage in the Gospel of Mark: “And when the disciples went, they found a colt of a she-ass tied outside by the gate, at the crossroads” [Note: [Col. 0965] 6 Mark XI, 4]. This means that the holy preachers, sent by the Lord into the whole world to preach, found the people of the sinful nations, without Christ, entangled in cords and involved in many errors [Col. 0965C].

The gate is understood as the conscience, as the Lord says in the Apocalypse: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” [Note: [Col. 0965] 7 Revelation III, 20]. The Lord stands at the door and knocks because, ready to help, he rouses the sleeping person by repeated admonitions, so that he may open his heart to him. Whoever obeys his admonitions hears his voice. He opens the door who, having driven back the bolts of his vices, cleanses his conscience for the Lord. The Lord enters that conscience whose heart he inhabits by grace. He is said to dine with the one in whose faith and work he delights. That person dines with the Lord whom divine consolation and heavenly recompense strengthen.

The gate is the understanding of divine Scripture, according to the passage: “And he commanded the clouds from above” [Note: [Col. 0965] 8 Psalm LXXVII, 23]—that is, the heralds of the highest Word—“and he opened the gates of heaven.” The Lord gave the apostles understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures.

All those through whom others enter into heavenly blessedness are called the gates of heaven. The Lord opens them when he causes them to come forth publicly from his secrets. Or the gates of heaven are those who open sacred Scripture to us; they are opened when they speak to our understanding [Col. 0966A].

Faith and repentance are called gates, according to the passage: “And the door was shut” [Note: [Col. 0965] 9 Matthew XXV, 10]. For, when the saints have first been established in rest with God, faith and patience will be useless to the impious. This is what blessed Job says: “Behold, the judge stands before the door” [Note: [Col. 0965] 10 James V, 9]. This is what the apostle Paul says: “The Lord is near” [Note: [Col. 0965] 11 Philippians IV, 5]. Or by the gate is meant mercy, as above: “and the door was shut”—that is, mercy was opened.

**Ibices** are preachers, as in Job: “Do you know the births of the ibices among the rocks?” [Note: [Col. 0965] 12 Job XXXIX, 4]. That is: Have you perceived when preachers ought to bring forth others through the examples of those who preceded them?

Ibices are perfect men, as in the Books of Kings: “And over the very precipitous rocks, which are passable only for ibices” [Note: [Col. 0965] 13 1 Kings XXIV, 3] [Col. 0966B]. This means that the impious torment the faithful with their persecutions more severely than do other tribulations, which only the perfect are able to endure with equanimity.

**Idumaea** is the Gentile world, as in the Psalms: “Into Idumaea I will extend my sandal” [Note: [Col. 0965] 14 Psalms LIX and CVII]. That is: I will cause the faith of my incarnation to reach as far as the Gentile world.

**Jerusalem**, by metonymy, expresses the inhabitants of that city. God the Father lamented it with affection, saying: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets” [Note: [Col. 0965] 15 Matthew XXIII, 37], and so forth.

According to allegory, Jerusalem is understood as the present Church of Christ, spread throughout the whole world, as in Isaiah: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen” [Note: [Col. 0965] 16 Isaiah LXII, 6]. That is: Upon your assemblies, O Church, I have placed rulers.

According to tropology—that is, the moral sense—every holy soul is rightly called Jerusalem, as in Isaiah: “Arise, shine, Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 0965] 17 Isaiah LX, 1]. That is: Raise yourself up from the darkness of ignorance and attain that brightness, O soul [Col. 0966C].

According to anagogy—that is, the understanding that speaks of higher things—Jerusalem is the dwelling-place of the heavenly homeland, which consists of holy angels and human beings, as in the Psalms: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city” [Note: [Col. 0965] 18 Psalm CXXI, 3]. This means that the heavenly homeland is built from innumerable people coming together as one.

These last three meanings appropriately correspond to one another, for Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace,” although the realities are greatly different. The peace of the saints journeying on earth cannot be equated with the peace of the saints in heaven and reigning with God.

**Fire** is the Holy Spirit, as in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” [Note: [Col. 0965] 19 Luke XII, 50]. The Holy Spirit is sent into the earthly heart. “Earth” is called the earthly conscience, which, while it continually heaps earthly and filthy thoughts within itself, is trampled by evil spirits. God sends fire into this earth when he sets it ablaze with the breath of the Holy Spirit. The earth burns when the conscience, previously cold, abandons its desires and grows fervent in love of God.

Fire is understood as charity, as in Leviticus: “Fire shall always burn upon the altar” [Note: [Col. 0965] 20 Leviticus VI, 12]. The ardor of charity must always be in our mind, according to the passage: “Fire shall go before him and shall burn up his enemies round about” [Note: [Col. 0967] 1 Psalm XCVI, 3]. It will burn those who had previously been enemies on every side, so that they may become friends.

Fire is good desire, as in Scripture: “From on high he sent fire into my bones” [Note: [Col. 0967] 2 Lamentations I, 13]. That is: He sent good desire into my vigorous thoughts.

Likewise, the bridegroom speaks in the Song concerning the power of love: “Strong as death is love, severe as hell is jealousy; its lamps are lamps of fire and flame” [Note: [Col. 0967] 3 Song of Songs VIII, 6]. It is as though he openly said to the bride: “The love which I have had for you was as effective as death, because through it my soul was separated by love; and just as hell is not altered from its severity by any torments of the wretched, so jealousy—that is, the execution of love—could not be turned back by any temptations of the enemy from concern for human salvation” [Col. 0967B].

Why say more? Whoever becomes a vessel of love burns inwardly with good desires and shines outwardly through the evident works of goodness.

Fire is the ardor of holiness, as in Isaiah: “God is a fire in Zion” [Note: [Col. 0967] 4 Isaiah XXXI, 9]. That is: He whose holiness burns in the Church.

Fire is the light of knowledge, as in Exodus: “The appearance of the glory of the Lord was like a burning fire” [Note: [Col. 0967] 5 Exodus XXIV, 17]. Knowledge that follows leads us toward the likeness of divine glory.

Fire is persecution, as in the Apocalypse: “Fire mixed with blood” [Note: [Col. 0967] 6 Revelation VIII, 7]. That is: The persecution of the Jews against the apostles proceeded as far as the shedding of blood.

Fire is envy, as in Job: “The fire of God fell from heaven” [Note: [Col. 0967] 7 Job I, 16]. That is: With God permitting it, envy proceeded from the highest leaders of the Jews [Col. 0967C].

Likewise, in the Apocalypse: “And the first angel sounded the trumpet” [Note: [Col. 0967] 8 Revelation VIII, 7]. This means that the assembly of the apostles thundered with a clear voice. “And there was hail, hard”—namely, a threat—“and fire mixed with blood.” This means that the envy of the Jews against the apostles proceeded as far as the shedding of blood. “And it was sent forth”: this happened in Judaea, cultivated by the plough of the Law.

“And a third of the trees was burned, and all green grass was burned up.” Earth signifies the lower among the Jews; trees, the higher, part of whom were blinded by the fire of envy. Green grass signifies the carnal, who, wholly devoted to the joys of the world, were all blinded. For, lest they lose their place and nation, they killed Christ and the apostles, and therefore they perished, entirely expelled from that land [Col. 0967D].

Fire is doctrine, as in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0967] 9 Revelation XI, 3]. In the voice of Christ, it is said concerning Enoch and Elijah: “And I will give to my two witnesses”—namely, Enoch and Elijah—the word of preaching, “and they will prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days, clothed in sackcloth.” This means that they will preach for three and a half years, displaying the garment of repentance—not because they themselves need repentance, since they fulfill in themselves by their works what they teach others.

“These are the two olive trees and the two shining lampstands standing before the God of the earth” [Note: [Col. 0967] 10 Revelation XI, 4]. They are filled with the Holy Spirit, contain within themselves the light of truth, and offer it to others, persevering immovably in God’s good pleasure.

“And if anyone wishes to harm them, fire will come out of their mouths” [Note: [Col. 0967] 11 Revelation XI, 5]. That is: Doctrine will proceed from their speech. “And it will devour their enemies” [Note: [Col. 0967] 12 Revelation XI, 5]. If anyone opposes their preaching or tries to turn them back from the truth, spiritual doctrine proceeds from their preaching and confounds those who oppose them.

Fire is temporal eminence, as in Job: “Nor will the flame of his fire shine” [Note: [Col. 0967] 13 Job XVIII, 5]. The flame of the impious person’s eminence will not last long.

Fire is the avaricious person, as in Job: “Fire devours their tents” [Note: [Col. 0967] 14 Job XV, 34]. That is, the heat of avarice torments the minds of the impious.

Fire is zeal: “To make fire descend from heaven”—that is, to cause zeal to proceed from the hearts of exalted men.

Fire is tribulation, as John says in the Apocalypse: “His feet were like aurichalcum, as though refined in a burning furnace” [Note: [Col. 0967] 15 Revelation I, 15]. The preachers of Antichrist will be purified through experience of the most severe tribulation. For aurichalcum is changed into the color of gold through extensive refinement.

Fire is vengeance, as in the song of Deuteronomy: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath” [Note: [Col. 0967] 16 Deuteronomy XXXII, 22]. Vengeance is prepared while I am angry, “and it will burn even to the lowest depths of hell, without any future remedy” [Note: [Col. 0967] 17 Deuteronomy XXXII, 22]. It is not the case that vengeance is exacted twice against the same person: here the peace is punishment brought to an end, but their guilt is prolonged for a short time.

Fire is the lower spirit, as in the Psalms: “We passed through fire and water” [Note: [Col. 0967] 18 Psalm LXV, 12]. That is: Through the heat of adversity and the relief of prosperity.

Fire is the madness of impatience, as in the Psalms: “He delivered their possession to fire” [Note: [Col. 0967] 19 Psalm LXXVII, 48]. He permitted the patience by which they ought to possess their souls to be destroyed through impatience. “Possession is delivered to fire” when patience, by which we possess our souls, is driven out through impatience [Col. 0968C].

Purgatorial fire, which will appear before the face of the Lord when he comes to judgment, is the understanding of which the Psalm speaks: “Fire will blaze before him” [Note: [Col. 0967] 20 Psalm XLIX, 3]. At the last judgment, fire will consume the earth, also burning the expanse of the air that the flood once occupied. “And around him a violent storm” [Note: [Col. 0967] 21 Psalm XLIX, 3], winnowing the chaff destined for the fire.

Fire is the deceit of Antichrist, as in the Book of Judges: “Let fire go out from the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon” [Note: [Col. 0967] 22 Judges IX, 15]. A great deceit will proceed from Antichrist and kill the holy men of the Church.

Fire is lust, as in Job: “Fire consumes even to destruction” [Note: [Col. 0967] 23 Job XXXI, 12]. Solomon likewise says: “Who hides fire in his bosom and his garments are not burned?” [Note: [Col. 0967] 24 Proverbs VI, 27]. To hide fire in one’s bosom is to conceal lust carefully in the heart; to burn one’s garments is to lose the virtues of the soul through lust.

Fire is desire, as above: “Who hides fire in his bosom?” [Note: [Col. 0967] 25 Proverbs VI, 27]. No one can conceal unlawful desire in his heart without its destroying his virtues.

Fire is eternal punishment, as in Job: “Fire will devour him that is not kindled” [Note: [Col. 0969] 1 Job XX, 26]. The fire of Gehenna, which is not consumed, will burn every reprobate.

Burning fire is the fervent spirit, as the Psalm says: “You make your angels spirits” [Note: [Col. 0969] 2 Psalm CIII, 4]. You establish spiritual men as messengers of truth. “And your ministers a burning fire”: you make those who serve you fervent in spirit.

Likewise: “You make your angels spirits” [Note: [Col. 0969] 3 Psalm CIII, 4]. Those who are incorporeal spirits become, whenever you will, messengers of your voice. “And your ministers a burning fire” [Note: [Col. 0969] 4 Psalm CIII, 4]. You also send the Seraphim into your service; *Seraphim* is interpreted as “burning.”

Fire is called indignation, according to the passage: “My heart grew hot within me” [Note: [Col. 0969] 5 Psalm XXXVIII, 4]. It began to be restless, “and in my meditation fire will burn”: fervent indignation gnaws at the mind. For I fear giving what is holy to dogs; I fear denying food to fellow servants; and while I reflect upon this uncertainty about keeping silent or speaking, I become indignant in vain.

By the name fire, desire is understood, as David says: “The voice of the Lord cleaving the flame of fire” [Note: [Col. 0969] 6 Psalm XXVIII, 7]. The preaching of Christ destroys the fury of fiery desire.

Fire expresses the wrathful, according to the passage: “Fire, hail, snow, and so forth, praise the name of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0969] 7 Psalm CXLVIII, 8]. The most poisonous dragons are the most despairing; fire, the wrathful; hail, persecutors; snow, hypocrites; ice, the hardened; storm winds, the turbulent. These carry out the word of God, either by conversion and fulfillment of righteousness or, if uncorrected, by suffering the misery they deserve [Col. 0969C].

Eternal fire is everything of which the Psalm says: “Coals will fall upon them” [Note: [Col. 0969] 8 Psalm CXXXIX, 11]. The saints, burning with zeal for God, will crush the wicked in judgment. “You will cast them into fire” [Note: [Col. 0969] 9 Psalm CXXXIX, 11]—the condemned in comparison with the saints. “They will not endure in miseries” [Note: [Col. 0969] 10 Psalm CXXXIX, 11], but will fail without relief.

By fire understand the divinity that consumes our vices. Hence it is commanded in the Law that Aaron should take live coals from the altar fire, place them in a golden censer, carry them into the Holy of Holies, and burn incense to God. Aaron is Christ; the priest is the sacrifice; the live coals are powerful virtues; the altar fire is the divinity of the Father; the golden censer is the heart full of divine wisdom and refined by the fire of passion; the Holy of Holies is the kingdom of heaven. To burn incense to God is to offer prayers acceptable to the Father.

**The Image** is the divinity itself, as in Genesis: “Let us make man in our image” [Note: [Col. 0969] 11 Genesis I, 26]. This means that, according to his soul, man is in some respect made like God.

The image is evil example, as in the Psalms: “In your city you will reduce their image to nothing” [Note: [Col. 0969] 12 Psalm LXXII, 20]. He destroys evil examples in the soul and heretical deceptions in the Church.

**Impetigo** is avarice, as in Leviticus: “If he has impetigo on his body” [Note: [Col. 0969] 13 Leviticus XXI, 20]. That is: If he has practiced avarice.

**The Impious One** is the Jewish people persecuting Christ, as in Job: “As the impious, my enemy” [Note: [Col. 0969] 14 Job XXVII, 7]. The Jewish populace, which persecutes Christ [the object of “imitates” is unclear in the source], is full of impiety.

The impious one is any reprobate, as in Job: “This is the portion of an impious man” [Note: [Col. 0969] 15 Job XX, 29]. Every reprobate has a portion in eternal punishment with the devil.

The impious one is Antichrist, as in the Psalms: “When the impious man exalts himself, the poor man is set on fire” [Note: [Col. 0969] 16 Psalm IX, 2]. When Antichrist is raised up to such heights, the humble are oppressed by him.

The impious one is the ancient enemy, as in Job: “The earth has been given into the hand of the impious” [Note: [Col. 0969] 17 Job IX, 24]. The flesh of Christ was delivered into the devil’s power for the Passion.

**Rain** is Christ, as in Hosea: “He came to us like the seasonal and latter rain upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 0969] 18 Hosea VI, 4]. Christ came and poured the moisture of his grace first into the Gentile world and afterward into Judaea.

Rain is the preaching of divinity, as in Job: “And the rain of his strength” [Note: [Col. 0969] 19 Job XXXVII, 6]—and of the preaching of his divinity.

Rain is abundant doctrine, as in Job: “Who gave a course to the most violent rain?” [Note: [Col. 0969] 20 Job XXXVIII, 25]. God alone causes abundant doctrine to be received by a human being.

Rain is humble doctrine, as in Isaiah: “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon it” [Note: [Col. 0969] 21 Isaiah V, 6]. That is: I will command my preachers not to pour humble doctrine upon it.

Rain is persecution, as in the Song: “The rain has gone away” [Note: [Col. 0969] 22 Song of Songs II, 11]. That is: The storm of persecution has ceased.

By rain are meant the words of teachers, as in Job: “Which the rains of the mountains water” [Note: [Col. 0969] 23 Job XXIV, 9]. The humble pour out the words of exalted teachers.

**The Anvil** is the devil, as in Job: “And he will harden like a smith’s anvil” [Note: [Col. 0969] 24 Job XLI, 15]. The devil has been handed over to the blows of eternal damnation.

**India** is the world, as in Job: “Wisdom cannot be compared with the colors of dyed India” [Note: [Col. 0969] 25 Job XXVIII, 16]. Christ cannot be compared with the nobles and rich people of this world.

**The Earring** is obedience, as in Job: “My golden earring” [Note: [Col. 0969] 26 Job XLII, 11]. Christ’s faithful offer him spontaneous obedience with charity.

**The Infant** is Christ, as in Isaiah: “The infant will delight at the breast” [Note: [Col. 0969] 27 Isaiah XI, 8]. Christ possessed the delight of holiness in his very birth.

The infant is every elect person, as in Genesis: “The infant shall be circumcised among you on the eighth day” [Note: [Col. 0969] 28 Genesis XVII, 12]. Every elect person will be freed from all corruption in the final resurrection [Col. 0970D].

The infant is the word of God, as in Exodus: “If the infant has committed fornication”—that is, if the word has already reached a good disposition in the soul.

**Hell** is the devil, as in Job: “The Almighty … is deeper than hell” [Note: [Col. 0969] 29 Job XI, 8]. God surpasses the devil by his omnipotence.

By the name hell, all the wicked are designated. Speaking in the Apocalypse about the future judgment, he says: “And hell and death were cast into the lake of fire” [Note: [Col. 0969] 30 Revelation XX, 14] [Col. 0971A]. When the Lord exercises his final judgment, all the wicked, who become only dwellings of demons without the remedy of repentance, and the devil himself, who is the cause of all our death, will be thrust into the punishments of Gehenna. Because of its darkness and depth, these punishments are called a lake.

Hell is avarice, as Solomon says in Proverbs [Note: [Col. 0971] 1 Proverbs XXX, 15]: “There are three things that are never satisfied, and the fourth never says, ‘Enough’: hell, the mouth of the womb, and the earth, which is not satisfied with water. Fire, moreover, never says, ‘Enough.’” Hell is the immoderate love of possessing, which is never satisfied; the mouth of the womb is the tireless opening of lust; fire is envy, which does not know how to cease. The devil may also be designated by the name hell here, since he cannot be satisfied with the destruction of human beings [Col. 0971B].

Hell is blindness of mind, as in the Psalms: “For there is no one in death who remembers you; but in hell, who will confess to you?” [Note: [Col. 0971] 2 Psalm VI, 6]. He calls criminal sin “death,” which is committed in contempt of the divine Law. A person is in that death when he is forgetful of God. He calls blindness of mind “hell,” because one who is blind in mind does not confess the Lord.

Hell is despair, as in the Psalms: “Nor do all those who descend into hell” [Note: [Col. 0971] 3 Psalm CXIII, 17]. Those who despair do not praise the Lord: “When the impious comes into the depth of evils, he despises.”

Hell is criminal sin, as in the Psalms: “They descend alive into hell” [Note: [Col. 0971] 4 Psalm LIV, 16]. That is: They knowingly commit criminal sin.
