Hell is this darkened air, as in Peter’s Epistle: “Drawn down by ropes of hell into Tartarus” [Note: [Col. 0971] 5 2 Peter II, 4]. The devil is bound by the chain of his wickedness in the dark region of this air.

**The Islands** are the Churches, as in the Psalms: “Let the many islands rejoice” [Note: [Col. 0971] 6 Psalm XCVI, 1].

**The Entrails** are the hidden words of God, as in Exodus: “The head with the feet and the entrails” [Note: [Col. 0971] 7 Exodus XII, 9]. You will understand spiritually the mystery of Christ’s divinity and humanity and the hidden words of God.

The entrails are the inner parts of our mind, as in Leviticus: “Having washed the entrails with water” [Note: [Col. 0971] 8 Leviticus IX, 14]. Our sacrifice is pleasing to God only when the inner parts of our mind have been cleansed by contrition.

**The Merchants** are the prophets, as in Job: “If they trample her, the sons of the merchants” [Note: [Col. 0971] 9 Job XXVIII, 5]. The apostles, who are sons of the prophets, did not bring the Synagogue to faith [Col. 0971D].

The merchant is Christ, as in Proverbs: “She has become like a merchant’s ship” [Note: [Col. 0971] 10 Proverbs XXXI, 14]. Christ leads his Church to the gate of eternal salvation.

**The Jordan** is the order of the baptized, as in Job: “He trusts that the Jordan will flow into his mouth” [Note: [Col. 0971] 11 Job XL, 18]. The devil is thought capable of carrying away not only unbelievers but also believers.

The Jordan is humility, as in the Psalms: “I will remember you from the land of the Jordan” [Note: [Col. 0971] 12 Psalm XLI, 7]. That is: From the stability of my humility I will remember you [Col. 0972A].

The Jordan is the instability of this life, as in the Books of Kings [Note: [Col. 0971] 13 4 Kings II, 8]. Elijah and Elisha crossed the Jordan. This means that Christ and his followers pass through the instability of this world, leaving behind its traces.

**The Reed** is any hearer, as in Isaiah: “The greenness of reed and rush will spring up in it” [Note: [Col. 0971] 14 Isaiah XXXV, 7]. In the Church this signifies the holiness of spiritual teachers and of disciples [fragment].

**The Juniper** is the stability of charity, as in the Books of Kings: “And when he sat beneath a single juniper tree, he asked that his soul might die” [Note: [Col. 0971] 15 3 Kings XIX, 4]. Every perfect person, when he humbles himself in perseverance in burning charity, desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ. The juniper is said to preserve fire for a long time.

Through the juniper are meant sins, as in Job: “The root of junipers will be their food” [Note: [Col. 0971] 16 Job XXX, 4]. The delight of the wicked is the desire of sins.

**The Yoke** is the dominion of Christ, as in the Gospel: “Take my yoke upon you … for my yoke is easy” [Note: [Col. 0971] 17 Matthew XI, 29]. To serve God is to reign; and “my burden is light,” because God’s commandments are not unbearable. Difficult steps over steep places become level ground for exalted souls.

The yoke is religion, as in the Psalms: “Let us cast their yoke away from us” [Note: [Col. 0971] 18 Psalm II, 3]. That is: Let us resist, lest they impose the Christian religion upon us. Or, from the perspective of the Jews opposing Christ: “Let us break their bonds”—that is, the words of the apostles—if we can, lest they bind us; and, if we cannot, “let us cast their yoke away from us,” that is, expelling them from our territories, lest the yoke of the Christian religion be imposed upon us.

Alternatively, from the perspective of Christ and the apostles: “Let us break” means that we should despise their weak torments, “and let us cast the yoke away from us,” that is, regard their blandishments as nothing.

“I have bought five yoke of oxen” [Note: [Col. 0971] 19 Luke XIV, 19]. That is: Like the covetous and foolish, I neglected concern for my salvation for the pleasure of the five carnal senses.

The yoke is captivity, as in Ecclesiasticus: “A heavy yoke upon the sons of [the] robe” [Note: [Col. 0971] 20 Ecclesiasticus XL, 1; the text is corrupt]. That is: Great desire holds the human race—[lacuna] of righteousness, as in Jeremiah: “It is good for a man that he has borne the yoke from his youth.” That is: When [lacuna] the practice of righteousness from his earliest age.

The yoke is sin, as there: “The yoke will rot before the face of oil” [Note: [Col. 0971] 21 Isaiah X, 27]. Sin will fail in the presence of the Holy Spirit.

The yoke is the burdensome dwelling of hell, as in Isaiah: “For you have overcome the yoke of his burden” [Note: [Col. 0971] 22 Isaiah IX, 4]. That is: In your elect you have conquered the burdensome dwelling.

The yoke is therefore fourfold: first, Christ’s; second, the world’s; third, sin’s; fourth, hell’s. The first is adorned by the holiness of righteousness; the second is renounced by the unity of pride; the third is polluted by the iniquity of wickedness; the fourth is afflicted by the calamity of punishment.

**Justice** is faith, as in the Psalms: “And my tongue will meditate upon your justice” [Note: [Col. 0973] 1 Psalm XXXIV, 28]. That is: My preachers will announce your faith “all day”—that is, continually praising you and referring everything they do to it.

Justice is a good action, as in the Gospel: “Take care that your justice is not done before human beings” [Note: [Col. 0973] 2 Matthew VI, 1]. That is: Do not perform your good work for human praise. It is as though he said: Let your good works be seen, not so that you may seek praise from them, but so that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven. Thus a good work should be done publicly, while the intention remains hidden, both so that you may offer your neighbors an example of good work and so that the mind may flee the desire for human praise.

The justice of God means the scourges that justify, concerning which it is said: “And I did not cast away his justices from me” [Note: [Col. 0973] 3 Psalm XVII, 23]. I did not refuse to be scourged by him in time, so that I might deserve to rejoice in eternity.

Justice is used emphatically for the just, as in the Psalms: “Your justice is like the mountains of God” [Note: [Col. 0973] 4 Psalm XXXV, 7]. Your just ones excel in virtues, not like the mountains of the world, swollen with pride.

**Judges** are the rulers of the Church, as in the Book of Judges: “He gave them judges to judge them” [Note: [Col. 0973] 5 Judges II, 16]. He appointed rulers over them to govern them.

Judges are wicked rulers, as in Job: “He brings judges into stupor” [Note: [Col. 0973] 6 Job XII, 17]. God permitted corrupt rulers to pursue their course.

Judges are the Jews judging Christ, as in Job: “He covered the face of their judges” [Note: [Col. 0973] 7 Job IX, 24]. God permitted the hearts of the Jews judging Christ to be [corruptly read: “cut down”].

**Judgment** is discernment, as in Isaiah: “Judge between me and my vineyard” [Note: [Col. 0973] 8 Isaiah V, 3]. That is: Discern between me and my people.

Judgment is separation, as in the Psalms: “Judge me in your strength.” That is: In your strength separate me from the wicked.

Judgment is condemnation, as in the song of Deuteronomy: “If I sharpen my sword like lightning” [Note: [Col. 0973] 9 Deuteronomy XXXII, 41]. That is: When I have prepared my terrible vengeance, “and my hand takes hold of judgment”—that is, when my power exercises condemnation—I will repay vengeance to my enemies who oppose me in word or deed.

There are two judgments of God: one hidden, the other manifest. A third judgment is that the wicked prosper and the good are scourged: some wicked flourish, others suffer want; likewise, some good people live in peace, while others endure adversity. One person is chosen in evil; another is abandoned in evil. One completes a good undertaking; another is abandoned in the evil he began. One wishes to perish but is not permitted; another wishes to be saved but is not granted this.

Concerning these judgments the Psalm says: “The judgments of God are a great abyss” [Note: [Col. 0973] 10 Psalm XXXV, 7]. They are, as the Apostle says, incomprehensible. The manifest judgment, however, is to repay each person according to his works, so that no sin remains unpunished and no rightly performed deed remains unrewarded.

**Beasts** that come together once a year for the generation of offspring signify chastity, as in the Psalms: “He delivered their beasts to hail” [Note: [Col. 0973] 11 Psalm LXXVII, 48]. That is: He permitted their chastity to be given over to violence—namely, when wives, who were given to men as helpers, are violently seized, as though the beasts were being pelted with hail.

Beasts receive their name from *juvare*, “to help”; hence they also signify aids. Therefore it is written: “He made a path for the way of his anger” [Note: [Col. 0973] 12 Psalm LXXVII, 50]. He gave breadth to the smallness of his vengeance. For anger seems to have a path when human beings are scourged in their possessions. God makes a path for his anger when, justly abandoning sinners, he permits them to sin in small matters. He adds a way to that path when he allows them to fall into criminal sins.

Thus it is appropriately added: “He did not spare their souls from death”—their death being the greater criminal sin—“and he shut up their beasts in death.” He entangled all their aids—whether fasts, almsgiving, or prayers—in their sins, so that they could not benefit them.

Or by beasts are meant virtues, as was said above in the Psalms: “He shut up their beasts in death.” That is: He permitted their spiritual virtues to be entangled in sins.

Beasts are preachers, as in the Psalms: “The earth brings forth grass for beasts” [Note: [Col. 0973] 13 Psalm CIII, 14]. The lower multitude supplies temporal support to its preachers.

The Samaritan placed the wounded man upon his beast [Note: [Col. 0973] 14 Luke X, 34]. Christ permitted human nature to be fastened to the cross.

Beasts are understood as the simple, as is said of the primitive Church of the Gentiles through the Psalmist: “And he blessed them” [Note: [Col. 0973] 15 Psalm CVI, 38]. God increased them in virtues: “And they multiplied exceedingly,” so that the net was broken and many fish escaped; “and he did not diminish their beasts.” He did not diminish their simple ones; rather, he improved their simple ones, or did not permit their simple ones to be diminished.

Beasts are the lustful, as in Joel: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” [Note: [Col. 0973] 16 Joel I, 17]. The carnal have ended their life in the stench of their lust. For beasts rotting in their dung means that some foolish person serves vice for so long that it can be said of him: “Behold, you already stink.”

Beasts are the flesh of Christ, as in the Gospel: “He placed the wounded man upon his own beast.” He bore the sins of the human race in his body. Thus in the Psalms: “I became as a beast before you” [Note: [Col. 0973] 17 Psalm LXXII, 22]. That is: I am humble in your sight.

**Young Men** are to be understood as the strong, as the apostle John says: “I write to you, young men, because you have conquered the evil one” [Note: [Col. 0973] 18 1 John II, 14]. That is: I write to you who are spiritually strong, because you have overcome the devil.

The Psalms say: “Young men and maidens, old men with the young” [Note: [Col. 0973] 19 Psalm CXLVIII, 12]. “Young men” are those who are steadfast in virtue; “maidens,” those who excel in chastity; “old men,” those mature in counsel; “young men,” novices—that is, those recently converted.

Young men are the wanton, as in the Psalms: “Their young men he consumed” [Note: [Col. 0973] 20 Psalm LXXVII, 6]. That is: The flame of lust consumed their wanton ones [Col. 0975A].

Young men are the frivolous, as in Job: “Young men saw me and hid themselves” [Note: [Col. 0975] 1 Job XXIX, 8]. That is: Those who were frivolous in conduct did not dare appear before me.

**Youth** is the earliest age, as in the Psalms: “O God, you have taught me from my youth” [Note: [Col. 0975] 2 Psalm LXX, 17]. That is: From my earliest age.

Youth is the beginning of good conduct, as in Deuteronomy: “As the days of your youth, so also will be your old age” [Note: [Col. 0975] 3 Deuteronomy XXXIII, 25]. That is: What brightness of fervor you possessed at the beginning of your way of life, the same you now possess at its end.

Youth is a return to goodness, as in the Psalms: “Your life will be renewed like the eagle’s” [Note: [Col. 0975] 4 Psalm CII, 5]. That is: Like an eagle, from corrupt old age [fragment].

**The wrath of God** is not a disturbance of mind but the experience of just vengeance. Or the wrath of God is the movement of a soul that sees God’s law being disregarded by an evil person, through which movement many things are avenged. Or the wrath of God is the darkness that follows transgressors. The wrath of God is purgatorial punishment.

Fervor is eternal condemnation in body and soul. Hence in the Psalms: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury,” and so forth [Note: [Col. 0975] 5 Psalms VI and XXXVII, 1].

Just as being rebuked is harsher than being corrected, so our fury is harsher than wrath. To be rebuked is to be accused. Here one must fear that the accusation may end in condemnation. To be corrected, however, serves amendment.

At the judgment they will be rebuked—that is, condemned—because they will be found without the foundation, which is Christ. But those will be corrected—that is, cleansed—who build wood, hay, and straw upon the foundation. They suffer loss, but they themselves will be saved, yet only as through fire.

This penitent person therefore existed not merely so that he might in no way be condemned to eternal punishment, but also so that he might not be cleansed by purgatorial punishments; rather, he might experience the medicine of a merciful mind, if he should feel the severity of the angry judge.

Iniquity is properly called whatever differs from equity. Hence John says in his Epistle: “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity; and sin is iniquity” [Note: [Col. 0975] 6 1 John 3:4.]. But since every person at some time commits iniquity, who is without sin? According to the Psalmist’s saying, “Those who work iniquity do not walk in the law of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0975] 7 Psalm 14:4.], and therefore they have not been set free. Who, then, has been set free?

There is, therefore, one iniquity—that is, the sin without which no one is—and there is another iniquity: those who * work it do not walk in the law of the Lord, nor are they blessed, since that sin is the illicit desire of the flesh and * violent desire. This latter is the most obstinate persistence in an evil deed; it operates in those who will it to such an extent that the Apostle, speaking either in his own voice or in that of the weak, declares concerning it: “I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I practice” [Note: [Col. 0975] 8 Romans 7:19.]; that is, “I desire what is illicit.”

How, then, do you walk in the way of God, O Paul? “But,” he says, “if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me. For I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh. Thus with my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin.” Therefore that desire is called sin in the just, because it is both the punishment of sin and the cause of sin: while it urges * us toward something by giving pleasure, if we consent, we act in sin; but if it acts in us, although we are nevertheless said to do it, this is not the vigor of another nature but the weakness of our own.

Those, therefore, who consent to illicit desire and act along with it do not walk in the law of the Lord, which says: “Turn away from evil and do good” [Note: [Col. 0975] 9 Psalm 33:15; 1 Peter 3:11.]. But whoever feels this within himself and does not consent to it by resisting it walks in the law of the Lord and is, finally, blessed. For temptation is the life of the good upon earth, and although we are far from criminal acts, temptation is not absent, since we sometimes consent even to a slight sin. But those who deviate from the way of God only in this manner are to be regarded as non-sinners and blessed. For “blessed is the one to whom God has not imputed sin” [Note: [Col. 0975] 10 Psalm 31:2.].

Sacred Scripture therefore commonly signifies by “iniquity” not only slight sins but also abominable crimes, as it does concerning the Lord’s death. Hence David, in the person of Christ: “Attend to visiting all the nations” [Note: [Col. 0975] 11 Psalm 58:6.], that is, “Present yourself for judgment, Father, so that the fleece may be drenched”: “do not show mercy to all who work iniquity,” that is, “do not drench the fleece that has rejected from itself the rain of grace”; and they say to this one that I did not come, as do others concerning not returning evil for evil. “Lord, if I have done this”—that is, this abominable thing—what is this? “If there is iniquity in my hands,” that is, in my works, what iniquity do you mean? He states it openly: “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil.” Here is the iniquity which, according to the prophet Zechariah’s saying [Note: [Col. 0975] 12 Zechariah 5:7–8.], sits upon the talent of lead.

There are also those who work iniquity who, wishing to justify themselves, pour their guilt upon the Creator, asserting that the stars created them under the Lord’s dominion so that they cannot abstain from sin. Such, finally, are those who work iniquity with such obstinate persistence that they persevere in it to the end of life and will never be free from guilt. Of such it is said: “And all who work iniquity will be scattered” [Note: [Col. 0975] 13 Psalm 91:10.].

“Iniquity” is used emphatically for “the iniquitous,” as David says: “And every iniquity will close its mouth” [Note: [Col. 0975] 14 Psalm 106:42.], because all the iniquitous—whether Jews or heretics—when they have nothing to say against manifest truth, will be convicted and fall silent.

## K

Kalends are sometimes understood in a good sense, as in the Book of Numbers: “At your festivals and Kalends and Sabbaths” [Note: [Col. 0975] 15 Numbers 28:11.]; sometimes in a bad sense, as in Isaiah: “My soul has hated your Kalends” [Note: [Col. 0975] 16 Isaiah 1:14.].

## L

[Col. 0977A]

Lips. Wild grapes. Pit. Lizard. Flask. Lamia. Light. Lamp. Loins *. File. Mud. Cloak. Lebanon. Spears. Torch. Coffering. Side. Robbers. Basin. Milk. Lettuce. Little flask. Tear. Wood. Lily. Thong. Bed. Law. Embassy. Hare. Lepers. Leviathan. Wool. Stone. Snare. Brick. Breadth. Line. Shore. Lucifer. Wood. Flax. Blear-eyed. Book. Locust. Length. Lion. Bed. Reader. Legate. Leprosy. Place. Little chamber. Light.

[Col. 0977B] Lips are the judgments of God, as in Job: “And that he might open his lips to you” [Note: [Col. 0977] 1 Job 32:20.], that is, “reveal his judgments to him.”

Lips are the words of Christ, according to the passage in which the bride praises the bridegroom: “His lips are lilies dripping first myrrh” [Note: [Col. 0977] 2 Song of Songs 5:13.], because the words of Christ’s teaching, which promise the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom, everywhere spread contempt for and mortification of carnal pleasures, so that those who desire glorious things willingly drink what is bitter.

Lips are preachers, when the bridegroom says to the bride: “Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your speech is sweet” [Note: [Col. 0977] 3 Song of Songs 4:3.]. They are preachers insofar as they are lips, and while they grind the teeth, others restrain them. While by preaching they restrain fluid thoughts, they are scarlet: they do not cease to preach and imitate the price of the Lord’s blood by which they were redeemed, and, like twice-dyed scarlet, they burn with the fervor of a twofold charity. Their speech is sweet because they finally do what they say, setting their preaching before people like flavorful food *.

Lips are the speech of the mouth, as in Job: “Only my lips are around my teeth” [Note: [Col. 0977] 4 Job 19:20.], because when Christ suffered, they had * only this concerning him.

A basin is baptism, as in the Books of Kings: “Twelve oxen carried the basin” [Note: [Col. 0977] 5 1 Kings 7:25.], because the twelve apostles preached baptism. A basin is compunction, as in Exodus: “A bronze basin made from the mirrors of the women” [Note: [Col. 0977] 6 Exodus 38:4.], that is, from examples of souls.

Wild grapes are vices, as in Isaiah: “He expected it to produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes” [Note: [Col. 0977] 7 Isaiah 5:24.], that is, “I hoped that it would bring forth virtues, but it produced vices.”

Milk is the order of our conception, as in Job: “You milked me like milk,” that is, “I was conceived from flesh.” Milk is simple teaching, as in Paul: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” [Note: [Col. 0977] 8 1 Corinthians 3:2.], that is, “I preached simple things to you, not difficult ones.” And elsewhere: “You have become people who need milk, not solid food” [Note: [Col. 0977] 9 Hebrews 5:12.].

By the name “milk” understand simple hearers, when the bridegroom says in the Song: “I drank my wine with my milk” [Note: [Col. 0977] 10 Song of Songs 5:1.], because I led both the strong preachers of heavenly things and simple hearers inward, into the kingdom of heaven, drawing them as though they were my own entrails. Milk is innocence, as in the Song: “Those washed with milk” [Note: [Col. 0977] 11 Song of Songs 5:12.], that is, “those cleansed through innocence.”

Milk is good action, as in Isaiah: “Drink wine and milk” [Note: [Col. 0977] 12 Isaiah 55:1.], that is, “practice contemplative theory and good action.” Milk is the flattery of sin, as in Exodus: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” [Note: [Col. 0977] 13 Exodus 23:19.], that is, “you shall not cherish the sinner in the flattery of his guilt.”

Milk is the teaching of the Law, as in Genesis: “His teeth are whiter than milk” [Note: [Col. 0977] 14 Genesis 49:12.], because Christ’s words are deeper than the teaching of the Law. Milk is temporal administration, as in Jeremiah: “The Nazarites were whiter than milk” [Note: [Col. 0977] 15 Lamentations 4:7.], because contemplatives are * spiritual in relation to those who administer temporal affairs.

[Col. 0978B] The pit is hell, as in Isaiah: “With those who descended into the pit” [Note: [Col. 0977] 16 Isaiah 38:18.], that is, “with those who were in hell.” Likewise John in the Apocalypse: “And the angel thrust his sickle into the earth, and harvested the vineyard of the earth, and cast it into the winepress of the wrath of the great God” [Note: [Col. 0977] 17 Apocalypse 14:19.]. For the order of preachers, exercising its judgment against earthly people, [lacuna] of evils [lacuna] which they had nourished on earth, and [lacuna] them into hell, where countless persons will suffer God’s vengeance: “And the winepress was trodden outside the city” [Note: [Col. 0977] 18 Ibid., verse 20.], because those who were outside holy Church were punished in hell; or hell was filled with the faithful. “And blood came out of the winepress as far as the horses’ bridles,” because on account of the sin that is in hell it overflowed as far as the demons themselves, who are to be punished *, since they draw their subjects [Col. 0978C] toward evil. How far? “For one thousand six hundred stadia,” that is, through all secular persons, whether lesser, greater, or great.

A stadium was said to be as far as Hercules ran in a single breath, and the Greeks measured by a stadium the squares in which they played. “Stadium” signifies those devoted to worldly variety; six, the lower; one hundred, the more excellent; one thousand, the most excellent.

The pit is the world’s calamity, as in the Psalms: “He brought me out of the pit of misery” [Note: [Col. 0977] 19 Psalm 39:3.], that is, “out of the calamity of the world.” The pit is this world, when we do not see the depth of its miseries.

The pit is the corruption of the flesh, when Christ says to the Father: “To you, Lord, I will pray intently in the time of my passion. My God, through whom I was made from a woman” [Note: [Col. 0977] 20 Psalm 85:7.], * do not be silent, saying: “From me, Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” [Note: [Col. 0977] 21 Matthew 27:39.]; do not at any time be silent when I cry: “Father, glorify your Son” [Note: [Col. 0977] 22 John 17:1.]; “and if you wish to be silent, I shall become like those who descend into hell” [Note: [Col. 0977] 23 Psalm 27:1.], that is, “I shall be like those who fall into the corruption of the flesh.” He is said to be silent or keep silent when he does not grant what is asked.

The pit is this world, whose depth of miseries we do not see. The greatest descent is to deviate from God and incline oneself toward the miseries of this world; the ascent to heaven, on the other hand, is to hasten from those miseries toward everlasting goods.

[Col. 0979A] Concerning this pit, when he was to be drawn out of it in Jeremiah, not only ropes but also old rags were given to him [Note: [Col. 0979] 1 Jeremiah 38:11–12.]. Whoever desires to pass from the depths of this world’s miseries to heavenly joys must hold firmly in his hands the ropes of God’s commandments, wrap himself in them, and cling to them.

But because the things commanded seem hard, let old rags be added to the ropes: that is, let the examples of the ancient Fathers, who fulfilled in deed what they taught by hearing, be applied to the commandments of God. In this way each person is drawn toward a good life, when the lives of the saints are brought forward after the Lord’s commandments for his strengthening; for everyone more readily strives to imitate what he sees another doing.

The pit is vices, as in the Psalms: “You saved me from those descending into the pit” [Note: [Col. 0979] 2 Psalm 29:4.], that is, “from the depth of vices.”

Lettuces are afflictions, as in Exodus: “With wild lettuces” [Note: [Col. 0979] 3 Exodus 12:8.], that is, “with bitter afflictions.”

A lizard is the way of the wicked, as in Leviticus: “You shall not eat the lizard” [Note: [Col. 0979] 4 Leviticus 11:30.], because we must not imitate the life of the ungodly.

A little flask is the body of Christ, as in Isaiah: “He will shatter the flask” [Note: [Col. 0979] 5 Isaiah 10:33.], because Christ’s body was crucified. Through a little flask [are meant] consciences, as in Job: “He bursts new flasks” [Note: [Col. 0979] 6 Job 32:19.], that is, “the renewed person wounds consciences.”

A flask is the faith of baptism, as in the Gospel: “A man carrying a flask of water will meet you” [Note: [Col. 0979] 7 Mark 14:13.], that is, “the Christian people possessing the faith of baptism.” Through the flask are meant earthly bodies, as in the Book of Judges [Note: [Col. 0979] 8 Judges 7:20.], where Gideon’s companions broke the flasks, because Christ’s martyrs handed over their bodies to death.

A plate is the splendor of divinity, as in Exodus: “A plate of purest gold” [Note: [Col. 0979] 9 Exodus 28:36.], that is, “splendor from the exalted God.” A plate is the hearts of the Jews, as in Job: “And the people’s * plate” [Note: [Col. 0979] 10 Job 19:24.], that is, “in the heart of the Jewish people.” Through plates are meant works of piety, as in the Books of Kings: “He fastened the plates with nails” [Note: [Col. 0979] 11 1 Kings 6:21.], that is, “he rewarded good works with eternal prizes.”

A lamia is pretence, as in Isaiah: “The lamia lay down” [Note: [Col. 0979] 12 Isaiah 34:14.], that is, “pretence came to rest.”

Wool is simplicity, as in Deuteronomy: “You shall not wear a garment woven of linen and wool” [Note: [Col. 0979] 13 Deuteronomy 22:11.], that is, “do not display simplicity outwardly while possessing duplicity within.”

Wool is the Virgin Mary, as in the Book of Judges: “I shall place this fleece of wool on the threshing floor” [Note: [Col. 0979] 14 Judges 6:37.], because Mary’s virginity is honored in the Church.

Wool is good action, as in Proverbs: “She sought wool and flax” [Note: [Col. 0979] 15 Proverbs 31:13.], that is, “she practiced action and contemplation.” Wool is the gentle, as in the Psalms: “He gives snow like wool” [Note: [Col. 0979] 16 Psalm 147:16.], because he sometimes makes gentle those who were previously untamable. “He scatters mist like ashes” [Note: [Col. 0979] 17 Ibid.], because he makes some who were previously blinded into penitents.

Through wool are meant temporal means of support, as in Ezekiel: “You clothed yourselves with wool, but you did not feed my flock” [Note: [Col. 0979] 18 Ezekiel 34:3.], that is, “you received temporal means of support from your subjects, but you did not provide for their salvation.”

[Col. 0980A] Spears are darts of temptation, as in Job: “He surrounded me with his spears” [Note: [Col. 0979] 19 Job 16:13.], that is, “with his temptations.” Spears are premeditated deceits, as in Isaiah: “They will beat their spears into sickles” [Note: [Col. 0979] 20 Isaiah 2:4.], that is, “they will cast aside premeditated deceits and devote themselves to the benefit of their neighbors.”

The stone signifies Christ, concerning whom it is written in Zechariah: “On one stone there are seven eyes” [Note: [Col. 0979] 21 Zechariah 3:9.], because the fullness of spiritual gifts dwells in Christ.

Daniel also understood this stone as coming from the mountain without hands [Note: [Col. 0979] 22 Daniel 2:34.], because here * Christ was begotten from the Jewish people without conjugal intercourse; afterward, having been made into a great mountain *, he filled the whole face of the earth, because by the word of his teaching he made both the Gentiles and the Jews fruitful.

Stones signify the prophets, according to the passage: “For your servants have loved its stones” [Note: [Col. 0979] 23 Psalm 101:15.], namely, the stones of Zion, because the prophets pleased the apostles, who understood their words through the Holy Spirit: “and they will have compassion on its dust,” that is, mercy will be bestowed through the apostles’ teaching upon the lower members of the Jews; or, the synagogue pleased the apostles, and therefore they also had compassion upon its lower members.

Or, through stones are meant the prophets, as in the Books of Kings: “Great stones for the foundation of the temple” [Note: [Col. 0979] 24 1 Kings 5:17.], because holy [Col. 0980C] Church was founded upon prophets distinguished by life and knowledge.

The stone is the Law, which was written only on stone, as the Psalm speaks concerning Christ, and which is also grasped by the members: “They will carry you on their hands, lest you perhaps strike your foot against a stone” [Note: [Col. 0979] 25 Psalm 90:12.]. This means that they will support his members with their ministries and assistance, lest they understand the Law carnally, lest they neglect to fulfill it spiritually, and lest they fulfill the Law out of fear of punishment rather than love of righteousness.

The tempter said this to Christ, doubting his divinity. The devil wished to test by this whether he was truly only human: whether, as though assistance were necessary to him, he might be sent downward and lifted up by the aid of angels. The angels therefore ministered to God, not from necessity, as though he were powerless, but as a matter of office. They did not carry him ascending into heaven because he would fall if they did not carry him, but in order to render the service of due submission.

“Foot” signifies the mind’s affection.

The stone is the devil, hard through impenitence and heavy through iniquity. Concerning him Moses says in the Song of Exodus: “His chosen leaders were drowned in the sea” [Note: [Col. 0979] 26 Exodus 15:4.], because the devil’s ministers, including those of higher rank, are submerged in the burning hell through Christ’s coming. “The deeps covered them” [Note: [Col. 0979] 27 Ibid., verse 5.], because profound wickedness crushed them. “They descended into the depths like a stone,” that is, without hope of resurrection, like an exceedingly hard stone.

The stone is any wicked person, as in the Apocalypse: “And one mighty angel lifted up a stone like a great millstone and cast it into the sea, saying: ‘With this force Babylon, that great city, will be thrown down’” [Note: [Col. 0981] 1 Apocalypse 18:21.], and so forth.

The angel is Christ, the messenger of the Father’s voice; he is mighty, and no one can resist him. Hence: “No one is found like him” [Note: [Col. 0981] 2 Psalm 88:7, 9.].

The stone is any ungodly person, because of the hardness of his heart and the weight of his sins. He is called a millstone because of the rolling movement of worldly affairs, which alone he follows, as in the Psalms: “The wicked walk about” [Note: [Col. 0981] 3 Psalm 11:9.]. He is also called great because of his power, since he sometimes rules even over the good.

The sea is the burning hell. Babylon is the gathering-place of the wicked. Thus, just as the angel lifted the stone high and cast it into the sea with great force, so Christ sometimes raises the wicked to honors and dignities in order to plunge them more severely into the punishments of hell. For the reprobate, the more they are exalted, the more grievously they will fall, unless they humble themselves beforehand.

Or in this way: the angel lifted up the great stone, like a millstone, and sends the rolling stone into hell.

The stone is hardness of heart, as in the Gospel: “Will he give him a stone?” [Note: [Col. 0981] 4 Luke 11:11.]

“The foundations of the city adorned with every precious stone”: this means that the prophets and apostles are adorned with every steadfastness of virtue.

Through stones are meant preachers, as in Isaiah: “Behold, I will lay your stones in order” [Note: [Col. 0981] 5 Isaiah 54:11.], that is, “I will place your preachers in an orderly arrangement.”

Through stones are meant the minds of the saints, as in Job: “The shore of sapphire, its stones,” because the minds of the faithful think upon heavenly things.

Through stones are meant religious persons, as in Jeremiah: “The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” [Note: [Col. 0981] 6 Lamentations 4:1.], because some who ought to have been religious are more entangled in earthly business than secular people.

Through stones are meant the apostles, as in Exodus, where twelve stones were in the breastpiece of the high priest: this means that the twelve apostles excelled in the faith of Christ [Note: [Col. 0981] 7 Exodus 28:17.].

Through stones are meant the Gentiles, as in the Gospel: “From these stones * raise up children for Abraham” [Note: [Col. 0981] 8 Matthew 3:9.], that is, “from the Gentiles, represented by these stones, * those whom you lead before you as true believers.”

A lamp is any simple person, as in Job: “A despised lamp” [Note: [Col. 0981] 9 Job 12:5.], in the thoughts of the rich, because any simple person is regarded as hopeless in the sight of the proud.

A lamp is the examination of judgment, as in Genesis: “A fiery lamp passed between those divisions” [Note: [Col. 0981] 10 Genesis 15:17.], because the terrifying judgment of God will distinguish between the elect and the reprobate.

Through the lamp are meant good works, as in the Gospel: “Oil in their vessels with their lamps” [Note: [Col. 0981] 11 Matthew 25:4.], that is, “charity in their hearts with good works.”

Through the lamps are meant the gifts of the Holy Spirit, as in the Apocalypse: “Seven burning lamps before the throne” [Note: [Col. 0981] 12 Apocalypse 4:5.], because the seven * gifts of the Holy Spirit illuminate the Church.

Through the lamps are meant the hearts of the saints, as in the Song: “Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame” [Note: [Col. 0981] 13 Song of Songs 8:6.], because those who are vessels of truth possess within themselves a good desire and within themselves a good action.

Through the lamps are meant the deceits of the reprobate, as in Job: “From his mouth come forth lamps” [Note: [Col. 0981] 14 Job 41:10.], because from the devil’s suggestion come tricks and deceits.

Through the lamp is meant the splendor of miracles, as in the Book of Judges: “Lamps and empty flasks in the midst of the flasks” [Note: [Col. 0981] 15 Judges 7:16.], because the bodies of the holy martyrs * and miracles from them.

A snare is suggestion, as in the Psalms: “He himself delivered me from the snare of the hunter” [Note: [Col. 0981] 16 Psalm 90:3.], that is, “from the suggestion of tempting demons.”

Through the snare are meant deceptions, as in the Psalms: “He will rain snares upon sinners” [Note: [Col. 0981] 17 Psalm 10:6.], that is, “he will pour deceptions upon the ungodly.”

[Col. 0982B] Coffering signifies the simple in the Church, as in the Song: “Our coffering is of cypress” [Note: [Col. 0981] 18 Song of Songs 1:16.], because the simple who are in the Church emit from themselves the good fragrance of holiness [Note: [Col. 0981] 19 Song of Songs 1:3.].

A brick is an earthly mind, as in Ezekiel: “Son of man, you shall draw the city of Jerusalem on a brick” [Note: [Col. 0981] 20 Ezekiel 4:1.], because a prelate ought to depict the joys of the heavenly homeland in the earthly heart of his subject.

Bricks are earthly affairs, as in Exodus: “With hard labor in clay and * of the altar” [Note: [Col. 0981] 21 Exodus 1:14.], that is, “with burdensome acts of lust and secular occupation.”

Through bricks are meant lustful minds, as in Genesis: “They had bricks for stones” [Note: [Col. 0981] 22 Genesis 11:3.], because the reprobate, having cast aside good works, possess lustful minds.

A side is the crown of the just, as in the Psalms: “A thousand will fall at your side” [Note: [Col. 0981] 23 Psalm 90:7.], that is, “countless people will fall away from the crown of the just.”

A side is protection, as in Proverbs: “The Lord will be at your side, lest you * be caught” [Note: [Col. 0981] 24 Proverbs 3:26.], that is, “God will be present as protection for you, lest in temptation you * be avenged.”

A side is the meditation of contemplation, as in Ezekiel: “Water flowing out of the temple from the right side” [Note: [Col. 0981] 25 Ezekiel 47:1–2.], that is, “water of compunction proceeding from the soul in the meditation of contemplation.”

A side is the mind, as in the Acts of the Apostles: “And when he struck Peter’s side, the angel awakened him” [Note: [Col. 0981] 26 Acts 12:7.], because when the sinner’s heart is struck through repentance, he rises from sin; or inward inspiration raises him from sin.

Through the two sides are meant the two Testaments, as in the Psalms: “On the sides of your house” [Note: [Col. 0981] 27 Psalm 127:3.], that is, “in the two Testaments of your Church.”

Through sides are meant powerful intimates, as in Job: “His soul hangs from his sides” [Note: [Col. 0981] 28 Job 15:27.], that is, “it proceeds from his intimates.”

Through sides are meant unbelieving peoples, as in Isaiah: “I shall sit on the sides of the North” [Note: [Col. 0981] 29 Isaiah 14:13.], that is, “I shall rest among those peoples who are cold through unbelief.”

Through sides are meant the Jewish people, as in Exodus: “In the sides of your board there shall be projections” [Note: [Col. 0981] 30 Exodus 36:22.], because in * the peoples of the synagogue, terrible persons, both priestly and royal, were joined to one another.

Through sides are meant the Gentiles, as in the Psalms: “Mount Zion, the sides of the North, the city of the great King” [Note: [Col. 0983] 1 Psalm 47:3.], because one Church consists of Jews and Gentiles.

Breadth is charity, as in Exodus [Note: [Col. 0983] 2 Exodus 27:9.]. “The breadth of the court is one hundred cubits,” because charity possesses the perfection of virtues in the soul.

Stonecutters are teachers, as in the Books of Kings: “Eighty thousand stonecutters” [Note: [Col. 0983] 3 1 Kings 5:15.], that is, “teachers who, together with the teaching of the Decalogue, preach the resurrection.”

Robbers are evil spirits, as in the Gospel: “He fell among robbers” [Note: [Col. 0983] 4 Luke 10:30.], that is, “he fell among evil spirits.”

The lion is Christ, as in the Apocalypse: “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” [Note: [Col. 0983] 5 Apocalypse 5:5.], that is, “Christ, born from the tribe of Judah, overcame the devil.”

The lion is God the Judge, as in the prophet: “The lion will roar”—that is, “God will judge”—“who will not fear?” [Note: [Col. 0983] 6 Amos 3:8.]

The lion is anyone spiritually strong, as in Proverbs: “But the just person, confident like a lion, will be without terror” [Note: [Col. 0983] 7 Proverbs 28:1.], because the holy person, relying upon his conscience, will be without terror.

The lion is the Jewish people, as in the Psalms: “They surrounded me like a lion ready [for prey]” [Note: [Col. 0983] 8 Psalm 16:12.], because the cruel people were ready to kill Christ.

The lion is the austerity of the Law, as in the Book of Judges: “A swarm of bees in the mouth of the lion” [Note: [Col. 0983] 9 Judges 14:8.], that is, “a multitude of sweet and threatening teachings from the utterance of the Law.”

The lion is the Roman emperor, as in Paul: “And I was delivered from the mouth of the lion” [Note: [Col. 0983] 10 2 Timothy 4:17.], that is, “from fear of the emperor Nero.”

The lion is any cruel person, as in the Books of Kings: “A lion or a bear carried off a ram” [Note: [Col. 0983] 11 1 Samuel 17:34.], because the cruel and unclean seek to crush the humble.

The lion is the Antichrist in his deceitfulness. * The lion himself, the roaring devil, trembles, because the devil always strives to seize the faithful [Note: [Col. 0983] 12 1 Peter 5:8.].

A lioness is the Church, as in Job: “Nor has the lioness passed through it” [Note: [Col. 0983] 13 Job 28:8.], because the holy Church is dishonored by the Jewish people.

A lioness is the human mind, as in Job: “Because of pride you will seize me like a * lioness” [Note: [Col. 0983] 14 Job 10:16.], that is, “you will tame my mind so that it may not be proud.”

A lioness is this world, as in Job: “The roar of the lioness and the voice of the lioness” [Note: [Col. 0983] 15 Job 4:10.], that is, “the enemy’s suggestion and the world’s desire.”

A bed is the flesh, as in the Psalms: “May the Lord help him upon the bed of his pain” [Note: [Col. 0983] 16 Psalm 40:4.], that is, “may God make him superior to his flesh.”

A bed is desire, as in the Psalms: “I will water my bed with tears” [Note: [Col. 0983] 17 Psalm 6:7.], that is, “by weeping over each of my sins I will cleanse my conscience.”

A bed is the pleasure of the flesh, as in the Psalms: “If I climb onto the bed of my couch” [Note: [Col. 0983] 18 Psalm 131:3.], that is, “if I take my being to consist in the pleasure of my flesh.”

A bed is a reprobate sense, as in the Apocalypse: “I cast Jezebel onto a bed” [Note: [Col. 0983] 19 Apocalypse 2:22.], because God * never permits the unclean sinner to fall into a reprobate sense.

A little bed is holy leisure, as in the Song: “Our little bed is flowering” [Note: [Col. 0983] 20 Song of Songs 1:16.], that is, “inward leisure flourishes in virtues.”

A little bed is inward hope, as in Job: “My little bed will console me” [Note: [Col. 0983] 21 Job 7:13.], that is, “I shall receive inward consolation through our hope.”

A little bed is inward rest, as in the Song: “On my little bed during the night I sought him whom my soul desired” [Note: [Col. 0983] 22 Song of Songs 3:1; ibid., verse 7.], because the devoted soul seeks God in its rest amid the darkness of the present life.

A little bed is eternal blessedness, as in the Song: “Sixty mighty men surround Solomon’s little bed” [Note: [Col. 0983] 23 Matthew 5:17.], because they contemplate the eternal blessedness in which Christ is, those who are like him in teaching and perfect in action.

The Law is the Old Testament, as in the Gospel: “I have not come to destroy the Law but to fulfill it” [Note: [Col. 0983] 24 John 10:34.], that is, “to destroy the Old Testament.”

The Law is the Book of Psalms, as in the Gospel: “Is it not written in your law”—that is, in the law of the Psalms—“‘I said, You are gods’?” [Note: [Col. 0983] 25 Psalm 81:6.]

The Law is the Pentateuch, as in the Gospel: “Everything written in the Law must be fulfilled” [Note: [Col. 0983] 26 Luke 24:44.], that is, “in the Pentateuch of Moses.” * The Law is Christ’s words, as in the Epistle of James: “Whoever keeps the whole Law” (that is, Christ’s words, which are called the Decalogue) [Note: [Col. 0983] 27 James 2:10.].

The Law is * corruption, as in the Psalms: “He will give the Law to those who offend on the way” [Note: [Col. 0983] 28 Psalm 24:8.], because God will scourge his guilty ones in the present life.

The Law is charity, as in Job: “How manifold is his law” [Note: [Col. 0983] 29 Job 11:6.], that is, “how innumerable are the good things that will come from charity.”

The Law is the goadings of the flesh and good desire, as in Paul: “The law in my members opposing the law of my mind” [Note: [Col. 0983] 30 Romans 7:23.], that is, “the goading of the flesh opposing the desire * of the flesh.”

[Col. 0984C] The Lawgiver is Christ, as in the Psalms: “The Lawgiver will give” [Note: [Col. 0983] 31 Psalm 83:7.], that is, “the one who gave the Law will also give grace.”

The Lawgiver is the Antichrist, as in the Psalms: “Appoint a lawgiver over them” [Note: [Col. 0983] 32 Psalm 9:21.], that is, “the Antichrist, the one whom the lost deserve to have.”

The legate is Christ, as in Jeremiah: “He sent a legate to the nations” [Note: [Col. 0983] 33 Jeremiah 49:14.], because Christ was sent by the Father to human beings.

Through legates are meant preachers, as in the Psalms: “Legates will come from Egypt” [Note: [Col. 0983] 34 Psalm 67:32.], because preachers will proceed from the Gentiles.

Through legates are meant the preachers of the Antichrist, as in Isaiah: “He sent his legates into * the sea” [Note: [Col. 0983] 35 Isaiah 18:2.], that is, “into the world, his preachers.”

[Col. 0984D] Embassy is the reconciliation of sinners, as in Paul: “We act as ambassadors for Christ” [Note: [Col. 0983] 36 2 Corinthians 5:20.], that is, “in Christ’s place * we undertake the reconciliation of sinners.”

Embassy is the tears of penitents, as in the Gospel: “He sends an embassy, asking for terms of peace” [Note: [Col. 0983] 37 Luke 14:32.], that is, “sending ahead tears of repentance, he seeks pardon.”

The hare is any iniquitous person who is nevertheless learned in the Law. * “The hare, for it too chews the cud” [Note: [Col. 0983] 38 Leviticus 11:6.], because some iniquitous people are nevertheless learned.

[Col. 0985A] Leprosy is sin or false doctrine, as in Leviticus: “If the plague of leprosy is in a person” [Note: [Col. 0985] 1 Leviticus 13:9.], that is, “if sin or heresy is in a person.”

Lepers are heretics, as in the Gospel: “Ten leprous men met him” [Note: [Col. 0985] 2 Luke 17:12.], because many come to Christ who, previously understanding the Decalogue to have perished, had been stained by heretical filth.

The left hand signifies temporal gifts, as in the Song: “His left hand is under my head” [Note: [Col. 0985] 3 Song of Songs 8:3.], that is, “Christ’s temporal gifts console my soul.”

Leviathan is the devil, as in Job: “They are ready to stir up Leviathan” [Note: [Col. 0985] 4 Job 3:8.], because holy men provoke the devil by living well.

Lebanon is Christ, as in the Song: “His appearance is like Lebanon” [Note: [Col. 0985] 5 Song of Songs 5:15.], because Christ’s spiritual form [Col. 0985B] is beautiful.

Lebanon is the Church, as in the Song: “They flow swiftly from Lebanon” [Note: [Col. 0985] 6 Ibid., verse 8.], because salutary teachings proceed from the Church.

Lebanon is baptism, as in the Song: “Come from Lebanon, my bride,” that is, “my Church, made white through baptism.”

Lebanon is this world, as in the Books of Kings, where Solomon’s servants cut wood from Lebanon [Note: [Col. 0985] 7 1 Kings 5:18.], because the Savior’s preachers converted people in the world to the faith.

The tongue is the Son, as in the Psalms: “My tongue is the pen of a swift writer” [Note: [Col. 0985] 8 Psalm 44:2.], that is, “my Son, together with the Holy Spirit, is my fellow worker.”

The tongue is Christ’s voice, as in the Psalms: “My tongue cleaves to my jaws” [Note: [Col. 0985] 9 Psalm 21:16.], that is, “my voice became silent before the Jews.”

The tongue is heretical doctrine, as in Job: “You will bind his tongue with a rope” [Note: [Col. 0985] 10 Job 40:20.], that is, “through Sacred Scripture you will overcome heretical doctrine.”

The tongue is the mind, as in the Psalms: “All day long your tongue devised injustice” [Note: [Col. 0985] 11 Psalm 51:4.], that is, “your mind continually devised iniquities.”

The tongue signifies God’s preachers, as in the Psalms: “And my tongue will meditate upon your justice” [Note: [Col. 0985] 12 Psalm 34:28.]. *

The tongue is secular learning, as in Isaiah: * “The Lord will dry up the tongue of the sea of Egypt” [Note: [Col. 0985] 13 Isaiah 11:15.], because he will destroy the world’s dark learning.

Wood is Christ, as in the Apocalypse: “From the wood of life, which is in the paradise of my God [Note: [Col. 0985] 14 Apoc. II, 7.] *”—to enjoy Christ, who gives life to the Church. [Note: [Col. 0985] 15 Jer. XI, 29.] Wood, the cross, as in Jeremiah: “Let us put wood into his bread,” that is, let us present the cross to his heart. Wood, the incarnate Wisdom, as in Proverbs: “She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her [Note: [Col. 0985] 16 Prov. III, 18.],” because whoever confesses God’s Wisdom by faith in [lacuna] is nourished by her with inward sustenance. Wood, any righteous person, as in Job: “A tree has hope [Note: [Col. 0985] 17 Job XIV, 7.],” because the righteous person is always made safe by hope. Wood, any exalted person, as in the prophet: “I, God, have humbled the lofty tree [Note: [Col. 0985] 18 Ezek. XVII, 24.],” because whoever exalts himself will be humbled. Wood, any humble person, in the same passage: “and I have exalted the lowly tree,” because whoever humbles himself will be exalted. Wood, the human heart, as in the Books of Kings: “He cut down a tree and put it there, and the iron floated [Note: [Col. 0985] 19 IV Kings VI, 6],” because Christ humbled the heart and restored grace. Wood, spiritual delights, as in Genesis: “You shall eat from every tree of paradise [Note: [Col. 0985] 20 Gen. II, 16.],” that is, acquire for yourself the spiritual delights of the holy Church. Wood, the holy angels, as in Ezekiel: “No tree of paradise was likened to it [Note: [Col. 0985] 21 Ezek. XXXI, 8.],” that is, none among God’s angels could be compared with it.

Woods are holy men, as in the Song: “With all the woods of Lebanon [Note: [Col. 0985] 22 Song IV, 14.],” that is, with all the saints who are in the Church. Woods, the Gentiles, as in the Psalms: “The trees of the field will be filled [Note: [Col. 0985] 23 Ps. CIII, 16.],” that is, the Gentiles of the world will be refreshed through faith. Woods, penitents, as in the Psalms: “All the trees of the forests will rejoice [Note: [Col. 0985] 24 Ps. XCV, 12.],” because at the Lord’s coming the penitents, who had previously been uncultivated, rejoiced spiritually after receiving pardon. Woods, spiritual virtues, as in the Law: “You shall plant fruit-bearing trees in it,” that is, you shall place spiritual virtues in your mind [Note: [Col. 0985] 25 Lev. XIX, 23.]. Woods, vices, as in Deuteronomy: “When, in the cutting of wood, the axe has flown from [its] handle [Note: [Col. 0985] 26 Deut. XIX, 5.],” * that is, when the rebuke of corrected vices has exceeded its proper measure. Woods, envious thoughts, as in Exodus: “The people offered acacia wood [Note: [Col. 0985] 27 Exod. XXXV, 24.],” because each faithful person offers to God incorruptible thoughts. Woods, good works, as in Paul: “Upon this foundation, gold, silver, wood [Note: [Col. 0985] 28 I Cor. III, 12–13.],” that is, in the faith of Christ, purity of thoughts, brilliance of speech, and energy in action. Woods, the wicked, as in the Book of Judges: * “They put forward wood to anoint the king [Note: [Col. 0985] 29 Judg. IX, 8.],” because those who wish to have as ruler someone governed by the desire of their carnal pleasure [do so].

The lily is the brightness of divinity, as in the Song: “I am the lily of the valleys [Note: [Col. 0985] 30 Song II, 1.],” that is, in my divinity I am the reward of the humble. The lily, the holy Church, as in the Song: “As a lily among thorns [Note: [Col. 0985] 31 Ibid., v. 2.],” because the holy Church is pierced by the teachings of heretics. The lily, heavenly blessedness, as in Exodus: “After the cup, the sphere, and the lily [Note: [Col. 0985] 32 Exod. XXXVII, 17.],” because that flourishing strength rightly rewards you, the preachers and those who do good. By the lily, good works, as in the Song: “He who feeds among the lilies [Note: [Col. 0985] 33 Song VI, 2.],” because they rejoice in the sweet fragrance of good works. By the lilies, the sacred Scriptures, as in the Song: “Those who feed among the lilies, until the day breathes [Note: [Col. 0985] 34 Song II, 16.],” and holy souls are nourished in this way by the sacred Scriptures until the brightness of the life to come appears. By the lilies, the brightnesses of truth, as in the Song: “His lips are lilies [Note: [Col. 0985] 35 Song V, 13.],” because the holy preachers of Christ proclaim the truth. By the lilies, the perfect, as in the Song: “Your belly is like a heap of wheat, enclosed with lilies [Note: [Col. 0985] 36 Song VII, 2.],” because the faithful of the holy Church perform good works and adorn [or: abhor?] the works of the flesh.

The threshold is the first assembly of the Old Testament, as in Ezekiel: “He measured the threshold of the gate [Note: [Col. 0987] 1 Ezek. XL, 6.],” because Christ reckons with himself the merits of the ancient fathers. The threshold, faith, as in the Books of Kings: “The hands of Dagon had been cut off upon the threshold [Note: [Col. 0987] 2 I Kings V, 4.],” because the works of the devil—which, through superstitious curiosity, lead toward eternal [lacuna] justice—have been destroyed through faith. For Dagon is interpreted as “fish of sadness,” [both] on the doorposts of houses and in the intentions of souls.

Flax is the Gentile people, as in Isaiah: “He will not extinguish the smoking flax [Note: [Col. 0987] 3 Isa. XLII, 3.],” that is, he will not condemn the Gentile people. Flax, subtlety, as in the Law: “You shall not wear a garment woven of linen and wool [Note: [Col. 0987] 4 Deut. XXII, 11.],” that is, you shall not conceal inwardly the subtlety of malice while displaying holiness outwardly. Flax, spiritual understanding, as in Proverbs: “She sought wool and flax [Note: [Col. 0987] 5 Prov. XXXI, 13.],” because the holy Church, or the devout soul, seeks a simple and spiritual understanding in sacred Scripture.

A line is God’s hidden judgment, as in Job: “Who stretched a line over it [Note: [Col. 0987] 6 Job XXXVIII, 5.]?” because God exercises his hidden judgment in the human soul. A line, the rule of suitable instruction, as in the Books of Kings: “A line of twelve cubits for the columns [Note: [Col. 0987] 7 III Kings VII, 15.],” because the rule of the apostles suggests other preachers.

The shore is the end of the world, as in the Gospel: “Sitting beside the shore [Note: [Col. 0987] 8 Matt. XIII, 48.],” that is, dwelling at the end of the world. The shore, the faithful, as in Genesis: “Zebulun will dwell on the shore of the sea [Note: [Col. 0987] 9 Gen. XLIX, 13.],” because the faithful people rested in the birth of faith. The shore, the stability of immortality, as in the Gospel: “While the disciples were laboring on the sea, Jesus stood on the shore [Note: [Col. 0987] 10 John XXI, 4.],” because, while they were enduring the burdens of mortal life, he himself had already reached the solidity of immortality.

Blear-eyed is mental darkness, as in Leviticus: “If he is blear-eyed, if he is hunchbacked [Note: [Col. 0987] 11 Lev. XXI, 20.],” that is, if he is weighed down by worldly occupation, if he is darkened in mind.

A book is God’s presence, as in the Psalms: “Let them be blotted out of the book of life [Note: [Col. 0987] 12 Ps. LXVIII, 29.],” that is, let it appear that they were never written in God’s presence among those to be saved. The book, Christ, as in the Apocalypse: “Another book was opened, which is the book of life [Note: [Col. 0987] 13 Apoc. XX, 12.],” because Christ, who is our life, will appear in judgment to all the Jews. The book, the Old Testament, as in the Apocalypse: * “Written within and without [Note: [Col. 0987] 14 Apoc. V, 1.],” that is, the Old Testament, containing within itself a mystical and a historical sense. The book, the Gospel, as in the Apocalypse: “He had in his hand an open book [Note: [Col. 0987] 15 Apoc. X, 2],” because Christ completed his Gospel in deed. By the book, the hidden things of a person, as in Daniel: “The court sat, and the books were opened [Note: [Col. 0987] 16 Dan. VII, 10.],” because at the last judgment the secrets of our hearts will be made manifest.

A place is Christ, as in the Apocalypse: “The woman fled into the wilderness, where she had a place prepared [Note: [Col. 0987] 17 Apoc. XII, 6.],” because the holy Church, finding the solitude of the mind, finds Christ. A place, innocence, as in the Psalms: “He will no longer know his place [Note: [Col. 0987] 18 Ps. CII, 16.],” that is, * if the spirit of one in authority rises against you, do not leave your place; that is, if the * present *sibilis* [uncertain] in a[lacuna] prevails against you, do not abandon the humility of repentance. A place, the holy Church, as in Job: “There is a place where gold is smelted [Note: [Col. 0987] 19 Job XXVIII, 1.],” because the testing of martyrdom is of no benefit except in the Church. A place, * love of the present life, as in Job: “The impious man will be carried away by the delight of life [Note: [Col. 0987] 20 Job XXVII, 21.].” A place, the heart of flatterers, as in Job: “Nor will his place look upon him again [Note: [Col. 0987] 21 Job XX, 9.],” because after death the flatterers who used to flatter the wicked man will no longer praise him. A place, the human mind, as in Job: * “Where is the place of understanding [Note: [Col. 0987] 22 Job XXVIII, 12, 20.]?” because understanding dwells in the human mind. A place, pride, as in Job: * “Turn the wicked from his place [Note: [Col. 0987] 23 Job XX, 7.],” that is, destroy the proud in their very pride. A place, the hearts of the righteous, as in Ezekiel: * “Blessed is the glory of the Lord from his place [Note: [Col. 0987] 24 Ezek. III, 12.],” because his praise proceeds from the hearts of the righteous, in which he dwells. A place, holy conduct, as in the Law: “In his place he shall eat these meats [Note: [Col. 0987] 25 Lev. VII, 6.],” because those who live in holy conduct are worthy to handle the divine mysteries. A place, holiness of life, as in the Psalms: “Until I find a place for the Lord,” that is, until my soul is sanctified to such a degree that God deigns to rest in it. A place, the heavenly homeland, as in the Psalms: “I will pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle [Col. 0988C] [Note: [Col. 0987] 26 Ps. XLI, 5.],” that is, I will reach the heavenly homeland, where there is a house not made by hands, eternal in the heavens. By place, the anxieties of the mind:

[fragment]

The locust is the resurrection, as in the Psalms: * “I am exalted like a locust [Note: [Col. 0987] 27 Ps. CXCVIII, 23.],” that is, I have escaped death incorruptible. The locust, the Gentiles, as in Ecclesiastes: “The locust will be burdened [Note: [Col. 0987] 28 Eccl. XII, 5.],” that is, the Gentiles converted to the Lord will be sanctified. The locust, empty glory, as in the Psalms: “And the locust devoured their labors [Note: [Col. 0987] 29 Ps. LXXVII, 46.],” that is, empty glory devoured their good works. By locusts, the Jews, as in the Gospel: “He ate locusts and wild honey [Note: [Col. 0987] 30 Mark I, 6.],” because God incorporated Jews and Gentiles into himself through faith. By locusts, heretics, as in the Apocalypse: “Locusts came out of the smoke of the pit upon the earth [Note: [Col. 0987] 31 Apoc. IX, 3.],” because heretics proceeded in the Church from the obscurity of profound error. By locusts, flatterers, as in Exodus: “The burning wind lifted up the locusts [Note: [Col. 0987] 32 Exod. X, 13.],” because an earthly enemy stirred up flatterers. By locusts, preachers, as in Job: “Will he raise him up like locusts [Note: [Col. 0987] 33 Job XXXIX, 23.]?” because holy preachers at one time leap up to contemplation and at another return to action.

[Col. 0989A] A bier is an evil conscience, as in the Gospel: God touched the bier [Note: [Col. 0989] 1 Luke VII, 14.], because through repentance God moves the sinful conscience. A bier, a good conscience, as in Genesis: “Embalmed with spices and placed in a bier [Note: [Col. 0989] 2 Gen. L, 25.],” because every saint, refreshed by virtues, rests in his conscience.

Length is long-suffering, as in Ezekiel: “He measured the court at one hundred cubits in length,” because the perfection of the saints consists in long-suffering [Note: [Col. 0989] 3 Ezek. XL, 47.]. Length, eternity, as in Proverbs: “Length of days is in her right hand [Note: [Col. 0989] 4 Prov. III, 16.],” because the joy of the heavenly homeland will endure without end. Length, faith, as in Genesis: “Its length shall be three hundred cubits [Note: [Col. 0989] 5 Gen. VI, 15.],” because the faith of the Church consists in the mystery of the holy Trinity.

A thong is the commandment of discipline, as in Job: “For plowing with your thong [Note: [Col. 0989] 6 Job XXXIX, 13.],” because God can bind the proud rulers of the world by the commandment of his discipline. By the law, the bonds of our custody, as in the Books of Kings: “Bronze thongs hanging down [Note: [Col. 0989] 7 III Kings VII, 29.],” because when the bonds of custody are despised, superiors [lacuna].

Light is God the Father, as in the Book of Wisdom: “He is the creator of eternal light [Note: [Col. 0989] 8 Wis. VII, 26.],” because Christ is the glorification of God the Father. Light, Christ, as in the Gospel: “He was the true light [Note: [Col. 0989] 9 John I, 9.],” because no one is illuminated except through him. Light, the apostles, as in the Gospel: “You are the light of the world,” that is, the brightness of the Church. Light, the faithful, as in Paul: “But now you are light in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0989] 10 Eph. V, 6.],” that is, now there is brightness in the Lord. Light, a good action, as in the Gospel: “Let your light shine before men [Note: [Col. 0989] 11 Matt. V, 16.],” [Col. 0989C] that is, let your good action shine before the wicked. Light, evangelical preaching, as in Isaiah: “The people who sat in darkness saw a great light [Note: [Col. 0989] 12 Isa. IX, 2.],” that is, let the people of the Gentiles, who were in error, understand evangelical preaching. Light, the glory of the present life, as in Job: “Why was light given to the wretched [Note: [Col. 0989] 13 Job III, 20.]?” that is, the glory of the present life to a holy man, who considers himself wretched in this age (sic). Light, * the sword of the heart, as in Job: “His light will grow dark in his tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0989] 14 Job XVIII, 6.],” that is, joy will fail in his heart. Light, the holy angels, as in Genesis: “God saw the light, that it was good [Note: [Col. 0989] 15 Gen. I, 4.],” that is, he approved the good angels.

Lucifer is Christ, as in Job: “Do you bring forth Lucifer in his time [Note: [Col. 0989] 16 Job XXXVIII, 32.],” that is, Christ in the fullness of time. Lucifer, a holy man, as in Job: “You will rise like Lucifer [Note: [Col. 0989] 17 Job XI, 17.],” that is, you will shine like a holy man. Lucifer, the devil, as in Isaiah: “Lucifer, who rose in the morning [Note: [Col. 0989] 18 Isa. XIV, 12.],” that is, the devil, who at the beginning was brightness. Lucifer, clear understanding, as in Peter’s Epistle: “Let Lucifer rise in our hearts [Note: [Col. 0989] 19 II Pet. I, 19.],” that is, let clear understanding shine in our minds.

A lamp is Christ, as in the Gospel: “A lamp is not brought in order to be placed under a bushel [Note: [Col. 0989] 20 Mark IV, 21.],” that is, Christ did not come to be hidden among the Jews alone. A lamp, the friend of the bridegroom, as in the Psalms: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ [Note: [Col. 0989] 21 Ps. CXXXI, 17.],” that is, I have prepared John, who would precede Christ. A lamp, the righteousness of the saints, as in Proverbs: “Her lamp will not be extinguished at night [Note: [Col. 0989] 22 Prov. XXXI, 18.],” that is, the righteousness of the Church will not fail in the present adversity. A lamp, a good work, as in Exodus: “Let the lamp burn continually in the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0989] 23 Exod. XXVII, 20.],” that is, let a good action appear in a person. A lamp, divine grace, as in Job: “His lamp shone over my head [Note: [Col. 0989] 24 Job XXIX, 3.],” that is, divine grace shone over my mind. A lamp, sacred Scripture, as in Peter’s Epistle: “Like a lamp shining in a dark place [Note: [Col. 0989] 25 II Pet. I, 19.],” that is, sacred Scripture in the obscurity of the present life. A lamp, the word of preaching, as in the Psalms: “Your word is a lamp to my feet [Note: [Col. 0989] 26 Ps. CXVIII, 104.],” that is, your preaching shines in my works. A lamp, anyone’s good life, as in the Gospel: “They do not light a lamp and put it under a bushel [Note: [Col. 0989] 27 Matt. V, 15.],” because a good life must not be hidden but set before others as an example. A lamp, inward visitation, as in Proverbs: “The lamp of the Lord is the breath of a person [Note: [Col. 0989] 28 Prov. XX, 27.],” because inward visitation gives a person life. A lamp, the glory of the reprobate, as in Job [Note: [Col. 0989] 29 Job XXIV, 20.]: “The lamp of the wicked will be extinguished,” that is, the glory of the perverse will be destroyed.

Light is Christ, as in the Gospel: “A light for the revelation of the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0989] 30 Luke II, 32.],” because Christ illuminates the Gentiles. Light, the apostles, as in the Psalms: “Clothed with light as with a garment [Note: [Col. 0989] 31 Ps. CII, 2.],” that is, surrounded by the apostles clinging to your side. Light, knowledge of truth, as in Job: “They were rebellious against the light [Note: [Col. 0989] 32 Job XXIV, 13.],” that is, they refused to receive knowledge of the truth. Light, preaching, as in Job: “His light is over all the boundaries of the earth [Note: [Col. 0989] 33 Job XXXVII, 3.],” that is, his Gospel is preached throughout the whole world. Light, a miracle, as in Job: “Light will shine upon your ways [Note: [Col. 0989] 34 Job XXII, 28.],” that is, there will be signs and miracles in your works. Light, God’s grace, as in Job: “Upon whom does his light not rise [Note: [Col. 0989] 35 Job XXV, 3.],” that is, who is there in whom his grace is not present? Light, intention, as in the Gospel: “See, therefore, lest the light that is in you become darkness [Note: [Col. 0989] 36 Luke XI, 35.],” that is, beware lest your intention be darkened. Light, God the Father, as in the Gospel: “In your light we shall see light [Note: [Col. 0989] 37 Ps. XXXV, 10.],” because through the Son we recognize the Father. [Col. 0990D] Light, doctrine, as in the Apocalypse: “That city will have no need of the light of the sun [Note: [Col. 0989] 38 Apoc. XXI, 23; XXII, 5.],” because that assembly of the heavenly homeland will not need to be taught by any teacher.

Through the loins, the succession of mortality, as in Paul: “He was still in the loins of his father [Note: [Col. 0989] 39 Heb. VII, 10.],” that is, he was still to be begotten. Through the loins, lust, as in Job: “His strength is in his loins [Note: [Col. 0989] 40 Job XL, 11.],” because the devil greatly conquers the male sex through lust. Through the loins, lust of the heart, as in Peter: “Gird the loins of your mind [Note: [Col. 0991] 1 I Pet. I, 13.],” that is, drive lust out of your heart.

A loincloth is the holy Church, as in Jeremiah: * “The loincloth is possessed [Note: [Col. 0991] 2 Jer. XIII, 1.],” because Christ chose the Church for himself.

The moon is the Church, as in the Psalms: “Until the moon is taken away [Note: [Col. 0991] 3 Ps. LXXII, 7.],” that is, until the Church is transferred. The moon, fame accompanied by praise, as in Job: “And the moon proceeding brightly [Note: [Col. 0991] 4 Job XXXI, 26.],” that is, fame raising itself on high. The moon, instability of mind, as in Ecclesiasticus: “A fool changes like the moon,” because the brightness of a foolish mind fails through instability. The moon, this world, as in the Apocalypse: “The moon beneath her feet [Note: [Col. 0991] 5 Apoc. XII, 1.],” because the holy Church despises this world. The moon, knowledge, as in the Psalms: “The moon and stars for the rule of the night [Note: [Col. 0991] 6 Ps. CXXXV, 9.],” because in the present life we need knowledge and good examples. The moon, adversity, as in the Psalms: “Nor the moon by night [Note: [Col. 0991] 7 Ps. CXX, 6.],” that is, nor may adversity break you through * impatience.

By wolves, fraud and deceit, as in the Gospel: “But inwardly they are ravenous wolves [Note: [Col. 0991] 8 Matt. VII, 15.],” that is, inwardly they are fraudulent and deceitful.

Mud is the Word made flesh, as in the Gospel: “He made mud from spittle [Note: [Col. 0991] 9 John IX, 6.],” because Christ is God and man. Mud, the first condition, as in Job: “That you made me like mud [Note: [Col. 0991] 10 Job X, 9.],” because the human being was made from earth. Mud, the Jewish people, as in Job: “He will be restored like a clay seal [Note: [Col. 0991] 11 Job XXXVIII, 14.],” because the Jews, who were God’s seal, are trampled like mud on account of unbelief. Mud, worldly things, as in the prophet: “Heavier than thick mud [Note: [Col. 0991] 12 Hab. II, 6.],” that is, he strives excessively to multiply earthly things. Mud, doctrine, as in the Apocalypse of Habakkuk: “In the mud of the waters [Note: [Col. 0991] 13 Hab. III, 15.],” that is, in the wicked doctrine of many peoples. Mud, the enticement of the flesh, as in the Psalms: “Rescue me from the mud, so that I may not become stuck [Note: [Col. 0991] 14 Ps. LXVIII, 15.],” that is, guard me from carnal pleasure, lest I be overcome. Mud, the stench of vices, as in Job: “He will spread gold beneath himself like mud [Note: [Col. 0991] 15 Job XLI, 12.],” because the devil strives to trample holy men through vices.

A laver is baptism, as in the Books of Kings: “The thickness of the laver was three inches [Note: [Col. 0991] 16 I Kings VII, 26.],” because in holy baptism there is the confession of the persons together with one Godhead.

## M

[Col. 0991D]

Wall. Myrrh. Jaw. Pomegranate. Myrrh. Honey. Stain. Moab. Members. [Col. 0992A] Marble. Evil. Necklaces. Midday. Sheaves. Woman. Wonders. Pearl. Breasts. Mountain. Hireling. Mandrakes. Mule. Soldiers. Male. New wine. Marrow. Manna. [Col. 0992A] Fly. Myrtle. Millstone. Mortar. Months. Morning. Mulberry. Harlot. Bushel. Table. Hand. Death. Harvest. Sea. Mule. Kite. Hammer. Pomegranate. [Col. 0992A] Border. Fortification. Warfare. Mother. Weasel. Walls. Reapers.

A wall is discipline of the heart, as in Proverbs: “And [it was] on the wall of stones [Note: [Col. 0991] 17 Prov. XXIV, 31.],” that is, the discipline of stable thoughts “had been destroyed.” A wall, the side [of Christ], as in the Song: “In the cleft of the wall [Note: [Col. 0991] 18 Song II, 14.],” that is, in the wound of Christ’s side. A wall, the Jewish kingdom, as in the Psalms: “Why have you destroyed its wall [Note: [Col. 0991] 19 Ps. LXXIX, 13.]?” because the Lord permitted the kingdom * to be brought upon that people, by which it ought to have been governed *. By the wall, faith and action, as in the Book of Numbers: “Between the two walls with which the vineyards were enclosed [Note: [Col. 0991] 20 Num. XXII, 24.],” because the faithful souls are united through faith and action.

A stain is sin, as in Paul: “Not having stain or wrinkle [Note: [Col. 0991] 21 Eph. V, 27.],” that is, sin or hypocrisy.

The pomegranate is Christ’s blood, as in the Song: “As the rind of a pomegranate, so are your cheeks [Note: [Col. 0991] 22 Song VI, 7.],” because through the shedding of Christ’s blood the holy Church assumed patience for herself. By pomegranates, good works, as in Exodus: “You shall make pomegranates of violet [Note: [Col. 0991] 23 Exod. XXVIII, 33.],” that is, good works for the sake of the heavenly reward. By pomegranates, those who hold the one faith, as in the Song: “A paradise of pomegranates [Note: [Col. 0991] 24 Song IV, 13.],” that is, the Church, containing within one faith diverse [lacuna] of profession. By pomegranates, martyrs, as in the Song: “If the pomegranates have blossomed [Note: [Col. 0991] 25 Song VII, 12.],” that is, if martyrs have appeared.

Pomegranates are the ranks of the elect, as in the Books of Kings: “There were two hundred rows of pomegranates [Note: [Col. 0991] 26 I Kings VII, 18.],” because the elect possess perfect love of God and neighbor. Pomegranates, virtues, as in the Song: “The wine of pomegranates [Note: [Col. 0991] 27 Song VIII, 2.],” that is, the holiness that proceeds from the virtues of the saints.

Evil is adversity, as in the prophet: “Is there evil in the city which the Lord has not made [Note: [Col. 0991] 28 Amos III, 6.]?” because the Lord permits adversity to arise in the Church for its correction.

Breasts are preachers, as in the Song: “How beautiful are your breasts, bride [Note: [Col. 0991] 29 Song IV, 10.],” that is, how holy are your preachers, O Church, who pour forth the milk of preaching? Breasts, the natural senses, as in the prophet: “Your breasts became those of puberty [Note: [Col. 0991] 30 Ezek. XXIII, 3.],” because in many within the human race the natural senses have been darkened.

Morning is the time of the Incarnation. * Morning, the beginning of faith, as in Exodus: “In the morning they will be filled with bread [Note: [Col. 0991] 31 Exod. XVI, 8.],” because at the beginning of faith those who were in the primitive Church were refreshed by the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Morning, prosperity in the present life, as in Ecclesiastes: “Whose rulers eat in the morning [Note: [Col. 0993] 1 Eccl. X, 16.],” that is, whose leaders rejoice in the prosperity of the present life. Morning, the beginning of each person’s present life, as in Job: “From morning until evening they will be cut down [Note: [Col. 0993] 2 Job IV, 20.],” because from the beginning of their life to its end the wicked do not cease to be deprived. Morning, the illumination of the Holy Spirit, as in the Song: “Let us rise early to the vineyards [Note: [Col. 0993] 3 Song VII, 12.],” that is, illuminated by the Holy Spirit, let us rise toward the examples of the saints. Morning, inward consolation, as in Genesis: “There was evening and there was morning [Note: [Col. 0993] 4 Gen. I, 5; VIII, 13; XIX, 23, 31.],” because at one time the soul is darkened by temptation, and at another it is illuminated by inward brightness. Morning, the brightness of the future life, as in the Psalms: “In the morning I will stand before you, and I will see [Note: [Col. 0993] 5 Ps. V, 4.],” because in the future the holy Church will stand before the face of God and contemplate him. Morning, what comes first, as in Genesis: “In the morning he will devour the prey [Note: [Col. 0993] 6 Gen. XLIX, 27.],” because he afflicted the holy Church first. Morning, Christ’s resurrection, as in the Psalms: “Evening and morning [Note: [Col. 0993] 7 Ps. LIV, 18.],” that is, in the Passion and resurrection. Morning, the first age of the world, in the Gospel: “At first light he hired workers for his vineyard [Note: [Col. 0993] 8 Matt. XX, 1.],” because in the first age of the world God did not cease to exalt his Church. Morning, childhood, as in Ecclesiastes: “In the morning sow your seed [Note: [Col. 0993] 9 Eccl. XI, 6.],” that is, begin to live well from childhood itself.

The morning-time is prosperity, as in the Psalms: “The departures of morning and evening you will make delightful [Note: [Col. 0993] 10 Ps. LXIV, 9.],” that is, you make the rejection of prosperity and adversity delightful to your faithful. The morning-time, exercise, as in the Psalms: “In the morning I will meditate on you [Note: [Col. 0993] 11 Ps. LXIII, 7.],” that is, in my exercise I will strive to serve you. The morning-time, * righteousness, as in the Psalms: “And joy in the morning [Note: [Col. 0993] 12 Ps. XXX, 6.],” because joy is given to those who strive toward Christ’s righteousness. The morning-time, delay, as in the Psalms: “And my chastisement in the mornings [Note: [Col. 0993] 13 Ps. LXXII, 14.],” that is, I was chastised without * love. The morning-time, the day of judgment, as in the Psalms: “In the morning I was killing all the sinners of the earth [Note: [Col. 0993] 14 Ps. C, 8.],” that is, I understood that all the wicked would be condemned on the day of judgment, when eternal light will begin to rise.

A hand is Christ coming into the world, as in the Psalms: “Send forth your hand from on high [Note: [Col. 0993] 15 Ps. CXLIV, 7.],” that is, send your Son from heaven. A hand, Christ ascending, as in Deuteronomy: “I will lift up my hand to heaven [Note: [Col. 0993] 16 Deut. XXXII, 40.],” because Christ was lifted up to the heavens. A hand, divine consolation, as in Ezekiel: “The hand of the Lord was with me [Note: [Col. 0993] 17 Ezek. V, 14.],” that is, divine consolation was present to me. [A hand], power, as in the Psalms: “From the hand of apostate sons [Note: [Col. 0993] 18 Ps. CXLIII, 7, 11.].” A hand, the members of Christ, as in Exodus [Note: [Col. 0993] 19 Exod. IV, 6.]: Moses’ hand was brought out from his bosom, leprous, and when it was returned to his bosom it became as it had been before; because the members of Christ become unclean when they depart from grace through sinning, but when they return through repentance they are cleansed. A hand, impulse, as in the Psalms: “Let the hand of the sinner not move me [Note: [Col. 0993] 20 Ps. XXXV, 12.].” A hand, discipline, as in the Psalms: “Day and night your hand was heavy upon me [Note: [Col. 0993] 21 Ps. XXXI, 4.],” that is, your discipline continually presses me down. A hand, grace, as in the Psalms: “The Lord supports him with his hand [Note: [Col. 0993] 22 Ps. XXXVI, 24.],” that is, he bestows his assisting grace. A hand, generosity, as in the Psalms: “You open your hand [Note: [Col. 0993] 23 Ps. CXLIV, 16.],” that is, you lavishly expend your generosity. A hand, vengeance, as in the Psalms: “You have strengthened your hand against me [Note: [Col. 0993] 24 Ps. XXXVII, 3.],” that is, you have increased your vengeance against me. A hand, a good work, as in Job: “I will place my hand over my mouth [Note: [Col. 0993] 25 Job XXXIX, 37.],” that is, through a good work I will cleanse my illicit speech. A hand, the force of heavenly virtue, as in Ezekiel: “The likeness of a hand seized me [Note: [Col. 0993] 26 Ezek. VIII, 3.],” that is, the force of heavenly virtue seized me. A hand, Christ’s action, as in Ezekiel: “The hand of a man was beneath their wings [Note: [Col. 0993] 27 Ezek.
