Palms signify spiritual victories, as in the Books of Kings: “And he made cherubim and palms in them [Note: [Col. 1017] 9 1 Kings 6:29],” meaning that God grants holy preachers both the fullness of true knowledge and spiritual victory over [text uncertain] vices. The palm signifies eternal rewards, as in the Apocalypse: “And palms were in their hands [Note: [Col. 1017] 10 Rev. 7:9],” that is, eternal rewards for their good works.

A vine-shoot signifies anyone who holds the sevenfold faith, as in the Gospel: “Every vine-shoot in me that does not bear fruit shall be cut off [Note: [Col. 1017] 11 John 15:2],” that is, he will condemn anyone who has faith in me alone and no good work. Vine-shoots signify the apostles, as in the Gospel: “I am the vine, you are the vine-shoots [Note: [Col. 1017] 12 ibid., v. 5],” that is, I, Christ, possess the fullness of grace, whereas you apostles possess a portion. Vine-shoots signify faithful men, as in the Psalms: “He extended his vine-shoots to the sea [Note: [Col. 1017] 13 Ps. 80:12],” meaning that the holy Church extended its faithful to the ends of the earth.

The cloak signifies the exaltedness of Christ’s humanity, as in the Books of Kings: “Christ lifted up Elijah’s cloak, which had fallen from him [Note: [Col. 1017] 14 2 Kings 2:13],” meaning that the assembly of Christ’s faithful greatly honored the sacraments of his humanity, which he left to them on earth. The cloak signifies the holy Church, as in Genesis: “And with the blood of the grape his cloak [Note: [Col. 1017] 15 Gen. 49:11],” meaning that Christ [text uncertain] extends his Church through the sacrament of his passion. The cloak signifies the letter of the Old Testament, as in Genesis: “Leaving his cloak in her hands, he fled [Note: [Col. 1017] 16 Gen. 39:12],” meaning that Christ, leaving behind the veil of the letter in the works of the Synagogue, came to the Gentiles through knowledge of faith. [Col. 1018A] The cloak signifies reverence, as in Genesis: “They placed the cloak upon his shoulders [Note: [Col. 1017] 17 Gen. 9:23],” meaning that Christians reverently honor in Christ the weakness of the humanity he assumed. The cloak signifies gladness of heart, as in Isaiah: “A cloak of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow [Note: [Col. 1017] 18 Isa. 61:3],” that is, I shall give you exultation, you who were previously in sadness. The cloak signifies repentance, as in Genesis: “She quickly took her cloak and covered herself [Note: [Col. 1017] 19 Gen. 24:65],” meaning that the Church from the Gentiles, as soon as it came to know through faith, covered by repentance the depravity of its former way of life. The cloak signifies help, as in Proverbs: “Whoever takes away a cloak on a cold day [Note: [Col. 1017] 20 Prov. 25:20],” that is, whoever has no help in a time of need. The cloak signifies consideration of one’s own weakness, as in the Books of Kings: “He covered his face with his cloak [Note: [Col. 1017] 21 2 Kings 19:13],” meaning that when we [text uncertain] in contemplation, we ought to humble ourselves through consideration of our weakness. The cloak signifies outward sins, as in the Gospel: “Let him have your cloak [Note: [Col. 1017] 22 Matt. 5:40],” [text uncertain], and cast your outward sins away from you. The cloak signifies corrupt antiquity, as in the Song: “The guards of the walls took away my cloak [Note: [Col. 1017] 23 Song 5:7],” that is, the rulers of the Churches removed from me the depravity of my old way of life. The cloak signifies pride, as in the Book of Joshua: “Achan saw among the other spoils a scarlet cloak, very beautiful [Note: [Col. 1017] 24 Josh. 7:21],” meaning that among the other sins the reprobate desire the splendor of pride most intensely. The cloak signifies actions, as in the Book of Numbers: “That they may make tassels at the corners of their cloaks [Note: [Col. 1017] 25 Num. 15:38],” that is, that they may strive to persevere in the connections among their good actions. The cloak signifies exultations, as in Isaiah: “God will remove *ointment-containers and cloaks [Note: [Col. 1017] 26 Isa. 3:22],” that is, he will destroy in the reprobate instability and pride.

The eyelids signify the judgments of God, as in the Psalms: “His eyelids examine the children of men [Note: [Col. 1017] 27 Ps. 10:4],” meaning that the judgments of God make us attentive and anxious concerning him, since in some matters they conceal themselves from us and in others reveal themselves. The eyelids signify the rulers of the Church, as in Job: “And my eyelids grew dim [Note: [Col. 1017] 28 Job 16:16],” that is, my rulers went astray in certain matters. The eyelids signify the wise of this world, as in Job: “His eyes are like the eyelids of dawn [Note: [Col. 1017] 29 Job 41:9],” meaning that the wise of this world glory in empty splendor. The eyelids signify thoughts, as in Proverbs: “Nor let your eyelids sleep [Note: [Col. 1017] 30 Prov. 6:4],” that is, let your thoughts not go astray. The eyelids signify inward counsels, as in Proverbs: “Let your eyelids go before your steps [Note: [Col. 1017] 31 Prov. 4:25],” that is, let your inward counsels precede your actions.

Straw signifies holy men, as in Genesis: “We have an abundance of straw and hay [Note: [Col. 1017] 32 Gen. 24:25],” meaning that holy men, lightened of the burden of sin and green in good works, abound in the holy Church. Straw signifies the teachings of sacred Scripture, as in the Book of Judges: “We have straw and hay for fodder for the donkeys [Note: [Col. 1017] 33 Judg. 19:19],” that is, possessing sacred teachings and examples for the refreshment of the simple. Straw signifies the necessities of this life, as in Exodus: “Straw shall not be given to you, and you shall deliver the customary number [Note: [Col. 1019] 1 Exod. 5:18],” meaning that the malign spirits desire the elect to be deprived of the necessities of this life and crushed by harsh afflictions. Straw signifies all unstable persons, as in Job: “They shall be like straw before the face of the wind [Note: [Col. 1019] 2 Job 21:18],” meaning that unstable persons are scattered when the breath of temptation arrives. Straw signifies unbelievers, as in Isaiah: “The lion shall eat straw like an ox [Note: [Col. 1019] 3 Isa. 11:7],” meaning that the devil incorporates unbelievers into himself. Straw signifies the condemned at the judgment, as in the Gospel: “But the straw you shall burn with unquenchable fire [Note: [Col. 1019] 4 Matt. 3:12; Luke 3:17],” meaning that the reprobate condemned at the judgment shall be tortured without end in the underworld.

Marshes signify associations of the reprobate, as in Exodus: “The marshes were turned into blood and brought forth frogs [Note: [Col. 1019] 5 Exod. 7:19],” meaning that the gatherings of the reprobate contain cruelties and poisonous talkativeness.

The paliurus signifies excuse, as in Isaiah: “And the paliurus in their fortifications [Note: [Col. 1019] 6 Isa. 34:13],” meaning that the excuse of sin dominates the arrogance of the reprobate.

A wound signifies a harsh blow, as in Job: “The hand of my wound [text uncertain] is heavier than my groaning [Note: [Col. 1019] 7 Job 23:2],” that is, the blow is greater than what I feel, greater than the pain I display. A wound signifies passing tribulation, as in Isaiah: “The Lord will strike Egypt with a wound and heal it [Note: [Col. 1019] 8 Isa. 19:22],” meaning that while his elect remain in the darkness of the present life, the Lord sometimes wears them down through tribulation and sometimes raises them up through consolation. A wound signifies eternal condemnation, as in Jeremiah: “With the wound of an enemy I have struck you [Note: [Col. 1019] 9 Jer. 30:14],” meaning that the Lord has made the reprobate subject to the eternal condemnation owed to the devil. A wound signifies corrections, as in the Psalms: “Remove your wound from me [Note: [Col. 1019] 10 Ps. 38:11].” A wound signifies sins, as in the Gospel: “And after laying wounds upon him, they went away [Note: [Col. 1019] 11 Luke 10:30],” meaning that the demons, after inflicting sins upon our first parents, departed. A wound signifies afflictions, as in Exodus: “I shall send all my wounds upon your heart [Note: [Col. 1019] 12 Exod. 9:14],” meaning that the Lord imposes all afflictions upon *the devil. A wound signifies present adversities, as in the Books of Kings: “I shall rebuke him with the rod of men and with the wounds of the children of men [Note: [Col. 1019] 13 2 Sam. 7:14],” that is, I shall correct him through rebuke and present adversities, by which I customarily correct my *elect.

The sole of the foot signifies discernment of heart, as in Ezekiel: “The sole of their foot was like the sole of a calf [Note: [Col. 1019] 14 Ezek. 1:7],” that is, their discernment is mature. The sole signifies the lowest action, as in Isaiah: “From the sole of the foot to the crown there is no health in him [Note: [Col. 1019] 15 Isa. 1:6],” [text uncertain], from the lowest action to the highest there is nothing praiseworthy in him. The sole signifies the end of each person, as in Job: “His sole shall be caught in a snare [Note: [Col. 1019] 16 Job 18:9],” meaning that the devil strives especially to deceive every reprobate person at the end. The sole signifies the end of the world, as in Genesis: “The other, coming out, held his brother’s heel in his hand [Note: [Col. 1019] 17 Gen. 25:26],” meaning that at the end of the world, when the final judgment arrives, the elect will hold primacy over the reprobate.

Plane trees signify holy men, as in Genesis: “Jacob took rods from plane trees [Note: [Col. 1019] 18 Gen. 30:37],” meaning that a good ruler takes good examples from holy men in order to instruct his subjects. Plane trees signify holy angels, as in Ezekiel: “The plane trees were not equal to its branches [Note: [Col. 1019] 19 Ezek. 31:8],” meaning that the other angels could not equal that first angel in the prerogatives of his gifts. The plane tree signifies anyone standing upright in contemplation, as in the Book of Ecclesiasticus: “And like a plane tree I was exalted in Kadesh [Note: [Col. 1019] 20 Sir. 24:19],” meaning that a person approaches an exalted heart, and God exalts him.

The street signifies a multitude of peoples, as in Job: “And in the street they prepared a seat [Note: [Col. 1019] 21 Job 29:7],” that is, among the multitude of subjects I exercised authority. Streets signify hearers, as in Proverbs: “And divide your waters in the streets [Note: [Col. 1019] 22 Prov. 5:16],” that is, distribute your preaching among your hearers. Streets signify secular people, as in the Song: “Through the lanes and streets I shall seek the one whom my soul loves [Note: [Col. 1019] 23 Song 7:2],” that is, I shall seek Christ in the ways of life of religious and secular people. Streets signify the hearts of the elect, as in the Book of Ecclesiasticus: “I was exalted beside the water in the streets [Note: [Col. 1019] 24 Sir. 24:19],” meaning that wisdom is elevated through deep contemplation in the minds of the saints, which have been expanded by charity. Streets signify the ranks of heavenly citizens, as in the Book of Tobit: “Your streets, Jerusalem, shall be paved with pure gold [Note: [Col. 1019] 25 Tob. 13:22],” meaning that the ranks of the good citizens are adorned with the pure brightness and bright purity of eternal wisdom. Streets signify the glory of the wicked, as in Job: “May his name not be celebrated in the streets [Note: [Col. 1019] 26 Job 18:17],” meaning that the wicked, although they are always honored in the eminence and glory of the present life, are not renowned.

Bread signifies Christ, as in the Gospel: “I am the living bread [Note: [Col. 1019] 27 John 6:35, 41, 48],” meaning that in Christ, by the testimony of the living soul [fragment]. Bread signifies the sacrament that we receive on the altar, as in Proverbs: “Let her not eat idle bread [Note: [Col. 1019] 28 Prov. 31:27],” that is, let her not receive the body of Christ without the fruit of good works. Bread signifies spiritual grace, as in Isaiah: “His bread shall be given him; his waters are sure [Note: [Col. 1019] 29 Isa. 33:16],” that is, spiritual grace has been granted to him; his contemplations are not erroneous. Bread signifies sacred doctrine, as in Jeremiah: “The children asked for bread [Note: [Col. 1019] 30 Lam. 4:4],” that is, the simple and humble asked to hear doctrine. Bread signifies a good action, as in Isaiah: “We shall eat our bread [Note: [Col. 1019] 31 Isa. 4:1],” meaning that the sevenfold Spirit delights in the good work that he inspires us to perform. Bread signifies the strength of charity, as in the Gospel: “Which of you, if his father asks for bread [Note: [Col. 1019] 32 Luke 11:11]?” [text uncertain]. Bread signifies humility, as in the Books of Kings: “And behold, at his head was a cake baked under ashes [Note: [Col. 1019] 33 1 Kings 19:6],” meaning that in the mind of the holy man, humility from consideration of his own weakness [fragment]. Bread signifies a holy man, as in the Psalms: “For I ate ashes like bread [Note: [Col. 1021] 1 Ps. 102:10],” meaning that the Lord incorporates into himself not only the saints through righteousness, but sinners through repentance. Bread signifies anyone who perseveres in sin, as in Hosea: “Ephraim has become a cake not turned [Note: [Col. 1021] 2 Hos. 7:8],” meaning that the unclean sinner lies in his sins and does not repent of them. Bread signifies carnal delight, as in Job: “Unless he rises to seek bread [Note: [Col. 1021] 3 Job 15:23],” that is, when he has turned to acquiring carnal delight. Bread signifies consolation, as in Jeremiah: “The people groaning and seeking bread [Note: [Col. 1021] 4 Lam. 1:11],” that is, grieving and desiring to have consolation. Bread signifies support for the present life, as in Genesis: “If you give me bread to eat [Note: [Col. 1021] 5 Gen. 28:20],” that is, if you grant me support for strengthening. Bread signifies heretical doctrine, as in Proverbs: “And stolen bread is sweeter,” meaning that heretical doctrine is clearer to the reprobate than sound doctrine. Bread signifies spiritual graces, as in the Psalms: “I shall satisfy its poor with breads [Note: [Col. 1021] 6 Ps. 132:15],” that is, I shall confer the gifts of my graces upon the humble. Bread signifies spiritual instructions, as in Isaiah: “You spend silver not on breads [Note: [Col. 1021] 7 Isa. 55:2],” that is, in your speech you do not devote sufficient attention to instruction. Breads signify the apostles, as in Exodus: “Twelve loaves of the Presence on the table [Note: [Col. 1021] 8 Exod. 25:30],” that is, the twelve chosen apostles in the Church. Bread signifies understanding of the Holy Trinity, as in the Gospel: “Friend, lend me three loaves [Note: [Col. 1021] 9 Luke 11:5],” that is, O Christ, grant me understanding of the Holy Trinity. Breads signify the legal books, as in the Gospel: “There is one boy here who has five loaves [Note: [Col. 1021] 10 John 6:9],” that is, the Jewish people, childish in understanding, who possess the five books of Moses closed. Breads signify inward consolations, as in the Psalms: “My tears were my breads *with wild lettuces [Note: [Col. 1021] 11 Ps. 42],” that is, good works without malice amid bitter compunctions.

Cloths signify the sacraments of Christ’s humility, as in the Gospel: “She wrapped him in cloths and laid him in a manger [Note: [Col. 1021] 12 Luke 2:7],” meaning that [lacuna] concealed the Lord beneath the sacraments of the humanity he assumed, and thus manifested him to the world. Cloths signify the commandments of the Law, as in Job: “I would wrap him in the cloths of infancy [Note: [Col. 1021] 13 Job 38:9],” meaning that God bound the Synagogue by the commandments of the Law. Cloths signify the examples of the righteous, as in Jeremiah: “Place old cloths beneath the elbows of his hands [Note: [Col. 1021] 14 Jer. 38:12],” that is, employ the examples of the ancient Fathers to strengthen your works.

Papyrus signifies secular knowledge, as in Isaiah: “And in vessels of papyrus upon the waters [Note: [Col. 1021] 15 Isa. 18:2],” meaning that the Antichrist will adorn his preachers with words of secular knowledge in order to seduce the peoples. Papyrus signifies the Synagogue, as in Exodus: “Seeing the basket in the papyrus marsh, she sent one of her maidservants [Note: [Col. 1021] 16 Exod. 2:5],” meaning that the Church from the Gentiles, when it saw the faith of Christ among the Jews, sent forth its devouring power and, by believing, received Christ.

Paradise signifies the holy Church, as in Genesis: “God had planted a paradise [Note: [Col. 1021] 17 Gen. 2:8],” meaning that God established the holy Church. Paradise signifies serenity of mind, as in the Song: “Your shoots are a paradise [Note: [Col. 1021] 18 Song 4:13],” meaning that whatever you produce from your mind is delightful and pleasing. Paradise signifies temporal glory, as in Genesis: “Which watered all of it, like paradise [Note: [Col. 1021] 19 Gen. 13:10],” meaning that all temporal glory appears to shine for a time. Paradise signifies heavenly joy, as in the Apocalypse: “From the tree of paradise, which is in the paradise of my God [Note: [Col. 1021] 20 Rev. 2:7],” meaning that whoever conquers the world, the flesh, and the devil will enjoy Christ without end *in heavenly joy.

[Col. 1022B] The wall signifies Christ’s humanity, as in the Song: “He himself was behind our wall [Note: [Col. 1021] 21 Song 2:9],” meaning that divinity lay hidden beneath the veil of the humanity he assumed. The wall signifies sacred Scripture, as in *the Song: “We groped for the wall like the blind [Note: [Col. 1021] 22 Isa. 59:10],” meaning that blinded heretics are exposed in sacred Scripture through error. The wall signifies the hearts of subjects, as in Ezekiel: “Son of man, dig through the wall [Note: [Col. 1021] 23 Ezek. 8:8],” meaning that rulers ought to scrutinize the hearts of their subjects through sharp investigation. The wall signifies obstinacy, as in Ezekiel: “They were building the wall, while they were plastering it [Note: [Col. 1021] 24 Ezek. 13:10],” meaning that the wicked build obstinacy within themselves, while flatterers nourish it with smooth flatteries. The wall signifies past sins, as in the Books of Kings: “Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall and wept [Note: [Col. 1021] 25 2 Kings 20:2],” meaning that the elect turn toward their sins in repentance, the sins they have built between themselves and the Lord.

The leopard signifies anyone full of a variety of vices, as in Isaiah: “And the leopard shall lie down with *the kid [Note: [Col. 1021] 26 Isa. 11:6],” that is, the sinner full of a variety of vices, converted through repentance, shall rest in the Church with the one who continually sacrifices himself in the service of God. The leopard signifies hypocrites, as in the Song: “From the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards [Note: [Col. 1021] 27 Song 4:8],” that is, from the secret places of the proud and from the heights of criminals.

Pasture signifies the sublimity of sacred Scripture, as in Genesis: “Either give the sheep drink, and then lead them back to pasture [Note: [Col. 1021] 28 Gen. 29:7],” that is, first preach simple things to your hearers, and then lead them on to understand higher matters. Pasture signifies instruction, as in Genesis: “The sons were occupied with pasturing the flocks [Note: [Col. 1021] 29 Gen. 34:5],” that is, the rulers were devoted to instructing the peoples. Pasture signifies refreshment by inward wisdom, as in Job: “Their young go out to pasture; they go forth and do not return to them [Note: [Col. 1021] 30 Job 39:7],” that is, the subjects of rulers go out to the refreshment of the heavenly banquet and do not return to them in this life.

The sparrow signifies Christ, as in the Psalms: “I kept watch, and became like a sparrow [Note: [Col. 1021] 31 Ps. 102:8],” that is, I rose from death and flew to heaven. The sparrow signifies a holy man, as in the Psalms: “The sparrow found a house for itself [Note: [Col. 1023] 1 Ps. 84:4],” that is, the holy man chose a heavenly dwelling for himself. The sparrow signifies anyone converted from sin, as in the Psalms: “Our soul was rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters [Note: [Col. 1023] 2 Ps. 124:7],” meaning that sinners are freed from the seduction of demons. The sparrow signifies the unstable person, as in the Psalms: “Flee to the mountain like a sparrow [Note: [Col. 1023] 3 Ps. 11:1],” because heretics strive to draw to their own excellence what they behold. Sparrows signify the humble, as in the Psalms: “There the sparrow builds its nest [Note: [Col. 1023] 4 Ps. 104:17],” that is, the especially humble place their hope in Christ. The sparrow signifies the twofold substance of the human being, namely body and soul, as in Leviticus [Note: [Col. 1023] 5 Lev. 14:49], where two sparrows are taken for the cleansing of the leper: one is sacrificed, while the other is allowed to fly away free. Thus, for a sinner to be completely cleansed, it is necessary both that his body be slain through mortification and that his soul be lifted to the heights through contemplation.

The Father signifies God the Creator, as in Proverbs: “The eye that mocks its father [Note: [Col. 1023] 6 Prov. 30:17],” that is, the heretic who mocks God the Creator. The father signifies any ruler, as in the Books of Kings: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer [Note: [Col. 1023] 7 2 Kings 2:12],” that is, my *ruler, who carries and leads. The father signifies the first-created man, as in the Psalms: “My father and my mother have forsaken me [Note: [Col. 1023] 8 Ps. 27:10],” that is, Adam and Eve exposed me to sin. The father signifies any superior, as in the Books of Kings: “Who is his father [Note: [Col. 1023] 9 1 Sam. 10:12]?” that is, who is superior to him? The father signifies this world, as in Jeremiah: “Cursed is the one who announced to my father, saying: A male child has been born to you [Note: [Col. 1023] 10 Jer. 20:15],” that is, the one who through flattery caused me to be praised by the world for my work. The father signifies the devil, as in the Gospel: “You are from your father the devil [Note: [Col. 1023] 11 John 8:44],” meaning that although the devil did not create or beget them, he nevertheless persuaded and held them.

The floor signifies our flesh, as in the Psalms: “My soul clung to the floor [Note: [Col. 1023] 12 Ps. 119:25],” that is, my reason consented to the flesh. The floor signifies a humble heart, as in the Books of Kings: “He covered the floor with foreign boards [Note: [Col. 1023] 13 1 Kings 6:15],” meaning that the Lord adorns the humble heart with spiritual gifts. The floor signifies any hearer, as in Ezekiel: “Treasuries around the floor [Note: [Col. 1023] 14 Ezek. 40:17],” meaning that the examples of the Fathers who preceded them stir the hearer toward the good.

The stake signifies compunction, as in Deuteronomy: “Carrying a stake on your belt [Note: [Col. 1023] 15 Deut. 23:13],” that is, possessing the goad of compunction in the mind. Stakes signify rulers, as in Exodus: “You shall make the stakes of the court from bronze [Note: [Col. 1023] 16 Exod. 27:19],” that is, you shall establish rulers of the Church who are strong in action and resounding in preaching.

The breast signifies an upright heart, as in Exodus: “The teaching and truth that shall be on Aaron’s breast [Note: [Col. 1023] 17 Exod. 28:30],” that is, in the ruler’s thought. The breast signifies pride, as in Genesis: “You shall walk upon your breast [Note: [Col. 1023] 18 Gen. 3:14],” that is, you shall overcome the arrogance of the reprobate.

The little breast signifies an upright heart, as in Exodus: “The little breast shall belong to Aaron [Note: [Col. 1023] 19 Exod. 29:27–28; Lev. 7:31],” meaning that it pertains especially to the ruler to possess an upright heart.

Cattle signifies the heretic, as in the Song of Habakkuk: “The flock shall be cut off from the sheepfold [Note: [Col. 1023] 20 Hab. 3:17],” that is, the heretic shall be cut off from the Church. Cattle signifies both sinner and righteous person, as in Ezekiel: “Behold, I judge between cattle and cattle [Note: [Col. 1023] 21 Ezek. 34:17],” that is, I distinguish between sinner and righteous person. Cattle signify peoples, as in Genesis: “Appoint them as masters of my cattle [Note: [Col. 1023] 22 Gen. 47:6],” that is, rulers of my peoples. Cattle signify the covetous, as in the Psalms: “And also the cattle of the field [Note: [Col. 1023] 23 Ps. 8:8],” that is, you subjected to him also the covetous of the world.

[Col. 1024B] Sin is the commission of evil, whereas transgression is the omission of good. Sin signifies a sacrifice for sin, as in Paul: “He who knew no sin, for our sake he made sin [Note: [Col. 1023] 24 2 Cor. 5:21],” meaning that God the Father appointed Christ, free from every sin, as a *sacrifice and priest for our sins. Sin signifies the punishment of sin, as in Isaiah: “He himself bore the sin of many [Note: [Col. 1023] 25 Isa. 53:12],” meaning that Christ underwent the punishment of death for us sinners. Sin signifies the tinder of sin, that is, desire, as in Paul: “I did not know sin except through the Law, *when the Law said, ‘You shall not covet’ [Note: [Col. 1023] 26 Rom. 7:7].” Sin signifies the devil, as in Paul: “The man of sin shall be revealed, *the son of perdition [Note: [Col. 1023] 27 2 Thess. 2:3],” that is, the Antichrist, the man of the devil, prepared for eternal damnation, shall be manifested.

[Col. 1024C] A foot is any preacher, as in the Psalms: “That your foot may be dipped in blood” [Note: [Col. 1023] 28 Psalm 67:24], meaning that a preacher is sometimes afflicted by tribulation. A foot is preaching, as in the Psalm: “They will pass through the river on foot there” [Note: [Col. 1023] 29 Psalm 65:6], that is, they will go into the world through preaching. A foot is any friend, as in the Gospel: “If your foot causes you to stumble” [Note: [Col. 1023] 30 Matthew 18:8], that is, if your necessary friend suggests evil to you, do not follow him. Feet are the works of heavenly commandments, upon which both peoples ought to lean, as in Isaiah: “Leaning the foot of the ox and the donkey” [Note: [Col. 1023] 31 Isaiah 32:20], that is, setting forth the works of heavenly commandments upon which both peoples—the Jewish and the Gentile—ought to lean. A foot is Christ’s example, as in Isaiah: “The foot of the poor man will trample it” [Note: [Col. 1023] 32 Isaiah 6:6], meaning that the example of humble [Col. 1024D] Christ cast down the proud of the world. A foot is a bad example, as in Job: “He will forget that the foot tramples them” [Note: [Col. 1023] 33 Job 39:18], meaning that a negligent prelate does not care that a bad example corrupts his subjects. By feet are meant the sacraments of the Incarnation, as in the Gospel: “She began to bathe his feet with tears” [Note: [Col. 1023] 34 Luke 7:38], meaning that the converted Gentile world began to venerate the lowliness of Christ’s Incarnation. Feet are the apostles, as in Job: “I washed my feet with butter” [Note: [Col. 1023] 35 Job 29:6], meaning that Christ, [Col. 1025A] who bore our sins, cleansed his apostles with the Holy Spirit. By feet are meant preachers, as in Isaiah: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace!” [Note: [Col. 1025] 1 Isaiah 52:7], meaning that through holiness preachers are made beautiful—those who announce repentance to the people. By feet are meant preachers, as in the Gospel: “Shake the dust from your feet” [Note: [Col. 1025] 2 Matthew 10:14; Mark 6:11; Luke 9:5], that is, do not accept earthly things from those who despise us in return for your preaching. By feet are meant the weak who are in the Church, as in Job: “They have overthrown my feet” [Note: [Col. 1025] 3 Job 30:12], that is, the heretics have overthrown my weak ones who are in the Church. By feet are meant thoughts, as in Jeremiah: “Her uncleanness is on her feet” [Note: [Col. 1025] 4 Lamentations 1:9], that is, her impurities are in her thoughts. By feet are meant intentions, as in Proverbs: “Their feet run toward evil” [Note: [Col. 1025] 5 Proverbs 1:16], [Col. 1025B] that is, their intentions are inclined toward sins. By feet are meant afflictions, as in Leviticus: “With his entrails and feet washed in water” [Note: [Col. 1025] 6 Leviticus 1:9], meaning that, in order that we may be God’s sacrifice, we must cleanse our relationships and * afflictions with the water of compunction. By feet are meant deeds, as in Jeremiah: “He spread a net for my feet” [Note: [Col. 1025] 7 Lamentations 1:13], meaning that the devil strives in many ways to corrupt our works. By feet are meant the actions of the saints, as in Ezekiel: “Their feet were straight feet” [Note: [Col. 1025] 8 Ezekiel 1:7], meaning that the actions of the saints are not twisted toward iniquity. By feet are meant holy men, as in the Psalms: “We will worship in the place where [his feet have stood]” [Note: [Col. 1025] 9 Psalm 131:7], that is, in contemplation of the holy way of life in which your perfect servants persist profitably, we humble ourselves. By feet are meant those saints who are in the heavenly homeland, as in the Psalms: “You have set my feet in a spacious place” [Note: [Col. 1025] 10 Psalm 30:9], meaning that those who, departing from here, settle in the heavenly homeland are in the breadth of grace. By feet are meant the ministers of the wicked, as in the Psalms: “Their feet are swift to shed blood” [Note: [Col. 1025] 11 Psalms 13:3 and 59:7], that is, their ministers are ready to practice cruelty.

A skin is the movement of the flesh, as in Job: “You clothed me with skin and flesh” [Note: [Col. 1025] 12 Job 10:11], that is, you surrounded me with the movement and sensations of the flesh. A skin is the reality of our body, as in Job: “Again I shall be clothed with my skin” [Note: [Col. 1025] 13 Job 19:26], that is, I shall again appear in the reality of my body. A skin is a small adversity, as in Job: “Skin for skin” [Note: [Col. 1025] 14 Job 2:4–5]; and therefore he accepts these few adversities calmly, because he fears suffering greater ones. A skin is the very outward surface of our action, as in Leviticus: “The priest who offers the burnt offering shall have its skin” [Note: [Col. 1025] 15 Leviticus 7:8], meaning that only the * exterior is assigned to the person in a good work. A skin is the weak things of the world, as in Job: “Will you fill a * net with his skin?” [Note: [Col. 1025] 16 Job 40:26], meaning that the Lord chose the weak things of this world, * who clung to the enemy, and established his Church from them. Skins are holy women, as in Job: “My skin and flesh being consumed” [Col. 1026A] [Note: [Col. 1025] 17 Job 19:20], that is, with devoted women surrounding me, while the disciples who seemed to be closer were fleeing, the strength of my Passion clung to me. A skin is the literal understanding, as in Leviticus: “After removing the skin of the victim, they shall cut its limbs into * pieces” [Note: [Col. 1025] 18 Leviticus 1:6], meaning that preachers, once the veil of the letter has been removed, ought subtly to examine the inner things. A skin is human mortality, as in the Psalms: * “You stretch out the heavens like a skin” [Note: [Col. 1025] 19 Psalm 103:2], meaning that through the mouths of mortal preachers the Lord has opened the sacred Scriptures to us. Skins are the bodies of martyrs, as in Exodus: “From the skins of rams dyed red” [Note: [Col. 1025] 20 Exodus 26:14], that is, from the bodies of martyred saints. By skins are meant the ancient fathers, as in the Books of Kings: “I walked in the midst of skins,” meaning that the Lord dwelt in the ancient fathers. By skins are meant bodily virtues, [Col. 1026B] as in Jeremiah: “Suddenly my skins were laid waste” [Note: [Col. 1025] 21 Jeremiah 4:20], that is, my external scars were suddenly broken open. By skins are meant the citizens of heaven, as in the Song: “Like Solomon’s skins” [Note: [Col. 1025] 22 Song of Songs 1:5], meaning that the devout soul strives even in the present life to possess in part the spiritual beauty that the citizens of heaven possess. By skins are meant the reprobate, as in the song of Habakkuk: “The skins of the land of Midian will be troubled” [Note: [Col. 1025] 23 Habakkuk 3:7], that is, the reprobate, condemned at the judgment, will be punished, for Midian is interpreted as “judgment.”

The pelican is any hermit, as in the Psalms: “I have become like a pelican” [Note: [Col. 1025] 24 Psalm 101:7], that is, he dwells in solitude after the manner of that bird.

Plaited work signifies concord, as in the Books of Kings: “Between the little wreaths and the plaited work, lions and oxen” [Note: [Col. 1025] 25 3 Kings 7:29], meaning that among holy men zeal and gentleness exist with charity and concord.

A feather is the external action, as in Job: “The ostrich’s feather is like the feathers of the heron” [Note: [Col. 1025] 26 Job 39:16], meaning that the hypocrite’s external action appears similar to the actions of a holy man. By feathers are meant the admonitions of the prophets, as in the Psalms: “Under his feathers you will have hope.” [Note: [Col. 1025] 27 Psalm 90:4]. * By feathers are meant the commandments of charity, as in the Psalms: “If I take the feathers” [Note: [Col. 1025] 28 Psalm 138:9], that is, if I strive to fulfill the commandments of charity. By (feathers) are meant moral virtues, as in the Psalms: “The feathers of a dove” [Note: [Col. 1025] 29 Psalm 67:14], that is, in your virtues I shall have the gentleness of simplicity and the brightness of knowledge. By feathers are meant the contemplations of the saints, as in Ezekiel: “And their faces and their feathers were extended above” [Note: [Col. 1025] 30 Ezekiel 1:11], meaning that holy men, with regard to their inward reward, devote themselves both to action and to contemplation.

Small feathers are holy desires, as in Leviticus: “Everything that has small feathers you shall eat” [Note: [Col. 1025] 31 Leviticus 11:9; Deuteronomy 14:19], meaning that those enter the body of the elect who, through holy desires, transport themselves to heavenly things.

Melons are earthly sweetnesses, as in the Book of Numbers: “The cucumbers and melons came to mind” [Note: [Col. 1027] 1 Numbers 11:5], that is, carnal pleasures and earthly sweetnesses.

A purse is the burden of the world, as in the Gospel: “Do not carry a purse or a bag” [Note: [Col. 1027] 2 Matthew 10:10; Mark 6:6; Luke 9:3 and 10:4], that is, do not hide knowledge, nor take upon yourselves the burden of the world. A purse is the understanding of the apostles, as in the Books of Kings: “He put five stones into the shepherd’s bag which he had with him” [Note: [Col. 1027] 3 1 Kings 17:40], meaning that he entrusted the five books of Moses to the understanding of the apostles. A purse is a devout mind, as in the Books of Kings: “Carrying a new vessel for the man of God in his purse” [Note: [Col. 1027] 4 4 Kings 4:42], meaning that we ought to bring Christ nourishment of holy newness in our devout mind.

A pilgrim is Christ, as in Job: “And I am like a stranger in their eyes” [Note: [Col. 1027] 5 Job 19:15], meaning that the Jews regarded Christ as altogether alien to them. A pilgrim is anyone who despises the world, as in the Psalm: “And a pilgrim, like all (my fathers)” [Note: [Col. 1027] 6 Psalm 38:13], that is, after the manner of the ancient fathers, I consider myself * foreign, so long as I live in the present exile. A pilgrim is concupiscence, as in the Books of Kings: “When a certain pilgrim had come to the rich man” [Note: [Col. 1027] 7 2 Samuel 12:4], that is, when the concupiscence of the flesh tempted King David.

The partridge is the devil, as in Jeremiah: “The partridge gathered what it did not hatch” [Note: [Col. 1027] 8 Jeremiah 17:11], meaning that the devil persuaded those whom he did not create and retained those whom he did not beget.

Prey is the salvation of the elect, as in Genesis: “You have gone up to the prey, * my son” [Note: [Col. 1027] 9 Genesis 49:9], meaning that Christ went up onto the cross for the salvation of the elect. Prey is the praise of hypocrites, as in Job: “The tiger perishes because it has no prey” [Note: [Col. 1027] 10 Job 4:11], meaning that the hypocrite comes to an end before he loses his praise. Prey is the souls of the wicked, as in Job: “He promises prey to his companions” [Note: [Col. 1027] 11 Job 17:5], that is, he promises his companions that he will acquire the souls of the wicked. By prey is meant persecution, as in Genesis: “In the morning he will devour the prey” [Note: [Col. 1027] 12 Genesis 49:27], meaning that Saul pursued the persecution of the godly.

A manger is sacred Scripture, as in Job: “Or will he remain at your manger?” [Note: [Col. 1027] 13 Job 39:12], that is, will an earthly and proud ruler obey your Scripture by your strength? By a manger is meant the Lord’s Incarnation, as in Isaiah: “And the donkey knows its master’s manger” [Note: [Col. 1027] 14 Isaiah 1:3], meaning that the Gentile people recognized the Incarnation of their Redeemer. A manger is heavenly blessedness, as in Job: “Or will the ox bellow when it stands before the manger?” [Note: [Col. 1027] 15 Job 6:5], meaning that the preacher of the Church has no need to groan when he has reached the fullness of heavenly happiness. By mangers are meant the various orders of the Church, as in the song of Habakkuk: “There will be no herd in the mangers” [Note: [Col. 1027] 16 Habakkuk 3:17], meaning that at that time there will scarcely be a commendable fellowship in certain orders of the Church.

Robbers are plunderers, as in Job: “The tents of robbers abounded” [Col. 1028A] [Note: [Col. 1027] 17 Job 12:6], that is, the possessions of plunderers.

A bolt is human pleasure, as in the Song: “I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved” [Note: [Col. 1027] 18 Song of Songs 5:6], that is, I offered the desire of my heart to my God.

The rock is Christ, as in the Psalms: “He struck the rock, and waters flowed” [Note: [Col. 1027] 19 Psalm 77:20], meaning that the Jewish people struck Christ crucified, and gifts of grace flowed from him. The rock is faith, as in Exodus: “There is a place with me, and you shall stand upon the rock” [Note: [Col. 1027] 20 Exodus 33:21], that is, you will find a dwelling with me if you persist in the firmness of faith. The rock is the confession of faith, as in the Gospel: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” [Note: [Col. 1027] 21 Matthew 16:18], that is, upon this confession of faith I will build my Church. The rock is the firmness of good action, as in [Col. 1028B] the Psalms: “And he set me upon a rock” [Note: [Col. 1027] 22 Psalm 39:3], that is, he stirred my affections toward firm action. The rock is any steadfast man, as in Proverbs: “The way of a serpent upon a rock” [Note: [Col. 1027] 23 Proverbs 30:19], meaning that the devil’s suggestion cannot prevail against a spiritual man. The rock is spiritual strength, as in the Psalms: “He exalted me upon a rock” [Note: [Col. 1027] 24 Psalm 60:3], that is, he raised me up in true strength. By rocks are meant the holy angels, as in Job: “The eagle dwells in the rocks,” meaning that the devout soul dwells in contemplation of the holy angels. By rocks are meant holy men, as in the Psalms: “From the midst of the rocks they will give forth voices” [Note: [Col. 1027] 25 Psalm 103:12], that is, they utter preaching from the life of the holy fathers. By rocks are meant good examples, as in Job: “Do you know the time when the wild goats give birth (among the rocks)?” [Note: [Col. 1027] 26 Job 39:4], that is, do you know when the saints ought to bring forth a good action from good examples? By the rock are meant great contemplations, as in the Books of Kings: “Upon the very steep rocks, which are accessible only to wild goats” [Note: [Col. 1027] 27 1 Samuel 24:3], that is, upon the greatest contemplations, which are open only to the perfect.

Paintings are the varieties of virtues, as in the Books of Kings: “Various paintings, as if projecting” [Note: [Col. 1027] 28 1 Kings 6:29], the powers appearing.

Hairs are the humility of penitents, as in Exodus: “He made eleven curtains of goats’ hair” [Note: [Col. 1027] 29 Exodus 36:14], meaning that God causes *[uncertain: pervisorum aeternorum] to repent of transgression after the manner of humble penitents. Hairs are afflictions, as in the Gospel: “John was clothed in camel’s hair” [Note: [Col. 1027] 30 Matthew 3:4; Mark 1:6], meaning that he preached the affliction of the flesh. Hairs are weak thoughts, as in [Col. 1028D] Job: “The hairs of my flesh bristled” [Note: [Col. 1027] 31 Job 4:15], that is, the thoughts of my weakness were stunned. Hairs are sins, as in the Book of Numbers: The Levites shaved all the hairs of their flesh [Note: [Col. 1027] 32 Numbers 8:7], meaning that, when they undertake divine service, they ought to cast away their former sins.

The hairy beings are unclean spirits, as in Isaiah: “And the hairy beings will leap there” [Note: [Col. 1027] 33 Isaiah 13:21], meaning that in the reprobate mind its unclean spirits rejoice in its destruction. A hairy man is anyone devoted to excess, as in Genesis: “Esau is hairy, and I am smooth” [Note: [Col. 1029] 1 Genesis 27:11], meaning that the reprobate love excess, while the elect strive to restrain excess from themselves. A hairy man is anyone humble * and base, lowly in [lacuna] his own affairs and strengthened by bodily chastity.

* The Pleiades are the elect, as in Job: “Can you reach the shining stars of the Pleiades?” [Note: [Col. 1029] 2 Job 38:31], that is, can you assist all the elect of the Church in heavenly blessedness?

The pine is the truth of faith, as in Isaiah: “The fir and the box tree will come to you [and the pine together]” [Note: [Col. 1029] 3 Isaiah 60:13], meaning that in the Church there are those who are exalted in contemplation, strong in action, and verdant in faith.

[Col. 1029B] The firstborn is faith, as in the Psalms: “And he struck every firstborn in Egypt” [Note: [Col. 1029] 4 Psalm 77:51], meaning that in the mind of the reprobate the Lord sometimes even permits faith * to be destroyed. The firstborn is the beginning of a good work, as in Deuteronomy: “You shall not work with the firstborn of your ox” [Note: [Col. 1029] 5 Deuteronomy 15:19], that is, do not place your confidence in the beginning of your good work. The firstborn is pride, as in Job: “May death consume the arms of the firstborn” [Note: [Col. 1029] 6 Job 18:13], meaning that pride, the beginning of every sin, sometimes corrupts the good works that the wicked man performs.

A prince is Christ, as in Isaiah: “Father of the future age, Prince of Peace” [Note: [Col. 1029] 7 Isaiah 9:6], meaning that Christ gives peace of conscience here to those for whom he has prepared future joy. A prince is any prelate, as [Col. 1029C] in Isaiah: “He who is foolish will not be called a prince” [Note: [Col. 1029] 8 Isaiah 32:5], meaning that he who does not possess wisdom in himself ought not to preside over others in governance. A prince is the human belly, as in Jeremiah: “The prince of the cooks destroyed the walls of Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 1029] 9 Jeremiah 39:3], that is, the belly, which cooks serve with great care, corrupts the virtues of the soul. A prince is our understanding, as in Leviticus: “If a prince sins” [Note: [Col. 1029] 10 Leviticus 4:22], that is, if the understanding in a person goes astray. A prince is the devil, as in the Gospel: “The prince of this world has nothing in me” [Note: [Col. 1029] 11 John 14:30], meaning that the devil, who rules over the reprobate, finds nothing of his own in Christ. By princes are meant angels, as in Daniel: “And behold, Michael, one of the princes” [Note: [Col. 1029] 12 Daniel 10:13], meaning that Michael is one among the angels. By princes are meant the apostles, as in the Psalms: “You will appoint them princes over all the earth” [Col. 1029D] [Note: [Col. 1029] 13 Psalm 44:17], meaning that Christ appointed the apostles as prelates over the whole Church. By princes are meant the rulers of the Church, as in the song of Hannah: “He raises the poor man up, that he may sit with princes” [Note: [Col. 1029] 14 1 Samuel 2:8], meaning that God exalts the humble so that he may preside with the rulers of the Church. Princes are the proud, as in Job: “He does not accept the persons of princes” [Note: [Col. 1029] 15 Job 34:19], that is, he does not honor the persons of the reprobate. By princes are meant heretics, as in Job: “The princes will cease to speak” [Col. 1030A] [Note: [Col. 1029] 16 Job 29:9], meaning that the Church destroys the errors of heretics.

A pool is the Jewish people, as in the Gospel: “A pool having five porticoes” [Note: [Col. 1029] 17 John 5:2], that is, the Jewish people holding the five books of Moses. A pool is compunction, as in Isaiah: “To the end of the watercourse of the upper pool” [Note: [Col. 1029] 18 Isaiah 7:3], that is, to the summit of inward compunction, which the desire of love produces. By a pool is meant the doctrine of preaching, as in the Song: “Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon” [Note: [Col. 1029] 19 Song of Songs 7:11], meaning that the preachers of the holy Church stir their hearers to compunction and sorrow, for Heshbon is interpreted as “a girdle of mourning.”

A fish is Christ, as in the Gospel: “They offered him a piece of grilled fish and a honeycomb” [Note: [Col. 1029] 20 Luke 24:42], that is, they honored the sacraments of the suffering Christ by believing rightly and living holily. A fish is faith, as in the Gospel: “Will he give him a serpent instead of a fish?” [Note: [Col. 1029] 21 Luke 11:11], that is, “Will he give him unbelief instead of faith?” A fish is death, as in Jonah: “God prepared a great fish to swallow Jonah” [Note: [Col. 1029] 22 Jonah 2:1], meaning that God the Father permitted cruel death to attack Christ. A fish is the devil, as in the Book of Tobit: “A monstrous fish came out to devour him” [Note: [Col. 1029] 23 Tobit 6:2], meaning that the devil circles about, seeking someone to devour. By fishes are meant human beings, as in the Gospel: “Gathering fish of every kind” [Note: [Col. 1029] 24 Matthew 13:47], meaning that without any distinction he gathers everyone into the faith of the Church. By fishes are meant the faithful, as in Job: “Or will you pierce his head with a fish-hook?” [Note: [Col. 1029] 25 Job 40:26], meaning that God made faithful through the faith of the Church those very rulers of the world who were the highest members of the devil’s body. By fishes are meant these two * purses, namely, the priestly and the royal, as in the Gospel: “A boy here who has five barley loaves and two fishes” [Note: [Col. 1029] 26 John 6:9], meaning that the Jewish people, childish in understanding, were adorned with the five books of Moses and fortified by priestly and royal rule. By fishes are meant curious people, as in the Psalms: “The birds of heaven and the fishes” [Note: [Col. 1029] 27 Psalm 8:9], that is, those lifted up and raised by pride, and the curious, immersed in the depths of this life.

Fishermen are preachers, as in Jeremiah: “Behold, I am sending fishermen to you” [Note: [Col. 1029] 28 Jeremiah 16:16], that is, I shall send preachers to you.

Apples are prophets, as in Job: “Like ships carrying apples” [Note: [Col. 1029] 29 Job 9:26], that is, like the ancient fathers possessing the teaching of the prophets. Apples are good works, [Col. 1030D] as in the Song: “With the fruits of apples” [Note: [Col. 1029] 30 Song of Songs 4:13], that is, with the virtues of good works. Apples are the commandments of both Testaments, as in the Song: “All new and old apples, my beloved, I have kept for you” [Note: [Col. 1029] 31 Song of Songs 7:13], that is, I have believed that all the commandments instituted by you belong both to the Old and to the New Testament. Apples are the marks of humaneness, as in the Song: “That I might see the apples of the valleys” [Note: [Col. 1029] 32 Song of Songs 6:11], that is, that I might choose the sweetness of a humble heart. Apples are holy men, as in the Song: “That he may eat [Col. 1031A] the fruit of his apples” [Note: [Col. 1031] 1 Song of Songs 4:16], that is, that he may delight in the holiness of his elect.

The high priest is Christ, as in Paul: “Christ, appearing as high priest of the good things to come” [Note: [Col. 1031] 2 Hebrews 9:11], meaning that, offering himself upon the altar of the cross, he bestowed eternal goods upon the redeemed.

The gate is Christ, as in Job: “His sons will be far from salvation and * will be turned at the gate” [Note: [Col. 1031] 3 Job 5:4], meaning that the synagogue of the people, distancing itself from true salvation, was corrupted through unbelief when Christ came. The gate is the Virgin Mary, as in Ezekiel: “This gate was closed * and shall not be opened” [Note: [Col. 1031] 4 Ezekiel 44:2], meaning that Mary remained undefiled both before giving birth and after giving birth. The gate is faith, as in the Psalms: “When he speaks with his enemies at the gate” [Note: [Col. 1031] 5 Psalm 126:5], that is, when he disputes with heretics in defense [Col. 1031B] of the faith. The gate is the work of righteousness, as in Job: “When I went out to the gate * of charity” [Note: [Col. 1031] 6 Job 29:7], that is, when I went forth outwardly before others to the work of righteousness. The gate is departure from this life, as in Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 1031] 7 Ezekiel 11:1]: The prophet standing inside had his eyes directed outward toward the gate, meaning that every elect person living in the faith of the Church ought to extend his desire toward his departure from this life, so that he may be with Christ. By gates are meant preachers, as in Isaiah: “And your gates in stones sculpted” [Note: [Col. 1031] 8 Isaiah 54:12], meaning that the Lord adorns the preachers of the holy Church with good works. Gates are moral virtues, as in the Psalms: “Open to me the gates of righteousness” [Note: [Col. 1031] 9 Psalm 118:19], that is, make the virtues of my good works known to me. Gates are evil works, as in the Psalms: “You who lift me up from the gates of death” [Note: [Col. 1031] 10 Psalm 9:14], [Col. 1031C] that is, you who free me from evil works, through which entry into perdition is made. Gates are the five bodily senses, as in Esdra: * “Would that they did not bring burdens through their gates on the Sabbath day” [Note: [Col. 1031] 11 2 Esdras 17:19], meaning that all of us who are in the brightness of inward repose ought not to admit vanity through sight, curiosity through hearing, pleasure through smell, gluttony through taste, or impurity through touch. By gates are meant evil habits, as in the Psalms: “He shattered the gates of bronze” [Note: [Col. 1031] 12 Psalm 106:16], that is, he destroyed the hard habits of wickedness. By gates are meant the doctrines of heretics, as in the Gospel: “And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” [Note: [Col. 1031] 13 Matthew 16:18], meaning that heretical doctrines cannot resist the confession of the true faith. By gates are meant wicked teachers, as in Job: [Col. 1031D] “Who opened the gates of his face?” [Note: [Col. 1031] 14 Job 41:5], meaning that the Lord revealed to his Church the deception of wicked teachers. By the gate is meant the Last Judgment, as in Proverbs: “Her husband is renowned at the gates” [Note: [Col. 1031] 15 Proverbs 31:23], meaning that at the Last Judgment Christ will appear exalted and glorious, though here he was humble and judged.

A portico is the ancient fathers, as in the Books of Kings: “There was a portico before the temple” [Note: [Col. 1031] 16 1 Kings 6:3], meaning that before it was built among the Gentiles, the ancient fathers were in Judaea. A portico is the Synagogue, as in the Gospel: “Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s portico” [Note: [Col. 1031] 17 John 10:23], meaning that Christ was in the world, in the Synagogue among the Jews. Porticoes are the legal books, as in the Gospel: “A pool having five porticoes” [Note: [Col. 1031] 18 John 5:2], that is, the Synagogue devoted to the five books of Moses.

Leeks are the occupations of this world, as in the Book of Numbers: “The leeks, melons, and cucumbers came to mind” [Note: [Col. 1031] 19 Numbers 11:5], meaning that they admit into themselves worldly pleasures, vanities, and the curiosities of worldly occupations.

Swine are despisers of the truth, as in the Gospel: “Do not cast your pearls before swine” [Note: [Col. 1031] 20 Matthew 7:6], that is, do not share the secrets of sacred Scripture with despisers of the truth. Swine are unclean [Col. 1032B] spirits, as in the Gospel: “He sent him into his estate to feed swine” [Note: [Col. 1031] 21 Luke 15:15], that is, he raised him up in pride, so that by living wickedly he might feed unclean spirits. Swine are evil people, as in the Gospel: * “Send us into the herd of swine” [Note: [Col. 1031] 22 Matthew 8:31], meaning that demons choose for themselves a dwelling in the hearts of the reprobate.

The steward is Christ, as in the Gospel: “The lord said to the steward of his vineyard” [Note: [Col. 1031] 23 Matthew 20:8], meaning that Christ, whom the Father appointed over his Church, will render to each person according to his work at the end of the world.

The propitiatory is Christ, as in Exodus: “And you shall make a propitiatory of purest gold” [Note: [Col. 1031] 24 Exodus 25:17], meaning that Christ was born for us pure and free from every sin.

The champion is Christ, as in Isaiah: “And he will be a champion for salvation” [Note: [Col. 1031] 25 Isaiah 63:1], meaning that, in order to save us, Christ overcame the devil.

Bulwarks are miracles, as in the Song: “And it was built with bulwarks” [Note: [Col. 1031] 26 Song of Songs 4:4], meaning that sacred Scripture displays the miracles of the saints to us. Bulwarks are the defenses of the Scriptures, as in the Song: “Upon it bulwarks * of silver” [Note: [Col. 1031] 27 Song of Songs 8:9], meaning that the holy Church has been strengthened by the defenses of Scripture.

Doorposts are the body and soul of a human being, as in Exodus: “And they shall put some of the lamb’s blood on both doorposts” [Note: [Col. 1031] 28 Exodus 12:17], so that we may receive Christ’s body both with the mouth and grasp it with the mind. Doorposts are the books of the Gospels, as in the Books of Kings: “He made doorposts at the entrance of the temple” [Note: [Col. 1031] 29 1 Kings 6:3], meaning that through the books of the Gospels we have entrance into the faith of the Church.

The powerful are holy men, strong in goodness, as in Job: [Col. 1032D] “God does not despise the powerful” [Note: [Col. 1031] 30 Job 36:5], that is, he does not abandon holy men who are strong in good works; * powerful in * themselves, that is, the proud, he casts down from his election.

A child is Christ, as in Isaiah: “The little child will lead them” [Note: [Col. 1031] 31 Isaiah 11:6], meaning that Christ, humble through his fear, inwardly terrifies his elect, lest they cling to the world through affection. A child is the Jewish people, as in the Gospel: “There is one child here” [Note: [Col. 1031] 32 John 6:9], that is, the Jewish people, childish in understanding. By children are meant all the innocent, [Col. 1033A] as in the Psalms: “Praise the Lord, children” [Note: [Col. 1033] 1 Psalm 112:1], meaning that those rightly praise the Lord who are innocent and simple like children. By children are meant the citizens of the heavenly homeland, as in the Gospel: “My children are with me in the bedroom” [Note: [Col. 1033] 2 Luke 11:7], meaning that the citizens of heaven rejoice with the Lord in eternal rest. By children are meant the Jews, as in the Books of Kings: “And they nursed from them forty-two children” [Note: [Col. 1033] 3 4 Kings 2:22], meaning that, after forty-two years had passed since the Lord’s Passion, emperors laid waste to the Jews.

A colt is the Gentile people, as in the Gospel: * “You will find a donkey tied up and a colt with her” [Note: [Col. 1033] 4 Matthew 21:2], meaning that the apostles found both peoples, Jewish and Gentile, bound by the cords of sins. By colts are meant the apostles, as in Job: “For his colts . . . . .” meaning that [Col. 1033B] the apostles ardently desired the salvation of the Gentiles. By colts are meant people from the Gentiles, as in the Psalms: “And the young ravens that call upon him” [Note: [Col. 1033] 5 Psalm 46:9]. By colts are meant hearers, as in Job: “His colts lick up blood” [Note: [Col. 1033] 6 Job 39:33], meaning that faithful hearers absorb the sacraments of Christ’s Passion by believing faithfully.

Dust is the fruitfulness of holiness, as in the Song: “And all the dust of the perfumer” [Note: [Col. 1033] 7 Song of Songs 3:6], that is, all the fruitfulness of * virtues. By dust is meant light-mindedness, as in the Gospel: “Shake the dust from your feet” [Note: [Col. 1033] 8 Matthew 10:14; Mark 6:11; Luke 9:5], that is, cast light-mindedness away from your affections. Dust is every unstable person, as in the Psalms: “Like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth” [Note: [Col. 1033] 9 Psalm 1:4], that is, every unstable person whom the breath of temptation casts down. Dust is inward thought, as in Isaiah: “Sit in the dust, daughter of Babylon” [Note: [Col. 1033] 10 Isaiah 47:1], that is, rest in earthly thought, barren soul abiding in the confusion of vices. Dust is worldly desire, as in Job: “And together they will sleep in the dust” [Note: [Col. 1033] 11 Job 20:11], that is, they will rest together in worldly desire. Dust is worldly action, as in Job: “My flesh is clothed with corruption and the filth of dust” [Note: [Col. 1033] 12 Job 7:5], meaning that the weak who are in the Church are now defiled by unclean vices and * entangled in worldly actions. Dust is any sinner, as in Job: “When the dust was poured upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 1033] 13 Job 38:38], meaning that a sinner is sometimes converted from his softness to steadfastness through God’s inspiration. Dust is weak action, as in Job: “Perhaps you will warm them in the dust?” [Note: [Col. 1033] 14 Job 39:17], meaning that God alone can inflame with heavenly love those who are subject to a negligent evil prelate in a lowly way of life and have been abandoned. Dust is spiritual weakness, as in Jeremiah: “He will put his mouth in the dust” [Note: [Col. 1033] 15 Lamentations 3:29], that is, he will spiritually confess his weakness. Dust is inward discernment, as in Exodus: “When he has crushed everything into the finest dust” [Note: [Col. 1033] 16 Exodus 30:36], that is, when you have distinguished everything you do by the most subtle discernment. Dust is human frailty, as in the Psalms: “And they will return to their dust” [Note: [Col. 1033] 17 Psalm 103:29], that is, you will take the spirit of pride away from them, and they will attend to their frailty in order to humble themselves. Dust is the decay of the human race through death, as in Job: “As clay you made me” [Note: [Col. 1033] 18 Job 10:9], that is, from earth you made my body, and after death you will reduce it to * decay.

A cushion is flattery, as in Ezekiel: “Those who sew cushions under every elbow” [Note: [Col. 1033] 19 Ezekiel 13:18], that is, those who arrange flatteries in every perfection of action.

Lead is the Synagogue, as in Job: “And a plate of lead, or at least” [Note: [Col. 1033] 20 Job 19:24], meaning that in the Synagogue * they received eight words of God and quickly cast them away, whereas the Gentiles received them slowly [Col. 1034B] and retained them for a long time. Lead is the weight of sin, as in Zechariah: “Behold, a talent of lead was being carried” [Note: [Col. 1033] 21 Zechariah 5:7], that is, the magnitude of sin was causing distress. Lead is the devil, as in Exodus: “They sank like lead in the mighty waters” [Note: [Col. 1033] 22 Exodus 15:10], meaning that just as the devil fell, so the reprobate, who are his members, rush into infernal punishments.

Rain is holy preaching, as in Job: “Who is the father of rain?” [Note: [Col. 1033] 23 Job 38:28]—namely, God, who through his inspiration pours preaching into teachers. Rain is inward grace, as in the Psalms: “You will set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance” [Note: [Col. 1033] 24 Psalm 67:10], that is, you will pour gratuitous grace into the elect. This rain is temptation, as in the Gospel: “The rain descended, and the rivers came” [Note: [Col. 1033] 25 Matthew 7:25, 27], that is, temptation and persecution flowed upon him.

Punctus is the brevity of this life, as in Job: “And the joy of the hypocrite is like a point [Note: [Col. 1033] 26 Job XX, 5],” because the joy of the present life is not lasting. Punctus, haste, as in Job: “And in a moment they descend to the underworld [Note: [Col. 1033] 27 Job XXI, 13],” because the reprobate descend hastily, without any delay, to the underworld.

The pupil is Christ, as in the Psalms: “As the pupil of the eye [Note: [Col. 1033] 28 Ps. XVI, 8],” that is, “Guard me, O God the Father, as though I were a member of your Son.” The pupil, the elect, as in the Prophet: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye [Note: [Col. 1033] 29 Zech. II, 8],” that is, just as that tender member is delicate, so tenderly do I love you, my elect.

An orphan is any humble person, as in the Psalms: “Be a helper to your orphan,” that is, “You will help the humble.” [Col. 1034D] By orphans are meant the weak who are in the Church, as in Job: “They drove away the donkey of the orphans [Note: [Col. 1033] 30 Job XXIV, 3],” because heretics strive to deceive the simple teacher of the weak.

Purple is the passion of Christ, as in the Song: “The locks of your head are like the purple of a king [Note: [Col. 1033] 31 Song VII, 5],” that is, the thoughts of your mind are constantly occupied with the passion of the Redeemer. Purple, the splendor of chastity, as in Exodus: [Col. 1035A] “And bronze, and hyacinth, and purple [Note: [Col. 1035] 1 Exod. XXV, 4],” that is, resonant preaching, pure action, and shining chastity. Purple, pride, as in the Gospel: “He was clothed in purple and fine linen [Note: [Col. 1035] 2 Luke XVI, 19],” because lovers of this world love both the beauty of arrogance and the softness of lust.

Frost is heavenly beauty, as in Exodus: “In a likeness upon the earth [Note: [Col. 1035] 3 Exod. XVI, 14],” because the beauty of the spiritual word is in some respect like the beauty above. Frost, temporal adversity, as in Job: “Upon those who fear the frost snow will fall [Note: [Col. 1035] 4 Job VI, 16],” because those who refuse to be afflicted temporally for the Lord are struck by eternal vengeance. Frost, the maturity of religious life, as in the Psalms: “I have become like a wineskin in the frost [Note: [Col. 1035] 5 Ps. CXVIII, 83],” that is, “I have been mortified in the maturity of religious life.”

[Col. 1035B] Coals are the hearts of the wicked, as in Job: “His breath makes the coals burn [Note: [Col. 1035] 6 Job XLI, 12],” because the devil’s suggestion inflames the minds of the wicked through desire. Coals, worldly consolations, as in the Gospel: “They were standing by the coals, because it was cold, and they were warming themselves [Note: [Col. 1035] 7 John XVIII, 18],” because lovers of this world, when they suffer adversities, run to worldly consolations.

A well is the secret place of contemplation, as in the Song: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters [Note: [Col. 1035] 8 Song IV, 15],” because the holy Church possesses the fecundity of good works and the secret place of life-giving contemplations. A well, sacred Scripture, as in Genesis: “He sees a well in the field, and three flocks of sheep lying beside it [Col. 1035C] [Note: [Col. 1035] 9 Gen. XXIX, 2],” that is, he looked upon sacred Scripture in the Church, and the three orders of the faithful attentive to it. A well, the secret place of the heart, as in Genesis: “Isaac dug a well [Note: [Col. 1035] 10 Gen. XXVI, 18–22],” because every holy person carefully searches out the secret of his conscience. A well, any heretic, as in the Apocalypse: “The sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the well [Note: [Col. 1035] 11 Rev. IX, 2],” that is, faith and the holy Church were shaken by the error of the heretic. A well, our mortality, as in the Gospel: “You have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep [Note: [Col. 1035] 12 John IV, 11],” because Christ did not commit sin in the nature of the mortality he assumed, and our mortality was honored in him by the sublimity of holiness. A well, the depth of vices, as in the Psalms: “Let not the well close its mouth over me [Note: [Col. 1035] 13 Ps. LXVIII, 16],” that is, “Let not the depth of vices rule over me”; as in the Psalms: “You will lead them down into the well of destruction,” that is, “You will plunge them into the depth of eternal perdition.”

## Q

Quadrigae. Oak. Quadrans.

Quadrigae are the apostles, as in the Song of Habakkuk: “And your chariots are salvation [Note: [Col. 1035] 14 Hab. III, 8],” because the apostles, who came through the world to Christ, saved the people through faith. Quadrigae, holy teachers, as in the Song: “Because of the chariots of Aminadab * [Note: [Col. 1035] 15 Song VI, 11]”; Aminadab is interpreted as “spontaneous people.”

An oak is the hardness of despair, as in the Books of Kings: “His head caught fast in the oak [Note: [Col. 1035] 16 II Sam. XVIII, 9],” that is, his mind persisted in the hardness of despair. An oak, barrenness of mind, as in Isaiah: “When you are like an oak with falling leaves [Note: [Col. 1035] 17 Isa. I, 30],” that is, when you are barren in mind, with your external goods also failing *. Oaks, the lustful, as in Isaiah: “And upon all the oaks of Bashan [Note: [Col. 1035] 18 Isa. II, 13],” because God will condemn the authors of shamefulness; for Bashan, as they say, is interpreted as “shamefulness.”

A quadrans is the fourfold understanding of sacred Scripture, as in the Gospel: “She put in two small coins, [Col. 1036B] * which is a quadrans [Note: [Col. 1035] 19 Mark XII, 42]”; because the holy Church honors the two Testaments, in which the understanding is fourfold: historical, allegorical, tropological, and anagogical. Quadrans, minor sins, as in the Gospel: “Until you repay the last quadrans [Note: [Col. 1035] 20 Matt. V, 26],” that is, “Until you are punished for your minor and final sins.”

## R

Root. Reclining-place. Creeping things. Rational. Rust. Thornbush. Rhinoceros. Rule. Branch. Laughter. Ruler. Buckthorn. Dew. Little cord. Streamlet. Net. King. Roar. Streams. Wheel. Frogs. Redness. Retribution. Governance. Rock. King.

[Col. 1036C] A root is Christ, as in Isaiah: “The root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples [Note: [Col. 1035] 21 Isa. XI, 10],” that is, Christ, who was born from the stock of Jesse and gave eternal salvation to his people. Root, the incarnation of Christ, as in Job: “My root is open beside the waters [Note: [Col. 1035] 22 Job XXIX, 19],” because the mystery of the incarnation was revealed to the faithful. Root, holy preaching, as in Job: “If its root grows old in the earth [Note: [Col. 1035] 23 Job XIV, 8],” that is, if its preaching becomes despised among the reprobate. Root, the human soul, as in the Psalms: “And your root from the land of the living [Note: [Col. 1035] 24 Ps. LI, 7],” that is, “Your soul from the dwelling-place of the heavenly.” Root, the offspring of the wicked, as in the Gospel: “The axe has been laid at the root of the tree [Note: [Col. 1035] 25 Matt. III, 10],” that is, the full measure of rejection has been fulfilled in the children of the Jews. Root, intention, as in Isaiah: “He will send down a root and produce [Col. 1036D] its fruit * [Note: [Col. 1035] 26 Isa. XXXVII, 31],” that is, “He will display a good * action in secret and show a good action publicly.” Root, human suggestion, as in Isaiah: “From the root of the serpent a ruler will come forth [Note: [Col. 1035] 27 Isa. XIV, 29],” that is, desire proceeds from the devil’s suggestion. By root are meant the faithful, as in the Psalms: “You planted its roots, and it filled the earth [Note: [Col. 1035] 28 Ps. LXXIV, 10],” because God called the faithful of the Church, and it multiplied to the ends of the earth. By roots are meant good * thoughts, as in Job: [Col. 1037A] “Let its roots below dry up [Note: [Col. 1037] 1 Job XVIII, 16],” that is, let the good thoughts it has in its * inmost parts be deprived of the moisture of grace.

A branch is a good affection, as in Genesis: “Carrying an olive branch * with falling leaves [Note: [Col. 1037] 2 Gen. VIII, 11],” because the holy soul bears a good affection toward a tranquil mind through pure thoughts. A branch, carnal pleasure, as in Ezekiel: “Behold, they apply the branch to their noses [Note: [Col. 1037] 3 Ezek. VIII, 17],” because the reprobate delight in the will of the flesh. By branches are meant sacred doctrine, as in the Gospel: “So that the birds of heaven may come and dwell in its branches [Note: [Col. 1037] 4 Matt. XIII, 32],” because, when God calls them, the proud of this world come to faith and rest in its sacred doctrines. By branches are meant good works, as in Job: “And its branches sprout [Note: [Col. 1037] 5 Job XIV, 7],” that is, its good works appear. By branches are meant sacred Scriptures, as in the Gospel: “They were cutting branches from the trees [Note: [Col. 1037] 6 Matt. XXI, 8],” that is, they were receiving sacred teachings from the holy Fathers. By branches are meant wicked people, as in Job: “Its branches he will dry up with flame [Note: [Col. 1037] 7 Job XV, 30],” because eternal condemnation will lay waste wicked people.

A buckthorn is the Antichrist, as in the Book of Judges: “Let fire come forth from the buckthorn and devour the cedars of Lebanon [Note: [Col. 1037] 8 Judg. IX, 15],” because cruelty will come forth from the Antichrist and kill the eminent men of the Church. Buckthorn, the delight of sin, as in the Psalms: “Before your thorns understood the buckthorn [Note: [Col. 1037] 9 Ps. LVI, 10],” that is, “Before your pricks reach the delight of sin.”

Frogs are heretics, as in the Psalms: “Their land brought forth frogs [Note: [Col. 1037] 10 Ps. CIV, 30],” because the gatherings of the blind and ignorant, being talkative, produce heretics and the unclean.

Plunder is presumption, as in Paul: “He did not regard equality with God as plunder [Note: [Col. 1037] 11 Phil. II, 6],” that is, it was not presumption for him to say that he possessed equality with God, since the Son is naturally equal to the Father.

The breastpiece (rationale) is inward purity, as in Exodus: “The priest’s breast must have a breastpiece [Note: [Col. 1037] 12 Exod. XXVIII, 4, 15, 22, 23, 26, 28, 29, 30, etc.],” that is, pure reason will adorn the priest’s mind.

A king is God the Father, as in the Gospel: “The king who made a wedding feast for his son [Note: [Col. 1037] 13 Matt. XXII, 2],” that is, God the Father, who joined the Church to Christ. King, Christ, as in Job: “And when I sat like a king, with the army standing around me, I was nevertheless a comforter of the dying [Note: [Col. 1037] 14 Job XXIX, 1],” because [Col. 1037D] Christ, although he reigns over the blessed in heaven, nevertheless comforts penitents on earth through the hope of forgiveness. King, the Holy Spirit, as in Proverbs: “A king who sits on his throne disperses every evil by his gaze [Note: [Col. 1037] 15 Prov. XX, 8],” because the Holy Spirit destroys sin in the mind of a holy man through his inspiration. King, the holy Trinity, as in Isaiah: “His eyes will see the king in his beauty [Note: [Col. 1037] 16 Isa. XXXIII],” because the elect will contemplate the holy Trinity * in its inward glory. King, the preacher, as in Proverbs: “The locust has no king [Note: [Col. 1037] 17 Prov. XXX, 27],” because the Gentiles had no preacher to proclaim the coming of the Antichrist *. King, any holy man, as in the Psalms: “The king will rejoice in your strength [Note: [Col. 1037] 18 Ps. XX],” because the holy man knows that his strength is not his own but divine, by which, like a strong king, he powerfully suppresses the tyranny of vices within himself. King, any wicked person, as in Job: “Like a king prepared for battle [Note: [Col. 1037] 19 Job XV, 24],” so is any wicked person who prepares himself through pride to resist God. King, sin, as in Job: “And destruction will trample him like a king [Note: [Col. 1037] 20 Job XVIII, 14],” because sin presses down every wicked person without any opposition and leads him to eternal death. King, the devil, as in Job: “He is king over all the sons of pride [Note: [Col. 1037] 21 Job XLI, 23],” because all who are proud against God and their neighbor are under the devil’s dominion. By kings are meant angels, as in Job: “With the kings and rulers of the earth [Note: [Col. 1037] 22 Job III, 14],” because, if human beings had not sinned, they would rest with the angels who reign with God in heaven and * provide counsel for us on earth. By kings are meant prelates, as in the Psalms: “And now, kings, understand [Note: [Col. 1037] 23 Ps. II, 10],” that is, “Consider carefully through understanding, O prelates, how you ought to rule your subjects.” By kings are meant holy men, as in Job: “And he sets kings upon the throne forever [Note: [Col. 1037] 24 Job XXXVI, 7],” because those who, by resisting unlawful movements within themselves, rule themselves well in the present will reign forever with the Lord. By kings are meant the inner senses, as in Proverbs: “Do not give wine to kings [Note: [Col. 1037] 25 Prov. XXXI, 4],” that is, “Do not allow your rational senses to be made foolish by the pleasure of the flesh.” By kings are meant those who grow proud of chastity, [Col. 1038C] as in Job: “He loosens the belt of kings [Note: [Col. 1037] 26 Job XII, 18],” because in those who vainly boast of chastity he sometimes permits the belt * of their modesty to be loosened. By kings is meant any proud person, as in the Apocalypse: “And they go out to the kings of the whole earth * to prepare them for battle [Note: [Col. 1037] 27 Rev. XVI, 14],” because unclean spirits, through suggestion, go out to the elect of this age in order to stir them up to oppose the divine commandments. By kings are meant the bodily senses, as in the Book of Joshua: “Put your feet upon the necks of these kings [Note: [Col. 1037] 28 Josh. X, 24],” because men * rule over the bodily senses within themselves through the purity of their inner affections.

A queen is the holy Church, as in the Psalms: “The queen stood at your right hand [Note: [Col. 1037] 29 Ps. XLIV, 10],” because the holy Church, standing in uprightness of life, was chosen by Christ. A queen, the pride of this world, as in the Apocalypse: “I sit as queen [Note: [Col. 1037] 30 Rev. XVIII, 7],” because the lovers of this world devote themselves confidently to pride. By queens are meant devoted souls, as in the Song: “The queens praised her [Note: [Col. 1037] 31 Song VI, 8],” because devoted souls venerate the holy Church as their mother.

A kingdom is the heavenly homeland, as in the Gospel: “Blessed is the one who eats bread in the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 1037] 32 Luke XIV,],” that is, happy is the one who reaches that sweetness of delight which exists in the homeland of the blessed citizens. Kingdom, the present Church, [Col. 1039A] as in the Gospel: “And they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals [Note: [Col. 1039] 1 Matt. XIII, 41],” because the holy teachers destroy all the errors of heretics in the Church. Kingdom, sacred Scripture, as in the Gospel: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits [Note: [Col. 1039] 2 Matt. XXI, 43],” because the spiritual understanding of sacred Scripture will be taken away from the Jews and given to the Gentile people, who both understand it correctly and live holy lives according to it. Kingdom, the holy mind, as in the Gospel: “The kingdom of God is within you [Note: [Col. 1039] 3 Luke XVII, 21],” because God reigns in the devout mind. By kingdom are meant the various orders of the faithful, as in the Psalms: “Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God [Note: [Col. 1039] 4 Ps. LXVII, 33],” that is, “O various orders of the faithful of the holy Church, praise God.”

A rule is the eloquence of philosophers, as in the Book of Joshua: [Col. 1039B] “A scarlet cloak, very good, and a golden rule [Note: [Col. 1039] 5 Josh. VII, 21],” because the lovers of this world approve proud and empty eloquence.

A ruler is desire, as in Isaiah: “From the root of the serpent a ruler will come forth [Note: [Col. 1039] 6 Isa. XIV, 29],” because an unlawful movement of desire proceeds from the devil’s suggestion. A ruler, the Antichrist, as in Isaiah: “He will put his hand into the den of the ruler [Note: [Col. 1039] 7 Isa. XI, 8],” because the Lord sometimes visits by his grace the wicked mind that is the dwelling-place of the devil.

A reclining-place is inward rest, as in the Song: “He made its pillars of silver, its reclining-place of gold [Note: [Col. 1039] 8 Song III, 10],” because the preachers of the Church are strong and illustrious, and those who live in holy rest shine with the brightness of wisdom.

[Col. 1039C] The loins are works of lust, as in the Psalms: “And my loins have been changed [Note: [Col. 1039] 9 Ps. LXII, 1],” that is, the works of lust in me have been changed into the practice of chastity. Loins, genital works, as in Job: “And he will gird their loins with a cord [Note: [Col. 1039] 10 Job I, 18],” because the Lord permits condemned sin in the genital members * of the proud. Loins, the pleasure of the flesh, as in the Psalms: “Burn my loins and my heart [Note: [Col. 1039] 11 Ps. XXV, 2],” that is, “Extinguish pleasure in my flesh and purify thought in my heart.”

Creeping things are unclean spirits, as in the Psalms: “There are creeping things without number [Note: [Col. 1039] 12 Ps. CIII, 25],” because our enemies, who tempt us in the present, are innumerable. Creeping things, earthly thoughts, as in Ezekiel: “And every likeness of creeping things [Note: [Col. 1039] 13 Ezek. VIII, 10],” [Col. 1039D] because in the wicked mind thoughts are inclined toward the desire for earthly things.

A net is the Church in exile, as in the Gospel: “Their net was breaking [Note: [Col. 1039] 14 Luke V, 6],” because so many now enter the holy Church that they tear it apart through heresies. A net, the Church in the kingdom, as in the Gospel: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat [Note: [Col. 1039] 15 John XXI, 6],” because when the holy Church was in the kingdom, it possessed nothing of left-hand work. A net, sin, as in Job: “He has put his feet into the net [Col. 1040A] [Note: [Col. 1039] 16 Job XVIII, 8],” that is, “He placed his affections in sin.”

A little cord is the commandments of God, as in the Book of Kings: “A cord thirty cubits long surrounded the sea [Note: [Col. 1039] 17 III Kings VII, 23],” because the divine commandments, proclaiming faith in the holy Trinity, adorn baptism.

Retribution is fourfold: first, when good things are repaid for good things; second, when evil things are repaid for evil things; third, when evil things are repaid for good things; fourth, when good things are repaid for evil things. The first and second belong to justice, the third to wickedness, and the fourth to glory.
