Whoever gives good for good is good; whoever does not give evil for evil is better; whoever does not give good for evil is bad; whoever gives evil for evil is worse; whoever gives good for evil is best; whoever gives evil for good is worst.

[Col. 1040B] Laughter is spiritual joy, as in Genesis: “The Lord has made laughter for me [Note: [Col. 1039] 18 Gen. XXI, 6],” that is, God has bestowed spiritual joy upon me. Laughter, the joy of the world, as in Proverbs: “Laughter will be mixed with sorrow [Note: [Col. 1039] 19 Prov. XIV, 13],” because the joy of this world will end in grief. Laughter, heavenly joy, as in Job: “Until your mouth is filled with laughter [Note: [Col. 1039] 20 Job VIII, 21],” that is, “Until your heart is filled with heavenly joy.”

Streams are preachers, as in the Psalms: “Water its streams, multiply its shoots [Note: [Col. 1039] 21 Ps. LXIV, 11],” that is, “Fill the preachers of the Church with your grace, so that the people may be increased in number * s. a.” Streams, the faithful peoples, as in Isaiah: “Broad and * powerful streams [Note: [Col. 1039] 22 Isa. XXXIII, 21],” that is, faithful peoples opening their hearts to faith.

Streamlets are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, as in Job: “May he not see the streamlets of the river [Col. 1040C] [Note: [Col. 1039] 23 Job XX, 17],” that is, “May he not be worthy to receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit.” Streamlets, the teachings of sacred Scripture, as in the Song: “Doves above streams of waters [Note: [Col. 1039] 24 Song V, 12],” that is, “Simple souls attending to the teachings of the Scriptures.”

Dew is heavenly contemplation, as in Genesis: “May God give you of the dew of heaven [Note: [Col. 1039] 25 Gen. XXVII, 28].” Dew, the grace of God, as in Job: “And the dew will remain in my harvest [Note: [Col. 1039] 26 Job XXIX, 19],” that is, the grace of God will persevere in my work. Dew, the fullness of holiness, as in the Book of Judges: “Let there be dew on the fleece alone [Note: [Col. 1039] 27 Judg. VI, 37],” because, more than all others, the fullness of holiness was in the Virgin Mary. Dew, infidelity, as in the Song: “My head is full of dew [Note: [Col. 1039] 28 Song V, 2],” that is, “Preach the word, O faithful friend”; because some have an erroneous opinion concerning his divinity.

[Col. 1040D] A rose is an assembly of martyrs, as in the Book of Ecclesiasticus: “Like a * palm tree, a rose in Jericho [Note: [Col. 1039] 29 Sir. XXIV, 18],” that is, perseverance in the world—for Jericho is interpreted as “Jerusalem” and signifies the instability of this world. By roses are meant the delights of the present life, as in the Book of Wisdom: “Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither [Note: [Col. 1039] 30 Wis. II, 8],” that is, “Let us satisfy ourselves with the pleasant pleasures of this age and its luxurious delights before they fail.”

[Col. 1041A] A wheel is the Old and New Testament, as in Ezekiel *: “A wheel within a wheel [Note: [Col. 1041] 1 Ezek. I, 16],” that is, the New Testament prefigured in the Old. A wheel, this world, as in the Psalm: “The sound of your thunder is in the wheel [Note: [Col. 1041] 2 Ps. LXXVI, 19],” because the voice of divine threat resounds through preachers in the world. A wheel, the conduct of the reprobate, as in the Psalms: “Make them like a wheel [Note: [Col. 1041] 3 Ps. LXXXIII, 14],” because the reprobate rush toward punishment in the end. By a wheel are meant preachers, as in Daniel: “Its wheel was burning fire [Note: [Col. 1041] 4 Dan. VII, 9],” because holy preachers are inflamed with divine love.

Redness is the passion of Christ, as in the Song: “My beloved is white and ruddy [Note: [Col. 1041] 5 Song V, 10],” because he who is white in the glory of divinity is red in the distress of the passion. Redness, heavenly desire, as in Jeremiah: [Col. 1041B] “More ruddy than ancient ivory [Note: [Col. 1041] 6 Lam. IV, 7],” that is, possessing a greater desire than some of the ancient Fathers.

The thornbush is the Virgin Mary, as in Exodus: “The bush was burning and was not * consumed [Note: [Col. 1041] 7 Exod. III, 2],” because Mary conceived and gave birth to Christ, and was neither corrupted in conception nor harmed in childbirth.

Rust is anger, as in Joel: “What the locust left, the rust ate * [Note: [Col. 1041] 8 Joel I, 4],” because when gluttony ceases to infect the reprobate mind, the madness of rage afflicts it. Rust, malice, as in the Prophet: “And its great rust did not go out from it [Note: [Col. 1041] 9 Ezek. XXIV, 12],” that is, its immense malice did not cease.

A roar is the lamentation of the penitent, as in Job: “And my roar is like overflowing water [Note: [Col. 1041] 10 Job III, 24],” that is, just as I grieve in the thought of my heart, so I lament in the speech of my mouth. Roar, the devil’s suggestion, as in Job: “The roar of the lion and the voice of the lioness [Note: [Col. 1041] 11 Job IV, 10],” that is, the suggestion of the enemy and the movement of desire. Roar, the devil’s savagery, as in Peter’s Epistle: “Like a roaring lion [Note: [Col. 1041] 12 I Pet. V, 8],” because the devil, raging cruelly, prowls about seeking someone to devour. By roaring are meant the anxieties of prelates, as in Job: “The does bend down to their young, give birth, and utter roars [Note: [Col. 1041] 13 Job XXXIX, 6],” because holy preachers humble themselves in order to draw others through preaching and to provide spiritual care for their subjects.

A wrinkle is perfidy, as in Paul: “Having neither spot nor wrinkle [Note: [Col. 1041] 14 Eph. V, 27],” because the catholic Church knows neither the spot of malice nor the wrinkle of perfidy. [Col. 1041D] By wrinkle are meant all hypocrites, as in * Genesis: “My wrinkles bear witness against me [Note: [Col. 1041] 15 Job XVI, 8],” that is, those who pretend to love me in prosperity resist me in adversity.

Rocks are the holy angels, as in Job: “And upon inaccessible rocks [Note: [Col. 1041] 16 Job XXXIX, 31],” because the devout soul contemplates the joy of the angels through desire, although it is not yet able to approach them in spirit. Rocks, preachers, as in Job: “The rocks are moved from their place [Note: [Col. 1041] 17 Job XVIII, 4],” because the holy preachers, leaving Judea, migrated to the Gentiles. Rocks, the powerful of this world, as in Jeremiah: “The wild asses stood upon the rocks [Note: [Col. 1041] 18 Jer. XIV, 6],” because the Jews * relied upon the powerful of this world. Rocks, anyone hardened, as in Ezekiel: “Thus says the Lord to the rocks and valleys [Note: [Col. 1041] 19 Ezek. VI, 3],” because the Lord sometimes visits the hardened, just as he visits the humble, through the speech of his inward inspiration.

## S

Sabbath. Ears of grain. Old age. Shoulder blade. Thirst. Cave. Archer. Drippings. Appearance. [Col. 1042B] Brackishness. Sleep. Star. Putrefaction. Scorpion. Hissing. Drops of perfume. Seal. Pod. Shunammite woman. Proud man. Juice. Seed. Sack. Frying pan. Awl. Thread. Furrows. Fine flour. [Col. 1042C] Axe. Pig. Sparks. Old man. Fixed position. Siren. Tomb. Covering. * Silla. Den. Salt. Solitude. Stellion. Blood. Robe. Sneezing. Stable. Spheres. Arrow. Mother-in-law. Servant. Saliunca. Sound. Barren. Scales. Sister. Sycamore. Pond. Sulfur. Flint. Rock. Pride. Left hand. Path. Little bag. Reed. Seat. Hedge. Footstool. * Structure. Stylus. Watchman. Spirit. Thorny places. Scab. * Stilio. Mirror. Dragnet. Sun. Serpent. Flintstones. Spoils. Dung. Sculpture. Forest. Stature. Ephod (shoulder-piece). Fine linen. Fine linen. Segor. Priest. Thorn. Senators. Beetle. Stubble. Sapphire. Throne. Saw. * Psalter. Broom. Dungheap. Sardonyx. Clear sky. Stakes. Balance. Symphony.

The Sabbath is rest of mind and rest of eternity, as in Isaiah: “There will be Sabbath after Sabbath [Note: [Col. 1041] 20 Isa. LXVI, 23],” because whoever [lacuna] rests in mind from iniquity will afterward rest in eternal happiness. By Sabbath are meant sluggishness and negligence, as in Jeremiah: “And they mocked her Sabbaths [Note: [Col. 1041] 21 Lam. I, 7],” because the evil spirits make those whom they see growing sluggish and idle through negligence in useful work carry about certain unclean things through affection in thought. By Sabbath are meant works of holiness, as in Leviticus: “Keep my Sabbaths [Note: [Col. 1041] 22 Lev. XIX, 3, 30],” [Col. 1042D] that is, “Practice the works of holiness in which I rest *.”

A priest is Christ, as in the Psalms: “You are a priest forever [Note: [Col. 1041] 23 Ps. CIX, 4],” because Christ offered himself for us in the ark of the cross. A priest, our very reason, as in Leviticus: “If the priest who * has lied sins [Note: [Col. 1041] 24 Lev. III],” that is, if the rational sense, which is both enlightened through understanding and purified through affection, should go astray. By priests are meant wicked prelates, as in Job: “He leads priests * without glory [Col. 1043A] [Note: [Col. 1043] 1 Job XII, 19],” because eternal glory does not reward prelates who do not glory in the benefit of their subjects.

A sack is penance, as in Job: “I sewed sackcloth upon my skin [Note: [Col. 1043] 2 Job XVI, 15],” that is, through the harshness of penance I chastised my softness. Sack, our mortality, as in the Psalms: “You tore my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness [Note: [Col. 1043] 3 Ps. XXIX, 12],” that is, “You tore away my mortality and clothed me with the glory of immortality.” Sack, the human mind, as in Genesis: “He found * the cup in Benjamin’s sack [Note: [Col. 1043] 4 Gen. XLIV, 12],” because the wisdom of Christ rested in the heart of the * apostle.

A little bag is the negligent soul, as in the * Law: “He put them into a pierced bag [Note: [Col. 1043] 5 Hag. I, 6],” because the negligent soul immediately loses the good it acquires at the present moment. [Col. 1043B] A little bag, the heart of the penitent, as in Job: “You have sealed my sins as though in a little bag [Note: [Col. 1043] 6 Job XIV, 17],” that is, “You inspired me, by repenting, to carry my sins about in my mind.”

A ladder is charity, as in Genesis: “A ladder standing upon the earth, with its top touching heaven [Note: [Col. 1043] 7 Gen. XXVIII, 12],” because charity joins us to our neighbor through compassion and unites us to God through desire.

The shoulder blade is the practice of good work, as in Genesis: “She placed her jar * upon her shoulder blade [Note: [Col. 1043] 8 Gen. XXIV, 45],” because the Church called to Christ from the Gentiles, which had previously tasted Christ, humbly turned toward the humility of good action. By the shoulder blade are meant defenses, as in the Psalms: “He will overshadow you with his shoulder blades [Note: [Col. 1043] 9 Ps. XC, 4],” that is, Christ will defend you with his protections.

[Col. 1043C] The beetle is Christ, as in the Prophet: “He created the beetle from wood,” because Christ, appearing in the lowliness of our flesh, was suspended upon the cross.

Scab is lust, as in Leviticus: “If he has a lasting scab [Note: [Col. 1043] 10 Lev. XXI, 20],” because whoever is continually defiled by lust is forbidden to approach the altar of the Lord. Scab is a stain of the heart, as in Leviticus: “He will cleanse him, because it is a scab [Note: [Col. 1043] 11 Lev. XIII, 6],” that is, the one who is polluted only in mind will easily be purified.

A footstool is the sacrament of the incarnation, as in the Psalms: “Worship the footstool of his feet [Note: [Col. 1043] 12 Ps. XCVIII, 5],” that is, “Honor the sacrament of his humanity, by which he touched the earth of our mortality.” A footstool is anyone who serves God in good action, as in Isaiah: “Heaven is my throne, and earth is the footstool of my feet [Note: [Col. 1043] 13 Isa. LXVI, 1],” [Col. 1043D] that is, “I rest in contemplative things, and in active things I remain through good works.”

Coverings are the rulers of the Church, as in Exodus: “He also made eleven coverings of goats’ hair [Note: [Col. 1043] 14 Exod. XXVI, 7],” because holy rulers strive, through repentance, to correct whatever transgression they perceive in themselves through their occupations.

An archer is any preacher, as in Job: “No archer will put him to flight [Note: [Col. 1043] 15 Job XLI, 19],” because a preacher cannot drive the devil from the human mind by himself, without God’s help.

An arrow is the word of God, as in the Book of Kings: “Jonathan’s arrow returned backward [Note: [Col. 1043] 16 II Sam. I, 25],” because the word of the Lord will not return to him empty but will accomplish whatever he wills. An arrow, the Lord’s chastisement, as in the Book of Kings: “The arrow of the Lord’s salvation against Syria [Note: [Col. 1043] 17 IV Kings XIII, 17],” that is, “For your salvation and that of the people of Israel, the Lord will strike Syria through his chastisement.” An arrow, open persecution, as in the Psalms: “From the arrow flying by day [Note: [Col. 1043] 18 Ps. XC, 5],” that is, “From adversity striking openly.” By arrows are meant words of preaching, as in the Psalms: “The sharp arrows of the mighty [Note: [Col. 1043] 19 Ps. CXIX, 4],” that is, “The lofty words of the Creator.” By arrows are meant the Lord’s acts of vengeance, as in the Song of Deuteronomy: [Col. 1044B] “And my arrows [Note: [Col. 1043] 20 Deut. XXXII, 23],” that is, “I will complete my acts of vengeance in them.” By arrows are meant afflictions, as in the Psalms: “Their teeth are weapons and arrows [Note: [Col. 1043] 21 Ps. LVI, 5],” that is, “Their words strike and afflict me.” By arrows are meant the Lord’s commandments, as in the Song of Habakkuk: “In the light of your arrows [Note: [Col. 1043] 22 Hab. III, 11],” that is, “In the brightness of your commandments they walk in this life.” By arrows are meant God’s threats, as in the Psalms: “For your arrows are fixed in me [Note: [Col. 1043] 23 Ps. XXXVII, 8],” that is, “I already grieve over what you threatened me.” By arrows are meant ambushes, as in the Psalms: “The arrows of the little ones became their wounds [Note: [Col. 1043] 24 Ps. LXIII, 8],” because the Jews deceived themselves in the very thing by which they thought to deceive Christ. By arrows are meant the Lord’s blows, as in Job: “For the arrows of the Lord are in me [Note: [Col. 1043] 25 Job VI, 4],” that is, “The arrows of the Lord afflict me.”

A dragnet is the holy Church, as in the Gospel: “A dragnet was cast into the sea [Note: [Col. 1043] 26 Matt. XIII, 47],” that is, “The Church journeying in the deep of the present age.” By the dragnet are meant the many Churches that make one catholic Church, as in Job: “Will you fill the dragnets with his skin [Note: [Col. 1043] 27 Job XL, 26]?” because the Lord mercifully calls to the Church those in whom the devil was.

Sapphire is the brightness of the angels, as in Job: “Not to the most precious sardius stone, nor to sapphire [Note: [Col. 1043] 28 Job XXVIII, 16],” because neither any human being on earth nor any angel in heaven can be compared with the Son of God. Sapphire, holy contemplation, as in Jeremiah: “More beautiful than sapphires [Note: [Col. 1043] 29 Lam. IV, 7],” that is, * they are more excellent than contemplatives. By sapphire are meant Christ’s miracles, [Col. 1044D] as in the Song: “His belly is ivory, adorned with sapphires [Note: [Col. 1043] 30 Song V, 14],” because Christ’s chaste humanity was adorned with miracles.

Salt is spiritual understanding, as in Job: “That which is not seasoned with salt” [Note: [Col. 1043] 31 Job VI, 6]; that is, Holy Scripture is of no benefit unless it is understood spiritually. Salt is wisdom, as in the Books of Kings: “Bring me a new vessel, and put salt into it” [Note: [Col. 1043] 32 IV Kings II, 20]; for our old Elisha desires that we be renewed through holiness and seasoned through wisdom. Salt is discernment, as in Leviticus: “With every *offering you shall offer salt” [Note: [Col. 1045] 1 Lev. II, 13]; for it is necessary that we have discernment in all our activity. Salt signifies the angels themselves, as in the Gospel: “You are the salt of the earth” [Note: [Col. 1045] 2 Matt. V, 13]; that is, you are the seasoning and *bearer of the Church. Salt is admonition, as in Genesis: “She was turned into a pillar of salt” [Note: [Col. 1045] 3 Gen. XIX, 26]; for the destruction of the reprobate is a great heavenly admonition.

Brine is good desire, as in Job: “And his dwelling-places in a land of salt” [Note: [Col. 1045] 4 Job XXXIX, 9]; for he rests delightfully in the mind that ardently desires him. Brine is holiness, as in the Psalms: “A fruitful land into salt” [Note: [Col. 1045] 5 Ps. CVI, 34]; for the Lord sometimes permits the soul that used to bear the fruit of good works to fall into barrenness.

[Col. 1045B] Saltwort (saliunca) is earthly thought, as in Isaiah: “Instead of the reed, the fir shall rise” [Note: [Col. 1045] 6 Isa. LV, 13]; for the Lord sometimes forms, by his grace, exalted contemplation in the mind in which there had been earthly thought.

Willows are holy men, as in the Prophet: “They shall sprout like willows among the green herbs” [Note: [Col. 1045] 7 Isa. XLIV, 4]; that is, they will be among other people in good works. Willows are those who are barren in good works, as in Job: “Willows of the *torrent shall surround him” [Note: [Col. 1045] 8 Job XIV, 17]; that is, people who love this passing world will favor him. Willows are the proud, as in the Psalms: “Upon the willows in the midst of it” [Note: [Col. 1045] 9 Ps. CXXXVI, 2]; that is, before the proud, who are in the midst of confusion, *we wished to display our preaching.

*The psaltery is the Old Law, as in the Psalms: “Upon the psaltery [Col. 1045C] of ten strings” [Note: [Col. 1045] 10 Ps. XXXII, 2]; that is, strive to please him in contemplation of the Old Law, which consists in the ten commandments. *The psaltery is good action, as in the Psalms: “A pleasing psaltery with the harp” [Note: [Col. 1045] 11 Ps. LXXX, 3]; that is, spontaneous action together with abstinence from the flesh.

Blood is Christ’s passion, as in Job: “Earth, do not cover my blood” [Note: [Col. 1045] 12 Job XVI, 18]; that is, O Church, do not be ashamed to confess my passion. Blood is the examples of the martyrs, as in Exodus: “But he took the blood and sprinkled it upon the people” [Note: [Col. 1045] 13 Exod. XXIV, 8]; for prelates ought to display to their subjects the examples of the holy martyrs. Blood is a carnal understanding, as in Proverbs: “He who squeezes hard brings out blood” [Note: [Col. 1045] 14 Prov. XXX, 33]; for whoever examines Holy Scripture too indiscreetly falls into a carnal understanding. [Col. 1045D] Blood is the wrath of God, as in the song of Deuteronomy: “I will make my arrows drunk with blood” [Note: [Col. 1045] 15 Deut. XXXII, 42]; that is, I will exercise my vengeance with fury. Blood is Christ’s death, as in Genesis: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth” [Note: [Col. 1045] 16 Gen. IV, 10]; that is, the confession of the death of Christ, who survived the Jewish people, cries to the Father from the Church. Blood is sin, as in Isaiah: “And the earth shall reveal its [Col. 1046A] blood” [Note: [Col. 1045] 17 Isa. XXVI, 31]; that is, the devout soul will confess its sin. Blood is anguish, as in the Psalms: “That your foot may be dipped in blood” [Note: [Col. 1045] 18 Ps. LXVII, 24]; for preachers who bear Christ will be afflicted by tribulation. Blood is vengeance for sin, as in the Psalms: “He shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner” [Note: [Col. 1045] 19 Ps. LVII, 11]; for then the righteous person carefully corrects his actions when he sees the sinner punished for his guilt. Blood is cruelty, as in Isaiah: “Your hands are full of blood” [Note: [Col. 1045] 20 Isa. I, 15]; that is, your actions are filled with cruelty. Blood is the punishment of hell, as in the Apocalypse: “And blood came out of the winepress as far as the horses’ bridles” [Note: [Col. 1045] 21 Apoc. XIV, 15]; for among the assemblies of the reprobate, infernal punishment will extend as far as the rulers of the peoples. Through blood are signified works of lust, as in the Psalms: “Deliver me from blood” [Note: [Col. 1045] 22 Ps. L, 16], [Col. 1046B] that is, from lustful works. Through blood are signified any malicious persons, as in the Psalms: “Men of blood and deceit” [Note: [Col. 1045] 23 Ps. LIV, 24]; that is, people intent upon malice and treachery.

Pus is carnal delight, as in Job: “He scraped the pus with a potsherd” [Note: [Col. 1045] 24 Job II, 8]; for by considering our mortality we ought to extinguish in ourselves illicit delight.

Scales are the strength of good works, as in Leviticus: “Everything that has fins and scales” [Note: [Col. 1045] 25 Lev. XI, 9]; for we ought carefully to imitate those who exercise agility in *contemplation and strength in action. Scales are perverse excuses, as in Job: “Compacted with scales pressing one upon another” [Note: [Col. 1045] 26 Job XLI, 6]; for the reprobate incline their hearts toward words of malice, to make excuses for sins.

The frying-pan is zeal for souls, as in Ezekiel: “And you, take an iron frying-pan” [Note: [Col. 1045] 27 Ezek. IV, 3]; for every prelate ought to examine his zeal for God and maintain it firmly toward his subjects. The frying-pan is tribulation, as in Leviticus: “That which is broken in the frying-pan, sprinkled with oil” [Note: [Col. 1045] 28 Lev. VI, 21]; for the holy mind is afflicted in tribulation, not without the richness of inward consolation.

Sardonyx is a holy man, as in Job: “Nor to the most precious sardonyx stone” [Note: [Col. 1045] 29 Job XXVIII, 16]; for no person, however holy, could have been compared with Christ. Sardonyx is Christ’s humanity, as in the Apocalypse: “And he who sat there was like the appearance of a jasper stone and a sardius” [Note: [Col. 1045] 30 Apoc. IV, 3]; for Christ is God from God and man from man.

[Col. 1046D] The stable is the present Church, as in the Gospel: “He brought him into the stable and took care of him” [Note: [Col. 1045] 31 Luke X, 34]; that is, into the Church, and he was concerned for him.

*Stacte is prayer, as in Exodus: “Take for yourself stacte” [Note: [Col. 1045] 32 Exod. XXX, 34]; that is, practice constancy in prayer.

Tin is false doctrine, as in Isaiah: “And I will remove all your tin” [Note: [Col. 1045] 33 Isa. I, 25]; that is, the false doctrine that is in you.

[Col. 1047A] The warp is the human soul, as in Leviticus: “That which has leprosy in the warp” [Note: [Col. 1047] 1 Lev. XIII, 48]; that is, the stain of sin in the mind.

The balance is Christ, as in Job: “And the calamity that I suffer on the balance” [Note: [Col. 1047] 2 Job VI, 2]; for in Christ it can be discerned how grievous is the misery that a human being endures. The balance is discernment, as in Leviticus: “A just balance shall be yours” [Note: [Col. 1047] 3 Lev. XIX, 36]; that is, right discernment. Through the balance are signified judgments, as in the Psalms: “The sons of men are liars in the balances” [Note: [Col. 1047] 4 Ps. LXI, 10]; that is, they are not upright in their judgments.

Stature is holy conduct, as in the Song: “Your stature is like a palm tree” [Note: [Col. 1047] 5 Song VII, 7]; that is, in your conduct you exercise victory over vices. Stature is strength, as in the Book of Numbers: “The people whom we saw are of great stature” [Note: [Col. 1047] 6 Num. XIII, 33]; [lacuna] is strength. Stature is pride, as in the Books of Kings: “They were of great stature, knowing war”; that is, upright in pride and loving. Stature is progress, as in the Gospel: “He could not see because of the crowd, since he was small in stature” [Note: [Col. 1047] 7 Luke XIX, 3]; that is, he could not contemplate purely because of the tumult of unstable thoughts, since he was not great in perfection.

*The bed is the state of our life in which we have remained for a long time, as in the Psalms: “I watered my bed with my tears” [Note: [Col. 1047] 8 Ps. VI, 7. *]; through the old compunction of my life I shall water my bed. The bed is our mind, as in the Psalms: “You have turned his whole bed” [Note: [Col. 1047] 9 Ps. XL, 4]; that is, you have troubled his mind in contemplation of your infirmity. The bed is inward contemplation, as in Job: “And I shall reveal myself, speaking [with myself] in my bed” [Note: [Col. 1047] 10 Job VII, 13]; that is, I shall have relief as I think about myself in my inward contemplation.

The rock is Christ, as in the song [of Deuteronomy]: “And oil from the very hard rock” [Note: [Col. 1047] 11 Deut. XXXII, 13]; that is, after the resurrection they received the Holy Spirit from Christ. The rock is a steadfast mind, as in Job: “And the rock is moved from its place” [Note: [Col. 1047] 12 Job XIV, 18]; for when temptation assails, even a steadfast mind is sometimes drawn back from its good purpose. Through rocks are signified the holy angels, as in Isaiah: “The height of the rocks shall be his refuge” [Note: [Col. 1047] 13 Isa. XXXIII, 16]; for the holy man approaches the strength of the angels through contemplation.

The axe is Christ, as in the Gospel: “The axe has been laid at the root of the tree” [Note: [Col. 1047] 14 Matt. III, 10; Luke III, 9]; for Christ uprooted the unbelieving Jews. The axe is a good man, as in Isaiah: “Shall the axe boast against him who cuts with it?” [Note: [Col. 1047] 15 Isa. X, 15]; for the holy man will not prevail against the Lord, who bestowed upon him the holiness that he possesses. The axe is correction, as in Deuteronomy: “[If] the axe slips from the hand while cutting wood” [Note: [Col. 1047] 16 Deut. XIX, 5]; that is, if correction exceeds its proper measure in prohibiting vices. The axe is the gift of grace, as in the Books of Kings: “So that the iron of the axe fell into the water” [Note: [Col. 1047] 17 IV Kings VI, 5]; for the gift of grace is sometimes lost through pride. The axe is severe persecution, as in the Psalms: “With axe and hatchet they cut it down” [Note: [Col. 1047] 18 Ps. LXXIII, 6]; that is, through greater and lesser persecution the wicked disturbed the Church.

The seat is the kingdom of Israel, as in the Gospel: “And the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father” [Note: [Col. 1047] 19 Luke I, 32]; that is, the kingdom of Israel will be subjected to him through the many Jews who believe in him. The seat is the holy mind, as it is written in Wisdom: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” [Note: [Col. 1047] 20 Verse 25]; for the Father’s Wisdom, Christ, rests in the holy mind. The seat is the holy Church, as in the Psalms: “And you have cast his throne down to the ground” [Note: [Col. 1047] 21 Ps. LXXXVIII, 45]; that is, you have permitted Christ’s Church to be disturbed in the present age. Through seats are signified the apostles, as in the Psalms: “There the seats sat in judgment” [Note: [Col. 1047] 22 Ps. CXX, 3]; for the apostles will sit upon thrones, that is, *the twelve tribes of Israel. Through seats are signified the conduct of the saints, as in the Apocalypse: “The elders who sit before God upon their seats” [Note: [Col. 1047] 23 Apoc. XI, 16]; that is, holy men who humble themselves in their conduct through contemplation of the Godhead.

Segor is the married state, as in Genesis: “And Lot entered Segor” [Note: [Col. 1047] 24 Gen. XIX, 23]; for a person can be saved in the married order, although there is not great holiness in it.

Seed is Christ, as in Genesis: “And all nations shall be blessed in your seed” [Note: [Col. 1047] 25 Gen. XII, 3; XVIII, 18; XXVIII, 14]; that is, in Christ. Seed is *holy preaching, as in the Gospel: “You sowed good seed in your field” [Note: [Col. 1047] 26 Matt. XIII, 27]; that is, you placed holy preaching in your Church. Seed is evil and good people, as in Genesis: “Between you and the woman, and your seed and her seed” [Note: [Col. 1047] 27 Gen. III, 15]; for there is great discord between the devil and the holy Church, and between the members of Christ and those of the devil. Seed is the elect, as in the Gospel: “The good seed truly are the children of the kingdom” [Note: [Col. 1047] 28 Matt. XIII, 38]. Seed is a good work, as in the Psalms: “And his seed shall be in blessing” [Note: [Col. 1047] 29 Ps. XXXVI, 26]; that is, his work will be worthy of reward. Seed is the incitement of a holy man, as in the Psalms: “His seed shall be powerful upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 1047] 30 Ps. CXI, 2]; that is, he who imitates the righteous person in goodness shall be exalted in heaven. Seed is speech of the mouth, as in Leviticus: “A man who suffers an issue of *blood” [Note: [Col. 1047] 31 Lev. XV, 2, 10]; that is, he does not avoid an excess of speech; “he shall be unclean.” Seed is sin, as in Isaiah: “And his seed shall devour the flying creature” [Note: [Col. 1047] 32 Isa. XIV, 29]; that is, sin, from which desire proceeds, *gives birth to sin; and sin, when it has conceived, gives birth to death.

The path is humility, as in the Psalms: “Lead me in the path” [Note: [Col. 1047] 33 Ps. CXVIII, 35]; that is, make me possess true humility, which is the foundation of the other virtues. The path is inward thought, as in Proverbs: “She considered the paths of her house” [Note: [Col. 1047] 34 Prov. XXXI, 27]; that is, she carefully examined the inward thought of her mind. The path is Christ’s ascent, as in Job: “The bird has not known the path” [Note: [Col. 1047] 35 Job XXVIII, 7]; for the Synagogue did not recognize the ascent of our Redeemer. The path is perfection, as in Genesis: “Let Dan be a *serpent in the path” [Note: [Col. 1049] 1 Gen. XLIX, 17]; for the Antichrist shows himself cruel toward holy men who constrain themselves in the perfection of life. The path is the human will, as in Job: “And his snare is upon the path” [Note: [Col. 1049] 2 Job XVIII, 10]; for the devil strives especially to deceive the human will. The path is worldly pride, as in Job: “Do you wish to keep the path of the ages?” [Note: [Col. 1049] 3 Job XXII, 15]; that is, do you desire to imitate the pride of worldly people? The path is the anguish of death, as in Job: “And I walk the path by which I shall not return” [Note: [Col. 1049] 4 Job XVI, 22]; that is, I am heading toward the anguish of death, from which I cannot return. Through the path are signified religious actions, as in the Psalms: “And know my paths” [Note: [Col. 1049] 5 Ps. CXXXVIII, 23]; that is, make my inward thoughts acceptable to you.

An old man is any perfected person, as in Genesis: “Abraham died old and full of days” [Note: [Col. 1049] 6 Gen. XXXV, 29]; he departed from this life perfect in holiness and filled with the glory of good works. An old man is one who persists in the oldness of malice, as in the song of Deuteronomy: “*The nursing child with the aged man” [Note: [Col. 1049] 7 Deut. XXXII, 25]; for he will devastate the one small in understanding together with the vice of evil days grown old. Through elders endowed with the maturity of life are signified the holy men who will appear as judges with Christ in judgment, as in Isaiah: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” [Note: [Col. 1049] 8 Isa. III, 14]. Through elders are signified prelates, as in the Psalms: “And that he might teach his elders wisdom” [Note: [Col. 1049] 9 Ps. CIV, 22]; for Christ, who is the true Joseph, teaches wisdom to prelates.

Old age is the maturity of perfection, as in Genesis: “*You shall go to your fathers in peace, buried in a good old age” [Note: [Col. 1049] 10 Gen. XV, 15]; that is, you will imitate the lives of the ancient saints, devoting yourself to the repose of contemplation and mature in perfection. Old age is the loss of strength, as in the Psalms: “Do not cast me away in the time of old age” [Note: [Col. 1049] 11 Ps. LXX, 9]; that is, do not abandon me when my strength fails me.

The senators are the holy angels, as in Proverbs: “When he sits with the senators of the earth” [Note: [Col. 1049] 12 Prov. XXXI, 23]; for the Lord will come to judgment with the angels, with great power and majesty.

Thorns are perverse delights, as in Job: “They considered delights to be beneath the thorns” [Note: [Col. 1049] 13 Job XXX, 7]; for they regard subjection to carnal delight, which damnably pierces the soul, as a great sweetness.

*The hedge is angelic protection, as in Isaiah: “And he surrounded it with a hedge” [Note: [Col. 1049] 14 Isa. V, 2; Matt. XXI, 25; Mark XII, 1]; for the Lord assigns *angelic protection to his people. Through the hedge are signified good commandments, as in Isaiah: “You shall be called the builder of hedges, turning aside the paths of iniquities” [Note: [Col. 1049] 15 Isa. LVIII, 12]; that is, an establisher of good commandments, prohibiting wicked actions. Through hedges are signified the gentile peoples, as in the Gospel: “Go out into the *streets and hedges, and compel them to enter” [Note: [Col. 1049] 16 Luke XIV, 23]; for when the Jews were *unwilling to believe, the Gentiles were called to faith by frequent miracles inviting them to faith.

The tomb is the secret of contemplation, as in Job: “You shall enter the grave in abundance” [Note: [Col. 1049] 17 Job V, 26]; that is, by perfection in good action, *reaching as far as the secret of contemplation. The tomb is perverse speech, as in the Psalms: “Their throat is an open tomb” [Note: [Col. 1049] 18 Ps. V, 10, 15]; that is, just as their thought is unclean, so their speech is foul-smelling. Through the tomb are signified earthly works, as in the Psalms: “He leads out those who provoke him from the tombs” [Note: [Col. 1049] 19 Ps. LXVII, 7]; for by his grace the Lord makes those who have clung to bodily pleasures leave their wicked way of life. Through the tomb are signified the reprobate, as in *Isaiah: “And Assyria all around, its tomb” [Note: [Col. 1049] 20 Ezek. XXXII, 22]; for in the devil they are dragged into eternal punishments, in which they dwell through the perpetration of sin.

The cave is Christ’s human nature, as in the Books of Kings [Note: [Col. 1049] 21 I Kings XXIV, 4 and following]: David, fleeing Saul, hid himself in a cave; for Christ, on the cross, concealed the knowledge of his human nature from the devil and the Jews, his ministers. The cave is holiness of life, as in Genesis, where the dead Sarah is *buried in the double cave [Note: [Col. 1049] 22 Gen. XXIII, 19]; for the faithful soul, extinguished by a life-giving death to the desire for visible things, is hidden in the holiness of contemplative and active life. The cave is a perverse mind, as in the Gospel: “Now it was a cave, and a stone had been placed over it” [Note: [Col. 1049] 23 John XI, 38]; that is, the sinner’s conscience was deep through malice and dark through ignorance, and the insensibility of hardness was present in it. The cave is our body, as in the Books of Kings: “And his going forth stood at the entrance of the cave” [Note: [Col. 1049] 24 III Kings XIX, 19]; for, standing in uprightness *[lacuna], he might break the barriers of his dwelling; he was going forth through contemplation. The cave is a wicked dwelling, as in the Gospel: “But you have made it a den of thieves” [Note: [Col. 1049] 25 Matt. XXI, 13; Mark XI, 17; Luke XIX, 46]; that is, you have made your soul, in which I ought to dwell, a dwelling-place of unclean thoughts.

Small spheres are the revolutions of thought, as in Exodus: “Rods and *cups and small spheres” [Note: [Col. 1049] 26 Exod. XXV, 31]; that is, preachers, hearers, and the revolving movement of preaching.

The mirror is faith, as in Paul: “Now we see through a mirror and in a riddle” [Note: [Col. 1049] 27 I Cor. XIII, 1]; that is, through faith. Through the mirror are signified good examples, as in Exodus: “He made the basin from the mirrors of the women” [Note: [Col. 1049] 28 Exod. XXXVIII, 2]; for the Law sets before us *spiritual cleansing in the examples of holy men. The mirror is the favor of worldly people, as in Isaiah: “The Lord will take away the mirrors from the daughters of Zion” [Note: [Col. 1049] 29 Isa. III, 23]; for in the reprobate, in whom they delight, he will destroy what is worldly.

The watchman is the preacher, as in Ezekiel: “I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel” [Note: [Col. 1049] 30 Ezek. III, 17]; that is, I have appointed you as preacher to the people, so that you may live in a *lofty manner yourself and announce what is right to others by preaching.

[Col. 1051A] The caves are the inner recesses of the heart, as in Job: “And they lie in ambush in the caves” [Note: [Col. 1051] 1 Job XXXIX, 2]; for spiritual prelates foresee in the inner recesses of their hearts how they may gain souls.

Appearance is Christ’s divinity, as in Isaiah: “He had no appearance or beauty” [Note: [Col. 1051] 2 Isa. LIII, 2]; for in his passion Christ did not display the beauty of his divinity. Appearance is holiness in Christ, as in the Song: “His appearance is like Lebanon” [Note: [Col. 1051] 3 Song V, 13]; for the radiance of ineffable holiness is in Christ. Appearance is our neighbor, as in Job: “And when you visit your appearance, you shall not sin” [Note: [Col. 1051] 4 Job V, 24]; that is, you will not sin if you do *not show compassion to and assist your neighbor.

[Col. 1051B] The servant is Christ, as in Isaiah: “Behold my servant; I will receive him” [Note: [Col. 1051] 5 Isa. XLII, 1]; that is, in Christ it pleases me that he serves me with filial love. The servant is an angel, as in the Apocalypse: “I am your fellow servant and one of your brothers” [Note: [Col. 1051] 6 Apoc. XXII, 9]; that is, I serve the same Lord whom you serve together with the other Christians. The servant is the Jewish people, as in Job: “I called my servant, and he did not answer me” [Note: [Col. 1051] 7 Job XIX, 16]; that is, I invited the Jewish people to faith by preaching, but it did not receive me as I preached. The servant is anyone placed in temptation, as in Job: “As the *stag desires the shade” [Note: [Col. 1051] 8 Job VII, 2]; that is, as one who is being tempted awaits the refreshment of consolation. The servant is our body, as in the Gospel: “And to my servant, ‘Do this’” [Note: [Col. 1051] 9 Matt. VIII, 9]; that is, I do not permit my body to resist me. The servant is the devil, as in Job: “And you shall receive him as an everlasting servant” [Note: [Col. 1051] 10 Job XL, 23]; for, *although the devil always serves the judgments of God, who disposes all things.

The serpent is Christ, as in the Book of Numbers: “Make for yourself a bronze serpent” [Note: [Col. 1051] 11 Num. XXI, 8]; for Christ came in the likeness of sinful flesh, but he did not possess the poison of sin. The serpent is unbelief, as in the Gospel: “Will he give him a serpent instead of a fish?” [Note: [Col. 1051] 12 Luke XI, 11]; that is, if we ask the Lord, he will not give us unbelief instead of faith. The serpent is the devil, as in Isaiah: “Dust shall be the serpent’s bread” [Note: [Col. 1051] 13 Isa. LXV, 25]; for those who love earthly things against the Lord themselves feed the devil. Through the serpent are signified slanders, as in the Psalms: “They have sharpened their tongues like serpents” [Note: [Col. 1051] 14 Ps. CXXXIX, 4]; for the words uttered by slanderers are poisonous. Through serpents are signified sins, as in the Book of Numbers: “The Lord sent fiery serpents among them” [Note: [Col. 1051] 15 Num. XXI, 6]; for the Lord permits sins to rule over the proud and murmurers. Through serpents are signified demons, as in the song of Deuteronomy: “With the fury of those who drag along upon the earth and of serpents” [Note: [Col. 1051] 16 Deut. XXIII, 24]; that is, I will permit wicked people and the demons themselves to afflict them.

The saw is the devil, as in Isaiah: “Shall the saw exalt itself against him by whom it is drawn?” [Note: [Col. 1051] 17 Isa. X, 15]; that is, shall the devil rise up against Christ, through whom he is cast out of human hearts?

The stellion is any wicked person, as it is forbidden in Leviticus: “The stellion shall not be eaten” [Note: [Col. 1051] 18 Lev. XI, 30], lest one *imitate a wicked person.

The star is Christ, as in the Apocalypse: “And I will give him the morning star” [Note: [Col. 1051] 19 Apoc. II, 28]; for whoever overcomes the devil will have Christ, who exists from eternity with the Father and the Holy Spirit, in a *moment. The star is the Virgin Mary, as in *Leviticus: “A star shall arise from Jacob” [Note: [Col. 1051] 20 Num. XXIV, 17]; for the Virgin Mary was born from the stock of Jacob. The star is faith, as in the Gospel [Note: [Col. 1051] 21 Matt. II, 2, 9, 10]: the star led the Magi to Christ; thus through faith we attain to hope. Through the star are signified the gifts of the Holy Spirit, as in Job: “Can you join together the shining stars of the Pleiades?” [Note: [Col. 1051] 22 Job XXVIII, 31]; for in Christ alone the fullness of the seven spiritual gifts comes together. Through the stars are signified the apostles, as in the Apocalypse: “And upon his head a crown of twelve stars” [Note: [Col. 1051] 23 Apoc. II, 1]; for the doctrine of the twelve apostles shines in the faith of the Church. Through the stars are signified prelates, as in the Apocalypse: “The seven stars are the angels,” that is, the prelates, “of the seven churches” [Note: [Col. 1051] 24 Apoc. I, 20]. Through the stars are signified the virtues of the saints, as in Job: “And he seals up the stars as though under a seal” [Note: [Col. 1051] 25 Job IX, 7]; for the Lord first strengthens the virtues secretly in his elect, so that afterward they may be displayed publicly as an example. Through the stars are signified holy men, as in Genesis: “I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven” [Note: [Col. 1051] 26 Gen. XXII, 17]; for the faithful, who are Abraham’s spiritual children, shine with heavenly brightness through faith and love. Through the stars are signified hypocrites, as in the Apocalypse: “Its tail dragged a third of the stars” [Note: [Col. 1051] 27 Apoc. XII, 4]; for the Antichrist associates with himself many who appear to shine before human beings. Through the stars are signified the holy angels, as in Daniel: “And those who instruct many in righteousness shall shine like the stars for everlasting eternities” [Note: [Col. 1051] 28 Dan. XXII, 3]; for those who here undertake the office of angels, announcing true knowledge to others in piety, will in the future shine together with them in everlasting beauty.

Barren is our flesh, as in Job: “For he fed the barren woman and her who does not bear” [Note: [Col. 1051] 29 Job XXIV, 21]; that is, he cherished his flesh, which does not desire to produce the fruit of good works.

Dung is humanity, as in the Psalms: “And raising the poor man from the dung” [Note: [Col. 1051] 30 Ps. CXII, 7]; for whoever humbles himself will be exalted. Dung is a worldly thing loved in an disorderly manner against God, as in the Book of Ecclesiasticus: “The lazy man shall be stoned with the dung of oxen” [Note: [Col. 1051] 31 Ecclus. XXII, 2]; for lovers of the world who are lazy in good works are scourged because of their love of worldly things, as though they regarded as dung the good works in which holy men labor diligently like the oxen of the Lord, in order to gain Christ. Dung is the stench of lust, as in Joel: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” [Note: [Col. 1051] 32 Joel I, 17]; for the carnal have ended their earthly existence in the stench of lust. Through dung are signified hidden evils of the heart, as in the Book of Judges: “Immediately the dung of the belly burst forth through the secret passages of nature” [Note: [Col. 1053] 1 Judg. III, 22]; that is, the foul malice of the heart became known in secret. Through dung is signified remembrance of sins, as in the Gospel: “Until I dig around it and put dung on it” [Note: [Col. 1053] 2 Luke XIII, 8]; that is, until by the interposition of humility I make it remember its former happiness. Through dung are signified sins of the flesh, as in Jeremiah: “And those who were nourished in *scarlet embraced dung” [Note: [Col. 1053] 3 Lam. IV, 5]; that is, those who delighted in spiritual goods practice carnal sins.

The dunghill is human weakness, as in Job: “Sitting on a dunghill” [Note: [Col. 1053] 4 Job II, 8]; that is, humbling himself in the recognition of his weakness. The dunghill is the stench of inward things, as in Job: “Like a dunghill he will be destroyed at the end” [Note: [Col. 1053] 5 Job XX, 7]; for every reprobate, full of the stench of vices, will finally be destroyed.

Sneezing is disturbance, as in Job: “His sneezing is the splendor of fire” [Note: [Col. 1053] 6 Job XLI, 9]; for the Antichrist, in whom the devil will be fully aroused, will deceive through miracles and proceed through cruelty.

Whistling is wonder, as in Job: “He will whistle over him, looking upon his place” [Note: [Col. 1053] 7 Job XXVII, 23]; that is, he will be astonished at him when he sees his dwelling. Whistling is divine inspiration, as in Isaiah: “The house of the fly will whistle” [Note: [Col. 1053] 8 Isa. VII, 18]; for he inspires the unclean person so that he may come to him. Through whistling are signified admonitions, as in the Book of Judges [Note: [Col. 1053] 9 Judg. V, 16], so that he *may hear the *sons of the flocks; that is, so that you may receive in your mind the admonitions of fools.

The sycamore is Christ’s cross, as in the Gospel: [Col. 1053C] “He climbed up into a sycamore tree” [Note: [Col. 1053] 10 Luke XIX, 4]; for whoever desires to contemplate God purely should set the crucified Christ before himself for imitation. Through sycamores are signified the unbelieving Jews, as in Isaiah: “They have cut down the sycamores, but we shall replace them with cedars” [Note: [Col. 1053] 11 Isa. IX, 10]; that is, the sins of unbelief destroyed the Jews, but we shall have exalted men from among the Gentiles.

The shekel is Holy Scripture, as in Exodus: “The shekel contains twenty obols” [Note: [Col. 1053] 12 Exod. XXX, 1]; for Holy Scripture, in the perfection of the two Testaments, consists, as it were, in a double denarius. Through the shekel are signified our body and soul, as in Leviticus: “Let him offer a ram that can be bought for two shekels” [Note: [Col. 1053] 13 Lev. V, 15]; for we must give body and soul so that we may acquire Christ.

The seal is the first angel, as in Ezekiel: “You are the seal of the likeness of God” [Note: [Col. 1053] 14 Ezek. XXVIII, 12]; for in him the image of God’s likeness was impressed. The seal is the confirmation of the elect, as in Haggai: “And I will set you like a seal, for I have chosen you” [Note: [Col. 1053] 15 Hag. II, 24]; that is, I will confirm in myself that I have predestined you for the kingdom. The seal is the virtue of chastity, as in the Song: “Set me as a seal upon your heart” [Note: [Col. 1053] 16 Song VIII, 6]; that is, confirm me upon your mind through charity. The seal is the gentile people called to faith, as in Job: “And he shut up the stars as though under a seal” [Note: [Col. 1053] 17 Job IX, 7]; for now he appoints holy preachers among the gentile people, until at the appointed time they proceed to convert the remnant of Israel. The seal is the once-elect people, as in Job: “It will be restored like clay under a seal” [Note: [Col. 1053] 18 Job XXXVIII, 14]; for that people, once chosen through faith, is now rejected and despised because of unbelief.

The forest is this world, as in the Psalms: “The boar from the forest has ravaged it” [Note: [Col. 1053] 19 Ps. LXXIX, 14]; for the Roman emperor, who held power throughout the world, uprooted the Jewish people. The forest is the human mind, as in Deuteronomy: “With a friend simply into the forest” [Note: [Col. 1053] 20 Deut. IX, 5]; that is, if he concerns himself with the building up of his subject. The forest is Holy Scripture, as in the Book of Kings: “Let each one take one piece of timber from each one” [Note: [Col. 1053] 21 IV Kings VI, 2]; for each of us ought, according to our understanding, to extract individual teachings from Holy Scripture.

Pods are secular doctrines, as in the Gospel: “From the pods that the pigs were eating” [Note: [Col. 1053] 22 Luke XV, 16]; that is, they wish to learn secular doctrines, which the unclean loved.

Flint is Christ, as in the Book of Numbers: “Striking the flint twice” [Note: [Col. 1053] 23 Num. XX, 11]; for Christ was subjected to reproaches in his passion. Flint is the hardness of the Gentiles, as in Job: “They shall be carved in flint” [Note: [Col. 1053] 24 Job XIX, 24]; for the words of Christian faith have now been received in the hearts of the Gentiles. Flint is good action, as in Job: “He will give flint instead of earth” [Note: [Col. 1053] 25 Job XXII, 24]; for in place of a soft way of life the Lord grants his elect a steadfast action. Through flints are signified the holy angels, as in Job: “And he dwells among the broken flints” [Note: [Col. 1053] 26 Job XXXIX, 31]; for the holy man perseveres in contemplation of the strength of the angels, who have been shattered in those who fall.

Fine flour is purity of heart, as in the Book of Maccabees: “And we offered sacrifice and fine flour” [Note: [Col. 1053] 27 Macc. I, 8]; outwardly, mortification of the flesh, and inwardly, purity of mind.

Symphony is the preaching of the Gospel, as in the Gospel: “And he heard the symphony and the chorus”; for the Jewish people now hear the Gospel preached in the Church, but scorn to believe.

*Sindon* is subtle preaching, as in Proverbs: “She made and sold a sindon [Note: [Col. 1053] 28 Prov. XXXI, 24],” meaning that the holy Church sends forth subtle preaching and gains some for God. *Sindon*, a pure mind, as in the Gospel: “And he wrapped him in a clean sindon [Note: [Col. 1053] 29 Matt. XXVII, 59],” meaning that Christ dwells in a pure mind. *Sindon*, worldly occupation, as in the Gospel: “Having cast away the sindon, he fled from them naked [Note: [Col. 1053] 30 Mark XIV, 52],” meaning that, having cast off every worldly occupation, we ought to flee, freed from spiritual persecutors.

*Bosom* is the substance of the Godhead, as in the Gospel: “The Only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father [Note: [Col. 1053] 31 John I, 18],” that is, who is with the Father in one and the same substance of the Godhead. *Bosom*, our mind, as in Job: “And in my bosom I hear the words of his mouth [Note: [Col. 1055] 1 Job XXIII, 12],” that is, I have hidden his words in my mind. *Bosom*, that which properly belongs to us, as in the Psalms: “And my prayer shall return into my bosom [Note: [Col. 1055] 2 Ps. 34:13],” that is, what I pray for others shall properly rebound upon myself. *Bosom*, security, as in Job: “This hope of mine is laid up in my bosom [Note: [Col. 1055] 3 Job XIV, 27],” that is, I possess the most certain security in the hope of my resurrection. *Bosom*, the grace of God, as in Exodus concerning Moses: “He put his hand into his bosom and drew it out leprous; he put it in again, and it became like the rest of his flesh [Note: [Col. 1055] 4 Exod. IV, 6–7],” meaning that Christ cast the Jews out from his grace because of the *uncleanness of their unbelief; yet, when again cleansed in faith, they will attain that same grace through faith. *Bosom*, secret rest, as in the Gospel: “And he was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom [Note: [Col. 1055] 5 Luke XVI, 22],” that is, into the secret rest of the *Father.

*Left* is the present life, as in Proverbs: “In her left hand are riches and glory [Note: [Col. 1055] 6 Prov. III, 16],” meaning that in the present life the Lord grants his elect both the riches of merits and glory in a pure conscience. *Left*, the pleasure of human praise, as in the Gospel: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing [Note: [Col. 1055] 7 Matt. VI, 3],” that is, in your good work do not seek the favor of human praise. *Left*, adversity, as in Proverbs: “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left [Note: [Col. 1055] 8 Prov. IV, 27],” that is, let neither prosperity exalt you nor adversity break you. *Left*, an evil deed, as in Job: “If I go to the left, what shall I do? I shall not see him [Note: [Col. 1055] 9 Job XXIII, 9],” that is, if I do an evil deed, I shall not be able to reach God. *Left*, reprobate angels, as in the Books of Kings: “All the army of heaven standing by him on his right and on his left [Note: [Col. 1055] 10 III Kings XXII, 19],” meaning that not only do the good angels serve God, but the evil also minister to his just judgments. *Left*, reprobate human beings, as in the Gospel: “The goats on the left [Note: [Col. 1055] 11 Matt. XXV, 32],” meaning that sinners will somehow be the left-hand part, because they will be condemned.

*Sparks* are the preachers’ words, as in Ezekiel: “And sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze [Note: [Col. 1055] 12 Ezek. I, 7],” that is, words of preaching set aflame.

*Ears of grain* are the pronouncements of Sacred Scripture, as in Job: “They took away the ears of grain from the hungry [Note: [Col. 1055] 13 Job XXIV, 10],” meaning that heretics strive to take sacred pronouncements away from those who eagerly desire the word of life from good preachers. *Ears of grain*, good works, as in the Books of Kings: “Taking ears of grain, they struck him in the groin [Note: [Col. 1055] 14 II Kings IV, 6],” meaning that evil spirits take away the good works possessed by anyone who is negligent, and kill him through the pleasure of the flesh. The ears of grain were years of fertility, such as existed in Joseph’s time, as in Genesis: “The seven ears of grain are seven years of abundance [Note: [Col. 1055] 15 Gen. XLI, 26].”

[Col. 1056A] *Thorn* is a preacher, as in Isaiah: “I shall give in the wilderness a cedar and a thorn [Note: [Col. 1055] 16 Isa. XLI, 19],” that is, I shall place in the Church one who contemplates and one who preaches. *Thorn*, the compunction of sins or vices, as in Job: “And instead of barley, a *thorn [Note: [Col. 1055] 17 Job XXXI, 40],” that is, if I have done this evil, may good activity fail in me and the prick of vices grow in me. *Thorn*, pride of heart, as in the Psalms: “While the thorn is pierced [Note: [Col. 1055] 18 Ps. XXXI, 4],” that is, while pride is humbled in me. By *thorns*, the malice of the heart, as in Isaiah: “Thorns shall spring up in his houses [Note: [Col. 1055] 19 Isa. XXXIV, 13],” that is, malice shall grow in his thoughts. By *thorns*, suspicions of fears, as in Proverbs: “The way of the wicked is like a hedge of thorns [Note: [Col. 1055] 20 Prov. XV, 19],” because suspicions surround the wicked on every side, so that they do not dare to walk along the way of righteousness. By *thorns*, preachers, as in the Song: “As a lily among thorns [Note: [Col. 1055] 21 Song II, 2],” meaning that the holy Church dwells *here in the midst of the wicked. By *thorns*, riches, as in the Gospel: “And when the thorns sprang up together, they choked it [Note: [Col. 1055] 22 Matt. XIII, 7; Mark IV, 7; Luke VIII, 7],” meaning that earthly riches destroy the word of life. By *thorns*, heretics, as in the Gospel: “Do they gather grapes from thorns [Note: [Col. 1055] 23 Matt. VII, 16]?” meaning that the grace of holiness does not proceed from heretics.

*Spirit* is God himself, as in the Gospel: “God is Spirit [Note: [Col. 1055] 24 Luke VI, 44; John IV, 24].” *Spirit*, the soul of a human being, as in the Gospel: “And, bowing his head, he gave up the spirit [Note: [Col. 1055] 25 John XIX, 30],” that is, the soul. *Spirit*, our mind, as in Paul: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind [Note: [Col. 1055] 26 Eph. IV, 23],” that is, exercise spiritual renewal in your mind. *Spirit*, our reason, as in Paul: “I will pray with the spirit [Note: [Col. 1055] 27 I Cor. XIV, 15],” that is, I will pray rationally. *Spirit*, the sinner’s desire, as in Ecclesiastes: “And the spirit of beasts descends downward [Note: [Col. 1055] 28 Eccles. III, 21],” because beasts desire nothing except earthly and lower things. *Spirit*, the devil, as in the Books of Kings: “An evil spirit from the Lord [Note: [Col. 1055] 29 I Kings XVI, 14],” because the devil is both “of the Lord,” insofar as he serves his judgment, and evil, insofar as he always has wickedness in his will. *Spirit*, the wind of the air, as in the Psalms: “And stormy winds, which do his word [Note: [Col. 1055] 30 Ps. CXLVIII, 8],” that is, storm winds, which obey his will. *Spirit*, divine inspiration, as in the Psalms: “*He breathed his spirit, and the waters flowed [Note: [Col. 1055] 31 Ps. CXLVII, 18],” meaning that inward inspiration visits us, and tears of compunction *flow*. *Spirit*, fear of the Lord, as in the Books of Kings: “A great spirit of the Lord, overthrowing mountains and *turning rocks [Note: [Col. 1055] 32 III Kings XIX, 11],” meaning that fear of the Lord casts down every height in us and melts hardness. *Spirit*, human strength, as in the Psalms: “You take away their spirit, and they fail [Note: [Col. 1055] 33 Ps. CIII, 29],” that is, you permit their strength to be weakened, and they do not endure. *Spirit*, human pride, as in Job: “Whose indignation has drunk up my spirit [Note: [Col. 1055] 34 Job VI, 4],” meaning that divine affliction will destroy all arrogance in us. By *spirit*, all spiritual persons, as in the Psalms: “Who makes his angels spirits [Note: [Col. 1057] 1 Ps. CIII, 4],” that is, he makes his preachers spiritual.

*Rush* (*sirpus*) is the life of hypocrites, as in Job: “Can the *rush flourish without moisture [Note: [Col. 1057] 2 Job VIII, 11]?” meaning that a hypocrite cannot have a good work without the grace of God.

*Sirens* are heretics, as in Isaiah: “And *sirens in the temples of *pleasure [Note: [Col. 1057] 3 Isa. XIII, 22],” meaning that heretics [in their] conventicles of truth *[text uncertain]*.

*Thirst* is good desire, as in the Psalms: “In my thirst they gave me drink [with vinegar] [Note: [Col. 1057] 4 Ps. LXVIII, 22],” that is, while I desired their salvation, they gave me the bitterness of the Passion to drink. *Thirst*, desire or covetousness, as in Job: “And thirst *burns against him [Note: [Col. 1057] 5 Job XVIII, 9],” meaning that desire inflames the wicked person more and more.

[Col. 1057B] *Stubble* is human weakness, as in Job: “And you pursue dry stubble [Note: [Col. 1057] 6 Job XIII, 15],” that is, you attack my fragile weakness with temptations. *Stubble*, an unstable mind, as in the Psalms: “And he comes like stubble before the wind [Note: [Col. 1057] 7 Ps. LXXXIII, 14],” because the wind of temptation drives an unstable mind here and there. *Stubble*, the reprobate, as in the Song of Exodus: “Which devoured them like stubble [Note: [Col. 1057] 8 Exod. XV, 7],” meaning that the *judgment of God condemns the reprobate as dry and light.

*Lizard* (*stellio*; the source reads *stillio*) is any simple person, as in Proverbs: “The lizard supports itself on its hands [Note: [Col. 1057] 9 Prov. XX, 28],” meaning that every simple person is *overcome by good works [text uncertain].

*Stylus* is the firm sentence of God, as in Job: “That they may be engraved in a book with an iron stylus [Note: [Col. 1057] 10 Prov. XIX, 24],” meaning that the words of God are bound in the hearts of the elect by his firm judgment.

*A drop* is human weakness, as in Isaiah: “Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket [Note: [Col. 1057] 11 Isa. XL, 15],” meaning that human beings continually flow downward in the skin [or: shell] of their weakness. By a *drop*, preachers, as in Job: “Who begot the drops of dew [Note: [Col. 1057] 12 Job XXXVIII, 28]?” meaning that through his grace the Lord produces *preachings* of truth.

*Drippings* are the faithful, as in the Psalms: “In his drippings she shall rejoice, the one who sprouts [Note: [Col. 1057] 13 Ps. IV, 11],” meaning that the holy Church rejoices in the increase of her faithful.

*Mother-in-law* is the Synagogue, as in the Gospel: “A mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law [Note: [Col. 1057] 14 Luke XII, 53],” meaning that the Synagogue dissents from the Church, and the Church from the Synagogue.

*Sun* is God, as in the Book of Wisdom: “The sun of righteousness has not risen for us [Note: [Col. 1057] 15 Wis. V, 6],” that is, the Lord has not shone upon us either through knowledge of the truth or through love of virtue. *Sun*, Christ’s resurrection, as in the Psalms: “The sun has risen, and they have gathered together [Note: [Col. 1057] 16 Ps. CIII, 22],” that is, when Christ’s resurrection appeared, the disciples who had been scattered were brought together. *Sun*, the holy Church, as in the Song: “Fair as the sun [Note: [Col. 1057] 17 Song VI, 9],” because the Lord chose for the Church a beautiful brightness and a bright beauty. *Sun*, the Virgin Mary, as in the Psalms: “He set his tabernacle in the sun [Note: [Col. 1057] 18 Ps. XVIII, 5],” because his body, in which the Godhead dwelt, was conceived in the Virgin. *Sun*, preaching, as in the Apocalypse: “The sun became black like sackcloth [Note: [Col. 1057] 19 Rev. VI, 12],” because holy preaching is also regarded as contemptible by certain people. *Sun*, any preacher, as in Job: “Who commands the sun, and it does not rise [Note: [Col. 1057] 20 Job IX, 7],” because by God’s just judgment every preacher departed from Judea. *Sun*, baptism, as in the Apocalypse: “A woman clothed with the sun [Note: [Col. 1057] 21 Rev. XII, 1],” namely, the holy Church cleansed by the inundation of baptism. *Sun*, the priestly order, as in the Psalms: “The sun for the authority of the day [Note: [Col. 1057] 22 Ps. CXXXV, 8],” because the Lord imposed the priestly charge upon the clergy. *Sun*, any wise person, as in Ecclesiasticus: “*The wise person endures like the sun [Note: [Col. 1057] 23 Sir. XXVII, 12],” that is, he perseveres in the brightness of his wisdom. *Sun*, charity, as in the Song: “Because the sun has *darkened me [Note: [Col. 1057] 24 Song I, 6],” that is, because I am afflicted, this is my charity. *Sun*, joy, as in the Psalms: “By day the sun shall not burn you [Note: [Col. 1057] 25 Ps. CXX, 6],” that is, in the time of prosperity, joy shall not exalt you. *Sun*, the exalted in the Church, as in the Apocalypse: “The angel poured out his bowl upon the sun [Note: [Col. 1057] 26 Rev. XVI, 8],” that is, affliction struck those exalted ones of the Church. *Sun*, contemplation, as in Job: “If I saw the sun when it shone [Note: [Col. 1057] 27 Job XXXI, 26],” that is, because of the brightness of contemplation, as in the Apocalypse: “The angel standing in *heaven [Note: [Col. 1057] 28 Rev. XIX, 17],” that is, those exalted ones of the Church, “and he cried out to all the birds,” that is, behold the teacher living in holy conduct and preaching to all holy men. *Sun*, the fervor of righteousness, as in Genesis: “When the sun had set, darkness came to be [Note: [Col. 1057] 29 Gen. XV, 17],” meaning that when the fervor of righteousness fails in the mind, the mind itself is immediately darkened. *Sun*, the heat of temptation, as in Leviticus: “When he has washed his flesh with water and the sun has set, then he shall eat of the sanctified things [Note: [Col. 1057] 30 Lev. XXII, 7],” that is, when he has cleansed his unlawful acts through compunction and the heat of temptation has subsided, then he will be able to approach the divine sacraments. *Sun*, tribulation, as in the Gospel: “But when the sun had risen, they were *scorched [Note: [Col. 1057] 31 Matt. XIII, 6],” that is, when the heat of tribulation grew fierce, they suffered. *Sun*, the acuities of the wise, as in Job: “Under him are the rays of the sun [Note: [Col. 1057] 32 Job XLI, 21],” meaning that the devil sometimes makes those who seem to be wise serve him. *Sun*, the present time, as in the Psalms: “His name endures before the sun [Note: [Col. 1057] 33 Ps. LXXI, 17],” because he existed unchangeably before all times. *Sun*, the brightness of the heavenly homeland, as in Genesis: “The sun rose upon him after he had crossed Phanuel [Note: [Col. 1057] 34 Gen. XXXII, 31],” meaning that after we cease to see God through faith, we shall see him face to face in the heavenly homeland; for *Phanuel* is interpreted as “the face of God” and signifies faith.

*Throne* is the glory of the heavenly kingdom, as in Job: “He holds the face of his throne [Note: [Col. 1057] 35 Job XXVI, 9],” that is, he still conceals from us the sight of his glory. *Throne*, the holy angels, as in Job: “And I shall come even to his throne [Note: [Col. 1057] 36 Job XXIII, 3],” that is, through contemplation I shall reach even to the angels, in whom he himself reigns. *Throne*, both the angelic and human nature, as in Isaiah: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and exalted [Note: [Col. 1059] 1 Isa. VI, 1],” meaning that the Lord presides intellectually both over the angel remaining in his original exaltation and over the human being raised up through Christ’s redemption after his fall. *Throne*, the holy exaltation of the mind, as in Job: “And he sets kings upon the throne [Note: [Col. 1059] 2 Job XXXVI, 7],” meaning that the Lord leads his elect, who *intelligently resist their unlawful impulses, to great heights of holiness in the mind. *Throne*, the seat of counsel, as in Isaiah: “There is no *throne of the daughter of the Chaldeans [Note: [Col. 1059] 3 Isa. XLVII, 1],” meaning that the reprobate have no sound counsel. *Throne*, worldly elevation, as in Jonah: “The king rose from the throne of his kingdom [Note: [Col. 1059] 4 Jonah III, 6],” meaning that the highest rulers, having recognized the truth, humbled themselves through repentance and faith before the preaching of Christ.

*Wilderness* is paganism, as in Isaiah: “I shall give in the wilderness a cedar and a thorn [Note: [Col. 1059] 5 Isa. XLI, 1],” that is, I shall place contemplatives and preachers among the pagans. *Wilderness*, rest of mind, as in the Psalms: “And I remained in the wilderness [Note: [Col. 1059] 6 Ps. LIV, 8],” that is, I persevered in the inward rest of the mind.

*Sleep* is the death of the flesh, as in the Psalms: “When he gives sleep to his beloved [Note: [Col. 1059] 7 Ps. CXXVI, 2],” that is, when he leads his elect to death. *Sleep*, rest of mind, as in Job: “And I would rest in my sleep [Note: [Col. 1059] 8 Job III, 13],” that is, I would rest in the tranquility of my heart. *Sleep*, the torpor of negligence, as in Proverbs: “When will you rise from sleep [Note: [Col. 1059] 9 Prov. VI, 9]?” that is, when will you shake yourself free from the torpor of negligence? *Sleep*, any hypocrite, as in Job: “Like a fleeting *sleep, he shall not be found [Note: [Col. 1059] 10 Job XX, 8],” because in the future the hypocrite will vanish before the sight of the Judge.

*Sound* is the Holy Spirit, as in Job: “And a sound proceeding from his mouth [Note: [Col. 1059] 11 Job XXXVII, 2],” because the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. *Sound*, faith, as in Ezekiel: “And they walked, and it was like the sound of a multitude [Note: [Col. 1059] 12 Ezek. I, 24],” because, as the apostles went forth preaching, many confessed the true faith with complete freedom. *Sound*, the groaning of repentance, as in Job: “After him a roaring sound will resound [Note: [Col. 1059] 13 Job XXXVII, 4],” that is, the groaning of penitents will echo.

*Spoils* are divine utterances, as in Genesis: “And in the evening he shall divide the spoils [Note: [Col. 1059] 14 Gen. XLIX, 17],” that is, at the end he will preach divine words. *Spoils*, holy men, as in the Psalms: “And they divide the spoils of the beautiful house [Note: [Col. 1059] 15 Ps. LXVII, 13],” because the holy men of the holy Church receive different forms of holiness as their portion. *Spoils*, sinners, as in the Gospel: “And he shall distribute his spoils [Note: [Col. 1059] 16 Luke XI, 22],” because the Lord has released many through the gifts of his graces—those whom the devil had acquired through the gain of sin.

*Baskets* are the hearts of teachers, as in the Gospel: “Seven baskets from the fragments [Note: [Col. 1059] 17 Matt. XV, 37],” because preachers are filled with the delights of Sacred Scripture through the sevenfold Spirit.

*Stole* is Christ’s flesh, as in Isaiah: “This one is beautiful in his stole [Note: [Col. 1059] 18 Isa. LXIII, 1],” because he had no stain of sin in his humanity. *Stole*, the holy Church, as in Genesis: “He shall wash his stole in wine [Note: [Col. 1059] 19 Gen. XLIX, 11],” that is, through the sacrament of his Passion he will cleanse his Church. *Stole*, the virtue of innocence, as in the Gospel: “Bring out the stole quickly for him and put it on him [Note: [Col. 1059] 20 Luke XV, 22],” that is, crown him with the virtue of innocence that he previously possessed. *Stole*, new joy, as in the Gospel: “Sitting at the right hand, covered with a white stole, and they were astonished [Note: [Col. 1059] 21 Mark XVI],” *and he announced the eternal life and new joy of our Savior. By *stole*, heavenly glory, as in the Apocalypse: “And individual white stoles were given to them [Note: [Col. 1059] 22 Rev. VI, 11],” because the saints, stripped of their bodies, have already received individual stoles in the joy of their souls. By *stoles*, good works, as in Genesis: “He also ordered two stoles to be brought out for each one [Note: [Col. 1059] 23 Gen. XLV, 22],” because the true Joseph, the Lord Jesus, commanded his elect to be holy both in body and in spirit. By *stoles*, thoughts, as in the Apocalypse: “Blessed are those who wash their stoles [Note: [Col. 1059] 24 Rev. XXII, 14],” that is, those who cleanse their thoughts. By *stoles*, the adornment of the external senses, as in Genesis: “Three hundred silver pieces with five excellent stoles [Note: [Col. 1059] 25 Gen. XLV, 22],” because the Lord granted Paul perfection of faith in the Holy Trinity and of holy preaching, together with purity of the external senses.

[Col. 1060C] *Scorpion* is despair, as in the Gospel: “Will he offer him a scorpion [Note: [Col. 1059] 26 Luke XI, 12]?” meaning that if we ask God *himself, he will not give you despair. By *scorpions*, teachers, as in Ezekiel: “And you dwell with scorpions [Note: [Col. 1059] 27 Ezek. II, 6],” that is, with those who slander from behind, since the scorpion is feared in its rear. By *scorpions*, demons, as in the Gospel: “Over serpents and scorpions [Note: [Col. 1059] 28 Luke X, 19],” that is, over wicked human beings and evil spirits.

*Sister* is the primitive Church, as in the Song: “Our sister is little, and she has no breasts [Note: [Col. 1059] 29 Song VIII, 8],” because the primitive Church possessed little strength at the beginning and had not yet been strengthened by doubled charity. *Sister*, the rottenness of the flesh, as in Job: “My mother and my sister to the worms [Note: [Col. 1059] 30 Job XVII, 14],” because we come from corruption and walk together with corruption.

*Awl* is the subtlety of the word, as in Exodus: “He shall pierce it with an awl [Note: [Col. 1059] 31 Exod. XXI, 6],” that is, he shall transfix the mind with the subtlety of the divine word.

*Shield* is protection, as in the Psalms: “With the shield of your good will you have crowned us [Note: [Col. 1059] 32 Ps. V, 13].” *Shield*, judgment, as in Jeremiah: “Give them, Lord, the sorrow of heart, your shield [Note: [Col. 1059] 33 Lam. III, 65],” that is, according to your just judgment, cause them to have *sorrow. *Shield*, the reprobate, as in Job: “His body is like cast shields [Note: [Col. 1061] 1 Job XLI, 6],” because the reprobate, who are the devil’s body, are *… fragile* [text defective]. By *shields*, excuses, as in the Psalms: “And he will burn the shields with fire [Note: [Col. 1061] 2 Ps. XLV, 10],” that is, through love of God he will destroy excuses for sin.

*Carving* is the example of the saints, as in the Books of Kings: “And carving ran around it above the bronze rim [Note: [Col. 1061] 3 III Kings VII, 24],” because the examples of the saints adorn the baptized together with their confession of faith.

*Palisades* are the counsels of the saints, as in Job: “And with palisades he shall pierce his nostrils [Note: [Col. 1061] 4 Job XL, 19],” because through the sharp counsels of his saints the Lord destroys the devil’s cunning. *Palisades*, the wicked, as in the Book of Joshua: “Let them be palisades in your eyes [Note: [Col. 1061] 5 Josh. XXIII, 13],” because the reprobate take away the brightness of true light from the saints if they imitate them.

*Sulfur* is the stench of vices, as in Job: “Let sulfur be sprinkled upon his tabernacles [Note: [Col. 1061] 6 Job XVIII, 15],” because in the mind of every wicked person the stench of lust dominates. *Burning sulfur*, the stench of punishment, as in the Psalms: “He will rain snares, fire, and sulfur upon them [Note: [Col. 1061] 7 Ps. X, 6],” and so forth; that is, he will inflict punishments on the *wicked, so that both heat will *burn them and stench will afflict them.

*Furrows* are holy men, as in Job: “And when its furrows *weep [Note: [Col. 1061] 8 Job XXXI, 38],” that is, just as the holy men of the *Church weep [text uncertain].

*Shunammite* is the Synagogue, as in the Song: “Return, return, O Shunammite [Note: [Col. 1061] 9 Song VI, 12],” that is, return to faith, return to good works, captive Synagogue—for *Shunam* is interpreted as “captive.”

[Col. 1061C] *Shoulder-piece* is the strength of a good work, as in Exodus: “You shall make a shoulder-piece of gold [Note: [Col. 1061] 10 Exod. XXVIII, 6],” because the fruit of true wisdom is the strength of a good work.

*Proud one* is the devil, as in Job: “And his wisdom struck down the proud one [Note: [Col. 1061] 11 Job XXVI, 12],” because the wisdom of the Father, Christ, cast down the devil.

*Pride* is swelling of the mind, as in Job: “He is king over all the sons of pride [Note: [Col. 1061] 12 Job XLI, 25],” because the devil rules over those who swell up in mind against God or their neighbor. *Pride*, authority, as in Isaiah: “And I shall set you in the pride of *lords [Note: [Col. 1061] 13 Isa. LX, 15],” because the Lord raised his Church up to the establishment of great authority.

[Col. 1061D] *Pig* is an unclean sinner, as in Peter: “And the washed pig returns to wallowing in the mud [Note: [Col. 1061] 14 II Pet. II, 22],” that is, a sinner wrapped up in the uncleanness of sin.

*Ostrich* is any negligent preacher, as in Job: “The ostrich’s feather is like the feathers of the heron and *the hawk [Note: [Col. 1061] 15 Job XXXIX, 16],” because the external activity of a negligent preacher sometimes seems similar to the works of the saints. By *ostrich*, dissemblers, as in Job: “I was a brother to dragons and a companion of *ostriches [Note: [Col. 1061] 16 Job XXX, 29],” that is, I was a dweller with the faithful and with dissemblers.

## T

Tabernacle. Lathe. Incense. Bulls. Turtledove. Dyes. Tent. Trowel. Potsherd. Talent. Throne. Tympanum. Cloth. Censer. Wheat. Treasure. Topaz. Beams. Bridal chamber. Tunic. Bells. Topaz. Temptation. Trunk. Breastplate. Tablets. Winepress. Tiara. Roof. Tower. Thistle. Earth. Incense. Tiger. Consumption. Trumpets. Moth. Temple. Torrent. Thunder.

*Tabernacle* is the heavenly homeland, as in the Psalms: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle [Note: [Col. 1061] 17 Ps. XIV, 1]?” that is, who will be worthy to be placed in the heavenly kingdom? *Tabernacle*, Christ’s humanity, as in the Psalms: “He set his tabernacle in the sun [Note: [Col. 1061] 18 Ps. XVIII, 6],” that is, he placed his humanity in the Virgin. *Tabernacle*, the Virgin Mary, as in the Psalms: “The Most High sanctified his tabernacle [Note: [Col. 1061] 19 Ps. XLV, 5],” that is, Christ purified his mother through the Holy Spirit. *Tabernacle*, the holy Church, as in the Apocalypse: “Behold, the tabernacle of God with human beings [Note: [Col. 1061] 20 Rev. XXI, 3],” because the holy Church dwells in the midst of the carnal. *Tabernacle*, our body, as in Peter’s Epistle: “But I consider it right, as long as I am in this tabernacle, to *stir you up [Note: [Col. 1061] 21 II Pet. I, 13],” that is, as long as I live in this body, to teach you. *Tabernacle*, our mind, as in Job: “God will be secretly in my tabernacle [Note: [Col. 1061] 22 Job XXIX, 4].” *Tabernacle*, one’s manner of life itself, as in Job: “And you shall put iniquity far from your tabernacle [Note: [Col. 1061] 23 Job XXII, 23],” that is, from your manner of life. *Tabernacle*, the flesh of the wicked, as in Job: “He shall be afflicted, abandoned in his tabernacle [Note: [Col. 1061] 24 Job XX, 26],” that is, the rejected person will be punished in his flesh. *Tabernacle*, earthly happiness, as in Job: “And the tabernacle of the wicked shall not endure [Note: [Col. 1061] 25 Job VIII, 22],” that is, the earthly happiness on which the wicked rely with such great eagerness will fail. *Tabernacle*, the holy angels, as in the Psalms: “How beloved are your tabernacles, Lord [Note: [Col. 1061] 26 Ps. LXXXIII, 2]!” that is, with what great love *…* the angels in whom you dwell belong to you, O Lord! By *tabernacles*, the saints of old, as in the Book of Numbers: “How beautiful are your tabernacles, Jacob [Note: [Col. 1061] 27 Num. XXIV, 5]!” because the saints of old shone with great spiritual beauty. By *tabernacles*, the Gentiles, as in Job: “And their tabernacles are in a land of salt [Note: [Col. 1061] 28 Job XXXIX, 9],” because Christ God the Father gave the Gentiles a heart in which he might dwell through faith. By *tabernacles*, the crimes of any reprobate, as in the Psalms: “And let there be no one dwelling in his tabernacles [Note: [Col. 1061] 29 Ps. LXVIII, 26],” because the elect scorn to imitate the crimes of the reprobate.

*Tablets* are the apostles, as in Exodus: “And he made the standing tablets of the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 1063] 1 Exod. XXVI, 15],” because Christ made the apostles exalted in the Church through uprightness of faith and works. *Tablets*, knowledge and power, as in Exodus, where the Lord gave Moses “two tablets [Note: [Col. 1063] 2 Exod. XXIV, 12],” because these two things are especially necessary to every prelate: namely, knowledge for understanding and power for acting. *Tablets*, breadth of heart, as in the Song: “Let us panel it with cedar tablets [Note: [Col. 1063] 3 Song VIII, 9],” because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit adorn the holy soul inwardly with exalted breadth. *Tablets*, breadth of work, as in the Book of Kings: “And he covered the floor with fir tablets [Note: [Col. 1063] 4 III Kings VI, 15],” because God adorns the humble man outwardly with the breadth of good works.

*Talent* is understanding, as in the Gospel: “He hid the talent in the earth [Note: [Col. 1063] 5 Matt. XXV, 18, 25],” because every negligent person spends on earthly affairs the understanding he received for the salvation of others. *Talent*, the weight of sin, as in Zechariah: “And behold, a talent of lead was carried [Note: [Col. 1063] 6 Zech. V, 7],” that is, the weight of sin was being exercised. *Talent*, a good weight, as in Exodus: “The lampstand, with all its vessels, had a talent of pure gold [Note: [Col. 1063] 7 Exod. XXV, 39],” because Christ and his elect possess the greatness of true knowledge. By *talent*, the bodily senses, as in the Gospel: “Lord, you delivered five talents to me [Note: [Col. 1063] 8 Matt. XXV, 20],” namely, the gift of the five senses; that is, you delivered to me knowledge of external things. By *talents*, understanding and action, as in the Gospel: “Two talents [Note: [Col. 1063] 9 ibid., v. 27],” that is, you delivered understanding and action to me.
