*Beam* is hatred, as in the Gospel: “Cast out the beam from your eye [Note: [Col. 1063] 10 Matt. VII, 5],” that is, cast hatred from your heart. By *beams*, the apostles, as in the Books of Kings: “And he placed beams throughout the house [Note: [Col. 1063] 11 Luke VI, 42],” that is, he placed the apostles in the Church: “And their sound went out into all the earth.”

*Bridal chamber* is Mary’s womb, as in the Psalms: “Like a bridegroom proceeding from his bridal chamber,” that is, the pure one coming forth from the virginal womb. *Bridal chamber*, a devoted mind, as in Deuteronomy: “He shall remain all day as in a bridal chamber [Note: [Col. 1063] 12 Deut. XXXV, 12],” because the holy man dwells in contemplation within his mind. By *bridal chambers*, holy men, as in Ezekiel: “And between the bridal chambers, five cubits [Note: [Col. 1063] 13 Ezek. XL, 8],” because holy men burn inwardly with love of God and outwardly exercise the ministry of the five senses.

[Col. 1063D] *Bulls* are the Jews, as in the Psalms: “Fat bulls surrounded me [Note: [Col. 1063] 14 Ps. XXI, 13],” that is, proud and fierce Jews afflicted me. *Bulls*, the fathers of the Old Testament, as in the Gospel: “My bulls and my fattened animals have been killed [Note: [Col. 1063] 15 Matt. XXII, 4],” that is, the fathers of old have already offered good examples, through which they were granted the ability to love their enemies. *Bull*, the neck of pride, as in Job: “Take for yourselves seven bulls [Note: [Col. 1063] 16 Job XLII, 10],” that is, wholly slaughter within yourselves the leader of pride. *Bulls*, heretics, as in the Psalms: “The assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples [Note: [Col. 1063] 17 Ps. LXVII, 31],” that is, the conventicles of heretics among the fecundities of human beings.

*Roof* is a *roof*, [the term is repeated in the source], as in the Psalms: “Like a solitary sparrow on the roof [Note: [Col. 1063] 18 Ps. CI, 8],” because Christ alone, with his body—which is the Church—will reign in heaven, the reprobate having been excluded. *Roof*, the subtlety of Sacred Scripture, as in the Gospel: “They uncovered the roof where Jesus was [Note: [Col. 1063] 19 Mark II, 4],” that is, they expounded Sacred Scripture, in which our true salvation lies. *Roof*, our flesh, as in the Gospel: “And let the one who is on the roof not come down [Note: [Col. 1063] 20 Matt. XXIV, 17],” that is, let the one who exercises dominion in the flesh not prostrate himself beneath the flesh.

*Cloth* is the brevity of this life, as in Job: “*Like a cloth cut off by a weaver [Note: [Col. 1063] 21 Job VII, 6],” because the more of our life that has passed, the less remains for the future. By *cloth*, the condition of the wicked, as in Isaiah: “And they *weave spiders’ webs [Note: [Col. 1063] 22 Isa. LIX, 5],” because the reprobate labor in every way to seize the gain of the present life, like a spider, which stretches out its entrails for the purpose of catching worthless prey, namely, a fly.

*Temple* is the heavenly homeland, as in the Psalms: “*They shall be filled with the good things of your house; your temple is *holy [Note: [Col. 1063] 23 Ps. LXV, 6],” that is, the heaven where your dwelling is shall be filled with joys, and it shines with complete holiness. *Temple*, Christ’s body, as in the Gospel: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up [Note: [Col. 1063] 24 John II, 19],” that is, kill my body, and on the third day I shall raise it up. *Temple*, the Virgin Mary, as in the Psalms: “And in his temple all shall speak glory [Note: [Col. 1063] 25 Ps. XXVIII, 9],” because in the Church the elect confess the true faith. *Temple*, our body, as in Paul: “Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1063] 26 I Cor. VI, 19]?” because the Holy Spirit dwells in pure hearts. *Temple*, a devoted mind, as in Paul: “If anyone violates the temple of God [Note: [Col. 1063] 27 I Cor. III, 17],” that is, if anyone violates his mind, in which God ought to dwell. *Temple*, the capacity of angelic and human understanding, as in Isaiah: “And the things beneath him filled the temple [Note: [Col. 1063] 28 Isa. VI, 1],” because angelic and human understanding marvels even at the wonders of God’s creatures. *Temple*, holy men, as in Paul: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are [Note: [Col. 1063] 29 I Cor. III, 17].”

Temptation is either human—that is, thinking otherwise than the matter stands in what is good, and then only in the mind—or diabolical—that is, defending too stubbornly one’s own opinion, which one knows to be perverse—or for good, since God tests us in order to know, that is, to make known, that you love him—or a temptation of seduction, since God tempts no one. Of the first it is said, as in Paul: “Let no temptation overtake you except what is human” [Note: [Col. 1063] 30 1 Corinthians 10:13]. Of the second, likewise in Paul: “Nor let us tempt Christ, as they tempted him.” Of the third, in Genesis: “God tested Abraham” [Note: [Col. 1065] 1 Genesis 22:1]. Of the fourth, the Lord says in the Lord’s Prayer: “Do not lead us into temptation” [Note: [Col. 1065] 2 Matthew 6:13; Luke 11:4], that is, do not allow us to be led into diabolical deception.

A tent is the holiness of the primitive Church, as in Exodus: “He also made a tent at the entrance of the tabernacle” [Note: [Col. 1065] 3 Exodus 26:36], because the primitive Church was adorned with great beauty of holiness. A tent is any holy person, as in Job: “If he wishes to spread his tent like a cloud” [Note: [Col. 1065] 4 Job 36:29], that is, to enlarge a holy man in holiness after the likeness of the holy Fathers. A tent is the Synagogue, as in the prophet: “There is no one any longer who will stretch out my tent” [Note: [Col. 1065] 5 Jeremiah 10:20], because now no preacher proclaims the true faith to the Jewish people. By the tent of the righteous, as in the book of Numbers: “How beautiful are your tents, O Israel” [Note: [Col. 1065] 6 Numbers 24:5], is meant: “How very splendid are the assemblies of the Lord’s saints, intent through faith on beholding.” By the tent are meant all the wicked, as in the song of Habakkuk: “I saw the tents of Ethiopia” [Note: [Col. 1065] 7 Habakkuk 3:7], that is, I contemplated wicked people covered by the blackness of sin.

Earth is Christ, as in Job: “The earth has been given into the hand of the wicked” [Note: [Col. 1065] 8 Job 9:24], because Christ, at the time of his Passion, was handed over to the servants of the devil. Earth is the kingdom of heaven, as in Isaiah: “In their land they shall possess double” [Note: [Col. 1065] 9 Isaiah 61:7], because in the heavenly kingdom the elect will rejoice both in blessedness and in the body. Earth is the Virgin Mary, as in the Psalms: “And our earth shall give its fruit” [Note: [Col. 1065] 10 Psalm 66:7], that is, Mary bore her Son. Earth is the Church, as in Job: “When I laid the foundations of the earth” [Note: [Col. 1065] 11 Job 38:4], that is, when I established the apostles of the Church. Earth is the Israelite people, as in Job: “Who shakes the earth from its place” [Note: [Col. 1065] 12 Job 9:6], because the Lord allowed the Jewish people to be driven from the land. Earth is the company of the scribes and priests of the Synagogue, as in Job: “The earth, from which bread arose in its place, was overturned by fire” [Note: [Col. 1065] 13 Job 28:5], that is, the priests and scribes, from whom the nourishment of holy preaching ought to have proceeded, were turned by envy against Christ. Earth is the Gentile world, as in Job: “That they might rain upon the earth where no man is, in the wilderness” [Note: [Col. 1065] 14 Job 38:26], that is, that he might preach among the Gentile people, who, abandoned by God, were instructed by no preacher. Earth is any holy person, as in Job: “The earth is longer than its measure for you” [Note: [Col. 1065] 15 Job 11:9], because the greatness of God exceeds the contemplation of a holy man. Earth is any subject, as in Job: “The hoof digs the earth” [Note: [Col. 1065] 16 Job 39:24], because a superior, strong in example, covers and softens his subordinate. Earth is our body, as in Genesis: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” [Note: [Col. 1065] 17 Genesis 3:19], because our body was taken from the earth and will return to the earth. Earth is a holy mind, as in Genesis: “And let the earth bring forth green grass” [Note: [Col. 1065] 18 Genesis 1:11], that is, let a devout mind openly display an action that corresponds to it. Earth is a perverse mind, as in Job: “It is not found in the land of those who live in pleasure” [Note: [Col. 1065] 19 Job 28:13], because wisdom does not dwell in a mind subject to carnal desires. Earth is those who think earthly thoughts, as in Job: “Speak to the earth, and it will answer you” [Note: [Col. 1065] 20 Job 12:8], because even those who think earthly thoughts bring us some instruction through our contemplation of them. Earth is a weak action, as in Job: “For earth he will give flint” [Note: [Col. 1065] 21 Job 22:24], that is, in place of a weak action he will bestow a strong one. Earth is any person, as in Paul: “For earth, receiving the rain that comes upon it” [Note: [Col. 1065] 22 Hebrews 6:7], that is, a hearer embracing the preaching that instructs him. Earth is the household, as in Job: “If my land cries out against me” [Note: [Col. 1065] 23 Job 31:38], that is, if my household complains about me. Earth is the lesser members in the Church, as in the Song: “Let the earth hear the words of my mouth” [Note: [Col. 1065] 24 Deuteronomy 32:1], that is, let the lesser members listen to my preaching. Earth is the Antichrist, as in Isaiah: “Woe to the land of the whirring wings” [Note: [Col. 1065] 25 Isaiah 18:1], that is, cursed is the Antichrist, who will sound the flight of pride. Earth is hell, as in Job: “To a land of darkness and covered with the gloom of death” [Note: [Col. 1065] 26 Job 10:21], that is, to hell, full of darkness and enveloped in deadly obscurity.

Treasure is the heavenly reward, as in Job: “As though they were digging for treasure” [Note: [Col. 1065] 27 Job 3:21], that is, as though they were seeking the heavenly reward. Treasure is good desire, as in the Gospel: “A treasure hidden in a field” [Note: [Col. 1065] 28 Matthew 13:44], that is, a good desire hidden in the mind. Treasure is holy speech, as in Proverbs: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” [Note: [Col. 1065] 29 Proverbs 21:20]. Treasure is good intention, as in the Gospel: “From the good treasure he brings forth good” [Note: [Col. 1065] 30 Matthew 12:35], because where good intention proceeds, good action follows. By treasure are meant holy men, as in the Psalms: “Who brings forth the winds from his treasures” [Note: [Col. 1065] 31 Psalm 134:8], because among holy men some bring forth others. By the treasures of the wicked, as in Job: “Have you entered the treasures of the snow?” [Note: [Col. 1065] 32 Job 38:22], is meant that the Lord sometimes enters, through the grace of his inspiration, the cold hearts of wicked Jews. By treasure is meant the providence of God, as in Deuteronomy: “And sealed up in my treasures” [Note: [Col. 1065] 33 Deuteronomy 32:34], that is, established and confirmed in my providence.

A potsherd is the flesh of Christ, as in the Psalms: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” [Note: [Col. 1065] 34 Psalm 21:16], because Christ’s flesh grew strong through the fire of the Passion. A potsherd is the force of strict discipline, as in Job: “He scraped the discharge with a potsherd” [Note: [Col. 1065] 35 Job 2:8], because holy men, through the force of strict discipline, wipe away the flow of unlawful pleasure.

A tiger is a hypocrite, as in Job: “The tiger perished because he had no prey” [Note: [Col. 1065] 36 Job 4:11], because a hypocrite thinks himself somehow to perish when he cannot seize the prey of human approval. A tiger is our mortality, as in the book of Tobit: “He remained beside the river Tigris” [Note: [Col. 1067] 1 Tobit 6:21], because Christ assumed the flow of human mortality.

Timbers are teachers, as in the Song: “The timbers of our houses are cedars” [Note: [Col. 1067] 2 Song of Songs 1:17], because the preachers of the Churches are both pleasing in good works and lofty in contemplation.

Incense is the devotion of prayer, as in Exodus: “And incense of a pleasing fragrance” [Note: [Col. 1067] 3 Exodus 25:6], that is, prayer of great devotion.

A tiara is the adornment of virtues, as in Exodus: “And you shall make a linen tiara” [Note: [Col. 1067] 4 Exodus 28:39], that is, an adornment of virtues shining with chastity.

A timbrel is the affliction of the flesh and harmony of the mind, as in Exodus: “Mary, the sister, immediately perceived a timbrel [reading uncertain]” [Note: [Col. 1067] 5 Exodus 15:20]. A timbrel is a good work, as in the Psalms: “Take up the psalm and give the timbrel” [Note: [Col. 1067] 6 Psalm 80:3], that is, add preaching and exhibit good action.

A moth is any heretic, as in Job: “He has built his house like a moth” [Note: [Col. 1067] 7 Job 27:18], because heretics always gnaw away at the conscience through their wickedness. A moth is temptation, as in Job: “Like a garment that is consumed by the moth” [Note: [Col. 1067] 8 Job 15:28], that is, the body, which is worn down by temptation. A moth is the torment of hell, as in Isaiah: “Beneath you the moth shall be spread” [Note: [Col. 1067] 9 Isaiah 14:11], that is, the punishment of hell will roll you about.

Bells are the sounds of preaching, as in Exodus: “And bells of pure gold” [Note: [Col. 1067] 10 Exodus 28:34], that is, true preaching and true wisdom.

Dyed stuffs are the adornments of virtues, as in Job: “The purest dye-stuffs shall not be compared” [Note: [Col. 1067] 11 Job 28:19], because the adornments of our virtues, whatever they may be, cannot be compared with the virtues of Christ. Dyed stuffs are philosophers, as in Job: “It is not compared with all the colors of India” [Note: [Col. 1067] 12 Ibid., verse 16], because the philosophy of this world ought not to be compared with Christ.

A thorn is the piercing of the heart, as in Job: “Let a thorn grow up for me instead of wheat” [Note: [Col. 1067] 13 Job 31:40], that is, let the refreshment of exultation depart from me, and let the wound of pain pierce me. By thorns are meant heretics, as in the Gospel: “Or figs from thorns?” [Note: [Col. 1067] 14 Matthew 7:16], because we can find no true sweetness in heretics. By thorns are meant perverse pleasures, as in Genesis: “But it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” [Note: [Col. 1067] 15 Genesis 3:18], that is, your flesh will produce temptations and unlawful pleasures for you.

Wheat is the word of preaching, as in the Gospel: “To give them their measure of wheat at the proper time” [Note: [Col. 1067] 16 Luke 12:42], that is, to minister to them the fullness of preaching when the time is most suitable. Wheat is a good work, as in the Song: “Your belly is like a heap of wheat” [Note: [Col. 1067] 17 Song of Songs 7:2], that is, your affection produces a fullness of good effects. Wheat is good men, as in the Gospel: “But gather the wheat into my barn” [Note: [Col. 1067] 18 Matthew 13:30], that is, admit my elect into my kingdom.

Thunder is the incarnate Lord, as in Job: “And the way of resounding thunder” [Note: [Col. 1067] 19 Job 38:25], because the Father inspired the hearts of those who hear, so that they may give faith to Christ who preaches. Thunder is any preacher, as in the Psalms: “At the voice of your thunder they will fear” [Note: [Col. 1067] 20 Psalm 103:7], that is, having heard the word of your preaching, they will fear and repent. Thunder is a threat, as in the Psalms: “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel” [Note: [Col. 1067] 21 Psalm 76:19], because the divine threat resounds in Holy Scripture. By thunder are meant rebukes, as in the Apocalypse: “And there were voices and thunderclaps” [Note: [Col. 1067] 22 Revelation 16:18], that is, miracles, preachings, and rebukes appeared.

A breastplate is the virtue of patience, as in Job: “The spear cannot stand, nor the breastplate” [Note: [Col. 1067] 23 Job 41:17], because no one’s endurance can resist the malice of the devil without the grace of God.

A torrent is the wisdom of God, as in the Psalms: “And you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight” [Note: [Col. 1067] 24 Psalm 35:9], that is, you will refresh them with the wisdom of divinity. A torrent is the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, who pours into a person both sweetness in the mind and richness in the mind. A torrent is the Passion of Christ, as in the Psalms: “From the torrent he shall drink on the way” [Note: [Col. 1067] 25 Psalm 109:7], that is, he will allow himself to be afflicted by much present suffering. A torrent is the Last Judgment, as in Job: “He divides the torrent from the traveling people” [Note: [Col. 1067] 26 Job 28:4], because the final judgment will separate from the elect the reprobate, hardened by wickedness and hardened by ignorance. A torrent is the course of this life, as in Job: “The willows of the torrent surround them” [Note: [Col. 1067] 27 Job 40:17], because unfruitful lovers of this passing life favor the devils. By torrents are meant preachers, as in Job: “And instead of a willow, torrents of gold” [Note: [Col. 1067] 28 Job 22:24], because the Lord sometimes makes even preachers desolate those whom he finds strong in good work. By torrents are meant preachers, as in Proverbs: “Let the ravens of the torrent dig it out” [Note: [Col. 1067] 29 Proverbs 30:17], that is, let humble teachers who dwell in divine preaching root it out.

Topaz-stones are holy men, as in Job: “Topaz from Ethiopia shall not be compared with it” [Note: [Col. 1067] 30 Job 28:19], because holy men from this world can in no way be compared with Christ. Topaz is the precious things of this age, as in the Psalms: “Above gold and topaz” [Note: [Col. 1067] 31 Psalm 118:127], that is, above the exalted things and all the precious objects of this world.

A lathe is uprightness of action, as in the Song: “His hands are turned like a lathe” [Note: [Col. 1067] 32 Song of Songs 6:14], because Christ’s works were upright in every respect.

A winepress is the cross of Christ, as in Isaiah: “I have trodden the winepress alone” [Note: [Col. 1067] 33 Isaiah 63:3], that is, while my disciples fled, I alone endured the cross.

Thrones are the holy angels, as in Ezekiel: “And above all of them was the likeness of a throne, with the likeness of a human being above it” [Note: [Col. 1067] 34 Ezekiel 1:26], because above all the angels is the glory of our Redeemer. A throne is the holy Church, as in the Psalms: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever” [Note: [Col. 1069] 1 Psalm 44:7], because the holy Church will endure forever. Thrones are holy preachers, as in Daniel: “Your throne was a flame of fire” [Note: [Col. 1069] 2 Daniel 7:9], because preachers proclaim both love of virtue and pour in the light of truth. A throne is the tribunal of the future judgment, as in the Psalms: “You sit upon the throne, judging justice” [Note: [Col. 1069] 3 Psalm 9:5], because at the future judgment he will repay each person according to his works.

A trumpet is the sound of preaching, as in Joel: “Blow the trumpet in Zion” [Note: [Col. 1069] 4 Joel 2:1, 15], that is, cry out the voice of preaching in the Church. A trumpet is the voice of secular power, as in Job: “He does not regard the trumpet’s blast” [Note: [Col. 1069] 5 Job 39:27], because a holy preacher fears no threats of secular power. A trumpet is human approval, as in the Gospel: “Do not sound a trumpet before you” [Note: [Col. 1069] 6 Matthew 6:2], that is, do not perform good works with regard for human approval. By trumpets are meant the two commandments of charity, as in the book of Numbers: “Make for yourself two silver trumpets” [Note: [Col. 1069] 7 Numbers 10:2], that is, fulfill the two commandments of charity with the splendor of preaching. By a trumpet are meant preachings, as in the book of Judges: “They held torches in their left hands and sounding trumpets in their right” [Note: [Col. 1069] 8 Judges 7:20], because holy teachers consider what they do little in comparison with their preachings.

A tunic is the flesh of Christ, as in Leviticus: “The priest is clothed in a linen tunic” [Note: [Col. 1069] 9 Leviticus 16:4], that is, Christ will be clothed in human garb. A tunic is the Catholic Church, as in the Gospel: “The tunic was seamless” [Note: [Col. 1069] 10 John 19:23], because the holy Church insists above all upon unity and entirely avoids being torn by scandals. A tunic is a completed action, as in Genesis: “And he made him a long tunic” [Note: [Col. 1069] 11 Genesis 37:3], that is, an action persevering in goodness. A tunic is worldly occupation, as in the Song: “I have taken off my tunic” [Note: [Col. 1069] 12 Song of Songs 5:3], that is, I cast away from me the worldly occupation by which I was once entangled. A tunic is the human body, as in Jude: “Hating even the tunic stained by the flesh” [Note: [Col. 1069] 12 Jude 23], that is, shunning the body polluted by what is subject to carnal desires. A tunic is inner sins, as in the Gospel: “And if anyone takes your tunic, let him have your cloak also” [Note: [Col. 1069] 14 Matthew 5:40; Luke 6:29], that is, if someone admonishes you to cast away your inner sins, cast away the outer ones as well.

A turtledove is the holy Church, as in the Song: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” [Note: [Col. 1069] 15 Song of Songs 2:12], that is, the desire of the holy Church is heard in the heavenly homeland. A turtledove is love of God, as in Genesis: “A turtledove and a dove” [Note: [Col. 1069] 16 Genesis 15:9], that is, love of God and neighbor. A turtledove is the flesh of a human being, as in the Psalms: “And the turtledove has found a nest for itself” [Note: [Col. 1069] 17 Psalm 83:4], that is, our flesh has found hope in which to cherish its actions. A turtledove is hidden compunction, as in Leviticus: “Let him offer two turtledoves, one for sin and the other for guilt” [Note: [Col. 1069] 18 Leviticus 5:7], that is, let him sacrifice to God hidden compunctions of tears for having committed evil and omitted good.

A tower is the strength of preaching, as in the Song: “Your neck is like an ivory tower” [Note: [Col. 1069] 19 Song of Songs 7:4], because holy preachers are strong through courage and radiant through chastity. A tower is the virtue of humility, as in the Gospel: “Which of you, wishing to build a tower” [Note: [Col. 1069] 20 Luke 14:28], that is, to construct humility within himself. A tower is the pride of this world, as in Genesis: “And a tower whose summit may reach” [Note: [Col. 1069] 21 Genesis 11:4], that is, pride whose fame will fly to the heights.

A censer is the flesh of Christ, as in the book of Numbers: “Take the censer, and, having taken fire from the altar, put incense on it” [Note: [Col. 1069] 22 Numbers 16:46], because our old Aaron, the Lord Jesus, when he endured in his flesh the ardor of the Passion at the Father’s command, offered that same Father a pleasing fragrance for us. Censers are good workers, as in Exodus: “And bowls, and mortars, and censers” [Note: [Col. 1069] 23 Exodus 25:29], that is, preachers, martyrs, and authors of righteousness. By censers are meant the apostles, as in the Apocalypse: “And the angel took the censer in his hand, filled it with fire from the altar, and cast it upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 1069] 24 Revelation 8:7], because Christ chose his apostles through his grace and, filled with the Father’s Spirit, sent them into the world.

A trunk is the human body, as in Job: “And its trunk will have died in the dust” [Note: [Col. 1069] 25 Job 14:8], that is, if its body has been killed.

A trowel is divine protection, as in Amos: “And in his hand was a builder’s trowel” [Note: [Col. 1069] 26 Amos 7:7], that is, in his work there is the protection of Christ.

Frankincense is the devotion of prayer, as in the Gospel: “Gold, frankincense, and myrrh” [Note: [Col. 1069] 27 Matthew 2:11], that is, wisdom of mind, sweetness of prayer, and mortification of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 1069D] a These seem rather to belong under “Penitence” in the letter P.]

There are three kinds of penitence: cruel and despairing, as in Cain and Judas; simulated and impure, as in Saul and Esau; and useful and complete, as in Zacchaeus and Mary. The last contains these five elements: contrition, confession, maturation, correction, and perseverance. The first is in the heart, the second in the mouth, the third in the flesh, the fourth in action, and the fifth in virtue.

Three rivers obstruct us: the goad of desires, which washes over us; the mass of temptations, which suggests; and the barb of troubles, which pierces. The first is like a sea, surging stormily around us with swollen and tempestuous waves of thoughts; the second is like the Jordan exceeding the limits of its channel and wishing to overwhelm the land of our heart by denying passage; the third is like the Jordan meeting Elisha on his way and denying him passage. The waters of the first were divided by Moses’ staff, namely, discernment of judgment; those of the second by the ark of the covenant, that is, knowledge of the truth; those of the third by Elijah’s cloak, namely, meditation on the incarnation of Christ.

There are three arrows by which the enemies of God are pierced: the goad of lost excellence; the plague of bodily distress; and the hammer of infernal memory. There are three by which the elect are gently wounded: chaste fear, devoted love, and the strength of desire.

There are three paradises: the pleasurable sweetness of invisible things, which is watered like a garden of delights; the sincere purity of spiritual things, which preserves a person within itself; and the delightful truth of heavenly things. Hence Paul hears words that it is not permitted to a human being to speak.

There are three girls who overturn our senses: the tenderness of the flesh, which is Delilah and tore out Samson’s eyes; the beauty of worldly glory, which is Jezebel and killed Naboth; and distrust of the future life, which is the daughter of Herodias and takes away the head of John the Baptist.

## V

Vah. Sheath. Vapor. Bar. Fleece. Poison. Belly. Brambles. Spring. Uterus. Valley. Cow. Ointment. Garment. Face. Elm. Fox. Ulcer. Clothing. Footprints. Evening. Evening-time. Bladder. Virtues. Inward parts. Life. Watchers. Birds. Travelers. Widow. Estate. Vineyard. Urn. Shadow. Vineyard. Viper. Virgin. Little rod. Calf. Glass. Plowshare. Hoof. Man. [Uncertain reading: “Ulae.”] Wife. Bear. Uterus. Cow. Valley. Green things. Bat. Veins. Wind. Winnowing shovel. Worm. Ram. Heifer. Wine. Vestibule. In the evening. Vision. Way. Bonds. Vulture. Navel. Life. Rod. Vessel. Veil. Vine. Voice. Grape. Nettle. Womb.

Vah is joy of mind, as in Job: “When he hears the trumpet, he says, ‘Vah!’” [Note: [Col. 1071] 1 Job 39:28], because the spiritual athlete shines forth when tribulation arrives. Vah is reproach of the wicked, as in the Gospel: “Vah, you who destroy the temple of God” [Note: [Col. 1071] 2 Matthew 27:40], that is, he is to be reproached who boasts such things about himself.

A cow is Christ, as in the book of Numbers: “A red cow of full age, which has not borne a yoke” [Note: [Col. 1071] 3 Numbers 19:2], that is, Christ, marked by the female sex on account of the weakness of the assumed nature, yet wholly complete in perfection and, as it were, subjected to sin. A cow is the Israelite people, as in the prophet: “Israel has turned aside like a wanton cow” [Note: [Col. 1071] 4 Hosea 4:16], that is, because of wantonness Israel rushed into evil. A cow is sensuality, as in Genesis: “Take for yourself a three-year-old cow” [Note: [Col. 1071] 5 Genesis 15:9], that is, bring sensuality, as a servant, under the rule of the Holy Trinity. By cows are meant holy men, as in the books of Kings: “The cows went straight on, going and lowing” [Note: [Col. 1071] 6 1 Kings 6:12], because the saints, by living well, advance toward religion and show discerning compassion to those who are related to it. By cows are meant the rulers of Israel, as in Amos: “Hear this, you fat cows” [Note: [Col. 1071] 7 Amos 4:1], that is, listen, you arrogant rulers. By cows are meant foolish souls, as in the Psalms: “The assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples” [Note: [Col. 1071] 8 Psalm 67:31], that is, gatherings of heretics for deceiving foolish souls.

A sheath is perverse thought, as in Job: “Drawn out, and going forth” [Note: [Col. 1071] 9 Job 20:25], into evil action from thought. A sheath is mercy, as in the Gospel: “Put your sword into its sheath” [Note: [Col. 1071] 10 John 18:11], that is, turn your destruction into mercy.

A valley is the present life, as in the Psalms: “He has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears” [Note: [Col. 1071] 11 Psalm 83:7], because in the present life the holy man strives daily to ascend through merits. A valley is a humble mind, as in the Gospel: “Every valley shall be filled” [Note: [Col. 1071] 12 Isaiah 40:4], that is, a humble mind will have the fullness of grace. By valleys are meant the minds of the wicked, as in Job: “Like a torrent that swiftly passes through the valleys” [Note: [Col. 1071] 13 Job 6:15], that is, the impulse of love will suddenly plunge itself into the minds of the wicked. By valleys are meant the humble, as in the Psalms: “And the valleys will abound in grain” [Note: [Col. 1071] 14 Psalm 64:14], because the humble will be filled with the divine word.

Vapor is blindness of heart, as in Joel: “Blood and fire and vapor of smoke” [Note: [Col. 1071] 15 Joel 2:30], that is, the cruelty of wickedness, the heat of desire, and the blindness of ignorance. Vapor is the condition of the present life, as in the Epistle of James: “It is a vapor appearing for a little while” [Note: [Col. 1071] 16 James 4:14], that is, having no stability.

A vessel is understanding of the Divinity, as in Exodus: “Every golden vessel set apart as an offering to the Lord” [Note: [Col. 1071] 17 Exodus 35:22], because whatever we understand concerning his divinity, we must ascribe all of it to grace. A vessel is God’s approval, as in the Acts of the Apostles: “This man is a vessel of election for me” [Note: [Col. 1071] 18 Acts 9:15], that is, he was received into the company of the elect with my approval. A vessel is our body, as in Paul: “Let each one know how to possess his vessel in sanctification” [Note: [Col. 1071] 19 1 Thessalonians 4:4], that is, to preserve his body in chastity. By vessels are meant the holy angels, as in Exodus: “And all the vessels for its service” [Note: [Col. 1071] 20 Exodus 25:9], because, as far as we are able, we ought also to imitate those angels in serving God. By vessels are meant the prophets, as in Job: “Nor shall vessels of gold, lofty and eminent, be exchanged for it” [Note: [Col. 1071] 21 Job 28:17], because the prophets cannot be compared with Christ, faithful in life and renowned in reputation. By vessels are meant heretics, as in the Psalms: “And in it he prepared vessels of death” [Note: [Col. 1071] 22 Psalm 7:14], because heretics, prepared for the punishment of destruction, stumble against Holy Scripture. By vessels are meant our hearts, as in the Gospel: “But the wise took oil in their vessels” [Note: [Col. 1071] 23 Matthew 25:4], because the elect possess true glory in their consciences. By vessels are meant our bodies, as in the books of Kings: “And the vessels of the young men are holy” [Note: [Col. 1073] 1 1 Kings 21:5], because the bodies of the gentle and humble are clean. By vessels are meant human beings, as in the books of Kings: “And pour it into all these vessels” [Note: [Col. 1073] 2 2 Kings 4:4], because holy Mother Church administers the fluid of grace to human beings called to the faith. By vessels are meant the reprobate, as in Isaiah: “And in vessels of papyrus upon the waters” [Note: [Col. 1073] 3 Isaiah 18:2], because the Antichrist will establish preachers for himself from reprobate people, whom he will appoint over others as the latter flow toward death.

A bar is the cross of Christ, as in the book of Numbers: “Which two men carried on a bar” [Note: [Col. 1073] 4 Numbers 13:24], that is, two peoples believed in Christ on the cross. A bar is the humanity of Christ, as in Job: “And I set its bar and doors” [Note: [Col. 1073] 5 Job 38:10], because Christ incarnate and his apostles restored the wickedness of this age [reading uncertain]. A bar is the devil, as in Isaiah: “Against Leviathan, the serpent, the bar” [Note: [Col. 1073] 6 Isaiah 27:1], that is, against the poisonous devil. And holy men are called bars, as in Exodus: “You shall also make bars of acacia wood” [Note: [Col. 1073] 7 Exodus 25:13], that is, men adorned with strong virtues. By bars are meant evil spirits, as in the Psalms: “And he broke the iron bars” [Note: [Col. 1073] 8 Psalm 106:16], that is, he overcame evil spirits hardened by wickedness.

A veil is the obscurity of the letter, as in the Gospel: “The veil of the temple was torn” [Note: [Col. 1073] 9 Matthew 27:51; Mark 15:38; Luke 23:45]. A veil is heaven, as in Leviticus: “The high priest shall enter within the veil,” that is, Christ penetrated heaven.

Fleece is the Virgin Mary, as in the Psalms: “He shall descend like rain upon fleece” [Note: [Col. 1073] 10 Psalm 71:6], that is, through the Holy Spirit Christ will come into the Virgin’s womb.

A vein is Christ the Lord, as in Jeremiah: “The fountain of living waters, the Lord” [Note: [Col. 1073] 11 Jeremiah 17:13], that is, the source of unfailing virtues, the Lord. By veins are meant the books of the divine page, as in Job: “It has the sources of its silver in its veins” [Note: [Col. 1073] 12 Job 28:1], because the divine page contains holy books. By veins are meant the exalted things of inner speech, as in Job: “The veins of his whisper” [Note: [Col. 1073] 13 Job 4:12], that is, the subtleties of inner speech. By veins are meant sins, as in Hosea: “And he will dry up its veins,” because Christ, born of a virgin, took away the sins of the world.

Poison is wickedness, as in the Psalms: “The poison of asps is under their lips” [Note: [Col. 1073] 14 Psalm 139:4], that is, the malice of demons in their minds.

Wind is the Lord, as in Hosea: “The Lord will bring a scorching wind” [Note: [Col. 1073] 15 Hosea 13:15], that is, the Lord will bring forth Christ, who rebukes the world. By wind is meant iniquity of mind, as in Job: “Against a leaf carried away by the wind” [Note: [Col. 1073] 16 Job 13:25], that is, against a mind held in its iniquity. Wind is the present life, as in Job: “A passing wind will drive them away” [Note: [Col. 1073] 17 Job 37:21], because the instability of the present life removes from holy men the desire to remain here for long. Wind is persecution, as in the Psalms: “And like straw before the face of the wind” [Note: [Col. 1073] 18 Psalm 82:14]. Wind is great tribulation, as in Ezekiel: “A whirlwind was coming from the north” [Note: [Col. 1073] 19 Ezekiel 1:4], that is, a massive tribulation of persecution proceeded from the unbelief of the wicked. Wind is inward temptation, as in the Psalms: “Like dust which the wind drives away” [Note: [Col. 1073] 20 Psalm 1:4], that is, like a joyful spirit stirred by the breath of temptation. Wind is an evil spirit, as in Ecclesiastes: “Whoever watches the wind will not sow” [Note: [Col. 1073] 21 Ecclesiastes 11:4], because whoever fears diabolical opposition too much does not devote himself to good work. By wind are meant the gifts of the Holy Spirit, as in the Psalms: “Who brings forth the winds from his treasures” [Note: [Col. 1073] 22 Psalm 134:8], because the Lord brings forth spiritual gifts for good from the hearts of his elect. By winds are meant holy souls, as in Job: “Who gave weight to the winds” [Note: [Col. 1073] 23 Job 28:25], that is, he bestowed the maturity of holiness upon the minds of the elect. By winds are meant malice, as in Jeremiah: “They drew up the winds like dragons” [Note: [Col. 1073] 24 Jeremiah 14:6], because cruel men brought forth malice for wicked action.

The belly is the humanity of Christ, as in the Song: “His belly is ivory” [Note: [Col. 1073] 25 Song of Songs 5:14], because Christ’s humility was free from all pollution of sin. The belly is the Church, as in the Psalms: “In the midst of my belly” [Note: [Col. 1073] 26 Psalm 21:15], that is, in the midst of my Church. The belly is the font of baptism, as in the Song: “Your belly is like a heap of wheat” [Note: [Col. 1073] 27 Song of Songs 7:2], because the fruit of baptism is sanctified by the word of God. The belly is the human mind, as in Proverbs: “Who searches all the secret things of the belly” [Note: [Col. 1073] 28 Proverbs 20:27], because the radiance of inner light searches out all the hidden things of the mind. The belly is our manner of life, as in the Apocalypse: “It will make your belly bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey” [Note: [Col. 1073] 29 Revelation 10:9], because the sweeter Holy Scripture tastes to us on the palate of the heart, the more austerely we conduct our life, having rejected every carnal pleasure. The belly is a compunctious heart, as in Jeremiah: “I am in pain in my belly” [Note: [Col. 1073] 30 Jeremiah 4:19], that is, because I omitted good and admitted evil, I am pierced in my heart by a twofold pain. The belly is avarice, as in Job: “Nor is his belly satisfied” [Note: [Col. 1073] 31 Job 20:20], that is, his avarice is not filled. The belly is human memory, as in Job: “And from his belly God will draw them out” [Note: [Col. 1073] 32 Ibid., verse 1], because by just judgment God removes holy words from the memory of the wicked, who is seen to refuse to preserve them in life.

A winnowing shovel is the distinction of judgment, as in the Gospel: “His winnowing shovel is in his hand” [Note: [Col. 1073] 33 Matthew 3:12; Luke 3:17], that is, the distinction of judgment is in his power.

Brambles are the pricks of vices, as in Isaiah: “Upon the shoulder of my people, thorns and brambles” [Note: [Col. 1073] 34 Isaiah 32:13], because temptations of vices afflict even the elect with their pricks. Brambles are the persecuting Jews, as in Genesis: “Caught by the horns among the brambles” [Note: [Col. 1075] 1 Genesis 21:13], because Christ was crucified by the persecuting Jews.

The worm is Christ, as in the Psalms: “But I am a worm, and not a man” [Note: [Col. 1075] 2 Ps. XXI, 7], that is, because to some I was regarded not as a man but as something so contemptible as a worm. The worm is lust, as in Job: “His sweetness is worms” [Note: [Col. 1075] 3 Job XXIV, 20], because the sweetness of an impure mind is lust. The worm is the conscience of the condemned: the conscience of the reprobate will gnaw them eternally. By worms are meant the corruptions of our body, as in Job: “And my sister, to the worms” [Note: [Col. 1075] 4 Job XVII, 14], because our body lives amid corruptions and tends toward corruptions. By worms are meant the garments of hell, as in Isaiah: “And your covering shall be worms” [Note: [Col. 1075] 5 Isa. XIV, 11], because infernal beings will torment the devil and the reprobate.

[Col. 1075B] Spring is the beginning of a good work, as in the Psalms: “You formed summer and spring” [Note: [Col. 1075] 6 Ps. LXXIII, 17], because the Lord formed the perfect and the foolish.

The crown of the head is the reasoning faculty of the mind, as in the Psalms: “And upon his crown his iniquity shall descend” [Note: [Col. 1075] 7 Ps. VII, 17], that is, he will exercise the reasoning of his iniquity. The crown of the head is holiness, as in Deuteronomy: “From the crown of the ancient mountains” [Note: [Col. 1075] 8 Deut. XXXIII, 15], that is, from the sublime holiness of the first parents.

A garment is Christ’s humanity, as in the Apocalypse: “On his garment he had written: King of kings and Lord of lords” [Note: [Col. 1075] 9 Rev. XIX, 16], because Christ as man rules all things and exercises dominion over every creature. A garment is the holy Church, as in Job: “In the multitude of them my garment is consumed” [Col. 1075C] [Note: [Col. 1075] 10 Job XXX, 18], because the holy Church is disturbed by the multitude of heretics. A garment is a good work, as in Isaiah: “You have a garment; be our ruler” [Note: [Col. 1075] 11 Isa. III, 6], that is, you practice good works; be our leader. A garment is our body, with which our soul is clothed, as in Isaiah: “And the garment mixed with blood shall be for burning, and food for fire” [Note: [Col. 1075] 12 Isa. IX, 5], because a body polluted by lust will be burned in Gehenna. By a garment is meant the order of the faithful, as in the Psalms: “Which descended upon the hem of his garment” [Note: [Col. 1075] 13 Ps. CXXXII, 2], that is, the grace that reaches even the one who is last in the order of the faithful. By a garment is meant a holy man, as in the Song: “And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense” [Note: [Col. 1075] 14 Song IV, 11], because the holiness of the faithful is made equal to the holiness of prayer. By a garment are meant works of righteousness, as in Job: “And he tore his garments” [Note: [Col. 1075] 15 Job I, 20], that is, through discernment he deferred his good works. By garments are meant divine works, as in Job: “He has indeed prepared garments, but the just man will put them on” [Note: [Col. 1075] 16 Job XXVII, 16–17], because the wicked person sometimes possesses the divine utterances through understanding, but the just will put them on through their effect. By garments are meant the members of our body, as in Ecclesiastes: “Let your garments be white at all times” [Note: [Col. 1075] 17 Eccl. IX, 8], that is, keep the members of your body clean from the filth of lust. By garments are meant good examples, as in the Gospel: “And they placed him upon their garments, * so that he might not walk naked” [Note: [Col. 1075] 18 Matt. XXI, 7; Mark XI, 7; Luke XIX, 35; John XII, 13], that is, unless he preserves the gifts of grace bestowed upon him, he will appear deprived of them.

A robe is Christ’s flesh, as in the Apocalypse: “And he was clothed in a robe sprinkled with blood” [Note: [Col. 1075] 19 Rev. XIX, 13], because Christ appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh. A robe is charity, as in the Gospel: “And over my garments they cast lots” [Note: [Col. 1075] 20 Matt. XXVII, 35; Mark XV, 24; Luke XXIII, 34; John XIX, 23], because charity is so great a reality that no one can possess it except whole and by lot—that is, through divine grace. A robe is the holy Church, as in Paul: “A glorious Church, [Col. 1076B] not having spot or wrinkle” [Note: [Col. 1075] 21 Eph. V, 27], because God has clothed himself, as it were, with a certain robe, namely the Church, in which he practices neither depravity in action nor dissimulation in intention. A robe is anyone who strives for purity, as in the Gospel: “But Herod despised him, clothed in a white robe” [Note: [Col. 1075] 22 Luke XXIII, 11], because the devil, through the reprobate, despised Christ in his elect, who strive for the victory of purity. A robe is Christ’s martyrs, as in the Gospel: “And they wrapped him in a scarlet robe” [Note: [Col. 1075] 23 Matt. XXVII, 28], because the Lord is clothed in the holy martyrs who resist unto blood. By garments are meant the sentences of sacred Scripture, as in Genesis: “And Rebecca clothed Jacob in Esau’s very fine garments, which she had with her at home” [Note: [Col. 1075] 24 Gen. XXVII, 15], because, through the sentences of sacred Scripture that the Jewish people preserve secretly within themselves, the mother of grace spiritually adorned the gentile people.

Footprints are the works of God, as in Job: “My foot has followed his footprints” [Note: [Col. 1075] 25 Job XXIII, 11], that is, I have completed his works in their effect. Footprints are God’s visitations, as in Job: “Perhaps you will comprehend his footprints” [Note: [Col. 1075] 26 Job XI, 7]. * Footprints are God’s presence, as in the Psalms: “And your footprints will not be known,” because God’s presence is indeed perceived in the mind through affection, but is not comprehended through the intellect. By footprints are meant bad examples, as in the Song: “And I went after the footprints of your flocks” [Note: [Col. 1075] 27 Song I, 8], that is, imitate the depraved examples of fools.

The vestibule is eternal life, as in Ezekiel: “But the vestibule of the gate was on the inside” [Note: [Col. 1075] 28 Ezek. XL, 9], because eternal life, the reward of faith, will be in the heavenly homeland.

Evening is the Antichrist, as in Job: “And you cause evening to rise over the children of the earth” [Note: [Col. 1075] 29 Job XXXVIII, 32], because the Lord permits the Antichrist to rule over earthly and reprobate people.

Evening is the time of the Incarnation, as in Exodus: “In the evening they shall eat flesh” [Note: [Col. 1075] 30 Exod. XVI, 12], that is, at the time of the Incarnation you will have spiritual refreshment. Evening is perfection, as in Genesis: “And evening came and morning came” [Note: [Col. 1077] 1 Gen. I, 5], that is, perfection and the beginning of a work.

Eventide is temptation, as in Job: “And again I shall await eventide” [Note: [Col. 1077] 2 Job VII, 4], that is, I shall await temptation securely. Eventide is the end of life, as in Isaiah: “From morning until evening you will bring me to an end” [Note: [Col. 1077] 3 Isa. XXXVIII, 12], that is, you who caused me to have a beginning through birth will bring me to completion at the end of my life through death. Eventide is adversity, as in Job: “From morning until evening they are cut down” [Note: [Col. 1077] 4 Job IV, 20], because the reprobate tend toward ruin both in prosperity through intemperance and in adversity through impatience. Eventide is the end of the world, as in the Psalms: “They shall return toward evening” [Col. 1077B] [Note: [Col. 1077] 5 Ps. XXXVIII, 7, 15], because at the end of the world the remnant of the Jews will be saved.

The bat is an error of the mind, as in Leviticus, where it is forbidden that anyone eat a bat [Note: [Col. 1077] 6 Lev. XI, 19], that is, follow error.

A blister is swelling, as in Exodus: “Swollen blisters” [Note: [Col. 1077] 7 Exod. IX, 9], that is, swelling produced by pride.

The way is Christ, as in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” [Note: [Col. 1077] 8 John XIV, 6], because for us in hope he is the way in example, the truth in promise, and life in reward. The way is good conduct, as in Proverbs: “The way of the righteous is without stumbling” [Note: [Col. 1077] 9 Prov. XV, 19], that is, the conduct of the good, without criminal sin. The way is the rectitude of the Churches, as in Job: “Nor does he walk by the way of the vineyards” [Note: [Col. 1077] 10 Job XXIV, 18], that is, he does not live according to the rectitude of the Churches. The way is our life, as in the Psalms: “Direct my ways in your sight” [Note: [Col. 1077] 11 Ps. V, 9], that is, make my life pleasing to you. The way is the condition of the reprobate, as in Proverbs: “The way of the wicked is dark” [Note: [Col. 1077] 12 Prov. IV, 19], because the condition of the reprobate is dark through error. The way is the rarity of the present life, as in Genesis: “Let Dan be a serpent on the way” [Note: [Col. 1077] 13 Gen. XLIX, 17], because, to those who love the sweetness of the present life, the devil will display himself in the Antichrist as soft and slippery. By the way are meant the works of the Creator, as in Job: “He is the beginning of the ways of the Lord” [Note: [Col. 1077] 14 Job XL, 14], because God made the angel before all his other works. By ways are meant the divine commandments, as in the Psalms: “Show me your ways, Lord” [Note: [Col. 1077] 15 Ps. XXIV, 4], that is, inspire me with your commandments, Lord. By ways are meant our inward thoughts, as in the Psalms: “I have declared my ways to you” [Note: [Col. 1077] 16 Ps. CXIX, 26], that is, through confession I have revealed my hidden thoughts to you. By the way are meant our actions, as in Job: “Does he not himself consider my ways?” [Note: [Col. 1077] 17 Job XXXI, 4], that is, my thoughts.

Travelers are holy men, as in Job: “Ask any one of the travelers” [Note: [Col. 1077] 18 Job XXI, 29], that is, consult one of the holy men who regard the present life as a journey.

The lanes are religious people, as in the Song: “Through the lanes and streets I will seek him whom my soul loves” [Col. 1078A] [Note: [Col. 1077] 19 Song III, 2], that is, in the conduct of religious and secular people I will seek something belonging to the Lord that I may imitate. The lanes are heavenly citizens, * as in Tobit: “And through all its lanes they sang Alleluia” [Note: [Col. 1077] 20 Tob. XIII, 22], because those dwelling in that house of the Lord will praise you forever and ever.

A widow is the Church, as in Job: “And they took the widow’s ox as a pledge” [Note: [Col. 1077] 21 Job XXIV, 3], that is, the heretics, so that they might later subvert their hearers, first endeavored to take away the preacher of the Church. A widow is a wicked soul, as in Leviticus: “A widow and a divorced woman” [Note: [Col. 1077] 22 Lev. XXI, 13], because a soul departing from God and rejected for its evil works is not worthy of Christ’s companionship. A widow is a human soul, as in Job: “And he did not do good to the widow” [Note: [Col. 1077] 23 Job XXIV, 21], that is, he brought no benefit to his own soul. By widows are meant peoples subject to heretics, as in Job: “You sent away widows empty” [Note: [Col. 1077] 24 Job XXII, 9], that is, under the heretics you left peoples empty of good works.

The watchers are holy angels, as in Daniel: “This has been decreed in the sentence of the watchers” [Note: [Col. 1077] 25 Dan. IV, 14], that is, it has been arranged in the ministry of the angels. The watchers are holy shepherds, as in the Song: “The watchers who guard the city found me” [Note: [Col. 1077] 26 Song III, 3], that is, the shepherds who govern the Church worshiped me.

The farm is the mass of the wicked, as in the Gospel: “He sent him to a farm to feed pigs” [Note: [Col. 1077] 27 Luke XV, 15], that is, he associated him with gatherings of the wicked, so that he might nourish impure thoughts. The farm is the lord of pride, as in the Gospel: “I have bought a farm, and therefore I cannot come” [Col. 1078C] [Note: [Col. 1077] 28 Luke XIV, 18], because those who swell with the arrogance of pride do not at all strive toward the heavenly homeland. By the farm are meant the gentile peoples, as in the Song: “Let us dwell in the farm” [Note: [Col. 1077] 29 Song VII, 11], because Christ admonishes his preachers among the peoples of the nations.

Wine is the secret of the Godhead, as in Proverbs: “She mixed the wine” [Note: [Col. 1077] 30 Prov. IX, 2], because Wisdom, appearing through the flesh, revealed to us the secret of the Godhead. Wine is the fervor of the Holy Spirit, * which pours true joy into the human mind. Wine is knowledge of the Law, as in the Song: “Your breasts are better than wine” [Note: [Col. 1077] 31 Song I, 2], because the wisdom of the Church surpasses knowledge of the Law. Wine is the word of the Gospel, as in the Song: “Your throat is like the finest wine” [Note: [Col. 1077] 32 Song VII, 9], because the preachers proclaim his Gospel. [Col. 1078D] Wine is each contemplative person, as in the Song: “I drank my wine with my milk” [Note: [Col. 1077] 33 Song V, 1], that is, I incorporated contemplatives together with active persons. Wine is spiritual understanding, as in the Gospel: “But you have kept the good wine” [Note: [Col. 1077] 34 John XI, 10], that is, you have preserved spiritual understanding for spiritual persons. Wine is Christ’s blood, as in Genesis: “He will wash his robe in wine” [Note: [Col. 1077] 35 Gen. IV, 11], that is, by the outpouring of his blood he will cleanse his Church. Wine is compunction, as in the Psalms: “You gave us wine of compunction” [Note: [Col. 1077] 36 Ps. LIX, 5]. * Wine is correction, [Col. 1079A] as in the Gospel: “Pouring in oil and wine,” that is, consolation and correction. Wine is contemplation, as in the Apocalypse: “And do not harm the wine and the oil” [Note: [Col. 1079] 1 Rev. VI, 6], that is, do not harm contemplation and action; that is, do not corrupt them. Wine is love, as in the Song: “And I will give you a cup of spiced wine” [Note: [Col. 1079] 2 Song VIII, 2], that is, I will give you joy from true love. Wine is the delight of sin, as in Joel: “And howl, all you who drink wine in sweetness” [Note: [Col. 1079] 3 Joel I, 5], that is, repent, all of you who consent to the delight of sin. Wine is love of this world, as in Proverbs: “Do not look upon wine when it grows red, when its color shines in the cup” [Note: [Col. 1079] 4 Prov. XXIII, 31], that is, do not take delight in love of the world when it entices, when its beauty smiles with fragile charm. [Col. 1079B] Wine is vengeance, as in the Apocalypse: “He too will drink of the wine of God’s wrath” [Note: [Col. 1079] 5 Rev. XIV, 10], that is, he will experience God’s vengeance before God brings judgment.

A vineyard is Christ, as in the Song: “Let us see whether the vineyard has blossomed” [Note: [Col. 1079] 6 Song VII, 12], that is, whether Christ has blossomed in human beings through faith. A vineyard is the Church, as in the Gospel: “Go, you also, into my vineyard” [Note: [Col. 1079] 7 Matt. XX, 4, 7], that is, by living well in the Church, labor in my Church. A vineyard is sacred Scripture, as in Job: “And they harvest his vineyard, which they have violently oppressed” [Note: [Col. 1079] 8 Job XXIV, 6], because the heretics claim for themselves the Scripture of the Catholic man whom they have afflicted. A vineyard is the human soul, as in Joel: “He has made my vineyard a wilderness” [Note: [Col. 1079] 9 Joel I, 7], that is, he has emptied my soul of spiritual goods. A vineyard is the Church from the gentiles, as in the Psalms: “You brought a vineyard out of Egypt” [Note: [Col. 1079] 10 Ps. LXXIX, 9], that is, you led the Church of the gentiles from the darkness of ignorance into the light of truth, since “Egypt” signifies darkness. A vineyard is the Synagogue, as in the Song: “I did not guard my vineyard” [Note: [Col. 1079] 11 Song I, 6], because on account of unbelief the Lord rejected the Synagogue from himself. A vineyard is the life of anyone who is negligent, as in Proverbs: “And I passed by the vineyard of a foolish man” [Note: [Col. 1079] 12 Prov. XXIV, 30], that is, I observed the life of a negligent person. A vineyard is a hypocrite, as in Job: “His cluster will be harmed as a vineyard in its first flowering” [Note: [Col. 1079] 13 Job XV, 33], because the hypocrite’s action is corrupted at its first appearance through the favor of human praise. By the vineyard are meant faithful peoples, as in the Song: “They appointed me keeper of the vineyards” [Note: [Col. 1079] 14 Song I, 6], that is, they chose me as leader over the peoples.

Bonds are the weaknesses of the humanity assumed in Christ, as in Job: “And who will loose his bonds?” [Note: [Col. 1079] 15 Job XXXIX, 8], because through the resurrection God the Father changed every weakness in Christ into power. Bonds are sins, as in the Psalms: “You have broken my bonds” [Note: [Col. 1079] 16 Ps. CXV, 16], that is, you have dissolved my sins.

The viper is the devil’s temptation, as in Job: “And the viper’s tongue will approach him” [Note: [Col. 1079] 17 Job XX, 16], that is, the devil’s suggestion will cast him down to the death of the soul through consent. [Col. 1080A] The viper is the act of sin, as in Isaiah: “The lion and the lioness, and from them the viper” [Note: [Col. 1079] 18 Isa. XXX, 6], that is, the devil suggesting, lust raging, and the evil act proceeding from them.

A man is Christ, as in Jeremiah: “A woman will surround a man” [Note: [Col. 1079] 19 Jer. XXXI, 22], that is, the Virgin Mary will conceive Christ. A man is understanding, as in the Gospel: “Call your husband here” [Note: [Col. 1079] 20 John IV, 14], that is, gather your understanding to yourself and understand me spiritually. A man is our spirit, as in Genesis: “And she gave it to her husband, who ate” [Note: [Col. 1079] 21 Gen. III, 6], because the flesh, polluted by delight, also draws the spirit into consent. A man is the devil, as in the Psalms: “Deliver me, Lord, from the iniquitous man” [Note: [Col. 1079] 22 Ps. CXL, 2], that is, from the devil, who loves iniquity, deliver me. A man is the error of the soul, as in the Gospel: “And the one whom you have is not your husband” [Note: [Col. 1079] 23 John IV, 18], that is, you are not joined to a bridegroom—namely, sound * understanding—but you prostitute yourself in the adultery of error. By men are meant all who are strong and spiritual, as in Job: “Of whom men sang” [Note: [Col. 1079] 24 Job XXXVI, 24], * whom teachers strong in good work proclaimed. By men are meant heretics, as in the Psalms: “Men of blood, depart from me” [Note: [Col. 1079] 25 Ps. CXXXVIII, 19], that is, O heretics, who drink blood through the deception of souls, flee from me. By men are meant the five bodily senses, as in the Gospel: “For you have had five husbands” [Note: [Col. 1079] 26 John IV, 18], that is, you have clung to the five senses of your body.

The virgin is that ornament of all virgins, as in Isaiah: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” [Note: [Col. 1079] 27 Isa. VII, 14], that is, Mary bore Christ without injury, just as she conceived him without corruption. A virgin is the holy Church, as in Paul: [Col. 1080C] “For I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” [Note: [Col. 1079] 28 2 Cor. XI, 2], because that same eminent preacher was intent on offering the Church, without spot or wrinkle, to your Savior. * A virgin is a holy soul, as in Leviticus: “He takes a virgin as his wife” [Note: [Col. 1079] 29 Lev. XXI, 13], because he will join a faithful soul to himself through love. A virgin is a wicked mind, as in Isaiah: “Sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon” [Note: [Col. 1079] 30 Isa. XLVII, 1], because the soul, dwelling softly in earthly thought and barren of good work, has been subjected to the confusion of vices. * A virgin is the Jewish people, as in the prophet: “The virgin of Israel has been cast down” [Note: [Col. 1079] 31 Amos V, 2], that is, the Jewish people, barren and fruitless on account of unbelief, has been rejected.

The rod is the abiding Word, as in Exodus: “He grasped its tail, and it became a rod” [Note: [Col. 1079] 32 Exod. IV, 4], because the elect believe that God and man are Lord in one and the same Christ. [Col. 1080D] The rod is Christ’s humanity, as in Paul: “And the rod of Aaron, which had blossomed” [Note: [Col. 1079] 33 Heb. IX, 4], because Christ’s humanity, that of the true priest, shone with every adornment of holiness. The rod is Christ’s power, as in the Psalms: “The Lord will send forth the rod of your strength from Zion” [Note: [Col. 1079] 34 Ps. CIX, 2], that is, he will bring forth the power of his strength from the Jewish people. The rod is the banner of the cross, as in Exodus: “And Aaron took the rod before Pharaoh” [Col. 1081A] [Note: [Col. 1081] 1 Exod. VII, 10], because the order of preachers proclaimed the banner of the cross before kings and princes. The rod is Christ’s mother, as in Isaiah: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse” [Note: [Col. 1081] 2 Isa. XI, 1], that is, Mary will proceed from the offspring of Jesse. The rod is faith, as in Exodus: “Take the rod in your hand, with which you will perform signs” [Note: [Col. 1081] 3 Exod. IV, 17], that is, fulfill right faith in action, through which you must perform miracles. The rod is correction, as in the Psalms: “Your rod and your staff” [Note: [Col. 1081] 4 Ps. XXII, 4], that is, your correction and consolation: “They themselves have comforted me.” The rod is the congregation of the righteous, as in the Psalms: “You have redeemed the rod of your inheritance” [Note: [Col. 1081] 5 Ps. LXXIII, 2], that is, you have stripped the heirs of your kingdom from the power of the devil. The rod is divine chastisement, as in Jeremiah: “I see a watching rod” [Note: [Col. 1081] 6 Jer. I, 11], that is, I behold the divine election touching the elect. The rod is the terror of the Law, as in Job: “Take your rod away from me” [Note: [Col. 1081] 7 Job IX, 34], that is, legal fear. The rod is divine persecution, as in Jeremiah: “With the rod of his indignation,” that is, with the blow of his strictness. The rod is the judge’s sentence, as in Isaiah: “And he will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth” [Note: [Col. 1081] 8 Isa. XI, 11], that is, he will condemn sinners by the sentence of his judgment.

The little rod is the holy Church, as in the Song: “Like a little column of smoke from * Aaron” [Note: [Col. 1081] 9 Song III, 6], that is, the holy Church, sending forth a reputation of virtue from itself.

Green things are eternal goods, as in Job: “And he seeks out every green thing” [Note: [Col. 1081] 10 Job XXXIX, 11], that is, he strives to possess those things that are eternal goods.

The Powers are angels, as in the Gospel: “For the powers of heaven will be shaken” [Note: [Col. 1081] 11 Luke XXI, 26], that is, the angels will be shaken at the judgment.

A vision is revelation, as in Daniel: “A vision appeared to me” [Note: [Col. 1081] 12 Dan. VIII, 1], that is, a revelation of God’s secrets became known to me. A vision is the life of hypocrites, as in Job: * “He will pass away like a vision of the night” [Note: [Col. 1081] 13 Job XX, 8], that is, the obscure life of hypocrites will fail.

The inward parts are human minds, as in Job: “Who placed in the inward parts of human beings” [Note: [Col. 1081] 14 Job XXXVIII, 36], that is, in human minds, “wisdom, if not I?” The inward parts are the affections of the heart, as in Job: “He has poured out my inward parts upon the earth” [Note: [Col. 1081] 15 Job XVI, 14], that is, he has allowed my affections to dissipate among earthly things. The inward parts are the pride of the wicked, as in Job: “His inward parts are full of fat” [Note: [Col. 1081] 16 Job XXI, 24], that is, proud movements are full of earthly pleasure.

The vine is Christ, as in the Gospel: “I am the vine” [Col. 1081D] [Note: [Col. 1081] 17 John XV, 1, 5], because he himself is the source and * strength of every good. The vine is faith, as in Genesis: “And to the vine, O * my son, your donkey” [Note: [Col. 1081] 18 Gen. XLIX, 11], that is, they bind his Church to the sacraments of faith. The vine is anyone who has been perverted, as in Jeremiah: “How have you been turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” [Note: [Col. 1081] 19 Jer. II, 21], that is, how have you been changed from good and holy into something evil and perverse?

Life is temporal glory, as in Job: “And life to those who are in the bitterness of life” [Col. 1082A] [Note: [Col. 1081] 20 Job XXXIX, 20], that is, those whose glory is bestowed temporarily upon holy men who devote themselves to continual lamentation. Life is the external approval of action, as in Proverbs: “The life of the flesh is the health of the heart” [Note: [Col. 1081] 21 Prov. XIV, 30], because goodwill of mind commends the practice of external action.

A ribbon is holy preaching, as in the Song: “Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon” [Note: [Col. 1081] 22 Song IV, 3], because through their preaching preachers restrain the wandering thoughts in the minds of their hearers. A ribbon is hope of heavenly things, as in Exodus: “And you shall bind it with a violet ribbon” [Note: [Col. 1081] 23 Exod. XXVIII, 37], that is, you shall strengthen virtue in your mind through hope of heavenly things. By ribbons are meant the divine commandments, as in the book of Numbers: “Putting violet ribbons on them” [Note: [Col. 1081] 24 Num. XV, 38], that is, having divine precepts in their hearts. [Col. 1082B]

The calf is Christ, as in Genesis: “He took a calf from the herd” [Note: [Col. 1081] 25 Gen. XVIII, 7], that is, Christ born from the race of the patriarchs. The calf is pride of heart, as in Leviticus: “Let him offer a calf for his sin” [Note: [Col. 1081] 26 Lev. IV, 3], that is, for forgiveness of his offense, let him humble the proud movement in his heart. The calf is the suffering Redeemer, as in the Gospel: “He killed the fattened calf” [Note: [Col. 1081] 27 Luke XV, 27], because the Lord Jesus Christ, adorned with the fullness of every holiness, died for sinners. The calf is the devil, as in Exodus: “They made a calf and worshiped it” [Note: [Col. 1081] 28 Exod. XXXII, 8], that is, they received the devil into themselves and served him. The calf is our flesh, as in the books of Kings: “And they sacrificed the calf and presented the boy to Eli” [Note: [Col. 1081] 29 1 Kings I, 25], because purity is then worthily offered to God if the wantonness of the flesh is first slain. By calves are meant the Jews, as in the Psalms: “Many calves surrounded me” [Note: [Col. 1081] 30 Ps. XXI, 13], that is, proud Jews persecuted me. By calves are meant wanton movements of the heart, as in the Psalms: “Then they shall place calves upon your altar” [Note: [Col. 1081] 31 Ps. L, 21], that is, in their mind they will mortify wanton movements.

The heifer is Christ’s flesh, as in the book of Numbers: “That they should bring you a red heifer” [Note: [Col. 1081] 32 Num. XIX, 2], that is, Christ’s flesh, called by that color on account of the likeness of sin. The heifer is a man’s wife, as in the book of Judges: “Unless you had plowed with my heifer” [Note: [Col. 1081] 33 Judg. XIV, 18], that is, unless you had acquired it from my wife. The heifer is a wicked mind, as in Hosea: “Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing” [Note: [Col. 1081] 34 Hos. X, 11], that is, a wicked mind accustomed to earthly unrest.

[Col. 1082D] Glass is the condition of the citizens of heaven, as in Job: “Gold or glass shall not be compared with it” [Note: [Col. 1081] 35 Job XXVIII, 17], because neither the saints shining in this life nor the heavenly citizens, who foresee one another’s thoughts, can be compared with Christ. Glass is the deceptive allure of this age, as in Proverbs: “When its color shines in the glass” [Note: [Col. 1081] 36 Prov. XXIII, 31], that is, when the appearance of worldly love smiles with deceptive allure.

[Col. 1083A] Birds are holy souls, as in Job: “The birds of heaven also lie hidden” [Note: [Col. 1083] 1 Job XXVIII, 21], because even holy souls in this life cannot attain full knowledge of God. Birds are the rulers of this age, as in the Gospel: “So that the birds of heaven may rest in its branches” [Note: [Col. 1083] 2 Matt. XIII, 32], that is, the highest rulers of this age may rest in its mysteries. Birds are all who are proud, as in the Psalms: “The birds of heaven and the fish of the sea” [Note: [Col. 1083] 3 Ps. VIII, 9], that is, the proud of the world and all the curious in the depths. Birds are malignant spirits, as in the Gospel: “And the birds of heaven ate it” [Note: [Col. 1083] 4 Luke VIII, 5].

A plowshare is the sharpness of holy religion, as in the book of Judges: “He struck six hundred men of the Philistines with a plowshare” [Note: [Col. 1083] 5 Judg. III, 31], because the holy man overthrows the powers of darkness through the sharpness of his religion. By plowshares are meant preachings, [Col. 1083B] as in Isaiah: “And they shall beat their swords into plowshares” [Note: [Col. 1083] 6 Isa. II, 4], that is, they will change the harshness of their tongues into health-giving thoughts.

The voice is the Son of God, as in the Psalms: “The voice of the Lord is over the waters” [Note: [Col. 1083] 7 Ps. XXVIII, 3], because the Son of God spoke to human beings in the flesh. The voice is contemplation, as in Ezekiel: “When a voice came over * the grain” [Note: [Col. 1083] 8 Ezek. I, 25], that is, when in contemplation of truth it surpassed the angelic nature. The voice is the preaching of teachers, as in the Song: “Let your voice sound in my ears” [Note: [Col. 1083] 9 Song II, 14], that is, let your preaching be heard by those obedient to me. The voice is the movement of desire, as in Job: “The roar of the lion and the voice of the lioness” [Note: [Col. 1083] 10 Job IV, 10], that is, the devil’s suggestion and the movement of desire. The voice is compunction, as in Ezekiel: “And the sound of a great commotion” [Note: [Col. 1083] 11 Ezek. III, 10], that is, the cry of great sorrow. [Col. 1083C] The voice is divine exhortation, as in Isaiah: “And your ears shall hear the voice of one admonishing behind your back” [Note: [Col. 1083] 12 Isa. XXX, 21], that is, you who have turned your back on God through sin will receive inwardly a salutary admonition, so that you may turn your face toward him through repentance. The voice is the enemy’s suggestion, as in Job: “They did not hear the voice of the taskmaster” [Note: [Col. 1083] 13 Job III, 18], that is, they did not consent to the suggestion of temptation. The voice is the terror of persecution, as in the Psalms: “The rivers raised their voice” [Note: [Col. 1083] 14 Ps. XCII, 3; Ps. LXVI, 2], that is, proud persecutors raised their threat.

The face is knowledge of the truth, as in the Psalms: “Let him illuminate his face upon us” [Note: [Col. 1083] 15 Job IX, 24], that is, let him infuse knowledge of the truth. The face is a wicked mind, as in Job: “He covers the face of its judges” [Note: [Col. 1083] 16 1 Cor. II, 8], because error obscured the minds of those who judged Christ: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” [Note: [Col. 1083] 17 Job XXVIII, 7].

The vulture is our Redeemer, as in Job: “Nor has the vulture’s eye looked upon it” [Note: [Col. 1083] 18 Lev. XI, 14], because the Synagogue did not approve the Savior’s commandments through obedience. The vulture is any plunderer, as in the Law we are forbidden to eat the vulture [Note: [Col. 1083] 19 Job XVI, 15], that is, imitate a plunderer.

[Col. 1084A] A wound is sin, as in Job: “He tore me with wound upon wound” [Note: [Col. 1083] 20 Prov. XX, 30], that is, he permitted sin upon sin in certain people who cling to me through faith [lacuna] permitted it. A wound is tribulation, as in Proverbs: “The bruise of a wound will wipe away evils” [Note: [Col. 1083] 21 Song II, 5; V, 8], because the harshness of tribulation cures sins. A wound is charity, as in the Song: “I am wounded by charity” [Note: [Col. 1083] 22 Job V, 18], that is, I am wounded by the point of love. A wound is the pain of the scourge, as in Job: “He himself heals and wounds” [Note: [Col. 1083] 23 Job IX, 17], that is, he scourges and consoles. By a wound are meant our distresses, as in Job: “And he multiplied my wounds” [Note: [Col. 1083] 24 Luke XIII, 32], because the distresses that the holy Church suffers in the present life are many.

A fox is Herod, as in the Gospel: “Go, tell that fox” [Note: [Col. 1083] 25 Matt. VIII, 20], that is, the deceitful Herod. By foxes are meant all who are crafty, as in the Gospel: “Foxes have dens” [Note: [Col. 1083] 26 Song II, 15], because fraud and deceit are in the minds of the wicked. By foxes are meant heretics, as in the Song: “Catch for us the little foxes” [Note: [Col. 1083] 27 Judg. XV, 4–5], that is, beware of deceitful heretics. By foxes are meant persecutors, as in the book of Judges: “Samson made foxes with burning torches run through the fields of the Philistines” [Note: [Col. 1083] 28 Ps. LXII, 11], because Christ sometimes permits persecutors to destroy the goods of the wicked. By foxes are meant malignant spirits, as in the Psalms: “He will be delivered into the hands of the sword; they will become portions of foxes” [Note: [Col. 1083] 29 Song IV, 5], that is, they will be condemned at the judgment, “and they will go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.”

The breasts are the two Testaments, as in the Song: “Your two breasts are like two fawns” [Note: [Col. 1083] 30 Prov. XXX, 33], because from the two Testaments two peoples arise through understanding. The breasts are the mystical words of sacred Scripture, as in Proverbs: “He who presses the breasts strongly to draw out milk expresses butter” [Note: [Col. 1083] 31 Song I, 12; IV, 10], that is, whoever carefully examines profound words in order to extract rich sweetness gathers understanding from them. The breasts are the two commandments of charity, as in the Song: “Your works are more beautiful than wine” [Note: [Col. 1083] 32 Job III, 12], that is, the signs of the twofold charity are far better than carnal love. The breasts are illicit blandishments, as in Job: “Why was I suckled at the breasts?” [Note: [Col. 1083] 33 Prov. VII, 18], that is, why did harmful blandishments cherish me? The breasts are illicit desires, as in Proverbs: “Come, let us drink deeply of the breasts and enjoy desired embraces” [Note: [Col. 1083] 34 Lev. XIII, 20], that is, let us be refreshed by lawful desires, and let us take our stand in desirable pleasures.

[Col. 1084D] An ulcer is a bad habit, as in Leviticus: “Leprosy has arisen in the ulcer” [Note: [Col. 1083] 35 Luke XVI, 21], that is, an ingrained fault appears as wickedness. By ulcers are meant sins, as in the Gospel: “But dogs also came and licked his ulcers” [Note: [Col. 1083] 36 Isa. XIII, 22], because preachers taught and healed the sins of the gentile people.

Ululae are the wicked, as in Isaiah: “And * the screech-owls answered in his presence” [Note: [Col. 1083] 37 This note is missing in Migne’s printed edition], meaning that, apart from the transformation of the wicked, they somehow speak in the thoughts of the impious.

Ulmus is any worldly person, as in Isaiah: “I will plant in the desert the fir tree and the elm” [Note: [Col. 1085] 1 Isa. XLI, 19], that is, among the Gentiles I will establish a contemplative and faithful worldly preacher who gives support.

The navel is the order of the Church’s preachers, as in the Song: “Your navel is a turned bowl” [Note: [Col. 1085] 2 Song VII, 2], meaning that the preachers of the Church, with uprightness of conduct, pour out the cup of preaching. The navel is lust, as in Job: “And his strength is in the navel of his belly” [Note: [Col. 1085] 3 Job XL, 11], meaning that the devil rules both women and men chiefly through lust. The navel is carnal affection, as in Ezekiel: “Your navel was not cut off” [Note: [Col. 1085] 4 Ezek. XVI, 4], that is, carnal affection was not removed from you.

The shadow is humanity, as in Jeremiah: * “Under his shadow we shall come among the nations” [Note: [Col. 1085] 5 Lam. IV, 20], that is, through the sacraments of his incarnation we shall receive the life of our souls in the present age. The shadow is Christ’s protection, as in the Song: “I sat under the shadow of him whom I desired” [Note: [Col. 1085] 6 Song II, 3], that is, I rested in the protection of Christ, whom I love. The shadow is the refreshment of consolation, as in Job: “As * the stag longs for the shade” [Note: [Col. 1085] 7 Job VII, 2], so the one under trial longs for refreshment amid trial. The shadow is the harshness of the Law, as in Job: “And * he will bring his shadow into the light” [Note: [Col. 1085] 8 Job XII, 22], that is, they change the rigor of the Law into the gentleness of grace. The shadow is any impious person, as in Job: “The shadows protect his shadow” [Note: [Col. 1085] 9 Job XL, 17], meaning that sinners defend a sinner in his guilt. The shadow is forgetfulness, as in Job: “Let darkness and the shadow of death obscure him” [Note: [Col. 1085] 10 Job III, 5], meaning that only the death of the body kills the holy martyrs. The shadow is infernal darkness, as in Job: “A land of misery and darkness, where there is the shadow [of death]” [Note: [Col. 1085] 11 Job XXXIX, 14], meaning that hell is full of every misery and gloom, where there is the darkness of eternal damnation.

The hoof is perfection, as in Job: “The hoof digs the earth,” meaning that the holy preacher softens the hardness in his subjects through the perfection of virtue. The hoof is final works, as in Exodus: * “And it will remain as a hoof indeed” [Note: [Col. 1085] 12 Exod. X, 26], meaning that we must not abandon even our final works, provided that they are good. The hooves signify the ends of this world, as in Genesis: “Biting the horse’s hooves” [Note: [Col. 1085] 13 Gen. XLIX, 17], meaning that through his knowledge the devil will curse in the Antichrist at the end of the world.

The only one is our soul, as in the Psalms: “And my only one from the hand of the dog” [Note: [Col. 1085] 14 Ps. XXI, 21], that is, my soul from the power of the enemy.

The ointment is repentance, as in the Gospel: “She brought an alabaster flask of ointment” [Note: [Col. 1085] 15 Luke VII, 37], that is, the devotion of a repentant spirit. The ointment is holy conduct, as in the Gospel: “And the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” [Note: [Col. 1085] 16 John XII, 3], that is, the Church was sprinkled with the reputation of her conduct. Ointments signify the gifts of the Holy Spirit, as in the Song: “We shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” [Note: [Col. 1085] 17 Song I, 4], that is, we shall live well according to the examples of your virtues. Ointments signify the delights of the flesh, as in the Book of Wisdom: “Let us fill ourselves with the wine of * wisdom and ointments” [Note: [Col. 1085] 18 Wis. II, 7], that is, let us refresh ourselves with the world’s sweetness and the pleasure of the flesh.

The urn is Christ’s humanity, as in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Having a golden urn containing manna” [Note: [Col. 1085] 19 Heb. IX, 4], that is, Christ’s humanity, full of the sweetness of every virtue.

The nettle is the harshness of vices, as in Isaiah: “And in place of the nettle the myrtle will grow” [Note: [Col. 1085] 20 Isa. LV, 13], that is, in place of the harshness of vices there will be the self-control of virtues. Nettles signify depraved affections, as in Isaiah: “In his houses thorns and nettles will grow” [Note: [Col. 1085] 21 Isa. XLIV, 13], that is, in his thoughts there will be pleasures that * fatten and affections that bite.

The bear is any cruel person, as in Isaiah: “The calf and the bear will feed together” [Note: [Col. 1085] 22 Isa. XI, 7], that is, the one who was cruel will be nourished by the feasts of sacred Scripture. The bear is impurity, as in the Books of Kings: “I, your servant, killed both the lion and the bear” [Note: [Col. 1085] 23 1 Kings XVII, 36], that is, I extinguished pride and lust. The bear signifies the Roman emperors, as in the Books of Kings: “Two bears came out of the forest” [Note: [Col. 1085] 24 2 Kings II, 24], meaning that emperors who came out from Rome devastated the Jews.

The womb is the substance of the Father, as in the Psalms: “From the womb, before the dawn, I begot you” [Note: [Col. 1085] 25 Ps. CIX, 3], meaning that from his own substance the Father eternally begot his Son. The womb is the Synagogue, as in Job: “And I entreated the sons of my womb” [Note: [Col. 1085] 26 Job XIX, 17], that is, I addressed the people of the Synagogue humbly. The womb is the grace of God, as in Job: “From the * womb the ice came forth” [Note: [Col. 1085] 27 Job XXXVIII, 29], meaning that the hardened Synagogue proceeds from the grace of God.
