The wineskin is the holy Church, as in the Psalms: “Gathering the waters of the sea as into a wineskin” [Note: [Col. 1085] 28 Ps. XXXII, 7], meaning that Christ united his Church with the people of the Gentiles. The wineskin is the letter of the Law, as in Genesis: “And taking the boy and the wineskin of water, he placed it on her shoulders” [Note: [Col. 1085] 29 Gen. XXI, 14], meaning that God gave the precepts and the letter of the Law to the people of the Synagogue. The wineskin is a depraved mind, as in the Psalms: “He set the waters as though in a wineskin” [Note: [Col. 1085] 30 Ps. XXXII, 7], meaning that, lest they come to fruition, the Lord sometimes enclosed wickedness in a depraved thought. The wineskin is this mortal body, as in the Psalms: “I have become like a wineskin in the frost” [Note: [Col. 1085] 31 Ps. CXVIII, 83], that is, my body is subject to mortal corruption. Wineskins signify the hearts of spiritual people, as in the Gospel: “They put new wine into new wineskins” [Note: [Col. 1085] 32 Matt. IX, 17], meaning that hearts renewed through holiness receive the grace of God. Wineskins signify the minds of the wicked, as in the Gospel: “Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins” [Note: [Col. 1085] 33 Matt. IX, 17], meaning that God does not pour the gift of his grace into minds grown old through the habit of sin.

The grape is the love of the present life, as in Jeremiah: “Everyone who eats the unripe grape—his teeth will be set on edge” [Note: [Col. 1087] 1 Jer. XXXI, 30], meaning that the sharpness of his spiritual senses diminishes for one who enjoys the world, which is an untimely fruit. The grape is an evil work, as in the Song of Deuteronomy: “Their grape is a grape of gall” [Note: [Col. 1087] 2 Deut. XXXII, 32], that is, their work is a work of bitterness. Grapes signify the fervor of love, as in the Gospel: “Do they gather grapes from thorns?” [Note: [Col. 1087] 3 Matt. VII, 16], meaning that we cannot receive from heretics the fervor of true love.

The wife is the Church, as in the Apocalypse: “The bride, the wife of the Lamb” [Note: [Col. 1087] 4 Rev. XXI, 9], that is, the Church, the bride of Christ. The wife is the wisdom of the righteous, as in the Psalms: “Your wife is like a fruitful vine” [Note: [Col. 1087] 5 Ps. CXXVII, 3], meaning that the wisdom of the saints is enriched by the moisture of inward grace. The wife is a good example, as in Leviticus: “He shall take a virgin as wife” [Note: [Col. 1087] 6 Lev. XXI, 13], that is, he will join to his good conduct the chaste example of another. The wife is a good action, as in Exodus: “I love my wife and children; I will not go out free” [Note: [Col. 1087] 7 Exod. XXI, 5], that is, I wish to persist in good action, and through the fruits of good works * I still wish to go forth into the freedom of contemplation. The wife is a good will, as in Genesis: “Enter the ark, you and your wife” [Note: [Col. 1087] 8 Gen. VII, 1; Luke XIV, 20], that is, enter into the repose of your mind with a good and devoted will. The wife is the pleasure of the flesh, as in the Gospel: “I have taken a wife” [Note: [Col. 1087] 9 Ps. II, 2], and therefore I cannot * hasten toward the kingdom of God.

## X

XPS is the Lord Jesus, as in the Psalms: “Against the Lord and against his Christ” [Note: [Col. 1087] 10 Ps. CIV, 15], meaning that King Herod and the Jews, with their rulers, conspired against God the Father and his Son. The christs signify holy men, as in the Psalms: “Do not touch my christs” [Note: [Col. 1087] 11 Job IX, 9], that is, do not trouble the holy men anointed by the grace of my Spirit.

## Y

YADES.—YDRIAE.—YDROPICUS.—YSOPUS.

The Hyades are holy teachers, as in Job: “Who makes Arcturus, Orion, and the Hyades” [Note: [Col. 1087] 12 John II, 8], meaning that the Lord established the holy Church and produced in her martyrs and spiritual teachers.

The water-jars are the hearts of the faithful, as in the Gospel: “Fill the water-jars with water” [Note: [Col. 1087] 13 Gen. XXIV, 18], meaning that preachers ought first to pour fear into the hearts of the faithful, since “the * fear of the Lord” is the beginning of wisdom. The water-jar is wisdom, as in Genesis: “She placed her water-jar upon her shoulder” [Note: [Col. 1087] 14 Luke XIV, 2], meaning that the Church called to Christ from the Gentiles humbly bent her wisdom, of which she had previously boasted in lofty fashion, toward spiritual usefulness.

The dropsical person is any greedy person, as in the Gospel: “And behold, a dropsical man” [Note: [Col. 1087] 15 1 Kings IV, 33], meaning that the greedy person, the more he has, the more he desires to have, just as the dropsical person thirsts more the more he drinks.

Hyssop is Christ’s humanity, as in the Books of Kings: “From the cedar that is in * Lebanon even to the hyssop that comes forth from the wall” [Note: [Col. 1087] 16 Num. XIX, 6], that is, from the divinity he has in the Father even to his humanity, which proceeded from the Virgin. Hyssop is baptism, as in the Book of * Numbers: “Cedarwood, hyssop, and scarlet” [Note: [Col. 1087] 17 Lev. XIX, 4, 49], that is, martyrdom and baptism. Hyssop is humanity, as in the Psalms: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop” [Note: [Col. 1087] 18 Ps. L, 9], that is, you shall humble me, and thus I shall be cleansed.

## Z

ZEAL.—TARES.—BELT.

Zeal is spiritual fervor, as in the Psalms: “The zeal of your house has consumed me” [Note: [Col. 1087] 19 Ps. LXVIII, 10], that is, spiritual fervor has shaken me. Zeal is envy, as in Paul: “For while there is zeal and contention among you” [Note: [Col. 1087] 20 1 Cor. III, 3], that is, worldly envy.

The tares are the reprobate, as in the Gospel: “Gather the tares first, and bind them” [Note: [Col. 1087] 21 Matt. XIII, 30], meaning that the angels will gather the reprobate together and place them under a like punishment, since here they were in like guilt.

The belt is the bond of charity, as in the Apocalypse: “And girded about the breasts with a golden belt” [Note: [Col. 1087] 22 Rev. I, 13], that is, he is adorned in his actions with spontaneous charity. The belt is discipline of the mind, as in Leviticus: “He shall be girded with a linen belt” [Note: [Col. 1087] 23 Lev. XVI, 4], that is, he will be strengthened by spiritual discipline. The belt is mortification of the flesh, as in the Books of Kings: “And girded at his loins with a leather belt” [Note: [Col. 1087] 24 2 Kings I, 8], that is, with the mortification of the flesh in the members of the reprobate.

# COMMENTARIES OF BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, ON THE CANTICLES SUNG AT MATINS

To the most reverend and most zealous in the cultivation of true religion, King LOUIS, RABANUS, your devoted little servant in Christ, wishes eternal salvation.

Recently, when I came to you at your summons in the small cell of our monastery called Ratestorph, and we were speaking together about the sacred Scriptures, you deigned to persuade me to expound for you in an allegorical sense the canticles that the holy Church sings at the praises of matins. At that time I replied that I had already done this in my little works, which, as far as I could, I had composed in my treatment of the divine books, and that there was no need to repeat it again. But when I had returned to the monastery and asked whether I had already provided an exposition of all those canticles, I discovered that I had not yet applied my hand to those which come from the prophets—namely, Isaiah and Habakkuk. Therefore I thought that I should combine these with the others into a single volume and send it to you for reading, especially during these days of Lent.

I did this, and placed both editions together: namely, the one according to which the Roman Church sings, and the one translated from the Hebrew truth, which most of the other Churches of the West possess. Wherever the meaning of the two editions seemed to differ from one another, I explained the sense of each, and completed the work according to what I found already expounded in the sayings of the holy Fathers, or what, with the help of divine grace, I was able to investigate myself. I ask the reader that, if anything in it displeases him, he not condemn it hastily, but first consider whether it agrees with the understanding of our predecessors and is not contrary to the truth. Thus, weighing my devotion of mind more than the eloquence of my words, let him judge it with fair judgment, knowing what is written: “In the measure with which you measure, it shall be measured to you” (Matt. VII).

If anyone is troubled that the canticles themselves do not preserve the order in which they were composed by their authors, but that those published later are placed first—for the canticle of Exodus and the canticle of Deuteronomy were issued by the Lawgiver before the other canticles—let him recognize that this was not done without reason, but in a fitting order and according to a rationale, so that they might correspond in every respect to the divine mysteries and institutions.

For on Sunday, which is altogether honorable and worthy of praise, the praises of the three youths are sung in the Church. In them all creatures are summoned to praise and bless their Creator. On Monday, however, the canticle of Isaiah is sung, in which the coming of the Savior and the sacrament of baptism are proclaimed, because these are the beginnings of our salvation. On Tuesday as well, the canticle or prayer of Hezekiah is sung; in it, recovering from his illness, he offered God thanksgiving for his salvation, admonishing us that, after receiving God’s grace and the cleansing of holy baptism, and being released from the bonds of death, we should strive to give thanks to God throughout the whole time of our life.

On Wednesday the canticle of the prophetess Hannah is sung, in which the expulsion of Jewish unbelief is indicated and the election of the Church from the Gentiles is demonstrated. On Thursday, appropriately, the canticle of the Israelites is sung, which they sang after celebrating the Passover, when they had been led out of Egypt and crossed the Red Sea on dry ground. On that same day our Savior, celebrating the typical Passover with his disciples, likewise consecrated the mystical Passover continually in the sacrament of his body and blood and in the offering of that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world.

Therefore, on Friday, the canticle of the prophet Habakkuk is suitably sung in the Church. It contains the sacraments of the Lord’s Passion and declares the mysteries of his resurrection and ascension into heaven, so that it may be known to all how, on Friday—the day on which the first man was formed—the human race was restored to eternal life through Christ.

On Saturday, too, it was rightly and suitably established that the canticle of Deuteronomy should be sung. In it God’s benefits toward the former people are set forth, and how ungratefully that same people received and abused them is most clearly expressed. For on that day it was anciently established that Deuteronomy of the Law should be read in the synagogue, lest the people forget God’s commandments, but rather be stirred to observe his precepts. Hence, when James spoke, we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “For Moses from ancient times has in every city those who proclaim him in the synagogues, where he is read every Sabbath” (Acts XV). We, therefore, are likewise instructed spiritually by the same song, so that we may not be ungrateful for God’s benefits, but may rather devote ourselves to his praises throughout the whole time of our life, until that Sabbath comes in which we shall eternally possess rest with Christ.

The canticles taken from the Gospel, however, were fittingly and suitably decreed by the teachers of the Church to be sung every day in the Church. Thus the canticle of the prophet Zechariah, where the rising of light in the darkness is recalled, is to be sung at the praises of matins; and the canticle of Mary, the Mother of God, in which the scattering of the proud, the overthrow of the powerful, and the exaltation of the humble by the arm of the Lord are proclaimed, is rightly sung last in the evening office. For in the evening of the world—that is, at the end of the age—through the coming of the Savior, the proud will be cast into the fire of hell, and the humble will be exalted into eternal glory.

These things, then, we have brought forth in writing according to what we have understood and received as handed down by the teachers, without prejudging those who understand better and know how to express such matters more eloquently. But you, most wise king, well instructed in all things, graciously receive what has been offered to you by your devoted servant, and use it according to what you perceive will benefit you and your people. For my part, I shall gladly render you whatever service I can, and shall even devote myself to it, praying and entreating God for your safety and for the stability of your kingdom, so that you may live here long in health and, after the end of this present life, enjoy eternal life in the heavenly kingdom. May the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve you here and everywhere, now and always, sound and unharmed.

# THE CANTICLE OF THE PROPHET ISAIAH BEGINS

After the prophet Isaiah had discussed in mystical expressions the Lord’s incarnation, the calling of the Church, and the destruction of idolatry—first relating the flower of the shoot rising from the root of Jesse, upon whom the grace of the sevenfold Spirit would rest, and then proclaiming in the Church the harmony and dwelling together of wild beasts with cattle, that is, of the rich with the poor, and of the fierce and proud with the gentle and humble—and had testified that the sign of the cross summoned the nations everywhere to the unity of faith, he finally made clear that the desolation of the river of Egypt, that is, the error of the Gentiles who dwelt in the darkness of unbelief, was to be undone. Thus he summons the people of the Church, or the faithful soul, to praise God, so that it may attribute to his grace the fact that, having been liberated from its enemies and separated from the children of wrath, it has become a daughter of reconciliation and mercy. Therefore he says:

“I will confess to you, Lord, because you were angry with me. Your wrath has turned away, and you have comforted me.” Confession, then, as we have often said, is an equivocal term and is understood differently according to the circumstances. Those who lament their sins confess—that is, those who perform worthy repentance for them—and those who give thanks to the Lord also confess. The former is expressed in tears, the latter in joy; the former is recognized in affliction, the latter in holy gladness of mind. Hence the faithful people here exult in overflowing joy, signifying a kind of image of the future age, where these voices are unceasing and they celebrate the Lord’s praises with devoted minds.

Great indeed is the joy of a soul that was once sinful when it remembers that, through the grace of holy baptism, it was snatched from the bonds of sins and the snares of error, and through the renewal of the Holy Spirit was transferred into the portion of the elect, possessing hope of future life and everlasting joy. But he shows from where this grace came to him, saying:

“Behold, God is my Savior: I will act confidently, and I will not fear.” For the whole cause of our redemption and salvation rests in the incarnation of Jesus Christ our Lord, because there is no other name given under heaven to human beings, as the apostle Peter testifies, by which we must be saved. Of him Paul also says: “For by grace we have been saved” (Eph. II). And again: “Who,” he says, “will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII).

Of him he says again: “We give thanks to God, who has made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in light, who has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love. In him we have redemption and the forgiveness of sins. He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, because in him all things were created in heaven and on earth” (Col. I).

Everyone who rightly believes in the Lord and hopes in him acts confidently in him, knowing that he is able to liberate and defend those who truly trust in his protection. For this reason he does not fear the adversary, since the adversary cannot harm him unless permitted to do so. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord is my helper, and I shall see my enemies” (Ps. CXVII). What is understood is that they will be made weak and powerless; for he means spiritual wickedness, which he says will be seen at that judgment where the devil, already destroyed and condemned with his other servants, will appear before human eyes.

“Because the Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation.” One whom the Lord’s help appears to strengthen cannot be overthrown and fall. But lest it be thought that the person whom the Lord’s gifts preserve merely avoids dangers, he adds: “He has become my salvation,” because through him they receive eternal life, and through him they are counted worthy to escape the ruins of this world. He himself is both the strength and the eternal praise of the blessed.

Let the most wicked heresy hear that the Lord has become such for those who are saved, for those to whom the Lord previously did not belong, so that in Scripture we may understand “creation” and “making” not always as the formation of things that did not exist, but sometimes as grace granted to those who have merited that God become theirs.

After this, the Prophet, under a figure, exhorts those who believe in God to strive attentively to learn his teaching, since they have received both his portion and his faith, and he says:

“You shall draw water with joy from the springs of the Savior.” Above he had called him Emmanuel and by other names—“Hasten to strip the spoils,” “Make haste to plunder”—so that he might not seem to be someone other than the one whom Gabriel announced to the Virgin, saying: “You shall call his name Jesus. For he will save his people” (Matt. I). Now he calls him the Savior and proclaims that water is to be drawn from his springs, by no means from the waters of the river of Egypt, which were struck, nor from the waters of the river of Rasni, but from the springs of Jesus. For in the language of the Hebrews this is what “Savior” expresses.

Hence he himself cried out in the Gospel: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” But the Evangelist says: “He spoke this about the Holy Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (John VII). And in another Gospel he himself says: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst forever, but the water that I shall give him will become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life” (John IV).

Let us understand the springs of the Savior as evangelical teaching, concerning which we read in the seventy-seventh Psalm: “Bless God in the assemblies, the God of the springs of Israel.” The apostles poured this teaching into the Gentiles; for from there the spring of religion flowed out among the other nations.

Hence it follows:

“You shall say on that day: Give thanks to the Lord and invoke his name. Make known his inventions among the peoples; remember that his name is exalted. Sing to the Lord, for he has acted magnificently. Announce this throughout the whole earth.”

The Lord’s “inventions” are the divine commandments, which have been brought forth solely from the counsel of supreme wisdom and become altogether saving for those who strive to fulfill them in their deeds. The apostles and the other teachers from Israel command these things to those from the Gentiles who have believed: that they should give thanks to the Lord alone, abandon their idols, invoke his name, and proclaim all his works to unbelievers, so that they may know that he alone is exalted, and that “in his name every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II). He must be praised because he has acted magnificently, and his mercy must be proclaimed throughout the entire world.

The beginning of the hundred and fourth Psalm also agrees with this passage, where it is written: “Give thanks to the Lord and invoke his name; announce his works among the nations.” The order of these words therefore consists of three parts. First he says: “Give thanks to the Lord,” that is, praise him and acquire for yourselves the grace of divinity through good works, because praising the Lord consists in both honoring him with the mouth and carrying out his commands through works. Here “confession” is to be understood as that which never ceases to celebrate the Lord’s praises, since what follows declares the same intention and action.

Then he urges that the Lord be invoked, so that after the service of the most holy praise we may render him worthy thanks. For the one truly invokes God who cries out to God more through action than through voice. Hence the Savior says in the Gospel to the proud and disobedient: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke VI). And elsewhere: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII).

Third he says: “Announce his works among the nations.” This can properly apply to the glorious evangelists, the most holy apostles, and now the priests, who are known to announce his mighty works throughout all the nations.

“Exult and praise, dwelling of Zion, because great is the Holy One of Israel in your midst.” First, this should be stated according to the literal sense: O dwelling of Zion, exult and praise your God, because he who previously seemed to be your God and was confined within the narrow limits of the small land of Judea has now filled the whole earth with his knowledge; rising from the dead, he reigns among the nations, and the nations entreat and worship him. This is so that he may also extend his hand a second time to possess what remains of his people, and that those who gather the fugitives of Israel and assemble the dispersed of Judah may collect them from the four quarters of the earth, because the seed of the Gospel proceeded from the springs of Israel through the apostles who were Jews.

It is better, however, to interpret Zion—that is, a watchtower set in the heights—as the Church, concerning which the fiftieth Psalm also sings: “Deal kindly with Zion in your good pleasure, so that the walls of Jerusalem may be built.” Thus a sacrifice of justice, offerings, burnt offerings, and the calf that the most merciful father sacrificed for his repentant son may become acceptable to the Lord in her.

# THE CANTICLE OF HEZEKIAH, KING OF JUDAH, BEGINS

The canticle designated under the name of Hezekiah—which some interpreters call a writing and others a prayer—seems to me better designated by the term “thanksgiving.” For it is written in the prophet (Isa. XXXVIII): “The writing of Hezekiah, king of Judah, when he had been sick and recovered from his illness.” The Septuagint, however, rendered it: “The prayer of Hezekiah, king of Judah, when he languished and rose from his illness.” It is clear that, after his health had been restored and he had risen from his illness, he composed this. Therefore it is not a prayer but thanksgiving for the benefit he had received.

This canticle can suitably apply to those who, after a long illness of soul, recover their senses from the snares of the devil, are healed from the burden of sins, strive to restore themselves through holy virtues, and proclaim the praises of God not only with their voice but also with their heart and actions.

“I said: In the midst of my days I shall go to the gates of hell.” He recounts what he silently thought during the time of pressing distress and impending illness. “I said,” he says, “in my heart: ‘In the midst of my days’”—or, as others have translated it, “in the illness and silence of my days,” or “in the blood of my days,” when my blood and my death were being observed. Therefore, in despair, I said: “I shall go to the gates of hell.”

Either he means the gates according to the common law of nature, or those gates of which the Psalmist sings that he was delivered: “You who raise me up from the gates of death, so that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. IX). I think these are the gates of hell that do not prevail against Peter, because he died in the fullness of his days.

The saints complete their days, as Abraham did, who died full of days in a good old age. Sinners and the impious, however, die in the midst of their days. Concerning them the Psalm also speaks: “Men of blood and deceit will not halve their days” (Ps. LIV), for they do not complete works of virtue and do not strive to amend their sins through repentance. Therefore, in the middle of life’s course and in the darkness of errors, they will be led to Tartarus.

“I sought the remainder of my years.” Not thinking that I would live any longer, I said: “I shall not see the Lord God any longer in the land of the living.” In place of “Lord” and “God,” the Hebrew has *Ia*, which sounds in the final syllable of *alleluia*. In its place the Septuagint translated: “I shall no longer see the salvation of God in the land of the living.” Concerning this it is also written elsewhere: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. CXIV); and again: “I shall please the Lord in the light of the living” (Ps. LV).

The region of the saints, therefore, is itself what is called the light of the living. “For he is not the God of the dead but of the living” (Matt. XXII). This is all that he fears: that, having been led to the underworld, he might not deserve to behold God’s salvation. It follows:

“I shall not see a human being any longer, nor an inhabitant; my generation has ceased. It has been removed and rolled up from me, like a shepherd’s tent. My life has been cut off as by a weaver; while I was still weaving, he cut me down.”

He fears, therefore, that he will not dwell in repose with the saints and the people of God; that he will not see God in the land of the living; that his generation will be dissolved like a tent; that he will be cut off, like a piece of cloth, at the very beginning of the light; and that Christ will not arise from his seed.

The Apostle also teaches that our body is called a tent, saying: “We who are in this tent groan, being burdened” (2 Cor. V). Human life, therefore, is not woven by the threads of the Fates, according to the fables of the Gentiles, but is ordered by God’s disposition. Hence Job says to the Lord: “The days of a human being are short; the number of his months is with you. You have appointed his limits, which cannot be passed” (Job XIV).

But it is asked how the fixed number of human life is known to the Lord if Hezekiah said that he would die in the midst of his days. It should be understood in this way: the prophet, by foretelling him that death was soon to come, showed what he had deserved. Nevertheless, God’s predestination accomplished what he willed, because, hearing his prayer and considering his repentance, he added the number of days that he had foreknown and predestined before the ages.

Therefore, lest Hezekiah’s heart should be lifted up after his unbelievable triumphs and victory in the midst of captivity, he was visited by bodily illness and heard that he was going to die; then he turned to the Lord and bent his sentence. We read the same thing in the prophet Jonah and in the threats against David that were said to be future but did not occur—not because God changed his sentence, but because he summoned the human race to knowledge of himself.

For the Lord relents concerning evils; thus the prophet was not false, since the time of death was made known at which that man deserved to die. Nor were the Lord’s decrees overturned, because the increase of his years of life through God’s generosity had also been fixed before the ages. The span of life that was unexpectedly added outwardly had been established inwardly without any increase in divine foreknowledge.

“From morning until evening you will finish me; from evening until morning, like a lion, so he crushed all my bones.” According to another edition it is read as follows: “From morning until evening you will finish me.” I hoped until morning, as Job also says that he endured in his distress and bodily torments, when by day he awaited night and looked for light in darkness, thinking that the punishments might be changed through the alteration of times.

The one who burns with great fevers knows this reality: his inward fire, like a lion, consumes all his bones, and because of the magnitude of his pain he does not think that he will live any longer.

“From morning until evening you will finish me; like a young swallow, so I shall cry out; I shall meditate like a dove.” These two birds customarily produce a moan instead of a song. Therefore Hezekiah adopts their likeness in the complaints and groans of his pain, pouring out prayer to God, so that his mournful supplication, mingled with tears, might immediately rise to the ears of the merciful Judge, and so that he might feel his help bestowed upon him more quickly. Hence it follows.

“**My eyes are weakened as I look upward. Lord, I am under oppression; be surety for me. What shall I say, or what will he answer me, since I myself have done it?**” [Col. 1096C] “My eyes,” he says, “have failed as I gazed toward the height of heaven, toward the Lord who delivered me and took away the anguish of my soul—and he did it himself. Even now death is imminent, together with sicknesses and the pain pressing upon me; like a lion, it was breaking the bones of my body. But, in the likeness of the swallow and the dove, I joined day to night with weeping and groaning, and, lifting my eyes on high toward God alone, who could help, I awaited assistance. I said to him: ‘I suffer more than my merits demand; but even if I have gone astray in anything, I will turn toward what is better. Be surety for me.’ ‘For it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy’ (Rom. IX).” Then he turns back to himself and says: “What shall I say, or what shall I plead against my Maker? Or what will he answer me, since he himself has done what he willed?” [Col. 1096D] Therefore, whatever he has decreed must be endured.

“**I will review all my years in the bitterness of my soul. Lord, thus one lives, and in such things is the life of my spirit: you will correct me and restore me to life. Behold, my bitterness is most bitter in peace; but you have delivered my soul, so that it would not perish.**” Nothing belonging to mortals is lasting, and every happiness of this world is lost even while it is being held. For when the time of tribulation arrives, everything that has passed provides no help to the one who is enduring it. Hence the foolish opinion of Epicurus, who asserts that present evils are alleviated by remembering past goods. Thus Hezekiah says that he is reckoning all the years of his reign, and of his former happiness—as he supposed it—in his present bitterness. And because [Col. 1097A] he is now secure and no longer suffers what he recounts concerning the human condition, he philosophizes and says: “Lord, this is how one lives, and such is the condition in which we were born.” You corrected me, but you restored me to life and granted me peace when Assyria had been driven away. Yet my peace was more bitter to me than any bitterness, because, when peace had been restored to the people and the city made secure, I alone entered the threshold of death. But you delivered my soul, so that it would not perish, either from the present life or from the life to come.

“**You have cast all my sins behind your back, because hell will not confess to you, nor will death praise you.**” “You have cast,” he says, “all my sins behind your back, so that I would not look upon them in sorrow, but contemplate your mercy. For hell and death will neither confess nor praise you, according to what is written: ‘But in hell, who will confess to you?’ (Ps. XXX).” The confession mentioned here is understood not as repentance, but as glory and praise, just as we also read in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. XI).

“**Those who descend into the pit will not await your truth; the living, the living—he himself—will confess to you, as I do today.**” “Those who descend into the pit,” he says, “will not await your truth.” For this fits the meaning better than what we read in the Septuagint: “Those who descend into the pit will not await your mercy,” especially since the Savior descended into hell in order to free the captives from the underworld. Instead of “pit,” the same translators rendered it more explicitly as “the underworld.” “The living, the living—he himself—will confess, as I do [Col. 1097C] today.” Here too “confession” is used for praise; for he is not confessing his crimes but giving thanks to God, and “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.” Since hell and death neither confess nor praise God, life and the living, by contrast, glorify the Lord. Hence what follows:

“**The father will make your truth known to his children. Lord, save me, and we shall sing our psalms all the days of our life in the house of the Lord.**” “The father will make your truth known to his children.” This signifies what is also said in Deuteronomy: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will say it to you” (Deut. XXXII), so that, through succession and each generation, God’s mercy may be proclaimed to those who come after. For this the Septuagint wrote: “From this day I will make children who will proclaim your righteousness.” The conjunction “for” links what follows with what precedes: namely, that the living, and he himself as one living, bless God because from that day he would make children who would proclaim his truth. But this certainly was not within Hezekiah’s power, for children were not promised to him through the Prophet; rather, present life was granted to him—especially since he fathered the most impious son, Manasseh, who filled Jerusalem with blood from gate to gate and did not bless God but cursed him, persecuting his holy ones.

Accordingly, following the Septuagint, we can say that he did not say, “I will make children,” but *PIDIA*, by which we understand either little ones, boys, infants, or descendants. Thus, because he himself obtained mercy, all future posterity, recognizing this, might praise his incredible clemency. “Save me, therefore, Lord, so that all who believe in you and have been delivered by your help may sing to you throughout all the days of our life in the temple.”

## HERE BEGINS THE SONG OF HANNAH, MOTHER OF THE PROPHET SAMUEL

The Song which Hannah, the mother of the blessed prophet Samuel, uttered in the prophetic spirit in the prophetic book of Kings and which is prefaced under the title of a prayer contains many mysteries concerning Christ and his Church. For by his gift these things were foretold prophetically, through whose aid the strength of the whole Church endures, its multitude increases, and its stability is confirmed. But it is asked why Scripture says that Hannah brought forth this song while praying, when it contains rather a proclamation of future things than a petition for anything. For it is written: “And Hannah prayed and said”:

“**My heart has exulted in the Lord, and my horn has been exalted in my God.**” She is not found to be praying in this song except through only two expressions, when she says: “I have rejoiced in your salvation,” and: “For there is no God besides you.” The Apostle, however, says: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. V). For those engaged in divine service count all their deeds and words as prayer; because when a righteous person continually does what is righteous, by this he prays continually as a righteous person. And in the Psalms he says: “The lifting of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXL). He lifts his hands who lifts up his deeds. In another sense, when Moses lifted his hands, Israel was victorious, but when he let them down, Amalek was victorious. For as long as the servant of God lifts his deeds toward the Lord, God’s people triumph; but when he lets his deeds fall, Amalek, the enemy of God, triumphs.

“‘My heart has exulted,’ Hannah says, and she necessarily added, ‘in the Lord,’ just as Paul said: ‘Rejoice in the Lord always’ (Phil. IV),” because someone can rejoice in carnal things. When people praise me, I do not rejoice in the Lord but rejoice in vanity. Therefore I am pierced by the word of God when it says: “My heart has exulted [Col. 1098D] in the Lord.” Let Hannah, then—whose name is interpreted as “grace,” namely the Church of Christ, the city of the great King, full of grace and fruitful in offspring—say what she recognizes as having been prophesied about herself long beforehand through the mouth of this devout mother.

“**My heart has exulted in the Lord, and my horn has been exalted in my God.**” Truly the heart has exulted because it has exulted in the Lord; and truly the horn has been exalted because it has been exalted not from itself but in the Lord its God. Elsewhere also he says: “The horns of the righteous will be exalted” (Ps. LXX), because these horns are bestowed upon the righteous from the points of Christ’s cross. With them we shall brandish and overthrow the hostile powers lying in wait for our soul.

“**My mouth has been enlarged over my enemies.**” [Col. 1099A] For even amid the straits of afflictions the word of God is not bound, nor is it bound in those who proclaim it, though they themselves may be bound.

“**For I have rejoiced in your salvation.**” This Savior is the Lord Christ Jesus, whom, as we read in the Gospel (Luke II), the old man Simeon embraced as a little child while recognizing him as great: “Now, Lord,” he said, “you dismiss your servant in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation.” If I rejoice in the Lord’s salvation, then my mouth is enlarged; through meditation on the word of God we shall come to the elevation of the heart. Hence the Apostle says: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart has been enlarged” (2 Cor. VI). For from the breadth of the heart wisdom is supplied to the mouth.

“**There is none holy like the Lord.**” He uses a distinction. He does not say, “There is no one except the Lord,” but rather that there is no one holy and sanctifying, just and justifying, as the Lord is.

“**For there is no other besides you, and there is none mighty like our God.**” “There is no one holy,” he says, “besides you, Lord, because no one becomes holy except through you.” Although there are those who are called many gods and many lords, none of them is by nature what God is, because he alone is the one who said to Moses his servant: “I am who I am” (Exod. III). For a shadow is nothing in comparison with a body, nor is smoke anything in comparison with fire.

“**Do not multiply lofty words, boasting.**” Solomon also says: “Do not seek what is too high for you” (Eccli. III). And elsewhere: “The Lord is in heaven and you are upon the earth; therefore let your words be few” (Eccl. V).

“**Let old things depart from your mouth.**” That is: let grandiloquence not proceed from your mouth. “Let every evil word,” the Apostle says (Eph. IV), “not proceed from your mouth.”

“**For God is Lord of knowledge, and thoughts are prepared by him.**” He knows you, even where no one else knows. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. Hence whoever thinks himself to be something when he is nothing deceives himself. These words are directed against the adversaries of the city of God who belong to Babylon and presume upon their own strength, glorying in themselves rather than in the Lord. Among them are also the carnal Israelites of earthly Jerusalem, earthborn citizens who, as the Apostle says (Rom. X), “being ignorant of the righteousness of God”—that is, the righteousness God gives to a human being, he alone being just and justifying—“and seeking to establish their own,” that is, as though prepared by themselves for themselves rather than bestowed by him, “have not submitted to the righteousness of God.” Certainly, they are proud, thinking that they can please God by what is their own and not by what belongs to God.

But because God is the Lord of knowledge, and therefore also the judge of consciences, he himself sees the thoughts of human beings, because they are vain. And why are they vain, if not because they are peculiarly human, deriving from the one through whom human beings themselves exist?

“**The bow of the mighty has been overcome, and the weak have been girded with strength.**” The bow has been weakened—that is, their purpose, by which they seem so powerful to themselves that, through human sufficiency and without God’s gift and help, they can fulfill divine commandments. But the weak have been girded with strength: those who trust entirely in God’s mercy and seek support from him, saying with the Prophet: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak” (Ps. XXX).

The Gentile people were weak when they had been strangers to God’s covenant. Now, therefore, they have been girded with strength, clothed with the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation, and with the sword of the Spirit they trample underfoot the fiery darts of the ancient enemy.

“**Those who were formerly filled have hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry have been filled.**” Who are to be understood as those filled with bread except those very people who, as though powerful—that is, the Israelites—were entrusted with the utterances of the Lord? But among that people the sons of the slave woman were diminished when they withdrew from believing in the Savior. And in those loaves—that is, in the divine utterances that they alone at that time received from all the nations—they understand only earthly things.

But the nations, to whom that law had not been given, after they came to those utterances through the New Testament, traversed the earth in great hunger, because they tasted in them not earthly but heavenly things. And this is as though the reason why it happened were being sought.

“**Until the barren woman has borne seven, and she who had many children has grown weak.**” In the Hebrew and in the Septuagint translation, not “many” but “seven” is read. The Jews understand this passage as follows: when Samuel was born, Peninnah’s firstborn son died, and as each of Hannah’s children was born, one of Peninnah’s sons died. But it must be asked how this can stand, since Peninnah had seven children, whereas Hannah had no more than five.

The Hebrews solve this question by counting Samuel’s two sons together with Hannah’s children: “For the barren woman,” he says, “has borne seven, and she who was rich in children has grown weak.” Here everything that was being prophesied becomes clear to those who recognize the number seven, by which the universal protection of the Church is signified. For this reason the Apostle John writes to seven churches, thereby showing that he is writing to the fullness of one Church; and Solomon prefigured the same thing earlier in Proverbs: “Wisdom built herself a house and supported it with seven columns” (Prov. IX).

The city of God was barren among all the nations before this offspring, which we see, came forth. We also see that Jerusalem of the earth, which had been rich in children, has now grown weak, since whoever among its children were children of the free woman constituted its strength. But now, because there is the letter and not the spirit, it has lost its strength and grown weak.

“**The Lord puts to death and gives life.**” He puts to death the one that had been rich in children, and gives life to this barren woman who bore seven. Yet it can more suitably be understood that he gives life to the very ones whom he put to death, for he repeated the thought by adding what follows.

“**He leads down to the underworld and brings back.**” Those to whom the Apostle says, “If you have died with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Rom. VI), are beneficially put to death by the Lord. He adds to them: “Set your minds on the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth,” so that they may be the ones who passed beyond the earth while hungry.

“For you have died,” he says—this is how God beneficially puts them to death—and then [Col. 1101A] it follows: “And your life is hidden with Christ in God.” Behold how God gives life to those same people. But did he lead those same people down to the underworld and bring them back? Without controversy among the faithful, we see both things fulfilled rather in him, our head, with whom the Apostle said that our life is hidden in God. For he who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all—this one, certainly, now puts to death; and because he raised him from the dead, he again gave him life. And because his voice is recognized in prophecy—“You will not abandon my soul in the underworld” (Ps. XV)—he led him down to the underworld and brought him back. By his poverty we have been enriched.

“**For the Lord makes poor and enriches.**” To understand what this means, let us hear what follows.

[Col. 1101B] “**He humbles and exalts.**” Certainly, he humbles the proud and exalts the humble. For what is read elsewhere—“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV)—is contained throughout this discourse, whose name is interpreted as “his grace.”

Now, what is added—“**He raises the poor man from the earth**”—I understand better of no one than of him who became poor for our sake, although he was rich, so that we might be enriched by his poverty, as was said shortly before. For he raised him from the earth so quickly that his flesh did not see corruption. Nor will I separate from him what is said:

“**And he lifts the needy man from the dung heap.**” The needy person is, of course, the same as the poor person. The dung heap from which he was raised is most correctly understood as the Jewish persecutors. Among them, when the Apostle had said that he had persecuted the Church, he says: “What were gains to me, these I counted as losses for Christ; and not only as losses, but I also considered them dung, so that I might gain Christ” (Phil. III).

Therefore, he was raised from the earth; the poor man was lifted above all the rich; and from that dung heap the needy man was raised above all the wealthy.

“**So that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory.**” To them he says: “You will sit upon twelve thrones” (Matt. XIX), giving them the seat of glory as an inheritance. “**For the foundations of the earth belong to the Lord, and he set the world upon them.**” For he himself rules from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the world [Col. 1101D] (Ps. LXXI). “The foundations of the earth belong to the Lord”: that is, the four regions of the world, in which he will enlarge the sphere of his Church, which praises his name from the rising of the sun to its setting.

“**He will guard the feet of his holy ones.**” That is, he directs the works of his chosen ones along the way of righteousness.

“**And the impious will be silenced in darkness.**” They will be sent into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. There they will be silenced—that is, they will cease from the arrogance of their pride.

“**For a man will not be strengthened by his own strength.**” That is, a man—the people of believers—is powerful not through his own strength but through divine power.

“**The adversaries of the Lord will fear him.**” For [Col. 1102A] the Lord will make his adversary weak. From the ambiguity of the Greek, this can also be understood as “his own adversary.” For when the Lord begins to possess us, the adversary who had been ours becomes his; and he will be overcome by us, not by our strength, since a man is not powerful through his own power. Therefore the Lord will make his adversary weak.

The Lord is holy, so that he may be overcome by the holy ones whom the Lord, the Holy One of holy ones, makes holy. Therefore let the powerful person not glory in his own power, nor the prudent in his own prudence, nor the rich in his riches. Rather, let him glory who glories in understanding and knowing the Lord and in doing judgment and righteousness in the midst of the earth. He does not understand and know the Lord only in some small part who also understands and knows that this very ability to understand and know the Lord is given to him by the Lord.

But because a just recompense will come from the Lord on the sons of Adam on the day of judgment, it follows:

“**In the heavens he will thunder over them.**” He will judge the ends of the earth, because he is just. This prophetess maintained the order of the confession of the faithful with complete precision: for the Lord Christ ascended into heaven, and from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. “For who ascended,” as the Apostle says (Eph. IV), “except the one who also descended into the lower parts of the earth? The one who descended is himself the one who ascended above all the heavens, so that he might fulfill all things.”

Therefore he thundered through his clouds, which he filled with the Holy Spirit when he ascended. Concerning these clouds he threatened earthly Jerusalem—that is, the ungrateful vineyard—through the prophet Isaiah, lest they rain [Col. 1102C] upon it.

Thus it is said:

“**The Lord will judge the ends of the earth.**” It is as though it were said: “The Lord will judge the extremities of the human being,” because what is changed for better or worse during the intervening time will not be judged, but rather the state in which the one being judged was found at the end.

“**And he will give sovereignty to his king**”—that is, to the Christian people. He gives them the power by which, like kings, they rule the flesh and, in the one who shed his blood for them, conquer the world.

It follows:

“**And he will exalt the horn of his Christ.**” How will Christ exalt the horn of his Christ? We may rightly call all those anointed with his chrism “Christs,” although together with their head the whole body is one Christ. Hannah, the mother of the holy and greatly praised man Samuel, prophesied these things. In him the change of the former priesthood was then represented figuratively, and now has been fulfilled, when she who had been rich in children grew weak, so that the barren woman who bore seven might have a new priesthood in Christ.

## HERE BEGINS THE SONG OF EXODUS

“**Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified.**” We read of many songs being composed in the divine Scriptures, yet this is the first of them all: after the Egyptians and Pharaoh had been submerged, the people of God sang this song after their victory. For it is the custom of the saints, whenever the adversary is defeated, to offer a hymn of thanksgiving to God, as though they knew that the victory had been secured not by their own power but by God’s grace.

When they sing the hymn, they also take tambourines in their hands, as is related concerning Mary, the sister of Moses and Aaron. Therefore, if you cross the Red Sea, if you see the Egyptians submerged, Pharaoh extinguished, and hurled into the depths of the abyss, you too can sing a hymn to God, you can utter a voice of thanksgiving and say: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored; horse and rider he has cast into the sea.”

You say this better and more worthily if you have a tambourine in your hand—that is, if you have crucified your flesh with its vices and desires, and if you have put to death your members that are upon the earth. Yet let us see what he says: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored,” as though “he has been glorified” were not sufficient. Thus he added: “He has been glorified gloriously.” And, as far as we can conjecture—for it seems to me that one thing is to be glorified and another to be glorified gloriously—my Lord Jesus Christ, when he assumed flesh from the Virgin for our salvation, was indeed glorified because he came to seek what had perished. Yet he was not glorified gloriously. For it is said of him: “We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty, and his face was dishonored beyond the sons of men—yet glorified” (Isa. V). When he came to the cross and endured death, he was, so to speak, glorified humbly, not gloriously.

But because “it was necessary for Christ to suffer these things and thus enter into his glory” (Luke XXIV), when he comes in the glory of the Father and of the holy angels, when he comes in his majesty to judge the earth, and when he will also destroy the true Pharaoh—that is, the devil—by the breath of his mouth; when he shines forth in the majesty of his Father and, after his coming in humanity, shows us his second coming in glory, then he is not merely glorified. Then all will honor the Son just as they honor the Father.

“**He cast horse and rider into the sea.**” The people who pursue us are horses; and, so to speak, all who are born in the flesh are figuratively horses. But those who have riders are horses whom the Lord rides, and they travel through the whole earth. Of them it is said: “And your riding is salvation.”

There are also horses who have the devil and his angels as riders. Judas was a horse, but as long as he had the Lord as his rider, he belonged to the cavalry of salvation. For he was sent with the other apostles and granted salvation and healing to the sick. But when he submitted himself to the devil—for after the morsel Satan entered into him—Satan became his rider, and, led by Satan’s reins, he began to ride against the Lord and our Savior.

All, therefore, who persecute the saints are neighing horses, but they have riders, evil angels by whom they are driven; therefore they are fierce. The Lord cast horse and rider into the sea, and he became salvation for me.

“**The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation.**” Another edition has: [Col. 1104A] “He has become my helper and protector for salvation.” The Lord, therefore, is the strength and praise of his servants. He helps them in tribulations and protects them from all enemies, and he becomes the salvation of those who hope in him. For, according to the statement of the Apostle Peter, salvation is not in anyone else; he himself is the Savior of all, and especially of believers.

“**This is my God, and I will glorify him; the God of my father, and I will exalt him.**” This, then, is both my God and the God of my Father. Our Father, who made and begot us, is Christ. And he himself says: “I am going to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John XVI). If I recognize that God is my God, I will glorify him; but if I also recognize how he is the God of my Father, Christ, I will exalt him.

“**The Lord is like a warrior; Almighty is his name.**” Or, according to another edition: “The Lord, crushing wars; the Lord is his name.” Truly our Lord is almighty. He is mighty in battle and will crush his enemies, and there is no one who can resist him.

Do not think that the Lord crushes only visible battles. He will also crush those battles that are waged against us not against flesh and blood but against principalities and powers and against the rulers of the darkness of this world. The Lord is his name, and there is no creature of which he is not Lord.

“**Pharaoh’s chariots and his army he cast into the sea; his chosen princes were submerged in the Red Sea.**” Leaders and subjects alike—chariots, horsemen, infantry, and Pharaoh’s entire army—were submerged in the Red Sea. Of this it is written that “not even one of them remained; but the children of Israel went through the midst of the dry sea, and the waters were to them like a wall on their right and on their left” (Exod. XIV).

For everyone who opposes God’s will and perseveres in wickedness to the end is enveloped in eternal torments. But whoever follows the true Moses—that is, the law of God—will escape his enemies safely and walk across dry ground, because he does not mingle with the enticements of the world.

The wave is forced into a heap, and the water, held back within itself, bends; the liquid receives solidity, and the floor of the sea dries into dust. Understand the goodness of God the Creator: if you obey his will and follow his law, he compels the elements themselves to serve you even against their nature.

The Apostle therefore shows what the passage of the children of Israel through the Red Sea signifies when he says: “All indeed passed through the sea, and all indeed were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. X). This, therefore, represents mystically the baptism prefigured through Moses in the cloud and in the sea. Thus you, who are baptized in Christ in water and the Holy Spirit, should know that the Egyptian powers pursue you and wish to recall you to their service—namely, the rulers of this world and spiritual wickedness, whom you formerly served. They do indeed try to pursue you, but you descend into the water and escape unharmed. After your sins have been washed away, you ascend as a new human being, prepared to sing a new song.

But the Egyptians, pursuing you, will be drowned in the abyss, even if they seem to be begging Jesus not to send them into the abyss for the time being.

It should be noted, however, that according to another edition it reads: “Pharaoh’s four-horse chariots and his army he cast into the sea. He plunged his chosen riders, three by three, into the Red Sea.” Pharaoh, as more powerful in wickedness and holding the kingdom of evil, drives four-horse chariots. It is not enough for him to mount one horse; he drives many at once and compels many at once with blows and tortured lashings. Whenever you see people more shameful in lust, fiercer in unbelief, more repulsive in greed, or more criminal in impiety, know that these belong to Pharaoh’s quadrigas. He also harnesses them to his chariot; he is carried and flies along in them, driving them with loosened reins through the open fields of crimes.

There are other chosen riders, undoubtedly chosen for wickedness. But we have already spoken above about the riders; now let us see who the three-by-three “standers” are. It seems to me that the three-by-three standers are so called because there are three ways by which human beings sin: either in deed, in word, or in thought. Therefore, three standers are said to be present in each person, occupying these three avenues of sin within us, always watching and lying in ambush, so that one may draw an evil word from the wretched human being, another may force out an unjust deed, and another may seize a wicked thought.

Indeed, the seed of God’s word, where it falls and perishes, is also described as having three locations: one beside the road, where it is trampled by people; another among thorns; and another on rocky ground. Conversely, good soil is said to produce a threefold harvest: a hundredfold, a sixtyfold, or a thirtyfold.

These three-by-three standers, therefore, are wicked angels from Pharaoh’s army. They stand in such ways, watching each one of us and seeking through these avenues to lead us into sin. The Lord will drown them in the Red Sea and, on the day of judgment, hand them over to fiery waves and cover them with a sea of punishments.

“**The abysses covered them; they descended into the depth like a stone.**” These abysses are surely those of which it is written in Job, where Leviathan is described: “He will regard the abyss as though it were growing old” (Job XLI). In the Gospel also the demons begged Jesus not to command them to go into the abyss. They descended into the depth like a stone.

Why did they fall into the depth like a stone? Because they were not stones of the kind from which children could be raised up for Abraham, but stones of the kind that loved the depth and cherished the liquid element—that is, they desired the bitter and fleeting pleasure of present things.

“**Your right hand, Lord, has been magnified in strength; your right hand, Lord, has struck the enemy.**” What is this right hand except the one of which it is written in the Psalm: “The right hand of the Lord has done strength; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me” (Ps. CXVII)?

According to another edition, this right hand was glorified in power when, through the mystery of the cross, it broke and destroyed the ancient enemy and true adversary, and through death destroyed him who held the power of death—that is, the devil—“binding the strong man and plundering his goods” (Matt. XII). It also destroyed the dragon, namely the ancient serpent, which with its tail dragged down a third of the stars and cast them into the lake of burning fire, which has been prepared for it and its angels. Hence it follows:

“**And in the multitude of your glory you cast down my adversaries.**” The glory of the Lord’s resurrection was indeed the confusion and crushing of the devil, who, together with the Jews, plotted Christ’s death.

“**You sent your anger, which devoured them like stubble.**” The final vengeance inflicted upon the devil and his angels appears as anger to those who suffer it. Yet it is inflicted justly upon sinners, without disturbance of spirit, by the one who judges all things with complete tranquility. It devours them like stubble because it violently lays them waste and torments them on every side.

“**And in the spirit of your fury the waters were gathered together.**” The lake of sulfur, corresponding to their deserts, is assigned to them, beneath which they groan, submerged forever. But since this punishment will be paid in full at the final judgment, and the hour of vengeance is still being delayed, he seems to grant the enemies an opportunity to persecute. They abuse God’s patience, storing up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment.

Yet he will most certainly come to grant his saints the rewards of eternal blessedness and to give his adversaries vengeance in flaming fire. Hence it follows:

“Moving waters stood still; the abysses were gathered together in the midst of the sea. The enemy said: ‘I will pursue and overtake them; I will divide the spoils; my soul shall be filled; I will draw my sword; my hand shall destroy them.’ Your spirit blew, and the sea covered them; they sank like lead in mighty waters.” [Col. 1106C]

“‘You sent,’ he says, ‘your spirit, and the sea covered them.’ Here the Spirit of God is now mentioned for the fifth time, so that in this number we may also understand what was said: ‘This is the finger of God’ (Exod. 8). First, where it is written: ‘The Spirit of God was borne over the waters’ (Gen. 1). Second, where it says: ‘My Spirit shall not remain among these men, because they are flesh.’ Third, where Pharaoh says to Joseph: ‘Since the Spirit of God is in you.’ Fourth, where the Egyptian magicians say: ‘This is the finger of God.’ Fifth, in this song: ‘You sent your Spirit, and the sea covered them.’” [Col. 1106D]

Let us remember, however, that the Spirit of God is mentioned not only in relation to benefits but also in relation to vengeance. For what else did he say above? “By the spirit of your anger the water was divided.” Was this Spirit of God therefore against the Egyptians—the spirit of his anger—which harmed them through the division of the waters, so that, when they entered, they could be overwhelmed by the returning waters? Yet was it not the same spirit of God’s anger for the children of Israel, whom the division of the water benefited? Hence it is signified that, because of its different operations and effects, the Spirit of God is called by different names, although he is one and the same—the one who is also understood as the Holy Spirit in the unity of the Trinity.

Accordingly, I do not think that anyone other than this same Spirit is signified when the Apostle says: “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the spirit of adoption, in which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8). [Col. 1107A] For by the same Spirit of God—that is, by the finger of God—by which the law was written on stone tablets, fear was instilled in those who did not yet understand grace, so that through the law they might be convicted of their weakness and sins, and the law might become their tutor, by whom they would be led to the grace that is in faith in Jesus Christ.

Of this spirit of adoption and grace—that is, of this work of the Spirit of God, by which grace and rebirth into eternal life are bestowed—it is said: “The Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3), whereas it was said above, “The letter kills,” that is, the letter merely written and issuing commands without the assistance of grace.

“They sank,” he says, “like lead into exceedingly mighty water.” Sinners are heavy; indeed, iniquity is shown to sit upon a talent of lead, as the prophet Zechariah says: “I saw,” he says, “a woman sitting upon a talent of lead, and I said, ‘What is this?’ And he answered, ‘Iniquity’” (Zech. 5). Therefore the wicked have sunk into the depths like lead in exceedingly mighty water. [Col. 1107B] The saints, however, do not sink but walk upon the waters, because they are light and are not weighed down by the burden of sin.

Indeed, the Lord and Savior walked upon the waters. He is the one who truly knew no sin. His disciple Peter also walked upon them, although he was briefly afraid; for he was not yet so great and such that he had nothing at all of the nature of lead mixed into him. He possessed some of it, though little, on account of which the Lord said to him: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14.) [Col. 1107C]

Therefore the one who is saved is saved through fire, so that, if he happens to have some of the nature of lead mixed into him, the fire may boil it away and dissolve it, until all become good gold. For the gold of that land, which the saints will inhabit, is said to be good; and just as a furnace tests gold, so temptation tests righteous people.

Everyone must therefore come to the fire; everyone must come to the smelting furnace. For the Lord sits and smelts and purifies the sons of Judah. When one comes there, if someone has brought many good works and a little iniquity, that little is dissolved and purified by the fire like lead, and all that remains is pure gold. If someone has brought more lead there, more is burned away, so that it may be boiled down more thoroughly, until perhaps a little purified gold remains. [Col. 1107D] But if someone comes there wholly made of lead, what is written will happen to him: “He sinks into the depths like lead in exceedingly mighty water.”

“Who is like you among the mighty, O Lord? Who is like you, magnificent in holiness, awesome and praiseworthy, doing wonders?”

Another edition reads: “Who is like you among the gods, O Lord? Who is like you, glorious among the holy, wondrous in majesty, doing marvels?” [Col. 1108A]

When it says, “Who is like you among the gods,” or “among the mighty,” it does not compare God with the idols of the nations, nor with demons, who falsely claim for themselves the name of gods or mighty beings. Rather, it calls gods those who are named gods through generation and participation in God, concerning whom Scripture says elsewhere: “I said, ‘You are gods’” (John 10). Again: “God stood in the assembly of gods.”

Yet although these beings are capable of receiving God and seem to be granted this name by grace, no one is found to be like God, either in power or in nature. Although the apostle John says: “Little children, we do not yet know what we shall be; but when he is revealed”—speaking of the Lord—“we shall be like him,” this likeness is nevertheless attributed not to nature but to grace. For example, we may say that a painting is like the person whose image is represented in the painting. Insofar as grace is concerned, it is called similar in appearance; insofar as substance is concerned, it is utterly dissimilar. One is the form of flesh and a living body; the other is a coloring applied with wax to lifeless boards. [Col. 1108B]

No one, therefore, among the gods is like the Lord. No one is invisible, no one incorporeal, immutable, without beginning and without end, or creator of all things, except the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit, who alone performs wonders.

“You stretched out your hand, and the earth devoured them.”

“Earth” is evidently put in place of “water.” For this whole outermost, or weaker, part of the world is designated by the name “earth,” according to what is often said: “God, who made heaven and earth.” And in the division of that psalm, after the heavenly things have been mentioned, it says: “Praise the Lord from the earth” (Ps. 148), and then it proceeds in praise to include things that also belong to the waters.

Even today the earth devours the ungodly. Or does it not seem to you that the one who is always thinking about earth, whose actions are always earthly, who speaks of earth, quarrels over earth, desires earth, and places all his hope in earth—who does not look toward heaven, does not think about the future, does not fear God’s judgment, and does not desire his blessed promises, but is always thinking about present things and sighing after earthly things—is devoured by the earth? [Col. 1108C] When you see such a person, say: “The earth has devoured him.”

And if you see someone devoted to the lusts of the flesh and the pleasures of the body, in whom the soul has no strength but the desire of the flesh has gained complete control, say of him also: “The earth has devoured him.”

I am still moved by the words: “You stretched out your right hand, and the earth devoured them,” as though the reason they were devoured by the earth were that the Lord stretched out his right hand. If you consider how the Lord, exalted upon the cross, stretched out his hands all day toward the unbelieving and rebellious people, and how the unbelieving people who cried, “Crucify him, crucify him,” were overwhelmed by the death deserved for their crime, you will clearly see how he stretched out his right hand and the earth devoured them. [Col. 1108D]

Yet one must not despair completely. For if the one who has been devoured should perhaps come to his senses, he may again be vomited forth, as Jonah was.

“You were a guide in your mercy to the people whom you redeemed, and you carried them in your strength to your holy dwelling.”

In another edition it reads: “You governed this people of yours in your righteousness, whom you redeemed. You encouraged them by your power and by your holy refreshment.”

The Lord leads in righteousness the people whom he has liberated through the bath of regeneration. [Col. 1109A] He also comforts, or refreshes, them through the consolation of the Holy Spirit by his power and in his rest. For the image of future things gives rest to those who labor, just as, for those engaged in the contest, the hope of the crown mitigates the pain of their wounds.

“The peoples rose up and were angry; pains seized the inhabitants of Philistia. Then the rulers of Edom were troubled; trembling seized the mighty men of Moab; all the inhabitants of Canaan grew numb.”

Another edition reads as follows: “The nations heard and were angry; pains seized the inhabitants of Philistia. Then the leaders of Edom and the princes of the Moabites hastened; fear seized them; all the inhabitants of Canaan melted away.” [Col. 1109B]

As far as the historical account is concerned, it is clear that none of these nations was present at the wonders that occurred. How, then, will they be seen to have been frightened by trembling, or to have hastened, as it says, or to have become angry—the Moabites, Edom, and the other nations it enumerates?

But if we return to the spiritual meaning, you will find that the Philistines—that is, “those falling upon the people”—and Edom, which is interpreted as “earthly,” tremble; and all their rulers hurry about and are terrified, bound by pains, when they see their kingdoms, which are in the underworld, penetrated by the one who descended into the lower regions of the earth to rescue those held by death. Fear and trembling seized them when they perceived the greatness of his arm.

Hence also all the inhabitants of Canaan melted away. They are interpreted as “changeable” and “mobile,” when they see their kingdoms being shaken, the strong man bound, and his vessels plundered. [Col. 1109C]

“Let strength and terror fall upon them through the greatness of your arm.”

What do the demons fear? What makes them tremble? Without doubt, the cross of Christ, on which they were triumphed over, on which their principalities and powers were stripped away.

Fear and trembling will therefore fall upon them when they see the sign of the cross faithfully fixed in us, and the greatness of that arm which the Lord stretched out upon the cross, as he says: “All day long I stretched out my hands toward a people who did not believe and contradicted me” (Rom. 10). [Col. 1109D]

They will not fear you in any other way, nor will your trembling come upon them in any other way, unless they see the cross of Christ in you, unless you too can say: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6).

“Let them become immovable like a stone until your people pass over, O Lord, until this people of yours pass over, whom you have acquired.”

To become like a stone does not mean to be stone by nature; for something would not become what it was not. We say this on account of those who claim that Pharaoh or the Egyptians were of an evil nature and were brought into these things not by the freedom of their will, and also on account of those who accuse God the Creator as cruel because he turns human beings into stones.

Before they blaspheme, let them carefully consider what has been written. For he did not say, “Let them become like a stone,” and then remain silent; rather, he established a time and determined a measure for their condemnation. He said: “Until your people pass over.” [Col. 1110A] This plainly means that after the people have passed over they will no longer be like stones. Here, I think, something prophetic is concealed.

For I see that the earlier people, who existed before us, became like a stone—hard and unbelieving—not so that they would remain permanently in the nature of stone, but until this people should pass over, the people whom he acquired.

“For a partial blindness has happened to that Israel which is according to the flesh, until the fullness of the nations enters; then all Israel, which had become like a stone through the hardness of unbelief, will be saved.”

And do you wish to see how it will be saved? “God,” he says, “is able to raise up children for Abraham from stones.”

The stones therefore remain for now, until this people of yours passes over, whom you acquired. Yet the Lord himself is the Creator of all things. We must consider how he is said here to have acquired what is unquestionably his own. [Col. 1110B]

“You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain of your inheritance.”

God does not wish to plant us in Egypt, nor in low and depressed places. He wishes to plant those whom he plants on the mountain of his inheritance.

The prophet says: “You brought a vine out of Egypt, you drove out the nations, and you planted it. You made a path before it; you planted its roots, and it filled the land. Its shadow covered the mountains, and its branches were like the cedars of God” (Ps. 79).

You now perceive how God plants and where he plants. He does not plant in valleys but on mountains, in lofty and elevated places. Those whom he leads out of Egypt, whom he brings from the world to faith, he does not wish to place again in lowly regions. Rather, he wishes their way of life to be lofty; he wishes us to dwell on the mountains. [Col. 1110C]

But even on those mountains he does not wish us to creep along the ground, nor does he wish his vine to have its fruit cast down upon the earth. He wishes its branches to be led upward, placed on high, and trained—not on just any lowly trees, but on the lofty and highest cedars of God.

I think, therefore, that the cedars of God are the prophets and apostles. If we are joined to the vine that God brought out of Egypt, and if our branches spread through their branches, leaning upon them and becoming trained branches joined together by the bonds of mutual love, we will undoubtedly bear abundant fruit. For “every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 3). [Col. 1110D]

“To the most secure dwelling that you have prepared, O Lord.”

See the goodness of the merciful Lord. He does not wish to lead you into labor, nor does he wish you yourself to make a dwelling for yourself; rather, he leads you to a habitation already prepared.

Hear the Lord saying in the Gospel: “Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor” (John 4).

“The sanctuary, O Lord, which your hands established.”

A sanctuary, or holy place, is called the dwelling of God, like a temple, because it sanctifies those who approach it. He does not say that this was made by human hand, but by the hand of God.

Therefore, because God plants and builds for your sake, he becomes a farmer and a builder, so that you may lack nothing. Hear Paul also say: “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (1 Cor. 3). [Col. 1111A]

What, then, is this holy place, which was not made by human hands but prepared by the hands of God? Hear Wisdom saying that she “built herself a house” (Prov. 9).

I think, however, that this is more rightly understood of the Lord’s incarnation. It was not made by human hand—that is, the temple of flesh was not built in the Virgin by human workmanship. Rather, as it is written above in Daniel: “A stone cut without hands grew and became a great mountain” (Dan. 2).

This is the holy place of the assumed flesh, cut without hands—that is, without human activity—from the mountain of human nature and the substance of flesh.

“The Lord will reign forever and beyond.”

Another edition reads: “You who reign forever, and throughout the age, and still beyond.” [Col. 1111B]

Whenever “throughout the age” is said, it indicates a length of time but also suggests that some end exists. Even if it refers to another age, that age undoubtedly has a longer duration, yet still comes to an end. And whenever “ages of ages” are named, perhaps some limit established by God is indicated, although it is unknown to us.

But when he added here “and beyond,” or “and still further,” he left no sense of any limit or end. Whatever you may imagine as the point at which an end could stand, the prophetic word always says to you, “and still further.” It is as though it were speaking to you and saying: Do you think that the Lord will reign throughout the age of the age?
