And still further. Do you think he will reign through ages of ages? And still further. Whatever you may say about the spans of his reign, the prophet always says to you, “and still further.” [Col. 1111C]

“For Pharaoh entered into the sea with his chariots and horsemen, and the Lord brought the waters of the sea back over them; but the children of Israel walked on dry ground in the midst of it.”

And you, if you are a son of Israel, can walk on dry ground in the midst of the sea if you are in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, holding the word of life like the light of the sun for glory.

It can happen that, although you walk in the midst of sinners, the moisture of sin will not soak you. It can happen that, as you pass through this world, no wave of lust will sprinkle you, and no heat of desire will strike you.

For the one who is an Egyptian and follows Pharaoh is submerged in the waves of vices. But whoever follows Christ and walks as he walked, for that person the waters become a wall on the right and on the left. [Col. 1111D] He himself walks along the middle road on dry ground, turning neither to the right nor to the left, until he comes out into freedom and sings a hymn of victory to the Lord, saying: “I will sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored” (Exod. 15).

## HERE BEGINS THE SONG OF THE PROPHET HABAKKUK

“The prayer of Habakkuk the prophet concerning ignorances.”

The Septuagint reads: “The prayer of Habakkuk the prophet with a song.”

We read in the sixteenth psalm, “A prayer of David”; in the eighty-ninth, “A prayer of Moses, the man of God”; and in the one hundred and first, “A prayer of the poor man, when he is anxious and pours out his prayer before the Lord.” And wherever else the name of prayer occurs, nowhere is it read together with a song. [Col. 1112A]

I do not know whether it is fitting to pray with a song, unless perhaps, according to the Septuagint, we say that the prophet prays for the coming of Christ and prophesies this very thing with delight, with psalms and a song: in that it is a prayer, he entreats the Father; in that it is a song, praise is offered to the Father who sent the Son and to the Son who came.

But it is better to read according to the Hebrew truth: “The prayer of Habakkuk the prophet concerning ignorances.”

For the prophet, contemplating the condition of the present world, had seen the peace of sinners and the afflictions of the righteous. He had seen the wicked abound in riches and the innocent subjected daily to scourges. He had seen wickedness in the place of judgment and iniquity in the place of justice. He had seen the tears of the innocent, with no one to comfort them, and those deprived of every human aid unable to resist the violence of their accusers. [Col. 1112B]

Knowing that these and countless other things could not happen without divine providence, he was troubled in spirit. Sighing deeply from the innermost part of his heart, he cried out to the Lord: “How long, O Lord, shall I cry out and you will not hear? I shall shout to you while suffering violence, and you will not save?” (Hab. 1.) And again: “Your eyes are pure, so that you cannot see evil, and you cannot look upon iniquity. Why do you look upon those who act unjustly and remain silent while the wicked devours one more righteous than himself? You make human beings like the fish of the sea, like a creeping thing that has no ruler” (ibid.).

Yet amid these things he immediately recalled the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation and passion, which he had known through the spirit of prophecy. He understood that he had complained much more sharply than was fitting about the afflictions of the saints in this life, to whom eternal rest had been promised in the future, since even the Son of God, appearing in the flesh, was not to depart from the world without the punishment of the cross—he who was to be born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mother and to live in the world without any sin. [Col. 1112C] Making prayer to the Lord for his own ignorances, he begins thus:

“Lord, I heard your report and was afraid; Lord, in the midst of the years revive your work.”

The Septuagint reads: “Lord, I heard your report and was afraid. Lord, I considered your works and was astonished; in the midst of two living beings you will be known.”

The Hebrews explain this passage according to its historical sense as follows: [Col. 1112D]

“Lord, I heard your report and was afraid.” I heard, he says, the punishments that you prepared for Nebuchadnezzar and the devil, in which you said to him: first, “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his own”; second, “Woe to him who gathers evil greed for his house”; third, “Woe to him who builds a city with blood and establishes a town in iniquity”; fourth, “Woe to him who gives drink to his companion, sending his gall and making him drunk”; and fifth, “Woe to him who says, ‘Awake, arise,’ to the silent stone.”

And just as one terrified by fear that the great dragon must be pierced by such wounds, so I entreat you, Lord, to fulfill what you promised and, when the time is complete, restore your Christ. For you said: [Col. 1113A] “Because the vision is still for a distant time, and it will appear at the end, and it will not lie.”

Therefore revive what you promised—that is, fulfill your promise. Let your word not die in vain, but be completed in deed. This may also be understood, in our view, of the Savior’s resurrection, so that the one who died for us may rise from the dead and be brought to life.

According to the Septuagint, however, the meaning is quite different: “Lord,” he says, “I heard your report and was afraid; I considered your works and was terrified.”

The Lord and Savior’s report is what he heard from the Father: that he should come, be born in the flesh, live in the world, almighty among the weak, righteous among sinners, and God among human beings; that he should perform heavenly works, teach heavenly commandments, be tempted and scourged; that our death should be destroyed by his death; that, rising from the dead, he should ascend into heaven; and that, having sent the Spirit from above, he should illumine the world with the grace of truth. [Col. 1113B]

He himself frequently recalls this report in the Gospel, saying: “But the one who sent me is true, and what I heard from him, these things I speak in the world” (John 8). Again: “I have called you friends, because everything I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15). Concerning this, John the Baptist also says: “The one who comes from heaven is above all, and what he has seen and heard, this he testifies” (John 3).

The prophet heard this report of the Lord in the spirit, and he was afraid because he had complained about the afflictions endured by the righteous in the world, although even the Lord’s own departure from the world by death was for us a prosperous path to salvation and life. He was afraid because he had complained about the tribulations of the saints, who are not merely to be rescued by the Lord from tribulations but are eternally to be crowned with the Lord. [Col. 1113C]

“I considered your works and was terrified”—namely, those works by which he redeemed the world, “becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross,” so that, as the Apostle again says, “through death he might destroy him who held the power of death” (Phil. 2; Heb. 2), that is, the devil.

The more attentively one considers these works, the more one trembles at the works of one’s own weakness.

As for the reading according to the Septuagint, “In the midst of two living beings you will be known,” some interpret this as referring to the two cherubim made through Moses in Exodus, which stood beside the ark and had the oracle in their midst.

Others refer it to the two seraphim according to Isaiah, covering God’s head and feet, which fly only in the present age, and each cries out to the other the mystery of the Trinity. [Col. 1113D]

Some think that this was said of the first Church, which was gathered from circumcision and from uncircumcision, so that the Savior is understood and believed to be in the midst of the two peoples surrounding him on either side.

There are those who understand the two living beings as the two Testaments, the New and the Old, which truly are living and life-giving, breathing, and in whose midst the Lord is known.

It can also be understood as “in the midst of two living beings,” in the midst of Moses and Elijah. There he was made known to the three disciples on the holy mountain because he was to die, as they told him what he would suffer in Jerusalem. There he was made known as one who would rise again and become immortal, when his face was glorified like the sun and his garments shone like snow. [Col. 1114A]

There he was made known as the Son of God, when a paternal voice from heaven said to him: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 3).

It may also suitably be understood as referring to the midst of two robbers, between whom he was crucified. By dying, he was made known as a human being. When the sun was darkened, the earth was shaken, and the other miracles occurred around the cross that the Gospel recounts, he was made known as God. By interceding with the Father for his executioners, he made known how merciful he was.

By this example the prophet, who foresaw these things in the spirit, was admonished not only to endure patiently the afflictions inflicted by evil people but also to extend the grace of his kindness to his persecutors. [Col. 1114B]

The Septuagint reads: “When the years draw near, you will be known; when the time comes, you will be shown.”

“When the time comes,” he says, “and you have fulfilled your promises in deed, you will show that what you promised is true.” Or: “When the consummation draws near, and your Son comes in the final hour to destroy sins, you will be known more clearly.”

Alternatively, according to the historical sense, “years” and “time” may designate that fullness of time of which the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. 4).

The prophet saw these times and years as still far away and greeted them from a distance, because when the years drew near and the time came, the Lord would be shown and known. [Col. 1114C]

For above also he heard the Lord say to him: “The vision is still for a distant time, and it will appear at the end and will not lie. If it delays, wait for it, because it will surely come and will not be late.”

Hearing this report and considering the works of his passion, he was afraid and terrified, because he had been troubled by the temporary prosperity of the wicked and the temporal affliction of the good. Yet when he had made fitting repentance for his ignorances, he immediately became confident that he could obtain pardon for his errors. Therefore he adds:

“When my soul is troubled, you will remember mercy in anger.”

“When my soul is troubled,” he says, shaken by the grief proper to satisfaction and repentance, through fear of your anger and judgment, which I, unwary, fear that I have incurred, I believe that I shall quickly obtain the mercy of the forgiveness I have desired from you. [Col. 1114D]

Here we should observe the wonderful speed of divine compassion. He said only that he was troubled in spirit on account of the Lord’s anger, and immediately added that the Lord had been turned from anger to mercy.

Such indulgence, however, may apply to the smallest faults. As for our offenses, the graver they are, the more they require prolonged repentance, tears, and almsgiving.

According to the Hebrew, the passage reads: “When you are angry, you will remember mercy.” We must not think that God forgets and, after his anger, remembers his mercy. Rather, it means that, when we are placed under punishment, we think that he has forgotten us, according to the words: “How long, O Lord, will you forget me to the end?” [Col. 1115A]

And when we are overwhelmed by temptations like waves, and the raging storm of demons lashes out against us, we speak as though to one sleeping: “Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord?”

At the same time, consider God’s clemency. He did not say, “When you inflict punishments, you will remember mercy,” but “When you are angry.” One who is angry does not always strike; sometimes he merely threatens. The Apostle also understood this when he said: “The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of human beings” (Rom. 1). Where it is revealed, however, it is not inflicted; it does not strike, but is revealed in order to frighten, so that it may not be inflicted upon those who have been frightened.

“God will come from the South, and the Holy One from Mount Paran.”

The Septuagint reads: “God will come from Theman, and the Holy One from a shadowy and dense mountain.”

Theman is therefore interpreted as “South” and signifies Bethlehem, the city of David, in which the Lord was born. [Col. 1115B] It is situated south of Jerusalem. From there, on the fortieth day after his birth, the Lord himself was brought to Jerusalem by his parents, so that an offering might be made for him according to the law.

Paran is a place near Mount Sinai, on which mountain the Lord gave the law to Moses. The Lord, therefore, will come from the South—that is, he will be born in Bethlehem and will arise from there. And because the one who was born in Bethlehem is the one who formerly gave the law on Mount Sinai, he is the Holy One who comes from Mount Paran.

According to the Hebrews, the word that follows is a *diapsalma*, that is, “always.” Its meaning is this: The one who was born in Bethlehem, and who gave the law at Sinai—that is, on Mount Paran—is always, in all past, present, and future things, their author and giver. [Col. 1115C]

Paran is interpreted as “mouth of the seer,” and signifies that knowledge of the Son of God comes from the speech of an instructed man.

In some copies, however, we read: “God will come from Lebanon, and the Holy One from a shadowy and dense mountain.” This has the following meaning:

Lebanon is the highest mountain of Phoenicia, distinguished by lofty, incorruptible, and aromatic trees. Scripture testifies that the Lord’s temple in Jerusalem was made from them. Therefore, in Scripture, the temple itself is sometimes also designated by the name Lebanon.

Hence the passage in Zechariah concerning the army of the Chaldeans that was to come against it: “Open your doors, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars” (Zech. 11). [Col. 1115D]

God therefore comes from Lebanon because the Lord, appearing in the flesh, sowed the first seeds of the Gospel in the temple itself, and from there filled the whole world with the growth of his faith and truth.

Hence Isaiah says: “For the law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2).

He sowed there the first seeds of faith not only through the apostles, who after his passion and resurrection, filled with the Holy Spirit, laid the first foundations of the Church there by preaching, whose sound afterward went out into all the earth and whose words reached the ends of the world, but also through himself. [Col. 1116A]

For in that same temple he first bore witness to the faith that was to be held in him, when, sitting among the teachers at the age of twelve, he questioned them as though he were a human being of tender age, yet answered those who taught as though he were God of eternal majesty.

When his parents sought and found him, he himself also indicated that he was God and the Son of God, saying: “Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?” (Luke 2.)

“The Holy One,” he says, “from a shadowy and dense mountain.”

The Holy One is the same mediator between God and humanity who above is plainly called God. Concerning him Gabriel, announcing the Gospel to his Virgin Mother, says: “Therefore also the holy thing that will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1). [Col. 1116B]

The mountain from which this Holy One is sung as coming can be understood as the kingdom of the Jews, from which he derived the origin of his flesh. From this mountain Daniel saw a stone cut without hands—that is, Christ, brought forth without human activity—who, crushing the kingdoms of the world, would fill the whole earth with the glory of his name.

This mountain is rightly called shadowy and dense. For it has many fruitful trees, that is, many holy men laden with the fruits of virtues. They nourish the hunger of our minds with the most delightful taste of their teaching, and by the protection of their intercession they overshadow our weakness, lest the heat of tribulations cause it to wither from the inner freshness of love.

“His glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise.”

The Septuagint reads: “His power covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise.”

After describing the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation, he immediately adds the mystery of the ascension, by which the same humanity was to be glorified, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “His going forth is from the end of heaven, and his course reaches to its end” (Ps. 18). [Col. 1116C]

“His glory,” he says, “or his power, or his majesty, covered the heavens.” For the one who through the incarnation was made a little lower than the angels was himself, through the resurrection, crowned with glory and honor, and through the ascension was set above the works of the Father’s hands. All things were placed beneath his feet.

When the apostles preached, the whole earth was filled with his praise. But even before his passion and resurrection, when the Word made flesh dwelt among us, his majesty covered the heavens, because the assumed humanity, though still mortal, already surpassed the heavenly powers, and the earth was full of his praise, since those same heavenly powers truly knew that he was the creator of the earth, as he is of the whole creation through his divinity, although at that time he dwelt and was seen on earth through his humanity.

Hence, when he was born, they sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among people of good will” (Luke 2). [The supplied source ends here; its closing quotation mark is absent.]

[Col. 1116D] “His splendor will be like light; horns are in his hands. There his strength is hidden.”

The splendor of the virtues and teaching of the Lord and Savior will illuminate believers; hence in Scripture he is also called the sun of righteousness. But because that same splendor could not shine upon the world perfectly unless he first tasted death for a time, overthrew the kingdom of death, and, rising from the dead, granted the world the hope and faith of resurrection, his splendor too shone forth like the sun of righteousness in bright light. The horns in his hand are the banners and trophies of the cross, and in those horns his strength is hidden.

“For although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil. II). On the cross, therefore, his strength was hidden for a little while, when he said to the Father: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. XXVI); and, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (ibid.); and on the cross itself: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.”

According to another edition, however, the passage reads: “Horns are in his hands; there the strength of his glory has been confirmed.” By “horns” he means the crossbeam of the wood of the cross, which, fastened to it, he held in his hands; by this kind of death he conquered every death and thus confirmed the strength of his glory in the hearts of the elect, so that they could not be held back from his love by any terrors or enticements, while the promised glory of future incorruption was also set before them, through which the last enemy, death, would be destroyed. [Col. 1117B]

Finally, on the holy mountain, in the presence of Peter, James, and John, his splendor shone like light. They certainly delighted in the sight of this splendor, but how fragile and weak they still were was demonstrated at the time of his passion. After he had received the horn of the cross into his hands, however, the strength of his glory was confirmed there to such an extent that neither terrors nor death itself could drive it from the hearts of the faithful.

The kingdoms of this world may be suggested by “horns,” as is customary among the prophets. The loftiness of the human mind, whether good or rejected, may also be designated by the word “horns.” Horns are in Christ’s hands “because he is King of kings and Lord of lords” (I Tim. VI). Horns are in his hands so that, humbling one and exalting another, he may break all the horns of sinners, by which they are vainly puffed up. And may the horns of the righteous be exalted—their desires devoted to God, by which they strive to overcome every struggle against the wicked and against vices.

What we read according to the LXX—“He placed a strong love of his strength”—is also to be understood of Christ. God the Father opened the heavens by his strength, filled the earth with praise, and caused his splendor to exist in order to place light and kingship in the hand of his Son, so that he might cause his beloved to be loved by all, and not lightly but ardently and firmly. Those who loved him firmly and remained in his love no one could take from his hand.

Conversely, the devil causes us to love the world and, in place of love for strength, to love vices—not lightly but firmly—so that it may be said of us: “The devil placed a strong love of his vices.” Likewise, where certain copies read, “He placed the firm charity of his strength,” this signifies that the saints loved Christ’s strength with an inward charity even before his passion, but this charity was not firm until, after his passion and resurrection had been completed, he granted them more fully the grace of his Holy Spirit. Then it became so firm that not even their horn—that is, the power of insolent kings—could break it.

“Death will go before his face, and the devil will come forth before his feet.”

According to the Hebrew truth, this verse is read in the following way. Blessed Jerome explained it as follows:

“The Hebrews relate that, just as in the Gospel the prince of demons is called Beelzebub, so Resheph is the name of a demon who holds authority among the others. Because of his great speed and his wandering in different directions, he is called a bird and a winged creature. They say that he is the one who spoke to the woman in paradise under the form of a serpent, and that from the curse by which he was condemned by God he received his name: for Resheph is interpreted as ‘creeping on the belly.’”

This, then, is what is meant: as soon as the Lord came, was baptized in the Jordan, and, at the descent of the dove, the Father’s voice thundered, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III), the devil will meet him as he comes out of the waters, and death will stand before his feet like the ancient serpent; for forty days he will tempt him in the wilderness. [Col. 1118B]

If, however, we read according to the LXX, “Before his face the Word will go, and he will come forth into the fields,” this signifies that the word of God precedes and prepares the hearts of believers before his visitation—which is now allegorically called his “face”—so that it may make crooked things straight and level uneven places, and so that the soul of the hearer, like a cultivated field, may be able to receive spiritual seed.

Before the Lord came in the flesh, the words of the prophets went before him and bore witness to his coming. These same words went out into the fields when, through the preaching of the apostles, they were proclaimed throughout the whole world. The word of preaching preceded the Lord not only in the prophetic writings but also in the apostles, when they announced to the world that Christ’s coming in the flesh had been fulfilled. [Col. 1118C]

The Word went before his face because, plainly, the teaching of truth first reaches the ears of those who are to be instructed; then faith and understanding of the word illuminate their hearts and make them worthy for God to dwell in them.

“He stood and measured the earth; he looked and dissolved the nations; the mountains of the age were crushed, and the hills of the world bowed down before the paths of his eternity.”

The Savior stood, surveyed everything, and measured the universe of the world with his eyes; he scattered the multitude of the nations. Once they had been scattered and dissolved, the mountains of this age were crushed and the hills of this world bowed down. There are other mountains and hills, however, over which the bridegroom leaps and bounds in the Song of Songs. Of them the Psalm of Ascents also says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help will come” (Ps. CXX). [Col. 1118D]

The mountains of the age are the same as the dark mountains, concerning which Jeremiah commanded that our feet should not stumble upon them. “The hills of the world,” he says, “were bowed down.” Before the Savior’s coming, they walked with their necks erect, and no one could humble their pride.

They were crushed and bowed down before the paths of his eternity—that is, the eternity of God—because his eternity deigned to come to us. Or this may mean that from the beginning of the world until his incarnation he continually came to the saints, and that the word of God became present in the hand of each of them. In all who conquered, he himself triumphed, bending the path of his eternity and crushing the hills and mountains.

The mountains may also be understood as demons who operate in heretics and exalt themselves against the knowledge of God. The hills may signify other demonic powers, which cause human beings to admire the beauty of their bodies, honors, riches, nobility of birth, and the other goods of the world.

We may observe, after the coming of the word of God and of God the Father’s presence, how human souls are shaken, how everything earthly is dissolved, and how former thoughts are reduced to nothing. Then the demons are destroyed; then the heights of the world are brought to nothing; and all the knowledge of heretics, which had first swelled up, is humbled, crushed, and consumed at the coming of the word of God.

According to another edition the passage reads: “His feet stood, and the earth was shaken; he looked, and the nations melted away; the mountains were violently broken; the everlasting hills melted away.” [Col. 1119B]

When, through the preaching of a teacher, the traces of truth are fixed in the mind of the hearer, the mind itself is immediately shaken and disturbed as it considers itself. The Lord’s feet may appropriately be understood as the teachers through whom the word is ministered, since he who is everywhere present by himself is carried throughout the whole world through them as through his feet.

They stand on their feet, and the earth is moved, because the more firmly holy teachers persist in proclaiming and guarding the truth, the more quickly earthly hearts are shaken into repentance for their errors. Since this act of repentance must be attributed not to the human preacher but to the grace that illuminates, it is rightly expressed by saying: “The Lord had mercy, and the nations repented.” By that very gaze he looked upon Peter after Peter had denied him, and Peter, pierced with remorse at the memory of his sin, immediately melted into tears.

He calls proud people “mountains”—those who exalt themselves through the kingdom, wisdom, or riches of this age. When the Lord looked upon them, they were not merely broken but violently broken. When he showed mercy, some such people abandoned not only their empty and arrogant elevation but also attacked it by the way they lived and preached.

Saul and Matthew were mountains: the one was exalted by the wisdom of carnal learning, the other by unrighteous mammon. But when each was turned toward the discipline of humility and became a disciple of Christ, the mountains were indeed violently broken.

The name “hills,” like that of “mountains,” expresses proud people. Perhaps they are inflated with less arrogance, yet are not free from the guilt of swelling pride. They therefore need to be healthfully bent down, so that they may deserve to be raised up by the Lord. They are rightly called “everlasting hills,” because, while humbled in time and melting away from the swelling of pride, they are raised up and glorified forever by him who says: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted.”

The same edition continues: “I saw the paths of his eternity because of the labors.”

The paths of the Lord’s temporality are those by which he came into the world, so that he might appear to human beings for a time. The paths of his eternity are those by which, having left the world bodily, he returned to the Father, with whom he remained eternally even while he dwelt temporally in the world. The Lord himself desired these paths when, approaching his passion, he said to the Father: “I have glorified you upon the earth; I have finished the work that you gave me to do” (John XVII).

Immediately afterward he added, concerning the paths of his eternity: “And now glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed.” The prophet saw these paths of eternity through the labors of the incarnation and passion. Concerning them it was said above: “God will come from Lebanon, or from the south, and horns are in his hands,” and other expressions of this kind, many of which are found in this same Song.

“For iniquity I saw the tents of Ethiopia; the skins of the land of Midian will tremble.”

The LXX: “Because of labors I saw the tents of the Ethiopians; they will fear, and the tents of the land of Midian.”

The Ethiopians are dark, lovers of darkness, and estranged from every light; they feed on the flesh of the dragon, concerning which it is written: “You gave him as food to the Ethiopian peoples” (Ps. LXXIII). They signify demons. Whoever in this age labors for honors and riches becomes their tent or dwelling, as is significantly shown under the single word “iniquity.” For every rich person is either unjust or the heir of an unjust person.

Consider people crossing seas, keeping watch before the doors of the powerful, and enduring everything that the condition of slaves scarcely endures, in order to gather riches or obtain some office. After they have attained this, they surrender themselves to luxury, pleasures, and every form of iniquity, so that what avarice gathered luxury may consume.

These people, therefore, become a lodging place for demons because of their labors. Those who ought to have been the temple of God become tents of the Ethiopians. The following statement—“the skins of the land of Midian will tremble”—should also be understood of the same people: the tents of the Ethiopians and the tents of the land of Midian.

Midian in our language means “from judgment,” that is, “for condemnation.” This indicates that they are always in fear of judgment and eternal punishments, and that they endure the torments which they know they sustain through daily terror.

Alternatively, the tents of the Ethiopians and the tents of the land of Midian will be afraid when the nations, after the Gospel has been announced to them by the apostles, begin, through that same hearing and through the completion of the same works, to serve the Lord in fear and to rejoice before him with trembling.

It is fitting that he placed the Ethiopians first, since they are at the ends of the world, thereby mystically indicating that the sound of the preachers would go out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world. Let the Ethiopians, then, fear at the name of Christ, and let it be marked that his faith will reach the ends of the earth. Let the Midianites also fear, so that the peoples of the interior regions may likewise be shown to be destined for salvation.

When he does not say, “The Ethiopians and Midianites will fear,” but, “The tents of the Ethiopians will fear, and the tents of the land of Midian,” he uses the same figure of speech found in the Gospel: “The whole city went out to meet Jesus,” although it was not the city itself that went out, but those who were in the city.

“Were you angry, Lord, with the rivers, or was your fury against the rivers, or your indignation against the sea, when you mounted your horses and your chariots were salvation? You will surely rouse your bow; the oaths sworn to the tribes, which you spoke.”

The LXX: “Were you angry, Lord, with the rivers, or was your fury against the rivers, or your onslaught against the sea? For you will mount your horses, and your riding is salvation; bending, you will stretch your bow over scepters, says the Lord.”

This may be understood literally as follows. Just as you dried up the Jordan and the Red Sea when you fought for us—for you were not angry with rivers or the sea, nor could insensible things incur any offense—so now, mounting your chariots and taking up your bow, you will grant salvation to your people and fulfill forever the oaths that you swore to our fathers and tribes.

When he says, “Were you angry, Lord, with the rivers, or was your fury against the rivers, or your onslaught against the sea?” he speaks ambiguously, both in the language of one asking a question and of one making an assertion. For there are good rivers and bad rivers; there is a very evil sea and a very good sea.

An example of good rivers is: “The river’s streams make glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV); and: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him, rivers of living water will flow from his belly into eternal life” (John VII). An example of bad rivers is what Pharaoh says in Ezekiel: “The rivers are mine, and I made them,” in which the dragon dwells, along with many similar passages.

The sea likewise may be understood in a good sense, as when the Psalmist says of the Church: “He founded it upon the seas and prepared it upon the rivers” (Ps. II). It may also be understood in a bad sense, as in: “This is the great and spacious sea; there are creeping things without number” (Ps. CIII), and so forth.

If the rivers and the sea are good—the rivers and sea upon which Jesus places and prepares his Church—and if, when understood in a bad sense, they are the sea and rivers of which it is written, “The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned back” (Ps. CXIII), then we may appropriately understand that there are good horses and bad horses, and likewise good chariots and chariots that are bad, placed in some passages in one sense and in others in another.

For in Exodus we read that Pharaoh’s chariots and four-horse teams were submerged in the waves of the sea. Conversely, in the Song of Songs the bridegroom says to the bride: “I have compared you, my beloved, to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots” (Song I). Christ does not compare the Church, or the word of God the soul whom he calls his bride, to Pharaoh’s chariots; rather, every soul, however holy and perfect, is, in comparison with God, like Pharaoh’s chariot and beast of burden.

Hence Moses says to God: “I am irrational”; and David: “I became like a beast before you” (Ps. LXXII)—not that he was simply a beast, but that before God he was as a beast.

“Therefore the Lord rouses his bow and aims his arrows at the scepters,” that is, at the kingdoms of the devil, which oppose the Lord through various vices and sins: avarice, luxury, envy, slander, thefts, and perjuries. Against these the word of God, seated upon his horses and chariots—that is, upon the souls of the saints, upon whom the divine word mounts—raises the bow of the holy Scriptures. From them the shafts of divine testimonies are sent forth, and he fulfills the oaths sworn to the tribes of the Lord, which he spoke to their fathers.

These are the tribes concerning which the Psalmist, discussing the mystical Jerusalem, says: “For there the tribes of the Lord went up, a testimony for Israel, to give thanks to the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXXI).

In the LXX edition, the words “Were you angry, Lord, with the rivers, or was your fury against the rivers, or your onslaught against the sea?” may also express by the names of rivers and sea the hearts of unbelievers. They are rightly called rivers because, with the whole force of their intention, they flow downward toward lower things. They are called sea because they are darkened within by turbid and bitter thoughts and exalt themselves above others through the swollen currents of boastful self-display.

Does he therefore ask whether those who drag their minds down from heavenly desires into the pursuit of weak and inferior things, and who in the instability of their pride raise themselves against their neighbors, have sinned so grievously that the anger they deserve will remain forever unrelieved in such people? Or does he mean that, to all who sin throughout the world—whether more lightly or more seriously—he manifests the grace of his mercy in the world?

For I see that you will send apostles to proclaim your glory to the nations; but who will believe is a matter of your thought, not of human thought. This is what follows: “For, ascending, you will ascend upon your horses, and your riding is salvation”—that is, ascending into the hearts of your elect through the illumination of grace, by which, under your guidance, they may walk the path of virtue and, carrying you throughout the whole world by evangelizing, proclaim to the world the life of perpetual salvation.

The figure of this riding was also shown literally in the Lord, when, going toward Jerusalem, he sat upon a donkey while the crowds before him, behind him, and coming to meet him sang: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. XXI).

Salvation resounded in this riding, because it signified their spiritual journey: under the Lord’s leadership, through the apostles, they are led toward the Jerusalem above, which is our mother, so that they may behold its kingdom.

“Bending, you will stretch your bow over the scepters, says the Lord.”

By “bow” he means the unexpected arrival of the divine scrutiny, by which he also foresaw that the scepters—that is, the kingdoms of the world—would be examined.

The Prophet therefore indicates what our Lord accomplishes in the apostles and their successors, mounting his horses—that is, filling and governing them by his grace: “Bending, you will stretch your bow over the scepters.” That is, through the teachers you will threaten that your judgment will come suddenly. Whoever is terrified by the threat of wrath, as by a drawn bow, and hastens to implore your mercy will not experience the shooting of the arrows—that is, the threat of everlasting punishments.

When, after first saying, “Bending, you will stretch your bow over the scepters,” he adds, “says the Lord,” he signifies God the Father, concerning whom the Son himself says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V).

“Splitting the rivers of the earth.”

Let us first set forth an example, so that by this step we may ascend to higher things. We read in the works of those who compiled books about marvels and brought the Olympiads of Greece down to the memory of our own time, explaining what new event occurred in the world in each year, that among other things rivers burst forth during earthquakes—rivers that had not existed before—while others were swallowed up and disappeared. All the veins of the earth, like the blood in a human body, contain hidden waters within themselves, which break open when the earth is shaken and flow as rivers.

If we understand this, let us see that the human soul naturally contains waters and rivers, but that through our sluggishness they are hidden and do not flow. When the soul is shaken by the preaching of the word of God and moved from its former condition, what was hidden then bursts forth and flows to refresh those who drink.

According to another edition the passage reads: “The earth will be split by rivers.” The rivers here are not the same as those with which he feared the Lord’s anger and fury above, but rather those of which he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” And the Evangelist explains: “He said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive” (John VII).

By these rivers, then, the earth will be split. When the hearts of the carnal are watered by the words of those who teach, they crush the hardness of their unbelief by humbling themselves and open the bosom of their inner thought—which had been wrongly closed—to receive the words of saving reproof or exhortation.

“God, they saw you, and the mountains were in pain; the torrent of waters passed by; the abyss uttered its voice; the height raised its hands. The sun and moon stood in their dwelling. In the light of your arrows they will go; in the brightness of your flashing spear, in your fury you will trample the earth; in your wrath you will astonish the nations. You went forth for the salvation of your people, for salvation with your Christ; you struck the head from the house of the wicked; you stripped its foundation as far as the neck, forever.”

We have set down only our edition, so that, weaving together the sequence of the passage according to it—that is, according to the Hebrew—we may afterward discuss the LXX by clauses and sections.

“They saw you, God, and the mountains were in pain”: that is, the exalted kingdoms and lofty powers of this age, and the four chariots in Zechariah that come forth from the bronze mountains. These saw you and trembled. “The torrent of waters passed by”: that is, all their force and persecution by which they afflicted your people passed away after they saw you.

Then “the abyss”—that is, the underworld—praised you. Then the heights also, that is, the angels, clapped their hands and, as it were, demonstrated the victor by a gesture and dance with uplifted hands.

Your sun and moon, and all the splendor by which you had previously illumined your people, but which afterward had been covered by the weight of evils with the horror of universal darkness, received their light again and regained their former radiance. Your arrows and your flashing spear—that is, your blows and your instruction—gave light to your people.

Finally, “in the light of your arrows and in the brightness of your spear,” which corrected them for the purpose of amendment, your people walked in your fury. When, therefore, you avenge the wrongs done to your people, you will trample earthly kingdoms and make all nations marvel, because you went forth for the salvation of your people and came to them with your Christ. For Jesus is interpreted as “Savior.”

When Jesus Christ, your Son, comes, you will strike the Antichrist from the house of the wicked—that is, from this age, which lies in wickedness—or you will strike the devil himself, who is the head of impiety. You will strip his foundation as far as the neck: that is, you will reveal what was hidden, not for a brief time but forever. For this is what *Sela* means, namely, “forever.”

According to another edition, however, the passage reads:

“They will see you, and the peoples will be in pain.”

The sense is as follows. The hearts of sinners, split open for recognition and confession of the truth by the frequent exhortation of teachers, see the Lord for the time being through faith, as though washed by repeated torrents, and grieve that they have so long withdrawn from him through guilt. When the pain of repentance has ended, they will see him more fully in the future, by sight, and will rejoice forever in his blessed vision.

It continues:

“Sprinkling waters on his paths, the abyss gave its voice from the height of its imagination.” [Col. 1124C]

The same teachers are represented above by the name “abyss” and by that of “rivers.” They are called rivers because of the force of their more vigorous attack, by which they cut through the hardness of the earthly mind and move it to repentance for its errors. They are rightly called an abyss because of the height of the knowledge with which they themselves are inwardly filled, as Solomon testifies when he says: “Deep water is the word from a man’s mouth” (Prov. XVIII).

Thus the abyss gives its voice while sprinkling waters on its paths, when holy preachers, inwardly filled in their hearts with a deep knowledge of the truth, present the ministry of the word outwardly to their hearers. They bring forth gradually and in portions, according to the capacity of the weak, what they themselves inwardly comprehend all at once and in abundance.

By “paths” he means the works either of the teachers themselves or of their hearers. For they sprinkle waters on their paths when, wherever they walk, they continually display examples of right living to those who look upon them, together with the voice of preaching. They sprinkle waters on the paths of those who watch them when, by teaching and living alike, they show them beforehand by what ways of action they ought to walk.

It is fitting that, after saying that the abyss gave its voice, he added, “from the height of its imagination,” because what the holy preachers proclaim outwardly as marvelous proceeds from that fountain of wisdom by which they themselves are inwardly illuminated through the more marvelous contemplation of heavenly joys.

Did not the great abyss give its voice from the height of its imagination when the apostle Paul said: “Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted in us, but you are restricted in your own inward parts. I speak as to children: be enlarged yourselves also”?

How and in what order it came about that the world was sprinkled with saving waters and that the abyss of heavenly wisdom thundered upon the earth is shown next, when it says:

“The sun was lifted up, and the moon stood in its order.”

The Lord, the sun of righteousness, was lifted up into heaven after his passion and resurrection. Having been sent by the Father, the Spirit illuminated the Church and spread it throughout the whole world, so that the Church, in its order—that is, after the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation had been fulfilled—might rise from its long illness of unbelief, stand firm in faith, act courageously, and be strengthened in his love.

Since he had compared Christ to the sun and the Church to the moon, he appropriately turned again to the same sun and immediately added:

“In the light your arrows will go, in the brightness of the gleam of your weapons.”

The arrows of Christ are his words, by which human hearts are pierced, so that, after receiving a saving wound, the faithful soul may say: “I am wounded by love.” These arrows go in light because, through the ministry of teachers, the words of truth have been openly made known to the world, according to what Truth himself commanded them: “What I tell you in the darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops” (Luke XII).

Because the brightness of miracles also followed the words of light, he added: “In the brightness of the gleam of your weapons.” With arrows combatants strike their adversaries; with weapons they protect themselves from being wounded. Hence the sayings of preachers, by which they overcome the perversity of unbelievers, are appropriately signified by arrows, while the miracles by which they confirm the truth of their preaching are signified by weapons.

The arrows of Christ therefore go in light, and they go in the brightness of the gleam of his weapons, because the mighty deeds he performed, the mysteries he revealed, the commandments he set forth, and the rewards he promised have now become known throughout the world, brighter than the sun, through the writings of the Gospel.

The holy teachers too, because they are children of light, shine with clear light and splendor in whatever they do or say by his gift.

“In your threat you will diminish the earth, and in your wrath.”

By threatening the strictness of the judgment by which the wicked will be condemned, you will bring down the nations. You will healthfully humble those who were accustomed to place earthly things before heavenly things, so that, as their earthly desires are gradually diminished, they may begin to think about and seek the things that are above. And by bringing wrath upon them, you will condemn forever those who, for the sake of their eternal exaltation, refused to be humbled for a time.

“You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your christs.”

The mediator between God and human beings went forth from the Father and came into the world, not to judge the world but so that the world might be saved through him.

By “christs” he means all the elect, because they are rightly called by this name from the anointing of spiritual grace. Hence the Psalmist speaks of those who wished to harm the saints but were restrained by divine prohibition. “He rebuked kings for their sake: ‘Do not touch my christs’” (Ps. CIV).

He saved his christs—not those whom he found already to be christs, but those whom, by going forth from the Father and appearing in the flesh, he made his christs, that is, his anointed ones, through the Spirit of adoption.

Concerning this anointing the apostle John admonishes his hearers: “Let the anointing that you received from him remain in you” (I John II).

“You sent death upon the heads of the enemies; you raised up bonds as far as the necks.”

The Lord killed sin, sending death upon the heads of his enemies so that he might give life to righteousness. I shall say something more boldly: Christ came into the world for this purpose, to send death upon the heads of his enemies. Just as he himself died to sin once for all, so they too might die to iniquity, and those who had become partakers of death might also become partakers of this life.

The Lord raised up the bonds of charity, so that, having laid aside our former burden and cast off the very heavy yoke under which we were oppressed, we might take up Christ’s easy yoke and, placed upon his chariot, carry an excellent charioteer.

This may also be understood in another way. To his elect, whom he had called “christs” through the Prophet, he offered the joy of salvation; but to those who neglected to be anointed by his grace, he sent eternal death. This was also fulfilled bodily in the Jewish people, which persecuted the Lord who had appeared in the flesh even unto death.

After it crucified him, not many years passed before the Roman army descended upon it. With the sole exception of those who had withdrawn into faith in the grace of the Gospel, the nation was condemned by an enormous disaster and was deprived even of its kingdom and homeland. [Col. 1126C]

This is what he says: “You raised up bonds as far as the neck,” namely, the neck of the kingdom which they had raised in opposition to the Lord. Concerning this the most blessed protomartyr Stephen says to them even while they raged against him: “You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts V).

The Lord raised up the bonds as far as this neck when he sent a hostile army to overthrow the proud nation. Hence it is written: “The righteous Lord will cut down the necks of sinners” (Ps. CXXVIII).

“You cursed his scepters, the heads of his warriors, when they came like a whirlwind to scatter me. Their exultation was like that of one who devours a poor man in secret. You made a way in the sea for your horses, in the mud of many waters. I heard, and my belly was troubled; at the sound my lips trembled. Let putrefaction enter my bones, and beneath me let it seethe, so that I may rest on the day of my tribulation, so that I may ascend to our armed people.”

And now I have set down only the Hebrew, so that we may discuss separately the edition of the Septuagint. For the Septuagint differs greatly from all the other translations.

“You cursed his scepters”—that is, his kingdoms, undoubtedly those of the impious one of whom he had said above, “You struck the head from the house of the wicked; you laid bare the foundation even to the neck.” We understand the wicked one either as Nebuchadnezzar or as every adversary of God’s people. And not only his scepters, but also the heads of his warriors, whom he had struck. “They came,” he says, “like a whirlwind to scatter me”—that is, to overthrow Israel and lead it captive in different directions—so that they exulted while devouring the poor man, namely, Israel subjected to them, as though they were doing this in secret and devouring us while we knew nothing.

You therefore came to battle for your people, and by sending your chariots into the waters—that is, among many nations—you made a way for them in the mud of many waters, so that you might trample them down and crush them as the mud of your horses and chariots beneath hoof and wheel.

As for what follows, “I heard, and my belly was troubled at the sound”—with the following understood: “my lips trembled; let putrefaction enter my bones, and beneath me let it seethe, so that I may rest on the day of tribulation, so that I may ascend to our armed people”—the sense is this: Now we gladly endure every hardship and tremble with all our inward parts at your threat. Now my lips tremble, and the fear of my anxious mind is marked upon my mouth. And not only this, but I willingly seek and desire something else as well: “Let putrefaction enter my bones, and above me let it seethe.” That is, I gladly endure what Job endured. I desire not only my flesh but even the marrow of my bones to waste away, and my bed to teem with bodily corruption and countless worms, so that, after I have endured these things here for my sins, I may rest on the bitter day, on the day of tribulation, on the day of necessity and distress. “And I shall ascend to our armed people”—that is, to the strong, warlike, and fighting people. And beautifully he says “I shall ascend,” for one always ascends to an armed people; and fittingly he says “our people,” for the one who has been afflicted, willingly endured hardships, and exchanged present evils for future rewards speaks boldly as “ours,” so that, like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, he too may sleep in a good old age, full of days, and be gathered to his fathers.

Another edition:

“You cut off, in alienation, the heads of the mighty; nations shall be moved in it.” In Greek, instead of “in alienation,” it is written “in ecstasy” (*in exstasi*). Some have interpreted this as “in astonishment,” others as “in a mental rapture.” Whether it is called astonishment, alienation, or mental rapture, it signifies one and the same thing: when someone, struck and stupefied by a sudden miracle, is so disturbed that he becomes alienated from the perception of his own mind. This happened to the Jews, as the Gospel’s frequent testimony reveals, saying that they were astonished and amazed at Jesus’ teaching and mighty works, and said: “Where did this man get all these things, whose father and mother we know?” (John VI).

And in the Acts of the Apostles, after the lame man had been healed by Peter and John at the temple gate: “They were filled,” it says, “with astonishment and ecstasy” (Acts III). In this ecstasy—that is, in this amazement or alienation of mind—many from the people were moved to believe in the Lord. But the heads of the mighty, that is, the chief priests and elders, were cut off from the lot of the faithful through their unbelief. Nations also were moved in it, for when they heard or saw the mighty works of the Lord and his apostles, they were so astonished and amazed that, having anathematized and cast away those whom they had worshiped as gods, they received the new faith of Christ with devoted minds.

“They shall open their mouths like a poor man eating in secret.” For just as a poor man, remaining hungry for some time, if he happens to find food somewhere, immediately hastens to refresh himself with it in secret and does not wish to bring it out in public, lest someone else seize it and he himself perish of hunger, so—indeed, so—the peoples of the nations, when the apostles offered them the bread of the word from which they had long remained hungry, at once opened the mouths of their hearts and began to taste it with complete eagerness.

The order by which the poverty of the nations came to receive the feasts of the word is indicated when what follows is immediately added:

“You sent your horses into the sea, troubling many waters.” He calls the sea the world, God’s horses the holy preachers, and the many waters the peoples of the nations. When God’s horses were sent into the sea, the many waters were troubled, because, when heralds of the word were scattered throughout the world, the hearts of the nations were disturbed—some to believe and receive the sacrament of faith, others to contradict or even persecute the heralds of that same faith.

He appropriately speaks above also of these horses, namely, the holy preachers: “For, mounting, you shall mount upon your horses”; and here he adds concerning them: “You sent your horses into the sea.” From both statements it may be gathered that the Lord sent preachers into the world in such a way that he himself was never absent while they preached. Rather, just as a charioteer guides horses, so he continually presided over the direction of their minds.

[Col. 1128C] “My belly guarded and trembled at the sound of the prayer of their lips.” In the customary manner of the prophets, he calls his belly his mind. For just as food is received by the belly, by which the body’s strength and life are restored, so holy thoughts are received in the mind, by which the life of the inner person is sustained and preserved lest it fail.

“I guarded myself,” he says, “with a trembling mind and with greater vigilance, lest I should sin in my heart or, while preaching to others, myself become disqualified.” It should be noted that he says he trembled at the sound of the prayer of his lips, although throughout this entire song he appears to have prayed nothing at all, but only, in fear and trembling, to have described the mysteries of Christ and the Church that were to come. Yet the one who calls his song a prayer is not mistaken, since he gave it precisely this title: “The prayer of the prophet Habakkuk concerning ignorances.” For whatever the holy man says is wholly prayer to God. Everything you do, when its sincere intention is to please the Lord, intercedes with the Lord on his behalf and commends you to him.

“And trembling entered my bones.” Just as Scripture sometimes designates our carnal actions by the name “flesh,” so by the word “bones” it is accustomed to signify strong and spiritual deeds. “My heart therefore trembled,” he says, “at what I foresee is to come upon the world; and whatever spiritual strength I thought I possessed trembled as something fragile when I contemplated the greater virtues and sufferings of Christ and of the blessed apostles.” This is explained more clearly in the following words:

“And beneath me my strength was troubled.” He appropriately says that his strength was troubled not in him but beneath him. For, carried away into contemplation of heavenly mysteries, the prophet saw that he had somehow been raised above himself; and the higher he is made by the light of contemplation, the more clearly he perceives his imperfection. Raised up to behold heavenly things, he is rightly troubled by what he had done in the lowest regions.

The prophet’s strength was troubled, his bones trembled, and his belly was terrified—not only because he recognized himself as less than perfect in action, but also because he learned that all who wished to live devoutly in Christ would suffer persecutions. He also saw that Christ himself, who would enter the world without sin, would leave the world not without the punishment of sin.

“I shall rest on the day of my tribulation, so that I may ascend to the people of my exile.” He rests on the day not only of recompense but also of tribulation, because he does not doubt that through temporal afflictions he will increase his eternal joys, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “For by hope we were saved” (Romans VIII). And again: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Romans X).

This is the rest of the elect in this life: having abandoned the desire for earthly things, they strive with the whole intention of their minds and by the daily steps of good works to ascend and migrate into the fellowship of those who preceded them in Christ. Even before that final and universal judgment, the saints rest on the day of tribulation, ascending to the people of their exile, when, after good works, they are transferred from the world and joined in heaven to the joys of the earlier righteous, while their persecutors, likewise removed from this life, undergo the torments of Gehenna, where they will be troubled forever.

The day of tribulation may also be understood as belonging to this life, when, as the scarcity of temporal goods grows heavier, those who loved such things grieve as though surrounded by misery. But every elect person, although suffering the same hardships bodily, has rest, with the hope of his mind fixed upon the Lord, knowing that the more heavily he is pressed down in the lower regions, the more exaltedly, after his sufferings, he will ascend to the eternal fellowship of the citizens above. The following agrees suitably with this interpretation:

“For the fig tree shall not blossom, and there shall be no bud on the vines; the work of the olive shall lie, and the fields shall yield no food; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls.”

The Septuagint: “For the fig tree shall not bear fruit, and there shall be no generation in the vines; the work of the olive shall lie, and the fields shall not produce food; the sheep have failed from food, and there shall be no cattle in the manger.”

According to the Hebrew, where we said above, “Let putrefaction enter my bones, and beneath me let it seethe, so that I may rest on the day of tribulation, so that I may ascend to my armed people,” the preceding words are joined to what follows. Therefore I wished to endure tribulation in the present and afterward ascend to the strong people, because the day of tribulation and necessity will come. While the rest are placed in distress, I shall rejoice in your majesty: “The fig tree shall not blossom, and there shall be no bud on the vines; the work of the olive shall lie, and the fields shall yield no food,” and so forth. Since these words do not differ greatly from the Septuagint, let us discuss them together with that interpretation.

When the day of tribulation comes and I ascend to the people who once journeyed as exiles with me—or certainly, when the day of the overthrow of the Jews and of the former people comes, and the daughter of Zion is abandoned like a shelter in a vineyard, like a hut in a cucumber field, and like a city under siege—then, while that people perishes, I shall be chosen as part of the people of whom it was said: “Unless the Lord had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom, and we would have been made like Gomorrah” (Romans IX). I shall join myself to the disciples of Christ. Since he teaches them on the mountain, while the crowds and the weak are left below, I shall ascend to the mountains.

If someone asks what these verses signify figuratively, they may be explained as follows. The fig tree, vine, and olive were the synagogue of the Jews when it offered to God the sweetness of good works, the ardor of fervent love, and the richness of a merciful spirit devoted to him. The sheep and oxen were symbols within that same people: sheep, namely, those who humbly listened to the voice of the supreme Shepherd; oxen, those who diligently bore the yoke of the law and, in order to produce the fruits of good works, prepared the hearts of their hearers by teaching and correcting them assiduously, as though plowing the Lord’s soil.

While these lived spiritually, they made spiritual food from the broad fields of the divine Scriptures. Their pasture delighted the one who had become like a beast before God and always clung to him, saying: “The Lord rules me, and I shall lack nothing; in a place of pasture he has set me” (Psalm XXII).

But when this fig tree failed to bear the fruit of good works for the Lord when he came to it a third time—that is, in the giving of the law through Moses, in diligent rebuke and exhortation through the prophets, and in the bestowal of grace through himself—it was condemned to eternal dryness in consequence of his curse. The generation failed in the vineyards once belonging to the Lord, that is, the fruit of charity among the crowds of the Jews. Therefore, when he was thirsty, they offered him vinegar instead of wine: seeking in them the sweetness of virtues, they produced the bitterness of vices.

“The work of the olive lied,” when that same people fattened the heads of the wretched with the oil of flattery and, with false lips, made the prophet’s truthful declaration resound, saying: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God; I have hoped in the mercy of God” (Psalm LI). Therefore, at the time of the final recompense, it will bring lamps that have been extinguished and, together with its darkness, will be excluded from entry into the heavenly homeland.

“The fields do not produce food,” when that same people cannot, by rightly understanding, find the pasture of truth in the open pages of the divine writings. “The sheep fail from food,” because where the inward refreshment of sweetness is absent, there is no source from which the innocence of a simple life might arise.

Thus it is said, “The sheep have failed from food,” that is, because food was lacking, just as the prophet says in the Psalm: “And my flesh,” he says, “was changed because of the oil” (Psalm CVIII)—that is, because there was no oil by which I might be refreshed or anointed. Finally, some manuscripts read: “They failed because they did not eat the sheep.”

“There are no oxen in the stalls,” because although among the Jews there are abundant stalls of heavenly writings, those who do not perceive in them the nourishment of heavenly understanding, and who might bear the gentle yoke of the Gospel, are absent.

Considering all these things that were to come upon the faithless part of his people, the prophet immediately showed what he himself would do with the faithful of that people—or rather, with the fellowship of the whole Church that was to be gathered throughout the world in Christ or had already been gathered—saying:

“But I shall rejoice in the Lord, and exult in God my Jesus.”

Another edition: “But I shall glory in the Lord; I shall rejoice in God my Jesus.”

“But I,” he says, “shall glory not in my own righteousness but in faith in divine protection. I shall rejoice in my God Jesus, for I consider salvation to be not in myself but in him.” And as though we were asking him why he gloried in the Lord and in God Jesus, whom he called “my own” out of great affection, he immediately indicated the most just cause of that joy and brought his song to an end as follows:

“God the Lord is my strength, and he will set my feet like those of deer, and upon my high places he will lead me, singing to the victor in Psalms.”

“God the Lord,” he says, “is my strength. I shall have no other power except in Christ, and I shall count all the righteousnesses of the law as refuse. He will set my feet like those of deer, so that I may tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and, like a little child, cast [it] into the hole and draw Judah, the serpent, out of the viper.”

“For my kinsman is like a doe or a fawn of the deer.” And because he himself is the deer, he also granted me to become a deer: lofty in horns, cleaving hooves, chewing the cud, and causing serpents to flee at my scent. Of him it is said in the Psalm: “He made my feet like those of a deer and set me upon high places” (Psalm XXVIII). And again: “The voice of the Lord perfecting the deer.”

He will therefore set my feet among his other deer and lead me to heavenly things, so that among the angels I may sing the glory of the Lord and announce peace on earth to people of good will. I shall sing his victory, triumph, and trophy of the cross.

According to another edition, this prophetic statement is read as follows:

“Lord God, my strength, establish my feet for completion, and set me upon high places, so that I may conquer in his glory.”

As though he were saying plainly: “My strength beneath me was troubled,” that is, when I look upon the condition of human frailty that lies below, and when I raise the eyes of my mind to the grace of divine assistance, I trust that in him I can perform acts of strength. He alone can bring the steps of my works to a firm conclusion. He alone can set me upon high places, so that I may despise as nothing every elevation of worldly power through contemplation of eternal goods. I shall conquer in his glory every temptation that comes upon me, whether from adversity or from the allurements of the world—that is, while in everything I do I seek not my own glory but his, remembering that whatever good I do I have received from him.

Those who, having conquered temptations, have been proved worthy, are rightly assisted by the Lord so that they may attain the palm of the heavenly calling, when they attribute the whole cause of their victory to his praise. Some manuscripts read, “so that I may conquer in his song,” which refers to the same sense. Whoever knows how to give thanks to the Lord from the heart in all the tribulations he endures conquers in the Lord’s song, knowing that “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans VIII).

Nevertheless, according to the historical sense, the prophet’s statement may have this meaning, as though he were saying: “I shall conquer in song; my hands shall compose the cithara, the psaltery, and every kind of instrument; I shall write a panegyric for the triumphant one. Though at the beginning I said, ‘How long shall I cry, and you will not hear? I shall call out to you, suffering violence, and you will not save’—and though I argued about justice and judgment—afterward I shall praise equity and surpass the other singers with my song.”

Beautifully, then, he responds at the end to the beginning of this prophetic song. For the one who, after hearing and considering the works of the Lord appearing in the flesh, faithfully fears and trembles will consequently despise the things that fluctuate in this life like the waves of the sea in their varied movement, and glory and rejoice in him alone.

## HERE BEGINS THE SONG OF THE BOOK OF DEUTERONOMY

It is read in Deuteronomy that Moses, after writing the words of the law in a scroll and completing them, spoke, in the hearing of the whole assembly of Israel, the words of this song and brought it to its conclusion. Hence it may be inferred that this song, which Moses sang as a testimony to the children of Israel, does not merely express a simple history but is filled with spiritual understanding.

In part, according to the historical sense, it reproves the Israelites’ faithlessness for the exceedingly abundant benefits bestowed upon them by the Lord. In part, through allegory, it instructs the holy Church of God concerning heavenly mysteries. In part, through tropology, it calls each of the faithful to moral uprightness.

Therefore the sober reader ought to preserve the truth of Scripture in the historical sense; in allegory, to consider the meaning of the heavenly mysteries; and in tropology, to learn the usefulness of good disciplines. Thus instructed by this threefold distinction, he may be advanced to that heavenly theory—that is, to the contemplation of secret things and to the sublimity of divine contemplation.

It must also be carefully examined that Moses is said to have spoken the words of the song and completed them to the end. Perhaps this admonishes us that whoever strives to praise God with his mouth should not contradict him in his works. For praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner. Therefore the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does and teaches them shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XIX).

The beginning of this song is as follows:

“Hear, O heavens, what I shall speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth.”

Following the opening of the prophet Isaiah, it is written: “Hear, O heaven, and perceive with your ears, O earth, because the Lord has spoken” (Isaiah I). Above, in the same book, the title showed which prophet he was, whose son he was, against Judah and Jerusalem—or through Judah and Jerusalem—and at what time he saw these things. Now he calls heaven and earth to hear, signifying by heaven the heavenly and angelic powers, and by earth the human race. He indicates the things contained by means of those that contain them—*metonymically* (*metonymikōs*).

For since, through Moses, the Lord had called heaven and earth as witnesses when he gave his law to the people of Israel, saying, “Give attention, O heaven, and I shall speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth,” after the people’s transgression he again calls the same witnesses, so that all the elements may know that God has been justly provoked to anger in avenging the violation of his commandments.

“Let my teaching gather like rain; let my speech flow like dew, like a shower upon grass and like drops upon the herbage, because I shall invoke the name of the Lord.”

Another edition: “Let my speech be awaited like rain, and let my words descend like dew, like a shower upon a young plant and like snow upon hay, because I have invoked the name of the Lord.”

He compares the word of God’s law to rain and dew, because it seeks the shoots of spiritual fruits from the hearts of the faithful. For these hearts are the Lord’s vineyard, from which he seeks fruit pleasing to himself—that is, good works.

We find a similar comparison in the prophet Isaiah: “As rain,” he says, “and snow descend from heaven, and do not return there again, but water the earth, saturate it, and make it germinate, giving seed to the sower and bread to the eater, so shall my word be that goes forth from my mouth. It shall not return to me empty, but shall do whatever I have willed, and it shall prosper in the things for which I sent it” (Isaiah LV).

But because Moses said that his teaching should gather into rain, in order to show openly what this rain was, he added: “Because I shall invoke the name of the Lord.” To invoke the name of the Lord, therefore, is to preach the Gospel of Christ. Whoever hears and obeys it will undoubtedly possess the fruit of good works in heaven.

“Give greatness to our God; God’s works are perfect, and all his ways are judgments.”

Another edition: “Give majesty to our God. God—true are his works—and all his ways are judgments.”

To magnify the Lord is to proclaim the majesty of the Savior with believing heart and devout mouth, together with good works. Hence Mary, the mother of the Lord, says in the Gospel song: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior” (Luke I).

“God’s works,” he says, “are perfect.” What, then, are those works? Hear Moses speaking in Genesis: “Thus the heavens and the earth were completed, and all their adornment. And God completed on the seventh day his work that he had made, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done” (Genesis II).

The work of God, therefore, is the redemption of the human race. When he completed it, resting in the tomb, he showed us a spiritual Sabbath.

“All his ways,” he says, “are judgments,” because all his commandments are true. Hence the Psalmist says: “The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the simple” (Psalm XVIII). And again: “The judgments of God are true, justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “With my lips,” he says, “I have declared all the judgments of your mouth” (Psalm CXVIII).

“A faithful God, and just and upright, without any iniquity.”

Another edition: “A faithful God, and there is no iniquity in him; the Lord is just and holy.”

He is faithful because he undoubtedly fulfilled what he promised. He is without any iniquity because supreme equity in no way admits fellowship with iniquity. He is just because he will repay sinners who do not repent with punishment for their evils. He is upright because he will give eternal life to those who act worthily and have deserved well. He is holy because he is most proven in all his judgments and actions. For “holy” also signifies one who is pious, patient, and a giver of all good things, since whatever he accomplishes is completed with the praise of virtue.

“They sinned against him—not his children—in their filth.”

Another edition: “They sinned; they are not his children, but defiled.”

How are they not God’s children? Because they are not so through faith: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John I).

Therefore the Lord said to the Jews who refused to receive his faith and despised his teaching: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father; he was a murderer from the beginning and a thief.” And Stephen said to those same Jews: “Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold the coming of the Just One, whose betrayers and murderers you have now become, you who received the law through the disposition of angels and did not keep it.”

Whoever sins incorrigibly proves that he is not a son of God.

The edition produced by the seventy interpreters, however, reads: “They sinned; they are not his children, but blameworthy.” Some have translated this from the Greek as “defiled children”; others, “idle children.” Hence there is no great question—indeed, no question at all.

But this deserves to be asked: if the statement is general, “They sinned; they are not his children,” does it mean that whoever sins does not sin against God—that is, that he does not harm God but himself? How, then, is what we read in the Psalm to be understood: “Against you alone have I sinned” (Psalm L)? And in Jeremiah: “We have sinned against you, O patience of Israel, Lord” (Jeremiah XIV). And again in the Psalm: “Heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” (Psalm XL). Is this the same as sinning against God, or sinning into God, as the priest Eli says: “If he sins against God, who will pray for him?” (1 Samuel II).
