To sin against God is to sin in matters pertaining to the worship of God. Thus we read that God said to Abimelech concerning Sarah: “Therefore I spared you, lest you should sin against me” (Genesis XX).

But as for sinning against the Lord—or rather, having sinned against the Lord—unless some passage should be found that resists this interpretation, I think that those are rightly so called who do not perform worthy repentance for their sin, so that God may be glorified in forgiving them. For David gives the reason why he said, “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you” (Psalm L). He adds: “So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged,” because it plainly appears to all who think rightly that the Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works: “He does not desire the death of a sinner, but that he should turn and live” (cf. Psalm XL).

Likewise, when David said, “Heal my soul, because I have sinned against you,” the same purpose is at work: that God may be glorified by forgiving, because his mercy is great toward those who confess to him and return to him.

In this song the prophet foresaw that there would be some who would sin in such a way—offending God by their great iniquities—that they would not wish either to repent or to return to God to be healed. Of them it is also said: “For they are flesh, a spirit that goes and does not return.” Therefore he said that they were not children of God, because they had become incorrigible.

“A crooked and perverse generation—do you repay the Lord in this way?”

Another edition: “For a crooked and perverse generation—you have repaid the Lord in this way.”

The Savior marked their faithlessness with a similar condemnation in the Gospel. When they tested him and sought a sign from him, he replied: “A crooked and perverse generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given it except the sign of Jonah” (Matthew XII).

Likewise John the Baptist said to the crowds of Jews coming to him: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance, and do not wish to say, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.”

The generation of the Jews was always crooked and perverse. It was ungrateful for God’s benefits and did not repay him with fitting praises; indeed, on the contrary, it continually returned various transgressions, the filth of idols, and provocations.

“Foolish and senseless people, is he not your Father, who possessed you, made you, and created you?”

Another edition: “So, foolish and unwise people—is he not himself your Father? He possessed you, made you, and created you.”

According to the power of nature, there is one Father and creator of all, God, because all things are from him, through him, and in him. God created the human being when he formed the material from which he could be fashioned; he made him when he formed him in his own image and likeness; he possessed him when, after expelling errors through faith and grace, he claimed him for himself.

The foolish and senseless people, therefore, were the Jewish nation, which neither revered its Creator and Maker—whom the law given to it most clearly revealed—with worthy worship, nor remembered the benefit by which he had specially possessed it in Egypt, rescuing it from the hands of its enemies through miracles and signs. He gave it manna from heaven and water from the rock, and provided guidance through the Red Sea and in the desert by angelic ministry—that is, in the pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night.

But this crooked and perverse generation did not repay its Lord with fitting thanks for such great benefits. Rather, it fashioned idols for itself and most foolishly offered them divine honor and sacrifices, saying: “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus XII).

“Remember the days of old; consider the generations one by one; ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you.”

Another edition: “Keep in mind the days of the age; understand the years, the nations of nations; ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you.”

He recalls ancient deeds to their memory, commanding them to question their fathers and learn from them how, in past ages and generations, they were freed by divine aid and repeatedly protected from their enemies. In this way at least they might be summoned to repentance for their sins and more readily consider stripping themselves of every error and drawing near to the truth.

The fathers here are not to be understood as any dull or foolish people, but mystically as teachers of the law and preachers of the Gospel. Through their doctrines and examples a person can advance toward divine understanding. Hence the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: “For if you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, yet not many fathers. For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Corinthians IV).

And to the Hebrews: “We indeed had fathers of our flesh as educators, and we respected them. Shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live? And they indeed instructed us for a few days according to their own will, but he does so for what is useful, in order that we may receive his sanctification” (Hebrews XII).

“When the Most High divided the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel. But the Lord’s portion is his people, Jacob the cord of his inheritance.”

Another edition: “When the Most High divided the nations, as he dispersed the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of God’s angels; and the Lord’s portion became his people, Jacob the cord of his inheritance, Israel.”

For the order of the historical account gives the reason for the distribution of the human race. Since the multitude of human beings is so great that their number cannot be comprehended by human reckoning, the Lord chose the sons of Israel alone from so great a multitude as his inheritance, so that he might make his name and his power known among them and reveal the secrets of his will through the judgments of the Law and the writings of the prophets. Thus Moses, earlier in the present book, bore witness, saying (Deut. VII):

“The Lord your God chose you to be his special people from all the peoples who are upon the earth—not because you surpassed all the nations in number did the Lord join himself to you and choose you, since you are fewer than all the peoples, but because the Lord loved you and kept the oath that he swore to your fathers, and brought you out with a strong hand and redeemed you from the house of slavery, from the hand of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, so that you might know that the Lord your God himself is the strong and faithful God, keeping his covenant and mercy with those who love him and those who keep his commandments for a thousand generations, and repaying those who hate him immediately, so that he destroys them and does not delay, at once rendering to them what they deserve. Therefore keep the commandments, rites, and judgments that I command you today to perform.”

And these words may be understood in this way according to the Hebrew truth. According to the other edition, however, where it reads, “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God,” and in Daniel’s vision, where the angel told the Prophet about the prince of Persia who resisted him, it seems to suggest something else to us. For the ministries of angels are believed to have been appointed over individual nations and over individual human beings, so that human nature might be guarded under their governance and protection according to the dispensation of almighty God, and defended from enemies. Hence, when the Lord teaches in the Gospel that the little ones must not be scandalized, he immediately adds:

“Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XII).

Since that heavenly city consists of angels and human beings, and we believe that as many from the human race will ascend there as the number of elect angels who remained there, just as it is written, “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God,” we too ought to draw something from those distinctions among the heavenly citizens for the practice of our way of life, and kindle ourselves through good pursuits toward an increase in virtue. Since a multitude of human beings is believed to be destined to ascend there as great as the multitude of angels who remained, it follows that those very human beings who return to their heavenly homeland should, in returning there, imitate something from those ranks. For the distinct ways of life of human beings correspond to the orders of the individual ranks, and by the likeness of their conduct they are assigned to their lot.

But the Lord’s portion is the spiritual people Jacob, and the cord of his inheritance is true Israel, namely, the Catholic Church, of which the Psalmist says:

“The cords have fallen for me in pleasant places—for indeed my inheritance is pleasant to me” (Ps. XV).

“He found him in a desert land, in a place of horror and vast solitude. He surrounded him, taught him, and guarded him like the pupil of his eye.”

Another edition: “He made him sufficient for himself in the wilderness, in the thirst of heat, where there was no water. He surrounded him, instructed him, and guarded him like the pupil of the eye.”

The Lord is said to have found Israel in a place of horror and vast solitude because, when giving the Law on Mount Sinai, he entered into a covenant with him, distributed manna from heaven to them, brought forth water from the rock, gave them the flesh of quail, and provided them with every sufficiency of food according to what seemed appropriate to him. During those same forty years, as he led them around in the wilderness, he taught them his commandments. But it is rightly asked how he says that he protected them like the pupil of his eye, when so many of them fell in the wilderness—unless perhaps we say that they were protected and guarded for as long as they kept God’s commands; but when they transgressed them, they were immediately struck by plagues and ravaged by enemies.

In the mystical sense, however, the Lord found Israel in the wilderness when he brought the Church out of the error of the world, where there was the horror of idolatry and no remembrance of God. The Lord therefore leads the Church around when, extending her through all the regions of the world, he directs her along the path of his commandments; and, making his will known to her through the Holy Spirit, he guards her everywhere with complete protection, which is signified by the pupil of the eye, against heretics and persecutors.

Another comparison follows:

“Like an eagle urging its young to fly and hovering over them, it spread its wings, took them up, and carried them upon its shoulders.”

Another edition: “As an eagle covers its nest and settles over its young, it spread its wings, took them, and received them upon its shoulders.”

Natural philosophers report that the eagle, which is so called from the sharpness of its eyes, has such keen vision that, when it is carried over the sea on motionless wings and is hidden from human sight, it can see fish swimming in the water from such a height; then, descending like a projectile, it seizes its prey and draws it to shore on its wings. It is also said that it does not turn its gaze away from the sun’s rays. Hence it exposes its young, suspended in its claws, to the sun’s rays, and preserves those whom it sees holding their gaze steady as worthy of their lineage; but those whom it sees turning their gaze away it casts aside as degenerate.

Eagles are also said, when they see their young growing feathered in the nest, to strike them with their wings and urge them from the nest to fly. They build their nests in rocks and trees, and in their nests a stone called *echites* is placed, which some have called *gaietes*; it is useful for many remedies and loses nothing through fire. These same investigators of nature report that eagles do not usually die so much from old age or illness as from hunger, because their upper beak grows so much that its hooked shape can no longer open. But when the eagle sees that danger threatens it on this account, it blunts its beak against the hardest rock until it returns again to its former use.

Therefore, in mystical speech, it is written in the Psalm, when the Prophet says to the faithful soul:

“Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. CII).

According to the literal sense, the likeness of the eagle shows that the Lord helped his people by urging them on to possess the land of Canaan through warfare, and protected them from enemies by assisting them. According to the mystical sense, however, this eagle signifies the Lord and Savior, who resembles an eagle in that by his death he rescued the prey from the malignant enemy, and after his resurrection carried on high into heaven the flesh that he had assumed for the redemption of the human race. By his words and examples he exhorts us to follow there in faith and strive in devotion, where he ascended bodily. Hence he says in the Gospel:

“Where the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Luke XVII).

The other examples that we have mentioned about the eagle can likewise be figuratively transferred to him and to his children. For just as the eagle has such keen vision that, lifted over the sea on motionless wings and invisible to human eyes, it sees fish swimming from such a height in the depths and seizes them as prey, carrying them to shore, so our Redeemer, exalted above all the heavens and bodily removed from human sight, nevertheless sees in the sea of this world, through the vision of his majesty, those whom he may rescue as saving prey and draw by the cord of his love to the shore of eternal blessedness. Hence he himself says in the Gospel:

“And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John XII).

He exposes his young—that is, his children reborn to him through the grace of baptism—to the rays of the eternal sun through contemplation. Those whom he sees possessing a steadfast mental gaze as they look upon it, or as worthy of his lineage, he preserves forever; but those whom he sees turning the gaze of their mind downward toward earthly and carnal desires, he casts aside as degenerate.

This eagle nests in rocks and trees because it produces the fruitfulness of spiritual offspring in those whom it sees as firm in faith and fruitful in virtues. There is born there that gem and most precious pearl which the sacred text of the Gospel says the spiritual merchant acquires after selling all his possessions.

But when the eagle rubs its excessive beak against a rock and thus restores it to its former condition, this signifies that holy men break against the rock, Christ, whatever they perceive to be excessive and harmful in their way of life; renewing themselves through grace and good effort, they make themselves fit again for their former service.

[Col. 1139C] “The Lord alone was his leader, and there was no foreign god with him.”

Another edition: “The Lord alone taught them, and there was no foreign god with them.”

It is clear that the one and only God delivered Israel from Egypt, not the false idols worshiped by the Egyptians. Likewise, in our deliverance from spiritual Egypt, it is no other than the same God who formerly rescued the Israelites: namely, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one and triune, great and almighty God, who through the incarnation of Jesus Christ our Lord brings about the mystery of our salvation. From this let heretics recognize how miserably they wander, straying from the true faith, when they separate themselves from the Catholic Church through schisms; for they are subject to as many idols as they have errors.

[Col. 1139D] “He established him upon a lofty land, so that he might eat the fruits of the fields.”

Another edition: “He brought them into the strength of the land; he fed them with the produce of the fields.”

He calls Palestine a lofty land because, in comparison with the land of Egypt, which is flat and watered, it appears mountainous and rugged. It has strength because it is not barren but exceedingly fertile in producing the fruits of the earth for the satisfaction of its inhabitants.

In another sense, the lofty land is the holy Church, which is very exalted in virtues and knowledge and most fertile in the growth of good works. There, all the faithful who have been established eat the fruits of spiritual fields, because there the good seed of God’s word germinates, producing in one case thirtyfold, in another sixtyfold, and in another a hundredfold fruit, so that each person finds sufficient nourishment according to his capacity.

[Col. 1140A] “So that he might suck honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone.”

Another edition: “They sucked honey from the rock and oil from the firm rock.”

Yet nowhere is anything of this kind recorded according to the historical sense. If the whole of the Old Testament is reviewed, nowhere do we read that that people sucked honey from a rock, or oil from a firm rock or hardest stone. But, according to Paul’s statement, “The rock was Christ” (I Cor. X), they sucked honey from the rock who saw the deeds and miracles of that same Redeemer of ours. They sucked oil from the firm rock who, after his resurrection, deserved to be anointed through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit.

Thus, as it were, he gave honey in the firm rock when the mortal Lord still displayed the sweetness of his miracles to his disciples. But the firm rock poured forth oil because, after his resurrection, having become impassible, he caused the gift of holy anointing to flow forth through the breathing of the Spirit.

The prophet also speaks of this oil:

“The yoke will rot from the face of the oil” (Isa. X).

They were held under the yoke of demonic domination; but we have been anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit. Because the grace of freedom has anointed us, the yoke of demonic domination has rotted away.

“Butter from cattle and milk from sheep, with the fat of lambs and rams, the sons of Bashan, and goats, with the marrow of wheat and the blood of the grape.”

Another edition: “Butter of cattle and milk of sheep, with the fat of lambs and rams, the sons of bulls, and goats, with the fat of kidneys, wheat, and the blood of the grape.”

Although these words, according to the historical sense, indicate the fertility of the land of Canaan, in a deeper sense they demonstrate the abundance of Christ’s grace, which the holy Church has received through the gift of her benefactor.

They brought butter from cattle who learned the fullness of faith from the examples of the patriarchs. They received milk from sheep who took simplicity of mind, or ease of instruction, from the innocent life of the Fathers for their own edification. They received these things with the fat of lambs and rams—that is, with the richness of the apostles’ charity and of those whom the apostles had instructed in the faith—for the nourishment of their minds.

For by the name “rams,” the apostles and men of apostolic dignity are signified, because they are the leaders of God’s flock. Hence it is said in the Psalm:

“Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. XXVIII).

What is added, “the sons of Bashan,” belongs to the same meaning, because *Bashan* is interpreted as “fatness.” The sons of fatness are those who have been instructed in the disciplines of the New Testament, where an abundance of knowledge and greatness of virtues reside.

What is read in the other edition, “the sons of bulls,” may likewise be referred to the persons of prophets and apostles, as well as other holy teachers, because they are leaders of God’s flock and preside over spiritual herds. From their teachings they receive the seed of the word, from which they can produce offspring of good works.

Nor were these gifts sufficient unless goats were also added. Goats represent penitents, because they were offered for sin in the Law. For it is not enough for the faithful to possess the gifts of virtues unless they also do penance for their offenses. Hence the one who was both king and prophet, and to whom it was promised concerning Christ’s incarnation that he would be born from his seed, entreats the Lord for his sins, saying:

“Wash me more fully from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin, for I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. L).

And so that all the benefits mentioned above might be increased by a more eminent gift, he added the marrow of wheat and the blood of the grape. For what is signified by the marrow of wheat except the body of Christ? And what by the blood of the grape except the cup of the New Testament, represented in Christ’s blood?

Among the many gifts granted through God’s mercy to the ecclesiastical people, this excels them all: that he ministers to them, for eternal salvation, the sacraments of his body and blood in the preparation of bread and wine.

The text continues:

“He drank the purest wine; he grew fat, and the beloved kicked.”

Another edition: “Jacob drank wine and ate, and was satisfied, and the beloved kicked.”

Certainly all God’s gifts are bestowed upon believers who receive them worthily and understand them rightly, without any dregs of wickedness or reproach. But just as the carnal Israelites once abused God’s gifts and, made worse by the benefits of the most generous giver, fell into idolatry, so, alas, not a few among the ecclesiastical people, ungrateful for God’s benefits, relapse into vices and turn that which was bestowed upon them for salvation into their own destruction.

Hence it follows:

“He grew fat, became stout, and expanded; he abandoned God his creator and departed from God his salvation. They provoked him with foreign gods and stirred him to anger with their abominations. They sacrificed to demons and not to God, to gods whom they did not know; new and recent ones came to them, whom their fathers had not worshiped.”

Another edition: “He became fat and stout, expanded, abandoned God who made him, and departed from God his salvation. They provoked me with foreign things; with their abominations they stirred me to anger. They sacrificed to demons and not to God, to gods whom they did not know; new and recent ones came to them, whom their fathers did not know.”

The ancient Israelites did this historically, as is sufficiently expressed in their books. But modern Israelites also, when they turn the gifts of God granted to them in knowledge and virtues for divine service toward heresy or hypocrisy, are proved to serve idols and not God. They offer worship to demons and not to God—something our fathers, that is, the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and evangelists, certainly never did. Thus it happens to these idolaters that, provoking the most merciful Lord by their evil deeds, they will suffer him as severe and strict because of their wicked works, though they could have had him as favorable had they acted well.

“You abandoned the God who begot you, and you forgot the Lord your creator.”

Another edition: “You abandoned the God who begot you, and you forgot the God who nourished you.”

In a certain sense the Lord begot the Israelites through the Law and circumcision; he also begot the ecclesiastical people through the grace of baptism and the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, and sufficiently supplied them with nourishment from heavenly food, that is, evangelical teaching. But whoever does not fear to forget these things will justly feel God angry with him through punishment.

Hence it follows:

“The Lord saw and was provoked to anger, because his sons and daughters provoked him, and he said: ‘I will hide my face from them, and I will consider their end.’”

Another edition: “The Lord saw, and he was jealous, and he was angered because of the anger of his sons and daughters, and he said: ‘I will turn my face away from them and show what will happen to them at the end.’”

Nothing is more grievous among punishments than to be deprived of God’s presence and vision. Hence the Psalmist beseeches the Lord, saying:

“Do not cast me away from your face” (Ps. L).

And again:

“Do not turn your face away from me.”

Job likewise speaks to the Lord:

“Do not hide me from your face” (Job XIII).

Since, then, sons and daughters—that is, human beings of both sexes—provoked him by the evil things they do and do not deserve his mercy, they are rejected by him as ungrateful at their end. This will be proved when they are cast into the eternal punishments of Gehenna. For this is what it means to consider their end: to reveal their torments, which he justly inflicts upon them—not with a troubled mind but with tranquillity.

[Col. 1142C] “For it is a perverse generation, and faithless sons; they themselves provoked me with what was not God, and they stirred me to anger with their vanities, and I will provoke them with what is not a people, and with a foolish nation I will anger them.”

Another edition: “For the generation is crooked and perverse; the sons in whom there is no faith in them have themselves compelled me to jealousy, not toward God; they stirred me to anger with their idols, and I will drive them out in jealousy, not into a nation; with a foolish nation I will anger them.”

Since the Israelites, abandoning the worship of their Lord, worshiped idols, and, forsaking the true and living God, served the vanity of images among nations that at that time had not yet deserved to be called the people of God, they were handed over to plunder.

Likewise, ecclesiastical people who, abandoning the truth, have turned toward errors will be handed over, unless they repent of their evil deeds, to malignant spirits who, through pride, lost their angelic dignity, so that they may be thrust into the prisons of hell. Demons may rightly be called a foolish nation, because they hate justice and love iniquity.

“Fire has been kindled in my anger, and it will burn to the depths of hell.”

Another edition: “For fire has blazed up from my anger, and it will burn down to hell below.”

Of those whom scourges condemn and do not liberate it is written:

“You struck them, and they did not grieve; you consumed them, and they refused to accept correction” (Jer. V).

For such people the scourges begin in this life and continue in eternal punishment. Hence, through Moses also, the Lord says:

“Fire has blazed up from my anger, and it will burn down to hell below” (Deut. XXXII).

With regard to the punishment of the present life, it is rightly said, “Fire has blazed up from my anger.” With regard to eternal damnation, what follows is appropriately added: “And it will burn down to hell below.”

Although some commonly say what is written, “God does not avenge the same thing twice,” they nevertheless fail to consider what is said by the Prophet concerning the wicked: “And crush them with a twofold destruction,” as well as what is written elsewhere: Jesus, while saving the people from the land of Egypt, destroyed a second time those who did not believe.

If we grant assent to those who hold that no fault can be struck twice, this must be understood of those who are struck on account of sin and die in their sin. Their punishment begins here and ends there. Thus, in the uncorrected, there is one scourge: it begins temporally but is completed in eternal punishments, so that for those who altogether refuse to be corrected, the striking of present scourges becomes the beginning of the torments that follow.

The text continues:

“It consumed the land and its produce, and it will burn the foundations of the mountains. I will heap evils upon them, and I will exhaust my arrows against them. They will be consumed by hunger, and birds will devour them with the most bitter bite. I will send the teeth of beasts against them, together with the fury of those that drag themselves across the earth, and of serpents. Outside, the sword will lay them waste, and inside, terror—the young man together with the virgin, the suckling with the old man.”

Another edition: “The land consumed the produce of the fields, and it burned the foundations of the mountains. I will heap evils upon them, and I will exhaust my arrows against them. Fading away through hunger, they will become food for birds, and an incurable stretching of the back; I will send the teeth of beasts against them, together with the fury of those that drag themselves across the earth. Outside, the sword will deprive them of children, and in their storehouses there will be fear: young men with virgins, sucklings with established old men.”

“It consumed,” he says, “the land and its produce.” It consumes the land and its produce when the flame of eternal vengeance burns sinful flesh because of the works of lust. The produce of the flesh properly consists of the works of carnal desire:

“What are fornications, impurities, immodesties, luxuries, the service of idols, sorceries, enmities, contentions, rivalries, angers, quarrels, dissensions, sects, envies, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. Those who do such things,” as Paul testifies, “will not obtain the kingdom of God” (Gal. V).

“And it will burn the foundations of the mountains” when it consumes in eternal torments the wicked plans of the proud, by which they believed they could sin with impunity. “He will heap evils upon them” when he brings to mind for their punishment not only evil deeds but also perverse thoughts and wicked words. “He will exhaust his arrows against them” when he displays the anger of his indignation through various torments.

“They will be consumed by hunger”—that is, not by a lack of food or drink, but by perpetual barrenness of good works. “And birds will devour them with the most bitter bite”: namely, malignant spirits will tear them apart with the most savage mouth, reproaching them for their past sins.

What is added after the devouring by birds—“an incurable stretching of the back”—signifies the most severe wounds that sinners suffer in the torment of demons. These afflict them without any mercy and compel them to pay heavy penalties in hell.

The same malignant spirits are the beasts and serpents: they are called beasts because of their savagery and serpents because of their cunning. The beasts and serpents drag the reprobate across the earth with their teeth and in fury when, with furious intent, they demand from sinners what they previously persuaded carnal people to do by flattery in order to seduce them.

“Outside, the sword will lay the impious waste, and inside, terror,” when, in the final vengeance, the body is tormented on every side by the burning of eternal fire, while inwardly the greatness of anguish oppresses the mind. Hence it is written:

“Their worm will not die, and the fire will not be extinguished” (Mark IX).

“The young man together with the virgin, the suckling with the old man.” By listing every age, he shows that no age will be spared in the final vengeance—those whom the defilement of idolatrous worship had polluted.

Allegorically, in the young man he shows one who is wanton and lustful; in the virgin, one barren of good works; in the suckling, one dull; and in the old man, one sluggish and useless. Just vengeance will therefore consume all these in the final punishment, whom warning and correction do not now restrain from sins.

“And I said: ‘Where are they? I will cause their memory to cease from among human beings.’”

Another edition: “And he said: ‘I will destroy them; but I will remove their memory from among human beings.’”

God’s question is not ignorance but correction. Anyone who sees that the Jews were expelled from the promised land and scattered throughout the whole world can easily recognize the fulfillment of this sentence.

More generally, what is destined for all sinners and impenitent people is that they will be removed from the land of the saints and that their memory will not be counted among the assembly of the elect. Hence the Psalmist foretells that punishment will come upon the head of all the wicked together with the whole body. After enumerating the individual kinds of vices, he adds:

“Therefore God will destroy you forever; he will uproot you and remove you from your tent, and your root from the land of the living” (Ps. LI).

[Col. 1144D] “But because of the anger of the enemies I delayed, lest perhaps their enemies should become proud and say: ‘Our hand is exalted, and not God has done all these things.’”

Another edition: “Except for the anger of the enemies, lest they remain for a long time upon the earth, lest the adversaries agree and say: ‘Our hand is exalted, and not God has done all these things.’”

For this reason the Lord often endured a sinful people for a long time, lest the nations bordering them blaspheme his name and power. Hence Moses also said to the Lord, who was angry over Israel’s sin and wished to destroy them:

“Please, Lord, let the Egyptians not say, ‘He brought them out deceitfully in order to kill them in the mountains and wipe them from the earth.’ Let your anger rest, and be gracious toward the wickedness of your people. Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants, to whom you swore by yourself, saying: ‘I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven, and I will give all this land of which I have spoken to your seed, and you will possess it forever.’ And the Lord was appeased, so that he would not do the evil that he had spoken of doing to all his people.”

Likewise, when we have sinned, he sustains us because of his great patience and long-suffering, unwilling that anyone should perish, but that all should be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. In accordance with the statement of the Apostle Paul, who writes to the Romans:

“Do you suppose, O man, who judges those who do such things and yet does them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering, not knowing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Rom. II), and so forth.

And lest malignant spirits perhaps glory in our destruction because of their own strength, as though they had won the victory by their power—for they always strive to overturn the sentence of the Most High, who has determined that human beings should occupy in heaven the place of the fallen spirits—

“[This is] a nation without counsel and without understanding. Would that they were wise, understood, and considered their end.”

Another edition: “For it is a people lost in counsel, and understanding is not in them; they have not learned discipline; they will understand in the time to come.”

The Jewish nation, and likewise all the impious, are without the counsel of salvation because they do not know how to provide for their future, so as to escape the vengeance impending because of their sins and avoid the eternal torment of infernal punishments. And because they neglect to live according to discipline, they will endure tribulation and anguish in the future, in accordance with what is written about them (Prov. I):

“When sudden calamity falls upon them and destruction comes upon them like a storm, when tribulation and anguish come upon them, then they will call upon me, and I will not hear; they will rise early and will not find me, because they hated discipline and did not accept the fear of the Lord.”

“How does one pursue a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight? Is it not because their God sold them, and the Lord shut them up?”

Another edition: “How does one pursue a thousand, and two move ten thousand, unless the Lord has subjected them and God has delivered them?”

Whoever truly recognizes the greatness of the Lord will clearly prove that the destruction of his people occurs not through any weakness of his power but through the permission of his just judgment. For it could in no way happen that one would pursue a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight unless the Lord had delivered them and, casting them away as hated, had shut them into the hands of their enemies.

“For our God is not like their god. And our enemies are judges.”

Another edition: “He who is not our God is like their gods; but our enemies are senseless.”

The Lord our God is true and just, whereas the idols of the nations are false and useless. This is approved not only by us but also by our adversaries. Hence it is often read that when the Jews were delivered into the hands of enemies because of their faithlessness and injustice, they were deservedly reproved by them, as Jeremiah says in his lamentation:

“Enemies saw her and mocked her sabbaths” (Lam. I).

For this reason we must take the greatest care lest our enemies—who, through the error of idolatry, are rightly called senseless—provoked by our evil deeds, break out into blasphemy against the Lord when they see us defeated and reduced to nothing because of our sins. They may then attribute this to their own strength, although it was accomplished not by their power but by the Lord’s judgment.

“For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their grape from the outskirts of Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is most bitter.”

Another edition: “For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their offspring from Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is a cluster of bitterness to them.”

In the sacred Scriptures, the synagogue or Jerusalem is often compared with Sodom and Gomorrah, because just as those cities wickedly abused God’s gifts, so these have always proved ungrateful for God’s benefits. Hence Isaiah says of them:

“Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah. Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; listen with your ears to the law of our God, people of Gomorrah,” and so forth (Isa. I).

The Lord’s vineyard, as it is written in the same prophet, was the house of Israel. It was then changed into the bitterness of gall when it plotted Christ’s death. Hence, to him hanging upon the cross, they themselves offered vinegar mixed with gall on a reed. This demonstrated that the knowledge of the Law, which they had rightly received, had been corrupted by the gall of their malice, since they refused to receive the giver of the Law when he came to them; indeed, they provoked him and fastened him to the cross.

In another sense, this sentence also strikes at the wickedness of heretics. Although they originally received the pure doctrine of spiritual grace from holy preachers, they nevertheless did not fear to stain it with their errors. Therefore their entire teaching has been turned into gall and the bitterness of wormwood.

“Their wine is the gall of dragons, and the incurable venom of asps.”

Another edition: “Their wine is the fury of dragons, and the fury of asps is incurable.”

The faithlessness of the Jews and the cunning of heretics are aptly compared with the gall of dragons and the venom of asps. Just as serpents conceal bitterness and poison within themselves so that they may unexpectedly injure the unwary, so Jews and heretics conceal their malice beneath deceit and fraud in order more easily to destroy the unsuspecting.

It is therefore rightly said, “The incurable venom of asps,” because whoever is invaded by the error of heretics, unless he frees himself from it, is undoubtedly destroyed forever.

But what is read according to the other edition—“Their wine is the fury of dragons, and the fury of asps is incurable”—shows that it is not the disposition of a sound mind but of one more truly insane to despise eternal life and choose perpetual death, to abandon the truth of the Gospel and prefer to follow the deceit of error.

[Col. 1147A] “Are not these things stored up with me and sealed in my treasures?”

Another edition: “Are not all these things gathered with me and sealed in my treasures?”

It is characteristic of the human race quickly to forget the past, and for things that once seemed great gradually to fade from memory as time passes. But it is not so with God, where there is neither past nor future but everything is present and always at hand. What passes away from us is preserved there and will not be handed over to oblivion.

Therefore it is necessary that we strive to erase before God’s eyes, through immediate repentance, the sins we committed long ago, lest perhaps in the future, when the time of vengeance comes, he reckon our debts to us and say:

“You have done these things, and I was silent. You thought that I was altogether like you. I will accuse you and set them before your face.”

“Vengeance is mine, and I will repay them in due time, when their foot slips.” Another edition reads: “On the day of vengeance I will repay them, at the time when their foot has slipped.” With the Lord, both the time and the manner of vengeance are certain, by which sinners are to be tormented if they do not correct themselves from their sins. But because his mercies are many, “let us come before his face with confession, and let us rejoice to him with psalms (Ps. 94).” Let us humble our souls with fasting, let us watch and pray, for who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and leave a blessing behind him?

“Near is the day of destruction, and the times hasten to arrive.” Another edition reads: “For the day of their destruction is near, and these things are prepared for you.” The day of vengeance is near for each person, because it is certain, and what eventually comes to an end cannot be long-lasting. For whatever is temporal—the human lifespan and the course of the present life—becomes small when compared with eternity. Therefore it is said, “and the times hasten to arrive,” because temporal things quickly end, and torments prepared for the wicked come upon them, in accordance with what is written: “Judgments are prepared for mockers (Prov. 19).”

According to the historical sense, vengeance drew near for the Israelites, because from the time they began to rebel they never completely ceased, until they lost their kingdom, their place, and the prosperity of their life all together. For after they had killed the prophets and crucified the Savior, adding new offenses to their ancient seditions, they provoked the Romans against themselves by rebelling. The Romans destroyed the city, burned the temple, killed the people by famine and the sword, and scattered their survivors throughout the whole world. There they wander in uncertain settlements, remaining uncertain of the hope of future things.

“The Lord will judge his people, and will have mercy on his servants.” Another edition reads: “For the Lord will judge his people, and will console his servants.” The Lord will therefore judge his people when he separates his elect from the reprobate, for “to judge” sometimes means “to distinguish”; at other times it means “to condemn.” Thus in the psalm the prophet said to the Lord: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation; deliver me from the unjust and deceitful man (Ps. 42).” Here “to judge” is used for discrimination. Elsewhere the same prophet, crying out to the Lord, says: “Judge, O Lord, those who harm me; fight against those who fight against me (Ps. 34).” Here, however, judgment is understood as condemnation.

The Lord will judge his saints when, separating them from sinners on the day of judgment, he places them at his right hand. Their enemies and persecutors he will set at the left, so that they may receive certain condemnation with the devil and his angels in hell: “These will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.” Then what follows in the aforementioned verse will be perfectly fulfilled: “And he will have mercy on his servants,” because in heavenly blessedness he will grant his faithful eternal mercy.

As for the reading in another edition that the Lord will be consoled in his servants, this is said by metonymy, in which what is produced is indicated through the one who produces it. For by nature the Lord is always joyful and tranquil, and is never changed into the sorrowful grief of sadness. Of him it is written: “You, Lord, judge and dispose all things with tranquility (Wis. 12).” It is therefore rightly said that the Lord is consoled in his servants, because after the end of the present sadness he consoles his elect with eternal peace and joy.

This verse may also be referred to the final conversion of the Jews, when, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, the whole of Israel will be converted to the same faith and saved by divine grace, God having mercy on his people.

“[He] will see that the hand has been weakened, and that even the confined have failed, and the remnants have been consumed; and he will say, ‘Where are their gods, in whom they trusted, from whose sacrifices they ate the fat and drank the wine of their libations? Let them rise and help you, and protect you in your need.’” Another edition reads: “For he saw them wearied and exhausted in captivity and scattered, and he said: ‘Where are their gods now, in whom you trusted, whose sacrificial fat you ate and whose libation wine you drank? Let them rise now and help you and become your protectors.’”

“He will see,” he says, “that the hand has been weakened,” when he causes it to be seen that the works of evil which they committed in idolatry or in other transgressions have been weakened—when they have been reduced to nothing and have benefited nothing those who made them. “Even the confined have failed”: that is, either the Jews who were led into captivity by their enemies and consumed there, or all the impious who, handed over to the power of demons, will no longer prevail. “The remnants have been consumed,” because, when they depart from this life, they will no longer have the power or ability to do anything.

For this reason it is written in Ecclesiastes: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it earnestly, because there is neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge in the underworld, where you are hastening (Eccles. 9).”

What follows—“Where are their gods, in whom they trusted?” and the rest—signifies that idolaters will have no help in the day of need from the idols to which they formerly offered worship. Nor will worldly lovers, who through greed—which is the service of idols—had amassed money in the world, and who had devoted themselves to pleasures and luxury, whose god was their belly and whose glory was their shame, and who set their minds on earthly things, carry anything with them from all their labor when, because of their sins, they are dragged by evil spirits into Tartarus.

“See that I alone am, and there is no other God besides me.” Another edition reads: “See, see, that I am God, and there is none besides me.” This admonition applies generally to all human beings: they must abandon the falsehood of idols and the deception of heretics, reject the filth of every kind of iniquity, and turn by catholic faith to the one and only God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, whom they must worship. They must love him with their whole heart, soul, and strength, and carefully keep his commandments and judgments, so that they may deserve to become heirs of the heavenly kingdom.

“I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I heal; and there is no one who can deliver from my hand.” Another edition reads: “I kill, I make alive; I strike, and I heal; and there is no one who can rescue from my hands.”

Almighty God wounds in two ways those whom he intends to restore to salvation. At times he strikes the flesh, and the hardness of the mind melts away in fear of him. Thus, by wounding, he recalls them to salvation, when he afflicts his elect outwardly and gives them life inwardly. Rightly, therefore, he speaks through Moses, saying: “I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I heal.” He kills in order to give life; he strikes in order to heal. For this reason he inflicts blows outwardly, so that he may inflict wounds inwardly: he strikes the hardness of our mind with the desire for him, but by striking he heals, because, pierced by the dart of his fear, he recalls us to an awareness of righteousness.

Our hearts are unhealthy when they are not wounded by any love of God, when they do not feel the distress of their pilgrimage, and when they do not languish even with the smallest affection for the weakness of their neighbor. But they are wounded when God strikes insensitive minds with the arrows of his love, and immediately makes them sensitive through the ardor of charity.

“I will lift my hand to heaven and say: I live forever.” Another edition reads: “For I will lift my hand to heaven, and I will swear by my right hand, and I will say: I live forever.”

To lift or raise one’s hand to heaven is to display the power of one’s eternity, which surpasses all things. To swear by the right hand is, through the Son—who is called the right hand of God—to confirm his promises in the sight of human beings and to reveal his eternity to those who believe in him, because his power is eternal and his kingdom will not perish.

“If I sharpen my sword like lightning, and my hand seizes judgment, I will repay vengeance upon my enemies, and I will repay those who hate me.” Another edition reads: “For I will sharpen my sword like lightning, and my hand executes judgment; I will repay judgment to my enemies, and I will repay those who hate me.”

To sharpen the sword of God like lightning is to exercise sudden vengeance against his enemies. For the divine hand to seize judgment is to render to each person, through just repayment, according to his own merits, as it is written: “For the Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each one according to his works (Rom. 2).” And the Apostle says: “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each one may receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5).”

“I will intoxicate my arrows with blood, and my sword will devour flesh.” An arrow strikes a person when he is not paying attention, and when he has not foreseen it, it suddenly kills him. The arrows of the Lord are his swift acts of vengeance. Although they are now hidden from the eyes of the wicked, they will nevertheless suddenly be revealed in the condemnation of the lost. The sword of God devours flesh because, at the final judgment, his sentence kills those who think according to the flesh.

“From the blood of the slain and from the captivity of the naked enemy’s head.” Another edition reads: “From the blood of the wounded, from captivity, from the head of the enemy’s princes.”

In the phrase “from the blood of the enemies,” what was stated above is understood: “I will intoxicate my arrows.” The Lord intoxicates his arrows with the blood of the slain when he exercises vengeance upon the multitude of his enemies. Then the heads of the enemies will be stripped bare, when the plans of wicked minds—by which they trusted that they could sin with impunity—are proved vain.

The heads of the wicked may also be understood as the teachers of those who go astray, upon whom the final vengeance rebounds, because those who were the cause of sins will experience the losses involved in the repayment of punishments. Hence it is written in the Apocalypse: “And blood came out of the winepress as far as the horses’ bridles (Rev. 14),” that is, the vengeance of torments extended to the rulers of peoples. The vengeance for the blood of the saints that was poured out extended, in the final struggle, even to the devil and his angels, as it is written: “You sinned through blood, and blood will pursue you (Ezek. 35).”

It should be noted that in this passage the edition of the Seventy Interpreters inserts certain statements that are not found in the Hebrew text, as follows:

“Rejoice, heavens, together with him, and let all the angels of God adore him. Rejoice, nations, together with his people, and let all the sons of God strengthen him.”

Nevertheless, these words are shown to have been rightly brought forth from canonical authority, since the Apostle Paul is found to have taken testimonies from them. In the Epistle written by him to the Hebrews, as well as in the Epistle addressed by him to the Romans, he is found to have drawn testimonies from this passage.

Finally, writing to the Hebrews, he says: “And when he again brings the firstborn into the inhabited world, he says: ‘And let all the angels of God adore him’ (Heb. 1).” To the Romans, discussing the calling of the Gentiles and the fullness of the Jewish people, he says: “For I say that Christ Jesus became a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers (Rom. 15).” He also says that the Gentiles should honor God because of his mercy, as it is written: “For this reason I will confess to you among the Gentiles, O Lord, and I will sing to your name (2 Sam. 22).” And again he says: “Rejoice, Gentiles, with his people (Rom. 15).”

It is therefore clear that the apostles approved equally both the edition derived from the Hebrew text and the edition of the Seventy Interpreters, since they took testimonies from both.

When he speaks exhortatively to the heavenly creation, saying, “Rejoice, heavens, together with him, and let all the angels of God adore him,” he shows that after the Savior’s coming in the flesh and his universal judgment—by which the righteous are crowned and sinners condemned—the heavenly and earthly creatures are united together in the praise of their Creator. They adore and venerate Christ the King, who reigns and rules over all, forever.

What follows—“Rejoice, nations, together with his people, and let all the sons of God strengthen him”—means the same thing. The Church of Christ, gathered from Jews and Gentiles, after it truly receives immortality and incorruption in the resurrection of the flesh, confirms by its deed what it previously testified in words. The text continues:

“Praise, nations, his people, because he will avenge the blood of his servants and repay vengeance upon their enemies.” Another edition reads: “For the blood of his sons is defended, and he defends it; I will repay judgment to the enemies, and he will repay those who hate him.”

All the nations will praise God’s people when they see the Church of God appear glorious in the sight of its Creator, and when its persecutors, because of the blood of the martyrs that they shed and all the evils they committed in this life, are thrust into the fire of eternal Gehenna through the ministry of evil spirits.

Then the good will praise the good that they see, because the reward they receive is pleasing. The impious, established in punishments, will repent—though too late—for the evil they committed when they see the glory of the saints shining, a glory they did not expect:

“For, groaning and placed in anguish, they will say within themselves, repenting: ‘These are the ones whom we once held in derision and as an object of reproach. We, fools that we were, considered their life madness and their end without honor. How, then, have they been counted among the sons of God, and their lot is among the saints?’ (Wis. 5).”

“And the Lord will be propitious to the land of his people.” Another edition reads: “And he will cleanse the land of his people.”

The Lord will therefore cleanse the land of his people, or will be propitious to the land of his people, when he causes his Church—which he has hitherto governed amid adversities through his ministers—to live amid the prosperity of the heavenly kingdom, rescued and purified from every scandal and enjoying perpetual peace. There it will rejoice without end and sing praises to the Lord together with the saints forever.

## The Hymn of the Three Young Men Begins

The hymn of the three young men, which is contained in the book of the prophet Daniel, is not found in the Hebrew text, as our blessed interpreter, namely Jerome, testifies. Rather, it was added from the edition of the Seventy or of other interpreters. There it is also related beforehand that the angel of the Lord descended with Azariah and his companions into the furnace, drove the flame of the fire out of the furnace, and made the middle of the furnace like a wind blowing with dew. The fire did not touch them at all, nor distress them, nor cause them any harm.

This angel of the Lord, who descended with the three young men into the furnace of burning fire and protected them from the heat of the flames, may also typologically signify the Lord Savior, whom the prophet called the angel of great counsel, because he is the announcer of his own and his Father’s will. He too descended into this world, where the king of confusion—that is, the devil—sets the furnace, namely the hearts of the wicked, ablaze with the fire of desire and luxury. By the breath of the Holy Spirit and through his grace, he preserves his elect unharmed from this fire, so that, intent upon his praises, they may give thanks to their deliverer for their rescue. Concerning him the text continues:

“Then these three, as though with one mouth, praised, glorified, and blessed the Lord in the furnace, saying.”

These three men, therefore, who praised, glorified, and blessed the Lord as though with one mouth, signify God’s elect. Established in faith in the Holy Trinity, they adore, worship, and proclaim one God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. They praise him through right belief, glorify him through true confession, and bless him through good works. Hence they also say together:

“Blessed are you, Lord, God of our fathers, and praiseworthy and glorious and exalted above all forever.”

The Lord God of our fathers is therefore Christ, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one almighty God. The patriarchs worshiped him, the prophets praised him, the apostles proclaimed him, and the whole Church of Christ confesses him. He always was, is, and will be praiseworthy and glorious; exalted above all creatures, he reigns forever and ever.

“All works of the Lord, bless the Lord.”

After first stating in general praise that every creature ought to praise the Lord, the text proceeds to exhort, individually and in turn, the angels and the heavens; the waters and the powers; the sun and the moon; rain and dew; spirit, fire, and heat; cold and warmth; and the rest, which would take too long to enumerate. It summons springs, seas, and rivers; sea creatures, birds, beasts, and cattle to the praise of the Lord; then the sons of men; and after all these, Israel; and from Israel, the priests and servants of the Lord; the spirits and souls of the righteous; the saints and humble of heart; and finally Ananias, Azariah, and Misael, who are summoned to the praises of the Lord by the benefit presently bestowed upon them.

Every creature praises the Lord not with its voice but by its work, because from creatures the Creator is consequently understood, and God’s magnificence is displayed in each of his works and effects.

But because David in the Psalter likewise summons all the works of the Lord—that is, all creatures—to bless and praise God, it remains that, just as this order of blessing and praise exists historically, so its spiritual, mysterious meaning should be fittingly applied to each species.

At the end of Psalm 102, which he composed for blessing God, David says:

“Bless the Lord, all his works, in every place of his dominion.”

He teaches that the works of the Lord themselves ought to praise their author, so that he might include both earthly and heavenly things. Since everything is his work, all things ought to bless their Creator, and this is to occur “in every place of his dominion,” because just as no creature is commanded to be excluded from the praises of the Lord, so no place is left outside such a duty.

For when it says, “in every place of his dominion,” nothing is excluded, because he rules everywhere. This may perhaps signify the catholic Church, which, by the Lord’s will, was to believe throughout the whole world. It blesses the Lord everywhere, praises him everywhere, and celebrates him with hymnic rejoicing.

What is added to each verse in the blessing of the three young men—

“Praise and exalt him above all forever”—

shows that his proclamation of praise should be uttered in such a way that he is proclaimed as reigning forever, exalted above all things.

“Bless the Lord, heavens; bless the Lord, angels of the Lord.”

According to the historical sense, the heavens bless the Lord because by their arrangement they show their Creator to be praiseworthy and blessed. Although we read in Genesis that one heaven was made, the Apostle Paul nevertheless also names the heavens in the plural. He relates that he was caught up to the third heaven and there learned things that it was not permitted a human being to utter; here too they are named in the plural.

This perhaps has the following explanation. We say that there is one palace surrounded by many members and many spaces. In the same way, we may call the parts of heaven “heavens,” while its structure and interior reveal it to be one. The substance of heaven, although it must be considered pure, bright, and excellent, and worthy of such and so great inhabitants, nevertheless is not, as far as I have discovered, a living being. It is rash, on the basis of human opinion, to say what the authority of the heavenly writings does not transmit.

In Scripture, moreover, we find apostles and prophets designated by the name “heavens.” By discussing the Lord’s coming, they filled the world with holy admonitions. In them God dwells as in the heavens, embracing all things broadly—not partially, but with the whole fullness of his majesty. For there is no part in God; he is everywhere wholly and completely present.

“Bless the Lord, waters that are above the heavens.”

Genesis reports that waters are above the heavens. It says: “And he divided the waters that were above the firmament (Gen. 1).” Both of these things reveal a mystery of immense praise: the thinness of the heavens remains firm, while the waters placed above them, though heavier, do not descend unless commanded.

As for the waters that are above the heavens, there is no doubt, in my opinion, that these are the waters that flow downward, since the book of Genesis testifies that the cataracts of heaven were opened and that rain fell upon the earth for forty days and forty nights, and so forth. It is not necessary to investigate this too closely, since all things are urged to praise the Lord either by themselves or through rational substances.

“Bless the Lord, all the powers of the Lord.”

Of the powers of God it is said in the psalm: “Bless the Lord, all his powers, and his ministers who do his will (Ps. 102).” That sublime and spiritual substance of the blessed angels, when it beholds the Lord, recognizes there the truth of his will. There is no need for speech where the divinity, having been reconciled, reveals itself. God does not speak by striking the air; rather, by his inspiration he turns their wills toward his own will.

“Bless the Lord, sun and moon. Bless the Lord, stars of heaven.”

Of these the Psalmist also says: “Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light (Ps. 148).” The sun, moon, and stars, as some say, although they may be governed by some spirit of their own, are nevertheless manifest to bodily eyes and are therefore considered inferior to the powers that are not seen. This conclusion is not unreasonable.

Although they appear to adorn the appearance of heaven with a beautiful light, whatever our sight reaches—even if bright and subtle—is plainly corporeal, and must yield to things that subsist by invisible power. Therefore the prophet exhorts the sun, moon, and stars—whether through their own rational principle or through other perceptible and discernible substances—to praise the Lord, because they have deserved to exist through the Creator’s gift.

When so many lights are considered, they can arouse immense admiration: they make mortal eyes behold them, and they themselves remain in such splendid brightness. Light is added here in general so that other things possessing light, which have not been enumerated, might likewise be summoned to the Lord’s praises by this comprehensive expression.

“Bless the Lord, rain and dew.”

In rain and dew, heavenly gifts, precepts, and commandments of the Lord are expressed. They water the earth—that is, human beings—and stir them to produce the sprout of good works. It is fitting that what is beneficially offered to human beings as a heavenly gift should contribute to the blessing and praise of the Lord.

“Bless the Lord, all spirits.”

This is what is finally written in the Psalter: “Let every spirit praise the Lord (Ps. 150).” It is not flesh and blood, nor worldly ambition, nor worldly enticements that should praise him, but that which is higher in nature; that which knows heavenly things when it desires eternal rewards. Therefore he gave the whole work a brief and perfect conclusion: all things should spiritually praise the Lord Savior.

“Bless the Lord, fire and heat.”

Fire sometimes signifies charity and sometimes tribulation. Likewise, heat sometimes expresses the ardor of love and the freshness of good works, and sometimes the heat of persecution. These bless the Lord when they cause human beings to bless their Creator, because holy men praise the Lord always, both in prosperity and in adversity.

Hence the Apostle exhorts us “that God may be glorified in all things through Jesus Christ.”

The following four verses may likewise be understood in this way:

“Bless the Lord, nights and days. Bless the Lord, light and darkness. Bless the Lord, cold and heat. Bless the Lord, dews and frost.”

Through things opposed to one another, he urges the Lord’s praise and summons them to bless him. Day, light, heat, and dew signify prosperity; night, darkness, cold, and frost, by contrast, signify tribulation.

Not only the elements and seasons of the world are suited to praising God. Human beings themselves, who live temporarily under the elements of the world, become debtors to bless God, because the Creator of all things so orders present circumstances for his elect that they never cease from divine proclamations of praise.

Hence Paul says: “I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me (2 Cor. 12).” And again: “This momentary and light affliction of ours is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, while we do not contemplate the things that are seen,” and so forth (2 Cor. 4).

“Bless the Lord, frost and cold. Bless the Lord, ice and snow.”

In frost and cold, ice and snow, the adversity of the present age or the hardness of the human mind is signified. But often the Lord turns these things into his praise, when people who are numb with the cold of unbelief are converted to the service of Christ through the warmth of faith and zeal for good works. Hence it is written in Solomon: “As ice in fair weather, so your sins will melt away (Sir. 3).”

And in the psalm: “Fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy wind, which perform his word (Ps. 148).” Allegorically, these things signify human beings who in this world have passed from turbulent and very wicked ways to the most tranquil pursuits of devotion. How do they perform his word, unless because they have deserved to come from stormy and wicked conduct to the grace of confessing him?

“Bless the Lord, lightning and clouds.”

What, then, are signified by clouds if not the preachers of the Gospel, and by lightning if not the flashes of miracles shown to us? Of these the Psalmist says: “You will multiply the lightning and trouble them (Ps. 17).”

Through these clouds, therefore, the Lord flashes his light from above, because through holy preachers he illumines even the darkness of our insensibility by miracles. When these clouds rain words, and when through miracles they reveal the power of flashing light, they turn even the farthest boundaries of the world toward divine love.

“Let the earth bless the Lord; praise and exalt him above all forever.”

Here the earth signifies the holy Church, of which it is written in the psalm: “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it (Ps. 23).” Although we know that “earth” is often used both in a good and in an evil sense, here we must understand the Church, which serves the Lord especially with a pure mind.

Although all things were created from the abyss, we properly call that his own which venerates him as its author. Therefore the Church is rightly understood as a fruitful earth, because it nourishes and contains the Christian people.

This earth always praises God and exalts him above all forever, because it praises him not only in the present age but also in the future, and proclaims him as ruling over all.

“Bless the Lord, mountains and hills. Bless the Lord, all things that grow on the earth. Praise and exalt him above all forever.”

For this reason the Psalmist too, when he summons all creatures to praise the Lord, says among other things: “Mountains and all hills, fruitful trees and all cedars (Ps. 148).”

Here “mountains” signifies people raised high by their proud power; “hills,” those who conduct themselves with moderate equality; and “fruitful trees,” those who, converted from the hardness of sins, have produced the sweetest fruits of good works. Cedars, in turn, simply signify the proud and exalted.

But because he commands all things growing from the earth to praise the Lord, he shows that from every kind of person Christ’s grace prepares elect ones who can be joined to the assemblies of angels in the final resurrection and associated forever in the praises of their Creator.

“Bless the Lord, springs.”

In Scripture, a spring mystically signifies either the Lord Christ, the grace of the Holy Spirit, the baptismal washing, or the origin of virtues.

It signifies Christ in the passage of Genesis where a spring is said to be in the middle of paradise. From it four rivers proceeded—that is, the four Gospels proceeding from the fountain of salvation for the watering of the human race.

Likewise, the spring signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit in what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever drinks the water that I will give will have in him a spring of living water welling up into eternal life (John 4).”

The sacrament of baptism is indicated by the passage in Zechariah which says: “On that day there will be a fountain opened for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and of the menstruating woman (Zech. 12).” This spring, proceeding from the house of God, is said to flow toward the Church and toward knowledge of the Scriptures, so that we may all be reborn in Christ and, through the water of baptism, our sins may not be imputed to us [the Latin is corrupt or uncertain].

Here, however, we can understand the springs as the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures uttered through the mouths of preachers. Hence it is written in the psalm: “The springs of waters appeared (Ps. 17),” that is, the truth of preachers, who poured forth springs of eternal life through the mouth of holiness. When the Lord himself came, what had been concealed by the obscurity of divine speech became manifest.

“Bless the Lord, seas and rivers.”

When he says “seas,” he generally includes all collections of waters together, whether salt or fresh, in accordance with what is written: “He called the gatherings of waters seas (Gen. 1).” From them rivers proceed, as it is written: “All the rivers enter the sea, and the sea is not filled; to the place from which the rivers flow, there they return, so that they may flow again (Eccles. 1).”

Here, metaphorically, by “waters” the mud of the earth is understood, and by “rivers” human beings, who return to the earth from which they were taken; but the earth is not filled by their multitude.

Human beings are therefore commanded to bless the Lord—that is, to recognize their author and worship him through faith and good works—because they were created by him and all return to his judgment, “so that each one may receive according to what he did in the body, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5).”

“Bless the Lord, sea creatures and all that move in the waters; praise and exalt him above all forever.”

In the sea creatures, which because of the greatness of their bodies are compared with mountains and surpass the other animals that inhabit the sea, the powerful of this world may be represented. Together with the other human beings who live in this age, they are summoned to praise their Creator, by whose gift all subsist and all are nourished. For it is fitting that great and small should praise their almighty Creator and bless him forever.

“Bless the Lord, birds of heaven.”

By birds, philosophers may be understood, who, because of the swiftness of their thoughts, judged that they should investigate the natures of things and the courses of the stars. Or, in a higher sense, angels may be understood as designated by the name of birds. God sends them into the world for the protection of human beings, so that they may care for them and defend them against spiritual wickedness.

For it is right that all rulers and subjects together should bless the ruler of all, “who made heaven and earth, the seas and everything in them.”

“Bless the Lord, all beasts and cattle; praise and exalt him above all forever.”

In beasts, cruel and untamed human beings are signified; in cattle, the whole common people and the countless masses. The prophet exhorts such people, when they have turned from cruelty and pride, to return to humility and innocence, so that in heart, mouth, and deed they may bless their Maker, by whom the heavens and the earth and all their adornment were perfected.

“Bless the Lord, sons of men; let Israel bless the Lord.”

By the sons of men, those who live rationally are signified; by Israel, those who devote themselves to divine contemplation. He therefore invites them to bless God, because it is most fitting and just that those who, by the generosity of their Maker, have received this above the other earthly creatures—namely, the ability to recognize him truly, worship him with right faith and good works, contemplate him with a pure heart and sincere intention, and love him—should never cease from his praises, but should bless and proclaim him forever.

“Bless the Lord, priests of the Lord; bless the Lord, servants of the Lord.”

In the priests he expresses the teachers of the Church; in the servants, the people subject to them. He therefore exhorts all, rulers and subjects alike, always to bless the Lord Christ, by whose gift they have been sanctified and cleansed, who reigns together with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever.

“Bless the Lord, spirits and souls of the righteous.”

By the words “spirits and souls,” he comprehends the whole condition of the inner person, who understands through the spirit and lives through the soul. The prophet therefore commands the spirits and souls of the righteous to bless the Lord, because only those truly bless the Lord who keep the rule of justice and truth. The divinity gladly accepts the blessings of those who, living justly through right faith, true confession, and good works, praise him together.

[Col. 1158B] “Bless the Lord, holy and humble in heart.” This verse also teaches us to possess humility of heart, as does what is read in the Gospel: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11). That humility of heart is meant which elsewhere is called poverty of spirit, so that we are not lifted up by pride, nor seek earthly glory through feigned humility, but incline ourselves with our whole heart [the supplied source breaks off here].

“Bless the Lord, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael; sing a hymn to him, praise him, and exalt him above all forever. For he has rescued us from hell, saved us from the hand of death, delivered us from the midst of the burning flame, and rescued us from the midst of the fire.” Finally, the three youths exhort one another to bless the Lord, and rightly did he alter the order of creation for their deliverance, so that neither could the fire harm their bodies nor the flame burn their garments. To him a hymn is owed and fitting praise, because he always remains worthy of praise and exalted above all, forever and ever. After these blessings the holy Fathers also added what is now sung in the Church, namely, the praise and confession of the Holy Trinity, in the following form:

“Let us bless the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit; let us praise and exalt him above all forever.” For there is one and only one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, three in persons and one in substance. He created heaven and earth, the sea, and everything that is in them. It is right for all who believe in him, desire to receive eternal life from him, and wish to enjoy his goodness in the heavenly kingdom, to proclaim his praise and confess his name above all things.

What follows in this Canticle was previously placed in the prophetic book, where, before the works of the Lord were summoned to bless the Lord, it is written: “He is blessed in the firmament of heaven, and worthy of praise and glorious forever.” The firmament of heaven signifies either the angelic powers, in whom the Lord perpetually reigns, or knowledge of the holy Scriptures, where the foundation of all goodness and truth is found, and the majesty and goodness of the Creator are continually praised and proclaimed. Hence it is also written: “Heaven will be folded up like a rolled book”; and elsewhere: “The Lord is a firmament for those who fear him, and his covenant, so that it may be revealed to them.” For all who here truly love God, desire to keep his commandments, and strive to devote themselves continually to God’s praises not only with their mouths but also with their hearts, will advance from day to day by receiving fitting consolation from the holy Scriptures; and thus, without any doubt, after the end of this life, through God’s grace, they will receive without end in the heavenly kingdom what they had long sought here.

[Col. 1159A]

## HERE BEGINS THE CANTICLE OF ZECHARIAH, FATHER OF BLESSED JOHN THE BAPTIST

[Col. 1159B]

Accordingly, although Zechariah, the father of blessed John the Baptist, had for a long time been deprived of speech because of his doubt, he was not deprived of the divine gift. Rather, when the child whose name he had written down in silence had been born, he was enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit and prophetically declared what would happen in God’s people, saying:

“Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and accomplished the redemption of his people.” We can appreciate how great is the abundance of the heavenly gift, if the devotion of our faith is ready to receive it.
