Behold: speech, which had alone been taken from the doubter, was restored together with the spirit of prophecy to the believer. The Lord visited his people as though they were wasting away from a long illness, and, as though sold under sin, redeemed them by the blood of his only Son. Since blessed Zechariah knew that this was shortly to be accomplished, he relates it in prophetic fashion as though it had already happened. It should also be noted that he is said to have visited and redeemed his people—not because, on coming to them, he found them to be his, but because by visiting them he made them his own.

“And he raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant.” He calls the horn of salvation the firm height of salvation. All bones, indeed, are enclosed in flesh; the horn rises above the flesh. Therefore the horn of salvation is called the kingdom of Christ the Savior, by which a spiritual height, surpassing the joys of the flesh, is proclaimed to the world. As a figure of this, David and Solomon were consecrated to royal glory with the horn of oil.

“As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets, who have been from the beginning.” “From the beginning,” he says, because prophecy concerning Christ proceeded from the whole of the Scripture of the Old Testament. It was not spoken only by Jeremiah, Daniel, Isaiah, and the others who are specially called prophets and who spoke openly of his coming; rather, the father Adam himself, Abel, Enoch, and the other Fathers each bore witness to his dispensation by their deeds. Hence the Lord himself, rebuking the hardness of the Jews, says: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me, for he wrote about me” (John 5).

“Salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us.” This should be joined to the preceding verse: “He raised up for us”—that is, he raised up for us salvation from our enemies. For after briefly saying, “and he raised up for us a horn of salvation,” he immediately explains, as though more clearly, what he raised up: “Salvation,” he says, “from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us.” By all who hate us he signifies either wicked human beings or unclean spirits. From their hand we have been saved meanwhile in hope, and in the future we shall truly be saved. In some churches the verse is sung, “and he delivered us from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us.” This has the same meaning, because we shall receive complete salvation from our enemies when we have been perfectly freed from their plots and seductions, so that in the future life we may fully possess the mercy which here we receive in part through God’s grace and the merits of the Fathers. Hence it follows:

“To show mercy to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, the oath which he swore to Abraham our father, that he would grant us that, delivered from the hand of our enemies without fear, we might serve him.” He had said that the Lord would be born in the house of David, in accordance with the words of the prophets; he now says that this same Lord would free us in order to fulfill the covenant that he established with Abraham. For it was especially to these patriarchs that either the gathering of the nations or the incarnation of Christ from their offspring was promised. Matthew also wished briefly to indicate this when he began his Gospel in the following manner: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.”

Here it should be noted that in both Evangelists David is placed before Abraham. Although David was later in time, he was greater by the privilege of the promise. Abraham, while still in uncircumcision, abandoned his former way of life, came to know God, and merited the testimony of faith. To him only the faith of the nations and the most holy gathering of the Church were promised, when the Lord said to him: “And in you all the kindreds of the earth shall be blessed.” David, however, heard through a more exalted oracle that Christ would be born from him according to the flesh: “When your days are fulfilled,” he says, “and you go to your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, which shall come from your sons, and I will establish his kingdom. He himself shall build me a house, and I will establish his throne forever. I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me” (1 Chron. 17).

“In holiness and righteousness before him all our days.” He plainly and briefly indicates how the Lord must be served: in holiness and righteousness, before him, and all our days. For whoever departs from his service before death, whether through any impurity or through injustice, stains the sincerity of his faith; and whoever strives to remain holy and righteous only before human beings, and not also before the Lord, is not yet perfectly freed from the hand of spiritual enemies but, like the Samaritans of old, attempts to serve the gods of the nations and the Lord alike.

“And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High. For you will go before the face of the Lord, to prepare his ways.” Beautifully, while speaking about the Lord, he suddenly turns his words to the prophet, so that this too might be shown to be a benefit of the Lord. But one may ask how he addresses an infant eight days old. Yet why should we think that one who was born could not hear his father’s voice, when he heard Mary’s greeting while still enclosed in the womb? Unless perhaps Zechariah is to be understood as wishing, for the sake of those who were present, to instruct them concerning the future offices of his son, which he had learned earlier through the angel, and, as soon as he was able to speak, to proclaim them.

Let the Arians hear and blush; let the meek hear and rejoice: Christ the Lord, whom John preceded by prophesying, he calls the Most High. In agreement with this, the Psalmist, praising God and the perfect man in one person, says: “Mother Zion will say: ‘A man and a man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her’” (Ps. 86), calling him the Most High who was made—the one who founded that same man.

“To give knowledge of salvation to his people for the remission of their sins.” As though wishing to explain and commend more carefully the name Jesus, which is the same as “Savior,” he repeatedly mentions salvation when he speaks of the horn of salvation to be raised up, salvation to come from enemies, and knowledge of salvation to be given to the people. But lest you think that temporal and bodily salvation is being promised, he says: “For the remission of their sins.” Yet the Jews do not for that reason wish to receive Jesus Christ; rather, they prefer to await the Antichrist, because they desire to be saved not inwardly but outwardly, and to be freed not from the dominion of sin but from the yoke of human servitude.

“Through the merciful compassion of our God, in which the dawn from on high has visited us.” The prophet too, speaking of the Lord, says: “Behold the man; his name is Dawn” (Zech. 6). He is rightly called Dawn because, opening for us the rising of the true light, he made children of light out of children of night and darkness, as blessed Zechariah next explains, saying:

“To enlighten those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, to direct our feet into the way of peace.” For the Lord to enlighten those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death is to pour the rays of knowledge and love of himself into those who have lived in sins and the blindness of ignorance. To such people the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5). Our feet are directed into the way of peace when the course of our actions in every respect conforms to the grace of our Redeemer and Illuminator. With proper order, he testifies that hearts must first be enlightened and deeds then directed, because no one can practice a peace he has not first learned. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “Seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. 33)—which is to say: “You who sat in darkness, be enlightened, and enter the way of peace from which you had long been exiled.”

## HERE BEGINS THE CANTICLE OF MARY, MOTHER OF THE LORD

After the most blessed Virgin Mary realized that she was pregnant with a heavenly birth, she did not exalt herself at all as though these gifts from heaven were hers by her own power. Rather, so that she might become increasingly suited to divine gifts, she fixed her steps in the guardianship of humility of mind, remembering the Scripture’s command: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3). As soon as the angel who had announced the divine birth to her returned to heaven, she arose and climbed into the hill country. Carrying God in her womb, she sought the dwelling places of God’s servants and desired their conversation. At her arrival Elizabeth heard the greeting of the mother of the Lord, immediately prophesied about her, and testified that the mother of the Lord had come to her. She declared her blessed among women and the fruit of her womb blessed; moreover, she related that, at her voice, the infant in her womb had leaped, filled with the Holy Spirit.

Hearing this, Mary did not exalt herself boastfully in empty glory. Rather, with humility and the full intention of her heart, she gave thanks to God, saying:

“My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God my Savior.” “The Lord,” she says, “has exalted me with so great and unheard-of a gift that it cannot be expressed by any service of the tongue, but can scarcely be grasped even by the innermost affection of the heart. Therefore I offer all the powers of my soul in songs of thanksgiving. Whatever I live, perceive, and discern, I gladly devote entirely to contemplating the greatness of the One who has no end. For my spirit rejoices in the eternal divinity of that same Jesus—that is, the Savior—whose flesh gladdens me through its temporal conception.” Similar is the Psalmist’s saying: “My soul will rejoice in the Lord and delight in his salvation” (Ps. 34), for he himself venerated the Father and the Son with equal love.

“Because he has looked upon the humility of his handmaid; behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed.” She rejoices that her humility has been regarded and that she is rightly to be called blessed by all. Conversely, the woman whose pride was despised is condemned and wastes away under the name Eve—that is, woe or calamity. For it was fitting that, just as death entered the world through the pride of our first mother, so the entrance of life should be opened through Mary’s humility.

“Because he who is powerful has done great things for me, and holy is his name.” This looks back to the beginning of the song, where it was said: “My soul magnifies the Lord.” Only that soul to which the Lord deigns to do great things can magnify him with worthy praises and exhort those who share the same desire and purpose by saying: “Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together.” For whoever among us, having come to know him, neglects to magnify him as far as he is able and to sanctify his name will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.

His name is called holy because, in the height of his unique power, he transcends every creature and is set far apart from all that he has made. This is better understood in Greek, where the very word used—ἅγιον (*hagion*)—seems to signify “as though outside the earth.” In imitation of him, we too are commanded, according to our measure, to be separated from all who are not holy and not dedicated to God, as the Lord says: “Be holy, because I too am holy” (1 Pet. 1). Whoever consecrates himself will rightly be regarded as being outside the earth and outside the world. He too can say: “While walking upon the earth, we have our manner of life in heaven.”

“And his mercy is from generation to generation toward those who fear him.” Turning from particular gifts to the general judgments of God, she describes the condition of the whole human race and explains in alternating verses what the proud and the humble deserve, what the children of Adam possess through free choice, and what the children of God possess through grace. “Therefore,” she says, “he has not done great things only for me, he who is powerful; in every nation and generation, whoever fears him and does righteousness is acceptable to him.”

“He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts.” “With his arm” signifies in the Son of God himself—not that God the Father is represented by the form of human flesh and that the Son clings to him like a bodily limb, but because all things were made through him, he is therefore called the arm of the Lord. Just as your arm is the means by which you work, so God’s Word is called his arm, because he worked the world through the Word. Why does a human being extend his arm in order to perform some action? Because what he says does not immediately come to be. But if he possessed such power that what he said came to be without any movement of his body, his word would be his arm. Therefore, when we hear that the Son of God is the arm of God the Father, let carnal custom not obstruct us; rather, insofar as he grants us the ability, let us contemplate the power and wisdom of God through which all things were made.

“He has cast down the powerful from their throne and exalted the humble; he has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty.” Through his arm, therefore, the Lord casts down throughout all the generations of the world the powerful—that is, the proud—from the throne of their vainglory, and exalts the humble, who trust not in their own power but in God’s goodness: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matt. 23). Likewise, he fills those who hunger and thirst for righteousness with eternal goods, while he allows the avaricious and stingy rich to perish empty of good works.

“He has taken up Israel his servant, remembering his mercy.” He beautifully calls Israel the Lord’s servant, because Israel has been taken up by him for salvation—obedient and humble, in accordance with Hosea’s saying: “Because Israel was a child, and I loved him” (Hos. 11). For whoever refuses to humble himself cannot be saved, nor can he say with the Prophet: “For behold, God helps me, and the Lord is the protector of my soul” (Ps. 53). “Whoever humbles himself like a child is greater in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18).

“As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever.” He signifies not the bodily but the spiritual offspring of Abraham: not merely those descended from his flesh, but those who, whether in circumcision or in uncircumcision, followed the traces of his faith. For Abraham himself believed while still in uncircumcision, and it was counted to him as righteousness; he then received circumcision as the sign of that same faith, so that through faith he might become the father of both peoples, as the Apostle fully explains in his letter to the Romans.

Therefore the coming of the Savior was promised forever to Abraham and his offspring, the children of promise, to whom it is said: “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. 3). It is also fitting that the mothers prophetically anticipate the arising either of the Lord or of John, so that, just as sin began through women, good things might also begin through women; and that she who perished through the deception of one woman might have life restored to her by two women proclaiming in rivalry.

## HERE BEGINS THE BLESSING OF SIMEON THE PROPHET

[Col. 1164B]

The Evangelist Luke relates that, when the parents of Jesus our Lord brought the child into Jerusalem to the temple of the Lord, to do for him according to the law and to offer sacrifices as it is written in the law of the Lord, the righteous Simeon took him into his arms and blessed him, prophesying about him.

Great indeed is the Lord’s power, but no less illustrious is his humility: he whom heaven and earth cannot contain is carried whole in the arms of an aged man. But Simeon also receives Christ figuratively: an old man receives an infant, to teach us to put off the old man, who is corrupted together with his deeds, and, with the spirit of our mind renewed, to put on him who was created according to God in righteousness, holiness, and truth. This means laying aside falsehood, speaking the truth, and accomplishing by mouth, heart, and deed the other things that belong to the state of the new man.

The righteous and God-fearing elder, in accordance with the law, takes the child Jesus into his arms to signify the righteousness of works that came from the law—for who does not know that works are commonly represented by hands and arms? The elder receives the infant Christ in order to be transformed by the humble grace of saving evangelical faith, suggesting that this age, already weighed down as if by old age and long duration, would return to the innocence and, so to speak, infancy of Christian conduct, and that its youth would be renewed like that of an eagle.

“And he blessed God and said: ‘Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace.’” You see that not only the righteous of the New Testament but also those of the Old Testament desired, in hope of future life, to be released from the body; indeed, they regarded laying aside the earthly burden as the way of peace, since they did not doubt that they would possess perpetual rest in Abraham’s bosom.

Finally, Idithun—that is, “the one who leaps over the desires of worldly things”—after silently contemplating for a long time the many evils of the world and becoming inwardly inflamed through meditation in his heart, at last spoke with his tongue and brought forth what he had pondered within: “Make known to me, Lord,” he says, “my end, and the number of my days, what it is, so that I may know what I lack. Behold, you have made my days old” (Ps. 38). By these words he plainly reveals how great a consolation he hopes to obtain at the end of his present afflictions, whose arrival he desires for so long.

“Because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples.” Blessed are the eyes that see what Simeon saw. “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.” “That very thing,” he says, “which you later prepared to be seen in mind and faith by all nations, peoples, and languages, and which you foresaw as something to be sought through hope and love, I now behold as your desired salvation with the eyes both of flesh and of heart.”

“A light for revelation to the nations and the glory of your people Israel.” Christ is God’s saving light for both peoples, prepared by God the Father. Yet he is more especially the glory of Israel, for whom he was long awaited and from whom, having been foretold, he came. He is called the revelation of the nations because he himself deigned to visit, reveal, and enlighten the eyes of their minds, which had already been sunk in profound blindness and were raised by no hope of the Lord’s coming.

The revelation of the nations is rightly placed before the glory of Israel, because “when the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved.” Thus also the Psalmist, after saying, “The Lord has made his salvation known; in the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness” (Ps. 97), adds: “He remembered his mercy to Jacob and his truth to the house of Israel.”

[Col. 1165B]

# THE BOOK OF BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, ON THE SACRED ORDERS, DIVINE SACRAMENTS, AND PRIESTLY VESTMENTS, TO THIOTMAR

[Note: [Col. 1165] a. This little work is in many respects identical with Book I of *On the Instruction of Clerics*, but the prefixed letter is different.]

[Col. 1165]

## PREFACE

[Col. 1165B]

Rabanus, servant of Jesus Christ, sends greetings to his brother Thiotmar.

As you asked me, dear brother, to resolve for you by explanation certain questions concerning the divine sacraments and sacred orders, as well as priestly vestments, I have done as much as I could. I have explained partly by interpretation and partly by clarifying their meaning what mysteries they contain. Since I have chosen you as my fellow worker in the sacred ministry, I urge you to make known to those ordained to the priesthood and required to carry out the priestly ministry what I cannot explain publicly before many people because of bodily weakness—you who are younger in age and stronger in body—and to persuade them, indeed to command them, diligently to learn what is written in this little work and pertains to their office.

Thus they may know what it is fitting for them to know, and may make known to the people entrusted to them what they must believe, do, and hold in the Christian religion. In this way both groups—those who preside and those who are subject—may be saved, provided that they attentively meditate on the law of the Lord and strive in all things to keep the divine commandments.

For the Apostle taught this when writing to his disciple in his letter, saying (1 Tim. 4:14): “Attend to reading, exhortation, and doctrine. Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. Meditate on these things; devote yourself to them, so that your progress may be manifest to all. Pay attention to yourself and to doctrine; persist in them. For by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.”

May divine grace enable you to keep this in a pure mind, complete it in sound speech and good works, so that here you may become sufficiently useful in his service, and, after the end of this life, may share in eternal joy with God’s elect in the heavenly kingdom.

## CHAPTER I — On the One Catholic Church of God

(*On the Instruction of Clerics*, Book I, chapter 1.)

The Catholic Church of God, spread and extended throughout the whole world, is ennobled and glorified by the name of Christ. Every person who participates in the right faith and is regenerated through holy baptism is called a Christian from Christ and is recognized as a son of God the Father and of the Church his mother.

“Church” is a Greek word which is translated into Latin as *convocatio* or *conventus*, “assembly” or “gathering,” because it calls everyone to itself. It is called “Catholic,” that is, “universal,” because throughout the whole world there is one Church of Christ, which is both his bride and his body.

## CHAPTER II — On the Three Orders of the Church

(Ibid., chapter 2.)

There are nevertheless three orders of those living within the Church: laypeople, monks, and clerics. The first, the lay order, is interpreted as the order of the people. For *laos* in Greek means “people” in Latin. The second is the monastic order, that is, living separately, removed from worldly society. For *monas* in Greek means “singleness,” and a monk is one who is solitary or alone.

The third is the clerical order. In Greek, *cleros* means “lot” or “inheritance.” Our teachers say that clerics are called by this name because Matthias was chosen by lot; he is the first whom we read was ordained by the Apostles. Likewise, those whom the leaders of the churches ordained in those times were chosen by lot.

“Inheritance” is also called *cleronomia* in Greek, and an heir is called *cleronomus*. Therefore they are called clerics either because they belong to the Lord’s lot or because they have the Lord as their portion, as it is written concerning them, with the Lord speaking: “I am their inheritance” (Ps. 36:18). Therefore those who possess God as their inheritance ought, without any impediment from the world, to strive to serve God, so that they may appropriately say with the Psalmist: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. 15:5).

This order is rightly placed first in the Church because it serves in holy things and dispenses the sacraments to the people. Just as in the Old Testament the tribe of Levi was specially chosen by the Lord above the other tribes to serve him through various offices in the tabernacle, so now the clerical order has been specially chosen to minister to God in the true tabernacle of God, which is the present Church.

They are to serve him day and night in his holy temple; to serve the people in matters pertaining to God; to offer gifts and sacrifices to God for their own ignorance and that of the people; to judge between the just and the unjust; to distinguish between the holy and the profane, between the polluted and the clean; and to teach God’s people all his statutes and the commandments that he gave them.

## CHAPTER III — On the Tonsure of Clerics

(Ibid., chapter 3.)

The custom of ecclesiastical tonsure arose, unless I am mistaken, from the Nazirite men. After first allowing their hair to grow, they shaved their heads again when the devotion associated with a life of great continence had been completed, and they were commanded to place their hair in the fire of the sacrifice, so that they might consecrate the perfection of their devotion to the Lord.

Following their example, the Apostles introduced the custom that those who are devoted to divine worship and consecrated to the Lord should, like Nazirites—that is, holy men of God—be renewed by cutting their hair. This is also commanded to the prophet Ezekiel, when the Lord says: “You, son of man, take a sharp sword and draw it over your head and your beard” (Ezek. 5:1). [The supplied reading “Larbam” is evidently an OCR corruption of *barbam*, “beard.”]

We also read in the Acts of the Apostles that the Nazirites Priscilla and Aquila were the first to do this; likewise the Apostle Paul and certain disciples of Christ, who are shown to have imitated them in this form of religious observance.

Among clerics, the tonsure is a certain sign that is represented in the body [perhaps supplied], but enacted in the soul. Through this sign, vices are cut away in religious life, and we are stripped of the sins of our flesh as though of hair. Thus, with our minds renewed, we shine with new growth, “putting off,” according to the Apostle, “the old man with his deeds, and putting on the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God” (Col. 3:9). This renewal must take place in the mind but be shown on the head, where the mind itself is understood to dwell.

As for the fact that, after the upper part of the head has been shaved, a circular crown is left below, I think that the priesthood and kingship of the Church are signified in them. In former times the *tiara* was placed on the heads of priests. Made of linen, it was round like half a sphere; this is signified in the shaved portion of the head. The golden crown is the breadth of a circle that encircles the heads of kings. Thus both signs are expressed on the heads of clerics, so that, through a certain likeness of the body, what the Apostle Peter wrote may also be fulfilled: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:9).

It may be asked why, unlike the ancient Nazirites, the hair is not first allowed to grow and only afterward cut. Those who inquire about this should consider the difference between that prophetic veil and the revelation of the Gospel, concerning which the Apostle says: “When you turn to Christ, the veil is taken away” (2 Cor. 3:16).

What the veil placed between Moses’ face and the sight of the children of Israel signified, the hair of holy men signified in those times. The Apostle also says that hair is a veil. Therefore the heads of those consecrated to the Lord should no longer be veiled with hair, but merely revealed, because what was hidden in the mystery of prophecy has now been disclosed in the Gospel.

There are also certain teachers who assert that the Apostle Peter first adopted this rite for various reasons. First, so that he might bear on his head the form and likeness of Christ, who, as he was about to undergo the punishment of the cross for our redemption, was cruelly crowned by the wicked Jewish nation with the sharp points of thorns. Second, so that the priests of the Old and New Testaments might be distinguished by their tonsure and dress. Finally, so that the same Apostle and his successors and followers might carry among the Roman people the ridiculous mockery of derision, because their barons and the enemies of their army were accustomed to sell conquered enemies under a crown.

But concerning these matters we leave the decision to the judgment of the reader.

## CHAPTER IV — On the Sacraments of the Church

(Ibid., chapter 24.)

Concerning the sacraments that exist in the Church, this work must first explain and clarify the priestly rite, because the ecclesiastical ministry must be ordered through the priests of Christ and, with God’s help, brought to completion.

The sacraments are baptism and chrism, the body and the blood. They are called sacraments because, under the covering of bodily things, divine power secretly works the salvation associated with those same sacraments. They are called sacraments from secret or sacred powers. They are fruitfully administered in the Church because the Holy Spirit, who remains in her, secretly brings about the same effect of the sacraments.

Therefore, whether they are administered within the Church of God by good or by bad ministers, these gifts are neither increased by the merits of good ministers nor diminished by those of bad ones, because “neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7). Hence in Greek it is also called a *mysterion*, because it contains a secret and hidden meaning.

## CHAPTER V — On the Sacrament of Baptism
*(Same work, ch. 23.)* The first of the sacraments is baptism, because before anyone is anointed with the holy chrism, so that he may become a partaker of the body and blood of Christ, he must be cleansed by sacred regeneration and then proceed duly to the other rites. *Baptismus* is Greek; in Latin it is rendered *tinctio*, “dipping” or “immersion.” It is called *tinctio* not only because a person is immersed in water, but because there he is changed for the better by the Spirit of grace and becomes something altogether different from what he was. At first we were foul through the deformity of sins; in that immersion we become beautiful through the whitening of virtues. Hence it is written in the Song of Songs: “Who is this that comes up as though whitened?” (Song III, 6).

Its mystery is completed in no other way than under the designation of the Trinity—that is, through knowledge of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—for the Lord says to the apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19). For just as every word stands upon three witnesses, so the threefold number of the divine names confirms the sacrament.

The reason baptism is administered through water is this: the Lord wished that, through suitability and efficacy, an intangible and invisible element should be bestowed [the text is corrupt], [Col. 1169D] over which also, in the beginning, the Holy Spirit was borne.

[Note: [Col. 1169D] Read: *per congruentiam et profectum incontrectabili et invisibili impenderetur elemento* (“that it should be bestowed, through suitability and efficacy, by an intangible and invisible element”); or: *per congruens et perfectum contrectabile et visibile impederetur elementum* (“that a suitable and perfect tangible and visible element should be supplied”). If the former reading is preferred, in which the least alteration is made, perhaps *propter* may be read for *per*, although *propter* is also understood in this passage.]

For just as oil, by its natural weight, floats above every liquid, so in the beginning the Holy Spirit was borne above the waters. As water cleanses the body outwardly, so through its mystery the soul is secretly purified by the Holy Spirit. Its sanctification occurs as follows. When God has been invoked, the Holy Spirit descends from heaven and, as though healing the waters, sanctifies them from himself; they receive the power of purification, so that in them flesh and soul polluted by sins may be cleansed. Both things must necessarily be applied in baptism: the washing of baptism and the purification of the Holy Spirit, since the Savior says: “Unless someone has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.”

Before baptism, however, the ministry of catechizing must precede in a person, so that the catechumen may first receive the rudiments of faith. [Col. 1169D] For in the Gospel according to Matthew it is read that after the resurrection the Lord commanded the apostles to teach and baptize all nations in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, first to impart the faith of that God, and then to baptize those who believed for the remission of sins. Hence, according to Mark, the same Lord is read to have placed faith before baptism, when he said: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark XVI, 6). And, as John bears witness, Jesus first smeared the eyes of the man born blind with mud made from spittle, and then sent him to the waters of Siloam, because the person to be baptized must first be instructed in faith in the incarnation of Christ and then, already believing, be admitted to baptism, so that he may know whose grace he is receiving and to whom he is henceforth made a debtor.

## CHAPTER VI — On Catechumens

*(Ibid., ch. 26.)* A catechumen is so called because he is still hearing the teaching of the faith but has not yet received baptism. For *catechumenus* is interpreted in Greek, and *auditor* in Latin, as “hearer,” etc., to the end of the chapter.

## CHAPTER VII — On the Order of Catechizing

*(Ibid., ch. 27.)* The order of catechizing is as follows: first the pagan is asked whether he renounces the devil and all his damnable works and deceitful practices, etc., to the end of the chapter.

## CHAPTER VIII — The Meaning of the Creed According to the Latins

Accordingly, *symbolum* is interpreted in Latin as “indication,” “sign,” or “collation.” It is an “indication” because by it the integrity of the faith is indicated; a “sign” because, when it is rightly retained and understood, the faithful are distinguished from the unfaithful; and a “collation” because in it the apostles brought together the whole integrity of the faith.

All of them retained it in their hearts with equal sincerity of faith and confessed it with their mouths; and, contributing their individual formulations, they produced the *symbolum*, that is, the collation of the whole faith. As they were about to depart from one another, [Col. 1170C] they established together the rule of their future preaching, lest, departing from one another in different places, they should preach anything diverse or discordant. For it was most fitting and useful that those who had one soul and one heart in the Lord, and whom the breath of the Holy Spirit quickened, should also be adorned by one confession of faith. Those who were bound together by the bond of one faith could neither be nor ought to be divided in anything.

Moreover, many wish the “abbreviated word” prophesied through Isaiah to be understood in the Creed and in the Lord’s Prayer. In the one, the integrity of faith is contained; in the other, the integrity of prayers. Thus, in the twelve words, the teaching of the twelve apostles is contained, and in the seven petitions, everything is contained that pertains to the ordering of the present and future life.

Yet the whole word of the teaching may also be called “abbreviated,” because what the Law and the Prophets formerly contained in the breadth of their commandments, the Lord, when he came, pronounced and stated: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend” (Mark XII, 30). In these two sayings he evidently abbreviated the Prophets and the Law.

Let this suffice concerning the Creed and its name.

## CHAPTER IX — On Belief: How One Must Believe in God the Almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ His Son, Born and Suffering, and in the Holy Spirit, the Catholic Church, and the Other Things That Follow in the Same Creed

[Col. 1171A]

The faith contained in this Creed must be understood by those who are to be baptized in such a way that they believe in God the Almighty Father, creator of all visible and invisible things. He alone, because he is not from another, is therefore called “unbegotten.” They must believe in Jesus Christ, his Son, through whom all things were made: true God, the only-begotten, and true Son of God—not made or adopted, but begotten and of one substance with the Father. He is in every respect equal to God the Father, so that he cannot be inferior in time, rank, or power, and the one who was begotten is as great as the one who begot him.

They must also believe that he was born of the Holy Spirit from Mary, ever-virgin—that is, that, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, the Son of God assumed from the virgin a true body; so that he who in divinity was the Son of God the Father became in humanity the Son of a human mother.

They must also believe that in the last age he descended from the Father for the redemption of the world, although he never ceased to be with the Father; that he became truly human so that a human being might set the human race free; and that he, who without beginning possesses eternity with the Father and the Holy Spirit, assumed at the end of the ages a complete human nature, and that the Word became flesh by assuming humanity, not by changing his divinity.

They must also believe that he endured suffering and death, [Col. 1171C] not through the power of divinity but through the weakness of humanity; that he died a true death of the flesh; that he rose again in a true resurrection of the flesh; and that by his resurrection he bestowed upon us the hope of resurrection—solely in such a way that, just as he rose alive from the dead on the third day, so we too may rise at the end of the ages in the same flesh in which we now live.

They must also believe that in the same body which he assumed from the Virgin, in which he endured suffering and rose again, he ascended into heaven, that he is now there in the same body, and that he will come for judgment. When all have been raised, he will assign to some the sentence of eternal punishment for their sins, and to others the reward of eternal blessedness for the merits of their righteousness.

They must also believe in the Holy Spirit, true God, proceeding from the Father and the Son, equal in every respect to the Father and the Son in will, power, [Col. 1171D] eternity, and substance. There are no degrees in this holy Trinity by which anyone can be called inferior or superior.

They must also believe in the holy Catholic Church, that is, the universal Church—not “in” the holy Church in the same way as believers believe in the Trinity. They must believe that the holy Church is the house of that same holy Trinity. Those who depart from its communion are called schismatics and heretics and are punished with eternal damnation; but those who remain in its communion are both members of Christ, receive the remission of sins, and belong to eternal life.

Since, therefore, infants who do not yet possess the use of reason cannot at all grasp these things, when they reach an age capable of understanding, they must be taught the sacraments of faith and the mysteries of their confession, [Col. 1172A] so that they may both truly believe them and carefully preserve them.

We have expressly spoken of “their confession,” because although they are not yet able to speak, those who receive them from the laver of the font confess and speak on their behalf. Nor is it without good reason that those who are liable to the sins of others should, through the mystery of baptism, receive the remission of original sins through another’s confession.

## CHAPTER X — On Examination

Those who are already of such an age that they can give an account of their belief must be examined with diligent scrutiny, to determine whether they truly believe or whether some stain of falsehood is concealed in them. Otherwise, while—whether through fear or favor toward earthly powers, or through the acquisition of certain things—they come to the sacrament of baptism while the ministers of the Church are ignorant of their condition, what is holy may be given to dogs, pearls may be thrown before swine, and wolves may be clothed in sheep’s clothing.

The Church has been accustomed to observe this practice: over a period of several days, those who are to be baptized at the solemnity of Easter are examined, so that the sacraments of life may be imparted to those who come to the true faith instructed, taught, and pure in heart. In order that they may be found more suitable for the sacrament of baptism and that their faith may be more credible, certain things are performed bodily which, when tasted with spiritual discernment, convey something mystical and spiritual.

## CHAPTER XI — What Renunciation Is

We must now speak of renunciation and of what renunciation is. For *abrenuntiare* is customarily used to mean “to despise,” “reject,” “oppose,” or whatever else may be expressed by this verb in this sense. Although the meaning of the verb *nuntio* (“announce”) is clear when it is used without a preposition, and although with a preposition it sometimes does not depart far from its meaning—as in *narrabo et renuntiabo* (“I shall tell and announce”)—at other times it turns to another sense, as in: “Thus, therefore, whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 33), *abrenuntiare* is nevertheless always customarily used in the sense stated above.

A person therefore confesses that he renounces Satan and all his works and all his pomps; this renunciation is rightly followed by the confession of the holy Trinity. And [possibly: “so that”] where sin abounded, grace may abound still more; and where the yoke of the devil has rotted away before the face of the anointing of the Holy Spirit, there may come the yoke of him who said: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. XI, 29).

The faithful renounce Satan, who is also called the devil, so that they may serve the Lord Savior more freely, because, according to the word of that same Lord: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI, 24).

## CHAPTER XII — On the Renunciation of Satan and All His Works and Pomps, and on Which Works and Pomps Belong to the Devil

His works are also renounced, because his works are opposed to the works of the Savior. Since he subjected the human race to himself by his weapons—that is, by vices—the Lord conquered him by his own weapons—that is, by virtues. In the devil’s service, that is, in our sins, lasting slavery received death; in Christ’s service, that is, in virtues, we receive eternal life.

We may therefore appropriately call the seven principal vices, by which the devil assails the human race, the works of Satan. Opposed to them are the seven principal virtues, which are undoubtedly saving works. Meanwhile, his pomps are also renounced. These too are works of Satan, but they seem to be distinguished from his other works in this respect: through them pride, whose author he is and which cast him down, is in some way represented.

His pomps, therefore, are ambition, arrogance, vainglory, and other things of this kind, which are recognized as proceeding from the fountain of pride. That *pompa* is to be understood as ambition, ostentation, and similar things is shown by the prophetic text, which says: “Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion and trust in Mount Samaria, nobles, leaders of the peoples, entering pompously into the house of Israel” (Amos VI, 1).

The most eloquent and thoroughly Christian poet Clemens Prudentius also used *pompa* in this sense in the book *Psychomachia*, where he says:

> The ostentatious pomp of empty splendor  
> Is stripped bare of its empty robe.

Although every sin may be called pride, because when someone sins he appears to oppose God, who prohibited sinning, it is nevertheless one thing to sin lazily, another maliciously, another knowingly, another ignorantly, another negligently, and another arrogantly. Whatever the manner in which a person sins, if he scorns repentance, he plunges himself into a great abyss of pride, from which he can emerge only through confession of his sins, amendment of his conduct, and the aid of saving repentance.

A person is proud against God in two ways: either when, being disobedient to his commands, he commits what has been prohibited, or when he neglects to repent of what he has committed. Therefore, whether those who are to be baptized or we who have already received the sacrament of baptism must keep before our eyes the covenant made with God in baptism, in which Satan, his works, and his pomps are renounced. That covenant is then made void if someone, while remaining in the faith, submits to vices, or, departing from the faith, submits to the worship of idols or to the errors of heresies.

## CHAPTER XIII — On the Order of Holy Baptism

Since, therefore, it is established that there are two covenants of believers—one in which the devil, his pomps, and all his works are renounced, and another by which they confess that they believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—these must be held with unwavering attention of mind. In order that they may be preserved undefiled, we must always seek the help of him who bestowed the sacrament of baptism for the salvation of the human race.

Its mystery was prefigured in the Old Testament through Moses, when the people were baptized in the cloud and in the sea, and was most clearly demonstrated for us in the New Testament through the mediator between God [Col. 1174A] and humanity. For he himself says: “Unless someone has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III, 5). And John says of him: “Behold, I baptize with water; but one stands among you whom you do not know. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (John I, 26).

Through this, we who are born into the world are reborn to God; and we who through sin were children of wrath become through grace children of God. Through this immersion and this washing the Church is invigorated. For just as a woman was built from the bone of the sleeping first-created man, so the Church was formed from the side of Christ sleeping on the cross: “For blood and water flowed from his side”—the two chief sacraments of the holy Church, so that consecration might be granted to that Church through the one, and cleansing through the other. We are regenerated from the washing and consecrated by the blood.

Hence also the people crossed the Red Sea, because the baptism of Christ is consecrated by blood. Since, therefore, the element of water in this world is, among all the elements, suited to the grace of cleansing, giving life, and restoring, the dignity of baptism is not unfittingly conferred upon it. [Possibly, “which” is to be referred to water.] For it conceived the efficacy of regenerating human beings when the Spirit of God was borne over it at the beginning of the world, and it received the dignity of cleansing when it flowed from the side of Christ. Through this visible element, that invisible reality is signified: just as water cleanses the body outwardly, so through its mystery the soul is secretly purified by the Holy Spirit.

When God has been invoked, the Holy Spirit descends from heaven and, having sanctified the waters, grants them the power of purification. [Col. 1174C] Thus the human being, restored according to the image of the holy Trinity in whose image he had been created, is cleansed; and the one who had entered those waters old through the sin of the first human being emerges from them new through the grace of Christ. Changed for the better by the Spirit of grace, he becomes something altogether different from what he had been: foul through the deformity of sins, he is there restored beautiful through the whitening of virtues.

The mystery of baptism can in no way be completed except under the invocation of the holy Trinity, because the Lord also said to the apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” The same Lord confirmed this sacrament when, in his own baptism, the Father was declared by the voice, the Son in the body, and the Holy Spirit in the manifestation of a dove.

O glorious and wondrous sacrament, which makes children of God from children of wrath, new people from old, and beautiful people from foul ones; in which we are both regenerated and cleansed, and imitate the example of Christ’s death.

How, then, are we to imitate this example? Let the Apostle say: “Do you not know,” he says, “that all of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI, 3).

We die to sin, therefore, when we renounce the devil and all that belongs to him. We are buried with Christ when, under the invocation of the holy [Col. 1175A] Trinity, in a threefold immersion, we descend into the font of washing as into a certain tomb. We rise with Christ when, stripped of all sins, we emerge from the font as from a tomb.

Nor is the mystery of the three days and nights during which the Lord is said to have been in the tomb passed over, when, after the holy Trinity has been invoked—which is certainly the true light—we descend into the font. For here the Father is light, and in the light of him who is the Son we see the Holy Spirit as light.

We do not, however, make three nights when we oppose the father of darkness and ignorance, together with the lie born from him—which is false just as its father is—and when he speaks a lie, he speaks from what is his own. In the third place, we destroy the spirit of error, which inspires false prophets to say, “Thus says the Lord,” although the Lord did not send them. We destroy and trample these things down if we have also been buried with Christ, according to what he himself says: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke X, 19).

Each of these things is so opposed to the holy Trinity as night to day, darkness to light, and falsehood to truth. The baptismal font also bears the likeness of Christ’s tomb, which is said to have been new, because whoever is buried with Christ in it and rises with him, according to the same Apostle, must walk in newness of life.

The seven steps of this font—three in the descent, signifying the three nights, and three in the ascent, signifying the three days—seem to signify the things mentioned above. The seventh, which is also the fourth, is the one of whom someone said: “And the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God, who extinguishes the fiery furnace, who is the support of the feet, [Note: [Col. 1175] A manuscript reads “foundation of the water”; but the former is better.] and the foundation. In him,” according to the Apostle, “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II, 9).

Baptism is not repeated because Christ also dies no more than once. Sins committed after baptism are erased by tears of repentance, almsgiving, and the performance of other good works, not by repeating baptism.

Meanwhile, very clean linen cloths and spices are used for burying the Lord’s body, because the person who desires to be buried with Christ, if his age permits it, although he is dead through original sin—which he still bears—must nevertheless burn with the performance of good works and be clothed in clean garments.

The Prophet prays that the priests be clothed in these things when he says: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI, 9). If, therefore, before he is reborn, cleansed of original sin, and buried with Christ, a person ought to burn with spices and be clothed in the cleanest garments, how much more, once reborn, cleansed, made alive together with Christ, walking in newness of life, and made a new creation, ought he to abound in the fragrance of good works and shine with the brightness of white garments?

The order and examination of catechizing having thus been properly completed, we must now speak of the immersion of baptism and the anointing with chrism.

## CHAPTER XIV — On the Immersion of Baptism and the Anointing with Chrism

[Col. 1176A]

*(On the Instruction of Clergy, book I, ch. 18.)* After this, therefore, the font is consecrated, and the catechumen approaches baptism itself; then he is baptized in the name of the holy Trinity by a threefold immersion. And rightly: the human being, created in the image of the holy Trinity, is renewed to that same image through the invocation of the holy Trinity; and the one who fell into death by the third stage of sin—that is, by consent—may, raised from the font on the third occasion, rise again through grace to life.

This threefold immersion can also signify the Lord’s three-day burial, as we have already said above, especially since the Apostle says: “All of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been grafted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be united with him in resurrection” (Rom. VI, 3), and so forth.

Baptism must therefore be completed with the invocation of the holy Trinity and under a threefold immersion, so that the mystery of baptism may be celebrated according to the distinction of the persons, while, according to the unity of substance, there may be one baptism. Hence the Apostle says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV, 5), and so forth.

After the baptized person has risen from the font, he is immediately signed on the head by the presbyter with the sacred chrism, accompanied at the same time by prayer, so that he may become a partaker of Christ’s kingdom and may be called a Christian from Christ.

It is also written in the Gospel: “When Jesus had been baptized, he immediately rose from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him” (Matt. III, 16).

The anointing with chrism rightly follows baptism, because the Holy Spirit, who through that chrism sanctifies believers by the admixture of his power, immediately descended upon baptized Jesus in the form of a dove. That dove prefigured the type of the dove which, during the flood, brought back to the ark a branch of olive with green leaves, signifying that the Holy Spirit, through the anointing of chrism in baptism, grants believers the greenness of heavenly grace.

But we shall speak more fully about this in what follows.

We also read in the Acts of the Fathers that Pope Sylvester established in the Roman Church that, just as the power and privilege belong solely to the bishop—that he himself prepare the sacred chrism and sign the baptized person with that chrism through the laying on of hands, because of heretical persuasion—so the presbyter should anoint with the same chrism the baptized person after he has been raised from the water, because of the possibility of death’s approach. For it is written in the Apostle: “But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. VIII, 11), and so forth.

It is therefore plainly evident that whoever does not belong to Christ cannot become a partaker of his kingdom. For this reason it is necessary to come immediately to the aid of the baptized person with the anointing of chrism, so that, receiving a share in the Holy Spirit, he may not remain alien to Christ.

## CHAPTER XV — On the Garment of the Baptized Person and the Eucharist

*(Ibid., ch. 29.)* After baptism, a white garment is given to the Christian, signifying Christian innocence and purity, which, after the washing away of …, etc., to the end of the chapter.

## CHAPTER XVI — On the Bishop’s Laying on of Hands and the Sacrament of Chrism

*(Ibid., ch. 30.)* Finally, through the laying on of hands by the high priest, the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, is bestowed upon him, so that he may be strengthened through the Spirit, etc., to the end of the chapter.

## CHAPTER XVII — On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Body and Blood

[Col. 1177B]

*(Ibid., ch. 31.)* But since above we have discussed, insofar as the Lord has granted us, the two sacraments—that is, baptism and chrism—etc., to the end of the chapter.

## CHAPTER XVIII — On the Office of the Mass

*(Ibid., ch. 32.)* We have, as I think, said enough above concerning the sacraments; now we must speak of the office of the Mass, in which the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood are consecrated, etc., to the end of the chapter.

## CHAPTER XIX — On the Order of the Mass
*(Ibid., chap. 33.)* First, in the celebration of the Mass, at the priest’s entrance to the altar, an antiphon is sung by the clergy, so that a sound may be heard when he enters the sanctuary in the sight of the Lord, just as in the Old Testament the entrance of the high priest was made known by the sound of bells. Thus, appropriately, at the priest’s entrance, as the choirs resound, a melody of divine praise is heard, so that the harmony of the ministers may piously precede the mysteries of the Lord’s celebration, and the sacrifice of worthy praise may precede the venerable sacrament of Christ’s body and blood.

A choir is a multitude gathered for sacred purposes; and it is called *chorus* because at first they stood around the altars in the form of a crown and thus sang psalms. Hence the book of Ecclesiasticus also writes of a priest standing before the altar, with a crown of brothers around him. Others have said that *chorus* derives from concord, which consists in charity and true peace. Or it may derive from the harmony of sound: when one person sings, it is called in Greek *monodia*, in Latin *sicinium*; when two sing, it is called *bicinium*. When many sing, it is called a choir.

*Antiphon* is a Greek word meaning “reciprocal voice,” that is, a song sung alternately by two choirs. *Introit* is so called from entering, for by this song one enters into the duties of sacred melody; or, at that time, the congregation of the Christian religion, entering the church of God, prepares itself to proceed to the other praises of the offices. For just as the *invitatory* is so called from inviting, when the nocturnal office begins and “Come” is said, so the *introit* is named from entering, when the daytime office begins.

Pope Celestine, a Campanian by birth and bishop of Rome, established that the antiphon at the introit should be celebrated before the sacrifice. Previously this was not done; only Paul’s Epistle and the holy Gospel were read. [Col. 1177C–D]

Then *Kyrie eleison* is said, which is translated from Greek into Latin as “Lord, have mercy on us.” Likewise, *Christe eleison* means “Christ, have mercy on us.”

The angelic hymn, namely, *Gloria in excelsis Deo*—“Glory to God in the highest”—was sung by the angels when the Lord was born. Pope Telesphorus, a Greek by birth, established that it should be sung before the sacrifice. He also established that Masses should be celebrated throughout the night on the Lord’s Nativity.

Then the lector reads the canonical lesson, so that the minds of the hearers, instructed by it, may rise more attentively to the remaining things. Yet a reading from the Epistles of Saint Paul is more often read in the office of the Mass. Everyone knows Paul to be the teacher of the nations; and because he merited from the Lord to be a chosen vessel, therefore, while he remained in the body, he taught the nations for a time through the doctrine by which he wrote certain epistles. Consequently, now, whenever he is read each day, he strengthens the minds of all the faithful with the firmness of sound faith. [Col. 1178A–B]

After the reading, the cantor says the responsory, in order to summon the hearers to compunction and make their minds gentle. It is called a *responsory* because, when one person has finished, another responds. There is also this difference between responsories and antiphons: in responsories one person sings the verse, whereas in antiphons the choirs alternate in the verses. The Greeks are said to have discovered antiphons first, and the Italians responsories. Some call this responsory a *gradual*, because it is sung beside the steps of the ambo.

After the responsory, “Alleluia” is sung, so that the people may lift their minds to heavenly things and raise them to divine contemplation. *Alleluia* is an interpretation consisting of two words: “praise God”; and it is Hebrew. *Ia* is one of the ten names by which God is called among the Hebrews.

Likewise, *Amen* is Hebrew, to which the faithful people respond after every prayer or blessing of the priest. *Amen* may also be translated into Latin as “truly,” “faithfully,” or “let it be.” For, as Jerome testifies, where the Psalter has “Let it be, let it be,” the Hebrew reads *Amen, amen*. Nevertheless, these two words—*Amen* and *Alleluia*—may not be transferred at all into the language of the Greeks, Latins, or barbarians, nor pronounced in another language. For although they can be translated, the antiquity of their own proper language has been preserved by the apostles because of their more sacred authority.

They are such sacred names that John also reports in the Apocalypse that, through revelation by the Spirit, he saw and heard the voice of the heavenly host, like the sound of many waters and mighty thunder, saying “Amen” and “Alleluia.” Therefore both words ought to be spoken on earth just as they resound in heaven.

Then the Gospel is read by the deacon with the greatest authority in the ears of the people, so that the teaching of the one toward whom all their attention is directed may be heard there, and his power may be understood through the Gospel—the power of him whose most holy mystery of body and blood is then celebrated.

After this, offerings are presented by the people, and the offertory is sung by the clergy. It receives its name from the very act, as if it were the song of those offering. That offertory songs are sung in honor of the sacrifices is attested by the book of Ecclesiasticus, which says that the ancients used to sing when victims were sacrificed. It reads as follows:

> “The priest,” it says, “stretched out his hand for the libation, and poured out the blood of the grape, and poured forth upon the covering of the altar a fragrance to the divine and exalted Prince. Then the sons of Aaron shouted on their beaten trumpets, and sounded them and made a great voice heard as a memorial before the Lord” (Ecclus. 50:16).

Likewise now, with the sound of the trumpet—that is, in the proclamation of the voice—we worthily bring forth a song, so that, proclaiming praises to the Lord in heart and deed alike, we may exult before him on high, celebrating the true sacrifice by whose blood the world has been saved. [Col. 1178C–D; 1179A]

A corporal is placed upon the altar—that is, a cloth—which signifies the linen in which the Savior’s body was wrapped. It ought to be woven from pure linen, not from silk or purple, nor from dyed cloth, as we find established by Pope Sylvester. For in the Gospel it is written that Joseph wrapped the Savior’s body in a clean shroud (Matt. 27:59), and that after the Lord’s resurrection the headcloth was found not lying with the linen wrappings but folded separately.

At that time the sacred vessels are also placed upon the altar: the chalice and the paten. These in some manner represent the Lord’s tomb, because just as Christ’s body was then anointed with spices and placed in a new tomb through the service of the devout, so now, in the Church, his mystical body, seasoned with the ointments of sacred prayer, is administered in the sacred vessels through the ministry of the priests, for reception by the faithful.

Afterward the Mass is sung by the priest. First, when he has secretly completed the prayer called “Upon the Offerings,” he greets the people and prays, saying: “The Lord be with you”—that is, may almighty God be with his people. The people respond: “And with your spirit.” This response and prayer of the people are appropriately offered: just as the priest prayed that the Lord might be with the people, so the people pray that the Lord might be with the priest’s spirit.

When the priest says, “Let us pray,” he asks everyone to pray that his prayer may be heard by the Lord. When, near the end of the prayer, he says, “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son,” the priest prays to God the Father that the prayer itself may be brought to completion through his Son, who is our Lord and is equal to the Father.

When he says, “Who with you lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit,” he wishes the people to believe and understand that the Son lives and reigns as God with the Father, without beginning and without end. Just as the Father is God and the Son is God, so also the Holy Spirit has one majesty, one power, and one substance with the Father and the Son; and in all three this unity of the Godhead remains forever and ever. That is, just as the Son lived and existed with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit before all ages, so also in the present age and in the future age, where the righteous will remain with the holy angels and the unrighteous will be tormented with the devils, he is to be believed to live equally with the Father and the Holy Spirit, bounded by no end. [Col. 1179B–D; 1180A]

“Amen” follows, by which the responding people conclude the prayer just spoken. As we said above, *Amen* is the confirmation of the prayer, spoken by the people, and in Latin it is translated “let it be.” Here it sounds as if everyone were saying, “Let it be as the priest has prayed.”

Then the priest says: “Lift up your hearts.” He admonishes the people to lift all their hearts upward—that is, above themselves—to the Lord almighty, and to pray faithfully that help may come to them from above, from the heavenly God by whom they were created. The people respond: “We have them with the Lord”—that is, just as the priest commanded them to keep their hearts above, so they profess that they do.

Then the priest exhorts the people to give thanks to their Creator, saying: “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.” The people respond: “It is worthy and just.” For it is a just and worthy reason that all should give thanks to God, because we have received every good thing from him—or rather, we shall receive them if we persevere in right faith and good works to the end.

After this the priest begins the preface, saying: “It is truly worthy and just, right and salutary.” He confirms the profession of the people and says that it is truly worthy and just to give thanks to God for everything, and that it is right—that is, correct—and salutary, that is, full of salvation, to give thanks to him who gave us eternal salvation.

“We give you thanks,” he says, “always and everywhere.” After the profession of the people, the priest turns toward the Lord and speaks as though to one present, because we are always in the Lord’s presence and he sees our thoughts; that is, we are so before him at all times and in every place.

Immediately, turning the speech of the prayer itself toward God the Father, he completes it as follows: “Lord, holy Father, almighty and eternal God, through Christ our Lord.” He calls him “Lord” because he rules over all and everything exists under his dominion. “Holy,” because he is holy and through him all things are sanctified, since he created all things holy and good.

“Father” is called *pater* in Greek and *genitor* in Latin, because he begot the Son without any defilement or corruption. In Latin, *father* is said to derive from *patrando*, that is, from accomplishing or helping, because he completed all things that were made and helped all things that were helped. He also willed us to become his adopted sons through the sanctification by which he sanctified us.

“Almighty”: because he can do all things, he is called almighty, since no word is impossible with God.

“Eternal God.” There is this distinction between the eternal, the perpetual, and the temporal: the eternal is that which had no beginning and will have no end, but always was, is, and will be. The perpetual is that which began to exist but will have no end. The temporal is that which had a beginning and will have an end. Therefore he is called “eternal God” because God alone is eternal: he neither began to be nor ceases to be, but always is.

“God” is said to derive from loving, because he loves everything and governs what he created. Alternatively, *Deus* is said from *divinity*, because he is divine, knows all things, and disposes of all things according to his will. [Col. 1180B–D; 1181A]

“Through Christ our Lord.” *Christ* is Greek and means “anointed” in Latin. This is Christ, who was ineffably begotten by the Father before all beginnings. Then, at the time pleasing to him, the Holy Spirit came upon the virgin Mary and anointed her womb with divine anointing; from this he was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary.

In the Old Testament, priests and kings were also anointed; therefore they were called *christs*, because they had been anointed with temporal anointing. This Christ, through whom we give thanks to the Father, is eternally Christ and, with the Father, eternal God. Through him we have been redeemed, and he is our Lord because he rules over us.

“Through whom the angels praise your majesty.” Through that Christ, through whom we give thanks to the Father, the angels praise the Father’s majesty, because he is equal to the Father in divinity. *Majesty* is said as if meaning “greater power,” because God’s power is greater than human power. The angels praise God’s majesty through Christ because Christ, together with the Father, created the angels.

*Angel* is Greek and is translated into Latin as “messenger.” *Angel* is the name of an office, not of a nature, for angels announce things; by nature they are spirits.

“Dominions adore.” The dominions praise and adore the majesty of God the Father through the Son. *Dominions* is the name of one order among the nine orders of angels. There were ten orders of angels, but the tenth order fell and, through pride, was changed into the devil. Nine, however, remained in their holiness. These are their names: angels, archangels, virtues, principalities, powers, thrones, dominions, cherubim, and seraphim.

The names of two of these orders are not Latin. *Cherubim* is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge”; *seraphim* means “burning.” The remaining names of the orders mentioned above are Latin, except for angels and archangels. For angels are called messengers, while archangels are called exalted messengers.

Pope Gregory the Roman, in his homily on the Gospel reading in which it is written, “The tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to Jesus to hear him” (Luke 15:1), explained the aforesaid orders most fully. But let us return to our subject.

“Powers tremble.” He speaks of the orders mentioned above. He does not say this because those orders are bodily, but he speaks according to our manner of expression: we customarily tremble and fear before our lords. He says that they tremble and fear so that we may understand that all heavenly, earthly, and infernal things tremble and fear before the sight of the divine majesty.

“Heavens and the powers of the heavens.” The heavens themselves obey the divine command, because they have no power to show themselves clear or cloudy. The powers of the heavens are the angelic orders mentioned above, as Gregory testifies in his homily on the Gospel reading where it is written: “There will be signs in the sun, moon, and stars” (Luke 21:25).

“And blessed seraphim.” The seraphim have been discussed above.

“With united exultation they celebrate together.” All the aforesaid orders equally celebrate the majesty of God the Father through Christ with united exultation.

“With them we ask that you command our voices also to be admitted.” This is our supplication: that the heavenly Father himself, through his Son Christ, through whom we give him thanks for everything, may deign to admit our voices and join them to the voices of the angelic orders mentioned above.

“Saying with humble confession.” That is, with humble confession. What is more humble than to commend ourselves to the eternal Father through the eternal Son, to presume nothing from our own conscience or goodness, and, in accordance with the angelic voices, always to believe and proclaim him to be holy in his very essence, saying:

“Holy, holy, holy.” John the Evangelist wrote in the book of the Apocalypse that he saw “before the throne of God and of the Lamb twenty-four elders and four living creatures standing there and incessantly saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Sabaoth,” and so forth (Rev. 4:4).

He is called holy three times in order to signify the holiness of the Father, the holiness of the Son, and the holiness of the Spirit of the Father and the Son. Yet although “holy” is said three times, it is not said in the plural, “holies,” but in the singular, “holy,” so that one holiness and one eternity may be understood in these three persons.

“Lord God Sabaoth.” Many customarily interpret *Sabaoth* as “almighty,” while many others interpret it as “of hosts.” Thus he is Lord God, and he orders all the hosts of angels and human beings.

“Heaven and earth are full of your glory.” That is, the heavens and the earth are governed by his glory, and those who are in heaven and on earth glorify his holy name.

“Hosanna in the highest.” What is now said corruptly as *Osanna* was formerly said as *Osianna*. *Osi* is an interjection of one praising, or magnifying without cause; *anna* means “save.” But it is corruptly said as *Osanna*, and it may be understood as “save” or “grant salvation.” “In the highest” means “in the heights.”

“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” When Christ came to Jerusalem and descended from the Mount of Olives, the children of Israel shouted, saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (John 12:13). But what did Christ’s coming into Jerusalem signify except the future resurrection, when he will come to judge the living and the dead and will appear to us in the same flesh in which he suffered for us? Then “at the name of the Lord Jesus every knee shall bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2:10), and so forth, as he said to the apostles. [Col. 1181B–D; 1182A–D]

After the angelic hymn, which the entire clergy sings together with one voice, a prayer follows through which the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood is effected. It begins as follows:

> “Therefore, most merciful Father, through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, we humbly pray and ask you to regard as acceptable and bless these gifts, these offerings, these holy and unblemished sacrifices.”

He speaks to God the almighty Father, calling him most merciful because he is most compassionate and most pious. *Clement* is said as if meaning “bright mind” or “abundant.” Therefore, when he calls him “most merciful,” that is, “of the clearest mind,” he means that God is clearest in mind and most merciful in heart. When we call him merciful, we must not understand this bodily, as though he were composed of bodily members, a heart, or a mind like a human being. Rather, we call him merciful and compassionate because he is naturally pious and merciful, always ready to save us if we turn to him with our whole heart, right faith, and good works.

“Through Jesus Christ your Son.” *Jesus* is Greek and is translated into Latin as “Savior” or “saving.” He is called Savior because he saves his people from their sins. He saves from sins because he has authority to forgive sins, as he himself said: “But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins” (Matt. 9:6).

He is called “saving” because he gave us salvation, so that, if we keep his commandments, we may be able to attain eternal life.

“Your Son, our Lord.” He calls him his only-begotten Son because he is the only-begotten Son from the substance of the Father. We, however, are adopted sons through him, who is the only-begotten Son proceeding from the Father and coeternal with the Father. Therefore, through him we ought to ask the Father, humbly saying:

“We humbly pray and ask”—that is, we ask humbly—“that you regard as acceptable and bless these gifts, these offerings, these holy and unblemished sacrifices.” “That you may regard as acceptable,” that is, that you may receive and bless them.

Gifts are things given voluntarily; offerings are things presented in return for some gift or reward, just as we offer to God so that our sins may be forgiven. Sacrifices are things that are consecrated together with prayers. “Unblemished” means immaculate and free from every stain of envy or malice.

The gifts and sacrifices are holy and unblemished when they are offered without the stains of scandals and acquired through honest labor. It is not as many err, saying that “unblemished” means “not dedicated.” Read the seven Conferences of the Fathers, and in the second conference of Theonas, chapter nine, you will find what “unblemished” means. [Col. 1183C]

> “In the first place, the things we offer to you for your holy catholic Church, which you may deign to pacify, guard, unite, and govern throughout the whole world, together with your servant, our pope, and our bishop.”

“In the first place,” he says, “the things we offer to you,” because this offering is to be offered to God alone. He indicates for whom it should be offered: namely, first of all it should be offered for the holy catholic Church.

*Church* is Greek and is translated into Latin as “assembly.” *Catholic* means “universal,” because all who believe in the Lord ought to be in one assembly.

“Which you may deign to pacify, guard, unite, and govern throughout the whole world.” We offer this first of all for her, so that you may deign to preserve your aforesaid assembly throughout the whole world in peace and unity, “together with your servant, that one”—that is, together with him who occupies the see of the apostle Peter, because the Church in which Peter, the chief of the apostles, sits is the head of all the catholic Churches. This is because Christ said to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church,” and so forth (Matt. 16:18).

Because of this statement, we ought all to pray for the one who presides over that Church.
