“And our bishop”—that is, for our bishop, in whose diocese we are. We ought to pray for him because he is the shepherd and preacher of our Church.

“Remember, Lord, your servants and handmaids, and all who stand around.” The priest has already prayed for the apostolic see and for his bishop. If a bishop celebrates Mass, he should not say “our bishop,” because he himself is the bishop. If a presbyter celebrates Mass, he ought to say “our bishop.”

Prayer has already been offered for the pope and the bishops; afterward prayer is offered for the people when the priest says: “Remember, Lord, your servants and handmaids.” He beseeches God the Father to deign to remember all the men and women who have come to the office of the Mass. By “those who stand around,” he means the men and women who stand around.

The priest has now prayed for all who have come to hear the Mass. Finally, he prays for those who bring their offerings:

> “Who offer you this sacrifice of praise for themselves and all who belong to them, for the redemption of their souls, and for the hope of their salvation and well-being. To you, the eternal, living, and true God, they render their vows.”

He calls it a sacrifice of praise because they offer it first for the praise of God. Then he adds: “For themselves and all who belong to them, for the redemption of their souls, and for the hope of their salvation and well-being they render their vows to you, the eternal, living, and true God.”

They offer because the faith of all who stand around, and the devotion even of those who do not offer, are known and understood by the living and true God. All render their vows. Vows are promises made willingly, because we ought willingly and gladly to vow to God and fulfill what we have vowed.

> “In communion and venerating the memory, first of all, of the glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and also of your blessed apostles and martyrs.”

He says that he is in communion with them—that is, that he has communion with them—and that he venerates their memory, that is, honors them reverently in memory. He means that the holy virgin Mary became the mother of the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, through the coming of the Holy Spirit. Christ is God and man. Through him we beseech the Father, and, sharing in sound faith, we firmly believe that, when the Holy Spirit came, the Son of God was born from her, yet her virginity was not violated.

“And also of your blessed apostles and martyrs.” *Apostle* is translated in our language as “one sent,” while *martyr* means “witness.” The apostles are so called because they were sent by Christ. Martyrs are so called because they are witnesses that Christ suffered for them and for all who rightly believe in him, and that they themselves suffered for Christ, namely, in confessing his name. [Col. 1184C–D]

> “Therefore, this offering of our service, and also of your whole household, we ask you, Lord, graciously to accept.”

The priest commends his offering and that of all who serve the Lord—that is, who are his servants—in order that they may please the Lord and that he may be favorable toward them.

> “And order our days in his peace, rescue us from eternal condemnation, and command that we be numbered among the flock of your elect, through Christ our Lord.”

Because the priest offers this, the people ought to pray that the priest may be heard, that all our days may be ordered in peace, and that we may thus be rescued from eternal condemnation. Concerning this, our Lord will say to the wicked at the end of the world: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire,” and so forth (Matt. 25:41). May we merit to be numbered by the holy angels among the flock of his elect, to whom he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid., v. 34).

It follows:

> “Which offering, O God, we ask you to deign to make blessed, approved, ratified, reasonable, and acceptable in every respect, so that it may become for us the body and blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ,”

and so forth.

The priest supplicates that the offering he makes for himself and for the people may be accepted by the almighty Father as blessed, and that he may regard it as approved—that is, assigned to himself, so that it may please him.

“Ratified,” that is, judged, so that he may judge it worthy to be offered in his sight. “Reasonable,” that is, full of right reason. He may deign to make it so, because it is acceptable to him when we who rightly believe offer it according to right reason.

It is just to ask that the offering which we reasonably make may be made acceptable to the almighty Father through sanctification:

> “So that it may become for us the body and blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.”

The Son is beloved by the Father, as the Father himself testified from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son,” and so forth. We ought to love him because he first loved us and suffered for us.

> “Who, on the day before he suffered, took bread into his holy and venerable hands, and, with his eyes lifted toward heaven, to you, God his almighty Father, giving you thanks, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and eat from this, all of you, for this is my body.  
> 
> “In like manner, after supper had ended, taking also this glorious chalice into his holy and venerable hands, likewise giving you thanks, he blessed it and gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and drink from this, all of you, for this is the chalice of my blood, of the new and eternal Testament, the mystery of faith, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of all sins. Whenever you do these things, you shall do them in remembrance of me.”

What we omitted—“who, on the day before he suffered”—means “on the day before he himself suffered for us.” He wished to hand over to his disciples the mystery of his body, so that they might hand it over to us.

Who would ever believe that bread could be changed into flesh or wine into blood, unless the Savior himself had said so—the one who created bread and wine and made everything from nothing? It is easier to make something from something than to create everything from nothing.

The Savior himself wished to assume a human body and join humanity to God, so that the man Christ Jesus might become the one mediator between God and human beings. He also wished bread and wine to be offered to him through us and to be consecrated divinely by him, and he wished the faithful people to believe that the mystery he had handed down to his disciples was true, saying: “Take and eat from this, all of you.”

Likewise, concerning the chalice he said: “Take and drink from this, all of you.” When he lifted his eyes toward heaven and gave thanks to the Father, he taught us by this that we must always beseech the Father to deign to accomplish so great a sacrament through our hands.

And when he said, “Whenever you do these things, you shall do them in remembrance of me,” he commanded us to remember continually the passion he endured for us, especially at the time when we celebrate this sacrament, and to commend ourselves to his mercy and goodness. [Col. 1185D–1186A]

> “Therefore, mindful, O Lord, we your servants and also your holy people, of Christ, your Son, our Lord and God,”

the priest professes that he has done what was commanded him by the Lord. The priests themselves must faithfully remember the Son of God, namely Jesus Christ the Lord, because they celebrate the Mass and offer the sacrifice, instructed by Christ’s example. They must know what they celebrate, because it is foolish to ask for what one does not know.

The holy people must likewise remember together because Christ suffered not only for the priests but also for the people. They are called holy because, having received the faith and baptism of Christ, they have been sanctified.

He now indicates what they ought to remember: the blessed passion, the resurrection from the dead, and the glorious ascension into heaven of Christ, the Son of God.

We ought to remember his passion because he deigned to suffer for us; his resurrection from the dead because righteous souls were freed from the underworld through his resurrection; and likewise his glorious ascension, because the human body he had assumed, joined to divinity, he carried into heaven by his own majesty, without the aid of anyone.

We said “without the aid of anyone” so that it might be understood that he did not ascend into heaven by any vehicle of human beings, angels, or any creature, but was lifted up by the majesty of the Father. Concerning this he himself said in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one.”

> “We offer to your glorious majesty, from your gifts and grants, a pure victim, a holy victim, an immaculate victim, the holy bread of eternal life, and the chalice of everlasting salvation.”

“O Lord, remembering all the goodnesses mentioned above, we offer to your majesty a pure victim”—that is, with a pure heart, because your body, which we believe is made from this bread, is pure.

“A holy victim,” because you sanctified your body when you assumed humanity into God; and now sanctify this bread so that it may become your body.

“An immaculate victim,” because you suffered for us without the stain of sin.

“The holy bread of eternal life,” because you are the living bread who came down from heaven. You wished us to receive your body in this bread sanctified by you, and through the chalice of your passion you wished us to receive your blood.

Sanctify this victim so that it may become for us your body and your blood.

> “Upon these offerings deign to look with a favorable and serene countenance.”

We pray for this: that you, holy Father, may deign to look with a gracious, kindly, and radiant countenance upon the gifts offered by us [perhaps “presented”], and “to accept them, just as you deigned to accept the gifts of your righteous servant Abel, the sacrifice of our patriarch Abraham, and what your high priest Melchizedek offered to you, a holy sacrifice and an immaculate victim.”

The Lord accepted Abel’s gifts because he offered to the Lord whatever best thing he found. We too ought to offer just and pure gifts to God with a pure heart.

Abraham did not spare his son but, obedient to the Lord’s command, wished to offer him. Melchizedek was the first priest to offer bread and wine to the Lord. Therefore it is written in the Psalm: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4), because just as Melchizedek offered bread and wine, so Christ in his passion offered his body and blood to God the Father for us.

In bread and wine he wished us to imitate the mystery of his passion, when, giving bread and the chalice to his disciples, he said: “This is my body, and this is the chalice of my blood” (Matt. 26:26). We too ought to pray that just as the gifts of the fathers mentioned above were acceptable to God, so ours may also be acceptable.

> “We humbly ask you, almighty God: command that these offerings be carried by the hands of your holy angel to your sublime altar, in the presence of your divine majesty.”

We therefore ask humbly that the heavenly Father command our gifts, offered upon this altar that can be seen, to be carried by the hand of his holy angel to that lofty altar which is before his divine majesty and which we cannot see with our eyes, because it is not bodily but spiritual.

Just as we cannot investigate the divine majesty of the Father, so we ought not to investigate the things that are in his presence, but rather believe:

> “so that all of us who receive the most holy body and blood of your Son from participation in this altar may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace, through Christ our Lord.”

We ought indeed to pray to the heavenly Father that all of us who receive the body and blood of the aforesaid Son of God from participation in this altar—which we offer to God the Father in remembrance of his Son, our Lord and God Jesus Christ—may merit to receive every heavenly blessing through Christ himself, our Lord.

> “And to us sinners, your servants, who hope in the abundance of your mercies, deign to grant some part and fellowship with your holy apostles and martyrs and with all your saints.”

We also beseech you, most merciful one, not to look upon our sins, but according to the abundance of your goodness to deign to grant us eternal joys and to confer upon us perpetual participation in joy and eternal gladness with all your saints.

> “Admit us into their company, we ask you, not weighing our merits, but as the giver of forgiveness.”

We ask this of the one who said: “On whatever day the sinner turns and does penance, all his sins will be forgotten before me.” May he not weigh the retribution due for sins, but himself be the giver of forgiveness, and send us into the fellowship of the saints.

> “Through Christ our Lord. Through him, Lord, you always create, sanctify, make alive, bless, and grant us all these good things.”

We pray that through this same Christ, your only-begotten Son, through whom all good things were created, sanctified, and made alive, you may bless these sacraments and provide them to us for the reception of eternal healing.

> “Through him, and with him, and in him, to you, God the almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, is all honor and glory, forever and ever. Amen.”

After this—
Therefore, in order to introduce the Lord’s Prayer, the priest urges the people, saying:

“Having been admonished by saving precepts and formed by divine instruction, we dare to say.”

For Christ’s precepts are full of salvation, because he himself is eternal salvation. [Col. 1188B] Formed by his admonition, command, and divine instruction, we have dared to offer prayers to almighty God, following the model by which the Savior himself taught his disciples to have a prayer pleasing to God and to make humble supplication to the almighty Father on our behalf.

“Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come; thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth; give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors; and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.”

In these seven petitions, therefore, we ask God the Father to grant us what is beneficial for our salvation and to drive far from us what is harmful. We have decided [Col. 1188C] briefly to set down here an exposition of this petition according to the understanding of the holy teachers.

“Our Father,” he says, “who art in heaven.” After his resurrection Christ said to his disciples: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father.” He spoke of his Father in one way and of our Father in another: his own Father, because he is truly the Father’s own Son, begotten from the substance of the Father before all ages and co-eternal with the Father. He is also our Father because he created us in time, so that we might be his adopted children and might possess without end the heavenly inheritance of our heavenly Father, first fulfilling through our works what we previously promised that we would do when we received the faith.

“Heaven” (*coelum*) is said to derive from *caelare* (“to conceal”), because it conceals divine secrets. Alternatively, heaven is said to derive from height (*celsitudo*), because it is higher than earthly things. We therefore [Col. 1188D] say, “Our Father who art in heaven,” to show that we believe in the heavenly Father; and just as devoted children desire to fulfill their father’s commands, so we too should desire to fulfill his commandments and always strive toward heaven.

“Hallowed be thy name.” That is, may we be worthy to hold his holy name in our hearts. Just as the holy angels who are in heaven know and understand the holiness of his name, so may we who are on earth, with his help, deserve to recognize the holiness of his name, so that his name may be hallowed in heaven and likewise on earth.

“Thy kingdom come.” That is, may we deserve to recognize his kingdom and his power, and may [Col. 1189A] the devil no longer reign over us because of our sins; rather, may his kingdom come, as it is written in the Gospel: “The kingdom of God is within you.”

“Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth.” That is, just as those who are in heaven do his will, so may we who are on earth do it. “Earth” (*terra*) is said to derive from *terere* (“to wear down”), because it is worn down by feet.

“Give us this day our daily bread.” Among the Greeks, *bread* is interpreted in our language as “all,” and we pray that the almighty Father may graciously bestow on us at all times every kind of spiritual and bodily nourishment.

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” For one who demands repayment of a debt owed to him does nothing unjust. But if almighty God demands all debts from us, no one [Col. 1189B] will be found without a debt. Therefore we ought to forgive the debts of our debtors, so that the almighty God may forgive ours, because he said: “If you do not forgive each one his brother from your hearts, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matthew 18:35). And elsewhere: “All scandals are removed from his kingdom,” he says (Matthew 13:41). And again: a sacrifice is not received if it is offered with a scandal; rather, it is commanded to be left before the altar until one has been reconciled to one’s brother, and then it is to be offered with a clean heart.

“And lead us not into temptation.” That is, may we not enter the temptation in which the devil tempts us, nor consent to him; rather, may the Lord himself defend us, so that we are not led into diabolical temptation. If God abandons us, [Col. 1189C] we are immediately brought into the devil’s snare. Therefore we ask that he himself deliver us from evil—that is, from every assault of the devil.

“Deliver us, we beseech you, Lord, from all evils, past, present, and future.” In this prayer he asks that the one who created us good and pure, in whom there is no evil, may himself deliver us from all evils. Past evils are those which we committed earlier when we sinned, and for which we endure scourges. Present evils are those which we commit daily; future evils are those which may yet come at the devil’s urging. Therefore we pray to be delivered from them all, because before God’s presence there are neither past nor future things, but all things are present.

“Through the intercession of the blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, and of your blessed apostles [Col. 1189D] Peter, Paul, and Andrew.”

We invoke the Mother of God as our helper—she who was a virgin before childbirth, a virgin in childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth—and the blessed apostles, who handed down to us the celebration of these mysteries, so that they may intercede for us. We ourselves are not worthy to obtain pardon for past and present sins, nor protection against future things, unless this is granted to us through their prayer.

We have now prayed to be delivered from evils; we pray next that, through the intervention of the saints mentioned above, he himself may grant peace.

“Graciously grant peace in our days”—you who are powerful enough to deliver us from evil; grant us peace from evil people, so that we may not suffer their scourges.

“So that, aided by the help of your mercy”—that is, aided by God’s help—“we may always be free from sin [Col. 1190A] and secure from every disturbance.” That is, may our sins be forgiven, so that in the present age we may not again be disturbed by sinning, nor in the day of judgment suffer eternal disturbance.

“Through our Lord.”

Through him, therefore, the Son of the almighty God the Father, if we desire to attain eternal life, we must obtain access to the heavenly kingdom. For without him we can in no way prosper here or reign happily in the future life with his holy angels, because he is the beginning and completion of every good, “who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever.”

Then, asking peace for the people, the priest says:

“The peace of the Lord be always with you.”

For Christ is eternal peace. Through his Passion he reconciled us to the Father, [Col. 1190B] so that we would not be held in hell because of the sin of the first man. Here the priest prays that this peace may remain with the people and make them all harmonious, so that we may deserve to reign peacefully with Christ in heaven.

Therefore, at that time let us make peace before receiving the Lord’s body and blood, so that in harmony we may receive the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ into our bodies. For without harmony we are not worthy to receive holy communion; and if we are in discord with our neighbors, our gifts are not accepted by God until we have been reconciled.

Then the clergy pray by singing:

“Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.”

He is called a lamb because of his innocence: he harms neither human beings nor beasts, but after his slaughter he refreshes the one who killed him. [Col. 1190C] So too Christ harmed no one, as the apostle said: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22). But after his Passion he refreshed many of his persecutors, once they had been converted, through the holy communion of his body and blood, and made them believers.

He took away the sins of the world when he gave us the forgiveness of sins, because before his Passion the righteous and sinners descended into hell. In the Old Testament we nowhere read of the forgiveness of sins; but Christ, through repentance, promised us not only pardon for sins but also angelic joy, saying: “There will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:7).

We ask that Christ himself, the Lamb of God [Col. 1190D] innocent and suffering for the salvation of the world, have mercy on us, saying: “Have mercy on us.”

For in the Old Testament a lamb was offered for the sins of the people; in the New Testament Christ offered himself to God the Father, so that through his Passion he might free the human race from sin. Therefore the “Lamb of God” is sung when the Lord’s body and blood are received, so that we may all believe that the body and blood of that Lamb who took away the sins of the world by dying are then received. And by rising again he gave us eternal life.

“Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.”

And after the Mass has ended, the deacon says to the people: [Col. 1191A]

“Go, the dismissal has taken place.”

“Deacon” is said in Greek; in Latin it means “minister.” He announces to the people that the prayers have ended, because no one ought to leave the church before the completed [Col. 1192A] service has been announced by the minister. And let everyone respond:

“Thanks be to God.”

[Note a: The remaining chapters are missing from the manuscript of the Fulda codex, perhaps deliberately omitted because, as the headings indicate, the chapters of Book One, from the fourth through the twenty-third inclusive, of *On the Instruction of the Clergy* would be found in the same wording.]

[Col. 1191A]

**Three Books on Ecclesiastical Discipline by Blessed Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda and Archbishop of Mainz** [Note: [Col. 1191] a In the first two books there are several chapters that correspond with the books *On the Instruction of the Clergy*, as is noted in their proper place.] **to Bishop Reginbald.**

[Col. 1191]

## Preface

[Col. 1191B] One day, while I was sitting quietly in my little cell, free from every worldly concern, and was devoting myself to reading the divine Scriptures, the recollection of your good zeal came to my mind, holy priest of Christ: the zeal that you possess in instructing the flock divinely entrusted to you—how you invite those who are still outside and continuing in pagan error to receive the faith of Christ; how you strengthen by Catholic teaching and exhortation those who have already been brought into the Church through baptism and confession of the true faith, so that they may put into good practice what they have professed with their mouths; and how, when they go astray through various transgressions, you strive to restrain them by evangelical discipline and restore them to their former state through repentance.

Reflecting carefully on all this in my mind, I decided to compose a little work [Col. 1191C] and dedicate it to your name. In it, in accordance with the authority of the holy Scriptures and the teaching of the Catholic Fathers, you would be able to find what the calling of those who are still outside should be like, so that they may receive the faith of Christ; what sort of approach should follow once they have received the faith, so that they may receive the regeneration of sacred baptism and the sanctification of the divine sacraments; and how they may understand the order of sacred teaching and preserve the Christian religion faithfully.

Therefore, we have decided first to instruct the teacher himself concerning his office and training, and then to speak about instructing the uneducated in the faith of Christ. Next, we shall explain how those who have already been summoned ought, through the office of preaching, to be made catechumens, washed in the baptism of Christ, [Col. 1191D] confirmed by the divine sacraments, and strengthened in the truth of the faith. After this, we shall explain how those who are already Christians should be instructed in Catholic doctrine and corrected by ecclesiastical discipline, and how, once enrolled in the army of Christ, they ought to fight against vices with the virtues and persevere in the practice of a good way of life to [Col. 1192B] the end of their lives, insofar as the Lord grants us the ability to set this forth.

For you know very well how the Apostle Paul, when writing to Timothy, admonished and instructed him concerning how he ought to conduct himself in the Church of God. Among other things, he says (1 Tim. 4:12):

> “Command and teach these things. Let no one despise your youth, but be an example to the faithful in word, in conduct, in charity, in faith, in chastity. Until I come, attend to reading, exhortation, and teaching. Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbyterate. Meditate on these things; devote yourself to them, so that your progress may be manifest to all. Pay attention to yourself and to your teaching; persist in them. For by doing this you will save both yourself [Col. 1192C] and those who hear you.”

And elsewhere he says (2 Tim. 2:1):

> “You therefore, my son, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus; and what you have heard from me through many witnesses, entrust to faithful men who are capable of teaching others also. Work as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.”

And again he says (1 Tim. 5:22):

> “Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure.”

Thus, as he was going to instruct him concerning each of the orders—how he ought to ordain presbyters, deacons, and the other ranks—and to teach and fully train persons of every kind, age, and sex, he instructed him completely. Therefore, it is necessary that you diligently teach and discipline those whom you desire to promote to the divine ministry, so that they may know how [Col. 1192D] ministers of the divine word ought to be and what it is fitting for them to know and possess, so that, once they have been ordained and raised to the sacred orders, they may benefit the people of God more than they harm them.

## Book One: On the Sacred Orders

[Col. 1193]

### On Receiving the Sacred Orders

But since those who occupy a certain position of eminence and hold the helm of governance in the Church ought above all to possess fullness of knowledge, uprightness of life, and perfection of learning, and so forth, as in the book *On the Instruction of the Clergy*, book 3, chapter 1, through the end of that chapter.

### On Reading the Divine Scriptures

(*On the Instruction of the Clergy*, book 3, chapter 2.) The foundation, stability, and perfection of prudence is knowledge of the holy Scriptures, and so forth, through the end of the chapter.

### That Reaching the Summit of Wisdom Is the Same as Reaching the Summit of Charity

[Col. 1193B] (*Ibid.*, chapter 5.) Whoever, therefore, reaches the summit of wisdom reaches the height of charity, and so forth, through the end of the chapter.

### On Acquiring the Virtues

(*Ibid.*, chapter 27.) Meanwhile, while he desires to attain spiritual knowledge through attentive meditation, it is necessary, and so forth, almost to the end of the chapter, up to the words: “But since concerning the manner…”

### What a Teacher Ought to Do in Teaching

(*Ibid.*, chapter 28.) The interpreter and teacher of the divine Scriptures, the defender of the true faith, ought, and so forth, through the end of the chapter.

(*Ibid.*, chapter 30.) But although there is, or ought to be, such great care for teaching in good teachers [Col. 1193C] that, and so forth, through the end of the chapter.

(*Ibid.*, chapter 31.) The best manner of speaking is that by which the hearer comes to know the truth, and so forth, through the end of the chapter.

And indeed, he must move [the hearer] in order to prevail. Thus, observing these principles in the delivery of his discourse, the evangelical preacher, with the help of divine grace, will be able to find the fruit of his labor and praise.

### How the Uneducated Should Be Catechized

Since, in accordance with the tradition of our predecessors, we have thus far given some instruction concerning the teaching of doctrine and the formation of morals for preachers of the word of God, let us now proceed to explain how the uneducated should be catechized. This office, therefore, should be carried out through narration, [Col. 1193D] exhortation, and cheerfulness.

Narration is complete when someone is first catechized from what is written—“In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1)—down to the present time of the Church. Yet for that reason we should not recite from memory the whole Pentateuch, all the books of Judges and Kings and Ezra, the entire Gospel, and the Acts of the Apostles, even if we have learned them word for word; [Col. 1194A] nor should we unfold and explain in our own words everything contained in these volumes by narrating it. Neither time permits this nor does any necessity require it.

Rather, we should embrace everything in summary and in general terms, choosing certain especially marvelous events that are heard with greater pleasure and that stand as principal points within the narrative, and display them as though through a covering. We should not immediately snatch them away from sight, but linger over them for a while, as though untying and unfolding them, and offer them to the minds of the hearers for examination and wonder; the remaining material, however, should be woven in by touching upon it briefly. In this way, the matters we especially wish to commend stand out more prominently through the subordination of the others. Nor does the person whom we wish to stir by our narration arrive at them exhausted, nor is the memory of the one whom we must instruct confused as we teach.

[Col. 1194B] In everything, certainly, we must not merely keep in view the goal of the commandment—which is “charity from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith”—to which we should refer everything we say; we must also direct and turn toward that goal the attention of the person whom we instruct by speaking. For everything that we read in the holy Scriptures was written before the Lord’s coming for no other reason than to commend that coming and foreshadow the future Church—that is, the people of God among all the nations, which is his body, with all the saints joined and numbered among it. Those who lived in this world before his coming believed that he would come, just as we believe that he has come.

What greater reason is there for the Lord’s coming than that God might demonstrate his love by commending it to us with overwhelming force? For while we were still enemies, Christ died for us. This happened because the end of the commandment and the fullness of the law is charity: so that we may love one another, and just as he laid down his life for us, so we too may lay down our lives for our brothers; and so that we may love God, because he first loved us and did not spare his only Son, but handed him over for us all.

If one is reluctant to love, let him at least not be reluctant to return love. For there is no greater invitation to love than to anticipate another by loving, and a spirit is exceedingly hard that, if it was unwilling to bestow love, is unwilling also to return it. Thus Christ came above all for this purpose: that the human being might know how greatly God loves him, and might know it in order to burn with love for the one by whom he was first loved; and that, [Col. 1194D] at his command and following his example, he might love his neighbor—he who, by loving not a neighbor but one who was traveling far away, made himself a neighbor.

Every divine Scripture written beforehand to announce the Lord’s coming, and everything subsequently committed to writing and established by divine authority, proclaims Christ and stirs up love. It is clear that not only do the whole Law and the Prophets hang upon [Col. 1195A] those two commandments of love of God and neighbor—the only sacred Scripture then existing when the Lord said this—but also all the volumes of divine writings that were later beneficially consecrated and committed to memory.

Since nothing is opposed to charity more than envy, and pride is the mother of envy, the same Lord Jesus Christ, God and man, became both the proof to us of divine love and the example among us of human humility, so that our great swelling might be healed by a greater medicine opposed to it. Great is the misery of a proud human being, but greater is the mercy of humble God.

With this love, therefore, set before you, reader, as a sign to which you should refer everything you say, narrate whatever you narrate in such a way that the person to whom you speak may, by hearing, believe; by believing, hope; and by hoping, love.

[Col. 1195B] Once the narration has ended, the hope of the resurrection should be declared. In proportion to the capacity and strength of the hearer, and to the amount of time available, one should address the resurrection of the body against the empty mockery of unbelievers, and the goodness of the future final judgment toward the good, its severity toward the wicked, and its truth toward all.

After recalling the punishments of the ungodly with abhorrence and horror, the kingdom of the just and faithful, that heavenly city of his, and its joy should be proclaimed with longing. Then human weakness should be instructed and encouraged against temptations and scandals, whether outside or within the Church itself: outside, against pagans, Jews, or heretics; within, against the chaff of the Lord’s threshing floor.

This should not be done by arguing against each individual kind of perverse person or refuting all their evil opinions through proposed [Col. 1195C] questions. Rather, in a short time it should be demonstrated that these things were foretold, what benefit temptations have for the instruction of the faithful, and what medicine is found in the example of God’s patience, since he has determined to permit these things to continue until the end.

When instruction is given against those whose perverse crowds fill the churches bodily, the commands of Christian and honorable conduct should also be recalled briefly and appropriately, lest the person being instructed be so easily led astray by drunkards, the greedy, swindlers, gamblers, adulterers, fornicators, lovers of spectacles, those who invoke sacrilegious remedies, enchanters, astrologers, diviners of every kind of vain and evil art, and others of the same sort, and think that such conduct will go unpunished because he sees many who are called Christians loving, practicing, defending, and recommending these things.

What end has been appointed for those who persevere in such a life, and how such people are to be tolerated within the Church, from which they are to be hoped for [Col. 1195D] at the end, should be taught from the testimonies of the divine books. It should also be foretold that he will find in the Church many good Christians, most genuine citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem.

If he himself begins to be such a person, he must finally be earnestly warned not to place his hope in a human being. For it is not easy for one human being to judge who is righteous; and even if it were easy, the examples of the righteous are not set before us so that we may be justified by them, but so that, by imitating them, we may know that we too are justified by the one who justified them.

From this will follow what must be especially commended: when the one who hears us—or rather, through us hears God—begins to make progress in conduct and knowledge and to enter the way of Christ eagerly, he should attribute this neither to us nor to himself. Instead, he should understand that he himself, we ourselves, and all other friends whom he loves are loved in him and on his account who loved him as an enemy in order to make him a friend by justifying him.

[Col. 1196A] This point must certainly not be passed over: if someone comes to you to be catechized who has been educated in the liberal disciplines, has already decided to become a Christian, and has therefore come in order to become one, it is altogether difficult for him not to know much of our Scriptures and writings, since he has already been instructed and has come only to participate in the sacraments.

Such people usually investigate everything carefully before the hour when they become Christians, and share and discuss the movements of their minds with those whom they can. [Col. 1196B] With such people, therefore, one must proceed briefly, not tediously impressing upon them what they already know, but touching upon it modestly. We should say that we believe they already know this or that, and in this way run rapidly through everything that must be impressed upon the uneducated and ignorant. Thus, if the educated person knows something, he will not hear it as though from a teacher; and if he perhaps still does not know something, he will learn it while we recall what we believe he already knows.

There are also some who come from the commonly frequented schools of grammarians and orators. You would not dare to number them among the ignorant, but neither among those most learned whose minds have been exercised by investigations into great matters. To these, then, who seem to excel other people in the art of speaking [Col. 1196C] when they come in order to become Christians, we ought to impart something more than to the unlettered: they should be earnestly warned that, clothed in Christian humility, they must learn not to despise those whom they know; to avoid faults of character more than faults of speech; and not to dare even to compare a practiced tongue with a chaste heart, though they have been accustomed to prefer it.

Above all, such people must be taught to listen to the divine Scriptures, lest solid eloquence offend them because it is not inflated. They should not suppose that the words or deeds of human beings read in those books, wrapped and concealed in bodily coverings, should not be unfolded and opened in order to be understood, but should instead be received merely as the letters sound.

Rather, the benefit of the hidden meaning—from which these things are also called “mysteries”—and the power of the concealment of riddles to sharpen [Col. 1196D] the love of truth and shake off the torpor of weariness should be demonstrated through actual experience, when something that is set out plainly and does not move them greatly is brought forth by means of an allegorical explanation.

For it is especially useful for such people to know that meanings should be preferred to words just as the soul is preferred to the body. Hence they should prefer to hear more truthful rather than more eloquent speeches, just as they should prefer to have wiser rather than more handsome friends.

They should also know that there is no voice for God’s ears except the disposition of the soul. Thus they will not mock if they happen to notice certain bishops and ministers of the Church invoking the Lord with barbarisms and solecisms, or failing to understand the very words they pronounce and distinguishing them confusedly—not that these faults should not be corrected, so that the people may say “Amen” to what they understand clearly, but that such faults should nevertheless be borne with piety [Col. 1197A] by those who have learned that just as one is blessed by sound in the marketplace, so one is blessed by intention in the church.

Cheerfulness is also of the greatest value in the office of catechizing, because it makes the hearer devoted, well-disposed, and attentive. The preacher’s speech accomplishes little if the hearer’s attention is not present and delighted. An unmoving hearer also makes speaking wearisome—not because it is fitting for us to be desirous of human praise, but because what we administer belongs to God; and the more we love those to whom we speak, the more we desire that what is offered for their salvation may please them. If this does not happen, we become sorrowful and are weakened and broken in the very course of our work, as though we were exhausting our effort in vain.

[Col. 1197B] Sometimes, too, we are called away from something we desire to do, whose performance either delighted us or seemed more necessary to us, and are compelled—either by the command of someone whom we do not wish to offend or by the unavoidable insistence of others—to catechize someone. We approach a task that requires great tranquility already disturbed, grieving that we are neither permitted to maintain the order of activities we desire nor able to suffice for everything. Thus, as the speech proceeds from sadness itself, it is less welcome because it flows less abundantly from the dryness of sorrow.

At times, too, grief occupies the heart because of some scandal, and then we are told: “Come, speak to this person; he wants to become a Christian.” Those who do not understand say this, to whom we ought not to disclose our feelings. We undertake unwillingly what they desire, and that speech will certainly be weak and unpleasant, having passed through a feverish and smoking vein of the heart.

When any of these many causes obscures the serenity of our mind, we must seek, in accordance with the Lord, remedies by which that constriction may be relaxed; and in the fervor of the spirit we should rejoice and be glad in the tranquility of good work. “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7).

And since it makes a great difference whether one is weary of speaking and desires silence, let us consider what has been entrusted to us by the one who showed us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps. However much our articulated voice differs from the liveliness of our understanding, the mortality of the flesh differs still more greatly from the equality of God. Yet, although he existed in the same form, “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” and so forth, even to the death of the cross (Phil. 2:7). Why did he do this, except because “he became weak to the weak, in order to win the weak” (1 Cor. 9:20)?

Hear his imitator also saying elsewhere: “For whether we were beside ourselves, it was for God; or whether we are self-controlled, it is for you; for the love of Christ constrains us, judging this: that one died for all” (2 Cor. 5:13). For how would he have been ready to expend himself for their souls if he had been reluctant to bend down to their ears?

Therefore he became a little one in our midst, like a nurse tenderly caring for her children. If the person proves receptive and offers himself to be healed, he should be healed without delay by an abundance of authorities and arguments. But if the offense is silent and hidden, God’s medicine can help. If he recoils and refuses to be healed, let us be consoled by that example of the Lord who, when people were offended by his word and withdrew from it as though it were harsh, said even to those who remained: “Do you also wish to go away?” (John 6:68).

We must hold firmly and immovably in our hearts that, when the appointed times have passed, captive Jerusalem will be liberated from the Babylon of this world; and that none of it will perish, because whoever perishes did not belong to it. For the firm foundation of God stands, bearing this seal: “The Lord knows those who are his,” and “Everyone who names the name of the Lord must depart from iniquity.”

As we reflect on these things and invoke the Lord in our hearts, we shall fear less the uncertain outcome of our speech because of the uncertain reactions of our hearers. Even the endurance of difficulties for a merciful work will delight us, provided that we do not seek our glory in it.

For a work is truly good when the intention of the one doing it is launched forth by charity and, as though returning to its proper place, comes to rest again in charity. If, however, the person is exceedingly slow and wholly unreceptive and alienated from every such pleasure, he must be borne with compassion. The other matters should be passed over briefly, while those most necessary—concerning the unity of the Catholic Church, temptations, and Christian conduct in view of the future judgment—must be impressed upon him with solemn force. More should be said to God on his behalf than many things about God.

If, however, a mind disturbed by some scandal cannot produce a serene and joyful speech, there must be such great charity toward those for whom Christ died, desiring to redeem them by the price of his blood from the death of worldly errors, that the very news brought to us in our sadness—that someone wishes to become a Christian—should be able to serve for our consolation and to dispel our grief, just as the joy of profit usually eases the pain of losses.

For we are saddened by someone’s scandal only when we believe or see that someone is perishing, or that a weak person is perishing through that individual. When the darkness of weariness has been driven away by thoughts and considerations such as these, the mind is made ready for catechizing, so that what bursts forth energetically and cheerfully from the abundance of charity may be absorbed with pleasure.

For it is not so much I who say these things to you as the love itself, which says them to all of us and has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

If anyone wishes to know the complete practice of catechizing, he can learn it from the words of blessed Augustine, who, among other things, wrote to a friend concerning the catechizing of the uneducated and said:

> You perhaps already demand from me as something owed what I ought not to have promised beforehand: that I should not shrink from setting forth and proposing for your consideration some example of a speech, as though I myself were catechizing someone. Before I do this, I want you also to consider that the intention of a person writing is one thing when a future reader is being imagined, and the intention of a speaker is another when a present hearer is attentive. It is one thing when someone privately gives an admonition while no one else is present to judge us; another when he openly teaches something while the hearing of people who think differently [Col. 1199A] surrounds him; and in this category it is one thing when one person is being taught while the others listen as though judging or bearing witness to what they know; another when everyone together waits for what we are going to say to them.

> Again, within that same situation, it is one thing when it is considered almost privately that a conversation is being carried on; another when a silent crowd gazes attentively at someone about to speak from a higher place. It makes a great difference whether only a few are present or many; whether they are educated or uneducated; whether they are mixed from both groups; whether they are townspeople or country people; whether these and those are present together; or whether the people are composed of every kind of human being. For it is impossible that these circumstances should not affect the person who is about to speak in different ways.

> Thus the speech that is delivered bears something like the face of the speaker’s state of mind and affects the hearers differently in accordance with that diversity, while the hearers themselves also affect one another differently by their presence.

> [Col. 1199B] But since we are now dealing with the instruction of the uneducated, I have testified to you from my own experience that I am moved in different ways when I see before me someone to be catechized who is educated, dull, a citizen, a foreigner, rich, poor, of private status, honored, placed in some position of authority; a person of this or that social class, of this or that age or sex; someone coming from this or that sect, or from this or that popular error. In accordance with the diversity of my own reaction, the speech itself proceeds, advances, and comes to an end.

> Although the same charity is owed to everyone, the same medicine is not to be applied to everyone. That same charity gives birth to some, grows weak with others, cures some in order to build them up, trembles [Col. 1199C] lest it offend others, bends down to some, rises up toward others; it is gentle toward some, severe toward others, the enemy of no one, and the mother of all.

> A person who has not experienced what I am saying through that same charity may see that we take pleasure in becoming commendably known in the mouths of the crowd because some ability has been granted to us, and may therefore think us blessed. But may God, before whose sight the groaning of those in chains enters, see our humility and our labor, and forgive all our sins.

> Therefore, if anything in us pleased you so that you wished to hear from us some account of how we conduct our speeches, you would learn better by seeing and hearing us while we are doing these things than by reading us while we dictate them.

> Nevertheless, let us suppose that someone has come to us who wishes to become a Christian. He belongs to the class of the uneducated, though not to country people but to townspeople, such as you must often encounter at Carthage. When asked whether he wishes to become a Christian for some advantage in the present life or for the rest that is hoped for after this life, he has replied that it is for the future rest. Perhaps he would be instructed by us with an address such as this:

[Col. 1199D] “Thanks be to God, brother. I rejoice greatly and am glad for you, because amid the many and perilous storms of this world you have thought about some true and certain security. In this life also, people seek rest and security through great labors, but they do not find them because of their perverse desires.

[Col. 1200A] “They wish to rest in things that are troubled and do not endure; and because those things are taken away and pass with time, fears and pains agitate them and do not allow them to be at rest.

> “If a person wishes to rest in riches, he becomes more proud rather than more secure. Do we not see how many have suddenly lost them, and how many have perished because of them—either while they desire to possess them, or when, weighed down by them, they are taken away by people still more greedy? Even if riches remained with a person throughout his whole life and did not abandon their lover, that person’s own death would abandon them.

> “For how long is a human life, even if it reaches old age? Or when people wish for old age for themselves, what else are they wishing for except a prolonged infirmity?

> “So too, what are the honors of this world except a shadow, emptiness, and the danger of ruin? For the holy Scripture says: ‘All flesh is grass, and the glory of man is like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and the flower falls; but the word of the Lord [Col. 1200B] remains forever’ (Isa. 40:6).

> “Therefore, whoever desires true rest and true happiness must remove his hope from mortal and passing things and place it in the word of the Lord, so that, clinging to what remains forever, he too may remain forever with it.”

There are also people who can neither be rich nor attain the vain pomp of honors, but wish to rejoice and rest in taverns, fornications, theaters, and spectacles of frivolity, which they have freely available in the great cities. Yet even these, as they consume their means through indulgence, later advance from destitution to theft, housebreaking, and sometimes even robbery, and suddenly become filled with many great fears; [Col. 1200C] those who shortly before were singing in the tavern now dream of the laments of prison.

Through devotion to spectacles they become like demons, inciting people by their shouts to slaughter one another and arranging contentious combats among those who have not injured each other, while they desire to please the insane crowd. But if they notice that the contestants are in agreement, then they hate and persecute them, and cry out that they are accomplices, so that they may be beaten with clubs; and they compel the judge, who is also the avenger of wrongdoing, to commit this injustice. If, however, they discover that the contestants are exercising dreadful hostility toward one another—whether they are those called *sintae* [uncertain reading], or stage performers and orchestra performers, or charioteers, or hunters, whom wretched men make fight and contend not only human beings against human beings but also human beings against beasts—the greater the discord with which they perceive them raging against one another, the more they love and enjoy it. They cheer them on, and by cheering incite them to rage more fiercely against one another; the spectators themselves, each on behalf of one contestant, are more frenzied than those whose madness they provoke, and in their own madness desire to watch it.

How, then, can a mind retain the health of peace when it feeds upon discord and contests? For whatever kind of food is taken, such is the health that follows. Finally, although insane pleasures are not pleasures, nevertheless—whatever they may be, and however much one may be delighted by the ostentation of riches, the swelling of honors, the abyss of taverns, the wars of theaters, the filth of fornications, and the itch of bathhouses—one little fever takes all these things away and, while people are still alive, deprives them of their entire [Col. 1201A] false happiness. What remains is an empty and wounded conscience, about to experience as judge the Lord whom it refused to have as guardian, and about to find a harsh Lord whom it scorned to seek and love as a gentle Father.

But you who seek the true rest promised to Christians after this life will taste it even here, sweet and pleasant amid the bitterest troubles of this life, if you love the commandments of the one who promised it. You will quickly perceive that the fruits of righteousness are sweeter than those of wickedness, and that a person rejoices more truly and pleasantly in a good conscience amid troubles than in a bad conscience amid delights, because you did not come to be joined to the Church of God in order to seek from it some temporal advantage.

For there are some who wish to be Christians for this reason: either to win the favor of people from whom [Col. 1201B] they expect temporal benefits, or because they do not wish to offend those whom they fear. But these are reprobate. Even if the Church bears with them for a time, just as the threshing floor bears the chaff until the time of winnowing, if they do not correct themselves and begin to be Christians for the sake of the future eternal rest, they will at the end be separated. Let them not flatter themselves that they can be on the threshing floor with God’s grain, for they will not be with it in the granary; rather, they are destined for the fire they deserve.

There are also others with better hope, but nevertheless in no less danger. They already fear the Lord and do not mock the new Christian, nor do they enter the Church of God with a pretended heart; but in this life they await happiness, so that they may be more prosperous in earthly matters than those who do not worship the Lord. Therefore, when they see certain criminals [Col. 1201C] and ungodly people enjoying and excelling in this worldly prosperity, while they themselves either possess less of it or lose it, they are troubled, as though they worshiped the Lord without cause, and easily fall away from the faith.

But the person who wishes to become a Christian for the sake of the eternal blessedness and everlasting rest promised to the saints after this life—so that he may not go into eternal fire with the devil but enter the eternal kingdom with Christ—is truly a Christian. He is watchful in every temptation, lest he be corrupted by prosperity or broken by adversity; in the abundance of earthly goods he is moderate and self-controlled, and in tribulations strong and patient. By making progress, he reaches such a disposition that he loves the Lord more than he fears Gehenna. Even if God were to say to him, “Enjoy [Col. 1201D] everlasting carnal delights, and sin as much as you can; you will neither die nor be sent into Gehenna, but only you will not be with me,” he would recoil in horror and would not sin at all—not now so that he might avoid falling into what he feared, but so that he might not offend the one whom he loves in this way, in whom alone there is the rest “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II, 9).

Concerning this matter Scripture indicates, and does not keep silent, that from the beginning of the world, when God made heaven and earth and everything in them, he worked for six days and rested on the seventh day (Gen. II, 1). For the Almighty could have made everything in a single moment of time. He had not labored in order to rest, when “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created,” [Col. 1202A] but did this to signify that after the six ages of this world, in the seventh age, as on the seventh day, he would rest in his saints. They will rest in him after all the good works by which they served him—works that he himself performs in them, he who calls, commands, forgives past sins, and justifies the one who was previously ungodly. Just as, when they perform good works by his gift, he is rightly said to work, so, when they rest with him, he is rightly said to rest. For insofar as he himself is concerned, he does not seek cessation, since he experiences no labor.

He made all things through his Word, and his Word is Christ himself, in whom the angels and all the purest heavenly spirits rest in holy silence. But human beings, having fallen through sin, lost the rest they had in his divinity and received it [Col. 1202B] in his humanity. Therefore, at the fitting time when he himself knew it ought to happen, he became human and was born of a woman. He could not be defiled by flesh; rather, he was going to cleanse flesh. The ancients recognized through the revelation of the Spirit that he would come, and they prophesied it; thus they were saved by believing that he would come, just as we are saved by believing that he has come. This was so that we might love the Lord, who loved us in such a way that he sent his only Son, clothed in the humanity of our mortality, to die both from sinners and for sinners.

From the beginning of the ages the depth of this mystery has never ceased to be prefigured and foretold. For almighty God—good, just, and merciful—who made all good things, whether great or small, whether highest or lowest, made the things that are seen, such as heaven, earth, and the sea, and in heaven the sun, moon, and the other stars, and on earth and in the sea trees, shrubs, and animals, each according to its own nature, and all bodies, whether heavenly or earthly; [Col. 1202C] and he made the things that are not seen, such as the spirits by which bodies are endowed with strength and made alive.

He also made human beings in his own image, so that, just as he rules over all creation through his omnipotence, so human beings, through the understanding by which they also know and worship their Creator, might rule over all earthly animals. He also made a woman as a helper for the man, not for carnal desire—since at that time they did not yet have corruptible bodies, before mortality invaded them as the punishment for sin—but so that the man might have glory through the woman when he led her to the Lord, and might [Col. 1202D] offer himself to her as an example in holiness and devotion, just as he himself would be the glory of God when he followed God’s wisdom.

Thus he established them in a certain place of perpetual blessedness, which Scripture calls paradise, and he gave them a commandment: if they did not transgress it, they would remain forever in that blessed immortality; if they transgressed it, they would undergo the punishments of mortality. God knew beforehand that they would transgress, but nevertheless, because he is the creator and maker of every good thing, he made them all the more readily, just as he made the beasts, so that he might fill the earth with earthly goods. In any event, even a sinful human being is better than a beast. He gave the commandment that they would not keep precisely so that they might be without excuse when he began to punish them.

[Col. 1203A] Whatever a human being does, he finds God praiseworthy in his deeds. If he acts rightly, he finds God praiseworthy through the justice of rewards; if he sins, he finds God praiseworthy through the justice of punishments; if, having confessed his sins, he returns to living rightly, he finds God praiseworthy through the mercy of forgiveness.

Why, then, would God not make the human being, even though he knew beforehand that he would sin, since he would crown him if he stood, order his condition when he fell, and help him when he rose again—being everywhere glorious in goodness, justice, and clemency? This is especially so because he also knew beforehand that from the stock of his mortality there would arise saints who would not seek glory for themselves but would give it to their Creator, and who, by worshiping him, would be freed from all corruption and would deserve to live forever and happily with the holy angels.

For the one who gave human beings free [Col. 1203B] choice, so that they might worship the Lord not through servile necessity but by a freeborn will, gave it also to the angels. Therefore the angel who, in his pride, deserted the obedience of God together with the other spirits who served as his attendants and became the devil did no harm to God, but to himself. For God knows how to order souls that desert him and, from their just misery, to adorn the lower parts of his creation with laws most fitting and harmonious, in an arrangement worthy of wonder.

Thus neither did the devil do any harm to God, whether he himself fell or seduced the human being into death; nor did the human being in any way diminish the truth, power, or blessedness of his Creator, because he consented by his own will with his wife, who had been seduced by the devil, to what God had forbidden.

By the most just laws of God all were condemned: [Col. 1203C] God was glorified through the equity of his vengeance, while they themselves were made shameful through the degradation of punishment. Thus the human being, turned away from his Creator and defeated by the devil, was subjected to him, while the devil was set before the human being as one to be defeated when the human being turned back to his Creator. Accordingly, all who consent to the devil to the end will go with him into eternal punishments, while all who humble themselves before God and through his grace conquer the devil will deserve eternal rewards.

Nor should this disturb us: that many consent to the devil while few follow the Lord. For grain is also very few in number in comparison with chaff. But just as the farmer knows what to do with a huge heap of chaff, so the multitude of sinners is nothing to God, who knows what to do with them, so that the administration of his kingdom may be neither disgraced nor disturbed in any respect. [Col. 1203D] Nor should the devil be thought to have conquered because he drew many with him, by whom he would be defeated by the few.

## On the Two Cities

(Augustine.) Thus two cities—one of the wicked and the other of the saints—are carried forward from the beginning of the human race to the end of the age: now mingled in bodily existence but separated in their wills, while on the day of judgment they will also be separated bodily.

All human beings who love pride and temporal domination, together with the vain appearance and pomp of arrogance, and all spirits who love such things and seek their own glory through the subjection of human beings, are bound together in one society. [Col. 1204A] But although they often fight among themselves for these things, they are nevertheless hurled by an equal weight of desire into the same depth and joined together by the similarity of their character and merits.

Conversely, all human beings and all spirits who humbly seek God’s glory rather than their own, and pursue it with devotion, belong to one society. Yet the most merciful God is patient even with ungodly human beings, and grants them an opportunity for repentance and correction.

For although he destroyed everyone in the Flood except one righteous man together with those whom he wished to preserve in the ark, he knew that they would not reform. Nevertheless, while the ark was being built over a hundred years, the coming wrath of God was certainly being proclaimed to them; and if they had turned to the Lord, he would have spared them, just as he later spared the city of Nineveh [Col. 1204B] when it repented, after he had announced through the prophet its coming destruction.

God does this even for those whom he knows will persist in wickedness, granting time for repentance so that he may exercise and instruct our patience by his example. Through it we learn how patiently we ought to endure the wicked, since we do not know what they may later become, whereas he spares them and allows them to live, although nothing concerning the future is hidden from him.

The sacrament of the Flood, however, also foretold that the righteous were saved through the wood, prefiguring the future Church. Its king and God, Christ, suspends it from the submersion of this world through the mystery of his cross. God was not ignorant that even among those who had been preserved in the ark there would be born wicked people who would fill the face of the earth with iniquity. Nevertheless, he both gave an example of the future judgment [Col. 1204C] and foretold the deliverance of the saints through the mystery of the wood.

After this, wickedness did not cease to sprout again through pride, lusts, and unlawful acts of ungodliness. Having abandoned their Creator, human beings fell not only toward the creature that God had made, so that they worshiped in place of God what God had made, but also bent their souls toward the works of human hands and the crafts of artisans. There the devil and demons triumphed over them more shamefully, rejoicing to be adored and venerated in such images while feeding their errors on human errors.

Even then there were righteous people who devoutly sought the Lord and conquered the pride of the devil—citizens of that holy city whom the future humility of their king Christ, revealed through the Spirit, healed. From among them Abraham, [Col. 1204D] a devout and faithful servant of God, was chosen. To him the mystery of the Son of God was revealed, so that, because of the imitation of his faith, all the faithful of every nation might be called his children.

From him was born the people among whom the one true God, who made heaven and earth, was worshiped, while the other nations served images and demons. In that people the future Church was represented much more clearly. For there was a multitude concerned with the flesh, which worshiped the Lord because of visible benefits. Yet there were also a few who considered the future rest and sought the heavenly homeland. Through prophecy the future humility of God, their king and our Lord Jesus Christ, was revealed to them, so that through that faith they might be healed from all pride and arrogance.

The speech, life, marriages, children, and deeds of these saints [Col. 1205A] who preceded the Lord’s birth in time were all prophecy of the present age. In this age, through faith in Christ’s passion, the Church is gathered from the nations. Through those holy patriarchs and prophets, the carnal people of Israel—later called the Jews—were provided with visible benefits, which they desired carnally from the Lord, and with restraints of bodily punishments by which they were terrified for a time, as suited their hardness.

Yet in all these things spiritual mysteries were signified, pertaining to Christ and the Church. The members of this Church included those saints as well, although they lived in this life before Christ the Lord was born according to the flesh.

For he himself, the only-begotten Son of God, the Word of God the Father, equal and coeternal with the Father, [Col. 1205B] through whom all things were made, became human for our sake, so that he might be the head of the entire Church as of an entire body. But just as a whole human being, when born, remains joined and compacted under the head with the entire body, even if he brings forth a hand first in birth—just as some, in the patriarchs themselves, were born with a hand emerging first as a sign of this very thing—so all the saints who lived on earth before the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ, although they were born earlier, remained joined under the head to the entire body of which he is the head.

That people, therefore, was brought into Egypt and served a very harsh king. Trained through the most grievous labors, it sought the Lord as liberator. A holy servant of God, Moses, was sent to them from that same people. Through God’s power, [Col. 1205C] terrifying the impious nation of the Egyptians by great miracles, he led God’s people out from there through the Red Sea. There the descending water provided a path for those crossing; but when the Egyptians pursued them, the waves returning upon themselves submerged and destroyed them.

Thus, just as through the Flood the earth was cleansed by water from the wickedness of sinners, who were then destroyed in that inundation, while the righteous escaped through the wood, so the people of God, departing from Egypt, found a path through the waters, by which their enemies were consumed. Nor was the mystery of the wood absent there, for Moses struck with his staff so that the miracle might occur.

Both signs refer to holy baptism, through which the faithful pass into new life, while their sins, like enemies, are destroyed and perish.

More clearly, Christ’s passion was prefigured in that people when they were commanded to kill a sheep, eat it, mark their doorposts with its blood, celebrate this every year, and call it the Lord’s Passover. For the Prophet most plainly says of the Lord Jesus Christ: [Col. 1205D] “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter” (Isa. LIII, 7). By the sign of this passion and cross the Christian is today to be marked on the forehead, as on a doorpost; indeed, all Christians are marked with it.

From there that people was led through the desert for forty years. It also received the law written by the finger of God. By this name the Holy Spirit is signified, as the Gospel makes abundantly clear. God is not defined by bodily form, nor are members and fingers to be imagined in him [Col. 1206A] as we see them in ourselves. But because the gifts of God are distributed to the saints through the Holy Spirit, so that although they possess different abilities they do not depart from the love of charity—for a certain division is especially apparent in the fingers, though not a severance from unity—the Holy Spirit was called the finger of God, whether for this reason or for some other. Nevertheless, when we hear this, we must not imagine the form of a human body.

That people therefore received the law written by the finger of God on stone tablets, signifying the hardness of their hearts, since they would not fulfill the law. Desiring bodily gifts from the Lord, they were held more by carnal fear than by spiritual love; but it is love that fulfills the law. Therefore they were burdened with many visible sacraments, so that they might be pressed under a servile [Col. 1206B] yoke in observances of food, sacrifices of animals, and innumerable other practices. Yet these were signs of spiritual realities pertaining to the Lord Jesus Christ and to the Church. At that time they were understood by a few saints for the fruit of salvation and observed in keeping with the age. By the carnal multitude they were merely observed, not understood.

Through many and various signs of future realities—which it would take too long to enumerate in full, and which we now see being fulfilled in the Church—that people was led to the promised land, where it would reign temporarily and carnally, according to the measure of its desire. Yet that earthly kingdom bore the image of the spiritual kingdom.

There Jerusalem was established, the most famous city of God, serving symbolically [Col. 1206C] the free city called the heavenly Jerusalem. This is a Hebrew word and is interpreted as “vision of peace.” Its citizens are all sanctified human beings—those who were, those who are, and those who will be—and all sanctified spirits, including all who in the lofty regions of heaven obey God with devout dedication and do not imitate the impious pride of the devil and his angels.

The king of this city is the Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of God the Father by whom the highest angels are governed, and the Word taking on humanity, so that human beings might also be governed by him. All of them together will rejoice with him in eternal peace.

As a prefiguration of this reality, among the people of Israel in that earthly kingdom, King David shone forth especially. From his seed according to the flesh came our truest king, the Lord Jesus Christ, “who is God over [Col. 1206D] all, blessed forever.”

Many things took place in that promised land as figures of the coming Christ and the Church; you will be able to learn them gradually in the holy books.

After several generations, however, another type was displayed, one especially pertinent to the matter. For that city was captured, and a large part of it was led away to Babylon. Just as Jerusalem signifies the city and fellowship of the saints, so Babylon signifies the city and fellowship of the wicked; its name is understood to mean “Confusion.”

Concerning these two cities, which from the beginning of the human race to the end of the age proceed amid changing times, mingled together and to be separated at the final judgment, we have already spoken shortly before.

That captivity of the city of Jerusalem, and that people [Col. 1207A] led into Babylon, was commanded by the Lord through Jeremiah, the prophet of that time, to go into servitude. Kings of Babylon arose under whom they served; moved by what happened to them, they came to know through certain miracles the one true God who created all creation, worshiped him, and ordered that he be worshiped.

They were also commanded to pray for those by whom they were held captive and to hope for peace in their peace, so that they might beget children, build houses, and plant gardens and vineyards. After seventy years, liberation from that captivity was promised to them.

All this signifies figuratively that the Church of Christ, in all its saints who are citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, would serve under the kings of this age. For apostolic teaching says that “every soul must be subject to the higher [Col. 1207B] authorities” (Rom. XIII, 1), and that there must be rendered “to all their due: tribute to whom tribute, tax to whom tax” (ibid., V, 7), and so forth—all those things which, without compromising the worship of our Lord, we render to the rulers of human government. The Lord himself, to provide us with an example of this sound teaching, did not disdain to pay the tribute required of that part of the human being with which he was clothed.

Christian servants and faithful believers are also commanded to serve their temporal masters with equanimity and fidelity. They will judge those masters if they find them wicked to the end, or they will reign equally with them if those masters also turn to the true Lord. Nevertheless, everyone is commanded to serve human and earthly authorities until, after the appointed period signified by the seventy years, the Church is liberated from the confusion of [Col. 1207C] this age as from the captivity of Babylon, just as Jerusalem was liberated.

Through the occasion of this captivity, even the earthly kings themselves, abandoning the idols for which they had persecuted the Christians, came to know and worship the one true God. On behalf of these kings the apostle Paul commands prayer, even when they were persecuting the Church. For he says (I Tim. II, 1): “I urge, then, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for kings, for all people, and for all who are in positions of authority, so that we may lead a secure and tranquil life in all devotion and charity.”

Thus, through those kings, peace was granted to the Church, although it was a temporal tranquility of the age for the spiritual building of houses and the planting of gardens and vineyards.

“‘For behold, by this discourse we are now building and planting you’ [Col. 1207D]. And this is done throughout the whole world under the peace of Christian kings, as the same Apostle says: ‘You are God’s field, God’s building’ (1 Cor. 3:9).

After seventy years, which Jeremiah had prophetically foretold in a mystical sense to prefigure the end of the ages, the restoration of the building of God’s temple was indeed carried out in Jerusalem, so that the figure itself might be fulfilled. But because everything was being done figuratively, firm peace and liberty were not restored to the Jews. Thereafter they were defeated by the Romans and made tributary—from the time, certainly, when they received the promised land and began to have kings—so that they would not imagine that in any of their kings had been fulfilled what Christ the Liberator was promised to them.

Christ was prophesied more plainly through many prophecies, not only by David himself in the Book of Psalms, but also by the other great and holy prophets, down to the time of the captivity in Babylon.
