Even during that captivity there were prophets who foretold the coming Lord Jesus Christ, the liberator of all. After the temple had been restored when the seventy years had elapsed, the Jews suffered such great pressures and calamities from the kings of the nations that they understood that the Liberator had not yet come. They did not understand him as one who would liberate spiritually, but desired him for bodily liberation.

Thus, when the five ages of the world had been completed, the first of which extends from the beginning of the human race—that is, from Adam, the first man who was made—until Noah, who built the ark during the Flood, the second extends from then until Abraham. He was chosen as the father of all the nations that would imitate his faith, yet from the offspring of his flesh there was to arise, before the faith of the nations in Christ, the Jewish people, who alone among all the peoples of all the earth worshiped the one true God, and from whom Christ the Savior was to come according to the flesh.

These are the defining events of the first two ages in the ancient books. The remaining three are also declared in the Gospel, when the bodily descent of the Lord Jesus Christ is recalled. The third extends from Abraham to King David; the fourth from David to that captivity in which the people of God were deported to Babylon; the fifth from that deportation to the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

With his coming the sixth age is enacted, so that the spiritual grace, which was then known only to a few patriarchs and prophets, might be revealed to all nations. Thus no one would worship the Lord except freely, desiring from him not visible rewards for his service or the happiness of the present life, but eternal life alone, in which he would enjoy God himself. In this sixth age the human mind is renewed according to the image of God, just as on the sixth day humanity was made according to the image of God.

Then the law is also fulfilled, when whatever he commands is done not out of desire for temporal things but out of love for the one who gave the command. Who would not desire to love in return the most just and most merciful Lord, who first loved the most just and most proud of human beings in such a way that for their sake he sent his only Son, through whom he made all things? He, without any change in himself but by assuming humanity, became man, so that he might not only live with them but also be killed for them and by them.

Thus he revealed the new covenant of an eternal inheritance, in which the human being, renewed by God’s grace, would live a new life—that is, a spiritual life. The old covenant showed what came first: the carnal people, living as the old human being, desired carnal rewards from the Lord God, apart from the few perceptive patriarchs and prophets and certain hidden saints who lived spiritually and received those rewards as figures of spiritual goods.

Therefore the Lord Christ, having become human, despised all earthly goods, to show that they were to be despised; and he endured all earthly evils that he commanded to be endured, so that happiness would not be sought in the former, nor unhappiness feared in the latter.

He was born of a mother who, although she conceived without being touched by a man and remained untouched forever—virgin in conceiving, virgin in giving birth, virgin in dying—was nevertheless betrothed to a craftsman. Thus he extinguished all conceit of carnal nobility. He was also born in the city of Bethlehem, which among all the cities of Judea was so small that even today it is called a village; he did not wish to glory in anything belonging to the eminence of any earthly city.

He also became poor, although all things belong to him and were created through him, so that no one who believed in him would dare to become exalted through earthly riches. He did not wish to be made king by human beings, because he was showing the way of humility to the wretched, whom pride had separated from him, although all creation bears witness to his eternal kingdom.

He was hungry, though he feeds everyone; he thirsted, though through him every drink is created, and though spiritually he is the bread of the hungry and the fountain of the thirsty. He was wearied by an earthly journey, though he made himself the way for us to heaven. He was as though mute and deaf before those who reviled him, though through him the mute spoke and the deaf heard. He was bound, though he frees from the bonds of infirmities. He was scourged, though he drove the scourges of every pain from human bodies. He was crucified, though he brought our torments to an end. He died, though he raised the dead.

Yet he rose again, never to die, so that no one would learn from him to despise death as though he would never die. Then, after strengthening his disciples, he lived among them for forty days and, while they watched, ascended into heaven. When fifty days had been completed from the resurrection, he sent them the Holy Spirit. He had promised the one through whom, once love had been poured into their hearts, they would be able to fulfill the law given to the Jews in ten commandments—not only without burden but also with joy. This is what they call the Decalogue.

These commandments are again reduced to two: that we love the Lord ‘with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind,’ and that we love our neighbor as ourselves. For the Lord himself both said in the Gospel that the whole law and the prophets depend upon these two commandments and demonstrated it by his own example.

The people of Israel, from the day on which they first celebrated the Passover symbolically, killing and eating the sheep whose blood had already marked their doorposts for protection, completed the fiftieth day from that very day and received the law written by the finger of God. By that name, as we have already said, the Holy Spirit is signified.

Likewise, after the Lord’s passion and resurrection—which is the true Passover—the Holy Spirit himself was sent to the disciples on the fiftieth day. This time he no longer signified hard hearts by tablets of stone. Rather, when they had gathered in one place in Jerusalem, ‘Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a mighty wind being borne along, and divided tongues as if of fire appeared to them, and they began to speak in tongues, so that each of those who had come to them recognized his own language’ (Acts 2:2).

For Jews were coming to that city from every land in which they had been scattered, and they had learned the different languages of the various nations. Then, with complete confidence, they preached Christ and performed many signs in his name, so that when Peter passed by, his shadow touched a certain dead man and he rose again.

When the Jews saw such great signs being performed in his name, some crucified him out of envy, others out of error. Some were provoked to persecute his preachers, the apostles; others, admiring even more that such miracles were being performed in the name of the one whom they had mocked as though they had overpowered and bound him, repented and were converted, and thousands of Jews believed in him.

They no longer desired temporal benefits and an earthly kingdom from God, nor did they carnally await the promised King Christ. Rather, they understood and loved him immortally—the one who had suffered so much mortality for them and by them, who forgave them their sins even to the shedding of his blood, and who by the example of his resurrection showed them that immortality was to be hoped for and desired from him.

Thus, now putting to death the earthly desires of the old human being and burning with the newness of spiritual life, they sold everything they possessed, as the Lord had commanded in the Gospel, and laid the proceeds of their possessions at the apostles’ feet, so that they might distribute them to each person according to need. Living together in Christian love, they did not call anything their own, but everything was common to them, and they were of one heart directed toward the Lord (Acts 4:34).

Then they themselves also suffered persecution from the carnal Jews, the citizens of their own flesh, and were scattered, so that Christ might be preached more widely through their dispersion and so that they themselves might imitate the patience of their Lord. For the one who had suffered meekly for them commanded them, once made meek, to suffer for him.

The apostle Paul himself had been among those persecutors of the saints and had raged especially against Christians. But afterward he believed, became an apostle, and was sent to preach the Gospel to the nations, suffering more grievously for the name of Christ than he had previously done against the name of Christ.

As he established churches throughout all the nations in which he sowed the Gospel, he earnestly commanded that, since these people, newly converted from the worship of idols to the worship of the one Lord, could not easily serve God by selling and distributing their possessions, they should make offerings for the poor among the saints who were in the churches of Judea that had believed in Christ.

By apostolic teaching he appointed some as soldiers and others as provincial taxpayers, inserting Christ among them as the cornerstone, as he had been foretold through the prophet. In him the two walls, coming from different directions—from the Jews and from the nations—were to be joined in genuine love.

Later, heavier and more frequent persecutions arose from unbelieving nations against the Church of Christ, and the word of the Lord was fulfilled day by day: ‘Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves’ (Matt. 10:16). But that vine which, as had been prophesied concerning it and foretold by the Lord himself, spread fruitful branches throughout the world flourished all the more abundantly the more it was watered by the blood of martyrs.

When innumerable people died throughout all the lands for the truth of the faith, the very kingdoms that persecuted them yielded, and, with the neck of their pride broken, were converted to know and honor Christ.

Yet it was necessary that the same vine, as the Lord had repeatedly foretold, should be pruned, and that fruitless branches should be cut from it. In various places these became heresies and schisms, seeking under Christ’s name not his glory but their own. Through their opposition the Church would be exercised more and more, and both its teaching and its patience would be tested and made manifest.

Thus, just as we read that all these things were foretold so long beforehand, so we recognize that they have happened. Just as the first Christians, because they did not yet see these things come to pass, were prompted by miracles to believe, so we, because all these things have been fulfilled as they were written in books composed long before their fulfillment, where everything was said to be future but is now seen as present, are built up in faith, so that we may believe without doubt that the things still remaining will come, while enduring them and persevering in the Lord.

Indeed, future tribulations are still read about in those same writings, as is the final day of judgment, when all the citizens of those two cities will rise again with their bodies restored and give an account of their lives before the tribunal of Christ the Judge.

For the one who first deigned to come in the humility of humanity will also come in the glory of power, and he will separate all the godly from the ungodly—not only those who altogether refused to believe in him, but also those who believed in him fruitlessly and without result. To the former he will give an eternal kingdom with him; to the latter, eternal punishment with the devil.

Just as no joy in temporal things can in any respect be compared with the joy of the eternal life that the saints will receive, so no torment of temporal punishments can be compared with the everlasting torments of the wicked.

Therefore, brother, strengthen yourself in the name and assistance of the one in whom you believe, against the tongues of those who mock our faith, concerning whom the devil speaks seductive words, especially wishing to mock faith in the resurrection.

But believe from your own case that you will be among those who are to come, since, although previously you did not exist, you now see that you exist. Where, a few years ago, before you were born—or even before you were conceived in your mother’s womb—was this mass of your body, this form and joining together of your limbs? Where were this mass and stature of your body?

Did they not come forth from the hidden secrets of this creation into the light, invisibly formed by the Lord God, and rise through the fixed increases of age into this size and form? Is it therefore difficult for God, who in a moment draws together masses of clouds from the hidden depths and covers the sky in an instant, to restore this quantity of your body as it was, when he was able to make it from what it was not?

Believe, therefore, firmly and without wavering that everything which he seems to remove from human eyes as though it were perishing remains safe and intact in the omnipotence of God. Whenever he wills, he will restore it without any delay or difficulty—at least those things which the right of justice judges ought to be restored—so that human beings may give an account of their deeds in the bodies in which they performed them, and in those same bodies may deserve either the transformation into heavenly incorruption according to the merits of their piety, or the corruptible condition of the body according to the merits of their wickedness: not a condition saved by death, but one that provides material for everlasting pains.

Flee, therefore, through immovable faith and good conduct—flee, brother, those torments where neither the torturers fail nor the tortured die, where death without end consists in being unable to die amid torments.

And kindle yourself with love and desire for the everlasting life of the saints, where action will not be burdensome, nor rest idle; where the praise of God will be without weariness and without defect; where there will be no tedium in the soul, no labor in the body, and no need—neither your own need, which you might wish to remedy, nor that of your neighbor, to whose aid you might hasten.

God will be every delight, and the fellowship of the holy city will live wisely and blessedly in him and from him. For we shall become, as we hope and await according to his promise, equal to the angels of God, and with them we shall equally enjoy that Trinity by sight, in which we now walk by faith.

For we believe what we do not see, so that through the very merits of faith we may deserve both to see what we believe and to cleave to it: the equality of the Father and the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and the unity of the Trinity itself.

How these three are one God—we shall no longer proclaim it in the words of faith and the clamor of syllables, but in that silence we shall absorb it through the purest and most ardent contemplation.

Hold these things fixed in your heart, and call upon the Lord in whom you believe, so that he may protect you against the temptations of the devil. Be watchful, lest that one who seeks companions to be condemned with him creep upon you from some other direction, for the consolation of his most foul condemnation.

He does not dare to tempt Christians only through those who hate the Christian name, who grieve that the world is occupied by that name, and who still desire to serve idols and the occult practices of demons. He also attempts this through those whom we mentioned shortly before, who, like pruned branches, have been cut off from the unity of the Church and are called heretics or schismatics. At times he also attempts to tempt and seduce through the Jews.

But above all, one must beware lest anyone be tempted and deceived through people within the Catholic Church itself, whom God endures like chaff until the time of his winnowing. For God is patient toward them so that, by exercising the faith and prudence of his elect through their perversity, he may strengthen those virtues.

Since many of them make progress and turn with great force toward pleasing God, having taken pity on their own souls, not all of them are storing up wrath for themselves through God’s patience for the day of his just judgment. Rather, that same patience of the Almighty leads many to the most salutary sorrow of repentance. Until this happens, those who already hold the right path are exercised through them not only in endurance but also in mercy.

You will therefore see many drunkards, greedy people, swindlers, gamblers, adulterers, fornicators, people binding upon themselves sacrilegious remedies, devoted to enchanters, astrologers, or diviners of any impious arts. You will also notice that the crowds who fill the churches on the feast days of Christians are the same kind of crowds who fill the theaters on the solemn days of pagans. By seeing these things you will be tempted to imitate them.

And what shall I say? You will see what you already certainly know, for you are not unaware that many who are called Christians practice all the evils I have briefly mentioned. Perhaps you also know people called Christians who commit even worse acts.

But if you have come with the intention of doing such things as though you were secure, you are greatly mistaken. The name of Christ will not benefit you when the one who first deigned to come mercifully to your aid begins to judge with the utmost severity.

He foretold these things and said in the Gospel: ‘Not everyone who says to me, “Lord, Lord,” will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father. Many will say to me on that day, “Lord, Lord, in your name we ate and drank”’ (Matt. 7:2).

For all who persist in such works have condemnation as their end. When, therefore, you see many not only doing these things but also defending and recommending them, hold fast to the law of God and do not follow its transgressors. You will not be judged according to their opinion but according to his truth.

Join yourself to the good whom you see loving the King together with you. You will find many, if you too begin to be such a person. If you wanted to be with those in the spectacles and to cling to those who, together with you, loved either a charioteer, a hunter, or some actor, how much more should the fellowship of those delight you who, together with you, love the Lord, concerning whom his lover will never be ashamed?

For he cannot himself be conquered, and he will also make his lovers unconquerable. Yet even in those good people who either precede you or accompany you toward the Lord, you must not place your hope, just as you must not place it in yourself, however much you may have progressed. Place it in the one who makes both them and you such people by justifying you.

You are secure concerning God, because he does not change; but concerning a human being, no one is wisely secure. If we ought to love those who are not yet just so that they may become just, how much more ought those who are already just to be loved!

But it is one thing to love a human being and another to place hope in a human being. The difference is so great that God commands the former and forbids the latter.

If, after suffering insults or tribulations for the name of Christ, you do not fail in faith or deviate from the good life, you will receive a greater reward. But those who yield in such things to the devil lose even the lesser reward. Be humble before God, so that he may not permit you to be tempted beyond your strength.

After these things have been said, he must be asked whether he believes them and desires to observe them. When he has answered, he must certainly be solemnly signed and treated according to the custom of the Church.

Regarding the sacrament he has received, once it has been properly explained to him that visible signs are signs of divine realities, but that the invisible realities themselves are honored in them, it must be said that he is not to regard the sanctified blessing merely according to its outward appearance, as one regards an ordinary object. It must also be explained what the discourse he heard signifies, what it contains, and of what reality that object bears the likeness.

Then, on this occasion, he must be warned that if he hears anything in the Scriptures that sounds carnal, he should nevertheless believe, even if he does not understand it, that something spiritual is signified which concerns holy conduct and the life to come.

He learns this briefly as follows: whatever he hears from the canonical books that cannot be referred to the love of eternity, truth, holiness, and the love of neighbor, he should believe to have been said or done figuratively. He should try to understand it in such a way as to refer it to that genuine love—understanding “neighbor” not in a carnal sense, but as everyone who can be in that holy city with him, whether already manifest or not yet manifest—and so that he does not despair of the correction of any person whom he sees God’s patience allowing to live, for no other reason, as the Apostle says (Rom. 2:4), than that the person may be led to repentance.

## How Someone Should Be Catechized Briefly

(Augustine.) If this discourse seems long to you, by which I instructed a person newly come to the faith as though he were present, you may say these things more briefly. I do not, however, think it should be longer, although much depends on what the matter itself suggests while it is being conducted and on what the presence of the hearers shows that they not only can endure but also desire.

When speed is needed, see how easily the whole matter can be explained. Suppose again that someone is present who wishes to become a Christian and who has therefore been questioned about what he was shown above to have answered. If he does not give that answer, it must be explained that he ought to have given it. Then the rest should be connected in this manner:

“Truly, brother, that is the great and true blessedness promised to the saints in the age to come. All visible things pass away, and all the splendor, pleasures, and curiosity of this age will perish, dragging their lovers with them into destruction. From that destruction—that is, from eternal punishments—the merciful God wishes to free human beings, provided they are not enemies to themselves and do not resist the mercy of their Creator. For this reason he sent his only-begotten Son, that is, his Word, equal to himself, through whom he made all things.

“Remaining in his divinity, not departing from the Father, and not changed in any respect, he nevertheless came to human beings by assuming humanity and appearing to them in mortal flesh. Thus, just as through one human being, the first who was made—that is, Adam—death entered the human race because he consented to his wife, who had been deceived by the devil, so that they might transgress God’s command, so through one human being who is also God, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, all who believe in him might enter eternal life, with all past sins blotted out.

“All that you now see being done in the Church of God and throughout the whole world under the name of Christ was foretold before the ages. As we read, so we see. Through this we are built up in faith.

“Once there was a flood over the whole earth so that sinners might be destroyed. Yet those who escaped in the ark signified the sacrament of the future Church, which now floats amid the waves of the age; and through the wood of Christ’s cross we are delivered from drowning.

“It was foretold to Abraham, the faithful servant of God, a single man, that a people would be born from him who would worship the one God among the other nations that worshiped idols. Everything foretold as destined to happen to that people occurred just as it had been foretold.

“Among that people Christ, King of all the saints and God, was also prophesied as coming from the seed of Abraham according to the flesh which he assumed, so that all who imitated Abraham’s faith would be children of Abraham. And so it happened: Christ was born of the Virgin Mary, who belonged to that lineage.

“The prophets foretold that he would suffer on the cross at the hands of that same Jewish people, from whose lineage he came according to the flesh, and so it happened. It was foretold that he would rise again; he rose again. In accordance with the very prophecies of the prophets, he ascended into heaven and sent the Holy Spirit to his disciples.

“It was foretold not only by the prophets but also by the Lord Jesus Christ himself that his Church would exist throughout the whole world, spread through the martyrdoms and sufferings of the saints. This was foretold when his name was still hidden from the nations and, where it was known, was mocked. Yet, as these things were proclaimed and believed through the power of his miracles, whether performed by him directly or through his servants, we already see that what was foretold has been fulfilled, and that the very kings of the earth who once persecuted Christians have now been subjected to the name of Christ.

“It was also foretold that schisms and heresies would arise from his Church and would seek their own glory, not Christ’s, under his name wherever they could. These things too have been fulfilled.

“Are those things that remain, then, not going to come? It is clear that, just as these foretold things came, so those things too will come: whatever tribulations of the just still remain, and the day of judgment, which will separate all the ungodly from the just in the resurrection of the dead. It will separate not only those who are outside the Church but also the chaff of the Church itself, which the Church must endure most patiently until the final winnowing, when it will be separated for the fire it deserves.

“Those who mock the resurrection, thinking that this flesh cannot rise because it decays, will rise again in it for punishment. God will show them that the one who was able to make these bodies before they existed is able in an instant to restore them as they were.

“All the faithful, however, will rise to reign with Christ in the same body, so that they may also deserve to be changed into angelic incorruption and become equal to the angels of God, as the Lord himself promised. They will praise him without any defect or weariness, living forever with him and from him, with a joy and blessedness such as no human being can either express or imagine.

“You, therefore, who believe, beware of temptations, because the devil seeks those who will perish with him. Do not let that enemy seduce you only through those outside the Church, whether pagans, Jews, or heretics, but also through those whom you see within the Catholic Church living wickedly—whether in immoderate pleasures of the belly and throat, in impurity, in empty curiosities or illicit practices, whether spectacles, remedies, or demonic divinations, or in the pomp and conceit of greed and pride, or in any way of life condemned and punished by the law. Do not imitate them.

“Rather, join yourself to the good, whom you will easily find if you too become such a person, so that together you may worship and love the Lord freely, for he himself will be our entire reward, and in that eternal life we shall enjoy his goodness and beauty.

“He must be loved not as something seen by the eyes, but as wisdom, truth, holiness, justice, love, and whatever else is called by such names—not as these qualities exist in human beings, but as they exist in the very source of incorruptible and unchangeable wisdom.

“Therefore, join yourself to all whom you see loving these things, so that through Christ, who became human in order to be the mediator between God and human beings, you may be reconciled to God.

“Even if wicked people enter the walls of churches, do not think that they will enter the kingdom of heaven, for at the proper time they will be separated unless they change for the better.

“Imitate the good, tolerate the bad, and love everyone, because you do not know what the person who is bad today will be tomorrow. Do not love their injustice, but love the people themselves so that they may attain justice.

“For we are commanded not only to love God but also to love our neighbor; on these two commandments the whole law and the prophets depend. No one fulfills them except the one who has received the gift of the Holy Spirit, who is equal to the Father and the Son, because the Trinity itself is God, in whom all hope must be placed.

“Hope must not be placed in a human being, whoever he may be. The one by whom we are justified is one thing; those with whom we are justified are another.

“The devil tempts not only through desires but also through the terrors of insults, pains, and death itself. Whatever a person suffers for the name of Christ and for the hope of eternal life, and endures steadfastly, will receive a greater reward. If he yields to the devil, he will be condemned with him.

“But works of mercy, together with devout humility, obtain from the Lord that he not permit his servants to be tempted beyond what they can endure.”

Since the preceding discourse has, as I think, sufficiently explained how the person who has professed his desire to come to the faith of Christ should be instructed, we shall now explain, in the following discourse, as the Lord grants, how he himself should be introduced into the order of catechism, so that he may become a catechumen and thus proceed to receive Christ’s baptism and the divine sacraments.

# BOOK TWO. ON CATECHISM AND THE DIVINE SACRAMENTS

[Col. 1217A] (On the Instruction of Clergy, Book 1, chapter 26.) “A catechumen is so called because he is still hearing the instruction of the faith, though not yet…” Up to the end of the chapter.

For the weakness of human nature does not obstruct the grace of almighty God.

Although infants, because of their age, cannot understand conversion itself to God or belief, we nevertheless believe that they are converted to God because of the sacrament of conversion, and that they have faith because of the sacrament of faith. Thus we read in Augustine’s Letter to Bishop Boniface, in response to his inquiry about infants, where he says—the response itself concerns the celebration of the sacrament—as the Apostle says of baptism itself: “We were buried with Christ through baptism into death” (Rom. 6:4).

He did not say, “We shall signify burial,” but plainly said, “We were buried with him.” Therefore he named the sacrament of so great a reality by the very term belonging to that reality.

Thus, although the infant does not yet possess that faith which consists in the will of believers, the sacrament of faith itself already makes the infant faithful. For just as they are said to respond, “I believe,” so they are also called faithful—not by mentally assenting to the reality itself, but by receiving the sacrament of that reality.

When a person begins to understand, he does not repeat that sacrament but understands it, and his will is joined to it by a corresponding act of will. As long as he cannot do this, the sacrament serves for his protection against hostile powers. It serves so effectively that if he departs from this life before reaching the use of mature reason, then, through that sacrament, commending the Church’s love to him, he is freed by Christian aid from the condemnation that entered the world through one man.

At the scrutiny, the sign of the cross must be made over boys or girls, as we find written in the Roman Order, together with kneeling for prayer. The Lord’s Prayer must be explained to the godfathers and godmothers, so that they too may do the same for those whom they are to receive from holy baptism.

Likewise, the Creed must be explained. In our language, *symbolum* is translated as “sign” or “recognition.” When the apostles were being sent throughout the whole world for the sake of preaching, they gave this sign of preaching, so that if anyone confessed the things stated in it, he would show that he had learned them from Christ’s apostles or their successors.

For this reason we make the sign on the forehead: the seat of shame is ordinarily on the forehead. Indeed, the Jews are ashamed to believe in the one whom they know was crucified, as the apostle Paul says: “But we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to the Jews, etc.” (1 Cor. 1:23). We, however, believe that we are saved through the one who was crucified.

The Jews are ashamed of his name; we believe that we are protected by his name. Therefore we make the sign on the forehead, where the seat of shame is, as we have already said. We mark it with no other sign than the sign of the cross, because the Lord, born in the flesh, brought the standard of the cross by which he would mark the foreheads of his own, in order to destroy the dominion of death. Through this sign the opposing power recognizes that it is losing its authority over those whom God has called to the grace of baptism.

The priests, acolytes, godfathers, and godmothers also make that sign on their foreheads.

It must therefore be explained and proclaimed with the greatest insistence to the godfathers and godmothers themselves that they are sureties for those whom they receive from baptism, and for whom they have made a profession. They will give an account to God concerning them: whether, when they reach the age of understanding, they have taught them the faith of Christ and true religion, or not.

## On the Order of Catechizing

(On the Instruction of Clergy, Book 1, chapter 27.) “The order of catechizing is as follows. First the pagan is asked whether he renounces the devil, etc.” Up to the end of the chapter.

He is also anointed between the shoulder blades with the same oil, so that he may be protected on every side and strengthened by God’s grace to perform good works.”

*(Same work, near the end, chapter 25.)* For this reason, before baptism the office of catechizing must come first: so that the catechumen may first receive the rudiments of faith and thus approach the washing of baptism already prepared. [Col. 1218C] For in the Gospel according to Matthew we read that after his resurrection the Lord commanded the apostles “to teach and baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19)—that is, first to instill faith in them, and then, when they believed, to baptize them for the remission of sins. Hence, according to Mark, the same Lord is read to have placed faith before baptism, when he said: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16). And according to the testimony of John, Jesus first “smeared the eyes of the man born blind with mud made from spittle, and then sent him to the waters of Siloam” (John 9). For the person to be baptized must first be instructed in faith in Christ’s incarnation, and thus admitted to baptism already believing, so that he may know of what grace he is made a participant and to whom he thereafter becomes a debtor. [Col. 1218D] But since these matters, as we said, must precede the office of baptism, it remains for us first to speak of the sacraments themselves of the Church.

## On the divine sacraments

*[Note: [Col. 1217] a He deals only with those sacraments by which a person becomes a Christian, as the author himself testifies below at the beginning of Book III.]*

*(Same work, chapter 24; Isidore, Etymologies.)* The sacraments are [Col. 1219A] baptism, chrism, the body and blood. They are called sacraments for this reason: because, beneath the covering of bodily things, divine power secretly brings about the salvation belonging to those same sacraments. Hence they are called *sacramenta* either from secret powers or from sacred things. They are performed fruitfully within the Church because the Holy Spirit, remaining in it, secretly effects the same result of the sacraments. Thus, whether they are administered within the Church of God by good or by wicked ministers, these gifts are neither increased by the merits of good administrators nor diminished by those of wicked ones, “for neither is the one who plants anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7). Hence, in Greek it is also called *mystērion*—“mystery”—because it contains a secret and hidden deposit.

## On the rite of baptism

[Col. 1219B]

*(Same work, chapter 25.)* The first sacrament is baptism, because before anyone is anointed with holy chrism or becomes a participant in the body and blood of Christ, he must be cleansed by sacred regeneration and thereafter approach the other rites properly. *Baptism* is interpreted from Greek into Latin as *tinctio*, “dipping” or “immersion.” It is called *tinctio* not merely because a person is plunged into water, but because there he is changed for the better by the Spirit of grace and becomes something altogether different from what he was. At first we were ugly through the deformity of sins; in the immersion itself we become beautiful through the whitening of virtues. Hence it is also written in the Song of Songs: “Who is this who ascends as though whitened?” (Song 7, according to the Septuagint).

[Col. 1219C] This mystery is completed in no other way than under the designation of the Trinity, that is, through knowledge of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as the Lord says to the apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). For just as every word stands by three witnesses, so the threefold number of the divine names confirms the sacrament. The reason baptism is given through water is this: the Lord willed that the invisible reality should be imparted, by fitting correspondence and efficacy, through an intangible and invisible element: “Over which also, in the beginning, the Holy Spirit was borne” (Gen. 1). For just as oil, by its natural weight, floats above every liquid, so in the beginning the Holy Spirit was borne above the waters. Just as water cleanses the body outwardly, so through the hidden mystery of the Holy Spirit the mind is purified inwardly.

[Col. 1219D] Its sanctification takes place as follows: when God has been invoked, the Holy Spirit descends from heaven and, as though medicating the waters, sanctifies them from himself; and they receive the power of purification, so that in them flesh and soul polluted by sins may be cleansed. Both things must be applied to the person being baptized: the washing of baptism and the purification of the Holy Spirit, because the Savior says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

*(On the Instruction of Clergy, Book I, chapter 28.)* Finally, after the office of catechizing has been fully carried out, the font is consecrated; the catechumen approaches it and is baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity by a threefold immersion.

[Col. 1220A] Certainly, a person who was created in the image of the Holy Trinity is renewed into that same image through invocation of the Holy Trinity; and the one who fell into death at the third stage of sin—that is, through consent—will, when raised up from the font for the third time, rise through grace to life. This threefold immersion can also signify the Lord’s three-day burial, especially since the Apostle says: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be so in the likeness of his resurrection,” and so forth.

[Col. 1220B] Therefore baptism must be completed with invocation of the Holy Trinity and under a threefold immersion, so that the mystery of baptism may be celebrated according to the distinction of the Persons, while one baptism is effected according to the unity of substance. Hence the Apostle says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism,” and so forth (Eph. 4:5).

After the baptized person has come up from the font, he is immediately signed on the forehead by the presbyter with sacred chrism, with prayer accompanying it, so that he may become a participant in Christ’s kingdom and may be called a Christian from Christ. It is also written in the Gospel: “But when Jesus had been baptized, he immediately came up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him” (Matt. 3:16).

[Col. 1220C] The anointing with chrism rightly follows baptism, because the Holy Spirit, who through that chrism sanctifies believers by the admixture of his power, descended immediately upon baptized Jesus in the form of a dove. The dove which, during the flood, carried back to the ark a branch of olive with green leaves was clearly a type of him [the Holy Spirit], signifying that through the anointing of chrism the Holy Spirit bestows on the faithful, in baptism, the freshness of heavenly grace. But we shall speak more fully of this in what follows.

We also read in the deeds of the Fathers that Pope Sylvester established in the Roman Church the following practice: just as the authority and privilege belong solely to the bishop—that he himself prepare the sacred chrism and, by the laying on of hands together with that chrism, seal the baptized person because of heretical persuasion—so the presbyter should anoint the baptized person, washed with water, with the same chrism, because of the danger of the passage of death. For it is written in the Apostle: “But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you; but if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him,” and so forth.

[Col. 1220D] It is therefore plainly evident that whoever does not belong to Christ cannot become a participant in his kingdom. For this reason it is necessary that the baptized person should immediately be assisted by the anointing of chrism, so that, receiving a share in the Holy Spirit, he may not remain estranged from Christ.

*(Same work, chapter 29.)* After baptism, a white garment is given to the Christian. This signifies the innocence and Christian purity which, after the various stains of his former life have been washed away, he must preserve undefiled through devotion to holy conduct, in order to present it before the tribunal of Christ.

[Col. 1221A] All who have been reborn are clothed in white garments as a mystery of the Church’s resurrection. Thus the Lord himself was transfigured before his disciples, so that it was said: “His face shone like the sun, and his garments became white like snow.” By this event he prefigured, as has been said, the future splendor of the Church as she rises. They therefore use white garments so that, whereas the infancy of their first birth had been darkened by the cloth of ancient error, the clothing of their second generation may display the garment of glory.

After the sacred anointing, his head is covered with a mystical veil, so that he may understand himself to be the bearer of the diadem of royal and priestly dignity, in accordance with the Apostle: “You are,” he says, “a royal and priestly race, offering yourselves to God as a living, holy sacrifice pleasing to God,” and so forth (1 Pet. 2:9). For in the Old Testament the priests always adorned their heads with a certain mystical veil.

[Col. 1221B] Then the entire preceding sacrament is confirmed in him through the body and blood of the Lord, because he ought to receive these so that he may be worthy to have God dwelling within him and may be a member of that Head who suffered and rose for us. For Truth itself says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57). And again: “Unless you eat,” he says, “the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (ibid., v. 54).

## On the episcopal laying on of hands

*(Same work, chapter 30.)*

[Col. 1221C]

Finally, from the supreme priest, through the laying on of hands, the Paraclete [Holy Spirit], and so forth, to the end of the chapter.

For this reason the Holy Spirit is called sevenfold, because of the gifts which, from the fullness of his divinity, each person is deemed worthy to obtain in due measure.

## On the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord

*(Same work, chapter 31.)* But since we have now said as much as necessary about the two sacraments, namely baptism and chrism, and so forth.

For whoever has ceased from sinning must not cease from receiving Communion.

When someone has been imbued with the divine sacraments, has become faithful, and has become a participant in the Christian name and true religion, it is necessary that he prove by his works the faith which he holds by profession and strive with all his strength, through devotion to holy conduct, to please him who by his grace called him to the Catholic faith and willed to incorporate him into his body.

[Col. 1221D] He must also earnestly ask this every day in sacred prayers: that the one who willed to enroll him, together with the other elect, among the number of sons may, by his assistance, bring him to the sight of his eternal glory. Hence he must learn the Lord’s Prayer thoroughly, so that he may not merely utter it with his voice but understand it, fulfilling what the Apostle taught when he said: “I shall pray with the spirit, and I shall pray with the mind; I shall sing psalms with the spirit, and I shall sing psalms with the mind” (1 Cor. 14:15).

This prayer itself contains fully everything that is necessary for us in the present life and beneficial in the future. Therefore it is not necessary to speak at length in prayer in order to be heard, as the pagans do, because, as Truth itself testifies, “our heavenly Father knows what we need before we ask him.” We must not deal with God through words in order to obtain what we want, but through the realities which we carry in our hearts and through the intention of our thoughts, with pure love and a simple disposition. Nevertheless, our Lord had to teach us those very realities in words, so that, committing them to memory, we might recall them at the proper time for prayer.

[Col. 1222A] We have therefore decided to insert here, interwoven with the prayer itself, the meaning of this prayer according to the exposition of the holy Fathers, so that the one praying may know what he prays and what it is fitting for him to request. “You shall pray,” he says, “in this way.”

## On the Lord’s Prayer

[Col. 1222B]

“Our Father, who are in heaven.” We have therefore received a great gift from God, that we are permitted to say to God, “Our Father.” For what will he not now give to sons who ask, when he has already granted this very thing—that they should be sons? Finally, how greatly this ought to touch the mind: that the one who says “Our Father” should not be unworthy of so great a Father.

God, however, never falls into sordid behavior. Thanks therefore be given to his mercy, which requires us to make him our Father—a status that can be acquired at no cost, but solely by good will.

“Who are in heaven,” he says—that is, in the holy and just. For God is not confined by the extent of places. Rather, just as the sinner was called “earth” when it was said to him, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go,” so, conversely, the just person can be called “heaven.”

[Col. 1222C] For the just person is called: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3:17). Therefore, if God dwells in his temple, and if they are his temple, it is rightly said, “who are in heaven”—that is, who are in the holy.

“Hallowed be your name.” This is not requested as though God’s name were not holy, but so that it may be regarded as holy by human beings: that is, so that God may become known to them in such a way that they do not imagine anything holier, and therefore fear offending anything more. In another way we ask and pray that God’s name may be hallowed in us, so that we who have been sanctified in baptism may persevere in what we have begun to be.

“Your kingdom come.” “Come,” then, should be understood as “be manifested to human beings.” For just as present light is absent to the blind and to those who close their eyes, so the kingdom of God, although it never departs from the earth, is nevertheless absent to those who do not know it.

[Col. 1222D] No one, however, will be permitted to remain ignorant of the kingdom of God, since the Only-Begotten came from heaven not only intelligibly but also visibly in the Lord’s humanity, to judge the living and the dead.

“Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth.” That is: just as your will is in the angels who are in heaven, so that they adhere to you completely and enjoy you, with no error clouding their wisdom and no misery hindering their blessedness, so may it be done in your saints who are on earth and who, with regard to the body, were made from earth; and although they are destined for heavenly dwelling and transformation, they will nevertheless be taken from the earth.

[Col. 1223A] Likewise, “Your will be done” is rightly understood as “May your commands be obeyed”—“as in heaven and on earth,” that is, by angels and by human beings alike.

The will of God is what Christ did and taught: humility in conduct, steadfastness in faith, modesty in speech, justice in deeds, mercy in works, discipline in habits; being unable to inflict injury and able to endure injury when it has been inflicted; maintaining peace with one’s brothers; loving God with one’s whole heart; loving in him the fact that he is Father and fearing the fact that he is God; placing nothing before Christ, because he placed nothing before us; adhering inseparably to his love; standing bravely and confidently by his cross; when there is a contest concerning his name and honor, displaying the steadfastness with which we confess, the confidence with which we engage in the struggle, and the patience with which we are crowned in death.

[Col. 1223B] This is to will to be a co-heir of Christ; this is to do God’s commandment; this is to fulfill the will of the Father.

“Give us this day our daily bread.” “Daily bread” may refer to all those things which sustain the needs of this life, concerning which he commanded when he said, “Do not worry about tomorrow” (Matt. 6:34), and for this reason “give us this day” was added. Or it may refer to the sacrament of Christ’s body, which we receive daily. Or it may refer to spiritual food, concerning which the same Lord says: “Work for the food that does not perish” (John 6:27), and: “I am the bread of life who came down from heaven” (ibid., v. 51). But which of these is more probable may be considered.

[Col. 1223C] Someone may perhaps be troubled about why we pray to obtain the things necessary for this life, such as food and clothing, when the Lord himself says: “Do not be anxious about what you will eat or what you will wear.” As for the sacrament of the Lord’s body, let those not raise the question who know that very many people in the eastern regions do not partake daily of the Lord’s Supper. Since this is daily bread, it remains that we should understand daily bread as spiritual: namely, the divine commands, which must be meditated upon and practiced every day.

For concerning these the Lord says: “Work for the food that does not perish.” This food is daily God’s food, for as long as this temporal life is carried on through passing and succeeding days; and, indeed, for as long as the mind’s affections alternate now toward higher things and now toward lower things—that is, now toward spiritual things and now toward carnal things—this bread is necessary every day, as it is for one who is sometimes nourished by food and sometimes suffers hunger: it restores the hungry and raises up the faint.

[Col. 1223D] As for the fact that in other copies we read “supersubstantial bread,” or “special” or “pre-eminent” bread, this likewise signifies that bread of which he says: “I am the living bread who came down from heaven” (ibid.). It is above all substances and surpasses every creature.

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” After the provision of food, forgiveness of sin is requested, so that the one who is nourished by God may live in God, and so that provision may be made not only for present and temporal life but also for eternal life.

[Col. 1224A] One can reach eternal life if sins are forgiven—sins which the Lord calls debts, as he says in his Gospel: “I forgave you the whole debt because you asked me” (Matt. 18:32). How necessarily, wisely, and beneficially we are reminded that we are sinners, since we are compelled to ask for our sins; he who taught us to pray for our debts and sins taught us to seek the Father’s mercy and promised that forgiveness would follow.

He plainly added and imposed a law, binding us by a definite condition and pledge: we are to ask that our debts be forgiven in accordance with our own forgiveness of our debtors. We know that what we ask for our sins cannot be obtained unless we ourselves have done the same toward our sinners.

“And do not lead us into temptation.” God does not himself lead anyone into temptation, but he allows the person whom he has abandoned to his own aid to be led into it, according to a most hidden order and according to merits. He often judges, even for manifest causes, that the person whom he abandons is worthy to be abandoned and permits him to be led into temptation.

[Col. 1224B] To be led into temptation, however, is one thing; to be tempted is another. For no one can be proved without temptation. We do not therefore pray here that we may not be tempted, but that we may not be brought into temptation. If someone who must necessarily be tested by fire were praying, he would not pray that he be touched by fire, but that he not be burned.

“But deliver us from evil. Amen.” When we say, “Deliver us from evil,” nothing remains that ought still to be requested after we have once asked for God’s protection against evil. For once it has been obtained, we stand secure and safe against everything that the devil and the world do.

## On the Creed

*(On the Instruction of Clergy, Book II, chapter 56.)* Our ancestors, therefore, report that the Creed was instituted for the following reason. After the Lord and our Savior had ascended to the Father, and after the arrival of the Holy Spirit his disciples, inflamed, spoke in the languages of all nations—so that, by this sign, no foreign nation and no barbarian language seemed inaccessible or impassable to them—the Lord commanded them, as they were sent to preach the word of God, to go to every nation.

[Col. 1224D] As they were therefore about to depart from one another, they first established together a rule for their future preaching, so that, when they separated locally from one another, nothing differing or discordant would be preached to those who were being invited to the faith of Christ.

All of them therefore gathered together in one place and filled with the Holy Spirit composed, by bringing together into one the brief statement of preaching, what each of them held. They determined that this rule should be given to believers.

They wished it to be called the *symbol* for many and very proper reasons. For *symbol* in Greek can mean both “sign” and “contribution”—that is, something which many people contribute into one whole. This is what the Apostles did in these statements, each contributing into one whole what he believed.

[Col. 1225A] It is called a sign or token for this reason: at that time, as Paul says and as is reported in the Acts of the Apostles, many pretended to be apostles of Christ, naming Christ indeed but not proclaiming him according to the complete lines of the traditions. Therefore they established this token by which the one who truly preached Christ according to the apostolic rules could be recognized.

The Creed is a sign by which God is recognized, and believers consequently receive it so that they may know how to prepare the struggles of faith against the devil. It contains few words, but all the sacraments are contained in it. For these words were collected briefly by the Apostles from the whole of Scripture, so that, since many believers do not know letters, while those who do know them cannot read the Scriptures because of the distractions of the world, they may retain these words in their hearts and possess sufficient saving knowledge.

[Col. 1225B] It is a brief word of faith, formerly foretold by the Prophet: “For the Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth.” It is recited in the following form.

“I believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth.” It begins, therefore, with “I believe.” You see that our Lord does not command us to scrutinize divine judgments, but to believe; nor to demand an explanation, but simply and immovably to offer faith.

“In God the Father.” Observe that, by joining the name of Father to that of God in the confession, he shows that God did not first begin to be God and afterward become Father, but that, without any beginning, he is always both God and Father. Since he was always Father, he always had a Son to whom he is Father.

“Almighty”—he says this because he is almighty, and nothing is impossible for him. He created heaven, earth, the sea, human beings, and all animals and reptiles not by some laboring process, but solely by the command of his word. Therefore we should not wonder in our thoughts how this or that could have come to be, when we are commanded to confess the creator of heaven and earth as almighty.

[Col. 1225C] This is what I said above: “He accomplished everything solely by the power of his word.”

“And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.” Observe that just as we must believe in the Father, so we must believe in the Son; and because he is equal to the Father in majesty, we know that we owe him as much honor and as much obedient service as we owe the Father.

“Jesus Christ”: Jesus is interpreted as “Savior.” Christ, however, is named from *chrism*, because, just as ancient kings were anointed by priests with sacred oil, so our Lord Jesus Christ was filled through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit.

“Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit.” He could not have been conceived from anywhere but God, since he was worthy to bring forth God.

“Born of the Virgin Mary.” She, who was to remain a virgin after giving birth, could not have had any other kind of conception.

“Suffered under Pontius Pilate.” Pilate was the judge appointed at that time by the emperor over Judaea, under whom the Lord suffered. His mention refers to the indication of the time, not to the dignity of that person.

“Crucified, dead, and buried.” We bear on our foreheads the cross on which he was crucified in the body. Just as he was truly born, so he was truly dead and truly buried.

[Col. 1226A] “He descended to the underworld; on the third day he rose from the dead.” The duration of the three-day burial clearly shows that while the body lay in the tomb, that soul triumphed over the underworld.

“He ascended into heaven; he sits at the right hand of God the almighty Father.” For this reason he placed above the heavens, at the right hand of God the Father, the condition of our nature which he assumed when he was born of a human mother.

The Father’s right hand, where he is said to sit, is not bodily; it would be impious to think this about God, since the divine majesty does not have a side according to human form. Rather, the Father’s glory and blessedness are called his right hand, at which the Son sits according to his humanity—that is, he reigns forever.

[Col. 1226B] “From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.” He will come to judgment in the very body in which he ascended to heaven, in order to judge Christians and pagans, the just and sinners, the faithful and the impious.

“I believe in the Holy Spirit.” Observe that, just as we must believe in the Father, so we must believe in the Son and in the Holy Spirit. For whoever does not believe in one Person of the Trinity will gain nothing by believing in two.

“The holy Catholic Church.” *Church* is called in Greek *ekklēsia*; in Latin it is said to mean “assembly” or “calling,” because it calls everyone to itself and gathers them together into one.

[Col. 1226C] It must be understood that we are to believe the Church, but not to believe in the Church, because the Church is not God but the house of God. It says “Catholic,” meaning spread throughout the whole world. The churches of the various heretics are not called Catholic because they are confined to particular places and to their respective provinces. This Church, however, is spread from the rising of the sun to its setting by the splendor of one faith.

“The communion of saints”—that is, let us maintain fellowship and communion of hope with those saints who have died in the faith which we embrace.

“The remission of sins.” The first remission of sins is through the grace of baptism, the second through martyrdom, and the third through the satisfaction of penance. Nevertheless, these remissions of sins do not occur at all outside the faith and unity of the Church.

[Col. 1226D] There are also other remissions of sins: through the forgiveness of enemies, through true love, through works of mercy, and through the word of preaching, if someone causes a sinner to turn back from the error of his way.

“The resurrection of the flesh.” Let us believe that the flesh which we bear in this life under mortal conditions will rise immortal and will give an account for its fellowship with the soul.

“Eternal life.” Let us confess without any doubt that we shall attain eternal life if we faithfully hold these sacraments which we expound to you and preserve them through good works. For this is the correct and true interpretation of the Apostolic Creed.

[Col. 1227A]

*(On the Instruction of Clergy, Book II, chapter 57.)* It must be understood that, according to the Apostolic Creed, this is the most certain faith of Christians, which our teachers have handed down: that we confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be of one essence, and of the same power and eternity—one invisible God—so that, while the distinct properties of the Persons are preserved in each, the Trinity must neither be divided substantially nor confused altogether personally.

We must confess the Father as unbegotten, the Son as only-begotten, and the Holy Spirit as neither begotten nor only-begotten, but proceeding from the Father and the Son. The Son proceeds from the Father by being born; the Holy Spirit, however, proceeds without being born.

[Col. 1227B] We must confess also that the Son himself, perfect from the Virgin, assumed a human nature without sin, so that he might mercifully restore, by his own will, what he had created by pure goodness and what had fallen of its own accord.

We must confess that he was truly crucified, rose from the dead on the third day, and ascended into heaven with that same glorified flesh, in which he is expected to come for the judgment of the living and the dead.

The divine and human substance were borne by one perfect Christ in both respects, because the integrity of the two substances neither multiplied the person into two nor did the unity of the Person confuse the two substances. For neither excluded the other, since each of the two preserved its proper integrity unimpaired. The authority of the New and Old Testaments soundly commends this: the former having been fulfilled through prophecy, the latter truthfully through history.

[Col. 1227C] We must not agree with pagans or heretics concerning God or the world’s creature in those matters in which they dissent from the truth. We must believe only what the divine utterances testify in both Testaments.

God created neither human beings nor the universe out of any necessity. There is no visible or invisible substance except either what God is or what, having been created by the good God, is good. God is supremely and unchangeably good, whereas the creature is good in a lower and changeable manner.

The origin of souls is uncertain. The nature of angels and of souls is not a part of the divine substance, but a creature of God, created from nothing; it is incorporeal because it was created in the image of God.

[Col. 1227D] Everyone must strive after piety of conduct, without which faith in divine worship grows idle and torpid, and with which the integrity of divine worship is perfected. Each person must love God for God’s sake and his neighbor in God, advancing even to love of enemies, so that by advancing he may arrive.

Nor can the sin of one person pollute another where an equal consent of the will is not present.

Lawful marriages must not be condemned, although the offspring born from them is also believed to be liable to original sin, and although the integrity of faithful virgins or of those who practice continence is taught to be preferred to them.

The one baptism of the Trinity, which it would be impious to repeat, must not be repeated. Nor should it be thought that, because the ministers who administer it differ, it is conferred separately by each of them; rather, it is bestowed by the single power of the one of whom we read: “The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit. And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John 1).

[Col. 1228A] We must not think that we have no need of the remedies of penance. For the daily offenses of human frailty, without which we cannot exist in this life, let us acknowledge that all sins are wiped away through fruitful contrition in penance, as it is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. 31).

No one is joined to Christ the Head by his own powers, but through divine grace; and he is strengthened in the unity of the Church by perseverance in unbroken peace. No good thing should be attributed to the free choice of the human will; rather, the entire number of the elect is acquired according to the purpose of God’s good will.

[Col. 1228B] Temporal goods are created by God and are common to the good and the wicked; by his dispensation they are either granted or denied to each person. In the case of each believer, it is not the possession of these goods but their use that is either to be condemned or approved.

The remaining and eternal goods can be attained in the future only by the good. We believe that the Church is now held in their pledge, possessing here the first fruits of the Spirit and in the future its perfection; here sustained in hope and afterward nourished in reality; here seeing through a mirror in an enigma, but in the future face to face, when through faith it has been brought to vision.

[Col. 1228C] Until this is perfected, so that we may enjoy the eternal goods of the supreme God, temporal goods must be used in such a way that we do not harm either ourselves or our neighbors.

We also have this hope of resurrection: that we shall rise as the Lord himself rose from the dead, in the same order and in the same form; that we shall rise in the same body in which we exist and live, not changing our nature or sex, but laying aside only frailty and vices.

Satan himself, together with his angels and worshipers, is to be condemned to eternal fire. He is not, according to the sacrilegious argument of certain people, to be restored to his former—that is, angelic—dignity, from which he fell through his own wickedness.

This is the true integrity of the faith of Catholic tradition. If any single part of it is rejected, the whole belief of the faith is lost.

## On various heresies

[Col. 1228D]

*(On the Instruction of Clergy, Book II, final chapter.)* It is therefore necessary that every soul who fears God take care and guard against falling away from the Catholic faith and abandoning the teaching of truth, lest it fall into the errors of the heretics, and so forth, to the end of the chapter.

But anyone who understands Holy Scripture otherwise than the sense of the Holy Spirit, by whom it was written, may nevertheless be called a heretic, even if he has not withdrawn from the Church.

# BOOK THREE. ON THE CHRISTIAN STRUGGLE

[Col. 1229]

[Col. 1229A] Having set forth, then, the divine sacraments by which a person becomes a Christian, as well as the Lord’s Prayer, by which prayers are poured forth to God, and also the creed and the truth of the faith, together with the errors from which one must beware lest one be led astray, we think that it should next be written how such a person must afterward contend in the Christian struggle.

For we read in the Gospel that our Savior, appearing to his disciples in Galilee after his resurrection, said: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you (Matt., last chapter).”

In this there is a perfectly correct order of preaching, and one that the Church’s preachers today must follow most diligently: first, the hearer is to be taught; then he is to be imbued with the sacraments of the faith; [Col. 1229B] after this, he is to be instructed more freely and fully in due time to observe the Lord’s commandments. For it cannot happen that the body receives the sacrament of baptism unless the soul has first received the truth of the faith; nor can an uneducated person ignorant of the Christian faith be washed by the sacraments of that same faith. Nor is it enough to cleanse anyone from sins by the washing of baptism if, after baptism, he does not strive to devote himself to good works.

He therefore commands that the nations first be taught—that is, instructed in knowledge of the truth—and then baptized, because without faith it is impossible to please God, and unless someone has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. Finally he adds: “Teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you.” And lest we think that what was commanded is trivial or limited, he added: “Everything that I have commanded you,” so that all who believe and have been baptized in the Trinity may do everything that has been commanded; for just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead.

How great a reward for this pious way of life, and what a pledge of future blessedness awaits the faithful even in the present, he subsequently indicates when he says: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age.”

It is also pleasing to compare with this testimony what Mark says: “And indeed the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God (Mark, last chapter).” Since he is himself both God and man, he was taken up into heaven in the humanity that he had assumed from the earth; yet he remains with the saints in his eternal divinity, [Col. 1229D] by which he fills earth and heaven alike.

He remains with them all days, until the consummation of the age. From this it is understood that, until the end of the age, there will not be lacking in the world those who are worthy of the divine dwelling and inhabitation. Nor should we doubt that, after the struggles of this age, those who, while contending in the world, have deserved to have Christ dwelling in the lodging-place of their hearts will remain with Christ in the kingdom.

Meanwhile, it must be noted that the divine majesty, present everywhere, is with his elect in one way and with the reprobate in another. He is present to the reprobate through the incomprehensible power of his nature, by which he knows all things, the last and the first, understands thoughts from afar, and foresees the ways of every individual.

He is present to the elect through the grace of loving protection, by which he trains them spiritually through present gifts or through chastisement, as a father trains his children; and by training them he advances them toward possession of future blessedness. He is present to the elect, as it is written: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit (Ps. XXXIII, 19).”

He is present to the reprobate, as was stated above: “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their remembrance from the earth (ibid., v. 17).”

Therefore, if the eyes of the Lord observe the good and the wicked, and the Lord looks down from heaven upon the children of men to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God, each person purified by the water of baptism and adorned with the dignity of the Christian name ought, while diligently exercising himself in the service of the eternal King, to fight not with bodily weapons against flesh and blood, but chiefly against the principalities and powers of this air, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, and against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.

In all things he must take up the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, the breastplate of righteousness, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; and he must put to death the desires of his flesh daily, according to the Apostle’s saying (Col. III, 5):

“Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is idolatry; because of these the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief. Among them you also once walked, when you lived in them. But now you too must put away all these things: anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy; do not let shameful speech come from your mouth. Do not lie to one another. Strip off the old person with his deeds, and put on the new, the one who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who created him, where there is neither gentile nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all.”

For it is clear that blessed Paul the Apostle wrote these words to the faithful, not to pagans, just as he also admonished the Ephesians in his Epistle, [Col. 1230D] saying (Eph. IV, 23): “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new person who has been created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth.”

He also says elsewhere (Gal. III, 17): “All of you who have been baptized have put on Christ.” And to show how Christ must be put on, he says (Col. III, 12):

“Put on, therefore, as God’s elect, holy and beloved, compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, [Col. 1231A] patience, bearing with one another and forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another; just as Christ forgave you, so you also must forgive. Above all these things have charity, which is the bond of perfection. And let the peace of Christ rejoice in your hearts; in that peace you were also called in one body. And be grateful. Let the word of Christ dwell in your hearts abundantly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing in your hearts to God in grace. Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God the Father through him.”

From this, then, it is clear that the aforementioned Doctor of the Gentiles wished his hearers to live in a disciplined manner, [Col. 1231B] and, by believing rightly and doing good, to possess the hope of eternal life.

## On Christian Discipline

Discipline is the guardian of hope, the support of faith, the guide of the way of salvation, the kindling and nourishment of a good disposition, and the teacher of virtue. It makes us remain always in Christ and live continually for God; it brings us to the heavenly promises and divine rewards. To follow it is salutary; to turn away from it and neglect it is deadly.

Thus the Holy Spirit speaks in the Psalms: “Hold fast to discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the right way when his anger is quickly kindled against you (Ps. II, 12).” And again: “But God says to the sinner: Why do you declare my ordinances and take my covenant upon your lips? Yet you hate discipline and have cast my words behind you (Ps. XLIX, 16).”

Again we read: “Whoever rejects discipline is unhappy.” And from Solomon we receive the commands of Wisdom, which admonishes: “My son, do not neglect the discipline of God, and do not lose heart when you are corrected by him; for whom God loves, he corrects (Wis. III, 11).”

But if God corrects the one whom he loves, he corrects him in order to reform him. Brothers also, and especially priests, do not hate but love those whom they correct in order to reform them, since God had already foretold this through Jeremiah and indicated the times in which we live, saying: “And I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will feed you”—feeding you with discipline.

If discipline is so often and everywhere commanded in the Holy Scriptures, and if the whole foundation of religion and faith proceeds from obedience and fear, what ought we to desire more eagerly, what ought we to wish for and fear more, than that, with our roots fixed more firmly and our dwellings solidly established upon the rock by a massive structure, we may stand unshaken against the storms and whirlwinds of the age and come to God’s gifts through the divine commandments?

At the same time, we must consider and know that our members are God’s temples, cleansed from all the filth of former thought by the sanctification of the life-giving bath; and that it is not lawful for them to be violated or polluted, since the one who violates the temple is himself also violated.

We are the worshipers and guardians of these temples. Let us serve him whose we have already begun to be. The Apostle Paul says in his Epistles, by which he formed us for the course of life through divine instruction: “You are not your own; for you were bought at a great price. Glorify and bear God in your body (I Cor. VI, 20).”

Let us glorify and bear God with a pure and clean body and with better observance; and we who have been redeemed by Christ’s blood must in every service obey the command of our Redeemer. Let us take care that nothing unclean or profane be brought into God’s temple, and that he not depart in anger from the dwelling-place in which he inhabits.

These are the words of the Lord who restores health, teaching, healing, and also admonishing. “Behold,” he says, “you have been made well; now do not sin any more, lest something worse happen to you (John V, 14).”

After granting health, he gives the fear of living and the law of innocence. He does not afterward allow anyone to wander about with free and loosened reins; rather, he threatens more severely the very one who has been healed, knowing, of course, that he had sinned less grievously before, when he did not yet know God’s discipline. After you have begun to know God, there is no forgiveness for continuing to sin.
