Indeed, both men and women, boys and girls, every sex and every age, must observe and attend to this according to the religion and faith they owe to God, so that what is received as holy through the Lord’s favor may not be held less carefully because of insufficient fear.

Teachers must not neglect their pupils, nor parents their children; rather, they must educate them in every discipline, though with discernment, because it is written: “Nothing in excess”—lest, while they desire to scrape away too much rust, the vessel be broken.

The Apostle says: “Bring up your children in the discipline and correction of the Lord [Col. 1232C] (Eph. VI, 4).” Hence Wisdom also exhorts through Solomon, saying: “Do not withdraw discipline from a child. If you strike him, you will save his soul from death; you will strike him with the rod, and he will not die (Prov. XXIII, 14).”

All persons in authority ought to be diligent in guarding their subjects through discipline and must not neglect to govern them, because only in this way will they be freed from responsibility for them at the divine judgment.

Thus Wisdom exhorts and says to us: “My son, if you have become surety for your friend, you have pledged your hand to a stranger. You have been ensnared by the words of your mouth and captured by your own speech. Do therefore, my son, what I tell you, and free yourself, since you have fallen into the hands of your neighbor. Run, hasten; rouse your friend. Do not give sleep to your eyes, [Col. 1232D] nor slumber to your eyelids (Prov. VI, 2).”

Hence also the Lord speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, saying: “Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. You will hear a word from my mouth, and you will announce it to them from me. If, when I say to the wicked, ‘You shall die the death,’ you do not announce it to him, nor speak so that he may turn from his wicked way and live, that wicked man will die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand. But if you announce it to the wicked, and he does not turn from his wickedness, he will die, but you will have saved your own soul (Ezek. XXXIII, 7).”

Discipline must therefore be adjusted by teachers according to the character of the person. Hence Paul, writing to his disciple, says: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all authority (II Tim. IV, 2).”

It is as though he said: Show the harsh severity of a teacher and the loving affection of a father, so that you may rebuke the undisciplined and restless more severely, but entreat the obedient and gentle, so that they may advance toward better things; rebuke and correct the negligent and contemptuous.

Nor is it without reason that the Savior is read in the Gospel to have driven from the temple the hard and unbelieving Jews, who were buying and selling, making a whip of cords, and to have said: “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of thieves (Matt. XXI, 13).”

Nor was it without reason that the Apostle Peter condemned Ananias and Sapphira, corrupted by the plague of greed, lying and testing the Spirit of God through hypocrisy, to the sentence of death. It was so that what is written might be fulfilled: [Col. 1233B] “Strike the pestilent man, and the fool will become wiser (Prov. XIX, 25),” so that through the forceful correction of a few, many might be corrected and reformed from error.

For this reason our holy Fathers also established various forms of discipline and excommunication in their councils for those who sinned, so that, according to the measure of the fault, the extent of excommunication might provide a remedy for the sick and a warning for the healthy.

## On Meditation upon the Divine Law

For the more diligent observance of this discipline, the study of learning true wisdom and the continual meditation upon the divine law are of great help. Each person ought to investigate this law with a pure heart and chaste body, because in this way he can attain its sober understanding.

For it grants knowledge of God to those who faithfully and earnestly seek and meditate upon it. [The supplied Latin here is textually uncertain: *Ipsa enim cognitionem Dei se fideliter quaerentibus et instanter meditantibus tribuit.*]

Nothing is better than knowledge of God, because nothing is more blessed; indeed, it is true blessedness itself. Hence the Savior says to the Father: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John XVII, 3).”

Therefore, above all, a person must seek to know what true knowledge and true wisdom are, because the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God. True knowledge is to withdraw from the service of the devil, which consists in sins; and perfect wisdom is to worship God according to the truth of his commandments. For blessed life is acquired in these two things, as the Psalmist says: “Turn away from evil and do good (Ps. XXXIII, 15).”

Nor is it enough for anyone not to do evil unless he also does good; nor is it enough to do good unless he also abandons evil. Therefore, everyone who is wise in this way will undoubtedly be blessed forever.

Blessed life is knowledge of divinity; knowledge of divinity is the virtue of good work; and the virtue of good work is the fruit of eternal blessedness.

For this good, then, we have the comfort of reading the divine Scriptures. The reading of the Holy Scriptures is a divine foreknowledge—not a small one—of blessedness. In them, as in a certain mirror, a person can consider himself: what he is and toward what he is tending.

Constant reading purifies the soul, instills fear of Gehenna, and urges the heart of the reader toward heavenly joys. Whoever wishes always to be with God ought frequently to pray and to read. [Col. 1234A] For when we pray, we speak with God; but when we read, God speaks with us.

The reading of the Holy Scriptures confers a twofold gift, both because it trains the understanding of the mind and because, drawing a person away from the vanities of the world, it leads him to the love of God. The labor of reading is honorable and contributes greatly to the reform of the soul.

Just as flesh is nourished by bodily food, so the inner person is nourished and fed by divine words. As the Psalmist says: “How sweet are your words to my throat, Lord, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth (Ps. CXVIII, 113).”

But the truly blessed person is the one who, while reading the divine Scriptures, turns words into works. All the Holy Scriptures were plainly written for the salvation of souls, so that we may advance in them in the knowledge of the truth.

A blind person stumbles more often than one who sees; likewise, the person who is ignorant of God’s law sins more often in ignorance than the one who knows. Just as a blind person scarcely walks along the right path without a guide, so a person scarcely walks along the right path without a teacher. Therefore, whoever is able to read the sacred books must devote himself to them, so that he may frequently make use of meditation upon them.

Those who cannot grasp the meaning of sacred speech from reading should listen more attentively to one who explains it, so that they may at least receive it for their edification.

But when, instructed by heavenly teaching, they learn what must be done and what must be avoided, there should be no delay in doing what they inwardly understand through discernment. For, as blessed James the Apostle says, “It is not the hearers of the law who will be justified, but the doers of the law (Rom. II, 13).”

Truth itself also says: “The servant who knows the will of his master and does not act accordingly will be beaten many times (Luke XII, 47),” and so forth. Elsewhere it is also written: “For the one who knows to do good and does not do it, it is sin.”

Therefore, we must strive with all diligence to know the will of God. Once we have come to know it, we must strive with the utmost effort to do it, fulfilling his commandments, and earnestly ask that, persevering in this, we may reach his promises.

## On Faith, Hope, and Charity

It is therefore necessary that everyone who bears the Christian name and has been imbued with the sacraments should know the doctrine of the Christian religion and recognize the truth of the faith, as well as that faith which, as the Apostle says, “works through love,” which strengthens and confirms believers in the present and leads them to the contemplation of God in the future.

For blessed Paul, the distinguished Doctor of the Gentiles, set forth certain things necessary for our soul, saying: “Now these three remain: faith, hope, and charity; but the greatest of these is charity (I Cor. XIII, 13).”

First, then, Catholic faith is necessary for the Christian, because by it the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil, and the children of light from the children of darkness. Through it we are reborn in baptism and obtain eternal salvation, as it is written: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved (Mark XVI, 16).”

This is the door of life; this is the gate of the kingdom. Through it the knowledge of truth is learned and knowledge of divinity is received. Through it we find the grace of God; otherwise we cannot please God, because without faith it is impossible to please him.

Truly blessed is the person who lives well by believing rightly and, by living well, preserves the right faith. Therefore, just as faith without good works is useless, so good works accomplish nothing without right faith.

Hence blessed James the Apostle also said: “What good is it, my brothers, if someone says that he has faith but does not have works? (James II, 14).” Can faith save him? Faith without works is dead. For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead.

Above all, it is necessary to possess faith that is right and undefiled; to hold by heart the creed established by the holy Fathers according to the rule of apostolic instruction; to strive to live religiously; [Col. 1235B] to flee the poisonous doctrines of heretics; to shudder at the deadly poisons of sorcerers and enchanters; utterly to reject the wicked traditions of diviners and those who practice lots, which have fellowship with demons; and to hold in mind and confession, and also to display in conduct, nothing other than what the Catholic faith praises, loves, and proclaims.

After this faith, one must possess and learn firm hope, which draws our soul toward invisible things, directs our intention toward heavenly and eternal realities, and binds it, as it were, with unbreakable bonds. Hope does not deceive but leads those who faithfully serve it to eternal blessedness.

Therefore, no one, however heavily burdened by the weight of sins, ought to despair of the goodness of God’s mercy. Rather, he ought daily to beseech for himself the hope of certain mercy and forgiveness through tears, which he may rightly hope for if he ceases from evil action.

For this reason, we must not sin persistently on account of the hope of pardon; nor, because God justly punishes sins, must we despair of forgiveness. Instead, avoiding both dangers, let us turn away from evil and hope for forgiveness from God’s mercy.

Likewise, in every distress of tribulation, we must run through hope to the consolations of heavenly mercy, because in God alone all hope and salvation undoubtedly consist, as the Prophet says: “In God is my salvation and my glory; God is my help, and my hope is in God (Ps. XLI, 8).”

When we urge people to possess right faith and firm hope, we especially exhort them to strive in every way to possess charity within themselves and to demonstrate it in their works. Through charity and in charity, we must know that we shall have true blessedness, because without it no one will see God.

The Apostle says that charity is greater than faith and hope because, when the others depart, it alone will remain. Faith gives way to hope, and hope to blessedness; but charity does not change—only its perfection remains.

Charity is the art of all virtues; it is the promise of the kingdom; it is the highest reward of the saints in heaven. For in everlasting joy the saints have nothing more pleasing or sweeter than the perfected love of God. When they see him present, they love him more sweetly and enjoy that good more deeply.

## On Charity

We must know that charity holds primacy in all things. The Apostle Paul testifies that without its perfection nothing can please God. He shows that neither martyrdom, nor contempt for the world, nor generosity in almsgiving can accomplish anything without the duty of charity.

Thus, when a certain scribe asked the Lord which commandment was greatest, he answered: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.” He added a second commandment like it: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets (Matt. XXII, 37).”

When he says “with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind,” that is, with the whole understanding, the whole will, and the whole memory, he means that God must be loved. The love of God consists entirely in observing his commandments, as he says above: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words (John XIV, 23).”

Hence Truth itself says elsewhere: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another (John XIII, 35).” The Apostle likewise says: “Love is the fullness of the law (Rom. XIII, 10).”

The evangelist John also says: “We have this commandment from God: that whoever loves God should love his neighbor also.”

If someone should ask who one’s neighbor is, let him know that every Christian is rightly called one’s neighbor, because in baptism we are all sanctified as children of God, so that we may be brothers spiritually in perfect charity. Spiritual generation is nobler than bodily generation.

Concerning this, Truth itself says in the Gospel: “Unless someone has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God [Col. 1236C] (John III, 15).”

Whoever understands his neighbor in this way and loves him will undoubtedly possess true charity within himself. Its evident sign and outstanding virtue is true peace. Through peace, the children of God are especially recognized, because perfect peace can exist nowhere unless the charity that produces it is present. The whole sequence of the Holy Scriptures also shows this to us.

## On Peace and Unity

For we read in the Gospel that, when our Savior and Lord was approaching his Passion and announcing to his disciples his departure from this world to the Father, among the other words he gave to his beloved companions for their remembrance, he especially commended the good of peace and, as a special gift, unity, saying: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace (John XIV, 27).”

It was as though he said: “I left you in peace; I will find you in peace.” As he departed, he wished to give what he desired to find in everyone when he returned.

He gave this peace to his own as an inheritance; he promised all the gifts of his pledge and all rewards in a life of peace. Therefore, if we wish to be heirs of Christ, we must remain in his peace.

Christ gave us peace and commanded us to be concordant and united in mind. He ordered that the bonds of love and charity remain uncorrupted and inviolate. Elsewhere he wonderfully shows the adornments of this peace, saying: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called the children of God (Matt. V, 9).”

Behold, the one who has begun to be peaceable begins to be called a child of God. Whoever refuses to embrace peace does not wish to be called a son; whoever disdains to be peaceable denies God as his father.

The children of God must therefore be peaceable: gentle in heart, simple in speech, faithfully united in affection, and joined to one another by the bonds of harmony.

But this peace is to be maintained with the good and with those who keep God’s commandments, not with the wicked and criminal, who have peace among themselves in their sins. The peace of Christ contributes to everlasting salvation; peace must be maintained with the good and war must always be waged against vices.

The evil deeds of impious people must indeed be hated, but the people themselves, although evil, must be loved because they are God’s creatures. Peace among the good joins together the harmony of brothers and the love of neighbors. Peace especially wins the favor of God’s Spirit. Peace is the mother of love. Peace is the sign of holiness, concerning which the Lord says through the Prophet: “Love peace and truth.”

Peace is the health of the people, the glory of the priest, the joy of the homeland, and the terror of enemies, whether visible or invisible. Peace must be guarded with all one’s strength. It always remains in God, and whoever remains in holy peace has fellowship with God’s saints.

It is the priest’s duty to admonish the people in peace concerning what they ought to do; it is the people’s duty to listen humbly to what the priest advises. Whatever is not permitted, the shepherd must forbid lest it be done; the people must listen lest they do it.

All leaders and subjects alike must preserve the bond of unity in faith and love in every respect, because without peace neither the priest’s prayer nor the people’s offering is accepted.

If, therefore, we wish to be heard quickly by God and to have our gifts accepted by him with favor, we must certainly live in peace. Concerning this, Truth itself graciously instructs us:

“If you offer your gift before the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then come and offer your gift (Matt. V, 23).”

Because God desires our unity and concord, the Savior himself shows this in the Gospel when he speaks to the Father: “Holy Father,” he says, “keep them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may be one as we are (John XVII, 11).”

Hence the Apostle also exhorts the faithful, saying: “I beseech you, brothers, that you all have the same mind and speak as one (I Cor. I, 10).” And again: “Let there be no jealousy and contention among you; let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice (Eph. IV, 31).”

Elsewhere he says: “Bearing with one another in love, be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling (ibid., v. 3).”

Such unity once existed among the apostles. The Scripture proves that the new people of believers, keeping the Lord’s commandments, maintained their charity; it says: “The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and one soul.” And again: “They all persevered with one accord in prayer with the women and Mary, who was the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers (Acts I, 14).”

For this reason they prayed with effective prayers; for this reason they could confidently obtain whatever they requested from God’s mercy.

But among us unity has been so diminished that generosity in action has also been weakened. At that time people sold their houses and estates and offered the proceeds to the apostles for distribution to the needy, so that treasures might be stored up for them in heaven. But now we do not give even tithes from our patrimony; and although the Lord commands us to sell, we instead buy and increase our possessions.

Just as the vigor of faith has withered in us, so the strength of believers has grown weak. Therefore, looking upon our times, the Lord says in his Gospel: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on the earth? (Luke XVIII, 8).”

We see happening what he foretold: in the fear of God, in the law of righteousness, in love, and in works, there is no faith. No one, through fear of the future, considers the day of the Lord, the wrath of God, the punishments awaiting unbelievers, or the eternal torments established for the faithless—things which our conscience would fear if it believed. But it does not believe at all, and therefore it does not fear.

If it believed, it would beware; if it took heed, it would escape.

We must therefore rouse ourselves as far as we can. Breaking away from the sleep of former lethargy, let us keep watch to observe and carry out the Lord’s commandments. Let us be what he himself commands us to be, saying: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning, and be like people waiting for their lord when he returns from the wedding, so that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him (Luke XII, 35).” And again: “Blessed are those servants whom the lord, when he comes, finds watching (ibid., v. 37).”

We must be girded, lest, when the day of departure comes, it find us hindered and entangled. Let the desire for good works shine within us and radiate as a light, so that this very light may lead us from the night of this age to the light of eternal glory, where, with Christ, the author of true peace, and with his holy angels, we may enjoy eternal peace and everlasting happiness.

## On the Virtue of Continence
And so, in order that we may accomplish this promptly, we must strive to acquire for ourselves the consolation of the sacred virtues and take care to proceed along the way of justice and truth, so that, escaping unharmed by God’s grace the ambushes of spiritual enemies and the tumult of vices, we may reach heavenly blessedness. [Col. 1238D] For accomplishing this, continence against the desires of the flesh and the allurements of pleasures is especially necessary to us. Therefore Scripture admonishes us, saying:

> “Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your will. If you grant your soul its desire, it will make you a joy to your enemies” (Ecclus. XVIII, 30).

For love of this world produces hostility toward God. Hence it is written:

> “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this age is made an enemy of God” (James IV, 4).

Knowing this, the apostle John, our fellow apostle, urges and says:

> “Do not love the world. The Father’s love is not in it, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (I John [Col. 1239A] II, 15).

His fellow apostle Paul likewise warns us again and says:

> “Those who buy should be as though they did not possess, and those who use this world as though they did not use it. For the form of this world is passing away” (I Cor. VII, 30).

Therefore the Savior himself also shows in his parable that the riches and pleasures of the age choke the word, so that it bears no fruit. Elsewhere he commands, saying:

> “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. XVI, 24).

And again:

> “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses,” he says, “cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 33).

Considering these things, then, it is right for us to weigh how necessary continence is for us, by which we may become worthy of Christ’s discipline and be able to come with him to the everlasting kingdom. [Col. 1239B]

Continence and sobriety, however, do not consist solely in bodily chastity. They consist also in dress and adornment, and likewise in life and conduct. Every continent person ought to abstain from all that is unlawful; but what is lawful he ought to use with modesty and sobriety. For it is not fitting that a Christian, to whom the heavenly kingdom has been promised, should yearn for the profits of this world. Rather, through continence he should live worthily for his Lord, so that he may rejoice with him forever.

He ought to love charity and flee fornication; not devote himself to greed, but be content with food and clothing; not be proud, nor place his hope in the uncertainty of riches, but think humbly and despise the pomp of the world. He must not be boastful or arrogant, nor deceitful or abusive, [Col. 1239C] neither double-tongued, whispering, nor defamatory. Rather, he must speak the truth from mouth and heart and restrain his tongue from excessive speech, because it is written:

> “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Prov. X, 9).

He should close his eyes against vanity; turn his hearing away from obscenity and falsehood, indeed from every evil utterance; not love loud and uproarious laughter; not readily devote throat and nose to the allurements of sweet foods and pleasant smells, but rather desire the good and sweet fragrance of the virtues.

He must carefully guard his hands, feet, and all the members of his body, lest they become weapons of iniquity for sin, but rather that they may become powerful weapons of God for destroying the spiritual enemy. The soldier of Christ must above all keep his heart [Col. 1239D] under vigilant guard, lest boasting lift it up, anger inflame it, envy pierce it, greed harass it, lust burn it, sadness weigh it down, sluggishness and indolence burden it, and—what is more serious—lest heresy tear it apart through presumptuous novelties [the wording is uncertain].

For whoever strives through continence to keep the hidden places of the heart tranquil will certainly also guard the members of his body more easily from outwardly wicked acts. For it is written:

> “Guard your heart with all vigilance, because from it life proceeds” (Prov. IV, 23).

Again, elsewhere:

> “Death is placed beside the entrance of pleasure.”

And the Savior says in the Gospel:

> “The good man brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart, and the evil man brings forth evil from the evil treasure of his heart” (Matt. X, 35).

And again he says:

> “From the heart come evil thoughts, murders, [Col. 1240A] adulteries, fornications,”

and so forth.

Since, then, fruits both good and evil come forth from the root of the heart, we must first cleanse the heart and then discipline our flesh itself through fasts, vigils, and useful labor, lest the lust of the flesh stain the mind. For it is difficult for those who live in indulgence to have a pure heart. Therefore the Apostle said:

> “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected” (I Cor. IX, 27).

And again:

> “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. Let us live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us in order to redeem us and cleanse for himself from all [Col. 1240B] iniquity a people acceptable to him, devoted to good works, so that when he comes in his majesty with thousands of holy angels, he may grant us rewards for good labors and holy conduct, rather than repay us with everlasting torment for the desire and pleasure of the present life.”

Therefore, in order that we may be able to fight and resist the devil’s temptations and the desires of the flesh in an orderly and courageous manner, we must first know that there are eight principal vices through which the devil seeks to corrupt and deceive the human race: “pride with vainglory, anger, envy, greed, gluttony, lust, sadness, and acedia.”

From these roots the offspring of all vices arises and grows. Conversely, there are four principal virtues. These are “prudence, justice, temperance, and fortitude,” from which all the adornment of the virtues proceeds, and with which, aided by divine grace, every multitude of vices is overcome and crushed by Christ’s soldier.

## On Pride

The first and chief of the fiery darts of the ancient enemy is pride. Wherever it has entered, it drags behind it the troops of every vice. Its first offspring, and almost its partner in every iniquity, is vainglory. Our Creator especially detests this also. Hence it is written of it:

> “Every arrogance is an abomination before God” (Prov. XXVI, 5).

And again:

> “Pride is hateful before the Lord and before human beings” (Ecclus. X, 7).

And again:

> “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6).

The first and greatest sin of the devil was pride, and by it he deceived the first human beings. Hence it is written:

> “The beginning of pride made human beings apostatize from God, because their heart withdrew from the one who made them. For pride is the beginning of every sin; whoever holds fast to it will be filled with curses, and it will overthrow them in the end. Therefore the Lord dishonored the assembly of the wicked and destroyed them to the end. He destroyed the seats of proud leaders, and in their place made the meek sit. God dried up the roots of proud nations and planted the humble among those nations. The Lord overturned their lands and destroyed them to their foundations. He dried them up from among themselves and scattered them, and caused their memory to cease from the earth. God destroyed the memory of the proud and left the memory of the humble in understanding” (Ecclus. X, 14).

For this reason pride is worse than every vice. It often arises even from good actions, when a person takes pride in his good works; and through pride he loses what he had through charity. Pride is also the last of all vices, because when a person is adorned with virtues and begins to grow proud in them, he falls from a height.

As we have said, pride is the beginning of every sin: when the soul despises the Creator’s commandment, it immediately falls into the pit of some sin. For every pride lies so much lower the higher it raises itself, and falls so much more deeply the higher it has been lifted. Whoever is raised up by his own pride is condemned by God’s justice. Hence it is written:

> “Before a person’s fall, his spirit is exalted” (Prov. XVI, 18).

Therefore a Christian must avoid nothing more than pride, which provokes God’s anger. Pride made demons from angels, whereas humility made human beings like the holy angels.

The proud desire to be praised for things they do not do; the humble shrink from having whatever good they perform recognized. Let no one, then, become exalted in his goodness or seek praise for himself, even if he does something good. Rather, let him desire that God be praised in his gifts, since no one does anything good except what God has granted him to do. Therefore he ought to refer to God everything he does well, not to himself.

## On Anger

Since the Christian soldier strives to avoid the glory that pride, the source of every evil, has produced, he must necessarily also beware the vice of anger, which that same pestilence likewise engenders, lest, hurled by it into fury, he become opposed to God’s clemency and mercy. For our Lord and Savior, instructing us by his word and example in gentleness and patience, completely rejected obstinate anger and rage, so that what could not be fulfilled by the commandment of the Law might be perfected by the commandment of the Gospel.

The Law prohibited murder; but because it allowed the thing that is the seed of murder to arise, it did not entirely remove the vice itself. Our Redeemer, therefore, who came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, completed by his command what was lacking in the Law. He removed the occasion of anger and commanded us not only not to become angry or kill, but also to endure with the greatest patience whatever adversities others inflict upon us.

Anger is a certain suffering of the mind which, if it is not governed by reason, turns into fury, so that a person becomes unable to control himself and does what is unfitting. If anger takes hold in the heart, it removes all foresight from the person. He will be unable to seek the judgment of right discernment, to possess the virtue of honorable contemplation, or to have mature counsel; rather, he seems to do everything through a kind of precipitous impulse.

From it grow mental swelling, quarrels, insults, shouting, indignation, presumption, blasphemies, the shedding of blood, murders, the desire for vengeance, and the memory of injuries. It is overcome by patience and long-suffering, [Col. 1242A] by the intellectual reason that God implants in human minds, and by recalling the Lord’s Prayer, in which we say to God:

> “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

Therefore, if we desire to attain that supreme divine reward of which it is said,

> “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8),

we must not merely cut these things away from our hearts, but also uproot them from the innermost roots of the soul.

It will not greatly profit us if the fury of anger is restrained in speech and not brought into action, if God, who is not unaware of the secrets of hearts, perceives that anger remains hidden in the secret places of our breasts. It is as though every kind of poisonous serpent or wild beast, while remaining in the wilderness and in its lair, continued harmless, yet could not on that account be declared harmless simply because it harmed no one. This is not due to a disposition toward goodness in them, but to the necessity of their solitude. When they obtain an opportunity to harm, they immediately pour forth and display the venom stored within them and the savagery of their nature.

The Gospel teaching commands that the roots of vices be cut away rather than merely their fruits, which, once the sources have certainly been torn out, will never grow again. In this way the mind will be able to remain continually in all patience and holiness, when these things have been uprooted not from the surface of our actions and deeds but from the inner chambers of our thoughts.

For this reason, so that murder may not be committed, anger and hatred are cut down; without them the vice of murder cannot in any way be admitted. For:

> “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matt. V, 22).
>
> “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer”—

namely, insofar as he desires in his heart that the other perish, although it is recognized among human beings that he has shed none of his brother’s blood by his own hand or weapon.

The Lord declares a person to be a murderer through the feeling of anger, because he will repay each person with reward or punishment not only for the outcome of an action but also for the desire of the will and intention.

The distinguished preacher to the world says:

> “Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you” (Eph. IV, 31).

For the anger of a man cannot accomplish God’s justice, because anger without moderation is devoid of reason. A gentle answer calms anger; a harsh word stirs up fury.

> “An angry man,” says Solomon, “provokes quarrels; a patient man calms those that have been stirred up” (Prov. XV, 18).

Who could endure a spirit of pride that is easily provoked to anger? Such a person has no mercy, and erupting fury knows no end to vengeance.

If anger, O human being, has overtaken you, calm it. That anger is evil which disturbs the mind so that it loses sound counsel. Anger is just and necessary when a person becomes angry at his own sins and is indignant with himself when he acts wrongly. Hence the Prophet says:

> “Be angry and do not sin” (Ps. IV, 5).

He granted what belongs to nature and removed what belongs to guilt.

But there is something even more serious: one person asks for the death of an enemy, and the one whom he cannot pursue with a sword he pursues in prayer. The one who is cursed continues to live, yet the person who curses is already held guilty of his death. God commands that an enemy be loved, yet God is asked to kill an enemy. Whoever prays in this manner fights against the Creator with his impious prayers. Hence it is said under the figure of Judas:

> “Let his prayer become sin.”

For a prayer becomes sin when one asks for what the one being invoked himself forbids.

Therefore the Truth says:

> “When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you have in your hearts” (Mark XI, 25).

But suppose an enemy has seriously offended us, inflicted losses, harmed those who help us, and persecuted those who love us. These things would have to be retained if our sins did not also need to be forgiven. For our Advocate composed a prayer for us in our case, and he himself is the judge of that same case—the one who is our Advocate. He inserted a condition into the prayer he composed, saying:

> “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

Since, then, the very Judge who came is the one who became our Advocate, and the one who made the prayer is the one who hears it, we either say, without doing what we say, “Forgive us our debts,” and the rest, thereby binding ourselves by these words; or perhaps we omit this condition from the prayer, and our Advocate does not recognize the prayer he composed and immediately says to himself: “I know what I taught; this is not the prayer I made.”

What, then, must we do except show true affection of charity toward our brothers and, just as we keep our hands outwardly innocent of slaughter, keep our hearts inwardly innocent of hatred?

## On Envy

So much for anger. Now we must speak of envy, because through the devil’s deception some people regard being jealous of what is good and envying those who are better as a slight and insignificant crime. Since it is thought slight and insignificant, it is not feared; what is not feared is despised; what is despised is not easily avoided. Thus it becomes a blind and hidden destruction which, because it is not clearly perceived, secretly afflicts minds that are unable to guard against it.

From the very beginning of the world, through it the devil was the first both to perish and to destroy. No one should think that this evil is confined to a single form or enclosed within brief boundaries and a narrow limit. Envy has wide scope, many forms, and a fertile destructiveness. It is the root of all evils, the fountain of disasters, the seedbed of offenses, and the material of sins.

From it hatred arises; from it hostility proceeds. Envy inflames greed: when someone could be content with his own possessions, he envies another whom he sees to be richer. Envy arouses ambition when someone sees another greater in honors, while it blinds our senses and brings the secrets of the mind under its own power. The fear of God is scorned, Christ’s teaching is neglected, and the day of judgment is not anticipated.

Pride is inflated, savagery embittered, impatience shaken, discord driven into frenzy, and anger heated. The person who has become subject to another’s power can no longer restrain or govern himself.

From this the bond of the Lord’s peace is broken; from this fraternal charity is violated; from this truth is adulterated and unity divided, leading to heresies and schisms—when priests are disparaged, bishops are envied, and someone either complains that he himself was not ordained or disdains to accept another’s appointment. Hence he kicks back and rebels: proud through envy, perverse through rivalry, an enemy not of the person but of the person’s honor through hostility and resentment.

What kind of soul is that, and what corruption of thought in the breast, what rust, to envy in another either his virtue or his happiness—that is, to hate in him either his own merits or the divine gifts; to turn another’s good into one’s own evil; to be tortured by the prosperity of the illustrious; to make another’s glory one’s own punishment?

Other evils have an end, and whatever crime is committed is terminated when the crime is completed. In the adulterer, the offense ceases once adultery has been committed; in the robber, the wickedness comes to rest once murder has been committed; the plunderer sets a limit to his rapacity once the booty has been obtained; and the forger’s deceit reaches its measure once the fraud has been completed.

Envy has no limit. It remains an enduring evil and a sin without end. The more the person who is envied advances through better success, the more fiercely the envious person burns in the fire of resentment. Hence come a threatening face, a grim expression, pallor in the countenance, trembling lips, gnashing teeth, rabid words, unrestrained insults, and hands ready for violent slaughter—even if they are presently empty of a sword, they are armed with the hatred of a frenzied mind.

Whoever conceals [his hatred] and hates his brother is stained by the crime of murder. The Apostle John declares this in his Epistle, saying:

> “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has life abiding in him” (I John III, 15).

And again:

> “Whoever says that he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness; he walks in darkness and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes” (I John II, 19).

> “Whoever hates his brother,” he says, “walks in darkness and does not know where he is going.”

Thus, ignorant, he is hurled into Gehenna; unaware and blind, he is cast into punishment, withdrawing from the light of Christ, who warns and teaches:

> “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness but will have the light of life” (John VIII, 12).

We shall undoubtedly please him if we now remain free from all envy and resentful jealousy and love our neighbors with true affection, because the peacemakers are sons of God, and whoever loves his brother is born of God and sees God.

Thus, since we have shown in a few words how great the evil of envy and hatred is—

## On Greed

We must not remain silent about how harmful the plague of greed is. It is therefore entirely fitting for the Christian who is striving toward the heavenly kingdom and eager to receive the riches above to restrain himself from present things and flee, like deadly poison, the evil of love of money—which especially captivates the human race—lest he desire to obtain something through fraud or retain through rapacity what he has acquired for his own use. For every fraud displeases God, and the Apostle compares greed with idolatry.

> “Nothing is more wicked than a greedy person,” says Scripture. “Why are earth and ashes proud? Nothing is more unjust than to love money. For such a person has sold his own soul” (Ecclus. X, 9).

Greed, which the Greeks call *philargyria* (love of money), is an excessive desire to acquire or retain riches. This plague is insatiable and resembles and is compared to the disease of dropsy. Just as a dropsical person becomes thirstier the more he drinks, so the greedy person, the more money he acquires, the more he desires to possess; and while he has no limit in possessing, he has no limit in desiring.

From this arise envy, thefts, robberies, murders, lies, perjuries, plunder, violence, restlessness, unjust judgments, contempt for truth, forgetfulness of future blessedness, and hardness of heart, which is opposed to mercy and almsgiving toward the poor and competes with every form of piety.

Our Lord, therefore, who admonishes us to be generous from our possessions toward the poor and wretched, himself forbids us every form of greed and every unjust acquisition of money. The one who says:

> “Give alms from your just labors,”

himself urges us through his Apostle, saying:

> “Do not defraud one another” (I Cor. VII, 5).

For whoever acquires anything through any kind of fraud loses the equity of justice.

The Lord himself also says in the Gospel:

> “Beware of all greed, because a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of what he possesses. Do not the rich die in the same way as the poor?” (Luke XII, 15).

Riches cannot help on the day of vengeance, nor will they free those who use them wrongly from everlasting punishments.

If we wish to know how pernicious and harmful this fuel is, unless it is carefully cut out, and how, if it is seized, it bears fruit for the destruction of the one who has seized it and sprouts with every kind of branch of vice, let us look to Judas, counted among the number of the Apostles. Because he did not wish to crush the deadly head of this serpent, let us see how it killed him with its poison and, entangled in the snares of desire, drove him into the crime of so precipitous a fall that he persuaded himself to sell the world’s Redeemer and the author of human salvation for thirty pieces of silver.

He would never have fallen into so wicked a crime of betrayal if he had not been infected with the disease of love of money; nor would he have become guilty and sacrilegious through denying the Lord, unless he had first been accustomed to pilfer the money entrusted to him. Yet although many detest Judas’s crime, few strive to avoid it.

Everyone judges the man who sold the Lord to be guilty, but the one who exchanges truth for a lie is scarcely reproached by anyone. For whoever sells truth for love of money or earthly advantage loses Christ and becomes a participant in Judas’s crime. The Lord himself says:

> “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6).

The one who sells truth for money abandons life, and through this wretched bargain he merits not eternal life but is plunged into the punishment owed to falsehood.

Therefore the Apostle Paul warns us and says:

> “The time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they did not have them; those who weep as though they did not weep; those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice; those who buy as though they did not possess; and those who use this world as though they did not use it. For the form of this world is passing away” (I Cor. VII, 29).

The man who has a wife as though he did not have one is the one who strives to please his spouse without displeasing the Creator. He weeps, but as though he did not weep, when he is afflicted by temporal losses in such a way that he nevertheless continually consoles his mind with eternal gains. He rejoices, but as though he did not rejoice, when he takes delight in temporal goods while always considering everlasting torments and immediately weighs down with prudent fear the mind that temporal joy lifts up.

He buys, but as though he did not possess, when he prepares earthly things for use but carefully foresees that he will soon leave them behind. He uses the world, but as though he did not use it, when he gathers externally all that is necessary for the service of his life but does not allow these same things to rule his mind, so that they serve outwardly as subjects and never break the intention of the soul that strives toward higher things.

Therefore, all such people have all earthly things present not for desire but for use. They use what is necessary, but desire to possess nothing together with sin. From the very things they possess they acquire daily rewards, and they take greater joy in a good work than in a good possession.

With these matters understood and seen according to the truth, we must now consider bodily sins and how serious they are.

## On Gluttony

The first bodily sin is gluttony, that is, the immoderate pleasure of food or drink. Through it the first parents of the human race lost the happiness of paradise and were cast into the wretched misery of this life, where every human being is born through sin, lives through labor, and dies through sorrow.

Who could adequately enumerate what, and how much, contempt for abstinence took away from our first parent? He had been endowed with the dignity of an intellectual mind and received the image of his Creator; subject only to his God, he saw all visible things subject to himself; by divine command the abundance of every tree in paradise served him freely for the necessities of life; and the tree of life supplied, by the gift of its Creator, a mystical food—not merely by which he might live, but by which the life of his body would not come to an end.

As long as it was received, this food preserved the one who received it in a single condition through the figurative meaning of a hidden sacrament, so that it would not allow him to be corrupted by any illness, changed or aged by time, or dissolved by death.

Troublesome anxiety did not disturb the tranquil; anxious labor did not weary the idle; sleep did not oppress the unwilling; fear of losing life did not torment one secure in immortality. His body, healthy in every part, had easy nourishment and tranquil movement; his heart was pure; he was ignorant of punitive evil; he was an inhabitant of paradise, free from sin, capable of God.

Finally, who could be happier than one to whom the world was subject, who was hostile to none, whose mind was free, and to whom God was visible? For unless Adam had been accustomed, before sin, to see God in the assumption of visible creation, how could he, after becoming a sinner, hide from the face of a God whom he had never seen?

Adam could therefore see God before he sinned, just as the holy patriarchs saw him. But when he said:

> “I heard your voice, and I was afraid” (Gen. III, 10),

he had already fallen from that holiness of seeing God, having transgressed God’s command through gluttony.

Gluttony appears to reign in a person in three ways: when someone desires to anticipate the canonical and appointed hour for eating on account of gluttony; when he orders more elaborate foods to be prepared than the body’s need or the condition of his person requires; or when, in eating or drinking, he takes more from the desire of his immoderation than benefits his health.

But this must be understood: no delicacies cause harm if they are consumed without desire, and cheap foods often contribute to the progress of abstinence when they are taken appropriately. Thus the holy David chastised the desire for water within himself and poured out the water offered to him by his men, lest he seem to satisfy his desire through it; and the holy Elijah was not harmed by eating meat when he had not desired it.

From this it is understood that those who truly abstain condemn not the natures of foods but their desires, and mortify their own wills through deprivation of desired food or drink. Those who wish to abstain not only from the quality but also from the quantity of foods strive for nothing else than to indulge only as much as seems sufficient to refresh the stomach and remove hunger. They do not satisfy their appetites through greedy consumption, but restrain them; and they allow their will, rather than satiety in eating, to set the limit. Thus they will abstain both from craving expensive foods and from the mind’s desire for cheap ones.

What should I say now about abstaining from or consuming wine? The holy Apostle established a definite rule, saying:

> “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Eph. V, 18).

As though he were saying: it is excessive consumption of wine, not its nature, that produces and nourishes debauchery. Therefore I prohibit you not from using wine but from becoming drunk. For moderate use of wine strengthens a weak stomach, whereas drunkenness weakens both mind and body.

Those who, while wine is denied them, flood themselves with portions of various other drinks do not seem to me to fulfill abstinence. Perhaps they abstain from wine for this very reason: to earn praise from people, while compensating themselves for the forbidden wine with more pleasant drinks.

Likewise, those who abstain from quadrupeds but enjoy fattened birds or fish do not seem to me to cut away the pleasures of the body but to change them. For there are some among the number of false abstainers who wish to appear more sparing in this respect and seek glory for themselves as though from a distinctive abstinence. They judge that one must abstain from all animals, yet fill the appetite of their body with exotic fruits, delicate little drinks, and other such things, whereas spiritual abstinence urges the restraint not of the use of certain foods but of desire.

Those should be considered more devoted to frugality who forbid themselves not the consumption of certain things but the pleasures of the body.

We do not say these things, however, as though we were criticizing the rule of monks that prohibits the eating of quadrupeds, or as though we were forbidding penitents to abstain from eating meat. We say them to teach how the vice of gluttony must be avoided. For one who abstains from wine and meat must not be excessively greedy with other foods or drinks, but must be sober and moderate in everything.

What benefit is it for someone to abstain from wine and meat yet consume other foods or drinks to the point of indigestion or vomiting, when it is not the kind of food but merely gluttony and drunkenness that constitutes the vice?

Therefore let us consider how carefully we should strive to observe the laws of sobriety at our meals. Just as we must beware of gluttony and drunkenness, so we must also be continent with respect to defamatory speech and foolish talk, as well as empty jokes.

Let us reject the games and songs of mimes and actors as deadly poison, because they are the devil’s seduction and fabrications. Let us always remember that rich man of the Gospel who, buried in hell, begged that his burning tongue be cooled, because during his banquets he had previously devoted himself to gluttony and empty talk.

Let us hear the Apostle speaking to us:

> “Whether we eat or drink, or do anything else, let us do everything for the glory of God” (I Cor. X, 31).

## On Fornication
These things concerning gluttony may suffice. Now let us proceed to see what Holy Scripture teaches concerning its companion, namely fornication. The holy apostle Paul, writing to his disciples, says: “Flee fornication. Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the fornicator sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6:18) [Col. 1248C].

He wished to magnify the evil of fornication above all other sins. Although other sins also involve the body, they do not bind and subject the human mind to carnal desire in the way that the act of bodily fornication does: for through lust it causes the mind to become involved with the body itself, to be somehow joined and fastened to it, so completely that at the very moment and in the experience of so great a crime a person can think of or attend to nothing except what he has given himself over to. The very submersion—and, so to speak, absorption—of lust and carnal desire makes the mind captive.

Therefore the Apostle commanded that this great evil be fled, not so much in place as in disposition, because it is difficult to resist once it has taken the heart captive through desire. Hence God, the Creator and Maker of the human race, knowing above all the nature and correction of his workmanship, applied the remedy precisely where he knew the causes of the disease chiefly arose: “Whoever,” he says, “looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28) [Col. 1248D].

By pointing to wanton eyes, he rebukes not so much the eyes themselves as the inner sense that misuses their service in looking. For the heart, sick and wounded by the dart of lust, looks in order to desire; and, unwillingly turning to the service of wicked deeds the benefit rightly granted to it by the Creator, it brings forth within itself the hidden disease of desire on the occasion of looking.

For this reason he gave it a saving commandment: the worst sickness of this vice proceeds from the occupation of sight. It is not said, “Guard your eyes with all vigilance”—though they certainly ought principally to be guarded if the inclination to desire proceeded from them—but, “Guard your heart with all vigilance.” The remedy was applied especially to that which everywhere can misuse the ministry of the eyes.

Therefore let us strive to extinguish the wanton movements of our thoughts at their beginning, before they bring forth the fruits of sin, and let us dash the little ones of the daughter of Babylon against the rock—that is, let us immediately crush the suggestions of fornication and thoughts of impurity by recalling Christ’s commandments [Col. 1249A].

No virtue so properly enables carnal people to follow spiritual angels in their manner of life as the merit and grace of chastity. Through it, while still dwelling on earth, they possess, according to the Apostle, citizenship in heaven—the condition which is promised to the saints in the future, once carnal corruption has been laid aside, but which they already possess here in fragile flesh.

Let us therefore hear how the aforementioned Apostle of the Gentiles, writing to the Thessalonians, placed this virtue above all others: “This is the will of God, your sanctification” (1 Thess. 4:3) [Col. 1249B]. And lest he leave us uncertain or unclear about what he wished to call sanctification—whether justice, charity, humility, or patience, since sanctification is believed to be acquired through all these virtues—he immediately explains and plainly indicates what he specifically wished to call sanctification: “This is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication; that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God.”

You see with what praises he commends it, calling it the honor and sanctification of our vessel, that is, of our body. Conversely, the person who is in the passion of desire remains in dishonor and impurity and is estranged from sanctification.

A little later he again declares it to be holiness: “God has not called us to dishonor, but to holiness. Therefore whoever despises these things does not despise a human being, but God, who has also given us his Holy Spirit” (1 Thess. 4:7–8) [Col. 1249C]. He thus binds inviolable authority to his command, saying, “Whoever despises these things”—that is, the matters concerning holiness of which I have spoken—“does not despise a human being”—that is, me, who command these things—“but God,” who speaks through me and who has also appointed our heart as a dwelling place for his Holy Spirit [Col. 1249D].

Let us therefore discuss these matters among ourselves, turn them over frequently in our minds, and hasten with all our strength to accomplish this: that, chaste in body, we may deserve to become a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit.

Those who are joined in marriage should preserve conjugal chastity and not defile themselves in the brothel of prostitutes or concubines. Let the man know only his lawful wife, and the woman only her lawful husband [Col. 1250A]. Whoever transgresses this is without doubt held guilty of adultery.

Those who are not yet joined in marriage and lead a celibate life should observe chastity until the proper time for marriage and not pollute themselves with the disgrace of fornication, because it is written: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. 13:4).

Those who have undertaken the purpose of virginity should preserve it without any reproach, lest they be shut out from the wedding feast of the eternal King with the foolish virgins. Rather, together with the prudent, shining with the merits of good works, let them enter adorned into the banquet of the heavenly Bridegroom.

Likewise, those who have professed widowhood should not turn back, but should direct their attention to the reward of the heavenly calling, so that they may attain it. Therefore, all of us together who hold the Catholic faith, let us hear the Apostle saying to us: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2) [Col. 1250B].

## Concerning sadness

We must be no less vigilant against the plague of worldly sadness, because, unless it is avoided, it is the surest bringer of death. Hence the Apostle admonishes us, saying: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice. Let your moderation be known to all. The Lord is near. Be anxious about nothing, but in every prayer and supplication let your requests be made known to God” (Phil. 4:4–6) [Col. 1250C].

Since those who seek God and believe his promises are commanded always to be joyful and to rejoice, they are plainly forbidden to be sorrowful in a destructive manner.

There is also a kind of sadness that is pestilential and deadly. It seems to have the power to seize our soul indiscriminately through its successive courses and various occasions; at every moment it removes us from the contemplation of God and utterly weakens and depresses the mind, cast down from its entire state of purity. It does not allow the mind to complete its prayers with the accustomed cheerfulness of heart; it does not permit it to rest upon the remedies of sacred reading; it does not allow it to be tranquil and gentle toward the brethren; and it makes it impatient and harsh in every work and religious duty. When every wholesome counsel has been lost and the steadfastness of the heart disturbed, it makes a person appear insane and drunk [Col. 1250D].

It breaks and overwhelms the understanding with punitive despair. Therefore, if we care properly for the contests of spiritual struggle, we must labor no less attentively here to cure this disease.

For just as the moth harms clothing and the worm wood, so your sadness harms the heart. The divine Spirit has expressed the force of this harmful and destructive vice with sufficient clarity and precision. A garment consumed by moths can no longer, when touched, have any value or honorable use; and wood bored through by worms will no longer deserve to be assigned to ornament or even to an ordinary building, but only to the burning fire.

There is also a still more detestable kind of sadness, which inflicts upon the sinner not correction of life or amendment of vices, but the most destructive despair of the soul [Col. 1251A]. It did not make Cain repent after the murder of his brother, nor Judas hasten after his betrayal to the remedies of satisfaction; rather, through despair it dragged him to the noose of hanging.

Therefore only one kind of sadness should be judged useful to us: when we are stirred by repentance for sins, by the desire for perfection, or by contemplation of future blessedness. Concerning this the blessed Apostle says: “The sadness that is according to God produces repentance leading to enduring salvation; but the sadness of the world produces death” (2 Cor. 7:10).

That sadness which produces repentance leading to enduring salvation is obedient, gracious, humble, gentle, sweet, and patient, since it descends from the love of God. It extends itself tirelessly, through desire for perfection, to every bodily pain and contrition of spirit; and, in a certain sense, joyful and invigorated by the hope and progress of its advancement, it retains all the sweetness of graciousness and patience, possessing within itself all the fruits of the Holy Spirit, which the same Apostle enumerates: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, faith, gentleness, kindness, self-control” (Gal. 5:22–23) [Col. 1251B].

The other kind of sadness, however, is extremely harsh, impatient, fruitless, full of bitterness and fear, hard and despairing. It breaks and turns back from industrious and salutary sorrow the person whom it has embraced, as irrational sadness that not only interrupts the effectiveness of prayer but also empties all the spiritual fruits mentioned above, which the other kind knows how to bestow [Col. 1251C].

Therefore, apart from that sadness which is undertaken either for salutary repentance, or for the pursuit of perfection, or from desire for future things, all sadness—as belonging to the world and bringing death—must equally be rejected and utterly driven from our hearts, just like the spirit of fornication, avarice, or anger.

We can drive this most destructive passion from ourselves if we continually occupy our mind with spiritual meditation and raise it through hope for the future and contemplation of the promised blessedness. In this way we shall be able to overcome every kind of sadness: whether it descends from preceding anger, arises from the loss of profit or injury inflicted upon us, is generated by an insult committed against us, proceeds from irrational confusion of mind, or brings deadly despair upon us. We shall overcome them when, always joyful and steadfast through contemplation of external things and of the future, we are neither cast down by present circumstances nor elated by prosperity, regarding both as fleeting and soon to pass away [Col. 1251D].

## Concerning acedia

The eighth and final poison among the eight principal vices is acedia. From it arise tepidity of mind and harmful sluggishness, which make a person useless for every good work and inclined toward destruction.

Hence it is written: “Idleness is the enemy of the soul.” The devil, the enemy of every good thing, injects it into a person through the aforementioned disease of acedia, so that he causes the person to grow torpid uselessly and not labor at all in good works [Col. 1252A].

Acedia is a pestilence that is shown to do great harm to those who serve God. An idle person grows sluggish in carnal desires: he neither rejoices in spiritual work, nor delights in the salvation of his soul, nor takes pleasure in assisting his brother’s labor. Instead, he merely covets and desires, moving aimlessly through everything while occupied in idleness.

When it besieges a wretched mind, it infects it with many miseries, which teach many evils. From it arise sleepiness, laziness in good work, instability of place, wandering from one place to another, tepidity in labor, weariness of heart, murmuring, and idle talk. The soldier of Christ conquers these through devotion to reading, constant good work, desire for the rewards of future blessedness, confession of the temptation present in his mind, steadfastness in his place and purpose, exercise in every kind of skill and labor or prayer, and persistence in vigils, so that the servant of God may never be found idle [Col. 1252B].

For the devil finds it more difficult to discover an opportunity for tempting a person whom he finds engaged in good work than one whom he finds idle and doing nothing good.

The wisest Solomon also very clearly notes this vice of idleness in many passages, saying: “Whoever pursues idleness will be filled with poverty,” whether visible or invisible, “because every idle person must be held entangled in every vice and must always remain estranged from the contemplation of God, or from spiritual riches” (Prov. 28:19).

Concerning these the blessed Apostle says: “In everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge” (1 Cor. 1:5) [Col. 1252C].

Idleness has taught many evils. The Apostle plainly enumerates them, saying: “We hear that some among you walk disorderly, doing no work but acting as busybodies” (2 Thess. 3:11).

Immediately he adds a certain remedy for this vice: “We ask you, brothers, to make it your endeavor to be quiet, to attend to your own affairs, to work with your hands, and to walk honorably before those who are outside, desiring nothing from anyone” (2 Thess. 3:12).

And noting those who are disorderly and rebellious, he commands the diligent to separate themselves from them, saying: “We command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly and restlessly, and not according to the tradition which you received from us” (2 Thess. 3:6) [Col. 1252D].

He immediately explains what that tradition was, saying: “You yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, because we were not disorderly among you, nor did we eat anyone’s bread without paying for it; rather, in labor and toil, working night and day, we labored so as not to burden any of you—not as though we had no authority, but so that we might give you ourselves as an example for you to imitate” (ibid., v. 7).

What kind of Christian, then, is the person who, when he rises in the morning from the bed of his drunkenness, does not devote himself to some useful work, does not go to church for the sake of prayer, does not hurry to hear the word of God, does not strive to give alms, and does not endeavor to visit the sick or assist those who suffer injury [Col. 1253A]—but either goes out hunting, or stirs up quarrels and disputes at home, or spends himself uselessly at dice, in stories, and in jokes, until his food is prepared by servants who are laboring?

And if something has been prepared by the servants according to his wishes in a lesser quantity because of some unavoidable circumstance, he suddenly blazes up and immediately rushes to exact vengeance. Thus, while he enjoys himself at the banquet, the servant is tortured outside.

But why do they act in this way, except that they do not think about the future and do not consider God’s judgment in their minds? If they rightly foresaw the day of their death, they would never entangle themselves in such madness.

Does not the wise die in the same way as the foolish, the rich as the poor, the noble as the ignoble? Does not the flesh of the rich swarm with worms just as does that of the beggar? Behold, the rich man is led with pomp to the tomb, but none of those who attend him deigns to remain with him in the grave. Just as he was born here alone, so he will leave here alone.

Why is this? Before burial, mortals do not willingly take thought for what everyone will necessarily be forced to do after death. Behold, every day, willingly or unwillingly, we hasten toward death, yet we do not consider what our end will be after death.

For we must all be brought before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what is proper to the body according to what he has done, whether good or evil. But since no one can properly fight against vices unless he strives to have the assistance of holy virtues:

## Concerning the four principal virtues

It must be understood that these four kinds of principal virtues which we enumerated above—namely prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance—from which the entire order and sequence of the virtues arises, are necessary for every Christian. For the pestilential diseases of vices are overcome in no other way than by the remedies of spiritual medicines [Col. 1253C].

The authority of the holy Scriptures strongly commends to us the exaltation and nobility of these sacred virtues, so that through their abundance we may strive to be fit for the service of Christ.

That these four are principal virtues, and as it were certain fountains from which the other virtues flow, is held not only by philosophers but also by our own teachers. As we have already shown, they wished their names to be prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance [Col. 1253D]. They confer such holiness upon the Christian soul that there is no perfection whatsoever that is not found in these virtues.

For if prudence makes a person prudent, justice just, fortitude courageous, and temperance temperate, I do not know what could be more perfect than one who acts prudently, justly, courageously, and temperately.

Virtue is a disposition of the soul, the beauty of nature, the rule of life, and the nobility of character. Its principal parts are four, as has often been said. The first is prudence, which consists in the investigation and discovery of truth.

It awakens memory in the mind, grants understanding to the intellect, and adorns foresight with counsel. It enlightens spiritual people who have been cleansed of carnal vices, and illuminates with the desire to contemplate truth those who have been overturned by every harmful pleasure of curiosity, so that, having attained knowledge of human and divine matters, they may truly become prudent and wise [Col. 1254A].

Let them foresee impending evils and guard against them at the same time. Let them understand prudently that there are no evils except those that make people evil, and let them accept that nothing in this world happens by chance or unjustly, but that all things happen either by God’s will or by his permission. Let them either teach others wisely when they understand matters differently, or correct them; let them neither harm others nor promise harm to themselves.

The Lord commanded in the Gospel that people become such, saying: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16), because the simple cannot deceive others, nor do the prudent allow themselves to be deceived.

But if, in any contract, conversation, or other matter, a person does not allow himself to be deceived yet deceives someone else, he does not possess prudence, which is the cause of salvation rather than destruction. He is merely pretending. For virtue differs from vice in this respect: vice corrupts what is sound, whereas virtue heals what has been corrupted by the inflammation of vice [Col. 1254B].

If someone thinks about another’s destruction or rejoices in the downfall of one who is perishing, he himself must perish first, before he destroys the other; and the destruction that he desires for another begins with him.

Justice, the second principal part of virtue, is a disposition of the soul that assigns to each thing its proper dignity. In it are preserved the worship of God, the rights of humanity, and the equity of the whole of life.

Therefore, if in this life we strive to fulfill justice—whose proper work is to give each person his due—let us render ourselves to God, by whom we were made, and let us not permit those things over which we have been naturally placed to rule us [Col. 1254C]. Let reason rule the vices; let the body be subjected to the soul, and the soul to God—and the whole perfection of the human being has been fulfilled.

There are, conversely, two kinds of injustice: one, when we inflict injuries; the other, when we neglect to repel injuries inflicted by others, even though we are able to do so, and refuse to defend the oppressed when we can rescue them from oppression. It benefits me nothing that I do not deceive or defraud anyone if I permit another to be deceived or defrauded.

The same may be understood concerning sins. If I see someone sinning and not only fail to rebuke him but even consent to his sin, I make myself a participant in his condemnation. I sin in all sins when, through a certain cruel wickedness of heart, I do not rebuke those whom I know to have sinned or to be sinning [Col. 1254D].

Fortitude, the third in the order of the principal virtues, is the endurance of dangers and labors with greatness of spirit. Its parts are magnificence, confidence, patience, and perseverance.

Magnificence is the thoughtful planning and administration of great and exalted matters, accompanied by a certain broad and splendid purpose of mind.

Confidence is that by which the mind places a firm trust in itself, together with sure hope, in great and honorable matters.

Patience is the voluntary and prolonged endurance of difficult or arduous things for the sake of honor or usefulness.

Perseverance is steadfast and perpetual continuance in a course of action that has been carefully considered.

These qualities are especially fitting for those who are distinguished by the honor of the Christian name, so that they may bring beginnings undertaken well to a good end through pious and discerning effort [Col. 1255A].

Temperance, then, is the fourth kind of virtue: a rational, firm, and moderate dominion over lust and over other disordered movements of the soul. Its parts are self-restraint, clemency, and moderation.

Self-restraint is that by which every evil desire is governed and subdued through the powerful direction of deliberation.

Clemency is that by which quarrels and hatreds are restrained with a gentle spirit.

Moderation is that by which concern for propriety preserves the proper measure of the whole of life, whether in the movements of the soul or of the body.

Great honor before human beings and praise before God belong to the person who observes these things.

Therefore let us strive through good zeal and pious labor to observe them and worthily perform the service of Christ, and above all to walk in the way of justice and truth [Col. 1255B], because it is written: “The righteous Lord loves righteousness; his face beholds equity” (Ps. 10:7). And elsewhere: “Justice delivers from death” (Prov. 10:2). Again: “Whoever follows justice and truth will find life, justice, and glory.”

We therefore have a strong helper and a merciful protector, namely the Mediator between God and human beings, concerning whom it is written: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and justice has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84:12).

Therefore let us despair in nothing and lose hope in nothing, but place all our hope of salvation in him, because it is written of him: “He will not forsake all who hope in him” (Ps. 33:23), and, “His mercy is from generation to generation for those who fear him.”

Since these things are truly so, we now think that we must speak of the fraud of the ancient enemy and of the vigilance you need against his snares [Col. 1255C].

Everyone who is enlisted in the Christian service must vigilantly and cautiously watch against the wickedness of the ancient enemy, lest he be led astray by his deceitful fabrications. For the cunning enemy, seeking various wounds with which to strike the heavenly soldier, sometimes wounds him by stealth with an arrow from his quiver, and sometimes brandishes a spear before his face. For he conceals some vices under the appearance of virtues and places others, in their open form, before the soldier’s eyes.

Wherever he sees God’s soldier growing weak, he does not seek coverings for his fraud. But wherever he sees him resisting firmly, there he undoubtedly prepares deceit against his strength.

When he sees someone weak in the allurements of the flesh, he openly places before his eyes the appearance of a body capable of being desired. But if he happens to see someone strong against avarice, he persistently suggests to his thoughts the poverty of his household, so that while the mind is bent, as if piously, toward providing for them, it may be secretly led astray and unjustly seized by the pursuit of possessions [Col. 1255D].

Often he proposes a temptation of lust and then, suddenly withdrawing with greater deceit, suggests pride concerning the chastity that has been preserved. There are some who, seeing many fall from the stronghold of chastity into the pit of pride, neglect the guardianship of their life and sink into the impurity of lust.

Others, conversely, while fleeing the impurity of lust, fall through the height of chastity into the abyss of pride [Col. 1256A].

Thus, guilt arising from vice is like a spear striking openly, while guilt arising from virtue is like an arrow wounding secretly from the quiver. But the prudent discernment of the saints, looking carefully in every direction, detects guilt placed on high before it arrives; and the more watchfully it marks it beforehand, the more firmly it avoids it.

The first concern of the soldier of Christ must be not to commit any evil. In the second place, he must consider how not to perform good things carelessly; and after he has subdued wickedness, he must also strive to subdue what is right within himself, lest, if these things pass beyond the dominion of the mind, they turn into the guilt of pride.

For, as was said above, evils often arise from good things through the vice of negligence. Therefore he carefully observes how arrogance arises from teaching, cruelty from justice, laxity from piety, anger from zeal, and sluggishness from gentleness [Col. 1256B].
