When he performs these good works, he observes what enemies may rise against him through them. When he labors to attain the studies of teaching, he prepares his anxious mind for the battle against arrogance. When he desires justly to punish the faults of sinners, he most carefully avoids allowing the cruelty of vengeance to exceed the measure of justice.

When he strives to restrain himself through piety, he diligently watches lest he be overcome by some dissolution of discipline. When he arouses the goads of righteous zeal, he takes the greatest care lest the flame of anger kindle him more than necessary. When he moderates himself with great tranquility of gentleness, he watches attentively lest he grow cold through sluggishness.

Because every vice is perceived by the thought of the spiritual soldier before it can steal upon him, it is rightly said of him in the Book of Job: “He smells the battle from afar” (Job 39:25) [Col. 1256C].

Let us, according to the Apostle, put on the breastplate of justice and the helmet of salvation, carrying the shield of faith, with which we can extinguish all the fiery darts of the evil one, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

Let us restrain ourselves from wicked actions; let us guard our mouths from harmful and idle speech; and let us beware lest we be wounded by evil thoughts, lest we lose through the folly of pride the victory we have gained through steadfastness.

Let us also strive to preserve patience in all adversities that come upon us, because our enemy is defeated in no other matter more effectively; every day he plots how he may destroy us. For our Lord says: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19) [Col. 1256D].

Patience is enduring the evils of another with equanimity and not being wounded by pain against one’s neighbor who inflicts evil.

It must nevertheless be understood that patience is usually exercised in three ways. Some things we endure from God, others from the ancient adversary, and others from our neighbor. From our neighbor we endure persecutions, losses, and insults; from the ancient adversary, temptations; from God, chastisements.

But in all three forms the mind must watch over itself with vigilant attention: lest, in response to the evils of a neighbor, it be dragged into repaying evil with evil; lest, in response to the temptations of the adversary, it be seduced into delighting in or consenting to sin; and lest, in response to the chastisements of the Creator, it rush into excessive murmuring [Col. 1257A].

The adversary is perfectly defeated when our mind, amid his temptations, is guarded against delight and consent; amid our neighbor’s insults, is guarded against hatred; and amid God’s chastisements, is restrained from murmuring.

## Concerning confession and repentance

Nevertheless, if the soldier of Christ is in any way led astray by the deceitful enemy or overcome by the frailty of the flesh, he must not despair. Rather, he must strive through true confession, worthy repentance, and the compunction of tears to recover himself, obtain pardon for his sins from the merciful Judge, and, through vigorous practice of good works, deserve to return to the state of his former life and attain the reward of the promised recompense.

## Concerning compunction

Compunction of heart arises from the virtue of humility. From compunction comes confession of sins; from confession, repentance; and from repentance proceeds the forgiveness of offenses [Col. 1257B].

Compunction of heart is humility of mind accompanied by tears, remembrance of sins, and fear of judgment. Tears usually flow from the genuine spring of compunction when the mind carefully considers the evil of its deeds, or when it sighs with desire for eternal life.

Hence the Prophet says: “My soul thirsted for the living God. When shall I come and appear before the face of God? My tears have been my bread day and night” (Ps. 42:2–3).

There are likewise four qualities of affection by which the thought of the just person is pierced with salutary grief: the memory of past crimes, remembrance of future punishments, consideration of one’s pilgrimage amid the misery of this life, and desire for the heavenly homeland, so that one may reach it as quickly as possible [Col. 1257C].

When these things take place in a person’s heart, it must be understood that God is then present to the human heart by grace. Hence it is also said in the Psalm: “I have declared my life to you, and you have placed my tears in your sight, as in your promise” (Ps. 56:8).

The promise of forgiveness that we have from God arouses the tears of repentance in our hearts. But compunction is salutary only when it urges a person to confess his sins and to turn toward a better life.

Therefore Holy Scripture frequently urges us to flee to the remedy of confession—not because God needs our confession, since everything we think, say, and do is already present to him, but because we cannot otherwise be saved unless, in repentance, we confess what we have done wickedly through negligence [Col. 1257D].

Whoever accuses himself of his sins gives the devil no opportunity to accuse him again on the day of judgment, provided that, by confessing and repenting, he wipes away what he has done and does not renew the deeds he committed.

“Confess,” says the apostle James, “your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James 5:16).

Likewise the blessed Apostle Paul says: “With the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

Solomon also spoke concerning confession of sins: “Whoever hides his crimes will not be set right, but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy” (Prov. 28:13) [Col. 1258A].

It is a great remedy of salvation not to repeat the wicked things we have done, nor to reopen the former scar of our wounds.

Hence the evangelist John says: “If we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (1 John 1:9).

Likewise the Psalmist says: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Ps. 32:5).

## Concerning not delaying conversion to God
While alive, let the sinner confess what he has done, because confession is not fruitful in hell, nor is repentance effective for salvation. Behold, now is the time of salvation; behold, now is the acceptable time before God. Now is the time of forgiveness for those who repent, but after death there will be a time of vengeance for those who neglected to confess their crimes. For all the ungodly have bitter repentance amid their punishments, but their repentance does not benefit them for forgiveness; rather, their conscience torments them, increasing the punishments they suffer. They could have guarded themselves against the enormity of their torments through confession, but they neglected to do so. Thus, just as they are tormented outwardly by flames, so inwardly they are tormented by their own conscience.

How can a physician heal what the sick person is ashamed to show? For God desires our confession, so that he may have a just reason to forgive. Whoever conceals his sins and is ashamed to confess them for his own healing will have God, whom he has as witness, again as his avenger. A person judges himself most wisely in this life, lest he be judged by God with everlasting condemnation.

Every sinner ought to have a twofold lament in repentance: either because through negligence he failed to do good, or because through boldness he committed evil—because he failed to do what should have been done, and did what ought not to have been done. For the Savior displayed the power of repentance in the Gospel, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. III, 2). And John the Baptist said: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (ibid., v. 8). A worthy fruit of repentance is to mourn past sins and not commit them again, as Scripture says: “Do not add sin upon sin and say, ‘The mercy of God is great,’ since mercy and wrath come from him” (Ecclus. V, 5).

[Col. 1258B]

“Wash yourselves,” says the Lord through the prophet Isaiah, “and be clean” (Isa. I, 16). Therefore, the one who both mourns past deeds and does not again commit deeds requiring mourning is washed and clean. The one who mourns what he has done but does not abandon it, and after his tears repeats the things he had wept over, is washed but not clean.

Concerning those who return to their former crimes after their tears, blessed Peter says terrifyingly: “A dog has returned to its own vomit” (II Pet. II, 21). “Son, if you have sinned,” it is said in Holy Scripture, “do not add to it again, but pray concerning your former sins, that they may be forgiven you” (Ecclus. XXI, 1).

True repentance is not measured by the number of years but by the bitterness of the heart. Hence blessed Peter immediately received forgiveness from the Lord, because he wept most bitterly over the guilt of his threefold denial. Repentance, even if it lasts only a short time, is not despised by God, the just judge, if it is undertaken with the innermost bitterness of heart, for he considers the secrets of the heart. God does not require so much the length of time as he weighs the sincerity of the penitent’s devotion.

Whoever trusts in Christ with his whole mind, even if he dies with many sins, has a faith that lives forever, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John XI, 25). He spoke of the death of the soul, which comes upon it because of the sickness of sins.

God is merciful by nature. Through mercy he is ready to save those whom he did not come to save through justice; he desires all human beings to be saved and no one to perish. Through the Prophet he says: “On whatever day the sinner turns, he shall live and shall not die” (Ezek. XXXIII, 12). However sinful and ungodly a person may be, if he turns to repentance, let him not doubt that he can obtain forgiveness through God’s mercy.

In this age, God’s mercy comes to the aid of those who repent; in the future, however, repentance is of no benefit, and we shall give an account of our deeds. Only in this life is the freedom to repent available; after death there is opportunity for correction. Therefore, each of us must hasten to turn to God while he can, lest, when he wishes too late, he be wholly unable to do so. We must always fear the final day, which we can foresee.

[Col. 1259B]

Behold, we have received this very day on which we are speaking as a postponement for conversion, and yet we refuse to mourn the evils we have committed. We not only fail to lament what we have done, but also increase the things that will require lamentation. Yet if some illness were to seize us, if signs of sickness announced approaching death, we would seek a postponement of death so that we might mourn our sins; and we would beg for it with great ardor of desire—though, when granted now, we regard it as worthless.

Let us now weigh the riches of our Creator’s goodness toward us. He saw us sinning and endured it. He who prohibited us from sinning before the offense does not cease, even after the offense, to await us for forgiveness. Behold, he himself, whom we despised, calls us. We have turned away from him, yet he does not turn away from us. Hence it is said through Isaiah: “Your eyes shall see your teacher, and your ears shall hear the voice of one admonishing you from behind” (Isa. XXX, 20).

A person was admonished face-to-face when, created for righteousness, he received the commands of uprightness. But when he despised these same commands, he gave his mind’s back, as it were, to his Creator’s face. Yet behold, the Creator still follows behind and admonishes him, because although he has already been despised by us, he nevertheless does not cease to call us. We have, as it were, turned our backs to the face of him whose words we disregard and whose commands we trample underfoot. But he stands behind us and calls us back, seeing what is despised and nevertheless crying out through his commands and waiting with patience.

Let us therefore consider whether, if a servant of any one of us suddenly became arrogant toward his master and turned his back to his face, that master, having been despised, would not strike down his arrogance and inflict wounds in strict punishment.

[Col. 1259C]

Behold, by sinning we have turned our backs to the face of our Creator, yet we are endured. He kindly calls back those who have arrogantly turned away; and although he could strike us as we turn away, he promises gifts so that we may return. May such great mercy from our Creator, I beg, soften the hardness of our guilt, and may a person who, when struck, could have been made to experience the evil he did at least be ashamed when granted time to wait.

Let us therefore have confidence in the mercy of our Creator. Let us consider what we are doing and reconsider what we have done. Let us look upon the generosity of heavenly goodness and come with tears to the merciful judge while he still waits. Let us consider that he is just, and therefore not neglect our sins. Let us consider that he is compassionate, and therefore not despair.

The God-man gives a human being confidence before God; he is great hope for us who repent, because our judge has become our advocate. Therefore, we must hear that he is merciful and turn away from sins, remembering that he is just. Let us fear to depart from righteousness, lest, having begun good works, we abandon them without bringing them to completion, lest what is written come to pass: “All who see it will begin to mock him, saying, ‘This man began to build and was unable to finish’” (Luke XIV, 29).

For, in accordance with Paul’s statement, we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings; and in everything we do we must consider our hidden adversaries, who are always intent upon our works and always rejoice in our failure. Observing them, the Prophet says: “My God, in you I trust; I shall not be put to shame, nor shall my enemies mock me” (Ps. XXIV, 2).

For if, while intent on good works, we do not watch carefully against evil spirits, we suffer mockery at the hands of those whom we have as agents of evil. Therefore, we must consider carefully lest we perish through faintheartedness, lest our spiritual enemies—of whom we have countless numbers—when they see that we have fallen from the state of righteousness, make all our labor, at the end of our life, a mockery for themselves and turn our life into reproach against us.

[Col. 1259D]

For whatever sort of people we are found to be when the soul departs, such we shall certainly be judged by our Creator. Hence it is written: “The Lord will judge the ends of the earth” (I Sam. II, 10). It does not help us to have begun well if we happen to end badly.

## On Good Perseverance

[Col. 1260D]

Therefore, so that we may persevere patiently in the good we have begun, divine mercy must be implored, so that the mercy that went before us may follow us through all the days of our life.

We must think deeply about how terrifying the hour of our dissolution will be: what fear and sorrow there will then be, how great the memory of all evils, what forgetfulness of past happiness, and what dread and contemplation of the judge. What, then, ought to be a source of delight to us in the present, when, although all things are passing away together, what is imminent cannot pass away; when what is loved is completely coming to an end, and that begins where pain never ends?

[Col. 1261A]

Then, when the soul departs, evil spirits seek their own works; they repeat the evils they suggested, so that they may drag their companion with them to torments. But why do we speak of this only concerning a wicked soul, when they come even to the departing elect and, if they prevail, seek something of their own in them?

For there was one person who, before his passion, said openly: “I will no longer speak much with you. For the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV, 30). Because he saw this man as mortal, the prince of the world believed that he could find something of his own in him. But Christ departed from the corruption of the world without any sin, just as he came into the world without sin.

Neither did Peter presume to say this about himself, although he deserved to hear: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 19). Nor did Paul presume to say it, although before he paid the debt of death he reached the mysteries of the third heaven. Nor did John dare to say it, although because of his exceptional love he reclined at the breast of his Redeemer at the supper.

For when the Prophet says: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Ps. L, 7), no one who came into the world with guilt could be in the world without guilt. Hence the same Prophet says: “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII, 2). Hence Solomon says: “There is no person on earth who does good and does not sin.” Hence John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I, 8). Hence James says: “For we all offend in many ways” (James III, 2).

[Col. 1261B]

It is certain, and we cannot deny it, but confess it truthfully: the prince of this world has much in us. Nevertheless, at the time of our death he is no longer able to seize us, because we are members of the one in whom he has nothing.

But what does it profit that we are joined to our Redeemer by faith if we are separated from him in our conduct? For he himself says: “Not everyone who says to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII, 21).

Therefore, right works must be joined to right faith. Let us mourn through daily lamentation the evils we have committed. Let our past wickedness be overcome by the upright works that arise from love of God and neighbor. Let us refuse no good that we are able to bestow upon our brothers.

For we cannot otherwise become members of our Redeemer except by cleaving to God and sharing in the suffering of our neighbor. The one fit for the kingdom of heaven is the person who strives above all to possess love of God through keeping his commandments to the end of life, and who openly demonstrates love of neighbor through works, helping him in his needs as far as he is able.

[Col. 1261C]

Considering these things, let us fight the good fight, strive to complete the course of our contest, and take care to preserve the faith. Let none of us presume upon his own righteousness, but, forgetting what lies behind, let each continually reach forward to what lies ahead, pursuing the prize of the heavenly calling until he attains it.

No one knows what is being decided concerning him in God’s hidden judgments, for “many are called, but few are chosen.” Since no one is certain that he himself is chosen, it remains that all should tremble, all should fear concerning their conduct, all should rejoice in divine mercy alone, and no one should presume upon his own strength.

There is one who perfects our confidence: namely, the one who deigned to assume our nature in himself.

[Col. 1261D]

# Three Books of Blessed Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda and Archbishop of Mainz, On Seeing God, Purity of Heart, and the Manner of Repentance, Addressed to Abbot Bonosus

[Col. 1261]

# Book One: On Seeing God

[Col. 1261D]

The apostolic saying admonishes us (Rom. XII, 3) “not to desire to be wiser than one ought to be,” but to be wise unto sobriety and according to the rule of faith. The same apostle also urges us to strive to do whatever we do prudently and according to order, saying: “Let everything of yours be done honorably and according to order” (I Cor. XIV, 40).

Therefore, I am astonished that some of our people, observing neither time nor proper measure, debate during their banquets, amid their cups, about the secrets of God and heavenly mysteries—how, after this life, the elect will see the Lord in the heavenly kingdom—as though the occupation of a tavern and that of contemplation were the same, and as though a cup of wine could confer upon its lovers in a single hour what they previously refused to meditate upon attentively and for a long time in the Sacred Scriptures.

[Col. 1262D]

This is especially astonishing since the Psalmist calls blessed those “who walk blamelessly in the way, in the law of the Lord, and who search out his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart” (Ps. CXVIII, 1). And lest anyone suddenly or imprudently presume to debate about the invisible and ineffable God, the same prophet says in the person of the Lord: “Be still and see how I am God” (Ps. XLV, 11).

For whoever neglects to be still for God hides from himself, by his own judgment, the light of God’s vision. Whoever indiscreetly involves himself in disturbances and permits the tumult of temporal affairs to revolve within his mind becomes altogether incapable of searching out the secrets of the invisible God. Those who have learned from the Lord God Jesus Christ to be meek and humble of heart make greater progress by thinking and praying and by seeking him with a simple heart than by debating and contending in superfluous discussions.

That one must not devote oneself to contentious questions in this way Paul shows when, writing to his disciple, he says: “Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they generate quarrels. But the servant of the Lord must not quarrel; rather, he must be gentle toward all, teachable, patient” (II Tim. II, 23).

Therefore, whoever wishes to search out or discuss heavenly mysteries ought first to strive to cleanse his heart of worldly desires and the filth of vices, and only then hope, through God’s grace, to be able fully to perceive spiritual gifts. Hence the aforementioned apostle teaches, saying: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind and put on the new person, who was created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth” (Eph. IV, 23).

[Col. 1263A]

And again: “Put to death,” he says, “your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols. Because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience. In these things you too once walked, when you lived among them. But now you too must put away all these things: anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, and shameful speech from your mouth. Do not lie to one another. Strip off the old person with his deeds, and put on the new person, who is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of the one who created him. There is neither gentile nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all” (Col. III, 5).

[Col. 1263B]

For the image of God, who is incorporeal, is not in the human body, which is subject to corruption and weighed down according to the desires of error, but in the spirit and soul. For God is spirit, and he searches all things; nor is it possible for anything earthly and fragile to be compared with his height and eternity, because he is the life that gives life to all things. He alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light.

For he is the true light “which enlightens every person coming into this world.” Therefore, whoever desires to enjoy contemplation of that light in eternal blessedness must cleanse his heart during the pilgrimage of this life, because otherwise he will not be able to attain the vision of the one concerning whom the Truth itself says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8).

[Col. 1263C]

But because our friends requested this of me, and especially because King Louis urged me, I have been compelled to write something about the future vision of God. I shall attempt to undertake this not according to my own opinion but according to the tradition of the holy doctors and Catholic Fathers; and, either by setting forth their judgments or, for the sake of brevity, explaining their meaning in my own words, I shall strive to show as far as I understand it.

Blessed Augustine wrote about this in many places, especially in his letter to Paulina on seeing God, where he does not conceal what he himself thought or what the other holy Fathers before him had written. For in that same letter he says:

“So we believe that we shall see God—not because we have seen him either through the eyes of the body, as we see this sun, or through the mind’s inward gaze, as each person sees himself within: sees himself living, sees himself willing, sees himself seeking, sees himself knowing, sees himself not knowing.

“Thus, when you have read these words, you remember that you have seen the sun through the eyes of the body. You can also see it immediately, if it is the appropriate time and you are in a place where the sky is open before your eyes in the direction of the sun.

“But for seeing those things that I have said are perceived by the mind—that you are alive, that you wish to see God, that you seek this, and that you know yourself to be alive, willing, and seeking, while you do not know how God is seen—for seeing all these things, I say, you do not use the eyes of the body, nor do you sense or seek any interval of place through which your gaze might be extended so as to reach them and perceive them.

[Col. 1263D]

“Thus you see your life, your will, your seeking, your knowledge, and your ignorance, because you see all these things in yourself and possess them within yourself. Without any outlines of figures or brilliance of colors, you perceive them all the more clearly and certainly the more simply and inwardly you contemplate them.

“Since, then, we do not now see God either with the eyes of the body, as we see bodies, whether heavenly or earthly, or with the mind’s gaze, as we see those things—some of which I have mentioned—that you contemplate with complete certainty within yourself, why do we believe that he is seen, unless we give faith to Scripture, where it is written, ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God,’ and to whatever else has been written with the same divine authority in this sense? We consider it impious not to believe that authority, while we have no doubt that believing it is an act of devotion.

“Let us also say that seeing and believing differ in this respect: present things are seen, absent things are believed. Perhaps it is sufficient if here we understand ‘present things’ to mean those that are available to the senses, whether of the mind or of the body; hence they are also called ‘present,’ from the word itself.

“Thus I plainly see this bodily light through the senses, and I likewise plainly see my own will, because it is available to the senses of my mind and is present within me. But if someone tells me his will, although his mouth and voice are present to me, nevertheless, because the will he reveals to me is hidden from my bodily and mental senses, I believe it; I do not see it. Or, if I think he is lying, I do not believe it—even if what he says should happen to be true.

“Therefore, things that are absent from our senses are believed if the person who bears testimony concerning them appears trustworthy. Things that are present are seen through the senses, whether of the mind or of the body, and are therefore called ‘present.’

[Col. 1264A]

“Our knowledge, then, consists of things seen and things believed. In matters that we have seen or see, we ourselves are witnesses; in matters that we believe, we are moved to faith by other witnesses, when signs of things that we neither remember having seen nor see are given in voices, writings, or any other records, through which unseen things are believed when the signs are seen.

“We are not without reason said to know not only what we have seen or see, but also what we believe because we have been moved by suitable testimonies or witnesses concerning each matter. Moreover, if we are correctly said to know even what we believe with complete certainty, this is why we may also rightly be said to see with the mind what is not present to our senses.

“For knowledge is attributed to the mind, whether it retains and recognizes something perceived through the bodily senses or through the mind itself; and faith itself is therefore seen by the mind, although by faith one believes what is not seen.

“Hence the apostle Peter says: ‘In him, though you do not now see him, you believe’ (I Pet. I, 8); and the Lord himself says: ‘Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed’ (John XX, 29).

[Col. 1264B]

“For the things that one sees are present to the senses, whether of the mind or of the body; but the things that one believes are absent from both the mental and bodily senses. Nevertheless, the will of the one from whom he hears that he should believe is not past but remains in the speaker; the speaker himself sees it within himself. The one who hears, however, does not see that will but believes it.

“The resurrection of Christ, however, is past, and not even those human beings who were present at that time saw it as it occurred. For those who saw the living Christ, whom they had seen dying, nevertheless did not see the resurrection itself as it was taking place; rather, they believed it with complete certainty by seeing and touching alive the one whom they had known to be dead.

“We believe the whole: that he rose again, that he was then seen and handled by human beings, and that he now lives in heaven, no longer dies, and that death no longer rules over him. The reality itself is not present to the senses of our body, as this heaven and earth are present, nor to the gaze of our mind, as the faith itself is present by which we believe this.

“Let us come to the matter at hand. We know that God can be seen, because it is written: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’ (Matt. V, 8).

[Col. 1264C]

“Or perhaps I ought not to have said ‘We know,’ but ‘We believe,’ since we have never seen God with the body as we see this light, nor with the mind as we see within ourselves the faith by which we believe this. Have we not merely believed, because it is written in the Scripture to which we are faithful, that this is true, without the slightest doubt?

“Yet when the apostle John said something of this kind, he said: ‘We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is’ (I John III, 2). Behold, he said that he knew what had not yet happened and what he had come to know not by seeing but by believing.

“Thus we rightly said, ‘We know that God can be seen,’ although we have not seen him but have believed the divine authority contained in the holy books.

“What, then, is the meaning of that same authority when it says, ‘No one has ever seen God’?

[Col. 1264D]

“Or perhaps the answer is that those testimonies concern seeing God, not having seen him. For it says, ‘They shall see God,’ not ‘They saw’; and not ‘We have seen,’ but ‘We shall see him as he is.’ Therefore, these statements are not contrary to: ‘No one has ever seen God’ (John I, 18). Those who wished to be children of God with pure hearts shall see the one whom they have not seen.

“What, then, is the meaning of: ‘I saw God face to face, and my soul was saved’ (Gen. XXXII, 30)? Is this also contrary to what was said, ‘No one has ever seen God’?

“And what of what is written about Moses, that ‘he spoke with God face to face, as one speaks with his friend’ (Exod. XXXIII, 11)? And what of what the prophet Isaiah says about himself: ‘I saw the Lord of Hosts sitting upon a throne’ (Isa. VI, 1)? And if there are other similar testimonies that are customarily brought forward from the same authority, how are they not contrary to the statement that ‘no one has ever seen God’?”

The Gospel itself too may seem to contradict itself. For how is it true when it says, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father also” (John XIV, 9), if no one has ever seen the Lord? How is it true: “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matthew XVIII, 10), if no one has ever seen God? By what rule of interpretation, then, shall we prove that these statements, which seem contrary and opposed, are neither contrary nor opposed? For it is in no way possible that the authority of these Scriptures should lie in any respect.

If we say that, in the statement “No one has ever seen God,” only human beings are to be understood, just as it is said: “No one knows what is happening in a person except the spirit of the person that is in him” (1 John IV, 12)—that is, no one among human beings—then certainly this cannot be understood of God, since it is written of Christ that he had no need for anyone to bear witness to him concerning a person, because he himself knew what was in a person. The Apostle, explaining this more clearly, says: “Whom no human being has seen or can see” (1 Timothy VI, 16). If, then, “No one has ever seen God” was said as though it meant “No human being has ever seen him,” that question will seem resolved to this extent: the Lord’s statement, “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matthew XVIII, 10), will not be contrary to it, since we are to believe that angels see God, while “no one has ever seen God” is understood to mean: no human being.

How, then, did Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Job, Moses, Micah, Isaiah, and all the others—if there are any—see God, concerning whom the most truthful Scripture bears witness that they saw him, if no human being has ever seen God or can see him? Yet some, wishing to prove that even the ungodly will see God, think that God was seen even by the devil himself, understanding what is written in the Book of Job: that he came with the angels and that the devil came into God’s presence. Thus the question also arises how it was said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew V, 8), and: “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Hebrews XII, 14).

I am greatly astonished if those who suppose that the ungodly will see God, and that God was seen by the devil, go so far as to assert that such people are pure in heart and pursue peace and holiness with all. For the Lord’s saying, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John I, 9), may, on closer consideration, not appear contrary to what he said: “No one has ever seen God” (John I, 8). For he did not say, “Because you have seen me, you have seen the Father also”; rather, by saying, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also,” he wished to show the unity of the Father’s and the Son’s substance, lest they should be thought in any respect unlike one another.

And so, since it is true that “Whoever sees me sees the Father also,” then, since no human being has ever seen God, no one should be thought to have seen either the Father or the Son, insofar as the Son is God and, with the Father, is one God. But insofar as he is human, he was certainly seen on earth and lived among human beings.

Yet the great question is how it is not contrary to the statement that so many of the ancients saw God, if no human being has ever seen God, nor can see him. You see what a difficult question you have set before me, from which you wanted me to write at length and in abundance, taking the occasion of my brief letter, which seemed to you to require more careful and fuller explanation.

Would you therefore be willing to attend to what I have meanwhile discovered among other distinguished interpreters of the divine Scriptures concerning what they thought about the vision of God, in case it should satisfy your desire, although perhaps you already know it? Attend, then, if you please, to these few points.

When blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan, was expounding the Gospel and had come to the passage where the angel appeared in the temple to the priest Zechariah, observe how much and how important a discussion he offered on the vision of God as well.

“Not without reason,” he says, “the angel is seen in the temple, because the coming of the true priest was already being announced and a heavenly sacrifice was being prepared, in which the angels would minister. And he is rightly said to have appeared to the one who suddenly saw him. Scripture commonly maintains this especially concerning angels and God: that what cannot be foreseen is said to appear. Thus you have: ‘God appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mamre’ (Exodus VI, 3). Because he is not perceived beforehand, but is seen by a sudden glance, he is said to appear.

“For sensible things are not seen in the same way as the one whose will determines whether he is seen, and whose nature is not to be seen, though it is his will to be seen. For if he does not wish it, he is not seen; if he wishes it, he is seen. God appeared to Abraham because he wished to; to others, because he did not wish to, he did not appear.

“It also seemed to Stephen, when he was being stoned by the people, that heaven was opened; Jesus was also seen standing at the right hand of God, yet he was not seen by the people. Isaiah saw the Lord Sabaoth, but he could not be seen by others, because he appeared to the one to whom he was pleased to appear.

“And why should we speak of human beings, when we have even read concerning the heavenly powers and authorities themselves that ‘no one has ever seen the Lord’ (John I, 8)? And he adds that, beyond the heavenly powers, the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, himself declared him. Therefore it must either be accepted that, if no one has ever seen God the Father, the Son was seen in the Old Testament—and let heretics cease to assign a beginning to him from the Virgin, since he was seen before he was born from the Virgin—or else it cannot be denied that either the Father, or the Son, or certainly the Holy Spirit—if indeed there is a vision of the Holy Spirit—is seen in whatever form the will has chosen, not in one formed by nature, since we also understand that the Spirit was seen in the form of a dove.

“And therefore ‘no one has ever seen God,’ because no one has looked upon or comprehended with mind or eyes that fullness of divinity which dwells in God. ‘Saw’ must indeed be referred to both. Finally, when we hear, ‘The only-begotten Son himself declared him,’ this signifies a vision of minds more than of eyes. A form is seen, but power is declared: the former is grasped by the eyes, the latter by the mind.

“But what shall I say about the Trinity? The seraph appeared when he wished to, and Isaiah alone heard his voice. An angel appeared, and is now present, but is not seen. For it is not in our power to see, but in his power to appear. Nevertheless, although the power of seeing is not ours, there is a grace by which we may merit the ability to see; and therefore the one who has received grace has merited the opportunity. We do not merit that opportunity, because we do not possess the grace of seeing God.

“And what wonder is it if, in the present age, the Lord is not seen unless he wishes to be? Even in the resurrection itself it is not easy to see God except for those who are pure in heart; and therefore: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’ (Matthew VIII, 5). How many blessed people had he already numbered, and yet he had not promised them the ability to see God?

“If, then, those who are pure in heart will see God, certainly others will not see him. The unworthy will not see God, nor can the one who has not wished to see God see him. Nor is God seen in a place, but by the pure in heart; nor is he sought with bodily eyes; nor is he circumscribed by sight; nor held by touch; nor heard through speech; nor perceived by his walking. When he is thought absent, he is seen; and when he is present, he is not seen.

“Finally, not even all the apostles saw Christ, and therefore he said: ‘I have been with you so long, and you still do not know me’ (John XIV, 9)! For whoever has understood what is the length and breadth and height and depth, and the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, has seen Christ and has seen the Father.

“For we no longer know Christ according to the flesh, but according to the spirit. For Christ the Lord is the Spirit before our face; may he deign by his mercy to fill us with all the fullness of God, so that he may be seen by us.”

God, then, is invisible in nature—not only the Father, but the Trinity itself, the one God. And because he is not only invisible but also immutable, he appears to those to whom he wishes, in whatever form he wishes, in such a way that his invisible and immutable nature remains intact with him. But the true desire of the godly, by which they long and burn ardently to see God, does not, I think, burn to contemplate that form in which he appears as he wishes, which is not himself, but that substance in which he is what he is.

The holy Moses, his faithful servant, displayed the flame of this desire when he said to God, with whom he spoke face to face as with a friend: “If I have found favor before you, show me yourself” (Exodus XXXIII, 13). What, then? Was that not himself? If it is not himself, Moses would not say to him, “Show me yourself,” but rather, “Show me God.” And yet, if he were seeing his nature and substance, he would even less say, “Show me yourself.”

He himself, therefore, was present in the form in which he had wished to appear. But he was not appearing in his own nature, which Moses desired to see and which is promised to the saints in the life to come.

Thus the answer given to Moses is true: “No one can see my face and live” (ibid., v. 20)—that is, no one living in this life can see him as he is. For many saw him, but they saw what the will chose, not what nature formed; and what John says, if it is rightly understood—“Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John III, 2)—does not mean that we shall see him as human beings saw him when he wished to be seen, in the form in which he wished to appear, not in his nature, which remained hidden in itself even when he was seen. Rather, we shall see him as he is—the very thing Moses asked of him when he said, “Show me yourself,” he who spoke with him face to face.

This does not mean that anyone has ever comprehended the fullness of God, not only with the eyes of the body but even with the mind. For it is one thing to see, another to comprehend the whole by seeing. That is seen which is present and perceived in both respects; but the whole is comprehended by seeing when it is seen in such a way that nothing of it is hidden from the one who sees, or when its boundaries can be surveyed. For example, nothing of your present will is hidden from you, while the boundary of your ring can be surveyed.

I have given two examples: one pertains to the mind’s vision, the other to bodily eyes. For sight, as he said, must be referred to both—that is, to eyes and to the mind.

Moreover, if “no one has ever seen God” for this reason: as the interpreter whose words we are considering says, no one has looked upon or comprehended the fullness of his divinity, either with mind or eyes—“saw” must be referred to both.

It remains to inquire how the angels see God, because of the statement he recalled from the Gospel: “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matthew XVIII, 10). For if he appears even to them not as he is, but in a form he chooses, while his nature remains hidden, then it must be asked all the more how we shall see him as he is, just as Moses desired when he asked God, who was present before him, to show him himself (Exodus XXXIII, 13).

For this is promised to us as the supreme reward in the resurrection: that we shall be equal to the angels of God. And so, if they themselves do not see him as he is, how shall we see him in that way when we have become equal to them in the resurrection?

But observe what our Ambrose says next. “Finally,” he says, “when it is added, ‘The only-begotten Son himself will declare him,’ this signifies a vision of minds more than of eyes. A form is seen, but power is declared. The former is comprehended by the eyes, the latter by the mind.”

Shortly before, he had said that vision must be referred to both; now he assigns it not to the mind but to the eyes—not, I think, because he was heedless in considering his own words, but because in ordinary speech we are accustomed to attribute vision to the eyes, just as we attribute form to the body. This manner of speaking is also used more frequently with respect to things contained in places and distinguished by colors.

But if there were no form to be contemplated by the mind, it would not be said of him: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Psalm XLIV, 3). For this was not said according to the flesh, but according to spiritual form.

Therefore, when the Only-Begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, declares him, rational, pure, and holy creation is filled with an ineffable vision of God, which we shall attain when we have become equal to the angels. For no one has ever seen God in the way these visible things, known through the senses of the body, are seen. If he was ever seen in some way, he was not seen as this nature is seen, but was seen by his will, appearing in the form he wished, while his nature remained hidden and immutable in itself.

In the manner in which he is seen as he is, he may perhaps now be seen by certain angels. But he is not thus seen [will not thus be seen] by us when we have become equal to them. Then, after adding that “the heavenly powers, like the seraphim, are not seen unless they wish to be and in whatever manner they wish,” so that from this too the great invisibility of the Trinity might be inferred, he nevertheless says: “Although the power of seeing is not ours, there is a grace by which we may merit the ability to see”; and therefore the one who has received grace has merited the opportunity. We do not merit that opportunity, because we do not possess the grace of seeing God.

In these words, then, by which he is not teaching his own doctrine but explaining the Gospel, he did not wish it to be understood that some of those who believed and were given power to become children of God would see God while others would not, since the statement “we shall see him as he is” applies to all of them. But by saying, “We do not merit the opportunity, because we do not possess the grace of seeing God,” he indicated that he was speaking of this age, in which God has deigned to appear to some—not in his own nature, but in whatever form he wished—such as to Abraham, Isaiah, and others like them.

To countless others, however, although they belong to his people and to the eternal inheritance, he does not reveal himself even in such a form. But in the age to come, all who will receive the kingdom prepared for them from the beginning will see him with pure hearts; and no others will be in that kingdom.

Pay attention, then, to what he adds, beginning to speak of that age: “And what wonder,” he says, “if in the present age the Lord is not seen except when he wishes to be? Even in the resurrection it is not easy to see God except for those who are pure in heart. And therefore: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.’ How many blessed people had he already numbered, and yet he had not promised them the ability to see God? If, then, those who are pure in heart will see God, certainly others will not see him. The unworthy will not see God, nor can the one who has not wished to see God see him.”

You see how carefully he speaks now of those who will see God in the age to come: not everyone, but those who are worthy.

For both the worthy and the unworthy will rise for that kingdom in which God will be seen, since all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come forth, but with a great distinction. Those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment. Here “judgment” signifies eternal punishment, as in the statement: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John III, 18).

When blessed Ambrose says, “Nor can the one who has not wished to see God see God,” what else did he wish to be understood except that the one who is unwilling to devote himself to purifying his heart—a task worthy of so great a matter—does not wish to see God? Observe, therefore, what he adds: “Nor is God seen in a place, but by the pure in heart.”

What could have been said more clearly and explicitly? From this vision, then, the devil and his angels, and all the ungodly with them, are excluded without any shadow of doubt, because they are not pure in heart. Accordingly, when it is written in the Book of Job that the angels came into God’s presence and that the devil came with them, the devil should not for that reason be believed to have seen God. For they are said to have come into the presence of God, not God into their presence.

Nor is it necessary to linger here and try, to the extent of our abilities, to show how this too occurs temporally, since all things are always in God’s presence. The question now is how God is seen—not in the form in which, even in this age, he wished to appear to certain people, when he spoke not only with Abraham and other righteous persons but also with Cain the fratricide, but how he is seen in that kingdom where his children will see him as he is.

Then their desire will be satisfied with good things. Moses burned with this desire; speaking to God face to face was not enough for him, and he said: “Show me yourself plainly, so that I may see you” (Exodus XXXIII, 13), as though he were saying what is sung in the Psalm from the same desire: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Psalm XVI, 15).

Philip too burned with this desire and wished to be satisfied in this way when he said: “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John XIV, 8–9).

Speaking of this vision, Ambrose himself, its lover and desirer, says: “God is not seen in a place, nor as at the oak of Mamre, nor as on Mount Sinai”; but by the pure in heart. He continues, knowing what he desires, what he burns for, and what he hopes for:

“God is not sought with bodily eyes,” he says, “with which he showed himself to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and others in this age; nor is he circumscribed by sight, because of the statement, ‘You shall see my back’; nor held by touch, as when he wrestled with Jacob; nor heard through speech, as he was heard not only by so many saints but also by the devil; nor perceived by his walking, as when he once walked in paradise toward evening.”

You see how this holy man strives to call our minds away from all bodily senses, so as to make them fit for seeing God. Yet what does such an external planter and waterer accomplish, unless God, who gives the growth, works within? For who, without the help of the Spirit of God, could think that there is something which is greater than all the things perceived through the body—something that is not seen in a place, not sought with the eyes, not heard through speech, not held by touch, not perceived by walking, and yet is seen by the pure in heart?

He was not speaking of this life when he said these things. For, by distinguishing with complete clarity the life of the future age from this age in which God appeared—not as he is, but in the form he wished, to those to whom he wished—he said: “And what wonder if in the present age the Lord is not seen except when he wishes to be? Even in the resurrection it is not easy to see God except for those who are pure in heart. And therefore: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.’”

At this point he began to speak of that age in which they will see God—not all who will rise, but those who will rise to eternal life; not the unworthy, concerning whom it is said, “Let the ungodly be taken away, lest he see the glory of the Lord,” but the worthy, of whom the Lord himself spoke when he was not seen in this way: “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments”; and: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and show myself to him” (John XIV, 21).

Nor will they be the ones to whom it will be said, “Depart into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew XXV, 41), but those to whom it will be said, “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world” (ibid., v. 34).

The former will go into eternal punishment, but the latter into eternal life. And what is eternal life except what Life itself says elsewhere: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3)?

But they will know him in the way he promised to show himself to those who love him, as one God with the Father—not as in this age, when he was seen in the body by the good and the wicked. For in the future judgment, when he will come in the same way in which he was seen going into heaven—that is, in the same form of the Son of Man—those to whom he will say, “I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matthew XXV, 42), will see that same form. For the Jews too will see the one whom they pierced, not that form of God in which he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized.

In that divine form those who see him as he is will then see him. They will not see him merely because in this life they were poor in spirit, meek, mourning, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, merciful, peacemakers, or persecuted for righteousness’ sake—although those who are pure in heart are indeed the same people who possess all these qualities. For this reason, among all those beatitudes, although those with a pure heart possess them all, nowhere is it stated, “They shall see God,” except where it says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, because he who is not seen in a place, is not sought with bodily eyes, is not circumscribed by sight, is not seen by touch, is not heard through speech, and is not perceived by walking will be seen by the pure in heart” (Matthew V, 8). “No one has ever seen God” (John I, 8)—either in this life as he is, or even in the life of the angels, in the manner in which these visible things are perceived by bodily sight—for the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, himself declared him.

Thus the statement that he declares him pertains not to the vision of bodily eyes but to the vision of minds. Yet again, lest our desire should pass from one bodily sense to another—from the eyes to the ears—after saying, “God is not sought with bodily eyes, nor circumscribed by sight, nor held by touch,” he also added, “nor heard through speech.” In this way, if we are able, we may understand the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, declaring him as the Word—not a sound resounding in the ears, but an image made known to minds—so that there, in inner and ineffable light, what was said, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV, 9), may shine clearly. This was said here to Philip when he was seeing and yet not seeing.

The distinguished lover of this vision, Ambrose, continues:

“And when he is thought absent, he is seen; and when he is present, he is not seen.”

He did not say, “When he is absent,” but, “When he is thought absent.” For the one who fills heaven and earth is nowhere absent; he is not enclosed by spaces, nor spread out through small or great regions, but is wholly everywhere and contained by no place.

Whoever understands this with a transcending mind sees God even when he is thought absent. But the one who cannot do so should pray and act in order to merit the ability, and should not knock at the door of a human interpreter so that he may read what he has not read, but at the door of God the Savior, so that he may become able to do what he cannot do.

Yet the question may arise how the very substance of God could already have been seen by certain people living in this life, because of what was said to Moses: “No one can see my face and live” (Exodus XXXIII, 20). This is possible only because the human mind can, by divine action, be carried away from this life into the life of the angels before it is separated from the flesh by the common death.

Thus was carried away the one who heard there ineffable words that it is not permitted to a human being to speak. There the mind was so turned away from the senses of this life that, whether he was in the body or outside the body—that is, whether, as commonly happens in a more intense ecstasy, the mind had been withdrawn from this life into that life while the bodily bond remained, or whether a complete dissolution had occurred, as happens in full death—he said that he did not know.

Thus both statements are true: “No one can see my face and live,” because the mind must be withdrawn from this life when it is taken up into the ineffability of that vision; and it is not unbelievable that certain saints, although they had not yet died in such a way that their bodies remained to be buried, were nevertheless granted this surpassing revelation.

Furthermore, when the Apostle writes to the Ephesians (Ephesians III, 14):

“For this reason I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person; that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, rooted and founded in love, so that you may be able, with all the saints, to comprehend what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled into all the fullness of God”—

I am accustomed to understand these words of the Apostle Paul in this way: in breadth, the good works of love; in length, perseverance unto the end; in height, hope of heavenly rewards; in depth, the inscrutable judgments of God.

From this source grace comes to human beings. May he deign by his mercy to fill us with all the fullness of God, so that he may be seen by us.

Now, however, carefully consider what you had proposed to me and what seemed difficult to explain, whether it has been explained, by recalling what has been said. If you ask whether God can be seen, I answer: He can. If you ask how I know this, I answer: because it is written in the most truthful Scripture: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8), and other passages of this kind.

[Col. 1274B] If you ask how He is said to be invisible if He can be seen, I answer that His nature is invisible, but that He is seen whenever He wills; for He has appeared to many—not as He is, but in whatever form He was pleased to appear. If you ask how the wicked Cain saw Him, when Cain was questioned and judged by Him concerning his crime, or how the devil himself saw Him when he came with the angels to stand before Him, if “the pure in heart shall see God,” I answer that it does not follow that those who sometimes hear voices produced by Him also see God. For those who heard Him say to the Son, “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John 12:28), did not see Him.

Nevertheless, it should not be surprising if even some who are not pure in heart see God in a form produced by His will, while His invisible and intrinsically unchangeable nature remains concealed.

[Col. 1274C] If you ask whether He can at some time be seen as He is, I answer that this has been promised to the sons of God, concerning whom it is said: “We know that when He appears, we shall be like Him, because we shall see Him as He is” (1 John 3:2).

If you ask from where we shall see Him, I answer: from the same place from which the angels see Him, for then we shall be equal to the angels. Just as the things called visible are seen, “no one has ever seen God” (John 1:18), nor can He be seen, “because He dwells in inaccessible light.” His nature is invisible just as it is incorruptible, as the Apostle placed these qualities together when he said: “To the King of the ages, invisible, incorruptible” (1 Tim. 1:17). For just as He is incorruptible now and will not become corruptible later, so He is not only invisible now but always invisible.

[Col. 1274D] He is not seen in a place, but by the pure in heart; He is not sought with bodily eyes, nor heard through speech, nor perceived by movement. The only-begotten Son, however, who is in the bosom of the Father, declares the nature and substance of the Godhead in an ineffable manner and therefore also invisibly displays it to eyes worthy and fit for so great a sight.

These are the eyes of which the Apostle says: “The eyes of your heart having been enlightened” (Eph. 1:18); concerning which it is said: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Ps. 12:4). For “the Lord is Spirit”; hence, whoever cleaves to the Lord is one spirit with Him. Therefore, whoever can see God invisibly can cleave to God incorporeally.

[Col. 1275A] Moreover, if the things within our mind, although resembling bodily places, are nevertheless not contained by the dimensions or boundaries of places, nor stored in our memory according to spatial intervals, how much more do those things that bear no resemblance to bodies—love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control—occupy no spatial extent, are not separated by any interval, and do not seek out distances for the eyes of the heart to which they might send their rays and by which they might see them?

Are not all these things present together in one without restriction, and known within their own limits without any circuit of regions? Or tell me in what place you see love, which nevertheless is known to you in proportion as you can contemplate it with the mind’s gaze. You do not know it to be great because, by looking upon it, you have surveyed some enormous mass. Nor, when it speaks inwardly to you so that you may live according to it, does it make any noise; nor, in order to see it, do you raise the light of bodily eyes; nor, in order to hold it firmly, do you prepare the bodily strength of your arms; nor, when it comes to mind, do you sense its movement.

[Col. 1275B] Behold, even love, however small it may be, exists in our will and is visible to us, yet it is not seen in a place, is not sought with bodily eyes, is not circumscribed by sight, is not grasped by touch, is not heard through speech, and is not perceived by movement. How much more is this true of God Himself, whose pledge is within us!

For if our inner person, however small an image of Him it may be—not begotten from Him but created by Him—although it is still being renewed day by day, already dwells in such a light that no bodily sense of sight can approach it; if the things we contemplate with the eyes of the heart in that light are distinguished within themselves and are not separated by any spatial distances, how much more is this true of God, who dwells in light inaccessible to bodily senses, to which there can be access only for a pure heart!

[Col. 1275C] Since, therefore, we have set this light before every bodily light—not only by the judgment of reason but also by the desire of love—the more we see it, the better shall we be able, until all the illnesses of our soul are healed by Him who is merciful toward all our iniquities.

I think that, after considering all these matters, you now concede that it was rightly said that God is not seen in a place but by the pure in heart; that He is not sought with bodily eyes, is not circumscribed by sight, is not grasped by touch, is not heard through speech, and is not perceived by movement. And if we understand anything in these matters inadequately or think about it differently, God will also reveal that to us, provided that we walk in what we have attained.

[Col. 1275D] We have attained the belief that God is not a body but Spirit. We have also attained the belief that no one has ever seen God; that God is light and there are no darknesses in Him; that with Him there is no change or shadow caused by a moment’s turning; that He dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see; that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, without any diversity or separation of nature; that the pure in heart shall see Him; that we shall be like Him because we shall see Him as He is; that God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God and God remains in him; that we must pursue peace and sanctification, without which no one will see God;

[Col. 1276A] that this corruptible and mortal body of ours will be changed at the resurrection and will put on incorruption and immortality; that, since an animal body is sown, a spiritual body will rise; that the Lord will transform our lowly body so as to make it conform to the body of His glory, so that He may subject all things to Himself; that God made human beings in His image; and that we are renewed in the knowledge of God through the spirit of our mind, according to the image of Him who created us.

Walking by faith in these and similar authorities of the holy Scriptures, those who, through divinely granted or assisted understanding, made spiritual progress and were able to compare spiritual things with spiritual things, saw that God is seen better by the mind than by the body; that the mind sees things which are not contained in places, are not separated by earthly spatial intervals, and are not smaller in a part than in the whole.

[Col. 1276B] Therefore, since the holy Scriptures commend His substance as invisible, while in those same authorities He is found to have been seen by many, either through the body and in bodily places or by the spirit through which bodily images are perceived, through some likeness of a body, although incorporeal, as in dreams or ecstasy, that holy man distinguished the nature of God from visions of this sort. He said that these were forms which God’s will had chosen, not forms which His nature had fashioned.

For God produces such things for whomever He wishes, in whatever manner He wishes, for whomever He wishes, and whenever He wishes, so that His substance may appear while remaining hidden and intrinsically unchangeable. If our own will, remaining and hidden within us without any alteration of itself, expresses voices through whatever means it can make itself known, how much more easily can almighty God, with His nature hidden and intrinsically unchangeable, appear in whatever form He wishes and to whomever He wishes—He who created all things from nothing and, while remaining in Himself, renews all things?

[Col. 1276C] He admonished us to cleanse our hearts for that vision in which we shall see God as He is. Because bodies are called visible in ordinary speech, God is therefore called invisible, so that He may not be believed to be a body—not because He has deprived pure hearts of the contemplation of His substance. This is the great and supreme reward promised to those who worship and love God, as the Lord Himself said when He visibly appeared to bodily eyes and promised that He would be contemplated by pure hearts: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21).

[Col. 1276D] His nature is invisible together with the Father, just as it is equally incorruptible. As was said above, the Apostle placed these qualities together, commending the divine substance to human beings insofar as he could by his preaching.

If bodily eyes will behold this substance at the resurrection after the bodies have been changed, let those who can establish this prove it. I am more moved by the opinion of the one who attributed this vision, even at the resurrection, not to bodily eyes but to pure hearts.

I do not refuse either to learn more about or to inquire into the quality of the spiritual body promised to those who will rise, provided that, in discussing this matter, we can remain free of those vices which are often aroused by human studies and disputes, when “one is puffed up on behalf of one against another beyond what is written” (1 Cor. 4:6).

[Col. 1277A] For while we argue in our search to discover how God can be seen, we might lose the peace and sanctification without which no one will see God. May He Himself avert this from our hearts, making them pure for the contemplation of Him and preserving them so.

There is one matter, however, about which I have no doubt and therefore do not inquire: God’s nature is never seen in a place. Whether something that is not seen in a place can be seen by the eyes of this body, I am prepared to hear from those who can demonstrate this through argument, in the peace of love, and to discuss with them what troubles me for the common good.

Finally, what I said in that letter of mine concerning the eyes of our flesh—that they can neither now nor then see God—is true even in this sense. It was said only of bodily eyes, which will no longer exist if the body itself will be spiritual. Consequently, bodily eyes will never see God, because when Spirit is seen, it will not be the body that sees Him.

[Col. 1277B] The whole question, therefore, now concerns the spiritual body, although this corruptible and mortal body indicates incorruption and immortality, and although it is changed from an animal body into a spiritual one.

This matter must be treated more carefully and attentively, especially because of the body of the Lord Himself, who transforms our lowly body so that it conforms to the body of His glory, enabling Him to subject all things to Himself.

Since God the Father sees the Son and the Son sees the Father, those who refuse to attribute vision to anything except bodily beings certainly must not be heeded. For it is not permissible to say that the Father does not see the Son; nor, if sight pertains only to bodies, that the Father is clothed in a body in order to see.

[Col. 1277C] What, then, is meant by the fact that, at the very beginning of creation, before the Son had assumed any form of a servant, “God saw the light, that it was good,” and saw the firmament, the sea, the dry land, every plant and every tree, the sun, the moon, the stars, creeping creatures possessing living souls, the birds of heaven, and the living soul? Finally, “God saw everything that He had made, and behold, it was very good” (Gen. 1:4, etc.).

Therefore, until careful inquiry, with the Lord’s help, discovers what should more probably be believed according to the Scriptures concerning the spiritual body promised at the resurrection, let it suffice for us meanwhile that the only-begotten Son, who is also the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, sees the Father just as He is seen by the Father.

[Col. 1277D] As for that vision of God which is promised to us at the resurrection, let us not attempt to transfer to it from this world the desire of the eyes. Rather, let us devote ourselves with devout affection to cleansing our hearts. Nor should we imagine a bodily face when the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12).

This is especially so because the Apostle expressed himself more clearly when he said: “Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I have been known” (ibid.). If, then, we shall know God with a bodily face, we have now been known with His bodily face, for he says: “Then I shall know even as I have been known.”

[Col. 1278A] Who, therefore, would not understand that in this passage he also intended to signify our face of which he says elsewhere: “But we, with unveiled face contemplating the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18)—that is, from the glory of faith into the glory of eternal contemplation?

To state not only what Blessed Ambrose thought but also what Saint Jerome thought: not only the divinity of the Father, but also that of the Son and the Holy Spirit—for there is one nature in the Trinity—cannot be looked upon by the eyes of the flesh, but by the eyes of the mind, concerning which the Savior Himself says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

For, as the same Jerome briefly and truthfully defined elsewhere, an incorporeal reality is not seen by bodily eyes.

[Col. 1278B] I have inserted these opinions of such great men concerning so great a matter, not so that you should regard anyone’s human judgment as an authority equal to that of canonical Scripture, but so that those who think otherwise may strive to see mentally what is true and seek the Lord in simplicity of heart, rather than rashly criticize such learned interpreters of the divine words.

Nor should you be troubled by what some say with insufficient consideration: “What will bodily eyes see then, if they will not see the Lord? Will they perhaps be blind, or will they exist without purpose?”

Those who say such things do not understand that, if there are no bodies, those eyes will certainly not be bodily; but if there are bodies, there will be something that bodily eyes can see.

We have taken these matters from the letter which Blessed Augustine wrote to Paulina concerning the vision of God. Now, from the same teacher’s letter to Italica concerning the body of the Mediator—whether he sees the substance of God with bodily eyes—we shall append a few things, as a kind of conclusion.

[Col. 1278C] But what tongue could express, or at least what human mind could apprehend, the nature or greatness of that very light by which all these things that are now stored in our hearts will be illuminated?

Certainly that light itself is God, since “God is light, and there are no darknesses in Him” (John 1:4); but it is the light of purified minds, not of these bodily eyes.

The mind, therefore, will then be fit to see that light—something which I would not say now [perhaps: “which is not now said to be”]. But the bodily eye can neither now see this nor see it then.

For everything that can be seen by a bodily eye must exist in some place; it cannot be wholly everywhere, but occupies a smaller place by its smaller part and a larger place by its larger part. The invisible and incorruptible God is not like this. He alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light; no human being has seen Him or can see Him.

[Col. 1278D] For the reason that He cannot be seen by human beings is the same reason by which human beings see bodies through the body. If He were inaccessible also to the minds of the devout, it would not be said: “Draw near to Him, and you will be enlightened” (Ps. 33:6). And if He were invisible to the minds of the devout, it would not be said: “We shall see Him as He is.”

For consider the whole sentence in John’s Epistle: “Beloved,” he says, “we are children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared. We know that when He appears, we shall be like Him, because we shall see Him as He is” (1 John 3:2).

[Col. 1279A] Therefore, we shall see Him to the extent that we shall be like Him, because even now we do not see Him to the extent that we are unlike Him. We shall see Him, then, from the same source by which we shall be like Him.

What madman would say that we either are or shall be bodily like God? This likeness, therefore, exists in the inner person, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of Him who created him. The more we progress in knowledge and love of Him, the more like Him we become. For although our outer person is being corrupted, our inner person is being renewed day by day.

This is true even though, in this life, however great our progress may be, we remain far from that perfection of likeness which will make us capable of seeing God, as the Apostle says: “Face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12).

[Col. 1279B] If in these words we wish to understand a bodily face, it will follow that God also has such a face, so that there is some interval between our face and His when we see Him face to face. And if there is an interval, then there must be boundaries, the form of limbs, and a limit—ideas absurd to say and impious to conceive. With such deceitful vanities the animal person, who does not perceive the things of God’s Spirit, is mocked.

Some of those who babble such things say, as far as I have been able to learn, that we see God now with the mind and then with the body. They even assert that the wicked will see Him in the same way. See how much worse they have progressed, while unrestrained by fear or shame, as this wandering and unpunished loquacity is carried here and there.

Earlier they said that Christ had granted this only to His flesh: that it would see God with bodily eyes. Then they added that all the saints, once they had received their bodies in the resurrection, would see God in the same way.

[Col. 1279C] Now they have granted this possibility even to the wicked. Let them grant it, then, as much as they wish and to whomever they wish. For who would dare contradict people who give from their own possessions? “Whoever speaks a lie speaks from his own resources.” But you, together with those who hold sound doctrine, must dare to claim none of these things from your own resources.

When you read, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8), understand that the wicked will not see Him, for the wicked are not pure in heart.

Again, when you read, “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12), from the same source from which we now see through a mirror in an enigma, we shall then see face to face.

[Col. 1279D] Both of these belong to the inner person, whether one still walks by faith in this pilgrimage, in which one uses a mirror and an enigma, or whether, in that homeland, one contemplates by direct vision, for which the expression “face to face” is used.

Let the flesh, drunk with carnal thoughts, hear this: God is Spirit, and therefore those who worship God must worship in spirit and truth. If He must be worshiped in this way, how much more must He be seen in this way?

Who would dare affirm that the substance of God is seen bodily, when He did not wish to be worshiped bodily?

But they think they speak cleverly and seem to press the matter by asking: “Could Christ grant His flesh the ability to see the Father with bodily eyes, or could He not?” If we answer that He could not, they will proclaim that we have detracted from God’s omnipotence; but if we agree that He could, they will conclude their argument from our answer.

[Col. 1280A] How much more tolerable is the error of those who assert that flesh will emerge into the substance of God and become what God is, so that at least by seeing they may make it capable of this, although now it is so greatly unlike Him!

I believe that these people derive such vanity from their own faith—or perhaps from their ears. Yet if they are similarly pressed by the question whether God can accomplish this or cannot, will they detract from His power if they answer that He cannot, or will they admit that this will happen if they agree that He can?

How, then, would they escape from someone else’s snare? Let them escape from their own in the same way.
