Moreover, why do they insist that this gift was attributed only to the bodily eyes of Christ, and not also to His other senses? Will God, then, be a sound, so that He may also be perceived by the ears? Will He be a breath, so that He may be sensed by smell? Will He be some liquid, so that He may also be drunk? Will He be a mass, so that He may also be touched?

[Col. 1280B] “No,” they say. “What, then? Can God do that, but not this?” If they say He cannot, why do they detract from God’s omnipotence? If they answer that He can but does not wish to, why do they favor the eyes alone and begrudge the other bodily senses of Christ?

We have excerpted these matters from the works of Saint Augustine, Ambrose, and Jerome. Now we shall set forth in succession what Blessed Gregory thought concerning the future vision of God. In the eighteenth book of his exposition of Blessed Job, while treating of the vision of the divine essence, he brought forward explicitly the statement from the Book of Exodus in which the Lord addressed Moses when Moses asked Him to manifest Himself, saying:

[Col. 1280C] To the Lord’s statement addressed to Moses, “For no human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:20), John agrees when he says: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18).

But when I consider the fathers of the Old Testament, I recognize that many of them saw God, as the history of sacred reading itself bears witness. Jacob saw the Lord, for he said: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my soul has been preserved” (Gen. 32:30).

Moses saw the Lord, concerning whom it is written: “The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend” (Exod. 33:11).

Job saw the Lord, for he said: “I heard you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you” (Job 42:5).

Isaiah saw the Lord, for he said: “In the year when King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up” (Isa. 6:1).

Micaiah saw the Lord, for he said: “I saw the Lord sitting upon His throne, and all the host of heaven standing by Him on His right and on His left” (2 Chron. 18:18).

[Col. 1280D] What, then, is the meaning of the fact that so many fathers of the Old Testament testified that they had seen God, while He Himself says, “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:20), and John says, “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18)?

It is this, plainly understood: as long as one lives here in mortal existence, God can be seen through certain images, but He cannot be seen through the very form of His nature. Thus the soul, breathed upon by the grace of the Spirit, sees God through certain figures, but does not reach the actual power of His essence.

[Col. 1281A] Hence Jacob, who testified that he had seen God, saw Him only in an angel. Hence Moses, who spoke with God face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend, turned his words toward the one with whom he was speaking and said: “If I have found grace in your sight, show me yourself plainly, so that I may see you” (Exod. 33:13).

Certainly, if the one with whom he was speaking was not God, he would have said, “Show me God,” and not, “Show me yourself.” But if the one with whom he spoke face to face was God, why did he ask to be able to see the one whom he was seeing?

From this request of his it is gathered that he thirsted to behold, through the splendor of God’s uncircumscribed nature, the one whom he had already begun to see through certain images, so that the heavenly essence might be present to the eyes of his mind in such a way that no created image belonging to time would intervene between him and the vision of eternity.

[Col. 1281B] Thus the fathers of the Old Testament saw the Lord; yet, in accordance with John’s statement, “No one has ever seen Him,” and in accordance with the Lord’s own statement, “No one has seen God and lived,” those who remain in mortal flesh cannot see Him through the uncircumscribed light of eternity.

But if some who are still living in this corruptible flesh, while growing through immeasurable virtue, can see the eternal splendor of God through a certain sharpness of contemplation, this too does not conflict with the statement of that same Virtue: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:20). For whoever sees Wisdom, which is God, dies completely to this life, so that he is no longer held by love of it.

[Col. 1281C] No one sees Wisdom while still living carnally, because no one can embrace God and the world. Whoever sees God dies by that very act, because in the intention of the heart or in the effect of action he is separated with his whole mind from the pleasures of this life.

Thus, “No one has seen God and lived,” as though it were plainly said: No one has ever seen God spiritually and lived carnally in the world.

We shall therefore see God if, through a heavenly manner of life, we are found worthy to rise above human beings; yet we shall not see Him as He sees Himself. The Creator sees Himself in a manner utterly unlike that in which a creature sees the Creator.

[Col. 1281D] So far as God’s immensity is concerned, a certain measure of contemplation is fixed for us, and we are circumscribed by that very weight by which we are creatures. Certainly, we do not behold God as He beholds Himself, just as we do not rest in God in the way that He rests in Himself.

Our vision or rest will be in some way like His vision or rest, but it will not be equal to it. Perfect rest is that in which God is seen; yet our rest must not be made equal to His, because He does not pass from Himself into another in order to rest.

There is therefore a rest that is both like and unlike: what His resting is, our rest imitates. The vision of God begins now through faith, but is perfected then through direct vision, when we shall drink from the very source the Wisdom coeternal with God which we now receive through the works of preachers, as though through flowing streams.

It should also be known that some have said that, even in that blessed region, God is indeed seen in His glory but is not seen in His nature. They were deceived by a less subtle inquiry. For in a simple and unchangeable essence, glory is not one thing and nature another; rather, His nature itself is His glory, and His glory itself is His nature.

[Col. 1282A] For when this Wisdom of God at some time reveals Himself to those who love Him, He promises this in Himself, saying: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21). It is as though He plainly said: “You who see me in your own nature, it remains for you to see me in my nature.”

Again, He says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

[Col. 1282B] Paul says: “Now we see in a mirror through enigmas, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I have been known” (1 Cor. 13:12).

But because the Church’s preacher first says concerning God, “Into whom the angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1:12), there are some who suppose that not even the angels see God. Yet we know that Truth itself has said: “Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.”

Does Truth, then, speak one thing and the preacher of truth another? But if both statements are compared, it is recognized that they in no way disagree.

[Col. 1282C] The angels both see God and desire to see Him; they thirst to contemplate Him and they contemplate Him. For if they desired to see Him in such a way that they were never able to enjoy the fulfillment of their desire, desire without fruition would contain anxiety, and anxiety would contain punishment.

But the blessed angels are far removed from every punishment of anxiety, because punishment and blessedness never coexist.

Again, when we say that they are satisfied by the vision of God—for the Psalmist also says, “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 16:15)—we must consider that satiety is usually followed by disgust.

[Col. 1282D] Therefore, so that both statements may rightly agree, let Truth say that they always see, and let the outstanding preacher say that they always desire to see. So that desire may not contain anxiety, they are satisfied while desiring. And so that satiety may not contain disgust, they desire while satisfied.

In this way the chosen among human beings are satisfied by the divine vision during this life and yet desire it. This happens without weariness, because desire is accompanied by satiety; and they are satisfied without disgust, because satiety itself is continually kindled by desire.

So shall we also be when we come to the very fountain of life. Thirst and satiety will be delightfully impressed upon us at the same time. Necessity will be far from that thirst, and disgust far from that satiety, because we shall thirst while being satisfied and be thirsty while satisfied.

We shall therefore see God, and He Himself will be the reward of our labor, so that after the darkness of this mortality we may rejoice in the light kindled by Him.

# BOOK TWO: ON PURITY OF HEART
In the preceding book we completed, as far as we could, our discussion—according to the teaching of the holy Fathers—of the future vision of God [Col. 1283A]. Now, following the tradition of our elders, we think it appropriate to discuss purity of heart, through which contemplation of God rises, because the vision of God has been promised only to those who are pure in heart. Therefore it is necessary for us to put to death the desires of the flesh within us and devote ourselves to sacred virtues, so that, through their assistance and by the gift of divine grace, we may be able to attain the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom and the contemplation of eternal light.

Although we have been born bodily from Adam, we ought not to imitate Adam, but Christ, in whom we have been reborn and in whom we live, when, salutarily renewed, we lay aside our former way of life. What does it mean to imitate Adam except to be condemned to death on account of carnal lusts and desires? And what does it mean to imitate Christ [Col. 1283B] except to be crucified with respect to carnal lusts and desires? For laying aside the former way of life is nothing other than living not according to the flesh—which grows old and dies—but according to God, who alone can continually renew and bless those who persevere in him.

Therefore, just as when we were in Adam we all fell when he fell, so now that we have begun to be in Christ, who graciously consented to die for us all, let us also die spiritually with him to our sins and rise again with him. In Adam we lost every good thing we could possess; in Christ we shall receive again even greater things, to be possessed without end, if we steadfastly follow in his footsteps.

Adam made us liable to every evil through his own fault; the coming of Christ, by grace, freed us from them. [Col. 1283C] Adam transmitted his guilt and punishment to us, whereas Christ, since he was conceived and born without sin, could not take upon himself our guilt; but by taking on our punishment he simultaneously abolished both our guilt and our punishment. In short, Adam snatched paradise from us, while Christ gave us heaven as well.

Therefore, if we wish to be in him what we ought to be, let us spiritually walk as he walked, as the holy apostle John says: “Just as he walked, let us also walk spiritually.” What does it mean to walk as he walked except to despise all the prosperity that he despised; not to fear the adversities that he endured; gladly to do what he did; to teach others to do what he commanded; to hope for what he promised; to follow where he went before us; to bestow benefits even on the ungrateful; not to repay the ill-disposed according to their deserts; to pray for our enemies [Col. 1283D]; to love the good; to show mercy to the perverse; to invite those who oppose us; and to receive in charity those who have been converted?

To this also pertains what the holy apostle Paul says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (Col. 3:1). Those rise with Christ who die as he did to sin, with this distinction preserved: he died to sin not his own but ours, whereas each one of us dies not to everyone’s sin but to his own.

What is it to die to sin except entirely to cease living for works that deserve condemnation, to desire nothing carnally, and to covet nothing? For just as a person dead in the flesh no longer slanders anyone, hates or despises anyone, corrupts anyone’s chastity through cunning deception [Col. 1284A], uses violence against no one, calumniates or oppresses no one, does not envy the good or insult the afflicted, does not serve the luxury of the flesh, and, being addicted to wine, does not inflame the thirst for drinking within himself by drinking more and more; just as he does not burn with the torches of hatred, pursue unjust gains, flatter the powerful or the rich, get carried away by restless curiosity, become distracted by the cares of household affairs, take pleasure in the dutiful greetings of those who approach him, or become wearied by the insults of the proud; just as pride does not inflate him, vainglorious ambition does not hurl him headlong, empty glory does not shamefully boast through him, desire for a celebrated reputation does not inflame him, and distinction in another’s conduct does not entangle him; just as love of disgrace does not invite him into the company of the disreputable, mad fury does not drive him on, [Col. 1284B] the expense of hateful lawsuits does not destroy him, and the heat of contentious anger does not take his life; so too, among those who are dead to sin, these vices do not live at all.

They do not become shameless through audacity, unjust through injustice, savage through harshness, changeable through fickleness, stubborn through obstinacy, insane through madness, self-indulgent through gluttony, rebellious through disobedience, vain through boastfulness, faithless through treachery, frivolous through ease, savage through cruelty, a glutton through disgraceful greed for food, impatient through volatility, volatile through instability, wandering through spiritual weakness, angry through contentiousness, suspicious through perversity, talkative through vanity, a mocker through malice.

Such a person is entirely removed from worldly allurements, removed from hostilities, removed from the snares of others, removed from thefts—whether hidden or open—removed from lies and perjuries, and, finally, removed from every kind of shameful act and crime by which those who live according to the flesh offend God and, being dead to sin, do not serve him.

Just as one dead in the flesh can neither do nor suffer the things I have mentioned, so those who have crucified their flesh, with its vices and desires, in order to live for God do not live at all in such vices. They put to death their members that are upon the earth when they restrain their appetite within its necessary bounds; when they refrain, with disciplined moderation, not only from more delicate foods but also from ordinary foods, allowing their flesh nothing for the sake of desire, but only what is necessary to sustain life.

They are certain that no delicacies do harm if they are taken without desire, while cheap foods often impede the progress of abstinence if they are consumed greedily. This is why holy David checked his desire for water within himself and poured out the water offered to him by his men, lest he appear to satisfy his desire through it; whereas the holy Elijah’s consumption of meat, since it was not desired, did him no harm.

From this it is understood that those who truly abstain condemn not the natures of foods but their lusts, and put their desires to death by abstaining from the food or drink they long for. Those who wish to abstain not only from the quality but also from the quantity of food strive for nothing other than to allow themselves as much as seems sufficient to restore the stomach and relieve hunger [Perhaps “enough” is missing], but not to satisfy their appetites from the pleasure of consuming. They restrain them, so that it is not satiety in eating that brings their desires to an end, but their will.

Thus they will abstain both from a craving for expensive foods and from excessive consumption of cheap ones [Col. 1285A]. They do not wish to be dissolved in sensuality by richer foods, nor burdened with cheap foods through distension of the belly; for men who abstain are not usually either luxurious or greedy.

What should I say now about abstaining from wine or taking it? The holy Apostle established a firm rule when he said: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Eph. 5:18). It is as though he said: “Excessive consumption of wine produces and nourishes debauchery, not the nature of wine itself. Therefore I forbid you not to use wine, but to become drunk.” For moderate use of wine strengthens a weak stomach, whereas drunkenness weakens both mind and body.

Finally, he instructed his disciple Timothy, who had already weakened himself greatly through the rigor of abstinence and had damaged his stomach by drinking water, to use a little wine, saying: “No longer drink water [Col. 1285B], but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses” (1 Tim. 5:23). Accordingly, those who take wine not for drunkenness but only for the health of the body do nothing contrary to abstinence. It is not their will that offers this to them, but illness permits it; and if illness is absent, they must abstain from wine.

For every use of wine that sustains a sick person inflames a healthy body. In any case [or perhaps read: “for certainly”], no one would say that using wine and making use of oil is a sin. Nevertheless, we must not grant these things to the flesh when it desires them, lest, once we begin to grant it what is lawful, it demand what is unlawful and compel those who indulge it in small matters to commit punishable crimes; and lest, with the natural order overturned, the body rule the spirit, and the spirit serve the body.

Moreover, the fruit of abstinence makes the mind itself cheerful. It also makes the flesh active, not exhausted to the point of weariness, but properly subjected to the spirit. The habit of frugality relieves the senses, which accumulated luxuries are said to render dull or burden, and, as though by a kind of polishing through religious discipline, makes them finer.

Nevertheless, we ought to abstain or fast in such a way that we do not subject ourselves to the necessity of fasting or abstinence, lest we do something voluntary no longer as devoted persons but unwillingly. If, when visitors arrive, I refresh them after interrupting a fast, I am not breaking the fast but fulfilling the duty of charity.

But if, on account of abstinence, I distress spiritual brothers whom I know to take pleasure in my leniency, my abstinence should not be called a virtue but a vice. For if the continuity of abstinence and fasting is not interrupted when circumstances require it, and it inflates me while distressing my brother, whom charity commands me to serve, or at least demonstrates that I have no fraternal charity, then it is defective; for charity alone perfects any Catholic person even without abstinence. Every abstinence without the addition of charity either destroys or perishes.

Since even the Manichaeans and other heretics can abstain—indeed, because they detest all flesh not for the sake of abstinence but because they consider it unclean, they wear out their bodies through a meager diet of bread and water—we should not consider it a great thing when we abstain from what they too reject. Rather, our abstinence must be commended by faith and completed by charity [Col. 1286A]. Lacking these virtues, they may kill themselves, but by abstaining they cannot be built up or brought to perfection.

As for Catholic Christians, however, who—whether unable or unwilling to abstain—receive with thanksgiving everything granted for our use, we should not place ourselves above them on account of abstinence. Perhaps they possess greater humility and other virtues, by which they may rightly be preferred to us despite our abstinence.

Therefore, if we wish our abstinence and fasts to benefit us, let us first turn away from pride—which either drives out all virtues or diminishes them—and from boastfulness, which is hostile to every virtue, and from every vice altogether. Then it will benefit us that we abstain from pleasurable foods. For it will benefit us to chastise our bodies—or rather the incitements of our bodies—with the severity of stricter abstinence only if, freed from carnal desires, we flourish in holy virtues.

But I plainly declare that true virtues are separated from imitations of virtues by as great a distance as falsehood is separated from truth. For an imitation of virtue, which appears to be virtue although it is not, is nothing other than falsehood; and therefore it must not be called virtue but vice.

True virtue is truth. Whoever clings to it lovingly, having been raised from the death of sin, cannot die again unless he withdraws from it through a corrupted will. Conversely, the pretense of virtue—which, as I have said, is falsehood opposed to truth—separates the soul from God, its life. The soul will not perish, but it will live forever in punishment, which is its death, enduring penal suffering without end, as Scripture says: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11) [Col. 1286C].

Accordingly, just as true virtue justifies the soul that genuinely clings to it, so false virtue condemns it. And what is the justification of the soul except its perpetually blessed life and its blessed perpetuity? Likewise, the condemnation of the soul must be understood as its punishment, which is shown to be death, and itself perpetual.

Thus the soul is guilty in two ways: if it does not do the good by which it may live spiritually, and if it desires the likeness of good under which it may live wickedly and remain hidden.

The proud man wants to be believed steadfast, the prodigal generous, the miser diligent, the inhuman frugal, the glutton humane, the lazy tranquil, and the fearful cautious. Shamelessness writes the name “confidence” for itself; impudence conceals itself under the title “freedom”; verbosity imitates eloquence; and the evil of curiosity lurks under the appearance of spiritual study [Col. 1286D].

Although these things can be discerned by human intelligence, nevertheless, as far as I can see, without God’s gift neither virtues can be desired or possessed, nor can their imitations—which are vices imitating virtues—be avoided. Thus we must believe that even if unbelievers have performed certain virtues bodily, these have profited them nothing, since they neither believed that they had received them from their God nor wished to refer them to him who is the end of all good things.

And what do I mean? They did not merely fail to benefit from them; they were even harmed by them, as the holy Apostle says: “Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23). He did not say, “Everything that is not from faith is nothing”; rather, by saying, “Everything that is not from faith is sin” [Col. 1287A], he made clear that all good deeds performed from faith are virtues, and these certainly justify; but if they are performed without faith, they must not be regarded as any kind of good, but as vices, which do not help their practitioners but condemn them, cast them down in their pride, and drive them away from the boundaries of eternal salvation.

But why do I elaborate these matters concerning unbelievers, about whom no one seems to have doubts, when the holy Apostle also calls certain believers carnal—those who, although they believe in God, live not according to God but according to human standards? He says: “And I, brothers, when I came to you, could not speak to you as spiritual people but as carnal people” (1 Cor. 3:1). “For you were not yet able; indeed, even now you are not able, for you are still carnal.”

And as though we were asking what he means by “carnal,” he continued: “For while there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human standards?” (ibid., v. 3) [Col. 1287B]. What could be found worse than these two plagues of the soul, jealousy and contention, by which those who live carnally according to human standards are tormented even in this life? Contention makes them heretics, while jealousy makes them imitators of the devil who envied the first human beings their paradise.

Accordingly, when believers rejoice in justice, piety, mercy, gentleness, humility, innocence, and the other virtues, either they are living according to God, and must be believed to possess true virtues, which sanctify those who obtain them by living spiritually and commend them to God; or they are living according to human standards, and these are not true virtues but likenesses of virtues, which profit those who live carnally nothing [Col. 1287C].

Therefore, whoever lives religiously, chastely, soberly, and mercifully, if he ascribes this to God, by whose gift he is enabled to live well, lives spiritually according to God. But if he ascribes everything he does well to his own powers, as though he were sufficient to act well without God’s help, he lives carnally according to human standards. Thus he either does not live well, or whatever good he does for the sake of human beings will profit him nothing, because, delighted by human praise, he receives here and now the temporal reward of works he performed temporally.

The person who lives according to human standards therefore lives according to himself, since he too is human. He lives according to himself when, if he can, he stays with whomever he wishes, goes wherever he wishes, sleeps when and as long as he wishes, speaks what he wishes and where he wishes [Col. 1287D], eats and drinks when he wishes, whatever he wishes, and as much as he wishes, laughs and plays among whomever he wishes.

Finally, whatever is pleasant to his nostrils, whatever is agreeable to his touch, whatever delights his eyes, and whatever is pleasant to the other senses of his flesh, he practices and pursues as he wishes, because he desires carnally all things, lawful and unlawful.

But the person who lives according to God does not do what pleases him carnally, but what builds him up spiritually. He restrains every desire of the flesh through the delight of spiritual desire; he places future things before present things; he subjects the flesh to the spirit; and whatever he desires or does, he wishes to proceed not from his own will but from the will of his God, whom he longs with all his strength to please.

Thus, if it has become clear in some measure that those who pretend do not appear to possess true virtues, and that those pretend who perform something good not from faith or for God’s sake but only for the sake of human beings—engaging in almsgiving, fasting, abstinence, and other good works not in order to become good but to pretend to others that they are good, and not to receive an eternal reward but to acquire popular glory—let us now consider the preceding causes and subsequent stages by which vices usually arise or grow, and the remedies, with the Lord’s help, by which they can be reduced or healed as by medicines.

Every holy virtue is a divine reality, wholly incorporeal and utterly pure. Defiled minds do not defile it; rather, it cleanses those who are defiled through it. By participation in it, shapeless things are formed, the dead are raised, the weak are healed, the crooked are corrected, and those who are estranged are reconciled [Col. 1288B].

No one possesses it except God and the one to whom God gives it. It dwells in the soul, but sanctifies both soul and body. No one approaches it unwillingly, and no one loses it except one who has been deceived by his own will. No one can bestow it upon himself, though one may be able to give it—or fail to give it—to another; nor can anyone take it away.

Therefore, when such a great virtue has shone upon someone who is still languishing amid his pleasures and has stirred within him a salutary desire to long for it, immediately a struggle between two contrary pleasures arises in his soul. The will, divided against itself by a twofold and conflicting delight, leads the mind back and forth in opposing directions: at one moment reproving what it had chosen, at another choosing what it had reproved.

As it turns from one side to the other amid the variety of its thoughts, it is tormented and torn apart by a kind of lukewarm middle state between virtue and vice. For as long as a person has not confirmed himself in what he has chosen by a firm decision—as long as he sometimes does not want what he wanted and sometimes begins to want what he did not want—the very diversity of his wills rends him apart, as though he were standing at a crossroads of uncertain deliberation [Col. 1288C].

From one side virtue reminds him of his salvation and calls him; from the other, vicious habit delays and recalls him as he tries to depart. When he has turned away from it for a little while but has not yet fully turned toward virtue, vicious desire flatters him with reminders of its former state and displays all the enticements in which he once indulged to his ruin. It also introduces shameful desires by which he may be conquered [Col. 1288D].

When he is already nearly weary of them, it softens and whispers something deceptively pleasant, begging him not to exchange softness for hardship, joy for sadness, certainty for doubt, or future things for present pleasure. It tells him to consider how painful and difficult it is to do without sweet luxuries, to renounce carnal allurements, to be weighed down by the constant labor of abstinence, to be tormented by continual fasting and vigils, and to seek the reward of uncertain recompense through certain affliction of the flesh.

It tells him to consider the taking up of weapons to resist the devil, an expert in deception, and the avoidance of his snares and frauds through the watchful caution of the mind. It then tells him how miserable it would be, after being overcome by the enormity of such harshness and deceived by the devil’s fraud, to return to what he had rejected, to enjoy the pleasures he had cast away, and to delight in all the things he had despised when he rashly undertook a laborious undertaking [Col. 1289A].

Through these and similar arguments, vicious habit disturbs the uncertainty of the holy decision. Virtue, however, which is called continence, boldly rebukes the one who hesitates. It invites him to pure pleasures and chaste delights, enjoyed by all who love it; it offers the naked person the garment of justice; it displays the beauty of its illuminated attire; and it promises the one who distrusts himself the help of its protection.

It urges and summons him, once the uncertainty of his decision has been set aside, to undertake a spiritual purpose and to persevere in the labor he has assumed. It tells him to trust not in his own ability but in the Lord’s mercy, and, relying not on his own strength but on the help of almighty grace, to take up the weapons of victory against the devil’s attacks.

Let him also consider how many people, and how great they were, have been able—and still are able—to do what he despairs of being able to do [Col. 1289B]. From the fact that they were able, let him firmly believe, with certain hope, that he too can be able. Let him place spiritual things before carnal things, heavenly and future things before earthly and present things.

All arts and disciplines have a certain aim—that is, a destination—and a *telos*, that is, their proper end. Looking toward this end, the diligent pursuer of each art patiently and willingly endures all labors, dangers, and expenses. Thus, those skilled in the use of weapons, when they wish to display their mastery of this art before the king of this world, strive to hurl spears or arrows at a very small target on which prizes, javelins, or arrows are painted, confident that they can reach the desired prize only by the straight line of their intended destination. [Col. 1289C] So too our way has a certain end, the kingdom of God. But what its aim is must be carefully investigated. If this is not similarly discovered by us, we shall tire ourselves by striving in vain, because for those traveling without a road the labor of the journey brings toil, not progress. The end of our profession, as we have said, is the kingdom of God, or the kingdom of heaven; its destination, however—that is, its aim—is purity of heart, without which no one can reach that end.

Fixing the gaze of our direction upon this destination, therefore, we guide our course along a definite line, perfectly straight. If our thought should turn even slightly away from it, we immediately return to its contemplation and correct it again with the utmost precision, as though by a rule. [Col. 1289D] This continually recalls all our efforts to this one sign and at once reproves us if our mind has deviated even slightly from the direction we have set. Thus, just as the end of our purpose is, according to the Apostle, “eternal life,” so, as he declares in the same passage, “having your fruit in sanctification, and the end eternal life” (Rom. VI, 22), the purity of our heart must be our aim, which he rightly called sanctification, without which the aforementioned end cannot be attained.

It is as though he had said in other words: “Having purity of heart as your aim, and eternal life as your end.” Teaching us about this destination, the same blessed Apostle expressly used the very word—that is, “aim”—when he said: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the destination, the prize of the heavenly calling of the Lord” (Phil. III, 14). This is expressed more clearly in Greek as the printed text has it, “rato ciro iconatui rui κατά σκοπόν διώκω etc.,” [the initial printed words are materially corrupt and cannot be reconstructed from the supplied text] that is, “I pursue according to the destination,” as though he had said: “By this destination—that is, by forgetting what lies behind, the vices of the former person—I strive to reach the end, the heavenly prize.” [Col. 1290A]

Whatever, therefore, can direct us toward this aim, namely, purity of heart, must be pursued with all our strength; whatever draws us away from it must be avoided as pernicious and harmful. For its sake we do and endure everything. For its sake parents, country, honors, riches, the pleasures of this world, and every form of enjoyment are despised, so that purity of heart may be retained perpetually. [Col. 1290B]

With this destination set before us, our actions and thoughts will always be directed most precisely toward attaining it. If it is not continually established before our eyes, it will not only render all our labors equally empty and unstable, but will also cause them to be poured out uselessly and without any benefit, like the efforts of those who do not possess apostolic charity and are thereby rendered barren and fruitless in everything. Foreseeing this in the Spirit, the blessed Apostle said: “And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. XIII, 3).

From this it is plainly demonstrated that perfection is not immediately attained through nakedness, nor through the renunciation of all possessions or the rejection of honors, unless one possesses that charity whose members the Apostle describes and which consists in purity of heart alone. [Col. 1290C] For what else is meant by “not being jealous, not being puffed up, not being provoked, not acting wrongly, not seeking what is one’s own, not rejoicing over iniquity, not thinking evil,” and the rest, except that one continually offer to God a perfect and most pure heart and guard it untouched by every disturbance?

All gifts are granted for a time, according to use and necessity, and, once their purpose has been fulfilled, they undoubtedly pass away through the course of God’s dispensation. Charity, however, will never be interrupted. For it does not merely work beneficially in us in the present world; in the future, when the burden of bodily necessity has been cast aside, it will remain far more effective and excellent. It will never be corrupted by any decay, but through perpetual incorruption will cleave to God more ardently and intently. [Col. 1290D]

Charity, then, is, as it seems to me, a right will utterly withdrawn from all earthly and present things, inseparably joined to God and united to him by a kind of fire of the Holy Spirit—from whom it comes and toward whom it is directed—kindled by that Spirit; foreign to every defilement, incapable of corruption, subject to no fault arising from change, exalted above everything that is loved carnally, supremely desirous of divine contemplation among all affections, always unconquered in everything, the summit of good actions, the salvation of morals, the end of heavenly commandments, the death of crimes, the life of virtues, the strength of those who fight, the palm of the victorious, the soul of holy minds, the cause of good merits, and the reward of the perfect.

It raises the dead in their sins, heals the sick, restores the lost, inspires hope in the despairing, pacifies minds, dwells fruitfully in penitents, joyfully in those making progress, gloriously in those who persevere, victoriously in martyrs, and actively in all the faithful without exception. [Col. 1291A] Faith conceives it; hope runs toward it; the progress of all serves it; from it every good work derives life; under it obedience grows; through it patience conquers; for its sake religious devotion despises carnal allurements. Without it no one has pleased God; with it no one could sin, nor will anyone be able to sin.

This is true, genuine, perfect charity, which the holy Apostle calls “the more excellent way.” Truly, it is the way that leads those who walk by it to their homeland. For just as no one reaches the place toward which he is traveling without a road, so without charity—which has been called the way—people cannot walk but only wander. [Col. 1291B]

Therefore, if we show charity toward God and toward our neighbor from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith, we easily resist sin, abound in every good thing, despise the allurements of the world, and accomplish with delight everything that is difficult or harsh for human weakness—provided that we love with our whole heart, soul, and strength the perfect charity of the Lord, which comes to us from him. For a person sins in that part in which he loves God less.

If we love him with our whole heart, nothing will remain by which we might serve the desires of sin. And what is it to love God except to occupy the mind with him, to conceive an affection for enjoying his vision, to hate sin, to despise the world, and also to love the neighbor whom he himself judged should be loved; to preserve the proper measure within that love and not overturn the established order of affection? [Col. 1291C]

Those overturn the order of love and do not preserve the proper measure of loving who love the world, though it ought to be despised; or who love their own bodies, which ought to be loved less, too much; or who do not love their neighbors as themselves; or who perhaps do not love God more than themselves.

Regarding the world, which ought not to be loved at all, the voice of our Lord himself speaks through the holy Apostle John: “Do not love the world” (I John II, 15).

Our body, because it is part of us, ought to be loved so that we may naturally care for its well-being and weakness and act in such a way that, properly subjected to the spirit, it may reach eternal salvation by receiving immortality and incorruption—not by dissolving in its own pleasures, softening the firmness of the soul that yields to it, polluting purity, and corrupting its entire dignity through the sickness of pleasure. [Col. 1291D]

We love our neighbors as ourselves when we love them not for any advantage of our own, not for benefits hoped for or received, not for family connection or blood relationship, but solely because they share our nature. For we do not love them as ourselves when we love them for the reasons mentioned above.

No one loves himself merely because another is his brother or sister, father or son, mother or daughter, nephew or niece. Whoever loves in this way loves carnally. For we must not believe that only those are our neighbors whom degrees of blood relationship join to us; all human beings who share our nature, as I have said, must be regarded as our neighbors.

Now, if we love our relatives—though they may be disorderly, disgraceful, and badly behaved—more than any saints whom we call strangers because they are unrelated to us by blood, we love them not only carnally but also sin gravely in such love. [Col. 1292A]

Accordingly, we love all people as our neighbors when we care for their salvation, as we do for our own, so that they may acquire good morals and eternal life; when we are concerned about their sins and dangers; and when, just as we would wish to be helped, we help them according to our ability—or, if we lack the means, retain the will to help them.

Therefore the whole of love for one’s neighbor is this: that you should wish for your neighbor the good that you wish to be conferred upon yourself.

Those love God more than themselves who, for his love, do not spare their temporal welfare; who give themselves over to tribulations and dangers; who are ready to be stripped of their possessions, driven into exile from their country, and to renounce parents, wives, and children; and, to say everything, do not merely refuse to flee bodily death but willingly embrace it, desiring to depart from the life of their body rather than from God, who is the life of their life. [Col. 1292B]

This, then, is the order of love that we must preserve, in accordance with what the Holy Spirit says: “Order charity in me.” Just as ordered charity demands, we must love God above all; and for his sake, in him, we must love the things that ought to be loved, and love them only to the extent that he commands.

For he commands us to love our bodies for our own sake, our neighbors as ourselves, and himself more than ourselves. We should, however, give more of ourselves to those whom greater familiarity makes closer to us, provided that their reputation does not condemn them and their life commends them. We should regard the progress of all as our own and mourn the sins of others mercifully as though they were our own. [Col. 1292C]

Thus those can be perfect in this life who love God perfectly. And they love God perfectly who desire what God desires, do not desire what he does not desire, do not consent to any sins by which he is offended, and continually strive to love and possess the virtues that he deigns to grant.

These are the people who truly believe that they have been enabled by him to accomplish all the good things they can accomplish; who attribute whatever evil they commit to the fault of their own will; who continually ask him to enable them to accomplish whatever good they have been unable to accomplish; who give him thanks whenever they have been able to do so; who wish the good things they have obtained from him to be shared with others; and who extend the breadth of their love even to their enemies, desiring that everyone should become what they themselves are. [Col. 1292D]

Everything, therefore, must be desired and undertaken for the sake of this. We must understand that for its sake we ought to undertake fasts, vigils, bodily labors, nakedness, reading, and the other virtues, so that through them we may prepare and preserve our heart unharmed by every harmful passion, and climb toward the perfection of charity by these steps.

We must not, however, because of these observances fall into sadness, anger, or indignation if, prevented by some honorable and necessary occupation, we are unable to fulfill the strict observance of our discipline—the observance we had intended to undertake in order to overcome those emotions. The gain from fasting is not as great as the loss caused by anger; nor does reading yield as much fruit as the harm incurred through contempt of a brother. [Col. 1293A]

We ought therefore to practice the things that follow—fasts, vigils, anchoritic solitude, and meditation on the Scriptures—for the sake of the principal aim, namely, purity of heart, which is charity. We must not, for the sake of those practices, disturb this principal virtue. For while it remains whole and unharmed, it will do us no harm if, because of necessity, something among the secondary practices must be omitted. Indeed, it will not help us to have done all those things if this principal cause, for whose sake everything must be undertaken, has been removed. [Col. 1293B]

This, then, must be our principal effort: this must be the immovable destination of the heart, continually desired, so that the mind may always cling to divine things and to God. Whatever differs from this, however great it may be, must nevertheless be judged secondary, or even least of all, or certainly harmful.

The figure of this state of mind or activity is beautifully represented in the Gospel by Martha and Mary (Luke X, 41). Martha was serving in a holy ministry as best she could, ministering to the Lord himself and to his disciples, while Mary, intent solely upon spiritual teaching, clung to the feet of Jesus, kissing them and anointing them with the ointment of a good confession. [Col. 1293C] Yet the Lord preferred Mary, because she had chosen the better part, and the part that could not be taken away from her.

For the Lord said to Martha: “You are anxious and troubled about many things” (ibid.); “but few things are necessary, or even one.” He placed the highest good not in active work, however praiseworthy and abounding in many fruits, but in contemplation of himself [the text reads *sua*; perhaps read *sui*, “his own”], which is truly simple and one. Declaring that few things are necessary for perfect blessedness—or even one thing—he referred to that *theoria* which first consists in the contemplation of a few things. But the person who is still advancing, when he climbs upward, will also reach, with God’s help, that which is called “one thing,” namely, the vision of God alone, so that, having surpassed even the wonderful activities and ministries of the saints, he may now be nourished solely by the beauty and knowledge of God. [Col. 1293D]

Mary therefore chose the good part, which will not be taken away from her, and this deserves careful consideration. For when he says, “Mary chose the good part,” although he says nothing about Martha and does not appear to reproach her at all, by praising one he nevertheless declares the other inferior. Again, when it is said, “which will not be taken away from her,” he shows that Martha’s portion can be taken away. Bodily ministry cannot remain perpetually with a person; but he teaches that Mary’s devotion can never come to an end.

Therefore it seems appropriate to me to consider what this good thing is that the Apostle Paul described in his Epistle as though he were seeking it and unable to accomplish it, saying: “For I do not do the good that I desire; but the evil that I hate, that I do” (Rom. VII, 15); and again: “If I do what I desire, it is no longer I who perform it, but sin dwelling in me” (ibid., v. 15); and what follows: “For I delight in the law of God according to the inner person, but I see another law in my members opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members” (ibid., vv. 22–23). [Col. 1294A]

Although some think that he spoke these words in the person of sinners, it is clear that they cannot in every respect apply to the person of sinners, but concern only those who are called “perfect” and correspond only to the holiness of those who follow the merits of the Apostles. [Col. 1294B]

For how could this statement apply to the person of sinners: “I do not do the good that I desire, but the evil that I hate, that I do”? Nor does this other statement fit them: “If I do what I do not desire, it is no longer I who perform it, but sin dwelling in me.” For who among wrongdoers is polluted by adultery and fornication against his will? Who, unwillingly, lays snares for his neighbor? Who is compelled by unavoidable necessity to crush a person with false testimony, deceive by theft, desire another’s possessions, or shed blood?

On the contrary, as it is written, the human race has been diligently devoted to wickedness from its youth. The prophet Jeremiah says that people not only willingly and without any rest of heart or body commit crimes of depravity, but that they labor with such strenuous efforts to accomplish them that they sweat in reaching their fulfillment and are not recalled from their deadly appetite for wickedness even by the obstacles of great difficulties. [Col. 1294C] He says: “They have labored to act wickedly” (Jer. IX, 5).

Who could say that this also applies to sinners: “Therefore I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin”? It is evident that they serve God neither in mind nor in flesh. Or how could those who sin in body serve God in mind, when the flesh conceives the fuel of vices from the heart, and the author himself declares that the source and origin of sins in both natures flow from the heart: “From the heart,” he says, “proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, thefts, and so forth” (Matt. XV, 19)?

It is therefore plainly shown that this cannot in any way be understood as referring to sinners, who not only do not hate evil but love it, and who serve God neither in mind nor in flesh to such a degree that they sin in mind before they sin in body and are overtaken by the sin of their thoughts before they fulfill the desire of the body. [Col. 1294D]

It remains, then, that we measure the force of the meaning from the speaker’s innermost feeling and examine what the blessed Apostle called good and what he pronounced evil by comparison—not through the bare meaning of the words, but with the same intention with which he examined them. Let us also investigate his outlook according to the dignity and merit of the one who spoke. Finally, we must carefully inquire what this principally good thing was that the Apostle could not accomplish even when he wished to do so. [Col. 1295A]

For we know many good things that we cannot deny the blessed Apostle and all men of his merit to have possessed by nature and acquired by grace. There is good chastity, praiseworthy continence, admirable prudence, generous kindness, watchful sobriety, moderate self-restraint, devout mercy, and holy justice. All these virtues were so full and perfect in the Apostle Paul and his companions that it is beyond doubt that religion was taught by their example of virtue more than by their words.

What a great good of mercy it was that they were always consumed by constant care for the churches and sleepless concern! What perfection it is to burn for those who cause scandal and to become weak with the weak!

Since the Apostle abounded in so many goods, we cannot recognize what that good was whose perfection he lacked unless we advance into the feeling in which he himself spoke. [Col. 1295B] All the virtues we have mentioned, although they shine like splendid and beautiful gems, nevertheless, when compared with that glorious and outstanding pearl which the merchant in the Gospel sought and desired to purchase by selling everything he possessed, become so diminished and despised in value that, once they have been sold without hesitation, possession of the one good enriches the seller of countless goods.

What, then, is that one thing which is placed so incomparably above so many and such innumerable goods that, with everything else despised and cast aside, it alone ought to be possessed? Surely it is that best part whose magnificence and permanence Mary preferred when she abandoned the task of hospitality and service. For the Lord says: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; but few things are necessary, or even one. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her” (Luke X, 41). [Col. 1295C]

There is therefore, as we have said, one and only one *theoria*, that is, contemplation of God, to which all forms of justification and every practice of virtue are rightly subordinated. All those things that we said shone in the Apostle Paul are not only good and useful but also great and distinguished. Yet just as the metal tin, which was thought to possess some usefulness and value, becomes worthless when silver is considered, and silver’s value in turn vanishes in comparison with gold, and gold itself is despised when gems are contemplated, and the multitude of gems, however remarkable, is surpassed by the splendor of a single pearl, so all those merits of holiness, although they are not only good and useful for the present but also acquire the gift of eternity, will nevertheless be judged worthless and, so to speak, saleable goods when compared with the merits of divine contemplation. [Col. 1295D]

For who, however eminent among all the just and saints and however bound by the chains of this body, can be believed to have possessed this highest good in such a way that, never descending from divine contemplation, he was thought to have been withdrawn even for a brief time from him who alone is good? Who has never cared about food, clothing, or any other bodily matter; who has never been concerned with receiving brothers, changing his place, or constructing his cell; who has never desired human assistance; or who, afflicted by the barrenness of poverty, would not incur the rebuke of the Lord’s sentence: “Do not be anxious for your soul, what you shall eat, nor for your body, what you shall wear”? [Col. 1296A]

Finally, we confidently assert that the Apostle Paul himself, who surpassed the labor of all the saints in the number of his sufferings, could not fulfill this. He himself testifies to it in the Acts of the Apostles, saying to his disciples: “You yourselves know that these hands ministered to the things that were necessary for me and for those who were with me” (Acts XX, 34). And when writing to the Thessalonians, he testifies that he worked in labor and weariness, night and day.

Although these things prepared great rewards of merit for him, nevertheless his mind, though holy and exalted, could not avoid being drawn away at times from that heavenly theory—the contemplation of God—by earthly work. [Col. 1296B]

Finally, when he saw himself enriched with such and so many fruits, and weighed in his heart the good of contemplation, setting, as it were, the gain of such great labors in one scale and the delight of divine contemplation in the other, after a long examination and a kind of chastening of his heart—while on one side the immense rewards of his labors delighted him and on the other the desire for unity and inseparable fellowship with Christ invited him even to the dissolution of the flesh—he finally cried out anxiously and said: “I do not know what to choose; I am pressed between the two, having the desire to depart and be with Christ, for that is much better, but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. I, 22). [Col. 1296C]

Although he had placed the excellence of this good above his many other goods and above all the fruits of his preaching, nevertheless he submits it to charity, without which no one can win the Lord’s favor. For the sake of those to whom he was still giving milk, as a nurse from evangelical breasts, he did not refuse separation from Christ, harmful to himself but necessary for others.

It is impossible for a mind stretched by such frequent cares and hindered by such various and violent anxieties always to enjoy the vision of God. For what study of the saints is so persistent, what purpose so difficult, that the crafty enemy cannot mock it in some way? Who has pursued the solitude of the desert and avoided the company of all mortals so completely that he has never slipped into superfluous thoughts or departed from the contemplation of God, which alone is truly good, through the sight of things or the occupation of earthly activities? [Col. 1296D]

Who has ever been able to retain such fervor of spirit that he was not at times carried away by slippery thoughts from the very concentration of prayer and suddenly fell from heavenly things to earthly ones? Who among us, to omit the other periods of wandering, does not even in that moment when, praying to God, he raises his mind to higher things, collapse through some stupor and, even against his will, offend God through the very act by which he hoped to obtain forgiveness of sins?

Who has ever been so experienced and watchful that, while singing a psalm to God, his mind was never drawn away from the meaning of Scripture? Who is so familiar with God and so closely joined to him that he can rejoice in having fulfilled, even for one day, the apostolic command by which we are instructed to pray without ceasing? [Col. 1297A]

Although all these things may seem light and almost unrelated to sin to some who are entangled in grosser vices, to those who know the good of perfection even the multitude of the smallest matters is extremely burdensome. The saints therefore despise everything from which this world is constituted, but it is impossible that they should not be carried away toward such things even by a brief excess of thought.

No human being in this life, except our Lord and Savior, has held the natural wandering of the mind so constantly fixed upon the contemplation of God that he never, seized by the delight of some worldly thing, sinned through being drawn away from it. Scripture says: “The stars themselves are not clean in his sight”; and again: “If he does not trust in his saints and finds perversity in his angels”; or, according to the corrected translation: “Behold, among his saints no one is unchangeable, and the heavens are not clean in his sight.” [Col. 1297B]

Rightly, therefore, I would compare the saints, who retain the memory of God steadfastly and are borne along as though walking suspended upon lines stretched upward, to *schoenobatae*, whom the common people call rope-walkers. They place the whole of their safety and life upon the extremely narrow path of that rope and do not doubt that they will immediately encounter a most terrible death if their foot deviates through even a slight wavering or goes beyond the measure of that saving direction.

While they attempt with marvelous skill to make their aerial steps through empty space, if they do not preserve that path, narrower than a footprint, with cautious and anxious control, the earth—which is naturally the basis of all things and the firmest and safest foundation for everyone—becomes for them immediate and evident destruction. This is not because its nature has changed, but because they fall upon it under the precipitous weight of the flesh. [Col. 1297C]

So too the tireless goodness and unchanging substance of God itself harms no one; but by turning away from the highest and striving toward the lowest, we bring death upon ourselves. Indeed, the very turning away becomes death for the one who turns away.

“For woe to them,” he says, “because they have departed from me; they shall be devastated, because they have transgressed against me” (Hos. VII, 13). And again: “Woe to them when I depart from them; for your wickedness shall rebuke you, and your apostasy shall reprove you. Know and see that it is evil and bitter for you to have abandoned the Lord your God” (Hos. IX, 12). [Col. 1297D]

Since the saints therefore daily feel themselves weighed down by the burden of earthly thought, withdrawing from that sublimity of mind and being led unwillingly—or rather, even without knowing it—into the law of sin and death, and since, to omit everything else, they are recalled from the sight of God by those good and just but nevertheless earthly works mentioned above, they certainly have reasons to sigh continually to the Lord.

They have reasons to declare themselves sinners in truth, humiliated and contrite, not merely in words but in feeling; to ask forgiveness for all that they daily incur after being overcome by the weakness of the flesh; and, continually seeking the Lord’s grace, to pour out genuine tears of repentance without ceasing. For they see that they remain entangled until the very end of life in the same surges by which they are continually tormented with sorrow, and that they cannot offer even their prayers without anxiety of thought. [Col. 1298A]

Having therefore learned by experience that human strength cannot attain the desired end because of the burden of the flesh, nor be joined, according to the desire of the heart, to that chief and highest good, but is led captive from its contemplation toward worldly things, they flee to the grace of God, which justifies the ungodly, and proclaim with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII, 24). [Col. 1298B]

They feel that they cannot perfectly accomplish the good that they desire, but continually fall into what they do not desire and what they hate: the evil of the movements of thought and the care of bodily things. They indeed delight in the law of God according to the inner person, who, transcending all visible things, strives always to be united with God alone. But they see “another law in their members,” that is, one implanted in the nature of the human condition, which “opposes the law of their mind” and violently drags their understanding captive under the law of sin.

This law compels the mind, after abandoning the principal good, to submit to earthly thought. Although such thought may seem necessary and useful when it is undertaken for the sake of some religious necessity and with proper order, it is nevertheless judged evil and to be avoided by those who are withdrawn through it, even for a short time, from the joy of that perfect blessedness, which delights the contemplation of all the saints. [Col. 1298C]

*(Moses in Cassiodorus, Conferences, Conference I, chapter 15.)*

The contemplation of God, however, is conceived in many ways. God is known not only through admiration of that incomprehensible substance of his—although this remains hidden for the present in the hope of the promise—but also through the greatness of his creatures, through consideration of his justice, and through the assistance of his daily dispensation.

This occurs when, with the purest mind, we examine what he has done with his saints through each generation; when we contemplate his power by which he governs, orders, and rules all things; when, with trembling heart, we marvel at the immensity of his knowledge and at the eye from which the secrets of hearts cannot be hidden; when we think with awe that the sand of the sea and the number of the waves have been measured and known by him; when we contemplate with astonishment that raindrops, the days and hours of the ages, and all past and future things stand before his knowledge. [Col. 1298D]

It occurs when we consider his ineffable clemency, by which he sustains with tireless patience countless crimes committed every moment beneath his gaze; when we contemplate the calling by which, without any preceding merits, he summoned us by the grace of his mercy; and, finally, when we observe with a kind of excess of wonder how many opportunities for salvation he grants to those whom he adopts. [Col. 1299A]

It occurs when we consider that he commanded us to be born in such a way that, from our very cradles, the grace and knowledge of his law might be given to us; that, by conquering the adversary within us, he rewards us with eternal blessedness and everlasting prizes for the sole assent of a good will; and finally, when he undertook the dispensation of his incarnation for our salvation and spread the wondrous mysteries of his divine purposes among all nations.

There are also innumerable other contemplations of this kind, which arise in our minds according to the quality of our life and the purity of our heart. Through them God is either seen by pure eyes or held by them.

No one, however, will retain these contemplations perpetually if any affection for carnal things still lives within him. For the Lord says: “You cannot see my face; for no human being shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII, 20)—that is, no one attached to this world and to earthly affections. [Col. 1299B]

The soul, therefore, has its food and its clothing when it clings to that supreme good which is divine, which the Apostle Peter urges us to seek, so that through acquiring knowledge of it we may become partakers of the divine nature. The good God discloses knowledge of this to his saints and gives it from his good treasury, as the sacred law testifies, saying: “For the Lord swore to their fathers that he would give you and open for you his good treasury, from which heavenly treasure he gives rain to his land, to bless all the works of his hands” (Deut. XVIII). This rain is the word of the law, which sprinkles that fertile and fruitful soul with good works, so that it may possess the moisture of grace. David sought knowledge of this good, as he himself indicates, saying: [Col. 1299C] “One thing I asked of the Lord, this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, and behold the delights of the Lord and contemplate his temple” (Ps. XXVI, 4). Finally, he immediately explained in the same psalm that this is the supreme good: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (ibid.). Here it is sought; there it is fully seen face to face. This good is in the house of God, in that secret place and retreat of his. Hence he says again: “We shall be filled with the good things of your house” (Ps. LXIV, 6). Elsewhere, too, he declared that this is the supreme blessing, saying: “May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem” (Ps. CXXVII, 5). Blessed, therefore, is the one who dwells there, by the progress of faith, the lodging of the mind, the dwelling-place of devotion, and the practice of virtue. [Col. 1299D]

Let us therefore remain at once in that place and in him of whom Isaiah also says: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” (Isa. LII, 7; Rom. X, 15). Who are those who proclaim good things, if not Peter, if not Paul, if not all the Apostles? What good things do they proclaim, if not the Lord Jesus? He is our peace; he is that supreme good, because he himself is good from the Good—for from a good tree, Scripture says, comes good fruit. His Spirit, too, is good; receiving from him, it leads God’s servants along the straight path. But who, possessing the Spirit of God within him, would deny the Good, when he himself says: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matt. VI, 23).

May this Good come into our soul, into the inmost depths of our mind. [Col. 1300A] The merciful God gives it to those who ask him. This is our treasure, this is our way, this is our wisdom, our righteousness, our shepherd—and the Good Shepherd. This is our life. You see how many goods there are in the one Good. The evangelists proclaim these goods to us. Seeking these goods, David says: “Who will show us good things?” (Ps. IV, 6). And he shows that he himself is the good when he adds: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us.” But who is the light of the Father’s countenance except the radiance of glory and the image of the invisible God? In him the Father is both seen and glorified, just as he himself glorifies his Son.

The Lord Jesus, therefore, is the supreme Good, announced to us by the prophets, proclaimed by the angels, promised by the Father, and preached as good news by the Apostles. He came to us like ripeness; and he came not only like ripeness, but is present in our minds as ripeness, so that nothing unripe or immature may be found in our counsels, nothing harsh or rough in our works and conduct. He was the first to proclaim good things and was present; hence he says: “Here I am, the one who was speaking” (Isa. LII, 6)—that is, “I, who was speaking in the prophets, am present in the body that I assumed from the Virgin. I am present as the inner image of God, the impress of his substance; and I am present as man. But who recognizes me? They saw the man, but they believed in the works that were beyond man.”

Was he not as man when he wept for Lazarus, and again beyond man when he raised him? Was he not as man when he was scourged, and again beyond man when he took away the sin of the whole world? Let us therefore hasten to him in whom the supreme Good exists, [Col. 1300C] since he is goodness itself, the patience of Israel, who calls you to repentance so that you may not come into judgment but receive forgiveness of sins. “Repent,” he says (Matt. III, 2). He is the one of whom the prophet Amos cries: “Seek the good.” He is the supreme Good, who needs nothing and abounds in all things.

He easily abounds in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily; he easily abounds from whose fullness, the Evangelist says, we have all received and in whom we have been filled. This, therefore, is the true and supreme Good. As soon as the soul has tasted it with its desire and delight, and has drunk deeply from these two affections, banishing grief and fear, it burns with unbelievable ardor. Having kissed the Word of God, it knows no measure and cannot be satisfied, saying: “You are sweet, Lord, and in your delight teach me your ordinances” (Ps. XCIX, 5). Having kissed the Word of God, it desires him above every beauty, loves him above every joy, delights in him above all spices, longs to see him frequently and gaze upon him often, and longs to be drawn so that it may follow:

“Your name is poured-out perfume; therefore the young women love you, therefore we strive, but we cannot grasp you. Draw us, so that we may be able to run, so that by the fragrance of your perfumes we may receive the strength to follow.”

It hastens also, amid the mysteries, to see the very rest of the Word, the dwelling-place of that supreme Good itself, and its light and splendor. In that paternal bosom and retreat it hastens to hear his words, and when it has heard them, it receives them as sweeter than all sweetness. Let the prophet teach you, he who tasted them and said: “How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII, 103).

For what else would the soul desire once it has tasted the sweetness of the Word and once seen his splendor? Moses, stationed on the mountain for forty days while receiving the law, did not seek bodily food. Elijah, hastening toward that rest, asked that his soul be taken from him. Peter, gazing on the mountain at the glory of the Lord’s resurrection, did not want to descend, saying: “Lord, it is good for us to be here” (Mark IX, 3).

How great, then, is the glory of the divine substance! How great are the good things of the Word, into which the angels long to look! The soul that sees him does not seek this body; it understands that it ought to have the least possible familiarity with it, renounces itself to God, withdraws from the bonds of the flesh, and strips itself of all the chains of these pleasures. Thus Stephen saw Jesus and was not afraid to be stoned; indeed, while he was being stoned, he prayed not for himself but for those by whom he was being killed. Paul, too, caught up to the third heaven, did not know whether he was in the body or outside the body. Caught up, I say, into paradise, he no longer experienced the body in its ordinary way; and when he heard the words of God, he was ashamed to descend to the weaknesses of the body. Thus, knowing what he had seen or heard in paradise, he cried out, saying: “Why are you still making decisions as though you were living in this world: ‘Do not touch, do not handle, do not taste,’ things which all lead to corruption through use” (Col. II, 21)? [Col. 1301C]

For he wanted us to exist in the image of this world, not in its possession and use, so that we might use this world as though we did not use it—as passing through, not as settling down; walking as in an image of the age, not in desire—so that with the utmost speed we might pass through the very image of this world. Finally, walking by faith and not by sight, he was a stranger to the body but present with God; and while he was on earth, he lived not in earthly things but in heavenly ones.

Therefore let our soul, which wishes to draw near to God, lift itself above the body and cling always to that supreme Good which is divine, which always is, which was from the beginning, and which was with God: this is the Word of God. He is that divine one in whom we live and move and have our being. He is the one who was in the beginning; he is the one who is. “For Jesus Christ, the Son of God,” he says, “is in you; in him there was no Yes and No, but Yes was in him.” He told Moses to say: “He who is has sent me.”

Since our soul is with him and, if possible, always with him, so that one may say of ours too, “My soul will always be in your hands,” it will be so if it is not in the flesh but in the spirit and does not mingle with earthly things. For when it turns back toward carnal things, the enticement of the body creeps upon it; then it burns with anger and indignation; then it is afflicted with sorrow; then it is laid low through arrogance; then it is tormented by grief. These are the grave illnesses of the soul, by which it is often driven toward death, while its eyes are blinded so that they do not see the true light of glory and the riches of the eternal inheritance.

But if it continually directs its eyes toward God, it will receive from Christ the radiance of wisdom, so that, enlightened in knowledge, it may possess a clear vision; so that it may see the hope of our calling, and behold what is good, perfect, and pleasing. What is good and pleasing to the Father, and what is perfect, you have in the Gospel, where the Lord says: “Love your enemies, so that you may imitate the Father who rains upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. V, 44). This is surely an act of goodness. Then he concludes, saying: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (ibid., v. 48). For love is perfect; indeed, it is the fullness of the law. What, then, is as good as love, which thinks no evil?

Therefore flee the lands in which there is envy, where there is ambition, where there is strife. Let your soul make itself capable of that Good, so that it may fly above the clouds like an eagle, be renewed like an eagle, and put forth wings, so that, with the oars of its wings renewed, it may not fear to seek the heights. Let it leave this dwelling-place, for an earthly habitation weighs down the soul. Let it strip off the old things, cast away the desires of error, and wash its eyes, so that it may see the fountain of true wisdom, the fountain of eternal life. It flows forth and overflows for all, needing no one—for who has given anything to him, since all things are from him, through him, and in him?

The supreme Good, therefore, is the fountain of life, from which the substance of life is supplied to all. Yet it possesses enduring life in itself; it receives from no one as though it were needy. It gives good things to others; they do not come to it from elsewhere. For it does not need our goods, and hence he says in the person of a human being: “You have no need of my goods” (Ps. XV, 2). What, then, is more beautiful than to draw near to him and cling to him? What greater pleasure is there? Once someone has seen him and freely tasted from the fountain of living water, what else can he desire? What kingdoms, what powers, what money, when he recognizes how miserable are even the conditions of kings here, how changeable the states of authority, how brief the spans of this life, and how much servitude exists within power itself, since rulers live according to the will of others, not their own?

Who, moreover, passes into eternal life possessing wealth, unless supported by the wealth of virtues—which is declared impossible for the merely rich to possess? It is not blessedness, therefore, to use these things, but to see the one by whom you despise them and judge them truly vain, empty, and worthless; to love the beauty of naked truth, which rebukes these fleeting vanities of the age.

Raise your eyes, therefore, O soul—those eyes of which the Word of God says to you: “You have captured us in the heart, my sister, my bride; you have captured us with one of your eyes” (Song IV, 9). Ascend the palm tree; conquer the world, so that you may grasp the height of the Word. Leave that image of the world outside; leave wickedness outside, but bring in goodness of mind, which possesses grace in the tree of life, if it washes its robe and enters the city that is the true homeland of the saints. There is the Lord’s tabernacle, around which the Lord’s scribes spread their covering. There neither day, nor sun, nor moon supplies light; the Lord himself is its light, illuminating the whole city. For he is the light of the world—not visible light, of course, but the intelligible splendor of souls [Col. 1303A] that are in this world, into whom rational prudence pours itself with shining light, proclaimed in the Gospel “in the body of virtue, inflaming with its vapor the hidden places of minds and the inner chambers of souls.”

If anyone, therefore, begins to be an inhabitant of that heavenly city—an inhabitant, that is, in conduct and character—let him not depart, withdraw, go out, or turn back his step—not, I say, the step of the body, but the step of the mind. Let him not turn back. Behind him is luxury; behind him is impurity. Thus Lot, ascending the mountain, left behind the Sodomite crimes. But because he looked back, he could not escape to the higher places.

Therefore let your feet not turn back, but neither let your conduct turn back. Let your hands not become slack, nor the knees of your devotion and faith grow weak. Let there be no relapse of your will, no interruption through crimes. You have entered: remain. You have arrived: stand firm. Save yourself by saving your soul. Ascend directly; raise your step. Let no one sit safely there [perhaps read: “depart”]. Here there is a way; there, ruin. Here there is ascent; there, a precipice. There is labor in ascending, but danger in descending.

Yet powerful is the Lord, who can guard you when you are established there, enclosed by prophetic walls and apostolic towers. Therefore the Lord says to you: “Enter, tread the grapes, for the vintage is at hand; let us be inside, not outside.” And in the Gospel the Son of God says: “Let the one who is on the housetop not come down to take his vessels” (Matt. XXIV, 17). This is not said of this roof, but of that one: “He stretches out the heavens like a chamber.”
