Be inside, therefore; within Jerusalem; within your soul, peaceful, gentle, [Col. 1303C] and tranquil. Do not leave it, nor descend from it in order to lift up this vessel of yours through honors, riches, or arrogance. Remain inside, so that foreigners may not pass through you; so that sins may not pass through your soul; so that vain actions and empty thoughts may not pass through.

But if you consecrate [perhaps read: “have consecrated”] the struggle for the contest of devotion and faith, for the pursuit of truth, against the enticements of the passions, and if you take up the armor of God against spiritual wickedness and the cunning of the devil, who tests our senses by fraud and deceit, then the gentle warrior will easily be able to overcome him—the one who does not sow quarrels, but, as befits a servant of the Lord, teaches the faith with modesty and rebukes those who oppose it. Scripture says of this: “Let the gentle warrior rise, and let the weak say: ‘I can do all things in him who strengthens me’” (Phil. IV, 13).

Relying on this faith, even the weak will prevail, his soul will be holy, and the prophetic or apostolic mountains will drip sweetness for him, and the hills will flow with milk (Amos IX, 13)—such as that hill which gave the Corinthians a drink of milk. And there will flow for him “waters from his own vessels, and springs from his own wells,” or “living waters from his belly”—that is, spiritual waters which the Holy Spirit supplies to his faithful. May he also deign to water your soul, “so that within you there may abound a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John IV, 14).

# BOOK THREE: ON THE MANNER OF REPENTANCE

[Col. 1304A]

## CHAPTER I — On True Repentance

Since the greatest good is for a person, humbling himself, to submit himself wholly to his Creator, and, obeying his commands, not to place confidence in himself but firmly to trust in God’s goodness; and since he should disclose in confession to a priest whatever he remembers having done wickedly, and for this very reason perform worthy penance, hoping in the mercy of his Maker—for he who created him from nothing is able, after his fall, to restore him again, to make him righteous from a sinner, and to make him a participant in the eternal kingdom together with his holy angels—alas, there are many [Col. 1304B] who are not afraid to sin and do not cease to live in sins almost until the end of their lives, flattering themselves in their danger and saying: “The mercy of God is great. Even if I spend all the days of my life in sins, and at the point of death finally confess my sins and receive penance, I shall immediately be saved.” They do not know whether they will be granted to live upon earth even the span of a single day.

Others, after committing many crimes, despair of themselves and, distrustful of God’s goodness, say that if, after receiving baptism, they pollute themselves with the filth of vices, they can in no way be restored to their former state or earn complete forgiveness. But since this error has spread widely and has taken deeper and deeper root in many places, it seems fitting to me [Col. 1304C] to gather together, for its eradication, the canonical judgments and the sayings of orthodox Fathers in a single volume, and to make clear what the holy Fathers judged should be believed concerning this matter, and what I myself think about it.

For although the sayings of the holy prophets in some passages threaten sinners with punishments, nevertheless they plainly give hope of forgiveness to those who turn away from sins and truly do penance, and proclaim remission of sins to them. Hence the Lord himself, coming into the world and born without sin through a virgin, graciously summoned sinners to himself. At the very beginning of his preaching, as Matthew the Evangelist testifies, he preached the same words that his forerunner John, namely the Baptist, had previously proclaimed while teaching in the desert of Judea. Of him it is written: “When Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he began to preach and say: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is drawing near’” (Matt. III, 2).

If he had been unwilling to forgive sinners who worthily did penance for their sins, he would certainly not have commanded them to repent. It is rightly said, therefore, through the Savior, that the kingdom of heaven draws near to those who repent, because through him we are lifted from the depths to the heights. The kingdom of heaven will truly draw near to those who repent when, at his coming, our Savior promised eternal life to all who, through repentance, renouncing their former errors, have fled to his faith and baptism: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John I, 12).

It draws near even now, because after his resurrection he commanded his disciples to preach repentance and the remission of sins in his name to all nations: “And behold,” he says, “I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20).

It is necessary for everyone who recognizes himself to be a sinner and guilty to come to his own aid through the remedy of repentance and not delay turning to better things from day to day. While he has the opportunity and remains in this life, he should strive to devote himself more to good works than to lie idle in the torpor of negligence. Scripture teaches this, saying: “Do not add sin upon sin and say: ‘The mercy of God is great,’ for mercy and wrath are with him” (Ecclus. V, 6–7).

## CHAPTER II — On Those Who Live Uprightly

[Col. 1305B]

For I am certain that a baptized person who has led a life—not, I dare not say, without sin, for who is without sin?—but without crime, and who has other sins that are forgiven him daily in the prayer in which he says, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” if he does what he desires God to do for him, when he finishes this life does not end life but passes from life to life, from laborious life to restful life, from wretchedness to blessedness, from temporal life to eternal life. Whether such a person runs of his own will to baptism, or is baptized while in danger so that he may pass over, he goes to the Lord; he goes to rest.

But if a baptized person afterward becomes a deserter and violator of the sacrament, and by sinning drives the Lord away from himself, let him repent with his whole heart and truly do penance, seeing in himself what David’s heart saw when, severely rebuked by the prophet and after terrifying threats, he cried out to God, saying: “I have sinned.” And immediately he heard: “The Lord has taken away your sin; you shall not die.”

How powerful is this word! It consists of three syllables: “I have sinned.” Yet in these three syllables the flame of the sacrifice of his heart rose to heaven. Therefore the one who truly does penance, and is released from the bond by which he had been bound, and lives well after penance, will go to the Lord when he dies after reconciliation; he will go to rest. He will not be deprived of the kingdom of God; he will be sown [perhaps read: “separated”] from the people of the devil.

## CHAPTER III — On Those Converted Late

[Col. 1305D]

But if someone, placed in the final crisis of his illness, receives penance, is immediately reconciled, and then departs from the body, I confess that I do not deny him what he asks; but neither do I presume to say that he has departed well. I do not presume, I do not promise, I do not say it. I deceive no one; I mislead no one. It is not promised outright.

The faithful person who lives well departs from this world securely if, while healthy, he does penance and afterward lives well after reconciliation. But someone says: “What does ‘lives well’ mean? Teach us this too, good priest, so that we may know it. You say that you do not know whether, if someone receives penance and departs at that moment, God will forgive his offenses and release him from his sins on the day of judgment. In that case you give us no assurance whatever; at least you ought to teach us how we should live well after penance.”

I say, therefore: abstain from drunkenness, from lust, from theft, from evil speech, from immoderate laughter itself, and from idle words, for which people will have to give an account on the day of judgment. See how trivial are the things I have mentioned—and yet all those things are serious and destructive. I say something else: a person must guard himself from those vices not only after penance but also before penance, while he is healthy, because he does not know whether he will be able to receive that penance and confess his sins to God and to the priest.

That is why I said: one must live well before penance, and better after penance. But if someone does penance at the very end, is reconciled, and departs from the body, I do not know whether he departs securely. I can give penance; [Col. 1306B] I cannot give security. Pay attention to what I am about to say; I must explain it more clearly so that no one may misunderstand me.

Do I say that he will be condemned? But neither do I say that he will be delivered. And what do you say to me, holy bishop? What shall I say to you? I do not know. I have already said: I do not presume; I do not promise. I simply do not know God’s will.

But do you wish, brother, to be freed from uncertainty? Do you wish to escape what is doubtful? Do penance while you are healthy. For if, while healthy, you do true penance, and the final day finds you, people will hasten to reconcile you. If you act in this way, you are secure. Why are you secure? Do you want me to tell you? Because you did penance at a time when you were able to sin.

There: I have told you why you are secure. But if you wish to do that penance only when you are no longer able to sin, your sins have left you, not you your sins. But someone replies: “How do you know whether perhaps God will have mercy and forgive my sins?” You speak truly, brother; you speak truly. How do I know? And for that reason I give you penance, because I do not know.

“Then,” you say, “leave my case to the Lord. Why do you distress me with words and leave me to God as judge?” I entrust you to the judgment of the one to whose judgment I commend myself. For if I knew that penance would benefit you not at all, I would not give it to you. Again, if I knew that it would benefit you, I would not terrify you.

There are two possibilities: either you are forgiven or you are not forgiven. Which of these will happen to you, I do not know. But I give this counsel: leave aside what is uncertain and hold fast to what is certain. While you live, while you are healthy, perform true penance, so that when you come to God’s judgment you may not be put to shame by him but may be led into the heavenly kingdom.

These words of admonition concerning those who, while they have a suitable time, postpone doing penance, so that they may not delay it until the end of life, should suffice. Now it remains to repeat the teachings of the orthodox Fathers for the correction of those who do not wish to do penance but utterly despair of salvation.

## CHAPTER IV — That One Must Not Despair of God’s Goodness

You must not, therefore, O human being, distrust God or despair of his mercy. I do not want you to doubt or despair that you can be changed for the better. For if the devil had such power that he could lead you from the lofty traces of virtue into the depths of evil, how much more will God be able to recall you to the highest summit of goodness—not merely to restore you to what you were, but also to make you much more blessed than you previously appeared to be?

Do not grant such power to your mind, I beg you, nor hide from yourself the hope of good things, lest what commonly happens to the impious happen to you. For it is not the multitude of sins that leads the soul into despair, but impiety. Hence Solomon said: “Everyone who comes into the depths of evil despises” (Prov. XVIII, 3). It belongs, therefore, to the impious to despair of salvation and to despise when they have come into the depths of sins.

Impiety does not allow them to look toward the Lord and return to the place from which they have fallen. This thought, therefore, which cuts off the hope of conversion, descends from impiety. Like a very heavy stone resting upon the neck of the soul, it continually forces it to look downward toward the earth [Col. 1307B] and does not allow it to raise its eyes toward its Lord.

But it is the mark of a manly spirit and a noble mind to throw off from the neck of one’s soul that most hostile burden—or rather, to cast away the devil who is pressing one down—and to command one’s soul, singing the prophetic words, to say to the Lord: “As the eyes of servants are on the hands of their masters, as the eyes of a maidservant are on the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us. Have mercy on us, Lord, have mercy on us, for we have been filled exceedingly with contempt” (Ps. CXXII, 2).

There is a splendid and heavenly teaching of philosophy in these words: “We have been filled,” he says, “with contempt.” This is what he wanted to teach us: even if, because of the multitude of our sins, we have been filled with contempt and covered with reproaches, nevertheless our eyes are toward the Lord our God until he has mercy on us; nor should we cease our supplication before we deserve to obtain forgiveness of our sins.

For this truly belongs to a steadfast and persistent soul: not to be driven away from perseverance in asking by despair of obtaining, but to persevere and persist in prayers until God has mercy on it. And lest you suppose that you incur a greater offense before the Lord if, although you do not deserve to be heard, you persist too insistently in prayer, remember the Gospel parable. There you will find that the Lord did not regard persistent and importunate petitioners as ungrateful. He says: “Even if he will not give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence he will rise and give him as much as he needs.”

Understand, therefore, dearest one, that the devil introduces despair of obtaining precisely in order to cut off from us hope in God’s goodness, which is the anchor of our salvation and the foundation of our life, the guide of the journey by which one goes to heaven. Finally, the Apostle says: “In hope we have been saved” (Rom. VIII, 24).

Hope, therefore, is where our salvation rests. It lifts souls from the earth, as though they were fastened to it by chains hanging down from heaven, and carries them upward to the heights. It restores to the heavenly seats those who cling to it more firmly, and makes them loftier than the storms of this life and of earthly evils.

If, amid these things, anyone’s spirit should be weakened and let go of the anchor of saving hope, it must fall into the abyss [Col. 1308A] and perish in the depths of evil. When the enemy senses this, and sees us terrified by the multitude of our sins and frightened even by the rebukes of conscience itself, he approaches and implants in us thoughts of despair, heavier than all lead and all sand. If we accept them, we must immediately be submerged by their very weight into the depths of evil, the moorings of our salvation having been torn away.

For we know that many, both in our own times and in the memory of former generations, have slipped from the right path and been hurled from the entrance of the narrow way, yet have afterward been restored in such a manner that they surpassed their former state in their later one, reached the palm, and the crown, and are believed to have been enrolled again among the number and chorus of the saints.

But while someone still remains in the very flame and furnace of lust, these things seem impossible to him, even if he is challenged by a thousand examples. If, however, even a small conversion begins to take place and he gives a beginning to returning, advancing little by little and directing his foot toward the higher things, then the flame that had been more intense will remain behind him. Before his feet, the more vigorously he begins to advance, the more he will find everything lulled to sleep by the cooling refreshment of a certain divine dew. The only point is that we guard against the one thing that is especially hostile to salvation.

## CHAPTER V — How Dangerous Despair Is

Despair is hostile to conversion and repentance. If it settles in the mind, no matter how great the desire for salvation or how immense the resolve to be saved, when despair intervenes every access to salvation [Col. 1308C] will be blocked. Once the path of repentance has been obstructed, the entrance into the struggle is likewise closed. How can someone who is outside the path, and for whom the door is closed, accomplish any good work, since despair prevents him from entering upon good works?

For this reason the devil strives by every means to plant such thoughts in our hearts. If fear of despair keeps us far from the path of virtue, no contest against us will remain for him. For whom would he attack when no one resists? But if someone can loosen this bond, his strength immediately returns to him, the vigor of his spirit grows warm, and he will delight in beginning his contests anew. For he will see that the one from whom he had been fleeing is now fleeing him, and that he is pursuing the one who was pursuing him.

And even if, as the condition of the struggle requires, he should again slip and fall, he must not immediately despair through shame at his fall. Rather, let him remember that this is the law of struggle and combat: not that no one ever fall, but that no one ever yield. For it is not the one who has often fallen who is called defeated, but the one who has yielded at the end. The person conquered by thoughts of despair—how can he recover the strength to struggle, or resist and fight, when he flees and does not return at all to the contest?

I do not want you to suppose that I am speaking only of those who have sinned in a few and lesser matters. I am speaking of the one who has succumbed to every evil, who by the enormity of his crimes has shut the way to the kingdom of heaven against himself, and who has been not an unbeliever but a believer—one of those who previously pleased God but afterward fell either into adultery or into every kind of impurity, things which, as the Apostle says, are shameful even to mention.

I do not say that even this person ought to despair of salvation, even if he has reached old age besieged by such evils. But listen to the reasoning behind this statement. If God’s anger were a passible emotion, we would rightly say that the flame kindled by so many and such great evils of sins could no longer be extinguished. But since the truth of the faith establishes that the divine nature is impassible, we must understand that even if God punishes and even if he inflicts penalties, he does so not with passible anger but with ineffable clemency, with the disposition of one who heals, not one who destroys.

Therefore we ought to repent very willingly. For if the medicine of repentance comes first and heals the soul, it does not allow it to reach the medicines of wrath on account of what it has committed against God. For God does not, as we have said, take vengeance on the sinner for his own sake, as though avenging a personal injury; the divine nature receives nothing of that kind in itself. Rather, he does everything for our benefit and introduces corrections and punishments not to avenge himself but to amend us.

If someone persists in hardness, like one who turns his eyes away from the light, he has indeed inflicted no damage upon the light, but has condemned himself to darkness. Likewise, the one who, through an unrepentant heart, thinks that he despises God’s power makes himself alien to salvation.

If a physician suffers insults from those who are delirious or deranged, he neither grieves nor becomes angry because of them, but does everything that the method of healing requires, even though the one who suffers may seem to be tormented by it. That torment, moreover, is not vengeance for insults but care for the sick person. Indeed, if the patient begins to make even a little progress toward health, you immediately see the physician rejoice, become glad, and carry out the rest of the treatment more eagerly. He never remembers the insults at all, but in everything he gives attention to the patient’s recovery.

How much more, then, does God, even when we have fallen into the utmost madness, act toward us not from a desire for vengeance on account of what we have committed, but desiring to heal the illnesses of vices that have grown old in our inmost being? For this reason he teaches and does everything, desiring our health, not our punishment. Although reason itself sufficiently demonstrates this truth of piety, nevertheless, so that no doubt about such a judgment may arise in you, [Col. 1309D] we can also prove from the divine Scriptures that these things are so.

## CHAPTER VI — Testimonies of Sacred Scripture and Examples of the Penitent Drawn from Them
Tell me, what was more wicked than the king of Babylon? Although he had experienced the Lord’s power in many ways, so that he worshiped His prophet and ordered incense and myrrh to be offered to him, nevertheless he again fell back into his former arrogance against God, and cast into a furnace of burning fire those who refused to worship his image, preferring the veneration of God. Yet God calls even this man, so savage and impious, to repentance and gives him means of conversion [Col. 1310A]. First, by the very fact that He appeared to him in the furnace of fire, joined to the three boys; then by the vision which he saw and which Daniel interpreted—one that by itself would have been sufficient to soften even hearts of stone. But after he had been admonished by these events, an exhortation through prophetic words was also added: for he received the prophet’s counsel, who said:

> “Therefore, O king, let my counsel please you, and redeem your sins by almsgiving, and your iniquities by mercy toward the poor; perhaps there will be patience with your prayers” (Dan. IV, 24).

What do you say to this, wise and blessed man? Even after such great falls he was restored. Believe me: after the most grievous illness, health returns from the very brink of death, and after desperate madness many recover their senses. For behold, as we mentioned above, this Babylonian king had already closed every avenue of salvation against himself by provoking God, who had made him, raised him to the heights of royal power, revealed heavenly mysteries to him, granted him knowledge of future things, and opened to him the secrets of the whole kingdom; He had confounded the magical, astrological, Gazæan, and Chaldaean deceits through the divine interpretation of His prophet, and disclosed the ineffable mystery to the captive boy through his supremely wise discernment. Thus he seemed not merely to believe in the Most High God, but proclaimed throughout the whole world that Daniel’s God was the true God. Yet afterward he not only denied this very God, but again fell into such madness that he cast the servants of God who would not worship his image into a furnace of burning fire [Col. 1310C].

Nevertheless, even there divine mercy does not forget His care and remedy for him. In the very midst of the fire, where he had handed over the boys who worshiped God to the flames, He there too calms him, not by terrors but by wonders. He could have extinguished the fire and poured down rains from heaven, but He does not do this, lest He inflame his madness still further. Instead, He permits the flame to be increased to the extent that the fury of the raging king demanded. He not only does not prevent punishments from being inflicted, but deprives the punishments inflicted of their power to torment. And lest anyone, seeing that the boys were not burned, should think that the flames were an apparition, He allowed the ministers of punishment—namely, those standing around the furnace—to be consumed, so that He might show that the fire which was seen was truly fire.

But the Lord’s command was stronger than the power of the fire. Everything that exists necessarily serves Him from whom it received the origin of its existence. That fire, therefore, received the bodies of the saints and, forgetting by God’s command and will the nature by which it burns, exercised only that part of its nature by which it gives light, so that it did not render the saints and faithful men who had been cast into it corrupted, but illuminated. For they came forth from the fiery furnace like men emerging from a royal palace, objects of wonder and veneration to all. Then no one turned his eyes toward the king, resplendent in purple and diadem; he was abandoned by everyone as though he did not exist, because the wondrous boys seized all eyes for themselves. Who would not be astonished that flames had fed upon the bodies of young men, yet not only shrank from the limbs of the saints, but did not even singe a hair of their heads—the most fragile part of all—or even the outermost hem of their clothing? Who would not marvel that their limbs were stronger than mountains, their garments stronger than metals, and their hair stronger than adamant?

But the height of the wonder increases because, placed in the midst of the flames, they sang a hymn to God. It is well known that those handed over to the flames are consumed as soon as they open their mouths. Those blessed boys, however, remained glorious with God and wondrous among human beings. The impious king, meanwhile, was moved neither by the wonders nor astonished by the mysteries of his vision and humiliation; he remained unbelieving. Yet he was not punished, for God’s patience was not overcome in him. After sustaining him for a very long time, God eventually chastised him—but not punishing what was past, rather looking toward his future amendment. In the end, he was not condemned forever; after being chastised for a short time and corrected for only a few years, he was restored again to his former condition, so that he suffered no loss from the punishment but gained very much through his correction [Col. 1311B].

Such, believe me, such is God’s mercy toward human beings. He never despises repentance when it is offered to Him sincerely and faithfully. Even if someone reaches the greatest depths of evil and then wishes to return from there to the path of virtue, He gladly receives and embraces him, doing everything that may restore him to his former condition. And what is still more excellent and remarkable: even if someone cannot complete the whole process of making satisfaction, God does not reject whatever repentance he has shown, however small or brief its duration. He receives it also and does not allow the reward of even a very slight conversion to perish [Col. 1311C].

## CHAPTER VII — On Isaiah

Isaiah seems to indicate this to me when he says the following concerning the Jewish people:

> “Because of his small sin I grieved him, and I struck him, and I turned my face away from him; and he was grieved and walked sadly before me. I saw him and healed him, and I comforted him” (Isa. LVII, 18).

That impious king also gives us an even clearer testimony: through the wickedness of his wife he sought the prey of his desire, but, shaken by the enormity of the crime itself, repented; clothed in sackcloth, he wept over his deed, and thus stirred up God’s mercy toward himself, so that God absolved him from all his evils. For He says:

> “And he said to Elijah: ‘Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he wept in my presence, I will not bring evil in his days’” (III Kings XXI, 29) [Col. 1311D].

After him came Manasseh, who had surpassed all tyrants in the enormity of his crimes, who had overthrown the worship of divine religion and observance of the law, and who had filled the temple of God with idols, emptying it of heavenly worship. Yet this man, surpassing every form of wickedness in the impiety of his crimes, was nevertheless later counted among God’s friends because he repented.

If these men, or those whom we mentioned above, had considered the enormity of their crimes and despaired of returning through conversion and repentance, they would certainly have fallen away from all the good things that followed their correction. Rather, by looking toward the ineffable mercies of God and the depth of His immeasurable goodness, they broke the devil’s chains of despair from their necks; then, raising themselves up, they turned to the path of virtue and, recalling their steps from the precipice, completed their good course once more [Col. 1312A].

## CHAPTER VIII — On prophetic sayings and Gospel examples concerning the conversion of sinners

These things have been said to us from the examples of the saints. Now hear how the Lord also invites us to conversion through words spoken by the prophets:

> “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts” (Ps. XCIV, 8).

When he says “today,” he indicates the whole time in which we live, even up to the final period of old age, if matters should reach that point [Col. 1312B]. Repentance is measured not by the length of time but by the sincerity of one’s disposition. Or have we not read that the Levites washed away that exceedingly grave sin in the wilderness not through a long period of time but within the brief space of a single day? And that thief who hung upon the cross did not need an extended period to deserve entry into paradise; only as much time was sufficient as could elapse before he was able to utter a single word. Thus, within a moment, he was absolved from the crimes of his entire life and deserved to precede even the Apostles into paradise.

And what of the martyrs? Did they not often receive crowns of immense rewards in a single day, and sometimes within the space of a single hour? Therefore we must only dare, and with ready and eager minds undertake the struggle, so that, moved as if by a kind of indignation, we may become angry against our deceptive lust and turn our desire and love toward the virtue of God [Col. 1312C]. This is what God also asks of us. He does not seek a long duration of time or the affliction of the cross; He looks especially to whether our conversion is true and sincere. Therefore we have sometimes seen those who began last become, by merit, first.

It is not so great an evil to have fallen as, after falling, to lie there and refuse to rise; to sin with a certain deliberate resolve; and to conceal the fault of an evil purpose under words of despair. Against such people the prophet cried out with a kind of indignation:

> “Shall one who falls not rise again? Or shall one who has turned away not return?” (Jer. VIII, 4) [Col. 1312D].

But if you say, “It is asked whether one of the faithful has fallen and has been able to be restored,” hear this: by the very statement that we say he “fell,” we confess that he stood before he fell. No one says that a person has fallen if he has always lain there and never stood.

Let us also bring forth from the divine Scriptures whatever they contain on this subject, whether in parables or in explicit sayings, and whatever is found in the examples of our forebears. What else does that sheep signify which, after straying from the ninety-nine sheep, was later sought and carried back on the shepherd’s shoulders? Does it not plainly display both the fall and the restoration of a believer? It too is a sheep, just as the ninety-nine are; it belongs not to another flock but to one and the same flock, and not to another shepherd but to one and the same shepherd. It had previously used the same pastures as the others, the same drinking places, and the same resting places. But it went astray—and not slightly, for it wandered across mountains and hills, driven far away through the difficult twists and turns of error [Col. 1313A].

Yet the good shepherd did not abandon it to perish in its errors. He sought it and brought it back—not violently forcing it forward or compelling it with blows, but carrying it on his own shoulders. Just as the best physicians moderate the severity of their treatment in some cases toward those whom they see afflicted by the wasting disease of a long illness, dealing with them more gently and tenderly, so God does not recall those whom He sees to be more deeply corrupted by sins by a strict and excessively demanding observance of the path, but gradually and little by little. Thus He supports them in many things and raises them up in many things, lest a sudden conversion seem harsh and difficult to them; lest they appear to remain in their errors not because they are held back by a love of sinning, but because they have been frightened away by the austerity of conversion [Col. 1313B].

Nor does this alone show us, with equal moderation, the manner of conversion. The same is shown by the account written about the return of the prodigal son. He too was a son; he was not a stranger. He was the brother of the one who had never departed from his father. He is therefore a son who is said to have reached the furthest extremities of evil. He had gone away into a distant region and had become very far from God. Though he had been rich and noble, he became worse than a servant and a hired laborer. Yet when he returned and repented, he was received into his former condition and restored to his former glory [Col. 1313C].

If he had despaired and, ashamed of what had happened to him, had blushed to return to his father, but had remained in that distant and alien region, he would certainly not have obtained what he did obtain; rather, he would have perished from hunger and suffered a most miserable death. You see, therefore, how great is the usefulness of repentance and how great is the hope of conversion through repentance. The prodigal son received the state of his former glory, which his elder brother had possessed through perseverance. If one may dare to say such a thing, it seems to me that through his conversion he even gained something more. For see how the elder brother says:

> “Behold, for so many years I have served you, and you have never given me a young goat, so that I might feast with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has consumed your substance with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf” (Luke XV, 29) [Col. 1313D].

How, then, does he not seem to have received more, who returned through repentance, when the elder brother never received a young goat, whereas a fattened calf was killed for him?

Therefore, beloved, having these examples of repentance, let us not persist in evil, nor despair of reconciliation. Rather, let us say: “Let us too return to the Father and draw near to God.” Believe me, He will never turn away those who have converted to Him. We are the ones who have made ourselves far from God. For He Himself says: “I am God who draws near,” and not “a God from afar.” And again, through the same prophet:

> “Sins separate me and you.”

If sins are what separate us from God, let us remove this obstacle, and nothing will prevent us from being joined to God.

Do you wish me to show you that these things were not spoken only in parables but were also fulfilled in actual events? Among the Corinthians there was a certain man who, it seems, was not insignificant. He had committed a sin such as is not ordinarily permitted even among the Gentiles, and he belonged to the number of God’s sons and household. Some report that he was from the priestly order.

What, then? Did Paul remove him from the number of those who hope for salvation? Certainly not. After sufficiently rebuking the Corinthians on his account, wishing again to show that there is no wound and no illness that does not yield and become healed through the medicine of repentance, he ordered the man to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. But he gave this command before he knew of the man’s repentance [Col. 1314B].

When, then, he repented, Paul said:

> “This rebuke, which is inflicted by many, is sufficient for him.”

And he added:

> “I beg you to confirm your love toward him, lest he be possessed by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his devices” (II Cor. II, 8).

What else, then, is taught through all these things except that, even if someone has fallen into the ultimate destruction of sins, Christ can again be restored in him through repentance?

> “For I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11).

Nor should those people be heard in any way who say that the faithful, after a fall into sin—and especially those who have been promoted to an ecclesiastical rank—cannot be completely restored to their former condition.

Concerning this, what the holy pope Gregory thought and replied to a friend who asked him, I judge should be inserted here for the confirmation of our understanding. In the letter which he wrote to Secundinus, a servant of God living in confinement, he says among other things:

“For your holiness asked us to write back to you concerning the priestly office and the possibility of rising again after a fall, since you say that you have read different canons on this matter and different opinions—some allowing restoration, others declaring that restoration is entirely impossible. For our part, beginning generally with the Nicene Council, we venerate it together with the other four councils, because the later councils, following it, agree unanimously with it in all their decisions. We therefore follow both it and the Fathers who preceded us, since, with God as author, we do not depart from their sacred teaching.

“Beginning, then, at the head and proceeding to the fourth ministry of the altar, we recognize that this rule must be observed: since the lesser is preceded by the greater, just as one is greater in honor, so one should be greater in guilt; and the greater the fault that follows upon a person of higher rank, the greater the punishment that should be imposed upon him. After this, repentance should be believed to be fruitful. For what benefit is there in sowing wheat and not gathering its fruit, or in building a house and not dwelling in it? After worthy satisfaction, we believe that one may return to honor, as the prophet says:

> ‘Will one who falls not add that he may rise again? And will one who has turned away not return?’” (Isa. XXIV, 20) [Col. 1314D].

The same prophet says to the sinner:

> “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, then he will be saved” (Ezek. XXXIII, 12).

Therefore the Psalmist says:

> “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. L, 12) [Col. 1315A].

When he asks not to be cast away by God because of the guilt of his fall, the king and prophet, shaken with fear after having taken another man’s wife, added, after the prophet had pointed out his crime and he had begun to repent:

> “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit” (Ps. L, 14).

For if he himself had not offered worthy repentance to God, he would certainly not have proclaimed it to others. He says:

> “I will teach transgressors your ways, and the impious will be converted to you” (Ps. L, 15).

When the prophet saw that his own sins had been cleansed through repentance, he did not hesitate to chastise the sins of others by preaching, and thus he sought to offer sacrifice from himself, saying:

> “The sacrifice to God is a broken spirit” (ibid., v. 19).

These things would have been sufficient. But the more every judgment is confirmed by the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures, the more readily it is believed. Concerning this the prophet says:

> “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.”

To sinners it is said:

> “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, all his iniquities will be delivered over to oblivion.”

If our Redeemer, who came not to destroy sinners but to justify them, leaves the offenses of sinners in oblivion, what human being would reserve them for condemnation? For the Apostle says:

> “If God justifies, who is he that condemns?”

Returning to the fountain of mercy, let us bring forth the Gospel saying:

> “I will rejoice,” He says, “over one sinner doing penance more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Matt. XVIII, 13).

And, leaving the ninety-nine who had not strayed, He carried the lost sheep back to the fold on His shoulder. If the wandering sheep, after being found, is carried back to the fold on the shepherd’s shoulder, why should a minister not be recalled to the ministry of the Church after punishment?

What, then, is more serious: to commit a carnal offense, from which not many but only a few are found to be free, or to deny the Son of God out of fear? We know that the blessed chief of the Apostles, Peter, to whose body we now sit unworthy, fell into this sin. But repentance followed his denial, and mercy was granted after repentance; for Christ did not cast him out of the apostolate, although He had foretold that Peter would deny Him [Col. 1315C].

Let us therefore turn, my dearest friends, and return to the fulfillment of God’s will. For God created us and made us exist when we did not exist so that He might confer eternal goods upon us and grant us the kingdom of heaven. He did not make us for the purpose of handing us over to Gehenna and everlasting fire. The kingdom of heaven was prepared for us; Gehenna was prepared for the devil. Let us prove from the Gospels that this is so. The Lord Himself says to those who are at His right hand:

> “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34).

But to those who are at His left He says:

> “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., 41).

He did not say “for you,” but “for the devil.” If the fire of Gehenna was prepared for the devil, and the kingdom of heaven was prepared for humanity from the foundation of the world, let us take care only not to exclude ourselves from entry into these blessings by stubbornly persisting in evil [Col. 1316A].

As long as we are in this life, whatever sins may befall us, it is possible for everything to be washed away through repentance. But when we have been taken away from this world, even if we then repent—and we shall indeed repent greatly—our repentance will be of no benefit. Though there may be gnashing of teeth, wailing, and weeping; though we pour forth prayers and cry out with countless supplications, no one will hear and no one will help. Not even the tip of a finger will anyone dip in water to moisten our tongue, which lies in the flames. Rather, we shall hear what the rich man heard from Abraham:

> “A great chasm has been fixed between us and you,”

and neither can anyone cross from here to there nor from there to here [Col. 1316B].

## CHAPTER IX — On the time of fruitful repentance

Therefore we ought to consider more attentively and handle more carefully the fact that God has given human beings the time for acquiring eternal life only in this present life. Here He also wished repentance to be fruitful. Repentance is fruitful here because a person can, after laying aside wickedness, live well; by changing his will, he can change both his merits and his works, and in the fear of God perform those things that please God.

Whoever does not do this in the present life will indeed have repentance in the future age for his evils, but he will not find forgiveness in God’s sight. For although there will be there a goad of remorse, there will be no correction of the will. Such people will blame their iniquity in such a way that they will be entirely unable either to love or to desire righteousness. Their will will be such that it will always contain within itself the punishment of its own wickedness, yet it will never be able to receive an inclination toward goodness [Col. 1316C].

For just as those who will reign with Christ will have no remnants of an evil will within them, so those who will be assigned with the devil and his angels to the punishment of eternal fire will have no rest thereafter and will in no way be able to possess a good will. And just as the perfection of grace will be given to Christ’s co-heirs for eternal glory, so wickedness itself will increase the punishment of the devil’s companions, when, assigned to the outer darkness, they will be illuminated by no inner light of truth.

Therefore repentance can be useful to every human being in this life, whenever he practices it—however wicked or advanced in years he may be—if he renounces his past sins with his whole heart, pours before God tears not only of the body but also of the heart on their account, and takes care to wash away the stains of evil deeds by good works. He will immediately obtain forgiveness for all sins. For the Lord promises this to us in prophetic speech:

> “If you turn and groan, you will be saved” (Ezek. XXXIII, 12).

And elsewhere it is said:

> “Son, you have sinned; do not add again” (Eccli. XXI, 1).

But pray also concerning past sins, that they may be forgiven you. Prayer for sins would never have been commanded to one who had not sinned if forgiveness were not to be granted to the one who prays [Col. 1317A].

Repentance also benefits the sinner only if he practices it in the Catholic Church, to which God granted, in the person of blessed Peter, the power of binding and loosing, saying:

> “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 18).

At whatever age, therefore, a person practices true repentance for his sins and corrects his life with God’s illumination, he will not be deprived of the gift of forgiveness. For God, as He says through the Prophet, does not desire the death of the dying person, but rather that he turn from his evil way and that his soul may live (Ezek. XXXIII, 11).

Nevertheless, no one should remain any longer in his sins under the pretext of God’s mercy. Even in the body, no one wishes to remain ill for long in hope of future health. Those who neglect to depart from their iniquities and promise themselves forgiveness from God are sometimes overtaken by God’s sudden anger, so that they find neither time for conversion nor the benefit of forgiveness [Col. 1317B].

Therefore Holy Scripture kindly warns each one of you:

> “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day. For His wrath will come suddenly, and at the time of vengeance He will destroy you” (Eccli. V, 8).

Blessed David also says:

> “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts” (Ps. XCIV, 8).

Blessed Paul agrees with him in these words:

> “See, brothers, lest perhaps there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, leading you to depart from the living God. Rather, exhort one another each day, as long as it is called ‘today,’ so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.”

A person therefore lives with a hardened heart either when he converts while despairing of forgiveness for his sins, or when he hopes for God’s mercy in such a way that he remains until the end of his present life in the perversity of his crimes.

Therefore, loving God’s mercy and fearing His justice, let us neither despair of the forgiveness of sins nor remain in sins. We know that the equity of the most just Judge will exact from all human beings whatever the mercy of the most merciful Redeemer has not forgiven. For just as mercy receives and absolves those who convert, so justice will reject and punish the hardened. These are the people who, having sinned against the Holy Spirit, will receive forgiveness of their sins neither in this age nor in the future [Col. 1317D].

## CHAPTER X — Comparison of Gehenna with the pleasures of the present life

Remember these things, my friend, and set the fire of Gehenna against the flames of lust and desire that now torment you. For this is a remarkable kind of medicine: that fires may be extinguished by fires. If these lusts which now torment you are not quenched, they will make those eternal fires more fierce and inextinguishable for you.

How long do you think the pleasures of the present life can last for you? In my judgment, even if you live to extreme old age, you cannot have fifty years remaining until the end. But during even this period, see how many things can intervene. First, no one is certain of reaching even evening. Second, the condition of human affairs is always changeable. Often life is prolonged for a long time, yet possessions and riches do not remain reliably with a person; it frequently happens that someone loses his wealth before he loses his life.

Nevertheless, let us grant that you can live for many years without suffering any change of circumstances. And how much, I ask, is that span compared with eternal punishments? How much is this matter of desire [voluntatis; perhaps read voluptatis, “pleasure”] compared with those execrable and intolerable punishments? In this life, whether good or evil, both know their own limit and quickly reach it. In the future age, however, both are extended through immortal spans [Col. 1318B].

Add also that the condition of the punishment itself is altogether different. The fire that exists in the present life consumes everything it receives; but that fire forever torments those whom it has received and preserves them perpetually intact for its punishment. It is called “inextinguishable” not only because it is itself not extinguished, but because it neither extinguishes nor destroys those whom it has taken in. Therefore let us not think that the excessiveness of the punishments themselves will bring an end to the sufferings. Rather, as we have said, sins kindle the punishments, while the incorruptibility of soul and body will grant no end to the torments.

Tell me, then, how long a period of luxury do you wish to compare with such punishments? Suppose you wish to give a hundred years to pleasure; add another hundred, if you like; add ten times a hundred. What comparison will these have with eternity? Does not the whole time of this life, during which one seems to enjoy pleasures and indulge lust, appear, in comparison with eternity, like the dream of a single night?

If, then, there were someone who chose to undergo eternal punishments merely to see a pleasant dream for one night, and to receive the one in exchange for the other, or to exchange this for that, would he not be insane? I am not yet turning to the condemnation of pleasures, nor am I now exposing the bitterness that is in them, because this is not the time for such a discourse. That will come when perhaps you are able to escape from them. For now, while you are painfully held in their grip, you think us delirious if we declare that the gifts of lust—which appear pleasing and delightful to everyone—are harsh and bitter. But if, through God’s mercy, you are able to escape from this illness, then you will perceive what bitterness—or rather what poison—lust contained [Col. 1318D].

## CHAPTER XI — On not delaying conversion to God

Why do we delay? Why do we linger and fail to use God’s generosity? God’s ineffable and immense goodness also provided this: He did not extend the time of labor and struggle, making it long or eternal, but made it brief—indeed, so to speak, a moment of a single hour. For such is this present life when compared with the eternal one.

God’s goodness therefore provided that in this brief and insignificant life there should be struggles and labors, while in the eternal life there should be crowns and rewards for merits, so that the labors might quickly end, but the rewards of merit might last without end [Col. 1319A]. Yet just as this gladdens those who are crowned through patience in their labors, so in the future it afflicts and torments those who see that, for a brief and insignificant time of pleasure, they have lost eternal goods and sought everlasting evils.

Therefore, lest we too come into this torment of the soul, let us awaken at last while we have time. Behold, now is the acceptable time; now is the day of salvation; now is the opportunity and time for repentance, when repentance also receives its fruit.

Yet these are not the only evils that await us if we neglect our life and endure in Gehenna what we have brought upon ourselves. There is an evil far more serious than these: to be excluded from eternal goods and made strangers to those things prepared for the saints. This produces such torment and such grief that, even if no external punishment tortured us, this alone would be sufficient. That punishment surpasses all the torments of Gehenna: to lack the goods over which you once had the power to rejoice [Col. 1319B].

## CHAPTER XII — On the condition of the future life

Consider, I beg you, the condition of that life, insofar as it is possible for you to consider it. No speech will truly suffice to comprehend it, but let us gather from what we read and receive through riddles at least a faint conception of it. It is said of it in one passage that “there pain, sorrow, and groaning will flee away.”

What could be more blessed than that life? There is no fear of poverty, no illness; no one unjustly harms or is harmed; no one becomes angry; no one envies; no desire burns; no craving for food exists; no ambition for honor or power strikes the heart [Col. 1319C]. Every stain of vice has been laid aside and utterly extinguished. Peace and joy contain everything; all things are tranquil and quiet. There is a perpetual splendor—not like the one that exists now, but as much brighter and clearer as the sun is brighter than a lamp.

There is no night there, no darkness, no storm of clouds, no harshness of cold or heat. Rather, there will be such a tempering of all things as only those who have been found worthy to enjoy it will know. There is no old age there, nor the misery of old age; everything that belongs to corruption is removed [Perhaps read: is absent], and the glory of incorruption surrounds everything.

Above all these things is fellowship with the company of angels and archangels, and the enjoyment of companionship with all the heavenly and higher powers [Col. 1319D]. Beyond all this is the glory of attaining the ineffable sight of our Lord Jesus Christ Himself and being irradiated by the indescribable splendor of His majesty.

## CHAPTER XIII — On the splendor of Christ’s glory

Let us turn our eyes toward that mountain on which Christ was transformed and contemplate the splendor with which He then shone in His transformation. Even so, we shall not find the whole glory of the future age disclosed to us. That transformation was revealed not to the extent that the reality of future blessings possesses, but only to the extent that the eyes of those who looked upon it could bear. Thus the Gospel says:

> “He shone like the sun” (Matt. XVII, 2) [Col. 1320A].

But the glory of incorruptible bodies will emit not merely as much splendor as proceeds from this corruptible light, nor will it be a light of the kind that mortal eyes can now receive. Rather, the splendor of the future light will be as great as corporeal sight cannot bear—although the one who shone in the transformation of the mountain bore it. From this it is shown that as much was revealed as mortal eyes could bear; yet they did not endure even that entirely, for, as the Gospel says, “they fell on their faces upon the earth.”

What then, tell me, shall we deprive ourselves of all these blessings, and deprive others as well, merely so that we may not undertake some small labor or reject the allurements of lust for a brief time? If it were necessary for us to endure torments every day, or to tolerate Gehenna itself for a short time, in order to see Christ coming in glory and to be joined to the number of His saints, would it not be worthwhile to suffer everything grievous, provided that we might become participants in so great a good and so great a glory? Hear what blessed Peter says:

> “It is good for us to be here” (Matt. XVII, 4).

If he, seeing only a faint image of the future glory, suddenly cast everything else from his mind, bound by the sweetness of the vision he perceived, what will someone say when he contemplates the very reality of things as it truly is? This will be when the heavenly court is opened, and the King of heaven is revealed for us to behold—not now through a mirror and in a riddle, but face to face; not now through faith, but by sight [Col. 1320B].

Some of the uninstructed think it sufficient and desirable for them merely to escape Gehenna. But I say that it is far more grievous than the torments of Gehenna to be removed and cast away from that glory. I do not think the punishments of Gehenna are as bitter as those by which the person is tormented who is shut out from the sight of Christ. Believe me, this is more grievous than every punishment.

## CHAPTER XIV — Prophetic testimonies concerning the coming of the future Judge and the terror of judgment
Heed not to think that this king whom we have mentioned will come, when he comes to judge the world, borne along by teams of mules or golden chariots, adorned with purple, or accompanied by the terrifying power of a diadem. Rather, hear how he now commanded that his coming be announced to all through the proclamation of the prophets. One of them therefore says:

> “God will come manifestly; our God, and he will not keep silent. Fire will burn before him, and a mighty storm around him; and he will summon heaven from above and earth, to distinguish his people” (Ps. XLIX, 3).

Another, Isaiah, who also shows us the forms of punishment, hear how he speaks:

> “Behold, the day of the Lord will come, incurable—a day of fury and wrath—to make the world desolate and destroy sinners from it. For the stars of heaven, Orion, and all the adornment of heaven will not give their light; the sun will be darkened at its rising, and the moon will not give its light. I will command evils against the whole world, and their sins against the impious. I will destroy the insolence of the wicked, and humble the outrage of the proud. Those who are left will be more precious than gold, even gold without fire; and a human being will be more precious than a sapphire stone. For heaven will be shaken, and the earth will be moved from its foundations because of the fury of the wrath of the Lord of Sabaoth, on the day when his fury overtakes it” (Isa. XIII, 9).

And again he says:

> “The windows of heaven will be opened, and the foundations of the earth will be shaken. The earth will be utterly troubled; the earth will be utterly stupefied. The earth will be utterly bent and has been bent; it will be utterly shaken by shaking. It will be tossed about like a drunken and intoxicated man; it will be shaken out like a guardhouse of apples. The earth will fall and will not be able to rise, for iniquity has prevailed over it. On that day God will bring his hand against the adornment of heaven on high, and against the kingdoms of the earth; and he will bind their assembly in fetters and shut it up in a fortified place” (Isa. XXIV, 18).

When these things therefore begin to take place, the gates of heaven will undoubtedly be opened—or rather, heaven itself will be removed from the midst, as the covering of some tent is gathered up—so that it may be restored and transformed for the better. Then everything will be possessed by fear; dread and trembling will fill all things. Then fear will shake even the angels themselves—not only the angels, but also the thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers of heaven. This is indicated by the statement:

> “The powers of heaven will be shaken,”

for they are fellow servants of those who are to be judged and who will render an account of this life.

Add to all these things also the pains of punishments—not merely confusion, nor only the mark of disgrace—but set before your eyes that road by which human beings are dragged to the fire and by which they are dragged to punishments. Consider those savage and horrifying ministers of punishment who hurl sinners into torment, at the very time when others who have lived well, supported by most glorious and gentle angels, are rewarded before the lofty throne of the eternal King with crowns of glory and immortal gifts. These things, indeed, will belong specifically to that day and to the time of judgment.

## CHAPTER XV — The joy of the future life, and that present tribulation is not to be compared with it

But who will be able to explain what will follow afterward? What pleasure, what joy it will be to be with Christ, when the soul, restored to its own nobility, begins with confidence to see its Lord! The greatness of that joy cannot be explained. For it rejoices not only in those things of which it presently partakes, but much more in this: that it knows there will be no end to its blessings.

I beg you, therefore, let us not despise so great a blessedness, nor neglect this precious treasure that is within us—especially since our return can be easy and the soul’s dignity restored with little labor. For once you have conceived hope of future things, the soul immediately returns to its beauty. The apostle Paul says:

> “For our present momentary and light tribulation is producing in us an incomparably immense and eternal weight of glory, as we look not to the things that are seen but to those that are not seen; for the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (II Cor. IV, 17).

If Paul calls tribulations light and easy because we look not to the things that are seen but to those that are not seen, how much more will it be light and easy for you to cease from the foul burdens of unchastity?

For we are not now inviting you to those labors, dangers, tribulations, or daily deaths that the apostles endured; nor to those persecutions, blows, chains, prisons, the theater of the whole world, hunger, nakedness, many vigils, dangers of travel, shipwrecks at sea, dangers from robbers, dangers from one’s own kindred, dangers from false brothers, and all those struggles through which the apostles toiled. We ask none of these things of you now. We ask only that, abandoning this most shameful slavery, you return to your former freedom, considering the punishment that follows luxury and the glory reserved for virtues.

For if those who do not believe in the future resurrection neglect their lives, have no fear of the future judgment, and feel no compunction in their hearts, it is not surprising. But for us, who contemplate future things with much greater certainty than present things, to live so unhappily and so miserably, to retain no remembrance of judgment, and to fall into utter contempt is the height of madness. Nothing could be added to this evil if we believers were like unbelievers—indeed, among the unbelievers not a few have been found who flourished in the virtues of the soul during this life.

What excuse or consolation will remain for us if, on the day of judgment, such people are brought forward as examples for us? Moreover, we see that some merchants have suffered shipwreck and lost their entire fortune, yet they have not therefore been cast down and remained idle; instead, they have undertaken the same path again, restored the same occupations, and rebuilt what they had lost. These losses, indeed, they suffered not through sloth of spirit but through the violence of the winds.

How then shall we, who are certain about the end of all things and clearly know that, if we wish, we can suffer neither shipwreck of the soul nor loss, fail to take up again our former exercises and restore the affairs that we negligently lost? Instead, we shall lie on our backs in idleness and apply idle hands to our breast—and would that they were merely idle and not working toward our destruction! This is plainly madness, as if, for example, someone were to turn his hands against his own head on behalf of his adversary [perhaps: his adversary’s], striking his own neck. “The devil has repelled us and dashed us to the ground.” Therefore we must rise and stand against him again. For if, once thrown down, you not only refuse to rise from the ground but also cast yourself headlong, that is to help your adversary and favor his side.

## CHAPTER XVI — The fall of David and his repentance

For blessed David, whom we have already mentioned somewhat above, perhaps fell into the same misfortune in which you now find yourself. Not only that: he added something else more serious, for he joined homicide to adultery.

And after this, did he remain lying there? Did he not rise and stand once more against the enemy, and so subdue him that even after his death his merits benefited his descendants?

When Solomon had committed that monstrous crime and was considered worthy of a thousand deaths, the Lord nevertheless says that, because of David, he would leave his kingdom intact to him. For he says:

> “I will surely tear the kingdom from your hands and give it to your servant Jeroboam. Nevertheless, in your days I will not do this, for the sake of David your father; rather, I will take it from the hands of your son” (III Kings XI, 11).

But when Hezekiah had come into extreme dangers, although he too was just, the Lord nevertheless says that, for the sake of blessed David, he would bring him aid. For he says:

> “For I will protect this city and save it, for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant” (IV Kings XIX, 34).

You see how great is the power of repentance; you see how much merit conversion restored.

If David had wished to consider the things that now occupy your mind and to say, “It is now impossible for God to be gracious to me. He honored me with great honor, bestowed prophetic glory upon me, and also gave me a kingdom. He rescued me from countless dangers. How, after all these great benefits, now that I have fallen, offended him, and descended into the most extreme crimes, can I again merit God’s favor?”—if David had thought such things, he would have lost both his former blessings and his latest ones.

For it is not only bodily wounds, if neglected, that bring death; the same is true of wounds of the soul. Shall we then be so foolish that, when the body suffers a wound, we immediately apply medicine, but never treat the wounds of the soul? In bodily wounds there are many that cannot be healed at all, and yet we do not immediately despair. Rather, to the extent possible, we apply care; even if we hear physicians say that such a wound cannot be healed [the word *non*, “not,” is absent], we nevertheless persist and beg the physicians to seek for us at least some comfort and support.

But with wounds of the soul, where nothing is incurable—for the soul does not suffer by necessity of nature, as though its affliction were alien to us—we are so negligent, so despairing, and give no thought to the soul’s care. Where the nature of the illness necessarily brings about treatment, we nevertheless do not omit care, as though diligence could offer some hope; yet here, where there is no reason for despair, we abandon treatment entirely, as though there were no healing.

Even if you despair of yourself a thousand times, we will never despair of you. For we are not doing to you what we condemn in others, although it is not the same thing when someone despairs of himself and when another despairs of him. The one who despairs of another has an excuse; but the one who has despaired of himself has no excuse, because the former is not master of another’s mind, whereas the latter controls his own purpose. We therefore do not despair that you can return to the state of your former life and to those virtues of spirit that we know to have been in you.

## CHAPTER XVII — The repentance of the Ninevites

We add still this point: the Ninevites heard the prophet speaking with certainty and threatening:

> “Three days more, and Nineveh will be destroyed” (Jon. III, 4).

Yet even then they did not lose heart, although they were not confident that they could persuade God to go against his own pronouncement—which they saw was not suspended under any condition of pardon but concluded by a direct sentence. Nevertheless, they fled to repentance, saying:

> “Who knows whether God will have mercy, and whether God will relent concerning the evil that he has spoken of doing?” (Amos V, 15).

If barbarous and uneducated people could possess so much understanding of divine goodness, ought we not much more to do so, who have been instructed in the divine Scriptures and who know that many such examples preceded these, and have learned from the divine Scriptures that similar examples are contained both in present circumstances and in deeds that have been performed?

For God says:

> “My counsels are not like your counsels, nor are my ways like your ways. As far as heaven is from earth, so far are my thoughts from your thoughts and my counsels from your counsels.”

Moreover, if we receive our servants who have perhaps offended us when they promise that they will be better, restore them to their former position, and sometimes even give them greater confidence after their offense because of reconciliation, will God not do this much more for us?

For if he made us for the purpose of punishing us, you would have been right to despair and doubt your salvation. But if he made us solely because of his goodness, so that we might enjoy his eternal blessings and gifts, and if everything he has done from the beginning of the world to the present he has done and set in motion for this purpose, what reason for despair or doubt will remain for us?

“But,” you say, “we have offended him so grievously that no human being has ever offended him so.” For that very reason, then, we must make satisfaction and repent of our offense more quickly and more earnestly, and promptly withdraw from those actions by which God is offended. For even the gravest injury of a crime does not offend upright and noble minds as much as contempt for making satisfaction. To sin is human; to persist in sins is diabolical.

Finally, see how God reproves this more than the other through the prophet:

> “And I said: After you had played the prostitute, after all these things, return to me—and you did not return.”

And elsewhere again:

> “Even after all these things, faithless Judah did not return, and her hand was still excessive.”

In another passage, after the prophet had reproved the people’s offenses and they had promised amendment, God shows how lovingly he receives the conversion of sinners and says:

> “Who will grant that their heart may be such that they fear me and keep my commandments all the days of their life, so that it may be well with them and with their children forever?” (III Kings VIII, 40).

Moses too, wishing to teach the people what God requires of human beings, says:

> “And now, Israel, hear what the Lord your God requires of you: that you fear the Lord your God, walk in [lacuna] his ways, and love him with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Deut. XIX, 9).

Since God desires to be loved by us and does everything for this purpose, and since for our salvation and love he does not even spare his Only-Begotten Son, and desires, so to speak, that we be reconciled to him by whatever means and at whatever time, how could he not gladly receive us when we repent and turn back to him, and love us as sons?

What do you think he meant when he said through the prophet:

> “Speak first of your iniquities, so that you may be justified”?

## CHAPTER XVIII — The hope and confidence to be placed in God’s goodness

Come, then; let us now set out upon the way of life. Let us return to the heavenly city in which we have been enrolled and appointed citizens. Despair closes the gates of this city to us, but hope will open them, and confidence will provide a broad entrance. If we despise these, we incur not only the guilt of sloth but also that of pride.

The devil too became such as he is for no other reason than that, after his sin, he first resorted to despair, and afterward, from despair, fell into pride and arrogance. Likewise, if the soul once begins to despair of its salvation, it no longer understands into what evils or how far it is being plunged. It fears doing or saying nothing that is contrary to salvation. As we often see among those who are insane, once they have lost a state of soundness, they fear nothing further and are ashamed of nothing; they readily dare to say and do everything.

If they rush into fire, they do not turn aside; even if they move toward a precipice or into the depths, they do not draw back their foot. So too those seized by despair become irreclaimable; they run through every path of wickedness. Shame prohibits nothing, fear restrains nothing. They fear nothing present and dread nothing future. Only death remains, which they cannot escape.

Therefore, before you become more deeply intoxicated by the poison of this evil, rise, I beg you; wake up at last and put aside this diabolical affliction. If you cannot do so suddenly, gradually and little by little recover your courage. Although, as it seems to me, the easier way is to break everything off at once, sever all the restraints of this evil together, and turn back wholly to the practices of repentance.

But if this seems difficult to you, at least make some beginning. Take up a desire for a better and eternal life, and then, with the Lord’s help, climb toward greater and more perfect things. First, therefore, through humble confession, declare your offenses before God and the priest, and diligently carry out the small measure of repentance imposed upon you by him. Do not return to your former vices, but always strive along the path of righteousness to reach the citadel of the virtues.

## CHAPTER XIX — Humble confession

Signs of humility are that each person recognizes his own iniquity and, once recognized, discloses it by confession. It is a customary vice of the human race both to commit sin by falling and, after committing it, not to disclose it by confession, but to defend it by denial, and, once convicted, to multiply it through further defense.

From the fall of the first human being we derive these increases of wickedness, since from that fall we drew the very root of guilt. For this reason the first human being was summoned: so that what he had committed by transgressing he might erase by confessing. When asked where he was, he was being made to look upon the guilt he had perpetrated and, by confessing, recognize how far he was from the presence of his Creator.

Indicators of true confession are present if, when each person calls himself a sinner, he does not contradict another who says the same thing about him. It is written:

> “The righteous person is his own accuser at the beginning” (Prov. XVIII, 19).

When someone confesses himself a sinner without anyone accusing him, he desires to appear not a sinner but righteous. The truth of confession is shown when another reproves the evil we have done and we proudly defend it; it is clear [the manuscript reads *licet*; perhaps *liquet*, “it is clear”] that we were falsely saying that we are sinners.

We must take the greatest care both willingly to admit the evils we have done and not to deny them when others reproach us for them. It is a vice of pride that what one deigns to confess, as though voluntarily, one disdains to have said about oneself by others. A confession is the pledge of a debtor: a pledge is received from a debtor when the confession of sin is obtained from a sinner.

## CHAPTER XX — That it is of no benefit to call oneself a sinner while refusing to amend

Repentance is corrupted if someone again becomes entangled in the same evils for which he confessed. For it is said:

> “One building and another destroying—what do they gain except labor? And one who is baptized from the dead and again touches the dead—what does he gain from his former washing? So too the person who fasts for his sins, and then goes away and does the same things: who will hear his prayer?” (Eccli. XXXIV, 29).

And again he says:

> “Whoever turns back from God’s righteousness to sin, the Lord casts him into the sword; and just as a dog, when it returns to its vomit, becomes hateful, so a fool, when he returns to his sin, becomes hateful.”

It is therefore not enough merely to appear to expose your sins by accusing yourself. Rather, do this with such an attitude that you hope repentance will bring you some justification. In this way you will be able to instill shame in your confessing soul, so that it does not again fall into the things for which it confesses.

To condemn oneself and call oneself a sinner is common to everyone; this is the repentance of unbelievers. Indeed, many men from the stage, and especially immodest women, call themselves sinners and criminals. They do not say these things because they desire to be corrected. Therefore this confession ought not to be called confession. Such words do not come from a contrite heart or from the bitterness of tears; nor are they spoken with the attitude of those who hate the things they accuse and who no longer wish to do them—or even to hear them mentioned. The matter exists only in speech, and the speech comes from the tips of the lips, not from the inward grief of the heart. Sometimes they even expect to be praised for this, as though they deceive no one.

Although they speak truly against themselves, they do so as though sin appeared especially serious among human beings when it is spoken of by the person who committed it, rather than when another accuses him. But those who do this are so deeply given to despair that they lack even the feeling of pain. They no longer fear the judgment of human beings, but with a certain confidence pronounce their own evils as though they belonged to someone else.

I do not want you to do any of these things, nor to come to confession through despair, but with good hope and confidence in pardon, having utterly cut out the root of despair. For the root of despair is sloth—not merely its root, but also its nurse and mother. Just as clothing generates and nourishes moths, so sloth not only gives birth to despair but also feeds and fosters it. Thus these two things draw strength from one another and grow together; if someone cuts off one of them, the other will undoubtedly perish through the destruction of its companion, and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXI — How repentance should be practiced

Every sinner ought to have a double groaning in repentance, because he both failed to do the good he ought to have done and did the evil he ought not to have done. When we do not add good works, it is necessary that we mourn ourselves doubly: we did not do what was right, and we practiced what was wrong.

Through blessed Moses, one turtledove is commanded to be offered for sin and another as a burnt offering; a burnt offering is so called because it is wholly burned. We offer one turtledove for sin when we express a groan over our guilt; we make the other a burnt offering when, because we neglected good things, we set ourselves wholly ablaze and burn with the fire of grief.
