Blessed Job, advancing after his afflictions and dissenting from himself in severe reproof, says:

> “Therefore I rebuke myself and do penance in dust and ashes” (Job XLII, 6).

To do penance in dust and ashes is, after contemplating the supreme essence, to recognize oneself as nothing other than dust and ashes. In sackcloth there is harshness and compunction for sins; in ashes the dust of the dead is shown. For this reason both are customarily applied to repentance: in the compunction of sackcloth we recognize what we have done through guilt, and in the scourging of ashes we consider what we have become through judgment.

Therefore, in the ashes, let the sentence of death that follows be considered, corresponding to the punishment of the vices that arose after the sin of the flesh. Let a person see in the harshness of sackcloth what he did through pride; let him see in the ashes how far he reached by sinning. The sinner is pricked, as it were, by sackcloth, while he is constricted in his mind by the sharp goads of reproof. He does penance in ashes when he carefully considers what he became through the just judgment resulting from his first sin.

We turn day into darkness when, sternly punishing ourselves, we torment the very enticements of wrongful pleasure through the severe laments of repentance, and pursue with tears whatever we silently sin in our heart through pleasure.

Every faithful person, while carefully examining his thoughts in judgment, does not remain unaware of himself. By examining his inward self, he scrutinizes himself severely before judgment, so that the strict Judge may come all the more peacefully to the heart he wishes to examine, insofar as he sees it already punished for its guilt.

Almighty God examines our deeds minutely, yet mercifully releases them for those who repent. He sees the hardness of sinners, but through preceding grace softens it for repentance. God counts our offenses when he turns us toward mourning each thing we have done; he mercifully releases them because, while we punish ourselves, he does not judge them at the final examination, as Paul testifies when he says:

> “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged.”

What we do outwardly, unless we wipe it away through repentance, is kept hidden in the secrecy of God’s judgments, so that one day it may emerge from the seal of secrecy into public judgment. But when we are worn down by the scourge of discipline for the evils we have done and mourn them through repentance, he both seals and heals our iniquity: he neither leaves it unpunished here nor preserves it to be punished in the judgment.

God seals our offenses because he carefully attends to them here, in order to strike; but he heals them because, through the scourge, he wholly releases them.

Blessed Job, assuming the role of the human race, says:

> “You have sealed up my offenses as in a bag” (I Cor. XI, 21).

Our sins are sealed as in a bag when we continually weigh the evils we have done with an anxious heart. For what is the human heart except God’s bag? When we carefully observe how greatly we have sinned, we carry our sins sealed as in God’s bag, because the Creator releases our offenses all the more when we recognize them by looking upon them and repenting of them. After “you have sealed my offenses in a bag,” it is rightly said:

> “But you heal my iniquity,”

as though he plainly said: “You now seal it so that I may see it through repentance; you act so that it may not be seen in retribution.”

## CHAPTER XXII — The difference between the good and the evil

It often happens that someone corrects many great things through repentance, yet among the good things he has corrected through repentance also commits sins. This is what most especially brings despair into the mind, because he seems to himself to have destroyed what he had built and poured out all those labors in vain. This is the thought that chiefly lays the burden of despair upon the soul.

But we must again consider the thought by which this very worst and life-hostile thought may be driven away. For if those good things we did, and that amendment sought through repentance, had not existed—if it had not stood like a counterweight against this weight that has been introduced into our account—there would have been nothing to prevent us from falling into the depth of evils. But now, like a strong breastplate that does not permit a heavy and bitter missile to penetrate to the vital organs, it has broken the force of the deadly weapon to a very great extent.

It is certain that the person who carries more good deeds and more evil deeds with him into that place will have some relief amid the punishments. But what awaits the person who brings with him no good works and a great abundance of evil need not be said.

There will undoubtedly be a balancing there between good and evil works; as though placed on a scale, whichever side rises will claim for itself the weight of those works toward which the balance inclines. If the multitude of evil works surpasses the quantity of good works, it drags the person to Gehenna. But if the sum of good works is greater, they will resist and oppose the evils with all their strength and recall their author to the land of the living even from the very boundary of Gehenna.

Yet these things are affirmed not so much from our own reasoning as from the words of the divine Scriptures. For Scripture declares:

> “He will repay each person according to his works” (Matt. XVI, 27).

There will be many distinctions not only in the Gehenna of punishments but also in the heavenly kingdom:

> “There are many dwelling places,” he says, “in my Father’s house” (John XIV, 2);

and again:

> “One glory belongs to the sun and another to the moon” (I Cor. XV, 41).

And what is truly more astonishing, to show that even in the smallest matters the proportion and measure of merits will be weighed, he says:

> “Star differs from star in glory” (ibid.),

thereby showing that there will also be a distinction among the individual people who will be in the kingdom.

Knowing all these things, therefore, let us not withdraw from good works, nor surrender ourselves to sloth and idleness under the pretext of despair. Nor, if we cannot attain the splendor of the sun and moon, should we despise even the glory of a star, though it be lesser.

Let it be enough that we seek at least a little light through the merit of virtues; let it be enough that, however small, we may deserve to complete some adornment of heaven. If we cannot be gold or a precious stone, let us at least fill the place of silver. Only let us not be turned into that material which fire easily consumes; let us not be found to be wood, hay, or straw. Let us at least be among the last of the good, and not among the first of the evil.

## CHAPTER XXIII — The sayings of Abbot Pinophus
Moreover, it should be noted that, after that general grace of baptism and that chief gift of martyrdom, which is obtained through the washing away of blood, other remedies for our sickness are likewise found recorded in the Holy Scriptures. For there are many fruits of repentance, through which expiation of sins is attained. Eternal salvation is promised not only under that simple name “repentance,” of which the apostle Peter says, “Repent, he says, and turn back, so that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 3:19), nor only by John the Baptist or the Lord himself: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 3:2), but also through the affection of charity, by which “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

Likewise, healing for our wounds is shown through the fruit [Perhaps add: of almsgiving], since, just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin. The obliteration of offenses is also obtained through an outpouring of tears: “For every night I wash my bed; I water my couch with my tears” (Ps. 6:7). Then he adds, showing that those tears had not been poured out in vain: “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping” (ibid., v. 9). Through confession of sins also forgiveness is granted: “I said,” he says, “I will declare my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Ps. 31:5); and again: “First declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26).

Through affliction of heart and body, too, remission of the crimes committed is similarly obtained. For he says, “See my humility and my labor, and forgive all my sins” (Ps. 24:18); and especially through amendment of conduct: “Take away,” he says, “the evil of your thoughts from my eyes; cease to act perversely; learn to do good; seek judgment; assist the oppressed; judge the orphan; defend the widow; and come and accuse me, says the Lord. And if your sins are like scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; if they are red like a worm, they shall be made clean like wool” (Isa. 1:16–18).

At times, pardon for offenses is also obtained through the intercession of the saints: “If anyone knows that his brother is committing a sin not unto death, let him ask, and life will be given to him who sins not unto death” (1 John 5:16); and again: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up, and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (Jas. 5:14–15).

Sometimes, too, the labor of vices is burned away through the merit of mercy and faith, according to this saying: “Sins are cleansed through mercy and faith, and often through the conversion and salvation of those who are saved by our admonition and preaching; for whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (ibid., v. 19).

Likewise, through our own pardon and remission we attain the pardon of our offenses: “For if,” he says, “you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses” (Matt. 6:14).

You see, therefore, how many entrances to mercy the Savior’s clemency has opened, so that no one who desires salvation may be broken by despair, when he sees himself invited to life by so many remedies. For if, because of the weakness of the flesh, you claim that sins cannot be blotted out through the affliction of fasts, nor can you say, “My knees have grown weak from fasting, and my flesh has been changed because of oil; I ate ashes as bread and mixed my drink with weeping” (Ps. 101:9), redeem them by the generosity of almsgiving.

If you do not have anything to give to the needy—although no lack of means or poverty excludes anyone from this work, since even the widow’s two small coins were preferred to the great gifts of the rich, and the Lord promises to repay a cup of cold water—surely you can be purified by amendment of conduct. If you cannot attain perfection in the virtues by extinguishing every vice, devote your pious concern to the salvation of another. If you complain that you are not fit for this ministry, you can cover your sins through an affectionate charity. If even here some sluggishness of mind has made you weak, at least with prayer and the intercession of the saints, humbly and devoutly, implore remedies for your wounds.

Finally, who cannot simply say, “I have made my sin known to you, and I have not covered my injustice” (Ps. 31:5), so that through this confession he may also deserve confidently to add, “and you forgave the wickedness of my heart” (ibid.)? But if, because shame draws you back, you are embarrassed to reveal them before human beings, do not cease to confess them through continual supplication to the one from whom they cannot be hidden, and say to him: “I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me; against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you” (Ps. 50:5).

He is accustomed both to heal without any public exposure causing shame and to forgive sins without reproach. After that assistance, so ready and certain, the divine goodness has also granted us another, still easier one, and has entrusted the power of this remedy to our own will, so that we may presume upon the pardon of our offenses according to our own disposition, saying to him: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

Whoever, therefore, desires to attain pardon for his offenses should strive to equip himself with these instruments, and should not, through the obstinacy of a hardened heart, turn away from the saving remedy, the fountain of such great compassion. Yet even if we do all these things, they will not be sufficient for the expiation of our sins unless the Lord’s goodness and clemency blot them out. When he sees the services of our religious efforts offered with a humble mind, he follows our small and meager endeavors with immense generosity, saying: “I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities for my own sake, and I will no longer remember your sins” (Isa. 43:25).

But you, O man, considering these things, strive to recover yourself through repentance and to separate yourself far from vices. Thus, applying yourself to good works, you will be able to bring yourself near to God. Whatever good you can do while you have the time, do it earnestly. For just as the wealth of this world is increased most greatly when no profit, however small, is rejected [Perhaps: despised], so in spiritual riches no good work, however small, is to be despised.

Otherwise it seems utterly absurd that, although our Judge has promised that he will not refuse the reward even of a cup of cold water, we should say that unless the things we do [Perhaps: and have done; Col. 1332A] are great and mighty, small things will be of no benefit. Indeed, I add this as well: if anyone despises small and insignificant things, it is certain that he will gradually fall even into greater ones. “Whoever despises small things,” as Scripture says, “will gradually fall” (Ecclus. 19:1). For this reason I think that God our Savior has established great rewards for small things. What is as light and easy as visiting the sick? Yet for this very small work he has appointed a magnificent reward. Again, what is as easy and as pleasing as offering food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, and visiting one confined in prison?

These things, though so small and insignificant, he regards as so great and exalted that God counts them as having been done not for a human being but for himself, and on their account he has promised the heavenly kingdom.

Therefore begin, dearest friend, begin the journey of eternal life; once again take up Christ’s yoke, which is sweet, and his burden, which is light. Recover the virtues of your soul within yourself, and make the end resemble the beginning. Do not allow the wealth of spiritual graces, acquired for you at such cost and through such great labor, to be plundered. You will perish if you persist in sins and provoke God by your deeds.

But if, before your wealth suffers great loss and before your land is filled with destructive floods, you block the mouths of the breaches and the entrance of the vices that are pouring in, you will be able to restore your former cultivation and once again work the fallow fields of the excellent countryside that was once yours for its accustomed fruits.

Rise, therefore—rise, as the Prophet says—and “shake off your dust” (Matt. 10:14). Rise from the earth, and, believe me, your adversary will immediately be terrified. For he cast you down as though you would never rise again; but if he sees you risen from the earth and once more stretching out your arms for combat, your very boldness will terrify him. The readier you are, the more fearful he will become; the greater the things you dare, the weaker and more fragile he will be made.

Consider also that God will be present to you when you dare, whereas the consciousness of his crimes will undermine both his boldness and his strength. Thus, by the generosity of divine grace, being superior to your enemy in all things, you will depart as a strong victor, greatly enriched by the aid of the virtues, to receive the glory of the heavenly kingdom, where you will rejoice eternally with Christ and the holy angels.

[Col. 1333]

## THREE BOOKS ON QUESTIONS CONCERNING THE PENITENTIAL CANONS

(See among the works of Halitgarius, *Patrologia*, vol. 105, cols. 677–694; here we give only Rabanus’s preface, which he placed before the books of the Penitential Canons. [Col. 1333])

## PREFACE OF RABANUS

[Col. 1333]

[Col. 1333A] A person ought first, through the humility of confession, to disclose his debts before God and the priest, and then carefully carry out the measure of penance imposed upon him by the priest. He must not return to his former vices, but must always strive to reach the citadel of the virtues along the path of justice.

For it is evidence of humility for each person to recognize his own iniquity and, once recognized, to disclose it by confessing it aloud, since it is a customary vice of the human race both to commit sin by falling and, after committing it, to betray it by refusing to confess it, defending it by denial, and then, by defending what has been proven against him, multiplying it.

From the fall of the first man we derive these increases of wickedness, since from that fall we drew the very root of guilt. Thus the first man, who had committed sin by transgressing, was summoned so that, by confessing it, he might erase it; and when he was asked where he was (Gen. 3), he was to look upon the guilt he had committed and, by confessing, recognize how far he was from the presence of his Creator.

The signs of true confession are that, when a person calls himself a sinner, he does not contradict another who says the same thing about him. Therefore, we must take the greatest care both to confess willingly the evils we have done and not to deny them when others accuse us of them. For it is a vice of pride that what a person deigns to confess voluntarily, he disdains to have said about him by others.

The confession of a sinner is the pledge of a debtor. A pledge is taken from a debtor when confession of sin is obtained from a sinner. And because the children of God, as long as they live mortally, struggle with death—just as they are stirred by the Spirit of God so that, as children of God, they may advance toward God—so also, because of the burden of corruptible flesh, as children of human beings they fail in certain human behaviors and fall back upon themselves, and therefore they sin.

There is, however, a distinction as to degree; for not every sin is a crime, although every crime is a sin. Thus the life of holy people, which is lived in this death, can be found without crime, but never without sin, as the apostle John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1). Nevertheless, Scripture is accustomed to use one term for the other.

In the practice of penance, when a crime has been committed of such a kind that the person who committed it is separated from the body of Christ, the measure of time should not be considered as much as the measure of grief: “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50). Since, however, another person’s grief is often hidden from another, those who preside over the Churches rightly establish periods of penance, so that satisfaction may also be made to the Church in which sins are forgiven.

Therefore, when the wound of sin is so great that the medicines of the body and blood of the Lord must be deferred, each person ought, by the authority of the bishop, to withdraw from the altar in order to perform penance, and by that same authority to be reconciled. For this is to receive the body and blood of the Lord unworthily (1 Cor. 11), if one receives them at a time when one ought to be doing penance.

For penance itself, when the cause is worthy enough that it should be performed according to the custom of the Church, is often not performed because of weakness, since there is shame and fear of displeasing. When a person values reputation more than justice, by which each person humbles himself in doing penance, let him remember—whoever he is—that “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. 5; Jas. 4).

For what is more perverse, or more wretched, than not to be ashamed of the very wound that cannot be hidden? No one should suppose that he ought to despise the salutary counsel of this penance merely because he notices and knows that he approaches the sacraments of the altar while retaining within himself such crimes.

Many are corrected, like Peter; many are tolerated, like Judas; many remain unknown until the Lord comes, illuminates the hidden things of darkness, and reveals the thoughts of hearts. We, however, cannot prohibit anyone from communion, although this prohibition is not deadly but medicinal, unless the person has either confessed voluntarily or has been accused and convicted in some secular or ecclesiastical court.

One ought, therefore, to approach penance with complete confidence and to believe without doubt, in faith, that sins can be blotted out through penance, even if a person repents of sins committed at the final breath of life. Sins should be disclosed through public lamentation, because God’s purpose—by which he has decreed to save what had perished—remains unshaken. Therefore, since his will does not change, whether through amendment of life when time is granted, or through humble confession when life immediately comes to an end, pardon for sins should be confidently sought from him who does not desire the death of a sinner, but that he should turn back from destruction through repentance and, saved by God’s mercy, live.

The keys of the Church are most certain and most trustworthy; through them, “whatever is loosed on earth is also promised to be loosed in heaven” (John 20).

These things have been said concerning the twofold satisfaction by which a person humbles himself not only before God but also before the Church, which possesses the key of the kingdom of heaven and in which the remission of sins takes place.

We do not deny that mortal crimes can also be loosed through secret satisfaction, provided that a person first changes his secular way of life and, through correction of life and continual—indeed perpetual—mourning, devotes himself tirelessly to religion, with God showing mercy, and provided that he does the opposite of the things for which he repents.

Daily and lighter sins, without which this life is not lived, are cleansed by the Lord’s Prayer, in which one says, “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. 6), and so forth, including the words, “Forgive us our debts,” because it is itself an almsgiving to forgive a repentant person.

Hence the Lord says: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.” There are therefore many kinds of almsgiving by which, when we perform them, we are helped so that our sins may be forgiven. Yet none is greater than that by which from the heart we forgive what anyone has sinned against us.

There are, however, certain sins that are thought to be extremely light, unless the Scriptures demonstrated them to be more serious than people suppose. Who would have thought that the person who says to his brother, “Fool,” was guilty of hell, unless the Truth had said so? Or who would have judged it such a great sin to observe days, months, years, and seasons, as those do who, on particular days, months, or years, wish either to begin something or refuse to begin it, unless the Apostle had said: “I fear that I have labored among you in vain”?

How many other sins there are, whether in speaking about the affairs and business of others, which do not concern you; or in empty laughter; or even in the foods prepared for the necessities of this life, in which appetite becomes excessive; or in selling and buying things, when desires contrary to charity and usefulness arise.

There are also other sins of this kind, committed through offenses in words and thoughts, as the apostle James says: “For we all offend in many things.”

We ought daily and frequently to entreat the Lord and say, “Forgive us our debts,” lest in what follows we lie: “as we also forgive our debtors.” For these sins, too, they should not cease to offer sacrifices of almsgiving and fasting according to their strength.

For those sins contained in the Decalogue, concerning which the Apostle says, “Neither the greedy, nor the rapacious, nor adulterers, nor those who lie with males,” and so forth—for “those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 11)—the practice of penance must be undertaken in which each person exercises greater severity upon himself, so that, judged by himself, he may not be judged by the Lord.

The canons do not establish the duration of penance for each crime with sufficient exactness, but rather determine that it should be left to the judgment of the bishop, because with God the measure of grief is worth more than the measure of time, and not merely abstinence from food but rather the mortification of vices. For this reason, during the period of penance, the prescribed time is to be shortened for the penitent according to faith and conduct, and prolonged for negligence.

Nevertheless, modes of penance imposed by the canons exist for certain faults; according to these, other faults are to be weighed, since through those same modes it is easy to estimate the punishment and severity of the canons.

[Col. 1335C]

## OF THE BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, ON VICES AND VIRTUES AND THE SATISFACTION FOR SINS

[Col. 1335]

## PREFACE

[Col. 1335D] Therefore, considering [Note: [Col. 1335D] a. *Ergo* (“therefore”) is a word characteristic of the author at the beginnings of his books.] how I might provide some consolation to the Christian people, by which they could fight more effectively against the ancient enemy and, by the gift of Christ’s grace, attain true victory, I selected from the writings of holy and catholic Fathers certain testimonies from which those who wished to read our little works—and before whom our labor is not despised—might receive some assistance for governing themselves and correcting others toward a better life.

First, we shall write about the eight principal vices and the remedies to be set against them. Then we have resolved to write about the holy virtues and their praise, and thus we intend to turn our style toward the true humility of confession and the remedy of penance.

For although, through the grace of the Mediator granted in baptism, all original sins are truly believed to be blotted out—for that spiritual generation alone is sufficient—nevertheless, when a person reaches the age at which he already receives the commandment and can be subjected to the authority of the law, war must be taken up against vices and waged fiercely, lest he return again to damnable sins.

Very few are so fortunate that, from the beginning of adolescence, they commit no damnable sins, whether in disgraceful acts, crimes, homicides, or the wicked error of any impiety. Rather, through the great generosity of the Spirit, it is necessary to suppress whatever carnal pleasure can or could dominate within them.

Those vices are then to be considered overcome when they are conquered through the love of God—love which no one gives except God himself, and which is given only through the Mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ, who became a participant in our mortality in order to make us participants in his divinity.

Nevertheless, under the grievous yoke placed upon the children of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all, this evil too is found, miserably. Therefore, let us be sober and understand that this life was made punitive for us because of that exceedingly wicked sin committed in paradise, and that everything done with us concerns nothing other than the inheritance of the new age, so that, having received here the pledge, we may in its proper time obtain that of which it is the pledge.

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 1337]

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1337]

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 1337]

## PREFACE

[Col. 1337B]

This third little book, with the Lord’s favor, now begins. As we stated in the prologue to this work, it has been culled from the sayings of the holy Fathers and concerns mortal sins and crimes, their repentance and satisfaction; the origin, affliction, judgments, objections, and remedies of the eight principal vices; the struggle of the virtues against the assault of the vices; and the ways in which sins are committed in thought, speech, and deed.

Therefore, encouraged by your merits and prayers, most devoted Father, although not as I ought, nevertheless, as I am able, I will humbly strive, with God’s favor, to fulfill your commands.

## CHAPTER I — On Serious Mortal Sins and Crimes, and on Their Repentance and Satisfaction
[Col. 1337C] What, then, are grave and mortal sins? The excellent preacher Paul made them known in his Epistle to the Romans when he listed the most abominable crimes, adding:

> “Filled with all iniquity, wickedness, fornication, greed, depravity; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malice; whisperers, detractors, hateful to God, insulting, proud, arrogant, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, senseless, disorderly, without affection, without covenant, without mercy. Although they knew the justice of God, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Rom. 1:29).

Consider, therefore, with all fear that those who perpetrate the crimes written above and similar ones, or consent to them, unless they redeem them before the end of life through repentance, almsgiving, and other good works, are, according to the definition of the blessed apostle Paul, [Col. 1337D] most worthy of death—that is, everlasting death, death without remedy, death without end.

The same Apostle also speaks of mortal crimes in his Epistle to the Galatians:

> “Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, lust, service of idols, sorcery, enmities, contentions, rivalries, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envy, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these, which I foretell to you, as I foretold them, because those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:19).

For he did not say, “Those who have done such things have not obtained the kingdom of God,” but, “Those who do such things,” or those who persist in these crimes, “will not obtain the kingdom of God.” Many, indeed, have committed the crimes written above and similar ones, and before death cleansed them through repentance, almsgiving, [Col. 1338C] and other good works; afterward they attained the kingdom of God, and every day they deserve to attain it.

In his Epistle to the Ephesians the same Apostle says, among other things, concerning criminal sins:

> “But fornication and every uncleanness or greed must not even be named among you, as befits saints” (Eph. 5:3).

A little later:

> “For know this: no fornicator or unclean person or greedy person, which is service of idols, has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God” (ibid. 5).

He also commanded this in his Epistle to the Colossians, saying:

> “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is service of idols; because of these the anger of God comes upon the sons [Col. 1338D] of unbelief” (Col. 3:5).

This Apostle also instructed his beloved disciple Timothy to avoid people entangled in serious vices, saying in the Second Epistle to that same disciple:

[Col. 1339A]

> “But know this: in the last days dangerous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves, greedy, arrogant, proud, blasphemous, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, incontinent, savage, without kindness, traitors, reckless, swollen with pride, lovers of pleasure rather than of God, having indeed an appearance of piety but denying its power. Avoid such people” (2 Tim. 3:2).

According to the definition of the canons, these are also capital crimes.

First is “pride,” which is the mother and queen of all vices, whether lesser or principal, as Sacred Scripture bears witness:

> “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10).

For pride is the cause of all sins, since it is itself not only sin, but no sin could be, can be, or will be committed without it. Indeed, every sin is nothing other than contempt of God, by which his commandments are trampled underfoot; and nothing else persuades people to this contempt of God except pride.

Next comes “evil desire,” of which the apostle Paul says:

> “Greed is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10).

When, therefore, the Holy Spirit declares through the prophet that pride is the beginning of every sin, and through the Apostle affirms that greed is the root of all evils, this signifies that they are one and the same thing. For greed and pride are so great an evil that a proud person cannot be found without greed, nor a greedy person without pride.

Those who discuss sins and vices should carefully consider that pride is the beginning of every sin, whereas greed is the root of all evils. For each thing first has a beginning and afterward sends out a root; nevertheless, just as beginning and root are one and the same thing and substance, so pride and greed, although one comes first and the other later, are nevertheless one evil.

Next, among the principal vices, is placed envy, that most destructive plague, which is always tormented by another’s happiness. Afterward come “gluttony of the belly, fornication, anger, worldly sorrow,” which brings about death, “empty glory, greed, sacrilege”—that is, theft of sacred things—adultery, theft, robbery, false testimony, perjury, idolatry, drunkenness, effeminates, men who have intercourse with males, sodomites, slanderers, murderers.

Among other things, the apostle Paul makes capital crimes known in his First Epistle to the Corinthians, saying:

[Col. 1339D]

> “Do not err: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor effeminate men, nor men who have intercourse with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:9).

That is, if they persist in these crimes. But concerning those who have destroyed them before the final day of this life by repenting, redeemed them through almsgiving, and persevered in good works, we believe and affirm that they can possess the kingdom of God, for the Lord says:

> “But the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

(Augustine.) Certainly, one must beware lest anyone suppose that those abominable crimes—of the sort whose perpetrators will not possess the kingdom of God—are to be redeemed daily in order to improve. For life must be changed, and God must be appeased through almsgiving for present sins. The purpose is not to be reformed in some way so that one may always commit them with impunity. For God has granted no license to sin when, in his mercy, he erases sins already committed.

A suitable course of action must not be neglected. Those who live most wickedly, who do not care to correct such a life and such conduct, and who continue frequently to give alms amid their crimes and disgraceful deeds, flatter themselves without cause concerning such an act. For whoever wishes to give alms in an orderly manner must begin with himself and give alms first to himself. Almsgiving is an act of mercy, and it is most truly said:

> “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30:24).

Therefore, let those who remain in the enormity of their crimes and the wickedness of their disgraceful deeds not deceive themselves by imagining that, through the most lavish almsgiving of their produce or any money whatsoever, they can purchase impunity. For they not only commit these things, but love them so much that they always wish, if only they can do so with impunity, to remain involved in them.

Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul; and whoever hates his own soul is not merciful but cruel. For by loving it according to the world, he hates it according to God. If, therefore, he wished to give it alms by which all things might be made clean for it, he would hate it according to the world and love it according to God. Yet no one gives alms of any kind unless he receives from the one who does not need, that from which he may give.

(Bede.) Therefore it is said:

[Col. 1340C]

> “His mercy will go before me” (Ps. 58:11).

For mortal sins, as has already been said, are so utterly opposed to every share in justice and are committed with such great iniquity that, unless corrected, they plunge their perpetrator without any contradiction into eternal punishment. Concerning such people it is written:

> “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. 18:4, 20),

and the apostle Paul says that:

> “Those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:21).

Hence the apostle John says:

> “Everyone who is born of God does not sin” (1 John 5:18).

We can understand this concerning every capital crime: “Everyone who is born of God does not sin,” that is, he does not commit a sin leading to death. A sin leading to death is a sin prolonged until the time of death; the one who is born of God does not commit such a sin.

Indeed, King David committed a mortal crime—that is, adultery and murder—but because he was born of God and belonged to the fellowship of the children of God, he did not sin unto death, since by repenting he soon obtained pardon for his guilt.

There are, moreover, certain sins that would be considered extremely slight unless the Scriptures showed them to be more serious than people suppose.

(Augustine.) For who would think that one who says to his brother, “Fool,” is guilty of hell, unless Truth said so? Or who would judge how great a sin it is to observe days, months, seasons, and years—as those do who, on fixed days, months, or years, wish or refuse to begin something because they regard certain times as fortunate or unfortunate according to the vain teachings of men—unless we weighed its seriousness in the fear expressed by the Apostle when he said:

> “I fear for you, lest perhaps I have labored among you in vain” (Gal. 4:11).

Often certain great and dreadful sins, once they become habitual, are believed to be small or nothing at all. Indeed, they seem not only not to be concealed but even to be proclaimed and advertised, as it is written:

> “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who does iniquity is blessed” (Ps. 10:2).

In Sacred Scripture such iniquity is called a “cry.” Hence the statement in Genesis:

> “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied” (Gen. 18:20),

because among them those disgraceful acts were not only no longer punished, but were practiced publicly, as though sanctioned by law. Thus it is written:

> “They proclaimed their sin as Sodom and did not hide it” (Isa. 3:9).

This is a very grave sin, because it leads not only its own perpetrators but also those whom it draws into sin through deadly words and deeds to everlasting punishment. When someone commits this or something similar, he is worthy of as many deaths as he transmits examples of destruction to others.

No one would think that the desire of lust was so great a sin unless the Lord said:

> “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28).

Who would think it such a great sin uselessly to hoard wealth unless the apostle James said:

[Col. 1341C]

> “Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that will come upon you. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you, and it will consume your flesh like fire” (Jas. 5:1).

(Gregory.) Those sin greatly who are able to proclaim the word of sacred preaching profitably, yet hide it in silence. Hence Solomon says:

> “Whoever hides grain will be cursed among the peoples” (Prov. 11:26).

To hide grain is to retain within oneself the words of holy preaching. Such a person is cursed among the peoples because he is condemned to the punishment of the many whom he could have corrected, through the sole fault of his silence.

Perhaps no one would think the word of cursing such a dreadful sin, although it separates its followers from the kingdom of God, unless the apostle Paul said:

> “Nor will slanderers possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6).

This is an extremely common and very grave sin, attributed to frivolity. Almost no one restrains his tongue from such an utterly monstrous crime—neither rich nor poor, noble nor wise, foolish nor cleric, layman nor old person, young person nor male, female nor free person, slave.

The speech of cursing is not only what is said—“May the Lord curse him,” or “Cursed one, do this or that,” or “Let him be cursed”—but also every statement uttered in order to defame someone, disparage him, or speak of him maliciously. Although it may not appear insulting, it is cursing, as in the case of the blind man:

> “The Jews cursed him and said to him: ‘You are that man’s disciple’” (John 9:28).

(Basil.) Who would believe that worldly sorrow is a deadly sin unless the apostle Paul said:

> “Worldly sorrow produces death” (2 Cor. 7:10)?

Worldly sorrow is when we grieve over something belonging to human affairs or pertaining to the world. Sorrow according to God, however, is when we grieve over our own errors and those of our neighbors. Concerning this the same Apostle says:

> “Sorrow according to God produces lasting salvation” (ibid.).

There are also many other grave sins, which a diligent reader, if he wishes, will find scattered throughout the various pages of the Sacred Scriptures. When these become habitual, as written above, they are believed to be small or nothing at all.

Therefore the illustrious doctor, Saint Augustine the bishop, was compelled to cry out with profound grief in his exposition of Saint Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, saying:

> Woe to the sins of human beings, which we shudder at only when they are unusual, but which, when habitual, we are often compelled to tolerate by living with them and, by tolerating them, sometimes even to commit—although the blood of the Son of God was shed to cleanse them, and although they are so great that they altogether cause the kingdom of God to be closed against them. And would that, O Lord, we did not do everything we might be able to prohibit!

In no way, however, should we despair of God’s mercy concerning the remission in the holy Church of these crimes, however great, for those who do penance according to the measure of each sin. In the practice of penance, when something has been committed such that the perpetrator is separated even from the body of Christ, the measure of time should not be considered so much as the measure of grief:

> “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. 50:19).

But because the grief of one heart is often hidden from another and does not come to the knowledge of others through words or any other signs, although it is before the one to whom it is said:

> “My groaning is not hidden from you” (Ps. 37:10),

those who preside over the Churches rightly establish periods of penance, so that satisfaction may also be made to the Church, in which these sins are forgiven; for outside it they are not forgiven.

Therefore, whoever bears the great leprosy of more serious sin, so that he is separated not in spirit but bodily from the most health-giving medicine of the Lord’s body and blood, should, by the counsel and authority of the bishop, remove himself from the altar and from communion at the Lord’s table—not in despair but in humility—to perform penance of satisfaction, and afterward, according to canonical institution, be reconciled by the authority and prayer of the priest.

Penance must first be performed, and then this saving sacrament must be received:

> “Whoever eats unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29).

To receive unworthily means to receive it at a time when one ought to be performing penance.

(Prosper.) But if some people established in an ecclesiastical rank secretly commit a crime, they deceive themselves through a vain persuasion if they think that they ought for this reason to communicate and fulfill their office because they deceive people by concealing their crime. Those who have committed such things and fear to disclose them lest they receive the sentence of just excommunication communicate without cause—or rather, they aggravate the anger of divine indignation against themselves twofold: they pretend innocence through their dignities, and, despising God’s judgment, they are ashamed to abstain from the altar for the sake of human beings.

Therefore those will more easily reconcile God to themselves who, not convicted by human judgment, voluntarily acknowledge their crime. They either reveal it through their own confessions, or, while others do not know what they secretly are, they themselves pronounce upon themselves the sentence of voluntary excommunication. Separated from the altar at which they ministered not in spirit but in office, they mourn in penance, living their life as though it were dead.

(Augustine.) Even penance, when the cause is such that it ought to be undertaken according to the custom of the Church, is often not undertaken because of weakness. Shame is also a fear of displeasing, when human opinion is more pleasing than the justice by which a person humbles himself through repentance.

Thus not only when penance is performed, but also so that it may be performed, God’s mercy is necessary. Otherwise the Apostle would not say of certain people:

> “Lest perhaps God grant them repentance” (2 Tim. 2:25),

and, so that Peter might weep bitterly, the Evangelist would not have stated beforehand:

> “The Lord looked upon him” (Matt. 26:75).

(Prosper.) Those whose sins escape human knowledge, who have neither confessed them themselves nor had them made public by others, if they refuse to confess or amend them, will have as their avenger the very God whom they have as their witness. What does it benefit them to avoid human judgment, when, if they persist in their evil, they will go into eternal punishment, with God rendering recompense?

But if they make themselves their own judges and, as avengers of their own iniquity, impose upon themselves here a voluntary punishment of the strictest correction, temporal punishments will replace eternal penalties, and tears flowing from genuine contrition of heart will restrain the fires of eternal fire.

All who are entangled in mortal crime, whether secret or public, and for whom the life-giving medicines of the Lord’s body and blood must consequently be deferred, nevertheless presumptuously approach to receive the sacraments of the altar without the satisfaction and reconciliation of their bishop because they perhaps see many receiving the Lord’s communion whose such crimes they know about. They do not consider that many are corrected like Peter, many are tolerated like Judas, and many remain unknown until the Lord comes, illuminates the hidden things of darkness, and reveals the thoughts of the heart.

But those who have voluntarily confessed some mortal crime, or have been accused and convicted of one before either a secular or ecclesiastical judgment, and for this reason have been separated from the Lord’s communion by medicinal prohibition—if, when the necessity of death is pressing, they ask for viaticum and reconciliation, such a request must in no way be denied them.

(Leo.) It is exceedingly useful and necessary that the guilt of sins be released before the final day through priestly supplication. To those who, in a time of necessity and amid the urgency of imminent danger, implore the help of penance and immediate reconciliation, neither satisfaction should be forbidden nor reconciliation denied, because we can impose neither measures nor times upon the mercy of God, before whom conversion tolerates no delay.

(Coelestine.) For we most certainly believe that God’s clemency can suffice to assist the dying even in a single moment. The thief hanging at Christ’s right hand would have lost his reward if the repentance of one hour had not helped him. While he was undergoing punishment, he repented, and through the confession of a single statement he obtained, at God’s promise, a dwelling in paradise.

Therefore genuine conversion to God in those placed at the end of life must be judged more by the mind than by the time, as the prophet declares:

> “When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved” (Ezek. 33:12);

and:

> “On whatever day the sinner turns, his sins will not be counted against him” (ibid. 18:21);

and again:

> “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live”;

and:

> “You first declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26).

Likewise:

> “With the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption” (Ps. 129:7).

In distributing God’s gifts, therefore, we must not be difficult, nor neglect the groans and tears of those who accuse themselves, since we believe that the very disposition to repent is conceived by God’s inspiration. The Apostle says:

> “Lest perhaps God grant them repentance, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil” (2 Tim. 2:26),

by whom they are held captive to his will.

As the most holy martyr Cyprian says in the letter he wrote to the Romans, concerning those whose approaching end of life cannot endure delay: after penance has been undertaken and professed, if, through tears, groans, and weeping, they display [proderint; variant: prodiderint] signs of a grieving and truly penitent mind (dolentes ac vere poenitentes animi; variant: dolentis ac vere poenitentis) over the haste of their actions—when, humanly speaking, no hope of living remains—then help is finally provided carefully and anxiously. God himself knows what he does concerning such people and how he weighs them in his judgments. We, however, are anxious that wicked people should neither praise our excessive readiness nor truly penitent people accuse us of a supposedly harsh cruelty.

Those penitents whose life is known to be secure should weep over sins as great as those they committed, and seek counsel as great as the offense appears to be in its extent. The medicine should not be less than the wound; the remedies should not be less than the deaths.

As the aforementioned martyr Cyprian says in his book On the Lapsed, penitents ought to pray and plead more earnestly, pass the day in mourning, spend the nights in vigils and tears, occupy all their time with tearful lamentation, cling to the ground spread with ashes, roll about in sackcloth and filth; after losing Christ’s garment, desire no garment any longer; after the devil’s food, prefer fasting; devote themselves to righteous works, by which sins are cleansed; and frequently devote themselves to almsgiving, by which souls are freed from death.

For, as the same doctor says in his third letter to Cornelius, bishop of the city of Rome, there are people who do not understand their own offenses: their mind is stricken, their spirit deranged, and their perception alienated. God’s anger toward them is that they do not understand their sins, lest they follow repentance, as it is written:

> “God gave them a spirit of compunction, so that they would not return,”

be healed, and be cured of their sins through prayers and righteous acts of satisfaction.

The apostle Paul explains this in his Epistle and says:

> “They did not have a love of the truth so that they might be saved; and therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie, so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but took pleasure in injustice” (2 Thess. 2:10).

The first degree of happiness is not to sin; the second is to recognize sins. In the former, complete and undefiled innocence proceeds, preserving a person; in the latter, healing follows, restoring him.

[Col. 1345B] There are, moreover, some who consider the greatness and countless number of their sins and, despairing of the ineffable and incomprehensible mercy of almighty God, lose hope. Therefore they refuse to do penance for their sins and crimes, but remain hardened in their evils with an impenitent heart, unhappily rebellious against the grace of the Holy Spirit. Concerning them the Apostle says:

> “Do you not know that God’s patience leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Rom. 2:5).

This hardness of an impenitent heart is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which will not be forgiven any human being. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “Whoever speaks blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven” (Mark 3:29).

Concerning this blasphemy, the most cautious and distinguished doctor Augustine, when speaking to the people about unforgivable blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, says among other things:

> This impenitence certainly has no forgiveness, neither in this age nor in the age to come, because repentance obtains forgiveness in this age, a forgiveness that avails in the future. But this impenitence, or impenitent heart, cannot be judged as long as a person lives in this flesh, for no one is to be despaired of so long as God’s patience leads him to repentance.

A little later he says:

> Every sin and blasphemy will certainly be forgiven human beings, wherever this sin of an impenitent heart against the Holy Spirit is absent. Through the Holy Spirit sins are loosed in the Church, and all other sins are forgiven. But how will that be forgiven which also prevents the forgiveness of other sins? Everything, therefore, is forgiven in those in whom that sin is absent which will never be forgiven. But in those in whom it is present, because it will never be forgiven, neither are the other sins forgiven, since the forgiveness of all sins is obstructed by the bond of this one.

Concerning this blasphemy—that is, impenitence or an impenitent heart—the aforementioned father Augustine discoursed most clearly and at great length, as is his custom, in a sermon to the people, in accordance with the testimony of the Sacred Scriptures.

Let no one, therefore, despair because of the multitude and enormity of his sins. Rather, trusting in God’s mercy, let him do penance for his sins while he lives in this body, lest in the future examination of the eternal Judge he be condemned, as has already been said, because of the hardness of an impenitent heart, which is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, and remain without any forgiveness according to the judgment of the Lord and Savior.

(Chrysostom.) There is no crime and no iniquity that cannot be healed by the medicine of repentance, provided that the sinner returns to God, from whom he departed by sinning, with a contrite and humbled heart, with tears, groans, vigils, prayers, fasts, and almsgiving, according to the measure of his strength.

The most distinguished doctor John, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, wrote an excellent book on the restoration of the fallen through repentance. I think that no sinner who reads it will afterward, with God’s gift, be able to despair because of the number of his sins.

The most holy martyr Cyprian also wrote an elegant book On the Lapsed. Whoever possesses these two authors as physicians of souls and properly understands their books will be able, with the help of God, who is the physician of physicians, to apply saving medicine to every wound of the soul.

Nor do I think that in this present excerpt something should be left unsaid which blessed Augustine says in the fourteenth book of The City of God concerning the proud and those who sin secretly:

> It is useful to fall into some open and manifest sin by which those who had already fallen through pleasing themselves may become displeased with themselves. For Peter’s displeasure with himself when he wept was more salutary than his pleasure with himself when he presumed.

The sacred Psalm also says:

> “Fill their faces with disgrace, and they will seek your name, O Lord” (Ps. 82:17),

that is, so that they may please you while seeking your name, whereas they had pleased themselves by seeking their own.

But there is a worse and more damnable pride in those who, amid manifest sins, seek the support of excuses, inquiring as did the first human beings. One of them said:

> “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (Gen. 3:13),

and the other said:

> “The woman whom you gave as my companion—she gave me from the tree, and I ate.”

Nowhere here is there a request for pardon; nowhere an imploration of healing.

Nor should we pass over what the same Saint Augustine says in his book On Faith and Works concerning those who make people falsely secure, so that they will not be condemned on account of correct faith even if they persist in crimes:

> Let us carefully beware, with the help of the Lord our God, lest we make people falsely secure by saying to them that, if they have been baptized in Christ, however they may have lived in that faith, they will come to eternal salvation.

For the apostle James says:

> “If someone says that he has faith but does not have works, can faith save him? For faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:14).

Just as correct faith without good works benefits no one, so good works without faith cannot benefit anyone, as Sacred Scripture bears witness:

> “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6).

And to affirm that correct faith without good works cannot save anyone, the same distinguished doctor Augustine, in the fourth book of On Baptism, confirms it through divine testimonies, saying:

> Let us suppose someone who is a fornicator, unclean, lustful, greedy, a sorcerer, quarrelsome, contentious, factious, envious, drunk, a reveler—but Catholic. Will he possess the kingdom of God merely because he is Catholic, while doing such things as the Apostle concludes in this way: “These things I foretell to you, as I foretold them, because those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:21)? And elsewhere he says: “Know this, understanding that every fornicator or unclean person or greedy person, which is service of idols, does not have an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God” (Eph. 5:5).

For true is the statement of the holy apostle James, who says:

> “Faith without works is useless” (Jas. 2:20, 26).

Many ask whether parents harm baptized infants when they try to associate them with sacrifices to demons, or how greatly the parents themselves sin in this matter.

Saint Augustine teaches us more fully concerning this in his Epistle to Bishop Boniface, written in response to an inquiry about infants. He says that one who has once been born through the spiritual will of others cannot thereafter be bound by the bond of another’s iniquity, since he has consented to it by no will of his own.

Parents, however, or any elders who try to bind baptized sons or any little children to the sacrilege of demons are spiritual murderers. They do not indeed kill them physically, but, insofar as it lies within them, they become killers.

There are many other innumerable testimonies in the authority of the divine Scriptures concerning crimes and mortal sins, which our poor pen could not collect in this present excerpt. For it is exceedingly long and difficult even for wise and highly learned men to gather together all the statements of the Old and New Testament and of all Catholics concerning this subject—how much more difficult for me, who am entirely unlearned in speech and life.

But because, as I believe, I ought not to appear disobedient to your holy charity, I presumed beyond my strength to do what neither skill supplies me, nor ability grants me, nor weakness permits.

Thus far, if it pleases you, let these few excerpts concerning grave and mortal sins, drawn from many authorities of the Sacred Scriptures, suffice. Now, concerning the origin of the eight principal vices and their remedies, insofar as the author of eternal light deigns to grant them to your merits, I shall endeavor, according to the modest capacity of my ability, to append to this work testimonies from the little works of the holy Fathers.

**CHAPTER II.—Concerning the matter of the eight principal vices and the origin of their offspring.**
God, the creator and founder of the human race, wishing, because of the immense mercy of his compassion, to free his people from present and everlasting evils and happily bring them to a blessed life, gives commandments and salutary admonitions concerning what they ought to do or observe. Thus, among other commandments, he says to Israel in Deuteronomy (Deut. VI, 10):

> “When the Lord your God has brought you into the land which you are about to enter and possess, and has destroyed before you many nations—the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites—seven nations much more numerous than you and stronger, and when the Lord has delivered them to you, you shall strike them down to complete destruction.”

(Cass.) These seven nations are the seven principal vices, which every spiritual soldier is admonished to overcome through God’s grace and utterly exterminate. But the reason they are said to be more numerous is that vices are more numerous than virtues; and therefore, while seven nations are counted in the catalogue, in the account of their conquest they are mentioned without an enumeration. For it is said: “And he has destroyed many nations before you.” The people of carnal passions, which proceeds from this sevenfold fuel and root of vices, is more numerous than Israel.

From *gastrimargia* arise revelries and drunkenness. From fornication arise filthy speech, buffoonery, frivolity, and foolish talk. From *philargyria*—that is, avarice or, more precisely, love of money—arise lying, fraud, thefts, perjuries, the pursuit of shameful profit, false testimony, violence, inhumanity, and rapacity. From anger arise murder, shouting, and indignation. From sadness arise rancor, faintheartedness, bitterness, and despair. From *acedia* arise idleness, sleepiness, importunity, restlessness, wandering, instability of mind and body, verbosity, and curiosity. From *cenodoxia* arise disputes, heresies, boasting, and presumption concerning novelties. From pride arise contempt, envy, disobedience, blasphemy, murmuring, detraction, and many other similar things, which together are far more numerous than the virtues.

Nevertheless, once those seven principal vices, from whose nature these things proceed, have been conquered, all the others immediately become quiet and are likewise destroyed in perpetual annihilation along with them. That these plagues are also stronger we clearly perceive from their very assault upon nature: the delight of carnal passions fights more powerfully in our members than the pursuit of virtues, which are acquired only through the greatest contrition of heart and body.

The command that we should beneficially possess the territories of these destructive nations is understood as follows. Each vice has its own station in our heart. But if, together with the people of Israel—that is, with the virtues fighting against them—the vices are overcome, then the place in our heart which the spirit of lust or fornication had occupied will thereafter be possessed by chastity; the place which fury had seized will be reclaimed by patience; the place which sadness, working death, had occupied will be possessed by health-giving and joy-filled gladness; the place which *acedia* had laid waste will begin to be cultivated by fortitude; and the place which pride had trampled will begin to be cultivated by humility. Thus, once each vice has been expelled, the children of Israel—that is, souls who see God—will possess their places, namely, their contrary dispositions.

But when the Lord spoke with Abraham about future events, Scripture records not seven nations but ten, whose land was promised to be given to his descendants. This number is most clearly completed by adding the idolatry of the nations, the blasphemy of the Jews, and the error of heretics. Before the knowledge of God and the grace of baptism, the multitude of the impious Gentiles or the blasphemous Jews was subject to these powers, so long as it dwelt in intellectual Egypt.

If someone, however, renounces that place, departs from it, and by God’s grace reaches the spiritual wilderness, he is freed from the assault of three nations and will undertake battle only against the seven counted by Moses.

Thus far these few remarks have been spoken concerning the eight principal vices, from the works of Cassian, a most eloquent teacher. But it may be asked why Cassian and Gregory disagree with one another in their catalogue of these same principal vices, so that Cassian counts *philargyria* and *acedia* among them, whereas Gregory does not place these two vices—namely, *philargyria* and *acedia*—among them, but instead counts envy and avarice among the same vices, which Cassian does not do at all.

For Cassian says that, with the Lord’s help, we must undertake the struggle against eight principal vices. They are as follows: first, the vice of *gastrimargia*, which is interpreted as the desire of the throat or the greed of the belly; second, fornication; third, *philargyria*, understood as avarice or, more accurately expressed, love of money; fourth, anger; fifth, sadness; sixth, *acedia*, which is anxiety or weariness of heart; seventh, *cenodoxia*, interpreted as vainglory; eighth, pride.

But blessed Pope Gregory counts and describes the principal vices in this order: first, pride; second, empty glory; third, envy; fourth, anger; fifth, sadness; sixth, avarice; seventh, gluttony of the belly; eighth, lust.

This question has been truthfully resolved by learned teachers in the following manner. “Avarice,” they say, “is called *philargyria* in Greek.” Hence Cassian likewise says: “The Apostle declared not only that it is the root of all evils, but also that it is the service of idols,” saying: “And avarice, which in Greek is called *philargyria*, ‘which is the service of idols’” (Col. III, 5).

It is therefore clear that these two teachers, Gregory and Cassian, although one said *philargyria* and the other avarice, did not differ at all concerning the name, because avarice and *philargyria* are one and the same.

They say that the envy which Cassian did not count among the other vices he understood under the title of pride, because the devil fell from heaven through pride and, through envy, expelled the first human beings from the seats of paradise. For this reason they wish the two to be one disease. Hence Prosper says: “It is so completely one evil that neither can a proud person be found without envy nor an envious person without pride.”

As for *acedia*, about which Gregory said nothing in the aforementioned enumeration of the principal vices, they say that he wished to understand it under the name of sadness. Hence Cassian also says: “*Acedia*, which we can call weariness or anxiety of heart, is akin to sadness.”

These statements clearly prove that Gregory and Cassian held a uniform opinion concerning the eight principal vices.

It may also be asked why Gregory places pride first in his enumeration of the vices, while Cassian places it last. Cassian himself says: “Although the disease of pride is eighth and last, and in the conflict and order of the vices is placed at the end, in origin and time it is first.” He says likewise elsewhere that, although pride is later in the order of the conflicts, in origin it is earlier than all sins and crimes, and is the destroyer of all virtues.

From this point onward, with the Lord’s help, let us pursue how the eight principal vices and their offspring have been set forth and arranged by blessed Pope Gregory in his exposition of blessed Job. He says:

> “The vices that tempt us and fight against us in invisible battle serve under pride. Some go before like commanders; others follow like an army. For pride itself, the queen of vices, as soon as it has taken possession of the conquered heart, immediately hands it over to the seven principal vices, as though to its commanders, to be devastated. The army follows these commanders, because from them, without doubt, innumerable crowds of vices arise. We shall show this more clearly if, as far as we can, we enumerate and set forth the commanders and the armies themselves.
>
> “Pride is the root of every evil, concerning which Scripture testifies: ‘Pride is the beginning of every sin’ (Eccl. X, 15). From this poisonous root the seven principal vices emerge: empty glory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony of the belly, and lust. Because our Redeemer grieved that we had been captured by these seven vices of pride, he came, full of the Spirit of sevenfold grace, to the battle of spiritual liberation.
>
> “But each of these has its own army. From empty glory arise disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, disputes, stubbornness, dissensions, and especially presumption. From envy arise hatred, whispering, detraction, exultation at one’s neighbor’s misfortunes, and distress at his prosperity. From anger arise quarrels, swelling of mind, insults, shouting, indignation, and blasphemies. From sadness arise malice, rancor, faintheartedness, despair, sluggishness concerning the commandments, and wandering of the mind toward unlawful things. From avarice arise betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjury, restlessness, violence, and hardness of heart against mercy. From gluttony of the belly arise foolish merriment, buffoonery, uncleanness, excessive talk, and dullness of understanding. From lust arise blindness of mind, lack of consideration, inconstancy, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to the present world, and dread or despair concerning the future.
>
> “Since, therefore, the seven principal vices produce such a multitude of vices from themselves, when they come to the heart they drag along, as it were, the troops of a following army. Of these seven, five are spiritual and two carnal. Yet each is joined to the next by such kinship that one is produced only from another.
>
> “The first offspring of pride is empty glory. When it has corrupted the oppressed mind, it immediately gives birth to envy, because while a person seeks the power of an empty name, he wastes away lest someone else should attain it.
>
> “Envy likewise gives birth to anger, because the more deeply the soul is wounded by the inward injury of spite, the more it loses gentleness and tranquility. And because a painful limb is being touched, the hand of the opposing action is felt as though it were pressing more heavily.
>
> “From anger, sadness arises. For the disturbed mind, the more disorderly its agitation, the more it confounds itself by its very agitation; and when it has lost the sweetness of tranquility, nothing nourishes it except the sorrow that follows from disturbance.
>
> “Sadness, in turn, derives from avarice. When the confused heart has lost inwardly the good of joy, it seeks outside itself something by which it may be consoled; and the more it desires to acquire external goods, the less it possesses anything inward to which it may return.
>
> “After these, the two carnal vices remain: gluttony of the belly and lust. Yet it is clear to everyone that lust is born from gluttony of the belly, since in the arrangement of the bodily members the genitals appear to be supported by the belly. Thus, when one is improperly nourished, the other is undoubtedly aroused to shameful acts.
>
> “They are rightly called commanders when they exhort, and armies when they howl, because the first vices insinuate themselves into the deceived mind under the appearance of a kind of reasoning, while the countless vices that follow, dragging the mind toward every madness, confuse it with something like a beastly roar.”

Since thus far we have extracted and set forth a few things concerning the eight principal vices, I now consider it very necessary that, from the many works of the holy Fathers, and as much as the Lord may grant, we investigate more fully, first, their origins and natures, however minute and obscure; then their causes and torments; and finally, as we began, their appropriate cures and remedies.

## Chapter III — On the Nature and Origin of Pride

(Cass.) We can learn how to avoid the most destructive poison of this disease if we pursue the causes and origin of its ruin. For sickness can never be cured, nor can remedies be applied to diseases, unless their origins and causes have first been investigated by careful inquiry.

That archangel who, because of the excess of his splendor and beauty, was called Lucifer was cast down from that blessed station of the angels and fell into hell through no other vice than pride. Clothed in divine brightness and shining, by the Creator’s generosity, among the other heavenly powers, he believed that the splendor of wisdom and the beauty of the virtues with which the Creator’s grace had adorned him were possessed through the power of his own nature, not through the benefit of the Creator’s munificence.

For this reason, exalted as though he did not need divine assistance to persevere in this purity, he judged himself like God. This thought alone became his ruin. Abandoned by God on account of it, he lost the blessedness which he had enjoyed as God’s gift.

This is the cause of the first fall and the principal origin of the disease. For the fuel of all vices sprang from pride, as Holy Scripture testifies: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Eccl. X, 15). It does not say “of a particular sin,” but “of every sin,” because, as Prosper says, pride is not merely itself a sin, but no sin has been, is, or can be committed without it.

This, then, is the nature and origin of pride, through which its inventor fell from heaven and afterward corrupted the first human beings and brought the entire human race from immortality to mortality. Concerning this the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings.”

## Chapter IV — That There Are Two Kinds of Pride

(Cass.) There are two kinds of pride: one that assails spiritual and advanced persons, and another that embraces beginners and carnal persons. Although both kinds of pride inflate people with a harmful exaltation against God and against human beings, the first is especially directed against God, while the second properly concerns human beings.

Since, as has been said, there are two kinds of pride, one is called spiritual because it assails spiritual and holy people; the other is carnal because it attacks carnal people.

First, however, we must speak of spiritual pride. Spiritual pride usually assails only those who, after conquering the higher vices, have already been placed almost at the summit of the virtues. Since the most subtle enemy could not overcome them through a carnal fall, he attempts to cast them down and overthrow them through spiritual ruin, striving by this means to strip them of all the merits of their former labors, acquired with great toil.

Carnal pride makes carnal people disobedient and harsh and does not allow them to be gentle and approachable. It makes their life long, and, lest they confess their sins, it infuses them with shame and embarrassment. When rebuked for their negligences, they rebel and murmur. And what is more? Once it has taken possession of the miserable mind, it does not permit that mind to descend to the true humility of Christ. We shall discuss more about its most wretched fall when we begin to treat its signs.

## Chapter V — That Pride Is So Great an Evil That It Deserves to Have God Himself as Its Adversary

(Cass.) Pride is so great an evil that it deserves to have not an angel or other virtues as its adversaries, but the Lord himself, as Scripture testifies: “God opposes the proud”; and again: “Everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before God.” It should indeed be noted that Scripture never said of those entangled in the other vices that they have the Lord resisting them, but only of the proud.

## Chapter VI — How Pride Torments the Proud

(Cass.) Those whom pride torments do not have fitting speech, but light and foolish laughter; they have unrestrained and undisciplined exaltation of heart. It makes disciples incautious and haughty toward the holy rulers of God’s churches; it makes its followers proud in prosperity, despairing and sad in adversity, slow in prayer, lazy in vigils, tight-fisted in giving alms, greedy in fasting, sluggish in obedience, inhuman in hospitality, and—what is more—in every good thing dishonorable and without mercy.

## Chapter VII — By What Signs Pride Can Be Recognized

(Cass.) Pride is revealed by the following signs. At first there is forceful shouting in one’s speech; in silence, bitterness; in joy, high and excessive irrational laughter; in seriousness, sadness; in one’s answer, rancor; ease and looseness in speaking; words bursting forth everywhere without any gravity of heart; patience absent; charity toward others lacking; boldness in inflicting insults but faintheartedness in enduring them; difficulty in obeying; implacability in receiving exhortation; weakness in cutting away one’s own desires; extreme harshness in yielding to those of others; and a continual effort to establish one’s own judgments, while oneself never agrees to yield or give place to another.

Thus it happens that, even after becoming capable of receiving sound counsel, a person trusts his own opinion in everything rather than the judgment of his elders. Hence Prosper says:

> “Those whom the virulent corruption of pride of mind has infected do not obey the commands of their elders but judge them. When rebuked for their negligences, they either rebel or murmur. They contend for the higher place, strive to be preferred to their betters, boldly flaunt their own opinions, and do not preserve reverence in service. These are the signs of the swelling of pride, by which God is offended and at which the devil, nourished by these evils, rejoices.”

## Chapter VIII — That No Vice Departs So Far from God’s Commands as Pride, nor Provokes the Lord’s Anger More

(Hilar.) In the exposition of a certain psalm, the most excellent teacher Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, cried out with grief, saying:

> “O wretched pride, which disdains to live under heavenly commandments, which, through the swelling of an unbelieving mind, scorns the divine commands. There are many crimes belonging to human vices and diverse, innumerable operations of sinners, but nothing provokes God’s anger against us more than pride. Through pride many despise human things and scorn to obey God.
>
> “Yet although the other works of faith may be excellent and devotion may persist in the keeping of all the divine commandments, when pride creeps in, the memory of the things we have done rightly is erased.
