Through it that evangelical Pharisee, saying, ‘I am not a sinner like this tax collector’ (Luke XVIII, 11), fell from great works into guilt. For the Apostle Paul received an angel of Satan to buffet him, lest he should be exalted by the greatness of his revelations (I Cor. XII, 7).”

(Cass.) Pride is a most serious vice. Through it we despise human things and neglect divine things; it drains all the virtues alike; it strips a person of justice and holiness; it is the destroyer of all virtues. It is the fiercest beast, more savage than all the vices that precede it. Without it no sin existed, exists, or can exist: “Pride,” he says, “is the beginning of every sin” (Eccl. X, 15).

[Prosper.] Every sin is nothing other than contempt for God, by which his commandments are trampled underfoot. Indeed, the devil himself, the inventor of pride, fell from heaven through it, although God had made him without any sin. This is the cause of all evils. Through it the crafty serpent, the devil, destroyed our first parent; through it he brought death into the world.

Pride is the mother and queen of the vices, whose king is the devil, as Scripture says: “He is king over all the sons of pride” (Job XLI, 25).

## Chapter IX — An Admonition or Rebuke Addressed to the Proud, with Various Testimonies on the Subject

Therefore the proud must be told:

> “Why is earth and ashes proud?” (Eccl. X, 9);
>
> “God resists the proud” (I Pet. V, 5);
>
> “Everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before God”;
>
> “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke XIV, 11);
>
> “Before ruin, the spirit is exalted” (Prov. XVI, 18);
>
> “The Lord knows the lofty from afar” (Ps. CXXXVI, 7);
>
> “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Eccl. X, 15).

God became humble; let the human being blush to be proud.

The occasion of our destruction, therefore, was the devil’s pride, while the foundation of our redemption was found in God’s humility. Our enemy, although created among all things, wished in his exaltation to be seen above all things; but our Redeemer, remaining great above all things, deigned to become little among all things.

Therefore let it be said to the humble: when they abase themselves, they ascend to the likeness of God. Let it be said to the exalted: when they raise themselves up, they fall in imitation of the apostate angel.

## Chapter X — How We Can Overcome Pride

We can escape this snare of the most wicked spirit if, whenever we feel that we have advanced in any virtue, we say the Apostle’s words:

> “Not I, but the grace of God with me; and by the grace of God I am what I am; and it is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure” (I Cor. XV, 10; Phil. II, 13).

The author of our salvation himself also says:

> “Whoever remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, because without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5),

and other sayings of the same kind.

Pride, the despoiler of all virtues, can be extinguished through true humility. Therefore God, the creator and physician of the universe, recognizing that pride is the cause and beginning of diseases, arranged to heal opposites with opposites, so that the things which had fallen through pride might rise again through humility.

The devil says: “I will ascend into heaven” (Isa. XIV, 13); the Lord says: “My soul was humbled to the earth” (Ps. XLIII, 25). He says: “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 14); the Lord, “although he was in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. II, 7). He says: “I will exalt my throne above the stars of God” (Isa. XIV, 13); the Lord says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29).

If we have perceived the cause of the first ruin and the foundations of our salvation—by whom and how the one was brought about and the other arose—then by the ruin of one and the example of the other we may learn how we ought to avoid pride’s terrible death.

## Chapter XI — Remedies Against the Disease of Pride

(Cass.) If we hasten by every means to extinguish pride, that most savage beast and devourer of all virtues, let us judge ourselves inferior and more contemptible than all human beings, and let us endure with the greatest patience everything inflicted upon us by those above us, even if it is insulting, sad, or harmful, as though it had been imposed by our superiors.

Let us continually recall in our minds the sufferings of our Lord and of his saints, considering that we are assailed by injuries so much lighter as we stand farther from their merits and manner of life. Let us also reflect that we shall soon depart from this world.

Afterward let us hold this same humility toward the Lord with the greatest firmness. This will be accomplished in us when we recognize that, without his help and grace, we can accomplish nothing pertaining to the perfection of the virtues, and when we truly believe that even the understanding we have been permitted to possess is his gift.

The holy Father Basil also speaks as follows about the cure and remedy of pride:

> “It is impossible for this vice to be cured unless a person withdraws and departs from every occasion of exaltation. Just as it is impossible to extinguish the speech or language of any tongue or nation, or any craft, unless a person withdraws in every way not only from doing, speaking, or moving, but also from hearing those who do what he wishes to forget, so this must be observed concerning all vices.”

## Chapter XII — On the Nature and Origin of Empty Glory

(Cass.) *Cenodoxia*, which we call vain or empty glory, is a multifaceted, varied, and subtle passion, so much so that it can scarcely be avoided, anticipated, or detected even by the most discerning eyes.

As has been said, it arises from pride. Through this vice of vanity the devil was expelled from angelic blessedness when he said, “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 14). Through this disease of empty glory he deceived the first human beings when he said to them, “You will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III, 5).

Empty glory is a multiple, multifaceted, and varied passion, as has been said, confronting the victor from every side like an enemy in battle. In clothing and appearance, in gait and voice, in work, vigils, prayer, withdrawal, reading, knowledge, silence, obedience, humility, and patience, it attempts to wound the Christian.

Through this vice of vanity, whoever desires to be praised for his good deeds is deceived and does not give honor, praise, and thanksgiving to the Lord God. Nor does he attribute to divine grace whatever good he has thought, said, or done. Rather, as though he possessed from himself what he has rightly thought, said, or accomplished in deed, he boasts that he has acquired either earthly honor and dignity, or spiritual distinction and the beauty of wisdom, through his own merit or effort.

Yet no human being could, can, or will be able to think, say, do, or possess anything good without God’s grace, help, or inspiration, as the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5).

## Chapter XIII — By What Comparison the Nature of *Cenodoxia*, That Is, Empty Glory, Is Shown

(Cass.) The elders aptly describe the nature of this disease by comparison with an onion and *pultorum* [the latter term is uncertain], which, adorned with one covering, is found again clothed in another, and is found covered as many times as it has been stripped.

## Chapter XIV — How and in What Ways Empty Glory Attacks and Torments Its Followers

(Cass.) Empty glory attacks a person not only in the carnal part, like the other vices, but also in the spiritual part. It insinuates itself into the mind with more subtle wickedness, and when it cannot deceive someone through carnal vices, it attempts to wound him through spiritual goods. It is more dangerous in combat because it is more difficult to guard against.

It does not cease to attack the Christian from the right and from the left. The wisest Solomon says: “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left” (Prov. IV, 27).

Those who exalt themselves over their virtues and good works and flatter themselves vainly turn aside to the right. Those who seek glory for themselves from their vices, in their shame, turn aside to the left through the vice of exaltation and empty glory.

When *cenodoxia* cannot ensnare someone through the appearance of a close-fitting and clean garment, it tries to bring him down through one that is filthy, neglected, and inferior. When it cannot overthrow him through honor, it trips him through humility. When it cannot exalt him through the adornment of knowledge and speech, it strikes him down through the gravity of silence.

If he fasts, he is openly assailed by the glory of vanity. If he conceals his fasting in order to despise glory, he is dulled by the same vice of exaltation. If he practices secret prayers, he does not escape the prickings of vanity, since he has no human witness to the deed.

This disease does not cease to pursue even those who have fled the company of all mortals in solitude for the sake of glory. The more someone has looked away from the whole world, the more eagerly it pursues and harries him. It tries to exalt one because he is especially patient in work and labor, another because he is especially ready to obey, another because he surpasses others in humility. One is tempted through knowledge, another through reading, another through the length of his vigils.

This disease of empty glory also often exalts certain men in the clerical order because of the sound of their voice—because they chant more loudly—or because they are handsome in bodily form, or because they have rich and noble parents, or because they are learned in wisdom, or because they are eloquent and most fluent in speech, or because they are versed in various arts and disciplines.

And what is more? This plague of vanity always attacks every person—cleric or layman, man or woman, old or young—in order that he may seek praise from human beings for the good things he does.

## Chapter XV — By What Signs Empty Glory Can Be Recognized

(Basil.) Empty glory is recognized by these signs: when someone performs a good work in the presence of those who can praise him, but, when no such person is present—or even in the presence of those who can criticize him—is sluggish and slower in the work.

If he truly wished always to please the Lord, he would be the same everywhere and would do the same things in every place, fulfilling what is written: “By the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through evil report and good report, as deceivers and yet true” (II Cor. VI, 7–8).

Vanity is a kind of inflated affection surrounding the various pleasures of a sick soul. It is at once ignorant of and greedy for honor; inflated by the disease of empty distinction, turbulent, mistress of frivolous minds, flattering toward all who are badly grounded, smoky toward those who resist, seductive toward those whom it can capture, unconquered by its captives. It is a kind of imitation of the virtues and an appetite for dignities, sweet to the wretched and bitter to the perfect.

The timid serve it; the exalted lie beneath it. These boast shamefully of works of which they are not conscious in themselves; they wickedly desire to be praised by human beings; they disparage holy men in comparison with themselves. Soothed by these and similar things, vanity oppresses them and does not permit them to perceive their disease or come to the physician.

And what is it to come to the physician except for a sick person to recognize his illnesses? The fire of human praise inflames them so greatly that they take up laborious works which the people admire and through which their reputation spreads as though without labor, and willingly perform them. Hence, although fasting, abstaining, keeping vigils, frequenting the church, and chanting all require labor, they perform these things even with delight, so that they may appear before human beings, whom they desire to please rather than God.

Thus Truth says: “Truly, I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 2, 5).

## Chapter XVI — A Rebuke Addressed to Those Tormented by the Disease of Empty Glory, with Various Testimonies on the Subject

(Cass. and Hieron.) The outstanding preacher Paul admonishes us, saying: “Do not become desirous of empty glory” (Gal. V, 26). And the Lord, rebuking the Pharisees, says: “How can you believe, who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone?” (John V, 44).

The blessed David also speaks of them with a threat: “For God has scattered the bones of those who please themselves” (Ps. LII, 6).

(Hieron.) The same prophet teaches that it is not our glory but the Lord’s that must be implored when he says in prayer: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. CXIII, 1). And the Apostle Paul says: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31). And again: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Cor. XV, 10).

Instructed by these statements, beware, O lover of empty glory, lest you seek praise from human beings for the good things you do. Believe firmly that, even if you give many alms, offer long prayers, undertake many fasts, preserve chastity or virginity, or do any other good thing, if you do these things for human praise, you will receive no reward from God for them.

## Chapter XVII — Remedies by Which We Can Overcome Empty Glory

(Cass.) We can escape this many-sided and varied beast of empty glory by applying the following remedy. Let us consider the saying of David: “The Lord has scattered the bones of those who please human beings” (Ps. LII, 6). First, let us do nothing for the sake of obtaining vanity and empty glory.

Then, whatever we have begun well, let us strive to preserve with the same vigilance, lest the disease of *cenodoxia*, creeping in afterward, drain away all the fruits of our labors. Let us avoid those things which can make us conspicuous among others, and for which praise may be sought from human beings as though we alone had done them.

To avoid this disease, we must consider not only that we shall lose whatever fruits of our labors we have performed with the intention of empty glory, but also that, having become guilty of a great crime, we shall pay eternal penalties like sacrilegious persons. For, to God’s injury, we preferred to perform for the sake of human beings the work which we ought to have done for God’s sake. We shall be convicted by him who knows what is hidden of having preferred human beings and the glory of the world to God and the Lord’s glory.

According to the holy bishop Basil, the medicine of this vice is that we do all good things for God and at his command, and seek human praise in nothing. He says elsewhere that if someone is certain of God’s presence, has a fixed concern to please God, and is held by a great desire for the blessedness promised by the Lord, then, with the Lord’s help, he can be cured of this vice of vanity.

## Chapter XVIII — On the Nature and Origin of Envy
(Cypr.) Nothing should be more carefully avoided by a Christian, nothing more prudently guarded against, than being seized by envy and ill will—lest anyone, entangled in the blind snares of the deceiving enemy, while fraternal zeal is turned into hatred of a brother, unknowingly perish by his own sword. To understand and perceive this more fully and clearly, let us return to its head and origin. Let us see where, when, and how envy and jealousy began; for this most destructive evil will more easily be avoided by us if we recognize both its origin and its magnitude. From this source the devil was the first to fall and to destroy, at the beginning of the standing world. He, upheld by angelic majesty, accepted and beloved by God, when he saw the human being made in the image of God, burst forth into jealous ill will—not casting down the other first through the impulse of jealousy, but having himself first been cast down by jealousy. A captive before he captured, ruined before he ruined, while by goading ill will he robbed humanity of the grace of immortality, he too lost what he had previously been. From then on envy rages upon the earth, while the teacher of destruction, ruined by ill will, carries out his task; while those who belong to his party imitate the devil who envied, as it is written: “But through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wis. II, 24). Thus they imitate him who are on his side. From this source heinous parricides began: the unjust Cain envied the righteous Abel, and Esau became the enemy of his brother Jacob through envy. Joseph too was sold by his envious brothers, and King Saul persecuted David because of envy; and the Jews perished for this reason, preferring to envy Christ rather than believe in him.

### CHAPTER XIX — How envy torments the envious

Let no one suppose that this evil is contained in a single form, or confined within brief limits and a narrow compass. The manifold and fertile destruction of jealousy extends widely. It is the root of all evils, the source of great [Al.: general] evils, the seedbed of transgressions, and the material of faults. From it hatred arises; from it hostility proceeds. Jealousy inflames greed, when someone cannot be content with what is his, seeing another richer. Jealousy arouses ambition, when someone sees another more exalted in honors. When jealousy excites our senses and brings the hidden things of the mind under its dominion, the fear of God is scorned, Christ’s teaching is neglected, the day of judgment is disregarded, pride is inflated, savagery is aggravated, faithlessness transgresses, impatience is blinded, discord rages, and anger seethes. The person who has become subject to another’s power can neither restrain nor govern his anger. From this the bond of the Lord’s peace is broken; from this fraternal love is violated; from this truth is adulterated and unity is torn apart.

Envy is the moth of the soul, which wastes the breast through its infection. The envious person envies in another either his virtue or his happiness—that is, either his personal merits or the divine gifts. The envious turn another’s good into their own evil; they are tormented by the prosperity of the distinguished and make another’s glory their own punishment. For them neither food is pleasant nor drink delightful. They constantly sigh, groan, and grieve; and since the envious never cast off their ill will, their afflicted breast is torn without interruption, day and night. Other evils have an end, and whatever wrongdoing is committed comes to an end with the completion of the offense. Envy has no end: it is an evil that persists continually and a sin without conclusion. The more the person whom he envies advances through improving circumstances, the more the envious and ill-disposed person burns in the greater fire of his resentful passion.

Who can easily express in words what sort of evil this is—an evil in which the envious person persecutes, through hatred of a human being, the divine gift present in that human being, when instead a person ought to be loved even for the holiness of his merit? The envious person has as many torturers of just punishment as the envied person has praisers: excellence of merit makes the other envied, while punishment for sin makes the envious one so. (Hieron.) There is this distinction between *invidus*, “the envious,” and *invidiosus*, “the envied”: the envious person envies one who is more fortunate, whereas the envied person is one who suffers envy from another. Envy is always tormented by another’s happiness and is divided into a double passion: either one is himself what he does not want another to be, or, seeing another to be better, grieves that he is not like him. A certain poet aptly played upon envy when he said:

> Nothing is more just than envy, which at once  
> gnaws its very author and torments his mind.

### CHAPTER XX — By what signs the envy of the envious is recognized

(Cypr. and Prosp.) The face of the envious is threatening and his expression gloomy; there is pallor in his face, trembling on his lips, and gnashing of teeth. His words are rabid and unrestrained insults; his hands are ready for the violence of slaughter, even if they are presently empty of a sword, being nevertheless armed with the fury of his hateful mind. The envious hide their hatred within themselves and nourish it for their own torment. They envy those who are advancing and favor those who are sinning. They rejoice in the misfortunes of the good and grieve over their progress. They burn with gratuitous hostility; they fear that the malice of their hearts will be detected; they are never sure of being loved. They are friends of the devil and enemies even of themselves. They stain the reputation of the good; in spiritual matters they praise carnal things, so as to persuade them that spiritual goods are likewise carnal.

### CHAPTER XXI — Rebuke against the envious

[Col. 1360B] (Cypr.) Whoever you are, envious and malignant person, consider how treacherous, destructive, and hostile you are toward those whom you hate, and how you are the enemy of no one’s salvation more than your own! Whoever it is whom you pursue with jealousy may be able to evade and avoid you; you cannot flee from yourself. Wherever you are, your adversary is with you; the enemy is always in your breast, and destruction is enclosed within. You are bound and chained by an inescapable link of fetters; with envy also ruling, you are held captive. No comfort comes to your aid. To pursue a human being who belongs to the grace of God is an enduring evil. To hate the fortunate is a calamity without remedy.

If you have begun to be a person of light, do the things that are Christ’s, because you are Christ’s light and day. Why do you rush into the darkness of jealousy? Why do you wrap yourself in the cloud of ill will? Why, through the blindness of envy, do you extinguish every light of peace and love? Why do you return to the devil, whom you had renounced? Why do you become like Cain? Why do you lurk as a wolf beneath a sheep’s clothing? Why do you disgrace Christ’s flock while falsely claiming to be a Christian? To put on the name of Christ and not proceed along Christ’s way—what else is this than a violation of the divine name and an abandonment of the path of salvation?

Therefore consider, envious person, how great is the blindness in which you live: you waste away at another’s advancement and wither at another’s joy. Consider how great is your unhappiness, since you become worse through your neighbor’s improvement. Reflect, I beg you, that while you do not guard yourself at all from ill will, you yield to the ancient wickedness of the crafty enemy. For if you had wished to love another’s goods, you could have made them as your own.

### CHAPTER XXII — Remedies against the disease of envy

[Col. 1360D] (Cypr.) The medicine and treatment of this vice can be as follows: the mind must be strengthened through divine meditation and exercises against all the darts of the devil; divine reading must be in our hands, the Lord’s thought in our understanding; constant prayer must never cease; salutary work must continue; and the mind must always be occupied with spiritual actions. Thus, whenever the enemy approaches or attempts to draw near, he will find the breast closed against him and armed.

You who were possessed by envy and ill will, cast away all the malice by which you were formerly held. Restore yourself to the way of eternal life by salutary steps. Tear thorns and thistles from your breast; spit out the poisons of bile. Expel the venom of discord. Let the mind that the serpent’s ill will had infected be cleansed. Heal yourself from the place where you were wounded. Love those whom you formerly hated; cherish those whom you envied through unjust slanders. Imitate the good, if you are able to follow them; if you cannot follow them, at least rejoice with and congratulate those who are better. Make yourself a participant with them through united love; make yourself a coheir through the fellowship of love and the bond of brotherhood.

Think upon the things that are divine and just. You have many things to think about: think upon paradise, to which Cain did not return after killing his brother through envy. Think upon the heavenly kingdom, [perhaps something is missing after *ad*] to which the Lord admits only those who are harmonious and of one mind. Think that only those may be called the children of God who are peacemakers, who in their birth and under the divine law correspond, united, to the likeness of God the Father and of Christ. Think that we stand beneath the eyes of God, and that our conduct and the course of our life unfold while he himself watches and judges. Think that we shall soon depart from this world. For if you think upon these things that have been stated and fulfill them in action, then, with God’s protection, you will be able to be healed of the disease of envy.

### CHAPTER XXIII — The nature and origin of anger and rage

Anger is generated from envy. When the mind is wounded by the external injury of ill will, it loses the gentleness of tranquility in proportion to the extent to which envy has occupied it. After the devil was expelled from heavenly blessedness because of pride, envious and angry, he drove humanity from the blessed dwellings of paradise by seducing it through the deceitful art of his wickedness. This is the nature and beginning of anger, which is a form of rage. (Basil.)

The difference between rage and anger is this: the person who is angry has willed this within his mind, as is indicated by the saying: “Be angry and do not sin” (Ps. IV, 5). But the person who rages already manifests something more through his agitation; for, he says, “their rage is like that of a serpent.” The difference between irascibility and anger is that the irascible person is always angry, whereas the angry person is aroused for a particular occasion.

### CHAPTER XXIV — How anger torments the angry and the furious

(Cass.) When anger has taken up residence in our hearts, we will be unable to acquire sound judgment and discernment, possess the insight of honorable contemplation, or have mature counsel; we will be neither participants in life nor steadfast in justice, nor even capable of spiritual and true light, “because my eye is troubled by anger,” he says (Ps. VI, 8). Nor shall we become participants in wisdom, even if we seem, in the opinion of all, to be declared wise, because anger rests in the bosom of fools.

(Hieron.) The name “anger” is understood in a twofold way, not only among us but also among philosophers: either when, provoked by an injury, we are stirred by natural impulses, or when, after the impulse has subsided and the rage has been restrained, the mind can exercise judgment and nevertheless desires vengeance against the one believed to have caused the injury. This vice of anger removes humanity, clemency, and gentleness from the person who possesses it intimately.

### CHAPTER XXV — By what signs the angry person is recognized

[Col. 1362A] (Cass.) When this pitiable disease of anger has occupied the mind, the angry person preserves resentment against the one who has provoked him. He denies in words that he is angry, but in reality and in action he is plainly shown to be deeply indignant. He does not address the other with fitting speech [or: “nor does he address him”], nor speak to him with his customary friendliness. Instead, his reply is bitter, his speech harsh, his face gloomy, his gaze turned away, and his mind troubled and hostile. The person whom anger restrains is always ready to mock, exasperate, and criticize, and to speak of the other’s good qualities incorrectly. This vice disorders the mind, scatters sound counsel, and alienates justice.

### CHAPTER XXVI — Rebuke against the disease of anger

(Cass.) If you are striving toward perfection and wish to contend lawfully in the spiritual contest, remain free from all anger and rage. Hear what our Lord commanded when he said: “Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matt. V, 22). And the Apostle Paul says: “Let all anger and indignation and shouting and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice” (Eph. IV, 31). When he says, “Let all anger be removed from you,” he excludes none of it as necessary or useful to us.

But when the Psalmist says, “Be angry and do not sin” (Ps. IV, 5), he commands us to be angry with ourselves, with our vices, and with our evil suggestions, and not to sin—that is, not to bring them to a harmful outcome. Take care that this vice of anger does not reside even lightly in your heart. Wherever it is found, it removes the holy company of many virtues. Scripture says: “An angry man is dishonorable”; and again: “Anger rests in the bosom of fools”; and: “The angry person acts without counsel, and the hot-tempered man produces quarrels, but the angry man digs up sins” (Prov. XV, 18); and the Apostle says: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (Jas. I, 20).

### CHAPTER XXVII — Remedies by which we can eradicate anger from our hearts

(Cass.) The perfect medicine for this disease is first to believe that we are in no way permitted to become angry, whether for unjust or just reasons; second, to know that we absolutely cannot become a temple of the Holy Spirit while the spirit of anger dwells within us; and finally, to consider that we are not at all permitted to pray or to pour out prayers to God while angry. Considering the uncertain condition of human life, we should believe each day that we will depart from the body. Then we will understand that continence and chastity, the labors of fasting, prayer, almsgiving, and vigils will profit us nothing if, because of anger alone and hatred, the Judge of all promises us eternal punishments.

### CHAPTER XXVIII — The nature and origin of deadly sadness

Sadness also arises from anger, because the more a troubled mind agitates itself disorderly, the more it confounds itself by yielding to that agitation. Once it has lost the sweetness of tranquility, nothing feeds it except the grief that follows from its disturbance.

Sometimes, however, sadness arises from the preceding vice of anger, or from desire, or from having obtained less of some gain than one had hoped for, when someone sees that he has fallen away from these things, having conceived some expectation of them in his mind. At other times, even when no causes exist, we are suddenly plunged by the devil’s instigation into such great grief that whatever anyone says with kindly friendliness or suitable conversation seems to us intrusive and unnecessary, and we return no gracious reply, because every recess of our heart has been occupied by the bitterness of gall.

### CHAPTER XXIX — The nature and origin of salutary sadness

(Cass.) The excellent preacher says of this sadness: “The sadness that is according to God produces repentance for lasting salvation.” For it either grieves over another’s sin or over one’s own. It does not grieve because divine justice is being carried out, but mourns over what is committed through human wickedness.

This sadness arises in three ways: first, from repentance for sins; second, from the desire for perfection; third, from contemplation of future blessedness. Salutary sadness is recognized by these signs: it is obedient, friendly, humble, gentle, sweet, and patient, possessing within itself all the fruits of the Holy Spirit that the same Apostle enumerates: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control” (Gal. V, 22).

This, as has been said, is healthy sadness according to God, which produces repentance for lasting salvation. It separates its followers from worldly and harmful deeds and directs them toward the citadel of heaven. Apart from this, every sadness—as worldly and as bringing death—must alike be rejected. Now we must return to the intended order concerning deadly anger.

### CHAPTER XXX — How deadly sadness torments and drives away its followers

(Cass.) Whoever is possessed by this pestilential disease is separated from every contemplation of the divine and is shaken and cast down from every state of purity. It does not allow him to complete his prayers with gladness of heart; it does not permit him to devote himself to the remedies of sacred readings; it does not allow him to be tranquil and gentle. It makes him impatient and harsh toward every duty of action or religion. When every salutary counsel has been lost and the steadfastness of his heart disturbed, it makes him like a madman and a drunkard, breaks his understanding, and overwhelms it with punitive despair.

### CHAPTER XXXI — By what signs deadly sadness is recognized

(Cass.) This sadness is exceedingly harsh, impatient, hard, full of resentment, unfruitful grief, and punitive despair. Whoever it possesses, it separates from the practice of prayer; it draws him away from the exercise of reading; it makes him negligent and sluggish in sacred meditation; it makes him slow and lazy in the holy practice of vigils; and it empties out all the spiritual fruits that the sadness according to God is known to bestow.

### CHAPTER XXXII — Rebuke against the disease of deadly sadness

(Cass.) Whoever you are, entangled in this pestilential disease, remember that just as a moth harms clothing and a worm harms wood, so sadness harms your heart. Spit out, therefore, this poison of bitterness. Why are you sad over the loss of present gain? Why over an injury inflicted? Why over wrongs committed against you? Why are you shaken by deadly despair over the multitude of your sins, grieving like Cain after the murder of his brother and Judas after his betrayal?

Hear the Lord saying: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11). Whenever and wherever, and in whatever matter, worldly sadness rises up against itself, say in word and deed: “Rejoicing, I will rejoice in the Lord, and my soul will exult in my saving God” (Isa. LXI, 10).

### CHAPTER XXXIII — Remedies by which we can drive deadly sadness from our hearts

(Cass.) We can expel this most destructive passion from ourselves if we continually occupy our mind with spiritual meditation and raise it through hope of the future and contemplation of the promised blessedness, always remaining joyful and steadfast through the contemplation of eternal things, neither cast down by present misfortunes nor elated by prosperity. We must contemplate both as things passing away and soon to disappear.

The Apostle James suitably teaches us the medicine for this vice, saying: “Is anyone among you sad? Let him pray. Is anyone of good cheer? Let him sing psalms” (Jas. V, 13). In these ways, with the Lord’s help, we can overcome every kind of harmful sadness, if we are willing.

### CHAPTER XXXIV — The nature and origin of greed

(Cass.) Greed, which in Greek is called *philargyria* (φιλαργυρία), “the service of idols,” is, according to the Apostle, the root of all evils. For he says: “The root of all evils is desire; by craving it, some have wandered from the faith and entangled themselves in many sorrows” (I Tim. VI, 10).

This insatiable pest arises from pride, which is contempt for God. That angelic order which unhappily fell from heaven collapsed because of pride and greed. There this insatiable madness of greed—which is also called desire—first took its origin, when it desired to be like the Lord, saying: “I will set my throne toward the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 14). For greed concerns not only money but also exaltation.

Through this vice the devil drove the first human beings from the enclosure of paradise; through it he also insolently tested the Lord, when he showed him all the kingdoms of the world and said: “All these I will give you if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. IV, 9). As Prosper, that illustrious teacher, says, this insatiable destruction cannot be found without pride. For he says that desire and pride are so completely one evil that neither can the proud person be found without desire nor the desirous person without pride.

Finally, if I cannot commit any sin unless I consent to my own pleasure, which is characteristic of desire, and unless I despise God’s commandments, which is the evil of pride, how can every sin not proceed from desire, which is the root of all evils, and from pride, which is called “the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. X, 15)?

### CHAPTER XXXV — How greed torments the greedy

(Cass.) Greed torments some of its followers through public acclaim and praise of a good name; some through the height of honor; some through the acquisition of superfluous possessions; some through the seizure of other people’s goods; and others by driving them to retain their own wealth uselessly.

The greedy person commonly thinks or says: “If I do not have money stored away, what will my children do after my death? What if illness should befall my body? What if prolonged old age should continue?” [Jerem.?]

While considering these and similar matters, the greedy desire to gather money by any means and to possess coins by right or by wrongdoing; they delight in a full money-bag. They run and rush about, now here, now there, conducting business, seizing, lying, swearing, and quarreling. The greedy person thinks he has had a good day when he deposits a coin in his chest. Therefore, insatiable and inexhaustible, he runs through every kind of shame and wantonness: he worries where to put his money, to whom to entrust it, and then what to purchase with it and what kind of transaction might double it. When this desire has been fulfilled for him [and this desire has been fulfilled for him], his hunger for greed increases, and it is aroused more violently in proportion as a greater sum of profit is added.

(Cass.) As money increases, the madness of desire grows. Just as the dropsical person becomes thirstier the more he drinks, so the greedy person desires to have more the more he possesses. He regards nothing else with the gaze of his heart except how he may acquire money. Greed is the producer of all evils: wherever some hope of money has shone for its followers, it permits them to show no loyalty and, for its sake, they shrink from neither lying, perjury, nor theft. In every respect, as the belly is a god to others, gold and the hope of profit become a god to the greedy person.

Hence the blessed Apostle pronounced greed “the service of idols” (Col. III, 5), because, abandoning the form and image of God—which he ought, as one devotedly serving God, to have kept undefiled within himself—he preferred to love and preserve, in place of God, the figures of human beings impressed upon gold.

Greed agitates nearly everyone and permits no one among them to be at rest. Those who have nothing are tormented by desire; those who possess riches are tortured by anxiety. Things are not well even for those who lie upon their hidden gold; indeed, things are worse for them. They are always anxious, sad, and worried lest a servant take it away or a thief dig it out. Therefore they shut it away in darkness and hide it so that it may escape everyone’s notice, never bringing any of it forth for use, lest opening the darkness become the cause of its loss. They preserve it but do not use it. They preserve it, I say; should I call such people guardians [perhaps *non* should be inserted], rather than masters? They diligently attend to what belongs to another, instead of suitably spending what belongs to themselves.

The greedy person guards more anxiously than he acquires and protects more painfully than he seized. He sighs while awake as he acquires, sighs while asleep as he preserves. His waking is not joyful, his sleep is not secure, his day is not happy, and his night is not peaceful. He rushes about, is tormented, and groans, as though it did him no good to acquire.

With possessions spread far and wide, he does not allow another to possess land beside him. He joins boundaries, extends limits, brings accusations against the poor, oppresses the ordinary person, excludes his neighbor, and drives away all those placed around him by harassing and persecuting them. He acquires only when another has wept; he stores up profit only when another has groaned. For him alone what is a public evil is good: he either stores up produce, hoards grain, inflates prices, or increases interest. He seeks the profits of acquisition through devices of harm. The wailing of orphans is sweet to him, and the weeping of widows is pleasant, while he feeds upon such plunder and delights in the spoils of such people.

He is rich in his chest, not in merit; in possession, not in birth; in name, not in dignity. For his greed, neither what is his own suffices nor what belongs to another sets a limit. Greed commonly encourages a conquered mind as though by reason, saying: “It is entirely without fault that you desire certain things to be possessed, because you do not seek to multiply them but fear to be in need; and what another keeps badly, you yourself spend better.”

### CHAPTER XXXVI — By what signs greed is recognized

[Col. 1366C] (Cass.) Whoever is possessed by greed is urged to hurry to the marketplace rather than to the Church. He looks at gold with more attentive eyes than at heaven. He considers garments woven with gold and *holoserica*—silken cloth—more than the virtues of his soul. He loves a coin more than a poor person, the profit of this life more than the remedy of his soul, and gold more than God.

He displays no humility, obedience, love, reverence, or virtue. Instead, he is indignant at everything, murmurs and sighs at every task, and, like an exceedingly hard-mouthed horse, is carried without a bridle toward the precipice.

### CHAPTER XXXVII — Rebuke against the greedy, with various testimonies on the subject

[Col. 1366D] O whoever you are, greedy and covetous person, hear the Lord saying in his Gospel: “Beware of all greed” (Luke XII, 15), and hear the Apostle threatening: “Neither the greedy nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI, 10).

Hear Solomon also saying: “He will not receive fruit from them” (Ecclus. V, 9); likewise: “Nothing is more wicked than a greedy person” (Ecclus. X, 9); and Scripture says elsewhere: “The greedy person will not be filled with money” (Ecclus. V, 9).

Fear, greedy person, these statements of the divine Scriptures, and do not store your riches in the chest of an earthly bedroom. Instead, send them through the hands of the poor, orphans, and widows into heavenly treasuries.

Hear, greedy and covetous person, the Apostle Paul saying: “Let greed not even be named among you” (Eph. V, 3). Likewise: “Greed, which is the service of idols” (Col. III, 5). Hear further how harmful this madness is to the human race, as the same Apostle says: “Those who desire to become rich fall into temptation and into the devil’s snare and into many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge people into ruin and destruction” (I Tim. VI, 9).

Hear also the Apostle James, exposing its harmful wounds: “Come now, you rich; weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted; your garments have been eaten by moths; your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will eat your flesh like fire” (Jas. V, 1).

Terrified by these sacred statements, beware, wretched greedy person, lest you retain gold in your chest and sin in your soul; lest you have garments in your chamber and wickedness in your conscience; lest you store grain and provisions in your storerooms while reserving your wretched soul in hell, to be miserably tormented without end with the devil.

Give to the poor, greedy person, what you have on earth, so that you may find preserved in heaven by the angels what, for Christ’s love, you distributed to the poor on earth. For if you do not distribute your substance to the poor in this life, know that after death you will be tormented in hell with the purple-clad rich man, greedy and without mercy.

“For what does it profit if you gain the whole world and afterward suffer the loss of your soul?” Thus the Lord says (Matt. XVI, 26).

Beware lest you trouble anyone or unjustly take what is theirs from the powerful or the poor, from neighbors or strangers, from widows or orphans. For their cries and tears rise to God, the just and strict judge.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII — A remedy against the disease of greed

(Cass.) The perfect medicine and treatment for this most destructive calamity is to consider above all the condition of human frailty and beware, lest, when the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night, we hear what was said to the rich man in the Gospel: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke XII, 20).

Whoever desires to be healed of this vice should continually think beforehand of the day of death before his eyes, and should consider that after a person comes the worm in the grave, and after the worm comes dust. He should reflect where his riches will then be. By reflecting upon these and similar things, he should be generous in almsgiving, contrite in prayer, adorned with fear of the Lord, fervent in repentance, and burning with love.

Thus far, with divine grace assisting, we have inserted into this excerpt, as briefly as our small ability allowed, eternal testimonies from the works of orthodox fathers concerning the five spiritual vices. Now it remains for us to discuss, as we began, the two carnal vices—gluttony and lust—by the gift of him who loves abstinent and chaste minds.

### CHAPTER XXXIX — The nature and origin of *gastrimargia*, interpreted as gluttony

Apart from pride, which is the principal ruin, queen, and mother of all vices, there are seven offspring of pride: five spiritual—namely, vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, and greed—and two carnal, namely gluttony of the belly and lust. Together there are eight principal vices. The five vices, together with their mother as the sixth, have already been discussed above. From this point we must discuss gluttony and lust, so that the number eight may be completed.

Prosper more fully explains where, when, and how gluttony of the belly, which is also called the desire of the appetite, took its origin. He says:

“Let us see how those first human beings committed so great a sin that it also expelled them from paradise into the misery of this penal life, and in them condemned the entire human race by origin. The Lord had forbidden them to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, but, deceived by the vice of appetite, they ate. If they had not eaten, they would have remained immortal forever; if, living under their God, they had kept the commandment they received, they would not have been abandoned by God unless they had first abandoned God themselves. Therefore, cast down and handed over to misery and death by the offense of appetite, they were delivered into this wretched misery of the present life, where every human being is born through sin, lives through labor, and dies through sorrow.”

### CHAPTER XL — How gluttony of the belly torments and drives away its devotees

(Cass.) Gluttony of the belly torments the person whom it possesses in three ways. First, it makes him taste food and drink before the canonical and appointed hour for eating, for the sake of his appetite. Second, it makes him rejoice solely in the gluttony and satiety of the belly, whatever the food may be. Third, it makes him delight in more carefully prepared and more expensive foods, although neither the need of his body nor the quality of his person warrants this.

As Isidore says, there are four kinds of excess in the appetite of the belly: what, when, how much, and how one desires. “What” concerns the thing desired; “when” concerns desiring something before the proper time; “how much” refers to immoderation; and “how” refers to the impatience of haste.

*Gastrimargia*, that is, gluttony of the belly, does not permit the person it possesses to live patiently. It frequently makes him rise from his bed during the night and drives him with great force to hurry to the privy.

(Hieron.) The belly and throat are engaged in the one work of digestion. At such a time, lustful thoughts surround the person excessively, because wherever satiety and drunkenness are found, there lust rules. I will never consider a drunkard chaste: even if he sleeps in a stupor from wine, he could nevertheless sin through wine.

After rising from his miserable sleep, he rushes here and there, anxious and searching for how, in what way, and with what foods and drinks he might load his belly again. At whatever hour he rises from sleep—whether in the middle of the night, at cockcrow, or when day is dawning—he immediately feels excessive headache and burning thirst. Then, like a most voracious wolf, he eagerly seeks drink and food with complete anxiety. Once he has found them, by devouring them like a glutton and a *gastrimargus*, he cools his dry lips, bitter throat, inflated lungs, and colliding entrails.

### CHAPTER XLI — By what signs the *gastrimargus*, that is, the devotee of gluttony, can be recognized

The person whom this pitiable beast tears apart can be recognized by these signs. He is always fond of delicacies and avid, for he seeks more sumptuous and expensive foods. However many dishes of food he sees set before him, he considers how he might take some of everything. He anxiously and carefully investigates the time and hour of eating by means of clocks. He repeatedly goes out and enters his cell, and gazes frequently at the sun, as though it were hastening too slowly toward setting.

If he hears any discussion of abstinence and fasting, he turns away his ear, obtains stories from elsewhere, and flees from that place as quickly as possible. By every means he can, he flies here and there, searching for how he may prepare various foods and cups of drink for himself, and waits for a secret hour so that he alone may consume them.

### CHAPTER XLII — Rebuke against those devoted to gluttony
Against you, O gluttons and belly-slaves, the divine saying thunders through the Gospel, saying: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34); and the Apostle Paul cries out against you: “Food is for the belly and the belly for food, but God will destroy both the one and the other” (1 Cor. 6:13). For the same Apostle also says of you: “Whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things” [Col. 1369C] (Phil. III, 9).

[Cass.] Consider that the Sodomites were overwhelmed not by drunkenness from wine but by satiety of bread; hear the Lord’s prophet rebuking Jerusalem: “For what did your sister Sodom commit, except that she ate her bread in satiety and abundance?” Consider, therefore, if the Sodomites fell through the mere excess of bread, what will those do who, being sound in body, indulge with unrestrained freedom in the consumption of meat and wine, taking not as much as weakness requires, but as much as the desire of the mind suggests.

(Isidor.) Hear likewise, O slaves of the appetite, O drunkards and wine-bibbers, how vigorously feasting and lavish banquets are reproved through the prophet, so that the Lord threatens that he will not forgive this iniquity to those who willingly pursue it. For he says through Isaiah: “Behold, joy and gladness, killing calves and slaughtering rams, eating meat and drinking wine; if this iniquity is forgiven you, until you die” (Isa. 22:13). Just as all carnal desires are cut away by abstinence, so all the virtues of the soul are destroyed by the vice of gluttony. Hence the same Prophet also says: “The chief of the cooks destroyed the walls of Jerusalem,” because the belly that is served by cooks destroys the virtues of the soul.

Therefore let drunkards hear: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is debauchery” (Eph. 5:18); let them also hear the prophetic saying: “Fornication and drunkenness will take away the heart” (Hos. 4:11). Drunkenness, as in the case of Lot, captivates the understanding of reason. Let those who drink much and are not intoxicated hear: “Woe to those who are mighty for drinking wine and strong men for mixing drunkenness” (Isa. 5:22); and let those devoted to much wine and living luxuriously hear through the prophet Isaiah: “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness, continuing until evening, so that they burn with wine” (ibid., 11).

Let gluttons hear, let drunkards hear the Apostle Paul saying: “Not in feasting and drunkenness” (Rom. 13:13); and again: “Food does not commend us to God” (1 Cor. 6:8). Therefore those devoted to gluttony must be warned not to pierce themselves with the sword of debauchery while they devote themselves to the pleasure of food. Let them observe how much talkativeness during eating, how much frivolity of mind, lies in wait for them, lest, while they serve the belly softly, they be cruelly bound in the snares of vices.

## CHAPTER XLIII — Remedies against the disease of gluttony, that is, the belly’s voracity

[Col. 1370B]

Whoever desires to overcome this vice completely should practice moderation not only in taking food—so that hunger always restrains his refreshment—but should also despise more carefully prepared and more delicious dishes, except in bodily illness and in receiving guests.

(Cass.) He should not only constrain his mind and body with fasts, but also with vigils, reading, frequent compunction of heart, an abundance of tears, constant prayer, generosity in almsgiving, and assiduity in every good work. Let him fix his mind upon divine contemplation, taking delight rather in the love of virtues and the beauty of heavenly things; thus he will despise all present things as fleeting.

For against the threefold assault described above in connection with this vice, a threefold discipline must likewise be maintained: first, he must await the lawful time and hour of release from fasting and of refreshment; second, without the greatest necessity of the body, as was said above, he must not order delicious dishes to be prepared for himself; third, he must be content with any foods, even the cheaper ones.

## CHAPTER XLIV — On the nature and origin of debauchery and fornication

(Cass.) From what source this most unclean spirit of debauchery and fornication arises is declared by the Lord’s word [Col. 1370D]: “From the heart,” he says, “come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies,” and the rest (Matt. 15:19). For this most hostile disease of fornication, since it begins to attack the human race from the earliest time of puberty, is not extinguished until the other vices have first been overcome.

(Isid.) Debauchery arises from the vice of pride, following the example of the first man, who, as soon as he swelled up through pride against God, immediately experienced the desire of the flesh and covered his private parts. Among the seven vices generated by pride, the mother of vices, fornication is the greatest of crimes, because through the uncleanness of the flesh it violates God’s temple and, taking away the members of Christ, makes them members of a prostitute.

There are, however, different kinds of fornication. There is carnal fornication, in which the body is defiled [Col. 1371A], and there is spiritual fornication, in which the body is not polluted but the mind is defiled. Concerning this Christ says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). Every unclean pollution is called fornication, although each person prostitutes himself to a different pleasure of shame.

(Hier.) For from the pleasure of fornication various crimes are born, by which the kingdom of God is closed and a human being is separated from God. Hence also, in the old law, Scripture generally embraced those unspeakable crimes that are committed in secret and are most shameful even to name, lest both the mouth of the speaker and the ears of the hearers be polluted, saying: “Make the sons of Israel modest or reverent toward every uncleanness.” Of this the Apostle Paul also speaks: “But fornication and every uncleanness or greed must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints” (Eph. 5:3).

For we also find it prophesied in many places that idolatry is called fornication, as in the passage: “They fornicated after their idols, and they were led astray by the spirit of fornication” (Ezek. 6:9).

## CHAPTER XLV — How debauchery afflicts the debauched

For the most part, those whom this most unclean passion afflicts produce shameful and lewd speeches. Inflamed by the excessive heat of lust, they cast wanton eyes upon the beautiful forms of women; and, anxiously running about here and there, they seek how, where, and in what manner—even in the most unspeakable crimes, which it is exceedingly shameful to mention—they might satisfy their most unclean desire [Col. 1371C].

For this reason they often dress themselves in garments adorned with precious things, so that they may be loved by those whom, in their own misery, they wish to make participants in it; and with whatever demonic cosmetics and adornment they can, they disfigure their faces.

## CHAPTER XLVI — By what signs the debauched person may be recognized

(Cypr.) Those whose life is debauched and immodest frequently speak vain, false, and lewd words. They always allow their eyes to wander over alluring and beautiful forms; they walk with a pompous and seductive gait; they love wantonness, love lust, applaud desire, multiply their words, pursue the cravings of the appetite, love drunkenness, do not avoid quarrels and anger, do not restrain avarice and love of money [philargyria], love idleness, take no delight in good morals, remain silent among those who speak of chastity and continence, disdain the divine Scriptures and the chaste life, do not possess an orderly appearance and suitable way of life, as is proper, either in their hair or their clothing, and do not avoid every uncleanness but love it.

## CHAPTER XLVII — Rebuke against the debauched and fornicators

Let the debauched, who pursue carnal debauchery, hear the Apostle Paul threatening terribly: “Neither fornicators,” he says, “nor those who serve idols, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, [Col. 1372A] nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:9). And again: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. 13:4). Again the same Apostle says: “Flee fornication, brothers: every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but whoever fornicates sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6:18).

Let those also hear who pursue spiritual debauchery—that is, those who consent to lust in the heart but do not proceed to the act of the desired lust: “Whoever looks,” says the Lord, “at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. XXVIII [as printed]). And it is said through blessed Job: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin. For what portion would God have in me from above, and what inheritance would the Almighty have from on high?” (Job 31:1).

Unless the thought of wrongful consent were displeasing to our creator [the printed text has actori; perhaps auctori], he would certainly not say through Isaiah: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes” (Isa. 1:16). And in the Gospel he says to the Pharisees: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matt. 9:4).

[Isid.] For fornications must first be removed from the heart, so that they do not burst forth into deeds. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Gird your loins over your breasts” (Isa. 22:11), that is, cut away in the heart the lusts that pertain to the loins. For the heart is above the breasts, not in the loins.

Let those also hear who pursue uncleanness—that is, those who do not consider it a great crime when, without intercourse between man and woman, they arouse their lust in various demonic prostitutions. Let them hear the Apostle Paul saying: “Neither will the unclean possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10); and again: “Fornication and every uncleanness must not even be named among you” (Eph. 5:3).

[Hier.] For he would not say “every uncleanness” unless the emission of semen occurred in various ways and the most filthy titillation of the flesh also took place.

(Cass.) Let all adulterers, the debauched, fornicators, the unclean, and those who lie with males hear the Apostle Paul saying: “For God did not call you to uncleanness but to holiness.” Therefore whoever despises these things does not despise a human being but God, who also gave his Holy Spirit in us. And this: “This is the will of God,” he says, “your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication; that each of you know how to possess his vessel in honor and sanctification, not in the passion of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God” (1 Thess. 4:3).

And also in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Pursue peace,” he says, “and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Heb. 12:14). Here too he clearly declared that without holiness—which he usually calls integrity of mind or purity of body—God cannot be seen at all. Indeed, here likewise he explains the same meaning, adding: “Let there be no fornicator or profane person, like Esau.”

Let those who sin not through corruption of the flesh but of the heart hear the judgment of Saint Basil, bishop of Caesarea. “I do not know a woman,” he says, “and I am not a virgin,” where it is understood that abstinence concerns not so much women as the integrity of the heart. Hence also Bishop Augustine says: “Virginity of the flesh is an untouched body; virginity of the soul is an incorrupt faith.”

## CHAPTER XLVIII — Remedies against the disease of debauchery and fornication, and against all unclean and unspeakable crimes

(Cass.) There is a twofold assault of fornication and debauchery, rising armed with vice for battle; therefore it must likewise be resisted with a twofold battle line. For just as it acquires a poison compounded of the flesh and the soul as though it were a disease, so it cannot be conquered [variant: *nequit*, “cannot/is unable”] unless both are fighting together.

Nor is bodily fasting alone sufficient for one who desires to be healed of this most unclean vice, unless contrition of spirit, prayer, and continuous meditation on the Holy Scriptures precede it [Col. 1373B]. Spiritual understanding and knowledge also contribute greatly to cleansing this most impure passion. Labor and the work of the hands likewise provide excellent assistance in restraining this vice. Above all there must be true humility, without which victory over any vice can never be obtained.

With the greatest diligence, moderation through fasting must be pursued for the elimination of this disease, lest flesh refreshed by an abundance of food cast down its ruler, the spirit. This disease requires bodily affliction and contrition of heart, as well as solitude and withdrawal, so that, once the harmful fever of its heats has been laid aside, it may reach complete health.

It is exceedingly dangerous for the eyes of fornicators to have beautiful forms before them—not only beautiful ones, but any forms whatever [Col. 1373C] where fornication or suspicion of fornication may exist.

(Hier.) For holy David, chosen according to the heart of the Lord, was captivated by Bathsheba’s nakedness; therefore he joined murder to adultery. Solomon, because he refused to withdraw from women, withdrew from the Lord. And lest anyone trust in blood relationship, Amnon, the brother of Tamar, burned with an unlawful passion.

(Cass.) It is exceedingly beneficial for extinguishing the heat of fornication to withdraw far from those whose appearance can draw us on and provoke us to the incitement of lust. For that source from which the fountain of life and death is known to flow must first be purified, as Solomon says: “Guard your heart with every care” (Prov. 4:23). For from it lewd thoughts proceed, as the Lord says: “From the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, etc.” (Matt. 15:19).

Whoever wishes to extinguish completely the suggestion of this diabolical cunning should first hasten to drive the memory of all women from his heart and avoid their company by whatever suitable means he can. Hence the most blessed bishop Ambrose also says, among other things: “If you enter a fortress, do not approach women and do not linger in conversation with her; for just as one who swallows a hook is drawn in, so your soul is drawn in.”

The continual remembrance of eternal condemnation and everlasting fire, the recollection of past crimes, and the premeditation of death and the dreadful day of future judgment are also of great help in extinguishing the flame of fornication. For the remission of past sins and the attainment of perpetual purity of mind and body, the pious distribution of alms is likewise a great aid.

What is more important, we must believe, with the whole attention of our minds and without relying on our own powers, that we can conquer this most unclean spirit of fornication. Human diligence cannot accomplish this, but only the Lord’s assistance and mercy. We must not believe that we can obtain victory through our own labor and effort unless we are supported by divine help and protection. For it is impossible for a human being, so to speak, to fly up on his own wings to such a lofty and heavenly reward, unless God’s grace draws him out of the mud and mire of the earth through the gift of chastity.

Therefore, to repeat briefly all the remedies for this disease: whoever wishes to be cured of this pestilential illness must first and foremost ask the Lord unceasingly, through nightly and prolonged prayers, to purify him. He must remain watchful through vigils, sacred readings of the Scriptures, meditations, namely compunction and contrition of heart, withdrawal from the body, work of the hands, and unfailing fasting.

Up to this point, in accordance with the way in which the holy teachers of the churches described the eight principal vices, and insofar as the smallness of our understanding has permitted, with the Lord’s generosity we have excerpted a few testimonies from the statements of various Fathers concerning the origin, affliction, signs, rebukes, and remedies of these same vices. Now it remains for us, following the tradition of the holy Egyptian and Eastern Fathers, briefly to treat the same vices and their order by selecting passages, as the author of all good things may deign to grant.

## CHAPTER XLIX — Recapitulation of gluttony and the other principal vices

(Cass.) Gastrimargia [Greek: γαστριμαργία], in Latin, is called “desire of the appetite,” or “the belly’s voracity.” It is the first bodily sin, through which the first human beings were expelled from Paradise and through which Esau sold his birthright by desiring a dish of lentils.

This vice appears to rule in a person in three ways: first, when a person, not from necessity but from desire of the appetite, wishes to anticipate the appointed hour of refreshment; second, when he desires to load his belly merely with the swallowing and satiety of any kind of food; third, when he takes delight in more precious and carefully prepared dishes.

Against this threefold frenzy, a threefold remedy must be applied: first, he should await the lawful time of refreshment. For, unless bodily illness intervenes, the lawful time of refreshment for a Christian is not canonically established before the third hour of the day but is prohibited. Second, he should take even the cheaper foods [variant: *de ipsis*, “from those very foods”] not for the sake of desire but for the necessity and sustenance of the body. For, according to the divine testimonies of Scripture, even water and the cheapest food, if taken for the desire of the appetite and not for the body’s necessity, are recognized as the sin of gluttony. Third, he should be content with any foods, even the cheaper ones. This most wretched vice is also overcome through prayer, fasting, abstinence, and constant engagement in every kind of good work.

## CHAPTER L — On fornication

(Isid.) Fornication is every unclean pollution. The first arrows of fornication are those of the eyes; the second are those of words.

There are two principal kinds of fornication. The first is that in which it is committed [perhaps read: “I mean,” *inquam*] through the joining of the flesh, whether with a woman or through any other uncleanness for satisfying the heat of lust. This is called carnal fornication. The second is called spiritual fornication, which is committed through desire and longing alone. Concerning this the Lord says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28).

The perfect cure for this most impure passion is to withdraw by every means from the company and sight of those among whom this most wretched passion lurks; and, with constant prayer, frequent reading, and unceasing vigils, to fear without interruption the memory of eternal fire, the fear of God’s presence, and the day of death; to love fasts and hunger, and to shun satiety of the belly.

Saint Ambrose, bishop, as a most experienced physician, beautifully gave someone this advice: “Weigh your bread, and drink your water by measure, and the spirit of fornication will flee from you.”

## CHAPTER LI — On love of money

(Isid.) Philargyria [Greek: φιλαργυρία], which is interpreted as avarice or love of money, is the source of all crimes. Hence the Apostle says: “Desire is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10). Avarice and love of money are worse than every sin. Therefore it is said through Solomon: “There is nothing more wicked than loving money” (Ecclus. 10:9). For it makes the soul itself saleable, since in its life it has cast away its inmost things.

Philargyria is an insatiable plague, as someone says: “The miser is always in need, because the more he acquires, the more he seeks.” He is tormented not only by the desire to increase his possessions but also afflicted by fear of losing them. This insatiable beast operates in acquiring, possessing, and holding; and just as a dropsical person thirsts more the more he drinks, so this passion, as has been said, desires more the more it possesses.

(Cass.) Although this passion is hostile to the entire human race, it is especially destructive to monks and to all clergy consecrated to divine offices. For it attacks them in three ways. First, it makes them want to acquire what they had not previously possessed, as in the case of Gehazi, the disciple of the holy Elisha. Therefore they are drenched with eternal leprosy by the curse of the holy Elisha. Second, it makes them take back money which, when they followed Christ, they had previously abandoned, as Judas, the Lord’s betrayer, did. Third, it makes them reserve some portion when they pass from the riches of the world to the poverty of Christ, as Ananias and Sapphira did; for this they are punished with death by the apostolic word together with them.

The perfect cure for this vice is to remember the apostolic saying: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6:8); and what was said in the Gospel to the rich man: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20).

Constant fear of God, remembrance of past crimes, brotherly love, works of mercy, pious distribution of alms, hope of future blessedness, and constant prayer with kinship or connection of heart (*cognatione*) [perhaps *contritione*, “contrition”] also mortify this serpentine and poisonous passion.

## CHAPTER LII — On anger

(Cass.) There are two kinds of anger, one health-giving and the other deadly. Righteous anger occurs when a person is angry against his own sins and indignant with himself when he acts wrongly; when he angrily rages against the wanton movements of his heart; and when, fearing the presence of the angels and of God himself, from whom no secrets are hidden, he is indignant that he has allowed what is shameful to do or say before human beings to rise up in the hiding places of his breast.

That we should become angry in this way is also taught by the prophet who says: “Be angry and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5)—that is, be angry at your vices and evil suggestions, and do not sin: do not bring your evil and wicked thoughts and suggestions to evil effect and action.

For when he had desired water from the cistern of Bethlehem and it had been brought to him, he, angry against the desires of his own craving, immediately poured it upon the ground, saying: “The Lord be gracious to me; shall I do this? Shall I drink the blood of these men and the danger of their lives, who have gone?” (I Reg. XXIV, 7).

There is another kind of anger, however, which is deadly and generates many evils. If it settles in the heart, it blinds the eye of the mind with harmful darkness and does not permit a person to acquire sound judgment, possess the insight of honorable contemplation, or attain maturity of counsel. Those entangled in this disease cannot be participants in life, steadfast in justice, or capable of the true light.

This anger sometimes arises from one’s own bitterness and sometimes from another’s provocation through diabolical instigation. It disturbs the mind, destroys sound counsel, and, if it is not governed by reason, turns into fury, so that a person loses control of his own spirit and his face becomes distorted [Col. 1376D].

The perfect medicine for this disease is first to believe that we are in no way permitted to become angry, whether for just or unjust causes, as the Apostle says: “Let all anger and indignation be taken away from you” (Eph. 4:31). He left no anger of this kind remaining. It is also conquered most effectively through patience, gentleness, and long-suffering; through true contrition of heart; through the intellectual reason that God implants in human minds; through fear of that Gospel saying [variant: *illius*, “of that”]: “Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matt. 5:22); and through remembrance of the Lord’s Prayer, in which we say to God: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12).

## CHAPTER LIII — On sadness

[Col. 1377A]

(Basil.) There are two kinds of sadness: one according to God and the other according to the world. Sadness according to God is health-giving; sadness according to the world is deadly.

Sadness according to God occurs when we grieve over neglect of a commandment or over transgression, according to what is written: “Sadness has taken hold of me because of sinners who abandon your law.”

(Cass.) This sadness arises in three ways: first, through repentance for sins; second, through desire for perfection; third, through contemplation of future blessedness. Concerning this blessed Paul the Apostle says: “The sadness that is according to God,” he says, “produces repentance leading to lasting salvation, but the sadness of the world produces death” [Col. 1377B] (2 Cor. 7:10).

When someone is saddened by human affairs belonging to the world, this wretched passion can accomplish nothing in a good work. It disturbs the mind, often inflicts the most destructive despair upon the sinning soul, and removes hope of future good things.

This worldly sadness arises in six ways: sometimes it descends from preceding anger; sometimes from the loss of profit; sometimes it comes from an injury inflicted; sometimes it is generated by insults suffered; sometimes it proceeds from irrational confusion of mind; and sometimes it arises as mortal despair from the magnitude of crimes.

All these kinds of sadness are overcome through spiritual joy and meditation, through hope in future good things, through the consolation of the ancient Scriptures [Col. 1377C], through brotherly conversation in spiritual gladness, and through the practice of holy works.

## CHAPTER LIV — On acedia

(Cass.) Acedia [Greek: ἀκηδία], in Latin called weariness, anxiety of heart, or even idleness, is akin to sadness. For acedia blinds the mind and makes the soul drowse away from all contemplation of virtues and from every perception of spiritual things, as blessed [David] elegantly expressed it: “My soul has slumbered from weariness” (Ps. 118:28)—that is, from acedia.

He properly said not that the body but that the soul had slumbered. For this sometimes occurs in the mind, sometimes in the body, and sometimes in mind and body together. It is shown to harm greatly those who serve God in every way, rendering them idle and empty of every spiritual activity.

The holy teachers of the churches did not list this vice among the eight principal vices but placed it under the heading of sadness. In the catalogue of the aforementioned vices, in place of acedia, they placed envy, so that the vices would remain eight. But, conversely, the holy Egyptian and Palestinian Fathers and those of the eastern regions, who especially described the instructions and corrections of monks, rightly placed envy under the heading of pride in their enumeration of the principal vices. They affirmed acedia to be one of the eight principal vices, because this passion is more familiar to monks and solitaries and is a more hostile and frequent enemy to those living in the desert.

But since in the first description of these principal vices we touched on nothing concerning acedia, it remains for us, with the Lord’s help, to select suitable brief testimonies from the works of the holy Fathers concerning its origin, affliction, signs, rebukes, and remedies, just as we did concerning the other principal vices.

## CHAPTER LV — On the nature and origin of acedia

The spirit of acedia arises from interruption and neglect of good work, from slowness in reading and prayer, from the sadness of this world, and from disdain and contempt for the divine and principal commandments.

## CHAPTER LVI — How acedia afflicts the acedious

[Col. 1378B]

(Cass.) Whoever is possessed by this wretched passion it makes sluggish, lazy, and inactive toward every good work. It does not allow him to remain in his own place. At the fifth or sixth hour it raises up such great weariness of body and hunger for food that, as though exhausted by a long journey and the most burdensome labor, he seems weary to himself.

Then he anxiously walks about here and there, frequently enters and leaves his cell, and repeatedly gazes at the sun as though it were moving slowly toward sunset. He becomes idle and empty of every spiritual activity, arranging nothing else except where or by what means he may prepare an opportunity for the coming refreshment. For the mind of the idle person knows how to think of nothing except food and the belly: “For every idle person is in his desires,” as Holy Scripture testifies (Prov. 21).

## CHAPTER LVII — By what signs the acedious person is recognized

(Cass.)
