The blessed Apostle Paul, as a true and most skilled physician, fully exposes the wounds of acedia in the Epistle to the Thessalonians, saying: “We ask you, brothers, to abound more, and to strive to be quiet, to attend to your own affairs, to work with your hands, and to walk honorably and desire nothing belonging to another” (1 Thess. 4:1, 10).

The acedious person is recognized by these signs: first, because he is restless; second, because he takes care of other people’s affairs, which is the evil of curiosity; third, because he disdains working with his own hands; fourth, because he walks dishonorably; fifth, because he desires what belongs to others.

In another place the same Apostle identifies the acedious: “We hear,” he says, “that some among you walk restlessly,” and he immediately adds the second symptom, which is the root of this restlessness (2 Thess. 3:11): “doing nothing,” and the third disease, which arises from it like a little branch, “but acting inquisitively.”

Behold, in this statement he confirms that the acedious are restless, idle, and curious. Whoever is tormented by this wretched and most evil passion it makes lazy and sluggish in the pursuit of prayer and strikes down with the weapon of sleep; it renders him tired, inactive, drowsy, and lazy in the exercise of reading; it makes him slow and lazy in every good work; and, so that he may quickly withdraw from prayer, reading, preaching, honorable and holy conversation, and the practice of good work, it seeks out by thought and deed various and manifold opportunities and causes.

## CHAPTER LVIII — Rebuke against the spirit of acedia; various testimonies on the subject

(Cass.) Why, unhappy soul, impeded by such devices of the enemies, do you fall, wearied by the spirit of acedia as by a most powerful battering ram, struck down by the weapon of sleep? Or why do you cut yourself off at the doors of your little cell? You will not flee the attack of acedia by avoiding it, but you will overcome it by resisting.

Whoever you are, O monk, who are afflicted by the spirit of acedia, hear the ancient and most truthful saying handed down by the holy Fathers: “The working monk is struck by one demon, but the idle monk is devastated by innumerable spirits.”

Hear the holy and most truthful saying of the Fathers: “Whoever desires to overcome acedia should neither love sleep nor abandon his cell, but should devote himself to vigils and prayers and remain within the enclosure of his cell, intent upon the work of his hands.”

Hear also holy Bishop Ambrose saying: “If the spirit of acedia rises up in you, do not leave your house, and do not abandon the beneficial mourning at its proper time. Tears drive away the spirit of acedia, but prayer troubles the spirit of sadness. Do not give yourself over to much sleep, because the sleepy and acedious monk walks in evils; but whoever keeps watch will be like a sparrow. Much sleep brings temptations, but whoever keeps watch will escape them.”

(Cass.) Let all who are established in the bosom of holy Mother Church and are struck by the most evil spirit of acedia hear together; let them attentively hear the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures.

Solomon says: “Every idle person is in his desires” (Prov. 31)—that is, in evil desires. Concerning this disease of inactivity the same Solomon says again: “The roads of those who do no work are paved with thorns” (Ecclus. 33:29)—that is, with vices. Likewise: “Idleness has taught many evils” (Prov. 28:19); and again: “Whoever pursues idleness will be filled with poverty,” whether visible or invisible.

Elsewhere the poverty of the idle is described in this way: “Every sleepy person will be clothed [*veste*, “with a garment”] in a torn and ragged garment”—that is, he will not deserve to be adorned with the garment concerning which the Apostle commanded: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13:14), and again: “Clothed with the breastplate of righteousness and charity” (1 Thess. 5:8), and concerning which the Lord also speaks to Jerusalem through the Prophet: “Arise, arise, Jerusalem; put on the garments of your glory” (Isa. 52:1).

Let all the acedious and idle hear the Apostle Paul: “If anyone does not wish to work, let him not eat” (2 Thess. 3:10); and again: “Let the one who was stealing steal no longer, but rather let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to those suffering necessity” (Eph. 4:28).

For the Apostle condemns idleness not only by words but also by examples. When he came to Corinth, he went to Aquila and Priscilla, “because they were of the same trade, and he stayed with them and worked, for he was of the trade of tentmaking.” Elsewhere he says: “These hands have provided what was necessary for me and for those who were with me.”

Idleness generates many and infinite evils in the mind of a Christian; conversely, the work of the hands cuts away many vices. Therefore Christians should flee the evil of inactivity and idleness with all their strength, as though it were a serpent, and, occupied with the work of their hands and every good pursuit, persist in divine praises, in heart, mouth, and deed, saying with the holy prophet David: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways. You shall eat the labors of your hands; you are blessed, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. 127:1).

## CHAPTER LIX — Remedies by which we may overcome acedia

[Col. 1380B]

The exceedingly wicked disease of acedia is overcome by earnestness in prayer and vigils, by devotion to the reading of divine Scripture, by holy conversation with good people and their admonition, by remembrance and confession of sins, by desire for future blessedness, by stability of place and of one’s devotion, by the practice of any craft and labor, by bodily weakness, by silence of mouth and speech, and by fear of the Lord—so that one believes God to be present, searching hearts and kidneys. It is also overcome by restraining vain thoughts, for which reason it is said: “I kept the Lord always before my eyes, for he is at my right hand, that I may not be shaken” (Ps. XV, [Col. 1380C] 8), by separation from those who pursue boasting and idleness, and by contemplation of the divine majesty, so that one always believes oneself to be standing before the eyes of God.

## CHAPTER LX. — On Cenodoxy, That Is, Vain Glory

(Cass.) Cenodoxy, in Greek, is called in Latin *inanis gloria*, or vain glory. It is a varied, manifold, and subtle beast, exceedingly harmful to all whom it overcomes. It assails the Christian not only in the carnal part, as do the other vices, but also in the spiritual, so that if it cannot deceive him through carnal vices, he is wounded more sharply through spiritual successes. According to the definition of the ancient Fathers, it attempts to wound Christ’s soldier in fifteen ways and more: in clothing, [Col. 1380D] appearance, gait, voice, work, vigils, fasts, prayer, withdrawal, reading, knowledge, silence, obedience, humility, and patience. This disease is all the more dangerous in combat the more obscure it is to guard against.

(Isid.) It arises both in deeds and in words, when a person strives to please himself rather than God and to obtain praise from human beings, although no one ought to claim anything for himself because of sin.

(Cass.) The more this madness has been cast down, the more fiercely it rises again for combat. All the vices that have been overcome wither and become weaker day by day, but this one, once cast down, rises more powerfully for battle; when it is thought to have been extinguished, it recovers with greater vitality through its own death. It does not grow lukewarm through age [Col. 1381A] or solitude; it knows neither exclusion from any place [Perhaps: “exstinguishing”] nor withering through age. Rather, it is nourished by the successes of the virtues, and it casts down from the summit of virtue not only the small but also the great—even angelic—men.

(Joannes.) The vice of boasting and vain glory is grave and exceedingly dangerous; it casts souls down even from the very summit of perfection.

(Jesus?) This evil has a certain twofold form. In some people it appears immediately at the beginnings of good works, when they have contributed a little either in abstinence or in money given to the poor. Although they ought to think that they have merely added what they have contributed, they act and think as though they were superior to those to whom they have given something. The other form of boasting and vain glory occurs when someone has reached the highest virtue but attributes it not wholly to God, rather to his own labors and studies. While seeking glory from human beings, he loses the glory that comes from God. Therefore let us flee the vice of boasting in every way, lest we perhaps fall into the fall into which the devil fell.

(Prosp.) Those afflicted by this passion desire to receive human praise for the good things they do; they shamefully boast even of works of which they are not conscious, and wickedly long to be praised by human beings. They disparage holy men by comparing themselves with them, and sometimes perform good deeds with great labor so that they may receive praise from those whom they desire to please—not from God. Hence Truth also says: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 2, 5). For when, as holy Pope Gregory says, passing praise is sought for a righteous work, a thing worthy of eternal recompense is sold for a cheap price. The perfect and salutary medicine for this wretched passion is constant remembrance of divine goodness, through which all good things have been, are, and will be conferred upon the human race; also continual prayer with tears and compunction of heart; the most attentive reading of divine Scripture; remembrance of past sins; recollection of those good men who were cast down by the disease of vain glory; and remembrance of the Lord’s saying: “How can you believe, who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that is from God alone?” (John V, 44); and of the apostle Paul’s: “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. I, 10); and: “Let us not become desirous of vain glory” (Gal. V, 26); and of the holy prophet David’s: “For God has scattered the bones of those who please human beings” (Ps. LII, 6). Above all, let the most fervent praise of divine goodness be continually present in heart, mouth, and deed, together with fear of death and with the present life always before one’s eyes in tears.

## CHAPTER LXI. — On Pride

Pride is the mother, origin, and queen of all vices, through which the angels fell from heaven. Just as it is the origin of all crimes, so it is the ruin of every virtue. It is first in sin and last in conflict. It either lays the mind low through sin at the beginning, or finally casts it down from the virtues. It is therefore the greatest of all sins, because through both virtues and vices it destroys the human mind. Everyone who sins is proud, since by doing what is forbidden he holds the divine commandments in contempt. Thus it is rightly said: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Eccli. X, 15), because unless disobedience to God’s commandments has preceded, the guilt of transgression does not follow.

There are two kinds of pride: one attacks the spiritual and the advanced; the other embraces even beginners and the carnal. Although both kinds of pride swell with an elevation harmful both to God and to human beings, the first is especially directed toward God, while the second properly concerns human beings. Pride, as has been said, empties all virtues alike and strips a person of every form of justice and holiness.

(Prosp.) What is more, pride is not only itself a sin; no sin could be, or could have been, or could be committed without it.

(Cass.) Although this disease is last in the conflict of the vices and is placed last in order, it is nevertheless first in origin and time. It is the fiercest and most monstrous of all the preceding vices, testing the perfect above all and, with a more savage bite, devouring those who have almost reached the completion of virtue.

(Basil.) This exceedingly wicked disease is recognized by the fact that it always seeks and desires what is more elevated and despises everyone, so as to make itself superior to all.

(Cass.) It is cured if one believes the sentence of him who said: “God resists the proud” (Jas. IV, 6); if one withdraws and distances oneself from every occasion of elation; if, in true and humble heart, one believes and declares in mind and voice that one is more worthless and lower than everyone else; if one endures with the utmost patience everything that is imposed upon one, whether grievous or harmful; if one always recalls the sufferings of the Lord and his saints; if one considers that one will soon depart from this world; if one believes with complete certainty that without God’s help one can think, speak, or do nothing good; and if one persists assiduously in prayer and reading with compunction of heart.

## CHAPTER LXII. — On the Concord of the Six Vices and the Kinship of the Two That Differ from Them

(Serap.) These eight vices, although they have different origins and dissimilar effects, are nevertheless connected among themselves by a certain kinship—and, so to speak, by a chain—in their first six members: gluttony, fornication, avarice, anger, sadness, and acedia. Thus the excess of the earlier becomes the beginning of the next. From the abundance of gluttony, fornication necessarily springs; from fornication, avarice; from avarice, anger; from anger, sadness; and from sadness, acedia. Therefore one must fight against them in a similar manner and according to the same reasoning, and we should always begin our battles against the later vices from the preceding ones. The harmful breadth and height of any tree withers more easily if its roots, on which it rests, are first exposed or cut away, and the waters that infest it are continually dried up when the spring and flowing channels from which they arise have been stopped by skillful effort.

Accordingly, to overcome acedia, sadness must first be conquered; to drive away sadness, anger must first be expelled; to extinguish anger, avarice must be trampled down; to uproot avarice, fornication must be restrained; and to overthrow fornication, the vice of gluttony must be corrected.

The remaining two—cenodoxy and pride—are indeed joined to each other by the same reasoning that we described concerning the preceding vices, so that the increase of the first becomes the origin of the second. For the excess of cenodoxy gives birth to the fuel of pride. Yet these two differ completely from the first six vices and are not bound to them by a similar association. They not only receive no occasion for their generation from those vices, but are also aroused in the contrary manner and order. When those six have been uprooted, these two flourish more vigorously and, through the death of the others, sprout and grow more vigorously.

Therefore we are attacked by these two vices in a different way. We fall into each of the six vices when we have been overwhelmed by those that precede them; but into these two, when victorious—and especially after triumphs—we are in danger of falling. Thus, just as all the vices are generated by the growth of those that precede them, so they are cleansed by the diminution of those same vices. Accordingly, for pride to be driven out, cenodoxy must be strangled. Once the earlier vices have always been conquered, the later ones will subside; and as the preceding passions are extinguished, the remaining passions too will wither through labor.

Although these eight vices, as we have said, are connected and intermingled with one another in the manner described, they are nevertheless more specifically divided into four pairings and unions. Fornication is joined by special relation to gluttony; anger to avarice; acedia to sadness; and pride is familiarly joined to cenodoxy.

## CHAPTER LXIII. — On the Origin and Character of Each Vice

(Serap.) Now, to discuss the kinds of each vice individually, there are three kinds of gluttony. The first drives a person to hasten toward food before the appointed and proper hour. The second rejoices in filling the belly and in the voracious consumption of every kind of food. The third desires more carefully prepared and especially delicate foods. These three strike the Christian with no small harm unless he strives to free himself from all of them with equal zeal and observance.

For just as the breaking of the fast must in no way be presumed before the canonical and proper hour, so the greed of the belly and the expensive and elaborate preparation of foods must likewise be cut away. From these three causes different and exceedingly bad illnesses of the soul are generated. From the first arises hatred of the community, and from that hatred grow dread and intolerance of the same dwelling; without doubt, departure and very swift flight will soon follow. From the second arise the burning goads of luxury and lust. The third weaves unbreakable snares of avarice around the necks of its captives and never permits a person to be established in the complete nakedness of Christ.

We detect traces of this passion in ourselves by the following indication. When we happen to be detained for a meal by one of the brothers, we are not content to eat the food with the flavor in which it was prepared by the person serving it; instead, with an intrusive and unrestrained freedom, we demand that something be poured over it or added to it. This must not be done at all for three reasons.

First, the Christian’s mind must always be engaged in every exercise of endurance and moderation and, according to the Apostle, must learn to be content with what is sufficient. For no one will be able to restrain either hidden or greater bodily desires if, offended by the taste of a slight blandness, he has not been able even for a moment to discipline the delicacies of his throat.

Second, it sometimes happens that the particular item requested is unavailable at that moment, and we bring shame upon the need or frugality of our host by making public his poverty, which he would rather have been known to God alone.

Third, the flavor we acquire may at times displease others, and we are found to inflict injury upon many while attempting to satisfy our own appetite and desire. For this reason this freedom must be disciplined in us in every way.

There are three kinds of fornication. The first is accomplished through the intercourse of the two sexes. The second occurs without the touch of a woman; for this, the patriarch Judah’s son is recorded as having been struck down by the Lord, and in Holy Scripture it is called impurity. Concerning it the Apostle says: “But I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I do; but if they do not exercise self-control, let them marry, for it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. VII, 9). The third is conceived in the soul and mind, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 28).

The blessed Apostle declares that these three kinds must be extinguished in the same way: “Put to death,” he says, “your members that are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, and so forth” (Col. III, 5). Again, concerning two of them, he says to the Ephesians: “Fornication and impurity must not even be named among you” (Eph. V, 3). Again: “But know this, that every fornicator, or impure person, or avaricious person—which is idolatry—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. V, 5). The same exclusion from the kingdom of Christ warns us to avoid these three with equal vigilance.

There are three kinds of avarice. The first does not allow those who renounce their wealth and possessions to be stripped of them. The second persuades us, with even greater desire, to take back what we have scattered or distributed to the needy. The third compels us to desire or acquire things that we had not previously possessed.

There are three kinds of anger. One burns inwardly; in Greek this is called *thymos* (θυμός). Another bursts forth into word, deed, and action; this is called *orgē* (ὀργή). Concerning these the Apostle says: “But now put away from yourselves all anger and indignation” (Col. III, 8). The third is not discharged as those two are, by boiling up for an hour, but is stored up for days and periods of time; this is called **ILHNIC** [uncertain reading]. All these must be condemned by us with equal horror.

There are two kinds of sadness. One arises either when anger comes to an end, or from damage inflicted, or from a desire that has been obstructed and frustrated. The other descends from irrational anxiety of mind or from despair.

There are two kinds of acedia. One drives those who are in distress toward sleep; the other urges them to leave and flee their cell.

Although cenodoxy is varied and manifold and is divided into different forms, it nevertheless has two kinds. The first is that by which we are exalted on account of carnal and manifest things. The second is that by which we are inflamed with desire for vain praise on account of spiritual and hidden things.

## CHAPTER LXIV. — On the Varied Assault of All the Vices

[Col. 1385B]

(Cass.) Although these eight vices assail the entire human race, they do not attack everyone in the same way. In one person the spirit of fornication holds the chief place; in another, fury dominates; in another, cenodoxy claims tyranny; in another, pride holds the citadel. Although it is certain that everyone is attacked by all of them, each of us struggles in a different manner and order.

## CHAPTER LXV. — On Establishing the Battle against the Vices According to Their Assault

(Serap.) Therefore we must take up battles against these vices in such a way that each person, examining which vice most greatly assails him, undertakes the principal struggle against that one, directing all the care and concern of his mind toward its assault and observation. Against it he must aim the daily arrows of fasts; against it, at every moment, he must hurl the frequent sighs and darts of his heart’s groans; against it, he must devote the labors of vigils and the meditations of his heart; and he must pour out to God unceasing tears of prayer, continually asking him especially for the destruction of that assault.

For it is impossible for anyone to deserve victory over any passion before understanding that he cannot obtain victory in the struggle through his own skill or labor. Nevertheless, if he is to be cleansed, it is necessary for him to remain day and night in every care and concern. When he senses that he has been freed from that passion, he should again inspect the hiding places of his heart with similar attention, select for himself whichever he perceives to be more savage than the rest, and turn all the weapons of the spirit against it with particular force.

In this way, once the stronger vices have always been conquered, he will have a swift and easy victory over the remaining ones. For the mind will become stronger through the progress of its triumphs, and the struggle that follows against weaker opponents will bring him a more ready outcome in battle.

It is customary among those who, before the kings of this world, have learned to fight every kind of beast for the sake of prizes—a spectacle commonly called *pancarpum*—that when they see any wild animals more formidable either in strength or in the fury of their savagery, they begin the contest of the first encounter against those beasts. Once these have been destroyed, they overthrow the rest, which are less terrifying and less violent, with an easier conclusion. So also, when the stronger vices have been conquered and weaker ones follow, perfect victory will be prepared for us without any danger.

Nor should one think that someone fighting principally against one vice, and therefore watching the weapons of the others less carefully, can more easily be wounded by an unexpected blow. This will by no means happen. It is impossible for someone who has armed the attention of his mind for the assault of any vice, being concerned for the cleansing of his heart, not also to possess a general horror of the other vices and a similar vigilance against them.

For how will one deserve to obtain victory over the passion from which one desires to be freed, if one makes oneself unworthy of the reward of purification through contamination by the other vices? But when the principal intention of our heart has taken up a special battle against one passion, we will pray about that one more attentively, entreating God with particular concern and zeal so that we may observe it more carefully and thereby deserve to obtain a swift victory over it.

That we ought to practice this order of battles, while nevertheless not trusting in our own strength, the Lawgiver also teaches in these words:

“You shall not fear them, because the Lord your God is in your midst, a great and terrible God. He himself will consume these nations before you, little by little and in separate parts. You will not be able to destroy them all at once, lest the beasts of the earth multiply against you. And the Lord your God will deliver them before you and kill them until they are completely destroyed.”

## CHAPTER LXVI. — On the Two Kinds of Vices and Their Fourfold Mode of Operation

[Col. 1386C]

(Cass.) These vices therefore have two kinds. Some are natural, such as gluttony; others are contrary to nature, such as avarice. Their mode of operation, however, is fourfold. Some cannot be completed without carnal action, such as gluttony and fornication. Others are completed without any bodily action, such as pride and cenodoxy. Some receive the cause of their agitation from outside, such as avarice and anger; others are stirred up by internal movements, such as acedia and sadness.

## CHAPTER LXVII. — A Recapitulation of the Passion of Gluttony and Fornication and Their Cure

Gluttony and fornication are naturally present in us, since they sometimes arise without any prompting of the mind, through the mere stimulation and itching of the flesh. Nevertheless, they require external material in order to be completed, and thus they reach their effect through bodily action.

These two vices in particular, which are fulfilled through the service of the flesh, require, beyond that spiritual care of the soul, a more particular bodily continence. This is accomplished through fasts, vigils, and the mortification of labor, together with withdrawal from a place. For just as both vices are generated through the defect of both soul and body, so they cannot be overcome except through the labor of both.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. — Which Vices Are Called Carnal and Which Spiritual

(Cass.) Although the blessed apostle Paul declared all vices generally to be carnal, since he numbered enmities, angers, and heresies among the works of the flesh, nevertheless, in order to gather their cures and natures more carefully, we distinguish them by a twofold division. We say that some are carnal and others spiritual.

Those are carnal that specifically pertain to the movement and perception of the flesh. The flesh delights in and feeds upon them so greatly that it even stirs up minds at rest and sometimes drags them unwillingly into consent to its will. Concerning these the blessed Apostle says: “Among whom,” he says, “we all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the pleasures of the flesh and of our thoughts, and we were by nature children of wrath, even as the others” (Eph. II, 3).

We call those spiritual which arise from the impulse of the soul alone. They not only contribute no pleasure to the flesh, but also afflict it with the gravest illnesses, while nourishing only the sick soul with the wretched nourishment of a miserable delight. Therefore these require the simple medicine of the heart.

Carnal vices, however, reach health only through a twofold cure, as we have said. Hence it is of great benefit to those who strive for purity to remove from themselves first the very materials of these carnal passions, through which either the occasion or the recollection of those passions may be generated in a soul that is still sick.

A twofold illness requires a twofold correction. In the case of the body, so that desire may not attempt to burst forth into action, the image and enticing material must necessarily be removed. Likewise, for the soul, so that it may not conceive the thought, more attentive meditation upon Scripture, watchful concern, and withdrawal into solitude should usefully be applied.

In the other vices, however, human association does no harm; indeed, it contributes greatly to those who truly desire to be free from them. For in the frequent presence of people they are more strongly rebuked, and when provoked they are revealed more often, so that they reach salvation through a swifter cure.

## CHAPTER LXIX. — Various Testimonies Concerning the Meaning of the Eight Vices

The eight vices are also signified in the Gospel in this way:

“When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it walks through dry places, seeking rest, and does not find it. Then it says: ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds it empty, swept with brooms, and adorned. Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself; and entering in, they dwell there, and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first” (Matt. XII, 43).

Just as there we read of seven nations, excluding the Egyptians from whom the children of Israel had gone out, so here too seven unclean spirits are said to return, except for the one said earlier to have gone out from the person.

Solomon also describes this sevenfold source of the vices in Proverbs as follows: “If your enemy asks you with a loud voice, do not consent to him, for there are seven wickednesses in his soul.” That is: if the spirit of gluttony, having been overcome, begins to flatter you through its humiliation, asking, so to speak, that you relax something of your initial fervor and grant it what exceeds the measure and standard of disciplined continence, do not be weakened by its submission or suggestion. Do not, because of the apparent security of the assault, by which you seem for a little while to have become more peaceful regarding carnal incentives, return to your former laxity or to your former desires for gluttony.

For this is what that spirit whom you had conquered says: “I will return to my house from which I came.” Then the seven spirits of the vices that proceed from it will immediately be there, more fierce than the passion that had been overcome at the beginning, and they will soon drag you toward worse kinds of sins.

## CHAPTER LXX. — That, Once the Passion of Gluttony Has Been Conquered, Labor Must Be Devoted to Acquiring the Other Virtues

[Col. 1388B]

Therefore, while we are devoted to continence, we must hasten, so that once the passion of gluttony has been overcome, we do not immediately allow our soul to remain empty of the necessary virtues. Rather, we must occupy all the recesses of our heart with them more zealously, lest the spirits of desire, when they return, find us empty and unoccupied by those virtues. Then, not content merely to prepare an entrance for themselves, they will bring with them into our soul this sevenfold fuel of the vices and make our last state worse than the first.

After this, the soul will be more disgraceful and impure and will be punished with a heavier penalty if it boasts that it has renounced this world while the eight vices rule it than it once was when it existed in the world, before it had professed the discipline or name of a monk.

These seven spirits are said to be worse than the first spirit that had gone out for this reason: the desire for food—that is, gluttony—is not harmful in itself unless it lets in other, more serious passions: fornication, avarice, anger, sadness, and pride. It is beyond doubt that these are harmful and destructive to the soul in themselves.

Therefore no one will ever be able to attain the purity of perfection if he hopes to acquire it through this one continence alone, that is, bodily fasting. He must know that he ought to practice it for this purpose: so that, with the flesh humbled by fasts, he may more easily enter the battle against the other vices, rather than allowing the flesh to grow insolent through the fullness of satiety.

## CHAPTER LXXI. — That the Order of the Battles Is Not the Same as the Order Set Out in the Catalogue of the Vices

[Col. 1388D]

It must nevertheless be understood that the order of the battles is not the same for all of us. As we have said, we are not all attacked in the same way, and each of us must undertake the struggles of combat according to the character of the battle by which he is chiefly assailed. Thus one person must first engage in conflict against the vice placed third, another against the fourth or fifth, and so on, according to which vices hold primacy in us. As the manner of the assault requires, so must we establish the order of our battles. In accordance with that order, the outcome of victory and the triumph that follows will bring us to purity of heart and the fullness of perfection.

## CHAPTER LXXII. — How the Number of the Eight Nations Is Fulfilled According to the Eight Vices

[Col. 1389A]

There are eight principal vices that attack the human race; figuratively, they are named under the designation of nations. For after the children of Israel had gone out from Egypt, the Lord promised that he would give them the lands of seven nations. It is said:

“When the Lord your God brings you into the land which you are entering to possess, and destroys before you many nations—the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite—seven nations much more numerous than you and stronger than you, and when the Lord delivers them to you, you shall strike them down to destruction” (Deut. VII, 1).

Seven nations are therefore counted here because, after they had already gone out from Egypt and had been freed from one exceedingly powerful nation, namely the Egyptians, they were to have a similar conflict against the remaining seven nations mentioned above.

The first nation, which had already been conquered, is not counted, and its land is not given to Israel as a possession. Rather, by the Lord’s command, Israel is ordered to abandon it forever and depart from it. One nation—the Egyptian—is to be abandoned, while seven are commanded to be destroyed.

The Egyptian nation, which is commanded to be abandoned, is the vice of gluttony, from which we cannot wholly free ourselves through our daily dealings. We must receive food out of necessity, not out of desire, as the apostle Paul says: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. XIII, 14). When we reject the desires of the flesh, we abandon the Egyptian nation.

The remaining seven nations, which are the seven vices—fornication, avarice, anger, sadness, acedia, cenodoxy, and pride—are commanded to be utterly destroyed.

Since, by God’s gift, we have excerpted from the works of the holy Fathers a few testimonies concerning the eight principal vices, let us now take up the battle of the virtues and consider how sins are committed in thought, speech, and deed.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. — That Individual Virtues Must Be Set against Each Vice

(Isid.) Accordingly, individual virtues must be set against the individual vices, and the assaults of the vices must be opposed by contrary virtues. Against the greed of the belly, moderation and abstinence must be set; against the luxury of the heart, purity of heart must be applied; against carnal lust, chastity of heart and body must be displayed; against covetousness (*avaritia*), generosity; against *philargyria*, that is, love of money, nakedness and the stripping away of wealth; against envy, charity and fraternal rejoicing; against hatred, love; against the fires of anger, gentleness; against the sadness of the world, spiritual joy; against acedia and disordered wandering, firm stability; against vain glory, fear of God; against the devil’s pride, the humility of Christ.

Thus, against the remaining vices also, let the virtue proper to each good work be opposed. For pride is the queen and mother of the seven principal vices, and these seven principal vices give birth to many others from themselves, since they are joined to one another by a certain kinship, so that one arises from another. Thus David, because he did not avoid adultery, committed murder; and whoever does not restrain excessive greed of the belly falls unhappily into lust.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. — The Ways in Which Sin Is Committed
Four ways sin is committed in the heart, and four ways it is carried out in deed. It is admitted into the heart through the suggestion of demons, the delight of the flesh, the mind’s consent, and the defense of pride. In deed it is committed now secretly, now openly, now through habit, now through despair. Thus, by these stages one sins in the heart, and wickedness is perpetrated in deed.

Sin is committed in three ways: ignorance, weakness, and deliberate intent [Col. 1390B]—with differing danger of punishment. Eve sinned in Paradise through ignorance, as the Apostle says: “The man was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and was in transgression” (1 Tim. 2:14). Eve therefore sinned through ignorance. Adam, however, sinned deliberately, because he was not deceived but sinned knowingly and with full awareness. Whoever is deceived evidently does not know what he is consenting to.

Peter sinned through weakness when, fearing the servant girl who questioned him, he denied Christ, and afterward wept most bitterly over his sin. For it is more serious to sin through weakness than through ignorance, and more serious to sin deliberately than through weakness. One sins deliberately when he does evil through the determined purpose and deliberation of his mind [perhaps corrected from: “through study and deliberation”]; through weakness, however, when he sins by accident or rashness [Col. 1390C].

Those who sin deliberately are more wicked: they not only fail to live well but, if they can, turn away from the truth even while living well. Some sin unknowingly, some knowingly, and some do not wish to know, under the pretext of ignorance, so that they may be considered less culpable; yet they do not lessen their guilt but rather deceive themselves. Simply not knowing belongs to ignorance. Not wishing to know, however, belongs to obstinate pride. To refuse to know the will of one’s own Lord is nothing other than, through pride, to wish to despise the Lord.

Let no one excuse himself through ignorance of God, because God judges not only those who turn away from knowledge of him, but also those who have failed to know him, as the same Lord testifies through the prophet: “I will destroy human beings from the face of the earth, and those who turn away from following the Lord, and those who have not sought the Lord or investigated him” (Zeph. 1:3). And the Psalm says: “Pour out your wrath upon the nations that have not known you” (Ps. 78:6).

There are some who commit slight and minor sins in thought, speech, and deed; and there are others who perpetrate grave crimes in thought, speech, and deed. Those who delight in slippery and empty thoughts commit slight sins in thought. Hence the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes” (Isa. 1:16).

Those sin gravely in thought who so delight in perverse and destructive thoughts that they desire to carry them through to the accomplishment of a wicked deed [Col. 1391A]. Concerning them Holy Scripture testifies: “Perverse thoughts separate from God” (Wis. 1:3).

One sins lightly in speech when one speaks an idle word, for, as the Lord says, “an account must be given.” One sins gravely in speech when one incurs the crime of falsehood, because “the mouth that lies kills the soul.” One sins lightly in deed when one pursues idleness; gravely when one commits theft or robbery; lightly when one irritates a poor person; gravely when one strips him; lightly when one fails to bury the dead; gravely when one kills a human being. You will find many similar sins in speech and deed.

## CHAPTER LXXV — On Those Who Sin in Thought

[Col. 1391B] (Isidore.) Although someone may abstain from an evil deed, he is nevertheless not innocent on account of the wickedness of his thought alone. Hence the Lord says through Isaiah: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes” (Isa. 1:16). We sin not only by deeds but also by thoughts, if we take delight in them when they arise unlawfully.

For unlawful thoughts arising is the work of demons; delighting in perverse thoughts is our own work. It must be understood that there are three kinds of wicked thoughts. The first consists of those that contaminate the mind through deliberation and the intention to sin. The second consists of those that disturb the mind through the pleasure of sin but do not draw it into consent to sin. The third consists of those that pass through the mind by natural impulse and do not so much entice it to commit vices [Col. 1391C] as hinder us from thinking about what we ought to think about.

This occurs, for example, when we recall to memory images of things that we know were once done or said needlessly. Their frequent reconsideration, like the annoying persistence of flies, habitually circles around the eyes of the heart and disturbs its spiritual vision more than it blinds it.

Solomon warned that we should be disciplined against all these kinds of wicked thoughts when he says: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds” (Prov. 4:23). Following his admonition, let us be diligent: if we have sinned inwardly by consenting to commit a crime, let us quickly cleanse this away through confession and worthy fruits of repentance; if we feel ourselves being tempted by the pleasure of sin, let us drive away that harmful delight through frequent prayers and tears and through frequent, continual remembrance of bitterness [Col. 1391D]. If we do not find ourselves sufficient to repel it unaided, let us seek the help of our brothers, so that what we cannot accomplish by our own strength we may obtain through their counsel and intercession.

For persistent prayer has great power, as the same apostle has already said: “The prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (Jas. 5:15).

Since we cannot wholly free ourselves from superfluous thoughts, let us drive them away as far as we can by introducing good thoughts, especially through frequent meditation on the Scriptures, following the example of the Psalmist, who says: “How I have loved your law, O Lord; all day long it is my meditation” (Ps. 119:97). [Col. 1392A]

Great vigilance, therefore, must be applied to guarding the heart, because the origin of either good or evil is located there. For as it is written: “Evil thoughts come out of the heart” (Matt. 15:29). Therefore, if we resist a wicked thought at the outset, we do not fall into the resulting deed.

### How Dangerous It Is to Take Pleasure in Evil Thoughts

There was a holy man named Eulogius who had received such great grace from the Lord in offering the sacraments that he recognized the merits and faults of each person who approached. Accordingly, he held back certain people who wished to approach communion, saying: “How have you dared to approach the divine sacraments when your mind and intention are set on evil?”

He would say to one: “You have entertained thoughts of fornication.” To another: “You said in your heart, ‘It makes no difference whether a righteous person or a sinner approaches the sacraments.’” And another had doubt in his heart, saying: “What can communion do to sanctify me?”

He therefore removed each of them from communion in the sacrament and said to them: “Withdraw for a little while and do penance, so that, purified through satisfaction and tears, you may be deemed worthy of communion with Christ.”

## CHAPTER LXXVI — That All the Secrets of Thought Are Open to the Divine Gaze

To know the secrets of thoughts is an evident sign of divinity. Solomon affirms this when, praying, he says: “For you alone know the hearts of all the children of human beings” (Prov. 15:11). The apostle Paul likewise says: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. No creature is invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. 4:12).

Jeremiah also says: “But you, Lord of hosts, who judge justly and test the kidneys and hearts” (Jer. 11:20).

These matters should not be mentioned casually or carelessly. Rather, my brothers, we must keep watch diligently so that we may render worthy of the divine gaze not only our words and deeds but also the very secrets of our hearts. Let not hatred dwell in the temple of our breast; let not the rust of envy remain there; let not the root of shameful or insulting speech arise from it; let not the contemplation of a harmful deed take root there.

Let us remember the Lord’s threat, in which it is said: “I am coming to gather their deeds and thoughts”; and, once the rubble of vices has been expelled, [the text appears incomplete:] “such a fitting dwelling of our heart,” in which he himself may graciously deign to dwell, since he is its unavoidable observer and judge.

## CHAPTER LXXVII — On Those Who Give Offense in Speech

Holy Scripture says: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue.” Therefore we must take great care not to say things by which death for our soul may be acquired.

Sin is committed in speech in many ways: through idle words, empty talk, excessive talk, shameful talk, buffoonery and words that provoke laughter, and—what is worse and more serious—through lies, falsehoods, mockery, insults, detraction, whispering, curses, perjury, and the words of the prophet: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isa. 5:20), along with other similar offenses [Col. 1393A].

We must diligently guard not only against perverse and criminal speech, for which eternal punishment is paid, but also restrain the tongue from idle and other superfluous words. Just as those who are making progress fear the crime of falsehood, so perfect men avoid idle words.

For, as someone has said, an account is demanded for an idle word, and punishment is paid for unjust speech. We sin either by speaking evil wrongly or by speaking good wrongly. We speak evil wrongly when we try to persuade someone to commit any kind of wickedness [Col. 1393B]. We speak good wrongly when we arrogantly proclaim anything that is right.

We also speak wrongly in the heart when inwardly we contemplate and devise harmful thoughts. We speak wrongly with the tongue when, being scourged for doing evil, we complain and grumble. We speak wrongly by our deeds when, living badly, we instruct others through our example to act perversely.

The forms of speech written above, and similar ones, must be avoided in every way. If, contrary to the commandment of the Lord and his saints, it is wrong to speak idle and buffoonish words and the like—since, as the Lord says, an account must be given—how much more must we avoid perjury, falsehoods, curses, and other such things, for which damnation and eternal punishment are imposed?

For example, the Savior of the world says: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12:36). An idle word is one that benefits neither the speaker nor the hearer.

Of lies, hear this: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11). Of detraction: “The one who detracts will be uprooted.” Of curses: “Nor will those who curse inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10). And there are other such statements concerning similar words.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII — On Lying

Every lie is either formed by deliberation or by rashness. Sometimes it is worse to deliberate a lie than to speak one. At times someone, being incautious, speaks a lie in haste. But one cannot deliberate a lie except through serious intention [Col. 1393D]. Therefore the person who lies deliberately is considered worse than the one who lies through mere rashness.

Every lie must be avoided with the greatest care, although sometimes a certain kind of lie may be a lesser fault—for example, when someone lies for the sake of human safety. Yet because it is written: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11), and: “You will destroy those who speak lies” (Ps. 5:7), perfect men diligently avoid even this kind of lie, so that the life of another may not be defended through their deception, nor may they harm their own souls while striving to preserve another person’s flesh.

Nevertheless, we readily believe that this kind of sin is easily forgiven. For if any fault is cleansed by a subsequent reward, how much more easily is this fault wiped away when a reward accompanies it [Col. 1394A].

In every way, however, lying must be avoided, whether it seems to be uttered for evil or even for good, because every lie is not from God but, as the Savior says, “is from evil.”

## CHAPTER LXXIX — On the Various Kinds of Lies

There are eight kinds of lies, as Saint Augustine, bishop, says in his book *On Lying*.

“The first,” he says, “is the capital lie, which must be avoided above all: a lie made in teaching religion. No one ought to be brought to this lie under any condition.

“The second is one that unjustly harms someone; it is such that it benefits no one and harms someone.

“The third benefits one person in such a way that it harms another, though not by causing bodily impurity.

“The fourth is told solely from the desire to lie and deceive; this is a sheer lie.

“The fifth is told from the desire to please.

“The sixth is one that harms no one and benefits someone—for example, if someone knowingly lies that he does not know where a person’s money is, when that money is unjustly being sought.

“The seventh is one that harms no one and benefits someone—for example, if someone lies because he does not wish to betray a person who is being sought for execution, whether that person is not only just and innocent but also guilty and subject to Christian discipline, so that hope of correction may not be abandoned for anyone and the way to repentance may not be closed to anyone.

“We have treated these two kinds, which commonly provoke much controversy, sufficiently, and have shown what seems right to us: these kinds too should be avoided by brave, faithful, and truthful men and women, through their willingness to endure disadvantages honestly and courageously.

“One must not lie to someone asking where a person is who has entrusted himself to another’s protection. Rather, one should answer courageously: ‘I will neither betray him nor lie.’

“This was done by Firmus, formerly bishop of the church of Tagaste, a man firmer in will. When a man who had taken refuge with him was being sought by the emperor’s order through officers sent for that purpose, and Firmus was concealing him as carefully as he could, he replied to those who asked that he could neither lie nor betray the man. He endured many bodily tortures—for the emperors were not yet Christian—and remained firm in his resolve. Then, when he was brought before the emperor, he appeared so remarkable that he obtained without difficulty the pardon of the man whom he was protecting [perhaps: obtained pardon for the man].

“What could be stronger or more steadfast than this?

“The eighth kind of lie is one that harms no one and even benefits someone by protecting him from bodily impurity.

“In these eight kinds, the less one sins by lying, the closer one rises toward the eighth; the more one descends toward the first, the more one sins. Whoever thinks that there is some kind of lie that is not a sin shamefully deceives himself, imagining himself an honorable deceiver of others. For a lie—and any other sin—is grave [variant: “graver”] when it is produced by the mind of one who harms rather than by the mind of one who helps. Nevertheless, no lie is without sin. For it is written: ‘The mouth that lies kills the soul,’ and every lie is not from God but ‘is from evil’ (Wis. 1:11).

“Therefore, for every lie, according to the quality and degree of the lie, suitable satisfaction and repentance must be performed, lest we be judged severely by God, the judge of truth, who neither deceives nor is deceived.”

## CHAPTER LXXX — On the Various More Serious and Mortal Sins and Crimes Perpetrated in Speech

The distinguished preacher Paul, wishing generally to restrain everyone from all evil and destructive speech, says: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only such as is good for the building up of faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Eph. 4:29). And he adds: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (ibid., v. 30). Nothing, of course, could be a more serious evil than this.

It is therefore clear that every word uttered which does not contribute to the building up of the hearers’ faith grieves the Holy Spirit of God. If speech that does not build up is forbidden by the Apostle of Christ so that it may not grieve the Holy Spirit, how much more is speech forbidden that destroys and pollutes the mouth of the speaker and the ears of the hearer, such as falsehood, detraction, cursing, and similar things?

### On Falsehood

“A false witness,” says Solomon, “will not go unpunished. Whoever gives false testimony against his neighbor, his lamp will be extinguished in the final day” (Prov. 19:9; 20:20).

### On Detraction

“Whoever detracts from his brother,” Scripture says, “detracts from the law” [Col. 1395C] (Jas. 4:11). And the Psalmist says: “The one who secretly detracts from his neighbor, him I pursued” (Ps. 101:5). Elsewhere it is said of the person who willingly listens to a detractor: “Do not listen to the detractor,” Scripture says, “lest you be uprooted.”

### On Cursing

The apostle Paul says: “Nor will those who curse inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10). Every evil word spoken for the purpose of defaming someone or commending him in an evil manner is a curse, even if it does not seem insulting. This is confirmed by the statement: “They cursed him and said to him, ‘You are that man’s disciple’” (John 9:28).

### On Grumbling

The apostle Paul says: “Do not grumble, as some of them grumbled in the wilderness and perished by the destroyer” (1 Cor. 10:10).

These testimonies of divine Scripture make clear that for these and similar vices committed in speech, perpetual punishment threatens unless they are removed in this life through satisfaction and repentance.

## CHAPTER LXXXI — On Those Who Sin in Deed and Act in Various Ways

There are many slight sins perpetrated in deed, for which it is necessary to do penance in the present life, lest after the end of this life they be brought before our eyes as grounds for accusation. For, as Scripture says, the Lord leaves nothing unpunished [Col. 1396A].

Therefore not only grave but also slight sins must be avoided. Holy men mourn slight sins as though they were most serious, for many slight sins make one great sin, just as immense rivers commonly grow from small and tiny drops. A multitude gathered into one produces an overflowing abundance.

There are also many grave and mortal sins and crimes perpetrated in act and deed, for which the kingdom of heaven is closed to those who have committed them and have not redeemed them in this life through repentance, tears, almsgiving, and other good works. These include sacrilege, homicide, adultery, theft, robbery, drunkenness, and similar offenses, which the apostle Paul enumerates.

Whoever recognizes that any of these sins rules within him will, unless he reforms himself worthily, performs penance for a long time if he has the opportunity, and gives abundant alms, be destroyed by eternal fire without any remedy [Col. 1396B].

The following are minor and slight sins: whenever someone takes more food or drink than is necessary; whenever he speaks more than he ought or is silent more than is useful; whenever he irritates a poor person who asks insistently; whenever, although physically healthy, he wishes to dine while others are fasting; whenever, devoted to sleep, he rises late for church; whenever, apart from the desire for children, he has intercourse with his wife; whenever he is slow to visit someone in prison or slow to visit the sick; whenever he neglects to reconcile those who are at odds; whenever he irritates a neighbor, wife, or servant more than he ought; whenever he flatters someone more than he ought; whenever he wishes to flatter someone of greater status, whether voluntarily or out of necessity; whenever, while the poor are hungry, he prepares excessively sumptuous or expensive banquets; whenever he speaks idle stories either in church or outside it.

There is no doubt that these and similar things belong to minor sins, which can scarcely be enumerated. Although we do not believe that these sins kill the soul, they nevertheless make it deformed by filling it, as it were, with pustules and a dreadful scab.

Whatever of these sins is not redeemed in this life through prayers, fasting, almsgiving, and especially forgiveness of those who sin against us must be purified by fire. The Apostle speaks of this fire: “It will be revealed in fire, and whoever’s work is burned will suffer loss” (1 Cor. 3:13).

## CHAPTER LXXXII — Likewise, On the Various and Many Ways in Which People Sin

(Isidore.) There are some who sin knowingly; others unknowingly; others secretly; others out of necessity; others through habit; others through love of sin; and others sin not from love of sin but from fear of human beings.

### On Those Who Offend Knowingly and Unknowingly

The anger of God that is provoked is more serious than that which is deserved. We deserve it when we sin through ignorance; we provoke it when we know how to do good but do not wish to do so.

### On Manifest and Hidden Sins

It is a greater fault to sin openly than secretly, for the person is guilty in two ways: he sins personally and both practices and teaches what he does. Isaiah speaks of such people: “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom and did not hide it” (Isa. 3:9). To perpetrate sin is a crime; to proclaim sin is a public outcry. Concerning this the apostle Paul says: “Let every outcry be taken away from you, along with all malice.”

### On Those Who Sin from Necessity

Many fear temporal poverty and sin not willingly but only from the necessity of sinning; while fleeing the necessity of the present age, they are deprived of future goods.

### On Those Who Sin Willingly and Not from Necessity

Some commit sin willingly and not from necessity. Compelled by no poverty, they remain wicked, simply wishing to be evil gratuitously.

### On Those Who Sin through Habit

To sin is exceedingly wicked; it is worse to make a habit of sins. From the former one rises easily; from the latter one rises only with difficulty, because one must struggle against an evil habit.

### On Those Who Sin from Love of Sin

Some both love sin and commit it; some love it but do not commit it; some do not commit sin and nevertheless hate righteousness. The one who not only loves sin but also commits it sins more seriously than the one who does not commit it but loves it; and sometimes the one who loves it but does not commit it sins more seriously than the one who commits it but hates it. It is most serious not only to commit sin but also to love it.

Some are immediately ashamed after committing a crime; others not only do not grieve that they have done evil but even glory in the evil deed itself.

### On Those Who Sin from Fear of Human Beings

Some wretched people, fearing an earthly human being like themselves more than God their creator, perpetrate crimes, giving no thought to the saying: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5:29). It would have been better for them to lose temporal life than to commit sin.

### That Sometimes One Sin Gives Rise to Other Sins

Often one sin is the cause of another. When it is committed, another arises from it like its offspring [Col. 1398B], as lust commonly arises from excessive gluttony.

Sin is admitted as the punishment of sin when, in accordance with the merit of a particular sin, God abandons a person and he proceeds into another, worse sin, by which the one who committed it is further defiled. Thus a preceding sin is the cause of a subsequent sin, while the subsequent sin is the punishment of the preceding offense. Preceding sins are therefore the cause of subsequent crimes, so that those which follow are the punishment of those which preceded them.

The punishment of preceding sins is itself called hardening, which proceeds from divine justice. Hence the prophet says: “You have hardened our heart, so that we would not fear” (Isa. 63:17). For God does not drive those who are just to become evil; rather, when people are already evil, they are hardened so that they may become worse.

Thus far, from the many pronouncements of the holy Fathers, we have excerpted, with the Lord’s permission, a few passages concerning how sins are perpetrated in thought, speech, and deed. These may perhaps be useful to the more simple.

---

[Col. 1397D]

# THE BOOK OF RABANUS MAURUS, BLESSED ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, ON PENITENTS, ADDRESSED TO OTGAR

## PREFACE

[Col. 1397D]

To the most beloved Lord in the Lord of lords, OTGAR, archbishop, RABANUS, a sinner in Christ, wishes salvation.

For as long as we hoped, holy Father, that you would come to us, we looked forward to your arrival all the sooner. But after you departed from us and left us saddened by your absence, we considered that we ought to pray that the divine majesty, preserving you unharmed, might grant us to see you safe and well again, because your health is our security. If, however, anything adverse should happen to you, it would undoubtedly make us sad and troubled.

Moreover, while you were physically present here, your holiness was pleased to discuss and consider with my smallness the various transgressions in which human weakness violates the divine commandments, and how through repentance those who transgress the law of God in various crimes might be restored and reconciled to God [Col. 1398D]. Therefore you ordered me to excerpt briefly from the canons and the judgments of the holy Fathers and gather into one work the provisions promulgated by the teachers of the Church for such persons, for the correction of their vices.

I did what you commanded and wrote these things in a small book, so that you might have readily before your eyes for reading what I had to gather from various books into one place, and so that our labor might in some way satisfy your wishes.

And so that it might not perhaps be necessary for you to search through different volumes for what you now clearly have carefully collected in brief, I have appended to this book another work that I recently composed concerning marriages between relatives, the tricks of magicians, and false divinations, so that you might have together works that the order of the discussion has made compatible [Col. 1399A].

Read, then, the little work that has been sent to you. If anything in it seems incorrectly stated, may your sacred diligence correct it for the benefit of readers. Farewell in good health, and remember me, a sinner, in your holy prayers, in the name of the Lord.

## CHAPTER I — On Those Who Commit Capital Crimes after Sacred Ordination, and on Their Repentance or Excommunication

First, then, it seemed to you that I should write about those who hold sacred orders and acknowledge that they have been contaminated by capital crimes either before or after ordination. In my view, the following distinction must be observed.

Those who are publicly discovered or apprehended in perjury, theft, fornication, or other such crimes should, according to the provisions of the sacred canons, be deposed from their proper rank. It is a scandal to the people of God to have such persons placed over them when they are clearly excessively vicious. For on this account people disparage the sacrifice of God; and, becoming rebellious and hostile, they grow worse each day through their evil examples, as the sons of Eli are once read to have done when they sinned.

Those who, through secret confession, confess before the eyes of God—and in the presence of the priest who is to impose penance upon them—the evil deeds they have secretly committed, and who accuse themselves of having sinned grievously, should, if they truly repent and strive to purify themselves through fasting, almsgiving, vigils, sacred prayers, and tears, be promised hope of forgiveness from the mercy of God while retaining their rank. He desires all human beings to be saved and to come to knowledge of the truth, and he does not desire the death of a sinner but that he should turn and live.

For concerning those who have been advanced to the honor of the priesthood without examination, the following is written in the Council of Nicaea, canon 8:

“If certain presbyters have been advanced without examination, or, when examined, have confessed their sins, and people, stirred up against the canons, have attempted to impose hands upon those who have confessed, the rule does not admit such men, because the Catholic Church defends what is irreproachable.”

Likewise, in the Council of Neocaesarea, canon 8, the following was determined concerning this matter:

“If a presbyter has been advanced while burdened by a bodily sin and confesses that he sinned before ordination, he shall not consecrate the offerings, but shall remain in the other offices on account of his good discipline. For many have said that other sins can be forgiven through the laying on of hands. But if he has not confessed concerning himself and cannot be openly convicted, he is to be left to the judgment of his own authority.”

Likewise, in the same council, canon 10:

“In the same way, if a deacon has fallen into the same sin, he shall be removed from the order of ministry.”

Concerning those who have sinned after receiving their rank, the Apostolic Canon likewise says:

“Let a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has been caught in fornication, perjury, or theft be deposed, but let him not be deprived of communion. For Scripture says: ‘The Lord will not take vengeance twice for the same thing’” (Nah. 1).

Likewise, in the same council, canon 28:

“If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon, justly deposed for certain crimes, dares to take up again the ministry formerly entrusted to him, let him be completely cut off from the Church.”

The Apostle teaches that an accusation against men of sacred orders should not easily be received, but that the case must first be carefully examined and judgment then rendered. Writing to Timothy, he says: “Do not accept an accusation against a presbyter except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. Those who are sinning, rebuke before everyone, so that the others may have fear” (1 Tim. 5).

What kind of witnesses these must be is made clear in the African Council, canon 96, where it is written:

“It has been decided that slaves or personal freedmen may not be admitted to bring an accusation, nor anyone whom the public laws do not permit to accuse of public crimes. Nor may anyone marked by the stains of infamy be admitted, that is, actors and persons subject to disgraceful practices; nor heretics, pagans, or Jews. Nevertheless, all those who are denied the right of accusation in their own cases must likewise be denied permission to accuse.”

Likewise, in the same council, canon 98:

“Those witnesses are not to be admitted for testimony who, according to the precept, are not admitted for accusation, nor those whom the accuser himself has produced from his own household. No one under fourteen years of age is to be admitted as a witness.”

Likewise, in the same council, canon 97:

“It has been decided that whenever many crimes are brought against clerics by their accusers, and the accuser is unable to prove one of those charges—the one he brought forward first—he is not to be admitted to the others.”

Concerning those whose sins are hidden and cannot be openly accused by anyone: if, moved to salutary contrition for their sins, they secretly confess them to a bishop or priest, it seems good to me that they should do penance according to whatever has been prescribed for them by the bishop or priest—not lukewarmly or tardily, but fervently and diligently—and thus trust that they will receive from the Lord forgiveness of their sins and recover their rank.

The blessed Pope Gregory also confirms this in a letter that he wrote to Secundinus, a servant of God confined in seclusion, saying:

“For your Holiness requested of us that I write back to you concerning the priestly office and rising again after a fall, since you say that you have read differing and divided opinions about this canon: some saying that one may rise again, others that this is by no means possible. For our part, beginning with the Council of Nicaea, we venerate this council together with the other four; and those that followed it agree unanimously with it in all their decisions. We therefore follow the fathers who preceded us, because, with God as author, we do not depart from their sacred teaching.

“Beginning at the head, therefore, and proceeding to the fourth minister of the altar, we know that this rule must be observed: whoever is preceded by a greater, just as he is greater in honor, so must he be greater in guilt. And whoever is followed by a greater fault must also receive a greater punishment. In this way, penance afterward may be considered fruitful. For what benefit is there in sowing wheat and not gathering its fruit, or in building a house and not dwelling in it?

“After worthy satisfaction, we believe that he can return to his honor, as the prophet says: ‘Shall not he who falls add this also—to rise again? And shall not he who has turned away return?’ (Isa. XXIV, 20). The same prophet says to the sinner: ‘On whatever day you turn and groan, you shall be saved’ (Ezek. III). Hence the Psalmist also says: ‘Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me’ (Ps. L).”

[Col. 1401B] When, having fallen into guilt, he asked not to be cast away from God—for the king and prophet, terrified that he had seized another man’s wife when the prophet exposed his crime—he added, doing penance: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit.” For if he himself had not done penance worthy of God, he would certainly not have preached to others. He says: “I will teach the unrighteous your ways, and the impious will turn to you.”

When the prophet saw that his own sins had been cleansed through penance, he did not hesitate, by preaching, to rebuke the sins of others; and so he sought to offer himself as a sacrifice to God when he said: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit” (ibid.).

These things would suffice; but the more fully a judgment is confirmed by testimonies from Holy Scripture, the more readily it is believed. Concerning this the prophet says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XVIII). And concerning sinners it is said: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, all his iniquities are given over to oblivion.”

If our Redeemer, who came not to destroy sinners but to justify them, has left the offenses of sinners in oblivion, who among human beings would preserve them for condemnation, when the Apostle says: “If God justifies, who is he that condemns?”

Let us also return to the fountain of mercy and bring forward the evangelical saying: “I will rejoice,” he says, “over one sinner doing penance more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of penance” (Luke XV). He also carried the lost sheep—the ninetieth and ninth—not leaving the others who had not strayed, but bringing it back to the fold on his shoulders.

[Col. 1401D] If a wandering sheep, once found, is carried back to the fold on the shoulders, why should such a person not be recalled to the ministry of the Church after punishment? What is more serious: to commit a carnal offense, without which not many but only a few are found, or to deny the Son of God out of fear? We know that the blessed Peter himself, the foremost of the apostles, at whose body we now sit unworthy, fell into this sin. But after the denial came penance, and after penance mercy was granted; for the one who had foretold that Peter would deny him did not cast him out of the apostolate.

Let these words, dearest son, suffice for you, so that when you see him erasing his offenses with tears, you may not doubt that he obtains mercy in the sight of the Godhead; for the one who came to redeem sinners with his blood despises no sinner who returns.

[Col. 1402A] Hence also the blessed Augustine, writing to the deacon Peter concerning the faith, says:

“Penance can be useful to every person in this life. Whenever a person undertakes it—however wicked, however advanced in years—if with his whole heart he renounces his former sins, and before God sheds for them tears not only of the body but also of the heart, and takes care to wash away the stains of evil works through good works, he will immediately obtain forgiveness of all his sins. For the Lord promises this to us in prophetic speech, saying: ‘If you turn and groan, you shall be saved.’ And elsewhere it is said: ‘Son, you have sinned; do not add to it again, but pray concerning your former sins, that they may be forgiven you’ (Eccli. XXI).”

[Col. 1402B] Prayer for sins would never have been prescribed to the sinner if forgiveness were not to be granted to the sinner.

But penance benefits the sinner only if he performs it within the Catholic Church. To this Church God, in the person of the blessed Peter, granted the power of binding and loosing, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVIII).

Therefore, at whatever age a person performs true penance for his sins and, with God’s illumination, corrects his life, he will not be deprived of the gift of forgiveness; for God says through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the one who dies, but only that he return from his evil way and that his soul may live” (Ezek. XVIII).

Nevertheless, no one ought, under the hope of God’s mercy, to remain longer in his sins [Col. 1402C], since no one even in the body wishes to remain ill longer in the hope of future health. For such people, who neglect to withdraw from their iniquities and promise themselves forgiveness from God, are sometimes overtaken by God’s sudden wrath, so that they find neither time for conversion nor the benefit of forgiveness.

Therefore Holy Scripture kindly warns each one of you, saying: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not defer it from day to day. For his wrath will come suddenly, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you.” The blessed David also says: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Ps. XCIV).

The blessed Paul likewise agrees, saying: “See, brothers, that there not perhaps be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, departing from the living God; but exhort one another each day, as long as it is called ‘today,’ so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Heb. III).

[Col. 1402D] A person therefore lives with a hardened heart whether he does not turn, despairing of forgiveness of sins, or whether he hopes in God’s mercy in such a way that he remains to the end of his present life in the perversity of his crimes.

Accordingly, loving God’s mercy and fearing his justice, let us neither despair of the forgiveness of sins nor remain in sins, knowing that the justice of the most righteous Judge will exact all those debts which the mercy of the most compassionate Redeemer has not forgiven. For just as mercy receives and absolves those who turn, so justice will reject [Col. 1403A] and punish those who remain hardened. These are the ones who sin against the Holy Spirit and receive forgiveness of sins neither in this age nor in the age to come.

Concerning this, Isidore, bishop of Hispalis, wrote in reply to Bishop Massio’s inquiry as follows:

“Indeed, concerning what your venerable Fraternity subsequently made known in your letters, no diversity of decision is to be understood in such judgments: in one place it is read that after penance the rank of honor is to be restored following a bodily fall; elsewhere, that after such an offense the dignity of the former order is by no means to be restored.

“This difference is distinguished in the following way: the Canon commanded those to return to their former offices who had been preceded by satisfaction through penance or by a worthy confession of sins. But those who are not corrected by their vice of corruption, and who even attempt, with a certain superstitious recklessness, to justify the very carnal offense they commit, receive neither the rank of honor nor the grace of communion.

“Thus both judgments must be reconciled: those who have merited reconciliation through penance by divine mercy must necessarily be restored to their place of honor. Nor do those who are known through the correction of penance to have received the remedy of life obtain the status of their acquired dignity undeservedly.

“To make this still less ambiguous, let it be confirmed by a judgment of divine authority. For the prophet Ezekiel, under the figure of faithless Jerusalem, shows that after the satisfaction of penance one may have one’s former honor restored. ‘Be ashamed, O Judah,’ he says, ‘and bear your disgrace’ (Ezek. XVI). And shortly afterward: ‘You and your daughters,’ he says, ‘return from your iniquity.’

“When he said ‘be ashamed,’ he showed that after confessions it is the work of sin for anyone to blush, and, because of the crimes committed, to lower a shamefaced brow to the ground for the deed worthy of shame that he had perpetrated. Then he commanded her to bear the disgrace of her deposition, mourning with humility for what she had done. Thus, according to the prophet, she can be recalled to her former state.”

The evangelist John likewise wrote something similar to the angel of the church at Ephesus, among other things: “Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance, and do the first works; otherwise I will come to you and move your lampstand from its place” [Col. 1403D] (Apoc. II).

By the angel of the Church he plainly indicates its superior, that is, its priest, in accordance with Malachi, who says: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord” (Malach. II).
