Therefore the superior who has fallen into vice is warned by the evangelist to remember from where he has fallen, to do penance, and to perform his first works, so that his lampstand may not be moved.

For the lampstand of the angel is priestly teaching; or it may be understood as the honor of the authority that he bears, in accordance with what is written in Samuel concerning the condemnation of Eli: “His eyes had grown dim, and he could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished” (I Reg. III).

The lamp of God had been his when, endowed with priestly dignity, he shone with the brightness of justice. The prophet asserts that it was extinguished when, because of the crimes of his sons, he lost the authority of the priesthood and the light of his merits.

The priest’s lampstand or lamp, understood as the gifts of honor, is extinguished or moved, according to John, when, after a fall into sin, the admitted crimes are not mourned because penance has been neglected. For he did not say, “Because you have fallen, I will move your lampstand,” but, “Unless you do penance, I will move your lampstand.”

Therefore, if penance comes first for a sinful superior, forgiveness of the offense necessarily follows. It is also written in Proverbs: “Whoever hides his crimes will not prosper; but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy” (Prov. XXVIII).

For even the fact that the discipline of the canons commanded the penitent to return to his former state after seven years was not decreed by the holy Fathers according to their own choice, but rather sanctioned in accordance with the judgment of divine justice.

For we read that Maria, the prophetess and sister of Aaron, when she had incurred guilt through slander against Moses, “was immediately covered with the mark of leprosy. And when Moses asked that she be cleansed, the Lord commanded her to go outside the camp for seven days, and after her cleansing to be admitted again into the camp” (Num. XII).

Maria, therefore, sister of Aaron, is understood as the flesh of the priest. When, devoted to pride, it is stained by the most filthy contagion of thoughts, it is to be cast outside the camp for seven days—that is, outside the fellowship of the holy Church for seven years—where, after the cleansing of its vices, it will receive the merit of its place or former dignity.

Behold, insofar as I have been able, I have explained the ancient and fully authoritative judgment of the council through sacred testimonies, showing that the person who knows how to mourn his own offenses through the satisfaction of penance can be restored to his own honor; but that the person who neither mourns what he has done nor, without any religious shame or fear of divine judgment, commits what ought to be mourned cannot be restored.

At the end of the letter I thought this should also be added: whenever a discordant judgment is found in the records of councils, the judgment of the one whose authority was older and weightier should rather be retained.

In the Council of Hilerdum, therefore, chapter 5, concerning those who serve at the altar, if they should suddenly fall through the weakness of the flesh and, with the Lord looking favorably upon them, do worthy penance, so that, mortifying the body, they offer to God the sacrifice of a contrite heart, it is written that they are to remain under the authority of the bishop. He may either not suspend for long those who are truly afflicted, or separate the negligent from the body of the Church for a longer period; but in such a way that, when they recover their offices, they cannot afterward be promoted to higher offices.

If, however, they should return again like dogs to their vomit, they shall lose not only the dignity of their office but also holy communion, unless they receive it at the point of death.

Likewise, in the Council of Carthage, canon 27, it is written that priests and deacons convicted of a grave offense are by no means to receive the laying on of hands as lay penitents. It was confirmed that, whenever priests or deacons have been convicted of some grave offense for which they must be removed from the ministry, hands are not to be laid upon them as upon lay penitents; nor is it to be permitted that those who have been rebaptized be promoted to the clerical rank.

## CHAPTER II—Concerning Incestuous Unions

Concerning incestuous unions, the Council of Agde, chapter 61, states:

“We reserve absolutely no forgiveness for incestuous marriages, unless they have remedied the adultery by separation. Those involved in incest are not to be counted as belonging to any marriage, and it is even a deadly thing to designate them. We judge the following to be incestuous: if anyone violates through carnal union his brother’s widow, who had previously been almost like a sister; if anyone takes his brother’s full sister as a wife; if anyone marries his stepmother; if anyone joins himself to his cousin.

“We prohibit these things in the present time, but we do not dissolve what was established before us. If anyone joins himself to a widow or daughter or uncle’s daughter, or is polluted by intercourse with his father’s daughter or his stepdaughter.

“Those, however, whose illicit union is forbidden shall have the freedom to enter into a better marriage.”

Likewise, concerning the same matter, the Council of Orléans, chapter 14, states:

“Let no brother ascend upon the bed of his deceased brother. Let no one, having lost his wife, dare to join himself to her sister. If he does so, let him be struck by ecclesiastical discipline.”

Likewise, concerning the same matter, the Council of Hilerdum, chapter 4, states:

“Those who stain themselves with the pollution of incest are to be permitted in the church only as far as the Mass of the catechumens, for as long as they persist in that detestable and illicit carnal cohabitation. With such persons, no Christian ought even to take food, as the Apostle commanded (I Cor. V).”

Likewise, concerning such persons, the Council of Ancyra, chapter 24, states:

“A certain man who had a fiancée violated her sister and made her pregnant; afterward he took as his wife the woman to whom he had been betrothed. The woman who had been violated then killed herself by hanging. Those who had been aware of the matter were ordered, after ten years of satisfaction, to receive the established stages of penance.”

Likewise, in the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 2, concerning women who marry two brothers, or men who take two sisters as wives, it is stated:

“If a woman marries two brothers, she is to be cast out until death. Nevertheless, at the point of death, out of mercy, if she promises that, once restored to health, she will dissolve the bonds of this union, she shall obtain the fruit of penance. If a woman or man dies while in such a marriage, penance will be difficult for the survivor while life remains.”

Likewise, concerning those who are joined to two sisters, the Council of Elvira, chapter 61, states:

“If anyone, after the death of his wife, takes her sister, and she is a believer, he is to abstain from communion for five years, unless perhaps the necessity of illness compels peace to be granted more quickly.”

Likewise, concerning a woman who takes two brothers in marriage, or a man who has two sisters as wives, the Council of Bishop Martin, chapter 78, states:

“If a woman marries two brothers, or if a man marries two sisters, they are to abstain from communion until death. At death, communion is to be granted to them out of mercy. But if they survive after receiving communion and recover from their illness, they are to perform full penance for the prescribed period.”

Likewise, in the Apostolic Canon, chapter 19, it is written:

“Whoever takes two sisters in marriage, or his brother’s daughter, cannot be a cleric.”

## CHAPTER III—Concerning Those Who Commit Adultery

Adultery is condemned not only by the law, but is also altogether forbidden by evangelical authority. Therefore the holy Fathers, instructed by heavenly teaching, decreed what must be observed concerning it.

For in the Council of Ancyra, chapter 18, it is written:

“If someone’s wife has committed adultery, or if he himself has committed adultery, he must perform seven years of penance and afterward be restored according to his former rank.”

Likewise, in the Council of Carthage, chapter 69, concerning those who leave their wives, or women who leave their husbands, so that they may remain apart, it is written:

“It has been decided that, in accordance with evangelical and apostolic discipline, neither a man dismissed by his wife nor a woman dismissed by her husband is to be joined to another, but they are to remain as they are or be reconciled to each other. If they refuse, they are to be reduced to penance; and in this matter it is to be promulgated that the imperial law should be sought.”

Likewise, in the decrees of Pope Innocent, chapter 24, it is written that husbands should not associate with adulterous women. It was desired to know why believing husbands do not associate with adulterous wives, while wives appear to remain in the company of adulterous husbands.

In this matter Christian religion condemns adultery equally in both sexes. But women do not readily accuse their husbands of adultery, and hidden sins do not receive punishment. Men, however, more freely customarily report adulterous wives to priests; and therefore communion is denied to women once their crime has been exposed. But when men’s offense remains hidden, no one is easily deprived of communion on the basis of suspicions. He will certainly be removed if his crime is revealed. Since the cause is therefore the same, when proof is lacking, the reason for punishment sometimes remains inactive.

Likewise, in the same decrees, chapter 27, it is written:

“Those who, after a divorce has intervened, have undergone separation and then joined themselves to other marriages are shown to be adulterers. Your affection also inquired about those who, after a divorce had intervened, joined themselves to another marriage: it is clear that they are adulterers on both sides.

“Those who, while their wife is still alive—even though the marriage appears to have been dissolved—hurry to another union cannot fail to be regarded as adulterers. Indeed, even those persons to whom such people are joined appear themselves to have committed adultery, according to what we read in the Gospel: ‘Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery. Likewise, whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery’ (Matt. V).

“Therefore all are to be kept from communion. Nothing of this kind can be decreed concerning their parents or relatives unless they are discovered to have encouraged the illicit union.”

Likewise, in the Council of Elvira, chapter 9, concerning women who have left adulterous husbands and marry others, it is written:

“A believing woman who has left an adulterous husband, himself a believer, and takes another husband is to be prohibited from marrying. If she marries, she is not to receive communion before the man whom she left has departed from this world, unless perhaps the necessity of illness compels communion to be granted.”

## CHAPTER IV—Concerning Those Who Commit Fornication

Likewise, in the Council of Elvira, chapter 30, concerning fornicators, it is written:

“Those who committed fornication in their youth are not to be ordained subdeacons, because they were being promoted to a higher rank through deception. If any have been ordained in the past, they are to be removed.”

Likewise, in the same council, chapter 31, concerning young men who commit fornication after baptism, it is written:

“Young men who have committed fornication after receiving the faith of saving baptism are, once they have taken wives and completed legitimate penance, to be admitted to communion.”

Likewise, in the same council, chapter 42, concerning one who, while having a wife, commits fornication repeatedly, it is written:

“If a believer who has a wife has committed fornication not once but repeatedly, he is to be confronted at the point of death. If he promises that he will cease, communion is to be given to him. If, after being restored, he commits fornication again, it has been decided that he is no longer to be granted the communion of peace.”

Likewise, in the same council, chapter 13, concerning virgins consecrated to God who commit adultery, it is written:

“Virgins who have dedicated themselves to God, if they have broken their pledge of virginity and served the same lust, not understanding what they have committed, are not to be given communion even at the end of life. But if, once persuaded by her own desire, such a woman has fallen through the weakness of the body, and after committing the vice has done penance during her lifetime so that she abstains from intercourse, it has been decided that she ought to receive communion at the end of life.”

Likewise, in the same council, chapter 14, concerning secular virgins who commit fornication, it is written:

“Virgins who have not preserved their virginity, if they marry and retain as husbands those who violated them, because they have violated only the marriage bond, are to be reconciled after one year without penance. But if they have known other men, because they have committed fornication, it has been decided that, after five years and after completing legitimate penance, they ought to be admitted to communion.”

Likewise, in the Council of Ancyra, chapter 18, concerning those who have professed virginity, and concerning those who are reported to live with certain persons under the guise of sisters, it is written:

“All who, promising virginity, invalidate their pledge are to be counted among those who have married twice. We prohibit virgins from living together with certain men as though they were sisters.”

## CHAPTER V—Concerning Those Who Join Themselves to Consecrated Virgins, and Concerning Veiled Virgins Who Commit Fornication

Likewise, in the decrees of Pope Gelasius, chapter 20, concerning those who join themselves to consecrated virgins and commit incestuous unions, and concerning the fact that they cannot receive communion unless they have perhaps performed public penance, it is stated:

“We have learned that certain men rashly join themselves to sacred virgins and, after their dedication to God, mingle incestuous and sacrilegious unions with them. It is immediately just that these virgins be cast out from sacred communion and not received at all except through public and approved penance. Nevertheless, communion as viaticum is not to be denied to those who are departing from this world, provided they have done penance.”

Likewise, in the decrees of Pope Innocent, chapter 20, concerning virgins who are not veiled but have gone astray, it is written:

“Those who, although not yet covered with the sacred veil, had always professed to remain in the purpose of virginity—if they should perhaps marry, although they had not been veiled—must perform penance for some time, because their pledge was held by the Lord.

“For if among human beings a contract made in good faith is ordinarily dissolved for no reason whatsoever, how much more can this promise, which she made with God, be dissolved without punishment? For if the Apostle Paul said that those who departed from their profession of widowhood had condemnation because they had broken their first faith (I Tim. V), how much more do virgins deserve this who have attempted to break faith with their former promise!”

## CHAPTER VI—Concerning Those Who Fornicate Unnaturally

In the Council of Ancyra, chapter 15, concerning those who fornicate unnaturally—that is, those who have intercourse with animals or are polluted with males—it is written:

“Concerning those who have acted unnaturally, or who do so: all who committed such a crime before the age of twenty are to merit the communion of prayers after completing fifteen years in penance. Then, remaining for five years in this communion, they may at last receive the sacraments of the offering.

“Their manner of life is also to be examined, namely, what sort of persons they were during the time of their repentance; and thus they are to obtain mercy. But if they have clung to these crimes insatiably, they are to spend a longer period in performing penance.

“All who, after reaching the age of twenty, have fallen into this sin while having wives are to be received into the communion of prayers after performing twenty-five years of penance. Remaining in that communion for five years, they may then at last receive the sacraments of the offering.

“But if some, while having wives and having passed their fiftieth year of age, have sinned in this way, they are to obtain the grace of communion at the end of life.”

Likewise, in the same council, chapter 16, concerning those who have formerly been polluted with beasts or males, or who still languish in this vice, it is written:

“Those who have lived unnaturally and have polluted others with the leprosy of an unjust crime, the holy synod commanded to pray among those who are endangered by an unclean spirit.”

## CHAPTER VII—Concerning Married Persons, If One of Them Is Taken Captive

Likewise, in the decrees of Pope Innocent, chapter 37, it is written:

“If someone’s wife has been carried away into captivity and the husband has taken another wife, when the first returns, the second woman must be excluded.”

Innocent wrote to Probus:

“The storm of barbarian violence brought misfortune upon the order established by the laws. For, when a marriage had been properly established between Fortunius and Ursa, the invasion of captivity would have caused a blemish unless the provisions of sacred religion had taken care of the matter.

“Since the aforementioned woman Ursa was being held in captivity, the said Fortunius is known to have entered into another marriage with Restituta. But, by the Lord’s favor, Ursa returned and approached us, proving without anyone’s doubt that she was the wife of the aforesaid man.

“Therefore, illustrious lord and deservedly my son, with the Catholic faith supporting us, we have decreed that the marriage founded originally by divine grace is the valid marriage. The union with the second woman, while the first survives and has not been rejected by divorce, can in no way be legitimate.”

## CHAPTER VIII—That a Wife Is One Thing and a Concubine Another, and That There Is No Duplication of Marriage When, After a Slave Woman Is Rejected, a Wife Is Taken

[Col. 1409B]

In the decrees of Pope Leo, chapter 19, it is written that a wife is one thing and a concubine another.

Let no one err who gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has had a concubine. Not every woman joined to a man is the man’s wife, just as not every son is his father’s heir. The covenants of marriage are legitimate among freeborn persons and among equals. This was established by the Lord long before the beginning of Roman law.

Thus a wife is one thing and a concubine another, just as a slave woman is one thing and a free woman another. Therefore, to make clear the distinction between these persons, the Apostle also adduces testimony from Genesis, where it is said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son. For the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Gen. XXI).

Since the partnership of marriage was established from the beginning in such a way that, beyond the union of the sexes, it contained within itself the sacrament of Christ and the Church, there is no doubt that a woman does not belong to marriage in whom it is shown that there was no nuptial mystery.

Therefore, if a cleric of any place gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine, this must not be understood as giving her to a married man, unless perhaps that woman is seen to have been made free, legally endowed with a dowry, and honored by a public marriage. Women joined to men by their fathers’ decision are without guilt if the women whom the men keep were not wives, because a married woman is one thing and a concubine another.

Likewise, in the same decrees, chapter 20, it is written that there is no duplication of marriage when, after a slave woman is rejected, a wife is taken:

“To cast a slave woman away from the marriage bed and take a wife of certain free birth is not a duplication of marriage but an advancement in honorable conduct. Certainly the negligence of such men is blameworthy, but they are not to be driven to utter despair, so that, encouraged by frequent exhortations, they may faithfully carry out what they necessarily sought.

“For no one is to be despaired of while he remains in this body, since what is sometimes postponed through lack of confidence arising from age is accomplished through more mature counsel, and appears to be rightly established in marriage.”

## CHAPTER IX—Concerning One Who Takes as Wife a Woman Whose Husband Has Been Taken Captive

[Col. 1410A]

Likewise, in the decrees of Pope Leo, chapter 43, it is written that the man who takes as wife a woman whose husband has been taken captive does not appear to be blameworthy; nevertheless, he is not to be judged culpable or regarded as an invader of another’s rights because he assumed the place of a husband who was thought no longer to exist.

For many things belonging to those who had been taken captive could thus pass into another’s possession; nevertheless, it is entirely just that, when the same persons return, their own possessions should be restored to them. If this is rightly observed with regard to slaves, fields, houses, and possessions, how much more must it be observed in the restoration of marriages, so that what was disturbed by the necessity of war may be restored through the remedy of peace.

## CHAPTER X—Concerning One Who Has a Concubine in Addition to His Wife

[Col. 1410B]

In the Council of Toledo, chapter 7, it is written concerning one who has a wife and also has a concubine, that he is not to receive communion:

“If a believer who has a wife has a concubine, he is not to receive communion. But one who does not have a wife and has a concubine in place of a wife is not to be excluded from communion, provided only that he is content with the union of one woman, whether wife or concubine, as he prefers. If he lives with others, however, he is to be cast out until he ceases, and he is to return to penance.”

## CHAPTER XI—Concerning Parricide and Those Who Kill Their Own Children

[Col. 1410C]

How detestable a crime parricide is, the Lord himself demonstrated in the judgment passed between Cain and his brother Abel, when he said to Cain the parricide: “You shall be cursed upon the earth, which has opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand. It shall not give you its fruits. Wandering and fugitive you shall be upon the earth” (Gen. IV).

In this he also placed a sign, namely, that he should live forever as a trembling and groaning fugitive and should no longer dare to establish a settled dwelling anywhere.

But because in modern times fugitive parricides roam through various places and devote themselves to various vices and the allurements of gluttony, it seems better to me that, remaining in one place, they should chastise themselves with strict penance, if perhaps they may merit receiving forgiveness for their crime from the Lord’s goodness.

[Col. 1410D] For they may no longer take up the military belt or enjoy weddings and the bond of marriage, because the sacred Canons do not allow this for them—as we shall now show when the synodal decrees concerning penitents for the guilt of grave crimes are set forth.

Accordingly, in the Council of Ancyra, chapter 20, concerning those who kill their own children conceived through fornication by various means, it is written:

“Concerning women who fornicate and kill their own children, or who act to expel from the womb what has been conceived, the ancient decision indeed removes them from the Church until the end of life. But now we define more humanely that we grant them a period of ten years, according to the prescribed stages of penance.”

Likewise, in the Council of Elvira, chapter 63, concerning women who kill children conceived in adultery, it is written:

“If a woman has conceived through adultery while her husband is absent and, after the crime, kills the child, it has been decided that communion is scarcely to be given even at the end of life, because she has doubled her crime.”

Likewise, in the Council of Hilerdum, chapter 2, concerning those who cause abortions or kill their newborn children, it is written:

“Those of either sex who strive to kill children wrongly conceived through adultery, whether conceived or born, or who crush them in their mothers’ wombs with certain potions, are to be given communion after seven years have elapsed, provided that throughout the whole of their lives they persist in tears and humility.”

## CHAPTER XII—Concerning Voluntary Homicide

In the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 21, concerning homicides, it is written:

“Those who have committed voluntary homicide are to submit themselves continually to penance, but they are to attain perfection near the point of death.”

## CHAPTER XIII—Concerning Homicides and False Witnesses

Likewise, in the Council of Agde, chapter 34, concerning homicides and false witnesses, it is written:

“Therefore we have decreed that homicides and false witnesses are to be removed from ecclesiastical communion unless they have washed away the crimes they committed through the satisfaction of penance.”

## CHAPTER XIV—Concerning Those Who Kill Their Slaves Without a Judge, and the Mistress Who Kills Her Slave Woman Out of Jealousy

Likewise, in the Council of Agde, chapter 62, concerning those who kill their slaves without a judge, it is written:

“If anyone kills his own slave without the knowledge of a judge, he shall cleanse himself of the guilt of bloodshed through excommunication or two years of penance.”

[The supplied source ends here.]

Item, in the Council of Eliberitanum, canon 5, it is written concerning a mistress who kills a maidservant out of jealousy:

“If any woman, inflamed by jealous fury, beats her maidservant with blows so that she gives up her life amid torment within the third day—since it is uncertain whether she killed her intentionally or by accident—if intentionally, she shall be admitted to communion after seven years; if accidentally, after five years, once the prescribed penance has been performed. But if she should become ill during the appointed period, she shall receive communion.”

### CHAPTER XV.—Concerning homicides committed involuntarily, and those who excuse themselves as innocent of homicide committed in battle by order of rulers

[Col. 1411D] In the Council of Neocaesarea, canon 22, it is written concerning those who have committed homicide involuntarily:

“Concerning homicides committed involuntarily, the earlier ruling ordered that perfection be attained after seven years of penance; the second, however, prescribed completion of a period of five years.”

But since some excuse a homicide recently perpetrated in the revolt and battle of our rulers, as though everyone ought necessarily to do penance for it because it was carried out by order of the rulers and brought to an end by God’s judgment, we know that God’s judgment is always just and worthy of no reproach. Concerning this it is also written: “The Lord is righteous in all his ways, and holy [Col. 1412A] in all his works; he judges the world with equity and the peoples in his truth; without him not even a sparrow falls upon the earth” (Psalm 144).

Yet no one can penetrate all God’s judgments, since it is written: “The judgments of God are a great abyss” (Psalm 35). Therefore those who wish to defend this wicked killing ought to consider whether they can excuse before God’s eyes as innocent those who, because of avarice—which is the root of all evils and is compared with the service of idols—and because of favor toward their temporal lords, despised the eternal Lord and, scorning his commandments, committed homicide not by accident but deliberately.

For concerning those who killed people involuntarily, we read that God, through the lawgiver, appointed cities of refuge [Col. 1412B], so that those who fled to them might be saved from the avenger of their kinsman’s blood and might not die. Thus it is written in Deuteronomy:

“This shall be the law concerning the homicide whose life is to be preserved. If someone strikes his neighbor unknowingly, and it is established that he had no hatred against him either yesterday or the day before, but that he went simply with him into the forest to cut wood, and, when cutting the wood, the axe should slip from his hand, or the iron fall from the handle, and strike and kill his companion, he shall flee to one of the cities mentioned above and live, lest his neighbor, whose blood has been shed, should, driven by the sting of grief, strike his soul” (Deuteronomy 19).

But concerning one who has killed someone deliberately, it is commanded in Exodus:

“If anyone deliberately and by ambush [Col. 1412C] kills his neighbor, you shall drag him away from my altar, so that he may die” (Exodus 21).

And in Deuteronomy:

“If anyone,” he says, “hating his neighbor, lies in wait for his life, and rises up against him and strikes him, so that he dies, and he flees to one of the cities mentioned above, the elders of that city shall send and take him from the place of refuge; they shall hand him over to the hands of his neighbor whose blood has been shed, and he shall die. You shall not pity him” (Deuteronomy 19).

If, then, someone says that the one whom the Lord judged worthy of death is not guilty, how is he not opposing the law of God, since he asserts that what the Lord commanded is null and void? He must therefore see to it that he does not perhaps belong to the number of those to whom it is said through the prophet:

“Woe to you who sew pillows under every elbow [Col. 1412D] and make cushions for deceiving souls” (Ezekiel 13).

And elsewhere:

“Woe to you,” he says, “who call evil good and good evil, who make light darkness and darkness light, who call bitter sweet and sweet bitter. Such people kill souls that do not die and give life to those who do not live” (Isaiah 5).

Whoever, therefore, says that anyone can obtain forgiveness from God for evil deeds without worthy penance is completely mistaken. And when, having been deceived, he hastens to deceive others, he is bound by a double offense: namely, his own error and the deception of another.

But amid these matters it must be understood that there is a great difference between a legitimate ruler and a rebellious tyrant; between one who seeks to overturn the tranquility of Christian peace [Col. 1413A] and one who strives with weapons to defend justice against iniquity. Concerning this, many examples of brave men are found both under the ancient Law and under the New Testament, and these can instruct us what we ought to think about such an act.

### CHAPTER XVI.—Concerning administrators and those who dictate criminal petitions

It is easy to discover what the sacred canons think concerning administrators who exercise secular judgments according to the law of their forebears. For in the decrees of Pope Innocent, canon 23, it is read:

“It was therefore asked concerning those who, after baptism, served as administrators and either exercised torture alone or also pronounced a capital sentence. Concerning these, we read that nothing was defined by our predecessors. For they remembered [Col. 1413B] that these powers had been granted by God, that the sword had been given for the punishment of the guilty, and that God’s minister had been appointed as an avenger in such matters. How, then, could they condemn an action which they saw had been granted by the authority of the Lord? Concerning these matters, therefore, we hold to what has hitherto been observed, lest we appear either to overturn discipline or to act against the authority of the Lord. They themselves, however, shall preserve a record of all their actions when they render an account.”

Again, in the same decrees, canon 30, it is written that those who dictate criminal petitions are to be considered exempt from guilt:

“You wished to inquire whether, because of the regeneration of baptism, permission is granted to those who dictate petitions to ask rulers for someone’s death or for bloodshed on account of guilt. Rulers never grant this without an investigation; rather, they always refer the matters or crimes in question to judges [Col. 1413C], so that punishment may be imposed after the case has been examined. When these matters have been delegated to the investigator, either acquittal or condemnation is pronounced according to the nature of the case. And while the authority of the laws is exercised against the wicked, the one who dictated the petition will be exempt.”

### CHAPTER XVII.—Concerning the necessary crime committed by the people

Concerning how the necessary crime of the people is usually allowed to pass unpunished, the same pope, responding to questions from certain bishops of Macedonia, wrote as follows:

“Let your love therefore foresee that such matters have remained thus far, and observe that, as you indeed say, necessity compelled it; even churches established in peace cannot presume to do otherwise. But, as often happens [Col. 1413D] whenever sin is committed by peoples and crowds, because punishment cannot be exacted from everyone on account of their multitude, such matters usually pass unpunished. I therefore say that the former matters must be left to God’s judgment; for the future, the greatest care must be taken to prevent them.”

Here, as it seems to me, this apostolic teacher is not saying that the people need not do penance for their evil deeds, but that because punishment cannot be exacted from everyone on account of the multitude, the earlier matters must be left to God’s judgment; for the future, the greatest care must be taken to prevent such things from occurring.

### CHAPTER XVIII.—Concerning theft

Concerning theft, it is written in the Council of Agde, canon 5:

“If a cleric commits theft against the Church, let him be granted communion as a stranger.”

[Col. 1414A] Again, in the same council, canon 26, it is written:

“If any clerics should presume, with blameworthy and punishable obstinacy, either to suppress, deny, or perhaps hand over to adversaries documents by which the Church’s possession is secured, let them restore from their own resources whatever loss has been inflicted upon the Church through the withholding of the documents, and let them be deprived of communion. The same applies to those who, wickedly solicited to the Church’s detriment, have accepted such documents from traitors.”

### CHAPTER XIX.—Concerning conspiracy or collusion

Concerning conspiracy or collusion, it is written in the Council of Chalcedon, canon 14:

“The crime of conspiracy or collusion is altogether prohibited even by secular laws; much more should it be admonished that it must not occur in the Church of God. Therefore, if any clerics [Col. 1414B] or monks are found conspiring or colluding, or laying snares for bishops or clerics, let them be completely expelled from their own rank.”

### CHAPTER XX.—Concerning those who bind themselves by oath not to return to peace

Concerning those who bind themselves by oath not to return to peace, it is written in the Council of Hilaria, canon 7:

“Whoever binds himself by oath to quarrel with anyone and never in any way to return to peace shall, on account of perjury, be separated for one year from communion of the body and blood of the Lord, and shall expiate his guilt by almsgiving and tears, and by fasting insofar as he is able. Let him hasten to come quickly to charity, which covers a multitude of sins.”

### CHAPTER XXI.—Concerning those who make harmful oaths, and how they ought to do penance

[Col. 1414C]

Concerning an unjust oath that pertains to harm against one’s neighbor, the following is contained in the Council of Toledo, canon 26:

“For when we are compelled to swear falsely, we offend the Creator, but stain only ourselves. When, however, we fulfill harmful promises and proudly despise God’s commands in order to injure our neighbors with wicked cruelty, we ourselves slaughter ourselves with the more cruel sword of death. There we are struck by the twofold weapon of sins; here we are slain in three ways.

“Therefore it remains that our judgment should proceed in the direction where a path of mercy has opened. This is so acceptable to the Lord that he desires it more than venerable sacrifices, as he himself says: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’ (Matthew 9).

“Now that this permission for clemency has been granted, we commit the work of mercy itself to the power of the glorious ruler, so that, because God has opened to him an avenue for showing mercy, he too may not deny the remedies of compassion. Let these be regulated with such princely discretion that, through the mercy granted to them, no people or country may suffer any danger or loss through them; let it be sufficient that these matters have been moderated under the pretext of mercy.

“Nevertheless, because oaths have either already been exacted or may henceforth be exacted for the safety of royal power, for the constitution of the people and the country, we decree that they are to be observed indissolubly with every safeguard and vigilance, even though the religious prohibition against mutilation of limbs [Col. 1415A] and the sentence of death be wholly set aside.

“But lest the crafty wickedness of depraved minds should at some time provoke us into the guilt of perjury, or claim that this judgment departs from the rule of holy faith, we have taken care to attach to this account both the testimonies of divine authority and those of the Fathers who preceded us.

“Thus he spoke through Jeremiah:

‘Suddenly I shall speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to uproot and destroy it. If that nation repents of its evil, concerning which I spoke against it, I too shall repent of the evil that I had thought to do to it’ (Jeremiah 18).

“And through Ezekiel:

‘If,’ he says, ‘I tell the righteous that he shall live, and he, trusting in his righteousness, commits iniquity, all his righteousness shall be forgotten, and in the iniquity that he has committed [Col. 1415B], in that he shall die. But if I tell the wicked, “You shall surely die,” and he does penance, he shall live and shall not die’ (Ezekiel 18).

“If, then, our conversion changes the divine judgment in this way, why should the abundant tears or distress of the wretched not, through mercy, moderate so harsh a vengeance? For this reason punishment is often promised even to the Israelite people and then suspended, and the destruction of the Ninevites is calmed by a change in the divine judgment.

“For Saint Ambrose, in the third book of *On Duties*, chapter 12, says:

‘The disposition ought therefore to be pure and sincere, so that each person may speak plainly and possess his vessel in holiness, lest he mislead his brother through guarded wording; let him promise nothing dishonorable. But if he has promised something, it is more tolerable not to fulfill the promise than to do [Col. 1415C] what is disgraceful.

“‘Often many people bind themselves by the oath of a solemn promise; and although they themselves recognize that the oath ought not to have been made, nevertheless, out of regard for it, they do what they promised. Thus, as we wrote above concerning Herod, he shamefully promised a reward to the dancing girl and cruelly paid it (Matthew 14). Shameful was the kingdom promised for a dance; cruel was the prophet’s death granted out of reverence for an oath! How much more tolerable would such perjury have been than keeping the oath.’

“And shortly afterward, distinguishing the case of Jephthah, he says: ‘A pitiable necessity, which is discharged by parricide.’ It is better not to vow what the person to whom the promise is made would not wish to be fulfilled.

“And a little later: ‘Therefore not every promise must always be fulfilled. Indeed, the Lord himself, as Scripture indicates, frequently changes his judgment.’

[Col. 1415D] “Likewise, the most holy man Augustine, sharp in the keenness of his investigation, says: ‘The way of discovery lies open: the lesser alternatives should always be chosen. For even one who is enclosed so that he cannot escape by the circuit of walls rushes toward escape where the shorter wall is found.’

“For this reason Isidore also says: ‘It is more tolerable not to fulfill an oath than to remain in the disgrace of fornication.’ Likewise, in the *Synonyms*: ‘In evil promises, withdraw your pledge; in a shameful vow, change your decision; what you rashly vowed, do not do. The promise that is fulfilled through crime is impious.’

“Therefore one who has sworn wrongly must necessarily perform worthy penance, because he has taken the name of the Lord in vain, against his command; for it is written in Exodus:

‘The Lord will not hold innocent the one who takes the name of the Lord his God in vain’ (Exodus 20).

“And in Leviticus:

‘You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of the Lord your God: I am the Lord’ (Leviticus 19).

“Nevertheless, he must not do at all the evil that he had sworn by oath to do, since foolish vows must be broken.”

### CHAPTER XXII.—Concerning those who flee to the protection of the Church, so that they may not be handed over to their pursuers without a pledged agreement

Concerning those who flee to the protection of the Church and must not be handed over, it is written in the Council of Orange, canon 5:

“Those who have fled to the church must not be handed over, but must be defended by reverence for the holy place [Col. 1416B] and by intercession.”

In the Council of Orléans, canon 1, concerning murderers, adulterers, and thieves who flee to the church, it is written:

“We decree that what the ecclesiastical canons have established and Roman law has enacted must be observed: that it is altogether unlawful to drag such persons from the atria of the church or from the bishop’s house; nor may they be removed from the altar unless, after oaths have been given upon the Gospels, they are secured against death, bodily harm, and every kind of punishment, in such a way that the criminal may make satisfaction to the person against whom he is guilty.

“But if the guilty person is convicted of violating his oath, he shall be separated not only from communion with the Church and all clerics, but also from the table of Catholics. If he does not wish to settle with the person to whom he is liable, and, driven by fear, the guilty person [Col. 1416C] leaves the church, he is not to be pursued by the church’s clerics.”

Again, in the same council, canon 2, concerning abductors who flee to the church, it is written:

“Concerning abductors, we have judged that the following must be established: if an abductor comes to the church with the woman he has abducted, and it is established that the woman herself suffered violence, she shall immediately be freed from the abductor’s power. The abductor, with immunity from death or punishment granted, shall be subjected to service, or shall have the option of ransoming himself.

“But if it is established that the abducted woman has a father, and the girl consented to the abductor, she shall be restored, excused to the authority of her father; and the abductor shall be held liable to the father for satisfaction according to the father’s superior status.”

Again, in the same council, canon 3, concerning slaves who flee to the church, it is written [Col. 1416D]:

“If a slave flees to the church for any offense, and, once the offense has been waived by his master, receives an oath from him, he shall immediately be compelled to return to his master’s service. After he has been handed over to his master upon the giving of the oath, if he is proved to have suffered any punishment for the same offense for which he had been excused, he shall, on account of contempt for the Church and violation of faith, be regarded as excluded from communion and from the table of Catholics, as stated above.

“But if a slave, defended by the Church on account of his offense, has received, at the clerics’ insistence, sacred assurances guaranteeing immunity, it is permitted for his master to seize him if he refuses to leave.”

### CHAPTER XXIII.—Concerning those who seek divinations and serve incantations or auguries

[Col. 1417A]

In the Council of Ancyra, canon [lacuna], concerning those who seek divinations and follow the customs of the pagans, or introduce such people into their homes to inquire into something by magical art or for the purpose of purification, let them lie under the rule of five years, according to the established degrees of penance.

In the Council of Laodicea, canon 36, concerning those who use incantations and amulets, it is written:

“It is not fitting for those devoted to sacred offices or for clerics to be magicians or enchanters, or to make amulets, which are demonstrably bonds for their souls. We command that those who use such things be expelled from the Church.”

[Col. 1417B] In the Council of Agde, concerning diviners and those who observe auguries, so that they may be separated from the Church, canon 43, it is written:

“Lest it perhaps appear that we have omitted what especially attacks the faith of the Catholic religion: some clerics or laypeople devote themselves to auguries, and, under the name of a fictitious religion in which they profess the knowledge of divination through the lots of the saints, or promise the future by inspecting any sort of objects. Whoever, whether cleric or layperson, is discovered either consulting or teaching such practices shall be regarded as an outsider to the Church.”

In the Council of Toledo, canon 29, it is written:

“If any bishop, priest, or deacon, or anyone from the clerical order, is caught consulting magicians, haruspices, diviners, or lot-casters, or those who profess some form of occult art, or anyone practicing similar things [Col. 1417C], he shall be deposed from the honor of his dignity and shall assume the care of a monastery. There, devoted to perpetual penance, he shall atone for the sacrilege he has committed.”

In the synod of Martin, canon 59, it is written:

“Priests and clerics must not be enchanters or make bindings, which are a binding of souls. If anyone does these things, let him be expelled from the Church.”

### CHAPTER XXIV.—That Christians may not preserve pagan traditions or participate in any of their festival observances

Again, in the same synod, canon 72, it is written:

“Christians must not retain the traditions of the pagans or observe the course of the moon or stars. Christians must not observe or worship the elements, or the course of the moon or stars [Col. 1417D], or the empty deception of signs, for building a house, for crops, for planting trees, or for joining marriages. For it is written: ‘Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God’ (1 Corinthians 10).”

Again, in the same council, canon 72, it is written that the Kalends must not be observed:

“Christians must not practice the wicked observances of the Kalends or devote themselves to idle pursuits; nor may they go around houses with laurel or the greenery of trees. All such observance is paganism.”

Again, in the same council, canon 75, it is written that medicinal herbs must not be gathered with any observance [Col. 1418A]:

“When gathering medicinal herbs, it is not permitted to employ any observances or incantations, except solely with the divine creed and the Lord’s Prayer, so that only God, the creator of all things and the Lord, may be honored.”

In the Council of Laodicea, canon 39, it is written concerning those Christians who celebrate pagan festivals:

“It is not fitting to celebrate festivals with pagans or to participate in the wickedness of those who are without God.”

### CHAPTER XXV.—That one must not feast with pagans

In the Council of Africa, canon 27, concerning the abolition of pagan banquets, it is written:

“It should also be requested that, since contrary to the divine commandments banquets [Col. 1418B] are held in many places which have been drawn from pagan error, so that now Christians are compelled by pagans to celebrate them, and from this it secretly appears that a second persecution is being carried out in the times of Christian emperors, they should order such things to be prohibited and forbidden by penalties imposed in cities and estates.

“This is especially necessary since in certain cities they do not hesitate to commit such acts even on the birthdays of the most blessed martyrs and in the sacred places themselves. On those days also—shameful as it is to say—they hold utterly wicked dances through the streets and public squares, so that the honor of married women and the modesty of countless women who devoutly come to the most sacred day are assailed by the insults of the wanton, and even access to that holy religion is almost shunned.”

[Col. 1418C] In the decrees of Pope Leo, canon 30, concerning those who have taken part in pagan banquets and sacrificial foods, it is written:

“If some have merely taken part in the banquet of pagans and eaten sacrificial foods, they can be cleansed by fasting and the laying on of hands; if they abstain from idol-offerings, they may participate in the sacraments of Christ. But if they have either worshiped idols or been defiled by homicides or fornications, they must not be admitted to communion except through public penance.”

### CHAPTER XXVI.—Concerning Christians who eat with Jews, and that Jews may not have Christian wives or concubines, or a Christian slave

In the Council of Eliberitanum, canon 55, concerning Christians who eat with Jews, it is written [Col. 1418D]:

“If any cleric or member of the faithful eats food with Jews, it has been decreed that he is to abstain from communion, so that he may be cleansed.”

In the Council of Toledo, canon 14, concerning Jews, it is written:

“At the Council’s suggestion, our most glorious Lord ordered the following to be inserted into the canons: Jews must not be permitted to have Christian wives or concubines, nor to purchase a Christian slave for their own use. But the children born from such a union must be brought to baptism. They must not perform public offices through which an opportunity might be given them to inflict punishment upon Christians.

“But if any Christians have been defiled by those Jews in their rite [Col. 1419A], or have even been circumcised, they shall return, without repayment of the price, to freedom and to the Christian religion.”

### CHAPTER XXVII.—That it is not fitting for Christians to attend drinking parties, become actors, or dance at weddings or banquets

In the Council of Laodicea, canon 55, it is written that it is not fitting for Christians to attend drinking parties:

“It is not fitting for priests or clerics to hold banquets arising from gatherings or drinking parties. Nor can this be fitting for laypeople.”

In the Council of Africa, canon 30, concerning actors who have become Christians, it is written that the following should also be requested:

“If anyone wishes to come to the grace of Christianity from any kind of theatrical or public entertainment and to remain free from that stain, no one may again lead or compel him to practice the same activities.”

In the Council of Laodicea, canon 53, it is written that people must not dance at Christian weddings:

“It is not fitting for Christians who go to weddings to applaud or dance, but to dine or lunch reverently, as befits Christians.”

### CHAPTER XXVIII.—That the divine Scriptures should be read at the bishop’s table, and that men devoted to the sacred orders ought not to pursue drunkenness

In the Council of Toledo, canon 7, it is written that the divine Scriptures should be read at the bishop’s table:

“Out of reverence for God and the priests, the entire holy synod established that, since idle stories are often inserted into meals, the reading of the divine Scriptures should be interwoven into every priestly banquet. Through this, souls are built up toward goodness and unnecessary stories are restrained.”

In the Apostolic Canon, canon 42, it is written that a bishop, priest, or deacon must not be a gambler or a drunkard:

“A bishop, priest, or deacon who devotes himself to dice or drunkenness must either desist or certainly be condemned.”

### CHAPTER XXIX.—Concerning the continence and chastity of clerics

In the Council of Carthage, canon 3, concerning the continence and chastity of clerics, it is written:

“Bishop Aurelius said: When the regulation of continence and chastity was discussed in the preceding council, it was decided that these three ranks, which are joined by a certain obligation of chastity through consecration [Col. 1419D]—namely, bishops, priests, and deacons—should, as is fitting for holy overseers and priests of God, as well as for levites and those who serve the divine sacraments, be continent in all things, so that they may simply obtain from God what they ask.

“Let us also preserve what the apostles taught and antiquity itself maintained.”

### CHAPTER XXX.—That priests must not carry out mutilations among the Church’s dependents or judge anything worthy of death

In the Council of Toledo, canon 6, it is written that priests must not carry out any mutilations among the Church’s dependents or judge anything worthy of death [Col. 1420A]:

“Those to whom the Lord’s sacraments are to be administered may not exercise a judgment of blood. Therefore such excesses must be prohibited with the greatest care, lest, driven by impulses of indiscriminate presumption, they presume either to judge by their own sentence something deserving death or to inflict any mutilation upon persons themselves or order it to be inflicted.

“If any one of these, forgetful of the commandments, does such a thing either among the Church’s dependents or upon any persons, let him be deprived both of the honor and position of the order he has received and remain bound in a perpetual prison of condemnation. Nevertheless, communion must not be denied him when he departs this life, on account of the Lord’s mercy, who does not desire the death of a sinner but that he should turn and live.”

### CHAPTER XXXI.—Concerning clerics who rush into mutual slaughter

[Col. 1420B]

In the Council of Hilaria, canon 11, concerning clerics who rush into mutual slaughter, it is written:

“If any clerics rush into mutual slaughter, let the bishop punish the offense with the greater severity according to the indignity that the rank of their offices has suffered in such an excess.”

### CHAPTER XXXII.—Concerning avarice and greed, and that interest must not be demanded

In the Council of Carthage, canon 5, concerning avarice, it is written:

“Bishop Aurelius said: The greed of avarice is detestable; no one doubts that it is the mother of all evil things. Therefore it must be prohibited that anyone should usurp another’s boundaries or, for a payment, cross the limits [Col. 1420C] established by the fathers. Nor may any cleric receive interest on any matter.

“Although new proposals, whether obscure or concealed under some category, will receive a ruling after we have examined them, nevertheless, concerning matters on which divine Scripture has spoken most clearly, judgment must not be postponed but rather carried out. Therefore what is condemned in laypeople ought to be condemned much more severely in clerics.”

The entire council said:

“No one acts against the prophets or against the Gospels without danger.”

In the Council of Toledo, canon 23, concerning the evil of avarice, it is written:

“Avarice is the root of all evils, and its thirst also possesses the minds of priests. For many of the faithful, out of love for Christ and the martyrs [Col. 1420D], build basilicas in the bishops’ parishes and record offerings. The priests take these away and convert them to their own uses. Hence the worshipers of sacred things decline, while they lose their support. Hence the ruins of falling basilicas are not repaired, because everything is taken away by priestly avarice.

“Therefore the present council has decreed that bishops govern their dioceses in such a way that they presume to take nothing away from their rights, but, according to the authority of earlier councils, receive a third part both of offerings and of dues and crops. If they should presume to take anything more, it shall be restored through the council, either at the appeal of the founders themselves or, if they have already departed from this world, of their relatives.

“Let the founders of basilicas know, however [Col. 1421A], that they possess no authority over the things they confer upon those churches; rather, according to the institutions of the canons, just as the church itself belongs to the bishop’s administration, so does its endowment.”

In the Council of Nicaea, canon 17, concerning clerics who receive interest, it is written:

“Since many under the rule pursue avarice and shameful profits, and, forgetting divine Scripture, which says, ‘He who has not given his money at interest,’ lend money and demand hundredfold returns, the holy and great synod has justly decreed that if anyone is found, after this definition, receiving interest, or conducting business in any transaction or manner whatsoever, or demanding *hemiola*, that is, one-and-a-half times the amount, or devising anything of this sort for the sake of shameful profit, he shall be deposed from the clergy and [Col. 1421B] shall be excluded from the rule.”

In the decrees of Pope Leo, canon 3, it is written that not only clerics but also Christian laypeople must not demand interest:

“We have judged that we must not pass over the fact that certain people, seized by a desire for shameful profit, are already practicing usury. We grieve over this not only in the case of those established in clerical office, but also among laypeople who desire to be called Christians. We decree that those who are convicted of this are to be punished more severely, so that every opportunity for sinning may be removed.”

### CHAPTER XXXIII.—Concerning apostates

In the decrees of Pope Siricius, canon 3, concerning apostates, it is written:

“It has also been added that certain Christians [Col. 1421C] have passed into apostasy—a thing forbidden to say—and have been profaned by the observance of mourning and the pollution of sacrifices. We command that they be cut off from the body and blood of Christ, through which they had formerly been redeemed by being reborn. If at some time they should come to their senses and turn to lamentation, they must do penance for as long as they live. At the end of their life, the grace of reconciliation is to be granted them, since the Lord teaches: ‘I do not desire the death of a sinner; only that he should turn and live’ (Ezekiel 18).”

In the Council of Arles, canon 22, concerning apostates, it is written:

“Those who return late must not be received except through worthy penance. Concerning those who apostatize and never present themselves to the Church, nor even seek to do penance, and who, later seized by illness [Col. 1421D], request communion, it has been decreed that communion must not be given them unless they have confessed and produced fruits worthy of penance.”

Again, in the same council, canon 25, concerning apostates who do not return, it is written:

“Those who, after professing the holy religion, apostatize and return to the world, and afterward do not seek the remedies of penance, must not receive communion at all without penance. We also command that they not be admitted to clerical office. Nor may anyone, after penance, presume to resume secular dress; if he presumes to do so, he shall be regarded as separated from the Church.”

### CHAPTER XXXIV.—Concerning the profession of a monk

In the Council of Toledo, canon 59, concerning the profession of a monk, it is written [Col. 1422A]:

“A monk is made either by paternal devotion or by his own profession. Whichever of these bonds has been formed, it shall hold. Therefore we forbid such persons access to return to the world, and we forbid every return to the secular life.”

### CHAPTER XXXV.—Concerning the regulation of penance, and when penitents themselves are to be reconciled

In the Council of Africa, canon 10, it is written concerning penitents:

“Let the periods of penance be determined by the bishop’s judgment according to the differences among sins. Let a priest not reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop, except when the bishop’s absence makes necessity compelling. If the crime of any penitent is public and notorious and has disturbed the whole Church [Col. 1422B], let hands be laid upon him before the apse.”

In the decrees of Pope Innocent, canon 7, concerning penitents, it is written:

“Concerning penitents who are doing penance either for graver offenses or for lesser ones, Roman ecclesiastical custom shows that, if no illness intervenes, they are to be released on the Thursday before Easter. The priest, however, must judge the weight of the offenses, attending to the penitent’s confession and to the weeping and tears of the one who is correcting himself; then he must order him to be released when he has seen his satisfaction.

“Certainly, if anyone falls ill and reaches the point of despair, he is to be released before the time of Easter, lest he depart from the world without communion.”

### CHAPTER XXXVI.—Concerning those who die while placed under penance

[Col. 1422C]

In the Council of Arles, canon 12, concerning those who die while placed under penance, it is written:

“It has been decided that no one is to be sent away without communion; rather, because he prayed while doing penance, his offering is to be received.”

In the Council of Orange, canon 3, concerning penitents who depart from the body, it is written:

“Those who depart from the body after receiving penance are, it has been decided, to receive communion without the laying on of the hand of reconciliation. They called this, in accordance with the appropriate definition, the viaticum, which is sufficient consolation for the dying. If they survive, they shall remain in the order of penitents, so that, after displaying the necessary fruits of penance, they may receive legitimate communion with the laying on of the hand [Col. 1422D] of reconciliation.”

### CHAPTER XXXVII.—Concerning those who, violating penance, despise it and again transgress
In the Council of Orléans, chapter 4, it is written concerning those who violate penance:

“Those who, having forgotten the penance they undertook and the religious profession they made, relapse into secular pursuits are to be suspended from communion and separated from the banquets of all Catholics. If, after the prohibition, anyone should presume to eat with such a person, he too is to be deprived of communion.”

In the Council of Toledo, chapter 55, it is written concerning secular persons who accepted penance, had their hair tonsured, and, again becoming transgressors, returned to the lay state:

[Col. 1423A] “Those apprehended by their bishop are to be recalled to the penance from which they withdrew. If some cannot be reclaimed by penance and, after admonition, do not return, they are indeed to be condemned thereafter before the Church by the sentence of anathema. The same rule applies to those who were tonsured by their parents, or who, after sending their parents away, voluntarily devoted themselves to the religious life, but afterward assumed secular dress; when apprehended by a priest, they are to be recalled to the observance of religion after first performing penance. If the apostates cannot return, they are to be cast out by the sentence of anathema. This rule is also to be observed with widows, consecrated virgins, and women doing penance who put on the holy monastic habit and afterward either changed their clothing or entered into marriage.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII — That final penance is to be denied to no one

[Col. 1423B]

In the decrees of Pope Celestine, chapter 15, it is written that final penance is to be denied to no one:

“We have learned that penance is not to be denied to the dying, nor their desire to be granted—the desire by which, at the time of their death, they ask that their souls be aided by a remedy. I confess that we shudder to find anyone guilty of such great impiety as to despair of God’s mercy, as though He could not at any time come to the aid of one who hastens to Him, and rescue a person endangered beneath the horror of sins by the burden from which that person longs to be freed.

“What else, I ask, is this than to add death to one who is dying, and by one’s cruelty to kill his soul, lest it be able to be absolved? God, however, is most ready to come to our aid, and, inviting us to penance, promises:

“‘On whatever day the sinner is converted, his sins shall not be counted against him’ (Ezek. XVIII).

“And again:

“‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he be converted and live’ (ibid.).

“Whoever denies penance at the time of death therefore takes salvation away from a person. He despairs of God’s mercy who does not believe that God is sufficient, even in a moment, to aid the dying. The thief hanging at Christ’s right hand would have lost his reward if the penance of one hour had not helped him. While suffering punishment, he repented; and through the promise contained in a single utterance, with God’s promise, he earned a dwelling in paradise.

“True conversion to God by those placed at the end of life must therefore be judged by the mind rather than by the length of time, as the prophet declares in these words:

“‘When, having turned, you groan, then you will be saved.’

“Since, therefore, the Lord is the examiner of the heart, penance is not to be denied at any time to one who requests it, since that person binds himself to the Judge to whom he knows that all hidden things are revealed.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX — That one who asks pardon for illicit acts must also abstain from many lawful things; and that during the time of penance he ought not to engage in commercial profits

[Col. 1424A]

In the decrees of Pope Leo, chapter 22, it is written that one who asks pardon for illicit acts must also abstain from many lawful things.

“It is one thing to demand back what is justly owed; it is another to disdain one’s own possessions out of love for perfection. But one who asks pardon for illicit acts must also abstain from lawful things, since the Apostle says:

“‘All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial’ (1 Cor. VI).

“Therefore, if penitents have a case which they perhaps ought not to neglect, it is better for them to seek ecclesiastical judgment than a secular court.”

Likewise, in the same decrees, chapter 23, it is written that it is not fitting for a penitent to engage in commercial profits.

[Col. 1424B] “The quality of profit either excuses or accuses the merchant, because there is dishonest and shameful gain. Nevertheless, it is more advantageous for a penitent to suffer losses than to become entangled in the dangers of commerce, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene in the exchange between buyer and seller.”

## CHAPTER XL — That after penance one ought not to return to secular military service

Likewise, in the same decrees, chapter 24, it is written that after penance one ought not to return to secular military service:

“It is altogether contrary to ecclesiastical rules, after performing penance, to return to secular military service, since the Apostle says:

“‘No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs’ (2 Tim. II).”

Therefore, one who wishes to entangle himself in worldly military service is not free from the snares of the devil.

## EPILOGUE

I have taken care, holy Father, to collect for you these few chapters from the councils of the holy Fathers, so that you might have at hand, from their judgments, the means by which you could judge the uncultivated and untamed minds of the new people among whom you now reside. Thus they may know that they cannot sin with impunity, but that a sentence is always ready from you; that you may cut away the emerging vices of the wicked more swiftly, and grant timely consolation to the humble who weep over their sins with worthy satisfaction.

For since your holiness now dwells among them, it is fitting that, through the preaching of God’s word and the guardianship [Col. 1424D] of true religion, your sacred zeal should become known to all, so that the fruit of this good labor may win you praise here and bring forth an everlasting reward and glory in the future. Amen.

[Col. 1425]

# A LITTLE WORK OF THE BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, ON THE PASSION OF THE LORD

(Pez, *Anecdota*, vol. II, part II, p. 8.

[Col. 1425]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1425A]

If you wish to enter into life through Jesus, who is the way and the door; if you wish to eat from the tree of life and taste the hidden manna, do not let it frighten you, nor let it seem worthless to you, that everywhere you find the approach difficult and contemptible. He has thorns on his head, nails in his hands and feet, a lance in his side, scourges on his arms; he is wholly lacerated in body, and, like a leper, hideous to behold and difficult to follow.

But take care not to throw away the nut because of its bitter shell: for the more bitter it appears outwardly, the sweeter a kernel you will sometimes find within. Therefore, so that you may in some measure comprehend, with all the saints, what is the length, breadth, height, and depth of the mystery of the holy cross and of the Lord’s Passion—[Col. 1425B] which God hides from the wise and prudent of the world and reveals to little ones—understand the weight of the words that are spoken. For, with God’s cooperation, they prepare the soul to possess devotion in prayer, consolation in tribulation, and revelation in contemplation; and learn not only what has been given to us by God, but also Him who has been given to us.

In this meditation the fire will blaze forth if you also meditate upon these things simply and according to the literal sense. Here, therefore, carefully recognize the face of your Creator and Redeemer, and look upon the face of your Christ with the whole gaze of heart and body, with your entire intellect and affection, and with a deeply humbled spirit. Attend to this image as though Christ were presently dying on the cross, and consider in your heart whose image and inscription this is: [Col. 1425C] for He is God and man.

## CHAPTER II

Consider first, if you can, and as much as you can, how great is the interior length of clarity in the divinity—a length that lay hidden in Him for so many years, extending from end to end, having neither beginning nor end, in which God the Father chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world.

Consider also how great is the exterior length of that same reality in His humanity, in which He endured so long and so many things, throughout His whole body and over so long a period: from the sole of His foot to the crown of His head, from the Incarnation to the Resurrection.

Consider not only the length but also the breadth of His love, because He loved us not only with perpetual but also with immeasurable love. [Col. 1425D] Thus God, needing nothing, who made all things for Himself and subjected all things to humanity, after humanity had lost everything through sin, did not wish to lose humanity. [Col. 1426A] Instead, He established a lawgiver over it, carefully instructing it through the prophets, and at last coming personally Himself—or rather, mercifully showing Himself to us—and humbly putting on the lowliness of our flesh.

After the examples of perfect holiness, after words of saving knowledge, after miracles of singular power, doing good to all and suffering evil for all, He did this so that we might not die by an eternal death.

He wished to die in this way, with His hands extended, embracing everyone, calling everyone to Himself, rejecting no one, bowing His head and offering the kiss of peace to His enemies, wholly overlooking His own injury—or rather, making satisfaction for it. With His body pierced on every side and His side opened, He gave us and each of us most generously His body and blood, His heart and soul, indeed the whole God and man, and with Him life and inspiration [Col. 1426B] and all things. For evil He returned so many good things and endured so many evils.

## CHAPTER III

Attend and see how great was His love—how astonishing His love—that God wished to become man for humanity, and that, in order to exalt human beings, the Most High humbled Himself.

Therefore, just as a human being abhors and flees shame, labor, and pain, so God chose and embraced these things for humanity when, setting aside joy, He endured the cross, confusion, and reproach.

See, then, and consider how lofty was the depth of that love, which the Wisdom of God so united to Himself that love in Him was not only long and broad but also high and deep: the kind of love that it was fitting for God to display and necessary for humanity to discover.

See how great was that sublimity and glorious majesty from which He came, and how deep and contemptible the humility to which He descended: from the highest heaven to the lower regions of the earth; from the throne of glory to a place of misery; from the delights of the angels to all human troubles; from the bosom of the Father into the womb of a poor mother; from the narrowness of a virginal womb into the wretched stable of an ass and an ox; and afterward, because of Herod’s fear, into Egypt.

From there He remained in His homeland without honor, humbly enduring so many blasphemies, insults, injuries, and snares. In the midst of the disciples, like a servant of servants, He served even to the cleansing of sins and the washing of feet—including the feet of Judas the traitor, who could be appeased neither by such service, nor by a gracious meal, nor by gentle conversation, nor by the kiss of peace, but sold Him to His enemies for a contemptible price, to the death of the cross.

There He emptied Himself so completely that He descended from the gallows of thieves, His body into the tomb and His spirit into the underworld: at once rich and poor, living and dead, exalted and humbled; lofty above the heads of the angels, humble beneath the feet of sinners; regarded as a contemptible and weak sinner, mad, and the least of men.

## CHAPTER IV

Consider how great was the labor of His body, in which He had been so poor from His birth: fasting, keeping vigil, traveling about, preaching, and finally, because of the anguish of impending death, remaining in the agony of prolonged prayer until His sweat became blood.

He was deceitfully captured, bound most indecorously, and throughout the night shamefully beaten from house to house. Before the chief priests and nobles He was smeared with spittle and struck with blows. In the morning He was led to Pilate’s house and handed over to secular justice as though guilty of death. [Col. 1427B]

Then He was presented to Herod and regarded by Herod and his army as a fool. Again, before Pilate, He was mocked as the king of fools, and as a criminal He was treated with [harsh] words and beatings. Before so many Jews and Gentiles He was accused in the most contemptible manner, scourged with great severity, judged without cause, and compelled to carry the cross like a thief and murderer.

The Just One was condemned for the unjust and wicked, and condemned with the wicked—not to exile, imprisonment, or the loss of foot or hand, but to death, and to the most shameful death. He was lifted up before friends and enemies, on a solemn feast and in a prominent place, amid the vile arms of the cross, with His hands and feet stretched out and pierced with iron nails, and, hanging there, was mocked by everyone.

There the ears of His enemies heard blasphemies; His eyes saw them laughing and insulting Him; His nostrils could sense the stench; and to His thirsty mouth they offered a deadly drink. As Jerome says in his commentary on Isaiah, they had already plucked out the hairs of His beard.

## CHAPTER V

Look upon the letters of the crown—that is, the punctures by which the crown impressed itself around His head—and upon His entire face, hidden and despised, disfigured by spittle and blows, and bloodied by the sharp points of thorns.

His whole body was filled with black and red letters, as numerous as the wounds inflicted by scourging; it was bruised and sprinkled with drops of blood. Finally, the very beauty of the angels, the one more beautiful in form than the sons of men, was treated more shamefully than a leper and more cruelly than any criminal.

Amid these things, consider how great was His shame before the world: so many nations were scandalized by Him; how great was the shame for so great and such a Lord, the King of kings, to be abandoned at such a moment by so few servants. Everyone had fled from Him out of fear; they hid themselves in terror and mourned in grief.

In so great a solemnity, in His own city, where shortly before He had been honored so magnificently, while others were more decently clothed, He was stripped so shamefully and so often before everyone, and assailed by so many insults and mockeries.

How little clothing covered the shame of nature in Him who is Lord of heaven and earth and the splendor of glory, whose beauty and radiance the sun and moon admire! And lest anyone should see so great a disgrace, the earth, in wondrous compassion, was darkened by darkness spread everywhere.

[Col. 1428A] But, to complete the shame, look at the multitude of letters on the tablet of the page, as though representing the innumerable people of the Jews and Gentiles standing around the cross for such a spectacle.

There the centurion with his soldiers and guards, the chief priests and Pharisees, the elders with the teachers of the law and their attendants, seemed to stand beneath the arms of the cross with power and authority. The whole people—not only of that great city but also gathered from many regions—stood without compassion before the face of the dying Lord.

The soldiers divided His garment among themselves in play. The chief priests and Pharisees, who ought to have taught others, mocked among themselves with the scribes the best miracles He had performed and the sweetest words He had spoken, as much as they could; and the thieves hung before Him, blaspheming.

## CHAPTER VI

All His acquaintances also stood at a distance, while His mother and many other women stood near the cross. And the more numerous the enemies were and the fewer the friends, the more they brought Him to shame.

But how great was the pain of His heart in enduring such bitterness of death for so long, since the grief of His friends who stood there—and especially that of His mother—pressed upon Him no less?

How could such a mother stand there, seeing such a son die in this way? Did she not possess a mother’s heart and compassionate entrails?
