What was the Mother of Mercy thinking, she who felt everything and saw her son suffering? How could she bear the pressure of His death, when many people, after so many years, cannot even endure the memory of the Passion?

Where is the mother who could see and endure her son hanging on the gallows, even if that son had deserved it? Do not mothers love their sons so greatly that they cannot even bear to hear a harsh word spoken against them?

How, then, could the Mother of the Lord stand there, rather than fall down a hundred times after being struck, or fall down dead? What was she doing? How could she stand and remain silent, when everyone was speaking among themselves and she heard her son speak so many times?

Why did she not run to the cross, crying out and wailing, tear her son away from them, or at least ask through her tears that he be given back to her? Why did she not compel her sisters, Mary Magdalene, and the others to weep and mourn through cries and tears?

If Mary Magdalene later stood outside the tomb on the third day, weeping for so long over the dead man that not even the angels could console her, how could she not have wept when she saw Him die in this way—He who had so kindly forgiven her sins, who shortly before had raised her brother Lazarus, and for whose love she had abandoned everything?

Much more forcefully and bitterly should the sisters of the Lord’s mother have wept and mourned, both for the Passion of their nephew and out of compassion for their sister. Who, then, can doubt that the mother grieved infinitely more for her son?

## CHAPTER VII

But whatever was a cause of pain and sorrow for her, by God’s power she held it all most tightly within herself, and inwardly she was bodily tormented. And the less she dared to cry out, lest she lose patience and, dying with her son, burden her dying son more heavily, the sharper were the rending pains she felt in her heart.

But when she saw that He, so badly treated, prayed to God the Father for them and even excused them because they did not know what they were doing, how could she not say to Him:

“Most beloved and sweetest Son, why do you say this? They crucify you, mock you, and curse you, while you, in return, bless them? How do they not know what they are doing, when you have done them no evil?”

And what could she say when, dying, He commended her to the care of the young man? What consolation was this for the most sorrowful mother at the death of her most beloved son: “Receive the son of Zebedee in place of the Son of God”?

What could mother say to son, and son to mother, if at that time they had been able to speak with one another at length? And how, finally, could she see the sword approaching which she had awaited each day for so many years after Simeon’s prophecy, the sword that then pierced her maternal entrails through her son’s side?

How could John then support her so that she would not fall, when he himself could not have been without the greatest pain?

The Lord also saw, to increase His sorrow, such blood poured out so contemptibly and uselessly, because He labored in such a way seemingly in vain that He scarcely gained one thief at that time and lost one apostle.

He saw also, in those present and in those yet to come, the general ingratitude by which He was to be given over to oblivion even by Christians as though He were dead. Very few are those who give Him thanks for so great a benefit, even while looking upon Him crucified and saying:

“Glory, praise, and honor be to you, Christ the King and Redeemer.”

The Lord also saw the worst return of present and future generations, from those who hate Him without cause and repay evil for good. For if He could still suffer, He would suffer worse things from evil Christians than He then suffered from the Jews. By adding transgression to the pain of His wounds, they renew His wounds daily, crucify Him again, and expose Him to contempt.

## CHAPTER VIII

He could grieve greatly for those of the present age whom He foresaw, whom the Apostle also wept over: enemies of the cross of Christ, ungrateful for such great benefits, occupied with the pleasures of the flesh, boasting in empty things, and yearning for worldly matters.

It is not enough for them that they are heading toward destruction; by persecuting the good, they mock, reproach, and despise them, indeed they strip and kill them, just as the soldiers of the king, the teachers of the law, and the people who agreed with them did to the Lord. Of these it is said in Malachi:

“You crucify me, O people, all day long.”

Nor are the many wicked pleasing who have committed and continue to inflict many evils, blaspheme God, and murmur in adversity, like the thief hanging on the left.

Few, however, patiently endure evil for their sins and are saved, like the thief hanging on the right. Even fewer truly sympathize with Christ’s Passion in the manner of the holy women.

And yet the wicked were not satisfied with His sufferings. With unheard-of rage they raged against the dead man and pierced His side through with a lance.

When darkness came, the veil of the Temple fell, the rocks split and the earth trembled, the tombs opened, the thief confessed, and the centurion glorified the righteous Son of God, the faithless Jews still refused either to believe or to feel compassion. Instead, they called Him a deceiver, guarded the buried body in order to erase His name and memory, and declared that the disciples had stolen it away.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 1430B]

O soul, weigh and reconsider these things: how narrow and harsh is the way that leads to life, and how much He had to suffer in order to enter into His glory. If He purchased His glory in this way, who will possess it entirely without payment?

Finally, if these things do not move you, consider that He is your heavenly Father, your brother according to the flesh, and your faithful, beneficent, useful friend. Even for you, who were condemned before He died in this way, because of your great and manifold guilt He was punished in all His limbs, so that He might make satisfaction for all your iniquities.

He endured so many wounds in order to heal all your infirmities. He redeemed your wretched, useless, detestable, condemnable life from destruction by a redemption so precious, so abundant, so gracious, and so glorious in divinity.

In this way He destroyed the guilt of sin and hell through the destruction of His own body. In this way He crowned His head with thorns, so that He might crown you with mercy and compassion. His soul was filled with evils, and He possessed no good thing of the world, so that He might fill your desire with good things.

In this way His flesh dies on the cross, so that your youth may be renewed like the eagle’s.

And you, senseless, hardened, and ungrateful in all these matters, see these things and laugh, wicked and degenerate servant, who without shame and without sorrow see before you the gallows and your Father hanging upon it.

You do not consider, wretched and pitiable person, by what judgment and punishment you deserve to be condemned, since you have pierced His body, hanging upon the gallows, so many times with an arrow or lance as often as you have sinned mortally.

It was not enough for you not to return your soul to your Redeemer; you even took other souls away from Him.

Ask, therefore, that God be merciful and propitious to you, and turn to Him with your whole heart, who lives forever and ever.

[Col. 1431]

# THE LIFE OF BLESSED MARY MAGDALENE AND OF HER SISTER, SAINT MARTHA, BY THE BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

(*Unpublished Monuments concerning the Apostolate of Saint Mary Magdalene in Provence, etc.*) (G)*

[Col. 1431]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1431A]

The contemplative life of the most blessed Mary Magdalene—Christ’s sweetest beloved, and greatly beloved by Christ, whose name must be spoken with the highest reverence—and likewise the active life of her glorious sister Martha, Christ’s servant; the friendship of their venerable brother Lazarus; and his resurrection through Christ—these things the Catholic Church throughout the world believes and venerates.

They were not recently discovered from the tradition of modern writers [Note b], but were publicly proclaimed long ago by the authentic testimonies of the four Gospels themselves, as it were from the very swaddling clothes of our faith.

[Note a: These two sisters, beloved by the Lord, display the two spiritual lives by which the holy Church is exercised in the present age. Martha represents the active life, by which we are joined to our neighbor in charity; Mary represents the contemplative life, by which we sigh in the love of God. Rabanus, *Homily on the Assumption*, from Bede on Luke, book III, chapter 10; *Homily on the Assumption*, vol. V.]

Devotion that has been approved by such divine oracles does not need the proclamation of human speech. Let the one who has ears to hear listen to what the Spirit says to the churches [Col. 1431B] (Matt. IX, 15; Rev. II, 17), through the mouth of blessed John the evangelist, concerning the greatness of the love, the abundance of familiarity, and the fullness of sweetness that existed mutually between the Son of the glorious Virgin and His friends Martha and Mary and their brother Lazarus.

According to the saying:

“I love those who love me” (Prov. VIII, 17).

“The Lord Jesus loved Martha and her sister Mary and Lazarus” (John XI, 5).

This is the testimony borne by John (John I, 19–32), borne by that disciple whom Jesus loved more than the others (John XXI, 7). This is the testimony borne by the apostle who reclined upon the Lord’s breast at supper (John XIII, 25; XXI, 20), borne by the evangelist to whom, [Col. 1432A] from the cross, Christ entrusted the Virgin Mother to the virgin.

Truly happy, truly blessed are those to whom the holy Gospel has borne so magnificent, so illustrious, and so evident a testimony.

To demonstrate this more fully, I consider it worthwhile to recount the many categories [Note c] of the evangelists, in which they agree on this very matter. Then I shall discuss in truthful prose what our fathers handed down to us concerning what happened after the Savior’s ascension among His friends and what they also left in their writings.

[Note b: “Moderns,” that is, more recent writers—a phrase familiar to Rabanus. “Both of these cities are without surrounding walls in modern times.” Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book II, chapter 4. “Christ could grieve greatly when foreseeing those of the present age.” Rabanus, *On the Passion of the Lord*. *Newest Treasury of Anecdotes* by Blessed Pez, vol. IV, part II, p. 14.]

To pursue this matter more clearly, we shall begin somewhat further back and attempt briefly to report what the ancient histories relate concerning their origin and lineage, their birth and upbringing, their diligence and character, to the praise of the Lord the Savior and to the honor and glory of His friends. [Col. 1432B]

[Note c: “Categories,” from *categorare* or *categorizare*, meaning “to proclaim” or “to teach.” Thus, it seems to me, “categories” means “proofs” or “evidences.”]

## CHAPTER I — Where and from what lineage the Savior’s friends, Mary, Lazarus, and Martha, were born

In the territory of Jerusalem, on the Mount of Olives, fifteen stadia from the holy city [Note d], toward the rising of the sun, lies Bethany, a most famous village among the evangelists, belonging to Mary Magdalene, Lazarus, and Martha.

[Note d: The city is called holy because of the Temple and the Holy of Holies, and to distinguish it from the other cities in which idols were worshiped. Rabanus, on Matthew, book VIII, chapter 27, from Bede on Matthew, book IV, chapter 27, vol. III. See Jerome, *To Hedibia*, vol. IV, part I, col. 176.]

It was made most noble by the frequent bodily presence of the Lord and Savior (John XI, 1) [Note g: Bethany, which the Savior, when about to come to Jerusalem, exalted by the condescension of His presence. Rabanus, *On Matthew*, ibid., from Bede, vol. III.], consecrated by His lodging there, celebrated for its banquets, illustrious for its miracles, memorable for its tears [that is, worthy of remembrance], magnificent for His procession, distinguished by His footprints, and remarkable for His ascension.

[Note e: The ancients called a *castrum* a settlement situated in a very high place; its diminutive is *castellum*, “castle” or “village.” Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book XIV, chapter 1.]

From this town came the venerable hostess and most devoted servant of the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, the most blessed Martha (Matt. XXI, 17; XXVI, 6; Mark XI, 1, 11, 12; XIV, 3; Luke XIX, 29; XXIV, 50; John XI, 1, 18; XXI, 1).

[Note f: Bethany was a village or town on the side of the Mount of Olives, about fifteen stadia from Jerusalem, as the evangelist John makes clear; there Lazarus was raised from the dead. Rabanus, on Matthew, book VI, chapter 21, from Bede on Mark, book III, chapter 11, vol. III. “Bethany, a village two miles from Aelia, on the side of the Mount of Olives, where the Savior raised Lazarus.” Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book XIV, chapter 1.

“A mile is measured by a thousand paces. A stadium is the eighth part of a mile, consisting of one hundred and twenty-five paces. They say that Hercules first established this measure and defined it by the distance he could cover in a single breath; hence it was called a stadium, because at its end he would have finished breathing and stood still.” Ibid., chapter 21. See Bede on Luke, book VI, chapter 24, vol. III.]

Her mother, the most noble Eucharia, derived her illustrious lineage from the royal stock of the Israelite people. Her father, Theophilus, a Syrian by nationality, possessed a line of nobility distinguished not only by birth but also by title and renowned by office.

For, holding the first position among the satraps of the province—which the sons of this age regard as a great thing—he was the renowned leader and prince of all Syria and of the entire coastal region.

Afterward, however, in what was more important, he became a disciple of Christ through the preaching of Christ. Abandoning the honors of the world, he humbly followed Christ’s footsteps.

Martha had a uterine sister of remarkable beauty named Mary and a brother of outstanding character and flourishing youth named Lazarus.

In these three, natural talent and good diligence flourished together, and during their childhood they acquired a complete knowledge of Hebrew letters.

Integrity crowned the gifts of nature and their cultivation of the arts. For in each of them there was found admirable beauty of body, most pleasing grace of character, and most agreeable brilliance of speech. Thus they seemed to compete with one another in virtuous excellence—in appearance, character, and grace.

[Note a: In the copy, “of those investigating,” evidently through the carelessness of the scribes.]

## CHAPTER II — That Martha acted as mistress of the household on the estates, and concerning Mary’s character

As I have said, they were noble by birth and distinguished by kinship. By hereditary right they possessed a great quantity of property, a large number of estates, riches, and servants, as well as the greater part of the city of Jerusalem and three estates:

Bethany in Judea (John XI, 18), nearly two miles from Jerusalem; Magdala in Galilee [Note b], situated on the left side of the Sea of Galilee, in a hollow of the mountain, two miles from Tiberias; and “Bethany beyond the Jordan,” likewise in Galilee, “where John was baptizing” (John I, 28; X, 40).

[Note b: Although the entire province of the Jews was generally called Judea to distinguish it from the territories of other nations, more specifically its southern region was called Judea, to distinguish it from Samaria, Galilee, the Decapolis, and the other regions within the same province: “Jesus departed from Galilee and came into the borders of Judea” (Matt. XIX, 1). Rabanus, on Matthew, book V, chapter 19.]

Living together harmoniously in all these places, they abounded in delights. Yet the brother and sister wished Martha, as the firstborn, to possess the management of all their affairs and estates.

She did not abuse this position arrogantly, but used it generously, bearing a “manly spirit” in a “womanly” breast. Lacking the companionship of a husband, she flourished in the honor of continence. To her family she was sweet and lovable; to the poor, gentle and approachable; and finally, to everyone, merciful and generous.

In short, Martha was a woman respected and revered by all, because she was noble by birth and rich in possessions, celebrated for her beauty and glorious for her chastity, hospitable and lavish, and pleasing to everyone.

But when Mary reached marriageable age, she shone with extraordinary bodily beauty and appeared exceedingly lovely, with graceful proportions of limb, a beautiful face, remarkable hair, extraordinary charm, and a honey-sweet mind.

The beauty of her face and the “grace of her lips” (Prov. XXII, 11) were like the whiteness of lilies mingled with roses. Finally, her form and beauty shone with such brilliance that she was said to be a singular and wondrous creation of God the Maker.

## CHAPTER III — How Mary misused the gifts of nature and diligence

But since the brilliance [Note c] of appearance is rarely joined to chastity, and abundance of possessions is usually hostile to continence, the young woman, abounding in pleasures (Song VIII, 5), began, as that age is accustomed to do, to take joy in the nobility of her spirit and also to be drawn by the pleasure of the flesh.

[Note c: In the copy, “modesty.”]

Youth in its vigor, becoming beauty, and abundance of wealth can soften good morals. A beautiful body and a wanton spirit are a sweet evil that breathes love. Nobility of birth, beauty of face, and abundant possessions commonly uproot modesty from the heart. Finally, the heat of youth, the incentives of the flesh, and the weakness of the sex can utterly overthrow bodily chastity.

Alas, what grief! The gold was darkened (Lam. IV, 1), the best of her possessions, by love of earthly things. The finest color of the good produced by her diligence was changed by the stench of carnal desires.

Enticed by seductive impulses, wavering in spirit toward every unlawful thing, she turned toward the lusts of a life that enticed her whatever God had bestowed on her as evidence of honor: she abused the sweetness of her spirit to the danger of her soul, the beauty of her body to the disgrace of her heart, and the vigor of youth to the destruction [Col. 1434C] of chastity.

“All her beauty has departed from the daughter of Zion; all that work of divine generosity has been poured out in her” (Lam. I, 6; II, 11), while she sinned against the Lord all the more gravely because she owed Him greater things.

But why should we linger over these matters any longer? The young woman’s mind became estranged and dwelt temporarily in love of the world. She abused the pleasures of the flesh and returned [perhaps, “went”] to the region of unlikeness. The younger daughter, having gone far away from God into a foreign land (Luke XV, 13), quickly squandered both the good gifts of nature and the fruits of her diligence.

But as soon as she discovered that she had suddenly been deprived of divine virtues, recalling how many precious things she had lost and from whom she had received so many and such great gifts, she hastened quickly to return to His favor.

## CHAPTER IV — That at that time the Lord and Savior, having become a young man, performed miracles and healed sinners

[Col. 1434D]

Indeed, the time of grace had now arrived; indeed, by that time the Virgin had given birth; for Emmanuel had already come from heaven to accomplish his work (Isa. 28:21) on earth. But his work was foreign to him, so that God might be brought into difficulty, the healthy might be wounded, and life might die. [Col. 1435A] This is wisdom. “Whoever has understanding, let him give a portion to seven and also to eight” (Eccl. 11:2).

[Note: [Col. 1435C] a “By these words of Ecclesiastes, ‘Give a portion to seven and also to eight,’ it is mystically commanded that we believe with equal reverence in both Testaments, namely, the Old as well as the New,” says St. Jerome in his Commentary on Ecclesiastes, vol. II, p. 778. St. Augustine interprets it similarly, *To the Inquiries of Januarius*, book II, letter 55, vol. II, p. 137. — Salonius, bishop of Vienne, in *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. VIII, p. 419. After St. Augustine, Alcuin, Rabanus’s own teacher, likewise says: “The Jews gave a portion to seven, but they did not give one to eight. Conversely, the heretics Marcion and Mani give a portion to eight, accepting the Gospel; but they do not ascribe the same to the number seven, rejecting the old law. But let us believe and venerate both, whatever each presents.” [Col. 1435D] Alcuin, *Commentary on Ecclesiastes*, chapter 10, verse 2, vol. I. Rabanus seems to have followed this interpretation here in the *Life of St. Mary Magdalene*, just as below, in chapter 30: “Much more blessed is the soul that, ascending with you, O wondrous contemplative and most devoted minister, from the feet of the humanity to be embraced to the head of the desirable divinity, gives a portion to seven and also to eight,” attributing the sufferings to humanity and assigning the miracles to God.]

—so that injuries might touch the man, while miracles might reveal the Lord. By then Jesus, growing through the natural stages of life, had reached youthful years.

[Note: [Col. 1435D] b “When John began to preach and baptize . . . at which time Christ is found to have been of youthful age.” Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book I, chapter 3, vol. V, p. 17.]

Already baptized through the ministry of his precursor, he had fasted for forty days, but afterward he became hungry (Matt. 3:16; 4:2)—not symbolically, not phantasmatically, not merely in appearance, but truly: “He himself bore our infirmities” (Isa. 53:4). He had already chosen many disciples for himself from the province; already, being more than thirty years old,

[Note: [Col. 1435D] c Christ is related to have been nearly thirty years old when he was baptized by John. Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book I, chapter 3, vol. V, p. 17.]

he had changed water into wine. From then on he shone most gloriously through signs and miracles, as befitted the Son of God, diligently doing what he had come to do: to cure the sick and heal sinners.

[Note: [Col. 1435D] d “He went about the cities, having this as the work entrusted to him by the Father: to save unbelievers . . . and after teaching, he healed every infirmity, so that those whom speech had not persuaded might be persuaded by deeds.” Rabanus, cited above, book III, chapter 9, p. 59; *Homily for Wednesday of the Thirteenth Week after Pentecost*.]

“For I have not come,” he says, “to call the righteous, but sinners” (Mark 2:17). “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. 9:12). For the Son of Man came “to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10). And reports about him spread throughout all Syria, through both Galilees, and as far as the coastal regions, and Tyre and Sidon (Matt. 4:24).

One day, while preaching the kingdom of God in Galilee, he compared the Jews to children who call out as they play: “We piped for you, and you did not dance; we lamented for you, and you did not weep” (Matt. 11:17).

[Note: [Col. 1436C] e What he says, “We lamented, and you did not weep,” refers to John, whose abstinence from food and drink signified the mourning of repentance. But what he says, “We piped for you, and you did not dance,” refers to God himself, who, by eating and drinking with the others, represented the joy of the kingdom. Yet they were unwilling either to humble themselves with John or to rejoice with Christ, calling the former demon-possessed and the latter a glutton, a drunkard, and a friend of tax collectors and sinners. Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book IV, chapter 11, p. 70, from Bede on Luke, book II, chapter 7, vol. III.]

Then, explaining why he had said this, he continued: “John the Baptist came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Behold, a glutton and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners’” [Col. 1435C] (Luke 7:32–34).

## Chapter V. How the fame of Christ’s miracles changed Mary’s mind

[Col. 1436A]

Then behold, the Savior was invited to dinner by a certain Pharisee, whom our evangelist calls Simon (Luke 7:36). I believe this man was a citizen of the town of Magdala, closely associated with blessed Martha through great affection and kinship. While he was dining in his house with many who had gathered there, the report of the Savior’s arrival immediately filled the entire city.

This was the report about him: that a holy and kind man was present, gentle and modest, devout and merciful; moreover, that he was familiar with the humble, approachable to sinners, beloved by penitents, a supporter of sobriety, and a lover of chastity; and that some believed him to be the Son of God and the Christ.

This saving rumor [Col. 1436B] reached the ears of the young woman whom I mentioned above, Mary, who was known as Magdalene because of Magdala, her own estate, a name meaning “Tower.”

[Note: [Col. 1436D] f “Mary Magdalene, the sister of Lazarus and Martha . . . is called Magdalene from the place Magdala; for Magdalene is interpreted as ‘Tower.’” Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book IV, chapter 1, p. 82, from Bede, *Interpretation of Hebrew Names*. Bede in his *Ephemerides*: “Mary, whose origin from Magdala is indicated by her surname.” — “Magdalene: tower; but it is better to say *turrensis*—‘of the tower’—just as one says *montanus*—‘of the mountain’—from *mons*.” Bede on Luke, book III, chapter 8.]

As we said, through the exceptional beauty of her appearance she had lost her own chastity and attacked that of others; with an attractive form, flourishing youth, and abundant possessions, she had everywhere waged war against good morals, so that, because of the countless number of her vices, she was said to have been possessed by seven demons.

[Note: [Col. 1436D] g St. Gregory the Great, *Homilies on the Gospels*, homily 33: “What else are the seven demons but the universal vices?” — “Seven demons are said to have gone out from her, so that she might be shown to have been full of countless, indeed universal, vices. For Scripture often uses the number seven to signify totality. Hence the prophet also comprehends the grace of the Holy Spirit under a distinction of seven virtues.” Bede on Luke, book III, chapter 8, vol. III, p. 305.]

Drawing faith, therefore, from the report she had heard of the most merciful prophet whose arrival she had learned, she turned toward herself and directed her inner eyes upon herself; and setting herself before herself, she remembered the transgression of all the desirable things she had possessed (Lam. 1:7) from the years of childhood—namely, both natural gifts and those acquired through personal effort.

Remembering these things in her heart (Lam. 3:21), she found herself far from God and utterly unlike him; and she began to weep. God gave her to drink of the wine of compunction (Mark 14:72),

[Note: [Col. 1437C] a “Wine: compunction,” as in the Psalms: “You have given us wine of compunction.” Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*, vol. V, p. 821.]

so that she might flee from the face of the bow (Ps. 59:5). “Unless you turn back,” he says, “he will sharpen his sword; he has bent his bow and prepared his deadly weapons in it” (Ps. 7:13–14).

Immediately, through the free and sudden prompting of the Holy Spirit, who, “when he wills and where he wills, breathes” (John 3:8)—who breathes upon whom he wills and as much as he wills, who has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills (Rom. 9:18)—the young woman, inspired and speaking to herself, said:

“Recognize yourself, Mary, and remember what you were, what you are now, and what you will be. Blush that you have so shamefully degenerated from your noble origin; repent that you have abused yourself; grieve that you have lost your own chastity; and weep that you have been a scandal to those nearest you. Groan that you have despised the Lord for so long, and let it shame you that you have responded so wickedly to God’s best gifts.

“Do not do this superficially or for a brief hour; take it seriously, because life is short and death certain, while its hour is uncertain. Health is deceptive, and beauty is vain. A woman who fears the Lord will herself be praised, and on the day of death her works will praise her (Prov. 31:33).

“You, therefore, Mary, fear eternal destruction; look toward the heavenly Judge; forestall the Lord your accuser; detest your former life; hasten toward a better one. Thus, indeed, by wisdom the hawk grows feathers, spreading its wings toward the south (Job 39:26).”

[Note: [Col. 1437D] b “Every elect person is a hawk,” as in Job: “Does the hawk grow feathers through your wisdom?” The holy man acquires the feathers of virtues through the power of God alone. Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.]

## Chapter VI. How Mary took the alabaster jar and went to Simon’s house

[Col. 1437C]

Then Mary rose as quickly as possible, took a vessel of spices made of Indian alabaster, which is a kind of white marble streaked with various colors,

[Note: [Col. 1437D] c Alabaster is a kind of white marble streaked with various colors. They hollow it out for perfume vessels because it is said to preserve their contents unspoiled particularly well. It grows around Egyptian Thebes and Damascus in Syria, but the whitest and finest is found in India. Rabanus on Matthew, book VIII, chapter 26, from Bede on Matthew, book IV, chapter 26, vol. III, p. 76, and on Luke, book III. Also in the *Homily on the Nativity of Blessed Mary Magdalene* and the *Homily for Tuesday of Holy Week*, vol. V.]

and filled it with choice and especially fine ointment of marvelous fragrance—so precious that she thought it could fittingly and honorably be applied to the feet of the prophet whom she intended to approach, whom rumor declared to be the Son of God, and whom she already loved with the greatest ardor.

She possessed a large supply of spikenard and aromatic substances, as well as balsam and every fragrant liquid. From childhood she had applied such sweet-smelling substances to herself to increase the fragrance of her flesh.

Carrying the fragrant vessel in her hands—for it is written that one may not appear before the Lord empty-handed (Exod. 23:15 and elsewhere)—and carrying, more importantly, a breast full of faith and hope of pardon, she wept most bitterly within herself, with a loud cry of the heart that God sweetly hears:

“Woe is me,” she said, “for I have miserably abused [MS.: *cauca*] the years of my youth. See, Lord, and consider, for I have become worthless” (Lam. 1:11). My God, let what I have sinned up to now be enough for me. I renounce the allurements of heart and flesh and worldly pomp; I detest continuing to go astray; from now on I profess that I will amend my life.”

Repeating these words within herself, with the mouth of her heart and conscience, she went to the banquet where she had learned that the Son of God was reclining.

This did not escape the one whom she approached, from whom no secret is hidden. Rather, with the sevenfold Spirit he went before her as she came, “with blessings of sweetness” (Ps. 20:4), and drew her toward himself as she hastened to him.

Then, once the seven demons had been thrown into confusion and expelled from her heart and body, permanently forbidden to return and separated from her,

[Note: [Col. 1437D] d “Mary Magdalene herself is the sister of Lazarus and Martha, from whom the Lord drove out seven demons. She is also the very woman—not another—who, as Luke writes, while still a sinner, came and watered the Lord’s feet with tears of repentance and anointed them with the ointment of devout confession; and because she loved much, she obtained pardon for many from the devout Judge.” Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book IV, chapter 1.]

he filled her with the good gifts of the sevenfold Spirit. Made fertile by these gifts, she conceived good hope through faith and gave birth to fervent charity, since the external sign was the offering from the fragrant alabaster,

[Note: [Col. 1438C] e *Exenium* or *exennium* means the same as *xenium*: a gift, present, or offering, as in Hincmar of Rheims, Rabanus’s contemporary.]

of the burning holocaust of compunction within.

[Note: [Col. 1438D] f “The logs burn on the altar when the love of God is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. And this holocaust, placed upon that fire, is consumed when everything we have resolved to do well is made acceptable through the power of love of God, by the gift of the grace of the Holy Spirit.” Rabanus, *Commentary on Exodus*, book III, chapter 16.]

With her conscience thus pregnant through complete repentance for her former life, laden with the offspring of devotion most pleasing to God,

[Note: [Col. 1438D] g “The ointment is repentance,” as in the Gospel: “She brought an alabaster jar of ointment,” that is, the devotion of a repentant soul. Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.]

and animated by a sure hope of forgiveness,

[Note: [Col. 1438D] h “Useful and complete repentance,” as in Mary, in whom five things are present: contrition, confession, mortification, correction, and perseverance. The first is in the heart, the second in the mouth, the third in the flesh, the fourth in works, and the fifth in virtue. Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.]

she arrived at the Savior’s banquet. [Col. 1438C]

## Chapter VII. How Mary performed unprecedented services at Christ’s feet, and why Christ defended her against the Pharisee

Entering the banquet, Mary looked around and, behold, saw from a distance the Son of the Virgin Mary reclining. Immediately she prostrated herself and worshiped him; then she rose and reverently approached the couch on which the Savior was reclining.

Standing boldly behind the Messiah, whose paths she grieved to have abandoned, she began to wet his feet with the eyes that had desired earthly things, crushing them with tears. And with her hair (Luke 7:38), which she had displayed for arranging the appearance of her face, she wrapped his feet and wiped away her tears.

With the mouth that she had abused for vanity and lust, she also kissed his feet. With the ointment she had brought, she anointed them—an ointment she grieved having once used for the fragrance of her own flesh.

[Note: [Col. 1439C] a “Previously . . . she used ointment for the fragrance of her own flesh. What she had therefore shamefully offered to herself, she now laudably offered to God. With her eyes she had desired earthly things, but now, crushing them through repentance, she wept. She had displayed her hair for arranging her face, but now she wiped away her tears with that hair. With her mouth she had spoken proudly, but now, kissing the Lord’s feet, she fixed it upon the footsteps of her Redeemer.” Bede on Luke, book III, vol. III, p. 301; *Homily on the Nativity of Blessed Mary Magdalene*, vol. V, p. 114; from St. Gregory the Great, *Homilies on the Gospels*, book II, homily 33.]

At this the Pharisee who had invited the Lord to dinner became indignant and jealous,

[Note: [Col. 1439D] b “But the Pharisee sees this and is jealous, because when the Jewish people see the gentiles preaching God, they waste away inwardly through their own wickedness.” St. Gregory the Great, *Homilies on the Gospels*, book II, homily 33.]

having no natural compassion for Mary and forgetting his own frailty. He reproved the woman who was to be saved, because she had come to be saved, and he reproved the Savior for coming to her aid.

[Note: [Col. 1439D] c The manuscript copy reads *subvenit* (“he came to her aid”), but *subvenire* (“to come to her aid”) should be read, as is clear from Bede: “The Pharisee reproved the sick woman for her sickness and the physician for his assistance.” On Luke, book III.]

He muttered to himself: “Is this man a Jew? Surely, if he were a prophet, though absent understanding the past and the present and prudently foreseeing the future, he would know for certain what sort of woman this is, whose services he gladly accepts and by whom he does not disdain to be touched.”

Responding to these thoughts of the Pharisee, God, the discerner of thoughts and examiner of intentions,

[Note: [Col. 1439D] d God is understood here as referring to the person of the Son, as in Paul: “Who is God over all, blessed forever.” Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.]

said, “Simon, I have something to say to you.”

But he smoothed down his Pharisaic brow, as was customary,

[Note: [Col. 1439D] e “The brow of the scribes and Pharisees is certainly indicated here.” Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book III, chapter 9, from Bede on Luke, book II, chapter 5. — “Bishops and priests take something of the Pharisees’ brow for themselves.” Rabanus, *Homily on the Nativity of St. Peter*.]

and, speaking inwardly and secretly as though he had whispered no murmur at all, answered plainly

[Note: [Col. 1440C] f *Maniacus*, that is, “insane.” Bede, whom Rabanus follows, says at this point: “The Pharisee, like a madman, carries the rope by which he will be bound.” On Luke, book III, vol. V, p. 302; *Homily on the Nativity of St. Mary Magdalene*, from St. Gregory the Great.]

—that is, briefly: “Teacher, speak.”

And the Lord said: “Two debtors owed money to a certain creditor. One owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty. When they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave the debt of both. Which of them will love him more?”

[Note: [Col. 1440D] g “A paradigm drawn from St. Gregory the Great: a paradigm concerning two debtors is set before him.” *Homilies on the Gospels*, book II, homily 33.]

Simon, like a madman, wound the rope around himself, not realizing that the paradigm had been spoken about him,

[Note: [Col. 1440D] h “The Lord gladly enters and reclines in the affection of the one who believes. This is the spiritual banquet of good works.” Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book III, chapter 9.]

and, in a reply that could not have expressed the parable either more concisely or more clearly, answered: “I suppose, the one to whom he forgave more.”

The Lord said to him: “You have judged rightly.”

Then, turning away from the table and toward Mary, in whose heart he was dining more delightfully than at the table,

[Note: [Col. 1440D] i “We owe God . . . that we have lived well and justly, and that we understand rightly and according to the Catholic faith. We owe everything to God. Nothing is ours except the sin and evil that we have committed.” In Smaragdus, *Commentary on the Rule of St. Benedict*.]

he presented his desirable face for her to see and looked upon her most kindly with his serene eyes.

But before addressing her, he rose to defend her against the Pharisee. Looking at her but speaking to him, he said:

“Do you see this woman?”

Then, recalling in orderly succession the services of washing, wiping, anointing, and kissing, he indicated that he had accepted them all most gratefully; and he openly reproached Simon for having failed in these and similar duties, setting each omission against each service:

“I entered your house, invited by you. But you did not give me water from a cistern or river for my feet, the service customarily offered to guests. But she, in a service unheard of throughout the ages, washed my feet with her own tears and wiped them with her hair, a towel more precious than any other.

“You did not give me a kiss, an indication of love. But she, not merely once or repeatedly, has not ceased kissing my feet from the moment she entered.

“You did not anoint my head with oil, which would have been a sign of devotion. But she has anointed my feet not with ordinary oil, but with ointment mixed with the dew of balsam.

“Therefore I tell you: Her many sins are forgiven, and rightly so, because she loved much. But the one to whom little is forgiven loves little”—although the one whom God preserves from falling into sins is bound to love the Lord no less.

[Note: [Col. 1440D] j The manuscript reads *enervari*; perhaps *enumerari* (“to be enumerated”) should be read, as appears from Bede: “The good deeds of the sinful woman are enumerated, and the evils of the false righteous man are enumerated, when it is said, ‘I entered your house,’ and so forth.” Bede on Luke, book III.]

## Chapter VIII. How Christ forgave Mary’s sins and sent her away in peace

After saying this, the Savior understood that he had given Mary “joy and gladness” to hear (Ps. 50:9), since she heard the services she had rendered to Christ being enumerated

[Note: [Col. 1440D] j The manuscript reads *enervari*; perhaps *enumerari* (“to be enumerated”) should be read, as appears from Bede: “The good deeds of the sinful woman are enumerated, and the evils of the false righteous man are enumerated, when it is said, ‘I entered your house,’ and so forth.” Bede on Luke, book III.]

and approved; greater joy because she knew that the gifts of her devotion had been preferred to Simon’s banquet; and the greatest joy because she had learned that the living sparks of her love were seen by God and that the forgiveness of her sins was being discussed.

With wondrous cheerfulness and ineffable sweetness, comforting her as she wept and tirelessly kissed his feet, he said to her: “Your sins are forgiven. For the ardor of your love has consumed”—that is, erased—the rust

[Note: [Col. 1440D] k The manuscript reads *aeruginem*; Bede has *rubiginem* (“rust”): “Her many sins are forgiven because she loved much.” [Col. 1441C] “What do we believe love to be except fire, and sins except rust? It is as though it were said plainly: She has completely burned away the rust of sin, because she burns fiercely with the fire of love. For the rust of sin is consumed all the more as the sinner’s heart is burned by the great fire of charity.” On Luke, book III; *Homily on the Nativity of Blessed Mary Magdalene*, from St. Gregory the Great, *Homilies on the Gospels*, book II, homily 33.]

of all your sin.”

When the fellow guests reclining at table heard this, they were scandalized and began saying to themselves: “Who is this man who even forgives sins?” For this is the work of God alone.

But he left them to such thoughts. Turning to Mary, he said: “Your faith, by which you believed that you would obtain what you devoutly sought,

[Note: [Col. 1441C] a Because she did not doubt that she could receive what she had asked for. Bede, cited above, on Luke and in the *Homily*, from St. Gregory the Great.]

has saved you. Go in peace.”

Strengthened by this most blessed declaration, Mary worshiped the Savior. Then, filled with ineffable joy, she left the banquet and withdrew to her own home, carrying the sevenfold Spirit in her breast. The rush of her tears was not suppressed, but diminished.

For the tears that had previously been bitter because of punishment became joyful because of the pardon she had received. Then the river’s current

[Note: [Col. 1441C] b “The river signifies the Holy Spirit,” as in the Psalms: “The river’s current makes glad the city of God”—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit. Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.]

made glad Mary’s mind, the city of God,

[Note: [Col. 1441D] c “The city is the holy soul . . . The city is the gentile people,” as in the Psalms: “The river’s current makes glad the city of God,” that is, the fruitfulness of the Holy Spirit gladdens the gentile people. Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.]

and then the Most High sanctified his tabernacle

[Col. 1441B]

within her (Ps. 45:5).

[Note: [Col. 1441D] d “The tabernacle is our mind.” Ibid.]

From then on there was no vice of mind or body in her. From then on she was chaste—none more chaste! From then on she conquered nature, and even she herself yielded to herself. From then on she so expelled her former ways that every part of her was good and no portion evil.

To know such a Mary is good; to speak of her is worthy. I count this alone among her praises as worthy: that I confess myself unable to speak worthily of her.

## Chapter IX. How Mary gratefully and diligently ministered with her companions

After this, while the Lord Savior traveled through cities and villages and preached the kingdom of God with the twelve apostles, noble matrons followed him. Among them was their leader, the Lord Savior’s special friend, Mary Magdalene, as well as Joanna, Susanna, and many others who ministered from their possessions for the Lord’s needs

[Note: [Col. 1441D] e “They ministered to the Lord from their substance, so that he might reap their material things, while they reaped spiritual things—not because the Lord of creation needed food, but so that he might provide a model for teachers, namely, that they should be content with food and clothing from their disciples.” Rabanus on Matthew, book VIII, chapter 27; Bede, *Lenten Homilies*.]

and for the needs of the apostles,

[Col. 1442A]

responding with marvelous affection and diligent devotion to the benefits they had received from him.

[Note: [Col. 1441D] f “Twelve-year-old,” that is, twelve years of age. It should be noted that the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue was also twelve years old. Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book III, chapter 9.]

For he had cured them of evil spirits and infirmities. He raised the twelve-year-old daughter of Jairus, the ruler,

[Note: [Col. 1441D] g “He commanded that food be given to her.” He ordered food to be given to her as evidence that she had been restored to life, so that she would be believed to be not a phantom but a real person. Rabanus, *Homily*.]

saying, “Talitha cumi” (“Little girl, arise”), and commanded that food be given to her (Mark 5).

[Note: [Col. 1442C] h *Emoroydam*, that is, the woman with a hemorrhage.]

Accepting the faith of the Syrophoenician woman, he cleansed her daughter from a demon (Luke 8). He cured the woman with a hemorrhage

[Note: [Col. 1442C] i Rabanus presents these two examples—the daughter of Jairus and the woman with a hemorrhage—as signifying the Jewish Church and the Church from the gentiles. While the Lord was going to heal the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter, before he reached her, the woman suffering from a flow of blood touched him from behind and was healed. The ruler’s daughter represented Judea; the woman suffering from the flow of blood represented the Church from the gentiles. When the latter believed after Christ’s ascension, she touched the Lord, as it were, from behind, and obtained salvation before the synagogue. Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book IV.]

through the touch of his fringe and most emphatically commended her faith.

This woman was a citizen of Caesarea Philippi

[Note: [Col. 1442D] j The Caesareas are cities of Judea in the Promised Land. One is Caesarea Palestinae, situated on the seacoast; the other is Caesarea Philippi, which Scripture mentions in the Gospel. Philip, the brother of Herod and tetrarch of the regions of Ituraea and Trachonitis, named Caesarea Philippi, now called Paneas, in honor of Tiberius Caesar. He imitated his father Herod, who, in honor of Augustus Caesar, named Caesarea, previously called the Tower of Strato, and who, after his daughter, built Julias beyond the Jordan. This is the site of Caesarea Philippi, where the Jordan rises at the foot of Lebanon. It has two springs, one called Jor and the other Dan; when joined together, they produce the name Jordan. Rabanus on Matthew, book V, chapter 16, p. 98, vol. V; *Homily on the Nativity of St. Peter*, vol. V, p. 704, from St. Jerome on Matthew, chapter 16, vol. IV, part I, col. 73. See Josephus, *Antiquities*, book XVIII, chapter 2, vol. I, p. 872; book I, chapter 10. There is also a third Caesarea, the metropolis of Cappadocia, which Luke mentions as follows: “Coming down to Caesarea, he greeted the Church.” Rabanus, *Homily for the Feast of St. Paul*.]

and was called Martha.

“Her house is still visible there. In front of it stands a base in an elevated place, on which an image in bronze of the woman herself, as if prostrate on her knees and extending her hands suppliantly, is visibly represented. Beside it stands another bronze statue, in the form of a man, dressed in a finely arranged robe and extending his right hand toward the woman.

“At the feet of this statue a certain plant grows from the base. It is of an unusual kind and normally grows upward as far as the fringe of that bronze garment. When the growing plant reaches the very top of the fringe, it acquires power to drive away every disease and infirmity; a small draught of the moistened healing herb dispels them. But it has no power at all if it is plucked before it has grown upward and touched the summit of the bronze fringe.

“They say that this statue was fashioned in the likeness of the face of the Lord Jesus Christ. Nor is it surprising that, in return for the benefits she received from the Savior, the woman wished to offer something of this kind as a memorial gift. Even to this day, although observed as an inherited pagan custom, it is practiced indiscriminately by Christians; thus they customarily honor those whom they have judged worthy of honor. For preserving the memorials of ancient people for the remembrance of posterity is a sign of their honor and of the love of those who preserve them (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, from Rufinus’s translation).”

## Chapter X. How Martha received Christ as a guest, and Christ vindicated Mary as she philosophized

[Note: [Col. 1443C] a “Mary philosophizing.” This expression is taken from St. Chrysostom. Speaking of Mary hastening to Jesus when he came to Bethany to raise Lazarus, Chrysostom says: “Behold, then, a woman philosophizing” (*Homilies on John*, homily 63).]

[Col. 1443A]

Around this same time, the Savior was transfigured in Galilee on Mount Tabor. When the days of his journey were nearing completion, he resolutely set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), seeking without fear the place where he had determined to suffer.

As he went, he entered a certain village (Luke 10:38)—namely, the village of Magdala, distinguished by the possession and name of Mary Magdalene. There Martha received him as a guest and prepared, with every desire of her heart, the arrangements for hospitality and the abundance of the banquet.

With the Lord Savior were the twelve apostles, the seventy-two disciples, and a multitude of noble matrons. While Martha was occupied with the things required by domestic care, her most holy sister chose to sit beside the Savior’s feet and listen to his word, rather than offer assistance to her sister, who was busy with the extensive service.

Martha therefore approached the Savior and said: “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me alone to serve? Tell her, then, to help me.”

Hearing this, Mary did not answer her complaining sister but entrusted her defense to the Savior, who was already dining in the banquet of her contemplation. “I sit beneath the shadow of the one I desire,” she said,

[Note: [Col. 1443D] b “The shadow is Christ’s protection,” as in the Song: “I sat beneath the shadow of the one whom I desired,” that is, “I rested in the protection of Christ, whom I love.” Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*. In the Song, the bride’s voice says: “I sat beneath the shadow of the one whom I desired,” because she found rest under Christ’s protection. Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.]

“and his fruit is sweet to my throat” (Song 2:3).

[Note: [Col. 1443D] c “The throat stands for the heart. The Bridegroom’s throat is the inner savor of Christ’s words, which few taste.” Ibid.]

“Remembering these things in my heart, therefore I will hope” (Lam. 2:21).

The Savior answered: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious.”

The repetition of her name is a sign of affection.

[Note: [Col. 1443D] d “The repetition of the name is a sign of affection, or perhaps of arousing attention.” St. Augustine, sermon 26, *On the Words of the Lord*.]

For he loved her as well, for her charitable actions, as he loved Mary for her devotion to contemplation, with marvelous affection.

“You are anxious,” he said, “about managing domestic affairs, and you are troubled about many things necessary for the weak and afflicted. Yet, above all else, one thing is necessary: to cling continually to God.

“This is the best portion. Your sister Mary has chosen it, and it will not be taken away from her. Her contemplation, love, and desire have begun faithfully here and will never fail; rather, they will finally be perfected in heaven.”

[Note: [Col. 1443D] e Although the active life is good, the contemplative life is better. For the former comes to an end with mortal life, whereas the latter grows more fully in immortal life. Hence it is said: “Mary has chosen the best portion, which will not be taken away from her.” Rabanus, *Commentary on Ezekiel*, book I, chapter 1. “Behold, Martha’s portion is not condemned, but Mary’s is praised. Why Mary’s portion is the best is added when it says, ‘It will not be taken away from her.’ For the active life ends with the body. Who will offer bread to the hungry in the eternal homeland, where no one hungers? Who will give drink to the thirsty, where no one thirsts? Who will bury the dead, where no one dies? With the present age, therefore, the active life will be taken away, but the contemplative life begins here so that it may be perfected in the heavenly homeland, because the fire of love that begins to burn here grows hotter when it sees the one whom it loves.” Rabanus, *Homily on the Assumption*, from Bede on Luke, book III, chapter 10; *Homily on the Assumption*.]

He spoke and reclined, as did the twelve apostles, the seventy, and the devout matrons. Most blessed Martha served the tables generously, as was her custom; so did the manager of her household, the distinguished Marcella, Susanna, and Joanna, whose husband was steward and administrator of the kingdom of Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee.

[Note: [Col. 1444D] f To prevent the kingdom of Judea from becoming too powerful, Augustus arranged for it to be divided into tetrarchies, which he caused the four brothers of Archelaus—Herod, Antipater, Lysanias, and Philip—to hold, as the historians of the period relate. Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book I, chapter 2.]

## Chapter XI. How the Queen of Heaven arrived, and blessed Marcella blessed the Virgin Mother’s womb and breasts
[Col. 1444B] From that time onward, the Savior often traveled through the cities and estates of Galilee and repeatedly returned to Magdala. With his most blessed company, he stayed as a guest with Martha and Mary; the sisters ministered to him diligently and generously, supplying everything necessary from their own resources. Whenever, as household concerns required, they remained at home while the Lord was preaching farther away, they sent people to carry to the Savior and his companions whatever they knew would be useful. These things were also entrusted to one of the Twelve, Iscariot, who, having the Lord’s money box, carried what was sent (John XII, 6) and secretly conveyed it away.

One day, after the Savior had healed a demon-possessed man who was also blind and mute [Note: [Col. 1444D] g Rabanus introduces the healing of the blind and mute as typological. The demon-possessed man who was blind and mute signifies those who are converted from the idolatry of the nations to faith in the Lord. Yet, when the worship of demons has been driven from their hearts and they have received the former light of faith, their tongue is afterward released to praise the Lord, so that they confess him whom previously they denied. Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book IV, chapter 1.] (Matthew XII, 22), the crowds gathered, marveled, and cried out in praise of God; but the Pharisees blasphemed and maliciously claimed that this had been done by Beelzebub. [Note: [Col. 1444D] h The crowds were always marveling at the Lord’s deeds; but the Pharisees and scribes, on the contrary, strove either to deny them or to distort what they could not deny by a sinister interpretation, as though these were not works of divinity but of an unclean spirit—namely, Beelzebub, who was the god of Ekron. For *Bel* itself is *Baal*, while *Zebub* means “fly,” hence “the man of flies,” evidently because of the filth of sacrificial blood; from its most foul rite or name they called the prince of demons by this designation. Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book IV, chapter 11; from Bede, *On Luke*, book IV, chapter 11.]

But the Savior, reasonably asserting [Note: [Col. 1445C] a “How can anyone enter the house of a strong man and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man? Then he will plunder his house.” By “the strong man” he means the devil; by “his goods,” human beings deceived by him; by “his house,” the world. The Lord therefore shows through this parable—now made entirely plain—that he freed human beings from demons not by a deceitful agreement with them, as they alleged, but by a wholly different and contrary power, namely, the power of divinity. Rabanus, *on Matthew*.], that he cast out demons by the finger of God [Note: [Col. 1445C] b “The finger of God,” as the Gospel plainly says, is understood to mean the Holy Spirit. Rabanus, *On Exodus*, book I, chapter 15, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.], the Queen of Heaven arrived there with her sisters and relatives to see and address the Son of God, the Savior.

Since, because of the crowd, they could not approach him, a certain man who was standing at the doors rose and said to the Savior—not by chance or innocently, but testing whether he preferred flesh and blood to spiritual work: “Behold,” he said, “your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking you” (Matthew VII, 46). When the Savior heard this, he refrained from going out, pretending not to know his mother—not because he denied her as his mother, but because he was answering the one who was setting a snare for him: “Who is my mother,” he said, “and who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hands toward the disciples, he said: “Behold my mother and my brothers,” through the special anointing; “for whoever, whether man or woman, does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.” [Note: [Col. 1445D] c The Lord was occupied with the work of speaking, teaching the peoples, and carrying out the office of preaching. “Mother and brothers are standing outside and wish to speak with him”; then someone announces to the Savior that his brothers and mother are standing outside, seeking him. It seems to me that the man who announces this does not do so accidentally or simply, but lays a trap, testing whether he prefers flesh and blood to spiritual work. Therefore he pretends not to know his mother, so that he may indicate who is his mother and who are his relatives—not through kinship of flesh, but through union of the Spirit. *Ibid.*]

For whoever preaches me to the heart of a hearer gives birth to me; she becomes my mother, through whose voice my love is generated in others. [Note: [Col. 1445D] d Whoever does the will of God is called the Lord’s sister and brother because both sexes are gathered into the faith. But we must understand that the one who is Jesus’ brother and sister by believing becomes his mother by preaching. For she gives birth, as it were, to the Lord when she pours him into the heart of a hearer. She becomes his mother if, through her voice, the Lord’s love is generated in the mind of her neighbor. [Col. 1446B] Rabanus, *ibid.*, p. 79; from Bede, *On Mark*, book I, chapter 4. “These are my mother, who daily generate me in the minds of believers. These are my brothers, who do the works of my Father.” Therefore, contrary to Marcion and Manichaeus, he did not deny his mother so that he might be thought to have been born from a phantom; rather, he preferred the apostles to kinship, so that we too might prefer the spirit to the flesh in the ordering of our love. *Ibid.* “Mother”: any preacher, as in the Gospel: “He is my brother and sister and mother,” because a preacher, by teaching others in the faith, gives birth. Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.]

At these words the multitude of believing men and women rejoiced. Among the other devout matrons who ministered to the Savior was Marcella, whom we mentioned above, the steward and companion of blessed Martha, [Note: [Col. 1446C] e *Comitissa* here seems to mean the same as *procuratrix*, “steward” or “manager.”] a woman of great devotion and faith. With extraordinary sincerity she believed in the Savior’s Incarnation, and with extraordinary confidence she trusted in it [Note: [Col. 1446C] f This woman is shown to possess great devotion and faith: with such extraordinary sincerity, more than all others, she recognizes the Lord’s Incarnation, and with such confidence she confesses it. Bede, *On Luke*, book IV, chapter 11.]. Confounding the calumnies of the rulers and Pharisees who were present, she raised her voice from the crowd and said to the Savior:

“Blessed is the womb that bore you, which supplied you, who would prevail in the flesh, with the seed-material of its own flesh; and blessed are the breasts that nursed you, which, from the same origin—the seed of its flesh—offered you milk for nourishment.”

The Savior replied: “Not only, as you say, is that mother blessed who gave birth from her flesh to me, who am the Word of God, and nourished me with her milk; rather, blessed are those who hear, receive, and conceive the Word of God in the womb of their mind.” [Note: [Col. 1446C] g In our copy the reading at this point is *valituro*, perhaps “about to be born,” as in Bede: “Mary supplied the Only-Begotten Son of God, about to be born from human limbs, with the material of her flesh … for by what reasoning should he be believed to have been nourished by her milk when it is denied by heretics that he was conceived from her seed? For, according to the physicists, both fluids are demonstrably derived from the origin of one and the same source. Unless perhaps the Virgin could be thought capable of supplying the seed-material of her flesh to nourish the Son of God in the flesh, but incapable of doing so in the Incarnation, as though that were the greater and more extraordinary miracle.” Bede, *On Luke*, book IV, chapter 11.]

At the mention of this same gift of grace, they rejoice [Note: [Col. 1446D] h In the copy one reads: “The grace of remembering both things is given to her mind.”], and nourish and guard the seed of the Word, born through faith, with the breasts of hope and charity.

## CHAPTER XII—Where Christ frees a sinful woman.

On the fourth day of the Feast of Booths [Note: [Col. 1446D] i The days of the Feast of Booths—that is, of Tabernacles—were especially celebrated. For seven days the Hebrews lived in shelters, taking for themselves palm fronds, branches of trees with dense foliage, and willows from the stream, and rejoiced before the Lord their God in commemoration of their departure from Egypt, because the Lord had made them dwell in booths when he led them out of the land of Egypt. Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clergy*, book II, chapter 47.], Jesus went up into the Temple and was teaching. When evening came, he went out with his disciples and went up to the Mount of Olives, to Bethany, the village of Mary and Martha, where Lazarus, his friend, lived and where he stayed as a guest. For they had deserved his intimacy and continually received him as a guest: at Magdala, a city [Col. 1447A] of Galilee; at Bethany beyond the Jordan; and in Judea, at Bethany near Jerusalem. O truly happy and greatly blessed were those who deserved to have so great a guest, feeding on the bread of angels, by whom they themselves were fed!

On the eighth day of the Feast of Booths, the Savior descended from Bethany and came early to the Temple. All the people came to him, and, sitting down, he taught them (John VIII, 2). How mercifully and wisely he freed a certain sinful woman from the danger of death we shall briefly relate, although it may seem that we are exceeding our limits.

The peoples were exceedingly pleased with the Savior because he commended mercy and compassion. [Note: [Col. 1447C] a The codex reads *misericordias*; in Alcuin, “the mercy which he always taught.”] But the Pharisees were always lying in wait for him and envying him because he received sinners. Seeking to trap him by something from his mouth for which he might either justly be reproached or condemned, they brought him a woman who had just been caught in adultery, saying among themselves:

“Let us test him concerning justice, to see whether he will speak against her, since he is a preacher of mercy. If he says that the adulteress must be stoned, the people will despise his teaching, against which he will have pronounced sentence. If he says that she should be released, we shall shout: ‘He is an enemy of the Law, opposed to Moses, an enemy of God, guilty of death, and he must be stoned together with the adulteress.’” [Note: [Col. 1447C] b Rabanus has a similar passage in his *Commentary on Matthew* concerning the Pharisees who asked the Savior whether it was lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason: “Here too the difference of mind between the crowds and the Pharisees must be noted: the crowds come together to be taught and to have their sick healed. The others approach in order to deceive the Savior and teacher of truth by testing him. Thus they ask him whether it is lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason, so that, as though holding him fast in a horned syllogism, whatever he answered he would suffer entrapment. If he said that a wife could be divorced for any reason and another married, the preacher of chastity would seem to be teaching the opposite. But if he answered that a wife ought not to be divorced for every reason, he would be held guilty of sacrilege and of acting against the teaching of Moses and, through Moses, of God.” Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book VI, chapter 19. See Bede, *On Matthew*, book III, chapter 19; Alcuin, volume I, p. 541. “Here we find an occasion for accusing him and make him guilty as a transgressor of the Law, saying to him: ‘You are an enemy of the Law; you answer against Moses, indeed against the one who gave the Law through Moses. You are guilty of death and must be stoned together with her.’” Augustine, *On John*, chapter 8, Tractate XXXIII, no. 4, volume III, part II, p. 531.]

Approaching him, they said: “Teacher, this woman has just been caught in adultery. Now Moses in the Law commanded us to stone such women. What then do you say?”

To this Wisdom of God, who is God, did not judge immediately, nor did he immediately answer. Instead, with his face turned away as he sat, he bent down and wrote on the ground with his finger the sins of those who were accusing the sinful woman. He had no personal sins of his own to write. The Savior gave us here a most useful example: when we hear of another’s sins, not to judge immediately, but first to examine ourselves with the finger of discernment [Note: [Col. 1447D] c “The finger” means discernment. As in the Gospel, “he was writing with his finger on the ground”; by humble discernment we ought to search our earthly heart. Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.], to see whether we have fallen, or might fall, into similar or worse things. Meanwhile the Pharisees persisted, seeking his judgment, already muttering [Codex: *praemasticantes*, “chewing beforehand”], already laughing loudly, convinced that he could not escape, since he would judge either against justice or against mercy.

But “there is no wisdom, no prudence, and no counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs XXI, 3). Therefore Christ straightened up, about to pronounce judgment. Teaching that those who wish to condemn the guilty must themselves be righteous, he rose and, while preserving mercy, rendered a judgment of justice [Note: [Col. 1448C] d “Behold, in answering the Lord will preserve justice and will not depart from gentleness.” Saint Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 4.]: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.”

Having thus wisely given his judgment, he bent down again and wrote on the ground, turning his face away so that the Pharisees would be free to leave [Note: [Col. 1448C] e Saint Augustine interprets this differently in *On John*, chapter 8, Tractate XXXIII, no. 5: “But after the Lord had struck them with that weapon of justice, he did not even deign to notice them as they fell; but, turning his gaze away from them, he again wrote with his finger on the ground.” Rabanus, however, the disciple of Albinus, follows his teacher, who himself adheres to his teacher Bede, saying that he turned his face elsewhere in order to give them freedom to leave. Alcuin, *On John*.], for he knew that at that moment they preferred to remain farther away rather than ask further questions. He teaches us as well: after a judgment has been given, he again bends down and writes, so that not only before we judge, but also after judgment has been delivered, we may humbly and tremblingly examine our conscience, lest we should deserve a worse sentence [Note: [Col. 1448D] f Similar material is found in Alcuin, *ibid.*].

They departed, clothed as though in a double cloak of shame. Thus mercy and misery remained, standing in the midst [Note: [Col. 1448D] g “The two were left behind: misery and mercy.” Saint Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 5.]. Finally the Savior rose, about to give the judgment of mercy, just as earlier, when he had risen, he had given the judgment of justice:

“Woman, where are those who accused you? Perhaps I drove them away? Has no one condemned you?”

She replied: “No one, Lord; for none of them was without sin. But you, who alone are without sin, can condemn me if you wish.”

The Savior said to her: “No one? Neither will I condemn you for what is past” [Note: [Col. 1448D] h “Neither will I condemn you”: “Having been made secure concerning the past, beware of the future.” Saint Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 8.]. “Go, beware of what is to come, and sin no more.” [Note: [Col. 1448D] i Rabanus inserts this account of the adulterous woman because she was a type of the Church from the nations, just as Mary Magdalene was. The adulterous woman, who is brought by the Jews to the Lord to be stoned, is the Church. Having first abandoned God, she had committed fornication with idols; the jealous synagogue wanted to kill her. Christ saves her by forgiving her sin and does not allow her to perish, for he knows how to pardon sinners. Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book IV, chapter 1.]

## CHAPTER XIII—Where Lazarus grows ill and dies, and Christ is summoned.

In the middle of winter, on the fifteenth day of the month Casleu, the Dedication took place in Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1449C] a The Dedication was the festival of the Temple’s consecration. The Jews solemnly celebrated the day on which the Temple was dedicated by Solomon. Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clergy*, book II, chapter 45.]. The Savior was walking in the Temple, in Solomon’s Portico, where, while preaching and saying, “I and the Father are one,” the Jews picked up stones in order to stone him (John X, 22, 30).

But he escaped from their hands and went again across the Jordan to Bethany of Galilee, the village of Mary and Martha, where John the Baptist had first been baptizing, and he remained there. Meanwhile, behold, his friend Lazarus was ill in Bethany of Judea, likewise the village of Mary and Martha, his sisters. His sisters therefore sent across the Jordan [Note: [Col. 1449D] b “They sent” to where the Lord was, namely, across the Jordan. Bede, *On John*, chapter 11; from Saint Augustine, *On John*, chapter 11, Tractate XLIX, no. 5.] to the Savior in Bethany, saying: “Behold, the one whom you love is ill” (John XI, 1–2).

“It is enough,” they said, “to announce the illness of the beloved to the beloved. He is our friend; Jesus loves Lazarus and will not easily abandon one whom he loves tenderly.” [Note: [Col. 1449D] c “Behold, the one whom you love is ill.” It is enough that you know; for you do not love and then abandon. Bede, *ibid.*, from Saint Augustine, *ibid.*]

When the Savior heard this, he said: “This illness will be for a miracle, not for death” [Note: [Col. 1449D] d “It is not for death, but rather for a miracle.” Bede, *ibid.*], but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.

Now Jesus loved Martha, her sister Mary, and Lazarus. He was ill, they were sorrowful, and all were beloved; but beloved by whom? Jesus loved them—the Savior of the sick, indeed the raiser even of the dead and the consoler of the sorrowful. [Note: [Col. 1449D] e “He was ill, they were sorrowful, and all were beloved. But he loved them as the Savior of the sick, indeed as the raiser even of the dead and the consoler of the sorrowful.” Alcuin, *Commentary on John*, book V, chapter 11, from Saint Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 7.]

For Jesus loved Martha, her sister Mary, and Lazarus. O happy and glorious family! Although Truth says, “I love those who love me,” faithful people who are specifically identified in Scripture as being specially loved by the Lord are nevertheless rarely found.

When the Savior heard that Lazarus was ill, he delayed going; he delayed coming to his aid, so that he might bring him back from death. At that time he remained where he was, in Bethany of Galilee, for two days, so that the four days might be completed. [Note: [Col. 1449D] f The time was prolonged until the four days were completed. Bede, *ibid.*, from Saint Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 7.]

Meanwhile a terrible fever burned Lazarus’s body. The physicians could do nothing; medicines were of no help. Thus the sick man had no remedy unless the Lord wished to heal him. His sisters sat beside the young man’s bed, promising that Jesus would come and assuring the man who was breathing that health would come. At last, when the vapor of his breast had been dried up by the force of the fevers, his vital spirit evaporated. They mourned the young man, tearing their garments. The holy sisters embraced the dead man and leaned over his corpse. One could see cheeks wet with blood, eyes darkened by tears, and the air filled with funeral wails.

Finally, after the funeral rites had been performed, the body was carried out in a solemn procession. Lazarus was enclosed in a marble tomb; the stone with which he was enclosed was moistened with tears. Since he was noble by birth and even nobler in character—innocent in conduct, discreet in speech, generous in hand, and openhearted—men of distinction from Jerusalem had come to Bethany to console him, and they too attended his funeral.

## CHAPTER XIV—Where the Lord rebukes the apostles who feared for themselves, discusses the sleep of his friend, approves Thomas’s devotion, and commends Martha’s faith.

[Col. 1450B] Meanwhile, after two days, the Savior said to his twelve disciples: “Let us go again into Judea” (John XI, 7).

The apostles were frightened and offered the Lord advice not to die, although he had come in order to die, lest they themselves should die. [Note: [Col. 1449D] g See how frightened the disciples were. They wanted to advise the Lord not to die, although he had come to die, lest they themselves should die. Bede, *ibid.*; Alcuin, *ibid.*, on John, chapter 11, p. 575; from Saint Augustine, *On John*, chapter 11, Tractate XLIX, no. 8.] They said: “Rabbi, just now the Jews were seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?”

Jesus answered: “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light of the world is not in him. But if he walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. I am the day; I am the light of the world. You are the twelve hours. It is mine to go before; it is yours to follow, as the hours follow the day.” [Note: [Col. 1450C] h Christ, the Sun of Justice, illuminates the whole world at all times. And just as the day turns through twelve hours until sunset, so the true day, Christ, illuminates the faithful through his twelve apostles. Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book IV, chapter 1. The twelve hours complete the day, as the Lord testifies when he says: “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” Although allegorically he calls himself the day and the disciples, who were to be illuminated by him, hours, and so forth. Rabanus, *ibid.*, book X, chapter 3.]

“Allow me, therefore, to suffer. Do not give me advice; but follow me, if you do not wish to stumble.” [Note: [Col. 1450D] i “The hours follow the day.” Alcuin, *ibid.*] [Note: [Col. 1450D] j “Do not give me advice, since you ought to receive advice from me.” Saint Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 8. “If I am the day,” he says, “and you are the hours, do the hours give advice to the day? The hours follow the day, not the day the hours.” This, then, is what he says in brief: “Follow me, if you do not wish to stumble.” Saint Augustine, no. 8.]

He said this, and afterward said to them: “Lazarus our friend sleeps, but I am going to awaken him from sleep.”

The disciples replied according to their understanding: “Lord, if he sleeps, he will be well, for sleep is usually a sign of recovery among the sick.” [Note: [Col. 1450D] k They answered according to their understanding: “Lord, if he sleeps, he will be well.” For the sleep of the sick is usually a sign of recovery. Alcuin, *ibid.*; Bede, *ibid.*, from Saint Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 11.]

Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he was speaking of ordinary sleep. Then Jesus told them plainly: “Lazarus is dead; and I am glad for your sake, so that you may believe that nothing is hidden from me, because I was not there, yet I know that he is dead.” [Note: [Col. 1450D] l “I am glad for your sake, so that you may believe,” because I was not there. “So that they might begin to marvel that the Lord could say that he was dead whom he had neither seen nor heard. ‘So that you may believe’: so that you may believe more fully and more firmly.” Saint Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 11.] “But let us go to him.”

Thomas therefore said to his fellow disciples: “Let us also go, and let us die with him.” [Note: [Col. 1451C] a In a certain manuscript of Alcuin: “and let us die.” In the Vulgate: “that we may die.”] Behold the true affection of lovers: either to live with him or to die with him.

Christ then came and found that Lazarus had already been four days in the tomb. Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia—two miles less a stadium. Many Jews had come to Mary and Martha to console them concerning their brother.

When Martha heard that Jesus had come, she went to meet him. But Mary remained sitting at home. Martha therefore said to Jesus: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you. And I know that you can raise him if you wish; but I leave this to your judgment, Lord.
