I do not ask you to raise him, for I do not presume to do so, because I do not know whether his resurrection would be beneficial.” [Note: [Col. 1451D] b She did not say, “Even now I ask you to raise my brother.” For how did she know whether it would be beneficial for her brother to rise? She said only: “I know that you can. If you wish, you do it.” Whether you do it is a matter of your judgment, not of my presumption. “But even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.” Bede, *On John*, chapter 11, from Saint Augustine, *On John*, chapter XI, Tractate XLIX.]

Jesus said to her: “Your brother will rise again.”

Martha said to him: “I know that he will rise in the general resurrection, on the last day.”

Jesus said to her: “I am the resurrection and the life. Because I am life, he will rise through me; through me he will rise then, if I wish, and now as well.” [Note: [Col. 1451D] c Through the one by whom he will rise then, he can rise now, because “I am the resurrection and the life.” Bede, *ibid.*]

“Whoever believes in me will live, even if he has died in the body, just as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob live, whose God I am, as the God of the living. Whoever believes in me, even though dead, lives; whoever does not believe in me, even though alive, is dead. And everyone who, while living in the flesh, believes in me, even if he dies for a time according to the flesh, will not die forever, because he will live in the soul in the meantime, until he rises again in the body.” [Note: [Col. 1451D] d Similar material is treated more fully by Alcuin, from Saint Augustine: “Therefore believe: even if you have died, you will live. But if you do not believe, even while you live you are dead. Whoever believes in me, even if he has died in the flesh, will live in the soul until the flesh rises, never afterward to die.” Bede, *ibid.*, from Saint Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 15.]

When he had said this, he added: “Do you believe this?” Knowing Martha’s faith, he sought her confession; for “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” [Note: [Col. 1451D] e “And Jesus said to them: ‘Do you believe that I can do this for you?’ Knowing their faith himself, he questions them so that faith may bring forth confession, confession may be followed by power, and salvation may accompany power; for, as the Apostle says, ‘with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.’” Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book III, chapter 9.]

She said to him: “Indeed, Lord, I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, who came into this world for the salvation of the world.”

## CHAPTER XV—Where the Savior sees Mary weeping and himself sheds tears.

After these words Martha went away and called her sister in a subdued voice, saying: “The Teacher is here and is calling you.” These words show that the Lord called Mary—something John passed over, preserving the brevity of his narrative, without saying where, when, or how he called her. [Note: [Col. 1452C] f It should be noted how he called a subdued voice silence; and it should also be noted how the Evangelist did not say where, when, or how the Lord called Mary, so that this might rather be understood from Martha’s words, while the brevity of the narrative was preserved. Saint Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 16. Alcuin, however, preserves the truth of the matter. *Ibid.* Bede likewise preserves the truth. *Ibid.*]

When Mary heard that the Lord was asking for her, she rose quickly and came to him. Jesus had not yet come into the village but was still in the place where Martha had met him.

The Jews who were with her in the house and were consoling her, when they saw that Mary had risen quickly and gone out, supposed that she was hurrying to seek comfort for her grief through tears. They followed her, saying [Note: [Col. 1452D] g The Jews supposed that she was hurrying for this reason: to seek comfort for her grief through tears; so they followed her. Saint Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 17.]: “She is going to the tomb to weep there.”

When Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet and said to him: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. In your presence no illness ever dared appear among those in whose company life was accustomed to dwell.”

When Jesus saw Mary weeping, he groaned in spirit and troubled himself, because he did so when he wished and in the manner he wished, although no one else could trouble him. Even today, when a sinner considers what good things he has received from God and what evils he has repaid God for those good things, he groans in spirit, is pierced with remorse, and is troubled. Faith groans within a person when it reproves him for his sins: Christ groans in him; Christ is troubled, because faith concerning Christ is Christ in the heart. [Note: [Col. 1452D] h “You considered yourself; you saw yourself guilty; you reckoned with yourself: ‘I did this; I committed that … What shall I do? Where shall I go? Where shall I turn?’ When you say these things, Christ is already groaning, because faith is groaning. If faith itself is within, Christ is there groaning; if faith is in us, Christ is in us. For what else does the Apostle mean when he says, ‘that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith’? Therefore your faith concerning Christ is Christ in your heart.” Saint Augustine, *On John*, chapter 11, Tractate XLIX, no. 19. Similar material is found in Bede and Alcuin.]

Jesus said: “Where have you laid him?”

They said to him: “Lord, come and see.”

And Jesus wept.

O great expression of compassion! O great proof of love! O unfathomable sign of intimacy! Who could be capable of estimating that mutual love which then burned between the Lord and Savior and his friend Mary, whose sign we know to have been that most sweet ardor of tears? I truly believe that love to be incomprehensible to every human creature, indeed even to the angelic creation.

“And Jesus wept.” O tears most worthy of reverence, not to be named without tears! Tears of the Son of God, which welled from his purest pupils, which trickled from his most beautiful eyes, which watered his most serene face, when, seeing Mary weeping, he groaned in spirit and troubled himself!

“And Jesus wept.” For Jesus loved Martha, her sister Mary, and Lazarus.

The Jews therefore said: “See how he loved him.”

But some of them said: “Could not this man, who opened the eyes of the man born blind, have caused this man not to die? He could have, but he did not wish to, because it is greater to raise the dead than to heal the sick.” [Note: [Col. 1453C] a He who did not wish to prevent his death will do something greater: he will raise the dead. Saint Augustine, *ibid.*, no. 21.]

## CHAPTER XVI—Where Christ prays and raises Lazarus.

Jesus therefore, again groaning within himself, came to the tomb. Let him groan within you also, whoever you are who are weighed down by the habit of sin, if you wish to come back to life [Note b: “Jesus therefore, again groaning within himself, came to the tomb. Let him groan within you also, if you intend to come back to life.” This is said to every person who is oppressed by the worst habit. St. Augustine, same work, no. 22.].

[Col. 1453B] It was a cave, and a stone had been placed over it [Note c: “The cave is the perverse mind,” as in the Gospel: “It was a cave, and a stone had been placed over it”—that is, the sinner’s conscience was deep through wickedness and dark through ignorance, and insensibility arising from hardness was present in it. Hrabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*]. Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha said to him, “Lord, by this time there is a bad odor, for he has been dead four days.” Jesus said to her, “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?” [Note d: Lazarus, whom the Lord raised from the tomb after four days, when he already stank, signifies the world, which had been corrupted by the most grievous habit of sin, yet is raised on the fourth day of death. The first day of death is the mortality derived from Adam, the race of death. The second day of death is the transgression of the natural law. The third day of death is the violation of the law that was given. The fourth day of death is contempt for the preaching of the Gospel; on that day, looking mercifully upon his work, the Lord deigned to raise his own. Hrabanus, *On the Universe*, book IV, chapter 1. Similar passages occur in Bede, *On John*, and more fully in Alcuin, drawing on St. Augustine, same work.]

And what is the glory of God? [Note e: Something may perhaps have been omitted by the scribes and could be restored from Augustine. For he says: “What does ‘you will see the glory of God’ mean? That he raises even one who is putrefying and has been dead four days. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God”; and: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more.” St. Augustine, same work, no. 23. The words “the glory of God,” duplicated here, seem to indicate a copyist’s error.] That where transgression abounded, grace abounded still more (Rom. 5:20); and that she loves more to whom more is forgiven (Luke 7).

So they took away the stone. But Jesus, lifting his eyes upward, said, “Father, I thank you because you have heard me. I knew, indeed, that you always hear me; but because of the people standing around I said this, so that they may believe that you sent me.” When he had said this, he cried out with a loud voice. He cried out with a loud voice, because [Col. 1454A] the one weighed down by the mass of an evil habit rises with difficulty [Note f: “He cried out with a loud voice. How difficultly does one rise whom the mass of an evil habit weighs down.” From St. Augustine, same work]; and in Zechariah: “Iniquity sits upon a talent of lead” (Zech. 5:7) [Note g: Lead signifies the weight of sin, as in Zechariah: “Behold, a talent of lead was being carried”—that is, the enormity of sin was increasing. Hrabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.].

Therefore he cried out with a loud voice; therefore he groaned, therefore he was troubled, therefore he wept. And he said, “Lazarus, come out.” And immediately the one who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with strips of cloth, and his face bound with a napkin [Note h: Some people corrupt themselves by burying themselves, as it were, not only by thinking or doing unlawful things but also by the very habit of sinning . . . For this reason he raised Lazarus, who had been four days in the tomb and already stank . . . But when the dead man of four days sought to escape the long confinement of the pressing tomb, Jesus groaned in spirit, troubled himself, shed tears, groaned again, and cried out with a loud voice: “Lazarus, come out.” And thus at last the one who had been beyond hope, having shaken off the weight of darkness, was restored to life and light. Hrabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book III, chapter 9.].

Thus, thus is the sinner bound: in the inner darkness of a hardened mind; and in the outer darkness he will be held by the debt of future condemnation [Note i: By inner darkness we mean blindness of heart; by outer darkness, the eternal night of condemnation. Same work, book VI.]. But the one whom Christ first absolved inwardly, by himself, from the bond of death, he immediately commanded the apostles to release outwardly. And he said to them, “Unbind him and let him go” (John 11:44): “For I have said, ‘You are gods’” (Ps. 81:6); “You shall not revile the gods”; and “You shall bring the servant, so that he may be free, to the gods” [Col. 1454B] (Exod. 22:28; 21:6).

Therefore those who attribute the forgiveness of sins to God alone in such a way as to deny that human beings share in it are mistaken [Note j: Similar passages occur in Alcuin. Therefore, when the dead man came out still bound, confessing and still guilty, he said to the ministers—that is, to the disciples—that his sins might be loosed: “Unbind him.” Bede, *On John*, chapter 11, drawing on St. Augustine, same work. “Who can forgive sins,” they say, “except God alone?” Although they spoke unknowingly, they spoke the truth, because no one can forgive sins except God. He also forgives through those to whom he has given the power of forgiving. Thus the Jews err . . . but the Arians err far more madly . . . Hrabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book III, chapter 9; and *Homily for Friday in Pentecost*. From Bede, *On Luke*, book II, chapter 5. From this resurrection, which took place in his body, is signified how we are raised in our hearts: when it is said to the dead man, “Come out,” so that the person dead in his sin and already buried beneath the mass of an evil habit—lying hidden within his conscience through wickedness—may come out of himself through confession. St. Gregory the Great, book XXII, on chapter 31 of Job.].

And contrary to God’s prohibition they revile the gods when they take away the authority God has given them. God alone is good; God alone performs wonders; God alone forgives sins (Matt. 19:17; Ps. 71:18; Luke 5:21). Without God, no one is good; without God, no one performs wonders; without God, no one can forgive sins. No one is good except God alone; no one performs wonders except God alone; no one can forgive sins except God alone.

Therefore he lies who says of the righteous Joseph, “A good and righteous man” (Luke 23:50); who says of the blessed man, “For he performed wonders in his lifetime” [Col. 1455A] (Ecclus. 31:9); or Christ, who says, “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John 20:23).

No. Rather, God himself does what a human being does through him; indeed, much better and more truly, a human being does what God does through him. For God did not say to Peter, “What has first been loosed in heaven, you shall afterward loose on earth” (Matt. 16:19), but the reverse. Therefore Peter’s judgment does not precede but follows the judgment of heaven. For the Lord’s giving a human being the power to forgive sins means nothing other than that God himself forgives sins through the human being.

And if a person truly repents of his sins but nevertheless cannot reach confession [Note a: Confession is the acknowledgment of sin, as in the Psalms: “I will confess my iniquity against myself.” Hrabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture.], I confidently declare that, when the supreme Priest completes with that person what the mortal was unable to do, it is reckoned before the Lord as accomplished: the person truly wished to do it but was unable to fulfill it—provided that necessity, rather than contempt, prevented confession [Note b: Holy Scripture frequently urges us to seek the remedies of confession—not because God needs our confession, since everything we think, say, and do lies open to him, but because we cannot otherwise be saved unless, in penitence, we confess what we have wickedly done through negligence. Hrabanus, *On Christian Struggle*, book III, “On Compunction”.].

## CHAPTER XVII — Where Martha serves at the supper, Lazarus reclines, and Mary anoints the feet

Many of the Jews who had come to Mary and had seen what Jesus did believed in him. But some of them went to the Pharisees and told them how much Jesus had done. So the chief priests and Pharisees assembled a council, in which Caiaphas, the high priest, prophesied that Jesus was going to die for the Jewish people. From that day onward—indeed, there is no doubt that they had thought of it earlier, but from then on definitively—they resolved to kill him.

But Jesus did not walk openly among the Jews [Col. 1455C]; he went away into the region near the desert, to a town called Ephraim, and there remained with his disciples. The Passover, the Jewish festival, was near. The chief priests had issued an order that if anyone knew where Jesus was, he should report it, so that they might seize him (John 11:45–56).

Jesus, knowing that they had conspired against him, returned to Bethany, near Jerusalem [Note c: As the time of his Passion approached, the Lord wished to approach the place of his Passion and to remain nearby, where, at the time established and predetermined before the ages, he could be found by those through whom the Passion was to be accomplished. Hrabanus, *On Matthew*, book VI, chapter 21.], like a lamb going to sacrifice [Note d: Our Savior, led like a lamb to slaughter and offered as a sacrifice upon the altar, granted the remission of sins to the whole world. Hrabanus, *On Numbers*, book IV, chapter 19.], to be sacrificed six days before Passover, on the following Friday, and crucified at the sixth hour. He who had created all things in six days had formed the human being on the sixth day, and he had come in the sixth age to redeem the human being [Note e: God completed all his works in six days. The six ages of the human race in this world, through the succession of times, signify God’s works. The first extends from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the Babylonian captivity; the fifth then extends to the humble coming of our Lord Jesus Christ; the sixth, which is now in progress, continues until the world’s end. The seventh is understood as the rest of the saints. Hrabanus, *On Genesis*, book I, chapter 10. The sixth age has now arrived with the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. For just as on that sixth day the first human being, Adam, was formed [Col. 1456C] . . . so in this sixth age of the world Christ was born. Same work; similar passages occur in Alcuin.].

It was then the solemn Sabbath, and they prepared a supper for him there, in the house of Simon the leper (John 12:2; Matt. 26:6), whom he had cleansed from leprosy some time before [Note f: “In the house of Simon the leper”: not because he remained leprous at that time, but because he had formerly been a leper and was afterward cleansed by the Savior, his former name remaining so that the power of the healer might be displayed. Hrabanus, *On Matthew*, book VIII, chapter 26; from Bede; from St. Jerome.].

Jesus reclined, along with the twelve apostles and many who had gathered. Lazarus, however, was one of those reclining with him (John 12:2), so that it might be proved that he was truly alive, not a phantom [Note g: So that those who contrived slanders might not say that Lazarus had been raised as a phantom, a supper was held there for the Lord, and Lazarus himself was one of those reclining with him. Bede, *On John*, chapter 12. So that people might not think that it was a phantom, since a dead man had risen, he was one of those reclining at table. St. Augustine, same work, treatise 50, no. 5.].

And blessed Martha, as was her custom, served at the tables with generous hand, cheerful face, and openhearted spirit. But Mary Magdalene, chief among all those who served Christ, did not forget herself—for immense zeal and the ardor of Christ’s love would not permit her to rest. She took a pound of precious ointment and, approaching the Savior with the utmost reverence, anointed his feet as he reclined (John 12:3; Matthew 26).

That ointment was genuine, *pistic*—that is, faithful—not adulterated with similar herbs or roots, as is the custom of perfumers, who fraudulently deceive both the sense of smell and the sight [Note h: The ointment is called *pistic*, that is, faithful, because physicians often adulterate precious ointments with similar herbs. Just as perfumers, who are accustomed to sell perfumes, frequently mix various sprouts into their preparations through fraud, deceiving the sight of purchasers. But this ointment was not adulterated; it was genuine, and with it Mary anointed the Lord’s head and feet. Hrabanus, same work, book VIII, chapter 26; see Alcuin on John and Bede on Matthew, book IV, chapter 26.].

It was composed of nard, an aromatic shrub that smells of *situm*, or of cyperus [Note i: The codex reads, “It smells of *cethim* or cypress”; Hrabanus on Matthew has, “*citum* or cypress”; and Bede on Mark, “*sinum* or cypress.” But Pliny, whose words Bede and Hrabanus quote in these passages, is discussing *situm* and cyperus.]; with a heavy, thick, fragile root, though fatty, harsh in taste, and with a small, dense leaf. It was also spiked, for the tops of nard spread out into ears, and perfumers celebrate both its spikes and its leaves. Mary’s perfume for Christ was not made merely from the root of nard; rather, to make it more precious, its fragrance and efficacy were enriched by the addition of its spikes and leaves [Note a: Nard is an aromatic shrub, they say, with a heavy and thick root, but a short, black, fragile one, though fatty, smelling of *situm* or cypress, harsh in taste, and with a small, dense leaf whose tips spread out into an ear. Therefore perfumers value both the spikes and the leaves of nard. This is what Mark means by “precious ointment of spiked nard”: the ointment Mary brought to the Lord was made not only from the root of nard, but, to make it more precious, its fragrance and efficacy were also enriched by the addition of its spikes and leaves. Hrabanus, *On Matthew*, book VIII, chapter 26; from Bede, *On Mark*, book IV, chapter 14.].

For nard is foremost among perfumes. That ointment, therefore, was precious and Indian—nothing is more precious than it—and worthy of the Lord’s feet and head [Note b: Natural philosophers report of nard that it is foremost among perfumes, and so it was rightly offered for anointing the head and feet. There are indeed many kinds of it, but all are herbs except the Indian variety, which is more precious. Hrabanus on Matthew, from Bede.]. Thus the three evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and John—testify (Matt. 26; Mark 14:3; John 12:3).

Finally, after pouring the precious nard over the Savior’s feet, she rubbed it all around them with her hands and fingers. Then she very gently wrapped her hair around them—the hair whose sheen had made her beautiful—and, applying it also to his breast and mouth, she wiped them most tenderly. At last, drawing him to herself, she cherished him for a long while and then let him go.

## CHAPTER XVIII — Where Mary anoints Christ’s head, Judas rages, and Christ praises her

This intimacy of the chief among Christ’s attendants with the Lord Savior is small in comparison with what follows. Once his feet had been anointed, her spirit kindled by the immense fire of love that he kindled in her whom she served, trusting boldly in the intimacy she had been granted and trusting well in God—for, unless I am mistaken, she had often been admitted to such acts—she reverently approached the sacred head of the Savior, worthy of reverence from angels and archangels, principalities and powers.

Parting the hair of almighty God with her fingers, she broke the alabaster jar [Col. 1457C] and poured the remainder of the nard over the crown of the Son of God (Matt. 26:7; Mark 14:3). Then, rubbing his hair with her hands, she drenched his curls with drops of nard [Note c: “Drenched,” that is, “moistened.”]; and with her most delicate fingers she spread the outpouring of the sacred liquid with the greatest care as far as his forehead, temples, and the borders of his neck, like a noble maker of balm. Thus Mary fulfilled by her devout works what King Solomon had once sung in her person in the Songs of Love: “While he was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (Song 1:11) [Note d: Mystically, this devotion of Mary serving the Lord signifies the faith and piety of the Church, which speaks in the Song of Love, saying: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.” These words she fulfilled once, literally, through Mary’s hands, and she does not cease to fulfill them spiritually every day in all her members. Hrabanus, *On Matthew*, book VIII, chapter 26; from Bede, *On Mark*, book IV, chapter 14, and *On John*, chapter 12, homily for Tuesday in Holy Week. Nard signifies faith, as in the Song: “Our nard gave forth its fragrance”; that is, the faith of the holy Church manifests itself publicly. Hrabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.].

How great then was the fragrance of Mary’s hair, hands, and lips from contact with Christ’s feet, whose perfume is above all spices (Song 4:10)! [Note e: Fragrance is the sweetness of holiness, as in the Song: “The fragrance of your perfumes is above all spices”—that is, the sweetness of your virtues surpasses all the pleasant things of this life. Same work.] For the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment, and the world with the fame of the deed [Note f: The ointment signifies holy conduct, as in the Gospel: “The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment”—that is, the Church is sprinkled with the fame of its conduct. Same work; see Bede on John, chapter 12.].

How great was the abundance of the gifts of the Holy Spirit in Mary’s mind when it was granted her from above by the Father of lights (John 12:3) to enjoy such intimacy with the Son of God! Finally, how pleasing Mary’s devotion was to the Son of almighty God, how sweet her love and how acceptable her service, the evangelists testify. They say that Judas Iscariot [Note g: “Scarioth.” Thus it is commonly written by Hrabanus, or also “Scharioth.” *Commentary on Matthew*, book III, chapter 10.], indignant when he perceived how sweetly the feet and head of the Lord Savior had exhaled the balsam that remained, cried out with both the voice of his mouth and the disposition of his traitorous heart: “Why this waste? For this ointment could have been sold for much and given to the poor” (Matt. 26:8).

And he raged against Mary, so that what David says might be fulfilled in him: “The sinner will see and be angry; he will gnash his teeth and waste away” (Ps. 3:9). He was full of the noonday demon and of the business that walks about in darkness (Ps. 90:6), disguising the feelings of his greed [Note h: “Feelings,” in French *sentiment*; or perhaps it is derived from the word *sentis*, meaning “thief.”] under concern for the poor.

He said this not because he cared about the needy, but because he was a thief and, having the Lord’s money box, carried what was given to the Savior in the course of his ministry, while as a thief he carried it away [Note i: “But because he was a thief, and having the money box, he carried what was put into it.” Did he carry it, or carry it away? He carried it as part of his ministry; as a thief, he carried it away. St. Augustine, *On John*, chapter 12, treatise 50, no. 9.].

The Lord did not wish to endure the traitor’s rage any longer; yet he did not rebuke him for greed. Instead, he heaped praises upon the beloved woman, his own perfumer, while quietly intimating that he was soon to die: “Leave her alone,” he said, “so that she may keep it for the day of my burial”—quietly indicating that he knew Mary would shortly come with spices to anoint his body. Although she did not complete this in fact, she completed it in devotion; for what you wish to do but cannot, God counts as done.

Meanwhile, everyone at the banquet was watching in wonder, and their minds were fixed upon Mary: they admired her intimacy and her tender affection [Note a: Here “tender affection” is opposed to spirituality, to designate the tenderness of love.], inhaled the fragrance of the nard, and approved her love and devotion. Some of them, persuaded by Judas’s words—not, however, with his disposition but with an innocent concern for the poor—became indignant against her, saying (Matt. 26:8; Mark 14:4; John 12:5): “Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” [Note b: “When the disciples saw this, they were indignant, saying, ‘Why this waste? For it could have been sold for much and given to the poor.’” Matthew and Mark speak in this way, using *synecdoche*—that is, employing the plural number for the singular. John, speaking more distinctly, testifies that Judas said this, and that he did so out of greed, because he was a thief and, having the money box, carried away what was put into it. It may also be understood that the other disciples either felt or said this, or were persuaded by Judas when he said it, and that Matthew and Mark expressed the will of all in their words. Judas said it because he was a thief; the others because of their concern for the poor. John wished to mention it only of Judas, since he believed that the occasion revealed his habitual practice of stealing. Hrabanus on Matthew, book VIII, chapter 26; in Bede on Mark, book IV, chapter 14. In printed editions, *laetari vero* is incorrectly read for *caeteri vero*. Homily for Tuesday in Holy Week. Finally, from St. Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, book II, no. 156.].

Immediately the Savior opposed himself to them: “Leave her alone,” he said. “Why do you trouble her? She has performed a good work for me. For you will always have the poor with you, and whenever you wish you can do good to them; but you will not always have me. What she had, she did: she anticipated anointing my head for burial. She did this for my burial, putting this ointment on my body and anticipating the service of my burial” [Note c: “What she had, she did; she anticipated anointing my body, for she could not touch it after I was dead. She did the only thing she could do. She anticipated giving the living the service of burial.” Bede on John, chapter 12.].

“Amen I tell you: Wherever this Gospel is preached throughout the whole world, what this Mary has done for me will be told in memory of her” (Mark 14:6–8; Matt. 26:12).

## CHAPTER XIX — Where the crowd meets Christ, Christ weeps and hungers, and why he returned to Bethany every day

A great crowd of the Jews learned that Jesus was in Bethany and, led by curiosity rather than charity, came [Note d: “Curiosity, not charity, brought them to Jesus.” Alcuin, from St. Augustine, same work, treatise 50, no. 14.], not because of Jesus, but to see Lazarus, whom Jesus had raised.

The chief priests also resolved to kill Lazarus, because many of the Jews were going away on his account and believing in Jesus (John 12:9; Matt. 21:7; Mark 2:7; Luke 19:35)—as though the one who had raised a man dead four days could not raise one who had been killed [Note e: “O foolish thought, O blind savagery! The Lord Christ, who could raise the dead, could he not raise one who had been killed?” St. Augustine, same work, no. 14.].

On the following day, the Savior, seated on a donkey and accompanied by palm branches and the praises of the people, descended from the Mount of Olives. When he saw the city, he wept over it [Note f: It should be noted that this entrance of his into Jerusalem took place five days before Passover, in which he had determined to fulfill the mystery of his most sacred Passion. John relates that six days before Passover he came to Bethany, where a supper was prepared for him . . . and on the following day, seated on a donkey, he came to Jerusalem, met by a very large crowd with palms. Hrabanus on Matthew, book VI, chapter 21.].

Entering the city, he went first to the temple [Note g: “Entering the city, he first went to the temple.” Hrabanus on Matthew, book VI, chapter 21.], from there drove out the money changers and merchants, healed the blind and the lame, and disputed with the chief priests.

After so many tears shed over the city destined to perish, as a sign of the soul destined to perish [Note h: “When he saw the city, he wept over it.” He did this once when he announced that the city would perish; our Redeemer does not cease to do this daily through his chosen ones when he observes that some have passed from a good life into depraved behavior. Hrabanus, *Homily for the Eleventh Sunday after Pentecost*, from Bede on Luke, book V, chapter 19.]; after so many cries of praise—“Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matt. 21:15); after the pomp of the procession, with garments, flowers, and branches spread along the road; after so many miracles; after the radiance of divinity visible to all in his face, from whose presence the merchants fled [Note i: Most people consider it the greatest of the signs that Lazarus was raised . . . To me it seems more astonishing that he could, with the blows of a single whip, drive out such a multitude, overturn tables, break seats, and do other things that an entire army could not have done. For something fiery and star-like radiated from his eyes, and the majesty of divinity shone in his face. Hrabanus on Matthew, from St. Jerome’s *Commentary*, book III on Matthew, chapter 21.]; and finally after a long period of disputation and teaching, he found nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58) among all the people who had gathered for the feast.

After looking around to see whether anyone would invite him to lodging, when evening had already come [Note j: “After looking around, he went out to Bethany.” The inward judge of all examines hearts; when he finds nowhere to lay his head, he withdraws to the faithful and rejoices to make his dwelling with the Father in those who obey the word. Bethany means “house of obedience.” Hrabanus, *Homily for Friday of the Fourth Week after Pentecost*, from Bede on Mark, book III, chapter 11.], he was so poor and had so utterly refused ever to flatter anyone that in so great a city he had no lodging and no dwelling. He went out to the Mount of Olives with the twelve apostles, so that what he did not have in Jerusalem he might have in Bethany: lodging with blessed Lazarus and his sisters [Note k: This too should be understood: he was so poor and had flattered no one that in the greatest city he found neither a host nor a dwelling, but lived in a small village with Lazarus and his sisters. Their village is Bethany. Hrabanus on Matthew, same work; from St. Jerome’s *Commentary*, book III on Matthew, chapter 21.].

And on another day, as he went out, he was hungry (Matt. 21:17), because he wished to be; and seeing a fig tree beside the road, he came to it, looking for fruit. Finding nothing but leaves, he cursed it: “May fruit never grow from you again forever” (Mark 11:19) [Note l: When he was returning to the city, he was hungry, either showing the reality of his human flesh or hungering for the salvation of believers. When he saw a certain tree, which we understand as the synagogue . . . he came to it . . . and found nothing on it but leaves: the noise of promises, Pharisaic traditions, and boasting of the Law. And he said to it, “May fruit never grow from you again,” either forever or for the age. Just as the Lord often spoke many things in parables, so he also used to enact some things in parables . . . The fig tree was withered from its roots to signify that the wicked people were to be utterly deprived not only of outward human glory but also of inward divine favor. Hrabanus, *Homily for Friday of the Fourth Week after Pentecost*; Bede on Mark, same passage.].

He spent the whole day teaching in the temple. When evening returned, he returned to Bethany, to Martha and Mary. Again, in the morning, on the third day of the week, he went back to the city with the apostles. They saw that the fig tree he had cursed had withered. By this example the Savior taught the apostles how to pray and to trust in obtaining whatever they might ask with confidence, even if they wished mountains to be moved [Note a: Pagans who have written slanders against the Church—Julian the Emperor and Porphyry—often reproach us for not having complete faith in God, since we have never been able to move mountains. They should be answered . . . that this too could have happened: a mountain could have been removed from the earth and cast into the sea if necessity had demanded it. We read that something similar occurred through the prayers of the blessed father Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, a man distinguished in merits and virtues: a mountain withdrew from its place on the earth by as much as the inhabitants of the city required. Hrabanus on Matthew, same work; St. Jerome on Matthew.].

When evening came, he left the city and returned to his familiar lodging. On the fourth day of the week, returning to the temple at dawn, he spoke at length to his apostles about the end of the world, while Judas Iscariot meanwhile promised the chief priests that he would betray Jesus [Note b: “When Jesus had finished all these words”—namely, the words he had delivered by preaching concerning the consummation of the world and the discernment of judgment—“he said to his disciples: You know that after two days the Passover will take place . . .” From the day on which he came to Bethany and the event concerning the ointment occurred, until the day on which all these things were done and said, we understand that four days had elapsed. Hrabanus, same work, book VIII, chapter 26.].

Meanwhile the Lord Jesus completed the sermons of that day, saying this to his disciples: “You know that after two days”—that is, today and tomorrow—“the Passover of the typical lamb will take place, and immediately the true Lamb, the Son of Man, will be handed over, so that on the third day he may be crucified” [Col. 1461B] (Mark 13; Matt. 24; John 14:10; Matt. 26:1–2).

He spoke; and when evening returned, he left the temple and returned to Bethany, intending to take his final lodging with his attendants and friends, Lazarus, Mary, and Martha [Note c: “After looking around, when it was already evening, he went out to Bethany with the twelve.” He did not do this only once, but throughout all five days from the time he had gone up to Jerusalem until the time of his Passion he always did the same: by day he taught in the temple, while at night he went out and stayed on the Mount of Olives, as we read in Luke. Hrabanus, *Homily for Friday of the Fourth Week after Pentecost*.].

He was like a young stag among the deer (Song 2:9), which, wherever it has gone away during the day, returns to its former bed when evening comes [Note d: Christ is the young stag among the deer, as below, from Hrabanus’s allegories.]. Thus the Savior, both about to suffer and about to ascend, returned to Bethany, the house of obedience, indicating that above all he seeks obedience from his friends [Note e: He left the unbelievers and, going out of the city of those who contradicted him, went to Bethany, which is interpreted as “house of obedience,” already prefiguring the calling of the Gentiles. He remained there because he could not remain in Israel. Hrabanus on Matthew, from St. Jerome, same passage. Similar passages occur in Alcuin. From Bede, *Interpretation of Hebrew Names*.].

## CHAPTER XX — Where Christ, after dining, is betrayed and led away bound; the apostles flee; Peter denies him; Mary clings to Christ
On the first day of Unleavened Bread (Matt. 26:17), Thursday, bidding his dearest guests, Lazarus, Mary, and Martha [Col. 1461C], a final farewell, when evening came he celebrated supper in Jerusalem with his twelve disciples. That celebrated supper was a blessed supper, at which he washed the feet of his apostles and made his body and blood from bread and wine. Immediately afterward [that is, as soon as it could be; French, *incontinent*] [Col. 1462A] came the Savior’s betrayal and passion. One of his apostles went forth and betrayed him with a kiss in the garden beyond the torrent Kidron, to the cohort and the attendants of the chief priests whom he had brought, with lanterns, torches, and weapons. And when he was led away bound, his disciples abandoned him and all fled (Matt. 26:56).

But Mary Magdalene’s devotion did not fail. Then, while the Savior’s bones clung to his skin as the flesh was consumed (Job 19:20), because Judas betrayed him, Peter denied him, and the ten apostles fled, the strength of the Redeemer always found Mary Magdalene at his side. Who could express the sorrow of her heart and the bitterness of her mind? Her inmost being seethed when she saw her beloved betrayed with a kiss, bound with chains, and led away to the palace of the high priest Annas [Col. 1462B]. There he was accused, interrogated, judged, proclaimed guilty of death, spat upon, struck with blows [that is, beaten with slaps], blindfolded, punched, and blasphemed.

Who could recount Mary’s laments and the tears with which she followed her beloved from the house of the high priest to the praetorium of the governor Pontius, and then from the governor’s praetorium to the palace of King Herod? Who could unfold Mary’s sobs and varied cries of mourning with which she was overcome while before Herod he was accused by the chief priests, questioned by the king, despised by the soldiers, mocked by the army, and, dressed in a white garment, sent back to the governor’s hearing?

Who could recall without tears Mary’s tears, which she poured forth abundantly, when she saw him standing before the tribunals, accused yet silent, the chief priests persistently accusing him, the governor excusing him at length and striving for his release, proving him innocent in every respect, and asking with many prayers that, at least out of reverence for the Paschal day, he might be allowed to depart [Col. 1462C]?

[Note: Pilate gave many opportunities for releasing the Savior. First, he compared the robber with the righteous man; then he asked: “What, then, shall I do with Jesus? [lacuna]” He himself also answered: “For what evil has he done?” By saying this, Pilate acquitted Jesus. Pilate took water [lacuna], in a certain sense bearing witness and saying: “I indeed wished to release an innocent man. [lacuna]” He does not condemn the one brought before him, but accuses those who brought him, declaring righteous the man who is to be crucified. Rabanus, on Matthew, book VIII, chapter 27.]

Yet the chief priests opposed this, offered their pleas on behalf of the robber Barabbas [Col. 1463A], and shouted concerning Jesus: “Crucify, crucify!” Then Mary’s grief was renewed when she saw her Lord stripped, tied to the column, and torn over his entire body by scourges. The column itself also bears witness to this: the column to which the Lord was bound still displays to those who see it unmistakable traces of the Lord’s blood.

Then Mary’s sorrow and the bitterness of her mind burned more fiercely when Pilate decreed that the chief priests’ request should be carried out, and the soldiers summoned the entire cohort. They ironically worshiped Christ, clothed in purple, crowned with thorns, holding a reed in his hand instead of a scepter, and greeted him with mockery [Col. 1463B].

[Note: The soldiers do this in mockery: after stripping him of his former garments, they dress him in a scarlet cloak instead of the purple garment used by ancient kings; instead of a diadem they place a crown of thorns on him; instead of a royal scepter they give him a reed; and they worship him as though he were a king. Rabanus, on Matthew, book VIII, chapter 27.]

They gave him vinegar and gall to drink; they struck his head with a reed; they spat in his face; and finally they removed the scarlet cloak and dressed him in his own garments. Carrying his cross, he went out of the city crowned with thorns. The queen of heaven, her sisters, Mary Magdalene, and the other matrons followed him, weeping and lamenting. They had followed him not only from Galilee but also from Judea and Jerusalem.

But Jesus turned his eyes and face toward the women who loved him and said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves and over your children; for if they do this to the green wood, what will happen to the dry?” (John 19:17; Luke 23:27; Mark 15:40; Matt. 27:55; Luke 23:28) [Col. 1463C].

[Note: The green wood signifies himself and his elect; the dry wood signifies the impious and sinners. Bede, on Luke, book IV, chapter 23.]

## CHAPTER XXI — Where Christ is crucified while Mary stands by; he is taken down and wrapped while Mary is present

“Love is strong as death” (Song 8:6): the Lord’s passion is seen [Col. 1463C], and Mary’s devotion does not cease. Christ is led away to be crucified; Mary follows and proves her affection by her weeping. Christ is raised upon the cross; Mary cries out and is tormented. Christ is fastened to the cross with nails; Mary’s soul is pierced by the goads of sorrow [Col. 1464A]. Christ is mocked by the chief priests, derided by the soldiers, and reviled by the robbers.

[Note: “The robbers and those who were crucified with him also reproached him.” How did they reproach him, since one of them believed in God, unless we understand Matthew and Mark to have used the plural number for the singular, just as in the Epistle to the Hebrews we read in the plural, “They closed the mouths of lions,” although only David is understood, and in the plural, “They were cut apart,” although tradition speaks only of Isaiah? What is more common, for example, than for someone to say, “The peasants insult me,” even if only one insults him? The two robbers may also signify both peoples, the Gentiles and the Jews. At first both peoples blasphemed the Lord, when Jews and Gentiles alike consented to the Lord’s death. Later, however, one of them outwardly repented because of the greatness of the signs and, even to this day, rebukes the blaspheming Jews. Rabanus, on Matthew, book VIII, chapter 27.]

He is blasphemed by passersby who shake their heads and shout, “Ha!” [Col. 1464B]

[Note: “Ha!” is a reproach directed against evils, as in the Gospel: “Ha, you who destroy the temple of God”; that is, reproach is directed at one who makes such claims about himself. Rabanus, *Allegories of Sacred Scripture*.]

Meanwhile he himself prays to the Father for those crucifying him (Matt. 27:40).

How great was Mary’s sorrow amid all this; what sobs, what sighs, when she saw the sufferings of her beloved, the one she loved, hanging among robbers! Yet she endured seeing the sufferings of her so-beloved Lord—so harsh and so prolonged. With what bitterness and anguish was she overcome when she heard the Messiah cry from the cross, “I thirst”; when she saw a sponge dipped in wormwood, vinegar, myrrh, and gall placed on a reed; when the stalk of hyssop was fixed to the sponge; when the sponge was brought to his mouth on the reed; when the hyssop stalk was applied to his lips; and when, after tasting it, he refused to drink [Col. 1464C]!

[Note: Rabanus combines two events without preserving their chronological order. He had already said in chapter 20 that the soldiers greeted him with mockery, gave him vinegar and gall to drink, and struck his head with a reed, although Christ was not given vinegar to drink in the praetorium. Here likewise, setting aside the chronological order, he joins to Christ’s later drinking the circumstances of the earlier event described by Matthew and Mark: “And they gave him wine mixed with gall to drink, and when he had tasted it, he would not drink.” “But what is meant by ‘when he had tasted it, he would not drink’ is that he indeed tasted the bitterness of death for us, but on the third day he rose again. And what Mark says, ‘wine mixed with myrrh,’ should be understood as Matthew’s ‘mixed with gall.’ For he used gall to signify bitterness, and wine mixed with myrrh is also exceedingly bitter. It is possible, however, that both gall and myrrh made the wine extremely bitter.” Rabanus, on Matthew, book VIII, chapter 27.]

At last Mary’s grief [*recendit*; perhaps, “began anew”] when she heard the Son of God bid farewell to his mother from the cross; entrust the care of his mother to holy John, who was then twenty-three years old; repeat, “Eloi”; cry out, “It is finished”; commend his soul into the Father’s hands; and finally, with a loud cry, expire when he willed.

[Note: *Recendit*, a word not found in ancient manuscripts. It may be derived from *recentia*, which signifies a beginning; hence *recendere* would mean “to begin.” This is so, however, only if the reading is not corrupt.]

And after the sun’s eclipse, after three hours of darkness, after the temple veil was torn, after the earthquake, after the rocks were split, after the tombs were opened, after the centurion and the whole multitude had departed; when she saw soldiers sent to break the legs of the robbers who were still alive—who would deny that Mary was terrified at the breaking of her Lord’s legs? Her sorrow grew immeasurably [Col. 1464D] when one of the soldiers pierced the Savior’s side with a lance, and immediately blood and water flowed from the recesses of his cold breast.

Oh, how welcome to Mary was the arrival of the noble man Joseph of Arimathea [Col. 1465C] and of Nicodemus the ruler, with one hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes [Col. 1465A], preparing them for the Lord’s burial [possibly: “with them prepared”]!

[Note: Joseph is described as rich not out of the evangelist’s boastfulness in presenting him as a noble man who was Jesus’ disciple, but to show why he was able to obtain Jesus’ body from Pilate. Poor and unknown men could not approach Pilate, the governor representing Roman power, and obtain the body of a crucified man. Rabanus, on Matthew, book VIII, chapter 27, from Bede on the Gospel.]

[Note: Myrrh is a tree of Arabia, up to five cubits tall, resembling a thorn tree … Aloe grows in India and Arabia; it is a tree of exceedingly sweet and noble fragrance … In the Gospel the Lord’s burial is described thus: “Joseph came and took the body of Jesus. Nicodemus also came … bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds.” Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book XIX, chapter 7.]

How gladly she looked upon the nails being drawn from the Savior’s hands and feet, his body being taken down and embalmed, his body being wrapped in linen, and his head in a cloth! All these things took place while Mary stood by, Mary gazing on, Mary lamenting pitiably and inconsolably.

## CHAPTER XXII — Where Christ was buried, and when Mary bought the spices

There was a certain little garden in a pasture (*phastio*) of the city, near the place where Jesus was crucified.

[Note: *Phastio*, perhaps *pascio*, with the same meaning as *pascum*, that is, pasture or meadow. Supplement to Du Cange’s *Glossary*.]

In this garden Joseph, a noble member of the council, had hewn out for himself a tomb, round, cut from the underlying rock, reddish and white in color, and so high that a man standing inside on the pavement could scarcely touch the top with his outstretched hand (John 19:1; Matt. 27:60) [Col. 1465B].

The entrance and doorway of the tomb were on the eastern side. On the north was the mausoleum, cut out of the very pavement of the tomb above the floor, seven feet long, not open above but solid; on the southern side, however, it was open along its entire length.

[Note: Those who in our time have been in Jerusalem report that the Lord’s tomb was a round chamber cut from the underlying rock, so high that a man standing inside could scarcely touch the top with his outstretched hand. It had an entrance on the east, to which that great stone was rolled and set. In the northern part of the tomb was the sepulcher itself, that is, the place of the Lord’s body, made from the same rock. It was seven feet long and rose three palms above the rest of the floor. This place was open not from above but along the entire southern side, through which the body was carried in. The color of the tomb and the burial chamber is said to be a mixture of reddish and white. Rabanus, on Matthew, book VIII, chapter 27. This description is taken from Bede, on Matthew, book IV, chapter 28; on Mark, book IV, chapter 15. See also Bede, *On the Holy Places*, chapter 2.]

They carried the embalmed and wrapped body of the Savior into the tomb from the east and into the mausoleum from the south; there they laid it on its back [the text reads *collatum*; perhaps *collocatum*, “placed”], with its head toward the west, its left side against the solid northern wall, and its right side toward the open south.

[Note: Since the body lay on its back with its head toward the west, it necessarily had its right side toward the south. Bede, on Mark, book IV, chapter 16, and *Homily for Easter Day*.]

When these things had been done, they left the tomb with many tears and great anguish of heart, with all speed lest the evening of the first day of the Sabbath overtake them. The men who were present rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb [Col. 1466C].

[Note: “Joseph … rolled a great stone to the entrance of the tomb and departed.” The great stone could not have been removed from the tomb without the help of many. Bede, in the same place.]

They immediately returned to their homes.

Mary Magdalene, however, with her companions [Col. 1466A], sat facing the tomb, lamenting and weeping for the Lord. After examining more carefully the arrangement of the tomb, which they intended to visit frequently, they went to the city market and to the sellers of spices, bought the most precious spices and balsams, and kept them with them until the evening of the second day of the Sabbath.

For although they mourned inconsolably and repeated their laments with the loudest cries, the greatness of their sorrow could not obliterate the memory of their religious duty toward their friend. It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was dawning (Luke 23:54). The chief priests persuaded the governor Pilate to place guards at the tomb, lest the last error become worse than the first. He said to them: “Let the first and the last error be yours; it is enough for you that I consented with you to his death; you have a guard—go, secure it if you wish” [Col. 1466B].

[Note: Pilate said to them: “You have a guard; go and secure it as you know how.” As though he had said: “Let it be enough that, compelled by force, I have completed with you the killing of an innocent man; let the error remain with you.” Rabanus, on Matthew, manuscript of the Royal Library, 2439.]

Therefore the Jews went away, secured the tomb, and sealed the stone with the guards (Matt. 27:64–66).

## CHAPTER XXIII — When Christ kept the Sabbath, how Mary did so, concerning the preparation of the spices, and the account of the times

It was a great day of that Sabbath (John 19:51) on which, after so many and such great torments, Christ’s flesh rested in hope of the resurrection (Ps. 15:10), without the stain of any corruption [Col. 1466D].

[Note: “The Sabbath … on that day the Lord rested in the tomb,” to confirm the mystery of that rest. Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book IX, chapter 16. Since man was made on the sixth day and the whole creation of the world was completed, while on the seventh the Creator rested from his work, rightly was the Savior crucified on that same sixth day and fulfilled the mystery of humanity’s restoration. Therefore, when he had received vinegar, he said, “It is finished”—that is, the work which I undertook on the sixth day for the restoration of the world is now entirely completed. On the Sabbath, resting in the tomb, he awaited the outcome of the resurrection that was to come on the eighth day. Rabanus, on Matthew, book VIII, chapter 27. See Bede, on Matthew, book IV, chapter 28, and elsewhere. The veneration of Holy Saturday is celebrated for this reason: on that same day the Lord rested in the tomb. Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, book II, chapter 38.]

Thus Mary Magdalene kept the Sabbath according to custom and was silent on the Sabbath (Luke 23:56), though she was silent without silence; for the sobs of the heart and the tears of the eyes do not accord with Sabbath observance.

But when the desired evening of the Sabbath arrived, with Joanna and Susanna and the other Marys standing by [Col. 1466C], she began to crush chosen and select spices and to mix balsam with the finest substances of every powder sold by the spice merchants (Song 3:6) [Col. 1467A]. One could see in the woman the courage of men as she completed the work that King Solomon had sung in her person: “My hands dripped with myrrh, my fingers with the finest myrrh and aloe and all the chief perfumes” (Song 5:5; 4:13).

Tears continually burst forth while she mixed them, from the fullness of her heart, in remembrance of her beloved, the one she loved; and as her breast grew warm with the fire of love, the remaining fat of devotion within her flowed out through her eyes. You would have seen ears of grain moistened by the dew of her eyes, shaken out gradually amid sobs; tears mingled with the spices; her hands wet with showers of tears; drops flowing from her eyelids, each drop more precious than myrrh and cassia, and certainly more pleasing to God.

Indeed, the illustrious maker of the Savior’s spices, together with her companions, made the night of the Lord’s resurrection so celebrated, so bright, and so radiant through the works of her devotion [Col. 1467B], that from that time God, the creator of times, willed the order of times to be narrated and day to follow night.

[Note: We must ask why, in describing the night of the Lord’s resurrection, the Evangelist says: “On the evening of the Sabbath, which dawns toward the first day of the Sabbath,” since the customary order of times makes evening grow darker into night rather than dawn toward day. But the Evangelist, speaking mystically, wished to indicate how much dignity this most sacred night received from the glory of death conquered: he declared that its beginning, when the women devoted to Christ began to keep vigil in his service, was already dawning into the following day. For the Lord, the author and arranger of times, who rose in the final part of this night, made the entire night festive and shining with the light of the resurrection.

From the beginning of the world’s creation until this point, the course of times had been distinguished so that day preceded night, according to the order of the first creation. On this night, however, through the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection, the order of times was changed. Since he rose from the dead at night but displayed the effect of that resurrection to his disciples on the following day [lacuna], that night was most properly joined to the light of the following day, and the order of times was established so that day should follow night.

Previously night appropriately followed day, because humanity, having fallen through sin from the light of paradise, descended into the darkness and distress of this world. Now day most appropriately follows night, because through faith in the resurrection, Christ granting it, we are brought back from the darkness of sin and the shadow of death to the light of life. Rabanus, on Matthew, manuscript of the Royal Library, 2439; *Homily on the Easter Vigil*; from Bede, on Matthew, book IV, chapter 28; *Homily on the Easter Vigil*.]

## CHAPTER XXIV — Where Christ rises, the angel descends, and the women meet at the tomb

After the sorrowful Sabbaths, a joyful day dawned; and the sun, rising from below along the straight path of the east and illuminating the sky, sent ahead a rosy dawn. Meanwhile the true sun of righteousness, Christ, rose victoriously from the lower regions (Mal. 4:2), and at the hour he willed rose immortal from the dead [Col. 1468C].

[Note: Our Lord could raise his flesh from the tomb when he wished and in whatever manner he wished. Rabanus, *Homily for Tuesday of Easter Week*.]

At that hour there was a great earthquake, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose (Matt. 28:2; 27:52).

Meanwhile Mary Magdalene, the noble maker of balsams, having prepared before dawn her compounds of the first and finest genuine liquids, filled her alabaster vessels—so precious that they could fittingly embalm the price of the world, and so abundant that they would amply suffice for embalming the body. Very early, while the darkness had not yet been removed [Col. 1468A] and her arms were laden with spices, she hurried most swiftly to the Savior’s tomb; every speed seemed slow to her. The fervor of love had found the delays of night hard to bear.

Other Marys followed Magdalene, the Savior’s chief woman: Mary of Cleophas, Salome, Joanna, Susanna, and the others who were with them, each carrying the spices she had prepared.

The Evangelists also describe different times of visitation, not falsely or superficially, but deliberately, as evidence of their assiduous visits: they repeatedly run back and forth, go and return, and cannot endure being away from the Savior’s tomb for long or at any distance.

[Note: The fact that different times are described for these women in the Gospels is not a sign of falsehood, as the impious allege, but of their diligent service of visitation: they repeatedly go and return and cannot endure being away from the Lord’s tomb for long or far away. Jerome, book III on Matthew, chapter 38.]

Therefore, lest I should rashly—God forbid—depart even slightly from the Evangelists’ meaning, I have taken care, after setting out the names of each, to write down the very words of each [Col. 1468B].

[Note: I beseech readers that if any should judge these little works of ours, whatever their quality, worthy of transcription, they should remember to append the aforementioned signs of the names as they find them in our exemplar. Rabanus, preface to his work on Matthew.]

I considered this the better course because of certain commentators who so heap together and confuse the visions of the angels, which the individual Evangelists report differently, that they scarcely admit that the Marys had visions of angels not four times, not three, but twice—as though it were impossible for God, or unsuitable to so great a solemnity, that at least six angels should have stood beside the risen Christ or appeared to the women: one sitting outside, according to Matthew; another sitting inside, according to Mark; and two sitting, seen by Mary Magdalene alone, according to John [Col. 1468C].

[Note: Here words such as these may be missing: “And two seen inside by Mary Magdalene and the other women, according to Luke.”]

Matthew (Matt. 28:1): “On the evening of the Sabbath, which dawns toward the first day of the Sabbath in the glory of the resurrection”—the order of times being changed—“Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the tomb.”

Mark (Mark 16:1): “And very early, on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome came to the tomb, when the sun of righteousness, Christ, had already risen after the setting of his bodily form.”

[Note: The setting of the sun signifies Christ’s passion and death; he said: “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” Rabanus, commentary on Matthew, book III, chapter 8.]

And they said to one another: “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” For it was very large. And as they approached the tomb, looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away (Matt. 28:2–4), to show that the Savior had already departed, while the entrance of the tomb remained closed and the seal of the chief priest intact—just as he entered the world while the womb of the Virgin remained closed, with the seal of chastity [Col. 1469A].

[Note: The angel rolled away the stone not to open the door for the Lord as he emerged, but to provide human beings with evidence that his departure had already occurred. For he who, while still mortal, could enter the world by being born while the Virgin’s womb remained closed, could certainly, having become immortal, rise and leave the tomb while it remained closed. Rabanus, on Matthew, manuscript of the Royal Library, 2439; Rabanus, *Homily for the Easter Vigil*, from Bede. See Bede.]

For this reason he rolled away the stone and sat upon it. At the sight of him the guards were terrified and became like dead men. His appearance was like terrifying lightning, and his clothing white like snow.

## CHAPTER XXV — Where Mary brought Peter and John, and the angel speaks to them outside and inside

John: “Mary Magdalene came in the morning, while it was still dark, to the tomb and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb” (John 20:1) [Col. 1469B]. Fearing that his body had been removed, she was, as though informed by the relics of a head so dear to her, thrown into confusion of mind, burned with anguish, and was distressed.

Running back quickly, she came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved [Col. 1469C], so that they might either search with her or grieve with her.

[Note: As John says, Mary Magdalene undoubtedly came before the other women who had ministered to the Lord, being much more fervent in devotion; thus John not improperly mentions her alone, passing over those who were with her, as the others testify. She came, and when she saw the stone taken away from the tomb, before examining anything more carefully, without doubting that Jesus’ body had been removed from there, she ran, as John himself says, and announced it to Peter and to John. Rabanus, on Matthew, manuscript of the Royal Library.]

And she said: “They have taken my Lord from the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him” [Col. 1469D].

[Note: “So she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved and said to them: ‘They have taken the Lord from the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.’ Agitated by excessive love, when she did not find the one she sought, she ran to announce it to the disciples, so that they might either search with her or grieve with her over the Lord who had been taken away. Rabanus, *Homily for the Saturday in Easter Week*. Similar material is found in Alcuin, from Augustine.]

Here, where he says, “They have taken the Lord from the tomb,” the Greek manuscripts add “my,” with a more ardent feeling of love or service.

[Note: Some Greek manuscripts also read, “They have taken my Lord,” which may be understood as spoken with a more ardent feeling of love or service; but this reading is not found in most of the manuscripts available to us. Augustine, on John, chapter 20, tractate 210, no. 6. Although Rabanus seems to have taken this from Augustine, he repeatedly adds similar notes in his writings, being knowledgeable in Greek letters: “For the time of dissolution—or, as we read in the Greek manuscripts, of return—is at hand.” Rabanus, on Numbers, book IV, chapter 1.]

Then Simon Peter and the other disciple went out, and they went to see what they had heard. The disciples ran; Mary followed. Each disciple entered the tomb; they saw the linen cloths, and they saw the napkin, wrapped separately. They saw the tomb empty and believed that the Lord had been taken away, as Mary had said [Col. 1470A].

The disciples therefore returned to their own homes, from which they had run.

[Note: “The disciples returned again to themselves,” that is, to the places where they lived and from which they had run to the tomb. Rabanus, *Homily for the Saturday in Easter Week*, from Augustine, tractate 121, no. 1.]

But Mary, when they had departed, fixed her affections more firmly in the same place [Col. 1470C].

[Note: We must consider how great a force of love had inflamed this woman’s mind: even when the disciples withdrew from the Lord’s tomb, she did not withdraw; she sought the one whom she had not found, wept while seeking, and, kindled by the fire of her love, burned with longing for the one whom she believed had been taken away. Rabanus, *Homily for Thursday of Easter Week*. While the men were returning, her weaker sex was held more firmly in the same place by a stronger affection. Bede, on John, chapter 20.]

She stood outside at the tomb, wasting away in tears and anxious with longing. Troubled in mind and eyes by grief and tears, she wept while seeking Christ, and sought him while weeping, panting with desire for him. She sought him diligently; she sought him, looking around everywhere and asking questions. When she did not find him, she avenged herself upon her own eyes with tears, for they sought the desire of her soul but did not find it. They saw but did not recognize.

Later the other devout matrons also came to this, distraught in mind and dissolved in tears. Nor did the angel endure any longer—he who sat outside upon the stone he had rolled away from the entrance of the tomb, beneath the slope, on the right of those entering [Col. 1470B]. Taking pity on their grief, he began to console them more carefully, exhort them not to be afraid, and address them familiarly.

[Note: “The angel who sat upon the rolled-away stone by which the entrance of the tomb had been closed … refreshes its most devout visitors with kindly consolation, strengthens them not to be afraid, and, moreover, first addresses them familiarly, saying that he knew they were seeking Jesus and adding that he had already risen. Rabanus, on Matthew, manuscript of the Royal Library; Rabanus, *Homily for the Easter Vigil*, from Bede.]

Matthew (Matt. 28:5): “The angel answered and said to the women: ‘Do not be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. For it is impossible that what he said should not happen.’” And he ordered them to enter the tomb and see the place where the Lord had been laid: “If you do not believe my words, believe your own eyes” [Col. 1470C].

[Note: “He has risen,” he says, “as he promised you, for it is impossible that what he foretold should not come to pass. Come and see the place where the Lord was laid. And if you do not believe my words, believe the empty tomb.” Rabanus, on Matthew, manuscript of the Royal Library.]

Mark (Mark 16:5): “And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right, on the southern side of that place where the body of Jesus had been laid” [Col. 1470D].

[Note: “Sitting on the southern side of that place where the body of Jesus had been laid.” Bede, on Mark, book IV, chapter 16, and *Homily for Easter Day*.]

He was covered with a white robe, and they were astonished. He said to them: “Do not be terrified; you should not be afraid. Those whom you see are your fellow citizens” [Col. 1470C].

[Note: “Let those be afraid who, oppressed by carnal desires, despair of being able to reach the fellowship of the citizens above. But why are you afraid, when you see your fellow citizens?” Rabanus, *Homily for Easter Day*.]

“You are unmarried women; we are dwellers in heaven. You are ministers; we are messengers of one and the same Lord. You seek Jesus the substantial Savior, the Nazarene, crucified the day before yesterday” [Col. 1471A].

[Note: “You seek Jesus the Nazarene.” In Latin discourse *Jesus* is interpreted as “salutary,” that is, “savior.” Indeed, many could then be called Jesus, but not substantially, only by name. Therefore the place is added so that it may be made clear of which Jesus he is speaking: the Nazarene. He immediately adds the cause: crucified. Rabanus, on Matthew, manuscript of the Royal Library, in the same place, from Bede on Mark, book IV, chapter 16, and *Homily for Easter Day*.]

“He has risen; he is not here”—although he is also everywhere.

[Note: He added: “He has risen; he is not here.” He is said not to be here with respect to the presence of his flesh, although he was nowhere absent with respect to the presence of his majesty. Rabanus, on Matthew, manuscript of the Royal Library, in the same place.]

The Marys were standing inside the tomb they had entered, on the eastern side, before the sepulcher; the angel sat before them on the right side of the burial place. Extending his hand and pointing out to them, almost with his finger, the mausoleum empty of the body, he said: “Behold the place where the leaders of the Jews, the noble member of the council, and the others who devotedly buried him laid him.

“But because he truly has risen from the dead, go and tell his disciples who, when he was seized, were afraid and abandoned him, and all fled; and tell Peter, who, while the others were fleeing, followed him from a distance and afterward, when he had denied him three times and Christ had mercifully looked upon him in his denial, went out from the courtyard of the high priest and wept bitterly” [Col. 1471B].

[Note: We must ask why, after naming the disciples, the angel identifies Peter by name. But if the angel had not named the man who had denied his Master, he would not have dared to come among the disciples. He is therefore called by name so that he might not despair because of his denial. Rabanus, *Homily for Easter Day*, from Bede, in the same place.]

“Tell them, I say, so that they may not despair either because of their flight or because of their denial, that he has risen. And behold, he goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him, as he told you.”

But they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and fear had seized them; and they said nothing to anyone, because they were afraid.

## CHAPTER XXVI — Where Mary Magdalene alone first sees two angels sitting, and then Christ
## John

“Mary Magdalene stood outside at the tomb, weeping” (John 20:11), grieving more because he had been taken away from the tomb than because he had been hung upon the cross. She had lost the living presence of her beloved Beloved, and she retained no memory of the dead man in any of his remains.

> **Note d.** Mary’s eyes, which had sought the Lord and had not found him, were already overflowing with tears. She grieved more because he had been taken away from the tomb than because he had been killed on the wood, since no memory remained of so great a teacher, whose life had been taken from them (or: her). Rabanus, *Homily for Easter Thursday*. This is found word for word in Alcuin, from Bede on John, chapter 20.

She therefore wept inconsolably, because she feared that she had irrecoverably lost the one whom the soldiers, after crucifying him, and the Jews, after sealing the tomb, had left for her. Yet she did not believe herself, although before dawn she had seen the empty mausoleum; nor the apostles, who had searched for him with her; nor the apostles to whom she had announced that he had been taken away; nor the women companions, who had often been frustrated in their searching; nor the angels, from whom she had heard not that he was absent from that place but that he had risen. While she was weeping, she bent down and looked into the tomb—truly at the prompting and inspiration of the one who was urging her to seek him.

> **Note e.** She herself had already announced to the disciples that he had been taken away, and they had come to the tomb; they had sought the Lord’s body not only by looking but also by entering, and had not found it. Yet, because she was grieving excessively, did she not easily believe either her own eyes or theirs? Or rather, was it brought about in her mind by divine prompting that she should look? Rabanus, from Saint Augustine, same passage, *Tractate* 121, no. 1.

He was also kindling her mind with the fire of his love. Under his instruction she considered that she should not easily trust the eyes of the apostles, of the women, or even her own. And she saw two angels in white, seated, one at the head and the other at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been placed.

They said to her: “Woman, why are you weeping?” Mary, thinking that they were inquiring and not ignorant of the reason for her tears, replied: “Because they have taken away my Lord”—so that, by speaking of the whole, she might signify a part—and “I do not know where they have placed him.” This increased the sorrow of her grief, since she did not know where to seek the comforter of her pain.

> **Note f.** “Because they have taken away my Lord.” She calls the lifeless body of her Lord “her Lord,” signifying a part by the whole, just as we all confess Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, our Lord. He is at once Word, soul, and flesh; yet it was flesh alone that was crucified and buried. Rabanus, *Homily for Holy Thursday of Easter*. This is found in Bede and Alcuin, from Gregory the Great, *Homilies on the Gospels*, book II, homily 25, and ultimately from Saint Augustine, same passage.

> **Note g.** “And I do not know,” she says, “where they have placed him.” This was the cause of her greater grief: she did not know where she should go to console her sorrow. Rabanus, same passage; Bede, same passage; from Saint Augustine, *Tractate* 121, no. 1.

When Mary had said this to the angels, bending toward the entrance—for the door of the tomb was low, and one could see inside only by humbling oneself—she straightened again and turned backward, toward the rising sun. She saw the Lord Jesus standing in the garden, but she did not know that it was Jesus.

She loved intensely the one she desired and had sought for so long. Because she had not found him, her hope of finding him had now grown weak; and therefore she saw him but did not recognize him.

> **Note h.** It should be noted that Mary was still doubting the Lord’s resurrection. Yet because she loved and doubted, she saw but did not recognize him: love had shown him to her, while doubt concealed him. Her continuing ignorance is likewise expressed when it is added that she did not know that it was Jesus. Rabanus, same passage, from Gregory the Great, *Homilies on the Gospels*, book II, homily 25, no. 4.

Thus she seemed rightly to utter that prophetic saying: “My eyes have grown dim from my weeping” (Job 16:17), because he who consoled me has withdrawn far from me.

Jesus said to her: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?”

> **Note i.** Jesus says to her: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” He asks the cause of her grief so that her desire may increase, in order that, when she named the one she was seeking, she might burn more ardently with love for him. Rabanus, same passage.

When she heard this, Mary’s desire flared up. Repeating her sighs and speaking in half-broken words, she reverently—or perhaps tearfully—answered the one whom she supposed to be the gardener. She did not say why she was weeping or whom she was seeking, as is natural among those who love deeply: they think constantly of what they themselves love and hope [perhaps: think] that everyone else thinks of it as well.

> **Note a.** This is the power of love; this is what it habitually does in the mind: whoever is always in one’s own thoughts is believed to be unknown to no one else. Rightly this woman does not say whom she is seeking, yet she says: “If you have taken him away,” because she does not think that the one whom she continually mourns in longing could be unknown to another. Same passage.

She prepared her shoulders to carry back the one whom she believed had been carried away, and said: “Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have placed him, and I myself will take him.”

“O love as strong as death!” Truly, nothing is difficult for one who loves. The strength of the love with which Mary burned for Christ persuaded her that she alone could carry the Savior’s body, anointed with one hundred pounds of aloe and myrrh.

At this the Savior, when he had come to console Mary, kindled her still more by asking whom she was seeking, no longer able to remain hidden, to look upon her panting, or to hear her lamenting. For the abundance of her grief had already grown to the point of exhaustion, arising from the greatness of her desire: while he whom she sought was himself present, he concealed himself from the one who saw him and revealed himself to the one who did not see him.

He called her by name, “in the abundance of his sweetness” (Psalm 30:20), saying: “Mary, recognize me, the one by whom you are recognized. I know you by name (Exodus 32:12); I know who you are and what you desire. Here I am—do not weep; here I am, the one you seek.”
