> **Note b.** “Mary says to him,” as though he were saying openly: “Recognize the one by whom you are recognized.” To the perfect man also he says: “I know you by name,” as though the Lord were saying openly: “I know you specifically, not generally like the others.” Rabanus, same passage, and in Alcuin, from Gregory the Great, same passage.

At once Mary’s bitterness of grief was stilled when the comfort of the friend’s voice and the sweetness of the Lord sounded. She recognized the familiar voice and felt the customary tenderness with which he had been accustomed to call her “Mary.”

Then, lowering her face and humbly worshiping, the disciple greeted her Teacher, saying: “Rabboni”—that is, “Teacher” (John 20:16).

> **Note c.** She says to him, “Rabboni.” Here she remembered the teacher from whom she had learned to distinguish human things from divine things. Saint Augustine, same passage, *Tractate* 121, no. 2. Since Mary recognizes the author when she is called by name, she immediately calls him “Rabboni,” that is, “Teacher,” because he was both the one whom she was seeking outwardly and the one who was teaching her inwardly to seek him. Same passage and in Alcuin, same passage, from Gregory the Great, same passage.

As she approached, intending to humble herself at Christ’s footsteps, she embraced his feet, as she had done nine days earlier. The Lord said to her: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.”

“Do not touch me with bodily embraces; for you do not yet believe that I have escaped the bonds of death, since you are seeking the living among the dead. Rather, first touch me with the embrace of your heart, firmly holding the faith in my resurrection. For I have not ascended to the Father in your heart, since you do not yet believe that I have risen or that I am equal to God the Father.”

> **Note d.** “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.” These words show that Mary wished to embrace the feet of the one whom she had recognized. But the Teacher says to her: “Do not touch me”—not because after the resurrection the Lord refused to be touched by women, since it is written concerning two women at his tomb: “They approached and held his feet.” The reason why he should not be touched is added when it follows: “For I have not yet ascended to my Father.” Jesus ascends to the Father in our heart when he is believed to be equal to the Father. For whoever does not believe him equal to the Father still does not have him ascended to the Father in his heart. Rabanus, *Homily for Easter Thursday*, and in Alcuin, from Gregory the Great, same passage. Similar material is found in Bede on John, chapter 20.

When Mary heard this, she no longer doubted but believed Christ. She drew faith from hearing the Lord’s desired voice and from seeing his desirable face. For the mustard seed that Jesus, the good gardener, had sown in the garden of her heart immediately took root and grew into a great tree of the firmest faith (Matthew 13:31; Luke 13:19). Without hesitation she believed that the Christ whom she saw, the Son of God, was truly God—the one whom she had loved while he was living—and that he had truly risen from the dead, whom she had seen dying; that he was truly equal to God the Father, whom she had sought lying in the tomb.

> **Note e.** She thought that he was the gardener. Perhaps this woman was not mistaken even in thinking that Jesus was a gardener. Was he not spiritually a gardener to her, who planted in her breast, through the seeds of his love, the flourishing crops of virtues? Rabanus, *Homily for Holy Thursday of Easter*. Christ compares perfect faith to a mustard seed. *Homily*, same passage. The man who sowed a mustard seed in his field is Christ, who sowed faith in the world; in that faith the birds of heaven—that is, spiritual souls—rest. Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book IV, chapter 1. The tree is strong faith, as in the Gospel: the mustard seed grew and became a great tree, just as faith grew and received great strength. Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*. When Jesus answered her thus, he was teaching faith; and that gardener was sowing a mustard seed in her heart as in his garden. Bede on John, chapter 20, from Saint Augustine, same passage, *Tractate* 121, no. 3.

## CHAPTER XXVII — Where Christ sends Magdalene to the apostles as an apostle

At last, persuaded by the exceedingly sweet privilege of that former love which had never ceased to burn in the heart of his chief and special friend, and knowing with absolute certainty—for no secret is hidden from him—that he had already ascended to the Father in the heart of his believing spice-bearing woman, the Savior appointed her as the apostle of his ascension to the apostles. He rewarded his standard-bearer with a worthy recompense of grace and glory and with the first and chief privilege of honor, since she had shortly before been appointed evangelist of the resurrection. He said to her:

“Go to my brothers and say to them: ‘Thus says the Lord: I ascend to my Father by nature and to your Father by grace; to my God, under whom I am human, and to your God, between whom and him I am mediator’” (John 20:17).

> **Note f.** “Go to my brothers and say to them: ‘I ascend to my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God.’” He does not say “our Father”; therefore he is my Father in one way and your Father in another. He is my God, under whom I too am human; he is your God, between whom and him I am mediator. “I ascend to my Father,” namely, by nature, “and to your Father,” by grace. Rabanus, *Homily for Easter Thursday*. Bede on John, chapter 20; also in Alcuin on John, from Saint Augustine, same passage, *Tractate* 121, no. 3.

He said this, and immediately vanished from her eyes.

But she, raised to such great and singular dignity of honor and grace by the Lord and Savior himself, the Son of God, and illumined alone by his first and most excellent appearance—being, among all the female sex, after the unique Virgin Mother of God, the one most familiar to God, most devoted, and most beloved—did not delay in carrying out the apostolic office with which she had been honored. Rather, she hurried at once to the apostles and said to them:

“Rejoice with me, all you who love the Lord, because the one whom I was seeking appeared to me. While I was weeping at the tomb, I saw my Lord, and he said this to me: ‘Go to my brothers and say to them: Thus says the Lord: I ascend to my Father, who begot me before the ages, and to your Father, who adopted you as sons for himself; to my God, because I descended, and to your God, because you have ascended.’”

> **Note a.** “I ascend to my God, because I descended; to your God, because you have ascended.” Rabanus, same passage.

Behold, the life that was taken from the world through Eve and announced as restored through the Virgin Mary. At that time Eve intoxicated the man in paradise with the poisonous drink; now Magdalene offered the cup of eternal life to the apostles.

> **Note b.** Behold, the guilt of the human race is cut off at the point from which it proceeded. Because in paradise a woman offered death to a man, from the tomb a woman announces life to men and recounts the words of her life-giver, she who had recounted the serpent’s deadly words. It is as though the Lord were saying to the human race not in words but in deeds: “From the hand by which the drink of death was brought to you, receive the cup of life.” Rabanus, on Matthew, Royal Library manuscript, and in Alcuin, same passage, from Gregory the Great, *Homilies on the Gospels*. Just as at the beginning the woman was the author of guilt for the man, and the man the executor of error, so now the one who had first tasted death was the first to see the resurrection, and the one who had transferred guilt to the man transferred grace as well. Rabanus, *Homily for the Saturday of Easter Octave*. See also Bede on Mark, book IV, chapter 16.

Eve first drank the asp’s gall in the garden of delights (Job 20:14).

> **Note c.** The asp is the devil, as in the Psalms: “You will tread upon the asp and the basilisk”—that is, you will crush the one who deceives secretly and rages openly. The asp is the devil’s hidden ferocity. Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*. Gall is the persuasion of demons, as in Job: “Into the gall of asps.” Same passage.

Mary was the first to see the victor over death in the garden of burial. Eve persuaded her own husband through the serpent’s promise: “You will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). Mary proclaimed to her fellow apostles the resurrection of the Messiah: “I have seen the Lord,” and prophesied his ascension: “He said this to me: ‘I ascend to my Father and your Father’” (John 20:18).

Mary was a far truer prophetess than Eve, and the last cupbearer was far better than the first. “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Psalm 76:11).

Mary had come to the tomb burdened with spices, as a woman skilled in perfumes, in order to embalm the dead. Finding him alive, she gladly changed the office she had intended to perform: she became the cupbearer of the living Savior and offered the apostles the balsams of true life.

That the Savior appeared first to Mary Magdalene alone, as we explained according to John, is also testified by the evangelist Mark: “Rising early on the first day of the week, Jesus appeared first to Mary Magdalene” (Mark 16:9). And because we read of many Marys, lest we should suppose that there were also several Magdalenes, as some have wished, he adds a celebrated benefit and certain identifying sign: “The woman from whom he had cast out seven demons.”

He testifies that she not only saw the risen Lord first but also first proclaimed him to the apostles, adding: “She went and announced it to those who had been with Jesus, as they mourned and wept. And when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe.”

When she could not persuade them, she returned to the tomb, hoping—as happened—to see the Lord again.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — Where two angels standing and Christ appeared a second time, and concerning the remaining appearances

Thus far we have recounted the Savior’s first appearance, in which he first wished to be seen by Mary Magdalene alone among mortals; the appearance of the two angels, whom Mary alone saw seated and addressed; and Mary’s apostleship, by which, exalted by the Son of God himself on the day of so great a solemnity—than which none has ever been happier or more celebrated, nor is, nor will be—she first proclaimed to her fellow apostles that the resurrection had already occurred and alone prophesied the future ascension. We have also recounted how, first offering the drink of life to the apostles, she purified Eve’s cup, on the testimony of the evangelists John and Mark.

Now we shall briefly explain, according to Luke, the vision of the two angels whom she saw standing together with the other women, and at the same time the Savior’s second appearance, in which, according to Matthew, he wished to be seen by the two Marys.

Luke (Luke 24:4): “And it happened, while the women were bewildered in mind because the body of the Lord Jesus had not been found, that behold, two men stood beside them in shining clothing.”

When the women were afraid and lowered their faces toward the ground, this custom also arose in the Church of God: throughout the whole Easter season, we pray not on bent knees but with only the face inclined toward the ground.

> **Note e.** It should be noted that the holy women, when angels stood beside them, are said not to have fallen upon the ground but to have lowered their faces toward the ground. Nor do we read that any of the saints, during the Lord’s resurrection, worshiped prostrate on the earth when either the Lord himself or angels appeared to them. Hence the ecclesiastical custom arose that, whether in memory of the Lord or in hope of our resurrection, on all Sundays and throughout the season of Pentecost we should pray not with bent knees but with our faces inclined toward the ground. Rabanus, *Homily for the First Sunday after the Easter Octave*, from Bede on Luke, book VI, chapter 24.

The angels said to them: “Why do you seek the living among the dead? The places of the dead are tombs. He is not here, but has risen.”

> **Note f.** “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” “Do not,” they say, “seek among the dead—that is, in the tomb, which is properly the place of the dead—the one who has already risen from the dead to life.” Rabanus, same passage.

“Remember how he spoke to you. For he had foretold not only to the men but also to the holy women that he would rise, while he was still in Galilee,” saying: “It is necessary that the Son of Man be handed over to the hands of sinners, be crucified, and rise on the third day.”

The women remembered the words of the Lord Jesus.

Matthew (Matthew 28:8): “And Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went out from the tomb with fear and great joy, running to announce it to his disciples. And behold, he met them and said: ‘Greetings!’” Thus the curse of Eve was dissolved: first through the mouth of Gabriel in the case of the singular Virgin, and now through the mouth of the Savior himself in the case of the Marys.

They approached, held his feet—which he had previously forbidden one of them to touch because she did not yet believe—and worshiped him. Like the universal Church, they kissed the Lord’s footprints.

> **Note b.** Behold, Jesus meets them and says: “Greetings,” so that the curse of Eve, the woman’s curse among women, might be dissolved. They approached, held his feet, and worshiped him. They approach and hold his feet because they worshiped him. But the woman who sought the living among the dead and did not yet know that the Son of God had risen rightly heard: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.” Rabanus, on Matthew, Royal Library manuscript, *Homily for the Friday of the Easter Octave*.

Then Jesus said to them: “Do not be afraid. Go and announce to my brothers that they should go to Galilee; there they will see me.”

Luke (Luke 24:9): “And they went out from the tomb and announced all these things to the eleven and to all the others. There were Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary of James, and the other women who were with them; they were telling these things to the apostles.”

> **Note c.** This Mary Magdalene is the sister of Lazarus who anointed the Lord with ointment; Joanna was the wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward; Mary of James was the mother of James the Younger and Joseph, and the sister of the Lord’s mother. Rabanus, *Homily for the First Sunday after the Easter Octave*.

These words seemed to them like nonsense, and they did not believe them. But Peter rose and ran to the tomb. Bending down, he saw only the linen cloths lying there, and he went away wondering to himself at what had happened.

Then the Savior appeared to him, for he appeared third to Simon Peter.

Mark (Mark 16:12): “After this he appeared in another form to two who were walking, as they went into a village that is now Nicopolis, a distinguished city of Palestine,” sixty stadia from Jerusalem, which is seven and a half miles. They went and announced it to the others, but they did not believe them.

> **Note d.** “Emmaus”: this is now Nicopolis, a distinguished city of Palestine. Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book XIV, chapter 1, from Bede on Luke, book VI, chapter 24. This city, after the conquest of Judea, was restored under the emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus; when its status changed, it also changed its name. Bede, *Homily for Easter Monday*.

Luke (Luke 24:33): “And they found the eleven gathered together and those who were with them, saying: ‘The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon Peter.’”

He appeared first of all the men to Peter.

> **Note e.** Thus the Lord is understood to have appeared first of all the men to Peter. Bede on Luke, book VI, chapter 24.

While they were saying these things, Jesus stood in their midst and said: “Peace be with you.”

These, then, are the Lord and Savior’s five appearances by which, on the day of his resurrection, he wished to console those whom he loved and to be seen by his greatly beloved ones.

After eight days he appeared to them for the sixth time and offered his side to the apostle Thomas to touch (John 20:26). He appeared for the seventh time to those fishing by the Sea of Tiberias (John 21:1). He appeared for the eighth time to them on the mountain of Galilee, as he had commanded through Mary Magdalene.

> **Note f.** On that day the Lord was seen first by Mary Magdalene at the tomb, when, as she desired to embrace his feet, he said to her: “Do not touch me.” Then, while she and the other Mary were running from the tomb to announce to the disciples what they had learned from the angels concerning the completion of his resurrection, he was seen by them; concerning them it is written: “They approached, held his feet, and worshiped him.” He appeared also, as evening fell on that same day, to the two who were going to the village of Emmaus. He appeared to Peter. Immediately the evangelist adds his fifth appearance: “While they were saying these things, Jesus himself stood in their midst and said to them: ‘Peace be with you.’” Rabanus, on Matthew, book VIII, chapter 28, from Bede, *Homily for Easter Tuesday*. He is said to have appeared five times on the very day of his resurrection. He appeared sixth after eight days, when Thomas was also with them; seventh to those fishing by the Sea of Tiberias; eighth on the mountain of Galilee. In Alcuin on John. Ninth, he appeared to the eleven while they were reclining, on the day when he ascended into heaven. Tenth, they saw him on that same day no longer placed upon the earth but lifted into the air and seeking heaven, while the angels said to them: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.” Rabanus, same passage. Rabanus discusses the final two appearances below, in chapter 31.

## CHAPTER XXIX — Recapitulation: how pleasing Mary’s services were to Christ and how they were rewarded in the present life

Nor should we pass over what many rightly wonder at; rather, we should recall it from the beginning and review it carefully with great sweetness of spirit: that each service which Mary Magdalene offered to her Beloved, the Lord and Savior, was not, as is customary with the other saints, silently accepted and reserved for eternal recompense with the Father of lights, who sees in secret (James 1:17; Matthew 6:4), but was immediately disclosed, praised, and magnified by the Savior’s own mouth. And if anyone dared to distort or accuse any of them, she was immediately vindicated [or: “reviewed/enumerated”] and approved, so that, in accordance with the evangelist Mark (Mark 10:30), she received a hundredfold grace here in the present life for grace (John 1:16), until she might enjoy eternal glory in heaven.

And when her most holy sister complained about her, she sat under the shadow of the one whom she loved and, gathering the fruits of his mouth, sweet to her throat (Song of Songs 2:3), she “tasted and saw how sweet the Lord is” (Psalm 33:9). With splendid eagerness she drank from the veins of life (Proverbs 10:11), from the fountain of his breast, which multiplied its enrichment of her with spiritual riches, making the streams of her understanding and heart drunk with the drops of his utterances. In them she produced holy affections and rejoiced, while God multiplied the offspring of her devotion (Psalm 64:10–11).

> **Note g.** The manuscript has *enceriata*, through the carelessness of scribes. Perhaps *recensata* should be read, from *recensare*, that is, “to enumerate.”

“Many daughters have gathered riches” (Proverbs 31:29), but Magdalene, foremost among his attendants, surpassed them all.

She prepared in her breast a resting place for the fawn of the stags—whose spirit rests nowhere except upon the humble and peaceful—where it might lie, roam, feed, and be fed (Song of Songs 1:6), and where it might be intoxicated by the services of her devotion.

> **Note a.** The holy Church says in the Song of Songs to the one whom she seeks under the figure of the fawn of the stags: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you rest at midday.” The Lord is called the fawn of the stags according to the flesh he assumed, the son of the ancient fathers. Gregory the Great, *Homily on the Gospels*. “The fawn of the stags”: by the stags are meant the ancient fathers, as in the Song: “My beloved is like a fawn of the stags,” because Christ was born from the flesh of the ancient fathers. The stag is the faithful soul. Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*. The supper is the sweetness of contemplation, by which every perfect person is refreshed in contemplation by the wisdom of Christ. Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*. Whoever receives Christ within as a dwelling is nourished by the greatest delights of overflowing pleasures. Therefore the Lord gladly enters and reclines in the affection of the one who believes. This is the spiritual banquet of good works. Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book III, chapter 9.

Leaving aside these matters, by which the wondrous contemplative woman tasted in advance what the glory of the saints is, already worshiping the true joys that she now enjoys in her heavenly homeland, I wish to recall that she first, as a sinner, in the house of Simon the Pharisee, watered the Lord’s feet with tears, wiped them with her hair, cherished them with her eyes, and anointed them with ointment. She was not rejected according to Simon’s judgment; rather, fully recompensed for her sins, she departed to her home, filled with the sevenfold grace of the Spirit.

What a blessed recompense for a service unheard of through the ages!

Second, the holy lover, in the house of Simon the leper, broke the alabaster jar and poured nard over the Lord’s feet and head. She did not, according to the judgment of Judas the traitor, waste the ointment; rather, she earned grace, glory, proclamations of praise from the mouth of almighty God, and the promise of eternal remembrance through the Gospel.

> **Note b.** Mary Magdalene is the sister of Lazarus and Martha, the one from whom the Lord cast out seven demons. She, and no other, is the woman who watered the Lord’s feet with tears of repentance. Near his Passion, justified and made familiar to the Lord, she anointed not only his feet but also his head with holy oil. Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book IV, chapter 1, and *Commentary on Matthew*, book VIII, chapter 26. “Amen, I say to you, wherever the Gospel is preached throughout the whole world,” and so forth. It is not so much this woman as the Church that is proclaimed throughout the world, because it buried the Savior and anointed his head. Mary attained glory throughout the whole world wherever the holy Church has spread. On Matthew, same passage.

Now, for the third time, the famous woman skilled in perfumes prepared and hastened to anoint Christ’s body with the most precious spices, with an affection of devotion no less—and perhaps even greater—than before. Although the Savior, not despising but anticipating her intention, rose again, she nevertheless received no less the reward of her recompense.

For she was enriched by a manifold reward of divine condescension: she was glorified by being alone at his first appearance; she was exalted by the honor of apostleship; she was appointed evangelist of Christ’s resurrection; and she was sent to the apostles as prophetess of his ascension.

## CHAPTER XXX — On the three ointments: of the feet, the head, and the body
Therefore the precious ointments were reserved for Mary Magdalene, and sold and distributed at great price to the disciples of the Lord and Savior.

> **[Note: [Col. 1480D] c]** You will find this inserted in Saint Bernard, *Sermon* 12, no. 7, on the *Song of Songs*.

The Son of God did not wish them to be spent upon his dead body, so that he might preserve them for the living. For the Church of God lives, and it eats the living bread. It is itself the dearer body of Christ, and so that it might not die, that other body was handed over to death. Mary devoted her spices to the uses of this body—that is, to the needs of the disciples—carefully presenting to its members what could not be offered to its head.

The Savior, who is the fountain of compassion, knew that Mary’s spices had been prepared for him, mingled not only with the dew of balsam but also with the rich oil of great compassion. Therefore he wished them to be reserved not for himself—already immortal and, as recently as yesterday, needing no one’s compassion—but for his members, whose poverty needs to be relieved by the compassion expressed in words.

Blessed is that soul which, together with you, O blessed sinner and most ardent lover of Christ, recalling all its years in the bitterness of its soul (Isa. 38:15), embraces the feet of the judge and, filled as with fat and richness (Ps. 62:6)—with the hope of pardon—appeases the strict judge by the sacrifice of a contrite and humbled heart and a troubled spirit (Ps. 50:18), in the fire of sorrow and true repentance!

Such a soul receives from God the gift of understanding, the Lord saying:

> “Because I ate ashes like bread, incorporating penitents into myself, and mixed my drink with weeping” (Ps. 101:10).

> **[Note: [Col. 1480D] d]** “Ashes” means the sinner, as in the Psalms: “I ate ashes like bread,” because God incorporates the sinner—but the penitent sinner—into himself as he incorporates the righteous. Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.

But far more blessed is she who, together with you, O wondrous contemplator and most devoted minister, ascends from the feet of the humanity to be embraced to the head of the desirable divinity,

> **[Note: [Col. 1480D] e]** The head is Christ’s divinity, as in the *Song of Songs*: “His head is the finest gold.” In Christ’s divinity there is incomparable splendor. Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*. If Christ’s head is God, then consequently his feet are to be understood as the Incarnation, by which he touched the earth of our mortality. Rabanus, *Homily*. See Bede on Luke, book III; and Saint Gregory the Great, *Homilies on the Gospels*, book II, homily 33: “What does it mean that, at the place of the Lord’s body, two angels are seen, one sitting at the head and the other at the feet, except that he was to be announced who is both God before the ages and man at the end of the ages? As though at the head … because ‘in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.’ And as though at the feet, when … ‘the Word was made flesh.’” Rabanus, *Homily for the Thursday of Easter Week*.

assigns “seven and also eight portions” (Eccl. 11:2), attributing sufferings to humanity and ascribing miracles to God; and, for all his benefits, offers God a sacrifice of praise with a voice of rejoicing and confession (Ps. 49:14), offering precious pistik nard,

> **[Note: [Col. 1481C] a]** Nard signifies the fragrance of the virtues of the saints in the Church. Thus the bride says in the *Song of Songs*: “My nard gave forth its fragrance.” Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book XIX, chapter 8. Nard signifies charity, as in the *Song of Songs*. Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.

of many nations,

> **[Note: [Col. 1481C] (b)]** Saint Paulinus, *Letter to Severus*, volume VI of the *Library of the Fathers*. “The Church … had brought [in Mary’s person] an ointment fragrant with the grace and virtue of many grasses or flowers mixed together. The Church, fragrant with the various flowers and juices of heavenly graces, breathes forth to God manifold sweetnesses from diverse nations, and exhales the prayers of the saints like spices burning in fragrant bowls, through the Spirit of truth; so that the Bridegroom himself may rejoice in her, overflowing with the scents of such flowers and the dews of such liquids, with that joy with which he addresses her tenderly in the *Song of Songs*: ‘My dove,’ he says, ‘my perfect one, for my head is filled with dew.’” Saint Ambrose likewise, in *On Luke*, chapter 7.

offers it to God the Father of human beings [perhaps “of lights”], from whom every good gift comes (Jas. 1), enriched with the oil of devotion and burning with the unquenchable fire of divine love.

Such a soul receives grace from God in return for grace, the Lord saying:

> “The sacrifice of praise will honor me” (Ps. 49:23). “Whoever glorifies me, I will glorify; but those who despise me will be held in contempt” (1 Sam. 2:30).

But most blessed is the joyful person who shows mercy and lends (Ps. 111:5), who, together with you, O celebrated Balsam-bearer and chief minister of the Savior, carrying in the box of his breast the spices of compassion that benefit the whole body of Christ, gives himself to the Almighty; who diligently seeks out the innumerable needs of the poor and pours into them the balsam of mercy. In whose heart charity will always burn like fire upon the altar (Lev. 6:12),

> **[Note: [Col. 1481D] c]** Fire signifies charity, as in Leviticus: “The fire on the altar shall always burn.” This means that the ardor of charity must always be present in our mind. Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.

which neither the frost of love of money

> **[Note: [Col. 1481D] d]** *Philargyria*, which means avarice, or love of money. Rabanus, *On Satisfaction for Sin*, book III, chapter 51, on *philargyria*. This attribution to Rabanus is erroneous.

will be able to constrict nor the wind of vanity blow out.

Such a person is made a god by transformation. For nothing makes one a god by transformation [*deiparat*, so in the manuscript]

> **[Note: [Col. 1481D] e]** *Deiparat*, thus in the manuscript. The word may perhaps have the same meaning as “to make God” or “to deify.” It is not found in the ancient authorities, but the following forms are commonly used: *deificare*, “to deify”; *Deum facere*, “to make God”; *deificus*, *deicus*, “divine”; *deiloquus*, “speaking of God”; *deividus*, “one who sees God”; *deiformis*, “conformed to the divine will”; *deipassiani*, *patripassiani*; *deiferi*, “apostles”; *deicolae*, “monks.”

except the person who lives in such a way that his goodness benefits the community.

Let this suffice as a philosophical treatment of the three ointments of Christ’s special friend—the ointments of the feet, the head, and the body—with which she ministered to the Son of God in her love: the great lover, the wondrous contemplator, the blessed maker of spices.

Blessed is the person who sweetly hears these things about Mary Magdalene, happily believes them, and recalls them with the greatest devotion! More blessed is the person who, while piously admiring these things about Mary and reverently cherishing them, also imitates her with the most ardent zeal! Most blessed, surely, is the person who is so moved and delighted by Mary’s finest fragrances that he imitates the pattern of her conduct, is stamped with the form of her way of life, is intoxicated with the spirit of her devotion, and becomes a sharer in the “better part” that she chose (Luke 10:42).

## CHAPTER XXXI — On Christ’s Ascension, with the Apostles and the Marys Present

As the Savior was about to ascend into heaven, on the fortieth day after his resurrection, he wished to revisit his own who were in the world (John 13:1; Matt. 27:53) and to be seen by them. He appeared to them while they were eating in the holy city (Mark 16:14); and then, reclining at table, he ate with them, so that through the act of eating the truth of his flesh might be made evident.

> **[Note: [Col. 1482C] f]** While eating with them, he instructed them not to depart from Jerusalem. He took food with the disciples in order to show, by touching and handling it, that the same flesh which he had raised after death was real. Rabanus, *Homily for Ascension Day*. “To make known the truth of his resurrection, he deigned not only to be touched by the disciples but also to eat with them … so that in this way he might establish the nature of the body after resurrection, lest they think it was not a body but a spirit, and that he appeared to them not solidly but merely as an image. He ate by power, not by necessity.” Rabanus, *Homily for the Tuesday of Easter Week*, from Bede on Luke, book VI, chapter 24.

It was therefore a festival of solemn joy to behold, a meal memorable to the whole world, a banquet to be proclaimed to angels and human beings. Reclining with the Son of God were his blessed and glorious mother, the queen of heaven, the Virgin Mary; and John, the apostle and evangelist, prophet and virgin, whom Jesus loved more than the others (John 21:7); and Mary Magdalene, the Savior’s special friend and chief of his female ministers; and Martha, his most devoted hostess; and Lazarus, whom he had recalled from the dead; as well as Mary of Cleophas, Salome, Joanna, and Susanna.

Peter was also present, recently a “walker on the sea” near Tiberias,

> **[Note: [Col. 1482C] g]** *Mariambulus*. This perhaps alludes to Peter walking upon the Lake of Gennesareth, which Rabanus often calls by the name of Tiberias: the Lake of Gennesareth, also called the Sea of Tiberias after the city of Tiberias. The land of Gennesareth lies beside the Lake of Gennesareth and, according to some, is the same as the Sea of Galilee or Sea of Tiberias. The Sea of Galilee was named from the neighboring province; the Sea of Tiberias, from the nearby city, formerly called Gennesareth but rebuilt by Herod the Tetrarch and named Tiberias in honor of Tiberius Caesar. Rabanus, *On Matthew*, book V, chapter 14, from Bede on Luke, book II, chapter 5.

and, during the meal, joined to Christ by a threefold confession,

> **[Note: [Col. 1482D] h]** The Lord asks Peter three times whether he loves him, so that by this threefold confession he might release the bonds with which Peter had been bound by denying him three times. As often as Peter, terrified by Christ’s Passion, had denied knowing him, so often, restored by Christ’s resurrection, he testified that he loved him with his whole heart. Rabanus, *Homily for the Vigil of Saint Peter*.

as well as Andrew, the gentlest of the saints,

> **[Note: [Col. 1482D] i]** “Andrew, the gentlest of the saints.” The author may perhaps allude to the *Acts of Saint Andrew*.

James, the brother of John; Philip also, the son of that very gentleness; and that twin Thomas, the most vigorous investigator of Christ’s wounds; as well as Bartholomew, the mediator of the apostolic number,

> **[Note: [Col. 1483C] a]** “Bartholomew, the mediator of the apostolic number”—that is, he always occupies the middle place in the list of the apostles. In Matthew, Mark, and Luke he holds sixth place, and in Acts seventh place. Matt. 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14; Acts 1:13.

and Matthew, who is also Levi,

> **[Note: [Col. 1483C] b]** In the manuscript: “Matthew, who is Levi’s son, the son of Alphaeus, the first writer of the Gospel.” These words appear interpolated. Rabanus certainly wrote “Matthew who is also Levi,” following Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 3, which he knew very well—not “who is Levi”; he would have written “who was Levi,” and still less would he have written “who is Levi’s son,” since Rabanus himself, in *On the Universe* and in his *Commentary on Matthew*, says that this evangelist was surnamed Levi from the tribe, not from his father. Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book IV, chapter 1; *Commentary on Matthew*, book I, preface.

the first writer of the Gospel.

> **[Note: [Col. 1483D] c]** “Matthew the evangelist took the surname Levi from the tribe … and was the first to compose the Gospel in a language—that is, in Hebrew letters.” Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, preface.

Also present were James of Alphaeus, the Lord and Savior’s cousin, later patriarch of Jerusalem, who is called Oblias and Justus, a Nazirite from his mother’s womb;

> **[Note: [Col. 1483D] d]** James of Alphaeus is the one who is called the Lord’s brother in the Gospel. Because Mary, the wife of Alphaeus, was the sister of Mary the Lord’s mother—whom the evangelist John calls Mary of Cleophas—this may be because Alphaeus was also called Cleophas, or because Mary herself, after Alphaeus’s death following James’s birth, married Cleophas … After the Lord’s Passion, the apostles immediately appointed James of Alphaeus bishop of Jerusalem. He drank no wine or strong drink, ate no meat, and was never shaved, as Hegesippus testifies. Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book III, chapter 10, from Bede on Luke, book II, chapter 6.

Simon the Zealot,

> **[Note: [Col. 1484C] e]** Simon the Cananaean is the same person who is called the Zealot by another evangelist. *Cana* means “zeal.” Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book IV, chapter 1.

and Judas, the brother of James, who is also called Thaddeus and “Little Heart.”

> **[Note: [Col. 1484C] f]** Judas of James, elsewhere called Lebbaeus, has a figurative name derived from the heart; we may call it diminutively *corculum*, “little heart.” In another Gospel he is called Thaddeus. He was the brother of James, the Lord’s brother, as he himself writes in his Epistle. Thus he too was called the Lord’s brother, as his fellow citizens testify. Astonished at his miracles, they said: “Is this not the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, Joseph, Judas, and Simon?” Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book III, chapter 10.

There were also many others who had gathered and who were related to Christ by kinship and familiar to him. At that time they were already sharers in the faith, though before the Passion it had been said: “For even his brothers did not believe in him” (John 7:5; Mark 16:11).

The Son of God deigned to dine with them and, after reproaching their unbelief, said:

> “I will send the promise of my Father upon you; but remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high. For you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Luke 24:49; Acts 1:5).

Finally, assigning them the duty of preaching, he said that it was first to be carried out in Jerusalem, Judea, and Samaria; and then, when the Jews rejected the word of life, he commanded that the Gospel be preached throughout the whole world,

> **[Note: [Col. 1484D] g]** It was necessary that Christ’s coming first be announced to the Jews, so that they would not have a legitimate excuse, saying that they had rejected God because he had sent the apostles to the Gentiles and Samaritans. Thus the preaching, first rejected by Judea, would afterward become our assistance. Rabanus, same work.

promising those who evangelized the efficacy of all signs (Mark 16:17).

After he had spoken these and similar words to the leaders of his people, while he was “a king upon his couch” (Ps. 112:7; Song 1:12), the meal was finished and he arose. Going out, he led his companions to Bethany, on the Mount of Olives, near Jerusalem—a journey of one thousand paces, the distance prescribed for the Sabbath.

Finally, with the queen of heaven, the accompanying Marys, the apostles, and a crowd of nearly one hundred and twenty disciples present (Luke 24:50; Acts 1:12, 15), he gave them his final farewell:

> “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age.”

Then, raising his hands, he blessed them (Luke 24:50). Immediately, while they watched, he was lifted into the air and carried into heaven. At once an exceedingly bright cloud appeared; it received the Savior and bore him into the ether, while the queen of heaven, the apostles, and the holy women watched together with the beloved of God and the accompanying Marys (Acts 1:9).

## CHAPTER XXXII — On Those Who Ascended with Christ and on the Excellence of John the Baptist of Christ

Therefore, when Christ ascended on high (Eph. 4:8), he raised into the heavens the captivity which he had led out from the underworld: thousands of rejoicing souls of the first-formed human beings (Ps. 67:18), and all those who had pleased God from the beginning of the world (Wis. 9:19).

For he did not wish to ascend alone, since he had not wished to rise alone. The witnesses of his resurrection, whose tombs were opened when the Lord was crucified (Matt. 27:50, 53), and those who rose when he rose, and who afterward appeared to many in Jerusalem when the Lord appeared, ascended into heaven together with the Lord.

> **[Note: [Col. 1484D] h]** As testimony to the Lord’s resurrection, many bodies of the saints rose, in order to show that the Lord Jesus had risen; yet, when the tombs were opened, they did not rise before the Lord rose, so that he might be the firstborn from the dead. Those who rose from the dead when the Lord rose are to be believed to have ascended together with him when he ascended into heaven. When it is said, “They appeared to many,” this shows that the resurrection was not general, appearing to everyone, but particular, appearing to many, so that those who deserved to see might behold it. Rabanus, *On Matthew*, book VIII, chapter 27.

They would not truly have been witnesses of the resurrection if they had risen fantastically, shadowily, imaginatively, and not in reality.

An army of angels met the triumphant King. Immediately they were sent by the Lord upon the Mount of Olives, where, while he stood there and they watched him penetrating the heavens, they announced his return together with the queen of heaven, the apostles, and the holy women:

> “He will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

No one should think it absurd that we have related these matters so carefully and inserted them into the deeds of blessed Mary Magdalene, because she participated in all of them with complete devotion. Just as she was conscious of the resurrection in the garden, so she was a witness of the ascension on the mountain; just as she evangelized the apostles that the resurrection had already taken place, so she prophesied to them the ascension that was to come. Standing with the apostles as he ascended, and pointing him out as though with her finger, she demonstrated the one ascending, in the likeness of John the Baptist,

> **[Note: [Col. 1485C] a]** In this John is greater than the other prophets: those prophets preached that he was to come, but John pointed him out with his finger as having come. Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book IV, chapter 11.

more than a prophetess.

She was celebrated throughout the whole world for her astonishing conversion to Christ and her incomparable intimacy with Christ, just as John was incomparable among all the saints for his life in the wilderness and holiness from the womb.

John says that he is unworthy to loosen the strap of Christ’s sandal (Luke 3:16)—behold great humility!

> **[Note: [Col. 1485D] b]** In speaking of the Lord’s sandals, John intended nothing other than to express Christ’s excellence and his own humility. Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book I, chapter 3.

Mary drenched, washed, dried, warmed, and anointed his feet with tears, hands, hair, eyes, and ointments—behold wondrous intimacy.

When John baptized Christ, he trembled and did not dare touch the holy crown of God (Matt. 3:14).

> **[Note: [Col. 1485D] c]** John was astonished that Christ came to him to be baptized with water. He rightly feared—a human being, however holy—to baptize the Lord. Rabanus, *Commentary on Matthew*, book I, chapter 3.

But she poured ointment upon the head of the Lord, the most precious head of the price of the world, exceedingly precious; she, herself more precious.

> **[Note: [Col. 1485D] d]** Rare indeed is the person who deserves to anoint Christ’s head with pistik nard. Yet great was the one who declared himself unworthy to carry his sandals; and great also was the woman who deserved to anoint his feet and wipe them with her hair. Same work, book III, chapter 9.

The four evangelists record the deeds of both him and her. John is commended because he heard the Father’s voice and saw the Holy Spirit; she is commended because she continually ministered from her resources to the Son of the Virgin Mother with wondrous affection; because she stood by Christ when he was crucified and when he was being prepared for burial; and because she was the first to see and hold him when he rose from the dead.

Christ magnified John and commended his angelic life (Matt. 11:7, 10). He defended Mary when the Pharisee murmured, excused her when Martha complained, praised her when Judas raged, and appointed her as an apostle to the apostles themselves.

John the Baptist, “among those born of women” (ibid. 11:11), after the King of heaven, is equal to those above him, or superior to all.

> **[Note: [Col. 1485D] e]** “Among those born of women,” he says. He is therefore preferred to human beings born of women and of intercourse with a man, but not to the one born of the Virgin and the Holy Spirit. Yet when he said, “There has not arisen among those born of women anyone greater than John the Baptist,” he did not rank John above all the other prophets, patriarchs, and human beings, but made the others equal to John. It does not immediately follow that, if others are not greater than he, he is greater than all the others; he may instead possess equality with the other saints. Rabanus, *On Matthew*, book IV, chapter 11, from Bede on Luke, book II, chapter 7. It should nevertheless be noted that Rabanus, in his homily on Saint John the Baptist, held the common opinion, which he perhaps later corrected in his *Commentary on Matthew*: “There has not arisen among those born of women anyone greater than John the Baptist. For he surpasses all and everyone, precedes the prophets, exceeds the patriarchs, and whoever is born of a woman is inferior to John. But the one born of a Virgin is greater than he.” It should certainly be observed that, in the *Life of Saint Mary Magdalene*, while asserting the earlier view—at least John’s equality with the other saints—the author neither affirms nor denies John’s superiority over all, saying: “Equal to those above him, or superior to all.”

Magdalene, among the daughters of human beings, after the queen of heaven,

> **[Note: [Col. 1486D] f]** The Virgin Mary, the Lord’s mother, holds the primacy among all women. Rabanus, *Homily for Easter Day*.

is equal to those above her and inferior to none.

## CHAPTER XXXIII — How Christ’s Friend Grieved His Absence

Yet amid these celebrated glorifications of Christ, Mary Magdalene openly rejoiced beyond words in the glory of her Lord and Redeemer, while inwardly she grieved beyond measure over the bodily absence of her beloved Beloved.

It is natural—indeed, I say, natural and necessary—to be affected by friends pleasantly and joyfully when they are present, but tearfully and painfully when they are absent. The tears of the one who remains measure the magnitude of love for the one who departs; the extent of love among those present is perceived from the distress of those who are separated.

Mary alone, however, endured what lovers usually endure when they lose one another, although she had not lost her beloved but had sent him ahead to prepare a dwelling for her.

Who could estimate how sweetly and delightfully, while eating, walking, and speaking, she had heard the Savior; how she had gazed with unblinking eyes upon the Son of the Virgin, whose face she could never see enough, he who is “beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44:3)? What did she feel after the final farewell, after the solemn words of blessing, when he was suddenly carried into the air with raised hands? What did she feel when she followed with unbroken gaze the one received by the milk-white cloud as he penetrated the inner regions of the ether? What did she feel when, received into the open heaven, he could no longer be seen? (Luke 24:50–51.)

I believe that she stood there for a long time—or scarcely stood at all, or not at all. Rather, I believe she fainted and collapsed with panting breath; that, with her limbs chilled, she grew pale; and then, as her breast warmed again and tears arose, she wept most abundantly.

Could Mary, I ask, remember her beloved Beloved, the Lord Jesus, without sorrow and without tears? Could there henceforth be any time without pain, any moment without delay, any hour without weeping, although she knew that she ought not to grieve—especially when she remembered his promise: that he was going to prepare a place for his own, and would return to take them to himself, so that where he was, they too might be with him? (John 15:1.)

Recalling these things within her heart (Lam. 3:21), she turned mourning into joy (John 16:20). Through continual contemplation she saw the Son of God present to her in the spirit (1 Cor. 5:3), and so moderated her longing for his bodily presence, resting sweetly in the honey of his memory. At last, after many sighs, after longings, after the prolonged hunger for that most blessed vision, satisfied by the face of her beloved, she gave her neck to his sweetest and most delightful embraces upon the bed of eternal contemplation.

## CHAPTER XXXIV — On Pentecost and the Holy Spirit, on the Canonical Life of the Primitive Church, and on Mary’s Contemplation

Finally, after the vision and words of the angels, the apostles worshiped at the place where the feet of the Lord and Savior had stood and accompanied the queen of heaven as she returned to Jerusalem, with great joy.

> **[Note: [Col. 1487C] a]** When the Lord ascended into heaven, the disciples worshiped at the place where his feet had last stood and immediately returned to Jerusalem. Rabanus, *Homily for the Friday after the Sunday after Ascension*.

They entered the Temple, praising and blessing the Lord. Then they went up into the upper room with the Mother of God, the accompanying Marys, the other holy women (Luke 24:52; Ps. 131:7; Acts 1:1 and following), and Christ’s relatives. In great joy they devoted themselves unanimously to prayer.

> **[Note: [Col. 1487C] b]** “They were all together in the same place”—that is, in the upper room, where they gathered immediately after the Lord’s ascension. Rabanus, *Homily for Pentecost Sunday*. “Upper room” is so called from the sharing of food. In ancient times people ate publicly and communally; no one had a private banquet, lest hidden indulgence produce luxury. Rabanus, *On the Universe*, book XIV, chapter 20.

There were about one hundred and twenty of them altogether (Acts 1:15).

After the holy Matthias had been appointed to the number of the apostles, the day of Pentecost arrived. The Holy Spirit descended upon them at the third hour of the day in bodily form, in fiery tongues, with a mighty sound; and they began to speak in the languages of all nations (Acts 2:1 and following) and to prophesy.

> **[Note: [Col. 1487C] c]** The Holy Spirit appeared in fiery tongues because he makes all whom he fills both burning and speaking. *Homily for Pentecost Sunday*; Bede, *On the Acts of the Apostles*, chapter 2.

Whatever language any one of those hundred men and women spoke, each hearer—whatever his or her own language—seemed to hear that person speaking in his or her own language.

> **[Note: [Col. 1487C] d]** Their speech possessed this power: although hearers of different nations were present, each received and understood, according to his own language, the one speech that had been uttered by the apostles. Rabanus, *Homily for Pentecost Sunday*; Bede, *On the Acts of the Apostles*, chapter 2. “The grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out on the one hundred and twenty believers on the day of Pentecost.” Rabanus, *Homily for the Wednesday of Pentecost Week*.

At that time there were dwelling in Jerusalem, celebrating the feast, devout men from every language and nation under heaven.

> **[Note: [Col. 1487D] e]** “Celebrating”—that is, observing the feast. These were religious men who had gathered in Jerusalem from various nations for the celebration of the Paschal festival. Rabanus, *Homily for Pentecost Day*.

Among them five thousand immediately believed.

> **[Note: [Col. 1487D] f]** “Five thousand”: some words may be missing here in the manuscript—for example, “three thousand,” followed shortly by “five thousand.” For five thousand did not believe on the day of Pentecost, but only three thousand (Acts 2:41), as Rabanus knew very well. In his *Homily for the Sunday after Ascension* he says: “When the Holy Spirit came, the prince of the apostles preached to many thousands of Jews, so that we read that at his preaching three thousand men believed and were baptized, and not long afterward five thousand also believed.”

And afterward countless others …

All who believed were together and held everything in common. As many as owned fields or houses sold everything, converted it into money, and laid the price at the apostles’ feet (Acts 2:44; 4:34).

Lazarus also, the friend of the Lord and Savior, together with his sisters Mary and Martha, possessed a great abundance of estates and riches in Jerusalem and Bethany of Judea, as well as at Magdala and Bethany of Galilee. They sold everything and offered the proceeds at the feet of the chief of the apostles.

Noble matrons and widows also ministered with wondrous devotion and fitting affection to the queen of heaven, the glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God. In accordance with ancestral custom, they provided services to the holy apostles of Christ and were honored.

> **[Note: [Col. 1488C] g]** It was a Jewish custom, and according to the ancient practice of the nation it was not considered blameworthy, for women to provide food and clothing from their own means for their teachers. Because this could cause scandal among the nations, Paul records that he had rejected it: “Do we not have the right to take along believing women, as do the other apostles?” Rabanus on Matthew, from Bede on Luke, book III, chapter 8, *Homily 40*. “But let us see what companions she had: Mary Magdalene; Mary the mother of James and Joseph, his maternal aunt, the sister of Mary the Lord’s mother; the mother of the sons of Zebedee; and the others whom we read of in the Gospels.” Rabanus, *On Matthew*, book VIII, chapter 27; Bede, same work.

They had once been familiar with and devoted to the Lord and Savior: namely, Mary Magdalene, the special friend of the Son of God and chief of his female ministers, the apostle to the apostles; Martha, Christ’s most blessed hostess and daughter of his generosity; and the Lord’s maternal aunts, Mary of Cleophas and Salome, as well as Joanna and Susanna, his ministers and relatives of the queen of heaven, whom the evangelists call his sisters.

> **[Note: [Col. 1488C] h]** We understand the Lord’s brothers not as Joseph’s sons but as the Savior’s cousins, the children of Mary, the Lord’s maternal aunt, who is said to be the mother of James the Lesser, Joseph, and Judas; these are called the Lord’s brothers elsewhere in the Gospel. That cousins are called brothers is demonstrated throughout Scripture. Thus Abraham and Lot are called brothers, although Lot was Abraham’s nephew, and there are many similar examples. Rabanus, *On Matthew*, book IV, chapter 12; also book V.

For this reason, as zeal grew hot—

> **[Note: [Col. 1488D] i]** Zeal is spiritual fervor. Rabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.

a complaint arose among the Jews who had come from Greece, because their widows were being placed behind the widows from Galilee and Judea in the daily service of the saints (Acts 6:1 and following).

> **[Note: [Col. 1488D] j]** A complaint arose among the Greeks against the Hebrews. The reason for the complaint was that the Hebrews, as the more educated, preferred their own widows to the Greek widows. Bede, *On the Acts of the Apostles*, chapter 6.

When this became known, the chief of the apostles convened a council. He chose seven deacons, placed them over the tables and over those who ministered at the tables: Stephen, Philip, Parmenas, Timon, Prochorus, Nicanor, and Nicolaus (Acts 6:5).

Immediately the most blessed Stephen became renowned for miracles, and soon he was crowned with martyrdom.

All the Savior’s disciples, however, together with Philip the deacon,

> **[Note: [Col. 1488D] k]** It should be noted that Philip, who evangelized Samaria, was one of the seven deacons. If he had been an apostle, he himself would certainly have been able to lay hands on them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit. Rabanus, *Homily for the Tuesday after Pentecost* and *Homily for the Thursday*. From Bede, *On the Acts of the Apostles*, chapter 8.

were driven out from Jerusalem, except for the apostles who were with the queen of heaven and the illustrious matrons who ministered to them (Acts 8).

Mary Magdalene, however, clung to the glorious Virgin Mary as to the queen of heaven and mother of the eternal King, with unspeakable devotion. She ministered to her as a handmaid with wondrous affection and devoted herself with her to heavenly contemplation. The angelic visions and visitations which the Virgin continually enjoyed as their mistress, Mary Magdalene deserved to experience frequently, to be comforted and refreshed by them as their handmaid and as the special friend of her Son, Jesus Christ, God and our Lord.

When she was repeatedly illumined by their vision and conversation, she continually recalled, in her customary manner, “the memory of the abundance of the sweetness” of Christ (Ps. 144:7), her beloved Beloved; and in meditation upon him the fire of love blazed within her (Ps. 38:4), an unquenchable fire with which she burned herself daily as a whole offering, in an insatiable longing for her Redeemer.

## CHAPTER XXXV — Recapitulation: How Dear Christ’s Friend Was to the Queen of Heaven and the Holy Apostles
This holy woman was equally an object of love and honor to the glorious Mother of God and to the holy apostles, because of the manifold, magnificent, and immeasurable intimacy which she had enjoyed with the Lord and Savior. They loved her more fervently than they knew they had loved the Son of God, their divine Master; they honored her more insistently than they knew they had honored the Creator and Redeemer of the world; they consoled her more attentively than they had seen God, the God of all consolation and comfort (2 Cor. 1:3; Rom. 15:5), customarily console her more lovingly through angels and through himself. They constantly recalled and frequently proclaimed to the people how she had been converted from worldly vanity to discipleship of the Savior, and they set her repentance before sinners—for whom Christ willed to die—as an example of conversion, so that sinners might come to their senses. And because, if hope of pardon is absent, repentance is fruitless and superficial, indeed punishable, they presented Mary’s faith and trust as proof of a sure hope of forgiveness, so that penitents might breathe again.

Yet because the one who turns away from evil is not sufficiently dear to God unless he also undertakes to do good (Ps. 36:27), they displayed Mary’s life as a mirror of complete holiness, “to give knowledge” (Luke 1:77) and a pattern of good conduct, so that the faithful might run after the fragrance of her ointments (Song 1:3) and be transformed.

[Note: [Col. 1489D] a Through “ointments,” the gifts of the Holy Spirit are meant, as in the Song: “We will run after the fragrance of your ointments”; that is, “let us live well according to the examples of your virtues.” Hrabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.]

But because the hope of perfected conduct and the fruit of devout conduct are heavenly reconciliation and abundant reward, they brought forward Mary as an argument for divine mercy, so that all might rejoice in her. The apostles also very frequently recalled and publicly proclaimed to the people the unfathomable devotion of her most holy sister Martha toward the service of the holy Savior, their own needs, and the spirit filled with every grace of generosity and kindness: how intimate, gracious, and acceptable these two devout sisters had been to the Son of God above all women; with what inward love they had loved him; how tenderly they had been loved by God; how kindly he had often visited their house; how affectionately they had supplied him and his companions with everything necessary from their own resources; how confidently they had sent him word through their brother, “Behold, he whom you love is ill”; how lovingly he himself, revealing their brother’s death to his apostles, had said, “Lazarus, our friend, sleeps”; how mercifully, seeing them weeping, he had wept, and had wept with those who wept, so that the Jews said, “See how he loved him,” with the testimony of that disciple whom Jesus loved more than the others: “The Lord Jesus loved Martha, and her sister Mary, and Lazarus” (John 13:23; 21:7, 20; 11:5).

The apostles also decreed that this house of Christ’s friends—namely, Lazarus, Mary, and Martha—should become a house of prayer (Mark 11:1). They constantly recalled that the Son of almighty God and of the Virgin Mother had very often walked there, sat, reclined, slept, spent the night, prayed, and performed many miracles; and that the Savior himself had sanctified and dedicated it by his holy dwelling, residence, and extended sojourn.

As the number of the faithful increased, they appointed the holy Lazarus bishop of his own city in that same basilica.

[Note: [Col. 1489D] b “Basilicas” are royal dwellings. They are now called basilicas because in them worship and sacrifices are offered to God, the King of all. Hrabanus, *On the Universe*, book XIV, chapter 21.]

Later, when the Jewish persecution raged, he went to Cyprus, preaching the word of Christ; there he became the first bishop, and lived for twenty-four years after his resurrection. His memory, and that of his sisters, is still reverently celebrated at Bethany on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January [December 17].

## CHAPTER XXXVI  
### The Division of the Apostles and of the Twenty-Four Elders and Friends of Christ

After the martyrdom of blessed Stephen, the protomartyr, Saul was called from heaven to the faith (Acts 9); nevertheless, he was not called Paul until twelve years later.

[Note: [Col. 1489D] c “Nevertheless, he was not called Paul until twelve years later,” namely, after a proconsul had been converted to the faith, as Hrabanus supposes. For just as Scipio, after Africa had been brought under his power, assumed the name Africanus, and Metellus, after subjugating the island of Crete, received the distinction Creticus for his family, and Roman emperors are still named after the peoples they have subdued . . ., so Saul, sent to preach to the Gentiles, brought back trophies of his victory from the first spoils of the Church, the proconsul Sergius Paulus, and raised a standard so that he might be called Paul instead of Saul. Hrabanus, *On Paul’s Epistle to Philemon*. “It appears that Saul, according to the order of the history, received the apostleship in the thirteenth year after the Lord’s Passion together with Barnabas, and received the name Paul.” Bede, *On the Acts of the Apostles*, chapter 13.]

Those who had been scattered with Philip and the other companions of holy Stephen went about evangelizing the kingdom of God until they came to Antioch; there a great Church of disciples was gathered (Acts 11). There the name “Christians” first arose. There blessed Peter’s patriarchal chair was established. After Evodius had subsequently been ordained patriarch,

[Note: [Col. 1491C] a The old Martyrology, commonly called the Little Martyrology, 11 May: “Evodius, bishop, who was first ordained by the apostles at Antioch.”]

he returned to Jerusalem to the fellow apostles, who, at the Savior’s command, preached for twelve continuous years in the promised land (Heb. 11) to the twelve tribes alone.

[Note: [Col. 1491C] b Just as Jacob fathered twelve sons to possess the promised land, so Christ chose twelve apostles, to whom he entrusted the promised land—that is, the blessing of the heavenly kingdom. Hrabanus, *On the Universe*, book IV, chapter 1. There are two cities called Caesarea in the promised land, ibid., book XIV, chapter 1. Homily for Thursday of Easter week.]

In the thirteenth year after the Ascension, James, the brother of John, was killed by the sword; Peter was imprisoned; and Saul, through the Holy Spirit, received the apostleship of the Gentiles and the name Paul. In the fourteenth year the apostles were divided among themselves (Acts 12:2; 13:2).

[Note: [Col. 1491C] c “In the fourteenth year, according to the agreement of James, Cephas, and John, he departed to teach the Gentiles. Nor does ecclesiastical history contradict this when it says that the apostles were commanded to preach in Judea for twelve years.” Bede, *On the Acts of the Apostles*, chapter 13.

“He wrote a lie who, presenting a book on the death of the blessed Mother of God in the person of Melito, bishop of Asia, says that in the second year after the Lord’s Ascension all the apostles were divided throughout the whole world to preach, each in his own province; and that, as the death of blessed Mary approached, they were lifted from the places where they preached the word of God and carried on clouds to Jerusalem, where they were set down before the door of her house . . . The same writing also specifically reports concerning the apostle John that at that time he was preaching at Ephesus. All this contradicts the words of blessed Luke, who relates that the apostles remained there after the other faithful had been driven out of Jerusalem . . . Yet far be it from us to believe that the blessed apostle John, to whom the Lord, from the cross, entrusted his Virgin Mother to the virgin, abandoned her alone and cast down for so long a time.” Bede, *Retractions on the Acts of the Apostles*.]

The East fell to Thomas and Bartholomew; the South to Simon and Matthew; the North to Philip and Thaddeus; the central region of the world to Matthias and James; the provinces of the Mediterranean Sea to John and Andrew; the kingdoms of the West to Peter and Paul.

At that same time Paul came to Jerusalem to see Peter (Gal. 1:18; 2:9). He gave and received the right hands of apostolic fellowship from James, John, and Peter. From there, with his fellow apostle Barnabas, he went to Syria and Illyricum to evangelize. Peter, intending to leave the East and go to Rome, designated as preachers of the Gospel for the regions of the West which he himself could not visit men of noble standing in Christ and senior disciples of Christ: for the region of Gaul, which has seventeen provinces and as many bishops; and for the region of Spain, which has seven provinces and as many teachers.

[Note: [Col. 1492C] d Under the prefect of the Gauls’ praetorium, there were seven provinces of Spain and seventeen of Gaul, as recorded in the *Notitia Imperii* beyond the times of Arcadius and Honorius, as may be seen in Pagi, year 37, IV, VII, vol. I.

**Spain**

Under the diocese of Spain were seven provinces: Baetica, Lusitania, Gallaecia, Tarraconensis, Carthaginensis, Tingitana, and the Balearic Islands.

**Gaul**

Under the diocese of Gaul were seventeen provinces: Viennensis, Lugdunensis I, Germania I, Germania II, Belgica I, Belgica II, the Maritime Alps, the Pennine and Graian Alps, Maxima Sequanorum, Aquitania I, Aquitania II, Novempopulana, Narbonensis I, Narbonensis II, Lugdunensis II, Lugdunensis III, and Lugdunensis Senonia.]

[Note: [Col. 1492D] e *The Old Life of Saint Magdalene*.]

Of these twenty-four elders, the first and chief was Maximinus, one of the seventy disciples of the Lord and Savior, an outstanding teacher, illustrious through the grace of every kind of miracle, and, after the apostles, the standard-bearer of the Christian army, chosen above the rest.

[Note: [Col. 1492D] f Ibid.]

Blessed Mary Magdalene joined herself to his religious devotion and holiness by the bond of charity, so that wherever the Lord should call him, she would not be separated from his company or fellowship. For the Queen of Heaven had already been assumed into heaven. She had served her, devoting herself to contemplation and sharing in the delights of paradise. The division of the ten apostles had already taken place, and they had remained with them in pious devotion for so long, until, when the envy of the Jews stirred up persecution against the Church, Herod beheaded the apostle James, imprisoned Peter, and drove the believers from their own lands.

[Note: [Col. 1492D] g Ibid.]

When this storm of persecution raged, therefore, the scattered faithful went to the various regions of the earth assigned to them by the Lord, so that they might steadfastly preach the word of salvation to nations ignorant of Christ. When they departed, noble matrons and widows who had ministered to them in Jerusalem and the East joined them, unable to bear being separated any longer from the company of the Savior’s special friend and from the chief of all his female ministers.

Among them was Martha, the most blessed and venerable hostess of the Son of God. Her most reverend brother Lazarus was then bishop in Cyprus, and she followed in her sister’s footsteps. With them was blessed Marcella, a woman of great devotion and faith, the attendant of blessed Martha, who, greeting the Lord, had said: “Blessed is the womb that bore you” (Luke 11:27).

Saint Parmenas was also present, a deacon full of faith and the grace of God (Acts 6:8). Blessed Martha entrusted herself in Christ to his guardianship and care, just as holy Mary entrusted herself to the holy bishop Maximinus. Thus, by the wondrous counsel of divine providence, they directed their journey toward the western regions of the world, so that not only would the praise and memory of blessed Mary and her sister become known throughout the whole world through the Gospel, but also, just as the East had been made blessed by the example of their devout conduct, so the western region would be illumined by their bodily presence and their most holy relics.

## CHAPTER XXXVII  
### How the Twenty-Four Elders Received Gaul and Spain by Lot

Having therefore taken to the waves of the sea, the glorious Mary Magdalene, beloved of God,

[Note: [Col. 1493D] a Perhaps the word *friend* is missing.]

together with her sister, the most blessed Martha; holy Maximinus, chief bishop; blessed Parmenas, archdeacon; the bishops Trophimus and Eutropius; and the other leaders of the Christian army, left Asia with the east wind blowing. Passing between Europe and Africa through the Tyrrhenian Sea, and sailing around and downward, they left the city of Rome and all Italy on their right, as well as the Alps, which rise from the Ligurian Gulf and the Gallic Sea and extend eastward to the Adriatic Sea.

[Note: [Col. 1493D] b The manuscript first reads *Lugiristio* and then *Ligurio*, certainly through the carelessness of scribes. In Hrabanus, *On the Universe*, book XII, chapter 5, one finds *Ligurian waters*.]

[Note: [Col. 1493D] c *The Old Life of Saint Magdalene*.]

With a favorable voyage they landed on the right in the province of Gaul called Viennensis, at the city of Massilia, where the Rhône enters the Gallic Sea. There, having invoked God, the great ruler of the world (2 Macc. 12:25), they divided among themselves, under his inspiration, the provinces of the region to which the Spirit had brought them. Soon they set out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word by the accompanying signs (Mark 16:20).

The King of virtues, the Beloved of the beloved, gave the word to those who evangelized with great power; he gave them to divide the spoils of the strong man armed, the glory of the house of God (Ps. 67:12–13).

Saint Maximinus, chief bishop, received Aquae, the metropolis of the province of Narbonensis II, in which blessed Mary Magdalene completed the course of her pilgrimage. Paul received Narbo, the metropolis of Narbonensis I. Austregisilus received Bourges, the metropolis of Aquitania I. Irenaeus received Lyon, the metropolis of Lugdunensis I. [Gatianus received Tours, the metropolis of Lugdunensis III.]

[Note: [Col. 1493D] d “the First; Gatianus received Tours, the metropolis of Lugdunensis”—these words are absent from the manuscript, certainly through the copyist’s carelessness, because of the repeated words “the metropolis of Lugdunensis.” For, first, Hrabanus would certainly not have said that Lyon was the metropolis of the province of Lugdunensis III, since he himself notes below, and rightly, that Le Mans is situated in Lugdunensis III. Second, “these ten provinces of Gaul believed while these men preached. The other teachers preached not in the remaining seven provinces, but in the cities,” and so it follows that Hrabanus had already designated ten provinces by name. Yet only nine are enumerated in the manuscript. One must therefore have been omitted there; and the omitted one was Tours. For Hrabanus admits seventeen provinces in Gaul, whereas only sixteen are enumerated in the manuscript, Tours having been omitted. It follows incontrovertibly that Tours was the province omitted.]

Sabinus and Potentianus received Sens, the metropolis of Lugdunensis IV. Valerius received Trier, the metropolis of Belgica I. Feroncius received Besançon, the metropolis of Maxima Sequanorum. Eutropius received Saintes, a city of Aquitania II, whose metropolis is now Bordeaux. Trophimus received Arles, then the metropolis of the province of Viennensis. These ten provinces of Gaul believed through their preaching.

The other teachers preached not in the remaining seven provinces, but in seven cities of the provinces: Eutropius at Orange, a city of the province of Viennensis; Frontinus at Périgueux, a city of Aquitania II; Georgius at Velay, a city of Aquitania I; Julianus at Le Mans, a city of Lugdunensis III; Martialis at Limoges, a city of Aquitania I; Saturninus at Toulouse, a city of Narbonensis I, where he was thrown from the Capitol for the faith of Christ; Parmenas at Avignon, a city of the province of Viennensis, where he withdrew with Martha, the venerable minister of the Lord Savior. Marcella, also his minister, withdrew with him.

Epaphras and Sosthenes, Germanus and Euchodia, and Syntex received the following cities: Rouen, with its province of Lugdunensis II, which is now Normandy; Mainz, with its province, Germania I; Cologne, with its province, Germania II; Octodurus, with its province of the Graian and Pennine Alps; Auch, the metropolis with its province of Novempopulana; Embrun, the metropolis with its province of the Maritime Alps; and Reims, the metropolis with its province of Belgica II. These were reserved for other teachers.

The names of those whom the apostles sent to Spain are as follows: Torquatus, Thesiphus, Secundus, Indalecius, Caecilius, Esicius, and Euphrasius. These seven joined the seven provinces of Spain to the Christian faith.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII  
### How Blessed Mary Devoted Herself Both to Preaching and to Contemplation at the Metropolis of Aquae

[Col. 1494C]

When blessed Maximinus entered the metropolis of Aquae, he scattered the seeds of heavenly teaching in the hearts of the Gentiles. Day and night he devoted himself to preaching, prayer, and fasting, so that he might lead the unbelieving people of that region to knowledge and worship of almighty God.

After a new harvest of faith had grown through evangelical preaching, blessed bishop Maximinus, presiding over the Church of Aquae, shone forth through many different miraculous works. With him in the same Church was the glorious and special friend of the Lord Savior, Mary, devoting herself to heavenly contemplation. She was truly the Redeemer’s most ardent lover and the wisest chooser of the better part, which, as God bears witness, was never taken from her after she had obtained it at Christ’s feet.

Mary in a wondrous manner aroused and, by arousing, refreshed her mind’s hunger for the Word of God. Drawn by the sweetness of her beloved Beloved, intoxicated in the Lord with longing for the cup,

[Note: [Col. 1495D] a “Intoxication” is the joy of heavenly grace, with which the elect will be filled when they enjoy the happiness of both body and soul. Intoxication is the inward satiety of the saints, as in the Psalms: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house,” that is, with the fullness of your heavenly house; and here also, at times, your saints are nourished. Hrabanus, *Allegories on Sacred Scripture*.]

she gathered herself entirely within herself and raised herself above herself. Dissolved by the warmth of the purest love, she tasted inward joys; while still placed on earth, she wandered through ethereal choirs,

[Note: [Col. 1495D] b Mary exemplifies the contemplative life, by which we sigh for the love of God. The contemplative life is to retain the love of God and neighbor with the whole mind; to cling solely to the desire for the Creator, so that the soul may burn to see the face of its Creator; so that it may already know how to bear with sorrow the burden of corruptible flesh, and with all its desires long to take part in those hymn-singing choirs of angels, to be joined to the heavenly citizens, and to rejoice in incorruption everlasting in the presence of God. Hrabanus, *Homily on the Assumption*. From Bede, *On Luke*, book III, chapter 10.]

walking in spirit among the angels.

Such was her inner life. Yet concerned also for the salvation of her neighbors, for whose sake she had come to the western ends of the world, she would sometimes lay aside the sweetness of contemplation and preach to unbelievers, or, in the end, strengthen believers with a honeyed mind, instilling honey-sweet words into the hearts of her hearers. For “the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart” (Matt. 12:24), and thus all her preaching was truly contemplation of God.

She always presented herself to sinners as an example of conversion, to penitents as a sure hope of forgiveness, to the faithful as a pattern of mercy, and to the whole Christian people as an argument for divine compassion. She displayed her eyes, whose tears had watered Christ’s feet, and which had first seen Christ risen from the dead; her hair, with which she had first dried his feet after washing them with her tears, and later wiped the feet anointed with precious nard at the supper; her mouth and lips, with which she had kissed the feet—of the living Christ, of the dead Christ, and of Christ risen from the dead—thousands upon thousands of times; her hands and fingers, with which she had first held, washed, and anointed the feet of almighty God; and with which she had again poured over them pure nard, pouring the remainder of the nard over the head of the Son of God.

Why should I recall each detail? Which of the evangelists is silent about Mary Magdalene’s merits? Which of the apostles clung more familiarly to the Lord? Which of them drank more eagerly from the streams of his teaching?

[Col. 1495C]

It was therefore fitting that, just as she was appointed the apostle of Christ’s resurrection to the apostles and its prophetess of his Ascension, so she should also become the evangelist of believers throughout the world. He knew this—he who, seeing and approving her devotion at the anointing of his head, said: “She has performed a good work upon me. Amen, I say to you, wherever this Gospel is preached throughout the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her” (Matt. 26:10, 13; Mark 14:9).

## CHAPTER XXXIX
