### Where Blessed Martha Preached, and Concerning the Miracles of Both Sisters

Blessed Martha, together with her companions, preached the Lord Savior to the people in the city of Avignon, in the city of Arles, and in the villages and towns around the Rhône, in the province of Viennensis. She publicly testified to what she had seen concerning him and what she had learned from his mouth; and whatever she preached about divine powers, she confirmed by miracles of her own.

Whenever occasion required, after prayer had been offered and the sign of the holy cross had been made, the grace of healings was present with her (1 Cor. 12:30): the cleansing of lepers, the healing of paralytics, the raising of the dead, and the granting of benefits to the blind, mute, deaf, lame, weak, and sick.

This was Martha’s work. In the same way, Mary performed miracles with ineffable ease, to confirm the truth of her words and to stir her hearers to faith. In the faces of both sisters there was a venerable beauty, in their conduct honesty, and in their speech a most ready grace for persuasion. Scarcely ever, or never, was anyone found who went away from their preaching unbelieving or without tears; no one failed to be inflamed by their faces with love for the Lord Savior, or to weep at the consideration of his own misery.

Their food was frugal; their dress combined propriety with religious devotion. Mary, however, cared little about food and clothing after she had lost the bodily presence of the Lord Savior, although the matrons who were with her and clung to her with wondrous affection provided her abundantly with necessities.

From this, too, that apocryphal story arose—if indeed it is wholly apocryphal—that, as poisoners customarily mix in more honey so that they may administer gall more secretly, the story perhaps arose that she was lifted daily into the heavens by angels, lowered again by angels, and refreshed with heavenly foods supplied by angels. If this is understood mystically, it is not entirely incredible. In truth, and without doubt, she was very frequently refreshed by the sight of angels, relieved by their services, and soothed by their words.

It was fitting—indeed, certainly fitting—that the God of all consolation (2 Cor. 1:3) should console Mary in a wondrous and unheard-of manner, since Mary herself had offered on earth acts of devotion wondrous and unheard-of throughout the ages.

But the claims that, after the Savior’s Ascension, she immediately fled into the desert of Arabia; that she hid naked in a cave; that afterward she never saw a man; that, visited by some priest or other, she asked for clothing; and other things of this kind are utterly false, borrowed by fabricators of tales from the deeds of the Egyptian penitent.

Indeed, at the beginning of their story, they themselves accuse themselves of falsehood by attributing their narrative to Josephus, the most learned historian, although Josephus never mentions Mary Magdalene in his books.

[Note: [Col. 1496D] c These writings of Flavius were well known to Hrabanus, who also cites them many times. In the *Commentary on Matthew*, book I, chapter 2: “It is read in Josephus that Herod killed several of the Jewish nobles before his death.” Ibid., book V: “Nor should we pass over what Josephus relates: that John, having been bound, was taken to the fortress of Machaerus and there beheaded.” Ibid., book VIII: “Josephus also reports that the angelic guardians of the temple once cried out together: ‘Let us depart from these dwellings.’”]

Let this suffice concerning these matters. Now let us return to the order of the narrative and, setting aside Mary’s contemplation for the moment, continue with the deeds and miracles of her most blessed sister Martha.

## CHAPTER XL  
### How Blessed Martha Freed the Province of Viennensis from the Tarasque

Between Arles and Avignon, cities of the province of Viennensis, along the banks of the Rhône, amid barren thickets and the river’s gravel beds, there was a wilderness of poisonous beasts and reptiles. Among the other venomous creatures, a dreadful dragon roamed there, of incredible length and great bulk. It emitted pestilential smoke from its breath, sulfurous sparks from its eyes, shrill hisses from its mouth, and horrible roars from its hooked teeth.

[Note: [Col. 1497D] a “For your almighty hand was not powerless . . . to send them among them” (Wis. 11:18).]

Whatever came within its reach it tore apart with claw and tooth; whatever came nearer it killed with the stench of its breath. It is incredible how many animals and shepherds it devoured, and how great a multitude of people it drove to death, dying from its foul odor.

One day, while the most blessed woman was preaching the word of God to the crowds who had gathered, the conversation turned entirely to the dragon. Some earnestly begged her, while others, as is customary, spoke testingly, saying that if she possessed any power through her Christ, the blessed woman should display it; for it could not be done by any human effort to remove this dragon from their midst.

She said to them: “If you are prepared to believe, all things are possible to the one who believes” (Mark 9:22).

Immediately, they promised faith, and she cheerfully went ahead of the people. She boldly approached the dragon’s lair and, making the sign of the cross, subdued its ferocity. She fastened her own girdle around the dragon’s neck and, looking at the people watching from a distance, said: “Why are you afraid? Behold, I hold the serpent, and you still hesitate. Come boldly in the name of the Lord Savior and cut this venomous beast to pieces.”

Having thus forbidden the dragon, by her powerful authority, to harm anyone with its breath or teeth, and having rebuked the crowds of little faith (Matt. 8:26) and urged them to strike courageously, she immediately restrained the dragon, but only with difficulty encouraged the crowds. At last, taking up weapons and exerting their strength, they tore the beast apart piece by piece, marveling at the faith and steadfastness of the most blessed Martha: she had held so enormous a beast motionless, without any fear, with her fragile girdle while it was being cut apart.

That wilderness had previously been called “the Black Hearth”; from then on it was called Tarascon, after the dragon, which was called the Tarasque. Thus, when they saw or heard of the miracle, the people of the province of Viennensis believed in the Lord Savior and were baptized, glorifying God in the miracles of his servant. From that time, because of her exceptional merits, she became an object of love and honor to all the people of the province.

## CHAPTER XLI  
### How Blessed Martha Lived at Tarascon

After the wilderness of Tarascon had been cleared by God’s power of every venomous reptile, most holy Martha chose it as her dwelling. She made habitable, pleasant, and beloved a place that had previously been hateful and detestable. There she established for herself a house of prayer (Mark 11:17), which she sought to enrich with virtues and miracles rather than with useless feminine ornaments. She lived there alone for seven years.

For all that time, her only food was roots of vegetables, green herbs, and the fruit and produce of trees. Yet she considered it wrong to refresh herself with this food more than once a day—though she did not impose this rule on her neighbors. For she did not wish her daily fast to be a punishment without compassion for herself or a burden to those living with her. Always mindful of her former hospitality, she was never without the poor, to whom she most gladly gave whatever was provided for her.

She always made the needy participants at her table, providing herbs for herself but necessary foods for them, with pious concern and her customary devotion. She did this with greater eagerness and more frequent care than if she had wished food to be set before herself, remembering that the one whom she had once been accustomed to serve on earth—who hungered and thirsted because he willed to do so—no longer needed temporal services as he once had, and therefore now wished to refresh herself in the poor.

The servant of Christ remembered what Christ would say concerning his own: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. 25:40). Thus, just as she had once ministered to the Head of the Church, she now sought to provide for the members of Christ. She was always beloved by everyone and approachable by all.

And because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7), he provided for his servant with his customary mercy, so that an unfailing spring of renewed abundance might arise (Ecclus. 24:6) and fill her storerooms (Deut. 28:8), emptied by daily charity, without any concern on her part. The devotion of the faithful supplied all the more what she could give abundantly, because she herself, through the generosity innate in her, gave cheerfully. Nor did she send the rich away empty (Luke 1:53); many of them flocked to her and received benefits for body and soul.

Her clothing was rough: sackcloth and haircloth, worn for seven years, fastened tightly against her flesh with a knotted belt made of horsehair, so that worms issued from her rotting flesh. O incomparable endurance—that a woman living in the flesh should become food for worms while still alive! She was always barefoot and wore a white tiara; her head was veiled with camel hair. Her bed was spread on the ground with branches and twigs, with a coarse cloth laid over them; a stone served as a pillow beneath her temples.

Amid such delights, Martha, martyred a thousand times over, gazed inwardly toward heaven. Her soul, wholly devoted to God, was lost in sacred prayers and kept vigil through the night. The one whom she had once seen humble in her house she now worshiped, with unwearied knees bent, reigning in heaven.

She also frequently went out to cities and towns, preaching to the people the faith of the Lord Savior. Returning to her solitude, she brought back many sheaves of believers. Whatever she taught in words, she immediately proved by wonders and signs: by prayer alone, with the laying on of hands, she expelled demons from possessed bodies and performed every kind of miracle through the power of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XLII  
### How Blessed Martha Raised a Young Man Drowned in the Rhône

One day, at Avignon, a city of the province of Viennensis, before the city gates, in a pleasant place between the currents of the Rhône and the city’s fortifications, most blessed Martha sat preaching the word of life to crowds of citizens and healing the sick.

A young man who was on the other side of the Rhône saw the gathering of the people and wished to hear the word of God. Since he had no opportunity to use either a bridge or a boat, he was nevertheless driven by eagerness to hear and see the miracles. Trusting in his skill at swimming, he stripped off his *pericia* [perhaps: *perizoma*, “loincloth”] and committed himself to the currents of the Rhône; then he began to swim.

All the eyes of the citizens across the Rhône were fixed upon him (Luke 4:20), when suddenly he was caught by the swelling waves of the boiling Rhône. He was submerged and drowned. A public outcry arose; the young man’s devotion was praised, and his misfortune was lamented.

Why say more? The entire people had one mind, one will, and one wish: that, with fishermen and nets sent out, the young man’s body should be sought with every effort, if by chance the mercy of the Lord Savior should permit it to be found.

On the following day, at the ninth hour, after a great deal of labor, it was found, brought back, and presented to most holy Martha. The entire city gathered for this spectacle (Acts 13:41). The city’s nobles, men and women alike, knelt and earnestly begged the servant of Christ to allow them to behold the mighty works of Christ the Savior in the raising of this young man.

She consented, as she was most willing to do—provided that all who were present would give their hands to the Christian faith. They all cried out with one voice: “We will believe that the Lord Savior is the true Son of God, and that he is God, who chose you as such a servant.”

At this, most blessed Martha rejoiced and, trusting in the piety and power of the Lord Savior, prostrated herself with tears and prayed. The people also prostrated themselves at her urging, and with a great lamentation (Gen. 27:38) they implored the mercy of almighty God, that, for the honor and glory of his name, he might deign to manifest his power in this miracle (Ps. 78:9; 79:3).

When the prayer was completed, the servant of Christ rose and approached the body. “In the name of the Lord Savior Jesus Christ, Son of God,” she said, “arise, young man, and tell us how great a kindness the Redeemer has shown you.”

Why delay with further details? At this voice, as his soul returned, the young man revived and sat up (Acts 3:6; Luke 8:39; 7:15; Acts 9:40). Immediately he confessed his belief in Christ and was baptized. After great rejoicing among the celebrating people, he returned home sound and unharmed.

When the people saw this, they all cried out with one accord: “Christ Jesus is the true God, and there is no other besides Christ God” (Jdt. 9:19). From that time, the fame of Martha, the most holy servant of Christ, was on every tongue; from that time she became an object of love to men and of honor to women.

## CHAPTER XLIII  
### How Blessed Martha Changed Water into Wine at the Dedication of Her House
[Col. 1500B] At that same time, throughout all the provinces of Gaul, and especially those of Vienne, Narbonne, and Aquitaine, a most distinguished report and the sweetest fragrance of a good reputation, like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed (Gen. XXVII, 27), stirred the hearts of all the inhabitants of those provinces toward faith in Christ and toward love for Christ’s handmaid, the most holy Martha. Her most blessed sister, Mary Magdalene, who must be named with the greatest reverence, rejoiced and congratulated her. Archbishop Maximinus, the organizer and guardian of the most holy contemplative life, set aflame in spirit, went from his second Narbonese province into the province of Vienne, as far as Tarascon, in order to see and address Christ’s handmaid (Acts XXVIII, 20). The same intention and desire also brought Archbishop Trophimus from the city of Arles, and Bishop Eutropius from Orange, to Tarascon: the same longing and vow brought them together on the same day and at the same hour. Yet at that time none of them suspected that the others were coming; nevertheless, under the inspiration of God, who orders all things sweetly (Wis. VIII, 1), they assembled together.

The sacred heroine received them honorably, entertained them generously, and forcibly detained them. On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, which is the seventeenth day of the month Casleu, called December by the Latins [Note: [Col. 1499D] The month Casleu, which is called December by the Latins. Rabanus, Commentary on Maccabees, Book I, chapter 1], they dedicated to the Lord Savior the basilica of the most blessed Martha’s house, distinguished by her signs, her miracles, and her holy way of life. After the dedication of the church, when the bishops had gone to dinner, the most holy Martha served them [Col. 1500D] with her extraordinary and customary devotion. Many who had gathered were reclining at table. When the wine ran out (John II, 3), the Lord Savior’s hostess ordered water to be drawn in the name of Jesus Christ and poured abundantly for everyone. When the bishops tasted it at the banquet, they perceived that the water had been changed into the finest wine.

The bishops therefore decreed together that this day should be solemnly observed every year, both on account of the dedication of the basilica [Note: [Col. 1500D] The day on which the temple was dedicated by Solomon, as the Book of Kings and Chronicles recount, the Jews solemnly celebrated; that day was considered a feast among them. This custom has evidently died out among those who have been deprived both of worship and of the temple. Christians, however, preserve the custom of those Fathers in whom the glory seems to have been transferred. Rabanus, On the Instruction of Clergy, Book II, chapter 45], and on account of the wonderful transformation of water into wine.

## CHAPTER XLIV.—Where blessed Martha greets Mary, entertains the bishops, and foretells that the day of her departure is near

[Col. 1501A]

After the death of blessed Martha, on account of this miracle a custom arose whereby, on the day of the dedication of her house, people also celebrated the feast of her passing, as well as the passion of her brother, Saint Lazarus, the bishop. We see the same practice to this day concerning blessed John the Baptist [Note: [Col. 1501D] It is gathered from the Evangelists that John was beheaded as the Paschal feast was approaching … and because the Book of Sacraments records his birthday on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, while in the Martyrology marked with the names of Eusebius and Jerome it reads: “On the fourth day before the Kalends of September, in the city of Emesa in the province of Phoenicia, the birthday of John the Baptist, on the day on which he was beheaded.” It does not specifically designate the day of his beheading, but rather the day on which his head was found in that same city of Emesa and buried in the church. Rabanus, On Matthew, Book V, chapter 19], and concerning Christ’s apostles John and James, Simon and Jude, and very many martyrs: their passions are celebrated not on the days on which they suffered, but on the days on which their churches were dedicated or their relics discovered.

At last, the blessed bishops took leave of Christ’s handmaid, commending themselves to her sacred merits and prayers. After giving and receiving a mutual blessing, they departed from one another (Acts XV, 39) [Col. 1501B]. Blessed Martha then greeted her venerable sister, proclaimed throughout the whole world, Mary Magdalene, earnestly asking her to deign to visit her while she was still alive. When the archbishop reported this to the blessed lover of God, Mary returned her sister’s greeting and granted what had been requested, although she fulfilled it not in the body but after the body. From this it may be understood that God’s saints remember their own people after death, granting them what they promised while alive.

At about the same time, a savage persecution of the pagans arose in the province of Aquitaine, and many Christians were driven into exile. Among them, Frontinus, bishop of Périgueux, and Georgius, bishop of Velay, fled to Tarascon and to the most blessed Martha. As a sign of charity, she kindly welcomed them, entertained them magnificently, and diligently retained them honorably until they were permitted to return to their own dioceses [Col. 1501C].

When at last they were hastening home, Christ’s handmaid gave them her final farewell: “O bishop of Périgueux, know that when the coming year is complete I shall depart from this body of death (Rom. VII, 24). I ask you, if it pleases you, to come and bury me.”

The bishop replied: “I shall be present, daughter, to serve you, God willing, with my life still accompanying me (Gen. XVIII, 10, 14).”

The bishops therefore returned to their own places (Acts XXI, 6). Martha, the most blessed, summoned her people to her and foretold that the day of her departure would come after a year. Then, lying on her noble bed made of branches, she was afflicted with fever for almost the whole year, as gold is tested by fire in a furnace (Sup. III, 6).

## CHAPTER XLV.—Where blessed Mary sees Christ; she departs and is buried

[Col. 1502A]

Meanwhile, blessed Mary Magdalene, devoted to heavenly [Note: [Col. 1502D] Rabanus’s codex always reads “heavenly.” But in the royal codices 5281 and 5360, where this passage is found—apparently taken from Rabanus—the reading is “heavenly.” Likewise, above, in chapter 38, Rabanus has “devoted to heavenly contemplation.”] contemplation and preserving the better part which she had chosen (Luke X, 42), although she still wandered in the body on earth, nevertheless walked in spirit through the beauty of paradise [Note: [Col. 1502D] Paradise means heavenly joy, as in the Apocalypse concerning the tree of Paradise. Rabanus, Allegories of Sacred Scripture], and fed upon that ineffable sweetness insofar as it is permitted to mortals.

Who could adequately explain with what sighs she was drawn, with what desires the Savior’s beloved yearned toward heavenly things [The royal codices 5281 and 5360: “toward heavenly things”], although even here she already enjoyed the company of angels? With what desires, I say, did she burn, longing to be with Christ (Phil. I, 23), so that she might see reigning in majesty the one whom she had seen humble in the form of a servant (ibid. II, 7) [Col. 1502B] [Note: [Col. 1502D] Ancient Life of Saint Magdalene].

At last, as the time approached when her most holy soul would be released from the prison of the flesh and enter those courts [The royal codices: “to”] which she desired and for which she languished (Ps. LXXXIII, 3), and be joined more fully to the Lord, the Son of God, the Lord Savior, appeared to her and showed her the object of her desire: namely [The royal codices: “namely”], Christ Jesus himself, with a multitude of angels, mercifully and graciously calling her to the glory of the heavenly kingdom (Rev. III, 21):

“Come, my beloved, and I will place you upon my throne, because the king has desired your beauty; you are beautiful in form above the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV, 12, 3). Thus, to you who, while he dwelt among human beings on earth (Bar. III, 38), diligently ministered the necessities of temporal life [The royal codices: “had ministered”], he grants the rewards of heavenly life, so that, rejoicing and exulting among the choirs of angels [Col. 1502C], you may receive them without end [The royal codices: “might receive them”].

The Lord’s intimate friend and the Savior’s apostle therefore departed on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, while the angels rejoiced: she became a fellow heir of the heavenly powers, worthy to enjoy with them the glory of everlasting brightness, and to see the King of the ages in his beauty (Isa. XXXII, 17) [Note: [Col. 1502D] Ibid.].

Blessed Maximinus the bishop placed her most holy body, embalmed with various spices, in a magnificent mausoleum [The royal codices: “most sacred body”], and afterward built a basilica of honorable architecture over her blessed remains. Her tomb, made of white marble, is displayed; carved upon it is the account of how, in Simon’s house, she obtained forgiveness of sins, together with the act of humanity which she devoutly performed concerning the Lord’s burial [The royal codices: “his burial”].

## CHAPTER XLVI.—Where blessed Martha saw her sister’s soul carried into heaven by angels

[Col. 1503A]

While these things were happening at Aix, the metropolis of the ecclesiastical province of Narbonne [Add: “the second”], at that same hour, in the province of Vienne, at Tarascon, Martha, the most holy handmaid of the Lord Savior, lay detained by fever. Yet she was intent upon divine praises. While meditating on heavenly things, she saw choirs of angels carrying the soul of her sister Mary Magdalene into heaven.

She called those who were attending her and told them what she had seen, asking them to share her joy. Then she cried out: “O most beautiful sister, what have you done? (Gen. XII, 18.) Why did you not visit me, as you had promised and instructed me? Are you then enjoying the embraces of the Lord Jesus without me—the Lord who greatly loved us who loved him greatly [Col. 1503B]? I shall follow you wherever you go (Luke IX, 57). Meanwhile, may you live the eternal life and be happy without end [Note: [Col. 1503D] The Breviary of Autun, 1550. Office of Saint Martha, fol. XC, where it is made known to the brothers and sisters, saying: ‘O most beautiful, blessed, and beloved sister of mine, you did not consider what you had vowed to me, that you would visit me.’ [Col. 1504D] ‘May you live with our master and true host in the blessed seat.’ These words seem to have been taken from Rabanus, or at least from an old document used by Rabanus], and do not be unwilling to remember my soul, which remembers you.”

The sacred heroine, gladdened by this vision, desired more than usual to be released and to be with Christ, grieving that she remained longer in the flesh (Phil. I, 23–24) and was deprived of the companionship of her sister and of the angels whom she had seen. Knowing that she would soon depart, she admonished, instructed, and encouraged the faithful.

When it became known through the report of others that Christ’s handmaid’s departure was near, a great multitude of believers gathered (Acts II, 6), and they remained with her until she was buried, tents being spread through the woods and fires lit everywhere.

## CHAPTER XLVII.—Where Christ and Magdalene, his beloved, appeared to blessed Martha

[Col. 1503C]

On the following seventh day, as evening approached, she ordered them to light seven candles and three lamps [Something may be missing here in the manuscript, for example: “that they should pray,” or something similar]. Around midnight, the watchers were overcome by deep sleep (John I, 5) and fell asleep everywhere. Behold, a violent blast of a whirlwind rushed in with a mighty wind (Ps. XLVII, 8) and extinguished all the candles and lamps.

Understanding this, Christ’s handmaid, making the sign of the cross, prayed against the snares of the demons. Then she woke the guards and asked them to relight the lamps. As they ran to do so and were delayed for a long time, suddenly a light poured down from heaven and shone. In that very light, Mary Magdalene, the apostle of Christ the Lord [Col. 1503D], Savior, appeared, carrying a fiery torch in her right hand. She immediately lit the seven extinguished candles and the three extinguished lamps with her heavenly light.

Then, standing beside her sister’s bed, she said: “Hail, holy sister.”

Immediately, after her sister returned the greeting, she said: “Behold, I have visited you in the body while you are still living in the body, as you sent word to me through the blessed bishop Maximinus. And behold, your beloved (Song II, 9, 10), the Lord Savior, is here, to call you from this valley of misery (John XI, 28), just as he appeared to me before my departure and summoned me to the palace of his glory. Come, therefore, and do not delay (Ps. LXIX, 6).”

She spoke. The Lord entered, and Martha joyfully went to meet him. Drawing near and looking upon Martha with a most peaceful countenance, he said:

“To the one to whom you once ministered most devotedly from your possessions, to whom you offered most gracious hospitality, and for whom, after my passion, you did many good things in my members, behold, I am here (Gen. XLVI, 11)—to the one to whom you once said, prostrate: ‘I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, who has come into this world’ (John XI, 27). Come, therefore, my hostess; come from exile; come, you shall be crowned (Song IV, 8).”

Hearing this, she tried to raise herself, get up, and immediately follow the Savior. But the Savior said to her:

“Wait, for I am going to prepare a place for you, and I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be with me” (John XIV, 2–4).

He spoke and disappeared; but her holy sister Mary also vanished. The light, however, remained—the light which had appeared with them. Then the watchers arrived and marveled at the lamps which they had left extinguished, now shining with an extraordinary light.

## CHAPTER XLVIII.—Where, when, and how, and in whose presence, blessed Martha departed from the body

When day dawned, she ordered them to place her outside under the open sky. Every haste seemed slow; that morning seemed to last a thousand years. Straw was spread beneath a leafy tree, and a haircloth was placed upon the straw, upon which [Col. 1504C] a cross was made from ashes. As the sun rose, Christ’s handmaid was carried out and placed upon the ashes. At her own request, an image of the crucified Savior was raised before her face.

After she had rested there for a little while, she looked upon the multitude of the faithful and asked them to pray that her departure might be hastened. As they wept abundantly, she raised her eyes to heaven and said:

“O guest, why, Lord Savior, do you delay? What is the reason for your lingering? (Acts XXII, 16.) When shall I come and appear before your face? From the moment you spoke to me at dawn, my soul has melted (Ps. XLI, 5; Song V, 6). Since then, out of desire for you, all my limbs grow stiff, my sinews are numb, my bones waste away, my marrow fails, and all my inward parts dry up. Do not put me to shame, Lord, by frustrating my expectation. My God, do not delay; Lord, do not linger” (Ps. CXVIII, 116; Ps. XXXIX, 18; Ps. LXIX, 6) [Col. 1504D].

While she was meditating on these things, she remembered that she had once seen how Christ expired on the cross at the ninth hour and that she had once brought with her from Jerusalem an account of Christ’s passion written in Hebrew. She summoned Saint Parmenas and asked that it be brought out and read aloud before her, so that in this way she might lessen the weariness of waiting.

And it happened as she had hoped. As she listened to him reading in her own language, one by one, the sufferings of her beloved [Col. 1505A] which she had once seen, tears arising from compassion, she began to weep. Forgetting her own departure for the moment, she fixed her whole attention upon the course of the passion.

When she had heard that Christ, commending his spirit into the hands of the Father, released his spirit (Luke XXIII, 46), she sighed deeply and expired.

She slept in the Lord on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, the eighth day after the passing of her holy sister Mary Magdalene, on Friday, at the ninth hour of the day, in the sixty-fifth year of her age.

Her companions, who had come with her from the East and had steadfastly remained with her until that day, buried and wrapped her body with due honor in her own church: namely, Saint Parmenas; also Germanus, Sosthenes, and Epaphras, who had been companions of Saint Trophimus, archbishop of Arles; and Marcella, her handmaid, together with Euchodia and Syntex [Col. 1505B].

These seven kept three days of vigil at her funeral with the multitude of peoples who had gathered from every direction. Until the third day they watched around the holy body in the praises of God, candles being lit in the church, lamps throughout the houses, and fires throughout the woods.

## CHAPTER XLIX.—Where, when, and how she was buried by the Lord Savior and by the holy bishop Frontinus, although he was bodily absent

On Saturday, a distinguished burial was prepared for her at her own basilica, which the bishops had dedicated. On the following Sunday, at the third hour of the day, everyone had gathered to embalm the holy body properly, on the day before the Kalends of August [Col. 1505C].

Behold, at that same hour, at Périgueux, a city of Aquitaine, while the holy bishop Frontinus was about to celebrate Mass, awaiting the people and dozing in his chair, Christ appeared to him and said:

“Son, come and fulfill what you promised: that you would assist at the funeral of Martha, my hostess.”

He spoke, and immediately, together in the twinkling of an eye (1 Cor. XV, 52), they appeared at Tarascon in the church, holding little books in their hands: Christ stood at the head and the bishop at the feet. They alone placed the body in the mausoleum [Note: [Col. 1505D] Mausolea are the tombs or monuments of kings, named from Mausolus, king of Egypt. After his death, his wife built a tomb of extraordinary size and beauty for him, so that to this day all costly monuments are called mausoleums from his name. Rabanus, On the Universe, Book XIV, chapter 28] [Col. 1506D], while all who were present marveled.

When the funeral rites were complete, they went out. One of the clergy followed them, asking the Lord who he was and where he had come from. The Lord gave him no answer, but handed him the book he was holding [Col. 1505D]. The cleric returned to the tomb and showed the book to everyone. On every page he read:

“Martha, Christ’s hostess, shall be in everlasting remembrance; she shall not fear an evil report” (Ps. CXI, 6).

Nothing else was contained in the book.

Meanwhile, at Périgueux, a deacon woke the bishop, informing him that the hour of the sacrifice was passing and that the people were growing weary. The bishop said to him:

“Do not be troubled (Acts XX, 10), and do not be annoyed that you have waited longer. For I have now been carried away in spirit—or in the body, or outside the body, I do not know; God knows (2 Cor. XII, 2–3)—to Tarascon with the Lord Savior, to bury his handmaid, the most holy Martha, dead, just as I promised her while she was alive. Send someone now to bring back our ring and the crimson gloves which I placed in the hands of the sacristan while I arranged the holy body in the mausoleum.”

The people, astonished at hearing this, sent messengers as far as Tarascon. The people of Tarascon wrote back to the people of Périgueux that they did not know the day or hour of her burial; that a venerable person had attended her funeral with their bishop, whom they knew well; and that, concerning the little book and its inscription—lest this have escaped the bishop’s notice—the ring which the sacristan had received should be returned, together with one of the gloves, while the other was retained as testimony [Col. 1506B] to so great a miracle.

Some of those who had ministered to the Savior’s handmaid returned to the East, evangelizing the kingdom of God: Epaphras, with Saint Marcella, and blessed Syntyche, who lies buried at Philippi, about whom the Apostle writes. Syntex rested in a blessed death. Parmenas (Acts VI, 5), full of faith and the grace of God, attained the glory of martyrdom. Germanus and Euchodia, laboring for the consolation of the faithful, assisted the blessed apostles, together with Saint Clement and their other fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life (Phil. IV, 2).

In the basilica of the most blessed Martha, from the day of her falling asleep, miracles without number occurred. Complete healings came to the blind, deaf, mute, lame, paralytic, withered, leprous, demoniac, and those afflicted by various illnesses [Col. 1506C].

Clovis, king of the Franks and Germans, the first to bear the insignia of the Christian faith, was moved by the number and greatness of the miracles of the most holy Martha and came to Tarascon. As soon as he touched the saint’s tomb, he was freed from the severe kidney disease from which he had suffered miserably.

As a testimony to so great a power, he gave the land extending three leagues around Martha’s church, on both banks of the Rhône, together with villages, castles, and forests, to God and marked it with his own ring. The sacred heroine possesses all these lands to this day under perpetual immunity.

Theft, robbery, sacrilege, and false judgments are immediately and horribly punished there by God’s sudden judgment, to the praise of the Lord Savior.

## CHAPTER L.—On the death and burial of the holy archbishop Maximinus

[Col. 1506D]

It is enough to have narrated thus far the religious life and precious death of Martha, the venerable handmaid of the Son of God, the Lord Savior. Now, reserving for a new beginning the miracles performed by her or around her after her sacred departure, as well as the life filled with virtues and the passion of her brother, blessed Lazarus, bishop and martyr [Col. 1507A], we shall briefly recount the miracles performed through Mary Magdalene, the beloved of God; and first we shall touch upon the departure of the most holy archbishop Maximinus.

When the time was approaching at which, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, he learned that he would be taken from this light and would receive the reward of his labors from the merciful Judge [Note: [Col. 1507B] Ancient Life of Saint Magdalene], he ordered that the place of his burial be prepared within the basilica which, as we related above, he had built with magnificent workmanship over the most holy remains of blessed Mary Magdalene [The royal codices 5281 and 5360: “the aforesaid”]. He ordered his sarcophagus to be placed beside the mausoleum of Mary Magdalene, the beloved of God [The royal codices: “the body of Mary Magdalene”] [Note: [Col. 1507B] “Sarcophagus” is Greek, because bodies are consumed there: *sarx* means “flesh” in Greek, and *phagein* means “to eat.” Rabanus, On the Universe, Book XIV, chapter 28, p. 199].

After his holy departure, when the faithful had honorably deposited his sacred body there, both saints adorned the place with great miraculous powers, granting healing through their intercession to those who asked for it, both for soul and body [The royal codices: “for the body”] [Note: [Col. 1507B] The following passage, through the end of Rabanus’s text, is found in the royal codices containing the Life of blessed Mary Magdalene: 3820, 5312, 5347, 5551, and 5368 [Col. 1508B]].

That place was afterward held in such great religious reverence that no king or prince, nor anyone endowed with secular pomp, dared enter their church to ask for benefits until he had first laid down his weapons and abandoned every bestial ferocity, and then entered with complete devotion and humility [Note: [Col. 1508B] Rabanus’s codex reads “and his soul”; many copies of the Life of Saint Mary Magdalene read “and his spirit.” The reading must certainly be “and every …,” as we have corrected it from royal codex 5268] [Note: [Col. 1508B] This passage is found only thus far in royal codices 5296 B, 5278, 5345, and 5323].

No woman, however, ever presumed to enter that most holy temple with the audacity of any rashness, whatever her condition, order, or dignity might be.

That monastery is called the Abbey of Saint Maximinus. It was built in the aforementioned County of Aix and is richly endowed with every possession and honor.

Blessed Bishop Maximinus departed on the sixth day before the Ides of June and was happily crowned in heaven [In the aforementioned codices: “by the Lord”].

[Col. 1507] Here ends the Life of blessed Mary Magdalene and of her sister Saint Martha.

[Col. 1507]

[Col. 1507]

[Col. 1507D]

# LETTERS OF BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ (G)*

[Col. 1507]

## LETTER ONE. TO REGIMBALD, CHOREPISCOPUS OF MAINZ

(Baluze, *Capitularia*, vol. II, p. 1378.)

[Col. 1507B]

To the most reverend and most religious priest of Christ in divine worship, Regimbald: Rabanus sends greetings in the Lord.

Recently a certain brother came to us from the monastery called Herolvesfeld, near us. He brought, written on a little slip, several brief questions and asked, in your name, that we resolve them by our answers. We willingly gave ear to his request and began, insofar as we could, to resolve them from the judgments of the Fathers.

1. First, it was asked what judgment should be imposed upon a man who, while flogging his wife, killed two of his children during childbirth, so that they could not attain the grace of baptism, and so weakened a third child that, after birth, it was baptized and soon afterward died [Col. 1509A].

It is clear that by excessive correction he fell into the crime of parricide. What the sacred canons decree concerning homicide is not unknown to you, since the following is written in the Council of Ancyra:

“Those who have committed voluntary homicide shall continually submit themselves to penance, but they shall attain perfection toward the end of life. Concerning homicides committed involuntarily, the earlier ruling ordered that perfection be attained after seven years of penance, while the second prescribed completion of a period of five years.”

The weakness of the penitent’s person and the manner of his penance must also be considered. Whoever performs penance for his sins fervently will obtain pardon more quickly through the Lord’s mercy [Col. 1509B].

2. The second question concerns a man whose foot was torn by the bite of a mad dog. To cure him, certain people, without his knowledge, gave him the liver of that same dog to eat, as though he could thereby be restored to health.

Here human error produced the guilt of wrongdoing in those who, wishing to heal a sick man, did not know the power of the remedy. Such people must therefore be corrected from this error, so that they do not commit such an act again; and for what they have done they must be disciplined by some correction or fast, so that the others, being afraid, may not afterward presume to commit such a crime.

3. The third question concerned a man who had intercourse irrationally with a female dog; and the fourth concerned one who had repeatedly fornicated with cows. What judgment should be made concerning such men, and what should be done with such animals and their offspring?

Here the greatest madness of the human mind and misery are evident. The deed is all the more detestable because the crime is shown to be so great: a rational animal, driven by lust, joins himself against nature to an irrational animal.

In the Law, therefore, the Lord decreed that such a crime should be punished by the judgment of death, saying:

“Whoever lies with a beast or an animal shall surely be put to death. You shall also kill the beast. A woman who lies with any animal shall be killed together with it. Their blood shall be upon them.”

But if someone thinks he must ask how the animal can be guilty, since it is irrational and in no way capable of the law, let him understand that the animals are ordered to be killed because, having been polluted by such an outrage, they perpetuate an unworthy memory of the deed and are not fit for human use where the greatest abomination is manifest [Col. 1509D].

The sacred canons prescribe the following concerning those who fornicate irrationally—that is, who have intercourse with animals—or who defile themselves with males: whoever committed such a crime before the age of twenty shall, after completing fifteen years in penance, be deemed worthy of communion in prayers; then, remaining in this communion for five years, they may finally receive the sacraments of the offering. Their way of life during the time of repentance must also be examined [Col. 1510A], and thus they may obtain mercy. But if they have clung to their crimes without restraint, they must spend a longer period in penance.

Those who, after completing twenty years of age and having wives, have fallen into this sin shall, after performing penance for twenty-five years, be admitted to communion in prayers; remaining in it for five years, they may then receive the sacraments of the offering. If some who have wives and are over fifty years old have committed such a crime, they shall receive the grace of communion at the end of life.

4. As for the calves born from those polluted cows, I do not know what prevents them from being used for human purposes. But if anyone has scruples about whether their milk or meat may be eaten, and if some scandal arises because of the pollution of their mother, let them be killed together with their mother, or sold to pagans, so that the scandalous memory of the former disgrace may not arise.

For the Apostle says: “If food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat.” Again: “If your brother is grieved because of food, you are no longer walking according to love. Do not destroy by your food the one for whom Christ died. Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food. All things are clean. But it is evil for the person who eats through giving offense” [Col. 1510B].

5. Finally, you asked about the man who kills his uncle, whether unwillingly or willingly, and what he should suffer. Enough has already been said above concerning homicide, according to what the sacred canons contain. But it is clear that the crime of parricide is subject to a greater penalty [Col. 1510C]. Therefore the holy Fathers decreed that parricides, laying aside the military belt, should remain in penance for the whole time of their lives and serve God in a monastery.

We have written all these things according to what we have found expressly stated in the sacred Scriptures or in the canons of the Fathers. But you, most holy one, should temper your judgment according to what you see to be expedient for each person, preserving discernment in all things, because discernment is the mother of all virtues.

For the Lord has given you understanding in all things, and he will grant an eternal reward in the heavenly kingdom with the holy shepherds to the one who fights the good fight and carefully guards his flock [Col. 1510D].

## LETTER TWO. TO HERIBALD, BISHOP OF AUXERRE

See the letter prefixed to Rabanus’s *Penitential*.

## LETTER THREE. TO EGIL, ABBOT OF PRÜM. On the body and blood of the Lord, against Ratpertus

[Note: [Col. 1509D] The work on the Eucharist published here was extracted from a manuscript codex at Gembloux, in which it is contained together with other writings of the same kind. First comes Ambrose, *On the Mysteries* and *On the Sacraments*; then, after several other works, Paschasius Radbertus, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*; next, a little book or letter by someone bearing the same title and treating the same subject, beginning with the words “Considering the Apostle’s judgment,” etc., published in volume XII of the *Spicilegium* [Col. 1511B]; afterward, *Sayings of a Certain Wise Man on the Body and Blood of the Lord against Ratbertus*; and also a fragment on the body and blood of the Lord. Appended to these in the same codex are *Sayings of Lord Abbot Herigerus on the Body and Blood of the Lord*, beginning: “As a certain wise man said before us,” etc.; this work was published by Cellot under the title *Anonymous*.

The first anonymous author, whom I call Acherian, is concerned to prove that the Lord’s body in the Eucharist is not subject to evacuation or corruption. The second anonymous author, namely ours, advances two arguments against Paschasius: first, that the Eucharistic body is not entirely identical with that which was born from the Virgin; second, that Christ does not suffer as many times as the solemn rites of Mass are celebrated.

The first of these indeed conflicts with Paschasius; the second was wrongly attributed to Paschasius, as Herigerus, or the Cellotian anonymous author, acknowledges in chapter 6 in these words: “As for what they again object, that he said Christ suffers as often as it happens that Mass is celebrated everywhere each day, I certainly did not find this in his book,” and so forth.

There is no doubt that Herigerus directs this accusation against our anonymous author, for I do not remember reading anything similar in Ratramnus. Certainly Herigerus had seen this anonymous author, since he transferred quite a few words and several arguments from him into his own little book [Col. 1511C].

From this I am readily led to think that the following anonymous writing is none other than Rabanus’s letter to Egilus, or Egilo, abbot of Prüm, whom Rabanus himself mentions in his letter to Heribald. There, while arguing against those who had said that the Eucharistic body of Christ is the very body that was born of the Virgin Mary, he adds:

> “Against this error, insofar as we have been able, while writing to Egilus the abbot, we have explained what ought truly to be believed concerning the body itself.”

What chiefly moves me is that Herigerus, whom I have said was not unfamiliar with our anonymous author, when speaking of this question sets only two opponents of Paschasius against him, namely Rabanus and Ratramnus:

> “Against him,” he says, “Rabanus argues sufficiently in his letter to Egilo the abbot, and a certain Ratramnus in a book composed for King Charles.”

Since Herigerus had read our anonymous author, who expressly opposed Paschasius on this matter, he certainly would not have passed him over here if he had been someone other than Rabanus and Ratramnus.

Furthermore, the age of our anonymous author agrees remarkably well with that of Rabanus. The author was writing at a time when the controversy concerning the threefold body was still new. For, after reporting Paschasius’s opinion concerning the one body, he adds:

> “I plainly confess that I had never before heard, seen, or read this.”

This novelty, or ignorance, could apply to that author only either because, being Paschasius’s contemporary, he witnessed the first beginnings of the question, or because, having been born much later than Paschasius, he had not received from his elders any memory of a matter already largely forgotten. Yet he lived before Herigerus, who made use of his writing, and he was not even a century and a half removed from Paschasius. Thus this dispute appeared new and unfamiliar to that anonymous author because, being Paschasius’s contemporary, he had learned it from Paschasius himself.

Finally, our anonymous author was writing at a time when the Bulgarians—who are known to have come to the faith under Pope Nicholas I—were still partly heathen, that is, still held by pagan errors. For, wishing to prove the Catholic faith concerning the Eucharist, he says that it is so evident to everyone that “even part of the heathen know it.” He continues:

> “For once, in the land of the Bulgarians, a certain noble and powerful pagan humbly begged me to drink, for love of that God who makes his blood from wine.”

This could not be turned into an argument if, after the others had been converted, some one pagan alone had learned this after the preaching of our mysteries among the Bulgarians. They could not properly be called “part of the heathen” unless all of them had then still remained in the darkness of unbelief.

All these circumstances fit the age of Rabanus very well. He was Paschasius’s contemporary and died two years before the pontificate of Nicholas I, to whose time we have said that the conversion of the Bulgarians must be assigned. The author of this little work, therefore, may not unreasonably be identified in this way. If so, I do not doubt that it is Rabanus’s letter to Egilus the abbot, which has come down to us stripped of the ordinary epistolary formulas, just as happened with Herigerus’s writing, which Abbot Gerard calls a letter in the prologue to the *Life of Saint Adalhard*.

Nor is it beyond conjecture that our anonymous author’s work is found not only in the Gembloux manuscript but also—as I learned from the report of friends—in a parchment book of the monastery of Saint Hubert in the Ardennes. That place is not very far from the monastery of Prüm, over which Abbot Egilus presided, and to whom Rabanus wrote the letter.

I offer these points as conjectures, which I willingly submit to the judgment of learned men.

Moreover, when this author charges Paschasius with having said that Christ suffers as often as the solemn rites of the Mass are celebrated, he undoubtedly derives this only as a consequence, not from Paschasius’s explicit words. For, as Paschasius himself complains in Book XII on Matthew, some people maliciously interpreted his statements as though, in his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, he

> “wished to attribute more to Christ’s words than the Truth itself promises; perhaps fearing,” he says, “what those to whom he was speaking feared at that time—namely, that I might wish to divide him into parts and cut up or distribute his members one by one,”

and so forth.

In the same way, Paschasius’s opponents inferred from his opinion concerning the one and identical body of Christ in the Eucharist that Christ would suffer as often as Masses were celebrated.

*Mabillon.*

*[Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, vol. VI.]*

### 1

[Col. 1511A] Every faithful person ought to believe, know, hold, confess, and likewise assert without hesitation that the body and blood of the Lord are true flesh and true blood. Whoever denies this is plainly known and proved to be an unbeliever, since he does not believe the Lord himself, who says:

> “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54);

and:

> “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (ibid., verse 57);

and:

> “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (ibid., verse 56).

Explaining this, blessed Augustine says:

> “Therefore, if it is truly food and true flesh, and if it is truly drink, then it is certainly true blood. Otherwise, how will what he says be true: ‘The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world,’ [Col. 1511B] unless it is true flesh? This, then, I most faithfully [Col. 1512A] affirm and add: just as Christ is the Truth and the true Lamb of God, who is mystically sacrificed each day for the life of the world, so undoubtedly true flesh is created from bread and his true blood from wine by the consecrating power of the Holy Spirit. For, as Saint Augustine most truly testifies, just as true flesh is created from the Virgin through the Holy Spirit without intercourse, so through that same Spirit the same body and blood of Christ are mystically consecrated from the substance of bread and wine.”

Since all these things are most certain, and no Christian who believes Christ can doubt them, even part of the heathen knows that this is true. For once, in the land of the Bulgarians, a certain noble and powerful pagan humbly begged me to drink for love of that God who makes [Col. 1512B] his blood from wine.

### 2

[Note: Col. 1513D, a. In the interlinear space, namely, Paschasius.]

[Col. 1513A] I plainly confess that I find in this book something wholly unheard-of under the name of Saint Ambrose: namely, that this is not another flesh of Christ than that which was born of Mary, suffered on the cross, and rose from the tomb.

> “This is that very flesh,” he says, “and therefore it is Christ’s flesh, which is still offered today for the life of the world.”

This is placed in the second chapter (in the edition, chapters 1 and 4). Likewise, in the eighth chapter it is said:

> “Believe truly that this which is effected by the word of Christ through the Holy Spirit is his body from the Virgin.”

I plainly confess that I had never before heard, seen, or read this. I was greatly astonished that Saint Ambrose had said it; and I am even more astonished that the author of this volume [Note: Col. 1514D, b. Namely, Paschasius.] had inserted it there.

For, in the seventh chapter, blessed Augustine says somewhat earlier:

> “Because it is not lawful for Christ to be devoured by the teeth, he willed that this bread and wine should truly be created as his flesh and blood in the mystery, through the consecrating power of the Holy Spirit, and that, once created, it should be mystically sacrificed each day for the life of the world; so that, just as true flesh is created from the Virgin through the Spirit without intercourse, so through that same Spirit the same body and blood of Christ are mystically consecrated from the substance of bread and wine.” [Col. 1513B]

For if it is true—indeed, because it is undoubtedly true—what so great an authority confessed, namely, that it is not lawful for Christ to be devoured by the teeth, how can it be lawful for this flesh of Christ to be devoured if it was born of Mary, suffered on the cross, and was raised from the tomb? Especially since that flesh of Christ, rising from the tomb, was so glorified that it can in no way now be devoured.

Therefore, although these statements appear so contradictory to one another, I would never again have wished to place them in any of my writings unless I knew that they belonged together and, with God’s gift, could immediately explain them clearly. [Col. 1513C]

### 3

There is also something much more troubling and altogether more difficult: namely, that in the twelfth chapter (in the edition, chapter 7), where the body of Christ is said in three ways—that is, the Church, this mystical body, and that which sits at the right hand of God—blessed Augustine argues as though he did not approve what Saint Ambrose had said.

He says:

> “That body which was born of Mary—into which this is transferred—hung upon the cross, was buried in the tomb, rose from the dead, penetrated the heavens, and, having become High Priest forever, daily intercedes for us. To him, if we communicate rightly, we direct our mind, so that from him and by him we may receive his body, his flesh, while he remains whole. This flesh is itself also the fruit of that flesh, so that he may always remain the same and feed all who are in the body.” [Col. 1513D]

If you read these statements of the teacher of all the Churches after the Apostles, as was said before us, faithfully, fervently, carefully, intelligently, and frequently—as indeed is necessary—you will clearly understand that there is a distinct body of the Lord—not naturally, God forbid, but specifically—which is consecrated daily through the Holy Spirit from the substance of bread and wine for the life of the world and is afterward humbly offered by the priest to God the Father; [Col. 1514A] another body of Christ, specifically, which was born of the Virgin Mary and into which this is transferred; and another body of Christ, specifically—namely, the holy Church, we who are the body of Christ—while it is bestowed and conferred by Christ himself, the supreme High Priest, as he extends it.

Augustine made this sufficiently clear when he says of that pious High Priest himself that “from him and by him we receive his body, his flesh, while he remains whole.” What else does this mean than that we, who are the body of Christ, receive the body of Christ, which is given to us by Christ himself and from no one other than himself? It has been transferred into him, so that what is in him may be given by him to us, who are from him; yet he himself remains whole, because the whole body of Christ born from Mary, into which this has been transferred—that which is divinely consecrated on the altar—is afterward offered and sacrificed to God. [Col. 1514B]

### 4

At the words of the Lord, “This is my body,” the body of the Lord comes to be. At the priest’s supplication, the body of the Lord that can be received is transferred into the body of the Lord born of the Virgin, which is wholly incapable of being consumed, so that it may truly be given to us by Christ himself, the High Priest.

For just as he himself is the one who baptizes, so he himself is the one who gives us—his body—his body to receive healthfully: that is, for healing, not, as the reprobate receive it, for judgment.

He himself, I say, is the one who gives, just as he says:

> “The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:52), [Col. 1514C]

not for the life of two worlds.

He is plainly our High Priest, himself truly the blessed man who is “like a tree planted beside streams of water” (Psalm 1:3). He gives his fruit only to his elect. For he is also Wisdom because of the unity of person, of whom it is said in praise: “She is a tree of life to those who grasp her.”

Therefore he truly says, being himself the tree of the tree of life:

> “To the one who conquers I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” (Revelation 2:7).

For, as blessed Augustine subsequently explains in the same chapter, he gives this in the mystery to no others than those who conquer.

He himself is the grain of wheat which, falling into the earth, died and bears much fruit. He gives none other than his chosen conquerors to eat of it. He found them to be hay, but, having become man, he himself changed our hay into wheat; and he alone fed, feeds, and will feed this wheat of his—namely, his elect—from the richness of wheat.

Hence it is also said in another psalm to Jerusalem and Zion:

> “He satisfies you with the richness of wheat” (Psalm 147:14).

And the prophet Zechariah, speaking of the Church, says:

> “What is its goodness, and what is its beauty, if not the grain of the elect and wine that produces virgins?” (Zechariah 9:17.) [Col. 1514D]

### 5

Behold, it is perfectly clear that this is food only for the elect. Let us therefore place before the eyes of faith our blessed High Priest, the blessed Son and Wisdom, and joyfully, yet tremblingly, receive how he, who is truly the tree of life, as though plucking it, bestows the fruit of life on his elect as they approach to communicate with fear and humility.

Thus we shall be able, very easily and consistently, to believe by the true light of our faith, which graciously enlightens our eyes, that the day before he suffered the Lord gave his true body and blood to his disciples, while his own body remained whole—the body that, from the day of his resurrection, he bears immortal. [Col. 1515A]

It was therefore most suitably and divinely ordained and accomplished that this sacrament was celebrated before the Lord’s passion, so that the body of the Lord which was sown might, rising again, remain forever whole and incorrupt; and yet that, from this same tree of life, we might daily partake until the end of the age of the fruit that we received when his death was imminent.

For this fruit of life springs, flows, and overflows forever from the tree of life. Hence, after Saint Augustine had said, “that from him and by him we may receive his body, his flesh, while he remains whole,” he immediately added:

> “This flesh is itself also the fruit of that flesh, so that he may always remain the same and feed all who are in the body.” [Col. 1515B]

I believe that he said this because the human body of the Lord, which was sown in death, was like a grain and seed of life, and because afterward, from him rising again as from the tree of life, it would forever spring forth—and still springs forth—for us to receive, so that we may have eternal life abiding in us.

Therefore, the reprobate are absolutely not permitted to receive it, as blessed Augustine again testifies earlier in the same chapter:

> “This body of Christ, so that it may be true flesh of Christ for the life of the world, is consecrated daily through the Holy Spirit; and those who are opposed do not have the power to eat from it.” [Col. 1515C]

Those who are in his body feed upon it worthily, so that, while the body of Christ is still on its journey, it may be refreshed by his flesh alone and learn to hunger for nothing other than Christ, to perceive nothing other than Christ, to savor nothing other than Christ, to live from no other source, and to be nothing other than the body of Christ.

Hence the Lord, the Bridegroom of the Church, from whom the bread is given, is given, and will be given—that is, his flesh—says not to the reprobate and unclean, but to those who have been cleansed and are being cleansed more and more, to the clean who alone possess life, his elect:

> “Eat, friends; drink and be intoxicated, beloved” (Song of Songs 5:1). [Col. 1515D]

For the tree of life gives its body from its body only to its own members, that is, to its own body.

Likewise, he who is the true vine gives his blood to the branches that remain in him to drink, just as he says:

> “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57).

But the reprobate world, eating and drinking unworthily, eats and drinks judgment upon itself. It is not nourished by the grain of the elect, because it is not wheat but chaff, even though it is physically present on the threshing floor. Nor does it drink the Lord’s blood, because the sterile branch does not remain in the vine, even though it appears to be in the vineyard.

### 6

[Col. 1516A] Let the person who proclaims that, as often as the solemn rites of the Mass are celebrated throughout the whole world, Christ the Lord suffers just as often—apparently for no other reason than that he may say that all the reprobate, whom he knows to have been redeemed by the Lord on the cross, are redeemed, are being redeemed, and will be redeemed by the very communion of Christ’s body and blood—open his eyes and ears, if he can, and see and hear these things (Herigerus, chapter 4).

Rather, every reprobate who receives the sacrament itself unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.

Yet I would like him who proclaims this to the ruin—God forbid!—of both himself and those who eat, to answer us and say who has inflicted, does inflict, and will hereafter inflict the Lord’s passion so often: is it the priest who sacrifices, or the Father who sanctifies what has been sacrificed, or the Son who gives life to those who communicate, or the Holy Spirit through whom he creates and consecrates these things and in whom the priest asks that they be accomplished, or the people—that is, the Church and bride of Christ—which communicates? [Col. 1516B]

Since nothing except something most deceitful and destructive can be said concerning these possibilities, it is plainly evident that the Lord, having suffered and died once, could not afterward have suffered or be able to suffer—God forbid—as blessed Peter the Apostle says:

> “Christ suffered once for our sins” (1 Peter 3:18).

The Apostle Paul likewise says:

> “Christ was offered once to exhaust the sins of many” (Hebrews 9:28).

Yet lest the reprobate say to the elect, “He suffered once for your sins, but he suffers frequently for ours”—then, specifically, to exhaust the sins of many, but now generally, for everyone—only the reprobate can invent such ravings within themselves, according to the Apostle’s words:

> “Crucifying again for themselves the Son of God” (Hebrews 6:6). [Col. 1516C]

Far be it from his Church and bride to inflict suffering upon him. But so that the reprobate may not say such things thereafter, let them hear what the Apostle says:

> “Jesus did not enter into holy places made by hands, representations of the true ones, but into heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God for us; nor does he enter in order to offer himself often, as the High Priest enters the holy places every year with another’s blood. Otherwise, he would have had to suffer often from the foundation of the world. But now, once, at the consummation of the ages, he has appeared for the destruction of sin through his sacrifice” (Hebrews 9:24). [Col. 1516D]

From this it is altogether clear and perfectly evident that the Lord Jesus neither ought nor ought ever to have suffered frequently from the foundation of the world.

For if Christ had suffered when Cain killed his brother Abel, and, rising again on the third day, could again have been crucified and killed, and had thus suffered on the cross every third day until the end of the age, then he could not and would not have suffered as often as he had suffered and would suffer if, from the time when the solemn rites of the Mass began to be celebrated, he had wished—and were to wish until the end of the world—to suffer at each Mass, which are celebrated daily in thousands and countless [places]. [Col. 1517A]

But just as he did not suffer at that time in his Supper when he first deigned to create, consecrate, and give his true body and blood from bread and wine to his disciples, while his human body remained whole, so afterward he did not, does not, and will not suffer whenever he creates his body from bread and his blood from wine.

The Apostle proves this most clearly. After he had distinguished the statement quoted above—“but now once he has appeared”—he immediately adds:

> “And just as it is appointed for human beings to die once, and after that comes judgment, so Christ was offered once to exhaust the sins of many; he will appear a second time, without sin, to those who await him for salvation” (ibid., verse 27).

Thanks be to God: the truth is clear, pleasing, and welcome; falsehood lies prostrate and destroyed. For when the Lord, in his Supper, gave his body to be eaten and his blood to be drunk, he suffered no evil, although he was still capable of suffering and mortal. How much less, then, did he suffer afterward when he had risen from the dead, and how much less does he suffer or will he suffer, remaining incapable of suffering and immortal, as the Apostle says:

> “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer rule over him” (Romans 9 [as printed]).

Behold the kind of solemn rites of the Mass celebrated by that exceedingly and widely praised pontiff [Note: Col. 1517D, a. Namely, Paschasius, whom he ironically calls “pontiff”], who wishes and proclaims that our Lord God should endure his passion for the reprobate alone as often as the priest strives to offer the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood upon the altar.

Yet the Apostle says again:

> “By the will of God we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.”

And again:

> “But this man, having offered one sacrifice for sins, sits forever at the right hand of God, henceforth awaiting until his enemies are placed as a footstool beneath his feet. For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are sanctified” (Hebrews 10:10). [Col. 1517C]

### 7

But, in order finally to bring this little disputation against the enemy of truth to a close with God’s help, let the person who says this know that the Lord Jesus did not come to suffer there again, since that cannot happen. Rather, he came to transform bread and wine into his body and blood by consecrating them, which is exceedingly necessary for us.

Therefore the elect world—the Church of God, the bride of Christ—neither ought nor can desire the Lord to die again there, where he comes in a new body and blood to give it life, feed it, give it drink, and truly *renew it at the same time every day*. [Col. 1517D]

We must know above all that, although there is one body of Christ in a specific sense—the body of which I spoke above, which sits at the right hand of God—and another, specifically, which is divinely created and consecrated daily as something new, nevertheless there are not two bodies together, God forbid, but one.

For just as there are body and an embodied being, so also there is a human being. This body, however, is not a human being, although it is true flesh; nevertheless, both that body and this body—which, as Saint Augustine says, is transferred into that—are bodies. Therefore they are not two bodies but one, although one is specifically that body and the other specifically this one.

For that richness of wheat—that is, the divinity of the Word—makes there be one body of one Lamb. This is because both that body and this body are true bodies and likewise true flesh. [Col. 1518A]

To make this clearer, I shall prove it by evident examples.

In the Lord Christ himself there is one spirit naturally according to his divinity and another spirit naturally according to his humanity—not, God forbid, personally, but naturally. Yet together they are not two spirits but one spirit personally, because of the unity of person.

For the Spirit who is God, the Son of God, is wholly everywhere and nowhere absent; while the spirit of the human being is created and therefore local and bounded. Concerning this latter the Gospel says:

> “And bowing his head, he gave up his spirit” (John 19:30).

In each of us there is one human being naturally, the outer, and another, the inner, as the Apostle says:

> “Even though our outer person is being corrupted, the one within is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). [Col. 1518B]

Yet together they are not two human beings but one human being, as Christ himself testifies, who made the whole person healthy on the Sabbath.

There is one Spirit of God and another spirit of a human being, and yet:

> “Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17).

The flesh of a man is personally one thing and the flesh of a woman another; yet together they are one flesh, as Scripture says:

> “And the two shall be one flesh” (ibid., verse 16).

Explaining this, the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh” (Matthew 19:6).

The Apostle knew that this had occurred historically in Adam and Eve, yet he interprets it spiritually as a great mystery in Christ and the Church.

Therefore, let it now be evident, pleasing, and welcome, I ask, that God made man, the Word made flesh, gives flesh to his Church, his bride—that is, to his own flesh—to eat: his flesh from himself, the Lamb of God, while he always remains alive and whole. [Col. 1518C]

Therefore, his own.

It is clear, pleasing, and welcome that one flesh is specifically incapable of being consumed, another is capable of being received, and another is specifically subject to corruption (Herigerus, chapter 5). Yet the flesh that receives the flesh given by the flesh that gives, by receiving it healthfully, will become incorruptible.

It ought likewise to be clear, pleasing, and welcome that together there is naturally one flesh: the flesh that gives, the flesh that is given, and the flesh that receives—namely, the invisible flesh to be eaten and eating, the incorruptible flesh to be received and receiving—until the incorruptible flesh, by nourishing the flesh that receives it, perfects it so that it may present it to itself glorious, “not having spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind,” and may graciously bring one flesh with itself to glory, as it is. [Col. 1518D]

Amen.

## LETTER IV. TO HINCMAR OF RHEIMS

*[From Sirmond.]*

To the most reverend and most beloved brother, deservedly and rightly venerated by all Catholics for his true faith and sound confession, Hincmar, bishop, Rabanus, servant of the servants of God, wishes eternal salvation in the Lord.

[Col. 1519A] In the following spring, that is, in the month of March, during the days of Lent, as the solemnity of Easter was approaching, your messenger came to me and brought your letter, together with the little work you composed for the recluses and simple people residing in your parish, against Gottschalk’s error. He also brought with him the writings of others who to some extent follow the doctrine of the aforementioned heretic, though not entirely.

For Prudentius, bishop of the city of Troyes, writing to you and to Pardulus, collected in his booklets many testimonies of the Fathers of earlier times. In some respects these agree with our own understanding—namely, where he says that God is not the author of sin and compels no one to sin; that he mercifully bestows immeasurable grace as a reward upon the just; and that he justly repays the wicked with a punishment proportionate to their evil deeds, because “the Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works.”

[Col. 1519B] But when he says that, just as God by his predestination brings the elect to eternal reward, so by his predestination he compels sinners to go to destruction, he seems to me, in his collection of testimonies, to be trying to make us believe and confess, in accordance with Gottschalk’s teaching, that there is a twofold predestination: namely, that just as God, foreknowing and predestining the elect, leads them to life, so, foreknowing and predestining the reprobate, he leads them to punishment. But since I have nowhere found this set forth in this combined manner in the sacred Scriptures, I do not consent to accept his teaching.

[Col. 1519C] My bodily weakness and the infirmity of old age do not permit me to answer each of his propositions individually, point by point, or to place contrary testimonies alongside the statements he himself has gathered from many books. What I have learned about God’s foreknowledge and predestination, however, and the statements that I found approved by canonical writers in the divine Testaments, I inserted, as they came to mind, into the little works that I previously composed for Bishop Notting and Count Eberhard against Gottschalk’s error. I have now sent these works to you for reading, just as they were dictated by me, since you said that the aforementioned Gottschalk was corrupting and falsifying them. If anything in them requires correction, I prefer that it be corrected according to your judgment rather than according to that of the heretic.

[Col. 1519D] I have thought it appropriate to insert here a few further testimonies from the apostles and prophets, so that those who wish to twist God’s predestination into so perverse a meaning as to say that God, by his predestination, is the author of the lost may test whether they can or cannot affirm their inventions from divine authority.

For my part, so far as I remember, I have nowhere found predestination spoken of in relation to evil, but always in relation to good. Thus the blessed apostle Paul wrote in his Epistle to the Romans:

> “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called saints according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified. What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all—how will he not also, together with him, graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:28.)

[Col. 1520A] In his Epistle to the Ephesians he speaks as follows:

> “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and blameless before him in love. He predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, with which he has graced us in his beloved Son. In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, [Col. 1520B] according to the riches of his grace, which he has lavished upon us in all wisdom and understanding, making known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him for the dispensation of the fullness of times: to restore all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth, in him. In him you also, when you had heard the word of power, the Gospel of your salvation, and had believed, were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance, for the redemption of the possession, to the praise of his glory” (Ephesians 1:3).

[Col. 1520C] The blessed Ambrose and Jerome explained this passage as follows: God decreed that those who believed in Christ should be adopted as sons of God. God, who foreknew all things, knew who would believe in Christ, as he says in Romans: “Those whom he foreknew and called”—not only from the Jews, but also from the nations.

Those whom God is said to call persevere in faith. These are the ones whom he chose in Christ before the foundation of the world, so that they might be undefiled before God in love—that is, so that the love of God might make their conduct holy.
