The statement, “In love he predestined us,” may be read in two ways, according as “love” is joined either with what precedes or with what follows. Joined with what precedes, it reads: “so that we might be holy and blameless before him in love,” followed by: “predestining us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ in him.” Joined with what follows, it reads: “in love predestining us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ in him”—that is, in Christ, who was never anything other than a son; whereas we were not sons before we were predestined with him.

[Col. 1520D] This, then, is what he predestined: that everyone who wished to believe in him should have the power to become a son of God, since no one could become a son of God without possessing faith and love, which works through charity.

Therefore deception and the ruin of human beings, through which a person falls into everlasting death, must not be attributed to God, who is the author of human salvation and of every good thing. Rather, they must be attributed to the person himself, who, consenting to his own desire or to the devil’s suggestion, commits sin and refuses to perform worthy repentance before death.

The apostle James makes this clear when he says:

> “Let no one, when he is tempted, say, ‘I am being tempted by God.’ For God is not a tempter of evils, and he himself tempts no one. Rather, each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire. Then, when desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and when sin has been brought to completion, it produces death” (James 1:13).

[Col. 1521A] Earlier he discussed the temptations that, with the Lord’s permission, we endure externally for the sake of being tested. He now begins to deal with those that we endure internally, when the devil instigates them or the weakness of our nature persuades us toward them.

First he refutes the error of those who think that, just as it is evident that good thoughts are inspired in us by God, so bad thoughts are also generated in our minds at his instigation.

“Let no one, therefore, when he is tempted, say, ‘I am being tempted by God’”—that is, by the temptation through which a rich man, proceeding along his own paths, withers. In other words, when someone has committed robbery, theft, false testimony, murder, adultery, or anything similar, let him not say that, because God compelled him, he was obliged to perpetrate these things and therefore was entirely unable to avoid carrying them out.

[Col. 1521B] “For God is not a tempter of evils”—the word “temptations” being understood. “He himself tempts no one”—namely, with the temptation that deceives the wretched so that they perish.

There are, however, two kinds of temptation: one that deceives and another that tests. God tempts no one with the kind that deceives; with the kind that tests, God tested Abraham. Concerning this latter kind the Prophet also asks: “Test me, Lord, and try me” (Psalm 25:2).

[Col. 1521C] “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire”—drawn away, that is, from the right path, and enticed toward evil.

Concerning this verse Jerome writes against Jovinianus (Book II, near the beginning):

> “As in good works,” he says, “God is the one who brings them to perfection—for it is not the one who wills or the one who runs, but God who shows mercy and assists, so that we may be able to reach the finish—so in evils and sins our own seeds are the incentives, while the devil brings them to completion. When he sees that we have built hay, wood, and straw upon the foundation of Christ, then he sets the fire beneath it.”

It is therefore not right for us to assert that our Savior is the author of our destruction. Rather, we should love him as a merciful Father, fear him as a just Judge, and continually beseech him to rescue us from evils and defend us against all enemies.

[Col. 1521D] In the Lord’s Prayer he commanded us to ask the heavenly Father to forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors; not to lead us into temptation, but to deliver us from evil. He will not lead us into the temptation by which we are deceived. Rather, we ask that he not permit us to be led into the harmful temptation through which we might fall into the ruin of sins; indeed, that he deliver us from evil—that is, from the devil—and from everlasting destruction (Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*, Book II, chapter 9).

[Col. 1522A]

> “Therefore God does not himself lead a person into temptation, but permits the one whom he has abandoned to be led into it, according to a most hidden order and according to merits. Often, for reasons that are also evident, he judges the one whom he abandons worthy of this, and permits him to be led into temptation. To be led into temptation, however, is one thing, and to be tempted is another. No one can be tested without temptation. We do not therefore pray here that we may not be tempted, but that we may not be brought into temptation—as if someone who must be tested by fire were not to pray that he might not come into contact with fire, but that he might not be burned. The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and the temptation of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclesiasticus 27:6).

Many people, when praying, say: “Do not permit us to be led into temptation,” thereby explaining how the command “lead us” is to be understood (Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*).

> “This shows that the adversary can do nothing against us unless God has first permitted it, so that all our fear, devotion, and vigilance may be turned toward God, since in our temptations evil is permitted nothing unless power is granted to it from that source.”

[Col. 1522B] The monk of Corbie, in his letter, also censured us, writing to his friend that we had not correctly explained Fulgentius’s statement. He said:

> “As for what Fulgentius is said to have declared—‘God prepared the wicked to undergo punishments’—instead of saying ‘he permitted them to be prepared,’ he found something to say, but did not say what he ought to have said. He also asserts that you were led astray by the style of a certain little book said to be by Jerome, concerning the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart, so that you would say that God did not harden Pharaoh’s heart but permitted it to be hardened.”

It seems to me that he does not rightly criticize you. For God does not harden anyone’s heart by his own action, so that the person cannot correct himself from error; rather, by a just judgment he permits it to be hardened, either by the person’s own wickedness or by the devil’s malice.

This can be proved by clear evidence. For when the apostle Paul had mentioned Pharaoh in his Epistle to the Romans, he added:

[Col. 1522C]

> “For Scripture says to Pharaoh: ‘For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you and that my name might be proclaimed throughout the whole earth’” (Romans 9:14) (Origen, *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*, chapter 9).

> “Observe that he did not say, ‘For this very purpose I made you’; otherwise the fault would seem to be referred to the Creator. Rather, he says, ‘For this very purpose I raised you up’: through the wickedness of your mind, which you acquired by living foolishly and without fear of God, useful and fruitful correction might be inflicted upon others, and upon yourself a notorious destruction might be brought as an example for posterity” (Ambrose, *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*, chapter 9).

[Col. 1522D]

> “For this purpose Pharaoh was preserved, so that many signs and plagues might be displayed against him as though he were already dead. He is said to have been raised up because, although he was dead before God, he received a short period of time in which he might appear to live. Thus there would be someone upon whom, until death, punishment and various kinds of torment could be inflicted, and all who were without God, terrified by fear of him, might confess with the greatest wonder that this was the one true God from whom these acts of vengeance came. In this respect the physicians of old also examined people who were worthy of death or had received the sentence of death, seeking to discover how what lay hidden in a person might be exposed for the benefit of the living, so that they might learn the causes of the illness and the punishment of the dying might contribute to the salvation of the living” (Augustine, *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*, chapter 62).

[Col. 1523A]

> “That Pharaoh no longer obeyed God’s commands was already a consequence of punishment. No one can say that the hardening of his heart happened to Pharaoh undeservedly, but rather by the judgment of God, who repaid his unbelief with the punishment it deserved. It is therefore not held against him that he did not obey at that time, since, with his heart hardened, he could not obey; rather, it is held against him that he had made himself worthy of having his heart hardened by his earlier unbelief. For in those whom God justly condemns, unbelief and ungodliness begin the merit of punishment, so that through the punishment itself they also perform evil deeds. As the Apostle says above: ‘And because they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a debased mind, to do what is improper’ (Romans 9:18).”

For this reason the Apostle concludes:

[Col. 1523B]

> “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Origen, *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*, chapter 9).

> “When he says, ‘Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills,’ he appears to derive this from what is written in Exodus. There he says: ‘I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, so that he will not release the people’ (Exodus 4:21).

> “Pharaoh’s heart was hardened in the following manner. God did not wish to inflict sudden and complete vengeance upon him. Although Pharaoh was utterly wicked, God, in his patience, had not even deprived him of the opportunity for conversion. Therefore he first used milder blows against him, and then gradually intensified them. But what God was doing through patience hardened Pharaoh toward contempt; he stored up greater wrath for himself. Thus the words written by the Apostle apply to him: ‘Do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience? [Col. 1523C] Do you not know that God’s patience leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath?’ (Romans 2:4.)

> “It is not, therefore, that God hardens the one whom he wills; rather, the one who refuses to obey his patience is hardened” (Augustine, *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*, chapter 62).

> “For the one upon whom he has mercy he causes to do good works; and the one whom he hardens he leaves to do evil. Yet that mercy is attributed to a preceding merit of faith, and that hardening to preceding ungodliness, so that we perform good works through God’s gift and evil works through punishment. Nevertheless, free choice is not removed, whether for believing in God, so that mercy may come to us, or for ungodliness, so that punishment may come to us.”

[Col. 1523D] After presenting this conclusion, he introduces a question as though from an opponent:

> “You will say to me, then, ‘Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?’” (Romans 9:19.)

He answers this inquiry in such a way that we understand that even spiritual people—those who do not live according to the earthly human being—can perceive the preceding merits of faith and ungodliness: how God, by his foreknowledge, chooses those who will believe and condemns unbelievers, choosing neither group on the basis of works nor condemning either on the basis of works; rather, granting the former faith so that they may do good works, and, by abandoning the latter, hardening their ungodliness so that they may do evil works.

Since this understanding, as I have said, is accessible to spiritual people but far removed from carnal wisdom, he rebukes the questioner so that he may understand that he must first lay aside the name of clay before he can investigate these matters through the Spirit. Thus he says:

[Col. 1524A]

> “Who are you, O human being, to answer back to God? Will what is formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Romans 9:20.)

As long as you are something formed, he says, and belong to a mass of clay, not yet brought to spiritual things so that you are spiritual, judging all things and judged by no one, you ought to restrain yourself from such inquiry and not answer back to God. Whoever desires to know his counsel must first be received into his friendship; and this cannot happen except to spiritual people, who already bear the image of the heavenly human being.

> “I no longer call you servants, but friends. For everything that I have heard from my Father [Col. 1524B] I have made known to you” (John 15:15).

As long, therefore, as you are a potter’s vessel, this very vessel must first be broken within you by that iron rod of which it is said:

> “You shall rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you shall shatter them” (Psalm 2:9),

so that, once the outer person has been corrupted and the inner person renewed, you may be rooted and grounded in love and comprehend the breadth, length, height, and depth, and know the surpassing greatness of the knowledge of Christ’s love.

Now, when God makes some vessels from the same lump for honor and others for dishonor, it is not yours to investigate this, whoever still lives according to that same lump—that is, whoever thinks in a carnal manner according to an earthly understanding (Origen, *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*, chapter 9).

[Col. 1524C]

> “The Apostle adds these words from the perspective of one who holds the contrary opinion: ‘You will say to me, then, “Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?”’” and so forth.

Certainly no one can resist God’s will; but we must understand that his will is just and upright. Whether we are good or evil is a matter of our own will; but whether the evil person is destined for such punishments and the good person for such glory—that is a matter of God’s will.

> “O human being,” he says, “who are you to answer back to God?” (Gregory, *Moralia*, Book IX, chapter 8.)

The one called a human being is shown to be unable to answer back to God, because, having been taken from the earth, he is not worthy to scrutinize the heavenly judgments. Hence it is written in Job:

> “Or who can say to him, ‘Why do you do this?’” (Job 9:12.)

[Col. 1524D] The deeds of the Creator must always be revered without being questioned, since they can in no way be unjust. To seek an explanation for his hidden counsel is nothing other than to grow proud against his counsel. When the causes of his deeds cannot be grasped, it remains for us to be silent in humility before his deeds, since the understanding of the flesh is wholly insufficient to penetrate the secrets of his majesty.

Therefore, whoever does not see the reason in God’s deeds should recognize, by considering his own weakness, why he does not see the reason. Thus Paul also adds:

> “Does what is formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’” (Romans 9:20.)

The more clearly one sees oneself to be a work of the divine hand, the more one rebukes oneself for resisting the hand of the one who works. For he who graciously made what did not exist does not unjustly abandon what does exist.

[Col. 1525A] After being struck, therefore, the mind should return to itself and not seek what it cannot grasp. Otherwise, if it investigates the cause of divine wrath, its investigation may provoke that wrath still further, and pride may kindle beyond extinguishing the one whom it could have placated through humility.

With these matters standing as they do, it seems good to me that human weakness should not presumptuously scrutinize the divine judgments indiscriminately, but should rather strive to revere them. For the person who does not attend to the limits of his own measure places his foot on a precipice.

God alone knows his will and power perfectly and in every respect. Therefore it is not fitting for us to scrutinize the divine judgments that are unknown to us. Nevertheless, we must firmly believe that God did not make death and does not rejoice in the destruction of the dying; and that he who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth will redeem the souls of his servants and will not abandon all who hope in him.

[Col. 1525B] Let us firmly hold what we read in the sacred Scriptures and the divine Testaments concerning predestination, and let us not presume to add anything of our own. It is enough for us that the Apostle and teacher of the nations taught concerning the predestination of the elect; let us not introduce anew what he himself did not wish to say concerning the predestination of the reprobate.

For it is not right for us to dispute about God’s will and deeds without charity, or to contend presumptuously with one another to the scandal of the weak, lest perhaps, through this, we be condemned to everlasting punishment according to the judgment of the Truth.

[Col. 1525C] For our salvation and for the sobriety of right faith, it is sufficient that we follow what apostolic teaching instructs us, and that we entirely abandon foolish questions, in accordance with the command of the same Apostle, who wrote to Timothy:

> “Do not quarrel about words; it is useful for nothing except the ruin of those who hear. Take care to present yourself as one approved by God, a worker without shame, rightly handling the word of truth. Avoid profane and empty talk and novelties of words, for they contribute greatly to ungodliness, and their speech spreads like a cancer” (2 Timothy 2:14 and following).

And again:

> “Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they produce quarrels. The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward everyone, teachable, patient, correcting with modesty those who resist the truth, in the hope that God may perhaps grant them repentance for the knowledge of the truth, [Col. 1525D] and that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will” (ibid., verses 23–26).

Let us pray for one another so that we may be saved, as the aforementioned Apostle teaches us to do:

> “I urge, then, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and for all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and chastity. For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for many, the testimony [Col. 1526A] at the proper times. For this I was appointed a preacher and apostle—I speak the truth, I do not lie—a teacher of the nations in faith and truth” (1 Timothy 2:1 and following) (Rabanus, *Commentary on the Epistles of Paul*, Book XXIII).

> “He commanded them to be concerned in common for everyone. For the one who is commanded to do these things for all people is plainly also commanded to expend concern for all. Then he proceeds to those who seem to be highest among human beings: ‘For kings,’ he says, ‘and for all who are in high positions.’

> “And showing that this too is to their advantage, he says: ‘so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life with all piety and [Col. 1526B] sobriety.’ For if, as is fitting, they live in peace, it is possible for us also, by fostering tranquility, to devote ourselves to piety and to a sober life.

> “By persuading them to do these things as he himself commanded—to expend a common concern for all people who appear to exist throughout the whole world, and to consider as common goods those things that belong to everyone—he says: ‘For this is good and acceptable before our Savior God’” (Ambrose).

He sufficiently persuaded them to think in this way, since this also pleases God. To demonstrate that these things please God, he adds:

> “Who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.”

Since God wills these things for all people, no one can contradict this. It is evident that he wills all to be saved, because he also protects them all. Therefore it is necessary for us to imitate his protection of everyone, provided that we hasten fully to think in a manner like God.

[Col. 1526C] To demonstrate this in every respect, he adds:

> “There is one God.”

That is, he is the God of everyone; it is not the case that he is Lord of some people but not of others. It is therefore impossible for him to despise certain people as though they were alien to him.

[Col. 1526D]

> “There is one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (Augustine).

The deceptive mediator—that is, the devil, through whose hidden judgments God permitted human pride to be mocked—has one thing in common with human beings: sin. He wishes to appear to have something else in common with God, so that, because he is not covered by the mortality of the flesh, he may present himself as immortal. But since the wages of sin are death, he shares this with human beings, so that together they may be condemned to death.

The true mediator, however, is the one whom, Lord, your mercy [the printed reading *secuta* is uncertain] revealed to the humble and sent, so that by his example they might also learn humility itself.

That mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, appeared between mortal sinners and the immortal righteous: mortal with human beings, righteous with God. Thus, since the reward of righteousness is life and peace, by the righteousness joined to God he might abolish the death of those whom he justified from ungodliness, a death that he chose to share with them.

He was revealed in this way to the holy people of ancient times, so that they might be saved through faith in his future passion, just as we are saved through faith in his past passion. Insofar as he is human, he is mediator; insofar as he is the Word, he is not a mediator, because he is equal to God, God with God, and, together with the Holy Spirit, one God” (Ambrose).

[Col. 1527A]

> “Most appropriately, and especially in this passage, he called him a human being, so that he might show from his nature the common character of the gift, since everyone must necessarily confess that, as a part of the whole and according to a nature common to all, he can bestow the gift through likeness of nature.

> “Accordingly, taking up what had already been brought almost to the point of confession, he adds: ‘who gave himself as a ransom for all, the testimony at the proper times.’

> “For he gave himself for everyone. He did not consent to undergo death for only some, but, wishing to confer a common benefit upon all, he deigned to undergo the passion according to the time at which he suffered. For he calls the passion itself ‘the testimony.’ When he says ‘at the proper times,’ he asserts that this occurred according to the time at which he suffered.

[Col. 1527B]

> “And to demonstrate that Christ’s passion was necessary for everyone, he shows that it is fitting to exercise a common concern for all people, since God also cares for everyone, since he is the common Lord of all, and, what is greater, since Christ himself likewise appears to draw near to everyone through the shared property of his nature. For he bestowed a benefit upon all by undergoing the passion for all.

> “He further confirms this from what concerns himself: ‘For this I was appointed,’ he says, ‘a preacher and apostle; I speak the truth, I do not lie, a teacher of the nations in faith and truth.’

[Col. 1527C]

> “For this reason I too was appointed an apostle: to bring this teaching to the knowledge of all people and to lead everyone to approach the faith of Christ, through whom these things have been bestowed upon us. Indeed, I was made an apostle for the instruction and proclamation of the nations, so that I might preach to all people who are in every place.”

Therefore, concerning God’s foreknowledge and predestination, and concerning the fact that God himself wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, I have here collected, briefly and concisely, as I was able and as my continual weakness allowed me, the sense of the apostolic statements in accordance with the exposition of the Fathers mentioned above, at your request. I know that you can gather more from this, since your learning and good health, surpassing my ignorance and weakness in every respect, enable you to do so.

For my part, insofar as I presume to do so, I admonish you [Col. 1527D] to prevent these harmful disputes from arising among the Christian people, and not to permit Gottschalk himself, the author of this error, to harm so many any longer, either by writing or by speaking. For I wonder at your prudence: you permitted this harmful man—namely Gottschalk, who has been found blameworthy in every respect, since he has properly observed neither the monastic vow nor the rite of the sacred order, nor even the duty of preaching—to write something, in which capacity he could do more harm than by speaking aloud. Consequently, as I have heard, in many places he has intoxicated not a few with a cup of his poison and turned them toward the madness of error.

This ought by no means to happen, as is written in the Epistle that he sent to his disciple Titus (Tit. 3:10): “Avoid a heretical person, he says, after the first and second admonition, knowing that such a person is subverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment” (Rabanus, *On the Epistles of Paul*, book XXV).

“Blessed Ambrose,” he says, “explained this statement as follows: ‘Avoid him completely who has chosen in preference those things that are contrary to godliness; for he calls such a person a heretic. After you have instructed him once and twice, and have shown him those things that accord with his salvation, it is superfluous to dispute any longer with such a person, since it is evident that he accepts no admonition: although he has heard once and twice those things that did not suit him, he was unwilling to recognize the truth. Therefore leave such a person to await the just punishment from the Judge, because, persisting in his obstinacy, he is unwilling to accept from instruction any counsel for his correction.’

“Concerning him blessed Jerome likewise says: ‘He gives the reasons why such a person is to be avoided after the first and second admonition, saying that he is subverted and sins, since he is depraved in himself. For whoever, after being admonished once and twice, does not wish to be corrected when he has heard his error, considers the one correcting him to be in error; and, preparing himself instead for quarrels and verbal disputes, he wishes to win over the one by whom he is being taught. He is said to be condemned by himself because fornicators, adulterers, murderers, and other offenders are expelled from the Church by priests, whereas heretics pronounce sentence upon themselves, withdrawing from the Church by their own decision; this withdrawal appears to be a condemnation by their own conscience.

“They judge this to be the difference between heresy and schism: heresy possesses a perverse doctrine, while schism separates itself from the Church because of episcopal disagreement. This may indeed be understood as partly true at the beginning. But no schism fails to devise some heresy for itself, so that it may appear to have withdrawn rightly from the Church.’”

Therefore, if it pleases you, it seems good to me that the heretic mentioned above should be given no opportunity or license to write or to dispute with anyone, until, if possible, his mind and understanding return to Catholic doctrine. Let prayer be offered for him, that the Lord, who is almighty, may work salvation for the sick brother, grant him a teachable heart consenting to the right faith—the faith that the Catholic Church preserves throughout the whole [Col. 1528D] world—and that he may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom he has been captured for the devil’s own will; that he may return to holy Mother Church, think and profess with her as one, and preserve throughout the rest of his life that unity of peace and right faith.

Meanwhile, until this happens, I do not approve of communion being granted to him, because, according to the testimony of the apostle John, everyone who departs and does not remain in the doctrine of Christ does not have God; whoever remains in the doctrine has both the Son and the Father. “If anyone,” he says, “comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, and do not say ‘Greetings’ to him; for whoever says ‘Greetings’ to him shares in his evil works” (2 John 10).

Behold, I have warned you, so that you may not be put to shame on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1529A]. Recall how the teacher of the Gentiles speaks about himself: “If I rebuild the things that I destroyed, I show myself to be a transgressor” (Gal. 2:18). And consider how you can be without blame, since in your synod you condemned this wicked sect together with the heretic, if you now communicate with him while he remains uncorrected.

You ought to be correctors of evils, not followers of those who err, so that our office and teaching may be without reproach and may please God as well as human beings.

Furthermore, let your holiness know that I approve the little book which you dictated against Gottschalk’s error for the simple and secluded people residing in our parish, and that I hold the opinion expressed there. As for Gottschalk’s most obstinate [Col. 1529B] and incorrigible error, I judge it superfluous to write anything against it, since I was unable to draw him away from his wickedness when he was present, and now, after your sound correction, I have found nothing sound in his understanding, but only pride. For Moab is exceedingly proud, and his pride and arrogance exceed his strength.

What should I write against a man who casts away the whole Church as something foul, filthy, and unworthy of his conversation, and directs his speech solely to God who presides in heaven, judging whatever is on earth unworthy of his address? As though it were lawful, while despising the members of Christ’s body, to direct words to the head itself, although in no way can the head be separated from the members.

“For no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.” While praying to his Father concerning his disciples, he said: “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, so I sent them into the world. And for their sake I sanctify myself, so that they too may be sanctified in truth. I do not pray for these alone, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, so that all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I am in you, and so that they too may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me. And I have given them the glory that you gave me, so that they may be one, just as we are one: I in them and you in me, so that they may be perfected into one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them as you loved me. Father, I desire that those whom you gave me may be with me where I am, so that they may see my glory, which you gave me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world” (John 17:17).

For whoever can have the saving communion of the holy Church—for he himself says to his elect in the Gospel: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10:16)—

But this request, which the same misguided man makes, as though speaking to God, for a trial by fire, so that by it the truth of his faith—or rather of his faithlessness—might be demonstrated, seems to me to have been uttered more from an elated heart than from firmness of faith. After the blasphemy that he proclaimed with shameless mouth, he desires that, before a multitude of peoples gathered from every direction, with the ruler of the kingdom also present, together with a host of bishops and priests, monks, or canons, he might be permitted to pass through four barrels set one after another and filled individually with boiling water, thick oil, pitch, and, finally, a very large blazing fire, in order to test his teaching, so that the truth of his profession might thereby be proved. I have read of no one besides him who has wished for this.

For the three youths of whom it is written in Daniel—Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego—did not ask for a trial by fire with similar obstinacy. Rather, leaving everything to God’s judgment, they answered the king of Babylon, who compelled them to worship the golden statue he had made, saying: “We have no need to answer you concerning this matter. Behold, our God whom we worship is able to rescue us from the burning furnace of fire and to deliver us from your hands. But if he does not, let it be known to you that we do not worship your gods, and that we will not adore the golden statue that you have set up” (Dan. 3:17).

Thus, through steadfastness of faith and humility of confession, they deserved to be delivered from the fire. What end this man’s obstinacy will have, however, remains unknown. May the Lord do with him what is good in his eyes, deliver us from every evil, defend us against every error, and grant us, through his grace, by right faith and good works, to merit eternal blessedness in his presence and to enjoy everlasting life.

Let these things, dearest brother, dictated now for you in a rustic style but with devoted spirit, suffice. Know, moreover, that as long as I live I shall always be ready to obey your good will and to consent to sound doctrine. [Col. 1530C] May almighty God grant that, while we are here, we may render him acceptable service together with you, and that after the end of this life we may rejoice perpetually in the heavenly kingdom.

## LETTER V. TO NOTTING, WITH A BOOK ON THE PREDESTINATION OF GOD

*(From Sirmond.)*

To the venerable and in every respect most worthy man Notting, bishop-elect: Rabanus sends greetings in Christ.

Recently, when you came to the most serene Emperor Louis, while he was passing through the district of the Logana, on a hostile expedition, and there spoke with me about the heresy which certain people wickedly maintain concerning God’s predestination, erring and leading others into error, you and I agreed that I should compose, from the divine Scriptures and from the opinions of orthodox Fathers, a short work to refute the error of those who think so wickedly concerning the good and just God that they say his predestination causes neither a person predestined to life to be able to fall into death, nor one predestined to death to be able in any way to recover life—although God, the author of all things and creator of natures, is the cause of no one’s ruin or destruction, but is the source of salvation for many.

Therefore receive now the little work that you asked our insignificance to compose for you. If you find anything in it agreeable and clearly expressed in a Catholic sense, attribute it to the one from whom you know that every good thing comes; and know that, in everything and in every respect, I am ready to contribute whatever I can by his grace to the benefit of your charity. Farewell, and love one who loves you; and do not fail to remember our lowliness in your holy prayers.

*The preface ends.*

## ON PREDESTINATION
If a rational human being recognized the power of his own nature and properly understood the power of his Creator, he would in no way entangle himself in foolish questions, nor would he retain in his mind or utter aloud anything contrary to the Christian religion. But because the ancient enemy, who from the beginning has envied the salvation of the human race, never ceases to sow weeds among Christ’s wheat, he therefore speaks through empty talkers words that are not merely idle but harmful and full of blasphemies [Col. 1531B]. Thus some of them assert that the author of their own destruction is its creator, saying that, just as those who have been called through God’s foreknowledge and predestination to receive the glory of eternal life cannot fail to be saved, so those who go to eternal destruction are compelled by God’s predestination and cannot escape destruction.

How absurd this is even the uneducated can understand, since in no way does he who created all good things, made the nations of the world capable of healing, and wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, compel anyone to perish. Rather, he causes the person who believes rightly and acts kindly to attain eternal salvation. For if, according to those who think such things, God’s predestination makes a person sin against his will, how does God justly condemn the sinner, when he sinned not voluntarily but under compulsion? Or how will God judge the world—he who is a just judge—and repay each person according to his works? “He will judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in his truth.” If by such reasoning God is deprived of being a just judge, then consequently his royal dignity and divine majesty are also taken away.

But, on the contrary, prophetic Scripture cries out: “For God is a great Lord, and a great king above all gods” (Ps. XCIV, 3); and again: “The Lord will reign over all the nations; God sits upon his holy throne” (Ps. XIII, 1). Therefore, when this matter is clearly explained according to the foregoing argument, it remains that the person who thinks such things belongs to the number of those of whom the Psalmist says: “The fool has said in his heart, ‘There is no God.’ They are corrupt and have become abominable in their pleasures” (Ps. XLVI, 9).

The teaching of the holy Fathers refutes this error in many ways and proves that those who think in this manner rely neither on the authority of Scripture nor on sound reasoning. For faith in predestination is firmly fortified by the authority of the holy Scriptures; yet it is in no way lawful to attribute to it the evil deeds committed by human beings, who have fallen into the inclination to sin not through God’s creation but through the transgression of our first father. From the punishment arising from that transgression no one is freed except by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, prepared and predestined in God’s eternal plan before the foundation of the world. (Prosper, *Against the Gauls*, ch. 3.)

[Col. 1532A] “Every person who, believing in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is reborn in baptism is absolved both from his own sins, which he contracted through evil will and action, and from original sin, which he inherited from his parents. But one who, after baptism, falls back into unbelief and impious ways, and who denies that he was cleansed from original sin, holds an opinion as false as the person who asserts that he was not condemned to eternal death. For whoever withdraws from Christ and, alienated from grace, ends this life, falling into destruction, does not fall back into what was remitted, nor will he be condemned on account of original sin; rather, because of his later crimes he will suffer the death that was due to him on account of those things that were remitted. Since this did not escape God’s foreknowledge or deceive it, he certainly never chose such a person, never predestined him, and never separated him from eternal destruction as one who would perish.”

Therefore, just as good works are to be attributed to the inspiration given to those who perform them, so evil works must be attributed to those who sin. They were not abandoned by God so that they might abandon God; rather, they abandoned him and were abandoned, and by their own will they changed from good to evil. For this reason, although they had been reborn and although they had been justified, they were nevertheless not predestined by the one who foreknew that they would become such.

It is most foolishly said that God’s predestination—whether to good or to evil—operates in everything. Nor is it true that people fulfill certain things by necessity, since in good actions the will must not be understood apart from grace. What reason is there, then, for any sensible person to say: “I do not need to labor for my rest and salvation, because if I have been predestined by God to eternal life, I shall arrive there whether I wish it or not; but if I have not been predestined, it does me no good to act well and devote myself to virtue, because I shall not possess the rewards of eternal blessedness”? This would be as though, by tempting God and despising his promises, one could please him, rather than by serving him devoutly through faith and love. (*Hypomnesticon*, book VI.)

[Col. 1532C] “Let us first explain what the very name ‘predestination’ signifies; then we shall prove, by the authority of the divine Scriptures, that predestination exists with God, who shows no partiality. Predestination is so called from foreseeing, anticipating, or foreordaining something future. Therefore God, for whom foreknowledge is not an accident but has always been and is his essence, predestines whatever he foreknows in advance, before it exists; and he predestines it because he foreknows what it will be. Hence the Apostle also says: ‘Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined’ (Rom. VIII, 29).”

But he does not predestine everything that he foreknows. He foreknows evil things only, but does not predestine them; good things he both foreknows and predestines. Thus, whatever is good, foreknowledge predestines—that is, it ordains it beforehand before it exists. When it begins to exist together with its author, he calls it, orders it, and disposes it. Hence what follows: “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.”

Let us therefore discuss more openly what we are saying. How, then, does God, in whom there is no iniquity, make general use of his foreknowledge and predestination with regard to the human race? The mass of the human race, made damnable and mortal through the transgression of Adam and Eve, is generally subject not to divine condemnation but, by what is owed, to the punishment and torment of Gehenna. Pardon, however, is bestowed not as a merit but through the generosity of the mercy of God, the just judge.

Since God is both just and merciful and foreknows the future, from this damnable mass he prepares—through his gratuitous mercy, not through partiality toward persons but by the irreproachable judgment of his equity—those whom he foreknows; that is, he predestines them to eternal life. The others he punishes with the penalty that, as I have said, is owed, because he foreknew what they would be. Yet he himself did not make them punishable or predestine them to punishment; he merely foreknew them, as I said, within the damnable mass.

[Col. 1533B] If you ask me to explain why God makes these two distinctions, if he is not a respecter of persons—since, in general, he must either punish by justice or free by mercy—argue with Paul; indeed, if you dare, argue against Paul, who spoke with Christ speaking in him: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me this way?’ Or does the potter not have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. IX, 30.)

But I say what I have already said: whatever God does, he does mercifully, justly, and holily, because he alone knows through foreseeing what a human being, through ignorance, does not know. For “who has known the mind of the Lord? Who has instructed him? Or who has been his counselor? Or who first gave to him, so that he might be repaid? Or who says to him, ‘What have you done?’”

God cannot be called merely just, or merely merciful, but both just and merciful. So we read, and so we believe. Therefore, when together with David we sing of mercy and judgment, we sing in fear; we do not question what his will may be, but rest in his judgment and mercy.”

For the whole divine law teaches that we reach our Creator through obedience to God’s commandments; and no one possessed of reason can please God without right faith and good works. Thus both prophetic and apostolic utterances resound with this message and exhort us to reach our Creator by the straight course of a holy way of life.

Accordingly, Moses says: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God, as you tempted him in the place of temptation. Keep the commandments of the Lord your God, his testimonies, and his ordinances, which he commanded you; and do what is pleasing and good in the sight of the Lord, so that it may be well with you, and so that you may enter and possess the excellent land which the Lord swore to your fathers he would give you, driving out all your enemies before you, as he has spoken” (Deut. VI, 16 ff.).

The Psalmist says concerning this: “Who is the person who desires life and longs to see good days? Let him restrain his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit. Let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Ps. XXXVIII, 13).

For this reason it is also said through Isaiah: “Thus says the Lord: Keep judgment and practice righteousness, for my salvation is near to come and my righteousness to be revealed. Blessed is the person who does this, and the son of man who holds fast to it, keeping the Sabbath so as not to profane it, guarding his hands from doing any evil” (Isa. LVI, 1 ff.).

Of this it is also said through Jeremiah: “Thus says the Lord to Israel: Cursed is the person who will not listen to the words of this covenant, which I commanded your fathers on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace, saying: Listen to my voice and do everything that I command you; then you shall be my people, and I shall be your God. And I shall confirm the oath that I swore to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey” (Jer. XI, 3 ff.).

To Ezekiel the Lord says: “You therefore, son of man, say to the house of Israel: Thus you have spoken, saying, ‘Our iniquities and our sins are upon us, and in them we waste away; how, then, can we live?’ Say to them: Thus says the Lord God: I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live. Turn, turn from your very evil ways; and why will you die, house of Israel?

“You therefore, son of man, say to the children of your people: The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him on whatever day he sins, and the wickedness of the wicked shall not harm him on whatever day he turns from his wickedness; nor shall the righteous be able to live by his righteousness on whatever day he sins.

“Even if I say to the righteous that he shall surely live, and he, trusting in his righteousness, commits iniquity, all his righteousness shall be forgotten, and in the iniquity he has committed, in that he shall die. But if I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he repents of his sin, practices judgment and righteousness, restores the pledge, returns what he has stolen, walks in the commandments of life, and does nothing unjust, he shall surely live and shall not die. None of all his sins that he has committed shall be held against him” (Ezek. XXXIII, 10 ff.).

To Nebuchadnezzar also the prophet Daniel said: “O king, may my counsel please you: redeem your sins by almsgiving and your iniquities by mercy toward the poor; perhaps God will forgive your offenses” (Dan. IV, 24).

For this reason it is also said through Hosea: “Sow for yourselves in righteousness, and reap at the mouth of mercy; renew your fallow ground. It is time to seek the Lord, when he comes who will teach you righteousness” (Hos. X, 12). And again: “Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have fallen through your iniquity. Take words with you and return to the Lord, and say to him: ‘Take away all iniquity, and receive what is good, and we shall repay the fruit of our lips’” (Hos. XIV, 2–3).

For it is written in Joel: “For the day of the Lord is great and exceedingly terrible, and who can endure it? Now therefore, says the Lord: Return to me with all your heart, in fasting, weeping, and mourning; tear your hearts and not your garments, and return to the Lord your God, for he is gracious and merciful, patient and rich in mercy, and relenting from evil. Who knows whether he may turn and forgive, and leave behind him a blessing, a sacrifice and a drink offering for the Lord our God?” (Joel II, 11.)

For this reason it is also said through Amos: “Seek good and not evil, so that you may live; and the Lord God of hosts will be with you, as you have said. Hate evil and love good, and establish judgment at the gate; perhaps the Lord God of hosts will have mercy on the remnant of Joseph” (Amos V, 14 ff.).

Thus also the prophet Obadiah says: “The day of the Lord is near upon all the nations. As you have done, so shall it be done to you; your retribution shall be turned back upon your own head” (Obad. I, 15).

Jonah likewise preached in the great city of Nineveh that they should do penance. The Ninevites proclaimed a fast and clothed themselves in sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. God saw their works, that they had turned from their evil way, and God had mercy concerning the evil that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it (Jonah III, 3–10).

For this reason Micah says: “I shall show you, O man, what is good and what the Lord your God requires of you: surely to practice judgment, to love mercy, and to walk attentively with your God” (Mic. VI, 8).

Finally, Nahum proclaims: “God is jealous and the Lord takes vengeance; the Lord takes vengeance and possesses wrath; the Lord takes vengeance upon his enemies and is angry with his adversaries” (Nahum I, 2).

Concerning this Habakkuk says: “Behold, the unbelieving person is not upright in himself; but the righteous shall live by his faithfulness” (Habac. II, 4). And again: “Woe to him who gathers evil greed for his house, so that he may set his nest on high and think to escape from the hand of evil” (ibid., v. 9).

And again: “Woe to him who builds a city with blood and establishes a town in iniquity. Woe to him who gives drink to his friend, sending his gall and making him drunk so that he may look upon his nakedness. He is filled with disgrace instead of glory. Woe to him who says to wood, ‘Awake,’ and to a silent stone, ‘Arise.’ Can it teach? Behold, it is covered with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all within it. But the Lord is in his holy temple; let all the earth be silent before him” (ibid., vv. 12–20).

For this reason Zephaniah says: “Seek the Lord your God, all you humble of the earth who have practiced his judgment; seek righteousness, seek humility, if perhaps you may be sheltered on the day of the Lord’s anger” (Zeph. II, 3).

Haggai likewise says: “Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Set your hearts upon your ways. Go up to the mountain, bring wood, and build the house; then it will be acceptable to me, and I shall be glorified, says the Lord. You looked for more, and behold, it became less; you brought it home, and I blew upon it. Why is this, says the Lord God of hosts? Because my house lies deserted, while each of you hastens to his own house” (Hag. I, 7 ff.).

Through Zechariah also the Lord says: “Judge true judgment and mercy, and show compassion each to his brother. Do not oppress the widow, the orphan, the foreigner, or the poor; and let no one of you devise evil against his brother in his heart” (Zech. VII, 7 ff.).

And again: “Do not be afraid. These, then, are the words that you shall do: Speak the truth, each one with his neighbor. Judge truth and the judgment of peace in your gates, and let none of you devise evil against his friend in your hearts; and do not love a false oath. For all these are things that I hate, says the Lord” (Zech. VIII, 16 ff.).

Through Malachi he also says: “You shall return and see what difference there is between the righteous and the wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not serve him” (Malach. III, 18). “For behold, the day will come, burning like a furnace, and all the proud and all who practice iniquity will be straw. The coming day will set them ablaze, says the Lord of hosts, and will leave them neither root nor branch. But for you who fear the name of the Lord, the sun of righteousness will rise, and healing will be in its wings; you shall go out and leap like calves from the herd, and you shall tread down the wicked when they have become ashes beneath the soles of your feet, on the day when I act, says the Lord God of hosts. Remember the law of Moses my servant, which he commanded them at Horeb for all Israel: the commandments and judgments” (Malach. IV, 1 ff.).

In Proverbs also Wisdom teaches as follows: “My son, do not forget my law, and let your heart keep my commandments. For they will add length of days and years of life and peace to you. Let mercy and truth not forsake you; bind them around your throat and write them on the tablets of your heart, and you will find grace and good discipline before God and human beings” (Prov. III, 1 ff.).

Likewise Ecclesiastes teaches: “Rejoice, therefore, young man, in your youth, and let your heart be joyful in the days of your youth; walk in the ways of your heart and in the strength of your eyes, and know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment. Remove anger from your heart and put away wickedness from your flesh, for youth and pleasure are vanity. Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the time of affliction comes and the years approach of which you will say, ‘They do not please me’; before the sun and the moon and the stars grow dark, and the clouds return after the rain” (Eccl. XI, 9; XII, 1 ff.).

The book called Wisdom begins in this way: “Love righteousness, you who judge the earth. Think of the Lord with goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart, for he is found by those who do not tempt him, and he reveals himself to those who have faith in him. For perverse thoughts separate from God, but tested virtue rebukes the foolish, because wisdom will not enter a soul that plots evil, nor will it dwell in a body subject to sins. For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that lack understanding; it will be rebuked when iniquity arrives” (Wis. I, 1 ff.).

And again: “Therefore, guard yourselves from murmuring, which profits nothing, and spare your tongue from slander, for an obscure accusation will not pass into emptiness; but a lying mouth kills the soul. Do not seek death through the error of your life, nor acquire destruction by the works of your hands, because God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living. For he created all things to exist, and made the nations of the world capable of healing; there is no destructive poison in them, nor is the kingdom of Hades upon the earth” (Wis. I, 11 ff.).

Likewise, in the book of Jesus son of Sirach, Wisdom teaches what must be avoided and what must be done: “You who fear the Lord, believe in him, and mercy will come to you as a delight. You who fear the Lord, love him, and your hearts will be enlightened. Look, children, at the nations of human beings, and know that no one who hoped in the Lord was put to shame. For who has remained in his commandments and been abandoned, or who has called upon him and been despised? For God is compassionate and merciful, and he forgives sins in the time of tribulation; he is a protector of all who seek him in truth.

“Woe to the double-hearted and deceitful lips, to hands that do evil, and to the sinner who walks upon the earth by two paths. Woe to those who are fainthearted, who do not believe God and therefore are not protected by him. Woe to those who have lost endurance, who have abandoned the straight ways and turned aside into crooked paths; what will you do when the Lord begins to inspect you?

“Those who fear the Lord will not be incredulous toward his word, and those who love him will keep his way. Those who fear the Lord will seek what is pleasing to him, and those who love him will be filled with his law. Those who fear the Lord will prepare their hearts and sanctify their souls in his sight. Those who fear the Lord keep his commandments and have patience until his visitation” (Eccli. II, 8 ff.).

All these passages, then, teach the rule of sound faith; they either proclaim punishments to sinners for evil works or promise rewards to the righteous for good deeds. How, then, does anyone dare to say that good merits do not help the righteous and that sins do not harm the wicked, but that each person is either crowned or punished by the necessity of predestination?

Let us therefore see what the New Testament indicates to us concerning this. The Truth itself says in the Gospel: “Enter through the narrow gate, because the gate is wide and the way is broad that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter through it. How narrow the gate and constricted the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it” (Matt. VII, 13–14). “Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke XIII, 20). “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII, 21).

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I shall refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart; and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. XI, 28, 30).

“For the Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each person according to his works. But concerning that day or hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, except the Father. Watch, be vigilant, and pray, for you do not know when the time will be. It is like a man who went abroad, left his house, and gave his servants authority over each task, commanding the doorkeeper to keep watch. Watch, therefore; you do not know when the master of the house will come, whether in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning, lest, when he comes suddenly, he find you sleeping. What I say to you, I say to all: Watch” (Matt. XXIV).

Paul the Apostle, writing to the Romans, says: “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those who hold back the truth of God in unrighteousness. But for those who are contentious and do not obey the truth, yet believe in iniquity, there will be wrath and indignation, tribulation and anguish upon every soul of one who practices evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek; but glory, virtue, honor, and peace for everyone who practices good, for the Jew first and also for the Greek. For there is no partiality with God. For all who have sinned without the law will perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” [Col. 1538C] (Rom. I, 18 ff.).

“Therefore, let sin not reign in your mortal body so that you obey its desires; nor present your members as weapons of iniquity to sin, but present yourselves to God as those living from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness for God. For sin will not rule over you, because you are not under the law but under grace” (Rom. VI, 12 ff.).

James says: “Be doers of the word and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves” (James I, 22). And again: “What does it profit, my brothers, if someone says that he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him?” (James II, 14.)

And again: “Therefore submit yourselves to God; resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to the Lord, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded. Be miserable, mourn, and weep; let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow. Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you in the time of tribulation” (James II, 7–10).

How the power of faith saves a person, and that our ruin must not be attributed to God, from whom every good thing comes, the same apostle shows in that Epistle, saying: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach anyone, and it will be given to him. But let him ask in faith, without doubting. For the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind. Therefore let that person not suppose that he will receive anything from God” (James I, 5–7).

“Let no one, when he is tempted, say, ‘I am tempted by God.’ For God cannot be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one. Rather, each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire. Then, when desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and when sin has been completed, it brings forth death. Therefore, do not err, my most beloved brothers. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration” (ibid., vv. 13–17).

Peter also wrote concerning this: “Therefore, girding the loins of your mind, being perfectly sober, hope in the grace that is offered to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ, as obedient children, not conforming yourselves to the desires of your former ignorance, but according to the one who called us, the Holy One, be holy in all your conduct, for it is written: ‘You shall be holy, because I am holy’” (I Pet. I, 13–16).

And again: “Therefore humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation, casting all your anxiety upon him, because he cares for you. Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil prowls around, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, strong in faith, knowing that the same sufferings are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world” (I Pet. V, 6–9).

John also says: “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world. By this the Spirit of God is known: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of Antichrist, of which you have heard that it is coming, and now it is already in the world.

“You are from God, little children, and you have conquered him, because greater is the one who is in you than the one who is in the world. They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them. We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we recognize the spirit of truth and the spirit of error” (I John IV, 1–6).

And again: “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born from God; and everyone who loves the one who begot him also loves the one who has been begotten by him. By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and do his commandments. For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments; and his commandments are not burdensome. For everything that has been born from God conquers the world; and this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith. Who is the one who conquers the world, except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” (I John V, 1–5.)

For if the love of God helps no one, and if the children of God are not children of light, how does that which is born from God conquer the world? And how is the victory over the world faith in Christ? But if faith in Christ, which works through love, is the true salvation of human beings—for “whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame”—as he himself says, “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me will never die” (John XI, 25)—how do these empty talkers babble that right faith and good works benefit human beings nothing, because, unless someone has been predestined, he will not come to life, when predestination is nothing other than the granting of life, not the condemnation of anyone to destruction?

Hence Scripture plainly says: “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living. For he created all things to exist, and made the nations of the world capable of healing” (Wis. I, 13). And the Lord himself says through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11).

But if the Lord does not desire the death of the wicked and the sinner, how does he predestine him to death, [Col. 1540B] when his willing is nothing other than predestining? For the will of God is the cause of all things, and his willing is; nor does the simple nature possess any opposition within itself. Yet the same Lord of all is rich toward all who call upon him.

Therefore predestination is read of in connection with good, not evil. Hence the Apostle says: “Those whom he foreknew, he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. VIII, 29–30).

Notice that he says, “Those whom he predestined, he also called,” not “Those whom he predestined, he also condemned.” For the good Maker loves his creature, and he does not condemn anyone without cause. Concerning this it is written elsewhere: “You have mercy on all, Lord, and you hate nothing that you have made, overlooking the sins of human beings for the sake of repentance and sparing them, because you are the God of all” (Wis. XI, 24).

This person, therefore, is bound by multiple guilt, because he turns the good of predestination into an evil meaning and presumes to blaspheme in impious words.

First, he dares to call his Creator, who is supremely good, malevolent, and claims that he decrees his own work to perish uselessly and without cause.

Second, he attempts to assert that the Truth itself is deceiving, although through the holy Scriptures it promises the rewards of eternal life to those who believe rightly and act well, and foretells the punishments of death for sinners who do not repent.

Third, he proclaims unjust the just judge who will judge the living and the dead in equity, because he claims that the Lord does not repay rewards to those who act well or torments to those who act badly.

Fourth, through his error he does not fear to pretend that the Redeemer of the world shed his blood in vain, since, because of the necessity of predestination, he would be unable to help those who believe and hope in him.

Fifth, he claims that our Savior does not complete, through the creation of human beings, the number of the good angels that the devil diminished when he fell through pride.

Sixth, by his opinion he favors the devil more, because he has handed over to the devil’s lot of destruction those whom divine grace has decreed to reach eternal salvation.

Seventh, he shows himself to be the greatest enemy of the entire human race, since he says that through faith in Christ and the sacrament of baptism humanity cannot be rescued from the fall of its first parent, from the guilt of its own crimes, or from the power of its enemies, but, bound by the harmful predestination of its Maker, must be plunged into Tartarus.

When all these points have thus been demonstrated, he is proved to be above all his own enemy, since he not only prepares for himself the fire of Gehenna by this teaching, but also, by leading others away from the way of truth through the doctrine of his error, makes them participants in his condemnation. For them, without doubt, he will pay fitting punishments in the eternal fire.

Hence the shepherd of the Church says: “There were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will introduce destructive sects, even denying the Lord who redeemed them, and bringing upon themselves swift destruction. Many will follow their immoralities, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. In greed they will exploit you with deceitful words. Their judgment has not been idle for a long time, and their destruction does not sleep” (II Pet. II, 1–3).

Concerning them Jude also writes in his Epistle: “For certain people have infiltrated among you, who long ago were designated for this judgment: ungodly people who turn the grace of our Lord into immorality and deny the only ruler and our Lord Jesus Christ” (Jude, 4).

And again: “In the same way they indeed defile the flesh, but they reject dominion and blaspheme majesty. When Michael the archangel, disputing with the devil, argued about the body of Moses, he did not dare to pronounce a judgment of blasphemy, but said: ‘May God rebuke you.’ Yet these people blaspheme whatever they do not understand; and whatever they know naturally, like animals without reason, by these things they are corrupted” (ibid., 8–10).

A little later: “Behold, the Lord has come with his holy myriads to execute judgment against all and to convict all the ungodly concerning all the works of their ungodliness that they have committed ungodly, and concerning all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him. These are grumblers and complainers, walking according to their desires; their mouth speaks arrogance, and they admire persons for the sake of gain” (ibid., 14–16).

The testimonies that we have brought forward from the divine Scriptures to confound the error of those who say that God’s predestination is the cause of the destruction of the lost, and to show that God wills the rewards of the heavenly kingdom to be acquired through right faith and good works, selected from among many, should suffice for the prudent reader.

Next, we shall state what we have found set forth concerning God’s predestination in the opinions of the holy teachers and catholic Fathers. (Prosper, *Against the Objection of Vincent*, II.)

[Col. 1541D] “For those who say that God does not wish all to be saved, even if all wish to be saved, how greatly they err, ...

It is clear to everyone, since Truth says: “If you, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him?” (Matt. 7:11). How can it be that God, who even saves those of whom it cannot be said that they wish to be saved, should not wish some to be saved even if they wish to be saved—unless there exist certain causes about which, although they are unknowable to us, he nevertheless judges, and of him it cannot be said that he ought to have acted otherwise than he did? Once this distinction, therefore, which divine knowledge holds within the secrecy of its justice, has been set aside, we must most sincerely believe and profess that God wills all human beings to be saved. For the Apostle, whose statement this is, most earnestly commands—and this is devoutly observed in all the churches—that supplication be made to God for all human beings. Of these, the fact that many perish is the merit of those who perish; the fact that many are saved is the gift of the one who saves. That the guilty person is condemned is the justice of God, who is without blame; that the guilty person is justified is the ineffable grace of God.

But those who say that God creates the greater part of the human race for the purpose of destroying it eternally, on the grounds that many go by the broad and spacious way that leads to death, while few go by the narrow way that leads to eternal life; and that the number of unbelievers is very great, as is the number of those who pass from this world without the remedy of baptism and therefore cannot be released from the bond of original sin—as though all these things belonged to the Creator of the human race, as though he himself wished those who perish to perish in this way—do not think rightly. [Col. 1542A]

(Objectio Vincent. IV.) “God is indeed the creator of all human beings; but no one was created by him in order to perish, because the cause of birth is one thing, and the cause of perishing another. That human beings are born is the Creator’s gift; that they perish is the transgressor’s merit. For in Adam, in whom the nature of all human beings was prefigured, all sinned, and they were bound by the same sentence that he received. Nor are they released from this bond, even if they are free from personal sins, unless they are reborn in the Holy Spirit through the sacrament of the death and resurrection of Christ. He is therefore exceedingly impious and ignorant who does not distinguish the defect of nature from the author of nature, from whom everything that must be condemned in each person is entirely alien. He creates human beings, nor does he withdraw his workmanship from the succession by which generations are multiplied, according to the purpose of his good will; and in many he will restore what he himself did not make.” [Col. 1542B]

(Objectio Vincent. V.) “When they say that God is the author of our sins because he makes the human will evil, this is blasphemy against the substance, as though by its natural impulse it could do nothing but sin. We wholly reject this from our understanding. We know God as just and good, and as the creator of human substance and of its inward and outward faculties, so that whatever is contrary to nature is utterly alien to him. Sin, however, is contrary to nature; from it arise death and all things belonging to death. Human beings put on these evils when the devil, finding them deprived of faith and obedience, led them away from God’s law into his own promises and, through the ruin of the corrupted stock, bound all the offspring of posterity to himself. God, therefore, is not the author of anyone’s sin, but the creator of nature. Although nature possessed the power not to sin, it sinned of its own accord [Col. 1542C] and voluntarily subjected itself to its deceiver. It is moved in sin not by a natural impulse but by a captive one, until it dies to sin and lives to God—which it cannot do without the grace of God, since it cannot recover the freedom it lost unless Christ sets it free. For there is no other name under heaven given to human beings by which they must be saved.”

(Objectio Vincent. X.) “When some say that a man committed adulteries, the violation of consecrated virgins, murders, and other crimes because he could not avoid committing them—as though God had predestined those persons for the purpose that at a fixed time they should fall into various vices—this opinion is detestable and abhorrent to every Christian, since it believes God to be the author of anyone’s evil will or evil action. His predestination is never outside goodness and never outside justice. For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. Holy divinity does not establish the adulteries of married women or the violation of virgins, but condemns them; nor does it ordain them, but punishes them. When human beings commit such evils, they serve their own lusts and desires, which they inherited from that first stain of voluntary transgression. But when they turn away from evil and do good, the steps of human beings are directed by the Lord, and they desire his way. Therefore the Apostle says: ‘We pray to the Lord that you do nothing evil—not so that we may appear approved, but so that you may do what is good’ (2 Cor. 13:7).

“Therefore the predestination of God neither aroused, persuaded, nor impelled the fall of those who plunge into ruin, the wickedness of the unrighteous, or the desires of sinners; rather, it plainly predestined his judgment, by which he will repay each person according to what he has done, whether good or evil. That judgment would certainly not exist if human beings sinned by the will of God. It will, however, most manifestly take place, and every person whom the discrimination of divine knowledge has placed on the left will be condemned, because he carried out not God’s will but his own.” [Col. 1543A]

(Vinc. XI.) “God therefore predestined none of the affairs of evil to occur, nor did he prepare any soul that would live wickedly and shamefully for the purpose of living in that manner. But he was not ignorant that such a soul would be such, and he foreknew that he would judge such a one justly. Thus nothing else can be referred to his predestination except what pertains either to the due retribution of justice or to the due bestowal of glory.” [Col. 1543B]

(Objectio Vinc. XII.) “Therefore those who say that, by God’s predestination, children of God become children of the devil, holy temples become temples of demons, and members of Christ become members of a prostitute are perniciously deceived, and in their error they deceive others.”

(Vinc. XII.) “God’s predestination, although it is uncertain to us while we are involved in the dangers of the present life, nevertheless remains immutable with him who made the things that are to come. He does not blind the one whom he has illumined; he does not destroy what he has built; he does not uproot what he has planted. For ‘the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable’ (Rom. 11:29), and God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are his’ (2 Tim. 2:19).

“God’s predestination therefore in no way makes some who are children of God into children of the devil, or makes temples of demons out of temples of the Holy Spirit, or turns members of Christ into members of a prostitute. Rather, predestination makes children of God out of children of the devil, makes a temple of the Holy Spirit out of temples of demons, and makes members of Christ out of members of a prostitute. For he binds the strong man and seizes his possessions, rescuing them from the power of darkness and transferring them from dishonor to glory.

“But those of whom it is said, ‘They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us’ (1 John 2:19), ‘went out by their own will and fell by their own will.’ Because they were foreknown as destined to fall, they were not predestined; they would have been predestined if they had been destined to return and remain in holiness and truth. Consequently, God’s predestination is for many a cause of standing; it is the cause of falling for no one.” [Col. 1544A]

(Vinc.
