XIII.) “To all who have fallen back from faith into unbelief and from holiness into ungodliness, and who have not been cleansed by any correction before the end of life, nothing but eternal death is owed. But it is impious to ascribe the cause of such collapses to God. Although, from his eternal knowledge, he has foreknown what he will repay each person according to that person’s merits, he has nevertheless, by the fact that he cannot be deceived, imposed on no one either the necessity or the will to sin. If, therefore, someone falls away from justice and piety, he is driven headlong by his own choice, drawn by his own desire, and deceived by his own persuasion. [Col. 1544B] The Father does nothing there, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit; nor does anything of the divine will intervene in such an affair. By its work we know that many are held back lest they fall, but that none are impelled to fall.”

(Vinc. XIV.) “Finally, there is absolutely no predestination of God to transgress the law, neglect religion, corrupt discipline, abandon the faith, or commit any kind of sin; nor can it happen that through him by whom one rises from such evils one falls into such evils. If, therefore, a person lives in holiness, advances in virtue, and perseveres in good pursuits, this is manifestly a gift of God, without whom no fruit of good works is acquired. But if a person withdraws from these things and passes over to vices and sins, God does not introduce any evil temptation there. He does not abandon the one who is about to depart before that person departs, and he often causes him not to depart—or, even if he has departed, to return. Why he holds one person back and does not hold another back cannot be comprehended, nor is it lawful to investigate it, when it is enough to know both that our standing comes from him and that our falling does not come from him.” [Col. 1544C]

(Objectio Vinc. XV.) “Those who say that all those faithful—and indeed holy—people who have fallen through sin into eternal death were so predestined and so ordered by God after they had fallen that they could neither be freed nor wished to be freed through repentance do not speak truthfully or wisely. Those who fell away from faith and holiness fell by their own will; by their own will they do not rise, and they voluntarily endure the domination of the desires to which they surrendered. But if some grieve over their captivity and, judging themselves, flee with changed hearts to the mercy of God, they do this not without the spirit of divine compassion. This is the transformation wrought by the right hand of the Most High, who grants repentance to countless fallen people so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they were held captive for his will.

“God deprives no one of the path of correction, nor does he strip anyone of the possibility of doing good; for the person who turns away from God has himself taken away from himself both the will and the power to do what is good. Therefore it does not follow, as those who raise such objections think, that when God has not given certain people repentance, he has taken away their recovery, or that when he has not raised them up, he has struck them down. It is one thing to have led an innocent person into crime, which is alien to God; it is another not to have granted forgiveness to a guilty person, which is attributable to the sinner’s merit.” [Col. 1545A]

But since these people disagree among themselves—those who say that God’s predestination makes it impossible for anyone to be saved even if he wishes to be saved, and the Pelagians, who attribute to human beings alone, by virtue of the condition received at the beginning, everything pertaining to their state of salvation, even without divine grace to assist them—and although their error is different, their impiety is equal, we therefore think it necessary to establish by testimonies from the Scriptures that human beings were created good by God at the beginning, because “God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good”; but that no one can be saved by his own merit without the grace of God, because Truth says in the Gospel: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6), and: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Accordingly, Paul, writing to the Ephesians, says: “For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we might walk in them” (Ephes. II, 8). And again: “Peace to the brothers and love with faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption” (Ephes. VI, 23). [Col. 1545B]

To the Romans he likewise says: “Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII, 24). And again: “‘The remnant,’ he says, ‘has been saved according to the election of grace. But if by grace, then not by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace’” (Rom. XI, 5).

To the Corinthians he likewise speaks in this way: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not empty; rather, I labored more abundantly than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10). James the Apostle also wrote about this, saying: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17). And again: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

Peter also commends the grace of God to his hearers in his Epistle, saying: “Grace and peace be multiplied to you” (2 Pet. 1:2). And again: “Grace be with all of you who are in Christ Jesus” (1 Pet. 5:14). And once more: “You therefore, brothers, since you know these things beforehand, guard yourselves, lest, carried away by the error of the foolish, you fall from your own steadfastness. Rather, grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (II Petr. III, 17).

John too wrote in his Apocalypse, saying: “Grace to you and peace from him who is, who was, and who is to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne, and from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth, who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Apoc. I, 4). [Col. 1546A]

No rightly believing person can deny that free choice was given to human beings. But if it reaches the accomplishment of a good work, this is the gift of God’s grace. When the divine admonitions say, “Do not do this” and “Do not do that,” and when they require the work of the will for doing or not doing something, free choice is sufficiently demonstrated.

(Augustine, On Grace and Free Choice, ch. 2.) “Let no one therefore blame God in his heart, but let each person blame himself when he sins; nor, when he does something according to God, let him attribute this to anything other than his own will. For when he acts willingly, then the work must be called good, and then the reward of the good work must be hoped for from him of whom it is said that he ‘will repay each person according to his works’ (Matt. 16:27).”

The will is always free in us, but it is not always good. For it is either free from righteousness when it serves sin—and then it is evil—or it is free from sin when it serves righteousness—and then it is good. The grace of God, however, is always good, and through it a person who previously had an evil will becomes a person of good will. Through it also the good will itself, once it has begun to exist, is increased and becomes so strong that it can fulfill the divine commandments when it wills to do so, and wills to do so very fully and perfectly.

This is the point of what is written: “If you will to keep the commandments, the commandments will preserve you” (Ecclus. 15:16): a person who wills but cannot do so should recognize that he has not yet fully received the will to do it, and should pray that he may obtain as much good will as is sufficient for fulfilling the commandments. For in this way he is helped to do what is commanded. It is useful to will when we are able, and it is useful to be able when we will. For what benefit is there if we will what we cannot do, or do not will what we can?” [Col. 1546B]

(On Ecclesiastical Dogmas, ch. 20.) “From the very first creation of the world, human beings were entrusted to the freedom of their own choice, so that, if they wished to remain in that for which they had been created, they might persevere in keeping the commandment by the sole exertion of an attentive mind. But after they fell through the serpent’s deception by means of Eve, they lost the good of nature and likewise the strength of free choice—not, however, the power of choosing, lest the sin they corrected should not be their own, nor what they had not washed away by choice be forgiven by merit.

“Freedom of choice, that is, rational will, therefore urges them to seek salvation, but God first admonishes it and invites it to salvation, so that, through the opportunity of salvation—that is, through God’s inspiration—it may choose, follow, or act. But that it may attain what it chooses, follows, or undertakes through this opportunity, we freely confess to be God’s work. Thus the beginning of our salvation comes from God’s mercy, so that we may consent to saving inspiration; that we may attain what we began by consenting to the admonition is a divine gift; that we may not fall after receiving the gift of salvation belongs both to our diligence and to heavenly assistance; but that we fall belongs to our own power and negligence.” [Col. 1547A]

(Hypomnesticon VI, to the end.) “Holy Scripture openly opposes those who criticize God’s predestination in very many passages. But I should like to ask them to explain by what judgment Paul and Barnabas, preaching the word of God at Lystra, said: ‘In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways’ (Acts 14:15), so that they might perish in the idolatry of images, while the Lord chose for himself one nation alone, namely Jacob, and Israel as his possession (Ps. 34:4)—to which alone, as I have said, he gave the law for knowing him, setting aside the other generations.

“Or why again did the loss of the Jews take place so that the reconciliation of the world—that is, of all the nations—might occur, as the Apostle says: ‘For if their loss is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?’ (Rom. 11:15). As though it were impossible for almighty God to give the law to the whole world, confer the salvation of Christ’s grace, or, so to speak, accomplish from the beginning of Adam’s fall what he decided should take place according to his will at different times.

“Let them also explain why, when Paul and Barnabas had been sent by the Holy Spirit to carry the name of the Lord for the salvation of the nations, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit, as they passed through Phrygia and the region of Galatia preaching, to speak the word in Asia; and when they came to Mysia and wished to go into Bithynia, ‘the Spirit of Jesus,’ he says, ‘did not permit them’ (Act. XVI, 7). God knew, he says, that they would not believe; and therefore he did not permit them to go and speak the word. Does this prohibition by the Holy Spirit not show something other than the word of the Lord Jesus spoken in the Gospel: ‘The Spirit breathes where he wills’ (John 3:8)? Let them reflect on this and explain why he breathes where he wills and not everywhere.

“Let them also say why, when the aforesaid Paul and Barnabas were preaching salvation at Pisidian Antioch to Jews and Gentiles, no one believed except those whom the Lord had previously ordained to believe. For the sacred text itself testifies concerning them: ‘And they believed,’ it says, ‘as many as had been ordained to eternal life’ (Acts 13:48)—that is, predestined.” [Col. 1547D]

Behold, in all that we have brought forward on the authority of divine Scripture, you have both mercy and judgment; and it is certain that God is not a respecter of persons, nor does he show regard for anyone’s person. Descend, then, if you are able, into the depth of God’s mercy; ascend, if you are sufficient, into the height of his judgment; stretch out into the length and breadth of his unsearchable ways; and, if you have clearly penetrated these secrets—which are so fearful and incomprehensible, and before which Paul himself trembled—then disclose them to us without fear.

For however much you may strive to know, you cannot comprehend God’s judgments, nor will you be able to, because just as no one knows what belongs to a human being [Col. 1548A] except the human spirit within that person, so no one knows what belongs to God except the Spirit of God (Rom. XI, 33). Therefore, if we are able to reach anything, we must acknowledge that it has been revealed not by our own cleverness but by the gift of the Holy Spirit. But if we have not been granted knowledge of what is above us, let it not be sought from our littleness. For Holy Scripture has said: “Do not seek things higher than you, and do not investigate things stronger than you in vain” (Ecclus. III, 32). And again: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. XI, 20).

We have said that, from the damnable mass of the human race, God foreknew—through mercy, not through merits—those whom he predestined to life by the election of grace. As for the others, who by the judgment of his justice are made without this grace, he merely foreknew that they would perish through their own fault; he did not predestine them to perish.

[Col. 1548B] But, as I have said, those whom he foreknew would rush into works of ungodliness and death he did not preordain, nor did he drive them into them. These are the people who provoke God to anger, refusing to accept the faith brought and preached to them—or, with God as judge, are unable to accept it—or who misuse it once accepted. For this reason they are handed over to a depraved mind, so that they may do things that are not fitting; and we rightly confess that punishment was predestined for them.

To prove this, I think Judas alone is a sufficient example. For when God foreknew that he would be utterly wicked through the vices of his own will—that is, that he would misuse the discipleship graciously bestowed on him by Christ, and, burning with avarice, would betray the Lord to the Jews for money—he predestined punishment for him according to his merit. Through David the Holy Spirit says:

“God, do not keep silent about my praise, for [Col. 1548C] the mouth of the sinner and the deceitful man has been opened against me” (Ps. CVIII, 2).

That is, against Judas, or against the Jews, in relation to Christ. Against Judas, when he says: “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” (Matt. XXVI, 15). And after the promise of money, giving the sign of the betrayal: “Whomever I kiss, he is the one; seize him.” Therefore he says, “the mouth of Judas has been opened against me.” For when he gave the kiss, he revealed by his deceitful mouth whom they were to seize.

Likewise, against the Jews, when, wishing to destroy him by deceit, as the Gospel relates, they cried out: “Crucify, crucify!” (John XIX, 6). And shortly afterward it says: “Appoint a sinner over him”—that is, over Judas—“and let the devil stand at his right hand. When he is judged, let him go forth condemned, and let his prayer become sin. Let his days [Col. 1548D] be few, and let another receive his episcopate.”

And after the other things that follow concerning him:

“Because,” it says, “he did not remember to show mercy, but persecuted the poor and needy man, and the brokenhearted, to put him to death.”

The remaining passages that were spoken concerning his person follow.

For, as the book of the Acts of the Apostles relates, the holy apostle Peter proves that these things had been foretold concerning him and fulfilled in him, when he declares that one of those who had gathered with the apostles, for the sake of bearing witness to the resurrection of Jesus Christ, ought to be appointed in his place. He says:

“Men, brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became leader of those who arrested [Col. 1549A] Jesus. He was numbered among us and received his share in this ministry. This man indeed acquired a field from the reward of his iniquity; and, hanging, he burst open in the middle, and all his bowels were poured out. It became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that that field was called in their language Acheldemach—that is, ‘the field of blood.’ For it is written in the Book of Psalms: ‘Let his dwelling become desolate, and let there be no one inhabiting it; and let another receive his episcopate’” (Acts I, 16 ff.).

Therefore, when the Holy Spirit recalls his evil deeds in the Psalms, before he existed he was foreknown—not made—to be such an adversary of the Son of God. For if he had been made such, he would be blameless, and it would be attributed to God’s workmanship, not to Judas. [Col. 1549B] His condemnation would also have been pronounced unjustly against him. But far be this from the supremely good Judge, God, the author of all good things and the condemner of all evil. For, as I said, he foreknew Judas’s evils; he did not make them. Yet, in those things which he foreknew, he justly handed him over to a depraved mind and permitted him to fulfill them. He permitted this because, through the Holy Spirit, he had foretold beforehand that Judas would perish.

For just as Christ had to suffer through Judas, with the Holy Spirit announcing it beforehand through the prophets, so Judas had to perish, with the same Holy Spirit proclaiming it beforehand. For it was said concerning him: “No one has perished except the son of perdition” (John XVII, 12). Punishment was therefore predestined for him on account of his evils, in which, as I have often said, he was merely foreknown, not predestined.

[Col. 1549C] But that what we have said is true—namely, that punishment was predestined for those who would perish—hear the apostle Peter, when he says that there would be false prophets, lying teachers, and apostates in the Church, just as there had been among the ancient people:

“For them,” he says, “judgment from of old does not cease, and their destruction does not sleep” (II Pet. II, 3).

Likewise the apostle Jude says:

“Certain men have slipped in unnoticed, who long ago were designated for this judgment as ungodly, transferring the grace of our Lord into sensuality, and denying the only Master and our Lord Jesus Christ” (Jude 4).

And in the Gospel the Lord says to sinners:

“Depart into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 34).

But to the predestined he says:

[Col. 1549D] “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid., verse 41)—that is, predestined.

This rule of our discussion, therefore, must be held firmly and without wavering: it is made clear by the testimonies of Scripture that sinners, in their own evils, were foreknown before they existed in the world, but not predestined; whereas punishment was predestined for them according to the condition in which they were foreknown.

Infants who have not been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit are likewise subject to predestined punishment. They were foreknown, not through their own wills—for they possess no wills that are either good or evil—but only in Adam’s sin, which they drew with them at birth and in which they remained until they completed the term of their present life.

[Col. 1550A] For anyone who believes with pure faith, when the Lord says, “Whoever does not eat my flesh and drink my blood will not have life within himself” (John VI, 54), understands what justice does with those whom mercy does not assist and withdraws from contention.

But concerning those who live according to God’s purpose, it must be said without hesitation that they were foreknown and predestined by the election of his gratuitous grace, and that the kingdom of heaven was predestined for them. The Apostle proves this when he testifies that they were predestined and elected before the foundation of the world.

Writing to the Ephesians, he says:

“Just as he chose us in him”—that is, in Christ—“before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and blameless in his sight; he predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ in himself” (Eph. I, 4).

[Col. 1550B] Let the human tongue be silent, and let it not exalt itself at all over merits in the matter of predestination. Let it attend to the words, “before the foundation of the world.” This gift belongs to the divine will, not to the merit of human weakness.

Finally, consider what follows:

“In him,” he says, “we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which has abounded toward us in all wisdom and prudence, making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, those in heaven and those on earth, in him. In him we too have been called by lot, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to his will, so that we may be [Col. 1550C] to the praise of his glory—we who first hoped in Christ” (ibid., verses 7–12).

Hear the words, “according to the riches of his grace, which has abounded toward us”—that is, which went before us. For what purpose? Namely, so that he might make known to us the mystery of his will. Is it my will, or yours, or someone else’s, so that it might rest on merits? Far from it. It is his will, which also prepares works of good will in those whom he has predestined, so that they may walk in them.

Accordingly, he says in the same Epistle:

“For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves. It is God’s gift, not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them” (Eph. II, 8–10).

Hear the words, “in good works which God prepared.” [Col. 1550D] And if you see that you are able to do anything good, give thanks to the one who prepares what you are able to do; do not give thanks to your own will, which without him can do absolutely nothing—he who says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5).

Therefore, do not think that by saying these and similar things we abolish freedom of the will, although it is nevertheless clear that what we say rests upon divine authority—or, as you accuse us, that we prevent those intent on doing good and diligent in God’s purpose.

Rather, we exhort those who recognize that through the gift of grace they belong to God’s mercy to devote themselves diligently to prayers, fasts, vigils, and every work of the divine will.

For the Apostle says this to the predestined, although what is said to him by Christ is general—Christ [Col. 1551A] predestined according to the flesh from the seed of David, but himself predestining according to the power of God the Father, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit:

“Watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation” (Matt. XXVI, 41).

Likewise:

“Watch at all times, praying that you may be considered worthy to escape all these things that are to come, and to stand before the Son of Man” (Luke XXI, 36).

Likewise:

“Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke XIII, 24).

Likewise:

“You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John XV, 14).

And there are many other passages that it would take too long to recount.

But, as I recalled above, he who said to them, “Without me you can do nothing” (ibid. XV, 5), enables them through himself to do what is commanded.

The Apostle says that God’s elect are of this kind in Christ:

“In whom you also have been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things” (Eph. I, 11).

[Col. 1551B] Understand the words, “who works all things,” and believe that the works of those who walk according to his purpose are God’s work.

Therefore, those who are without the grace of predestination—that is, strangers to God’s purpose—and who persist in evil works, even if they have departed from this life, we do not say, as you suppose, that God, the maker of all things, ordered them to perish, as though he himself had created their evil character and himself compelled them unwillingly toward every work of death.

Far be this from the divine purpose. For God is not willing iniquity; he commanded no one to act impiously, nor did he give anyone permission to sin. He made all things to exist, and the nations of the world to be healable; but through the devil’s envy death entered the world. [Col. 1551C] Those who belong in part to the devil imitate him.

Nor do we say, as you invent, that even if they wish to believe or to devote themselves to God’s good works, God does not wish to grant these things to them, since such willing is itself God’s gift. If what they will is from God, God wills that what he has granted should be brought to perfection. But if it is not from God, but arises from the boasting of their own will—if they think that by their merits they can win God’s favor—they plainly cannot attain what they will, because, as the Apostle says, it is “not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX, 16). And a human being cannot do anything from himself unless it has been given to him from above.

The supremely good God does not bring this about through malice, but through justice—not by respecting persons, but by distinguishing hidden causes.

[Col. 1551D] We know that at times some people wish to receive faith in eternal life and to attain it, while others do not. We know also that some unwilling people attain it, when divine grace changes their will so that they become willing. We know that some who had become perfect through the labor of many years have fallen at the end of their life and perished, while others have persisted in every crime and damnable conduct from their earliest age into extreme old age, and then, suddenly seized by salvation inspired from heaven, have been carried away to the rest of the heavenly kingdom.

We also know that infants, who do not possess the use of free will by which we might judge their merits, whether good or evil, have been carried by their parents’ hands to the grace of holy baptism; and while in the case of one of them the mystery of faith was being completed through the hands of the priest, on several occasions another, still in its parents’ hands, became lifeless and was deprived of the grace of the Savior.

[Col. 1552A] Who is wise enough to understand these things, or who will be capable of giving an account of them?

Let us say with David:

“The Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works” (Ps. CXLIV, 17);

and:

“How greatly your works have been magnified, O Lord! Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep” (Ps. XCI, 6).

Let us also say with the apostle Paul:

“O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. XI, 33).

But if, even after an explanation has been given, you still wish to be contentious and refuse to submit to the truth, cease accusing us as though we thought wrongly of the just and most merciful God. Rather, accuse the Lord Christ himself, whose Gospel we follow, if you dare. [Col. 1552B] Quarrel with him; engage him in dispute; accuse him—God forbid—of having thought wrongly about God his Father, since he says:

“Many are called, but few are elect” (Matt. XX, 16);

and:

“No one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John VI, 66);

and:

“Not all receive this word, but those to whom it has been given” (Matt. XIX, 11).

There are very many other passages as well.

“You will say, then, that what the Apostle says is false: ‘He wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of his truth’” (I Tim. II, 4).

It is certainly not false, because God can do everything he wills, and human will cannot in any way prevent what he wills. But I ask you to say why God, who wills all human beings to be saved, blinds the eyes of some, as the prophet Isaiah says (Isa. VI, 10), so that they may not see; hardens their hearts [Col. 1552C] so that they may not understand; and prevents them from turning and being healed.

The evangelist John confirms that this is true when he says concerning the Jews:

“For this reason they could not believe, because Isaiah said: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they would not see with their eyes, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them’” (John XII, 40).

Likewise, in the Gospel according to Mark, when the disciples questioned Jesus about the parable of the seed, he said:

“To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to those who are outside, everything is presented in parables, so that, seeing, they may not see, and hearing, they may not understand, lest they should ever turn and their sins be forgiven” (Mark IV, 11).

[Col. 1552D] Tell us, then, why God, who is not a respecter of persons and wills all human beings to be saved, opens the hearts of some for believing, illuminates their eyes for seeing and for knowing the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, by which they may be saved; while, as the text of the reading says, he veils the truth from others in parables, dulls their hearts, blinds their eyes, and closes their ears, so that they may not recognize the Gospel of salvation or receive forgiveness of sins?

Tell us, I beg you, how you understand these passages of the Gospel. Teach us what you think here about God, who wills all human beings to be saved.

Behold, then, they are not all saved in a general sense, since some are granted knowledge of the way of salvation and others are not. Therefore, when God does these things, he does not do them by respecting persons, nor through injustice, but through ineffable justice and undeserved mercy.

[Col. 1553A] Since we are plainly unable to say anything definitive about either side of this matter, let us believe only that the person guilty of death depends upon the judge’s will.

But lest anyone think that it is not by divine judgment that all human beings are not saved, the Apostle said: “He wills all to be saved” (I Tim. II, 4). Therefore, all human beings who are saved are saved by God’s will. For our God is the God who saves, and the Lord’s are the ways out of death. And because “there is wrath in his anger, and life in his will,” understand that justice is in his anger and mercy in his will.

To deny predestination, which we have proved exists with God, is therefore a monstrous blasphemy. We must not understand it, as you are accustomed to say, as applying only to the apostles, but also to the patriarchs, prophets, martyrs, confessors, and all the saints and those who serve God worthily.

[Col. 1553B] Let no one boast on this account; let no one despair. For the Lord alone knows who are his. But insofar as we are able, let us exhort all people to good works; let us give no one cause for despair; let us pray for one another; and let us humble ourselves before God, saying: “Your will be done.”

It belongs to his power to change the judgment due to us of condemnation and to bestow the undeserved grace of predestination.

Behold, beloved brother, you have what you requested: the understanding of the orthodox and catholic Fathers, briefly arranged in a single little book, concerning foreknowledge and predestination, grace and free will.

It remains for you to believe and confess—or rather, with firm faith and sound doctrine, to preach to others so that they may believe and understand—that God foreknew that the good and the wicked would come to be. He predestined the good only so that they might receive eternal life; but he merely foreknew that [Col. 1553C] the wicked would perish eternally—he did not predestine them to perish.

As for God’s grace, all who would be saved attain salvation through it. As for free will, which had been corrupted by the fall of the first human being: when divine goodness chooses to govern it according to its own pleasure, it can earn an everlasting reward. But when a human being abuses it through pride, it is worthy not of glory but of everlasting punishment.

No one ought to scrutinize God’s hidden and secret matters, which are open only to divine knowledge, lest, wishing to know more than one ought to know, they fall into everlasting destruction by pursuing falsehood instead of truth and the greatest error instead of the right faith.

## LETTER VI. TO COUNT HEBERARD

[From Sirmond.]

To the most reverend and highly approved man, Count HEBERARD, RABANUS, the most unworthy of the servants of Christ, sends greetings.

Our brothers, the priests Ascrihus and Hudpertus, who recently traveled to Rome, reported to us your good health and the kindness that you customarily show not only toward them but also toward many others. I confess that I rejoiced greatly, and, giving thanks to almighty God for this, I prayed that he who began the good work in you might bring it to completion until the day of Jesus Christ, so that by God’s grace you might be deemed worthy to receive the full reward for your good works [Col. 1554A] in the life to come.

And because our aforementioned brothers reported to us that you had requested our little work composed some time ago in praise of the cross of Christ, asking at your word that I send it to you, I willingly did what they requested. Last year, through the messenger Gagauzardus, who came to us and made the same request, I sent the work to you. I ask that you keep it, have it read before you, and, if you find anything in it worthy and pleasing to you, attribute it to divine grace, not to human skill. But if you find anything otherwise in it, attribute it rather to my ignorance and human frailty than to malice. For, insofar as by God’s gift I understand and am able, I desire to offer agreeable service to Christ’s servants and to those who fear and love the Lord, [Col. 1554B] so that they may pray for me, asking that the most merciful Judge of all the ages grant me forgiveness of my sins and bestow eternal life upon me.

Furthermore, because it is known to have been widely reported in these regions that a certain sophist named Gottschalk is staying with you, who teaches that God’s predestination so constrains every human being that, even if someone wishes to be saved and strives for this with right faith and good works in order to attain eternal life through God’s grace, he labors in vain and without result if he has not been predestined to life—as though God, by his predestination, compelled a person to perish, although he is the author of our salvation, not of our destruction.

This sect has already driven many here into despair concerning themselves, so that they say: “Why must I labor for my salvation [Col. 1554C] and eternal life? For if I do good and am not predestined to life, it profits me nothing; but if I do evil, it harms me nothing, because God’s predestination causes me to attain eternal life.” This teaching is a scandal to many in these regions and makes people disobedient to the preachers of the Gospel, because it has caused them to despair of themselves.

It is said that your teacher himself has excerpted many testimonies from the works of the most blessed and learned Father Augustine, by which he endeavors to affirm his own opinion. Yet that same Father and catholic teacher, writing against the Pelagians, who were preachers opposed to God’s grace, was a defender of that grace, not a destroyer of right faith. For, writing to Prosper and Hilary and discussing predestination [Col. 1554D] and foreknowledge in the following manner, he says (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, ch. 10):

> “Predestination is something that cannot exist without foreknowledge; foreknowledge, however, can exist without predestination. For by predestination God foreknew those things which he himself was going to do; hence it is said: ‘He made the things that are to come.’ But he can also foreknow things that he himself does not do, such as sins—for although there are certain things that are sins in such a way that they are also punishments of sins, as it is said: ‘God handed them over to a reprobate mind, so that they might do things that are not fitting’ (Rom. 1:28), the sin there is not God’s, but his judgment. Therefore God’s predestination, which concerns what is good, is the preparation of grace. Grace, however, is the effect of predestination itself.”

[Col. 1555A] Saint Jerome agrees with this Father. In his exposition of Ezekiel, he explains the statement in which the Lord says to the prophet: “Speak and say to them: Thus says the Lord God: If perhaps they themselves will hear, and if perhaps they will desist, for they are an embittering house.”

God speaks in this manner with the disposition of one who leaves the matter open, in order to show the freedom of the human will, so that foreknowledge of future evil or good may not make immutable what God knows will happen. For it is not because he knows that those things will come to pass that we must do what he has foreknown; rather, as God, he knows beforehand what we are going to do by our own will.

The aforementioned Father Augustine also wrote two books *On the Predestination of the Saints*, in which he most wisely demonstrates from passages of Holy Scripture that everything good bestowed upon a human being comes from God’s grace, not from human [Col. 1555B] free will. But there were some who, either because they did not understand what was rightly written there or because they did not wish to understand it, attempted to lead it into a perverse interpretation.

Against them blessed Prosper, who was a faithful executor of Augustine’s teaching, resisted most vigorously in his replies and convicted them of having formed an incorrect opinion of that teacher of the holy Church. For the aforementioned man, blessed Prosper, wrote to Rufinus on grace and free will; he wrote against the chapters of the Gallic calumniators concerning predestination; likewise against the chapters of the Vincentian objections concerning the same predestination; and he also gave a most appropriate response to the excerpts on predestination that had been sent to him from the city of Genoa. In all these works [Col. 1555C] a faithful reader can establish that he understood God’s predestination to be made for the salvation of the human race, not for its condemnation.

Accordingly, it has pleased us now to excerpt some passages from the writings of this aforementioned man and place them in this letter. To the Vincentian objections he responded as follows (*Vincentian Objections*, 11):

> “How can it be established as true that God does not wish all to be saved, even if all wish to be saved, when the Truth says: ‘If you, though evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him?’
>
> “How can it be that God, who even saves those of whom it cannot be said that they wish to be saved, does not wish to save some even if they wish to be saved—unless there are certain reasons which, although they are unknowable to us, [Col. 1555D] he nevertheless judges rightly, since it cannot be said that he ought to have done anything other than what he did?
>
> “Once this discrimination, which divine knowledge holds hidden within the secrecy of its justice, has been set aside, we must sincerely believe and confess that God wishes all human beings to be saved. For the Apostle, whose statement this is, most earnestly commands—and this is devoutly observed in all the churches—that supplication be made to God for all human beings. Of these, the fact that many perish is the merit of those who perish; the fact that many are saved is the gift of the one who saves. For the condemnation of the guilty displays the blamelessness of God’s justice; the justification of the guilty is the ineffable grace of God.”

(*Objection* 4.)

> “They also say that the greater part of the human race [Col. 1556A] was created by God for the purpose of doing not God’s will but the devil’s. It is altogether insane and contrary to reason to say that God’s will does not come about from God’s will, and that God—the condemner of the devil and his servants—wishes the devil to be served.
>
> “But the Pelagians think that they can consistently raise this objection against Catholics, because they deny that Adam’s sin has passed into all. For if original guilt does not bind a person from his first birth, infants are not subject to the devil and do not need to be rescued from the power of darkness, since they have never departed from their own author.
>
> “We, however, who confess that all perished in Adam—for the Son came to seek and save what had perished—do not say that anyone is created for the purpose of doing the devil’s will. We acknowledge that every unredeemed [Col. 1556B] human being is held captive by the devil. The human transgression, however, could not disturb the order of creation established from the ages; and rightly the sinful creature suffers the punitive domination of the one to whom, having abandoned the true Lord, it willingly sold itself.”

(*Objections* 7, 8, 9, 10.)

> “This slavery is not God’s institution but his judgment. Those who say that it is God’s will that a large part of Christians neither wish nor are able to be saved; or that God does not wish all Catholics to persevere in the Catholic faith, but wishes a large part of them to apostatize or fall from their purpose of holiness; or that the adulteries of married women and the corruption of consecrated virgins occur because God predestined them to fall—these people think most perversely and speak wickedly.
>
> “For it is a detestable [Col. 1556C] and abominable opinion to believe that God is the author of anyone’s evil will or evil action. His predestination is never outside goodness, never outside justice. ‘All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.’
>
> “That Divinity does not know how to institute the adulteries of married women and the corruption of virgins, but to condemn them; not to ordain them, but to punish them. When human beings commit such evils, they serve their own lusts and desires, which they have drawn from that first stain of voluntary transgression.”

Yet it must in no way be believed that such people fell into this despair by God’s will, since the Lord rather lifts up all who fall and raises all who are bowed down. No one is established except by his grace. It is therefore God’s will [Col. 1556D] that they remain in a good will, and he abandons no one before being abandoned.

In the little book that the aforementioned man wrote against the chapters of the Gallic calumniators, he appended the following near the end of the work:

(*Sent.* 1.)

> “Whoever, therefore, says that human beings are driven into sins by God’s predestination as though by a fatal necessity and thus compelled to death is not a Catholic. For God’s predestination in no way makes human beings wicked, nor is it the cause of anyone’s sin.”

(*Sent.* 2.)

> “Whoever says that, among those who are not predestined to life, original sin is not removed by the grace received in baptism is not a Catholic. For the sacrament of baptism, by which all sins whatsoever are blotted out, is true even in those who will not remain in the truth [Col. 1557A] and therefore are not predestined to true life.”

(*Sent.* 3.)

> “Whoever says that those who are not predestined to life, even if they have been regenerated in Christ through baptism and have lived piously and justly, gain no benefit from this, but are preserved only until they fall, and are not taken from this life before that happens—as though the fall of such people were to be attributed to God’s decree—is not a Catholic. For God did not prolong anyone’s period of life so that, by living long, he might fall and fail in the true faith through his longevity, since longevity itself is to be counted among God’s benefits, by which a person ought to have become better, not worse.”

(*Sent.* 4.)

> “Whoever says that not all are called to grace—if he is speaking of those to whom Christ has not been announced—should [Col. 1557B] not be blamed. For we certainly know that the Gospel has been destined for all the ends of the earth, but we do not suppose that it has already been preached in every part of the earth. Nor can we say that the call of grace exists where there has as yet been no regeneration through the mother Church.”

(*Sent.* 5.)

> “Whoever says that those who were called were not called equally, but that some were called in order to believe and others in order not to believe—as though the call were a cause for anyone not to believe—does not speak rightly. For although faith comes only from God’s gift and the human will, unbelief comes only from the human will.”

(*Sent.* 6.)

> “Whoever says that free will is nothing in a human being, but that God’s predestination operates in human beings either toward good or toward evil, is not a Catholic. For God’s grace does not abolish human [Col. 1557C] choice but cultivates it; it recalls and leads it back from error into the way, so that what was perverse through its own freedom becomes upright through the action of God’s Spirit.
>
> “God’s predestination is also always directed toward what is good. It knows the sin committed solely by the human will either to be forgiven with praise of mercy or punished with praise of justice.”

(*Sent.* 7.)

> “Whoever says that God did not give perseverance to certain of his children whom he regenerated in Christ and to whom he gave faith, hope, and love, because by God’s foreknowledge and predestination they were not separated from the mass of perdition—if he intends to affirm that God did not wish such people to remain in the good things he had given them, and that he himself was the cause of their [Col. 1557D] turning away—has an opinion contrary to God’s justice.
>
> “Although God’s omnipotence could have supplied the strength to stand to those who were going to fall, his grace nevertheless did not abandon them before they abandoned it. And because he foresaw that they would make this defection voluntarily, he did not include them in the choice of predestination.”

(*Sent.* 8.)

> “Whoever says that God does not wish all human beings to be saved, but only a definite number of the predestined, speaks more harshly than one ought to speak about the height of God’s inscrutable grace. For he both wishes all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, and he fulfills the purpose of his will in those whom he foreknew and predestined, predestined and called, called and justified, justified and glorified.
>
> “He omits nothing of the fullness of the Gentiles and of all Israel’s offspring, for whom an eternal kingdom was prepared [Col. 1558A] in Christ before the foundation of the world. For from the whole world the whole world is chosen, and from all human beings all human beings are adopted.
>
> “Nor can God’s promise waver in any way because of the unbelief and disobedience of many—the promise he made to Abraham: ‘In your seed all nations shall be blessed.’ What he has promised, he is powerful enough to accomplish, so that those who are saved are saved because the Lord wished to save them, while those who perish perish because they deserved to perish.”

(*To the Genoese Excerpts*, 6.)

> “When the Apostle says, ‘For faith is not possessed by all,’ the believer should not be troubled by the question of why faith is not given to all. He believes without doubt that all proceeded from one person into a [Col. 1558B] condemnation that was entirely just, so that there would have been no just reproach against God even if no one had been delivered from it.
>
> “Hence it is clear that great is the grace by which many are delivered, and that those who are not delivered should recognize what was owed to them, so that those who boast may boast not in their own merits—which they see to be equal to those of the condemned—but in the Lord.
>
> “Why he delivers one person rather than another—his judgments are inscrutable and his ways unsearchable.”

(*Objection of the Gauls*, 8.)

> “Why, in past ages, did God allow all the nations to walk in their own ways, when the Lord chose Jacob for himself and did not deal similarly with every nation, nor manifest his judgments to them? Why was one who had once been called ‘not a people’ now called the people of God; why did he now show mercy to those on whom he had once not had mercy; and where it was said, ‘You are [Col. 1558C] not my people,’ why were they there called children of the living God? Why did Israel fail to obtain what it sought, while the elect obtained it and the rest were hardened? This is impossible to comprehend, and it is dangerous curiosity to inquire into it.
>
> “Nevertheless, no one may be permitted to remain ignorant that there is no iniquity with God. Nor should it be believed that anyone, whether before the Law or during the time of the Law, was justified by any other grace or faith than this same grace and faith, by which our Lord Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will, came at the end of the ages to seek and save what had perished.
>
> “But whoever refers the causes of God’s works and judgments entirely to human wills and actions, although he finds no such causes in the adoption [Col. 1558D] or rejection of infants; whoever wishes God’s dispensations to vary according to the mutability of free will—such a person declares God’s judgments to be searchable and his ways traceable, and thinks that he can proclaim as disclosed what Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, did not dare to touch.”

(*Sent.* 9.)

> “Whoever says that the Savior was not crucified for the redemption of the whole world looks not to the power of the sacrament but to the portion of the faithful, although Christ’s blood is the price of the whole world. Those who are excluded from that price are those who either, delighting in captivity, did not wish to be redeemed, or returned to the same slavery after redemption.
>
> “The word of the Lord has not failed, nor has the redemption of the world been made void. For although the world did not know God in the vessels of wrath, the world nevertheless knew God in the vessels of mercy, [Col. 1559A] which God, with none of their merits preceding, rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of his beloved Son.”

(*Sent.* 10.)

> “Whoever says that the preaching of the Gospel is withheld by the Lord from certain people so that they may not be saved after receiving the preaching of the Gospel can avoid the reproach of this objection by appealing to the Savior himself. He did not wish to perform signs among certain people whom he said would have believed if they had seen his miraculous signs; he forbade the apostles to preach the Gospel to certain peoples; and even now he allows certain nations to live outside his grace.
>
> “Nevertheless, we have received with the firmest faith that the Church is to be extended through all parts of the world, and that this age will not end before the Gospel is directed to all the ends of the earth and every [Col. 1559B] tongue confesses that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father.”

(*Sent.* 11.)

> “Whoever says that God compels human beings to sin is rightly condemned. For God, who is the author of justice and goodness and whose statutes and commandments are all directed against sin, must not be believed to compel anyone to sin or to drive anyone from innocence into crimes.
>
> “If some people are of such profound impiety that they are considered beyond the remedy of correction, they do not receive an increase of wickedness from God. Rather, they become worse through themselves. Because of their preceding sins, they deserved to be abandoned by God and handed over to themselves and to their deceivers, so that sin itself became for them the punishment of sin.”

(*Sent.* 12.)

> “Whoever says that obedience is withdrawn from certain people who have been called and who live piously and [Col. 1559C] justly, so that they cease to obey, forms a bad opinion of God’s goodness and justice—as though he compelled the pious to impiety and took innocence away from the good, although he himself is the giver and guardian of piety and innocence.
>
> “Whoever therefore adheres to God is moved by God’s Spirit; whoever withdraws from God ceases to obey through his own will.”

(*Sent.* 13.)

> “Whoever says that certain human beings were not created by God for the purpose of attaining eternal life, but only to adorn the condition of the present age and to be born for the benefit of others, would speak better if he said that God, who is the creator of all things, does not create even those whom he foresees will not become participants in eternal life without purpose. For even in wicked people, nature itself [Col. 1559D] is God’s good work, and justice is praiseworthy in the condemnation of the impious.
>
> “Nor can the person who says that the world is adorned even by the condition of such people rightly be reproached, or that those who will harm themselves by their own wickedness are born for the benefit of others. For no innumerable multitude of the impious is disgraceful to the world or useless to God’s kingdom, since even through their offspring a generation destined for regeneration comes forth, and through the toleration and love of them God’s people become more illustrious, learning goodness and patience from the one who makes his rain fall upon the just and the unjust and causes his sun to rise upon the good and the evil.”

(*Sent.* 14.)

> “Whoever says that those who do not believe the preaching of the Gospel do not believe by God’s predestination, and that God [Col. 1560A] has determined that whoever does not believe should not believe by his own decree, is not a Catholic. For just as faith, which works through love, is God’s gift, so unbelief is not God’s decree, because God knows how to ordain punishments for crimes, not crimes themselves.
>
> “Nor does it follow that what he has not forgiven he himself committed. The predestined person therefore lives by the faith given to him; the non-predestined perishes through voluntary, not compelled, unbelief.”

(*Sent.* 15.)

> “Whoever says that foreknowledge and predestination are the same undoubtedly mixes these two things together in our good works. For what we possess from God’s gift, and what is called foreknown, cannot fail to be predestined; and what is called predestined cannot fail to be foreknown.
>
> “But in our evil works only God’s [Col. 1560B] foreknowledge is to be understood. For just as he foreknew and predestined what he himself does, and gave us the ability to do it, so he merely foreknew—but did not also predestine—what he neither himself did nor required us to do.”

Since all these matters have thus been established from the sacred teachers and demonstrated in their various works in different styles but with no different faith, it seems good to me that recent teachers should follow the footsteps of the holy Fathers and catholic teachers, rather than depart from the straight path of their tradition and fall into the byways of error. For, as Holy Scripture says, those who wish to attain eternal life must walk along the royal road and must not rashly turn aside either to the right or to the left. Just as the straight way leads to life, so the byways of error tend toward [Col. 1560C] everlasting death.

Therefore the prophet prays to the Lord, saying:

> “Lead me, Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth.” (Ps. 85:11.)

And again:

> “Lead me, Lord, in the straight path, because of my enemies.” (Ps. 26:11.)

And again:

> “Remove from me the way of iniquity, and in your law have mercy on me. I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments.” (Ps. 18:29–30.)

What this straight way and way of truth is, Truth himself shows in the Gospel, saying:

> “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” (John 14:6.)

> “Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” (John 8:12.)

And elsewhere:

> “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved; he will go in and out and find pasture.” [Col. 1560D] (John 10:9.)

But the person who says that, just as piety, chastity, charity, and the other virtues are to be preached, so predestination must be preached, so that whoever hears these things obediently may glory not in a human being—and therefore not in himself—but in the Lord, speaks rightly, provided that he moderates his preaching with discretion according to the character of his listeners, lest a weak hearer take scandal from the very thing from which he ought to have drawn life.

In investigating and meditating upon the sacred Scriptures, a reader ought to act cautiously and prudently, lest he wish to be wiser than he ought to be, but rather possess sober wisdom and act according to the rule of faith. Hence Wisdom also teaches through parables, saying:

> “You have found honey; eat what is sufficient for you, lest, having been filled, [Col. 1561A] you vomit it up and profane the name of God.” (Prov. 25:16.)

Likewise, one who teaches another must moderate his doctrinal discourse in such a way that the hearer hears the truth and understands what he hears. Thus he preserves the apostolic pattern in teaching. The Apostle says to certain of his hearers:

> “I could not speak to you, brothers, as spiritual people, but as carnal—as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not solid food. For you were not yet able, nor indeed are you able even now. We speak wisdom among the mature: wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing; but we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the wisdom hidden, which God predestined before the ages for our glory.” (1 Cor. 3:1ff.)

Hence the same [Col. 1561B] Apostle elsewhere exhorts us, saying:

> “Let everything of yours be done for edification, and let everything be done decently and according to order.” (1 Cor. 14:40.)

For this reason one of the teachers most rightly says: “It is the mark of a deceitful or incompetent physician to bind even a useful medicine in such a way that it cannot be undone by skill.”

Therefore in the old Law the Lord commands through Moses:

> “If someone opens a cistern, or digs one and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it, the owner of the cistern shall repay the price of the animals.” (Exod. 21:33.)

Blessed Gregory explains the mystery of this figure as follows (*Moralia* 27.14):

> “What does ‘to open a cistern’ mean except to penetrate the secrets of Scripture with a powerful intellect? What is signified by the ox and the donkey—that is, by the clean and unclean animal—except the faithful and the unbeliever? [Col. 1561C]
>
> “Therefore let the one who digs a cistern cover it, lest an ox or a donkey fall into it. That is, whoever already understands lofty meanings in sacred discourse should conceal sublime senses through silence from those who cannot grasp them, lest through the scandal of the mind he destroy either a faithful little one or an unbeliever who might have been able to believe.
>
> “For the death of the animals entails a price for the one who is convicted of having allowed what makes him liable to punishment and obligated to do penance. Whoever reaches the deep waters of knowledge but fails to veil these things from the brutish hearts of his hearers becomes liable to punishment if, through his words, either a pure or an impure mind is caught in scandal.
>
> “The cistern must therefore be covered, because profound knowledge must be veiled before [Col. 1562A] childish minds, lest, from the very point at which the heart of the teachers is lifted toward the heights, the weakness of the hearers should descend into the depths.”

We cannot all do everything. Each of us has his own gift from God: one in this way, another in that. Therefore the Savior, divinely perceiving the weakness of his disciples for this purpose, says to them in the Gospel:

> “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will teach you,” and so forth. (John 16:12.)

If our Lord considered the capacity of his hearers, who are we to think that everything must be preached to everyone equally? Especially since the Lord himself says:

> “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble,” and so forth.

[Col. 1562B] An unwise physician is one who prepares his poultice in such a way that, when applied, it harms the sick person more than it benefits him. A wise physician first examines the nature of the illness and then, carefully adjusting the treatment to the character of the disease, applies the medicine of salvation.

I have therefore written these things to you, dearest friend, so that you might understand what kind of scandal the opinion coming from those regions has generated among this people. If anyone staying with you teaches things contrary to right faith, restrain him so that he may cease from this sect, and say to him: “Look, brother, lest your license in preaching become an occasion of offense to the weak; and by your doctrine do not destroy the one for whom Christ died, for his blood will be required at your hand.”

For I am confident, venerable sir, that you are a good Christian and do not wish to [Col. 1562C] have in your household anything opposed to Christ’s Gospel, but rather whatever pleases God and pertains to the salvation of souls. In this will and devotion may the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ deign to preserve you safe forever.

## Letter VII. To Louis, King of Germany

He sends the acts [Note: [Col. 1561D] The occasion for celebrating this council was the same as that of the council of Meaux: namely, because laymen were continually invading the property of the churches, as well as their rights and persons, and frequent complaints concerning these matters were being made before the king. He therefore caused a provincial synod to be assembled to free the Church from these evils. Rabanus, archbishop, a man highly distinguished for learning, uprightness, and knowledge, was to preside over it.

Which and how many bishops attended this council, what they discussed, and what they determined should be observed through its canons, the synodal letter—which was sent to Louis, king of Germany, together with the chapters appended below—makes sufficiently clear.

The following also pertains to this council. The Frankish annals, in their account under the specified year, report the following concerning a woman who boasted that she was a new prophetess and usurped the office of publicly teaching and preaching:

> “In the same year, 847, a certain woman from the regions of Germany, named Thiota, a false prophetess, came to Mainz and greatly disturbed the parish of Bishop Salomo. For she professed that she knew, as though divinely revealed to her, the certain day of the consummation of the age and many other things known only to God; and in that same year she preached that the final day of the world was imminent.
>
> “Consequently, many common people of both sexes, struck with fear, came to her, brought her gifts, and commended themselves to her prayers. What is more serious, men of the sacred order, setting aside ecclesiastical teaching, followed her as though she had been appointed from heaven as a teacher.
>
> “She was brought before the bishops at Saint Alban’s and carefully questioned about her assertions. She confessed that a certain priest had suggested these things to her and that she had related them for the sake of profit. Therefore, by synodal judgment, after being publicly beaten with whips, she disgracefully lost the ministry of preaching, which she had irrationally seized and presumed to claim for herself contrary to ecclesiastical custom; and at last, confounded by her prophecies, she brought them to an end.”

SEV. BIN.]

Of the Mainz council, held for the rights and immunities of the churches, with Rabanus himself presiding, in the year of the Lord 847, in the time of Pope Leo IV and Emperor Lothair.

(From Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XIV, p. 900.)

To the most serene and most Christian king Louis, the most vigorous ruler of the true religion and defender of God’s holy Church, together with his wife and offspring and his faithful people: life and salvation, honor and blessing, with victory destined to endure forever.

We, your most humble servants—namely Rabanus, unworthy archbishop of the Church of Mainz, together with my fellow bishops who belong to the diocese of that Church, namely Samuel, Egorbold, Baturat, Hebo, Gorbrath, Hemmo, Waltgar, Ansgar, Otgar, Lanto, Solomon, and Gebehard, together with the rest of our colleagues, the chorepiscopi, abbots, monks, priests, and the other ecclesiastical orders—have made known to your most worthy reverence that we came, according to your command, to the city of Mainz. There, assembled together [Col. 1563B], after a three-day fast, which we observed with litanies while humbly imploring the divine mercy that by his holy grace he might deign to make the gathering and proceedings of this synod acceptable to him, beneficial to the Christian people for salvation and eternal life, and to you for everlasting honor and glory, we decreed that in each parish prayers should be offered by the bishops and clergy, by the abbots and monks, for you and for your wife, together with your most noble offspring. The total of these prayers was three thousand five hundred Masses and one thousand seven hundred psalters.

With all devotion we asked that almighty God grant you lasting health and prosperity, establish your kingdom for a long time, defended on earth from every enemy [Col. 1563C], and, after the end of this life, grant you everlasting glory in the heavenly kingdom together with his saints.

Then, sitting in the cloister of Saint Alban the martyr, according to the custom by which in former times, under the emperor Charles, Hildebold and Richolf, together with the other bishops and abbots who had assembled there, had proceeded, we began in God’s name, with common agreement and consent, to deliberate together about the condition of true religion and the well-being and progress of the Christian people.

We agreed among ourselves, in our common college of clerics and monks, to form two groups, as we indeed did. In one group the bishops sat with certain notaries, reading and examining the holy Gospel, as well as the Epistles and Acts of the Apostles, the canons [Col. 1563D], and various works of the holy Fathers, together with the other sacred teachings. With diligent care they sought to determine by what means, with God’s gracious assistance, they could establish and preserve the condition of the Church of God and the progress of the Christian people, secure in sound doctrine and examples of justice.

In the other group the abbots and approved monks sat, reading the Rule of Saint Benedict and carefully discussing how, with God’s grace, they might bring the life of monks to a better condition and greater flourishing, and how, wherever the regular order had fallen into decline through the negligence and sloth of its rulers, it might again be completely restored according to the norm of the Rule of Saint Benedict.

When these matters had thus been arranged and completed [Col. 1564A], we first decreed that fitting honor should be shown to every person and sex, according to the words of Saint Peter, the first shepherd of the Church:

> “Honor everyone, love the brotherhood, fear God, honor the king. Servants, be subject with all fear to your masters, not only to the good and gentle but also to the harsh; for this is grace in Christ Jesus our Lord” (I Peter II).

The teacher of the nations, writing similarly to his disciple Timothy, says:

> “Pay attention to yourself and to your teaching; persist in them, for by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you. Do not rebuke an older man, but entreat him as a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters, in all chastity” (I Timothy IV).

Moreover, it seemed fitting that priests and the churches of God should be honored by lawful and inviolable right. Concerning them the Lord says:

> “Whoever hears you hears me; whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me” (Luke X; Matthew X).

And the Apostle says to the Hebrews:

> “Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over your souls as those who will have to give an account” (Hebrews XIII).

Regarding reverence for churches, the Lord says:

> “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations” (Isaiah LVI).

It is also read in the Gospel (Mark XI; John II) that when the Lord himself came to Jerusalem and entered the Temple, he made something like a whip from cords and drove out all those who were carrying on earthly business there, engaging in illicit buying and selling [Col. 1564C].

Alas, in these times neither are holy places revered nor are God’s ministers honored as they ought to be. Instead, in an inversion of the proper order, those who ought to be honored are beaten, stripped, and crushed by various accusations.

Therefore great necessity has compelled us to appeal to you on this matter and to ask that, just as the holy Church of God was honored under your predecessors, the kings and emperors who ruled before you, and just as ecclesiastical possessions remained secure through their immunities and continued to remain unharmed within them, so may they remain undefiled in your time.

You ought to defend the churches of Christ with zeal for God, since he has granted you a kingdom and dominion on earth. Do not allow your grant, which you bestowed upon the churches of Christ as your alms, to be altered through anyone’s wicked suggestions [Col. 1564D]. For it is disgraceful that what was granted to the honor of God—not only by Christians in Christian times and by Christian emperors, but also by pagan kings in the time of paganism—should in your time and within your kingdom be exchanged.

For we read in Ezra that King Artaxerxes commanded Ezra, the scribe of the law of God, by letter, saying:

> “I, King Artaxerxes, have established and decreed for all the keepers of the public treasury who are beyond the River: Whatever Ezra the priest, the scribe of the law of the God of heaven, requests from you—whatever pertains to the worship of the God of heaven—let it be carefully provided in the house of the God of heaven, lest anger arise against the kingdom of the king and his sons [Col. 1565A]. We also make known to you concerning all the priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, and ministers of this house of God, that you have no authority to impose tax, tribute, or provisions upon them. And you, Ezra, according to the wisdom of your God which is in your hand, appoint judges and magistrates, so that they may judge all the people who are beyond the River—namely, those who know the law of your God—and teach those who do not know it freely. Whoever does not carefully observe the law of your God and the law of the king, judgment shall be executed against him, whether unto death, exile, confiscation of his property, or imprisonment” (I Ezra VII).

As for Christian kings and emperors, it is not necessary to set forth examples [Col. 1565B], since all who have possessed right faith and sound doctrine, from the emperor Constantine—who was the first of the emperors to begin defending the Christian religion and enlarging the honor of the churches of God—down to you, have always labored diligently in this endeavor, so that the Church of God might have peace and tranquility, the worship of God might remain undefiled, and his servants might serve God delightfully and without hindrance.

What punishment is appropriate for those who, through greed, bring trouble upon the churches of Christ contrary to God’s commands and your order, we have demonstrated in what follows, at the proper place, through the canons of the holy Fathers and the teaching of the divine Scriptures.

Following the example of the Lord and Savior, we do not fear to impose suitable judgment upon corrupters of God’s temple and defilers of sacred places [Col. 1565C]. For if those who violated the holy place through earthly greed were driven out of the house of God by Christ the Lord, it is not unjust to impose canonical judgment upon the insolent and those unwilling to correct themselves, so that when corrected they may experience what, when gently admonished, they previously refused to perceive.

May almighty God strengthen you in his justice and protect you unharmed from every enemy.

## ARTICLES

### Chapter I—On the Catholic faith

We decreed that the beginning of our proceedings should concern the faith, which is the foundation of all good things. Although, as the Apostle says, “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews XI), faith nevertheless requires works, “for faith without works is dead” (James II).

Therefore blessed Gregory says: “That person truly believes who practices in action what he believes.” For this reason all Christians ought continually to admonish and teach one another concerning our faith, but the Lord’s priests especially ought to labor in this struggle so that it may be firmly held by everyone.

### Chapter II—On ecclesiastical doctrine

Since all the canonical councils that are received ought to be read and understood by priests, and since they ought to live and preach according to them, we considered it necessary that the passages relating to the faith, and those in which the uprooting of vices and the planting of virtues are discussed, should be frequently read and well understood by them, so that they may preach them to the people.

Every bishop [Note: [Col. 1565D] The text lacks *habeat* (“should have”) or something similar.] should have homilies containing the necessary admonitions by which those subject to him may be instructed: concerning the Catholic faith, according to what they are able to understand; concerning the everlasting recompense of the good and the eternal condemnation of the wicked; concerning the future resurrection and the last judgment; concerning the works by which blessed life may be merited and those by which it may be forfeited.

Each person should also make an effort to translate these homilies clearly into the rustic Roman language or into the Germanic language, so that everyone may more easily understand what is said.

### Chapter III—On the sacrament of baptism

We wish the sacraments of baptism to be celebrated and maintained continually, harmoniously and uniformly, in every parish according to the Roman order. This includes the scrutiny belonging to the order of baptism, as it is set forth in two chapters of the decrees of Pope Leo.

In chapter five:

> “These two seasons, namely Easter and Pentecost, have been lawfully appointed by the Roman pontiff for baptizing.”

Likewise, in chapter six:

> “Permission is not forbidden, since at whatever time those in danger are assisted by the administration of baptism.”

And Siricius says:

> “Whenever the sacred water of baptism is required in any necessity, we wish assistance to be provided with all speed” (Epistle I, to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona). [Note: [Col. 1566D] b Epistle 1, to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona.]

Therefore bishops ought to hand over the sacrament of baptism to their priests with great diligence, together with what is to be renounced and what is to be believed in it.

The devil and his works are renounced. The works of the devil are understood to be works of the flesh, namely murders, fornications, adulteries, drunkenness, and many other things like them. These are first conceived in the mind through the devil’s instigation before they are carried out in action.

His pomp consists in pride, boasting, arrogance, vainglory, haughtiness, and very many other things that appear to arise from these.

### Chapter IV—On peace and concord

It is certainly necessary that there be peace, concord, and unanimity among the Christian people, because we have one God the Father in heaven, one mother, the Church, one faith, and one baptism. Therefore we ought to live together in one peace and unanimity if we desire to reach the one true inheritance of the heavenly kingdom.

“For God is not a God of dissension but of peace” (II Corinthians XIV), as he himself says.

If peace and concord must therefore be maintained among all the faithful, as the Apostle says,

> “Pursue peace with everyone, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Hebrews XII),

then peace and concord ought all the more to exist between bishops and counts, who govern God’s people after the dignity of imperial office.

They ought to agree with one another in such a way that they not only do not harm one another in carrying out God’s service and rightly fulfilling their ministry, but rather assist one another [Col. 1567A].

### Chapter V—On conspiracy

If peace and concord are judged the greatest good among human beings, especially among Christians, and worthy of the highest reward—namely, that by their merit we may be called children of God (Matthew V)—then, conversely, discord and dissension are the greatest evil and deserving of the highest punishment.

Thus the wise man says that the Lord detests the person who sows discord among brothers (Proverbs VI), and therefore such a person is not undeservedly called a son of the devil.

Accordingly, we decree and confirm by ecclesiastical authority that those who form conspiracies and rebellious associations against the king, ecclesiastical dignities, or the lawful arrangements of the powers of the commonwealth established in each order, are to be removed from the communion and fellowship of Catholics who love true peace.

Unless they are incorporated into ecclesiastical peace through repentance and correction, we decree that they are to be exiled from all the children of peace.

[Note: [Col. 1567B] *Forte, legitima dispositione.* “Perhaps, by a lawful arrangement.” HARD.]

### Chapter VI—On the immunity of ecclesiastical property

Whoever, lifted up by the arrogance of pride, treats the house of God with contempt, or dishonorably handles or presumes to violate possessions consecrated to God and placed under the protection of royal immunity for God’s honor, shall be excommunicated as an invader and violator of the house of God.

He ought also to experience the indignation of the king himself, whose goodwill he has despised and whose constitution he has violated [Col. 1567C].

Nevertheless, the king should order that the immunity granted by him be preserved unharmed by all subject to his authority. He should not rashly give credence to those who assert that the Lord’s possessions—that is, possessions given to the Lord of lords—ought not to be under the king’s protection in the same way as his own inheritances.
