He should rather take into account that, just as God is more excellent than a human being, so the divine cause is more excellent than mortal possession.

Accordingly, anyone who takes greater pride in his own possessions than in the Lord’s possessions is deceived. The defender and guardian of these divine things, appointed by God, must care diligently not only to preserve them but also to increase them. He ought to defend and enlarge what we have mentioned as more excellent rather than his own property [Col. 1567D].

Therefore, if some madman, through the importunity of his wickedness, attempts to turn the king away from a right purpose and appears unable to be softened by any remedies, then, even if he is needed for some passing services, he must be rejected and cast away from him in fact, according to the Gospel saying:

> “If your foot, hand, or eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it away from you” (Matthew XVIII).

### Chapter VII—On the bishops’ authority over ecclesiastical property, their cooperation with laymen, and the rejection of corrupt rewards

We wish bishops to have authority to foresee, direct, govern, and administer ecclesiastical property according to the authority of the canons [Col. 1568A].

Laymen should obey bishops in their ministry, for the governance of the churches, the defense of widows and orphans, and the preservation of their Christianity. Counts and judges should cooperate with their prelates in carrying out justice according to the commands of the divine law.

Under no circumstances should a just law be corrupted through anyone’s lie, false testimony, perjury, or reward.

[Variant: “divine law” instead of “just law.” HARD.]

### Chapter VIII—On property acquired by bishops or priests after ordination

It is written in the Council of Carthage (Council of Carthage III, canon 49) that priests, deacons, or any clerics who are ordained possessing nothing, and who during their episcopate or clerical office acquire fields or any estates in their own name, are to be held guilty as invaders of the Lord’s property, unless, after being admonished, they transfer those same things to the church [Col. 1568B].

If something of their own comes to them through someone’s generosity or through inheritance from their family, they should use it in a manner suitable to their purpose. If they deviate backward from their purpose, they are to be judged unworthy of ecclesiastical honor, as reprobates.

Priests should not sell a possession of the church in which they have been established without the knowledge of their bishops and without necessity. Nor may a bishop appropriate a possession of the mother church in the name of his own title.

### Chapter IX—On manumissions

The Council of Carthage contains the following (African Council, canon 31):

> “Concerning manumissions celebrated in the church: if our fellow priests in Italy are found to carry this out, it will also be our trust to follow their order. Permission has plainly been given to the envoy, so that whatever trustworthy action they are able to undertake for the condition of the Church and the salvation of souls, we may know that we shall commendably accept before the Lord” [Col. 1568C].

### Chapter X—On giving tithes and dividing them into four portions

We wish the tithes given to each church to be distributed by the priests, after consultation with the bishops, with the greatest care for the use of the church and of the poor [Col. 1568D].

Four portions should be made both from revenues and from the offerings of the faithful, according to the resources of each church, as was long ago reasonably decreed: one portion for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth to be applied to the fabric of the church, according to episcopal regulation.

It must nevertheless be admonished that the tithe should not be neglected but given wholly to God, since God himself ordained that it be given to him. For it is to be feared that if someone withholds from God what is owed to him, God may through that person’s sin take away what is necessary for him.

### Chapter XI—That ancient churches should retain their privileges

Churches established in ancient times are not to be deprived of tithes or of other possessions for the sake of new oratories without the consent and deliberation of the bishops [Col. 1569A].

### Chapter XII—That priests should neither be established nor received in churches without the bishops’ consent

Whoever has obtained a church for payment is to be completely deposed. Anyone who, contrary to the discipline of ecclesiastical rule, expels a priest lawfully ordained to a church by means of money and claims that church for himself in this way is plainly acting unlawfully. This widely spread vice must be corrected with the greatest care.

Likewise, it seems necessary to forbid clerics and laymen from presuming to give a church to any priest without the permission and consent of his bishop.

### Chapter XIII—On the life of clerics and monks

Every bishop must take necessary care concerning how canons ought to live, and likewise monks, so that they strive to live according to the regular order, as the Apostle says:

> “Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called” (I Corinthians VII).

They must also abstain entirely from secular business.

There are many forms of secular business, but we have touched upon a few of them. These include every form of lust—not only bodily impurity but also whatever a person desires beyond what is just in every carnal concupiscence; sordid profit; receiving or giving unjust gifts for anything secular; hiring someone for profit and payment; contentions, lawsuits, and loving quarrels [Col. 1569C]; disputing in secular courts, except in defense of orphans and widows; serving as contractors or agents for secular affairs; being a maker of shameful jokes in word or deed, or loving secular amusement; loving dice; seeking adornment inappropriate to one’s purpose; wishing to live in luxury; pursuing gluttony and drunkenness; possessing unjust weights or measures; conducting unjust business.

Yet just business is not to be forbidden because of various necessities, since we read that the holy apostles engaged in trade, and the Rule of Saint Benedict commands that care be taken through whose hands the business of the monastery passes.

Also included are pursuing dogs and birds for hunting; indulging in excessive feasts and drunkenness; and refusing to avoid excess in any matter [Col. 1569D].

We forbid all these things to the ministers of the altar, urging them to observe the apostolic saying:

> “No one serving as a soldier for God involves himself in secular business” (II Timothy II).

They should also consider the Lord’s judgment:

> “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with overeating and drunkenness” (Luke XXI).

They should moderate food and drink so that, according to the Apostle (I Timothy III), they may be sober and ready for the Lord’s service. They should not permit secular or shameful jokes to be made in their presence. Rather, they should have the poor and needy at table with them, hear divine reading there, and take food with the blessing of the Lord, according to the Apostle’s words:

> “Whether you eat or drink, do everything to the glory of God” (I Corinthians X) [Col. 1570A].

### Chapter XIV—On the monastic vow

No monk may possess anything as private property. He must in no way appropriate to himself secular things to which he has renounced his claim, nor may he presume to accept the parishes of churches without the bishop’s consent.

Regarding the titles in which they have been established, they must render an account to the bishop or his representative and come when summoned to a synod.

### Chapter XV—On clerics who grow their hair long

It is written in the decrees of Pope Gregory:

> “If any cleric lets his hair grow long, let him be anathema.”

Therefore we decree that such men be compelled to return to their former condition [Col. 1570B].

### Chapter XVI—On the life of nuns

An abbess who has a monastery in a city must not leave the monastery at all without the permission of her bishop or of the person who acts in his place, unless perhaps she is compelled by royal command.

Whenever she goes outside, she must exercise care and vigilance over the nuns whom she takes with her, so that no permission or occasion for sinning is given to them.

When she leaves, she must appoint in the monastery someone to act in her place, who will care for and watch over the souls of the nuns.

The abbess must also be diligent in building and restoring those things necessary for the nuns.

The nuns established in the monastery must devote themselves to reading and singing, to the celebration of the psalms and prayer, and must likewise celebrate the canonical hours—namely, Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline [Col. 1570C].

All of them, except those whom illness keeps from it, must sleep in the dormitory. Every day they must come together for consolation, and they must observe the other requirements contained in the rule for nuns and those established there by the holy Fathers.

### Chapter XVII—That the poor should not be oppressed

We admonish the royal piety concerning the oppression of poor free persons: they must not be oppressed unjustly by the more powerful through any evil device, nor compelled to sell or surrender their possessions.

Otherwise their parents might perhaps be unjustly disinherited, royal service diminished, and the poor themselves, through want, become beggars, robbers, or criminals. They should also not be summoned so frequently to public hearings, except as prescribed in the capitulary formerly issued by the lord king [Col. 1570D].

[Note: [Col. 1569D] a That is, “summoned individually.”]

### Chapter XVIII—On not taking the property of the poor through wrongful pretexts

For the protection of the poor, whose care we ought to undertake, we have decided that neither bishops, abbots, counts, vicars, judges, nor anyone at all may, under a wrongful pretext or through an evil device, purchase or take the property of the poor or of those with less power [Col. 1571A].

Whoever wishes to purchase something from them must do so in a public hearing before suitable witnesses and with due process. Wherever the contrary is found to have occurred, it must be entirely corrected by royal command.

### Chapter XIX—On those who accept gifts to overturn justice

Those who accept gifts from two parties in order to overturn justice—that is, from the person who justly seeks what has been unjustly taken from him and from the person who unjustly seized the same thing—are to be admonished and strongly rebuked, lest they irrevocably close themselves out from the kingdom of Christ, which is open to all who act justly.

### Chapter XX—On parricides

How detestable a crime parricide is, the Lord himself demonstrated in the judgment passed between Cain and his brother Abel, when he said to Cain the parricide:

> “You shall be cursed upon the earth, which has opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand. When you cultivate it, it shall not give you its produce; wandering and fugitive you shall be upon the earth.”

He also placed a sign upon him, namely that he should live forever as a trembling and groaning fugitive and should not dare to have a settled dwelling.

But because in modern times parricides wander as fugitives through various places and devote themselves to various vices and the allurements of gluttony, it seems better to us that they should remain in one place and chastise themselves with strict penance, if they deserve to receive from the Lord’s goodness forgiveness for their crime [Col. 1571C].

They may not thereafter take up the military belt or be joined in marriage or wedlock, since the sacred canons do not permit this to them.

[Note: [Col. 1571D] a This is canon 20 of the Council of Ancyra.]

### Chapter XXI—On women who kill their children

Concerning women who commit fornication and kill their offspring, or who act against themselves so as to expel what has been conceived in the womb, the ancient definition removes them from the Church until the end of their lives. We now define the matter more humanely, granting them a period of ten years according to the prescribed stages of penance.

Likewise, in the Council of Elvira, chapter 63, it is written concerning those who kill children conceived in adultery:

> “If a woman has conceived through adultery and has killed the child after the crime, it has been decided that communion should scarcely be granted to her at the end of her life, because she has doubled the crime.”

[Variant in the text: “that communion should be granted to her neither at the end” (*ei nec in fine*), rather than “scarcely at the end.”]

Likewise, in the Council of Lérida, chapter 2, it is written concerning those who cause abortions or kill their newborn children:

> “Those who strive to kill fetuses conceived in adultery, or children who have been born, or who crush them in their mothers’ wombs with various potions, shall receive communion, in either sex, after seven years of penance, as adulterers; nevertheless, throughout the whole time of their lives they must devote themselves to tears and humility” [Col. 1571D].

### Chapter XXII—On homicides

In the Council of Ancyra, chapter 21, the following is written concerning homicides [Col. 1572A]:

> “Those who have committed voluntary homicide must continually submit themselves to penance, but they shall attain completion near the end of life.”

In the Council of Agde, chapter 37, the following is read concerning homicides and false witnesses:

> “Therefore we have decreed that homicides and false witnesses are to be removed from ecclesiastical communion, unless they cleanse the crimes they have committed by the satisfaction of penance.”

Likewise, in the Council of Agde, canon 62, it is written concerning those who kill slaves without a judge:

> “If anyone kills his own slave without the knowledge of the judge, he shall cleanse the guilt of bloodshed by excommunication or by two years of penance.”

Likewise, in the Council of Elvira, chapter 5, it is written concerning a mistress who kills her maidservant through jealousy:

> “If a woman, inflamed by the fury of jealousy, beats her maidservant with whips so that she gives up her life in torment within the third day—since it is uncertain whether she killed her intentionally or accidentally—if intentionally, after seven years; if accidentally, after five years of duly performed penance, it has been decided that she may be admitted to communion. But if she becomes ill during the appointed period, she shall receive communion” [Col. 1572B].

### Chapter XXIII—On involuntary homicides

In the Council of Ancyra, chapter 22, it is written concerning homicides committed unintentionally that the earlier definition prescribed attaining completion after seven years of penance, while the later one required completing a period of five years.

### Chapter XXIV—On priests killed while holding office

Whoever kills a priest shall be assigned twelve years of penance according to the statutes of the ancients. If he denies the deed, then, if he is free, he must swear with twelve others; if he is a slave, he must clear himself by passing over twelve red-hot plowshares.

Once convicted of the offense, he must lay aside the military belt until the end of his life and lose his wife.

### Chapter XXV—On priests killed after degradation

It has been reported to us that certain men who formerly claimed to have been priests, and who were later degraded for their sins, went about various places seeking the intercession of the saints while doing penance, and were murdered [Col. 1572D].

We deny all ecclesiastical communion to the perpetrators of such killings [The text reads *interrectionibus*; perhaps *interfectoribus*, “to the killers”], until they have discharged a fitting penance for their guilt according to the judgment of the bishops.

### Chapter XXVI—On the sick who are in danger of death

From the sick who are in danger of death, priests must seek a sincere confession. A fixed amount of penance is not, however, to be imposed upon them; rather, it is to be made known, and the burden of penance is to be lightened through the prayers of friends and the practice of almsgiving.

Thus, if they should happen to die, they will not be bound by excommunication or become separated from the fellowship of the good [Perhaps: “bound by excommunication, or separated from communion, or deprived of the fellowship of forgiveness or of the good.” HARD.].

If they recover after being divinely rescued from this danger, they must diligently observe the measure of penance imposed by their confessor.

Therefore, according to canonical authority, so that the door of mercy may not appear closed to them, they should be strengthened by prayers and ecclesiastical consolations, receive sacred anointing [Perhaps, “anointing with oil”], and, according to the statutes of the holy Fathers, be refreshed with communion as viaticum [Col. 1573A].

### Chapter XXVII—On those who are hanged on the gallows

Certain brothers have asked concerning those who are hanged on the gallows for their crimes after making confession to God: whether their corpses should be brought to the churches, whether offerings should be made for them, and whether Masses should be celebrated.

We answer them: If communion is to be given at the end, according to canonical ordinance, to all who make a sincere confession of their sins and do worthy penance, why should it not be given to those who pay the ultimate penalty for their sins?

For it is written:

> “God does not avenge the same thing twice” (Nahum I, according to the Septuagint).

The Lord himself says:

> “On whatever day the sinner turns, his sins shall not be counted against him” (Ezekiel XXXIII).

And again:

> “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (ibid.).

[Note: [Col. 1573D] a These words are from Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Vienne and Narbonne. HARD.]

Whoever denies penance to a person at the time of death deprives that person of salvation and despairs of the mercy of God, not believing that it can suffice to assist the dying even in a single moment.

The thief hanging at Christ’s right hand on the cross would have lost his reward (Luke XXIII) if the penance of one hour had not helped him. While undergoing punishment, he repented, and through the confession of a single statement, with God’s promise, he merited a dwelling in paradise.

True conversion to God among those placed at the end of life must therefore be judged by the mind rather than by the length of time, as the prophet affirms:

> “When you have turned and groaned, then you shall be saved” (Ezekiel XXXIII) [Col. 1573C].

### Chapter XXVIII—On incestuous persons

We have decreed that bishops must diligently investigate incestuous persons. If they refuse to repent, they are to be expelled from the Church until they return to penance.

If they refuse to lend an ear to the admonitions of the priests and wish to persist in their former crimes, they must be restrained from such a depraved custom through the discipline of secular power [Col. 1573D].

### Chapter XXIX—On condemned marriages

If anyone marries a widow and afterward commits fornication with her daughter; or marries two sisters; or if a woman marries two brothers, or a father and son; likewise, if anyone violates through carnal union his brother’s widow, who previously was nearly [uncertain]; if anyone takes his niece in marriage; if anyone marries his stepmother or daughter-in-law; if anyone shamefully joins himself to his female cousin; or if anyone is polluted by intercourse with the widow or daughter of his maternal uncle, with his father’s daughter, or with his stepdaughter, or is defiled by contact with any such union [Col. 1574A]—we decree that such persons are to be separated and never again joined in marriage, under severe discipline.

### Chapter XXX—Within which degree marriages may be contracted

We also prohibit anyone from entering marriage within the fourth degree. Wherever such a marriage is found after this prohibition has been issued, it must be dissolved.

The same rule of the law of marriage that is observed in the man’s family relationship must likewise be observed in the woman’s.

Since it is established that the two are one flesh, their relationship on both sides must be regarded as common, as it is written:

> “The two shall be one flesh” (Genesis II).

### Chapter XXXI—On the manner of assigning penance

The measure and duration of penance for those who confess their sins must be imposed by priests either according to the institution of the ancient canons, the authority of the holy Scriptures, or ecclesiastical custom [Col. 1574B].

For those who impose certain light and unusual forms of penance for grave sins sew together cushions, according to the prophetic saying (Ezekiel XIII), under every elbow, and make pillows beneath the head of people of every age in order to capture souls.

A distinction must be observed between penitents who ought to do penance publicly and those who ought to do it secretly. Whoever sins publicly ought to be punished with public penance and, according to the order of the canons, both excommunicated and reconciled according to the merit of his offense [Col. 1574C].

Penitents must desire both the completion of the appointed period and the remission of their crime. It is not enough for them to abstain from receiving certain things unless they also withdraw from harmful pleasures.

Let those who turn away from evil do good; let them seek peace and pursue it.

Many other matters were brought before us in various inquiries, but because of the brevity of the time we could not at the present council answer and settle them all. We ask, however, that these matters which have been transmitted to you be confirmed by your authority; and, if anyone should wish to oppose them, let him not be permitted to prevail. For you ought to be God’s fellow workers [Col. 1574D] and helpers of his holy Church, so that the Christian religion may be preserved undefiled throughout the time of your reign and unto the end.

## EPISTLE VIII, SYNODAL, TO HINCMAR, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, CONCERNING GOTHESCALC

*(In Mansi, Councils, vol. XIV, p. 914.)*

To the most reverend brother and fellow priest Hincmar, archbishop, Rabanus, servant of Christ and of his servants, sends greetings in the Lord.

Let your affection know that a certain wandering [Col. 1575A] monk named Gothescalc, who claims that he was ordained a priest in your diocese, came to us at Mainz from Italy, introducing new superstitions and a harmful doctrine concerning God’s predestination, and leading the people into error. He says that God’s predestination applies to evil just as it does to good, and that there are certain people in this world who, because of God’s predestination—which compels them to go to death—cannot correct themselves from error and sin; as though God had made them incorrigible from the beginning and destined them to go to destruction, liable to punishment.

When we recently heard this opinion from him at the synod held at Mainz, and found him incorrigible, with the consent and command of our most pious king Louis we decided to send him to you, condemned together with his pernicious doctrine, so that you may confine him [Col. 1575B] within your diocese, from which he first departed unlawfully. Do not allow him to teach error any longer or [Col. 1576A] lead the Christian people astray. For, as I have heard, he already has many deceived and less devoted to their salvation, who say:

“Of what benefit to me is it to labor in the service of God? For if I am predestined to death, I shall never escape it; but if I do evil and am predestined to life, I shall go without any doubt to eternal rest.”

We have therefore written these things to you briefly, informing you what we found his doctrine to be. You will also be able to hear more fully from his own mouth what he thinks and to decide justly what ought to be done about it. May almighty God deign to preserve your holiness in good health, and praying for us, forever.

## B. RABANUS’S LATIN-BARBARIAN GLOSSARY OF THE PARTS OF THE HUMAN BODY

WALAFRID STRABO, DISCIPLE OF MAURUS

Thus does man exist; thus I shall hold forth the limbs of his body, as Strabo, displaying them to Maurus, points them out.

[Col. 1575C] Man—*homo*—is so called from *humus*, earth.

The soul derives its name from the winds; hence in Greek **ἄνεμος**, “wind,” is so called, because man draws air through his mouth.

The body—*corpus*—is so called from corruption.

The head—*caput*—is named from *capere*, “to take,” because it receives all the bodily senses and is the first part of the body.

The crown of the head: *scheitila*, *nuilla*.

The back of the head: *hail ancha*.

The hair: *loccha fahs*.

The flowing hair: *gischoram fahs*.

The locks: *ungischoran fahs*.

*Crines* properly refers to women’s hair, because it is divided by ribbons.

The temples: *thunuuengiu*.

The face is so called from *effigies*, “image,” for in it is the whole figure of a human being [Col. 1575D] and the recognition of every individual person.

The countenance—*vultus*—is so called because through it the will of the mind is shown.

The forehead: *endi*. The forehead—*frontispicium*—is so called from the openings of the eyes.

The eyes—*oculi*—are so called as if from *ocior lux*, “swifter light,” because they quickly receive light.

The pupil: *seha*, the central point of the eye.

The circle by which the white parts of the eye are separated from the pupil is called a crown, because of its distinct blackness.

The eyelids are the folds of the eyes, named from blinking: *augbrâuuа*.

The eyelashes—that is, coverings by which the eyes are covered—are so called because they conceal the eyes.

The eyebrows—that is, *windbrâuua*.

[Col. 1576C] The cheeks, the lower parts of the eyes: *hiufilon*.

The cheekbones—that is, *bracchom*; the jaws are likewise called this, diminutively.

The ears are named from drawing in, because they draw in the voice.

The little ear: the uppermost part of the ear.

The nostrils: *nasa*. The straight part of the nostrils is called the column; its extremity is called *pirula*, from the shape of a pear-apple. The parts to the right and left are called little wings; the middle partition is called the dividing wall.

The mouth—that is, *mund*—is called as if it were a doorway, because food enters there and speech goes out.

Men’s lips are called *labra*, women’s lips *labia*.

The tongue is named from licking, just as the lips are named from lapping.

[Col. 1576D] The teeth: *ceni*. The front ones are called incisors because they cut food. The next are called canine teeth because, just as dogs break bones with them, human beings give to these teeth what the front teeth cannot cut, so that they may break it. The last are the molars: *chinni ceni*. The number of teeth differs according to sex: men have more, women fewer.

The gums—that is, *bilorna*.

The palate: *giumo* or *huruuua*.

The throat is named from pouring forth voices.

The arteries—that is, *weisunt*.

The windpipe: *quercha*, *chela*. It takes its name from the throat, whose passage extends toward the mouth and nostrils.

The *pumen* [perhaps *rumen*], next to the windpipe, through which food and drink are swallowed, is the sublingual part, that is, *hracho*.

The chin: *Chinni*.

The neck: *hals*. Its front part is called the throat; its rear part the nape.

The shoulders: *scultyrra*.

The elbow: *helina*.

According to some, the ulnae are the extension of both hands; according to others, the elbow.

The arm: *arm*.

The muscles: *musi*.

The armpit: *oahchasa*.

The palm is the extended hand.

The thickened middle of the palm: *ir*.

The first finger is the thumb; the second, the index or pointing finger; the third, the modest or middle finger; the fourth, the annular or medical finger; the fifth, the little finger.

The fingernail: *nagal*.

The breasts: *prusti*.

The nipples: the heads of the breasts.

The chest, beneath which is the firmness of the human being.

The skin is the outer part of the body, as is the hide.

*Arvina* is the fat adhering to the skin.

*Pulpa* is flesh without fat.

The limbs are the parts of the body.

The joints are the parts by which they are connected.

The vertebrae are the uppermost parts of the bones.

Cartilages are soft and without marrow; the outer ear, the partition of the nostrils, and the ends of the ribs are of this kind.

[Col. 1577C] The ribs: *ribbi*.

The side: *sita*.

The shoulder blade: *ah sala*.

The back, or rear, is the posterior part of the body from the neck to the kidneys.

The spine is the joining of the back. It is so called because it has sharp little roots and contains the joints of the ribs. A part of the brain is said to pass through it in a long tract. It is also called the sacred spine, because it is formed first in the conceived infant; therefore this first part was also offered by the nations to their gods as a sacrifice.

The viscera: *hinnuouili*.

The heart is named from care.

The lung: *lungun*.

The veins are so called because they are the paths of the blood as it flows.

[Col. 1577D] The liver: *lebera*.

The fibers are the extremities of the liver.

The spleen—that is, *miltzi*.

The gall—that is, *galla*.

The stomach—that is, *mago*.

The intestines—that is, *tharma*.

The omentum is a membrane that contains part of the large intestines.

The belly—that is, *huuanba*. The belly, the abdomen, and the uterus differ from one another. The belly is that which digests the food it receives and appears externally. The abdomen is that which receives the food and is accustomed to being cleansed. Only women have a uterus, in which they conceive children.

[Col. 1578A] The abdominal fat visible externally: *aquilicus*.

The matrix is the place in the uterus where the fetus is produced.

The bladder: *blatra*.

The kidneys: *lendibraton*.

The loins: *lendin*.

The navel: *nabulo*.

The flanks: *lancha*.

The buttocks or hips: *hufphi*.

The anus: *arsloch*.

The buttocks: *arsbelli*.

The lower intestines: *crozdarm*.

The genitals are the parts of the body that received their name from the begetting of offspring. They are also called the shameful parts, either from modesty or from puberty, and therefore are covered by clothing. They are also called “dishonorable,” because they do not possess the appearance of beauty [Col. 1578B] like the other limbs. The same is true of the penis, either because it belongs only to the man or because fluid is emitted from it.

The testicles: *hodon*, which pour the seed into the vessels carrying it.

The scrotum is the skin in which the testicles are placed.

The thighs: *deon*; their inner parts are called the femurs.

The knees: *chniu*.

The legs: *bein*.

The calves: *wadon*.

The marrow: *marc*.

The ankles—that is, *ancli*. From them socks worn beneath the feet are called *subtalares*, because they are beneath the ankles.

The foot: *phuoz*.

The soles are the front parts of the foot, which consist of many bones.

[Col. 1578C] The heel is the first lower part of the sole of the foot, with which we tread the earth.

The heel-bone is the lower part of the foot, so called because we impress footprints upon the earth.

## B. RABANUS: ON THE INVENTION OF LANGUAGES, FROM HEBREW TO THEODISC, AND ON ANCIENT LETTERS

[Col. 1579]

First of all, the letters of the Hebrew language were invented by Moses and renewed by Ezra after their captivity and return. We have noted below their elements and figures, insofar as we have been able to discover them; their total consists of twenty-two letters.

Cadmus, son of Agenor, first brought some Greek letters to Greece from Phoenicia. After him others added several, which are considered suitable for making numbers; and the total of those letters with which one can write comes to twenty-four. Three other characters were added so that the number one thousand could be reached.

The Latin letters were invented by the nymph Carmentis, the mother of Evander, who was also called Nicostrata. She first brought them to Italy. Later the Latins added three Greek letters out of necessity, because they needed to pronounce certain words as they are found in Greek, such as **ΧΡΣ** [perhaps X, Y, Z], *Ymnus*, and *Zelus*, and the rest. I have resolved to write these letters out for you with the greatest care.

We have also found the letters of the philosopher and cosmographer Aethicus, a Scythian by nation and of noble lineage. The venerable presbyter Jerome brought them down to us, explaining them together with his own statements, because he held Aethicus’s knowledge and ingenuity in high esteem; for this reason he preferred to publish his letters. If we are still mistaken in these letters, and if we make errors in some places, correct us.

[Col. 1581] We have written below the letters used by the Marcomanni, whom we call Northmen. Those who speak the Theodisc language derive their origin from them. Those still entangled in pagan rites use them to signify their songs, incantations, and divinations.

This kind of writing is called “Caesar’s Notes.” It is made with letters called “the ancient hand.” When one of the Romans wished to entrust something to letters by carving it on buildings, walls, towers, or stone monuments in memory of himself and his family, he bound the letters with dots and headings so that no ignorant person could immediately read them, as was shown above in a few examples.

This type of writing, both that given above with dots, **V**, and vowels, and that contained below with vowels other than the customary ones, is said to have been demonstrated to our predecessors by the holy archbishop and martyr Boniface, who came from the Angles and Saxons. Yet it was not first begun by him; rather, we have discovered that the use of this kind had grown among the ancients.

## THE FINAL PART OF ALL THE WORKS OF THE BLESSED RABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

Poems first published and illustrated with notes by Christopher Brower.

[Col. 1583]

[Col. 1583C]

## CHRISTOPHER BROWER TO THE READER

Here, friendly reader, are Rabanus’s verses, wrested from the hands of gravediggers; they have come to life again from a reliable and very ancient manuscript, though its owner wished to remain concealed, and I thought them worthy to be brought back, as it were, from Libitina or the underworld and restored to their master. The inscription of the parchment book, though badly preserved, was: “Verses of Rabanus on Various Matters, XIV: order XIX.” These are plainly signs of theft and of a plundered library, like **σημεῖα κλοπῆς**, “signs of theft.” Meanwhile, although help was solicited everywhere to heal these mutilated poems, little hope has so far appeared from learned men. Thus, although at present I cannot, in accordance with Cato’s saying, offer what neither turns sour nor grows moldy, nevertheless within the next three days, as he puts it, you will be able, at the judgment of a good man, to taste Rabanus’s piety and wisdom like wine. Farewell and enjoy.

[Col. 1583D]

## SECTION ONE — POEMS ON VARIOUS SUBJECTS

### I

[Note: [Col. 1583B] a PREFACE. That more monuments of Rabanus’s talent exist, written in richly measured prose, than have become commonly known, may be inferred from the verses we are publishing. Would that those poems had reached us complete! For not only are many of this number missing, but also many epic poems, which they say he composed in heroic verse about the deeds of the children of Louis the Pious—Lothair, Charles, and Louis—and which are now forgotten and held shut in the prisons of libraries. This loss of the present works may therefore be borne somewhat more lightly by us.

I confess that in the poems we are publishing the song of the meter is harsh, rustic, and unpolished, and that it would even grate unpleasantly upon the melodious swans of Latium. But I ask you to remember that Rabanus lived at a time when people scarcely knew by what laws meters properly sounded, and did not concern themselves with the words and thoughts by which they should be clothed. It was considered sufficient that the meaning be understood: the first praise of gifted minds was that, without relaxing their pursuit of wisdom, integrity of life and innocence of character shone through.

THE METHOD OF THESE NOTES. We must often proceed along a narrow path, because in the darkness of that age our view is easily obstructed, and the memory of the people and events to which the titles of the poems refer is either obscured or at least greatly entangled. Nevertheless, the poet’s meaning is not so hidden that it cannot be perceived without our assistance and understood by anyone. We shall therefore provide the notes more tightly and sparingly, in the manner of the ancients, since we are no longer permitted to be so eloquent, being devotees of sterner Muses.

To Pope Paschal. Paschal, a pontiff of illustrious name and outstanding generosity, occupied the see for seven years beginning in 817 and crowned Lothair, the son of Louis the Pious, with the diadem. Rabanus therefore began composing poems at an early stage and chose Paschal as the guardian of his first page.

To Gregory, etc. This is Gregory IV, whose pontificate began in the year of Christ 842. Baronius did not hesitate to establish Gregory’s praise from this poem, which Rabanus composed as an acrostic in praise of the holy cross, and to raise him up in his panegyric as a shining star newly risen over Germany. The books say that the work was prepared as a gift for Gregory but was not presented because of an impediment. I readily believe, in accordance with the title prefixed here, that it was both sent to Gregory and offered to Gregory, prince of the apostles. For what would prevent the same book, transcribed in several copies and eagerly desired at that time, from being sent and inscribed alike to Pope Gregory and to his successor Sergius?

Let the Pithaean, or Fulda, Annals therefore retain their credibility; some make Strabo their author. Under the year 844 they say: “Rabanus the sophist, and a poet second to none of his time, sent through Aserichus and Theodbertus, monks of the monastery of Fulda, to Pope Sergius, to be offered to Saint Peter, the book which he composed concerning the praise of Christ’s holy cross, distinguished by a variety of figures and fashioned in difficult and wondrous poetry.”

In the Wimpheling copy, published a hundred years ago, the title of this little poem is given as: “Commendation of the Pope.” Nor does our manuscript recognize the intermediate inscription before the verse “Prelate beloved of God”: “He offers a gift to the pontiff.”

“Peoples wage wars,” etc. Anastasius the Librarian writes: “In the times of this most holy Father Gregory, the impious, wicked, and God-hated race of the Agarenes, or Saracens, rising from its own borders and spreading through nearly all the islands and regions of the earth, was savagely carrying out the plundering of people and the devastation of places.”

To these evils were added the civil wars throughout Gaul—or rather, I should say, the parricidal hatred and wars of the royal sons against Louis their father.

“What belongs to the praise of Christ,” etc. The subject of the work is the vindication of human salvation; its end is the glory of Christ, to which everything is referred. Its mode of composition is an esoteric art, involving the scattered and manifoldly subtle arrangement of letters as though they were numbers, an art once used by the Sibyls, the royal Psalmist, and other prophets. Even now, we see the hidden matters of our religion represented admirably in the mind, so that although they are furthest removed from the judgment of sight, they are nevertheless offered to the unlearned through images, figures, and a certain configuration, and are very easily marked, so that they may present themselves, quickly strike the inner senses, and move people to piety.

Therefore, you should not rashly use everything.

“It is shameful to have difficult trifles,

and foolish labor is labor spent on absurdities.”

When Rabanus began scattering little letters, Serarius investigates in his Mainz writings, following the example of Porphyry; yet he could scarcely establish anything certain about it. In writing to Gregory, Rabanus testifies that he had played with such things in ancient times.

Gregory sat for sixteen years and reached the year of Christ 843. Trithemius, in his Hirsau chronicle, and others who followed him, report that Rabanus resigned the administration of the monastery of Fulda in 842. Other earlier writers, among them Lambert, remember that he was treated more harshly and expelled in that same year. Hence, according to the index of ecclesiastical writers, he fled for the favor and protection of Louis, king of Germany, or of the emperor Louis the Pious. But the emperor Louis died in 840; and Caesar Baronius demonstrated from the letters of Lupus of Ferrières that Rabanus withdrew voluntarily from the administration in 838, out of a desire for leisure and quiet. For Lupus writes in letter 40 that he laid down the burden of administration so that he might devote himself more fully to divine matters.

We have observed elsewhere that Rabanus attended to the secret affairs of Louis the Pious, whether this was done through counsel or through duties concerned with the direction of conscience. The year in which he resigned was the eleventh year of Gregory’s pontificate and the twenty-fifth of the emperor Louis. It was around this time, we think, that this acrostic work came to Rome. But how many years earlier he had begun the work on the holy cross is not equally easy to determine. Let us suppose twenty years, so as to arrive at 817, when he himself was already entering his thirtieth year; for he had completed six lustrums when he wove together these literary figures.

The remaining summary is therefore this. Rabanus was made abbot in the place of Haistulf in the year of the Lord 822, in the thirty-fifth year of his age. He presided for twenty-four years—or, as Rudolph records in his Acts, twenty years—so that, after completing his retirement on Mount Saint Peter, he entered the see of Mainz in 847, where he sat for nine years. He therefore lived approximately sixty-three years.

“Verses of Maurus,” etc. The title of these verses removes a widespread error. A common inscription misled the reader: “Intercession of Albinus for Maurus.” Hence there is a double mistake: that of those who attribute this poem to Albinus, whom we followed in the first book of the Fulda Antiquities, and that of others who wish it to have been inscribed to Pope Gregory. For the father of the poem is Maurus himself, Rabanus, though he assumes the persona of Albinus; and the patron whom he invokes is Saint Martin.

The city to which he sends a copy of the book as a gift is Tours, among whom there existed a famous monastery and school, where Albinus the teacher and Rabanus his disciple lived.

“His own abbot,” etc. The clearest meaning of this couplet—although those who subtly transferred the sense to Pope Gregory took great pains to explain it—is this: the abbot who directed him was Ratgar; the Father to whose dwelling he was sent was Saint Martin, to whom the people of Tours owe everything.

“That he might read with me,” etc. Serarius aptly noted in his Mainz writings that “to read with someone” is a form of speech taken from vernacular usage. Rabanus used it elsewhere of his disciples, as Alcuin did of Ludger. The ancient custom of the schools should also be noted, when grammarians and rhetoricians alike, as Fabius testifies, taught by reading aloud.

“Who arrange symbolic numbers,” etc. This was done after the example of the ancient lyric poets: first, that poet whom our Simonides, playing Christ upon the lyre, joins to Pindar and Alcaeus in his ten-stringed psalter and who often arranges numbers in the letters at the beginnings of verses (Psalms VII, XXIV, XXXIII, XXXVI, CX, CXI, CXLIV, CXVIII); and second, the poet who follows the destruction of his city and the captivity of his people with laments, joining a fourfold alphabet in different meters in the Lamentations.

Why should I mention the Erythraean or Cumaean Sibyl, who, many centuries ago, as Saint Augustine records in *The City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 23, expressed so clearly at the beginnings of verses **Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς Θεοῦ υἱὸς Σωτήρ**, “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior”? In the same verses she also enclosed the Fish, **ἰχθύς**, in words charged with a notable mystery.

I pass over Sedulius in his hymn for Christ’s birth, and our Fortunatus, Christian poets who did not reject this kind of poem as empty **περιεργία**, “curiosity,” but accepted it as **εὐρυθμία**, “well-rhythmed form,” because it was customary among the ancients.

“And because he remembers that he was nourished in an illustrious dwelling.” There is no trace of this dwelling to seek either at Paris, where Rabanus is thought to have studied under Alcuin, or in any of that city’s schools. Rather, as I have said, it was at the monastery of Saint Martin at Tours, where Rabanus, as a disciple, listened to Alcuin the teacher.

No ancient writer known to me has reported that Rabanus lived in Paris, much less that he served there as teacher or student, although the author of the published catalogue of the abbots of Fulda asserts this.

“Gentle patron, receive the care of the work,” etc. He again commends the work to Saint Martin, whose library he hopes may be adorned by the craftsman’s ingenuity, and his own life fortified through prayers and intercession.]

## TO PASCHAL AND GREGORY, SUPREME PONTIFFS

[Col. 1583B]

### On the Praises of the Holy Cross

*(See the dedicatory poem prefixed to the book on the Praises of the Holy Cross, vol. I of this edition, col. 103.)*

### II — TO GERFRID, BISHOP

[Col. 1584B]

May your love be long-lived; may you remain safe for many years,

Reigning with Christ for everlasting time.

This lowly Raban asks this everywhere for Gerfrid;

Hear him, O Christ; may you be well forever.

### III — MAURUS’S PRAYER TO GOD

[Col. 1585A]

Almighty Father, greatest author of all things,

Co-equal Son, and Spirit of God,

[Col. 1586A] One in nature, threefold in persons,

God, blessed life, giving life to all things.

Look upon me, wretched as I am, and stand near me in mercy as I grieve,

[Col. 1587A] For I live in the world as one sick, grievously sinning.

Deliver me from these evils, unconquered one; drive far away all

The dreadful crimes that hold mind and body:

For I did not fear to stain my whole life

With various errors of defilement, nor to scorn your law.

With tongue, mind, and hand I committed many harmful deeds,

Everything that the text of the Gospel usually forbids.

And what did I then desire, deceived by the wicked one’s fraud?

Whom did I madly follow, loving the enemy’s snare?

Unhappy me! I chose to love the sulphurous pools of hell,

Its fire and worm, with perpetual groaning,

More than the sweet joys of heaven,

More than your incense-bearing fields, O paradise.

Alas, wretched and mad, where would your life now perish?

What groans would you utter, tortured in fierce fire?

[Col. 1587B] Unless the God of boundless goodness, the true lover

Of human nature, in mercy drew me back.

What the Psalmist once loudly sang has also come to pass,

When, amazed, he marveled at God’s heavenly gifts.

Unless the Lord had been my helper, hell would already possess

My guilty soul, cruelly tormenting it.

Now, gracious God, receive your servant in your accustomed mercy,

A penitent whom sorrow torments.

Heal the contrite; comfort the mourning one who weeps,

Forgiving, I beg you, all his crimes.

Give me hope of pardon; make hearts deserving of joy;

Change what is torn and make it peaceful now.

Give me full faith, give hope, give the pledge of love,

So that I may carry your commandments in heart and hand.

I have bound myself by a vow; merciful judge of the world, fulfill

What fragile nature cannot hasten to accomplish.

Let every work be yours, whatever you expend upon your servant;

To you alone be praise, and yours be the glory.

When you wish to set an end to life and to labor,

Then have mercy on your wretched servant.

May the savage encounter not harm me, nor burning Tartarus;

Instead, may a messenger of light lead me to the stars of heaven.

When you come as judge, repaying each according to the law of merits,

Then, I pray, justify your servant yourself.

[Col. 1587C] Place me on the right hand, when you give rewards to the just,

So that in the citadel of light I may behold your face.

I pray you, good Jesus, Ruler, Savior, and Author,

To receive whatever I have uttered here in prayerful speech.

Receive your wretched servant mercifully and hear him;

Grant also the lofty realms of heaven to one who asks.

May I be part of the people and sing in their order,

Rejoicing and singing pleasing songs to you among the saints.

Great glory to God; glory always to you, O Christ;

Amen: great glory to God forever.

### IV — VERSES TO A FRIEND

Hail, faithful love; hail, happy affection.

Remain safe in the world; remain safe, and counsel me with your voice.

For I say that your poems are better than the poems of Maro,

[Col. 1588B] Better than the songs of lofty Ovid:

Better than the odes sung by Flaccus and the verbose Homer,

[Note: [Col. 1588D] a “Whom Corduba produced,” etc. Perhaps he means one of those whom Martial praises as fellow countrymen, **συμπατριώτας**. “Corduba speaks with eloquence …” It produced two Senecas—one the father, a rhetorician, the other the son, a philosopher—and the single Lucan. “Africa held him,” as I understand the passage, but it is unclear whom he means if the reference is different. Africa held several others as well: Publius Terentius, the comic poet; Septimius Severus; Tertullian; and Terentianus Maurus.]

Whom Corduba produced and Africa held.

Because these men uttered falsehoods through their pompous Muses,

They rightly wasted away under the bites of envy.

You join bonds devoted to the pious with faithful words,

Singing calmly and marking friendly hearts.

This is what I ask our love to accomplish; I ask and pray in verse

That diligent ardor may flow through our writings.

Let elegant speech flourish, let rule be preserved in words,

And let the verse move according to the art in fixed connections.

Then your pipe will be adorned with sober song,

And you will rightly be praised as a good poet.

May the highest tongue of the Father give you eloquent speech;

May Christ, God in heaven, be a pious ruler in the world.

[Col. 1588C] May his Spirit make your heart kind,

So that in mind and words you may please the Lord.

As a traveler now hastening along the road, I was compelled

To write these brief words to you. Farewell forever.

### V — TO BATURICUS, BISHOP OF REGENSBURG

[Note: [Col. 1588D] b Baturicus, called *Baterich* in the Theodisc vernacular, which we interpret with Rabanus as “rich in benefits.”]

From the person of [Note: [Col. 1588D] c Concerning Isanbertus, more fully in the epitaphs. He seems to have been a priest and monk, a Boian by origin, living at Fulda and familiar with Bishop Baturicus because of their shared homeland. [Col. 1589B] A bishop of Regensburg, he was rich in resources, helpful to many, and useful. Lupus Servatus, a weighty authority, appears to indicate in the Life of Saint Wigbert that he emerged from Saint Wigbert’s discipline and grew up at Fritzlar under Bishop Albuin. There he names him among the monks entrusted with the mission of secretly transferring the saint’s body to Hersfeld.

I also find in Rabanus’s synodal letter that Baturicus—or “Baturatus,” as it seems to be written there corruptly—was present at the synod of Mainz, which Rabanus held in 816. Although the Church of Regensburg is not today within the province of Mainz, it was then subject to the metropolitan of eastern Francia.

Wiguleius commemorated the memory of Bishop Baturicus in the *Metropolis of Salzburg*. He counts him as the fourth bishop of the Church of Regensburg, successor to Adalbinus, and says that he held the see for twenty-eight or thirty years, beginning in the year of Christ 814 or two years later.

He claimed the monastery of Saint Emmeram for himself and for the Church, since he possessed exceptional favor and authority with Louis, king of Germany, the son of Louis the Pious. That king recorded him in grants as his chief chaplain and bestowed many gifts upon him for the splendor and advancement of his see. See the aforementioned *Metropolis* concerning these matters.

One thing surpasses all else in the praises of Baturicus: he prepared the way for the Bohemian people to embrace the Christian faith, having initiated fourteen rulers and washed them in the bath of holy baptism.]

Isanbertus.

Go willingly, paper; you are commanded to cross over on my behalf.

Go yourself to the dwelling of the Father and greet him.

[Col. 1589A] [Note: [Col. 1589D] a “The city of Regensburg,” etc. No city in Europe is prouder of its titles than Regensburg, concerning which G. Ligurinus writes:

“Then Regensburg, which has borne its ancient name from this,

because it is good for ships, or because the sailor

has been accustomed to place ships there. This city is the chief joy

of the Noric duchy,” etc.

The commentator says: “Among the cities along the Danube, it was once famous for wealth and power, so that it did not fear the strength of the emperors. Irenicus indicates it was Hiaspalim; Aventinus, the Augusta of Tiberius; Petrus Appianus, Reginoburgum. I think that it received its name from the river Rego—here called the Regen—which the Danube receives there.”

So much for him. Ortelius also gathered several more names in his *Geographical Treasury* and in his *Synonyms*. Indeed, the very ancient writer of the Life of Saint Emmeram, Meginfredus, says: “He recognizes the city of Regensburg as foremost in all Germany both in name and dignity, and still the metropolis of that people and the head of an ancient lineage.” There is also a note saying that it was called Germanisheim from Germanicus and Tiburnia by the Romans.

But the writer of the most refined judgment, the distinguished Marc. Welser, investigates with suspended hand and mind, in the third and fourth books on the Boians and in his notes on the Life of Saint Severinus, whether Reginoburgum was the Augusta of Tiberius, the Tiburnia of Eugippius, or Tigurina. He freely inclines rather to the view that the camp called Regina, mentioned in the little book *The Notice of Both Empires*, gave its name to Reginoburgum. For the river Regen at that place was adopted into the name of the camp, just as Quintana was named from the river Quintanica. Arnulfus certainly calls this same city Reginum in book I, chapter 5, of the Miracles of Saint Emmeram and elsewhere.]

The city of Regensburg, whose threatening walls rise toward heaven,

Where the river Regen flows, watering the fields.

There, I ask, seek the illustrious man Baturicus,

[Note: [Col. 1590D] b “For whom house and homeland, the Noric land, rejoices.” The commentator on the Life of Saint Severinus, when describing the location of ancient Noricum, aptly notes that in later centuries barbarian writers added to the name Noricum everything contained within the territory of Bavaria. He cites Paul the Deacon, book III, chapter 19: thus, in the soil of Noricum, Regensburg—or, as Rabanus says, the city and diocese of Regensburg.]

For whom house and homeland, the Noric land, rejoices.

If you find him there, say to him as a suppliant, “Hail,

Honored prelate of God, lofty glory of the people.

A humble monk addresses you, lofty one;

A holy priest, he addresses you in writing, seeking heavenly gifts:

That the body may thrive in strength, that wisdom may imbue the mind,

And that you may remain wholly safe everywhere.

He freely offers thanks; he praises your most generous heart;

He proclaims the gifts which you have bestowed upon him.

He asks the High-Throned One, who reigns richly everywhere,

To repay your merits with the reward due to them.

Receive, holy Father, what your pupil offers with his lips;

He humbly offers you what he offers in mind and hand.

Consider your name, therefore, and handle with reverence

The office which the Almighty has given you.

You are the people’s honor; you yourself are called a bishop,

An overseer; you are the leader and shepherd of the flock.

You are the salt of the earth, the light of the world, and a burning lamp;

A firm city, set upon the summit of a lofty mountain.

Lead the people along the narrow way, and go before them;

Carrying the standard, be first to advance into battle.

As victor, overcoming the enemy’s camps,

You display to the King the rich rewards that you reap.

The supreme Shepherd has appointed you shepherd
Feed Christ’s flock; behold, he comes nearby.

[Col. 1590A] Thus, sagacious and watchful, you keep guard around the sheepfolds,

lest the wolf break in, lest the lion tear them apart;

lest the thief, digging through and entering, slaughter the lamb,

but may the Shepherd, when he comes, possess the whole flock.

May the girded Judge, on his way, rightly minister to you,

and exalt all his gifts;

where joyful bands rejoice, where the Lamb of the Virgin

feeds, together with his entire flock, in due order.

Hasten here, here, pastor, hurry to proceed,

and bring your own here with you, holy Father:

thus you will rightly be judged the author of your name,

if you show yourself to be a Batorich by admonishing your people.

If you assent to Christ’s heavenly kingdom, if you assent to the citadel,

if you remove vices, if you give sacred gifts.

These things too, a poor and needy man, although you are highest in honor,

[Col. 1590B] has sent, gathered together; receive them with a kindly mind,

and do not despise the lowly gift, since, though it carries treasures in a chest,

may my devoted mind bring you acceptable offerings.

Therefore, if any concern for my name has touched you,

know that I am called by the name Isanbert.

You are the altar-stone, you the jewel in the king’s diadem,

you are the key of the kingdom; open the thresholds of heaven.

Then, devoted to you, may Christ’s grace save you;

I am devoted to you in mind; God hears from his citadel.

O nourishing Father of heaven, always protect your friend—

this I ask of you, Son of God, and Spirit of God.

[Note: [Col. 1590D] c “He who is threefold and simple.” After he had invoked the Persons of the holy Trinity three by name, he declares God to be “threefold”—whether this is acceptable in the peaceful judgment of theologians, let the schools decide. That Rabanus possessed a sound mind is clear from every quarter, and immediately afterward in his prayer he says:

“One in nature, three in Persons.”

I know that those who cling more tenaciously to the Second Council of Toledo, and who, with Saint Augustine and Doctor Thomas, deny that God can be called “threefold,” will here brand the expression with their censor’s line and mark this manner of speech as improper. Nevertheless, since the simple nature of God is here affirmed and every composition of several things is excluded, you may take “threefold” here as equivalent to “triune” and “a threefold number of Persons.” Thus our Gabriel Vasquez, an outstanding theologian, thinks that the term “threefold,” when referred to the Persons, may altogether legitimately be used of divine things (*Disputation* 131, on question 31 of Saint Thomas, *First Part*); and rightly did the Mirandulan mark with black charcoal the verse in which the term belonging to the essence was used by you in this fashion:

“Having one divinity in the threefold God.”]

You who are threefold and simple, who rule the scepters of heaven,

who encompass the world without end and grant light from your citadel.

[Col. 1591A] May he live here in safety and seek life above the ether;

may he always possess your life in your citadel.

May I see him joyful, while I too remain joyful with him,

in heaven, with you, supreme God, in your citadel.

Amen—may this come to pass; may this truly be “Hosanna.”

Let us both ask this, sweet friend; farewell.

## VI. — PRAYER TO GOD

O eternal God, most holy Ruler of the world,

my mind seeks you, and my soul’s living power,

my praise, love, and glory; you, the honorable light of my heart,

restore the movement of my limbs and the use of my eyes,

and grant hearing to my ears and beloved work to my hands.

Whatever the earth contains, whatever the sea and heavens enclose,

and whatever everywhere feels, understands, exists, and lives,

[Col. 1591B] all things, created by your wisdom, have shone forth;

you give life to all, preserve all, and govern all by your mighty command.

Make me, supremely merciful, confess you with my whole heart,

speak of you with my tongue, learn of you in sound doctrine,

seek you with my hands, and pray to you with a pure mind.

You are the way, the power, the life, and the door of life;

you are the reward of work, the creator, and also the teacher.

Grant me now, wretched as I am, forgiveness, and release me from my sins;

make me willing to do good, able to know it in action, and rightly to approve it,

so that you may then grant me to behold your joyful face forever

and to gather the true fruits of joy.

## VII. — TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS BISHOP

[Note: [Col. 1591D] a He gives these verses to a distinguished bishop: for the most part admonitory and exhortatory, though without the assistance of the Graces of the Muses, and in accordance with what someone said of the parent of Roman eloquence:

“Without the Muses and Apollo, but nevertheless by the weight of their subject, if not by poetic genius, they will survive.”

This bishop, moreover, living in a distant region and carrying the torch of Christian faith before barbarian peoples, is indicated by the verse:

“This people is uncultivated, this people whom you yourself rule is harsh.”

And by another verse concerning the bond of mutual affection:

“Neither sea nor land, mountains, forest, or Alps

can obstruct him.”

It occurs to me that in this period the use of rare Latin names at baptism among the Franks was customary, although such names were often adopted for native persons, either in jest or for elegance and distinction. Thus this Praeclarus—whose memory is otherwise not very illustrious—may have had another personal name, just as the blessed Witta was called Wittanus Albinus, and Alcuin called John, bishop of Salisbury, “the Eagle.”]

Bishop of the Lord, living forever through your merits,

devout teacher in the world, great love of the people.

Praeclarus by name, illustrious also in skill as a teacher,

illustrious in authority, illustrious in office.

Holy priest, resplendent with apostolic mind,

you possess the joys of Christ as shepherd of the flock.

Cultivator of justice and lover of holy piety,

firm in duties, truthful in speech.

You are the Church’s distinction, the people’s praise, the clergy’s glory,

an example of life, a pattern of salvation’s aid.

Salt of the earth, or light of the world, and renowned city of Christ,

a jewel shining in the diadem of the eternal King.

May the eternal God graciously grant you, for many years,

to multiply the sacred flock.

Your tongue has power to open and close heaven,

[Col. 1592A] while you are placed on earth as heaven’s key-bearer.

Christ kindled you and set you as a lamp among the people,

so that you might shine for all through doctrine, peace, and faith.

Open for all the way of salvation through sacred teachings,

so that you may be the path of everlasting light for the people.

The times of this life are now full of dangers;

now the world’s honor falls, and it itself declines.

Those things that holy God foretold would come upon the world—

terrible signs—are arriving again and again.

Now the leafy fig tree sends forth blossoms from its bark,

signaling that summer days are hastening.

Thus these signs testify that the day of the Lord is near,

on which God, the pious and just King, will come.

Rescue, holy man, through pious admonitions and consecrated prayers,

the flock entrusted to you as shepherd, from the enemy,

[Col. 1592B] whose concern is to move around the sheepfolds

in order to slaughter, destroy, scatter, and injure.

Let your effort always be directed toward Christ’s flock,

so that you may preserve it unharmed and help it by gathering it together.

He, swelling with pride, fell from his lofty seat;

you, humble, climb to the heavenly kingdoms of heaven.

He urges what is lowly, but you always urge heavenly things;

he is full of deceit, while you are full of the love of God.

This was the work of the ancient Fathers throughout the world,

whose sayings the sacred page now sings.

The honor of their virtue is celebrated throughout the broad world,

and the heavenly page preserves their names.

This, this is the work and concern of a great shepherd in the world:

to multiply the talents entrusted to him.

For the heavenly Judge watches over human deeds,

[Col. 1592C] so that he may judge all according to their own merits.

The Lord will come, breathing flame and flashing with a cloud,

and he will examine human deeds together with their words.

Then the faithful servant will receive the gifts of his merits,

and joyful will enter the highest joys of God.

So that you may then deserve to be happy among the blessed,

let no labor in the world now be hard for you.

This people is uncultivated, this people whom you yourself rule is harsh,

but through the mercy of the gracious Lord it will become gentle.

Let gentle commands of salvation first be handed on

to minds ignorant in the newness of faith.

As tender infancy rejoices in milk,

so a strong man is able to retain strong sayings.

[Col. 1593A] Be everywhere a pious and prudent teacher of the peoples,

recognizing what is suitable for each person.

Give milk to the little ones, cherish those who are strong with bread;

with piety care for, nourish, and teach them all.

Let no dreadful temptation break your mind;

remain steadfast, and thus you will be able to conquer.

Fire tests gold, and temptation purifies the just,

so that the purer soul may seek the lofty stars.

This is the whole life of the just man: temptation;

but the patient person endures all things for the love of God.

What soldier will seize the palm without combat?

Unholy wars will provide great rewards for their own.

He already rejoices in his diadem who wins in the arena of war;

after the battles of earth he reigns in the citadel of heaven.

May Christ’s grace grant you to reign with Christ,

[Col. 1593B] supreme Father, shepherd, for all time.

And may your praise, reward, and glory remain forever,

with the saints in heaven, and fare well without end.

Remember me yourself; may Christ’s grace remember you,

bishop in the house of God; remember me yourself.

## VIII. — THE SAME TO THE SAME

At every hour, holy priest, the holy eyes of God

will see you devoted.

May the law of the Lord be sweeter to you than all honey,

and more precious than many thousands of gold.

Let the lights of the mind precede the steps of action;

do whatever you command with counsel.

Be a gentle ruler, everywhere mild and just,

an example to all through excellent conduct.

What you are accustomed to condemn, do not do yourself,

and let your speech be seasoned with wisdom and salt.

Let what God himself has given you suffice.

That servant is rich enough who possesses the Lord.

The devouring end destroys all the joys of the world;

then the poor just man gains the heavenly kingdoms.

Christ the illustrious King will come,

so that he may render to all their own merits,

and lead you and yours together above to the citadel,

so that you may live joyfully, possessing the blessed kingdoms.

## IX. — ALSO TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS BISHOP

Go more swiftly, my little sheet, to our Praeclarus,

who now serves God prosperously and peacefully,

and seek the illustrious dwelling of the illustrious teacher Praeclarus;

bring the holy peace of the bishop, the good man.

Love has penetrated our breast with an abiding flame;

love itself always burns with new warmth.

Neither sea nor land, mountains, forest, or Alps

can obstruct or impede its way,

so as to prevent this love, dear Father, from always surrounding

and penetrating your heart, beloved one.

Everyone is rich who abounds in friends;

no one can have more than is expedient.

[Col. 1594A] The best friend is clothed in Christ’s love;

a friend always loves, and will always be loved.

The Almighty always loves wisdom that loves him,

since wisdom is better than all treasures.

The knowledge of good things is always worthy of love;

the devoted teacher will be dear to the Lord.

Love not yourself, nor the world, but Christ alone,

so that no one may rightly reproach you in words.

Good reputation is not given by wealth, but by noble conduct;

piety does not lose whatever it gives to the wretched.

Eyes are of no use for seeing when the mind is blind;

deprived of light, they seek blind and wandering paths.

The greater you are, the more moderate you should be;

be fair to all, everywhere a pious ruler.

Live for God, live happily, and live forever;

a true, blessed, good life is life for God.

You will be joined as a joyful citizen to Christ forever;

he remains forever, and you too will always exist.

## X. — THE SAME TO PRAECLARUS

[Note: [Col. 1593D] a In this poem he shows that whatever is outstanding among the types of the Old Testament is wonderfully fulfilled in Christ the Lord. He uses a serpentine pattern in which the half-lines that begin a hexameter finish a pentameter—often in an inelegant and constrained fashion, but with ingenious variety of figures and an apt correspondence of likeness.]

Almighty Creator, gentle Ruler, stand by me;

grant gifts of the word, almighty Creator,

so that I may say what ancient things signify through figures,

and what Christ reveals, so that I may say it.

Your only Son, who with you created all things,

now recreates all things, your only Son.

In the beginning the Lord plants paradise in the East;

in the beginning the Lord forms the Church.

Fourfold rivers flowed forth from the face of paradise;

from Christ the fountain, fourfold rivers flow.

[Col. 1594C] God brought forth Adam, born of virgin earth;

he brought forth Jesus from a virgin mother.

He formed Eve from Adam’s side and gave her as wife to the man;

thus he formed the bride for Christ from his side.

Savage death subdued the wretched world to itself from the tree;

now savage death lies prostrate from the tree.

Thus the envious brother once brought death upon the just man;

so Judas, envious of Christ, brought death.

The earth felt the words of the curse through man;

through man the earth found peace.

The ark carries back the righteous, lest the swollen sea swallow them;

lest they perish in the world, the ark carries back the righteous.

For the wicked brother shamefully laughed at his naked father;

the wicked brother laughed at him hanging on the cross.

The only heir of the old man had been an acceptable sacrifice to the Father;

[Col. 1594D] the Savior of the world is the Father’s acceptable sacrifice.

Rebecca herself was properly married to a distinguished man;

the Church herself was married to Christ, the distinguished man.

Behold, the younger brother forestalls his elder brother with a gift;

behold, the younger people forestall the ancient people.

Joseph, bought in Egypt, drove away the famine;

Jesus was sold, and drove away the famine.

Pharaoh’s daughter found Moses in the river;

the barbarian people found Christ in the river.

[Col. 1595A] The sacred Lamb redeemed the fathers from the enemy in his blood;

the sacred Lamb has rescued us from the enemy by his blood.

The wave overwhelmed wickedness while the people walked across the sea;

now the wave has overwhelmed the wickedness of the whole world.

The spring of Marah was made sweet by the sweetness of the wood;

thus the spring of Marah was sweet from the wood of the cross.

Impiety murmurs, restored when manna comes;

Christ the bread is present, and impiety murmurs.

After the rock, twice struck with the rod, had brought forth streams,

Christ too, having suffered, afterward brought them forth.

The first law is written by the Lord on tablets of stone;

now it is written by the Lord on the tablets of the heart.

The law gave an indication that sinners would pay their penalties;

the law gave an indication that salvation would come.

The splendid tabernacle of God, constructed among the former people,

[Col. 1595B] is the Church of Christ, the splendid tabernacle of God.

This too is a lampstand distinguished by seven lamps,

which shines upon the world; this too is the lampstand.

[Note: [Col. 1595D] a “The ark of God is covered,” and so forth. The upper part of the ark, or its cover, was called *kappōreth* by the Hebrews, from *kāphar*, which includes the sense both of covering and of making propitiation. Here it is called a tablet; others call it the oracle or mercy seat. Cherubim in the form of male and female sat upon it, looking at one another. For its description, see Blessed Arias Montanus, in his book *On Sacred Structures*.]

The ark of God is covered by the propitiatory tablet;

the Church and Christ cover the ark of God.

It contains the tablets, the urn, and the scepter of triumph;

with Christ it contains the two tablets.

Here is the acceptable victim, and the altar, and he himself the priest;

for the offenses of the world, here is the acceptable victim.

He himself is preferred in honor to all his brothers

through chrism and gift; he himself is so to his brothers.

The bridal chamber of the virgin received him, while the harlot was rejected;

the bridal chamber of the virgin, the Church, received him.

Behold, two bearers bring back the cluster on a tree;

[Col. 1595C] behold, two peoples bring back Christ.

The offering and vow of the former people is consumed by sacred fire;

the rebellious tribe is consumed by sacred fire.

The heir of the law did not attain the Father’s blessed kingdoms;

Jesus dispenses the blessed kingdoms of the Father.

And the wicked possessor is driven outside by blows,

[Note: [Col. 1595D] b “When the devil is driven out together with vices,” and so forth. *Zabulus*, in place of *diabolus*, is frequently used by the holy Fathers; or it may derive from Greek *kakoboulia* (κακοβουλία), “craftiness and evil counsel,” and from such formations as *zátheos*, *zákotos*, and *zagreus*, in which, as Hesychius testifies, *za* (ζά) is intensive. Others observe, however, that *za* among the Aeolians and Attics sometimes also has the force of *dia* (διά), as in *zakoros*, “temple-keeper,” which Plutarch has as *diakoros*; and *zaballein* or *ziaballein*, in place of *diaballein*. Hence, by an easy derivation, comes *zabolos*, or *diabolos*. This is also what J. Lipsius had in view in book 1, chapter 16, *On Correct Pronunciation*, and the commentator on Martial, when in connection with *diaeta* in Epigram 43 of book II he observes that, in this form, Lampridius calls them *zetas* in the Aeolic dialect. And the great critical detractor of Saint Jerome, in his commentary on chapter 6 of the Letter to the Ephesians, says that among the Greeks *diabolus* means “accuser,” while among the Hebrews it means *katarrheonta* (καταρρέοντα), “one who flows downward,” because it has a certain similarity to *zabulon*, which signifies *katarrheonta*. He rejects this derivation as forced, recognizing only the division of the word which we call *diairophthō*, such as the common people use when they say *zeta* for *diaeta*. But the earlier etymology is more strongly confirmed by the ancient Scriptures, which express *zabulus* as though it came from *boulē* (βουλή), “counsel,” rather than *zabolus*.]

when the devil is driven out together with vices.

The ark of God destroys the walls while it circles the city;

thus the ark of God destroys the city of the world.

For a woman pierced the enemy’s temples with a stake;

and on the nail of the cross the enemy was likewise pierced.

The ark has a fleece, but the fleece is dry though drenched;

thus the fleece, dry while the whole threshing-floor is wet, is present.

The pitcher, lamp, and rattle drive away the hostile camp;

the Victor of victors drives away the hostile camp.

Jephthah, by the promised offering, overcomes his affection for his daughter in honor of God.

Samson, dying, struck down more hostile troops;

our Savior, dying, struck down more hostile troops.

You are every honor to your own people, who bring down Goliath by slaughter;

you, who conquer the world, are every honor to your own people.

You too are strong of hand, who crush the jaws of the lion;

strong of hand against the monstrous beast.

The peaceful king also built the walls of the temple;

Christ, the peaceful King, also built the Church.

Once the prophet, rejoicing, reached the stars in a golden chariot;

Christ, rejoicing, reached all the stars above.

[Col. 1596B] The prophet restores the boy from death, which the rod could not do;

what the law could not accomplish, the prophet restores from death.

For Jonah, swallowed, lay hidden in the belly of a fish;

thus Christ was swallowed in the belly of the earth.

He was indeed a good leader, to whom the peoples return from prison;

to life the just return; he was indeed a good leader.

All the prophets sang of the greatest gifts of God;

Christ fulfilled the greatest gifts of God.

The virgin Mary bore God, and a true human being;

the virgin, made pregnant by God, bore God.

The chaste heroine shines, with no one violating her modesty;

after the Child’s birth the chaste heroine shines.

The only one who came fulfilled the vows of those before him;

the only one who came confirmed our vows.

Thus this man, who is God, the long-desired hope of the righteous,

[Col. 1596C] is the hope of the righteous at the end—this man who is God.

Your presence, Christ, becomes glory for all the good;

for the wicked, every torment; for the good, every glory.

Great glory to you, truly triune and one God;

almighty Creator, great glory to you.

## XI. — TO FREDERIC, BISHOP

[Note: [Col. 1596D] c Frideric ascended from humble circumstances to the height of pontifical dignity, but he does not mention the cathedral in which he sat. The etymology of the German name *Friederich* yields a double meaning: it may signify the author of an initiated peace or alliance, and the avenger of one violated. Rudolph mentions in his catalogue of Rabanus’s books that Frideric wrote commentaries on the Octateuch at the request of Bishops Frecholtius, Frideric, and Humbert, the last of whom was bishop of Würzburg.]

Come, nourishing Spirit, and compose sweet verses for me,

so that you may grant me to send gifts to my beloved Father.

As soon as he became known, he clung to me as a faithful friend,

not because of my merit, but because of his goodness.

The Spirit, seeing him full of the gift of piety,

[Col. 1597A] raised him from a humble to an exalted position.

In him the true Gospel saying was proved,
