which remains established by the Savior’s spoken word:

“He who makes himself humble will be exalted on high,

but he who seeks proud things falls headlong into the depths.”

Thus, dear Father, holy bishop and priest,

the Lord has raised you far above many,

so that with clear speech you may proclaim the word in faith,

and be the way and leader of the people to God’s sacred kingdoms.

Christ called you the light of the world and also the lamp;

he called you the salt of the earth—remember this devoutly.

Let your light shine upon the world like the radiant sun;

let your work become great glory to God.

Establish good doctrine in wavering hearts of sinners,

lest they putrefy in evil and the worm consume them.

I ask you to consider your name and see what it contains,

and thus immediately you can learn what your deeds should be.

It admonishes you piously, resounding: “Avenge the covenant”—

a phrase which properly bears a double meaning.

May your vengeance sever the covenant with human vices,

and may it piously strengthen Christ’s covenant everywhere.

For your parents gave you this name long ago,

when at your baptism you received your allotted name.

Now too may this name greatly suit you;

ponder it and learn the mystical gifts of God.

For you are called, piously, a bishop or overseer,

which admonishes you always to act prudently.

Thus, good Father, make yourself now what you are called,

and your action is worthy of either meaning of your name.

Be diligent, an honorable shepherd over all,

and let a worthy vengeance defend God’s covenant.

Remember us, and persist in consecrated prayers

for those who are devoted to you, pious one, always and everywhere.

For by constant prayer and vows we knock upon Christ,

asking that he rightly govern your years from heaven.

This too we all ask with faithful mouth;

this I, Rabanus, also ask, Frideric:

that you may live safely for a long time on earth,

and afterward climb to the heavenly kingdoms of heaven.

What I ask, do at the sacred altars as you stand,

that you may return me to Christ, holy Father, through your prayers;

may Christ, King of heaven and King of earth, Creator of the world,

grant me with you a place in the realm of light.

## XII. — TO OTGAR, ARCHBISHOP

[Note: [Col. 1598D] a This is the fifth archbishop of Mainz after Saint Boniface. Concerning him see book IV of the *History of Mainz*, where he is said to have occupied the see from the year of the Lord 826 until 847. Consult also the *Fuldensian Antiquities*. Because of the friendship he had with the distinguished bishop, Rabanus wrote for him not only these verses and an epitaph, but also a commentary on Wisdom and, as Sigebert reports under the year 827, one on Ecclesiasticus, and dedicated them to him.]

[Col. 1597D] Nourishing Spirit, come, sent down from the heavenly citadel,

so that you may grant sacred gifts to your servant.

Fill the secret places of my breast; grant gifts to my tongue,

so that I may sing pleasing verses to my beloved Father.

From the first moment I saw him, I loved him always;

to him I now wish good things, joyful things, and a place in heaven’s citadel.

O Father, O shepherd, to whom Christ has already given heavenly gifts

and the task of feeding the people in his place,

you are the renewer, hope, ruler, and honor of your homeland,

[Col. 1598A] sweet love to all, worthy of God’s love.

Open for all the way of salvation through sacred teachings,

so that you may be the path of everlasting light for the people.

The times of this life are now full of dangers;

now the world’s honor falls, and it itself will soon collapse.

Those things that God and Christ foretold would come upon the world—

terrible signs—arrive again and again.

Nation rises against nation, kingdom against kingdom;

they arise for war, peace perishes, the enemy rejoices.

Famine and pestilence torture and press hard,

and death, bitter death, weighs upon the peoples on earth.

Thus these signs testify that the day of the Lord is near,

on which God, the pious and just King, will come.

Rescue, holy man, through pious admonitions and consecrated prayers,

the flock entrusted to you as shepherd from the enemy,

[Col. 1598B] lest the fierce one destroy him whom the true Son of the Most High

rightfully redeemed with his own blood.

Behold, the king of earth commands that firm covenants be preserved,

and wishes his law and commands to be obeyed.

Thus the heavenly King commands that divine precepts be taught

and that his admonitions be rightly followed.

Nor does he permit human things to be preferred by wicked judgment

to divine things; rather, he wishes the latter to prevail.

He prefers the law of heaven to excel and to be held in heaven’s citadel

over worldly law and business alike.

Earthly law is indeed useful here in many matters,

but heavenly law alone will be wholesome.

In it alone true wisdom shines,

in which lie praise, reward, life, and the salvation of human beings.

Love this law above all perishable riches and treasures,

[Col. 1598C] Father, and hold it firmly.

It exalts you unharmed, preserves and protects you,

and is itself pleasing to all.

He who follows Christ will rejoice in the heavenly citadel,

possessing the kingdoms of heaven together with the saints.

Follow him rightly, as I ask, and preserve his footsteps;

always in this life, and thus you too will be victorious.

You will crush your enemies and yourself penetrate heaven;

freed, you will always rejoice while remaining in the citadel of light.

May eternal God, the gentlest creator of the world,

may Christ the Savior himself, grant this to you.

May he protect and govern you in soundness for a long life,

increase you in the titles and merits of your virtues,

so that your glory may grow through manifold praise

with the Lord and the saints, always in heaven’s citadel.

[Col. 1598D] Behold, I have sung these sixty verses,

wishing you the highest blessings, holy Father.

May you be sound in doctrine and perfect in conduct,

a servant rightly following the perfect Lord.

Live gratefully for God; thus live happily forever,

for a blessed and good life is life for God.

May your life prosper in safety, most holy shepherd;

may your life prosper forever.

And may you help me by praying, commending me

[Col. 1599A] to the Lord as you pray before the heavenly scepters; may you help me by your prayers.

May I, remaining in the citadel of light, share joys with you—

remaining in the citadel of the light of eternal life.

## XIII. — TO BRUNWARD, CHOREPISCOPUS

[Note: [Col. 1599C] a In the usage of nearly this period, *chorepiscopus* or *coepiscopus* meant what we now commonly call a suffragan: a bishop’s vicar in pontifical functions. Examples are readily found, including in Rabanus’s own books. As for Brunward, whom Rabanus praises as bishop and shepherd, it is not stated whether he served Haistulf or Otgar at Mainz, or whom elsewhere he may have served. Lambert, in his *Chronicle* under the year 846, mentions a Brunwart who was otherwise the celebrated abbot of the monastery of Hersfeld. From this you may recognize him as a contemporary and associate of Rabanus, since the church of Hersfeld was dedicated by Rabanus. The examples of Saint Wigbert and Albuin of Fritzlar show that abbots at that time also held the office of chorepiscopus. You may therefore reasonably suppose that this Brunward served as a bishop in Thuringia under Otgar and afterward obtained the governance of that very great monastery. Flodoard, in book III, chapter 24 of his *History*, mentions that Hincmar, archbishop of the Church of Rheims, wrote to this Brunward when he entrusted to him the possessions of Saint Remigius and the tenants of the Church of Rheims established in Thuringia.]

By these few verses, let me commit greetings to you,

beloved teacher; sweet friend, farewell.

O, what should I call you, so that there may be no dispute?

Do you seek what everyone calls you, or something else?

Tell me, Pierian Muses, by what name should I name him,

whom I commemorate in song, with mouth, mind, and hand?

In this powerful appearance, in this sacred order,

I do not know what deception of the name lies in the first part.

[Note: [Col. 1599D] b “The last … syllable.” There is a pun on *Brunward*, a disyllable, as with the names formerly given to slaves. For *bruin* in German means “dark” or “black.” It is necessary to investigate what *ward*, “bright,” signifies in this alteration of languages. But *wurt* or *wurd*, “that which is valued,” easily opens a path to this source. Hence among the Germans *endoxoi* (ἔνδοξοι) and *eugeneis* (εὐγενεῖς), “illustrious” and “noble,” are called, by an equivalence of meaning, *lieb und wardt*, “dear and worthy,” for distinguished men.]

The last makes him illustrious, while the first makes him dark;

the syllable itself gives no certain rule.

[Col. 1599B] The Pierian Muses say so, and Maurus himself agrees;

there is neither disagreement nor deception hidden in the name.

God exalted you from humble circumstances to the highest place in the world,

so that you might be a ruler, love, and glory to the peoples.

The first syllable reminds you of what you were;

the last praises what you are: light, mirror, bishop in God’s house.

Thus I think the bride sings in the Song of Songs

what virtue and what labor confer upon her.

“I am black, but beautiful,” daughter of the heavenly kingdom,

and “terrible as an army arrayed in beauty.”

I ask you to be a gracious maker of your name,

so that word may agree with work and faith:

you are God’s eternal city and the lights of the world;

Christ appointed you to guard his camp.

You are living fountains and the sacred rivers of paradise;

[Col. 1599C] teachers of the people, the flock’s praise and leaders,

salt of the earth, precious stones in Christ’s diadem;

you are his mother, brother, and sister.

[Col. 1600A] Therefore multiply the talents through pious labor and teaching,

so that you may receive the greatest rewards in heaven.

Lest the Judge, coming and ready to seek out the treasure,

find it shamefully buried in the earth.

Be an example and model of right conduct to all,

a cultivator of justice and a lover of piety.

I ask that your innermost heart be drunk with divine praise;

let no impious cups of Bacchus weigh upon your heart.

Visit Christ’s walls more often in your vigils,

and pray to God yourself for both yourself and your own people.

Remember to praise the Lord seven times a day,

as the Psalmist David sings from the mouth of God.

From this your glory grows through manifold praise,

with Christ and the saints, enduring in heaven’s citadel.

Remember me also, I testify by the scepters of the Thunderer.

[Col. 1600B] You, Father and shepherd, remember me yourself.

Live happily for God; live happily forever,

possessing the blessed kingdoms with Christ and the saints.

## XIV. — TO RATGAR, HIS ABBOT

[Note: [Col. 1599D] c Concerning Ratgar, the third abbot of the Church of Fulda, although much is found in the books of the *Fuldensian Antiquities*, I shall nevertheless provide some material here, thanks to a very ancient manuscript catalogue of abbots:

“Ratgar was born in the German regions of noble parents and was received by Saint Sturm into the monastery of Fulda. He succeeded Bangulf in the governance of the abbey in the year of the Lord 802 and was deposed in the year of the Lord 817. He governed the monastery nobly for sixteen years and, like a wise architect, joining the western church to another with marvelous skill and immense size, made one church. He sent Rabanus and Hatto to Albinus the teacher at Tours, to learn the liberal arts; Brunus to Einhard, a most skilled teacher of various arts; Modestus Candidus, with others, to Clement the Scot, to study grammar. But through gold and silver, crowns, lamps, and all good things, he gloriously advanced this place. This venerable Father also built a monastery of praiseworthy and well-proportioned dimensions on the mountain which the precious martyr Boniface named Mount of the Bishop; he had it dedicated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, by Haistulf, archbishop of the Church of Mainz, and at the entrance to the cloister of that church, on the right, he was committed to burial, old and full of good days. Aegil succeeded him.”

As for Clement the Scot: if he is the same man who in 745 was condemned for heresy by Saint Boniface and Pope Zacharias in a Roman synod, was shut away in a monastery somewhere, came to his senses there, and in extreme old age lived as a penitent, I might say that he gnawed his nails and fingers over the rules of grammar. Here Rabanus shows his devotion to vowed poverty, since he would not even claim the fruits of his own ingenuity without his prelate’s gracious permission.]

You, gracious Father, excellent man and shepherd of monks,

I, your servant, call upon you favorably.

May your gracious goodness now hear me, wretched as I am,

as I cry to you, everywhere a pious ruler.

Your goodness has already granted me the opportunity to study books,

but poverty suffocates my ingenuity.

Whatever my teachers have taught me orally,

lest my wandering mind lose it, I committed it all to leaves.

Hence glosses and little books now remain,

[Col. 1600C] which I ask you to order returned to the unworthy man.

Whatever servants possess is held by right under their masters’ authority;

thus everything I have written is yours by right.

[Col. 1601A] I do not arrogantly claim these writings as my own,

but submit them all to your judgment.

Whether you grant these things to me or not, nevertheless may the Divinity

of the Almighty always give you every good thing,

and may you complete the good contest in an honorable course,

so that you may remain forever with Christ in heaven’s citadel.

## XV. — TO AEGIL, ON THE BOOK HE WROTE

[Note: [Col. 1601D] a He appears to have inscribed these verses to Aegil, who was still his contemporary. We have already made public the Life of this Aegil, written by Candidus.]

When the pious law of God rules the broad world as its lord,

how holy indeed it is to write the law of God.

That labor is pious; no other work is worthy

to be compared with it by human hands.

For the eyes rejoice in seeing what the fingers have written,

and the mind turns over the mystical words of God in understanding.

No work arises that ancient age will not assail,

that wicked time will not overturn.

Letters alone are free from fate and repel death;

letters alone renew what has passed in books.

For the finger of God carved letters on suitable rock

when he gave the law to his people.

Things that are, that were, and that perhaps will come in the world—

writing displays them all in its speech.

## XVI. — ALSO TO THE SAME

A priest in age and merits, gracious priest,

Aegil, may Christ our God save you in the world.

Be for me what I ask and desire; be kind:

teacher, shepherd, always my friend and honor.

Let your correcting words not distress me,

since I know that you always hold a friendly heart.

I tell you the truth, and my judgment does not deceive me:

I wish to hold you alone, above many, in my heart.

Remain always the same for me, since I am always the same for you;

a friend always loves, and will always be loved.

May the Almighty Lord, supreme ruler of Olympus,

protect you unharmed at every hour.

May he preserve you on earth and lead you to heaven’s citadel;

may he bring me there with you as well, sweet friend.

## XVII. — TO GERHOH, THE PRIEST

[Note: [Col. 1601D] b He adorns Gerhoch the librarian with his verses and says that his name derives from bearing an arrow. I do not know whether *Gerhoch* meant “arrow” among the ancient Germans; certainly, by the usage of this vernacular speech, it clearly expresses the effect of an arrow: *garhoch*, that is, “very high.” Hence some report that an arrow is so called because, shot from the bowstring, it travels a considerable distance.]

Powerful with keys, brother, and sharing a name with the arrow,

may I be permitted to bring these little verses to you.

The pen suddenly snatched them from the mouth of the dictating speaker,

and the weary Muse gave them at an unusual time.

May sacred verses resound for you, dearest brother;

may Christ always be a song in your mouth.

[Col. 1602A] He himself was the chosen arrow in the mouth of the prophets;

he is the key of David, the wisdom and height of God.

May he mercifully preserve you through unending years,

always rejoicing with him in heaven’s citadel.

What can I say about the great praise of the books

which you, beloved brother, hold under your key—

whatever God directed from heaven into the world

through the pious words of sacred Scripture for human beings?

There you will find whatever the wisdom of the world

brought forth into public view at various times.

May these delights, overflowing with abundant piety,

delight, hold, and possess you.
may they hold.

Have nothing to do with the world, since the whole world passes away,  
and likewise its splendor and its beauty.  
For the Word of God, and the honorable student of the Word,  
endure forever in perpetual light.

Live for God a happy life, and live throughout the ages.  
Indeed, blessed and good is life lived for God.

May the sweet love of Christ, and the sweet little dwelling,  
be your sweet song, sweet friend, your own.  
As you stand at the sacred altars, remember me also;  
may the great grace of God likewise remember you.

As you read these things, may you prosper happily for many years,  
and, as you read these things with the choir of brothers, may you prosper.

### XVIII.—Also to the Same Man

May almighty God, dearest brother,  
always preserve you safely and prosperously through every season.

May you remain unharmed, and ask for safety for us as well,  
so that God himself, the author, may grant peaceful things.

Thus the Psalmist teaches: “Ask for the things that belong to peace”;  
this abundance belongs to the city of God and to the one who loves it.

May your mind, disturbed by no fear, preserve peace,  
and may it not fear the crimes of wicked discord.

So may you always love, brother, and so may you again always be loved,  
so that mutual love may never cease.

Let us persist in prayers and in praise of the Thunderer;  
may the Evening Star see this, may the Morning Star see this.

Let us ask pardon, let us ask Christ for gifts:  
may he free us from punishments and increase our merits.

Almighty Creator, Redeemer of heaven and the world,  
I ask that Christ preserve us together in peace;

so that, just as he and the Father are truly always one,  
he may likewise make us one in himself.

### XIX.—To Samuel the Priest

**Note:** The seven epigrams that follow were written in memory of and friendship for Samuel the priest. Of him I have discovered nothing else, except what Rabanus himself transmitted: that he had once been Rabanus’s fellow student and companion at Tours, had Albinus as their common teacher, and finally, separated from Rabanus by great distances of lands and rivers, had held the office of teacher somewhere. But on examining the matter more carefully, it appears that this same Samuel was afterward raised from being abbot of the once highly distinguished monastery of Lorsch, in the Rhenish region of the Palatinate, to the see of Worms; and in the year 847 he sat with Rabanus among his fellow bishops at the celebrated synod of Mainz, as can be gathered from the synodal letter, which is read in volume III of the Councils and elsewhere. (See above among the letters of Rabanus.) The records of the Church of the Vangiones agree, reporting that in this same year, on 15 October, he dedicated a church at Neuhausen in honor of Saint Cyriacus.

My strength and the anchor of my weary affairs,  
my shipwreck and my safe shore and land:

you alone are our honor, ever most faithful city,  
safe rest for my mind amid its afflictions and cares.

Although mountains and fields with waves lie between us,  
my mind is with you, confined by no earthly soil.

My mind follows you, and the song of love follows as well,  
wishing in my heart every good thing for you.

May Christ, who made you known to me and granted you as a friend,  
preserve you everywhere safe for me.

Before the revolving cycle of earth and heaven itself  
passes away, may our love also never cease.

This I have advised you, Father; I advise it now and shall advise it again:  
remember me, just as I myself remember you.

May God join in the palace of heaven, rejoicing together,  
those whom he here on earth joined as friends.

### XX.—Also to the Same Man

May the eternal God, the holiest creator of human beings,  
the Most High who holds the starry citadel of heaven,

who sees and, as mighty ruler, governs every abyss,  
exalt, save, preserve, love, and adorn you;

and grant you the merit and place of your namesake  
[Note: Samuel the prophet],

who was here a servant and lover of the symbolic temple,  
and grant that you possess all the honor of Samuel, Samuel’s namesake.

Remember the one whom the final syllable of your own name indicates  
[Note: ED, “the name of God”];  
and let this praise of your heart be the ardor of love.

May life be yours, salvation yours, and the way, glory, and strength yours;  
May your Protector and Ruler preserve you through all the ages.

### XXI.—Also to Samuel the Priest

He who holds the summit of heaven and the earth together,  
who governs the waves of the sea and the stars,

before whom stand all things that were, that are, and that will be,  
and who himself sees all things—

may he guard your fruitful labor,  
preparing worthy rewards for you in the kingdom of heaven.

Remember me, then, as you stand at the sacred altars,  
holy bishop of God; may God likewise remember you.

But if I can secretly bring you something by whispering it,  
I shall willingly accomplish something worthy in my prayers.

May the Lord grant to both of us the gift of life, already brought to completion by prayers.  
Farewell, sweet friend.

### XXII.—To Samuel the Priest

My mind is ready, my senses are ready; receive my vow.  
Do not despise your companion: a friend always loves.

Neither storm will shake this man, nor the turbulent South Wind,  
nor, surely, can the North Wind bind him with ice.

Freedom of spirit spends the gift of love;  
it is worthy that love itself summon the devout mind.

There was no one in the world whom age did not consume;  
for whoever can do so, always obeys the friend.

I, Rabanus, ask you, Samuel, as my elder,  
to weigh these things and read them all with justice.

May Christ God in the heavenly citadel always preserve you both;  
ask this yourself, Father, and farewell without end.

Once I rejoiced that you were my companion,  
among the readers, beloved brother, to me.

Now also I rejoice that you retain the rights of a teacher,  
that you grow in virtue and occupy the place of a father.

Remember me, then, as you stand at the sacred altars;  
I remember you—so remember me.

May your heart hold what Albinus, the proper teacher, once taught,  
and may your whole work approve it.

Thus may the gracious favor of Christ remain with you;  
thus may it lead me with you to the stars. Farewell.

### XXIII.—Also to the Same Man

You are my beloved; may you please Christ above the heavens;  
may you be dear to the saints—you are my beloved.

Be my one and only, and may the one Author protect you;  
be my one and only together with many.

May Christ the lover fill you with every good thing,  
and may the Spirit of God himself fill you with every good thing.

May divine power grant you every best thing;  
in my prayer I ask every best thing for you.

May you remain and flourish safely forever;  
here and in eternity may you remain and flourish.

Illustrious Samuel, live, prosper, and hear in the greatest joy:  
this is the end of the word—illustrious one, live and prosper.

### XXIV.—To Samuel the Priest

Please gratefully receive these tablets,  
which your devoted junior has presented to you.

The boxwood signifies old age, and the secluded cloister  
the counsel of the heart. You, gracious Father, farewell.

### XXV.—To Samuel the Priest

May you be happy, safe, and always joyful everywhere;  
may the almighty Lord protect and guide you.

You live in my mind; may you live for Christ through the ages,  
living with the saints and possessing the blessed kingdoms.

I copied these six verses in a short time;  
may the heavens receive you, perfected in old age  
[Note: In the neuter plural, as in Fortunatus].

### XXVI.—To Isanbert the Priest

**Note:** Isanbert, whose name Baturicus wrote shortly before, is said according to its Latin derivation to be “famous through iron”; his epitaphs show the man more fully.

Receive, Father, the first fruits of my Muse, this brief poem,  
and favor our studies as a pious man.

Since you are worthy to resolve learned poems,  
forgive ours when you see that they are rustic.

All the insignia of virtues indeed establish a name for you,  
by which you may become famous and worthy of honor:

iron marks you as strong, renowned, and adorned with virtue;  
through many paths of skill you grow.

May the Lord enthroned on high, the gracious Creator of all things,  
bless you with virtue and increase you in merits,

and may the grace of Christ preserve you mindful of me.  
Always and forever, sweet friend, farewell.

### XXVII.—To the Exiled Priest

You spoke strong words, exhortatory sayings,  
bringing such an example of the belly upon your lips.

For the Apostle commands the members to be concerned for themselves,  
and does not exclude the sluggish belly from this.

It is right for the feet to run, for the eyes to see,  
for the ears to hear, and for the mouth to utter words.

Therefore, if only the hands offer food to the belly,  
all the members together strive to satisfy it.

One prepares coverings and seeks suitable adornment;  
another takes up a shield for battle, another seizes weapons.

Let the belly have food, let food serve the belly;  
God himself will quickly destroy both this and that.

But to me it seems common and just  
that the care and labor of the members should be equal.

Just as the hand serves its work, so also let the belly  
compete in giving counsel and admonishing all things.

A house defended on one side lies open to the enemy;  
but whatever is fortified on every side remains safe.

Be provident in mind, cautious always in action;  
prudently beware of all things and fear no sadness.

May Christ be victorious; such is true victory:  
whoever follows this King remains himself victorious.

I have written as many verses as there are hours in the day,  
always wishing that you yourself may be safe.

### XXVIII.—To Irmingild

Christ, almighty Wisdom of the Most High Father,  
who rules all things by holding together the lowest with the highest,

preserve forever for me the friend whom I love,  
so that he may flourish safely, seeking the heavenly kingdoms.

May he increase in merits as he grows through the passage of time,  
gathering blessed gifts after death.

I pray, holy Mary, that you, Virgin and untouched Mother  
of the Thunderer God, obtain this by your prayers.

And you, apostolic band, with Peter first in your order,  
ask God earnestly with your summoned brethren.

You, forerunner and prophet of God, bridegroom's friend, and martyr,  
with the company of prophets, repeatedly ask this.

So I ask you to do this, Levite and protomartyr,  
and you, Stephen, with your companions, praying for the heavenly scepters.

All you righteous, chosen, and blessed, ask this:  
that God grant Buolo a kingdom above the stars.

**Note:** Either Buolo received the name Irmingild by another designation, or he is praying well for a third friend. The middle of the poem has been cut away, and therefore the beginnings of the following, quite long poem, *On the Patience of the Saints*, have also been lost.

In this way, loving Father, while there is time, seek the kingdom;  
do not cease seeking it, so that you may grasp and desire it.

The power of the heavenly court suffers violence, and the violent seize the stars;  
whoever struggles well now receives future gifts.

You have struggled bravely, and now strive to bring down the enemy;  
a crown is rightly given at the end to the victor.

Let your mouth resound with Christ, and let your palm feed the needy.  
Let your foot visit the sick; let your heart think upon God.

Let the Author perceive that you serve him wholly outwardly;  
and let God himself claim you wholly inwardly.

These things I have depicted for you, holy Father, in a wishing poem,  
so that you may become happy through knowing the sacred teachings.

This also I ask of God, while properly singing through the psalms:

[lacuna]

*(The rest is missing, approximately four leaves having been lost.)*

### XXIX.—To Bonosus

**Note:** I interpret this man as having been Rabanus’s equal in studies and as having succeeded him in the office of abbot, under the different name Hatto. The hexameters that he wrote to him sufficiently indicate that he excelled in the art of painting. Concerning Hatto, an old manuscript catalogue of abbots says: “Hatto, called Bonosus and glorious, took up the governance of the abbey in the year of the Lord 841 and governed it for twenty-two years discreetly and modestly, in the manner of Moses, of whom it is written: ‘He was the meekest of all human beings.’ He was discreet and gentle toward his subjects, but toward the powerful of the world he had been exceedingly serious and just. Endowed with perpetual virginity, he brought the monastery to great prosperity and ended his present life with a glorious death in the year of the Lord 842.” Nor would I rashly affirm that this was the abbot Bonosus to whose questions Rudolphus reports, in the Catalogue, that Rabanus composed a book on the intermixture of kinship and on avoiding magical art.

One day smiles; tomorrow, stripped of all, laments;  
there is nothing fixed—how can a happy die provide it?

Bright summer gleams; autumn will bring shadows.  
Spring blossoms with jewels; savage winter takes them away.

What, then, is there that does not flee swiftly on hurried wings,  
and what is not varied beneath the vault of heaven?

Sluggish old age bends the lofty pines;  
it dissolves rocks and dries up rivers.

While we speak, the tall crop is green, will ripen, and wither  
[Note: *Maturet et*, “and will ripen”; from the unusual verb *matureo*].

The violets turn white; the dark lilies fall.

The rose itself sooner lays aside its lovely garments,  
and the wild flowers soon follow it.

Brief is the use of all these things, and all are under a stepmother’s law;  
they alternate in turn and perish together.

Yet you believe that what the deceitful hour lends you  
you will always possess forever and in the same condition.

Little by little old age raises wretched people to their desires;  
and just now we were—now we cease to be.

The child suddenly rises higher from the nurse’s lap  
and marvels to produce a sound with his harsh voice.

Already the beard is swift to appear, already the hair is dyed by death;  
already he will lean toward the earth and become death’s prey.

Age carries everything away, and the end has deprived everything;  
nothing remains eternal, and the ages pass.

All things have their appointed time—except the one Author of time,  
who was, is always, and remains without end.

Love him always; confess him with your whole heart;  
ask him in prayers, and he will give you gracious things.

Do not let worldly instability disturb you, holy brother,  
with its many-changing whirlpools.

Thus it was, is, and will be: the order of the changeable age;  
let no one place certain trust in joy.

The people of the saints suffer many things in the world,  
by a hidden judgment—and I cannot know why.

I believe that he has never despised his servants,  
and that he has helped them sufficiently when they ask for what they desire.

For another life is reserved for his own in the citadel of the heavens,  
where gracious peace flourishes and no battles are fought.

This life has always been a just trial,  
as the flame of a furnace tests golden vessels.

Thus almighty God tested the saints through savage  
blows, afterward returning joyful rewards to heaven.

Stand firm, I pray; remember Christ, and remember the fathers  
whom the gracious page has sung into your ears.

Be strong in spirit, provident in word and action;  
the saints were such—be close to them.

Remember, I pray, that Abel, the most righteous, was the first victim  
of fratricidal slaughter.

Remember how Noah was shamefully mocked and cursed  
by his wicked offspring, through whom the human race was restored.

Remember how the holy Abram defeated kings after capturing Lot,  
and what sufferings he himself endured at their hands.

Remember the losses Isaac often suffered in wells,  
when the Philistine land was raging with envy.

How many tears did Jacob shed for his offspring?  
And how much did Joseph suffer in the world?

That pious leader—he laid all Egypt low  
while rescuing the people of God from the scourges.

How he was despised, and what he provided for his people;  
how he was dragged through disgraceful insults.

For how often did Samuel endure Saul’s afflictions?  
And did not David, hiding, flee the impious scepter?

How did he afterward suppress the anger of his offspring toward the kingdom,  
and endure very many shameful words from others?

Indeed, my Muse cannot recount all the thousands of punishments  
that the saints suffered.

Elijah, Daniel, Isaiah, Micah, Jonah,  
Jeremiah, Jaddo, the father Job, and Tobias—

those who once were like the lights of the world:  
what savage punishments they endured in the body.

Flaming heat consumed very many others,  
and stones others, and the sword still others.

Thus the saints, strong in faith, conquered their battles  
and performed the greatest works of righteousness.

Why recall ancient things, when the holy Catholic Church  
now rejoices throughout the world, shining with martyrdom?

She gleams brightly, illuminated by the apostolic trophy,  
and bears the banner of the cross while Christ reigns.

Therefore the Lord wished so many of his own  
to endure labors here, whom he carries to the heavenly kingdoms.

For this reason let us always love heavenly things,  
which will remain in heaven, rather than things that will perish on earth.

Let us now raise no murmuring voices to heaven,  
but sing of the Lord, who is merciful and good.

For God is not to be blamed for these blows;  
rather, our life must quickly be led toward what is better.

His mercy must be piously bent by our prayers,  
so that he may remove the scourges from us.

The father embraces with devoted love the son whom he has begotten;  
yet he will often give him harsh and grievous lashes.

Therefore let no dreadful temptation ever overcome your mind;  
be strong everywhere.

If anything has displeased Christ, who now sees all things,  
in your conduct and character, correct it quickly.

The heavenly law commands this, as do the fatherly ordinances;  
brotherly love commands it—strive to do this.

Make yourself now ready with all your strength,  
so that wherever you arrive no sadness may arise.

May the holy power of the Author grant this to you,  
and may the Most High God in his citadel grant it to us with you.

The pipe of old Maurus has sung these things in its hours,  
for you, beloved holy Bonosus.

### XXX.—Also to the Same Man

**Note:** “Although painting is dearer to you than every art…” The writer’s art contends here with the art of painting, which Bonosus vaunted more highly. He greatly prefers writing to the delicate invention of painting, demonstrating that writing is useful, pleasant, necessary to the human race, and even shown by God himself.

Although painting may be more pleasing to you than every art,  
I ask you not to despise, ungrateful man, the labor of writing.

nor the effort, study, and care of singing and reading;  
for writing is worth more than a vain form in an image,

and provides more beauty for the soul than false painting of colors,  
which displays representations of things improperly.

For sacred Scripture is the perfect rule of salvation,  
and has greater power in matters and greater usefulness in all things.

It is readier for tasting, more perfect in meaning,  
and easier for human senses to retain through its art.

It serves the ears, lips, and eyes;  
painting offers only a few consolations to the eyes.

Writing shows truth in appearance, truth in speech,  
truth in meaning; it is pleasing for a long time.

Painting feeds the sight while fresh, but burdens it when old;  
it soon fails and is not a reliable guarantor of truth.

Consider who the authors and followers of these things were;  
then you will be able most certainly to know

which things ought to be produced for you by art.

**Note:** “At first Egypt painted the lights of shadows…” Thus Pliny, *Natural History* XXXV.3, and his interpreters, although they report that painting was invented six thousand years ago before it passed into Greece, as a vain boast. He first places among the stages of the art the outline of a human shadow drawn around its edges; then an image expressed in single colors, called monochrome; finally, the Babylonians interwove various colors in paintings. On these matters see Caelius Rhodiginus, books VIII.11 and XXIX.24, and the *monogrammoi* in the *Adages*. Rabanus is supported here against Bonosus by the distinctive praise of the art: when the painter himself speaks, he speaks badly; but when the painting speaks, it speaks well indeed, for the work then speaks and commends its maker. The etymology of Egypt given here is traced more deeply to the Hebrew *Misraim*, the name of Ham’s son, said to signify tribulation and straits, as is clear from the root.

At first Egypt painted the lights of shadows;  
it formed the lights by varying them with dyes and shadows.

This word sounds like “narrowing,” like “tribulation”;  
it becomes and signifies what narrows and afflicts—little help from an art that has been discovered.

But the Lord carved the rock of the Law together with writing;  
he conferred its distinctions and entrusted the people’s commands to their teacher.

**Note:** “The mountain signifies that measure of mine and a just amphora…” This obscure verse may be understood if, by “mountain,” it receives Sinai or Sinai in the wilderness of Paran, on whose summit God gave Moses the Law written on stone tablets. For the Hebrews, Sinai or Sin means “thornbush”; in Syriac it means “enmity.” Rabanus, however, interprets it here as “measure” or “amphora.” Since *Sin* is far removed from the meaning of *middah* or *ḥad*, one may suspect that Rabanus confused *Sin* and *Hin*, since the well-known *hin* is a kind of measure in Scripture and the Latin translator rendered it somewhere as a sextarius; through careless use of such matters he may have assigned this word’s etymology to Mount Sin and Sinai. A theologian friend skilled in the language explained it in this way, conjecturing that this etymology may perhaps have been presented to Rabanus because, with *vel* understood as “or,” *Zehina*—“Behold, my hin,” that is, “measure or amphora”—may perhaps have sounded so to him. But I would more readily ask that Saint Augustine be believed here than that Rabanus had the secrets of that language in mind and before his eyes. Augustine, in commenting on Psalm 67, interpreted Sinai as a boundary and a kind of enclosure of the region of Judea; Jerome Lauretus also observed this in his *Forest of Allegories*.

The mountain signifies that measure of mine, and a just amphora.

An amphora signifies justice, a life measured with moderation.

The commands also show that we are bound to the Lord by the Law.

**Note:** “Why labor to proclaim more written compositions?” Although Rabanus is not a very careful observer of quantity in his poetry, I thought he must rather have written: “What labor is it?” Otherwise the verse could not be scanned in any other way:

“What labor is it to proclaim more compositions in writing?”

He commends the ability to write, praised by us elsewhere (*Antiquities of Fulda*), which, for Rabanus and the Middle Ages, was desired by noble monasteries and libraries, indeed by the commonwealth itself, before the invention of printing, and was supremely necessary. He makes God its author: God, who gave the Law and the tablets written by his own finger to Moses. This also permits us to refer to the most ancient prophets and to their leader Moses, who, according to Isaiah’s wording, wrote for the Lord with his own hand. “And what in this field is more divine?” Jesus, bending down, was writing with his finger on the ground (John 8). “I, Paul, have written with my own hand.” And: “The greeting is in the hand of Paul.” Among the opinions of the ancients is the statement that hands are certain ministers of reason and wisdom. From their easy and innate movement innumerable arts have flowed into the human race: architecture, cultivation of the fields, the making, use, and harmonious music of instruments of every kind; the abundant resources of clothing, armor, metalwork, and navigation, for ornament and utility; finally, all things subject to human authority in the world are perceived and managed through the skill of hands. But our subject is the two broadly extending arts of painting and writing; and since Rabanus prefers the latter to the former, let anyone who wishes read Caelius Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings* IV.3, where, after praising the hands, he commends the gift of writing. The Greeks established two kinds of writing: one belonging to those whom they called *τοὺς γράφοντας εἰς κάλλος*—“those who write for beauty”—whence they had *calligraphy*, while we call such men scribes and elegant copyists; and another belonging to those whom the ancients called *γράφοντες εἰς τάχος*—“those who write for speed”—our notaries. Martial writes of them:

> As yet the tongue has not completed its work, but the right hand has.

But let us not here enter the harvest of others. It is enough for our purpose to remember that the emperor Theodosius the Younger wrote letters so beautifully that, whether by making a living from it or otherwise, he earned the name *Alligraphus*; and that in this age there was found a noble writer who wished the pen, the symbol of the more noble art of writing, interpreter of his mind, and instrument of knowledge, prudence, and wisdom, consecrated to the honor of the glorious Mother of God, to be an everlasting gift. By it those who rashly and most ineptly scatter “winged words” (*ἔπεα πτερόεντα*, as Homer often says) through the evil habits of this age might learn that such words endure through the help of heaven, not only through the aid of the pen. It is often asked whether our ancient monks who were scribes, and who filled so many chests of libraries with skins and parchment, used pens—as writers now commonly do—from the wings of geese, cranes, and swans, or rather reeds, from which the ancients fashioned their pens. I confess that I have not read authors who settle the matter with certainty; the dispute cannot be ended from the mixed meaning of *arundo* and *calamus*, as some writers of a later age use them. If there is room for conjecture, I would dare to say that the large letters and uncial strokes with which older parchments were generally written were made with reeds, while smaller letters and shorthand (*ταχυγραφία*) were executed more easily with feathers. We think this meaning is suggested in Albinus’s verses dedicated to the scriptorium:

> By the straight path along which the flying pen proceeds.

Our ancestors also record that both reeds and feathers were widely used in monasteries for liturgical books and ecclesiastical chant.

Why labor to proclaim more compositions in writing?  
*(Another lacuna is noted after page IV.)*

### XXXI.—A Poem on the Catholic Faith, Composed in Rhythm

**Note:** The poet struggles greatly with the arrangement and effect. The verses are iambic, but in them, as the great poet also said of Pindar:

> He is carried along in rhythms released from law.

I believe it should be called rhythm because, according to the testimony of Venerable Bede, rhythm is modulation without formal measure, examined not by metrical law but by the number of syllables according to the judgment of the ears. Here the iambic harmony is therefore only a kind of imitation of sound. The subject is deeply devout, embracing the ordering of the whole human race in its creation and restoration and presenting the chief articles of the Christian religion to the reader’s mind with no weak force of meaning.

Eternal Creator of all things,  
glorious Fashioner of the world,  
God, turn your attention  
to the humble, for their help;

hasten to the aid  
of the heart devoted to you.  
Give faithful governance to the mind  
and the clear gifts of speech;

give the heart’s finest prayers  
and the many gifts of action.

Grant me the purest understanding in my heart  
and peaceful speech upon my lips,

so that I may first be able  
to speak your praise in speech,

great, wondrous, and glorious,  
most righteous, in worthy language;

and that I may be mindful, pierced with remorse,  
of the final hour of my misery.

God, salvation of believers,  
God, life of the living,

God of all gods,  
God and prince of princes,

God, supreme and lovable,  
God, beyond estimation,

high Creator, ancient  
of Days, and unbegotten,

you existed without origin,  
without beginning or foundation;

you are, and you will be through the ages  
of endless ages.

You have the Only-Begotten,  
Christ, your dearest offspring,

the Word spoken from the heart  
of the One who speaks,

begotten before the Morning Star,  
coeternal in the perpetual glory

of the Godhead.

With him, and likewise with the Son,  
through the everlasting age,

the Holy Spirit, equal  
and worthy of honor,

reigns in the same substance,  
remaining God through the ages.

I do not proclaim three gods,  
but I preach one God,

while preserving the faith in three persons,  
most glorious,

supreme, just, and utterly righteous,  
most gentle above all.

The most loving God of the fathers,  
the almighty Lord,

maker of visible things  
and likewise of invisible things,

source of the Godhead  
and creator of all things.

Christ Jesus, most beloved,  
Son of the Almighty,

the truest image,  
the Wisdom of God,

the Power through whom he made  
all the things he had formed.

And the Holy Paraclete,  
the life-giving Spirit,

who from the Father and the Son  
proceeds from the beginning,

the most gracious pledge and gift,  
the most radiant promise.

The essence of the Three is one,  
and their power is one;

one *homoousion*, one Godhead,  
and one eternity;

blessedness and holiness,  
greatness and goodness are one.

God alone through the ages,  
enclosing all times,

in which he formed the heavens,  
the earth, and the seas together.

Exalted in the heavenly places,  
rejoicing as first among the hosts,

he created good angels,  
orders and archangels,

principalities and virtues,  
thrones and dominions,

powers and cherubim,  
glorious seraphim.

So that goodness and majesty  
of the Trinity would not be idle

in the bestowal of all gifts,  
but would have heavenly beings

to whom it might grant privileges.

But at the summit of the heavenly kingdom,  
because of the splendor

of the angelic station  
and the beauty of his appearance,

Lucifer, whom he had formed,  
fell through pride.

And the apostate angels,  
in the same mournful fall,

became the authors of boastful presumption  
and obstinate envy,

while the others remained  
in their own principalities.

The great and most dreadful dragon,  
terrible and ancient,

who was the slippery serpent,  
wiser than all the beasts,

more savage than the living creatures  
of the earth—

he dragged a third part of the stars  
with him into the abyss,

into infernal places  
and various prisons,

a fugitive from the true light,  
plunging parasitically downward.

While the gracious one, foreseeing  
the structure and harmony of the world,

had made the vault of heaven and the dry land  
and separated the waters,

he formed the shoots of herbs,  
the shrubs and little trees;

the sun, moon, and stars,  
fire and the necessities of life,

birds, fish, and cattle,  
beasts and animals;

then at last he himself created  
the honorable human being.

He firmly commanded him  
to remain immortal,

to preserve reverently  
his sacred image,

and to follow the commands of the Lord,  
since he was God’s vicar.

“Be,” he said, “most humble,  
ruler and lord of the world,

for I have handed all things over to you  
and subjected them to your dominion—

all that lives in the world  
and grows from the earth.

Use them wisely,  
eating every kind of thing,

the fruit of the fruitful tree  
and likewise the life-giving fruit;

but do not eat the fruit  
of the forbidden tree,

lest you consume  
a deadly thing for yourself.”

When the savage Chelydros had heard this  
and had grown envious,

the dreadful plague had feared  
what had caused that fall:

that the human being might possess heaven,  
whom he had already seen formed.

He attempts to approach the woman,  
whom the Creator had joined in union;

he persuades her to eat the fruit  
and to hand it to her husband.

He promises that they will be like gods  
if their hunger is satisfied.

She consents more quickly,  
as though this were the better course;

she eats and gives it to her husband,  
and deceives them both together,

while, against the Lord’s command,  
both eat the fruit of the forbidden tree.

Most wretchedly, both see  
that they are shamefully naked;

they strive to cover the crime they have committed  
with a covering around their waists,

with a leaf of *kataphronysis* (“contempt”)  
[Note: Greek *καταφρόνησις*, “contempt”],

but it is not hidden from the Lord.

The Most High had visited them,  
whom he had previously left unharmed.

Adam, fearing, hid beneath a tree  
under its shade,

and the Lord rebuked him  
with a harsh and forceful voice.

“Adam, do you now see where you are?  
You have fallen through disobedience.”

But he excused himself  
by seeking protection elsewhere,

and assigned the cause of the crime  
and the guilt of the sin to another.

After this the Most High, as was just,  
made garments for them;

he girded them with leather  
[Note: That is, “hide”],

and most appropriately with a skin  
for the one who was to die,

so that they might be clothed  
with the garment of mortality.

Then Adam left the paradise  
from which the Lord had expelled him.

God also made the obstinate man  
now a cultivator of the hard earth,

so that it might produce for him sweat  
[Note: Greek *ἱδρῶτα*, “sweat”; the note also mentions *ὕδρα*, “water-serpent”],

thorns, and thistles.

He begot offspring,  
two in number, with disastrous consequence:

one struck down the other  
with the most impious wound.

Thus the poison of envy,  
the serpent, rages in humankind.

When the two primordial parents  
had thus gone astray,

the whole offspring afterward fell,  
and, without assistance,

the author had increased sin  
and dragged it down to hell.

Murders increased  
as love of money increased;

lust abounded  
as belly-rule increased;

the whole mass already possessed  
unspeakable crimes.

In Noah’s time God drowned  
the whole race of the world

in avenging waters,  
Adam and his glorious offspring,

except those whom the ark had carried  
and the Most High had preserved.

But again the earth-dwellers began  
to defile their wings  
[Note: Greek *πτέρυξ*, “wing”; perhaps “wings” or “tabernacles”],

and the rivers did not wash them clean  
so that their crimes might not increase,

nor had experience subdued  
those whom death had swallowed  
[Note: Greek *ἐπιστήμη*, “knowledge” or “experience”].

Abraham had afterward seen this,  
yet it had not helped him;

nor Isaac and Jacob,  
with the company of the exalted fathers;

nor the lawgiver Moses,  
nor David together with the prophets.

Nor did the diligence  
or the elements of learning  
[Note: Greek *στοιχεῖα*, literally “elements,” here perhaps the art itself, especially geometry]

of anyone help: after death  
they would enter the infernal chambers.

Death reigned most widely  
and most harshly over all.

Unless the mercy and power  
of the sole Author

had come to the aid of the wretched  
lying in the lowest depths,

the whole human race with its offspring  
would have perished in sin.

The most gentle Almighty Father  
sent his Only-Begotten Son from heaven,

beloved and most sweet,  
so that he might most mercifully

raise the human being  
from the earth.

The darts of the dreadful dragon  
wounded the heart of the human being,

whom another’s cunning  
had seduced by deceit.

And the thief subdued to himself  
one whom he himself had not created.

How great the mercy of God,  
and how everlasting his goodness!

God had taken upon himself  
the human being whom he had created;

he had sought for himself the one  
whom he had not justly lost.

The Virgin had conceived God,  
whom Gabriel had foretold;

and after nine courses  
and cycles of months,

the Word came incarnate from the Virgin  
with salvation.

The shepherds rejoiced to see  
Jesus newly born in the manger;

the blazing star, with its light,  
led the Magi with their gifts.

Herod began to seek  
the infant Christ in order to kill him.

He raged with slaughter  
among thousands of little children.

Such things at the beginning  
the world offered to the Lord:

it sought to destroy by death  
the one who had come to restore life.

After thirty great cycles  
of years and months had passed,

he was bound by baptism  
by John in the Jordan.

The broad wave washed him,  
as though it itself had become purer.

The Spirit remained over Jesus  
in the form of a dove;

the Father bore witness to the Son  
before the world, which had not believed.

Thus he consecrated  
the mystery of the Trinity in baptism.

Jesus went into the wilderness,  
the dwelling place of wild beasts,

and there completed  
a salutary period of fasting.

For forty nights  
he joined the days to the fast  
[Note: *Inesis*, used for “fasting”].

There the crafty serpent was present  
with his deceits  
[The supplied text has *doloribus*; the bracketed correction gives “deceits”],

and persuaded him to make bread  
for himself from a stone.

*Dipsitis* wishes, beneath a veil  
of words, to recognize Christ  
[Note: The supplied word *Dipsitis* is uncertain; perhaps related to *dipsas*, “thirst,” or to *deipnizō*, “to dine”].

From the lofty summit of the temple  
he orders Jesus to descend.

On the mountain he shows him  
the glory of the world and sovereignty;

he promises to give him everything  
if he will fall down and worship him.

He spoke as perversely  
as he had been perverse;

the serpent himself had applauded himself  
[Note: Perhaps for *plauserat*, “had applauded,” unless one prefers “had praised”],

claiming that he could do  
what he had never been able to do.

But he desired to overthrow  
the one whom he hoped to conquer.

Here he had conquered the first Adam;  
the Second had cast him down—  
through gluttony and love of money,  
and likewise through vainglory.

With these weapons Jesus drove him back  
and handed him over to the fire.

After the devil had been expelled,  
he was ministered to by angels.  
He summoned his disciples,  
now more numerous, and the apostles.

Among them he performed many signs  
and accomplished miracles.

At Cana he made wine,  
and at the same time strengthened  
the still inexperienced faith of his companions,  
when he completed the miracle;  
and he opened before them  
the profound abyss of his teachings.

Throughout the boundaries of Judea  
his miracles flashed forth,  
while the power sent from heaven  
performed its divine work.

He showed himself to be human—  
he who reigned in heaven.

Many thousands of blind people  
saw the light clearly.  
Many deaf men through the crowds  
ran and sought healing.  
The lame man danced joyfully;  
the healed man and the leper rejoiced.

The dragon’s whole horrid, cunning force fled altogether [Greek ὁμῶς, “together”; or ὠμά, “cruelly”],  
when demons came out of many people,  
crying aloud,  
bearing witness to Christ the Lord,  
whom the ages cannot contain.

Now the time of the Lord’s saving death arrived,  
when the Most High resolved within himself  
to redeem the human race,  
to repay the savage one his deserts  
and the punishments he fully deserved.

Judea stirred up conflict  
and gathered the mass of the people.  
They led the holy man  
before tribunals and councils.  
The most savage companion, Judas,  
ratified this with the rulers.

Christ was handed over, bound,  
by the chief priests to the Gentiles.  
With spittings, scourges, and blows,  
mocked and crowned with thorns,  
the innocent man was crucified;  
the foolish king consented.

The earth shuddered,  
quickly marking this crime by its convulsion.  
The elements trembled,  
and the stars concealed themselves.  
Man alone did not fear  
what he alone had brought about.

Then the dead came back to life,  
and the dark prison-places  
of the underworld were opened,  
when the author of light arrived.  
Bars and bolts were shattered;  
the righteous were set free.

The enemy groaned in chains,  
when the King pronounced his judgments  
and granted deliverance to the holy,  
because Tartarus had suffered.  
Christ the Victor ascended  
and led his own with him.

The third day had returned,  
and Christ had risen again,  
now destined to live in glory,  
the radiant Victor throughout the ages,  
God, Lord of hosts,  
the most powerful King of kings.

After forty days,  
having lived among those who rejoiced,  
he showed himself to his disciples  
by miracles to be truly alive.  
He removed every doubt  
that remained in their wondering hearts.

He commanded them to travel  
through the regions of the world with his teaching:

“Go,” he said, “among the peoples  
and bear very abundant fruit.  
Teach them by the faithful word  
to observe what I have taught.

Wash those who wish to believe  
in the sacred stream,  
in the name of God the Father,  
and of the Son together with the Spirit,  
releasing all sins,  
and teach them the remedies.

But I am with you forever  
as your consolation,  
when you see the world boiling  
with wars and error.  
Then do not be afraid,  
nor yield to evil blows.

The whole earth with its offspring,  
the sea as well as the sky,  
given into my rule,  
submits and serves as a gift.  
The bound enemy has been expelled,  
and the world has been set free.

Now I ascend, radiant,  
to the throne of my dear Father,  
who sent me from heaven  
to redeem the whole world,  
to seize the kingdoms owed to me,  
and to be at the Father’s right hand.

Let no sorrow of yours  
now hold your hearts captive.  
I am sending you the most joyful  
Spirit, the Paraclete;  
he himself will be your teacher forever,  
as I am.

They retain what he taught;  
he has gone where he had to go.  
Above the highest stars  
he sits at the Father’s right hand,  
indeed the Judge who will come at the end,  
and who will appear in heaven.

He himself, when the Most High Lord  
descends from heaven,  
will shine forth as the brightest sign  
and banner of the cross.

Then excessive mourning  
will be upon all nations.  
The two chief lights,  
their coverings withdrawn,  
will fall to earth—  
like a fig from the fig tree.

And the end of the world will be  
like the burning of a furnace.  
A fourfold trumpet-blast  
will resound through the regions of the earth.  
Flashing lightning and thunder  
will race about.

Then, in the caves of the mountains,  
the armies will hide themselves.  
Therefore that day will be  
a day of lamentation and tears,  
a day of wrath and vengeance,  
of darkness and cloud,  
a day of great distress,  
of toil and sorrow.

On that day the love and desire  
of women will cease,  
as will the contention of men  
and the desire for this world,  
when heaven and earth,  
through heat and light,  
burn together.

At the wondrous tumult  
of the first archangel,  
the most strongly fortified barriers  
and the burial chambers will burst open.  
Man will rise from the earth,  
restored from dust.

As the structures of the limbs  
are gathered together from every side,  
the ethereal souls coming to meet them,  
the saints strive, with their reward,  
to meet Christ the King.

The King enthroned on high  
will sit upon his glorious throne.  
Trembling hosts of angels  
will stand around him.  
As judge, he will render to all  
according to their individual merits.

We too will stand trembling  
before the tribunal of God,  
and we will give an account  
of all our desires,  
seeing our sins placed  
before his eyes,  
and the books of conscience  
opened in his presence.

We will break into sobs  
and groan with dreadful weeping,  
with the necessary opportunity  
for action taken away.

Then the faithful will be lifted  
to the heavenly homeland,  
to the supreme city of Jerusalem;  
they will enter into glory,  
where the true light of peace shines:  
Christ, the wondrous sun.

With the songs of hymns  
ringing out diligently,  
and the saints rejoicing  
among thousands of angels,  
in the Father’s glory  
they will rejoice to behold Christ.

Thus, with the twenty-four blessed elders  
already casting their crowns  
beneath the feet of the Lamb of God,  
the eternal Trinity is praised  
three times over.

With the four living creatures  
standing before him as one,  
sounding a threefold praise:  
“Holy, Lord Sabaoth [of hosts].”

In this glory the saints remain  
from age to age.

The raging zeal of fire  
will consume the adversaries—  
those unwilling to believe  
that Christ came from God the Father.

The impious will fall backward forever  
into the flames of fire,  
where there are darkness,  
worms, and dreadful beasts;  
where sulfurous fire  
burns with devouring flames;  
where there are the howling of men,  
weeping, and gnashing of teeth;

where there are the groans of Gehenna,  
thunder and horror;  
where blazing heat  
is joined to the greatest thirst and hunger;  
where the harshest torturer  
increases the punishment together with the household spirits.

Satan, with his dark host,  
will be submerged among the peoples  
in the whirlpools of Cocytus and Charybdis,  
where he is held in prison,  
bound in Tartarus  
for eternal fires.

O God, author of true light  
and of every human being,  
wretched that I am, what shall I do?  
Where then shall I be, and where shall I flee,  
when the structure of the world trembles  
beneath the dominion of flames?

Where can I then turn  
and seek intercession,  
when the sentence against me  
is pronounced amid great anguish?

I am accused, guilty of crime,  
since there is no favor earned by my works.  
My own deeds condemn me:  
the many thousands of my words,  
evil love with shame,  
anger, quarrels, and stains—  
all are exposed in the light  
and laid bare to the mind.

Trembling, I see what I had done  
and what I had long concealed.  
Nor do consolations help me—  
the words of father and mother;  
nor does the friendly crowd  
provide assistance to the weak.

From where, then, O Lord,  
will salvation come swiftly to me,  
apart from your mercy alone  
and your true grace?  
Or who grants forgiveness  
apart from your power?

I beseech you, good Jesus,  
author and restorer of life:  
save your servant,  
and grant an everlasting gift,  
so that by your truthful word  
you may be justified, O Lord.

To you, redeemed from danger,  
I shall give thanks from my heart;  
to the living God I shall proclaim  
victory with joyful voice,  
following you, my own King,  
snatched from the enemy to the Lord.

Now I ask that you command  
and accomplish this in me:  
as long as I am shut  
in the prison of the flesh,  
may I sing you continually  
with mouth, heart, and deed:  
“Praise, Kyrie.”

Glory to you, enthroned on high,  
most holy King of heaven.  
You will console me  
with your excellent help.

Praise and honor with glory  
through ages of ages.

Whoever you are who read these verses,  
remember to pray for me.  
I am called Rabanus;  
farewell forever.

## XXXII.—Poem on the Departure of the Monks

[Editorial note] He describes in this ode the secession carried out under Abbot Ratgarius; concerning it, see Book I of the *Life of Abbot Eigil* in the *Fuldensian Antiquities*.

Run, paper; carry far to the beloved brother  
the grievous gifts  
that the unhappy hour of time had brought.

Long ago, by a wicked fate,  
fate, deceit, grief, and immense labor  
had compelled [us] to seek distant lands.

One part was taken away, another remained,  
when one man—alas, a divided man!—  
was separated in vow and soul,  
in two bodies.

After you, my like-minded brother, had departed,  
I soon became a casualty of every kind,  
wounded by black hatreds.

But now I grieve with sorrowful heart  
that general evil can do so much—alas!—  
and that I alone must store up the damage for myself.

Ever since harmful sedition  
arose among us long ago,  
no one could soften it by prayers  
or bring it to an end.

But, increasing over a very long time,  
it grew day by day through evil fortune  
and devastated the people because of the Father’s anger.

He who hardens his heart and does not know how to yield,  
the savage man, drives away the sheep,  
blood-stained by slaughter;  
he pities no one and rages against all.

Moved by these evils, the crowd abandoned  
the ancient fold and became a wandering people;  
for the injured, the only salvation  
is to set out upon a long journey.

The final day came, the bitter time,  
when the crowd, forced to endure the extremity,  
and overcome by evils, had to leave its dwelling.

All the brothers assembled from every side,  
whose mind was one and whose will was equal,  
to strive by prayers to bend the pitiless man.

He, hardened in heart and having despised everyone,  
provoked the people and drove them from the church.  
He gave them cause to despair of the Father’s love.

Meanwhile the walls resound with varied grief;  
cymbals clash, and the church’s signal  
calls everyone together.

They rush to the tomb of the holy martyr.  
The younger people weep together with the old;  
they draw groans from the depths of their hearts.

They stretch out their hands with poured-out prayer.

*[The text is defective after the final page of quire VI.]*

[Editorial note] Another kind of poem follows. Because of the excellence of his talent and the reputation for learning that flourished in him, Rabanus adorned in verse the illustrious basilicas erected throughout his age, sometimes spontaneously and sometimes at the request of others. Those who love ancient history and the origins of their churches may rightly lament the fate of this mutilated and gaping codex. For, besides the inscriptions and headings that the copyist repeatedly neglected, several parchment leaves have been cut out; thus many titles and subjects of poems have perished. Nor do I conceal that many names of heavenly beings are read here and celebrated by Rabanus whose memory one would not easily recover elsewhere. Since it would be too long and dense a task to investigate the translations, relics, and repositories of the saints who are brought forward in such processions, and, from grapes so closely clustered, to press out must, we shall be content with poor posca: whenever anything worthy of remembrance comes into our hands, we shall, insofar as possible, kindle a light for the recognition of ancient history.

One warning will not be out of place. On the authority of titles and translations, unless the matter is made clearer elsewhere, this collection does not establish or compel us to conclude from Rabanus’s words that the saints’ entire bodies were translated, deposited, or entombed here; their relics, ashes, and remains were sufficient for preserving their memory and establishing the inscriptions.

Nor do I see that I must labor before fair-minded critics to explain how they will receive this rustic Muse from refined poets, who ought to remember that every age has its own ornaments and faults, and that the benefits and disadvantages of these should be assessed together. Yet, lest they kill Rabanus unheard, I shall ask them by what right Virgil and Propertius were permitted to contract *Italia* and *Arabia* at the end of a line; Juvenal to introduce *Stoicidas* with its penultimate syllable short; Ovid to contract and lengthen *Tuticanum*, and so forth. Why, I ask, was it permitted to other poets to indulge themselves so freely? Was it because, rebellious against the many words and syllables, they shook off the poetic yoke, and therefore could not be forced into verse without the rod? Or, having renounced the law of Latium, did they prefer to pass over to the laws of the Greek poets,

> for whom nothing is forbidden,  
> and whom it suits to sound *ares, ares*?

Thus in their works one finds everywhere *Lucianos*, *Claudianos*, and *Julianos* with the penultimate syllable shortened. I ought not to have been silent about these matters, because, once they are observed, I see that gentler judgments are being prepared for the whole nation of Christian poets—not only for Fortunatus and Rabanus—and that the grammarians’ rods are at least somewhat restrained.

# Titles and Inscriptions

[Editorial note] We have recalled, in chapter 3 of Book II of the *Fuldensian Antiquities*, the memory of the Fuldensian basilica dedicated in the year of Christ 818, in the twelfth indiction, on the first day of November. By God’s singular favor, since Rabanus’s epigrams had been separately committed to writing there, we were able to infer from them that the altar inscriptions abruptly transmitted here all belong to the adornment of the Fuldensian basilica, which was consecrated in honor of the Savior.

As in that description chief attention was given to the church’s dimensions and location, so here it was given to the altars, which stood beautiful with the relics of the saints and illustrious verse inscriptions. Hence more epigrams are read here than in the acts of the dedication. But such is the changeability of all things that neither the church’s arrangement nor the memory of its altars or poems survives in later works except in these writings. For the present I shall recall only those things that have recently come to light, so that the reader may know from them that the former can be adorned and the latter completed through these texts.

## Altars of the Basilica of Saint Savior at Fulda

### XXXIII

This altar shines for God with new honor.  
Fair Wirina [Old Fuldensian and Saint Gall litanies have *Verena*; perhaps Berenice, commonly Veronica], Concordia, and Mederisma  
stand here with you, together with Gertrude herself.  
For Theophila, beloved of God, duly mingles her prayers here  
and favors our petitions.  
Virgin flowers, strike the Thunderer by your merits;  
I beg you, render God propitious to us.

### XXXIV.—And on the right altar

This altar holds the blessed apostle Timothy,  
the martyr Vitalis, and Vitus also,  
Fortunatus, Felix, Tiburtius,  
Servilianus the beloved, and pious Sulpitius.  
Marius and Martha, together with their two children,  
and the martyr Martial with Diogenes likewise.  
Saint Firminus, Liberalis, and Fuscianus,  
Rusticus and Firmus, Castulus and Zeno.  
With these, Victoricius also fittingly rejoices;  
the martyr Gentianus remains, sharing their joy.  
I ask you, worshipper, to appease these patrons by prayers,  
if you wish to ascend to the kingdom of the Most High Father.

### XXXV.—At the altar of Saint Stephen

The deacon Stephen, together with Laurence,  
adorns this altar by his merits, and pious Pancratius also.  
Donatus, Victor, Vincentius, and Cyriacus,  
the martyr Quintinus and Sebastian,  
and Ferrutius himself, with forty others,  
press their request upon the martyrs: ask for the help of light.

[Editorial note] According to the order among the published basilica inscriptions, whose heading there is: “In the northern portico, on the left, of the eastern apse.”

### XXXVI.—At the altar of Saint Clement

[Editorial note] Fourth in the published collection; it was written or carved: “On the right of the eastern apse, in the southern portico of the basilica.”

Here the martyr Clement stands, together with the martyr Linus;  
Saint Alexander and Fabian are present.  
Marcellus, Stephen, Cornelius, and Cyprian,  
and Lactantum [reading uncertain], with the throng stained with its own blood.  
Here the golden bishop Justin, himself also a martyr,  
duly helps by prayers and good merits;  
with them, Saturninus and the martyr George  
joined together fittingly entreat the Lord for the peoples.

[Editorial note] The act of dedication says: “In the northern part of the transept.” And there this distich was omitted:

> When you cherish us, holy Praxedes, virgin Basilla,  
> so too, holy Pudentiana, [cherish us] by your pious merits.

### XXXVII.—At the altar of Saint Agatha the Virgin

Martyr Agatha of God, Petronilla, and you, Juliana,  
Lucy, Perpetua, and Sabina, cherish us.  
Holy Praxedes, virgin Basilla, cherish us with you;  
so too, holy Pudentiana, by your pious merits.  
Virgin Regina, joined with these sisters,  
open heaven’s kingdoms to us by your prayers.

### XXXVIII.—At the altar of Saint Luke the Evangelist

[Editorial note] This epigram was once given a title from its location: “On the left of the arch facing the eastern building.” You now see the poem enlarged by a new quatrain.

Luke, who wrote Christ’s teachings together with his deeds  
in Greek, places here the spoils mingled with Peter’s bonds.  
Augustine is present, Germanus, Remeius himself [Remigius],  
the bishop Maximinus, and Medardus rejoice.  
The teacher Ambrose, Eusebius, and Vedastus  
ask that the presence of the Most High be with us.  
With these, the martyr Hermes, joined to us,  
entreats the Lord and asks forgiveness.

### XXXIX.—At the altar of Saint Mark the Evangelist

[Editorial note] Heading of the published poem: “On the right of the same.” The poem must be completed with two verses omitted there:

> Candidus, Exuperus, and others …  
> The martyr Silenus and Timothy rejoice.  
> Abdo with Senne, the martyr Protus, and Hyacinthus,  
> whom for us … etc.

Mark, who wrote the Gospel with Greek skill,  
dwells here with the martyr Paul and John.  
Valentinus himself, Gorgonius, and Nazarius,  
Germanus, the Seven, and Gordianus likewise.  
Candidus, Exsuperus, Victor, Mauritius,  
the martyr Silenus, and Timothy rejoice.  
Abdo with Senne, the martyr Protus, and Hyacinthus—  
make them, O Christ, rightly favor us.

### XL.—At the altar of Saint Agnes the Virgin

Agnes and Euphemia, Genevieve, Susanna, Columba,  
adorn this altar duly with their prayers.  
With them, Bridget, and you, virgin Scholastica,  
ever make the enthroned One propitious to us.

### XLI.—At the altar of Saint Benedict in the western crypt

[Editorial note] This edition adds a distich suppressed in the acts of the dedication:

> Eucherius, Trudo, Arnulf, Servatius,  
> Cuthbert, Bede, and Equitius remain here.

You, Father Benedict, will protect this crypt and altar;  
Saint Honoratus himself also venerates it.  
Eucherius, Trudo, Arnulf, and Servasius [Servatius, unless it is Gervasius],  
Cuthbert, Bede, and Equitius remain here.  
Here Columbanus stands duly as a fixed pillar  
and will offer fitting support at the martyr’s tomb.

### XLII.—At the altar of Saint Ignatius

The martyr Ignatius and Florianus guard this inscription,  
together with Ursicinus and Rogatianus.  
Emmeramus is present, Julianus, and Patricius,  
Saint Wigbert, and the martyr Hippolytus.

### XLIII.—In the brothers’ cemetery, in the church of Saint Michael, at the first altar

[Editorial note] This cemetery, with its church of singular workmanship, was dedicated in 822 by Heistolf, archbishop of Mainz; we have preserved the verses’ ornament in Book II, chapter 5 of the *Fuldensian Antiquities*. Between it and the basilica lies a hill to the north, together with the provostship and church of Saint Michael, raised from the ruins of an old church, and not without distinction.

This altar is dedicated chiefly to God Christ,  
whose tomb here assists our graves.  
A portion of Mount Sinai, worthy of Moses’ memory,  
and this place of the birth of Christ the Lord.  
Here Michael, the Lord’s chief companion of John,  
and the three boys, victorious over the furnace, together.  
The martyr Privatus and Habundius himself  
receive vows and render them to God.  
The bishop Sulpitius and the confessor Amandus together,  
here the monk Mammas, and here Simeon rejoices.  
With them, we pray you always to stand here with your vows,  
consecrated virgin of God, martyr Anastasia.

### XLIV.—At the left altar

Here Anianus is present, and the martyr Desiderius;  
King Sisemund rejoices, and Genesius likewise.  
You too, pious Christopher, be present to our minds;  
with your companions, help our prayers.

### XLV.—At the right altar

Bishop Paulinus, Brixius also, Perpetuus,  
the holy Isidore, and Father Martial  
adorn this altar with ever-living merits;  
they assist the prayers that each will piously offer.

### XLVI.—In the church of Saint Mary, on the hill called Bishop’s Hill, at the right altar

[Editorial note] Concerning the Bishop’s Hill, which retains that name from Saint Boniface, its occupant, the books of the *Fuldensian Antiquities* speak often. The church, besides its former afflictions, was recently so shaken by many injuries that it seemed close to collapse. The beauty of the site, on a steep hill to the north in view of the town, and the famous sanctity of the place moved Balthasar, the abbot of blessed memory, to repair its damage, and he had already begun the work. Not only the church building but also a suitable monastic dwelling was rising, when envy and the perverse rivalry of factions broke the admirable effort of his spirit midway. At last John Frederick, his successor, restored the church and extended a kindly hand to the work. Meanwhile, no trace of Ratgarius’s works or of Rabanus’s monuments remains in the body of the church or even in its towers, although Ratgarius’s gravestone is still shown there. Thus everything we once recalled from Rudolph, in Book III of the *Antiquities*, concerning relics of saints brought to this place and other adornments has disappeared.

The priest Boniface himself, holding this altar,  
and the martyr of Christ, duly stands as patron.  
With him, let Pope Gregory also be joined here;  
equal in merits, they possess the heavenly kingdoms.  
Therefore the martyr Laurence is no less faithful than these;  
here he rejoices and himself helps the devout by prayers.

### XLVII.—At the left altar

Here, holy Father, greatest shepherd of monks,  
you, Benedict, duly help your own by prayers;  
your sister, the holy virgin Scholastica, is joined to you:  
ask salvation’s aid for those devoted to you.  
Martyr Anastasia, you too, we pray, pour forth  
prayers for us to Christ forever.

### XLVIII.—On Bishop’s Hill, in the tower of the church of Saint Mary
