Grant assent, Christ God; may the archangel Michael  
stand by this place’s vows and help us with prayers.  
May Bishop Martin, the martyr Dalmatius,  
make you propitious to us by their merits.  
Cassius, Anthimus, and holy Florentius stand here;  
the bishop Memmius, and here Sister Etpumia [Ethymia; perhaps Euprepia, found in ancient litanies, volume V of the *Ancient Lessons*].  
We therefore believe that you will be sufficiently propitious to us  
if these, by their prayer, strive duly to cherish us.

### XLIX.—In the apse of the church of Saint Peter situated on the hill

[Editorial note] In this work Rabanus magnificently equipped the church dedicated by Reginbald, chorepiscopus of Otgar, bishop of Mainz, with the relics of the saints, their repositories, and epigrams. Rudolph’s commentary, which establishes this fact, is found in Book III of the *Fuldensian Antiquities*.

Behold, the sower of men, victorious, ascends above heaven  
and opens to his disciples the sacred thresholds of the kingdom.  
The angelic oracles promise that he will come here in this way;  
the apostolic assembly, together with the faithful people,  
receives the gifts of the Paraclete in gleaming fire.

### L.—In the same place

[Editorial note] This epigram, inscribed on a reliquary chest with verses extending on both sides, was woven by Rudolph, the author of Rabanus’s acts, into his narrative.

Behold, this place duly holds the bones of the saints;  
remembering them, it venerates their holy deeds.  
Mother Felicitas, and holy Concordia the nurse,  
here rest Candida and Eutropia of Hippolytus.  
For Paul’s host, Aquila and Prisca [Priscilla], rest here;  
the virgin Eugenia and Basilla remain here.  
Here stands Emerentiana, Agnes’s foster-sister,  
herself a holy martyr.

### LI.—At the right altar

This altar is placed for all Christ’s martyrs,  
especially for those whom the inscription names.

### LII.—At the left altar

The company of Christ’s confessors possesses this altar,  
those whom the court of heaven possesses and holds.

### LIII.—In the crypt, beneath the first altar

At this sacred altar the mighty Baptist is venerated;  
at this one the throng of prophets and Fathers is honored.

### LIV.—At the middle altar

The Virgin Mother of God duly hold this altar;  
with you may the virgin choir possess it.

### LV.—At the third altar

The archangel Michael adorns this altar of God;  
angelic hosts likewise venerate it.

### LVI

He who rules the world’s empire and contains the stars  
himself dedicates this hall by his coming.  
With him, the Baptist and John the Lord’s companion  
inhabit this church, O Christ, your servants.

### LVII

The gracious Marcellus, Boniface, and Cyprian,  
with Sixtus and Linus, behold, are present here with their companions.  
I beg you, reader, whoever you are who enter with bowed head,  
strive duly to appease God with your vows.

### LVIII

The apostolic assembly, with its ministers duly depicted,  
holds this altar and helps by its merits.

### LIX

The Virgin Mary, Mother of God, contains this altar;  
the heavenly martyrs Agnes and Agatha are here together.

### LX

Lucy, Juliana, and the virgin Scholastica  
greatly help by prayers and make atonement by their merits.

### LXI

Bishop Martin, Antonius, and Benedict  
inhabit this crypt and retain its inscription.  
Here Pope Gregory, here Gallus and Equitius,  
receive pious vows together with Columbanus.

## LXXII.—An exhortation of the brothers to prayer

Run, brothers, ready toward heaven’s heights;  
Christ, seated in the citadel, prepares great rewards.  
Saint Anastasius promises true joys,  
which Christ the pious King himself will give you.  
We too, together with you, where you seize the blessed joys,  
ask this of you; behold, farewell together.

If you, reader, love to know the church’s guardian,  
the Lord’s own servant John is present here.  
Here is James, the Lord’s brother; here the virgin Mary;  
here is Boniface, martyr and bishop.  
Clement the merciful, Pancratius, and Julian  
receive vows here and render them to God.

## LXIII.—Verses in the church of the Mother of God

Sweeter and far redder than the rose-colored purple,  
you surpass fragrant locks in the scent of the mind.  
Dear, kind, shining, pious, holy, reverend, lovely—  
flower, glory, altar, splendor, palm, crown, modesty.

## LXIV.—In the church of Saint Mary built at Holzkyricha, these verses are inscribed beside its entrance

[Editorial note] In the region of Waldztaia by the Main, near Odo’s forest, once of immense size, we showed in the books of the *Fuldensian Antiquities* the location of this church and monastery, which is still counted among the provostships of the chief congregation. The place is called Holtzkyricha because the church—named from the Greek *κυριακόν*, German *kyricha*—was built in wooded ground rich in timber, called *holz* in the same language. The people of those districts are rightly called *waldsassen*, or inhabitants of the forest. The origins of the place are recorded elsewhere, and Rudolph, often praised by us, admirably described the translation of Saints Januarius and Magnus, who are named here by Rabanus. The zeal of Humbert, bishop of Würzburg, in whose diocese the monastery was established, moved him reverently to deposit the martyrs’ bones. Rabanus then added the verses read here as Epigram 65 to a finely constructed wooden structure over the tomb, covered with various metals. Behold these men, whom Rudolph likewise included in the Acts.

Whoever enters this hall with steps  
intending to visit it,  
let him first recognize what this place contains.  
Here the sacred relics of the Virgin Mother  
are duly placed;  
by her merits she consecrates this entire hall.  
With her, a noble throng of saints  
stands here piously,  
receiving vows and rendering them to God.  
Therefore it is most fitting that the pure intention of the heart  
and speech together with deeds  
should seek heavenly gifts.

### LXV.—In the tomb of the holy martyrs who rest there

Behold these men, most illustrious patrons,  
whom Rome, the world’s glory, sent here together.  
The humble abbot Rabanus received them,  
and duly placed them here with Bishop Humbert.  
Here rests Magnus, and the martyr Januarius,  
distinguished by office and sacred merits;  
slain by the sword together with Bishop Sixtus,  
they, deacons, gave their souls back to heaven.

### LXVI.—At the first altar

Virgin Mary, Mother of God, this hall resounds for you;  
behold, it shines entirely with honor to you.  
This sacred altar is adorned by the presence of virgins,  
which joyful piety marks above in the apse;  
with them Praxedes and Basilla rejoice,  
and Candida the virgin together with Pudentiana.

### LXVII.—At the right altar

The apostolic assembly holds this sacred altar,  
helps it by prayers, adorns it, and honors it with love.  
You too who have entered, bow your necks;  
with devout heart ask here for the aid of light.

### LXVIII.—At the left altar

The renowned martyr Boniface throughout the world  
holds this altar with his companions.  
If you, reader, wish to know their names,  
look at the painting and read the inscriptions again.

### LXIX.—At the cross

The shrine of the cross holds the wood of the cross  
by which Christ blessed the ages, enclosed in an emblem.  
The consecrated altar holds the relics  
of the Baptist and of Christ,  
and likewise the remains of Paul the teacher.  
Mark, the writer of the Gospel, with his companion Luke,  
and Senne and Abdo, venerate it with love.  
Saint Hippolytus, Protus, and the martyr Hyacinthus,  
joined to these, place their mingled relics here.

### LXX.—In the crypt

Bishop Martin and gracious Gregory  
duly venerate this altar by their own merits;  
with them Equitius rejoices, and Abbot Antonius,  
and holy Maximinus, himself a pious shepherd.

### LXXI.—In the chapel

The apostolic summit, Peter and Paul the teacher,  
duly dedicate this altar with their relics.  
The supreme pontiffs Sixtus and Boniface,  
distinguished by martyrdom, dwell here together.  
Felicissimus and Agapitus remain here with them,  
holy deacons, each a witness of God.

Bend your knees, you who have entered the sacred threshold;  
Christ the ruler is present; ask for the aid of light,  
through which all the ends of the earth earned salvation.  
The whole world rejoices—earth, sea, sand, and sky.

Whiter than fleece, more radiant than yellow gold,  
brighter than a ray, sweeter to the mouth than honeycomb,  
these words, though I am unworthy, I murmur to you with heart and mouth:  
may you who carry the world’s salvation be my hope of forgiveness.

## LXXII.—[Defective]

[Editorial note] After a great lacuna and several removed parchment leaves, these remnants of poems are read. They are excerpted from Book VIII, poem 5 of Fortunatus, entitled “In Praise of Saint Mary, Virgin and Mother of the Lord.” For what is given here under title 63, “Verses in the church of the Mother of God,” is wrongly mixed with the material extending under number 73. In Fortunatus, however, the following are read in this order:

> Beautiful, overshadowing the sun’s splendor above gems, etc.

We shall readily endure this loss if, as we suppose, Fortunatus’s lengthy poem was woven into this work.

*[Defective.]*

You also who stand here, bow your necks;  
loose the bonds of your feet and shut out the world’s cares.  
Christ the ruler is present, with the entire army of the saints;  
ask for the aid of light and leave behind the cares of darkness.

## LXXIII

[Editorial note] Here is expressed a notable rite of the ancient litany, which has continued into our own age: beginning with the invocation of the most holy Trinity, the supplication proceeds gradually through definite classes of saints and ends with an appeal for the aid and mercy of the Lamb of God, that is, Christ our Lord.

It seems to have been customary in Rabanus’s age to compose litanies in meter for easier singing and harmony. Examples of this kind, made by two learned monks of Saint Gall distinguished by rare piety, Ratpert and Notker, are presented in volume V of the *Ancient Lessons*. We now publish one that we had supposed proceeded from Rabanus’s genius or that of one of his contemporaries, and that we knew had once been sung in the *Barefoot Procession of Saint Mark* and was still used to this day in the rural supplication from the monastery of Fulda.

But after examining the monuments of the monastery of Saint Gall, we noticed that it is in fact attributed to Hartmann, or Hartmund, a disciple of Rabanus, as shown by Trithemius and the notes of Henricus Canisius in volume V of the *Ancient Lessons*.

The heading of those litanies is:

> For procession on Sundays.

Their wording is as follows:

> With humble prayer and sincere devotion,  
> crying to you, hear us always.  
> Most high and almighty Father, who created all things,  
> eternal, Christ the Son, and God, etc.

When these were compared with the commonly circulated Fuldensian manuscripts, great variety of reading and order was discovered, so that one might suspect that the monks of Saint Gall transferred a litany perhaps arranged by Rabanus for their own monastery’s use, altering several verses.

Common version:

> Ever shining with the virginity of modesty.

Fuldensian version:

> Ever and always shining with virginity.

Then, after the invocation of the apostles, beginning with the words “Make all good things follow,” the Fuldensians insert this quatrain:

> Great Boniface, most powerful soldier of Christ,  
> [or: “Gallus, soldier of the Most High God”],  
> now aid us, your servants.  
> Nothing obscure can be clearly spoken;  
> let a clear voice be returned,  
> as is fitting in such service of the Father.

Again, after the verse:

> And may pious Chrysogonus help us with compassion,

the Fuldensians alter the order and add the patronage of various martyrs:

> Here your halls resound with perpetual songs;  
> honor is always held in the sacred strongholds [or: bones].  
> When your kindly servants joyfully celebrate these festivals,  
> they persist in your praises night and day.  
> Direct our hearts, O pious one; direct our times,  
> and grant your servants to lead joyful days,  
> so that they may always be able to serve you in peace  
> and behold you in the heavenly light of heaven.  
> Basilides, Nabor, Gorgonius, and Cyrinus [Quirinus],  
> radiant through martyrdom, who are in heaven’s citadel,  
> pour forth prayers duly with unceasing voices,  
> so that the Lord may make us innocent.  
> O beloved of God, shining and flashing with virtue …

Holy Albanus (Vulgate, Othmar), Father, join your prayers likewise.

Intercede by seeking pardon for the pious poor,

and with ears receive songs so gentle.

Bishop Adalbert, who suffered for Christ’s name,

assist unworthy servants with your support.

To Christ the Lord, who saves the world by his blood,

that he may be gracious toward human sins.

[Col. 1630D] Holy prince Hammeran, and shepherd in the ecclesiastical order,

who, having shed your blood, stand as witness for the Lord,

always pray for every sin together with the people,

that he may preserve his servants from the harmful enemy. Here the following is now added:

“Ovos martyrio, etc.”

Vulgate: “O holy and gracious Father Benedict.”

Fulda: “O Father Benedict, join your prayers likewise.” The monks of Fulda close the Litany with a Greek distich:

Κύριε παντοκράτωρ, Ἰησοῦς σωτήριε παντὸς, Εὐ βασιλεὺς ἠμῶν, Ξριστε, ἐλείσον.

“Lord Almighty, Jesus, Savior of all; O our good King, Christ, have mercy.”

And Jodocus Motzler, a monk of Saint Gall and an ornament of his monastery, acknowledges that this rhythmic litany was still used on the Rogation weekdays, as it is today at Fulda; he also says that this formula was approved by Pope Nicholas III. See *Ancient Readings*, vol. V.] Verses composed in the manner of a litany.

[Col. 1630A]

All-ruling Judge, supreme creator of all things,

look down from heaven, almighty Father.

Almighty Father, from whom all things truly exist,

eternal Beginning, have mercy on your own.

You yourself, Son of God, through whom all things were made,

mercifully receive, I pray, our prayers.

Holy Spirit of God, finder of heaven and earth,

in whom all things exist, regard our devout vows.

One creator in three persons,

O God enthroned on high, always be graciously present.

Glorious Mother of God, most holy Virgin Mary,

pray for us, rightly showing favor with God.

May the archangel Michael himself plead for us,

and strong Gabriel and healing Raphael.

[Col. 1630B] Together with the heavenly hosts, appeasing the powers above,

make the Most-High-Throned One favorable toward us.

The son of Zechariah, the herald, and all the prophets,

[Col. 1631A] and the holy Fathers, reconcile God;

apostolic company, honorable retinue of Christ,

open for us by your prayers the gates of heaven.

Heavenly key-bearer Peter and Paul the teacher,

Andrew, and James and John, the beloved one;

Thomas with James, Philip, Bartholomew,

Matthew and Simon, Thaddeus and Matthias.

Joyful in doctrine, radiant and red with blood,

holy choir of the victorious, guide us by your teachings.

Barnabas, Silas, Stephen, Mark and Titus,

Luke and Clement, holy Apollinaris.

Sixtus, Alexander, Cornelius and Cyprian,

Felix, Urban, and Mauritius also.

Together with you, illustrious martyr Boniface, teacher,

we ask you to pour forth prayers, appeasing the Most-High-Throned One.

[Col. 1631B] Holy Martin, we pray that you admonish your companions

to ask the merciful Lord rightly for us.

Leo, Sylvester also, and the confessor Amandus,

Bishop Ambrose and Pope Gregory.

Augustine the honored one, the teacher Jerome,

and Maximinus the shepherd, together with Eusebius, may protect us.

Benedict, we pray that you bestow this upon your monks,

while holding blessed kingdoms with Antony and Paul.

Martyr Agatha of God, we rightly pray that you cherish us;

so may the virgin Agnes, and so Anastasia:

Lucy, Balbina, Petronilla, Eulalia, Thecla,

Regina, Euphemia, Cecilia, Soteris,

Eugenia, Prisca, Monegundis, Praxedis, Afra,

Christina, Bridget, and the chaste host of heaven.

All heavenly citizens, the entire army of the saints,

[Col. 1631C] bring this about by your prayers, that God himself may help us.

In his mercy may he cleanse, exalt, love, adorn,

preserve us unharmed, protect us, and guide us.

May he grant true peace, the full gift of love,

peaceful deeds, and good hope and faith.

May he bestow an abundance of virtues and a kindly mind,

and a chaste body, time, and every good thing;

[Col. 1632A] food and clothing from God, faithful friends always,

and may he himself keep all enemies far away.

May he drive away hunger and remove all diseases at once,

and crush the snares of the devil far off.

May we run joyfully, so that we may attain blessed kingdoms,

always on high with Christ in heaven’s citadel.

Holy Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world,

always and forever have mercy on your own.

Christ, hear us; Christ, hear us, we pray;

we follow you, Christ; we desire and long for you.

O Lord, save us, because we seek life from you;

restore your countenance, and then it will indeed be enough.

You, Christ, are power; you are eternal life.

You, Christ, have mercy; you, Kyrie, have mercy.

Amen.

### LXXIV. On Prudence

[Col. 1632B]

Prudence first reveals the forms of the virtues;

it recalls all things and dictates what is honorable and good.

### LXXV. On Justice and Piety

Justice and piety preserve an equal compact

and themselves order every judgment according to their own rule.

### LXXVI. On Fortitude of Patience

The virtue of patience bravely endures adversity;

confident in victory, it drives away every sorrow.

### LXXVII. On Temperance

Thus the virtue of moderation now temperately governs all things,

and mercifully, in peace, will grant the laws above.

*(The text breaks off at page VIII.)*

## Titles and Inscriptions of a Church N., Furnished by Otgar and Rabanus with Relics and Other Ornaments

[Col. 1632C]

### LXXVIII.

[Note: [Col. 1631C] The martyrs Sergius and Bacchus are frequently commemorated in ecclesiastical tablets. We cannot equally attest that they were brothers, or that their relics were transferred from Rome to Germany, although this is poetically—but truly—sung here. On 7 October the Roman Martyrology records their martyrdom; the place where Sergius rests is said to be Sergiopolis. Caesar Baronius, in his notes, also observed other matters in praise of these [Col. 1631D] martyrs from Greek commentaries. But who will clear a path for us to investigate when and how they came from the eastern Euphratesian province into the West and, as Rabanus says here, penetrated into the city of Romulus, where so many histories of the saints are clouded by darkness? Gregory of Tours sufficiently teaches, in book VII, chapter 31 of the *History of the Franks*, that their relics became known to the Gauls; Anastasius sufficiently shows that, under Pope Gregory III, a deaconry arose under their title. Yet it remains obscure whether their bodies, whole or in their greater part, were brought to Rome. Nevertheless, Otgar, the fifth archbishop of Mainz after Saint Boniface,

“From the city of Rome this bishop brought both of them,

and, after building a basilica, publicly placed a monument to Saint Sergius as a sign of veneration and honor.”

It was certainly pleasant to read in *Ancient Readings*, volume V, a hymn that bears witness to their arrival in the western world and expresses the praises and burial place of these martyrs, although not so clearly as to remove every ambiguity:

“Therefore, pursuing the reward of the age,

we ask you to favor us by your merits,

so that *nosos* (‘disease’) may not harm

these citizens of yours.

This place of yours is called Alba (*topus* [*tocus*]),

a city adorned with sacred treasures,

which the holy ashes adorn:

holy bodies (*somata*).”

The form belongs to the age of the grandsons of Charlemagne, with an affectation of Hellenism. But what geographer will mark out this Alba for us with his measuring rod? In his catalogue he does indeed list many cities of that name. More recent hagiologists, such as Wicelius in the *Choir of the Saints*, and the Martyrology commonly attributed to Peter Canisius, report that these martyrs rest among the Venetians, although Wicelius is unwilling to affirm this consistently. Following Rabanus, I am compelled to believe that they were brought into the diocese of Mainz.

From the following epigrams I infer that the body or principal bones of Saint Sergius were deposited in a celebrated basilica. For Rabanus had a reliquary made for him (epigram 79) and adorned the tomb’s confession with verses (epigram 80). Finally, he completed the ciborium begun by Otgar and placed above the altar of Saint Martin, dedicating it to the honor of both saints—Saint Martin, who remains the patron of the church of Mainz, and the martyr Saint Sergius (epigram 81).

Incidentally, I note that *ciborium*, in Athenaeus, book XI, and in his interpreter J. Casaubon, is a name used by the Egyptians for a particular kind of cup. Hence Hesychius writes: κιβώριον αἰγύπτιον ὄνομα ἐπὶ ποτηρίου—“ciborium, an Egyptian name for a drinking cup.” Ecclesiastical usage early adopted the word for a repository or reliquary that received the body of Christ or the bones of the saints; later it also used it for those larger structures which, raised above the altar-table like towers and chests, retain the name “altar.” In this sense Rabanus here called the ciborium’s structure an “arx,” or citadel. Consult Stephen Durand on ecclesiastical rites, book I, chapter 16.

But I return at once to the martyrs, and also pursue their memory in Eisfeld, in the not insignificant town of Heiligenstadt. This town, situated in central Germany and bounded by Mount Melibocus, is a borderland of many noble provinces—Hesse, Thuringia, and Brunswick—and is subject to the rule of the archbishop of Mainz. Through the college of the Society, with manifold cultivation, he polished and preserved in the Catholic religion the region’s rough and weakened people, impoverished by the hardships of the times.

While the history of Mainz is silent on this matter, ritual books nevertheless attest that in a very ancient collegiate church dedicated to Saint Martin the patronage of the holy martyrs Sergius and Bacchus is frequently invoked. When I consulted the clergy of that place, I discovered there truly distinguished and well-attested memorials of their account, which can easily rescue the titles of these verses and the fading memory of the martyrs from oblivion, and can place the origins of the town in a better light after clearing away the clouds of fable.

Indeed, a manuscript concerning the tombs of the martyrs Aureus and Justin, Sergius and Bacchus, and the relics of Saint Martin’s basilica, attributes the munificence by which the church was built and founded to Dagobert, king of the Franks. It relates that the king, abandoned by his people because of the disfigurement of leprosy, left his kingdom and went into unknown lands; that, having found and established a dwelling in Eisfeld, he went hunting, as is customary; that, exhausted, he surrendered to sleep on a pleasant couch of grassy earth, softened by flowers; that, when he awoke, he placed dew-moistened hands upon his eyes; and that health returned through contact with the dew—but only to his hands and face.

Thereupon, falling forward upon his whole body again at the urging of his queen, he immersed himself in the dewy grass. He learned from the answer of a hermit that, when the leprosy had been completely wiped away, the cure had been granted through the prayers of Justin and Aureus, whose relics were preserved unburied at that place where the king had been healed. At the hermit’s urging, he therefore dedicated the place to religion, donated money and estates so that a church might arise and a clergy devoted to God might grow there. He also left the place a name derived from the saints, which sounds as “Heiligenstadt.”

Yet, after so many wounds inflicted on this place by wars and fires, can we believe—as those who committed these matters to memory themselves admit—that traces of a church and clergy survived in this region, so close to Thuringia, from the time of Dagobert? In any case, the stories that the martyrdom of Aureus and Justin took place there in the wilderness, or that their heads, severed from their trunks, were carried to Mainz at Attila’s command, deserve no credence. This is not because they celebrate Justin as Justina, but because the account directly contradicts the provincial history of Aureus’s passion, deprives the metropolis of the glory of the contest, and finally sells fictions more worthy of poets than sacred writers as true history.

Thus we pronounce our judgment on the whole matter: while Louis the Pious ruled, Archbishop Otgar won exceptional honor and favor for Heiligenstadt by transferring there the relics of the martyr Saint Sergius and the presbyter Saint Justin, and by augmenting them with those of Bacchus and Bishop Aureus.

From the worship and veneration of these saints, celebrated by large gatherings of people—as great as those times allowed—the place received distinction and renown, especially when a more splendid and enlarged basilica, built at Otgar’s expense, succeeded the ancient church of Saint Martin, which had perhaps collapsed or fallen into obscurity, and when it flourished still more through Rabanus’s care.

We rightly wish here to restore the memory of the presbyter and confessor Justin, whom Rabanus teaches in more than one place that Otgar brought from Rome, in numbers 107 and 130 and following. Without these verses and the testimony of the clergy of Heiligenstadt, antiquity would have buried his name and title. Since the story of Aureus and his sister Justina is better known among the people, many thought it religiously safer to invoke the patronage of Saint Justin because of the suspicion of error and mistaken identity.

But apart from the consistent writing of the old book made available to me—even though that book incorrectly calls him a deacon and martyr—the stone covering the tomb in the middle of the basilica speaks of Justin. Two images carved upon this stone show him in Levitical vesture, as well as the blessed Aureus in pontifical dress. Although the inscription is silent, indeed nonexistent, the voice of our ancestors nevertheless interprets Justin and Aureus as saints.

The manuscript I have mentioned, although polluted by many—and, in my judgment, fabulous—narratives, nevertheless explains, on the basis of ancestral tradition, the memory of the four patrons resting at Heiligenstadt as follows:

“In this distinguished church are preserved, besides the precious relics of the blessed martyrs Aureus and Justin [of the martyr Aureus, the confessor Justin], with no less reverence and worship the venerable bones of the most valiant martyrs of Christ, Sergius and Bacchus, once transferred by royal diligence. The mausolea of all of them are visible to those entering the choir, on the right and left, remarkable in material and workmanship.”

So much is related there, with due adaptation to the basilica’s ancient appearance and its happier beginnings, after which many disasters and ruins followed.

Finally, everything that we have said seems to be confirmed by the confession of Sergius’s tomb, the reliquary made for the martyr, and the title joining Saint Martin, the church’s former patron, to the ciborium; also by the inscription of Saint Justin’s tomb, which we shall give later. It is additionally reported that Rabanus dedicated the more distinguished basilica, which he is said to have carried out on the Kalends of November in a year erased by the ravages of time.

I also think it should be considered whether the name Alba may have adhered to this region of Eisfeld before the name of the saints became widespread, in the way we remember it was earlier recorded in ancient Sapphic verses. But, I think, the inhabitants will readily forgive us that civic glory, since even under Willigis, the distinguished bishop of the see of Mainz—whose generosity greatly increased the fortunes of the clergy there—the place did not deserve the name of a city or town.

For the author of the *Life of Burchard*, bishop of Worms, writing in the age of Otto III, says that Burchard arrived with Willigis at a place called Heiligenstat and was there venerably consecrated by Willigis through the anointing of pontifical blessing.

This is what we have thought fit to say concerning those saints and the city of the saints.]

Verses on the tomb of Saint Sergius.

The greatest honor exists throughout the world for the holy martyrs,

who deserved to die for the name of Christ.

[Col. 1633A] Among them the holy Sergius rejoices as the outstanding one,

who endured severe punishments with his brother Bacchus.

From the city of Rome Bishop Otgar brought both of them,

but here he placed Sergius alone.

### LXXIX

For you, most holy martyr Sergius, Rabanus made

this reliquary—he himself, a little servant of God.

Though made at small expense, yet with devout labor,

it seeks you as its patron and its own.

Ask that the Almighty, in mercy, grant pardon for his offense and the gifts of rest to the unworthy man.

### LXXX. Above the Confession of His Tomb

[Col. 1635A]

Whoever wishes rightly to obtain the gifts of the Thunderer,

let him humbly ask here for aid and the help of the martyrs.

### LXXXI. These Verses Are Written above the Ciborium of the Altar of Saint Martin

Otgar began it; Rabanus rightly completed it—

this lofty structure of a ciborium, O Christ, by your servants.

May you, in your kindness, grant them a reward in heaven

and, almighty Lord, eternal rest.

Bishop Martin and the holy martyr Sergius

assist them with their sacred merits and prayers,

that they may receive pardon for sin and the gifts of light,

and, with the saints, joys and blessed kingdoms.

### LXXXII. Verses on a Tablet Placed among the Seraphim

[Col. 1635B]

Here is Christ the Lord, God, who reigns everywhere,

and, fastened to the cross, broke the harmful chains.

### LXXXIII. Verses …

[Note: [Col. 1635C] This concerns the succession of the bishops of Mainz, apparently only those who assumed office after the Hunnic disaster, roughly from the year 451 of Christ onward. Our Serarius, after adopting from Trithemius the opinion of those who admit forty bishops before Boniface—whereas more recent writers acknowledge only sixteen—and after investigating their chronology at great length and with considerable subtlety in book II of *The Affairs of Mainz*, had no stronger authority with which to support the entire discussion than Meginfrid, a monk of Fulda, whom Trithemius praises both elsewhere and in the preface to the *Life of Saint Maximinus*, bishop of Mainz.

Trithemius writes that Meginfrid lived at Fulda during the time of Otto II and Otto III, composed twenty-four books of histories covering the age of grace, and himself recorded forty bishops of Mainz before Saint Boniface, clearly setting out their names, the dates, and the years of their rule in order.

We have often regretted that none of Meginfrid’s books is found here at Fulda, nor can they be recovered elsewhere, in a matter so useful to the Christian commonwealth. Yet if Trithemius’s credibility is sound, it is no less astonishing that Rabanus should have been such a stranger and outsider to the antiquity of his own church that, although such illustrious documents were available at Fulda almost a century later in Meginfrid’s time, he himself—liberally trained in every branch of learning—should have been surpassed by some little trickle from a secluded spring, from which the entire stream might otherwise have burst forth.

Nevertheless, our Serarius, as though intending to point out gold buried in many places, was content to display the signs and marks of hidden sites, so that, once they had been explored, the reader might dig for himself. For that reason he thought that no numbers assigned to the bishops should be erased, but rather preserved. In very obscure matters, even the slightest ray of light often contributes greatly.

Nor does he deny, or consider contrary to truth, that the Church of Mainz experienced interregna or vacant intervals through various changes of time. The more carefully corrected Acts of Albinus and Theonestus, the ritual books themselves, and our own observations in the metropolitan church of Trier all acknowledge this. We have shown from the history of the Venerable Bede that the diocese in First Germany, in which Mainz lies, was at one time open to the bishops of Trier.] These bishops rightly held this see

after the Huns had ravaged this place.

But I could nowhere find the exact number of years

during which each one ruled the church.

Yet after the supreme bishop Boniface

was sent here from Rome as a pious ruler everywhere,

these men rightly held this see after him,

in succession, and likewise in episcopal office.

[Note: [Col. 1636C] This passage was explained by our Serarius in his *Affairs of Mainz*, book III, note 47. But the hitherto unknown verses, which bring the greatest honor and illumination to the place, and the ancient title of the church—which is now Saint John’s, but was formerly that of the holy Mother of God—rightly suggest that the neighboring fabric of the metropolitan church is older. It is probable that the veneration of the repository did not change its location, even though it was restored several times.]

In the Church of Saint Mary, beside the Tomb of Saint Boniface

After the holy Boniface had completed his martyrdom,

[Col. 1636A] the martyr and bishop, seeking the heights of heaven,

[Note: [Col. 1636C] He was brought here from Frisia and properly placed here with this reliquary. If the reliquary still exists, it is perhaps sunk into the ground and not conspicuous. The old inscription calls it a tomb, composed in a Leonine verse and carved into stone.] brought here from Frisia, he was properly laid here with this reliquary;

when he departed, he left behind here a portion of his blood.

[Note: [Col. 1636C] “Above this tomb …” In the year 857 this tomb had collapsed, [Col. 1636D] but it was restored through the efforts of Archbishop Gerlac. Later, when our memory was fading, it flourished again through the piety of the Reverend Suffragan Stephen, with paintings and ingenious verses inscribed on the southern wall, one of which is this:

“When the quarrel of different men,

a Frisian, killed the father,

Mainz rejoices to possess the slain.

It cannot possess the body, but receives the breathing entrails,

so that here the piety and faith of the bishop may breathe.”

For on the thirtieth day after the martyrdom, 5 July, as the ancients relate, the body of the slain martyr came spontaneously to Mainz against the current of the river.] Above this tomb Rabanus ordered it to be built,

an insignificant servant in praise of the saint.

Though an unworthy native bishop, nevertheless for him,

reader, pour forth prayers to the Lord.

### LXXXV. In the Church of Saint Michael

[Note: [Col. 1636D] Concerning the Fulda churches and the adornment of the prince’s basilica, he writes about the chapel, altar, or chest of Maurus, its figures, Count Guntram’s cross, and other crosses. Since more certain evidence has appeared, I report all these matters here.]

The archangel Michael adorns this hall with prayers;

[Note: [Col. 1637D] The words “In the church of Vodilhohi,” although I confess that investigation has not brought the place to light, may reasonably be expected to receive judgment from elsewhere.]

Behold, in one part I minister a temple to the Lord;

### LXXXIX. Likewise in the Same Chapel, Concerning the Figures

[Col. 1637C]

Behold the banner of the Lord Christ, who conquered hell,

This venerable cross of God shines from the rising of the sun;

Merciful Lord Christ, direct the heart’s sight with your right hand;

God, give your servant approved words.

[Col. 1638A] Here worthy honors are celebrated for all the saints;

### C

Behold those whom the old and the new Law possessed, the devout ones:

### CI

Here the piously buried limbs of the holy martyr rest,

whom Christ wishes to glorify through miracles.

### CII. At the Altar of Saint Peter

holding this altar, dedicates the church.

### CIII. Verses beside the Body of Permenius

[Note: [Col. 1637D] Pirminus, Permenius, Pyrminius, and other forms are found in the ancient sources for the name of this bishop. Whether he was from Meaux or Metz is disputed; we investigate the matter in the registers of the metropolitan church of Trier. Whether you call him from Meaux or Metz, you will establish neither by the authority of the ancient indexes. Trithemius declares for Meaux without hesitation; we prefer Metz.

Marcus Welser touches upon this controversy in book V of *Bavarian Affairs* and says that he came into Germany during the time of Charles Martel. I pass over here Molanus’s chronology, in which he wishes him to have died on 3 November, the day on which Saint Pirminius’s deposition is celebrated, in the year 1034.

In his *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*, Eisengrein names as authors of Pirminius’s life Warmannus, bishop of Constance; Count Henry of Cahye; and the abbot of Reichenau. Walafrid Strabo warmly praises Pirminius as the founder of the monastery on the island of Lake Acronius, called rich Reichenau, and Walafrid himself was not entirely remote from Pirminius’s age and was archimandrite of that flock. He often cites him from *Ancient Readings*, volume VI:

“Where the Rhine, led down from the Alps, mingles with the Ausonian sea,

spreading vast through the western regions,

an island hangs in the midst of its current,

called Augia; Germany lies around it.

This place is wont to produce distinguished companies of monks.

Here the holy bishop Pirminius first built walls

and protected his flock for three years.”

Since the verses we are explaining were requested from Rabanus to preserve the memory of the place where the dead bishop’s body was deposited, Walafrid lights a splendid torch for us by revealing the place of burial. He adds these verses:

“Whoever wishes to know this man’s holy life

should seek the tomb itself; he will prove it sufficiently at Hornbach.”

Now Hornbach is a monastery of Saint Benedict in the diocese of Metz, in the region of Hunsrück, not far from the town of Deux-Ponts. Trithemius mentions it in the *Hirsau Chronicle* under the year 1083 and in the *Spanheim Chronicle* under the year 1470; our table of the bishops of Metz mentions it under Bishop Stephen.] Written for Permenius.

Bishop Permenius of Christ, himself a confessor,

[Col. 1639A] inhabits and consecrates this church and place.

For Christ’s sake, rejecting the present joys of the world,

Here he sought the Frankish people with clear doctrine

and built many holy places for God.

Here too he now rests, laying down his bodily limbs,

while his soul holds blessed kingdoms above.

He also assists [those] who worthily seek heavenly things

and rightly preserves his own servants.

### CVI. Verses on the Tomb of the Holy Martyr Ferrutius

[Note: [Col. 1639D] The author of *The Affairs of Mainz* draws much concerning the martyr Ferrutius from Meginhard’s sermon, book II, chapter 34, and book IV, in the *Life of Saint Lullus*. Since Ferrutius is said to have spent six months in the squalor of imprisonment at Castellum, opposite Mainz, and was then transferred by Lullus to the monastery across the Rhine—now a college of canons—called Bleidenstadt, the matter deserves more careful consideration by the people of Mainz.

For how he died a martyr together with Albanus, when Rabanus says,

“a martyr bearing witness together with Albanus his companion,”

no one after Rabanus, so far as I know, whether ancient or modern, includes Ferrutius in the fellowship of that martyr’s victory.

Meginhard rightly admits that the Acts of Saint Ferrutius were hidden in his own time, either through a lack of written records or because they had perished in the turmoil of wars; hence he touched only upon the memory of the translation. After writing that Bleidenstadt had been founded and adorned by Lullus, he adds that Lullus’s successors Richolf, Haistulf, and Rabanus cultivated the holy place with the same devotion, enlarged the church, decently arranged the tomb of the sacred remains, and comforted Christ’s poor, who kept vigil over the sacred bones, with the utmost human kindness.

Rabanus expressed these matters in the following two epigrams; in addition, following the example of his predecessors, he made a chest and inscription there for the martyr and wrote praises through his own devotion and love.] of the holy martyr Ferrutius.

Long ago, therefore, Bishop Lullus, the honor of the city,

transferred here the bones of the holy martyr Ferrutius.

Afterward Bishop Richolf, and likewise Bishop Haistulf,

enlarged the church and built the tomb.

Their successor, the insignificant Rabanus, following

the example of his predecessors, made this chest and inscription.

### CVII

[Col. 1640A]

Great honor exists everywhere for the worshipers of Christ,

One of these was the holy and worthy Ferrutius,

eternal life and the heavenly kingdoms.

Rabanus produced these verses, compelled by love

for the saints. Almighty God, have mercy on him.

### CVIII. Verses at the Tomb of the Holy Confessor Justin

[Note: [Col. 1640D] We shall later discuss, at number 130, the four altars of the confessor Justin, erected by Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, after the basilica or church of Saint Justin was built; he sought to transmit them to posterity as monuments of his ingenuity.

The ordinary losses caused by time and oblivion would have taken Justin from us completely, had not traces impressed upon him remained in the basilica of Saint Martin at Heiligenstadt. Otgar transferred his body from Rome, and, after the bones had been placed in the tomb, Rabanus inscribed the epitaph. He records that Justin was a presbyter who assisted in burying martyrs during the persecution of Christians.]

An outstanding presbyter and honorable confessor,

here Justin rests with honor.

Bishop Otgar brought him here from the city of Rome

and, building a church, placed his sacred bones here.

Although this holy man was not a martyr in the flesh

who had been slaughtered in the flesh for Christ’s name.

For this he earned praise on earth, and, beyond that,

I, Rabanus, made these verses; and I pray that you,

reader, commend me to the Lord in your prayers.

[Note: [Col. 1641D] Five epigrams were offered to the honor of this church and sent to Nemetes. The monastery of Clinga is situated in the diocese of Speyer, though its former appearance has been altered and it now has another aspect. Trithemius, in his *Chronicle of Hirsau*, under the year 985, praises magnificently Adalbert, abbot of the monastery of Clinga, who had been summoned there from the monastery of Hirsau and whose fame for virtue and wisdom shone throughout all Germany. He also celebrates the monastery of Clinga—he himself calls it “Clingemünster”—in many places: under the year 1041, as united to Hirsau by a brotherly pact; again under 1237, and in the *Chronicle of Sponheim*. Finally, he relates that in 1491 it had abandoned the rule of its original institution, Saint Benedict, and passed to secular Canons, to the great detriment of the abbot, who, fearing stricter discipline, had yielded to the Canons.]

### CXX.—

[Note: [Col. 1641D] The worship and veneration of the martyrs Alexander, Eventius, and Theodulus endure in the Church on the fifth day before the Nones of May. Here Rabanus relates—something not easily found elsewhere—that the body of Theodulus was transferred by Charlemagne from Rome, from the Via Nomentana, into Germany, and perhaps into the diocese of Mainz. He says that the memory of the martyr, and the church built over it, had been weakened by flames and fire, but that he restored it and established a new resting-place for the martyr, with an inscription in verse. From the martyrs’ Acts in Notker’s martyrology, this notable detail has been excerpted: Severina, a devout woman, collected the blessed Alexander and Eventius in one tomb, while she carefully and diligently entrusted Saint Theodulus separately to another. Would that, together with Rabanus, it might be possible to renew the obscure and apparently hidden memory of this martyr and to prostrate ourselves at those holy thresholds—or at least at their traces!]

In the tomb of the holy martyr Theodulus.

The bodies of the saints who suffered for Christ’s name,  
who were accustomed to despise the luxury of the world—  
behold, they are rightly venerated, buried in many places;  
they themselves will be present here in sufficient answer to the people’s prayers.

Their chief is the gracious martyr Theodulus,  
who suffered in Italy with the pope Alexander.  
Summoned and brought here from the Roman city  
through Charles’s devotion, he rests here to help many.

But at a varied turn of events, a wicked flame consumed  
all these things, including the covering of the church.  
For many years this place remained disgracefully burned,  
and no one restored it;  
until the unworthy Rabanus, pierced by love of Christ,  
undertook to renew it.

For this church he diligently restored this building  
and constructed the altar;  
he constructed [a resting-place for] the saint’s body and brought it back here.

### CXXI.—

[Note: [Col. 1643A] Friteslar and Herolsfeld are again mentioned here, places dear to apostolic men and often needing to be rescued from oblivion by us, especially because they are increasingly trampled underfoot by heresy. We have treated this matter in the books of the *Fuldensian Antiquities*. Here the great size of the basilica is set before us, formerly built beside the monastery of Herolsfeld. Its origins are owed to the Fuldensian congregation. Saint Lullus, disciple and successor of Boniface, enlarged it. Its beginnings, like those of all things, and likewise those of the monastery and this church, were slight and obscure, when, at Lullus’s command and with Charlemagne’s approval, the body of Saint Wigbert was brought there from Friteslar. After some time Bruno of Hersfeld and Rabanus, abbots of Hersfeld and Fulda, laid the foundations of a larger basilica. Lambert of Hersfeld, a native witness, records this under the year of Christ 831.

That Saint Wigbert was received into a sacred and worthy resting-place, though not into this larger one adorned with the inscriptions here, is clear. We formerly brought to light a notable inscription, marking a later dedication, although we did not wish to regard it as absolutely certain. It names Emperor Louis the Pious as builder of the basilica and exceeds Lambert’s chronology by only two years; Lambert asserts that it was dedicated in the fiftieth year of that century. I would certainly have accomplished something useful if, in my interpretation, I were able to shed some light on Lupus Servatus’s obscure account of the translation of Saint Wigbert, an excellent writer in my judgment.

He therefore recognizes two translations: the first from the monastery of Friteslar to the town of Buriburg, and from there the second to the monastery of Hersfeld. Moreover, in the extensive Hessian district bordering Saxony, near the village of Friteslar, the beginnings were gathered of the Hessian Church. The Hessians, a people converted to the Christian faith before the Saxons, together with the Thuringians, and settled on the frontier of the kingdom against the Saxons, their perpetual enemies, were diligently cultivated by Saint Boniface and his disciples and rendered vigorous military service to the Frankish empire.

I describe this frontier as all the land extending northward between the banks of the Eder, Fulda, and Weser toward the winter-solstice sunset. In this region, especially from the Lippe and Pader districts, the Saxons threatened the Hessians, or Hessi, with hostility. Thus, when Saint Boniface had built a monastery for the Hessians beside the river Eder at the place called Friteslar, the settlers and community of religious men were often harassed by the savage enemy after the frontier had been violated. The inhabitants could scarcely defend their position until it was decided to build a more strongly fortified town across the river, on higher ground; it received the name Buriburg.

This place obtained episcopal dignity, and Boniface wished Saint Wigbert to administer it. At the same time Wigbert was abbot of the monastery of Friteslar and, as Lupus Servatus says—the source from which we draw all this—held the dignity of a priest of the second order, that is, among the Hessians, in the town of Buriburg. For a priest of the second order was either a suffragan, or the same as a bishop’s vicar and archdeacon, as we formerly noted.

Indeed, Blessed Vitta, also called Albuin, Wigbert’s successor, is explicitly called bishop of the church of Buriburg by Pope Zachary, Lupus Servatus, and others. It is therefore clear that Buriburg was honored as an episcopal see even by the public rescripts of Pope Zachary.

The writer of the *History of Mainz* suspects that the name Buriburg was changed, or passed into another form of sound, making it less easy to determine the site. But those who have examined Friteslar more carefully deny that it was founded where it is now seen. They place it in the region called Frauenmünster, or the monastery of the Blessed Virgin, and report that Buriburg stood nearby on a lofty mountain, still visible across the river from the neighboring area.

Lupus Servatus seems to bear decisive witness to this. In his account of the translation of Saint Wigbert, he clearly remembers that the body was taken from the monastery’s old dwelling at Friteslar; he says that a depressed valley lay between, and that, after crossing the intervening river, one easily reached the neighboring mountain where the recently fortified town of Buriburg could be seen, and where the saint’s body was received into safety.

Therefore the more careful topographers place Buriburg on the nearby mountain beyond the Eder, facing the Saxons in hostile territory. They describe Friteslar in the nearest region toward Fulda and the Weser, where today the countryside below joins both banks of the Eder by a bridge.

Buriburg, then, stood near the village and monastery of Friteslar as a fortress against the Saxons, though it too was liable to fall through its own disasters. After the ashes of Bishop Wigbert had been transferred there and came to rest in this town, memorable defeats were inflicted upon the Saxons by an incursion of the Hessians, even when the Saxons received aid from above; and a great radiance of miracles shone forth at the saint’s new tomb.

Meanwhile the chief church which Boniface had once established beside the monastery in honor of Saint Peter remained for a time desolate and neglected because of the Saxons’ continual raids and devastation. It was repeatedly profaned by the enemy, who made mangers and stalls for horses there. Yet heavenly signs were seen, and the church was protected from fires and other disasters of war. Terrified by these signs and driven into flight, the pagans were forced to abandon their desire to do harm.

These events were transmitted and celebrated for posterity in the public Frankish annals and in the writings of Lupus Servatus and other authors, because of the magnitude of the miracle. Regino, under the year 774—which better manuscripts assign to 773—recognizes Buriburg as a fortress and fortified position. He notes Frideslar as a place distinct from the fortress, where a basilica consecrated by the holy martyr Boniface of blessed memory stood, with the buildings of villages spread around it.

But beware of joining Friteslar to the town in chapter 24 of Lupus Servatus, where Albuin is called bishop of Friteslar and of the same town. Friteslar is called only a place by him and by other ancient writers; the name of the town must be understood as referring to nearby Buriburg, whose bishop Albuin was, while he was merely abbot of the monastery of Friteslar.

Lupus Servatus gives an even fuller account of the second translation and asserts that it was divinely commanded, perhaps lest the barbarians finally make booty of the sacred treasure. Nevertheless, the ashes had to be carried out secretly, so that the inhabitants of Buriburg, inflamed by desire for their beloved relic, might not wrest it from the bearers or completely prevent its removal.

Therefore, when Archbishop Lullus and the great Charles had given their assent, Bishop Albuin of Buriburg finally decreed that three faithful monks should carry Saint Wigbert away from Buriburg and that the monks of Hersfeld should receive him with due honors. This was done, and he was magnificently entombed in the principal place of the Hersfeld church.

Lullus erected a shrine as a monument of his devotion to the saint; Rabanus called it a ciborium, and Eginhard, in the translation of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, a wooden roof. Following the custom then established in Gaul and Germany, Lullus placed it above the tomb, beautifully covered with gold, silver, and other metals, on the Ides of August, while Emperor Charles himself favored the work.

Although Lupus does not state the year of this translation, one can infer from his words that it occurred not long after the Saxon incursions. He says that the translation took place after several years had intervened, namely after the Saxons, considering Charles’s absence—he was waging war in Italy against Desiderius the Lombard—a favorable opportunity, had violated the frontier and attacked Friteslar with renewed devastation.

The Frankish annals, together with Anastasius, Regino, and others, refer this event to the year 773 or 774. Since the period of Saint Lullus’s episcopate extends from 754 to 787, one may reasonably conjecture that the translation took place around the year 780.

The basilica to which the epigrams presently in hand belong was dedicated, as Lambert writes, in the year 850 or 851, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November, by Rabanus himself, then archbishop of Mainz. At the same time—or rather in the following year—the bones of Saint Lullus were transferred to another part of the basilica.

For in the old catalogue of the relics of the Hersfeld church these titles are found:

“Saint Wigbert the abbot is wholly present here in body.”  
“Saint Lullus the bishop rests here in body.”]

These verses were written in the church of Saint Wigbert the Confessor, that is, in the eastern apse, where the saint himself rests bodily.

This gracious house of God has been consecrated in Christ’s name,  
whose dedicated altar holds his relics.  
Here remains a portion of the manger and a sacred part of the tomb;  
the Mount of Olives and the beloved table also remain.

The Lord’s disciple Thomas, and Simon the Zealot,  
together with Jude of James, place their sacred remains here.  
Mark, the writer of the Gospel, and the martyr Boniface,  
Sixtus and Albanus, and Ferrutius remain here.

Beloved Landebertus, Pancratius, and Georgius,  
together with Valentinus, their companion, are present here.

### CXXII.—In the southern apse, beside the altar of Saints Peter and Paul, these verses are contained.

This altar is rightly aided by the merits  
of Peter the prince, Paul the teacher, and holy Andrew.  
Here Clement the shepherd, blessed Pope Marcellus,  
Saint Alexander, and Callistus rejoice.

The illustrious Urban, Sylvester, and Fabian,  
the supreme pontiffs, receive devout vows here.

### CXXIII.—Above the nearest altar, on the left side, these have been placed.

This altar holds Stephen and Laurence,  
sacred in the office of levite and in martyrdom.  
Agapitus likewise, and gracious Felicissimus,  
hold this inscription and speak through their merits.

Here Zeno also rejoices, and Vincent, both ministers  
who once belonged to Christ and now remain in the heavenly citadel.

### CXXIV.—Above the altar on the right, these have been inscribed.

Venantius and Quirinus, illustrious in martyrdom,  
famous pontiffs, hold this inscription.  
Saint Alexander and blessed Cornelius,  
the supreme rulers of the apostolic see.

Here Isidore rejoices, and the gracious bishop Theodulus,  
who was a renowned witness of Christ throughout the world.  
Maximus, Hippolytus, Victor, and Candidus himself  
will be present here with forty martyrs.

### CXXV.—In the northern apse, beside the altar of the Mother of God, these verses are contained.

Virgin Mother of God, consecrate this altar yourself;  
may the virginal choir remain here with you.  
Agnes, Cecilia, Juliana, and the martyr Agatha,  
Euphemia, Eutropia, and Pudentiana;

Rufina, Prisca, Emerita, and blessed Lioba—  
may Brigid and Eugenia also stand here in response to vows.

### CXXVI.—The altar nearest it, situated on the northern side, contains these verses.

O Father Benedict, supreme shepherd of monks,  
rightly help this altar by your prayers.  
Bishop Cuthbert and gracious Bishop Arnulf,  
may they be present here with you and help us by their merits.

Felix, Justinus, Goar the gracious priest,  
and Fortunatus—may they do the same here.

### CXXVII.—On the right side, these verses were written above the altar.

This altar holds Gervasius and Protasius,  
distinguished by martyrdom, and likewise Sebastian.  
Vitus, Sinizius, Cosmas, and Damian together,  
Gordianus likewise and Epimachus, love it.

Sergius and Bacchus, Protus and Hyacinthus together,  
and holy Nazarius, himself a devout martyr.

### CXXVIII.—It contains these relics at the cross placed opposite the altar.

Here is a part of the Lord’s cross, by which Christ blessed the ages,  
a portion of the sweat-cloth and of the sacred cloak.  
Behold Pope Gregory, Bishop Martin the gracious,  
Ambrose the teacher, and Medard rejoice.

Maximinus is present, Germanus, and here Remigius,  
with the illustrious virgin and martyr Anastasia.

### CXXIX.—In the western apse of the same church, beside the altar of the Lord’s Forerunner, these verses were written.

Here is the illustrious herald of Christ, John the Baptist,  
and John the writer of the Gospel rejoices.  
Here also Dionysius and Chylianus, the gracious martyr,  
pray together with their companions.

The martyr Marcellinus is present, and honorable Peter,  
Nereus, Achilleus, Prisca, and Aquila himself.  
Mark, Romanus, Crispinus, and Crispinianus,  
joined together, stand here for sacred prayers.

Behold Tiburtius, present here with Valerian  
and Caesarius together; they receive devout vows.

Therefore I admonish all who rightly approach this place  
for the purpose of prayer: let them do so with a sound mind.

### CXXX.—At Fulda, the church of Saint Mary situated on the mountain contains these relics in the eastern crypt.

Behold, here is a sacred portion of the tablets of Mount Sinai,  
and of the Lord’s manger and of his own [relic—text uncertain].  
Here Pope Sixtus, great Januarius,  
and the sacred levites, strong in martyrdom.

Here remain Hermes the martyr, Quirinus, and Sulpitius,  
Eustratius and Romulus, with perpetual praise.  
The martyr Theodulus, Bishop Humbert the gracious,  
and gracious Wigbert together rejoice here.

The worthy sacred virgin and Emerita alike shine here,  
equal in merits and in sacred prayers.

### CXXXI.—In the church of Saint Justin the Confessor, these verses were written, namely, on the first altar.

This altar truly declares the tomb of Christ,  
and the relics of the Virgin and Mother bring help.  
Mark, the writer of the Gospel, and the martyr Boniface,  
and the martyr Albanus receive the prayers.

### CXXXII.—On the northern altar, these.

Here the martyr Stephen and likewise the martyr Laurence  
place their sacred remains and hold the altar.  
Saint Alexander and blessed Pope Urban,  
and Bishop Severus, place their relics together.

### CXXXIII.—On the southern side, these.

Here most holy Fabian holds this altar,  
with Marcellinus and Peter as companions.  
Here Agapitus rejoices, and the martyr Felicissimus,  
and Saint Felicity herself, the sacred martyr.

### CXXXIV.—At the cross, these.

Here is placed a gracious portion of the cross of Jesus Christ,  
and likewise a portion of the place from which he ascended to heaven.  
Here remain the sacred pledges of Prince Peter,  
of Andrew his brother, and of many others, for life.

Behold Tiburtius here with his brother Valerian;  
Martin and Benedict stand rejoicing.  
Here the martyr Cecilia, Lioba, and the most holy virgin  
receive devout vows and offer them back to God.

### CXXXV.—

[Note: [Col. 1647D] a We are still investigating this in the diocese of Mainz.]

In the church of Saint Philip.

In the church of Philip this altar fittingly holds sacred relics;  
read them, honorable reader.  
Here is a portion of the Lord’s table, here a sacred part of the tomb;  
here is a most venerable portion of Christ’s ascension.

Here Michael, prince of the heavenly host,  
shares the honor with holy men.  
The martyr Albanus, gracious Boniface himself,  
with Marcellinus and Peter, rejoice here.

Bishop Martin and Benedict, the noble abbot,  
rejoice in prayer and receive prayers.  
Whoever you may be who wish to fulfill pleasing vows,  
see that you do so here with a pure heart.

### CXXXVI.—At the altar in the middle of the church.

This altar contains the sacred pledges of the saints  
and the very gracious gifts of the Lord Christ.  
For here is a portion of the cross by which Christ blessed the ages,  
a portion of the place where he was crucified, and of Calvary.

The Lord’s Forerunner remains here, and gracious Cyriacus;  
the martyr Fabian and Cyprian are present.

### CXXXVII.—On the right altar.

Twelve companions of blessed lot are venerated here;  
they rightly consecrate this altar and help us by their prayers.

### CXXXVIII.—On the left altar.

Here holy Mary, the Mother of Christ, is venerated;  
she remains associated with the sacred virgins.  
Here Agnes the martyr, and Juliana, herself a martyr,  
Cecilia and Lioba, and the martyr Agatha together.

### CXXXIX.—In the church of Saint Saturninus, on the high altar.

This temple of the Lord has been consecrated in Christ’s name,  
whose gifts here shine, rightly deposited.  
A sacred portion of the Lord’s manger, table, and tomb,  
and of his ascension, remains here.

Here Prince Peter is powerful, and Paul the teacher;  
illustrious men shine with martyrdom.  
Behold Albanus is present, and the martyr Boniface,  
who deserved to die for Christ’s name.

The supreme pontiffs Martin and Remigius,  
and likewise the confessor Philip, rejoice here.

### CXL.—On the right altar.

The twelve companions, illustrious through Christ’s gift,  
rightly dedicate and make holy this altar by their prayers.

### CXLI.—On the left altar.

Virgin Mary, Mother of God, consecrate this altar yourself,  
being present and helping it by prayer;  
may the virginal choir also rejoice, graciously,  
and rejoice with you here, helping by its merits.

Here remain Cecilia the virgin, Agnes, and the martyr Agatha,  
Lucia, Lioba, and Juliana.

### CXLII.—At the cross in the middle of the church.

Here is a portion of the Lord’s cross, who reigns supreme in the citadel,  
who, by the blood he shed, blessed the ages in triumph.  
Here Michael rejoices, and John the Baptist,  
and illustrious men pleasing through martyrdom.

Here Saint Stephen, Fabian with Cyriacus,  
and Sebastian shine through martyrdom.  
Here Benedict rejoices; here Pope Gregory stands;  
they receive vows and offer them back to God.

### CXLIII.

The inviolate Virgin Mary, Mother of God, mother of the Thunderer,  
holds and consecrates this hall with her Son.  
Peter and Andrew, brothers, Paul also, and the gracious  
writer of the Gospel, John, rejoice here.

Here is the illustrious herald and Baptist, John,  
and Bishop Martin and Boniface.  
Here are the levite Stephen, Laurence, and Cyriacus,  
present with Albanus and Dionysius.

### CXLIV.

Saint Maximinus, Germanus, and Gregory,  
illustrious pontiffs, and Ferrutius remain here.  
Here Agnes the virgin and the martyr Agatha  
stand in response to vows and devout prayers.

Among these saints the sacred remains of Cosmas and Damian,  
whose feast is celebrated today, also remain here.  
Saints pleasing through martyrdom hold such companions as these,  
whose members rest here.

Therefore I ask you rightly to seek such great patrons,  
if you wish to have God favorable toward you.

### CXLV.

Let the companions and witnesses of the Thunderer consecrate this altar,  
adorning it with merits and sacred prayers:  
Matthew and Simon, Thomas and Bartholomew,  
Cornelius, Sixtus, Sergius, and Bacchus.

### CXLVI.

Confessors and chaste women consecrate this altar  
with prayers and good merits.  
Here are Augustine, Jerome, and Hilary,  
Praxis [Praxedis], Cecilia, Lucia, and Eugenia.

Here Fabian is present and guards his own pledge,  
the supreme bishop, himself also a sacred martyr.  
With him rejoices and here stores sacred relics  
the man powerful in virtue, Sebastian.

### CXLVII.

For Agnes, the gracious virgin, consecrates this altar,  
she who follows Christ the Lamb as God’s bride.  
With her, Cecilia the martyr and the holy woman  
stands here, rightly helping the devout by her prayers.

### CXLVIII.

Marcellinus honorably holds this altar,  
and consecrates it with his companion Peter by their merits.  
Christ led them both to the heavenly citadel,  
illustrious in martyrdom, deeds, and goodness.

Behold the martyr Agatha occupies this distinguished place  
and commends it by her own devout merits.  
The virgin Lucia, Christ’s sweetest bride,  
rightly honors it, dwelling here and helping by her prayers.

### CXLIX.—These verses were written on the chapel altar.

With outstretched hands, Christ, God in the citadel,  
nailed to the cross, thus embraces the whole world.  
He extinguished death, shattered the tyrant’s scepters,  
and himself restored eternal rest to his own.

[Col. 1649C]

## SECTION TWO.—HYMNS

[Note: [Col. 1649D] a In Book II of *On the Instruction of Clerics*, chapter 49, Rabanus says that hymns are all songs composed in praise of God. He commends their use by the example of Christ and the apostles, saying that they are effective for moving the mind toward piety and inflaming the affection of divine love: some are made by heavenly inspiration, others by human ingenuity.

The Church has especially notable authors of hymns: in the Western Church, Saints Hilary and Ambrose. Thus far Rabanus, who, imitating these and others, undertook to weave together a hymnody, from which the Church has chosen to dedicate not a few songs to public use even to this day, or to retain those received from earlier generations.

How greatly Rabanus stirred enthusiasm for the singing of hymns in the minds of his disciples, and spread the example to other monasteries, is shown by the hymns of the ancient Fathers that have recently appeared from the library of Saint Gall, in volume V of the *Ancient Readings*. I readily admit that some hymns found here could be attributed to other writers. Because we observed that several had been inserted into an ancient parchment manuscript by a hand that was not especially old, we have marked them with asterisks to distinguish them. Since most of the remainder are written in the same script and are headed with Rabanus’s name, we do not hesitate to ascribe them to that same parent as legitimate offspring.]

(C)*

[Col. 1649]

### I.—HYMN ON CHARITY  
*(composed in Sapphic meter with a dactylic pentameter)*

A lofty thing, a great and saving good,  
the heavenly gift coming from above,  
the supreme right of the mighty Creator,  
the holy light of the world.

The splendid charity of the Thunderer,  
the ardor and communion of the Trinity,  
the mighty law rightly governing every power,  
the hosts of heaven.

This was the gracious origin of creation,  
for by it heavenly things were established,  
and the beginnings found alike in sea and land  
stand firm.

By this he first enabled Adam to possess within himself,  
behold, God’s likeness, so that he might become  
the image of the Creator; and the Creator set him  
over the whole world.

By this he made the prophets and the patriarchs  
together with the holy Breath, filling them  
so that they might piously proclaim  
Christ as saving doctrine.

By this he caused the Son of the highest Father  
to descend here for healing,  
so that the author might join together  
the heavenly and earthly people.

By this he granted Christ to suffer on the cross,  
to bear scourges, spitting, and thorns,  
to endure the tomb, and to become victorious,  
and he caused him to rise from death.

By this he opened the kingdom to Paul;  
from the time Christ sought the heights, he made  
all who followed his footsteps  
climb to heaven.

By this he gave the Holy Spirit from the ark of Pentecost,  
and thus consecrated  
the first company, when the Paraclete  
visited the world.

This directs the saving company,  
first the companions of Christ and then  
the preachers of the faith, so that the world  
might have salvation.

It prepared martyrs together with virgins  
for the honor of the great King in the citadel,  
and leads the Christian people to the stars,  
to the joys of life.

Joining and uniting the body of Christ,  
it powerfully binds member to member.  
It places the members beneath the head, and joins  
the head with the body.

Behold, this is love; this is the true citadel,  
the summit of virtues, the head and queen;  
this is the fullness of the law and the fountain  
of every goodness.

No living person will see the face of the eternal King  
without it, but he will enter the dark  
underworld, where burning hell  
scorches him.

The author calls this the new commandment;  
he ordered his companions to possess it greatly.  
Therefore let us all possess it  
with a pure heart.

### II.—

[Note: [Col. 1651D] a The distinguished jurist Henry Canisius, when reviewing the poem of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, which he had published in volume V of the *Ancient Readings*, publishes in volume VI, among other pieces, this very sweet hymn on the Nativity of the Lord, written in trochaic tetrameter. He candidly admits that in the book he used no author was identified, so that here we may properly follow the rule of the possessor: possession gives the better claim.]

### HYMN ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

The bright light rightly shines  
when the great star has risen,  
which shines throughout the world,  
driving away the shadows of night.  
When Christ is born, the great King,  
let the whole world rejoice.

The leader from Judah, whom the prophet  
had long ago foretold,  
has come to us in joy,  
born in illustrious Bethlehem.  
When Christ is born, the great King,  
let the whole world rejoice.

The royal virgin mother  
brought him forth, rejoicing in childbirth,  
him whom Gabriel announced  
as Savior of the nations.  
When Christ is born, and so forth.

While wakeful shepherds are troubled  
by concern for their flock,  
a brilliant messenger  
exhorts them to rejoice.  
When Christ is born, and so forth.

The joyful host of angels  
sang together in praise.  
Proclaiming peace to earth,  
they return glory to heaven.  
When Christ is born, and so forth.

O astonishing and wondrous  
sacrament of glory,  
that the Virgin, a little one,  
bears the Thunderer above all things.  
When Christ is born, and so forth.

The Maker of heaven, the Maker of earth,  
is enclosed in a woman’s womb.  
The supreme Author of the angels  
is laid in a manger.  
When Christ is born, and so forth.

He who measures heaven by a span  
encloses earth in a little hand.  
Wrapped in a few swaddling clothes,  
the tiny infant cries.  
When Christ is born, and so forth.

The right hand of the Most High, which first divided  
light from darkness,  
behold, now touches its mother’s breasts,  
seeking a drink of milk.  
When Christ is born, and so forth.

The glorious mouth of the Creator,  
which formed the age,  
behold, now gladly brought near,  
sucks at its mother’s breasts.  
When Christ is born, and so forth.

O blessed mother of Christ,  
woman of David’s stock,  
you are the praise and queen of the world,  
joyful virgin Mary.  
When Christ is born, and so forth.

Be present to the vows of the devout,  
preserving every age.  
For patriarchs and prophets,  
you are the crown of praise and glory.  
When Christ is born, and so forth.

Behold, the rejoicing hosts  
of angels hope  
that you will govern Christ’s people,  
as one acquainted with hidden things.  
When Christ is born, and so forth.

For every sex longs for you,  
Virgin, unmarried yet wedded.  
By your intercession protect  
parents and their children.  
When Christ is born, and so forth.

Heaven rejoices with the heavenly beings,  
with thousands of angels;  
the whole fullness of earth,  
the sea, the stars, and the rivers.  
When Christ is born, the great King,  
let the whole world rejoice.

### III.—HYMN ON THE NATIVITY OF THE INNOCENTS

It is pleasing then to sing songs  
with the voice and lyre,  
to produce melody by art,  
when the milk-white host perishes,  
slain by the wicked deceit of the prince.

And it itself is stained  
with its own blood.  
But when the raging plague  
rouses itself and provokes  
the jealous heart of the ruler  
to bring about the Lord’s death,  
it compels him to send men quickly  
to lay many companies low in death.

For as a lion roars toward a crime,  
from whose mouth a tender lamb  
suddenly escapes far into the fields,  
so he turns his weapons against  
the innocent flock, crushes, tortures,  
and tears it apart.

Thus Herod, driven by chaos,  
mad and raging like a wolf,  
gave thousands of little ones  
to slaughter, swollen with pride,  
horrible, and fierce;  
but Christ avoided the wicked weapons.

What murderous fury was yours then,  
when you looked upon such things?  
What groans did you utter  
when, cutting apart infant limbs,  
you yourself made their mothers mourn?

Good leader, excellent judge,  
you feed upon innocent blood.  
Gasping for tiny bodies,  
you tear apart their innocent entrails.  
Another’s death will give you joy.  
Come, then, executioner: burn, cut.

Divide limbs compacted from clay;  
it is easy to dissolve a fragile thing.  
Pain does not penetrate inward,  
for the Lord remains in the citadel of the mind.

Because he was the cause of their death,  
he will give them rewards above the stars.  
But you too, mad lover of death,  
rightly fall into death’s outermost place  
and will utter a groan without end.

Let the love of weeping people give way.  
Let the mournful duty of those  
who customarily celebrate the dead  
give way, because the kingdoms are open  
to the martyrs, and joys remain forever.

O companions, let us now resound  
the God without end in song,  
him who rightly gave his gifts;  
he himself gladly sings our song:  
Christ is the best God here.

### IV.—

[Note: [Col. 1653D] a Thus, myrrh and gold from Ophir. The latter expression seems to allude to Solomon’s fleet, which brought gold from Ophir, and to other passages of the Old Scripture. The interpreters of Scripture have made extensive investigations concerning the location and meaning of Ophir. See Blessed Arias Montanus’s preface to *Phaleg*, Joseph Acosta, Book I, chapter 3, *On the New World*, Bochart on Psalm 119, and others.]

### HYMN ON THE EPIPHANY

Behold, the heavens glitter splendidly with light;  
they testify that the little one, the Lord, is born.  
He who forms small things and creates lofty things,  
holding the scepters of the kingdom, is God and man.

The mysterious star led the Magi  
to seek the cradle of the peaceful King,  
whom Judaea, holding him in the farthest part of the world,  
gloriously announces with spreading rays.

When wicked Herod heard  
that this King had been born in the cities  
of Judaea, he immediately ordered him to be sought,  
sadly intending soon to hand him over to death.

The Lord was found by the star that pointed him out,  
in Bethlehem together with his parents.  
At once the Magi brought him gifts:  
frankincense, myrrh, and gold from Ophir—  
to the king, the man, and God.

Although the savage Herod himself  
might rage terribly and order  
the little ones to be slaughtered,  
his kingdom is rightly preserved everywhere;  
the envious man collapses before the Lord.

Behold, this is a day noble through its gift;  
this also became a day made noble by the Lord’s baptism.  
The fact that the Lord made wine from water  
gently commends these sacred teachings.

Let us rejoice together in our hearts, I pray,  
because the gracious Lord has come to us here;  
because he wished to receive our gifts,  
because he gave baptism and bestowed the cups.

For Christ the King is present, and judge of the world,  
light from holy light, and Father of all.  
May he lead us to the best homeland  
and make us reap the joys of life.

### V.—HYMN FOR THE EPIPHANY

God came, made man;  
let every nation exult.  
Heaven gave a new star;  
the author of all appears.

The Magi brought gifts,  
the first ambassadors of the nations.  
With sacred mystery  
they signify the glory of the one who lies hidden.

Gold indicates the reign  
of the powerful one; frankincense, the sacred divinity;  
and myrrh, the mortal flesh  
that makes atonement for the fabric of the world.

Herod, the envious enemy,  
most savagely does not understand these things;  
Christ, for the salvation of the nations,  
providently supplies what is needed.

Best Jesus, we pray,  
direct us kindly.  
Ready, let us bring you  
the sacred gifts of praise.

### VI.—ANOTHER

Christ, Redeemer of the peoples,  
consecrates a new baptism.  
Come, all you burdened with sins,  
to wash away every stain.

He consecrates the river Jordan;  
the Savior purifies the waters.

[The springs of the abyss, the rivers,]

The Maker of the world consecrates.

Pour forth bitter tears;

Lay bare the secrets of the heart.

May salty tears from our mouths

Prepare sweet salvation.

May no dregs defile us,

No portion of ancient death;

But may the blessed dwelling of light

Grant everlasting life.

## VII. HYMN TO BE SUNG AT THE LORD’S PASCH

Let us sing to the Lord, our God,

United brothers, reverently,

[Col. 1655B] Singing praises from a devout heart,

Now that we celebrate the Paschal feast.

For Christ has risen from the tomb;

Let humanity rejoice with the choir of angels.

The sacred Lamb once led our fathers

Out of Egypt through the shed blood.

And now Christ himself has redeemed us

By his blood from infernal darkness.

He has risen, etc.

As he once led forth the former people,

After destroying the enemy in the Red Sea,

So also he has freed us by baptism,

The devil being submerged in the wave of his Passion.

He has risen, etc.

For raging Judaea prepared death,

To inflict the death of the cross on Christ the master by treachery;

A pious remedy cannot calm it,

Nor the teaching of the good parent’s word.

He has risen, etc.

By a new device they seize him, betrayed by his disciple;

They drag the teacher away, binding his hands;

Then they hand the innocent man over to the tyrant pontiff,
