That he may torture, scourge, and beat the devout one.

He has risen, etc.

After they slap him and spew saliva

Into his sacred face, and crown his head

With thorns, they suddenly fasten him to the cross;

They give him gall to drink and pierce his side.

He has risen, etc.

[Col. 1655D] As he gives up his spirit, he enters the realm of chaos;

Christ, triumphing over death, drives away the darkness.

He rescued the righteous, bound the enemy,

Giving the stars to the devout and pain to the wicked.

He has risen, etc.

[Col. 1656A] At dawn the Savior rises from the sleep of death,

Peacefully, with an angel as his minister.

The guards tremble, the devout rejoice,

The disciples rejoice, while the envious grieve.

He has risen, etc.

Mary recognizes the teacher by his voice;

Thomas, through the wound in his side, proclaims him God;

Peter, rightly burning with zeal, approaches the tomb;

And the eleven worship the Lord on the mountain.

He has risen, etc.

Why do you rage, Judaea, resisting God,

Fabricating wickedness through a contrived deceit—

Clattering that he was stolen, while he shines forth in triumph,

He who restores the world and slays Satan?

He has risen, etc.

[Col. 1656B] The stars of heaven, the sea, and the earth praise him,

Rejoicing that Christ the Lord lives.

You alone, wicked one, grieve, sadly inventing accusations,

Partner of demons, sharer in Gehenna.

For Christ has risen from the tomb;

Let humanity rejoice with the choir of angels.

## VIII. [Note]

*This is the first hymn received in many churches of Gaul and Germany. Georg Fabricius cautiously included it in his* Thesaurus, *under the title “of uncertain author,” if indeed it is to be read. We examined a book of hymns printed at Cologne about a hundred years ago by Heinrich Quentel, together with an exposition—for ecclesiastical poems were then held in great reverence—in which several of these are described as being used in the Church; for example, IX, “On the Ascension of the Lord,” and XVIII, “The illustrious herald, sacred prophet,” [Col. 1656D] on the nativity of St. John the Baptist; then XIII, “Christ’s accessible gate.” Finally, XII, “What the venerable choir of prophets once sang,” at the Purification of St. Mary. The others frequently used by the Roman Church are: “Come, Creator Spirit,” here X, attributed by others to St. Ambrose; “Golden light,” XVII, for the feasts of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, attributed to Elpis, the wife of Severus Boethius; “Christ of the saints,” XIV and XVI; and “To you, Christ, splendor of the Father,” sung in praise of the archangel Michael—these are attributed to an uncertain author.*

### AT VESPERS ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

The holy day of God is here,

Shining with radiant light,

On which the victorious and mighty

King Christ, exulting, seeks the heavens,

Whom the crowd then proclaims

In resounding praise as the mighty one.

Following the triumphant King,

[Col. 1656C] He enters the gates of heaven.

When the princes see this,

They are immediately astonished;

They ask who the Thunderer is,

And what this passage of so great a leader means.

At once the angelic hosts

Who go before him reply:

“This is the strong and mighty

King of glory, the God of hosts.”

Then all the barriers suddenly open;

The thousands on high rejoice

When they see Christ seated,

Glad in heavenly glory.

O King of heavenly glory,

[Col. 1656D] Who sit at the Father’s right hand,

Look kindly upon us, your servants,

Now entreating you;

Give us hope, faith, and catholic belief;

Give us the gifts of charity,

[Col. 1657A] So that in due manner we may render you

Devout thanks at all times.

## IX. [Note]

*If it is asked whether Rabanus is the author of this poem, this fact is certainly worth remembering: it exists in almost all the ancient breviaries of Germany, but not in those of Italy, England, and so forth. Everyone knows that it is absent from the Church’s modern books. Daniel.*

### ALSO ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

Now a famous feast and great joys

Urge our hearts to bring forth songs,

When Christ ascends the lofty throne,

The devout arbiter of heaven.

He ascends joyfully, exulting, to the ether;

The people of the saints proclaim his fame,

And the angelic choir sings together

The glory of the good victor.

As he ascends above the heavens, he had bound the bonds,

Granting countless gifts to earthly beings;

Returning as the stern judge of all,

He who has just passed over in gentleness.

[Col. 1657B] We pray, illustrious Creator and Lord:

Look upon and protect your devoted servants,

Lest the devouring envy of the devil overwhelm us

Or plunge us into hell.

When you return in a flame-emitting cloud,

Judging and laying bare the hidden things of humanity,

Do not impose dreadful punishments upon the guilty,

But good rewards upon the just.

Grant this, excellent and supreme Father;

You, Son of God, and good Spirit, grant it;

O radiant Trinity, reigning forever,

Through all ages in holiness.

## X. HYMN TO THE HOLY SPIRIT

[Col. 1657C] Come, Creator Spirit,

Visit the minds of your own.

Fill with heavenly grace

The hearts that you have created.

You are called the Paraclete,

The gift of God Most High,

Living spring, fire, charity,

And spiritual anointing.

You are sevenfold in your gift;

You are the finger of God’s right hand.

You are the Father’s promised one,

Enriching our throats with speech.

Kindle light in our senses;

Pour love into our hearts.

Strengthen continually

[Col. 1657D] The weakness of our bodies by your power.

Drive the enemy far away,

And grant peace at once.

With you as our guide before us,

May we avoid every evil.

Through you may we know the Father;

May we also know the Son;

May we believe at all times

That you are the Spirit of both.

Grant this, most holy Father,

[Col. 1658A] And only-begotten one equal to the Father,

With the Paraclete Spirit,

Reigning through every age.

## XI. HYMN ON THE NATIVITY OF CHRIST

Let all flesh rejoice

At Christ the Lord who has been born.

Because of the guilt of the first-created man,

He put on our flesh.

So that he might save those whom

The God of wisdom formed.

Through John he greatly commended

Grace.

Baptized in the Jordan,

He washed away the sins of the world,

So that he might cleanse

[Col. 1658B] The offenses of believing peoples.

The Father’s Word, made flesh,

Is born from a Virgin.

He did not lose his divinity,

But assumed the form of a servant,

So that the Almighty might condemn

Sin arising from sin.

The Father’s voice called him:

“Behold, my Son,

In whom I am well pleased,”

The Lord of heaven and earth.

Peoples, obey him;

Kings, submit yourselves.

## XII. HYMN AT THE PURIFICATION OF HOLY MARY

[Col. 1658C] What the venerable choir of prophets once sang,

Filled with the Holy Spirit,

Is shown to have been fulfilled in Mary,

The mother of God.

This Virgin conceived and gave birth

To the God and Lord of heaven and earth;

And after childbirth she deserved to remain

Unviolated.

The just old man Simeon

Joyfully took him in his arms

In the Lord’s house,

Because he had seen Christ, long desired,

With his own eyes.

Mother of the eternal King,

We earnestly ask you: favor us who pray.

You who, retaining the realms

Of lofty Olympus, have sought

[Col. 1658D] The heights—

To our God be glory and power;

May there be perpetual salvation and enduring honor

To him who dwells in the highest citadel of heaven,

Three and one.

## XIII. ALSO A HYMN ON THE SOLEMNITY OF HOLY MARY

Christ’s gate becomes accessible,

Filled full of grace;

The King passes through, yet it remains

Closed, as it was through the ages.

The offspring of the heavenly Godhead

Came forth from the Virgin’s chamber:

The Bridegroom, Redeemer, and Creator,

The giant of his Church.

The mother’s honor and joy,

The immense hope of believers,

Through the dark cups of death

Loosed our sins.

Glory to God the Father, etc.

## XIV. [Note]

*It is sung at Lauds on the Dedication of St. Michael. Do not be surprised that the other archangels and all the heavenly spirits, as well as Mary, who is the queen of the angels, are mentioned. For it is the feast of all the angels, as is clear from the Collect and from the fourth lesson and those that follow. Daniel.*

### HYMN ON SAINT MICHAEL THE ARCHANGEL

Christ, glory of the holy angels,

Ruler and creator of humankind,

Kindly grant us to ascend

To the eternal kingdom.

[Col. 1659B] We ask that Michael, the angel of peace,

Be sent from heaven to this dwelling;

So that, when he comes to us often,

All prosperity may increase.

May the mighty angel Gabriel

Drive away the ancient enemy;

May he often fly down from above

To visit this temple of ours.

Send us from heaven Raphael,

The angel, physician of salvation,

So that he may heal all the sick

And likewise direct our actions.

From this place may Mary, the mother of our God,

And the entire choir of angels

Always assist us,

Together with the whole blessed assembly.

[Col. 1659C] May the blessed Godhead grant this to us—

Of the Father and the Son,

And likewise of the Holy Spirit,

Whose glory resounds throughout

The whole world. Amen.

## XV. HYMN ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

Glory to God

In the highest today:

The heavenly host

First sang it.

The true peace of the angels

Has descended to earth

In voices.

Today the heavens

[Col. 1659D] Have become honey-sweet,

And the sea has made

Its waves equal in sweetness

To a gentle murmur,

With a calm breath

Blowing softly.

## XVI. ON SAINT MICHAEL THE ARCHANGEL

To you, Christ, splendor of the Father, life and strength of hearts,

In the sight of the angels we sing psalms with prayers and voice;

Alternating, we offer a melody with resounding voices.

[Col. 1660A] We all praise and venerate the soldiers of heaven,

But especially the commander of the heavenly host,

Michael, crushing Zabulon by his might.

With him as our guardian, drive far away,

Most merciful King Christ,

Every wickedness of the enemy;

Restore us to your paradise, pure in heart and body,

By your mercy alone.

Let us resound glory to the Father with melodious voices, etc.

## XVII. HYMN ON SAINTS PETER AND PAUL

*“Golden light and roseate beauty,” etc.*

*(See the Roman Office. At the end this stanza is added:)*

Two olive trees, one in piety,

See your devoted ones, strengthened by the greatest hope,

Filled from the twofold fountain of charity,

Obtain life after the death of the flesh.

[Col. 1660B] To the Trinity, etc.

## XVIII. HYMN ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

The illustrious herald, sacred prophet,

Blessed paranymph of the eternal King,

And voice of one crying powerfully to the Lord:

“Make straight the path.”

You who pointed out the Redeemer with your finger,

Rightly declaring that he was taking away every crime of the world,

Announcing the Lamb, wholly merciful,

Who would free the world;

And you sensed the Father resounding,

The Holy Spirit hovering above,

When you deserved to baptize

The Redeemer Christ in the waters.

We believe that you were made a shining lamp,

With the angel as witness, the glory of Elijah,

Born on this day—

You whom the world honors.

Behold the people piously asking;

Make us rightly count the reigning Lord as our parent,

And, by merciful allotment, receive

The light and accept our prayers.

Since you are called the angel of the Most High,

Ask the Thunderer, who rightly forms all things,

That we may be joined to the holy stars

In the citadel of heaven.

Grant this also, heavenly Father;

Grant this, Redeemer, Son of the Supreme;

Grant this, guiding Spirit, we pray,

Throughout every age.

## XIX. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL

[Col. 1660D] Companions, celebrate together

The nativity of the holy chief apostles;

Sing it with praises,

And joyfully sound forth their distinguished triumph.

The illustrious glory of such great companions

Of the excellent King surely demands this,

With whom they joyfully remain forever

In the citadel of light.

For Peter raises up a lofty title,

When, as heaven’s key-bearer, he exults

In praise of God, powerfully holding

[Col. 1661A] The kingdoms of heaven.

His perpetual and illustrious companion is Paul,

A teacher and excellent man,

Christ’s precious vessel and ruler of God’s people.

Behold: those whom one calls, the other places above;

Those whom Paul receives, Peter admits.

Both are witnesses of Christ,

Citizens and inhabitants of heaven.

For Peter follows Christ through the death of the cross,

While Paul is horribly struck down at the head;

Both rightly hold one head—the victorious God.

By their most holy prayers, O Christ,

We ask that you quickly grant us

To seek you from heaven;

May every crime be absent,

And may all things go well.

May we be free from guilt in hand and deed;

Grant our hearts a devout and excellent mind,

So that, as flocks rightly worshiping you, we may behold you, Lord.

His is the honor of the world and of heaven;

His is life, salvation, and the greatest goods;

His is the name forever,

And his everlasting kingdom.

To the unbegotten Father be the greatest glory;

To the Son likewise be fitting glory;

And to the Holy Spirit together with them,

Through all ages in holiness.

## XX. HYMN IN PRAISE OF SAINT BONIFACE THE MARTYR

The illustrious glory of the saints grows everywhere,

And the splendor of their merit shines throughout the world.

Asia magnifies James, Ausonia also Peter,

And Ephesus John, Africa Cyprian.

Germany, no less, exalts and celebrates

The praises and life-giving work of the martyr Boniface.

[Col. 1661C] Rome ordained him, and Britain, his mother,

Sent this glory of the Church as a teacher to the peoples.

A supreme pontiff, renowned for the lightning of his signs,

Brilliant in speech and outstanding in character;

Whom so great a prophetic grace supports with honor

That he reported many future things as new events.

Let him be proclaimed a minister of eternal life

To the Franks, Frisians, and Saxons alike.

Although the Frisian people, always savage in character,

Polluted their hands with the martyr’s blood,

Christ’s most truthful voice foretold what is now

Seen fulfilled in many places.

As the earth dies, it produces abundant grain,

And strives to multiply its seed and fruit;

[Col. 1661D] So the most joyful harvest of the Lord’s priest grows,

To be glorified from a few grains.

Behold, though now dead, he lives as he formerly did,

Winning for Christ hosts of many kinds.

Signs move the peoples; the blind see great wonders,

And the sound of his sweat itself thunders in their ears.

The stains of diseases flee;

The impious madness of the dark demon withdraws

At the martyr’s prayers.

Thus Christ enriched his servant with honor,

So that he might reign in heaven

And command upon earth.

The Lord grants the eternal praises of many to increase—

Those whom the merit of faith had made holy.

But the teachers of the Church are rightly praised throughout the world,

Those whom work, word, and faith prepare.

Therefore this man of God, scorning worldly things, left them behind,

[Col. 1662A] For Christ, who would give all better things.

Here he receives a rich hundredfold harvest,

And, moreover, possesses eternal rest.

You are worthy of praise, indeed, leading a blameless life,

You who thus closed the limits and reckoning of your age.

Already a sojourner of the Lord, you had conquered the savage enemy;

Now, a sojourner of the Lord, you reign with Christ.

Joyfully he has already entered God’s great joys,

And he invites you to God’s great joys.

By his own blood he surely obtained blessed rest for himself;

By his own blood he surely commands it for us.

By his martyrdom he adorns whatever Germany nurtures,

And by his own martyrdom he adorns his offspring.

O fatherland, O people enriched by so great a patron,

Through whom life has come—O fatherland, O people!

[Col. 1662B] O you who were worthy, thrice and four times blessed,

Worthy to be ruled by this bishop!

Glory worthy of God, who granted that he should be such;

And great glory to God, who gave him to us.

Let us all say great glory to God forever,

Through all ages: Great glory to God.

## XXI. ON THE NATIVITY OF SAINT ANDREW THE APOSTLE

Behold, a day comes to us at its appointed time,

Now celebrated, bright, and beloved,

On which the victorious saint

Andrew, the Lord’s apostle,

Hastens to climb above the lofty stars;

He was the brother of Peter,

The illustrious chief,

And himself a manly leader,

[Col. 1662C] Sharing in martyrdom.

While the companions, equal in step and matched,

Together equaled Christ’s teachings,

They gathered them up and followed him in death,

And followed his footsteps through the cross.

Peter and Andrew had been fishermen;

Afterward both seized the world and its hosts,

Laid waste the seas of the world,

And drew them toward the kingdoms of heaven.

They rightly and bravely sought the praise of the cross,

While they proclaimed the glory of Christ from the cross;

They took possession of heaven’s kingdoms,

And gathered life from the cross.

When Andrew saw the cross,

[Col. 1662D] He suddenly exclaimed, crying out:

“Hail, holy triumph,

Perpetual honor of Christ.

Receive me now, your servant, kneeling—

You who once raised up the merciful Lord.

Now return to the Master

What you had sought out for me from God.”

By his most holy prayers, O Christ,

We ask you yourself to absolve us from guilt;

Give the redeemed to the light,

Cleansing the guilty by your blood.

Give us a sober mind, as you rule the stranger;

Give us the thread of work out of the dregs of the body;

Within, without, everywhere,

Protect us, illustrious one.

[Col. 1663A] Grant this, excellent and supreme Father;

You, Son of God, and good Spirit, grant it,

Reigning alone in the citadel,

Through all ages in holiness.

## XXII. HYMN ON A CONFESSOR  
*(Sapphic meter)*

Holy confessor, blessed in merits,

See the devout assembly gathered for you,

Resounding a song with melodious voice

And united minds.

It rejoices to celebrate your feast,

On which you, holy one, conquered bitter death,

Opening the prison of the body as you went,

Victorious to the stars.

Therefore, now present, we devoutly ask you:

Appeal to the Judge with your consecrated prayers,

So that the Creator, merciful and compassionate,

May remember us.

And may the Redeemer himself grant that we remain

Always faithful to him in heart,

Please him sufficiently through grateful deeds,

And merit forgiveness for every offense.

Holy Father, grant this through the prayers of the blessed;

With you, may your gracious Son

And the Spirit grant it also, we pray—

Three and one.

## XXIII. [Note]

*The glorious translation of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, full of miracles, took place; Eginhard, a most devout and learned abbot, formerly palatine to Charlemagne and his son Louis, accurately and piously described it in four books, which are read in volume VII of Surius. The author of the* Ecclesiastical Annals *added an excerpt in the year of Christ 826 and the following years. The martyrs’ first arrival was from the city of Michilunstadium, in the forest called Odonowald, between the Neckar and Main, about six leagues from the river Main. In that place Eginhard had recently established a retreat for a quieter life and had built a basilica, though at that time it had not yet been dedicated. There the deposited martyrs, by many heavenly admonitions, pressed for their departure until, after repeated commands over seven successive days, they obtained their conveyance by dripping an unceasing stream of bloody moisture. They were buried in the basilica of Mülinheim, where now, together with the great monastery over which Eginhard presided, stand the basilica and town of Seligenstadt, in the territory of Mainz, on the river Main. Rabanus therefore delights in the patronage of these martyrs and venerates their memory with special devotion—for Fulda is little more than a day’s journey away.*

### HYMN ON THE HOLY MARTYRS MARCELLINUS AND PETER

Brothers, sing the bright and salutary praises

Which the glory of the saints aptly compels us to utter.

[Col. 1663C] O glorious victors, celebrate with these praises!

How many strong martyrs have I seen through the power of the blessed King?

Marcellinus and Peter have now conquered the world.

O glorious victors, etc.

Those whom the citadel of the world and queen Rome once produced,

She herself sent to the heavenly throne of Christ the King.

O victors, etc.

Peter is an exorcist; Marcellinus, a priest.

Together they summon the sacred people and prepare them for Christ.

O victors, etc.

By their word they heal and offer remedies to sick limbs,

[Col. 1664A] Driving the dreadful power of the demon out of the insane.

O victors, etc.

They are tortured, beaten with scourges, and scored with claws;

Bound in foul chains, they are shut into prison.

O victors, etc.

For Peter is in a narrow pillory, Marcellinus on shards;

Lying down on broken glass, naked over his whole body.

O victors, etc.

The dark judge Serenus strives to conquer them with punishments;

They sing praises fully worthy of Christ the King.

O victors, etc.

An angel sent from heaven soon brought them consolation,

So that, freed from their bonds, they might go wherever they wished.

O victors, etc.

Strengthened and encouraged, the martyrs themselves,

[Col. 1664B] Ready now to appear before Serenus, hasten onward.

O victors, etc.

Then the very angry and agitated Serenus commands

That they be dragged out into the forest and beheaded.

O victors, etc.

From there they proceed rejoicing and climb the lofty stars;

There they sing everlasting praises to Christ the King.

O victors, etc.

This poor hymn-writer offers you this song, martyrs;

Whatever it may be, accept it: your servant has offered it.

O glorious victors, celebrate with these praises!

## XXIV. THE SAME VERSES ON THE SAME MARTYRS

Savior of the world, who govern the scepters of heaven,

And, ruling by your own authority, govern all things,

Be present in kindness and favor the prayers of your servants;

In mercy grant whatever your servants ask.

And add this honor to your martyrs:

That they may be able to return abundant gifts to their own.

A good man, Ainhardus, brought these witnesses of Christ

From the city of Rome and established this place.

[Note: [Col. 1664D] *He recalls Eginhard, the founder of the basilica; his successor, Ratlaicus, priest and abbot, added a new building or hall to the basilica, so that the martyrs might rest there more suitably, and asked a poet friend, whose skill he knew, to compose this tribute. It will be learned from his epitaph how Ratlaicus later flourished at the palace of Emperor Louis through his excellence in counsel, courage, and learning. We believe him to be the very same man whom Eginhard calls his notary in the Acts of the translation of the holy martyrs, and by whose keen industry and skill their bodies were first extracted from the crypt of the basilica of St. Tiburtius in Rome and then transported to the Main over great distances, through an undertaking no less bold than fortunate, under heavenly guidance. Everywhere, and wherever they traveled, traces appeared of the ancient saints’ miracles that customarily occur on such a journey. With one letter changed, he is often called Ratlaicus by Eginhard.]*

His successor, the priest Ratlaicus, after completing the hall,

Composed this inscription for the saints.

May you, Christ God, preserve them through eternal ages,

And grant them, with your saints, the rewards of heaven.

[Col. 1665A] Before the ages and the world’s beginning,

Holy Father, you begot the Son,

Who reigns with you and the Holy Spirit;

You made nine orders of angels.

Look, God, from your heavenly dwelling

Upon these verses composed by Deudofredus [Note: [Col. 1665D] *On the six ages.*],

From the beginning of the world, from the first-created man,

To the final age.

The first age begins with Adam’s creation,

Whom that dragon deceitfully deceived

Through Eve’s tasting of the forbidden tree,

And both were expelled from paradise.

A cruel war arises between two men:

Cain kills Abel without a sword;

He first committed murder,

[Col. 1665B] And its origin follows the innocent man.

## XXV. VERSES ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF MARY

The angel of the Lord came to the Virgin:

“Hail, Mary; the Lord is with you,

Blessed Virgin and mother of God.”

Blessed Virgin and mother of God,

You who deserved to bear the Lord.

Blessed, etc.

For virginity is always chaste,

Upon which heavenly grace came.

Blessed, etc.

God, restorer of the world, light of eternal glory,

Kindly grant me, I beg, forgiveness in my penitence,

So that the heaps of the crime I have committed may lie concealed,

Under whose heavy mass my spirit is compelled to suffer anguish.

Behold, I am not worthy to raise my unhappy eyes

To the furthest stars of heaven for my offenses,

Unless you, merciful one, deign to regard

The streams of my tears by the help of your goodness.

Christ rose from the sleep of death,

And, bowed down and fastened [to the cross], raised the dead.

By his death he redeemed the human being whom he had created;

Judas betrayed the Redeemer of the world,

Then received the price of his deceit,

Rejected it, and hanged himself with a noose.

Therefore the Jews seized the Lord,

And led him, after scourging, into the praetorium;

And they led him, after crowning him, before the governor.

The governor Pilate investigated the charges,

[Col. 1665D] But found no crime in him;

Christ, by keeping silent, freed Adam from death.

In the third flowering of the world,

While it was still growing toward maturity,

In the beauty of youth,

The age of the world was becoming fair.

And beneath all the heavenly axes

The human race would happily

Germinate and sprout forth,

Bringing forth offspring.

[Col. 1666A] A man was born into the world,

A noble patriarch,

Abraham, the friend of God,

A most faithful child,

Born from the golden Hebrew stock.

From him the Hebrew people

Began to be spoken of,

And let us all proclaim glory

To the eternal Lord,

Who through his goodness

Made us celibates.

Let us also rejoice together,

And praise the Only-Begotten

And the holy Paraclete,

[Col. 1666B] Now and through everlasting ages.

Wisdom of the Father,

Christ the Teacher,

Give sweet gifts

To our tongue,

God, Creator

And King, Redeemer.

Scatter the seeds of the word

Throughout the world

Among the nations,

So that, rightly singing

Your praises, they may adorn you,

Lover of light.

Sing psalms to the Highest,

Sing psalms to the King,

[Col. 1666C] Sing psalms to Jesus,

Sing psalms to Christ,

Sing psalms to the living,

Sing psalms to the true one:

Hosanna in the highest.

Hosanna in the stars,

Hosanna in the fields,

Hosanna in the waves,

Hosanna in these things,

O God, whom you hate [text uncertain].

Glory to the Father,

Glory to the Son,

Glory to the Holy

Spirit, who are

[Col. 1666D] Supreme power

And holy strength.

## XXVI. [Note]

*The poem is unmetrical* (ἄμετρον) *and acrostic, following the sequence of the alphabet. It sets before the eyes charity, equally good, and the filth of avarice; it was teeming with errors, and its awkward meter and barbarous language prompt doubt whether it ought to be counted among Rabanus’ works.*

### HYMN ON CHARITY

Noble, true, and excellent undivided charity,

Whoever has it loves God and loves his neighbor.

Whoever does not have it gains no increase of forgiveness—

The savage, brutal beast, avarice,

Which forever drags those who consent to it

With itself into dark infernal places, where they suffer punishments.

The beloved Apostle called charity

[Col. 1667A] The true, supreme, and just God, who created all things;

Whoever fears him possesses the bond of charity.

A dreadful hunger, a double evil, is the worst desire,

Always anxious to relinquish and to increase;

For even Gehenna itself never says, “It is enough.”

From the root of charity all good things proceed,

For the language of angels and of human beings

Is comparable only to it, which is the mother of all things.

A savage deceiver, an evil stench—this is avarice,

Which is sad, wrinkled, and intolerable;

It helps itself alone and gives no support to any of the brothers.

This greatest virtue is pleasing, joyful, and eager;

It believes, loves, hopes, and endures everything,

Patiently bearing all things, it loosens our sins.

[Col. 1667B] Alas! How greatly to be lamented is this empty straw,

Always hissing, biting, and gnashing upon its lips!

It neither pities itself nor comes to the aid of others.

For he follows the footsteps of charity

Who loves his brothers and, for the Lord’s sake,

Venerates the Lord in his neighbor,

As the law teaches by commanding continual love.

Likewise, a miserly cleric is infernal steel [*Kalips*; text uncertain],

Who turns the examples of Scripture into vice—

One whom Paul did not even judge worthy to name among the saints.

Yet the Lord loves the cheerful giver,

Who always eagerly distributes his own goods to the poor;

For his righteousness endures forever.

[Col. 1667C] But one who distributes badly loves the Lord himself [text uncertain]:

When one gives while murmuring with the mouth

And grieving also in the heart,

The gift will no longer be pleasing to the Most High God.

The happy man, born of God, rejoices with his brothers—

With the wretched, the orphans, the needy, and the fatherless.

In these, lofty men have received the Lord.

The sacred pages tell that this existed long ago;

Nor, I think, is any poor or rich person hidden from this.

Whoever wishes to consider them . . . [lacuna]

The happy poor man is placed in the bosom of the supreme patriarch Abraham,

Gathered in honor among the holy dwellings;

But the rich man, chained, is handed over to the fires.

Why, therefore, Christian brother, after such an end

Are you forgetful of the eternal reward of both?

You who, because of this brief life, acquire your merit,

The eternal King, ruler of kings and disposer of laws,

Himself return [returns] to all what is just according to their deeds and merits,

Which, after the night of this age, penetrate to us below.

With sound faith, holy man [or “man of holy hope”; text uncertain], attend carefully:

For faith and hope themselves cease at the end,

But joyful charity reigns brightly forever.

With all your strength, O blessed heart of charity,

Always retain it in your mind, always proclaim it with your mouth,

And expend it upon your neighbors in word and deed.

The living trumpet, the holy trumpet, and the hosts of the saints

Have sung this to peoples through sacred examples and words,

[Col. 1668A] From which they may always gain—or possess—the joyful kingdoms of their homeland.

Christ, favor our prayers, Jesus, King and Lord of kings;

Draw to yourself those who wish to follow you through charity,

For you are life, light, and the everlasting way.

We now sing a hymn to you, holy sacred charity,

For you are blessed, ascending the lofty heavens;

You are the omen and the name of the glory of God the Father:

Brighter than emerald, more radiant than every gem.

Shining brilliance, seated above the ether on a lofty throne,

Make us reign with you in glory through charity.

## XXVII. ON THE FEAST OF ALL SAINTS

*(In Thomasius, volume II.)*

Christ, Redeemer of all,

Keep your servants,

Appeased by the holy prayers

Of the blessed ever-virgin.

You blessed hosts also

Of heavenly spirits—

Drive away past, present,

And future evils.

Prophets of the eternal Judge

And apostles of the Lord,

We humbly ask

To be saved by your prayers.

Illustrious martyrs of God

And radiant confessors,

By your prayers

Carry us into the heavenly places.

[Col. 1668C] Choirs of holy virgins

And all monks,

Together with all the saints,

Make us sharers in Christ.

Remove the faithless people

From the borders of believers,

So that we may joyfully render

The praises owed to Christ.

Glory to the unbegotten Father

And to his Only-Begotten,

Together with the Holy Spirit,

Through everlasting ages.

Amen.

## XXVIII. ON THE SAME FEAST

Jesus, Savior of the world,

Come to the redeemed with your aid,

And, holy mother of God,

Ask salvation for the wretched.

Let all the angelic assemblies,

The bands of patriarchs,

And the merits of the prophets

Pray forgiveness for us.

The Baptist, Christ’s forerunner,

And the heavenly key-bearer,

Together with the other apostles,

Release us from the bond of sin.

The sacred choir of martyrs,

The confession of priests,

And virginal purity

[Col. 1669A] Wash us from our sins.

The intercession of monks

And all citizens of heaven

May favor the prayers of suppliants

And ask the reward of life.

[Col. 1670A] Praise, honor, power, and glory

To God the Father and the Son,

And to the Holy Paraclete together,

Through ages of ages.

Amen.

[Col. 1669]

# SECTION THREE. EPITAPHS

[Col. 1669]

## I. EPITAPH OF HILTIBRAT, BISHOP

[Note: [Col. 1669C] *Raised from the bosom of the Fulda community to episcopal dignity; when he held it cannot easily be established from any ancient evidence. I find not a few Hildeberts, whom I associate with the name Hiltebrat. But what “Hilt” signified to the ancient Germans in such a compound is investigated by our Gretser in the prolegomena to his commentary on Paul of Bernried’s* Life of Gregory VII.]

[Col. 1669A]

Here lie buried the remains of the renowned bishop,

Called Hildibrath, truly a servant of God.

France, his mother, gave him birth; Fulda nourished him,

And by election established him as its father.

[Col. 1669B] For afterward, having become a bishop with humble governance,

He continually wiped away his sins with tears.

Make his soul blessed now, O Christ, God;

Say this, O reader—say it: the Father himself asks it.

## II. EPITAPH OF EINHARD

[Note: [Col. 1669D] *This epitaph was written for the basilica at Seligenstadt, in which Eginhard received his tomb. In his own age, this man was by far the most distinguished in practical experience and learning, and his fame among scholars is brighter than any that needs to be enhanced by scholia. Caesar Baronius defended his chaste marriage against the charge of improper love in volume IX of the* Annals, *under the year of Christ 826. He was still alive in 848, when he attended the second synod convened by Rabanus, together with the other abbots. The year of his death is not known to me.]*

You who enter this temple, I ask you not to disdain learning

What this place contains and what its occupant teaches.

Behold, a noble man lies buried in this tomb,

Einhard, the name his father gave him.

Here he was wise in intellect, upright in conduct, and eloquent in speech,

And through his skill he benefited many.

Prince Charles nourished him in his own court,

And through him he completed many works.

[Col. 1669C] For, having undertaken the fitting honor of these saints

[Note: [Col. 1669D] *Of the saints Marcellinus and Peter.*],

He sought out their bodies at Rome and brought them here,

So that they might benefit many by prayers and healing,

And grant the kingdoms of heaven to his own soul.

Christ God, Savior, Ruler, and Creator of humankind,

Kindly grant him eternal rest above the stars.

## III. EPITAPH OF THE EMPEROR LOTHAR

[Note: [Col. 1669D] *This monument, more precious than a jewel, is sought in vain among the later monks of Prüm. Regino, in his* Chronicles *under the year 855, says: “Lothar, having arranged and ordered the affairs of the kingdom, bade farewell to his people, left the world, and came to the monastery of Prüm. There he cut off the hair of his head, received the habit of holy religious life, and ended his final day in the profession of religion on the third day before the Kalends of October.” This date is expressly appended to the epitaph, whereas the author of the* Ecclesiastical Annals, *following his own opinion and that of others, gave the fourth day before the Kalends of October and, by another reckoning, the sixth. He mentions Lothar, praised by Rabanus in the book* On the Soul, *and by Angelomus in the preface to the* Song of Songs.]

This tomb contains the bones of the memorable Caesar,

Lothar, a great and devout prince,

Who ruled the Franks, Italians, and Romans themselves,

[Col. 1670A] But despised everything and departed from here poor.

For thus, as a monk, he reached twice thirty years,

And changed his way of life; afterward he died well,

On the second day before the Kalends of October.

## IV. Epitaph of Haistulf, Archbishop

[Note e: Concerning him, consult *The Affairs of Mainz*, book IV, under Haistulf. Although the tomb is not explicitly displayed there, the words indicate that it was once exhibited together with this epitaph in the monastery of St. Alban and elucidated by Rabanus. The place was later destroyed, as the memory of our ancestors records, by sacrilegious fire during the Brandenburg war.]

[Col. 1670B]

You who have entered the church, you who have filled your mouths with prayers,  
Do not disdain to learn who lies in this tomb.

Here in this sepulchre lie the remains of Archbishop Haistulf,  
Who discharged his episcopal office well.

For twice six years he had ruled this city as its shepherd and king,  
And brought forth apostolic doctrine by mouth and hand.

A guardian of justice, upright, patient, and kind,  
Faithful in speech and pleasing in devotion.

A disciple of Lullus, and duly the successor of Riculphus,  
He was inferior to neither of them in merit.

Who, holy Father, would not know that you are with Christ,  
Whom your splendid life proves to have been with you?

## V. Epitaph of Otgar, Archbishop

[Note f: He too is celebrated in the monuments of the Church of Mainz. Having departed this life in the year of Christ 847, he was buried in the chapel of St. Alban, which bore the title of St. Boniface, and was honored by his successor Rabanus with this epitaph.]

You who have entered the church, you who bend before this altar,  
Reader, do not disdain to read this inscription.

[Col. 1670C]

For this tomb soon reveals to you whose it is,  
And here it will disclose Otgar’s name and illustrious deeds.

Within whose breast victorious patience reigned,  
An anchor fixed amid such mighty waves.

Free from gall, tranquil in spirit, nourished by sweetness,  
He joyfully fulfilled the office of a bishop.

Here he completed four lustres and two years,  
And soon, when the appointed day pressed upon him, he was snatched from the world.

I believe that he was carried by the better way to the heavenly realms;  
The urn does not hold him beneath the funeral pyre, but the palace of heaven contains him.

[Col. 1671A]

Christ, King of kings, be ever gladly present to him,  
And be merciful to us without end, O God.

## VI. Epitaph of Rabanus, Archbishop

[Note a: Nicolaus Serarius published this epitaph almost word for word in his *Affairs of Mainz*. He shows that it was written by Rabanus while he was still alive, and he establishes this, among other things, from the arrangement of the verses. Melchior Hittorp had already published it in his *Commentary on the Divine Offices of the Catholic Church*, where it is prefixed to Rabanus’s books *On the Instruction of Clerics*, with this heading: “The funeral lament of Rabanus Maurus concerning his own life.” More than a hundred years ago Jacob Wimpheling placed it at the end of his work *Acrostics on the Holy Cross*, saying that it had been dug out of the ruins of the monastery of Mount St. Alban, which had already been transferred to the Canons. He adds that Rabanus had occupied the see of Mainz for nine years, had died in 856, and had been buried on Mount St. Alban, then transferred to Fulda. Trithemius disagrees, writing that St. Maximinus and St. Rabanus were carried from Mainz into Saxony by Cardinal Albert and buried in the Basilica of St. Maurice at Halle in 1515. Although some private writers count Rabanus among the saints, this is neither approved nor acknowledged publicly—not even here at Fulda.]

### Of Rabanus, Archbishop

Honorable reader, if you wish to know my life  
During my mortal time, you can learn it thus.

I was indeed born in this city and reborn in the sacred font;  
Afterward, at Fulda, I learned sacred doctrine.

There I became a monk and followed the commands of my elders;  
The holy rule was the standard of my life.

But although I did not always keep it carefully and firmly,  
My cell was nevertheless a pleasant dwelling for me.

But when many years of time had already passed,  
Men gathered to alter the destiny of this place.

They drew me, weak as I was, from my home and led me to the ruler,  
Asking me to undertake the office of bishop,

In which neither the merit of my life nor my doctrine was found,  
Nor the work of a shepherd rightly approved.

My spirit was ready, but my body was weak and slow;  
I did what I could, and what God had granted me.

Now, from my tomb, I ask you, beloved brother:  
By your prayers commend me to Christ the Lord,

That the grace of the eternal Judge may save me forever,  
Looking not to merit, but to the work of devotion.

For Rabanus is my name, and the reading  
Of divine law was always sweet to me everywhere.

To him, O almighty God, grant the heavenly kingdoms,  
And perpetual rest in the citadel of heaven.

## VII. Epitaph of Alcuin

[Note b: Who does not know the praises and commendations of Alcuin, or Albinus Flaccus, a man supreme in the knowledge of the greatest matters in his age? Trithemius rightly placed him in his catalogue of illustrious writers. Many monuments of his genius have been brought to light in our own time, among them those published in volumes I, V, and VI of the *Ancient Readings* by the learned jurist and expert in ancient memory, Henry Canisius. He also inserted this epitaph, whether composed by Albinus or by Rabanus. We investigated the matter in book I of the *Fuldensian Antiquities*, since the neighboring church of Hersfeld claims for itself the ashes and urn of Albinus. He is said to have died in 804, and Canisius gives an inscription stating that “the lord Alcuin, abbot of blessed memory, died in peace on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June.” In volume VI of the *Ancient Readings*, and on the same day in Rabanus’s Martyrology, his deposition is commemorated.]

[Col. 1671C]

Here, traveler, I ask you, stop for a little while as you pass,  
And examine my words with your heart.

So that from my likeness you may recognize your own fate,  
And my condition may be changed into yours.

What you are now, I once was—a famous traveler in the world;  
And what I now am, you too will one day be.

I pursued the world’s delights with empty love;  
Now I am ash and dust, food for worms.

[Col. 1672A]

Therefore remember to care for your soul  
Rather than for the flesh, since the soul remains while the flesh perishes.

Why prepare fields for yourself, when you see how small a chamber  
Holds me in rest here, and how small yours too will become?

Why long to clothe your body in Tyrian purple,  
Which a hungry worm will soon eat as dust? [The printed text has *edet*, “will eat.”]

As flowers perish when the threatening wind comes,  
So all the glory of your flesh perishes.

Reader, I ask you to repay me with a response in this poem,  
And say: “Give pardon, O Christ, to your servant.”

I beg that no pious hand violate the rights of the tomb  
Until the angelic trumpet sounds from the heavenly citadel:

“You who lie in the tomb, rise from the dust of the earth;  
The great Judge is present with countless thousands.”

My name was Alchuuin; I always loved wisdom.  
For this, pour out prayers as you read the inscription.

## VIII. Epitaph of Reginbald, Chorepiscopus

[Note c: Without Rudolf’s commentary, no memory of this Reginbald would now survive. It is therefore reported in the *Acts of Rabanus* that he was Otgar’s suffragan, or chorepiscopus, and it is clear that he diligently and devoutly assisted Rabanus in transferring and entombing the relics of Saints Venantius, Urbanus, Quirinus, and other saints.]

Behold, Reginbald the chorepiscopus rests here,  
But only in body; his spirit seeks the stars.

He who rightly governed this people by word and hand alike  
Will receive a full reward from the Almighty.

## IX. Epitaph of Eigil, Abbot

[Note d: The matter concerning Eigil, abbot of Fulda and Rabanus’s educator, has been treated above.]

Reader, entering through the passage of this small house,  
Read the inscription, look, and learn the fate of the man.

This was Eigil, abbot of famous name,  
Who lies in the tomb but remains above the stars.

He himself ruled this monastery successfully  
And joyfully accomplished many good works in due order.

Therefore, together with the bishop, he transferred  
The sacred bones of the martyr [Note e: St. Boniface],

[Col. 1672C]

And likewise dedicated these two churches [Note f: St. Saviour’s and St. Michael’s].

After this he sought the heights and sent his soul to the stars,  
While he laid the members of his feeble body here.

For him too I, Rabanus, his unworthy successor,  
Out of love composed this inscription: May Christ help them both.

## X. Epitaph of Walachfred, Abbot

[Note g: The abbot of rich Augia, more commonly known by the name Walafrid Strabo, a disciple of Rabanus, was educated in the monasteries of St. Gall and Fulda. Henry Canisius collected much concerning him from various sources in volume VI of the *Ancient Readings*, and in book I of the *Fuldensian Antiquities* we honored him with due praise. He is held to have been the twelfth abbot in succession, to have died at Augia in the year of Christ 842, and to have had this epitaph sent there in 849, in the eighth year of his administration, as Jodocus Metzler, in his book *On the Illustrious Men of St. Gall*, learned from Hermannus Contractus.]

Whoever wishes to know who is buried in this tomb,  
Let him read through this inscription, and so learn everything.

Therefore Walachfred, buried by fate, rests here,  
A priest and monk, strong in intellect.

Abbot of this monastery and its faithful guardian,  
He had carefully read and understood sacred doctrine.

For he taught many, skilled in the rules of metre;  
He composed verses and was eloquent in prose.

Earnestly inviting the sheep to the pastures of the King,  
He distributed sweet salt to the brothers from his mouth.

Himself upright in conduct, he left examples of virtue,  
A shepherd to his disciples and a nourishing love to the people.

But savage death snatched the young man away  
And brought loss to many; Christ, however, carried him to heaven.

Whoever reads this inscription, I ask that for him the faithful  
Pour out prayers to Christ, and thus please the Lord.

## XI. Epitaph of Adalhard

Here lies enclosed Adalhard, so called by name,  
One of the clergy, whom savage death snatched away.

Hartnandus himself composed this inscription with prayer;  
Let the reader say to him: “Have mercy, O God.”

## XII. Epitaph of Isanbert, Priest and Monk

I am Germanic, descended from Norican ancestors, an exile from my homeland,  
Born in Wasconia, a priest and monk.

If, honorable reader, you ask my name,  
I am called Isanbert. Have mercy on me, O God.

## XIII. The Same

I had been Norican by descent and Aquitanian by birth;  
France nurtured me, and there I became a monk.

My parents once called me “Bright Iron,”  
But now the dreadful bonds of death confine me in the tomb.

## XIV. The Same

My first parent was Norican, my mother Aquitanian;  
France carried me away, and I became a priest.

I lived as a monk, called by the name Isanbert;  
Reader, remember me in your prayers.

Behold, as you asked, I have willingly written out of affection  
These verses for your tomb, dear friend:

Composing the inscription in threefold form, and praying to the Trinity,  
That the Most High God from his citadel may preserve you.

Remember me while you live in health in the world,  
So that after death I may gladly seek the stars with you.

## XV. Epitaph of Wigfrid

[Note a: The word *nonna*, repeated from the earliest antiquity of Christianity, was used by the Fathers for a religious woman consecrated to God. This is expressed very significantly by St. Jerome, *Letter* 22, to Eustochium: “Those who have experienced the rule of husbands prefer the freedom of widowhood. They are called chaste women and nuns.” Consult the passage.]

[Col. 1674A]

Behold, here lies buried the noble woman Wigfrid,  
Whom the Saxon and the Thuringian are glad to claim as kin.

She too entered into marriage and brought forth children,  
And after her husband’s burial became a nun dedicated to God.

Her daughter Theotfrid also caused this inscription  
To be written, gladly joining her own funeral to her mother’s.

## XVI. Epitaph of Irmingard

[Note b: Regino’s *Chronicle* agrees entirely with this epitaph: “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 851, Herimingardis, queen, wife of the emperor Lothar, a venerable matron acceptable to God, died.” We have also observed that ancient charters give her the title of empress. Moreover, Irmingard Augusta was buried in the very noble Alsatian monastery of virgins called Ehrinstein. This monastery is said to have been generously endowed around the year 819 by Hirmingardis, wife of Louis the Pious, while Lothar and his wife Irmingard are said to have enriched it with many resources. Hence one should not conceal the views of Brusch in his catalogue of the bishops of Strasbourg: when he attributes the foundation of the nunnery to Lothar’s queen, he understands that she and her daughter of the same name were buried there. But here I prefer to follow the judgment of a more recent writer of no ordinary reputation, Francis Guillimann; he may be consulted under Hatto, the twenty-first bishop of the Church of Strasbourg.]

Whoever enters and properly visits this building,  
May wish to learn what lies hidden in this tomb.

Here rests a woman, Augusta and noble by birth,  
Whose given name was Irmingard.

She began this work and ordered this church to be built here  
To the praise of Christ and for her own repose.

[Col. 1674B]

For, piously receiving the relics of the saints from the city  
Of Rome, she brought them here and placed them here,

So that through their merits she might receive the joys of life  
And obtain pardon for her sins through their prayers.

Living chastely, she despised worldly joys,  
Generous to the poor and suited to every good work.

She lived nobly and left examples of virtue to others,  
Preparing joyful rewards for herself.

While she was still completing the years and time of youth  
And beginning to enter mature age, she died.

Leaving behind the kingdoms of earth, she entered the kingdoms of heaven,  
Holding true joys with Christ and the saints.

Reader, I ask you to commend her properly to the Thunderer  
With continual prayers, so that Christ may receive her.

May she live happily with him in shared rejoicing,  
Blessed forever among the angelic choirs.

[Col. 1674C]

I, Rabanus, composed these odes in verse,  
Sorrowful at her death and rejoicing at her rest.

Irmingard the empress died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 851, in the fourteenth indiction, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, on Good Friday, at approximately the sixth hour, and rested in peace.

## XVII. Epitaph of Tutin

Here lies buried the distinguished man called Tutin,  
Completing the common day when fate summoned him;

Born from the lofty stock of illustrious parents,  
In every custom he matched his noble ancestors,

In intelligence, uprightness, faith, and dignity of speech;  
He lived among royal men with honor.

That he fell as a young man bravely amid the battle  
Was brought about by the great grace of his Lord.

He was the brother of a bishop, swiftest in arms,  
Who brought here the bones of his brother.

Bend your knee and raise your hands, good reader, and pray;  
Say, I ask: “O God, be merciful to them both.”

## XVIII. Epitaph of Gundramn

This place—behold—properly holds gathered in its tombs  
The ashes of its worshipers and itself covers its own.

For Gundramn is here, and below, in body,  
He lies hidden in a sarcophagus; his spirit seeks the heights.

For him, reader, I ask that you deign to pour out  
Prayers to Christ the Lord, that he may favor his servant.

## XIX. Epitaph of Otdruda, His Wife

[Note a: In the obscure memory of private persons, nothing more readily presents itself for conjecture than what is recorded in book III, chapter 13 of the *Fuldensian Antiquities*, concerning the origins of the monastery of Solnhofen. There mention is made of Guntram, Rabanus’s nephew, by whose donation that tract of land, situated on the boundaries of the dioceses of Bamberg and Eichstätt, came to the monastery of Fulda. Nor does it prevent him from being called a chaplain and a sacred lord there. Since he is said to have served at the palace and, through royal generosity, to have obtained the court of St. Sola, it could have happened that, already advanced in years, after renouncing the world following his marriage, he embraced monastic life and was then again summoned to the service of the kings. This little verse supports our conjecture:

“Boniface, by the gift of these men, possesses this place;  
The martyr rightly consecrates it to the Lord.”]

[Col. 1675B]

For this woman was the wife of that man, called Otdruda by name;  
Covered by the turf, she lies properly buried here.

By the gift of these men Boniface possesses this place;  
The martyr rightly consecrates it to the Lord.

Christ God, Savior, Ruler, and Creator of humankind,  
In your mercy grant them eternal rest in heaven.

## XX. Epitaph of Ratlaicus, Priest

[Note b: We have mentioned him in the hymns, as the successor of Eginhard and abbot of Seligenstadt; here Rabanus bestows upon him the honors he deserved.]

Behold the servant of Christ called Ratlaicus by name;  
Here his body rests, but his spirit seeks the heights.

He had been a priest and a devoted lover of wisdom,  
And he discharged the office and work of an abbot well.

Skilled and energetic in the teaching of divine law,  
He learned by investigation and taught others.

Coming from Cologne, he joined King Louis  
And was of great use to him.

For he taught many by his words and caused them to write  
Many things that were suitable for various offices.

Leaving this life while still young, he departed to the heavens,  
And there he holds true joys with Christ.

There is a happy place, remote in the first East,  
Where the greatest gate of eternal heaven stands open.

Yet it is neither near the summer or winter risings,  
But where the sun pours forth the day in spring from its axis.

There a plain spreads out its open spaces;  
No hill rises and no hollow valley gapes.

[Col. 1676B]

But that place towers above our mountains,  
Whose ridges are thought to be lofty, by twice six cubits.

There is a grove of the sun, planted with many trees,  
A woodland ever green with the glory of foliage.

When the Phaethontean fire had blazed from the sky,  
That place remained untouched by the flames.

And when the flood had submerged the world in waves,  
It rose above the waters of Deucalion.

Bloodless disease does not approach it, nor sickly old age,  
Nor cruel death, nor harsh fear.

# Doubtful and Spurious Works

Certain scattered and dispersed pieces of Rabanus and others, similar in subject and style, worthy to be gathered together for the memory of antiquity.

## I

Eulogy of Alexander and Fabian, Roman pontiffs, written for them by Rabanus after he brought their relics into the monastery and church of the Blessed Mother of God at Fulda, on the northern hill, which, devastated by the misfortunes of the preceding age, the most reverend abbot Johann Friedrich now adorns with new buildings.

Supreme pontiffs, whom Rome sent here to be honored,  
Were rulers of the apostolic see.

Rabanus received these servants of Christ with joy,  
And placed their bones in this tomb.

Therefore two Levites, having followed the aforesaid men from the city,  
Came here, worthy of their own honor.

The servant of the Lord, meeting them at once and standing before them,  
Received them humbly and placed them here together.

The martyr Alexander and the martyr Fabian likewise,  
Both holy teachers, came here together.

Disciples of Christ, popes, and worthy ministers,  
Felicissimus and Agapitus remain here.

All these together adorn this church sufficiently with their bones;  
May the Virgin Mother of God commend it through their merits.

You also who have entered the church, seek these men,  
With poured-out prayer, as patrons to aid you.

## II

The bones of Saints Urbanus, Quirinus, and Venantius are buried in the church on the Mount of St. John the Baptist; the following verses were inscribed by Rabanus on the canopy erected in their honor.

The Forerunner of the Lord, who baptized Christ in the waters,  
Inhabits this church and sanctifies the building.

Four men of Christ, who once expressed his mighty deeds in writing,  
Behold, dwell here together.

But these very holy men, distinguished by sacred rank,  
No less exalt and ennoble the place.

The strenuous love of the servants of the Lord  
Led them here from different parts of the world.

Rome sent Quirinus [F.: Urbanus]; Siscia sent Quirinus;  
This place, piously receiving them, holds them.

The distinguished holy bishop Venantius also,  
Coming from Aliminium, remains here with them.

Rabanus likewise received these men and placed them by lot  
In this sarcophagus, and worthily composed the inscription,

Asking all who enter the church with their feet  
To commend him properly to God in prayer.

## III

Inscription of Saints Tiburtius, Valerianus, and Cecilia, engraved on their reliquaries when Rabanus deposited their venerable bones in the collegiate church at Rathesdorf, now under the jurisdiction of Fulda.

After Christ, King of kings, had victoriously ascended  
Above the lofty heavens as almighty judge,

He left here a throng of servants and a faithful people  
Who would bring very many gains by word and deed.

Among them were these men, whose limbs rest here,  
Outstanding in the titles of their virtues.

Despising the pomp of the world, they rightly held  
The palm of martyrdom and virgin honor.

Behold, two brothers rest here, whom the blessed virgin Cecilia  
Won for Christ by her teaching.

Valerianus is here, one; Tiburtius, the other,  
Illustrious in name and still more illustrious in merit.

Your servant, Christ, Rabanus received  
These three persons coming from the Roman citadel;

Desiring them to become his patrons, and with skill,  
He adorned the tomb and composed the inscription.

## IV

Rabanus inscribed the following quatrains on the four-sided structure, built like a tower at Fulda in the Basilica of the Saviour in honor of the saints. The first inscription ran around it; the following ones were attached to its sides.

Here, identified by name and image, are marked  
The illustrious servants of Christ God:

Men who, fearless in heart, reddened with sacred blood  
And offered their lives for Christ.

### On the first side

For the martyrs of Christ whose bones rest here,  
The humble Rabanus built this tomb.

If you wish, reader, to know their names,  
The chest placed above reveals them to you.

### On the second side

Rome, glory of the world, praise of all things, supreme power,  
Once had these men as readers and pontiffs,

Men taken from different parts of the world who rest here,  
Illustrious in virtue, O Christ, your servants.

### On the third side

Most fortunate and blessed are those  
Whom Christ the King, rejoicing in his heavenly citadel,  
Places among the stars for their holy merits  
And restores to them the highest life.

### On the fourth side

You who enter the Lord’s temple with your feet,  
I now admonish you with a kindly heart:

Ask Christ humbly in prayer  
That he may grant you the stars together with the martyrs.

## V

To Haistulf, Archbishop of Mainz, when he dedicated to him the books *On the Instruction of Clerics* as a token of gratitude.

Holy Father, I bring these gifts to you with devotion;  
Receive them graciously, whatever their worth.

You are our glory, the supreme teacher and priest,  
Sacred leader and prince, light, way, shepherd, and honor.

Because you dedicated the temple of the gracious martyr,  
The martyr himself gave this gift through his servant.

For it is the eight-hundred-and-nineteenth year  
Since the gracious Saviour came into the fields of earth.

May he appoint you as ruler and make you blessed,  
And admit you joyfully to the angelic choirs.

For my abbot, and your faithful friend,  
Eigil wished these gifts to be returned to you.

He offers himself wholly, and freely presents all that is his;  
May the Most High God save him with you in his heavenly citadel.

## VI

Concerning the same books, addressed to the monks of Fulda, with an exhortation in which he encourages them to study the divine Scriptures.

See what the judgment of the Law has desired, brothers:  
What words of God it rightly commands us to learn.

“Whoever has ears here, let him hear,” it says,  
What the Holy Spirit says to the churches.

The Psalmist agrees with this in a similar verse,  
Commanding the people to behold rightly the Law of the Lord.

Thus it is always proper for us, brothers,  
To learn the words of God with attentive eyes and ears:

What he commands in words, what he indicates by his deeds,  
What that twofold book of his contains;

What Christ’s dearest Bride signifies by celebrating  
The sacred mysteries in pious rites and varied studies.

For you asked me to set these matters down in writing for you;  
I have presented them myself in these three small books.

What worship signifies, what the holy Church of God announces  
By gracious steps, by prayer, and by festivals;

What sacred doctrines it is fitting for all orders to learn,  
And what mystical sayings of God they should teach.

Although I cannot gather all these things in writing,  
I have nevertheless included very many of them here with skill.

I, the sinner Rabanus, receive these gifts of the Thunderer,  
And now share them devoutly with you.

I humbly ask you, calling upon the power of the Thunderer,  
To commend me in your prayers to the Lord,

So that he in his mercy may grant the gifts of salvation  
And, with you, the blessed kingdoms of heaven to me.

Christ your leader, Christ your king, Christ your beloved,  
May the Most High God always save you in his heavenly citadel.

## VII

An old writing on the Holy Cross, perhaps attributable to Rabanus. From the library of the abbey of Hersfeld.

Behold, through the position of its limbs, the image of the Saviour consecrates for us the most salutary, sweetest, and most beloved form of the holy cross, so that, believing in his name and obeying his commandments, we may through his passion have hope of eternal life; so that whenever we look upon the holy cross, we may remember him who suffered upon it for us, to rescue us from the power of darkness, swallowing death so that we might become heirs of eternal life.

Having gone up into heaven, with angels, authorities, and powers made subject to him, we are to remember that we were not redeemed from the empty conduct handed down by our fathers with corruptible silver or gold, but with his precious blood, like the blood of an unblemished and spotless lamb, Christ, so that we too may be spotless in his sight in love; and that through these things we may become participants in the divine nature, fleeing the corruption of the desire that exists in the world.

Indeed, on the painted cross itself there are also names of the Redeemer, our same Lord: some derived from the substance of his divinity, others assumed from the dispensation of the humanity he took upon himself. This was to show that the same mediator between God and human beings was consubstantial and co-equal with the Father in divinity, and, in the humanity he assumed, of the same nature and likeness as his mother, because he perfectly assumed our whole nature without human sin.

The character of these names can easily be recognized by the reasoning set out below, whether each pertains to his divine or to his human nature.

**CHRIST** is called in Greek *chrismate*, that is, “anointed.” Among the Jews, priests and kings were anointed with sacred anointing in the Old Testament, and therefore Christ is called *anointed* in Latin; or he is called “anointing” because he is king and priest. He was anointed not with material oil but with the oil of joy, that is, the Holy Spirit, above all his companions. In the Hebrew language Christ is called **Messiah**.

**JESUS**, in Hebrew, **Sother** in Greek, means “saving” or “Saviour” in Latin, because he came as the bringer of salvation to all nations.

**IMMANUEL**, or Emanuel, means in Latin from Hebrew, “God is with us,” namely, that God, born through the Virgin, appeared to human beings in mortal flesh.

[Col. 1679B]

He is called **GOD** because of the substance united with the Father. **LORD**, because of his lordship over creatures. He is God and man because he is at once Word and flesh.

He is called **ONLY-BEGOTTEN** because of the excellence of his divinity, since he was begotten without brothers. **FIRST-BEGOTTEN** because of his assumption of humanity, in which, through the adoption of grace, he deigned to have brothers, being the firstborn son among them.

**HOMOUSION.** He is so called with the Father from the unity of substance. For substance, or essence, is called *ousia* in Greek. *Homousion*, joined together, means “one substance.”

**BEGINNING**, because all things are from him, and because nothing exists before him.

**END**, because at the end of the ages he deigned humbly to be born and die in the flesh; or because whatever we do we refer to him, and when we reach him we have nothing further to seek.

He is the **MOUTH OF GOD**, because he is his Word. Just as we often say of words made through the tongue, “that language” or “this language,” so “mouth” is used for the Word of God, because it is customary for words to be formed by the mouth. He is called **WORD** because through him the Father created or commanded all things.

He is also called **TRUTH**, because he does not deceive but grants what he promises.

He is **LIFE**, for he gives life to all things. He is called **IMAGE** because of his equal likeness to the Father. **FORM**, because, taking the form of a servant, he displayed in himself the image and immeasurable greatness of the Father through the likeness of his works and virtues.

He is the **HAND OF GOD**, because all things were made through him. Hence also **RIGHT HAND**, because of the effect of the work of the whole creation, which was formed through him. He is called **ARM**, because all things are held together by him.

**POWER**, because he possesses within himself all the power of the Father and can do all things.

[Col. 1679D]

**WISDOM**, the Greek word *sophia*, because he himself reveals the mysteries of knowledge and the secrets of wisdom. **SPLENDOR**, because he makes things manifest.

**LIGHT**, because from on high he illuminates the world. **LIGHT**, because he opens the eyes of the heart to contemplate virtue. **SUN**, because he enlightens righteousness and prudence.

**RISING**, because he is the source of heavenly things and the author of light, and because he causes us to rise to eternal life. **FOUNTAIN**, because he is the origin of all things in nature, or the advocate of knowledge, since he makes people truly knowledgeable.

**PARACLETE**, that is, “comforter,” “advocate,” and “one who calls,” because he intercedes for us with God the Father and takes care to remove our sins.

**BRIDEGROOM**, because, descending from heaven, he joined himself to the Church, so that the two might be one flesh. He is called **ANGEL** because he announces the Father’s will and his own; hence the prophet speaks of “the angel of the great counsel,” although he is God and Lord of angels.

[Col. 1680A]

He is called **SENT**, because the Word became flesh. He is **MAN**, because he was incarnate.

**MEDIATOR**, because he leads us from death to life. **PROPHET**, because he revealed the future. **PRIEST**, because he offered himself as a sacrifice for us. **SHEPHERD**, because he is the guardian. **TEACHER** and **RABBI**, because he is the one who shows the way.

**NAZARENE** from the place; **NAZIRITE** from merit, that is, “holy” or “pure,” because he committed no sin. Indeed, Christ also takes names from lower things so that he may be more easily understood.

He is called **BREAD**, because he is life-giving flesh. **VINE**, because we were redeemed by his blood. **FLOWER**, because he was chosen above the sons of men. **WAY**, because through him we go to God the Father. **DOOR**, because through him we enter to God. **MOUNTAIN**, because he is exalted and strong.

**ROCK**, because he is the greatest firmness of those who believe devoutly. **CORNERSTONE**, because he joins two walls from opposite directions—that is, from circumcision and uncircumcision—into one structure of the Church; or because he makes peace between angels and human beings. **STONE OF OFFENSE**, because, coming in humility, unbelievers took offense at him, and he became a rock of stumbling. He is called **FOUNDATION** because our faith is founded upon him, or because the catholic and apostolic Church and its divinely constructed teaching are built upon him.

**Alpha and Omega**, because Christ is the beginning and the end. He is also called **LAMB** because of his innocence. He is likewise called **SHEEP** because of his gentleness or patience. **RAM**, because of his pre-eminence. **KID**, because of the likeness of sinful flesh. **CALF**, because he was sacrificed for us.

**LION**, because of kingship and strength. **SERPENT**, because of death and wisdom. **WORM**, likewise, because he rose again. **EAGLE**, because after the resurrection he joyfully returned to the stars.

[Col. 1680C]

Nor is it surprising that he is represented by humble symbols, since, although he is the Son co-eternal with the Father before the ages, he did not disdain the lowliness of our nature but was born in time as the son of man. For the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

### The Holy Cross

The right hand of the Most High God created all things: Jesus.  
Christ, thus placed upon the cross, will release the world from its debts through blood,  
Dissolving the tyrant’s bonds.  
The eternal Lord led the blessed to the stars,  
And God gave them a life-giving crown from his citadel.

Here he is covered by a small garment, though he contains the stars,  
And with his palm he encloses the whole earth everywhere.

This is the King of Justice. The just order, sacred to God.  
I.N.R., Lord of kings, Lord of lords.  
A.M. Ω: Beginning, Middle, End.

## VIII. Verses Read in the Basilica of the Illustrious Monastery of Hersfeld beside the Fulda River

### On the left, at the front of the lower choir, which they called the laypeople’s choir

As drops of dew are erased by the heat of the sun,  
As a flower or leaf dissolves into nothing,

So every glory perishes that wandering man seeks,  
Which he enjoys briefly and, dying after a short time, loses.

The machinery of the world brings nothing sincere or lasting;  
What stood yesterday totters today or tomorrow.

But the joys that are above do not know the passage of time;  
Reader, hasten toward them, following righteous works.

Light, solemn praise, and everlasting peace are there for all;  
No beauty is absent, and the supreme King is everywhere present.

Cease pursuing empty things; as a reward from the just Judge,  
May you be granted life there for your good deeds.

[Col. 1681A]

Ah, how joyful, harmonious, sacred, and peaceful  
Is the whole assembly there: no deceit, anger, or fear.

### Inscribed in stone on the right

As with the flowers of the fields, so the honors of the world  
Are destined to stand for a brief time, by a fragile condition.

The world will pass away, but it will not perish altogether;  
Its state will be changed into something better.

Moreover, by divine care two things were created:  
The angel and the soul, neighboring by covenant.

Both are without end, but all other things are subject to an end—  
Things covered by the waves of the sea, or carried by earth or air.

Therefore, human being, discern what you are;  
As you strive toward the homeland of heavenly peace, seek and keep the way.

Though your body will fall, your soul will never die;  
Joined to the hope of faith, love the gifts of God.

### An old epitaph in a cemetery

Stop, read, consider what you are and what your deeds have been;  
For a short and uncertain span one lives here.

Behold, like a flower you fall; soon you will go from ash to ash.

[Col. 1681B]

Whether seeking the highest or the lowest, reap worthy gains.

[Col. 1682A]

Now, while you live, strive to become a citizen of the heavenly homeland;  
Let death and hope there be fixed frequently in your mind:

There where life is perpetual and joys are established,  
Rest is without labor and day is without night.

You who read this, pray for me; labor for yourself;  
As I am guilty, offer your vows to God for yourself and me.

Ask the one who pities the wretched to pity me,  
And to make me a participant in true good.

### In the vestibule of the upper choir, around the Apostles, on the right

They seek to know what rewards they will possess—  
Those who leave everything behind and follow Christ,

Whom he promises will sit as judges and assessors with him  
When he comes again into the world.

### In the same vestibule, on the left

The twelve Fathers, filled with the divine Spirit,  
Behold, proclaim, foretell, and testify

By heart, speech, deeds, writings, and reason  
The birth of the One born from the closed womb of his mother.

### Verses to be read downward, beside the tomb of Albinus
