Why the Alleluia is sung at particular times, IV, 36. What it signifies, III, 352–353.

The Allophyli, struck down by Shamgar with an ox-goad, III, 1132. An allusion to the name Friedrich, VI, 1596; likewise to the name Brunward, VI, 1599. Suffragan of Mainz, VI, 1597. Abbot of Hersfeld, ibid. Etymology, ibid. The Alps: Hannibal crossed them, V, 363. A copious explanation of the Hebrew alphabet, V, 1183.

The altar, or description of the burnt offering, II, 179. A type of the hearts of the elect, ibid. Why God commanded that an altar be made of earth, II, 107. The golden altar signifies the hearts of the perfect, III, 179. Its construction and use, ibid. What was offered upon it, ibid. The two altars of the Old Testament, their distinction and meaning, V, 393. The command and description of the altar of incense, II, 208. Its figure, II, 211. To whom the golden altar corresponds, II, 208. The rejection of the Lord’s altar, literally and mystically, V, 1203. What the altar signifies mystically, VI, 856. The bronze altar as a figure of various mysteries, III, 458–459.

Altfrid, Saint, a monk and bishop of Hildesheim, IV, I, 96. Alum: its meaning and kinds, V, 459. The battle with Amalek, II, 84, 945. Why the people are called “the licking ones,” V, 53. Amalek as a type of the demon, III, 1144. The Amalekites are commanded by God to be destroyed, together with their beasts, III, 44. Why, ibid. Haman as a type of the proud, III, 652; likewise of the bloodthirsty Jews, ibid. Through enduring bitterness one passes to pleasant things, II, 813.

Amasa, now called the son of Jether the Ishmaelite, now of an Israelite: how this is to be understood, III, 292. Why Amasias is called “the one who removes the people,” and whom he denotes, V, 62. The various terms for Amath, III, 283–284. Who the ambidextrous are mystically, II, 1129. Detestation of ambition, II, 700, 863; III, 812. [Column 1685]

To walk and to go about: what these mean, I, 577. In what sense “Amen” is used, V, 991. Those struck with madness, II, 957. The various kinds of friendship, III, 852. How friendship should be fostered, III, 914–916. The benefits of true friendship, ibid. The power of false friendship, V, 1195; III, 847. Who is the friend rising at night and asking his friend for loaves on behalf of a guest, IV, 224–226. What a friend is, VI, 837; and what a female friend is, ibid. Whence the word is derived, III, 797, 899. Job’s friends represent heretics, V, 50. Friends are of many kinds, but a true friend cannot be valued sufficiently, III, 795, 797, 915. Which friends are to be corrected, III, 891.

One commending money or a vessel to a friend for safekeeping: whom he allegorically represents, II, 119; likewise one commending an ox or an ass, ibid. Why Ammon the idolater is called faithful or honorable, V, 63. A type of the Jews and heretics, V, 380. Ammon and Amalek make a treaty with Eglon against the Israelites, II, 1128–1129. Ammon’s incestuous love for Tamar: what lessons it gives us, III, 103. His outrage against David’s messengers, III, 97. A type of the devil, ibid. and III, 371–372. Ammon in Hebrew means “son of my people,” or “people of sorrow,” II, 1187. Jephthah goes to war against them, ibid. They are a type of the damned and of demons, ibid.

Isaac loved Rebekah so greatly that he forgot the death of his mother, I, 578. The effects of self-love, IV, 657. Its power, VI, 1593. The Amorites resist the sons of Dan and do not permit them to descend into the level places, II, 1117. The Amorites make peace with Israel under Joshua, III, 34. In Hebrew, “bitter,” ibid. Anagogically, that alliance signifies the union of the Gentiles and the Jews in Christ, ibid. Amos is rightly called “the people torn away,” V, 68. An amphitheater: what it is, V, 387.

Ana, the first discoverer of hot springs, III, 286. While feeding his father’s asses, he was the first to bring wild asses to female asses and asses to mares in order to produce mules, III, 286–287. Anaglyphs: what they are, III, 159; whose type they are, ibid. Ananias: what he signifies, V, 70. Breaking a wooden yoke and making iron chains: what he intended, V, 1015. After being convicted by Jeremiah of falsehood, death is announced to him, ibid.

What an anathema signifies, II, 712. The distinction between anathematizing and sanctifying, II, 573 and 582. Anathoth: what it signifies literally and mystically, V, 896. The maidservants sent to the citadel bear the type of weak preachers, V, 710. The encomium and integrity of Saint Andrew’s life, IV, 65. Who the androgyne are, V, 196. Anfinia: what it is, V, 237; its kinds, ibid.

The three angels who came to Abraham: what they were like, V, 35. The angels ascending Jacob’s ladder: whom they signify, I, 591. At an angel’s command Lot, with his wife and two sons, escapes the burning of Sodom, I, 556. A type of Christ’s body, ibid. Why he chose to be saved at Segor rather than on the mountain, I, 556. Why he went up from Segor to the mountain, I, 558. The angels are solicitous for us, III, 156. Their nine orders, IV, 60. [Column 1686]

The angels rejoice over the repentance of sinners, II, 1222. They avoid divine honors, ibid. They now refuse to be worshiped because of the human nature assumed by the Word, ibid. What sort of angels the apostles are to judge, VI, 54. Angels lead the Israelite by the hand, II, 130. Why Joshua is called an angel, II, 130. Angels were created with heaven and earth, I, 445. Why they were created, II, 1127. How angels ate with the patriarchs, I, 463. They assume an airy body, I, 552. The number of angels who fell from heaven will be filled by human beings, VI, 1137. Their creation, VI, 1611. The angels have various offices and names, which can sometimes also be applied to human beings, V, 28. See ibid. for an explanation of each.

An angel appears to Gideon, promises victory, and strikes fire from the rock with his staff, II, 1158. Who the “crudens” angel is and his office, V, 736. The angel sent to aid Hezekiah caused a great slaughter in the Assyrian camp, III, 258, 521. The angel of the Lord appears to the Jews at the place of weeping and rebukes them because they had not destroyed the inhabitants of the promised land according to God’s command, II, 1117. The angel who met Moses: whom he threatened with death, II, 26. Who the angel was who spoke to Hagar and her son, I, 564. Mystically, he sometimes represents Christ, priests, and evil spirits, VI, 851. The angel protecting the three children from the heat of the flames aptly expresses our Savior, VI, 1157. An angel appears to Manoah, Samson’s father, and announces a son to him, II, 1190–1191. His conversation with Manoah, ibid. He represented Christ, ibid.

Snakes hear more quickly than they see; see “serpent,” V, 228. The origin of eels, V, 238. The meaning of a corner, V, 401. A corner denotes a kingdom, and why, V, 1001. What should be done by those pressed by distress, III, 612. Whether, as some maintain, the soul is a part of God, I, 475. Why the soul of God abhors the Jews, II, 564. Whether the soul can properly be called dead, II, 477, 480. What the hot soul, burning as if with fire, is, III, 919–920. The soul must be tested; and if it is wicked, power must not be granted to it, III, 1029. Comparison of the rational soul with the Holy Trinity, III, 875. “The soul that sins shall itself die,” IV, 703, 710. It denotes the whole human being, II, 257. How every soul worthy of peace can be called Jerusalem, V, 926. The lamentation of the soul deprived of divine grace, V, 1185. The properties and effects of the human soul, VI, 1085.

God is the father of the Christian soul, and Christ its husband, III, 910. How many souls of Jacob entered Egypt, I, 646 ff. The happiness of the soul clinging to Christ its bridegroom, and the misery of the soul that abandons him, II, 766. The souls of subjects will be required from the hands of wicked shepherds, IV, 575–576. What order must be observed in speaking of it, ibid. How weak souls are to be strengthened, V, 845. [Column 1687]

How “soul” is understood in the Old and New Testaments, V, 843. The nature of the soul, IV, 1109–1110. Its etymology, ibid. Its kinds and effects, ibid. Its immortality, ibid. Its origin, ibid. Whether it has a form, IV, 1113. Whether it is believed to be smaller in children and larger in the stronger, ibid. Where its seat is, ibid. Its moral virtues, ibid. Its various names, VI, 352.

Who strikes a person’s soul, II, 909. The soul must be preserved in gentleness, III, 535. For one wishing to save the soul, the conduct of philosophers and heretics must be avoided, and how, V, 1114, 1173. “Soul” often expresses the present life, I, 837. What those who undertake the care of souls gain, V, 718.

A harmful animal must be killed, II, 115, 467. Its allegorical meaning, V, 199. Animals that do not chew the cud are sinners, V, 199, and holy people, ibid. Animals of the raven kind are without affection, V, 352. Whence they received their names, I, 483. What the animals offered by Abraham signify, I, 541. Whence the production of creeping, swimming, and flying animals arose, I, 456. The mystical interpretation of animals to be sacrificed, V, 397. Why sacrifices of various animals were instituted, IV, 1039–1040. The mystical interpretation of the animals full of eyes, IV, 281. The separation of clean from unclean animals, II, 351. Since elsewhere all things are said to be good, why are some considered unclean? ibid. The various kinds and meanings of animals, V, 199. Carnal and wicked people persecute spiritual people, II, 1133.

The remarkable affection of Joseph’s heart, I, 641. Anna, Elkanah’s wife, grieves because her rival torments her on account of her barrenness, III, 12. Her fervor in prayer, III, 13. The mother of Samuel, by God’s singular gift, ibid. Anna in Hebrew means “grace,” III, 14. Her song, full of piety and pure joy, III, 16. Why, with each of Anna’s sons being born, one of Peninnah’s seven sons is said to have died, although it is certain that Anna had five, VI, 1100.

What the rest of the seventh year and the seventh day signify typologically, II, 126, 890. The three hundred and ninety years during which Ezekiel was commanded to lie on his left side are calculated, IV, 592–593. How, according to some, the years of the Israelites’ sojourn in Egypt amount to four hundred; according to others, four hundred and thirty, III, 259. The meaning and significations of a year, V, 304; VI, 858. The great scarcity of grain in Germany, I, 100. One who nods with his eyes devises evil, III, 965–966. The ring received from Haman and given to Mordecai mystically signifies the seal of faith taken from the Jews and offered to the Gentiles, III, 661. The ring: whence it is named, its ancient use among the Romans, and its distinction, V, 582. What it signifies mystically, VI, 858.

The common year, the intercalary year, and the bissextile year, V, 127. Whether Catholics observing fixed years and days according to Jewish custom sin, [Column 1687] VI, 318. Superstitions concerning this matter, VI, 319. How irregular forms are lengthened and shortened, V, 652. What they are, V, 675. What geese denote, V, 248. How something is said to be before God, II, 86. What proceeding before one’s face signifies mystically, IV, 514, 519. No one is crowned before victory, III, 844.

Antichrist will be born from the Jews, and his tyranny against the good, II, 1171. He is signified by Nhamnum, who blows upon and consumes trees, II, 1172. God raises the Shechemites against him, ibid. Whence he is named, ibid. What the coming of Antichrist will be like and its effects, VI, 569. He will arise wholly from the tribe of Dan, V, 44. The punishment of Antichrist and heretics, V, 1147.

Antiochus, “sinful root,” and why, III, 1133. A notable instigator of sedition, ibid. He devastates and profanes the walls and shrines of Jerusalem, and is an apt type of Antichrist, III, 1134–1138. His etymology, III, 1139. He constructs an abominable idol: whom he denotes, III, 1138. He dies, III, 1173. He breaks faith, III, 1176. He orders Apollonius to be killed, III, 1134. Why he ordered the festival of the Father Liber to be celebrated, III, 1125. He forces Eleazar, an old man, to eat pork, ibid.

The monstrous Antipodes in Libya, V, 198. The first authors of antiphons were Greeks, I, 352. The frugal food of the ancients, III, 979. An old friend must not be abandoned, III, 821–822. Mystically, this signifies that one must not pass from the Catholic faith, once abandoned, to sectarians, ibid. Antistes: whence the name derives, V, 92. The life and death of Saint Antony, IV, 1127. The grave error of the Anthropomorphites, V, 813. An old woman: who she is, VI, 676; what is fitting for such women, ibid.

Ehud, the second judge in Israel, ambidextrous, brings gifts to Eglon, king of Moab, and kills him by cunning, II, 1129. Whether he lied to Eglon, king of Moab, II, 1130. By God’s command he killed the king, ibid. In Hebrew his name signifies “praise,” ibid. Because of the people’s sins he dies before his time, II, 1132. A type of good ecclesiastical prelates, II, 1133.

The boar, called so from its fierceness, signifies wicked rulers, V, 207. Apher, after conquering Libya, gave Africa its name, III, 285. The origin and various kinds of bees, V, 255; VI, 859. Detestation of the apocryphal books, V, 612. The apodyterium: whence it is called so, V, 388. The life and martyrdom of Saint Apollinaris, IV, 1158. The heresy of the Apollinarists, II, 556. Aporiae and Ymon, III, 961. The punishment of apostates according to the decree of Pope Siricius and the Council of Arles, VI, 1421. The two kinds of apostasy, IV, 551–552. Those returning to the Church must not be reproached, IV, 643. What harm apostates inflict upon the Church, III, 273. They were prefigured by Joram, ibid.

The catalogue of the apostles and a fuller explanation of them, V, 85. What possessions they had, II, 539, and the effects of their seed, ibid. They confessed Christ by voice and tongue with great fruit, II, 1201. They led Jews and Gentiles to Christ, ibid. Their books are craftsmen of the Church and weapons against demons; they are called “craftsmen of light,” and why, [Column 1688] II, 1118. They offer themselves to God and are like sheep among wolves, II, 1142. Their praiseworthy actions, III, 666. Why, together with many others, they were preserved from captivity, IV, 605. Their work and fruit in the Church, III, 502–503. Their four kinds, VI, 247. By what things they were prefigured, I, 891. They receive the power to perform miracles, and poverty is commended, ibid. Why they were ordered to shake the dust from their feet, I, 896. What they signified by plucking ears of grain, I, 918.

What the appearance of the Lord at Pharan signifies mystically, III, 986. Where and when the appearance of Christ sometimes occurred, I, 1148, 1154. How the various apparitions of different angels took place and what they signified, VI, 1267–1268. The Apennines: whence they were named, V, 363. Appetite, not food, is vicious, I, 584. What being gathered to one’s fathers or one’s people signifies, I, 666. What sunny places are, V, 372. A copious enumeration of the festivals and saints of April, IV, 1138.

The various diversity of waters, V, 309. Their multiple meanings, III, 860, 1030–1031; V, 1247 ff. They were created by God, III, 860. How waters, naturally flowing, stood above the heavens, I, 449. Where all the waters covering every part of the earth were gathered, I, 451. Where they returned after the flood had ended, I, 519. What the waters made sweet by Moses signify typologically, II, 75–76; III, 1030. What those seen by Ezekiel from the temple signified mystically, IV, 1151–1152. Water and earth are the two elements of the world, to which fire and air are added as the other two, I, 446. Water from the forests mystically signifies the abundant grace of evangelical teaching, II, 552. What water sprinkled on journeys signifies, VI, 1124. “Stolen waters are sweet,” and so forth, signifies heretics, who prefer their private errors to the universal Catholic religion, V, 711–712. What drawing water from the fountains of the Savior signifies, VI, 1092.

Descriptions and various meanings of eagles, V, 241–242, 246. Whence they received their names, VI, 1138. Their nature, ibid. They gaze at the sun with an unbroken directness of vision, ibid. They suspend their young by their claws and expose them to the sun’s rays, testing whether they are genuine or degenerate, ibid. They teach their fledglings to fly, ibid. They bring forth from their nests a stone of remarkable power, VI, 1138. By sharpening their hooked beaks on a rock they are types of Christ, ibid. Their nature and description, II, 974; V, 1258; VI, 862. The enigmatic eagle seen by Ezekiel represented Nebuchadnezzar, IV, 694–696; another represented Pharaoh, ibid. Various conditions of human beings are expressed under the name “eagle,” IV, 696–697. Whom the north wind figures, V, 261; VI, 860.

Ar is interpreted as “he raised up,” V, 368. The altar seen by Ezekiel: what it was like, IV, 978. It is compared with Solomon’s Temple altar, IV, 993. Altars: whence they are named, V, 391. Arabia signifies “sacred” or “blessed,” because of its abundance of frankincense, myrrh, and so forth, V, 338. Why it was called Saba, ibid. The distinction between a pledge and a surety, VI, 392–393. The location and description of the island of Aradus, IV, 774. The spider is a figure of human frailty, V, 235, and a type of diabolical deceit, ibid.

Ararat is interpreted as Armenia; in its mountains the ark first came to rest after the flood, [Column 1689] V, 343. The beautiful mystical meaning of Ararat, ibid. See V, 359. It is shown that no one is ruled by his own will against the new preachers, V, 885. Grace does not at all remove freedom of choice, II, 1204. What free choice is, V, 972.

The location and description of Arboch, V, 376. There stood the oak that was seen until the time of Constantine; its trunk can still be seen, and a temple was erected there, ibid. Its abuse, ibid. What sort the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was, I, 476–477. Whom it denotes, I, 930. The meaning of a tree, VI, 865. Which trees must be cut down for constructing siege machines, and which must be left, II, 912. From what a tree is bent, V, 507. All its parts are beautifully applied to the human race and to Christ the Lord, ibid. The various kinds of mystical trees, II, 553. The trees’ counsel and deliberation concerning the choice of a king, II, 1171–1173.

Many Bethshemites were killed because they looked irreverently upon the ark, III, 30. From the field of Joshua of Bethshemesh to the house of Abinadab at Gibeah, III, 31. How long it remained in Abinadab’s house, III, 32. The Ark of the Covenant, V, 1592. Noah’s ark expresses the form of baptism, III, 517. Just as no one outside it was saved, so no one outside baptism and the Church is saved, ibid. The construction of Noah’s ark, I, 514. What shape it had, ibid. Why it had a window, ibid. Why it had two and three chambers, I, 514. It contained five compartments, ibid. What it denotes mystically, I, 515. A beautiful figure of the Church, ibid.; V, 605. Whether [reading uncertain] and all the animals were contained in it, I, 517. It is compared with the Lord’s Incarnation, II, 141–145.

The secrets of God are not to be investigated curiously, III, 737. Citadels are so called from restraining the enemy, V, 387. Their various mystical meanings, ibid. Archippus, Paul’s fellow soldier: what he was like, VI, 698. How the daughter of the synagogue ruler, whom the Lord was to raise, could be called dead by Matthew, while Mark and Luke said that she was already near death, V, 879. What this signifies, V, 76. Architects are especially necessary to the state, III, 1037. What Arcturus signifies, V, 272.

The bow is a sign of the covenant between God and human beings, V, 277; III, 1073; IV, 547. Its various literal and mystical meanings, V, 1225, 541. The bow of the mighty denotes intention, VI, 1099. What it means to draw the bow, VI, 1122. Why David taught Judah’s sons to use the bow, III, 71. The heron signifies the elect, V, 246. The threshing floor: what it is and why it is compared with Holy Church, V, 411. What sand signifies allegorically, VI, 949.

The literal and mystical interpretation of silver, V, 476. What is rejected, V, 355. Clay soil is an exemplar of Sacred Scripture, III, 455. Its use, V, 458. Argob: what it is, V, 351; mystically it signifies pride, ibid. Sinners are to be reproved in a spirit of gentleness, III, 816. The man with the withered hand, healed by the Lord: what he prefigured, I, 922. What sort of man he was, ibid.

Rams signify the leaders of the Churches, V, 202; III, 778. The ram: what it is and how one must resist its attack, V, 542. The ram that cannot be resisted denotes the order of priests, V, 778. [Column 1689]

The Areopagus is interpreted as “the village of Mars,” and why, V, 382. Definition of arithmetic, I, 399. It was invented by Abraham, ibid. Its necessity and usefulness, ibid. What the armor of God is, III, 691. What our weapons are, II, 1141. What the weapons of righteousness on the right and left signify, V, 778. An armarium: what it is, V, 405. Those invincible in arms are softened and overcome by the beauty of women, II, 765–766. The literal and mystical meaning of weapons, V, 536. Armenia: whence it was named and its location, V, 343. Whom the overseers of herds denote, III, 404. The use and meaning of bracelets, III, 622.

The right shoulder and breast, consecrated from peace offerings to the priest, II, 318. Why, ibid. and II, 905. Spices: whence they received their name, V, 523. The various meanings of aromatic trees, ibid. What the spices and prostitutes’ perfumes are, III, 487–488. The various meanings and powers of aromatic herbs, V, 525. Azotus, one of the five cities of the Allophyli; in Hebrew, “fire of my father,” III, 27.

Arphaxad, king of the Medes and founder of the city of Ecbatana, III, 541, 601. He defeats Nebuchadnezzar, ibid. Who he was according to Philo’s opinion, III, 599. The confusion of the Arians and Manichaeans concerning the frankincense, myrrh, and gold offered to Christ, I, 760; and that of other heretics, I, 759. The error of those who assert that the Son is lesser than the Father, VI, 13.

Jacob, by a marvelous art, makes Laban’s sheep multicolored, I, 603–604. What this signifies mystically, ibid. The enemies of art are ignorant, V, 411. An enumeration of the liberal arts, V, 395. The craftsmen of Solomon’s Temple are compared with philosophers and teachers, and so forth, III, 135. They were chosen from all Israel, III, 136. Their distribution, III, 137, 419–423. The craftsmen of vanity are heretics, II, 950. The literal and typological meaning of a reed, V, 521. Why the citadel of Zion is called the city of David, III, 82, 327.

Why Asa is called “the one who raises up”: a figure of those who begin well and end badly, V, 59. While worshiping God he had every prosperity; after abandoning him and relying too much, in illness, upon physicians’ art, he died, III, 487. Whom he denotes mystically, ibid. Asahel’s swiftness, III, 76. His encounter with Abner, ibid. Seized by excessive fury, he was killed when pierced by the butt end of a spear, III, 76. A beautiful type of the furious, III, 77.

Why Asaph is called “the synagogue,” V, 70. He is interpreted as “gathering,” III, 352. Why, ibid. He was appointed by the Lord prince of those who confess, ibid. and III, 395. Asasonthamar: what it is, I, 538. The power of asbestos, V, 359, 462. Ascalon, a city of Palestine assigned to the tribe of Judah but not obtained by it, III, 291; V, 377. To ascend from the opposite side, and not flee from the wolf: what this signifies mystically,
V, 1105. Why the solemnity of the Lord’s Ascension is celebrated, I, 353. Moses’ ascent to the mountain prefigured Christ, II, 84–86. David’s ascent with his wives to Hebron is compared with the holy Church, III, 74. What Ascopera is, III, 623. [Col. 1690]

What Aser signifies, I, 597. A type of Christ and the saints, II, 1114; V, 46. What Aseroth signifies, V, 367. Description of Asia and its provinces, V, 343. Who the Assidaeans are, III, 1253. Balaam’s she-donkey bears the type of the Gentile world, II, 731. The donkey is so called from sitting; much is said about it, V, 212. What its burial signifies, V, 981. A symbolical type of those who pursue earthly things, III, 37. Where Asiongaber is and what it is, III, 192, 472.

Appearance often deceives, III, 820. And beauty likewise, ibid. The asp is described, with its various kinds and meanings, V, 231. David filled by a single heavenly breath, III, 347. Ashtaroth and Juno are the same goddess, II, 1122. Whether several Junos were worshiped, and how this is to be understood, ibid. Astaroth, an idol worshiped by the Jews, III, 33. The Hebrew form of *explorers*, ibid. The same goddess as Juno, ibid. Whom the morning stars signify, I, 445.

What astronomy is and its effects, I, 403. Some of it is superstitious, some natural, ibid. Who Ahasuerus was, III, 636. He limits the decree issued against the Jews, III, 661–662. By making the whole earth and all the islands tributary, he signifies Christ, III, 670. The celebration of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, IV, 433, 455. Its encomium, ibid.

Asshur is interpreted as “the rod of God’s fury”; he is a type of the devil, III, 583, 632. A figure of the Antichrist, IV, 818. The origin of Assyria, V, 335. Assyria first seized supremacy, V, 335. Athaliah signifies impiety, V, 61. Her cruelty in killing all the royal offspring, III, 498.

Atlas, the first inventor of astrology, V, 363. Whom Atlas represents as a type, V, 363. What Atheraim signifies—the way of the spies—and why, V, 368. What atoms are, V, 262. They consist in three things, ibid. The construction and form of the court of the tabernacle, II, 184. Its length and breadth, II, 1186. From where it received its name, V, 389. Mystically, it denotes the Church, ibid. Its literal and typological interpretation, III, 162.

Why avarice is called idolatry, VI, 446. Detestation of avarice, VI, 1244–1245. It is compared with dropsy, ibid. It led Judas astray, ibid. The remedy against it, VI, 1364–1367. Its nature and origin, ibid. Whom it torments among the envious, ibid. Its characteristics, VI, 1364–1367; III, 829, 853. It is guarded against by three kinds of adversity, I, 1151. Because of it, the salvation of souls must not be neglected, I, 834; III, 244. Wealth is destructive to the miserly and the envious, III, 856. The miser, by living frugally, hoards wealth for another to devour, III, 843.

The pious accounts of presbyters and elders are to be heard, III, 816. How “to hear” and “to perceive with the ears” differ spiritually, III, 1138. What the unclean birds signify, II, 356. They are born twice, V, 242. Which birds serve for sacrifice, and which are useless, II, 355–360; II, 885–888. Their mystical meaning, VI, 871. The innumerable kinds and meanings of birds and winged creatures, V, 240. The rite for sanctifying birds, II, 255. Birds of the same color fly together, III, 963. The corpses of birds and beasts of the earth are devoured by the teeth of the rebellious, IV, 878–879.

Omens taken from the flight of birds, V, 242. How auguries differ from the servant of Abraham’s requesting signs, I, 572. What an augury is, V, 423. The Phrygians were its inventors, ibid. Description of the famous witnesses of Augustus, IV, 1160. The miraculous life of Saint Avitus, IV, 1151. The literal and mystical interpretation of halls or courts, V, 389. A gentle breeze signifies tranquility of mind, V, 282. The ears must be carefully guarded, III, 972. What they signify mystically, VI, 871. Who those drinking from golden cups are, III, 640. What “to perceive with the ears” means, V, 909. The literal and typological meaning of gold, V, 475; VI, 869–870.

Solomon, rejecting gold and riches and asking for wisdom—whom does he represent as a type? III, 415–416. Excessive hunger for gold is destructive, III, 987. Many people fall through it, III, 988. The origin and meaning of the word *auspicia*, V, 423. By the name “the South,” the Jewish people are understood, III, 398; V, 261. The author of the Book of Wisdom, III, 1119. He ascribes praise, exaltation, and thanksgiving to God, ibid. The authors of the books of the Old and New Testaments, V, 109. Supported by the Lord’s help, he will not fall, VI, 1092. The impiety and cruelty of Hazael, III, 506. Azariah means “the help of the Lord,” V, 70. See Uzziah, V, 62. What Azekah is and its location, III, 51. What eating unleavened bread means, II, 53.

## B

Whether Baalam was Jupiter, II, 1122. Baal means “Lord” in Punic, ibid. Baalim, an idol worshiped by the Jews: what the Hebrew word means, III, 33. The disagreement between Baasan and Asa, V, 1088. From where Babylon derives its name, V, 337. Its founder and destroyer, ibid. A figure of Antichrist, ibid. Its founder, V, 1164. Its greatness, ibid. Its various meanings, VI, 872. How its kingdom passed to the Medes, III, 520. Why the Babylonians carry a decalogue written on little membranes and hung from the forehead, IV, 755; II, 866.

The staff, invented by Bacchus, V, 609; and what it signifies, VI, 872, 873. Bala, preserved alone through Lot’s prayers, V, 377. Its various names, ibid. The traditional interpretation, V, 40.

Balaam is sent to curse the people of Israel, II, 725. He is forbidden by God, II, 727. He is killed, II, 795. He is rebuked by the speaking she-ass, II, 729. Why Balaam was forbidden by the Lord to curse the Israelites, although the curse of demons cannot harm the blessed, and the Lord himself could have protected them, II, 727–730. He represents the person of the Pharisees and scribes, II, 729. He had the word of God in his mouth and not in his heart, II, 733. He is filled with the Spirit of God, II, 746. Why the people are called vain, V, 53. Those who embrace his teaching, II, 765.

What *Bale* means in Hebrew, I, 537. The Balearians, inventors of slings, V, 358. The distinction between *Balim* and *Baal*, V, 873. What a ballista is, V, 541. From where baths derive their name, V, 388.

A beautiful description of balsam, and its species and nature, III, 935, 936. Where it grows, ibid. Its use, ibid. Why it is called a vineyard, ibid., 937. It most aptly represents the Redeemer, [Col. 1691] ibid. Its remarkable nature and power, V, 526.

What a belt signifies, II, 203–206; VI, 873. Banaiah, who killed a lion in a cistern, is a type of Christ and the Church, III, 118. He killed Shimei, who was cursing David, III, 119. Bangolius, second abbot of Fulda, I, 72, 86.

The sacrament of baptism, and how many kinds there are, V, 134, 135. From where it derives its name, I, 309; VI, 1168. Why it is effected through water, ibid. Faith and doctrine precede it, VI, 1170. Its order, VI, 1173. Its office, VI, 1219. Its effects, III, 1166; VI, 748. It is of no benefit unless received for salvation, IV, 668. How those initiated by it formerly performed penance, II, 302. What we ought to do after receiving it, II, 828, 1162. Its threefold sense, IV, 357. If validly conferred, it is not to be repeated even when conferred by a schismatic or heretic, IV, 283. What it means to be baptized by a dead person, III, 1012.

Barak, commander of the army under Deborah, who refused to enter battle without Deborah and was deprived of the glory of victory, II, 1134. In Hebrew, his name means “flashing” or “lightning,” II, 1135. He is a type of the Jewish people, ibid. He pursues the fleeing Sisera in vain, II, 1136. A type of the Jewish people, II, 1143. Whether he should rightly be considered a saint, VI, 804.

What the abyss is, V, 374. Why priests are forbidden to shave the beard and head, II, 474. Who shave it, IV, 103. Its various meanings, VI, 873. Why the bodies of barbarians are straighter than those of Romans, V, 1457.

Baruch means “flashing” or “lightning,” V, 56. He receives Jeremiah’s prophecy while shut up in prison and recites it to the people, V, 1071. It is burned by Jehoiakim, and another volume is written against him, V, 1072.

Bashan means the same as “confusion,” “fatness,” or “cankerworm,” V, 48. Bases and columns are types of the sacred books, V, 397. Likewise of the apostles and teachers of the holy Church, ibid.; III, 173, 443, 445. What a basilica figuratively signifies, III, 164. The inscriptions of the altars of the Basilica of Fulda, VI, 1622–1625.

The nature and meaning of the basilisk, V, 231. The bronze fire-pans represent divine Scripture, which heretical doctrine attempts to lay waste, II, 683.

Baturicus, bishop of Regensburg, and his glory, VI, 1599. His various deeds, ibid. His praise, ibid.

The eternal life of the blessed, III, 1029. What it is, VI, 1594. Who should truly be considered blessed, III, 193. What bdellium is, and the nature and use of its fruit, I, 478. The joys of the blessed, III, 456. The distinctive character of the true blessed, V, 1585. The blessedness of those who fear God, III, 1009. It is acquired through carefulness in speech, III, 854. And through observance of the commandments of Christ and the apostles, II, 1118.

From where the province of Belgica derives its name, V, 350. Ninus, king of Assyria, the first author of war, V, 531, 532. Its division into four kinds, and their meanings, ibid. Its etymology, V, 533. What is the war of Christians, and what is the new war, II, 1141. How its laws are to be observed, II, 910. A just war, free from sin, III, 622. Not every war is unjust, II, 1124.

The perpetual war between the kings of Judah and Israel signifies the conflict of the holy Church with heretics, III, 486. The arrogance of Ben-hadad when attacking Samaria, III, 213. Defeated and returning home in disgrace, he is a type of the devil, ibid., III, 236. [Col. 1692]

God’s blessing upon the good and his anger against the wicked, III, 1044. Spiritual and temporal blessing is bestowed upon Judith, III, 631. Aaron’s blessing signifies the rite of the priesthood, III, 755. That blessing and cursing cannot coexist in one mouth is shown by various comparisons, III, 1063. The effect of the Lord’s blessing, II, 534, 535. The rite of blessing owed to priests, and its origin, I, 383. Its effect, I, 384. What David blessing his household signifies, III, 363. The blessings of the sons of Israel, II, 626. Those who bless Christ are blessed, and those who curse him are accursed, II, 754. Moses’ blessings upon each of the tribes of Israel, II, 984–988. St. Augustine’s extensive commentary on these blessings, II, 988 and following. The blessings gathered together, concerning the elect, II, 952–955. What the blessings bestowed by fathers upon their sons signify mystically, I, 655–658.

One should do good from one’s substance before death, since it does not delay, III, 857, 878, 884. Ecclesiastical benefices, especially those belonging to others, are not to be eagerly sought, II, 119. The benefits bestowed upon the people of Israel in the desert, III, 749. How great are the benefits of God and his grace, VI, 404, 423.

Benjamin, “son of the right hand,” is an image of blessed Paul and, allegorically, of Christ, V, 48. Benjamin pouring out Amalek signifies allegorically the apostle Paul, II, 1144. “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf,” etc.: a most fitting prophecy concerning the apostle Paul, I, 665. The crime of the Benjamites avenged, II, 1116. Why they twice slaughtered the others, ibid. The Benjamites occupy Jerusalem but do not destroy the Jebusites, II, 1115. This city was shared by them with the tribe of Judah, ibid.

The monstrous torture of St. Benignus, IV, 1176. Why severity is mingled with God’s kindness, V, 828, 843. A commendation of kindness and humanity, IV, 97. What Ben-oni signifies, I, 617. Why Benjamin was so called, ibid.

Beersheba, a village in the tribe of Judah, III, 26. In Hebrew, *Be’er-shebaʿ* means “well of satiety,” ibid. What it signifies literally, III, 98. A type of the Church, ibid.

Where the city of Berech is situated; in Hebrew, “poverty,” III, 39. Berith, the idol of the people of Shechem, with whom the Shechemites make a pact, II, 1174. Bezalel and Oholiab, craftsmen of the tabernacle, II, 220, 244.

To what creatures the name “beasts” properly applies, V, 217, 1122. What touches Mount Bestra, II, 90. Where Bethel is situated, and what its Hebrew name means, III, 55; V, 376, 616. From where Bethlehem derives its name, V, 377. Christ was born there, ibid. What Bethsaida is, V, 381. Beth-shan, and why it was called Scythopolis, II, 1116. Fifty thousand Beth-shemites were killed because they looked irreverently upon the ark of the Lord, III, 31. Bethany is famous for the tomb of Lazarus, who was raised from the dead, V, 380. The various names of different places, ibid. [Col. 1693]

There were two places called Bethsamis, III, 30. Bethsamis means “house of the sun,” III, 30; V, 381. Its location, ibid. Bethsura signifies the reading of sacred Scripture, III, 1195.

The various libraries of the world, V, 95. From where the two-day, or three-day, fast originated, I, 339. Why pairs of animals were brought into the ark, I, 517. Why Christ called pairs of disciples to the apostolate, I, 790. Whom they signify mystically, ibid.

The power and use of bitumen, V, 459; I, 514. Where it is found, ibid. The torture of St. Blandina and sixty-eight martyrs, IV, 1148. The punishment of blasphemers and the law of retaliation, II, 521–527. Their detestation, II, 862. The seriousness of blasphemy, VI, 685. When its sin is forgiven, ibid.

Boeotia derives its name from *bos*, “ox,” and why, V, 549. The good things bestowed upon David and Solomon, III, 467. In what sense good and evil, life and death, are said to have been made by God, III, 467. Goodness generally contains something of wickedness mixed with it, and conversely, V, 1583. What kind of good the apostle says he was unable to find, V, 1430. What is to be understood by one who does good in God’s sight but not with a perfect heart, III, 506. For the good, all things turn out for good; for the wicked, for evil, III, 1045. What “the good” signifies, V, 368. In this passage, the circumcised people of Israel, ibid. Interpretations of various passages of sacred Scripture, ibid.

The instruments of good works. With what intention and faith they should be performed, III, 844. The sanctity and praise of St. Boniface, pontiff and martyr, IV, 47. *Boos* means “in strength,” V, 57.

Boaz, a kinsman of Elimelech, powerful and wealthy, is a type of Christ, II, 1205. In Hebrew, “strength of God,” ibid. His piety and kindness toward Ruth, ibid. He consults a kinsman concerning Naomi’s field, II, 1207. He offers it to that kinsman and takes Ruth as his wife, ibid., 1216. With the whole people as witnesses, he takes Ruth as his wife and receives all the fields of Elimelech and the others, ibid.

The heresy of Botescalcus refuted by Rabanus, I, 98–99. Botescalcus proscribed by King Louis, I, 99.

The cluster brought back by the explorers to Moses is a type of Christ crucified, II, 845. The ox plowing represents the people of the circumcision, and the ass the people under the Law, II, 922. Why one who steals an ox is ordered to restore five oxen, but four sheep, V, 201. Oxen represent the apostles, V, 201, 208. The various kinds of oxen, ibid. Their meanings, VI, 876, 877. What kicking oxen signify, III, 85.

The arm signifies the supreme dignity of the priesthood, III, 22. Its mystical meaning, VI, 873, 874. The origin of the name Britain, V, 354. Its fertility and pleasantness, ibid. The meaning of *bruchi*, “cankerworms,” V, 258. The owl, V, 247. What a dry morsel signifies, V, 738. By the sound of the trumpet sinners are invited to repentance, IV, 831. Its use among the Romans, V, 355. Butter from the herd signifies the fullness of grace, VI, 1140. Its various meanings, VI, 877. [Col. 1693]

What it means to eat butter and honey, V, 594. *Byssus*, fine linen, is a type of chastity, V, 578; VI, 875.

## C
## C

Cacabus, whence the name is derived, V, 602. Caballus, see Equus. A corpse, so called from *cadere* (“to fall”), mystically signifies the body of an unbeliever, V, 195; VI, 878. What and where Cades-barne was, II, 448. The blind and the lame, whom they signify, V, 75; II, 485–496. Why, when Matthew mentions two blind men on the road, Mark says that there was one, I, 1033. Praise of celibacy, IV, 902; VI, 74. What should be done by one who violates ceremonies through error, II, 288. The various ways in which they are observed in eating, cutting the hair, and taking omens, II, 457. Their kinds and seriousness, II, 1459–1460. Cain is interpreted as “possession” or “lamentation,” V, 32–33. How Cain knew that his brother’s sacrifice had been pleasing to God, I, 501. The etymology of Cain, ibid. Why his offering was rejected by God, ibid. Cain, by killing his brother, departed from God and was reconciled again through wisdom, III, 716. The mystical interpretation of reeds and rushes, IV, 886–887. Reeds, see also VI, 879–880. How great the calamity of the Jews was at the time of the devastation, V, 936; III, 48; V, 1265. What the basket of good figs signifies, V, 989. Likewise the basket of bad figs, ibid. and following; V, 1020. What the heel represents, V, 1088. Whence spurs are called by their name, V, 612. The shoe of the Lord, a type of his incarnation, I, 800. What Moses’ removal of his shoes signifies, I, 19. Hebron was given to Caleb, II, 115. He destroyed the three sons of Anak while Joshua was still alive, ibid. What darkness signifies, VI, 879. The cup of virtues and vices, V, 906. What the golden cup, Babylon, which intoxicates the whole earth, signifies mystically, V, 1155. The first use of the cup in Sicily, V, 602. Its mystical meaning, VI, 873. Who drink the cup of the Lord’s wrath, V, 995–997. Who is to drink it undiluted, even down to the dregs, IV, 747. To whom this applies, ibid. The distinction between the cup of the New Testament and the cup of punishments, V, 906. Pope Saint Callistus was imprisoned; he healed a soldier covered with ulcers, but was put to death together with him, IV, 1173. Whence Mount Calvary received its name, I, 1136. When slander is committed, II, 448–449. What lime is, and its nature and remarkable power, V, 462. The allegorical meaning of lime and sand, ibid. Whence the chameleon and the camelopard received their names, V, 222. Their nature, II, 353. The camel, an apt type of the scribes and Pharisees, II, 883. Their kinds and meanings, V, 211. Gentiles are signified by the names of camels and asses, III, 405. Camon, the burial place of Jair, judge in Israel; in Hebrew, “useless resurrection”; it signifies heretics and impious persons, II, 177. Chemosh, god of the Ammonites: what sort of god he was, and how his weakness was mocked, II, 1178. Whence Chemosh received his name, V, 366. Its beautiful comparison with Sacred Scripture, ibid. Likewise with the world, ibid. It is taken in a good and a bad sense, ibid.

[Col. 1694]

The daughter of the Canaanite: whose type she bears, V, 73. The Canaanite woman: of what she is a figure, V, 73. The lampstand, a type of the Lord’s body, V, 691. The construction and use of the golden lampstand, II, 150 and following. Its mystical meanings, ibid. The description of the dog and its various meanings, V, 224; VI, 883. What the basket signifies, V, 604. What the basket of completion signifies figuratively, II, 331–332, 624. What the gray hair of old men signifies, V, 746. Honor must be shown to the gray-haired, and why, II, 460. Whether the authors of our canonical books should be called wise or eloquent, I, 413. The martyrdom of Saint Canus and his son, IV, 1146. Whence the canons of councils received their name, and how many were promulgated in various councils, V, 124. Which canons of the Gospels are recognized, V, 124. How singing and psalmody differ spiritually, II, 1139. Moses was the first author of song, I, 361. What it signifies, ibid. Why the custom of singing was instituted in the Church, ibid. What mysteries the Song of Moses contains, II, 967. Its literal and mystical explanation, II, 967 and following; VI, 1132. The song of a pure soul delights God, II, 1139. The Song of Deborah explained mystically, II, 1138. By what term the Song of Hezekiah should be designated, VI, 1094. The Song of Hannah, filled with sacred mysteries, VI, 1098. Why it acquired the name of prayer, although it is rather a prophecy of future things, ibid. The difference between a song and a prayer, VI, 1112. Whence a cantor is so called, V, 92. What the eighty-eight singers signify, III, 396. The scapegoat bears a figure of Christ, II, 420. What being captured by a beast signifies, II, 281. What being captured in the eyes signifies, III, 623. The use and meaning of hair, II, 384; IV, 1012. Who are said to have been counted, and how, I, 902; II, 590. Nodding of the head, an indication of joy, V, 1209. The mystical explanation of the head and hair, V, 144; VI, 883 and following. What five capitals represent, III, 167–168. Their diversity and structure, ibid., 169–171; III, 433, 436. Whence the Capitol received its name, V, 387. What Cappadocia is, V, 344. Its location, ibid. The nurse of horses, ibid. A type of Holy Church, ibid. Its mountains and provinces, with their meanings, ibid. Capus, see Falco. How Saul’s head was said to have been hung in the temple of Dagon and carried through different regions of the earth, III, 323. What sort of animal a goat is, and whom it denotes, V, 204. The captivity and liberation of the Apostle Peter: of what kind they were, IV, 350. His profession of faith concerning Christ, IV, 351. A coal sometimes signifies a sinner and sometimes a just person, V, 280. It also signifies Christ’s cross, ibid. Its various meanings, VI, 886. The twelve kinds of carbuncle and their figurative meaning, V, 471. Whence it is called thus, I, 478–479. How many hinges of heaven there are, and what they signify, V, 265. A hinge is a type of the slothful person, V, 400. Kiriath-jearim, the city of woods, situated in Gibeah and the native city of the prophet Uriah, killed by Jehoiakim, III, 32. A poem is interpreted in a good and a bad sense, IV, 560. A poem in honor of the Annunciation to the Virgin, VI, 1665. A poem on the death of Charles, ibid. Carnal and vain people rarely give ear to God in preachers’ sermons, II, 1149. Their destruction, ibid. What a heart of flesh is, IV, 644. Those who serve the flesh are stripped of grace, II, 1198. The flesh is figured by the woman, ibid. Why we are not debtors to the flesh although we owe it sustenance, V, 1446. When, and to whom, the use of meat and wine is permitted, V, 1588. Whom the flesh of unclean beasts denotes, II, 124. When the use of meat and the drinking of wine were permitted, I, 339. Why they were prohibited for a time, ibid. When and why the eating of flesh was first permitted, I, 524. The typological interpretation of flesh, V, 591; VI, 886–887. What a hut is, V, 376. The literal and mystical meaning of the little chasuble, I, 308. What the month Casleu signifies, III, 1130. The chestnut, a type of the continent, and why, V, 515. The Israelites, punished to some extent by the bites of serpents, were healed by the raising up of the bronze serpent, III, 746. What true chastity is, as prescribed to monks, ibid. Its reward, III, 684. The manner of cultivating it and its praise, V, 853–856; IV, 87. Its effects, ibid., 88. Whence beavers are called thus, and whom they signify, V, 222. What Jacob’s vision of the camp of God was, I, 608. The four camps of the people of Israel not inaptly designate the four orders in heaven, II, 604. In what order the camps of the Israelites moved in the desert, II, 650. The camps placed in the midst of the people represent Holy Church, III, 582, 632. A kind of bee called castrum, V, 256. The meaning of a camp, V, 383. The production and shortening of cases in the conjugation of pronouns, etc., V, 644–652. Which nominal cases are recognized from their endings, V, 634–642. How many cases there are and how they are recognized, V, 642–648. The fall of Lucifer, I, 445. Why Moses made no mention of the fall of the transgressing angel, I, 447. What falling on one’s face and falling backward signify, IV, 549. What a helmet signifies, V, 544. When and in what manner the Flood occurred, I, 519. What the cause of the Flood was, III, 1051. A catalogue of the Father’s virtues, divided into seventeen classes, which are not imputed to children who violate them, IV, 704–706. A catalogue of the uncleannesses and iniquities of Jerusalem, IV, 665–667. Likewise of its benefits and ornaments, IV, 670–676. The order for catechumens, I, 310. Its rite, ibid.; VI, 1193, 1198. Whence a catechumen receives this name, I, 310. The distinction between them and the competentes, ibid. The various meanings of chairs, VI, 889–890. Little chains denote the offices of charity, III, 426. What sort of friendship ought to exist between Catholics and heretics, III, 796. A Catholic who lives badly is a source of grief to others, V, 714. Puppies are a type of the gentiles, V, 221. A description of Mount Caucasus, V, 359. What cutting off the tail signifies, II, 761. The sheepfold is a type of Holy Church, and why, V, 407. Certain different causes for which we are afflicted in this life, I, 872. What a cautery is, and of what it is a type, V, 613. A precaution concerning secret murder and a corpse found, II, 913. Mystically it denotes the Savior, ibid. and following. Kedar is interpreted as “darkness,” V, 336. Whence it derived its origin, ibid. The torrent Cedron, V, 322. What the cedar signifies mystically, VI, 891; V, 517. Its nature, III, 482. The meaning of carved palms, IV, 934–935. What a shout of encouragement denotes, V, 1121. The serpent celidros makes the earth smoke, V, 227. Whence a cell is named, V, 389. What are called high places in Scripture, III, 277. The precious treasures of the region of Cene, V, 342. The severe punishment attending the census of the people, III, 93. Its appeasement, III, 123. A centaur, a man joined with a horse, V, 198. The number one hundred, a figure of heavenly life, III, 470. A type of the elect, I, 857. What the centurion signifies, V, 75. The profession and meaning of the centurion and his soldiers who guarded Christ’s tomb, I, 1144. Cerberus with three heads, V, 198. The does represent a type of teachers, IV, 45. Their habits, ibid. A type of the Church, II, 1171. Stags are so called from their horns; their various kinds and meanings, V, 204. Why Abraham married Keturah in his old age, I, 579. What this signifies, ibid. Who inhabit Chaldea, V, 1151. Why the Chaldeans expelled all the artisans from destroyed Jerusalem, III, 272. Why Chaleph is called “heart” or “dog,” V, 54. What Ham signifies, V, 34. Why, although he sinned in his father’s drunkenness, he was cursed not in himself but in his son Canaan, I, 525; II, 454. A figure of Christ and the Jews, I, 525. Canaan is interpreted as “their movement”; what the land promised to the Israelites signifies, II, 20; V, 94. The Canaanites are slaughtered, II, 1111. Why the Canaanite nations were left rather than all destroyed, II, 11. Which ones were left, ibid. Kirjath-sepher was conquered after Joshua’s death, II, 1113. What charity infused into hearts is, V, 1370–1371. Its praise, VI, 1235. Its strength and necessity, V, 1147. Its effects, III, 767; at length, IV, 83. The Cherubim and the flaming sword before paradise: what they signify, I, 500. What they signify mystically, III, 154. Why there were two Cherubim, and what they signify mystically, II, 144–145. The Chimera, a three-formed beast, V, 198. The meaning of *chod*, IV, 776. What the Chebar is, V, 322; IV, 499. Ezekiel’s visions occurred there, ibid. Choré is called “Calvary,” V, 72. His sons, V, 71. Why they were singers, ibid. What chrism signifies, V, 135. Christians united in Christ, III, 44. They need grace and a change of morals, ibid. Their strength and grace come from God, ibid., 16. And against our enemy the Devil, ibid. They subject their flesh to the spirit through the grace of the Holy Spirit, ibid., 20. All are anointed and belong to Christ, ibid. Their heart is the Lord’s tabernacle, III, 31. The excellence of the Christian name, IV, 82. Who are worthy and unworthy of it, ibid. Christians must not observe the practices of the gentiles, VI, 1417. Nor feast with pagans, ibid. Nor with Jews, VI, 1418. Feasting and dancing disgrace them, ibid. Their constancy and religion are greater than those of the Jews under the Law, II, 1221. Their bishops voluntarily offer themselves to death, II, 1144. The various names of Christians, V, 92.

Who Christ is, VI, 1102. How Christ was appointed for ruin and for a sign that would be opposed, V, 928. Why Christ is called sometimes a goat and sometimes a calf, V, 755. Christ remained in the tomb for forty hours, III, 1152. He is a horror to heretics, III, 1167–1168. Christ and Jesus Christ: how they differ, I, 992. Whether Christ may rightly be called God, V, 1483. For whom Christ was proscribed, and for whom he was crucified, VI, 283. How Christ is said to have been delivered up by God for us and to have delivered himself up, VI, 445. Christ is mystically a stone, V, 41. And our brother, V, 191. The Bridegroom of the Church, ibid. How his sitting on the shore and the disciples’ sitting in the boat should be understood, V, 373. A priest according to the order of Melchizedek, V, 397. He condemns and confounds pleasure, II, 1136. He threatens woe to the Jews and to people stiff-necked, II, 1149. He was represented by Gideon, II, 1177. Gideon’s sacrifice was a type of Christ’s offering on the cross, ibid. He is a calf, in whom are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, ibid., 1158. He is the Rock, ibid. He was born from a priestly and royal lineage, as was also the Virgin Mary, II, 1176. His resurrection is useless to the Jews, ibid., 1177. He is the light of the world, represented by Jair, ibid., 1176. And by Jephthah fleeing from his brothers, ibid., 1177. He offered himself, ibid. The martyrs imitate him, ibid. He frees the nations from the tyranny of the Devil and destroys his kingdom, II, 1162. He himself is the one who encompasses in the womb, ibid., 1163. Through his divinity he embraces all things; he casts down the enemies of the Trinity by perfect knowledge and faith, ibid., 1163. His soldiers—that is, those who are both learned and active in good works—, ibid. Where he sends his preachers, and with what purpose and outcome they contend against Satan, ibid., 1166. He destroys philosophers, gentiles, and heretics, ibid., 1167. He delivers obstinate Jews and mockers of the Gospel to the Roman emperors, ibid. The angels represent his person, II, 1192. He was represented by Samson, ibid., 1194. His triumph and strength are represented by Samson in almost every respect, ibid., 1198. By dying, he saved more people dead to vices than he had saved while living, II, 1197. He is a Nazarene, the sun of justice, ibid. Represented by Elimelech, he joins the Church to himself as his wife and begets children for himself from her, [Col. 1697] II, 1201. Born from the line of Ruth, ibid., 1199. Promised in the Law, ibid., 1204. His power and riches, ibid., 1206. He is concerned for the Church and inquires through the apostles concerning its teachers, ibid., 1207. He protects the Church, ibid., 1208. What his wings are, ibid. He opens to the gentiles the treasures of his knowledge, ibid. He admits the gentiles into the Church, ibid., 1213. He shakes and winnows the will of the Jews, II, 1211. He rejoices in the redemption and salvation of the gentiles, ibid., 1212–1213. He suffered and died because of the prophecies, ibid. He led forth from the underworld throngs of souls, ibid. How and why he marvels at the faith of the gentiles, ibid. His perfect gifts to the Church, ibid.
