His decree and infallible wisdom, II, 738. How he terrifies, II, 739. For Judah’s discipline and to restrain pride amid greater prosperity, he did not hand over to him the inhabitants of the valley, II, 1115. How he is the cause of sin, II, 1117. He asks love from human beings, and why, II, 1122. Whether, and in what manner, he should be said to become angry, ibid., 1122–1123. Whom God delivers into Satan’s hands, ibid. He delivers people over to passions of dishonor, ibid. He delivers them by abandoning them, ibid. When he dwells in us, ibid. He does not test as one ignorant and unaware of the future, but for our sake, II, 1125. Whether God’s promises are ineffective, ibid. Whom he delivers over to a reprobate mind, II, 1133. His astonishing mercy, ibid., 1128. No one can resist his power, II, 1140. He rages against his enemies with heaven, stars, and the elements, II, 1148. He is holy and just, III, 16. Indeed, he alone is strong, ibid. He searches hearts, III, 17. Power over death and life is in him, ibid. He led Christ down to hell and brought him back from there, ibid., 18. He raised him from the dust to glory, ibid. He allows the impious to fall and perish, ibid., 19. He resists the proud, ibid. Faith in him and knowledge of him come to us from him, not from ourselves, ibid. How he is said to have a soul, III, 29. Why he delivered Israel from the hand of Midian with a small army, II, 1160. He tests the soldier, ibid. He chooses contemptible things, ibid., 1166. How he sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem, II, 1173. He does not delight in human sacrifices, ibid., 1179. He crowns those who are slaughtered for justice and religion, II, 1179. Through the wicked he also performs wondrous deeds, II, 1183. He makes good use of our sins, ibid. He rejects Saul from the kingdom, together with his offspring, III, 41. He does not ask as one ignorant, ibid. He commands Saul to destroy the Amalekites, and why, III, 44–45. He is not changeable, ibid., 47. Faithful in his promises, III, 1214. He is present to those who invoke him in war, III, 310. His judgment is unchangeable, III, 522. He chastises his own; no limit is to be prescribed for him, III, 614. He is honored through the weaker, III, 621. He never forgets his mercy, VI, 1115. He made everything without intending death, III, 677. In the Gospel he is more often called “Son of Man” than “Son of God,” and why, and how he is to be invoked, III, 852. How he tests, III, 675. He is a severe avenger of crimes, III, 676. He does nothing contrary to nature, III, 677. What it means to sin against him, VI, 1134. His severe punishment of various sinners, III, 693. Why he is called faithful and upright, VI, 1134. In what respect eyes, ears, hands, anger, and so forth are applicable to God, III, 727. How he is seen by human beings, III, 1122. How he differs from the gods of the nations, V, 455. He became man, VI, 1614. Whether he is rightly called “threefold,” VI, 1590 (note). What this signifies, VI, 907.

How God, producing all things in six days, is elsewhere said to have created them all at once, I, 471.

God exists by nature, human beings by grace, III, 825.

God does not speak in order that something may come to be, but because it is going to happen he foretells it, V, 864.

How Moses was given as God to Pharaoh, II, 31.

When God alone is to be worshiped, how Abraham was permitted to do obeisance to the people, I, 570.

How God, not willing the death of a sinner, contemplated killing Amaziah, III, 508.

The contents of Deuteronomy, V, 111. Where it is written, V, 360. What it signifies, and why it says that the Lord spoke to Moses, when Moses himself is the author of this book, II, 839–840.

Remote places are types of heretics, III, 371.

Who are said to devour the saints, V, 746–747.

What the right hand laid upon Ephraim, the younger, and the left upon Manasseh, the elder, signifies mystically, I, 653.

Although the right hand is always understood in a favorable sense, why in Deuteronomy we are forbidden to turn either to the right or to the left, II, 953–955.

Why the right hand is anointed, II, 331. What it signifies, VI, 909.

The difference between the right and left hands, and what it signifies, V, 158.

What a right-handed diviner is, III, 621.

What the dextrocherium signifies, and its use, III, 621–622.

The devil, mystically represented by Adonibezek: his cunning against humanity, and how he is overcome by tyrants through faith and virtues. Various human limbs are attributed to him, V, 172. How he is to be bound and deprived of strength, II, 583. His wars, blandishments, and stratagems against the human race, II, 1147. He is signified by the king of Canaan, ibid. He was conquered by Christ, ibid. He attempts to hinder the efforts of teachers in the Church, and how, III, 42. He is envious and proud, ibid. Through his pride the human race was seduced; through Abraham’s wisdom it was restored, III, 716. Through his envy, human beings, created by God immortal, became mortal, III, 681. Why he burns with such fury against the human race, III, 483. From where he obtained the opportunity for evil, III, 487.

The etymology of “deacons,” I, 302. Their office, ibid. Why seven were instituted by the apostles, ibid.

A description of a diadem, V, 581.

The definition and excellence of dialectic, I, 397. Its effects and necessity, ibid.

What a didrachma is, II, 570.

The various meanings of “day,” V, 287–288; II, 513. The meaning of its parts, V, 289. An allegorical exposition of the six days, I, 466–468. What they signify, I, 469. Which days are long and which short, II, 1119. The seventh and final day, I, 464. What it signifies, I, 465–466. It has no evening, ibid. What is called the eighth day, ibid. Which day is most celebrated and most holy, II, 507–510. Which belongs to the strong, III, 669. How the statement that their days will be one hundred and twenty years is to be understood, I, 512. How the day of vengeance is just, II, 958. That days and times come from God, who also created and ordered everything else, III, 1000. What the day of man and the day of God are, V, 951. Why the day of death is unknown to us, IV, 911. When the day of death and the general judgment will occur, V, 560. How we ought to be prepared for it, ibid. Its terror, VI, 568.

The distribution of the fingers signifies the gifts of the Holy Spirit, V, 158–159.

What the finger of God is, and its power, I, 37.

The celebrated gods and goddesses of the various regions and places are described, V, 426. What their origin and function are, ibid.

What it signifies to disparage the gods, II, 123.

What sort of delay there should be, III, 356.

Reproach and envy repel love of one’s neighbor, III, 794. Sweetness in speech and peaceful conduct are helpful, III, 795.

The reward of those who love God and keep his commandments, IV, 255.

The meaning of the flood, V, 329. Noah’s flood, ibid. The flood in Achaea, ibid. Likewise Deucalion’s flood, ibid., 330.

What Dinah’s fall and her brothers’ zeal against the Shechemites signify spiritually, V, 42. Her abduction and violent violation, I, 614. The punishment of her rape, ibid.

What sort of persecution arose in the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, IV, 853–854.

What Christian discipline is, and its effects, VI, 1231. It is acquired through meditation on the divine law, ibid.

What it means to hear the discipline of father and mother, V, 682.

What it means to learn the discipline of the senses, III, 871.

The duty of a disciple is silence and attentiveness, II, 995–996.

The various gifts of Christ’s disciples, I, 1076.

What the mystical meaning is of the two disciples’ running to Christ’s tomb, IV, 171.

The weakness of the disciples before the coming of the Holy Spirit, IV, 176.

Discord surpasses all capital sins, V, 704.

Discretion in seeking counsel: who should be consulted, and from whom counsel should be concealed, III, 1025.

Discretion in distinguishing dreams, III, 1005. They occur in six ways, ibid., 1006. From where they arise, ibid.

Discretion must be observed in speech, III, 890.

Whether it is lawful for everyone to dispute about God, II, 297.

The disagreement between Rabanus and the monks, I, 97.

The distribution of the Promised Land among Israel by various lots, II, 828–833.

We should not readily associate with one who is richer and more honorable than ourselves, III, 850.

The diversity of the body reveals a corresponding diversity of the soul, II, 601.

The etymology of “inn,” V, 592. Its mystical meaning: the Church, ibid.

A sinful rich man must not be honored, III, 836.

Whom the rich man compared with a camel signifies, V, 77.

Divine things must be preferred to human things, VI, 1597.

The magicians use divinations, as the prophet uses the ephod, II, 727.

The division of the Holy Land among the twelve tribes, IV, 1065–1066.

The rich man does not agree with the poor man; when the latter is despised, the former is honored, III, 853.

Riches add friends, V, 740. What unjust riches are, and their evil, III, 792. Why they are compared with thorns, V, 80. What one’s own riches are, IV, 616. They can free no one, ibid. The two kinds of riches in Holy Scripture: some good, others evil, III, 987. Their disadvantages, V, 723. The riches of the holy Church, III, 489. The riches of God’s goodness and patience must not be despised, V, 1307. The commendation of the rich man without blemish, III, 988. The dangers and calamities of the rich, VI, 629. Their various conditions, I, 1021.

The very useful method of teaching and correcting, VI, 364–365.

The duty of teacher and hearer, IV, 836.

Why teaching is forbidden to women, VI, 677.

What a Catholic teacher should consider in teaching, I, 506–513. He should set kinds of virtues against kinds of vices, I, 414–415. A teacher must moderate his voice and cut into vices like a two-edged sword, III, 641. A teacher must beware lest his own fault rebuke him, IV, 557.

[Col. 1705] The teacher himself is often rebuked by his own fault, II, 364.

The teachers of the Church are generally objects of laughter to the perverse, V, 966. They should avoid obscurity, V, 1189. Their office, II, 650.

The doctrine of heretics is an empty tale, III, 898.

Doctrine is proven through patience, V, 740.

One must submit to the teaching and governance of priests, II, 578.

Christ’s teaching was a stumbling block to the Jews, V, 689.

What it means to teach sound doctrine, VI, 674.

Doeg, “bound” according to the interpretation, and why, III, 59. After Saul’s death he killed himself, III, 70. See III, 321–322.

Why God sometimes pretends not to hear the voice of those who grieve, V, 1217–1231.

What kind of grief is applicable to God, V, 729.

The plots of the deceitful, especially heretics, must be avoided, III, 845.

What the domestic Church is, II, 297.

The domestics clothed in double garments signify the holy Church, V, 787.

The dominion over fish and birds was given to the first parents as a reminder of mortality, I, 460.

From where the Lord’s Day is called so, V, 308. How and why its sanctification was instituted by the apostles, I, 355; IV, 76. It is also founded upon Holy Scripture, ibid.

In what manner the Lord spoke to Laban, I, 573.

How the Lord is found, IV, 380.

The etymology of “house,” V, 390. The unstable house of the proud, V, 731. What an alien house is, V, 679. What the house of God is, IV, 249–250.

What the house of David and Saul is like, III, 77.

A house destroyed signifies the synagogue of heretics, III, 907.

A house outside the walls denotes the Church of the nations, II, 539.

What the house of Jacob is, II, 749.

The house of the righteous expresses the Church, V, 719. It will not be destroyed, ibid., V, 727. Its strength, V, 728.

How and what sort of houses should be built for human beings, II, 541. Its various meanings, IV, 330.

What one who vowed a house to the Lord was formerly required to do, II, 574. And a field, ibid.

What gifts were to be offered for constructing God’s tabernacle, II, 139–140.

The gifts bestowed upon our first parents, III, 873. Their race was divided among various peoples and nations, III, 874.

Some gifts protect a person, others adorn him; which ones they are, V, 1199.

What it means to sleep with the uncircumcised, IV, 827.

What it means to sleep while traveling, I, 592.

In what manner sleep is applicable to God, V, 919.

What a doryx is, and from where it received its name, III, 875.

What Dothaim signifies, I, 624.

The dragon signifies the devil and his ministers, V, 230. The sea dragon, when struck, pours forth venom, V, 238. The sea dragon pours forth venom when struck, V, 238.

Which are the two hateful nations, III, 1118.

The two remarkable petitions of Solomon, V, 774.

What the two dangerous kinds are, III, 960.

Jacob’s two wives are a type of the two Testaments, III, 289. And of our present life, ibid.

Why and how God uses ambiguous expressions, IV, 553–554.

The type signified by leaders understood in a good and a bad sense, V, 448.

[Col. 1705] The leaders are commanded to offer gifts one each day, and the duty of each, II, 630.

Whom the two blind men sitting beside the road represent, V, 76.

Whom the two sons sent to work in the vineyard signify, V, 78.

What the two things that grieve the heart are, III, 948.

The two smoking firebrands are a type of the ending of two kingdoms, III, 248–249.

The twelve oxen of Solomon’s Temple represented the twelve apostles, III, 438.

What the twelve legions of angels signify mystically, I, 1118.

The twelve princes encamped around the tabernacle most aptly express the patriarchs and the twelve apostles, II, 602.

The twelfth month designated for the slaughter of the Jews expresses the final age of the world, III, 665.

What a double-minded person is, III, 370. What will happen to him, III, 374.

What the repetition of words signifies in Holy Scripture, II, 403.

Whether God strikes with a double blow, V, 840.

Who binds together double sins, III, 803.

## E
## E

Ebony, when cut, hardens into stone, V, 518. Drunkenness: what it consists in, V, 770. Its disadvantages and effects are proved from their opposites, III, 627. It often denotes satiety, I, 641. A supporter of lust, V, 756. What it signifies in priests and apostles, V, 1034. All vices accompany it, III, 888. It produces frivolity, ibid. Joy in iniquities and disgust at correction, ibid., 889. Loquacity, ibid. Exultation in evil, ibid.

The drunk are sons of Belial, III, 13. What must be concealed from a drunkard but disclosed to a sober person for correction, III, 65. Description of staggering drunkards, V, 1154.

Hebron is captured by the tribe of Judah; formerly it was called Kiriath-arba, III, 1112; V, 60. What ivory signifies, V, 464. Who are the inhabitants of ivory houses, V, 464.

Why the Church is called a congregation and why it is Catholic, V, 89. It is compared with a dragnet, V, 239. It alone prepares the way to heaven, II, 1140. Its praise: Christ the Bridegroom, signified through Jael as a most powerful woman, lays the devil low, II, 1136; ibid., 1115. With what weapons and stratagem, ibid. The Church is a virgin daughter, II, 1189. Its victory and weapons against Antichrist, II, 1175. Signified by Jephthah’s daughter, who mourned her virginity for sixty days, II, 1189. It is gathered through six ages, ibid. Its gates are the apostles and prophets, II, 1114. Made a most fertile mother by the grace of the Holy Spirit, ibid., 1189. After the Lord’s ascension and the death of the apostles, it was like a widow deprived of husband and children, II, 1202. Its zeal for souls, ibid. Its discernment toward its children, ibid., 1203. It is oppressed by tribulations, ibid., 1204. It imbues its own members with the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion, ibid., 1205. The bride and body of Christ, ibid., 1206. Grateful for and mindful of the bridegroom’s benefits, ibid., 1207, 1208. Its humility toward Christ, ibid. It proves Christ’s incarnation from the Old Testament, ibid. From the Law it elicits the spiritual meaning and confession of the Holy Trinity, ibid., II, 1209. Its knowledge and virtues, II, 1214. Through Ruth it patiently awaits the incarnation, ibid. How powerful its prayers are, III, 612. It always prays for the safety of its own, III, 662.

And for the gravest sins, by divinely granted authority it remits offenses, V, 867.

What “Catholic” means and from where it is derived, I, 297 and VI, 1166. Its three orders and what they are, ibid. Those who have benefited from it sometimes become its enemies, III, 1212, 1213. How it has been turned into a den of robbers, V, 865.

The simple Church rejoices in variety of clothing, V, 570, 597–598. Its enemies are compelled, unwillingly, to confess its truth, III, 658. One who is disobedient to the just decrees of the Church and priests must be punished with death, II, 902, 903. The children of the Church of the just are wisdom’s children, III, 776. The meanings of distinguished churches, VI, 1621 (note). Explanation of distinguished churches and patrons of Mainz, VI, 1636 (note).

What Ecclesiastes signifies, V, 775. To what the books Ecclesiastes and Ecclesiasticus chiefly serve, III, 363, 364. Their distinction, ibid. What impelled writers of ecclesiastical matters to write, I, 41. How many grades there are in the ecclesiastical order and from where they began, I, 301. Clergy must beware of surrendering themselves to earthly profits and pleasures, II, 639.

Edelhard, Rabanus’s cellarer, because of avarice and because he failed to provide alms for the dead, is horribly beaten by spirits, I, 92, 93. Edelhard dies after three days, I, 93. He appears to Rabanus after death, ibid.

The ivy has the figure of the Jewish people, and why, V, 528. To eat with a prince: what this means allegorically, V, 754.

What Edom is like, V, 1260. Whose type its daughters bear, ibid.

What the Ephnaim taught, V, 95. What poverty means, V, 700.

Why Eglah alone is called David’s wife, although it is certain that he had several wives, III, 78, 297. What Eglon signifies, V, 55. The king of Moab oppresses Israel under fifteen years of servitude, II, 1129. He is killed by Ehud, ibid. Whether he was thin or fat, III, 1130. What his name means in Hebrew, ibid.

Einhard, abbot, from a royal senator, VI, 1669 (note).

What is to be understood by “the expelled,” III, 1014.

El, the name of God, VI, 1593.

Elkanah, Samuel’s father, arose from the tribe of Levi, yet had a mother from the tribe of Judah, an Ephrathite, III, 77. His piety, ibid., 12. His wives were Hannah and Peninnah; he grieved over Hannah’s barrenness, ibid.; a type, in his piety, of those who remain steadfast, III, 13.

Elchias, inventor of Deuteronomy, III, 314.

Eleazar means strength, V, 53; III, 16. A specimen of other strong men, ibid. Why Eleazar is called at one time the son of Mattathias and at another the son of Sauras, III, 1174. The slayer of the elephant: a type of the proud, ibid.

Who are the elect of Israel, II, 135, 136. They are often tested for instruction, III, 100. They immediately suppress vain glory that stealthily creeps in, III, 344. Their compunctions according to the disposition of circumstances, V, 1235. Their glory, VI, 1619. Their diversity, VI, 656.

The testing of the elect and the reprobate, V, 1197. Their distinction, IV, 198. The condition of both, IV, 198. Why the former desire to pass over to the latter, IV, 294.

Jacob’s election and Esau’s rejection, [Col. 1707] V, 1485, 1486. Its obscurity, V, 1486. How they were elected and rejected before birth, ibid. The sign of election is charity, IV, 920. The pride of rejection, ibid.

From where electrum derives its name, and its nature, V, 478. A type of our Redeemer, ibid.

Almsgiving as redemption from sin, V, 747; III, 783. In what manner alms should be distributed, V, 696–698. Definition, I, 340. The Corinthians are urged to send alms to the poor of Jerusalem, VI, 207. They are to give them promptly and abundantly, VI, 211. The excellence of almsgiving and fasting, IV, 22. Various kinds of almsgiving, III, 788; I, 340. The gift of alms must not be postponed, III, 783. The orderly manner of distributing it, III, 807, 808, 845, 846, 877, 888, 896, 973.

All the elements and created things are stirred to praise God, IV, 637. The four elements, V, 262; VI, 317. How and when they were created, I, 446, 447.

Description of the elephant signifying the sinner, V, 221. The first use of elephants in war, III, 1174.

The fruits of raising one’s hands to God, VI, 1098. What this signifies, VI, 1149.

What Eliachim signifies and whom he represents, V, 67. Eliachim, a type of Christ’s resurrection, III, 550. His exhortation to the Israelites, III, 552; III, 606. What kind of man he was, ibid.

Whether Elijah sinned when he worshiped the impious king Ahab, III, 568. Elijah signifies Christ, III, 206. He was nourished by ravens, ibid. He blessed the widow’s oil and flour with whom he lodged, III, 207. In raising her son, he was a beautiful type of Christ, ibid. He was not irritated by the rebuke of his hostess, ibid. While building an altar and sacrificing to God after the drought had been driven away, he obtained water in abundance, III, 208, 209. The efficacy of his prayer, III, 209. He killed the prophets of Baal, ibid. Distinguished by great piety and virtues, he asked the Lord for death, III, 210. While sleeping, he was awakened by an angel, III, 211; he fasted for forty days and forty nights, ibid. Fleeing persecution, he hid himself in a cave, ibid. Why he was carried to the heavenly air in a chariot, and where he still dwells, III, 222. Having neither wife nor children, he was a suitable figure of Christ, the most chaste, ascending into heaven, III, 223. With his cloak he divided the waters, which allowed himself and Elisha to cross, III, 224. His praise, III, 1100, 1101.

How Elijah was permitted to sacrifice outside the temple of God, although this is forbidden, II, 431. Sought for death, he is thrown into a pit, V, 1078. He is rescued by Ebed-melech, ibid. A type of preachers, ibid. He is freed from captivity, V, 1085. Johanan foretells to Gedaliah his death at the hands of Ishmael, ibid.

Elimelech is a figure of Christ, II, 1201. In Hebrew, “my God is king”; he has Naomi as his wife, ibid. He dies in Moab, ibid.; and so do his sons, II, 1202.

Elisabeth is said to mean “the fullness of my God”; she is a type of the ancient Law, V, 74.

Elisha is interpreted as “the salvation of my God,” V, 67; III, 213. His praise, III, 213. Whom we should understand by the sword of Jehu, which was to kill the fugitives, ibid. Why, after Elijah’s translation, he asked for a double portion of his spirit, III, 223. With Elijah’s cloak left to him, he divided the waters a second time, III, 224. By means of salt alone he healed the malignant waters of Jericho, III, 225. The boys who mocked him were devoured by bears, [Col. 1707] ibid. A type of Christ, ibid. As he was dying, he promised King Joash victory over Syria by shooting an arrow, III, 243, 244.

Eliud signifies a proud teacher, V, 50.

The river Ella, V, 321.

The two provinces of Ellanos, V, 344.

What an eloquent person must observe, I, 408. One style belongs to the law courts and another to the Church, ibid. He must adapt himself to his subject, ibid. What it means to speak eloquently and wisely, I, 412.

Why eloquence is compared with rain, VI, 1149. What it means to illuminate wisdom, III, 941.

Heman, who is called David’s brother and singer, V, 70.

The Creator’s eminence shines out in the adornment and beauty of the heavens, III, 1070. And in the sun, ibid.; the moon, ibid.; the stars, III, 1071; the rainbow, ibid.; snow, hail, thunder, and mist, III, 1072, 1073; and in the frost from the north the Creator’s power shines forth, III, 1075, 1076.

What the flashes of lightning signify, III, 691. The buyer always disparages, V, 744.

When and why the feast of the Dedication was instituted, III, 1161; IV, 74; I, 358. The Dedication of the New Testament surpasses that of the Old, ibid.

What Enoch signifies, V, 33. Why he is said to have been transferred to the heavenly air rather than carried up, and why he did not die, III, 223; VI, 791. How he died according to faith, VI, 223. A type of Christ ascending into heaven, VI, 794. His encomium, III, 1084.

Enos is said to mean “man” or “male,” V, 32.

The enydros, an enemy of the crocodile, V, 232.

What an ephah is, II, 286. A type of the Holy Trinity and the Incarnation, II, 287, 298, 676.

What Gideon’s ephod, made from the spoils of the Midianites, was: a garment, pure gold, or a statue, II, 1168. The people fornicated with Gideon through it, ibid. The word ephod referred to the high priest’s garment, ibid. Samuel’s ephod was different, ibid. What it signifies, III, 64. There were two kinds under the old Law, III, 20.

Ephraim allegorically signifies the Church of the Gentiles, which conquers evil spirits, II, 1144. Why it is compared with a dove and not with other birds, V, 1102. It is interpreted as “increase,” V, 49. Ephraim in Hebrew means “fruitfulness,” III, 14.

Why Ephrath is called David’s city, V, 345; other names of regions and cities, ibid.

The etymology of Epiphany, IV, 18. Why it was instituted, ibid. Explanation of the gifts offered on that day, ibid. Its celebration, I, 344. From where it received its name, ibid.

Several distinguished bishops of Mainz are listed among the first; they imitate farmers, II, 1232. The name “bishop” or “cleric” benefits no one, V, 901. The name and office of bishop, V, 85. The rite of their creation, I, 299. Their orders are threefold, ibid. From where the name derives, I, 301. Their ornaments and epithets, VI, 1609. Their qualities, III, 21; VI, 597, 661. How it is to be understood that a bishop must be the husband of one wife, VI, 661. Why priests were formerly called presbyters, VI, 597. Their divisions, VI, 695. They are stewards of Christ, not rulers, VI, 664. They must pursue chastity, VI, 667. The ornaments and epithets of bishops, VI, 1599.

A letter of Bishop Hunbert to Rabanus, II, 1107. Why some reject Paul’s Letter to Philemon, II, 1134. For what purpose the Letter to the Romans was written, V, 1258.

Inscriptions of epitaphs and of various altars and churches, VI, 1632. [Col. 1708] At very great length, likewise, those of distinguished men, VI, 1670, 1671.

Why Abraham made a feast for Isaac not on the day of his circumcision or birth, but after he was weaned, I, 562.

What horses signify in Scripture, V, 213. Who are their riders, II, 68. Who disturb the sea, VI, 1128. Their interpretation in a good and bad sense, V, 214. Which horsemen are good and which evil, V, 214, 215. What it means to cast horse and rider into the sea, VI, 1103. The distinction between a horse and a mule, V, 613.

The eradication of the Jewish people, V, 1235.

The notion of Erebus, V, 374. The praise of hermits and perfect monks, V, 1227.

What ergasterium and ergastulum signify, V, 405. The Egyptian prison mystically signifies temptations, II, 30.

The ericius and erinacius are the same animal; see what they signify, V, 205 and 227.

Hermaphrodites conceive and give birth, V, 196.

How one ought to be ashamed of sins, III, 1061. What shame is praiseworthy and what is blameworthy, IV, 615. What kind of sign shame is, IV, 615, 690.

What the caterpillar denotes, V, 236, 258.

Esau has three names, V, 38. How he is said to have lived on Mount Seir, although his brother Jacob inhabited it, I, 619. What his name means in Hebrew, II, 1136. A type of the Jewish people, ibid., and II, 1139. Why he was born red and hairy, I, 582. Skilled in hunting, ibid. Whom Jacob’s selling his birthright to his brother signifies, I, 583. Led by an evil spirit, he intended his brother’s death and was prevented, III, 717.

Ezra means the same as “helper,” V, 70. What kind of man he was, III, 311. What sort of men Ezra, Jether, Mered, and others were, III, 305.

“Being” belongs to God alone, V, 1044–1046. He cannot be seen by us in this life, III, 420. What sort of being he is, V, 1158.

Esther, whose name is interpreted as “hidden,” V, 66, signifies the Church of the Gentiles, III, 446. Devoting herself to fasting and prayer, she attempts to avert destruction from the Jews, III, 653.

Ethan, who is called “the strong singer of David,” V, 70; III, 312.

The pagans, who, although recognizing God from created things, rejected his worship, deservedly abandoned by God because they worshiped images of creatures, and as punishment fell into detestable crimes, III, 338, 720.

Why the Ebionites reject the holy apostle Paul from the catalogue of the apostles, I, 918. Their heresy, VI, 337.

The seriousness of receiving the Eucharist unworthily, and the rite of receiving it worthily, VI, 103.

Saint Eugenia, living holily among monks in their habit, is exposed; finally she is endowed with the crown of martyrdom, IV, 236.

The river Euphrates, V, 321.

The error of Eunomius concerning knowledge of the Father and the Son, III, 88.

Eunuchs forbidden entry into the Church are a figure of those who live effeminately, II, 929; what kind they were, III, 407; three kinds, I, 1018. The eunuchs who threatened Ahasuerus’s death bear the type of the Jewish scribes and Pharisees, III, 651, 651. Likewise, of heretics and schismatics, III, 651. Joseph interprets the dreams of Pharaoh’s eunuchs in prison, predicting that one would be restored to office and the other punished by hanging; these things occurred on Pharaoh’s birthday, I, 633, 634.

What Europe is like, V, 347. From where it received its name, ibid. Its division, ibid.

Refutation of the heresy of the Eutychians, I, 1176.

The letter “Eva”: what it signifies, V, 31. Why Eve was made as Adam’s helper, I, 482. What she signifies mystically, I, 484. Made from his side, she is a type of Christ, ibid. Deceived by the serpent’s blandishments and fraud, II, 1148. Why, before she had yet been made, the man is spoken of as male and female, I, 474.

The actions of the Gospel are beautiful, V, 695. Its truth is to be sought by the prophets, II, 1138. By the evangelical word, the storms of the fluctuating world are calmed, III, 1078. The harmony of the Evangelists, IV, 510. Why one must stand when the Gospel is recited, and who instituted this practice, V, 823. The excellence of evangelists, V, 1292, 1514.

What Evilach means, I, 478.

What it means to be exalted in songs, III, 361. What it signifies to be exalted above the rooftops, II, 752.

What the lofty land is, VI, 1139. A detailed description of the destruction and devastation of the city of Jerusalem, III, 569.

Excommunication performs in the Church what execution once did, II, 938. Its usefulness, V, 908.

The watch-duty assigned to the Levites, II, 693.

By excusing our fault we increase our sin, I, 493, 494.

From where the model of the Temple arose, III, 411. What a ruler’s example accomplishes, VI, 1390.

What the Book of Exodus contains, V, 111, 1024.

From where exomologesis derives its name, I, 766. Its various kinds, ibid. How it differs from litanies, ibid.

The office, interpretation, and purpose of exorcists, V, 93, 156. King Solomon was the first inventor, ibid.

The praise of the experienced or tested, III, 1007.

How the sanctuary was expiated by the blood of a goat and a calf, II, 423. The most celebrated solemnity of the expiations was instituted, II, 509, 510. What it prefigured, ibid.

The Assyrian spies designate inquisitive investigators, III, 566. What the twelve spies prefigured, V, 54. The spies sent into the Promised Land and what happened there, II, 666, 667. They brought back a branch with a cluster of grapes and other fruits as a sign of fertility, II, 668, 669. They bear the type of the scribes and Pharisees, ibid. All except Caleb and Joshua grumble and despair, II, 669, 844. Their twofold kind, IV, 775.

The reproach of benefits granted and the exaggeration of Judah’s iniquities, III, 495. Christ’s reproach of the cities for their impenitence, IV, 442.

What ecstasy means, V, 1330. Who the destroyer is, III, 617.

External correction is often internal correction, V, 746. Who is a stranger, III, 818.

An elegant description of the Last Judgment, III, 1049.

Why Hezekiah, bearing the type of the Savior, is called “the strength of the Lord,” V, 63. By breaking the bronze serpent and removing many abuses of idolatry, he prefigured Christ, [Col. 1709] III, 252. Pressed by Sennacherib in war, he recognized his fault but did not disdain to ask pardon, ibid. His humility and prudence, III, 255. He asks the Lord God for Isaiah’s prayers on his behalf, ibid. His piety, III, 256. So that he would not become arrogant over his triumphs and victories, he was visited with illness, III, 258, 765. The various causes of his great weeping in his struggle, III, 260. Why he was called the son of David, ibid., 261. His life was prolonged beyond expectation, ibid. The miracles that occurred when he recovered, III, 261, 262. Error concerning the steps of his house, ibid. His encomium and piety, III, 517.

Ezekiel is interpreted as “the strength of the Lord,” V, 67. What his four creatures signify, ibid. When he wrote his prophecy, V, 1021; IV, 750. Since he had not yet said anything, how does he begin by saying that it occurred in the thirtieth year? IV, 497. He is strengthened by the Lord against adversaries, IV, 554, 555. Why he was ordered to eat the book shown to him and not to drink, IV, 561. Why he is forbidden to turn from the left side to the right, IV, 595. He prepares food and drink for the future famine, baked with human dung, and what kind, ibid. Gathering the vessels of migration and veiling his face, he is a figure of Christ, IV, 647. He prophesied at the same time as Jeremiah, ibid. He saw the glory of the Lord, IV, 957.

## F

From where “smith” derives its name, and the power of a smith’s fire, V, 558.

The martyrdom of Saint Fabian, IV, 1128. Who are to be understood allegorically as smiths, ibid. Their various instruments, ibid.; see V, 559.

Daedalus, inventor of building, V, 560.

Why Israel expelled blacksmiths from all its regions, III, 272. Smiths laboring night and day signify preachers of the divine word, III, 1035, 1036.

The deprivation of the divine face is the gravest punishment, VI, 1142. The Israelites cannot look upon Moses’ horned face without a veil, II, 239. Since God himself affirms that no one has seen God’s face, how did Jacob see him face to face? I, 612. Likewise Moses, II, 230–234. How Jacob said that he had seen Esau’s face as though it were the face of God, I, 613. One must not turn the face away from one’s neighbor, III, 1061.

Those who do the word, not those who merely hear it, are justified, IV, 219.

The falcon, V, 253.

Faleq is interpreted as “division,” V, 35.

Reproof of false friends, III, 1024.

Why the sickle is attributed to Saturn, V, 428. It denotes preaching the divine word, V, 611.

What the famine was like in the time of Elisha, III, 229. The famine of the word often arises from a scarcity of teachers, III, 1199. It occurred among the Jews, ibid., 1200. The distress of famine, V, 1384–1389.

From where temples derive their name, V, 391.

What Paran means, VI, 1115. What fascination means, VI, 282, 283. What the Fasti are, III, 403. What fate signifies, V, 453. Its threefold distinction, ibid.

What it mystically means to be “the fool of God,” V, 881. Who is a fool, V, 724.

What it means to scatter ashes from a furnace before Pharaoh, II, 39.

When and how God strikes with fever, II, 955.

The happiness of the just, who were despised here by the wicked and approved by God, III, 682. Happy is the one who runs along the way of God’s commandments, III, 855.

Woman made in the image of God, I, 461. Where women conceive at the age of five years, V, 197.

The use of thigh-coverings, II, 205. To whom they are prescribed, ibid.

Women are to be appointed to ministry in the Church, V, 1605–1606.

What striking the thigh signifies, V, 1037.

Why slanting windows were made in the Temple, and what they signify mystically, IV, 918, 919. Windows are compared with the five senses, V, 401.

Wild beasts signify paganism, V, 201.

What a bier means literally and mystically, V, 607.

For what purpose and when the Feast of Tabernacles was proclaimed, II, 511. With what rites it was to be celebrated, II, 511, 512.

What it means to offer the leaven of praise, II, 50. What the leaven of the Pharisees and Herod is, I, 988. The meaning of the word, VI, 924.

From where iron derives its name, V, 480. What it signifies mystically, ibid.; VI, 924.

Why the feasts of the apostles, martyrs, and the other saints are celebrated and in what manner they should be conducted, I, 356. With what worship, ibid. When Masses were first celebrated over their bodies, ibid.

Hasty combat is vicious, III, 970.

What the unending feast is, IV, 1030. When it is celebrated, IV, 1032.

How the Feast of Tabernacles is to be celebrated mystically, II, 899, 900.

The feast of Solomon and the Israelites after the Temple was completed, III, 186. The notable allegorical significance of this feast, once celebrated, III, 187, 454.

The feasts of Christians and Jews, V, 307. The feasts of the ancients, and from where they originated, I, 359, 360.

Why someone sees the speck in his brother’s eye sooner than the beam in his own, IV, 519.

Twin offspring: the two commandments of charity, V, 200. What kind of fetus is formed, V, 176.

The feigned humility of heretics, III, 893.

Why the Lord cursed the fig tree, IV, 330. The fig tree is a figure of the Jewish Synagogue, I, 1044; VI, 1129. From where it derives its name, V, 182.

What miracles occurred in the Old Testament through faith, VI, 803. A rhythmic description of the Catholic faith, V, 1609. A clear declaration of active faith, V, 1263; VI, 735. The praise and necessity of faith and hope, VI, 1325.

One should show gratitude to a guarantor and keep faith, III, 976. What is the goal of the labors of the faithful, III, 668. The number of the faithful is far smaller than the other number, II, 772, 773. The rarity of the faithful, V, 827. When true faith existed, ibid., 840, 871. The Catholic faith professed in baptism must not be abandoned, III, 806. What it means to have faith in the saints, V, 1262; VI, 701. Those who trust in God must not neglect works necessary for salvation, I, 609.

What faith is; see “Religion,” V, 90. What the most certain faith is, I, 369. Faith is the foundation of perfection, II, 747. Its definition and commendation, VI, 788.

Abraham’s faith and obedience were tested in the command to sacrifice his son, but an angel prevented the sacrifice, I, 566, 567. Who this angel was, I, 567. What it signifies mystically, I, 568, 569.

Faith is the source of all virtues, IV, 906, 909. What is most certain, I, 369.

What it means to walk confidently, V, 696. Confidence in earthly things produces poverty, III, 838.

Potters bear the type of the teachers of the Church, III, 1036, 1037. Potters dwelling in plantations and sacred hedges bear the type of teachers, III, 306. What the vessels of Jeremiah shown to him prefigured, V, 955.

Pharaoh’s daughter is a type of the Church of the Gentiles, V, 52. The daughter of a priest who commits fornication is to be burned in the flames, and why, II, 476. If she marries one of the people, she shall not eat the sacrifices, II, 492.

A daughter must be carefully guarded, III, 1066. Who are called the daughters of men, I, 512; likewise, of Christ and the Church, III, 750.

What the daughters of Zelophehad, who obtained an inheritance among their father’s kinsmen, mystically represent, II, 774–775. Why they are permitted, through the intercession of leaders, to marry their nearest relatives, II, 836.

To whom daughters are to be given in marriage, and why, III, 808.

In Scripture, sons are called by four modes, V, 187. What “daughters” means, III, 585. Who are the sons of Israel, III, 288, 289.

The sons of the Kenites, relatives of Moses, dwell with the sons of Judah, II, 1114. How sons are punished for the sins of their fathers to the third and fourth generation, V, 104.

After Joshua’s death the sons of Israel consult the Lord, II, 1111. Who were the sons of Israel who entered Egypt, II, 9. A figure of the apostles, II, 11.

Who are the sons of fatness, or of Bashan, VI, 1140.

The sons of Salma and others: how they are the crown of the house of Joab, III, 295.

A portion is given to the sons of Reuben and Gad and to half the tribe of Manasseh beyond the Jordan, provided that they precede their brothers into the Promised Land, II, 803 and following; 853, 854.

Whether the sins of children are to be imputed to righteous parents, VI, 664.

The learning and offices of the sons of Issachar, III, 336. A type of Christ, ibid.

Why the work of the Israelites is called “works,” but the service of the Levites is called “the work of works,” II, 614.

Why Laban called Jacob’s sons and daughters his own, I, 606.

Spiritual sons, just as much as natural sons, are to be educated by fathers in discipline, III, 981. How harmful it is to indulge them excessively, ibid.

The Son of God has certain names from the substance of divinity and others from the dispensation of humanity, V, 19. These are explained, ibid. Bodily members are also ascribed to him, ibid. In all things equal to the Father, he is the supreme good, II, 327; III, 701. The radiance of light and spotless mirror, ibid., 702. The Word of the Father, ibid. Light without darkness, ibid. He was predestined from eternity in God’s counsel, III, 765. Why he is sometimes called created and sometimes begotten, ibid., 766. Why he is said to have been made from a woman, although she was a virgin, VI, 315. How he is said, against certain heretics, not to know the day of judgment, V, 1436. Why he came in the likeness of sinful flesh, I, 1077.

The growing son of Joseph prefigures Christ, I, 663.

“The Son of Man” in the singular is taken in a good sense, and in the plural in a bad sense, IV, 807. Why Ezekiel is so often called “son of man” by God, IV, 889. Why he is commanded to attend with his eyes and ears, ibid.

What “son” signifies mystically, VI, 926. And “daughter,” ibid.

What fringes signify, V, 580. A type of the Lord’s Incarnation, ibid. By placing fringes and ribbons at the four corners of their cloaks, the Israelites remembered God’s commandments, II, 680. What this signifies allegorically, ibid.; II, 926.

What the firmament is and what its matter is, I, 449. Who are understood by its name and when it was made, I, 44.

The boundaries of Japheth: Africa, III, 603.

What “end” signifies mystically, VI, 932.

What a treasury means, V, 604.

Why the Lord’s scourges occur, V, 908.

The crime of the Roman commander Flaminius and a little prostitute, I, 960.

What flame means, VI, 921.

What weeping over the mountains and lamentation over the beautiful places of the wilderness signifies mystically, V, 872–873.

The effect and purpose of the flowering rod, IV, 611, 612. What a flower signifies, VI, 929.

Why the rivers of Egypt were turned into blood, II, 34. Why they are compared with the same things, V, 1099. The mystical interpretations of a river, VI, 933. The two kinds of rivers and their various meanings, V, 318. The various names and explanations of rivers, ibid. The various meanings of the principal rivers, IV, 1056.

From where hearth derives its name, V, 605.

The covenant and oath of the Israelites with the Lord, II, 961.

From where Phogor derives its name, V, 359.

What the fountain irrigating the whole surface of the earth signifies, I, 472–474. The distinction between a perpetual spring and cisterns, V, 814. Various mystical interpretations of a spring, V, 317; VI, 929, 1156.

What a hole means, VI, 930.

Various explanations of legal cases, V, 544, 545. The distinction between doors and gates, V, 389.

The twofold etymology of scissors, V, 610.

One must not abuse beauty and riches, III, 615; IV, 676.

The form of cultivating friendship, III, 779. Among whom it should exist, ibid. The stages by which it is attained, ibid.

Who is a formed infant, II, 114.

The ant-lion attacks ants, V, 227. Description and significance of ants, V, 227.

The timid must not be sent to war, II, 911.

Whether fornication is included under the commandment against adultery, II, 933. Its punishment and gravity, V, 707. Its worst kind is idolatry, III, 738. What spiritual fornication is, IV, 683. Its exaggeration, ibid. Its remedy, ibid. Its description and kinds, VI, 1375.

He is stronger who conquers himself than he who conquers the strongest walls, III, 1093.

[Col. 1712] Definition and usefulness of fortitude, IV, 1116; VI, 1362.

The location and description of the Fortunate Islands, V, 381. Why some thought that they were paradise, ibid.

From where forum derives its name, and its kinds, V, 544. What a forum signifies, V, 386.

The pit is a type of the condemned, the devil, and Antichrist, V, 409. The one who makes a pit will fall into it, III, 660, 669.

What Christ signified by the breaking of bread, I, 984.

What a spear means, V, 537.

The two names of the Franks, vernacular and Latin, VI, 1592.

The commendation of brotherly charity, V, 738; I, 830–844. The method of correction and granting forgiveness, I, 1011, 1012.

Who are the brothers of Christ according to the flesh, I, 622, 623.

Joseph’s brothers, oppressed by the need for grain, flee to Egypt, I, 631. Their supplication and apology to their brother, I, 640.

Rebecca’s brothers bless her as she departs to Isaac, I, 573.

Why God forbade the fratricide Cain to be killed, I, 505, 506. What his seven sins were, ibid.

Why God requires the soul of a brother from the hand of a man, I, 524. What is signified by this name, VI, 921.

Fraud is committed in three ways, V, 1114. What fraud belongs to the devil, V, 1089.

Freculph’s letter to Rabanus, I, 439.

The etymology of bridles, V, 612. What tribute signifies, III, 31.

The meaning of “strait” or “open sea,” V, 315.

The coldness of snow signifies hardness of heart, V, 712.

The fruit reveals the tree, and speech reveals the man, III, 962.

What the fruits of divine love are like, V, 694. What the fruit of light is, VI, 450. Why the fruits of the earth were stored up, III, 992. What fruit worthy of repentance is, I, 770. What the fruit of the mouth is, V, 721. What it signifies, VI, 937.

The various kinds of fruits and trees, V, 511, 512. Their literal and typological meanings, ibid., 512, 513, 514–523. A full explanation of the fruits of the Spirit, VI, 358.

How “to enjoy” and “to use” differ, IV, 151.

What is called grain, V, 504. Its kinds and typological interpretations, ibid. What those who hide and sell grain may expect, V, 718.

The drone, a counterfeit bee, V, 256.

The flight of Moses into Midian after the slaughter has the type of our Savior abandoning the Jews and calling the nations, II, 17, 18. The flight of the wicked and the security of the righteous, III, 1194. What it means to flee in winter or on the Sabbath, II, 277.

The fugitive slave denotes a man oppressed by the devil or by the weight of sins, II, 932.

How Ful is said to have transferred Reuben to the tribe of Manasseh, although elsewhere this is ascribed to King Shalmaneser, III, 310.

Saint Boniface, founder of the monastery of Fulda, I, 43. Its location and construction, ibid. Its estates and their distribution, [Col. 1713] I, 44, 54. In Rabanus’s time it supported one hundred and fifty monks, V, 175. The monks of Fulda live by the labor of their hands; see ibid. Their austerity of life and studies, I, 75. They abstain from wine and meat, ibid., 82.

The splendor of virtues shines forth only in the unity of the Church, III, 648.

Lightning signifies divine terrors, V, 277. The lightning and flashes that occurred on the mountain: what they signify figuratively, II, 91–95.

The coot, a bird, V, 248.

The meaning of smoke, V, 271.

Offices must not be determined by age, VI, 619.

From where sling and slingers derive their names, and what they signify, III, 611. Lyranus’s dream concerning the interpretation of this name, ibid. What a sling, as a weapon of war, signifies, V, 541.

What a foundation means, V, 400. Its allegorical significance, ibid.

A funeral sermon at vigils for the dead, IV, 128. Which priests were permitted to attend the funerals of citizens, II, 473.

From where ropes received their name, V, 556. How David is said to have measured the peoples with a cord, III, 94. What this means allegorically, ibid. The cord of inheritance is a type of the world’s twistedness, III, 355.

The life of Fureseus, VI, 180.

A nocturnal thief may lawfully be killed, II, 118.

What the Furies are like, V, 434.

Gentle anger is unworthy of a disciple of Christ, III, 790.

Penance for theft and sacrilege from the Council of Toledo and the opinion of other Fathers, ibid. Likewise, from the Council of Elvira, VI, 1413.

Since the law of theft in Exodus commands restitution of double, how does it here demand the principal and a fifth part? II, 618.

Whether theft can be committed without injury, II, 447.

How prophets foretell future contingencies and God foresees them, IV, 552, 832.

## G
Gaal attacks Abimelech, III, 1174. What Gaas is, V, 351. What Gabaon is, III, 415. The killing of the Gibeonites causes a three-year famine, III, 112. Gabaoth was a twofold city, III, 288. What Gad signifies, V, 45. The soldiers of Gad are compared with lions and wild goats, III, 332. Where Gadis is, V, 354. The marvelous power of the gagate stone, V, 463. What Galaad is, V, 360. A type of Sacred Scripture, ibid. Its distinctions, ibid. It denotes the synagogue of the Jews, II, 1146. Other meanings, II, 161. The Galatians’ swift transfer from evangelical truth, II, 1186–1188. Its condemnation, VI, 254. Why they were called senseless, VI, 282. Their attitude toward Paul, VI, 324. How they were begotten by the Apostle, VI, 326. What galbanum is, III, 934. The location of Galgal, V, 368. The Samaritans’ error concerning this place, ibid. Where Galilee got its name, V, 339. Its division, ibid.; its various mystical meanings, ibid., V, 541. The doctrine of the Galileans, V, 95. Where Gallatia got its name, V, 344. The Gauls were so called from the whiteness of the people, V, 350. The hen, V, 248. The nature of hens brooding their chicks, I, 1075. What the cock signifies, V, 248. [Col. 1713] What the cock girded about the loins signifies, V, 778. The Ganges, which is also the Phison, V, 320. A description of the Garamantes, V, 352. The effects of gluttony, II, 867. An encomium of heavenly joy, III, 270. Solid and true joy is from and in God alone, and likewise from the cross of our Lord, III, 16. The righteous rejoice in calamities, ibid. Gaza of the Euaeans, formerly a city of the Cappadocians; later giants lived there, III, 29. It was utterly destroyed, but another city of the same name was built, ibid. Which city Gaza is, V, 1110. How it is said in a certain Prophet that it will become an everlasting tomb, ibid. Where it got its name, V, 378. The etymology of “treasury,” IV, 922. Its description, ibid. Its typological meaning, IV, 945, 957, 959, 981, 982. What Gedeon signifies, V, 56. He cries to the Lord, lamenting the people oppressed by Midian, II, 1156. He was placed in command against Midian, ibid. Before God’s call he commanded a thousand soldiers, ibid. An angel appears to him and promises victory over Midian, ibid. He offers a sacrifice before the angel, ibid. It is kindled by fire leaping forth from a rock, ibid. From this sign he recognizes that it is the angel of God, ibid. Whether he legitimately and without a breastplate offered sacrifice outside Shiloh, and whether others did so as well, II, 1157. In the sacrifice he offered, he bears the figure of Christ, II, 1157, 1158. He kills the bull of his gentile master and another seven-year-old bull, ibid. The figurative meaning of this deed, ibid. He summons all the tribes of Israel, II, 1159. He trusts in God, yet seeks a sign of victory and does not sin in doing so, ibid. In the mystery he sees the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the nations, ibid. He sends messengers to Ephraim to seize the water crossings against Midian, II, 1166. He kills Oreb and Zeb, ibid. He takes possession of Sorhot and the Tower of Phanuel; he refuses the kingship offered by the Jews, asks for five earrings and whatever ornaments were collected from Midian, from which an ephod was made, II, 1167, 1168. Whether he sinned in making the ephod, ibid. He committed fornication through it, ibid. At the end of his life, ibid. He was called Jerobaal, II, 1170. He has Abimelech as a son by a concubine and dies full of days, ibid. What the sons and wives signify mystically, II, 1170, 1171. Because of the ephod that was erected, all his offspring perished, II, 1171. He sinned by asking the Lord for a sign, II, 1182. His fleece drenched with dew and the ark: what they typify, II, 1183. He is praised by the Apostle, ibid. A comparison of Gehenna with the luxury of the present life, VI, 1318. How great its fear ought to be, ibid. Where its name comes from, I, 901. The mountains of Gilboa withered when David cursed them, V, 360. Ice and cold signify the calamities of the present life, VI, 1155. The nations and kinds of gems, V, 464. What the cheeks of the Savior were like, V, 151. The genealogy from Adam to Abraham, III, 281. The genealogy of the sons of Esau, I, 618. An account of Christ’s genealogy, I, 731, 744; IV, 458. Why no mention of holy women occurs in it, ibid. Why Matthew placed the genealogy at the beginning, but Luke after the baptism, ibid. Why Matthew began from Abraham and Luke from Christ, ibid. Various difficulties and contradictions between them are reconciled, ibid. Genealogies and fables are not to be heeded, V, 582 and VI, 689. The generation of Abraham, I, 531. [Col. 1714] The chaste generation of the Catholic, and why, III, 685. Its blessedness, ibid. The generation of Jacob’s sons from two wives, I, 596–602. What is called a perverse generation, VI, 1135. Its condemnation, V, 1094. How many generations there are from Adam to Christ, I, 509. Two generations are explained, the first aptly applied to the Jews and the Father, the second to heretics who curse the Son, V, 776. What the generations of heaven and earth are mystically, I, 470, 471. What history Genesis encompasses, V, 111. What broom plants signify, V, 95. Where the word “nation” comes from, V, 437. The Gentiles expected more silver and ornament in their idols than they worshiped divinity, III, 733. They worshiped not only gold but also earthen vessels, III, 743. Who are to be called Gentiles, V, 486. The Gentiles search through the divine writings and satisfy their hunger from them, II, 1209, 1210. They are given grace through Christ, ibid. They are called to faith after Christ’s Passion, II, 1211, 1212. They are commanded to scrutinize the ancient law and the prophecies concerning Christ, II, 1212. They submit themselves to Christ, ibid. They receive a twofold mercy from him, ibid. They come after the Jews in time, but not in grace, II, 1214. They embrace the faith soon after Christ’s Passion, II, 1216. The constancy of converted Gentiles, II, 1204. Through Ruth drawing barley from the ears, II, 1206–1209. The promises of the nations concerning the reception of God’s grace, V, 1596. An explanation and division of the various nations, V, 438–445. Which are holy, II, 89. Which are without counsel, VI, 1145. The fellowship of the nations and idolaters is strictly forbidden to the Israelites, II, 236, 237. The origin and progress of the nations, V, 437. Knees are to be bent before God, II, 1421. Who do this and who do not, ibid. Some knees are bodily, others belong to the mind, ibid. What the chosen race is, V, 452.
