Its remedy, ibid. Its two kinds, V, 767. The seriousness of the anger of fools, VI, 1376. Its twofold distinction, and which kind is lawful, III, 768. Its twofold meaning, VI, 438. Explanation, VI, 439.

Anger must be absent from the judgment, III, 334. It is the gate of all vices, V, 773. Its detestation together with homicide, IV, 112. Its distinction from wrath, VI, 271. The seriousness of both, ibid. How God’s anger toward Moses is to be understood, II, 24, 25.

Iris: see “rainbow.”

Queen Irmingardis, wife of Lothair, VI, 1671. Irony, VI, 223; III, 627. The Egyptians ironically exhort the unwarlike to take up arms, V, 1099.

The penance of those who irrationally have intercourse with animals or with males, from the Council of Ancyra, VI, 1407, 1408. What the upper and lower irrigation channels signify mystically, II, 1114.

Isaac signifies “laughter,” V, 37. Where he was born, I, 565. He prays concerning Rebecca’s barrenness, I, 580. Walking alone across the field, he is an apt type of Christ praying in the garden, I, 573, 574. Whether only Isaac, and not also Ishmael, was born from Sarah according to the promise, VI, 329. The mystical exposition of both, VI, 331 ff. What their playing signifies, VI, 334.

Issachar is called “reward”; he signifies the Church of the Gentiles, its praise and type, V, 43. Why Isaiah is called “the sacrifice of the islands,” V, 58. Jesse is said elsewhere to have had eight sons, although in another place only seven are mentioned, III, 52. What moved Isaiah to sing a song to the Lord, VI, 1091. Why Isaiah is called “the salvation of the Lord,” V, 64.

Who the sons of the Ishmaelites were, and their dwellings, I, 580. Why they are called Midianites, ibid., 624. What Israel signifies, II, 1152, 1153. Israel abandons God, V, 38. It is oppressed by the Midianites, ibid. Its grain and seed are devastated, ibid., 1153. It enjoys peace under Gideon for forty years, II, 1170.

The more the Israelites were oppressed, the more they increased, II, 11. Whether they are to be accused of theft for asking their neighbors for golden vessels, ibid., 47. They defeat the Canaanites on Mount Hor, ibid., 711. They promise not to drink from the wells of King Sion; this is a type of Christians renouncing the devil in Baptism, II, 719, 720. Why they alone were chosen from among the incomprehensible, ibid., 972. How they are said to have been protected by God as the apple of his eye, although many perished, II, 973.

Their idolatry, II, 1121; ibid., 250; VI, 1141. Which idols they worshiped, ibid. See the description of the various ones, ibid. They are captured by their enemies, sold, and divine vengeance follows them everywhere because of their idolatry, II, 1123. How they were sold without a price, ibid. They dwell with the Canaanites, enter into marriages with them, and worship their gods, ibid., 1125. They are delivered into the hands of Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, and serve him for eight years—why, ibid.; under Othniel they enjoy forty years of peace, II, 1127. After his death they relapse into their former sins, II, 1128. They serve Eglon, king of Moab, for fifteen years; Ehud delivers them, ibid., 1129. They enjoy eighty years of peace; after Ehud’s death they return to their former crimes, II, 1131. God delivers them into the hands of Jabin, king of Canaan, ibid., 1132. Under Jabin’s tyranny the Canaanites cry out to God, II, 1133. Because they are stiff-necked, they are delivered into the hands of the fierce Sisera, ibid.

Their fasts and bodily mortifications were not fruitless, III, 556. They murmured against Uzziah, III, 557. How they conquered their enemies, III, 609. How God begot them, ibid., 610. When they repent, they are received back into favor; the Egyptians are scourged, III, 718. Their division into two classes, V, 1522.

Why Italy and Spain are called the Hesperides, and their distinction, V, 350. From where the name is derived, ibid. Why Italy is called Latium, ibid. Its fertility and pleasantness, ibid. From where the Ituraeans are named, V, 240. Why the sons of Izrai are said to have been five, although only four are counted, III, 313.

## J

What Jabesh signifies, III, 295, 296. A most learned teacher of God’s law, ibid. A type of God, ibid. Jabin, king of Canaan, oppresses the Jews, II, 1132. His commander is Sisera, ibid. His power, ibid. What his name signifies in Hebrew, ibid., 1133. A symbol of what, ibid.

What Jaboc signifies, I, 609. What we ought to hear while lying down and while standing, IV, 551.

For Jacob’s meaning, see the extensive discussion, V, 38. His dwelling, V, 357. What his covering his body with goatskins signifies, I, 589. As one avoiding Esau’s deceit, he is a type of Christ, I, 591. His vision and vow when he went to Mesopotamia, I, 591. What it signifies mystically, ibid. At God’s command he returns to his father with his wives and children, I, 605. Laban pursues him, ibid. He wrestles with the angel and, after his name is changed, is called Israel, I, 609, 610 and 615. An apt type of the suffering Christ, I, 610. Why, after being touched on the thigh, he became lame, ibid. He worships his brother seven times, I, 609. He descends into Egypt with all his household, I, 643. He is presented by his son before the king, I, 647. As he is dying, he asks his son under oath to bury him with his fathers, I, 650. Blessing each of his sons and reproving the faults of some, he foretells their future; finally, after declaring the place of his burial, he dies, I, 654, 655, 666. Taking a wife from Mesopotamia, he is a type of Christ, V, 339. Why, after his name was changed, he is so often still called by his former name, I, 616.

Jacobus Pamelius’s commentary on Judith, III, 599. Detestation of boasting, III, 794, 804. Darts bear the type of the divine word, VI, 1125.

Jael, a foreign woman, kills Sisera, whom she had fed with milk in her house, by driving a nail into his jaws, etc., II, 1136. A symbol of the Church, ibid. She forestalls Barak in killing Sisera, ibid. What this signifies, ibid. Her praise, ibid. What she signifies, V, 56.

Jair the Gileadite governs Israel for twenty-two years after Tola, II, 1176. He has thirty sons, ibid., 1177. He is a figure of Christ and Christians, ibid. In Hebrew, Jair means “illuminating”; he is buried at Camon, ibid. What he signifies, V, 57.

Why Jannes is so called, V, 52. The etymology of Jamnia, III, 1245, 1246. Who the doorkeepers are mystically and literally, III, 396. The gate is named from Janus, for whom every entrance is sacred, V, 339. What the gates of heaven signify, V, 265.

The feast days of January, IV, 1122. How Christ entered to the disciples when the doors were shut, IV, 173.

Why Japheth is the father of nations, I, 525, 526. His generations, ibid. The kingdom of his sons, III, 281. Japheth is called “expansion,” V, 34.

Jerusalem, formerly called Jebus, V, 295, 296. Why, ibid. Jeconiah: see Joachim, V, 64, 65. His sons, III, 301.

Jehu typologically represents the rule of the Gentiles, V, 61. He is anointed king at Elisha’s command, III, 238. His punishment of transgressors of the law, ibid. He is sent to eradicate the kingdom of Ahab and kill the priests of Baal, III, 238 and 498.

The commendation of the fast of the tenth month, IV, 13. The times of fasting, V, 136. Its definition and distinction from a station, V, 136, 137, and I, 334. Its various kinds, ibid. Why it was prescribed after Pentecost, ibid. And before the Nativity of the Lord, ibid. What the legitimate fasts are, I, 338. Likewise the fasts of the four Saturdays, ibid. Private fasts, ibid. Its praise and usefulness, IV, 90. When and why the fast of the fourth month was commanded, IV, 45. The seven-day fast instituted for the dead, III, 325. Why the fast of the seventh month was instituted, IV, 56.

Why Jephthah is called “opening”; he is a type of Christ, V, 57. He flees from his own people and is appointed leader, III, 1177, 1185. He sacrifices his daughter, ibid. He is a figure of Christ, ibid. Whether he sinned by sacrificing his daughter, III, 1179, 1180. Whether the Spirit of the Lord impelled him to sacrifice his daughter and make the vow, II, 1184. In Hebrew, “powerful in strength,” II, 1186. He refuses to be ruler, ibid., 1187. He judged Israel for six years, ibid., 1188. What his words to the elders of Gilead, as well as his journey and defeat of the enemies, signify mystically, ibid. His daughter mourns her virginity for sixty days, II, 1189. What this period signifies mystically, ibid.

Why Jeremiah is interpreted as “exalted of the Lord,” V, 76, 77. When and for how many years he prophesied, V, 797. His origin, ibid. Sanctified in the womb, ibid. He pleads childhood as an excuse, but is strengthened by the Lord, ibid. His lamentation before God, V, 959. He is struck and thrown into prison, V, 960. He complains that he is made a laughingstock, ibid. In the vestibule of the prison he foretells Zedekiah’s captivity, V, 1050. The mysteries and sayings revealed to him apply especially to Christ, V, 793.

From where Jericho received its name, V, 378; II, 1021. Its ruin, ibid., 1023. It mystically signifies the instability of life, ibid., 1009.

Why Jeroboam is interpreted as “division,” V, 59 and 64. A type of heretics, III, 199, 1099. He is called “judging the people,” V, 76.

From where Jerusalem received its name, V, 379. A type of the Church, ibid. Why it was devastated in the fifth month, on the fifth day, III, 276. What it signifies by metonymy, VI, 966. Jerusalem as a type of the present Church, V, 337. The cause of its destruction, I, 486. Its description, V, 108. It is captured and burned by the Chaldeans, V, 1173, 1174. The Temple is plundered, ibid. Its fourfold meaning, applied to a virgin fit for marriage, IV, 670. Who its father, mother, and sister are, IV, 687.

Jesse, the fruit of the root, V, 1595. How the inheritance of Jesus and Moses differs, II, 171 and 172. Who share in it, ibid. The praise and military courage of Jesus son of Nun, Moses’ successor, III, 1090. An apt type of the Savior, ibid., 1091.

Jesus the high priest, a figure of Christ, V, 65. Jesus Christ is the illuminating light, II, 1118. He lives in the devout, but is dead in the impious—indeed, he is crucified again by them, II, 1220.

What Jethro was like, II, 87, 88. Why Jezebel is called “empty flow,” V, 65. The valley of Jezreel, which is Hebrew for “seed of God,” II, 1154.

Joab, holding Amasa’s chin with his right hand and a sword with his left, is a type of flatterers, III, 112. Why Joahaz signifies “held back,” V, 63. Joahaz as a type of the devil, III, 530. Joachim and Eliakim are synonymous, III, 605. The more probable opinion concerning this name, ibid. Joachim’s sons and impiety, III, 272, 531. He is taken captive by Nebuchadnezzar, III, 532. Joachim’s death, V, 1073. Joachim, or Jeconiah, captured with his mother: whom he typifies, V, 64. Joachim: see Eliakim, V, 64.

What moved John the Evangelist to write the Gospel, I, 787. Why he is compared with an eagle, V, 71. The distinction between John the Baptist and Christ the baptizer, I, 901; IV, 252.

Why John the Baptist is called “the grace of the Lord,” V, 71. What form he had, V, 75. He denies that he is the Messiah, II, 1216. He gives Christ that honor, II, 1218. Why he mystically refused to loosen the sandal strap, ibid. His frank profession concerning Christ, ibid. He understood the father speaking after eight days, VI, 1160, 1161. The austerity of his life in food and clothing, I, 767. What sort of locusts and wild honey he had, ibid. Why he baptized only in water, I, 769. Why he is called an angel, I, 910.

The letter of Johann Trithemius to Albert of Brandenburg, archbishop of Mainz, dedicating his Life of Saint Rabanus, I, 71–106. [Col. 1723]

Joash, the only one rescued from Athaliah’s tyranny after the entire royal seed had been destroyed, III, 239, 499. He is placed on the throne by Jehoiada the high priest, III, 239, 500. He gives the priests money offered to the Temple by passersby out of generosity, ibid., 241. He restored the Temple’s damaged structures, III, 241, 500. The number of his age signifies perfection, III, 504. God was worshiped by the princes of Judah, but Joash incurred God’s displeasure by excessively seeking the honors of his subjects, III, 504. What he signifies, V, 62.

Why Jotham is interpreted as “perfect,” and is a type of Christ, V, 58; III, 513. The son of Gideon, by flight, preserves his life; his prudence, II, 1171. He is a figure of the Jewish people who will believe in the Church and escape the sword of Antichrist, ibid. He addresses the people on Mount Gerizim, ibid. He is a type of the saints, II, 1172.

From what lineage Job came, and why he is called “suffering,” V, 50. How he descended into hell, V, 1236. Synopsis of his book, V, 111. Jobab is believed to have been Job; how his sons and daughters, killed during the time of his testing, were restored to him twofold, III, 287.

Joel, Samuel’s wicked son, was a judge, III, 35. Joel is called “the fool of God,” V, 68. Joiada means the same as “beloved of the Lord,” V, 61. The piety of Jonadab’s sons, V, 1070. Why Jonah is called “dove” or “suffering,” V, 68. He raises the son of the widow of Sarepta, ibid.

Why Jonathan alone is said to have been a priest in the house of the Lord, although it is clear that there were several, III, 311. After tasting the honeycomb, how Jonathan is said to have been enlightened, III, 42. A figure of the elect, III, 54. When Bacchides was in turmoil, he typifies Christ withdrawing from the people with his disciples to pray and fleeing the fury of the Jews, III, 1187. Leaving his brother Simon in the city and pursuing the enemies: whom he signifies, ibid.

The Joppians as persecutors of the Jews: what they were like and what they signify mystically, III, 125. Joram as a type of apostates; why he is called “the one who is exalted,” V, 61. What Jehoshaphat signifies, V, 60. What his friendship with Ahab signifies: the familiarity of Catholics with heretics, ibid. His piety, III, 492, 493. What he signifies mystically, ibid.

What Joseph signifies; see the beautiful discussion of him, V, 44. Pharaoh honors him greatly and places him over all Egypt, I, 635. He is called “savior,” ibid. During the time of fertility he gathers grain to relieve the famine of the future, ibid., 636. He receives two sons before the seven years of famine, ibid. Worshiped by his brothers, he expresses Christ, I, 637, 638. Whether, when swearing by Pharaoh’s life, he is to be considered perjured, ibid. He orders money to be secretly placed in his brothers’ sacks, ibid., 639. After long affliction he reveals himself to his brothers, I, 643. Whether he incurred blame by subjecting all the land of Egypt to Pharaoh, I, 649. He visits his sick father, taking his two sons, whom Jacob adopts as his own and blesses, I, 652, 653. After his father is buried, he forgives the injury inflicted by his brothers and returns to Egypt, I, 668. After death he requests that his bones be carried out of Egypt, ibid., 669.

By accusing his brothers before his father, he incurs their envy, I, 621. Whether he was seventeen years old when he was sold into Egypt, I, 623, 625. A type of the Lord Christ, ibid., 622. He is sold by his brothers to the Midianites, I, 623. His mistress, attracted by his beauty, repeatedly invites him to adultery, but he firmly resists, I, 631, 632. Falsely accused, he is thrown into prison, I, 633. Sent to his brothers to care for them, he is an apt type of Christ sent into this world, I, 624, 625. Sold by his brothers and sent to prison because of a false accusation, he is freed solely by divine wisdom, III, 718.

Joseph the bridegroom: what he signifies, V, 75. Why Matthew calls him the son of Jacob but Luke the son of Eli, I, 735. Why he is not said to have been found by Mary with the child after the Magi arrived, I, 759. Why he is called just, I, 748. Why he is counted in the genealogy although he was not Christ’s father, I, 747.

Josiah as a mystical type of Christ: what he signifies, V, 63. His piety, III, 266, 267. He abolished the various images and idolatries of superstitious nations, ibid. Why he ordered the bones of the dead to be burned on the altar, ibid. A type of the Savior, ibid. He ordered the Passover to be celebrated for the Lord, III, 527. Killed by Pharaoh Neco, he bears a figure of the persecution of the wicked enemy against the holy preachers, III, 270 and 527. Rejecting idols, diviners, and pythonic spirits, he arranged for the ark of the Lord to be brought back into the Temple, ibid. His encounter with Neco, king of Egypt, and his death, III, 528. His praise, III, 1106, 1107.

Why Joshua is called “savior,” and whom he represents, V, 54. The history of his book, V, 112. Why he is called the servant of God, II, 137. A type of Christ, ibid.; 1118. He dismisses the people, each to his own possession, ibid. Why his death is repeated in the Book of Judges, ibid. He did not destroy certain nations by human, but by divine, counsel, II, 1124. He dies at the age of one hundred and is buried on Mount Ephraim at Timnath-heres, II, 1120. After his death he is a type of the dying Jesus, ibid.

The praise of Joshua and Caleb, III, 1092. They alone are preserved from the number of six hundred thousand, ibid. Joshua son of Nun is placed over the people of Israel, II, 778.

Jubal, the first inventor of music, the psaltery, and the lyre, II, 508. So that his discoveries would not perish, he engraved them on two pillars, ibid.

How, in the time of the Jubilee, sold land could be redeemed, II, 535–537. And whose land, ibid.; at what price, II, 541. In what sense “jubilation” is understood, V, 1000. It is shown that gladness of heart is useful and ought to be pursued, III, 985.

Judah is called “confession” and figures Christ, V, 43; II, 1220. Because of his brave conduct in war, the tribe of Judah had cities even in the territories of other tribes, III, 26.

Judas Maccabaeus, succeeding his father in the kingdom and killing Apollonius, figures the Lord Christ, III, 1148. He did everything by day, III, 1155. He defeats Gorgias and Lysias, ibid. After conquering the enemies, he orders the Temple to be purified, III, 1158. He distributes and sends his brothers to attack various nations, III, 1163. He establishes an embassy to the Romans, III, 1178. Why he is called “the tenth,” III, 1234. He institutes a sacrifice for the dead, III, 1251, 1252.

Judas, having had three sons by a Canaanite wife, joined first one and then another to Tamar, I, 625, 627. After they died, he unknowingly had intercourse with her as with a prostitute, ibid. What this signifies mystically, ibid.

Judas who went up against the Canaanite is not the name of a man but of a tribe, II, 1111. He captures Gaza and other cities, ibid., 1112.

Why Judaea is called Canaan, V, 339. Its location and length, ibid. Its mystical significance as the Church, V, 317.

In the time of Joshua and the Elders, the Jews serve God alone, II, 1118. Rebelling against God, they do not destroy the inhabitants of the Promised Land; they are rebuked by the angel and weep, II, 1117. Why they refused to destroy those nations, ibid. They are invited to the words of God, II, 1135. They refuse to come and believe in Christ, ibid. They are abandoned by God, ibid. They return at the end of the world, ibid., 1138. Mystically they are Barak, ibid. They delight in the Mosaic Law and rest in it and in temporal goods, II, 1146. After Gideon’s death they worship Baal, II, 1174. Likewise Astarte and the gods of Syria, Sidon, etc., II, 1177. They are delivered to the Philistines, ibid. They cast Christ out from themselves, II, 1187. From the wives of their deceased kinsmen they raise up a name without children, II, 1117. They had to appear before the Lord three times a year, III, 12. Their remnant is saved, III, 21.

How they are afflicted when they trust in weapons alone, V, 644. They vainly expect justice and salvation from themselves and the Law, III, 17. By God’s grace they are strong and just, ibid. They despise Christ because they are concerned with earthly things and do not search into the marrow of the Law, ibid. Many are converted to Christ, III, 21. Because of their sins, the gift of prophecy is taken away from them in the time of Eli, ibid., 25. Their blindness in recognizing Christ, ibid. They reject the Gospel, ibid., 32. After abandoning the Baals and Astarte, they serve God alone under Joshua, ibid., 33. They are at peace with the Amorites, III, 34. They ask for a king, III, 35. Saul is given to them, ibid. Having rejected Christ, they will never receive perfect freedom, ibid. Ungrateful to God, they yearn only for earthly goods, ibid. Although the prophets urge them toward true virtues, they do so in vain, ibid., 37. After the Philistines are slaughtered, they sin by eating blood under King and commander Saul, III, 43.

Their slaughter of enemies is admirable, III, 666. After conquering their enemies and establishing a solemn day of feasting, they represent the elect rejoicing eternally with Christ after the labors of the present life have been completed, III, 667. The weakness of their doctrines, II, 565–566. They are handed over to four plagues, and what these are, II, 723. They understand all figures literally, V, 984. Their delirium concerning the restoration of Sodom to its former state at the coming of their Christ, IV, 691. The Christian view on this matter, ibid. How they were under the elements of this world, although the Law commended the worship of one God to them, III, 766. Why we are called “Jews” in the Gospel, V, 827. How they differ from Christians, V, 1024.

Judith is called “praising” or “confessing,” V, 66. When and by whom her history was written, III, 541–543, 597. Wearing sackcloth and devoted to fasting, she recalled her people from surrender, III, 558, 618. Removing her mourning garments and clothing herself in joy, she bears the figure of Christ, III, 565, 621. Going forth into the contest and loading the necessary provisions for her journey upon her maidservant Abra, she signifies the holy Church strengthening her departing faithful with heavenly manna, ibid. In worshiping Holofernes, she did not sin through the fault of flattery, but by right of rank, according to the Apostle’s teaching, III, 567, 624. The words she reported concerning the destruction of the Jews were not flattering, but mysteries of future prophecy, III, 568. Rejecting royal banquets, she preferred to eat her own food, III, 570, 571, 627. Praying to God with tears, she beheads Holofernes while he is drugged with wine, III, 572. Returning and ascending to a higher place, and displaying Holofernes’ head with its canopy, she represents the holy Church, III, 575–628. Blessed by the Pontiff and the people, she is enriched with what belonged particularly to Holofernes, III, 579. Because of the victory won, she sings a song to God, III, 581. A distinguished model of chastity, III, 589. Full of days, she dies, and the days of this victory are perpetually celebrated among the Jews among the number of holy days, III, 590, 634, 636. She came from the tribe of Simeon, III, 614, 619. She notably deceived Holofernes concerning the cause of her flight, III, 624.

Why some remove her book from the canon of Sacred Scripture, III, 593. It is proved to be canonical, ibid. Why Origen did not mention it, ibid.

What a wise judge is, III, 35, 825–900. One who judges will not escape God’s judgment, V, 1306. “To judge” is interpreted in two ways, II, 981. Judges and teachers established at the gates of the city signify the leaders of the Church, II, 901. Description of the final judgment, VI, 720. Its twofold meaning, VI, 1147. Why all people from the foundation of the world are reserved for it, V, 1310. Its terribleness, VI, 1321. Its day, VI, 1619.

One must contend in judgment with those who deny their sins, IV, 112. Judgment according to outward appearances is dangerous, II, 1119. The judgment of the elect and the reprobate, III, 747, 754, 755. Rash judgment is dangerous, III, 87; V, 743. An example of condemned rashness, ibid. Its prohibition, I, 840. Its seriousness, ibid. It is dangerous to rely on one’s own judgment, III, 801. The commendation of the just person and the denunciation of false witnesses, IV, 108. What it signifies, VI, 973.

Why the Book of Judges is so called, II, 1127. It contains the crimes and virtues of the judges, ibid. Why it is so called, ibid.; V, 112.

When and how the perpetual sacrifice is to be celebrated, II, 779–780. What the yoke signifies, VI, 972. An account of the more notable festivals of July, IV, 1154. Various meanings of a beast of burden, V, 200. What reptiles and beasts are understood to signify, I, 458; VI, 973. What joints signify, III, 180. A description of the festivals of June, IV, 1148. What those who nourish a fire for a long time with juniper signify, II, 817.

The quarrels of the proud aptly signify heretics, V, 723. There must be no fuel for quarrels among friends, III, 914.

The oath of God in the Old Testament, IV, 688. In the New, ibid.; V, 1165, III, 1207. Its companions. Its kinds, I, 824. Why it was prohibited, I, 922. Abraham’s oath and covenant with Abimelech, I, 565. When this covenant was made, ibid. One who does not rebuke a person swearing, or report him to a superior, is to be punished in what manner, II, 279. How Abraham’s servant’s oath is called a curse, I, 572, 573.

The righteous alone are strong in war against enemies, human beings, and demons, II, 1143. Why they are often taken away by premature death, III, 686. They will judge with Christ, V, 755. They love tribulations, V, 771. Whether they foresaw everything, VI, 799. The elements serve them but oppose the impious, III, 758. When afflicted by necessities, they are permitted to acknowledge their good works, III, 260. They too fear death, and why, III, 524, 1095. They are of two kinds, V, 1505. Their glory and reward, III, 691. Their days are prolonged, whereas the days of the impious are shortened, III, 715.

Who is justified by faith, V, 1344. Justice prevails over mercy, II, 125. It comes from God alone, III, 17. Human justice is false, ibid. Its defense ought to be undertaken, III, 789. The distinction between Jewish and Christian justice, and what accounts for it, VI, 288. Its power, VI, 1254. What kind of justice the Jews possessed before the advent, VI, 686. What the invitation of the just and unjust will be like, V, 713. Whether a just person always leaves behind sons like himself, V, 745. Whether he should be called just when he can fall, V, 758. He is first the accuser of himself, V, 738.

A young bull, from “living,” is a sacrifice of Jupiter, V, 207. Who is called a young man, V, 705.

## K

How the solemnities and offerings of the Kalends are to be carried out, II, 782.

Laban: what he signifies and whose figure he is, V, 42. A type of the devil, I, 606, 607. The golden lip: what it is and its use, II, 146, 147. The bronze one figuratively expresses holy baptism, II, 215, 216. The river Laboch, V, 322. What the labor of the rich and poor is like, III, 987. Its end, VI, 440. The commendation of manual labor, VI, 575. The laver: what it is and its use, V, 602. It is aptly applied to Christ, ibid. Description of the labyrinth and its four kinds, V, 387. Milk: a symbol of simpler and more elementary doctrine, II, 1137; VI, 977; I, 551. The grace of tears is given by God, III, 47. For the penitent, tears are like baptism before God, I, 341. The praise and necessity of tears poured out, II, 216. Their various kinds, IV, 156. Lactantius’s prophecies concerning the Christ who was to be born, V, 421. What a lake signifies, V, 316, and VI, 978. The lakes Asphalt, Benacus, Tiberias, and Gennesaret, ibid. That “lake” is always taken in a bad sense is proved by examples, IV, 827; V, 1245, 849. What it means to rejoice in salvation, VI, 1099. What unleavened laganum is, II, 625. A broken earthen flask displays the destruction of the Jews, V, 959. Lamech signifies “striking,” V, 33. The order and construction of Jeremiah’s Lamentations, V, 1181. Why they were written in alphabetical order, ibid. Why they were composed, V, 1185. The lamia, with a human face and bestial body, is a figure of hypocritical Jews, V, 1249. And of heretics, V, 225. What the golden plate fastened to the forehead of the high priest signifies, II, 199 and 200. What a lamp signifies, V, 605. A type of the elect, ibid. What Lemuel denotes, V, 779. Wool, and the twisting of linen, V, 578. The lance: a type of the Lord’s Passion, V, 537. Minerva, the first inventor of wool-working, V, 568. Its use, ibid. Where the word “stone” comes from, V, 462. Its various mystical meanings, ibid. and VI, 980. Christ as the living stone, IV, 167. Whoever casts it upward, III, 967. What hailstones signify mystically, III, 1091. The uncorrupted stones from which the altar was built and on which Deuteronomy was inscribed mystically express the faithful of Christ, II, 917, 918. The saints who are stones, II, 713. The foundational stones signify the prophets and apostles, III, 138. The square stones, IV, 951. Why tables were made from them, ibid. Who are said to become stones, VI, 1109.

[Col. 1726] One ought not to reproach the fallen, III, 814. God raises them up, III, 871. David’s fall and the description of his repentance, VI, 1322. What the coffered ceilings signify, V, 404. A type of the prelates of the Church, ibid. The gull, living in water and on land: whose figure it is, II, 557 and 886. An explanation of the side, IV, 586. Whoever assumes it, IV, 588. The breadth, length, height, and depth of God, VI, 423. The breadth of the tabernacle, II, 169. To whom latria and dulia are owed, II, 133. The thief’s confession, V, 1510. Hezekiah, who did not sing praises to God after obtaining victories, is visited with bodily illness, III, 264. Freed from the disease, he is lifted up by pride and reveals to foreigners all his treasures and secrets; he is deprived of everything that both he himself and his fathers had gathered, and even of his sons, ibid. People are sometimes stirred to repentance by praises, but at other times by terrors, VI, 753. Where the laurel derives its name, V, 511. A sign of victory, and why, ibid. The praise and labor of apostles and teachers, II, 1144. Human praise is to be avoided, II, 1214. In the mouth of a sinner it is displeasing to God, III, 862. The praise and rarity of a virtuous woman, V, 380. She expresses the Catholic Church, V, 381. Her husband is the Lord and our Redeemer, ibid. She is like a merchant’s ship, ibid.; III, 954. That Paul did not abolish the law and free will is proved against certain persons, V, 1338. What reward awaits those who keep and violate it, II, 551–556. The ease and sweetness of the evangelical law, I, 874. It must be obeyed, VI, 721. The letter of the law is like a flying scroll, II, 565. The threefold meaning of “law,” V, 1340. And its fourfold meaning, 1424; III, 1341. It is a witness to God’s justice, ibid. The law that works wrath, 1352. What is written in the heart, V, 1422. The law of God in its many forms, 1568; VI, 367 ff. Its observance is earnestly commanded, II, 1194. The perfection of the whole law, I, 1062–1063. Its effects, V, 1388. How law, commandment, testimony, justification, and judgment differ from one another, II, 695, 696.

[Col. 1727] Whether the law of Moses contains goodness or justice, II, 685, 687. What it signifies when taken generally and specifically, II, 698. Concerning unintentional homicide, II, 834, 835. And intentional homicide, ibid., 907. The old vinegar made through the traditions of the Pharisees, III, 1208. It is imperfect and could heal no one, ibid., 1278. It yields to the new, ibid. Why it did not remove sin, VI, 779. The new law is symbolically wheat, and why, III, 1211. It is superior to the old, ibid., 1218. Since the law does not justify, why is one who violates it cursed? VI, 290. The law often denotes the history of Genesis, and why, VI, 327. What the proper time is, VI, 311. The etymology of legumes and their kinds, V, 506. Typologically they denote the mortification of the body, ibid. The lenticula, with which priests and kings were anointed: a type of the grace of the Holy Spirit, V, 602. What the lion denotes, V, 45 and 217; VI, 983. Sleeping with open eyes: a type of Christ, ibid. Lions standing beside the hands signify the Fathers of both Testaments, III, 197. How he is to be shut away for a fixed period so that he may be examined by the priest, II, 380. Why he was ordered to walk about with his garments torn, his head uncovered, and his mouth covered, II, 385. The hare, as though “light-footed”: whom it signifies, V, 205. The little hare, the weak populace: a type of the Church, V, 777. What “lesa” means, I, 529. How Leviathan is drawn out of the sea, IV, 822. Levi is called “added”; see ibid. Whose figure he is, V, 43. The Levites are taken into the service of the tabernacle, II, 605. They are received in place of the firstborn of Israel, ibid., 606. Their number, 609, 610 and 637. When they are ministers and when guardians of the vessels, ibid., 639. Exemption from possessions, II, 537–543. The subject of the book of Leviticus, V, 111. Praise, II, 245–247. Leah is interpreted “laboring,” V, 40. Leah is a type of labor, Rachel of eternal life, III, 1219. Likewise of the active and contemplative lives, II, 601, 602; II, 1219. The various figurative meanings of Lebanon, V, 362. What kind of book was given to Ezekiel by the Lord, IV, 558. What it signifies that it was written inside and outside, ibid. He is ordered to eat it, IV, 561. Christ, the liberator of souls, V, 726. Why we are called free, IV, 194. Free will, V. See Free Will. Where the balance derives its name, V, 482. Allegorically it denotes justice, etc., ibid.

[Col. 1727] Why one book of the deeds of purchase delivered to Baruch was open and the other closed, V, 1052. What the memorial books are, III, 651. What the smoothed timbers serving in the construction of the ark signify, I, 514. The distinction between the wood of paradise and the wood of Christ, III, 360. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil: why it is called evil, I, 481. What breaking it signifies mystically, III, 234. What is blessed and what is cursed, III, 736. The tree of offense, III, 988. What putting it into bread signifies allegorically, V, 895. Their four kinds and meanings, VI, 771, 985. Lilies clothing the columns signify the elect, III, 169, 437. And Christ, V, 528. Why some dogs are called Lincisci, V, 222. Where “straight line” derives its name, II, 191. The language by which God called the light “day” and the darkness “night,” I, 448. A tongue teaching sweetly surpasses every harmony, III, 1053. What the third tongue is and its effect, III, 971. Where the diversity of languages arose, V, 455; III, 284. Which are the more excellent, V, 455. Praise of Greek and Latin, and their divisions, V, 455, 456. The litanies of Fulda and Saint Gall, VI, 1122. What litanies and supplications are, V, 138. Litanies composed in verse, VI, 1629, 1630. Their formula, ibid. Approved and received in the monastery of Saint Gall, VI, 1630 (note). Immortal letters, VI, 1601. An exhortation to them, VI, 1679. A passage against Ziegler, III, 616. The place of the evil spirit: the hearts of sinners, IV, 569. Whom locusts signify, V, 257. A figure of the populace of the nations, V, 777. The distinction of divine speech, I, 749. What speech directed toward human beings is like, I, 553. The darnel denotes sinners, V, 529. Lot is interpreted “declining”; see ibid. Whose type he was, V, 36. Why he worshiped the men arriving at Sodom and received them hospitably, I, 555. Whom his daughters denote, V, 36. The emperor Lothair, I, 1674 (note). His death, ibid. How the law of Moses and that of Christ differ, II, 325. Where “slippery” derives its name, V, 372. It denotes vices, ibid.

[Col. 1728] Why Saint Luke bears before him the image of a calf, V, 71. Lucifer signifies the light of wisdom and understanding, V, 274. His exaltation and fall, III, 1046. Lamp: see light. What a lamp extinguished in the night signifies mystically, V, 785. The seven lamps denote the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, II, 635. What lamps placed under a bushel signify, I, 804. The distinction between lamps and lampstands, III, 181. Their order and mystical meanings, III, 447, 448. The rite of trimming them and offering oil in the tabernacle, II, 515–517. What Jacob’s wrestling with the angel signifies, V, 321. Joseph’s mourning over the departure of his father Jacob, I, 668. Its various signs, V, 864, 875, 935, 1124, 1262. The prohibition of excessive mourning for the dead, VI, 554. The prohibition against building a sacred grove and shrines beside the altar: what it signifies mystically, II, 901. Where “grove” derives its name, V, 371. Sometimes it denotes errors, ibid. What kind of people were playing with David before the ark, III, 338. Detestation of funeral games, V, 553. The gymnastic contest and its exercise, V, 549. Its kinds, ibid. What the loincloth or girdle is, V, 903. The succession of mortality is expressed by the term “loins,” IV, 546. What girding the loins with strength signifies, V, 709. Light—see “light”; what kind the daylight was before the creation of the heavenly bodies, I, 454. The lights of heaven, V, 267. Necessary for human uses, I, 453. Why, where, and how they were made, ibid. What their having been made on the fourth day signifies, ibid. Which are the great ones, ibid. and 454. The moon’s beautiful literal and mystical meanings, V, 268; VI, 991. Who is a lunatic, I, 1002. Why he is possessed by a demon, I, 1005. What a brothel is, V, 353. The wolf signifies Satan and heretics, and also Saint Paul, V, 293. What “lustra” signifies, V, 370. Lutberg, first abbot of Hirsau, I, 92. Luther’s measure, III, 176. Its mystical meaning, III, 41. The meaning of mud, V, 332. Whether the light before the creation of the heavenly bodies was the same as it is now; its various meanings, V, 265; VI, 989. Where it was placed, I, 448. The detestation and wickedness of lust, VI, 1371. A remedy against it, VI, 1372. Its nature and origin, VI, 1370. Whom it torments among its followers, VI, 1371. Its characteristics, ibid. M
[Col. 1729] Macedonia: whence it was named, and its situation and fertility, V, 348. It gave birth to Alexander the Great, ibid. Macellum: whence it received its name, V, 369. The mystical interpretation of walls, V, 407. The martyrdom of the seven Maccabean brothers and their mother, III, 1236–1237. Whom they signify mystically, ibid. Their swiftness, ibid. Their various effects, ibid. The gravity of magic is confirmed by various passages of Holy Scripture, V, 22. Its various kinds and effects, ibid. Rebuke of teachers who impose heavy burdens but do not touch them even with a finger, I, 1066–1067. The etymology and properties of the magnet, V, 463. What it means to magnify the Lord, VI, 1133. The greatness and terribleness of God, II, 868. Who is truly to be considered magnificent, V, 358. The description of the notable festivals of May, IV, 1142. The elder ought to speak first, III, 993. Catholic doctors are to be understood by this name, III, 994. What it means to find mandrakes, I, 600. Evils should be invoked not from delight in punishment but from love of justice, III, 620. The difference between evils and goods, VI, 1328. One who seeks wrongly does not deserve an answer, V, 727. Things badly acquired are badly dissipated, V, 752. The curse that remains upon the ungodly, III, 1055. The curse of the day of birth, V, 967. The curses heaped up against the ungodly, II, 948–961. [Col. 1729] The defense and interpretation of the apostle Paul’s curse against the persecutors of the Church, VI, 342. The accursed Cain is a type of the accursed Jewish people, I, 504. The malice of the Israelites is interpreted as punishment, II, 224. “The hammer of the whole earth,” V, 1148. Who broke it, ibid. When it is broken by God, and how it is broken by us, V, 1149. What it means to be between the hammer and the anvil, V, 1149. Why Mambres is called “sea in the head,” V, 52. The martyrdom is announced to Saint Mammes, who fled with his flocks to the mountain and lived there holily, IV, 1163. What “mammon of iniquity” means; its etymology, I, 836. Who serve it, ibid. The distinction between commandments, judgments, and ceremonies, II, 870. What the greatest commandment is, II, 507, 865–866, 899. The reward of those who remain in Christ, IV, 242. “Morning” signifies the final judgment, V, 686. See the various meanings, VI, 992. How God is said to rise in the morning, V, 859. The error of the Manichaeans, who established two natures in God, namely a good and an evil one, III, 365; the error arising from their denial that Christ was human, VI, 424. When manna rained down, II, 78. What it signifies, ibid. Its mystical interpretation, II, 869. He represents the apostle Paul, ibid., and the other doctors of the Church, ibid. Clothed in sackcloth and mourning the destined destruction of the Jews, he represents the teachers of the Church, III, 654. The molten sea bears the figure of the Savior’s laver, III, 171; its use, [Col. 1730] ibid. It is taken in both a bad and a good sense, VI, 1121. It signifies the hearts of unbelievers, ibid. Why Saint Mary is called “the illuminatrix,” or “star of the sea,” or “lady,” V, 75; her literal and mystical interpretation, I, 744. Marble: whence the name derives, and its various colors and multiple kinds, V, 463. Martha and Magdalene express the figure of the active and contemplative life, IV, 512. The celebrations of March, and the lives and martyrdoms of its saints, IV, 1134. The encomium of Saint Martin, confessor and bishop, IV, 63. His generosity toward the poor, ibid. Baptized, he is ordained bishop, ibid. There is no martyr outside the Church, V, 857. The apostle Paul foretells his own martyrdom, VI, 651. Why martyrs are called witnesses, and how many kinds of martyrdom there are; who was the first martyr, I, 951. They voluntarily offer their souls to God, II, 1138. They despise death, ibid. After conquering their enemies, they bless God, ibid. Their encomium, II, 1164. They despise their bodies and preach the word of faith everywhere, II, 1183. They are terrifying to the nations, ibid.; through their steadfastness, many from the nations, abandoning idolatry, were converted to the faith, III, 665. Why it is a more suitable place for prayer, III, 1153. Nature is the mother of every living creature, having beneath it every kind of sinner and righteous person, II, 498. The Mother of God repaired what Eve destroyed, IV, 54. Children readily absorb their mother’s character, IV, 687. What “mother” signifies, VI, 996. Whence the word is derived, V, 185. The punishment of Mattathias and his sons because of the affliction of the people, III, 1140, 1145. A type of our Savior, ibid.; his origin and sons, ibid.; their interpretations, ibid. and III, 1142. Mattathias dies, III, 1148. The etymology of mathematics and its division, I, 398–399. Methuselah is interpreted as “dead,” V, 33. How he lived fourteen years after the flood, I, 510–511. Instruction for conducting marriage peacefully, VI, 456; its excellence, VI, 461, 551. A noble matron enters a monastery, is seized by a demon, and dies, I, 92–96. Why Saint Matthew bears the symbol of a man, V, 71; why he wrote the Gospel in that order and style, I, 731; his etymology, I, 873; he is called to the apostleship, ibid. The upright life and martyrdom of Saint Maurus, IV, 1182. The origin of Mauretania, V, 352. [Col. 1731] The jaw signifies the doctors of the Church, V, 154. Why the Medes are called from measuring, V, 336. Media: whence it was named, and its situation, V, 336. Bodily and spiritual physicians are to be honored, III, 1080. Different people use different kinds of medicines, III, 1031. Their necessity, III, 235. The custom of lancing an ulcer, VI, 13. The beautiful meanings of medicine, V, 500; its requirements, ibid. Its inventor was Apollo, ibid. Hippocrates revived it after it had long lain dormant, ibid.; its dignity, ibid.; it was given to humanity by God, III, 1031. What it means to meditate like a dove, VI, 1096. Meditation on the divine law especially befits a churchman, III, 800. The Mediterranean is called the Great Sea, V, 312. The cruelty of the Medes and Persians, V, 1137. Why honey was not offered in God’s sacrifices, II, 823. It is compared with the teaching of a wise man, and why, V, 757. What Melchizedek signifies, V, 35. Offering bread and wine, he bestowed a blessing on Abraham and his victorious soldiers, I, 540. He is mentioned by the Apostle as without father and mother, ibid. A figure of Christ our priest, II, 505. Why the man who hides folly rather than wisdom is better, III, 1059. How “the iniquity of a man is better than a woman doing good” is to be understood, III, 1062. *Melo*, as though “catching honey,” V, 226. *Melos*, named from roundness, V, 356. What the members of the human body signify in Scripture, V, 163. Various interpretations are explained, V, 163 onward through V, 179. Those who sin more will be afflicted with greater punishment, V, 745. The reward of those who mortify them, V, 1541. Judith’s lies were not free from venial fault, III, 624. Its detestation, III, 899. It is preferred to theft, ibid. It imitates truth, V, 975. How it is committed, VI, 1394. Its various kinds, ibid. No lie, however slight, is without sin, VI, 1395. Who is a lying man, V, 1329–1330. The mind conscious of no evil laughs at everything, V, 941. How the mind is to be cultivated with virtues, IV, 563. [Col. 1731] What offspring a menstruating woman who has intercourse may bear, V, 1194. Her purification, II, 409–410. That it is unlawful to have intercourse with her, and why, II, 439, 468. What Micaiah signified when he ordered himself to be struck by the bystander, III, 216. His prophecy to Jehoshaphat and Ahab concerning the kingdom of Israel, III, 490. What his name signifies, V, 69. Michal, despising David in his humiliation, is a type of those who follow Christ in profession but Antichrist in conduct, III, 85–86. Since she was David’s wife, why is she called Saul’s daughter, ibid. The four kinds of military service, V, 451. The distinction between soldiers of the world and soldiers of Christ, V, 1227. The distinction and duties of each, V, 450. The number one thousand signifies perfection, III, 169. The kite, V, 252. Why Jesse’s younger son was raised to the kingdom after the elder sons had been rejected, III, 49. The commendation of the ministry of the New Testament, VI, 178 onward. The ministries serving the Old Testament are far inferior to those of the New, VI, 768–769. Ministers of God must observe the Decalogue, III, 389. Who the true ministers are, III, 352. What the Minocentaur was, V, 196. Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan, kindly received by David and chosen for divine service, III, 95–96. He is joined to David’s sons and admitted to the table, ibid. Miracles: see Saint Alexander and the letter “R,” under “relics.” Why God’s miracles must be proclaimed, III, 357. The miracles preceding Christ’s birth, I, 754. The greatest of all, I, 1043. Marah, or Mara: the place where the waters were changed to sweetness, V, 36. Misaac: see Mishael, V, 70. What it signifies, ibid. The mercy of God is above all his works, VI, 1147. It remits sins, V, 732. Its works are never without reward, III, 770. Its necessity, IV, 92. What good things are signified by its name, V, 1550. For one who desires it, it must be exercised toward the neighbor together with the forgiveness of offenses, IV, 25. The sacrifice of the Mass for the dead, I, 90. What it signifies, I, 321. Christ instituted it, ibid. Various pontiffs and bishops instituted its various ceremonies, VI, 1177. The order for celebrating it, ibid. Its parts carefully enumerated, ibid. They are explained, VI, 1179. The sending of Moses to Pharaoh: a type of the Lord sending the law, II, 21–22. What the sending of Jeremiah and Isaiah to the task of preaching was like, V, 797. Moab: from where the name is derived, V, 36, 379. It bears the type of the persecutors of the Church, III, 226. And of proud philosophers, III, 227; V, 1107. The fornication and idolatry of the Moabites with the Israelites, II, 767–769. The princes of Israel are therefore hanged, ibid. Phinehas, who avenged this crime, is given a perpetual priesthood, II, 770. They are oppressed by Ehud, II, 1131. Modesty must be maintained in speech, III, 963–964. And at the spiritual table, III, 989. An explanation of the limited vision of God, IV, 196, 218. Everyone must measure himself by his own measure, III, 817. What it means to commit adultery with wood and stones, V, 829. What adultery signifies, II, 104, 863. Its punishment according to the Council of Elvira, V, 1408. The obscurity of the history of the Church of Mainz concerning the succession, memory, order, and names of its bishops, VI, 1635, note. The millstone: whence its name derives, V, 603. A type of penitents, V, 1171. What the two women grinding at the mill, and the two in bed, signify mystically, I, 1079. One who sacrifices to Moloch must be punished by death, II, 451. A type of Lucifer, II, 461–462. The meaning of *momentum*, V, 286. The monks of Fulda are sent to Hirsau, I, 96. Why monks are so called, V, 93. Their many kinds; outside the cell they are like fish outside water, I, 72. After profession they may not return to the world, V, 1422. When their zeal begins to grow lukewarm, I, 86. The monastery of Hirsau, built by Count Erlafrid, V, 360. Its origin, V, 391. What it means to admonish someone to his face, V, 824. The monoceros: see unicorn. The Mount of Olives represents the grace of the Holy Spirit, V, 361. Who is pestiferous, V, 1169. Why the Mount of Offense was called the mount of idols, III, 269. “A very high mountain” is interpreted as Christ Jesus, IV, 882. What mountains signify, V, 559. The various names and interpretations of various mountains, V, 560. They bear the type of the proud, III, 586. And of the final judgment, III, 633. In what sense they are said to grieve, III, 307. How they are said to move or be disturbed, V, 814. Their various meanings, VI, 1000. The mountains of the Valentinians and Marcionites, IV, 822. Who their hills are, IV, 823. The various kinds of monsters, V, 196–197. The remarkable power of mulberry leaves, V, 513. What the moral virtues are, and their meanings, V, 417. The sources of various diseases, V, 501. Their various kinds, and which are understood mystically, ibid. Mount Moriah is interpreted as “mountain of vision,” and why, III, 423. What “you shall die and not live” signifies, III, 259. [Col. 1733] Why the apostle, desiring to die, feared to be stripped of the flesh, VI, 484. Death: whence the name derives, V, 194. Its three kinds, ibid. It will be destroyed at the end of the world, II, 1138. Whether anyone may inflict it upon himself, II, 1185; IV, 1253. How Razis and Samson, who inflicted death upon themselves, are to be excused, ibid. The death of the righteous is to be lamented, III, 634. Sin is its cause, III, 877. What the death of the saints is, ibid. It is preferable to a bitter life, III, 984. Its kinds, III, 912. For whom and for whom not its memory is bitter, III, 1055–1056. It is not to be feared, II, 1185; II, 1056. How it ruled over Christ, V, 1394–1395. It enters through the windows, V, 1395. It is not to be the enemy’s joy, III, 815. How it entered all human beings and the world together with sin, V, 1339. Why the Lord’s death is called death, but the death of his servants a sleep, VI, 554–555. The effects of Christ’s death and resurrection, IV, 34 and 42. What a mortal body is, V, 1395. What mortal sins are, VI, 1337. Their satisfaction, ibid., VI, 1339. The fruit of mortification, V, 1115. One who touches a carcass becomes unclean, II, 360, 363. Why cisterns and springs are not polluted by touching them, ibid. Nor are seeds, II, 365 and 888. One must abstain from carcasses and animals killed by beasts, and why, II, 434. What this signifies mystically, ibid. How the dead are to be mourned, III, 943. Their memory should be everlasting, ibid. Who are to be reckoned among the dead, V, 890. Their resurrection, VI, 213. Who are dead in Christ, VI, 556. The dead often receive honor that was denied to the living, III, 246. Why the Lord forbade the disciple to bury his dead parent, I, 862. The twofold movement of hearts, IV, 571–572. How Moses can say that the Lord was angry with him because of Israel, when elsewhere it is attributed to his own unbelief, II, 846. What the sanctification of Moses and of the Lord was like, II, 478. The literal and mystical interpretation of Moses, V, 52. The meaning of his Egyptian wife, ibid. What he signifies with Elijah on Mount Tabor, V, 77. Where his tomb is, III, 360. Exposed to the waters, then drawn out and nourished by his mother at Pharaoh’s daughter’s command, II, 14–15. He refused the milk of foreign women, ibid. From where he received his name, ibid. What this act signifies mystically, ibid. He kills an Egyptian fighting with a Hebrew, II, 16–17. Whom he represents while watering the flocks of the maidens beside the well, ibid. Pretending slowness of speech, he is rebuked by God, and the obstacle is removed, II, 24–25. His prophecy concerning Christ, II, 563. His various mystical meanings, II, 627–630. After being shown the promised land from the mountain, death is announced to him, II, 776–777. The reason for this vision, ibid. His praise, III, 1086. As leader of the chosen people, a figure of Christ, III, 719. With what faith he died, VI, 800. Because he did not believe the Lord with his brother Aaron, he is barred from entering the promised land, II, 740. When he declares everyone hanging on a tree accursed, is he to be considered insulting toward Christ, II, 921. Why he assisted Aaron in blessing the people and aided the synagogue, II, 340. He takes Aaron as his sole leader, II, 965. Why the Lord said that he would not hear Moses and Samuel, leaving aside the other Fathers, V, 922. Likewise Abraham and Daniel, IV, 661. The agility of the mugil fish, V, 238. The misery and servitude of woman after the Fall, II, 496. A type of the Church, ibid. Why one who takes a wife assumes the care of earthly affairs, II, 636. Her various meanings, VI, 1002. The woman suffering from a flow of blood: whom she typifies, V, 76; I, 857. Likewise the woman who lost the drachma, V, 77. The woman hiding leaven in three measures of meal, V, 81. Who is the woman crushing the serpent’s head, V, 495. The woman as a type of the Church, in what respect, V, 719. The encomium of the diligent woman, II, 1551. The blame of the quarrelsome woman, II, 751–746–764. Why she was made from the man’s side, III, 875. What she signifies, ibid. Why the beautiful woman captured in war, when marrying her captor, is ordered to shave her hair, cut her nails, and remove her garments, II, 915. What this means mystically, ibid. The woman mourning her husband’s death before Elisha beautifully designates Holy Church, III, 228. What a *multicola*—a worshipper of many gods—is, III, 820. The foreign woman: a type of heretics, V, 690. A beautiful but foolish woman is compared to one wearing a golden ring in her nose, V, 717. The harlot is compared with evil doctrine, III, 911. The woman building and destroying her house signifies the soul, V, 726. The woman seeking wool and flax mystically signifies the Church, V, 781. The woman considering a field: a type of the heavenly inheritance, V, 784. The foolish and loud woman is a notable figure of heretics, V, 711. Other men’s wives must not be looked upon, III, 1062. How cautious one ought to be in her company, III, 819, 1061. How the little women of the tribe of Judah were led by the elders from hope of the Messiah to illicit acts, V, 1021. Women are barred from entering the monastery of Fulda, I, 195. Why they must be silent in church, VI, 136. In sexual use, women and animals send external forms inward, V, 217. What women have eaten, and why, of the fruit of their womb, V, 1211. What this signifies mystically, V, 1254. Solomon’s love of foreign women led him into idolatry, III, 298. The names of women and matrons in the Gospel, V, 82. The punishment of women, II, 369. The mule, from *molando* (“grinding”), signifies fools, V, 216. The red mullet restrains lust and dulls the sight, V, 238. The distinction between clean and unclean animals, and their mystical meanings, II, 118. Through whom, how, and when the world was made, I, 443–445. Whether it existed from eternity, ibid. When it was made, ibid. Its formless matter, I, 446. Its division into two regions, I, 450–451. Why it began with light, I, 446. Its perfect adornment, I, 452. Why it is said to have been created in six days in one account and seven in another, I, 464. Its various meanings, V, 258. Its three evils, ibid. Its four regions, ibid. What it signifies mystically, V, 259. In which month it was formed, II, 641. Its delights abandon human beings at the end, II, 982. How Christ conquered it, IV, 173. How the Holy Spirit convicts it of sin, when Christ rebuked it on earth, IV, 209. Whether the world, heaven, and the seed of Israel are everlasting, IV, 89. The pure in heart shall see God, V, 751. How what is clean by nature becomes unclean, V, 1589. Burdens proportionate to one’s shoulders are to be taken up, V, 745; III, 892. Threefold gifts, V, 1115. What a muniment is, V, 406. The literal and mystical explanations of various fortifications, V, 384. The moray eel, entirely female, conceives from a serpent, V, 238. When the murmuring people complain, water flows from the rock of contradiction, II, 709. Those punished by the bite of the serpent, IV, 285. The gravity of murmuring, III, 676. The punishment of the perplexed Jews’ murmuring, II, [Col. 1734] 654–655. They obtain quail and other meats, ibid. Concerning their eating them, II, 661. What this signifies mystically, ibid. When the wall of Catholic faith is destroyed, the city of vice lies open, III, 1024. What the outer wall is, IV, 890. What it signifies, VI, 1003; V, 385. The mouse is named from the earth, V, 226. The significance of flies, V, 258. Why the Egyptians were afflicted by them, II, 37. The male whale, V, 237. The first use of music, V, 258. From where it arose, V, 495. Various opinions concerning its origin, ibid. Its use, effects, and distinction, ibid. It signifies the Church, III, 345. It is unsuitable for mourning, III, 910. Its pleasantness at a banquet, III, 994. It is aptly compared with a carbuncle, ibid. Its praise and necessity, I, 401. The Gentiles devised nine superstitions concerning it, ibid. The multiple mystical meanings of musical instruments, V, 499. The *musio* is so called because it catches mice; by the brightness of its light it overcomes the darkness of night, V, 226. The two kinds of weasel, V, 240; V, 226. The remarkable power of new wine, V, 596. See more, ibid. Since mutability is incompatible with God, why he did not remain with the sentence concerning Nineveh and similar matters, II, 739. What it means to open one’s mouth to the mute, V, 780. Whom the mute signify, V, 75. What the mysteries of the fourth day are like, I, 455. The various things in the Church impenetrable to the human mind, II, 613. How God made his mystery known in all wisdom and prudence, VI, 389. Whether it was hidden from Abraham, Jacob, and the other patriarchs, VI, 413. Since it is unsearchable, how it was revealed by the Apostle, VI, 418.

N

Nahash the Ammonite fights against Jabesh-gilead and makes a pact with each person concerning the removal of his right eye, I, 820. Allegorically he signifies heretics, ibid. What Naaman signifies literally and mystically, III, 231. His leprosy signifies idolatry, ibid. He is healed of leprosy by Elisha, III, 232. His indignation is calmed by his servants; his cleansing seven times in the waters of the Jordan is a type of Baptism, ibid. Nabal, “hard,” bears the type of the Jews, III, 64. What the *nablum* is, III, 344. A type of the Church, ibid. What Naboth signifies, V, 65. Refusing to give his vineyard to Ahab, he was stoned after false witnesses had been brought in, III, 217. Fittingly a type of Christ, falsely accused by the rulers and crucified, ibid. Nebuchadnezzar, enslaving Jehoiakim, displays the type of the prince of confusion and darkness, III, 272. He besieges Jerusalem, III, 276. He blinds Zedekiah’s sons, ibid. What this signifies, ibid. and III, 301. Sending messengers through various regions, he is a type of Christ our Savior, III, 545. Driven by fury and arrogance, he renews the war, III, 604. After exterminating the gods through Holofernes, he wished to be worshiped as God, III, 566. Cutting off the Israelites’ water supply, whom he imitates, III, 556, 611. Who this Nebuchadnezzar was according to Philo’s opinion, III, 372. A type of the Devil, V, 65. He is compared with the winds, V, 836. His hostile encounter with the Tyrians, IV, 803. He devastated the land of Judah three times, V, 1181. What Nabuzardan signifies, III, 276–277. He burned the temple of the Lord and of the King, III, 276. Nadab and Abihu are killed by the Lord when they offer foreign fire, II, 341 and [Col. 1735] 342. They bear the type of those who teach foreign doctrines, ibid. They are mourned by the people, not by the priests, II, 344. Naaman signifies the nations that are to be converted, V, 67. What Nahaliel signifies literally and mystically, II, 718. What Naid signifies, I, 507. What the things born of the flesh are, VI, 1143. Who is *nasoparvus*, II, 485. Nathan rebukes David as guilty of adultery, III, 1095. Why the Nativity of the Lord was instituted by the Fathers, I, 343. Why Masses are celebrated on that night, and by whose concession, ibid. How it should be celebrated, IV, 10. The birth of Adam’s two sons bears the figure of two peoples, I, 503. The mystical interpretation of the Nativity of John the Baptist, IV, 342. Nature is that which causes something to be born, V, 137. God’s nature is unsearchable, IV, 912. It is immutable, ibid. The Father worked two natures in Christ, V, 629. The heresy of those who posit two natures and substances, V, 1352. The gravity and detestation of those who change natural use into use against nature, V, 1303. Since God does not naturally become angry, how his indignation is said to drip, V, 864. Nahum, interpreted as “consoler” or “sprout,” V, 69. Sailors, after releasing oil from their mouths, make the sea luminous for themselves, I, 448. The definition of *navalia*, V, 372. Solomon’s and Hiram’s ships going to Tarshish to bring back treasures are a type of our Redeemer, III, 479. The ship is a true type of Holy Church, V, 372. One who abandons it drifts and is dashed against the rocks, VI, 1146. The names of ships and their parts, V, 554. Their mystical interpretations, ibid. A type of the Church, VI, 1004. God, the faithful pilot, does not allow the little ship of the Church, tossed by waves, to sink, I, 855. The consecration and offering of the Nazirite, II, 621–626. A type of those who abstain and practice continence, ibid. Why a razor did not touch their heads, ibid. Why iron did not come upon them, II, 376. What Mount Nebo was like and where it was, II, 984. What a cloud signifies, V, 329. Why it filled the ministering priests, III, 185. A type of the synagogue of the Jews, ibid. By denying sin, one increases it more than by committing it, V, 825. Who deny God before human beings, I, 904. Through neglect and sloth concerning the virtues, all labor and merit in the virtues is lost, II, 1153. How the sin of negligence is expiated, II, 617–619. How this is to be understood mystically, ibid. Nehemiah, the same as “he who is consoled by the Lord,” V, 70. A type of the apostles, ibid. No one is harmed except by himself, III, 747. No one is to be judged by appearance, III, 838. No one is sufficient to render God the praises due to him and to investigate his mighty works, III, 1080–1081. No one lives without fault, IV, 702. What the shady groves are, II, 749–750. Nimrod first seized tyranny in the kingdom after the flood had ended, I, 528–530. What he was like, ibid. The first author of the confusion of languages, ibid. Why he was called a hunter, ibid. What he signifies, V, 35. What the new moon is, II, 783. Their festival, ibid.; IV, 1037. [Col. 1735] The literal and spiritual meaning of Naphtali, V, 44. The remarkable detestation of the worthless woman, III, 949–950. Through her, sin began everywhere, III, 952. Her domination must not be endured, ibid. How not to know human beings, or to speak, can be fittingly said of God, V, 802–803. Nicanor, commander of the elephants, is a figure of the false prophets, III, 1178. The remarkable life of Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra, IV, 1183. What the discovery of a bird’s nest on the ground or in a tree signifies typologically, II, 923. The security of one who places his nest in a rock, II, 762–763. What a nest signifies, V, 242. There is nothing new in the world, III, 1070. The Nile, V, 319. What the repentance of the Ninevites was like, IV, 37. Ninus, the first king of the Assyrians, III, 544. He founded Nineveh, ibid. Nitrum: whence the name derives, V, 763. A type of the Church, I, 468. The significance of snow, V, 326; V, 1255. What it means to withstand the force of fire with snow and ice, III, 747. The various meanings of night, V, 290. Its seven parts, and what each signifies, ibid. The owl, V, 251. The owl and the sea-raven, V, 249–250. Introduced into the island of Crete, it dies, V, 251. Its type, ibid. Noah expresses Christ in all respects, V, 53. Tenth from Adam, III, 281. After the flood, together with his sons, he increased the human race, ibid. His praise, III, 1085. That he was righteous, I, 513. Noah and Christ, through a contemptible wooden instrument and under the guidance of wisdom, restored the human race, III, 716. Naomi, wife of Elimelech, a type of the Church, II, 1201. Beautiful, ibid. Her sons Mahlon and Chilion are types of the prophets and apostles, ibid. She returns from Moab to Bethlehem with Ruth, II, 1205. Her counsel concerning the marriage between Boaz and Ruth, II, 1210–1211. She is a type of the synagogue, II, 1221. How David made a name for himself, III, 95; III, 369. The names of various persons in the Gospel, with what they signify, V, 78–89. The excellence of the name Jesus, III, 1191. Why the most holy Fathers, except Joshua the son of Nun, were not called by it, ibid. The explanation of the Redeemer’s names expressed on the cross, VI, 1677. Who are unworthy of knowledge of God, V, 304. From where it can be established, V, 1286. The same is manifested by the construction of the world, III, 332. The heresy of the Novatians and Origen concerning obtaining forgiveness of sins, I, 929. The razor expresses the deceit of Antichrist, V, 610. What the nine unsuspected things are, III, 948. The festival days of November are described, IV, 1176. The memory of the last things is the most immediate antidote against all sins, III, 813; V, 1205; II, 263. What the festival of the new things is, and how it is to be celebrated, II, 785 and 895. What the new sacrifice is, II, 898. Who the new spirit is, V, 1270. Marriage is permitted to all, but in the Lord, II, 837. The clouds of the Gospel signify preachers; lightning and flashes signify miracles, VI, 1155. The various meanings of a cloud, II, 415; V, 1167. See its beautiful meanings, V, 276; VI, 1004. The mystical meaning of nuts, V, 514. The number is named from *nummus* (“coin”), from counting, [Col. 1736] or from the goddess Numaria; how many kinds there are, V, 672. Since the number of the days of human life is with the Lord, why Hezekiah said that he would die in the middle of his days, VI, 1094. Who are judged worthy of the divine numbers, II, 589. By doing what we shall be assigned to them, II, 591. God established the elect under a number, II, 590. What the Book of Numbers recounts, V, 111. The ordering of numbers, V, 489–490. They are types of many mysteries, ibid. What sort of people were the money-changers whom the Lord expelled from the temple, I, 1041. Who the messenger of Saul’s death was, and what reward he carried away, III, 71. Whom he signifies, ibid., 57. Who the messengers of death are, V, 734. Why a newly married man is exempted from war, II, 937. The mystical meaning of this statement, ibid. Marriage is not to be condemned, I, 461. The heresy of those who condemn marriage and the use of food, VI, 609–610 and 673. That marriage is lawful for the free, VI, 662 onward. What a movement of the eyes signifies, V, 713. The night-heron, V, 251. The origin of nymphs and the explanation of their various names, V, 454.

O
Obab is asked by Moses, his kinsman, to set out with them from Mount Sinai, II, 653. Obed, the son of Boaz by Ruth, II, 1222. In Hebrew, “serving”; also the father of Jesse, ibid. The outstanding praise of obedience, III, 45. More pleasing to God than sacrifices, ibid. Just as obedience means that nothing evil should be done, so at times it means that a good and virtuous deed should be omitted, ibid., 46. In adversity one may possess something of one’s own; not so in prosperity, III, 46.

Solutions to certain serious objections, II, 47–48.

The offering of rams at the consecration of the priests represents the Passover celebrated by the Lord with his disciples, II, 330. Its ritual and effects, ibid. and 338. What the offering of the firstfruits of the crops ought to be, II, 264. Its various kinds, II, 675–676. An offering made from unjust profit is despised, III, 109, 1015. The offering of the righteous, made from charity, enriches the altar, III, 1013. It should be offered with a cheerful countenance, ibid., 1016. The various offerings of the tabernacle are explained mystically, II, 242–243.

How harmful forgetfulness of our redemption is, II, 1120. Explanation of a more obscure apostolic passage, VI, 344–345. Observance of the Lord’s commandments and judgments is earnestly commended, by deterring people from vices, II, 434, 443, and 856.

What the obstacles to prayer are, V, 860–861.

The midwives ordered by Pharaoh to kill all the male children of the Hebrews, II, 13. Whom they signify, ibid. Because they were moved by compassion and refrained from the slaughter, they are rewarded by God, ibid. Whether, by lying to Pharaoh and refraining from drowning the Hebrews, they sinned, II, 13 and 447.

The obstinacy of the Jews in sin, V, 944. The fasts of the obstinate are not heard, V, 920. The occasion of sins must be avoided, V, 773. In what sense killing and giving life are appropriate to God, VI, 1149.

What “the west of the west” signifies, IV, 774. The sons of the west signify the impious and the children of darkness, as well as persecutors of the Churches, II, 1154. What kind of killing of God is meant, II, 982–983.

The human being infected with sin is subject to a great occupation, a heavy yoke, and various miseries, III, 1047.

From where Ocean is named, V, 312.

Ochosias, following the impiety of his father Ahab, pays the penalty, III, 221. The soldiers sent by him to seize Elijah are consumed three times by heavenly fire, ibid. He is a type of the Jewish people, V, 68.

An exposition of the eight beatitudes delivered on the mountain, properly adapted to the gifts of the Holy Spirit, I, 794–795. Since Exodus counts eight kinds of priestly garments, how does Leviticus mention seven? II, 328. A very full account of the festivals in October, IV, 1171.

“Eye has not seen, nor ear heard,” etc.—what this signifies, VI, 24. The eyes of heretics are sevenfold, III, 836. All things are naked to the eyes of God, III, 705, 865, 981, 1043. The look of the eyes and gentle words are very effective for winning the hearts of people, III, 620. The sense of sight is superior to the other senses, V, 955, 959. Its allegorical meaning, VI, 1009.

From where the hatred between David and Saul arose, III, 55. What hatred is praiseworthy, V, 155. What is detestable, ibid. The wicked should be pursued with hatred for correction, not out of envy, II, 451.

What the fragrance of Christ is, VI, 169–170. What *Oefi* is, IV, 1046.

An offense must be forgiven, III, 969. The difference between offense and a fall, V, 1526.

Who is the one offering in the sight of God, II, 305. Ecclesiastical or canonical offices: what and how many there are in the Church, V, 128. To whom ecclesiastical offices are permitted, III, 344. The names of various offices are explained, V, 446–447. The duties of a good ruler, III, 993.

Why Og is called “conclusion,” V, 53.

The various kinds and interpretations of vegetables, V, 530. Why the Israelites were commanded to offer olive oil, II, 188. Its mystical use, ibid., 515. Those who draw oil from the rock, III, 720. Who the keepers of olive groves and fig orchards are, III, 404.

From where *olla* is derived, and its mystical meanings, V, 602. A pot set alight and facing north: whom it typologically signifies, V, 806 and following. Whom the heat of this fire inflames, ibid. An erroneous opinion held by certain people concerning this pot, V, 808. A melted pot as a type of the burning of Jerusalem, IV, 749, and of the miseries of the world, ibid., 754–755.

The various kinds of swans, II, 589–590. From where *olus* is inflected, V, 530.

The height of Olympus, V, 349, 363.

All things are perishable and will return to the earth, III, 1058. Nothing is impossible for the Almighty, III, 723.

The wild ass aptly signifies heretics, V, 817. Their characteristics, V, 918. See *Asinus*, V, 213.

The burdens of priests, II, 691. How they are to be borne by one’s neighbor, following Christ’s example, V, 1591.

Onesimus: what sort of person he was and of what origin, VI, 698. Through the prayers of blessed Paul he returns to the favor of his master, VI, 703.

The historical meaning of Onias, III, 1227. And the mystical meaning, ibid. After withdrawing to Seleucus because of Simon’s slanders, he receives the high priesthood and corrupts the worship of God, etc., III, 1229–1230. Appearing to Judas in a vision, he hands him a sword, III, 1255.

The onocentaur, a monster, V, 196. The onocrotalus, a bird, V, 246.

The fornication and impurity of Oholah and Oholibah, IV, 741, 747. Their etymology, ibid. Whom they signify mystically, IV, 744. Their vengeance, ibid., 749. They represent the deserted Jews, ibid.

The etymology of shady places, V, 371.

The good works of the Fathers are counted to their children, II, 20. Good works are a sacrifice pleasing to God, II, 1222. It is fitting to praise the Author, II, 1153. What the works of the flesh are, and why they are so called, VI, 353, 355. Why, amid so many miracles of God, III, 839. The works of the Law are insufficient for salvation, and what they are, VI, 276. What religious people teach in words must be confirmed by their deeds, III, 1113. The distinct operations of humanity and divinity in Christ are established against Eutyches, I, 982.

The labor of good works is lost through any mortal sin, II, 1153. Their most just reward is given, II, 551–552; III, 684. The merits of mercy are infinite, III, 869. Who the laborers in the vineyard are, V, 77. What proud riches are, V, 709.

Why Ophni is interpreted as “barefoot,” V, 58. A description of Ophir, V, 342. David’s gold brought from there, ibid. The offense of Ophni and Phinehas, and its interpretation, III, 21.

Various opinions about the world, I, 443.

From where *oppidum* is derived, V, 375. Why it is enclosed by walls, ibid. Its origin, ibid.

A severe threat against nobles, priests, and kings on account of impiety, V, 866.

The work of the Holy Spirit in creation, I, 446. What the work of God is, VI, 1133. The various kinds of minor works, V, 122.

“Or” signifies anger, and why, V, 361.

What an oracle is, III, 152, 427. How we can always pray, III, 16. What an *orarium* is and to whom it was granted, I, 307.

Prayer and almsgiving benefit the dead, I, 93. What prayer is and at what time it ought to be made, ibid.; V, 136, 825; III, 885. What prayers are pleasing to God, III, 13. Its power, ibid., 616. It must be performed without interruption and with preparation, ibid., 606–607. The usefulness of ecclesiastical prayer, V, 1605. Its action, manner, and usefulness are taught at length, VI, 588 and following. Its various kinds, ibid., VI, 590 and following, at length. What legitimate prayer is, I, 139. Particular prayer, ibid. Their fourfold kind, ibid. and following. How compunction arises from them, ibid. How they are to be perfected, I, 816.

The prayer of the wise person, accompanied by recognition of his own weakness, for obtaining wisdom, III, 714. The prayer of the prophet Jeremiah, V, 1262. Its literal and mystical explanation, ibid. and following. Against pride, III, 817.

The distinction concerning the Lord’s Prayer, I, 332, 821. Saint Matthias includes seven petitions in it, while Luke has five, ibid. Its explanation, I, 817–886.

What nation is considered unworthy of the prayers of the faithful, V, 865. Two kinds of prayers that assist one another, VI, 811.

Definition of an orator, I, 409.

[Col. 1738]

What the world signifies and how many its parts are, V, 351–352. Its threefold mystical division, ibid. The remaining part of the world was illuminated with light while the Egyptians were oppressed by darkness, III, 754.

Enumeration and description of the Orcades Islands, V, 354.

What order must be observed in all things, II, 600. What the order of the resurrected will be, V, 883. Ecclesiastical order and rank, VI, 430. All things have been arranged by God in due order, III, 723.

What is necessary for one about to receive holy orders, undertake pastoral governance, and assume care of souls, I, 377–378. Who are to be initiated into each order, I, 306.

Oreb and Zeeb, Midianites killed by Gideon, are a type of the rulers of darkness, III, 1166–1167.

Orpah and Ruth, Moabite women: the former is a figure of the Jews, the latter of the Gentiles; and what their names mean in Hebrew, II, 1201. Orpah’s return to the Moabites is a type of apostates from faith and virtue, while Ruth is a type of those steadfast in faith, II, 1203–1204. She gathers ears of grain in the field, ibid., 1206. She is a type of the Gentiles seeking the faith and religion of Christ, ibid., and of the Church gathering ears of grain, ibid. She venerates Boaz and is praised by him, ibid., 1207. Her humility, ibid., 1208.

What the organ signifies mystically, V, 495. Who is hanged upon the willows, V, 1144.

What placing a hand over the mouth signifies, V, 778. The guarding of the mouth is praiseworthy, III, 917.

The grave error of the Origenists, who promise sinners and the devil himself a kingdom in heaven after the day of judgment, V, 696, 716.

Orion, V, 273. What it signifies, ibid.

What an ornament is, V, 580. The adornment of the Roman and Persian empires, ibid. Judith’s adornment was directed not toward adulterous love but toward the religious worship of God, III, 622.

What binding the mouth of the ox treading out the grain signifies mystically, II, 942; what opening it signifies, IV, 558, 561. The various meanings of *os* (“mouth”), *oris* (“of the mouth”), and *ossis* (“of bone”), VI, 1013.

What “Hosanna” signifies, I, 1039.

What birds are songbirds, V, 255. What harm the kisses of a prostitute imply, V, 751. The practice of the ancients, I, 595. The meaning, V, 760.
