Why Hosea is called “Savior,” V, 67.

The bones of Elisha, brought into contact with a corpse, restored it to life, III, 245. The dry bones coming to life signify the people of Israel being brought back to their land, or the resurrection of Jews and Christians, IV, 859–860. Whether this should be understood of the general resurrection, ibid.

Who the doorkeepers are, V, 93; I, 306. What “door opposite door” signifies, IV, 912. The house of Solomon facing east is a type of Christ’s body opened by the lance, III, 145. Why Christ is called the Door, V, 1367. Its various mystical meanings, VI, 1014.

Oysters conceive from mussels, V, 239.

Praise of Otagrius, archbishop of Mainz, VI, 1597 and note. Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, is buried, I, 97.

Othniel: interpreted as “response of God,” V, 55. Savior of the Israelites, he lays low Cushan-rishathaim, II, 1125. What it means in Hebrew, ibid. He restores peace to the people for forty years, II, 1127. The first judge of the people of Israel, ibid. Mystically, he signifies our guardian angels, ibid. Of what family he was, ibid.

[Col. 1739]

His remarkable praise, ibid. He dies while God is punishing the people, II, 1128. He is appointed in the place of Joshua, II, 1111.

The seriousness of idle words, IV, 42. Idleness must be avoided, III, 805.

What eggs signify mystically, V, 243. From where the word is derived, ibid., V, 255. What the eggs and chicks found in a nest signify mystically, II, 924.

The sheep are the chosen: Christians, V, 201, and the gentle, III, 405. Why the Egyptians abhor them, II, 38. While Moses is pasturing them, God appears to him in the bush and sends him, despite his resistance, to the children of Israel to free them from Pharaoh’s hand, II, 17 and following. Their various meanings, VI, 1015. The sheepfold signifies the Church, V, 203.

Uzzah, supporting the ark as it tilted, is a type of those who approach the Most Holy Eucharist unworthily, III, 83, 339. The ark placed upon a new cart is a figure of holy Baptism, III, 84.

Uzziah, about to offer sacrifice contrary to the law of Moses, is struck with leprosy, III, 246. He signifies the devil, ibid., III, 503. A dreadful earthquake occurs when he is struck with leprosy while unlawfully attempting to sacrifice in the temple, III, 512, 562.

P
Pachomius’s holiness, IV, 1145. His martyrdom, ibid. Our Savior, following the example of Solomon the Patriarch, offers peaceful beasts for us, III, 197, 349, 471. The rite of those offerings, II, 265, 445. The covenant between God and Abraham, II, 545. The office of a pedagogue, VI, 306. Its etymology, ibid. Description of the pagus, V, 384. Where pagans derive their name, and who were called by it, V, 426. How they oppose justice together with heretics, III, 855. How Catholics do so, III, 861. What Palatha is, III, 623. The meaning of palaestra, V, 549. Description of Palestine, V, 339. The literal and mystical interpretation of chaff and tares, I, 774. What the hyacinth-colored pallium signifies mystically, II, 166, 167. Its various meanings, VI, 1017. The various names of women’s cloaks, V, 575, 576. Interpretation of palms, V, 159, 511. Why Palm Sunday is celebrated, V, 347. Why it is called Capitulavium, IV, 29. The dove. See Turtur.

Why the Jews eat bread mixed with ox dung, IV, 597. The unleavened breads signify the books of the holy Apostles, II, 311. Their use, II, 312 and 313. The twelve in the tabernacle: a figure of the holy Apostles, II, 149. The various meanings of bread, II, 80; VI, 1020. What bread signifies of falsehood, V, 554; of life, III, 860. The manner of making the bread of the Presence, II, 517. Mystically, they represented Christ, ibid. Their various kinds, II, 517, 521. The origin of the name Pannonia, V, 350. Its length, ibid. The Panotii in Scythia, V, 198. The panther, friendly to every animal except the dragon, V, 219. Almost all the evangelical parables are explained together with their types, V, 85, 86. What a parable signifies, I, 939. Why Christ used them, I, 940. Explanation of certain parables, I, 951. Why we too often use them, I, 1013. Why Solomon’s sayings are called proverbs, and what benefit they provide, ibid. Interpretation of the ten foolish virgins compared with the kingdom of heaven, I, 1084. The parable of the lioness and the young lions signifies the captivity of the kings Jehoahaz and Jehoiachin, IV, 714. The parable of the vineyard describes Jerusalem’s calamity, IV, 715. The beautiful literal and mystical meaning of Paradise, V, 334. Its four rivers, ibid. What the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil signify there, ibid. Whom its four rivers signify, ibid. Where and when it was planted, I, 476. A type of the Church, I, 479. Its pleasantness, ibid. The waters of the Flood did not penetrate it, ibid. The divisions of its rivers, ibid. What the paralytic lying on a bed signifies, V, 75. Why Parasceve is numbered among the festivals, I, 348. How it is celebrated, ibid. The three Fates and their duties, V, 439. The leopard is a figure of Satan, and also of Antichrist and the sinner, V, 221. An exhortation to charity, IV, 236, 292; to repentance, III, 878. The increasing age of parents should come to rest when their children reach adolescence, III, 779. The mutual conduct of parents and children is taught at length, VI, 463; likewise that of masters and servants, VI, 538, 679. The wall is a type of Christ; likewise of hypocrites, V, 401. Where Mount Parnassus is situated, V, 340–362. The gravity and repentance of parricides at the Council of Mainz, VI, 1410. What the parts of the human body signify, and how many there are, V, 146–179; likewise in relation to the length of heaven, V, 265. Why the parts of the world were believed to be gods, I, 443. What participles are and where they derive their name, V, 661. The groaning of a woman in labor, V, 866. When lesser things are neglected, greater ones grow up, II, 222. Why the Apostle called himself little, VI, 432. Who the little ones are, V, 687–710. Why the uncircumcised soul of a little child perished, I, 546.

When and why the feast of Passover was first instituted, I, 350. Its etymology, ibid. Why it does not return to the same day of the year, ibid. Its excellences, IV, 34. Its sanctification and rites, II, 148, 149 and 696. The Passover season was commanded to be observed in four ways in the Old Testament, II, 639–643. Its lamb is a type of Christ, II, 49. What its eating signifies, II, 789, 958. The kinds and meanings of sparrows, II, 895–896; V, 250; VI, 1022. The distinction between passion and pre-passion, I, 810; IV, 328. The fruits of the Lord’s Passion, VI, 725. Its causes, I, 348. Its effects, ibid. Christ is the shepherd, V, 203; and so are the Apostles, ibid. Their office, II, 120 and 121. Whom the swineherds fleeing near Gerasa signify, V, 76. Lot’s shepherds represent heretics, II, 536. The distinction between shepherds and rams, V, 1001. Through the negligence and sins of shepherds, all vices and heresies are introduced into the Church, V, 1254. Reproof of shepherds who tear apart the Lord’s flock, V, 979, 840–842.

“Father” is used in Scripture in many ways, V, 184. The several kinds of fathers, V, 892. Who is called a paterfamilias in Scripture, V, 185. Who is the laborer hired in the vineyard, [Col. 1740] I, 1026; V, 76. What is signified by the one bringing forth old and new things from his treasury, V, 90. The counsels of fathers and elders are to be heard, III, 398. God’s patience is beautifully compared with the heat of the sun, V, 1490. The fruit of patience and its praise, V, 735. The Greek name patriarcha and what it signifies, V, 35. Certain patriarchs blessed their sons, while others cursed them, III, 778. Why Aaron carried the names of the patriarchs on his shoulders and breast during sacrifices, II, 195, 196.

Saint Paul resolves all things figured in riddles and teaches their forms, II, 664, 665. His victory and labor, II, 1144. Why an angel of Satan was given to him, IV, 551. His diligence in teaching and integrity of life, II, 1112. What oath he used, V, 1289. His fatherly affection toward his children, VI, 48. His zeal, VI, 86. His labors, VI, 227–228 and following. Why he commended himself, VI, 225, 367. Whether it should be held against him that, with human assistance, he was let down in a basket through a wall, VI, 230.

What kind of persons are the poor man and the creditor meeting one another, V, 772. Who is the poor man raised from the earth, VI, 1101. Whoever closes his ear to the poor will himself not be heard, V, 47. The poor must not be provoked, III, 784, 785. Whoever defrauds the poor is a man of blood, III, 1011. Whom the poor eating in secret signify, VI, 1128. What is represented by a pavement laid with precious marble and fitted with fir boards, III, 426. The peacock signifies paganism, V, 47.

Peace is to be maintained with many, but counsel is to be taken with one, III, 795. Which peace must be guarded, III, 1197, 1246, 1247. Those who accept it in wartime are to be spared, II, 911; against those who refuse it, especially heretics, force must be used, ibid. Its commendation, V, 1236. The judgment of holiness, ibid. It is to be announced to the people by priests, VI, 1236. Its various meanings, VI, 1016.

What it means to sin against God, II, 560. The sinner loves darkness, III, 920. Who is a sinner without the law, V, 1317. Why God endured the sinful Israelites for so long, VI, 1144. Sin kills the soul, I, 481; II, 227. One who conceals another’s sin is his helper, II, 281. What sin is unforgivable, II, 34 and 387. Why it must be avoided, II, 1123. It gives strength to enemies, ibid., 1123. What punishment is imposed on those who heap it upon sins, II, 203. Those infected by its stain are excluded from entry into heaven, III, 654. It must be confessed without shame, ibid., 789. It must not be attributed to God, but to the human being created by God, endowed with free will and given commandments that could be observed, ibid., 663–665. Those polluted by it place their trust in the temple in vain, V, 859. Its reward, V, 1406. Its nature and cause, V, 1545. How it is committed, II, 387; VI, 1394: in thought, ibid.; in speech, ibid. Its various kinds, VI, 1395; IV, 579, 817, 818. Whoever laments it without correcting it labors in vain, ibid. Its habit brings on despair, V, 737–738. The usefulness of remembering it, IV, 666. What it signifies to eat sin in a holy place, II, 305. Whether the legislator called the priest’s sin the sin of the people, II, 270 and 271. What Judah’s sin was, V, 944. Why the Jews falsified this text, ibid. What was written with an iron stylus on a diamond point, V, 945. How it is to be understood that sin reigned until the law, V, 1377. When it came to life again, V, 1418–1423. Who is said to have died without the law, ibid.

What are called the sins of the saints, II, [Col. 1741] 691. God is not harmed by the wicked, V, 860. Because of their merits human beings are afflicted, III, 614. What circumstances accompany adultery, III, 921. The gravity of sin against the Holy Spirit, and whether there is remission of sins outside the Catholic Church, III, 902. Whether it is remitted, III, 905. The prohibition and gravity of sins against nature, II, 439–441; III, 562. Because of the people’s sins, God removes good rulers from life prematurely, II, 1132. An account of those entangled in various sins, VI, 649. The distinction between a sinner and sinning, V, 1333. Who are sinners in the sight of God, I, 536, 537. They bend the knee before the Baals, II, 1221. Their inconstancy, III, 847. When they are freed from sins, II, 1127. Why they are called wicked, II, 496 and 497. In what way they deceive us, V, 682. Hated by God, III, 675. God does not hear the impenitent, ibid., 846; nor are they to be received by us, III, 847. They flee correction, ibid., 997. Why God is so greatly refreshed by the salvation of converts, I, 1010. How they are said to be alienated from the womb, to have gone astray from birth, and to have spoken falsehood, II, 607.

What distinguishes pecora and pecudes, V, 199; and whom these signify, ibid. What the priest’s breast was like, II, 319, 320. Wisdom is to be sought as money is sought, V, 688. Money was counted out to the Lord for the souls of individuals among the people, II, 214. What naked runners signify, V, 552. The Pelagianist heresy concerning presumption on one’s own strength, II, 847. The meanings of skin, VI, 1025. The pelican, an Egyptian bird, signifies hermits, V, 249. What feathers signify, V, 241. An inquiry concerning feathers, VI, 1610, note. What Pentapolis is and where it is situated, V, 341.

When and why the celebration of Pentecost was instituted, IV, 47. Sermons for that day, IV, 253. When its feast began to be celebrated in the Old and New Testaments, I, 354. How it is to be observed, ibid. Its Sabbath is equivalent to the Holy Saturday of Passover, I, 355. How God can say that he spared the Israelites when all except two perished, IV, 717. Whether those forbidden to enter the promised land were condemned to infernal punishments, ibid. The various kinds of blows, V, 1025, 1198; IV, 606; VI, 235. What kind of blows are divine among human beings, V, 842. What it signifies to lose money, III, 974. The partridge figures the devil, V, 249. Its nature, V, 948. Our destruction comes from ourselves, III, 864. The happiness of pilgrims and guests upon earth, VI, 795. What is necessary for one striving toward perfection, IV, 991, 992. Its power is in human hands, I, 1020. What it means to complete evil, V, 735, 736. Who is a lover of danger, III, 781. Dangers known to those sailing the sea, III, 1079. The obstacles and Charybdes of the historical sea, ibid. One must by no means remain in sins because of confidence in riches, III, 790; nor because of youth, strength, or the Lord’s mercy, ibid., 791.

A very difficult question concerning Joram and his son Ochoziah is unraveled, III, 497. The Persians and Medes, terrified by Judith’s boldness, signify the army of the devil, [Col. 1741] III, 554, 663. Their god is fire, V, 336; likewise the sun, ibid. Fortitude, IV, 774. Persecution is necessary for those living piously, III, 772. Perseverance in good works, II, 1132. Why Persia is so called, V, 336. Its location and breadth, ibid. There is no respect of persons with God, V, 720. Those of one substance, I, 459. What the foot mystically represents, VI, 1024. Which feet are to be gathered in poetry, and how many their kinds are, V, 675–678. What is to be asked in Christ’s name is explained, IV, 222. What human petitions ought to be, I, 1045.

The rock struck by Moses is a most fitting type of the Savior, II, 84. Whom it suits, V, 940. Its various meanings, VI, 1028. What it signifies when it quenched the thirst of the Israelites, III, 719; and when it is like melting wax, III, 586. The life and death of Saint Petronilla, IV, 1148. What rocky places signify, V, 341. Whether Peter was rebuked by the Apostle Paul, VI, 273. The reason for his rebuke, VI, 275. Why he is questioned before the other Apostles in difficult passages, I, 971, 988; IV, 366. Why he is called Baronia, IV, 52. His office and that of the Apostle Paul, I, 990. Why they died on the same day, in the same place, and at the hands of the same tyrant, yet by different kinds of death, ibid. How some Evangelists report that he denied the Lord after the third crowing of the cock, and others after the second, I, 1019, 1124.

What Phaedera is, V, 612. Refutation of those who ascribe a phantom body to Christ, IV, 365. Where Pharan is, III, 64. Pharao was formerly a title of honor and is a type of the devil, V, 52. What his vision signifies mystically, ibid., I, 634. His generosity toward Joseph’s brothers, especially Benjamin, I, 644, 647. He, despising God’s commandments, oppresses the Israelites more severely, II, 27 and 28. By the name Pharao all royal dignity among the Egyptians was expressed, IV, 795. The threat made against him, IV, 796. Why he was afflicted, IV, 798. He became a staff of reed to the house of Israel, and of what kind, IV, 798. By what plague he was struck when he claimed the rivers of Egypt for himself, IV, 800. His loftiness is compared with Assur, and a similar destruction is foretold for both, IV, 811–814. He is likened to a dragon, IV, 820, 821.

Why Phares is called “division,” V, 45. The etymology of Phareira, V, 151. Its mystical meaning: the golden one signifies heretical doctrines, III, 369. The meaning of phari, V, 386. Its use, necessary for sailors, V, 388–606. Where the Pharisees derive their name and what they teach, V, 95. Why they are called wise, V, 870. The madness of those who write the Decalogue on little membranes and bind them upon their foreheads, V, 1063, 1064. The institution of the Phase, II, 58 and 784. Its offering and feast, II, 895. The death of Pheltias, IV, 642. Phenenna, in Hebrew, means “conversion,” III, 14. She insults Anna but is punished, ibid. The effects of avarice, II, 867. Who Philemon was, to whom the Apostle Paul wrote a letter, what kind of man he was, and where he was born, V, 1258; VI, 698. Why Philip the apostle in Samaria was not permitted to lay on hands, IV, 262. Its effects, IV, 270.

Who the Philistines, also called Palestinians, were when they struck the Israelites after capturing the Lord’s ark, III, 27. They are severely punished by God, ibid., 28. Their counsel concerning the appeasement of God, ibid. [Col. 1742] They had five cities, ibid., 22. They place the ark on a new cart, adding golden images of tumors and mice in a little chest, ibid., 30. These were supplied by the five cities, while only mice were supplied by the villages and rural districts, ibid. They removed all the ironworkers from the Jews, III, 4.

The etymology of philosopher, V, 414. Pythagoras was the first author of this name, V, 357. The grave errors of many philosophers, V, 414. Their division into three classes, V, 414. What true philosophy is, V, 415. Its parts, ibid. The condemnation of pomp, VI, 521. The various opinions of pagan philosophers and theologians concerning God, V, 414. Their writings, together with those of the gentiles, are compared with the letters of Antiochus, III, 707. The various opinions of the Greeks and the holy Fathers concerning the creation of the world, I, 443. Some of these posit three principles, others two, and others still different principles, ibid., 1089.

The praise of Phinehas, son of Eleazar, III, 1095. Why he received the covenant of peace from God, ibid. He turned God’s anger away from the people, III, 1096. Whom he signifies mystically, ibid. There were two men named Phinehas, III, 21. The son of Eli, a despiser of divine and human law, ibid. In Hebrew, “the closing of the mouth,” ibid. He falls in battle, III, 27. His wife dies in childbirth when the news of his death is brought, ibid. What Phiton signifies, II, 12. Why Phinehas is interpreted as “sparing the mouth,” and whose type he bears, V, 58. “Mouth to mouth,” ibid. What Phison is and from where it derives its name, III, 942. The phoenix signifies the resurrection of the righteous, V, 246. The overthrow of the heresy of Photinus and the Manichaeans, VI, 247, 248. Why Phrygia was called Dardania, and its thirst, V, 344. Its division, ibid. Whether Phua, father of Thola, was Gideon’s uterine brother, II, 1176. The division of physics, logic, and ethics, V, 413. Their explanations, ibid. Whoever touches pitch is defiled, III, 849.

A description of piety and its benefit, VI, 613. The lazy person is urged to work by the example of the ant, V, 703. What the lazy man stoned on a muddy stone signifies, III, 909; and on ox dung, ibid. A description and amplification of laziness, V, 725, 731, 741, 751, 760, 766, 771. The manner of returning and reclaiming a pledge, II, 938. To whom it must be given, IV, 707.

Pious people aspire to the heavenly homeland, II, 1220. Those who have renounced the world must not look back, III, 30. They are not broken by adversity nor lifted up by prosperity, ibid. They groan, but nevertheless do not turn aside from the way of justice, ibid. They possess everything from God, III, 32. They renounce vices, ibid., 33. The enticements of pleasures must be avoided by them; to do so truly, they need the prayers of the saints, III, 43. What the hairs of the flesh are, II, 636. What the hair of Ezekiel’s head and beard, cut off and scattered in various ways, signifies mystically, IV, 598, 599. The office of cupbearer, I, 633. The fins and scales of fish signify the ignorant, II, 354; and also the elect, ibid.; II, 884, 885. What the pine tree signifies, V, 517. The various distinctions of pepper, V, 525.

Fish are so called from pascere, “to feed,” V, 237. The origin of their various names, V, 238, 239. Their various kinds, ibid. They represent the Old and New Testaments, ibid., and human beings, ibid. Their various mystical meanings, VI, 735. Why their names are not expressed in sacrifices, II, 354. What the fish with a stater in its mouth signifies mystically, [Col. 1743] I, 1005. What the fish roasted and given to the Lord by the disciples signifies, IV, 150. Whether and how one should please human beings, VI, 97.

The plagues of Egypt on account of the retention of the Hebrew people: the changing of the rivers into blood, II, 34; the production of frogs, ibid., 35; of gnats, II, 36; of flies, II, 37; likewise of pestilence, II, 39; the sending of hail, II, 41; of locusts, II, 42; of darkness, II, 43; and finally the death inflicted on the firstborn, II, 43 and 54. The mystical meanings of these plagues, II, 43–47. God’s lament over the city of Jerusalem, V, 837. Its cause, ibid. His lament over Egypt and its cities, IV, 804; over Pharao, IV, 819. The fourfold lament of the saints, I, 795. What the planting of the Rose in Jericho signifies, I, 930. What kind of planting belongs to the devil, V, 804. What planting and building ought to be, V, 1017. Where the plane tree derives its name, III, 931. A type of Christ the Lord, ibid. The definition of streets, V, 386. They are taken in a good and a bad sense, ibid. How God protects his people in a hostile land, II, 567. The Pleiades, V, 272. Where the complete joy of the holy Church is found, III, 655. What lead is and how many kinds there are, V, 479. The plural number used for the singular is common in Scripture, V, 1230.

Rain or a shower signifies heavenly gifts or God’s commandments, V, 325. Sometimes it signifies the devil, ibid. A type of the law of the Gospel, III, 39. What morning rain is, V, 734. The cup mystically signifies the Lord’s blood. Its various kinds, V, 599, 600. The mystical meaning of the priest’s tunic, V, 803. The punishment of sin committed through pride, II, 679. Eternal punishments are unavoidable, V, 1192. They correspond to sins, II, 1128. The punishment of those who do not release male and female servants whom they solemnly promised in the temple to set free, V, 1089.

The definition of repentance, V, 137. Its parts, V, 341; III, 21. It must be hastened, ibid.; and III, 792. Its manner is familiar to some, ibid., 606. When and why there is no place for it, VI, 820. What kind of repentance a sinner must undertake, VI, 1315. It must correspond to the quality of the sins, III, 21. Scriptural testimonies and examples of penitents, VI, 1306, 1312. The time of fruitful repentance, VI, 1314. When penitents are to be reconciled, VI, 1422. The punishment of those who violate repentance, ibid. The final opportunity is to be denied to no one, ibid. Its outstanding practitioners, I, 341. How it is to be practiced, ibid. Its two kinds, I, 342.

Where poets derive their name, and their origin, use, and duties, V, 419. What it means to profane God’s name, II, 463; and the earth, II, 937. Who are those eating fresh and aged fruit, II, 997. Weight and scales are the Lord’s judgments, V, 732. What the Lord’s weight and burden are, IV, 1025. The justice of weights and measures, IV, 1026. Certain kinds and explanations of them, ibid. The authors of different weights, V, 479, 480 and 481. Their names and interpretations, ibid.

The pontifical garments of Aaron and his sons are prescribed, II, 189, 191. What the name and office of pontiff are, V, 91. They were formerly kings, ibid. Their office, V, [Col. 1743] 797. Their qualities belong to Christ, ibid. What Pontus is, V, 347. The genuine interpretation of popina, V, 391. Where the word populus derives its name, V, 452. Who is the Lord’s people, III, 72; VI, 989. All the people hasten to Jerusalem with thanksgiving to offer holocausts, III, 587. The just people, oppressed by Pharao’s harsh slavery, are liberated through Wisdom, while their adversaries perish in the Red Sea, III, 718. Their salvation depends greatly upon presbyters, III, 56, 616.

The pig, as though “unclean,” signifies sinners, V, 206. Sea pigs dig into the earth beneath the waters, V, 238. Porphyrion, V, 255. Porphyry’s error and slander concerning the writings of Saint Matthew, III, 531. Where the word porta derives its name, V, 385. Taken in the right-hand sense, it signifies Christ and the Church; in the left-hand sense, the devil, heresy, and so forth, V, 386. The gate of heaven, V, 815. The new gate, ibid. The gate of the underworld, II, 1141. Its multiple meanings, IV, 347. What the Beautiful Gate of the sun-facing side of the temple, at which the lame man asked for alms, signifies mystically, IV, 347. The various kinds and meanings of portents, V, 199. What they sometimes foretell and when, III, 1232. What kinds appeared in the sky over Jerusalem, ibid. Why it endured prodigies, ibid. What a portico is, V, 399. A type of the Lord’s Incarnation, ibid. The portico of the Lord’s temple divided into three classes, III, 451. What they signify, ibid. Where the word portus derives its name, V, 372. Its mystical meaning, ibid.

How the possession of Canaan is called eternal, II, 546. How it differs from creation, VI, 406. The possession of a good woman signifies the Church, III, 1224. It is advised that possessions be distributed not during life but at death, III, 1003. What it means to see God’s “back,” I, 544, 545; II, 23. Why Abraham’s descendants were foreigners and wanderers, I, 542. The request should depend upon the will of the giver, not of the one asking, as shown by the example of Saul and David, V, 1491.

God’s power is joined with goodness, III, 724. What it means to make power in the arm, VI, 1163. One must flee from whoever has power, III, 822. Obedience to higher authorities is strongly commended, V, 1595. Whether God’s predestination is frustrated in Ezekiel, V, 1562. It is fulfilled through prayers, I, 581. Its effect, V, 1467. The preacher of God’s word must labor without ceasing, despising earthly things, III, 362. When and why the preaching of the word is sometimes withdrawn, IV, 585. What the Lord’s commandment is, II, 646, 647. The reward of those who observe it, II, 130 and 877. The commandment concerning observance of the Sabbath, II, 220, 240, 443, 459 and 501. A panegyric on an eminent bishop, VI, 1591. The preface of volume II to Bishop Hunbertus, containing an exhortation, II, 1139. Prelates of the Church ought at times to use gentle admonition and simplicity, II, 1132. Why evil men and bad shepherds sometimes exist in the Church, II, 1133. Under them there is a famine of the word of God, ibid.

What certain prepositions familiar to the holy Apostle Paul signify, V, 1346. How many there are, V, 666. Whether one should obey an evil superior, IV, 180. The law concerning removal of foreskins in the land of Canaan, II, 455. What it signifies mystically to remove the foreskin of the heart, V, 833. God is always present; he knows neither past nor future, VI, 1147. What Christ’s presence on earth was like, I, 1154, 1155: with the reprobate, VI, 1229; and with the elect, ibid. It is better to depart quickly than to live here without fruit, III, 1055. Presumption is seriously forbidden, III, 802. What a praetorium is, V, 388. Why transgressions are shown to human beings, V, 873. Why in one Gospel a meal, and elsewhere a supper, is said to have been prepared by a person, III, 659.

The prayers of the saints resist God’s anger, V, 860. Presbyters who do not diligently promote the worship of God deserve reproof, III, 616. Those formerly called presbyters are now called bishops, VI, 479. The commendation of good presbyters, VI, 623. Their office, VI, 626. At length, VI, 659. Where they derive their name, V, 301. Why they are called priests, ibid. Their office, ibid. See priest.

Payment must be made according to the means by which one has sinned, II, 549. The torments of the martyrs Primus and Felicianus, IV, 1149. The first fruits of all crops and all livestock are owed to the priests, II, 695, 904. Their various allegorical meanings, II, 698, 699. What kind are to be offered, II, 139. What it means literally and mystically to offer the firstborn, II, 59, 60. Why it was forbidden to vow them to the Lord, II, 580. What Jacob’s firstborn, sold by his brother Esau, signifies, I, 582, 583. The distinction between firstborn and only-begotten, V, 1469. Who is Israel’s firstborn, II, 26. Whether Jesus is rightly called the firstborn, I, 553. Where the Apostle found the names Principalities, Powers, Virtues, and Dominations, VI, 397. The various meanings of “beginning” in the creation of the world, I, 443.

Who is the prince of the strong, and his elegant comparison with the hornet, III, 721. Why the devil is called the ruler of the world, II, 116. Who are truly to be considered rulers, V, 447, 448. What they ought to be like, II, 1129. They are required to render an account of the people, II, 769. How they differ from kings, V, 1271. Evil rulers are given by God because of the people’s sins, II, 1128; good rulers are removed prematurely from life because of them, ibid. The people’s saviors are signified by destroying angels, II, 1189. Not all rulers are given by God, II, 1133. Evil rulers are either given by God because of the people’s sins or permitted to rule, ibid. The princes and nobles of the tribes of Israel in building the house of God, III, 412. What it means to sing “for the eighth,” III, 347. The storm signifies persecution, V, 283. Those who fall down through fear of the Lord are raised up by God, IV, 548, 581, 582. Lengthening and shortening of cases in declension, V, 665.

Ears must not be given to those teaching profane things, II, 406. What their purification ought to be, ibid. The multiple meanings of the deep, V, 373. Why Cain’s descendants produced only women, I, 508, 509. The literal and mystical interpretation of Christ’s ancestors, I, 739–744; IV, 461. The more suitable and mature age for procreation, and the years comprised by it, [Col. 1745] II, 569. What kinds of promises were made to Abraham, I, 533, 541. We shall not consider the remarkable promises concerning Solomon’s temple, holiness, and the perpetuity of his kingdom to have been empty or false, since they have been completely fulfilled in Christ, who was born from David’s seed, III, 90, 91, 364–366. Those who do not believe God’s promises will suffer severe punishments, II, 675. The various names of promontories and their meanings, V, 358, 359. Mystically, they signify the doctors of the holy Church, ibid. A beautiful comparison of storehouses with heretics, V, 405.

The prophet who ate food contrary to the Lord’s command and was devoured by lions, V, 190. Whose type he is, ibid. What the four major prophets treat, V, 112, 113. Why they are more obscure, V, 893; likewise the Psalms, ibid. A condensed history of certain prophets, V, 113, 114. The prophets and Apostles, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, were made ready and prompt in writing, V, 1072. Their two kinds, VI, 116. Their office and various kinds, V, 963–985. There are seven kinds of prophecy; see the discussion, V, 101. What it is, III, 611. It is not to be trusted easily, II, 730. A recapitulation of Jeremiah from beginning to end and an adaptation of it to our present morals and life, V, 1268. Its excellence surpasses the gift of tongues; whence it derives its name, VI, 129–137. Prophetic acts are sometimes called portents, V, 199. Prophetesses sewing little pillows beneath the elbow, and the spirit by which they are inspired to prophesy, IV, 655. Who is the neighbor of little children and orphans, V, 755. What the lesser propitiatory is, IV, 994. Its description, ibid.; likewise that of the greater, ibid., 995. The breads of the Presence represent holy teachers, II, 149; III, 318. Their use, II, 149.

Why the Israelites, otherwise the chosen people, are called proselytes and resident foreigners, II, 535. Where they derive their name, III, 422. Prosperity and adversity are to be endured with an even mind, V, 694. The wages of a prostitute and the price of a dog are not to be offered in the house of the Lord, II, 933. What evil is implied by the prostitution of a daughter, II, 459. Who are to be understood by the word neighbor, II, 465. God loves the charity and benefit of one’s neighbor, II, 432, 433. Why the wisdom of the flesh is death, and for whom, V, 1441. It is hostile to God, ibid. The effects of prudence, VI, 1253. What prudence is, IV, 1115; VI, 1632. Frost signifies the malice of the perverse, V, 328. Burning coals signify unlawful desires, V, 279. What it signifies to heap them upon the head, V, 764.

The contents of the Psalms, V, 112. Why Psalm XVII alone from the Book of Kings is found written down, III, 114. The ten-stringed psalter, a fitting type of the Decalogue, III, 1042. The reward of pseudo-apostles, V, 983; VI, 224. Their fellowship must be avoided, VI, 249. Why false prophets are called prophets, IV, 650. How they differ, ibid. They are compared with Samson’s foxes, IV, 652. Who they are tropologically, V, 1021. Those who turn people away from God are to be killed, II, 881. The parrot imitates human voices, V, 246.

Ptolemy Abobi is a figure of hypocrites, III, 1212. The generosity of Saint Pudentiana, virgin and sister, IV, 1115. What the boy of Elisha with the staff signifies, V, 61; and the boy of the centurion, V, 75. Why Christ is called a boy, V, 180. What the Egyptian boy found by David while he was fighting against the Amalekites signifies mystically, III, 695. The boys who mocked Elisha prefigure those who crucified Christ, V, 61. The uncleanness of a woman after childbirth, II, 367. Where this uncleanness arises, ibid. Its purification, ibid., 370. The beauty of the daughter of Zion, V, 848. A woman’s beauty is not to be coveted, V, 704–706. Grace is deceptive, V, 792. What young birds signify and whom they represent, V, 241. The two young pigeons, V, 248. Dust signifies the sinner, V, 331, 457. Its various meanings, VI, 1033. Who place pillows beneath every elbow, IV, 657. God’s punishment is a healing medicine, IV, 609. God faithfully pleads the cause of orphans, the injured poor, and the weeping widow, III, 1016. The interests of orphans and widows must be considered in judgment, III, 785. A remarkable proof of the fire of purgatory, I, 773, 930. What sins are cleansed by this fire, VI, 37. The purification of the Levites, II, 635. A figure of the ecclesiastical order, ibid. Why the feast of the Purification was instituted, IV, 19. How it is to be celebrated, I, 345. Why it is called Hypante, ibid. How one should strive for purity of heart, VI, 1285. A commendation of divine purity, II, 480, 481. The literal and mystical interpretation of the purple in which Christ was clothed, I, 1135. A type of martyrdom, V, 578. Why faintheartedness must be avoided, III, 803. The remedy for avoiding it is prayer, ibid., 804.

What the well of the oath is, and how many kinds there are, I, 565. What it signifies as “seeing” and “living,” I, 576. The well found by Jacob in a field, a figure of baptism, I, 594. The various names of wells and their beautiful significance concerning Christ, V, 324. What it means for those who are said to have wells within themselves, II, 716. What is the one fountain of many, ibid. Heretics boast that they are at this well, but they were not gathered by Moses; therefore their fountain is one of bitumen, II, 717, 718. The use of pyramids among the Egyptians, V, 408. The punishment of pythonesses, II, 472. How the prophet Samuel was raised through their assistance, III, 67.

## Q

The number forty always signifies affliction, IV, 801. This is confirmed by examples, ibid. Why the Lenten fast is observed for forty days, VI, 743. Its observance, IV, 20. The fast arose from the fasts of Moses and Elijah, I, 335, 779. Why it was instituted at that time, ibid. Its mystical interpretation, ibid. The forty-two encampments of the children of Israel through various places in the desert are listed, II, 809 and following. What they signify mystically, ibid. To what persons and how many years they are to be assigned, II, 825. Why a woman who has given birth is unclean for forty days, II, 368, 369. By what offering she is purified, II, 370. The meaning of a quadrans, IV, 328. Why quadrigae are joined to the sun and bigae to the moon, V, 550. What is included under the name quadrupeds, I, 458.

[Col. 1746] How God is rightly to be sought, VI, 688. How the qualities and terms of causes are to be expressed in the beginnings of narratives, II, 92. Who the four thousand men fed from seven loaves are, V, 77. Whom the four kings overcoming five signify, I, 539. What the four wives of Jacob signify, of whom two were free women and two slaves, I, 398 and following. The four golden rings of the altar of incense signify the four books of the Gospels, II, 210. Which regions of the world the four quarters properly signify, II, 603, 609. The four wheels are a figure of the four books of the Gospels, and why, III, 447, 1153. The four principal virtues, III, 706. They are bestowed by God alone, III, 707. What the four rivers of Paradise, proceeding from one source, signify mystically, III, 943. What four things arise from the heart, III, 727. What the four living creatures seen by Ezekiel prefigured, IV, 505. Their description, IV, 507, 514. How they are said to go and not to go, IV, 524. Why they are full of eyes, IV, 530. The description and mystical meaning of the four stone tables, IV, 940, 945, 948, 949, 951. Why their rims are turned back, IV, 955. What the four smallest things of the earth are, and which are most wise, V, 577. The complaining murmur of the people against Uzziah, III, 613; and against other superiors, III, 617. The description and mystical meaning of multiplied quinary numbers, IV, 909. The mystical meaning of numbers of fifty, II, 161, 189. The Jubilee is to be celebrated in the fiftieth year, II, 529. Its freedom from obligations, ibid. In it, interest is not to be taken from brothers on goods bought or sold, ibid. Why God promised to spare Sodom if fifty righteous persons were found, I, 554. Who the five thousand men fed with five loaves and two fish are, V, 77. David’s five stones bear the type of Moses’ five books, III, 52. The functions of the five senses, IV, 1119.

Rabanus presided over the monastery for twenty years, I, 66. He relinquished his office, ibid. He withdrew to the Church of Saint Peter, ibid. He wrote very many books; see them all, ibid. At the age of thirty he published two books in praise of the holy Cross, I, 66, 85. Rabanus, superior to all in learning, was sent by Abbot Ratgarius to Rome with Bishop Haimo, later bishop of Halberstadt, and Diedo, to Albinus the Englishman, in order to continue his studies, I, 76. Rabanus, another Augustine, terror and hammer of heretics, I, 76. Rabanus, cultivated in every kind of discipline, was recalled from Rome to Fulda with his companions, I, 76. Rabanus was ordained to the priesthood at the age of thirty, I, 78. He was loved by everyone, ibid. Rabanus was the first of all in Germany to teach publicly at the monastery of Fulda, at the age of twenty-five, ibid. Disciples from Germany and Gaul flocked to him, ibid. Several of his distinguished hearers are listed by Megenfrid, ibid. Rabanus was entrusted to the monk Rathgarius for instruction, I, 73. Rabanus excelled among all as a man of great promise, I, 73.

[Col. 1747] Rabanus became archbishop of Mainz, I, 97. He celebrated a synod, I, 99. The doctrines, fraud, and punishment of Thierda the false prophetess, I, 98. During his administration Rabanus built thirty oratories for relics, I, 65. At the age of nine Rabanus was solemnly committed to the monastery of Fulda under Abbot Bangolf, I, 72. Rabanus personally carried out all pontifical functions by preaching and teaching, I, 102. Rabanus became the fifth abbot of Fulda at the age of thirty-seven and presided for twenty-two years, I, 86. His diligence after his election, ibid. Rabanus was summoned to the court of King Louis of Germany, I, 97. When summoned to return, he declined, ibid. Rabanus’s profound humility, I, 76. His tireless diligence by night and by day, I, 76. Rabanus’s method and aim in teaching, I, 78. He repels the wandering and disorderly, I, 82. He was the first to teach the purity of the Greek and Latin languages, I, 83. Rabanus’s praise and eulogy among all, I, 86–97. Rabanus’s devotion to letters and monastic discipline, I, 44. Rabanus’s devotion to collecting holy relics, I, 44–55. Rabanus’s birth, education, gifts, and stature, I, 71. Rabanus’s generosity toward the poor and those oppressed by hunger, I, 100, 102. Rabanus’s dwellings or residences, I, 102. Catalogue of Rabanus’s books, I, 103. Rabanus’s diligence, praise, and learning, I, 104, 105. Rabanus’s death, foretold by an angel, I, 106. Rabanus’s passing, made glorious by the psalmody of angels, I, 106. Rabanus’s epitaph, miracles, and translation, I, 106. Another brief account of Rabanus’s life, I, 106, 107. Rabanus’s gentleness and severity in correcting, I, 88. Every day he meditates on the Lord’s Passion, ibid. He is the father of the destitute and the host of the needy, ibid. He has many rivals, I, 89, 90. His care for the dead, I, 90. Rabanus’s letter to Bishop Hemmo, V, 11. Rabanus’s letter to King Louis, V, 9. Rabanus’s examples for Freculphus concerning his Commentary on the Pentateuch of Moses, I, 541. Verses of Rabanus Maurus from the book on the holy Cross, addressed to Saint Martin, VI, 1583. A Frank by nationality but an Easterner, ibid. He lived among the people of Tours, ibid. 1587 (note). His prayer to God, VI, 1588 (note). Verses to a friend, VI, 1585. He embraces the more notable events and the names of the prophets and patriarchs of the Old Testament in a brief poem, VI, 1593. He requests a supply of books, VI, 1602. His devotion to poverty, VI, 1603. His epitaph, VI, 1671. His defense of his poems, VI, 1584 (note). His acrostics are praised, VI, 1585, 1586 (note). When it was written, ibid. The dates are noted, ibid. His intimacy with Bishop Frederick, VI, 1662. His Hymnody, VI, 1663 (note). Translation, VI, 1649 (note). He is numbered among the saints, ibid. Germany owes very much to Rabanus, I, 83. See there what disciplines he taught. Ambushes were laid for Rabanus, I, 99. The interpretation of the Pentateuch was imposed upon Rabanus, I, 489.

Rabshakeh—who he was, III, 252. Traitor of Jerusalem, III, 252. Blasphemer and liar, III, 253.

Racha—what it means, IV, 358; I, 806.

[Col. 1747] Rachel is called “sheep of God,” V, 40. As one who hides idols, she is a type of the Church, I, 607, 763. She dies because of the difficulty of childbirth, I, 903. How she mourns the sons of Judah as though they were her own, V, 773.

Patience—the root and guardian of all virtues, I, 903. The manner of practicing it, V, 425.

Ramath-sophim—the city where Elkanah lived, III, 11. It was the homeland of Joseph of Arimathea, ibid. In Hebrew, “their height,” III, 14.

Rameses—what land it was, I, 648; II, 62.

Branches of wisdom—what they signify, III, 769.

Frogs—the type of loquacious poets, II, 35; V, 228. They die while Moses is praying, II, 35, 36.

To rob the poor—what it means, V, 1225.

Paul’s rapture—the twofold kind of rapture, VI, 231, 232.

Eulogy of Ratgarius, Abbot of Fulda, VI, 1599 (note). His offices, ibid. Schism under him, VI, 1621 (note). He dies, I, 86.

Regensburg—where it is situated, VI, 1589 (note). The antiquity and splendor of its title, ibid.

The rationale—what it signifies, II, 193. Its construction, ibid.

The guilt of judgment, of the council, and of Gehenna—the distinction among them, I, 806; IV, 358.

Rebecca—why she was brought to Isaac on the back of a camel, I, 578. When she saw Isaac, she covered herself with a cloak: a type of the holy Church, ibid. How she learned of Jacob’s ambush, when Esau had conceived it in his thought, I, 590.

Reblatha is said to mean “multitude,” V, 63.

The obedience and blessing of the Rechabites, V, 1069. Whom they signify mystically, ibid.

To remember—how Jeremiah asks the Lord to remember, although everything is known to him, V, 1262.

To offer rightly—what it means figuratively, I, 504.

Rectitude and simplicity—inseparable companions, V, 689, 691.

The office of a ruler, V, 1237.

The merits of rulers and of the people are often joined together, III, 120. Their qualities and office, III, 121.

Reda—what it means, V, 608.

The entire cause of redemption and salvation consists in the Incarnation of Jesus, II, 1167. It was accomplished by Christ’s precious blood, and not by silver, VI, 1092.

Those who redeem the time, VI, 453.

The refreshment of the righteous seized by death beforehand—what it is like, III, 686.

Cities of refuge—which they are, II, 111. Their mystical explanations, II, 833, 907.

Spiritual and carnal regeneration—what they are, IV, 283.

Kings are interpreted as apostles and other saints, V, 708.

Kings, judges, and preachers of the word of God exhort people to pursue wisdom and justice, showing how severe a punishment threatens unjust rulers, III, 693.

The Queen of Sheba—an outstanding proclamation concerning her and Solomon’s wisdom, III, 195. A type of the Church, III, 469.

The region of the saints—what it is, VI, 1095; V, 1048.

The transfer of kingdoms from one nation to another—whence it comes, III, 827.

Kingdom—where the word is derived from, V, 445. The most eminent kingdoms are those of the Assyrians and Romans, ibid. The instability of a kingdom divided against itself, I, 927. The kingdom of death—what it is, V, 1381. Where its destruction began, ibid. In whom it exists, V, 1383. Why and to what earthly things the kingdom of heaven is compared, I, 954, 955. It is eternal, IV, 424. Its uncertainty, V, 709. Its terror, IV, 425.

[Col. 1748] The threefold rule of the Scriptures in our heart, VI, 565.

Why the order of kings and times is not observed in the prophecies of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, V, 968.

The mystical meanings of kings, V, 445. Who are truly to be considered kings, I, 1616. Subjects are formed according to their example, II, 222; III, 824. They must avoid excessive pomp, II, 903. Why wine must not be given to them, V, 779, 780. The destruction of fools, III, 825. Their office, V, 1146. Why the Assyrians are called lions, V, 967. The Roman Caesars, V, 1146. The contents of the books of Kings and Chronicles, V, 111.

Religion—what it is and what it requires. Its worship requires three things, V, 90.

Relics of Saints Alexander, pope and martyr, Urban, and various other saints, I, 50. Of Saints Quirinus and several others, I, 49. Those of the martyr Venantius shine with very many miracles; see them all. Many, dripping blood, are to be examined at length, I, 50–67.

The remains of sacrifices—to be burned, II, 644, 645.

Remissions of sins—how many there are, II, 261.

The rebuke between Saint Peter and Paul—what kind it was, IV, 924, 925. Rebuking friends, V, 1594.

The reprobate sometimes abound in delights, while the elect abound in tribulation—and why, III, 126. Why the reprobate are to be tormented in eternal fires, III, 1049.

The deeds of certain reprobate kings, in a manner not unfittingly, correspond figuratively to our Redeemer according to the testimony of Sacred Scripture and the holy Fathers, III, 638.

The various harms of the promise, III, 967.

The literal and figurative meaning of creeping animals, II, 365. When and why they were created, I, 456.

Those repudiated—which ones, IV, 1013. Why priests were forbidden to marry a repudiated woman, ibid. How the bill of repudiation was given by God to the Jews, V, 824. Why it was permitted by Moses, II, 935.

“Resting with the lion and its cubs”—Christ is understood on the cross, II, 754.

Three kinds of rest, VI, 730, 733. How one is to enter the heavenly rest, VI, 733. The rest of the elect in this life, VI, 1129.

Resheph—“creeping on the belly,” VI, 1118, 1119.

Resin figures repentance, V, 1097, 1163.

Moses’ answer to the people of Israel, II, 116.

The first inventors of responsories were Italians, I, 363.

The restoration of human beings—among whom it was accomplished, VI, 390.

How God is said to restore penitents, V, 935. When he does so by himself and when through other ministers, V, 1152.

When the restoration of the people of Israel was completed, V, 939.

The risen Christ—to whom he appeared, II, 642.

What the Lord’s Resurrection, called into question by the apostles, confers upon us, IV, 182. How it occurred, IV, 189. The commendation of its grace and evangelical teaching, V, 715, 718, 723. Its proof, IV, 140–288.

The reward of human favor is not to be sought, as Christ’s example shows, IV, 361.

The king who knew Joseph and the one who did not—who they were, and how the former is a fitting type of Christ, II, 11.

Christ mourning—and why, IV, 618.

The definition and usefulness of rhetoric, I, 306. It is a champion of truth, ibid.

The office of the rhetorician, I, 410. The holy Apostle Paul used its precepts, ibid.

The rhinoceros—whom it signifies; see V, 220.

The double-edged sword—what it is, III, 902.

The location and meaning of Mount Riphaeus, V, 363.

Sarah’s laughter at the son already promised—what it signifies, I, 552. It often reveals folly, III, 908.

One who asks rightly does not go away disappointed from God, III, 712.

The rite of cession in raising up offspring from the wife of a kinsman who died without children—what it was among the Jews, II, 1218.

Sacrifices and libations, II, 293, 295, 329 ff.

Description of the priesthood of the Old Testament, III, 1087. How many kinds of its vestments there were, and what they were, ibid.

The various kinds of quarrels and the punishments for each, II, 112. They are to be avoided, V, 767.

Rehoboam—how he can be called a young man when he was forty-one years old, III, 483. The etymology of his name, ibid. A type of wicked rulers of the Church, ibid. Because of his sins he is deprived of the treasures of the land of Egypt, III, 484, 1096. A typological note, V, 59.

Why the days of Rogations were instituted, IV, 37.

The spring of Rogel, V, 317.

The Passion of Saint Romanus the Martyr, IV, 1179.

The praise of the Romans, V, 1287.

Dew signifies the word of the Lord, V, 328. It also signifies the teaching of preachers, ibid.

The rose presents a type of Christ, V, 528.

The construction of the wheels seen by Ezekiel, IV, 525, 635. Their height and stature, ibid. Whom they typify, ibid. Their various mystical meanings, IV, 528. Their twofold spirit denotes the two Testaments and love of God and neighbor, IV, 637.

Reuben is interpreted as “son of vision,” V, 43. He violated his father’s bed, and what this signifies mystically, I, 618. What it means that he gave mandrakes to his mother, V, 43. He wages war against Christians, II, 1145. Because of unlawful intercourse he is deprived of the birthright, III, 309.

The bush—a type of the Blessed Virgin, V, 513.

Simple doctrine and milk are to be offered to the inexperienced and imperfect, III, 20.

The downfall of princes is rightly to be mourned, III, 73.

Heretics are compared with animals that chew the cud, and why, II, 352. Their discernment, II, 911.

Ruth—why she is called “hastening,” V, 111. Her history, V, 57. How she entered the Church, although entry into the Church was forbidden to Moabites, II, 1201. The various peoples who were not permitted to enter the Church, ibid. She lies at the feet of Boaz and covers herself with his cloak, 1212. She is praised by Boaz for her continence, ibid. A type of the Church gathered from the nations, II, 1215. She became Boaz’s wife, 1220. She bore Obed, II, 1221. Why she is counted in Christ’s genealogy, although Moabites were forbidden to enter the Temple, IV, 465.

## S

The Sabbath commandment properly pertains to the Holy Spirit, and why, II, 862. Its observance, IV, 722, 1015. What it is, II, 444. Its sanctification, II, 781. Why the holy day must also be observed with ritual, V, 60. What is signified by the man gathering wood on it, V, 308; II, 679–680.

The sackcloth of penitents is a type, V, 604.

Every priest was a Levite, but not every Levite was a priest, II, 938. Who should be ordained a priest, III, 21. He must be chaste, III, 20; holy and zealous against sinners, III, 21. His name and attire, V, 92. He must devote himself to virtue, II, 196, 475. When priests are punished for the sins of the people, III, 21. They sin more gravely in contaminating and despising sacred things and God, ibid. They are to be honored for God’s sake, III, 806. They must render an account of their subjects, III, 617. Hidden matters are to be revealed to them, II, 376–377.

The seven trumpets sounding before the ark represent the grace of the Holy Spirit and various other mysteries, III, 348. Firstfruits are owed even to ministers of the Gospel, II, 697–698 and 904; III, 807.

The power of distinguishing between clean and unclean was delegated to priests alone, III, 243. The priesthood of the Old Law was abolished through Christ, III, 23. The priests of the Old Law were indignant at Christ, ibid.

What the sanctuary signifies, V, 391.

One sacrifice is called “salutary,” another “of praise,” and another “of vow,” II, 312, 314.

Who is sacrilegious, V, 1383.

The doctrine of the Sadducees, V, 95. The etymology of the doctrine and heresy, I, 770.

The use of Cilician sackcloth garments, II, 164, 166. Mystically they represent the rulers of the Church, ibid.

What the arrows of the Lord’s salvation shot by Elisha signify, III, 244. Why they are called arrows, V, 539. The Cretans were their first inventors, ibid. Their mystical interpretations vary, ibid. What drunken arrows signify, VI, 1150. Which nation knew the art of archery best, V, 815.

What salt signifies allegorically, V, 460. Various opinions concerning its origin, ibid. Its use and nature, ibid. Why the Apostles are called “the salt of the earth,” I, 801. Its nature and use, ibid. [Col. 1750]

Salem is interpreted as “peace,” I, 166.

What the south signifies, IV, 729. Why Ezekiel was commanded to prophesy against it, ibid.

The superstition of the Samaritans, V, 95.

What “Samem” means in Punic, II, 1122.

The spring of Sames, V, 317.

Samgar is interpreted as “foreigner,” V, 55. He is a figure of the preaching of evangelical goods, II, 1131–1132, 1140. He frees Israel from impending war, II, 1131. He kills the Philistines with a plowshare, ibid. Likewise calves and oxen, ibid.

Samgar.

The Samian was the first to invent pottery vessels, V, 356.

Samson means the same as “strength of the sun,” and is a figure of Christ, V, 57. He avenges the abduction of his wife, II, 1193. The sons of Judah come to him and demand an account of this deed, ibid. He kills a thousand men with an ass’s jawbone, ibid., 1196. This jawbone signifies the person of humble preachers, ibid. He takes a prostitute at Gaza, ibid. He leaves the city after carrying away its gates, ibid. In this deed he was a figure of Christ, ibid. His riddle interpreted mystically, ibid. He kills thirty men at Ashkelon, ibid. He sends foxes into the grain, signifying the devil making war upon the strong through the weak, ibid. The jawbone with which he conquered a thousand men signifies the patience of Christians, ibid. What is indicated by his hair, ibid. The Holy Spirit departs from him, ibid. What he signifies, ibid. and 1197. His eyes are torn out, and what this means morally, ibid. His overthrowing the house is a type of Christ and of Christians conquering vices and demons, ibid. Whether he should rightly be numbered among the saints, VI, 804.

Samuel means “his name is God,” and is a type of the new priesthood, V, 58. Born of barren parents; in Hebrew, “petition of God,” or “his name is God,” III, 13. Weaned and brought to the temple, III, 15. Clothed in a linen ephod, III, 20. A priest most pleasing to God, III, 23. Chosen and praised by God, ibid. He had degenerate sons, ibid. Called three times by God during the night, he finally learns of the destruction of Eli and his sons, [Col. 1751] III, 23. How he is said not to have known the Lord, ibid. He is heard while interceding for the people, III, 33. His praise, ibid. He struck down the enemies as far as Beth-car, ibid. Each year he traveled through the cities, exercising judgment and administering justice, ibid. He built an altar at Ramah, III, 34. He had four degenerate and wicked sons, III, 35. God comforts him, ibid. He tells Saul about the lost she-asses and foretells the kingdom, ibid. He rebukes the people for asking for a king, III, 39. By his prayers he obtains rain, ibid. He rebukes Saul for sparing King Agag, III, 45. He declares that Saul has been rejected by God, III, 49. In anger he rejects the supplicant Saul, III, 49. His praise and piety, III, 1094. Since he did not see Saul until death, how is he said to have prophesied with him? III, 56. What kind of fellow student Samuel was with Rabanus, VI, 1601–1602, 1206.

The Holy of Holies: from where it obtained its name, V, 392. Its construction and mystical meaning, IV, 971, 974.

Descriptions of the relics of the saints and the monuments of Fulda, VI, 1677.

In what sense some are called both saints and sinners, II, 691. The holy Fathers help us by their prayers and strengthen us by their examples, II, 807. He intercedes for us, ibid.

Whether the holy patriarchs and prophets sinned by doing what belongs to the Law, VI, 317. How they lived under the Law, VI, 351.

The holiness of the Fathers often causes blessing for their children, V, 811.

The leech is Satan, V, 235. Its two daughters are luxury and avarice, V, 776.

No one is so wise that he cannot become wiser, V, 680. What their multitude means, III, 696.

Christ is God’s eternal wisdom, III, 765. It is incomprehensible, ibid. It is accessible to all, III, 694. Its acquisition is beneficial, ibid. The envious person is incapable of it, ibid. What steps are necessary for one who desires to acquire it together with charity, I, 380–381; V, 1193. These virtues are its inseparable companions, ibid.

What kind of person Shemaiah the Nehelamite was, V, 1082.

In what sense all things are said to have been created by God simultaneously, III, 880.

Mount Sinai represents the synagogue of the Jews, V, 360; II, 1140.

How “Leave me” is to be interpreted, II, 227.

Zion is translated as “watchtower” or “contemplation,” V, 360, 379. It aptly bears the type of the Church, ibid.

What Sior is, V, 324.

Sisera, commander of Jabin the Canaanite’s army: his power, II, 1152. In Hebrew, “vision of a horse”; a type of the impious and of animal-like people, II, 1153; V, 56. He is killed by Jael through cunning, ibid. The nail driven through his mouth: a type of what, ibid.

What the position and condition of the human body signify, V, 178.

From where the bucket received its name, V, 600–601.

What Shobal signifies literally and figuratively, III, 286.

The commendation of sobriety, III, 989. The condemnation of gluttony, ibid.

The fellowship of wicked people must be avoided, IV, 557.

Peter’s mother-in-law, suffering from fever and cured by the Lord, represents the synagogue of the Jews, I, 860; V, 75.

Sodom and Gomorrah, reduced to a wilderness because of unspeakable crimes; only Lot, accompanied by wisdom, escaped, III, 717. Their interpretation, V, 380, 688. The conflagration, ibid. Why Sodom is said to have been justified by comparison with Jerusalem, V, 829, 883, 1253. What their sins were, IV, 453–454. Their land resembled paradise, I, 536.

Why the sun and moon are called great lights, I, 455. How they are signs of times, days, and years, ibid. The origin of the eclipse of each, IV, 79.

What the sun signifies, V, 267. The sun represents preachers of the word of God, and why, V, 825. It stood motionless in its course for one day, III, 1091. Changing its course for Hezekiah’s safety, it was later superstitiously worshiped by some as a god, III, 261.

The comparison of sundials with the divine offices, V, 391.

The solemnities of weekdays and the Sabbath, II, 501. Of Passover, ibid. Why it was celebrated not on the fourteenth day but on the first day of unleavened bread, ibid. The manner of celebrating it, ibid. The solemnities of firstfruits, Weeks, and the harvest are also described, II, 503. Of the trumpets, II, 509. A type of Christ, ibid.

The first use of solid gold coins, V, 353.

A literal and mystical description of the ivory throne, III, 463. God’s throne, V, 1000.

The benefit of solitude and the harm of crowds, III, 887.

“Anxiety” has a twofold interpretation, V, 716.

What soil is, V, 366. Paternal soil is dear to all, V, 868.

From where Solurius received his name, V, 363.

The one who alone is to be sought, because he alone did not commit sin, II, 777.

Joseph is hated when he tells his dreams to his brothers, II, 623. What this signifies mystically, ibid., 630.

The sin and expiation of a nocturnal dream, II, 931.

Who is fit to interpret a dream, V, 986.

What sweet sleep is, V, 1039. It must be avoided, V, 744.

The literal and allegorical interpretation of Zophar, III, 278.

Those who speak sophistically are hateful to God, III, 1028. Their various kinds, ibid.

Why Zephaniah is called a mirror, V, 69.

What the sleep infused into Adam signifies, I, 484. Sleep attributed to the Lord, III, 50.

The shrew, called Saurix by the ancients, V, 225.

Everyone must use his lot well, II, 536. The nature of its assignment in the Old and New Testaments, IV, 1063. Lots are governed by the Lord, V, 736.

What a spectacle is, V, 553.

The various kinds of apparitions, V, 433.

What a watchtower is, II, 1188. Mystically, pride, ibid. What it means to set one up for oneself, V, 1038.

Who a watchman properly is, IV, 575–576.

What a cave signifies literally and mystically, V, 373. A cavern denotes the hardness of sinners, V, 373.

Cursed is the one who places hope in a human being, V, 946.

Thorns designate sinners, V, 256. What thorns growing in the hands of a drunkard signify, II, 168; V, 765. What the thorny ground is, VI, 750.

How Christians must fight against vices with the spiritual sword, II, 769.

Those who follow their own spirit easily stumble, IV, 650–651.

The spiritual person cries out to God in affliction, II, 1133.

From where the Holy Spirit proceeds and what names he bears, V, 23. He is signified by the south wind, V, 275. He is present in every action free from sin, I, 715. Without his grace we can do nothing, III, 660. The mind of heretics is incapable of his sanctification, I, 816. Why he appeared as fire among the Apostles but as a dove in Christ, I, 777. His various operations, ibid. Why he abandons a human being, V, 1545. Whether he comes from works of the Law or from hearing, VI, 285. Why our Lord gave him once while standing on earth and once while presiding in heaven, ibid.

The many meanings of “spirit,” V, 141–142; VI, 1056. How it differs from the soul, V, 141–143. At the creation of the world it moved over the waters; after the flood had ended, it was again brought over the earth, I, 519. The Lord’s spirits: in whom they rest, II, 658. The Lord’s spirit that departed from Samson: what kind and what sort, II, 1199. The spirit of the Lord that tormented Saul: in what sense it should be called evil, III, 50. What it signifies, V, 685. How the soul, while completing itself, can be both movable and stable, IV, 523–524. The spirits created for vengeance, III, 1045. The principal spirits and their effects, V, 880–883. When Moses’ spirit was troubled, God distributed his burden among the seventy elders, all of whom prophesied, II, 657. How God gave them some of Moses’ spirit, ibid.

The Israelites take spoil from the Egyptians, II, 22.

What a voluntary sacrifice is, II, 313. When it is lawful to eat from it, ibid. What the voluntary sacrifice of princes is like, IV, 1045. The gifts they bestow on their heirs, ibid.

One must labor to release a sponsor from the faith he has pledged, V, 702.

Who the “bridegroom of blood” is, II, 26.

The mystical meaning of the baskets containing the Lord’s fragments, I, 985.

What kind of animal a sponge is and what it signifies mystically, V, 238.

Hercules, founder of stadia, V, 412.

The nature and interpretation of a pond, V, 316–317. What Gennesaret is, V, 478.

How standing and sitting differ in human beings, V, 178. Likewise running, lying down, and so forth, ibid.

What the balance signifies, V, 485. What a deceitful balance is, V, 716–746.

What a station signifies, V, 372.

The star of Jacob: the star that appeared in the East, II, 757.

The stars are signs of the seasons, I, 455. How they differ from constellations and heavenly bodies, and what they signify, V, 272. Their various meanings, VI, 1052. They indicate the future condition of the air and the watches of the night, I, 455.

What it means to eat dung and drink urine, III, 254.

Why God imposed barrenness upon Hannah and upon holy men and women, III, 11. The barrenness of fields: whence it comes, V, 981.

Marks must not be branded on the body, II, 458.

The significance of dripping water, V, 326.

Why the apostle was given a thorn in the flesh, VI, 234.

For the various meanings of a robe, see VI, 1060.

The stomach is the gate of wind, V, 175. Its meaning in Scripture, ibid.

What storax signifies, III, 933.

Who Strabo was, Rabanus’s successor in the school at Fulda, and how distinguished. He wrote many works in prose and verse, I, 86.

The ostrich represents hypocrites, the synagogue, and heretics, V, 246, 1249. How it glorifies God, V, 246. Its hardening toward its young, V, 1249.

The task of ecclesiastical scholars is to contemplate the wisdom of the patriarchs and prophets, [Col. 1756] etc., III, 1038. They devote their hearts to vigilance and labor without interruption to propagate Christ’s vineyard, III, 1038. God is their helper, ibid. Their fruit, ibid.

The instability of fools, III, 963, 1000. How their questions should be answered, V, 764. Their various kinds, VI, 41.

The condemnation of foolish speech, VI, 447, 645.

Who is a fool, V, 714, 728, 736. Why he does not find wisdom, V, 727, 747.

One looking through a window into a house is a type of heretics, III, 908.

Saint Sturm, first abbot of Fulda, I, 73, 86.

Much must be granted to subjects so that their obedience may be more willing and they may not collapse under the burden, III, 46.

What those who mock their father are to be called, V, 776.

What the mockery and laughter of God will be like, V, 685.

Whether, according to the definition of Marcion and Valentinus, any substance is hostile to God, II, 626.

Whether it is lawful to investigate God’s name too curiously, II, 414–415.

The literal and typological interpretation of the suburbs, I, 104.

It is shown by the example of Moses that one must not always ascend to the helm of government by succession, II, 778. Likewise that of the Lord God, II, 903.

The boar fights with the asp, V, 225.

The power of sulfur, V, 457. Its four kinds, V, 458. Mystically it denotes carnal desires, ibid. What the sulfur consuming Sodom and Gomorrah signifies mystically, I, 518.

How the high priest is said to have been forbidden to attend his father’s funeral, although he succeeded him in office, II, 478.

The dead son of the Shunammite represents the human race, V, 67.

Why the serpent walks upon its breast, I, 495.

Pride is crushed by Christ’s humility, II, 1150–1151. Mortals scarcely escape it, III, 45. Still fewer are those who rule over or excel others, ibid. How it is to be avoided, ibid. Its seriousness and condemnation, III, 827; IV, 110, 689; VI, 1240, 1581. The remedy against it, VI, 1382. Its nature and origin, VI, 1351. Its two kinds, ibid. It is hated by God, ibid. The fall of our first parents must be attributed more to it than to the serpent’s cunning, I, 486–487. For what purpose their temptation was permitted, ibid. What sort of serpent this was, ibid. The various ways in which it tempted our parents, ibid. How the prophet calls it the root of all evils when the Apostle attributes this to greed, III, 829. The differing effects of both, III, 831–834.

The destruction of the proud, III, 1149. How they should be entreated, V, 723. Association with them is dangerous, III, 849.

What the shoulder-piece is and its use, II, 192–193. Why it was commanded first, I, 306.

Superiors and prelates must both live well and correct their subjects, III, 21. Their sins against God are graver than those of the people and must be expiated by greater repentance, ibid.

From where superstition received its name, V, 95. The condemnation of magical superstitions, IV, 80.

The tribulations of those who ask for punishments, III, 617.

Whom the deaf signify, V, 75.

How one must rise with Christ, IV, 141.

The sow. See Pig.

Susanna is called a figure of the Church; [her name signifies] its grace or lilies, V, 66. Her integrity, IV, 1161.

One hanged on a gallows, and the reason why he must be removed and buried, is a type of every baptized person, II, 918.

Who the whisperer and the double-tongued person are, III, 794.

From where shoemakers received their name, V, 526.

What a syllable is, V, 617–634. More concerning the joining of long and short syllables, ibid.

When and for what purpose the Apostles composed the Creed, I, 368. Its complete exposition, IV, 27; VI, 1224. What it contains and how many forms it has, V, 136, 746.

The torture of Saint Symphorosa and her sons, IV, 1157.

The etymology of synagogue, its distinction from the Church, and its mystical meaning, V, 90; III, 700, 762. It is a concubine and will believe Antichrist, who will be born from it, II, 1171. It is deserted and barren and asks about its own destruction, II, 1203. It can heal no one, II, 1216. It preceded the Church in time, but not in grace, ibid.

Syria: from where—
named, and its situation and length, V, 339. Its mystical interpretation, ibid. Its provinces, ibid. An inborn and insatiable passion for commerce, IV, 776.

## T

How that which touches the Tabernacle is said in Leviticus to be sanctified, whereas elsewhere a foreigner who touches it is said to die, II, 606. From what it was formed, V, 408. Its mystical interpretation, ibid. What is meant by the holy things of God, II, 615–616. All its parts are fitted to them, ibid. The form and construction of the Mosaic Tabernacle, II, 158–159. Its dimensions, ibid. A type of the holy Church, ibid. Its variety of colors, II, 245. When it was constructed, II, 245. Various meanings, VI, 1062.

Why taverns are so called, V, 388. Why the tablets of the covenant are said to have been written by the hand of God. The breaking and restoration of the Old and New Testaments as a type, II, 872. What the boarded floors are, and their use and prescription, III, 146. Why they were made of cedar, III, 149.

One must be silent when fruit does not follow words, III, 995. Praise of silence, III, 895. Its forms, IV, 574. How God is said to be touched by grief, I, 513. The twofold weariness of the ungodly, III, 722. The mole as a figure of evil people, V, 226. Why Thanatos is said to derive from the death of serpents, V, 364. Why Christ did not wish to be touched by Mary, IV, 162.

The fertility, latitude, and pleasantness of the island of Taprobane, V, 355. One must not delay in conversion to God, IV, 104. From where Tartarus derives its name, V, 374. The name and mysteries of the bull, V, 207. Bull-beetles, V, 256. Which month Tebeth is, III, 649. Nothing should be attempted rashly, I, 554. When Paul forbade rash judgment, whether he used the same expression in writing to the Philippians, VI, 1363.

A full description of temperance and its parts, VI, 1255. Its effects, III, 236–237. Tempest: see *Whirlwind*. The structure and proportions of Solomon’s Temple, III, 142, 424. The length of its beams, III, 144. In how many years it was begun and completed, III, 165, 424. From where “temple” derives its name, V, 392. What it signifies mystically, ibid. What is the true temple of the Lord, V, 858. The destruction of the material and mystical temple, V, 1006. Solomon’s distribution of those who stood by and administered the sacred matters into various divisions and offices, III, 240.

[Col. 1757]

Temporal things must not be accumulated with excessive zeal, III, 840. Nor should one trust or glory in them, ibid. A description and interpretation of the ages, V, 283. Their changes, V, 301. Whether they existed before the world, II, 454. Careful consideration must be given to them, III, 787. The meaning of darkness, V, 294. Its location, I, 448. Whether darkness was created before light, I, 445. Who are enclosed in darkness, III, 751. What it signifies mystically in the day. What the outer darknesses are, I, 859.

Temptation, VI, 1591. What Christ’s temptation in the desert was like, I, 780. Its twofold prayer, V, 1107, 1147. How the Apostle recalls that he did not despise it in his own flesh among the Galatians, VI, 333. The end of the righteous, III, 651. How God is said to have tempted Abraham, although according to others he tempts no one, I, 566.

What a tent is, V, 128. A figure of the Church, ibid. The misery and disadvantages of the lukewarm, VI, 350. How many kinds of terebinth there are, III, 938. It figures the Church, ibid. The boundaries of the Fathers must not be transgressed, V, 748. The number three signifies the Holy Trinity, II, 1162. The three hundred soldiers of Gideon signify those who take up Christ’s cross, ibid., 1163.

Before Adam’s fall the earth produced nothing harmful, I, 462. “Earth” is so called from *terere*, “to wear away,” I, 451. Mystically it signifies the hearts of earthly people, V, 829. What the earth of tribulation is, VI, 1108. It is taken for water, ibid. What the late earth is, V, 822. Also the earth flowing with milk and honey, V, 890. What the earth of tribulation is, V, 1093. The holy land inhabited by the ungodly, II, 669–670. It is cursed on account of Adam’s transgression, I, 497. Earthly things are often given so that affection may be stirred toward heavenly things, II, 21. How the saints abandon them, V, 779. What concern for earthly things belongs to spiritual people, VI, 55.

Why on the third day it was forbidden to eat the flesh of sacrifices, II, 314. From where Thessaly derives its name, V, 349. How many covenants there are, II, 314. The covenant placed between God and humanity is explained literally and mystically, I, 524. A careful enumeration of the books of the Old Testament, I, 364. Likewise of the New Testament, I, 365. Their individual authors, ibid. Their interpreters, I, 365. The covenant between God and the children of Israel, II, 220–221. From whom it is far removed, III, 870. What is signified by its being confirmed over the head of Jacob, III, 1086. When the New Testament is to be completed, IV, 907. The benefits displayed to us in it, ibid.

How heretics use the testimonies of Scripture, IV, 822. The various kinds of Christ’s testimonies, IV, 173. The requirements for witnesses, V, 546–547. The proper manner of hearing witnesses, II, 909. The punishment of false witnesses, according to the Council of Arles, VI, 1411; II, 909; V, 740. A corrupt text concerning the sale of land, II, 535–536. Concerning the origin of Judith, III, 558. Lyranus’s not implausible view of this, ibid.

The interpretation of Thabor as “the coming light,” V, 362. A type of Christ, ibid.; III, 38. See its various meanings, V, 1102. The word “bridal chamber” introduced through an oracle, V, 390. A type of the Blessed Virgin, ibid. A description of the temple’s surrounding structure, IV, 901–902. How Tamar is a type of the Church, V, 49. See also the historical account of Tamar, II, 1220. A type of the Jews, III, 289. What Thecua is, V, 847.

What Theman is and where it is situated, III, 287; VI, 1115. Praise of contemplation, V, 1228. What hot springs are, V, 388. What a *theristrum* is, I, 574. What the treasure hidden in a field signifies, V, 411, 1088. The Lord’s treasure is the Church, V, 1149. Buried treasure, like hidden wisdom, benefits no one, III, 901 and 1059. Semiramis, queen of Assyria, inventor of the tiara, V, 579.

Why the Apostle sent an epistle to the Thessalonians, VI, 540–541. Timothy is sent to advise them, VI, 549. The use of the tiara or mitre, II, 202–203. How it was made, ibid. Thile is said to derive from the sun, and why, V, 354. Topheth designates hell, III, 267, 515. Tola succeeds Abimelech as judge and judges Israel for twenty-three years, III, 1175. From where Thrace received its name, V, 348. Its location and breadth, ibid.

The ivory throne surrounded by lions signifies the Church, III, 195, 477. A description of frankincense, III, 934–935. The incense signifies the power of prayer, II, 211. What burning it morning and evening signifies, II, 211. Its composition, ibid., 219. The tiger as a figure of the devil, V, 219. The river, V, 319.

For one who fears God nothing is difficult, III, 767. One fear is called fear of punishment, another fear of the Lord, II, 41. Fear of the Lord brings many virtues with it, III, 767. Its various kinds, ibid. Without it we can do nothing, III, 168. It drives out sin, III, 770. The twofold fear, V, 679; IV, 99. Fear is more pleasing to God in beginners than the love of the perfect, V, 845.

Timothy represents the heretic, and how, III, 1242. He is overcome by Judah, ibid. How he is said to have been released alive by Judah’s commander, although earlier he is reported to have died in the garrison of Gazara, III, 1248. Whom moths represent, V, 236. Why bells and pomegranates were placed on the priest’s garments, II, 202. How immense a portent Titan was, V, 196. The goodness of Titus, son of Vespasian, VI, 375. Titus as a singular boar, V, 207.

The erection of inscriptions and idols is gravely prohibited, II, 550. Why Tobias represents an image of the ancient law, V, 66. His piety in burying the dead, III, 812. The younger Tobias as an image of Christ, V, 66. The use of the toga among the Romans, V, 573. From where thunder derives its name and what it signifies, V, 277. A type of the incarnate God, III, 1075. The nature and interpretation of the topaz stone, V, 465. What a burning log and firebrand signify, V, 281. The various meanings of the winepress, V, 406, 1193. The torments of some are remedies for others, V, 826. The difference between a beam and a rafter, V, 565.

How God is said to hand a person over, V, 1298. Why Christ was handed over, and by whom, VI, 280. One must firmly adhere to the traditions and teachings handed down from ancestors and parents, VI, 1136. How Matthew says that the Lord’s Transfiguration occurred after six completed days, whereas Luke and Mark mention eight, I, 996. Moses and Elijah appeared in it, I, 997. Its splendor, VI, 1319.
