What Christ’s passing was like, II, 231. The distinction and notation between transferred and proper expression, I, 390. The three most powerful enemies of humanity, I, 491. The three months of joy celebrated by Judith signify the three theological virtues, III, 588. Who the three men were who brought water from Bethlehem, III, 117. What they signify mystically, ibid. The three men in the Babylonian furnace represent the elect, VI, 1152. The three detestable kinds of vices, III, 945–946. The three things especially necessary, V, 232. The three principles of all things, I, 443. The three measures of meal set before the angels as a type of Noah’s three sons, I, 551. The three principal feasts and their observance, II, 127–128. The three insatiable things, V, 776. The three most difficult things, V, 776. What the three that walk well and the fourth that walks successfully signify, V, 778. The three things pleasing to the Lord and the three he hates, III, 945. The three things to be feared, III, 955.

What the three things in the world are, VI, 143. Whether tribulation is indifferent, V, 1371. It teaches us to invoke God, II, 1126. The literal and mystical sense of the tribe, V, 452. Why the tribe of Levi is not counted when the others are counted, but is placed over the Tabernacle, II, 599. Whom it signifies mystically, ibid., 600. The six tribes blessing the people on Mount Gerizim signify those who come to salvation, inflamed not by fear of punishment but by love of the heavenly promise; those cursing on Ebal represent people who do good works out of fear of punishment, II, 948–949. The tribes of Jacob signify the state of the Church, III, 1018. Except for three kings, all the kings of Israel sinned, III, 1007. The virtues and mystical meanings of the various tribes, II, 587, 599. Those who became distinguished among them, ibid.

The mystical tribunal signifies the power of the divine majesty, V, 392. In their thirtieth year Hebrew priests were initiated into sacred service, IV, 499. What a dining chamber is, V, 390. A type of the Holy Trinity, ibid. The thirty-day period for collecting the spoils of the Assyrians signifies the course of human life, III, 580. The reason for the Lord’s three prayers during his Passion, I, 1115.

From where the Holy Trinity derives its name and what it is, V, 26. Those who hold its faith are vigorous soldiers against the enemies of the Church, III, 40. It is often expressed by the number three, IV, 903. The whole Trinity cooperated in the creation of the world, I, 447. Why God always first promises sad things and afterward happier ones, V, 806, 1025. What the sadness of God is like, I, 1113. That of the Holy Spirit, ibid., VI, 441. The harm caused by sadness, III, 985; VI, 1250. Which forms are most dangerous, ibid. Which are lawful and necessary, ibid. Its nature and origin, VI, 1362–1364. How it harasses its followers, ibid. Its signs, ibid. Rebuke, ibid. The remedy against it, ibid. Its two kinds and what they are, VI, 1377.

Those who sow wheat and reap thorns, V, 901. The mystical meaning of the three gates in each of the four directions, IV, 934. A description of triumph and triumphal honors, V, 534. Who may triumph, ibid.

The trunk signifies weakness and inactivity, V, 161. Tryphon, commander of Asia, as a figure of proud heretics, III, 1199. He deceived Jonathan by treachery, ibid. The Gospel trumpet of preaching prevails over weapons and shields in putting enemies to flight, III, 577. What the blast of the trumpets, entrusted solely to the sons of Aaron, signifies, II, 651. Their use, II, 649. Why they were silver, ibid. Tubal-cain, highly skilled in warfare, I, 508. What a hut is, V, 400. The four kinds of swelling, IV, 416.

The tomb of the archbishop of Mainz at St. Alban’s, VI, 1670 note. Likewise that of Otgar and Raban, ibid. What kind of tunic Joseph’s father made for him, I, 622. What it signifies mystically, ibid. When Christ forbids having two tunics, whether one sins by wearing several, II, 225–226. Instructions for priests, V, 384. The whirlwind signifies tribulation, V, 283. The disgraceful practices and errors of the nations must be diligently avoided by God’s people, II, 442–443. The tower is mystically a type of the Blessed Virgin, V, 384. A literal and mystical description of the tower of Babylon, I, 530. The turtledove as a figure of Christ’s body, V, 244. And of others, ibid., II, 255. Various types of the apostles, V, 70–71. What tyrants are, V, 446.

The hospitality and benevolence of Tyre and Sidon, I, 914. Tyre is destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar because of its exaltation over the ruins of Jerusalem, IV, 764. Where it was situated, IV, 767. Its younger elect, while the elders were rejected, signify the Church and the synagogue, IV, 773. Its sailors and pilots are compared with the prelates of the Church, IV, 782–783. With heretics, ibid. They are lamented by Ezekiel, IV, 786.

What pressing the breasts firmly signifies, V, 779. The vengeance of the elect upon the reprobate, V, 742. What the owl signifies, V, 247. What the navel and bones signify, V, 673. Shadow: see *darkness*. Praise of unanimity, V, 1494. The use of anointing with chrism, I, 312; VI, 1176. The preparation of the finest ointment for consecrating the Tabernacle and its vessels, II, 218. Its effect, ibid. The hoof signifies the end of a matter, V, 154. The meaning of hoofs and drops, III, 934. What the unicorn is, II, 741. A type of Christ, II, 753, 998; V, 221.

One righteous person prevails over the whole world, II, 773. One sensible person dwelling in his homeland represents the Catholic; three ungodly deserters represent heretics, III, 867. What the bear with three rows in its mouth signifies mystically, V, 842. What kind of animal the bear is, V, 223. It signifies the devil, Vespasian, and the impious Titus, ibid.

## V

The various meanings of cows, V, 208; VI, 1071. The red cow, to be sacrificed outside the camp, aptly represents the Lord’s Incarnation, II, 703. From the cow’s ashes the water of purification was made, by which various impurities were washed away, II, 703–704. Who collected its ashes, ibid. One made unclean by touching a dead person was purified by this water, II, 708. Why its blood was sacrificed, V, 1119. Two cows with calves were harnessed by the Philistines to a cart for transporting the ark, III, 30.

## ORDER OF THE MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

Continuation of the works of Blessed Rabanus Maurus, Part Three: Expositions.

# Ninth Book on the Epistles of Paul

## Commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians

**Argument.** 9

**Chapter 1.**—The Apostle praises the Corinthians and exhorts those who say that they were baptized by different ministers to concord; and he explains that God has made the wisdom of this world foolish. 9

**Chapter 2.**—The Apostle shows that he did not use the excellence of secular speech, because only the perfect—those who are spiritual—can grasp it. 22

**Chapter 3.**—He removes the Corinthians’ error, because they attributed too much to certain ministers; he treats of building upon wood, hay, and straw, and of the foolish wisdom of the world. 29

**Chapter 4.**—The Apostle censures rash judgment and the contempt shown toward certain ministers, and insists on correcting them. 43

**Chapter 5.**—The Apostle censures the vice of fornication, together with its punishment, and reproves the root of the fault, along with negligence in correction. 47

## Book Ten 53

**Chapter 6.**—He censures his people concerning the judges before whom they bring lawsuits, and concerning the disputes they have among themselves; then he returns to correcting the vice of fornication. 53

**Chapter 7.**—He instructs those who are married and teaches that living in the virginal state is a greater good. 63

[Col. 1764]

**Chapter 8.**—The Apostle shows that knowledge is of no value unless it is ordered according to charity; he teaches the truth concerning foods sacrificed to idols and censures the rashness of those who cause scandal. 75

**Chapter 9.**—The Apostle leads the Corinthians toward perfection in virtue by his own example and by that of runners in the stadium. 78

**Chapter 10.**—The Apostle reproves participation in idolatrous rites and teaches how one should use things sacrificed to idols. 85

## Book Eleven 99

**Chapter 11.**—The Apostle reproves errors concerning the celebration of the most holy Eucharist and the pre-eminence of man; he sets forth the dignity of the Eucharist and the proper and fitting manner of receiving it. 99

**Chapter 12.**—The Apostle commends God’s grace by a general exposition of freely given grace, comparing the body of the Church with the natural body. 106

**Chapter 13.**—On the excellence, usefulness, and permanence of charity. 117

**Chapter 14.**—He shows the superiority of prophecy over the gift of tongues and how each gift should be used. 129

**Chapter 15.**—The Apostle treats of the grace of the resurrection, first commending evangelical doctrine. 137

**Chapter 16.**—The Apostle teaches how one should conduct oneself toward strangers and neighbors, and at the end of the Epistle adds a greeting. 158

## Book Twelve—Commentary on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians 159

**Argument.** 159

**Chapter 1.**—He wins the Corinthians’ goodwill through his tribulations in order to arouse their attention, and excuses himself concerning the promise he made to them. 159

**Chapter 2.**—There are two reasons why the Apostle did not come, lest he grieve them and so produce greater fruit elsewhere; he then explains what that fruit is. 165

**Chapter 3.**—The Apostle shows that he does not need, nor seek, commendation from men. He commends the ministers of Christ to the Church with regard to the dignity of their office and the excellence of their knowledge. 172

**Chapter 4.**—The Apostle commends the ministry of the New Testament both with regard to the working of good and with regard to the endurance of evil. 178

**Chapter 5.**—He treats of the reward of the righteous and of the desire and preparation for it. 185

**Chapter 6.**—The Apostle exhorts his people to do good in the future, with regard to outward conduct, inward devotion, and avoidance of unbelievers. 193

**Chapter 7.**—A useful admonition of the Apostle is given first, and the Corinthians are commended for their former good deeds. 200

## Book Thirteen 205

**Chapter 8.**—The Apostle exhorts the Corinthians to send alms to Jerusalem and treats of the collectors of this almsgiving. 205

**Chapter 9.**—The Apostle, removing suspicion, teaches that alms should be given promptly, cheerfully, and abundantly. 211

**Chapter 10.**—Paul excuses himself for the false charges brought against him by the evidence of his actions, by reasoning, and by examples. 215

**Chapter 11.**—After first presenting his case, the Apostle offers his commendation on the basis of his works and the evils he has endured. 219

**Chapter 12.**—The Apostle commends himself on the basis of visions and sets forth there a remedy against the danger of pride, and so forth. 231

## Book Fourteen—Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians 245

**Argument.** 245

**Chapter 1.**—The Apostle reproves the Galatians for their rapid turning away from the Gospel of Christ, which the Apostle received not from a human being but from Christ. 247

**Chapter 2.**—The Apostle shows that circumcision is not necessary, on the basis of the approval and authority of the other apostles. He opposed the Apostle Peter, who seemed in some way to excuse circumcision, concluding that the legal observances are not to be kept. 264

**Chapter 3.**—The Galatians are rebuked; the Apostle shows the imperfection of the Mosaic Law, says that righteousness comes from faith, and adds an explanation of the usefulness of the Law. 282

## Book Fifteen 297

**The continuation of Chapter 3.** 297

**Chapter 4.**—The Apostle shows the cessation of the legal observances through two comparisons, with the ingratitude of the Galatians inserted between them. 310

**Chapter 5.**—The Galatians are led not to observe the legal requirements in order to escape evils and attain good things; the works of the flesh and of the Spirit are distinguished. 334

## Book Sixteen 344

**The continuation of Chapter 5.** 344

**Chapter 6.**—The Apostle exhorts the Galatians to mutual support and confirms what he has said concerning the cessation of the legal observances. 363

## Book Seventeen—Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians 381

**Chapter 1.**—The divine predestination of certain persons is set forth, and God’s benefits bestowed upon the apostles and the Ephesians are recalled. 384

**Chapter 2.**—The Ephesians are led to give thanks because they have been freed from sin and separated from the other nations. 400

**Chapter 3.**—The Apostle first sets forth the disposition for praying for the Ephesians, and prays for them, attributing all their good to God. 412

## Book Eighteen 419

**The continuation of Chapter 3.** 419

**Chapter 4.**—The Apostle instructs the Ephesians to preserve ecclesiastical unity through the interconnection and distinction of the members; then he leads them toward upright conduct. 425

**Chapter 5.**—He leads the Ephesians to follow Christ in the fervor of charity, in the beauty of holiness, and in known truth, and instructs persons joined in marriage. 444

**Chapter 6.**—The Apostle teaches the mutual conduct of parents and children and returns to instructing the Ephesians generally concerning all the virtues. 463

## Book Nineteen—Commentary on the Epistle to the Philippians 478

**Argument.** 478

**Chapter 1.**—The Apostle gives thanks for the good things bestowed upon the Philippians; indicating his own situation, he sets forth distinctions among preachers and his own charity, and exhorts his people to endure persecution. 479

**Chapter 2.**—He instructs his people in unity of faith, true humility, and holiness, and sends his messengers to them. 486

**Chapter 3.**—He shows the abrogation of the legal observances in word and example; then he excuses himself and challenges them to imitate him. 495

**Chapter 4.**—The Apostle strengthens their patience by exhorting his people to spiritual joy and perseverance in good works. A greeting is placed at the end. 502

## Book Twenty—Commentary on the Epistle to the Colossians 507

**Argument.** 507

**Chapter 1.**—Having won their goodwill, he introduces the authority of the Gospel, which must be believed firmly. 508

**Chapter 2.**—He teaches them to guard against deceptions through false prophecy, through the authority of the Law, and through a pretense of holiness. 520

**Chapter 3.**—The Apostle instructs them generally concerning conduct: laying aside vices and acquiring virtues; and specifically concerning parents, children, married persons, and slaves. 530

**Chapter 4.**—The Apostle instructs masters; commends himself to the prayers of the Colossians; shows how they ought to conduct themselves toward unbelievers; and concludes the Epistle with a greeting. 538

## Book Twenty-One—Commentary on the First Epistle to the Thessalonians 539

**Argument.** 539

**Chapter 1.**—The Apostle gives thanks for the Thessalonians’ good beginning and for the spread of this goodness. 541

**Chapter 2.**—He consoles his people in adversity by their conformity to himself and to the Church of Jerusalem. 544

**Chapter 3.**—The Apostle sends Timothy to console the Thessalonians; the benefit of his return is set forth, and so forth. 548

**Chapter 4.**—He reproves his people for the vices of fornication, greed, idleness, and excessive mourning for the dead. 550

**Chapter 5.**—He admonishes his people concerning the future day of death and the general judgment, and urges them to conduct themselves well toward God and neighbor. 560

## Book Twenty-Two—Commentary on the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians 565

**Argument.** 565

**Chapter 1.**—The Apostle gives thanks for the Thessalonians’ good conduct, praying for its better completion. 567

**Chapter 2.**—The Apostle teaches his people concerning the coming of Antichrist and demonstrates the truth of this matter in several ways. 569

**Chapter 3.**—The Apostle asks for the support of their prayers, instructs them in the reform of evil, and urges them to manual labor. 574

## Book Twenty-Three—Commentary on the First Epistle to Timothy 580

**Argument.** 580

**Chapter 1.**—The Apostle warns Timothy not to attend to genealogies and legal observances. He gives thanks to God for his calling to the apostolate and urges him to resist teachers of falsehood. 581

**Chapter 2.**—Timothy is instructed concerning the act and manner of prayer; he speaks of prayer with regard to the people subject to it. 588

**Chapter 3.**—Timothy is taught to order the ranks of the Church, both bishops and deacons and their wives, and the reason for these instructions is given. 596

**Chapter 4.**—The Apostle excludes an erroneous manner of teaching and sets forth the true manner of teaching. 609

**Chapter 5.**—The Apostle instructs Timothy concerning elders, young men, and widows; teaches which women are true widows; and speaks of provision for the ministers of the Church, and so forth. 615

**Chapter 6.**—The Apostle urges bishops to care for the poor in the service of masters and urges them to pursue humility, piety, and the other virtues. 626

## Book Twenty-Four—Commentary on the Second Epistle to Timothy 635

**Argument.** 635

**Chapter 1.**—The Apostle urges Timothy to preach the Gospel of Christ steadfastly, on the basis of episcopal dignity and the scarcity of preachers. 637

**Chapter 2.**—The Apostle urges Timothy to carry out the duty of preaching and warns him to flee youthful desires. 642

**Chapter 3.**—Because false preachers are multiplying, he exhorts the Apostle to preach; an admonition concerning steadfastness is given to Timothy. 646

**Chapter 4.**—The Apostle foretells the multiplication of evil hearers, together with the announcement of his own martyrdom. He requests Timothy’s arrival and greets his friends. 650

[Col. 1767]

## Book Twenty-Five—Commentary on the Epistle to Titus 653

**Argument.** 653

**Another argument, from Jerome.** 654

**Chapter 1.**—Concerning the Lord the Father: before eternal times he promised us the Lord the Son, whom he later manifested at the proper times. Concerning the form of a bishop, and the fact that those once called bishops were also called presbyters. And concerning deceivers of the churches. 655

**Chapter 2.**—Titus is instructed to educate the old, the young, and slaves. 674

**Chapter 3.**—It is shown how the people ought to conduct themselves toward rulers, with an explanation of the statement, and toward heretics. A greeting is appended. 684

## Book Twenty-Six—Commentary on the Epistle to Philemon 693

**Argument.** 693

**Sole Chapter.**—Concerning Philemon, Appia, Archippus, and his household church. Concerning Philemon and the Apostle, who always remembers him in his prayers. Concerning the aged and imprisoned Apostle, who commands Philemon and at the same time entreats him on behalf of his slave Onesimus, and commends to him the preparation of lodging for himself. Concerning Epaphras, the Apostle’s fellow prisoner, and Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, Paul’s assistants. 696

## Book Twenty-Seven—Commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews 711

**Argument.** 711

**Chapter 1.**—The excellence of Christ is set forth: he is the giver of the new law, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, equal in power and dignity; and Christ is shown to be superior to the angels in these respects. 711

**Chapter 2.**—The Apostle shows that the new law given by Christ must be obeyed and that the humility of his passion is no obstacle. 721

**Chapter 3.**—It is shown that Christ surpasses Moses and must be obeyed firmly. 728

**Chapter 4.**—Concerning entering the heavenly rest, toward which one must hasten because of the excellence of Christ’s divinity and humanity. 732

**Chapter 5.**—The Apostle declares what is required in a high priest and shows that these things apply to Christ, indicating the difficulty of what is to be said about Christ. 741

**Chapter 6.**—The Apostle adds what he wishes to leave aside, namely, matters by which acceptance of his teaching is impossible, and those matters that are suitable and useful. 746

## Book Twenty-Eight 751

**The continuation of Chapter 6.** 751

**Chapter 7.**—The excellence of Christ’s priesthood is shown by comparing Christ with Melchizedek, whose priesthood is both more excellent than the Levitical priesthood and more necessary. 755

**Chapter 8.**—He shows Christ to be a better minister of the sacraments than the ministers of the Old Testament. 763

**Chapter 9.**—The Apostle touches upon the things that belonged to the ministry of the Old Testament and from them argues the dignity of Christ and of the new law. 768

**Chapter 10.**—It is shown that the old law cannot take away sin; the excellence of Christ’s priesthood is declared, and firm obedience to that priesthood is required. 779

## Book Twenty-Nine 787

**Chapter 11.**—The Apostle shows what it means to be subject to Christ; describing faith, he commends it in many ways. 787

**Chapter 12.**—The Apostle leads his people to endure evils that are punishments and to avoid evils that are sins, showing the conditions of the old and new laws. 807

**Chapter 13.**—He exhorts them to do good toward neighbors, themselves, and prelates; asks for prayer on his behalf; and offers the benefit of his prayer together with a greeting. 824
